abidlabs/wsw7Y085RY.paper_title: Capacity without Access: Reinterpreting the Mid-Depth Spectral Plateau in LLMs

claims.claim: Intermediate layers maintain broad representational span and rich spectral diversity indicating intact representational capacity
claims.evidence: The raw covariance effective rank is ~1.0 for all mid-depth layers (layers 2-11: 1.03-1.17), contradicting 'broad representational span'; only after switching to a correlation-matrix metric does effective rank become ~103-123, but this is on a single 124M-parameter model with 50 short sequences, and the logbook itself calls it 'directional' at gpt2 scale.

claims.claim: Intermediate layers project weakly onto output-relevant subspace indicating constrained accessibility despite high representational capacity
claims.evidence: Fraction of variance in the top-50 unembedding subspace is ~0.09-0.14 across layers, only ~1.5-2x over the ~6.5% random baseline; the logbook itself describes the effect as 'modest at gpt2 scale' with small K=50 and a single small model, which is too weak to confirm the claim.

claims.claim: Apparent stagnation in deeper layers is better accounted for by geometric limitations on accessibility rather than representational capacity deficit
claims.evidence: The logbook shows logit-lens accuracy rising slowly through mid-depth (0.03-0.12) while correlation effective rank stays high (~117-123), but this is purely correlational on one 124M model; the logbook explicitly marks it 'in-progress' and states that 'the causal/interpretive framing needs larger models and a proper accessibility intervention to settle.'

abidlabs/wsw7Y085RY.overall: The logbook provides toy-scale directional observations on GPT-2 124M (50 short sequences, 12 layers) that are loosely consistent with all three claims but far too weak to verify them: the standard covariance metric actually contradicts Claim 1, the accessibility effect is modest, and no causal intervention tests the accessibility-vs-capacity framing of Claim 3.

claims.evidence: The gallery edge audit uses an approximate visualization-edge F1 proxy on RGB depth visualizations (not official BF1 on raw depth), and on the Booster transparent/specular subset PointDiT (0.7444) actually slightly loses to PPD (0.7463), undermining the 'significantly better on transparent objects' claim; the 32×32 synthetic proxy further contradicts the claim with deterministic beating flow on edge F1 (0.4849 vs 0.2477).

abidlabs/QS0ZROPx8u.paper_title: Memory Savings at What Cost? A Study of Alternatives to Backpropagation

claims.claim: Backpropagation with checkpointing achieves up to 31.1% higher accuracy than FmAD and ZO variants
claims.evidence: The synthetic proxy (68,932-param model, synthetic Gaussian-mixture data) shows BP-Checkpoint at 93.52% vs FmAD/ZO at 84.93% (8.59-point gap), and the RoBERTa-base/AGNews run shows BP at 92.8% vs FmAD/ZO at ~24% (chance level). Both support the direction (BP > FmAD/ZO accuracy) but neither reproduces the specific 31.1-point maximum; the RoBERTa result is degenerate since FmAD/ZO never learn, unlike the paper's scenario where they partially converge.

claims.claim: 34.8% faster convergence and 3.8x fewer computations at comparable memory usage
claims.evidence: The synthetic proxy shows BP-Checkpoint reaching 80% accuracy in 20 steps/1.29 GFLOPs vs FmAD/ZO needing 306.7 steps/10.8–21.5 GFLOPs, and the RoBERTa run shows FmAD/ZO never reaching 0.85 in 2000 steps. The direction (BP converges faster with fewer computations) is clearly supported, but the specific 34.8% and 3.8× figures are not reproduced; the proxy ratios are much larger and scale-dependent.

claims.claim: FmAD and ZO trade memory for higher computational cost and longer wall-clock time to convergence
claims.evidence: On the RoBERTa experiment, ZO shows lower peak memory (635 MB vs 1788 MB vanilla BP) but never converges, partially supporting the trade-off. However, FmAD had the highest peak memory (14,089 MB), directly contradicting the memory-saving premise for FmAD. The synthetic proxy uses algorithmic live-set estimates rather than process RSS. The claim is only partially addressed for ZO and contradicted for FmAD in this implementation.

abidlabs/QS0ZROPx8u.overall: The logbook provides directional support for all three claims on simplified setups (a synthetic 68K-param proxy and a RoBERTa-base/AGNews run), but does not reproduce any of the paper's specific quantitative figures (31.1%, 34.8%, 3.8×). The RoBERTa experiment is degenerate—FmAD/ZO remain at chance level—and FmAD's memory advantage is not reproduced, limiting the strength of the evidence.

abidlabs/repro-cmollm-at-scale.paper_title: cMoLLM at Scale: Horizontal Scaling Laws for Convolutionally-Gated Mixture-of-LLMs

claims.claim: cMoLLM improves language modeling perplexity and downstream GLUE and SQuAD accuracy under matched compute compared to ParaScale and AltUp baselines
claims.evidence: A reduced-scale proxy (3 layers, width 128, ~7M params, 400 steps, 3M FineWeb tokens) compared cMoLLM N∈{1,2,4,8} against a dense baseline with matched nominal FFN MACs across 3 seeds, but no GLUE, no SQuAD, no ParaScale, and no AltUp baselines were implemented. claims.claim: Convolutionally-gated mixture reformulation improves stream utilization and reduces gradient collapse
claims.evidence: The proxy runs tracked gate entropy, effective streams, and utilization CV across gate types (simple, context_aware, adaptive, multi_head) at N=8, showing multi_head achieving normalized entropy 0.837 and effective streams 5.72/8, but gradient collapse was never directly measured or compared against a collapsing baseline, and all measurements are at toy scale (7M params, 400 steps).

abidlabs/repro-cmollm-at-scale.overall: The logbook provides a well-controlled but explicitly toy-scale architectural proxy (7M params, 3M tokens, 400 steps) that partially addresses perplexity scaling and stream utilization, while completely omitting GLUE, SQuAD, ParaScale, AltUp, and direct gradient-collapse analysis. The dynamic-convolution equivalence test is rigorous, but the two paper claims about downstream performance and gradient collapse are only touched at a scale far too small to verify or falsify them.

abidlabs/repro-olaf-world-spectral.paper_title: Olaf-World: Orienting Latent Actions for Video World Modeling

arthrod/repro-copyright-bench.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence from a from-scratch rebuild (4 models × 12 scenarios × 4 conditions × 3 reps = 576 episodes) that supports Claim 1 — agents do select copyrighted assets despite lawful alternatives — and partially supports Claim 2, with the user-intent effect reproducing robustly but the time-pressure effect being actively contradicted. The reproduction is limited by the absence of the paper's original code/data (none publicly available) and a scaled-down scenario count, and there are numerical inconsistencies between raw command output and summary tables.

rdubwiley/68AMoK2YNk.paper_title: Understanding Generalization and Forgetting in In-Context Continual Learning

claims.claim: Standard attention mechanisms inevitably induce inter-task interference through uniform or causal aggregation of historical contexts
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo simulation (d=20, T=5, M swept 1–5000, 2000 trials per M) shows unmasked multi-task MSE plateaus at 80.02, matching the independently derived closed-form interference floor of 79.70 (0.40% residual), while single-task oracle MSE shrinks to 0.086 at the same context length; masked/causal variant plateaus at 16.01 vs prediction 15.99 (0.10% residual), confirming a non-vanishing, quantitatively predictable interference floor rather than sampling noise.

claims.claim: In-context continual learning can exhibit both positive transfer and provable negative transfer depending on task structure
claims.evidence: Sweeping task-similarity angle theta over 0–180° (19 points, 1500 trials each, 28,500 total) with the masked multi-task predictor shows a clean monotonic sign flip: delta vs single-task baseline is negative (positive transfer, as low as −0.846 at theta=0°) for theta ≤ 70° and positive (negative transfer, up to +1.585 at theta=180°) for theta ≥ 80°, directly demonstrating both positive and negative transfer depending on task structure.

claims.claim: Theoretical framework reveals order sensitivity and performance degradation in long prompts as fundamental limitations of attention-based continual inference
claims.evidence: Exhaustive permutation of a fixed 5-task set (all 120 orderings, 30 trials each) shows the same task's forgetting ranges from mean 1.211 (first position) to 6.5e-5 (last position), a >18,000x spread purely from reordering; separately, sweeping T from 1 to 30 (300 trials each) shows forgetting of task 1 grows from 0.073 to ~33–37 and saturates rather than vanishing, confirming both order sensitivity and asymptotic long-prompt degradation.

rdubwiley/68AMoK2YNk.overall: This logbook implements the paper's exact closed-form linear/masked-linear self-attention expressions (Lemma 4.1, Theorems 4.3/4.4) in NumPy and verifies all three theoretical claims with substantial Monte Carlo simulations (thousands of trials per condition, full permutation enumeration), showing tight agreement between simulated and predicted interference floors, a clean positive-to-negative transfer sign flip, and strong order-dependent forgetting with asymptotic saturation. The reproduction is faithful to the paper's own theoretical model and analytical regime (Gamma=Lambda=I_d, N→∞), though the secondary GPT-2/Qwen neural-network experiments (Sec 5.4–5.5) were not attempted.

rdubwiley/UbzajT84Nd.paper_title: Domain-Shift-Aware Conformal Prediction for Large Language Models

claims.claim: DS-CP delivers more reliable coverage than standard conformal prediction under substantial distribution shifts.

The full-scale aggregation of 4,352 rows across 16 models corroborates (mean coverage 0.9375 vs 0.8927, under-coverage rate 16.9% vs 45.3%, DS-CP ≥ vanilla on 93.7% of pairs).

rdubwiley/J0y3sNbo9G.paper_title: Theoretical Investigation on Inductive Bias of Isolation Forest

claims.claim: Isolation Forest exhibits lower sensitivity to central anomalies while demonstrating greater parameter adaptability compared to k-Nearest Neighbor.

Test B (second run, psi=n matching the theorem) shows iForest threshold CV=0.208 across n_estimators vs k-NN threshold CV=0.534 across k, confirming greater parameter adaptability. A disclosed caveat shows subsampled (psi<n) sklearn IsolationForest can fail to meet the theoretical threshold, but this is outside the paper's idealized full-split assumption.

claims.claim: iForest scores points by considering both density and distances to endpoints, unlike k-NN.
claims.evidence: Standardized OLS across 400 datasets/2000 probe points shows iForest's closed-form h_bar has a significant boundary-distance coefficient (0.415, incremental R²=0.172 after controlling for density) while k-NN's mean-neighbor-distance has negligible boundary dependence (coefficient -0.029, incremental R²=0.0009), a ~200x gap confirming the density-plus-boundary vs density-only distinction.

claims.claim: Expected depth function derived from modeling iForest growth process as random walk using transition probabilities.
claims.evidence: Growing 480,000 actual randomized iTrees (60 configs: n=5–80, 3 distributions, 4 seeds, 8000 trees each) and comparing empirical average depth against the paper's closed-form h_bar yields max relative residual 0.95%, mean absolute residual 0.011, and mean Pearson correlation 0.99989 — consistent with pure Monte-Carlo sampling noise, confirming the closed-form derivation against an independent stochastic simulation.

rdubwiley/J0y3sNbo9G.overall: This logbook provides concrete, independently-computed experimental evidence supporting all three claims of the paper through from-scratch implementations of the iTree growth process, closed-form expected-depth calculations, sklearn IsolationForest/k-NN comparisons, and large-scale sweeps across synthetic 1D data matching the paper's own theoretical case-study scope. The reproduction is rigorous with honest disclosure of the practical limitation that subsampled iForest deviates from the idealized theory.

rdubwiley/jl2f2Y3iuC.paper_title: Fine-Tuning Without Forgetting In-Context Learning: A Theoretical Analysis of Linear Attention Models

claims.claim: Fine-tuning all attention parameters in linear attention models can degrade in-context learning.
claims.evidence: On the paper's exact single-layer linear attention model (d=5, σ²=0.1, n=20, 30k-sample Monte Carlo eval), full (V,Q) fine-tuning drove zero-shot error to 0.104 (vs theory prediction σ²=0.1, 3.6% relative residual) while few-shot error on the same target task rose from 0.357 (pretrained) to 1.286 (+260%), closely matching the theorem's prediction of σ²+θ₀ᵀΣθ₀=1.1 and demonstrating severe ICL degradation.

claims.claim: Restricting updates to the value matrix improves zero-shot performance while preserving in-context learning.
claims.evidence: Value-only fine-tuning (Q frozen) on the identical pretrained model improved zero-shot error from 1.430 to 0.369 (vs theory prediction 0.322, 14.6% relative) while few-shot error changed only from 0.357 to 0.346 (-3.2%), versus full fine-tuning's +260% degradation — an >80x gap in ICL degradation that directly confirms the theorem's ordering.

claims.claim: Incorporating an auxiliary few-shot loss enhances in-context learning on the target task but degrades performance on unseen tasks.
claims.evidence: Auxiliary-loss fine-tuning reduced target-task few-shot error from 0.357 to 0.210 (-41%), while the OOD sweep showed monotonic degradation from 0.215 (cos=1.0) to 1.971 (cos=-1.0) with Pearson r=-0.925 (R²=0.856); the pretrained control model remained flat (0.349–0.375 across all angles), confirming the anisotropic degradation is induced by the auxiliary loss itself.

rdubwiley/jl2f2Y3iuC.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous from-scratch reimplementation of the paper's exact linear-attention model with independent pretraining, three fine-tuning variants, and 30,000-sample Monte Carlo evaluation, yielding concrete numerical evidence that supports all three theoretical claims with large, correctly-signed, and correctly-ordered effects. A supplementary MMLU experiment on a 6x-smaller model with 150 training examples is honestly reported as statistically inconclusive at toy scale, but the synthetic experiments — which are the paper's own experimental domain — constitute the primary non-toy evidence.

rdubwiley/stability-beyond-bounded-diffe.paper_title: Stability beyond Bounded Differences: Sharp Generalization Bounds under Finite $L_p$ Moments

rdubwiley/stability-beyond-bounded-diffe.overall: The logbook provides solid independent evidence for the core concentration-inequality framework (Claim 1) and for two of three generalization paradigms (Claim 2) via a faithful from-scratch reimplementation of the paper's synthetic experiments at matching scale. claims.evidence: Across 12 (γ,B) cells with 200 seeds each, all directional predictions hold: at B=1 median escape falls 6,760→1,900→181 as γ goes 0→0.5→0.9, and MSD decreases monotonically in B at every γ. claims.claim: On the Beale test function, SAM is empirically shown to become stuck at a saddle point where vanilla gradient descent successfully escapes, matching the Case-III oscillation predicted by the theory (Section 5, empirical validation).
claims.evidence: On the Beale function, the saddle at (0,1) with Hessian eigenvalues ±27.75 is confirmed indefinite. claims.evidence: The claim page for Claim 3 is empty (header only). ai-sherpa/repro-vlm-robustbench.paper_title: VLM-RobustBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Robustness of Vision-Language Models

claims.claim: VLM-RobustBench evaluates 49 augmentations, including 42 severity-based corruptions across nine categories and 7 binary transforms (Table 1).
claims.evidence: An independent re-implementation (audit_taxonomy.py) enumerates 9 categories with per-category counts summing to 42 severity augmentations (blur 5, noise 4, weather 5, digital 2, geometric 5, occlusion 3, color_tone 10, resolution 5, vlm_specific 3) plus 7 binary transforms, totaling 49 augmentation types, matching the claim exactly.

claims.claim: The benchmark yields 133 corrupted settings per model-dataset pair by applying three severities to 42 corruptions plus seven binary transforms (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The same audit confirms the arithmetic 42×3 + 7 = 126 + 7 = 133 corrupted settings, and all 133 configurations were independently realized as deterministic valid RGB images (133/133 byte-identical on re-run, 133/133 valid RGB), with 135 total including clean and no-image baselines.

claims.claim: The evaluation covers 11 VLMs from Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5, Molmo2, and Gemma 3 families on MMBench and MMMU-Pro (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Cross-referencing the paper's Table 2 confirms 4 families (Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5, Molmo2, Gemma 3), 9 instruct checkpoints + 2 Qwen-Think = 11 total checkpoints, evaluated on 2 benchmarks (MMBench and MMMU-Pro). This is a structural claim about the paper's experimental scope, and the counts match.

claims.claim: Low-severity glass blur causes an average 8.1 percentage-point MMBench accuracy drop, larger than high-severity brightness reduction, illustrating a severity mismatch (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: At N=1000 on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct (MMBench dev, seed 0, parse rate 1.00), low-severity glass_blur (severity 1) causes a 1.4pp drop, not 8.1pp. The 8.1pp magnitude appears at mid severity (8.9pp at severity 3). Corroborated on InternVL3-8B where low-severity glass_blur costs 2.7pp. Both models are similar-class open-weight substitutes at the paper's real task and scale.

claims.claim: The study finds that spatial and resampling perturbations such as upsample and elastic_transform can cause drops up to 34 percentage points (Section 1).
claims.evidence: Across six geometric/resampling transforms at maximum severity on N=1000 (Qwen2.5-VL-7B), the largest drop is 12.2pp (elastic_transform s5), roughly one-third of the claimed 34pp. The paper's named transforms are mild: upsample ×8 = 8.7pp, rotate 45° = 2.7pp. Corroborated on InternVL3-8B where the maximum drop of any kind is 11.7pp.

claims.claim: Robustness is reported to vary by model family rather than simply by parameter count, producing family-specific vulnerability fingerprints (Section 1).
claims.evidence: At matched parameter count (Qwen2.5-VL-7B vs InternVL3-8B, 1.14× ratio), the two families invert their vulnerability ordering: Qwen shows geometric > photometric (4.8 vs 3.5pp mean drop) while InternVL shows photometric > geometric (7.2 vs 5.0pp), with the worst single corruption also inverting (elastic_transform vs glass_blur). Parameter count is held approximately constant and cannot explain the divergence.

ai-sherpa/repro-vlm-robustbench.overall: The logbook independently confirms the benchmark's structural composition (49 augmentations, 133 settings, 11 models across 4 families) and provides concrete GPU evidence at N=1000 that falsifies the two headline magnitude claims (low-severity glass blur = 1.4pp not 8.1pp; max geometric drop = 12.2pp not 34pp), while confirming the family-fingerprint finding via a matched-scale two-family contrast.

ancs21/repro-zeus.paper_title: Zeus: Towards Tuning-Free Foundation Model for Time Series Analysis

claims.evidence: The agent built the model from the released config and modeling code, confirming the multi-scale hourglass architecture (scales [1, 8, 32, 8, 1] with per-stage encoders, pooling/unpooling layers), point-wise tokenization (input_dim=1, no patch_size, gated MLP embedding each time step individually), and a parameter count of 102,104,841 matching the Zeus-100M name.

claims.evidence: The trained checkpoint was never released (README lists safetensors upload as TODO, nothing found on Hugging Face Hub), so no zero-shot inference experiments could be run to independently verify the reported GIFT-Eval performance numbers across any of the five tasks.

ancs21/repro-zeus.overall: The logbook concretely verifies Zeus's architectural design—multi-scale U-shaped Transformer with point-wise tokenization and ~102M parameters—through direct code inspection and model building. AceVikings/repro-13581-nb1-closed-form.paper_title: Continuous Variable Hamiltonian Learning at Heisenberg Limit via Displacement-Random Unitary Transformation

claims.claim: The Displacement-Random Unitary Transformation (D-RUT) protocol learns all coefficients of a generic multi-mode bosonic Hamiltonian with evolution time scaling as O(1/epsilon), achieving the Heisenberg limit (Theorem 1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: The reproduction tests the classical Chebyshev/IDFT estimator with an assumed noise model (std 0.05/T) yielding median-RMSE slope −1.0025 over T=25…800, but explicitly does not simulate the controlled quantum evolution or verify that RPE itself achieves 1/T scaling—the Heisenberg-limit mechanism is assumed, not demonstrated.

claims.claim: For single-mode Hamiltonians expressed in a first-quantization (position/momentum) basis, D-RUT recovers physical coefficients with RMSE epsilon_G using total evolution time O~(1/epsilon_G), under stated conditions on known zero coefficients, non-zero response to basis mismatch, and a sufficiently close initial guess (Theorem 2, Section 2).
claims.evidence: Physical coefficients [5.0, 2.5, 0.1] are recovered via exact linear inversion through a squeezing matrix (condition number 2.8577) with perturbations at 0.05/T, yielding slope −0.9878 over 256 trials per time point, but no oscillator quantum dynamics are simulated—only the classical inversion stage with assumed noise is tested.

claims.claim: The protocol's estimation error under state-preparation-and-measurement (SPAM) errors is bounded as ||delta g_SPAM||_2 <= (L_C/sigma_min(K)) ||delta beta||_2, where L_C is a Lipschitz constant and sigma_min(K) the smallest singular value of the Gram-like matrix K (Section 3.6, Eq. 43).
claims.evidence: The norm bound is numerically confirmed across 1,000 random displacement perturbations with a linear response map C(β)=Aβ (making L_C=‖A‖₂ exact), yielding zero violations and a maximum actual-to-bound ratio of 0.60728, providing concrete evidence that the inequality holds.

claims.claim: A hierarchical two-stage coefficient recovery strategy (learn single-mode coefficients first, then coupling coefficients) is proven to have covariance dominated by that of simultaneous estimation, Cov(delta g)_hierarchical <= Cov(delta g)_simultaneous, for all parameters (Section 4.1, Appendix A).
claims.evidence: Across 200 random 500-observation nested linear-regression designs, Cov_sim(active)−Cov_hier is positive semidefinite to 1e-12 with smallest eigenvalue 4.91e-11 and minimum trace ratio 1.00159, numerically confirming the covariance dominance property; the logbook also notes the source frames this as a worst-case error bound rather than literal matrix-covariance notation.

claims.claim: An iterative bisection search over the squeezing parameter R (relating the physical and reference bases via a Bogoliubov transformation) converges in O(log(1/epsilon_R)) iterations for first-quantization Hamiltonian learning (Section 5.3, Eq. 77-78).
claims.evidence: The downloaded primary source (main.tex, SHA-256 48ee31d7…1a81) contains no occurrence of 'bisection,' 'epsilon_R,' or the claimed Eq. 77–78; a generic bisection test shows the expected O(log(1/ε)) behavior but this cannot validate the claim's attribution of this algorithm to the paper.

claims.claim: The algorithm uses Chebyshev-node sampling of the displacement parameter combined with robust phase estimation and inverse discrete Fourier transform to reconstruct coefficients, as detailed in Algorithm 1 and illustrated for the single-mode case in Figure 1 (Section 2).
claims.evidence: The classical reconstruction algorithm is implemented with d+1 Chebyshev radial nodes and l+1 angular IDFT points, achieving zero-noise RMSE of 1.62e-13 for 14 degree-4 Hermitian coefficients; the RPE measurement subroutine is acknowledged as untested but the core Chebyshev/IDFT reconstruction is confirmed at machine precision.

AceVikings/repro-13581-nb1-closed-form.overall: The logbook provides solid numerical evidence for the classical components of D-RUT (Chebyshev/IDFT reconstruction, linear-inversion error propagation, SPAM norm bound, and nested-covariance dominance) and correctly identifies that the paper does not contain the bisection algorithm claimed in claim 5. However, the Heisenberg-limit scaling claims (1 and 2) are only tested on the classical post-processing layer with an assumed 1/T noise model, not through actual quantum dynamics simulation, making them toy-scale validations of the estimator rather than full reproductions of the quantum protocol.

AceVikings/repro-13581-nb2-lr-optimizati.paper_title: A Sketch-and-Project Analysis of Subsampled Natural Gradient Algorithms

claims.claim: For linear least-squares problems, subsampled natural gradient descent (SNGD) is shown to be directly equivalent to the regularized Kaczmarz method, and SPRING is equivalent to the Nesterov-accelerated regularized Kaczmarz (ARK) method (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: SNGD and regularized block-Kaczmarz updates were compared at batch sizes [1,2,4,6,9,11] with λ=0.17, yielding maximum Euclidean discrepancy 0.0e+00; the SPRING/ARK recurrence was also checked symbolically.

claims.claim: SNGD converges at rate (1-α)^t where α=λ_min(P̄), while SPRING converges at rate O((1-√(α/β))^t), giving up to a square-root improvement in iteration complexity over SNGD (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Complete enumeration of mini-batch subsets for a 12×5 system at k=3 gives α=0.137882, β=2.550361 (theoretical bases 0.862, 0.767); 400 sampled trajectories yield fitted bases 0.761 (SNGD) and 0.631 (SPRING), both below the conservative bounds and showing acceleration.

claims.claim: For general quadratic losses, SNGD requires the regularization parameter λ to exceed a threshold λ0 to guarantee convergence, and can diverge if regularization is insufficient (Proposition 3).
claims.evidence: A seeded 4×2 instance at λ=0 has ξ=-0.018633<0 and spectral radius 1.000373>1 (divergence), while ξ becomes positive at λ=0.1, demonstrating both the divergence and restoration-of-convergence halves of Proposition 3.

claims.claim: Under an assumption that the regularized projector P̄ shares an eigenbasis with J^T J, SNGD provably outperforms SGD by a factor of k^β when the spectrum of the Jacobian decays polynomially (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: 1400 Gaussian rows in 24 dimensions with eigenvalues i^-2, 2500 mini-batches per k, yield α scaling as k^1.857 (close to β=2) with 8.38× superlinear gain at k=12, directly testing the theorem's batch-size mechanism.

claims.claim: A unified algorithm (Algorithm 1) captures both SNGD (momentum μ=0) and SPRING (μ∈(0,1)) as momentum-based updates using subsampled Jacobians, enabling single-minibatch convergence guarantees of any batch size.
claims.evidence: A single-mini-batch implementation at k=[1,2,4,6,9,11] shows μ=0 reduces exactly to SNGD (discrepancy 0.0e+00) and μ>0 activates the projected-increment SPRING correction, with no batch-size-specific formula.

claims.claim: Analysis of SPRING's convergence for general (non-least-squares) quadratic losses is left open as Conjecture 7, despite numerical experiments showing large empirical performance gains over SNGD.
claims.evidence: Source audit confirms the general-quadratic SPRING result is explicitly labeled a conjecture; independent 240×20 LLQ experiments over 24 trials show SNGD/SPRING final-error ratios up to 28,272×, supporting the empirical-gains clause while preserving open status.

AceVikings/repro-13581-nb2-lr-optimizati.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence for all six claims: exact equivalence checks, complete enumeration of convergence rates, a seeded divergence counterexample, Monte Carlo scaling estimates, unified-algorithm verification, and independent LLQ experiments. System sizes are moderate but appropriate for testing theoretical claims about linear algebra identities and convergence rates.

Kiy-K/repro-modus-any-to-any.paper_title: MODUS: Decoder-only Any-to-Any Modeling of Diverse Modalities

claims.claim: MODUS treats all modalities symmetrically without modality-specific heads, losses, or task pipelines.
claims.evidence: The full 14.9B-parameter released checkpoint was loaded on an H200 and audited: 16 modalities registered, one shared lm_head, one shared llm2vae 2D projection, zero modules matching per-modality head patterns, and CE/flow-MSE as two shared (not per-modality) objective families — concrete architectural evidence on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: The decoder-only architecture naturally enables chained generation through intermediate modalities and cross-modal consistency verification.
claims.evidence: The full model executed RGB→Depth→Normal chained inference (4.179s, 10.86° angular proxy) and a caption→RGB→caption cycle (token-F1 proxy 0.65) on 2 preview samples at 512×512 with 10 flow steps, demonstrating the chaining mechanism functionally but not reproducing the paper's Table 14/15 benchmark gains or the best-of-four GenEval verification protocol.

claims.claim: MODUS demonstrates strong out-of-the-box performance and flexible multimodal composition within a single model.
claims.evidence: The same checkpoint produced depth, normal, and canny outputs for 2 RGB inputs (e.g., normal SSIM .801, angular proxy 10.13°) and composed ViT/VAE/both feature paths (angular proxies 11.99°/10.81°/10.73°), but no paper benchmarks (MMMU, GenEval, DIODE, NYUv2, RefCOCO, ImageNet) were run, so 'strong out-of-the-box performance' is not established — only functional breadth on a tiny preview subset.

Kiy-K/repro-modus-any-to-any.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous architectural audit of the full released 14.9B checkpoint that directly verifies the symmetric no-modality-specific-heads design (Claim 1), and functional demonstrations of chained generation and multimodal composition on 2 preview samples with proxy metrics (Claims 2–3), but does not reproduce any of the paper's headline benchmark results.

claims.claim: LatentMAS replaces text-mediated multi-agent communication with auto-regressive latent thought generation and a shared latent working memory (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook ran the official Gen-Verse/LatentMAS code and confirmed the architecture: 3 reasoning agents pass auto-regressive latent thoughts through a shared KV cache and emit no decoded text; only the Judger decodes. The latent_steps ablation (m=0 vs m>0) confirms the latent working memory is the unique component, matching the Figure 3 description.

claims.claim: The paper proves latent thoughts can be more expressive than equivalent text reasoning under a linear representation hypothesis (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Theorem 3.1's counting argument was reproduced step-by-step in exact integer arithmetic: |H|=3^dh confirmed by exhaustive enumeration (dh=1..12), the lower bound m'≥dh·m·log3/log|V| holds at all 588 grid points, tightness confirmed by explicit lossless encoder/decoder, and the paper's instantiated constants 235.7/377.1/471.4 reproduce to 4 significant figures from live model configs.

claims.claim: Latent working memory preserves information equivalently to directly inputting preceding agents' outputs under the paper's formal setup (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: On three real transformers (SmolLM2-135M, Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen3-0.6B) in float32, the KV-cache identity holds exactly (control: rel L2 err ~4e-6, 100% top-1 agreement), but equivalence to directly inputting the preceding agent's outputs fails by rel L2 err 0.3985 (latent) and 0.3817 (text)—8,952× and 8,574× the round-off floor—with next-token agreement dropping to 18.5%/14.8%.

claims.claim: LatentMAS reports higher accuracy, lower output token usage, and faster inference than single-agent and text-based MAS baselines across six general tasks in the sequential MAS setting (Table 1).
claims.evidence: On 5 of the paper's 9 benchmarks with Qwen3-4B (N=40, official code, A100), LatentMAS is the worst method on all 5, trailing the single agent by 22–45 pp (mean −35.0 pp) and near-random on code (MBPP+ 20%, HumanEval+ 22.5%), directly contradicting the claimed higher accuracy. Token reduction (53.4% mean) and speedup (3.69×) are directionally correct but below the paper's bands.

claims.claim: On AIME, GPQA-Diamond, and other reasoning-intensive tasks, LatentMAS is evaluated under both sequential and hierarchical MAS settings with accuracy, token, and speed metrics (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The arXiv e-print LaTeX source (tarball sha256 cd32da8c…) was parsed mechanically: Table 2 is confirmed as float #2, contains AIME24/AIME25/GPQA-Diamond, includes both Sequential MAS and Hierarchical MAS sub-blocks, and all 6 (task×setting) blocks report accuracy, token, and speed. All 108 numeric cells were extracted and all four structural assertions pass.

claims.claim: Input-output alignment improves downstream accuracy by 2.3% to 5.3% across three analyzed benchmarks (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: On tied-embedding backbones including the paper's own Qwen3-4B, W_a provably equals the identity (||W_a−I||/||I|| ≈ 1e-3, mean cos(v,vW_a)=1.000000), making the ablation a self-comparison. On untied backbones, W_a sends latent directions to near-orthogonal (mean cos 0.0097) with 91.5% residual. Running the official ablation on Qwen3-4B shows the latent stream is indistinguishable with W_a on vs off.

ai-sherpa/repro-latentmas.overall: The logbook provides rigorous evidence that the architectural method (Claim 1) and Theorem 3.1 (Claim 2) are sound, and that Table 2's coverage matches the paper's description (Claim 5). However, it falsifies the core empirical performance claims (Claims 4, 6) and Theorem 3.3's information-preservation equivalence (Claim 3) through concrete experiments on real models and exact algebraic analysis of the released code.

SabaPivot/repro-fair-regression.paper_title: A General Framework for Fair and Robust Regression

claims.claim: Optimal fair transformation guarantees demographic parity while achieving minimum population risk among rank preserving fair predictors.
claims.evidence: fair_verify.py shows W1-unfairness collapsing from 2.4049 to 0.004371 on an independent test set (x550 reduction), Spearman(g-hat, f-hat)=1.000000 within every group (exact rank preservation), and interpolation unfairness linear in λ with R²=0.999998 with risk monotone decreasing; claim1_table1.py over 30 trials confirms unfairness << RDNN and < FRWB, and claim4_crime.py on UCI Communities & Crime reproduces the paper's knee λ=0.52 exactly (per-trial 0.524±0.038).

claims.claim: General framework applies to wide class of M-estimators including Cauchy, Huber, least absolute deviation, quantile, and Tukey losses.
claims.evidence: claim2_losses.py runs all seven losses (LAD, Quantile 0.5/0.9, Huber, Cauchy, Tukey, MSE) end-to-end through the full framework on Sim 1 with 3 seeds each under both Gaussian and t(1.5) noise; unfairness collapses to ~0.005 for every loss in both regimes, confirming the framework handles each M-estimator.

claims.claim: Framework can be extended to conditional demographic parity to account for legitimate covariates.
claims.evidence: claim3_cdp.py over 15 trials shows the stratum-wise CDP transform reduces conditional unfairness from 2.5349 to 0.0123 (x206), while the marginal-only DP transform leaves conditional unfairness at 0.1590 (13x higher) despite collapsing marginal unfairness to 0.0056, demonstrating the necessity and effectiveness of the conditional extension.

SabaPivot/repro-fair-regression.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence from the official code supporting all three claims on non-toy setups (1000-sample simulations, 15-30 trials, UCI CRIME real data), with exact DP, rank preservation, interpolation linearity, multi-loss generality, and CDP extension all demonstrated with real numbers. Main limitations are reduced trial counts versus the paper's 200 and inability to access the PDF for theorem-level verification.

Sasikanth/repro-fairmerging.paper_title: FairMerging: Rethinking Model Merging through the Lens of Fairness

claims.claim: FairMerging substantially mitigates unfairness while retaining competitive multi-task performance across multiple datasets, backbones, and merging baselines.
claims.evidence: On the non-toy DistilBERT run, FairMerging clearly reduces loss-parity gap vs the best merging baseline on only 2/4 datasets (Adult-race 0.1507 vs 0.1657; COMPAS-sex 0.0182 vs 0.0281), while the Adult-sex improvement is negligible (0.1977 vs 0.1981) and COMPAS-race is worse (0.0289 vs 0.0152). Accuracy is competitive on 3/4 datasets but drops 5pp on COMPAS-sex (0.6374 vs 0.6868). The MLP run shows FairMerging worse than the best baseline on 3/4 datasets for loss-gap. The claim of 'substantially mitigates unfairness across multiple datasets' is not consistently demonstrated.

claims.claim: Fairness gap induced by model merging is governed by merging magnitude term and global sensitivity terms that determine how unevenly perturbation affects subgroup losses.
claims.evidence: On a 2-layer MLP across 24 configs (4 datasets × 2 base variants × 3 seeds), the fitted gap-slope correlates with signed global sensitivity at r=0.9998, and r(|induced gap|, |magnitude × sensitivity|)=0.9999 vs 0.53 for magnitude alone and 0.75 for sensitivity alone, with median(slope/sensitivity)=0.97. These strongly support the theoretical bound, but the setup is a small MLP on tabular data with ~200 examples/group, not at the paper's model or data scale.

Sasikanth/repro-fairmerging.overall: The logbook provides a thorough independent re-implementation testing both claims across MLP and DistilBERT backbones with multiple datasets and merging baselines. Claim 2's magnitude×sensitivity relationship is strongly confirmed but only at toy MLP scale, while Claim 1's practical effectiveness shows mixed results on the non-toy DistilBERT run with clear wins only on the high-sensitivity Adult-race configuration and inconsistent or negative outcomes elsewhere.

ai-sherpa/repro-medmosaic.paper_title: MedMosaic: A Challenging Large Scale Benchmark of Diverse Medical Audio

claims.claim: Benchmarking 13 audio-language systems shows Gemini-2.5-Pro is the strongest evaluated model but reaches only about 68.1% weighted accuracy (Table 1)

AceVikings/repro-14187-claim1.paper_title: Convex Basins in Single-Index Model Loss Landscapes: Applications to Robust Recovery under Strong Adversarial Corruption

claims.claim: The paper proves the existence of a dimension-independent convex basin of constant radius R around the true parameter beta* for single-index models whose link function satisfies the Lipschitz complexity condition in Assumption 2.1 (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Basin radii are reported for 6 links × 4 dims, but radii decrease with d (e.g., logistic 0.85→0.63, tanh 0.22→0.16 from d=50 to 500) and gelu/swish are capped at the binary search upper bound of 1.5, preventing assessment of their true basin size; the d=500 drop is attributed to MC artifacts without verification by increasing n_mc.

claims.claim: A robust recovery algorithm combining spectral initialization via robust PCA (Section 4.1) with robust gradient descent refinement (Section 4.2) runs in near-linear time n = O~(m + P*m~) and achieves parameter error ||beta - beta*|| = O(sigma*sqrt(epsilon)) under heavy-tailed noise and strong adversarial contamination (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: 73% of 72 contaminated runs meet a 2x threshold for O(σ√ε) error, but 27% fail without explanation; specific σ and ε values are not reported, making independent assessment of the error bound impossible; timing data does show linear scaling from 25k to 5M samples.

claims.claim: Spectral initialization is shown to produce an initial estimate beta_0 within distance O(C4*epsilon^{1/4}) of the ground truth, placing it inside the convex basin needed for the subsequent gradient descent step to converge (Theorem 4.2).

alinia/repro-epistemic-uncertainty-overp.paper_title: On the Epistemic Uncertainty of Overparametrized Neural Networks

claims.claim: Non-identifiability in overparametrized networks causes substantial parameter uncertainty even when function is fully identified
claims.evidence: Algebraic verification confirms weight-splitting (ω_m=√c_m·ω*) preserves both function and L2 norm to machine precision (max abs err 1.8e-15), and NUTS posterior sampling (8 chains, M=5, n=64→16384) shows tr(Cov)/d persisting at ~0.63 while within-mode Var_P(f) collapses 50× (0.36→0.0015) and MAP RMSE→f* drops to 0.139, directly demonstrating substantial parameter uncertainty despite near-complete function identification.

claims.claim: Characterizes discrete and continuous sources of residual uncertainty via variance-based decomposition
claims.evidence: The variance-based decomposition is demonstrated concretely: for M=5 (permutation-only), within-mode trace collapses (0.79→0.063) while mixture trace persists (~0.63), isolating the discrete component; for M∈{10,20,40}, the continuous splitting component is characterized by recovered coefficients matching Beta(3,(k−1)·3) with median KS D=0.060 across k=2..14, and tr(Cov)/d remaining ~0.66–0.80 across all overparametrized widths as n grows to 4096.

claims.claim: Thorough analysis of posterior structure for one-hidden-layer ReLU networks
claims.evidence: Posterior structure is analyzed via NUTS across 15 (n,M) settings: Dirichlet/Beta distributional fits hold (KS D median 0.060, means tracking 1/k across k=2..14 and M∈{10,20,40}), and Theorem 1's E[s²]→1/k shows clear n-convergence (M=10, k=2: 0.643→0.572→0.537→0.511 at n=256→16384, theory 0.500), though convergence remains incomplete at finite n for larger k and E[s] undershoots theory by ~20–30%.

alinia/repro-epistemic-uncertainty-overp.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all three claims at the paper's own scale (one-hidden-layer ReLU BNN, p=5, M up to 40, n up to 16384, NUTS with 8 chains), combining exact algebraic verification of the non-identifiability structure with posterior sampling that demonstrates persistent parameter-space uncertainty under function identification and confirms the Dirichlet splitting law. The main limitation is incomplete moment convergence at finite n for larger group sizes and widths, but trends are consistently in the predicted direction.

Sasikanth/repro-adversarial-rl-dlm-unlea.paper_title: Adversarial Reinforcement Learning for Robust Diffusion Large Language Model Unlearning

claims.claim: First comprehensive study of unlearning for Diffusion Language Models revealing new vulnerabilities
claims.evidence: A real 8-setting decoding sweep on NPO-unlearned Dream-7B shows a 0.230 ROUGE-L range (77% relative swing) across diffusion steps/temperature, demonstrating hyperparameter sensitivity on a genuine 7B DLM. However, this is tested on a single RWKU entity (Stephen King) with only 12 probes, far from a 'comprehensive study' — the claim's breadth is not addressed.

claims.claim: DLMs tend to reproduce unlearned information when target inputs embedded in informative contexts due to suffix conditioning
claims.evidence: The teacher-forced NLL probe provides genuine evidence for the mechanism: suffix-conditioned NLL of the unlearned answer barely moves after NPO unlearning (0.744→0.750), while bare NLL rises slightly. However, the actual free-generation recall metric — which directly tests 'reproduce unlearned information' — shows suffix recall drops the MOST after unlearning (−37.5% relative), contradicting the predicted resurfacing pattern. Reduced scale (1 entity, 47 probes, single seed) with a split between proxy and behavioral metrics.

claims.claim: Adversarial RL framework significantly improves unlearning effectiveness while preserving model utility
claims.evidence: On the fixed-passage forget/utility benchmark, vanilla NPO outperforms AdvNPO on every axis (lower forget ROUGE, higher neighbor ROUGE), directly contradicting the claim. Under a GCG-style optimized-suffix attack on 6 probes, AdvNPO shows lower ASR than NPO (0.667 vs 0.833), supporting the claim's robustness direction. The NLL gap reduction (1.617→1.147 nats) also supports the mechanism. However, training was only 300 steps with a simplified greedy-bandit context selector instead of a learned generator, on a single entity and seed — far below the paper's full RL framework.

Sasikanth/repro-adversarial-rl-dlm-unlea.overall: The logbook runs real experiments on Dream-v0-Instruct-7B with RWKU data for all three claims, but at greatly reduced scale (1 entity, 12–47 probes, single seed, 300-step LoRA training with a simplified adversarial policy). Claims 1 and 2 show partial mechanism-level support (hyperparameter sensitivity, suffix-conditioned NLL persistence), while Claim 3 yields genuinely mixed results — falsified on the standard benchmark but supported under adversarial-suffix attack — making none of the three clearly verified or falsified at full scale.

sugan04/ICML2026_3677_repro.overall: The logbook provides concrete full-scale evidence supporting Claims 1 and 3, with real model evaluations, large datasets, and appropriate metrics. agharsallah/8ewf5i4shw-logbook.paper_title: Causal Effect Identifiability in the Presence of Latent Confounders Without Auxiliary Variables

claims.claim: In linear SCMs without auxiliary variables, causal effect identifiability depends on Gaussianity of exogenous noises.
claims.evidence: The logbook tests exact population-level cumulant identities (Condition 1: cum(T,T,T,O)/cum(T,T,T,T)=alpha with non-Gaussian treatment noise) and Gaussian-component covariance ratios (Condition 2: Sigma_G[TO]/Sigma_G[TT]=alpha) across 144+32 configurations with 5 seeds each. Raw data shows alpha recovery errors at machine precision (≤1e-12) with 100% pass rates, confirming that identifiability holds under the stated non-Gaussianity conditions.

claims.claim: RGPO provides a complete characterization of conditions under which causal effect is identifiable vs. unidentifiable.
claims.evidence: All four Gaussianity regimes are tested: Conditions 1-2 (identifiable, from Claim 1) show unique alpha recovery, Condition 3 shows exactly m=2,3,5 feasible effects for m non-Gaussian sources with max_loading_residual=0.0, and Condition 4 shows 9 valid Gaussian-variance reallocations with covariance residual ~2.22e-16. Joshi2312/repro-masked-ssl-bbp-transitio.paper_title: A Random Matrix Theory of Masked Self-Supervised Learning

claims.claim: Masked modeling undergoes Baik–Ben Arous–Péché (BBP)-type phase transition, identifying when masked SSL begins to recover latent signals.
claims.evidence: 972 HF + 234 local runs of the exact SSR estimator at d=500–2000 (alpha=2, lambda=1e-5, matching Fig. 4) show the top eigenvalue matches the Prop. 1 closed form to mean abs error 1.7e-3 at d=2000, with the top eigenvector overlap^2 going from 0.004 below theta_*=0.707 to 0.80 above, and transition detection tightening toward the theoretical threshold as d grows (1.25→1.125→0.882 for d=500/1000/2000).

claims.claim: Provides explicit expressions for generalization error and characterizes spectral structure of learned joint predictor.
claims.evidence: Theorem 1 generalization-error formula matches simulation to mean rel. dev. 1.6% over 360 runs (Toeplitz rho in {0,0.5,0.9}, d=200, full double-descent grid), converging to 0.17% at d=1600; Theorem 3 spectrum matches at d=2000 with KS=0.041 (alpha=1.5) and two-atom locations to 2e-3 (alpha=0.6); Corollary 1 universality collapse across four power-law covariances with KS≤0.036.

claims.claim: Identifies structured regimes where masked self-supervised learning provably outperforms PCA on spiked covariance models.
claims.evidence: Both sides of the comparison are confirmed at full scale: on spiked covariance PCA strictly wins in 20/20 (theta,p) pairs (population and n=6000 empirical), consistent with Lemma 4.1; on AR(1)/Toeplitz covariances, SSR beats PCA below the phase boundary gamma_*(rho), which is reproduced to max error 3.3e-4 over 19 rhos at d=3000, with empirical finite-sample crossings at 0.150/0.1933 vs theory 0.1513/0.1950.

Joshi2312/repro-masked-ssl-bbp-transitio.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous, full-scale reproduction of all three core claims, implementing the paper's exact mathematical objects in numpy and validating them against Monte-Carlo simulation at dimensions matching or exceeding the paper's own figures (d up to 3000), with convergence-in-d studies and multiple seeds throughout. The quantitative agreement is strong across all claims (eigenvalue errors ~1e-3, risk formula deviations ~1%, phase boundary errors ~3e-4).

snaykey/repro-high-accuracy-sampling.paper_title: High-Accuracy Sampling for Diffusion Models and Log-Concave Distributions

claims.claim: The paper's First-Order Rejection Sampling (FORS) meta-algorithm (Theorem 3.1) produces samples with error δ using sample complexity bounded by 3Be^(2B)log(2/δ) with probability 1-δ (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: FORS (Algorithm 1) is implemented and run with T=200 calls across B∈{0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0}, measuring actual weight evaluations. Mean evaluations stay below the predicted bound B·e^{2B}·(T+log(1/δ)) with ratios 0.27–1.66, confirming the sample complexity scaling empirically rather than by formula evaluation.

claims.claim: Under only a finite second-moment assumption (minimal assumptions), the diffusion sampler achieves query complexity O(d·log²(1/δ) + log³(1/δ)), giving polylog(1/δ) dependence rather than the poly(1/δ) of prior work (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: v3/v4 implement a real VP DDPM backward sampler with FORS denoising steps on a bimodal Gaussian mixture (non-log-concave, finite second moment only). KS error decays geometrically in K (R²=0.92, slope -0.023/step), confirming K~log(1/δ). d-scaling sweep up to D=128 gives log-log slope 0.84, consistent with O(d·polylog(1/δ)).

claims.claim: Under a non-uniform Lipschitz condition on the score (Assumption 4.3), a DDPM-like sampler achieves total-variation error controlled via chi-squared divergence with complexity O(√(dL_δ log(d/δ))·log(d/δ) + L_δ log²(d/δ)) (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: v3/v4 test the Corollary 4.4 adaptive schedule on subspace mixtures in R^D with D up to 128. Measured speedup K(D)/K(k=2) matches the theoretical ratio (D+ℓ)/(k+ℓ) within 1% (7.27x vs 7.2x at D=64; 13.75x vs 13.6x at D=128), confirming d★ replaces ambient d in the complexity.

claims.claim: For distributions with low intrinsic dimension d★, an adaptive-step-size method attains complexity O(d★·log²((d+M₂²)/δ²)), replacing the ambient dimension d with d★ (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: The only evidence is arithmetic computation of speedup = d/√(d·L_op) for various d and L values—pure formula evaluation with no actual sampling experiment testing the non-uniform Lipschitz condition on a real sampler. No experiment measures TV error or chi-squared divergence under Assumption 4.3.

claims.claim: Section 5 extends the FORS framework to sample from general log-concave distributions using only gradient evaluations (no density evaluations), giving the first polylog(1/δ) sampler in this setting (Section 5).
claims.evidence: v3/v4 implement the proximal sampler (Algorithm 3) with FORS-based RGO using only gradient evaluations, tested on a non-Gaussian logcosh potential (d=8, quadrature ground truth, 1.1% final error) and anisotropic Gaussian (κ=10, max 4.1% coord error). Geometric error decay demonstrated at d=32,64,128 with rate ~1/d, confirming polylog(1/δ) steps for log-concave sampling via gradient queries.

snaykey/repro-high-accuracy-sampling.overall: The logbook provides real implementations of FORS, DDPM+FORS, and the proximal sampler with FORS-based RGO, tested on non-log-concave and non-Gaussian targets up to d=128, empirically confirming polylog(1/δ) scaling, d-dependence, and intrinsic-dimension speedup. Claim 4 (non-uniform Lipschitz refinement) lacks any actual sampling experiment and remains unverified.

IvanMiao/repro-phase-aware-moe-agentic-r.paper_title: Phase-Aware Mixture of Experts for Agentic Reinforcement Learning

claims.claim: In ALFWorld, single-policy RL agents exhibit simplicity bias: simple pick-and-place tasks consume roughly 75% of network capacity while complex heat/cool/clean tasks receive only about 5%, despite being critical to success.
claims.evidence: A real 3-seed RL experiment was run on a synthetic latent-regime MDP (not ALFWorld) with 4 experts, but dominant-expert occupancy was 36.61% in both conditions with no 75%/5% pattern emerging, so the claim was addressed on a clearly simplified setup without reproducing the paper's metric.

claims.claim: The phase router operates at the environment-step level (cross-attention over goal-conditioned observations plus a 3-layer LSTM over action-observation history) rather than per-token, using a switching penalty (λ_s=0.05) and temperature annealing (τ: 2.0→0.5) to keep expert assignment temporally consistent (about 8.4 switches/episode vs. 45 for token-level routing).
claims.evidence: A 3-seed L4 GPU proxy using frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B embeddings trained a paper-shaped router on 80 synthetic supervised episodes; the switching penalty alone reduced switches 11.2% and improved accuracy 1.3 points, but the combined penalty-plus-annealing recipe was not best (3.99 switches vs 3.71 for penalty-only, 71.8% accuracy vs 75.6%), and the specific 8.4 vs 45 switch counts were never validated on real ALFWorld RL.

claims.claim: On ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-1.5B, adding Phase-Aware MoE to a GiGPO baseline raises overall success rate from 86.1% to 93.8% (+7.7 points), enough for the 1.5B PA-MoE model to surpass a vanilla 7B baseline (90.2%).
claims.evidence: Only table arithmetic was checked (93.8−86.1=7.7); no ALFWorld training or evaluation was run because the release lacks checkpoints, data pipeline, and a working training entry point, so there is no empirical evidence supporting or contradicting the success-rate claim.

claims.claim: On WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B, PA-MoE improves success rate from 67.4% to 82.3% (+14.9 points), and ablations show K=4 experts with phase-level (not token- or trajectory-level) routing is optimal (93.8% vs. 85.7% token-level and 88.5% trajectory-level on ALFWorld).
claims.evidence: Only table values were verified from the paper (67.4→82.3, token 85.7, trajectory 88.5, phase 93.8); no WebShop training, ALFWorld routing ablation, or token/trajectory-level control was executed, as the release contains no WebShop data path or implemented routing-granularity controls.

IvanMiao/repro-phase-aware-moe-agentic-r.overall: The logbook provides a thorough source-and-code audit confirming table arithmetic and identifying that the released code materially differs from the paper (missing switch penalty, temperature schedule, wrong LSTM depth, bypassed router), but the only executed experiments are toy proxies on synthetic data that do not reproduce any benchmark claim. No ALFWorld or WebShop RL training was attempted.

Joshi2312/repro-tensor-schatten-dual-spa.paper_title: Refining Dual Spectral Sparsity in Transformed Tensor Singular Values

claims.claim: Tensor lp-Schatten-q quasi-norm enables explicit control of dual spectral sparsity
claims.evidence: On 40x40x32 tensors with planted (s=4, r=3) dual-sparse structure, the reweighted proximal scheme recovers exact support and ranks in 24/24 mid-grid runs, and calibrated control sweeps show effective active-slice count is monotone in p (1.00→1.17 at fixed q) while effective rank is monotone in q (1.00→1.17 at fixed p), with HF-scaled 64x64x48 runs confirming the same trends.

claims.claim: Strictly generalizes Tensor Nuclear Norm by coupling global frequency sparsity with local spectral low-rankness
claims.evidence: (p,q)=(1,1) equals TNN to 3.95e-16 max relative deviation over 50 tensors (3.46e-16 over 200 on HF); two tensors with exactly equal TNN (rel gap 0.0) but opposite dual-sparsity structure are separated by the quasi-norm by factors up to 2.96e5 at (0.3,0.3); oracle-tuned lp(Sq) denoising achieves 1.36% vs TNN's 2.16% relative error (37.3% improvement).

claims.claim: Establishes first minimax error bounds under this dual spectral sparsity model
claims.evidence: Both sides of the minimax statement are computed on the paper's own Gaussian location model and T_{0,0}(s,r) class across 180 problem sizes: the projection estimator risk tracks F=(σ²/n)(s log(em/s)+srd) with slope 1.03, R²=0.999, risk/F in [1.64, 2.11], while an independent Fano floor from explicit packings with exact Gilbert-Varshamov counts gives floor/F in [0.0181, 0.0209], slope 1.004, R²=0.9998, bracketing the minimax rate in a window flat in (s,r,d,m); the 'first' priority assertion is correctly noted as untestable by experiment.

Joshi2312/repro-tensor-schatten-dual-spa.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous from-scratch reproduction of the paper's core theoretical objects and algorithm, with both local and HF-scaled runs demonstrating exact special-case recovery to machine precision, strict separation beyond TNN, and two-sided minimax rate verification across 180 problem sizes. The main limitations—unavailable appendix, self-constructed converse, and untestable 'first' priority claim—are transparently disclosed.

agharsallah/4yrxhbbvdh-logbook.paper_title: Adaptive Multiscale Binary Expansion Tests for Independence

claims.claim: wa-dCoBET consistently matches or outperforms HSIC and distance covariance independence tests
claims.evidence: Across a 6-structure battery (n=128, 200 datasets, 2 seeds, permutation tests with 150 permutations), wa-dCoBET matches or outperforms both dCov and HSIC on 5 of 6 structures (linear, quadratic, sine, heteroscedastic, W-shape all at or above both baselines), with the sole exception being circle where wa-dCoBET (0.95) trails HSIC (1.00) by ~0.05, a small deficit on a structure where HSIC's radial kernel is ideally matched.

claims.claim: wa-dCoBET shows particular strength in higher-dimensional and non-monotone settings
claims.evidence: On non-monotone 1D structures, wa-dCoBET shows large power gains over the best baseline: sine (+0.50), W-shape (+0.46), high-frequency sine (+0.26), checkerboard (+0.09). In higher-dimensional non-monotone settings (p=2, p=3), wa-dCoBET retains full power (1.00 and 0.98), matching the strongest baseline rather than exceeding it, but confirming no degradation in higher dimensions.

claims.claim: wa-dCoBET maintains accurate type I error control while achieving strong power
claims.evidence: Type I error under independence is estimated at 0.060 (Gaussian marginals) and 0.033 (uniform marginals) across 400 datasets with nominal α=0.05, both within 2 Monte-Carlo standard errors of the nominal level (threshold 0.072). Power on the sine alternative remains strong at 0.81–0.87 with the same permutation test.

agharsallah/4yrxhbbvdh-logbook.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence across a 6-structure power battery, higher-dimensional non-monotone settings, and type-I error calibration experiments that collectively support all three claims. The setup (n=128, 200–400 datasets, permutation nulls, proper HSIC/dCov baselines) is at the standard scale for independence-testing power studies and is non-toy, though limited to 2 seeds and a reconstruction without official code.

claims.claim: GR-MoE preserves performance on retained capabilities while achieving 30% compute efficiency on forget capabilities for selective model access

snaykey/repro-profiling-irrational-agent.paper_title: Adaptive Estimation and Inference in Semi-parametric Heterogeneous Clustered Multitask Learning via Neyman Orthogonality

claims.claim: The adaptive orthogonal multitask estimator achieves exact recovery of the latent task clustering with high probability, established via Theorem 3.5 (Section 3, Cluster Recovery).
claims.evidence: On the paper's PLM DGP (m=9, K=3, R=20 reps), P(exact recovery) rises to 1.00 at δ=2/3 and 0.95 at δ=1 as N_k grows from 450 to 3000, with within-cluster spread ~1e-13 (bit-identical fused estimates) and cross-cluster gaps tracking δ — directly demonstrating the high-probability exact recovery of Theorem 3.5(1).

claims.claim: For tasks in cluster k with pooled sample size N_k, the estimator attains the rate ||θ̂_j − θ*_j||_2 = O_P(N_k^{-1/2}), matching pooled parametric convergence (Theorem 3.5, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Varying N_k over a 16× range (200–3200) with R=40 reps on the PLM DGP, the measured log-log slope of RMSE vs N_k is -0.551 (R²=0.980), close to the theoretical -0.5, while the personalized baseline achieves only slope -0.454 against its own n_j, confirming the pooled parametric rate with √m_k gain.

claims.claim: √N_k(θ̂_j − θ*_j) is asymptotically normal with covariance matching the oracle estimator that knows the true clustering in advance (Theorem 3.6, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Over R=160 replications at N_k=3000, the standardized statistic √N_k(θ̂−θ*) passes normality tests (KS p=0.834, QQ corr=0.9976) and its variance matches the clustering oracle to within 0.5% (ratio 1.005), with mean |adaptive−oracle| = 2.2e-10 and 2.8× variance reduction over the personalized estimator.

claims.claim: Extensions permit within-cluster heterogeneity bounded by ξ_k = O(N_k^{-1/2}) while preserving the estimation guarantees (Theorems 3.7–3.8, Section 3).
claims.evidence: With shrinking ξ_k=0.5·N_k^{-1/2}, the RMSE slope stays at -0.395 and the studentized statistic √N_k·|dev| remains bounded (1.18→1.45), while a constant-ξ=0.10 control collapses to slope -0.042 with diverging studentized statistic (2.35→6.88), empirically bracketing the O(N_k^{-1/2}) boundary of Theorems 3.7–3.8.

claims.claim: In simulations across three models (PLM, ATE, DID) and separation levels δ ∈ {1/3, 2/3, 1}, the method achieves Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) near 1, outperforming competing clustering approaches (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: Across all 9 cells (PLM/ATE/DID × δ∈{1/3,2/3,1}) with the paper's exact DGPs, orthogonal losses, and baselines (m=20, K=3), the adaptive method achieves ARI ≥ 0.98, while Personalized and MeTaG show ARI≈0 and ARMUL is competitive only with correct K (ARMUL(K±1) degrades), confirming ARI near 1 and superiority over competitors. Runs are reduced (R=6 vs 100) and n is smaller, but the task, models, metrics, and baselines are faithful to the paper.

claims.claim: On real electricity price elasticity data from 51 US states, the method recovers three clusters, e.g. Virginia at −1.138 ± 0.189 versus a 46-state cluster at −0.221 ± 0.009 (Table 1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: The RECS 2020 microdata was never downloaded and no real-data experiment was run; only a synthetic 51-task analog was tested, which the logbook explicitly states is not a reproduction of Table 1's numbers. The exact RECS elasticity estimates (VA −1.138±0.189, 46-state cluster −0.221±0.009) remain unverified.

snaykey/repro-profiling-irrational-agent.overall: The logbook provides strong concrete experimental evidence supporting claims 1–5 on the paper's own DGPs with proper baselines and controls, including exact recovery probabilities, measured convergence rates, normality tests, oracle variance matching, and heterogeneity boundary bracketing. Claim 6 (real RECS data) is inconclusive because the external dataset was never obtained and only a synthetic sanity check was performed.

sugan04/ICML2026_1_repro.paper_title: On the Epistemic Uncertainty of Overparametrized Neural Networks

claims.claim: Overparametrized one-hidden-layer ReLU networks (M>M* neurons) exhibit continuous non-identifiability through weight-splitting, where redundant neurons split a true neuron's contribution via coefficients constrained to a simplex, in addition to the discrete permutation symmetries present in exactly-specified models (Section 3.1, Section 3.2, Corollary 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook shows parameter variance persists under function identification (e.g., Layer 1 weight variance 42.15 with MSE ~0), but never demonstrates the specific weight-splitting mechanism with simplex-constrained coefficients. The ResNet-10/CIFAR-10 experiment uses an entirely wrong architecture (not a one-hidden-layer ReLU network), and the synth_regression run reports only aggregate variance bounds without showing the splitting structure or simplex constraints claimed.

claims.claim: Because standard information-theoretic uncertainty measures fail on these non-identifiable parameters, epistemic uncertainty is instead defined via the trace of the posterior weight covariance, EU(y|x) := tr(Cov_P(w|·)), enabling a variance-based decomposition into discrete (permutation) and continuous (splitting) sources of residual uncertainty (Section 2.1, Section 2.2, Example 1).
claims.evidence: The HMC-based variance decomposition on 50,000 samples separates discrete (65.2%) and continuous (34.8%) variance using Kuhn-Munkres alignment, which partially addresses the decomposition idea. However, the claim's core is the specific EU definition via tr(Cov_P(w|·)) and its theoretical justification; the experiments show decomposition numbers without verifying the trace-based definition or its properties. The reproduce.py script uses a tiny 5→50→50→1 network with 20 training points, clearly a toy setup.

claims.claim: For one-hidden-layer ReLU networks, Theorem 1 characterizes the induced posterior over splitting coefficients as following symmetric Dirichlet distributions with concentration parameter alpha=(p+1)/2 (Lemma 4), with posterior means of individual redundant neurons scaling as O(M^-1/2) and within-neuron covariance remaining constant while cross-neuron covariance decays as O(M^-1) (Theorem 1, Corollary 1, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook's Claim 3 experiments count unique activation patterns (12,458 modes) and compute Hessian spectra, but never test the actual mathematical claims: symmetric Dirichlet distributions with α=(p+1)/2, O(M^{-1/2}) scaling of posterior means, or O(M^{-1}) decay of cross-neuron covariance. None of the specific quantitative predictions of Theorem 1, Corollary 1, or Lemma 4 are evaluated.

claims.claim: The posterior over splitting coordinates remains non-degenerate even as the number of training samples n approaches infinity, showing that substantial parameter-space uncertainty persists despite the underlying function being fully identified (Section 3.2, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Claim 4 is never explicitly addressed in the logbook. While Claim 1's experiments loosely show parameter variance under function identification, no experiment systematically varies n toward infinity to show the posterior over splitting coordinates remains non-degenerate. The specific claim about the n→∞ limit of splitting-coordinate posteriors is untested.

sugan04/ICML2026_1_repro.overall: The logbook provides some experiments showing parameter variance persists under function identification and a variance decomposition into discrete/continuous components, but it fails to test the paper's core theoretical claims about weight-splitting simplex structure, Dirichlet posteriors, scaling laws, or the n→∞ limit. Most experiments use wrong architectures or toy setups, and key mathematical predictions are never evaluated.

claims.claim: RACO is an offline, reward-free preference-alignment method that accepts user-specified objective weights and explicitly handles conflicting objectives (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook shows a convergence run with user-specified weights [0.8, 0.2] on Qwen-3-7B and gradient norm decreasing to <1e-4, but this does not demonstrate the offline/reward-free nature of RACO or verify the Table 1 comparison of method properties. No evidence addresses the specific claim about being an offline, reward-free preference-alignment method.

claims.claim: The method uses CAGrad-Clip to limit correction gradients so updates better respect preferred objective trade-offs (Figure 1, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The Llama-3-8B gradient conflict logs show clipped CAGrad converting negative cosine similarities to positive ones (e.g., -0.85 to 0.12/0.16), and the reproduce.py toy script demonstrates a simple clipping mechanism on a 5x2 linear model. However, no experiment directly measures whether clipping causes updates to better respect preferred objective trade-offs as claimed in Figure 1/Algorithm 1.

claims.claim: On TL;DR summarization, RACO achieves better Pareto frontiers for conciseness-quality and faithfulness-quality trade-offs than AMoPO and weighted-loss DPO baselines (Figure 2, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports hypervolume metrics on summarization tasks but uses baselines PMTL, EPO, and Linear—none of which are the AMOPO or weighted-loss DPO baselines specified in the claim. No TL;DR dataset is explicitly identified, and the specific conciseness-quality and faithfulness-quality Pareto frontiers from Figures 2-3 are not reproduced.

claims.claim: On BeaverTails safety alignment, RACO improves harmlessness-helpfulness Pareto trade-offs across Qwen3 and Gemma3 setups (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: No experiments on BeaverTails or safety alignment (harmlessness-helpfulness) appear anywhere in the logbook. The Qwen-3 and Gemma-3 results shown are for summarization hypervolume, not safety alignment.

claims.claim: Ablations show clipping and the correction-radius constant affect validation margins and Pareto frontiers (Figure 5, Figure 6).
claims.evidence: No ablation experiments varying clipping on/off or sweeping the correction-radius constant are present in the logbook. No validation margins or Pareto frontier ablation results corresponding to Figures 5-6 are reported.

sugan04/ICML2026_2_repro.overall: The logbook provides only fragmentary evidence: a convergence run with user-specified weights, some gradient-conflict resolution logs on Llama-3-8B, and hypervolume comparisons against wrong baselines (PMTL/EPO/Linear instead of AMOPO/weighted-loss DPO). The majority of the paper's specific claims—TL;DR Pareto frontiers, BeaverTails safety alignment, and ablations on clipping/radius—are never addressed with matching experimental setups.

sugan04/ICML2026_4_repro.paper_title: Envisioning Beyond the Few: Disentangled Semantics and Primitives for Few-Shot Atypical Layout-to-Image Generation

claims.claim: The framework tackles representation fragmentation in few-shot atypical layout-to-image generation by disentangling category-level semantics from instance-level visual primitives through three modules: Semantic Anchoring, which aggregates DINOv2-based cross-attention features across exemplars into stable per-category anchors injected into U-Net layers; Primitive Imbuing, which models fine-grained appearance via learnable visual prototypes fit with closed-form ridge regression (T ≈ WP); and Conceptual Steering, which uses text-driven GradCAM to align generated and ground-truth foreground activation maps (Section 4.2, Section 4.3, Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook measures a proxy 'cross-attention leakage' metric on an unspecified 'atypical_layouts_v2' dataset comparing against GLIGEN, but never implements or tests the three claimed modules (Semantic Anchoring with DINOv2, Primitive Imbuing with ridge regression, Conceptual Steering with GradCAM). The specific architectural components central to the claim are not evaluated.

claims.claim: Evaluated in the 5-shot regime on three atypical layout-to-image benchmarks — DIOR (aerial imagery), RUOD (underwater scenes), and ExDark (low-light scenes) — the method outperforms prior SOTA layout-to-image baselines including MIGC, CC-Diff, and CC-Diff++, e.g. reducing FID by 8.17 versus CC-Diff on DIOR while improving mAP, AP50, and AP75 under Faster R-CNN evaluation across all three domains (Table 1, Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook evaluates on 'Fantasy Landscapes, Abstract Geometric, Surreal Portraits' instead of the paper's DIOR, RUOD, and ExDark benchmarks; uses GLIGEN and LDM-Layout as baselines instead of MIGC, CC-Diff, and CC-Diff++; and measures only FID and CLIP score instead of the claimed mAP, AP50, and AP75 under Faster R-CNN evaluation. None of the paper's experimental setup is reproduced.

sugan04/ICML2026_4_repro.overall: This logbook does not faithfully reproduce either claim: it substitutes entirely different datasets, baselines, metrics, and architectural components for those specified in the paper. The experiments are essentially unrelated to the paper's actual claims and setup.
