claims.evidence: Both sides of the rate F=(σ²/n)(s·log(em/s)+srd) are computed independently: achievability risk/F in [3.76,4.71] (slope 1.031, R²0.9936) over 32 configs and converse floor/F in [0.026,0.042] (slope 1.172, R²0.9966) via own Varshamov-Gilbert+Fano construction, with floor<F<risk holding in all 41 configs; the Le Cam two-point control yielding an identical flat floor confirms the rate genuinely comes from the packing argument.

ai-sherpa/tensor-schatten-dual-sparsity-.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all three claims by implementing the paper's theoretical objects from scratch at their native definitions: the quasi-norm's dual-axis sparsity control is demonstrated via calibrated monotone sweeps, the strict TNN generalization via machine-precision special-case matching and constructed separation examples, and the minimax rate via independently computed achievability and converse bounds with correct scaling. The reproduction is transparent about using its own algorithmic constructions for the unavailable appendix proofs, but the measured results on the paper's own Gaussian location model and dual-sparsity class constitute non-toy, faithful verification of the stated theoretical properties.

ai-sherpa/forest-matrix-signed-graphs-re.paper_title: Fast Estimation for Forest Matrix of Signed Graphs

claims.claim: GSCF (Generalized Spanning Converging Forest) generates spanning converging forests for signed graphs using loop-erased random walks in expected O(n) time, per Theorem 5.2 (Section 5.1, Algorithm 1, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Timed GSCF (Algorithm 1) on synthetic sparse signed graphs (avg out-degree 4, 20% negative edges) across n=1,000→2,000,000 with 7 repeats/size: OLS linear fit gives R²=0.9838 (slope 166 ns/node), and independent power-law fit gives exponent p=1.150 (R²=0.9800), both consistent with O(n) across 3 orders of magnitude. The OLS model also predicts n=4M timing within +19%, confirming linear generalization.

claims.claim: FMDE estimates the diagonal of the forest matrix via sampling in O(ln) time, where l is the number of samples (Section 6.2, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: On real Bitcoinotc (5,881 nodes/35,592 edges, exact Table-3 match) and Gnutella08* (6,301/20,777), FMDE and FMDE+ produce estimates with monotonically decreasing error as eps: 0.3→0.1, and independent OLS complexity fits give R²=0.9994 (time vs l, n fixed) and R²=0.9905 (time vs n, l fixed), both confirming O(ln) scaling.

claims.claim: FMDE+ incorporates additional network information to achieve the same O(ln) time complexity as FMDE but with lower variance, and Theorem 6.3 proves its superior performance on balanced signed graphs (Section 6.2, Theorem 6.3).
claims.evidence: Unit test directly evaluates Theorem 6.3's hypothesis on a balanced signed graph (l=1, 40 reps): MSE(FMDE)=0.1878 ≥ MSE(FMDE+)=0.0051. On real data, FMDE+ error is 11.5×–11.8× lower than FMDE on Bitcoinotc and 942× lower on Gnutella08* at matched l, with the same O(ln) time complexity confirmed by Claim 2's fits.

claims.claim: On the SlashdotZoo network, exact diagonal computation via direct matrix inversion takes 991.5 seconds while FMDE+ completes in under 1.1 seconds (Table 1).
claims.evidence: On the real KONECT SlashdotZoo graph (n=79,116, m=515,397), sparse-LU factorization of (I+L) alone took 961.9s single-threaded (same order as the paper's 991.5s on 72 cores), while FMDE+ completed in 1.32s at l=623 with the 0≤q_ii≤1 invariant holding for all 79,116 nodes and 0.54% mean relative error vs exact on 400 sampled nodes. Absolute numbers differ slightly due to single-thread Python vs 72-core Julia, but the ~1000× speedup ratio is corroborated.

claims.claim: The methods scale to the FullUSA network with roughly 2.3×10^7 (over twenty million) nodes, where exact computation fails but FMDE+ completes within one hour (Table 3).
claims.evidence: Ran the independently-implemented algorithm directly at n=23,947,300 (m=115,417,200 directed arcs, avg out-degree 4.82): GSCF completed 5/5 trials (median 12.72s), FMDE 5/5 (16.02s/trial), FMDE+ 5/5 (56.67s/trial), with 0≤q_ii≤1 holding for all 23.9M nodes, both estimators agreeing at q̄≈0.2058, and peak RSS 5,144 MB. Exact matrix inversion is categorically infeasible at this scale. The full Theorem-6.4 sample budget was not run (only 5 trials), but the method demonstrably scales to 20M+ nodes.

claims.claim: FMDE+ achieves roughly ten times lower average relative error than FMDE across tested networks (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: On Bitcoinotc at matched l, FMDE+ average relative error is 11.5× (eps=0.3) to 11.8× (eps=0.1) lower than FMDE, directly matching the 'roughly ten times' claim. On Gnutella08* the gap is even larger (942× at eps=0.1). The unit test on a balanced graph also shows MSE(FMDE+)/MSE(FMDE) = 0.0051/0.1878 ≈ 1/37.

ai-sherpa/forest-matrix-signed-graphs-re.overall: This logbook provides strong independent evidence for all six claims through a from-scratch numpy/numba reimplementation validated against brute-force combinatorial enumeration and exact matrix solves. The reproduction uses the paper's own real datasets (Bitcoinotc, Gnutella08*, SlashdotZoo) at exact node/edge counts, directly tests at the paper's native 23.9M-node FullUSA scale, and is transparent about implementation-dependent wall-clock differences (single-thread Python vs 72-core Julia) that affect absolute timings but not algorithmic complexity or accuracy ordering.

bertfil/IkjsHRpuYY.paper_title: Prescriptive Scaling Reveals the Evolution of Language Model Capabilities

claims.claim: Capability boundaries are estimated via smoothed pinball-loss quantile regression at quantile τ=0.98 with smoothing parameter κ=50 and regularization λ=10⁻³ (Section 2.1).
claims.evidence: The codebase confirms the exact hyperparameters (DEFAULT_LAMBDA_B=1e-3, kappa_train=50, tau=0.98 in skill_frontier/core/sigmoid.py and scripts), and C18 shows CV-tuned values cluster around these defaults with near-zero OOD pinball/coverage deltas, while C17 confirms coverage errors of ~1.8% IS and ~2.2% OOS on the full six-task, three-period setup.

claims.claim: Post-training capability boundaries are modeled as sigmoid functions of log10(FLOPs), q_τ^sig(z;θ)=y0+L·σ(a+βz), achieving in-distribution pinball loss of 4.08×10⁻³ versus 4.00×10⁻³ for a more flexible I-spline estimator, while generalizing better out-of-distribution (4.93×10⁻³ vs 4.92×10⁻³) (Section 3.1.1, Table 2).
claims.evidence: C5 reproduces Table 2 across 18 per-task CSVs (3 splits × 6 tasks): Sigmoid ID pinball 0.00408 vs I-spline 0.00400, OOD pinball 0.00493 vs 0.00492, and Sigmoid achieves the lowest OOD calibration error (0.0221 vs I-spline 0.0241), all within a fraction of a percent of paper values.

claims.claim: At 10²⁴ FLOPs, the estimated 0.98-quantile boundary reaches 0.539 accuracy on MATH Level 5 versus 0.563 on MMLU-Pro, 0.700 on BBH, 0.828 on IFEval, 0.535 on MUSR, and 0.424 on GPQA (Table 1).
claims.evidence: C3 interpolates the no-split 0.98-quantile sigmoid boundary CSVs at x=1000 (10^24 FLOPs), yielding IFEval 0.828, BBH 0.700, MATH Lvl 5 0.539, GPQA 0.424, MUSR 0.535, MMLU-Pro 0.563 — matching all six Table 1 cells to within ~0.001.

claims.claim: Unlike the stable boundaries for BBH, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and MUSR, the MATH Level 5 and IFEval capability boundaries are non-stationary over time, with later-period models exceeding earlier predicted boundaries (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: C2 reports OOD coverage errors below 2% for BBH (0.0143), GPQA (0.0188), MMLU-Pro (0.0167), MUSR (0.0186), while MATH Lvl 5 shows persistent under-coverage (mean 0.0294, signed errors -0.0496/-0.0123/-0.0314 across k1–k3) and IFEval shows early under-coverage recovering by k3; C6's regenerated temporal-drift figure confirms the same pattern.

claims.claim: A balanced I-optimal sampling design recovers near-full-data capability frontiers using roughly 20% of the evaluation budget, with GPQA and MUSR requiring as little as 5% (Section 4, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: C4's alpha-sweep shows MAE_OOS_macro decreasing 0.110→0.069→0.052→0.044→0.029 for alpha=5/10/20/50/100%, with the curve flattening after ~20%; GPQA at 5% (0.0236 vs full 0.0191, ratio 1.24) and MUSR at 5% (0.0297 vs full 0.0197, ratio 1.51) are near-identical to full-data.

claims.claim: A cross-benchmark shift test applied to AIME-2025 scores finds a positive but not statistically significant shift (p=0.15), giving no clear aggregate evidence of post-release contamination inflating math benchmark scores (Section 5.2.2, Equation 3).
claims.evidence: C10 ran the cross-benchmark logit-to-logit group-shift regression on MATH-500 vs AIME-2025 (n=90), producing gamma=0.576 (positive) with one-sided p=0.1484, matching the paper's p=0.15 and confirming non-significance at the 0.05 level.

bertfil/IkjsHRpuYY.overall: All six claims are supported by concrete numerical evidence from running the paper's own code on the full six-task, multi-period dataset with the specified hyperparameters, producing values that match the paper's tables and figures to within ~1% relative error. The reproduction is high-fidelity, with only trivial environment fixes (Python version selection) and no methodological changes.

bertfil/aGaBFE9pta.paper_title: Is Your LLM Overcharging You? Tokenization, Transparency, and Incentives

claims.claim: Under pay-per-token pricing, a provider that reports each output character as a separate token can overcharge users by approximately 344.9±3.8% on Llama-3.2-1B (Table 1, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook's C5 evidence shows the naive character-splitting overcharge for Llama-3.2-1B reaching 343.5% at maximum iterations, which falls within the paper's stated 344.9±3.8% range. Though the underlying output data was shipped rather than regenerated, the overcharge computation is a mechanical token-counting exercise that was independently executed by the agent.

claims.claim: Finding the longest plausible tokenization of a given output string that still matches the provider's claimed next-token distribution is NP-hard (Theorem 3, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Theorem 3 is a theoretical NP-hardness result. The logbook explicitly states no extracted claims test it, and no experiments or proof verification were attempted.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1, a heuristic that iteratively splits high-index vocabulary tokens into lower-indexed pairs in O(m(log m + σ_max)) time, lets a provider overcharge by up to 13% on Ministral-8B under nucleus sampling with p=0.99 without producing an implausible tokenization (Section 3.3, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook tested Algorithm 1 on Llama-3.2-1B (1B parameters) rather than the claimed Ministral-8B (8B parameters), and the specific 13% overcharge figure on M8B was never measured. Qualitative mechanisms (unimodality, temperature>1.0 requirement, plausibility ordering) were reproduced on the smaller model, but the headline quantitative claim on the specified model was not addressed.

claims.claim: Any incentive-compatible additive pricing mechanism must price purely as a function of the output string's character representation rather than the reported token sequence (Proposition 5, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Proposition 5 is a theoretical characterization result. The logbook states no veritas claims bear on it, and no experiments or proof verification were attempted.

claims.claim: The proposed incentive-compatible mechanism prices tokens linearly by character count, r(t) = |str(t)| × r_c, which provably removes the provider's incentive to misreport tokenization (Theorem 6, Section 4).
claims.evidence: C10 shows positive provider margins for 91.72%/93.79%/95.17% of outputs (vs paper's 92.4%/93.3%/94.1%, within ~1pp), and C11 confirms mean post-transition margins equal rho_o to 4 decimals, empirically demonstrating that character-based pricing preserves margins and removes tokenization-manipulation incentives as claimed.

bertfil/aGaBFE9pta.overall: The logbook provides concrete empirical support for the mechanical overcharge calculation (claim 1) and the character-based pricing mechanism's margin behavior (claim 5), but does not address the two theoretical claims (claims 2 and 4) and only partially tests Algorithm 1's headline overcharge claim on a smaller model than specified (claim 3).

arvkevi/graph-algorithms-exact-gnn-repro.paper_title: Learning to Execute Graph Algorithms Exactly with Graph Neural Networks

claims.claim: Local instructions can be learned from a small training set using Neural Tangent Kernel theory, enabling graph algorithms to be executed during inference without error.
claims.evidence: Closed-form infinite-width NTK kernel regression on the authors' unchanged orthogonal template datasets yields machine-precision training residuals (≤3.05e-14) and 0 bit errors across 16,554,746 certified bit decisions for all four algorithms; end-to-end composed inference through Equation (2) masks produces 0 NTK bit errors across 4,701,384 reachable-state bits with all 4/4 final algorithms exact, using the authors' official code commit and templates.

claims.claim: Learnability results established for the LOCAL model of distributed computation and algorithms like message flooding, BFS, DFS, and Bellman-Ford.
claims.evidence: The learned official-template GNN executes all four named algorithms (flooding, BFS, DFS, Bellman-Ford) exactly end-to-end with 0 bit errors, establishing learnability for each; a separate deterministic audit of synchronous LOCAL send/aggregate/update semantics confirms 544/544 exact reference executions on 136 graphs up to n=4096 with bounded degree 4 and no global reads, validating the LOCAL framework at scale beyond the paper's own validation range.

arvkevi/graph-algorithms-exact-gnn-repro.overall: This logbook provides concrete, reproducible evidence that the infinite-width NTK predictor learns the paper's local instruction templates with zero errors across millions of bit decisions, and that composed end-to-end execution of all four algorithms (flooding, BFS, DFS, Bellman-Ford) is exact. The reproduction uses the authors' official code and templates, computes the NTK in closed form, separates learned-model evidence from deterministic LOCAL-semantics audits, and honestly scopes what is and is not claimed.

binzhango/repro-less-token-more-signal-s.paper_title: Less Token, More Signal: MoE Expert Pruning via Critical Token Selection

claims.claim: On 30B Qwen3 MoE with 50% expert sparsity achieves nearly 50% reduction in memory usage with minimal performance degradation.
claims.evidence: On OLMoE-1B-active/7B-total (not the claimed Qwen3-30B), 50% expert pruning reduced parameter bytes by 46.5% and CUDA allocation by 46.4%, approximately matching the 'nearly 50%' memory direction, but C4 perplexity rose from 9.62 to 20.92 (loss delta +0.777, bootstrap 95% CI [0.555, 1.012]), contradicting 'minimal performance degradation' at this scale. The model is far below the paper's 30B class, making this a proxy-scale test rather than a direct reproduction or falsification.

claims.claim: Delivers 1.5× throughput improvement and completes entire pruning process within 10 minutes.
claims.evidence: On the same OLMoE-1B/7B proxy, the full 128-step STEP calibration completed in 246.9 seconds, supporting the under-10-minute direction, but median synchronized forward throughput improved only 1.233× (bootstrap 95% CI [1.225×, 1.248×]), well below the claimed 1.5×. The much smaller model prevents definitive falsification of the 1.5× throughput claim for Qwen3-30B.

binzhango/repro-less-token-more-signal-s.overall: The logbook provides real GPU experiments on A100 using the released STEP code at a specific commit, but on OLMoE-1B/7B rather than the claimed Qwen3-30B due to missing Qwen support in the release. Memory reduction and pruning-time directions were partially supported, but minimal quality degradation and 1.5× throughput were not reproduced at this proxy scale.

Sor0ush/repro-taming-aleatoric-impulse-o.paper_title: Taming Aleatoric Impulse in Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning

claims.claim: Aleatoric Impulse Damping mechanism achieves state-of-the-art results on Gym-MuJoCo and DeepMind Control Suite.
claims.evidence: Real DSAC-AID training was run on Ant-v4 for only 20k iterations (1.3% of the paper's 1.5M), achieving best eval return 983.1, but only on a single Gym task with no completed DSACT baseline comparison and no DMC tasks attempted—far too reduced in scale and scope to verify or falsify a SOTA claim across Gym-MuJoCo and DMC.

claims.claim: Disentangles return variance into epistemic and aleatoric components for adaptive weighting.
claims.evidence: Code audit of dsacaid.py confirms epistemic=Var(Q) and aleatoric=mean(sigma²) with adaptive (beta/lambda)² weighting, and a synthetic simulation (500 steps, fabricated Q/sigma tensors) demonstrates the disentanglement math, but no real training data shows the variance decomposition operating during actual RL.

claims.claim: Pessimistic lower confidence bound suppresses impulse while optimistic upper confidence bound drives exploration.
claims.evidence: Code audit confirms LCB in critic targets and UCB in behavior-policy targets, and a synthetic simulation shows lcb_penalty=1.015 and ucb_bonus=1.015 at the simulated aleatoric impulse peak, but these results come from a toy 500-step simulation with synthetic data, not from actual training demonstrating pessimism suppressing impulse and optimism driving exploration.

Sor0ush/repro-taming-aleatoric-impulse-o.overall: The logbook provides a useful code-level audit confirming the AID mechanism's implementation and a drastically scaled-down training run on a single Ant-v4 task, but no claim is verified at the paper's actual scale. Claims 2 and 3 are supported only by synthetic simulations on fabricated data, and Claim 1's SOTA assertion is untestable from a 1.3%-scale single-task run with no completed baseline.

claims.claim: Hamilton-Jacobi-based proximal operator (HJ-Prox) enables operator splitting for functions without closed-form proximal operators
claims.evidence: HJ-Prox is validated only on 1D λ|x| (which has a known closed-form soft-threshold proximal) via 1,800 Gauss-Hermite quadrature rows; the claim concerns functions WITHOUT closed-form proximals, so this is a proxy task at scalar scale, not a demonstration on a genuinely proximal-free function.

claims.claim: Replacing exact proximal steps with HJ-Prox preserves convergence guarantees under mild assumptions
claims.evidence: Theorems 3.2 and 3.3 error bounds are numerically checked on the same 1D L1 problem (worst ratio 0.662, zero exceedances in 4,000 MC trials), but these are finite witnesses on a scalar convex function, not a demonstration that convergence guarantees hold at the paper's intended scale or on non-trivial problems.

claims.claim: The framework applies to proximal point, proximal gradient descent, Douglas-Rachford, Davis-Yin, and primal-dual hybrid gradient methods
claims.evidence: All five schemes (PPM, PGD, DRS, DYS, PDHG) run for 300 steps on a scalar composite objective 0.5(x−1)²+0.5|x| and remain finite with final objective below 0.51 vs optimum 0.375, but this is a 1D problem rather than the paper's image benchmarks, confirming applicability only at toy scale.

Vassilbek/hj-proximals-repro.overall: The logbook provides clean, reproducible CPU-only numerical checks of HJ-Prox approximation bounds and five splitting schemes, but all experiments are confined to a one-dimensional scalar L1 problem that already possesses a closed-form proximal. This constitutes toy-scale evidence consistent with the paper's claims without verifying them at the paper's intended scale or on genuinely proximal-free functions.

claims.claim: Extends Follow-the-Prediction framework to parsimonious learning-augmented online metric matching
claims.evidence: 60 seeded n=40 instances with perfect action predictions yield cost/OPT = 1.0000 against exact Hungarian OPT, demonstrating a correct implementation of the Follow-the-Prediction framework on the actual online metric matching task.

claims.claim: Virtual predictions fill absence of actual predictions using online algorithm
claims.evidence: As real-prediction fraction varies 0→1, cost/OPT progresses 1.29, 1.29, 1.25, 1.16, 1.00, showing that missing predictions filled by the base online algorithm produce graceful degradation toward optimal as prediction availability increases.

claims.claim: Establishes lower bounds on performance of parsimonious learning-augmented algorithms
claims.evidence: 8,639 exact rational certificates (Python Fraction, no float/Monte Carlo) on the paper's own unit-star T_n hard instance cover all four Section 4 theorems at scale up to n=8192, k=4096: Thm 4.1 ratio 255, Thm 4.2 ratio 2047, Thm 4.3 ratio 1.1514, Thm 4.4 ratio 16.790, with detailed adversary audits matching each theorem's construction.

arvkevi/parsimonious-online-metric-match.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence for all three claims: empirical runs at n=40 with 60 seeds for the upper-bound claims, and 8,639 exact certificates at large scale for the lower-bound theorems. The lower-bound reproduction is particularly rigorous, using exact rational arithmetic on the paper's own hard instance with reproducibility hashes.

claims.claim: Framework converts online algorithm with competitive ratio ρ(k,·) into one with ρ(η,·) where η is prediction error
claims.evidence: 30 seeded instances at the paper's scale (1,000 elements, 100 sets, 500 requests) with exact scipy MILP OPT show ICE competitive ratio rising monotonically from 1.132 to 1.355 as normalized error increases from 0% to 70%, while the prediction-free classical algorithm stays flat at 1.364–1.412, demonstrating that the ratio depends on prediction error η rather than solely on k.

claims.claim: With accurate enough prediction, resulting competitive ratio breaks through worst-case online lower bounds
claims.evidence: An exact nested-family adversary construction through 65,536 sets (d=4..16) yields a deterministic online ratio of exactly log2(m)+1 (reaching 17), while perfect-prediction ICE achieves ratio 1 with η=0 at every scale, directly certifying the asymptotic separation between the worst-case lower bound and the learning-augmented algorithm.

claims.claim: Degrades smoothly as prediction error grows, applies to facility location, Steiner problems, set cover
claims.evidence: Smooth degradation is demonstrated by the monotone ICE means (1.132, 1.178, 1.208, 1.239, 1.260, 1.293, 1.315, 1.355) on set cover at paper scale; multi-domain applicability is supported by 128 exact NMFL reduction pairs (max gap 1.26e-11) and 224 exact rooted-k-Steiner cases (max decomposition ratio 1.063 < 4, zero violations), though metric facility location is only theorem-audited without an executable certificate.

arvkevi/learning-augmented-online-coveri.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence at the paper's scale for all three claims: exact MILP-based ICE runs on set cover showing η-dependent competitive ratios, an exact adversarial construction certifying lower-bound breakthrough with perfect prediction, and decomposition-premise certificates for NMFL and Steiner domains. Key limitations include 30 vs 100 instances, a simpler online heuristic than Alon et al., and theorem-only verification for metric facility location.

bertfil/dDkl5ZcyTl.paper_title: Markov Chain Monte Carlo without Evaluating the Target: an Auxiliary Variable Approach

claims.claim: Section 2 unifies the exchange algorithm (Algorithm 1), PoissonMH (Algorithm 2), and TunaMH (Algorithm 3) as instances of one common auxiliary-variable procedure (Section 2).
claims.evidence: No experiment in the logbook addresses the theoretical unification of exchange algorithm, PoissonMH, and TunaMH under a common auxiliary-variable procedure; the logbook itself acknowledges this framework-level claim was not targeted by any extracted veritas claim.

claims.claim: The proposed meta-algorithm (Algorithm 4) introduces two auxiliary variables, ω1 guiding the proposal and ω2 enabling target-ratio estimation, and Proposition 2 proves it preserves the target distribution Π as stationary (Algorithm 4, Proposition 2).
claims.evidence: No experiment tests Algorithm 4's construction with auxiliary variables ω1 and ω2 or verifies Proposition 2's stationarity proof; all extracted claims are empirical performance comparisons, leaving this theoretical claim unaddressed.

claims.claim: Proposition 1 gives a reversibility condition on the auxiliary-variable estimator, R_{θ→θ'}(ω)π(θ|x)P_{θ→θ'}(ω) = π(θ'|x)P_{θ'→θ}(ω), that guarantees the resulting kernel targets the correct posterior (Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: No experiment evaluates or verifies the Proposition 1 reversibility condition R_{θ→θ'}(ω)π(θ|x)P_{θ→θ'}(ω) = π(θ'|x)P_{θ'→θ}(ω); the replication tested only empirical metrics (ESS/s, KS, MSE) and never attempted to verify this theoretical guarantee.

claims.claim: The framework yields two new algorithms: Locally Balanced PoissonMH (Algorithm 5), which uses gradient-informed locally balanced proposals with balancing functions such as Barker's g(t)=t/(1+t) or the MALA-type g(t)=sqrt(t), and TunaMH with an SGLD proposal (Algorithm 6), which uses independent minibatches for gradient estimation and acceptance-ratio evaluation (Algorithm 5, Algorithm 6).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 5 (Locally Balanced PoissonMH) has real experimental support: Poisson-Barker and Poisson-MALA rank as top methods across all acceptance rates and metrics in the truncated Gaussian experiment (C1, C3 match) and per-iteration MSE in robust regression (C12 match), confirming gradient-informed locally balanced proposals with Barker and MALA balancing functions. However, Algorithm 6 (TunaMH with SGLD) was never tested — all MNIST experiments (C11, C15, C16) were not attempted due to compute constraints, so the claim's second algorithm remains entirely unverified.

claims.claim: The framework is designed to apply to both doubly-intractable distributions, where the likelihood f_θ(x)/Z(θ) has an intractable normalizing constant, and tall-data settings with millions to billions of observations, without needing to evaluate the full target density (Section 1).
claims.evidence: The minibatch-size check (C17, match) confirms the framework uses only ~5.86% of N=100,000 data points without evaluating the full target, and ESS/s experiments on the truncated Gaussian (C1, C3 match) and robust regression (C4 computed values showing 88–385x improvement over full-batch) demonstrate applicability to a doubly-intractable distribution and a tall-data setting. However, the KS correctness check (C6) was never completed at full scale, the claimed 'millions to billions' scale was not tested (largest dataset is N=100,000), and the MNIST experiments were not attempted.

bertfil/dDkl5ZcyTl.overall: The logbook provides real experimental evidence supporting Algorithm 5 (Locally Balanced PoissonMH) through ESS/s rankings and MSE comparisons on truncated Gaussian and robust regression experiments, and confirms the minibatch-based design avoids full target evaluation. However, Algorithm 6 (TunaMH-SGLD) was never tested, KS correctness checks were incomplete, the 'millions to billions' scale claim was untested, and all three theoretical claims (unification framework, Propositions 1–2) were not addressed at all.

bertfil/WNqIX3IFZU.paper_title: CausalGame: Benchmarking Causal Thinking of LLM Agents in Games

claims.claim: CausalGame includes 14 game settings with selection bias, noisy measurements, and hidden confounders to evaluate causal thinking in AI agents.
claims.evidence: The replication verified benchmark-design elements on a 5-of-14-scenario subset: selection-bias removal improved survival in both modes (C7 partial, +7.38pp agent / +8.57pp prompt), weather_noise produced the claimed low-survival range (C20 match, all 6 models in [15,32]%), and optimal designs for antenna_trap (82.5%) and deployment_zone (81.1%) matched the paper. However, the specific count of 14 game settings was never directly verified, hidden-confounder scenarios were not specifically tested, weather_noise's claimed ~78% optimal was contradicted (measured 44.2%, analytic ceiling 46.3%), an

bertfil/WNqIX3IFZU.overall: The logbook provides real but narrow evidence: 6 of 29 models and 5 of 14 scenarios were tested, with careful bug-fixing in the replication harness. SabaPivot/repro-minimum-distance-summari.paper_title: Minimum Distance Summaries for Robust Neural Posterior Estimation

claims.claim: Minimum-distance summaries (MDS) adapt the query summary s* = arg min_s D(P_{x|s}, Q) at test time while keeping the pretrained neural posterior estimator fixed, preserving amortization (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: SHA-256 hashes of NPE checkpoints matched before and after all test-time L-BFGS calls across Gaussian, HSP90, and exact-architecture campaigns, and the test-time optimizer only references summary parameters; MDS also reduced MMD² from 0.134071 to 0.044387 on 300 paired contaminated scenarios.

claims.claim: MDS is implemented via a Maximum Mean Discrepancy objective using random Fourier feature approximations of the Gaussian kernel, with a decoder mean-embedding network trained offline via MSE and the summary optimized at test time by L-BFGS (Section 3.2, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Decoder trained on 50,000 datasets with final MSE 1.752×10⁻⁶; RFF-512 vs exact Gaussian-kernel MMD² showed Pearson r=0.991278 and 6.878% normalized MAE; test-time code minimizes RFF discrepancy via L-BFGS, confirmed across multiple runs.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that under Huber's ε-contamination model Q_ε = (1-ε)Q + εδ_y, the KL divergence between posteriors under MDS-adapted summaries for Q and Q_ε is O(ε), bounding robustness to small contamination (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: In an exactly solvable Gaussian-location/RBF instance, the empirical small-ε KL log-log slope was 1.98870, consistent with O(ε) behavior (indeed locally O(ε²)); the theorem statement and assumptions were audited against the paper and official code.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 shows that when the model is correctly specified, posterior consistency under the original summary statistics implies posterior consistency under MDS-adapted summaries (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Independent finite-sample conjugate Gaussian evaluation over N=10–1,000 with 128 fresh datasets per N showed MDS posterior W₂² decreasing from 0.20035 to 0.0022268 (98.89% reduction) with log-log slope -0.97565, matching the original-summary slope of -0.97452.

claims.claim: On the Gaussian model, MDS outperforms NPE, NNPE, and NPE-OR baselines across a range of contamination proportions, with degradation only appearing at contamination levels above 40% (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The matched four-method run over ε=.1–.4 produced MDS 0.104075, NPE 0.174333, NNPE 0.208418, and NPE-OR 0.035457, showing MDS did not outperform NPE-OR; the five-seed campaign confirmed MDS beats standard NPE (48.62% reduction, CI excluding zero) but the blanket ranking including NPE-OR is contradicted.

claims.claim: On a 1024-dimensional Cryo-EM inference task, MDS substantially improves robustness to Gaussian noise contamination while maintaining performance in the well-specified regime (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The released 1024D cryoSBI HSP90 simulator was used but at reduced scale: 3,000 vs 15,000 training datasets, RFF-512 vs 1,024, one training seed, and a classifier-posterior substitution; results (MDS 3.565 vs NPE 6.192 at ε=.1–.4) are directionally supportive but not full-scale.

SabaPivot/repro-minimum-distance-summari.overall: The logbook provides strong concrete evidence for the MDS mechanism (frozen NPE verified by hash checks, RFF-MMD fidelity, L-BFGS optimization) and supporting numerical instance checks for both theorems, but falsifies the Gaussian benchmark ranking because NPE-OR outperforms MDS in the matched four-method run. The Cryo-EM claim is only addressed at substantially reduced scale (20% of training data, half the RFF dimensions, single seed).

snaykey/repro-self-distillation-ridge.paper_title: Optimal Unconstrained Self-Distillation in Ridge Regression: Strict Improvements, Precise Asymptotics, and One-Shot Tuning

claims.claim: Theorem 2.2 proves that for any nonstationary ridge penalty λ (i.e., R'(λ) ≠ 0), the optimally mixed self-distilled student strictly improves on the teacher's squared prediction risk, with optimal mixing weight ξ*(λ) = -(λ/2)·R'(λ)/D(λ) obeying sign(ξ*(λ)) = -sign(R'(λ)) (Section 2.3, Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: Three independent constructions of ξ* (direct 1-D minimization, (R-C)/D decomposition, and -(λ/2)R'/D derivative form) cross-check to <2.8e-7 across 78 grid points spanning 3 covariance designs (AR1 p=60, spiked p=80, isotropic p=100, γ=0.5); the core differentiation identity R-C = -(λ/2)R' holds to 9.2e-10; strict improvement and sign rule hold at 78/78 nonstationary points.

claims.claim: The optimal mixing weight ξ*(λ) can be negative, corresponding to a 'pro-learning' regime under over-regularization (λ > λ*), as opposed to the 'anti-learning' regime (ξ* > 1) identified in prior work by Das and Sanghavi (2023) (Section 2.3).
claims.evidence: A λ-census on AR1(0.25) with p=150, γ=0.75 over 60 grid points finds 28 points with ξ*<0 (all over-regularized with R'>0), 26 with ξ*>1 (anti-learning), and ξ* range [-67.4, 33.6]; constraining ξ∈[0,1] collapses to the teacher (ξ=0) in every negative-ξ* case, missing up to 0.355 absolute risk reduction.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 derives exact deterministic equivalents for the optimal self-distillation risk R*_sd(λ) and mixing weight ξ*(λ) in the proportional asymptotics regime (n, p → ∞, p/n → γ) under general anisotropic covariance and deterministic signals (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Independent re-implementation of the Eq. 12-16 deterministic equivalents (κ fixed point, resolvent, trace/alignment functionals, coefficients) compared against Monte-Carlo simulations across 3 designs (AR1, spiked, isotropic) at growing p∈{50,100,200} with γ=0.5; max relative error decreases from ~3.7% to ~1.8% as n grows, demonstrating proportional-asymptotic convergence.

claims.claim: In the isotropic-signal setting, Corollary 3.2 shows the optimal mixing weight changes sign exactly at λ* := γσ²/r², with ξ*(λ) < 0 for λ > λ* and ξ*(λ) > 0 for λ < λ* (Section 3.2, Corollary 3.2).
claims.evidence: Numerical root-finding of ξ*(λ)=0 using the Thm 3.1 deterministic equivalents under isotropic signal yields the crossing at γσ²/r² to max relative error 1.1e-14 across all 9 cases (3 covariances × 3 SNRs at p=300, γ=0.5); the crossing is identical across isotropic, AR1, and spiked spectra, confirming Σ-independence.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proposes a one-shot generalized cross-validation (GCV) estimator of the optimal mixing weight ξ* that is consistent in proportional asymptotics and avoids grid search, sample splitting, or refitting (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The Eq. 17-19 GCV estimators (training data only, single fit per λ, no grid/split/refit) compared per-realization to exact finite-sample optima at growing p∈{50,100,200,400} (n=2p, AR1 design, γ=0.5); median normalized |ξ̂*-ξ*| decreases monotonically 0.129→0.062 and median |R̂*_sd-R*_sd| decreases 0.165→0.059, demonstrating convergence in probability.

claims.claim: A curvature-based sufficient condition (Proposition 2.3, Eq. 10) predicts whether the self-distilled risk's global minimum over λ is strictly smaller than the teacher's; this test is verified exactly on all four real-data experiments (BlogFeedback, Communities and Crime, CIFAR10, Air Quality) in Table 2.
claims.evidence: Curvature test D(λ*) < (λ*²/2)R''(λ*) evaluated on all four real datasets (BlogFeedback n=2620/p=280, Communities n=399/p=99, CIFAR10 n=2000/p=512, Air Quality n=5175/p=8) with preprocessing per Section F; test outcome matches Table 2 exactly (✓/✗/✗/✓) and predicts the observed global gain in every case (0.54% and 39.8% where test holds; ~1e-5 where it fails).

snaykey/repro-self-distillation-ridge.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims through independent from-scratch implementations: exact identity checks at machine precision for Theorem 2.2 and Corollary 3.2, Monte-Carlo convergence studies for Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 4.1, a regime census demonstrating negative ξ* for Claim 2, and real-data curvature tests reproducing Table 2 for Claim 6.

arvkevi/santa-sparse-attention-repro.paper_title: Stochastic Sparse Attention for Memory-Bound Inference

claims.claim: SANTA achieves 1.5x decode-step attention kernel speedup over FlashInfer and FlashDecoding on NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada while matching baseline accuracy at 32k-token contexts.
claims.evidence: At n_k=32,768, H=32, d=128, BF16 with 40 CUDA-event trials and cache thrash, SANTA-Flash S=2048 measured 0.1754 ms vs FlashInfer 0.2634 ms (1.502x) and FA2 0.2678 ms (1.527x) on L40S (same Ada SM 8.9 as RTX 6000 Ada); accuracy on 48 exact-32k-token RULER QA2 rows with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct was identical at 28/48 for both dense and sparse with zero paired discordance.

claims.claim: Stochastic sparse value-cache access via post-softmax distribution sampling enables unbiased estimation while reducing bandwidth requirements.
claims.evidence: Exact CDF/stratum integration over 256 distributions at n_k=32,768 yields max |E[w]-p|=1.52e-14 (machine precision), confirming unbiasedness analytically rather than via Monte Carlo; official CUDA kernels at 32k geometry measured mean value-row coverage of 1.55% (Prop) and 22.70% (Flash) across 16 seeds, confirming bandwidth reduction.

arvkevi/santa-sparse-attention-repro.overall: The logbook provides concrete, at-scale experimental evidence for both claims: kernel speedups exceed 1.5x on same-architecture hardware at 32k context, accuracy is matched on real 32k-token prompts, unbiasedness is verified by exact computation at machine precision, and bandwidth reduction is measured on official CUDA kernels. The main caveats are a same-SM GPU transfer (L40S for RTX 6000 Ada) and a 48-row accuracy subset rather than the full private benchmark.

nielsr/repro-rethinking-genomic-modeling.paper_title: Rethinking Genomic Modeling Through Optical Character Recognition

claims.claim: OpticalDNA achieves best overall performance on genomic benchmarks with nearly 20x fewer effective tokens.
claims.evidence: No model inference or benchmark evaluation was run; the logbook only recomputed arithmetic means from the paper's own reported AUROC values and verified they round correctly. Checkpoints and evaluators are unavailable, so no independent performance evidence exists.

claims.claim: Surpasses models with up to 985x more activated parameters using only 256k trainable parameters on sequences up to 450k bases.
claims.evidence: The logbook verified the arithmetic ratio 252M/256K = 984.375 ≈ 985x, but no actual model comparison or inference was performed. The performance claim that OpticalDNA surpasses the larger model remains untested because checkpoints are unreleased.

claims.claim: Vision-based OCR framework retains fine-grained genomic information under reduced effective token budget.
claims.evidence: Compression ratios (19.0–21.2x) were arithmetically verified from page/token configurations, but no inference was run to confirm that fine-grained genomic information is retained under reduced token budgets. The claim's core performance assertion is untested.

nielsr/repro-rethinking-genomic-modeling.overall: This logbook is a source audit and arithmetic verification only—it recomputes means and ratios from the paper's own reported numbers and inspects code structure, but runs zero model inference or benchmark evaluations because checkpoints and evaluators are unavailable. No claim is independently verified with experimental evidence; all remain inconclusive.

kpshinnik/repro-split-vlm-icml2026.paper_title: SPLIT-VLM: Salience-Guided Partitioning towards Local Coverage for Importance-Aware Token Dropping in Vision-Language Models

claims.claim: SPLIT preserves over 99% accuracy with 192 vision tokens and 92.8% accuracy with only 64 tokens on image understanding with LLaVA-1.5-7B.
claims.evidence: Real runs on LLaVA-1.5-7B but only 3 of 10 benchmarks at n=60–150 (POPE, TextVQA, ScienceQA), yielding 92.44% relative accuracy at 192 tokens and 87.88% at 64 tokens—well below the paper's claimed 99.3% and 92.8%. The reduced benchmark count and tiny subset sizes make this a simplified setup, not a full reproduction.

claims.claim: Consistently outperforms state-of-the-art on image and video understanding benchmarks.
claims.evidence: Only 3 of 10 image benchmarks at n=60–150 were tested (no video benchmarks), and SPLIT did not outperform the attention-topk baseline on any of them at 64 tokens (POPE 77.3 vs 81.3, TextVQA 30.0 vs 40.0, ScienceQA 61.7 vs 65.0). The scale is too small to resolve the paper's sub-2% SOTA margins, so this is a simplified setup with real runs but not a full evaluation.

claims.claim: Estimates token importance via temporal shifts of hidden states across layers, eschewing attention scores and their biases.
claims.evidence: On the real CLIP ViT-L/14-336 (LLaVA-1.5's vision tower), temporal-shift importance computed from per-layer hidden states is spatially unbiased (center-of-mass row 11.4–11.6 vs grid center 11.5, Gini 0.03) and anti-correlated with CLS attention (Spearman −0.68 to −0.75), confirming it is a genuinely attention-free signal that eschews attention's position bias (CLS attention center-of-mass 12.7–13.6, Gini 0.43–0.47).

kpshinnik/repro-split-vlm-icml2026.overall: The logbook provides concrete evidence that SPLIT's temporal-shift importance mechanism is attention-free and spatially unbiased on the real CLIP ViT, but the accuracy and SOTA-comparison claims are only addressed at heavily reduced scale (3/10 benchmarks, n=60–150, no video), falling short of the paper's headline numbers and unable to resolve sub-2% SOTA margins.

agharsallah/amgjqp4vrr-logbook.paper_title: Clipping Makes Distributed and Federated Asynchronous SGD Robust to Stragglers

claims.claim: Gradient clipping removes dependence of maximum delay in oracle complexity for asynchronous SGD.
claims.evidence: The τ_max-independence is primarily demonstrated on a d=6 strongly-convex quadratic surrogate (clipped error flat at 0.373 across τ_max 4→128, R=96 reps), which is a simplified setup. The supplementary real ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 GPU run is single-seed and the clipped test loss is not flat across τ_max (1.203→1.089→1.192), so it does not clearly confirm τ_max-independence at scale.

claims.claim: Achieves convergence in expectation and convergence with high probability using sub-Weibull noise model.
claims.evidence: Convergence in expectation and high-probability polylog behavior are verified on the d=6 quadratic surrogate (R=500, polylog fit R²=0.992–0.995, θ-ordering confirmed). The sub-Weibull definition and θ-recovery methodology are verified on synthetic data, but the real GPU measurement of ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 gradient noise yields θ≈0.17–0.19, contradicting the paper's θ=2.71, so the empirical basis of the noise model is not reproduced at scale.

claims.claim: First analysis showing gradient clipping stabilizes asynchronous training for deep learning empirically.
claims.evidence: Real ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 GPU experiments (two independent scales) show clipped ASGD consistently beats vanilla: ~1.2x wall-clock speedup at D=4 (2720 vs 3280 steps to 65% accuracy), and 1.71–1.77x improvement under Dirichlet label-skew heterogeneity (41–55% vs 24–31% accuracy). The Shakespeare/LSTM experiments show a null speedup result (0.98x), but the CIFAR-10 evidence provides concrete non-toy support that clipping stabilizes asynchronous deep-learning training.

agharsallah/amgjqp4vrr-logbook.overall: The logbook verifies the structural form of the theoretical claims on a toy quadratic surrogate and provides supplementary real ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 experiments that partially support the empirical claims, though single-seed and with some null or off-target results (Shakespeare speedup, θ measurement). The core τ_max-independence and high-probability convergence are established only at toy scale, while the empirical deep-learning stabilization claim has genuine non-toy support from CIFAR-10.

Umong/repro-probabilistic-bisection-algo.paper_title: Probabilistic Bisection Algorithm Provably Achieves Exponential Convergence

claims.claim: The probabilistic bisection algorithm (PBA) converges at a geometric rate, matching the performance of classical binary search under noiseless responses.
claims.evidence: An independent exact continuous-posterior PBA implementation was run across 5 truths × 4 noise levels × 300 seeds (6,000 trajectories, 96 queries each), with all 20 configurations showing negative fitted log-error slopes (-0.3560 to -0.01729 per round) indicating geometric convergence. Separately, 1,000 noiseless roots obey the exact 2^-n half-interval bound through 40 rounds, directly confirming the binary-search-matching claim.

claims.claim: PBA queries oscillate around the truth but steadily draw closer, yielding an estimator that rapidly concentrates on the truth.
claims.evidence: Across all 20 truth/noise configurations, at least 91.7% of trajectories query both sides of the truth with a median of ≥11.5 sign changes (oscillation), mean absolute query error contracts in every configuration (steadily closer), and posterior mass within ±0.01 rises by more than 0.25 reaching at least 0.6009 in the hardest case (rapid concentration).

Umong/repro-probabilistic-bisection-algo.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from an independent exact-posterior PBA implementation across 6,000 noisy trajectories and 1,000 noiseless roots, supporting both geometric convergence with binary-search-matching noiseless behavior and the oscillation-plus-concentration query dynamics. The experimental scale and rigor are appropriate for a 1D search algorithm, making this a faithful non-toy reproduction.

SaiPavankumar22/repro-litreview-arena-ev.paper_title: LitReview Arena: Evaluating Literature Review Agents with Battle-style Peer Review Platform

claims.claim: The most advanced models win only 23.0% of decisive matches against humans on overall utility for literature review generation.
claims.evidence: The reproduction used the public snapshot (~60% of the full dataset), yielding 542 decisive D5 matches instead of the paper's 904, and computed an AI win rate of 14.6% versus the claimed 23.0% — a real but incomplete reproduction on a data subset that confirms the direction (AI far below 50%) without matching the specific magnitude.

claims.claim: Existing LLM-as-a-judge evaluation methods are severely misaligned with human experts (Spearman's ρ ≈ 0.467), while the provided LitJudge improves alignment to ρ ≈ 0.78.
claims.evidence: The logbook only reproduced the expert BT leaderboard (ground-truth side, Kendall τ = 0.911 vs. paper) but never executed the LLM judge inference (Qwen3-235B or equivalent) or LitJudge evaluation, so neither Spearman ρ value (0.467 or 0.78) was ever computed — the core experiment of the claim was not addressed.

SaiPavankumar22/repro-litreview-arena-ev.overall: The logbook provides a partial reproduction of Claim 1 on a public data subset, confirming the qualitative direction (AI loses overwhelmingly to humans) but not the specific 23.0% figure. Claim 2's central experiment — computing Spearman ρ between LLM-judge and expert rankings — was never executed, leaving the alignment claim unaddressed.

Umong/repro-a-linearly-convergent-proxim.paper_title: A Linearly Convergent Proximal Subgradient Algorithm for Sparse Portfolio Optimization with Transaction Cost

claims.claim: Establish R-linear convergence rate of proximal subgradient algorithm (PSGA) by showing Kurdyka-Łojasiewicz exponent is 1/2.
claims.evidence: The logbook tests convergence on a single synthetic 80×30 Gaussian ℓ0 problem (seed 13782, λ=0.012), observing log-gap slope −0.6049 and R²=0.999963, which is consistent with KL exponent 1/2 but on a small proxy instance rather than the paper's actual portfolio optimization problem at scale; a finite numerical run cannot establish the general theorem.

claims.claim: Achieve lower risk while keeping higher return than classical transaction cost optimization models on real-market data.
claims.evidence: On real market data (Kenneth French 10 Industry Portfolios, 2015–2025, 2,499 out-of-sample days), sparse PSGA achieves lower volatility (18.63% vs 18.82% for dense+TC and 20.94% for dense no-TC) but also lower net return (9.06% vs 10.22% and 16.60%), directly contradicting the 'higher return' part of the conjunction.

Umong/repro-a-linearly-convergent-proxim.overall: The logbook provides toy-scale empirical evidence consistent with KL-1/2 convergence on a small synthetic instance but cannot establish the general theoretical claim, while on real market data it finds lower risk but also lower return for sparse PSGA, falsifying the joint risk-return claim.

Umong/repro-inference-from-quantized-dat.paper_title: Inference from Quantized Data via Normal Variance-Mean Mixtures

claims.claim: ECM algorithm ensures all model parameters updated in closed form at each iteration for quantized ML estimation
claims.evidence: The reproduction implements closed-form ECM updates only for a discrete two-point mixing distribution W∈{0.5,2}, which is a simplified special case of the paper's general NVMM family; while 6,000 synthetic observations and a 442-sample diabetes dataset were used, the closed-form updates for finite discrete mixtures are standard EM mechanics and do not verify the paper's specific ECM algorithm for its intended continuous-mixture model.

claims.claim: Provides convergence guarantees and derives bounds on convergence rate and statistical error
claims.evidence: Empirical convergence behavior (monotone likelihood, contraction rate 0.872, R²=0.999999998) and statistical error scaling (slope −0.517 across 600 fits) were observed on the same simplified two-point special case, but the actual theoretical bounds, constants, and assumptions from the paper's theorems were never verified—the paper PDF was inaccessible (HTTP 403) and the logbook itself states it 'cannot validate constants or assumptions in the inaccessible paper theorem.'

Umong/repro-inference-from-quantized-dat.overall: The logbook provides a systematic empirical reproduction on a deliberately simplified discrete two-point NVMM special case, demonstrating closed-form ECM updates, monotone linear convergence, and approximately root-n statistical error scaling with real runs and public job verification. However, both claims are only addressed on this reduced model rather than the paper's general continuous-mixture framework, and the paper's actual theoretical bounds were never accessible or verified.

Umong/repro-a-control-theoretic-view-of-.paper_title: A Control-Theoretic View of Mamba on Stability and Robustness

claims.claim: Proves BIBO stability for selective state space models (Mamba) through control-theoretic framework
claims.evidence: The reproduction verifies BIBO bounds on a hand-crafted synthetic fixed-A diagonal SSM (n=64, T=4096) with simple tanh/sigmoid input-dependent maps, not on an actual Mamba model or trained checkpoint. The state-to-bound ratio of 0.184 confirms the bounds hold, but the system is constructed by design to satisfy the theorem's stability assumptions (negative eigenvalues, bounded maps), making the verification somewhat circular rather than a test on a real Mamba architecture.

claims.claim: Establishes two-term robustness bounds with linear growth in sequence length with practical certification algorithms
claims.evidence: The two-term certificate (K_force + t·K_warp)·delta is checked on the same synthetic system with worst error/bound ratio 0.077, and a scalar pure-clock-warp construction shows linear-fit R²=0.9988 at horizons up to 64. However, no actual Mamba model is certified, the perturbation radius is small (eps=0.02), and the 'practical certification algorithms' amount to direct formula evaluation on hand-set constants rather than a certification pipeline applicable to real models.

Umong/repro-a-control-theoretic-view-of-.overall: The logbook provides a clean numerical verification of the paper's theoretical BIBO and robustness bounds on a synthetic fixed-A selective SSM with hand-crafted parameters, but the setup is a simplified instantiation rather than a reproduction on actual Mamba models or trained checkpoints.

debrajsingha/repro-envisioning-beyond-th.paper_title: Envisioning Beyond the Few: Disentangled Semantics and Primitives for Few-Shot Atypical Layout-to-Image Generation

claims.claim: The proposed framework addresses representation fragmentation in few-shot atypical layout-to-image generation through disentangling semantics from primitives.
claims.evidence: The ridge regression closed-form solution is verified to machine precision (2.7e-15) on a synthetic Gaussian-mixture proxy, and all three modules (Semantic Anchoring, Primitive Imbuing, Conceptual Steering) are exercised on real DINOv2 ViT-L/14 and CLIP ViT-B/16 backbones on a T4 GPU (anchor separation 0.1015, recon MSE −62.7%, GradCAM foreground 0.72). However, these are module-level checks on isolated components — no end-to-end image generation pipeline is run, so the claim that disentanglement addresses representation fragmentation in the actual few-shot L2I task is not demonstrated at full

claims.claim: Demonstrates consistent improvements in the 5-shot regime over SOTA L2I methods in both visual fidelity and alignment across diverse atypical domains.
claims.evidence: The logbook only restates the paper's Table 1 numbers (e.g., FID 74.34 vs 82.51 for CC-Diff on DIOR) as targets and explicitly documents that no independent re-measurement was performed due to multi-GPU/multi-day training requirements and absence of released DSP checkpoints. No FID, mAP, AP50, or AP75 values were independently produced.

debrajsingha/repro-envisioning-beyond-th.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous mathematical verification of the Primitive Imbuing ridge formulation and demonstrates that all three framework modules run correctly on real pretrained backbones at the component level, but it does not execute the full few-shot layout-to-image generation pipeline on any of the three datasets. Claim 2's SOTA comparison numbers are cited from the paper without any independent experimental evidence.

agharsallah/ttogqk77go-logbook.paper_title: Beyond Temperature: Hyperfitting as a Late-Stage Geometric Expansion

claims.claim: Temperature scaling fails to replicate the diversity gains of hyperfitting, as demonstrated through entropy-matched control experiments.
claims.evidence: On a self-trained hyperfitted TinyLlama-1.1B (40 epochs, loss 0.021), entropy-matched temperature controls at T*=0.499–0.623 (bracketing the paper's 0.59) achieved TTR of only 0.212–0.323 versus 0.466 for hyperfitted greedy (p≤1.2e-4), with teacher-forced entropies 2.542/0.825 nats closely matching the paper's 2.083/0.862, confirming that temperature scaling at matched entropy fails to replicate diversity gains.

claims.claim: Hyperfitting relies on dynamic, context-dependent rank reordering mechanism rather than static vocabulary reweighting.
claims.evidence: Two independent lines of evidence support this: (1) hyperfitted model's full-vocab Spearman correlation with the original is 0.610 (vs 0.997–1.0 for any temperature scaling), with Top-1 agreement 0.547 and 14.6% of choices from rank >10, showing dynamic rank reordering; (2) static logit injection of the top-500 promoted tokens degrades diversity monotonically (Spearman ρ=−0.687 to −0.718, p<1e-4) and never exceeds TTR 0.13 under greedy vs 0.466 for real hyperfitting, falsifying the static reweighting explanation.

claims.claim: Terminal Expansion occurs in the final transformer block with a geometric expansion of feature space of approximately +80.8 dimensions.
claims.evidence: On the real hyperfitted checkpoint, per-layer L2 distance jumps from 22.615 (layer 21) to 92.58 (layer 22), a 4.09x spike matching the paper's 22.0→81.6 (3.7x), and Delta-Dim is +225.8 at the final block (maximal across all 23 layers) with all intermediate layers negative, confirming the compression-then-expansion pattern localized to the final transformer block; the magnitude exceeds the paper's +80.8 but the paper itself notes strong model/domain dependence.

claims.claim: Late-Stage LoRA updating only the final 5 layers achieves robust generation with minimal parameter updates.
claims.evidence: Exact trainable-parameter counts on real LoRA runs confirm 77.3–78.2% reduction on TinyLlama-1.1B (paper 78.3%) and 82.1% on Qwen2.5-1.5B (paper 82.7%), and rank-reordering dynamics replicate on both architectures (Top-1 agreement Qwen 0.474/0.489 vs paper 0.459/0.469; TinyLlama 0.554/0.545 vs paper 0.517/0.523), with generation metrics (TTR, bigram repetition) tracking Full LoRA closely, supporting robust generation with minimal parameter updates.

agharsallah/ttogqk77go-logbook.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous, full-scale reproduction on real self-trained checkpoints (hyperfitted TinyLlama-1.1B and four LoRA variants) using the paper's own training recipe and analysis protocols, with all four paper claims supported by concrete numerical evidence. The main deviations (WritingPrompts domain instead of unreleased Fiction-Stories, 18–40 epochs instead of 260) are consistently disclosed and justified by near-zero converged losses and the paper's own statement that effects emerge by epoch 20.

tpls/repro-chebyshev-mountain-car.paper_title: Chebyshev Policies and the Mountain Car Problem: Reinforcement Learning for Low-Dimensional Control Tasks

claims.claim: Theorem 2.4 gives the first closed-form optimal control solution for Mountain Car, α(t)=C·ẋ(t), a policy depending only on velocity, closing a 36-year-old open problem (Section 2, Theorem 2.4).
claims.evidence: The authors' own analytic policy code was run on the exact 100-start deterministic MountainCarContinuous-v0 protocol, yielding mean R=99.394 (paper 99.39), 100/100 starts reaching the goal, min 99.149, max 99.518. The C2 boundary falsifier confirmed a hard cliff: C2-0.1 drops to 0/100 goal-reaching, C2+0.1 does not improve. The 'first closed-form' and '36-year' priority claims are historical and not adjudicable by code, but the derived velocity-only policy's claimed numeric behavior is fully confirmed.

claims.claim: The derived analytical worst-case policy achieves returns of 99.15-99.52 on Mountain Car, versus 96.67 for ARS (regret 2.72), 93.91 for PPO (regret 5.48), and 94.61 for SAC (regret 4.78) (Section 2).
claims.evidence: All 8 named figures reproduce exactly at two-decimal precision using the authors' own code and shipped pretrained agents: π_ana 99.15–99.52, ARS 96.67 (regret 2.72), PPO 93.91 (regret 5.48), SAC 94.61 (regret 4.78). No direction reversal; both range endpoints hit. Negative controls (C2 perturbation, zero-gain policy) confirm the constants are load-bearing.

claims.claim: The degree-3 Chebyshev policy CH-3-ARS attains regret 0.65 on Mountain Car, a 4.18x improvement over neural ARS, using only 16 parameters versus 4,355 for a 2x64x64x1 MLP -- a 277x reduction in parameter count (Section 4, Section 5).
claims.evidence: CH-3-ARS was trained fresh (20 seeds, authors' hyperparameters) and evaluated on the 100-start protocol: best-of-20 mean R=98.950, regret 0.444 vs analytic optimum, improvement ratio 6.15x over ARS (regret 2.728). Parameter count confirmed at exactly 16; MLP introspection gives 4417 params, ratio 276.06x (paper 277x). The claim's specific numbers (0.65, 4.18x) differ from measurement (0.444, 6.15x) but match the paper's own v4 figures (0.44, 6.18x), indicating the contest text references a stale version; the underlying phenomenon—large regret reduction with 277x fewer parameters—is confirmed.

claims.claim: CH-3-PPO attains regret 1.29 on Mountain Car, a 4.24x improvement over standard PPO, and CH-3-REINFORCE attains regret 0.77, a 3.53x improvement over standard ARS (Section 5).
claims.evidence: CH-3-PPO best-of-10 on Mountain Car achieved R=93.929 (regret 5.47), within-noise of MLP-PPO (93.906) and far from the claimed regret 1.29; 4/10 seeds diverged. CH-3-REINFORCE best-of-5 reached the goal (1/5 seeds, mean 59.17) vs 0/5 for MLP-REINFORCE—a qualitative win—but the claimed regret 0.77 was not reached. Reduced seed budgets (10 and 5 vs paper's 20–30) may explain the shortfall, but the specific claimed numbers are not reproduced.

claims.claim: Table 2 shows Chebyshev policies generalize beyond Mountain Car: CH-ARS reaches -150.8 vs ARS's -218.3 on Pendulum, and on real-world Aero 2 hardware CH-PPO reaches -55.8 vs PPO's -182.0, indicating improved sim-to-real transfer (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The Pendulum CH-ARS comparison reproduces: CH-ARS −151.069 (paper −150.8) vs ARS −218.323 (paper −218.3 exact), Δ=+67.25 at 9.4x the 95% CI half-width on the 2500-point grid. However, the Aero 2 hardware comparison (CH-PPO −55.8 vs PPO −182.0) is declared-blocked due to physical hardware requirements and unvendored simulator, leaving the sim-to-real transfer claim untested. Additionally, CH-PPO on Pendulum missed by 52.4 units (−215.24 vs −162.8), a reversal below its own baseline.

tpls/repro-chebyshev-mountain-car.overall: The logbook provides strong reproduction evidence for the analytic policy (Claims 1–2) and the CH-3-ARS parameter/regret results (Claim 3), all using the authors' own code with negative controls. Claims 4–5 remain inconclusive: PPO and REINFORCE specific regret targets are not met under reduced seed budgets, and the Aero 2 sim-to-real claim is untestable without physical hardware.

tpls/repro-ppi-no-free-lunch.paper_title: No Free Lunch: Non-Asymptotic Analysis of Prediction-Powered Inference

Srishti280992/repro-minimum-distance-sum.paper_title: Minimum Distance Summaries for Robust Neural Posterior Estimation

claims.claim: Minimum-distance summaries provide a plug-in robust neural posterior estimation method that adapts test-time summaries independently of pretrained NPE using maximum mean discrepancy.
claims.evidence: State-dict hashes of the pretrained NPE remained unchanged across 420/420 (first run), 300/300 Gaussian, and 250/250 OUP adaptations, proving the NPE is frozen while only the 2D summary is optimized via an MMD/RFF objective (L-BFGS on decoder-predicted RFF embedding vs. observed RFF embedding). Both Gaussian (7,044-param ConditionalGaussianNPE) and OUP (10,180-param) models were tested with 100 observations across multiple contamination levels.

claims.claim: The algorithm is implemented efficiently with random Fourier feature approximations, yielding a lightweight, model-free test-time adaptation procedure.
claims.evidence: Implementation uses scikit-learn RBFSampler with 512 features, median-heuristic bandwidth, a 2x256-unit decoder trained to MSE ~9e-6, and L-BFGS strong-Wolfe optimization. RFF-vs-exact-MMD validation shows mean absolute gap 3.64e-05 (Gaussian) and 0.0120 (OUP) with correlations 0.9967 and 0.9983 respectively. Median adaptation times range 1-10 ms across contamination levels.

claims.claim: The method demonstrates substantial robustness gains with minimal additional overhead.
claims.evidence: Gaussian RMSE reductions of 86-91% (70 trials, eps=0.1-0.5) and OUP RMSE reductions of 18-46% (25 trials, eps=0.1-0.4) vs. frozen NPE, with median per-adaptation overhead of 1-10 ms. MDS beats NNPE at all contaminated levels and NPE-OR at eps>=0.2; the honest exception at eps=0.1 (NPE-OR 0.1279 vs MDS 0.1486) does not undermine the overall substantial-gains pattern.

claims.claim: Theoretical guarantees for the robustness of the algorithm are provided.
claims.evidence: Source audit confirms thm:robustness, thm:consistency, influence lemma, and all 8 robustness + 4 consistency assumption labels exist in the pinned arXiv TeX (SHA-256 ff81fd97...). Numerical corroboration: KL(post_Q||post_Qeps)/eps bounded at max 0.00139 across eps in [1e-4,1e-2], bounded-kernel influence sup 1.2131 with zero tail at |y|=60, and posterior RMS radius log-log slope -0.492 matching the N^{-1/2} contraction rate.

Srishti280992/repro-minimum-distance-sum.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all four claims through clean-room reproductions on Gaussian and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Process SBI tasks, with frozen-NPE hash verification, RFF-vs-exact-MMD validation, multi-contamination-level robustness curves, and source-audited theorem mechanisms. The main limitation is that all experiments use simplified 2D simulators rather than the paper's full-scale benchmarks (real Cryo-EM assets were unavailable).

kaustubhg73/repro-multilingual-safety-al.paper_title: Multilingual Safety Alignment via Representation-Space Separability

claims.claim: Large safety gap exists between high-resource and low-resource languages in existing LLMs
claims.evidence: 40 prompts per language (vs ~50 in paper) with different datasets (MaliciousInstruct+TDC23 instead of AdvBench), different judge (gpt-oss:20b vs GPT-4o), and different translation (NLLB-200 vs Google Translate) yield a gap of only 0.125 (vs paper's ~0.77), driven entirely by 'invalid' (garbled) responses with zero 'unsafe' verdicts across all languages.

claims.claim: SMO capable of substantially reducing attack success rates in low-resource languages to near zero while maintaining performance
claims.evidence: No SMO training was attempted; the logbook only documents that GPU-based SimPO fine-tuning was out of scope, with no experimental results produced.

claims.claim: Harmful prompts are significantly less separated from harmless prompts in low-resource languages compared to English
claims.evidence: Hidden-state distances on 40 prompts per language show EN D=70.81 vs BN D=22.43 (3.2x gap), supporting the directional claim, but the Pearson r=-0.881 correlation between ΔD and ΔASR is driven by only 2 non-zero ΔASR points (BN, SW) out of 5, making the correlation analysis unreliable; setup uses reduced prompt count and different translation pipeline.

kaustubhg73/repro-multilingual-safety-al.overall: The logbook provides directional evidence for the safety gap (C1) and representation separability (C3) on a reduced-scale setup with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, but C1's gap is small and driven by invalid responses rather than actual safety failures, C3's correlation rests on only 2 non-zero data points, and C2 (SMO training) was never attempted.

ProCreations/repro-approximate-proportio.paper_title: A Random Matrix Theory of Masked Self-Supervised Learning

claims.claim: Masked modeling undergoes Baik–Ben Arous–Péché (BBP)-type phase transition, identifying when masked SSL begins to recover latent signals.
claims.evidence: A 50-fit sweep at d=600, n=1200 across ten spike strengths with five seeds shows mean squared top-eigenvector overlap rising from 0.0322 below theta*=1/sqrt(2)≈0.7071 to 0.3688 above it, with per-point values (e.g., 0.026 at theta=0.5, 0.093 at 0.72, 0.303 at 1.0, 0.708 at 2.0) and a parallel eigengap separation, matching the predicted BBP transition.

claims.claim: Provides explicit expressions for generalization error and characterizes spectral structure of learned joint predictor.
claims.evidence: The joint-predictor identity A=I-Q(Q+λI)^{-1} matches explicitly fitted leave-one-coordinate masked ridge regressions to 3.22e-15 elementwise, with real eigenvalues and symmetric-similarity agreement to 3.89e-15; Theorem 1's asymptotic risk formula tracks 120 empirical fits across three covariance structures and eight sample sizes (d=200) with 0.918% median relative error, recovering the non-monotone interpolation peak near n=d.

claims.claim: Identifies structured regimes where masked self-supervised learning provably outperforms PCA on spiked covariance models.
claims.evidence: Across 192 comparisons on spiked covariance models (d=300, four spike strengths, four sample sizes, four seeds, three PCA ranks), PCA has lower reconstruction risk in every cell with margins ranging from 0.079 to 1.059; an AR(1) positive control where SSL wins 68/96 cells confirms the implementation is not biased toward PCA, indicating the superiority claim does not hold on spiked covariance models as worded.

ProCreations/repro-approximate-proportio.overall: The logbook provides concrete, non-toy experimental evidence supporting the BBP phase transition (Claim 1) and the explicit generalization error formulas plus spectral structure (Claim 2), while systematically falsifying Claim 3's assertion that masked SSL outperforms PCA on spiked covariance models through 192 independent comparisons with an AR(1) positive control.

ProCreations/repro-adaptive-multi-round-.paper_title: Adaptive Multi-Round Allocation with Stochastic Arrivals

claims.claim: Single-round allocation problem admits an exact greedy solution based on marginal survival probabilities.
claims.evidence: Clean-room greedy allocator compared against exhaustive enumeration over 2,090 frontier/budget cases (103,625 allocations) spanning 1–4 populations and six diverse finite-support PMFs with budgets 0–9; greedy matches oracle in every case with max gap 8.88e-16.

claims.claim: Multi-round problem can be solved via dynamic program using population-level surrogate value function with polynomial complexity in total budget.
claims.evidence: PGF-based DP cross-checked against Cartesian outcome enumeration through budget 8 (agreement to 8.88e-16, zero action mismatches); scaling table through budget 24 shows state count exactly (B+1)^2 with polynomial transition and coefficient counts, confirming both correctness and polynomial complexity.

claims.claim: Multi-round error bound decomposes into single-round frontier error and population-level transition error.
claims.evidence: Single-round term validated across 2,000 random cases (no positive violation, max signed violation −0.00651) and 7 tight witnesses (gap 1.78e-15); multi-round decomposition tested via exact MDP oracle across 12 controlled cases at budgets 3–6 with max positive violation exactly 0.0, including homogeneous controls where both bound and loss are zero and perturbation cases where named terms increase precisely.

ProCreations/repro-adaptive-multi-round-.overall: This logbook provides concrete, clean-room experimental evidence supporting all three claims through exhaustive oracle comparisons, exact DP cross-checks, and controlled error-decomposition tests, all without executing author code. The setups are mathematically rigorous with exact oracles, though budget scales are modest (up to 24), which is appropriate for verifying correctness and complexity properties rather than large-scale performance.

claims.evidence: Six exactly group-calibrated distributions (calibration residual 1.11e-16) all show PPV/FOR gaps after 0.5 thresholding (.2000, .1000, .11935, .16815, .16828, .27218), and exhaustive enumeration of all 180 deterministic per-bin rule pairs confirms none achieves parity (minimum gap .01818).

claims.evidence: The paper's boundary-trace construction was run on 6 distributions with 8–12 randomized variables, and an independently formulated SLSQP optimizer over raw per-bin probabilities agrees on accuracy within 4.74e-10 with sufficiency constraint violations below 1.7e-11 and PPV/FOR gaps at most 3.66e-15.

claims.claim: Geometric characterization identifies optimal classifier minimizing deviation from separation subject to sufficiency
claims.evidence: The geometric boundary construction's minimum separation deviation was independently confirmed by a raw-variable optimizer with separation-deviation objective across all six distributions, agreeing within 8.05e-10, with nonzero case-specific deviations (.02682–.17517) confirming the substantive tradeoff.

ProCreations/repro-fair-decisions-from-c.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence across six distributions (two from the paper, four fresh) using two independently formulated solvers and exact population-level computation, verifying all three claims with tight cross-method agreement.
