ProCreations/repro-lower-bounds-for-fran.paper_title: Non-Uniform Noise-to-Signal Ratio in the REINFORCE Policy-Gradient Estimator

claims.claim: For finite-horizon linear-quadratic systems with Gaussian policies, the noise-to-signal ratio of the multi-step REINFORCE estimator can be computed exactly in closed form via lifted dynamics (Theorem 5, Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements the double-integrator LQG system (horizon T=5) with lifted Gaussian dynamics and computes exact NSR via five-node tensor Gauss-Hermite quadrature, cross-validated against seven-node quadrature (relative discrepancy 9.56e-14) and against 3.2 million Monte Carlo trajectories (1.47% median error on well-conditioned cells), with a discriminating three-node control missing by 30.99%.

claims.claim: The NSR landscape is highly non-uniform: as the policy approaches the optimal deterministic policy (Σ→0, per Corollary 6), the NSR does not vanish uniformly and can blow up, as demonstrated for a double-integrator system (Figure 1, Section 2.3).
claims.evidence: An exact 41×41 covariance grid on the double-integrator shows NSR spanning 18.5 to 4.49e10 (9+ orders of magnitude); along a 40-step path interpolating toward the deterministic optimum K*=[0,-5] with shrinking policy std, expected return improves monotonically (-2.10 to -1.51) while exact NSR increases 4.48e11-fold (3,560 to 1.59e15), and the predicted sigma0²/sigma² scaling exponent is recovered as 0.999979.

claims.claim: Variance of the multi-step REINFORCE estimator grows exponentially with the control horizon when the closed-loop dynamics are unstable, i.e., when the spectral radius ρ(F)>1 (Theorem 8, Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: 155 exact horizon cells (T=2..32) across five closed-loop systems show unstable systems (rho(F)=1.08, 1.16) with log-linear variance growth (R²>0.999, fitted bases 1.54 and 2.48, spanning 7-13 orders of magnitude) while stable systems (rho(F)=0.78, 0.88) have tail bases near 1; lifted-state-map bases agree with rho(F)² within 2.65%, and exactness is confirmed by Gauss-Hermite cross-check (1.26e-16 error) with a destructive three-node control.

claims.claim: A general upper bound on REINFORCE gradient-estimator variance is derived for generic nonlinear dynamics with expressive neural-network policies (Theorem 10, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Two independently trained 4,417-parameter ReLU MLPs on nonlinear pendulum dynamics were tested with 4,096 50-step trajectories at two noise levels; the full-gradient second moment stayed below the theorem's upper bound in all four cells (RHS/LHS ratios 84-89x), with manual block-Jacobian agreeing with PyTorch autograd to 3.97e-16 and standard errors of 1.7-1.8% far below the bound margins.

claims.claim: The analysis is extended from linear to polynomial systems and polynomial feedback policies via a moment-evaluation approach (Proposition 9, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Eleven exact polynomial cells (six quadratic, five cubic) were evaluated via two independent routes—sparse multivariate polynomial expansion with Gaussian moment factorization and direct tensor Gauss-Hermite—agreeing to 5.01e-15 worst relative error, with high-degree propagation (gradient degree up to 64, 27,395 monomials) and destructive three-node controls missing by 44-98%.

ProCreations/repro-lower-bounds-for-fran.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, independently implemented numerical evidence supporting all five claims: exact NSR computation on the LQG double-integrator, non-uniform NSR landscape with blow-up near the optimum, exponential variance growth for unstable closed-loop dynamics, empirical validation of the nonlinear neural-policy variance bound, and exact Gaussian-moment evaluation for polynomial systems. Multiple cross-validation methods and destructive controls throughout make this a high-quality reproduction.

ProCreations/repro-magnitude-distance-a-.paper_title: On the Provable Suboptimality of Momentum SGD in Nonstationary Stochastic Optimization

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows momentum SGD's tracking-error bound scales as (1-beta)^-2 on the initialization term and (1-beta)^-1 on the noise floor, versus O(1) and O(sigma^2 gamma/mu) respectively for vanilla SGD in Theorem 3.1 (Section 3.1, Theorems 3.1 and 3.3).
claims.evidence: The full factorial at d=100, T=5000, 20 paired seeds shows HB/SGD error amplification growing from 2.02x to 96.92x as beta increases from .5 to .99, with a log-log slope of -0.9918 against (1-beta). The exact Fraction-arithmetic audit independently confirms the noise factor scales as exactly (1-beta)^-2 across 80 cells, and results match Appendix Table 3 values closely (0.0566/0.1040/0.1030 vs 0.056/0.103/0.100).

claims.claim: Theorem 3.7 gives a minimax lower bound decomposing regret into a noise-limited term and an inertia-limited term that worsens with beta and can dominate in drift-heavy regimes, establishing an information-theoretic (not just analytical) barrier for momentum methods (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence: A 200,000-trial two-environment Gaussian testing reduction yields optimal LR test error 0.307685 matching analytic Bayes error 0.308538, demonstrating an estimator-independent information-theoretic barrier. The exact characteristic polynomial audit across 32 cells recovers linear inertia window scaling (slope 1.057, R²=.990), and a 90-cell theorem grid shows the predicted crossover between information- and inertia-dominated regimes with the exact (1-beta)^(-2/3) exponent. Note: the logbook refers to Theorem 3.9 rather than 3.7, but the content tested matches the claim.

claims.claim: Under the stability constraint gamma <= (1-beta)^2/L, the paper proves vanilla SGD provably outperforms Heavy-Ball/Nesterov momentum SGD in drift-dominated nonstationary regimes (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: SGD beats HB and NAG in all 36 factorial cells at paper scale, and in all 16 cells with drift >= 0.05 under matched effective step sizes (gamma_mom=(1-beta)*gamma_SGD). Zero-drift controls correctly show momentum's stationary advantage (e.g., 0.02629/0.02477/0.02366 for SGD/HB/NAG at beta=.95), validating the experimental design. An exact deterministic Fraction-arithmetic recurrence confirms SGD < HB in all 12 nonzero-drift cells with exact ties at zero drift.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.6 shows the high-probability bound for momentum SGD exhibits an inertia horizon of order (1-beta)^-1 and drift-noise coupling scaling as (1-beta)^-2, both absent from the vanilla SGD high-probability bound in Theorem 3.5 (Section 3.2, Theorems 3.5 and 3.6).
claims.evidence: The noise-free step-response audit under the theorem's stability constraint shows horizons of 2, 5, 8, 12, 24 steps for beta 0/.5/.7/.8/.9 with log-log slope 1.0627 (R²=.9946) against 1/(1-beta), confirming the inertia horizon. Exact Fraction arithmetic across 80 cells confirms the noise term scales as (1-beta)^-2 and the coupling term as (1-beta)^-4, both absent when beta=0. The logbook explicitly notes a failed q95 quantile diagnostic was retained but not used as evidence.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments on quadratics, linear/logistic regression, and MLPs confirm that increasing nonstationarity (drift), momentum parameter beta, or condition number kappa systematically worsens Heavy-Ball and Nesterov tracking error while vanilla SGD remains comparatively robust (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Quadratics (d=100, T=5000, 20 seeds) show SGD wins all 36 cells. Logistic regression and MLP show monotone worsening with beta at every drift level (worst-case 2.86x and 7.94x SGD error respectively). Linear regression shows the predicted crossover: momentum helps at low drift (kappa=10) but worsens monotonically at drift 0.02, and condition number amplifies the penalty from 12.9x (kappa=10) to 1063x (kappa=100). NAG tracks HB closely (13.08x vs 12.93x worst-case). The MLP is a small 2-layer tanh network with only 5 seeds, slightly reducing rigor for that sub-setting.

ProCreations/repro-magnitude-distance-a-.overall: The logbook provides a thorough reproduction with full-scale factorial experiments, exact rational-arithmetic theorem-term audits, a 200,000-trial information-theoretic testing reduction, and matched-step controls across quadratics, linear/logistic regression, and MLPs. The evidence consistently supports the paper's claims about momentum SGD's suboptimality in nonstationary regimes, with minor limitations including a theorem number discrepancy (3.7 vs 3.9), a small MLP architecture, and reduced seed counts for non-quadratic experiments.

ProCreations/repro-on-the-power-of-sourc.paper_title: On the Power of Source Screening for Learning Shared Feature Extractors

claims.claim: Training on a carefully selected subset of sources suffices to achieve minimax optimality in subspace estimation
claims.evidence: On a paper-scale synthetic setup (d=30, k=6, M=99, imbalanced population [6,6,6,27,27,27]) across 30 seeds and 4 sample sizes, the screened 36-source subset achieves median errors within 1.105x of the full 99-source median, with a log-log slope of -0.5724 matching the n^{-1/2} minimax signature and scaled error constants in [1.775, 2.056].

claims.claim: Source screening plays a central role in statistically optimal low-dimensional subspace estimation
claims.evidence: Across 30 pilot draws, screening reduces condition number from 4.5 to at most 1.4 while retaining all six latent directions, and the random-subset and majority-only controls degrade sharply (e.g., random 36 at 320 samples has error 0.4080 vs screened 0.2219), isolating screening itself—not merely fewer sources—as the mechanism restoring admissible geometry.

claims.claim: Developed algorithms and heuristics for identifying informative source subsets are effective on synthetic and real-world datasets
claims.evidence: The heuristic passes 600 synthetic method/seed/sample cells, and on 1,797 real 8x8 digit images across 5 splits and 6 bootstrap replications, screened 30-source subsets achieve 0.7789 accuracy vs 0.7574 for all sources (paired improvement +0.0215, 95% CI [0.0087, 0.0341], 23/30 wins) and vs 0.7445 for random subsets (+0.0344, CI [0.0183, 0.0506], 24/30 wins).

ProCreations/repro-on-the-power-of-sourc.overall: This clean-room reproduction provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all three claims on a paper-scale synthetic regime and a real-world digit recognition task, with proper controls (random subsets, majority-only, genie-balanced) and statistical testing (30 seeds, bootstrap CIs). The main limitation is that the real-world dataset (8x8 digits) is relatively small and simple, and no direct comparison to the paper's original numerical results is provided.

ProCreations/repro-well-posed-kl-regular.paper_title: Well-Posed KL-Regularized Control via Wasserstein and Kalman–Wasserstein KL Divergences

claims.claim: Wasserstein-based KL divergence analogues remain finite under support mismatch, unlike classical KL divergence.
claims.evidence: Four explicit singular-support cases (displaced Diracs, shifted parallel lines/planes, orthogonal Gaussians) yield infinite classical KL but finite WKL and KWKL, and a 12-point regularization sweep from epsilon=1e-1 to 1e-12 shows classical KL rising from 20 to 2e12 (log-log slope -1) while WKL stays exactly 2 and KWKL converges to 1.999999999998.

claims.claim: Proposed variants remove singularity in classical KL as process noise vanishes in linear time-invariant systems with Gaussian process noise.
claims.evidence: Across 33 process-noise variances (1e-10 to 1e6) on the paper's double integrator (A=[[1,1],[0,1]], B=[[0],[1]], Q=I, discount 0.9), the classical KL control penalty changes by a factor 1e16 with feedback-gain norm collapsing to 1.63e-7, while WKL's penalty stays exactly 1 with limiting gain norm 1.24386 and KWKL tracks WKL to within 1e-10 at low noise and KL to within 1e-12 at high noise.

claims.claim: The resulting controls outperform KL-based regularization on double integrator and cart-pole examples.
claims.evidence: On the double integrator, WKL and KWKL beat KL in all 256/256 state/rho comparisons (e.g., at rho=1e-6, mean discounted state cost 130.44 for KL vs 3.7697 for WKL/KWKL); on nonlinear cart-pole with RK4 rollout for 25 seconds from 24 initial states, WKL and KWKL beat KL in all 96/96 comparisons (at rho=1e-6, cost 16.999 for KL vs 3.2845 for transport variants).

ProCreations/repro-well-posed-kl-regular.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from an independent NumPy/SciPy implementation supporting all three claims: finiteness of Wasserstein-based KL under support mismatch, singularity removal as process noise vanishes, and control outperformance on both double integrator and nonlinear cart-pole. The experiments use the paper's own benchmark systems with specific parameter values and report consistent quantitative results across hundreds of comparisons.

claims.claim: Wave-Induced Rotary Encodings (WIRE) rotate tokens based on the graph Laplacian spectrum to inject structural information into attention.
claims.evidence: Fifteen graphs (paths, cycles, stars, 6–33 nodes) show Laplacian diagonalization producing nonconstant off-diagonal attention (min std 0.238, ≥13 distinct scores), with permutation equivariance confirmed (max eigensystem residual 7.59e-15, attention permutation error exactly zero, absolute-vs-relative rotation agreement to 2.78e-16).

claims.claim: WIRE recovers regular RoPE on grids and depends asymptotically on the graph effective resistance.
claims.evidence: Paths of length 4–64 show first Laplacian mode matching 1-D RoPE closed form with correlation ≥0.9999999999999998; eight grids (3×4 to 8×10) show separable x/y modes with eigen-equation residual ≤5.14e-16; 45 node pairs match effective resistance to 5.33e-15 with log-log slopes in [3.9837, 3.9996] reproducing the predicted fourth-order term, corroborated by an 80-node Gauss-Hermite quadrature oracle agreeing to 3.33e-16.

claims.claim: WIRE is compatible with linear attention, unlike bias-based relative position encodings.
claims.evidence: Dense vs. associative linear-attention evaluation at 6 sizes (8–2048 tokens, feature dim 32, value dim 7) yields max relative error 2.16e-15, with the associative path avoiding a 4,194,304-element matrix at 2048 tokens (18,724.6× memory reduction), confirming that tokenwise Q/K rotations pass through the subquadratic contraction exactly.

ProCreations/repro-rotary-position-encod.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from a clean-room NumPy/SciPy implementation verifying all three mathematical claims about WIRE: Laplacian-spectral rotary structure with permutation equivariance, exact RoPE recovery on grids with effective-resistance asymptotics, and exact linear-attention compatibility. The verification is rigorous at the operator/mathematical level but includes no training or downstream-task experiments.

ProCreations/repro-no-free-lunch-non-asy.paper_title: No Free Lunch: Non-Asymptotic Analysis of Prediction-Powered Inference

neonforestmist/improved-dimension-bco-gr.paper_title: Improved Dimension Dependence for Bandit Convex Optimization with Gradient Variation

claims.claim: Theorem 1 establishes an Õ(d^{3/2}√V_T) regret bound for one-point bandit convex optimization with gradient variation V_T, improving the dimension dependence over Chiang et al. (2013)'s O(d^3√V_T) bound (Theorem 1, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Source audit of the pinned paper reveals Theorem 1 is stated for two-point BCO, not one-point as the claim asserts, and the prior comparison is to Chiang et al.'s d^2 dependence, not d^3. The algorithm was also executed over d=16–256 with two seeds and multiple V_T values, confirming the source mismatch.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 gives an O((d/λ) log V_T) regret bound for λ-strongly convex functions, improving the prior O((d^2/λ) log V_T) bound by a factor of d (Theorem 2, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Strongly-convex diagonal quadratics executed with λ=0.30, d=16–256, two seeds, V_T=1,16,256; maximum fixed-point residual 1.110e-16; recomputed source dependency (d/λ)log(dV_T) confirmed against prior (d^2/λ)log V_T with extra d factor.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 provides O(√(dW_T) + d) regret for linear functions and O(d√W_T + d) regret for convex functions in terms of the gradient variance W_T (Theorem 3, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Source proof (Appendices/Proof-of-Methods.tex lines 335–341) derives E[V_T] ≤ 4d^2 W_T + O(d^3) for convex losses, yielding O(d√(W_T+d)), not the claimed O(d√W_T + d); the O(d^3) remainder cannot be dropped. Linear part matches but the combined claim is contradicted for convex functions.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 delivers O(√(dF_T) + d) regret bounds for linear and convex functions using the small-loss quantity F_T (Theorem 4, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: F_T computed exactly as best-fixed cumulative loss on enlarged domain X+ via closed-form ball minimum (linear) and independently checked trust-region solve (convex); maximum realized-regret/envelope ratio 0.0595 < 1 across d=16–256 and two seeds for 6R√(d^2+16dLF_T).

claims.claim: Section 4 presents the first gradient-variation regret bound for one-point bandit linear optimization over hyper-rectangular domains (Section 4).
claims.evidence: One-point algorithm executed on [-1/√d,1/√d]^d with log-barrier Dikin perturbation, d up to 256, T up to 32,768; maximum implicit-solver residual 8.8e-15, minimum action-to-boundary margin > 0, median improvement over zero-action baseline 0.705.

claims.claim: Table 1 summarizes the dimension-dependence improvements across gradient-variation, gradient-variance, and small-loss metrics for linear, convex, and strongly convex function classes relative to prior best-known results (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Table 1 reproduced from pinned source with entries matching across V_T, W_T, F_T metrics for linear, convex, and strongly-convex classes; executed coverage spans V_T profiles (convex/strongly-convex), W_T rows (linear/convex), and F_T rows (linear/convex).

neonforestmist/improved-dimension-bco-gr.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence at d=16–256 and T up to 32,768 supporting claims 2, 4, 5, and 6, while source-text audits falsify claims 1 and 3 by showing the official claim sentences mischaracterize the paper's own theorems and proofs. The experiments use controlled linear and diagonal-quadratic stress families rather than fully general loss sequences, but the scale and source-audit methodology are substantive.

ProCreations/repro-row-stochastic-matric.paper_title: Row-Stochastic Matrices Can Provably Outperform Doubly Stochastic Matrices in Decentralized Learning

claims.claim: Row-stochastic matrix becomes self-adjoint while doubly stochastic one does not, creating penalty terms that amplify consensus error
claims.evidence: Direct operator audit across 12 graph/size cells (ring, grid, exponential, custom at n=16,32,64) measures the weighted-adjoint residual ||D_π W - W^T D_π|| at 1.59e-17 for row-stochastic W versus at least 0.005475 for doubly stochastic J, and explicitly computes the λ_max² penalty term at ≥10.196 with condition number 25, directly confirming the self-adjointness distinction and amplification term rather than inferring them.

claims.claim: Row-stochastic design convergence is strictly faster than doubly stochastic under tighter weighted Hilbert-space analysis
claims.evidence: Real-image stochastic nonconvex learning on the complete 1,797-image digits dataset with 16 nodes training a 2,410-parameter ReLU MLP across 5 stratified splits × 3 topologies (15 paired cells) shows Strategy II (row-stochastic) wins 15/15 on late held-out loss with median ratio 2.044× and 15/15 on loss AUC, plus 72/72 quadratic control wins. While smaller than the paper's CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 scale, the setup uses real data, nonconvex stochastic objectives, controlled pairing, and multiple topologies at the paper's 16-node configuration.

claims.claim: Derives sufficient conditions and topology guidelines for when row-stochastic design ensures faster convergence
claims.evidence: The audit computes spectral gaps and Theorem 7.1 thresholds for ring graphs at n=16,32,64, finding the row-stochastic gap satisfies the sufficient inequality in 3/3 cases. A falsifiable star-graph control shows degree-matched weights yield spectral gap 0.02 versus 0.000491–0.00828 for reversed weights, producing 2.4×–40.7× advantages that confirm the topology guideline.

ProCreations/repro-row-stochastic-matric.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all three claims through direct operator-norm measurements, paired real-image nonconvex learning experiments across 15 cells, and topology stress tests with falsifiable controls. The main limitation is reduced scale (digits/MLP vs CIFAR-10/ResNet-18), but the core theoretical distinctions and convergence comparisons are tested on non-trivial real-data setups with 16-node decentralized configurations.

ProCreations/repro-demystifying-llm-as-a.paper_title: Revenue Guarantees of No-Swap-Regret Dynamics in First Price Auctions

claims.claim: For exact correlated equilibria in discrete first-price auctions with k discretization levels, expected revenue is at least v2 - 4/k, where v2 is the second-highest valuation (Theorem 2.5).
claims.evidence: The fitted-dual certificate audit across 206 games (k=4..16, 2-3 bidders) checks all 96,612 pure profile inequalities and finds them feasible with worst slack 0.0625; at ε=0 the derived bound revenue ≥ v₂ - 3/k implies the claimed v₂ - 4/k for exact CE.

claims.claim: For ε-approximate correlated equilibria, expected revenue is at least v2 - 3/k - Θ(εk²) (Theorem 2.6).
claims.evidence: The dual certificate from Definition 3.6 is implemented directly and verified across 206 games with 96,612 enumerated profiles, yielding the explicit bound revenue ≥ v₂ - 3/k - 2εk² with sum(λ) ≤ 2k², matching the claimed Θ(εk²) dependence.

claims.claim: There exists an ε-approximate correlated equilibrium with revenue at most v2 - Θ(1/k) - Θ(ε), showing the ε-dependence in the revenue lower bound cannot be removed (Theorem 2.8).
claims.evidence: Exact Python Fraction arithmetic across 48 cells (k=4..128, ε=0.01..0.2) confirms a strengthened witness with revenue exactly 1 - 1/k - ε/2 + ε/(2k), containing both Θ(1/k) and Θ(ε) loss terms; the logbook transparently notes the paper's printed construction lacks the 1/k term, and 24 destructive controls are correctly rejected.

claims.claim: When bidders run no-swap-regret algorithms achieving swap regret O(√(kT)), the time-averaged revenue is at least v2 - 3/k - O(ε) after O(k^5/ε^2) rounds (Corollary 2.7).
claims.evidence: The rate composition R(T)=C√(kT) → CE error R(T)/T → revenue penalty 2k²R(T)/T ≤ 2ε is checked across 84 (k, ε, C) triples with identity error 2.22e-16, yielding T ≥ C²k⁵/ε²; a falsification control with T=k⁴/ε² fails by factors 2.83x–11.31x matching the predicted √k deficit.

claims.claim: Time-averaged bidder behavior under no-swap-regret dynamics converges to an ε-approximate correlated equilibrium with probability 1-δ (Theorem 2.3).
claims.evidence: Sixteen independently seeded Blum-Mansour swap-regret runs (k=8,16, 50,000 rounds each) show median max CE switching gain falling from 0.096 to 0.017 (82.8% reduction); the identity empirical CE gap = swap regret/T holds exactly at all 80 checkpoints, directly demonstrating the convergence mechanism.

claims.claim: The revenue lower bounds are proved via a dual-fitting approach that uses a linear program and weak duality to bound revenue of approximate correlated equilibria (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The fitted dual of Definition 3.6 is implemented directly from the paper and verified across 206 games with complete profile enumeration; weak duality is applied to derive revenue ≥ v₂ - 3/k - 2εk² from the feasible dual certificate, confirming the dual-fitting proof approach.

ProCreations/repro-demystifying-llm-as-a.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, exact-arithmetic verification of the paper's core mathematical claims through complete enumeration of dual certificates across 206 auctions, exact rational construction of a strengthened low-revenue equilibrium witness, and empirical convergence tests of Blum-Mansour dynamics with 16 seeded runs. Notably, it identifies that the paper's printed Theorem 2.8 construction lacks a standalone 1/k revenue loss term and supplies a corrected witness, demonstrating independent scrutiny rather than mere confirmation.

ProCreations/repro-positive-distribution.paper_title: Convergence Rate of the Last Iterate of Stochastic Proximal Algorithms

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes an Õ(1/√T) convergence rate for the last iterate of proximal SGD under componentwise convexity and L-smoothness of each fi (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Proximal SGD on a 64-dimensional, 800-component l1-regularized quadratic with the paper's Theorem 3.1 step size across 6 horizons (T=512–16384) and 128 independent runs yielded a last-iterate gap log-log slope of -0.466, consistent with Õ(1/√T), with all means below the literal theorem bound.

claims.claim: The analysis replaces the standard bounded-variance assumption with the weaker requirement of a finite second moment of the gradient at the solution, E||∇fi(x*)||² = σ*² < ∞ (Section 2, Assumption 1).
claims.evidence: An analytic two-component convex-smooth construction (f_s(x)=0.5(1+0.9s)x²-sx) has finite σ*²=1 at the solution x*=0 while its centered gradient variance grows as (0.9x-1)² with measured exponent 2.0002, directly demonstrating that finite second moment at the solution is strictly weaker than globally bounded variance.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 extends the Õ(1/√T) last-iterate rate to a randomized incremental proximal method when the regularizer decomposes additively and each component gj is Lipschitz continuous (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: A 24-node cycle graph with nonseparable edge regularizers g_e(x)=0.12|x_i-x_j| (Lipschitz continuous) was tested with the randomized incremental proximal method across 3 horizons and 384 runs, yielding slope -0.455 and all means below the Theorem 4.1 bound, with an independent primal-dual reference (gap 1.89e-8).

claims.claim: Section 4.4 applies the framework to a BlockProx algorithm for graph-guided regularizers used in multi-task and federated learning, proving last-iterate convergence without assuming bounded gradients (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: The graph-guided regularizer experiment on a 24-node cycle with nonseparable cycle-TV regularizers demonstrates last-iterate convergence (slope -0.455) using the randomized incremental proximal framework, directly instantiating the graph-guided applicability claim, though the logbook does not explicitly name or separately implement the 'BlockProx' algorithm from Section 4.4.

claims.claim: The obtained Õ(1/√T) rate matches, up to logarithmic factors, the last-iterate guarantees for unconstrained SGD under bounded variance from Garrigos et al. (2025) (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Direct head-to-head comparison of stochastic proximal SGD and unconstrained SGD on the same 40-dimensional least-squares problem with last-iterate measurements yielded fitted exponents of -0.5238 and -0.4842 (differing by 0.0396), both consistent with 1/√T, demonstrating rate matching; the logbook honestly notes that finite experiments cannot resolve the logarithmic-factor qualifier.

ProCreations/repro-positive-distribution.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all five claims through well-designed experiments with independent reference solutions, multiple runs, and honest scope limitations. The setups are moderate-scale but appropriate for verifying convergence-rate claims, with the variance-assumption claim demonstrated via an exact algebraic construction.

vissutagunawan/3KX1xU2bCC.paper_title: Lower Bounds for Frank-Wolfe on Strongly Convex Sets

claims.claim: Frank-Wolfe admits constructive lower bound of Ω(1/√ε) when both objective and constraint set are smooth and strongly convex
claims.evidence: A backward-constructed worst-case FW trajectory (T=74,993 steps, gap down to ~1e-10) satisfies the Eq 15 lower bound r_t ≥ r₀/(1+(8/3)r₀t) with 0 violations (min margin +7.50e-11), is certified as a genuine FW trajectory by a 150-digit forward replay matching to 2.7e-90, and yields gap slope -1.99941 vs t (target -2) and T-vs-ε slope -0.50664 (target -0.5), confirming T = Ω(1/√ε) at the paper's own model problem and parameters.

claims.claim: Known uniform O(1/√ε) guarantees in this regime are tight
claims.evidence: The Prop 3 one-step upper bound r_{t+1} ≤ r_t/(1+r_t) holds on 3,000,000 random feasible states with 0 violations (worst margin -6.66e-16), and the worst-case residual is sandwiched between the Eq 6 upper and Eq 15 lower envelopes with 0 violations on both sides over 74,993 steps, yielding fitted T-vs-ε slope -0.50275 (target -1/2) and t²·gap converging to 0.56232 ≈ 9/16, confirming the O(1/√ε) exponent is attained and thus tight.

claims.claim: Strong convexity of constraint set does not yield rates uniformly faster than O(1/√ε)
claims.evidence: On the same strongly convex unit ball, moving the optimizer so that ‖∇f(x*)‖>0 (q outside the ball) yields linear convergence (ρ=0.019–0.498, reaching 1e-10 in 5–31 iterations), while the hard case with ∇f(x*)=0 requires ~0.75·ε^{-1/2} steps (measured 68/743/7493 at ε=1e-4/1e-6/1e-8 vs theory 75/750/7500); dimension independence (d=2…500, max deviation 8.5e-12) and affine invariance across ellipsoids (max gap deviation ≤2.5e-11) confirm the result is not specific to the ball or low dimension.

vissutagunawan/3KX1xU2bCC.overall: This logbook provides strong numerical corroboration of all three claims through clean-room implementation of the paper's own equations on its model problem P_B at full paper parameters, including a 74,993-step backward-constructed worst-case trajectory certified by extended-precision forward replay, 3M-state upper-bound verification, and a clear linear-vs-sublinear contrast on the same strongly convex set. The evidence is concrete and at the paper's own scale, though it is numerical corroboration of analytical theorems rather than symbolic proof.

vissutagunawan/VnA5q5jXVz.paper_title: Why Self-Distillation Helps and Hurts: Denoising vs. Signal Forgetting

claims.claim: Derives deterministic-equivalent recursions for prediction risk and effective noise in self-training trajectories
claims.evidence: Clean-room Monte-Carlo of Algorithm 1 (p=1600, n=800, 40 seeds, spiked model) matches the deterministic recursion (Eq. 10) with NRMSE=0.0116 and max 2.01% relative error; the recursion reproduces the Thm 3.2 closed form to 0.80%; effective noise γ_t² matches D_t² to 0.57% median error; concentration slopes are -0.46 (risk) and -0.49 (gamma²), consistent with predicted p^{-1/2}; and a power-law covariance (p=1500, non-spiked) matches the recursion to 1.46% max error, confirming the recursions beyond the spiked special case.

claims.claim: Identifies U-shaped test-risk curve with optimal early-stopping time determined by denoising-forgetting tradeoff
claims.evidence: Across ρ∈{1.5,2,3} (s=20, p=1000, 24 seeds), every risk curve has an interior minimum with empirical t* matching theory within 0–1 iteration (ρ=1.5: t*=8/9, ρ=2: t*=4/4, ρ=3: t*=2/2), larger ρ gives earlier t*, and paired-seed 95% CIs confirm R(0)−R(t*)>0 and R(K)−R(t*)>0; the anisotropy gate shows isotropic s=1 is monotone (no interior minimum) while all s>1 cases are U-shaped, confirming the U-shape is gated by anisotropy as the denoising-forgetting tradeoff predicts.

claims.claim: Iteration acts as iteration-dependent spectral filter preserving strong eigendirections while suppressing weaker ones
claims.evidence: Multi-spike survival (spikes {80,16,4,1.5}, p=2000, 24 seeds) matches the predicted (s_j/(s_j+τ))^{t+1} to max deviation 0.0111, with a 166x strong/weak survival ratio at t=10; noise-only risk decays by 1/(1+τ) to <0.3% relative error across three aspect ratios; rotation by a random orthonormal Q leaves survival unchanged (max dev 0.0099); and the eigenvalue-swap control flips which direction survives (0.867→0.023 and 0.022→0.865), confirming the filter tracks eigenvalue magnitude rather than coordinate identity.

vissutagunawan/VnA5q5jXVz.overall: This logbook provides a clean-room reproduction of all three claims at the paper's own synthetic-covariance scale (p up to 2048, proportional regime), with Monte-Carlo validation against deterministic theory, proper statistical controls (paired CIs, anisotropy gate, rotation robustness, eigenvalue-swap), and concentration-rate checks. All three claims are supported by concrete numerical evidence with multiple seeds and falsifiable controls.

ProCreations/repro-lec-linear-expectatio.paper_title: LEC: Linear Expectation Constraints for Selection-Conditioned Risk Control in Selective Prediction and Routing Systems

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 proves that thresholding on a calibrated statistic derived from a linear expectation constraint yields a finite-sample marginal FDR guarantee, Pr(err=1 | u ≤ threshold) ≤ α, for a new exchangeable test sample using only calibration data (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides an exhaustive counterexample over all 2^9=512 binary error populations on nine fixed uncertainty ranks with nine held-out roles, showing conditional error of exactly 0.5 (121/242 at α=0.25, 428/856 at α=0.40) under a valid exchangeable distribution, directly violating the claimed bound Pr(err=1 | u ≤ threshold) ≤ α. This is a finite, deterministic, exhaustive construction—not an underpowered empirical test—that satisfies exchangeability and calibration-only conditions while exceeding the theorem's bound.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 extends this guarantee to two-model routing systems, showing that jointly calibrated thresholds for both models maintain system-level FDR control over routed predictions (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook applies the same exhaustive counterexample to the two-model routing system, noting it contains the single-model case as a special case (secondary threshold accepts no rows), yielding identical held-out conditional errors of 0.5 at both α=0.25 and α=0.40, exceeding the system-level bounds claimed by Theorem 3.2 under exchangeability-only assumptions.

claims.claim: On CommonsenseQA with LLaMA-3.2-3B at target FDR level α=0.05, LEC achieves power of 0.1959 compared to 0.1191 for COIN-CP, an improvement of roughly 8 percentage points at the same nominal FDR level (Table 1, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook independently executed LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct (Q4_K_M) on 10,000 CommonsenseQA examples across 100 seeded 50/50 splits at α=0.05, obtaining LEC power of 0.0111 and COIN-CP power of 0.0000, versus the paper's claimed 0.1959 and 0.1191 respectively—a gap of 1.1 points instead of the claimed ~8 points, with COIN-CP selecting zero test examples in all 100 splits.

claims.claim: LEC's calibration procedure relies only on exchangeable calibration data (no distributional assumptions beyond exchangeability) to compute the FDR-constrained, retention-maximizing threshold (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: While the algorithmic procedure does use only calibration data (verified by 200/200 permutation invariance), the logbook's exhaustive counterexample shows that exchangeability alone is insufficient for the FDR guarantee: the resulting threshold yields conditional error of 0.5 exceeding targets of 0.25 and 0.40 under a valid exchangeable construction, falsifying the distribution-free sufficiency claim.

claims.claim: The two-model routing evaluation (Section 4.3) shows a weaker model combined with a stronger one via LEC's joint threshold calibration accepts more correct predictions than either model used alone at the same FDR budget (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook ran Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Phi-3.5-mini-instruct on all 10,962 CommonsenseQA examples across 100 seeded partitions at α=0.10, showing the joint route accepts 2,561.19 correct predictions per held-out half versus 2,181.87 for Qwen-only and 2,106.10 for Phi-only, with both models materially participating (76.14%/23.86% split) and system error at 9.904% below the 10% target.

ProCreations/repro-lec-linear-expectatio.overall: The logbook provides strong evidence that the paper's empirical routing results (Claim 5) reproduce at scale with real instruction-tuned models, but presents exhaustive finite counterexamples that falsify the theoretical FDR guarantees (Claims 1, 2, 4) under exchangeability-only assumptions, and shows the specific LLaMA CommonsenseQA power numbers (Claim 3) do not reproduce. The reproduction is notably rigorous, using complete corpora, multiple models, exhaustive constructions, and full provenance tracking.

ProCreations/repro-inference-of-online-n.paper_title: Inference of Online Newton Methods with Nesterov's Accelerated Sketching

claims.claim: The proposed online Newton method using a sketch-and-project solver with Nesterov's acceleration (Algorithm 1, NASketch) matches the O(d^2) per-iteration time and memory complexity of first-order methods (Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: Operation-count audit across dimensions 32–512 fits exponent 1.976 (vs. 2.971 for dense solve), and 140 paired solves on an 18D system show accelerated mean relative squared error 1.64e-8 vs. 5.39e-5 unaccelerated, confirming both the O(d²) scaling and the accelerated solver's effectiveness.

claims.claim: The last iterate is proven asymptotically normal, with the limiting covariance characterized by a Lyapunov equation incorporating the sketching operator (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: 3,000 independent streams with non-Gaussian (centered-exponential) innovations at horizon 4,000 yield empirical covariance within 4.92% of the independently solved Lyapunov target, with all marginal QQ R² ≥ 0.99915 and low skewness/kurtosis, demonstrating emergent asymptotic normality with the claimed covariance.

claims.claim: A fully online covariance estimator achieves convergence rate E[||Sigma_hat_t - Sigma*||] = O(1/sqrt(t*phi_t)) without requiring matrix inversion (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: 600 independent 3D streams run to horizon 32,000 using only four recursive states (no matrix inversion) show mean Frobenius error decreasing 29.83% with fitted log-log slope −0.1037, reasonably close to the theoretical −0.125, supporting the stated O(1/√(t·φ_t)) rate.

claims.claim: Global convergence guarantees for the sketch-and-project Newton iterates are established (Theorem 3.8, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Theorem 3.8 conditions are explicitly instantiated on a globally strongly convex d=4 objective with bounded Hessian; 36 noisy trajectories starting from radii 1, 10, and 100 all contract to mean final distances ≤6.67e-4, with maximum final/initial ratio 0.001385.

claims.claim: A spectral radius recursion derived via the Cayley-Hamilton theorem proves contraction at rate 1 - sqrt(mu_t/nu_t) for the accelerated sketching operator (Lemma 3.6).
claims.evidence: Across 220,011 spectral cells spanning 11 (μ,ν) pairs and 20,001 z-values, the maximum spectral radius minus the claimed bound 1−√(μ/ν) is 3.33e-15, the Cayley–Hamilton matrix residual is ≤3.33e-16, and the scalar recurrence matches direct matrix powers through τ=64 within 8.69e-15.

claims.claim: The framework recovers exact Newton behavior and the unaccelerated sketching case (gamma=1) as special cases, clarifying computational-statistical trade-offs (Proposition 4.4).
claims.evidence: Exact Newton Lyapunov solutions match Ω/2, Ω, and (2/3)Ω across three φ/C_φ regimes with residuals ≤1.11e-16, full-rank sketch S=I recovers the direct Newton step to 3.99e-15, and 50 independent γ=1 sketch sequences match ordinary sketch-and-project to 2.22e-16.

ProCreations/repro-inference-of-online-n.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims through controlled instances with exactly computable theoretical targets, including operation-count scaling, stochastic-approximation limits, spectral verification, and special-case identities. While some tests use small dimensions (d=3–18), they directly probe the specific theoretical properties claimed rather than serving as proxy tasks.

noxeon/repro-on-the-variability-of-conce.paper_title: On the Variability of Concept Activation Vectors

claims.claim: CAV variance decreases as 1/N where N is number of random examples used in construction.
claims.evidence: A synthetic Gaussian experiment with Theorem 1's assumptions verifiably satisfied shows Var(CAV) ∝ 1/N from N=10 onward (log-log slope −0.925, R²=0.999), and real-data experiments across tabular (Adult MLP) and image (GoogLeNet) domains show asymptotic decay with tail slopes −0.51 to −0.75 (R²≈0.98–1.00) for N≳300, consistent with the theorem's asymptotic nature.

claims.claim: Variance follows universal 1/N relationship across different modalities and datasets.
claims.evidence: At the paper's own plotted scale (N≤200–300), CAV variance curves are flat or rising across all three modalities (slopes −0.11 to +0.00). Extended-tail slopes reach only −0.51 to −0.75 (never −1) in tabular and image, while text dense-layer slopes are merely −0.23 to −0.34 and the text pooled-conv layer shows variance increasing with N (+0.23 to +0.40). Assumption 1 is violated in all image and text settings, undermining the 'universal' characterization.

claims.claim: Provides practical recommendations for resource-efficient application of Concept Activation Vectors.
claims.evidence: The factual premises underlying the recommendation are directly measured: TCAV-score variance stays flat at ≈0.15–0.25 across N=10–3000 (Adult layer2/male, slope −0.01) while CAV variance falls ~10×, and multi-run averaging at fixed budget R=2000 yields variance decay with log-log slope −0.90 (R²=0.98), confirming that splitting budget into modest-N runs stabilizes TCAV while increasing N per run stabilizes the CAV direction.

noxeon/repro-on-the-variability-of-conce.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous independent reimplementation across three modalities with extended N ranges and a synthetic theory check, confirming the asymptotic 1/N CAV variance decay (Claim 1) and the practical multi-run averaging recommendation (Claim 3), but finding that the 'universal' 1/N relationship (Claim 2) does not hold at the paper's own plotted scale and is only approximate asymptotically, with text-domain results being particularly weak.

ProCreations/repro-dropout-universality-.paper_title: Dropout Universality: Scaling Laws and Optimal Scheduling at the Edge-of-Chaos

claims.claim: Dropout shifts perfect-alignment fixed point, making depth scale for information propagation finite even at critical initialization.
claims.evidence: A clean-room ReLU correlation map solved at critical initialization across eight dropout probabilities shows zero-dropout recovering c*=1 with infinite xi, while all seven positive dropout fields yield c*<1 with finite xi decreasing from 21.696 (p=0.0003) to 1.651 (p=0.2), with the same solver serving as the negative control.

claims.claim: Smooth activations and kinked activations constitute distinct universality classes with different critical exponents.
claims.evidence: Five critical exponents (ν_t, β, θ_rel, 1/δ, ν_ρ) independently fitted from full smooth-tanh (80-node Gauss-Hermite) and analytic kinked-ReLU maps produce distinct values matching theoretical targets (e.g., β=0.971 vs 1.964, 1/δ=0.512 vs 0.666) with all ten log-log fits at R²>0.999.

claims.claim: Predicted dropout schedules outperform constant dropout and maximize effective correlation length under fixed budget.
claims.evidence: The theoretical objective yields xi=5.086 for front-loaded [1,2,3] vs 3.204 for constant dropout (58.74% gain) across all 20 enumerated placements, and a 20-seed width-256 depth-6 CIFAR-10 MLP experiment shows front-loaded dropout wins 20/20 held-out loss pairs (10.22% reduction, p=6.24e-19) while the equal-budget late control loses all 20 pairs.

ProCreations/repro-dropout-universality-.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from clean-room mean-field computations and a 20-seed paired training experiment that independently support all three claims, including proper negative controls (zero-dropout critical recovery and reversed late-schedule control). The reproduction is limited to the paper's MLP setting and does not cover the additional Vision Transformer configurations mentioned in the paper.

vissutagunawan/MvuCgK0Qns.paper_title: Softmax as Linear Attention in the Large-Prompt Regime: a Measure-based Perspective

claims.claim: Softmax attention converges to linear operator in infinite-prompt limit for i.i.d. Gaussian inputs
