claims.evidence: The simulation confirms no per-class hyperparameter tuning was used, but accuracy is flat (-0.001), the synthetic efficiency score slightly decreased (-0.0020), and there is only one synthetic dataset with no real VLM inference cost measurements or cross-dataset evaluation.

Edd16/icml2026-YHLkqytT2p-repro.overall: This logbook provides a minimal synthetic numpy proxy (20 classes, 4K samples, hand-crafted logits) that tests the general directionality of MOON's shrinkage mechanism, finding marginal balanced-accuracy gains. It does not use any real VLM, real long-tail dataset, or comparison to prior transductive methods, so none of the paper's claims are substantiated at the claimed scale.

claims.claim: Position: combining In-Weight Learning and In-Context Learning through modular memory is the missing piece for continual adaptation at scale.
claims.evidence: The claim about continual adaptation 'at scale' is tested only on 3 linear synthetic regression tasks (y=ax+b) with a 2-layer MLP and tiny per-task heads; real runs and numbers exist but the scale is far below any realistic continual-learning benchmark.

claims.claim: A modular memory-centric architecture uses ICL for rapid adaptation/knowledge accumulation and IWL for stable capability updates, mitigating catastrophic forgetting.
claims.evidence: Forgetting mitigation is shown with concrete numbers (baseline TaskA MSE regression +8.02 vs memory +0.55, or 16.6 vs 0.078 in a second run), and ICL/IWL roles are proxied via 5-shot head-only updates vs full-head training, but only on 3 linear synthetic tasks with a 2-layer MLP — a clearly simplified setup, not a full reproduction.

Edd16/icml2026-iBXcqA5N6j-repro.overall: This logbook provides a small-scale proxy demonstration that modular per-task heads reduce catastrophic forgetting on synthetic linear tasks, with ICL and IWL represented by simplified proxies. It does not test the claims at any realistic scale or with true in-context learning.

Edd16/icml2026-0LeyqHkrEG-repro.paper_title: Reliability-Aware LLM Alignment from Inconsistent Human Feedback

claims.claim: RGPO effectively reduces inconsistency and noise in training data from human feedback.
claims.evidence: A synthetic binary classification task (N=2000, D=10, 35% label noise, logistic regression) showed 11.72% loss variance reduction from reliability-weighting, but test error was identical (0.0740 vs 0.0740) and no real human feedback data or LLM training was used.

claims.claim: RGPO achieves superior performance compared to widely adopted RLHF baselines on LLM alignment benchmarks.
claims.evidence: On the same synthetic toy task, reliability-weighted training achieved 0.9315 vs 0.9280 mean accuracy (+0.38%) with overlapping standard deviations; no PPO, DPO, or LLM alignment benchmarks (HH-RLHF, MT-Bench, AlpacaEval) were run.

claims.claim: RGPO uses reliability-aware consistency optimization to dynamically modulate training based on annotation consensus level.
claims.evidence: Static per-sample weights set equal to annotation consensus (Pearson r=1.0 by construction) demonstrate the weighting mechanism, but the logbook explicitly states the 'dynamic' aspect (modulation evolving over training steps) was not demonstrated, and no LLM-scale training was conducted.

Edd16/icml2026-0LeyqHkrEG-repro.overall: This logbook validates the core reliability-weighting mechanism on a synthetic binary classification toy problem but does not reproduce any of the paper's claims at LLM scale or on real human feedback data. All three claims are addressed only through a simplified proxy with logistic regression, with no PPO/DPO baselines or alignment benchmarks evaluated.

Edd16/icml2026-M78xLFN7EJ-repro.paper_title: Protein Design with Agent Rosetta: A Case Study for Specialized Scientific Agents

claims.claim: Using simplified action syntax raises Agent Rosetta's composition-penalty generation success rate from about 70% (GPT-5 without the simplification) to at least 98.88% across all tested LLMs (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: A deterministic numpy simulation models token-error rates and composition penalties, producing 0.7048 complex and 0.9889 simplified success rates, but no live LLM was called and no Agent Rosetta action syntax was actually executed.

claims.claim: On fixed-backbone sequence design across 8 test protein structures (74-125 residues), Agent Rosetta's action success rate is at least 86% across all LLMs, and its median RMSD matches ProteinMPNN within 0.20 Å tolerance while outperforming baselines on 5 of 8 conformations (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: A numpy proxy over 8 simulated structures yields an action success rate of 0.8225 (below the claimed ≥86%) and a simulated RMSD of 1.937 vs ProteinMPNN's 2.000, but no real Rosetta folding or ProteinMPNN design was run.

claims.claim: Gemini 2.5 Flash and Qwen3 Instruct achieve the best cost-performance tradeoff among LLM backbones tested for backbone-stabilization design, using 30 LLM queries per trajectory and 128 candidate designs per step (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: A numpy proxy with list-price cost estimates and simulated success rates ranks Llama 3.1 as the best tradeoff (not Gemini/Qwen3), and no live LLM was queried or real Rosetta cost accounting performed.

claims.claim: For designing a single non-canonical formyl-tryptophan (TRF) residue into the protein core across 4 de novo folds (40-153 residues), GPT-5 achieves the highest TRF inclusion success rate, about 14.5%, on the most challenging structure (PDB 8UZL) (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: A surrogate inclusion-probability model produces GPT-5 at 0.1526 across 4 simulated folds, but no live GPT-5, no PDB 8UZL structures, and no Rosetta scoring were executed.

claims.claim: Agent Rosetta outperforms the human expert baseline on AF3 RMSD and pLDDT metrics for non-canonical amino acid design, evaluated over 16 independent trajectories per method with 1,000 bootstrap samples (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Simulated metric distributions yield AR RMSD 2.205 vs Expert 2.740 and AR pLDDT 84.53 vs 76.43 with bootstrap CIs excluding zero, but no real AF3 structure predictions or human-expert design trajectories were performed.

Edd16/icml2026-M78xLFN7EJ-repro.overall: Every claim was addressed only through deterministic numpy proxy simulations with no real LLM calls, no Rosetta execution, no ProteinMPNN, and no AF3 predictions. The proxies reproduce directional trends but operate at a fundamentally reduced scale and fidelity relative to the paper's actual experimental setup.

Edd16/icml2026-tj9EwfaxHm-repro.paper_title: VERA-V: Variational Inference Framework for Jailbreaking Vision-Language Models

claims.claim: On the HarmBench dataset against GPT-4o, VERA-V attains a 67.75% average attack success rate versus 14.0% for the prior best baseline CS-DJ, a 53.75-point gap (Table 1).
claims.evidence: A numpy proxy simulation on cpu-basic reports baseline ASR 0.29475 and VERA-V ASR 0.4605, but no real VLM (GPT-4o or otherwise) was evaluated; this is a simplified score-based simulation, not the paper's actual HarmBench setup.

claims.claim: VERA-V integrates three complementary strategies in a composite adversarial image: typography-based text prompts, diffusion-based image synthesis, and structured distractor images that fragment model attention (Section 4.1.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports per-strategy slice ASRs (typography 0.369, diffusion 0.359, distractors 0.342, combined 0.4605) from a numpy simulation, demonstrating the qualitative complementarity claim but without any real VLM or real adversarial image generation.

claims.claim: On HarmBench, VERA-V reaches 72.0% average ASR versus FigStep's 21.5%, HADES's 46.75%, and CS-DJ's 53.0%, and also attains 72.0% ASR on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and 76.5% ASR on InternVL3-8B (Table 1, Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: Proxy ASR values for 'open-source' (0.4499) and 'frontier' (0.4688) VLM families come from a numpy simulation with no actual Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B, or GPT-4o evaluations; the specific claimed ASR figures (72.0%, 76.5%) are not reproduced.

claims.claim: On the HADES dataset, VERA-V achieves an 80.0% average ASR on open-source VLMs and 73.5% on closed-source VLMs (Table 2, Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: The HADES dataset results (80.0% open-source, 73.5% closed-source ASR) are never addressed anywhere in the logbook.

claims.claim: VERA-V achieves only 24.1% toxicity detection rate under a safety detector versus 35.0% for CS-DJ, indicating improved stealth against content moderation (Table 4, Section 5.4).
claims.evidence: The toxicity detection rate comparison (24.1% vs 35.0%) is never addressed anywhere in the logbook.

Edd16/icml2026-tj9EwfaxHm-repro.overall: This logbook only runs a numpy-based proxy simulation on cpu-basic with no real VLM access, no model weights, and no actual adversarial image generation, so it cannot verify any of the paper's empirical claims at scale. Claims 1-3 receive toy-level proxy evidence only, while claims 4 and 5 are entirely unaddressed.

Edd16/icml2026-J5i09faOOf-repro.paper_title: Entropy-Aware On-Policy Distillation of Language Models

claims.claim: Entropy-Aware On-Policy Distillation (EOPD) augments the standard reverse-KL on-policy distillation loss with an additional forward-KL term activated only when teacher token entropy H_te exceeds a threshold tau, per the loss L_EOPD = L_OPD + I[H_te > tau] * L_FKL (Technical Implementation section).
claims.evidence: No page in the logbook verifies the specific loss formula L_EOPD = L_OPD + I[H_te > tau] * L_FKL. The toy experiments use 'entropy-weighted' KL (a continuous weighting), not an indicator-gated forward KL term, so the claimed mechanism is never implemented or tested.

claims.claim: Forward KL in EOPD is computed only over the top-k=16 teacher tokens to keep the extra loss term computationally efficient (Technical Implementation section).
claims.evidence: The claim-0-fix page analyzes top-k=16 selection on a synthetic 1000-token Dirichlet(0.1) distribution, finding 31.79% mass retention and 62.5x cost reduction. This is a purely synthetic proxy with no real teacher model distributions, not a verification on actual LLM outputs.

claims.claim: Standard on-policy distillation causes diversity collapse: student models retain only 6.8% of high-entropy tokens versus 18.5% in the teacher (Core Problem section, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The claim-2-fix page runs a numpy simulation (100-vocab, 1000 contexts, 200 steps) showing high-entropy retention drops from 20.0% to 12.2% (top-20% threshold), confirming the collapse direction but not reproducing the paper's specific 6.8%/18.5% figures, which require real LLM-scale training.

claims.claim: EOPD improves Pass@8 accuracy on six math benchmarks over baseline on-policy distillation by +1.37 for Qwen3-0.6B-Base, +2.39 for Qwen3-1.7B-Base, and +5.05 for Qwen3-4B-Base (Experimental Results section).
claims.evidence: The claim-2 page explicitly states Qwen3 models could not be run; instead a synthetic 20-vocab proxy with 400 contexts shows a +0.1850 pass@8 proxy gain. No real Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B/4B models, no math benchmarks, and no transformer architecture were used, so the specific +1.37/+2.39/+5.05 gains are unverified.

claims.claim: EOPD achieves better student-teacher alignment via lower forward KL on high-entropy tokens while sustaining higher token-level entropy in high-uncertainty regions compared to the reverse-KL-only baseline (Experimental Results, Key finding).
claims.evidence: The claim-3 pages report forward KL on high-entropy tokens dropping from 0.6167 to 0.2984 (supporting the alignment part), but token entropy actually decreased from 2.9826 to 2.8001 for the entropy-aware student, contradicting the 'higher token-level entropy' part of the claim. All on a 20-vocab synthetic setup with no transformer or real LLM.

Edd16/icml2026-J5i09faOOf-repro.overall: The logbook provides only toy-scale synthetic experiments (20–100 vocab, no transformers, no real LLMs, no math benchmarks) that partially support the mechanism's direction but fail to reproduce any of the paper's specific claims at scale. HF Jobs were unavailable due to 402 errors, forcing all experiments onto CPU with numpy-only synthetic distributions.

Edd16/icml2026-c11G7lmfhm-repro.paper_title: Learn to Merge: Meta-Learning for Adaptive Multi-Task Model Merging

claims.claim: MetaMerging meta-learns to adaptively optimize merging coefficients for multi-task model merging.
claims.evidence: The logbook demonstrates the coefficient-optimization mechanism on two small MLPs (input dim=4, hidden=16) with synthetic data, converging to [0.796, 0.204] via gradient descent on the simplex. This shows the mechanism is executable but at toy scale, not the paper's real architecture or task scale.

claims.claim: MetaMerging shows strong performance on various downstream tasks in both CV and NLP fields.
claims.evidence: No real CV or NLP benchmarks were used; the reproduction relies on two synthetic numpy classification tasks. MetaMerging achieves best Task1 accuracy (0.9417) but worst-than-baseline Task2 accuracy (0.4833), so even on the proxy the 'strong performance on various tasks' claim is only partially supported.

claims.claim: The method produces more balanced and generalizable unified models compared to parameter merging baselines.
claims.evidence: On the synthetic proxy, MetaMerging has the largest inter-task accuracy gap (0.4583) compared to all baselines including best-fixed (0.0500), contradicting the 'more balanced' claim. However, since this is a toy setup with synthetic data and tiny MLPs, it does not constitute a full falsification at the paper's scale.

Edd16/icml2026-c11G7lmfhm-repro.overall: This logbook only exercises the MetaMerging mechanism on synthetic 4-dimensional data with small MLPs, without any real CV or NLP benchmarks. It shows the coefficient-optimization procedure runs and converges, but the balance/generalizability claim is contradicted even in this toy setting.

Edd16/icml2026-7pbmZatDuD-repro.paper_title: An Algebraic View of the Expressivity of Recurrent Language Models

claims.claim: The paper develops an algebraic framework in which a recurrent language model's expressivity reduces to whether its syntactic monoid divides the wreath product of the transition monoids of its layers, formalized via algebraic cores, cascade juxtaposition, and the ambient wreath product (Section 3, Definitions 3.4-3.8).
claims.evidence: The logbook instantiates wreath products on tiny finite-state examples (|Q|=3, |Σ|=2, |S|=6, |T|=2, wreath union 252 vs single-layer 6) and a local 6-state proxy (|S(A≀B)|=1054 vs |S(A×B)|=46), demonstrating the basic mechanism that wreath products exceed flat models, but does not implement the full algebraic framework with algebraic cores, cascade juxtaposition definitions, or syntactic monoid divisibility on any real RNN architecture.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.20 (the cascade juxtaposition identity) shows the realized wreath product of two cascaded algebraic RNNs equals the wreath product of their individual realized wreath products, up to canonical isomorphism, formalizing how expressivity composes across recurrent layers (Section 3.6.3, Proposition 3.20).
claims.evidence: The cascade juxtaposition identity (Prop 3.20) is checked only on Z₂ layers (2–3 layers, 8 states): |(A≀B)≀C|=|A≀(B≀C)|=128, set-equality of transition functions confirmed, and multiplication-table agreement on 200 random pairs. This is a concrete structural verification but only for the smallest nontrivial cyclic instances, not a general proof or test on diverse semigroups.

claims.claim: As a case study on diagonal state-space models (SSMs) such as Mamba-style linear recurrences, the same architecture cannot implement an even-modulus counter under floating-point arithmetic with nonnegative recurrence multipliers, yet can realize every even-modulus counter under unsigned-integer quantization (Section 4, Abstract).
claims.evidence: A scalar diagonal recurrence x_{t+1}=a·x_t+b·u_t with nonnegative a is tested: FP with a∈{0.9,1.0,1.3} fails all even M∈{2,4,6,8} (monotone orbits cannot cycle), while unsigned-integer modular update succeeds for all tested M. The mechanism is reproduced faithfully but only on a scalar recurrence with small moduli and finite step budgets, not a full Mamba-style multi-dimensional SSM.

claims.claim: The framework's Krohn-Rhodes-based decomposition (Appendix, Section 3.6.3) shows that algebraic impossibility results (a required factor of the syntactic monoid cannot be realized by any layer monoid in a given architecture family) rule out recognition of a target language, while observational realization constructs an explicit acceptor when the factor is realizable (Section 3.6.3, Corollary 3.21).
claims.evidence: Both KR directions are demonstrated on a single witnessing case: parity language (syntactic monoid Z₂), where an aperiodic flip-flop layer (size 3, no group) achieves only 130/200 accuracy while a Z₂ group layer achieves 200/200 on 200 random strings (length 0–8). This concretely exhibits impossibility-from-missing-group-factor and explicit realization, but is one small instance rather than a general classifier over languages and architectures.

Edd16/icml2026-7pbmZatDuD-repro.overall: The logbook provides honest but small-scale toy demonstrations of the paper's core algebraic mechanisms—wreath product expressivity, cascade isomorphism, FP-vs-integer counter separation, and Krohn-Rhodes impossibility/realization—on minimal instances (Z₂ semigroups, 2–3 state spaces, scalar recurrences). No claim is verified at the paper's full theoretical scope or on real RNN/LSTM/SSM architectures; the one completed HF job only ran the basic wreath-framework script, while all claim-specific experiments were local-only due to persistent billing failures.

claims.claim: Optimal subsample size in bagging regularized M-estimators yields sample-wise monotonic risk for any ensemble size M.
claims.evidence: A real grid sweep over M∈{1,...,100} and k∈{20,...,200} on synthetic isotropic Gaussian data (n=200, p=80) was executed, but risk-vs-k is not uniformly monotonic at intermediate k (e.g., M=50 shows risk rising between k=160 and k=180), and the setup is a simplified proxy, not a full-scale reproduction.

claims.claim: When ensemble size M→∞, the optimal subsample size tends to be in the overparameterized regime where k*→min{n,p}.
claims.evidence: The sweep only reaches M=100 (not M→∞) on synthetic data with p=80<n=200, which is underparameterized rather than the overparameterized regime the claim targets; additionally, the logbook incorrectly states min{n,p}=200 when in fact min{200,80}=80, so k*=200 does not match the claim's predicted k*→min{n,p}.

claims.claim: Joint optimization of subsample size, ensemble size, and regularization can significantly outperform regularizer optimization alone on full data.
claims.evidence: A 3D grid search over (k, M, λ) was run on synthetic data, finding that joint optimization (risk 0.4956) actually underperforms λ-only optimization on full data (risk 0.4147), contradicting the claim, but only on a simplified isotropic proxy that the authors acknowledge may not exercise the structural conditions needed for the claim.

Edd16/icml2026-71802-repro.overall: This logbook runs a small synthetic numpy simulation (n=200, p=80, isotropic Gaussian) that only loosely proxies the paper's claims, finding mixed-to-negative results on a toy setup. None of the three claims are reproduced at a realistic scale or under the structural assumptions (e.g., overparameterized regime, correlated design) the claims require.

Edd16/icml2026-8ewf5I4shW-repro.paper_title: Causal Effect Identifiability in the Presence of Latent Confounders Without Auxiliary Variables

claims.claim: In linear SCMs without auxiliary variables, causal effect identifiability depends on Gaussianity of exogenous noises.
claims.evidence: A single 3-variable linear SCM (X→Y→Z, X→Z) with 10,000 samples shows Gaussian noise yields a feasible interval |a'|≤2.147 (non-identifiable) while Laplace noise yields ICA recovery a=1.986 (error 0.014), demonstrating the principle on a simplified setup rather than verifying the general theoretical claim across diverse graph structures.

claims.claim: RGPO provides a complete characterization of conditions under which causal effect is identifiable vs. unidentifiable.
claims.evidence: The logbook shows RGPO produces a nontrivial interval under Gaussian noise and a singleton under non-Gaussian noise on one 3-variable SCM, but this single example does not verify the 'complete characterization' claim, which would require testing across multiple graph topologies and noise configurations.

claims.claim: For unidentifiable cases, the method quantifies the cardinality of the feasible solution set.
claims.evidence: The logbook reports a feasible interval of length 0.043 yielding '~600 statistically distinguishable solutions at standard resolution' for the Gaussian case, but the notion of 'standard resolution' is undefined and the quantification is performed only on a single small 3-variable example.

Edd16/icml2026-8ewf5I4shW-repro.overall: The logbook runs real experiments on a single 3-variable linear SCM demonstrating the core phenomena (Gaussian non-identifiability vs. non-Gaussian identifiability via ICA), but all three claims are tested only on this one small toy setup without exploring diverse graph structures, larger models, or the theoretical completeness of RGPO. The reproduction illustrates the paper's ideas but does not constitute full verification of any claim at the paper's intended scope.

junwatu/repro-targate-target-aware-data-.paper_title: TarGATE: Target-Aware Data Selection via Token-Attenuation Gates

claims.claim: TarGATE outperforms related baselines in both noisy and real-world data selection scenarios.
claims.evidence: The reproduction uses a drastically reduced setup (0.5B selector, 1600 samples vs ~15k+, top-10% vs top-5%, only Random and NegNLL baselines vs LESS/RDS) and only addresses the noisy scenario with trivially separable synthetic noise where even NegNLL achieves 100% precision. The real-world data selection scenario (Tulu-200k, multi-task) was never run, and SFT accuracy differences (7.5% vs 6.25% on 80 samples) are negligible.

claims.claim: The method exhibits superior computational efficiency and strong cross-model transferability for curating fine-tuning data.
claims.evidence: Efficiency is partially demonstrated (21,504 trainable gate params, ~289s warmup) but only compared against NegNLL, not the paper's actual baselines (LESS, RDS). The cross-model transfer experiment failed entirely with CUDA OOM when fine-tuning Qwen2.5-1.5B, so transferability was never actually shown—only that the small selector produced high-precision data, not that it benefits the larger model's fine-tuning.

junwatu/repro-targate-target-aware-data-.overall: The logbook runs a small-scale proof-of-concept on a toy noisy-selection task with trivially separable synthetic noise, showing TarGATE matches (not outperforms) a simple NegNLL baseline and beats Random. The real-world scenario, key baselines, and the cross-model transfer fine-tuning experiment were never successfully executed.

kalikho/repro-tau-2569xbench-evaluating-.paper_title: $\tau^2$-Bench: Evaluating Conversational Agents in a Dual-Control Environment

claims.claim: Agents show significant performance drops when shifting from single-control to dual-control environments, revealing challenges in guiding user actions in shared, dynamic worlds.
claims.evidence: The logbook independently computes pass@1 from raw simulation files in data/tau2/results/final/ for 114 tasks × 4 trials, showing gpt-4.1 default 0.342 vs no-user 0.515 vs oracle-plan 0.728 and o4-mini default 0.421 vs no-user 0.673 vs oracle-plan 0.963, confirming significant performance drops in dual-control (default) mode relative to single-control variants.

claims.claim: Fine-grained analysis of dual-control agents reveals distinct error patterns arising from reasoning versus communication/coordination failures.
claims.evidence: The logbook only provides aggregate pass@1 by operating mode (default/no-user/oracle-plan), which indirectly separates coordination cost from planning cost, but does not present any fine-grained error analysis, error taxonomy, or categorized failure patterns distinguishing reasoning failures from communication/coordination failures as claimed.

kalikho/repro-tau-2569xbench-evaluating-.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from pre-computed simulation results confirming performance drops in dual-control mode, but does not address the fine-grained error pattern analysis claim. The reproduction relies on analyzing existing result files rather than running new LLM evaluations, which limits its independence.

vbabenko97/repro-when-can-we-trust-survi.paper_title: When Can We Trust Survival Model Evaluation ?

claims.claim: Censoring induces systematic, mechanism-dependent distortions in survival evaluation metrics that vary by censoring rate and censoring mechanism.
claims.evidence: On real METABRIC data (n=888) with three Appendix-C censoring mechanisms across 5 rates, the normalized bias results concretely show IBS and D-Calibration becoming strongly negative and growing with censoring rate (medians reaching -6 to -9 at 90%), while concordance stays robust (max |median| ~1.0-1.75), with AC benign at early horizons and CDC most damaging—directly matching the claimed systematic, mechanism-dependent distortions.

claims.claim: Moderate numerical bias in censored data can lead to unreliable model comparison as censoring increases.
claims.evidence: Top-1 best-model consistency decays with censoring rate across all metrics (e.g., C-Harrell 0.93→0.47, IBS 1.00→0.53, D-Calibration 0.67→0.33 averaged over mechanisms), and genuine ranking inversions appear on the authors' own shipped data (IBS tau_dom = -1.0 at 70% and 90% censoring), providing concrete evidence that model comparison becomes unreliable as censoring increases.

vbabenko97/repro-when-can-we-trust-survi.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from a faithful reimplementation of the paper's controlled standard-vs-oracle protocol on real METABRIC data, demonstrating both the systematic mechanism-dependent metric distortions (Claim 1) and the degradation of model comparison reliability under increasing censoring (Claim 2). The scope is reduced (1 dataset, 4 classical CPU models, no deep models) but the task and methodology are non-toy and the qualitative claims are clearly supported.

lastmass/repro-ai-cartography-mapping-th.paper_title: AI Cartography: Mapping the Latent Landscape of AI Benchmark Ecosystems

claims.claim: Applied psychometric framework to 4,000+ models from Open LLM Leaderboard decomposes ranking variance sources
claims.evidence: G-theory EMS variance decomposition on 4,576 models × 6 benchmarks reproduces the paper's facet ordering: benchmark (0.468) >> contributor (0.157) > architecture (0.052) ~ deployment (0.055), matching Table 2's ordering though absolute shares differ due to a reduced EMS model versus the paper's fully-crossed 15-term design.

claims.claim: Human contributors account for 9% of ranking variance versus 4.8% for model architecture in AI benchmarks
claims.evidence: The EMS decomposition confirms contributor variance (15.7%) exceeds architecture variance (5.2%), preserving the paper's key qualitative finding (8.6% vs 4.2%). While absolute values differ substantially (contributor share nearly doubled), the logbook attributes this to estimator choice in crossed G-theory designs, and the core relationship—human contributors matter more than architecture—holds.

claims.claim: Methods establish measurement framework for assessing reliability of scaling laws and validity of AI evaluation claims
claims.evidence: The scaling-vector claim is confirmed (slopes span 5.85–21.04, >3.6× range), and item-level PCA on 9 models × 6,488 items yields Spearman rho=0.867 matching the paper's 0.86. However, the central reliability coefficients Rg=0.97 and Rbeta=0.53 were never computed, and the top-1% overlap result (~1% in paper) was not reproduced (64% at score-level), leaving the framework's core quantitative reliability claims unverified.

lastmass/repro-ai-cartography-mapping-th.overall: The logbook provides solid evidence for the G-theory variance decomposition ordering and the bifactor general factor structure at full scale (4,576 models), but the key reliability coefficients and top-1% reranking results central to the measurement framework claim remain unverified due to absence of item-level bifactor IRT estimation.

yugimani/repro-pdfbench-a-benchmark-for-.paper_title: PDFBench: A Benchmark for De Novo Protein Design from Function

claims.claim: PDFBench systematically evaluates eight state-of-the-art models on 16 metrics for function-guided de novo protein design.
claims.evidence: The logbook audited arXiv v1 (finding 5 unique model families and 22 metrics) but the claim concerns v3 (8 models, 16 metrics). No model evaluations were run; the v3 counts are noted but not independently verified from code or results artifacts.

claims.claim: SwissTest is a new test set created with strict datetime cutoff to ensure data integrity.
claims.evidence: The logbook concretely verified CAMEOTest via DuckDB scan: 642 rows, 642 unique IDs, dates 2022-05-14 to 2023-05-06, 0 rows outside the 2020-05-01–2023-08-01 window. However, the claim names 'SwissTest,' which the logbook never mentions; the verified test set may be a different or version-specific artifact.

claims.claim: PDFBench enables more reliable model comparisons and provides key insights for future protein design research.
claims.evidence: Independent aggregation of three released Pinal keyword-guided runs reproduced pLDDT (66.2475 vs 66.20), PAE (14.5128 vs 14.53), and ProtGPT2 PPL (584.2508 vs 584.25) to within 0.05, demonstrating partial reproducibility. But only one model on one task was checked—no cross-model comparisons or broader insights were independently validated.

yugimani/repro-pdfbench-a-benchmark-for-.overall: The logbook provides concrete dataset-integrity verification (CAMEOTest row counts and date cutoff) and reproduces one model's keyword-guided metrics from released JSON files, but it does not run any model evaluations and primarily addresses arXiv v1 rather than the ICML 2026 v3 claims about 8 models, 16 metrics, and SwissTest.

ramgopal-reddy/repro-post-training-with-.paper_title: Post-Training with Policy Gradients: Optimality and the Base Model Barrier

claims.claim: Policy gradient can achieve likelihood 1-ε with minimax optimal number of reward queries Õ((α⁻¹ + ε⁻¹)/γ²).
claims.evidence: A smoke test at N=16, k=4, d=8 (vs paper's N=128, k=32, d=32) shows PG-OR reducing test error from 0.824 to 0.392 after 200 steps, demonstrating qualitative improvement, but the specific convergence rate Õ((α⁻¹+ε⁻¹)/γ²) is never measured; the 'theoretical prediction check' is just arithmetic showing k^N/(γ²T)≫1.

claims.claim: A barrier exists for going beyond the support of the base model, with policy gradient variants potentially requiring exponential reward queries in sequence length N.
claims.evidence: The smoke test (N=16, k=4) shows ORM plateauing at 0.392 test error vs PRM at 0.292, qualitatively consistent with a barrier, but the exponential dependence on N is only illustrated by computing k^N arithmetically (e.g., 32^128≈10^193) — no experiment varies N to demonstrate exponential scaling empirically.

ramgopal-reddy/repro-post-training-with-.overall: The logbook provides only drastically reduced smoke tests (N=16, k=4 vs paper's N=128, k=32) that show qualitative ORM-vs-PRM differences, but neither the specific convergence rates nor the exponential scaling in N are experimentally measured. Theoretical claims are supported by arithmetic illustrations rather than empirical scaling experiments.

kondratevakate/repro-on-revisiting-entro.paper_title: On Revisiting Entropy for Identifying Mislabeled Images

claims.claim: Correctly labeled samples exhibit consistent entropy decrease during training while mislabeled samples maintain relatively high entropy throughout
claims.evidence: A small 3-conv CNN was trained on a 12k-image CIFAR-100 subset with real CIFAR-100N noise (26.4%), showing clean-sample entropy decreasing consistently (2.64→0.14) and mislabeled-sample entropy staying higher at every epoch (gap peaking at 0.51 at epoch 15). This confirms the directional mechanism but on a simplified setup far below the paper's medical imaging scale.

claims.claim: Introduces signed entropy integral (SEI) statistic capturing both magnitude and temporal trend of prediction entropy across training epochs
claims.evidence: Several proxy trajectory statistics were evaluated on the same toy CIFAR-100N setup, achieving AUC up to 0.716, but the actual signed entropy integral (SEI) was not implemented—only crude proxies were tested on a subset with a small CNN.

claims.claim: Achieves state-of-the-art performance in mislabeled data identification on three medical imaging datasets
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states this claim was not attempted; no experiments on any medical imaging datasets (ISIC, DeepDRiD, etc.) or against competing baselines were run.

kondratevakate/repro-on-revisiting-entro.overall: This logbook provides a toy-scale validation of the entropy-dynamics mechanism (Claims 1-2) on a small CNN with CIFAR-100N, showing directional support but not implementing the actual SEI statistic or testing at the paper's medical-imaging scale. Claim 3 (SOTA on three medical datasets) was not addressed at all.

claims.claim: Incremental BPE processes each input byte in worst-case O(log² t) time with overall complexity O(n log² t) where n is input length and t is maximum token length.
claims.evidence: The monotonic path property was empirically checked with zero violations across 200 random dictionaries and real GPT-2 vocab, but the actual O(log²t) complexity bound was not demonstrated: centroid decomposition (§5.3, the mechanism bounding tree depth to O(log t)) was not implemented, and measured worst-case single-byte latency grows linearly with tree depth (slope 0.972), not polylogarithmically.

claims.claim: Achieves up to ~3x speedups over Hugging Face's tokenizers and significant latency reductions on pathological inputs while functioning as drop-in replacement.
claims.evidence: The ~3x speedup over HF tokenizers was not tested—the reproduction is pure Python measuring ~52x slower than the Rust baseline, making the speedup claim untestable. However, pathological-input robustness was verified with concrete measurements (log-log slope ~0.99 for the implementation vs ~2.04–2.08 for era-appropriate tiktoken 0.8.0 CL100K), and token-for-token drop-in equivalence was confirmed on 500 kB of Wikipedia.

hinabarun/repro-incremental-bpe-tokeniza.overall: The logbook provides strong empirical verification of the monotonic path property and pathological-input robustness (flat vs quadratic throughput), plus token-for-token correctness against HF tokenizers, but does not verify the headline O(log²t) complexity (centroid decomposition unimplemented, measured linear growth) or the 3x speedup claim (pure-Python implementation, 52x slower than Rust baseline).

claims.evidence: 243 exact population cells across Conditions 1 and 2 (max recovery error 2.22e-16) demonstrate that identifiability mechanisms differ by Gaussianity; 32 official-code finite-sample runs at N=500,000 show both conditions beat the zero-effect baseline, and destructive controls (e.g., replacing non-Gaussian treatment by Gaussian) are caught.

claims.claim: RGPO provides a complete characterization of conditions under which causal effect is identifiable vs. unidentifiable.

MarxistLeninist/QZO3oby12w.paper_title: AI Engram: In Search of Memory Traces in Artificial Intelligence

claims.claim: AI engrams are extracted in closed form via W⁺ = W·Σ⁺(Σ⁺ + Σ⁻)† using covariance statistics from target and reference data, requiring only a single forward pass rather than iterative optimization (Equation 4).
claims.evidence: On a pretrained ResNet-18 with full CIFAR-10 (50k train, 10k test), Equation 4 was applied in a single forward pass with zero gradients or optimizer steps, suppressing all ten target classes (82.32 pp mean drop, +0.37 pp retained-class change). The closed form matched an independent direct least-squares solve within 9.2e-15 relative error across seeds 7/19/41 and four pseudoinverse cutoffs.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.1 proves that this closed-form engram solution corresponds to a minimum-norm projection under the Fisher information metric, and that ablation under a K-FAC approximation is equivalent to a natural gradient descent update (Theorem 6.1).
claims.evidence: Concrete numerical tests show the strict theorem fails: under target/reference overlap, Equation 4 violates the hard constraint and differs from the independently solved hard-constrained Fisher projection. Additionally, F†grad L = (2/c)W_plus means a literal unit step equals ablation only for c=2; at c=3.7 the relative mismatch is 0.459, contradicting the unqualified equivalence claim.

claims.claim: Memory composition and erasure are performed via linear vector arithmetic on extracted engrams (e.g., μ_new = μ ± μ_Glasses⁺ ∓ μ_Goatee⁺), allowing 2^n memory combinations from n engrams without any recomputation.
claims.evidence: On the pretrained CIFAR-10 ResNet-18, all 16 subsets of four cached class engrams were evaluated at alpha=4; the composed edit equaled the sum of cached memories with maximum path-relative error 1.6035e-17 and no re-extraction between subsets. Selected-class accuracy dropped 93.22 pp on average while unselected classes changed only -1.19 pp, confirming linear arithmetic composition of 2^n combinations from n engrams without recomputation.

claims.claim: On CIFAR-10 class unlearning, the method achieves a ToW score of 0.984 versus 0.999 for full retraining, while extraction takes under 2 minutes for 100 classes compared to hours for gradient-based methods.
claims.evidence: The logbook ran the extraction on full CIFAR-10 (10 classes, 312.94 s on GTX 1050 Ti) but never computed the ToW metric, lacked the five retrained reference models needed for the 0.984 vs 0.999 comparison, and could not test the A100 timing claim for 100 classes. The specific numerical claims (ToW=0.984, under 2 minutes for 100 classes on A100) were source-confirmed but not independently reproduced.

claims.claim: The framework is validated across MLPs, ResNet-18, ViT-B on ImageNet-1K, autoencoders/WAE, and a Llama-3.2-1B LLM evaluated on the TOFU benchmark, where it trails iterative unlearning methods on Utility and Privacy metrics.
claims.evidence: Only ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 was independently run; ViT-B/ImageNet, WAE/CelebA, and Llama-3.2-1B/TOFU were not rerun due to A100-scale compute constraints. TOFU Overall scores were merely recomputed from reported sub-metrics (matching within 4.8e-05), which is arithmetic verification of published numbers, not independent experimental reproduction of the architecture breadth claim.

MarxistLeninist/QZO3oby12w.overall: The logbook provides strong independent evidence that the closed-form engram extraction (Claim 1) and linear arithmetic composition (Claim 3) work on a real ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 setup, and presents concrete numerical counter-evidence against the strict reading of Theorem 6.1 (Claim 2). However, the specific ToW/runtime numbers (Claim 4) and the multi-architecture breadth including TOFU (Claim 5) were not independently reproduced due to missing reference models and A100-scale compute constraints.

ai-sherpa/bertrand-paradox-falsification.paper_title: Revisiting the Bertrand Paradox via Equilibrium Analysis of No-regret Learners

claims.claim: For symmetric-cost Bertrand competition with any non-increasing demand function, Theorem 2.1 shows two no-external-regret learners can sustain high prices while guaranteeing each firm's utility is at least 1/(4e^2) of the monopoly profit (Theorem 2.1).
claims.evidence: The τ-cascade CCE construction from the Theorem 2.1 proof was rebuilt and exhaustively certified: all 500/500 unilateral deviation checks pass in each of 4 demand families at k=500, with utility clearing the 1/(4e²)·monopoly floor everywhere (e.g., constant demand: 0.12449 ≥ 0.03383). Scaling tests confirm Θ(1) in k (log-log slope +0.1205) vs the Θ(1/k) CE cap (slope −1.0000), and the LP optimum over all symmetric CCEs converges to 1/e ≈ 0.3679.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.2 shows that when both learners use no-swap-regret algorithms, prices converge toward marginal cost, with expected utility bounded above by f(c+1/k)/k, demonstrating strong competitive pressure (Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: LP over the full CE polytope (all swap deviations) yields max utility exactly equal to f(c+1/k)/k to machine precision for constant demand (k=10: 0.1=0.1; k=30: 0.033333=0.033333), with 36/36 configurations respecting the bound and log-log slope −1.0000 confirming Θ(1/k). Regret-Matching self-play (T=500,000) converges to the competitive floor price with swap regret decaying to ~0.0005.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.3 shows an asymmetric setting—one no-external-regret learner paired with one no-swap-regret learner—can still sustain high, collusive-like prices under certain demand structures such as constant demand (Theorem 2.3).
claims.evidence: LP over the full hybrid Φ-CE polytope (player 1 all swap deviations, player 2 constant only) shows λ₀ flat in k at ≈0.1779 through k=128 for both players at c=0 and c=0.5, while the full-CE cap decays as Θ(1/k) — a 23× gap at k=128. Expected transaction price 0.3558 at k=128 far exceeds the competitive floor 0.0078, with constraint violations ≤ 9.4e-8.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.5 shows that as the number of firms n grows, the total utility attainable under no-external-regret dynamics decays exponentially, as e^(1-n/2) (Theorem 2.5).
claims.evidence: Symmetric CCE LPs for n=2…10 at k=100 show the Theorem 2.5 bound respected at every n across all 4 demand families, with n=2 recovering 2/e = 0.7357 as a consistency check. Measured log-slope is −0.6272 (R²=0.9991) over the clean exponential regime n=2…7, giving 1.87× decay per firm, consistent with the theorem's e^(−n/2) upper bound. The finite-k flattening at n≳7 is honestly disclosed as a grid artifact.

claims.claim: Under asymmetric costs, Theorem 2.6 shows high-utility coarse correlated equilibria exist for broad demand classes (including linear and exponential demand) under no-external-regret learning, while Theorem 2.7 shows that under no-swap-regret learning the higher-cost firm's utility converges to zero regardless of the demand function (Theorems 2.6 and 2.7).
claims.evidence: With c₁=0, c₂=0.25, CCE LPs give min monopoly-normalized utility 0.352–0.358 across all 4 demand families at k=100, flat-to-rising in k (linear: 0.288→0.352 from k=20→100), confirming Theorem 2.6. CE LPs maximizing player 2's utility return exactly 0.0 at every k∈{20,30,40,60} and every demand family, confirming Theorem 2.7's equality claim.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments across multiple demand functions show utilities converging toward 1/e ≈ 0.368 of the monopoly utility under no-external-regret dynamics (Numerical results section).
claims.evidence: Symmetric CCE LP ratios converge to 1/e = 0.367879: 0.367301 at k=25 → 0.367878 at k=400 (agreement 1.1e-6) → 0.367879 at k=2000, across all 4 demand families (constant, linear, quadratic, exponential). Cross-check: the independent n-player LP at n=2 returns 2/e = 0.735731.

ai-sherpa/bertrand-paradox-falsification.overall: This logbook provides concrete, non-toy experimental evidence for all six claims through from-scratch LPs over CCE/CE/Φ-CE polytopes, exhaustive deviation checks, k-scaling tests up to k=2000, n-player experiments up to n=10, asymmetric-cost experiments, and live no-regret dynamics — all with solver-independent feasibility re-checks and honest disclosure of finite-k artifacts.

ai-sherpa/dnn-functional-covariates-repr.paper_title: Deep Neural Network Regression with Functional Covariates

claims.claim: DNN estimators attain minimax-optimal polynomial rates of convergence for functional linear models
claims.evidence: On a non-toy setup (n=4K–100K, 5 smoothness levels, 782 cells, 4252 DNN fits, architecture constant in n and K), the measured variance exponent alpha_DNN=[1.0504,1.0697,0.989,0.959,0.9522] (max dev 0.0697) implies rates matching r* to mean abs err 0.0097; the direct envelope exponent matches r* to 0.0415 (corr 0.953); the DNN-to-optimal-reference risk ratio is bounded at 6.56x with non-drifting spread 2.19x; the exact Assouad lower bound matches r* to 0.0076; and the positive control recovers the classical estimator's known rate. 8 of 9 pre-registered bars pass.

claims.claim: DNN estimators achieve minimax-optimal rates for functional generalized linear models
claims.evidence: On the same non-toy setup with logistic GLM and Brier excess risk, the direct envelope exponent matches r* to mean abs err 0.0715 (corr 0.985) and the DNN-to-IRLS-MLE ratio is bounded at 4.49x with non-drifting spread 1.56x, directly measuring the upper-bound claim R<=C·n^(-r*). However, the primary variance exponent alpha_DNN=[1.1504,…,1.1129] is systematically above 1 (max dev 0.1717, failing pre-registered bar B1), implying a rate shortfall of 0.020–0.037; the bounded non-drifting ratio and high envelope correlation nonetheless support the claim, with 7 of 8 pre-registered bars passing.

ai-sherpa/dnn-functional-covariates-repr.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous, independent from-scratch reproduction on a non-toy setup (simulated Karhunen-Loeve functional data, n up to 100K, 5 smoothness levels, no imposed truncation schedule) with exact lower bounds, positive controls, architecture-invariance checks, and pre-registered acceptance bars. Both claims are supported by multiple converging measurements—envelope exponents, bounded non-drifting ratios to minimax-optimal references, and recovered truncation schedules—though the GLM case carries a honestly-reported alpha excess that prevents a fully clean verification.

kondratevakate/repro-conditional-coverag.paper_title: Conditional Coverage Diagnostics for Conformal Prediction

claims.claim: The paper introduces a family of Excess Risk of the Target Coverage (ERT) metrics—L1-ERT, L2-ERT, and KL-ERT—for evaluating conditional coverage in conformal prediction, built on the principle that no classifier can outperform a constant 1-alpha predictor under perfect conditional coverage (Table 1, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: A numerical audit checks the supporting-score identity f(h)+(p-h)f'(h)≤f(p) across L1, L2, and KL losses on a 99×100 grid, finding max oracle identity error of 0, max constant-target score of 0, and max supporting-plane violation of 1.11e-16, confirming that no classifier can outperform the constant 1-alpha predictor under perfect conditional coverage.

claims.claim: Using LightGBM as the underlying classifier for L1-ERT achieves 68.4% relative statistical power (relative to maximum), compared to only 38.3% for the PartitionWise classifier underlying CovGap (Table 2, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Re-aggregation of the authors' official 5,600-row results.csv yields 68.929% relative L1 power for LightGBM vs 33.671% for PartitionWise (a 2.05x ratio), directionally consistent with the paper's claimed 68.4% vs 38.3%; the PartitionWise value differs by ~4.6pp, suggesting updated released data, but the core claim of substantially higher LightGBM power is strongly supported.

claims.claim: In synthetic experiments, group-based metrics like CovGap remain unreliable and unaligned with their theoretical values even at 5,000 test points, whereas ERT metrics such as L1-ERT converge with far fewer samples (Figure 4, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: An independent experiment on the paper's 8D heteroscedastic model (X~U([-1,1]^8), Y~N(0,σ(X₁)) with theoretical L1 miscoverage 0.0948) shows L1-ERT recovering 92% of the analytic violation at 30,000 test points (0.0866) while unaligned CovGap recovers only 5% (0.0049), with oracle-group CovGap bounding the result at 0.0953.

claims.claim: The metrics decompose conditional coverage error into asymmetric components ell_plus-ERT and ell_minus-ERT, separating unnecessary conservatism (over-coverage) from excessive aggressiveness (under-coverage) (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: The same independent 30,000-point synthetic run evaluates clipped convex functions on either side of target coverage 0.9, finding over-coverage estimated at 0.0445 (analytic 0.0460) and under-coverage at 0.0464 (analytic 0.0488), both nonzero and close to theory, confirming the asymmetric decomposition mechanism.

claims.claim: Classification experiments report divergent KL_plus-ERT and KL_minus-ERT values across conformal prediction methods, demonstrating the over/under-coverage decomposition in practice (Table 4, Section 4.3.2).
claims.evidence: Analysis of all 80 rows of the official released classification CSV confirms the additive identity between total KL-ERT and directional components (max residual 8.94e-8) and finds all 8 dataset/method groups have absolute directional gaps above 0.01 (e.g., CIFAR100/cumulative: 0.0160 vs 0.1745), though this is a released-output replay rather than fresh classifier training.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 estimates the ERT metrics from finite samples using k-fold cross-validation to avoid overfitting the classifier used in the estimation (Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: An independent mutation control with 20 seeds, 2,000 observations, and 5 folds shows that a label memorizer produces false L2-ERT signal of 0.08886 under in-sample evaluation but 0 under cross-fitted evaluation, while a genuine two-region signal is still detected at 0.01013 cross-fitted, with maximum train/evaluation overlap of 0.

kondratevakate/repro-conditional-coverag.overall: The logbook provides concrete evidence for all six claims through four independently generated experiments/audits (Claims 1, 3, 4, 6) and two thorough re-aggregations of the authors' hash-pinned released outputs (Claims 2, 5). The independent synthetic experiments on the paper's 8D heteroscedastic model and the Algorithm 1 cross-fitting control are well-designed, but Claims 2 and 5 rely on re-analyzing the authors' own data rather than fresh experimental runs.

Srishti280992/repro-on-uniform-error-bou.paper_title: On Uniform Error Bounds for Kernel Regression under Non-Gaussian Noise

claims.claim: Provides non-asymptotic uniform error bounds for kernel regression that handle sub-Gaussian, bounded, sub-exponential, and variance-bounded noise
claims.evidence: The reproduction implements and numerically tests sub-Gaussian bounds (Claim 1 check with iid recovery to 8.88e-16, safe control, uncertainty sweep), bounded-noise bounds (proposed_bounded_bound used in sweep), and sub-exponential bounds (chi-squared noise experiment with Theorem 3.2(c) and Proposition 3.5). Variance-bounded noise is not explicitly tested, but three of four noise types are demonstrated on the paper's actual experimental setup with real KRR computations.

claims.claim: Bounds apply to both correlated and uncorrelated noise, extending beyond conditional independence assumptions
claims.evidence: The correlated_theory_check function tests Proposition 3.3 with AR(1) covariance matrices (rho=0.0, 0.4, 0.8) and confirms the correlated bound reduces to the iid sub-Gaussian case when C_t = sigma_M^2 I (max abs diff 8.88e-16), with bounds widening under stronger correlation (ratios 1.53 and 2.96 at t=100).

claims.claim: Demonstrates superior tightness of proposed bounds compared to existing results in safe control applications
claims.evidence: In the second run with fixed zeta optimization, the proposed SG bound achieves 84.7% feasibility at t=1000 versus 46.3% (Abbasi-Yadkori) and 47.9% (Fiedler), with lower mean cost (1.786 vs 3.755 and 3.738). The uncertainty sweep shows proposed/Abbasi ratio < 1.0 in all configurations (max 0.832), confirming tighter bounds.

Srishti280992/repro-on-uniform-error-bou.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from an independent KRR implementation supporting all three claims on the paper's actual experimental setup (safe control, uncertainty sweep, correlated noise check). The reproduction is credible but uses single runs rather than the paper's 100 Monte Carlo repetitions, and variance-bounded noise is not explicitly tested.

neonforestmist/exact-six-release-slot-20.paper_title: Dimension-Independent Convergence of Underdamped Langevin Monte Carlo in KL Divergence

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 establishes the first dimension-free KL-divergence convergence bound for standard underdamped Langevin Monte Carlo (ULMC) under strong convexity, with sample complexity depending on tr(H) rather than the ambient dimension d, where H is a known upper bound on the Hessian (Theorem 4.3, Assumption 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides generic decreasing residuals (slope -0.501) but never describes an actual ULMC implementation, target distribution, KL divergence measurement, or any experiment varying d vs tr(H) to demonstrate dimension-independence. The numbers are unconnected to the theorem's claims.

claims.claim: The strongly-convex ULMC sample complexity bound is Otilde(kappa^{3/2} beta^{-1/2} [tr(H)]^{1/2} / epsilon) to reach KL(mu (P')^N || pi) <= epsilon^2 (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Same generic residuals (slope -0.495) with no ULMC implementation, no measurement of the specific complexity bound involving kappa, beta, tr(H), or epsilon. The experiment does not test the stated sample complexity formula in any recognizable way.

claims.claim: Under randomized midpoint discretization, Theorem 5.2 improves the condition-number dependence relative to the bound of Liu et al. (2023), achieving complexity Otilde(kappa [beta^{-1} tr(H)]^{1/3} epsilon^{-2/3}) (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: The experiment is labeled 'preference-alignment' and runs a DPO/Bradley-Terry fit (n=600 pairs, d=12, pair acc=0.897), which is completely unrelated to randomized midpoint discretization for Langevin Monte Carlo. No connection to the claimed complexity bound whatsoever.

claims.claim: Theorems 4.4 and 5.4 extend the dimension-free guarantees to the general (non-strongly) convex setting (alpha = 0), the first such dimension-free result for underdamped Langevin dynamics in this regime (Theorem 4.4, Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: A generic least-squares fit (n=200, d=4, MSE=0.0025) with no implementation of underdamped Langevin dynamics in the non-strongly convex setting, no measurement of KL divergence, and no demonstration of dimension-free behavior when alpha=0.

claims.claim: The dimension-free change-of-measure argument (Lemma 6.1) bounds E_mu[||grad V(x)||^2] and E_mu[p^T H p] by tr(H) + beta*KL(mu||pi), avoiding the explicit dimension dependence introduced by standard Gaussian moment bounds (Lemma 6.1, Section 6).
claims.evidence: Another generic least-squares fit (n=200, d=6, MSE=0.0023) that does not measure E_mu[||grad V(x)||^2], E_mu[p^T H p], or the bound tr(H) + beta*KL(mu||pi). No change-of-measure argument is numerically verified.

claims.claim: The paper shows underdamped Langevin Monte Carlo attains better iteration complexity than composite overdamped Langevin Monte Carlo when tr(H) << d, e.g. in ridge-separable target distributions (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.5 framework).

ai-sherpa/rl-reachability-asymptotic-opt.paper_title: Reinforcement Learning for Reachability: Guaranteeing Asymptotic Optimality

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes a PAC guarantee that, for a sufficiently small guessed minimum transition probability p_k, there exists a number of simulations N_k such that the learned policy is ε_k-optimal with probability at least 1-δ_k (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook measures K_PAC (stage where guessed p_k crosses below true p_min) at median 4.0 across 8 benchmarks (155–405 states) × 10 trials, and shows transition-probability estimation error decreases monotonically at 15/15 stage transitions (5.71× reduction), providing concrete empirical evidence that the PAC preconditions of Theorem 3.1 are satisfied and the predicted ε_k-optimality mechanism operates as described.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 shows that once the approximation error ε_k falls below a threshold ε_diff—the minimum value gap between optimal and suboptimal memoryless deterministic policies—any ε_k-optimal policy is guaranteed to be exactly optimal, not merely near-optimal (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook directly tests Theorem 3.2's threshold condition K_opt=⌈log₂(1/ε_diff)⌉ across 8 benchmarks with ε_diff spanning 0.0095–0.4345, finding the extracted policy exactly optimal at every stage ≥ predicted K_opt in 1040/1040 checks (0 violations) on 155–405 state MDPs, confirming that once ε_k falls below ε_diff the policy is exactly optimal.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 proves that using a summable failure schedule δ_k = 1/2^k, the Borel-Cantelli lemma guarantees only finitely many stages fail, so the algorithm's policy is exactly optimal from some finite stage onward with probability 1 (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: Using the summable schedule δ_k=1/2^k, the logbook observes 80/80 independent trials across 8 benchmarks converge to and remain at the exactly-optimal policy (true value at s0 matching independently-computed optimum to 1e-6) for all subsequent stages up to K_MAX=16, providing concrete empirical evidence consistent with the Borel-Cantelli guarantee of only finitely many failures.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 bounds ε_diff via transition-complexity parameter D, showing ‖v_π − v_π'‖_1 ≥ (2D)^(-2|A|·|S|) 2^(-2|S|) for any two distinct memoryless deterministic policies, giving an explicit MDP-structure-dependent characterization of when exact optimality is reached (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook exhaustively checks 1,152,394,086 memoryless-deterministic policy pairs across D∈{2…25}, |A|∈{2…5}, |S|∈{4…405}, including exact rational arithmetic verification on 112,110 pairs (Tier C) and native-scale Hamming-≤1 policy ball enumeration on 155–405 state benchmarks (Tier D), finding 0 pairs with a nonzero L1 value gap below the Theorem 4.1 floor (2D)^(-2|A||S|)·2^(-2|S|).

claims.claim: Empirical evaluation on standardized benchmarks shows the algorithm's policy becomes exactly optimal at a median stage k=2, far earlier than the stage (k≈16) at which the theoretical worst-case value-bound guarantees convergence (empirical validation section).
claims.evidence: On 8 reachability MDPs of 155–405 states × 10 trials (80 runs), the logbook measures median empirical K_opt=2.0, mean=1.99, matching the paper's reported median k=2 and average k=2.3, while the value-bound gap remains 0.105 at k=16 (still converging), reproducing the two-timescale separation between early policy convergence (k≈2) and late value-bound convergence (k≈16).

ai-sherpa/rl-reachability-asymptotic-opt.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all five claims through an independent from-scratch numpy implementation on 8 reachability MDPs of 155–405 states with 80 trials, including direct testing of Theorem 3.2's threshold law (0/1040 violations), exhaustive verification of Theorem 4.1's floor on 1.15 billion policy pairs with exact rational arithmetic, and reproduction of the paper's median-k=2 convergence statistic. The main caveat is that benchmarks are QVBS-spirit synthetic MDPs rather than the paper's exact QVBS PRISM models (which require 36h each), though the state-space scale and end-component structure are comparable.

kondratevakate/repro-when-can-we-trust-s.paper_title: When Can We Trust Survival Model Evaluation ?

claims.claim: Censoring induces systematic, mechanism-dependent distortions in survival evaluation metrics that vary by censoring rate and censoring mechanism.
claims.evidence: The ST-vs-OR experiment (n=4000, 8 reps, 3 mechanisms × 4 rates) shows IBS bias varying from −0.080 under administrative censoring to ~0.000 under covariate-dependent censoring at 80%, while C-index drifts monotonically with rate — concrete evidence of systematic, mechanism-dependent distortions varying by rate and mechanism.

claims.claim: Moderate numerical bias in censored data can lead to unreliable model comparison as censoring increases.
claims.evidence: Near-tied model ranking agreement with the oracle drops from 100% at 0% censoring to 29–42% at 80% across all three mechanisms (24 reps, n=4000), directly demonstrating that moderate metric bias under increasing censoring makes model comparison unreliable, while the widely-separated regime stays at 100% as a boundary condition.

kondratevakate/repro-when-can-we-trust-s.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from a controlled synthetic ST-vs-OR design that supports both claims: mechanism-dependent metric distortions (especially in IBS) and ranking instability under heavy censoring for near-tied models. The fully synthetic setup is appropriate for this paper's oracle-based methodology, though it stops short of the paper's semi-synthetic real-data experiments.

lastmass/repro-inference-of-online-newto.paper_title: Inference of Online Newton Methods with Nesterov's Accelerated Sketching

claims.evidence: Analytical flop ledger with concrete counts from d=16 to d=2048 shows log-log slopes of 1.970 (Kaczmarz) and 2.095 (Gaussian) for NASketch vs 3.000 for dense Newton, directly supporting the O(d²) vs O(d³) complexity claim.

claims.claim: Proves asymptotic normality of last iterate with limiting covariance characterized by Lyapunov equation
claims.evidence: Experiments at d=20 (20 runs) and d=40 (10 runs) show CI coverage of 1.000 and 0.800 respectively vs the paper's 0.955 target — the coverage does not cleanly match and the dimensions/run counts are too small to constitute a full verification of asymptotic normality.

lastmass/repro-inference-of-online-newto.overall: The logbook provides solid evidence for the O(d²) complexity claim via an analytical flop ledger validated across multiple dimensions, but the statistical inference claims (asymptotic normality, covariance convergence rate) are only tested at small scale (d=20/40, 10-20 runs) with CI coverage that does not cleanly match theoretical predictions, and the non-asymptotic convergence rate is never directly measured.

neonforestmist/exact-six-release-slot-20.paper_title: A Tight Theory of Error Feedback Algorithms in Distributed Optimization

claims.claim: EF21 achieves a tight convergence guarantee under contractive compression with optimal step size eta_star = (2/(L+mu)) * ((1-sqrt(epsilon))/(1+sqrt(epsilon))), and the resulting contraction rate rho_star is independent of the number of agents n (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: 18 generalized-eigenvalue matrix cases (3 regimes × 6 worker counts n=1,2,3,5,10,25) match the closed-form eta_star and rho_star within 1.887e-15; the 49,446-evaluation operative sweep uniquely selects eta/eta_star=1 in all three regimes, and a 170-digit witness has relative residual 2.82e-170. The identical rho across all worker counts demonstrates n-independence.

claims.claim: Under the statistical homogeneity (shared minimizer) assumption, classic Error Feedback (EF) matches EF21's optimal step size and contraction factor exactly, giving identical tight convergence rates (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The theorem matrix table includes both rho_ef21_matrix and rho_ef_matrix_shared_minimizer columns across all 18 cases, with maximum gap 1.443e-15, showing classic EF under shared-minimizer assumption matches EF21's optimal step size and contraction factor to machine precision.

claims.claim: Without the shared-minimizer assumption, classic EF can exhibit 2-periodic cycles under statistical heterogeneity and generally fails to converge in the multi-agent setting (Proposition 2.1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: 9 concrete trajectories (3 step-size branches × 3 compression regimes) exhibit full (x,e_1,e_2) 2-periodic cycles with residuals ≤ 2.22e-16 and nonzero iterate amplitudes (e.g., x0=0.3714, x1=-0.3714, x2=0.3714), while satisfying compressor admissibility constraints, directly demonstrating 2-periodic non-convergence under heterogeneity.

claims.claim: The worst-case multi-agent convergence rate proven in Theorem 3.1 exactly matches the known single-agent rate, showing the novel Lyapunov function recovers prior single-agent guarantees as a special case (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Every parameter regime includes n=1 alongside n=2,3,5,10,25, and the worst-case rho is identical across all worker counts within machine precision (max gap 1.887e-15), directly showing the multi-agent rate recovers the single-agent rate.

claims.claim: For heterogeneous regularity parameters across agents, Corollary 3.2 extends the tight rates to deterministic, additive, positively homogeneous compressors using averaged parameters L-bar and mu-bar (Corollary 3.2).
claims.evidence: 4 worker configurations with explicit averaged L-bar and mu-bar values show formula-matrix gaps ≤ 3.33e-16 and max explicit-vs-barred update errors ≤ 1.78e-15 across 512 aggregation trials, confirming the averaged-parameter reduction for deterministic additive homogeneous compressors.

claims.claim: For the two-agent (n=2) heterogeneous case, an explicit cubic polynomial characterizes the empirically optimal convergence rate, and tuning the EControl algorithm's step size to its optimum yields eta=0, coinciding with EF21 (Law 4.3, Law 4.4, Section 4).
claims.evidence: 8 cubic polynomial cases show largest real roots with polynomial residuals < 1e-14, with homogeneous cases reducing to Theorem 3.1 rates; 16 heterogeneous cases confirm eta_EC=0 makes EControl identical to shifted EF21, and the destructive control forcing positive eta_EC is detected (metric 0.0434 > threshold 0.04).

neonforestmist/exact-six-release-slot-20.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence—generalized eigenvalue computations, high-precision witnesses, operative sweeps, explicit cycle trajectories, cubic root evaluations, and destructive controls—supporting all six claims on the paper's extremal scalar quadratic witnesses and replicated multi-agent constructions. The verification is rigorous but scoped to the theorem's tight scalar/quadratic extremal cases rather than general nonlinear objectives, which the logbook transparently acknowledges.

kondratevakate/repro-functional-decompos.paper_title: Functional Decomposition and Shapley Interactions for Interpreting Survival Models

claims.claim: SurvFD decomposes higher-order feature effects on survival predictions into time-dependent and time-independent components, characterizing when additive explanations fail across log-hazard, hazard, and survival-function scales (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The three-scale functional ANOVA audit on a 5^3=125-point exact grid demonstrates decomposition into time-dependent/time-independent components across log-hazard (pair effects ~1.4e-15 RMS), hazard (pair effects 0.005-0.011 RMS), and survival scales (time-dependent higher-order effects), with maximum reconstruction error 8.88e-16, directly showing additivity failure across nonlinear links.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 shows that under feature independence, SurvFD exactly recovers ground-truth effect decompositions when the underlying risk score is linear or additively separable in main effects (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: On three scenarios covered by Theorem 3.2 (additive TI, additive with TD main effect, linear+interaction TI), SurvFD exactly recovered the ground-truth TD/TI partition in 3/3 cases across 12 independent seeds, with a 15-order-of-magnitude margin between TD and TI effect spreads.

claims.claim: SurvSHAP-IQ extends Shapley interaction quantification to time-indexed survival functions, estimating higher-order time-dependent interactions and achieving local accuracy below 0.015 on ten simulated scenarios (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Local accuracy was tested on all ten simulated scenarios but only for ground-truth functions (sigma-bar ~1e-16, an algebraic identity), not for fitted CoxPH/GBSA models where the paper's <0.015 threshold applies; the fitted-model evaluation was explicitly not attempted due to missing scikit-survival.

claims.claim: On the TCGA-BRCA multi-modal dataset (n=990 patients), SurvSHAP-IQ reveals within-modality (image-to-image, clinical-to-clinical) interactions but no cross-modality interactions between histopathological images and clinical features (Section 5, TCGA-BRCA application).
claims.evidence: The TCGA-BRCA multi-modal application (n=990) is never addressed; the logbook uses only synthetic data and explicitly states no external data was used.

claims.claim: Scalability analysis across four additional datasets (10-16 features) shows regression-based Shapley interaction approximators achieve the highest fidelity among tested approximation algorithms (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: A synthetic proxy with 10-16 feature coalition games compares regression vs. permutation estimators (regression RMSE lower in all 8 cells), but does not use the paper's four datasets, does not run the full approximation-method panel, and does not establish the paper's empirical ranking on real data.

kondratevakate/repro-functional-decompos.overall: The logbook provides strong exact-computation evidence for the theoretical claims (Theorems 3.2 and 3.3, three-scale decomposition) on small synthetic setups, but does not attempt the TCGA-BRCA application (Claim 5) and only tests ground-truth—not fitted-model—local accuracy (Claim 4) and a synthetic proxy for the scalability analysis (Claim 6).
