AceVikings/repro-minimum-distance-summar.paper_title: Minimum Distance Summaries for Robust Neural Posterior Estimation

claims.claim: Minimum-distance summaries (MDS) adapt the query summary s* = arg min_s D(P_{x|s}, Q) at test time while keeping the pretrained neural posterior estimator fixed, preserving amortization (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Two independently trained NPEs (4,418-param Gaussian, 17,540-param OUP) had tensor hashes checked before and after every query and never changed, while being queried with optimized summaries—concretely demonstrating fixed-network test-time adaptation.

claims.claim: MDS is implemented via a Maximum Mean Discrepancy objective using random Fourier feature approximations of the Gaussian kernel, with a decoder mean-embedding network trained offline via MSE and the summary optimized at test time by L-BFGS (Section 3.2, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Hash-pinned official RFFTTAAdapter with Gaussian-kernel RBFSampler, offline MSE-trained mean-embedding decoder (final MSE 2.83e-05), and L-BFGS optimization over test summary at 512 RFF dimensions, with millisecond-scale adaptation timings.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that under Huber's ε-contamination model Q_ε = (1-ε)Q + εδ_y, the KL divergence between posteriors under MDS-adapted summaries for Q and Q_ε is O(ε), bounding robustness to small contamination (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Pinned 1,197-line TeX parsed with all 10 assumptions and R0→R1→R2→R3 dependency chain present; numerical check in Gaussian special case bounded max summary influence at 1.575812 across 20,001 contamination locations with KL/ε tending to zero.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 shows that when the model is correctly specified, posterior consistency under the original summary statistics implies posterior consistency under MDS-adapted summaries (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: All 4 consistency assumptions and C1→C2→C3→C4 chain found in source; across 300 replicates per sample size, MDS posterior RMS radius contracted from 0.4660 (N=10) to 0.0456 (N=1000) with log-log slope −0.5074, consistent with posterior consistency.

claims.claim: On the Gaussian model, MDS outperforms NPE, NNPE, and NPE-OR baselines across a range of contamination proportions, with degradation only appearing at contamination levels above 40% (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: 91.51% mean RMSE reduction across ε=0.1–0.4 with degradation to 5.38% at ε=0.5 reproduces the stated boundary; however, the logbook does not explicitly document comparisons against NNPE and NPE-OR baselines, only NPE and ordinary-summary controls.

claims.claim: On a 1024-dimensional Cryo-EM inference task, MDS substantially improves robustness to Gaussian noise contamination while maintaining performance in the well-specified regime (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Real 1,024-dimensional HSP90 Cryo-EM task with correct image size, conformational states, summary statistics, and RFF embedding, but trained on only 5,000 of 15,000 datasets (one-third scale), constituting a reduced-scope reproduction; MDS improved RMSE at all 5 contaminated levels (17–38%) and maintained clean performance.

AceVikings/repro-minimum-distance-summar.overall: The logbook provides concrete evidence for claims 1–5 through hash-pinned implementations, proof audits, and numerical experiments on Gaussian and OUP models. ProCreations/repro-on-densest-k-subgraph.paper_title: On Densest $k$-Subgraph Mining and Diagonal Loading: Optimization Landscape and Finite-Step Exact Convergence Analysis

claims.claim: Theorem 4 extends the Motzkin-Straus theorem to show the relaxed problem's maximum value equals 1+λ-1/ω, where ω is the largest clique size, establishing that diagonal loading parameter λ≥1 is the minimal value ensuring tightness of the penalty-based relaxation.
claims.evidence: A dimension-independent constructive rounding argument (pairwise mass transfer with gain delta*(lambda*x_i+s_i-lambda*x_j-s_j) + (lambda-A_ij)*delta^2, both terms nonnegative for lambda>=1) is encoded and tested in 2,304 exact cases through n=256 across six graph families and six lambda values, plus 61,440 exhaustive cases at n=5; 72 below-threshold controls at lambda<1 all produce strict relaxation gaps (smallest 0.004375), confirming the sharp lambda=1 boundary.

claims.claim: Corollary 1 proves that when λ≥1 there always exists a global maximizer of the relaxed objective that is integral, so the relaxed and combinatorial problems share the same optimal value.
claims.evidence: The same constructive rounding mechanism shows every relaxed feasible point maps to an integral k-hot point without objective decrease (all 2,304 trajectories through n=256 terminate integrally and nondecreasingly), directly establishing that an integral global maximizer exists and the relaxed and combinatorial optima coincide for lambda>=1.

claims.claim: Lemma 1 shows that for λ>1 there does not exist a non-integral local maximizer, establishing the strict dichotomy that all integral stationary points are local maximizers while non-integral stationary points are strict saddles.
claims.evidence: Exhaustive active-set KKT enumeration at n=5 over all 1,024 graphs yields 74,606 stationary points: 20,935 integral (all with positive swap slack, min 0.5) and 53,671 fractional (all with zero first derivative and positive curvature >=1.0); a dimension-independent argument (integral gradients are integer+lambda vs integer, so strict inequality; fractional KKT points have >=2 free coordinates with positive curvature 2(lambda-A_ij)) is verified through n=384 with exact rational arithmetic on 1,440 integral and 360 fractional certificates.

claims.claim: Theorem 5 shows that increasing the diagonal loading parameter beyond λ=1 introduces additional spurious local maxima, implying λ=1 optimally trades off relaxation tightness against optimization difficulty.
claims.evidence: On a perfect-matching family (n=2r, k=2), exact identities show r local maxima at lambda=1 (all global) versus binom(2r,2) strict local maxima for any lambda>1, yielding 2r(r-1) spurious maxima; 504 exact cells through n=128 with eight lambda values including 10001/10000 confirm this, while complete-graph controls (56 cells through n=128) show zero spurious maxima at all lambda, correctly bounding the claim's scope.

claims.claim: The saddle-escaping Frank-Wolfe algorithm (Section 3.1) has per-iteration complexity O(m+k log n) and is shown to converge in a finite number of steps to an integral local maximizer of the densest k-subgraph relaxation.
claims.evidence: At the paper's Section 5.2 scale (n=100, 10-regular, k=20, lambda=1.5), standard FW is stuck at the fractional saddle in 64/64 cases while the saddle-escaping variant escapes in exactly 1 step and reaches an exact integral stationary point in 12-30 iterations in 64/64 cases; an additional 64 Erdos-Renyi graphs with random starts converge in 6-19 iterations, all with monotone objectives.

claims.claim: Experiments show the Frank-Wolfe algorithm achieves denser subgraphs than competing methods LRBO, L-ADMM, and EXPP while incurring lower computational cost on real-world graphs with millions of vertices (Section 4).
claims.evidence: On com-Youtube (1,134,890 vertices, 2,987,624 edges), Frank-Wolfe is strictly densest at k=50/200/1000 (densities 0.731/0.353/0.086 vs best rivals) and uses 9.4x-47.1x less deterministic work than the cheapest comparable-density rival; across all three SNAP graphs FW leads or ties in 8 of 9 density comparisons, with one documented small-graph loss (Facebook k=100, EXPP ahead by 0.0002 density).

MarxistLeninist/repro-the-optimal-sample.paper_title: The Optimal Sample Complexity of Linear Contracts

claims.claim: Theorem 1.1 establishes uniform convergence: for sample size s ≥ 3456 ln(4/δ)/ε², with probability at least 1−δ, the empirical and expected utility of every linear contract differ by at most ε (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo over 80-type, 20-action, 8-outcome random instances shows median sup-error decaying as s^(-0.501) and 0.9-quantile as s^(-0.499), with the (1-delta)-quantile linear in sqrt(ln(1/delta)) at R²=0.993; at the prescribed s=3456 ln(4/delta)/eps², empirical failure probability is 0 with worst sup-error at 0.27% of eps.

claims.claim: Corollary 1.2 shows the Empirical Utility Maximization algorithm achieves an ε-approximation of the optimal linear contract using s ≥ 6912 ln(4/δ)/ε² samples and O(1/ε) oracle queries (Corollary 1.2).
claims.evidence: EUM grid sizes of 41, 81, 201 for eps=0.1, 0.05, 0.02 each satisfy ≤ floor(4/eps)+2 (confirming O(1/eps) queries), and at the prescribed s*=6912 ln(4/delta)/eps² the empirical failure probability P(subopt>eps)=0 across all tested configurations.

claims.claim: The O(ln(1/δ)/ε²) sample complexity matches the lower bound of Dütting et al. (2025) up to constant factors, and is independent of the action space size n and the number of outcomes m (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: Independence of n and m is verified on a non-toy setup (sup-error flat at ~0.0011 as n grows 6→500 with dominated-action padding, identical curves across m up to machine precision, with a negative control showing detectable n-dependence for other classes), but the matching of the Omega(ln(1/delta)/eps²) lower bound is demonstrated only on a 2-type, 2-action witness instance.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 shows the expected reward of a linear contract is non-decreasing in the contract parameter α, a structural property exploited to build fine-grained covering arguments where general pseudo-dimension bounds fail (Lemma 2.1).
claims.evidence: The test_lemma21_monotone_expected_reward checks non-decreasing expected reward R_{a*(theta,alpha)} in alpha on 300 random types (20 actions, 8 outcomes, 4001-point grid), yielding monotone fraction 1.000 and worst backward step 0.0 — no violations across all tested instances.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.2 constructs an L2 cover of the reward function class of size O(1/ν²), obtained by discretizing empirical rewards into ν-intervals, taking pullbacks to parameter space, and combining with grid discretization of the outcome axis (Lemma 2.2).
claims.evidence: An independent implementation of the L2 cover construction was exercised on 4 populations (24–120 types, 6–24 actions, 3–12 outcomes) at 5 precision levels (20 cells), with cover size ratio ≤ 0.2534 vs 12/nu², weighted L2 error ratio ≤ 0.2244 vs nu, zero missing pullback bins, and zero monotonicity violations — all hard assertions passed.

MarxistLeninist/repro-the-optimal-sample.overall: The logbook provides concrete Monte Carlo evidence verifying the uniform convergence rate, finite-sample guarantee, EUM algorithm properties, Lemma 2.1 monotonicity, and Lemma 2.2 cover construction on non-trivial random instances, while the lower-bound optimality matching is demonstrated only on a simplified 2-type witness.

imadreamerboy/repro-chb-hardness-aware-c.paper_title: CHB: A Diagnostic Toolkit for Hardness-Aware Clustering Evaluation

claims.claim: CHB maps dataset-representation pairs to interpretable hardness fingerprints capturing separation, cohesion, scale heterogeneity, and topology.
claims.evidence: A single real execution of chb.compute_fingerprint on sklearn's bundled digits dataset (1797×64) produced all eight named coordinates (S1–S3, C1–C2, T1–T3) and Regime C, demonstrating the mechanism works on one small dataset-representation pair, but not establishing the general mapping or interpretability across multiple pairs at paper scale.

claims.claim: Reveals reproducible structural regimes, regime-dependent ranking reversals across method families, and robustness signatures including topology-linked breakdowns.
claims.evidence: No method-family comparisons, ranking experiments, reversal analyses, robustness signatures, or topology-breakdown experiments were executed; the logbook only ran a single fingerprint computation.

claims.claim: Enables representation auditing by attributing gains to measurable shifts in hardness fingerprint rather than external performance changes alone.
claims.evidence: No alternate representations, performance comparisons, or attribution analyses were run; the logbook contains no evidence relevant to representation auditing.

imadreamerboy/repro-chb-hardness-aware-c.overall: This logbook provides only a single smoke-test execution of the CHB fingerprint computation on sklearn's bundled digits dataset, confirming the tool runs and emits eight coordinates. It does not reproduce any of the paper's substantive claims about regimes, ranking reversals, robustness, or representation auditing.

tpls/repro-mds-robust-npe.paper_title: Minimum Distance Summaries for Robust Neural Posterior Estimation

claims.claim: Minimum-distance summaries (MDS) adapt the query summary s* = arg min_s D(P_{x|s}, Q) at test time while keeping the pretrained neural posterior estimator fixed, preserving amortization (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Real upstream code confirms L-BFGS optimizes only [s_opt] (summary), NPE state_dict SHA-256 is byte-identical before/after adapt, and fit/adapt signatures take no NPE argument; MMD loss decreased 0.853→0.004 with ‖s−s*‖ 3.88→0.27, plus 3 negative controls that break as expected.

claims.claim: MDS is implemented via a Maximum Mean Discrepancy objective using random Fourier feature approximations of the Gaussian kernel, with a decoder mean-embedding network trained offline via MSE and the summary optimized at test time by L-BFGS (Section 3.2, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Real upstream rff.py uses scikit-learn RBFSampler with median-heuristic bandwidth; _compute_loss is squared L2 in finite RFF space; RFF→exact MMD² convergence slope −0.47 (theory −0.5) with 1.7% relative error at K=4096; decoder weights byte-identical after adapt; negative controls (wrong bandwidth, stepped decoder) fail as expected.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that under Huber's ε-contamination model Q_ε = (1-ε)Q + εδ_y, the KL divergence between posteriors under MDS-adapted summaries for Q and Q_ε is O(ε), bounding robustness to small contamination (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Theorem 4.1 and proof confirmed present (App A.3); bounded-kernel premise verified on real RFFTTAAdapter: single-point influence ≤0.0150 ≤ bound 0.0283, flat over radius 1→1e12 across 3 seeds; negative control (sample-mean) diverges to 1.4e10; adapted-posterior RMSE degrades smoothly 0.103→0.377 over ε=0→0.5 without blow-up.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 shows that when the model is correctly specified, posterior consistency under the original summary statistics implies posterior consistency under MDS-adapted summaries (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Theorem 4.2 and proof confirmed present (App A.5); at ε=0 (well-specified), adaptation is a no-op for 94.7% (284/300) of observations (n_steps=0), leaving the consistent NPE posterior untouched; clean-data RMSE improves 8.4%, within the ±10% no-op band.

claims.claim: On the Gaussian model, MDS outperforms NPE, NNPE, and NPE-OR baselines across a range of contamination proportions, with degradation only appearing at contamination levels above 40% (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: MDS vs NPE comparison is real and significant (+13.5% to +28.1% RMSE reduction, BCa lower bounds >0, perm p≤2e-4 at all ε), but scale is reduced (n_train 20000 vs 50000, n_eval 100 vs 500) and NNPE and NPE-OR baselines were not attempted, so the full three-baseline ranking claim is only partially addressed.

claims.claim: On a 1024-dimensional Cryo-EM inference task, MDS substantially improves robustness to Gaussian noise contamination while maintaining performance in the well-specified regime (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The 1024-dimensional Cryo-EM task was not attempted; no evidence was produced either way.

tpls/repro-mds-robust-npe.overall: The logbook provides strong code-level verification of the MDS mechanism (claims 1–2) and reasonable support for both theoretical guarantees (claims 3–4) via proof-existence checks, premise verification on real upstream code, and behavioural evidence from a 300-pair Gaussian benchmark. The Gaussian empirical claim (5) is only partially addressed at reduced scale with one of three baselines, and the Cryo-EM claim (6) was not attempted.

imadreamerboy/repro-data-manifold-under-.paper_title: The Data Manifold under the Microscope

claims.claim: The benchmarking framework repurposes and extends dSprites and COIL-20 with additional transformation dimensions and dense, axis-aligned sampling, pairing them with finite-difference estimators that recover curvature, reach, and volume at near-ground-truth accuracy (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook ran finite-difference volume and scalar-curvature APIs on analytic Circle (257-point grid, volume rel. error 9.96e-05) and Torus (64×64 grid, area rel. error 0.0032, curvature max abs error 0.0085) fixtures, but did not use dSprites/COIL-20, did not compute reach, and did not run any paper benchmark.

claims.claim: The extended dSprites dataset spans 3 shapes across 16^4 transformation combinations, yielding 196,608 images, while extended COIL-20 spans 20 objects times 18 views times 16^2 combinations, yielding 92,160 images (Table 1).
claims.evidence: No dataset construction, download, or enumeration was performed; the logbook explicitly states no dSprites or COIL-20 data was used.

claims.claim: The framework evaluates the scaling behavior of the minimax manifold estimation bound (Theorem 3.6) and the Fefferman et al. bound H(M_o,M) < C_1(log n/n)^(1/d) against measured Hausdorff error on dSprites of varying intrinsic dimension d=1 to 4 using MMLS (Section 5, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: No generalization-bound calculation, manifold fitting, MMLS run, Hausdorff measurement, or dSprites experiment of any dimension was performed.

claims.claim: Finite-difference curvature estimation error scales as O(h^2) = O((1/n)^(2/d)), and this scaling is validated on hyperspheres (S^2, S^3, S^4), a hyperboloid (H^2_2), and a torus (T^2) via scalar-curvature RMSE comparisons (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: A single torus scalar-curvature computation at one grid size was performed, but no scaling study varying h or n was conducted, and no hyperspheres (S², S³, S⁴) or hyperboloid (H²₂) were tested, so the O(h²) scaling claim was never addressed.

claims.claim: The framework tracks layer-wise evolution of manifold geometry (e.g., curvature and dimension) across a beta-VAE trained on dSprites and COIL-20 (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: No VAE construction, training, checkpoint loading, or layer-wise geometry measurement was performed; the logbook explicitly states no VAE-related work was done.

imadreamerboy/repro-data-manifold-under-.overall: The logbook only executed tiny analytic Circle/Torus finite-difference probes on a CPU-only host, producing volume and curvature error numbers on synthetic fixtures without touching any paper dataset, bound, scaling study, or VAE experiment. It provides minimal compatibility evidence for the released code but does not reproduce or falsify any of the five claims at the paper's scale.

algorise/repro-agora-toward-autonomous-b.paper_title: Agora: Toward Autonomous Bug Detection in Production-Level Consensus Protocols with LLM Agents

claims.claim: Agora is a three-agent system (Orchestrator, Strategy, TestGen agents, each with four subtasks totaling 12 workflow steps) that combines hypothesis-driven testing with domain knowledge to find protocol-level logic bugs in consensus implementations (Figures 1 and 2, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook maps all 12 subtasks (S.1–S.4, O.1–O.4, T.1–T.4) to specific code locations in agent/core/orchestrator.py with line numbers, and an actual EPaxos run log (session_20260717_192611.log, 2,212 lines) shows the full workflow executing end-to-end: Strategy agent → attack scenario → TestGen → test execution → confirmed bug → bug exploitation → additional bug found.

claims.claim: Agora discovers 15 zero-day protocol-level logic bugs across four consensus implementations (Raft/etcd, EPaxos, HotStuff, BullShark/Sui), with a 26.1% false-positive rate among 46 total bug reports (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The reproduction ran Agora with Qwen3-Coder-480B on all 4 protocols (~15–18 min each), producing 5 self-confirmed bug candidates, but adjudication found 0 substantiated: 3 test files were overwritten by later runs, 1 test never calls EPaxos code, and 1 asserts on a transient PREACCEPTED state. The 15-bug union and 26.1% FPR require 4 models and an adjudication ledger neither available nor shipped.

claims.claim: Baseline ReAct-style LLM agents augmented with code-reading tools find zero protocol-level logic bugs: GPT-5.2 finds 22 implementation-level bugs but 0 logic bugs, Gemini 3.0 finds 0/0, Claude Sonnet finds 0, and Qwen3 Coder finds 3 implementation bugs and 0 logic bugs, whereas Agora with Gemini finds 11 protocol-level logic bugs (baseline comparison results).
claims.evidence: The ReAct baseline was run with Qwen3-Coder-480B on 3 protocols, finding 5 implementation bugs and 0 logic bugs—matching the paper's Qwen3 row (3 EPaxos impl bugs) and confirming the '0 logic bugs' part. However, the Agora+Gemini 11-logic-bug contrast was not testable (Gemini unavailable), and Agora+Qwen3 produced 0 substantiated bugs. The reproduction used 1 of 4 models at ~1/10 runtime.

claims.claim: An ablation (Table 2) shows removing the state-analyzer or scenario-generator component drops discovered bugs to 0, removing the bug-exploitation component drops bugs found to 3 (a 73% reduction), and removing the reflection loop causes test-generation failures with 173 false reports.
claims.evidence: No ablation experiments were executed. The logbook only parsed Table 2 from the paper text (T1) and the artifact's table.tex (T2), noting that the artifact's 'Full' row (1/9/4/1/15) disagrees with the published Table 2's Agora row (1/6/3/1/11) and that ablation token counts contain impossible half-integer values. No component-removal runs were performed.

claims.claim: The discovered bugs span five categories, with Recovery & Execution Divergence and Persistence & Monotonicity Violations each accounting for 4 of the 15 bugs (26.7% each) (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Only text-matching checks against the paper PDF were performed (confirming 5 category names appear and counts sum to 15). No independent bug categorization was possible since the reproduction's own runs produced 0 substantiated bugs to categorize.

claims.claim: Agora's bug discovery process consumes 58.6M tokens in total, averaging roughly $40 per discovered bug (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The artifact's total_tokens_chart.py contains per-protocol values summing to 58,604,702 (rounding to 58.6M), but this is the authors' own shipped data, not independently measured. The reproduction's own runs consumed different token amounts at reduced scale. The $40/bug figure is derived from 58.6M/11, not independently verified.

algorise/repro-agora-toward-autonomous-b.overall: The logbook provides strong evidence that Agora's three-agent architecture exists in the released code and executes end-to-end, and partially confirms that ReAct baselines find only implementation-level bugs. However, the central empirical claims—15 zero-day logic bugs, the 26.1% FPR, the ablation results, and the Agora+Gemini 11-bug contrast—were not reproduced, as the reproduction used a single model at ~1/10 the paper's runtime and substantiated 0 of 5 self-confirmed bug candidates after careful adjudication.

AceVikings/repro-quantifying-llm-attenti.paper_title: Quantifying LLM Attention-Head Stability: Implications for Circuit Universality

claims.claim: Middle-layer attention heads show the lowest cross-refit stability, e.g., layer 5 drops to ≈0.70 stability versus ≈1.0 in layer 1, quantified via a layer-wise mean stability measure (Equation 5, Section 4.1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Layer-wise stability values (0.9745, 0.9067, 0.8576, 0.7753, 0.6210, 0.7021, 0.8658, 0.8195) confirm middle layers are least stable, with layer 5 at 0.621 vs layer 1 at 0.975, computed over 100 prompts with seed 1 as anchor and seeds 2–5 as refits using the paper's Equation 5 metric.

claims.claim: Middle layers also exhibit broader, less sharply defined off-diagonal head-to-head matching patterns across refits compared to early/late layers (Section 4.2, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Within-layer off-diagonal commonness for middle layers is lower by −0.311976 compared to edge layers, quantitatively supporting the claim that middle layers exhibit broader, less sharply defined head-to-head matching patterns.

claims.claim: In deeper architectures (8- and 12-layer models), the least-stable layer occurs at a relative depth r≈0.4–0.8, showing stronger mid-depth divergence than shallower models (Section 4.6.2, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: For depth-8 models, all 5 anchors show Gap2 < Gap4 < Gap8 with C_gap > 0.01 and minimum at layer 5/8 (r=0.625); for 12-layer GPT-2-small, all 5 anchors place the minimum at layer 5/12 (r=0.4167) with positive gaps (0.201–0.270), both within the claimed r≈0.4–0.8 band.

claims.claim: Using AdamW (weight decay) yields a clear increase in attention-head seed-stability for deeper MLP models (8- and 12-layer) without degrading task performance (Section 4.5, Figure 6).
claims.evidence: AdamW does increase mean head stability (0.815329 → 0.862876, +5.83%), but the compound claim includes 'without degrading task performance,' and WikiText-2 cross-entropy worsened by +0.179744 nats in 5/5 matched seeds, exceeding a 0.03-nat margin, directly contradicting the no-degradation clause.

claims.claim: Higher query-weight norms correlate with lower head stability, suggesting weight-norm control as a mechanistic driver of the weight-decay stability effect (Section 4.4.1).
claims.evidence: Negative observational correlations (Adam r=−0.700, AdamW r=−0.676) between per-layer query norms and stability are complemented by a controlled W_Q scaling intervention: reducing norms by 0.70× improved stability 8/8 layers for both optimizers, while increasing by 1.30× worsened 8/8, demonstrating a monotone causal relationship.

claims.claim: The residual stream is consistently more stable across refits than the corresponding attention heads, across all tested architectures and optimizers, as measured via Centered Kernel Alignment (Section 4.7, Figure 9, Appendix A.7).
claims.evidence: Residual RBF CKA means exceed corresponding head stability means for both Adam (0.885722 vs 0.815329, +0.070) and AdamW (0.904742 vs 0.862876, +0.042), computed across 32 comparisons (4 peers × 8 layers) per optimizer on depth-8 checkpoints.

AceVikings/repro-quantifying-llm-attenti.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence from official checkpoints, 100 released prompts, and multiple seeds supporting 5 of 6 claims, including a controlled W_Q scaling intervention for the weight-norm mechanism. The compound AdamW claim is falsified because while stability increases, task performance significantly degrades (+0.1797 nats in 5/5 seeds), contradicting the 'without degrading performance' clause.

ProCreations/repro-high-accuracy-samplin.paper_title: High-Accuracy Sampling for Diffusion Models and Log-Concave Distributions

claims.claim: The paper's First-Order Rejection Sampling (FORS) meta-algorithm (Theorem 3.1) produces samples with error δ using sample complexity bounded by 3Be^(2B)log(2/δ) with probability 1-δ (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: 120,000 FORS outputs on a non-uniform 1D target achieved pooled KS 0.001864 and acceptance-probability error 1.40e-4; the query-tail bound 3Be^(2B)log(2/δ) was never exceeded across five δ values (empirical quantiles 62–187 vs bounds 458–1162), directly testing both the output-law identity and the high-probability sample-complexity bound of Theorem 3.1.

claims.claim: Under only a finite second-moment assumption (minimal assumptions), the diffusion sampler achieves query complexity O(d·log²(1/δ) + log³(1/δ)), giving polylog(1/δ) dependence rather than the poly(1/δ) of prior work (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The Theorem-4.1 FORS chain was executed on a discrete four-point law with finite second moment (no smoothness/density assumptions), achieving KS 0.006339 at δ=0.05 versus 0.416 for the no-correction control; across a 20-cell grid (d=2–16, five δ values), score-query counts regressed against d·log²(1/δ)+log³(1/δ) with R²=0.991553, directly testing both dimension and accuracy scaling.

claims.claim: Under a non-uniform Lipschitz condition on the score (Assumption 4.3), a DDPM-like sampler achieves total-variation error controlled via chi-squared divergence with complexity O(√(dL_δ log(d/δ))·log(d/δ) + L_δ log²(d/δ)) (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: The Theorem-4.4 DDPM-like sampler was run on a non-Gaussian 2D mixture with Assumption 4.3 verified empirically (zero exceedances in 48,000 checks), achieving mean sliced KS 0.006752; across a 19-cell grid (d=2–8, five δ values, L_δ spanning 2.0–19.8), query counts regressed against √(dL_δ log(d/δ))·log(d/δ)+L_δ log²(d/δ) with R²=0.999840.

claims.claim: For distributions with low intrinsic dimension d★, an adaptive-step-size method attains complexity O(d★·log²((d+M₂²)/δ²)), replacing the ambient dimension d with d★ (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: The shifted-score Theorem-4.6 method was run on the same rank-2 support zero-padded to ambient dimensions 8, 32, and 128; score-query counts per draw varied by only 1.0073x across this 16-fold ambient-dimension range, the orthogonal shifted-score component cancelled to 1.80e-15, and output KS remained stable (0.012–0.018), directly demonstrating replacement of ambient d by intrinsic d★.

claims.claim: Section 5 extends the FORS framework to sample from general log-concave distributions using only gradient evaluations (no density evaluations), giving the first polylog(1/δ) sampler in this setting (Section 5).
claims.evidence: A gradient-only FORS/RGO chain (Algorithm 3) was run on a non-Gaussian strongly log-concave target through d=16 including a correlated non-product variant, with exactly zero density-oracle calls confirmed; a six-point accuracy sweep showed gradient-query log-log degree 1.78091 in log(1/δ) with R²=0.988987, providing finite-grid evidence of polylogarithmic accuracy dependence.

ProCreations/repro-high-accuracy-samplin.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence for all five claims through actual clean-room sampler executions on distributions satisfying the stated assumptions, with no-correction controls, query counting, blinded diagnostics, and byte-identical reproducibility. The evidence is finite-instance rather than proof-level, but directly tests the claimed mechanisms and scaling across varied dimensions, accuracy levels, and problem parameters.

AceVikings/repro-lower-bounds-for-frank-.paper_title: Lower Bounds for Frank-Wolfe on Strongly Convex Sets

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a constructive Omega(1/sqrt(epsilon)) lower bound on the number of iterations for Frank-Wolfe with short steps or exact line search when both the objective and the constraint set are smooth and strongly convex (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: The logbook independently reconstructed the paper's hard instance with 240-digit arithmetic over 16,384 forward steps, showing T·sqrt(gap_T) remains nonzero (0.606–0.749), zero lower-envelope violations across 32,713 states, forward inversion error ≤5E-242, and a direct 512-step 2D vector replay of the actual LMO and exact line search matching to 1.823e-91.

claims.claim: The lower-bound construction uses the specific instance of minimizing f(x) = ||x-p||_2^2 over the Euclidean unit ball B_1(0) with the unconstrained minimizer p on the boundary (||p||=1), showing this hard instance matches the known O(1/sqrt(epsilon)) upper bound of Garber et al. (2015) (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: The specific instance f(x)=||x-p||² over the Euclidean unit ball with boundary point p=(0,1) is used, and independent asymptotic fits over the five largest horizons yield slopes -1.990451308 (log gap vs log iteration, target -2) and -0.502396930 (log iteration vs log gap, target -1/2), demonstrating the construction matches the known O(1/√ε) upper bound exponent.

claims.claim: The lower bound is established via a 'backward reconstruction' technique that builds worst-case trajectories by working backward from terminal iterates, producing precise sequences over horizons of 10,000+ iterations (Section on Backward Reconstruction Strategy).
claims.evidence: Nine backward-constructed trajectories cover horizons 32–8,192, producing 16,384 forward steps (exceeding 10,000), with forward inversion error at most 5E-242, confirming the backward reconstruction technique produces precise worst-case sequences at the claimed scale.

claims.claim: The analysis reduces the dynamics to a two-dimensional invariant subspace parametrized by residual magnitude r and contraction factor s, revealing stable phases of monotonically increasing contraction followed by intermittent 'jumps' that explain the convergence stalling behavior (Section on Dynamical Analysis).
claims.evidence: On the backward-constructed horizon-8,192 trajectory, 16,384/16,384 transitions satisfy s_(t+1)>s_t (monotonically increasing contraction) with all residuals decreasing; a separate 40-step forward simulation from (r_0,s_0)=(1,0.44) exhibits three intermittent jumps at steps 6, 11, 24, each cutting the objective gap by more than fourfold and satisfying s_t>1/(1+r_t)².

claims.claim: The result shows strong convexity of the constraint set alone cannot yield convergence rates uniformly faster than O(1/sqrt(epsilon)), and this conclusion holds dimension-independently and extends to ellipsoidal constraints via affine invariance (Theorem 6, Implications).
claims.evidence: The Euclidean unit ball is a strongly convex set and f(x)=||x-p||² is strongly convex, yet the verified Θ(1/t²) gap (confirmed by the 512-step vector replay matching to 1.823e-91 with invariant coefficient in [1.724, 2.0]) demonstrates that constraint-set strong convexity alone cannot yield rates faster than O(1/√ε); the dimension-independence and ellipsoidal extension follow as theoretical consequences of this 2D construction and affine invariance of FW.

AceVikings/repro-lower-bounds-for-frank-.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous high-precision numerical verification of the paper's constructive lower bound, using 240-digit arithmetic, backward-constructed trajectories up to 16,384 steps, direct vector replays of the actual FW algorithm, asymptotic slope fits, envelope checks, and negative controls. All five claims are supported by concrete numerical evidence on the paper's specific hard instance rather than generic benchmarks.

svdrecbd/repro-fractal-state-space-model.paper_title: FRACTAL: State Space Model with Fractional Recurrent Architecture for Computational Temporal Analysis of Long Sequences

claims.claim: FRACTAL achieves an average score of 87.11% on the Long Range Arena benchmark, compared to 87.04% for S5 and 86.09% for S4 (Table 2).
claims.evidence: No actual training was performed; the logbook only conducted an arithmetic audit of Table 2's internal consistency. The FRACTAL average (87.11%) and S4 average (86.09%) are arithmetically consistent with the six task scores, but the S5 average is shown to be arithmetically inconsistent (computed 87.06% vs. printed 87.04%). This audits table consistency but does not empirically verify or falsify FRACTAL's achieved accuracy.

claims.claim: FRACTAL achieves 61.85% on the ListOps task, outperforming S5's 61.10% and S4's 59.60% (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The implementation gate failed before any training: the V⁻¹B construction produces non-finite values at N=64 in float32 and relative residuals of 2.22e27–1.02e32 in float64. No ListOps training was executed, so the 61.85% accuracy claim remains entirely untested.

claims.claim: On the Path-X task, FRACTAL scores 98.39%, slightly below S5's 98.62% but above S4's 96.35% (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Path-X was explicitly deferred and never evaluated; no compute was spent on it. The claim is not addressed in any form.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 proves that the diagonal elements A_nn = n+1 of the state transition matrix A(α) are independent of the fractional singularity index α, guaranteeing spectral stability, while off-diagonal coupling increases with α (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirms analytically and numerically (11,400 finite-difference checks on N=16, α=0:0.01:0.95) that the diagonal of the lower-triangular matrix is 1,…,N (independent of α) and that off-diagonal entries increase monotonically with α, with a closed-form expression and strictly positive logarithmic derivative. However, the logbook also shows this matrix does not govern the fractional projection coefficients for α>0 (Equation 6 predicts 1/3 where the true derivative is 2/3 for a counterexample), and eigenvector conditioning is catastrophic (κ₂≈1.84e11 at N=16), undermining the practica

claims.claim: FRACTAL's fractional-order measure uses power-law weighting (t-τ)^{-α} with tunable singularity index α in [0,1) to simultaneously achieve full history retention, recency sensitivity, and scale invariance, resolving a trade-off unmet by Scaled Legendre, Translated Laguerre, and Translated Legendre measures (Section on Technical Foundation).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides analytical proofs and executable numerical checks (normalization, full support, dilation invariance, recency monotonicity, Jacobi basis through N=12, α=0.99 with Gram error 9.66e-12) confirming that the power-law measure achieves full history retention (positive mass on every nonempty interval), recency sensitivity (mass of recent fraction p is p^(1-α), increasing in α), and exact scale invariance (λ·μ_{λt}(λx)=μ_t(x)). A correction to Appendix I.2's formula strengthens rather than overturns the result.

claims.claim: FRACTAL maintains O(N log L) parallel computational complexity through a diagonal state-space structure with multi-scale filter banks partitioning heterogeneous α values across channels (Section on Architecture Components).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirms that the diagonal recurrence forms an associative prefix scan, verified across 36 length/channel combinations (max error 1.78e-15) and 10,000 randomized associativity checks (agreement to 8.88e-16). The complexity analysis shows total work Θ(NL) and span Θ(log L) with parallel channels or Θ(N log L) with serial channels, making O(N log L) a valid upper bound for the parallel span.

svdrecbd/repro-fractal-state-space-model.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the three theoretical claims (fractional measure properties, spectral matrix structure, parallel scan associativity) through analytical proofs and numerical checks, but none of the three empirical accuracy claims (LRA average, ListOps, Path-X) were tested via actual training. MarxistLeninist/CHIsZDgdb6.paper_title: Solving Imperfect-Recall Games via Sum-of-Squares Optimization

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 establishes that sleeping bandits are a special case of 1-bounded K-OPSD, formally connecting the packet scheduling model to the multi-armed bandit framework (Section 2.2, Lemma 2.1).
claims.evidence: Two independently-coded environments (1-bounded K-OPSD buffer and a from-scratch Sleeping-Bandit simulator per Kleinberg et al. 2010) run on identical RNG streams across K∈{2,4,8,16,32}, T=3000, 8 seeds (40 runs), producing 0/3000 action mismatches per run and bit-for-bit identical cumulative rewards in all 120,000 round-decisions, confirming the structural identity claimed by Lemma 2.1.

DineshAI/dyRD6lBH8K.paper_title: A Tight Theory of Error Feedback Algorithms in Distributed Optimization

claims.claim: EF21 achieves a tight convergence guarantee under contractive compression with optimal step size eta_star = (2/(L+mu)) * ((1-sqrt(epsilon))/(1+sqrt(epsilon))), and the resulting contraction rate rho_star is independent of the number of agents n (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Independent reconstruction of the sum-of-squares identity on 672 cells (max residual 2.094e-15), exact generalized eigenvalues matching the closed-form rate on 294 cells across agent counts through n=64, and 8,064 endpoint/sign contraction cells, with lower-rate, wrong-step, and altered-Lyapunov controls all failing as expected.

claims.claim: Under the statistical homogeneity (shared minimizer) assumption, classic Error Feedback (EF) matches EF21's optimal step size and contraction factor exactly, giving identical tight convergence rates (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: EF sum-of-squares identity passes 672 independent cells (max residual 1.060e-15), exact tight rates pass 294 cells and 8,064 endpoint/sign cells, and a 3,500-cell covariance audit shows zero corrected-bound violations, demonstrating EF matches EF21's rate under shared minimizer.

claims.claim: Without the shared-minimizer assumption, classic EF can exhibit 2-periodic cycles under statistical heterogeneity and generally fails to converge in the multi-agent setting (Proposition 2.1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: 120 direct full-state constructions return to the initial state (x₀,0,0) with max error 4.547e-13 across three step-size regimes, and reversing prescribed compressor signs destroys all 72 nonboundary cycles, concretely demonstrating 2-periodic cycles under heterogeneity.

claims.claim: The worst-case multi-agent convergence rate proven in Theorem 3.1 exactly matches the known single-agent rate, showing the novel Lyapunov function recovers prior single-agent guarantees as a special case (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: 588 exact generalized-eigenvalue cells spanning n=1,2,3,5,10,25,64 attain the same closed-form ρ⋆ with largest discrepancy below 3.3e-13, and a corrected PEP grid explicitly checks n=1 and n=2, showing multi-agent and single-agent rates coincide.

claims.claim: For heterogeneous regularity parameters across agents, Corollary 3.2 extends the tight rates to deterministic, additive, positively homogeneous compressors using averaged parameters L-bar and mu-bar (Corollary 3.2).
claims.evidence: 640 random vector-quadratic cases confirm that linear contractive compressors satisfy additivity/homogeneity and the distributed averaged update equals the single-agent barred update to 1.884e-15, while a nonadditive contractive compressor breaks the reduction in 616 cells and extrema substitutions are detected in every case.

claims.claim: For the two-agent (n=2) heterogeneous case, an explicit cubic polynomial characterizes the empirically optimal convergence rate, and tuning the EControl algorithm's step size to its optimum yields eta=0, coinciding with EF21 (Law 4.3, Law 4.4, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Independent cubic implementation covers 10,500 configurations with max polynomial residual 1.742e-15 and rejects all 10,500 mutated polynomials; EControl formula and η=0 dynamics cover 7,050 configurations with zero alignment error, with all positive-η controls changing dynamics. Full MOSEK SDP grid was not locally rerun due to licensing, but high-precision SDPA certifies 2 reference cases.

DineshAI/dyRD6lBH8K.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical verification of all six theoretical claims through algebraic identity reconstruction, eigenvalue matching across multiple agent counts, explicit cycle constructions, and extensive negative controls, all at machine-precision residuals. The reproduction is rigorous for a theory paper, though the full SDP solver grid for Claim 6 was not independently rerun locally due to MOSEK licensing constraints.

ProCreations/repro-randomized-feasibilit.paper_title: Randomized Feasibility Methods for Constrained Optimization with Adaptive Step Sizes

claims.claim: Proposes Algorithm 2, a Gradient Method with Randomized Feasibility using an adaptive Polyak-type stepsize, and proves linear convergence in expectation to a prescribed tolerance ε for strongly convex, Lipschitz-smooth objectives, with iteration complexity O(log(1/ε)) (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: On the paper's Appendix G.1 scale (d=10, m=1000 quadratic constraints), 12 independent streams of Algorithm 2 show median |f(x̄)-f*| decaying from 1.33e-1 at iteration 25 to 5.55e-17 at iteration 500, with a semilog fit slope -0.1192 and R²=0.9991 over iterations 20–120, directly demonstrating geometric (linear) convergence to tolerance with zero final constraint violation.

claims.claim: Introduces Algorithm 3, DoWS (Distance over Weighted Subgradients) with Randomized Feasibility, a parameter-free adaptive-stepsize method for convex possibly-nonsmooth objectives, proving an O(1/√T) worst-case convergence rate in expectation (Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 3 was tested on a genuinely nonsmooth 24-dimensional absolute-loss objective with 288 linear inequalities and known optimum, using 24 independent streams at six horizons T=64–2048; the fitted log-log exponent of -0.606 (R²=0.925) is at least as fast as the claimed O(1/√T) worst-case rate, with infeasibility reaching zero by T=256.

claims.claim: Introduces Algorithm 4, T-DoWS (Tamed DoWS), which removes the requirement that the constraint set Y be bounded, retaining an O(1/√T) rate up to logarithmic factors (Theorem 5.5).
claims.evidence: T-DoWS was run on the same 24-dimensional nonsmooth instance but with Y=ℝ²⁴ (identity projection, no bounded-domain safeguard), directly exercising the unbounded-Y setting of Theorem 5.5; 24 runs per horizon yield fitted exponent -1.073 (R²=0.998) with zero final infeasibility, confirming the O(1/√T)-or-faster rate without boundedness of Y.

claims.claim: Proves (Lemma 3.1) that infeasibility of iterates under the randomized feasibility update decreases geometrically almost surely with the number of feasibility updates, without requiring compactness of Y.
claims.evidence: A controlled experiment with 16 orthogonal halfspaces (unbounded feasible region) and 4096 trials at each of 25 update counts matched the exact analytic geometric expectation 16·(15/16)^N: empirical semilog slope -0.06492 vs analytic -0.06454, R²=0.9998, relative RMSE 3.1%, confirming geometric infeasibility reduction without compactness of Y.

claims.claim: Validates the theory on quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP) simulations under strongly convex and convex objectives with known/unknown optimal value f*, confirming predicted function-value decay and geometric infeasibility reduction (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: All four QCQP cases (strongly convex × convex objectives crossed with known-f* Algorithm 2 and unknown-f* DoWS/T-DoWS) were run at d=10, m=1000 with 6 streams; Algorithm 2 reached 0.0 objective error in 140 iterations on both objective types, while parameter-free DoWS and T-DoWS reached 1.5e-16–3.9e-16 and 1.3e-8–3.5e-6 respectively in 1600 iterations, confirming predicted function-value decay across all cases.

claims.claim: Evaluates Algorithms 3 and 4 against a primal-dual baseline on SVM classification with three real datasets (Banknote Authentication, Breast Cancer Wisconsin, MNIST 3-vs-5), comparing test misclassification error (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: DoWS, T-DoWS, and a primal-dual baseline were evaluated on SVM classification with Banknote (n=1372, d=4), Breast Cancer (n=569, d=30), and MNIST 3-vs-5 (n=2000, d=784) using 70/30 splits, 3 seeds, and 3000 iterations; test misclassification error was reported for all methods on all three datasets, with DoWS and T-DoWS achieving 2.1–5.1% test error vs 9.4–44.1% for the baseline. However, the primal-dual baseline's near-random performance (0.44 on banknote) raises concerns about baseline implementation quality.

ProCreations/repro-randomized-feasibilit.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence at the paper's stated scale for all six claims, including geometric convergence of Algorithm 2, O(1/√T)-or-faster rates for DoWS and T-DoWS on nonsmooth problems, analytic verification of Lemma 3.1's geometric infeasibility reduction, all four QCQP cases, and SVM evaluation on three real datasets. The main weakness is the suspiciously poor primal-dual baseline in the SVM experiments, which may indicate an implementation issue rather than a faithful comparison.

Firemedic15/repro-beyond-text-to-sql-can.paper_title: Beyond Text-to-SQL: Can LLMs Really Debug Enterprise ETL SQL?

claims.claim: SQLBench (Squirrel) comprises 469 syntax-error tasks (Squirrel-Syntax) and 516 semantic-error tasks (Squirrel-Semantic), built from over 1,000 seed SQL scripts spanning 26 business scenarios, with scripts averaging over 140 lines, AST width >11, and AST depth >8.7 (Benchmark Construction section).
claims.evidence: The logbook generated a 10-script synthetic corpus mimicking the paper's construction pipeline, measuring 156 lines/script, 1403 tokens, AST depth 10, but the real 985-task benchmark is unreleased and the actual 469/516 task counts, 1,000+ seed scripts, and 26 scenarios were never independently recomputed from real data — only quoted verbatim from the paper.

claims.claim: Claude-4-Sonnet achieves only 36.46% Graph Match score on Squirrel-Syntax debugging and 32.17% on Squirrel-Semantic debugging, the best performance among evaluated models (Main Results table).
claims.evidence: The logbook ran a 20-task toy benchmark (10 syntax + 10 semantic) with 4 open-weight models via HF Inference Providers, but Claude-4-Sonnet was never tested and the real Squirrel Benchmark was never used; the toy results (50-100% GM-proxy) are not numerically comparable to the claimed 36.46%/32.17%, though the experiment does independently corroborate the EM-vs-GM gap motivation.

claims.claim: DeepSeek-V3 scores 30.28% (Graph Match) on Squirrel-Syntax and 21.32% on Squirrel-Semantic, while Qwen-2.5-Coder-32B scores 23.45% on Squirrel-Semantic, with most evaluated LLMs failing to exceed 20% success rate on enterprise SQL debugging (Main Results table).
claims.evidence: The same 20-task toy experiment shows DeepSeek-V3 at 100%/50% and Qwen-2.5-Coder-32B at 100%/60% GM-proxy — far from the paper's 30.28%/21.32%/23.45% — but does reproduce two qualitative patterns (32B > 7B on semantic; Semantic harder than Syntax for all models); the 'most models below 20%' check was arithmetic on the paper's own Table 2, not independent evidence.

claims.claim: SQLBench scripts contain on the order of 420+ tokens and 17.34-21.62 functions per script on average, reflecting enterprise-scale ETL SQL complexity rather than the short queries used in prior Text-to-SQL benchmarks (Benchmark Statistics section).
claims.evidence: The 10-script synthetic toy corpus yields 1403 tokens/script (different tokenizer) and 31 functions/script (regex over-count), which are order-of-magnitude consistent with the claimed 420+ tokens and 17.34-21.62 functions, but the real benchmark data was never accessed and exact figures were never independently re-derived.

Firemedic15/repro-beyond-text-to-sql-can.overall: The logbook confirms the paper's claims are internally consistent across abstract, tables, and body text, and a 20-task synthetic toy benchmark with 4 open-weight models corroborates two qualitative findings (Semantic > Syntax difficulty; model-scale effect within a family). However, the real Squirrel Benchmark is unreleased and Claude-4-Sonnet is unavailable, so no claim was independently reproduced at the paper's actual scale — all experimental evidence is from a clearly simplified toy setup.

MarxistLeninist/repro-approximate-propor.paper_title: Approximate Proportionality in Online Fair Division

claims.claim: Three natural greedy allocation rules (maximize relative item value, allocate to most unsatisfied agent, and minimize worst predicted dissatisfaction) each fail to guarantee any positive multiplicative approximation to PROP1 against an adaptive adversary (Section 3, Propositions 6-8).
claims.evidence: Greedy-1/2 yield realized PROP1 ratio of 0.008 at m=500 on the paper's n=2 adversarial constructions, exactly matching the paper's reported value; Greedy-3 via the Case-1/Case-2 alternation decreases monotonically from 0.870 (m=18) to 0.408 (m=576), consistent with the paper's ~0.385 at length ~500. Unit tests independently confirm greedy1/greedy2 fail below 0.05 on adversarial constructions at n=8, m=400.

claims.claim: Against a non-adaptive adversary, uniform random allocation achieves an Ω(1/log(n/δ)) approximation to PROP1 with probability at least 1-δ, specifically α = 27/(128·log(n/δ)), the first such multiplicative bound in the online setting without extra assumptions (Section 4, Theorem 9).
claims.evidence: Over a grid of n∈{2,…,64} and δ∈{0.2,0.1,0.05,0.02} with 20,000 random allocations per point, empirical failure probability is 0.0000 at the theoretical α, satisfying the ≥1−δ guarantee. Tightness is confirmed by regressing 1/α* on log(n/δ) yielding slope 1.02, R²=0.81, confirming α*=Θ(1/log(n/δ)). Note: the logbook tested α=3/(32·log(n/δ)) from the proof rather than the claimed 27/(128·log(n/δ)), but the empirical α* values far exceed both constants, so the core claim is supported.

claims.claim: Given perfect maximum-item-value (MIV) predictions, Algorithm 1 guarantees a 1/n-PROP1 allocation (Section 5, Theorem 11).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 with perfect MIV predictions achieves PROP1 ratio ≥ 1/n with zero violations across 400 random instances (n∈{2..6}, m∈{1..40}) and adversarial constructions (n∈{2,5,8}, m=200), confirmed by passing unit tests. Across four instance families (uniform, dense, correlated, specialist), Algorithm 1 maintains PROP1=1.0 in all cases, and the executive summary reports 0 violations over 6,009 instances.

claims.claim: Under one-sided MIV prediction error ε ∈ [0,1), the algorithm's approximation degrades gracefully to β = (1-ε)/(n-ε/n) (Section 5, Theorem 12).
claims.evidence: The β=(1−ε)/(n−ε/n) formula is verified to machine precision at ε=0 (recovering 1/n=0.167 for n=6), and across ε∈{0,0.1,…,0.9} with 400 trials each, the worst realized PROP1 ratio always exceeds β(ε). A mutation control (argmin→argmax selection) breaks the guarantee 125/400 times, confirming the mechanism is load-bearing. Unit test test_beta_formulas_consistent confirms formula consistency across multiple ε values.

claims.claim: Even with perfect MIV predictions, no online algorithm can achieve any non-zero approximation to EF1, MMS, or PROPX (Section 5, Proposition 10).
claims.evidence: An exact rational-arithmetic certificate (Python fractions.Fraction) evaluated 30 universal parameter cells (n∈{2,3,5,8,16}, α∈{1/2,…,1/64}) showing EF1, MMS, and PROPX ratios strictly below α in all cases, plus exhaustive enumeration of all 1,032 n=2 trajectory classes. The logbook audited the paper's printed proof, found and documented defects in the PROPX branch, provided a corrected construction, and verified it with exact arithmetic. A mutation control (removing the cap correction c) causes 6/6 cells to fail, confirming the correction is load-bearing.

MarxistLeninist/repro-approximate-propor.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental and exact-arithmetic evidence supporting all five claims: adversarial constructions drive greedy rules toward zero PROP1 ratio, RAND's logarithmic guarantee and tightness are confirmed across a parameter grid, Algorithm 1 achieves 1/n-PROP1 with zero violations on thousands of instances, the robust degradation formula is verified with mutation controls, and an exact certificate confirms the EF1/MMS/PROPX impossibility (with a corrected proof of the paper's printed PROPX argument).

Srishti280992/repro-lower-bounds-for-fra.paper_title: Lower Bounds for Frank-Wolfe on Strongly Convex Sets

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a constructive Omega(1/sqrt(epsilon)) lower bound on the number of iterations for Frank-Wolfe with short steps or exact line search when both the objective and the constraint set are smooth and strongly convex (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: The script instantiates the constructive proof recipe for T in {100, 1000, 10000}; for T=10000 it builds 20,000 forward states with min_lower_bound_ratio=1.0 (residual r_t >= r0/(1+8*r0*t/3) at every step, confirming gap >= Omega(1/t^2)), max one-step forward-backward error 7.62e-217, zero domain violations, and zero monotonicity violations, all at 220-digit precision.

claims.claim: The lower-bound construction uses the specific instance of minimizing f(x) = ||x-p||_2^2 over the Euclidean unit ball B_1(0) with the unconstrained minimizer p on the boundary (||p||=1), showing this hard instance matches the known O(1/sqrt(epsilon)) upper bound of Garber et al. (2015) (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: Source audit confirms the paper defines the instance as min_{x in B_1(0)} ||x-p||^2 with ||p||=1; the verifier uses p=(1,0), applies the closed-form ball LMO and exact line search, and confirms the resulting (r,s) dynamics match the paper recurrence with max forward-dynamics error 1.52e-11 against the released 1000-row CSV.

claims.claim: The lower bound is established via a 'backward reconstruction' technique that builds worst-case trajectories by working backward from terminal iterates, producing precise sequences over horizons of 10,000+ iterations (Section on Backward Reconstruction Strategy).
claims.evidence: The backward map G(r,s)=(r/(X+Y), X+Y) is implemented starting from (epsilon, 1-4*epsilon/3+2*epsilon^2); for target T=10000 it produces 20,000 constructed steps with max one-step forward-backward L1 error 7.62e-217 at 220-digit precision, independently confirmed by a Hugging Face CPU Job (max_one_step_l1=4.07e-85, constructed_steps=20000).

claims.claim: The analysis reduces the dynamics to a two-dimensional invariant subspace parametrized by residual magnitude r and contraction factor s, revealing stable phases of monotonically increasing contraction followed by intermittent 'jumps' that explain the convergence stalling behavior (Section on Dynamical Analysis).
claims.evidence: The (r,s) two-dimensional recurrence is implemented and verified with zero domain violations and zero monotonicity violations over stable phases for T up to 10000; the released 1000-row paper CSV confirms the forward recurrence (max error 1.52e-11) and exhibits 6 contraction decreases consistent with the claimed intermittent jumps.

claims.claim: The result shows strong convexity of the constraint set alone cannot yield convergence rates uniformly faster than O(1/sqrt(epsilon)), and this conclusion holds dimension-independently and extends to ellipsoidal constraints via affine invariance (Theorem 6, Implications).
claims.evidence: Source audit confirms the paper states Theorem 6 for every d>=2 with iterates confined to the 2D span of p and x0; the ellipsoid affine reduction is smoke-tested with A=diag(4,1) over 200 sampled states, yielding max affine commutation error 1.16e-16 and max constraint value 0.993, confirming the affine map commutes with exact line-search FW steps.

Srishti280992/repro-lower-bounds-for-fra.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all five claims through high-precision (220-digit) instantiation of the paper's constructive backward-reconstruction proof, forward-backward consistency checks at horizons up to T=10000, comparison with the released trajectory CSV, and an affine-invariance smoke test for the ellipsoid extension. This is a rigorous reproduction of a theoretical lower-bound construction rather than an empirical training experiment, and the evidence is appropriate for verifying constructive mathematical results.

Srishti280992/repro-exact-functional-ano.paper_title: Exact Functional ANOVA Decomposition for Categorical Inputs Models

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 establishes that any function in L^2 over categorical inputs admits a Fourier expansion using basis functions phi_A^(z), defined via a signed inverse-likelihood construction, that automatically satisfy hierarchical orthogonality (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: The revision run uses the official FullSupportAnova on a 5-variable, 243-state full grid under four structurally different PMFs (factorized, pair_dep, triple_dep, skew_dep), checking 54,728 hierarchical conditional-mean pairs with max residual 6.96e-13 and max reconstruction error 5.33e-15.

claims.claim: When the empirical support equals the full hypergrid, the exact ANOVA decomposition is obtained by solving the linear system Gamma c(f) = mu(f) (Section on full-support decomposition).
claims.evidence: A dense full-support solve on the complete Car Evaluation hypergrid (cardinalities (4,4,4,3,3,3), 1,728 states and 1,728 basis coefficients) under a nonuniform dependent PMF yields max absolute reconstruction error 5.77e-15 and weighted MSE 5.46e-30.

claims.claim: For sparse empirical support of cardinality r much smaller than the full hypergrid size |E|, Algorithm 1 greedily selects basis elements to yield decomposition computation in O(r^3) rather than O(|E|^3) (Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The extracted paper text states Algorithm 1 enumerates |E| candidate basis functions with per-step O(r^2) rank checks, yielding effective cost O(|E| * r_low^2) under a low-rank budget—not standalone O(r^3). The sparse mechanism itself works (selector reaches rank r without forming |E|×|E| systems), but the specific O(r^3) complexity claim is contradicted by the paper's own stated complexity.

claims.claim: On the Mushrooms dataset (22 categorical variables, hypergrid size approximately 10^14), the method achieves near-perfect reconstruction (R^2 approximately 1, MSE approximately 10^-15) in 0.3 seconds (Experimental results section).
claims.evidence: An authenticated HF Job reran the official Mushroom protocol with XGBoost (100 estimators, lr=0.1, max_depth=5) on all 8,124 samples: R²=0.999992 (near-perfect, as claimed), but MSE=1.967e-6 (vs claimed ~1e-15, off by 9 orders of magnitude) and ANOVA time=9.133s (vs claimed 0.3s, 30× slower).

claims.claim: On binarized MNIST (784 dimensions), the method achieves R^2 = 0.86 in 15 minutes using 10,000 basis elements (Experimental results section).
claims.evidence: An H200 HF Job used the official commit, all 60,000 binarized MNIST training images, the paper's MLP architecture (3 epochs), and the official BinaryBasisExtractor with n_set=10,000 (exactly 10,000 accepted basis elements over 59,984 unique patterns). For digit 3, R²=0.8657, matching the claimed 0.86; runtime was 25.06 min vs claimed 15 min, a plausible hardware difference.

claims.claim: Equation (5) defines generalized SHAP values as shap_i(x) = sum over sets A containing i of f_A(x_A)/|A|, which exactly recovers standard SHAP values in the independent-features setting (Equation 5).
claims.evidence: The official FullSupportAnova plus batch_shapley_values was compared against an independent exhaustive interventional Shapley enumerator on the full uniform binary (0,1)^3 grid (8 states, 3 features): max absolute disagreement 1.11e-16, mean 6.64e-17, and efficiency residual 1.67e-16, confirming exact recovery at machine precision.

Srishti280992/repro-exact-functional-ano.overall: The logbook provides concrete evidence verifying the algebraic claims (1, 2, 6) on non-trivial grids using the official code, and verifies the MNIST R² benchmark (5) at full scale via an H200 HF Job. Claims 3 and 4 are falsified: the paper's own text states O(|E|·r²) rather than O(r³), and the Mushrooms MSE and runtime are off by orders of magnitude from the claimed values.

svdrecbd/repro-fractional-is-better.paper_title: Fractional is Better: Learnable Derivative Orders in Neural Operator Learning
