amkkk/repro-fine-tuning-without-forgetti.paper_title: Fine-Tuning Without Forgetting In-Context Learning: A Theoretical Analysis of Linear Attention Models

claims.claim: Corollary 4.4 shows that full fine-tuning of all attention parameters in a linear attention model drives zero-shot error to σ² while few-shot (in-context) error converges to σ² + θᵀΣθ, a substantially larger value, formalizing the degradation of in-context learning after full fine-tuning (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Independent Monte Carlo at n=2000 reproduces the asymptotic predictions (ZS 0.099990 vs 0.100; FS 1.129446 vs 1.100) within tolerance, and the gradient-trained n=20 model shows the predicted few-shot degradation (FS 1.671 vs pretrain FS 0.363, and above ZS 0.104).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 shows that restricting fine-tuning updates to the value matrix reduces zero-shot error to σ² + (2/(d+4))θ₀ᵀΣθ₀ while Corollary 4.8 shows the asymptotic few-shot error only rises to σ² + 1/(d+4)²θ₀ᵀΣθ₀, i.e. value-matrix-only fine-tuning improves zero-shot performance with far less degradation to in-context learning than full fine-tuning (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Independent MC confirms the closed-form value-only predictions (ZS 0.322333 vs 0.322222; FS n=2000 0.115994 vs 0.112346), and the gradient-trained model shows ZS improvement (0.343 from pretrain 1.091) with far lower FS than full-FT (0.318 vs 1.671).

claims.claim: Proposition 4.10 proves that tuning the auxiliary few-shot loss weight w to optimize few-shot performance on the fine-tuning task θ₀ necessarily reduces few-shot performance on other tasks θ ≠ θ₀, formalizing a trade-off between target-task adaptation and generalization to unseen tasks (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: The finite-n formula and MC show the trade-off for θ=−θ₀ (target improves 0.470→0.326, OOD degrades 0.372→0.459), but the gradient-trained run does not reproduce the target improvement (aux 0.320 vs value-only 0.318), and only one OOD task is tested—insufficient for the claim's universal 'necessarily reduces.'

claims.claim: In synthetic linear-regression experiments (d=5, σ²=0.1, Σ=I₅, ‖θ₀‖₂²=1, m=n=20), Figure 4 confirms the theoretical zero-shot/few-shot error predictions across pretraining, full fine-tuning, and value-matrix fine-tuning regimes, and Figure 5 shows value-matrix fine-tuning attains the lowest error on the out-of-distribution task -θ₀ (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: At the paper's d=5 synthetic scale, the OOD ranking is confirmed (FT-value 0.394 lowest among fine-tuned regimes vs FT-all 1.344 and aux 0.462) and theory-derived MC curves match closed forms (max error 0.122), but the gradient-trained full-FT curve has a 46.8% max relative error, so Figure 4's broad confirmation is only partial.

claims.claim: On the MMLU benchmark using Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct fine-tuned on the Humanities category, full fine-tuning improves zero-shot accuracy but degrades 7-shot accuracy, whereas value-matrix-only fine-tuning preserves few-shot accuracy while still improving zero-shot performance (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: No MMLU experiment was run—no fine-tuning, no evaluation, no accuracy numbers. The local RTX 5070 (12 GB) was deemed insufficient for the paper's Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct LoRA setup, so the claim was never addressed.

amkkk/repro-fine-tuning-without-forgetti.overall: The logbook provides solid numerical verification of the core theoretical claims (Claims 1–2) through independent Monte Carlo and gradient-trained runs at the paper's synthetic scale, but the auxiliary-loss trade-off (Claim 3) has mixed evidence and the MMLU experiment (Claim 5) was never attempted due to hardware constraints.

amkkk/repro-unveiling-the-structure-of-d.paper_title: Unveiling the Structure of Do-Calculus Reasoning via Derivation Graphs

claims.claim: For a graph with no edges, the derivation graph decomposes into 2^|V|-1 connected components, one per distinct outcome variable (Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: Empty-graph component counts verified exhaustively for n=3,4,5 (7/15/31 = 2^n−1) plus subgraph property on two small ADMGs, but these are small instances of a universal mathematical proposition, not a full proof or large-scale verification.

claims.claim: The number of causally equivalent expressions reachable via do-calculus derivations is upper bounded by 3^|V\Y|, where Y is the set of outcome variables (Proposition 2).
claims.evidence: Bound |A^G_Q| ≤ 3^|V\Y| checked on 212 components across small graphs (empty-3, chain-3, napkin, Fig-1) with tightness on empty-3 (7/7), but the Sachs check (32 ≤ 59049) is trivially satisfied and the meaningful evidence comes from graphs with only 3–5 nodes.

claims.claim: Any two derivations of the same interventional distribution are connected by a path of length at most four in the derivation graph, using the canonical rule pattern R2-up, R3-up, R3-down, R2-down (Theorem 6, Corollary 2).
claims.evidence: Canonical 4-block pattern verified on 51810 ordered pairs across six small ADMGs (3–5 nodes) and 992 pairs on the Sachs 32-node component with 0 mismatches, but the primary evidence is from toy-sized graphs; the Sachs check covers only one component of one graph for a universal diameter claim.

claims.claim: Two expressions derivable from one another via arbitrary recursive do-calculus rule applications can always be connected using just two applications of Rule R2 and two applications of Rule R3, showing Rule R1 is redundant for this purpose (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: R1 redundancy verified on 2004 directed R1 labels across the same six small ADMGs (3–5 nodes) and canonical 2×R2+2×R3 completeness on 44600 equivalent pairs, but all substantive checks are on toy-sized graphs; the Sachs component check is supplementary and limited to one query.

claims.claim: On the Sachs protein-signaling dataset, the derivation-graph approach identifies 32 causally equivalent density expressions for the same query, yielding 11 distinct estimators whose bootstrap variance ranges from 0.000016 to 0.001032 (Table 1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: Full Sachs experiment reproduced at paper scale: 853 rows × 500 bootstraps yielding 32 equivalent densities → 11 adjustment sets, with measured bootstrap variance range 1.6400e-5 to 1.0324e-3 matching the paper's 0.000016 to 0.001032, variance ranking match, and individual estimator values agreeing to <5e-7.

claims.claim: Rule R2 applications commute with each other, and simultaneous or sequential insertions of multiple actions yield equivalent derivations, while R2 and R3 exhibit only weak commutativity that holds solely when applied in the same direction (Theorems 3, 4, 5).
claims.evidence: Commutativity properties checked on the napkin graph and specific paper counterexamples (R2 commutativity, R3 one-way, R2/R3 weak same-direction) with 33/33 unit tests passing, but these are representative checks on a single small example graph, not a general verification of the theorems.

amkkk/repro-unveiling-the-structure-of-d.overall: The logbook provides a full-scale, faithful reproduction of the Sachs experiment (Claim 5) with closely matching numerical results, but the five mathematical propositions and theorems (Claims 1–4, 6) are only verified computationally on small toy-sized graphs (3–5 nodes) or single example graphs, which constitutes partial evidence rather than full verification of universal claims.

Srishti280992/repro-solving-imperfect-re.paper_title: Solving Imperfect-Recall Games via Sum-of-Squares Optimization

claims.claim: For single-player imperfect-recall extensive-form games (IREFGs), the Sum-of-Squares/moment hierarchy converges to the optimal utility u* as the relaxation degree d goes to infinity, i.e. lim_{d→∞} u^d_sos = lim_{d→∞} u^d_mom = u* (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The hard_hierarchy.py run on the paper's G2 absentminded game (4 variables, two 3-action simplexes, quartic utility) computes certified upper bounds at orders 2, 3, 4: 1.0075070 → 1.0000086 → 1.0000040, monotonically converging toward the known optimum of 1.0 with 70×70 moment matrices at order 4.

claims.claim: Under a genericity assumption on the utility function u, the SOS hierarchy for single-player IREFGs achieves finite convergence at some finite degree d ≥ d0, rather than only asymptotic convergence (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The reproduction.py run solves 100 generic quartic single-player IREFGs (two information sets, three actions each, four reduced variables) with order-2 moment SDPs; all 100 achieve finite convergence with max SDP/oracle gap 4.37e-08 and max first-moment extraction error 1.71e-04.

claims.claim: For single-player non-absentminded IREFGs, the degree-(ℓ+1) SOS relaxation is exact, i.e. a single semidefinite program at that level solves the game exactly (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The NAM exactness suite tests 12 multiaffine games with 1–4 information sets at moment orders [2,3,4,5] matching d=ℓ+1, comparing against exhaustive pure-vertex enumeration over 90 vertices with max gap 2.80e-05, and symbolically verifies the SOS identity u*−u = Σ_b (u*−u(b))δ_b² modulo the Boolean ideal with zero coefficient residual.

claims.claim: A Select-Verify-Cut framework extends the KKT-based moment-SOS hierarchy to multi-player IREFGs, yielding analogous finite-convergence and single-level-solvability guarantees under genericity and non-absentmindedness (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: The Select-Verify-Cut suite runs 40 two-player polynomial IREFGs (each player: 2 info sets, 3 actions, 4 reduced variables) with 160 order-2 moment-SDP unilateral best-response solves and 0 non-SDP oracles; first KKT candidates are rejected in 40/40 cases, all traces terminate in two rounds, and max final unilateral improvement is 0.000.

claims.claim: Strictly concave/monotone single-player IREFGs are shown to admit finite SOS convergence, while SOS-concave/SOS-monotone IREFGs converge already at the first hierarchy level (Theorem 6.1).
claims.evidence: The concave suite tests 100 two-infoset three-action product-of-simplices games with u(z)=1−‖z−a‖² (negative Hessian 2I with explicit √2·I SOS factor); the first Moment-SOS level is exact in 100/100 with max objective gap 5.29e-09 and max first-moment extraction error 5.30e-05.

claims.claim: In the empirical comparison of Table 1 (Section 7), the SOS approach consistently recovers certified global optima across tested instances, whereas projected gradient descent only succeeds probabilistically, with reported success rates in the 70-89% range.
claims.evidence: Fifty degree-4 polynomial games over two 3-action simplexes are each solved with an order-2 moment SDP (max SOS/feasible gap 0.0) and challenged with 100 PGD restarts (eta=0.02, 5000 steps); PGD mean success rate is 75.88% with range 20%–100%, consistent with the paper's reported 70–89% band.

Srishti280992/repro-solving-imperfect-re.overall: The logbook provides concrete SDP-based experimental evidence on non-trivial game instances (product-of-simplices strategy spaces, quartic utilities, multi-information-set games) supporting all six claims, with 12–100 instances per claim and both numerical and symbolic verification. The main limitation is backend substitution from Julia/MOSEK to Python/CVXPY/CLARABEL-SCS, which preserves the polynomial/moment structure but introduces solver-precision warnings at higher hierarchy orders.

ProCreations/repro-revisiting-the-bertra.paper_title: Revisiting the Bertrand Paradox via Equilibrium Analysis of No-regret Learners

claims.claim: For symmetric-cost Bertrand competition with any non-increasing demand function, Theorem 2.1 shows two no-external-regret learners can sustain high prices while guaranteeing each firm's utility is at least 1/(4e^2) of the monopoly profit (Theorem 2.1).
claims.evidence: LP solutions at k={8,16,32,64,128} for constant demand find valid CCEs (max external deviation gain ≤1.03e-15) with per-player utility ~0.366-0.368, well above the 1/(4e²)≈0.034 floor; claims 4 and 6 extend comparable CCE results to linear, quadratic, and exponential demand.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.2 shows that when both learners use no-swap-regret algorithms, prices converge toward marginal cost, with expected utility bounded above by f(c+1/k)/k, demonstrating strong competitive pressure (Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: Complete CE polytope optimization at k={8,16,32,64,128} with c=0 yields maximum expected price exactly 2/k at every resolution (log-log slope −1), zero swap deviation gain, and no support above 2/k, confirming prices vanish toward marginal cost.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.3 shows an asymmetric setting—one no-external-regret learner paired with one no-swap-regret learner—can still sustain high, collusive-like prices under certain demand structures such as constant demand (Theorem 2.3).
claims.evidence: Hybrid equilibrium LPs at k={8,16,24,32} with player 1 under swap deviations and player 2 under external deviations yield minimum normalized utility 0.166-0.173 and transaction price 0.334-0.382, with both deviation gains ≤5.17e-17, directly certifying high-price equilibria in the asymmetric deviation-class setting.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.5 shows that as the number of firms n grows, the total utility attainable under no-external-regret dynamics decays exponentially, as e^(1-n/2) (Theorem 2.5).
claims.evidence: Symmetric-diagonal CCE LPs for n=2…10 at k=100 across four demand functions show negative log-utility slopes (−0.54 to −0.64) consistent with exponential decay; all 36 optima satisfy the Theorem 2.5 bound with minimum slack 0.204, and max recomputed deviation gain is 3.17e-15.

claims.claim: Under asymmetric costs, Theorem 2.6 shows high-utility coarse correlated equilibria exist for broad demand classes (including linear and exponential demand) under no-external-regret learning, while Theorem 2.7 shows that under no-swap-regret learning the higher-cost firm's utility converges to zero regardless of the demand function (Theorems 2.6 and 2.7).
claims.evidence: With c1=0, c2=0.25 across four demand functions at k={16,24,32,48}, CCE LPs yield minimum monopoly-normalized utility 0.261-0.319 (Theorem 2.6), while CE LPs maximizing the higher-cost firm's utility return exactly 0.0 in all 16 games (Theorem 2.7), with deviation residuals ≤2.70e-16.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments across multiple demand functions show utilities converging toward 1/e ≈ 0.368 of the monopoly utility under no-external-regret dynamics (Numerical results section).
claims.evidence: Utility-maximizing symmetric CCE LPs at k={25,50,100,200,400} for four demand functions converge to ratios of 0.36786-0.36788 at k=400, with absolute errors from 1/e of 1.11e-6 to 1.81e-5 and maximum deviation residual 1.61e-11.

ProCreations/repro-revisiting-the-bertra.overall: The logbook provides concrete LP-based equilibrium computations across multiple grid resolutions, demand functions, firm counts, and cost structures that independently verify all six claims with numerically certified deviation constraints. The methodology computes exact CCE/CE solutions rather than simulating learning trajectories, which is a faithful but indirect test of the no-regret convergence claims given the paper's equilibrium-to-learning bridge theorems.

AceVikings/repro-tucker-attention-a-gene.paper_title: Tucker Attention: A generalization of approximate attention mechanisms

AceVikings/repro-tucker-attention-a-gene.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical verification of the algebraic and scaling claims (claims 1, 5, 6) and a partial parameter-count verification for GPT-2 (claim 3), but does not run any actual model training, leaving the ViT and LLaMA3 performance claims (claims 2, 4) entirely unaddressed.

AceVikings/repro-multi-view-causal-disco.paper_title: Multi-View Causal Discovery without Non-Gaussianity: Identifiability and Algorithms

claims.claim: The Linear Multi-View Acyclic Model (LiMVAM) achieves identifiability of causal structure from multiple related datasets under Gaussian disturbances by exploiting noise-variance diversity across views (Assumption 1) rather than relying on non-Gaussianity (Section on Main Theorems).

claims.evidence: The output shows numerically distinct LSE and LSR phase boundaries at five temperatures (e.g., T=0.5: alpha_c^LSE=0.1489 vs alpha_c^LSR=0.0074; T=0.1: 0.3475 vs 0.3175). claims.claim: The lower-bound construction uses the specific instance of minimizing f(x) = ||x-p||_2^2 over the Euclidean unit ball B_1(0) with the unconstrained minimizer p on the boundary (||p||=1), showing this hard instance matches the known O(1/sqrt(epsilon)) upper bound of Garber et al. (2015) (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: The audit uses p=(0,1), Hessian 2I, unit-ball LMO, and exact line search; at iteration 10,000 the gap is 5.62e-9 with t²×gap=0.561650, and a 512-step Cartesian vector replay matches the scalar recurrence to 2.7e-152 with zero feasibility violation.

claims.claim: Section 4 numerical experiments show that existing Robust PCA methods fail to recover the true principal component even with only 5% outlier proportion when the aspect ratio d/n does not vanish (e.g., d/n=1), whereas MS-PCA consistently recovers it (Figure 2, Section 4).

ai-sherpa/adalina-shapley-semivalue-repr.paper_title: Adalina: Adaptive Linear Approximation for the Shapley Value and Beyond

claims.claim: Adalina (Algorithm 1) is a randomized adaptive linear-approximation algorithm achieving O(n/ε² log(1/δ)) utility-query complexity while using only Θ(n) space (Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Closed-form D* matches paper to 2.7e-15 at n=8; source-bound scaling sweeps show n-slope=1.000, ε-slope=-2.000, δ-spread=0.000 across n up to 1024; streaming memory log-log slope=0.9995 up to n=3072 (860KB vs 75MB for quadratic); seeded 1/T MSE slope=-0.983.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 shows that under an optimal sampling distribution q*_s, Adalina attains query complexity O(nD*C²/ε² log(2/δ)) where D*∈O(1) for both Beta Shapley and weighted Banzhaf semi-values, improving on OFA's O(n log n/(ε²δ)) bound (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: D* confirmed bounded for weighted Banzhaf (→4.760) and Beta(2,3) (→5.529) up to n=512; source bound T≥36nD*C²ε⁻²log(4/δ) verified with exact axis scaling; uniform/optimal D ratio grows from 1.03 to 1.50 (Shapley n=8→512), consistent with OFA's worse scaling.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 proves that paired sampling reduces the estimation problem to approximating (U−U^c)/2 and provably lowers MSE whenever E[U(S)·U([n]\S)] > 0 (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Exact paired-sampling identities computed: anti-complement utility (E[U·Uᶜ]<0) gives ratio 2.000 (worsens), positive-complement (E[U·Uᶜ]>0) gives ratio 0.280 (improves), confirming the sign of E[U·Uᶜ] governs MSE change as Theorem 3.2 states.

claims.claim: Experiments on spambase (n=57), FOTP (n=51), MinibooNE (n=50), and philippine (n=308) datasets, using 1000 queries per player averaged over 10 seeds, empirically validate the theoretical complexity/variance predictions (Figures 1-4).
claims.evidence: All four OpenML datasets downloaded with correct feature counts (57/51/50/308); GradientBoostingClassifier retrained with 10 trees at paper's depths; path-dependent U_f^x validated against model's decision_function to 1.3e-15; exact closed-form ground truth (efficiency identity 1.7e-13); 9.32M utility evaluations at 1000 queries/player × 10 seeds; MSE(Adalina)/MSE(oracle)∈[0.9998,1.0002]; closed-form MSE prediction within 7.4% across 31× MSE range.

ai-sherpa/adalina-shapley-semivalue-repr.overall: This logbook provides a thorough independent reproduction of all five claims, combining machine-precision closed-form verifications, scaling sweeps up to n=1024, memory measurements to n=3072, and 9.32M real utility evaluations on the paper's four OpenML datasets with exact ground truth. The scope limitations (2 semi-values per dataset, single test instance, MinibooNE subsampled to 20k rows, baselines characterized analytically) are honestly disclosed but do not undermine the core theoretical and empirical predictions.

kondratevakate/repro-accurate-evaluation.paper_title: Accurate Evaluation of Quickest Changepoint Detectors via Non-parametric Survival Analysis

claims.evidence: Independent derivation audit confirms the exponential H(t)^(N-1) factor in Eq. (8); numerical audit with 500,000 datasets per cell over N={2..64} shows bias contracting from +0.574 to +0.0016 with bound width shrinking 25.8x; destructive control removing independent censoring causes bound failure by >10x.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 establishes finite-sample bias bounds for the KM-ADD estimator under independent censoring.
claims.evidence: ADD-specific derivation audit confirms the reduction to Eq. (9) bounds; numerical audit with 500,000 datasets per cell over N''={2..64} shows all bias±5SE intervals inside independently computed bounds, with bias contracting from +0.435 to +0.001; destructive control confirms independent censoring is load-bearing.

claims.claim: Theorems 4.3 and 4.4 show that the truncation bias of KM-ARL and KM-ADD is smaller than that of conventional (non-censoring-aware) ARL/ADD estimators.

claims.claim: KM-ARL and KM-ADD are shown to be asymptotically unbiased (Equation 11) whenever the support of the detection-point distribution does not exceed the censoring boundary, without requiring parametric assumptions (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Both directions of the iff tested: with support satisfied (T=5000), KM-ARL relative bias converges -0.023→+0.005→+0.001→+0.003 as N grows 50→20000; with support violated (T=100), bias plateaus at ~-0.107 and does not vanish, confirming the support condition is load-bearing.

claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states the WISDM real-data variance claim was not attempted; no experiments on the 51,326-sequence WISDM Actitracker dataset were run.

kondratevakate/repro-accurate-evaluation.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting five of six claims through independent derivation audits, large-scale Monte Carlo bound checks (500K datasets/cell), multi-seed simulation sweeps on both Gaussian and Poisson processes, and destructive controls confirming key assumptions are load-bearing. The WISDM real-data variance claim (Claim 5) was never attempted, leaving it inconclusive.

MarxistLeninist/HMyCBL2yMV.paper_title: Beyond First-order Asymptotics in Sequential Mean Testing

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 establishes a central limit theorem for the empirical KL_inf statistic, showing sqrt(n)(KL_inf(q_hat_n, m_o) - KL_inf(q, m_o)) converges in distribution to N(0, sigma^2(q, m_o)) (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo with 5000 replicates at n=5000 shows KS distance 0.0132 for Beta(3,2) and 0.0202 for Bernoulli(0.6), variance ratios 1.0079 and 0.9480, and Gaussian 95% coverage 0.9490 and 0.9586 respectively, with clear convergence trend across n=50,200,1000,5000.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 extends this result to the stopping time tau_alpha, proving sqrt(log(1/alpha))(tau_alpha/log(1/alpha) - 1/KL_inf(q,m_o)) converges to a Gaussian limit N(0, sigma^2_bd(q,m_o)) as alpha to 0 (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: With 10000 replicates, the constant boundary shows KS decreasing from 0.1387 to 0.0266 and variance ratio approaching 1.0 across alpha=1e-2 to 1e-64; the theorem's exact growing boundary also converges (KS 0.5014→0.0585, variance ratio 2.3563→1.0224) but much more slowly, confirming the asymptotic claim while revealing slow finite-sample convergence.

claims.claim: The proof decomposes the normalized KL_inf statistic into a term from the dual optimization (shown to vanish in probability) and a standard empirical-mean term that converges to Gaussian, combined with verification of Anscombe's condition to transfer the CLT to the stopping time (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The T1 (dual optimization) RMS decreases from 0.1043 to 0.0124 for Beta and 0.1249 to 0.0115 for Bernoulli as n goes from 50 to 5000, T2 KS distances match the predicted Gaussian, and local-oscillation diagnostics at n=8000 show p90 of 0.1063 for delta=0.05 vs 0.2114 for delta=0.20, supporting the Anscombe mechanism.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.5 constructs asymptotically valid confidence intervals for the stopping time using only a single simulation run, without requiring multiple independent replicates (Proposition 4.5).
claims.evidence: Each interval uses only its own path (single run confirmed), and coverage of 1/KL_inf approaches 0.95 (0.9454 at largest growing-boundary scale, ~0.95 for constant boundary with variance ratio 1.0007); the interval targets the deterministic center 1/KL_inf rather than a future random stopping time, but the asymptotic validity and single-run property are supported.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments on synthetic Beta and Bernoulli distributions and on real crop-yield data show empirical stopping-time distributions converging to the theoretical Gaussian limit, with stronger agreement at smaller significance levels alpha (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Synthetic Beta/Bernoulli experiments reproduce with 5000-10000 replicates; the DSSAT public maize pool (44 yields, 8 experiment files, commit-pinned) with 3000 bootstrap paths shows KS decreasing monotonically (0.140→0.120→0.0920) across alpha=1e-2,1e-3,1e-4, variance ratio 0.9514, and coverage 0.9663 at alpha=1e-4, though using a different pool than the authors' unreleased one.

MarxistLeninist/HMyCBL2yMV.overall: The logbook provides rigorous Monte Carlo evidence with thousands of replicates supporting all five claims, including exact dual-score solver implementations, unit-tested decomposition identities, and a real-data extension on public DSSAT crop yields. The main limitations are the slow finite-sample convergence of the theorem's exact growing boundary and the inability to match the authors' private crop-yield pool exactly.

snaykey/repro-llapdiff.paper_title: Latent Laplace Diffusion for Irregular Multivariate Time Series

claims.claim: LLapDiff models irregular targets as low-dimensional latent trajectories, enabling horizon-wide generation without numerical integration over physical time (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: A real end-to-end trained LLapDiff on the crypto dataset (H=20, 16-dim latents) generates the full horizon in a fixed 24-step diffusion pass with no ODE/numerical integrator invoked, producing a genuine forecast (CRPS 0.3646, MSE 0.5750 below the trivial baseline).

claims.claim: The denoiser parameterizes mean evolution in the Laplace domain with stable complex-conjugate poles for direct evaluation at irregular timestamps (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: After real end-to-end training, all 512 learned Laplace poles are stable with discrete-time magnitudes in [0.809, 0.987] (stable fraction 1.0), directly confirming the stable complex-conjugate parameterization on a trained model.

claims.claim: A renewal-averaging analysis maps irregular sampling gaps to effective event-domain poles and motivates gap-aware history conditioning (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Gap-sensitivity is demonstrated only at the architecture level (untrained summarizer L2=3.27 for uniform vs irregular gaps); the trained-summarizer re-probe failed due to a window-size mismatch, and the renewal-averaging derivation was not independently re-derived, leaving the claim addressed via proxy mechanism checks rather than full validation.

claims.claim: Across seven real-world datasets, LLapDiff reports the strongest long-horizon probabilistic forecasting results on the main CRPS/MSE comparison (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Only 1 of 7 datasets (crypto) was evaluated with no baselines and a scaled budget (18 vs 600 epochs, 6 vs 25 samples), so the specific claim of strongest forecasting across seven datasets cannot be assessed; the ranking claim is unaddressed.

claims.claim: The same queried latent-trajectory model performs missing-value imputation by querying historical timestamps without retraining (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The same trained checkpoint with no retraining performs imputation on hidden historical timestamps under two masking regimes (regular-keep CRPS 0.367, random-mask-30% CRPS 0.370), with observed targets reconstructed better than hidden ones, directly confirming the claim on a real dataset.

snaykey/repro-llapdiff.overall: This logbook provides real end-to-end GPU training evidence on one real dataset (crypto) confirming the core architectural mechanism claims (latent trajectory generation, stable Laplace poles, same-model imputation without retraining), but does not address the multi-dataset ranking claim and only partially validates the gap-aware conditioning analysis. The reproduction is meaningfully scaled down (18 vs 600 epochs, 1 vs 7 datasets, no baselines).

ai-sherpa/statistical-evaluability-gener.paper_title: A Theoretical Framework for Statistical Evaluability of Generative Models

claims.claim: For binary-valued test function classes with finite VC dimension d, the corresponding IPM is strongly evaluable with sample complexity O((d log(1/epsilon) + log(1/delta))/epsilon^2), while unbounded VC dimension gives only 3-weak evaluability, with the constant 3 shown to be optimal (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Finite-VC half: KS convergence exponent fitted at -0.515 vs theory -0.5 (R²=0.9994) over n∈{50..3200}, and at theorem-prescribed m=9587 for (eps=0.05, delta=0.05) the empirical failure rate is 0.0 over 5000 trials. Unbounded-VC half: naive plug-in TV is exactly 1.0 for every n∈{10..3200} (impossibility of c=1), while a coarser √n-bin comparator's error shrinks 0.140→0.0094. The c=3 optimality constant is not independently tested (acknowledged as a cited external result).

claims.claim: For bounded real-valued test classes, finite gamma-fat-shattering dimension for all gamma in (0, 1/2] implies strong (arbitrary-precision) evaluability, whereas unbounded fat-shattering dimension yields only 3-weak evaluability (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Positive direction verified on a ramp class (Pdim=1): across a decreasing precision ladder eps∈{0.25,0.15,0.10,0.07}, theorem-prescribed n grows 684→15806, empirical failure rate is 0.0 ≤ delta=0.05 at every tier (200 trials each), and mean abs error decreases 0.0190→0.0040. The negative direction (unbounded fat-shattering → only 3-weak evaluability) is not directly tested for real-valued classes.

claims.claim: Alpha-Renyi divergences for alpha > 1, and KL divergence as their alpha->1 limit, are proven not weakly evaluable from finite samples because their values are dominated by rare, empirically undetectable events (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The paper's own 3-point adversarial construction (eta=1e-4, alpha=2) is implemented with independently derived closed forms: Rényi₂ grows 0.0001→190.79 matching M+log(eta) to 5 sig figs at M≥20, KL grows 6.3e-5→0.02 matching eta·M, while rare-point mass stays flat at ~1e-4 and empirical P(rare ever observed in m=1000) stays flat at ~0.09–0.125 across M∈{1..200} over 140k MC trials — divergence explodes while finite-sample distinguishability is M-independent.

claims.claim: Unlike VC theory for supervised learning, no finite taxonomy of sample-complexity functions characterizes all statistically evaluable IPMs, which admit infinitely many distinct complexity regimes (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Block-diagonal constructor against a 16-regime taxonomy verifies all 136 prefix inequalities c(N_k+log k)>M_i(1/k,1/k) by exact arithmetic (worst margin 5.0>0). The constructed IPM has finite γ-fat-shattering dim at every fixed γ (4, 11, 100, 8796, 384962 for γ=1/2..1/32) yet M*/M_lightest grows 946→2449→4617 across k=16,24,32, strictly exceeding all 16 candidate regimes. This is a numerical instantiation of the diagonalization mechanism, not a formal proof over all countable taxonomies.

claims.claim: Perplexity-based evaluation can fail to detect total variation distance or beta-restricted KL divergence without further assumptions, but total variation becomes evaluable under a Delta-closeness-in-ratio (bounded likelihood ratio) assumption (Section 5).
claims.evidence: 3-outcome counterexample (eps=0.1, M=30): q_bad is TV-worse (TV 0.200 vs 0.100) yet has lower NLL (1.0745 vs 3.6238), so perplexity selects the TV-worse model in 100% of 10,000 finite-sample trials; the same inversion holds for β-restricted KL (β=0.3). Under Δ-closeness-in-ratio (max ratio dev 0.053), NLL and TV agree on the closer model in 500/500 trials.

ai-sherpa/statistical-evaluability-gener.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all five theoretical claims at the theorems' own construction scale, with independent implementations (sorted-merge KS, hand-derived Rényi/KL closed forms, exact-arithmetic diagonalization) and honest acknowledgment of gaps (c=3 optimality not independently reproduced, Claim 2 negative direction not directly tested). The reproductions are non-toy: they operate at the paper's stated asymptotic regimes with adequate sample sizes and trial counts.

ProCreations/repro-the-relative-instabil.paper_title: The Relative Instability of Model Comparison with Cross-validation

claims.claim: For soft-thresholded least squares with penalty lambda_n = o(n), single-algorithm assessment satisfies relative stability, with loss stability gamma decaying as 1/n^2 so that r(h) = Theta(1/n) -> 0 (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Using exact Wishart sufficient statistics at n up to 90,000 with 6 seeds and 4,000 paired replications, the fitted log-log slopes are -2.0463 for gamma (theoretical -2) and -1.0461 for r(h) (theoretical -1), with sigma^2 converging to 20,000.017 against the theoretical limit of 2*tau^4=20,000, directly confirming the stated decay rates on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: When comparing two soft-thresholded least squares fits with tuning parameters lambda_n and lambda_n + delta_n where delta_n = Theta(1), relative stability fails: r(h) = Omega(sqrt(n)) does not vanish, invalidating the cross-validation central limit theorem needed for confidence intervals (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: With lambda_n=sqrt(n) and delta_n=1, the r(h) log-log slope is +0.4075 (positive across all six seeds, range +0.368 to +0.527), yielding a final r(h) of 404.108 versus 0.0004216 for the single model; the independent Lasso replication shows the same pattern (slope +0.3894, final r(h)=316.058), confirming that relative stability fails and r(h) does not vanish.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments confirm that cross-validation confidence intervals remain valid for single soft-thresholding assessment across moderate sample sizes but fail for pairwise soft-thresholding comparisons even at very large sample sizes (Empirical Validation section).
claims.evidence: Across 2,500 independent ten-fold CV datasets per cell with exact augmented-Wishart sampling, nominal-95% coverage at n=90,000 is 95.08% for ST single-model and 95.00% for Lasso single-model, but only 65.16% and 64.04% for the respective pairwise comparisons, with comparison pivot variances of 4.33 and 4.43 versus ~1.0 for single models.

claims.claim: Ridge regression is shown to satisfy relative stability for pairwise comparisons, in contrast to the Lasso and soft-thresholding, which exhibit relative instability even though each is individually (absolutely) stable (Critical Insight / Empirical Validation).
claims.evidence: Under the identical protocol, Ridge comparison r(h) has slope -1.0601 with final value 0.001041 and coverage 94.96% at n=90,000, while the dense-coefficient soft-thresholding control flips the comparison slope from +0.4075 to -1.2951 with final r(h)=0.000244, demonstrating that Ridge and dense-ST satisfy pairwise relative stability in contrast to sparse ST/Lasso.

ProCreations/repro-the-relative-instabil.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from exact distributional calculations (Wishart sufficient statistics) at the paper's full sample sizes up to n=90,000, with multiple seeds and proper controls, confirming all four claims: single-model stability, pairwise instability, CV coverage failure for comparisons, and Ridge/dense-coefficient stability as a contrasting control.

SabaPivot/repro-efficient-preference-poi.paper_title: Efficient Preference Poisoning Attack on Offline RLHF

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 shows that flipping a single preference label shifts the DPO gradient by a vector o_i·β·Δψ_i that is independent of the current policy parameter θ, enabling reformulation of preference poisoning as a binary sparse approximation problem in gradient space (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: On 20,000 real SHP pairs embedded with frozen DistilBERT [CLS] (768-dim), 100 random single-flip tests yielded max residual 4.11e-16 for g_flip−g_clean = o_i·β·Δψ_i, and 100 random 9-column sparse reformulation tests yielded max residual 7.44e-16 for (g_attacked−g_clean)−Vx, both at machine precision on the paper's actual feature construction.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 establishes a lower bound on the number of required label flips, |ℱ| ≥ ||g†||_2/(2β), showing flip requirements scale linearly with the target gradient norm (Section 3, Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: Constructed equality cases (ψ(a)=u, ψ(a')=−u, ||u||=1) for β∈{0.25,0.5,1,2} and K∈{1,2,4,8,16,32}; both the exact bound ||g†||/(2β)=K and the approximate bound (||g†||−ε)/(2β)=K were attained with max numerical gap 3.55e-15 and 7.11e-15 respectively across 48 boundary cases, confirming sharpness and linear scaling.

claims.claim: The Binary-Aware Lattice Attack (BAL-A) uses a penalty parameter M ≥ M_0(B,R,K*) so that the shortest lattice vector has coefficients constrained to {-1,0,1}^n, and under a separation condition ρ_k² > M²(K*-k), recovers the true K*-flip attack pattern exactly (Section 4.1, Lemma 4.1, Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Three distinct checks: (1) 40 exhaustive global integer optimizations at M=1.01·M0 found ternary optima 40/40 and binary nonnegative optima 40/40; (2) 40 random d=64,n=20,K*=5 targets with computed ρ_k showed positive separation margin (min 0.2271) and exact global binary recovery 40/40; (3) Algorithm 1 (real LLL+Babai) at d=64,n=20 with 200 supports and 25 M-values showed TPR=1.0 below the separation threshold and 99.4% Babai exactness; the real SHP d=768,n=50,K*=7 run also achieved TP=7,FP=0,FN=0.

claims.claim: The Binary Matching Pursuit Attack (BMP-A) recovers the exact flip support within K* iterations when the gradient dictionary's coherence satisfies μ(V) < b/((2K*-1)B) (Section 5.2, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: A fixed non-orthogonal d=n=200 dictionary with measured coherence μ=0.19710 (matching Appendix H.1) was tested across 12,000 BMP-A runs (200 trials × K=1..60); exact support recovery was 600/600 (100%) in the theorem-guaranteed region K≤3 (where μ<1/(2K−1)), with gradual degradation outside, and the SHP matched case also achieved TP=7,FP=0,FN=0.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.4 provides impossibility certificates against K-flip attacks under a spectral norm condition ||g†||_2 - ε > √K·||V||_2 and a coherence condition (||g†||_2 - ε)² > B²(K + μ(V)K(K-1)) (Section 5, Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: 240 non-orthogonal Gaussian dictionaries (d=10,n=16) with exhaustive binary attack enumeration up to K=4 found the spectral condition fired 59 times, the coherence condition fired 180 times, 120 certificates were within 2% of the theorem boundary, and exhaustive search confirmed zero false certificates across all fired cases.

claims.claim: On the SHP dataset, the crafted attack shifts the trained policy far closer to the intended target than clean training does (||π_θ†-π_θ̂||_1 ≈ 0.012 vs ||π_clean-π_θ̂||_1 ≈ 0.224), and BMP-A runs roughly four orders of magnitude faster than BAL-A (1.37×10⁻⁴s vs 0.6865s) on the same data subset (Section 6.2.3).
claims.evidence: On 20,000 real SHP pairs with DistilBERT 768-dim features, actual BAL-A and BMP-A on a matched n=50,K*=7 subset both recovered the planted support exactly (TP=7,FP=0,FN=0); measured wall times were 1.838s vs 2.874e-4s (6,395× ratio, consistent with the paper's ~4 orders of magnitude), and attacked-to-target policy L1 was 0.0 while clean-to-attacked L1 was 0.275, confirming the claimed direction and scale (paper: 0.012 vs 0.224), with exact decimals differing due to undisclosed λ and subset seed.

SabaPivot/repro-efficient-preference-poi.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all six claims: Claims 1–5 are verified through theorem-faithful algorithm implementations and boundary-case numerical checks at paper scale, and Claim 6 is verified on real SHP data with actual BAL-A/BMP-A algorithms confirming exact support recovery, correct policy-shift direction, and a ~6,395× timing advantage. The main limitation is that Claim 6's exact numerical values differ from the paper due to undisclosed hyperparameters (λ, subset seed), which is transparently reported.

SabaPivot/repro-asymptotically-optimal-s.paper_title: Asymptotically Optimal Sequential Testing with Markovian Data

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 gives a non-asymptotic instance-dependent lower bound on the expected stopping time, E_Q[tau_alpha] ≥ (log(1/alpha)/D_M^inf(Q,P) − 2C_Q/min_i pi_i)^+, where D_M^inf(Q,P) is a stationary-weighted projection distance and C_Q bounds a Poisson-equation solution (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: On a 3-state nonreversible Markov chain with nonconstant row KLs (D_M=0.0688207), the logbook computes C_Q=11.51047 from the pseudo-spectral gap, then runs 1,200 exact Algorithm-1 paths at five alpha levels (1e-2 through 1e-32); mean stopping times (e.g., 1595.19 at alpha=1e-32) exceed the conservative lower bound (974.07) at mean+2SE in all cases.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 bounds the Poisson-equation solution constant C_Q via the pseudo-spectral gap of the underlying Markov chain (Section 3, Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: Across 40 nonreversible kernels × 8 test functions (320 checks), every Proposition 3.1 inequality held with maximum ratio ||omega||inf/(C_P||f||inf) = 0.148435, using the pseudo-spectral gap explicitly rather than the ordinary eigenvalue gap.

claims.claim: The proposed Sequential Markov Chain Test (Algorithm 1) builds an empirical transition kernel and a martingale statistic L_t accumulating row-wise KL divergences from the null class, stopping when L_t exceeds an adaptive boundary beta_t (Section 4, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The implementation constructs Qhat_t from transition counts, computes L_t = sum_x N_x KL(Qhat_t(x)||P(x)), and compares against beta_t = log(1/alpha) + (m-1) sum_x log(e(1+N_x/(m-1))); a preregistered equivalence test on 1,024 random tables gives max discrepancy 1.14e-13, and 6,000 null paths at alpha=0.05 yield 0 false rejections while 1,500 alternative paths stop with mean 458.42 transitions.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves the proposed test is alpha-correct and asymptotically optimal, with limsup_{alpha->0} E_Q[tau_alpha]/log(1/alpha) ≤ 1/D_M^inf(Q,P), matching the Theorem 3.3 lower bound (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Alpha-correctness is supported by 0 false rejections in 6,000 null paths at alpha=0.05; asymptotic optimality is supported by a sweep of 1,000 paths at each of alpha 1e-32 through 1e-256 showing E[tau]/log(1/alpha) decreasing monotonically from 21.72 to 15.67, approaching 1/D_M=14.53 with a final relative gap of 7.85%.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 extends the one-sided asymptotic optimality result to the two-sided testing setting (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.4).

SabaPivot/repro-a-distributional-view-fo.paper_title: A Distributional View for Visual Mechanistic Interpretability: KL-Minimal Soft-Constraint Principle

snaykey/repro-decentralized-sgd-topology.paper_title: Improved Convergence Analysis of Topology Dependence in Decentralized SGD

claims.evidence: Real homogeneous D-SGD on a stochastic quadratic with the theorem's stepsize shows stationary consensus error matches the closed-form σ²η²Q to <1% across 5 Q-values at fixed spectral gap p (log-log slope 1.012, R²=0.999), and Xi_emp/(σ²η²Q) falls within the theoretical (0,3] band for line, ring, torus, and hypercube topologies.

claims.claim: Lemma 2 bounds stochastic noise propagation through the network using independence of gradient noise across nodes, showing (1/n)*sum_{i=2}^{n} lambda_i^2 <= max_{i>=2}(lambda_i^2), which yields tighter convergence bounds than prior spectral-gap-only analyses (Lemma 2).
claims.evidence: The inequality (1/n)Σλ_i² ≤ max λ_i² is checked on 25 mixing-matrix configurations (5 topologies × 5 sizes, all hold), and the max/avg gap is quantified as 2.0–5.6× for sparse graphs with equality only for the complete graph, demonstrating the non-trivial tightening Lemma 2 provides.

claims.claim: Table 1 shows the number of transient iterations improves for several topologies: ring from O(n^7) to O(n^5), torus from O(n^5) to O(n^3 log^2(n)), and hypercube from O(n^3 log^2(n)) to O(n^3) (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Computing the paper's transient-iteration object R∝n³Q² on real mixing matrices (n up to 512–1024) yields fitted log-log slopes: ring classical 7.01→new 5.08 (matching O(n⁷)→O(n⁵)), torus 5.15→3.68, hypercube 3.65→2.80, with the torus/hypercube offsets explained by log²n inflation.

claims.claim: Figure 1 compares the classical topology-dependence quantity (1-p)/p against the new all-eigenvalue quantity (1/n)*sum(lambda_i^2/(1-lambda_i^2)) across ring, torus, line, and hypercube topologies, showing the new quantity is considerably smaller for sparse networks (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: Both quantities are computed exactly as defined on Metropolis/lazy mixing matrices at n=64: the new Q is 20.4× smaller than (1-p)/p for line, 20.8× for ring, 8.0× for torus, and 5.2× for hypercube, with equality (both zero) for the complete graph.

claims.claim: Figure 2 experimentally validates on logistic and ridge regression over MNIST that convergence behavior depends on the full eigenvalue spectrum of the mixing matrix rather than only the spectral gap (Section 6, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Real MNIST D-SGD with logistic and ridge regression using the hold-p-vary-Q construction (n=100 nodes) shows final loss increases monotonically with Q at fixed p across all 6 configurations (3 base graphs × 2 models), with mean Spearman 0.95 and loss magnitudes matching the paper's range.

claims.claim: Figure 3 shows the improved topology-dependence prediction holds for neural network training (LeNet on Fashion-MNIST) under both homogeneous and heterogeneous data settings (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Real LeNet-5 D-SGD on Fashion-MNIST (n=16, 15k-image subset) reproduces both regimes: homogeneous case shows weak topology sensitivity (loss band 0.373–0.384 across 5× Q change, consistent with the paper's ζ≈0 observation), while heterogeneous label-sharded case shows strong topology effect (ring loss 0.947 vs complete 0.399, accuracy 0.63 vs 0.85).

snaykey/repro-decentralized-sgd-topology.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all six claims through spectral computations on real mixing matrices and end-to-end decentralized SGD experiments on stochastic quadratics, MNIST logistic/ridge regression, and LeNet on Fashion-MNIST. The key hold-p-vary-Q design directly isolates the paper's contribution, and quantitative results—consensus error matching σ²η²Q to <1%, loss increasing with Q at fixed p (Spearman 0.95), and fitted transient-iteration exponents matching Table 1—consistently support the paper's theoretical predictions.

snaykey/repro-lion-convergence.paper_title: Convergence Analysis of the Lion Optimizer in Centralized and Distributed Settings

claims.evidence: On a simple separable synthetic function (sum of x^2/2 - cos(2x), d=50), the measured power-law exponent is T^{-0.111} (R^2=0.946), far from the theoretical T^{-1/4}; the rate is slower than the upper bound, not matching the claim.
