claims.claim: Lemma 3.1 quantifies how missed detections cause 'endogenous confounding' by bounding the signal-to-noise ratio degradation as (SNR_j*(t) − SNR_j^eff(t;r))_+ ≤ C log((τ_j − r + 1)/α_r) + M² (Section 3.3, Lemma 3.1).
claims.evidence: 540 three-regime configurations × 200 real ATC paths (108,000 paths) showed the maximum observed (SNR*−SNR_eff)_+/log((τ_j−r+1)/α_r) ratio bounded at 5.606 on the conditioning set P(no alarm)>α_r; a 4,000-path intervention confirmed the mechanism by showing detection drop from 0.83 to 0.27 without restart.

claims.claim: Synthetic experiments with 5000 Monte Carlo runs confirm ATC's regret scales as O(log T), matching the theoretical rate (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Exact-scan ATC was run at the paper's stated 5,000 MC paths per horizon across T=600,1200,2400,4800,7000,9000, producing R²=0.9937 for the log T regression; the efficient geometric variant independently achieved R²=0.9976.

claims.claim: On the NAB benchmark using AWS CPU utilization data, ATC outperforms sliding-window and discounted-mean baseline detectors (Section 5).
claims.evidence: On the real NAB AWS CPU series (T=4032, SHA-256 verified), ATC achieved cumulative regret 9,061 versus 64,345 for sliding-window (W=30) and 157,940 for discounted-mean (ρ=0.98), a 7.1× and 17.4× improvement respectively; a variance-misspecification control produced 306 false alarms at σ=0.5 versus 11 at σ=1.

SabaPivot/repro-the-cost-of-learning-und.overall: The logbook provides concrete, non-toy experimental evidence for all five claims: 5,000-MC synthetic runs at paper scale confirm logarithmic regret scaling, 108,000 paths stress-test the endogenous-confounding lemma, an independent Bayes-risk audit validates the lower-bound construction, and the real NAB benchmark confirms ATC's superiority over baselines. The reproduction uses the authors' released code at a pinned commit with checksums and appropriate controls.

SabaPivot/repro-why-self-distillation-he.paper_title: Why Self-Distillation Helps and Hurts: Denoising vs. Signal Forgetting

claims.claim: Deterministic-equivalent recursions for prediction risk in overparameterized linear self-training decompose error into a systematic 'signal forgetting' term that grows with the number of self-training iterations and a stochastic noise term that decays exponentially in iterations (Section on risk decomposition; Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: An independent Monte Carlo implementation showed maximum relative disagreement of 4.69% between total risk and the sum of its two independently evaluated components, with signal forgetting increasing 0.04260→0.84675 and noise decreasing 9.31042→0.003326 across iterations, directly demonstrating the claimed opposing-motion decomposition at proportional scale.

claims.claim: Test risk as a function of self-training iteration count follows a U-shaped curve, with an optimal early-stopping iteration set by the tradeoff between decaying stochastic error and accumulating systematic (signal-forgetting) error, occurring strictly under spectral anisotropy of the feature covariance (Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: Anisotropic covariance spikes 3, 6, and 10 produced interior optimal rounds 7, 7, and 8 respectively, while the isotropic control (spike 1) monotonically improved to the boundary round 15, confirming both the U-shape and the strict-anisotropy qualification through a controlled contrast.

claims.claim: In spiked covariance models, each self-training iteration acts as a direction-dependent spectral filter that preserves eigendirections aligned with strong signal (survival factor near 1) while suppressing weaker, noise-aligned eigendirections at a rate of approximately (1+τ)^(−t).
claims.evidence: Across 48 independent trajectories (n=300, p=600), predicted round-10 retentions [0.90441, 0.67303, 0.15890, 0.01679] matched observed means [0.90352, 0.67225, 0.15966, 0.01657] with maximum deviation 0.00420 over all directions and rounds, and the strongest eigendirection retained 54.5× the coefficient of the weakest, confirming direction-dependent spectral filtering.

claims.claim: An iterated Generalized Cross-Validation (iGCV) estimator is proposed that achieves uniform consistency for estimating risk along the self-training trajectory, enabling data-driven selection of the optimal early-stopping iteration without a held-out validation set.
claims.evidence: A finite-sample convergence study (n∈{100,200,400}, 16 trajectories, 9 rounds, 5 λ values) showed median sup-absolute error decreasing 0.2789→0.1903→0.1751 and median selection regret decreasing 0.03119→0.00771→0.00496 with sample size, providing concrete evidence for uniform consistency and data-driven early-stopping selection without held-out validation.

claims.claim: The theoretical denoising-forgetting risk tradeoff, derived for linear regression, is empirically confirmed to hold for deep networks, specifically ResNet-50 trained on CIFAR-10 under repeated self-distillation.
claims.evidence: Six full ResNet-50/CIFAR-10 runs (3 seeds × hard/soft pseudo-labels, 10,000-image subsets, 40% noise, 4 rounds, 35 epochs each) failed to reproduce the reported U-shape: all 3 soft runs were minimized at round 0, and only 1/3 hard runs showed a marginal 0.30 pp improvement at round 1, contradicting the paper's reported 47.7%→43.6%→45.0% trajectory.

SabaPivot/repro-why-self-distillation-he.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence supporting the four linear-model theoretical claims through well-designed simulations with controlled contrasts (anisotropic vs. isotropic, multi-spike spectral filtering, finite-sample iGCV convergence), but falsifies the deep-network extension through six full-scale ResNet-50/CIFAR-10 runs that consistently fail to reproduce the reported U-shaped test-error trajectory under both hard and soft pseudo-label modes.

SabaPivot/repro-sample-complexity-bounds.paper_title: Sample Complexity Bounds for Robust Mean Estimation with Mean-Shift Contamination

claims.claim: Under a frequency-witness (spectral) condition on the contaminating distribution, Algorithm 1 estimates the mean of a mean-shift-contaminated distribution to error ϵ with probability at least 2/3 using O(d·log(...)/((1-α)A-2α)δ)²) samples (Theorem 3.2, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook executes the literal finite-cover Algorithm 1 exhaustively in d=3 (73,734 candidates × 504 active frequencies = 37M pairs per trial), using the complete Theorem 3.2 sample expression with C=1 at four δ values (n=1,821–7,186), achieving 12/12 successes with Wilson 95% lower bound 0.758 > 2/3 and median error 0.035–0.050 vs 0.700–0.784 for the contaminated sample mean. A destructive control at C=0.01 yields 8/12 failures with negative score gaps, confirming the mechanism is real.

claims.claim: The main upper bound states that under mild technical assumptions characterized by a Fourier-based parameter δ, an algorithm exists using Õ_α(d/δ²) samples to estimate the contaminated mean (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: The d=3 experiments directly vary δ across four Gaussian scales (δ=0.833–0.482) using the full displayed sample expression d·log(…)/(((1-α)A-2α)δ)², achieving 12/12 successes at each scale. The high-dimensional campaign varies d∈{4,8,16,32,64} with n scaling linearly in d, achieving 60/60 recoveries at C=1, while a lower-budget q-sweep shows the expected success transition and confirms δ-dependence cannot be omitted.

claims.claim: A matching one-dimensional lower bound shows any algorithm requires Ω(1/(δσ)^(1/3)) samples to achieve error ϵ under specific L2 Fourier-transform and tail-decay conditions, and more generally 1/δ^Ω(1) samples are required even in one dimension, qualitatively matching the upper bound (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Twelve LP-optimized Le Cam adversarial pairs are constructed varying δ and σ across four Gaussian scales and three target separations; the optimal likelihood-ratio test yields median error 0.4991 (near 0.5 = indistinguishable), with the smallest error minus two standard errors at 0.4704. The numerical log-log slope of the leading factor against δσ is −0.33333378, matching the claimed −1/3 exponent, and held-out TV divided by the Theorem 4.1 denominator is ≤0.0155 for 10 of 12 pairs.

SabaPivot/repro-sample-complexity-bounds.overall: The logbook provides concrete, non-toy experimental evidence supporting all three claims: exhaustive finite-cover Algorithm 1 runs in d≤3 with the full sample-complexity expression, high-dimensional score-separation audits through d=64 with exact witnesses, and Le Cam lower-bound constructions with optimal LR tests matching the predicted (δσ)^{-1/3} scaling. The reproduction includes destructive controls, checksums, and honest acknowledgment of limitations (exponential covers stop at d=3, sampled candidates used beyond).

claims.claim: Transported Conformal Calibration achieves reliable target-domain coverage without labeled target calibration data.
claims.evidence: A real run on Tiny-ImageNet-C (motion blur, severity 2) with 10k source-calibration, 10k target-pool, and 10k paired unlabeled examples showed TCC-KS recovering coverage from 87.45% (transported CP) to 90.67% at epoch 20 without target labels, but this is only 1 of 328 reported conditions, 1 of 20 corruption/severity settings, 1 transport objective, and 2 of 7 checkpoints, with absolute set sizes (121.35 vs paper's 136.6) and correction magnitude not matching the paper, and the target classifier reaching only 7.9% validation accuracy.

claims.claim: Target-domain coverage guarantees adapt to observable measure of mismatch between source and target distributions.
claims.evidence: Across two checkpoints in a single condition, the observable mismatch estimate δ̂ increased from 0 to 0.0012, causing δ+ to tighten from 0.02716 to 0.02836 and α* from 0.07284 to 0.07164, coinciding with TCC-KS recovering coverage; however, this demonstrates the correction mechanism on only two data points in one of 328 settings with a minimal mismatch change, which the logbook itself acknowledges does not support the broader cross-setting adaptation claim.

GwendalTsang/repro-conformal-calibration.overall: The logbook provides a genuine but extremely narrow spot-check on one Tiny-ImageNet-C condition at full sample scale, demonstrating that TCC-KS can recover target coverage above the nominal level and that the mismatch correction mechanism responds as designed. However, with only 1/328 conditions tested, significant numerical discrepancies from the paper, and a poorly trained target classifier (7.9% accuracy), this constitutes a partial mechanistic demonstration rather than a verification of the paper's broader claims.

agharsallah/yeyuprqtay-logbook.paper_title: Multivariate Distributional Reinforcement Learning Using Sliced Divergences

claims.claim: Theorem 1 proves that both uniform-sliced and max-sliced divergences retain the metric properties of the underlying base divergence when that base divergence is itself a metric on the reals (Section 4.1, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Numerical checks of all four metric axioms across 6 base×lift combinations (d=6, n=150, 300 directions, 40 triples) show identity d(X,X)=0.0, symmetry gap=0.0, minimum triangle slack +0.231, and minimum positive distance 0.215 for X≠Y, confirming metricity is inherited by both uniform-sliced and max-sliced lifts.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 proves the distributional Bellman operator is a contraction in the sup-sliced divergence metric under uniform slicing with shared scalar discounting γI_d, with contraction factor c(γ) (Section 4.2, Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Contraction ratios match predicted c(γ) to machine precision: sliced-Wasserstein ratios equal γ exactly (dev 3e-16), sliced-Cramér ratios equal √γ exactly (e.g., 0.9487 at γ=0.9, dev 3e-16), and sliced-MMD stays below √γ, across γ∈{0.5,0.7,0.9,0.95}.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 proves the max-slicing variant achieves a Bellman contraction under general dense per-state-action discount matrices Γ(s,a), resolving a previously open theoretical gap (Section 4.2, Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The paper's App-C.4.2 counterexample is reproduced to six digits (SW₁ 0.527393→0.567286, ratio 1.076 > ‖A‖_op=0.9), and over 60 random dense Γ matrices, max-slicing has 0/60 operator-norm violations while uniform slicing has 2/60, confirming max-slicing contracts under dense Γ where uniform slicing fails.

claims.claim: Propositions 5 and 6 show uniform slicing preserves the unbiased-sample-gradient property needed for one-sample TD bootstrapping, while max-slicing and Wasserstein-based objectives violate this property (Section 4.4, Propositions 5-6).
claims.evidence: One-sample (m=1) gradient bias measured via 8000 Monte-Carlo draws vs 40k-sample population proxy shows uniform-sliced Cramér at 1.4% and sliced-MMD at 2.1% relative bias (near-unbiased), while sliced-Wasserstein (108.5%), max-sliced-Cramér (49.4%), and max-sliced-Wasserstein (67.2%) are strongly biased, matching Propositions 5 and 6.

claims.claim: SDRL supports sliced Wasserstein distance and sliced Cramér distance, each computable in O(Ln log n), as well as sliced Maximum Mean Discrepancy at O(Ln^2), as base divergences within the particle-based critic of Algorithm 1 (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Runtime scaling exponents fitted across n=256–8192 (L=32, d=8) yield p=1.08 for sliced-Wasserstein and p=0.95 for sliced-Cramér (consistent with O(n log n)), versus p=1.99 for sliced-MMD (consistent with O(n²)), with concrete timing at n=4096 showing ~800× gap between sliced-W and sliced-MMD.

claims.claim: In the chain environment experiment, objectives satisfying the unbiased-gradient property (U) achieve a median Wasserstein distance of about 0.15-0.25 under standard TD updates, whereas objectives violating (U) degrade to roughly 0.4 or higher (Figure 2, Section 5).
claims.evidence: On the K=10 chain (γ=0.9, one-sample TD, 8 seeds, N=100 particles), (U)-satisfying objectives achieve full-OT W₂ of 0.41–0.59 (at the d=10 finite-sample floor of 0.40) and sliced W₂ of 0.046–0.075, while (U)-violating objectives degrade to 0.91 and 1.17 on full-OT W₂ and 0.112–0.337 on sliced W₂, confirming the qualitative separation and the ≥0.4 degradation threshold for violators, though the exact 0.15–0.25 band for satisfiers is not precisely matched on either metric.

agharsallah/yeyuprqtay-logbook.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims: four theoretical claims are verified to machine precision or six-digit agreement with the paper, the complexity claim is confirmed via fitted runtime exponents, and the chain experiment reproduces the qualitative separation between (U)-satisfying and (U)-violating objectives with (U)-violators degrading past 0.4. The main caveat is that the chain experiment's exact 0.15–0.25 band for (U)-satisfying objectives is not precisely matched, with sliced W₂ values falling below and full-OT W₂ values falling above that range, though the finite-sample floor explanation is reasonable.

amkkk/positive-distribution-shift-repro.paper_title: Positive Distribution Shift as a Framework for Understanding Tractable Learning

claims.claim: Noisy parities are D-DS-PAC learnable by an explicit efficient algorithm using m(epsilon) = O(d^2 log^2(d)/epsilon / (1-2eta)^2) samples, despite being conjectured computationally hard under the standard PAC model (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: At d=50, k=25 with 2M samples, the per-coordinate correlation gap under the PDS mixture D' is measured as in-support 0.1885 vs out-support 0.1738 (ratio 1.0846 vs theory 1.0851, 4-decimal match), while under uniform the correlations are ~0.0006 (pure noise), confirming the core mechanism the explicit threshold-based algorithm relies on.

claims.claim: Noisy parities are also D-DS-PAC learnable using a stylized layerwise SGD procedure on a 2-layer neural network with L1 regularization and sparsity-dependent initialization (Theorem 4.5).
claims.evidence: Standard SGD on a 2-layer MLP (1024 hidden, d=50, k=25, 200k iters, 3 reruns) achieves PDS mean final error 0.0099 vs no-PDS 0.4987 at eta=0, with PDS converging in 2/3 runs and no-PDS in 0/9 across all noise levels; this reproduces the paper's own Figure 1 empirical demonstration, though the stylized layerwise+L1 variant from the theorem was not directly implemented.

claims.claim: Noisy k-juntas are D-DS-PAC learnable via a Correlational Statistical Query algorithm using O(d^k + 2^k) queries, and are R-DS-PAC learnable via stylized layerwise SGD with a covariance loss using m = O~(d log(1/epsilon) / epsilon^2) samples (Theorems 4.6 and 4.8).
claims.evidence: A 9-junta over d=50 trained with standard SGD shows PDS convergence in 2/3 runs per noise level vs 0/9 without PDS, and the correlation signal (in/out ratio 1.0846 matching theory 1.0851) and the junta's minimum Fourier degree (7 = k-2) are verified; however, the specific CSQ algorithm and the stylized SGD with covariance loss from Theorems 4.6/4.8 were not directly implemented.

claims.claim: Any polynomial-size circuit with label noise is universally f-PDS learnable by SGD on specially constructed networks with polynomial sample complexity and runtime, though this construction requires designing the training distribution around the target function (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: No experiments were conducted; the logbook only restates a proof sketch from the paper's Section B describing how f is encoded in the training distribution D'_f and decoded by a non-standard network, with no runs, numbers, or artifacts.

claims.claim: The paper establishes a hierarchy of learnability notions showing D-DS-PAC learning implies non-adaptive membership query (NA-MQ) learning, and NA-MQ learners can be converted into R-DS-PAC learners with sample complexity m(epsilon) = O(m0(epsilon/2) * (log m0(epsilon/2) + log(1/epsilon))) (Theorems 5.2 and 5.3).
claims.evidence: No experiments were conducted; the logbook only restates proof sketches for the D-DS-PAC→NA-MQ and NA-MQ→R-DS-PAC conversions and the coupon-collector sample complexity bound, with no empirical validation of the hierarchy or the conversion formula.

claims.claim: The benefit of positive distribution shift for tractable learning is argued to be primarily computational rather than statistical, since PDS can enable polynomial-time algorithms without reducing information-theoretic sample complexity (Section 4, Abstract).
claims.evidence: Two independent experiments support the computational-benefit claim: (1) per-coordinate correlations under uniform are ~0.0006 (noise floor) vs 0.1885 under PDS at d=50, k=25, and (2) a scaling sweep shows PDS converges through d=50 while no-PDS stops converging at d>=40, demonstrating that the gap is computational (tractability) rather than statistical (sample complexity).

amkkk/positive-distribution-shift-repro.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence at non-trivial scale (d=50) supporting the core empirical claims (1, 2, 3, 6) through correlation analysis and SGD training reproducing the paper's Figures 1-3, though it substitutes standard joint SGD for the stylized layerwise/L1/covariance-loss algorithms specified in the theorems. Claims 4 and 5 receive no experimental treatment whatsoever, consisting only of restated proof sketches.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 proves that if the unconstrained network class universally approximates the target function class F, then CAffNet universally approximates the constrained target class {f_t in F | A(x) f_t <= b(x)}, with approximation error bound ||P* - f_t||_p < (3 + 3*sqrt(n_out))K (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: A single scalar target (clip(sin(2x),-2,0.5)) with a 64-wide 3-hidden-layer tanh network on 200 training points checks the error bound numerically (sup error 0.0522 < bound 0.9573, zero violations), but this is a simplified instantiation of a universal approximation theorem, not a proof or multi-function-class demonstration.

claims.claim: The CAffine layer's projection formula includes a trainable null-space component w_phi(x), P_gamma(x) = f_theta(x) - A_gamma^dagger(x)(A_gamma(x) f_theta(x) - b_gamma(x)) + (I - A_gamma^dagger(x) A_gamma(x)) w_phi(x), allowing joint optimization across multiple feasible projections rather than a fixed orthogonal projection (Section 3).
claims.evidence: A deterministic 2D test with A=[0,1], b=0, f_theta=[3,5] confirms the null-space component moves y1 from 3 to 13 while keeping Ay=0 across 21 w values, but this is a single small fixed example rather than a trained-network demonstration of joint optimization.

claims.claim: Unlike prior work (HardNet), CAffNet guarantees hard constraint satisfaction A(x)y <= b(x) without requiring A(x) to have full row rank, and handles arbitrary constraint cardinality via decomposition into sub-constraint combinations of at most min(m, n_out) constraints (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Three small deterministic constraint matrices (e.g., A=[[1,0],[2,0]], A=[[1,1],[2,2]], 3 constraints in 2D) show CAffNet violations at machine-epsilon (≤3.6e-15) while HardNet violates by 0.2 on the dependent-row case, but these are hand-crafted 2D cases, not a full experimental or formal-guarantee demonstration.

claims.claim: On the piecewise-constraint benchmark, CAffNet-TF (transformer variant) achieves a 73.33% MSE reduction relative to a soft-constrained neural network baseline while incurring zero constraint violations (Section on Experiments, piecewise constraints task).
claims.evidence: Official code run at paper scale (50,000 epochs, n_train=50, n_test=400, seed 1, float32) measures CAffNet-TF MSE=0.000542 vs NN MSE=0.012057 (95.5% reduction) with zero max inequality violation, exceeding the claimed 73.33% reduction and confirming zero violations; the one-seed vs five-seed and float32 caveats do not undermine the core finding.

claims.claim: In the safety-critical control experiment, CAffNet successfully avoids obstacles whereas both HardNet and the soft-constrained baseline fail to do so (Section on Experiments, safety-critical control task).
claims.evidence: The toy diagnostic uses 1 circular obstacle that does not block the nominal route, resulting in all three methods (NN, HardNet, CAffNet) showing collision=False and CAffNet not reaching the goal (final distance 1.19), which neither supports nor refutes the claim; the official CBF benchmark completed only 10 of 2,000 epochs, insufficient to evaluate obstacle avoidance.

amkkk/repro-caffnet-hard-constraint-affi.overall: The logbook provides toy-level numerical checks confirming the CAffine formula structure, null-space component, and rank-deficient constraint handling (Claims 1–3), and a completed official-code run at paper scale for the piecewise benchmark that exceeds the claimed MSE reduction with zero violations (Claim 4). The safety-critical control claim remains unaddressed due to an inadequate toy setup and an incomplete official run (Claim 5).

ProCreations/repro-the-optimal-sample-co.paper_title: The Optimal Sample Complexity of Linear Contracts

claims.claim: Theorem 1.1 establishes uniform convergence: for sample size s ≥ 3456 ln(4/δ)/ε², with probability at least 1−δ, the empirical and expected utility of every linear contract differ by at most ε (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: Across 81,920 independent empirical samples with sample sizes up to 16.5M, the exact supremum of |u_S(α)−u_D(α)| over all action-switch breakpoints and one-sided limits never exceeded ε; the largest deviation was 0.001283 (0.641% of applicable ε). A destructive control with n=16 produced failure rates up to 41.58%, confirming the audit can reject inadequate sampling.

claims.claim: Corollary 1.2 shows the Empirical Utility Maximization algorithm achieves an ε-approximation of the optimal linear contract using s ≥ 6912 ln(4/δ)/ε² samples and O(1/ε) oracle queries (Corollary 1.2).
claims.evidence: The EUM algorithm was implemented literally with the ε/4 contract grid (O(1/ε) oracle queries by construction), and across 81,920 independent samples with s ≥ 6912 ln(4/δ)/ε², zero selected contracts exceeded ε true regret; the largest regret was 0.016875 (16.64% of ε).

claims.claim: The O(ln(1/δ)/ε²) sample complexity matches the lower bound of Dütting et al. (2025) up to constant factors, and is independent of the action space size n and the number of outcomes m (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: A two-type, two-action lower-bound family with exact binomial tail calculations yielded normalized critical counts nε²/ln(1/δ) bounded between 0.1129 and 0.1780, while quarter-sized controls failed at 12.15%–34.38%. Action-count independence was tested across 4–24 actions with zero failures, and outcome-count independence was tested across 2–16 outcomes with expected rewards preserved to 2.23e-16.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 shows the expected reward of a linear contract is non-decreasing in the contract parameter α, a structural property exploited to build fine-grained covering arguments where general pseudo-dimension bounds fail (Lemma 2.1).
claims.evidence: The revealed-preference proof argument was implemented as an executable audit checking all 17,447 exact type/breakpoint paths across four models (5–16 types, 4–24 actions), finding zero reward decreases while principal utility was allowed to remain non-monotone, confirming the check is specific to the reward property.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.2 constructs an L2 cover of the reward function class of size O(1/ν²), obtained by discretizing empirical rewards into ν-intervals, taking pullbacks to parameter space, and combining with grid discretization of the outcome axis (Lemma 2.2).
claims.evidence: The L2 cover construction was implemented literally for four models and four ν values, with cover size ≤ 0.3334 × (12/ν²), L2 error ≤ 0.2469 × ν, zero missing reward pullback bins, and zero monotonicity violations across all 16 model/ν cells, with coverage evaluated at action-switch sides and Voronoi boundaries.

ProCreations/repro-the-optimal-sample-co.overall: This logbook provides concrete, exact-computation evidence supporting all five claims through finite but non-trivial models (up to 16 types, 24 actions, 16.5M samples), with destructive controls and a lower-bound construction that independently recovers the matching rate. The reproduction is rigorous in using exact breakpoint enumeration rather than grid approximations and includes both positive and negative controls.

ParetoOptimal/repro-rkvseuwbj0.paper_title: Posterior Sampling Reinforcement Learning with Gaussian Processes for Continuous Control: Sublinear Regret Bounds for Unbounded State Spaces

claims.claim: Theorem 4.11 establishes a Bayesian regret bound for GP-PSRL of order R_T = O(H^{3/2} sqrt((d_s+d_a) gamma_N(sigma^2, R̃) T log T)), giving tight sqrt(gamma_T) dependence on the maximum information gain rather than a linear dependence (Theorem 4.11).
claims.evidence: The logbook extracted the pinned theorem from manuscript_source/main.tex and found it states O(H sqrt((d_s+d_a) gamma_T(sigma^2,R̃) T log T)), contradicting the claim's H^{3/2} factor, gamma_N subscript, and 'maximum' (vs. expected) information gain terminology; the sqrt dependence itself is confirmed but the composite claim as written does not match the theorem.

claims.claim: Lemma 4.7 uses a recursive application of the Borell-Tsirelson-Ibragimov-Sudakov inequality to show that states visited by the algorithm remain within a ball of near-constant radius with high probability, enabling analysis without assuming bounded state spaces (Lemma 4.7).
claims.evidence: The logbook audited the proof chain in the source LaTeX, confirming the state-containment lemma gives P(sup ||s||_2 > R) <= 2/T with R = D sqrt(log(10(T+R_a) max(1,L/C))), and verified the proof constructs a sequential previous-state event, invokes the GP-norm-tail bound (which uses vector BTIS), and proves the radius recursion by induction.

claims.claim: The analysis requires only Holder continuity of the GP kernel with parameters L>0 and alpha in (0,1] (Assumption 3.4), removing prior requirements of four-times-differentiable kernels (Section 3, Assumption 3.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook extracted Assumption 3.4 from the source confirming |c(x,y)-c(x,z)| <= L ||y-z||_2^alpha with L>0, alpha in (0,1], confirmed the manuscript explicitly contrasts with prior four-times-differentiable kernel requirements, and tested a nondifferentiable Holder-1/2 toy function f(x)=|x|^0.5 with zero inequality residual; the caveat that bounded kernel variance is separately required does not undermine the smoothness claim.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.13 specializes the general regret bound to Matérn kernels, giving concrete polynomial-in-T rates for this standard kernel family (Corollary 4.13).
claims.evidence: The logbook extracted the pinned corollary giving the polynomial factor T^((nu+d)/(2nu+d)), independently verified the algebra sqrt(T * T^(d/(2nu+d))) = T^((nu+d)/(2nu+d)) across six parameter cases with max exponent error 1.11e-16, and confirmed all exponents lie strictly between 1/2 and 1 with correct boundary behavior.

claims.claim: The regret analysis assumes a bounded action space (Assumption 3.1) and a deterministic, uniformly bounded reward function (Assumption 3.2), while state spaces remain unbounded (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook extracted from the source that A subseteq B^{d_a}(R_a) (bounded actions), |r(s,a)| <= R_max (uniformly bounded reward), r is explicitly deterministic, and S = R^{d_s} (unbounded state space), with all four checks passing in the validation output.

ParetoOptimal/repro-rkvseuwbj0.overall: This logbook performs an analytic verification of the paper's theoretical claims by extracting formulas, assumptions, and proof structures from the manuscript LaTeX source and checking algebra, proof chains, and boundary cases. It finds Claim 1 falsified due to three concrete mismatches between the stated claim and the actual theorem, while Claims 2–5 are supported by source extraction, algebraic verification, and proof-chain auditing.

Srishti280992/repro-non-uniform-noise-to.paper_title: Non-Uniform Noise-to-Signal Ratio in the REINFORCE Policy-Gradient Estimator

claims.claim: For finite-horizon linear-quadratic systems with Gaussian policies, the noise-to-signal ratio of the multi-step REINFORCE estimator can be computed exactly in closed form via lifted dynamics (Theorem 5, Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: For a non-trivial multi-step LQG system (T=5, n=2, m=1, 7 Gaussian variables), 5-node and 7-node tensor Gauss-Hermite quadrature agree to 2.76e-14 on gradient mean and 8.03e-16 on second moment; lifted quadratic return matches rollout to 7.11e-15; Theorem-6 mean recursion matches quadrature to 3.41e-14, confirming exact closed-form computation via lifted dynamics.

claims.claim: The NSR landscape is highly non-uniform: as the policy approaches the optimal deterministic policy (Σ→0, per Corollary 6), the NSR does not vanish uniformly and can blow up, as demonstrated for a double-integrator system (Figure 1, Section 2.3).
claims.evidence: Exact closed-form NSR on a 41×41 grid for the double-integrator system spans 18.50 to 4.04e9 (2.18e8-fold range); along σ→0 at fixed initial std, the log-log slope is −1.9997, confirming NSR blows up as the policy approaches deterministic, directly supporting non-uniformity and blow-up.

claims.claim: Variance of the multi-step REINFORCE estimator grows exponentially with the control horizon when the closed-loop dynamics are unstable, i.e., when the spectral radius ρ(F)>1 (Theorem 8, Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: Exact polynomial-algebra computation of Var(G_K) for scalar LQG with ρ(F)=1.15 and 1.30 over T=1..12 shows exponential growth in horizon with per-step factors 2.58 (R²=0.9991) and 4.91 (R²=0.99996), directly confirming Theorem 8's exponential-growth claim for unstable closed-loop dynamics.

claims.claim: A general upper bound on REINFORCE gradient-estimator variance is derived for generic nonlinear dynamics with expressive neural-network policies (Theorem 10, Section 4).
claims.evidence: For nonlinear dynamics s_{t+1}=0.82s_t+0.35tanh(a_t)+0.04s_t³ with an 8-hidden-unit tanh MLP Gaussian policy, 220k rollouts at σ=0.2, 0.35, 0.6 show RHS/LHS ratios of 5.69–6.46 for the mean-parameter gradient and 16.89–20.20 for the log-std gradient, confirming the upper bound holds on a genuine nonlinear NN-policy system.

claims.claim: The analysis is extended from linear to polynomial systems and polynomial feedback policies via a moment-evaluation approach (Proposition 9, Section 3).
claims.evidence: For polynomial dynamics s_{t+1}=0.55s_t+0.12s_t²+0.35a_t with polynomial feedback a_t=θ₁s_t+θ₂s_t²+ε_t (T=3), exact monomial moment evaluation yields components of degrees 14–16 with 585–811 terms, exact NSR=15.18, and a 900k-rollout MC cross-check matches the second moment within 1.64%, confirming the moment-evaluation extension to polynomial systems.

Srishti280992/repro-non-uniform-noise-to.overall: The logbook provides concrete, exact-computation evidence supporting all five theoretical claims through Gauss-Hermite quadrature, closed-form NSR grids, polynomial-algebra variance scaling, nonlinear bound checks, and polynomial moment evaluation, each cross-validated by independent methods. The setups are low-dimensional but non-toy, directly addressing each theorem's mathematical content with high-precision numerical agreement.

Yashp2003/repro-no-data-no-problem-robus.paper_title: No Data? No Problem: Robust Vision-Tabular Learning with Missing Values

claims.claim: RoVTL (Robust Vision-Tabular Learning) is proposed in Section 3 as a contrastive vision-tabular pretraining method designed to remain robust across the full range of tabular data availability, from 0% to 100% of tabular attributes present (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The RoVTL architecture was reimplemented but on synthetic data (2000 train samples, 10 classes, 20 tabular attributes) with a simplified MLP tabular encoder instead of the paper's TARTE foundation model, running in ~9 seconds on a single A10. Pretraining loss decreased 3.81→3.54 and downstream accuracy reached 40.9% vs 10% random, confirming the pipeline trains, but at vastly reduced scale and scope compared to the paper's UK Biobank cardiac MRI setup.

claims.claim: RoVTL introduces random masking of tabular attributes -- simulating attribute-level missingness as a data augmentation during contrastive pretraining -- to make the learned joint representation robust to missing tabular values at test time (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Random tabular masking was implemented (augment_rate=0.95, random subset kept, rest zeroed) and pretraining loss decreased 7.1% over 5 epochs on synthetic data. However, the test-time robustness evidence is confounded: accuracy is identical (40.9%) at every missingness rate from 0–100%, which the logbook itself attributes to strong image-class correlations in the synthetic data rather than the masking strategy.

claims.claim: Section 5 evaluates RoVTL against baseline vision-tabular methods on UK Biobank cardiac MRI data, reporting comparisons in Table 3 across varying rates of tabular missingness (Section 5, Table 3).
claims.evidence: UK Biobank data was not accessed (requires institutional application) and no baseline methods (Early Fusion, Late Fusion, etc.) were compared. A missingness robustness curve was generated on synthetic proxy data showing constant 40.9% accuracy across 0–100% missingness, but this does not reproduce the paper's Table 3 comparisons on real cardiac MRI data.

claims.claim: An ablation isolating the contribution of the missingness-augmentation strategy versus standard contrastive pretraining is reported, evaluating its effect on downstream robustness (Table 6).
claims.evidence: An ablation was run on synthetic data with variants (w/o pretraining: 31.0%, w/o TabMoFe: 39.6%, w/o downstream missingness: 39.6%), but none of the variants isolate the specific comparison claimed — missingness-augmentation during pretraining vs. standard contrastive pretraining without masking. The 'w/o pretraining' variant removes all pretraining rather than just the masking augmentation, so the key ablation is not properly performed, and all results are on toy data.

claims.claim: Additional experiments on the German and time-based tabular datasets (cited as German et al. 2014 and Dugdale et al. 1999) are used alongside UK Biobank to assess generalization of RoVTL's robustness to missing tabular data (Section 4, Section 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook clarifies that German et al. 2014 and Dugdale et al. 1999 are motivation citations, not evaluation datasets. The actual generalization datasets (M&Ms, DVM) were not used: M&Ms and UK Biobank were blocked by access requirements, and DVM was publicly available but never downloaded or run. No experiments on any real additional dataset were executed.

Yashp2003/repro-no-data-no-problem-robus.overall: The logbook provides a minimal synthetic-data reimplementation of the RoVTL pipeline (2000 samples, 10 classes, simplified architecture, ~9 seconds compute) that confirms the method trains and produces above-random accuracy, but does not reproduce any of the paper's actual experiments on UK Biobank, M&Ms, or DVM data, nor any baseline comparisons. All claims are addressed only on a clearly toy proxy, with key ablation comparisons not properly isolated and generalization datasets entirely unrun.

GwendalTsang/repro-geometry-aware-probab.paper_title: Geometry-Aware Probabilistic Circuits via Voronoi Tessellations

claims.claim: Proposition 3.2 proves that a single Voronoi-gated node breaks tractability of probabilistic circuits even with fully factorized experts, because oblique Voronoi cell boundaries prevent the partition-function integral from factorizing (Proposition 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook computes the exact restricted mass P(Y≥X)=Φ(1/√2)=0.7602 for an oblique Voronoi boundary (centroids (0,1),(1,0)) with independent Gaussian experts, showing the product of coordinate projection integrals gives 1.0 (gap 0.2398), while an axis-aligned control region factorizes exactly (0.4207 both ways). This concretely demonstrates the non-factorizability structural property claimed in Proposition 3.2.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 shows that when Voronoi gating regions are geometrically aligned with the circuit's variable partition (Hierarchical Factorized Voronoi, or HFV, construction), the partition function decomposes and exact tractable inference is restored, with Theorem 3.14 giving inference time O(|C|K^m) for m-way factorizations with K cells per factor (Theorem 3.5, Theorem 3.14).
claims.evidence: For a 2-factor, 2-cell HFV node with nonuniform weights and unequal Gaussian experts, the factorized CDF computation gives Z=0.6433386432298214, matching independent piecewise numerical quadrature (0.6433386432298561, absolute error 3.47e-14). The complexity enumeration confirms exactly K^m joint cells for m∈{2,3}, K∈{2,...,10}, matching Theorem 3.14's operation count.

claims.claim: For the non-factorized Voronoi-gated PCs, Algorithm 1 provides an anytime refinement procedure yielding certified lower and upper bounds on partition functions, marginals, and conditionals that tighten monotonically at a rate of O(2^{-t/d}) after t refinement steps (Algorithm 1, Theorem 3.9).
claims.evidence: On a 2-cell diagonal tessellation of [-1,1]² with known Z=0.5, 128 adaptive refinement steps produced valid bounds (every interval contained Z), monotonically tightening (lower non-decreasing, upper non-increasing), with gap shrinking from 1.0 to 0.0996. Uniform refinement yielded a fitted log₂(gap) slope of -0.4964 per level versus the predicted -1/d=-0.5, and a conditional query produced a certified interval [0.4673, 0.6915] containing the exact value 0.5556.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.16 proves exponential convergence of the soft-to-hard Voronoi gate during temperature annealing: 1 minus the max soft gate weight is bounded by (K-1)exp(-alpha*gamma(u)) (Theorem 3.16).
claims.evidence: For 4 centroids in 2D with a fixed off-boundary point (margin γ=1.48), all 8 temperatures (α=0.5 to 64) satisfied the bound (K-1)exp(-αγ), with empirical log-error slope -1.5057 being at least as steep as the required -γ=-1.48, and the winning soft weight converging to 1.0.

claims.claim: On eight synthetic 2D/3D benchmarks (including CheckerBoard, Pinwheel, Spiral, and TwistedEight) compared against EinsumNet and HCLT baselines, VT-gated circuits attain certified lower bounds that often exceed baseline exact log-likelihoods, while HFV circuits match baseline performance with exact tractability preserved (Figure 1, experimental comparison).
claims.evidence: The logbook demonstrates algebraically that since log p(x)=log f(x)−log Z, using Z_lower (inner-box) yields an upper bound on log-likelihood, not a lower bound; the correctly directed lower bound uses Z_upper. In the paper-scale 48-run experiment (8 datasets × 2 families, 1 seed, 100 epochs), the correctly directed VT lower bound exceeded the exact baseline in only 2/16 comparisons, while the mislabeled inner-box-derived upper bound exceeded it in 16/16. HFV exact normalization was confirmed in 16/16 cases, but HFV performance matching was inconclusive (mean abs diff 0.16 on 2D, 2.47 on 3D) du

GwendalTsang/repro-geometry-aware-probab.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical verification of the paper's four theoretical claims (1–4) through executable code with independent cross-checks, and falsifies Claim 5 by showing the bound certification direction is algebraically inverted: the quantity reported as a 'certified lower bound' is actually an upper bound, and true certified lower bounds exceed baselines in only 2/16 cases.

squaredcuber/repro-loss-aware-distributi.paper_title: Loss-Aware Distributionally Robust Optimization via Trainable Optimal Transport Ambiguity Sets

claims.claim: The paper formulates learning the ambiguity set for OT-DRO as a bilevel problem in which the upper level tunes the ambiguity-set geometry parameter theta and the lower level solves a standard OT-DRO problem (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The bilevel structure (upper-level theta tuning wrapping a standard OT-DRO lower-level solve) was independently implemented and exercised end-to-end across 14,000 validated tasks spanning 50 portfolio and 10 regression distributions with multiple sample sizes; the 5,000-iteration cap affects convergence claims, not the formulation itself.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 establishes that the proposed hypergradient descent procedure converges to a critical point of the bilevel problem under mild conditions, including square-summable step sizes (Section 5.1, Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: A 12-item assumption audit was performed and source-bound, but no receipt establishes all theorem assumptions for the released instances, and the executed implementation is not the ideal recurrence analyzed in the theorem; finite capped trajectories cannot demonstrate asymptotic convergence.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 computes hypergradients through the nonsmooth conservative implicit function theorem, allowing differentiation through conic (OT-DRO) programs without assuming the solution map is continuously differentiable (Section 5, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: On the paper's exact Appendix A.2.1 W1 portfolio SOCP (2 assets, samples [1,0], radius 0.5, L=diag(t,1)), at the active-set boundary t=0.5 the solution derivative changes from (8,-8) to (0,0) yet every admissible generalized-Jacobian selection yields the same Algorithm 1 hypergradient of -2, confirmed by independent finite differences (-1.999996 at step 1e-6).

claims.claim: In portfolio optimization experiments with k=2, J=30, n_b=20, gamma=0.05, beta=0.1, the relative improvement of the learned ambiguity set over a fixed Wasserstein ball increases as sample size decreases (Section 6.1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Only 3 of the 5 anchored Figure 2 parameters (k=2, J=30, n_b=20, gamma=0.05, beta=0.1) are bound by the frozen plan, and the exact Figure 2 estimand is not source-bound; the available sample-size sweep is reported only as an extension and receives no claim credit.

claims.claim: Figure 3 shows the learned ambiguity set still enforces the coverage constraint, containing the true data-generating distribution with the specified high probability despite being shaped to reduce loss (Section 6.1, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Coverage values range from 0.752 to 0.868 across all ten sample sizes with every 95% upper bound below the 0.90 target, which is adverse to the claim, but 1,954 of 5,500 tasks hit the 5,000-iteration cap so the learned geometries are right-censored and a clean falsification of the converged method cannot be established.

claims.claim: Across 10 independent linear regression trials, the learned decision-focused ambiguity set consistently yields less conservative (lower average loss) decisions than baseline OT-DRO ambiguity sets (Section 6.2, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: The mean relative OOS improvement is positive at all five sample sizes (0.0403 to 0.1016 with positive 95% lower bounds), but Trial 5 is negative at every sample size (-0.0069 to -0.0005), contradicting the 'consistently' wording; however, capped training trajectories prevent determining whether the negative trial would persist with full convergence.

squaredcuber/repro-loss-aware-distributi.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting the bilevel formulation (Claim 1) and the nonsmooth hypergradient computation on a paper-native active-set boundary (Claim 3), but the 5,000-iteration cap on a substantial fraction of tasks prevents clean verification or falsification of the convergence theorem and the empirical performance and coverage claims.

agharsallah/2idtiht7w4-logbook.paper_title: A Sketch-and-Project Analysis of Subsampled Natural Gradient Algorithms

claims.claim: For linear least-squares problems, subsampled natural gradient descent (SNGD) is shown to be directly equivalent to the regularized Kaczmarz method, and SPRING is equivalent to the Nesterov-accelerated regularized Kaczmarz (ARK) method (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Independent implementations of SNGD (Eq. 8) and regularized block-Kaczmarz (Eq. 11) tested across 6 batch sizes, 12 lambda values, and 256 sketches per config yield max coordinate-wise discrepancy of exactly 0.0; SPRING(mu=0) vs SNGD trajectory difference is 0.0 over 220 iterations, confirmed by a sympy symbolic check with residual 0.

claims.claim: SNGD converges at rate (1-α)^t where α=λ_min(P̄), while SPRING converges at rate O((1-√(α/β))^t), giving up to a square-root improvement in iteration complexity over SNGD (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Exact enumeration of all 220 subsets on a 12x5 system gives alpha=0.2195, beta=2.5329; 400 trajectories per method yield fitted decay bases SNGD=0.6346 and SPRING=0.5773, both below their theoretical conservative bounds (0.7805, 0.7056), with SPRING strictly faster than SNGD.

claims.claim: For general quadratic losses, SNGD requires the regularization parameter λ to exceed a threshold λ0 to guarantee convergence, and can diverge if regularization is insufficient (Proposition 3).
claims.evidence: On a 4x2 general-quadratic witness (seed 70), exact spectral analysis of the expected iteration operator gives rho=1.0275>1 at lam=0 (divergence, paired trajectory median error 3.08e16) and rho=0.8447<1 at lam=0.1 (convergence, median error 2.60e-6), directly demonstrating both halves of Proposition 3.

claims.claim: Under an assumption that the regularized projector P̄ shares an eigenbasis with J^T J, SNGD provably outperforms SGD by a factor of k^β when the spectrum of the Jacobian decays polynomially (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: A 1400x24 Jacobian with i^{-1} singular values (J^T J eigenvalues decay as i^{-2}) with 2500 mini-batches per k yields a log-log exponent beta_hat=1.894 (theory 2), with a flat-spectrum control giving exponent 1.047, isolating spectral decay as the source of the superlinear k^beta advantage.

claims.claim: A unified algorithm (Algorithm 1) captures both SNGD (momentum μ=0) and SPRING (μ∈(0,1)) as momentum-based updates using subsampled Jacobians, enabling single-minibatch convergence guarantees of any batch size.
claims.evidence: A single unified recurrence across k in {1,2,4,6,9,11} over 200 iterations with shared state and random stream gives max trajectory discrepancy 0.0 at mu=0 (matching SNGD) and 0.0 at mu=0.6 (matching SPRING), while differing from SNGD by 32.16 at mu=0.6, confirming the momentum term is active.

claims.claim: Analysis of SPRING's convergence for general (non-least-squares) quadratic losses is left open as Conjecture 7, despite numerical experiments showing large empirical performance gains over SNGD.
claims.evidence: Source audit confirms Conjecture 7 remains open with no proof; independent 240x20 general-quadratic experiments with 24 trials across 5 batch sizes show SPRING beats SNGD in 99.2% of runs with median final-error ratio 5.74x (max 1715x), reproducing the large empirical gains described in the paper.

agharsallah/2idtiht7w4-logbook.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical and symbolic evidence supporting all six claims, using exact computations (subset enumeration, spectral radius, sympy symbolic checks) and statistical trajectory experiments at reasonable scale. Algebraic identities are confirmed to machine precision, convergence rate predictions are validated by trajectory fitting with appropriate controls, and the open conjecture status is confirmed alongside reproduced empirical gains.

agharsallah/q1khlimwkp-logbook.paper_title: Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader for Decoupled Bandits: Best-of-Both-Worlds and Practicality

claims.claim: In the adversarial regime, the proposed FTPL policy for decoupled bandits achieves O(sqrt(KT)) regret, matching the lower bound of Avner et al. 2012 (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: T-scan at K=8 shows Reg/sqrt(KT) ≈ 0.67–0.69 (constant across 16x T range) with log-log slope 0.507≈0.5; K-scan at T=10000 shows ratio bounded <0.84 for K∈{4,8,16,32}; Zimmert-Seldin non-stationary adversarial sequence also yields small ratios (0.095–0.049). 500 reps on the paper's actual algorithm.

claims.claim: In the stochastic (SCA) regime, with perturbation parameter alpha in (1,3], the FTPL policy achieves a time-independent regret bound of O(K/Delta_min), improving on the standard MAB O(sum log T/Delta_i) bound (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: On the paper's stochastic Bernoulli instance (K=5, Delta_min=0.05), at alpha=3 regret plateaus from 63.7 (T=10k) to 73.6 (T=80k) with tail slope 0.070, while UCB1 grows 247→494 (slope 0.333); slopes monotonically flatten across alpha∈{1.5,2.0,2.5,3.0} (0.258→0.070), and plateau value ~74 is same order as K/Delta_min=100.

claims.claim: Setting alpha=3 yields a near-optimal best-of-both-worlds regret bound of O(sqrt((K/Delta_min) * sum(1/Delta_i)) + K/Delta_min) (Corollary 3).
claims.evidence: K-sweep at fixed Delta_min=0.1 gives plateau regret 27.8→90.3 for K∈{3,5,8,12} (log-log slope 0.86, near-linear matching K/Delta_min term); Delta_min sweep shows regret increasing from 42.5 to 71.3 as gap shrinks (slope −0.39 vs Delta_min); same alpha=3 config achieves adversarial O(sqrt(KT)) per Claim 1 data.

claims.claim: The exploration probabilities q_{t,i} are computed via a closed-form approximation requiring only O(K log K) time per round through sorting, avoiding convex optimization or geometric resampling used by prior FTRL/FTPL decoupled-bandit methods (Equation 7, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Independent re-implementation of Eq.(7) matches production code with max deviation 0.0 over 300 random configurations; operation counters show FTPL uses 0 Newton iterations, 0 resampling draws, and 1 sort per round, vs 39.6 root-find iterations for Tsallis-INF-FTRL and 3.67 (up to 353) resamples for FTPL+Geometric-Resampling.

claims.claim: In adversarial-regime experiments, the proposed method runs approximately 2020 times faster than the Decoupled-Tsallis-INF baseline while achieving comparable regret.
claims.evidence: Per-step timing across K∈{2..512} shows FTPL at 7–25 μs (flat in K); speedup vs generic convex solver ranges 385x (K=8) to 4618x (K=64), bracketing the claimed ~2020x; regret comparison on K=8 adversarial instance is 194.8 vs 150.0 (same order). Caveat: against a specialized bisection solver the speedup is only ~14x, so the 2020x figure depends on baseline solver choice.

claims.claim: In stochastic-regime experiments, the method outperforms both the EB-TC pure-exploration policy and naive mixed exploration/exploitation policies.
claims.evidence: On the paper's stochastic instance (T=20000, 500 reps), FTPL regret is 76.6±6.0, strictly below naive eps=0.05 (283.9±17.4), naive eps=0.10 (422.6±12.1), and EB-TC (2291.6±6.5), with all gaps far exceeding confidence intervals.

agharsallah/q1khlimwkp-logbook.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from non-toy simulations (the paper's actual Algorithm 1, real bandit instances, 300–500 reps, horizons up to T=80k) supporting all six claims: adversarial sqrt(KT) scaling, stochastic constant regret, BOBW structure, closed-form O(K log K) computation, large speedups, and superior stochastic-regime performance. The main caveat is that the ~2020x speedup in Claim 5 is only reproduced against a generic convex solver, not a specialized one (which yields ~14x).

claims.claim: Do-Shapley values can be computed exactly in O(r(d+e+T)) time, where r is the number of irreducible sets, d the number of dimensions, e the number of edges, and T the value-function evaluation time, versus the naive 2^d complexity (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Across 60 SCMs (d=6-10) the exact r-class algorithm matches brute-force 2^d Shapley to max error 3.4e-14 with value-function evaluations exactly equal to r (not 2^d); runtime Pearson correlation with r is 0.9991 up to d=18 (r=230,400); Sachs DAG reproduced at 7.8e-16 error with r=72 vs 256; two negative controls (sham value function, dropped empty class) break the identity with median errors 0.444 and 0.68.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 shows the do-Shapley value phi_i is identifiable if and only if nu({j}) is identifiable for all j in [d], reducing identifiability checks from r coalitions to just d singleton coalitions (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: A Shpitser-Pearl ID algorithm validated on 5 canonical identifiability cases (all correct) confirms the iff characterization over 200 random ADMGs (d=4-8) with agreement rate 1.0 and zero counterexamples, with both branches exercised (31 identifiable, 169 non-identifiable); Sachs DAG reduces r=72 coalition checks to d=8 singleton checks.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.1 establishes that for any closed set with a basis, removing any basis element yields another closed set, enabling efficient lattice traversal via Algorithm 2 (Lemma 3.1, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: Both Lemma 3.1 statements (removing basis element yields closed set; existence of upward-closed neighbor) show 0 violations across chain/star/layered/random graphs (d=6-10) and Sachs; Algorithm 2's symmetric difference with exhaustive powerset enumeration is 0 on every graph; an independent semantic basis/closure oracle computed from graph paths matches Algorithm 1 with 0 mismatches.

claims.claim: Algorithm 3 (boundary sampling) guarantees discovery of min(m, r) distinct equivalence classes using m queries, running in O(m*d(d+e)) time (Section on estimator performance, Algorithm 3).
claims.evidence: Over 1,308 budget/graph configurations (d=6-7, m from 1 to 2r), the boundary sampler discovers exactly min(m,r) distinct classes with 0 deviations; the blind with-replacement baseline finds 35-45% fewer at m=r (e.g., 1024 vs 643, 976 vs 602), confirming the structure-aware sample-efficiency guarantee.

claims.claim: The doRegressionMSR estimator consistently outperforms baseline variants and exhibits a phase transition at m=r, where error vanishes to machine precision while structure-agnostic methods retain variance (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: The structure-aware estimator's relative MSE drops from 1.05e-2 at m/r=0.75 to 8.8e-30 at m/r=1.0 (machine precision) and stays there, while the blind baseline retains 1.6e-2 at m/r=1.0 and only reaches 4.4e-3 at m/r=2.0 — a 27.3-order-of-magnitude gap at the phase transition, with the structure-aware estimator monotonically dominating throughout.

claims.claim: Real-world causal structures tend to be sparse, so the number of irreducible sets r scales between the exponential worst case 2^d and the linear lower bound d (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Across 447 graphs the bound d ≤ r ≤ 2^d holds with 0 violations; chain graphs give r=d+1 (linear, verified d=2-14) and star graphs give r=2^d exactly (verified d=2-14, up to 16,384); the real Sachs DAG has r/2^d=72/256=0.281, well below the exponential ceiling, confirming sparsity of real-world structures.

agharsallah/peim0ky6ty-logbook.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from a self-contained CPU implementation testing all six claims against independent semantic oracles (linear-Gaussian SCMs, Shpitser-Pearl ID algorithm, exhaustive enumeration) on synthetic graphs up to d=18 and the real Sachs consensus DAG, with negative controls and brute-force comparisons throughout. All claims are supported by specific quantitative results in raw data tables rather than mere assertions.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.5 establishes that with step size ηk=1/(2Lm k^(1/2)) and penalty parameter ρk=k^(1/4), LCBO's stationarity residual satisfies rs(xk+1,λk+1) ≤ (C1,m + C2 εK)/√K and its feasibility residual satisfies rf(xk+1) ≤ C3/√K + (C4,m + C5 εK)/K (Theorem 5.5, Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides a valid finite counterexample (sequence (10,0,...,0) at K=100 has average 0.1=K^{-1/2} but maximum 10) demonstrating that Theorem 5.5 bounds averaged residuals K^{-1}∑r_s and K^{-1}∑r_f, not pointwise residuals as the claim states. A 50,000-step exact-oracle 1D quadratic recurrence yields tail slopes of -0.9959 (stationarity) and -0.4503 (feasibility), consistent with the corrected averaged rates but not the claimed pointwise bounds.

claims.claim: Corollary 5.6 shows that for RBF and Matérn (ν=2.5) kernels, LCBO's KKT stationarity residual bound scales as Õ(m^(5/2) d^(1/6) n^(-1/6) + σ m^(13/6) d^(7/6) n^(-1/6)), i.e., polynomially in dimension d rather than exponentially as in prior global constrained BO methods (Corollary 5.6, Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: Independent rational-exponent substitution of n=Θ(mdK³) into the paper's K-rate exactly reproduces the claimed exponents m^{5/2}d^{1/6}n^{-1/6} + σm^{13/6}d^{7/6}n^{-1/6}, confirmed by a 240-row 80-digit precision grid with maximum float64 relative error 4.64e-16. The cited Wu et al. gradient-variance lemma supplies the required E=O(σd^{3/2}b^{-1/2}) bound for RBF and Matérn-2.5 kernels.

claims.claim: LCBO is compared against CEI, EPBO, SCBO, and HDsafeBO baselines on synthetic constrained optimization benchmarks at d=25, 50, and 100, with LCBO's advantage over baselines growing more pronounced as dimension increases (Section 6.1-6.2).
claims.evidence: The only evidence is digitization of the paper's own published vector figure, yielding LCBO advantages of ~0.40 (25D), ~0.89 (50D), and ~2.46 (100D) at evaluation 950. No independent experimental runs were conducted; no official optimizer code, raw trajectories, seeds, or GP hyperparameters were available to enable a reproduction.

claims.claim: On the 50-dimensional Stepped Cantilever real-world task, LCBO sustains convergence to a feasible optimum while the EPBO baseline fails to find any feasible solution (Section 6.3).
claims.evidence: An independent 50D beam run (3 seeds, 250 evaluations, RFF surrogate replacing RBF-GP, 128 random candidates replacing Adam) found EPBO-like feasible in 2/3 runs, contradicting the claim that EPBO finds no feasible solution, but the substantial surrogate and budget deviations (250 vs 1000 evaluations, RFF vs RBF-GP/MLE) prevent a clean test. Digitization of the paper's Beam panel is consistent with the claim but is not independent evidence.

claims.claim: On the 102-dimensional MuJoCo HalfCheetah task, LCBO shows the most rapid initial descent and superior stability compared to baseline methods (Section 6.3).
claims.evidence: Digitized linear slopes from the paper's own published median plot over the preregistered window (evaluations 102–282) are: HDsafeBO -0.00523, SCBO -0.00418, EPBO -0.00390, LCBO -0.00296, CEI -0.00153. LCBO ranks 4th of 5 in initial descent speed, directly contradicting the 'most rapid initial descent' subclaim. The stability subclaim remains unaddressed due to undefined metrics and absent raw trajectories.

MarxistLeninist/iq8WrTozWy.overall: The logbook provides rigorous theoretical verification of Corollary 5.6's polynomial scaling exponents and a valid mathematical falsification of the pointwise reading of Theorem 5.5, but empirical claims are largely unaddressed due to missing official code and data. The only independent experimental run (50D beam, reduced budget with surrogate substitutions) yields mixed results that neither cleanly verify nor falsify the beam claim, while digitized slopes from the paper's own HalfCheetah figure contradict the fastest-initial-descent claim.

algorise/repro-cyberjurors-a-multi-agent.paper_title: CyberJurors: A Multi-Agent Simulation Task for E-Commerce Disputes Verdict

claims.claim: VerdictBench is introduced as a multimodal e-commerce dispute verdict benchmark comprising 6,000 real-world cases across five categories, each with crowdsourced jury verdicts and evidence averaging 14 images and 0.9 videos per case (Dataset section).
claims.evidence: The logbook programmatically inspected only the precedent database (2,953 cases in Social_Consensus.json), not the full 6,000-case benchmark. claims.claim: Lemma 1 shows that repeated evolutionary selection induces conditional dependencies among variables that are absent under static selection models, so applying static-selection graphical models to evolutionary data can yield false causal discoveries (Section 2, Lemma 1).

claims.claim: Theorem 1 proves that the clique-augmented DAG G^+ (Definition 2) fully captures all d-separation/conditional-independence constraints implied by the evolutionary selection model, without needing to explicitly model the selection variables (Section 3, Definition 2, Theorem 1).

claims.claim: Theorem 2 establishes that applying standard constraint-based algorithms such as PC or GES (Algorithm 1) to G^+ is sound and complete: oriented edges correspond to true causal relations, while unoriented edges may reflect the presence of selection (Section 3, Theorem 2, Algorithm 1).

GwendalTsang/repro-colorful-pinball-dens.paper_title: Colorful Pinball: Density-Weighted Quantile Regression for Conditional Guarantee of Conformal Prediction

claims.claim: Proposition 3.4 shows the optimal density weight for quantile regression equals the conditional density of the score evaluated at the true quantile, which for location-scale distributions is proportional to 1/sigma(x), capturing heteroscedastic structure ignored by standard pinball loss (Proposition 3.4).
claims.evidence: On synthetic Gaussian and Laplace location-scale data with 20,000 heteroscedastic draws, w(x)·sigma(x) has std 3.1e-17 (Gaussian) and 8.1e-18 (Laplace), confirming exact proportionality to 1/sigma(x) with constant f_0(z_tau). The Taylor identity (F(q_hat)-tau)^2 = 2*f(q_tau)*E(x) + O(eps^3) is confirmed: the weighted ratio approaches 1.0 as eps→0 (0.9915 at eps=0.01 for Gaussian) while the unweighted ratio converges to f(q_tau)=0.1755 instead, exactly as the proposition predicts.

claims.claim: The proposed three-stage framework estimates joint quantiles at levels tau-delta, tau, tau+delta, computes density weights via the finite-difference w(x) = 2*delta / (q_hat_{tau+delta}(x) - q_hat_{tau-delta}(x)), then fine-tunes the central quantile with a weighted pinball loss before conformalization (Section 3, three-stage framework).
claims.evidence: Using the authors' vendored MonotonicThreeHeadNet on synthetic and Naval data across 5 seeds: Stage 1 recovers all three quantile levels within ~1.7 points of nominal and maintains correct ordering; the finite-difference weight achieves Spearman r=0.9213 with the true density; Stage 2 fine-tuning shifts 99.99% of test predictions by ~6% of quantile magnitude; Stage 3 conformalization restores marginal coverage to 0.9097±0.0102 against target 0.9.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 gives a non-asymptotic excess risk bound with asymptotic rate O(R_n(G)^(2/3)) ≈ O(n^(-1/3)) under an optimal bandwidth choice delta* proportional to R_n(G)^(1/3) (Theorem 5.2).

claims.evidence: Softplus parameterization yields 0 ordering violations on 200,000 adversarial probes (|x| up to 1000); clipping at M=5.0 binds on all 8 datasets (0.03–6.5% of weights, raw max 21–67x mean); loss mixing at lambda=0.5 is confirmed algebraically as effective weight w_eff=0.5*w+0.5 with measured range [0.66, 1.84] on Naval. DineshAI/32XNOcwH1z.paper_title: Efficient Preference Poisoning Attack on Offline RLHF

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 shows that flipping a single preference label shifts the DPO gradient by a vector o_i·β·Δψ_i that is independent of the current policy parameter θ, enabling reformulation of preference poisoning as a binary sparse approximation problem in gradient space (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Across 1,125 single-comparison cells, the predicted gradient shift o_i·β·Δψ_i matches the actual DPO flip-induced shift with max error 8.88e-16, and parameter-independence is confirmed (max variation across θ values 8.88e-16); 225 nonlinear-logit controls correctly reject parameter-independence, confirming the result is specific to log-linear DPO as the paper claims.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 establishes a lower bound on the number of required label flips, |ℱ| ≥ ||g†||_2/(2β), showing flip requirements scale linearly with the target gradient norm (Section 3, Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The dedicated Theorem 3.4 verifier confirms ||v_i||≤2β (max 0.197≤0.2), zero lower-bound violations across 80 targets, tightness on an aligned dictionary (20 flips = ceil(4/0.2)), and a negative control showing inflated ||v_i||>2β reaches the target in 10<30 flips, directly supporting |ℱ|≥||g†||/(2β).

claims.claim: The Binary-Aware Lattice Attack (BAL-A) uses a penalty parameter M ≥ M_0(B,R,K*) so that the shortest lattice vector has coefficients constrained to {-1,0,1}^n, and under a separation condition ρ_k² > M²(K*-k), recovers the true K*-flip attack pattern exactly (Section 4.1, Lemma 4.1, Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Exact Fraction-arithmetic verification of Lemma 4.1, Theorem 4.2, and Theorem 4.3 on 48 complete binary instances (4,032 pattern certificates) plus an independent auditor (29 instances, 4,064 subsets) confirms that M≥M₀ forces binary coefficients and the separation condition ρ_k²>M²(K*-k) guarantees exact K*-flip recovery; the 15/96 LLL/Babai/truncation failures pertain to the practical heuristic, not the theoretical guarantee the claim references.

claims.claim: The Binary Matching Pursuit Attack (BMP-A) recovers the exact flip support within K* iterations when the gradient dictionary's coherence satisfies μ(V) < b/((2K*-1)B) (Section 5.2, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: On 240 non-normalized low-coherence dictionaries (48×10) with K*=1–4, BMP-A recovers the exact flip support in every cell when μ(V)<b/((2K*-1)B), with max final residual below tolerance (−0.12 margin).

claims.claim: Theorem 5.4 provides impossibility certificates against K-flip attacks under a spectral norm condition ||g†||_2 - ε > √K·||V||_2 and a coherence condition (||g†||_2 - ε)² > B²(K + μ(V)K(K-1)) (Section 5, Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: A concrete counterexample (V=I₂, g=0, ε=2, K=1) shows the squared coherence condition (||g†||−ε)²>B²(K+μK(K−1)) evaluates to 4>1 (true) while zero flips already achieve the tolerance, making the certificate a false positive; the spectral norm condition is separately verified (226 cells), but the coherence condition as stated in the claim is incorrect.

claims.claim: On the SHP dataset, the crafted attack shifts the trained policy far closer to the intended target than clean training does (||π_θ†-π_θ̂||_1 ≈ 0.012 vs ||π_clean-π_θ̂||_1 ≈ 0.224), and BMP-A runs roughly four orders of magnitude faster than BAL-A (1.37×10⁻⁴s vs 0.6865s) on the same data subset (Section 6.2.3).
claims.evidence: The timing claim is supported (BMP-A median 1.397e-4s vs BAL-A 2.296s, ratio 4.22 orders of magnitude), but the policy L1 values are not reproduced: attacked-vs-target is artificially 0.0 (not ≈0.012) due to identical clean-room setup, and clean-vs-attacked is 0.4169 (not comparable to the paper's ≈0.224 clean-vs-target), so the specific numerical policy claims remain unverified.

DineshAI/32XNOcwH1z.overall: The logbook provides strong finite-family verification of the mathematical theorems (Claims 1–4) with exact arithmetic and negative controls, falsifies the squared coherence impossibility certificate (Claim 5) via a concrete counterexample, and only partially reproduces the SHP empirical results (Claim 6) with timing confirmed but policy-distance values not matched.

ai-sherpa/why-deep-jacobian-spectra-sepa.paper_title: Why Deep Jacobian Spectra Separate: Depth-Induced Scaling and Singular-Vector Alignment

claims.claim: Theorem 5.3 gives closed-form Lyapunov exponents governing the top singular values of masked (fixed-gates) linear networks, including a finite-depth correction term (d_{i-1}-d_i)/L (Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: At native scale (n=128, 300 trials/depth, both p∈{1.0,0.5}), RMSE of (1/L)log s_i vs the closed-form γ_i decays monotonically from 0.420→0.018 (p=1.0) and 0.530→0.019 (p=0.5) over L=2..100, and s_2/s_1 falls from ~0.95 to 0.51/0.34, confirming the leading-order Lyapunov exponent convergence. The finite-depth correction sub-term was not tested (disclosed as ambiguous in the appendix), but the core theorem content is strongly supported.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.1 proves that sufficiently strong spectral separation between consecutive singular values forces alignment of dominant singular vectors across the matrix product, yielding an approximately shared singular basis for intermediate Jacobians (Theorem 6.1).
claims.evidence: At native scale (n=128, 100 trials, both p regimes), the block residual ‖R_L^{r,r}−I_r‖_F decreases monotonically from 2.91→0.71 (p=1.0) and 2.93→0.43 (p=0.5) over L=10..200, tracking the suffix-product separation ratio s_2/s_1 of A_l falling correspondingly. This directly tests the theorem's literal asymptotic content.

claims.claim: Proposition 7.1 shows that combining depth-induced scaling and spectral separation recovers deep-linear-like singular-value training dynamics for fixed-gates networks without the balanced-initialization assumption required by prior analyses (Proposition 7.1).
claims.evidence: At the paper's exact Appendix-G.1 scale (n=64, L=10, p=0.5, rank-10 target, non-balanced init, 5 seeds), 4/5 converged seeds show Jacobian effective rank rising from ~6 to 9.59–9.81, top-10 energy →>0.99999, and target-subspace alignment rising from ~0.15 to 0.998–1.0, confirming the predicted low-rank-in-correct-subspace implicit bias without balanced initialization. The 1 stalled seed is honestly disclosed.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.5 recovers the balanced deep-linear singular-value ODE of Arora et al. (2019), ds_k/dt = -L s_k(t)^{2-2/L} <grad_J L, u_k v_k^T>, as a special case of the paper's more general framework (Proposition 4.5).
claims.evidence: On exactly-balanced constructions (balance verified to ≤2.4e-15, reconstruction ≤9.5e-16) at L=2,3,5, the independently computed layerwise gradient-flow velocity ds_k/dt matches the Arora closed form −L·s_k^{2−2/L}·⟨∇_J L, u_k v_k^T⟩ to max relative error 3.6e-14 (top modes) and 1.6e-13 (all modes), confirming the algebraic identity to float64 precision.

claims.claim: On a synthetic rank-10 regression task with depth-10, width-64 networks, the top-15 Jacobian log-singular values during training converge toward the predicted theoretical Lyapunov exponents and finite-depth corrections (Figure 1, Figures 2-3).
claims.evidence: At native scale (n=64, L=10, p=0.5, 3 seeds), the initial top-15 log-spectrum follows the Lyapunov prediction, and under training the top-10 modes grow 16.6–28.1× while tail modes 11–15 shrink to 0.12–0.17×, with the s_10/s_11 gap sharpening from ~1.21 to 348–559. The finite-depth correction sub-claim is not tested (disclosed), but the main experimental content—Lyapunov match and separation dynamics—is reproduced at native scale.

claims.claim: Controlled MNIST experiments with square hidden layers of width n=128 validate the predicted emergence of depth-induced low-rank clustering and singular-vector alignment near a diagonal structure (Figure 4, Figures 5-6).
claims.evidence: On real MNIST at native width-128/depth-10 (3 seeds), the hidden-Jacobian effective rank collapses from ~14 to ~10, top-10 energy rises from ~0.93 to ~0.995, the s_10/s_11 gap sharpens in every seed, and the diagonal-correlation ρ remains high (~0.74). The alignment is moderate and largely pre-existing rather than training-driven, and an 8192-example subset is used, but the core low-rank clustering and near-diagonal alignment signatures are reproduced at native model scale on real data.

ai-sherpa/why-deep-jacobian-spectra-sepa.overall: The logbook provides strong, independently computed numerical evidence at the paper's native scale for all six claims, including machine-precision verification of the Arora-ODE identity (Claim 4) and robust multi-seed confirmation of Lyapunov convergence, singular-vector alignment, and implicit bias signatures. The finite-depth correction term (Claims 1, 5) is honestly disclosed as untestable due to ambiguity in the paper's appendix, and the MNIST alignment is moderate, but the core theoretical predictions are well-supported.

claims.claim: Definition 1 introduces ℓ*-smoothness, bounding the Hessian via a general norm and its dual, ‖∇²f(x)h‖* ≤ ℓ(‖∇f(x)‖*)‖h‖, generalizing prior ℓ-smoothness beyond the Euclidean/ℓ2 setting (Section 3.1, Definition 1)
claims.evidence: The ℓ*-smoothness inequality was tested on 1,200 random (x,h) samples across dimensions up to 256, in both Euclidean (ℓ2/ℓ2) and non-Euclidean (ℓ1/ℓ∞) geometries, with quadratics (constant ℓ) and exponential family (affine ℓ(t)). The inequality held at all 1,200 points with worst-case ratio 0.99986, demonstrating the bound is tight and operational beyond the Euclidean setting.

claims.claim: Theorem 8 shows mirror descent under ℓ*-smoothness attains O(1/T) convergence for both average-iterate and last-iterate suboptimality with an appropriately chosen learning rate (Section 4, Theorem 8)
claims.evidence: Mirror descent on a 1,024-dim non-strongly-convex quadratic (spectrum [1e-8,1]) run to T=4,096 over 3 seeds showed both average-iterate (slope −0.939, R²=0.9995) and last-iterate (slope −0.983, R²=0.9993) suboptimality satisfying the certificate gap(T) ≤ L·D²/(2T) at every horizon with 0 violations.

claims.claim: Theorem 9 shows an accelerated mirror descent variant attains the optimal O(1/T^2) convergence rate under ℓ*-smoothness via a time-partition analysis technique (Section 4, Theorem 9)
claims.evidence: Accelerated mirror descent on the same 1,024-dim quadratic run to T=4,096 showed the O(1/T²) certificate gap(T) ≤ 2L·D²/(T(T+1)) holding at every checkpoint with tail slope −2.018 (R²=0.9997), and a 564× speedup over plain mirror descent at T=4,096 (6.24e-6 vs 3.52e-3).

claims.claim: Theorem 10 and Theorem 11 extend the O(1/T) rate to optimistic mirror descent and mirror prox respectively, using a stability-tracking argument and a descent property for both update sequences (Section 4, Theorems 10-11)
claims.evidence: Optimistic mirror descent (slope −1.18) and mirror prox (slope −1.29) on a 200-dim quadratic over T=4,096 and 3 seeds both maintained average-iterate suboptimality below the L·D²/T certificate at every horizon. The mirror-prox descent property was audited across all 12,288 steps with 0 violations, confirming the monotone non-increasing function value required by Theorem 11.

claims.claim: Theorem 12 establishes an Õ(1/√t) anytime convergence rate for stochastic mirror descent under ℓ*-smoothness with a generalized bounded-noise assumption ‖ϵ_t‖* ≤ σ(‖∇f(x_t)‖*) (Section 5, Theorem 12)
claims.evidence: Stochastic mirror descent with anytime step size η_t=c/√t and gradient-scaled noise σ(α)=0.05α was run over 256 trajectories × 16,384 steps (4.19M updates). The tail log-log slope was −0.486 (R²=0.99983) and the √t-scaled 95% envelope remained bounded (4.82→5.25, <20% growth), confirming the anytime Õ(1/√t) rate under the generalized noise assumption.

claims.claim: Proposition 4 shows that on the simplex, ℓ*-smoothness yields a constant smoothness parameter whereas standard ℓ-smoothness has an O(n) dimension dependence, illustrating the benefit of the generalized notion (Section 3.2, Proposition 4)
claims.evidence: Exact operator norms for A=J_n−I_n computed across n up to 4,096 show the ℓ2 spectral norm equals n−1 exactly (fitted slope 1.029, R²=0.9994, confirming O(n) dependence) while the ℓ1→ℓ∞ operator norm equals 1 for all n (constant), yielding a 4,095× gap at n=4,096 that directly confirms Proposition 4.

agharsallah/j9aoifr5am-logbook.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims through non-trivial experiments: inequality verification across multiple geometries and dimensions, convergence-rate certificate checking with fitted slopes on 1,024-dim problems, 4.19M stochastic updates, and exact operator-norm computations up to n=4,096. claims.claim: Self-reflection alone produces only a minimal increase in visual attention (Delta=1.07), whereas explicit multi-turn user instructions to re-examine the image produce a much larger increase (Delta=2.21) and restore Qwen3-VL-235B-Thinking's accuracy from 34.1% to 85.4% (Section 5.2, Section 5.3).

claims.claim: A human baseline achieves 100% success in distinguishing the swapped VisualSwap image pairs, confirming the answer-relevant visual differences are readily detectable and the VLM failures reflect reliance on stale reasoning rather than genuine ambiguity (Appendix G).
claims.evidence: The human study (5 volunteers, 50 pairs each, 100% success) was not reproduced—C21 is marked not_applicable because a human annotation study cannot be re-run from code. The logbook checked that 799/800 pairs have distinct ground-truth answers and confirmed the textual-inertia failure mode (C22), but these are indirect supports, not a direct test of the human baseline claim.
