arvkevi/repro-dp-mixtures-of-gaussians.paper_title: Mind the Gap: Mixtures of Gaussians in Approximate Differential Privacy

claims.claim: Across 150 tested parameter settings in Table 1, multimodal (mixture-of-Gaussians) mechanisms achieve lower expected l1 noise loss than the analytic Gaussian mechanism in 142 of 150 cases, with mean reduction of 53.73% (std 34.86%) and median reduction of 61.86% (Section 5, Table 1).
claims.evidence: Running the official Julia code on all 150 cells yields 139/150 wins (not 142), mean 52.13% (not 53.73%), sd 32.76% (not 34.86%), median 62.99% (not 61.86%). Additionally, reconstructing the paper's own reported l1 values at four Table-1 cells gives hockey-stick divergence ~1.0, indicating the reported distributions violate the stated privacy budget.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.3 proves that for any delta in (0, 1/2) there exists an epsilon_0 such that the multimodal Gaussian mechanism has strictly lower l2 loss (variance) than the analytic Gaussian mechanism for all epsilon >= epsilon_0 (Section 3, Proposition 3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook reconstructs the Appendix B.5 proof: analytic Gaussian has L2 = 1/(2ε) + c_δ/ε^(3/2) + O(ε^-2) while a feasible K=1 mixture has L2 ≤ 1/(2ε) + 2exp(-ε), and since exp(-ε) = o(ε^-3/2), strict inequality holds for large ε. Numerical Balle-Wang witnesses across all 15 deltas confirm crossings at integer ε 3–15 with strict margins through ε=40.

claims.claim: In the low-privacy regime (epsilon >= 1), the proposed mixture mechanisms close up to 99% of the optimality gap between the analytic Gaussian mechanism and the theoretical lower bound, with l1-loss improvements of 79-99% depending on delta (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Independent dense integration of the mixture density at four high-ε cells yields hockey-stick divergence 0.9816–0.9990, far exceeding the stated δ, meaning the mechanism is not actually (ε,δ)-DP. A rigorous Geng et al. lower bound computation shows maximum certified gap closure of only 95.04%, below the claimed 99%.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.7 shows the multimodal Gaussian mechanisms satisfy the same zero-concentrated differential privacy guarantee (rho = Delta^2 / 2*sigma^2) as the standard Gaussian mechanism, preserving standard composition properties (Section 3, Corollary 3.7).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides an exact proof reconstruction: each Gaussian component pair has Rényi divergence α·shift²/(2σ²), mixture weights are identical for neighboring databases, and quasi-convexity of Rényi divergence under shared convex mixtures bounds the mixture divergence by the max component divergence, yielding ρ = Δ²/(2σ²) for all K and all α>1.

claims.claim: Table 2 compares the mixture mechanisms against truncated Laplace, Tulap, staircase, cactus, and flipped Huber mechanisms, finding the Gaussian mixtures competitive for epsilon >= 1 but inferior to non-Gaussian mechanisms for epsilon < 1 (Section 5, Table 2).
claims.evidence: The qualitative split is partially reproduced (75/90 wins at ε≥1, 1/60 wins below ε=1), but only 2 of 5 baselines were evaluated, the paper's specific cell values do not match, and the high-ε mixture outputs fail independent DP checks, undermining the validity of the comparison.

arvkevi/repro-dp-mixtures-of-gaussians.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous full-grid numerical audit and exact proof reconstructions, finding that the theoretical claims (Proposition 3.3, Corollary 3.7) hold but the empirical claims (Table 1, Table 2, optimality gap) are undermined by privacy violations in the official implementation and numerical discrepancies with the paper's reported values.

agharsallah/pyi0wjv5im-logbook.paper_title: Improved Convergence Analysis of Topology Dependence in Decentralized SGD

claims.claim: Theorem 1 gives improved convergence rates for Decentralized SGD in the strongly-convex, convex, and non-convex cases by replacing the spectral-gap-only dependency with the term (1/n)*sum_{i=2}^{n} lambda_i^2/(1-lambda_i^2), which depends on all eigenvalues of the mixing matrix (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Monte-Carlo D-SGD across 12 real topologies shows V_ss/(eta^2 sigma^2 T_new) ratios within 6% of 1.0 (raw CSV: ring16=1.007, torus16=1.001, hypercube32=0.998, etc.), and the decisive matched-gap control with 5 matrices sharing identical lambda_2=0.86 (T_gap spread 1.0000x) but T_new swept 15x shows V_ss varying 14.9x with Spearman=1.0, directly demonstrating all-eigenvalue dependence at fixed spectral gap.

claims.claim: Lemma 2 bounds stochastic noise propagation through the network using independence of gradient noise across nodes, showing (1/n)*sum_{i=2}^{n} lambda_i^2 <= max_{i>=2}(lambda_i^2), which yields tighter convergence bounds than prior spectral-gap-only analyses (Lemma 2).
claims.evidence: The inequality (1/n)*sum lambda_i^2 <= max lambda_i^2 holds across all 11 Metropolis matrices (raw CSV shows margins from 0.291 to 0.708), and 2M-draw Monte-Carlo confirms E[(1/n)||dev(W xi)||^2] matches the analytic all-eigenvalue trace to 0.026% relative error (measured 0.2101 vs analytic 0.2101, etc.), with averaged traces strictly below the worst-case max in every case.

claims.claim: Table 1 shows the number of transient iterations improves for several topologies: ring from O(n^7) to O(n^5), torus from O(n^5) to O(n^3 log^2(n)), and hypercube from O(n^3 log^2(n)) to O(n^3) (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Exact eigenvalues of Metropolis matrices computed up to n=1024 yield fitted growth exponents: ring T_gap~n^2.011 vs T_new~n^1.094, torus T_gap~n^1.079 vs T_new~log n (R^2=0.9991), hypercube T_gap~log n (R^2=1.0) vs T_new~O(1) (exponent -0.072); substituting into T_trans=Theta(n^3*term^2) recovers all six Table-1 entries (ring n^7->n^5, torus n^5->n^3 log^2 n, hypercube n^3 log^2 n->n^3).

claims.claim: Figure 1 compares the classical topology-dependence quantity (1-p)/p against the new all-eigenvalue quantity (1/n)*sum(lambda_i^2/(1-lambda_i^2)) across ring, torus, line, and hypercube topologies, showing the new quantity is considerably smaller for sparse networks (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: Exact spectra over ring/line (n=16-256), torus (n=16-400), hypercube (n=8-1024) show T_gap grows with exponents 2.011, 2.003, 1.082, 0.297 while T_new grows with exponents 1.094, 1.046, 0.421, -0.072 respectively, with T_gap/T_new ratios reaching 158x (ring), 314x (line), 63x (torus), 35x (hypercube) at largest sizes, confirming the new quantity is considerably smaller for sparse networks.

claims.claim: Figure 2 experimentally validates on logistic and ridge regression over MNIST that convergence behavior depends on the full eigenvalue spectrum of the mixing matrix rather than only the spectral gap (Section 6, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Real D-SGD on full 60,000-image MNIST with n=16 nodes over a matched-gap family (lambda_2=0.86 fixed, T_new swept 0.178-2.663) shows logistic regression consensus RMS rising 0.0259->0.0989 (3.81x spread, Spearman=1.0) and ridge regression consensus RMS 0.0040->0.0151 (3.81x, Spearman=1.0), with both losses monotonically ordered by T_new at identical spectral gap.

claims.claim: Figure 3 shows the improved topology-dependence prediction holds for neural network training (LeNet on Fashion-MNIST) under both homogeneous and heterogeneous data settings (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Real decentralized LeNet (~62k params) on full Fashion-MNIST with n=8 nodes over matched-gap family (lambda_2=0.86 fixed, T_new swept 0.355-2.485) shows heterogeneous (Dirichlet 0.1) accuracy dropping 55.3%->39.9% (15.4 points, Spearman=-1.0) while homogeneous accuracy is robust (67.5%->65.1%, 2.3pt range) yet model disagreement still tracks T_new (0.058->0.127, Spearman=1.0), reproducing the paper's homogeneous/heterogeneous asymmetry.

agharsallah/pyi0wjv5im-logbook.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all six claims through a combination of exact spectral computations, Monte-Carlo simulations, and real D-SGD training on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. The matched-gap control design—holding the spectral gap fixed while sweeping the rest of the spectrum—is a particularly rigorous experimental approach that directly isolates the all-eigenvalue effect from the classical gap-only prediction across all empirical claims.

arvkevi/repro-dp-submodular-knapsack.paper_title: Differentially Private Submodular Maximization with a Knapsack Constraint

claims.claim: For monotone submodular objectives under a knapsack constraint, DP-2GG (Algorithm 2) achieves the optimal (1-1/e)-approximation with query complexity O(β^{-1} n^3 k) and additive error scaling polylogarithmically in ground-set size (Theorem 4.1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 2 was executed at the paper's actual n=30/B=40/k=12 setup on the 100,000-row Uber dataset with finite ε=0.2, producing 206,693 measured oracle calls (consistent with O(n³k) for these parameters) and a DP/non-private ratio of 0.9742±0.0379, indicating small additive error consistent with the (1-1/e)-approximation claim.

claims.claim: A faster monotone variant, DP-DG+ (Algorithm 7), trades approximation quality for speed, achieving a 1/2-approximation with only O(nk) queries (Theorem 4.2, Appendix B.2).
claims.evidence: Algorithms 1+7 ran on all 100,000 pickups at n=100/k=8/ε=0.2 across 10 seeds, yielding a private/non-private ratio of 0.9922±0.0112 (well above 1/2) and measured query counts scaling with log-log exponent 0.865 against nk across n=20–100, consistent with O(nk).

claims.claim: The paper gives the first differentially private algorithm with provable guarantees for non-monotone submodular maximization under a knapsack constraint, DP-SDG (Algorithm 3), achieving a 1/4-approximation in expectation with O(nk) queries (Theorem 4.3, Section 6).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 3 with Bernoulli-1/2 retention ran on the full 100,000-row Uber graph-cut objective at n=100/k=8/ε=0.4 across 10 seeds, producing a private/non-private expected-value ratio of 0.7530±0.1680 (above 1/4) with 4,043 counted oracle calls, consistent with the O(nk) query claim.

claims.claim: The non-monotone algorithm handles DP-noise-induced negative marginal gains by continuing selection regardless and using Report Noisy Max post hoc to pick the best candidate solution (Section 6, Algorithm 4).
claims.evidence: A constructed n=100 nonnegative submodular star graph-cut hard instance at ε=0.05 forced negative marginal gains across 10 runs, observing 9,831 negative candidates and 307 selected negative marginals, with all runs continuing to RNM output rather than stopping early, directly demonstrating the claimed mechanism.

claims.claim: On the Uber Manhattan ride-sharing dataset with m=100,000 pickups, DP-DG+ achieves an objective value within 8% of the non-private baseline at privacy parameter ε=0.2 (Section 7, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: On the checksum-verified 100,000-pickup Uber dataset at ε=0.2, DP-DG+ produced a private/non-private ratio of 0.8798±0.0422 across 10 seeds, which is approximately 12% below the non-private baseline and thus outside the claimed 8% threshold (requiring ≥0.92).

arvkevi/repro-dp-submodular-knapsack.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence on the paper's actual 100,000-row Uber dataset with finite privacy parameters, supporting Claims 1–4 through measured oracle queries, approximation ratios, and direct mechanism testing, while falsifying Claim 5 by showing DP-DG+ falls outside the stated 8% bound at ε=0.2.

claims.evidence: Code inspection of the official implementation confirms the HVP via jax.jvp through jax.grad (train.py lines 78-83), stochastic column sampling with random one-hot vectors (data.py line 12), and the Hessian MAE loss matching DFT force constants (train.py lines 118-120), all consistent with the claimed O(N²)→O(N) reduction.

claims.evidence: Local evaluation on only 10 small structures (≤80 atoms) on CPU shows directionally consistent improvements (ωmax 9.5→4.4 K, S 20.8→5.7 J/K/mol), but absolute MAE values do not match the paper's claimed 24→12 K and 32→14 J/K/mol, and the full 1000-structure test set was not used.

claims.claim: PFT improves Nequix MP's Helmholtz free energy MAE from 12 to 5 kJ/mol (58% reduction) and heat capacity MAE from 6 to 3 J/K/mol (50% reduction), averaging to a 55% improvement across phonon thermodynamic properties (Table 1).

claims.claim: WaterSIC achieves a maximum rate gap of 0.255 bits per entry to the information-theoretic rate-distortion limit D*(R,Σ_X), uniformly over all input covariance matrices, with the gap equal to ½log₂(2πe/12) (Theorem, Rate-Distortion Bounds section).

arvkevi/repro-semi-knockoffs.paper_title: Semi-knockoffs: a model-agnostic conditional independence testing method with finite-sample guarantees

claims.claim: Semi-knockoffs avoids the train-test data split required by prior conditional-independence testing methods such as HRT while still yielding valid p-values, via nonparametric paired tests requiring only conditional expectations ν_j and ρ_j rather than exact knockoff construction (Theorem 3.3, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements the semi-knockoff paired test using conditional-mean regressions ν_j and ρ_j with residual permutation (no train-test split), and reports empirical type-I error of 0.055 at α=0.05 across 40 repetitions on a non-toy simulation (n=300, p=50, AR(1) design with known null set), which is within Monte Carlo variability of the nominal level.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 establishes that the Semi-knockoffs procedure controls the false discovery rate at level q, i.e. FDR(S_SKO) ≤ q (Theorem 3.4, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Using the known null set (last 0.75p coordinates), the knockoff+ selection yields empirical FDR of 0.176 ≤ q=0.2 across 40 repetitions with power 0.985, providing concrete finite-sample FDR control evidence on a non-toy simulation.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows that for null (non-relevant) features, regularized empirical risk minimizers trained with and without the feature remain close, with an ‖θ̃^j − θ̂‖₂ ≤ O_P(√(log(1/δ)/n)) bound, giving optimization stability guarantees for regularized models (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Ridge regression coefficients fitted with vs. without a null feature differ by ‖θ̃−θ̂‖₂ = 0.0769, 0.0304, 0.0174 at n=150, 600, 2400 respectively, with ratios approximately consistent with O(1/√n) scaling as the theorem predicts.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 provides a double-robustness property: the loss difference between imputed feature distributions decays at a compound rate O_P(a_n b_n) even when both the predictive model and the sampler have estimation error (Theorem 4.3, Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: The mean absolute null-feature statistic |W_j| decays 0.0172 → 0.0058 → 0.0013 across n=150, 600, 2400, with decay ratios (0.34, 0.22) faster than 1/√n (which would give 0.5), consistent with a compound product rate as claimed by Theorem 4.3.

claims.claim: On simulated data with adjacent-feature support, Semi-knockoffs maintains type-I error control while achieving higher power than HRT, and derandomization with 5 permutations under masked correlation further increases power (Figure 4, Figure 5, Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: Independent reanalysis of 360 authors' raw CSVs (60 seeds per setting, pinned to official commit) shows adjacent-support Semi-KO power exceeding HRT (GB: 0.997 vs 0.836; RF: 0.956 vs 0.789) with type-I near 0.05, and masked-correlation power increasing with 5 permutations (GB: 0.333→0.817, RF: 0.500→0.950, NN: 0.167→0.733), all exceeding HRT.

claims.claim: On the Wisconsin Breast Cancer real dataset, Semi-knockoffs is applied across Random Forest, Neural Network, and Gradient Boosting models to demonstrate model-agnostic feature selection (Figure 6, Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: On the Wisconsin Breast Cancer dataset with an injected conditionally-null feature, the method is applied across Random Forest, Neural Network, and Gradient Boosting models, with type-I rejection rates of 0.03 for all three, demonstrating model-agnostic applicability on real data with controlled error.

arvkevi/repro-semi-knockoffs.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all six claims through ground-truth-anchored simulations (n=300, p=50, 40 reps), scaling experiments (n up to 2400), an independent reanalysis of 360 authors' raw CSVs with hash verification, and a real-data application across three model classes. The reproduction is rigorous, with known-null-set evaluation, dual independent verification, and transparent reporting of a near-boundary type-I rate (0.055 vs 0.05).

claims.claim: Theorem 1 (Section 2) establishes finite-sample uniform validity of max-p aggregation, showing it yields coverage guarantees under any mixture distribution of the K sources.
claims.evidence: Numerical experiments with K=3 heterogeneous regression sources across 12 configurations (alpha in {0.1,0.2}, n_cal in {500,1000}, 3 seeds) show worst-source coverage consistently >= 1-alpha (0.9426-0.9491 at alpha=0.1; 0.8709-0.878 at alpha=0.2), confirming finite-sample uniform validity of max-p aggregation.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 (Section 3.1) characterizes the population-optimal prediction set as a superlevel set of a shared score function h_{λ*}(x,y) = Σ_k λ_k*(x) f_k(y|x), with complementary slackness ensuring exact 1−α coverage for at least one source.
claims.evidence: Covering LP solved as independent oracle for K in {2,3,4} Gaussian sources matches the analytic superlevel set {h_lambda*>1} with Jaccard 0.997-1.000, primal-dual gap at machine precision (~1e-15), and complementary slackness verified (at least one source tight at exactly 1-alpha, all active sources tight, 0 KKT violations) across 24 configurations.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 (Section 3.2) proves max-p aggregation with learned conformity scores is asymptotically optimal, converging to the oracle-optimal prediction set up to boundary regions.
claims.evidence: Learned-score prediction set converges to oracle optimum: symmetric-difference mass rho decreases monotonically from ~0.014-0.018 at n=250 to ~0.001-0.003 at n=8000 across 3 seeds, with Spearman rank-correlation of -0.94 to -1.0 between n and rho, demonstrating convergence up to boundary regions as Theorem 3 states.

claims.claim: In linear classification simulations, the method's prediction sets are 34.39% smaller than the naive max-p baseline while maintaining tight worst-case coverage (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: MDCP reduces mean set size from 10.06 to 5.35 labels (46.7% reduction, range 43.9%-49.8% across 3 seeds) versus naive max-p baseline in K=3, C=20-class linear-softmax simulation, while worst-source coverage holds at 0.897-0.9035; the reduction exceeds the paper's 34.39% in the same direction at valid coverage.

claims.claim: In linear regression simulations, the method achieves a 22.44% average reduction in prediction set size while maintaining valid ~90% worst-case coverage (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: MDCP reduces mean interval length from 12.15 to 9.20 (23.2% average reduction, range 14.2%-31.7% across 3 seeds) in K=3 heteroscedastic linear-Gaussian regression, closely matching the paper's 22.44%, with worst-source coverage at 0.899-0.913 (valid ~90%).

claims.claim: On the FMoW satellite imagery dataset spanning six geographic regions (with 249 countries in the training data), the method achieves near-tight worst-case coverage with smaller sets than single-source methods (Section 6.1, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: The FMoW satellite imagery experiment (6 regions, classification, deep features) is replaced with California housing tabular regression (4 regions, 20,640 samples), a different dataset, task type, and modality; while MDCP shows 10.2% smaller intervals at 0.899 worst-region coverage on this proxy, it does not reproduce the actual FMoW claim.

agharsallah/vv4xrzdmm0-logbook.overall: The logbook provides solid numerical evidence for the three theoretical claims (Theorems 1-3) and the two simulation-based efficiency claims (Figures 2 and 5), with real runs, multiple seeds, and raw data tables showing coverage validity and set-size reductions consistent with the paper. The FMoW real-data claim (Claim 6) is only addressed on a proxy dataset (California housing) with different task type and modality, constituting a toy-level substitute rather than a faithful reproduction.

jomasego/repro-a-noise-sensitivity-expon.paper_title: A Noise Sensitivity Exponent Controls Large Statistical-to-Computational Gaps in Single- and Multi-Index Models

claims.claim: The paper introduces a Noise Sensitivity Exponent (NSE), a quantity determined solely by the activation function, that governs the existence and magnitude of statistical-to-computational gaps in single- and multi-index models (abstract only).
claims.evidence: The logbook computes NSE values for 9 activations via Gauss-Hermite quadrature and matches the paper's classification, which verifies the definitional part of the claim. However, no experiments test whether the NSE actually 'governs the existence and magnitude of statistical-to-computational gaps' — that governing relationship is only addressed via circular analytical formula checks in claims 2–4.

claims.claim: In single-index models with large additive noise, the NSE fully characterizes the onset of the computational bottleneck separating statistically optimal from computationally efficient estimators (abstract only).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports 'fitted exponents' matching β⋆, but the executive summary confirms only 'analytical formulas from the paper's proofs' were used — no simulations of single-index learning were run. Fitting the exponent of the paper's own formula α^Alg_WR = (β⋆!/μ²)·λ^{-β⋆} is circular and does not independently verify the scaling law.

claims.claim: The NSE controls the statistical-to-computational gap that arises during the specialization transition in large separable multi-index models (abstract only).
claims.evidence: No multi-index committee machine simulations were run; the logbook only plugs into the analytical formula and reports that the exponent matches β⋆. The executive summary confirms the scope is 'analytical scaling law verification,' not simulation, making this circular rather than an independent test.

claims.claim: In hierarchical multi-index models, the NSE determines the optimal computational rate for sequentially learning the different index directions (abstract only).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports fitted exponents matching 2γβ⋆ for γ=1.0, but again no hierarchical multi-index learning experiments were conducted — only the paper's own analytical formula was evaluated. Without simulations at finite dimension, the scaling law is not independently verified.

claims.claim: The NSE is presented as a unifying quantity linking noise robustness, computational hardness, and feature specialization across these high-dimensional learning settings (abstract only).
claims.evidence: This meta-claim depends on the verification of claims 2–4, which are all inconclusive due to the absence of any learning simulations. The logbook's table asserting all three scaling laws are 'verified' is a self-reported conclusion, not backed by independent experimental evidence.

jomasego/repro-a-noise-sensitivity-expon.overall: The logbook computes NSE values correctly for 9 activation functions, confirming the paper's classification, but does not run any learning simulations to test the scaling laws. All scaling law 'verifications' are circular — plugging into the paper's own analytical formulas and checking that the exponents match — rather than independent experimental tests at finite dimension.

Deepakkambala/repro-a-tight-theory-of-er.paper_title: A Tight Theory of Error Feedback Algorithms in Distributed Optimization

claims.claim: EF21 achieves a tight convergence guarantee under contractive compression with optimal step size eta_star = (2/(L+mu)) * ((1-sqrt(epsilon))/(1+sqrt(epsilon))), and the resulting contraction rate rho_star is independent of the number of agents n (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The script evaluates eta_star and rho_star formulas for n in {1,2,4,16,64} and four epsilon values, confirming the computed values are identical across n, but this only verifies the formula as written contains no n-dependence; no actual EF21 optimization runs or PEP tightness certificates were performed.

claims.claim: Under the statistical homogeneity (shared minimizer) assumption, classic Error Feedback (EF) matches EF21's optimal step size and contraction factor exactly, giving identical tight convergence rates (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The CSV simply copies the same eta_star and rho_star values from the EF21 columns into columns labeled 'claim2_ef_*' with no separate EF algorithm computation, simulation, or PEP certificate; this is circular assertion, not evidence that classic EF achieves the same rate.

claims.claim: Without the shared-minimizer assumption, classic EF can exhibit 2-periodic cycles under statistical heterogeneity and generally fails to converge in the multi-agent setting (Proposition 2.1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: A 1D two-agent quadratic simulation with hardcoded contractive compressor responses demonstrates x returns to its initial value after 2 steps with zeroed error buffers for three step sizes, verifying the specific Proposition 2.1 construction, but only on a simplified 1D, 2-agent setup with no demonstration of general non-convergence.

claims.claim: The worst-case multi-agent convergence rate proven in Theorem 3.1 exactly matches the known single-agent rate, showing the novel Lyapunov function recovers prior single-agent guarantees as a special case (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The same formula table from Claim 1 trivially shows n=1 yields identical eta_star and rho_star to n>1 because the evaluated formula contains no n term; this confirms the code matches the formula but provides no independent verification that the Lyapunov function recovers single-agent guarantees.

claims.claim: For heterogeneous regularity parameters across agents, Corollary 3.2 extends the tight rates to deterministic, additive, positively homogeneous compressors using averaged parameters L-bar and mu-bar (Corollary 3.2).
claims.evidence: Computes L_bar, mu_bar, and checks the algebraic identity eta_star(mu_bar, L_bar, eps) = 2n/sum(L_i+mu_i) for two heterogeneous cases, but no actual distributed optimization with heterogeneous parameters or compressor runs were performed to confirm the rates hold.

claims.claim: For the two-agent (n=2) heterogeneous case, an explicit cubic polynomial characterizes the empirically optimal convergence rate, and tuning the EControl algorithm's step size to its optimum yields eta=0, coinciding with EF21 (Law 4.3, Law 4.4, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Evaluates the Law 4.3 cubic on a 12-point grid and confirms Q(rho)=0 to ~1e-15, but econtrol_eta_star is hardcoded to 0.0 rather than derived from any optimization or tuning procedure, and the full MOSEK/SDPA PEP certification sweep is explicitly not attempted.

Deepakkambala/repro-a-tight-theory-of-er.overall: The logbook provides formula-level numerical checks and one constructive 2-cycle simulation, but no actual distributed optimization experiments, no PEP tightness certificates, and no separate EF algorithm runs. Most claims are addressed only through trivial formula evaluation on simplified setups, and Claim 2 lacks any independent computation entirely.

arvkevi/repro-maximin-relative-improveme.paper_title: Maximin Relative Improvement: Fair Learning as a Bargaining Problem

claims.claim: Relative improvement is defined as the ratio of actual risk reduction to the maximum possible reduction from a baseline predictor, per Equation 1: ρ_P(f) = [R_P(f0) − R_P(f)] / [R_P(f0) − R_P(f*_P)] (Section 2, Equation 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook correctly implements the formula RI_g(f) = (R_g(f0) - R_g(f)) / (R_g(f0) - R_g*) and computes it on 400 random polytope instances, showing the MRI point has equal relative improvements across all groups (the KS property) and is Pareto-efficient on 400/400 instances.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves a no-harm guarantee: when the baseline predictor f0 is in the feasible class F, the maximin relative improvement solution f_RI satisfies R_g(f_RI) ≤ R_g(f0) for every group g (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: On 400/400 random polytope instances with the baseline feasible, every group's relative improvement RI_g >= 0 at the MRI solution, confirming no group's risk increases above the baseline.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.2 shows that, for two groups (m=2), relative improvement uniquely satisfies Pareto optimality, symmetry, scale invariance, and individual monotonicity simultaneously, and recovers the Kalai-Smorodinsky bargaining solution (Proposition 4.2).
claims.evidence: For two-group games, the logbook checks Pareto efficiency (400/400), symmetry on symmetrized games (400/400), and scale invariance under per-group rescaling (400/400), and shows KS recovery via equal relative improvements. However, individual monotonicity for m=2 is not explicitly tested in this section, and uniqueness is not checked.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.4 extends the axiomatic guarantees to more than two groups (m>2) via a leximin refinement that preserves scale invariance and a modified individual monotonicity property (Proposition 4.4).
claims.evidence: For m>2 groups, the leximin refinement is shown to refine the maximin (300/300), be Pareto-efficient (300/300), and be scale-invariant (300/300). However, the modified individual monotonicity property is not explicitly tested.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.4 establishes that the empirical maximin relative improvement estimator converges to the population solution at rate O(1/√n) under standard regularity conditions (Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: Solution errors of 0.0471, 0.0261, 0.0140, 0.0064 at n=100, 400, 1600, 6400 show approximate halving when n quadruples (ratios ~1.8-2.2), consistent with O(1/√n). The setup uses perturbed constraints with O(1/√n) noise rather than actual sampled empirical risks.

claims.claim: Table 1 shows relative improvement is the only compared fairness criterion (versus Group DRO, minimax regret, Nash bargaining, and explained variance) that jointly satisfies Pareto optimality, scale invariance, and individual monotonicity (Table 1, Section 3.1-3.3).
claims.evidence: RI is shown to be scale-invariant (200/200) and individually monotone (200/200); Group DRO fails scale invariance (200/200) and Nash bargaining fails individual monotonicity (7 witnessed cases). However, minimax regret and explained variance are not checked, and Pareto optimality is not explicitly tested for all criteria in this comparison.

arvkevi/repro-maximin-relative-improveme.overall: The logbook provides numerical verification of all six claims on a synthetic down-closed polytope model using exact linear programming, with 200-400 random instances per claim. The approach is appropriate for verifying mathematical properties (theorems, propositions, axiom checks) but does not include the paper's learning experiments on real fairness benchmarks, and some axiom checks (individual monotonicity for m=2, modified individual monotonicity for m>2, and two of four comparison criteria in Table 1) are incomplete.

arvkevi/repro-collaborative-fairness-bay.paper_title: Incentivizing Truthfulness and Collaborative Fairness in Bayesian Learning

claims.claim: Proposition 3.2 shows that a log-likelihood-based data valuation function (DVF), computed against a validation set unknown to sources, achieves i-strict-truthfulness for each source under assumptions A1-A3 (Section 3, Proposition 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook numerically verifies the proof identity E_q[log q - log p] = KL(q||p) > 0 across 10,000 arbitrary categorical posterior-predictive distributions (2–128 outcomes) with maximum residual 8.88e-16, plus 1,024 coalition certificates integrating over unknown coalition-data states with max residual 4.44e-16, directly testing the Proposition 3.2 identity at machine precision.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 establishes that combining this DVF with semivalues (a class generalizing the Shapley value) preserves strict truthfulness incentives at equilibrium even though sources' data valuations depend on other sources' unknown submissions (Section 4, Proposition 4.1).
claims.evidence: At n=9 sources, the reward gap is computed as the positive Shapley-weighted sum of coalition KLs across 256 random games with all 256 coalitions enumerated per deviator; the minimum truthful reward gap is 0.6579 with algebra/score identity residual 3.3e-16, providing concrete numerical evidence that positive semivalue weights preserve strict truthfulness.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.2 shows that an untruthful submission strategy causes a larger decrease to a source's own semivalue than to other sources' semivalues (Section 4, Proposition 4.2).
claims.evidence: Using the paper's paired C and C∪{k} formula, 2,048 comparisons across 256 nine-source games found 0 violations with a minimum own-minus-other decrease margin of 0.5650, directly testing that a deviator's own semivalue decreases at least as much as any other source's.

claims.claim: Section 5 extends the mechanism to a limited-reward-budget setting (Section 5.1) and to a setting with no dedicated validation set, where sources partition their own data and a modified reward excludes self-evaluation to prevent gaming (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: The limited-budget mechanism was tested across 1,000 random games with truthful reward optimal in 1,000/1,000 cases; the validation-free mechanism was tested with 3 sources over 20 splits × 64 posterior-predictive replicates, showing truthful strategy (mean reward 1.097948) highest against all five deviations, and the self-evaluation gaming attack was confirmed (value rising from 0.331 to 1.292).

claims.claim: Experiments across four Bayesian models compare truthful strategies against untruthful ones (duplication, noise injection, subsetting), reporting DVF and Shapley-value comparisons in Figures 1-2 and validation-free reward comparisons across 10 train-validation splits in Figure 3 (Section 6, Figures 1-3).
claims.evidence: All six strategies ran at real data scale (GP n=1,300; Heart n=920; Cycle Power n=9,568; BloodMNIST n=13,671), but only GP-FR uses the paper's exact model while the other three use substantially simplified inference (5-draw Bayesian bootstrap, last-layer Bayesian, PCA multinomial mode) instead of the paper's 4-chain NUTS protocol; additionally, the Heart model shows T rank 4/6 (a negative result), and Figures 1–2 DVF/Shapley comparisons are not explicitly reproduced.

arvkevi/repro-collaborative-fairness-bay.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification of the three theoretical propositions and both Section 5 mechanisms through large-scale random testing with machine-precision residuals, but the experimental reproduction of Figures 1–3 is only partial due to simplified inference methods for 3 of 4 models and a negative result on one dataset.

agharsallah/qo82qizesp-logbook.paper_title: Bulk-Calibrated Credal Ambiguity Sets: Fast, Tractable Decision Making under Out-of-Sample Contamination

claims.claim: Theorem 2.1 shows the worst-case risk under the support-restricted linear-vacuous (LV) ambiguity set has the closed form (1−ε)E[f_x] + ε·sup f_x, i.e., a finite mean+sup robust objective (Theorem 2.1).
claims.evidence: Closed-form worst-case risk compared against an independent adversary LP across 60 configurations (4 losses × 3 ε levels × 5 seeds, 40 support points in R⁴), with max absolute difference = 0.0 (machine precision); unbounded support case correctly shows sup blowing up to ~1.2e6, confirming the finiteness benefit of the bulk restriction.

claims.claim: Proposition 2.3 establishes that the bulk-calibrated credal ambiguity set coincides with the forward linear-vacuous ball, linking imprecise-probability and distributionally robust optimization (DRO) formulations (Proposition 2.3).
claims.evidence: Set equality tested via 12000 membership tests across 60 configs (ε∈{0.05,0.1,0.2,0.3}, |Ξ0|∈{10,25,50}, 5 seeds): forward direction saturates at 0.29993 for ε=0.30, reverse direction shows 0/12000 disagreements, and IP-vs-DRO worst-case risk gap ≤ 1e-15 on random loss functions.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.2 gives a DKW-based finite-sample calibration guaranteeing Pr{P*(Ξ0) ≥ 1−γ} ≥ 1−δ for the data-driven bulk set (Lemma 3.2).
claims.evidence: Monte-Carlo with T=3000 independent samples across 36 in-assumption configs (m∈{1000,2000,5000}, γ∈{0.1,0.05}, δ∈{0.1,0.05}) shows DKW-calibrated coverage = 1.000 in all configs, exceeding targets 0.90/0.95, while naive uncalibrated quantile covers only ~0.47, confirming the DKW inflation is load-bearing.

claims.claim: Section 3.1 and Table 1 derive closed-form suprema for linear, ReLU, absolute-value, and piecewise-linear losses over ellipsoidal and box bulk geometries, yielding tractable LP or second-order cone program (SOCP) reformulations (Section 3.1, Table 1).
claims.evidence: Closed-form suprema from Table 1 compared against independent cvxpy solutions across 40 configs (4 losses × 2 geometries × 5 seeds in R⁶), max abs error 7.2e-8; full robust objective assembled as DCP-valid LP (box, 0.014s) and SOCP (ellipsoid, 0.010s) with cross-solver agreement ~7e-8.

claims.claim: On the newsvendor experiment, the LV approach solves in 0.3s versus 2.6s for KL-BASPP and 23.5s for OR-WDRO, while remaining stable with only about 50 truncated samples (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: The ordering LV < OR-WDRO is confirmed (0.026s vs 0.086s, 3.3×) and sample stability is confirmed (1.2% OOS deviation at n=50 vs n=500), but the specific claimed timings (0.3s vs 2.6s vs 23.5s) are not reproduced (speedup ratio 3.3× vs paper's 78×), and KL-BASPP—one of the three baselines in the claim—is not tested at all.

claims.claim: On California Housing, LV reduces mean absolute error by 14% versus a Wasserstein DRO baseline and improves p98 and CVaR at 2% by about 10%, with end-to-end runtime of 1.58s versus 7.03s for the Wasserstein baseline (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: On the full 20640-row California Housing dataset with East→West 30% gap shift and 30 replications, LV achieves MAE 10.81 (paper 10.7), reducing MAE by 19.1% vs Wasserstein DRO (exceeding claimed 14%), p98 by 13.8% and CVaR@2% by 13.9% (exceeding claimed ~10%); runtime differs (0.115s vs claimed 1.58s) but this is hardware/solver-dependent and the accuracy claims are the core scientific contribution.

agharsallah/qo82qizesp-logbook.overall: The four theoretical claims (Thm 2.1, Prop 2.3, Lemma 3.2, Table 1) are verified with rigorous numerical checks at machine precision or via Monte-Carlo coverage on non-trivial setups, and the California Housing empirical results are reproduced on the full real dataset exceeding the paper's claimed improvements. The newsvendor timing claim is only partially addressed: the solve-time ordering is confirmed and sample efficiency is verified, but the specific timing numbers are not reproduced, the speedup ratio differs substantially, and the KL-BASPP baseline is missing entirely.

Deepakkambala/repro-box-thirding-anytime.paper_title: Box Thirding: Anytime Best Arm Identification under Insufficient Sampling

claims.claim: Box Thirding (B3) is analyzed under a formalized 'data-poor condition' where the candidate set size c0 cannot cover all potentially eps-optimal arms, decomposing error probability into non-inclusion probability and misidentification probability (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook only performs regex text-matching on the paper PDF to confirm the phrases 'data-poor condition,' 'non-inclusion probability,' 'misidentification probability,' and 'candidate set' appear. No independent mathematical derivation, numerical simulation, or formal verification of the error decomposition is provided.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 bounds the misidentification probability as P(mu_1 - mu_at > eps) <= exp{-Omega(max{N_(eps/2)/N, eps^2/N} * T)}, where N_(eps/2) is the count of eps/2-best arms (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirms via regex that 'Theorem 4.3' and the probability expression appear in the paper text, but the third pattern for the max{N_(eps/2)/N, eps^2/N} term was not found (found: false). No independent proof, derivation, or numerical verification of the bound was attempted.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.8 shows B3 attains candidate set size c0 = Theta(T), matching Uniform Sampling, while Bracketing Sequential Halving attains only c0 = Theta(T/(log_2 T)^2) (Proposition 4.8).
claims.evidence: Text pattern matching confirms the paper states the candidate-set scaling orders for US, BSH, and B3, and theory_checks.json records these orders. However, no independent mathematical derivation or multi-T simulation was performed to verify the asymptotic claims. The single-T=10000 simulation reports B3 candidate size 48 and BSH size 56, which does not test Theta(T) vs Theta(T/(log T)^2) scaling.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.9 shows B3 and Uniform Sampling share the same non-inclusion probability bound exp{-Omega(T*N_(eps/2)/N)}, while Bracketing Sequential Halving is slower by a log(T)^2 factor (Corollary 4.9).
claims.evidence: Only regex text-matching against the paper text confirms Corollary 4.9 and its stated bounds appear. No independent algebraic derivation from Proposition 4.8 and Theorem 4.7 was performed, and no numerical experiments tested the non-inclusion probability scaling.

claims.claim: On the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest dataset (contest 893, N=5,513 arms, budget T=10,000), B3 achieves consistently lower simple regret than Uniform Sampling, BUCB, and Bracketing Sequential Halving across high-noise (N(mu,0.5^2)), moderate-noise (N(mu,0.2^2)), and deterministic reward regimes (Section 5 experiments).
claims.evidence: The 200-repetition simulation on the real NYCCC 893 dataset (N=5513, T=10000) shows B3 does NOT consistently beat all three baselines: in deterministic regime Uniform Sampling achieves 0.0000 regret vs B3's 0.0223; in high-noise BUCB achieves 0.1009 vs B3's 0.2885 and BSH achieves 0.2444 vs B3's 0.2885; in moderate-noise BUCB achieves 0.0583 vs B3's 0.0633. The claim that B3 achieves 'consistently lower simple regret than Uniform Sampling, BUCB, and Bracketing Sequential Halving across' all three regimes is directly contradicted by these numbers.

claims.claim: The base sampling parameter r0 in B3 is set by solving r0 + r0^1.5 = 4, yielding r0 approx 1.728 (Section 4, Algorithm parameters).
claims.evidence: The logbook numerically solves r0 + r0^1.5 = 4 using scipy.brentq, obtaining r0 = 1.7281632013323833 with residual 8.88e-16, confirming the paper's stated approximate value of 1.728.

Deepakkambala/repro-box-thirding-anytime.overall: The logbook numerically verifies the r0 parameter (Claim 6) and runs a real-scale simulation on the NYCCC 893 dataset that contradicts the paper's central empirical claim (Claim 5). The four theoretical claims (1-4) are only addressed via regex text-matching against the paper PDF, providing no independent mathematical or numerical verification.

GwendalTsang/repro-identifying-connectiv.paper_title: Identifying Connectivity Distributions from Neural Dynamics Using Flows

claims.claim: The method trains a continuous normalizing flow via flow matching to learn a distribution p(m,b,d) over low-rank RNN connectivity parameters, rather than producing a single point estimate (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: A trained Connector checkpoint (1,000 neurons, 1,000 marginal + 1,000 conditional epochs, flow_matching=true) produced 5,000 CNF samples with minimum covariance eigenvalue 0.949, sliced Wasserstein 0.052 vs 0.100 for a moment-matched Gaussian, quadrant-mass L1 error 0.071, and four-cluster ARI 0.939, confirming a non-collapsed multimodal distribution rather than a point estimate.

claims.claim: The paper formally characterizes identifiability of the inferred connectivity structure, showing the latent variable z is identifiable only up to a linear transformation z' = Az under the model's conditions (Section 3, Equation 5).
claims.evidence: For a non-orthogonal A with det(A)=4.45, transformed networks preserve firing rates to 5.3e-15, latents obey z'=Az to 5.7e-15, the Eq. 5 Jacobian determinant is exactly 1.0, and importance integration of the RHS density yields 1.0009, numerically confirming the linear identifiability equivalence class.

claims.claim: Unique recovery of p(m,b,d) requires the data matrix to satisfy rank(z_{1:t}) = R + K_in and that the all-ones vector not lie in the row span of z_{1:t}, in the limit of infinite data (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Across 400 trials the two conditions are equivalent to augmented rank R+K_in+1; recovery error is 2.4e-13 when conditions hold; explicit one-parameter degenerate families produce identical rates (max|dr|<1e-9) with genuinely different distributions (mean shift up to 7.07); error decays at log-log slope -0.500 when conditions hold and plateaus at slope -0.005 when violated, up to K=256,000.

claims.claim: Degeneracy in the conditional distribution is resolved via a maximum-entropy optimization that yields a unique solution under stated regularity conditions (Section 3, Equation 7).
claims.evidence: Four moment-matched conditionals (Gaussian, bimodal, Student-t, skewed exponential) converge to the same flow field as K grows; the identity H(N)-H(p)=KL(p||N) holds with residuals ~2.5e-6 across Laplace, Uniform, bimodal, and Student-t families; every non-Gaussian has a strictly positive entropy gap (0.096–0.353) while the Gaussian equality case has gap ~0; ridge N_hat converges for small c (MSE 0.191→0.021) but not large c (0.095→0.179).

claims.claim: Applied to real neural recordings from rat frontal cortex, the inferred connectivity distribution is non-Gaussian, exhibiting heavy tails, multimodality, and skew (Section 6.3, Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: No experiment was run: the logbook identifies that the raw spike data (4.17 GB on Dryad) and Connector code are public, but the trained FINDR network, loading matrix, latent trajectories, and distilled lrRNN intermediates required before Connector can be fitted are absent from the public release, and no synthetic substitute was attempted.

GwendalTsang/repro-identifying-connectiv.overall: Claims 1–4 are supported by concrete experimental or numerical evidence at non-trivial scale: Claim 1 uses the official Connector at 1,000 neurons with distributional metrics, and Claims 2–4 are verified through careful algebraic/numerical constructions with convergence studies up to K=256,000. Claim 5 was never addressed because the trained intermediates needed to rerun the real-neural-data pipeline are missing from the public release.

claims.claim: Because standard information-theoretic uncertainty measures fail on these non-identifiable parameters, epistemic uncertainty is instead defined via the trace of the posterior weight covariance, EU(y|x) := tr(Cov_P(w|·)), enabling a variance-based decomposition into discrete (permutation) and continuous (splitting) sources of residual uncertainty (Section 2.1, Section 2.2, Example 1).

For an overparametrized M*=3→M=6 net, both components are non-zero: discrete=4.7324 (95.1%), continuous=0.2435 (4.9%). The EU=tr(Cov(w))=Συᵢ² identity (Lemma 1) is verified exactly (|diff|=0).

claims.evidence: Dirichlet splitting law with α=(p+1)/2=3 verified via 2M Monte-Carlo draws across k∈{2,…,14}: E[c]=1/k, Var(c)=(k-1)/[k²(kα+1)], Cov=-1/[k²(kα+1)], and μ_{k,α}=Γ(α+½)Γ(kα)/[Γ(α)Γ(kα+½)] all match closed forms to max abs err 2.10e-04. claims.claim: The posterior over splitting coordinates remains non-degenerate even as the number of training samples n approaches infinity, showing that substantial parameter-space uncertainty persists despite the underlying function being fully identified (Section 3.2, Figure 2).

ai-sherpa/proximal-last-iterate-repro.paper_title: Convergence Rate of the Last Iterate of Stochastic Proximal Algorithms

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes an Õ(1/√T) convergence rate for the last iterate of proximal SGD under componentwise convexity and L-smoothness of each fi (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Proximal SGD on a 64-dimensional, 800-component l1-regularized quadratic with 6 horizons (T=512–16384), 128 runs each, and 4.1M+ gradient queries yields a measured log-log slope of -0.5072 (R²=0.9998) with 0/6 envelope violations against C·log(T)/√T, using an independently computed ISTA reference minimizer (|Δ|<1e-14).

claims.claim: The analysis replaces the standard bounded-variance assumption with the weaker requirement of a finite second moment of the gradient at the solution, E||∇fi(x*)||² = σ*² < ∞ (Section 2, Assumption 1).
claims.evidence: A 2-component convex-smooth construction shows finite σ*²=1.0 at x*=0 while centred gradient variance grows quadratically (tail exponent 2.0020) from 1e-2 to 8.1e+11 over x∈[1,1e6], and the same phenomenon is corroborated on a 64-dim, 800-component instance where σ*²=1263.3 is finite but covariance trace grows 1.48e7×. This concretely demonstrates the assumption is strictly weaker than bounded variance.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 extends the Õ(1/√T) last-iterate rate to a randomized incremental proximal method when the regularizer decomposes additively and each component gj is Lipschitz continuous (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Randomized incremental proximal method on a 24-node cycle graph with 24 additive Lipschitz TV edge-terms, 8.26M edge-prox updates across 3 horizons (T=1024–16384, 384 runs each), yields measured slope -0.5055 (R²=0.9895) with 0/3 envelope violations and an independent ADMM reference (KKT residual 7.3e-15). Only 3 horizons limits robustness but evidence is consistent with the claim.

claims.claim: Section 4.4 applies the framework to a BlockProx algorithm for graph-guided regularizers used in multi-task and federated learning, proving last-iterate convergence without assuming bounded gradients (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: BlockProx on a 12-task, 8-dim/task multi-task instance with 32 graph edges and group-TV regularizer, with measured unbounded gradients (||g||≈541.8 at far iterate), yields slope -0.5376 (R²=1.0000) with 0/3 envelope violations against a consensus-ADMM reference. The slope deviation of 0.0376 from -0.5 is within noise, though only 3 horizons limits the fit's informativeness.

claims.claim: The obtained Õ(1/√T) rate matches, up to logarithmic factors, the last-iterate guarantees for unconstrained SGD under bounded variance from Garrigos et al. (2025) (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Head-to-head comparison on a 40-dim least-squares problem (n=400) across 4 horizons (T=512–32768, 128 runs each) shows proximal SGD slope -0.5119 and unconstrained SGD slope -0.5056 (difference 0.0063), both consistent with 1/√T. The logbook transparently acknowledges that finite-horizon experiments cannot resolve the logarithmic factor qualifier.

ai-sherpa/proximal-last-iterate-repro.overall: The logbook provides concrete, from-scratch experimental evidence on non-toy problem sizes supporting all five claims, with independent reference solvers and honest acknowledgment of limitations (synthetic problems, 3-horizon fits for some claims, inability to resolve log factors). The evidence is strongest for claims 1 and 2 and somewhat thinner for claims 3 and 4 due to fewer horizons.

ai-sherpa/muon-associative-memory-repro.paper_title: Muon in Associative Memory Learning: Training Dynamics and Scaling Laws

claims.claim: In the noiseless setting, Muon achieves loss L(t) decaying exponentially as K·e^{-(1+o_K(1))t}, versus gradient descent's L(t) ≍ K/t, giving an exponential-vs-polynomial speedup (Theorem 4.1, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: On the paper's own associative-memory model (K×K logit matrix, column-softmax, frequency-weighted CE), K∈{50,100,200}: GD log-log slopes are -1.043/-1.093/-1.213 (predicted -1, R²>0.9997) with prefactor L·t/K→1.02–1.18, while Muon exponential rates are 0.9991/0.9990/0.9962 (predicted →1), yielding a >10⁷× loss gap at t=20000 vs t=80. Cross-group uniformity (Muon lo/hi ratio 1.1–1.5 vs GD 10.5–12.7) confirms msgn strips per-column frequency scaling.

claims.claim: Under label noise with power-law frequency decay p̃ᵢ ∝ i^{-β}, GD's excess loss is lower-bounded by Ω̃(log K / T^{1-1/β}) while Muon's is upper-bounded by Õ((log K/T)^2), yielding a steeper scaling-law exponent for Muon (Theorem 5.7, Theorem 5.8).
claims.evidence: At β=2, α=0.1, sweeping M∈{4,6,9,13,19} (K=120–570, T=M²): GD excess-risk power-law slope is -0.398 (predicted -0.5, R²=0.9998) and Muon's is -1.819 (predicted -2.0, R²=0.9963), with Muon excess risk 4–5 orders of magnitude smaller at every budget. Both curves are clean power laws with the predicted ordering and steepness relationship.

claims.claim: Under label noise, Muon exhibits an Ω(C)-fold speedup over GD, where C is the size of each knowledge group in the associative memory model (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Fixing M=4, shared η=0.25, sweeping C∈{5,10,20,40,80}: the speedup ratio t_GD/t_Muon grows from 38.5× to 632.6×, with log(ratio) vs log(C) slope = 1.005 (predicted 1.0, R²=0.9997) and ratio/C ≈ 7.95 nearly constant. Muon step count stays flat (17→28) while GD scales with C (slope 1.19), directly confirming Ω(C)-fold speedup.

claims.claim: Muon is interpreted as an implicit matrix preconditioner arising from adaptive task alignment, distinguished from coordinate-wise SignGD by its exploitation of block-symmetric gradient structure; a Task-Representation-Aligned SignGD (TRA-SignGD) variant with oracle embedding access is shown to match Muon's performance (Section 5).
claims.evidence: At the paper's exact Section 7.1 scale (K=100, M=C=10, T=50, random orthogonal basis): TRA-SignGD(η) vs Muon(2η) trajectory RMSE = 0.00115 (0.12% relative), while TRA-SignGD vs misaligned SignGD RMSE = 1.71 (1494× larger). The disparity-gap ranking across 6 optimizers (Muon 0.0014, TRA 5.3e-14, SignGD 0.989) reproduces the paper's Fig 1b ordering, and Prop 6.1 residuals stay small and bounded in the noiseless and noisy-descent regimes.

claims.claim: On imbalanced MNIST and LLaMA pre-training experiments, Muon shows a steeper power-law decay slope than SGD across multiple data budgets, empirically confirming the derived scaling laws (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: On real MNIST with the paper's 2-layer ReLU MLP at native scale (784→128→10, geometric long-tail, balanced test, lr=0.005): Muon achieves per-class accuracy 0.87–1.00 (gap 0.13) vs SGD's 0.00–0.99 (gap 0.99, rarest classes at 0.00), and data-budget power-law slopes are Muon -0.772 vs SGD -0.395 (R²>0.96). A reduced-scale but genuine LLaMA-architecture pre-training run (3.3M params, real WikiText-103, 36 runs) additionally confirms the same ordering (Muon γ=-0.0626 vs SGD γ=-0.0489).

ai-sherpa/muon-associative-memory-repro.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from independent re-implementations supporting all five claims on the paper's own associative-memory model (Claims 1–4) and on real MNIST at native scale plus a reduced-scale LLaMA run (Claim 5). The theory claims are tested at the model's full stated scale with fitted exponents matching asymptotic predictions within disclosed finite-size tolerances, and the real-data experiments confirm the predicted qualitative ordering of Muon over SGD.

arvkevi/repro-autobidding-raic-oaic.paper_title: Risk-Averse and Optimistic Advertiser Incentive Compatibility in Auto-bidding

claims.claim: Risk-Averse Auto-bidding Incentive Compatibility (RAIC) requires that the worst-case equilibrium outcome under truthful reporting be at least as good as the worst-case outcome from misreporting, while Optimistic Auto-bidding Incentive Compatibility (OAIC) requires the same comparison using the best-case equilibrium outcomes (Definitions 1 and 2, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook exhaustively checks all 225 ordered pairs of nonempty welfare correspondences over {0,1,2,3}, producing a truth table (both=112, RAIC-only=43, OAIC-only=43, neither=27) with strict separating witnesses showing the min/min and max/max predicates are logically distinct and non-vacuous, correctly operationalizing Definitions 1 and 2.

claims.claim: For two tCPA auto-bidders under non-uniform bidding, the Second-Price Auction (SPA) is proven to satisfy both RAIC (Theorem 1) and OAIC (Theorem 2) (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook enumerates the full non-uniform equilibrium set over 1302 instances (6587 truthful/misreport pairs) and finds the worst-case (RAIC) and best-case (OAIC) truthful value won dominate every misreport with 0 violations, providing concrete numerical evidence for Theorems 1 and 2.

claims.claim: For two tCPA auto-bidders restricted to uniform bidding, SPA is proven to satisfy RAIC (Theorem 4) and OAIC (Theorem 5) (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook tests 24000 uniform-bidding truthful/misreport pairs for RAIC (Theorem 4) and 24000 for OAIC (Theorem 5), finding worst-case and best-case truthful value won dominates every misreport with 0 violations in both cases.

claims.claim: Existence of an equilibrium allocation under uniform bidding is characterized by inequality conditions (4)-(7) that depend only on reported tCPA targets and per-query values, after eliminating the bid multiplier variables (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook checks 3000 random two-advertiser instances and finds a prefix-cut equilibrium exists on all 3000/3000 via an exact interval-feasibility characterization that eliminates bid multiplier variables, matching Theorem 3's conditions (4)-(7).

arvkevi/repro-autobidding-raic-oaic.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence across thousands of random two-advertiser instances supporting all four claims, including exhaustive semantic verification of the RAIC/OAIC definitions and zero-violation checks for both uniform and non-uniform bidding incentive compatibility. The two-advertiser scope matches the paper's stated theorems, though the full paper's extension to arbitrary advertiser counts is not covered.

ICML-2026-agent-repro/repro-preserving-p.paper_title: Preserving Plasticity in Continual Learning via Dynamical Isometry

claims.claim: Plasticity is defined functionally as the capacity to reduce excess achievable loss under a task distribution and resource budget, and plasticity loss is linked to increasing anisotropy of the empirical neural tangent kernel, with layer-wise dynamical isometry (singular values near 1) proposed as a tractable surrogate for NTK isotropy (Section 2, Definition 2.1).
claims.evidence: A 4-layer MLP (784-128-128-10) NTK diagnostic was run for only 10 epochs on a single batch of 64 samples. AdamO's condition number (6.30) is actually worse than Adam's (3.88) at epoch 10, which does not support the claim that isometry regularization prevents spectral collapse.

claims.claim: GroupSort networks with orthonormal weights are shown to be almost-everywhere isometric while remaining universal 1-Lipschitz approximators, preserving expressivity through input-dependent permutations rather than gating (Section 3).
claims.evidence: A single 128×128 orthonormal layer with MaxMin was tested on 1000 random inputs. While singular value std is 0 (all equal), the singular values are 31.62 rather than near 1 as required for dynamical isometry, suggesting either an implementation issue or that the claim was not properly tested.

claims.claim: The proposed Gram-deviation regularization penalty (Eq. 16) penalizes deviations of squared singular values from one, and the AdamO optimizer (Eq. 20) decouples this isometry regularization from adaptive moment estimates, analogous to how AdamW decouples weight decay from gradient updates (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Basic correctness checks confirm the Gram-deviation penalty yields 0.0 for orthogonal matrices and 209.93 for random ones, and AdamO runs for 5 steps on a 10→20→5 MLP. This is a sanity check of implementation, not a demonstration at meaningful scale.

claims.claim: On supervised benchmarks (Pixel-Permutation, Random-Label Memorization, Label-Shuffling), isometry regularization with AdamO consistently outperforms the NaP baseline and other prior approaches (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: Pixel-Permutation MNIST was run at 20 tasks with 1 epoch/task (vs. paper's 1000 tasks, 40 epochs/task). AdamO (94.75% val) does not outperform NaP (94.82% val) at this scale. Random-Label Memorization was not run (CIFAR-10 download failed), and Label-Shuffling was not mentioned.

claims.claim: On Continual MinAtar over 20 task cycles, AdamO maintains performance while a standard PPO baseline degrades significantly, demonstrating plasticity preservation in a reinforcement learning setting (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states 'Not attempted locally' — no experiments were run for the MinAtar PPO benchmark. The claim requires 8 seeds × 4 games × 15M steps × 20 cycles, which was deemed infeasible on local MPS.

claims.claim: Isometry regularization substantially reduces dead ReLU unit buildup relative to baselines, coupling weight rows so inactive units reactivate as active neurons move, as measured in the dead-ReLU revival diagnostic (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: Dead ReLU ratio was tracked for 20 epochs on MNIST (vs. paper's 1000+ tasks). The difference between AdamO (23.53%) and Adam (23.84%) is only 0.31%, which is negligible and does not support the claim of 'substantial' reduction in dead ReLU buildup.

ICML-2026-agent-repro/repro-preserving-p.overall: The logbook provides small-scale sanity checks of core mechanisms (Gram-deviation penalty, AdamO, GroupSort, NTK diagnostic, dead ReLU tracking) but at drastically reduced scale compared to the paper's benchmarks, and no claim is verified at the paper's intended scale. The RL benchmark (Claim 5) was not attempted at all, and several results are either contradictory (Claim 1: AdamO worse than Adam) or problematic (Claim 2: singular values of 31.62 instead of ~1).

jomasego/repro-turning-back-without-forg.paper_title: Turning Back Without Forgetting: Selective Backward Refinement for Parameter-Efficient Continual Learning

claims.claim: SABER selects which prior task prompts qualify for backward refinement using two complementary criteria: a projection-based criterion requiring sufficient magnitude and positive alignment of the current task's prompt gradient onto the prior task's gradient subspace, and a loss-distribution-based criterion using Wasserstein distance between task loss distributions (Section 4.1.1, Section 4.1.2).

claims.evidence: The actual reward function in pipeline/rewards.py is tested with controlled token counts: Rd correctly counts newly-discovered nodes (Rd=2 for 2 new aware nodes), Re matches -min(λ·max(0,tokens-τ),1) exactly at token counts 0–5000 with λ=1e-3, τ=250, cap=1.0, and the combined reward increases with discovery and decreases with length (10/10 checks pass).

claims.claim: Compared against Base models, Prompted Base, and CollabLLM baselines, DiscoverLLM improves intent-discovery task performance by roughly 4%-14% while reducing token/conversation length by roughly 11%-45% across Creative Writing, Technical Writing, and SVG Drawing tasks (Table 1, Section 5).

tpls/repro-adam-degenerate-poly.paper_title: Towards Understanding Adam Convergence on Highly Degenerate Polynomials

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that on the degenerate polynomial loss L(x) = (1/k) x^k for k >= 4, Adam achieves local linear convergence when beta_1 < beta_2^(k/(2(k-2))), with asymptotic rate x_{t+1}/x_t -> beta_2^(1/(2(k-2))) (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Over 72 configurations (k∈{4,6,8,10}, β₂∈{0.9,0.93,0.99}), the measured asymptotic rate x_{t+1}/x_t matches β₂^(1/(2(k-2))) to max relative error 1.40e-20 in 80-digit arithmetic; 48/48 inside the Eq.(8) boundary pass and 25/25 outside fail (36-order separation); the negative control v_t:=g_t² inflates the error to exactly 1.0.

claims.claim: Gradient Descent and Heavy-Ball Momentum both exhibit only sublinear convergence of order Theta(t^{-1/(k-2)}) on the same degenerate polynomial objective, established in Theorems 5.1 and 5.3 respectively.
claims.evidence: GD at k∈{4,5,6,8,10}, T=200,000 gives log-log slope within 8.55e-05 of -1/(k-2) with BCa CIs excluding 0 and -1, and leading constant ratio within 3.25e-05 of 1; continuous Heavy-Ball (Theorem 5.3) matches exponent to 9.18e-06 at 6/6 configs; k=2 negative control gives exact geometric ratio 1-η.

claims.claim: Remark 5.8 quantifies the resulting complexity separation: Gradient Descent requires iteration complexity T_epsilon ~ epsilon^{-(k-2)} to reach accuracy epsilon, whereas Adam achieves T_epsilon ~ (k-2) ln(1/epsilon) (Remark 5.8).
claims.evidence: GD T_ε measured directly (up to 6M steps) gives log-log slope within 3.68e-03 of (k-2) at k∈{4,5,6}; Adam T_ε is linear in ln(1/ε) with R²≥0.999999994 and slope/(k-2) collapses across k∈{4,6,8} to 18.9812±0.02%; measured 15,385× separation at k=4, ε=1e-3; k=2 control removes GD's polynomial complexity.

claims.claim: Lemma 5.4 shows the second moment estimate satisfies v_t/v_{t-1} -> beta_2 asymptotically, decoupling v_t from the instantaneous squared gradient g_t^2 and producing an effective learning rate that grows as beta_2^{-t/2} (Lemma 5.4).
claims.evidence: Over 36 configurations, v_t/v_{t-1}=β₂ to max relative error 5.10e-22, g_t²/v_t < 5.10e-20 (decoupling), and d ln(v_t)/dt = ln(β₂) to 1.69e-15; the β₂=0 negative control gives g_t²/v_t = 1.0 exactly, confirming the decoupling is a property of the β₂-geometric recursion.

claims.claim: Section 6 identifies three convergence regimes governed by beta_1 relative to beta_2: stable exponential convergence, an intermediate regime with an initial exponential phase followed by loss spikes from fixed-point instability, and a SignGD-like oscillatory regime under tight v_t-g_t^2 coupling (Section 6, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Theorem 6.1's fixed-point criterion correctly assigns all 3 of the paper's Figure 6 settings (stable at β₂=0.91, unstable-exists at 0.895, non-existent at 0.8); coupling ratio g_t²/v_t is monotone across regimes (0.0, 9.2e-05, 5.0e-02); Regime II spike is preceded by effective sharpness crossing 2 at step 1,479 before the spike at 2,135; the β₂ sweep shows step size approaching η·sign(g) as coupling tightens.

claims.claim: Figure 3 shows the empirical phase diagram of stability boundaries across different degeneracy orders k matches the theoretical predictions of Equations 8-9 (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: On 25×25 grids at the paper's full 100,000-step settings, main-region agreement (excluding ±1% boundary layer) is 575/575 for k=4 and 569/569 for k=6; full-grid agreement is 99.84% and 99.68% with Wilson CIs above 98%; the single k=4 corner disagreement reproduces the paper's own Appendix G.1 caveat about convergence in theoretically unstable regions.

tpls/repro-adam-degenerate-poly.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims at the paper's own scale and hyperparameters, with pre-registered gates, negative controls, and high-precision arithmetic where needed. The scalar polynomial objective is exactly what the theorems address, so this is a faithful non-toy reproduction rather than a simplified proxy.

Srishti280992/repro-ski-rental-with-dist.paper_title: Ski Rental with Distributional Predictions of Unknown Quality

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows the algorithm achieves expected additive loss O(min(√b·max(EMD(p̂,p),1), b log b)), where EMD(p̂,p) is the Earth Mover's distance between the predicted and true distributions and b is the buy-ski-rental cost ratio (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 was implemented exactly (predicted optimal threshold, 1/√b tail cutoff, K*=min(K̂+√b, U+√b)) and tested on 83 exact finite-support instances with b up to 262,144 and N up to 16,777,216; the maximum ratio of additive loss to min(√b·max(EMD,1), b log b) was 0.9478, confirming the O(·) upper bound with a constant below 1 on all tested instances.

claims.claim: The algorithm attains consistency O(√b) when the prediction error (EMD) is 0 and robustness O(b log b) when the prediction is arbitrarily inaccurate, without needing to know the prediction error bound in advance (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: On EMD=0 rows, max loss/√b = 0.9478 supporting O(√b) consistency; across all shifted predictions with EMD up to 946,200, max loss/(b log b) = 0.1064 supporting O(b log b) robustness; the threshold function algorithm1_threshold(p_hat, b) takes only p_hat and b as inputs, with EMD computed solely by post-hoc audit code, confirming the unknown-quality aspect.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a Pareto-optimal consistency-robustness tradeoff: any algorithm achieving O(√b) consistency must incur Ω(b log b) robustness (Theorem 6, Section 4)
claims.evidence: The Section 4 geometric-tail construction with r=1−2/b and K=⌈0.5b log b⌉ was tested through b=2²⁰; with consistency budget 0.5√b, the minimum robustness threshold satisfying the budget was 0.2367·b·log(b) (deterministic) and 0.0360·b·log(b) (randomized), both bounded away from zero, supporting the Ω(b log b) tradeoff.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 introduces a parameterized algorithm with expected cost c(ALG_p) ≤ min{(1+λ)(c(OPT_p)+B), (1+1/λ)c(OPT_p)}, allowing explicit interpolation between trusting the prediction and worst-case guarantees via λ ∈ [0,1] (Theorem 2, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Algorithm 2 was swept over b∈{64,1024,16384,262144}, five prediction shifts, and 101 lambda values (0 to 1); all 2,020 exact expected-cost checks satisfied c(ALG) ≤ min{(1+λ)(OPT+B_emp), (1+1/λ)·OPT} with max violation = 0.0 and max cost/bound = 1.0.

Srishti280992/repro-ski-rental-with-dist.overall: The logbook provides exact (non-Monte-Carlo) numerical verification of all five theoretical claims on non-trivial scales (b up to 262K–1M, support sizes up to 16M), implementing the paper's algorithms and lower-bound constructions directly and confirming the claimed bounds hold with bounded constants throughout. claims.evidence: PDHG at n=40 with HJ-Prox for the primal L1 prox and exact dual quadratic update correlates 0.99987 with exact PDHG; the valid step condition (tau*sigma*||K||^2 = 0.25 < 1) is enforced and an invalid step (product 400) is correctly rejected as non-finite.

ai-sherpa/hj-prox-operator-splitting-rep.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all five claims through an independent numpy/scipy reimplementation at reasonable scales (n=24–256), with discriminating falsification tests (sign-flipped weights, invalid step sizes, naive baselines) and honest acknowledgment that almost-sure convergence theorems are witnessed rather than formally proven.
