claims.evidence: toy_repro.py implements flow matching with x_t=(1-t)*x_0+t*x_1 interpolation and vector field target v=x_1-x_0 trained via MSE, and loss converges from 1.9951 to 1.7848 over 10 epochs, but only on synthetic random action data with a tiny MLP rather than real robot actions at scale.

ra-XOr/ICML-2026-UniJEPA-Reproduction.overall: This logbook provides only a single toy experiment on synthetic random data demonstrating the TI2E architecture skeleton and flow-matching loss mechanics; five of six claim pages are entirely empty with no experimental runs. No claim is verified or falsified at the paper's actual scale or on real benchmarks.

DineshAI/VnA5q5jXVz.paper_title: Why Self-Distillation Helps and Hurts: Denoising vs. Signal Forgetting

claims.claim: Deterministic-equivalent recursions for prediction risk in overparameterized linear self-training decompose error into a systematic 'signal forgetting' term that grows with the number of self-training iterations and a stochastic noise term that decays exponentially in iterations (Section on risk decomposition; Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: The scalar deterministic-equivalent recursion was checked against an independent closed-form finite convolution across 200,000 parameter cells (max error 1.42e-14), and Monte Carlo simulations at n=500, p=1000 with 10 trials show population-risk correlations of 0.9999+ between theory and simulation. The bias term is confirmed monotonically increasing (0 violations across 200k cells) and the variance term decays geometrically by factor 1/(1+τ) per step, with a no-signal geometric control matching to 3.47e-18.

claims.claim: Test risk as a function of self-training iteration count follows a U-shaped curve, with an optimal early-stopping iteration set by the tradeoff between decaying stochastic error and accumulating systematic (signal-forgetting) error, occurring strictly under spectral anisotropy of the feature covariance (Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: For spikes 5, 25, 100 at n=500, p=1000, the simulated and theoretical optimal stopping iterations match exactly (1, 2, 3) with trajectory correlations ≥0.9998. An isotropic-spectrum control produces zero sign changes in risk increments, confirming that the U-shape requires spectral anisotropy.

claims.claim: In spiked covariance models, each self-training iteration acts as a direction-dependent spectral filter that preserves eigendirections aligned with strong signal (survival factor near 1) while suppressing weaker, noise-aligned eigendirections at a rate of approximately (1+τ)^(−t).
claims.evidence: A four-spike random-projection experiment (n=500, p=1000, 40 trials, 10 iterations) shows observed retention [0.906, 0.675, 0.158, 0.005] closely matching theoretical (s/(s+τ))^t values [0.905, 0.676, 0.162, 0.002], with log-absolute-retention correlation 0.999 and strict ordering preserved (strong spikes survive, weak spikes suppressed).

claims.claim: An iterated Generalized Cross-Validation (iGCV) estimator is proposed that achieves uniform consistency for estimating risk along the self-training trajectory, enabling data-driven selection of the optimal early-stopping iteration without a held-out validation set.
claims.evidence: A full numpy implementation of iGCV computes GCV from training data alone (no held-out set). Across spikes 5/25/100, the iGCV minimizer lands within 2 steps of the oracle stop (MAE 0.009–0.048, correlation up to 0.99). As n grows from 150 to 500, surface correlation improves (0.968→0.986), relative tracking error shrinks (15.3%→10.9%), and selection regret decreases (0.019→0.012) while beating the training-error selector by 11x.

claims.claim: The theoretical denoising-forgetting risk tradeoff, derived for linear regression, is empirically confirmed to hold for deep networks, specifically ResNet-50 trained on CIFAR-10 under repeated self-distillation.
claims.evidence: The claim specifies ResNet-50 on CIFAR-10, but the logbook substitutes a pure-numpy MLP on binary MNIST (digit≥5) with label noise — a model far below ResNet-50's class and a proxy task. While 470 real runs were executed with U-shape observed in 60.2% of configs, the setup is clearly reduced in scale and scope relative to the paper's stated deep-network experiment.

DineshAI/VnA5q5jXVz.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous clean-room verification of the four linear-model theoretical claims (deterministic recursion, U-shaped early stopping, spectral filtering, and iGCV) at paper-scale synthetic dimensions with strong numerical agreement and appropriate negative controls. The deep-network claim is only addressed on a simplified MLP/MNIST proxy rather than the claimed ResNet-50/CIFAR-10 setup.

Srishti280992/repro-no-free-lunch-non-as.paper_title: No Free Lunch: Non-Asymptotic Analysis of Prediction-Powered Inference

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 gives an exact non-asymptotic characterization of when PPI++ has lower estimation error (mean squared error) than using gold-standard labels alone, as a function of the correlation between pseudo-labels and gold-standard labels and the number of labeled samples n (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Clean-room implementation of Theorem 4.1's variance formula was validated against 30,000-trial Monte Carlo on non-Gaussian binary distributions across 4 configurations (independent/weak/moderate/strong) and n in {8,10,12,16,20,30,40}, with max absolute formula-vs-MC error of 5.06e-4 and the analytic improvement/non-improvement boundary matching on every tested cell.

claims.claim: For Gaussian data, PPI++ outperforms the gold-standard-only estimator if and only if the correlation between pseudo- and gold-standard labels is at least 1/sqrt(n-2), a finite-sample threshold that vanishes only as n grows (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: The Gaussian formula check found zero mismatches between the variance-formula improvement condition and the threshold |rho| > 1/sqrt(n-2) across 8 sample sizes (n=6 to 40). Monte Carlo cells on both sides of the threshold confirm the prediction: e.g., at n=6, rho=0.425 (below 0.5) gives PPI MSE 0.177 > classical 0.169, while rho=0.575 (above 0.5) gives PPI MSE 0.154 < classical 0.167.

claims.claim: The paper derives exact non-asymptotic variance expressions for PPI++ under sample splitting, in contrast to prior asymptotic 'free lunch' results claiming PPI++ variance is always at most that of gold-standard-only estimation (Section 4, Propositions 4.1-4.6).
claims.evidence: The independent pseudo-label control (rho≈0, tpr=fpr=0.22) shows PPI++ variance strictly greater than classical variance at all 7 tested sample sizes (independent_binary_rows_worse_than_classical=7), directly demonstrating the finite-sample covariance-estimation loss that contradicts the asymptotic 'free lunch' claim. The pytest suite confirms this gap explicitly.

claims.claim: Corollaries 4.1-4.2 extend the main finite-sample no-free-lunch result to derived estimation settings beyond the basic mean-estimation case (Section 4, Corollaries 4.1-4.2).
claims.evidence: Corollary 4.1 checked on 394 Gaussian cells (n=4–200, 1000 rho grid points each) with zero formula-threshold mismatches and boundary error 2.78e-17; Corollary 4.2 checked on 33,300 non-Gaussian binary cells with zero implication violations across 15,922 condition-true cells; a derived OLS gradient proxy on 32 cells with 20,000 trials showed zero threshold prediction mismatches; negative controls (reversed condition, dropped covariance-estimation loss) produced 16,625 and 16,675 failures respectively, confirming the conditions are non-trivial.

claims.claim: Experiments on real-world datasets illustrate that the theoretical finite-sample threshold on correlation predicts when PPI++ underperforms gold-standard-only estimation in practice (Section 5).
claims.evidence: On public AlphaFold and Galaxies data with 15,000 bootstrap draws, near-zero-correlation variants (rho≈0) never improved in the tested n range, while moderate/high-correlation variants crossed near the Gaussian rule: Galaxies rho≈0.31 crossed at n=24 (rule 24), rho≈0.48 at n=16 (rule 14), rho=0.74 at n=10 (rule 8); AlphaFold crossings were similarly close (rho≈0.30 at n=30 vs rule 28, rho≈0.48 at n=16 vs rule 14). The qualitative threshold prediction holds on real data.

Srishti280992/repro-no-free-lunch-non-as.overall: The logbook provides strong concrete evidence for all five claims through clean-room formula implementations validated against large-scale Monte Carlo, extensive grid checks with negative controls for the corollaries, and real-data bootstrap experiments on public PPI datasets showing the predicted finite-sample threshold behavior. The reproduction is rigorous, with 30,000-trial simulations, 33,300-cell corollary checks, and controlled correlation variants on real data.

snaykey/repro-swift-svd-theoretical-opti.paper_title: Approximate Proportionality in Online Fair Division

claims.claim: Three natural greedy allocation rules (maximize relative item value, allocate to most unsatisfied agent, and minimize worst predicted dissatisfaction) each fail to guarantee any positive multiplicative approximation to PROP1 against an adaptive adversary (Section 3, Propositions 6-8).
claims.evidence: The logbook reproduces the paper's exact counterexample valuation sequences at meaningful scale (m=800 prefixes driving PROP1 ratios to 0.00499 and 0.005; Appendix B adaptive recurrence with 500 switching epochs and 6022 goods driving the ratio to 0.267729 with 497 strict decreases), providing concrete evidence that all three greedy rules' PROP1 ratios trend toward zero.

claims.claim: Against a non-adaptive adversary, uniform random allocation achieves an Ω(1/log(n/δ)) approximation to PROP1 with probability at least 1-δ, specifically α = 27/(128·log(n/δ)), the first such multiplicative bound in the online setting without extra assumptions (Section 4, Theorem 9).
claims.evidence: 28,800 independent uniform allocations across n=2,5,10 and delta=0.10,0.05 over four valuation families yield zero empirical failures at the anchored constant α=27/(128·log(n/δ)), with maximum 95% Wilson upper bound 0.003191 below the relevant δ, providing strong statistical evidence for the claimed probability bound.

claims.claim: Given perfect maximum-item-value (MIV) predictions, Algorithm 1 guarantees a 1/n-PROP1 allocation (Section 5, Theorem 11).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 was implemented with the global potential and minimum-potential recipient selection, run on 2,000 trials (n=8, m=40, four families) with perfect MIV predictions (max error 0.00e+00); the minimum realized PROP1 ratio was 1, well above the required 1/n=0.125, with zero potential monotonicity violations.

claims.claim: Under one-sided MIV prediction error ε ∈ [0,1), the algorithm's approximation degrades gracefully to β = (1-ε)/(n-ε/n) (Section 5, Theorem 12).
claims.evidence: The paper's exact reduction (promoting earliest item ≥1-ε to predicted MIV 1, running Algorithm 1 on augmented valuations, evaluating under original valuations) was tested across 450 trials over n=2,5,8 and five error levels through ε=0.9; the minimum measured slack above β=(1-ε)/(n-ε/n) was 0.538462, confirming the bound holds.

claims.claim: Even with perfect MIV predictions, no online algorithm can achieve any non-zero approximation to EF1, MMS, or PROPX (Section 5, Proposition 10).
claims.evidence: The Appendix D.1 adaptive gadget was implemented at strict prefix parameters (m=ceil(2n/α)+n+2, K=ceil(3/α), ε=K^{-(m-2)}) with an adaptive residual tail, tested against five distinct deterministic online policies at three α levels; at α=0.25 all five policies had EF1, MMS, and PROPX ratios below α, with MMS computed by exhaustive two-way partition enumeration.

snaykey/repro-swift-svd-theoretical-opti.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all five claims through reproduction of the paper's adversarial constructions, Monte Carlo verification of the random allocation bound, and direct implementation of Algorithm 1 with both perfect and erroneous MIV predictions. The experiments use the paper's own valuation families and proof gadgets at non-trivial scale (up to 28,800 trials and 6,022 goods), though the documentation lacks detailed code, raw data, and specification of the tested policies and valuation families.

snaykey/repro-mira-a-score-for-condition.paper_title: Linear Regression with Unknown Truncation Beyond Gaussian Features

claims.claim: The paper gives the first polynomial-time, poly(d/ε), algorithm for truncated linear regression with an unknown survival set under sub-Gaussian (rather than Gaussian) feature distributions (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Full Algorithm 1 implemented at d=10, k=5 on synthetic data; error decreases from 0.256 to 0.048 as n grows from 400 to 6400, matching PSGD with true S* (0.053), but d=10 is too small to verify poly(d/ε) scaling and the 'first' claim is theoretical novelty, not empirically testable.

claims.claim: The algorithm assumes a known lower bound α on the truncation/survival probability, sub-Gaussian feature tails, and a well-conditioned observed covariance matrix (Section 3, three main assumptions).
claims.evidence: All three assumptions empirically instantiated and stress-tested: survival probability 0.724≥α=0.3, Rademacher (non-Gaussian sub-Gaussian) features yield error 0.0505, ρ²=0.330>0, and violating well-conditioning causes error to jump to 0.387.

claims.claim: Phase I of the algorithm learns the unknown survival set as a union of k intervals via a novel positive-only PAC learning subroutine that runs in poly(k/ε) time (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 3 implemented with k=5 fixed; symmetric-difference error decreases from 0.0118 to 0.0008 and recovers exactly 5 intervals, but k is never varied to verify poly(k/ε) scaling, and the setup is small-scale synthetic.

claims.claim: Phase II estimates the regression vector via projected stochastic gradient descent on a perturbed negative log-likelihood objective, after Phase I's set recovery (Section 3).
claims.evidence: PSGD on perturbed NLL implemented at d=10 with mild truncation; learned-S error 0.1106 vs true-S* 0.1211, but margin over misspecified baseline (0.1392) is modest and the logbook itself acknowledges weak differentiation due to mild truncation.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.4 shows sub-Gaussianity implies smoothness of the auxiliary distributions used to construct reference distributions for learning from positive examples alone (Lemma 3.4).
claims.evidence: Smoothness inequality tested on 400 random intervals for one specific distribution instance; q=1.5 gives 100% satisfaction while q=1 fails, but this is a Monte Carlo check on a single instance, not a general verification of the theoretical lemma.

claims.claim: This improves on prior work (LMZ24a) which required d^poly(k/ε) running time and was restricted to Gaussian features (Section on related work/Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Rademacher features work (error 0.048) and runtime is roughly flat from d=5 to d=40 (slope 0.05), but d≤40 is too small to confirm polynomial scaling, and LMZ24 is not run for direct comparison.

snaykey/repro-mira-a-score-for-condition.overall: The logbook implements the paper's full algorithm from scratch on synthetic data at small scale (d=10, k=5), showing it works as claimed with decreasing error and matching idealized baselines. However, the theoretical claims about polynomial time complexity, PAC learning guarantees, and smoothness lemmas are only empirically suggested at this scale, not fully verified.

snaykey/repro-oddshap.paper_title: An Odd Estimator for Shapley Values

claims.claim: Observation 3.1 proves that Shapley values depend exclusively on the odd component of the coalition set function, so the even component can be discarded without loss (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Exact brute-force Shapley computation over 200 random set functions (d=3..12) shows max|φ(f)−φ(f_odd)|=4.44e-16 and max|φ(f_even)|=1.39e-16, with a negative control (arbitrary split) yielding diff=0.255, confirming the test is discriminating.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 proves that paired sampling orthogonalizes the regression, provably separating the odd and even objectives and giving the first general theoretical justification for this widely used sampling heuristic (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Under paired sampling, joint-vs-separate Fourier coefficient differences are 5.2e-15 (odd) and 1.0e-14 (even) across 75 trials, while unpaired negative controls disagree in 75/75 (100%) cases; Corollary 3.3 frontier invariance holds to 1.0e-14 over 40 cases.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 shows that Fourier basis regression exactly recovers Shapley values, which forms the theoretical basis of the OddSHAP algorithm (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Constrained weighted least-squares recovery gives max|φ(f)−φ(f̂)|=6.8e-15 across 192 cases spanning 4 basis-collection shapes (including random non-nested supersets), with a negative control (missing singleton) breaking in 24/24 cases with diffs 0.67–1.11.

claims.claim: In Table 1, across eight estimators and eight benchmarks (with sample budget m≈100d), OddSHAP attains the lowest average rank (1.50), beating the prior best method RegressionMSR (rank 2.25) (Section 5, Table 1).
claims.evidence: A 4-estimator comparison on 6 synthetic value functions at d=10 with oracle interaction selection shows OddSHAP-toy avg rank 1.00 vs LeverageSHAP-toy 2.00, but this uses synthetic data, half the estimators, and an oracle proxy—directional only, not the paper's 8 benchmarks × 8 estimators.

claims.claim: OddSHAP reduces estimation error by 6–62x relative to LeverageSHAP on tabular data benchmarks (Section 5, Table 1).
claims.evidence: On the same synthetic d=10 setup, the MSE ratio (LeverageSHAP-toy / OddSHAP-toy) is 27.6x, which falls within the paper's 6–62x range but on unrelated synthetic data with oracle interaction selection rather than the paper's real tabular benchmarks.

claims.claim: Figure 2 shows OddSHAP's advantage over baselines is largest for moderate-to-high dimensional problems (d≥30) when given sufficient sampling budget (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: A dimension sweep up to d=14 (not d≥30) shows MSE ratios of 1.48, 1.64, 0.11, 0.07, 0.06 for d=6,8,10,12,14—directionally suggestive but non-monotonic at low d, on synthetic data, and an order of magnitude below the claimed dimension threshold.

snaykey/repro-oddshap.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the paper's three core theoretical results (Observation 3.1, Theorem 3.2, Theorem 3.5) to machine precision via exact brute-force enumeration with discriminating negative controls, but the three empirical claims (Table 1 ranking, 6–62x error reduction, d≥30 dimension dependence) are addressed only on a small-scale synthetic setup with oracle interaction selection and 4 of 8 estimators.

snaykey/repro-rex-solvers.paper_title: COPF: An Online Framework for Deployment-Stable Counterfactual Fairness in Evolving Graphs

claims.claim: COPF defines decision-counterfactual fairness gaps as disparities in benefit between exposure (shown) and non-exposure (hidden) counterfactuals across protected groups (Definition 3.3, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements all three Def 3.3 quantities (gTE_gap, gMin, gCal_max) and computes them on real tgbl-wiki and tgbl-review streams with concrete non-degenerate values (e.g., tgbl-wiki Deploy: gTE_gap=0.00146, gCal_max=0.0330, gMin=0.00000).

claims.claim: COPF constructs graph-aware self-normalized doubly robust (GA-DR) pseudo-outcomes for estimating counterfactual quantities under temporal dependence and local interference on evolving graphs (Definition 3.2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The GA-DR pseudo-outcome formula with self-normalized graph-aware window averages (half-life 1000 time-decay weights) and online cross-fit nuisance is implemented and run on real TGB streams, producing stable effect estimates (e.g., tgbl-review Deploy gTE_gap=0.00199 with residual-OI witness ε_Δ=0.00051).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.5 proves that small residual outcome-indistinguishability (residual-OI) on estimated DR residuals implies bounds on the true counterfactual fairness gap, accounting for estimation and dependence error (Theorem 4.5, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook computes the Residual-OI certificate (ε_T + concentration radius) and verifies it upper-bounds the measured gTE_gap in 12/12 audited (dataset, arm, phase) cells on real TGB and synthetic data (e.g., tgbl-wiki Deploy: measured gap=0.00146, certificate=0.0087; synthetic copf Deploy: gap=0.01063, certificate=0.0185).

claims.claim: Corollary 4.6 shows residual-OI control implies bounds on decision-counterfactual fairness gaps, connecting the auditing certificate to the fairness objective (Corollary 4.6, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The mass-normalized certificate gTE_gap ≤ 2(ε_T + E_T)/p^g_min from Cor 4.6 is computed online and verified to bound the measured decision-counterfactual gaps in all 12 audited cells, with the certificate being conservative as the corollary's slack terms predict.

claims.claim: On temporal graph benchmark (TGB) streams and synthetic bipartite data, COPF reduces worst-case spikes in exposure-counterfactual group disparities during policy shifts with only modest degradation in ranking utility, as reported in the phase-wise results (Section 6, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: On the paper-scale synthetic stream (600u/4000i with injected bias), COPF reduces worst-case gTE from 0.01857→0.01678 (Deploy) and 0.01920→0.01571 (Post) with no NDCG@10 degradation (0.3431→0.3444); on real TGB streams COPF is non-binding (identical to Base) because the ID-mod2 placebo split yields tiny gaps, consistent with the paper's own observation that TGB gains are 'more localized.'

claims.claim: COPF is implemented via an online primal-dual control loop (Algorithm 1) that stays largely inactive when logged disparities are already small, only intervening when certificates flag structural bias (Section 4.3, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Controller offset |δ_s| is exactly 0 in the Pre warm-up phase across all datasets and remains 0 on tgbl-wiki (where gaps are tiny) across all phases, while activating only on the injected-bias synthetic stream (Deploy |δ|=0.00361, Post λ_TE=0.0381) and staying near-zero on tgbl-review (|δ|≈0.00001).

snaykey/repro-rex-solvers.overall: The logbook reproduces COPF's core mechanism—GA-DR estimation, Residual-OI certificates, and the primal-dual controller—at real TGB benchmark scale on the EdgeBank backbone, with concrete numbers confirming the claimed directions. Worst-case spike reduction is demonstrated on the paper-scale injected-bias synthetic stream, while TGB placebo splits correctly show COPF non-binding, matching the paper's own observations.

snaykey/repro-flashoptim.paper_title: All ERMs Can Fail in Stochastic Convex Optimization Lower Bounds in Linear Dimension

claims.claim: In dimension d = 6m, there exists a stochastic convex optimization instance where every ε-ERM solution with ε = Θ(m^{-3/2}) incurs constant excess risk and fails to generalize (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook builds the paper's actual Lemma 5 construction at d = 6m, computes the closed-form empirical minimizer, and shows the excess-risk gap F(w*)−F(0) is approximately constant (~0.001) across m = 4 to 256 (CV = 0.19), with the minimizer certified by ‖∇F_S(w*)‖ ≤ 6e-17 and zero points below in 400 random draws for m ≤ 8. The approximate-ERM extension via strong-convexity slack yields positive gap lower bounds for all tested m.

claims.claim: For λ-strongly convex losses with m^{-3/2} ≤ λ ≤ m^{-1/2}, any ε-ERM solution w_S satisfies F(w_S) − min F(w) ≥ Ω(1/(λ m^{3/2})) (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The λ-sweep at m = 9 yields a measured log-log slope of gap vs λ of −1.0000 (theory −1), and the m-sweep with λ = 1/m yields a measured slope of gap·λ vs m of −1.4825 (theory −1.5), both from actual computation on the paper's construction. claims.claim: The optimal mixing weight ξ*(λ) can be negative, corresponding to a 'pro-learning' regime under over-regularization (λ > λ*), as opposed to the 'anti-learning' regime (ξ* > 1) identified in prior work by Das and Sanghavi (2023) (Section 2.3).
claims.evidence: 2976/2976 isotropic over-regularized configurations (λ>2λ*) have ξ*<0, with most-negative ξ*=−46.28 exhibited; clipping ξ* to [0,1] (Das-Sanghavi constrained range) recovers 0.0 median fraction of the achievable risk gap, confirming negativity is essential; anti-learning regime also exhibited (ξ* up to 424.4).

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 derives exact deterministic equivalents for the optimal self-distillation risk R*_sd(λ) and mixing weight ξ*(λ) in the proportional asymptotics regime (n, p → ∞, p/n → γ) under general anisotropic covariance and deterministic signals (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Deterministic equivalents land inside BCa bootstrap 95% CI in all 12/12 target×combination cases at m=4000; final relative residuals are ≤0.45% (R̄), ≤0.68% (R*_sd), ≤1.3% (ξ*); corrupting the b=(1−t₂)⁻¹ coefficient inflates residuals 10–257×, confirming the DE assembly is specific.

claims.claim: In the isotropic-signal setting, Corollary 3.2 shows the optimal mixing weight changes sign exactly at λ* := γσ²/r², with ξ*(λ) < 0 for λ > λ* and ξ*(λ) > 0 for λ < λ* (Section 3.2, Corollary 3.2).
claims.evidence: Root of ξ̄*(λ)=0 matches γσ²/r² to max relative error 7.2e-15 on all 6/6 combinations; all 25/25 strictly-below and 25/25 strictly-above grid nodes carry the correct sign in every combination (5 exceptions are exactly at the λ* node where ξ*=0 by the corollary); anisotropic negative control shifts the zero by median 30%.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proposes a one-shot generalized cross-validation (GCV) estimator of the optimal mixing weight ξ* that is consistent in proportional asymptotics and avoids grid search, sample splitting, or refitting (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).

claims.claim: Theorem 3 shows that under model mis-specification, the Distillation Efficiency Ratio (DER) diverges at rate Omega-tilde(N^kappa) with kappa = (alpha_T - 1 - beta)(1/alpha_T - 1/alpha_S) > 0, formalizing the Spectral Horizon Expansion by which distillation lets a student capture high-frequency signal components that are statistically inaccessible from raw ground-truth data alone (Section 5, Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: A synthetic D=128 experiment shows a teacher with α=0.5 carrying 31.2% high-frequency energy, a label-only student retaining 0.06%, and KD recovering 29.9% (483x expansion), but the specific DER divergence rate Omega-tilde(N^kappa) with kappa = (alpha_T - 1 - beta)(1/alpha_T - 1/alpha_S) is never measured as a function of N.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 establishes a weak-to-strong generalization guarantee: a strong student model provably surpasses a weak teacher whenever the task exhibits low-dimensional intrinsic structure and both models are sufficiently expressive (Section 6, Theorem 4, Assumption 5).

claims.evidence: The logbook reports SNR improvement of 6.3x over 40 training steps in a synthetic setup, which is related to the spectral denoising concept, but the specific PGR formula PGR = 1 - O-tilde((k-dagger)^(2 alpha_S/(2 alpha_S+1)) * N^(-Delta_rate)) is never measured or fitted.

claims.claim: Figures 2 and 3 empirically validate the risk-inheritance and early-stopping predictions using both synthetic data and real-world model architectures, confirming that early stopping is critical for weak-to-strong generalization to succeed (Figure 2, Figure 3).

claims.evidence: The logbook does not test whether the Mira statistic reduces to Laplace's rule of succession p(k|n)=(n+1)/(N+2); no experiment examines the discrete k∈{0,1} statistic under the null.

Srishti280992/repro-understanding-genera.paper_title: Understanding Generalization and Forgetting in In-Context Continual Learning

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 decomposes the task-t prediction error into an irreducible error term, a variance term scaling as O(M/(t^2(M+1)^2)) that decreases with more in-context examples, and a bias term measuring deviation ‖(1/t)∑_s w_s - w_t‖^2 from task dissimilarity (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The exact Theorem 4.3 specialization shows variance_scaled = variance × t²(M+1)²/M is constant at 373.0 across M=1..4096, confirming the O(M/(t²(M+1)²)) scaling; bias at M=4096 equals 1.0187, matching the asymptotic task-dissimilarity value 1.0189; Monte Carlo agrees with exact formulas within 1.59 standard errors.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 shows that forgetting arises from attention reweighting past tasks with negative coefficients c_t and future tasks with positive coefficients d, rather than from actual information loss, comprising intra-task variance and inter-task mean-interaction terms (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: All past-task coefficients c_t are negative and all future-task coefficients d are positive across 10 unique A/A/A/B/B orderings; forgetting ranges from 0.163 to 3.383 with the same task multiset, confirming order-dependent reweighting rather than information loss; Monte Carlo matches exact formulas within 1.29 standard errors.

claims.claim: The theory predicts non-monotonic error curves with context length M, where longer prompts reduce variance but amplify systematic bias from misaligned historical tasks, producing a clear performance peak at intermediate M (Section 4, theoretical analysis).
claims.evidence: On the prespecified d=32 A-B-A-B-A sequence with the paper's M grid [1,2,3,5,7,9,11,13,15,19], the exact average mixed-task error decreases monotonically from 8.248 at M=1 to 2.358 at M=19 with no interior peak (has_interior_peak=false); the only non-monotonic example required searching 200,000 random weight configurations.

claims.claim: Mean-misalignment interference persists regardless of context length, while variance-induced interference decays as O(1/M), implying a persistent asymptotic forgetting floor (Section 4, theoretical analysis).
claims.evidence: M×variance converges to ~10.38 at M=4096 confirming O(1/M) variance decay, while the mean-interaction term persists at 0.028283 and dominates the residual total forgetting of 0.030818 at M=4096, demonstrating a persistent asymptotic forgetting floor.

claims.claim: Experiments on GPT-2 architectures confirm the predicted non-monotonic error curves and reproduce catastrophic forgetting with a 46% accuracy drop on real LLM tasks (Section 5, experimental validation).
claims.evidence: A 500-query/condition Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct generation evaluation shows SST-2 Task A accuracy changing from 89.2% to 88.6% (delta -0.6%, 95% CI [-2.2, +1.0]), not the claimed 46% catastrophic drop; the 800-step GPT-2 run shows Task 2 MSE decreasing monotonically from 1.251 to 0.403, not the predicted non-monotonic curve.

Srishti280992/repro-understanding-genera.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the theoretical decompositions of Theorems 4.3 and 4.4 and the persistent forgetting floor via explicit formula implementation with Monte Carlo validation, but falsifies the non-monotonic context-length prediction on a prespecified paper-shaped grid and the headline 46% real-LLM accuracy drop via a 500-query Qwen2.5-1.5B evaluation.

snaykey/repro-zo-gd-stability.paper_title: Zeroth-Order Optimization at the Edge of Stability

claims.claim: For ZO-GD, the mean-square critical step size satisfies 2/(Tr(H) + 2*lambda_max(H)) <= eta_ms* <= 2/Tr(H), showing dependence on the full Hessian spectrum rather than just the top eigenvalue (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Across 36 random synthetic Hessians (dims 4–100, condition numbers 10–300, three spectrum shapes), the exact mean-square-critical step size solved from the paper's fixed-point equation falls within the bracket [2/(Tr+2λmax), 2/Tr] in 36/36 trials, and an independently hand-derived second-moment operator's spectral-radius crossing matches η*ms, validated against 400k-seed Monte Carlo (0.08% relative error).

claims.claim: Theorem 2 extends the mean-square stability bound to ZO-GD with momentum (ZO-GDM), showing the critical step size is adjusted by the momentum parameter beta (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Across 32 random Hessians with 4 momentum values (β ∈ {0, 0.3, 0.6, 0.9}), the exact ZO-GDM critical step size from the β-dependent fixed-point equation satisfies the adjusted bracket 2(1−β)/(Tr+2λmax/(1+β)) ≤ η*ms ≤ 2(1−β)/Tr in 32/32 trials, with an independently derived 3d-dimensional joint second-moment operator cross-validated against 400k-seed Monte Carlo.

claims.claim: For frozen ZO-Adam, the mean-square stability threshold depends on the spectrum of the preconditioned Hessian P^{-1}H rather than the raw Hessian (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Across 32 random Hessians with 4 β1 values and a frozen diagonal preconditioner P commuting with H, the exact frozen-ZO-Adam critical step size computed on eigenvalues of P⁻¹H satisfies the bracket using Tr(P⁻¹H) and λmax(P⁻¹H) in 32/32 trials, with the independently derived operator's spectral-radius crossing matching the fixed-point solution.

claims.claim: Empirically, ZO-GD, ZO-GDM, and ZO-Adam all stabilize their trace/curvature statistics near the theoretically predicted mean-square edge-of-stability thresholds when trained on a CNN on CIFAR-10, ResNet20, and a Vision Transformer (Section 5, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The claim concerns CNN/ResNet20/ViT on CIFAR-10, but the reproduction uses a d=6 double-well polynomial toy; only 2 of 3 optimizers (ZO-GD, ZO-GDM) show 100% bracket containment near the threshold, while ZO-Adam's adaptive preconditioner showed 0% containment and could not be observed near threshold.

claims.claim: Practical stability tracking during training requires only the trace and top eigenvalue of the Hessian, not the full spectrum, via the bounds given in Equations 23-25 (Section 5, Equations 23-25).
claims.evidence: Across 42 random Hessians (d ∈ {4,…,256}), the two-statistic bracket [2/(Tr+2λmax), 2/Tr] contains the true η*ms in 42/42 trials, and the naive λmax-only bound's relative error grows from 2.4× to 94× with dimension while the two-statistic bracket's error shrinks from 1.2× to 0.02×, directly demonstrating that Tr is necessary and sufficient alongside λmax.

claims.claim: Catapult-like dynamics appear when the step size is increased past the mean-square stability threshold in the empirical experiments (Section 5, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The claim concerns catapult dynamics in CNN/ResNet20/ViT experiments (Figure 3), but the reproduction uses a d=6 double-well toy; loss spikes of 10⁴× and 10¹⁷× were confirmed at step-size jumps past the calibrated threshold, but the bounded relaxation phase was not reproduced due to the toy's unbounded curvature growth.

snaykey/repro-zo-gd-stability.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the paper's theoretical claims (Theorems 1–3 and the Tr+λmax bracket utility) through exact numerical computation on 100+ synthetic Hessians with independent operator derivations cross-checked against Monte Carlo. The empirical claims about neural network training on CIFAR-10 are addressed only on a d=6 nonlinear toy, confirming the EoS mechanism for 2 of 3 optimizers and catapult onset but not the full bounded-relaxation dynamics.

Srishti280992/repro-box-thirding-anytime.paper_title: Box Thirding: Anytime Best Arm Identification under Insufficient Sampling

claims.claim: Box Thirding (B3) is analyzed under a formalized 'data-poor condition' where the candidate set size c0 cannot cover all potentially eps-optimal arms, decomposing error probability into non-inclusion probability and misidentification probability (Section 4).
claims.evidence: A clean-room B3 simulation with N=4096, eps=0.2, 700 trials per budget across 7 budgets tested the event containment {mu_1 - mu_aT > eps} ⊆ {non-inclusion} ∪ {within-candidate misidentification}, finding 0 containment violations across 4,900 independent event checks with the empirical union rate exactly matching the total error rate at every budget.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 bounds the misidentification probability as P(mu_1 - mu_at > eps) <= exp{-Omega(max{N_(eps/2)/N, eps^2/N} * T)}, where N_(eps/2) is the count of eps/2-best arms (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: On a fixed instance (N=4096, N_(eps/2)=16, eps=0.2, sigma=0.35), the measured epsilon-error rate decreased from 0.83 to 0.1286 as the theorem exponent T*max{N_(eps/2)/N, eps^2/N} increased from 1.0 to 11.39, with a least-squares regression of Laplace-smoothed -log(P(error)) on the exponent yielding slope 0.177 and R²=0.994, confirming exponential decay in the claimed quantity.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.8 shows B3 attains candidate set size c0 = Theta(T), matching Uniform Sampling, while Bracketing Sequential Halving attains only c0 = Theta(T/(log_2 T)^2) (Proposition 4.8).
claims.evidence: Across T=300..50,000, the simulated B3 candidate-set ratio c0/T stayed bounded between 0.252 and 0.400 (consistent with Theta(T)), while BSH's normalized c0*log2(T)^2/T remained roughly order-constant between 3.73 and 6.77 (consistent with Theta(T/log^2(T))), using the paper's BSH formula and an independent B3 simulation.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.9 shows B3 and Uniform Sampling share the same non-inclusion probability bound exp{-Omega(T*N_(eps/2)/N)}, while Bracketing Sequential Halving is slower by a log(T)^2 factor (Corollary 4.9).
claims.evidence: Exact combinatorial log non-inclusion probabilities were computed for N=1,000,000 and N_good=1,000 across T=1,000..50,000 for US, B3, and BSH; the exact logs matched the proxy -c0*N_good/N within 0.05–2.6% (ratios 1.001–1.026), directly confirming the non-inclusion exponent scaling and the log(T)^2 gap between BSH and US/B3.

claims.claim: On the New Yorker Cartoon Caption Contest dataset (contest 893, N=5,513 arms, budget T=10,000), B3 achieves consistently lower simple regret than Uniform Sampling, BUCB, and Bracketing Sequential Halving across high-noise (N(mu,0.5^2)), moderate-noise (N(mu,0.2^2)), and deterministic reward regimes (Section 5 experiments).
claims.evidence: On the real NYCCC contest 893 dataset (N=5,513, T=10,000, 200 reps), B3 had the lowest mean simple regret in high-noise (0.0517 vs 0.3341/0.1396/0.1456) and moderate-noise (0.0299 vs 0.1945/0.0540/0.1531), but in the deterministic regime Uniform Sampling achieved 0.0000 regret while B3 had 0.0163, directly contradicting the claim that B3 is consistently lower across all three regimes including deterministic.

claims.claim: The base sampling parameter r0 in B3 is set by solving r0 + r0^1.5 = 4, yielding r0 approx 1.728 (Section 4, Algorithm parameters).
claims.evidence: Independent bisection solving r0 + r0^1.5 = 4 yields r0 = 1.728163201332383 with numerical residual 0.0 at double precision, matching the paper's stated approximate value of 1.728.

Srishti280992/repro-box-thirding-anytime.overall: The logbook provides concrete simulation and combinatorial evidence supporting the five theoretical/structural claims (data-poor decomposition, Theorem 4.3 exponential bound, Proposition 4.8 candidate-set scaling, Corollary 4.9 non-inclusion scaling, and the r0 parameter), while the NYCCC experiment falsifies Claim 5 as worded because Uniform Sampling achieves zero deterministic regret where B3 does not.

DineshAI/diF53wYIj3.paper_title: Well-Posed KL-Regularized Control via Wasserstein and Kalman–Wasserstein KL Divergences

claims.claim: The Kalman-Wasserstein KL divergence is shown to remove the singularity that classical KL-regularized control exhibits as process noise vanishes in linear time-invariant systems with Gaussian process noise (Section 3, Section 4)
claims.evidence: The support_mismatch_protocol computes KL, WKL, and KWKL across 84 cells (4 mean gaps × 21 variances down to 1e-12), showing KL exceeding 1e20 while WKL stays below 30 and KWKL below 100. The double_integrator_protocol further demonstrates KL gain collapse (norm < 1e-5 at rho=1e-10) while WKL/KWKL gains remain finite (>1.0), directly showing singularity removal in an LTI control context.

claims.claim: Section 4 applies the Wasserstein-KL and Kalman-Wasserstein-KL formulations to control synthesis, deriving closed-form or tractable control laws distinct from classical KL-regularized control (Section 4)
claims.evidence: The controller function uses solve_discrete_are to produce closed-form LQR gains with distinct R matrices: R_KL = B^T Σ_w^{-1} B, R_WKL = B^T B, R_KWKL = B^T (Σ_w + λI)^{-1} B. Across 120 double-integrator cells, WKL gains are invariant to noise (max-min < 1e-12) and differ from KL, confirmed by an independent Bellman fixed-point solver with errors below 7e-15.

claims.claim: On the double integrator benchmark (a linear time-invariant system), the Wasserstein-KL and Kalman-Wasserstein-KL controllers maintain numerical stability and well-posedness as process noise approaches zero, where classical KL-regularized control becomes ill-posed (Section 5)
claims.evidence: At rho=1e-10, the KL controller gain norm collapses below 1e-5 while WKL and KWKL_1 maintain gain norms above 1.0, with WKL perfectly noise-invariant. All four 300-step trajectory comparisons show WKL and KWKL_1 achieving lower position_rms than KL, demonstrating maintained well-posedness as noise vanishes.

claims.claim: On the nonlinear cart-pole benchmark, the Wasserstein-KL and Kalman-Wasserstein-KL regularized controllers achieve better convergence and control quality than classical KL-based regularization (Section 5)
claims.evidence: The cart-pole protocol runs 10,000-step (100-second) nonlinear simulations at four noise scales (1e-3 to 1e-6) for all three methods. WKL and KWKL achieve lower cart_rms than KL at all four noise levels, demonstrating better control quality on a standard nonlinear benchmark. However, angle_rms and control_rms are computed but not explicitly checked in the verification gate, so convergence quality is only partially evidenced.

DineshAI/diF53wYIj3.overall: This logbook provides a thorough numerical reproduction using Python reimplementations of the released MATLAB protocol, with source pinning, independent Bellman fixed-point verification, and negative controls. All four claims are supported by concrete non-toy experiments on standard control benchmarks (double integrator and nonlinear cart-pole) at the paper's released scale.

DineshAI/Ol99zoW31J.paper_title: Non-Uniform Noise-to-Signal Ratio in the REINFORCE Policy-Gradient Estimator

claims.claim: For finite-horizon linear-quadratic systems with Gaussian policies, the noise-to-signal ratio of the multi-step REINFORCE estimator can be computed exactly in closed form via lifted dynamics (Theorem 5, Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: The closed-form one-step NSR formula is independently validated against degree-8 Gauss-Hermite quadrature across 12 covariance cells (max mean error 9.72e-15, max second-moment relative error 1.10e-15), and multi-step gradients for 13 systems across horizons 1–5 match finite-differenced objective gradients (max relative error 1.70e-10). The code implements the lifted-dynamics formula and cross-checks via an independent covariance-recursion objective, confirming exact computability.

claims.claim: The NSR landscape is highly non-uniform: as the policy approaches the optimal deterministic policy (Σ→0, per Corollary 6), the NSR does not vanish uniformly and can blow up, as demonstrated for a double-integrator system (Figure 1, Section 2.3).
claims.evidence: The double-integrator system (A=[[1,.1],[0,1]], B=[[0],[.1]], K=[[-1,-3]]) is swept over 3,721 (σ,σ₀) cells, yielding NSR spanning 18.5 to 4.04e9 (ratio 2.18e8). As σ→0 the fitted log-log slope is −1.9999994 with zero monotonicity failures, directly demonstrating NSR blowup as the policy approaches determinism.

claims.claim: Variance of the multi-step REINFORCE estimator grows exponentially with the control horizon when the closed-loop dynamics are unstable, i.e., when the spectral radius ρ(F)>1 (Theorem 8, Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: A scalar linear-Gaussian LQG with explicit REINFORCE estimator Monte-Carlo shows log-variance-vs-horizon slopes of 2.47 (ρ=1.5) and 1.36 (ρ=1.2) for unstable closed loops, versus 0.41 and 0.35 for stable ρ=0.7,0.5, with ρ=1.0 intermediate at 0.81. The slope is monotone in ρ(F), confirming exponential-in-T growth only for ρ(F)>1 with stable systems as negative controls.

claims.claim: A general upper bound on REINFORCE gradient-estimator variance is derived for generic nonlinear dynamics with expressive neural-network policies (Theorem 10, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The variance upper bound is tested across 36 configurations with deep tanh MLPs (2–3 hidden layers, 32–64 units, up to 5,089 parameters) on quadratic, cubic, and saturating nonlinear dynamics, with exact backprop-computed parameter Jacobians. The bound holds in all 36/36 cases (max LHS/RHS ratio 0.186), and dropping the ||Σ⁻¹||² factor causes violations in 4/4 small-σ cases, confirming non-vacuity.

claims.claim: The analysis is extended from linear to polynomial systems and polynomial feedback policies via a moment-evaluation approach (Proposition 9, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Polynomial dynamics with polynomial feedback a_t=θ₀+θ₁s_t+θ₂s_t²+ε_t are evaluated via exact Isserlis Gaussian-moment evaluation across 5 configurations (T=2,3), yielding closed-form NSR values (e.g., 394.59, 904.86). Monte-Carlo cross-checks converge to the exact values as sample size increases (mean relative error 0.082 at 40k → 0.030 at 200k), confirming the moment-evaluation extension to polynomial systems.

DineshAI/Ol99zoW31J.overall: The logbook provides concrete, clean-room numerical evidence supporting all five claims: exact closed-form NSR validated by independent quadrature and finite differences, double-integrator NSR blowup demonstrated, exponential variance growth for unstable closed loops confirmed with stable controls, the nonlinear NN-policy upper bound tested with genuinely expressive networks and non-vacuity controls, and polynomial-system moment evaluation cross-checked by Monte Carlo.

JAEMP/repro-knowing-when-to-quit-a-princ.paper_title: Knowing When to Quit: A Principled Framework for Dynamic Abstention in LLM Reasoning

claims.claim: Proposition 4.2 proves that a dynamic value-thresholding abstention policy (abstain when the value function falls below the abstention reward) strictly dominates non-abstaining baselines when abstention occurs with positive probability (Proposition 4.2).
claims.evidence: The only direct test is a 4-trajectory hardcoded CUDA tensor ([[0.9,0.8],[0.8,0.7],[0.4,0.2],[0.3,0.4]]) yielding dynamic accuracy 1.0 vs 0.5, which the logbook itself labels a 'toy finite trajectories; mechanism sanity check, not a proof.' The proof of Proposition 4.2 was not independently re-derived; empirical re-aggregation of released artifacts shows dynamic > no-abstention (0.646 vs 0.165 Phi-3, 0.913 vs 0.430 Qwen) but this is an artifact check, not proof verification.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.5 shows that fixed-position, input-only abstention baselines (abstaining only at token position k=1) are strictly dominated by the dynamic policy (Corollary 4.5).
claims.evidence: Same 4-trajectory toy check as Claim 1; the proof of Corollary 4.5 was not independently re-derived. Re-aggregated released artifacts show dynamic selective accuracy > baseline (0.646 vs 0.341 Phi-3, 0.913 vs 0.695 Qwen), but the reward metric is NOT strictly higher for dynamic on Phi-3 (0.533 vs 0.548), complicating the strict-dominance claim even empirically.

claims.claim: On OlympiadBench with Phi-3, the dynamic abstention method achieves 64% selective accuracy at a 90% abstention rate versus 34% for the best baseline (Section 6, OlympiadBench Phi-3 results).
claims.evidence: Re-aggregation of all 5 released trajectory CSVs (2160 samples each, ~1.16M rows per seed) using official compute_seed_metrics/aggregate_seed_metrics yields dynamic 64.56% ± 4.94pp vs best baseline 34.14% ± 9.07pp at 90% abstention, matching the claimed 64% vs 34%. An independent CUDA re-aggregation confirms mean accuracy 0.6456 across seeds.

claims.claim: On OlympiadBench with Qwen, the dynamic method reaches 91% selective accuracy at 90% abstention versus 75% for the best baseline (Section 6, OlympiadBench Qwen results).
claims.evidence: Re-aggregation of 5 released Qwen trajectory CSVs (2160 samples, ~1.67M rows per seed) yields dynamic 91.35% at 90% abstention, matching the claimed 91%. The best baseline among released models is 69.49% (baseline), which is lower than the claimed 75%, meaning the dynamic advantage is at least as large as claimed; the discrepancy likely reflects a baseline configuration not present in the released artifacts.

claims.claim: Probes trained on GSM8K generalize to OlympiadBench with minimal degradation in a cross-dataset transfer evaluation (Section 6.3).
claims.evidence: Re-aggregation of 5 released transfer trajectory CSVs (2160 samples each) shows GSM8K-trained probes on OlympiadBench achieve 64.28% (Phi-3) and 90.70% (Qwen) at 90% abstention, versus in-domain 64.56% and 91.35%—degradation of only 0.28pp and 0.65pp, consistent with 'minimal degradation.' The direct-model toy run (16 examples, 0% accuracy) is too small to be informative.

claims.claim: On RealToxicityPrompts, the method reaches a perfect 1.00 non-toxic rate at a 30% abstention rate (Section 6.5).
claims.evidence: Re-aggregation of 5 released RTP trajectory CSVs (500 samples each) yields dynamic non-toxic rate 1.00 (acc_ci 0.0) at 30% abstention, confirmed by independent CUDA re-aggregation showing accuracy 1.0 for all 5 seeds. Best baseline (self_assessment) achieves 99.71%.

JAEMP/repro-knowing-when-to-quit-a-princ.overall: The logbook independently re-aggregates the authors' released trajectory artifacts with official code and confirms the paper's headline empirical numbers on OlympiadBench (Phi-3 and Qwen) and RealToxicityPrompts at non-toy scale (2160 or 500 samples, 5 seeds each). The two theoretical claims (Proposition 4.2, Corollary 4.5) are only addressed with a 4-element toy tensor check and their proofs are not independently re-derived; the direct from-scratch model reproduction runs at toy scale (64 train / 32 eval examples) and does not reproduce headline numbers.

MarxistLeninist/repro-prior-diffusivenes.paper_title: Prior Diffusiveness and Regret in the Linear-Gaussian Bandit

claims.claim: Theorem 1 bounds the Bayesian regret of Thompson sampling in the linear-Gaussian bandit by dσ√T·C₂(d,T,σ,r,Σ₀) + 3rd√Tr(Σ₀^(1/2))·C₁(d,T) + √(2r²Tr(Σ₀)) (Section 2, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Over a 5-prior × 6-horizon grid (d=5, T≤16000, N=1000 replications, exact conjugate posterior), the worst BR/(σd√T + dr√Tr Σ₀) ratio is 1.003—within Monte Carlo noise of the constant-1 instantiation of the claimed bound; since C₁,C₂≥1 and the third term only add slack, the full bound holds a fortiori. Dimension scaling α∝d^1.30 vs predicted d^1 is modestly off but consistent with Õ log-factors on a 4-point grid.

claims.claim: Corollary 2 simplifies this to an additive decomposition Reg(T)=Õ(σd√T + dr√Tr(Σ₀)), separating a minimax term σd√T from a prior-dependent burn-in term dr√Tr(Σ₀) that does not multiply the √T factor, improving on the Kalkanli and Özgür (2020) bound where the burn-in term scaled as dr√(Tr(Σ₀))√T (Section 2, Corollary 2).
claims.evidence: A 256× prior-trace sweep (s=0.0625→16, d=5) moves the fitted late-√T coefficient by only 0.9% (x0.98) where multiplicative coupling predicts x16 growth; AIC decisively favors the additive model (75.0 vs 307.2), and matched-seed differencing shows the prior-driven burn-in is monotone in √Tr Σ₀ at every horizon.

claims.claim: Lemma 3, the generalized elliptical potential lemma, removes the standard requirement that the initial precision matrix V₀ ⪰ I_d and allows flexible exponents p∈[0,1], bounding the potential by 2^p T^(1-p)(log det V_T/det V₀)^p (Section 3, Lemma 3).
claims.evidence: Across 5 (d,prior) combos × 250 random sequences plus greedy and fixed-direction adversarial controls, T≤10⁴, p∈{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1}, the ratio LHS/RHS never exceeds 1 (worst 0.762 for p>0; exact equality 1.000 at p=0), including V₀=0.01I₁₀ (far below I) and anisotropic V₀ with eigenvalue spread 10⁴.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a matching lower bound showing the burn-in term dr√Tr(Σ₀) is unavoidable for non-pathological priors, via a bound of the form Reg^p(T) ≥ (r/π‖τ‖₂)Σᵢ₌₂^min{T,d}(i-1)τᵢ² (Section 4, Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: The explicit Theorem-6 formula L=(r/(π‖τ‖₂))Σ(i-1)τᵢ² was computed and compared against measured TS Bayesian regret over 200 grid cells (d∈{2,5,10,20} × 5 spectra × σ∈{0.1,1} × T∈{100,…,16000}, N=300): min BR/L=3.55, zero violations. Policy-comparison evidence shows forced exploration inflates the burn-in (~200×) and greedy fails differently, supporting unavoidability.

claims.claim: Theorem 9 extends the additive regret decomposition beyond Gaussian priors and noise to strongly log-concave distributions, preserving the same additive structure between the minimax and burn-in terms (Section 5, Theorem 9).
claims.evidence: At d≤2 with a grid-discretized parameter space (801 points for d=1, 51×51 for d=2), a single non-Gaussian strongly log-concave prior family and logistic noise, the 16× prior-trace sweep leaves the late √T slope at x0.45 vs x4 multiplicative prediction with burn-in growing monotonically—confirming the additive structure but at clearly reduced scale and scope relative to the theorem's arbitrary-dimension claim.

MarxistLeninist/repro-prior-diffusivenes.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting claims 1–4 on non-trivial setups (d≤20, T≤16000, up to 1000 replications, adversarial controls), with the additive decomposition (C2) and generalized elliptical potential lemma (C3) particularly decisively confirmed. Claim 5 is addressed only at toy scale (d≤2, discretized), confirming the structural prediction but not the theorem's full generality.

Girgie/repro-timespot-geo-temporal-under.paper_title: TimeSpot: Benchmarking Geo-Temporal Understanding in Vision–Language Models in Real-World Settings

claims.claim: TimeSpot defines a joint geo-temporal benchmark requiring structured prediction of four temporal and five geographic attributes from ground-level images (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook audited the pinned dataset release (kagnlp/TimeSpot at revision 976198f) and confirmed all nine structured prediction fields exist: four temporal (season, month, time of day, daylight phase) and five geographic (continent, country, climate zone, environment type, latitude/longitude).

claims.claim: The dataset contains 1,455 ground-level photos from 80 countries with broad season, daylight, month, continent, climate, and environment coverage (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The pinned release audit reports exactly 1,455 metadata rows, 1,455 unique image names, 1,455 hub image files, 80 countries, 12 months, zero missing/extra images, and matching Table 2 counts for season, daylight, continent, climate, and environment with specific continental counts (Asia 529, Europe 430, North America 326, South America 170).

claims.claim: TimeSpot includes hemisphere sanity, hard OOD, geo-temporal fusion, schema, calibration, and verifiable GPS/OSM-style scoring axes absent from many prior benchmarks (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirmed the nine diagnostic axes (hemisphere sanity, hard OOD, geo-temporal fusion, schema, calibration, GPS/OSM scoring, etc.) against both the released task schema and paper Tables 1 and 5; this is a design-feature claim appropriately verified by schema inspection rather than model evaluation.

claims.claim: Evaluated VLMs show substantially weaker temporal understanding than coarse geolocation, with top time-of-day accuracy far below top country accuracy (Table 3).
claims.evidence: An independent deterministic evaluation of Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct on 120 stratified TimeSpot images yielded 46.67% country accuracy vs 20.83% time-within-60-minutes accuracy, a 25.83-point paired gap with exact McNemar p=8.84e-5, confirming the claimed pattern of substantially weaker temporal than geographic performance on a real VLM with statistical significance.

claims.claim: The benchmark reports that the strongest VLMs can reach 77.59% country accuracy while still incurring a median geodesic error of 892.54 km and low time-of-day accuracy (Section 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirmed that Table 3 reports Gemini-2.5-Flash-Thinking at 77.59% country accuracy, 892.54 km median geodesic error, and 22.19% time-of-day accuracy; since the claim is about what the benchmark reports, matching the published table is appropriate evidence, and the cross-model aggregate (best country 77.59% vs best time 33.74%) further supports the mismatch.

claims.claim: Supervised fine-tuning improves TimeSpot performance but remains insufficient for robust physically grounded geo-temporal reasoning (Section 5.4).
claims.evidence: A rank-16 LoRA SFT experiment used only 160 training and 80 held-out examples (27.49% of paper training count) on Qwen2.5-VL-3B, showing improvement (country 46.25%→57.50%, time 18.75%→27.50%) followed by country regression at epoch 2; this demonstrates the mechanism at significantly reduced scale but does not constitute a full reproduction of the paper's SFT setup.

Girgie/repro-timespot-geo-temporal-under.overall: The logbook provides solid verification of the dataset and schema claims (1-3) through direct audit of the pinned release, and offers independent experimental evidence for the temporal-geographic performance gap (Claim 4) via a stratified 120-image evaluation with statistical testing. Claims 5-6 are supported by documentary matching and a reduced-scale SFT experiment respectively, with the SFT result being the weakest independent evidence due to its small training and evaluation sample sizes.

DineshAI/U1bxeLQLaK.paper_title: On the Provable Suboptimality of Momentum SGD in Nonstationary Stochastic Optimization

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows momentum SGD's tracking-error bound scales as (1-beta)^-2 on the initialization term and (1-beta)^-1 on the noise floor, versus O(1) and O(sigma^2 gamma/mu) respectively for vanilla SGD in Theorem 3.1 (Section 3.1, Theorems 3.1 and 3.3).
claims.evidence: Concrete numerical experiments on a 5-dimensional quadratic measure the lifted Heavy-Ball operator's worst-case transient growth G² scaling with log-log slope 2.115 vs 1/(1-β) (matching (1-β)⁻²), and noise-floor/SGD ratio with slope 0.987 (matching (1-β)⁻¹), with plain-SGD control showing G=1.0 (no amplification).

claims.claim: Theorem 3.7 gives a minimax lower bound decomposing regret into a noise-limited term and an inertia-limited term that worsens with beta and can dominate in drift-heavy regimes, establishing an information-theoretic (not just analytical) barrier for momentum methods (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence: Three scoped routes (symbolic p=∞,q=1 specialization, 16-way finite Fano family, d=100 pathwise witness) provide partial support for special cases, but the universal quantifiers over all p,q and every policy in Π_β remain open, and the Nesterov case lacks a source proof.

claims.claim: Under the stability constraint gamma <= (1-beta)^2/L, the paper proves vanilla SGD provably outperforms Heavy-Ball/Nesterov momentum SGD in drift-dominated nonstationary regimes (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: A full-dimensional (d=100) stochastic quadratic experiment with 20 seeds and 5,000 steps shows SGD tail tracking error ~0.0024 versus HB 0.021–0.236 and NAG 0.019–0.232 across β=0.5–0.98, with SGD+2SE below both momentum methods' mean−2SE at every β, plus a stationary negative control confirming HB accelerates when there is no drift.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.6 shows the high-probability bound for momentum SGD exhibits an inertia horizon of order (1-beta)^-1 and drift-noise coupling scaling as (1-beta)^-2, both absent from the vanilla SGD high-probability bound in Theorem 3.5 (Section 3.2, Theorems 3.5 and 3.6).
claims.evidence: Source algebra audit finds Theorem 3.5 (SGD) does contain a drift-noise coupling term (γ²σ²D_t⁽²⁾log(2T/δ)), contradicting 'both absent from vanilla SGD,' and after substituting γ=c(1-β)² the displayed forgetting horizon is Θ((1-β)⁻²), not (1-β)⁻¹ as claimed.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments on quadratics, linear/logistic regression, and MLPs confirm that increasing nonstationarity (drift), momentum parameter beta, or condition number kappa systematically worsens Heavy-Ball and Nesterov tracking error while vanilla SGD remains comparatively robust (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The β-effect is well-supported across quadratics, linear/logistic regression, and MLP (tracking error increases monotonically with β, SGD beats momentum), and the drift effect is supported on quadratics, but the condition-number experiment contradicts the claim: κ=1000/κ=10 ratios for HB (0.018) and NAG (0.069) are below 1, meaning high-κ improved momentum tracking, and the discrepancy cannot be resolved without the author's code.

DineshAI/U1bxeLQLaK.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting the (1-β)⁻² initialization and (1-β)⁻¹ noise-floor scaling (Claim 1) and the existential SGD-outperforms-momentum result (Claim 3), and falsifies Claim 4 via source audit showing the inertia horizon is (1-β)⁻² not (1-β)⁻¹ and SGD does contain coupling. Claims 2 and 5 remain inconclusive due to unclosed universal theorem quantifiers and contradictory condition-number results that cannot be resolved without the original author code.

agharsallah/cxdj2gyz4c-logbook.paper_title: Optimal and Scalable MAPF via Multi-Marginal Optimal Transport and Schrödinger Bridges

claims.claim: Anonymous multi-agent path finding is formulated as linear program P1 minimizing transport cost over per-timestep transport matrices subject to flow-conservation constraints (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The P1 node-split time-expanded LP was implemented and its optimum matched an independent brute-force Dijkstra oracle exactly (gap 0.0) on 40 random instances, while the variable count grows linearly in |V| (log-log slope 1.03), confirming the MMOT collapses to a polynomial-size LP recovering the exact MAPF optimum.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.3 proves the constraint set yields integral optimal solutions in {0,1}^(K×K) achieving minimum cost with polynomial-time complexity, and Theorem 3.4 confirms the resulting paths are collision-free and non-overlapping in space-time (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The continuous LP relaxation returned integral {0,1} solutions on 495/495 instances (max fractional error 0.0), with max vertex occupancy 1.0 and 0 swap conflicts, and on 40 enumerable instances the integral LP cost equaled the brute-force optimum exactly, empirically confirming Lemma 3.3 and Theorem 3.4.

claims.claim: Total unimodularity of the constraint matrix is proven via a node-splitting construction on time-expanded graphs (Appendix B).
claims.evidence: 360/360 randomly cost-perturbed LPs returned exactly integral optima (worst fractional error 0.0), and the constraint matrix was verified to be a node-arc incidence matrix with entries in {-1,0,1} and one +1/one -1 per column, confirming the TU property via the network-matrix theorem.

claims.claim: The Schrödinger bridge relaxation P2 adds entropic regularization parameter ε to P1, and Lemma 4.1 decomposes the KL divergence into transport and marginal terms enabling Sinkhorn iterations (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The multi-marginal Sinkhorn implementation achieved machine-precision residuals (endpoint ≤2.2e-16, consistency ≤1.8e-15, Gibbs 0.0) on small grids, showed monotone convergence of the entropic cost to the exact LP optimum as ε→0 (e.g., 5x5 grid: 4.31→0.0), and ran at the paper's full 150×150 scale (22,500 cells, 1,125 robots, T=30) with endpoint residual 4.65e-11 in 27.8s.

claims.claim: On grids with K up to 22,500 robots at 5% density, the entropic (P2+P3) pipeline scales as O(K^1.15) versus O(K^1.68) for the exact LP P1, yielding 3.6x-7.1x speedups (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The entropic pipeline's solve-time exponent (0.59, R²=0.95) is strictly smaller than the exact LP's (2.44, R²=1.00), speedups grow with scale (2.8x→702x up to 1,600 cells), and the entropic pipeline solves the full 22,500-cell grid in 0.44s where the LP is intractable; the specific exponents differ from the paper's 1.15/1.68 but the qualitative ordering and full-scale reach are confirmed.

claims.claim: Cost degradation from the entropic-to-integral projection stays under 10% while permitting 60-80% edge reduction in the graph pruning step (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Across 9 configurations in the 60–66% edge-reduction band (within the paper's 60–80% range), the reduced-LP cost degradation versus the full exact-LP optimum was 0.00% in every case, well under the 10% ceiling, on grids up to 28×28 (784 cells, 39 robots) where the full-LP baseline remains tractable.

agharsallah/cxdj2gyz4c-logbook.overall: The logbook provides comprehensive empirical evidence supporting all six claims through independent oracle verification, cost-perturbation stress testing for total unimodularity, ε→0 convergence analysis, and full-scale Sinkhorn demonstrations reaching the paper's 22,500-cell grid. The specific scaling exponents in claim 5 differ from the paper's reported values, but the qualitative ordering (entropic scales sub-LP with growing speedups) and the core scalability claim are confirmed.

agharsallah/jnuwpwbz8d-logbook.paper_title: Provably Data-driven Multiple Hyper-parameter Tuning with Structured Loss Function

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 establishes a general first-order-logic framework giving pseudo-dimension bounds of O(p*prod(d_k+1)*log M + p^2*prod(d_k+1)*log Delta) for multi-dimensional hyperparameter tuning by connecting logical complexity to learning-theoretic complexity via quantifier elimination (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Quantifier elimination is demonstrated on M≤5 polynomials with p≤5, yielding exact predicate counts of 3,6,10,15 and sign-cell counts growing linearly in p (R²=0.96). The mechanism is real but the scale is tiny (M≤5, p≤5, Δ≤4), and the pseudo-dimension values (~5-15) are too small to meaningfully test the asymptotic bound.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 bounds the pseudo-dimension of piecewise-polynomial training-loss objectives (with training loss f equal to validation loss g) as O(p*d*log(M_f+T_f+d) + p^2*d*log Delta_f) for p-dimensional hyperparameters (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Weighted LASSO is solved exactly via cvxpy for d≤16, with piece counts growing 7→87 and Pdim lower bound only 2→4. The upper bound (21→5808) is trivially satisfied with margins of 19-5803, providing no meaningful test of the bound's tightness or the O(pd) scaling.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.1 extends the framework to the bi-level validation-loss setting (f not equal to g), establishing Pdim(L) = O(p*d^2*log M_tot + p^2*d^2*log Delta_tot) without requiring identical training and validation objectives (Section 6).
claims.evidence: Bi-level f≠g setup is solved exactly for d≤8 only, with Pdim lower bounds of 3-4 and upper bounds of 29-3423 (margins 26-3419). The d-exponent comparison (1.55 vs 1.14) is based on just 6 data points at very small dimensions, and the bounds are trivially satisfied.

claims.claim: Theorem 7.2 shows that when the optimal parameter path theta*(x, alpha) is piecewise rational, the pseudo-dimension bound simplifies to O(p*log(M_total*Delta_total)) by bypassing quantifier elimination (Section 7).
claims.evidence: Ridge path rationality is confirmed to 1.8e-15 and complexity is flat in d (exponent 0.08) vs LASSO (0.85), but only 3-4 distinct pieces are observed across d=4-64, and the bound (6) vs measured Pdim (3-4) is trivially satisfied with no meaningful tightness test.

claims.claim: Theorem 8.1 provides the first learnability guarantee for weighted group LASSO regularization, a semi-algebraic (non-piecewise-polynomial) function class, with Pdim(L) = O(p^3*d + p^2*d^2), despite standard smoothness assumptions failing for this class (Section 8.1).
claims.evidence: Group LASSO is solved as SOCP for p≤5, d≤15, with KKT residual 3e-3 and pattern counts 8-91 (exponent 1.52). However, Pdim lower bounds are only 1-3 while the upper bound ranges 12-7500, making the bound check trivially satisfied and the super-linear p-scaling claim based on just 5 data points.

claims.claim: Theorem 8.2 derives a Pdim(L) = O(d^2) bound for weighted fused LASSO applied to signal denoising with spatially-varying regularization weights (Section 8.2).
claims.evidence: Fused LASSO is solved exactly for d≤32 with fusion pattern counts 24-3840 (exponent 2.46), but the logbook itself notes counts at d≥24 hit the sampling-grid ceiling, and Pdim lower bounds remain 3-4 while the O(d²) bound is 16-1024, trivially satisfied with margins of 13-1020.

agharsallah/jnuwpwbz8d-logbook.overall: The logbook constructs real instances of each structured loss class and solves them with exact algorithms (cvxpy, SOCP, sympy QE), providing genuine numerical illustrations of each theorem's mechanism (QE inflation, sign-pattern counting, rational-path bypass, semi-algebraic structure). However, all experiments run at very small scale (d≤8-64, p≤5, M≤5) with pseudo-dimension lower bounds of only 2-4 and upper bounds trivially satisfied by margins of 13-5803, making these toy-scale consistency checks rather than meaningful verifications of the asymptotic bounds.

claims.claim: The paper defines a Safe KL divergence with a bounded-density constraint (Definition 2.1, Equations 3-4) whose induced approximation to LogSumExp satisfies F_ρ − O(ρ) ≤ F ≤ F_ρ (Proposition 2.4, Section 2).
claims.evidence: Numerical check across 800 random inputs (n=5..120) × 6 ρ values confirms the sandwich inequality: max upper-bound violation (F_ρ − F) = −5.60e-05 ≤ 0 and normalized lower gap max (F − F_ρ)/ρ = 0.8112 ≤ 1, directly supporting F − ρ ≤ F_ρ ≤ F.

claims.claim: The rescaled SoftPlus-based conjugate of the Safe KL function is proven to be ρ-strongly convex, with its own conjugate being (1/ρ)-smooth (Lemma 2.7, Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: Numerical second-derivative evaluation over 6 ρ values shows min f_ρ'' = 4ρ ≥ ρ (strong convexity, worst ratio 3.999 ≥ 1) and max (f_ρ*)'' = 1/(4ρ) ≤ 1/ρ (smoothness, worst ratio 0.250 ≤ 1), matching Lemma 2.7's curvature claims.

claims.claim: The approximation family is shown to bound and connect to the CVaR functional, recovering CVaR and LogSumExp as limiting cases (Proposition 2.6, Section 2.1).
claims.evidence: Across 400 empirical measures (n=3000) × 5 ρ × 3 λ, the Proposition 2.6 two-sided CVaR bound holds with max lower-bound violation −2.24e-03 ≤ 0 and max upper-bound violation −2.09e-01 ≤ 0. The limiting-case recovery (CVaR/LogSumExp) is not separately tested numerically, but the core bound is confirmed.

claims.claim: In continuous entropy-regularized optimal transport experiments with regularization ε=0.01, the proposed semi-dual formulation (Equations 14-15) avoids the numerical overflow issues of the baseline and reaches a converged objective in roughly 10^4 iterations (Figure 2, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Real MNIST continuous eOT (2000+2000 samples, MLP potentials 256-128, ε=0.01, Adam): proposed semi-dual reaches 95% of plateau (100.4) within ~250 iterations and stays stable through 15,000; baseline raw-exp integrand overflows float64 (max exponent argument 842 > 709 limit) while proposed rescaled-SoftPlus integrand stays finite (max 83.95).

claims.claim: In KL-regularized distributionally robust optimization on California Housing, the proposed method converges with a stepsize of η=10⁻⁴ across batch sizes of 10, 100, and 1000, whereas the baseline requires a much smaller η=10⁻⁶ at batch size 10 (Figure 3, Section 3.2).

claims.claim: In unbalanced optimal-transport-based DRO on MNIST with label noise, the proposed approach (Equation 22) converges faster than the baseline (Equation 21) using η=10⁻⁴ versus the baseline's required η=10⁻⁵ (Figure 4, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: MNIST UOT-DRO with 25% label noise (8000 images, real CNN, 3 seeds, GPU): proposed at η=1e-4 converges (0/3 diverged, plateau in 483 iterations); baseline at η=1e-4 diverges (3/3) and only stabilizes at η=1e-5 (plateau in 833 iterations), confirming faster convergence at 10× larger stepsize.

agharsallah/tzqelzflxr-logbook.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical and experimental evidence supporting all six claims: theoretical propositions are verified via systematic numerical checks across parameter ranges, and experimental claims are reproduced on real datasets (MNIST, California Housing) with matching model architectures and hyperparameters. The reproduction is thorough, with multiple seeds, specific quantitative metrics, and direct overflow comparisons that align with the paper's central claims about numerical stability and stepsize advantages.

DineshAI/4T8vEVK79x.paper_title: Approximate Proportionality in Online Fair Division

claims.claim: Three natural greedy allocation rules (maximize relative item value, allocate to most unsatisfied agent, and minimize worst predicted dissatisfaction) each fail to guarantee any positive multiplicative approximation to PROP1 against an adaptive adversary (Section 3, Propositions 6-8).
claims.evidence: Clean-room greedy replays show Greedy-1 and Greedy-2 PROP1 ratios decreasing monotonically to ~0.008 at 512 goods (witness1/witness2 constructions), and Greedy-3's adaptive construction decreasing from 1.0 to 0.385 at 506 goods with a clear downward trend across 12 cycles, all matching the released stress CSV byte-for-byte.

claims.claim: Against a non-adaptive adversary, uniform random allocation achieves an Ω(1/log(n/δ)) approximation to PROP1 with probability at least 1-δ, specifically α = 27/(128·log(n/δ)), the first such multiplicative bound in the online setting without extra assumptions (Section 4, Theorem 9).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo simulation across 48 settings (n∈{2,3,5,8}, δ∈{0.1,0.05,0.01}, 4 adversarial non-adaptive instance families, 4000 trials each) using the claimed constant α=27/(128·log(n/δ)) shows empirical success probability ≥1−δ in every setting, with a negative control (absurdly large α) correctly failing.

claims.claim: On synthetic data, PT applied to Vanilla Conformal Prediction (PT-VCP) reduces average interval length from 22.894 to 22.614 at alpha=0.10 while preserving nominal coverage (Table 1)

claims.claim: Despite valid marginal coverage, the Prejudicial Trick yields highly unstable predictions: Proposition 2 proves its interval stability metric IS(C_PT) = p(1-p)(E(L))^2 > 0, meaning the same input can receive completely different interval outputs across repeated conformal calibration runs (Definition 1, Proposition 2)
claims.evidence: Interval stability IS(C_PT) was measured > 0 on 3 of 10 real datasets: bike 0.5859 (paper 0.58), concrete 1.1404 (paper 1.14), star 1.1383 (paper 1.14), all matching to <0.01.
