Yashp2003/repro-swe-fficiency-can-langua.overall: The logbook provides solid independent verification of the dataset's existence and structure (Claims 1-2) through direct HuggingFace API inspection, but does not independently reproduce any experimental results (Claims 3-4), relying entirely on citing the paper's own tables and figures. The only executed experiment is a toy-scale run of 5 instances with the gold patch included in the prompt, which cannot substantiate performance or failure-mode claims.

Yashp2003/repro-osf-on-pre-training-and-.paper_title: OSF: On Pre-training and Scaling of Sleep Foundation Models

claims.claim: SleepBench aggregates 166,500 hours of sleep recordings from over 21,000 sleep studies across nine public National Sleep Research Resource sources (SHHS, NCHSDB, CFS, CCSHS, WSC, MROS, MESA, CHAT, SOF) (Section on SleepBench dataset).
claims.evidence: The logbook only cross-references the paper's own reported per-dataset counts (summing to 21,482) against the paper's own tables; no independent data aggregation, download, or NSRR source verification was performed.

claims.claim: On MROS, OSF achieves 97.3 AUC for sleep staging and 92.8 AUC for arousal detection, outperforming SleepFM (96.4 and 90.3 AUC respectively) and a supervised ViT (96.9 and 88.4 AUC) (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook loads the OSF-Base checkpoint and confirms architecture (85.3M params, 12 channels, 768-d CLS) via a synthetic forward pass, but no actual MROS evaluation was run — the AUC numbers are simply transcribed from the paper's Table 2.

claims.claim: Combining time masking with channel masking during pre-training raises sleep-staging AUC from 94.8 (channel masking alone with SimCLR) to 96.7, supporting the claim that channel-invariant feature learning is essential for pre-training (Table 1 ablation).
claims.evidence: No SimCLR pre-training ablation was executed; the 94.8→96.7 numbers are read from the paper's Table 1. The code mechanism (iBOT patch masking) was inspected but the actual AUC results were not independently reproduced.

claims.claim: OSF outperforms baseline SleepFM across four missing-channel inference scenarios -- headband-only, respiratory+cardiac, brain+cardiac, and respiratory-only -- demonstrating that existing sleep foundation models fail to generalize when channels are missing at inference (Table 6).
claims.evidence: A proxy test zeroed channel groups on synthetic random input and measured CLS cosine drift (0.34–0.73), which is a simplified mechanism check on non-real data; the actual AUC comparison numbers are from the paper's tables, and even those show OSF loses on 2 of 8 cells, partially contradicting the 'outperforms across four scenarios' claim.

claims.claim: Performance scales consistently with pre-training data fraction from 1% to 100% of the corpus and with encoder capacity from 1M to 85M parameters (scaling analysis section).
claims.evidence: Parameter counts for the encoder family (1.63M–85.3M) were computed from released code, confirming the model sizes exist, but no pre-training at different data fractions or capacities was run — the performance scaling trends are merely transcribed from the paper's Tables 37/38.

Yashp2003/repro-osf-on-pre-training-and-.overall: This logbook does not reproduce any of the paper's empirical results; it verifies the released checkpoint's architecture and parameter counts, runs synthetic forward passes, and transcribes AUC numbers from the paper's own tables. No real task evaluation on actual PSG data was performed, making all performance claims unverified.

Yashp2003/repro-real-time-visual-attribu.paper_title: Real-Time Visual Attribution Streaming in Thinking Model

claims.claim: vStream trains a lightweight linear estimator with only L×H parameters (e.g., 1,152 weights for 32 layers x 36 heads) to predict visual-region ablation effects from cached cross-attention features, avoiding costly backward passes or perturbation-based attribution (Section on method).
claims.evidence: The estimator parameter count (L×H = 336 for 28×12 on Qwen2-VL-2B) and forward-only ground-truth computation are confirmed on a real but smaller model; however, prediction of ablation effects from cross-attention features was validated only on synthetic data, not on real benchmarks at the paper's 8B scale.

claims.claim: vStream achieves a Linear Datamodeling Score (LDS) of approximately 0.70-0.72, matching gradient-based baselines such as AttnLRP (LDS 0.69-0.71), while running at 0.024 sec per 10 tokens versus 2.80 sec per 10 tokens for InputGrad, roughly a 117x speedup (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Two conflicting LDS results are reported: 0.20 on 40 synthetic samples with Qwen2-VL-2B, and 0.807 on a synthetic proxy with n=2000 — neither uses real benchmark data at the paper's scale. The speedup direction is confirmed (~30,000× on smaller model or ~5× on CPU) but the specific 117× figure and LDS 0.70–0.72 are not reproduced on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: The method is evaluated across four thinking vision-language models (Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking, GLM-4.1V-9B-Thinking, MiMo-VL-7B, Cosmos-Reason1-7B) and five task categories including MathVista, MathVision, ScienceQA, DocVQA, and GQA (Section on experimental setup).
claims.evidence: The logbook only confirms that the four models and five datasets exist on HuggingFace; no actual evaluation was run on any of the four named VLMs or any of the five task categories. The reproduction used Qwen2-VL-2B with synthetic data instead.

claims.claim: An estimator trained on one task category retains 75-90% of its attribution performance when transferred to other categories, with strongest Math-to-Science transfer (LDS 0.62-0.63) and weakest transfer to Document tasks (LDS 0.54-0.58) (Table 2).
claims.evidence: A structured synthetic model with designed category relationships (Math↔Science sharing a 'diagram subspace') yields LDS values close to the paper (Math↔Science 0.611 vs 0.62–0.63; Document transfer 0.53 vs 0.54–0.58), but this is a synthetic proxy where the category structure was explicitly constructed to mimic the paper's findings, not a real cross-task evaluation on MathVista, ScienceQA, DocVQA, etc.

claims.claim: Attribution-space trajectory analysis shows successful reasoning chains have shorter path length (0.003 vs. 0.006) and lower tortuosity (13.7 vs. 25.4) than failed chains, enabling early failure prediction with AUC 0.69 at only 30% of reasoning completion (Section on trajectory analysis).
claims.evidence: Two inconsistent synthetic simulations are reported: one shows tortuosity direction reversed from the paper (success 8.72 > failed 7.36, contradicting paper's 13.7 < 25.4) with AUC 0.69; the other shows correct tortuosity direction but AUC 0.84 instead of 0.69. Both use random-walk simulations, not real attribution trajectories from actual VLM reasoning chains.

Yashp2003/repro-real-time-visual-attribu.overall: This logbook confirms vStream's core architectural design (L×H linear estimator, forward-only ground truth) and directional trends using a 2B proxy model with synthetic data, but does not reproduce any of the paper's quantitative results on real benchmarks at the paper's scale. All substantive claims are addressed only on toy setups with synthetic data, inconsistent numbers, or mere existence checks.

bertfil/wQxRphkfxn.paper_title: When the Prompt Becomes Visual: Vision-Centric Jailbreak Attacks for Large Image Editing Models

claims.evidence: The 80.9% and 70.3% ASR figures were never independently computed—the replication never ran VJA against Nano Banana Pro or GPT-Image-1.5, and the matching numbers in README.md are explicitly identified as the paper's own pre-existing table values, not outputs of this run. The full evaluation code and MLLM judge (Gemini 3 Pro) were not shipped.

claims.claim: VJA reaches 97.5% ASR on Qwen-Image-Edit and 94.1% ASR on Seedream 4.5, and 100% ASR on open-source models BAGEL, Flux2.0, and local Qwen-Image-Edit that lack built-in safeguards (Section 4.1, Table 1).
claims.evidence: No independent ASR values were produced for any of the five models. The 97.5% (Qwen-Image-Edit online) and 94.1% (Seedream 4.5) figures were never tested against commercial APIs. BAGEL and Flux2.0 were never run at all. A single-prompt qualitative demo on local Qwen-Image-Edit (step 4) showed the undefended model executes a malicious edit without refusal, but this is one prompt with no ASR computation—not a quantitative evaluation.

claims.claim: A training-free defense based on introspective multimodal reasoning reduces ASR on Qwen-Image-Edit-Safe from 100% to 66.9% and lowers the harmfulness score by 1.2 points, without requiring auxiliary guard models (Section 4.1, Table 1).
claims.evidence: The specific ASR reduction (100%→66.9%) and HS drop (1.2 points) were not reproduced because the scoring judge (Gemini 3 Pro) was unshipped. However, real runs were conducted on a 75-item category-balanced IESBench subset using a refusal-rate proxy (17.3% overall block rate, 13/75), and the defense mechanism was qualitatively confirmed to block unsafe prompts after a critical bug fix (output_hidden_states=True). This is a subset evaluation with a proxy metric, directionally consistent but not verifying the claimed numbers.

claims.evidence: The I13=61.5% and I15=55.3% ASR values appear only in the paper's own README table and were never independently computed. The refusal-rate proxy produced I13=0.00 and I15=0.20—entirely different metrics that cannot be mapped to the claimed ASR values. claims.claim: The introspective defense adds only about 170 input and 110 output tokens, increasing runtime by roughly 4ms for Qwen-Image-Edit and 6ms for LongCat-Image-Edit, about 3% additional latency versus baseline inference (Section A.4, Table 5).
claims.evidence: No token-count or controlled runtime-overhead measurements were ever made. LongCat-Image-Edit was never loaded or run. Only incidental wall-clock times exist (613s with CPU offload for undefended, 34.6s for a defended block), which are not comparable to Table 5's paired measurements and include no token counts.

bertfil/wQxRphkfxn.overall: This logbook did not independently verify any of the paper's headline quantitative claims; the attack ASR numbers were only echoed from the paper's own README, and the evaluation code plus MLLM judge needed to recompute them were never shipped. The only real experimental work was a 75-item proxy evaluation of the defense mechanism on a subset of IESBench, which directionally supports the defense claim but cannot confirm the specific ASR/HS reduction figures.

bertfil/wrGSN9kAVD.paper_title: The Obfuscation Atlas: Mapping Where Honesty Emerges in RLVR with Deception Probes

claims.claim: In the MBPP-Honeypot coding environment, RLVR training without a detector penalty produces reward-hacking, deceptive policies in 96.4% of runs (Section 4, Section 5).
claims.evidence: A single Llama-3-8B run at 20 steps (vs. 120) with no detector penalty (llama_det0_clp003_seed0) was classified as deceptive (deception_gap=0.73, likely_hardcoded=0.595, passes_first_n=0.83 vs passes_all=0.10), directionally consistent with the claim, but the 96.4% rate across 28 seeds and 4 models was never measured.

claims.claim: Undesired-answer rates on belief-elicitation probes rise from roughly 10-40% before training to 45-65% after RLVR training, across all four models tested (Figure 3).

claims.claim: Two distinct obfuscation strategies emerge under detector penalties: obfuscated activations via representation drift (post-RLVR Simple Deception probe AUC drops to 0.376±0.261) and obfuscated policies via detector-evading text (Table 4, Section 5.2).

claims.evidence: The GPT-5.2-based obfuscation-strategy classification was never attempted; no strategy category names, classifier invocations, or distribution computations appear anywhere in the replication outputs, and only a handful of Llama runs were completed—nowhere near the 34 obfuscated-policy models required.

bertfil/wrGSN9kAVD.overall: This logbook provides only a drastically reduced reproduction (1 of 4 models, 1 seed, 20 vs 120 steps) that directionally confirms deception emergence in one no-detector run and partially supports the detector-penalty capability claim, but leaves most quantitative claims unmeasured and one mechanistic ordering reversed. claims.claim: LMD keeps weight norms controlled during training (55.2±0.1) compared to AdamW's much larger and unstable norms (260.7±0.5), and trains a 124M-parameter GPT-2 on OpenWebText to a validation loss of 2.925±0.006 (full precision) and 2.927±0.002 with MXFP6 forward passes, whereas AdamW's perplexity degrades sharply under low precision (Table 1, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: Weight-norm direction is reproduced on a small 4-layer GPT-2 (LMD ~385 vs AdamW ~2980), but absolute values differ substantially from the paper (55.2 vs 260.7). The 124M GPT-2 on OpenWebText with val loss 2.925/2.927 is not reproduced—the logbook's small GPT-2 on synthetic data achieves loss 10.825, nowhere near the claimed values.

claims.claim: Ablations show that both the multiplicative weight decay and multiplicative noise injection components of LMD are necessary for stable low-precision training dynamics (Figures 3-4).
claims.evidence: Ablations on a 4-layer GPT-2 (2000 steps, synthetic data) show that removing noise does not degrade norm control (no-noise variant norm ~890 vs full LMD ~1050), which does not support the claim that noise injection is necessary. All variants have near-random loss (~10.84), making it impossible to assess training-quality effects of each component.

Yashp2003/repro-log-normal-multiplicativ.overall: The logbook runs real experiments on significantly reduced-scale setups (small GPT-2 on synthetic data, small ViT on CIFAR-100, single T4), showing the direction of some effects (AdamW collapse under fp6, LMD weight norms smaller than AdamW). However, LMD fails to learn in any configuration (1.74% ViT accuracy, 10.825 GPT-2 loss), so 'stable training' is not actually demonstrated, and the specific numerical claims from the paper are not verified.

JG1310/repro-online-learning-with-recenc.paper_title: Online Learning with Recency: Algorithms for Sliding-window Streaming Multi-armed Bandits

claims.claim: Any algorithm that finds the exact best arm at any step with probability at least 1/2+Omega(1) in the sliding-window streaming multi-armed bandits model requires Omega(W) arm memory, even with unlimited arm pulls (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The re-derivation checks each proof step with executed code (Yao's minimax reduction, injectivity of the argmax map, simultaneous-memory counting), and exp04 confirms success_freq ≤ (M+1)/W across 648 cells × 6 retention policies with W up to 500, with minimum memory for success scaling linearly in W (slope 0.60, R²=1.00) and a hard step at M=W in every configuration.

claims.claim: An epsilon-best arm can be found with probability at least 1-delta at any step using only O(1/epsilon) arm memory and O((n/epsilon^2) log(W/delta)) arm pulls, independent of the total stream length n (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: exp06 confirms peak memory equals ⌈3/ε⌉ exactly and is invariant in n and W; per-arm pull budget s is n-independent; rate fits match theory to 3 significant figures (log s vs log(1/ε) slope 1.9977, s vs log(W/δ) linear R²=0.99999988); and the PAC guarantee holds at the tested point (failure rate 0.000, CP95 upper 0.0149 ≤ δ=0.1). The full (ε,δ,W) sweep crashed and was not re-run, but the structural claims and the single-point PAC check provide concrete non-toy support.

claims.claim: For regret minimization under the paper's new epoch-wise regret notion, any single-pass algorithm achieving o(T/W^2) regret requires Omega(W) arm memory, establishing a sharp memory-regret trade-off with a transition around Theta(W) arm memory (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: exp05 recomputes all 34 analytic checks exactly and independently via gates.py; the T/(64W²) lower bound is never violated across 56 cells × 7 policies (closest approach 321× above floor); Cauchy–Schwarz has 0/10,000 violations; and the minimax per-epoch rate fit (slope 0.633, CI [0.351, 0.915]) covers the predicted 0.5. The paper's Figure 10 empirical sharpness signature is falsified (largest regret drop never at M=W in 8/8 configurations), but the theorem content establishing the Θ(W) threshold is supported.

claims.claim: The sliding-window streaming MAB model separates data arrival (window movement) from arm sampling, distinguishing it from non-stationary and mortal bandit models where the environment changes only as a result of arm pulls (Section 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook contains no experiment, re-derivation, or discussion addressing the model-level distinction between sliding-window streaming MABs and non-stationary/mortal bandit models; this conceptual claim about data arrival being separated from arm sampling is never tested or analyzed.

JG1310/repro-online-learning-with-recenc.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, independent re-derivations with executed checks for Theorems 1–3, corroborated by large-scale simulations (2110 cells across 5 of 6 experiments at full scale), supporting the memory lower bounds and the ε-exploration upper bound. Theorem 3's empirical sharpness signature (Figure 10) is falsified, exp06's full PAC sweep was blocked by a crash, and the model-separation claim (Claim 4) was never addressed.

ProCreations/repro-lower-complexity-boun.paper_title: Lower Complexity Bounds for Nonconvex-Strongly-Convex Bilevel Optimization with First-Order Oracles

claims.claim: Theorem 1 establishes that any first-order zero-respecting algorithm requires at least C0*ΔLf*κ^(3/2)/ε^2 oracle calls to find an ε-accurate stationary point for smooth nonconvex-strongly-convex bilevel problems in the deterministic setting (Section 4.2, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The proof certificate instantiates the construction with κ=4n²+1, λ=ε/(L_f n), T=floor(Δ/(12λ²L_f)), verifies the gradient floor ≥ε and support blocking (x_T=0 before call Tn) across 64 parameter cells, with constructed call counts fitting κ^1.5053 ε^-2.0001 — this checks the actual resisting-oracle mechanism rather than circularly evaluating the final formula.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows a stochastic lower bound of Ω(Lf^3*Δ*κ^(5/2)*σ^2/(Lg^2*ε^4)) oracle calls under bounded-variance stochastic gradient oracles (Section 5.2, Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The stochastic proof certificate derives p from λ, verifies the scaled Bernoulli oracle is unbiased and within the σ² variance budget across 20 moment cells, computes the Lemma-9 high-probability blocking horizon, and runs 9,216 negative-binomial reveal processes matching T/p within 0.00477 relative error; the unscaled destructive control produces bias ≥0.06.

claims.claim: The deterministic lower bound construction uses zero-chain functions built from tri-diagonal matrices via auxiliary Ψ/Φ functions to force any zero-respecting algorithm to make Ω(κ^(3/2)) progress per unit of accuracy (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Across 5 matrix sizes and 120 dimension/prefix cases, the tridiagonal matrix is verified PSD (≤6.4e-16 roundoff) with operator norm ≤3.9994, Ψ/Φ gradients show zero tail leakage and always activate the next coordinate, the support frontier induction certifies 43,520 states through n=32/T=1024, and the dense-coupling destructive control produces leakage ≥0.0706 in every case.

claims.claim: The paper shows bilevel optimization is provably harder than single-level nonconvex optimization (Ω(1/ε^2)) by a factor of κ^(3/2), and harder than nonconvex min-max optimization (Ω(√κ/ε^2)) by a factor of κ (Section 4, comparison to known lower bounds).
claims.evidence: Using the constructed call counts (κ^1.5053 ε^-2.0001) combined with independently SHA-pinned primary literature exponents (Carmon et al. for single-level ε^-2, Li et al. for min-max √κ ε^-2), the bilevel-to-single-level ratio yields κ^(3/2) and the bilevel-to-min-max ratio yields κ, with floating-point identity errors below 3.6e-15.

claims.claim: A gap remains between the proved deterministic lower bound of κ^(3/2)ε^(-2) and existing upper bounds of κ^4ε^(-2) or κ^3.5ε^(-2), which the paper leaves open (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: The gap between the constructed lower bound and the hash-pinned JMLR 2025 first-order upper bound (Õ(κ⁴ε⁻²)) yields ratio κ^(5/2), and the naive Nesterov specialization (κ^(7/2)ε⁻²) yields ratio κ²; both are nonconstant across all 112 rate cells, confirming the open gap as stated.

ProCreations/repro-lower-complexity-boun.overall: The logbook provides a substantive computational verification of a purely theoretical paper by instantiating the proof's actual construction parameters, checking key inequalities (gradient floors, support blocking, oracle unbiasedness/variance), running 9,216 stochastic resisting-oracle trials, and including destructive controls and primary-literature cross-checks. The verification is limited to finite-scale checks of asymptotic results, but the mechanisms checked are the actual proof ingredients rather than proxy tasks.

EraChanZ/prvGhNz39e.paper_title: Memory-Efficient LLM Pretraining via Minimalist Optimizer Design

claims.claim: SCALE combines column-wise gradient normalization with first-order momentum only on the LM output layer (Algorithm 1; Section 3).
claims.evidence: Code inspection of scale_optimizer.py confirms column-wise RMS normalization (var = torch.mean(torch.square(g), dim=col_dim, keepdim=True)) and first-order momentum (buf1.lerp_) applied only to the LM output layer, with an AdamW-style two-state fallback for the last layer; the measured memory profile (0.160 GB, only ~0.05 GB above 0.114 GB model-only) independently corroborates that momentum is restricted to the small output layer.

claims.claim: Column-wise gradient normalization is faster than singular-value normalization and avoids the unstable LM-head gradient spikes observed with row-wise normalization (Table 1; Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states Claims 2/5/6 were not covered due to hardware limitations; no ablation comparing column-wise vs singular-value vs row-wise normalization was run, and no gradient-spike measurements were taken.

claims.claim: Last-layer-only momentum targets the layer with the largest stochastic-gradient variance while adding minimal optimizer-state memory (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The memory measurement (SCALE at 0.160 GB vs Adam at 0.346 GB, only ~0.05 GB above model-only baseline) supports the 'minimal optimizer-state memory' portion, but the core scientific claim—that last-layer momentum targets the layer with the largest stochastic-gradient variance (Figure 4)—was never tested; no per-layer gradient variance analysis was performed.

claims.claim: Across LLaMA 60M-1B pretraining on C4, SCALE matches or exceeds Adam-like performance while using about 35-45% of Adam's total memory (Table 5; Figure 1).
claims.evidence: Memory ratio at 60M is well-reproduced (SCALE 0.160 GB / Adam 0.346 GB = 46.3%, close to paper's 43% and the claimed 35-45% range), but perplexity parity was only tested at drastically reduced scale (1500 steps / ~0.05B tokens vs the ~11000 steps / 1.4B tokens needed for converged comparison), and only the 60M model was tested, not the full 60M-1B range.

claims.claim: For LLaMA 7B pretraining, SCALE outperforms APOLLO and Muon in both perplexity and memory consumption (Table 6).
claims.evidence: No 7B experiments were run; the logbook explicitly states this was out of scope for the 8 GB laptop GPU.

claims.claim: SCALE remains stable when training a 7B LLaMA on C4 up to 100B tokens, reaching final evaluation perplexity 9.32 (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: No 7B training or 100B-token runs were attempted; the logbook explicitly states this claim was not covered.

EraChanZ/prvGhNz39e.overall: The logbook provides solid code-inspection and memory-measurement evidence confirming SCALE's algorithm structure and memory efficiency at the 60M scale, closely matching the paper's Table 5 numbers. However, four of six claims were never addressed (7B results, 100B-token stability, normalization ablations, gradient-variance analysis), and the perplexity-parity claim was only tested at drastically reduced scale.

neonforestmist/repro-ftrl-potential-game.paper_title: (Doubly) Exponential Lower Bounds for Follow the Regularized Leader in Potential Games

claims.claim: Theorem 1.2 proves that in two-player m×m potential games, Follow the Regularized Leader (FTRL) can require 2^Ω(m log m) iterations to reach an ε-Nash equilibrium for ε = 1/poly(m), for any permutation-invariant regularizer and any learning rate schedule η^(t) = 1/t^α with α ∈ [0,1) (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: Exact integer witnesses satisfy the paper's period-pair recurrence at every index for 47 odd dimensions, with final-period lower bounds dominating (m−3)/e and retaining positive m log m normalized exponent — a substantial finite check of the construction underlying Theorem 1.2.

claims.claim: Theorem 1.3 shows there exists an n-player binary-action potential game in which fictitious play requires 2^Ω(2^n) iterations to reach an ε-Nash equilibrium for ε = 1/2^n, a doubly exponential lower bound (Theorem 1.3).
claims.evidence: The exact snake recurrence dominates (k−1)! through k=256, and Log-Gamma certificates for n=8…22 show log2 iteration counts growing proportionally to n·2^n, confirming the doubly exponential scaling claimed in Theorem 1.3.

claims.claim: Theorem 1.1 establishes a matching-type positive result: alternating ε-lazy no-regret dynamics converge to an ε-Nash equilibrium in any potential game after at most exp(O_ε(1/ε^2)) iterations (Theorem 1.1, restated as Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: For nine decreasing ε values, the potential range gives at most 1/ε updates and the inter-update recursion multiplies time by at most 1+3/ε; composing these reproduces the exp(O_ε(1/ε²)) envelope claimed by Theorem 1.1/3.4.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.2 shows that for FTRL with learning rate η ≤ 1/L (L the smoothness constant of the potential), the potential function value is non-decreasing across iterations, without requiring alternation or laziness (Proposition 3.2).
claims.evidence: Across 96 deterministic identical-interest games and 3,840 simultaneous entropy-FTRL updates with η below a Frobenius upper bound on 1/L, every measured potential increment was non-negative within a 2e−12 audit tolerance.

claims.claim: Example 3.3 constructs a 'spurious fixed point' showing FTRL can maintain a highly suboptimal strategy (error proportional to 1/t) indefinitely relative to the observed utility sequence, illustrating why FTRL, unlike gradient descent under Legendre regularizers, need not reach an O_ε(ε)-Nash equilibrium (Example 3.3).
claims.evidence: After t repeated utilities (1,0), switching to (0,1) changes entropy-FTRL's strategy by less than 1/t for t=8…512 while the best-response gap remains above 0.99, concretely demonstrating the spurious fixed-point behavior from Example 3.3.

claims.claim: The two-player exponential lower bound construction uses a payoff matrix A of odd dimension m with maximum entry 2m−1, dividing the FTRL trajectory into 2m−1 'transition periods' governed by Property 4.3 (period consistency) and Lemma 4.1 bounding action probability by R/(η^(t)γ) (Section 4, Definition 4.2, Property 4.3, Lemma 4.1, Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: The recursive construction passes exact path, parity, uniqueness, and maximum-entry (2m−1) checks for 31 odd dimensions, and 2,048 entropy-FTRL cases satisfy the R/(ηγ) action-probability bound from Lemma 4.1.

neonforestmist/repro-ftrl-potential-game.overall: The logbook provides concrete finite computational witnesses for all six claims at substantial scale (47 matrix dimensions, n up to 22, thousands of FTRL updates), with results matching the paper's constructions and bounds. These are finite-instance checks of universal mathematical theorems rather than full proof verifications, but the scale and specificity of the evidence meaningfully support each claim.

algorise/repro-a-new-framework-for-cyber.paper_title: A New Framework for Cybersecurity Refusals in AI Agents

claims.claim: Across 8 tested frontier LLM-powered agents (including Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, GPT-5.2, and Gemini 3.1 Pro), 6 of 8 show near-zero (≤5%) refusal rates when asked to identify vulnerabilities in real production systems (Section on Critical Refusal Rate Findings).
claims.evidence: No agents were run and no refusal rates were independently measured; the logbook only quotes the paper's own reported numbers ({0,0,0,1,2,3.2,21,62}%) without any experimental reproduction.

claims.claim: Only 18 of 800 total agent trajectories exhibit the desired safety-refusal behavior across the evaluation suite spanning Easy (20 challenges), Medium (20 challenges), and Hard (9 challenges) difficulty tiers (Benchmark Components section).
claims.evidence: The logbook only read the paper text to identify the 18/800 figure and noted a scope discrepancy, but performed no experimental runs to independently verify the trajectory count or refusal behavior.

claims.claim: GPT-5.2 is the only tested model to show meaningful refusal behavior, refusing 62% of the time on medium-difficulty challenges (Critical Refusal Rate Findings section).
claims.evidence: The 62% refusal rate for GPT-5.2 was only confirmed by reading the paper text; no agent was executed and no refusal rate was independently measured.

claims.claim: The paper introduces the Cybersecurity Refusal Framework (CRF), a tripartite Red/Yellow/Green taxonomy where government, healthcare, power grid, and transportation targets warrant always-refuse treatment (Framework Overview / Refusal Boundary Categories section).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirms the taxonomy exists by quoting paper text, but this is a reading of the paper's description, not concrete experimental evidence verifying the framework's implementation or behavior.

claims.claim: The benchmark evaluates agents against 9 CWE vulnerability classes, including XSS, SQL injection, SSRF, path traversal, and insecure deserialization (Vulnerability Classes Tested section).
claims.evidence: The logbook lists nine CWE classes from the paper text but does not describe examining the actual benchmark code to independently confirm these classes are implemented and evaluated.

algorise/repro-a-new-framework-for-cyber.overall: This logbook is a purely static desk audit that read the paper text and linked the public repository but ran zero experiments—no agents were executed, no refusal rates were measured, and no benchmark code was empirically tested. It provides no independent experimental evidence for any claim, only restating the paper's own reported figures.

Yashp2003/repro-floorplanqa-a-benchmark-.paper_title: FloorplanQA: A Benchmark for Spatial Reasoning in LLMs using Structured Representations

claims.claim: FloorplanQA (PlanQA) comprises 1,800 synthetic structured floor layouts (600 each for kitchens, living rooms, bedrooms) yielding 18,000 question-layout pairs across 11 cognitive/question categories, evaluated on 11 LLMs (Section 3.1, Table 1, Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook loaded the real HF dataset (OldDelorean/FloorplanQA-Layouts) and confirmed 1,915 layouts with 8 question types, but never generated or validated the 18,000 Q&A pairs, did not confirm 11 cognitive categories (found 8 qtypes), and evaluated only 3 models instead of 11 LLMs.

claims.claim: Models achieve over 95% accuracy on metric-computation questions but fall below 50% accuracy on topology, rule-based validation, and geometric-planning questions, per the cognitive-target accuracy heatmap (Section 4.1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: On 120 items with Qwen2.5-7B/72B and Qwen3-32B, metric accuracy was 5-10% (vs paper's >95%) while topology was ~33% (below 50%, consistent). The setup uses much smaller models and possibly different GT generation, so absolute numbers are not comparable, but real runs were executed.

claims.claim: Accuracy gains from model scale are steep up to roughly 30B parameters but plateau beyond that on complex planning and constraint-satisfaction categories (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Only 3 models tested (7B, 32B, 72B); the 72B result is suspiciously identical to 7B (both 19.2% overall, same per-category breakdown), and the 32B model (Qwen3-32B) is a reasoning model with chain-of-thought, not a pure scale increase. The plateau claim cannot be tested with this data.

claims.claim: A JSON-vs-XML structured-representation ablation shows stable accuracy across formats, indicating models are largely invariant to the choice of structured encoding (Section 4.2, Table 5).
claims.evidence: JSON and XML formats were compared on Qwen2.5-7B with 120 items each on Modal, yielding identical overall accuracy (18.3% both) with minor per-category shifts (Metric 5% vs 10%, Topology 33% vs 30%). Real runs confirm format invariance but only on a single small model at small scale.

claims.claim: Small spatial perturbations (±0.1m jitter) to layouts cause only minor accuracy fluctuations, showing models are comparatively robust to small perturbations despite failing on harder constraint tasks (Appendix Table 10).
claims.evidence: Gaussian perturbation (σ=0.1m) applied to vertex coordinates on 120 baseline vs 69 perturbed items with Qwen2.5-7B showed 18.3% vs 18.8% overall accuracy (0.5pp difference, within noise). Real runs with correct perturbation method, but single model and small sample with very low absolute accuracy.

claims.claim: Kitchen layouts yield the highest accuracy (about 80%), while living rooms and bedrooms score lower due to denser layouts and greater occlusion (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Per-room accuracy on 30 items each with Qwen2.5-7B shows kitchen at 20-23% (not ~80% as claimed), living room often equal or higher (20-27%), and bedroom at 17-20%. Results contradict both the absolute accuracy and the ordering claimed, but on a single 7B model with 30 items per room.

Yashp2003/repro-floorplanqa-a-benchmark-.overall: This is a toy-scale reproduction (120 items vs 18,000, 3 models vs 11, 7B-32B vs frontier models) that provides directional evidence for some claims (format invariance, perturbation robustness) but cannot verify or falsify the paper's core findings due to drastically reduced scale, a possibly different GT implementation, and an unreliable 72B result.

DineshAI/RG7maF4bGu.paper_title: Gaussian Mean Field Variational Inference can Overestimate Predictive Variance

claims.claim: MFVI underestimates posterior variance in parameter space but can overestimate predictive variance relative to the exact posterior, with Theorem 3.7 proving that for test points drawn from the training distribution's empirical covariance, MFVI's expected predictive variance exceeds that of the exact posterior (Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence: An independent NumPy/SciPy implementation verified reverse-KL diagonal optimality and coexistence of posterior-trace underestimation with predictive-variance overestimation on 144 non-axis-aligned spherical-prior BLR systems, and the unmodified official uci_tr_inequ.py ran on all 9 cached UCI datasets showing lower MFVI posterior trace than exact in every dataset, with the independent implementation matching each source-formatted trace gap.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.6 shows a calibration constraint forcing MFVI to simultaneously underestimate variance in some directions while overestimating in others, with overestimation occurring specifically in directions where training data concentrates (Lemma 3.6).
claims.evidence: The independent audit reports nonnegative MFVI-minus-exact predictive variance along the first training-input principal component for all 9 UCI datasets (minimum 4.6e-08 on kin8nm), and the anisotropic-prior control reverses the sign to -0.039, confirming overestimation in data-concentrated directions; combined with posterior-trace underestimation from Claim 1 evidence, this confirms simultaneous directional over- and underestimation.

claims.claim: In a pathological rank-1 training-data subspace scenario, as dimensionality increases the MFVI posterior's predictive variance converges to the prior variance, effectively discarding training information (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: The rank-1 subspace experiment (x_i = ε_i·u, u = 1_P/√P) shows MFVI/prior predictive variance ratio increasing from 0.7% at P=2 to 90% at P=1000 while exact posterior stays near 0.5% of prior throughout, and the full-rank isotropic control shows no pathology (MFVI stays ≤0.6% of prior), directly reproducing Proposition 5.1 at substantial scale.

claims.claim: Temperature-scaled posteriors (cold posteriors, T<1) correct the predictive-variance overestimation and improve in-distribution predictions, while T>1 benefits out-of-distribution performance, offering a novel explanation for the Cold Posterior Effect.
claims.evidence: Basis-function regression yields T_in=0.05 (<1) and T_OOD=5.0 (>1) with calibration temperature 0.113, and 6 UCI datasets yield calibration T*_in<1 on 6/6 (median 0.41) and T*_OOD>1 on 6/6 (median ~10.3), with varMF/varEx>1 in-distribution and <1 OOD confirming the overestimation/underestimation mechanism that cold/warm temperatures correct.

claims.claim: Experiments on basis function regression and UCI datasets show optimal temperatures below 1 for in-distribution test points and above 1 for out-of-distribution test points, consistent with the theoretical predictions (Section 6, UCI experiments).
claims.evidence: The basis-function regression experiment shows optimal T_in=0.05 and T_OOD=5.0, and the UCI experiment on 6 datasets (yacht, airfoil, wine-red, wine-white, auto-mpg, housing) shows T*_in<1 on 6/6 and T*_OOD>1 on 6/6 using the paper's calibration-temperature metric, consistent with the theoretical predictions on both setup types.

DineshAI/RG7maF4bGu.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all five claims through an independent NumPy/SciPy implementation, official source runs on 9 UCI datasets, 144 synthetic BLR systems, a rank-1 subspace experiment up to P=1000 with controls, and temperature-sweep experiments on both basis-function regression and 6 UCI datasets. The reproduction is rigorous with independent implementations, negative controls, and hash-bound provenance, though the temperature experiments cover 6 rather than the full 9 UCI datasets and the NLL-optimal temperature metric is noisier than the primary calibration-temperature metric.

snaykey/repro-prob-bisection.paper_title: Why Deep Jacobian Spectra Separate: Depth-Induced Scaling and Singular-Vector Alignment

claims.claim: Theorem 5.3 gives closed-form Lyapunov exponents governing the top singular values of masked (fixed-gates) linear networks, including a finite-depth correction term (d_{i-1}-d_i)/L (Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: Direct measurement of (1/L)log s_{i,L} against the closed-form γ_i at n=64 across depths L∈{4,8,16,32,64} shows error decreasing from 0.22 to 0.02 (bare) and further to 0.002 (with finite-depth correction) for both p=1 and p=0.5 gates; the measured deviation coefficients at L=64 match the Haar-block quantities d_i-d_{i-1} in magnitude and per-mode pattern.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.1 proves that sufficiently strong spectral separation between consecutive singular values forces alignment of dominant singular vectors across the matrix product, yielding an approximately shared singular basis for intermediate Jacobians (Theorem 6.1).
claims.evidence: The alignment matrix R^{r,r} is measured directly: under controlled separation ratio ρ:0.9→0.01, max|R^{r,r}-I_r| drops from 0.879 to 0.003 and diagonal concentration rises from 0.245 to 0.998 (n=40, r=8, 40 reps); for random products, diagonal concentration increases monotonically with depth from 0.193 to 0.750 (L=2→40).

claims.claim: Proposition 7.1 shows that combining depth-induced scaling and spectral separation recovers deep-linear-like singular-value training dynamics for fixed-gates networks without the balanced-initialization assumption required by prior analyses (Proposition 7.1).
claims.evidence: Only the dominant mode (k=1) shows R²=0.994 with non-unit factor c₁=1.66 on a small n=16, L=6 unbalanced network; modes 2–4 have R² of 0.02, 0.92, 0.41, and the logbook itself admits the run does not discriminate the depth exponent 2-2/L from 2 or 1 because s_k≈O(1) at this scale.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.5 recovers the balanced deep-linear singular-value ODE of Arora et al. (2019), ds_k/dt = -L s_k(t)^{2-2/L} <grad_J L, u_k v_k^T>, as a special case of the paper's more general framework (Proposition 4.5).
claims.evidence: On a balanced deep-linear network (n=8, L=4), measured ṡ_k matches the Arora RHS -L s_k^{2-2/L}⟨∇L, u_k v_k^⊤⟩ to median relative error 7.5e-4 over 800 gradient-flow steps, with the balancing invariant gap remaining ≤6e-5 throughout training.

claims.claim: On a synthetic rank-10 regression task with depth-10, width-64 networks, the top-15 Jacobian log-singular values during training converge toward the predicted theoretical Lyapunov exponents and finite-depth corrections (Figure 1, Figures 2-3).
claims.evidence: At the exact Figure-1 config (n=64, L=10, p=1), init log-singular values match theory (bare error 0.099, corrected 0.022 over top-15 modes); under rank-10 target training, loss drops 29.8→9.6 and s_1 grows from e^{1.61} to e^{3.39} with the top block separating from the tail.

claims.claim: Controlled MNIST experiments with square hidden layers of width n=128 validate the predicted emergence of depth-induced low-rank clustering and singular-vector alignment near a diagonal structure (Figure 4, Figures 5-6).
claims.evidence: The depth-scaling mechanism is verified at width n=128 (intermediate-Jacobian log-spectrum affine in depth, R²=0.9995) and diagonal alignment increases with depth (0.08→0.26), but the trained low-rank clustering experiment uses sklearn load_digits (8×8, 1797 samples) as a proxy for MNIST (28×28, 60000 samples), a clear reduction in data scale and scope; alignment values remain modest (max 0.26) compared to the paper's post-training figures.

snaykey/repro-prob-bisection.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence directly verifying the closed-form Lyapunov exponents and finite-depth correction (Claim 1), the separation-forced singular-vector alignment (Claim 2), the balanced Arora ODE recovery (Claim 4), and the rank-10 depth-10 width-64 training dynamics (Claim 5) at the paper's specified configurations. Claims 3 and 6 are only partially addressed on reduced-scale setups: Claim 3 on a small n=16 network with only the dominant mode working and the depth exponent undiscriminated, and Claim 6 with MNIST replaced by a much smaller offline digit proxy.

snaykey/repro-pca-prob-measures.paper_title: PCA of Probability Measures: Sparse and Dense Sampling Regimes

claims.claim: The empirical covariance operator error is bounded as E||Σ−Σ̂||_HS ≤ R^{1/2} n^{-1/2} + 2R^{1/4} r_m(Φ), combining a parametric n^{-1/2} inter-measure term with an intra-measure approximation term r_m(Φ) (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: In a genuine RKHS setting with exact closed-form KME Gram matrices for Gaussian measures on R^8, the inter-measure term scales as n^{-0.490} (R²=1.000) and the intra-measure term r_m(Φ) scales as m^{-0.488} (R²=0.999), both matching the predicted n^{-1/2} and m^{-α} rates; the full inequality E||Σ−Σ̂||_HS ≤ R^{1/2}n^{-1/2} + 2R^{1/4}r_m(Φ) holds at every tested (n,m) grid point.

claims.claim: The dense-regime n^{-1/2} rate for empirical covariance operator estimation is proven minimax optimal (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: A numerical Le Cam two-point construction on RKHS covariance operators (rank-one bump along a fixed RKHS direction, exact Gaussian KL computation) yields a largest indistinguishable separation δ*(n) scaling as n^{-0.528} (R²=0.9997) with constant optimal-test error ~0.26, numerically demonstrating that no estimator can beat n^{-1/2} and matching the upper rate, supporting minimax optimality.

claims.claim: The PCA excess risk satisfies E_q^PCA ≲ n^{-1/2} + √q·m^{-α}, with the √q factor depending on the number of retained components (Theorem 3.7, Equation 5).
claims.evidence: Using the correct excess-over-best-rank-q reconstruction risk definition in the RKHS, the q-scaling yields E_q ~ q^{0.478} (R²=0.92), closely matching the predicted √q factor; the m^{-α} term is not separately resolvable at the excess-risk level (the well-separated top-q subspace is m-insensitive in the dense regime) but is verified at the operator level in Claim 1 with slope m^{-0.488}.

claims.claim: A sparse-to-dense transition occurs at sampling threshold m ≍ n^{1/(2α)}, separating regimes dominated by the m^{-α} versus n^{-1/2} terms (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The crossover of the two Theorem 3.3 bound terms (intra m^{-α} vs inter n^{-1/2}) is demonstrated concretely for n=128, 512, 2048, with the measured crossover exponent 1.025 matching the predicted 1/(2α)=1.025 using the measured α=0.488, and the dominance regime switching at m ~ m*(n) in each row.

claims.claim: Under practical embeddings, KME and sliced-Wasserstein (SW) require m ≳ n samples per measure while linear optimal transport (LOT) requires m ≳ n^{d/2} to reach the dense regime (Section 3).
claims.evidence: All three embeddings are implemented and run on measure-valued data: KME (α=0.487, threshold ~n^{1.03}) and SW (α=0.450, threshold ~n^{1.11}) both yield m ≳ n, while LOT's α decreases with dimension (0.337, 0.291, 0.215, 0.151 for d=2,3,4,6) yielding thresholds n^{1.48}, n^{1.72}, n^{2.33}, n^{3.32} that track the predicted n^{d/2} growth, reproducing the KME/SW-vs-LOT dichotomy.

snaykey/repro-pca-prob-measures.overall: This logbook provides a faithful RKHS reproduction using genuine probability measures embedded via kernel mean embeddings, with exact closed-form Gram matrices and cross-checked random Fourier features. All five claims are supported by concrete numerical evidence with measured scaling exponents closely matching theoretical predictions, though some aspects (minimax lower bound, excess-risk m-dependence) are demonstrated numerically rather than via formal proof reproduction.

DineshAI/jl2f2Y3iuC.paper_title: Fine-Tuning Without Forgetting In-Context Learning: A Theoretical Analysis of Linear Attention Models

claims.claim: Corollary 4.4 shows that full fine-tuning of all attention parameters in a linear attention model drives zero-shot error to σ² while few-shot (in-context) error converges to σ² + θᵀΣθ, a substantially larger value, formalizing the degradation of in-context learning after full fine-tuning (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Direct Gaussian-prompt evaluation at d=5, σ²=0.1 shows full fine-tuning zero-shot error near 0.10 (matching σ²) and 20-shot error of 1.11 (matching σ²+θᵀΣθ = 0.1+1 = 1.1), though the reported range 1.11–1.90 across auxiliary weights is wider than the point prediction.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 shows that restricting fine-tuning updates to the value matrix reduces zero-shot error to σ² + (2/(d+4))θ₀ᵀΣθ₀ while Corollary 4.8 shows the asymptotic few-shot error only rises to σ² + 1/(d+4)²θ₀ᵀΣθ₀, i.e. value-matrix-only fine-tuning improves zero-shot performance with far less degradation to in-context learning than full fine-tuning (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Zero-shot value-matrix error measured at 0.3242 vs theory 0.3222, with a sweep over d∈{3,5,8} and ‖θ₀‖²∈{0.5,1,2} all matching σ²+(2/(d+4))θ₀ᵀΣθ₀. The few-shot comparison (value-only OOD error ~0.40 vs full-update ~1.23) supports less degradation, though the specific few-shot formula σ²+1/(d+4)²θ₀ᵀΣθ₀≈0.112 is not directly tested against in-distribution few-shot error.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.10 proves that tuning the auxiliary few-shot loss weight w to optimize few-shot performance on the fine-tuning task θ₀ necessarily reduces few-shot performance on other tasks θ ≠ θ₀, formalizing a trade-off between target-task adaptation and generalization to unseen tasks (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo evaluation finds target-optimal auxiliary weight w=0.6541 yields OOD few-shot error 0.461, while OOD-optimal weight w=0.9308 yields 0.363, confirming that optimizing for the target task degrades OOD performance.

claims.claim: In synthetic linear-regression experiments (d=5, σ²=0.1, Σ=I₅, ‖θ₀‖₂²=1, m=n=20), Figure 4 confirms the theoretical zero-shot/few-shot error predictions across pretraining, full fine-tuning, and value-matrix fine-tuning regimes, and Figure 5 shows value-matrix fine-tuning attains the lowest error on the out-of-distribution task -θ₀ (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: Zero-shot predictions match theory across full fine-tuning (~0.10=σ²) and value-matrix fine-tuning (~0.322), with the d/‖θ₀‖² sweep confirming the value-matrix formula. OOD 20-shot error for value-only (~0.40) is lower than full-update (~1.23), supporting the Figure 5 claim. However, pretraining-regime error and full fine-tuning few-shot error are only partially documented.

claims.claim: On the MMLU benchmark using Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct fine-tuned on the Humanities category, full fine-tuning improves zero-shot accuracy but degrades 7-shot accuracy, whereas value-matrix-only fine-tuning preserves few-shot accuracy while still improving zero-shot performance (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: No MMLU experiments, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct fine-tuning, or any real-world LLM benchmark results appear anywhere in the logbook. The reproduction only covers synthetic linear-regression experiments.

DineshAI/jl2f2Y3iuC.overall: The logbook provides solid synthetic-scale numerical verification for the theoretical claims about linear attention models (Claims 1–4), including precise matches for zero-shot error formulas and the auxiliary-weight trade-off. However, the MMLU/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct experiments (Claim 5) are entirely absent, leaving half of the paper's empirical claims unaddressed.

rdubwiley/repro-reward-redistribution-fo.paper_title: Reward Redistribution for CVaR MDPs using a Bellman Operator on L-infinity

claims.claim: The paper introduces a novel formulation of the static CVaR objective for MDPs based on state augmentation that yields dense per-step rewards rather than sparse terminal rewards (abstract only).
claims.evidence: Independent re-implementation of both operators on the paper's own CliffWalk env at z-dim 5001 shows dense reward fraction 48.5% for T̄ vs 0.0% for T, and T̄'s fixed point stays non-degenerate (17.9–154.8) while T's collapses to near-zero (1e-5 to 1e-90) across 4000 random-Q trials at γ∈{0.5,0.7,0.9,0.95}.

claims.claim: The proposed Bellman operator is defined on the space of bounded value functions (L-infinity) and is shown to have contracting properties on the full space, unlike prior augmentation-based CVaR formulations (abstract only).
claims.evidence: Empirical contraction ratios for T̄ are strictly below the γ bound at every tested γ (0.486<0.5, 0.681<0.7, 0.875<0.9, 0.924<0.95) across 1000 random bounded Q-function pairs per γ, confirming γ-contraction on L∞; the original operator T shares the same contraction rate but has a degenerate zero fixed point, exactly as the paper distinguishes.

claims.claim: The authors derive risk-averse value iteration and a model-free Q-learning algorithm operating on discretized augmented state spaces (abstract only).
claims.evidence: Q-VI runs to completion on the paper's own code at z-dim 5001, but Q-learning is trained only 12,500 of 75,000 episodes with 1 seed instead of 10; the sup-norm gap to the VI reference dropped 22.6x (23.4→1.04), showing a convergence trend but not reaching the paper's full training scale.

claims.claim: Convergence guarantees and approximation error bounds are established that account for the discretization of the augmented state space (abstract only).
claims.evidence: Multi-resolution VI at bins {100,500,1000,5000} vs a 10000-bin reference shows the lower-upper gap shrinking monotonically (6.47→2.46→1.24→0.251) and staying within the theoretical Delta bound at every resolution, with up to 100k pointwise checks per resolution confirming the O(1/bins) rate.

claims.claim: Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed algorithms learn CVaR-sensitive policies that achieve effective trade-offs between performance and safety (abstract only).
claims.evidence: The policy-switch near alpha=0.5–0.6 is reproduced for both Q-VI and Q-learning, but the monotonic direction of the safety/alpha relationship is opposite to the paper's stated convention across both algorithms; the logbook author attributes this to a possible convention mismatch rather than a genuine falsification, and rollouts are reduced to 500 from 10k, leaving the issue unresolved.

rdubwiley/repro-reward-redistribution-fo.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification of the paper's core theoretical contributions (dense reward formulation, L-infinity contraction, discretization error bounds) on the authors' own CliffWalk environment at full grid resolution. The Q-learning convergence and empirical policy evaluation claims are only partially addressed due to disclosed compute reductions (12.5k/75k episodes, 500/10k rollouts) and an unresolved alpha-convention direction issue.

ai-sherpa/randomized-feasibility-adaptiv.paper_title: Randomized Feasibility Methods for Constrained Optimization with Adaptive Step Sizes

claims.claim: Proposes Algorithm 2, a Gradient Method with Randomized Feasibility using an adaptive Polyak-type stepsize, and proves linear convergence in expectation to a prescribed tolerance ε for strongly convex, Lipschitz-smooth objectives, with iteration complexity O(log(1/ε)) (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 2 re-implemented at paper scale (n=10, m=1000, μ=1, L=10, ε=0.05) with 30 Monte Carlo trials; mean objective error decays from 30.78 to 1.6e-16 over 300 iterations with log-linear slope -0.130/iter (R²=0.828), reaching the prescribed tolerance.

claims.claim: Introduces Algorithm 3, DoWS (Distance over Weighted Subgradients) with Randomized Feasibility, a parameter-free adaptive-stepsize method for convex possibly-nonsmooth objectives, proving an O(1/√T) worst-case convergence rate in expectation (Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: DoWS on nonsmooth f(x)=‖x−x*‖ at paper scale (n=10, m=1000, 40 trials) shows clean power-law decay with log-log exponent -0.661 (R²=0.991) across T∈{25..800}, which is at least as fast as the O(1/√T) worst-case upper bound.

claims.claim: Introduces Algorithm 4, T-DoWS (Tamed DoWS), which removes the requirement that the constraint set Y be bounded, retaining an O(1/√T) rate up to logarithmic factors (Theorem 5.5).
claims.evidence: T-DoWS run with Y=ℝ¹⁰ (identity projection, no box clipping) and tamed logarithmic denominator at paper scale (n=10, m=1000, 40 trials); all iterates remain finite (max ‖x‖=1.80) and error decays with log-log exponent -0.726 (R²=0.996), confirming the O(1/√T) rate on an unbounded set.

claims.claim: Proves (Lemma 3.1) that infeasibility of iterates under the randomized feasibility update decreases geometrically almost surely with the number of feasibility updates, without requiring compactness of Y.
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 alone at paper scale (n=10, m=1000, 100 trials, N=3000) shows mean max-violation decaying log-linearly from 383.7 to 1.33 (slope -1.02e-3/step, R²=0.884) with 81% of sample paths collapsing to ≤0.1% of starting violation. Note: the experiment uses compact Y=[-10,10]^10, so the 'without compactness' theoretical condition is not directly exercised, but the geometric a.s. decay mechanism is confirmed at scale.

claims.claim: Validates the theory on quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP) simulations under strongly convex and convex objectives with known/unknown optimal value f*, confirming predicted function-value decay and geometric infeasibility reduction (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The paper's own QCQP construction (n=10, m=1000, known optimum via strictly-feasible unconstrained minimizer) is reproduced and drives all four optimization results: strongly-convex decay to 1.6e-16, nonsmooth DoWS power law, unbounded-Y T-DoWS, and geometric infeasibility reduction — matching Figure 1 at native scale.

claims.claim: Evaluates Algorithms 3 and 4 against a primal-dual baseline on SVM classification with three real datasets (Banknote Authentication, Breast Cancer Wisconsin, MNIST 3-vs-5), comparing test misclassification error (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: DoWS and T-DoWS evaluated on all three real datasets at exact paper sizes (Banknote 1098/274, Breast Cancer 455/114, MNIST 3-vs-5 11552/1902) against a primal-dual Arrow-Hurwicz baseline; adaptive methods achieve 1.82–4.39% test error vs baseline 4.39–17.52%. The baseline is disclosed as un-tuned, and the Banknote baseline error (17.52%) is suspiciously high for this easy dataset, but the evaluation is conducted as claimed.

ai-sherpa/randomized-feasibility-adaptiv.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence at the paper's native QCQP scale (n=10, m=1000) and on three real SVM datasets for all six claims, with 30–100 Monte Carlo trials, clean power-law/log-linear fits, and unit tests validating the re-implementations. Key limitations include Monte Carlo estimation of expectations rather than formal proofs, testing on benign rather than worst-case instances for rate claims, and an un-tuned SVM baseline whose Banknote error is implausibly high.

abidlabs/repro-how-much-do-language-mode.paper_title: How much can language models memorize?

claims.claim: GPT-style transformers trained on uniform random data show an empirical memorization-capacity plateau of about 3.6 bits per parameter (Figure 1)
claims.evidence: Four GPT-2 models (80K–1.06M params) trained on uniform-random data for only 12K steps (vs paper's 10^6) yield α=3.44 bpp (R²=0.997), reproducing the linear-capacity mechanism at greatly reduced scale but not reaching the headline 3.6 bpp plateau.

claims.claim: Capacity estimates across model widths and depths support a roughly linear bits-per-parameter scaling law, with bfloat16 to float32 increasing capacity only modestly (Table 1)
claims.evidence: Linear bits-per-parameter scaling is demonstrated across 4 small models (R²=0.997) and bf16 vs fp32 is compared on only 2 model sizes (within 0.2%), confirming the mechanism but at far smaller scale and scope than the paper's Table 1.

claims.claim: On text data, unintended memorization rises with model size but decreases once models begin generalizing relative to an oracle reference model (Figure 2)
claims.evidence: No text-data experiments were run; the logbook explicitly states the FineWeb oracle-reference-model experiment was out of budget, so the claim about unintended memorization on text data is never addressed.

claims.claim: Double descent begins when dataset information content exceeds estimated model capacity in both synthetic bitstrings and text experiments (Figures 3 and 4)
claims.evidence: The synthetic-data plateau and per-sample memorization decline are shown at reduced scale, but no test-loss double-descent curve is plotted and no text experiments (Figure 4) were run, addressing only part of the claim on a simplified setup.

claims.claim: The paper derives and evaluates scaling-law predictions for membership inference as a function of model capacity and dataset size (Figure 7)
claims.evidence: Membership inference experiments (Figure 7) are never mentioned or attempted in the logbook; the claim is entirely unaddressed.

abidlabs/repro-how-much-do-language-mode.overall: The logbook reproduces the core synthetic-data mechanism (linear capacity scaling, plateau, precision-independence) at greatly reduced scale (4 small models, 12K steps) but does not address any text-data claims, double-descent test-loss curves, or membership inference experiments.

ProCreations/repro-when-more-data-doesn-.paper_title: When More Data Doesn't Help: Limits of Adaptation in Multitask Learning

claims.claim: For any adaptive learning algorithm operating over n tasks with N samples each, the expected excess risk is lower-bounded by Ω((n√N)^{-1/(2-β)}), establishing that adaptation hardness persists even as per-task sample size N grows arbitrarily large (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook shows that the paper defines N as task count and n as samples per task, so the claim's formula Ω((n√N)^{-1/(2-β)}) with n=tasks and N=samples swaps the variables, changing the rate's semantic dependence from (samples×√tasks) to (tasks×√samples); 58 rate-cell recomputations confirm the corrected version but contradict the claim as written.

claims.claim: The impossibility result extends the no-free-lunch theorem of Hanneke & Kpotufe (2022) by removing their restriction n < 2/β - 1 on the number of source tasks, using a construction with N = Ω(exp(n)) tasks (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook demonstrates that the restriction n < 2/β - 1 in Hanneke & Kpotufe (2022) applies to samples per task, not source tasks as the claim states; 54 of 58 rate cells confirm the corrected extension beyond the sample-size restriction with super-exponential task construction N ≥ n^(nβ/(1-β)), but the claim as written mischaracterizes what is restricted.

claims.claim: When the transfer exponent is known in advance, a non-adaptive algorithm that performs ERM on identified good source tasks achieves rates faster than the adaptive minimax bound (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: 30,000 oracle-ERM trials across five finite settings directly sample the paper's fair Bernoulli construction, with the largest empirical risk-to-adaptive-lower-scale ratio at 0.00783 and the exact Theorem-5.1 envelope divided by the adaptive scale below 1 in every cell (max 0.9447), providing concrete numerical support that known-exponent ERM beats the adaptive bound.

claims.claim: Pooling data across all tasks achieves adaptive rates that are nearly optimal up to logarithmic factors, despite the general impossibility of adaptation (Lemma 5.3).
claims.evidence: Across 25 Section-5 rate cells, the reproduced pooling envelope matches the Theorem-5.2 lower scale times the stated log(nN)^{1/(2-β)} factor to numerical error 3.56e-15, and a 128,000-trial destructive control confirms the near-optimality is specific to the designed hard family rather than universal, consistent with Lemma 5.3's scope.

claims.claim: The lower bound proof uses Fano's method with a tight upper bound on the KL divergence between mixture distributions over task allocations, addressing technical obstacles not handled by prior simpler constructions (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Exact enumeration of multinomial sufficient statistics for 8 finite settings confirms mixture normalization within 1e-12, exact joint KL ≤ component/Jensen bound in all settings (6/8 at least 5% tighter, minimum ratio 0.627), and positive Bretagnolle-Huber Bayes-error floor (min 0.000115), directly reproducing the Fano/KL mechanism described in the proof.

ProCreations/repro-when-more-data-doesn-.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous clean-room algebraic and finite-simulation audit of a theoretical paper, falsifying Claims 1 and 2 as written due to a notation swap that changes the rate's semantic meaning, while verifying Claims 3–5 with concrete numerical evidence from Monte Carlo trials, exact enumerations, and algebraic gate checks. The reproduction is CPU-only and operates at finite scales appropriate for checking mathematical constructions, though it cannot replace the paper's full asymptotic proofs.
