ProCreations/repro-complexity-of-decentr.paper_title: Complexity of Decentralized Optimization with Mixed Affine Constraints

claims.claim: For the smooth, strongly convex regime with mixed affine constraints, Theorem 4.1 gives an optimal communication complexity of O(√κ_f √κ̂_{C̃ᵀ} √κ_W log(1/ε)) that matches established lower complexity bounds (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: A 576-cell ledger spanning four values each of κ_f, κ̂_{C̃ᵀ}, and κ_W with three accuracies confirms fitted exponents of exactly 0.5 for κ_f and κ_W and constant scale/log(1/ε), numerically verifying the O(√κ_f √κ̂_{C̃ᵀ} √κ_W log(1/ε)) formula. The scope concern (Theorem 4.1 applying to shared-variable constraints rather than the full mixed problem) is a paper-interpretation issue, not an experimental falsification, and shared-variable constraints are a subclass of mixed affine constraints.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 provides a unified complexity bound O(√κ_f (√κ̃_{AC} + √κ̂_{C̃ᵀ}) √κ_W log(1/ε)) covering problems with simultaneously coupled (global) and local affine constraints (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: The full additive formula O(√κ_f (√κ̃_{AC} + √κ̂_{C̃ᵀ}) √κ_W log(1/ε)) is recomputed across 576 independent cells covering κ_f through 256, κ̃_AC through 36, and κ̂_{C̃ᵀ} through 64, with decomposition identity errors at most 4.55e-13, confirming the additive structure across dominance reversals.

claims.claim: The paper analyzes both smooth objectives (Theorem 2.4) and non-smooth objectives via a Gradient Sliding algorithm (Algorithm 2), each under mixed affine constraints (Section 2, Section 4, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: The smooth side runs Algorithm 1 on 12 strongly convex constrained quadratics with maximum final feasibility 1.52e-7, while the nonsmooth side solves 72 Algorithm-2 inner subproblems in closed form with optimality residual ≤1.48e-14, and three ℓ1-penalty trajectories improve feasibility by at least 15x over destructive controls.

claims.claim: The proposed framework is motivated by and applied to horizontal federated learning (consensus constraints), vertical federated learning (shared/global-variable constraints), and multi-task learning with node-specific local constraints (Section 1, Applications).
claims.evidence: Explicit constraint embeddings are constructed for all three applications: HFL via a path-incidence Kronecker matrix with consensus nullspace and rank (n-1)d, VFL via feature-partitioned coupled aggregation with shared top-model copy, and multi-task via block-diagonal node-local constraint matrices, each with zero residual and expected rank, with destructive perturbations yielding residuals 0.2236–0.5.

claims.claim: An accelerated proximal alternating predictor-corrector method (Algorithm 1, APAPC) is used as the core building block for achieving the optimal rates in Theorem 4.1 and Theorem 4.5 (Algorithm 1, Theorem 4.5).
claims.evidence: A 12-case direct implementation of Algorithm 1 (APAPC) spanning condition numbers 4–256 and three constraint scales shows predictor-corrector feasibility >1M times better than omitting the corrector, and Chebyshev preconditioning on path, cycle, and star graphs through 64 nodes compresses spectra to condition number ≤1.7115 versus ≥4.778x worse without acceleration.

ProCreations/repro-complexity-of-decentr.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence—576-cell formula audits, 12 algorithmic trajectories, 72 exact subproblems, and explicit constraint embeddings—verifying the complexity formulas and algorithmic mechanisms of this theory paper. The verification is rigorous within its scope but is limited to synthetic quadratics and computational formula audits rather than large-scale decentralized optimization runs.

Srishti280992/repro-fast-estimation-for-.paper_title: Fast Estimation for Forest Matrix of Signed Graphs

claims.claim: GSCF (Generalized Spanning Converging Forest) generates spanning converging forests for signed graphs using loop-erased random walks in expected O(n) time, per Theorem 5.2 (Section 5.1, Algorithm 1, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Timing sweep of GSCF on sparse signed graphs from n=1,000 to n=2,000,000 (out-degree 4, 20% negative edges, 7 repeats) shows linear fit R²=0.9947 and ~1.0 steps-per-node across the entire range, directly supporting expected O(n) time.

claims.claim: FMDE estimates the diagonal of the forest matrix via sampling in O(ln) time, where l is the number of samples (Section 6.2, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: Two independent timing sweeps support O(ln): fixed n=20,000 with l=50–2000 gives linear R²=0.989 vs l, and fixed l=200 with n=5,000–800,000 gives linear R²=0.981 vs n, with decreasing estimation error as l increases.

claims.claim: FMDE+ incorporates additional network information to achieve the same O(ln) time complexity as FMDE but with lower variance, and Theorem 6.3 proves its superior performance on balanced signed graphs (Section 6.2, Theorem 6.3).
claims.evidence: On a balanced signed ring graph (n=1,200, out-degree 4) with exact diagonal 0.2, FMDE+ returns 0.2 to numerical precision at l=623/1283/4674 while FMDE's average relative error ranges from 0.0633 to 0.0243; the same O(ln) sampler structure is confirmed by the Claim 2 timing sweeps.

claims.claim: On the SlashdotZoo network, exact diagonal computation via direct matrix inversion takes 991.5 seconds while FMDE+ completes in under 1.1 seconds (Table 1).
claims.evidence: On the real KONECT SlashdotZoo graph (n=79,116, m=515,397), 623 FMDE+ samples completed in 0.694s median (below 1.1s threshold); a 32-vCPU/256GB job running sparse LU factorization of the same I+L matrix exceeded 1,270s without completing, consistent with the paper's 991.5s exact-computation claim.

claims.claim: The methods scale to the FullUSA network with roughly 2.3×10^7 (over twenty million) nodes, where exact computation fails but FMDE+ completes within one hour (Table 3).
claims.evidence: A synthetic sparse signed graph at n=23,947,300 (matching FullUSA scale) was used rather than the actual FullUSA road network (unavailable); only 5 FMDE+ samples were run (18.67s total), with the l=623 full run projected to ~38.8 minutes rather than directly measured.

claims.claim: FMDE+ achieves roughly ten times lower average relative error than FMDE across tested networks (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: On real networks Bitcoin-OTC (5,881 nodes) and Gnutella08 (6,301 nodes) with 623 matched samples and 256 exact-diagonal ground-truth entries, FMDE-to-FMDE+ relative-error ratios are 10.95x and 8.21x respectively, bracketing the paper's roughly tenfold claim.

Srishti280992/repro-fast-estimation-for-.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting five of six claims through timing sweeps on graphs up to 2M nodes, real-network benchmarks (SlashdotZoo, Bitcoin-OTC, Gnutella08), and ground-truth error comparisons. The FullUSA scaling claim (Claim 5) is only addressed on a synthetic proxy graph with projected rather than directly measured full-run timing, making it a toy-scale verification rather than a full reproduction.

snaykey/repro-delayed-obs-mdp.paper_title: Asymptotically Optimal Sequential Testing with Markovian Data

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 gives a non-asymptotic instance-dependent lower bound on the expected stopping time, E_Q[tau_alpha] ≥ (log(1/alpha)/D_M^inf(Q,P) − 2C_Q/min_i pi_i)^+, where D_M^inf(Q,P) is a stationary-weighted projection distance and C_Q bounds a Poisson-equation solution (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: On a 4-state chain with independently computed D_M^inf=0.19398, C_Q=10.435, and π_Q, the measured E_Q[τ] over 200 runs at 7 alpha levels exceeds the eq-(3) lower bound at every α; the bound is mostly vacuous (0.0) due to the (·)^+ clip but becomes active at α=1e-8 (4.5 vs measured 326.3), and the regression slope 6.37 > 1/D_M^inf=5.155 supports the asymptotic lower bound.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 bounds the Poisson-equation solution constant C_Q via the pseudo-spectral gap of the underlying Markov chain (Section 3, Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: The inequality ‖ω_{P,f}‖∞ ≤ C_P‖f‖∞ holds in 60/60 random ergodic chains (m∈{3..6}) with Poisson-equation residuals ~1e-16, pseudo-spectral gap computed independently via time-reversal reversibilization, and C_P from the stated formula; the bound is loose (5–50× over-coverage) but valid in every instance.

claims.claim: The proposed Sequential Markov Chain Test (Algorithm 1) builds an empirical transition kernel and a martingale statistic L_t accumulating row-wise KL divergences from the null class, stopping when L_t exceeds an adaptive boundary beta_t (Section 4, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 is implemented from scratch with empirical kernel Q̂_t, penalty ψ_t, boundary β_t, and statistic L_t = inf_{P∈P} Σ N_x KL(Q̂_t,P); a worked trajectory shows L_t/t → 0.197 ≈ D_M^inf=0.194, and under the null E[M_t] ≈ 0 ≤ 1 over 300 trajectories at t∈{50,200,800}, confirming the e-process property.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves the proposed test is alpha-correct and asymptotically optimal, with limsup_{alpha->0} E_Q[tau_alpha]/log(1/alpha) ≤ 1/D_M^inf(Q,P), matching the Theorem 3.3 lower bound (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: α-correctness holds (0 false alarms in 400 runs at α=0.10 and 0.05 with 4000-step horizon) and power-one holds (100% stop rate at 7 alpha levels × 200 runs); the regression slope of E[τ] vs log(1/α) is 6.37 vs target 1/D_M^inf=5.155 (ratio 1.24), with the excess attributable to the log(τ)-drifting boundary offset that vanishes asymptotically, consistent with the paper's own finite-α tables.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 extends the one-sided asymptotic optimality result to the two-sided testing setting (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: The parallel two-one-sided-tests construction was implemented with α=β=1e-4 over 200 runs per hypothesis; both Type-I and Type-II empirical errors are 0 ≤ (α,β), and both directions stop with E[τ] affine in log(1/·) at rates consistent with 1/D_M^inf in each direction (29.5 vs 5.155 and 29.2 vs 5.069), in the same offset-dominated finite-α regime as Claim 4.

claims.claim: The framework is applied to detect MCMC transition-kernel misspecification (Section 5.1, Corollary 5.1) and to validate linear transition dynamics in MDPs (Section 5.2, Corollary 5.3).
claims.evidence: MCMC part uses the paper's exact Appendix-G.1 matrices: stationary distribution of Q_bad matches to 4 decimal places, Q_good stationary equals π, D_M^inf(Q_bad,P_π)=0.0474>0, and 40 runs show 100% detection under Q_bad and 0 false rejections under Q_good; MDP part uses a synthetic 6-state linear MDP (not MountainCar) but tests the identical KL-projection-onto-linear-manifold quantity, showing D_M^inf=0.0004 (linear, no stop) vs 0.152 (non-linear, stops at τ=1000).

snaykey/repro-delayed-obs-mdp.overall: The logbook implements Algorithm 1 from scratch and provides concrete numerical evidence from simulated ergodic Markov chains supporting all six claims, including exact reproduction of the MCMC application with the paper's own matrices. The main limitation is that asymptotic optimality (Claims 4–5) is only approximately verified at finite α, with the regression slope exceeding the theoretical target by 24%, though this is consistent with the paper's own offset-dominated finite-α behavior.

MarxistLeninist/repro-balancing-learning.paper_title: Balancing Learning Rates Across Layers: Exact Two-Step Dynamics and Optimal Scaling in Linear Neural Networks

claims.claim: For two-layer linear networks trained on single-index targets, Theorem 5.3 gives exact closed-form test-loss expressions after one and two gradient steps, with the one-step loss containing linear signal-alignment terms plus quadratic/interaction over-updating terms, and the two-step loss exhibiting higher-order dependence on the product η₁η₂ of the two layers' learning rates.
claims.evidence: Closed-form L1 and L2 formulas match Monte-Carlo empirical GD at h=600 with one-step rel-err ~1e-4 and two-step rel-err ~1e-3 to 1e-2 across alpha in {1.25, 1.4, 1.48}; two-step abs error shrinks with width (0.0109→0.0044 for h=250→500), consistent with the stated O(1/√h) finite-width correction.

claims.claim: Corollary 5.4 shows that for a learning-rate budget η₁+η₂=2h^α with 1<α≤3/2, symmetric learning rates η₁=η₂=h^α are suboptimal after one gradient step but become locally optimal after two steps in sufficiently wide two-layer networks.
claims.evidence: At h=600, alpha=1.3, the one-step empirical minimizer is at budget fraction 0.05 (asymmetric) while after two steps the symmetric point has positive curvature 4.58e-08, confirming it is a local minimum—directly demonstrating the asymmetry-to-balance transition for two-layer networks.

claims.claim: For three-layer linear networks, Theorem 5.5 derives analogous one- and two-step test-loss formulas under a critical learning-rate scaling η₁,η₂≤O(h), a stricter regime than the O(h√h) scaling used for two-layer networks.
claims.evidence: The three-layer one-step formula matches MC (rel-err ~1e-3) and the O(h) critical scaling is confirmed (threshold exponent 0.99 vs theory 1.0), but the two-step formula systematically overpredicts empirical loss by 7-10x near alpha=2/3, with the gap not closing with width (abs err 0.5727→0.2472 for h=250→500), contradicting the two-step portion of the claim.

claims.claim: Corollary 5.6 demonstrates a similar transition from asymmetric to balanced optimal learning rates in three-layer networks for 0<α≤2/3.
claims.evidence: At h=600, alpha=0.6, the three-layer two-step empirical minimizer is at fraction 0.27 (not symmetric), the symmetric-point curvature is -8.04e-06 (negative, not a local minimum), and empirical and closed-form disagree on minimizer location (0.27 vs 0.84), directly contradicting the claim that balanced rates become locally optimal after two steps.

claims.claim: Proposition 5.1 decomposes each layer's gradient as G_ℓ^t = B_ℓ^t - A_ℓ^t, where A terms capture data-aligned components and B terms capture self-interaction effects that are suppressed by a factor of 1/(√h - 1) below the critical learning-rate threshold.
claims.evidence: Gradient formulas match finite-difference to 1.2e-10 (machine precision), the decomposition G=B-A is verified as an exact algebraic identity to 1.3e-18 across h in [60,500], the residual bound ||B||/||G|| ≤ 1/(√h−1) holds at every width with fitted decay slope -0.46 vs theory -0.5, and critical-LR threshold exponents are 1.50 (2-layer, theory 3/2) and 0.99 (3-layer, theory 1).

MarxistLeninist/repro-balancing-learning.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence confirming the two-layer theory (Theorem 5.3, Corollary 5.4, Proposition 5.1) and the three-layer one-step formula plus scaling regime, but the three-layer two-step formula (Theorem 5.5 L2) is contradicted by empirical GD, which in turn falsifies the three-layer asymmetry-to-balance transition (Corollary 5.6).

ai-sherpa/online-packet-scheduling-deadl.paper_title: Online Packet Scheduling with Deadlines and Learning

claims.claim: For the deterministic algorithm EDF_Φ^L in 2- and 3-bounded K-OPSD, the Φ-regret upper bound is Õ(√(KT)), matching sleeping-bandit-style rates (Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: EDF_Φ^L was implemented and run on s∈{2,3}, K∈{2,4,8,16,32}, T up to 16,000 with 6 seeds; the cumulative confidence-width sum S(T) (the quantity the proof actually bounds) shows log-log slopes vs T in [0.484, 0.675] and vs K in [0.489, 0.503], with S/√(KT) bounded ≤6.641 across a 32× horizon range, confirming the Õ(√(KT)) rate on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: The deterministic algorithm ALG^θ achieves competitive ratio θ_K in [√2, Φ) for finite K packet types, breaking the classical golden-ratio Φ = (1+√5)/2 competitive-ratio barrier for 2-bounded deadline instances (Proposition 4.1).
claims.evidence: The θ_K recurrence (Eq. 1) was solved at 60-digit precision for K=2..32, yielding θ_2=√2 and θ_3=3/2 matching the paper, strictly increasing with all values in [√2, Φ); ALG^θ was tested against an exact transversal-matroid offline OPT over 60,000 instances with 0 violations of G_OPT ≤ θ_K·G_ALG, and an explicit edge sequence attains ratio θ_K to 6e-61 while a K=2 adversary forces √2.

claims.claim: The learning variant ALG^θ,U attains a θ_K-regret upper bound of Õ(√(KT)), which is shown to be nearly tight against a matching Ω(√T) lower bound (Theorem 4.2, Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Upper bound: confidence-width sum slopes vs T in [0.467, 0.543] for K∈{2,4,8}, T up to 32,000 with S/√(KT) bounded ≤6.845. Lower bound: on the hard gap Δ=√(K/T) construction, T·KL(0.5, 0.5+Δ) is horizon-constant ≈2K (16/32/64 for K=8/16/32) and the Bretagnolle–Huber floor cert/√T stays positive at ≈0.076, confirming Ω(√T) does not vanish.

claims.claim: The randomized algorithm ALG^R2 for 2-bounded instances achieves a 5/4-regret bound of Õ(√(KT)) (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: ALG^R2 was run on 2-bounded instances with K up to 32, T up to 16,000, 6 seeds; confidence-width sum slopes vs T in [0.522, 0.611] with S/√(KT) bounded ≤7.245, confirming the Õ(√(KT)) rate, and the competitive constant α=5/4 is verified as an exact identity.

claims.claim: The randomized algorithm ALG^Rs for s-bounded (unbounded slackness) instances achieves an e/(e-1)-regret bound of Õ(√(KT)) (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: ALG^Rs was run across s∈{2,3,5,8}, K up to 32, T up to 16,000, 6 seeds; confidence-width sum slopes vs T in [0.510, 0.636] with S/√(KT) bounded ≤7.150 across all slackness values, confirming the s-independent Õ(√(KT)) rate, and the competitive constant α=e/(e−1)=1.581977 is verified as an exact identity.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 establishes that sleeping bandits are a special case of 1-bounded K-OPSD, formally connecting the packet scheduling model to the multi-armed bandit framework (Section 2.2, Lemma 2.1).
claims.evidence: Two independently coded environments (OneBoundedKOPSD and SleepingBandit) driven by identical arrival streams and the same UCB policy produced 0 action mismatches, 0 reward mismatches, and 0 awake-set mismatches over 40 runs × 3,000 rounds = 120,000 rounds, confirming the operational equivalence of 1-bounded K-OPSD and sleeping bandits.

ai-sherpa/online-packet-scheduling-deadl.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all six claims on non-toy setups: exact 60-digit computation of the θ_K recurrence with empirical competitive-ratio validation over 60,000 instances, confidence-width sum rate measurements confirming Õ(√(KT)) scaling across all five learning theorems, a horizon-constant T·KL lower-bound certificate, and a bit-identical dual-environment reduction check. The main caveat is that the learning-rate claims (1, 3, 4, 5) measure the confidence-width sum proxy rather than raw regret, which the logbook justifies by noting the competitive constants are loose on i.i.d. instances.

ai-sherpa/anytime-oco-constraints-repro.paper_title: Optimal Anytime Algorithms for Online Convex Optimization with Adversarial Constraints

claims.claim: Algorithm 2 (Anytime Online Policy for COCO) achieves static regret bounded by 2GD(√t + 1) and cumulative constraint violation (CCV) bounded by 8GD√t·√(log t + 1)·(log(log t + 1) + 1)·log(4t), for any t ≥ 1 without prior knowledge of the horizon T (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 2 was implemented from scratch in numpy with the horizon-oblivious λ_t schedule, and both the regret bound 2GD(√t+1) and CCV bound were checked at all 1,080,000 checkpoints across 18 configurations × 20 seeds × T=3000, with zero violations. A representative config (d=2, G=0.5, D=2) shows regret_T=20.52 ≤ 111.54 and CCV_T=78.52 ≤ 39498.7. A long-horizon run to T=300,000 confirms the CCV growth tracks the bound curve's own finite-horizon slope.

claims.claim: The paper introduces a time-varying, horizon-oblivious Lyapunov function Φ_t(·) that replaces the fixed horizon-dependent Lyapunov functions used in prior anytime online convex optimization analyses (Section 4, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: The drift inequality (Eq. 8) was checked at 450,000 rounds with zero violations (minimum slack -2.22e-16, i.e., machine-epsilon boundary), and the slack was independently reduced to the convexity identity u·e^u − (e^u−1) ≥ 0 verified over 20,000 random u. Horizon-obliviousness was directly falsification-tested: T=5000 and T=2500 runs agree to 1e-10 on their entire shared 2500-round prefix, which would provably fail if λ_t depended on T.

claims.claim: Algorithm 3 (Anytime Online Policy for Dynamic COCO) attains dynamic regret of 2GD√(1+P_t)(√t + 1) and CCV of 8GD√(1+P_t)√t·√(log t + 1)·(log(log t + 1) + 1)·log(4t), where P_t is the unknown path length of the comparator sequence (Theorem 5.3, Section 5).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 3 was implemented from scratch with the path-scaled λ_t and path-weighted AdaGrad accumulator, and the dynamic-regret and CCV bounds were checked at all 360,000 checkpoints across 6 path-length regimes (δ∈{0,…,0.2}, mean final P_t from 0 to 1134) × 20 seeds × T=3000, with zero violations. The path-length sweep exercises genuinely different comparator-mobility regimes, and the √(1+P_t) bound inflates accordingly without being exceeded.

claims.claim: Algorithm 4 (Optimistic COCO) achieves regret O(√E_t(f̃)) and CCV Õ(√E_t(g̃)) that scale with the prediction error of the objective and constraint functions respectively, improving on the worst-case O(√t) bounds when predictions are accurate (Theorem 6.1, Section 6).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 4 was implemented from scratch with optimistic mirror descent and predicted-constraint projection; the Theorem-6.1 √E envelopes were checked at all 384,000 checkpoints across 6 noise levels × 16 seeds × 2 sweeps × T=2000 with zero violations. Perfect predictions yield median E=0 and CCV=0 (max 2.75e-14) versus the Õ(√t) worst case; regret and CCV are strictly ordered by prediction error; and both destructive controls (shuffled objective predictions, corrupted constraint predictions) causally degrade the corresponding metric as expected.

ai-sherpa/anytime-oco-constraints-repro.overall: The logbook provides a thorough from-scratch numpy implementation of all four algorithms with millions of bound-satisfaction checkpoints across multiple configurations, seeds, and regimes, plus direct falsification tests for the horizon-obliviousness and prediction-error mechanisms. The main limitation is that the worst-case bounds have very large headroom on random linear adversaries, but the implementations, unit tests, and destructive controls provide concrete evidence supporting each claim.

amkkk/repro-dataset-distillation-efficie.paper_title: Dataset Distillation Efficiently Encodes Low-Dimensional Representations from Gradient-Based Learning of Non-Linear Tasks

claims.claim: The paper proves (Theorem 4.6) that the memory complexity of dataset distillation for two-layer ReLU networks reduces from Θ(d³ ∨ d²/ε ∨ d/ε⁴ ∨ dL) to Θ̃(r²d + L), where r is the intrinsic dimensionality of the target function and L is the network width (Theorem 4.6, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook merely plugs d=10, eps=0.01, L=100, r=1 into the paper's stated Big-O formulas to compute a 9.09Mx ratio; this is arithmetic on the formulas themselves, not an independent verification of Theorem 4.6's proof or its scaling behavior across multiple dimensions.

claims.claim: The analysis targets multi-index models of the form f*(x) = σ*(B^T x), where B ∈ R^{d×r} encodes the intrinsic r-dimensional structure of the task, for two-layer networks trained via gradient-based optimization (Section 3, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Only the single-index special case (r=1, d=10) was implemented; teacher gradient alignment with beta was 0.04283 vs 6.83e-8 for random, confirming the mechanism at r=1 but not testing the general multi-index formulation with r>1.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 shows that for multi-index models with intrinsic dimension r, only M₁ ~ Θ̃(r²) synthetic points are needed in the first distillation phase to enable effective second-layer training (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Only r=1 was tested (M1=1), which is the trivial case where Theta-tilde(r^2)=O(1); the claim about M1~Theta-tilde(r^2) for general r was never tested with r>1, so the scaling in r is unverified.

claims.claim: The paper's main theoretical result (Theorem 4.1) shows distilled points align with the principal subspace of the target function via projections involving the Hessian matrix, formalizing how distillation encodes low-dimensional task structure (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Hessian H was computed via Monte Carlo (50k samples) for r=1 only, confirming rank=1, span(H)=S* (error 7.6e-8), and distilled-point alignment 0.99999 vs 0.362 random; this validates the mechanism at single-index scale but not for general r.

claims.claim: The work presents synthetic experiments in Section 5 validating the theoretical compression rates for gradient-based dataset distillation on two-layer networks (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Figure 1 and Figure 2 experiments were reproduced for single-index (r=1, d=10, L=100) only; distilled MSE converged to ~0.32-0.33 (paper reference ~0.26) and transfer learning showed marginal benefit at n=1000, but multi-index experiments and image tasks from the paper were not attempted.

amkkk/repro-dataset-distillation-efficie.overall: The logbook provides small-scale numerical checks (r=1, d=10, L=100) of the paper's theoretical mechanisms—Hessian subspace alignment, memory compression, and M1 sufficiency—but never tests the general multi-index case (r>1) or the paper's full experimental scope. All five claims are addressed only at toy scale with a single-index model, leaving the core scaling claims in r unverified.

amkkk/repro-a-task-centric-theory-for-it.paper_title: A Task-centric Theory for Iterative Self-Improvement with Easy-to-Hard Curricula

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 gives a finite-sample, high-probability lower bound on expected reward after one self-improvement iteration, showing the bound tightens as the accepted-data fraction (relative to total generated samples) increases (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook numerically evaluates Theorem 4.1's bound formula using a proxy Beta distribution with a single parameter set (V0=0.4, m=1, delta=0.1, tau=0.5), showing the bound increases monotonically with n (−0.63 to 0.14 across n=100–5000). This is a simplified numerical check of the bound formula, not a proof verification or test on real self-improvement data.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.4 and Remark 4.6.1 show that iterative self-improvement admits monotonic lower-bound guarantees across iterations only when initial task difficulty falls in a moderate regime, neither too easy nor too hard (Section 4, Corollary 4.4, Remark 4.6.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook iterates the F(x) map from Corollary 4.4 across multiple V0 values, showing monotonic chains for V0∈[0.05,0.65] and non-monotonic behavior for V0=0.85. However, V0=0.75 (labeled 'too_easy') still shows monotonic increasing trajectories, blurring the moderate-regime boundary. The setup uses a proxy formula evaluation with assumed constants (gamma=0.05, c=0.8), not the paper's full framework.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 proves that easy-to-hard curriculum scheduling achieves strictly better finite-sample guarantees than a fixed task mixture whenever a feasibility condition and an improvement condition (denoted ℳ<0) both hold (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook compares E2H vs baseline bounds with one parameter set (beta'=0.25, beta=0.4, L=3, n=2400) and shows E2H strictly dominates (gap ~0.11) for all tested V0. However, E2H dominance also holds when m_condition_holds=false (V0=0.05, 0.1, 0.7, 0.75), so the conditional nature of the theorem (M<0) is not precisely tested. This is a narrow numerical snapshot, not comprehensive verification.

claims.claim: Proposition 5.5 shows the region of initializations where easy-to-hard curricula provably beat fixed mixtures undergoes a sharp collapse near a critical sample-budget threshold ν_c, i.e., a phase transition in curriculum benefit (Section 5, Proposition 5.5).
claims.evidence: The logbook sweeps nu across a wide range and shows |I_N| collapsing from 0.44 to 0.01 near nu_c≈0.141, with derivative x'(nu) increasing. This is a direct numerical evaluation of Proposition 5.5's interval formula with specific constants, providing evidence of the phase transition but using proxy parameters rather than the paper's full setup.

claims.claim: Section 4.2 identifies an explicit feedback loop in which better-performing models accept a larger fraction of self-generated data per iteration, which in turn expands the training set and sustains further improvement (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook simulates the feedback loop using a custom update rule V_new = V + k_learn * accepted_fraction * (1-V) + noise with Beta-distributed acceptance, showing correlation 0.9985 between V0 and acceptance rate. The update rule is hand-crafted, not derived from the paper's theoretical framework, making this a proxy simulation of the feedback mechanism rather than a reproduction of Section 4.2's analysis.

amkkk/repro-a-task-centric-theory-for-it.overall: The logbook provides numerical Monte-Carlo checks of the paper's theoretical bound formulas using proxy distributions and narrow parameter snapshots, offering preliminary evidence consistent with all five claims. However, none constitute full reproductions: theorems are checked via specific numerical instances rather than proof verification, and Claim 5 uses an assumed update rule not from the paper.

snaykey/repro-accel-noisy-power.paper_title: Improved Analysis of the Accelerated Noisy Power Method with Applications to Decentralized PCA

claims.claim: Theorem 2.2 establishes accelerated convergence for the Accelerated Noisy Power Method under a noise magnitude condition that scales as Δ_k·ε rather than the stricter Δ_k·ε^μ requirement of prior work (Xu, 2023) (Section 2, Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: Synthetic setup (dimension 100, k=1, seven eigengaps, three seeds) shows ANPM gap exponent 0.536 vs theoretical 0.5 and standard 1.004 vs 1.0, with noise tolerance 186x–1.1Mx above Xu-2023 allowance. Real numerical evidence but clearly scaled scope, not a full theorem verification.

claims.claim: Theorems 2.4 and 2.5 prove that the noise conditions on the orthogonal component ||U_-k^T Ξ_t||_2 and parallel component ||U_k^T Ξ_t||_2 (Equations 3-4) cannot be relaxed without breaking the accelerated convergence guarantee (Section 2, Theorems 2.4-2.5).
claims.evidence: Adversarial phase-transition tests on dimension 100, k∈{1,3} show convergence fails when orthogonal noise multiplier exceeds 2 and parallel noise multiplier exceeds 1, while theorem-safe 1/32 converges. Demonstrates necessity direction on a simplified synthetic setup but does not test the exact universal constants.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 introduces ADePM, applying the improved ANPM analysis to decentralized PCA via an accelerated gossip protocol (Algorithm 1), achieving convergence rate O(sqrt(λ_k/(λ_k-λ_{k+1})) log(...)) with communication cost O(1/sqrt(γ_W) log(...)) comparable to non-accelerated decentralized methods (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: ADePM implemented over 8–64 agent rings with accelerated gossip, achieving graph exponent 0.508 vs 0.5 and eigengap exponent 0.607 vs 0.5 on Digits/MNIST subsets. Real multi-agent implementation but scaled scope with only ring topologies and limited datasets.

claims.claim: Section 3.1 shows the accelerated gossip subroutine attains O~(1/sqrt(γ_W)) mixing versus the O~(1/γ_W) rate of standard (non-accelerated) gossip (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Head-to-head comparison of accelerated (Chebyshev) vs standard gossip across 18 networks (rings, grids, ER graphs) up to 96 agents yields pooled mixing exponents 0.514 vs 1.015 (theory 0.5 vs 1.0), ring-only 0.5005 vs 0.9997, and 31.4x speedup at 96 agents. Directly tests the claimed scaling relationship at reasonable scale.

claims.claim: Section 4 experiments demonstrate that the optimal momentum parameter β* = λ_{k+1}^2/4 yields a square-root speedup over non-accelerated decentralized PCA methods, and that ADePM substantially outperforms DePM and DeEPCA baselines on real datasets (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The β* optimum is supported (48→23→22→78 iterations at 0/1.0/1.1/2.0·β*), and ADePM beats DePM decisively (2112 vs 29008 comm rounds). However, ADePM does NOT beat DeEPCA on total gossip rounds (2112 vs 1340 on Digits homogeneous, 2112 vs 1300 on Digits heterogeneous, 3096 vs 1640 on MNIST), directly contradicting the claim that ADePM 'substantially outperforms DeEPCA baselines on real datasets.'

snaykey/repro-accel-noisy-power.overall: The logbook provides scaled numerical evidence supporting the theoretical scaling predictions of the paper (noise conditions, gossip mixing rates, ADePM communication complexity), with Claim 4's gossip mixing rate being the strongest result across 18 networks. However, the DeEPCA baseline comparison on real datasets directly contradicts Claim 5's assertion that ADePM substantially outperforms DeEPCA, as ADePM uses more communication rounds than DeEPCA in all tested settings.

claims.claim: Proves (Theorem 1) that under diffusion scaling (residual weight ~1/sqrt(L)) with RMS token normalization, the discrete-depth Transformer token dynamics converge in distribution to a system of SDEs on the unit sphere driven by common matrix-valued Brownian noise (Section 3, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Numerical checks confirm key structural implications of the SDE limit: tangent projection orthogonality (2.98e-8), SDE step norm preservation (5.96e-8), and discrete dynamics maintaining sphere constraint over 500 steps (norm dev <1e-7); phase boundary matching from Claim 2 provides indirect validation of the SDE as correct continuous limit.

claims.claim: Proves (Theorem 2) a sharp phase transition for two-token dynamics: tokens collapse to a single cluster when d-2 >= cosh(2*beta), but antipodal (two-cluster) configurations emerge with positive probability when d-2 < cosh(2*beta), where d is token dimension and beta is the interaction/inverse-temperature strength (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: 20,000 trajectories per (d,beta) point across d=4..10 show sharp transition at beta_c=0.5*acosh(d-2): e.g., d=4 has P(A2)=0.006 at beta=0.33 (below beta_c=0.6585) vs 0.302 at beta=3.66 (above), with the same pattern across all 7 dimensions.

claims.claim: Shows via Proposition 1 that in a hybrid model, initialization noise below an explicit threshold epsilon^2 = 2*e^(-beta) still permits reaching cluster configurations unreachable by the corresponding deterministic (zero-noise) dynamics, demonstrating stochasticity prevents the single-cluster collapse predicted by deterministic mean-field models (Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: Threshold formula verified exactly via unit test, and hybrid simulations with 1000 trajectories per point confirm P(antipodal) increases monotonically with epsilon, but simulations use T=50 vs paper's T=500 and only d=3, making this a reduced-scale check rather than full reproduction.

claims.claim: Validates the theoretical phase boundary numerically with roughly 40,000 simulated trajectories, confirming antipodal clustering persists for N>=3 tokens as well as the two-token case (Section 6, experiments).
claims.evidence: Two-token phase boundary confirmed with 20K trajectories per point across 7 dimensions (1.68M total); multi-token simulations with N=3,5,10 at d=4 (5000 trajectories each) show P(antipodal pair exists)=1.0 at beta>=0.5, confirming antipodal structures persist beyond the two-token case.

claims.claim: Reports CIFAR-10 experiments in which random (stochastic) initialization of Transformer layers outperforms identity initialization, supporting the theoretical claim that initialization stochasticity is beneficial rather than merely a nuisance (Section 6).
claims.evidence: MiniViT with 6 layers (vs 128), d=32 (vs 96), 20 epochs (vs 300) over 3 seeds shows identity init 36.51% > random init 35.12%, opposite to the paper's claim; the drastically reduced scale means this is a toy-scale probe, not a full reproduction or falsification.

amkkk/repro-clustering-in-deep-stochasti.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical validation of the theoretical phase transition (Claims 2, 4) and structural SDE properties (Claim 1) at meaningful scale, while Claims 3 and 5 are addressed only at reduced scale with acknowledged limitations. The CIFAR-10 result at toy scale runs opposite to the paper's finding, but the setup is too small to constitute falsification.

vimarsh/repro-how-can-mamba-learn-in-con.paper_title: How Can Mamba Learn In Context with Outliers and Generalize Provably?

claims.claim: Theorem 2 proves that a trained one-layer Mamba generalizes on test prompts with distribution-shifted outliers whenever the outlier fraction α < min(1, p_a·l_tr/l_ts), allowing α to approach 1, whereas Theorem 4 shows a linear Transformer generalizes only when α < 1/2 (Theorem 2, Theorem 4, Section 3.4).
claims.evidence: Varying p_a ∈ {0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9} with 3 seeds, Mamba's empirical α-tolerance threshold rises monotonically (0.62→0.72→0.80→0.83) tracking the theory line min(1, p_a·l_tr/l_ts), while the linear Transformer stays pinned near 0.5 (0.42, 0.45, 0.40, 0.33) regardless of p_a, confirming the qualitative separation predicted by Theorems 2 and 4.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows one-layer Mamba requires T ≥ T_M = Θ(η^{-1}(1-p_a)^{-1}β^{-2}M_1) training iterations to reach ε generalization error, while Theorem 3 shows a linear Transformer converges faster, in T_T = Θ(η^{-1}(1-p_a)^{-1}β^{-2}l_tr^{-1}M_1) iterations, under the stricter outlier-tolerance constraint (Theorem 1, Theorem 3, Section 3.3-3.4).
claims.evidence: Sweeping l_tr ∈ {5,10,20,40} with 3 seeds, Mamba's iterations-to-ε remain high (1977, 897, 573, 443) while the linear Transformer's decrease rapidly (430, 60, 10, ~0), yielding ratios T_M/T_T of 4.6, 14.9, 57.3, and ≥44 (floored at l_tr=40 by eval granularity), confirming the Θ(l_tr) scaling predicted by Theorems 1 and 3.

claims.claim: Corollary 1 and Corollary 2 show the linear-attention component concentrates weight on context examples sharing the query's relevant pattern (attention sum ≥ Θ(1)), while the nonlinear gating component suppresses outlier-containing examples (G_i ≤ O(poly(M_1)^{-1})) and applies exponential decay by distance (G_h(j) ≥ Θ(1/2^{j-1})) (Corollary 1, Corollary 2, Section 3.5).
claims.evidence: Probing the trained Mamba on 30k test prompts: attention sum on same-pattern examples = +132.75 vs −26.54 on different-pattern (Corollary 1); gating on outliers = 0.0029 vs 0.0450 on clean, a 15.7× suppression (Corollary 2-i); clean gating decays by distance 0.227, 0.170, 0.127, 0.095, 0.071… staying above the Θ(1/2^{j-1}) lower bound (Corollary 2-ii).

claims.claim: Figure 2 empirically confirms that Mamba maintains test error below 0.01 at outlier fraction α ≈ 0.8 across label-flipping, targeted, and random outlier types, while the linear Transformer's error degrades once α > 0.5 (Figure 2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Across 8 seeds and three outlier types, Mamba error at α=0.8 is 0.005 (targeted) and 0.001 (random), both below 0.01; the flip type gives 0.020 at exactly α=0.8 but 0.0024 at α=0.75, so 'α≈0.8' is borderline for flip only. The linear Transformer degrades sharply past α=0.5 (flip→1.0, target→0.020, random→0.012 at α=0.6), matching Figure 2's qualitative pattern.

claims.claim: Table 1 shows Mamba's in-context accuracy is highly position-sensitive to outlier placement: 99.84% accuracy when outliers are placed farthest from the query (FQ) versus 73.28% when placed closest to the query (CQ) (Table 1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook reproduces the position-sensitivity mechanism in the one-layer synthetic setting (Mamba FQ=99.91% vs CQ=74.61% at α=0.85, closely matching the paper's 99.84% vs 73.28%), but explicitly acknowledges this is a 'synthetic proxy for the SST-2 table' using one-layer models rather than the paper's 3-layer SST-2 setup; the linear Transformer yields 0% everywhere, diverging entirely from the paper's SST-2 results.

vimarsh/repro-how-can-mamba-learn-in-con.overall: The logbook provides a thorough from-scratch reproduction of the paper's synthetic ICL setup, confirming the core theoretical predictions (outlier-tolerance separation, convergence scaling, mechanistic gating behavior) with multi-seed experiments and saved artifacts. Claims 1–4 are verified on the paper's own synthetic experimental scale; Claim 5 is reproduced only as a synthetic proxy for the SST-2-based Table 1, matching Mamba's numbers but not the full experimental setup.

snaykey/repro-admm-last-iterate.paper_title: Last-iterate Convergence of ADMM on Multi-affine Quadratic Equality Constrained Problem

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes sublinear convergence of ADMM to stationary points on multi-affine quadratic equality constrained problems under Assumptions 2.3 and 2.6, given a sufficiently large penalty parameter rho (Section 3).
claims.evidence: On the paper's q-sweep instance at q=1 scaled from nx=4 to nx=4096, the geometric contraction ratio stays at ~0.99 (non-geometric), k·gap decreases from 7.4e-05 to 3.7e-07 confirming gap ∈ o(1/k), and the sublinear signature is stable or sharpens across three orders of magnitude of problem size and across ρ≥1.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 proves a linear convergence rate when the nonlinearity norm ||C|| satisfies the bound in Equation 4 relative to Q's properties, provided the Lagrangian is second-order differentiable at limit points (Section 3).
claims.evidence: On Example 2.2 (β=1, ρ=3), the Lagrangian gap contracts geometrically at ratio 0.2667±0.0204 over 8 seeds (73% per-iteration reduction, 15 iters to 1e-10), the Eq. 4 matrix quantities (||C||=1, λ_min(QQᵀ)=q², ||(QQᵀ)⁻¹Q||=1/q) are recomputed in closed form showing the RHS grows ∝ q, and the linear ratio is stable to 4 significant figures from nx=4 to nx=512.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 achieves linear convergence without requiring second-order differentiability when the constraint indicator functions {I_i} are polyhedral (Section 3).
claims.evidence: With an active polyhedral lower bound on x₁ (creating a kink that voids second-order differentiability), the geometric ratio remains 0.266 (vs 0.246 for the smooth case), and across 12 configurations spanning 2–96 simultaneously-active faces at nx=32–512, all runs maintain linear ratios 0.05–0.13 and converge to 1e-8.

claims.claim: For robotic locomotion dynamics, Corollary 4.2 shows linear convergence holds when the discretization step Δt is below a threshold t0, since nonlinear terms decay as O((Δt)^3) (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The (Δt)³ scaling is verified to exponent 3.000 and a threshold t₀≈0.8 is demonstrated (ratio 0.94→0.56, iters 186→28), but on a synthetic surrogate where the bilinear term is literally multiplied by (Δt)³, not on the actual 2D locomotion dynamics of Eq. 6.

claims.claim: Empirically, ADMM outperforms PADMM, IPDS-ADMM, and IADMM baselines on multi-affine constrained problems, and toy-problem experiments show q≥10 is sufficient to transition from sublinear to linear convergence (Figures 2 and 4).
claims.evidence: The q≥10 sublinear→linear transition is well-verified (q=1 ratio 0.999 non-contractive, q=10 linear in 4 iters, stable across nx=4–512), but the baseline comparison uses standard-form reimplementations of PADMM/IPDS-ADMM/IADMM rather than the authors' exact code, and the paper provides no explicit update rules for these baselines.

claims.claim: The method is validated on 2D locomotion simulation and on real robot experiments including a humanoid jump and quadruped bounding task (Figures 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: No 2D locomotion simulation, no physics simulator, and no real robot experiments (humanoid jump, quadruped bounding) were conducted; only a synthetic T=6 and T=48 centroidal-chain surrogate of Eq. 6 was tested, showing linear convergence (ratio 0.25, 9–12 iters) on the proxy problem.

snaykey/repro-admm-last-iterate.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence for the three theoretical convergence-rate claims (Thms 3.1–3.3) on the paper's own multi-affine instances scaled up to 4096 variables, with systematic sweeps across problem size, q, ρ, and polyhedral configurations. The empirical and robot-validation claims (4–6) are only addressed on synthetic surrogates or approximate baseline reimplementations, falling short of full reproduction.

IvanMiao/repro-evaluating-relational-rea.paper_title: Evaluating Relational Reasoning in LLMs with REL

claims.claim: REL defines Relational Complexity (RC) as the minimal number of independent sources of variation that must be jointly bound to perform a reasoning step, and instantiates it across three domains: REL-A (algebra, RC 1-6), REL-B (biology/homoplasy detection, RC 2-25), and REL-C (chemistry, three tasks with RC from 2 upward).
claims.evidence: Full audit of 13,468 records across 28 JSONL files in the official release shows A1/A2 both labeled RC2 (not RC1-6 starting at RC1), only A1-A4 released (not full RC1-6 range), and C1-C4 present (not three chemistry tasks), contradicting the claimed inventory.

claims.claim: On REL-A, accuracy drops by 45% as RC increases from 3 to 9, with performance collapsing on tasks where RC scales with input size.
claims.evidence: Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct evaluated on 500 released A2/A3 questions (125 per condition) scored 23.2% at RC3 and 21.6% at RC9 — a 1.6pp drop, not 45pp; the fixed-RC2 control (24.8%→22.4%) also shows no collapse with input size.

claims.claim: On REL-B1 (homoplastic taxa detection), accuracy decreases by 93% as RC increases from 5 to 20.
claims.evidence: 334 successful Qwen3-4B responses on REL-B1 (177 at RC5, 157 at RC20) show 100%/100% under the released scorer and 0%/0% under strict exact-set scoring — a 0% decrease either way, not 93%; the released scorer's acceptance of partial taxa overlap is documented via a fixture test.

claims.claim: On REL-C, task completion rate decreases by 39.7% from complexity level C1 to C3 as relational complexity increases.
claims.evidence: 40 deterministic examples per C1/C2/C3 condition scored with paper task-completion metrics yield C1=57.5%, C3=2.91% — a 54.59pp drop, not 39.7pp; the C1>C3 direction is reproduced but the anchored magnitude is contradicted.

claims.claim: Giving models 4,096 to 16,384 tokens of test-time compute improves accuracy by only 2-3% on algebraic tasks and 0.4% on chemistry tasks, leaving the RC-driven performance gap largely intact (Section 5.4, Table A.8).
claims.evidence: 55 Qwen3-4B paired cases and 11 gpt-oss-20B paired cases show 0pp accuracy gain at 16k vs 4k tokens; gpt-oss mean completion usage rose from 3,334 to 12,221 tokens confirming the larger budget was consumed, but algebra gain was 0pp (not 2-3pp) and chemistry gains were 0/0/+0.68pp (not 0.4pp).

claims.claim: One-shot in-context learning improves performance at low RC but preserves the same hierarchical degradation, with accuracy at 77.0% (C1), 43.3% (C2), and 32.7% (C3), an average gain of only 3-6% (Section 5.4, Figure A.4).
claims.evidence: 30 paired zero/one-shot cases per chemistry task (180 responses) with Qwen3-4B yield one-shot accuracies of 63.33/33.33/1.67%, not 77.0/43.3/32.7%; mean gain is +0.74pp (not 3-6pp), with C2 and C3 actually worsening under one-shot.

IvanMiao/repro-evaluating-relational-rea.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence — 1,837 model responses across three models plus a 13,468-record benchmark audit — that contradicts the specific numerical magnitudes in all six claims, though qualitative directions (e.g., C1>C3 hierarchy, compute not closing the gap) are partially reproduced. The main limitation is model-class mismatch: most claims were tested with Qwen3-4B, far below the frontier models the paper likely used, though Claim 2 used the similar-class Llama-3.3-70B.

ai-sherpa/parameter-free-dynamic-regret-.paper_title: Parameter-free Dynamic Regret: Time-varying Movement Costs, Delayed Feedback, and Memory

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 establishes an improved comparator-adaptive dynamic regret bound for unconstrained OCO with time-varying movement costs that replaces a quadratic dependence on lambda_t with a linear interaction term lambda_t*||g_t|| relative to the bound in Theorem 3.1 (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Exponents of the sqrt bound fitted to 0.5 to 10+ digits (R²=1.0) across 37 configs and 1,092,000 rounds up to T=420,000; first-order vs quadratic separation of 1001× in the small-gradient regime; KKT residual 1e-14 on 2048 random states; worst regret/envelope ratio 0.0018.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 shows that for OCO with delayed feedback, the reduction to time-varying movement costs (via Lemma 5.1 and Algorithm 4) achieves regret depending on total delay d_tot rather than the worse max-delay times T (d_max*T) dependence of prior work, without requiring in-order feedback arrival (Section 5.1, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Out-of-order delay schedule with d_tot=60,443 vs d_max·T=1,260,000 (20.8× gap) over 20,000 rounds; reduction inequality holds with margin 106.16; counting lemma 74380 ≤ 120886; forced in-order feedback changes the stream digest, confirming the out-of-order regime is exercised.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.7 gives a comparator-adaptive dynamic regret guarantee for OCO with time-varying memory (loss functions depending on the last H actions) by reducing memory-dependent losses to movement costs via the effective memory coupling coefficients xi_t (Section 5.2, Lemma 5.6, Theorem 5.7).
claims.evidence: Memory coupling inequalities ξ_t ≤ B² (96 ≤ 576) and Σξ_t ≤ Σb_t² (241150 ≤ 454621) hold over 20,000 rounds; regret scale linear in B (exponent 0.9803); adversarial control shows replacing ξ_t by instantaneous b_t breaks the bound (RHS 2.0 < actual 3.769 ≤ valid ξ-RHS 12.0).

claims.claim: Algorithm 2 is a dynamic parameter-free subroutine that maintains parallel learning-rate instances on an exponential grid, used within the Composite Mirror Descent scheme (Algorithm 1) to obtain comparator-adaptive guarantees (Section 3, Algorithms 1-2).
claims.evidence: Grid sizes of 8, 8, 9, 11 instances at T=8k/16k/32k/420k match ½·log₂T growth; collapsing to single η changes the action trace and is rejected; closed-form radial inverse verified against root-finder to machine precision.

claims.claim: Setting the movement-cost weights lambda_t=0 in the derived bounds recovers the standard optimal static and dynamic regret guarantees for classical OCO as a special case (Section 3, following Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: With all λ_t=0 over 64,000 rounds, Algorithm-3-wrapped trace is bit-identical (SHA-256 match) to plain Algorithm-2 trace with movement paid 0.0; same trace scored against static (P_T=0.0) and dynamic (P_T=12.145) comparators isolates the specialization.

ai-sherpa/parameter-free-dynamic-regret-.overall: The logbook provides substantial numerical evidence at non-trivial scale (up to 420k rounds, multiple dimensions) supporting all five claims, including exponent fitting, reduction inequalities, destructive controls, and bit-exact special-case recovery. While these are theoretical claims verified numerically rather than symbolically, the experiments are well-designed with adversarial controls and honest scope limitations.

ai-sherpa/laplacian-connectivity-rl-repr.paper_title: Impact of Connectivity on Laplacian Representations in Reinforcement Learning

claims.claim: The approximation error of a rank-k learned Laplacian representation used for linear value function approximation is upper-bounded by ‖v−v̂_k‖_Φ ≤ ‖r̄‖_Φ√(1/(λ₂λ_{k+1})) + ‖v‖_Φ√(2ε/(λ_{k+1}−λ_k)), decomposing into truncation error and feature-estimation error (Theorem 3.3, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Theorem 3.3 was audited across 1000 random MDPs (476 gridworlds sized 6-11, 524 fully-random asymmetric dense MDPs) with exact computation of the Laplacian eigenbasis, eps from Assumption 3.1's own trace residual, and Phi-weighted least-squares projection. 0/1000 violations with min slack 1.645e-06; the truncation sub-bound also 0/1000 violations with min slack^2 1.14e-12.

claims.claim: The truncation error term is bounded by ‖v−v_k‖²_Φ ≤ ‖r̄‖²_Φ/(λ₂λ_{k+1}), showing the bound scales inversely with the algebraic connectivity λ₂ of the state-transition graph, so poorly-connected MDPs induce larger approximation error (Lemma 3.4, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Table 1 reproduced at native scale (15x15 gridworld, k=20, eta-sweep {0,...,0.9}, 5 seeds): analytical error matches paper to max 0.22% relative error, lambda2 to max 0.24%, and Spearman(lambda2, analytical_error) = -1.000 confirming perfectly monotonic inverse scaling with algebraic connectivity. Truncation sub-bound also 0/1000 violations in the Claim 1 audit.

claims.claim: The Graph Drawing Objective's feature-estimation error is bounded by ‖Π_Ψ−Π_Ψ̃‖₂ < √(2ε/(λ_{k+1}−λ_k)), depending on the spectral gap between the k-th and (k+1)-th eigenvalues (Lemma 3.5, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Lemma 3.5's projection bound isolated and tested on 1530 trials (867 RL Laplacians, 633 generic p.s.d. matrices, 30 actual NumPy-trained GDO feature sets) with eps computed from Assumption 3.1's residual: 0/1530 violations, min slack 0.2325. In the informative regime (RHS<1), 0/38 violations. Gap-scaling confirmed with Spearman(LHS, sqrt(2*eps/gap)) = 0.590.

claims.claim: The analysis defines a Φ-self-adjoint Laplacian L = I − (P+Φ⁻¹PᵀΦ)/2 (Equation 6, Section 3) and applies without assuming symmetry of the induced transition kernel, i.e., it holds for general non-uniform behavior policies (Lemma 3.6, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: 1000 trials across 4 non-uniform/asymmetric policy families (mixed, goal_directed, random_dirichlet, random_dirichlet_nongrid): 0/1000 had symmetric P_pi (min asymmetry 0.093, median 0.650), yet Phi-self-adjointness held to max |Phi L - (Phi L)^T| = 2.78e-17, and Theorem 3.3 held with 0/1000 violations (min slack 6.23e-08) on this exclusively-asymmetric population.

claims.claim: Propositions 4.1 and 4.2 establish that this matrix-based Laplacian formulation is equivalent to the operator-theoretic Laplacian representation formulation of Wu et al. (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Operator route built independently from P and its Htilde-adjoint P*=Phi^-1 P^T Phi across 1000 random MDPs. Prop 4.1 identities (adjoint, inner product, operator identity, Ltilde==L) all hold to <2e-15; Prop 4.2 eigenvalue equivalence to 5.2e-11, representation-subspace equivalence median 3.4e-15, trace-min optimum to 2.8e-15, and GDO re-derivation to 1.6e-14.

ai-sherpa/laplacian-connectivity-rl-repr.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all five claims through large-scale Monte Carlo audits (1000-1530 trials each) of the theoretical bounds and algebraic identities, plus a native-scale reproduction of Table 1 matching the paper's analytical error to <0.3%. The Phi-self-adjointness, symmetry-free generality, and operator-matrix equivalence are all confirmed to machine precision, with eps computed from the theorems' own residuals rather than proxies.

ProCreations/repro-a-direct-second-order.paper_title: A Direct Second-Order Method for Solving Two-Player Zero-Sum Games

claims.claim: Theorem 1 establishes a correspondence between fixed points of the Douglas-Rachford (DR) operator and Nash equilibria via the lifting transform z = ẑ − γF(ẑ) (Theorem 1, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: 108 test cells across three game families, three seeds, and four gamma values show lifting equilibria produces max DRS residual 1.10e-14 and back-projection recovers equilibria within 1.09e-14, with a 0.01 perturbation control moving residuals by ≥0.00152 and an unlifted-equilibrium control failing in 80 cells.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 proves local quadratic convergence of the hybrid semi-smooth Newton method, with residual bound ‖R^γ_DRS(z_{k+1})‖ ≤ C‖R^γ_DRS(z_k)‖² (Theorem 4, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: 36 nondegenerate trajectories with 72 local SSN steps all accepted, maximum finite residual-squared ratio of 1.367 (i.e., ‖R(z_{k+1})‖ ≤ 1.367·‖R(z_k)‖²), and final residuals reaching 7.14e-13, directly testing the quadratic convergence bound on concrete runs.

claims.claim: Lemma 1 shows the DRS residual operator is monotone and 1-Lipschitz continuous, which is the key property enabling application of a semi-smooth Newton (SSN) solver (Lemma 1).
claims.evidence: 4,320 deterministic point pairs across normal, uniform, and low-rank games with four step sizes yield minimum monotonicity product 0.6446 (positive, confirming monotonicity) and maximum Lipschitz ratio 0.95278 (≤1, confirming 1-Lipschitz), with a 1.25× residual multiplier control violating the bound in 1,353 pairs.

claims.claim: On 400x800 random zero-sum games, the hybrid PSSN methods reach a duality gap of 1e-12 in about 4.3-4.4 seconds versus 21.97 seconds for PRM+, an order-of-magnitude speedup in the high-precision regime (numerical results table, Section 4).
claims.evidence: At 400x800 scale, independent runs show the hybrid reaching 1e-12 in 8.51–19.29s (not the claimed 4.3–4.4s), while PRM+ runs 200,000 iterations in ~57s and remains at gaps 9.21e-4 to 4.09e-3 (not reaching 1e-12 in 21.97s as claimed), contradicting the specific timing and speedup numbers.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 performs a one-time switch from the first-order Predictive Regret Matching+ (PRM+) method to the Douglas-Rachford semi-smooth Newton (DRSSN) subroutine of Algorithm 2, combining global efficiency with local superlinear convergence (Algorithms 1-2).
claims.evidence: The one-time switch from PRM+ to DRSSN is demonstrated at 400x800 scale with the Newton phase taking 5–58 steps on Gaussian/uniform games and zero steps on low-rank games (where PRM+ already converged), and lengthening the PRM+ warm start from 400 to 800 iterations reduced Newton steps and total wall time as the two-phase design predicts.

ProCreations/repro-a-direct-second-order.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification of the three theoretical claims (Theorem 1, Theorem 4, Lemma 1) and the algorithmic one-time-switch mechanism through extensive testing with destructive controls, but independently falsifies the specific 400x800 timing comparison (4.3–4.4s vs 21.97s) with fresh runs showing 8.5–19.3s for the hybrid and PRM+ failing to reach 1e-12.

AceVikings/repro-quantifying-the-noise-s.paper_title: Quantifying the noise sensitivity of the Wasserstein metric for images

claims.claim: Theorem 2 bounds the expected signed 1-Wasserstein distance between a clean n-pixel image and its Gaussian-noise-perturbed counterpart by (2/√π)σn log2(n) + (1/(2√π))σn, i.e., growth roughly linear in n with a log factor, for zero-sum noise of standard deviation σ (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Exact W1 computed via POT emd2 on 32×32 toroidal cost for 20 HSP90 projections across 11 σ levels with 24 replicates each; all 11 bound cells passed (e.g., σ=0.02: mean W1 0.4172 vs bound 3.7914), fitted exponent 1.0007 (R² 0.99999).

claims.claim: Theorem 3 shows that for p-Wasserstein distances with integer p>1, the expected p-th power error is bounded by (4/√π) n σ, so the per-image error scales as (nσ)^(1/p), improving (becoming more noise-robust) as p increases, in contrast to the Euclidean (L2) metric's linear scaling in σ (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Same 264 corruptions evaluated with exact W2 and W3; 0/22 bound violations, fitted exponents W2=0.5035 (R² 0.99993), W3=0.3387 (R² 0.99977), L2=0.9999, matching predicted 1/p and linear scalings.

SabaPivot/repro-a-tight-theory-of-error-.paper_title: A Tight Theory of Error Feedback Algorithms in Distributed Optimization

claims.claim: EF21 achieves a tight convergence guarantee under contractive compression with optimal step size eta_star = (2/(L+mu)) * ((1-sqrt(epsilon))/(1+sqrt(epsilon))), and the resulting contraction rate rho_star is independent of the number of agents n (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: 768 high-dimensional configurations (dims 2–16, agents 1–8, condition numbers 2–50, ε∈{0.04,0.16,0.36,0.64}) all show squared spectral radius ≤ ρ_star at η_star, with largest ratio 0.999999516; sharpness embeddings in dims up to 64 attain ρ_star to 1.11e-16; replicated agent rates for n=1,2,4,8,16 show spread of only 2.33e-15, directly confirming n-independence.

claims.claim: Under the statistical homogeneity (shared minimizer) assumption, classic Error Feedback (EF) matches EF21's optimal step size and contraction factor exactly, giving identical tight convergence rates (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: Both EF and EF21 block iteration matrices were built for 768 random shared-minimizer problems with noncommuting compressors; at the common η_star, both satisfy ρ_star in 768/768 cases with rate-to-bound ratios matching to 15 decimal places (0.999999515805268 vs 0.999999515805271), and the embedded hard coordinate attains the common rate to 1.11e-16.

claims.claim: Without the shared-minimizer assumption, classic EF can exhibit 2-periodic cycles under statistical heterogeneity and generally fails to converge in the multi-agent setting (Proposition 2.1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: A 64-dimensional family of simultaneous 2-cycles was constructed with heterogeneous local minimizer shifts, distinct curvatures in [0.2,1.0], and a saturating diagonal compressor at ε=0.25; the maximum two-step state difference is 2.22e-16, the compression residual ratio is 0.2500000000000001 (within ε), and the iterate stays ≥2.374 from the global minimizer across all coordinates.

claims.claim: The worst-case multi-agent convergence rate proven in Theorem 3.1 exactly matches the known single-agent rate, showing the novel Lyapunov function recovers prior single-agent guarantees as a special case (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: 192 configurations per agent count (n=1,2,4,8) across all dimensions, condition numbers, and compression factors all fall below the single-agent ρ_star bound; the n=1 sharpness embedding reaches equality to 1.11e-16, and the multi-agent sweep shows no n-dependent degradation, directly testing the special-case recovery on full block systems.

claims.claim: For heterogeneous regularity parameters across agents, Corollary 3.2 extends the tight rates to deterministic, additive, positively homogeneous compressors using averaged parameters L-bar and mu-bar (Corollary 3.2).
claims.evidence: 288 heterogeneous-regularity systems (dims 2,8,16; agents 2,4,8) with independently drawn μ_i∈[0.25,2], condition numbers in [2,30], random SPD eigenbases, and noncommuting linear compressors all show measured block spectral rate ≤ the averaged-parameter (L̄, μ̄) prediction, with largest ratio 0.999056664.

claims.claim: For the two-agent (n=2) heterogeneous case, an explicit cubic polynomial characterizes the empirically optimal convergence rate, and tuning the EControl algorithm's step size to its optimum yields eta=0, coinciding with EF21 (Law 4.3, Law 4.4, Section 4).
claims.evidence: 10,500 cubic polynomial evaluations all yield valid rates in [0,1] with max |Q(ρ)|=1.67e-15; EControl(η=0) matches EF21 exactly over 30 steps (error 0.0); a fresh CVXOPT SDP campaign of 35,500 solves across 450 configurations found cubic_rate−10⁻³ infeasible in 450/450 cases and zero improving candidates among 34,600 in 346 nonempty search bands, with 61 ill-conditioned upper-bound non-certificates disclosed.

SabaPivot/repro-a-tight-theory-of-error-.overall: This logbook provides systematic numerical verification of all six theoretical claims through spectral radius computations on hundreds of high-dimensional distributed configurations, exact 2-cycle construction, and a fresh open-source SDP campaign for the EControl optimality search. The evidence is concrete, non-toy, and consistently matches the paper's formulas to machine precision, with limitations (61 unresolved SDP upper-bound cases) transparently disclosed.

MarxistLeninist/2kSBDoP1rE.paper_title: Why Deep Jacobian Spectra Separate: Depth-Induced Scaling and Singular-Vector Alignment

claims.claim: Theorem 5.3 gives closed-form Lyapunov exponents governing the top singular values of masked (fixed-gates) linear networks, including a finite-depth correction term (d_{i-1}-d_i)/L (Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: Across 20 configurations with 120 random products each, the printed finite-depth correction sign yielded lower RMSE in 0/20 cases while the appendix-derived opposite sign won 20/20; raw data shows wedge_derived_abs_error consistently far below paper_corrected_abs_error (e.g., 0.1076 vs 0.6882 at n=16,p=0.5,L=5,mode=1).

claims.claim: Theorem 6.1 proves that sufficiently strong spectral separation between consecutive singular values forces alignment of dominant singular vectors across the matrix product, yielding an approximately shared singular basis for intermediate Jacobians (Theorem 6.1).
claims.evidence: Ten fixed-seed trials over depths 1–40 under the theorem's explicit hypotheses (fixed right basis, fixed B, spectral gap) yielded median final Frobenius alignment error 9.37e-5 and fitted log-error slope -0.206 vs predicted -0.200; the no-gap control stayed at 0.502, confirming convergence is gap-driven.

claims.claim: Proposition 7.1 shows that combining depth-induced scaling and spectral separation recovers deep-linear-like singular-value training dynamics for fixed-gates networks without the balanced-initialization assumption required by prior analyses (Proposition 7.1).
claims.evidence: An exact diagonal depth-scaled construction satisfying the proposition's assumptions to 1.67e-16 precision produced up to 64.9% relative error in the proposition's predicted singular-value derivative, while the correct balanced deep-linear expression had 0% error on the same construction.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.5 recovers the balanced deep-linear singular-value ODE of Arora et al. (2019), ds_k/dt = -L s_k(t)^{2-2/L} <grad_J L, u_k v_k^T>, as a special case of the paper's more general framework (Proposition 4.5).
claims.evidence: Direct evaluation of the exact layerwise gradient recurrence for identity gates and balanced diagonal factors at depths L={2,3,5} matched the Arora et al. ODE ds_k/dt = -L s_k^{2-2/L} <grad_J L, u_k v_k^T> to maximum relative error 4.12e-16 (float64 rounding scale).

claims.claim: On a synthetic rank-10 regression task with depth-10, width-64 networks, the top-15 Jacobian log-singular values during training converge toward the predicted theoretical Lyapunov exponents and finite-depth corrections (Figure 1, Figures 2-3).
claims.evidence: Nominal dimensions (rank-10, depth-10, width-64, 3 seeds, 180 steps) were used, but author hyperparameters were unavailable; top-10 modes grew 5.62x vs 1.14x for modes 11–15, yet the critical s10/s11 gap amplification was only 0.719 (did not sharpen), and the fitted theory scale was itself estimated rather than confirmed.

claims.claim: Controlled MNIST experiments with square hidden layers of width n=128 validate the predicted emergence of depth-induced low-rank clustering and singular-vector alignment near a diagonal structure (Figure 4, Figures 5-6).
claims.evidence: Only a 4096-example MNIST subset was trained for 5 CPU epochs at width-128/depth-10; alignment correlation rose from 0.322 to 0.620 (predicted direction) but depth-affine R² fell from 0.976 to 0.864 and the s10/s11 gap decreased from 1.111 to 1.043, giving mixed evidence at far reduced scale.

MarxistLeninist/2kSBDoP1rE.overall: The logbook provides rigorous exact-algebra and Monte-Carlo evidence that two theorems (6.1, 4.5) hold while two printed formulas (Theorem 5.3's finite-depth sign, Proposition 7.1's derivative) are falsified by deterministic counterexamples. The two training experiments (synthetic regression, MNIST) run at reduced or incomplete scale with mixed diagnostics, yielding only toy-level support.

MarxistLeninist/repro-conditional-equiva.paper_title: Conditional Equivalence of DPO and RLHF: Assumptions, Failure Modes, and Provable Alignment

claims.claim: The paper proves DPO-RLHF equivalence is conditional on the RLHF-optimal policy preferring human-preferred responses (Section 3).
claims.evidence: E1 grid over 200k random Bradley-Terry preference pairs shows DPO population optimum equals RLHF-optimal margin to max abs error 1.07e-14; E2 Newton optimization converges to the same optimum from neutral init with max error 2.90e-12. claims.claim: When the equivalence assumption fails, DPO optimizes relative advantage over the reference policy rather than absolute human-preference alignment (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Of 66,812 pairs with delta_pi* < 0 (misaligned reference), all 66,812 have DPO optimum delta_theta* < 0, meaning the trained policy prefers the dispreferred response while still improving margin relative to pi_ref. This directly demonstrates DPO optimizing relative advantage over absolute alignment.

claims.claim: The paper characterizes undesirable solution spaces in which policies reduce DPO loss while preferring dispreferred responses (Section 3).
claims.evidence: For all 66,812 misaligned pairs, per-pair DPO loss L_DPO(delta_theta) is strictly monotonically decreasing across the interval (delta_ref, min(0, delta_pi*)) — entirely within the misaligned region — confirming loss reduction does not imply alignment.

claims.claim: Constrained Preference Optimization augments RLHF with constraints and derives a stationary DPO-like loss with an adaptive reference-based margin (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: E3 gamma sweep on a deliberately misaligned problem: derived gamma* = 6.40e-4, fraction of misaligned CPO optima drops to 0 for all gamma >= gamma*, with exactly one pair on the boundary at gamma* and at least one negative just below. The adaptive margin formula and its threshold guarantee are numerically confirmed.

claims.claim: The paper gives a soft-margin ranking interpretation showing DPO can implement margin ranking with potentially negative targets (Section 5).
claims.evidence: E4 numerically evaluates (1/beta)(-log sigma(beta(delta_theta - delta_ref))) for beta up to 500 on both sides: correct side converges to hinge 0 (error 2.7e-242), wrong side converges to hinge 1.4 (error 2.2e-16), confirming the beta->inf hinge limit with potentially negative target delta_ref.

claims.claim: Experiments on standard benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance for CPO (Section 6).
claims.evidence: Claim 6 concerns standard LLM benchmarks, but the reproduction only runs a synthetic contextual Bradley-Terry bandit (800 contexts, K=4, softmax policy) showing CPO alignment accuracy 0.987 vs DPO 0.647. No LLM fine-tuning or real benchmark data was used; the setup is a simplified proxy task confirming the mechanism's direction.

MarxistLeninist/repro-conditional-equiva.overall: The logbook provides rigorous numerical verification of all five theoretical claims (C1–C5) at machine precision on large-scale finite Bradley-Terry problems, including the conditional equivalence theorem, failure modes, undesirable solution spaces, CPO's adaptive margin guarantee, and the soft-margin hinge limit. AceVikings/repro-loss-aware-distribution.paper_title: Loss-Aware Distributionally Robust Optimization via Trainable Optimal Transport Ambiguity Sets

claims.claim: The paper formulates learning the ambiguity set for OT-DRO as a bilevel problem in which the upper level tunes the ambiguity-set geometry parameter theta and the lower level solves a standard OT-DRO problem (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The authors' pinned code (commit 6e8d18f) was executed with 15 portfolio and 100 regression bilevel runs, all finite, using the real Clarabel conic OT-DRO lower-level solver and upper-level Mahalanobis geometry L updates via optimize_transportation_matrix, directly instantiating the two-level formulation.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 establishes that the proposed hypergradient descent procedure converges to a critical point of the bilevel problem under mild conditions, including square-summable step sizes (Section 5.1, Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook only confirms via text search that the paper states the theorem, and runs 115 finite bilevel optimizations with fixed step sizes (not square-summable-but-not-summable). The proof itself was not checked, and finite fixed-step runs cannot establish asymptotic critical-point convergence as claimed by the theorem.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 computes hypergradients through the nonsmooth conservative implicit function theorem, allowing differentiation through conic (OT-DRO) programs without assuming the solution map is continuously differentiable (Section 5, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: A direct hypergradient check on the authors' Gaussian portfolio conic program compared the nonsmooth adjoint derivative against central differences (step 2e-5) for all lower-triangular coordinates of L, yielding max absolute error 5.87e-9 and max relative error 0.00587, with the dominant coordinate matching at -0.2401374.

claims.claim: In portfolio optimization experiments with k=2, J=30, n_b=20, gamma=0.05, beta=0.1, the relative improvement of the learned ambiguity set over a fixed Wasserstein ball increases as sample size decreases (Section 6.1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Using k=2, n_b=20, gamma=0.05, beta=0.1 with J∈{15,30,60} and 5 seeds each, mean worst-case relative improvement decreased monotonically with sample size: 4.807% at J=15, 2.770% at J=30, 0.723% at J=60, confirming the claimed trend.

claims.claim: Figure 3 shows the learned ambiguity set still enforces the coverage constraint, containing the true data-generating distribution with the specified high probability despite being shaped to reduce loss (Section 6.1, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Ten paired J=30 runs at 250 steps showed 80% coverage (8/10) in both constrained and unconstrained branches, below the nominal 90% implied by beta=0.1. The penalty reduced mean normalized distance (0.7026 vs 0.7136) but did not change the binary coverage rate; with only 10 runs this neither confirms nor refutes the paper's larger-scale Figure 3 claim.

claims.claim: Across 10 independent linear regression trials, the learned decision-focused ambiguity set consistently yields less conservative (lower average loss) decisions than baseline OT-DRO ambiguity sets (Section 6.2, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: The 10-model × 10-dataset regression design (100 runs) showed worst-case objective improvement in 100/100 runs (mean 0.925%) and OOS absolute error improvement in 95/100 runs (mean 0.267%, range -0.14% to +0.48%), confirming the average reduction in conservatism.

AceVikings/repro-loss-aware-distribution.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence from the authors' pinned code verifying the bilevel formulation (Claim 1), hypergradient correctness (Claim 3), the portfolio sample-size trend (Claim 4), and average regression improvement (Claim 6). The theorem convergence claim (Claim 2) is only text-checked and supported by finite runs, while the coverage constraint claim (Claim 5) is not reproduced at the reduced 10-run/250-step scale.
