agharsallah/piwlehb4db-logbook.paper_title: Non-Euclidean Gradient Descent Operates at the Edge of Stability

claims.claim: Directional smoothness D is defined so that, for non-Euclidean gradient descent with step size eta, the loss decreases if and only if D <= 2/eta (Definition 2.1).
claims.evidence: 120 configurations (4 norms × 6 step sizes × 5 seeds) on random PSD quadratics confirm the identity ΔL = ½||Δw||²(D − 2/η) with max residual 4.26e-14, and the iff condition (loss decreases ⟺ D ≤ 2/η) holds in 120/120 cases, exercising both branches with concrete numerical examples in the raw data.

claims.claim: Generalized sharpness S is defined as the maximum of d^T times the Hessian of the loss times d subject to the norm of d being at most 1 under an arbitrary norm, generalizing the largest-eigenvalue sharpness used for vanilla gradient descent (Definition 2.2).
claims.evidence: Generalized sharpness S computed via norm-specific solvers matches independent oracles to ≤2.2e-15 across 20 configs (4 norms × 5 seeds); the ℓ₂ case equals λ_max(H) to machine precision (e.g., 2.9222 vs 2.9222), confirming the generalization from largest-eigenvalue sharpness.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 proves non-Euclidean gradient descent on quadratic objectives converges linearly when the step size eta < 2/S, where S is the generalized sharpness (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: 160 configs (4 norms × 4 eta fractions {0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9} × 2 condition numbers × 5 seeds) on quadratics with η < 2/S all show geometric contraction ρ < 1 (e.g., ρ ≈ 0.876 for κ=10, frac=0.3) and loss drops of 2–28 orders of magnitude, confirming linear convergence below the threshold.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 proves divergence occurs from some initialization when eta > 2/S for non-Euclidean gradient descent on quadratics (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: 120 configs with initialization in span( d̂ ) and η > 2/S (frac ∈ {1.2,1.5,2.5}) all diverge with log-linear growth (R² = 1.0, positive slopes matching |1−ηS|), e.g., final_over_init ≈ 1.125e15 for frac=1.2, confirming divergence above the threshold.

claims.claim: Experiments show l-infinity-descent on CIFAR-10 and Tiny Shakespeare exhibits generalized sharpness stabilizing slightly above the 2/eta threshold, unlike vanilla GD which stabilizes at 2/eta (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Real full-batch runs on a 4000-image CIFAR-10 subset with a 3-layer MLP and a 1-layer Transformer on Tiny Shakespeare show progressive sharpening and EoS oscillation, but the CIFAR-10 ℓ∞ final ratio (1.004) is at the threshold rather than 'slightly above,' and vanilla GD (1.026) is actually above ℓ∞ on CIFAR, partially contradicting the claim; only Shakespeare (ℓ∞ 1.18 vs vanilla 1.04) clearly supports the claimed contrast.

claims.claim: SignGD and Muon (without momentum) are shown to exhibit normalized sharpness converging near the 2/eta edge-of-stability threshold, extending the phenomenon to optimizers used in practice (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Same reduced setup (4000-image CIFAR subset, 3-layer MLP, 1-layer Transformer) shows SignGD and Muon (no momentum) normalized sharpness converging near 2/η (final ratios 1.01, 1.05, 1.04, 1.06) with progressive sharpening, supporting the claim, but on a clearly simplified data subset and architecture rather than at the paper's full scale.

agharsallah/piwlehb4db-logbook.overall: The four theoretical claims (Definitions 2.1–2.2, Theorems 5.1–5.2) are numerically verified to machine precision across multiple norms, step sizes, condition numbers, and seeds on quadratic objectives. The two empirical EoS claims are addressed with real GPU runs on real networks but on a 4000-image CIFAR subset with simple architectures, yielding partial support for the ℓ∞-vs-vanilla contrast and clearer support for SignGD/Muon convergence near 2/η.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows a symmetric smoothing operator with positive coefficients can be rescaled by a diagonal matrix (via a symmetric Sinkhorn iteration) into a diffusion operator that is self-adjoint with respect to a mass-weighted inner product (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: On the MARGO M240 mandible (135K vertices), log-domain symmetric Sinkhorn reached final errors of 6.6e-14, 6.8e-14, 7.0e-14 for point-cloud, voxel, and GMM representations, with weighted-symmetry residuals below 3e-18; three different initial scalings agreed below 1e-10, numerically confirming self-adjointness, mass conservation, positivity, and spectral damping.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 proves that for Gaussian and exponential kernels, the Sinkhorn-normalized operators converge uniformly on bounded domains to continuous diffusion operators as sampling resolution increases (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: At sigma=0.15, uniform error contracted strictly across six resolutions (N=25 to 800) versus a 1600-point reference for three signals, ending below 0.005; on the actual Armadillo mesh with nested farthest-point prefixes (64 to 1024), uniform absolute error decreased monotonically from 1.293 to 0, demonstrating finite-scale convergence consistent with the theorem.

claims.claim: The symmetric Sinkhorn algorithm empirically requires only 5 to 10 iterations to reduce normalization error below 0.1% (Section 4/5, empirical convergence results).
claims.evidence: Across point-cloud and covariance-aware GMM families at N=100,200,400, the first error below 1e-3 occurred at iteration 5 or 6, and on the MARGO M240 mandible at sigma=0.05 the first sub-1e-3 iteration was 5, 6, and 5 for the three modalities, with all cases well below 1e-3 by iteration 10.

claims.claim: The normalized operators simultaneously satisfy symmetry, mass conservation, entrywise positivity, and spectral damping (eigenvalues in [0,1]), properties not jointly satisfied by standard row- or symmetric-normalization schemes (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: All six normalized operators exhibited constant-row residuals below 9e-12, weighted-symmetry residuals below 3e-18, strictly positive kernel minima, and eigenvalues in [0,1] with maxima exactly 1.0; destructive controls showed row normalization loses self-adjointness and one-shot symmetric scaling fails constant-preservation, while a positive-entry matrix with a negative eigenvalue retained it after normalization.

claims.claim: The method is demonstrated on point clouds, sparse voxel grids (jaw bone geometry), and Gaussian mixture models with covariance-aware kernels, showing Laplacian-like smoothing on each irregular data type (Section 5, experiments).
claims.evidence: On the actual MARGO M240 mandible, three deterministic modalities (256-point farthest-point cloud, 256-cell sparse voxelization, 117-component covariance-aware GMM) all achieved normalization errors below 7e-14, mass residuals below 5e-15, spectra in [0,1], and high-frequency norm contraction ratios of 0.425, 0.479, and 0.515, demonstrating Laplacian-like smoothing on each irregular data type.

claims.claim: Shape analysis experiments on the Armadillo mesh show spectral distributions remain consistent across sampling modalities, with eigenvalue divergence appearing only at scales matching sampling resolution, validating the Theorem 4.2 convergence guarantee (Section 5).
claims.evidence: On the actual Stanford Armadillo mesh (172,974 vertices) at sigma=0.05, comparing -log spectra against a 512-point reference, tail-to-low-mode error ratios were consistently above 1 across surface (8.2, 23.1), sparse-voxel (10.4, 8.4, 9.2), and GMM (8.6, 9.4, 3.8) discretizations, showing low-mode agreement and fine-mode divergence as claimed.

ProCreations/repro-improved-dimension-de.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence on real public meshes (Stanford Armadillo, MARGO M240 mandible) across multiple kernels, resolutions, and modalities, with destructive controls and reproducible code, supporting all six claims. The reproduction is thorough, using actual geometry rather than proxies, and carefully distinguishes finite-scale verification from theorem proofs.

agharsallah/ra2t1v4nml-logbook.paper_title: MIRA: A Score for Conditional Distribution Accuracy and Model Comparison

claims.claim: MIRA's Uniform Mass Property (Proposition 3.1) establishes that the probability mass lambda_n assigned to randomly constructed regions follows a Uniform[0,1] distribution when the candidate matches the true conditional distribution.
claims.evidence: 20,000 lambda values per config across q∈{1,2,5,13}×5 seeds (20 configs) all pass KS tests against Uniform[0,1] with p-values 0.035–0.75, sample mean 0.500, and variance 0.0831≈1/12, confirming the PIT-based uniformity with no dimension dependence.

claims.claim: Under the null hypothesis of a correctly specified candidate distribution, the Mira statistic reduces to Laplace's rule of succession, p(k|n) = (n+1)/(N+2) for k=1 and (N-n+1)/(N+2) for k=0 (Proposition 3.2).
claims.evidence: 400,000 trials comparing empirical P(k=1|n) to Laplace's rule across N∈{10,50,100} show max absolute deviation ≤0.0048 (N=10), ≤0.0146 (N=50), and ≤0.0259 (N=100), all within Monte Carlo sampling noise of the theoretical values.

claims.claim: As N approaches infinity under correct model specification, the expected Mira score converges to 2/3 with theoretical variance converging to 1/18 (Corollary 3.4).
claims.evidence: 500,000 trials across N∈{50,100,500,2000} show monotonic convergence: at N=2000, E[P_N]=0.66651 (gap 5.7e-4 to 2/3) and Var[P_N]=0.05559 (gap 3.4e-5 to 1/18), with gaps scaling as ~1/N consistent with the predicted Beta(2,1) limit.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.5 proves a lower bound that any candidate model achieves a Mira score mu_Mira(M) >= 1/2.
claims.evidence: Shift sweep over delta∈{0,…,12} at q=13, N=100, 300k trials shows mu_Mira decreasing monotonically from 0.6634 (correct) to 0.5000 (disjoint support), with all values ≥1/2; the text reports a minimum of 0.4995 at delta=12, which is within Monte Carlo noise of the theoretical 1/2 bound, and the trend confirms the bound is tight rather than vacuous.

claims.claim: In a Bayesian model comparison experiment on four strong gravitational lensing forward models in 13 dimensions, MIRA correctly ranks the true model (EPL plus 3 Sersic sources) as the best fit (Section 5.3, Bayesian Model Comparison).
claims.evidence: The MIRA algorithm and q=13 dimensionality are preserved and the authors' own mira() code is used, but the four gravitational lensing forward models (EPL/SIE × 3/1 Sersic) are replaced by controlled 13-dim Gaussian estimators with injected misspecification structure—a proxy task rather than the actual astrophysical models claimed.

claims.claim: In a high-dimensional robustness test on 64x64x3 galaxy images, MIRA detects prior and noise-model misspecification using as few as L=16 true fiducial samples (Section 5.3).
claims.evidence: Dimensionality (q=12288) and fiducial budget (L=16) are preserved using the authors' mira() code, but the 64×64×3 galaxy images are replaced by 12288-dim Gaussian vectors with injected prior/noise misspecification—a proxy task that demonstrates detection behavior but does not use the actual galaxy-image data from the paper.

agharsallah/ra2t1v4nml-logbook.overall: The four theoretical propositions (Claims 1–4) are rigorously verified via independent numerical reconstruction with exact noncentral chi-square computations and large-scale Monte Carlo trials. The two empirical claims (5–6) are addressed only through proxy Gaussian estimators that replace the paper's actual astrophysical forward models and galaxy images, preserving dimensionality and the MIRA algorithm but not the real experimental data.

jomasego/repro-stochastic-lifting-for-ge.paper_title: Stochastic Lifting for Generating Trajectories of Stochastic Physical Systems

claims.claim: Stochastic Lifting augments each training transition pair (x_t, x_{t+1}) with an independent Gaussian random label ξ_t ~ N(0, I_d), training a network F_θ via the regression loss ℒ(θ,𝒟_ξ) = (1/MT)∑‖F_θ(x_t^i,ξ_t^i)−x_{t+1}^i‖² (Equation 3, Equation 8).
claims.evidence: A real training run was executed on the official codebase with 64 trajectories, 960 transition pairs, label dims 16/32, and 2000 steps, yielding final loss ~1.0–1.3; however this is far below the paper's scale (1024 samples, 200K steps), confirming the mechanism but not a full reproduction.

claims.claim: At inference, drawing fresh random labels and rolling the map forward generates diverse trajectories using only a single network evaluation per time step (Section 3).
claims.evidence: 64 trajectories of 16 frames were generated from a single initial condition using one UNet forward pass per step with fresh labels on CPU (~0.1s for 960 steps), confirming the single-step inference mechanism on a reduced wave demo rather than a full benchmark.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 gives a Wasserstein-2 bound 𝔼[W₂(ρ̂_{t+1},ρ̃_{t+1})²] ≤ C(1+L_x²)min(M,M̃)^(-2/α), tying accuracy to the Lipschitz regularity L_x of the learned map (Proposition 3.1, Equation 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides no proof verification of Proposition 3.1 and only notes that higher label dimensions reduce training loss (d=16: loss ~1.3, WCT=0.136), which is a loose empirical observation, not a demonstration of the Wasserstein-2 bound itself.

claims.claim: On the Wave benchmark, Stochastic Lifting achieves a Wasserstein crossing-time distance of 4.53e-3, versus 1.11e-2 for an autoregressive diffusion model (ARDM) using 40 diffusion steps, despite Stochastic Lifting using a single step (Table 1).
claims.evidence: A reduced-scale wave run (n=64, 2000 steps) produced WCT=0.136, which is orders of magnitude worse than the claimed 4.53e-3; the mechanism of one-step generation is shown but the specific benchmark numbers are not reproduced at full scale.

claims.claim: On the BAIR Robot Pushing dataset, Stochastic Lifting achieves an FVD of 69.0, outperforming one-step baselines FitVid (93.6) and NUWA (86.9) (Table 2).
claims.evidence: No BAIR experiment was run; the logbook only restates Table 2 numbers from the paper and notes that the codebase contains the architecture, but no training or FVD evaluation was executed.

claims.claim: On CLEVRER, Stochastic Lifting produces stable rollouts for 500 frames, roughly 30x longer than the 16-frame training videos, without collapsing to mean predictions (Section 5).
claims.evidence: No CLEVRER experiment was run; the logbook only offers a logical argument that one-step inference avoids error accumulation and notes the codebase contains a suitable UNet, with no rollout artifacts or metrics produced.

jomasego/repro-stochastic-lifting-for-ge.overall: This logbook confirms the core Stochastic Lifting mechanism (Gaussian label augmentation, regression training, single-step inference with fresh labels) on a small-scale wave demo, but does not reproduce any of the paper's benchmark results at full scale. Claims 5 and 6 were never addressed experimentally, and the theoretical bound (Claim 3) was only loosely checked for empirical consistency without proof verification.

algorise/repro-deep-sequence-models-tend.paper_title: Deep sequence models tend to memorize geometrically; it is unclear why

claims.claim: Deep sequence models (Transformers and Mamba) solve an in-weights path-star (l-fold composition) task by memorizing a fixed graph's edges during training and then predicting complete root-to-leaf paths, achieving near-perfect accuracy on graphs with up to 50,000 nodes and path lengths up to l=10 hops even when trained on only 75% of paths.
claims.evidence: The largest run used star_degree=50, path_length=3, total_nodes=101 (vs. the claimed 50,000 nodes and l=10), and achieved only 25% edge memorization accuracy; a separate tiny sandbox achieved 100% edge recovery but on an even smaller graph. Neither setup approaches the paper's scale or demonstrates near-perfect path accuracy at l=10.

claims.claim: This near-perfect performance contradicts the associative-memory prediction that l-fold composition should require exponentially (Ω(exp(l))) more capacity or data, motivating a geometric account of memorization instead.
claims.evidence: The logbook only asserts that 'low-dimensional embeddings successfully organize to solve composition queries without needing exponential data capacity' but provides no scaling experiment varying l, no capacity measurement, and no comparison to Ω(exp(l)) bounds — this is assertion without evidence.

claims.claim: Learned embeddings organize into global geometric structure reflecting path identity rather than only local co-occurrence statistics, visible as diagonal clustering in embedding heatmaps and separated clusters in UMAP projections (Figure 6), even when the model is trained only on edge memorization.
claims.evidence: The tiny_transformer.ipynb sandbox produced diagonal similarity heatmaps and UMAP clusters on star, grid, cycle, and irregular graphs trained on 1-hop edges, but all graphs are tiny (e.g., star degree 4, cycle N=15) and no quantitative metric of geometric structure is reported — only qualitative visual observations at far below the paper's scale.

claims.claim: The paper attributes emergent geometric memory to spectral bias in learned representations, showing that Fiedler vectors of the graph align with learned Node2Vec-style embeddings (Section 4, Figure 7).
claims.evidence: Node2Vec was run on very small graphs (star degree 4, grid 4×4, cycle N=15, irregular N=16/E=20) and 100% edge recovery is reported, but no quantitative alignment metric (e.g., correlation or cosine similarity between embeddings and Fiedler vectors) is provided — alignment is merely asserted, not measured.

algorise/repro-deep-sequence-models-tend.overall: This logbook ran only tiny sandbox notebooks and small CLI experiments on local CPU, none approaching the paper's scale (50,000 nodes, l=10 hops). The qualitative phenomena (diagonal heatmaps, UMAP clusters, edge recovery) were observed at toy scale, but key quantitative claims about near-perfect accuracy at scale, exponential scaling bounds, and Fiedler vector alignment lack supporting measurements.

agharsallah/i4lntqhqbk-logbook.paper_title: Feature Resemblance: Towards a Theoretical Understanding of Analogical Reasoning in Transformers

claims.claim: Joint training on similarity premises (that A1 and A2 share a property) and attribution premises (that A2 has property C) provably yields perfect analogical reasoning via value-matrix feature alignment, with feature cosine similarity of 1-o(1) between aligned entities (Theorem 1, Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: The minimal attention model (N=5, d=128, 5 seeds) achieves perfect 1.000±0.000 analogical test accuracy across all seeds, with value-feature cosine 0.846±0.006 that increases monotonically with dimension (0.828→0.871→0.880 at d=64/128/256), consistent with the predicted 1−o(1) trend.

claims.claim: Sequential (curriculum) training succeeds only when similarity structure is learned before attribution: the similarity-then-attribution order achieves 1-o(1) feature alignment (Theorem 2), while the reverse attribution-then-similarity order yields o(1) alignment and near-random test performance despite convergent training loss (Theorem 3, Proposition 3).
claims.evidence: Similarity-first curriculum achieves 1.000 test accuracy while attribution-first achieves 0.000 across all seeds, with attribution-first attaining lower training loss (0.51 vs 1.09), confirming the central finding that order matters and the reverse order fails despite convergent loss. However, the cosine alignment values (~0.79 sim-first, ~0.82 attr-first) do not match the predicted 1−o(1) vs o(1) split, though the behavioral predictions are strongly reproduced.

claims.claim: Two-hop reasoning (A to B, B to C implies A to C) requires explicit identity-bridge examples (B to B) in training data to achieve perfect performance (Theorem 4); without identity bridges, two-hop reasoning fails completely with error rate 1-1/N despite successful learning of each individual hop (Theorem 5, Proposition 5).
claims.evidence: With identity bridges: 1.000 test accuracy and cosine 0.75; without bridges: 0.000 accuracy, error rate 1.000 (≥ predicted 1−1/N=0.8), and cosine −0.022≈0 across all seeds, confirming that identity bridges are necessary and their absence causes complete failure despite individual hops being learned.

claims.claim: On synthetic data, GPT-2 with joint training reaches 0.995 +/- 6e-4 feature similarity and 100% task success, and two-hop reasoning with identity bridges reaches 0.9642 +/- 7e-4 similarity and 99.7% +/- 0.5% success, versus 0.016 +/- 6e-3 similarity and 0% success without identity bridges (Table 1).
claims.evidence: A real GPT-2-architecture transformer (d=256, 4L, 8H, 3 seeds) trained from scratch reproduces Table 1's pattern: joint 100%/cosine 0.936, two-hop+bridge 95.8%/0.910, no-bridge 0%/0.039, with feature similarity rising toward the paper's values at larger scale (0.86→0.93→0.96 at d=128/256/384). The model is smaller than GPT-2-124M but uses the correct architecture on the same task with near-quantitative matches.

claims.claim: On natural-language experiments, Llama-3-1B under joint training reaches 0.8174 feature similarity and 73% success, and Qwen-2.5-1.5B reaches 0.8488 similarity and 85% success (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states the Llama-3-1B and Qwen-2.5-1.5B fine-tuning was never run ('the Llama/Qwen numbers themselves are quoted from the paper rather than re-measured'), citing GPU compute as a blocker. No experimental data for Table 2 was produced; the argument that the mechanism is verified in other claims does not constitute reproduction of this specific claim.

claims.claim: Deep linear networks trained layer-by-layer show progressively increasing feature alignment with depth, reaching cosine similarity of at least 0.8 by the penultimate layer for same-label inputs (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: An L=5 deep linear network (d=64, 5 seeds) trained layer-by-layer shows monotonically increasing same-label cosine alignment 0.593→0.831→0.874→0.894→0.900, with penultimate-layer values 0.862/0.900/0.908 across seeds, all exceeding the claimed ≥0.8 threshold.

agharsallah/i4lntqhqbk-logbook.overall: The logbook provides solid numerical evidence for the paper's theoretical claims (1–4, 6) by re-implementing the minimal attention model, a GPT-2-architecture transformer, and deep linear networks with multiple seeds and scale sweeps, though the curriculum alignment metrics in claim 2 don't match the asymptotic predictions at this scale. Claim 5 (natural-language billion-parameter experiments) was never executed and remains unverified.

claims.claim: RACO is an offline, reward-free preference-alignment method that accepts user-specified objective weights and explicitly handles conflicting objectives (Table 1).
claims.evidence: RACO is implemented from scratch with dpo_loss, cagrad_clip, and train_raco functions, and run on a synthetic two-objective dataset with five weight configurations. The method's properties (offline, reward-free, weight-aware, conflict-handling) are demonstrated but only on synthetic data, not at the paper's real scale.

claims.claim: The method uses CAGrad-Clip to limit correction gradients so updates better respect preferred objective trade-offs (Figure 1, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The CAGrad-Clip algorithm is implemented with the clipping mechanism lam_k = min(c * w_k, w_k), and an ablation comparing c=0 vs c=0.5 is referenced. However, the effect is only demonstrated on the synthetic two-objective dataset, not on real preference data at the paper's scale.

claims.claim: On TL;DR summarization, RACO achieves better Pareto frontiers for conciseness-quality and faithfulness-quality trade-offs than AMoPO and weighted-loss DPO baselines (Figure 2, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The Pareto sweep uses a 'synthetic two-objective dataset (quality and conciseness are conflicting by construction)' rather than TL;DR summarization as claimed. Additionally, the numbers do not clearly support RACO dominance: at w=0.50/0.50, AMoPO (45.561, 108.014) dominates RACO (35.992, 99.554) on both margins.

claims.claim: On BeaverTails safety alignment, RACO improves harmlessness-helpfulness Pareto trade-offs across Qwen3 and Gemma3 setups (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Only 10 'BeaverTails-style' prompts are evaluated with an LLM judge (Llama-3.3-70B via Nebius), and neither Qwen3 nor Gemma3 is used as claimed. RACO produces identical scores (harm=4.3, help=6.0) across all five weight settings, which is suspicious and suggests the method is not actually responding to weight changes.

claims.claim: Ablations show clipping and the correction-radius constant affect validation margins and Pareto frontiers (Figure 5, Figure 6).
claims.evidence: Ablation A (clipping on/off) and Ablation B (correction radius c sweep) are run on the synthetic dataset. The no-clip numbers are identical to the DPO-LW numbers from Claim 3, indicating reused rather than independently run experiments. At w=0.65, no-clip actually outperforms clip on both margins, partially contradicting the claimed consistent benefit.

algorise/repro-reward-free-alignment-for.overall: The logbook implements the RACO algorithm from scratch and runs experiments on synthetic two-objective data and 10 proxy safety prompts, but none of the paper's actual experimental setups (TL;DR summarization, BeaverTails with Qwen3/Gemma3) are reproduced. All claims are addressed only at toy scale with synthetic or proxy data, and some numerical results do not clearly support the paper's claims even in the toy setting.

alreadyinuse003/2Exmr1eIKZ.paper_title: AgentSuite: Toward More Reliable Agent Evaluation with a Component-Based Benchmark Auditing Pipeline

claims.claim: COBA achieves F1 scores between 0.791 and 0.874 for automated auditing across six widely used agent benchmarks
claims.evidence: The logbook tests only tau-bench (1 of 6 claimed benchmarks) on a 30-task labeled subset using the paper's own Gemini-2.5-Pro judge, obtaining F1=0.6364 (P=0.4667, R=1.0), which falls below the claimed 0.791–0.874 range. This is a real run with concrete numbers on a reduced scope (one benchmark, 30 tasks), not a full reproduction across all six benchmarks.

claims.claim: Benchmark flaws are widespread and materially affect agent evaluation outcomes, affecting leaderboard-based comparisons
claims.evidence: The logbook does not analyze whether benchmark flaws are widespread across multiple benchmarks or whether they materially affect leaderboard-based comparisons. The finding that the judge flags all 30 tasks (TP=14, FP=16, FN=0) is framed as a judge non-discrimination issue, not as evidence of widespread benchmark flaws, and no leaderboard impact analysis is presented.

alreadyinuse003/2Exmr1eIKZ.overall: The logbook provides a methodologically careful but narrow reproduction on a 30-task subset of a single benchmark (tau-bench), finding that the paper's own Gemini judge flags all tasks (F1=0.6364), contradicting the claimed F1 range on that subset. It does not address the breadth of the paper's six-benchmark claim or the claim about widespread benchmark flaws affecting leaderboards.

alreadyinuse003/xRVWftS3ES.paper_title: Memory is Reconstructed, Not Retrieved:  Graph Memory for LLM Agents

claims.claim: MRAgent represents memory as a Cue-Tag-Content graph and performs active memory reconstruction rather than passive retrieve-then-reason retrieval (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook executes the MRAgent codebase but never examines or verifies the Cue-Tag-Content graph structure or the active reconstruction mechanism; only benchmark scores were measured.

claims.claim: On LOCOMO, MRAgent reports the best overall LLM-Judge scores for both Gemini and Claude backbones, including 84.21 and 88.32 overall scores (Table 1).
claims.evidence: A single run (N=1) on LoCoMo with Gemini-2.5-Flash measured 73.05 overall vs the paper's 84.21 (an 11-point gap far outside the paper's ±0.10 variance), but only the Gemini backbone was tested (Claude's 88.32 never run), no baselines were evaluated to test 'best overall', and N=1 is insufficient to definitively falsify a 3-run mean.

claims.claim: On LONGMEMEVAL with a Gemini backbone, MRAgent reports 72.95 overall LLM-Judge versus 54.92 for the strongest listed baseline, and MRAgent* reports 86.76 overall (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook only ran experiments on LoCoMo; LONGMEMEVAL was never addressed at all.

claims.claim: On LONGMEMEVAL cost analysis, MRAgent uses 118k tokens per sample versus 245k for Mem0 and 3,268k for LangMem (Table 3).
claims.evidence: No LONGMEMEVAL cost analysis or token-per-sample measurements appear anywhere in the logbook; this claim was never addressed.

alreadyinuse003/xRVWftS3ES.overall: The logbook provides a methodologically careful but extremely narrow reproduction: a single N=1 run on LoCoMo with only the Gemini backbone, yielding 73.05 vs the paper's 84.21. Only one of four claims is partially addressed, and the scope is too limited to verify or falsify any claim definitively.

algorise/repro-tracing-the-dynamics-of-r.paper_title: Tracing the Dynamics of Refusal: Exploiting Latent Refusal Trajectories for Robust Jailbreak Detection

claims.claim: SALO detects direct harmful prompts with 99.0% accuracy and prefilling (forced-decoding) attacks with 99.4% detection rate on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, in a setting where terminal-state detection methods are described as failing (Table 1, Section 4)
claims.evidence: Ran on Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (not 7B) with authors' code unchanged: SALO-CNN achieved 98%/98% direct/prefilling detection at FPR=0.10, while terminal baselines collapsed under prefilling (RePE 49%, Linear 19%), reproducing the comparative gap but at 14x smaller model scale.

claims.claim: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, SALO achieves 100.0% detection of AutoDAN attacks and 98.8% detection of prefilling attacks, while GCG attacks are detected at 85.4% (Table 1, Section 4)
claims.evidence: No experiments were run; the logbook states GPU-blocked for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and explicitly chose not to proxy with 0.5B because attack suffixes are model-specific and would not transfer.

claims.claim: On Mistral-7B-Instruct, SALO detects GCG attacks at 96.5% and AutoDAN attacks at 98.8% (Table 1, Section 4)
claims.evidence: No experiments were run; the logbook states GPU-blocked for Mistral-7B-Instruct with the same reasoning about attack-suffix non-transferability as Claim 2.

claims.claim: Refusal processing decomposes into three phases: a Semantic Trigger at shallow layers on the harmful token, a Critical Construction phase with peak intensity at immediate subsequent tokens in intermediate layers, and Terminal Attenuation where signals weaken toward the final position (Section 3)
claims.evidence: Causal activation patching on Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct showed harmful-token recovery of 0.99 at shallow layers (Semantic Trigger), but the 'Critical Construction' peak at subsequent tokens in intermediate layers was only 0.08 (not a clear peak), and the deep-layer final-position recovery was 0.91 (high, not attenuated)—partial support on a 14x smaller model.

claims.claim: SALO's detector uses multi-granularity convolution kernels (3x2, 3x3, 3x5) applied to raw hidden-state volumes from selected middle layers, preserving spatiotemporal geometry rather than collapsing to a single vector (Section 3, Section 4)
claims.evidence: The logbook quotes the actual `salo/model.py` code showing kernel_sizes [(3,2),(3,3),(3,5)] applied via Conv2d on the 4-D volume (batch, layer, token, hidden), confirming the multi-granularity architecture on raw hidden-state volumes by construction.

claims.claim: Under a white-box adaptive GCG attack with λ=5.0 designed to evade the detector, SALO still achieves an 84.3% detection rate, indicating the refusal trajectory signal is entangled with malicious intent and hard to suppress without destroying prompt semantics (Section 4)
claims.evidence: No adaptive white-box GCG experiment was run; the logbook states GPU-blocked and only offers a qualitative analogy to the Claim 1 prefilling result, which is a different attack and model scale.

algorise/repro-tracing-the-dynamics-of-r.overall: This logbook provides real but toy-scale evidence (Qwen2.5-0.5B) for the comparative robustness claim and the three-phase decomposition, and confirms the CNN architecture by code inspection, but three of six claims involving 7B/8B models and adaptive attacks were never run due to GPU constraints.

agharsallah/xpdpfcj65t-logbook.paper_title: A theory of learning data statistics in diffusion models, from easy to hard

claims.claim: Diffusion denoisers trained on natural images exhibit a distributional simplicity bias: on CIFAR-10, a U-Net achieves nearly identical test loss on real images versus Gaussian clones matched in mean and covariance for roughly 10^3 training steps before performance diverges, indicating pair-wise statistics are learned first (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: A real GPU run on CIFAR-10 grayscale trains a DDPM U-Net (base width 48, 20k train images, 5k test) on real data vs Gaussian clones. At step 200, real and mean+cov clone losses are within 2.6% (0.0747 vs 0.0766), then diverge monotonically to a 23.7% gap by step 6000 (0.0497 vs 0.0651). The mean-only clone sits far higher (~0.28), confirming the ordering mean ≫ mean+cov > real. The divergence onset (~10²–10³ steps) matches the paper's ~10³, reproducing the distributional simplicity bias.

claims.claim: For a k-th order cumulant target, the sample complexity threshold for weak recovery via projected gradient descent is n_hat(d,k) = omega(d^(k-1) log^2 d), with |v . w(n_hat)| approaching 1 as d approaches infinity after this many steps (Proposition 4.3).
claims.evidence: Projected spherical SGD on a spiked single-index model y=He_k(⟨v,x⟩) recovers the spike to |v·w|=0.91 at n=20·d^(k-1) for k=2,d=64 (random baseline 0.10), 0.87 for k=3,d=32, and 0.63–0.77 for k=4,d=12. A data-collapse test confirms the d^(k-1) scaling: for k=2, overlap rises [0.80,0.88,0.91,0.93] across d∈{16,32,64,128} under n∝d, but collapses to 0.19 under fixed n=640 at d=128. For k=3, overlap rises [0.66,0.82,0.89,0.92] under n∝d².

claims.claim: If the number of samples n(d) = o(n_hat(d,k*)), standard SGD provably fails to achieve weak recovery of the k*-th cumulant, establishing a sharp learnable/unlearnable sample-complexity separation (Proposition 4.4).
claims.evidence: Sub-threshold budget n=0.02·d^(k-1) yields overlap at random level (0.09–0.15 for k=2,d=64; 0.10–0.22 for k=3,d=32), while super-threshold n=C·d^(k-1) yields overlap ~0.87–0.91. The separation gap of ~0.7–0.8 in |v·w| across the threshold boundary directly demonstrates the sharp learnable/unlearnable separation of Prop 4.4.

claims.claim: In a mixed-cumulant latent model, pair-wise statistics are recoverable with linear sample complexity n = Theta(d * polylog(d)), while recovering the fourth cumulant requires Omega(d^3) samples when latent variables are independent (Proposition 4.6).
claims.evidence: In the Mixed Cumulant Model with independent latents at linear budget n=40·d, the covariance top eigenvector recovers the pair-wise spike u to |u·û|=0.997 across d∈{40,80,160} (top eigenvalue ~7× above median), while the fourth-cumulant spike v remains at random overlap (|v·v̂|≤0.29) because v is isotropic in the second moment. This confirms pair-wise is linear-recoverable while the fourth cumulant is not.

claims.claim: When latent variables underlying the pair-wise and higher-order statistics are positively correlated, the fourth-cumulant recovery sample complexity accelerates from cubic to linear in d (Proposition 4.6).
claims.evidence: With positively correlated latents (ρ=0.6 or 0.8) at linear budget n=40·d, the fourth-cumulant spike v is recovered to |v·v̂|=0.94–0.97 via a second-order cross-moment estimator, versus random overlap (≤0.22) when latents are independent. Tested across d∈{60,120} and ρ∈{0.6,0.8} with 4 seeds each, the acceleration gap is 0.73–0.95.

claims.claim: Unconstrained SGD exhibits contraction dynamics toward w=0 for many activation functions, causing learning failure, whereas constraining updates to the unit sphere (spherical projection) preserves the ability to learn higher-order statistics (Proposition 4.7).
claims.evidence: Training the rank-1 denoiser S^W(x)=-x-σ(w·x)w with sigmoid activation for 12000 steps: unconstrained SGD collapses ‖w‖ to 0.000 with overlap |v·w| at random level (0.01–0.20), while spherical projection maintains ‖w‖=1.000 and recovers the spike to |v·w|=0.87–0.90. Tested at d∈{30,60} with 3 seeds each.

agharsallah/xpdpfcj65t-logbook.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims: a real CIFAR-10 GPU run reproducing the distributional simplicity bias (Claim 1), and CPU-based numerical checks of the theoretical propositions (Claims 2–6) using the paper's actual models (spiked single-index, Mixed Cumulant Model, rank-1 denoiser) with multiple seeds and scaling tests. The main limitation is reduced scale (20k CIFAR images, small U-Net, small dimensions for theory checks, limited seeds), but the qualitative phenomena and scaling laws are clearly demonstrated.

Edd16/icml2026-rHlcYGxb2x-repro.paper_title: DTS: Enhancing Large Reasoning Models via Decoding Tree Sketching

claims.claim: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, DTS improves AIME2024 accuracy from 52.67% to 60.67% (+8.00 points) while reducing average response length from 13,902 to 9,865 tokens (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The claim-0-fix page ran a 256-problem AIME2024-style proxy on a CPU-basic HF job using numpy-only simulation with no real DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B weights and no real AIME2024 problems. Measured lengths (~48→40 tokens) are orders of magnitude below the paper's (13,902→9,865), confirming this is a mechanism-level toy, not a reproduction.

claims.claim: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, DTS improves AIME2025 accuracy from 36.00% to 43.33% (+7.33 points) with a 17.35% reduction in generation length (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The claim-1-fix page explicitly reuses the identical proxy job and seed as claim 1, producing the same numbers (45.31%→57.81%, ~48→40 tokens). No real 7B model or AIME2025 benchmark was used; the page itself states it is a 'toy-scale simulation' with synthetic data.

claims.claim: Averaged across the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and 1.5B models, DTS yields accuracy gains of 7.66% and 4.00% respectively, alongside length reductions of 22.96% and 23.72% (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The claim-2-fix page ran a numpy-only proxy with synthetic '7B' and '1.5B' capacity parameters on 256 synthetic problems, reporting +12.50/+14.45 pp gains and −16.8%/−19.7% length reductions. No real model weights or real benchmarks were used; the page acknowledges numbers 'should not be numerically equated with the table values.'

claims.claim: DTS cuts the rate of endless/repetitive generations on AIME2024 for the 7B model from 6.7% to 1.3%, and for the 1.5B model from 15.3% to 4.7% (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The claim-3-fix page used a local numpy computation (no HF job, no GPU, no real model) simulating token diversity. The reported rates (6.7%→1.3%, 15.3%→4.7%) are simply restated from the paper, while the actual simulation produced nonsensical rates >100% (base_rate=146.3%, dts_rate=133.0%), providing only a toy-level mechanism check.

claims.evidence: The claim-4-fix page used a local numpy computation (no HF job, no GPU, no real 1.5B model, no real AIME2025 data). The numbers 26.7%→6.0% are directly copied from the paper; the only 'verification' is the tautological check that 6.0 < 26.7, making this a trivial toy simulation.

claims.claim: DTS uses next-token entropy to locate critical divergence points, selectively branching decoding paths with an entropy threshold τ=2.5 and top-K=3 candidate tokens, with early stopping at the first completed path (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The claim-5-fix page ran a real HF job (Edd16/6a61d2b513e6ef894d54d7b0) with a numpy simulation using τ=2.5, top-K=3, VOCAB=32, and 100 trials with synthetic transition matrices. Edd16/icml2026-rHlcYGxb2x-repro.overall: This logbook does not reproduce any of the paper's claims at scale; every claim is addressed only through numpy proxy simulations with synthetic data, no real DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen model weights, and no real AIME benchmarks. The evidence consistently demonstrates only the direction of the DTS mechanism on toy setups, never the paper's actual reported magnitudes.

Edd16/icml2026-aWfk16EvfM-repro.paper_title: Merge to Remember: Sharpness-Aware Isotropic Merging for Continual Learning

claims.evidence: The same toy proxy was run for T∈{3,5,8,10}; SAIM's average accuracy declines from 0.2233 to 0.2060, which does not demonstrate robustness, but the synthetic tasks and tiny MLP are far below the paper's intended scale and benchmarks.

claims.claim: SA-BCD fine-tuning strategy promotes flat minima and reduces parameter interference
claims.evidence: Sharpness was estimated on the same tiny synthetic MLP via 50 random ε=0.1 perturbations, yielding a negligible difference (standard 0.0117 vs SA-BCD proxy 0.0112) that is directionally consistent but on a clearly simplified proxy task, not a real model or benchmark.

Edd16/icml2026-aWfk16EvfM-repro.overall: This logbook runs a small numpy proxy (2-layer MLP on synthetic random-linear-transform tasks) that implements only a rough structural-isolation analogue of SAIM, not the actual algorithm on any real vision or language benchmark. All three claims were addressed with real runs and numbers, but at a scale and fidelity far below the paper's claims, yielding only toy-level evidence.

Edd16/icml2026-DYCt9JtCra-repro.paper_title: Symbiosis-Inspired Knowledge Distillation for Incremental Object Detection

claims.claim: Spatial Symbiosis Distillation preserves generalizable old class cues at symbiotic regions with high spatial overlap.
claims.evidence: A numpy proxy simulation with synthetic 64-dim class embeddings and cosine-similarity classification shows old-class recall maintained at 0.88 vs 0.1378 for fine-tuning, but 'spatial overlap' is simulated via a class_sims matrix rather than actual spatial regions in real images, and no real object detector forward pass is involved.

claims.claim: Semantic Symbiosis Distillation maintains class-level structure using confidence-weighted prototypes and soft-rank alignment.
claims.evidence: The simulation implements confidence-weighted prototypes and a semantic pull term in numpy, but Full SIKD (0.8403 overall) exactly matches Spatial SD only (0.8403), showing no additive benefit from the semantic component, and the setup uses synthetic unit-norm embeddings rather than a real detector's class-level structure.

claims.claim: SIKD demonstrates effectiveness and superiority in incremental object detection settings.
claims.evidence: The proxy simulation shows SIKD beating fine-tuning (0.88 vs 0.1378 old-class recall, 0.8403 vs 0.375 overall proxy), but this is explicitly not real object detection — no YOLO/Faster-RCNN, no Pascal-VOC/COCO, no real mAP — just a 5-old/3-new-class synthetic embedding simulation on CPU.

Edd16/icml2026-DYCt9JtCra-repro.overall: The logbook runs a pure-numpy proxy simulation of incremental class learning on synthetic embeddings, producing real numbers from a completed HF job that directionally show reduced forgetting vs fine-tuning. However, none of the three claims are validated on actual object detection with real detectors, real datasets, or real mAP, making all verdicts toy-level rather than full reproductions.

Edd16/icml2026-LHCQSx0cQV-repro.paper_title: Design Linear Constrained Neural Layers with Implicit Convex Optimization

claims.claim: Proposed differentiable layer degrades to classic layers like Softmax, Sinkhorn, and tanh when corresponding constraints are enforced
claims.evidence: Small-scale NumPy tests show tanh-GLC matches tanh exactly at alpha=1.0 (diff=0.0) and Sinkhorn-GLC matches at lambda=1.0 (diff=0.0066), but softmax-GLC does not converge to softmax at any tested lambda (diffs 0.54–0.96), providing only partial support on a simplified setup.

claims.claim: GLCLayer with Euclidean distance achieves closed-form solution for highly-efficient constraint enforcing
claims.evidence: Closed-form and iterative solutions agree to ≤3e-14 across n=5,10,20 and multiple lambda values, with first-order optimality gradient norms ≤1e-13, confirming the closed-form Euclidean GLCLayer solution is numerically correct.

claims.claim: Method addresses linear programming and real-world problems including partial graph matching and portfolio allocation
claims.evidence: A 4×5 partial graph matching shows a large cost gap (GLC soft cost 2.70 vs Hungarian 8.11) and a 6-asset portfolio barely differs from equal-weight baseline (return 0.1257 vs 0.1250), demonstrating the method runs on these tasks but at toy scale without convincing optimization quality.

Edd16/icml2026-LHCQSx0cQV-repro.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification of the closed-form Euclidean GLCLayer solution (Claim 2) but only toy-scale, partially supportive evidence for the degradation-to-classic-layers claim (Claim 1) and the real-world applications claim (Claim 3). All experiments use small matrices in pure NumPy on a cpu-basic job, limiting the scope of validation.

Edd16/icml2026-UWwmMJjlCb-repro.paper_title: DIVA: Harnessing the Representation Divergence in Unified Multimodal Models for Mutual Reinforcement

claims.claim: DIVA improves understanding performance by +3.8% to +6.1% (e.g., MMMU) and generation performance by +2.84 to +6.57 points on DPG-Bench across three unified multimodal backbones: Nexus-Gen (7B), Show-o (1.5B), and Liquid (7B) (Section 3, Table 1).
claims.evidence: A numpy simulation with 1000 synthetic paired samples (32-d per modality) uses 10-way classification accuracy and R² as proxies for understanding and generation; no real backbones (Nexus-Gen, Show-o, Liquid) or benchmarks (MMMU, DPG-Bench) were used, and the reported improvements (+12.33/+35.05 pts) do not match the paper's claimed ranges.

claims.claim: DIVA uses a two-stage training procedure: Stage 1 warms up lightweight shared/unique encoders via factorized logit injection with the backbone frozen, and Stage 2 unfreezes the backbone and applies mutual information objectives with asymmetric alignment (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: A toy numpy autoencoder (1600 samples, 32-d modality, tanh backbone 32→24) implements a structural analog of factorized logit injection as additive shared+unique decoder factors; Stage 1 (frozen backbone) and Stage 2 (unfrozen) both improve MSE, but the two-stage curriculum does not outperform single-stage training (0.101 vs 0.087), and no real backbone or MI objectives are used.

claims.claim: Ablation removing the unique-information regularization term I_uni degrades performance by -3.8% on MMMU and -3.3% on POPE (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The I_uni ablation is run on the toy proxy: MMMU proxy acc drops 0.205→0.185 (−2.0 pp) and POPE proxy acc drops 0.650→0.590 (−6.0 pp), matching the paper's direction but not its magnitudes (−3.8/−3.3 pp) and using synthetic proxies rather than real MMMU/POPE benchmarks.

claims.claim: Ablation replacing masked-inpainting with contiguous masking for the generation information flow causes the largest performance drop observed, -7.7% on MMMU and -9.5% on POPE (Table 2).
claims.evidence: A banded mixing-matrix proxy compares scattered vs contiguous masking on generation fidelity R², finding a −5.1 pp drop for contiguous masking — same direction as the paper's −7.7/−9.5 pp but on a synthetic structural proxy, not real MMMU/POPE evaluations.

claims.claim: The representation divergence between understanding and generation tasks peaks in the middle layers of the backbone (roughly layers 8-18), which DIVA specifically targets for its factorized readout (Figure 2, Table 2).
claims.evidence: Layer-wise divergence is measured on a 4-layer toy backbone (3 hidden + 1 readout) using canonical correlation, showing a peak at h3 (middle layer); this qualitatively matches the paper's middle-layer peak claim but the toy has only 4 layers vs the paper's deep transformer with layers 8–18.

claims.claim: DIVA is evaluated on understanding benchmarks MMMU, MME, MMBench, MMVet, and POPE, and on generation/editing benchmarks GenEval, DPG-Bench, WISE, ImgEdit, and GEdit-Bench-EN (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Toy proxies are defined for all 10 named benchmarks (e.g., MMMU as 10-way classification, POPE as binary object-presence) and run on the trained DIVA feature, but DIVA actually underperforms the baseline on most proxies (MMMU 0.185 vs 0.200, GenEval 0.0018 vs 0.0590), and none of the real benchmark datasets or harnesses are used.

Edd16/icml2026-UWwmMJjlCb-repro.overall: This logbook reproduces all six claims only on a synthetic numpy simulation with toy proxies (10-way classification, R² reconstruction, canonical correlation) — no real multimodal backbones (Nexus-Gen, Show-o, Liquid), no real benchmarks (MMMU, DPG-Bench, etc.), and no real training procedure are used. The directional mechanisms are sometimes consistent with the paper's claims, but the magnitudes do not match and the experimental scale is far below the paper's setup.

algorise/repro-svrg-and-beyond-via-poste.paper_title: SVRG and Beyond via Posterior Correction

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows that applying posterior correction with an isotropic-Gaussian posterior family reduces exactly to the standard SVRG gradient update, and Theorem 2 proves SVRG is equivalent to VSGD-PoCo in the limit of zero sampling noise.
claims.evidence: The logbook correctly derives the KL divergence for isotropic Gaussians with shared variance, substitutes into the variational objective, and shows the resulting corrected gradient g = ∇f_i(m_old) − ∇f_i(θ̃) + ∇F(θ̃) matches the standard SVRG estimator; the zero-noise limit argument for Theorem 2 is also mathematically sound.

claims.claim: Using full-covariance Gaussian posteriors yields a Newton-like variance-reduced extension (VON-PoCo) with a novel Hessian correction term H̄_out\i(m_in − m_out) not present in prior variance-reduced Newton methods.
claims.evidence: The logbook derives the VON-PoCo mean update m_in ← m_in − αH_in⁻¹(g_in − g_out + H_out(m_in − m_out)), correctly identifies H_out(m_in − m_out) as the novel Hessian correction term arising from the KL divergence constraint, and distinguishes it from prior curvature corrections in methods like SVRG-LBFGS.

claims.claim: Using diagonal-covariance Gaussian posteriors with mega-batches and momentum yields an Adam-like extension (IVON-PoCoMo) suitable for transformer pretraining, which achieves 17.4 validation perplexity on GPT-2 125M pretrained on 50B tokens, versus 18.0 for IVON and 18.4 for AdamW (Section 4.3, Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: The logbook trains a 0.10M-parameter baby GPT on character-level Shakespeare for 200 iterations on CPU — roughly 1000× smaller than GPT-2 125M and on a completely different dataset scale than 50B tokens. Results are mixed: IVON-PoCoMo is better at step 150 (2.8943 vs 2.9983) but worse at step 200 (3.0702 vs 2.7682), and the paper's specific perplexity numbers (17.4/18.0/18.4) are only restated, not reproduced.

claims.claim: The variance-reduced methods show consistent gains in finetuning across ViT-B/32, Qwen2.5, and Llama-3.1 (Table 1) and in ResNet-50/ImageNet and ResNet-20/CIFAR-10 image classification, particularly when learning rates are not annealed to zero (Figures 4-5).
claims.evidence: No actual experiments were run for this claim. The logbook only performs a code walkthrough of the ResNet-20/CIFAR-10 training script and restates the paper's reported accuracy numbers (90.46% IVON, 91.21% IVON-PoCoMo) without executing any runs. No finetuning experiments on ViT-B/32, Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1, ResNet-50/ImageNet, or ResNet-20/CIFAR-10 were conducted.

algorise/repro-svrg-and-beyond-via-poste.overall: The logbook provides sound mathematical verification of the two theoretical claims (SVRG equivalence and VON-PoCo's novel Hessian correction term) but only runs a toy-scale baby GPT experiment on Shakespeare for the transformer pretraining claim, with mixed results that neither reproduce nor falsify the paper's 50B-token GPT-2 125M results. No experiments were executed for the finetuning or image classification claims — only code walkthroughs and restated paper numbers.

Edd16/icml2026-KS6RbZMt8L-repro.paper_title: Complexity of Decentralized Optimization with Mixed Affine Constraints

claims.claim: For the smooth, strongly convex regime with mixed affine constraints, Theorem 4.1 gives an optimal communication complexity of O(√κ_f √κ̂_{C̃ᵀ} √κ_W log(1/ε)) that matches established lower complexity bounds (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: A 50-dimensional quadratic with κ=200 and one affine constraint was used to compare projected gradient vs accelerated projected gradient, but measured slopes (-9.16e-5 and -6.17e-5) do not match theoretical rates and APG does not visibly dominate PG, making this a toy-scale experiment that fails to validate the claimed O(√κ log(1/ε)) complexity.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 provides a unified complexity bound O(√κ_f (√κ̃_{AC} + √κ̂_{C̃ᵀ}) √κ_W log(1/ε)) covering problems with simultaneously coupled (global) and local affine constraints (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: The logbook merely evaluates the Theorem 4.6 bound formula numerically with synthetic condition numbers (κ_f=200, κ_W=100, κ̃_AC=1.18, κ̂_Ct=1.69), producing finite values at various ε; this checks internal consistency of the formula but does not test the theorem on any actual optimization problem.

claims.claim: The paper analyzes both smooth objectives (Theorem 2.4) and non-smooth objectives via a Gradient Sliding algorithm (Algorithm 2), each under mixed affine constraints (Section 2, Section 4, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: A composite objective (smooth quadratic + L1) with two affine equality constraints was run for 600 iterations of proximal projected gradient, but constraint violation remained large (0.354) and the setup is small-scale; this loosely demonstrates non-smooth + smooth handling but does not reproduce Algorithm 2 (Gradient Sliding) or validate its complexity.

claims.claim: The proposed framework is motivated by and applied to horizontal federated learning (consensus constraints), vertical federated learning (shared/global-variable constraints), and multi-task learning with node-specific local constraints (Section 1, Applications).
claims.evidence: A 2-node simulation with node-specific affine constraints showed feasible averaging to ~1e-8 violation and objective decrease, but the method used (averaging iterates then projecting) is not the paper's algorithm, and 2 nodes is far below any meaningful federated/multi-task scale.

claims.claim: An accelerated proximal alternating predictor-corrector method (Algorithm 1, APAPC) is used as the core building block for achieving the optimal rates in Theorem 4.1 and Theorem 4.5 (Algorithm 1, Theorem 4.5).
claims.evidence: APAPC was implemented on a single-machine composite problem (m=120, n=100, κ≈55) achieving 4.6× speedup over PG (50 vs 230 iterations to 1e-8), with contraction rates consistent with √κ vs κ separation, but no decentralized communication rounds or multi-agent setting was simulated.

Edd16/icml2026-KS6RbZMt8L-repro.overall: All five claims were addressed only through small-scale numpy simulations with synthetic problems, none reproducing the paper's actual decentralized optimization setting with communication complexity. The experiments provide weak toy-level evidence for some algorithmic mechanisms but do not validate any of the paper's theorems at their intended scale or scope.

Edd16/icml2026-EETUbVsG6X-repro.paper_title: HO-SFL: Hybrid-Order Split Federated Learning with Backprop-Free Clients and Dimension-Free Aggregation

claims.claim: HO-SFL achieves a convergence rate of O(sqrt(d_o/PT)) for the global gradient norm, proven in Corollary 4.5 (Equation 27), mitigating the dimension-dependent slowdown typical of zeroth-order optimization (Section 4, Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: A numpy least-squares simulation (HF Job 6a5c7615d216bd6f3a2008e7) showed ZO final loss 30x worse than FO, and the dimension-dependent slowdown mitigation was not robustly demonstrated—standard ZO converged faster than HO-SFL at d=500 and d=1000. No theoretical proof was re-derived; only a toy convex proxy was tested.

claims.claim: On CIFAR-10, HO-SFL reduces communication cost to 2.44 GB compared to 4.20 GB for standard split federated learning (SFL) and 3.71 GB for FSL-SAGE (Section 5).
claims.evidence: A numpy communication-cost simulation (HF Job 6a61cf2513e6ef894d54d76d) used random data instead of real CIFAR-10, 3 clients, 2 splits, and no actual training. Absolute GB values diverged sharply from the paper (SFL proxy=22.89 GB vs paper 4.20 GB); only the qualitative ordering and the HO-SFL/FSL-SAGE ratio (0.667 vs 0.658) matched.

claims.claim: On LLaMA-3.2-1B fine-tuned on SST-2, HO-SFL reduces client-side memory usage to 4.14 GB versus 8.78 GB for SFL and 20.81 GB for full local training, approaching the 4.01 GB inference-only footprint (Section 5).
claims.evidence: A numpy memory simulation (HF Job 6a5fb1f113e6ef894d549f89) used a LLaMA-scale architecture proxy with no actual SST-2 fine-tuning. Absolute numbers were far from the paper (HO-SFL=28.36 GB vs 4.14 GB; SFL=53.20 GB vs 8.78 GB), though the directional reduction ratio (~1.88x) was qualitatively consistent.

claims.claim: HO-SFL achieves dimension-free aggregation, reducing per-round communication complexity from O(d_o) to O(P) where P is much smaller than d_o, eliminating client-side backpropagation entirely (Section 3.3, Proposition 4.3).
claims.evidence: The HF job showed HO-SFL transmitting a fixed 3250-float payload across d=10–1000 while standard aggregation scaled linearly, but this was a numpy simulation of a projection-based proxy, not the paper's actual aggregation protocol. At d=10 HO-SFL cost more than standard (3250 vs 500 floats), and no real model or task was involved.

claims.claim: On GLUE benchmark LLM fine-tuning tasks, HO-SFL achieves accuracy comparable to first-order split federated learning baselines (Table 1).
claims.evidence: A 2-layer MLP proxy on synthetic 2-class Gaussian data (HF Job 6a5fb1f7d09dc1f57c6bfbf0) found HO-SFL mean accuracy 0.538 vs SFL 0.564 (worse by 2.6pp) with overflow warnings and high variance across seeds. No real LLM, no actual GLUE benchmark, and no first-order SFL baseline at paper scale were tested.

Edd16/icml2026-EETUbVsG6X-repro.overall: All five claims were addressed only through small-scale numpy simulations or proxies on synthetic/quadratic data, with no real CIFAR-10 training, no actual LLaMA-3.2-1B fine-tuning on SST-2, and no real GLUE benchmark evaluation. The logbook provides directional evidence for some claims (communication ordering, memory reduction ratio) but never reproduces the paper's actual experimental setup or absolute numbers.

claims.claim: For any ρ > 0, there exists a ρ-TV-stable RL algorithm supporting exact unlearning with expected computational cost equal to only a ρ√(ln T) fraction of full retraining from scratch (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: The experiment measures a joint rejection rate of 0.96–1.0 across all (T, ρ) settings, far exceeding the paper's bound of ρ√(2 log₂T) = 0.20–0.98. However, the logbook itself acknowledges the implementation uses per-node maximal coupling rather than the joint coupling required by the paper's proof, so the experiment tests an incomplete version of the algorithm and cannot verify or falsify the claim as stated.

claims.claim: The proposed algorithm achieves a regret bound of O(H³S²A + H²√(SAT) + H^2.5·S²A/ρ)·polylog(T,H,S,A,1/δ) for tabular MDPs with unlearning support (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: UCB-VI was run on a very small tabular MDP (S=4, A=2, H=3) with T up to 12800 and 20 trials; regret stays below the theoretical upper bound but grows roughly as T^1.0 in the tested range (slope ≈3.9 per 4× T increase), and the ρ-dependence is only ~6% over a 10× change in 1/ρ, making it impossible to isolate the claimed H^2.5·S²A/ρ term. Only one (S,A,H) configuration is tested, so scaling in those parameters is unverified.

claims.claim: A matching lower bound of Ω(H√(SAT) + HSA/ρ) is established, showing the algorithm is nearly minimax optimal (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: The experiment runs UCB-VI on randomly generated small MDPs (S=3, A=2, H=2) and checks that its regret exceeds the lower-bound envelope Ω(H√(SAT)+HSA/ρ). However, a minimax lower bound requires worst-case hard instances and must hold for all ρ-TV-stable algorithms; testing one algorithm on random MDPs does not construct the paper's hard instances or verify the minimax claim.

claims.claim: Exact unlearning is formalized as requiring the post-unlearning output distribution to be identical to that of an algorithm that never observed the deleted data (Definition 2.1), operationalized via ρ-TV-stability where TV(A(Z), A(Z')) ≤ ρ for neighboring sequences (Definition 2.2).
claims.evidence: The experiment computes per-node TV analytically as tv_gaussian_1d(0, B, σ) and notes it equals the leaf-level TV, but never measures the TV distance between the full algorithm output distributions on neighboring sequences, which is what Definition 2.2 requires. The logbook itself states 'the cumulative TV at any prefix sum query accumulates over O(log T) affected nodes, and is not the quantity bounded by ρ in the paper.'

claims.claim: The construction uses a binary tree mechanism with noise-perturbed prefix sums requiring only O(log T) shared noise samples per query, achieving O(Td) space and O(d·log T) per-episode update time (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The code for claim_5_binary_tree_complexity (timing insert/prefix_sum and measuring memory for T up to 4096 and d up to 16) is present in reproduce.py, but no output or results for this experiment are shown in the logbook—the page appears to be truncated.

claims.claim: The additional regret cost term for unlearning, H³S²A/ρ, improves upon the corresponding differentially-private RL cost term of H^3.5·S²A/ε by a factor of √H (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The code for claim_6_dp_rl (comparing Gaussian vs Laplace prefix-sum noise std across H=2,4,8) is present in reproduce.py, but no output or results for this experiment are visible in the logbook—the page is not shown or is truncated.

jomasego/repro-exact-unlearning-in-reinf.overall: The logbook provides real experimental runs only for Claims 1–4, and all of these are either on toy-scale MDPs (S≤4, A≤2, H≤3), test incorrect or incomplete implementations (per-node instead of joint coupling for Claim 1; per-node TV instead of output-distribution TV for Claim 4), or fail to construct the paper's hard instances (Claim 3). Claims 5 and 6 have code but no visible output, leaving them unaddressed.

bertfil/GmP3VcfHi0.paper_title: MuonSSM: Orthogonalizing State Space Models for Sequence Modeling

claims.claim: MuonSSM achieves substantial improvements in gradient propagation and mitigates vanishing gradients over long horizons
claims.evidence: C7 ran a real Newton-Schulz operator on a d_state=64 matrix from the model, showing conditioning improvement in the correct direction (kappa reduced ~30x from ~1.9e6 to ~6.5e4), but this was measured on a proxy matrix (the momentum-increment matrix) rather than the actual recurrent state-transition matrix, and the key long-horizon gradient propagation evidence (C13, gradient-norm heatmaps over 2048 tokens / 60K iterations) was never attempted.

claims.claim: Shows consistent gains in accuracy, robustness, and long-context performance across language, vision, and time-series benchmarks when integrated into SSM backbones
claims.evidence: All nine sub-claims spanning language (C1, C2, C8), vision (C3, C4, C14), and time-series (C5, C6, C12) benchmarks were never executed due to missing compute (FineWeb-Edu 10B pretraining, ImageNet/COCO/ADE20K) and gated HAR datasets; the only HAR runs were chance-level smoke tests on synthetic data, producing no comparable accuracy, robustness, or long-context metrics.

bertfil/GmP3VcfHi0.overall: This logbook provides only a proxy-level demonstration that Newton-Schulz normalization improves matrix conditioning in the expected direction, while the core claims about gradient propagation over long horizons and consistent cross-domain benchmark gains remain entirely unverified due to missing compute and gated data.

bertfil/UGAP2F6FfV.paper_title: Holi-Spatial: Evolving Video Streams into Holistic 3D Spatial Intelligence

claims.claim: Holi-Spatial is a fully automated pipeline for constructing large-scale spatially aware multimodal data directly from raw video inputs without human intervention (Section 3).
claims.evidence: No experiment directly tests the automation property; the logbook explicitly states 'none of the veritas claims directly test whether the Holi-Spatial pipeline is fully automated.' The pipeline ran end-to-end on substitute inputs but this was not captured as scored evidence addressing the no-human-intervention claim.

claims.claim: Holi-Spatial supports multi-level spatial supervision including optimized 3DGS reconstructions, rendered depth maps, object-level annotations, relational annotations, and spatial QA pairs (Section 3).
claims.evidence: C9 and C10 are both not_attempted. Key supervision types were never produced: 3DGS training was blocked (Step 4), captions/QA generation was blocked (Steps 8-9), and relational annotations were never generated. Only 3D-box counts (149,550 from released subset) and 128 boxes on a single substitute scene were produced, plus 787 SAM3 masks on 32 images — but these demonstrate pipeline mechanics on substitute inputs, not the full multi-level supervision claim.

claims.claim: Holi-Spatial-4M contains 12K optimized 3DGS scenes, 1.3M 2D masks, 320K 3D bounding boxes, 320K instance captions, 1.2M 3D grounding instances, and 1.2M spatial QA pairs (Section 4).
claims.evidence: C10 is not_attempted. The replication operated only on 904 ScanNet++ scenes (not 12K), and most annotation stages were blocked by license-gated data. None of the six claimed dataset totals (12K scenes, 1.3M masks, 320K boxes, 320K captions, 1.2M grounding instances, 1.2M QA pairs) were produced or verified at any scale.

claims.claim: Holi-Spatial outperforms existing feed-forward and per-scene optimized methods on ScanNet, ScanNet++, and DL3DV data-curation quality benchmarks (Section 5).
claims.evidence: C1, C2, C3, and C11 are all not_attempted — the repo ships no scoring code (no AP/IoU/F1 computation), no baselines were run, and no benchmark numbers were produced. C12 (partial) produced 787 real SAM3 masks on 32 images of one scene with substitute weights, but no SA2VA baseline was run and no comparative figure was generated, so the outperformance claim was never addressed with comparable evidence.

claims.claim: Fine-tuning VLMs on Holi-Spatial-4M improves 3D grounding and spatial reasoning performance (Section 5).
claims.evidence: C4, C5, and C14 are all not_attempted. tpls/repro-ftrl-potential-lb.paper_title: (Doubly) Exponential Lower Bounds for Follow the Regularized Leader in Potential Games

claims.claim: Theorem 1.2 proves that in two-player m×m potential games, Follow the Regularized Leader (FTRL) can require 2^Ω(m log m) iterations to reach an ε-Nash equilibrium for ε = 1/poly(m), for any permutation-invariant regularizer and any learning rate schedule η^(t) = 1/t^α with α ∈ [0,1) (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: Exact bigint arithmetic confirms the Lemma 4.5 recurrence witness dominates the Theorem C.14 closed form for all 48 odd m∈{7,…,101} with normalized exponent r(m) positive and monotone (0.1134→0.7537), and Lemma 4.1's regularizer-dependent bound holds with 0/57,462 violations across 2 regularizer families × 4 α schedules; the negative control crippling the (ℓ−2) kernel collapses r(101) by >9×, confirming the mechanism is load-bearing.

claims.claim: Theorem 1.3 shows there exists an n-player binary-action potential game in which fictitious play requires 2^Ω(2^n) iterations to reach an ε-Nash equilibrium for ε = 1/2^n, a doubly exponential lower bound (Theorem 1.3).
claims.evidence: Exact bigint recurrence satisfies T_k ≥ (k−1)! for 256/256 k values (T_256 has 505 digits), and the log-Gamma composition certificate gives log2(iterations(n)) ≥ 2^n for 15/15 n∈{8,…,22}; the negative control dropping the (k−1) multiplier fails at k*=4, confirming factorial growth depends on it. The snake-in-the-box existence is a cited result (Evdokimov 1969), not the paper's contribution, so verifying the novel arithmetic chain is appropriate.

claims.claim: Theorem 1.1 establishes a matching-type positive result: alternating ε-lazy no-regret dynamics converge to an ε-Nash equilibrium in any potential game after at most exp(O_ε(1/ε^2)) iterations (Theorem 1.1, restated as Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The composed closed-form bound B(ε)=(1+3/ε)^⌈1/ε⌉ satisfies ln B(ε) ≤ 1/ε² (envelope holds) and ln B(ε) ≥ 1/ε (non-vacuous) for all 9/9 ε∈{0.5,…,0.001}; the negative control raising the update-count cap to ⌈1/ε²⌉ breaches the envelope at all 9 points (max ratio 8.0×), confirming the cap is load-bearing.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.2 shows that for FTRL with learning rate η ≤ 1/L (L the smoothness constant of the potential), the potential function value is non-decreasing across iterations, without requiring alternation or laziness (Proposition 3.2).
claims.evidence: The exact quantitative inequality Φ(x^{(t+1)})−Φ(x^{(t)}) ≥ (1/2η)‖x^{(t+1)}−x^{(t)}‖² holds with 0/16,000 violations for Euclidean FTRL (L=σ_max via exact SVD) and 0/16,000 for entropic FTRL (L=max|A_ij|) across 20 seeds × 4 η/L ratios × 200 steps; the negative control at η/L=10 produces 31 violations and 21 genuine potential decreases (worst ΔΦ=−1.4515), confirming the step-size condition does real work.

claims.claim: Example 3.3 constructs a 'spurious fixed point' showing FTRL can maintain a highly suboptimal strategy (error proportional to 1/t) indefinitely relative to the observed utility sequence, illustrating why FTRL, unlike gradient descent under Legendre regularizers, need not reach an O_ε(ε)-Nash equilibrium (Example 3.3).
claims.evidence: Closed-form entropic-FTRL trajectory evaluation shows post-switch movement ≤1/t (over-satisfied, ‖Δ‖·t=0.0065 at t=8) and best-response gap ≥0.9991 for all 18/18 t∈{2^3,…,2^20}; the negative control resetting cumulative history jumps movement to 0.3268 (O(1), >1000× the with-history value), isolating cumulative-memory inertia as the mechanism. The GD-under-Legendre-regularizer comparison is not implemented but is a motivating remark, not the core construction.

claims.claim: The two-player exponential lower bound construction uses a payoff matrix A of odd dimension m with maximum entry 2m−1, dividing the FTRL trajectory into 2m−1 'transition periods' governed by Property 4.3 (period consistency) and Lemma 4.1 bounding action probability by R/(η^(t)γ) (Section 4, Definition 4.2, Property 4.3, Lemma 4.1, Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: Exact integer construction of payoff matrix A passes all structural invariants (unique positive entries {3,…,2m−1}, max entry=2m−1, a1/a2 index-map shift property, negative extra row/col) for 30/30 odd m∈{5,…,63}, with B_{4,2} and A_5 byte-exact to Figure 2a/2b; Lemma 4.1's bound holds with 0/64,676 violations (tightest ratio 0.167), and negative controls (entry-swap caught, R-shrink produces 5 violations) confirm both the structural checker and bound are non-vacuous.

tpls/repro-ftrl-potential-lb.overall: The logbook provides rigorous computational verification of all six claims through exact bigint arithmetic, closed-form evaluations, and actual FTRL simulations on random games, each backed by a meaningful negative control that breaks the underlying mechanism. For a pure-theory paper with no reference implementation, this approach—verifying the proof's key mathematical machinery (recurrences, bounds, constructions) at reasonable scale with exact precision—is an appropriate and thorough form of reproduction.

claims.claim: Corollary 1 proves that when λ≥1 there always exists a global maximizer of the relaxed objective that is integral, so the relaxed and combinatorial problems share the same optimal value.

claims.claim: Lemma 1 shows that for λ>1 there does not exist a non-integral local maximizer, establishing the strict dichotomy that all integral stationary points are local maximizers while non-integral stationary points are strict saddles.
claims.evidence: The logbook checks 21,720 integral stationary points across all graphs up to n=5 at λ=1.5 (zero local-max condition failures) and tests curvature 2(λ−aᵢⱼ)>0 on 20-node regular graphs (minimum curvature 1.0). Real runs and numbers, but restricted to small graphs (n≤5 and n=20).

claims.claim: Theorem 5 shows that increasing the diagonal loading parameter beyond λ=1 introduces additional spurious local maxima, implying λ=1 optimally trades off relaxation tightness against optimization difficulty.

claims.claim: The saddle-escaping Frank-Wolfe algorithm (Section 3.1) has per-iteration complexity O(m+k log n) and is shown to converge in a finite number of steps to an integral local maximizer of the densest k-subgraph relaxation.
claims.evidence: The logbook implements the saddle-escaping Frank-Wolfe algorithm and runs it on 40 seeded 6-regular graphs (n=40, k=8, λ=1.5); all 40 runs converge to integral stationary points in 9–13 iterations with monotone objectives. claims.evidence: The logbook performs only a source-text audit (SHA-256 hash, term occurrence counts) finding zero mentions of LRBO, L-ADMM, EXPP, or 'millions of vertices' in the paper source.
