ai-sherpa/set-preserving-p-to-e-repro.paper_title: Set-Preserving Calibration from Conformal P-Values to E-Values

claims.claim: A calibrator is defined as set-preserving when converting conformal p-values at level alpha into e-values yields prediction sets identical to thresholding the e-values directly at 1/alpha (Section 2.1, Definition 2.2)
claims.evidence: On 18 theorem-domain (n,α) cells covering 275 conformal grid atoms, the logbook reports 0/275 set-membership mismatches between P_n>α and F(P_n)<1/α, threshold identity |F(α)−1/α|=0.0, and exact-e-value error ≤4.44e-16. Classical calibrators inflate sets in 18/18 cells, confirming the motivating contrast.

claims.claim: Among left-continuous p-to-e calibrators, only the all-or-nothing calibrator can be exactly set-preserving, which motivates a new sigmoid-based P2E construction (Proposition 2.3, Theorem 2.6, Equation 9)
claims.evidence: The uniqueness argument is reproduced: set-preservation forces f≥1/α on (0,α], exhausting the budget ∫₀¹f≤1 and pinning f=F_AoN. Budget saturation ∫₀¹F_AoN=α·(1/α)=1 is verified exactly (error 0.0) for 4 α levels using rational arithmetic.

claims.claim: The proposed sigmoid-based P2E calibrator is exact (expectation equal to 1), smooth, invertible, strictly positive, and strictly dominates the all-or-nothing calibrator in aggregation settings (Theorem 2.6)
claims.evidence: Over 18 cells: |E[F]−1|≤4.44e-16 (exactness), analytic derivative max −5.01e-55<0 with finite-difference agreement <1e-4 (strict monotonicity/smoothness), inverse round-trip error 7.5e-15 (invertibility), min e-value 3.49e-57>0 (strict positivity), and F−F_AoN≥3.5e-57≥0 pointwise with P2E⊆AoN set inclusion in 18/18 cells (dominance).

claims.claim: Applied to e-Cross-Conformal Prediction (ECCP), the P2E calibrator preserves exact 1-alpha coverage, whereas standard cross-conformal-prediction variants only guarantee approximate 1-2alpha coverage (Proposition 4.1)
claims.evidence: Analytic e-merge exactness E[(1/K)ΣE_k]=1 is confirmed (MC ≈0.9999 over 20k draws). A transportation LP on the conformal grid at K=2 yields worst-case rejection 20/21·α≤α, certifying coverage ≥1−α=0.95 vs standard CCP's 1−2α=0.90. Synthetic e-CCP coverage is 1.000 over 4000 replicates.

claims.claim: Applied to Weighted Conformal Aggregation (WECA), data-dependent weighted merging of e-values across multiple models retains valid coverage (Proposition 4.2)
claims.evidence: Tuning-split weights are bit-identical under final-cal/test mutation in 6/6 trials; weighted e-merge E=1 (error 2.2e-16) confirms validity via Markov. Outcome-adaptive weights change in 6/6 trials and produce rejection tail 1.859·α>α, demonstrating the split-independence boundary.

claims.claim: Empirically, ECCP using the proposed P2E calibrator produces smaller prediction sets than baseline p-to-e conversion methods while maintaining valid coverage (Section 5)
claims.evidence: On the paper's real datasets (Boston, Abalone, Parkinsons) × 3 models × 13 methods × 100 seeds (11,700 cells), P2E ECCP is strictly shorter than every classical p-to-e baseline (sqrt/log/pow) in 9/9 dataset-model comparisons (worst-case shrink 1.32×, up to 9.2×) at coverage 0.893–0.900 ≈ nominal 0.9. P2E length ≈ AoN (14.40 vs 14.44), consistent with the set-preserving dominance mechanism.

ai-sherpa/set-preserving-p-to-e-repro.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims through an independent from-scratch numpy/scipy implementation. Theoretical properties (Claims 1–5) are verified to machine precision on the actual theorem domain, and the empirical efficiency claim (Claim 6) is reproduced at full paper scale on real benchmarks with 100 seeds.

Firemedic15/repro-pariskv-fast-and-drift.paper_title: ParisKV: Fast and Drift-Robust KV-Cache Retrieval for Long-Context LLMs

claims.claim: ParisKV projects queries and keys onto the unit hypersphere via L2 normalization and a shared random orthogonal (SRHT) rotation to construct data-independent analytic centroids that remain stable under decode-time distribution drift (Section 4.1.1, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Math checks confirm L2 normalization (norm=1.000000±0.000000) and SRHT rotation (orthogonality error 5.96e-08, pairwise distance error 0.000000) are correctly implemented, but the synthetic drift proxy (128-dim Gaussian, 16 steps) showed the full ParisKV mechanism (variant D) achieving 30.8% recall vs 41.1% for the stale baseline — the opposite direction from the claim, and the logbook acknowledges its analytic centroid construction is a guess at the paper's unspecified 'theoretical centroids.'

claims.claim: ParisKV achieves 2.1×-2.8× higher decoding throughput than full attention within full attention's runnable memory range, and scales to much larger batch sizes (e.g., batch size 88 at 128K context) where full attention runs out of memory at batch size 4 (Section 5.2, Figures 7-8).
claims.evidence: Benchmarked at 128K context on A10G 24GB with correct Llama3.1-8B GQA tensor shapes, but ParisKV measured ~9-10× slower than full attention (e.g., 10.4ms vs 1.2ms at batch 1) and OOM'd at batch 16 vs batch 32+ for full attention; the logbook explicitly attributes this to an un-fused Python implementation lacking custom CUDA kernels, so the implementation is not faithful enough to verify or falsify the throughput claim.

claims.claim: At the 1M-token scale on Llama3.1-8B, ParisKV reduces per-step decode latency to 49 ms, versus 830 ms for MagicPIG (17× reduction) and 2179 ms for PQCache (44× reduction) (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: Ran at 1M-token scale but only measured own full attention (16.9ms) vs own ParisKV (1659.7ms); MagicPIG and PQCache were not implemented at all, and the ParisKV implementation is acknowledged to be unoptimized, so the specific 49ms/830ms/2179ms comparison cannot be evaluated.

claims.claim: On MATH500 pass@1, ParisKV-equipped Qwen-3-4B scores 92.80 versus 58.80 for PQCache, a roughly 34-point gain, and on AIME25 pass@8 ParisKV improves 40-77 points over PQCache/MagicPIG across model families (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Explicitly not attempted — no MATH500 or AIME25 experiments were run; the logbook states that building generation-loop integrations of ParisKV, PQCache, and MagicPIG across multiple model families was infeasible within scope.

claims.claim: On LongBench-V2, ParisKV with DeepSeek-R1-Llama-8B achieves an overall score of 28.43 versus 19.90 for PQCache and 13.92 for MagicPIG (Table 3).
claims.evidence: Explicitly not attempted — no LongBench-V2 experiments were run; the logbook states the same blockers as Claim 4 (no baseline implementations, no generation-loop integration).

claims.claim: Ablations show that combining normalization, rotation, and theoretical centroids raises coarse-stage retrieval recall from 6% to 16.1% and final recall from 36.5% to 64.3% (Section 5.3).
claims.evidence: The synthetic drift ablation (128-dim Gaussian, 16 steps, 48 centroids) measured recall going 41.1%→33.4%→38.4%→30.8% across variants A→D, the opposite direction from the paper's claimed 6%→16.1% coarse and 36.5%→64.3% final recall; the setup is clearly simplified (synthetic data, not real LLM activations) and the centroid construction is acknowledged as a guess.

Firemedic15/repro-pariskv-fast-and-drift.overall: The logbook verifies the low-level mathematical primitives (L2 normalization, SRHT rotation) are correctly implemented and confirms the algorithmic sparsity ratio (~6.2% of keys touched), but cannot reproduce the paper's throughput, latency, memory, or recall improvements due to an unoptimized from-scratch implementation and an unconfirmed centroid construction, while the accuracy claims were not attempted at all.

GwendalTsang/repro-incremental-learning-.paper_title: Incremental Learning of Sparse Attention Patterns in Transformers

claims.claim: Shows transformers learn to attend over sparse, statistically-weighted historical positions through a sequence of distinct stages, each stage corresponding to acquisition of a specific attention pattern, without any explicit curriculum (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Attention mass per head at the paper's full configuration (d=50, T=20, 9000 train samples, batch 3000) shows uniform ~0.146 at step 0, all three heads on I(1) at step 60 (0.445/0.645/0.659), one head on I(2) at step 300 (0.618), and full specialization by step 990; ordering holds across 4 seeds (stage steps 55-63, 194-275, 566-995) and is confirmed by an independent CPU cross-check.

claims.claim: Proves (Theorem 1, Section 3.2) that under symmetric initialization, the coupled gradient dynamics of attention heads first converge to learning the single most statistically important pattern, and (Theorem 2) bounds how far the dynamics can deviate from this symmetric trajectory over finite training time.
claims.evidence: Numerical integration of the exact gradient flow (LSODA, rtol 1e-8) at the paper's reduced-model setup (h=3, T=40, m=1.7) shows Proposition 1 holds to 0.17% relative error via 400k Monte Carlo samples, Theorem 1's fixed point error decreases monotonically (0.083→0.0025 over horizons 1e3 to 1e6) with ordering invariance never breaking, and Theorem 2's deviation bound holds with a single universal c1=0.592 across four decades of eps (spread factor 2.2).

claims.claim: Proves (Theorems 3 and 4, Section 3.3) that after this initial competitive phase, a cooperative phase follows in which heads specialize onto distinct patterns, with dynamics provably converging to learning the second-most-important pattern once cooperation begins.
claims.evidence: Cooperative offsetting is exact to machine precision (spurious cross-term +1.09024 vs ensemble offset -1.09024, cancellation error 0.0), the free head learns the second pattern at strength 1.70000 = m_2* from every initialization, and the full 3-head system shows three separated stages (t≈32.5, 331, 83800) with complete head specialization; however, the logbook identifies that Theorem 4's literal parameter-space fixed point s'(∞)=s_2* is not reached by the reduction (the flow halts at b<1), though the function-space conclusion holds.

claims.claim: Empirically demonstrates the competitive-to-cooperative transition via attention-pattern snapshots at training steps t=0, 60, 300, and 1000 (Figure 2) and via KL-divergence curves showing stage-wise convergence to simpler hypothesis classes before more complex ones (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Both KL-divergence panels from the same full-scale run show minima arriving in strict order of increasing complexity: truncated ground truths at steps 56→275→995 and learned restricted-context models at steps 65→245→995, with each curve rising after its minimum as the model moves past that hypothesis class; attention snapshots at steps 0/60/300/990 quantitatively match the paper's Figure 2 progression.

claims.claim: Shows that reducing training dataset size causes models to learn fewer stages, interpreted as an implicit regularization effect of the finite-data training trajectory leading to a misspecified (simpler) learned model (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: A 7-point sweep (n=100 to 9000) on the paper's minimal architecture shows stage count increasing from 1 to 3: at n=100 all three KL minima coincide within 2 steps (1 stage), at n=2000 the second and third minima are 1 step apart (2 stages), and from n=3000 upward all three stages resolve with separation growing to 759 steps; stage order is correct in all 7 runs and excess loss decreases monotonically from 2.12 to 0.08.

GwendalTsang/repro-incremental-learning-.overall: This logbook provides concrete experimental and numerical evidence supporting all five claims at the paper's own scale, including attention mass measurements across 4 seeds, numerical integration of the gradient flow for the four theorems, and a 7-point dataset-size sweep. Two discrepancies in theorem statements (Theorem 2's validity window written backwards, Theorem 4's literal fixed point not reached by its own reduction) are identified but do not undermine the substantive claims.

rahit/repro-on-the-expressive-power-of-p.paper_title: On the Expressive Power of Permutation-Equivariant Weight-Space Networks

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 proves that the prominent permutation-equivariant weight-space architectures DWS, NP-NFN, HNP-NFN, GMN, and NG-GNN have identical expressive power for both invariant and equivariant mappings on compact sets (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies the commutant dimension (114 and 55) via two independent methods (Burnside and Reynolds SVD) on small architectures (2,3,3,2) and (1,4,4,1), confirming a structural prerequisite for expressive-power equivalence, but does not demonstrate that all five architectures realize the full commutant or can mutually approximate each other.

claims.claim: Proposition 5.3 shows Neural Functional Transformers (NFTs) differ in expressive power from the other architectures in general, but become equivalent under a general-position (GP) assumption requiring distinct bias terms per layer (Proposition 5.3).
claims.evidence: The NFT separation is exactly reproduced (wf(v1)=8/33, wf(v2)=16/33, error 0.00e+00) with verified equivariance and DWS-side non-separation, but the GP-equivalence part of the claim ('become equivalent under a general-position assumption') is explicitly not addressed.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.1 establishes that permutation-invariant weight-space networks are universal approximators of function-space functionals, i.e., maps depending only on the realized function and not the specific parameterization (Theorem 6.1).
claims.evidence: The separation property is verified on 5000 random function-distinct pairs (100% separated, min gap 0.5808) and the strict hierarchy ~DWS ⊊ ~func is shown exactly (1 vs 2.7), but the Stone–Weierstrass approximation step that establishes actual universality is not implemented or tested.

claims.claim: Proposition 6.2 proves a non-universality result showing invariant weight-space networks cannot approximate all permutation-invariant functionals, using a counterexample built from Weisfeiler-Leman graph indistinguishability (Proposition 6.2).
claims.evidence: The exact counterexample is reproduced: exhaustive orbit search over all 576 S4×S4 permutations finds 0 matches (min L1 distance 4.0), 1000 random NG-GNNs yield readout gap 0.000e+00, and 1-WL histograms are identical {0:4,1:1,2:1,3:4}, with destructive controls confirming the harness detects separation when it should.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.3 recovers universality for permutation-invariant functionals under the general-position assumption via continuous canonization maps that order neurons by bias value (Theorem 6.3).
claims.evidence: Canonization is verified to be orbit-constant (0.00e+00 over all 576 group elements), orbit-separating (min gap 1.785 over 2000 orbits), and continuous (linear scaling), with the exclusion-set destructive control breaking as predicted (1.884), but the actual approximation of canon by a DWS network—the step that yields universality—is not implemented.

claims.claim: Theorem 7.4 shows permutation-equivariant operators achieve universal approximation under the general-position assumption via canonization-based factorization, while Proposition 7.1 shows fixed-architecture equivariant networks cannot approximate function-space operators that increase geometric complexity (Proposition 7.1, Theorem 7.4).
claims.evidence: Prop 7.1's region-count ceiling (H+1) is exactly confirmed over 200k random nets per architecture and the complexity-increasing operator example is shown, and Thm 7.4's factorization identity is verified exactly (0.00e+00 over 3000 GP inputs) with exhaustive equivariance, but the pointwise-MLP universality step (fitting a DWS stack to approximate Φ) is not implemented.

rahit/repro-on-the-expressive-power-of-p.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies key finite mathematical constructions underlying all six theoretical claims—commutant dimensions, NFT separation values, separation properties, the WL counterexample, canonization maps, and region-count ceilings—with exact computations, exhaustive group searches, and destructive controls. However, with the sole exception of the Proposition 6.2 counterexample (which is the proof itself and is exhaustively verified), the logbook addresses structural prerequisites and specific instances rather than the full universality or expressive-power-equivalence theorems, leaving the Stone–Weierstrass approximation steps untested.

rahit/repro-on-the-power-of-approximate-.paper_title: On the Power of (Approximate) Reward Models for Inference-Time Scaling: Sequential Monte Carlo and Beyond

claims.claim: Under Assumption 3.2 (uniform Bellman error bound ε), if ε = O(1/T), SMC-based inference-time scaling attains a target TV error with particle/time complexity that is polynomial rather than exponential in the horizon T (Section 5, Theorem 5.1, Corollary 5.2).
claims.evidence: Exact closed-form evaluation shows (1+c/T)^{6(T-1)}→e^{6c} (bounded), with log-log slope of N(T) in T equal to 1.013 (c=0.5) and 1.032 (c=1.0), confirming polynomial scaling; TC slope 2.01/2.03 confirms O(T²). Destructive control with fixed ε yields exponential slope d(logN)/dT=1.1762 (ε=0.2) matching predicted 6ln(1.2)=1.0939. Small-scale SMC runs (N=256, T=2..6) confirm the trend.

claims.claim: Without reward guidance, the number of samples needed to hit the target region grows as Ω(L^(2T/3)), an exponential lower bound in T (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Full-leaf enumeration over 12 instances (L∈{2,3,4,5}, m∈{1,2,3}) confirms the mass identity p(A_u)=1/(2−L^{−2m}) to max error 4.8e-11, verifies Assumption 3.1 (ratio=L exactly), and recovers the Ω(L^{2T/3}) exponent as slope (2/3)ln(L) to relative error 2.4e-16. Monte-Carlo (20k trials) confirms the hit-probability bound Q/B^{2m}.

claims.claim: Even with a Bellman-error-bounded reward model, sampling complexity is lower-bounded by Ω((1+ε)^(2T/3)), showing guidance alone cannot remove exponential dependence unless ε shrinks with T (Section 4, Corollary 4.2).
claims.evidence: Exact enumeration over 6 instances (ε∈{1,2,3}, m∈{1,2}) confirms both Assumption 3.1 (ratio_bd=1+ε exactly) and Assumption 3.2 (bellman_bd=1+ε exactly), mass identity to error 7.2e-15, and exponent recovery as slope (2/3)ln(1+ε) to machine precision. The per-step base (1+ε)^{2/3}→1 only as ε→0, matching the paper's remark.

claims.claim: For single-particle guided SMC, the total-variation error is bounded by 2Tε, so guidance fails to control error once ε ≥ 1/(2T) (Section 4, Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: 31,500 exact (non-sampled) per-step TV checks across scale×B×T×seeds show 0 violations of TV≤2tε with max ratio 0.1161; at ε=0, TV=1.10e-15 (machine-precision exactness as predicted). Destructive control with mismatched high-Bellman-error reward yields 1631/6300 violations, confirming the bound requires the matched low-ε model.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 establishes a particle complexity bound N ≥ L^6 T(1+ε)^(6(T-1))/(2δ_TV) for SMC to achieve TV error δ_TV (Section 5, Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: Bootstrap PF on an explicit finite tree (B=2, T=3, L=4.288, ε=0.272) with 6000 SMC runs per N shows bias decaying as 1/N (log-log slope −0.914 vs theory −1), from 4.69e-2 (N=8) to 4.97e-4 (N=1024). The sufficient condition N*=5.57e5 for δ_TV=0.3 is validated since measured bias at N=1024 already ≪0.3. Destructive N=1 gives 755× worse bias.

claims.claim: A resampling-pool Metropolis-Hastings chain-based approach achieves the target accuracy with time complexity Õ(L T^3 log(1/δ) log(1/δ_TV)) (Section 6, Theorem 6.1).
claims.evidence: Three complexity ingredients verified by simulation on B=2, T=3 tree: (6a) MH invariant equals exact target (TV→1.52e-3 at 150k chains, 1/√K convergence); (6b) geometric mixing with fitted rate −0.470 (ρ≈0.625<1); (6c) pool relative-error ∝1/√M (slope −0.486 vs theory −0.5), confirming M=O(T²). Destructive no-MH-correction gives TV 0.1224, 57× larger.

rahit/repro-on-the-power-of-approximate-.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous clean-room reproduction of all six theoretical claims, using exact enumeration for the lower-bound and TV-bound claims (Claims 2–4, matching to machine precision) and simulation with matching scaling exponents for the complexity claims (Claims 1, 5, 6), each backed by destructive controls that fail as predicted. The evidence is concrete and independently computed from the paper's equations rather than re-parsing its tables.

rahit/repro-beyond-relu-bifurcation-over.paper_title: Beyond ReLU: Bifurcation, Oversmoothing, and Topological Priors

claims.claim: Proves a supercritical pitchfork bifurcation condition α·w·λ_k = 1 under which odd C^3 activation functions destabilize the homogeneous fixed point and create stable non-homogeneous patterns in GNN dynamics (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: 75 configurations across 5 graph families (N=200) show Jacobian spectral radius at w_k equals 1 to 3.55e-15, subcritical |x| collapses to 3.18e-12, supercritical |x| ≥ 0.8276 with cos(x*,u_k) mean 0.992, and ReLU control diverges (|x|=1e8) where sine converges — directly confirming the bifurcation threshold and stable non-homogeneous patterns.

claims.claim: Derives a √μ scaling law for the amplitude of emergent patterns near the bifurcation point, where μ measures distance from criticality, and validates this scaling empirically (Theorem 3.2, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Across 4 graph families (N=400) and 11 μ values, near-critical log-log slope of amplitude vs μ is 0.494 (theory: 0.5), and the closed-form prefactor ratio measured/predicted at μ=0.002 is 1.00057±0.00043; the wrong-exponent (μ^1) model fits 56x worse (RSS 3.18 vs 0.057), confirming both the √μ exponent and the full coefficient.

claims.claim: Shows Dirichlet energy stays at zero in the subcritical regime and grows linearly in the supercritical regime, quantifying departure from oversmoothing (Corollary 3.4).
claims.evidence: On 3 SBM community graphs with deflated interior modes (λ_k∈(0.888,0.921)), subcritical Dirichlet energy is 1.09e-25 (machine zero) and supercritical E_D/μ at μ=0.005 matches the predicted C_k = 6(1-λ_k)/(γ κ_k) to ratio 0.9869±0.0001, with the (1-λ_k)a² column matching E_D directly.

claims.claim: Proves that near the bifurcation point the NTK becomes asymptotically rank-one, dominated by the bifurcating eigenmode, explaining emergent topological learning priors (Corollary 4.1).
claims.evidence: On 3 graph families (N=160) and 4 μ values, the NTK eig2/eig1 ratio is ≤4.6e-16 (rank-one), dominant eigenvector cos(v_top,u_k) ≥ 0.9916 approaching 0.99999 as μ→0, top eigenvalue × μ converges to a constant per family (1/μ divergence), and finite-difference vs implicit-function-theorem derivatives agree to 1e-8; subcritical participation ratio drops from 133 to 1.06 near criticality.

claims.claim: Extends the scalar analysis to realistic multidimensional GNNs, proving emergent patterns are rank-one separable states aligned with graph and feature eigenmodes (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: Across 27 configs (3 graph families, d∈{4,8,16}, 3 μ values), the emergent state X* has s2/s1 ≤ 2.4e-2 approaching 5e-4 as μ→0 (rank-one), with left singular vector cos(.,u_k) ≥ 0.9991 and right cos(.,v_j) ≥ 0.9995 (separable), and subcritical control collapses to |X*|=3.18e-12; Ginibre critical variance check shows α·ρ(W)·λ_k → 1 as d grows.

claims.claim: Demonstrates that substituting bifurcation-inducing activations (e.g., sine) for standard monotone ones maintains performance in 64-layer GNNs on Cora, avoiding representational collapse under depth (Figure 5, Section 6).
claims.evidence: On the real CORA giant component (N=2485), an untrained forward-pass proxy metric (non-homogeneous energy fraction H) shows sin/tanh retain ~60% of energy at depth 64 vs ReLU's 4.8%, but the actual claim of maintained classification performance requires trained accuracy which was not attempted, and the feature dimension (d=16) is reduced from the paper's 64-256.

rahit/repro-beyond-relu-bifurcation-over.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification of all five theoretical claims (bifurcation threshold, √μ scaling, Dirichlet energy transition, NTK rank-one structure, and multidimensional separability) through clean-room implementations with destructive controls and cross-validated methods on multiple non-trivial graph families. The sixth claim about maintained performance on CORA is only addressed via an untrained proxy metric at reduced feature dimension, not the actual trained accuracy the claim requires.

rahit/repro-convergence-analysis-of-the-.paper_title: Convergence Analysis of the Lion Optimizer in Centralized and Distributed Settings

claims.claim: Theorem 1 proves centralized Lion achieves a convergence rate of O(d^{1/2} T^{-1/4}) under standard smoothness, without requiring the coerciveness assumption used in prior analyses (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: T-sweep over 2^11–2^17 (42 runs, 6 seeds) yields fitted slope −0.2511 vs theory −0.25 (R²=0.99983); d-sweep over 16–512 yields +0.4894 vs +0.5 (R²=0.99591); boundedness Lemma verified with 0/5000 violations; destructive control with wrong schedule collapses slope to −0.0435.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows that a variance-reduced Lion variant using STORM-based gradient estimators improves the rate to O(d^{1/2} T^{-1/3}) under an average smoothness assumption (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Lion-VR T-slope −0.2921 vs theory −1/3 (R²=0.9987), measurably steeper than v1's −0.2511; STORM estimator-error decay fitted at −0.658 ≈ −2/3 (R²=0.99988) vs momentum's −0.484; ablation removing STORM term while keeping v2 schedule degrades slope to −0.1898, confirming the mechanism.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 establishes that distributed Lion across n heterogeneous nodes matches the centralized rate, converging as O(d^{1/2} (nT)^{-1/4}) (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Distributed T-slope −0.2538 matches centralized −0.2511 (both ≈ −1/4); n-slope −0.2139 vs theory −0.25 (R²=0.9971) over n=1–32 heterogeneous nodes; destructive control removing n^{1/4} step-scaling collapses n-slope to −0.0687.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 shows that adding variance reduction to distributed Lion improves the distributed rate to O(d^{1/2} (nT)^{-1/3}) (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Dis-Lion-VR T-slope −0.3293 vs theory −0.333 (R²=0.99997, within 1.2%); n-slope −0.3045 vs −0.333 (R²=0.9968, ~9% off); both exponents steeper than non-VR Theorem 3 counterparts (−0.254→−0.329 for T, −0.214→−0.305 for n).

claims.claim: Theorem 5 gives a communication-efficient Lion variant with unbiased sign compression achieving either O(d^{1/2} T^{-1/2} + d n^{-1/2}) or O(n^{1/2} T^{-1} + d n^{-1/2}) depending on the learning-rate choice (Theorem 5).
claims.evidence: The unbiased sign identity E[S_R(v)]=v/R is verified to machine precision (1.1e-16) by exhaustive enumeration, and the two learning-rate regimes show correct qualitative behavior (decaying step → T-decay, constant step → plateau). However, the actual floor exponents are far from theory (n-slope −0.142 vs −0.5; d-slope +0.760 vs +1.0) and the regime-1 T-slope is −0.264 vs predicted −0.5, so the specific convergence rates are not recovered.

claims.claim: Theorem 7 shows that combining bidirectional unbiased sign compression with variance reduction attains a communication-efficient rate of O(d^{1/4} T^{-1/4}), improving over the non-variance-reduced Theorem 6 rate (Theorem 7, Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: The estimator-bias distinction is verified exactly (unbiased composed operator bias 0.0 vs biased sign∘sign bias L₂=6.67), and M(T) is monotonically decreasing. However, the fitted T-slope is −0.132 vs the claimed −0.25 (47% short, R²=0.977), acknowledged as floor-influenced, so the specific O(d^{1/4}T^{-1/4}) rate is not empirically confirmed.

rahit/repro-convergence-analysis-of-the-.overall: The logbook provides strong empirical support for Theorems 1–4, recovering the predicted T and n/d scaling exponents within 2–14% on controlled stochastic quadratics at non-trivial scale (d≤512, T≤131072, n≤32) with working destructive controls. The communication-efficient Theorems 5 and 7 are only partially supported: the unbiased sign identity is exact, but the actual convergence-rate exponents are not cleanly recovered due to floor effects on the quadratic test problem.

rahit/repro-the-interplay-between-interp.paper_title: The Interplay Between Interpolation and Aggregation in Regression: Optimal Sample Complexity

claims.claim: The paper defines the gamma-graph dimension d_γ (Definition 3.2) via a gamma-shattering condition (Definition 3.1) and uses it to characterize the sample complexity of aggregation-based regression procedures.
claims.evidence: Exhaustive enumeration of the γ-shattering condition on the Theorem 3.8 construction yields d_γ = D exactly for D=2,3,4 (k=4,6,8), with destructive controls confirming the >γ condition is load-bearing (collapses to 0 when violated) and a positive control on the full binary class returning d_γ=k.

claims.claim: Any interpolator-based aggregation using proper aggregation rules requires sample complexity Ω(d_γ/ε) to reach expected cutoff loss ε (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: The exact missing-mass identity E[loss]=Σpᵢ(1−pᵢ)ⁿ exceeds ε on all 48 grid configurations (D∈{2,…,200}, ε∈{1/8,…,1/1024}) at the boundary n=⌊d_γ/(32ε)⌋ with minimum ratio 3.09; MC cross-check matches to 2e-6 and destructive controls (n≫threshold→loss≪ε, benign interpolator→loss=0) behave correctly.

claims.claim: There exist hypothesis classes with γ-graph dimension d_γ and γ-OIG dimension at most 3 for which finite interpolating-aggregation algorithms still require sample complexity Ω(d_γ/ε), separating them from general learners that achieve Õ(1/ε) (Theorem 3.8).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive OIG computation on the Theorem 3.8 class shows max out-degree = 1 under both canonical and all-orientations minimisation for n=4,5 across k≤8, certifying γ-OIG dim ≤ 3 while d_γ grows; finite-aggregation lower bound exceeds ε with margin 7.0× on 20 configurations at n=⌊d_γ/(128ε)⌋ with k_u=10⁹.

claims.claim: For some hypothesis classes with constant γ-OIG dimension, no finite interpolating aggregation rule can achieve non-trivial cutoff loss regardless of sample size, requiring either infinite aggregation or non-interpolating rules (Theorem 3.10).
claims.evidence: Exact expected error of the best-effort finite-aggregation learner approaches 0.9998 as √k_u→10⁶ (n=100, m=100), matching the analytic lower bound 1−(n+m)/√k_u; destructive control with m=√k_u (effectively infinite aggregation) drives error to 0.00000, confirming the barrier is specific to finite aggregation.

claims.claim: Taking the median of three independently trained interpolators achieves expected cutoff loss O(d_γ/n), yielding optimal sample complexity O(d_γ/ε) that matches the lower bound (Theorem 3.11).
claims.evidence: Genuine Monte-Carlo run of median-of-three on the worst-case construction yields log-log slope −0.9964 vs n (theory −1, R²=1.0000) with n·loss/d_γ flat at ≈0.29, and slope 1.15 vs d_γ (R²=0.993) with loss/d_γ converging to a constant; MC matches exact formula to 3.8e-4 and identical-sample control collapses to single-interpolator loss.

claims.claim: Proper learners require sample complexity Ω((d_γ/ε)ln(1/ε)), strictly worse than the O(d_γ/ε) achieved by median-of-three aggregation, demonstrating aggregation's superiority over proper learning (Theorem 3.12).
claims.evidence: The coupon-collector construction recovers n·ε/d_γ = 0.4934·ln(1/ε) − 0.446 (R²=0.99992) across 7 values of ε from 1/16 to 1/1024, with MC validation matching exact to 3e-4; separation ratio n_proper/n_agg grows 3.15→10.23 tracking ln(1/ε), confirming the log factor absent from median-of-three.

rahit/repro-the-interplay-between-interp.overall: The logbook provides concrete computational verification of all six claims through clean-room implementations of the paper's explicit hard-instance constructions, with exact closed-form computations, Monte-Carlo cross-checks, and destructive controls for every claim. The evidence is non-toy: it uses the paper's actual constructions at meaningful scale (D up to 200, k_u up to 10¹², exhaustive enumeration where feasible) and every numerical result supports the corresponding theorem.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 proves the original DeepSets aggregation (Equation 4) is discontinuous in the natural any-dimensional topology because the infinite sum can diverge when the inner function ρ decays arbitrarily slowly, so standard DeepSets fails to be universal (Theorem 4.2, Section 4.1.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook constructs the exact mathematical witness: x_i=1/i² ∈ ℓ_1 (||x||_1=ζ(2)≈1.645), ρ(t)=|t|^{1/2}, giving S_n=H_n which diverges to 16.70 at n=10^7 while input distance ||X^(n)−x||_1=1e-7. The Cauchy-in-input/non-Cauchy-in-output demonstration (output gap 2.3026 vs input gap 9.0e-7) directly exhibits discontinuity, and the Lipschitz-ρ control converging to ζ(2) isolates the slow-decay mechanism.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.9 proves standard message-passing GNNs fail any-dimensional universality because their pointwise nonlinearities are discontinuous in the cut metric, since a pointwise map is continuous with respect to the cut norm only if it is linear (Theorem 4.9, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The Rademacher construction W_n=0.5+0.5·S shows input cut-distance →0 (spectral UB 0.130→0.025 over n=50–1600, exact for n≤12) while nonlinear φ=t² output stays ≥0.250 (mean lower bound) across all n. The linear φ=2t+3 control gives output →0.050 (vanishing), exhibiting both directions of the 'continuous iff linear' dichotomy with rigorous sandwich bounds.

claims.claim: A modified DeepSets-infinity architecture (Equation 5) that reweights terms by an ell_p norm factor is proven continuous and universal on ell_p(R^k) sequence space (Theorem 4.2, Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: On the exact input that broke original DeepSets (x_i=1/i², ℓ_1), the ||X_i||^p-reweighted DeepSets-∞ converges to ζ(2) with err 1e-7 at n=10^7. Permutation invariance holds to 8.9e-15 over 1000 relabelings, and the continuity modulus ratio ≤0.455 on 400 configurations confirms the Lipschitz bound. The destructive control (dropping the reweight) reverts to H_n=16.70, confirming the reweight is the active fix.

claims.claim: A measure-space variant DeepSets-bar-infinity (Equation 6), replacing the sum with a normalized integral under a growth condition, is proven universal on the Wasserstein space of probability measures (Theorem 4.5, Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: The Kantorovich–Rubinstein bound |Δ∫ρ dμ|/(Lip·W₁)≤0.778 holds across 2000 random measure pairs with exact 1-D optimal transport, confirming continuity. The growth-condition control (ρ=x², μ_n=(1−1/n²)δ_0+(1/n²)δ_n) shows W₁→1e-4 while ∫x²dμ_n=1≠0, demonstrating discontinuity when the condition fails. Permutation invariance holds to 4.2e-17.

claims.claim: A homomorphism-density-basis architecture (Equations 9-10) is proven continuous and universal on graphon space with the cut metric, restoring universality for graph architectures (Theorem 4.9, Theorem 4.10, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The counting-lemma Lipschitz bound |Δt(F)|/d_□≤e(F) holds on all 250 graphon pairs with exact brute-force cut norms (edge tight at 1.000, path3 1.104≤2, triangle 0.916≤3, 3-star 0.978≤3). The Eq-9 decorated density h_3^{a,b} has finite Lipschitz ratio 0.529. Separation is demonstrated (triangle+iso vs P4: same edge density 0.375 but triangle gap 0.094>0), and relabel invariance is exact (0.0).

claims.claim: A two-stage architecture combining a Gram-matrix map (Equation 12) with Invariant Graphon Networks (Equation 14) is proven universal on bounded point-cloud orbits under the group action (Theorem 4.12, Theorem 4.13, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: O(k) invariance of the Gram map holds to 4.4e-16 over 500 configs with random orthogonal Q. Completeness is verified: same-orbit Y=XQ gives |G(X)−G(Y)|=2.2e-16 with recovered T orthogonal (|T^T T−I|=1.1e-15), while a non-orthogonal shear gives gap 0.198. The two-stage hom-density readout is invariant to combined node-permutation × O(k) actions (6.4e-16 over 300 configs) and separates distinct orbits (gap 0.0094).

rahit/repro-any-dimensional-invariant-un.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims through clean-room implementations of the paper's exact mathematical constructions, with exact computations (cut norms, optimal transport, hom densities), machine-precision invariance checks, and destructive controls that isolate each claim's mechanism. The universality/denseness aspects of claims 3–6 are evidenced via necessary conditions (continuity, invariance, separation) rather than full density proofs, which the logbook honestly acknowledges.

GwendalTsang/repro-automatic-layer-selec.paper_title: Automatic Layer Selection for Hallucination Detection

claims.claim: Hallucination-related signals concentrate in intermediate layers of large language models rather than in the final layer, motivating automated layer selection over exhaustive per-layer evaluation (Section 1).
claims.evidence: Real runs on LLaMA CoQA (scaled 1,000/1,000) and paper-scale Mistral HaluEval both show oracle intermediate layers beating the final layer by +0.11 to +0.15 AUROC, but only 2 of 7 paper datasets are tested and the HaluEval test set is severely imbalanced (27 negatives).

claims.claim: First Effective Peak of Intrinsic Dimension (FEPoID), which uses a forward-horizon parameter w (default 7) to filter spurious early peaks in the intrinsic-dimension curve, achieves the highest average AUROC among four criterion families across five QA hallucination-detection datasets (CoQA, SQuAD, HotpotQA, TriviaQA, PsiloQA): 0.7253 for LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and 0.8531 for Mistral-7B (Section 3, Table 2).
claims.evidence: The five-dataset averages (0.7253 LLaMA, 0.8531 Mistral) were never computed; only scaled LLaMA CoQA was run, where FEPoID (0.5100 full / 0.6031 FST) does not lead Maximum ID (0.5160 / 0.6384), and SQuAD, HotpotQA, TriviaQA, PsiloQA, and Mistral QA were not completed.

claims.claim: On summarization hallucination-detection benchmarks (HaluEval, CNN/DM), FEPoID outperforms alternative layer-selection criteria with an average AUROC of 0.6080 for LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The claimed LLaMA average of 0.6080 on HaluEval/CNN-DM was never tested; the only summarization run is Mistral HaluEval, where FEPoID (0.7360) ranks below Maximum ID (0.8219), validation loss (0.8117), and SNR (0.7578), though all CIs overlap substantially.

claims.claim: FEPoID is training-free and computationally efficient, requiring only 10.14 seconds on average across benchmarks compared to 27-58 seconds for gradient-based alternatives, a 3-6x speedup (Table 4).
claims.evidence: On paper-scale Mistral HaluEval, FEPoID (54.29 s) is 5.38× faster than RGN (291.96 s) and 5.85× faster than SNR (317.50 s), matching the claimed 3–6× range for gradient-based alternatives, but the absolute 10.14 s mean was not reproduced (different hardware: Jetson Orin vs. FAISS-GPU), validation loss shows only 1.30× speedup, and RankMe/curvature were not timed.

claims.claim: First-Sentence Truncation (FST), proposed to remove end-of-sequence noise from inconsistent continuations, semantic drift, and degenerate repetition, yields consistent AUROC improvements of roughly 1-5% across tested layer-selection methods, with larger gains for LLaMA (more susceptible to such noise) than Mistral (Section 5, Figure 3, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: FST improves FEPoID AUROC by +0.0931 (LLaMA CoQA) and +0.0967 (Mistral HaluEval), and 6 of 7 Mistral selectors improve, but RGN declines (−0.0728), undermining across-method consistency; the deltas exceed the claimed 1–5% range, and the larger-LLaMA-than-Mistral contrast cannot be assessed across different datasets.

GwendalTsang/repro-automatic-layer-selec.overall: The logbook provides real runs on LLaMA-3.1-8B CoQA (scaled) and paper-scale Mistral HaluEval, showing directional support for intermediate-layer concentration and FST improvements, but the headline numerical claims (five-dataset QA averages, LLaMA summarization mean, absolute timing) were never computed, and FEPoID does not lead alternative selectors in the one summarization cell completed.

nathanael-fijalkow/repro-how-reasoning-e.paper_title: How Reasoning Evolves from Post-Training Data: An Empirical Study Using Chess

claims.claim: Fine-tuning a chess-playing LLM to directly predict only the single best move (Best Move data) enables effective downstream RL but produces an unfaithful reasoner, whose final chosen move often becomes disconnected from its own reasoning trace after RL (Section addressing Q2, Core Findings).
claims.evidence: A judge_pass.py script was executed (exit 0) on 10 sample generations from a bestmove-sft checkpoint, but no actual faithfulness scores, RL checkpoint results, or Best Move vs Best Line comparisons are shown anywhere in the logbook.

claims.claim: Fine-tuning on multi-move trajectories (Best Line data) yields RL performance comparable to Best Move training while retaining faithful reasoning traces and more stable RL training dynamics (Section addressing Q1/Q2, Core Findings).
claims.evidence: No page content for Claim 2 is visible in the truncated logbook; no Best Line generations, RL performance comparisons, or faithfulness measurements are present.

claims.claim: After RL, the Best Move model achieves 90% legal moves and an average move rank of 0.71, while the Best Line model achieves 85% legal moves and an average move rank of 0.63, with Best Line showing substantially higher reasoning faithfulness (Table comparing Best Move vs Best Line metrics).
claims.evidence: No table or numerical results showing 90%/0.71 or 85%/0.63 metrics for Best Move vs Best Line are visible anywhere in the logbook.

claims.claim: RL substantially shifts the move-quality distribution toward best moves and away from low-quality moves, and reduces hallucination rates as a side effect of reward maximization, consistent across experimental conditions (Section on core findings, move quality and hallucination).
claims.evidence: No move-quality distribution plots, hallucination rate measurements, or pre/post-RL comparisons are present in the visible logbook.

claims.claim: Referenced move accuracy and reasoning quality measured after SFT are identified as statistically significant predictors of downstream RL performance (Section addressing Q3, predictive SFT indicators).
claims.evidence: No statistical analysis, correlation results, or significance tests relating SFT metrics to RL performance are visible in the logbook.

claims.claim: The resulting 7B-parameter chess-playing model surpasses leading open-source reasoning models at chess, with code, model weights, and training data released publicly (Section on practical achievement).
claims.evidence: No comparison results between the 7B chess model and leading open-source reasoning models are present in the visible logbook.

nathanael-fijalkow/repro-how-reasoning-e.overall: The logbook is in an early stage: a scoring script was written and executed on 10 sample generations, but no actual results, metrics, or comparisons are shown for any claim. The logbook is truncated after the Claim 1 page, leaving Claims 2–6 with no visible evidence at all.

kshitijthakkar/repro-dynaschedbench-obse.paper_title: DynaSchedBench: Calibrated Dynamic Scheduling Benchmarks and Observability Paradox in LLM-based Scheduling Agents

claims.claim: Giving LLM scheduling agents oracle access to full structural information (level L3) yields a worse relative makespan gap (1.66%) than giving them concise statistical summaries (level L2, 0.65% gap), demonstrating an observability paradox (Section 7.2).
claims.evidence: The v2 experiment ran L2 CoT and L3 CoT on 3 non-degenerate toy instances (8 jobs, 3 job-family templates) with Qwen3-4B via CPU-only Ollama. Per-instance L2-vs-L3 comparison split 1 for paper's direction (seed_8101: L2=46.05 < L3=47.23), 1 against (seed_8102: L2=57.15 > L3=50.29), and 1 tie (seed_8103: both 44.31). Mean relative gaps were L2=5.52% and L3=1.71%, actually opposite to the paper's claimed ordering, but n=3 provides no statistical power.

claims.claim: L2 chain-of-thought agents show better tail stability (2.01% p95 relative makespan gap) than L3 chain-of-thought agents (2.92%), indicating LLMs struggle to distill useful signal from high-dimensional structural priors (Table 4).
claims.evidence: The specific p95 tail-stability metric (2.01% vs 2.92%) was never computed; with only n=3 instances per config, p95 is not meaningful and the logbook did not attempt it. The broader L2-vs-L3 comparison was mixed (1-1-tie), providing no evidence about tail stability specifically.

claims.claim: The best LLM agent (Qwen3-8B, 1.01% relative makespan gap) is statistically indistinguishable from the best hand-crafted priority dispatching rule (LIFO+LIT, 1.11% gap), with a paired difference of -0.099 percentage points (95% CI [-0.531, 0.389]) (Table 5, Table 6).
claims.evidence: The v2 parity test used Qwen3-4B (not the paper's Qwen3-8B) on 3 toy instances. The LLM was consistently worse than the best heuristic (LOPNR+LIT at 1.91%), with paired differences of +10.17, +3.28, and +4.56 percentage points—all positive, contradicting the paper's near-parity finding, but on a different model at toy scale with n=3.

claims.claim: Tool-augmented agents at reasoning level L1 consume 12.614 million tokens for 2.0% relative performance, versus 4.016 million tokens for 1.9% performance with chain-of-thought alone, a roughly three-fold token cost increase for worse results (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The v2 run compared L1+Tool vs L1 Direct (not L1 CoT as in the paper) on 2-3 toy instances. Token ratio was 2.10x input / 2.14x output (vs paper's ~3x), with L1 Tool performing worse (12.13% vs 6.00% mean gap). The qualitative direction—more tokens for worse results—matches, but the specific quantitative comparison (12.614M vs 4.016M tokens, 3x ratio, L1+Tool vs L1 CoT) was not reproduced.

kshitijthakkar/repro-dynaschedbench-obse.overall: The logbook provides a careful, honestly-reported reproduction attempt that fully verifies the paper's non-LLM calibrator claims at scale but only reaches toy-scale (3 instances, 8 jobs, Qwen3-4B) on the four LLM-dependent claims scored here. The observability paradox and p95 tail-stability claims remain unconfirmed at this scale, while the LLM-vs-heuristic parity and token-overhead claims show directional consistency with the paper but with different magnitudes and model identity.

akshitag001/repro-break-the-block-dynami.paper_title: Break the Block: Dynamic-size Reasoning Blocks for Diffusion Large Language Models via Monotonic Entropy Descent with Reinforcement Learning

claims.claim: b1 improves accuracy over fixed-size block baselines by +19.53% on Countdown (wd1 variant, 256-token setting), +1.97% on GSM8K, and +3.20% on MATH500, consistently across Diffu-GRPO, GDPO, and wd1 algorithms (Table 1).
claims.evidence: No training or evaluation runs were executed; the logbook only performed code-level inspection of the reward implementation (lines 414-455 in dynamic_generate.py) and confirmed checkpoints are downloadable. No accuracy numbers were independently produced to support or refute the claimed +19.53%/+1.97%/+3.20% gains.

claims.claim: Block-wise entropy trajectories are consistently descending for correct reasoning chains but fluctuate for incorrect ones, a pattern formalized as Monotonic Entropy Descent and quantified via Spearman's rank correlation coefficient in Table 3 (Section 4.3, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states this was not independently re-run due to no GPU budget. No entropy trajectories were computed, no Spearman correlations were measured, and no figures or tables were reproduced. Only the existence of official scripts and checkpoints was noted.

claims.claim: b1 raises the proportion of correct generations exhibiting positive Spearman rank correlation (rSCC) from a baseline range of 65-91% up to 75-98% (Section 4.4, Table 3).
claims.evidence: No evaluation runs were performed; the logbook only confirmed that official checkpoints are downloadable. The claimed shift from 65-91% to 75-98% positive rSCC was not measured or verified with any concrete data.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 proves that the local entropy reward used by b1's Monotonic Entropy Descent objective (Eq. 8) is equivalent to optimizing a global Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (Section 3.2, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides an independent mathematical derivation: by the Rearrangement Inequality, maximizing r_SCC (proportional to negative sum of squared rank differences) requires entropy ranks to be oppositely sorted to the index vector, i.e., strictly decreasing; R_ent also reaches its maximum of 1 only when every adjacent pair is strictly decreasing, so argmax R_ent = argmax r_SCC. This is a self-contained, correct proof requiring no experiments.

claims.claim: b1 generalizes beyond math reasoning, improving code generation and knowledge-task benchmarks by +1.22 to +9.39 points, while adding only about 2% training overhead and maintaining comparable inference throughput (~27 tokens/sec) (Table 4, Table 5).
claims.evidence: No code or knowledge benchmark runs were executed, and the logbook notes no pretrained checkpoints exist for HumanEval/MBPP/KodCode, making this the most expensive claim. No throughput or overhead measurements were taken. Zero empirical evidence was produced.

akshitag001/repro-break-the-block-dynami.overall: This logbook successfully verifies only the theoretical Claim 4 (Theorem 1) via an independent mathematical proof, and provides useful code-level corroboration of the reward implementation. All four empirical claims (1, 2, 3, 5) remain unaddressed because no GPU runs were performed, making the reproduction largely incomplete.

debo3/repro-manifoldkv-training-free-kv-.paper_title: ManifoldKV: Training-Free KV Cache Compression via Euclidean Outlier Detection

claims.claim: ManifoldKV scores tokens for retention using Euclidean (L2) distance from the key centroid, defined as s_i = ‖k_i − μ‖₂, rather than cosine similarity (Definition 3.1).
claims.evidence: The test script directly imports ManifoldKVPress and KeyDiffPress from the kvpress fork and verifies bit-exact equality between ManifoldKVPress.score and ‖k_i − mean(K)‖₂ (PASS 1), demonstrates that a radial outlier (cosine=0.999) receives the top L2 score but lowest KeyDiff score (PASS 2/3), and confirms WindowedManifoldKVPress matches per-window local centroids (PASS 4).

claims.claim: On the RULER benchmark at 4K–16K contexts with 20% compression, ManifoldKV (with the AdaKV framework) achieves 95.73% accuracy versus 95.66% for KeyDiff and 83.97% for the attention-based SnapKV (Table 4).
claims.evidence: On true per-length RULER data at 20% compression, AdaKV+ManifoldKV averages 93.51% across 4K–16K (not 95.73%), with 8K=93.70 and 16K=91.40; AdaKV+KeyDiff actually scores higher on average (94.10 vs 93.51), reversing the paper's claimed ordering. The logbook provides evidence that the paper's 8K/16K numbers were produced by re-running 4K data under a truncation cap, and control runs confirm true-16K is ~92.1±0.7 over 3 seeds, not ~95.7.

claims.claim: On 3-key NIAH multi-key retrieval at 8K context with 50% compression, ManifoldKV achieves 92.4% accuracy versus KeyDiff's 77.0%, a +15.4 point gain; on 2-key NIAH under the same setting it achieves 99.8% versus KeyDiff's 92.6%, a +7.2 point gain (Table 6).
claims.evidence: At 8K context, 50% compression, AdaKV+ManifoldKV scores 94.0 vs AdaKV+KeyDiff 79.0 on 3-key NIAH (+15.0 pts, paper +15.4) and 100.0 vs 93.0 on 2-key NIAH (+7.0 pts, paper +7.2), on 200 samples/task with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct — all within ~2 pts of Table 6.

claims.claim: At 64K-token contexts, global-centroid ManifoldKV suffers 'centroid dilution,' collapsing from 82.3% accuracy at 32K to 35.2% at 64K (Table 1, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Global-centroid ManifoldKV on true per-length RULER data shows 83.53% at 32K (paper 82.3) collapsing to 25.97% at 64K (paper 35.2), confirming the centroid dilution phenomenon with a −57.6 pt drop (paper −47.1), using data regenerated with the official NVIDIA/RULER pipeline at 50 samples/task × 13 tasks.

claims.claim: WindowedManifoldKV, using local 4K-token window centroids (Algorithm 2), restores accuracy to 84.3% at 25% compression and 64K context, a +49.1 point recovery over global ManifoldKV (35.2%) and +3.2 points over KeyDiff (81.1%) (Table 5).
claims.evidence: WindowedManifoldKV (4K window) scores 83.82% at 64K/25% compression (paper 84.3), recovering +57.9 pts over global ManifoldKV's 25.97% (paper +49.1) and +4.97 pts over KeyDiff's 78.85% (paper +3.2), with a paired t-test confirming significance (t=4.29, p=2e-5) on 649 paired samples.

claims.claim: Cross-architecture validation shows identical ManifoldKV code achieves 94–96% accuracy without tuning across Gemma-3-12B (95.2%), Qwen3-8B (95.0%), Ministral-8B (95.5%), and Llama-3.1-8B (95.7%) (Table 8).
claims.evidence: At 4K RULER with 20% compression and identical adakv_manifold_kv code with no per-model tuning, the four architectures score 95.70 (Gemma-3-12B, paper 95.2), 94.68 (Qwen3-8B, paper 95.0), 95.10 (Ministral-8B, paper 95.5), and 95.44 (Llama-3.1-8B, paper 95.7) — all within 0.5 pts and inside the claimed 94–96% band. The ΔSnapKV column also reproduces (mean +12.6 vs paper +13.1).

debo3/repro-manifoldkv-training-free-kv-.overall: The logbook provides concrete, non-toy experimental evidence verifying ManifoldKV's core mechanisms: Euclidean L2 scoring (Claim 1), multi-key NIAH advantage (Claim 3), centroid dilution collapse at 64K (Claim 4), windowed recovery (Claim 5), and cross-architecture generalization at 4K (Claim 6). However, Claim 2 is falsified because the headline 95.73% average across 4K–16K does not reproduce on true per-length data (93.51%), with evidence that the paper's 8K/16K numbers were generated by relabeling 4K evaluations under a truncation cap.

claims.claim: NeuralLog-UCB-1 achieves a regret upper bound of order Õ(d̃√(κT)), where d̃ is the data-adaptive effective dimension rather than the ambient feature dimension d, improving on the d√(κT) bound of Logistic-UCB-1 (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The effective dimension d̃≈54.4 vs p=441 is measured on a width-20 network (T=2000, diagonal design), confirming the dimensional mechanism at reduced scale, but the head-to-head regret comparison shows NeuralLog-UCB-1 winning only 2/6 datasets (h₃, mushroom) and losing on h₁, h₂, shuttle, and MNIST.

claims.claim: NeuralLog-UCB-2 achieves a regret upper bound of order Õ(d̃√(T/κ*)), matching the κ* dependence of ada-OFU-ECOLog (whose bound is d√(T/κ*)) while replacing the ambient dimension d with the effective dimension d̃ (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The d̃≪p dimensional advantage is measured on the same reduced setup, but NeuralLog-UCB-2 beats ada-OFU-ECOLog on only 3/6 datasets (h₂, h₃, mushroom) and loses on h₁, shuttle, and MNIST (1656 vs 718 on MNIST), so the empirical κ*-advantage is not demonstrated at this scale.

claims.claim: A novel Bernstein-type self-normalized martingale inequality (Theorem 3.1) yields concentration of order Õ(√d̃) without the extra κ factor required by the corresponding inequality in Verma et al. (2024), which scales as Õ(√(κd̃)) (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The martingale simulation (d=10, T=2000, 40 reps, κ swept 2→200) shows the Theorem 3.1 bound stays flat (~290) while the Verma-style bound grows from 418 to 1396, with the ratio increasing monotonically and the bound always covering the empirical statistic — concrete numerical evidence that the inequality removes the extra √κ factor.

claims.claim: NeuralLog-UCB-2 uses neural-network-based variance estimates in place of the true reward variance μ̇(xᵀθ*) within the design matrix, enabling the tighter T/κ* dependence while retaining d̃-scaling (Section on NeuralLog-UCB-2 / Condition 5.4).
claims.evidence: The code snippet confirms the NN-estimated variance mdot=σ(f)(1−σ(f)) weights the design matrix for NeuralLog-UCB-2 while other methods use unweighted V_t, but the implementation uses diagonal (not full) design matrices at width m=20, and the logbook itself notes the variance-adaptive W_t yields regret comparable to—not strictly below—the √κ design at T=2000, κ=10.

claims.claim: On synthetic nonlinear reward functions h1(x)=0.2(xᵀθ)^4, h2(x)=20cos(xᵀθ), and h3(x)=5xᵀθx, as well as on the MNIST, mushroom, and shuttle real-world datasets, NeuralLog-UCB-2 substantially outperforms baselines including the method of Verma et al. (2024) (Experimental validation section).
claims.evidence: All six datasets are run at T=2000 with 10 seeds, but at reduced scale (width-20 NN, diagonal design, PCA-d=20, ν-only grid search); NeuralLog-UCB-2 is the single best method on only 1/6 datasets (h₂), ties on mushroom, and dramatically underperforms linear baselines on MNIST (1656 vs 711) and shuttle (472 vs 400), contradicting the paper's headline claim at this scale.

shayekh/repro-neural-logistic-bandits.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting the theoretical mechanism of Claim 3 (κ-independent Bernstein inequality) and confirms the effective-dimension substitution (d̃≈54≪p=441) central to Claims 1–2, but all bandit experiments run at a clearly reduced scale (width-20, diagonal design matrices, T=2000) where NeuralLog-UCB-2 fails to dominate baselines on 4/6 datasets, making the empirical claims only partially addressed.

jomasego/repro-finite-time-convergence-a.paper_title: Finite-time Convergence Analysis of Actor-Critic with Evolving Reward

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 establishes finite-time bounds for single-timescale actor-critic with evolving rewards, with actor error G_T and critic error W_T each bounded by O(1/√T) + O(F_T·√T) + O(√(F_T/T)) + O(ε), where F_T measures cumulative reward-parameter variation over T iterations (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Real runs on a 5-state, 2-action MDP with 4-dim features show G_T·√T ≈ 0.4 across static, gradient, and random-walk modes, consistent with O(1/√T). However, F_T values are negligibly small (1.78e-11, 3.19e-8), so the F_T-dependent terms O(F_T·√T) and O(√(F_T/T)) are never meaningfully exercised, and the MDP is clearly a minimal toy setup.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.7 shows that when the reward parameter is updated via gradient-based steps with step size η^φ_t = c_φ/t and bounded gradients, F_T = O(1/T), so the bounds reduce to G_T = O(1/√T) + O(ε) and W_T = O(1/√T) + O(ε), matching the best-known rate for static-reward actor-critic (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Gradient-based reward updates with η^φ_t = c_φ/t yield F_T = 1.78e-11 on the 5-state MDP, which is technically O(1/T) but so close to zero that the reward parameter barely evolves, making the test uninformative about the actual scaling behavior. The setup is a minimal toy MDP.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.8 bounds the distribution mismatch under Markovian sampling without dependence on the mixing time, improving prior convergence rates by a factor of log²T in the static-reward case (Section 4.3).

claims.claim: Assumption 4.1 (sufficient exploration) requires the matrix A_θ to be negative definite with singular values bounded above by -λ, underpinning the actor-critic convergence analysis (Section 4, Assumption 4.1).
claims.evidence: A_θ is estimated via Monte Carlo at 5 random policy parameters on the 5-state MDP; the symmetric part of A_std has all positive eigenvalues (min ≈ 0.007), confirming negative definiteness of the paper's A_θ on this specific toy instance, but this only checks the assumption on one minimal MDP rather than verifying it in general.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 defines a single-timescale actor-critic scheme with step sizes η^θ_t = c_θ/√t and η^ω_t = c_ω/√t for policy and critic updates, alongside an arbitrary update rule for the evolving reward parameter φ_t (Section 3.3, Algorithm 1).

claims.claim: The proposed online Newton method using a sketch-and-project solver with Nesterov's acceleration (Algorithm 1, NASketch) matches the O(d^2) per-iteration time and memory complexity of first-order methods (Section 2.2).

claims.claim: The last iterate is proven asymptotically normal, with the limiting covariance characterized by a Lyapunov equation incorporating the sketching operator (Theorem 4.3).

claims.claim: A spectral radius recursion derived via the Cayley-Hamilton theorem proves contraction at rate 1 - sqrt(mu_t/nu_t) for the accelerated sketching operator (Lemma 3.6).
claims.evidence: Deterministic check over 11 parameter pairs (mu in [0.02,0.5], nu=1/mu), 20,001 spectral points, 64 Cayley-Hamilton recurrence steps: max recurrence error 7.0e-14 and max spectral-radius excess over 1-sqrt(mu/nu) of 1.1e-16, both at machine precision.

claims.claim: The framework recovers exact Newton behavior and the unaccelerated sketching case (gamma=1) as special cases, clarifying computational-statistical trade-offs (Proposition 4.4).

claims.evidence: The lp_round function and claim_one() verify both bicriteria inequalities (loss ≤ (1+κ)·ε·W and |K| ≤ (1+1/κ)·r) on 48 random instances, but only with n=5 vertices and ε=0.25, κ=1.0 — a clearly simplified setup far below the paper's intended scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 proves a monotonicity/nestedness property (Kτ1⊆Kτ2 for τ1<τ2), derived from a connection to parametric minimum cuts, which is required for valid conformal calibration (Theorem 2, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: A counterexample on two singleton hyperedges shows non-nestedness without canonical LP tie-breaking, while 32 instances with n=6 and grids up to 12×12 confirm nestedness under the maximal source-side parametric min-cut convention. Both the falsification and verification are on small-scale instances, not a full reproduction.

claims.claim: Corollary 1 shows the entire nested sequence of subgraphs across thresholds can be computed in Õ(γ(m+n)²) time (Corollary 1, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Runtime scaling is measured on grids from 4×4 to 12×12 (m+n from 40 to 408) with log-log slope 1.15, and finite sequence audits use n=6. The logbook itself notes 'no empirical run proves the source's asymptotic soft-O bound,' and the scales are too small to demonstrate the Õ(γ(m+n)²) complexity claim.

claims.claim: Lemma 1 establishes a distribution-free marginal coverage guarantee ℙ(B*⊆Kτ*(A*))≥φ−δ under exchangeability, without requiring model probability estimates (Lemma 1).
claims.evidence: Exact enumeration of all 40320 permutations with ncal=7 confirms coverage equals φ=0.75 exactly, and a 256-draw stage-1 filtering audit confirms coverage ≥ φ−δ. These are exact but very small-scale checks of the conformal rank guarantee, not a full-scale demonstration.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 proves NP-hardness of the conformal subgraph problem even for constant ε via reduction from clique detection, in Appendix B (Theorem 4, Appendix B).
claims.evidence: The reduction is verified answer-preserving on 60 random graphs (n=6–9) and one specific construction instance (K3 vs K1,3 with ε=0.5), confirming yes_max=31 ≥ target=31 and no_max=30 < 31. This is real but small-scale empirical support for the NP-hardness reduction, not a proof.

claims.claim: On a synthetic 6x6 grid navigation experiment with 50 train/test routes, the LP-based method compresses the calibration set to 52 edges at φ=0.75 coverage and outperforms greedy baselines for φ≤0.8 (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The campaign page reports 200 seeds at the paper's stated scale (6×6 grid, 50 train/test routes, 0.15 bypass probability), with LP mean 57.38 edges at φ=0.75 (20 seeds exactly 52) and paired CIs showing LP outperforms both greedy baselines for all φ≤0.8. This matches the paper's own experimental setup and confirms the qualitative claims, though the exact 52-edge figure is not the central tendency.

DineshAI/KqMqJpSMnQ.overall: The logbook provides toy-scale empirical checks for all five theorem-level claims (n=5–12 instances, exact small enumerations) and a faithful 200-seed reproduction of the paper's 6×6 grid navigation experiment confirming LP outperforms greedy baselines. The theorem verifications are too small to constitute full reproductions of universal mathematical statements, and the paper's lack of released code/seeds limits the fidelity of the experimental reproduction.

DineshAI/rZTiFcDihH.paper_title: Online Packet Scheduling with Deadlines and Learning

claims.claim: For the deterministic algorithm EDF_Φ^L in 2- and 3-bounded K-OPSD, the Φ-regret upper bound is Õ(√(KT)), matching sleeping-bandit-style rates (Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: Finite checks on 6,817 K=2/3 states (max ratio 1.25 < Φ) and a single T=65,536 stress run with zero positive Φ-regret, plus a 20,000-instance falsification search. These are real runs on small-scale instances, but the logbook explicitly acknowledges no route mechanized the complete universal 3-bounded charging bijection, so the asymptotic theorem is not verified.

claims.claim: The deterministic algorithm ALG^θ achieves competitive ratio θ_K in [√2, Φ) for finite K packet types, breaking the classical golden-ratio Φ = (1+√5)/2 competitive-ratio barrier for 2-bounded deadline instances (Proposition 4.1).
claims.evidence: A concrete three-type, two-bounded, six-packet counterexample yields independent OPT=8 and literal ALG^θ=5, giving ratio 1.6 > θ_3=1.5. The θ-system is independently solved with residual zero, and the offline DP is separate from the online rule. Since competitive-ratio claims are universal, a single valid counterexample suffices.

claims.claim: The learning variant ALG^θ,U attains a θ_K-regret upper bound of Õ(√(KT)), which is shown to be nearly tight against a matching Ω(√T) lower bound (Theorem 4.2, Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: K=3 bounded rewards in [0,1] with means (0.9,0.6,0.3), literal monotone UCB (δ=1/T), and independent offline DP show θ_3-regret growing from 62.25 at T=4,096 to 2,163.30 at T=65,536 with log-log slope 1.151 and positive tail regret/T=0.033, indicating linear rather than Õ(√(KT)) growth at non-trivial scale.

claims.claim: The randomized algorithm ALG^R2 for 2-bounded instances achieves a 5/4-regret bound of Õ(√(KT)) (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: Z3 proved 16 p_hat inequalities, 80-seed runs to T=32,768 showed nonpositive 5/4-regret, and 10,000 mean-pair integrations reached the 1.25 boundary without violation. However, the logbook states the source pseudocode omits single-set buffer cases and the full multi-round learning potential was not mechanized, so this is a partial check on simplified setups.

claims.claim: The randomized algorithm ALG^Rs for s-bounded (unbounded slackness) instances achieves an e/(e-1)-regret bound of Õ(√(KT)) (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Finite checks on 4,096–12,000 states stayed below e/(e-1), and 80-seed runs to T=32,768 aligned. However, the logbook identifies a proof gap in the displayed bound and notes the literal learning rule has undefined initialization (log(UCB/LCB) with LCB=0), meaning every executable run uses an unspecified deviation.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 establishes that sleeping bandits are a special case of 1-bounded K-OPSD, formally connecting the packet scheduling model to the multi-armed bandit framework (Section 2.2, Lemma 2.1).
claims.evidence: A parameterized mapping (sleeping action i → type-i packet with release=deadline=t) is formally checked via a quantified SMT query for action-set mismatch returning unsat, and a K=257, T=1000 round-trip simulation preserves all availability sets and cumulative reward. A negative control that changes a deadline away from its release is correctly detected.

DineshAI/rZTiFcDihH.overall: The logbook provides concrete falsifications of Claims 2 and 3 with specific counterexamples and non-trivial-scale experiments, and verifies Claim 6 via SMT plus simulation. Claims 1, 4, and 5 are addressed with real but incomplete finite-scale checks that do not constitute full verification or falsification of the asymptotic bounds.

ai-sherpa/sharp-io-nonlinear-adversarial.paper_title: On the Sharp Input-Output Analysis of Nonlinear Systems under Adversarial Attacks

claims.claim: The paper analyzes an ℓ1-norm (least-absolute-deviation) estimator and proves it achieves an estimation error bound of Θ(ρ^τ), where ρ is the system's contraction factor and τ is the input memory length (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook cites the paper's Eq. 12 as minimizing a sum of Euclidean (ℓ2) norms, not ℓ1/LAD, and quotes Theorem 3.1's bound as O(ρ^τ L/λ · (σ_u+σ_w)/(1-ρ) + ...) with multiple extra factors, not a standalone Θ(ρ^τ). Numerical experiments confirm the corrected ℓ2/geometric-median mechanism normalizes to ρ^τ (fitted power 1.0000, R²=1.0000), but this supports the corrected version, not the claim as written.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1's guarantee requires the adversarial attack probability to satisfy p < 1/(2τ), which ensures the probability (1-p)^τ of an attack-free observation window exceeds one half (Assumption 2.8, Remark 2.9).
claims.evidence: For τ=1..64 with five p values strictly inside p<1/(2τ), all 320/320 cells satisfy (1-p)^τ>½ (smallest margin 0.050). A destructive control at p=1.01·(1-2^{-1/τ}) yields 64/64 failures below ½, confirming the bound is sufficient and the check is falsifiable.

claims.claim: A matching lower bound of order Θ(ρ^τ L r/λ) is established, proving the upper bound of Theorem 3.1 is order-optimal and that no estimator can improve on this rate under probabilistic adversarial attacks (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook identifies the lower bound as Theorem 3.5 (not 3.4) with rate Ω(ρ^τ L/λ) and no r factor, citing Remark 3.4's explicit statement of r-independence. An indistinguishable-pair witness (h₁=0, h₂=s·max(1-z,0)·e₁, s=ρ^τL/λ) over 720 parameter combinations shows separation equals ρ^τL/λ exactly and is r-independent in 144/144 combos, contradicting the claimed Θ(ρ^τ L r/λ).

claims.claim: The estimation error is shown to decay exponentially with the input memory length τ through the contraction factor ρ ∈ (0,1) (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Direct measurement of fading-memory truncation error on a 100-dimensional nonlinear system across τ=1..8, ρ∈{0.4,0.6,0.8}, 40 seeds (960 runs) shows strictly monotone geometric decay with fitted rates 0.102/0.153/0.205 (≈0.256ρ) and R²≥0.99999, confirming the O(ρ^τ) form.

claims.claim: Section 3.2 first derives sufficient conditions for exact recovery in the case without past-state effects (Theorem 3.3, Section 3.2.1), then extends the analysis to the general case with nonzero past-state terms (Section 3.2.2).
claims.evidence: Theorem 3.3's sufficient condition (clean-window strict majority) matches independent geometric-median recovery on 4320/4320 worst-case paths, with every recovery failure coinciding with condition failure. For the general case (Section 3.2.2), 397/397 Eq.(17)-type certificates hold with recovery residual at the ρ^τ scale.

ai-sherpa/sharp-io-nonlinear-adversarial.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical and textual evidence falsifying Claims 1 and 3 as written (misstated estimator norm ℓ1 vs ℓ2, wrong theorem index 3.4 vs 3.5, and spurious r-factor), while verifying Claims 2, 4, and 5 through arithmetic checks, fading-memory decay experiments, and exact-recovery certificate evaluations on non-trivial setups.

SabaPivot/repro-approximate-proportional.paper_title: Approximate Proportionality in Online Fair Division

claims.claim: Three natural greedy allocation rules (maximize relative item value, allocate to most unsatisfied agent, and minimize worst predicted dissatisfaction) each fail to guarantee any positive multiplicative approximation to PROP1 against an adaptive adversary (Section 3, Propositions 6-8).
claims.evidence: Independent implementation of all three greedy rules with adaptive adversarial constructions at horizon ~500 goods yields ratios 0.007984, 0.008000, and 0.385269, closely matching the paper's stress-test values (0.008, 0.008, 0.385) and demonstrating the decreasing trend toward zero that supports the impossibility of positive multiplicative approximation.

claims.claim: Against a non-adaptive adversary, uniform random allocation achieves an Ω(1/log(n/δ)) approximation to PROP1 with probability at least 1-δ, specifically α = 27/(128·log(n/δ)), the first such multiplicative bound in the online setting without extra assumptions (Section 4, Theorem 9).
claims.evidence: Analytic re-derivation of the Bernstein bound with α=27/(128·log(n/δ)) checked across n∈{2,…,1024} and δ from 0.5 to 1e-6 yields a minimum exponent-to-L margin of 2.1826 (safely above 1), supplemented by 60,000 Monte Carlo allocations with zero failures, concretely confirming the probability guarantee and the stated constant.

claims.claim: Given perfect maximum-item-value (MIV) predictions, Algorithm 1 guarantees a 1/n-PROP1 allocation (Section 5, Theorem 11).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive testing of 11,084 instances (2-agent/4-good and 3-agent/3-good over {0,1/2,1}) all achieving exact PROP1, plus a rerun of the official experiment (n=8, m=40, 500 trials, seed 1428) reproducing PROP1=1.000 across all distribution families and adversarial prefixes, concretely supports the 1/n-PROP1 guarantee.

claims.claim: Under one-sided MIV prediction error ε ∈ [0,1), the algorithm's approximation degrades gracefully to β = (1-ε)/(n-ε/n) (Section 5, Theorem 12).
claims.evidence: 32,201 two-agent/three-good grid instances across ε∈{0.25,0.50,0.75} all yield worst-case PROP1 ratios exceeding the claimed β (e.g., 0.857>0.400 at ε=0.25, 0.667>0.286 at ε=0.50, 0.667>0.154 at ε=0.75), confirming the graceful degradation bound holds on exhaustive finite grids.

claims.claim: Even with perfect MIV predictions, no online algorithm can achieve any non-zero approximation to EF1, MMS, or PROPX (Section 5, Proposition 10).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive path enumeration (256 paths for α=0.5, 65,536 for α=0.25) with a repaired parameter choice (m>2n/α, ε=K^{-m}) shows every path violates EF1, MMS, and PROPX with worst ratios (0.2000,0.2500,0.4444) and (0.0909,0.1250,0.2353), confirming the impossibility mechanism; however, the paper's printed appendix parameters fail to establish PROPX violation (ratios 0.75 and 0.50), indicating a parameter gap in the original text.

SabaPivot/repro-approximate-proportional.overall: The logbook provides concrete computational evidence supporting all five claims through independent implementations, exhaustive finite-instance checks, analytic re-derivations, and reruns of the official codebase. Notably, Claim 5's impossibility mechanism is confirmed but the paper's printed appendix parameters contain a reproducible gap requiring repair to achieve the stated PROPX violation.

amkkk/repro-fixed-budget-is-no-harder-th.paper_title: Fixed Budget is No Harder Than Fixed Confidence in Best-Arm Identification up to Logarithmic Factors

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 establishes that the FC2FB meta-algorithm converts a fixed-confidence algorithm into a fixed-budget algorithm whose error probability decays exponentially in the budget (Section 3, Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: FC2FB was run on the paper's Section 6 setup (K=16 Gaussian arms, heterogeneous variances, 1000 trials) across budgets 5k–320k. Error probability decays from 0.362 to 0.005 to 0.0, with a negative log-linear fit slope, empirically supporting exponential decay in budget as claimed by Theorem 3.2.

claims.claim: When the fixed-confidence sample complexity is T*_delta = A*ln(1/delta) + C, FC2FB yields a fixed-budget sample complexity of O(A*ln(1/delta)*ln(A*ln(1/delta)/Q) + C), matching the fixed-confidence complexity up to logarithmic factors (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook only computes the ratio of the theoretical bound formulas (FB/FC ratio for various A, C, delta values) rather than measuring actual sample complexity from experiments. This is algebraic verification of the theorem's formula, not independent experimental evidence.

claims.claim: FCW2S (Algorithm 4) converts a weak fixed-confidence algorithm (Definition 4.1) into a strong one (Definition 3.1) via parallel execution and majority voting (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports P(error) < 1e-6 after FCW2S with L=31 and L=15 instances, but does not specify the number of trials run. Detecting error rates below 1e-6 empirically would require millions of trials; the results appear to be theoretical bound computations rather than measured outcomes.

claims.claim: FC2AT (Algorithm 6) is an anytime variant of the meta-algorithm using a doubling trick that requires no prior knowledge of the budget (Section 4).
claims.evidence: FC2AT is reported with P(error)=0.0 at every budget (B=1k–50k) with only 2000 trials, which is not credible as an empirical measurement. The comparison table also shows FC2FB with 0.8035 error at B=1000 but 0.0075 at B=2000 with no further decay, an inconsistent pattern suggesting possible implementation issues.

claims.claim: The framework's sample-complexity improvements are demonstrated on heterogeneous noise bandits (Corollary 5.2), linear bandits (Corollary 5.4), and unimodal bandits (Corollary 5.7) (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Only the heterogeneous noise setting (Corollary 5.2) has any numerical result (P(error)~0 at budget 5000). The linear bandit and unimodal bandit entries provide no error rates, sample counts, or quantitative measurements—only assertions that the algorithms 'run correctly' and 'elimination works.'

amkkk/repro-fixed-budget-is-no-harder-th.overall: The logbook provides genuine experimental evidence for Claim 1 (exponential error decay of FC2FB) on the paper's own bandit setup, but the remaining claims lack substantive experimental support: Claim 2 only checks algebra, Claims 3–4 report implausibly perfect results without adequate trial counts, and Claim 5 provides quantitative data for only one of three applications.

amkkk/repro-split-group-knockoffs-contro.paper_title: Split Group Knockoffs: Controlling False Discovery Rate in Transformational Group Sparsity

claims.claim: Establishes support recovery consistency under group-wise penalties in transformed spaces
claims.evidence: Support recovery tested at p=60, 30 groups, 3 active, n up to 12800 with 50 trials each, but Jaccard/precision/recall are 0.0000 at every sample size due to infinite knockoff threshold; active W>0 diagnostic noted but not shown in results table. Setup is clearly undersized for demonstrating asymptotic consistency.
