amkkk/repro-split-group-knockoffs-contro.overall: The logbook provides concrete synthetic-scale evidence that group-level FDR is controlled (Claim 1) and that a complexity proxy correlates with model disagreement (Claim 3), but support recovery consistency (Claim 2) is not demonstrated — zero recovery at all tested sample sizes. All experiments use small synthetic setups (p≤60, ≤30 groups) rather than the high-dimensional or real-data settings the paper likely targets.

amkkk/repro-understanding-the-gaps-in-sa.paper_title: Understanding the Gaps in Satisficing Bandits

claims.claim: The uncertain-UCB algorithm achieves satisficing pseudo-regret of O(sum_{i: Delta_i > Delta_*} log(K/Delta_*) / Delta_i).
claims.evidence: Across 4 bandit instances (K=4..10, T=50000, 15-20 runs, Bernoulli rewards), actual satisficing pseudo-regret is within constant factors of the claimed bound expression: ratios range from 0.009 to 7.89, with the worst case (all_below, K=5, S=0.6) showing regret 11733 vs bound 1487 (ratio ~7.9), consistent with big-O notation allowing a constant ~8. When satisficing arms exist, regret is near-zero (10-20), further supporting the bound.

claims.claim: A near-matching lower bound establishes the fundamental limits of satisficing bandits in the small excess-gap regime.
claims.evidence: The logbook uses a self-derived KL-divergence lower bound rather than reproducing the paper's theorem, and results are inconsistent: in 2 of 4 instances (three_arms_varying_gaps and many_arms_small_gaps), actual regret is far BELOW the computed lower bound (ratios 0.12 and 0.075), which would contradict a valid lower bound. While the two all-below-S small-gap instances show ratios of 2.47 and 5.42, the mixed results and non-reproduction of the actual theoretical lower bound leave the claim unverified.

amkkk/repro-understanding-the-gaps-in-sa.overall: The logbook provides reasonable empirical support for the uncertain-UCB upper bound (Claim 1) through from-scratch implementation at moderate scale, but the lower bound claim (Claim 2) is inadequately verified due to a self-derived proxy lower bound with contradictory results in half the tested instances.

amkkk/repro-commit-to-the-bit-reactive-r.paper_title: Commit to the Bit: Reactive Reinforcement Learning Done Right

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 proves that under Assumptions 3.1-3.3, the iterates of Algorithm 1 (Committed Q-learning) converge almost surely to Q*, with the resulting greedy policy optimal whenever the environment satisfies π-rewire-robustness (Theorem 3.5, Definition 3.7).
claims.evidence: A 4-state, 3-feature POMDP with 5 seeds and 20000 episodes shows both Committed and Standard Q-learning reach the optimal policy [0,1,0] (5/5 seeds), but mean||Q-Q*||=1.50 for both — this is a toy-scale empirical demonstration, not a verification of the almost-sure convergence theorem.

claims.claim: Rewire-robustness (Definition 3.7) is proven to be strictly weaker than the q*-realizability condition (Definition 3.4) used in prior work, admitting a broader class of environments (Section 3).
claims.evidence: An explicit counterexample with 3 features and 2D feature vectors shows Q* is not linearly realizable (residuals 0.73, 0.06) while rewire-robustness holds (margins >0.49), directly demonstrating strict inclusion of the condition classes.

claims.claim: Committed Q-learning differs from standard Q-learning by committing to a single sampled action upon entering a feature and only resampling when the observed feature changes, rather than resampling every step (Section 3, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Measured resample counts confirm Committed Q-learning resamples at 0.78/step (matching the 0.797 feature-change rate) vs Standard Q-learning at 1.0/step, directly confirming the algorithmic difference described in Algorithm 1.

claims.claim: Quasi-Markov environments are defined via an entrance matrix Σ satisfying p̄₀=ΣΦp̄₀, providing a structural condition analyzed alongside rewire-robustness (Definition 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: A constructed 3-state, 2-feature quasi-Markov environment satisfies p̄₀=ΣΦp̄₀ with residual 1.1e-16, while a 4-state non-quasi-Markov counterexample fails with residual 0.5, concretely verifying the definition.

claims.claim: In a corridor environment experiment, classical Q-learning fails to converge to the optimal reactive policy while Committed Q-learning converges quickly, illustrating the theoretical gap between the two algorithms (Section 4).
claims.evidence: In a 5-state, 2-feature toy corridor, Standard Q-learning converges 20/20 seeds to the optimal policy (mean||Q-Q*||=3.58) while Committed converges 19/20 (mean||Q-Q*||=4.19) — the claimed failure of standard Q-learning does not appear at this toy scale, so the claim is neither reproduced nor falsified at full scale.

amkkk/repro-commit-to-the-bit-reactive-r.overall: The logbook provides concrete analytical and small-scale empirical evidence for the structural/definitional claims (rewire-robustness strict inclusion, commitment mechanism, quasi-Markov definition), but the convergence theorem and corridor experiment are only addressed on toy POMDPs of 4-5 states where the key claimed failure mode of standard Q-learning does not materialize.

amkkk/repro-complexity-bounds-for-dirich.paper_title: Complexity Bounds for Dirichlet Process Slice Samplers

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 proves that the gap between the truncation level K_n and the number of occupied clusters H_n in Dirichlet process slice samplers satisfies K_n - H_n = O_P(log n) with probability at least 1-delta for any confidence level delta, uniformly over partitions (Theorem 3.3, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides a concrete table showing E[K-H]/log n bounded in [2.21, 4.75] across n=50–10000 with 1000 MC replicates, and P99/log n ≤ 8.58, with the Poisson rate λ_n/log n similarly bounded, numerically supporting the O_P(log n) claim at reasonable scale.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.4 gives exponential tail bounds and uniformly bounded moments for the normalized overhead K_n - H_n across all sample sizes n (Corollary 3.4).
claims.evidence: The detailed moment table lists N/A for all moments of order 2–4 at every n, directly contradicting the scorecard's claim that E[((K-H)/log n)^4] ∈ [65, 447]. The exponential decay rate (~1.06) is asserted without supporting tail probability data. The evidence is internally inconsistent and insufficient.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.5 shows an almost-sure guarantee that super-logarithmic overhead in slice sampling cannot occur infinitely often as n grows (Corollary 3.5).
claims.evidence: The almost-sure claim requires behavior as n→∞, which finite experiments (n≤2000, 100 trials) cannot establish. More critically, the table shows P(gap > 5·log n) increasing from 0 to 0.26 as n grows, suggesting the event rate is not decreasing, which undermines the Borel-Cantelli argument the logbook invokes.

claims.claim: Even in configurations where the number of occupied clusters H_n grows as O(n), the truncation level K_n remains O_P(n) with only vanishing probability of superlinear blow-up (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The claim concerns configurations where H_n = O(n), but the CRP-simulated partitions yield H_n/n ratios of 0.004–0.37 (i.e., H_n ~ α·log n, far from O(n)). The experimental setup does not test the regime the claim describes; P(K>2n)=0 is trivially expected when H_n is sublinear.

claims.claim: The complexity bounds hold without likelihood-specific assumptions and apply to any observed dataset, establishing favorable scalability of slice samplers relative to marginal CRP-based and truncated sampling methods (Table 1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The comparison uses simplified cost models (K_n·n vs H_n·n vs K_fixed·n) computed from simulated partition statistics, not actual MCMC sampler implementations or runtime measurements. This is a proxy analysis rather than an empirical scalability comparison at the paper's task scale.

amkkk/repro-complexity-bounds-for-dirich.overall: The logbook provides genuine numerical evidence supporting the core O_P(log n) gap bound (Claim 1) at reasonable scale, but the remaining claims suffer from missing or inconsistent moment data, failure to test the H_n=O(n) regime, inability to verify almost-sure guarantees with finite experiments, and a simplified cost-model comparison rather than actual implementation benchmarks.

amkkk/repro-near-optimal-regret-for-kl-r.paper_title: Near-Optimal Regret for KL-Regularized Multi-Armed Bandits

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 establishes a high-probability regret upper bound of O~(ηK log^2 T) for KL-regularized multi-armed bandits in the high-regularization regime where η ≤ sqrt(T/K) (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: 15 configurations with K∈{5,10,20}, T∈{500–10000}, η=0.5·sqrt(T/K) show regret consistently below the O~(ηK log²T) bound (ratios ≤0.27). K-scaling slope (0.40, R²=0.78) is imperfect but the overall evidence supports the claim.

claims.claim: In the low-regularization regime (η ≥ sqrt(T/K)), the same analysis yields a regret bound of O~(sqrt(KT log T)), which is η-independent (Theorem 4.2, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: 18 configurations with η=2·sqrt(T/K) show regret below O~(sqrt(KT log T)) in all cases (ratios ≤0.81). Log-log slope vs T = 0.53 (expected 0.5, R²=0.97). η-independence confirmed (CV=0.037). K-scaling slope of 1.08 vs expected 0.5 is discrepant, but with only 3 K values this regression is unreliable; the T-scaling and η-independence evidence are solid.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.3 provides a lower bound of Ω(ηK log(T/(η^2 K))) in the high-regularization regime, establishing near-tightness with the upper bound in Theorem 4.2 (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: The raw JSON data shows 'lower_bound_satisfied': 'False' for many of the 27 configurations with regret/LB ratios as low as 0.20–0.40, directly contradicting the markdown table which marks all 27 as '✓'. The experimental method (ε-greedy on a single hard instance) is inappropriate for testing a minimax lower bound, which requires showing no algorithm can beat the bound. The inconsistency between table and raw data undermines trust in the results.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 gives a lower bound of Ω(sqrt(KT)) in the low-regularization regime via a two-point construction method (Section 6.1, Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: 36 configurations using the two-point construction (optimal arm mean 0.5+ε, others 0.5, ε=0.5·sqrt(K/T)) show regret/sqrt(KT) ratios consistently in a stable range. Log-log slope vs K = 0.50 (expected 0.5, R²=0.94) and η-independence confirmed (CV=0.01). T-scaling slope of 0.65 vs expected 0.5 is somewhat off but could reflect log factors or limited range.

claims.claim: The KL-UCB algorithm uses an optimistic bonus term b_t(a) = sqrt(2 log(TK/delta) / (N_t(a) ∨ 1)) together with a novel peeling argument and Freedman's inequality to obtain tight high-probability bounds (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Bonus term b_t(a)=sqrt(2log(TK/δ)/N_t(a)) achieves 100% empirical coverage across 6 configs (expected ≥95%), confirming valid high-probability bounds. Peeling argument reduces log penalty by 2.4–4.1x across T∈{100–100000}. However, the raw data shows 'freedman_bound_is_tighter': 'False' for ALL 6 configs (Freedman bound consistently ~1 unit larger than Hoeffding), contradicting the markdown table's claim that Freedman is tighter for n≥100; this inconsistency weakens but does not falsify the overall claim that the algorithm uses all three components.

galexdav/repro-densesteer-steering-small.paper_title: DenseSteer: Steering Small Language Models towards Dense Math Reasoning

claims.claim: The steering vector is extracted from only 50 contrastive (dense vs. sparse) reasoning-trace pairs using GPT-5.1-rewritten dense variants of the small model's own outputs, avoiding the distribution mismatch of using larger-model references (Section 4.1)
claims.evidence: The 50-pair contrastive extraction pipeline was executed end-to-end: 50 GSM8K-train problems → target model's own sparse traces → dense rewrites → mean-difference steering vectors at layers {6,16,17,27,35} with non-trivial depth-increasing norms (1.835 to 17.685), confirming the extraction mechanism from the model's own rewritten outputs.

claims.evidence: Mean token-level NLL under Qwen2.5-3B on 200 GSM8K traces: self=0.239, dense_rewrite=0.384, qwen7b=0.345, llama8b=0.345 — the dense rewrite has the highest NLL (opposite of the claimed near-self-baseline ordering), and same-family vs cross-family references are indistinguishable rather than separated.

tpls/repro-linear-ar-latent.paper_title: Two-Layer Linear Auto-Regressive Models Estimate Latent States

Rank-deficient h=2 NC plateaus (slope -0.260), and ρ=1.0 cells are confounded as pre-registered.

claims.evidence: Squared Frobenius parameter error decays at slope -1.105 (ρ=0.9, CI [-1.154,-1.051]) and -1.084 (ρ=1.0, CI [-1.126,-1.037]), both containing -1 with R²≈0.998. claims.evidence: Exact identity x̂t=Cz̄t+Ā^L x̂t−L verified to worst residual 8.53e-14 over 112,680 cells (12 systems × L=1..20), 0 bound violations, decay-rate/ρ(Ā) median 0.997 (all systems in [0.87,1.01]). Wrong-gain NC blows residual to 0.105 median (~4e12x floor).

DineshAI/oqkiE71wrC.paper_title: Sharp Empirical Bernstein Inequalities for the Variance of Bounded Random Variables

claims.evidence: Four genuinely dependent bounded [0,1] processes (sign-switching martingale, random moving sign, block runs, two-state Markov chain) each with constant conditional mean 0.5 and variance 1/12 all achieve anytime coverage 1.000 >= 0.90, while the variance-blind negative control collapses to 0.475. The independent certificate also directly checks the supermartingale multiplier (max=1.0) across 3,800 high-precision cells.

ai-sherpa/spectral-learned-kernels-minim.paper_title: Alignment-Sensitive Minimax Rates for Spectral Algorithms with Learned Kernels

ai-sherpa/densest-k-subgraph-frank-wolfe.paper_title: On Densest $k$-Subgraph Mining and Diagonal Loading: Optimization Landscape and Finite-Step Exact Convergence Analysis

KKT conditions checked exactly in all cases, and the λ=1 sharp boundary demonstrated with destructive controls showing fractional>integral below λ=1 (min margin 5e-5) and integral>fractional above.

claims.claim: Corollary 1 proves that when λ≥1 there always exists a global maximizer of the relaxed objective that is integral, so the relaxed and combinatorial problems share the same optimal value.
claims.evidence: Constructive mass-transfer rounding executed in exact Fraction arithmetic over 864 cases (n=8..256, six graph families, multiple k and λ≥1 values): 0 non-monotone transfers, 0 failures to reach integral k-hot point, longest trajectory 255 transfers (=n-1 at n=256). Below-threshold controls on K_n show strict positive relaxation gap in 48/48 cases (min gap 0.075).

claims.claim: Lemma 1 shows that for λ>1 there does not exist a non-integral local maximizer, establishing the strict dichotomy that all integral stationary points are local maximizers while non-integral stationary points are strict saddles.
claims.evidence: Both halves of the dichotomy certified with exact arithmetic: 553/553 integral stationary points are strict local maxima (0 violations, min gap 0.01) at n up to 256; 135 swap directions at 45 fractional saddles have exactly-zero first derivative and curvature 2(λ-A_ij)≥1. Exhaustive enumeration of all 1,024 graphs at n=5 yields 15,815/15,815 integral stationary points as strict local maxima and 6,900 swap directions with zero derivative and min curvature 1.0.

claims.evidence: Perfect-matching family (n=2r, k=2) closed-form spurious count 2r(r-1) reproduced exactly for r=2..64 (63/63 matches, up to 8,064 spurious at n=128), with brute-force enumeration cross-check for r≤12. claims.claim: The saddle-escaping Frank-Wolfe algorithm (Section 3.1) has per-iteration complexity O(m+k log n) and is shown to converge in a finite number of steps to an integral local maximizer of the densest k-subgraph relaxation.
claims.evidence: At the paper's Section 5.2 setting (10-regular, n=100, k=20, λ=1.5), standard FW stalls at the fractional saddle in 64/64 graphs while SE-FW escapes in exactly 1 step and reaches an exact integral local maximizer (gap 0, integrality 1.0) in 14–35 iterations, 64/64. rahit/repro-a-stronger-benchmark-for-onl.paper_title: A Stronger Benchmark for Online Bilateral Trade: From Fixed Prices to Distributions

shayekh/repro-perceptrons-and-localizati.paper_title: Perceptrons and Localization of Attention’s Mean-Field Landscape

claims.claim: For analytic activation functions such as GeLU in d=2, strict second-order-positive-definite (SOPD) Wasserstein critical points are shown to be purely atomic with finite support (Theorem 3.2).

claims.claim: In dimensions d≥2, stationary measures are proved singular (zero Lebesgue measure), and for an open dense set of parameters with analytic activation they are purely atomic (Theorem 3.3).

claims.claim: In the descent (repulsive) regime, clusters forming at interaction scale sqrt(beta) are bounded in mass by approximately 0.5742 + O(e^{-beta}), preventing full collapse to single atoms (Theorem 3.5).

snaykey/repro-talda-minimax.paper_title: Revisiting Zeroth-Order Hessian Approximation: A Single-Step Policy Optimization Lens

claims.claim: ZoVH is introduced as a variance-reduced zeroth-order Hessian estimator that unifies One-Point, Two-Point, and Three-Point Stein-type estimators as special cases of a Gaussian sampling policy with different baseline choices (Proposition 3.2, Section 3).
claims.evidence: On a d=12 quadratic with K=400 directions, the general Gaussian-policy estimator with baselines b=0, b=f(θ), and antithetic+b=f(θ) recovers the One-Point, Two-Point, and Three-Point Stein estimators to Frobenius distances of 0.0, 0.0, and 8.1e-13 respectively (on a Hessian norm scale of ~42), directly confirming the algebraic unification.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 proves the ZoVH estimator is unbiased for the Hessian of the smoothed objective, E[Ĥ(θ)] = ∇²Fμ(θ), establishing the theoretical equivalence between the ZO Hessian estimator and the smoothed single-step Policy Optimization objective's Hessian (Theorem 4.6, Section 4).
claims.evidence: On a d=10 quadratic with R=4000 Monte Carlo draws, the ZoVH averaged-baseline residual decays with log-log slope −0.518 (matching the 1/√R unbiasedness signature), while the naive zero-baseline estimator shows a persistent bias of 752,847 matching the closed-form F(θ)/μ²·√d = 753,072 to 0.03%.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.7 shows the averaged-baseline estimator is variance-optimal, reducing in high dimensions to b* = E_u[F(θ+μu)], and Theorem 4.8 bounds the estimator's expected Frobenius-norm error as a sum of a K,d,μ-dependent variance term and an L2²μ²d bias term (Theorems 4.7–4.8, Section 4).
claims.evidence: On a d=8 quadratic, the empirical arg-min of the variance sweep over baseline b lands exactly on F_μ(θ)=85.1399 (matching the analytic value), and the MSE-vs-K log-log slope is −1.036 (theory: −1) while the smoothing-bias-vs-μ slope is +2.000 (theory: +2), confirming both theorems' key predictions.

claims.claim: On synthetic Quadratic and Rosenbrock functions, ZoVH with query-reuse parameter N=6 achieves an 8× accuracy improvement over central-difference Hessian estimators, and a 3.4× improvement on the Styblinski-Tang function (Figure 2, Section 6.1).
claims.evidence: Experiments run at d=50 (vs paper's d=5000, a 100× reduction); while ZoVH beats central-difference on Quadratic (7.68×) and Rosenbrock (8.29×) close to the paper's ~8×, the Styblinski-Tang ratio is 7.95× versus the paper's 3.4× — a major discrepancy inconsistent with the logbook's own √d scaling argument, which predicts lower ratios at lower dimensions.

claims.claim: On a black-box MNIST adversarial attack task, ZoVH with N=4 achieves a 4.04× speedup over the baseline, requiring 403±76 iterations versus 1629±610 iterations (Table 1, Section 6.2).
claims.evidence: The MNIST CNN adversarial attack is replaced with a d=15 ill-conditioned quadratic surrogate; the ordering Vanilla > ZoVH(N=1) > ZoVH(N=4) is reproduced but the speedup is 1.72× versus the claimed 4.04×, and the specific iteration counts (403±76 vs 1629±610) are not reproduced at all.

claims.claim: Across four synthetic convergence benchmarks (Quadratic, Levy, Rosenbrock, Ackley), ZoVH with N=4 achieves a 22× speedup versus vanilla zeroth-order optimization in reaching target accuracy (Section 6.2).
claims.evidence: At d=8 (vs paper's d=10000), ZoVH shows no speedup (mean 0.74×, with Ackley at 0.25× and Levy/Rosenbrock hitting iteration caps); the 1250× dimension reduction is too large to either confirm or refute the 22× claim at the paper's scale, and the logbook's mechanistic explanation for the gap is speculative.

snaykey/repro-talda-minimax.overall: The logbook provides strong, concrete verification of the paper's three theoretical claims (unification, unbiasedness, optimal baseline and error bound) through careful algebraic and Monte Carlo experiments at small but adequate scale. The empirical claims are tested at severely reduced dimensions (d=8–50 vs d=5000–10000) and with a quadratic surrogate replacing the MNIST attack, yielding partial directional agreement but no reproduction of the headline speedup magnitudes.

snaykey/repro-proximal-last-iterate.paper_title: Convergence Rate of the Last Iterate of Stochastic Proximal Algorithms

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes an Õ(1/√T) convergence rate for the last iterate of proximal SGD under componentwise convexity and L-smoothness of each fi (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Proximal SGD on a single L1-regularized least-squares problem (d=50, n=200, T up to 10000, 50 seeds) yields a fitted slope of -0.5245, close to the claimed -0.5, but the scale and problem diversity are too limited to constitute a full reproduction of the theorem's scope.

claims.claim: The analysis replaces the standard bounded-variance assumption with the weaker requirement of a finite second moment of the gradient at the solution, E||∇fi(x*)||² = σ*² < ∞ (Section 2, Assumption 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook measures sigma_star=0.2458 at the L1 solution and tests with Student-t(df=4) noise (which has finite variance), showing the tail slope remains -0.5101, but this does not demonstrate that the finite-moment assumption is strictly weaker than bounded variance—it only confirms the moment is finite in one synthetic instance.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 extends the Õ(1/√T) last-iterate rate to a randomized incremental proximal method when the regularizer decomposes additively and each component gj is Lipschitz continuous (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The true randomized incremental proximal method (sampling one smooth and one regularizer component per step) is run at three scales up to d=5000, n=20000, T=316228, 20 chains, float64; tail slopes approach -0.5 (-0.504, -0.938, -0.544) and gap·√T stays bounded or decreasing across all scales, supporting the Õ(1/√T) rate.

claims.claim: Section 4.4 applies the framework to a BlockProx algorithm for graph-guided regularizers used in multi-task and federated learning, proving last-iterate convergence without assuming bounded gradients (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: A real graph-guided BlockProx regularizer (pairwise edge penalties on a collaboration graph) is tested at three scales up to K=100 blocks, d=5000, n=20000, T=316228, 20 chains; tail slopes (-0.500, -0.792, -0.655) and bounded gap·√T confirm the Õ(1/√T) last-iterate rate without bounded-gradient assumptions.

claims.claim: The obtained Õ(1/√T) rate matches, up to logarithmic factors, the last-iterate guarantees for unconstrained SGD under bounded variance from Garrigos et al. (2025) (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: A paired head-to-head comparison of proximal SGD vs unconstrained SGD with identical noise streams at three scales (d up to 5000, T up to 316228) shows proximal tail slopes near -0.5 (-0.494, -0.956, -0.545), bounded prox/SGD suboptimality ratios (1.11, 0.46, 0.26), and bounded gap·√T for both methods, supporting the claimed rate match up to log factors.

snaykey/repro-proximal-last-iterate.overall: The logbook provides non-trivial scaled experimental evidence (d up to 5000, T up to 316228, 20 chains) supporting the Õ(1/√T) last-iterate rate for the incremental proximal method (C3), graph-guided BlockProx (C4), and the proximal-vs-unconstrained-SGD comparison (C5), all on synthetic finite-sum least-squares problems. Claims 1 and 2 are only addressed at small toy scale and do not fully verify the theorem's generality or the strict weakness of the finite-moment assumption.

claims.claim: MDS is implemented via a Maximum Mean Discrepancy objective using random Fourier feature approximations of the Gaussian kernel, with a decoder mean-embedding network trained offline via MSE and the summary optimized at test time by L-BFGS (Section 3.2, Algorithm 1).

claims.evidence: The logbook provides only textual verification that the theorem and proof exist in the paper ('textual/theorem verification only. I did not independently re-prove all Appendix A regularity assumptions'). No experimental or independent mathematical verification was performed.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 shows that when the model is correctly specified, posterior consistency under the original summary statistics implies posterior consistency under MDS-adapted summaries (Theorem 4.2).

tpls/repro-bc-action-quantization.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous clean-room verification of all six claims of a pure-theory paper using exact arithmetic (Fraction recursions, sympy symbolic algebra, exact binomial enumeration, deterministic quadrature) on the paper's own scalar constructions, with pre-registered gates, negative controls isolating mechanisms, and ratchets extending coverage beyond initial proxy scope. claims.evidence: Eq. (4) lazy alternating dynamics with entropic FTRL were run on 39 configurations (13 games × 3 epsilon values): all converged to 2ε-Nash, each accepted update raised potential by ≥ε, update count never exceeded floor(1/ε), and all convergence times were far below exp(4/ε²).

claims.claim: Proposition 3.2 shows that for FTRL with learning rate η ≤ 1/L (L the smoothness constant of the potential), the potential function value is non-decreasing across iterations, without requiring alternation or laziness (Proposition 3.2).
claims.evidence: 72,000 exact Proposition 3.2 inequalities checked across 72 random games (m=2..10) at η=c/L for c∈{0.05,0.25,0.5,1.0}: 0% violation rate, with violations appearing at c=2.0 (7 rounds) and c=3.0 (10 rounds), confirming the threshold is non-vacuous.

claims.claim: Example 3.3 constructs a 'spurious fixed point' showing FTRL can maintain a highly suboptimal strategy (error proportional to 1/t) indefinitely relative to the observed utility sequence, illustrating why FTRL, unlike gradient descent under Legendre regularizers, need not reach an O_ε(ε)-Nash equilibrium (Example 3.3).
claims.evidence: Example 3.3 was executed exactly (log-barrier FTRL, u=(1,0) then (0,1)) for t up to 1,000,000 at three learning rates: fitted error exponent −0.999933 to −0.999983 (i.e., 1/t decay), post-reversal suboptimality 0.999999 at t=10⁶, and movement O(1/t) after utility reversal.

claims.claim: The two-player exponential lower bound construction uses a payoff matrix A of odd dimension m with maximum entry 2m−1, dividing the FTRL trajectory into 2m−1 'transition periods' governed by Property 4.3 (period consistency) and Lemma 4.1 bounding action probability by R/(η^(t)γ) (Section 4, Definition 4.2, Property 4.3, Lemma 4.1, Figure 2b).

claims.evidence: The logbook demonstrates that best-response becomes discontinuous (0.50→1.00 jump) when MFCQ fails, which is tangentially related, but does not verify the actual proof technique of constructing a contractible feasible set and applying Begle's fixed point theorem; the scope table explicitly excludes 'the full contractibility/fixed-point proofs.'

claims.claim: A log-barrier regularized gradient ascent algorithm, using barrier B^eta_i(x) := u_i(x) + eta * sum_j log(c_j(x) - alpha_j), lets each player update using only its own gradient feedback while maintaining feasibility (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The simultaneous update x_i <- P[x_i + gamma grad_i(u_i + eta sum_j log(c_j - alpha_j))] is run with each player using only its own gradient, achieving best-iterate Nash-gap 0.0193 <= 0.02 with every iterate strictly feasible (True), converging to the boundary NE (0.375, 0.375); the 24 multi-player routing games also show feasible convergence on 24/24.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows that for constrained potential games, setting the barrier parameter eta = epsilon and running T = O(epsilon^-3) iterations yields an epsilon-approximate constrained Nash equilibrium (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Sweeping eps over [0.08, 0.04, 0.02, 0.01] yields iteration counts [400, 600, 750, 850] (log-log slope 0.36, well within the O(eps^-3) upper bound) on a 2-player identical-utility constrained potential game, directly testing the rate-iteration tradeoff claimed by the theorem.

claims.claim: The O(epsilon^-3) rate for the constrained setting is slower than the O(epsilon^-2) rate known for unconstrained potential games, an extra O(epsilon^-1) factor attributed to decreasing stepsizes needed near the feasible boundary (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook only tests the constrained rate (slope 0.36); it provides no unconstrained comparison run to demonstrate the O(eps^-2) vs O(eps^-3) gap, nor any analysis of stepsize behavior near the feasible boundary to verify the attributed mechanism for the extra O(eps^-1) factor.

arvkevi/repro-nash-concave-coupling.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting NE existence on nonconvex feasible sets and convergence of the log-barrier gradient-ascent algorithm with maintained feasibility, including a direct epsilon-sweep test of the O(eps^-3) rate. However, it does not verify the proof technique (contractible set + Begle's theorem) or the comparative rate claim against unconstrained games, leaving claims 2 and 5 unaddressed.

agharsallah/x8evkedmxb-logbook.paper_title: Causal Discovery for Irregularly Time Series with Consistency Guarantees

claims.claim: ReTimeCausal integrates an Additive Noise Model with an Expectation-Maximization loop that alternates E-step imputation of missing values (conditional expectation under the current causal estimate) and M-step sparse regression to refine the causal graph (Section on EM Framework / Method).
claims.evidence: Weight norms change across each EM iteration (0.958→1.058→...→1.406), confirming E-step imputation and M-step sparse regression alternate as described. F1=0.791/0.721 at MR=0.6/0.8 on the 20-var setup shows the mechanism recovers causal structure.

claims.claim: Proposition 1 (Structural Consistency) proves that under finite-order Markovity, time-invariant mechanisms, and causal sufficiency, ReTimeCausal recovers the true causal graph with probability one as sample size and iterations grow (Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: SHD drops from 123.1 to 7.8 as n grows from 250 to 4000 (94% reduction) at k=12, with log-log slope -0.94 consistent with the Theorem G.1 O(sqrt(log/n)) bound, empirically demonstrating the convergence-to-true-graph claim.

claims.claim: Noise-aware imputation injects noise into imputed values (X̂ᵢᵗ = fᵢ(Paᵢᵗ) + ϵᵢᵗ) to preserve the statistical independence assumptions needed for downstream edge pruning (Method, Eq. for noise-aware imputation).
claims.evidence: Noise-aware imputation yields |corr(residual, parent)|=0.006 (near-zero independence) and KS p=0.435 (matches empirical noise distribution), while deterministic imputation gives zero residual variance, directly confirming the mechanism and its purpose.

claims.claim: On a 20-variable linear-SEM benchmark with 60% missingness, ReTimeCausal attains F1 = 0.930 versus 0.205 for the best baseline PCMCI+EM, and at 80% missingness reaches F1 = 1.000 versus 0.190 for PCMCI+EM (Experiments/Results table).
claims.evidence: The ranking (RTC >> PCMCI+EM) is confirmed with F1=0.778 vs 0.099 at MR=0.6 and 0.730 vs 0.099 at MR=0.8, but the specific claimed F1 values (0.930 and 1.000) are not reproduced—the reproduction's absolute numbers fall significantly short, attributed to a simplified LASSO imputation instead of the paper's neural-network E-step.

claims.claim: On a 50-variable TANH nonlinear benchmark with 60% missingness, ReTimeCausal achieves F1 = 0.816 (SHD = 39), substantially above the best baseline PCMCI+EM at F1 = 0.258 (Experiments/Results table).
claims.evidence: ReTimeCausal achieves mean F1=0.963 (SHD=7.2) across 10 seeds on the 50-var TANH-laplace benchmark at 60% missingness, exceeding the paper's reported F1=0.816 (SHD=39) and well above the PCMCI+EM baseline of 0.258.

claims.claim: On the real-world CausalRivers dataset (10 nodes) with 60% missingness, ReTimeCausal reaches F1 = 0.436 versus 0.348 for the kernelized DYNOTEARS* baseline, both evaluated after TimeMixer preprocessing for the baselines (Experiments/Results table).
claims.evidence: Both ReTimeCausal and the baseline achieve identical F1_max=0.182 on CausalRivers, failing to reproduce the claimed 5pp ranking gap (0.436 vs 0.348); the logbook acknowledges the full kernelized RBF + neural-network pipeline was not implemented, so the specific claim remains untested at full fidelity.

agharsallah/x8evkedmxb-logbook.overall: The logbook provides solid empirical evidence for the architectural/mechanistic claims (EM alternation, noise-aware imputation, convergence) and the 50-var TANH benchmark, but does not reproduce the specific F1 values for the 20-var linear benchmark or the CausalRivers ranking gap, due to acknowledged simplifications in the imputation pipeline.

arvkevi/repro-speedcp-conditional-confor.paper_title: SpeedCP: Fast Kernel-based Conditional Conformal Prediction

claims.claim: SpeedCP is a kernel-based conditional conformal prediction method designed to reduce the computational cost of prior RKHS-based conditional conformal approaches while preserving coverage guarantees (Section 2, Methods).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements only the linear-feature instance (group-conditional conformal) on a synthetic K=3 admixture with a deliberately weak predictor, explicitly scoping out the full RKHS piecewise-affine path solver. Coverage (0.900/0.901/0.903) and speedup (0.2ms vs 20.8ms) are demonstrated but on a simplified special case, not the full kernel-based method.

claims.claim: SpeedCP's conditional coverage guarantees are established formally as a sequence of theorems covering the method's finite-sample and asymptotic properties (Section 2, Theorems 2.1-2.6).
claims.evidence: Numerical simulation on the K=3 admixture checks Theorem 2.6's prediction of exact per-cluster coverage (worst deviation 0.003 from target 0.9), but Theorems 2.1–2.5 are not individually tested and no mathematical proofs are examined. The setup is a synthetic toy with a weak predictor rather than a general verification of the theorem sequence.

claims.claim: SpeedCP is empirically compared against prior RKHS conformal baselines on interval length and runtime across multiple black-box predictors in the main experiments section (Section 3, Experiments; Table 7).
claims.evidence: Interval length (3.547 vs 6.088) and runtime (0.2ms vs 20.8ms) are compared against a single kernel-weighted CondCP baseline on the synthetic K=3 admixture, but the claim specifies comparison across multiple black-box predictors as in Table 7, which is not reproduced.

claims.claim: Additional experiments extend the comparison of interval length and computational speedup across further predictors and datasets (Section 4, Additional Experiments; Table 12; Table 13).
claims.evidence: No experiments extend the comparison to further predictors or datasets; Tables 12 and 13 are not reproduced. The logbook only uses the single synthetic K=3 admixture setup.

claims.claim: Theoretical proofs supporting the coverage guarantees, including extended theorem statements, are provided in a dedicated theory section and appendices (Section 5, Theoretical Proof; Appendix C, Theorems C.1-C.13).
claims.evidence: No theoretical proofs are checked or reproduced; Theorems C.1–C.13 are never addressed. The logbook provides only numerical evidence for Theorem 2.6's predictions, not any examination of the mathematical proofs in Section 5 or Appendix C.

arvkevi/repro-speedcp-conditional-confor.overall: The logbook provides a focused Monte Carlo verification of Theorem 2.6's exact-coverage prediction on a synthetic K=3 admixture with linear features only, but does not implement the full RKHS solver, reproduce the paper's real multi-predictor experiments (Tables 7, 12, 13), or examine any theoretical proofs. It is a narrow toy-scale check of one theorem's numerical implications rather than a reproduction of the paper's contributions.

arvkevi/repro-stable-localized-conformal.paper_title: Stable Localized Conformal Prediction via Transduction

claims.claim: Stable (localized) Conformal Prediction (StCP/SLCP) uses a conditional CDF estimator trained on labeled source-task data plus an empirical marginal distribution estimated from unlabeled target data, calibrated via a regularized optimization with parameter λ (Equation 7, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements a simplified 'lambda-weighted blend of source quantile and target calibration quantile' rather than the full conditional CDF estimator with regularized optimization of Eq. 7; the conclusion explicitly states the engression-network conditional-CDF estimator was not included.

claims.claim: StCP's coverage error is bounded by O(min(ε + λ^{1/2} + n^{-1}, δ_S + λ^{-1/2} + n^{-1})), establishing robustness of marginal coverage to the choice of λ (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: No experiment tests the Theorem 4.2 coverage-error bound involving ε, λ^{1/2}, δ_S, and λ^{-1/2}; the logbook only reports point coverage values (0.900, 0.923) related to Theorem 4.7, not the two-sided bound of Theorem 4.2.

claims.claim: Standard conformal prediction has set-size variance of order O(n^{-1}), while StCP achieves O(m^{-1} + {n(1+λ)²}^{-1}), yielding substantial stability gains when the unlabeled target sample size m greatly exceeds the calibration size n (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: On the synthetic LogAbs model, base set-size SD scales with slope -0.55 (~1/√n) over n=[30,60,120,240] and StCP SD decreases from 0.455 to 0.023 as λ grows from 0 to 20, qualitatively matching the variance-rate claim, but using a simplified quantile-blend implementation rather than the paper's full method.

claims.claim: On real data across five datasets, StCP/SLCP reduces prediction-set-size standard deviation by 20-48% when built on GLCP and by 6-29% when built on CQR, while maintaining marginal coverage near the nominal 90% level (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Only one of five real datasets (California Housing) was tested, with an induced covariate shift at n=30; the reported 59% SD reduction exceeds the paper's stated 20–48% GLCP range, and the CQR-based results and four other datasets were not reproduced.

claims.claim: On synthetic data, the largest stability gains occur at a small calibration size of n=30, with standard deviation reductions of 31.2% (GLCP-based) and 16.3% (CQR-based) (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports a 95% SD reduction at both n=30 and n=240, which contradicts the claim that the largest gains occur at n=30; the specific paper figures (31.2% GLCP, 16.3% CQR) are not reproduced, and GLCP/CQR bases are not separately tested.

claims.claim: A data-driven procedure for selecting λ maintains empirical coverage within the interval [1-α-α_tol, 1-α+α_tol+(n+1)^{-1}] (Theorem 4.7).
claims.evidence: A single data point on the synthetic LogAbs model shows StCP-sel coverage of 0.923 falling within [0.85, 0.95+1/(n+1)] for n=30, which is consistent with the Theorem 4.7 band, but only one configuration is tested with the simplified quantile-blend method.

arvkevi/repro-stable-localized-conformal.overall: The logbook provides partial numerical evidence on the paper's synthetic LogAbs model and one real dataset (California Housing) using a simplified quantile-blend implementation of StCP rather than the full conditional-CDF-estimator-plus-regularized-optimization method. Most claims receive only toy-level support, Theorem 4.2 is unaddressed, and the five-dataset real-data results are largely unreproduced.

arvkevi/repro-submodular-reward-marl.paper_title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Submodular Reward

claims.claim: MARLS formalizes cooperative multi-agent RL with submodular joint rewards, and finding the optimal policy is shown to be NP-hard even in the single-step setting via a reduction to submodular maximization under partition matroid constraints (Section 3.1, Section 4.1.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements the MAMDP-SR formalization and confirms the H=1 case has partition-matroid structure (each agent selects one action), but the NP-hardness claim is a proof-level result that is never verified or addressed experimentally; confirming the reduction structure is not the same as verifying NP-hardness.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows the greedy policy optimization algorithm achieves a 1/2-approximation guarantee, with value at least half the optimal value minus an error term of order epsilon*K*H with high probability, and time complexity polynomial in the number of agents K, O(K*H*|S||A|*max{|S|, epsilon^-2 log(K|S||A|H/delta)}) (Section 4.2, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: 160 random submodular MDPs at K=2, S≤4, A=3, H=5 (joint space up to 16×9) show greedy/optimal ratio min 0.902 ≥ 1/2 with 0 violations, providing real evidence for the core approximation bound, but at a clearly reduced scale; the epsilon·K·H error term is explicitly eliminated by using exact marginals, and the polynomial time complexity claim is not tested.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 gives a UCB-based greedy value-iteration algorithm for unknown dynamics achieving a 1/2-approximation regret bound of O(S^2*A*H^3*K^2*log(SATHK/delta)*logT + H^2*K*S*sqrt(A*T*log(SATHK/delta))), sublinear in T and scaling only linearly in the number of agents K (Section 4.3, Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: UCB-GVI regret is tested only up to T=400 episodes with a single configuration, showing qualitative sublinear growth (log-log slope ~0.50); the specific regret bound O(S²·A·H³·K²·... + H²·K·S·√(A·T·...)) and the claim of linear scaling in K are not verified, as no multi-K regret experiments are reported.

claims.claim: Lemma 1 introduces a marginal value decomposition that enables sequential per-agent optimization even though the optimal joint policy is not itself decomposable across agents (Section 4, Lemma 1).
claims.evidence: The marginal value decomposition is implemented and used in the sequential greedy algorithm on small instances (K=2, S≤4, A=3, H=5), and tightness is demonstrated via 6000 partition-matroid instances finding worst ratio 0.500, but the scale is clearly reduced and the structural claim is only validated on toy-sized problems.

claims.claim: The framework is presented as the first formal treatment of cooperative multi-agent RL with submodular rewards capturing diminishing marginal returns from adding agents, in contrast to standard additive-reward MARL formulations (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The 'first formal treatment' claim is a novelty/priority assertion relative to prior literature that cannot be established by running experiments; the logbook implements the framework but provides no evidence regarding whether this is the first such treatment.

arvkevi/repro-submodular-reward-marl.overall: The logbook provides small-scale empirical validation of the core 1/2-approximation guarantee and marginal value decomposition using exact brute-force methods, but at a clearly toy scale (K=2, tiny state/action spaces) and without addressing the NP-hardness proof, the specific regret bounds, or the novelty claim.

snaykey/repro-spectrally-sparse-jacobi.paper_title: Robust Bayesian Optimisation with Unbounded Corruptions

claims.claim: The Fixed-Center RCGP-UCB (FC-RCGP-UCB) algorithm achieves cumulative regret R_T = Õ(Ψ(T_c)(1+√T_c)√(β'_T T(γ_T+T_c))), yielding sublinear regret for corruption budgets T_c = O(T^α) with α < 1/4 (Theorem 2, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: The experiment uses a discretized 1-D Forrester function (100 candidates) with T up to 200 and calibrated constants rather than the paper's closed-form expressions. While R_T/T decreases from 0.268 to 0.097 (10 seeds), this is a simplified proxy for the theoretical bound in Theorem 2, not a full-scale verification.

claims.claim: The Anchor-Adapt RCGP-UCB (A2-RCGP-UCB) algorithm, which adaptively updates its centering function, achieves cumulative regret R_T = Õ((1+T_c Ψ(T_c)^2)√(β'_T T(γ_T+T_c))), yielding sublinear regret for α < 1/7 (Theorem 3, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Same simplified 1-D discretized setup as Claim 1, with T up to 200 and a fixed plateau threshold L=1.5 instead of the paper's adaptive closed form. R_T/T decreases from 0.268 to 0.089, showing the right qualitative trend, but on a clearly reduced-scale setup.

claims.claim: Both algorithms tolerate corruptions of possibly infinite magnitude, bounded only in frequency (number of corrupted points T_c), as formalized in the Frequency-Constrained Corruption model (Definition 1, Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: The magnitude sweep (|c| from 1e1 to 1e6) on the 1-D discretized Forrester (T=100, 100 candidates) shows FC-RCGP-UCB regret flat at ~15-17 while GP-UCB grows from 112 to 120, directly demonstrating the unbounded-magnitude tolerance property. However, the setup is small-scale and simplified.

claims.claim: When there are no corruptions (T_c = 0), both FC-RCGP-UCB and A2-RCGP-UCB recover the same asymptotic regret bound as standard GP-UCB, R_T = O(√(Tβ'_Tγ_T)), a zero-cost robustness property (Theorem 1, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: At T_c=0, the logbook shows bit-identical regret (8.393) for GP-UCB, FC-RCGP-UCB, and A2-RCGP-UCB across 10 seeds, with ratio 1.000. This confirms the algebraic identity that the P-IMQ plateau weight reduces the RCGP posterior exactly to the standard GP posterior, which is scale-independent and holds exactly.

claims.claim: Experiments on the corrupted Forrester function benchmark show RCGP-based methods (FC-RCGP-UCB, A2-RCGP-UCB) achieve lower cumulative regret than baselines using standard GP, Student-t process, or the heuristic DiagnosticsGP approach, even though the theoretical analysis conservatively requires α < 1/4 and α < 1/7 while experiments use corruption budgets as large as O(T^(1/3)) (Section 5.3, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: On the corrupted Forrester benchmark (T=100, T_c=5, 10 seeds, greedy clairvoyant adversary), the RCGP methods (A2: 15.53, FC: 15.78) clearly outperform all baselines (DiagnosticsGP: 93.22, GP-UCB: 119.19, Student-t: 159.67), reproducing the ordering from Figure 1 with the same experimental design including the O(T^{1/3}) budget exceeding theoretical thresholds.

snaykey/repro-spectrally-sparse-jacobi.overall: The logbook provides a from-scratch NumPy reproduction on the Forrester benchmark with real experiments and clear results: the zero-cost robustness property (Claim 4) and the benchmark ordering (Claim 5) are verified on the paper's actual task, while the theoretical regret bounds (Claims 1-2) and unbounded-magnitude tolerance (Claim 3) are demonstrated only on a simplified, small-scale setup.

snaykey/repro-ski-rental-dist.paper_title: Ski Rental with Distributional Predictions of Unknown Quality

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows the algorithm achieves expected additive loss O(min(√b·max(EMD(p̂,p),1), b log b)), where EMD(p̂,p) is the Earth Mover's distance between the predicted and true distributions and b is the buy-ski-rental cost ratio (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Exact expected costs for Algorithm 1 computed across many (b, distribution, prediction) cells through b=10,000; the loss-vs-EMD curve follows the min(√b·max(EMD,1), b log b) elbow with maximum implied constant ≤0.49, confirmed by an independent 252-cell grid (max constant ≤0.67).

claims.claim: The algorithm attains consistency O(√b) when the prediction error (EMD) is 0 and robustness O(b log b) when the prediction is arbitrarily inaccurate, without needing to know the prediction error bound in advance (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: With EMD=0, worst-case loss/√b=1.0000 flat across b=100–10,000 (consistency); with adversarial predictions, loss/(b log b)≤0.089 and declining (robustness). Algorithm fed only (p̂, b), verified by signature inspection and 300-truth invariance test showing single threshold K*.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 proves a matching lower bound showing no algorithm can achieve additive loss o(b)·EMD(p̂,p), establishing that the √b factor in Theorem 1 is necessary (Theorem 4, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Yao/concavity lower bound over confusable families (geometric hazard shifted by s≈0.25√b) fits LB/max(EMD,1) ∝ b^0.517 (R²=0.9992) across b=64–16384; Algorithm 1's own worst-case loss attains Θ(√b)·max(EMD,1) with fit b^0.519 (R²=0.9997), confirming the √b exponent is both necessary and tight.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a Pareto-optimal consistency-robustness tradeoff: any algorithm achieving O(√b) consistency must incur Ω(b log b) robustness (Theorem 6, Section 4)
claims.evidence: 18 algorithms (including paper algorithms, 9 lambdas, baselines) tested at b∈{100,400,2500,10000} with no Pareto frontier violator found, but the claim's universal 'any algorithm' quantifier is only checked on a finite family, not all possible algorithms.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 introduces a parameterized algorithm with expected cost c(ALG_p) ≤ min{(1+λ)(c(OPT_p)+B), (1+1/λ)c(OPT_p)}, allowing explicit interpolation between trusting the prediction and worst-case guarantees via λ ∈ [0,1] (Theorem 2, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: 2,016 exact cells across b∈{100,400,2500,10000}, 12 lambda values, 6 distribution families, 7 prediction variants; zero violations of the robustness bound c(ALG)≤(1+1/λ)c(OPT) with max ratio 0.99993, and consistency-side constants bounded and declining with scale.

snaykey/repro-ski-rental-dist.overall: The logbook provides rigorous exact (non-Monte-Carlo) numerical verification of the paper's upper-bound theorems (Claims 1, 2, 3, 5) across broad parameter ranges up to b=10,000–16,384, with the lower bound's √b scaling confirmed via Yao-type constructions. The main gap is Claim 4's universal 'any algorithm' quantifier, which is only checked on a finite family of 18 algorithms rather than proven.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.3 establishes that the rank-statistic approximation D^(K)_{f,ν}(μ) is monotone non-decreasing in the resolution parameter K and is always bounded above by the true f-divergence D_{f,ν}(μ) (Section 2, Theorem 2.3).
claims.evidence: Three Gaussian test pairs at K∈{8,…,512} all show strictly non-decreasing estimates in K and estimates ≤ true divergence (max overestimate 0.0045), directly confirming monotonicity and the lower-bound property of Theorem 2.3.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.5 establishes quantitative convergence rates of O(K^{-α/2}) for Hölder-continuous density ratios and O(K^{-1}) under higher regularity, as the resolution parameter K→∞ (Section 2.1, Theorem 2.5).
claims.evidence: Deterministic 65,536-node quadrature on smooth (C∞) and Hölder-α density ratios yields tail slopes of −0.997/−0.993 for smooth (matching O(K^{-1})) and −0.376/−0.717/−0.832 for Hölder-α (matching O(K^{-α/2})), with R²≈1.0 and correct α-ordering across KL, JS, and Hellinger generators.

claims.claim: On Gaussian-Uniform pairs across dimensions 2-10, the rank-statistic estimator shows superior stability with fewer samples compared to neural divergence estimators (Section 4.1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Across d=2–10 and n∈{250,1000,4000}, the rank-statistic estimator has across-seed std of 0.001–0.016 in all 15 configurations, while DV/MINE and NWJ neural critics are orders of magnitude noisier, especially at small n; rank is most stable in 15/15 configs.

claims.claim: Table 1 reports ratio estimates for KL, Jensen-Shannon, and Hellinger divergences across resolution values K ∈ {32, 64, 128, 256, 512} in a univariate convergence study (Section 4.2, Table 1).
claims.evidence: Ratio estimates for KL, JS, and Hellinger at exactly K∈{32,64,128,256,512} on a univariate Gaussian pair increase monotonically toward 1 (e.g., KL: 0.94→1.01), with noise-free population ratios staying ≤1 at every K, matching the Table 1 protocol and Theorem 2.3's lower bound.

claims.claim: The rank f-divergence estimator is used as a learning objective for generative transport dynamics on 2D toy examples (checkerboard, ring, spirals) and on CelebA image experiments (Section 4.4, Sections 4.4.1 and 4.4.2).
claims.evidence: The 2D toy transport experiments (checkerboard, ring, spirals) show the objective dropping to 2–6% of initial value and energy distance reaching the oracle floor, but the CelebA image-scale half of the claim is entirely unaddressed, and the 2D examples are themselves toy-scale.

snaykey/repro-rank-stat-fdiv.overall: The logbook provides solid computational evidence for the theoretical claims (monotonicity/lower bound, convergence rates) and empirical claims (stability vs neural baselines, Table 1 convergence) using non-toy setups with real numerical results. The generative transport claim is only partially addressed on 2D toy examples, with the CelebA image experiments explicitly excluded.

ParetoOptimal/repro-2vhdudz6mo.paper_title: A Risk Decomposition Framework for Pre-hoc Fine-tuning Prediction

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 decomposes the Bayes-optimal prediction risk at computation budget c into an irreducible intrinsic limit term L_int plus a reducible optimization variance term V_opt(c) (Section 4, Proposition 4.1).
claims.evidence: The decomposition L(c)=L_int+V_opt(c) is confirmed as an exact law-of-total-variance identity with residual 0.0 in a concrete hierarchical Gaussian filtration model, with V_opt properties (nonneg, monotone-decreasing, vanishing) all verified and Monte-Carlo Bayes risk matching closed form to 0.56% relative error over 200k samples.

claims.claim: Proposition 5.1 establishes an asymptotic lower-bound constraint on optimization-induced uncertainty decay of the form V_opt(c) ≳ K·c^(-α), implying a fundamental, task-dependent limit on how fast uncertainty can dissipate regardless of the predictor used (Section 5, Proposition 5.1).
claims.evidence: The decay exponent α=2ρ−1 is derived symbolically from the tail-sum integral and confirmed by log-log fits across 6 values of ρ (R²=0.999995, errors <0.004); a faithful stochastic-approximation simulation of Appendix C reproduces the rate (closed-form slope 0.5019, Monte-Carlo 0.4979), and the Bayes/MMSE floor is shown to bind for all 2000 random predictors tested.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.1 derives a budget-optimal probing equilibrium with closed-form optimal stopping point c* = (αK/γλ)^(1/(α+1)) for linear probing costs (Section 6, Theorem 6.1).
claims.evidence: The closed-form optimum c*=(αK/γλ)^{1/(α+1)} is derived in sympy with residual 0, confirmed as a second-order minimum (d²J/dc²>0), and cross-checked numerically across 4 trials with relative error <1.5e-8; the efficiency frontier is verified strictly decreasing and convex with 0/20000 counterexamples.

claims.claim: The framework organizes fine-tuning tasks into three predictability regimes -- Static-Sufficient (bias-dominant, rapid uncertainty collapse), Dynamic-Critical (variance-dominant, slow information revelation), and Noise-Dominant (intrinsic-limited, irreducible ambiguity dominates) -- visualized as an empirical phase diagram of intrinsic floor versus decay exponent (Section 7, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The (L_int, α) phase space is shown to partition into all three regimes via a 30×30 grid, with representative tasks separating correctly (Static-Sufficient: high α/low floor, Dynamic-Critical: low α/low floor, Noise-Dominant: high floor), and compute-to-target confirmed strictly decreasing in α — this verifies the theoretical structure of the three-regime organization, though the empirical visualization with real-task data is not reproduced.

claims.claim: Empirical validation shows power-law uncertainty decay across regimes on a log-log scale (Figure 2) and demonstrates that the marginal gain of additional probing decays monotonically at regime-dependent rates, consistent with the theoretical predictions (Section 8, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The real LLM fine-tuning experiments (Qwen/LLaMA-3-8B/Mistral-7B, LoRA, N=1500 seeds on SST-2/GSM8K/MMLU/SAMSum/TruthfulQA) are explicitly stated as out of scope; instead, the paper's estimation methodology is applied to a CPU simulation with SA surrogates, recovering structural predictions (power-law decay exponents, diminishing marginal gains, adaptive stopping regret 0.35%) but not reproducing the actual empirical validation on real benchmarks.

ParetoOptimal/repro-2vhdudz6mo.overall: The logbook provides rigorous symbolic and numeric verification of the paper's three theoretical claims (decomposition identity, decay-rate lower bound, budget-optimal equilibrium) and confirms the three-regime phase diagram structure. The empirical validation claim (Claim 5) is addressed only through a controlled CPU simulation with synthetic SA surrogates, not the real LLM fine-tuning experiments, making it a toy reproduction of the empirical content.

ParetoOptimal/repro-ykwn4lg9ve.paper_title: What Makes a Strong Model? A Unified Spectral Analysis of Knowledge Transfer over High-dimensional Linear Regression

ParetoOptimal/repro-1krpajnd6u.paper_title: FluxNet: Learning Capacity-Constrained Local Transport Operators for Conservative and Bounded PDE Surrogates

claims.claim: Proposition 1 shows that under periodic boundary conditions with symmetric stencils, FluxNet's flux-based update rule (the same flux serves as outflow for the sender cell and inflow for the receiver cell) exactly preserves the global sum of the transported quantity, yielding conservation errors at the machine-precision level (~1e-7 to 1e-8) (Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: The validate.py script tests 400 random periodic transports across stencil radii 1-8 with max absolute mass discrepancy of 1.42e-14, and a closed-boundary case with exactly 0.0 discrepancy, directly confirming the antisymmetric flux conservation property at machine-precision level.

claims.claim: The L-Head and U-Head mechanisms parameterize outflow as a fraction of the cell's available capacity above a lower bound (or below an upper bound), and Propositions 2 and 3 prove that this construction guarantees the next state stays within the prescribed bounds without any post-hoc clipping or projection (Propositions 2 and 3).
claims.evidence: 300 randomized cases show L-Head minimum of 0.013 (above bound 0.0) and U-Head maximum of 0.997 (below bound 1.0) without any clipping, plus boundary cases (all-zeros, all-ones) with zero error, confirming the single-bound architectural guarantees of Propositions 2 and 3.

claims.claim: On the shallow-water equations rollout task at horizon T=2, FluxNet-LAP achieves a depth MAE of 3.12e-3 versus 6.74e-3 for the best baseline (a post-hoc projection method), while also reducing conservation error from 3.3e-7 (baseline) to 3.3e-8 (Table 3).
claims.evidence: Across 4 independent test corpora (122 trajectories) using the authors' own harness, FluxNet-LAP beats all baselines on every corpus with mean improvement ratio 2.34 (paper: 2.16), and conservation drift of 2.3e-8 to 3.9e-8 (paper: 3.3e-8) vs baseline 2.7e-7 to 3.2e-7 (paper: 3.3e-7). Absolute MAE is ~20% higher than the paper's 3.12e-3 but the comparative claim holds robustly.

claims.claim: On the traffic flow benchmark at horizon T=2, FluxNet-D attains an MAE of 3.48e-3 compared to 15.9e-3 for a CNN-AR baseline, and reduces conservation error from 2.1e-2 to 7.7e-8, though FluxNet-D shows slightly higher upper-bound violation rates on some settings (1.87% vs 3.20% for CNN-AR) (Table 4).
claims.evidence: Across 3 training seeds and 4 rollout horizons on 100 test trajectories, FluxNet-D wins all 12 seed-by-horizon cells with mean improvement ratio 3.30 (paper: 4.57), and conservation drift of 6.5e-8 (paper: 7.7e-8). The measured CNN-AR baseline is stronger than the paper's (0.0094 vs 15.9e-3), explaining the smaller ratio, but the direction and ranking are fully reproduced.

claims.claim: On the spinodal decomposition experiment, a FluxNet model trained to take steps of 1000*dt achieves a 17.3x rollout speedup relative to the base timestep while preserving two-point correlation statistics of the simulated microstructure (Table 5).
claims.evidence: Using the authors' pure-PyTorch integrator (parity 0.0 vs their implementation over 300 steps), the 1000*dt surrogate's two-point autocorrelation error of 0.00069 is 3.5x smaller than the ground-truth's own seed-to-seed spread (0.00241), confirming statistics preservation. The 17.3x speedup falls within the measured range of 4.87x (grid 1024) to 33.5x (grid 256), landing near the grid-512 measurement of 15.2x.

claims.claim: The D-Head (dual bounds) variant enforces upper and lower capacity constraints via a dual consistency loss (DCL) rather than a strict architectural guarantee, achieving empirically near-zero bound violations rather than the exact guarantees proven for the single-bound L-Head and U-Head cases (Section on Bound Enforcement / D-Head).
claims.evidence: A feasible counterexample maps [1,1,1] to [0.501, 0.5005, 1.9985] via D-Head averaging, proving the bound violation is structural. The DCL ablation (dcl_weight=0) shows mean total violation rate of 1.25% vs 0.49% with DCL across seeds, confirming DCL reduces violations to near-zero without eliminating them (worst prediction 1.0067 at every seed).

ParetoOptimal/repro-mmlt3tq7ot.paper_title: AdamO: A Collapse-Suppressed Optimizer for Offline RL

claims.claim: The paper shows that optimizer dynamics themselves, independent of backup rule or network architecture, can directly trigger or suppress the value-collapse instability observed in offline RL, by analyzing frozen linearized TD-error dynamics (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook holds backup rule (gamma, X') and architecture (W, a, X) fixed while swapping only the optimizer preconditioner D, showing maxRe(S) flips from +1.1164 (collapse) to -0.0528 (stable) on a genuine 2-layer tanh critic with NTK Jacobian features. Stepsize and momentum sweeps further confirm optimizer knobs alone move the system across the stability boundary (eta*=1.9158; 18.9x threshold shift), and SL without bootstrapping never collapses (rho(A)<=1).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that frozen linearized TD error dynamics converge exponentially to zero if and only if the spectral radius rho(A(eta)) of the augmented update matrix is strictly less than one, giving a necessary and sufficient stability condition; Theorem 4.2 gives a practical sufficient condition via Hurwitzness of the underlying TD operator.
claims.evidence: The recurrence Eq. 10 is derived symbolically from Eq. 8 + Adam's EMA (sympy residual 0), the companion spectrum matches per-mode quadratic roots (max error 5.71e-14 over 200 random S), and the necessary-and-sufficient condition rho(A)<1 <=> exponential decay is confirmed with 0/3924 mismatches across random operator/stepsize pairs. The eta->0 perturbation gives dr/deta=mu exactly, and Remark 4.3 boundary cases reproduce (unit root at mu=0 to 5.6e-16).

claims.claim: Proposition 5.1 decomposes a sufficient condition for stability into a bootstrapped-amplification term and a feature-conditioning (near-orthogonality) term: gamma*||Phi||_2*||Phi*||_2 + ||Phi^T Phi - I||_2 < 1.
claims.evidence: The sufficient condition gamma*||Phi||*||Phi*|| + ||Phi^T Phi - I|| < 1 is tested over 20000 randomized near-isometry feature draws; in 2269 draws where the condition holds, there are 0 Hurwitz violations, and near-boundary samples remain Hurwitz, confirming the condition is genuinely sufficient and conservative as the paper states.

claims.claim: AdamO augments Adam with a decoupled, scale-normalized orthogonality correction subject to a budget constraint that provably bounds how much task progress the correction can sacrifice, with a closed-form scaling solution (Eq. 19, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The AdamO map (Eqs. 17-19) is implemented verbatim and verified: the task-alignment budget is met exactly (min residual -1.78e-15, 7962 clipped cases at equality), ratio clipping holds (||delta||<=kappa||u||), conflict-free non-inferiority has 0/3877 violations below the stepsize bound (407 failures at 5x confirming it is operative), worst-case degradation bound has 0/3000 violations, and the Hamiltonian identity dH_AdamO/dt - dH_Adam/dt = -<g,delta> holds to 2.89e-15.

claims.claim: Across offline RL benchmarks, AdamO improves average scores over standard Adam by roughly +112% on AntMaze with TD3+BC, +10-15% on MuJoCo locomotion tasks across algorithms, and +38% (IQL) to +6866% (TD3+BC) on Adroit, at a modest compute overhead (~28 extra minutes, 172 vs. 144 total minutes on TD3+BC) (Table 1, Figure 2).

ParetoOptimal/repro-mmlt3tq7ot.overall: The logbook provides rigorous symbolic and numerical verification of the paper's theoretical claims (Claims 1-4) on the frozen linearized TD-error dynamics and AdamO algorithm, with thousands of random instances and exact arithmetic checks. ParetoOptimal/repro-ugpfadssaa.paper_title: Distributionally Robust Markov Games with Average Reward

claims.evidence: Checks C1–C6 verify robust Bellman solvability (residual 0.00e+00, g=0.4228 matching independent ground truth to 2.22e-15), uniqueness up to constant vector (g spread 8.38e-15 over 5 inits), convexity of optimal policy set (interpolant gap 4.44e-16), and u.s.c. (max jump 2.55e-3 over 100-step path) on the same small 3-state, 2-action instance. Real numbers but clearly simplified scale.

claims.claim: The volume-contraction lemma shows that whenever the algorithm's prediction errs, the feasible volume fraction shrinks by at least a factor of 1 - 1/e, underlying the O(d log d) regret proof (Lemma 4.1, Section 4)
claims.evidence: The exact rational volume ratio L(A_{t+1})/L(A_t) was computed via integer subset DP over 223 mistake rounds across all CoG runs, never exceeding 0.5 (vs the lemma's threshold of 1-1/e=0.6321); the DP was validated against ground truth (returns d! for empty poset, CoG at 0.5 for unit cube), and volume endpoints L=d! at t=1 and L≥1 throughout were confirmed.

ParetoOptimal/repro-g7le4mukgq.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the finite content underlying all five theoretical claims using exact computation (integer DP for linear extensions, exhaustive strategy enumeration) rather than sampling, on the paper's own M-convex instance family. The main limitation is small dimensions (d≤20, d≤10, d=8, m≤8), inherent to exact computation, but the proof structures verified are dimension-independent and the scope is honestly acknowledged.

claims.claim: Definition 1 introduces ℓ*-smoothness, bounding the Hessian via a general norm and its dual, ‖∇²f(x)h‖* ≤ ℓ(‖∇f(x)‖*)‖h‖, generalizing prior ℓ-smoothness beyond the Euclidean/ℓ2 setting (Section 3.1, Definition 1)
claims.evidence: The logbook numerically checks the ℓ*-smoothness inequality ‖∇²f(x)h‖* ≤ ℓ(‖∇f(x)‖*)‖h‖ on the Prop-C.1 quadratic (n=64), finding max ratio 0.585 ≤ 1, confirming the bound holds and is valid. The standard ℓ2-smoothness ratio (0.482 with L=n-1=63) uses a much larger smoothness constant, illustrating the generalization.

claims.claim: Theorem 8 shows mirror descent under ℓ*-smoothness attains O(1/T) convergence for both average-iterate and last-iterate suboptimality with an appropriately chosen learning rate (Section 4, Theorem 8)
claims.evidence: Mirror descent on the Prop-C.1 quadratic (n=32) satisfies gap_T ≤ C/T with C=log(32)≈3.466 at all T∈{25,…,1600}, max ratio 0.0081. The hard ill-conditioned quadratic (cond=1e4) yields a log-log slope of -1.791, faster than the -0.65 threshold for O(1/T).

claims.claim: Theorem 9 shows an accelerated mirror descent variant attains the optimal O(1/T^2) convergence rate under ℓ*-smoothness via a time-partition analysis technique (Section 4, Theorem 9)
claims.evidence: Accelerated mirror descent satisfies gap_T ≤ C/T² with C=log(32) at all sampled T, max ratio 0.378. The hard-instance slope of -1.785 passes the -1.65 threshold for O(1/T²), though it is notably similar to plain MD's slope (-1.791), suggesting the hard instance may not fully discriminate the accelerated rate.

claims.claim: Theorem 10 and Theorem 11 extend the O(1/T) rate to optimistic mirror descent and mirror prox respectively, using a stability-tracking argument and a descent property for both update sequences (Section 4, Theorems 10-11)
claims.evidence: Both OMD (η=1/3) and MirrorProx (η=1/2) satisfy gap_T ≤ C/T at all T on the Prop-C.1 quadratic, with max ratios 0.061 and 0.031 respectively. Hard-instance slopes of -1.638 (OMD) and -1.748 (MirrorProx) both pass the -0.65 threshold.

claims.claim: Theorem 12 establishes an Õ(1/√t) anytime convergence rate for stochastic mirror descent under ℓ*-smoothness with a generalized bounded-noise assumption ‖ϵ_t‖* ≤ σ(‖∇f(x_t)‖*) (Section 5, Theorem 12)
claims.evidence: On a generalized-smooth log-sum-exp objective with gradient-scaled noise, SMD with η_t=1/√t yields suboptimality decaying with log-log slope -0.558 (≈-0.5), and gap·√t is uniformly bounded (~3.5) across t=200–20000, confirming the anytime Õ(1/√t) property. The separate hard-quadratic experiment gives a weaker slope of -0.326 but still within the pass band.

claims.claim: Proposition 4 shows that on the simplex, ℓ*-smoothness yields a constant smoothness parameter whereas standard ℓ-smoothness has an O(n) dimension dependence, illustrating the benefit of the generalized notion (Section 3.2, Proposition 4)
claims.evidence: Direct computation of operator norms for n∈{4,8,…,256} shows standard ℓ2-smoothness parameter equals n-1 (log-log slope 1.059, i.e., O(n)) while ℓ*-smoothness (ℓ1/ℓ∞ dual) equals 1.0 (slope 0.000, constant), exactly matching the proposition's prediction with exact arithmetic.

DineshAI/j9aoIFr5aM.overall: The logbook provides clean-room numpy verification of all six claims through bound checks with exact theorem constants, hard-instance slope fitting, and negative controls. However, the scale is modest (n=32–256, T≤16000), the mdgs module source is not shown, and some hard-instance slopes (notably AMD at -1.785 vs expected -2.0, and SMD on the hard quadratic at -0.326 vs expected -0.5) are not closely aligned with theoretical predictions.

arvkevi/repro-federated-causal-discovery.paper_title: Regret-Based Federated Causal Discovery with Unknown Interventions

claims.claim: I-PERI aggregates client CPDAGs via a modified regret computed on the graph intersection L(H∩C(GΦk),Dk)−L(C(GΦk),Dk), and Theorem 3.2 shows this converges to the true CPDAG C(G) common to all clients under consistent scoring (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies the Phi-MEC combinatorial characterization (Theorem 3.2 as labeled in the logbook) via brute-force d-separation on n=4 DAGs, but does not test the regret-based aggregation mechanism L(H∩C(GΦk),Dk)−L(C(GΦk),Dk) nor the convergence-to-true-CPDAG claim; it explicitly states it dodges the n→∞ asymptotics.

claims.claim: I-PERI introduces the Φ-Markov Equivalence Class, characterized by skeleton, v-structures, and intervention-induced structures, and proves convergence to the finer Φ-CPDAG Φ(G), letting it orient additional edges beyond the standard CPDAG using intervention-induced differences across clients (Definition 3.1, Theorem 3.4, Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: The Phi-MEC characterization is verified exhaustively over 32,400 (G,Phi) pairs on n=4 nodes with 0 mismatches, and the Phi-CPDAG uniqueness/nesting (CPDAG⊂Phi-CPDAG⊂I-CPDAG) is confirmed on 35/35 classes and 120/120 instances, supporting additional edge orientation. However, this is at toy scale (n=4, oracle level) and the convergence theorems (3.4, 3.5) are not tested.

claims.claim: I-PERI's regret statistic has bounded sensitivity of (2M+1)log r^2 + O(log n/n), which is used to achieve epsilon-differential privacy via Laplace noise injection (Lemma 3.1, Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirms the Laplace mechanism achieves eps-DP by computing a worst log-density-ratio of 0.4997 ≤ eps=0.5, but this is at oracle/population level on n=4 nodes and the sensitivity bound (2M+1)log r² + O(log n/n) is stated rather than independently derived or numerically verified against actual regret scores.

claims.claim: On synthetic Erdos-Renyi DAGs with K=5 clients and 1000-5000 samples per client, the recovered Φ-CPDAG attains lower structural Hamming distance and higher edge-orientation F1-score than the standard CPDAG baseline (Section 4, Figure 6).
claims.evidence: The logbook runs 400 ER DAGs at p=6 nodes, K=5 clients at oracle/population level (no finite samples), reporting SHD ≤ observational baseline on 400/400. However, the claim specifies 1000–5000 samples per client and F1-score; the logbook explicitly states it dodges 'the linear-Gaussian SHD/F1 experiments,' so neither the sample-size regime nor the F1 metric is addressed.

claims.claim: The federated CPDAG aggregation step assumes at least one client holds purely observational data (Assumption 2.1, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook's experimental setup explicitly includes 'one observational per Assumption 2.1' across its 400 ER DAG runs, confirming the assumption is integral to the federated aggregation procedure and exercised in the reproduction.

arvkevi/repro-federated-causal-discovery.overall: The logbook provides rigorous brute-force combinatorial verification of the Phi-MEC characterization and Phi-CPDAG uniqueness at n=4 oracle level, but does not test the regret-based aggregation mechanism, finite-sample convergence, or the specific SHD/F1 experimental regime (1000–5000 samples) claimed in the paper.

claims.claim: WeDLM implements diffusion-style parallel decoding entirely with standard causal attention to preserve prefix KV-cache compatibility (Section 3).
claims.evidence: On a custom TinyRoPETransformer (float64), incremental KV-cache decode matches full recompute to 6.1e-16 over 300 cases, committed K/V drift under causal attention is 2.8e-16, and the bidirectional control breaks with drift 0.082 — confirming the architectural property is scale-independent and holds exactly.

claims.claim: Topological Reordering lets each masked position condition on observed tokens under a strict causal mask by moving observed tokens into the physical prefix while preserving logical positions (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Across 1200 random configurations, topological reorder+causal forward equals explicit-mask forward to 6.7e-16 max diff, with both mutation controls (physical-index RoPE and no-reorder) breaking on 386/386 interior-mask trials, and connectivity principles (full observed-context visibility, directed mask dependence) holding in all trials.

claims.claim: WeDLM introduces a streaming decoding procedure that commits confident tokens into a growing left-to-right prefix while maintaining a fixed parallel workload (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1/Figure 3 invariants (fixed window ≤W, append-only left-to-right commits, no stop-and-wait, Figure-3 scenario reproduces) are verified across 80 configs, but predictions come from a deterministic synthetic confidence oracle rather than a real language model, making this a mechanism-level test on a simplified setup.

claims.claim: Against vLLM-served autoregressive baselines under matched deployment settings, WeDLM approaches 3x speedups on reasoning benchmarks and up to 10x speedups in low-entropy generation regimes (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Only a compute proxy was measured on a randomly-initialized 8-layer model (d=512): recompute penalty grows from 16.7x to 72.7x with length, but no vLLM baseline, no trained WeDLM weights, no reasoning benchmarks, and no low-entropy regime evaluation were attempted; wall-clock on T4 actually inverted (0.64–0.73x) at this scale.

MarxistLeninist/repro-wedlm-reconciling-.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies WeDLM's core architectural claims (causal KV-cache compatibility, topological reordering equivalence) to machine precision with appropriate mutation controls on small but scale-independent models. The streaming decoding invariants are verified with a synthetic oracle (toy), and the 3x/10x speedup claim is only addressed via a compute-cost proxy without vLLM, trained weights, or real benchmarks (toy).

radhakrishnadeshpande/repro-iworld-bench.paper_title: iWorld-Bench: A Benchmark for Interactive World Models with a Unified Action Generation Framework
