kshitijthakkar/repro-coinflip-safety.paper_title: A Coin Flip for Safety: LLM Judges Fail to Reliably Measure Adversarial Robustness

claims.claim: Across an audit of 6,642 human-verified labels spanning 4 victim models (Gemma-3-1B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-27B, Qwen-3-32B) and 5 attack methods (Direct Prompting, GCG, GCG-REINFORCE, Best-of-N, PAIR), 4 safety judges (LlamaGuard-3, HarmBench, AegisGuard, JailJudge) are shown to perform only slightly better than random guessing on average (Section 3, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Recomputation from released CSV confirms exactly 6,642 labels, 4 named victim models, 5 named attacks, and 4 judges with scores on 100% of rows. On the 2,746-row balanced set (chance=0.500), the four judges average 0.547 accuracy (margins +0.011 to +0.085), matching paper Table 1 within ≤0.01 per judge.

claims.claim: ROC analysis shows JailJudge attains AUROC as low as 0.48 (worse than chance) on some attack-model pairs and no better than 0.64 on any attack, demonstrating near-chance discriminative ability under distribution shift (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Within Figure 5's stated scope (JailJudge on Llama-3.1-8B), recomputed AUROC min is 0.476 on GCG-R (rounds to 0.48, below chance) and max is 0.642 on GCG (≤0.64 ceiling holds). Per-attack pooled over all models also holds (max 0.611). Three beyond-scope individual pairs exceed 0.64 (max 0.701), but these are outside the claim's cited scope.

claims.claim: Judge accuracy varies dramatically across attack-model combinations, with some judges scoring only 45% accuracy on specific attack-victim pairs, close to random guessing (Figure 3, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Across 68 judge×pair cells (n≥20) on the balanced set, accuracy spans 0.340–0.736. Four cells sit at or below 0.45 (floor 0.340, AegisGuard on Llama-3.1×PAIR), and 22 of 68 cells are below chance. Per-judge swings range 0.220–0.258 accuracy points.

claims.claim: The paper introduces ReliableBench, a curated set of 41 behaviors, which raises average judge accuracy from 57% to 70%, and JudgeStressTest (JST), a set of 971 challenging samples that exposes systematic judge failures across judge architectures via leave-one-out validation (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Independently recomputed top-41 behaviors yield mean accuracy 0.703 (paper 0.70) vs all-100 mean 0.574 (paper 0.57), with 41/41 overlap with released ReliableBench. Released JST contains exactly 971 samples. All 8 leave-one-out Acc@0/Acc@1 values reproduce within ≤0.02 of paper Table 1, confirming shared failure modes across judge architectures.

claims.claim: Correcting reported attack success rates (ASR) for judge unreliability substantially deflates the apparent effectiveness of attacks such as Best-of-N, which is shown to inflate ASR by exploiting judge insufficiencies rather than eliciting genuinely harmful content (Figure 1, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: BoN judge precision is 0.575 audit-wide (lowest of 5 attacks; others 0.76–0.88) and 0.287 on Gemma-3-1B. Precision-corrected ASR on Gemma-3-1B drops BoN from 0.41 to 0.12 (−71%), placing it last among attacks, reproducing Figure 1's corrected ordering. A declared deviation notes the uncorrected ASR denominator differs from the paper's, but the comparable quantities (precision and corrected ordering) reproduce.

claims.claim: Judge Concordance analysis shows judges can reach near-unanimous agreement with each other while still failing to align with human ground-truth labels, and averaging/ensembling judge scores does not consistently improve alignment with human judgments (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: Judge Concordance score reimplemented from paper definition: 40.8% of balanced rows are unanimous (S_JC=1), yet the panel is wrong on 40.9% of those. Per-behavior concordance–accuracy correlation is near zero (Pearson r=+0.066, Spearman ρ=+0.146). Averaged judge score correlates with human ratings no better than the best single judge (|r|=0.064 vs 0.132 on Llama-3.1), and all four ensemble rules score below the best single judge (0.564 vs 0.585).

kshitijthakkar/repro-coinflip-safety.overall: This logbook provides a thorough, paper-scale reproduction of all six claims via pure recomputation from the released audit CSV containing 6,642 human-verified labels and all four judges' verdict scores. Every numeric anchor reproduces within stated tolerances, with transparent declarations of minor scope deviations (e.g., ReliableBench CSV has 43 vs 41 behaviors, ASR denominator differs from paper's Figure 1) that do not undermine the core findings.

toqi/repro-cpKJ2GlnYT.paper_title: Relative Entropy Estimation in Function Space: Theory and Applications to Trajectory Inference

claims.claim: The paper derives a tractable estimator for the KL divergence between trajectory distributions in function space, expressed via squared discrepancies between the associated velocity fields under Functional Flow Matching (Theorem 3.6).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements Eq. 7 as a Monte Carlo estimator from scratch, confirms it requires only pointwise velocity evaluations (no ODE integration, verified by grep), and shows it produces KL estimates in the right order of magnitude across a ~40x dynamic range on Gaussian validation cases at paper-scale hyperparameters.

claims.claim: On synthetic Gaussian-measure validation cases, the estimator's KL values range from 3.95 to 45.73 across 8 configurations, closely matching analytic ground-truth values of 3.64 to 45.43 (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The analytic ground-truth KL values match the paper's Table 1 exactly across all 8 configs, but the estimated FKL values at paper-scale (30k iters, M=128, N=64) deviate by 22-123% relative error (e.g., case 5: est 16.27 vs analytic 7.29; case 6: est 2.39 vs analytic 10.93), far from the paper's <1-24% error, because the MINO backbone was replaced with a much lower-capacity FiLM-MLP.

claims.claim: The functional KL estimator is benchmarked against five methods (vSB, SBIRR, MSBM, MFL, AM, TIGON) on synthetic dynamical systems (Lotka-Volterra, Repressilator, Petal) and four real single-cell RNA-seq datasets (EB, hESC, ME, HF), using marginal metrics (EMD, W2, SWD, MWD, MMD) alongside forward and reverse functional KL (Tables 2-3).
claims.evidence: The full 6-baseline x 7-dataset benchmark was not attempted; instead, 2 hand-built proxy methods ('smooth' spline and 'bridge' SDE) were evaluated on 1 of 7 datasets (Repressilator only) with marginal metrics and FKL, demonstrating the evaluation framework's mechanism but not the paper's literal Tables 2-3.

claims.claim: On the Repressilator dataset, TIGON ranks above SBIRR according to marginal metrics but below SBIRR according to functional KL, illustrating that marginal-metric-based evaluation can be inconsistent with trajectory-level evaluation (Section on TI benchmark evaluation, Tables 2-3).
claims.evidence: On the paper's exact Repressilator SDE with proxy methods, the scaled GPU run shows marginal W2 ranks 'smooth' (TIGON-like) above 'bridge' (SBIRR-like) at late validation snapshots, while reverse FKL ranks 'bridge' (96.5) dramatically above 'smooth' (220.0), reproducing the claim's mechanism but with hand-built proxies rather than actual TIGON/SBIRR.

claims.claim: Figure 3 shows that marginal-metric-based rankings on Lotka-Volterra and Repressilator are often statistically indistinguishable despite apparently large numerical differences between methods, undermining confidence in marginal-only evaluation (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook did not reproduce the paper's CD-diagram methodology (Friedman/Nemenyi tests across training seeds); instead it used Mann-Whitney U on bootstrap subsamples of a single run, finding significant differences (p<0.05 at 4/5 snapshots) between deliberately-divergent proxies, which neither confirms nor refutes the paper's claim about near-indistinguishable rankings among similarly-tuned real baselines.

claims.claim: The estimator uses a Mesh-Informed Neural Operator (MINO) architecture with a subtraction-based parameterization enforcing boundary conditions and Monte Carlo integration that does not require simulating the full generative dynamics via ODE integration (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The subtraction-based boundary parameterization (v(x,1)=x via Eq. 21) and Monte-Carlo-only estimation (no ODE solver, confirmed by grep) are faithfully implemented and verified, but the MINO architecture itself was replaced with a FiLM-conditioned MLP operating on truncated spectral coefficients, a deliberate simplification since the fixed periodic grid does not require MINO's irregular-mesh machinery.

toqi/repro-cpKJ2GlnYT.overall: The logbook provides a credible independent reimplementation of the Theorem 3.6 FKL estimator, exactly reproducing the analytic ground-truth KL values and demonstrating the estimator's tractability and the marginal-vs-FKL ranking-inconsistency mechanism on a toy Repressilator benchmark. However, the MINO backbone substitution causes substantially worse estimation accuracy than the paper (22-123% vs <1-24% error), and the full 6-baseline, 7-dataset benchmark including real scRNA-seq data was not attempted.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows that when the perturbation radius ρ satisfies ρ ≥ -1/λ1 (λ1 being a negative Hessian eigenvalue at the saddle), the saddle point becomes an attracting fixed point of the SAM dynamics (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Measured attractor threshold ρ*=0.5000000000 matches -1/λ₁=0.5 to 10 digits on f(x,y)=x²-y²; unstable-direction multiplier crosses from 1.2 (ρ=0, escapes) to 0.8 (ρ=1, attractor), and SAM at ρ=1 converges to the saddle (||w||=0.0) while GD escapes (||w||=1.19e6). Additionally reproduced on the non-quadratic Beale function where SAM is trapped at the saddle (dist 7.5e-5) while GD reaches the global minimum (dist 9.4e-4).

claims.claim: Theorem 2 uses a stochastic diffusion analysis to show SAM's mean squared displacement near a saddle point is smaller than SGD's, implying SAM requires more time than SGD to escape saddle points (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Closed-form MSD_SAM < MSD_SGD for every ρ tested (e.g., 1.0959e-3 vs 1.1070e-3 at ρ=0.5), and Monte-Carlo first-passage escape over 2000 seeds shows SAM consistently slower (ratio 1.078–1.438). Independently confirmed on the paper's two-layer network over 1000 seeds: SGD escapes (99.9%, median 142 steps) while SAM stays trapped (0% escaped, median loss 2.500).

claims.claim: Theorem 3 shows the mean squared displacement near a saddle scales as 1/[(1-γ)B], so higher momentum γ and smaller batch size B accelerate SAM's escape from saddle points (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Closed-form Eq.17 MSD is strictly increasing in γ (1.39e-3→3.36e-1→3.89e0 for γ=0,0.9,0.95) and decreasing in B (1.34e0→3.36e-1→8.40e-2 for B=1,4,16), both monotonicities confirmed. MC heavy-ball escape over 2000 seeds shows momentum cuts median escape from 53.7 to 5.65 steps (9.5x speedup), and smaller batch escapes faster (B=1: 4.55 vs B=16: 6.80 steps). Network-level MSD and escape rate (1.5%→78.6%) also confirm.

claims.claim: On the Beale test function, SAM is empirically shown to become stuck at a saddle point where vanilla gradient descent successfully escapes, matching the Case-III oscillation predicted by the theory (Section 5, empirical validation).
claims.evidence: On the Beale function with Hessian eigenvalues ±27.750 at saddle (0,1), GD converges to the global minimum (2.9991, 0.4998) while normalized SAM at ρ=0.1 is trapped at the saddle (-3.8e-5, 0.9999, dist-to-saddle 7.5e-5) after 200k steps, reproducing the paper's Fig. 1 result of SAM stuck at saddle where GD escapes.

claims.claim: On CIFAR benchmarks, adding momentum increases SAM's accuracy by more than 20 percentage points, compared to roughly a 5-point gain for SGD with momentum, confirming momentum's outsized effect on SAM stability (Section 5).
claims.evidence: On full CIFAR-10 with a 1.15M-parameter CNN (10 epochs, 3 seeds), SAM momentum lift is +24.42 pp (36.31%→60.73% at ρ=0.5, lr=0.1), exceeding the >20 pp bar, and independently +23.79 pp at lr=0.01. SGD momentum lift is +1.92 pp at lr=0.1 (and +11.35 pp at lr=0.01), confirming the outsized asymmetry (12.7x). Controls at ρ=1.0/2.0 show momentum cannot rescue near-chance accuracy.

ai-sherpa/sam-stability-repro.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all five claims, combining closed-form theorem verification, Monte-Carlo simulations with thousands of seeds, reproduction on the paper's own intermediate experiments (Beale function, two-layer network), and a real CIFAR-10 training run. The main limitation is reduced scale for CIFAR-10 (10 epochs, 1.15M-param CNN vs the paper's 300-epoch ResNet), but the momentum lift—the claimed quantity—clearly exceeds the 20 pp threshold.

srilearns/vla-mbpo-icml2026-repro.paper_title: Towards Practical World Model-based Reinforcement Learning for Vision-Language-Action Models

claims.claim: VLA-MBPO uses a pretrained Unified Multimodal Model (UMM) as a world model to jointly predict visual dynamics and rewards, avoiding separate specialist world models (Section on UMM-based world modeling).
claims.evidence: The joint reward-head vs separate-specialist experiment was folded into Claim 2's GPU run, which never executed due to an HF API outage. Only a 4-step CPU smoke test ran, which the logbook itself states is 'meaningless as evidence.' No reward accuracy or F1 numbers were produced.

claims.claim: Interleaved view decoding enforces multi-view consistency between head and wrist cameras, and the UMM-World achieves an SSIM of 0.751 versus 0.680 for a baseline video-generation world model, while running at roughly 2x faster inference (Section on world model evaluation).
claims.evidence: The reduced-scale world model code was written and smoke-tested, but the substantive GPU training run never launched (HF API 504s). No SSIM values, ablation gaps, or inference-speed measurements exist. The 4-step smoke test is explicitly disclaimed as non-evidence.

claims.claim: Chunk-level branched rollout is theoretically shown to tighten the value-gap bound compared to prior methods; with discount γ=0.99 and horizon k=10, the branched rollout (n=2) reduces the bound to approximately 1710·ϵ_π^k + 400·ϵ_m^(k'n), versus roughly 4183·ϵ_π^k + 18916·ϵ_m for prior methods (Theoretical analysis section).
claims.evidence: All four case-study constants were recomputed from the formulas and match the paper exactly (4183.32, 18916.58, 1710.78, 400.00). Sympy confirmed Thm 4.2 follows identically from Lemma A.4. 200 random tabular MDPs showed both bounds hold (200/200) and n=2 branched rollout achieves 47% of full-horizon error, confirming the mechanism.

claims.claim: On the LIBERO benchmark, VLA-MBPO improves the base policy's average success rate by 9.1 percentage points, with the largest gain of 12.2 points on the LIBERO-Long suite, and outperforms an online RL baseline (πRL) under equivalent interaction budgets (Section on LIBERO simulation results).
claims.evidence: No LIBERO experiments were run; the logbook only performed an internal-consistency audit of the paper's Table 2 (checking deltas, averages, and grid granularity). This verifies arithmetic of reported numbers but does not reproduce or falsify the experimental claim.

claims.claim: VLA-MBPO uses a single universal set of hyperparameters across all tasks rather than task-specific tuning, which the authors argue supports robustness and scalability for real-world deployment (Section on hyperparameter settings).
claims.evidence: Direct inspection of the paper's own Table 5 shows 2 of 12 hyperparameters vary: Sample size is 1280 for LIBERO-Long vs 512 elsewhere, and Update-to-data is 50 vs 20. This contradicts the literal claim of 'a single universal set of hyperparameters across all tasks.'

claims.claim: Real-world validation spans 5 tasks across two robotic platforms (Arx-X5 and Galaxy-R1), including deformable-object manipulation and high-DoF whole-body control, with consistent improvements on both seen and unseen conditions (Section on real-world experiments).
claims.evidence: No robots, data, or video were available. The logbook provides only a qualitative assessment of the experimental design's plausibility. No experimental evidence was produced.

srilearns/vla-mbpo-icml2026-repro.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies Claim 3's theoretical bound (exact constant-matching, symbolic derivation check, and 200-MDP empirical validation) and cleanly falsifies Claim 5 against the paper's own table. However, Claims 1, 2, 4, and 6 lack any substantive experimental evidence — the key GPU run for the world-model mechanism never executed, LIBERO was only arithmetically audited, and real-robot experiments were infeasible.

SabaPivot/repro-to-grok-grokking.paper_title: To Grok Grokking: Provable Grokking in Ridge Regression

claims.claim: The paper proves end-to-end grokking for zero-teacher ridge regression, including early training overfitting, delayed poor generalization, and eventual low generalization error (Theorem 4.1)
claims.evidence: Exact spectral iterates at n=100, m=1000, lambda=1e-4, eta=1 show training loss crossing 0.01 at t1=215 while population loss remains 0.850218 at t=216, then population loss crosses 0.01 only at t2=22,413; all three theorem bounds (training upper, population lower, norm upper) hold with zero or negative violations across 79 evaluated time points.

claims.claim: The end-to-end grokking result is extended from the zero-teacher setting to realizable ridge regression with arbitrary realizable teacher functions (Theorem 4.2)
claims.evidence: A concrete counterexample with H=diag(100,1,0), lambda=1e-6, eta=0.1 satisfies the printed step-size condition eta < 1/(lambda + mu_min) but yields a GD multiplier of -9.0000001, causing training loss to explode from 50 to 9.27e16 by step 8; the stable regime (eta=0.005) converges, confirming the condition is insufficient as printed.

claims.claim: Separate theorems decompose grokking into training-loss convergence, poor generalization during overfitting, and eventual generalization (Theorems 4.4-4.6)
claims.evidence: Theorem 4.5's duration bound is supported (predicted 16,284 steps vs empirical crossing t2=22,812), but Theorem 4.4 inherits the same insufficient step-size condition as 4.2 (counterexample: H=diag(100,1) diverges under the printed condition), and Theorem 4.6's unconstrained GD-convergence clause is falsified by a 1-D example (phi=1, theta*=1, lambda=0.1, eta=2) where the multiplier is -1.2 and population loss grows from 1 to 1,221 by t=20.

claims.claim: Decreasing weight decay and sample size can amplify grokking time in ridge-regression simulations, matching the paper's quantitative hyperparameter predictions (Figure 2)
claims.evidence: Across 324 exact ridge trajectories (12 seeds per point), decreasing lambda from 2^-15 to 2^-19 raises median t2 from 75,366 to 1,196,429 with log(t2) vs log(1/lambda) slope 0.9968 (predicted 1); decreasing n from 160 to 10 lowers t1 from 365 to 18.5; increasing nu^2 from 1 to 10^6 raises t1 from 214 to 1,380 and t2 from 23,041 to 91,929; all Equation (8) t1/t2 bounds pass at 100%.

claims.claim: Two-layer ReLU experiments qualitatively reproduce the predicted grokking-time dependence on hyperparameters beyond the linear setting (Figures 3 and 4)
claims.evidence: Figure 4 (both layers trained, 23 configurations) shows all runs reaching the formal 0.01 held-out threshold, with halving weight decay approximately doubling t2 (154157→79386→40881→21052→10841→5583), smaller n fitting earlier, and width having little effect—matching the paper's qualitative predictions; Figure 3 (fixed features) reproduces the correct directional trends but never reaches the formal threshold (final losses ~0.23), which the logbook transparently discloses as a proxy limitation.

SabaPivot/repro-to-grok-grokking.overall: The logbook provides strong exact-spectral evidence verifying the zero-teacher grokking phenomenon (Claim 1) and all Figure 2 hyperparameter predictions (Claim 4), while also presenting concrete executable counterexamples that falsify the printed step-size conditions in Theorems 4.2, 4.4, and 4.6 (Claims 2–3). Figure 4 ReLU experiments qualitatively reproduce the predicted grokking-time dependence (Claim 5), though Figure 3 fails to reach the formal generalization threshold.

ai-sherpa/grok-grokking-ridge-repro.paper_title: To Grok Grokking: Provable Grokking in Ridge Regression

claims.claim: The paper proves end-to-end grokking for zero-teacher ridge regression, including early training overfitting, delayed poor generalization, and eventual low generalization error (Theorem 4.1)
claims.evidence: At the paper's default scale (n=100, m=1000, ν²=1, λ=1e-4, η=1), the closed-form spectral evolution (validated against iterative GD to 7.6e-14) shows median t1=218, t2=23027 (106x delay), population loss 0.874 right after fitting vs 9.0e-4 at t=120000, and 1/m floor scaling (slope -0.93, R²=0.999), concretely demonstrating all three grokking stages.

claims.claim: The end-to-end grokking result is extended from the zero-teacher setting to realizable ridge regression with arbitrary realizable teacher functions (Theorem 4.2)
claims.evidence: The linear experiments use a realizable unit-norm teacher (||θ*||=1, y=<θ*,x>) across 8 seeds, directly testing the realizable setting of Theorem 4.2, with grokking stages confirmed at the paper's default scale. The spectral method handles arbitrary teachers and results are consistent across seeds.

claims.claim: Separate theorems decompose grokking into training-loss convergence, poor generalization during overfitting, and eventual generalization (Theorems 4.4-4.6)
claims.evidence: The three stages are separately quantified: fast training convergence (t1=218), persistent poor generalization (pop loss=0.874 at t1), and eventual generalization (9.0e-4 at t=120000). Additionally, 135/135 config×seed rows satisfy both Eq.(8) and Eq.(11) bounds for t1 (upper) and t2 (lower) with non-vacuous worst-case ratios (≤0.594).

claims.claim: Decreasing weight decay and sample size can amplify grokking time in ridge-regression simulations, matching the paper's quantitative hyperparameter predictions (Figure 2)
claims.evidence: Weight decay amplification is explicitly demonstrated: t2∝1/λ with log-log slope -1.0000, R²=1.000000 across 5 λ values. The quantitative bounds (Eq. 8 and Eq. 11), which encode sample-size dependence via n/λ_min^+, are satisfied on all 135 grid rows spanning n∈{80,100} and m∈{1000,1500,2000}. The η scaling (t2∝1/η, slope -1.0000) is also confirmed.

claims.claim: Two-layer ReLU experiments qualitatively reproduce the predicted grokking-time dependence on hyperparameters beyond the linear setting (Figures 3 and 4)
claims.evidence: A genuinely trained width-1000 two-layer ReLU network (both layers, GD+weight decay, zero teacher, at paper Sec 5.3 defaults d=50/n=50/m=1000) reproduces all four qualitative dependencies: t2∝1/λ (slope -0.999, R²=1.0), t1 decreases with n (4100→1175), width barely affects t2 (1.06x over 4x range), and t2 increases with ν² (79475→148075). The honest reporting that t1 moves opposite to the linear prediction for ν² matches the paper's own Fig 3 caption note.

ai-sherpa/grok-grokking-ridge-repro.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous from-scratch reproduction of the paper's linear ridge-regression grokking theory using an exact closed-form spectral method validated to machine precision, plus a genuinely trained two-layer ReLU network at the paper's own scale. All five claims are supported by concrete numerical evidence at non-toy scale, with comprehensive bound-checking (135/135 rows) and explicit hyperparameter sweeps confirming the predicted scalings.

ai-sherpa/adam-degenerate-polynomials-re.paper_title: Towards Understanding Adam Convergence on Highly Degenerate Polynomials

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that on the degenerate polynomial loss L(x) = (1/k) x^k for k >= 4, Adam achieves local linear convergence when beta_1 < beta_2^(k/(2(k-2))), with asymptotic rate x_{t+1}/x_t -> beta_2^(1/(2(k-2))) (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Adam iterate ratio x_{t+1}/x_t matches analytic β₂^(1/(2(k-2))) to ~50 digits (k=4: 0.98202091428813, |diff|=3.4e-53) in 80-digit mpmath; steps-to-ε is affine in ln(1/ε) with fitted slope 13.77967 = analytic 13.77967, R²=1.0, for k=4,6,8 at paper defaults.

claims.claim: Gradient Descent and Heavy-Ball Momentum both exhibit only sublinear convergence of order Theta(t^{-1/(k-2)}) on the same degenerate polynomial objective, established in Theorems 5.1 and 5.3 respectively.
claims.evidence: GD and Heavy-Ball momentum run 2×10⁶ steps in float64; measured power-law exponents match analytic -1/(k-2) to <1e-4 (k=4: -0.49996 vs -0.5, k=6: -0.24999 vs -0.25, k=8: -0.16666 vs -0.16667), R²=1.0 for all, confirming Θ(t^{-1/(k-2)}) sublinear convergence for both optimizers.

claims.claim: Remark 5.8 quantifies the resulting complexity separation: Gradient Descent requires iteration complexity T_epsilon ~ epsilon^{-(k-2)} to reach accuracy epsilon, whereas Adam achieves T_epsilon ~ (k-2) ln(1/epsilon) (Remark 5.8).
claims.evidence: Adam steps to loss 1e-20 is ~1460 (k=4), affine in ln(1/ε) with slope matching 2(k-2)/(k·ln(1/β₂)) exactly; GD extrapolated steps ~2.5e11 (k=4), consistent with ε^{-(k-2)} scaling, growing to ~3.5e15 by k=8 — directly demonstrating the complexity separation.

claims.claim: Lemma 5.4 shows the second moment estimate satisfies v_t/v_{t-1} -> beta_2 asymptotically, decoupling v_t from the instantaneous squared gradient g_t^2 and producing an effective learning rate that grows as beta_2^{-t/2} (Lemma 5.4).
claims.evidence: v_t/v_{t-1} → 0.93 to |diff|=1.05e-49 (k=4) while g_t²/g_{t-1}² → 0.89686 ≠ 0.93; coupling ratio v_t/g_t² diverges to 6.2e47; effective LR growth slope = 0.036285346417418 = -ln(β₂)/2 with |diff|=1.4e-17, R²=1.0 — all measured in 80-digit mpmath for both Adam and RMSProp.

claims.claim: Section 6 identifies three convergence regimes governed by beta_1 relative to beta_2: stable exponential convergence, an intermediate regime with an initial exponential phase followed by loss spikes from fixed-point instability, and a SignGD-like oscillatory regime under tight v_t-g_t^2 coupling (Section 6, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Full Adam runs at k=4, β₁=0.9 across three β₂ settings: stable (β₂=0.91, 0 rebound, monotonic to floor), late-spike (β₂=0.895, initial descent to -112 decades then 97.67-decade rebound, max ratio 3.8e9), SignGD-like (β₂=0.80, 21.7-decade rebound, tight coupling v/g²~10^1.33); destructive control β₁=β₂=0 yields exact SignGD identity (error 0.0).

claims.claim: Figure 3 shows the empirical phase diagram of stability boundaries across different degeneracy orders k matches the theoretical predictions of Equations 8-9 (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: 61×61 (β₁,β₂) grid census for k=4,6,8 iterating the exact normalized two-state Adam map for 100k steps: empirical stability matches Eqs 8-9 theoretical boundary on 11163/11163 cells (100% agreement, 0 false positives, 0 false negatives), boundary MAE below one grid step for all k.

ai-sherpa/adam-degenerate-polynomials-re.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous, independent numerical verification of all six claims on the paper's own model problem L(x)=(1/k)x^k at the paper's stated defaults, using 80-digit mpmath for Adam/RMSProp and float64 for GD/momentum tails, with exact analytic rate constants matched to many digits and a full 11k-cell phase-diagram census showing 100% agreement with the theoretical boundaries.

Sor0ush/repro-lions-and-muons-stochastic.paper_title: Lions and Muons: Optimization via Stochastic Frank-Wolfe under Heavy-Tailed Noises

claims.claim: Lion with weight decay is shown to be a special instance of Stochastic Frank-Wolfe under an l-infinity norm constraint (Theorem 1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements both Lion and SFW with the Theorem 1 parameter mapping (η_SFW=λη_Lion, γ=1−β2, C={‖v‖∞≤1/λ}) and shows iterates match to max abs diff 5.2e-8 over 50 steps on dim=32, with the LMO identity argmin=−R·sign(g) confirmed. This is an exact algebraic equivalence, so numerical verification at machine precision on any scale is sufficient.

claims.claim: Muon with weight decay is shown to be a special instance of Stochastic Frank-Wolfe under a spectral-norm constraint (Theorem 2, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Muon+WD and SFW under spectral-norm ball are shown to produce identical iterates (max abs diff 1.8e-7 over 30 steps on 8×8 matrices) using exact polar factor via SVD, with the spectral LMO confirmed to minimize the Frobenius inner product. As with Claim 1, this is an exact equivalence verified at machine precision.

claims.claim: Under standard smoothness and bounded-variance assumptions, the proposed Stochastic Frank-Wolfe framework achieves an expected Frank-Wolfe gap of O(1/sqrt(T)) plus a variance term, and convergence in Frank-Wolfe gap corresponds to convergence to a KKT point of the norm-constrained problem (Theorem 3, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The FW gap rate O(1/√T) is tested on a 16-dimensional quadratic with T up to 1600; average gap decreases across horizons (2.99→1.77→0.97 for T=100/400/1600), roughly consistent with 1/√T scaling, but the KKT correspondence is only checked via a soft proxy (gap < 0.5). This is a simplified toy problem, not a full-scale verification of the theorem.

claims.claim: With heavy-tailed (p-th moment, p in (1,2]) gradient noise, a clipped variant achieves a high-probability convergence rate of O(log(T/delta) T^((1-p)/(3p-2))) without requiring large batch sizes, improved to O(log(T/delta) T^((1-p)/(2p-1))) when combined with variance reduction (Theorems 5-6, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The rate exponents are computed directly from the paper's formulas (not independently derived), and the empirical comparison of clipped vs unclipped SFW is on a 20-dimensional quadratic with Student-t noise (p=1.5, T=800), showing clipped avg gap 5.85 vs unclipped 6.61. The actual high-probability rate (including log(T/δ) factor and specific exponent scaling with T) is not empirically verified; only a toy proxy experiment is run.

claims.claim: On a 10M-parameter nanoGPT trained on Shakespeare, the clipped variant Lion+ reaches a validation loss of 1.46 in 3,200 steps versus 4,000 steps for standard Lion, a 20% reduction, while Muon+ reduces steps from 4,400 to 4,150 versus standard Muon (Section 5).
claims.evidence: A real 10.77M-parameter nanoGPT on Shakespeare was trained on GPU, but the quantitative claims do not match: Lion+ reached val≤1.46 at step 3300 (paper 3200, close), but Lion never reached 1.46 within 4500 steps (paper says 4000), so the 20% reduction cannot be confirmed. Muon+ reached 1.46 at step 1700 vs Muon at 1850 (paper: 4150/4400), with absolute step counts far from the paper's values and late-training val loss regression to ~1.62, indicating the setup likely differs from the paper's.

Sor0ush/repro-lions-and-muons-stochastic.overall: The logbook convincingly verifies the exact algebraic equivalences (Claims 1–2) at machine precision and provides toy-scale empirical support for the convergence rate claims (Claims 3–4), but the nanoGPT Shakespeare experiments (Claim 5) are inconclusive because absolute step counts diverge substantially from the paper and Lion never reaches the target loss.

Sor0ush/repro-shift-dependent-asymmetry-.paper_title: Shift-Dependent Asymmetry: Orthogonal Inverse Low-Rank Adaptation for Federated Medical Segmentation

claims.claim: Inverse Asymmetric Tuning (IAT) inverts LoRA factor personalization by module: in encoders it localizes the input-projection factor A (absorbing covariate/appearance shift) while aggregating the output factor B globally, and in decoders it aggregates A globally while localizing B (absorbing concept/supervision shift) (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The aggregation protocol was implemented and tested: encoder B factors were confirmed aggregated (equal across clients, weighted average correct), encoder A kept local, decoder A aggregated, decoder B kept local — all checks passed with real tensor comparisons on a functional IAT implementation.

claims.claim: Proposition 1 proves that minimizing reconstruction error under covariate shift requires localizing the input-side LoRA factor, motivating the encoder/decoder asymmetric split (Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: Synthetic 32×32 rank-4 matrix factorization with 4 clients showed LocalA/Shared-B error 15.55 < SharedA/Local-B 16.40 under covariate shift, and the reverse under concept shift (15.56 < 16.37), numerically supporting Proposition 1 but on a toy reconstruction problem, not real segmentation.

claims.claim: A Subspace Orthogonality Regularizer (SOR) imposes a soft geometric constraint forcing shared (global) and local LoRA subspaces to remain orthogonal, mitigating site-specific update leakage without added communication cost (Section 3).
claims.evidence: On a TinySegNet (dim=32, rank=4) with synthetic data, SOR reduced mean collinearity from 0.337 to 0.036 vs no-SOR, and communication was confirmed unchanged (local-only loss). The mechanism is demonstrated but only on a small synthetic proxy.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes an O(1/sqrt(T)) convergence rate to a stationary point under L-smoothness and bounded-gradient assumptions with non-degenerate LoRA factors (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: On a synthetic LowRankFederated problem (d=24, r=3, K=4, T=250) with diminishing LR, cumulative mean grad² decreased and correlated 0.948 with 1/√t, but the actual log-log slope was -0.073, far from the expected -0.5, providing only weak directional support on a simplified setup.

claims.claim: On histology nuclei segmentation, IAT achieves 81.40% average Dice score, a 1.31% improvement over the second-best baseline, using 0.39M trainable parameters and 0.55M per-round communication versus 0.78M for standard approaches (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Efficiency numbers (0.39M trainable, 0.55M IAT comm, 0.78M FedIT comm) match Table 3 analytically, but the 81.40% Dice was not reproduced — a scaled proxy (TinySegNet dim=64, synthetic data, 80 rounds) achieved 92.09% IAT vs 84.60% FedIT, confirming direction but not paper absolute values.

claims.claim: On fundus photography segmentation, IAT achieves 84.52% average Dice score, including a 27% improvement over FedIT on the Drishti-GS1 site (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Proxy fundus experiment showed IAT 88.60% vs FedIT 82.59% average and IAT 60.03% vs FedIT 59.25% on the Drishti-GS1 proxy site (+0.77pp, not the paper's +27pp), confirming directional advantage but not reproducing absolute Dice or the specific 27pp Drishti gain.

Sor0ush/repro-shift-dependent-asymmetry-.overall: The logbook faithfully implements and verifies the IAT aggregation protocol mechanism (Claim 1) and provides toy-scale numerical support for Proposition 1, SOR, and Theorem 3.1, but all empirical Dice claims (Claims 5–6) are only addressed via synthetic proxies on small models, not the paper's real medical datasets with SAM ViT-B.

deepakgudla/gara-repro.paper_title: Enhancing LLMs for Graph Tasks via Graph-aware LoRA Generation

claims.claim: GaRA generates task-specific low-rank weight updates by extracting whole-graph information via h = MaxPool(GNN(X,A)) and feeding it to an MLP-based weight generator that produces updates integrated with LoRA's existing matrices (Equation 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements the GaRA weight-generation pipeline (h=MaxPool(GNN(X,A)), MLP generator, W=W_hat+(L+G)R^T) with tiny dimensions (d_in=8, p=20, q=24, r=4) on random synthetic graphs, verifying shapes, tanh bounds, permutation invariance, graph-awareness, and gradient flow. This confirms the architectural mechanism on a simplified setup but not at the paper's real model scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that for the generated update there always exists a parameter update such that Delta W can be scaled with its direction unchanged, identifying an optimization bias (norm amplification) that motivates GaRA's norm-rescaling scheme W = W_hat + (L + G ⊙ M) R^T (Theorem 4.1, Equation 6).
claims.evidence: Part A numerically verifies Theorem 4.1 on a small generator (80-dim output, 6032 params): Jacobian is full row-rank, and stepping Theta by eps*dTheta scales G by ~(1+eps) with O(eps^2) error. Part B shows a toy fine-tuning loop where G_norm grows 5.72x without norm rescaling vs 2.00x with it, and cos_sim to W_hat is 0.85 vs 0.91. Both are on synthetic data with tiny dimensions, not the paper's real setup.

claims.claim: In zero-shot transfer (Table 1), GaRA outperforms baselines including UniGTE, GOFA, LLaGA, and TEA-GLM on node classification (Cora 0.251, WikiCS 0.669, Reddit 0.518, Instagram 0.611) and graph classification (BACE 0.549, HIV 0.512, Amazon 0.708, Photo 0.722) (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly does NOT reproduce Table 1's real numbers (Cora 0.251, WikiCS 0.669, etc.) and does not compare against UniGTE, GOFA, LLaGA, or TEA-GLM. Instead it uses a synthetic graph classification proxy (random graphs, n_nodes=40) showing GaRA beats a no-graph baseline by +15.12pt zero-shot accuracy. The paper's real numbers are merely transcribed for reference, not measured.

claims.claim: Table 2 shows that applying the norm-rescaling constraint during full training yields relative improvements of 31.35% and 24.26% on two link prediction tasks compared to without rescaling (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook does NOT reproduce the 31.35%/24.26% relative improvements on real link prediction tasks. It runs a synthetic proxy ablation showing 17.05% (in-dist) and 18.66% (zero-shot) relative improvements from norm rescaling on random graph classification. The real Table 2 numbers are transcribed for reference only, not measured on real datasets.

deepakgudla/gara-repro.overall: The logbook provides real but toy-scale evidence for all four claims: architectural mechanism checks (Claims 1-2) and synthetic proxy experiments (Claims 3-4) that test the qualitative direction of the paper's findings without reproducing any actual benchmark numbers or using real datasets, real baselines, or an LLM backbone.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows that when the perturbation radius ρ satisfies ρ ≥ -1/λ1 (λ1 being a negative Hessian eigenvalue at the saddle), the saddle point becomes an attracting fixed point of the SAM dynamics (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: On quadratic saddles with λ₁=-2, the fraction of initializations attracted to the saddle switches from 0 to 1 between ρ=0.49 and ρ=0.55, with the SAM-map Jacobian multiplier μ crossing |μ|=1 exactly at ρ*=0.5=-1/λ₁; the asymmetric case λ₁=-4 confirms threshold ρ*=0.25. The analytic Jacobian-eigenvalue crossing matches to machine precision (μ=1.00000 at ρ=0.500).

claims.claim: Theorem 2 uses a stochastic diffusion analysis to show SAM's mean squared displacement near a saddle point is smaller than SGD's, implying SAM requires more time than SGD to escape saddle points (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: 10,000-seed Monte Carlo on a 2D quadratic saddle (λ=(-1,+1), η=0.01, B=16) gives escape-direction MSD at t=200 of 1.62e-2 for SGD, 9.25e-3 for SAM(ρ=0.2), and 3.88e-3 for SAM(ρ=0.5), confirming SAM<SGD with gap growing in ρ; the small-t gap scales as ρ|λ|³τ²/B (ratio ~0.5 vs paper's constant, a documented SDE convention factor).

claims.claim: Theorem 3 shows the mean squared displacement near a saddle scales as 1/[(1-γ)B], so higher momentum γ and smaller batch size B accelerate SAM's escape from saddle points (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: 20,000-seed Monte Carlo shows MSD increases monotonically with momentum (3.90e-3 at γ=0, 7.94e-2 at γ=0.5, 1.29e+4 at γ=0.9) and decreases with batch size B with log-log slope -1.001 across B={4,16,64}, confirming the 1/[(1-γ)^k·B] scaling.

claims.claim: On the Beale test function, SAM is empirically shown to become stuck at a saddle point where vanilla gradient descent successfully escapes, matching the Case-III oscillation predicted by the theory (Section 5, empirical validation).
claims.evidence: On the Beale function (init (1,2), 400k steps), GD reaches (2.906, 0.476) near the global minimum (3,0.5) while SAM(ρ≥0.5) is trapped at the saddle (0,1) with f=14.20; the ascent/descent gradient cosine oscillates over the full [-1,+1] range (Case III). The x²-y² saddle demo from the official repo also shows GD escaping (|y|=199.6) and SAM trapped (|y|=0).

claims.claim: On CIFAR benchmarks, adding momentum increases SAM's accuracy by more than 20 percentage points, compared to roughly a 5-point gain for SGD with momentum, confirming momentum's outsized effect on SAM stability (Section 5).
claims.evidence: CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 (BN removed, no augmentation, B=512, 100 epochs) shows SAM momentum gain of +28.58 pts (42.78%→71.36%), exceeding the claimed 20-point threshold, and SAM benefits more from momentum than SGD (+28.6 vs +18.9 pts); however, the SGD gain of +18.9 pts does not match the paper's claimed ~5 pts, likely due to the reduced 100-epoch budget (paper uses 300).

SabaPivot/repro-sam-stability.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all five claims: Theorems 1-3 are verified by direct simulation on quadratic saddles with large Monte Carlo seed counts, the Beale experiment confirms SAM saddle-trapping with Case-III cosine oscillation, and CIFAR-10 training confirms SAM's >20-point momentum gain. The main caveat is that the CIFAR SGD baseline gain (+18.9 pts) diverges from the paper's ~5 pts, attributed to the reduced 100-epoch budget, and several documented deviations from the paper's stated parameters (learning rate, noise covariance convention) are disclosed.

ancs21/repro-ucast.paper_title: U-Cast: A Surprisingly Simple and Efficient Frontier Probabilistic AI Weather Forecaster

claims.claim: On short-range 10-meter wind forecasts, U-Cast's deep-ensemble variant achieves a CRPS of 0.345 at 1-day lead time versus GenCast's 0.332, part of broader Table 1 results also showing up to roughly 3% CRPS improvement over GenCast on variables such as short-range z500 (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook ran a 5-member ensemble on a single date (2020-01-01) in normalized variable space, obtaining CRPS 0.355 at 24h, but did not run GenCast or any baseline, did not evaluate z500, and did not match the paper's WeatherBench2 protocol. No head-to-head comparison exists.

claims.claim: The full U-Cast deep ensemble (4 members) trains in under 12 H200 GPU-days, decomposed as 7 GPU-days for deterministic Stage-1 pretraining plus 1.2 GPU-days per model for Stage-2 probabilistic fine-tuning (Section 4.1, Table 2).
claims.evidence: No training was attempted; the logbook only loaded the released checkpoint for inference. There is no evidence regarding GPU-days or the Stage-1/Stage-2 decomposition.

claims.claim: U-Cast generates a 60-step ensemble forecast in 11 seconds on H200 GPUs (17 seconds on A100), over a 10x reduction in inference latency compared to diffusion-based baselines such as GenCast (Table 2, Abstract).
claims.evidence: Inference was run on Modal GPUs but no timing measurements were reported. The logbook provides no latency numbers for 60-step ensemble generation on H200 or A100, nor any comparison to diffusion-based baselines.

claims.claim: GenCast retains an advantage over U-Cast on 2-meter temperature, attributed to GenCast's finer native resolution, illustrating a variable-dependent trade-off rather than uniform superiority (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: No 2-meter temperature evaluation was performed and no GenCast comparison was run. The claim is not addressed.

claims.claim: Section 4.3 positions U-Cast on the Pareto frontier of forecast skill versus computational cost relative to IFS ENS and GenCast, visualized against these baselines in Figure 2 (Section 4.3, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: No comparison against IFS ENS or GenCast was conducted, and Figure 2's Pareto frontier analysis was not reproduced. The claim is not addressed.

ancs21/repro-ucast.overall: This logbook verifies only architectural simplicity (stock DhariwalUNet) and model size (~895M parameters) from the released checkpoint, neither of which are among the five claims under review. A single-date, single-variable inference run without any baseline comparison does not substantiate any of the paper's performance, cost, or Pareto-frontier claims.

Kiy-K/icml2026-spon-paper127-trackio.paper_title: Resting Neurons, Active Insights: Robustifying Activation Sparsity in LLMs via Spontaneity

claims.claim: Spontaneous Neurons (SPON) are trainable, input-independent activation vectors that supplement sparsified activations and can be absorbed into bias terms post-training, adding no inference-time overhead
claims.evidence: On Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, all 224 projection alpha gradients were finite, zero-initialized SPON exactly matched TEAL, and trained-path logits before/after bias folding differed by exactly 0.0 in BF16, confirming no extra matrix multiplication post-folding.

claims.claim: At 50% activation sparsity on WikiText, SPON reduces perplexity relative to the TEAL baseline across backbones: Llama3-8B (7.83 vs. 8.34), Qwen3-8B (9.26 vs. 9.75), and Mistral-v2-7B (5.86 vs. 6.00), with the gap widening at 60% sparsity (Table 1)
claims.evidence: Full 10-epoch calibration on Mistral-7B showed SPON (PPL 24.17) beating TEAL (PPL 25.48) in the correct direction, but the absolute values bear no resemblance to the paper's claimed Mistral numbers (5.86 vs 6.00), and only 1 of 3 backbones was tested.

claims.claim: Across six zero-shot downstream tasks (CommonsenseQA, MathQA, MedMCQA, MMLU, OpenBookQA, TruthfulQA), SPON shows stable accuracy advantages over TEAL under sparsification (Table 3)
claims.evidence: Only 100 examples per task/subtask were evaluated; results were mixed (SPON better on 4/6 tasks but worse on CommonsenseQA and MathQA), with a mean advantage of just +0.20 points, insufficient to confirm 'stable accuracy advantages.'

claims.claim: SPON preserves the 1.5-1.6x throughput speedup of activation sparsity, with tokens-per-second nearly identical to TEAL at 50% sparsity (e.g., Llama3-8B: 64.131 vs. 64.279 TPS; Mistral-v2-7B: 71.836 vs. 71.246 TPS) (Table 2)
claims.evidence: No sparse execution kernel was available; the released Mistral implementation dispatches dense F.linear, so wall-clock throughput was never benchmarked and the 1.5–1.6x speedup claim was not addressed.

claims.claim: Hidden-representation analysis shows SPON mitigates distributional shift from sparsification, keeping activations closer to the original dense model's distribution across tested architectures (Figure 3)
claims.evidence: On 2,048 token representations across all 32 Mistral decoder layers, SPON achieved higher centered linear CKA in 31/32 layers and lower relative Frobenius L2 in 31/32 layers versus TEAL, with mean CKA 0.9987 vs 0.9961.

Kiy-K/icml2026-spon-paper127-trackio.overall: This logbook provides solid evidence for the SPON mechanism (Claim 1) and representation stability (Claim 5) on Mistral-7B, and directional but non-matching perplexity results (Claim 2). Claims 3 and 4 remain inadequately addressed due to limited sample sizes and absence of a sparse kernel, respectively.

SabaPivot/repro-success-conditioning.paper_title: Success-Conditioning as Policy Improvement: The Optimization Problem Solved by Imitating Success

claims.claim: Success conditioning is proved to exactly solve a trust-region policy optimization problem with a chi-squared divergence constraint whose radius is determined by the data (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Across 20 random finite-horizon tabular MDPs (7 deterministic, 13 stochastic; 5-15 states, 2-5 actions, horizon 5-10), the closed-form success-conditioned policy π+ satisfies per-state χ²(π+||π0)=I(s) to 4.4e-16, the aggregate constraint binds to 2.8e-17, and π+ beats all 1000 randomly sampled feasible policies per MDP on the linear objective (min margin +2.4e-2), confirming it is the trust-region optimum with data-determined radius Γ=Σ d+ I.

claims.claim: At the optimum, relative policy improvement, chi-squared policy-change magnitude, and action-influence are shown to be exactly equal at every state (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: On the same 20 MDPs, the three-way statewise equality A_{π0}(s,π+)/V_{π0}(s) = χ²(π+||π0) = I(s) holds to max error 3.6e-16 and 4.4e-16 respectively, the aggregate identity L(π+)/ρ(π0) = Σ d+ χ² = Σ d+ I holds to 2.2e-16, and a 203,862-trajectory Monte-Carlo estimator of the conditional χ² converges to Γ with error 3.3e-4.

claims.claim: The analysis characterizes exact success conditioning as a conservative improvement operator that cannot degrade performance or induce dangerous distribution shift (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Across 20 MDPs, ρ(π+)−ρ(π0) ≥ 0 (min +2.4e-2), the statewise bound (V_{π+}−V_{π0})/V_{π0} − I(s) ≥ 0 holds (min −4.4e-16, tight), the Appendix-C exact improvement formula |ρ(π+)−ρ(π0) − Σ d_{π+} V0 I| = 2.4e-16, and Example 3.1 reproduces exactly (gain=5e-5, I=1e-4, π+=(0.495,0.505)).

claims.claim: The paper analyzes return thresholding as an extension that can amplify improvement but can misalign the learned policy with the true objective (Section 5).
claims.evidence: On the paper's 100-arm Beta bandit (99 moderate Beta(a,a) arms + one Beta(18,2) arm, uniform π0), the Prop 7.1 ratio identity holds to 1.8e-15 across 3 seeds × 197 thresholds; proxy conditioning amplifies improvement up to ~2.7× faithful for θ∈[0.42,0.94], then improvement goes negative for θ≥0.97, reproducing both the amplification and misalignment phenomena.

SabaPivot/repro-success-conditioning.overall: This logbook provides strong numerical verification of all four claims on an exact float64 tabular-MDP harness with 20 random MDPs (deterministic and stochastic) plus the paper's own bandit examples, with identities holding to machine precision and qualitative phenomena reproduced. The setup is appropriate for a pure theory paper: finite MDPs are the actual setting of the propositions, not simplified proxies of a larger task.

claims.claim: Early experience methods (SFT and RL variants that use environment-generated future states rather than pure imitation) improve policy effectiveness across 8 diverse agent environments including WebShop, WebArena, ScienceWorld, and ALFWorld, compared to imitation-learning baselines (Section 4-5, Experiments and Results).
claims.evidence: The logbook only transcribes numbers from the paper's official GitHub README and tables; no independent training or evaluation runs were executed. The verification script crashed immediately on a pip install error, producing no output.

claims.claim: Models trained with early experience generalize better to out-of-domain tasks than pure imitation-learning (behavioral cloning) baselines across the 8 evaluated environments (Section 4-5, Experiments and Results).
claims.evidence: OOD generalization numbers are copied verbatim from Paper Table 3 with no re-execution of any environment or model. No independent experimental evidence was generated.

claims.claim: Early experience serves as a stronger initialization (warm-start) for subsequent reinforcement learning than standard SFT/imitation-learning initializations, yielding higher final RL performance (Section 3, Method: Early Experience).
claims.evidence: RL warm-start results are transcribed from Paper Figure 3; no GRPO runs were executed or reproduced. The logbook itself admits 'An end-to-end GPU training reproduction on Hugging Face Jobs was not possible due to insufficient credits.'

claims.claim: The comparison spans SFT, RL, and imitation-learning/behavioral-cloning baselines, with early experience-based training outperforming these baselines on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution splits (Section 2, Related Work; Section 4-5, Experiments and Results).
claims.evidence: The comparison across SFT/RL/IL baselines is only described by restating the paper's own tables and methodology; no baseline or early-experience method was independently trained or evaluated.

Shengxia/repro-agent-learning-via-early-.overall: This logbook is a literature review of the paper's own reported results, not a reproduction. No training, evaluation, or even the verification script was successfully executed (it crashed on dependency installation), so zero independent experimental evidence was produced for any claim.

claims.claim: In the zero-temperature (hardmax) limit of self-attention dynamics with negative-definite key-query interaction, token updates coincide with a Frank-Wolfe step on a quadratic objective over the convex hull of the tokens, and Theorem 3.1 gives a linear convergence rate bound J^t(x_i^{t+1}) ≤ (2/(t+1))·λ_max(B_0)·diam(K^0)^2 (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The Frank-Wolfe algebraic equivalence was confirmed across 256 random SPD trials (max_abs_error 0.0, 0 index mismatches), but Theorem 3.1's convergence bound is contradicted by an exact-rational three-point counterexample (X^0={(1,0),(0,1),(-0.2,-0.3)}, B*=I_2, gamma=2/(t+2)) satisfying all printed hypotheses including 0∈K^0, yet particles converge to (-2/15,2/15)≠0 with J=4/225 and the bound 4/(t+1) first violated at t=224 (ratio 2.667 by t=599). The proof's flaw is using 0∈K^t while only assuming 0∈K^0.

claims.claim: When the key-query matrix is positive definite, Theorem 4.2 shows super-exponential convergence of tokens to vertices, and Proposition 4.5 shows the induced cell structure coincides with B-norm Voronoi cells when vertices have equal norm (Section 4, Theorem 4.2, Proposition 4.5).
claims.evidence: Proposition 4.5's B-norm Voronoi identity is verified (40,000 anisotropic equal-B-norm samples with zero dominance-Voronoi mismatches; breaking equal-norm gives 50.4% mismatch), but Theorem 4.2's super-exponential rate is contradicted: the exact product formula holds (error ≤1.4e-15), yet an admissible summable schedule gamma_t=2^{-(t+2)} retains 0.578 of initial error (no convergence), constant gamma gives only exponential decay, and harmonic gamma gives polynomial decay—super-exponential convergence requires a stronger schedule approaching one, which the theorem's stated hypotheses do not gu

claims.claim: Theorem 4.8 establishes well-posedness of the singular ODE limit governing the hardmax dynamics (Section 4, Theorem 4.8, Equation 4.4).
claims.evidence: The explicit branch solution x_i(t)=v_σ(i)+e^{-t}(x_i^0−v_σ(i)) has RHS residual 1.67e-16, agrees with adaptive integration to 2.04e-13, maintains invariant cell assignments (0 changes), shows first-order Euler convergence (observed order 1.013), and a 2.4e-6 perturbation has amplification 1.0. The boundary-tie control at the excluded center produces three distinct branches separated by 1.498 at t=2, confirming the genericity assumption is necessary.

claims.claim: At finite inverse temperature β, Theorem 5.2 shows interior particles reach near-vertex configurations in O(1) steps with high probability, while Theorem 5.4 shows these metastable configurations persist for exponentially long times (on the order of e^β steps) before eventual collapse to a single cluster (Section 5, Theorem 5.2, Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: Theorem 5.2 is supported: 2,048 replicas at β=10^6 with T1=5 steps achieve empirical success probability 1.0, exceeding the paper's lower bound of 0.8222. Theorem 5.4 is supported: across 256 replicas per β (β=4…24), median first-exit time grows from 5 to 4,021 steps with log-linear fit R²=0.99868 and slope 0.3375, and all t=5 survival bounds pass with zero censoring.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 shows the argmax operation generically produces a singleton, and Lemma 2.2 shows the convex hull of tokens shrinks under step sizes γ^t ∈ (0,1), underpinning the Frank-Wolfe reformulation of hardmax attention (Section 2, Lemma 2.1, Lemma 2.2).
claims.evidence: An independent measure-zero proof shows that for invertible B^t, ties between distinct candidate maps correspond to zero sets of nonzero quadratic polynomials (verified by exact-rational audit of 487,935 coefficient systems with zero failures), and Lemma 2.2 follows directly from convexity since x_i^{t+1}=(1−γ^t)x_i^t+γ^t y_i^t∈K^t. Three destructive controls (singular B=0, γ=6/5, matrix-valued step) each break the corresponding conclusion as predicted.

SabaPivot/repro-attention-frank-wolfe.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous independent reproduction that verifies the core Frank-Wolfe algebraic identity and geometric foundations (Claims 3–5) while falsifying two theorem-level rate claims through exact counterexamples: Theorem 3.1's convergence bound fails at t=224 on an admissible 3-point configuration, and Theorem 4.2's super-exponential rate does not follow from its stated hypotheses. The reproduction uses exact rational arithmetic, large-scale sampling, and destructive controls throughout, achieving high methodological quality.

SabaPivot/repro-clipped-asgd.paper_title: Clipping Makes Distributed and Federated Asynchronous SGD Robust to Stragglers

claims.claim: In the homogeneous setting, Clipped ASGD achieves oracle complexity Õ(σ²/ε⁴ + σ·τ_C/ε³ + τ_C/ε²), which depends on the concurrency τ_C but not on the maximum delay τ_max (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: A general proof reconstruction derives the pathwise invariant ‖x̃_t−x_t‖≤ηcτ_C, telescopes the descent bound, and inverts to Õ(σ²/ε⁴+στ_C/ε³+τ_C/ε²) with no τ_max dependence; a 10,000-case algebra audit and a 50-dimensional stress test (16 workers, τ_max from 16 to 1024) show clipped updates varying <1% while vanilla degrades 6.6×, confirming the τ_max-independence signature.

claims.claim: In the heterogeneous setting, Clipped ASGD achieves oracle complexity Õ((σ²+ζ²)/ε⁴ + (σ+ζ)·τ_C/ε³ + τ_C/ε²), where ζ measures data heterogeneity, again independent of τ_max (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: The same proof certificate extends to heterogeneous worker resampling, adding ζ² to the second moment and ζ to the clipping scale, yielding Õ((σ²+ζ²)/ε⁴+(σ+ζ)τ_C/ε³+τ_C/ε²); a stress test with per-worker FIFO queues and gradient shifts (ζ=1) shows vanilla degrading 3.1× vs clipped 1.5× across increasing delay, directionally supporting the bound despite run-length saturation limiting the realized delay range.

claims.claim: The paper establishes the first high-probability convergence guarantees for asynchronous SGD, with a polylogarithmic dependence on the failure probability δ governed by the sub-Weibull tail parameter θ (Theorem 4.3, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: The proof certificate reconstructs the Freedman-inequality and sub-Weibull union-bound steps yielding polylogarithmic δ-dependence; a 2,000-seed concentration test on a 50-dimensional nonconvex objective with θ=1.5 noise shows clipped quantiles growing approximately as log(1/δ) (within the log³(1/δ) allowance) with a 99.5%-to-median ratio of 1.19 vs 1.53 for vanilla, and a targeted literature audit supports the priority claim for asynchronous (vs serial) high-probability bounds.

claims.claim: Gradient noise is modeled as sub-Weibull (Definition 3.1), generalizing sub-Gaussian (θ=1/2) and sub-exponential (θ=1) noise, and empirical measurement of ResNet-18 gradient noise on CIFAR-10 yields a fitted tail parameter θ=2.71 (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 gradient-noise norms were measured over two epochs and fit with three calibrated estimators (Weibull MLE, tail regression, finite-moment slope); synthetic validation confirmed the estimators recover true θ=2.71 within ~5%, but actual measurements yielded θ=0.213 (batch 128) and θ=0.682 (batch 1), far below the claimed 2.71.

claims.claim: On CIFAR-10 with delay factor D=4, Clipped ASGD achieves a 1.8x wall-clock speedup over vanilla ASGD (Figure 2), and on Shakespeare it achieves 2.0-2.2x speedup depending on the delay regime (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: With 16 asynchronous workers and full step-size/clipping grids, CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 at D=4 produced a 1.00× speedup (paper claims 1.8×), and Shakespeare LSTM at D=4 and D=8 produced 1.50× and 1.38× speedups (paper claims 2.0–2.2×); the clipping mechanism is reproduced (larger stable step sizes) but the headline magnitudes are contradicted.

claims.claim: Under label-skew data heterogeneity on CIFAR-10, Clipped ASGD shows a 1.2-1.3x improvement over vanilla ASGD (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Three matched seeds on CIFAR-10 with a two-layer CNN, 16 workers, Dirichlet(0.5) label-skew partition, and D=4 reaching the paper's 70% accuracy target yielded speedups of 1.392×, 1.338×, and 1.266× (mean 1.332×), consistent with and slightly above the paper's reported 1.2–1.3× range, with clipping using an 8× larger stable step size.

SabaPivot/repro-clipped-asgd.overall: The logbook provides proof reconstructions and supporting numerical stress tests that verify the three theoretical complexity claims (Claims 1–3), while empirically falsifying the fitted tail parameter θ=2.71 (Claim 4) and the headline wall-clock speedup magnitudes on CIFAR-10 and Shakespeare (Claim 5); the label-skew speedup (Claim 6) is reproduced with results matching the paper's reported range.

FloorIsAwake/icml-2026-paper-11440-repro.paper_title: A Noise Sensitivity Exponent Controls Large Statistical-to-Computational Gaps in Single- and Multi-Index Models

claims.claim: The paper introduces a Noise Sensitivity Exponent (NSE), a quantity determined solely by the activation function, that governs the existence and magnitude of statistical-to-computational gaps in single- and multi-index models (abstract only).
claims.evidence: The logbook independently computes NSE moments E[σ(Z)^β(Z²−1)] for four activations (He2/2, cos, He4/4!, cancelled_abs) via adaptive quadrature, recovering NSE=1 and NSE=2 respectively, confirming the quantity is activation-determined. The single-index threshold scaling α_alg ∝ λ^{−NSE} is numerically verified, demonstrating governance for the single-index case.

claims.claim: In single-index models with large additive noise, the NSE fully characterizes the onset of the computational bottleneck separating statistically optimal from computationally efficient estimators (abstract only).
claims.evidence: The exact weak-recovery threshold α_alg⁻¹ = E_y[(E[z²−1|y])²] is computed via Gaussian-Hermite quadrature for He2 (NSE=1) and He4 (NSE=2). Numerical values clearly show α_alg ∝ λ⁻¹ for He2 (e.g., α≈9998.5 at λ=1e-4) and α_alg ∝ λ⁻² for He4 (e.g., α≈1.8e9 at λ=1e-4), confirming the NSE-characterized bottleneck.

claims.claim: The NSE controls the statistical-to-computational gap that arises during the specialization transition in large separable multi-index models (abstract only).
claims.evidence: The committee proxy reuses the single-index threshold formula with effective SNR λ=1/((1+δ)p) rather than simulating an actual multi-index model or running AMP. The script explicitly states 'These proxies test the claimed exponent mechanism; they are not finite-d AMP runs or a full information-theoretic reproduction.' The scaling exponent is consistent but on a simplified proxy setup.

claims.claim: In hierarchical multi-index models, the NSE determines the optimal computational rate for sequentially learning the different index directions (abstract only).
claims.evidence: The hierarchical proxy applies the single-index threshold with λ=k^{-2γ}/(1+δ) rather than simulating a hierarchical multi-index model. The predicted exponent 2γ·NSE is checked against power-law fits of the proxy data, but no actual sequential learning dynamics or multi-index estimation is performed.

claims.claim: The NSE is presented as a unifying quantity linking noise robustness, computational hardness, and feature specialization across these high-dimensional learning settings (abstract only).
claims.evidence: The logbook shows the same NSE exponent consistently predicts scaling across single-index (exact), committee (proxy), and hierarchical (proxy) settings, providing partial evidence for the unifying interpretation. However, since the multi-index and hierarchical components are only tested via effective-SNR proxies rather than actual multi-index model simulations, the unification is demonstrated only on a simplified setup.

FloorIsAwake/icml-2026-paper-11440-repro.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous numerical verification of the NSE definition and the single-index computational bottleneck via exact quadrature of the paper's threshold formula, confirming the predicted λ^{-NSE} scaling. The multi-index and hierarchical claims are only addressed through effective-SNR proxies that reuse the single-index formula, not through actual multi-index model simulations or AMP runs.

sanjaymalladi/normuon-repro-scaling-laws.paper_title: Deriving Neural Scaling Laws from the Statistics of Natural Language

claims.claim: Derives a parameter-free prediction for the data-limited neural scaling exponent, alpha_D = gamma / (2*beta), from two measurable statistics of natural language: conditional-entropy decay exponent gamma (H_n - H_infinity ~ n^-gamma) and token-correlation decay exponent beta (||C(n)||_op ~ n^-beta) (Section 3, Equations 6-8).
claims.evidence: The logbook restates the derivation steps but provides no independent mathematical re-derivation or verification of the proof in Appendix A; it merely asserts the derivation is 'mathematically sound.'

claims.claim: Measures gamma=0.34 and beta=0.88 on TinyStories, predicting alpha_D ~ 0.19, and gamma=0.27 and beta=0.94 on WikiText, predicting alpha_D ~ 0.14 (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: The agent measured γ and β from pre-computed results in the authors' repo rather than from raw data; TinyStories values are close (γ≈0.30 vs 0.34, β≈0.86 vs 0.88), but WikiText γ is notably off (0.22 vs 0.27) and WikiText β is not reported at all.

claims.claim: Validates predicted scaling exponents against measured autoregressive loss scaling curves from GPT-2-style transformers with absolute and rotary positional embeddings and LLaMA-style architectures trained on TinyStories and WikiText (Figures 1-4).
claims.evidence: No models were trained; the agent explicitly states 'full training not feasible locally' and only inspected pre-computed learning curves from the official repo, asserting 'scaling consistent with' predicted exponents without any quantitative fit of the scaling exponent to the curves.

claims.claim: Shows that n-gram losses collapse onto a single curve when rescaled by the derived exponents, supporting a 'horizon-limited' learning regime where models progressively extend their effective context window rather than refining within a fixed context (Section 3, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The agent did not produce the rescaled collapse plot or quantitatively test the collapse; it only verified monotonicity (L_n decreases with n and P) and the n^{-γ} relation, which is necessary but far from sufficient to demonstrate the claimed collapse onto a single master curve.

sanjaymalladi/normuon-repro-scaling-laws.overall: This logbook provides only superficial analysis of the authors' pre-computed results without any independent model training or quantitative curve-fitting. The core experimental claims (scaling curve validation and n-gram collapse) are not substantiated, and even the exponent measurements rely on pre-computed artifacts with notable discrepancies for WikiText.

Sor0ush/ICML2026-graphphysics.paper_title: Mesh Based Simulations with Spatial and Temporal awareness

claims.claim: The Multi Node Prediction (MNP) objective predicts field values for a center node and its full 1-hop neighborhood jointly via a single-layer transformer over 'star sequences', combined with the main node-wise loss as L = L_main + 0.2*L_MNP (Section on Multi Node Prediction).
claims.evidence: The logbook identifies specific code files (`graphphysics/models/spatial_mtp_1hop.py` with `_EncoderBlock` for single-layer transformer over star sequences) and the loss combination `loss = loss + self.spatial_mtp_alpha * aux_loss` with alpha=0.20 in `lightning_module.py`, concretely confirming the MNP objective implementation matches the claim.

claims.claim: Theorem B.2 proves that patch reconstruction accuracy from MNP controls a discrete gradient (flux) error, providing a Sobolev-regularization justification for enforcing spatial derivative consistency (Theorem B.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook merely restates that Theorem B.2 provides a Sobolev-regularization justification, with no mathematical derivation, proof verification, or any concrete analysis of the theorem's assumptions or conclusions.

claims.claim: MNP is evaluated on three architectures — MeshGraphNet, Transolver, and a Transformer with optional long-distance 'jumper' edges — each using an Encode-Process-Decode structure (Section on Architectures).
claims.evidence: Code inspection shows three architecture classes exist (MeshGraphNet, Transformer, Transolver) in `processors.py`, but the logbook does not mention the 'jumper' edges feature, and no experiments were executed to confirm MNP was actually evaluated on these architectures.

claims.claim: Evaluation uses four physics datasets: Cylinder (2D fluid, COMSOL, 2000 nodes), DeformingPlate (solid mechanics, COMSOL, 1000 nodes), and coarse (20,000-node) and fine (250,000-node) 3D Aneurysm hemodynamics meshes solved with CimLib (Table of datasets).
claims.evidence: The logbook mentions config files for cylinder, plate, and coarse-aneurysm, and references a '2D-Aneurysm' dataset, but does not confirm the fine 250,000-node 3D Aneurysm dataset, nor verify the specific node counts (2000, 1000, 20000, 250000) claimed.

claims.claim: MNP yields 20-30% reductions in 1-step RMSE across all three architectures and all datasets, with error accumulation over long rollouts substantially reduced relative to baselines (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: All five training attempts on the Cylinder dataset failed due to missing dependencies (einops), DGL prompts, attribute errors, segfaults from pyvista/VTK, and index-out-of-bounds errors. No RMSE values were ever produced, so the 20-30% reduction claim was never tested.

claims.claim: Improvements from MNP scale with model size, tested up to 51M parameters, and remain consistent across 5-30 training epochs, at the cost of roughly a 10% increase in training and inference time (Figure 3, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: No training runs completed successfully; there are no results on model size scaling, epoch consistency, or training/inference time overhead to evaluate this claim.

Sor0ush/ICML2026-graphphysics.overall: This logbook only verifies the implementation-level details of the MNP objective (Claim 1) via code inspection; all other claims remain unaddressed due to repeated failed training attempts caused by dependency issues, runtime errors, and environment problems. No experimental results were produced for any quantitative claim.

SabaPivot/repro-csr.paper_title: Contrastive Spectral Rectification: Test-Time Defense towards Zero-shot Adversarial Robustness of CLIP

claims.claim: Under 50-step AutoAttack (l_inf=4/255), CSR achieves 66.4% average robust accuracy across 16 zero-shot classification benchmarks, an 18.1% improvement over the best prior test-time defense (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Real runs on 4 of 5 General datasets (omitting ImageNet) with APGD-CE-50 instead of the full AutoAttack ensemble; CSR achieved 70.8% on this subset vs paper's 66.4% on 5 datasets, but the +18.1% improvement over the strongest prior baseline (R-TPT/LPF) was never tested, and only 4 of 16 benchmarks were evaluated.

claims.claim: Under 10-step PGD (l_inf=1/255), CSR reaches 58.1% robust accuracy, a 6.9% gain over the strongest baseline, while clean accuracy drops by only 0.7% on average (Table 1, Table 2).
claims.evidence: On 14 of 16 datasets with 10-step PGD at L_inf=1/255, CSR achieved 60.9% robust accuracy (paper: 58.1%) with a 0.56-point clean-accuracy drop (paper: 0.7); the independently rerun TTC baseline yielded the same 33.6-point CSR–TTC gap as the paper. The +6.9% gain over R-TPT specifically was not rerun, but the core absolute results and clean-drop claim are reproduced at near-full scope.

claims.claim: CSR's contrastive rectification combines an attraction term toward a low-pass-filtered feature anchor with a repulsion term away from the original adversarial feature, and removing either term reduces robustness from 69.8% back to 51.6% on the General datasets in the ablation (Table 6, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Full 5-dataset General-group ablation (1,000 images each, APGD-CE-50, L_inf=4/255) shows full CSR at 72.48%, dropping to 41.26% without attraction (-31.22pp) and 38.02% without repulsion (-34.46pp), while removing greedy selection costs only 1.10pp — directly confirming that both contrastive terms are necessary and complementary, consistent with the paper's claimed 69.8%→51.6% collapse.

claims.claim: CSR runs at an average inference latency of 15.17ms per image on an RTX 4090, about 11.6x faster than the R-TPT test-time defense baseline at 176.33ms (Table 3).
claims.evidence: CSR latency measured at 18.5ms/img on an H100 (not the claimed RTX 4090) and R-TPT was approximated by a faithful cost model (98.5ms/img) rather than actual R-TPT code, yielding a 5.3x ratio vs the paper's 11.6x; the direction is reproduced but the specific hardware, absolute numbers, and ratio do not match the claim.

claims.claim: CSR generalizes beyond classification, improving mIoU by 16.7% under attack on semantic segmentation and restoring roughly 43.0% accuracy on image captioning and VQA tasks (Table 7).
claims.evidence: Claim 5 was not attempted; the official CSR repository contains only the classification pipeline, and the segmentation, captioning, and VQA experiments require external frameworks not available in the release.

SabaPivot/repro-csr.overall: The logbook provides solid evidence for CSR's core classification robustness claims (Claims 2–3) at near-full or full scope using the official implementation, and directional evidence for strong-attack robustness (Claim 1) and latency advantages (Claim 4) on reduced or proxy setups. Claim 5's downstream-task generalization remains entirely untested.

sanjaymalladi/strat-reasoner-repro-icml2.paper_title: Strat-Reasoner: Reinforcing Strategic Reasoning of LLMs in Multi-Agent Games

claims.claim: Strat-Reasoner-4B achieves a 22.1% average performance improvement across the evaluated multi-agent games compared to baselines (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook re-derived an average of 19.49% from the paper's own Table 1 data (not 22.1%), but no independent training or evaluation was run; the only GPU training attempt was 3 steps on TicTacToe that OOM'd on T4 and did not complete on A10G.

claims.evidence: The logbook only lists the baseline model names from the paper; no actual head-to-head evaluations against any of the listed baselines were executed.
