ai-sherpa/repro-tau2-bench-oc2z7isqka.paper_title: $\tau^2$-Bench: Evaluating Conversational Agents in a Dual-Control Environment

claims.claim: tau2-bench introduces a telecom dual-control environment where both the conversational agent and simulated user can act with tools in a shared dynamic state (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: Direct AST inspection of the official `sierra-research/tau2-bench` repo confirms 13 agent-side and 30 user-side `@is_tool`-decorated methods in disjoint name sets, both mutating one shared world state (agent tools on carrier backend, user tools on customer device), with a designed single-control ablation (`llm_agent_solo` + `main_policy_solo.md`) — this is the authors' actual code, not a reimplementation.

claims.claim: The telecom domain is modeled with separate agent and user databases, 13 agent tools, 30 user tools, and 114 sampled tasks from a 2,285-task full set (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Script `claim2_counts.py` AST-parses the tool modules and TOML fixtures, confirming 13 agent tools (6 write, 6 read, 1 generic), 30 user tools (15 write, 15 read), two separate databases (`TelecomDB` with 5 plans/9 lines/4 customers vs `TelecomUserDB`), 2285 tasks in `tasks.json`, and 114 in the base split (strict subset), with all 16 automated checks passing and intent breakdown 29/36/49 matching Table 4.

claims.claim: The benchmark uses a compositional task generator that creates verifiable telecom tasks from intent and subtask components (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: AST analysis confirms `BaseTask` carries `init_funcs`/`fix_funcs`/`extra_env_assertions` matching the paper's triple, `compose_tasks()` uses `itertools.product` with `[None]` appended per group (at-most-one-subtask selection), and independently re-running the generator regenerates exactly 2285 tasks per intent (254/47/1984) when excluding one identifiable post-paper subtask; all 114 base tasks were replayed end-to-end confirming broken-after-init (114/114), no-premature-solution (114/114), and terminal-assertion-holding (114/114).

claims.claim: Agents show lower pass@1 in default dual-control telecom operation than in no-user and oracle-plan modes, isolating the cost of decentralized user coordination (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Recomputing pass@1 from the authors' released trajectory files (114 tasks × 4 trials) using the repo's own `compute_metrics` shows GPT-4.1 default 0.342 < no-user 0.515 < oracle-plan 0.728 and o4-mini default 0.421 < no-user 0.673 < oracle-plan 0.963, with the no-user-op ceiling at 0.722/0.989, isolating a 17–25 point communication/coordination cost and a 39–54 point reasoning cost; the independent open-model arm (Qwen2.5-72B, 23 tasks) honestly showed no net drop, but the effect is established from the strong-model trajectories.

claims.claim: Telecom performance declines as the number of required actions or distinct issues increases (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Recomputing pass@1 per complexity bin from raw `reward_info.reward` across 1824 simulations (4 series × 114 tasks × 4 trials) shows monotonic decline in all 8 breakdowns (Spearman rho −0.87 to −0.98), with pass@1 falling from ~0.4–0.6 at easiest bins to ~0 at hardest; three specific prose statements also reproduce: >7 actions Default pass@1=0.0263, No-User advantage shrinking from +0.34/+0.37 to +0.15/+0.09, and gpt-4.1 No-User beating o4-mini at ≥10 actions (0.179 vs 0.000).

ai-sherpa/repro-tau2-bench-oc2z7isqka.overall: This logbook provides strong verification of all five claims through direct structural analysis of the official repo (AST-parsing tools, databases, task files, generator code) and recomputation from the authors' raw per-simulation trajectories using the repo's own metric code, with 16/16 and 12/12 automated checks passing. The main limitation is that most numerical evidence derives from recomputing the authors' own released trajectories rather than fully independent agent runs, and the one independent open-model run was underpowered and showed a negative result, but the recomputations are transparent, use the repo's own binning/metric definitions, and honestly report discrepancies (14 vs 15 subtask groups, post-paper subtask drift).

claims.claim: tau^2-Bench introduces a Telecom dual-control domain formalized as a Dec-POMDP in which both the agent and user use tools in a shared dynamic environment (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Structural inspection of the official sierra-research/tau2-bench repo confirms 45 agent-side tools and 59 user-side tools acting on one shared dynamic world state, with the telecom domain registered as a first-class domain containing 114 tasks and a designed single-control ablation (llm_agent_solo).

claims.claim: The benchmark includes a compositional task generator that creates diverse, verifiable tasks from atomic components (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Independent re-running of compose_tasks() regenerates the paper's 2,285-task corpus exactly (254+47+1,984); exhaustive pairwise similarity over all 2,609,470 pairs shows 2,285/2,285 distinct signatures with 0 identical pairs and mean Jaccard 0.3038 (vs 49.98% near-duplicate rate for a 2-template control); 114/114 shipped tasks pass init→solution→assertion replay with a two-sided positive control on the checker.

claims.claim: The user simulator is coupled to the environment through tools and observable state to improve fidelity over passive-user simulations (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The claim-1 page documents 59 user-side tools in user_tools.py acting on the customer's physical device (airplane mode, roaming, SIM, APN, Wi-Fi, etc.) over the same shared world state, with the user simulator (user_simulator.py) only able to report/act via its tools and observable device state, confirming the structural coupling described in the claim.

claims.claim: Agents show substantial performance drops when moving from no-user or single-control settings to the dual-control setting (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Recomputation of the authors' own released trajectories with the repo's metric code on 114 telecom tasks × 4 trials shows GPT-4.1 dropping from 0.515 (single-control) to 0.342 (dual-control) and o4-mini from 0.673 to 0.421, both substantial 17–25 point drops; the independent Qwen2.5-72B arm (23 tasks, 1 trial) showed no net drop but is transparently reported as a small-scale negative due to reasoning bottleneck.

ai-sherpa/repro-tau2-bench-71171.overall: The logbook provides concrete, non-toy evidence supporting all four claims through structural verification of the official repo, recomputation of released GPT-4.1/o4-mini trajectories with the authors' own metric code, and 30/30 automated checks on the compositional task generator including exhaustive diversity measurement and full verifiability replay. The independent open-model arm is honestly reported as a small-scale negative that does not undermine the verification established by the authors' own full-scale runs.

Sor0ush/repro-distmatch-icml2026.paper_title: DistMatch: Adaptive Binning  via Distribution Matching for Robust Sequential Conformal Prediction

claims.claim: DistMatch recursively partitions residuals into leaves via a binary tree using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, targeting γ*-approximate local exchangeability within each leaf (Definition 5.1, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Synthetic two-regime Gaussian series (240 points, w=20, γ=0.1) produced a tree with 5 internal nodes and 6 leaves; all right-child patches satisfied KS<γ. This confirms the algorithm mechanism on a small synthetic setup, not at paper scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.4 shows the within-leaf KS diameter converges to at most 2γ under the local stationarity and patch-mixing assumption (Assumption 5.2, Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: On synthetic 3-regime Gaussian data (240 points, γ=0.1), max within-leaf KS diameter was 0.15≤0.20=2γ, with 0 triangle-inequality violations over 200 trials. This empirically checks the bound on toy data but does not constitute a proof of Theorem 5.4.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.6 establishes a coverage guarantee for DistMatch that avoids the reweighting step required by prior sequential conformal prediction methods (Section 5, Theorem 5.6).
claims.evidence: Only a code-pattern audit was performed (no banned reweighting tokens found, leaf QRF present). No experiment verified the actual coverage guarantee of Theorem 5.6; empirical coverage results from Claims 4/5 undershoot the 0.90 target at reduced scale.

claims.claim: With a random forest predictor at alpha=0.1, DistMatch attains 0.90-0.92 empirical coverage on Electricity, Solar, Wind, META and NVDA datasets, with Winkler scores such as 1.97±0.01 (Electricity) and 0.49±0.00 (NVDA) (Table 1).
claims.evidence: HF job on real datasets at reduced scale (max_calib_patches=400, max_test=800, n_trees=5) yielded mean coverage 0.811 vs paper 0.90–0.92; Winkler scores not on paper's normalized scale (e.g., Solar 356.9 vs 1.54). Real datasets but clearly reduced scope; numbers do not match.

claims.claim: With an LSTM predictor, DistMatch maintains an average 0.90 coverage across Electricity, Solar, and Wind, with Winkler scores of 1.15±0.02, 1.87±0.11, and 2.05±0.01 respectively (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Used sklearn MLPRegressor as a surrogate for the paper's Global LSTM, at reduced scale (calib=350, test=600). Mean coverage 0.786 vs paper 0.90; Winkler scores off-scale. Wrong predictor class and reduced scope prevent reproduction.

claims.claim: DistMatch's calibration cost is O(n^2 w log n) and its per-step online update cost is O(w log n), amortizing to O(Tw log n) over T steps (Table 3).
claims.evidence: Timing grid on synthetic data (n=40–100, w=20) shows calib_over_n2w roughly constant (~1.3e-4) and online time roughly flat in n, consistent with O(n²w log n) and O(w log n). Scale is small and synthetic; code-level argument supports the complexity but empirical timing is limited.

Sor0ush/repro-distmatch-icml2026.overall: The logbook confirms the DistMatch algorithm mechanism (KS binary tree, no reweighting) via code audit and small synthetic checks, but does not reproduce the paper's empirical Table 1/2 results at full scale—coverage undershoots 0.90 on all datasets and Winkler scores are off-scale. Theoretical claims (Thm 5.4, 5.6) receive only toy-scale or code-pattern checks, not rigorous verification.

arthrod/repro-mmbert-annealed-multilingu.paper_title: mmBERT: A Modern Multilingual Encoder with Annealed Language Learning

claims.claim: mmBERT is pretrained on 3 trillion tokens split across three phases: 2.3T tokens pre-training, 600B tokens mid-training for context extension, and 100B tokens in a decay phase (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Script reads released language_counts.csv and configs: mid-training 600.8B and decay 114.2B tokens match paper's 600B/100B; pretrain shows ~1989B unique tokens vs 2.3T claimed, explained by up-sampling/repetition counting. Three-phase structure with context extension (1024→8192) confirmed from configs.

claims.claim: Cascading Annealed Language Learning expands language coverage across training phases from 60 to 110 to 1,833 languages, with temperature sampling decreasing from 0.7 to 0.5 to 0.3 (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: CSV language counts: 61→110→1834 matching paper's 60→110→1833. Additionally, behavioral MLM NLL measurement across checkpoints shows languages partitioning into three arrival tiers (high-resource at pretrain, mid-tier at ext, low-resource at decay), confirming cascade structure from model behavior. Temperature 0.7/0.5/0.3 not encoded in configs but direction consistent with token proportions.

claims.claim: An inverse mask ratio schedule lowers the masking rate from 30% in pre-training to 15% in mid-training to 5% in the decay phase (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Script reads mlm_probability from released configs: mmBERT-small = 0.30/0.15/0.05 (exact match to paper's 30/15/5%); mmBERT-base = 0.25/0.15/0.05 (base pretrain uses 25% not 30%, but mid/decay match exactly and inverse direction confirmed for both sizes).

claims.claim: On GLUE, mmBERT Base scores 86.3 average versus 83.3 for XLM-R Base, and mmBERT Small scores 84.7 versus 78.3 for Multilingual MiniLM (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Ran 5/8 GLUE tasks (excluded MNLI/QQP/QNLI) with reduced 2-LR sweep, 3 epochs, maxlen 128. Relative ordering reproduces strongly (mmBERT-base 82.9 > XLM-R 76.3; mmBERT-small 79.6 > mMiniLM 67.6) but absolute scores are 3-9 pts below paper's claimed 86.3/83.3/84.7/78.3 due to excluded tasks and reduced sweep.

claims.claim: On XTREME, mmBERT Base averages 72.8 versus 70.4 for XLM-R, and on MTEB Multilingual, mmBERT Base averages 54.1 versus 52.4 for XLM-R (Table 3, Table 5).
claims.evidence: Only the XTREME classification component was addressed via scaled XNLI transfer (200k examples, 1 epoch, 9 languages): mmBERT-base 73.98 vs XLM-R 71.52 (+2.46 vs paper's +2.5 XNLI gap). MTEB Multilingual (54.1 vs 52.4) was not reproduced at all (out of budget). Full XTREME average not computed.

claims.claim: Adding low-resource languages during the decay phase yields a 68% relative increase (12.1 absolute F1 points) on Tigray despite only 100B decay-phase tokens (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Same-model ablation using released decay-mid (110 langs) vs decay-all (1833 langs) checkpoints shows Tigrinya MLM NLL drops sharply only at decay-all (base: 3.33→1.98) while controls barely move, confirming the mechanism. However, the specific claim of 68% relative increase / 12.1 F1 points on TiQuAD was not measured—MLM NLL is a proxy for TiQuAD F1.

arthrod/repro-mmbert-annealed-multilingu.overall: Claims 1-3 are verified from released training configs and per-language token CSVs, confirming the three-phase schedule, language cascade, and mask ratio schedule. Claims 4-6 are addressed only via reduced-scale proxy experiments (5/8 GLUE tasks, XNLI-only for XTREME, MLM NLL for TiQuAD F1) that reproduce relative orderings and mechanisms but not the paper's specific absolute numbers.

SabaPivot/repro-linearizer.paper_title: Who Said Neural Networks Aren't Linear?

claims.claim: A Linearizer is defined as f(x) = g_y^{-1}(A g_x(x)) for invertible neural networks g_x, g_y and linear operator A, making f linear under induced vector-space operations (Section 2.1-2.2).
claims.evidence: algebra_check.py --part 1 verified additivity, homogeneity, and full vector-space axioms to ~1e-14 (float64) using randomly-initialized 4-block RealNVP-style invertible networks g_x, g_y with a random core A, confirming the induced linearity of f(x)=g_y^{-1}(A g_x(x)) on non-trivial random instances.

claims.claim: The composition of two Linearizers with compatible spaces is itself a Linearizer, with the composed operator obtained by matrix multiplication of the underlying cores (Proposition 2.5).
claims.evidence: algebra_check.py --part 2 confirmed that composing two Linearizers f2(f1(x)) equals a single Linearizer with core A2@A1 to 4.26e-14 max error, and 5-fold self-application yields core A^5 to 1.11e-16, using three independent random invertible networks.

claims.claim: A Linearizer f is idempotent, i.e. f(f(x)) = f(x), if and only if its core matrix A is an idempotent matrix (A^2 = A), enabling architectural (rather than optimization-based) enforcement of idempotent generative networks (Lemma 4.2, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Algebraic lemma verified both directions to ~1e-16 (idempotent A gives f(f(x))=f(x); non-idempotent A gives gap ~47). Additionally, a 454,512-parameter bijection trained on 10,000 real MNIST images with a fixed rank-588 binary diagonal projector achieved idempotence to 3.815e-6 max error across 6,000 held-out and OOD inputs, with a non-idempotent control reaching 8.778e-3 RMS, confirming architectural enforcement on a non-toy image task.

claims.claim: In the one-step flow-matching application, the product of per-step update operators over hundreds of integration steps collapses into a single operator, enabling one-step diffusion sampling without retraining (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Exact Euler-step product collapse verified to 1.2e-14. Using the paper's official pretrained MNIST checkpoint (not retrained), one-step sampling vs. multi-step rollout achieved MSE 4.22e-4 at T=100 (paper reports ~3e-4, same order) and 7.79e-6 at T=1000, confirming one-step diffusion sampling without retraining.

claims.claim: Modular style transfer is achieved by fixing the shared encoders g_x, g_y while swapping only the style-specific core matrix A_style, allowing algebraic interpolation between styles from a single trained network (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: A single 3.7M-parameter StyleLinearizer with shared invertible g was trained from scratch (2000 epochs, final loss 0.002627) on 256×256 images. Swapping only the style-conditioned linear core reproduced four Johnson-style targets at 0.83–3.07e-3 MSE (25–31 dB PSNR). A separate direct matrix-blend audit confirmed A_alpha=(1-alpha)A1+alpha*A2 is affine in induced space to 5.96e-7, verifying algebraic style interpolation from a single trained network.

SabaPivot/repro-linearizer.overall: All five claims are supported by concrete experimental evidence: algebraic properties verified at machine precision on random invertible networks, a trained 454K-parameter MNIST idempotent projector with proper controls, one-step flow matching evaluated on the paper's released checkpoint, and a trained 3.7M-parameter modular style-transfer network with direct core-matrix interpolation. The reproduction is notably transparent about limitations (empty upstream IGN stub, approximate RK4 cached path) while still independently confirming each claim's substance.

kshitijthakkar/repro-ising-aggregation.paper_title: Dependence-Aware Label Aggregation for LLM-as-a-Judge via Ising Models

claims.claim: Theorem 1 proves a nonvanishing Bayes-vs-conditional-independence separation for class-conditional Ising judge models under a Curie-Weiss framework: conditional-independence (CI) predictors incur constant error while the Bayes-optimal aggregator's error vanishes as the number of judges grows (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Exact computation (no sampling) using the closed-form Curie-Weiss magnetization pmf shows the CI-predictor risk equals min(pi,1-pi)=0.300000 at every K from 10 to 10000, while the Bayes risk vanishes (3.5e-7 at K=100, effectively 0 by K=10000), confirming the nonvanishing separation of Theorem 1 at the paper's own parameter settings.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 extends the separation to settings with informative marginals, showing CI-based aggregation remains bounded away from Bayes-optimal performance asymptotically even when each individual judge outperforms random guessing (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Exact finite-K computation at both Figure-4 parameter sets (beta1=2,c=1.5 and beta1=5,c=1) shows q0<1/2<q1 (each judge beats random), condition (8) satisfied, CI risk converging to pi*(1-p)=0.0374704665 and 0.0834554046 (matched to 2.4e-6 and 1.3e-8 at K=10000), while Bayes risk vanishes — confirming Theorem 2's separation with informative marginals.

claims.claim: For the class-independent Ising model, the quadratic dependence terms cancel in the likelihood ratio, reducing the Bayes-optimal log-odds to a linear, correlation-adjusted weighted vote (Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: A SymPy symbolic derivation with fully uninstantiated parameters (K=4 judges) shows all 6 pairwise quadratic coefficients in the Bayes log-odds reduce to exactly 0 under shared couplings W^(1)=W^(0), and the full expression collapses to the linear form b0+sum_j Delta_h_j J_j; a negative control perturbing one coupling entry correctly breaks cancellation at exactly that pair and nowhere else, ruling out a tautological check.

claims.claim: CI-based label aggregation methods can flip the Bayes-optimal predicted label even while exactly matching each individual judge's marginal accuracy (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Deterministic exact enumeration over all 2^3=8 vote patterns reproduces 33/34 printed Appendix B values at the paper's precision (the 34th differs by 1.7e-7, a parameter-rounding artifact) and confirms both label flips: Example 1 gives Bayes P(Y=1|J)=0.038 (predict 0) vs CI P=0.968 (predict 1); Example 2 gives Bayes 0.031 vs CI 0.957, with the CI predictor fed the true class-conditional marginals in both cases.

claims.claim: On three real-world LLM-as-a-judge datasets (Relevance, Toxicity, Summarization) using six LLM judges (Claude Sonnet/Haiku 4.5, gpt-oss-120b, Llama variants, DeepSeek-R1), the class-dependent Ising aggregator attains test accuracies of 0.90, 0.79, and 0.68 respectively, exceeding the CI-weighted-majority-vote baseline's 0.82, 0.72, and 0.61 (Table 1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The paper's six-LLM-judge vote matrices were never released and were not regenerated; the logbook substitutes three public human-crowdsourcing datasets (Bluebirds, sentiment, ZenCrowd-US) with human annotators replacing LLM judges. On these proxy datasets the Ising aggregator wins on only 1/3 (sentiment: 0.7682 vs CI-WMV 0.6815, matching the paper's ordering), while CI-WMV wins on duck (0.9000 vs 0.8886) and UMV wins on zencrowd-us (0.8748 vs 0.8238). The paper's specific Table 1 numbers (0.90/0.82, 0.79/0.72, 0.68/0.61) are never tested.

kshitijthakkar/repro-ising-aggregation.overall: The logbook provides strong, machine-precision verification of all four theoretical claims (Theorems 1–2, quadratic cancellation, label-flip counterexamples) via exact computation and symbolic algebra, and also documents a reproducible internal inconsistency in the paper's Appendix-F figures. The empirical claim on real LLM-judge datasets is untestable from released artifacts and was only addressed on proxy human-crowd data with mixed results.

kshitijthakkar/repro-judge-eval-reportin.paper_title: How to Correctly Report LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluations

claims.claim: The plug-in bias-adjusted estimator θ̂ = (p̂ + q̂₀ − 1)/(q̂₀ + q̂₁ − 1) corrects the naive LLM-judge accuracy estimate p̂ using estimated judge specificity q̂₀ and sensitivity q̂₁ (Section 3, Equation 7).
claims.evidence: Independent reimplementation of θ̂=(p̂+q̂₀−1)/(q̂₀+q̂₁−1) matches released package bit-identically (max diff 0.0 over ~9.7k random inputs); Fig. 5 Monte Carlo at paper scale (n=1000, m=200, 10k reps) shows naive bias up to +0.300 corrected to max |bias| 0.0042 on θ∈[0.1,0.9].

claims.claim: A Wald-type confidence interval (Equation 8) is constructed that incorporates variance contributions from both the test dataset of size n and the calibration datasets of sizes m₀ and m₁ (Section 3, Equations 8-11).
claims.evidence: The adjusted Wald CI (Eqs. 6-8) incorporating variance from n, m₀, m₁ was independently reimplemented and verified bit-identical to released code; empirical coverage at paper scale is [0.9499, 0.9700] across all 21 θ values vs nominal 95%, while naive CI coverage is <5% at 16/21 θ values.

claims.claim: Proposition 1 shows that when the calibration sample size m satisfies m ≳ q/(2q−1)², the bias-adjusted estimator θ̂ has lower absolute bias than the naive estimator p̂ for all true accuracy values θ (Section 4.1, Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: Exact enumeration (no sampling) of E[θ̂] over full discrete support confirms |bias(θ̂)| ≤ |bias(p̂)| for all θ above the calibration threshold (0 violations at q=0.9,m=50 and q=0.6,m=60) and demonstrates failure below it (20/21 violations at q=0.6,m=8 vs threshold 30).

claims.claim: Proposition 2 characterizes the confidence-interval-minimizing allocation between the two calibration subsets, with optimal ratio m₀ ≈ (1/p̂ − 1)√κ · m₁ where κ = (1−q̃₀)/(1−q̃₁) (Section 4.2, Proposition 2; Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Closed-form roots of the allocation formula (Eq. 15) match numerical root-finding to max diff 3.8e-15 over 1,500 (q₀,q₁) pairs; the κ=3 worked example yields symmetric allocation at p≈0.634/θ≈0.557 matching the paper, and Algorithm 1 produces shorter CIs at 100% of θ values >0.15 from the symmetric optimum.

claims.claim: Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that the adjusted estimator reduces bias and achieves proper 95% confidence interval coverage across all true accuracy values θ, while adaptive calibration allocation yields shorter intervals than equal allocation (Section 5, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Fig. 5 reproduced at paper scale (n=1000, m=200, 10k reps, 21 θ): adjusted estimator max |bias| 0.0042 interior, CI coverage [0.9499, 0.9700], adaptive allocation shorter than equal allocation at 100% of θ >0.15 from optimum; all 8 Appendix J configurations (Figs. 12-19) reproduce with coverage [0.948, 0.975] and adaptive shorter in all 8.

kshitijthakkar/repro-judge-eval-reportin.overall: The logbook provides concrete, full-scale experimental evidence supporting all five claims: the plug-in estimator, its CI, both propositions, and the Monte Carlo simulation results are all verified at the paper's exact configurations using independent reimplementations cross-checked against released code. The only unaddressed items are the real-data Chatbot Arena/AlpacaEval panels, which require unreleased LLM-judge labels and are explicitly declared as gaps.

neonforestmist/adam-degenerate-polynomia.paper_title: Towards Understanding Adam Convergence on Highly Degenerate Polynomials

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that on the degenerate polynomial loss L(x) = (1/k) x^k for k >= 4, Adam achieves local linear convergence when beta_1 < beta_2^(k/(2(k-2))), with asymptotic rate x_{t+1}/x_t -> beta_2^(1/(2(k-2))) (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: At k=4, beta1=0.001, beta2=0.01, the stated condition beta1 < beta2^(k/(2(k-2))) holds (0.001 < 0.0316) and a fixed point exists, yet the computed Jacobian spectral radius is 3.055>1, indicating local instability—a concrete counterexample to the single-inequality sufficient condition as written. The rate prediction itself is confirmed for stable cases (27 trajectories with zero max error), but the claim's stated condition is incomplete.

claims.claim: Gradient Descent and Heavy-Ball Momentum both exhibit only sublinear convergence of order Theta(t^{-1/(k-2)}) on the same degenerate polynomial objective, established in Theorems 5.1 and 5.3 respectively.
claims.evidence: Continuous-time Gradient Flow and Heavy-ball exponents across k=4,6,8,10 match the predicted -1/(k-2) with maximum absolute errors of 4.05e-08 and 2.74e-05 respectively, using high-accuracy LSODA integration to t=10^8 with tail fitting from t>=10^6.

claims.claim: Remark 5.8 quantifies the resulting complexity separation: Gradient Descent requires iteration complexity T_epsilon ~ epsilon^{-(k-2)} to reach accuracy epsilon, whereas Adam achieves T_epsilon ~ (k-2) ln(1/epsilon) (Remark 5.8).
claims.evidence: Exact GD hitting times at seven epsilons recover complexity exponents 2, 4, 6 for k=4,6,8 with errors ~1e-15; full Adam steps to epsilon=1e-20 are affine in ln(1/epsilon) with R^2>=0.9999998 and slopes 55.12, 110.25, 165.36 proportional to k-2.

claims.claim: Lemma 5.4 shows the second moment estimate satisfies v_t/v_{t-1} -> beta_2 asymptotically, decoupling v_t from the instantaneous squared gradient g_t^2 and producing an effective learning rate that grows as beta_2^{-t/2} (Lemma 5.4).
claims.evidence: Six Adam/RMSProp configurations across k=4,6,8 with 1000 tail samples each show median v_t/v_{t-1}=0.93=beta2 with zero error, effective learning rate slope matching -ln(beta2)/2, and strictly growing log(v_t/g_t^2), confirming decoupling and the beta_2^{-t/2} effective rate growth.

claims.claim: Section 6 identifies three convergence regimes governed by beta_1 relative to beta_2: stable exponential convergence, an intermediate regime with an initial exponential phase followed by loss spikes from fixed-point instability, and a SignGD-like oscillatory regime under tight v_t-g_t^2 coupling (Section 6, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Three 100,000-step trajectories at k=4, beta1=0.9 exhibit distinct regimes: stable (log loss -688, no spike, 0 sign changes), intermediate (93.66 log10 rebound after minimum, spike detected), and oscillatory (6381 tail sign changes), matching the three described regimes.

claims.claim: Figure 3 shows the empirical phase diagram of stability boundaries across different degeneracy orders k matches the theoretical predictions of Equations 8-9 (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Complete 50×50 grids run for 100,000 steps each at k=4,6,8 show agreement rates of 98.08%, 99.88%, 99.88% with theoretical boundaries, with zero theory-stable/empirical-unstable cells; the ~2% k=4 discrepancy is in the empirical-stable/theory-unstable direction, consistent with the paper's noted discrepancy region.

neonforestmist/adam-degenerate-polynomia.overall: The logbook provides rigorous numerical evidence confirming claims 2–6 through high-precision ODE integration, exact hitting-time computations, tail-ratio analysis, long-horizon regime trajectories, and complete phase-diagram sweeps. Claim 1 is falsified as written because the single stated inequality is insufficient—a concrete counterexample shows instability at a point satisfying the quoted condition, though the rate prediction and the corrected two-condition theorem are independently confirmed.

baimamboukar/repro-trace-34030.paper_title: The Realignment Problem: When Right becomes Wrong in LLMs

claims.claim: TRACE performs realignment via a three-stage pipeline: programmatic triage of preference pairs into Invert (Type I), Punish (Type II), and Retain sets, followed by hybrid DPO/NPO objectives and alignment impact-weighted optimization (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The official trace.py code was executed end-to-end on a tiny model with 6 synthetic pairs, and a scaled proxy on Qwen2.5-0.5B with 12 PKU-derived examples per category implemented all three stages (triage, DPO/NPO objectives, gradient-dot-product impact weights). However, the model is ~7% of the paper's scale, data is a proxy, and TRACE did not outperform uniform or U2A baselines (61.1% vs 63.9%).

claims.claim: TRACE is evaluated for realignment robustness on Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and Llama-3.1-8B using the PKU-SafeRLHF and SynthValueBench datasets (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Only Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct was used instead of Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, or Llama-3.1-8B; SynthValueBench was entirely unavailable. The PKU-SafeRLHF data was used but with a self-constructed policy-shift proxy rather than the paper's original triage. This is a drastically reduced scope relative to the claim.

claims.claim: In a human preference study, TRACE is preferred over the U2A baseline 81.8% of the time on PKU-SafeRLHF and 85.3% on SynthValueBench (Table 1).
claims.evidence: No human preference study was conducted or independently reproduced. The logbook only confirms that the numbers 81.8% and 85.3% appear in the paper text; no annotation data, response triplets, or votes were available or generated.

claims.claim: On policy alignment, TRACE achieves 70.2% target policy agreement compared to U2A's 54.7%, versus 100% for a full re-training oracle (Table 4).

suehuynh/repro-context-invariant-safety-.paper_title: Towards Context-Invariant Safety Alignment for Large Language Models

claims.claim: GRPO+AIR improves in-distribution group accuracy by 12.71 percentage points and out-of-distribution consistency by 33.49 percentage points relative to GRPO alone (Table 1, Section 4.2).

amkkk/repro-online-conformal-prediction-.paper_title: Online Conformal Prediction via Universal Portfolio Algorithms

claims.claim: UP-OCP is a parameter-free online conformal prediction method requiring no stepsize tuning, whose regret analysis is built on universal portfolio algorithms (Section 4.2, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 was implemented with only alpha as input (zero hyperparameters), the closed-form update lambda_t = (N_{t-1} + 1/2)/t was verified to machine precision, and wealth remained positive throughout a T=1000 run.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 shows UP-OCP achieves linearized regret of order O(√(T ln T)) in the worst case, improving to O(ln T) as the miscoverage target α→1 (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Linearized regret was bounded by the Theorem 4.3 analytical bound for all T in {100,500,1000,2000,5000} with ratio ~0.23, and the log-log slope of 0.562 is consistent with O(sqrt(T ln T)) growth; the alpha=0.95 case showed reduced regret as claimed.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 establishes a finite-time miscoverage bound of the form MisCov_T ≤ ε_T + √(2α(1-α)ε_T), where ε_T grows only logarithmically in T (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: The finite-time miscoverage bound MisCov_T <= epsilon_T + sqrt(2*alpha*(1-alpha)*epsilon_T) held for all tested alpha in {0.05,0.10,0.20} and T in {100,500,1000,2000}, including polynomially growing scores (q=1); the log-log slope of epsilon_T vs T was -0.886, consistent with logarithmic-over-T growth.

claims.claim: On the AXP dataset at α=0.05, UP-OCP achieves 0.932 marginal coverage with an average prediction set size of 14.8 and a longest error streak of 4 days, versus 0.920 coverage, 16.9 average set size, and a 15-day longest error streak for the Kalman/KT baseline (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Real AXP data from Yahoo Finance was used, and marginal coverage matched (0.933 vs 0.932), but the base model was a rolling 20-day linear trend rather than Prophet, yielding avg set size 2.66 vs paper's 14.8 and KT longest error streak of 3 vs paper's 15—the key comparative advantage (shorter UP-OCP error streaks) was not reproduced.

claims.claim: Across miscoverage rates from 0.05 to 0.25, UP-OCP empirically achieves the best Pareto trade-off between coverage and set size compared to the parameter-free KT baseline (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The Pareto sweep was conducted on synthetic AXP-like data rather than real AXP; UP-OCP Pareto-dominates KT in only 11/21 alpha values and is strictly worse on both coverage and set size in several cases (e.g., alpha=0.05: UP coverage 0.9310 < KT 0.9317, UP size 38.86 > KT 37.75), undermining the 'best Pareto trade-off' claim.

claims.claim: On a synthetic sinusoidal nonconformity-score sequence, UP-OCP tracks periodic volatility—expanding prediction sets during high-noise phases and shrinking them afterward—matching the best hyperparameter-tuned P-Control baseline without any tuning (Figures 3-4).
claims.evidence: The sinusoidal tracking behavior is confirmed (high-noise set size 19.85 vs low-noise 3.24, ratio 6.12x), but the P-Control baseline is clearly broken (coverage 0.277 vs target 0.90), so the claim that UP-OCP 'matches the best hyperparameter-tuned P-Control baseline' is not demonstrated.

amkkk/repro-online-conformal-prediction-.overall: The logbook provides reasonable empirical support for the three theoretical claims (parameter-free design, regret bound, miscoverage bound) via synthetic experiments with proper scaling checks. However, the empirical claims are weakly supported: Claim 4 uses a different base model yielding mismatched set sizes and error streaks, Claim 5 uses synthetic data with mixed Pareto results, and Claim 6's P-Control baseline is broken.

Claims requiring real clinical datasets or human clinicians were not addressed at all.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows a symmetric smoothing operator with positive coefficients can be rescaled by a diagonal matrix (via a symmetric Sinkhorn iteration) into a diffusion operator that is self-adjoint with respect to a mass-weighted inner product (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: On the 5000-point Stanford Armadillo surface with Gaussian and exponential kernels at sigma=0.05, Sinkhorn mass residuals were ≤8.1e-13, self-adjointness held at machine precision, and largest eigenvalues ≤1+9e-16; smaller-scale tests across Gaussian 2D/3D/GMM, exponential, and heat kernels also confirmed all axioms.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 proves that for Gaussian and exponential kernels, the Sinkhorn-normalized operators converge uniformly on bounded domains to continuous diffusion operators as sampling resolution increases (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: The resolution-convergence experiment covers 60 cases across three densities, Gaussian/exponential kernels, resolutions 32–512, and 257 probes, with sup errors ≤6.75e-5, final/initial ratios ~0.0034–0.0043, and log-log slopes ~-1.95 to -2.08, numerically demonstrating convergence as sampling resolution increases.

claims.claim: The symmetric Sinkhorn algorithm empirically requires only 5 to 10 iterations to reduce normalization error below 0.1% (Section 4/5, empirical convergence results).
claims.evidence: On the 5000-point Armadillo surface using the paper's Eq.-34 mass-weighted mean absolute error metric with threshold 1e-3, both Gaussian and exponential kernels first crossed the threshold at iteration 6; small-scale point-cloud kernels required 6–8 iterations.

claims.claim: The normalized operators simultaneously satisfy symmetry, mass conservation, entrywise positivity, and spectral damping (eigenvalues in [0,1]), properties not jointly satisfied by standard row- or symmetric-normalization schemes (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: On the same 5000-point Armadillo matrices, Sinkhorn passed all four properties (mass error ≤8.1e-13, self-adjoint relative error 0, spectrum in [0,1], positivity), while row normalization failed self-adjointness (0.308/0.152) and classical symmetric normalization failed mass conservation (0.276/0.258).

claims.claim: The method is demonstrated on point clouds, sparse voxel grids (jaw bone geometry), and Gaussian mixture models with covariance-aware kernels, showing Laplacian-like smoothing on each irregular data type (Section 5, experiments).
claims.evidence: Point-cloud and full-covariance GMM demonstrations confirmed valid diffusion operators with smooth leading modes; a real OpenMandible jaw mesh (42,992 triangles, 1,813 voxels) showed Sinkhorn mass error ~1e-13 and monotonic energy decay across eight diffusion steps, covering all three stated data types.

claims.claim: Shape analysis experiments on the Armadillo mesh show spectral distributions remain consistent across sampling modalities, with eigenvalue divergence appearing only at scales matching sampling resolution, validating the Theorem 4.2 convergence guarantee (Section 5).
claims.evidence: On the full Armadillo protocol (5000 points, 500 GMM components, voxel comparison with P1 FEM reference), seed 20260723 showed eigenvalue divergence at mode 18, before the independently recomputed resolution boundary at mode 21, at dimensionless frequency 0.42 outside the pre-registered [0.5,1.0] interval; both primary and independent checkers rejected the contract.

DineshAI/LJdacnMXkr.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence on real-scale data (Stanford Armadillo, OpenMandible jaw) verifying claims 1–5, including the four-property comparison and resolution convergence. Claim 6 is falsified by a full-scale Armadillo surface/volume experiment showing eigenvalue divergence outside the predicted resolution-scale interval.

amkkk/repro-a-sketch-and-project-analysi.paper_title: A Sketch-and-Project Analysis of Subsampled Natural Gradient Algorithms

claims.claim: For linear least-squares problems, subsampled natural gradient descent (SNGD) is shown to be directly equivalent to the regularized Kaczmarz method, and SPRING is equivalent to the Nesterov-accelerated regularized Kaczmarz (ARK) method (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports a relative difference of 0.00e+00 (machine precision) between the SNGD update direction and the regularized Kaczmarz update on a 100×50 linear least-squares problem, directly confirming the algebraic equivalence stated in Theorem 1.

claims.claim: SNGD converges at rate (1-α)^t where α=λ_min(P̄), while SPRING converges at rate O((1-√(α/β))^t), giving up to a square-root improvement in iteration complexity over SNGD (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The empirical SNGD rate ρ=0.0027 is approximately 12x slower than the theoretical prediction -log(1-α)=0.0321 (with α=0.0316), a large discrepancy that is not explained. Additionally, SPRING's convergence rate O((1-√(α/β))^t) is never empirically measured—only the target value 0.735 is computed, with no actual SPRING convergence run to compare.

claims.claim: For general quadratic losses, SNGD requires the regularization parameter λ to exceed a threshold λ0 to guarantee convergence, and can diverge if regularization is insufficient (Proposition 3).
claims.evidence: On an adversarial problem (first row of J boosted 100x), SNGD clearly diverges for λ=0 (err=5.28e54), λ=1e-6 (3.50e52), and λ=1e-4 (2.82e32), while converging for λ=0.01 (0.826) and λ=0.1 (0.977), directly demonstrating the regularization threshold behavior of Proposition 3.

claims.claim: Under an assumption that the regularized projector P̄ shares an eigenbasis with J^T J, SNGD provably outperforms SGD by a factor of k^β when the spectrum of the Jacobian decays polynomially (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: On a problem with polynomial spectral decay (σ_i ∝ 1/i², n=30, m=200), SNGD increasingly outperforms SGD as batch size k grows: ratios of 1.04x, 1.10x, 1.59x, 3.59x, and 14636x for k=1,2,5,10,20, confirming the qualitative claim that SNGD's advantage over SGD scales with k under spectral decay.

claims.claim: A unified algorithm (Algorithm 1) captures both SNGD (momentum μ=0) and SPRING (μ∈(0,1)) as momentum-based updates using subsampled Jacobians, enabling single-minibatch convergence guarantees of any batch size.
claims.evidence: Both SNGD (μ=0, final error 0.283) and SPRING (μ=0.581, final error 0.075) are run under the same unified update formula using single-minibatch subsampled Jacobians on a 100×50 LLQ problem, demonstrating that Algorithm 1 captures both methods and SPRING achieves 3.8x faster convergence.

claims.claim: Analysis of SPRING's convergence for general (non-least-squares) quadratic losses is left open as Conjecture 7, despite numerical experiments showing large empirical performance gains over SNGD.
claims.evidence: The logbook confirms that Conjecture 7 is explicitly stated as an open problem in the paper. However, the numerical evidence for 'large empirical gains over SNGD' on general (non-least-squares) quadratics reuses the same LLQ numbers (0.075 vs 0.283) from Claim 5 rather than running a separate experiment with H≠I, so the empirical-gains portion is not independently demonstrated.

amkkk/repro-a-sketch-and-project-analysi.overall: The logbook provides solid numerical verification of the algebraic equivalence (Claim 1), regularization threshold (Claim 3), spectral-decay advantage (Claim 4), and unified algorithm formulation (Claim 5) on small-scale linear least-squares problems. However, Claim 2's convergence rate verification is weak—the empirical SNGD rate is 12x slower than predicted and SPRING's rate is never empirically tested—and Claim 6's empirical evidence for general quadratics appears to reuse LLQ results rather than testing on H≠I.

amkkk/repro-anytime-detection-of-strateg.paper_title: Anytime Detection of Strategic Deviations in Multi-Agent Systems

claims.claim: For normal-form games, the framework defines a per-round e-value E_{i,t}(a_i')(lambda) = 1 - lambda*X_{i,t}(a_i') requiring only observed payoff evaluations, not knowledge of the equilibrium strategies themselves (Section 2, Lemma 2.2).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo on a single 2x2 normal-form game (50000 runs) shows mean E-values near 1.0 (e.g., 1.0001145 for lam=0.05), consistent with the e-value definition, but all empirical means are slightly above 1 rather than <= 1, and the setup is a minimal 2x2 game rather than a general normal-form game.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.6 shows family-wise error rate (FWER) is controlled at level alpha when the accumulated test supermartingale threshold reaches sum_i |A_i| / alpha, where A_i is agent i's action set (Section 2, Theorem 2.6).
claims.evidence: FWER is controlled (empirical FWER of 0.01, 0.0, 0.0 for alpha=0.2, 0.1, 0.05) but only one lambda value (0.05) and one 2x2 game are tested, which is a highly simplified setup insufficient to confirm the general theorem.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.7 bounds the expected detection time of an equilibrium deviation at O(log(sum_i |A_i| / alpha) / eta^2), where eta is the deviation's payoff-improvement magnitude (Section 2, Theorem 2.7).
claims.evidence: Detection times (1214.43, 618.1, 414.63 for eta=0.05, 0.1, 0.15) yield a ratio of ~1.97x between eta=0.05 and eta=0.1, whereas O(1/eta^2) predicts 4x; the observed scaling is closer to O(1/eta), so the toy results do not clearly support the claimed bound.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.8 adapts a Benjamini-Hochberg procedure to the sequential e-value setting for false discovery rate (FDR) control, and the paper shows empirically in a 2x2 game that this FDR procedure detects deviations faster than the conservative FWER-controlling baseline (Section 2, Theorem 2.8).
claims.evidence: On a 2x2 game matching the paper's own empirical setup, FDR mean stop time (1513.17) is faster than FWER mean stop time (1735.65), a 1.15x speedup, directly supporting the empirical portion of the claim; however, FDR control itself is not separately verified.

claims.claim: For stochastic games, Theorem 3.4 bounds detection time by (log b + C_i) / KL-bar_i(mu), where KL-bar_i(mu) is a state-averaged Kullback-Leibler divergence, and Remark 3.5 extends this via mixture martingales to handle deviations of unknown magnitude (Section 3, Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The claim concerns stochastic games (Theorem 3.4), but the experiment uses a normal-form 2x2 game and only checks KL divergence scaling against Proposition H.1, not the actual detection-time bound for stochastic games; the stochastic game setting is never implemented.

claims.claim: Empirical validation on Grid Soccer and Predator-Prey environments shows detection times matching the theoretical O(1/epsilon^2) scaling, including under the mixture-martingale extension for unknown deviation magnitude (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The claim explicitly requires Grid Soccer and Predator-Prey environments, but the reproduction uses only a normal-form 2x2 game; the specified environments are never run, so the empirical validation claim is not addressed.

amkkk/repro-anytime-detection-of-strateg.overall: This logbook runs all experiments on a single 2x2 normal-form game, which is adequate only for claim 4 (whose paper setup is also a 2x2 game) but inadequate for claims about stochastic games, Grid Soccer, and Predator-Prey. The O(1/eta^2) scaling in claim 3 is not confirmed (observed ratio ~2x vs predicted 4x), and claims 5 and 6 are essentially unaddressed due to using the wrong environment.

amkkk/repro-the-catastrophic-failure-of-.paper_title: The Catastrophic Failure of *the* k-Means Algorithm in High Dimensions, and How Hartigan's Algorithm Avoids It

claims.claim: In the high-noise, high-dimensional regime where σ² > n, Lloyd's k-means algorithm fails catastrophically: essentially every partition of the data becomes a fixed point of the algorithm (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: At d=100,000, σ²=64 > n=40, Lloyd's first step returned the initial partition in 100/100 trials (100%), with mean NMI=0.019; the easy control (d=64, σ²=1) showed only 1/160 fixed, confirming the detector is non-vacuous.

claims.claim: In the same high-noise regime, Hartigan's k-means algorithm avoids this pathology, having no incorrect fixed points with high probability (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: At d=100,000, σ²=64, Hartigan escaped every initialization (0/100 fixed) and achieved NMI=1.000 in 100/100 trials; unweighted sequential moves froze in 100/100, isolating the weighting mechanism as essential.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.8 bounds the probability that any q-approximately balanced partition is not a fixed point of Lloyd's algorithm by 2^n · n · ρ_q^(d/4) (Corollary 3.8).
claims.evidence: The bound was checked via exhaustive finite partition census at n=6 (vs paper's n=40), q=1.1, d up to 1500, with 500 trials per dimension and zero violations; the reduced n is a clearly simplified scale though the runs are real.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.12 bounds the probability that any incorrect partition is a fixed point of Hartigan's algorithm by 2^n · ρ_h^(d/4), a substantially tighter bound than Lloyd's case (Corollary 3.12).
claims.evidence: The bound was checked via exhaustive finite partition census at n=6 (vs paper's n=40), d up to 160,000, 200 trials, zero violations; the large dimension is substantial but n=6 is a reduced-scale proxy for the full setting.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 shows Lloyd's single-sample reassignment step persists misclassification errors once the noise level exceeds σ > (2c̄τ(c−1))/√(c(c+c̄)) (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: At n=40, d=100,000, above the paper's exact threshold (σ²=36.1 > 18.05), Lloyd kept the misclassified point in 80/80 trials; below threshold (σ²=9.025), Lloyd corrected it in 80/80, confirming the threshold behavior at paper scale.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments empirically demonstrate the divergence between Lloyd's catastrophic-failure behavior and Hartigan's robustness as dimension grows, corroborating the theoretical bounds (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Dimension sweep from d=10 to d=100,000 above threshold shows Lloyd's P(wrong stays) rising from 0.607 to 1.000 while Hartigan's drops from 0.423 to 0.000, with divergence reaching 1.000 at d=100,000, directly demonstrating the predicted divergence.

amkkk/repro-the-catastrophic-failure-of-.overall: The logbook provides concrete, non-toy experimental evidence at paper scale (n=40, d=100,000) supporting claims 1, 2, 5, and 6, with clean controls and unit tests. Claims 3 and 4 are addressed only at reduced scale (n=6) via finite partition census, which is real but simplified relative to the paper's full setting.

amkkk/repro-revenue-guarantees-of-no-swa.paper_title: Revenue Guarantees of No-Swap-Regret Dynamics in First Price Auctions

claims.claim: For exact correlated equilibria in discrete first-price auctions with k discretization levels, expected revenue is at least v2 - 4/k, where v2 is the second-highest valuation (Theorem 2.5).
claims.evidence: The logbook solves the primal LP (Definition 3.1) with eps=0 to find the minimum-revenue exact CE, addressing the universal quantifier. For k=4,6,8,10 with v2=0.8, the LP minimum revenue (0.5, 0.667, 0.75, 0.8) exceeds the bound v2-4/k (-0.2, 0.133, 0.3, 0.4) in all cases. The LP approach is exact for each k, not an approximation.

claims.claim: For ε-approximate correlated equilibria, expected revenue is at least v2 - 3/k - Θ(εk²) (Theorem 2.6).
claims.evidence: The logbook solves the primal LP with eps>0 for 12 (k,eps) pairs (k=4,6,8,10; eps=0.01,0.05,0.1). The LP minimum revenue exceeds v2-3/k-2*eps*k^2 in all cases. However, for larger eps the bounds become very negative (e.g., -19.5 for k=10, eps=0.1), making the check trivially satisfied; the meaningful verification is at eps=0.01 where bounds are closer to actual revenue.

claims.claim: There exists an ε-approximate correlated equilibrium with revenue at most v2 - Θ(1/k) - Θ(ε), showing the ε-dependence in the revenue lower bound cannot be removed (Theorem 2.8).
claims.evidence: The logbook constructs a symmetric 2-bid distribution (bid 1-1/k with prob p=0.01, bid 1-2/k otherwise) for 2 bidders with v1=v2=1, verifies all swap constraints, and checks revenue <= 1-1/k-eps. The construction succeeds for 8 of 12 (k,eps) pairs, demonstrating existence. Failures occur only for larger eps (0.1-0.2) at larger k (8-10), but existence is confirmed for multiple configurations.

claims.claim: When bidders run no-swap-regret algorithms achieving swap regret O(√(kT)), the time-averaged revenue is at least v2 - 3/k - O(ε) after O(k^5/ε^2) rounds (Corollary 2.7).
claims.evidence: The logbook simulates regret matching for only k=4,6 with a fixed T=50000 rounds, but the theorem requires T=O(k^5/eps^2) which for k=6, eps=0.1 would be ~777,600 rounds—far more than 50,000. The bounds tested are also very weak (e.g., -0.05 for k=4, eps=0.1), making the revenue of ~0.71 trivially exceed them. Only 4 configurations tested.

claims.claim: Time-averaged bidder behavior under no-swap-regret dynamics converges to an ε-approximate correlated equilibrium with probability 1-δ (Theorem 2.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook simulates regret matching for k=4,6 with T=5000 rounds and checks empirical swap violations. Only 3 of 4 configurations pass: k=6, eps=0.1 has max violation 0.128 > 0.1, failing the eps-approximate CE condition. No delta parameter is specified, no multiple seeds are run, and the round count is far below what the theorem's rate suggests.

claims.claim: The revenue lower bounds are proved via a dual-fitting approach that uses a linear program and weak duality to bound revenue of approximate correlated equilibria (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook solves both the primal LP (Definition 3.1) and dual LP (Lemma 3.3) for k=4,6,8,10 with eps=0.01. Dual feasibility is confirmed (all lambda>=0) and weak duality holds (primal_opt >= dual_opt) in all cases, e.g., k=10: primal=0.457, dual=0.252. This numerically validates the dual-fitting approach and weak duality mechanism.

amkkk/repro-revenue-guarantees-of-no-swa.overall: The logbook provides exact LP-based numerical verification of the paper's revenue bounds (Claims 1, 2, 6) and existence construction (Claim 3) for small k values (4-10), using sound optimization methods. The simulation-based claims (4, 5) are at toy scale with insufficient rounds and one outright failure, providing only weak partial evidence.

claims.claim: Definition 1 introduces ℓ*-smoothness, bounding the Hessian via a general norm and its dual, ‖∇²f(x)h‖* ≤ ℓ(‖∇f(x)‖*)‖h‖, generalizing prior ℓ-smoothness beyond the Euclidean/ℓ2 setting (Section 3.1, Definition 1)
claims.evidence: 2,048 Hessian-action inequality checks across Euclidean (max ratio 0.315) and l1/linf (max ratio 0.292) geometries pass; a wrong-norm mutation produces ratio 256, demonstrating the dual-norm choice is essential.

claims.claim: Theorem 8 shows mirror descent under ℓ*-smoothness attains O(1/T) convergence for both average-iterate and last-iterate suboptimality with an appropriately chosen learning rate (Section 4, Theorem 8)
claims.evidence: On a 1,024-dimensional wide-spectrum diagonal quadratic through T=8,192, average-iterate and last-iterate gaps have fitted log-log slopes of -0.989 and -0.999 respectively, with all 20 gap-to-bound ratios below 0.08 and gradient norms below the theoretical ceiling G=0.234.

claims.claim: Theorem 9 shows an accelerated mirror descent variant attains the optimal O(1/T^2) convergence rate under ℓ*-smoothness via a time-partition analysis technique (Section 4, Theorem 9)
claims.evidence: Accelerated recurrence on the same 1,024-dim quadratic yields fitted slope -1.986 (R²=0.999985) with max gap-to-bound ratio 0.212; time-partition diagnostics (early displacement ≤0.017, late t-weighted displacement ≤0.325) and gradient ceilings all pass.

claims.claim: Theorem 10 and Theorem 11 extend the O(1/T) rate to optimistic mirror descent and mirror prox respectively, using a stability-tracking argument and a descent property for both update sequences (Section 4, Theorems 10-11)
claims.evidence: Optimistic MD and Mirror Prox on the 1,024-dim quadratic show fitted slopes -0.996 and -0.997 respectively, with zero trajectory violations across 16,384 descent-property checks and stability norms decreasing with T.

claims.claim: Theorem 12 establishes an Õ(1/√t) anytime convergence rate for stochastic mirror descent under ℓ*-smoothness with a generalized bounded-noise assumption ‖ϵ_t‖* ≤ σ(‖∇f(x_t)‖*) (Section 5, Theorem 12)
claims.evidence: A 1D analytic counterexample (X=[0,1], f(x)=(x-1)²/2, ψ(x)=x²/2, zero noise) with summable step schedule η_t=2^{-(t+3)} satisfies all stated assumptions and step upper bounds, yet the weighted-average gap remains ≥49/128 for all t, contradicting Õ(1/√t) convergence.

claims.claim: Proposition 4 shows that on the simplex, ℓ*-smoothness yields a constant smoothness parameter whereas standard ℓ-smoothness has an O(n) dimension dependence, illustrating the benefit of the generalized notion (Section 3.2, Proposition 4)
claims.evidence: Exact closed-form operator norms for the rank-one simplex Hessian A=vv^T show l2 norm = n-1 and l1→linf norm = 1 across dimensions 2 through 32,768, with fitted slope 1.000 and intercept -1.000, confirming the O(n) vs O(1) separation.

amkkk/repro-mirror-descent-under-general.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical and analytic evidence supporting claims 1-4 and 6 on a non-trivial 1,024-dimensional quadratic setup and exact simplex computations through n=32,768, while presenting an analytic counterexample falsifying claim 5's stochastic convergence guarantee under a summable step schedule. The main limitation is that the algorithm rate claims (2-4) are validated on a single quadratic instance rather than across diverse function classes.

DineshAI/0SGle5hjIf.paper_title: A Geometry-Aware Efficient Algorithm for Compositional Entropic Risk Minimization

claims.claim: Theorem 3.6 proves SCENT achieves an O(1/sqrt(T)) convergence rate for convex compositional entropic risk minimization objectives of the form log(E[exp(s(w;zeta))]), improving on SCGD's O(1/T^{1/4}) rate (Section 3, Theorem 3.6).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 shows that for fixed w, SPMD's convergence is characterized by the second-order moment ratio kappa = E[z^2]/E[z]^2, and is provably faster than standard SGD by a factor proportional to 1/e^{(nu*-c0)} (Section 4, Theorem 4.3).

claims.claim: On extreme classification benchmarks Glint360K and TreeOfLife-10M, SCENT consistently outperforms the SOX, U-max, and BSGD baselines on both training and validation convergence (Section 5, extreme classification experiments).

DineshAI/0SGle5hjIf.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the four theoretical claims (closed-form update, O(1/sqrt(T)) rate, dual boundedness, kappa-characterized SPMD advantage) through large-scale numerical experiments with negative controls and independent checkers, and falsifies the partial AUC claim at full CIFAR protocol, while the extreme classification claim remains unaddressed due to compute constraints.

snaykey/repro-steady-state-behavior-of-c.paper_title: Steady-State Behavior of Constant-Stepsize Stochastic Approximation: Gaussian Approximation and Tail Bounds

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 (i.i.d. noise) and Theorem 4.1 (Markovian noise) bound the Wasserstein distance between the centered-scaled steady state Y^(α) = (X^(α) − x*)/√α and its Gaussian limit N(0, Σ_Y) by U√α log(1/α) (Theorems 3.1 and 4.1).
claims.evidence: Exact quantile-coupling W1 against closed-form Gaussian limits across 4 settings (SGD iid, linear SA iid, contractive SA iid, SGD Markov) and dimensions d=1 to d=100 shows W1 decaying with α at slopes 0.44–1.09 (R2>0.95 except contractive), consistent with the O(√α log(1/α)) rate; 200k chains per config.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 establishes an explicit non-asymptotic Wasserstein bound of order O(α^{1/2} log(1/α)) for constant-stepsize SGD on smooth, strongly convex objectives (Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: SGD steady-state W1 to Lyapunov-equation Gaussian decays with log-log slopes 0.976 (1-D, R2=0.957), 1.026/1.043/1.086 (d=20/50/100, R2>0.97) across α grid 0.32–0.005, consistent with O(√α log(1/α)); exact quantile coupling with 200k chains.

claims.claim: Propositions 3.2 and 3.3 extend the same O(α^{1/2} log(1/α)) Wasserstein bound to linear stochastic approximation with a Hurwitz matrix and to contractive nonlinear stochastic approximation, respectively (Propositions 3.2 and 3.3, Section 3.2.2, Section 3.2.3).
claims.evidence: Linear SA W1 slopes: 1.030 (2-D), 0.863/0.775/0.779 (d=20/50/100), all R2>0.95. Contractive SA (1-D) slope 0.438 with R2=0.73 due to MC floor effects, but W1 values do decrease with α and direction is correct; both propositions have real experimental evidence.

claims.claim: For one-dimensional projections, the paper derives a non-uniform Berry-Esseen-type tail bound |P(⟨Y^(α),ζ⟩ > a) − P(Z_ζ > a)| ≤ C_d α^{1/4} log^{1/2}(1/α) / a, which improves as the deviation level a grows (Section 4).

snaykey/repro-steady-state-behavior-of-c.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence for the Wasserstein Gaussian approximation bounds (Claims 1, 2, 3, 5) and the Gibbs-regime rate (Claim 6) using exact quantile-coupling W1, 200k chains, and dimensions up to d=100 with discriminating negative controls.
