BeardedAmbivert/repro-worldcache-heterog.paper_title: WorldCache: Accelerating World Models for Free via Heterogeneous Token Caching

claims.claim: WorldCache achieves a 3.65x end-to-end speedup on HunyuanVoyager-13B while preserving WorldScore quality (45.43 vs. 46.40 baseline) (Section 5.2, Table 1).
claims.evidence: The HunyuanVoyager-13B experiment was never executed — the page explicitly states 'PENDING GPU RUN' and only describes a prepared script. No latency measurements, no WorldScore quality metrics, and no actual results exist for this claim.

claims.claim: On Aether-5B, WorldCache attains a 1.68x speedup for world generation and a 2.61x acceleration for 3D reconstruction (depth/pose estimation) while preserving geometry fidelity (Sections 5.2-5.3).
claims.evidence: World generation speedup was measured at 1.60x (180.28s→112.46s) on A100-80GB with a real image, close to the paper's 1.68x. However, the 3D reconstruction speedup (2.61x) was explicitly not measured: 'Not separately measured in this reproduction (requires depth estimation pipeline evaluation with GT data).' Since the claim asserts both speedups and one was never tested, the full claim cannot be verified.

claims.claim: The curvature score partitions tokens into stable, linear, and chaotic groups using percentile thresholds ps=0.3 and pc=0.7 on the normalized turning-rate metric κi = ||a||₂/(||v||₂²+ε) (Section 4.1, Eq. 7).
claims.evidence: Unit tests on the authors' code confirm the curvature formula κi = ||a||₂/(||v||₂²+ε) matches manual computation exactly (max diff 0.00e+00), and token grouping with ps=0.3, pc=0.7 produces a complete, non-overlapping partition (30% stable, 40% linear, 30% chaotic) with stable tokens below Q_0.3 and chaotic tokens above Q_0.7.

claims.claim: Chaotic-prioritized Adaptive Skipping (CAS) accumulates a dimensionless drift score per token and triggers a full backbone evaluation once accumulated uncertainty exceeds threshold η (Section 4.2, Eq. 12-13).
claims.evidence: Unit tests confirm: (1) the drift score κ·||δy|| is scale-invariant across scales {0.5, 2, 10, 100} with max relative error 1.31e-07, (2) prediction error is computed only over chaotic tokens (zero error with empty mask), and (3) E_acc accumulates monotonically and triggers a FULL evaluation when exceeding η, then resets to 0.

claims.claim: On HunyuanVoyager, WorldCache improves reconstruction fidelity over the EasyCache baseline, reaching PSNR 23.49 vs. 21.76, SSIM 0.770 vs. 0.737, and LPIPS 0.176 vs. 0.208 (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The HunyuanVoyager experiment was never run, and EasyCache was never executed as a baseline ('EasyCache is not integrated into the WorldCache codebase'). The only perceptual metrics measured were WorldCache vs. original on Aether-5B with a single real image (PSNR 35.25, SSIM 0.9693, LPIPS 0.0237), which does not address the claim's specific comparison of WorldCache vs. EasyCache on HunyuanVoyager.

BeardedAmbivert/repro-worldcache-heterog.overall: The logbook provides solid unit-test verification of the algorithmic mechanisms (Claims 3–4) and a partial real-hardware speedup measurement for Aether-5B world generation (1.60x vs. 1.68x), but the HunyuanVoyager-13B experiments (Claims 1 and 5) were never executed, the 3D reconstruction speedup was not measured, and no EasyCache baseline was run.

sanjaymalladi/repro-well-posed-kl-contro.paper_title: Well-Posed KL-Regularized Control via Wasserstein and Kalman–Wasserstein KL Divergences

claims.claim: The Kalman-Wasserstein KL divergence is shown to remove the singularity that classical KL-regularized control exhibits as process noise vanishes in linear time-invariant systems with Gaussian process noise (Section 3, Section 4)
claims.evidence: On the double integrator (the paper's own LTI benchmark), at ρ=1e-10 the KL feedback gains vanish (F(1)=-8.1e-09, F(2)=-1.6e-07, spectral radius 0.9999999) while WKL and KWKL(λ=1) maintain nontrivial gains (F(1)=-0.388, F(2)=-1.182, spectral radius 0.454). The anisotropic 4D case further shows KL spectral radius 0.926 vs WKL/KWKL 0.454.

claims.claim: Section 4 applies the Wasserstein-KL and Kalman-Wasserstein-KL formulations to control synthesis, deriving closed-form or tractable control laws distinct from classical KL-regularized control (Section 4)
claims.evidence: The three control laws are explicitly stated and implemented: R_KL = B^T Σ_w^{-1} B (singular as Σ_w→0), R_WKL = B^T B (noise-independent), R_KWKL = B^T(Σ_w + λI)^{-1}B (interpolating), all solved via DARE and shown to produce fundamentally different closed-loop behavior in the double integrator experiments.

claims.claim: On the double integrator benchmark (a linear time-invariant system), the Wasserstein-KL and Kalman-Wasserstein-KL controllers maintain numerical stability and well-posedness as process noise approaches zero, where classical KL-regularized control becomes ill-posed (Section 5)
claims.evidence: Concrete numerical results on the double integrator show KL spectral radius approaching 1.0 (marginal stability) as ρ→1e-10 with vanishing feedback gains, while WKL/KWKL maintain spectral radius 0.454 with constant gains. Cost at ρ≈1e-5: KL=1004.9 vs WKL=6.97. Anisotropic 4D case confirms the same trend.

claims.claim: On the nonlinear cart-pole benchmark, the Wasserstein-KL and Kalman-Wasserstein-KL regularized controllers achieve better convergence and control quality than classical KL-based regularization (Section 5)
claims.evidence: Cart-pole was simulated (dt=0.01, T=100s) but with only a single noise scale (1e-3), no statistical replicates, and marginal RMSE differences (KL=1.832 vs WKL=1.802 vs KWKL=1.801 rad). The LQR gains differ substantially but the actual nonlinear performance improvement is too small and under-tested to confirm the claim of better convergence and control quality.

sanjaymalladi/repro-well-posed-kl-contro.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting the core theoretical claims about singularity removal (Claims 1-3) on the double integrator benchmark at the paper's own scale, with multiple noise levels and anisotropic cases. The cart-pole claim (Claim 4) is only weakly supported with a single noise scale, no replicates, and negligible performance differences.

JacobLinCool/repro-chebyshev-policies-mo.paper_title: Chebyshev Policies and the Mountain Car Problem: Reinforcement Learning for Low-Dimensional Control Tasks

claims.claim: Theorem 2.4 gives the first closed-form optimal control solution for Mountain Car, α(t)=C·ẋ(t), a policy depending only on velocity, closing a 36-year-old open problem (Section 2, Theorem 2.4).
claims.evidence: A numerical certificate with 10,000 perturbations supports the velocity-proportional Cauchy-Schwarz mechanism under continuous unconstrained assumptions (min perturbed-loss gap 0.0083, max constraint residual 5.85e-18), but the executable controller uses two fitted constants and position-dependent bootstrap rather than a single C·velocity rule, discrete Gym global optimality was not tested, and the historical priority ('first,' '36-year-old open problem') was not established—prior work (ProPS arXiv Nov 2025) already mentioned velocity-proportional force.

claims.claim: The derived analytical worst-case policy achieves returns of 99.15-99.52 on Mountain Car, versus 96.67 for ARS (regret 2.72), 93.91 for PPO (regret 5.48), and 94.61 for SAC (regret 4.78) (Section 2).
claims.evidence: Full 100-start evaluation panel on HF GPU Job 6a57d4e3b shows analytical mean 99.394 (paper 99.39, range 99.149–99.518 matching 99.15–99.52), ARS 96.666 (96.67), PPO 93.906 (93.91), SAC 94.605 (94.61)—all within 0.01 of paper values with correct ordering analytical > ARS > SAC > PPO and regrets 2.73, 5.49, 4.79 recomputed from raw episode-level data.

claims.claim: The degree-3 Chebyshev policy CH-3-ARS attains regret 0.65 on Mountain Car, a 4.18x improvement over neural ARS, using only 16 parameters versus 4,355 for a 2x64x64x1 MLP -- a 277x reduction in parameter count (Section 4, Section 5).
claims.evidence: The 16 Chebyshev parameter count is confirmed, but the reproduction found regret 0.44 (not 0.65), improvement 6.15× (not 4.18×), and the parameter ratio is ~276× (4,417/16) or ~272× (4,355/16), not 277×; the paper's MLP parameter count of 4,355 is incorrect (correct dense 2→64→64→1 count is 4,417), and the released ARS comparator actually has only 65 parameters (4.06× ratio).

claims.claim: CH-3-PPO attains regret 1.29 on Mountain Car, a 4.24x improvement over standard PPO, and CH-3-REINFORCE attains regret 0.77, a 3.53x improvement over standard ARS (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Full 20-seed runs on HF GPU Job 6a57d4f1 show CH-3-PPO selected mean 84.58 (target 98.10) with regret 14.81 (target 1.29)—actually 2.7× worse than standard PPO with 14/100 starts returning below zero; CH-3-REINFORCE selected mean 96.01 (target 98.62) with regret 3.38 (target 0.77)—worse than standard ARS, with 2/100 fixed-grid starts timing out.

claims.claim: Table 2 shows Chebyshev policies generalize beyond Mountain Car: CH-ARS reaches -150.8 vs ARS's -218.3 on Pendulum, and on real-world Aero 2 hardware CH-PPO reaches -55.8 vs PPO's -182.0, indicating improved sim-to-real transfer (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Pendulum CH-6-ARS (30 seeds, 2M steps, 2500-state grid) achieved -150.50 vs target -150.80 (misses ±0.05 tolerance by 0.30, though slightly better and ordering reproduced) with ARS baseline -218.32 matching -218.30; the Aero 2 physical hardware subclaim was never tested due to lack of Quanser Aero 2 rig, sensors, calibration, and real-time interface, and no simulation substitute was attempted.

JacobLinCool/repro-chebyshev-policies-mo.overall: The logbook provides strong full-scale evidence that the analytical policy and neural baseline returns on Mountain Car (Claim 2) reproduce precisely, but falsifies the CH-3-PPO and CH-3-REINFORCE improvement claims (Claim 4) and finds incorrect parameter arithmetic in Claim 3. The theorem mechanism is supported only in a narrow continuous scope (Claim 1), and the Aero 2 sim-to-real claim remains untested (Claim 5).

ProCreations/diffusion-bridge-flow-match.paper_title: Gaussian Mean Field Variational Inference can Overestimate Predictive Variance

claims.claim: MFVI underestimates posterior variance in parameter space but can overestimate predictive variance relative to the exact posterior, with Theorem 3.7 proving that for test points drawn from the training distribution's empirical covariance, MFVI's expected predictive variance exceeds that of the exact posterior (Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence: 140 Gaussian linear-model problems (dimensions 2-64, 20 seeds each) show Tr(Sigma) >= Tr(S*) in 140/140 with minimum margin 7.88e-7 (parameter underestimation), and MFVI exceeds exact predictive variance along the minimum-eigenvalue direction in 140/140 with minimum margin 4.37e-9; the training-covariance-weighted identity E[x'(Sigma-S*)x] = -(sigma² alpha/N)[Tr(Sigma)-Tr(S*)] <= 0 is derived in closed form and checked on all 140 problems plus 158 additional fresh matrices, all nonpositive.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.6 shows a calibration constraint forcing MFVI to simultaneously underestimate variance in some directions while overestimating in others, with overestimation occurring specifically in directions where training data concentrates (Lemma 3.6).
claims.evidence: Eigen-direction diagnostics on 140 problems show MFVI overestimates variance along the minimum-eigenvalue direction of Sigma (direction of maximum data concentration) in 140/140 cases, while the maximum-eigenvalue direction reverses the comparison in 140/140 cases, demonstrating simultaneous under- and overestimation with overestimation located in high training-covariance directions; the calibration identity is verified matrix-exactly.

claims.claim: In a pathological rank-1 training-data subspace scenario, as dimensionality increases the MFVI posterior's predictive variance converges to the prior variance, effectively discarding training information (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: Rank-1 design with uniformly spread direction u_i=1/sqrt(d) swept from d=2 to d=131,072: exact/prior stays flat at 0.166667 while MFVI/prior rises monotonically from 0.285714 to 0.999962, validated against direct matrix inversion (max discrepancy 1.75e-15); sparse-direction negative control (u=e_1) shows no pathology, confirming the mechanism depends on spreading across coordinates.

claims.claim: Temperature-scaled posteriors (cold posteriors, T<1) correct the predictive-variance overestimation and improve in-distribution predictions, while T>1 benefits out-of-distribution performance, offering a novel explanation for the Cold Posterior Effect.
claims.evidence: Basis-function regression (n=40, d=40, 12 seeds) shows MFVI predictive variance 1.7267x exact, and temperature sweep over 60 values finds median optimal T=0.104 with 12/12 seeds below 1 for in-distribution; two fresh 16-seed regimes (n=80-120, d=80) confirm ID median T*=0.08-0.11 (32/32 below 1) and OOD median T*=8.2-10.3 (32/32 above 1), all scored by exact Gaussian predictive log-likelihood.

claims.claim: Experiments on basis function regression and UCI datasets show optimal temperatures below 1 for in-distribution test points and above 1 for out-of-distribution test points, consistent with the theoretical predictions (Section 6, UCI experiments).
claims.evidence: Basis-function regression shows ID median T*=0.104 (12/12 below 1) and OOD median T*=4.201 (10/12 above 1); UCI experiments on 9 datasets (27 paired runs) show ID T*<1 in 25-27/27 runs and OOD T*>ID T* in 27/27 runs, though OOD median T*=0.7197 does not itself exceed 1; the directional prediction (OOD warmer than ID) is confirmed across both experiment types.

ProCreations/diffusion-bridge-flow-match.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from 140+ Gaussian linear-model problems, rank-1 sweeps to dimension 131,072, and temperature sweeps on basis-function regression and 9 UCI datasets, all with closed-form validation and negative controls. The core theoretical claims about MFVI variance behavior are strongly supported, while the temperature-optimality pattern is confirmed directionally across both synthetic and real-data experiments.

ProCreations/repro-simplemem-efficient-l.paper_title: Optimal Unconstrained Self-Distillation in Ridge Regression: Strict Improvements, Precise Asymptotics, and One-Shot Tuning

claims.claim: Theorem 2.2 proves that for any nonstationary ridge penalty λ (i.e., R'(λ) ≠ 0), the optimally mixed self-distilled student strictly improves on the teacher's squared prediction risk, with optimal mixing weight ξ*(λ) = -(λ/2)·R'(λ)/D(λ) obeying sign(ξ*(λ)) = -sign(R'(λ)) (Section 2.3, Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: Across 3,456 nonstationary cells (12 designs × 4 risk metrics × 72 λ values at n=260, p=72), the closed-form ξ*(λ) yields strict risk improvement in every cell (minimum gain 3.69e-9), the reconstructed weight matches the direct quadratic optimum to 8.12e-11, and the sign rule sign(ξ*) = -sign(R') passes in all cells.

claims.claim: The optimal mixing weight ξ*(λ) can be negative, corresponding to a 'pro-learning' regime under over-regularization (λ > λ*), as opposed to the 'anti-learning' regime (ξ* > 1) identified in prior work by Das and Sanghavi (2023) (Section 2.3).
claims.evidence: 1,838 of 3,456 optimal weights are negative (most negative: -21.2065), with sign changes observed between λ=0.1862 (ξ*=0.1049) and λ=0.2154 (ξ*=-0.0536), and the sign identity to the ridge-risk derivative holding in all cells.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 derives exact deterministic equivalents for the optimal self-distillation risk R*_sd(λ) and mixing weight ξ*(λ) in the proportional asymptotics regime (n, p → ∞, p/n → γ) under general anisotropic covariance and deterministic signals (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The full κ-fixed-point and resolvent functionals of Theorem 3.1 are implemented and compared against simulation under AR1 anisotropic covariance with a deterministic misaligned signal; median relative errors are R: 1.11%, ξ*: 3.23%, R*_sd: 1.06%, and errors shrink with n (ξ* error from 6.40% at n=400 to 1.66% at n=1600), the signature of a correct asymptotic equivalent. Concentration at n^{-1/2} is also confirmed across four anisotropic spectra.

claims.claim: In the isotropic-signal setting, Corollary 3.2 shows the optimal mixing weight changes sign exactly at λ* := γσ²/r², with ξ*(λ) < 0 for λ > λ* and ξ*(λ) > 0 for λ < λ* (Section 3.2, Corollary 3.2).
claims.evidence: The zero-crossing of ξ*(λ) computed from the Theorem 3.1 deterministic equivalents (isotropic Σ=I, isotropic signal) is located by bisection without referencing the predicted threshold, and matches λ*=γσ²/r² to relative error ≤ 2e-15 across five configurations spanning γ∈{0.5,1,2}, σ²∈{0.5,1,2}, r²∈{1,2,4}, with the sign rule and strict-improvement statement holding in all cases.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proposes a one-shot generalized cross-validation (GCV) estimator of the optimal mixing weight ξ* that is consistent in proportional asymptotics and avoids grid search, sample splitting, or refitting (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: A one-shot GCV estimator (Eqs 17–19) is evaluated over 216 cells (4 sample sizes from n=200 to 1600, 3 λ values, 18 repeats, p/n=0.08 fixed) with no grid search, splitting, or refitting; mean weight error decays with log-log slope -0.502 and mean excess risk with slope -0.986, consistent with the claimed n^{-1/2} and n^{-1} rates.

claims.claim: A curvature-based sufficient condition (Proposition 2.3, Eq. 10) predicts whether the self-distilled risk's global minimum over λ is strictly smaller than the teacher's; this test is verified exactly on all four real-data experiments (BlogFeedback, Communities and Crime, CIFAR10, Air Quality) in Table 2.
claims.evidence: Paired native replays of pinned author code reproduce all four Table 2 rows exactly (BlogFeedback yes/yes, Communities 20/80 no/no, CIFAR10 no/no, Air Quality yes/yes), and independent spectral recomputation of the curvature condition D(λ*) < (λ*²/2)R''(λ*) and global minima agrees; the Communities protocol mismatch (paper 20/80 vs released 5/95) is disclosed and both protocols run separately without conflation.

ProCreations/repro-simplemem-efficient-l.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims through independent implementations, finite-sample diagnostics, and paired native replays, with error analysis showing convergence behavior consistent with the paper's asymptotic predictions. The reproduction is notably thorough in its controls, protocol-mismatch disclosure, and multi-spectrum anisotropic testing.

ProCreations/repro-nanoquant-efficient-s.paper_title: Fair Decisions from Calibrated Scores: Achieving Optimal Classification While Satisfying Sufficiency

claims.claim: Even perfectly group-calibrated scores, including true class-conditional probabilities, provably violate predictive parity after thresholding, per Definitions 2.1 and 2.3 of sufficiency and predictive parity (Section 2, Definitions 2.1, 2.3).
claims.evidence: Six exactly group-calibrated finite-score populations (calibration residual ≤1.11e-16) all show nonzero PPV/FOR gaps after a common 0.5 threshold (gaps up to 0.27218); an exhaustive control over 180 deterministic rule pairs on the paper example finds minimum achievable gap of 0.01818, confirming randomization is needed.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows that for a fixed selection rate, the optimal classifier applies a soft threshold to group-calibrated scores, with randomization needed at exactly one threshold boundary (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: The paper's soft-threshold construction was run on 6 distributions and cross-checked by an independently formulated SLSQP optimizer (14 multistarts) over raw randomization variables; agreement within 4.74e-10 accuracy and equality violations below 1.7e-11, with PPV/FOR gaps ≤3.66e-15.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 characterizes the boundary of the feasible region of achievable positive-predictive-value/false-omission-rate pairs as a continuous, piecewise curve composed of hyperbolic arcs and line segments (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The complete attainable PPV/FOR boundary was traced from finite score atoms across all six cases and agrees with the predicted hyperbolic-arc and line-segment structure at all sampled points.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 traces the intersection of group-specific feasible PPV/FOR regions to construct the optimal classifier satisfying sufficiency exactly (Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 was implemented to intersect group-specific feasible regions; returned classifiers have sufficiency gaps ≤3.66e-15 and match an independent raw-variable constrained optimizer within 4.74e-10 on accuracy and 8.05e-10 on separation-deviation objective.

claims.claim: A COMPAS case study demonstrates that optimal fair classifiers under sufficiency generally require group-specific decision thresholds rather than a single universal threshold (Section 7).
claims.evidence: COMPAS experiment on real ProPublica data (3,075 test records, isotonic-calibrated logistic regression) shows optimal group-specific thresholds differ by 0.08–0.13 across FPR-gap constraints, while forcing a single universal threshold causes utility losses of 52–341; the unconstrained sufficiency-only optimum uses one threshold, confirming the mechanism that an added fairness criterion necessitates group-specific thresholds.

ProCreations/repro-nanoquant-efficient-s.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence for all five claims: exact calibrated-score constructions and exhaustive controls for Claim 1, independent optimizer cross-checks for Claims 2–4, and a real COMPAS experiment for Claim 5. The main limitation is that theoretical claims are validated numerically on finite-score examples rather than via formal proof, and COMPAS calibration residuals (up to 0.08) are non-negligible but expected with finite data.

nkapila6/bA6BgSbaUi.paper_title: How much can language models memorize?

claims.claim: GPT-style transformers trained on uniform random data show an empirical memorization-capacity plateau of about 3.6 bits per parameter (Figure 1)
claims.evidence: Real training runs were executed on uniform random data, but at drastically reduced scale: 7,728-param and 824K-param models with 500–10K steps, versus the paper's millions of parameters and ~1M steps. Measured capacity was 0.80–1.24 bits/param, far below the claimed 3.6 bits/param, so the specific quantitative claim is not reproduced.

claims.claim: Capacity estimates across model widths and depths support a roughly linear bits-per-parameter scaling law, with bfloat16 to float32 increasing capacity only modestly (Table 1)
claims.evidence: No bits-per-parameter measurements across varying widths and depths are presented; the only evidence is a single 4.8M-param model showing test loss decreasing with dataset size, which does not address the linear scaling law or the bfloat16-vs-float32 comparison.

claims.claim: On text data, unintended memorization rises with model size but decreases once models begin generalizing relative to an oracle reference model (Figure 2)
claims.evidence: The experiment varies dataset size (not model size) with a single 824K-param reference model, so the core claim that memorization rises with model size is not tested. The description also references 'random data' rather than text, and the U-shaped memorization-to-generalization curve was not reproduced.

claims.claim: Double descent begins when dataset information content exceeds estimated model capacity in both synthetic bitstrings and text experiments (Figures 3 and 4)
claims.evidence: The claim page contains only the claim description and evidence-level notes; no experimental runs, outputs, or numerical results are shown for double descent on either synthetic bitstrings or text.

claims.claim: The paper derives and evaluates scaling-law predictions for membership inference as a function of model capacity and dataset size (Figure 7)
claims.evidence: The claim page contains only the claim description with no executed experiments or numerical outputs. The scorecard references 'source-level checks' and a 40.9% average error figure, but no training runs or membership inference measurements are documented.

nkapila6/bA6BgSbaUi.overall: This logbook provides only toy-scale experiments for Claim 1 (models 100–1000× smaller than the paper, yielding 0.80–1.24 bits/param vs. 3.6), and does not present substantive experimental evidence for Claims 2–5. The reproduction is insufficient to verify or falsify any of the paper's five claims at the intended scale.

nkapila6/2RJN5vDHG0.paper_title: Rare Event Analysis of Large Language Models

claims.claim: The paper formulates LLM text generation as a stochastic process and adapts rare-event methods including importance sampling, reweighted distributions, and transition path sampling (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook only performs a keyword search in paper.txt for the terms 'stochastic process', 'importance sampling', 'reweighted', and 'transition path'. No implementation is run or verified; this is a textual assertion check, not experimental evidence that the formulation or methods are correct.

claims.claim: Annealed transition path sampling generates biased text-completion trajectories that explore rare high- or low-observable completions (Figure 1, Figure 2, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook loads the authors' released trajectory data (ari_trajectories.json, 10 walkers × 400K steps) and computes that the high-ARI biased chain reaches ARI=15.0 (2.6× beyond the unbiased 99th percentile of 5.88), while the low-ARI chain reaches ARI=-3.76 (below the 1st percentile of -0.40), with monotonically increasing mean ARI across bias strengths.

claims.claim: MBAR reweighting reconstructs the true distribution of observables such as automated readability index from biased simulations (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements a clean-room importance sampling reweighting applied to the authors' released trajectory data. For ARI, the reweighted mean (2.524) closely matches the unbiased mean (2.542) versus the biased mean (2.749), with a KS test p-value of 0.277. The log-probs observable failed due to numerical overflow, but the claim specifically cites ARI as the example observable.

claims.claim: Error analysis compares confidence intervals for MBAR rare-event estimates against direct sampling estimates (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook computes bootstrap CIs for direct sampling and effective-sample-size-based CIs for MBAR reweighting on the authors' released data. For ARI, MBAR CI half-width=0.022 vs direct=0.106; for log-probs, MBAR=0.559 vs direct=2.088. However, only 20 bootstrap iterations and 500 subsampled points were used, and different CI methods were applied to MBAR vs direct, weakening rigor.

claims.claim: Biasing toward readability uncovers rare completions far beyond the training-data quantiles and correlates with token repetition behavior (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: The quantile analysis is supported by concrete numbers (30.9% of high-ARI biased samples exceed the 99th percentile, max ARI=15.0), but the token repetition correlation is verified only by checking that the paper text contains the word 'repetition' near 'Figure 5' — no token-level data was analyzed and no experimental correlation was computed.

nkapila6/2RJN5vDHG0.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from the authors' released trajectory data supporting claims 2, 3, and 4, but claims 1 and 5 rely on keyword searches of the paper text rather than experimental verification. The reproduction is an artifact audit of released data rather than an independent end-to-end re-run of the TPS simulations, and several implementations use small subsamples or simplified methods.

ashish-soni08/Repro-Data-Provenance-Audi.paper_title: Data Provenance Auditing of Fine-Tuned Large Language Models with a Text-Preserving Technique

claims.claim: The ranking-test detection procedure provides a provable false-positive-rate bound of FPR ≤ k/K, where k is the acceptance threshold and K is the candidate watermark set size (typically K=100) (Section III-E).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo simulation with 50,000 trials under H0 confirms FPR ≈ k/K for multiple (k,K) configurations: (1,100)→0.0095, (5,100)→0.0490, (1,20)→0.0505, (2,50)→0.0403, all within bound and close to theoretical value.

claims.claim: Across more than 18,810 document-level challenges using counterfactual (left-out) watermarks, the method achieves 100% TPR at 0% FPR, with no spurious detections from watermarks not actually used in fine-tuning (Section IV-E, Table III).
claims.evidence: The 18,810-challenge experiment was not reproduced. The logbook verifies the combinatorial union-bound argument (~1.13e-5 per output) and runs a random-stream proxy (5000 trials, 0 hits, not a fine-tuned LLM), plus a reduced-scale dense Mistral-7B LoRA probe (40 docs, 300 steps) showing 39/40 target hits and 0 counterfactual hits — a mechanism check, not the paper's empirical scale.

claims.claim: On the Blog1k dataset, first successful detection occurs with as few as 20 watermarked documents (2% of the fine-tuning corpus), while the Poems dataset requires 30-40 marked documents before initial detection (Section IV-B, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The first-detection threshold (20 docs for Blog1k, 30–40 for Poems) was never tested. No sweep over marked-document counts was performed. The dense Mistral probe shows 39/40 hits at 40 docs but uses a different (denser, marked-only) training recipe and does not establish the minimum detection threshold.

claims.claim: Per-document hit probability differs sharply by fine-tuned model on Blog1k with 50 marked documents: Mistral achieves p≈0.588 versus LLaMA's p≈0.940, yielding false-negative rates of roughly 10^-20 and 10^-42 respectively (Section IV-B, Table II).
claims.evidence: The formula p_FN=(1-p)^{λX} was checked against Table II values: Mistral's p=0.588 yields 5.56e-20 (matches table's 5.6e-20), but LLaMA's p=0.940 yields ~8.08e-62, inconsistent with the table's 7.7e-42. Critically, the per-document hit probabilities p were not independently re-estimated via fine-tuning, so the core empirical claim remains unverified.

claims.claim: The method remains detectable even when watermarked documents comprise less than 0.33% of a 15k-document fine-tuning corpus, maintaining an average per-document detection rate above 45% (Section IV-C, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The 15k-document fine-tuning experiment was explicitly not run ('Did not retrain on 15k-document corpora (cost)'). The scaled Mistral job uses only 200-document corpora as a mechanism probe and does not address the <0.33% marked-fraction regime at all.

claims.claim: The watermarking scheme uses an alphabet of 4 invisible Unicode characters (U+200B, U+200C, U+200D, U+2060) with watermarks of n=8 syllables (m=4 characters each, split into a 5-syllable cue and 3-syllable reply) (Section III-F).
claims.evidence: Concrete code checks confirm: alphabet is exactly [U+200B, U+200C, U+200D, U+2060], n=8 syllables of m=4 chars each, cue=5 syllables (20 chars), reply=3 syllables (12 chars), text-preserving embedding (visible text unchanged), cue-only challenges exclude reply, and candidate-set cue/reply uniqueness all pass.

ashish-soni08/Repro-Data-Provenance-Audi.overall: The logbook solidly verifies the theoretical FPR bound (Claim 1) via Monte Carlo and the watermarking scheme design (Claim 6) via code-level checks. Claims 2–5 are not reproduced at paper scale: Claim 2 has only a combinatorial argument plus a reduced-scale probe, Claims 3 and 5 were never experimentally addressed, and Claim 4 only checks formula-to-table consistency without re-estimating the key hit probabilities.

nkapila6/ww57OvgpP9.paper_title: SimulCost: A Cost-Aware Benchmark and Toolkit for Automating Physics Simulations with LLMs

claims.claim: SimulCost evaluates LLM agents on cost-sensitive parameter tuning across 13 physics simulators in single-round and multi-round modes (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The public dataset contains 12/13 simulators (CGYRO absent; dataset README also says 12), all with both single_round and multi_round parquet files. An LLM experiment was run with Llama-3.3-70B on only 297 tasks (198 SR + 99 MR) out of ~4878 total, confirming benchmark functionality but at substantially reduced scale and with one simulator missing.

claims.claim: The benchmark contains 2,947 single-round tasks and 1,931 multi-round tasks across 13 solvers (Table 2).
claims.evidence: No code or output is shown that counts rows in the parquet files to verify 2,947 SR and 1,931 MR tasks. The scorecard asserts '2916 SR' but provides no supporting script or output; the Claim 2 page only discusses a 99-task multi-round LLM experiment, not task counts.

claims.claim: SimulCost distinguishes benchmarks by whether they track external tool cost, define platform-independent cost, and provide an extensible toolkit (Table 1).
claims.evidence: There is no dedicated page, code, or output for Claim 3. The scorecard asserts 'ref_cost column + FLOPs cost models + toolkit confirmed' but no script or execution output is provided to substantiate the Table 1 feature comparison.

claims.claim: The paper reports 46-65% frontier-LLM single-round success, 35-55% under high-accuracy requirements, and 72-81% multi-round success with 1.5-2.5x slower cost than traditional scanning (Abstract).
claims.evidence: The LLM experiment used Llama-3.3-70B (not frontier models), achieving 27.3% SR and 12.1% MR—well below the paper's 46-65% and 72-81% ranges—but this neither verifies nor falsifies the paper's frontier-model claims. The '35-55% high-accuracy' and '1.5-2.5x slower cost' sub-claims are not addressed at all.

nkapila6/ww57OvgpP9.overall: The logbook confirms the benchmark is structurally functional (12/13 simulators with both modes, LLM evaluation pipeline works) via a small-scale experiment on 297 tasks with a 70B model, but does not verify task counts, Table 1 features, or the paper's reported performance numbers. Multiple inconsistencies exist between the scorecard, sources page, and actual experimental output (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B vs Llama-3.3-70B, '5%' vs 27.3%).

ashish-soni08/Repro-CapBencher-Give-Your.paper_title: CapBencher: Give Your LLM Benchmark a Built-in Alarm for Test-Set Overfitting

claims.claim: CapBencher caps Bayes accuracy by injecting randomness among logically correct answers, so above-cap performance can signal leakage or gaming (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook runs a synthetic simulation with random integers (0–999) and L=2 ±1 capping on n=1000 samples, showing an honest Bayes agent scores ~50.1% and a raw oracle scores 0% on capped labels. No real benchmark data or LLMs are used; this is a simplified demonstration of the capping mechanism, not a reproduction on actual GSM8K or other benchmarks.

claims.claim: Capped benchmark accuracy remains monotonically related to original benchmark accuracy for tracking and ranking LLM improvement (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Claim 2 is not listed in the logbook's pages and no experiment addresses the monotonic relationship between capped and original benchmark accuracy. The claim is entirely unaddressed.

claims.claim: The paper uses exact binomial-test p-values rather than asymptotic approximations for contamination detection (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements scipy.stats.binomtest (exact binomial) at n=1319 with 56.52% accuracy, yielding p≈1.39e-6, and compares it to a normal approximation (p≈1.43e-6), concretely demonstrating that exact binomial p-values are used and produce the expected flagging behavior at the 5% level.

claims.claim: In a model-merge hacking simulation, the merged model's 56.52% accuracy is flagged as contaminated at the 5% significance level (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The actual GPU merge-hacking experiment on Qwen2.5-0.5B failed (≤1.5% accuracy, not 56.52%). The 'statistical reconstruction' is a pure simulation with no model merging: it assigns 100% accuracy to a hypothetical merged agent and plugs the paper's 56.52% directly into the binomial test. This demonstrates the detection logic on a proxy setup but does not reproduce the model-merge hacking simulation from Table 1.

ashish-soni08/Repro-CapBencher-Give-Your.overall: The logbook verifies the exact binomial test methodology (Claim 3) at the paper's scale, but only provides toy/synthetic demonstrations of the Bayes capping mechanism (Claim 1) and merge-hacking detection logic (Claim 4), with the actual model-merge experiment failing entirely. Claim 2 (monotonicity for ranking) is never addressed.

neonforestmist/linearizer-repro.paper_title: Who Said Neural Networks Aren't Linear?

claims.claim: A Linearizer is defined as f(x) = g_y^{-1}(A g_x(x)) for invertible neural networks g_x, g_y and linear operator A, making f linear under induced vector-space operations (Section 2.1-2.2).
claims.evidence: The only visible evidence for this definitional/linearity claim is a d=36, n=640 synthetic experiment showing MSE dropping from 4.6938 to 0.1027 over 900 SGD steps; this demonstrates optimization convergence in a small-dimensional setting but does not directly verify the linearity property under induced vector-space operations.

claims.claim: The composition of two Linearizers with compatible spaces is itself a Linearizer, with the composed operator obtained by matrix multiplication of the underlying cores (Proposition 2.5).
claims.evidence: On 12 real photo/style pairs using official pretrained style networks, sequential application of two style cores (candy→mosaic) agrees with direct common-latent core composition to worst max error 3.576e-07, while a mismatched bridge map fails by at least 0.117 RMS, directly confirming that composition equals matrix multiplication of cores.

claims.claim: A Linearizer f is idempotent, i.e. f(f(x)) = f(x), if and only if its core matrix A is an idempotent matrix (A^2 = A), enabling architectural (rather than optimization-based) enforcement of idempotent generative networks (Lemma 4.2, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: A 454,512-parameter invertible MNIST model with a fixed rank-588 projector core achieves max global idempotence error 2.861e-06 across held-out digits and multiple OOD domains, while replacing projected eigenvalues 0→0.5 (breaking A²=A) yields non-idempotence of at least 0.0134 RMS, testing both directions of the iff on real data.

claims.claim: In the one-step flow-matching application, the product of per-step update operators over hundreds of integration steps collapses into a single operator, enabling one-step diffusion sampling without retraining (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Using the official 9.9M-parameter MNIST flow checkpoint without retraining, the cached Euler product over 100 and 256 steps matches iterative sampling to worst image max error 4.274e-05, with proxy-FID 134.89 vs 1141.43 for noise control and all 10 classes covered; the RK sampler fails (0.6135 difference) but is transparently reported as an implementation limitation of the cached RK matrix.

claims.claim: Modular style transfer is achieved by fixing the shared encoders g_x, g_y while swapping only the style-specific core matrix A_style, allowing algebraic interpolation between styles from a single trained network (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Modular style transfer is demonstrated on 12 real photo/style pairs at 64px with a 20,916-parameter model trained from scratch, showing correct-core wins (11/12 feature, 12/12 Gram) and style interpolation with zero endpoint error, but the reduced resolution and tiny model represent a clearly simplified setup that the logbook itself acknowledges does not match full-resolution paper panels.

neonforestmist/linearizer-repro.overall: The logbook provides strong non-toy evidence for the composition (Claim 2), idempotency (Claim 3), and Euler flow-matching collapse (Claim 4) claims using official checkpoints, real MNIST data, and real photos with negative controls. The definitional linearity claim (Claim 1) and modular style transfer claim (Claim 5) are only addressed on simplified or reduced-scale setups.

ofou/Repro-Neural-Thickets-tinygrad.paper_title: Neural Thickets: Diverse Task Experts Are Dense Around Pretrained Weights

claims.claim: The paper argues that large pretrained models are surrounded by dense neighborhoods of task-specialized perturbations, unlike smaller needle-in-haystack regimes (Figure 1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Only the paper's 1D signal MLP toy (width 128, depth 5, N=200-400) was run. The tinygrad AR-MSE version shows thicket has higher discordance (0.676 vs 0.247) and larger useful ensemble gain (0.099 vs 0.002) than needle, supporting the mechanism. However, the actual claim about large pretrained models (Figures 1-2, Qwen2.5 0.5B-32B) was never tested; HF Jobs returned 402 errors and no LLM-scale landscape experiment was executed.

claims.claim: Solution density and diversity around Qwen2.5 instruction-tuned models increase with model scale (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B were probed on GPU (N=48 perturbations, σ=0.001, teacher-forced NLL on synthetic arithmetic), yielding densities 0.3125, 0.4167, 0.3333 — the trend is non-monotonic (3B dips below 1.5B). This is heavily downscaled from the paper (N=48 vs 5000, synthetic arithmetic vs Countdown/GSM8K, only up to 3B vs 32B) and does not clearly reproduce the claimed monotonic increase with scale.

claims.claim: Randomly sampled perturbations exhibit diverse task specialties rather than all acting as generalists (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: In the 1D toy, specialist_frac among improving thicket seeds is 1.0 with discordance 0.676 vs 0.247 for needle. On downscaled Qwen2.5 (N=48, synthetic tasks), specialist_frac is 1.0 across 0.5B/1.5B/3B with discordance ranging 0.185-0.705. However, the specialist metric is nearly trivially satisfied (any improving seed whose best task exceeds the median counts), the LLM experiments use only 3 synthetic tasks at N=48, and the paper's full multi-task spectra (Figure 4) were not reproduced.

claims.claim: RandOpt samples random parameter perturbations, selects top performers, and ensembles predictions; it matches or exceeds PPO, GRPO, ES, and related baselines in many LLM post-training settings (Algorithm 1, Figure 6).
claims.evidence: Only a 1D signal prediction proxy was run: RandOpt vs ES vs SGD (no PPO, no GRPO, no LLM experiments). Results were inconsistent across configurations — in one tinygrad run RandOpt's best_mse (0.188) was worse than ES (0.104), while in another (AR-MSE ranking) RandOpt (0.024) beat ES (0.178). The claim specifically concerns LLM post-training settings where zero experiments were conducted.

claims.claim: RandOpt accuracy improves with population size and depends on sufficient pretrained model scale (Figure 7, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: Population scaling was tested only on the 1D toy: in the AR-MSE-ranked tinygrad run, best_mse improved from 0.039 (N=20) to 0.006 (N=200), but in the next-step-ranked run results were non-monotonic (0.059→0.430→0.188→0.051). Scale dependence was weakly probed via width 32 vs 128 on 1D MLPs, showing gains at both scales. No LLM-scale population or scale-dependence experiments (Figures 7-8) were run.

ofou/Repro-Neural-Thickets-tinygrad.overall: The logbook provides toy-scale mechanistic evidence on 1D signal prediction MLPs and heavily downscaled Qwen2.5 probes (N=48, synthetic arithmetic, up to 3B only), but none of the paper's core LLM-scale claims (Figures 1-2, 3 to 32B, Figure 6 PPO/GRPO comparison) were reproduced at paper scope due to persistent resource constraints. Results are mixed even within the toy setups, with several inconsistencies across metric choices and runs.

claims.claim: WIRE applies rotary position encodings to graphs by using Laplacian spectral coordinates to define graph-dependent rotation angles (Figure 1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Independent implementation of WIRE rotation on path graph P10 confirms the method computes Laplacian eigenvectors, uses them as spectral coordinates, and applies RoPE-style 2D rotations; spectral coordinates match Laplacian eigenvectors (diff < 1e-10) and norm preservation holds for all nodes.

claims.claim: The WIRE transformation is equivariant to node-order permutations up to sign flips and rotations in degenerate eigenspaces (Lemma 1).
claims.evidence: On non-degenerate path graph P10, equivariance error is 1.56e-15 after accounting for sign flips (exhaustive search over 2^3 sign combinations). On degenerate cycle graph C10, direct equivariance fails as expected (error 2.71), but degenerate eigenspace agreement is verified via projection test (diff < 1e-8), matching the lemma's statement about rotations in degenerate subspaces.

claims.claim: Regular RoPE is recovered as a special case of WIRE on grid graphs with appropriate learnable frequencies (Theorem 2, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Path graph P20 Laplacian eigenvectors match the DCT-II sinusoidal basis with correlations of 1.000000 for all 9 tested eigenvectors; 2D grid 5x4 eigenvectors factorize as products of 1D path eigenvectors (correlations 1.000000); first non-constant eigenvector is monotonic along the path, providing the bijective position mapping required by Theorem 2.

claims.claim: WIRE asymptotically depends on graph effective resistance under the paper's spectral-feature assumptions (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The theoretical identity R(i,j) = ||r_i - r_j||^2 (where r_i = [u_k[i]/sqrt(lambda_k)]) is correctly identified and numerically verified: Pearson correlations between WIRE spectral feature distance and effective resistance are 0.9989 (P10), 0.9907 (C10), and 0.9605 (G8), with the sub-1.0 values explained by using only m=5 of N-1 spectral features.

claims.claim: Experiments report WIRE improvements on synthetic monochromatic-subgraph and shortest-path tasks, point-cloud transformers, and efficient graph transformer benchmarks (Table 1, Table 2, Table 3, Table 4).
claims.evidence: Only 2 of 4 experimental settings were attempted, using a clearly simplified setup (d_model=32, 2 layers, 1 head, 50 epochs, 1000 train graphs). WIRE did not improve on either task (monochromatic: -5.5%, shortest-path: -1.2%); point-cloud and graph-transformer benchmarks were not attempted. The negative results on this toy setup are not definitive given the large gap from the paper's scale.

nkapila6/trn64znfNx.overall: The logbook provides strong independent verification of all four theoretical claims (WIRE definition, equivariance, RoPE special case, effective resistance dependence) through clean implementations and numerical checks on small graphs. The experimental claim was only partially addressed on a heavily simplified setup where WIRE failed to improve, leaving the full experimental validation unconfirmed.

ashish-soni08/Repro-Q-Sched-Quantization.paper_title: Q-Sched: Pushing the Boundaries of Few-Step Diffusion Models with Quantization-Aware Scheduling

claims.claim: Q-Sched modifies the few-step diffusion scheduler rather than the model weights for post-training quantization (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirms via code inspection of the upstream repo (TCDScheduler applying model_coeff/sample_coeff scaling) and a runtime demonstration that PCM-8Step LoRA weights are loaded unchanged, W4A8 quantization is applied to the UNet, and only scheduler coefficients are grid-searched — concretely showing the scheduler-not-weights paradigm.

claims.claim: The JAQ loss combines text-image compatibility with an image-quality metric and is described as reference-free with only a handful of calibration prompts (Abstract).
claims.evidence: The logbook used a proxy JAQ loss (CLIPScore + 2·CLIP-IQA) instead of the paper's full stack (HPSv2/AQMap), with 8 hand-curated prompts. While reference-free and few-prompt, the logbook explicitly states this verifies the protocol, not the exact JAQ formula.

claims.claim: On Stable Diffusion v1-5 few-step models, W4A8 Q-Sched reports lower FID than the listed FP16 original schedules for 4-step LCM and 8-step PCM settings (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Only PCM-8Step was tested (LCM-4Step blocked by missing lcm_scheduler.py), with N=256 images and non-COCO FID references. FID values of ~315–316 are anomalously high, indicating a broken evaluation pipeline. The direction (Q-Sched 315.16 < FP16 316.31) matches but only on a clearly reduced-scale, partial setup.

claims.claim: For SDXL-scale models, Q-Sched is evaluated under W4A8 and W8A8 compression, described as 4x and 8x model-size reductions compared with FP16 (Table 2).
claims.evidence: No SDXL-scale experiments were attempted; the logbook's scope table lists SDXL/FLUX under 'full replication' as not attempted.

claims.claim: The paper reports 15.5% FID improvement over FP16 4-step LCM and 16.6% improvement over FP16 8-step PCM (Abstract).
claims.evidence: PCM-8Step only was run at N=256 with non-COCO references, yielding a 0.37% FID improvement vs the claimed 16.6%; LCM-4Step (15.5%) was not run at all. The evaluation setup is too different from the paper's COCO-30k protocol to confirm or refute the specific percentages.

ashish-soni08/Repro-Q-Sched-Quantization.overall: The logbook provides code-level and runtime confirmation that Q-Sched modifies scheduler coefficients rather than weights (Claim 1), but all quantitative FID claims are evaluated on a severely reduced setup (N=256, non-COCO references, proxy JAQ loss, only PCM-8Step) with anomalously high FID values (~315) that undermine comparability. SDXL experiments (Claim 4) were never attempted.

nkapila6/7UEBX1KU1y.paper_title: Conditional Equivalence of DPO and RLHF: Assumptions, Failure Modes, and Provable Alignment

claims.claim: The paper proves DPO-RLHF equivalence is conditional on the RLHF-optimal policy preferring human-preferred responses (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Numerical verification on a 2-response bandit MDP (1 prompt, closed-form RLHF optimum) confirms: when assumption holds, delta_pi*=1.847>0 and DPO gradient weight=0.269 (strong); when assumption fails, delta_pi*=-1.197<0 and DPO gradient at U boundary=0.100 (vanishing). Multi-seed (1000 seeds) and Monte Carlo (5000 samples) show 14.6% and 61.9% violation rates. However, this is a clearly simplified setup, not a full proof verification.

claims.claim: When the equivalence assumption fails, DPO optimizes relative advantage over the reference policy rather than absolute human-preference alignment (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Toy 2-response bandit counterexample: with pi_ref(y_w)=0.1, delta_piref=-2.197, DPO loss at delta_pi=0 (indifferent policy) is 0.1054, already near zero, showing DPO achieves low loss without preferring y_w. This supports the claim but on a simplified setup.

claims.claim: The paper characterizes undesirable solution spaces in which policies reduce DPO loss while preferring dispreferred responses (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Toy 2-response bandit demonstration: with delta_piref=-2.197, the undesirable space U=(-2.197, 0) is non-empty. A policy at delta_pi=-0.5 has DPO loss 0.1682 < reference loss 0.6931 while preferring y_l. Gradient weight weakens as delta_pi approaches 0. Real numbers but simplified setup.

claims.claim: Constrained Preference Optimization augments RLHF with constraints and derives a stationary DPO-like loss with an adaptive reference-based margin (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Only source-level text matching (grep for labels like 'def:margin_rlhf', 'eq:cpo_loss_practical', 'cor:gamma_star' in .tex source). No numerical verification of the CPO derivation, the stationary property, or the guarantee theorems was performed.

claims.claim: The paper gives a soft-margin ranking interpretation showing DPO can implement margin ranking with potentially negative targets (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Only source-level text matching (grep for 'prop:dpo_hinge', 'hinge', 'negative target' in .tex source). No numerical verification of the soft-margin ranking interpretation or the negative target margin property was performed.

claims.claim: Experiments on standard benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance for CPO (Section 6).
claims.evidence: The SOTA benchmark claim (AlpacaEval 2 WR 25.15%, LC 26.57%, Arena-Hard 32.6% with Llama-3-8B-Instruct) was never independently verified—only text matching in the .tex source. The toy 2-response bandit experiments (1-parameter logistic policy, 200 trials) verify CPO's gradient properties but do not address benchmark performance at all.

agharsallah/ffuphw7jqx-logbook.paper_title: Minimax Optimal Strategy for Delayed Observations in Online Reinforcement Learning

claims.claim: For the known-delay-distribution setting, the proposed algorithm achieves regret O~(H√((D_max∧B)SAK) + HBSA) for tabular MDPs with delayed observations, where D_max is the maximum delay and B is the branching factor (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: 24 configurations (S∈{4,5}, A=2, B∈{2,3}, D∈{2,3}, H=5, K=5000) show empirical regret below the Theorem-1 bound with ratio ≤0.947; scaling to S=50, K=200000 yields √K exponent 0.442 (R²=0.972), and the (D_max∧B) saturation is directly reproduced (regret flat in D beyond B at fixed B=2: 48930→19243).

claims.claim: For the unknown-delay-distribution setting, the algorithm achieves regret O~(H√((D_max∧B)SAK) + H√(Δ_maxSAK) + H(B+Δ_max)SA), extending the known-delay result (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: 12 configurations show unknown-delay regret ≥ known-delay (mean ratio 1.467); a large-scale Δ_max sweep (S·A=250, K=100000) confirms the extra term scales as √Δ_max (fitted exponent 0.500, R²=0.9999) and each fixed-Δ_max curve grows as √K, isolating the H√(Δ_max SAK) term.

claims.claim: A matching lower bound of Ω(H√(D̃SAK/log D̃)) is established for constant-delay MDPs, where D̃ = min{D_max, H/4, B/2, S/4-1}, showing the upper bounds are optimal up to log factors (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The Fano/Assouad lower-bound floor is reconstructed and checked across configurations (S=20, D̃∈{2,3,4} and large-scale S=100, A=10, H=50, K=100000); the floor matches Ω(H√(D̃SAK/log D̃)) with √K exponent 0.500 (R²=1.0) and the log-penalized D̃ dependence (exponent 0.319, R²=0.999), and the delay floor exceeds the delay-free floor (722.7 vs 515.7).

claims.claim: The result improves on the prior bound of Chen et al. (2023) by a factor of H^(1/2) D_max^2, tightening O~(H^{3/2}D_max^{5/2}√(SAK)) down to O~(H√(D_maxSAK)) (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The ratio (Chen'23 bound)/(this-work bound) = H^{3/2}D^{5/2}√(SAK) / (H√(D·SAK)) = √H·D² is confirmed as an exact algebraic identity over 128 grid configurations with maximum deviation 0.0 (tol 1e-9).

claims.claim: The framework is generalized to MDPs with partially known dynamics, yielding regret O~(H√(K∑_{z∈Z_eff}(log|Y|)∧B(z)) + H∑B(z)) (Theorem 5, Section 8).
claims.evidence: 24 configurations with known+unknown kernel split show regret below the generalized bound (ratio ≤1.494); large-scale sweep (S=50, K=100000, |Z_eff|=1..5) confirms regret grows with |Z_eff| (936→7633) and stays below the Theorem-5 bound (ratio ≤0.77), with known states incurring zero learning cost.

agharsallah/ffuphw7jqx-logbook.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence on synthetic tabular MDPs at reasonable scale (up to S=50–100, K=100000–200000) supporting all five theoretical claims, including √K scaling, (D_max∧B) saturation, √Δ_max dependence, the lower-bound form, and the |Z_eff| generalization. The verification is primarily numerical checking of regret bounds rather than formal proof reproduction, but the experimental design is sound and the scales are non-trivial.

VINAY-UMRETHE/paper-ZVyd4r9Xl5.paper_title: Beyond Majority Voting: LLM Aggregation by Leveraging Higher-Order Information

claims.claim: The Optimal Weight (OW) algorithm assigns each LLM a weight ω_i = σ_k^{-1}(x_i) based on its accuracy x_i, and Theorem 1 proves OW is Bayes-optimal among all aggregators with access to the same first-order accuracy information (Algorithm 1, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: A 3-agent, K=3 toy simulation confirms the OW weight formula matches σ_K^{-1}(x_i) and that OW (82.43%) dominates MV (76.21%), but the setup is far smaller than the paper's and does not test optimality among all aggregators—only MV and heuristic weighting. The theorem's proof is only asserted via 'source audit,' not independently derived.

claims.claim: The Inverse Surprisingly Popular (ISP) algorithm uses only second-order information (pairwise prediction correlations, no ground-truth labels) to compute a counterfactual advantage score per label, and Theorem 2 proves the ordering E[Adv_ISP(s*)] ≥ E[Adv_MV(s*)] ≥ E[Adv_SP(s*)], i.e., ISP dominates majority voting which dominates the classical Surprisingly Popular algorithm (Algorithm 2, Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: A synthetic simulation with N=4 agents and a single correlation parameter ρ=0.4 confirms the ordering Adv_ISP (0.142) ≥ Adv_MV (0.085) ≥ Adv_SP (0.031) in one specific synthetic configuration. Theorem 2's proof is only asserted via 'source audit,' and the test covers only one correlation setting rather than a general verification.

claims.claim: In simulated experiments with N=4 agents and M=10,000 questions, ISP achieves 90.48% accuracy versus 85.13% for majority voting at K=2 answer options, and 94.45% versus 92.64% at K=4 options, with the gap shrinking at rate Θ(1/K) (simulation results section).
claims.evidence: Full reproduction at N=4, M=10,000 yields ISP 90.51% vs MV 85.15% at K=2 (paper: 90.48%/85.13%) and ISP 94.42% vs MV 92.61% at K=4 (paper: 94.45%/92.64%), closely matching. However, the Θ(1/K) rate is fit using only two K values (K=2, K=4), making the R²=0.991 fit trivially achievable and not a meaningful test of the shrinkage rate.

claims.claim: On real-world datasets, OW-L attains 73.66% accuracy on UltraFeedback, 90.37% on MMLU, and 85.78% on ARMMAN, each exceeding majority voting's 72.21%, 89.32%, and 85.24% respectively (Table 3).
claims.evidence: Evaluation uses 1,000-sample stratified subsets with cached predictions rather than full datasets. Results are close (UltraFeedback: 73.61% vs 73.66%; MMLU: 90.42% vs 90.37%; ARMMAN: 85.81% vs 85.78%), but the reduced sample size means standard errors (~1.1%) are comparable to the claimed improvements (0.6–1.4%), and the full-dataset numbers are not directly reproduced.

claims.claim: Across 16 model ensembles, OW-L outperforms majority voting in 97.92% of cases, with absolute accuracy improvements ranging from 0.54% to 14.20% (Section on real-world experiments).
claims.evidence: The reproduction finds OW-L outperforms MV in 15/16 configurations (93.75%), not the claimed 97.92%. The logbook speculates that the paper's 97.92% 'likely aggregates over finer-grained sub-splits or bootstrap samples' but provides no evidence for this. The improvement range [0.58%, 13.95%] is close to the claimed [0.54%, 14.20%], but the specific win-rate claim is not reproduced.

claims.claim: Corollary 1 connects the optimal aggregation weights to the Bradley-Terry model, showing that in the binary setting the optimal weights are proportional to the inverse logistic function of each model's accuracy (Corollary 1).
claims.evidence: The mathematical identity σ₂⁻¹(x) = logit(x) is correctly identified but only asserted, not independently proven. The empirical check is circular: OW weights are computed using the formula and then regressed against the same logit formula, yielding R²=0.999 by construction. This confirms implementation correctness but provides no independent evidence for the corollary.

VINAY-UMRETHE/paper-ZVyd4r9Xl5.overall: The logbook attempts all six claims but primarily relies on toy-scale simulations, data subsets, and source-level assertions rather than full-scale reproductions. ProCreations/repro-model-monotonicity-in.paper_title: Model Monotonicity in Autobidding Auctions: When Do Better Predictions Lead to Better Outcomes?

claims.claim: For target-CPA bidders without budget constraints using uniform bidding with multiplier mu=1 in first-price auctions, refining the prediction model (partitioning clusters into subclusters while preserving calibration) never decreases platform revenue, i.e., Rev(M_A) >= Rev(M_B) when M_A refines M_B (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: 240 calibrated coarse/fine prediction pairs with 2–5 bidders and 2–4 children per cluster show FPA revenue never decreases under refinement, with worst gap of -8.88e-16 (machine precision). Fine predictions average to coarse vectors, confirming the calibration-preserving refinement mechanism.

claims.claim: The first-price auction revenue monotonicity proof for tCPA bidders relies on convexity of f(p) = max_i(t_i · p_i) via Jensen's inequality, since model refinement corresponds to a mean-preserving spread of this convex function (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: The executable reconstructs f(p)=max_i(t_i·p_i) before and after mean-preserving splits across all 240 cells and records Jensen gaps; the minimum gap is -8.88e-16, confirming non-negativity consistent with convexity and the mean-preserving spread argument.

claims.claim: Uniform bidding at multiplier mu=1 is simultaneously conversion-maximizing, revenue-maximizing among equilibria, and welfare-maximizing for tCPA bidders in first-price auctions (Theorem 5.2), and welfare monotonicity follows as a corollary when per-conversion values equal targets (Corollary 5.3).
claims.evidence: 120 independently drawn FPA instances evaluate focal multipliers on a dense grid against uniform-equilibrium rivals and a separate allocation oracle; mu=1 is conversion-maximizing, revenue-dominant over deviations, and welfare-equal to the oracle when values equal targets in every cell.

claims.claim: There exist instances with tCPA bidders where second-price (VCG) auctions exhibit non-monotonicity in both revenue and welfare under model refinement, with a constructed counterexample showing a simultaneous 6.2% decrease in both metrics (Theorem 5.8).
claims.evidence: The VCG counterexample is reconstructed from the paper's coarse and refined instance, yielding revenue and welfare both falling from 3.23 to 3.03, a 6.19% simultaneous decrease matching the paper's stated values.

claims.claim: Introducing budget constraints breaks revenue monotonicity even in first-price auctions, as optimal bidder multipliers shift under refinement and reduce competitive pressure, exemplified by a counterexample with a 16.8% revenue loss (Theorem 5.10).
claims.evidence: Budget counterexample recomputed from source-displayed primitive inputs yields 5.5267555 before refinement and 4.5977168 after (16.81% loss), agreeing with the paper's four-decimal display (5.5268, 4.5977) within 6e-5.

claims.claim: A centralized, non-strategic linear-programming benchmark allocation guarantees welfare monotonicity under budget constraints via a 'lifting' construction that preserves feasibility across refined partitions (Theorem 5.11), and the paper's overall characterization identifies exactly three settings where monotonicity holds (Table 1).
claims.evidence: 80 independent coarse and refined allocation LPs explicitly lift each coarse allocation to child clusters, verify all supply/budget constraints, and reconstruct identical objectives (worst refined-minus-coarse gap -8.88e-16); table_characterization.csv records exactly three positive monotonicity settings matching Table 1.

ProCreations/repro-model-monotonicity-in.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence across 240 FPA refinement checks, 120 multiplier-optimality tests, two exact counterexample reconstructions, and 80 LP-lifting experiments, all using independently implemented executables rather than author code. The experiments test the actual auction mechanisms and refinement processes from the paper at reasonable scale with consistent results.

Firemedic15/repro-on-the-ability-of-tran.paper_title: On the Ability of Transformers to Verify Plans

claims.claim: For delete-free and well-formed planning domains with a fixed universe of objects, plan verification lies in C-RASP[Pos], which guarantees length generalization for decoder-only transformers (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies the proof mechanism (well-formed truth values = parity of touch-counts) on the Colors domain only, with 0 mismatches across 3,000 random plans. This confirms the key idea on one illustrative domain but does not constitute a full proof of the general theorem across all delete-free/well-formed domains.

claims.claim: For general STRIPS domains under a fixed universe, there exist instances where the verification language L_D,O falls outside C-RASP[Pos], meaning length generalization is not guaranteed (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook constructs concrete counterexamples showing that identical action multisets in different orders yield different final validity in 100% of 3,000 trials on the STRIPS Colors variant, directly demonstrating the FlipFlop signature that proves existence of instances outside C-RASP[Pos].

claims.claim: The paper introduces C*-RASP, an extension of C-RASP that supports simultaneous growth in sequence length and vocabulary (object count), and shows delete-free/well-formed domains satisfy L_D in C*-RASP across a variable universe of objects (Theorem 3.6, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The trained-transformer experiment intended to test variable-universe generalization was inconclusive (both variants near chance), and the logbook offers only a structural/logical argument that the parity mechanism is object-identity-independent, with no empirical or formal-proof evidence.

claims.claim: FlipFlop and PARITY-style languages are shown to lie outside C*-RASP even in the variable-universe setting (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: The vocabulary-invariance of the FlipFlop reduction was verified exactly across 3,000 trials and vocabulary sizes 2-50, confirming a component of the proof mechanism. However, the toy PARITY transformer experiment failed to learn even in-distribution (49.3% accuracy), and no full proof of Theorem 3.5 was provided.

claims.claim: Transformers trained on plans of 11-100 actions are evaluated out-of-distribution on plans of 101-200 actions across Heavy Grippers, Colors, and Lights Out domains, with well-formed variants achieving high OOD accuracy while STRIPS variants degrade and conditional-effects variants perform at chance level (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The trained GPT-2 transformers achieved only ~50-55% accuracy on both well-formed and STRIPS Colors variants with training loss still decreasing after 500 epochs, and only the Colors domain was attempted (not Heavy Grippers or Lights Out). The experiment never reached a regime where the predicted OOD gap could manifest.

claims.claim: 70% of IPC 2023 Learning Track domains are classified as well-formed, supporting broad applicability of the delete-free/well-formed length-generalization guarantee (Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: An independent semi-automated classification of all 10 IPC 2023 Learning Track domains (fetched from the official benchmarks repo) found 8/10 (80%) well-formed, closely matching the paper's reported 70%, with concrete per-domain reasoning and specific violations identified in Rovers and Satellite.

Firemedic15/repro-on-the-ability-of-tran.overall: The logbook provides exact symbolic audits that confirm the core proof mechanisms for Claims 1, 2, and 4 on the Colors domain, and an independent IPC-2023 classification that closely matches the paper's figure. However, the flagship empirical experiment (Claim 5) was undertrained and inconclusive, Claim 3 lacks empirical or formal-proof evidence, and the theory claims are verified only on illustrative domains rather than through full proofs.

ProCreations/repro-bridging-the-gap-betw.paper_title: Bridging the Gap Between Average and Discounted TD Learning

claims.claim: Under i.i.d. sampling in the double-chain formulation, the algorithm converges to a unique, sample-independent fixed point of the projected Bellman equation with sample complexity Õ(ε^-1 η^-2) (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Fixed-point certificates across 8 full-rank feature families show nonsingular matrices (min singular value 0.01636, residuals < 2.3e-17) with three separated initializations converging to the same solution; 64-state i.i.d. runs show all 16 cells improving with fitted horizon exponent -1.195 (close to the predicted inverse-T mechanism) and a duplicated-feature control confirming singularity destroys uniqueness.

claims.claim: Under Markovian sampling with constant stepsizes in the double-chain setting, the same Õ(ε^-1 η^-2) sample complexity is preserved (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Markov diagnostics run the literal update on genuine Markov trajectories (no i.i.d. resampling) across 5 chain sizes, feature dims 2–5, reversible and non-reversible transitions, with median 3.04x MSE improvement at longest horizons; the 64-state panel executes 112.64M transitions with fitted horizon exponent -1.006, directly reproducing the inverse-horizon mechanism.

claims.claim: With decaying stepsizes, the method attains convergence guarantees with no explicit dimension-dependent terms (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: A literal formula audit across 36 cells (4 condition numbers, 3 decay exponents, 3 horizons) reconstructs both branches of Theorem 4.3, confirming exponents of 1 in ε and 2 in η for ξ=1 and 1/ξ and 2/ξ for ξ<1, with explicit_dimension_factor=0 in every cell, directly verifying the absence of explicit dimension-dependent terms in the guarantee.

claims.claim: The paper reduces the condition-number dependence of average-reward TD learning from quartic (prior state of the art) to quadratic, matching the scaling known for discounted TD learning (Section 1, Table 1).
claims.evidence: Table 1 is reconstructed over 4 ε and 4 η values with the double-chain column exactly 1/(εη²) and the prior-work column exactly 1/(εη⁴), yielding ratio η⁻² in all 16 cells; the 64-state empirical panel independently shows eta1 exponents of -3.170 (i.i.d.) and -2.900 (Markov), confirming error worsens with conditioning while remaining consistent with the quadratic upper bound.

claims.claim: A single-chain variant of the algorithm is also analyzed but only attains quartic sample complexity Õ(1/η^4 T) due to decorrelation requirements, contrasting with the double-chain method's quadratic rate (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: Formula reconstruction across 16 cells shows single-chain η-exponent of 4 vs double-chain exponent of 2 (ratio exactly η⁻²); destructive controls replacing the independent second sample with the same state produce nonzero bias in all 8 systems (min norm 0.0550), directly demonstrating the need for decorrelation; the literal one-chain recursion with auxiliary state w_t runs successfully on all 16 cells.

claims.claim: The condition number η1, defined via min over unit vectors of ||Φx||²_Dir + (μᵀΦx)², is shown to satisfy η1 >= (1/2)η3 relative to prior condition-number definitions (Equation 3, Lemma B.3).
claims.evidence: Across 36 cells spanning 5–12 states, feature dims 2–6, 12 non-reversible and 24 reversible chains, η1 is computed as the smallest eigenvalue of the exact quadratic form and η3 as the product of the smallest ΦᵀDΦ eigenvalue and smallest Dirichlet Rayleigh quotient on the D-mean-zero subspace; all 36 satisfy η1 ≥ η3/2 with minimum margin 9.67e-4, following the exact definitions from Equation 3 and Lemma B.3.

ProCreations/repro-bridging-the-gap-betw.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence—including fixed-point certificates, 112.64M state transitions on a 64-state chain, formula reconstructions, destructive controls, and variational condition-number checks—across all six claims on non-toy setups. The empirical scaling exponents are honestly reported as observations consistent with (but not equal to) the paper's upper bounds, and the formula audits directly verify the theoretical complexity statements.

amkkk/repro-quantifying-llm-attention-he.paper_title: Quantifying LLM Attention-Head Stability: Implications for Circuit Universality
