ParetoOptimal/repro-63o9emyhxt.paper_title: Universal Representation of Generalized Convex Functions and their Gradients

claims.claim: Theorem 1 (Section V.A) establishes that finitely Ỹ-convex functions form a dense subset of all Ỹ-convex functions, giving a universal approximation property for generalized convex functions.
claims.evidence: A density sweep over 164 kernel-target-size instances (three 1-D kernels including nonsmooth Lipschitz, 8 random targets each, up to 4097 supports; 2-D bilinear up to 5041 supports) shows all sup-error curves monotonically decreasing to ~2e-7 (smooth) and ~2.4e-4 (Lipschitz), with fitted log-log slopes of -1.915/-1.969 matching the O(m^-2) rate and -1.037 matching O(m^-1).

claims.claim: Theorem 2 (Section V.A) shows that, under semiconvexity conditions on Φ, gradients of finitely Ỹ-convex functions densely approximate gradients of all Ỹ-convex functions.
claims.evidence: Gradient density sweep with 6 random targets per kernel, up to 4097 supports, shows uniform gradient convergence (worst sup error 0.0003) under semiconvexity conditions, while curvature-violating families stall at 0.2078 sup error at discontinuities—demonstrating the semiconvexity hypothesis is material and the density conclusion holds in the theorem's regime.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 (Section V.C) proves that the lean subset of finitely Ỹ-convex functions forms a convex parameter space, which is what allows bilevel objectives to be rewritten as single-level problems solvable with standard first-order optimization (Section I).
claims.evidence: 18305 exact convex-combination leanness checks across 1-D potential families (up to 1000 supports), 1-D random-breakpoint families (up to 2000 supports), and 2-D bilinear kernels (up to 400 supports) all pass, with 80/80 planted non-lean controls correctly detected, confirming the convex parameter space claim with exact algorithms.

claims.claim: Table I reports multi-item auction experiments for n in {1,2,5,10,20} goods in which, for n up to 10, the learned mechanism's revenue matches the Straight-Jacket auction benchmark exactly.
claims.evidence: The paper's own printed Table I values show n=5 (0.314 vs 0.315) and n=10 (0.346 vs 0.347) differ by 0.001 per item, yielding only 2/4 exact matches for n≤10, directly contradicting the claim of exact matching.

claims.claim: Figures 2-3 show the learned parametrization recovers the known optimal posted price of 0.5 in the single-item auction case and finds a mixed-bundling pricing scheme matching theoretical benchmarks in the two-item case.
claims.evidence: Independent training from scratch with the paper's convex intercept parametrization recovers the single-item optimal posted price to five decimals (0.500005–0.500009 across 5 seeds vs 0.5) and produces mixed-bundling menus in all 3 two-item seeds with revenues 0.549055–0.549532 vs the independently computed 0.549425 benchmark.

claims.claim: Kantorovich dual solutions for optimal transport are characterized as Ỹ-convex functions in Section IV, so gradients of the learned parametrization directly yield optimal transport maps via a diffeomorphism condition.
claims.evidence: Trained Kantorovich dual potentials via first-order semi-dual ascent show learned-map L1 errors to closed-form Monge maps decreasing monotonically (0.147→0.0035 in 1-D, 0.048→0.012 in 2-D) with support count, and finite-difference gradients of the learned potential reproduce the map on ≥98.78% of mass via the twist identity.

ParetoOptimal/repro-63o9emyhxt.overall: This logbook provides scaled, deterministic numerical evidence supporting five of six claims—density and gradient-density theorems verified across multiple kernels and dimensions, exact leanness certificates at up to 2000 supports, independent auction training reproductions, and trained OT dual potentials—while falsifying the Table I exact-match claim using the paper's own printed values.

ProCreations/repro-model-free-robust-ave.paper_title: Model-Free Robust Average-Reward Reinforcement Learning with Sample Complexity Analysis

claims.claim: Robust Halpern Iteration (RHI) achieves a sample complexity of tilde-O(S A H^2 / epsilon^2) for computing an epsilon-optimal robust policy in model-free robust average-reward RL, without requiring prior knowledge of the robust bias span H (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: 36 G(20,15) stochastic RHI runs across four epsilons, three H scales, and three MDPs yield empirical epsilon exponent -2.1164 and H exponent 1.9973, matching the theoretical tilde-O(S A H^2/epsilon^2); the algorithm receives only epsilon, delta, and ceil(2/epsilon), never H.

claims.claim: The reduction-to-discounted-MDP approach analyzed in the paper requires knowledge of the bias span H and yields a worse sample complexity of tilde-O(S A H^2 / epsilon^4) (Section 4, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: 36 G(20,15) discounted-reduction runs with gamma=1-epsilon/H (requiring H) show empirical epsilon exponent -3.99998 and H exponent 1.999996; an epsilon^-2-budget destructive control has at least 6.84x larger value error in all paired cells.

claims.claim: Lemma 5.1 bounds the sub-optimality of a greedy policy relative to Q by the span seminorm of the residual, 0 <= g*_P - g^pi_P(s) <= Sp(T_P(Q) - Q) (Section 5, Lemma 5.1).
claims.evidence: 220 checkpoints across 20 trajectories independently compute both sides of the inequality; all greedy-policy gaps are nonnegative and below the residual span certificate, with max gap-to-residual ratio 0.014393.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 establishes that RHI's iterates converge exactly, with Sp(T_P(Q_k) - Q_k) approaching 0 as k goes to infinity (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: 20 trajectories of 600-step Halpern iteration with beta_k=k/(k+2) show max final residual span 0.003050 and all final-to-initial ratios below 0.005229; a Picard-iteration destructive control retains residual 2.0 by cycling.

claims.claim: Instead of a multi-level Monte Carlo estimator (noted to induce unbounded sample complexity in this setting), RHI uses a recursive sampling scheme that estimates successive differences T_P(Q_k) - T_P(Q_{k-1}) (Section 5, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: 144,000 coupled recursive-difference estimates show MSE slope -0.99555 consistent with inverse-n scaling; breaking the coupling and using independent estimates increases MSE by at least 284.6x.

claims.claim: The paper's sample complexity result is claimed to be the first finite-sample guarantee for model-free robust average-reward MDPs, covering both contamination and l_p-norm uncertainty sets (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: Both contamination and L1 (lp-family) uncertainty sets are directly tested with 10 independent G(20,15) MDPs each, with finite-sample RHI runs returning epsilon-optimal policies; the logbook correctly identifies that the 'first' priority claim is a literature-positioning statement not experimentally verifiable, while the technical coverage of both families is demonstrated.

ProCreations/repro-model-free-robust-ave.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical experiments on G(20,15) Garnet MDPs with empirical scaling exponents matching theoretical predictions, destructive controls, and direct inequality checks across 20+ independent MDPs and both uncertainty families. The experiments are finite sufficiency audits on synthetic MDPs rather than universal proofs, but they directly test the claims' substantive content with real runs and numbers.

rahit/repro-why-are-linear-rnns-more-par.paper_title: Why Are Linear RNNs More Parallelizable?

claims.claim: Any language recognized by a linear RNN (LRNN) over the rationals lies in PNC1, meaning LRNNs can be simulated by log-depth arithmetic circuits (Theorem 3, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies the core mechanism exactly: 132 random LRNNs (d∈{2,3,5}, n≤64) show sequential fold == balanced parallel scan with max abs error 0 over ℚ, and balanced-scan depth == ⌈log₂ n⌉ on 132/132 instances. The convolutional form Eq.(1) also matches with error 0 on 50 configs, and a destructive reversed-order control produces non-zero error, confirming associativity is load-bearing.

claims.claim: LRNNs require only O(log n log* n) depth NC circuits, an O(log* n) overhead beyond the O(log n) depth of transformers/TC0 circuits (Corollary 5, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The three components of the O(log n · log* n) bound are each measured exactly: parallel-scan depth == ⌈log₂ n⌉ on 22/22 sizes up to n=65536; log*(n) computed exactly (≤5 for all n≤2^65536); and bit-growth of iterated 3×3 DPLR products shown to be poly-bit (linear in n), contrasting with constant 1-bit diagonal LRNNs. The full Datta et al. NC circuit is cited machinery, not re-derived, but the depth accounting is exact.

claims.claim: Log-precision nonlinear RNNs can solve sorted deterministic graph connectivity, an L-complete problem, requiring Omega(log^2 n) depth and revealing a fundamental parallelization barrier absent in LRNNs (Theorem 2, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive enumeration of all sorted deterministic graphs on k≤6 nodes yields 29,367 instances; both the Lemma 2 counter-machine and the Lemma 3 log-precision ReLU RNN match ground truth on 29367/29367 (0 mismatches). Length generalization to L=100/200/300 is perfect, and a destructive control (removing the zero-test guard) breaks the machine on 636/3000 k=5 instances.

claims.claim: Poly-precision nonlinear RNNs can express P-complete problems under FO reductions, implying no efficient parallel algorithm exists for them unless P=NC (Corollary 2, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The Siegelmann–Sontag stack-as-rational encoding achieves exact LIFO recovery on 200/200 random stacks; a 2-stack ReLU RNN decides aⁿbⁿcⁿ on 29524/29524 exhaustive strings; and a ReLU RNN evaluates monotone CVP (P-complete) on 1568/1568 exhaustive input assignments across 60 circuits. Destructive controls (wrong AND gate, broken pop) produce errors as expected.

claims.claim: DPLR-based LRNN architectures such as RWKV-7 and DeltaNet can solve the PNC1-complete iterated 3x3 matrix multiplication problem using only 4 layers (Theorem 5, Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: RWKV-7's iterated 3×3 product matches numpy's exact ∏Aₜ on 280 products (entries in {-1,0,1} and ℤ[-5,5]) with max abs error 0 and (0,0)-positivity agreement 280/280; all algebraic lemmas (Lemma 5, 6, Eq.2) verified exact over ℚ on 600+200+300 configs. DeltaNet's transvection identity (Lemma 10) and end-to-end product verified on 98+75 configs with error 0. Destructive controls (wrong κ, wrong scale) produce errors 6 and 1/3.

claims.claim: Experiments show nonlinear RNNs generalize on the L-complete graph connectivity task while transformers and Mamba fail to solve it, matching the theoretical complexity separation (Figure 2, Section 6).
claims.evidence: The logbook does not train any models (no RWKV-7, DeltaNet, Mamba, or Transformer). Instead it uses the constructed nonlinear RNN from Claim 3 (100% accuracy on 300 instances per length range) and a linearization ablation (82.0% ≈ majority baseline 82.8%) as a proxy for the expressivity separation. This demonstrates the underlying expressivity gap but does not reproduce Figure 2's trained-model generalization bars.

rahit/repro-why-are-linear-rnns-more-par.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, exact-arithmetric verification of the paper's five theoretical claims (Theorems 3, 5, 2, Corollaries 5, 2) via exhaustive enumeration, exact rational computation, and destructive controls. The sole experimental claim (Claim 6, Figure 2) is addressed only through a proxy expressivity ablation rather than actual model training, leaving the trained-model generalization result unverified.

rahit/repro-the-implicit-bias-of-depth-f.paper_title: The Implicit Bias of Depth: From Neural Collapse to Softmax Codes

claims.claim: In deep unconstrained feature models trained with cross-entropy loss, deep neural collapse (DNC) remains only a local optimum for depth L≥2 (or L≥3 depending on class count), while lower-rank configurations become globally optimal (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook computes the deep-matrix-factorization min-norm identity F_L(Z)=(L+1)Σσ_i^{2/(L+1)} and compares F_DNC vs F_LR = (L+1)(K/2)·2^{2/(L+1)} over a 42-cell grid (L∈{1..6}×K∈{4,6,8,10,12,16,32}), finding 0 mismatches with the theorem's regime {L=2,K≥6}∪{L≥3,K≥4}, with the L=1 row correctly showing DNC optimal as a negative control. The 'local optimum' part is acknowledged as not separately certified.

claims.claim: The ratio of Frobenius norms between the DNC logit matrix and a low-rank alternative decays exponentially in depth L, following exp(-(L/2) log((K-1)/r)), explaining why low-rank solutions are favored as depth increases (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly constructs Z~=Phat^{L+1} for normalized projectors and verifies ||Z~_DNC||_F=(K-1)^{-L/2}, ||Z~_LR||_F=r^{-L/2}, and their ratio exp(-(L/2)log((K-1)/r)) over 70 (K,L,r) configurations with max absolute error 3.3e-16, plus a destructive control where mis-scaling one factor by 1.5 breaks the identity by exactly 1.5×.

claims.claim: In the infinite-depth limit (L→∞), the globally optimal feature geometry converges to the d=2 softmax code, i.e., class means arranged as vertices of a regular K-gon, linking depth-induced bias to explicit width-2 bottlenecks (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook shows the minimizing rank r* collapses to 2 as L grows for K∈{6,8,12,16} using the exact F_L objective, and verifies the regular K-gon geometry (rank 2, equal singular values to 1.7e-13, circulant Gram to 2.3e-14, uniform angular gaps to 0.0). At L=256 the rank-2 K-gon has F=524.6 vs rank-K/2 cross-polytope F=1033.6. The honest scope note acknowledges that fine selection of the regular K-gon among rank-2 configs is degenerate at leading order.

claims.claim: Under Hadamard initialization, neural collapse becomes a dynamically unstable fixed point near the origin for depth L>1, with the region of instability growing monotonically with depth (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook reimplements the exact singular-value ODE and computes the Jacobian of normalized dynamics at the NC direction, finding the instability threshold A_crit matches (L-1)/(L+1)(K-1) to 1e-6 over 18 (K,L) cells, with the prefactor increasing monotonically in L. KL divergence is monotonically decreasing at L=1 (Lyapunov) but diverges at L=2,3, confirmed by 400,000-step Euler integration.

claims.claim: A 'rich-get-richer' effect causes larger singular values of the feature/classifier matrices to grow faster than smaller ones during early training, driving emergence of low-rank structure before the network exits the linearized regime (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook measures the linearization residual scaling slope (3.3351 vs predicted 3.3333 for L=2, etc.) and exhaustively checks the sign law over 200 random initializations per (K,L) cell across K∈{4,8,16}, L∈{1,2,3,5}, finding 100% of all mode pairs (up to 20,999 per cell) satisfy the rich-get-richer sign for L>1 and 100% opposite sign for L=1 as a destructive control.

claims.claim: Empirically on ResNet-20 (MNIST/CIFAR-10), the effective rank of learned features decreases as classifier head depth increases, while increasing network width increases effective rank at convergence, and lower effective rank correlates with worse generalization (Section 5, experimental results).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly did not run ResNet-20 on MNIST/CIFAR-10 (no GPU), instead training a deep UFM (deep linear network with orthogonal inputs, n=1) at K=10. The qualitative trends match (effective rank falls 7.52→2.00 with depth L∈{1,2,3}, rises 2.78→4.61 with width), but this is a simplified theoretical model on synthetic data, not the paper's actual ResNet-20 experiments. The generalization correlation sub-claim is not addressed at all.

rahit/repro-the-implicit-bias-of-depth-f.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, machine-precision verification of all five theoretical claims through exact computation, exhaustive enumeration, and destructive controls on the paper's actual mathematical framework. The empirical ResNet-20 claim was substituted with the paper's deep-UFM toy model, reproducing qualitative trends but not the actual architecture, real data, or generalization correlation.

gizaom/repro-diving-into-kronecker-adapt.paper_title: Diving into Kronecker Adapters: Component Design Matters

claims.claim: Increasing the component dimension r1 of Kronecker adapters tends to degrade fine-tuning performance, while increasing r2 consistently improves it, and increasing the number of components r does not yield sustained improvement beyond a threshold (Section on design principles).
claims.evidence: The (r1,r2) sweep on MRPC used a single seed, 1 epoch, and did not hold the parameter budget constant — a key condition of the claim. Results are non-monotone (r2: 85.78→75.49→87.01; r1: 85.78→87.99→84.80), and the effect of increasing component count r was never tested at all.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 shows that subspace alignment between Kronecker adapters and full fine-tuning gradients depends critically on component configuration, with bounds favoring maximizing r2 while minimizing r1 and r (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Theorem 3.2 and its subspace-alignment bounds are never mentioned or tested in the logbook. No theoretical verification or gradient-alignment experiment was attempted.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 introduces a scaling factor lambda proportional to 1/sqrt(r*r2) that ensures training stability across different component configurations, applied in practice as lambda = 16/sqrt(r*r2) (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: Theorem 3.4, the scaling factor lambda = 16/sqrt(r*r2), and training stability across configurations are never mentioned or tested in the logbook.

claims.claim: CDKA achieves 56.71% on GSM8K, state-of-the-art among compared methods, and 87.30% average on GLUE using only 0.18% trainable parameters, about 12.5% of the parameters used by LoRA-One (Experiments, GSM8k/GLUE results tables).
claims.evidence: Only MRPC (one GLUE task) was run with t5-base, reaching up to 87.99% — a single-task proxy, not the 87.30% GLUE average. GSM8K (56.71%) was explicitly deferred, and the released code's metric only handles binary tasks, precluding the full GLUE average.

claims.claim: CDKA's practical configuration guidelines recommend r1 in [2,4], maximizing r2 under the parameter budget, and using r around 8 as the boundary for allocation decisions (Section on practical guidelines).
claims.evidence: The sweep fixed r=8 and tested only r1,r2 ∈ {2,4,8} on a single seed/1-epoch MRPC run without matched budget. The specific guidelines (r1∈[2,4], maximize r2, r≈8 as boundary) were not systematically tested, and results were non-monotone.

gizaom/repro-diving-into-kronecker-adapt.overall: The logbook confirms CDKA runs and achieves paper-level accuracy on a single GLUE task (MRPC, up to 87.99% with t5-base) after fixing non-trivial code issues, but does not adequately test any of the paper's core claims: the directional component-design principle, theorems, GSM8K results, full GLUE average, or configuration guidelines. All central claims remain unverified at this fidelity.

rahit/repro-why-agentic-theorem-prover-w.paper_title: Why Agentic Theorem Prover Works: A Statistical Provability Theory of Mathematical Reasoning Models

claims.claim: Theorem 1 establishes that the space of finite measures with bounded mass forms a compact metric space under the bounded Lipschitz metric, providing the topological foundation for the measure-valued goal encoding of the reachability MDP (Theorem 1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The experiment uses a 5-point discrete space K with W=1, verifying d_BL metric axioms via LP and finite ε-net covering numbers (252/3003/142506). The logbook itself admits it does not verify completeness and that 'a finite point set K is itself compact,' making this a clearly simplified instance of the general compactness theorem for measure spaces.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 proves that under mild Feller-type continuity conditions on the transition kernel, optimal deterministic Markov policies exist for the finite-horizon time-bounded reachability MDP (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: A 3-state MDP (G, A, B) with 4 actions and horizon 4 is used; exhaustive enumeration of all 65,536 policies confirms the DP optimum equals the class maximum (gap 0.00e+00). However, on a finite state/action space, sup attainment and Feller continuity are trivially automatic, so the theorem's substantive content is not engaged.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 shows that sequences of functions satisfying Bellman sub-/super-solution inequalities yield provability certificates (upper and lower bounds on the optimal value function) without requiring the full MDP to be solved, with the certificate gap defined as UB(x0) - LB(x0) (Theorem 3, Definition 5, Section 5).
claims.evidence: A 7-state finite MDP with 4 actions and horizon 5 is used to test 3000 random super/sub-solutions, confirming the sandwich property (slack ≥ 0) and tightness (gap 0.00e+00). The Bellman operator is applied exactly on a small finite instance, which is a simplified proxy for the general measure-valued MDP setting.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 bounds the worst-case regret of score-guided planning under uniform score-approximation error εb as 0 ≤ V*_B(x0) - V^{πh}_B(x0) ≤ 2∑_{b=1}^{B} εb, showing performance degrades linearly with accumulated approximation error (Theorem 4, Section 6).
claims.evidence: A 9-state MDP with 4 actions and horizon 6 is used; 6000 random-noise draws show 0 violations of 0 ≤ regret ≤ 2Σε_b, with adversarial tightness attaining 0.11–0.22 of the bound. Real runs and numbers, but on a small finite MDP that is a simplified instance of the general score-guided planning setting.

claims.claim: Theorem 5 shows that under a margin condition on action-value separation, the expected regret improves to O(Bε^{β+1}) for β>0, i.e., faster than the worst-case linear-in-B rate of Theorem 4 (Theorem 5).
claims.evidence: The margin-condition mechanism is directly simulated (not on a real MDP) with 1.5M MC samples, recovering exponents 1.50/2.00/2.50/3.04 vs predicted β+1 (R²≥0.9995). This is a faithful proxy of the mathematical mechanism but not a reproduction on a non-toy MDP instance.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 derives a high-probability estimation-error bound of order O(L H d_D/(d_D+2) (log(n/δ)/n)^{1/(d_D+2)}) under a doubling-dimension assumption on the relevant problem domain, formalizing how statistical complexity of a biased real-world problem distribution governs sample efficiency (Theorem 6, Section 7).
claims.evidence: A synthetic regressogram on [0,1]^d (d=1,2,3) with n up to 32000 recovers exponents -0.329/-0.228/-0.208 vs predicted -1/(d+2). The setup uses a simple cosine target and piecewise-constant estimator as a proxy for the theorem's general doubling-dimension estimation setting.

rahit/repro-why-agentic-theorem-prover-w.overall: The logbook provides clean-room numerical experiments for all six theorems on small finite MDPs or direct mechanism simulations, each with real runs, measured numbers, and destructive controls. However, every experiment operates on a clearly simplified setup (3–9 state MDPs, 5-point measure spaces, synthetic proxy tasks) that does not engage the general measure-valued or function-class setting of the theorems.

rahit/repro-learning-rate-scaling-across.paper_title: Learning Rate Scaling across LoRA Ranks and Transfer to Full Finetuning

claims.claim: Under Init[A] with LoRA scaling factor alpha=1, the maximal-update-adaptation optimal learning rate scales as eta = Theta(n^{-1/2} r^{-1/2}), making it rank-dependent (Section 4, Corollary 4.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook recovers the predicted exponents on the exact object of Corollary 4.4: slope_n = -0.4848 (theory -1/2, R²=0.9999) and slope_r = -0.5163 (theory -1/2, R²=0.9999) across n∈{512..8192} and r∈{4..256}, with 32 seeds and destructive controls showing wrong exponents drift 4.5x–18.3x vs 1.1x for the correct law.

claims.claim: Under Init[A] with alpha=r^{-1}, the optimal learning rate scales as eta = Theta(n^{-1/2}), i.e. rank-invariant (Section 4, Corollary 4.4, Table 1).
claims.evidence: The full Table 1 is reproduced across all three tabulated alpha values: gamma=0 gives slope_r=-0.519, gamma=1/2 gives -0.254, and gamma=1 gives -0.0001 (rank-invariant), with the rank exponent tracing the predicted -(1-gamma)/2 line and width exponent staying at -1/2 throughout (R²≥0.999).

claims.claim: Under Init[B] with alpha=1, the optimal learning rate scales as eta = Theta(n^{-1}), matching the scaling of full finetuning and enabling direct learning-rate transfer from LoRA to full finetuning (Section 4, Corollary 4.6).
claims.evidence: Init[B] with alpha=1 recovers slope_n=-0.9862 (theory -1, R²=0.9998) and slope_r=-0.0119 (flat, rank-invariant) across n∈{512..8192} and r∈{8..256}, with the Theorem 4.5 magnitude law confirmed by branch exponents 1.023/1.999 and crossover at eta~1/r. The FFT matching is independently confirmed in Claim 6 (FFT slope -1.004, ratio InitB/FFT ~1.06x).

claims.claim: Learning rate sweeps on Llama-3.2-1B show three distinct scaling patterns for the three LoRA configurations, visually confirming the rank-dependence/invariance predictions of the theory (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is about LR sweeps on Llama-3.2-1B, but no GPU experiments were run. Instead, the rank-slopes of eta*(r) were computed on a single-LoRA-layer SignSGD system, recovering the predicted patterns (-0.516, -0.253, -0.000, -0.010) but on a simplified proxy of the actual Figure 2 setup.

claims.claim: SFT experiments across Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen3-VL-2B, RoBERTa-large, and ViT-Huge/14 confirm that Init[B] with alpha=1 yields rank-invariant optimal learning rates aligned with the full-finetuning optimum (Figures 3-5).
claims.evidence: No SFT experiments on Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen3-VL-2B, RoBERTa-large, or ViT-Huge/14 were run. The logbook instead verifies term-wise diagnostics (delta2 Lemma ratio, Z_A scalings) on a single-LoRA-layer system, which addresses the underlying mechanism but not the empirical claim about multi-model SFT.

claims.claim: RLVR experiments on Llama-3.1-8B trained on GSM8K confirm the rank-invariance pattern, with full finetuning requiring more than 2x the GPU memory of LoRA (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: No RLVR experiments on Llama-3.1-8B/GSM8K or GPU memory measurements were performed. The logbook verifies the necessary condition for transfer (matched n^-1 scaling between FFT and Init[B], ratio ~1.06x) on a single linear layer, and shows Init[A] fails transfer (4.26x drift), but the actual RLVR and memory claims are unaddressed.

rahit/repro-learning-rate-scaling-across.overall: The logbook provides rigorous numerical verification of the paper's three theoretical scaling laws (Claims 1-3) on the exact single-LoRA-layer SignSGD system the theorems describe, with strong fits (R²≥0.999), destructive controls, and machine-precision identity checks. However, the three empirical claims involving real model training (Claims 4-6: Llama-3.2-1B sweeps, multi-model SFT, and Llama-3.1-8B RLVR) are only addressed on this simplified single-layer proxy, not on the actual models.

rahit/repro-capacitated-fair-range-clust.paper_title: Capacitated Fair-Range Clustering: Hardness and Approximation Algorithms

claims.claim: For capacitated fair-range clustering with a constant number of demographic groups, the paper gives a polynomial-time O(log k)-approximation algorithm for k-median and O(log^2 k)-approximation for k-means running in (nk^t)^O(1) time (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: Two component lemmas of the O(log k)-approximation pipeline are verified on very small instances (4-6 clients/facilities, k=2-3): clique-star embedding bound held in 27/27 trials and tree-DP matched brute force in 270/270 trials. However, the full algorithm is not tested end-to-end, the FRT tree embedding (source of the O(log k) factor) is explicitly not reimplemented, and the instance sizes are far too small to meaningfully exercise the logarithmic approximation behavior.

claims.claim: For any epsilon>0, a randomized (3+epsilon)-approximation algorithm exists for capacitated fair-range k-median with running time (O(2^t k epsilon^-1 log n))^O(k)*n^O(1), and a corresponding (9+epsilon)-approximation for k-means, matching the best known guarantees for capacitated clustering without fair-range constraints (Theorem 5.5).
claims.evidence: The leader-guessing FPT algorithm was reimplemented and tested on 26 instances with 3-4 clients, 4-5 facilities, k=2-3, but the realized ratio was 1.000 in every trial (algorithm cost exactly equals brute-force OPT). The logbook itself acknowledges this does not exercise the algorithm's worst case or the (3+eps)/(9+eps) approximation guarantee, as the search space at these sizes is nearly exhaustive over all feasible solutions.

claims.claim: No polynomial-time algorithm can approximate capacitated fair-range k-median or k-means to any polynomial factor unless P=NP, and this hardness holds even on tree metrics and even when fair-range feasibility is trivially satisfiable (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The 3SAT→FRkMedO reduction is reimplemented clean-room and verified exhaustively: on a satisfiable instance (m=5), OPT=5.0 matches k=m exactly; on the extremal UNSAT gadget (m=8, all sign patterns), exhaustive search over 16,777,216 combinations yields OPT=57.0 matching the predicted identity ell_max+(m-ell_max)*D=7+50 exactly. Trivial fair-range feasibility is confirmed (100% of all 2^n' assignments yield feasible solutions in both cases), and the metric is verified to be a tree (star through dummy node).

claims.claim: Under P≠NP, no polynomial-time algorithm can approximate the problem to a factor better than (Delta-2)/16 on tree metrics, where Delta is the distance aspect ratio (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: The (Delta-2)/16 inapproximability factor is verified across a sweep of 10 D values {1,5,10,25,50,100,250,500,1000,5000}: at every D, the measured gap OPT/k exceeds the predicted bound (e.g., D=1000: measured 125.875 vs bound 125.00; D=50: measured 7.125 vs bound 6.25). A destructive control relaxing one clause collapses OPT to k exactly, confirming the gap is tied to satisfiability and not an artifact.

claims.claim: Assuming Gap-ETH, no f(k)*n^o(k)-time algorithm, for any computable function f, can approximate capacitated fair-range k-median to any polynomial factor, ruling out algorithms with running time subexponential in k (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The super-clause construction's parameter formulas (|F|, t) are verified to match the construction at k=1,2,4, and the brute-force combo count is observed to not shrink with k. However, this observation about brute-force search space size does not constitute evidence for the actual claim—a Gap-ETH-conditioned f(k)·n^{o(k)} time lower bound on approximation algorithms. The logbook itself states it 'does not and cannot verify the hypothesis itself or a formal time-complexity lower bound,' and the search-space observation is about exhaustive enumeration, not about the reduction's gap-preserving p

rahit/repro-capacitated-fair-range-clust.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, exhaustive verification of the two hardness reductions (Theorems 4.1 and 4.2), confirming exact cost identities, tree-metric structure, trivial feasibility, and the (Delta-2)/16 factor across a parameter sweep with destructive controls. The approximation algorithm claims (Theorems 5.1 and 5.5) are only tested at toy scale with tiny instances that do not exercise the approximation guarantees, and the Gap-ETH lower bound (Theorem 4.3) is not meaningfully addressed beyond verifying construction parameter formulas.

rahit/repro-sampling-and-identity-testin.paper_title: Sampling and Identity-Testing Without Approximate Tensorization of Entropy

claims.claim: Theorem 4 proves fast mixing of Glauber dynamics for mixtures of k distributions satisfying Approximate Tensorization of Entropy (ATE) when initialized from an empirical (data-based) distribution built from m = O(k/ε + log(1/δ)/ε) samples, reaching KL divergence at most ε in time t = c*n · O(log log(1/min μ(x)) + log(1/ε)) (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Exact Glauber chain diagonalization on n≤12 (up to 4096 states), k=3 shows t_needed flat in ε ([0.42,0.57] over 12x range) and linear in n (R²=0.992), with destructive controls (worst-case init 3-5x slower, reduced m breaks failure probability by ~35x). However, n≤12 is far below asymptotic regime and the log log(1/min μ) term barely varies across tested n, so this is a small-scale exact check, not a full-scale verification.

claims.claim: The analysis avoids standard Chernoff-bound arguments in favor of moment generating function bounds on the KL divergence of empirical distributions, removing dependence on the minimum mixture weight (Section on Theorem 4, Lemma 21-22).
claims.evidence: Full exact enumeration of 362,484 multinomial compositions across 72 (k,m,skew,λ) configs confirms the MGF bound E[exp(λ·KL)] ≤ (1/(1-λ/m))^(k-1) holds in all configs (min gap 0.097 nats). The destructive control shows exact tail probability stays flat (0.0001–0.0035) as ρ_min shrinks 300x, while naive Chernoff would require 300x more samples — directly demonstrating ρ_min-independence.

claims.claim: Theorem 5 gives an efficient identity-tester for mixtures of k ATE distributions in the coordinate-conditional sampling access model, resolving an open question posed by Blanca et al., with sample complexity O(c*n/ε)·log²(c*n/ε)·log(1/η)·log log(1/η)·|Σ| + O(√k·log(1/ρ*)/ε) (Theorem 5).
claims.evidence: End-to-end Monte Carlo of Algorithm 1 on n=6 (64 states), k=3 with 300 trials shows Type-II rejection rates above the 0.6 bound (0.73–0.92) and correct attribution of intra/inter-component alternatives to local/weight steps. However, Type-I error is 0.407 (above the theorem's ≤0.4 bound), the setup is very small, and oracle-call scaling is linear in 1/ε by construction rather than independently measured.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 combines a Local Testing step detecting large intra-component divergence via the coordinate oracle with a Posterior Weight Estimation step detecting mismatched mixture weights via a KL-test, both relying on the KL-Test subroutine of Theorem 24 (Section 4, Algorithm 1, Theorem 24).
claims.evidence: Exact enumeration of 15.2M compositions verifies that a plug-in empirical-KL test achieves both error types ≤0.1 at m=15–20 for d=3–5, at or below the paper's formula-predicted order (30.6–39.5). However, the logbook explicitly states this is 'a different (simpler) test construction than the paper's H²-test-based KL-Test,' so the paper's specific Theorem 24 construction is not directly tested.

claims.claim: Lemma 11's chain rule for entropy decomposes the entropy of a mixture μ = Σₐ ρ(a)μₐ into an intra-component term Eₐ[Entμₐ[f]] and an inter-component term Ent_ρ[Eμₐ[f]], underlying the paper's use of Modified Log-Sobolev Inequalities in place of the Poincaré inequalities used in prior work by KLV24 and HMRW24 (Lemma 11, Remark 17).
claims.evidence: Chain-rule identity Ent_μ[f] = Ent_ρ[E_a f] + E_ρ[Ent_{μ_a}[f]] verified to machine precision (max residual 1.83e-15) across 2000 random mixtures and 1296 exhaustive grid points, for both Φ(u)=u log u and Φ(u)=u². MLSI vs Poincaré constants computed exactly on the 2-point Bernoulli(p) space show MLSI constant (0.50–0.72) is genuinely different from Poincaré's exact 1.0, supporting Remark 17.

rahit/repro-sampling-and-identity-testin.overall: The logbook provides rigorous exact-computation evidence for the algebraic/analytic claims (MGF bound via full enumeration, chain-rule identity to machine precision) but tests the dynamic/algorithmic claims (Glauber mixing, identity-testing) only at small scale (n≤12, k=3) with some simplifications (different KL-test construction, Type-I error slightly above bound). Two claims are verified by exact enumeration; three are addressed on simplified setups with real numbers but reduced scope.

rahit/repro-diffusion-flow-matching-dime.paper_title: Diffusion Flow Matching: Dimension-Improved KL Bounds and Wasserstein Guarantees

claims.claim: For the non-early-stopping, constant step-size setting, Theorem 1 establishes KL convergence bounds for Brownian-motion-based diffusion flow matching scaling as O(d^3) in dimension, improving on prior O(d^4) results, decomposing into a drift-approximation term epsilon^2 and a discretization term scaling as O(h) (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: All experiments use a linear-Gaussian (separable, iid-across-coordinates) instance where the true discretization error scales as O(d), not O(d^3). The O(d^3) scaling is verified only for the bound's complexity coefficient formula (log-log slope 2.994), not for actual KL convergence in high dimensions. The eps^2 additivity (R2=1.0) and O(h) bound satisfaction (true error O(h^2)) are confirmed but on this simplified setup.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 relaxes the assumptions of Theorem 1 to require score integrability only of the conditional coupling pi_{0|1} rather than the full coupling pi, while preserving the O(d^3) dimensional scaling under early stopping (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Same linear-Gaussian toy engine. The pi_{0|1}=mu reduction is verified exactly to 0 error at rho=0, and the bound's d^3 coefficient scales as 3.000 (R2=1.0) at fixed delta. However, the true early-stopped KL stays bounded in [3.1e-6, 9.0e-6] and does not exhibit the delta^-4 blow-up of the bound, confirming only that the bound holds loosely on this simplified instance.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 introduces a novel non-uniform step-size schedule (h_k = h early, then h_k = h*min(t_k, 1-t_k) later) that yields faster convergence in the early-stopping regime while retaining O(d^3) complexity (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Direct equal-budget simulation on the linear-Gaussian instance shows the non-uniform schedule performs WORSE than uniform for all 5 delta values (improvements -65.7% to -576.5%), contradicting 'faster convergence.' The logbook attributes this to the instance lacking score blow-up near t=1. Supporting evidence for the theoretical advantage comes only from evaluating the paper's own budget formulas (ratio reaching 2.4e29x), not from independent simulation.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 extends the analysis to 2-Wasserstein distance, giving bounds that decompose into a drift error epsilon and a discretization error scaling as O(sqrt(h))*O(sqrt(d^3)), under a weak log-concavity assumption on the coupling and first-order score integrability (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Same linear-Gaussian setup. W2 h-scaling measured as O(h) (slope 1.000, tighter than claimed O(sqrt(h))), eps-additivity confirmed (R2=0.99999998), and sqrt(d^3) coefficient slope is 1.497 (R2=0.999999). Constant C computed exactly as 4.302e15 with a destructive control showing blow-up under coupling degeneracy. All on the simplified Gaussian instance where the Hessian is constant.

claims.claim: Corollary 3 specializes the Wasserstein result of Theorem 4 to the independent coupling pi = mu tensor nu*, allowing assumptions to be stated on the marginals rather than the joint distribution (Corollary 3).
claims.evidence: The alpha_pi=min(alpha_mu,alpha_nustar) identity is verified to 0 absolute error across 25 random SPD Gaussian instances, and the Minkowski ratio is always ≤1 (range [0.596, 0.690]). Destructive control confirms identities break under correlation. However, all instances are Gaussian (constant Hessian, M=0 trivially), so the weak-log-concavity specialization is not tested on any non-trivially non-log-concave distribution.

claims.claim: The dimensional improvement from O(d^4) to O(d^3) is obtained by using integration-by-parts to transfer derivatives onto the coupling instead of directly expanding three logarithmic-derivative terms, reducing the required differentiation order from three to two (Section on Key Methodological Innovations).
claims.evidence: The exponent-halving mechanism is illustrated by computing raw 8th moment (slope 3.976) vs its square root (slope 1.988) on a synthetic bounded spectrum, yielding a gap of ~2. The logbook explicitly states this is 'an independent quantitative illustration...not a literal re-derivation of the appendix's covariance identity.' The naive vs IBP complexity coefficient slopes (4.976 vs 2.994) are computed from the same synthetic coupling, not from the paper's actual analytical argument.

rahit/repro-diffusion-flow-matching-dime.overall: The logbook provides careful, exact, closed-form computations on a linear-Gaussian special case of the DFM framework, verifying structural properties (additive decompositions, bound coefficient scaling) and including honest scope limitations and controls. However, all six claims are tested only on this simplified separable Gaussian instance where the true error scales as O(d) rather than the claimed O(d^3), making this a toy-level reproduction rather than a full verification of the paper's general-dimensional claims.

claims.claim: For the independent Gaussian variance allocation problem, the paper gives a PTAS achieving E[max_i X_i] ≥ OPT - ε in polynomial time (Theorem 1.1, Section 1.2).
claims.evidence: Grid-search PTAS tested on only n=5 variables with 2 instances and ε∈{0.5,0.35,0.25}; gaps are ≤3e-3 (within ε) using exact quadrature, but the scale is clearly reduced and OPT_ref is a 25-restart local optimizer, not a certified global optimum.

claims.claim: For correlated Gaussian variables, a PTAS with the same additive ε guarantee is established (Theorem 1.2, Section 1.2).
claims.evidence: Correlated PTAS tested only at n=2 (Clark closed form, 6 configs, gap→0) and n=3 (191-point hand-picked grid, no full ε³-lattice sweep); cross-validation of closed form vs 2D quadrature is strong (1e-8 agreement), but the PTAS itself is only verified at n=2.

claims.claim: For the GraphVarAlloc problem with multiple constraint sets (general m>1), the paper gives an O(log n) multiplicative approximation guaranteeing Ω(1/log n)·OPT (Theorem 1.3, Section 1.2).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive enumeration of all 2^n subsets (n≤12, 17,248 evaluations) confirms greedy matches exact optimum (ratio 1.0) in all 14 level-checks, and full Algorithm 3 matches continuous optimizer on n=6; however, instances are small and structured, and the O(log n) guarantee is not tested at scale where the log factor matters.

claims.claim: Theorem 1.6 proves that in the optimal allocation, only Θ(1/p) variables receive variance Ω(p), i.e., the allocation concentrates on a shrinking subset as the constraint parameter p grows (Theorem 1.6, Section 1.3).
claims.evidence: n=400 with 7 seeds across 9 density levels gives log-log slope -0.79 (theory: -1, R²=0.99), but uses greedy Algorithm 3 as a proxy for the true optimal allocation, which is the actual object of Theorem 1.6; the exponent mismatch and proxy nature prevent full verification.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 bounds the contribution of small-variance variables by O(ε√ln(1/ε)), which is used to limit the number of high-variance variables to O(1/ε²) and underlies the PTAS construction (Lemma 2.1, Section 2.1).
claims.evidence: Exact quadrature on the extremal configuration (k=1/ε² variables at variance ε²) across ε∈{0.5,…,1e-4} shows the ratio E[max]/(ε√ln(1/ε)) converging to 2, matching the √(2 ln m) asymptotic; n-independence confirmed to 1e-10 precision across n up to 10⁶; destructive control confirms the variance cap is load-bearing.

claims.claim: Monte Carlo simulations on Erdős–Rényi random graphs with n=8 nodes and edge probabilities p ranging from 1/8 to 8/8 are used to illustrate the concentration and concavity results across independent, positively, and negatively correlated settings (Figures 1-2, Section 1.3).
claims.evidence: Part A exactly verifies concavity of g(k)=E[max of k iid N(0,1)] (498/499 second differences ≤0), but Part B's Erdős-Rényi Monte Carlo reproduction shows the predicted correlation ordering (neg≥ind≥pos) at only 5/8 density levels and concavity fails uniformly (max second difference +0.030 for independent); mixed results do not clearly illustrate the claimed concentration and concavity.

rahit/repro-allocating-variance-to-maxim.overall: The logbook provides rigorous small-scale numerical verification using exact quadrature, closed-form formulas, and exhaustive enumeration, with the strongest result being Claim 5's exact verification of the Lemma 2.1 bound. Most other claims are tested on toy-scale instances (n=2–12) or with proxy algorithms, and Claim 6's Monte Carlo reproduction yields mixed results that do not fully support the paper's illustrative figures.

rahit/repro-revenue-guarantees-of-no-swa.paper_title: Revenue Guarantees of No-Swap-Regret Dynamics in First Price Auctions

claims.claim: For exact correlated equilibria in discrete first-price auctions with k discretization levels, expected revenue is at least v2 - 4/k, where v2 is the second-highest valuation (Theorem 2.5).
claims.evidence: Exact LP (scipy/HiGHS) minimizing revenue over all exact correlated equilibria (Definition 3.1, eps=0) solved for 341 exhaustively enumerated valuation profiles (n=2, k∈{4,6,8,10}; n=3, k∈{3,4,5,6}). Zero violations of the v2-4/k bound at tolerance 1e-7. Destructive control confirms non-vacuity: the naive bound revenue≥v2 fails in 152/341 instances.

claims.claim: For ε-approximate correlated equilibria, expected revenue is at least v2 - 3/k - Θ(εk²) (Theorem 2.6).
claims.evidence: Same exact LP with eps>0, parameterized as eps=C/k² so the Θ(eps·k²)=C term is comparable across k. 854 exhaustively enumerated instances (n=2, k∈{4,6,8,10}, C∈{0,…,0.5}) all satisfy Z_LP* ≥ v2-3/k-2C (the proven constant from Lemma 3.6). Empirical worst-case ratio slack/C=0.198, well below the proven constant 2. Destructive control with constant 0.1 fails in 3/854 instances, confirming sensitivity.

claims.claim: There exists an ε-approximate correlated equilibrium with revenue at most v2 - Θ(1/k) - Θ(ε), showing the ε-dependence in the revenue lower bound cannot be removed (Theorem 2.8).
claims.evidence: Explicit construction of the proof's distribution (mu diagonal, eps/k for s1=s2≤1-1/k, 1-eps at s1=s2=1) built directly in code for 30 (k,eps) pairs with k up to 100. The eps-CE property is verified by exhaustive enumeration of all bid-pair deviations (max deviation gain ≤ eps in all instances, violation exactly 0.0). Revenue matches the independently rederived closed form 1-eps/2-eps/(2k) to machine precision (≤1.11e-16). Destructive control shows eps-free bound v2-4/k is violated at eps≥0.728.

claims.claim: When bidders run no-swap-regret algorithms achieving swap regret O(√(kT)), the time-averaged revenue is at least v2 - 3/k - O(ε) after O(k^5/ε^2) rounds (Corollary 2.7).
claims.evidence: Clean-room Blum-Mansour/Hedge simulation at the paper's own experimental scale (k=10, n=3, T=20000) confirms sublinear swap regret (fitted log-log slope 0.388) and matches the paper's Fig.1 qualitative finding (revenue surpasses v2-1/k) in 4/5 configurations. However, T=20000 is far below the O(k^5/eps²) rounds the corollary requires (k^5=100000 at k=10), making the functional bound vacuously negative (implied eps≈4.4). The v2=1.0 symmetric-tie case fails to reach v2-1/k. The claim's round-complexity guarantee is not directly tested.

claims.claim: Time-averaged bidder behavior under no-swap-regret dynamics converges to an ε-approximate correlated equilibrium with probability 1-δ (Theorem 2.3).
claims.evidence: 240 Monte Carlo trials (60 per T∈{500,1000,2000,4000}, n=2, k=10) computing the exact Definition-2.2 deviation gain of the time-averaged empirical distribution. eps_realized concentrates and shrinks with T (mean 0.0181→0.0058). P(eps_realized≤threshold) increases monotonically with T for all three thresholds tested (e.g., 0%→33%→100%→100%), directly demonstrating the w.p. 1-δ convergence claim. Destructive control with an unrealistically small threshold yields 0/240 successes, confirming non-vacuity.

claims.claim: The revenue lower bounds are proved via a dual-fitting approach that uses a linear program and weak duality to bound revenue of approximate correlated equilibria (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Independent implementation of both the paper's explicit dual variable assignment (lambda^i_{si,si'}=1 iff si+1/k≤si'≤v2-2/k for i∈{1,2}; mu_hat=v2-3/k) and the primal LP. Dual feasibility checked by brute-force enumeration over all bidding profiles in 414 instances (n∈{2,3}, multiple k, multiple eps): max feasibility violation exactly 0.0. Weak duality cross-validated: independently-solved Z_LP* ≥ dual objective in 414/414 instances. Lambda-count never exceeds 2k². Destructive control: inflating mu_hat by +0.2 breaks feasibility (violation 0.075).

rahit/repro-revenue-guarantees-of-no-swa.overall: The logbook provides strong, exact computational evidence for the paper's core theoretical claims (Theorems 2.5, 2.6, 2.8, and the dual-fitting framework of Section 3) via exhaustive LP enumeration and brute-force verification over 1,669 finite instances combined, with destructive controls confirming non-vacuity throughout. The simulation-based claims (Corollary 2.7, Theorem 2.3) provide qualitative support at the paper's own experimental scale but do not reach the round complexity required by the corollary's worst-case guarantee.

MarxistLeninist/repro-skill-neologisms.paper_title: Skill Neologisms: Towards Skill-based Continual Learning

claims.claim: Skill neologisms extend a model vocabulary with trainable skill-token embeddings while keeping pretrained model parameters fixed (Figure 2, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Parameter count 20×896=17,920 matches Table D2 exactly, and a SHA-256 hash over every base-model parameter was identical before and after skill-token training (`base_params_unchanged: true`), confirming the frozen-model property on a non-toy setup with Qwen2.5-0.5B.

claims.claim: The method uses skill-centered datasets whose examples require the new skill composed with existing pretrained skills (Section 3.3, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: An exact audit of the dataset generator on the actual 12,000-sample datasets used in experiments confirms all four invariants: every example contains the new skill (frac=1.0), co-occurring operations come from the pretrained set, the held-out skill has zero occurrences, and operation-count buckets are exactly balanced (4000/4000/4000).

claims.claim: Skill neologisms are compared with fine-tuning, LoRA, prompt tuning, and related approaches for skill-based continual learning properties (Table 1).
claims.evidence: P1 (no weight updates) is verified exactly via SHA-256, but P2 is contradicted (LoRA OOD 0.792 vs neologism 0.461, ordering reversed) and P3 shows no advantage over ICL (0.104 vs 0.137, intervals overlapping), all at ~1/37 of the paper's optimisation budget where the stated precondition of near-perfect ID accuracy does not hold.

claims.claim: On digit-sequence transformation tasks, independently learned skill neologisms transfer to held-out two-skill and three-skill compositions (Table 3, Table 4, Figure 4, Figure A2).
claims.evidence: Neologisms do show transfer above controls (OOD k=2: 0.461 vs ≤0.04 for all controls), but LoRA is substantially better (0.792, non-overlapping intervals), reversing the paper's Figure-4 ordering. However, this is at 1/37 the paper's training budget with no method reaching near-perfect ID accuracy—the explicit precondition for the paper's comparison—so the regime is too different to be conclusive.

claims.claim: Zero-shot composition of independently trained SHIFT and INV-POL skill tokens outperforms or complements in-context learning baselines in the reported setup (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Zero-shot composition of two independently trained banks works above chance (0.458 at length 2 vs ≤0.04 for controls), confirming the mechanism, but composed neologisms do not outperform ICL (mean 0.104 vs 0.137, all Wilson intervals overlapping). The comparison is underpowered and at reduced budget.

claims.claim: A natural-language Skill-Mix experiment shows two separately learned skill neologisms can be combined at inference to elicit both target skills (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: The natural-language Skill-Mix experiment was not attempted; it requires a proprietary GPT-5 grader and ~650 proprietary-API-generated training samples, which exceeds the reproduction's cost envelope. No experiments or artifacts were produced for this claim.

MarxistLeninist/repro-skill-neologisms.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the method's core mechanism—frozen-base-model vocabulary extension (C1) and skill-centered dataset construction (C2)—with exact audits and strong negative controls. However, the paper's comparative claims (C3–C5) are not reproduced at 1/37 of the paper's training budget where preconditions fail, and the natural-language experiment (C6) was never attempted.

abhishekkataria16/claim-LcSPuepCDU-logbo.paper_title: Disease-Centric Vision-Language Pretraining with Hybrid Visual Encoding for 3D Computed Tomography

claims.claim: CT-DiagVLM achieves 84.4% AUC on CT-RATE, a 5.1% absolute improvement over prior state-of-the-art methods such as fVLM (77.8%) and ViSD-Boost (79.0%) (Table 1, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook only performed a Hugging Face Hub search and found no attributable public artifacts; no experiment was run, no model was trained or evaluated, and no AUC measurement was produced.

claims.claim: On the external Rad-ChestCT validation set, CT-DiagVLM reaches 75.4% AUC, a 5.4% absolute gain over fVLM's 68.0%, demonstrating generalization to unseen data distributions (Table 1, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook searched HF Hub for Rad-ChestCT and related terms, found no attributable artifacts, and launched no experiments; no AUC or generalization result was measured.

claims.claim: On the 60-disease benchmark using LLM-generated pseudo-labels, the model attains 85.6% AUC, a 9.8% absolute improvement over the 75.8% base model result (Table 2, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: The 60-disease benchmark claim was bundled into the logbook's Claim 2 page, which only performed a Hub search with no experiments; no AUC measurement on the 60-disease benchmark was produced.

claims.claim: An ablation isolates each component's contribution to the 5.1% AUC gain: the CNN-ViT hybrid encoder contributes +1.0%, the diagnosis-aware prompt strategy +2.1%, and disease-level contrastive learning +2.0% (Table 4, Section 4.5).
claims.evidence: The ablation claim (Table 4) is not addressed anywhere in the logbook; no component-level ablation experiments were run or discussed.

claims.claim: When transferred to radiology report generation, the pretrained representation yields 45.5% F1 on CT-RATE and 37.3% F1 on Rad-ChestCT, substantially outperforming existing methods such as CT-CHAT (Table 3, Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook's Claim 3 page only searched HF Hub for report-generation artifacts and found none attributable to the paper; no F1 measurement or transfer experiment was conducted.

claims.claim: Initializing from SigLIP-2 Base is critical: training the visual encoder from scratch drops performance to 76.5% AUC versus 84.4% AUC with SigLIP-2 initialization, while additional DeepStack/MoE enhancements yield no consistent gains (Table 5, Section 4.5).
claims.evidence: The SigLIP-2 initialization ablation (Table 5) is not addressed in the logbook at all; no from-scratch vs. pretrained comparison was run.

abhishekkataria16/claim-LcSPuepCDU-logbo.overall: The logbook established only that no public artifacts attributable to the paper were found on Hugging Face Hub; it ran zero experiments and produced no numerical evidence for any of the six claims. Three of the six claims were not even addressed, and the three that were addressed consisted solely of unsuccessful artifact searches.

abhishekkataria16/claim-LCosvYhXvi-logbo.paper_title: Data Difficulty and the Generalization–Extrapolation Tradeoff in LLM Fine-Tuning

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 (the two-gap upper bound) decomposes fine-tuning test risk into a generalization gap G_gen = O(√(KL(π_train‖π_pre)/n)) and an extrapolation gap G_ext = O(TV(D_test, D_train)), formalizing why optimal data difficulty depends on data budget n.
claims.evidence: The logbook provides no mathematical derivation or verification of Proposition 4.1's two-gap decomposition; it only searched the HF Hub for artifacts and found none, which does not constitute any attempt to verify the theoretical claim.
