ai-sherpa/sgmcmc-accurate-uncertainty-qu.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical and algebraic evidence supporting four core theoretical claims (covariance bound, exact noise formula, Wasserstein bound, Algorithm 1) on non-trivial nonlinear setups with exact verifications to machine precision, and falsifies two claims on text-decidable grounds: the Boston CT method does not diverge as the plural claim asserts, and Proposition B.1 does not contain the error-bound result attributed to it.

ai-sherpa/bp-gaussian-convergence-sparse.paper_title: Belief Propagation Converges to Gaussian Distributions in Sparsely-Connected Factor Graphs

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that variables in pairwise chain factor graphs develop increasingly Gaussian-distributed beliefs as topological distance from prior factors increases, driven by repeated convolution via the Central Limit Theorem (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Exact 1024-bin sum-product on two 13-variable chains shows monotonic KL decrease (seed 11: 0.364→0.004703 by hop 3; seed 23: 0.382→0.003437), both below the 0.02 threshold, with a sharp-prior negative control correctly staying non-Gaussian (KL 0.571878).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 extends the Gaussian convergence result to tree-topology factor graphs, provided the message non-Gaussianity ε satisfies ε² ≪ ε with increasing distance from the nearest prior factor (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: Exact upward BP on two 127-node binary trees with 64 non-Gaussian leaf priors yields distance-3 median KL of 0.000646 and 0.000818, both well below 0.02, with the ε²≪ε diagnostic explicitly checked (ε=0.036, ε²=0.0013).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.5 uses computation-tree equivalence to show loopy factor graphs exhibit the same Gaussian convergence mechanism as tree graphs under identical assumptions (Theorem 4.5).
claims.evidence: On a 4×4 loopy grid, 4 synchronous BP iterations compared against independently coded non-backtracking computation-tree recursion yield max float64 message difference of 0.0 across all 48 directed messages, confirming the structural equivalence that underpins the shared convergence mechanism.

claims.claim: Lemma 4.2 identifies an 'exclusion zone' in which non-Gaussian prior factors prevent Gaussian convergence when the prior-to-pairwise variance ratio R is less than or equal to approximately 6 (Lemma 4.2).
claims.evidence: Analytic derivation of the Gaussian-BP variance fixed point gives R*=y*(y*+1)=6.0 at y*=2 (residual 0.0), matching the paper's 'approximately 6'; empirical repeated-prior chain shows stationary KL monotonically decreasing in R (0.0226 at R=3 down to 0.000573 at R=10), confirming smaller R yields more non-Gaussian beliefs.

claims.claim: Figure 4 shows all tested topologies reach a KL divergence below 0.02 within 3 hops from prior factors, and that higher node degree increases non-Gaussianity in star graphs while weaker priors enable faster Gaussian emergence (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: All three sub-claims are supported with concrete numbers: chain/tree/loopy all cross KL<0.02 within 3 hops; 31-seed star intervention shows degree-10 KL > degree-2 KL in 31/31 seeds; four chains with decreasing prior weight show strictly monotone final KL decrease (0.00122 down to 5.3e-05).

claims.claim: Figure 5 applies the theory to stereo depth estimation belief propagation, showing Gaussian convergence in textureless image regions while non-Gaussian beliefs persist at high-contrast edges (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Official Middlebury Cones stereo pair at 30,000 variables and 32 disparities with 80 loopy iterations yields textureless-region median KL of 0.00403 (88% below 0.02) versus edge median KL of 0.029828 (62% above 0.02), a 7.4× separation matching the paper's predicted pattern; the logbook honestly notes that smoothness hyperparameters are independently chosen.

ai-sherpa/bp-gaussian-convergence-sparse.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence across all six claims, including exact sum-product runs on chains and trees, bit-exact computation-tree equivalence on loopy grids, an analytic derivation of the R≈6 exclusion boundary, and a full-scale 30,000-variable Middlebury Cones stereo experiment. The reproduction is independently implemented in pure numpy/scipy with negative controls, multi-seed interventions, and honest disclosure of unreleased hyperparameters.

ai-sherpa/accuracy-first-renyi-dp-repro.paper_title: Accuracy-First Rényi Differential Privacy and Post-Processing Immunity

claims.claim: The paper reformulates mechanisms as returning pairs (y, ε) rather than separate output and privacy-loss functions, resolving prior notational obstacles to defining post-processing immunity for accuracy-first privacy (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: 1000 random finite mechanisms (output spaces size 2–6) show identical output mass and privacy loss (max error 0e+00) between the (y,ε) pair form and the separate output+bound-function form, with exact round-trip (0/1000 failures) and ε carried unchanged through random post-processings (0/1000 failures).

claims.claim: Pure ex-post privacy (δ=0) satisfies post-processing immunity, but δ-probabilistic ex-post privacy with δ>0 does not, even though the latter is shown equivalent to (ε,δ)-probabilistic differential privacy for constant ε (Theorem 3.2, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Pure ex-post PPI holds with 0/1000 violations across 1000 random finite mechanisms; an exact 4-output witness (P=[0.2,0.3,0.25,0.25], Q=[0.001,0.11,0.4445,0.4445]) demonstrates δ-probabilistic PPI failure: bad mass jumps from 0.2=δ to 0.5>δ after deterministic post-processing, with merged loss 1.505>ε₀=1.099; constant-ε probabilistic-DP equivalence passes 0/1000.

claims.claim: The paper introduces α-ex-post Rényi differential privacy (Section 4), proves it satisfies post-processing immunity (Theorem 4), and proves it composes adaptively with total privacy loss ε* = Σε_i (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: Rényi divergence contraction under coarse-graining holds with 0/1000 violations and max violation 0e+00 across 1000 random finite mechanisms; two-step adaptive composition yields ε*=ε₁+ε₂ with 0/1000 failures and max error 1.3e-15 (machine precision).

claims.claim: The sequential precision-weighted Gaussian mechanism (Algorithm 2, Appendix C.4) is shown to achieve α-ex-post RDP equivalent to the original Brownian mechanism (Theorem 5, Section 5).
claims.evidence: 250,000 simulated paths over 7 cumulative privacy levels show the precision-weighted Gaussian matches Brownian target Var=tᵢ and Cov=min(tᵢ,tⱼ) with max variance error 0.271% and covariance error 0.223%; the covariance identity is additionally verified analytically.

claims.claim: Table 1 summarizes that pure ex-post privacy has post-processing immunity but the Brownian mechanism does not satisfy it, whereas α-ex-post RDP satisfies both post-processing immunity and compatibility with the Brownian mechanism (Table 1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: All three operative Table 1 rows are independently checked: pure ex-post has PPI (0/1000 from Claim 2) but BM fails (Gaussian release failure probability 0.001350>0 at ε_T=3.5, Δ=1, σ=1); δ-prob lacks PPI (exact witness from Claim 2) but satisfies BM; α-ex-post RDP satisfies both (Claims 3–4).

claims.claim: On the Adult dataset, a data-dependent stopping rule (Algorithm 1) using a private validation set generates synthetic data while minimizing privacy budget over ε ∈ [0.01, 1] subject to maintaining classifier accuracy thresholds (Figure 1, Section 6).
claims.evidence: Full 45,222-row UCI Adult dataset, 30 runs, 20/40/40 split with disjoint private validation, 7 log-spaced ε∈[0.01,1]: median accepted ε=0.0464, mean val/test accuracy 0.810/0.809 (baseline 0.752), query RMSE strictly decreasing across all 7 ε levels — demonstrating budget minimization while maintaining accuracy thresholds.

ai-sherpa/accuracy-first-renyi-dp-repro.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence for all six claims at the paper's native scale: finite-mechanism algebra with 1000 random instances per theoretical claim, 250k-path Brownian equivalence simulation, and a full Adult-dataset experiment with 30 runs. Evidence includes exact counterexamples, machine-precision composition checks, and analytic covariance verification alongside Monte-Carlo results.

claims.claim: RDNGD achieves iteration and oracle complexity of O(d·ε⁻²) for smooth nonconvex problems and O(d·ε⁻¹) for smooth convex problems using only a pairwise comparison oracle on Riemannian manifolds (Table 1).
claims.evidence: At d ∈ {40,80,120} (paper's own regime), regression gives nonconvex d-exp=1.03 and ε-exp=1.23 (inside the O(ε⁻²) upper-bound envelope), and convex ε-exp=1.12, d-exp=1.02, with raw oracle counts reported (e.g., d=120: ε=0.05→76028, ε=0.02→208308).

claims.claim: The recurrent variant RRDNGD attains linear convergence for strongly convex objectives, requiring O(d log(1/ε)) oracle calls (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Per-phase gaps at d=8 halve exactly (0.0266, 0.0129, 0.0068, 0.0034), giving log-gap-vs-phase slope −0.698 = −ln2 with R²=1.000, confirming geometric/linear convergence; oracle d-exp=1.07 and total growth ~6× over two decades of ε is consistent with logarithmic scaling despite log(1/ε)-exp=1.74 from phase quantization.

claims.claim: RDFW, a projection-free Riemannian dueling Frank-Wolfe method, achieves O(ε⁻¹) iteration complexity with O(d·ε⁻²) oracle calls for smooth convex problems using only a linear minimization oracle (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Using the paper's theory batch Mₖ ∝ d·(k+3), gap-vs-t log-log slope = −0.91 at d=40 (matching O(ε⁻¹) iterations), and oracle regression over d ∈ {20,40,80} and four ε values gives ε-exp=2.04, d-exp=1.13 (matching O(d·ε⁻²)), with 12 concrete oracle-count records.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.1 and Lemma 3.2 show the comparison-based gradient direction estimator is unbiased for the normalized gradient with improved constants over prior Euclidean dueling optimization work (Section 3, Lemma 3.1, Lemma 3.2).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo with 4×10⁵ samples across d ∈ {5,10,20,40} confirms cos(E[estimator], v/‖v‖) ∈ [0.9999,1.0000] (unbiasedness), empirical Ĉ ∈ [0.813,0.950] inside the paper's [0.399,1] interval and ~16× above Saha's 0.05, and Lemma 3.1 mismatch probability 0.00000 ≤ bound 0.00885.

claims.claim: The framework is applied to a black-box adversarial attack on DNNs with sphere-constrained perturbations and to horizon leveling via SO(2) image rotation, both using only pairwise comparison feedback (Section on real-world applications).
claims.evidence: A real MLP(128,64) trained on real MNIST (test acc 0.952) is attacked via comparison-only sphere-constrained RDNGD, flipping 25/25 images (median true-class prob 0.000); SO(2) leveling recovers tilts {−9°,+12°,+20°,−30°} to within 0.21° using only pairwise comparison feedback. Substitutions (MNIST for CIFAR-10, synthetic landscape for real photos) are documented and preserve the DNN, sphere constraint, SO(2) geometry, and comparison-only feedback.

claims.claim: The method covers Hadamard manifolds and bounded-sectional-curvature spaces, with demonstrated applications including Rayleigh quotient maximization on the unit sphere and Karcher mean computation on SPD matrices (Section on synthetic applications).
claims.evidence: Rayleigh quotient at d=30 reaches cos(x, top eigenvector)=1.0000 with f=0.6316 matching ½·λ_max=0.6316; Karcher mean on SPD (affine-invariant, n=5, m=8) reaches geodesic distance 1e-5 to the fixed-point reference with f−f_ref=2.31e-11, both using only the comparison oracle.

michaldobiezynski/repro-riemannian-dueli.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence at the paper's own scale for all six claims: complexity exponents are recovered via regression over multiple dimensions and ε values, lemmas are Monte-Carlo-verified, and both real-world and synthetic applications reproduce with the correct manifold geometry and comparison-only feedback. The main caveats are documented backend substitutions (MNIST/MLP for CIFAR-10/CNN, synthetic landscape for real photos) that preserve the paper's algorithmic structure.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-online-conformal-pre.paper_title: Online Conformal Prediction via Universal Portfolio Algorithms

claims.claim: UP-OCP is a parameter-free online conformal prediction method requiring no stepsize tuning, whose regret analysis is built on universal portfolio algorithms (Section 4.2, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The closed-form update λ_t=(N+1/2)/t was compared against direct numerical integration of the general UP definition (Eq. 9-10 with arcsine prior) across 12 rounds, yielding max absolute difference 1.11e-9. The algorithm also ran unmodified across three distinct regimes (α=0.05/0.25/0.1, Gaussian/Cauchy scores, T=2000) with zero hyperparameter changes, confirming parameter-free operation.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 shows UP-OCP achieves linearized regret of order O(√(T ln T)) in the worst case, improving to O(ln T) as the miscoverage target α→1 (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The linearized regret bound F_T(|u|) from Theorem 4.3 held with 0/80 violations across a grid of α∈{0.05,0.1,0.25,0.5}, T∈{50,200,1000,5000}, u∈{-5,0,1,5,10} on adversarially-structured score sequences. Term-dominance analysis confirmed the sqrt(T ln T) term dominates for typical α, while the ln T term dominates for longer horizons as α→0.999, consistent with the claimed transition (with the nuance that it is a practical regime extension, not a permanent asymptotic change).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 establishes a finite-time miscoverage bound of the form MisCov_T ≤ ε_T + √(2α(1-α)ε_T), where ε_T grows only logarithmically in T (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: The finite-time miscoverage bound MisCov_T ≤ ε_T + √(2α(1-α)ε_T) held with 0/180 violations across 180 trials spanning i.i.d. Gaussian and non-stationary polynomially-growing (S_t ≤ D·t^0.5) score streams, with α∈{0.05,0.1,0.25}, T∈{200,1000,5000}, 10 seeds each.

claims.claim: On the AXP dataset at α=0.05, UP-OCP achieves 0.932 marginal coverage with an average prediction set size of 14.8 and a longest error streak of 4 days, versus 0.920 coverage, 16.9 average set size, and a 15-day longest error streak for the Kalman/KT baseline (Table 1).
claims.evidence: With a real daily-refit Prophet forecaster on 2669 AXP scores, coverage (UP-OCP 0.938 vs paper 0.932; KT 0.934 vs paper 0.920) and longest error streak (UP-OCP 4, matching paper exactly; KT 13 vs paper 15) are close and directionally consistent. However, the average set-size ordering is reversed: UP-OCP (0.179 log-price units) is marginally larger than KT (0.174), whereas the paper reports UP-OCP smaller (14.8 < 16.9). The near-tie in size and unit mismatch prevent confirmation or falsification of the specific Table 1 numbers.

claims.claim: Across miscoverage rates from 0.05 to 0.25, UP-OCP empirically achieves the best Pareto trade-off between coverage and set size compared to the parameter-free KT baseline (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: On real AXP data with Prophet, UP-OCP has a smaller-or-equal average set size than KT in 11 of 15 α configurations (0.05–0.25), with the 4 exceptions being near-ties (≤0.01 log-price units difference). This majority-but-not-unanimous result falls short of the clean Pareto dominance implied by 'best Pareto trade-off,' and the claim references Figure 1 which is on AXP data specifically.

claims.claim: On a synthetic sinusoidal nonconformity-score sequence, UP-OCP tracks periodic volatility—expanding prediction sets during high-noise phases and shrinking them afterward—matching the best hyperparameter-tuned P-Control baseline without any tuning (Figures 3-4).
claims.evidence: Using the paper's exact synthetic sinusoidal setup (P=200, S_mag=10, S_min=2, T=3000, 10 trials), UP-OCP achieved the smallest average prediction-set size at all 6 tested α values (0.05–0.25) versus KT and SF-OGD (6/6 dominance), and tracked periodic volatility in the window analysis (mean size 22.7 vs KT 29.5 and P-Control 31.5 at comparable coverage). The logbook did not grid-search P-Control's learning rate to find its true best setting, so the 'matching best-tuned P-Control' comparison is incomplete, but UP-OCP outperformed the P-Control setting tested without any tuning.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-online-conformal-pre.overall: The logbook provides strong, independent numerical verification of the paper's three theoretical claims (closed-form derivation exact to 1e-9, regret bound 0/80 violations, coverage bound 0/180 violations) and clean confirmation of the synthetic sinusoidal benchmark (Claim 6). The real-data AXP results (Claims 4-5) are directionally consistent but not exact: coverage and error-streak orderings match the paper, yet the average-set-size comparison is a near-tie that is technically reversed at α=0.05 and only majority-supported across the Pareto sweep.

DineshAI/HDBpda5Vih.paper_title: Efficient privacy loss accounting for subsampling and random allocation

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 gives a closed-form reduction of the privacy loss distribution (PLD) of k-out-of-t random allocation to t-wise convolutions of exponentiated PLD terms (Section 4, Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook describes exact rational arithmetic verification of the Theorem 4.4 PLD identity on 30 add/remove cases across finite-support mechanisms (t=1..5), plus 6 k=2 scope checks, with a formula mutation (t→t+1) rejected in 30/30 cases. For a mathematical identity theorem, exact rational verification on diverse small cases with mutation testing is concrete and direct evidence.

claims.claim: The proposed algorithm computes an (α,β)-accurate approximation of the random allocation PLD in time O(log³(t)·log(t/β)/α²), using exponentiation-by-squaring with geometric-grid rounding (Section 4, Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports 17 fast-vs-exact accuracy comparisons, 6 released Gaussian API cases, and empirical work-scaling fits of log(t)^2.487 and α^-1.984, consistent with the claimed O(log³(t)·log(t/β)/α²) upper bound. Four destructive rounding mutations were rejected. The α^-1.984 fit closely matches the claimed quadratic dependence.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 introduces transformation rules φ_λ that apply Poisson subsampling directly to PLD realizations, allowing subsampling and random allocation to be composed within one unified PLD framework (Section 3, Theorem 3.3, Definition 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports 24/24 exact rational φ_λ transformation identities matching an independent checker, 4 unified composition (allocation-then-subsampling) checks, and 24/24 mutation rejections. This directly tests Definition 3.1 and Theorem 3.3 rather than a proxy privacy-amplification observation.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments show the new random allocation privacy bounds are nearly identical to the Monte Carlo lower bounds of Chua et al. (2024a) and substantially tighter than RDP-based analytic bounds, for t ∈ {1000, 10000} and δ = 10⁻⁶ (Section 5, Figures 1-2).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports evaluation at t ∈ {1000, 10000}, δ=10⁻⁶ with 20/20 Figure-1 points and 80 Figure-2 points, PLD below RDP at every point (median improvement 83.03%), Chua deterministic lower-bound median log10 gap of 0.00484, and 44 statistically resolved Monte Carlo points with median log10 gap 0.01359. These are concrete numerical results at the claimed scale.

claims.claim: A toy Bernoulli mean-estimation experiment (n=10³, δ=10⁻¹⁰) shows random allocation requires strictly lower noise than Poisson subsampling for the same privacy level, demonstrating a genuine privacy (not just variance) advantage (Section 5, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports the Bernoulli experiment at n=1000, δ=10⁻¹⁰ with three (ε,d) panels showing strict allocation noise advantage: σ_alloc=0.889941 < σ_Poisson=0.891829 at ε=1, and σ_alloc=1.865726 < σ_Poisson=1.938765 at ε=0.1. The claim itself describes a toy experiment, and the reproduction runs it at the stated full parameters with variance audited separately from privacy.

claims.claim: Applied to a DP-SGD scenario with block-sparse coordinate sampling (n=6×10⁵, d=2²⁰, C=2¹⁵, E=10 epochs), the PLD accounting method improves privacy bounds over RDP composition even under heavy composition (Section 5, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports the PREAMBLE DP-SGD grid at exact parameters n=600,000, d=2²⁰, C=2¹⁵, E=10, δ=10⁻⁶ across 4 batch sizes and 10 block sizes, with PLD tighter than independently recomputed RDP at 40/40 grid points (min/median/max improvement 5.99%/26.55%/56.59%), plus a matched-privacy anchor showing ε_PLD=0.2723 vs ε_RDP=1.0292 at σ=1.8025.

DineshAI/HDBpda5Vih.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence for all six claims at or above the stated experimental scales, including exact rational verification of mathematical theorems (Claims 1, 3), algorithmic accuracy and scaling checks (Claim 2), and full-scale numerical experiments (Claims 4-6). The old verify_pld.py proxy is still present but explicitly disclaimed; the active evidence comes from separate per-claim verifiers with mutation testing, independent checkers, and negative controls.

DineshAI/DpIc1cpNKG.paper_title: The Implicit Bias of Adam and Muon on Smooth Homogeneous Neural Networks

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 proves that any limit point of the normalized parameter trajectory θₜ/‖θₜ‖ under normalized steepest descent is the direction of a KKT point of the corresponding max-margin problem (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: A degree-3 cubic network with 40 data points and 5 dimensions was used to test convergence to a KKT reference direction, achieving cosine 0.9983–0.9987, but this small-scale finite-horizon experiment cannot establish the universal theorem over all admissible trajectories and limit points.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 extends the margin-maximization convergence result to momentum steepest descent under decaying learning rates, using an Approximate Steepest Descent framework introduced in Definition 5.1 (Theorem 3.3, Definition 5.1).
claims.evidence: Momentum steepest descent was tested on the same small cubic network, achieving cosine 0.989–0.991 to the KKT reference, below the predeclared 0.995 threshold; the verify_ib.py script uses a toy linear model with 40 points and 5 dimensions.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.4 shows Muon, applied simultaneously across weight matrices, is a special case of normalized momentum steepest descent with respect to the matrix spectral norm ‖·‖_msp (Corollary 3.4).
claims.evidence: Five genuine rectangular and rank-deficient matrix gradients were tested; in every case the polar direction achieved spectral norm one and the nuclear dual norm with maximum duality error 3.6×10⁻¹⁵, directly verifying the mathematical identity underlying the corollary.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.5 shows Muon-Signum hybrid algorithms exhibit margin maximization with respect to the max of the spectral norm and the ℓ∞ norm (Corollary 3.5).
claims.evidence: A separate experiment combined matrix polar directions with vector sign updates, confirming the joint primal max norm equals one and the achieved objective equals the nuclear-plus-ℓ₁ dual norm at machine precision, with an infeasible elementwise-sign negative control rejected.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.6 shows Adam without a stability constant exhibits implicit bias toward ℓ∞-margin maximization under a decaying learning rate regime when c₁ ≥ c₂ (Theorem 3.6).
claims.evidence: The verify_ib.py script shows Adam's gap to l_inf direction (0.0354) is larger than its gap to l2-SVM (0.0045), partially contradicting the claim, while the campaign evidence shows cosine 0.980–0.987 to the l_inf KKT reference, below the 0.995 cutoff; neither result adequately supports the claim.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes that under normalized steepest descent with a learning rate schedule satisfying ∫₀^∞ η(t)dt = ∞, the soft margin γ̃(θₜ) increases monotonically (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The campaign tested log(1/L(θ))/‖θ‖³ on a small cubic network, finding 500/500 sampled steps nondecreasing with minimum analytic derivative +3.424, but the verify_ib.py script showed only 50% of steps nondecreasing on a toy linear model; the evidence is on a simplified small-scale setup.

DineshAI/DpIc1cpNKG.overall: The logbook provides direct machine-precision verification of the matrix-norm identities behind the Muon corollaries (claims 3–4), but the convergence theorems (claims 1, 2, 6) are only tested on small-scale cubic or linear setups that cannot establish the universal statements, and the Adam claim (5) has mixed and partially contradictory evidence.

DineshAI/418BWmKIzX.paper_title: Efficiently Learning Drifting Halfspaces with Massart Noise

claims.claim: The paper's polynomial-time algorithm learns margin-separable halfspaces under distribution drift with Massart noise achieving error eta + O~(Delta^{1/3}/gamma), where eta bounds the Massart noise rate, Delta is the drift rate, and gamma is the margin parameter (Theorem 1.1, Section 1.1).
claims.evidence: The proof certificate for Claim 1 discharges eight mathematical obligations (gradient bound, projected regret, regret-to-error with drift, iterate existence, independent validation, epoch transfer, runtime, success probability) and independently verifies the key algebraic identity that both 1/(γ√W) and WΔ/γ equal Δ^{1/3}/γ at W=Δ^{-2/3}, with a negative control (mutating the epoch exponent to -1/2) that correctly fails.

claims.claim: Under the low-degree polynomial hardness conjecture, any efficient algorithm for this drifting halfspace problem must incur excess error Omega(Delta^{1/3}), matching the algorithm's guarantee and establishing an information-computation gap (Theorem 1.2, Section 1.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook identifies that the proof route through Theorem 4.1 is contradicted by the Claim 5 counterexample (inconsistent null distributions), but provides no alternative verification of the conditional hardness conclusion; the claim remains blocked with an explicitly unresolved obligation for a valid low-degree certificate plus testing-to-learning reduction.

claims.claim: For general VC-dimension-d hypothesis classes under Massart noise, the statistically optimal (possibly inefficient) error rate is O~(sqrt(d*Delta)), better than the Theta((d*Delta)^{1/3}) rate achievable under adversarial noise (Theorem 2.1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: The proof certificate discharges five obligations (TV telescope, Massart-Bernstein, localized VC deviation, ERM basic inequality, between-epoch transfer) and independently verifies via SymPy that both d/(qW) and ΔW equal √(dΔ/q) at W=√(d/(qΔ)), with a negative control (mutating the window exponent to -1/3) that correctly fails.

claims.claim: A matching information-theoretic lower bound of Omega(sqrt(d*Delta)) is proved for halfspaces under random classification noise (RCN), establishing optimality at Theta~(sqrt(d*Delta)) (Theorem 2.2, Section 2).
claims.evidence: An independent corrected construction discharges seven obligations (halfspace realizability, RCN contract, TV drift, information budget via BSC capacity ≤ q², generalized Fano giving success <0.138 at d=40, risk reduction, all-horizon coverage), yielding the Ω(√(dΔ/q)) scaling; the logbook explicitly notes the paper's printed proof has an extra factor of d defect but verifies the theorem's statement through the separate construction.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 formally shows that no polynomial of degree less than O(gamma^{-c/4}) can distinguish the null from alternative hypothesis in the associated trajectory-testing problem, giving the formal low-degree hardness evidence for the Delta^{1/3} scaling (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Exact rational arithmetic shows Definition 4.1 specifies Pr(Y=+1)=1/3 while Definition 4.3 specifies Pr(Y=+1)=2/3, making the degree-one polynomial p=Σyᵢ a 1-distinguisher at T=2 with standardized gap squared = (4/3)²/(16/9) = 1, directly contradicting the theorem's assertion that no low-degree polynomial distinguishes the distributions.

claims.claim: In the realizable setting, the algorithm's error improves to O~(Delta*gamma^{-3/2}), surpassing the prior best known bound of O~(Delta*gamma^{-2}) (Theorem 3.2, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides a side-by-side comparison (with source hash and theorem anchor verification) showing the paper's Theorem 3.2 actually states Õ(√Δ·γ^{-3/2}) and compares against Õ(√Δ·γ^{-2}), whereas the imported claim uses Δ^1 instead of Δ^{1/2}; the ratio √Δ vanishes as Δ→0, so the claim as stated misrepresents the paper's actual theorem.

DineshAI/418BWmKIzX.overall: The logbook provides structured proof certificates with independent algebraic verification for Claims 1, 3, and 4, an exact rational-arithmetic counterexample falsifying Claim 5, and a source-transcription mismatch falsifying Claim 6 as stated, while Claim 2 remains unresolved due to a blocked proof route. The accompanying numerical experiments (d=5, N=500, 4 seeds) are toy-scale and only check trivial monotonicity trends, but the proof-level evidence is the substantive contribution.

DineshAI/M52jcbntdB.paper_title: A Stronger Benchmark for Online Bilateral Trade: From Fixed Prices to Distributions

claims.claim: Under a bounded-density assumption on buyer/seller valuation distributions, the proposed algorithm achieves Õ(T^{3/4}) regret against the best fixed price distribution satisfying Global Budget Balance (GBB) (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The end-to-end experiment fitted regret exponent 0.9903 (CI [0.9873, 0.9935]) across T up to 1,048,576, but Profit-Max never stopped so exploration and constrained-UCB phases never ran, meaning the full three-phase algorithm was not successfully executed and the T^{3/4} rate was never properly tested.

claims.claim: Without the bounded-density assumption, any algorithm suffers Ω(T) linear regret against the GBB benchmark, shown via a needle-in-the-haystack construction proving discretization is impossible (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Exact LP computation of the four-atom needle-in-the-haystack hard family yields a GBB comparator gap of 0.005211 > 1/200 between full optimum (0.0833) and no-needle optimum (0.0781), with needle GFT=1/8, needle profit=-1/8, and feedback-history identification upper bound=1/8, cross-checked with SciPy HiGHS.

claims.claim: Bounded density lets the learner restrict to a uniform K×K price grid with discretization error O(log(T)/K), showing no separation between one-dimensional SBB learning and two-dimensional GBB distribution learning (Lemma 5.1, Lemma 5.2).
claims.evidence: Comparator-only LP comparison of dense vs grid-restricted GBB optima on three bounded-density rectangle mixtures across K=5..257 shows zero directed-projection violations, SciPy HiGHS cross-checks pass, and maximum gap (0.0004503 at K=33) vanishes by K=33, confirming O(log(T)/K) discretization error.

claims.claim: In the profit-collection phase, regret is bounded by Õ(β + T/K + √(KT)) where β is the accumulated budget (Lemma 7.1, Lemma 7.2).
claims.evidence: Actual Exp3 Profit-Max phase run at T=2048..131072 with two beta coefficients and 12 seeds achieved 96/96 targets reached, normalized-regret exponent 0.1385, and largest mean regret/stated scale ratio of 0.072, directly supporting the Õ(β + T/K + √(KT)) bound.

claims.claim: The pure-exploration phase estimates all K² price-pair outcomes using only 2K exploration samples via sample reuse across the observable/non-observable GFT decomposition (Lemma 8.1, Lemma 8.2).
claims.evidence: Actual exploration phase run for K=8,16,32 with 128 trials each updated all K² cells in exactly 2KN rounds, with zero simultaneous failures (failure-probability upper bound 0.023 < 0.05) and GFT=L+R+PRO identity holding to 1.11e-16.

claims.claim: The UCB-based constrained-bandit optimization phase achieves Õ(K√T) regret while preserving GBB feasibility, combining with the other phases to yield the overall Õ(T^{3/4}) rate (Lemma 9.1, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Constrained-UCB phase isolated with exact L,R supplied, run over T=2048..131072 at K=8 and K=4..16 at T=32768 with 12 seeds; horizon regret exponent 0.779 (CI [0.762, 0.798]) and grid regret exponent 0.677 are sublinear, with maximum regret/stated scale 0.575, though profit shortfall/stated scale of 3.87 is a noted concern for GBB feasibility preservation.

DineshAI/M52jcbntdB.overall: The logbook provides rigorous LP-based and simulation-based evidence for claims 2–6, including exact hard-instance verification, grid discretization checks, and phase-isolated experiments with proper scaling and multiple seeds. Claim 1 remains inconclusive because the full algorithm never executed end-to-end (Profit-Max did not terminate), yielding near-linear regret exponent ~0.99 rather than the theoretical 0.75.

DineshAI/zl3akehFBq.paper_title: Diffusion Flow Matching: Dimension-Improved KL Bounds and Wasserstein Guarantees

claims.claim: For the non-early-stopping, constant step-size setting, Theorem 1 establishes KL convergence bounds for Brownian-motion-based diffusion flow matching scaling as O(d^3) in dimension, improving on prior O(d^4) results, decomposing into a drift-approximation term epsilon^2 and a discretization term scaling as O(h) (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Exact closed-form Gaussian recurrence across d=1–256 with steps 8–512 confirms the KL bound's source factor scales as d³ (SymPy: factor/d³→5) versus the cited prior d⁴ (SymPy: factor/d⁴→6), and the ε² drift-approximation term is verified exactly (KL increments in ratio 1:4:16 for ε=[0,.02,.04,.08]) alongside O(h) discretization refinement.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 relaxes the assumptions of Theorem 1 to require score integrability only of the conditional coupling pi_{0|1} rather than the full coupling pi, while preserving the O(d^3) dimensional scaling under early stopping (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The coupling π=N(0,I_d)⊗δ₀ provides a strict witness where H3 is genuinely false (singular joint support, zero Lebesgue measure) while H4 holds (conditional Gaussian score), and exact Euler recurrence across d=1–256 with four early-stopping δ values confirms KL convergence with O(d³) scaling (SymPy: factor/d³→1+δ⁻⁴), validated by a 50-digit Decimal independent checker agreeing to 5.55e-17.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 introduces a novel non-uniform step-size schedule (h_k = h early, then h_k = h*min(t_k, 1-t_k) later) that yields faster convergence in the early-stopping regime while retaining O(d^3) complexity (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The exact theorem schedule h_k=h·min(t_k,1-t_k) is implemented and verified (max identity residual 1.60e-16 across 80 rows), and an independent first-hit work search across d={1,16,256} shows the nonuniform schedule consistently requires less work than uniform (ratios 1.87–13.56), with SymPy confirming the δ⁻⁴-to-log(1/δ) improvement and retained O(d³) dimension order.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 extends the analysis to 2-Wasserstein distance, giving bounds that decompose into a drift error epsilon and a discretization error scaling as O(sqrt(h))*O(sqrt(d^3)), under a weak log-concavity assumption on the coupling and first-order score integrability (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Correlated Gaussian couplings (ρ∈{0,.25,.5,.75}) across d=1–256 certify H3/H6/H7 assumptions with explicit constants (α_π=1/(1+|ρ|), Hessian norm=1/(1-|ρ|)), and exact W₂ propagation confirms the decomposition into a drift term linear in ε and a discretization term scaling as O(√h)·O(√d³), with SymPy verifying the dimension term/d^(3/2) has a finite nonzero limit and an independent scipy.linalg.sqrtm implementation agreeing to 6.31e-16.

claims.claim: Corollary 3 specializes the Wasserstein result of Theorem 4 to the independent coupling pi = mu tensor nu*, allowing assumptions to be stated on the marginals rather than the joint distribution (Corollary 3).
claims.evidence: Unequal marginal Gaussians μ=N(0,σ₀²I_d), ν*=N(m,σ₁²I_d) are explicitly constructed as π=μ⊗ν* across d=1–256 (280 rows), with zero cross-covariance verified in every row, H8 checked on each marginal separately, and Lemma 1 block-Hessian/concavity identities certified both numerically and via general symbolic differentiation of log μ(x)+log ν(y).

claims.claim: The dimensional improvement from O(d^4) to O(d^3) is obtained by using integration-by-parts to transfer derivatives onto the coupling instead of directly expanding three logarithmic-derivative terms, reducing the required differentiation order from three to two (Section on Key Methodological Innovations).
claims.evidence: The integration-by-parts identity ∫(∂³_u K_s)π du = -∫(∂²_u K_s)(∂_u log π)π du is directly evaluated via adaptive quadrature, analytic Gaussian-convolution derivatives, and SymPy, all agreeing to residual 2.22e-16, with SymPy confirming the kernel derivative polynomial degree drops from 3 to 2 while one derivative transfers to the coupling score, and the resulting tensor count changing from d⁴ to d³.

DineshAI/zl3akehFBq.overall: The logbook provides exact closed-form Gaussian specializations across dimensions up to 256 with independent SymPy symbolic verification, multi-method numerical checkers, and rejected negative controls for all six claims, directly testing the dimensional scaling, error decomposition, assumption relaxation, schedule improvement, product-coupling specialization, and integration-by-parts mechanism. While limited to Gaussian-family couplings rather than the full generality of the theorems, the setup is non-toy in scale and directly probes the core mathematical content of each claim.

vimarsh/repro-revit-roto-reflection-equi.paper_title: REViT: Roto-reflection Equivariant Convolutional Vision Transformer

claims.claim: REViT introduces Group Convolutional Self-Attention (G-CSA), which achieves discrete roto-reflection equivariance via convolutional patch embeddings and convolutional attention without requiring explicit rotation-aware position encoding (Section 4.2, Equations 8-10).
claims.evidence: Numerical audit of the official Rot2DTransformer code shows equivariance error of exactly 0.0 after lifting and ~5e-8 after all G-CSA blocks for p4 (C4) and p4m (D4) groups, with no position encoding used, versus 0.49 for a non-equivariant plain-conv control — confirming roto-reflection equivariance by construction.

claims.claim: On Rotated MNIST, the p4-CSA variant (44.28K params) reaches 97.48% accuracy and the larger p8-CSA variant reaches 98.92% accuracy, outperforming a group-equivariant self-attention (G-SA) baseline with relative position encoding while using fewer parameters (Table 1, Table 3).
claims.evidence: The p4-CSA 44K config (43.66K params, matching paper's 44.28K) was trained from scratch on A10G and reached 97.52% accuracy at epoch 75, exceeding the paper's 97.48%; however, the p8-CSA run was interrupted at epoch 120 (97.82% vs paper's 98.92%) and the G-SA baseline comparison was never conducted, so only the headline p4 result is independently confirmed.

claims.claim: On PatchCamelyon, p4m-CSA attains 90.75% accuracy, surpassing the α_F-p4m-CNN baseline, and on CIFAR-10 p4m-CSA attains 92.68% accuracy (Table 3).
claims.evidence: Neither PatchCamelyon nor CIFAR-10 p4m-CSA models were trained to completion — the CIFAR run stalled on data download and GPU credits were exhausted; only parameter counts were verified locally, with no accuracy results produced.

claims.claim: p4-CSA reduces computation to 116.37M multiply-add operations and 35.84MB peak memory, versus 232.49M operations and 161.77MB for p4-SA with relative position encoding, roughly a 50% reduction in compute (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Measured p4-CSA MACs were 1244.67M versus the paper's 116.37M (~10× discrepancy), the G-SA+RPE baseline (232.49M/161.77MB) was not measured as it requires an external codebase, and memory figures were not independently reported; only the group-order scaling trend (p4/Z2 ≈ 3.5×) was approximately reproduced, which does not confirm the specific claimed numbers or the 50% reduction.

claims.claim: At ImageNet-1K scale, REViT (18M params) achieves 79.27% top-1 accuracy, exceeding augmented ViT-Small (72.08%) and RE-ResNet (77.37%) (Table 7).
claims.evidence: Only the parameter count was verified (18.54M matches paper's 18M) and a forward pass at 224×224 was confirmed to run; no training was performed and no accuracy was measured, so the 79.27% top-1 claim is unsupported by any experimental evidence.

claims.claim: Equivariance error analysis shows near-zero pre-classification errors (1.5e-5 to 2.8e-5) for p4/p4m configurations, with elevated errors for the p8 group attributed to interpolation artifacts from non-grid-aligned rotations (45°, 135°) rather than architectural limitations (Table 6, Section 5.5).
claims.evidence: Equivariance audit reproduces the qualitative pattern: p4/p4m show near-zero errors (0.0 after lifting, ~1e-7 after G-CSA), p8 shows elevated error (1.9e-2 at lifting, 6.3e-2 after G-CSA) originating at the lifting layer from 45°/135° interpolation, and the non-equivariant control gives 0.49 — all consistent with the paper's Table 6 and Section 5.5 explanation.

vimarsh/repro-revit-roto-reflection-equi.overall: The logbook provides solid numerical evidence for the architectural equivariance mechanism (Claims 1 and 6) and reproduces the headline Rotated MNIST p4-CSA accuracy (Claim 2), but Claims 3, 4, and 5 lack completed training runs or matching absolute numbers, leaving them inconclusive.

SabaPivot/repro-a-short-and-unified-conv.paper_title: A Short and Unified Convergence Analysis of the SAG, SAGA, and IAG Algorithms

claims.claim: A single unified proof framework analyzes SAG, SAGA, and IAG jointly by bounding sub-sampling staleness with concentration tools and constructing a novel Lyapunov function V_k = f(x_k) - f(x*) + L*alpha^2*W_k with a weighted delay window W_k (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: On the full a9a dataset (32,561 rows, d=123, N=32 components), the same Lyapunov function V_k = f(x_k) - f(x*) + L*alpha^2*W_k was applied to SAG, SAGA, and cyclic IAG with 33,262 trajectory-level contraction checks yielding zero violations and window identity errors below 1e-7, demonstrating that one unified Lyapunov object works across all three algorithms on a non-toy real dataset.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.11 provides the first high-probability convergence bounds for SAG and SAGA under strong convexity, with rate O(exp(-K/(tau*kappa))) where tau = O(N log(NK/delta)) (Section 3, Theorem 3.11).
claims.evidence: On the full a9a-derived problem (N=32, d=123, κ=13.74), 32 independent seeds per method showed 95th-percentile objective gap decaying log-linearly (SAG slope −0.678/epoch R²=0.993, SAGA slope −1.038/epoch R²=0.995), and an exact-constant audit with the paper's conservative τ and stepsize showed 0/24 bound violations across method/checkpoint cells with worst q95/bound ratio 0.0257.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.12 extends the unified analysis to non-convex objectives, obtaining an O(L^2 B^2 tau / K) convergence rate on the squared gradient norm for SAG/SAGA (Section 3.4, Theorem 3.12).
claims.evidence: A genuinely nonconvex finite sum built from all 32,561 a9a rows (139/160 probe points with negative Hessian curvature, min eigenvalue −0.0474) was optimized with SAG and SAGA over 12 runs totaling 240,000 steps, yielding 108 stationarity certificate rows with 0 bound violations against the O(L²B²τ/K) envelope, worst measured ratio 1.745e-7.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 improves the deterministic convergence guarantee for IAG from O(exp(-K/(kappa^2 N^2))) in prior work to O(exp(-K/(kappa N))) (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Cyclic IAG was run to a fixed 10⁻³ gap reduction on 9 worst-direction quadratic instances spanning N∈{8,16,32} and κ∈{2,4,8}; a power fit of steps versus Nκ gave exponent 1.00407 (R²=0.999981) with steps/(Nκ) stable in [54.41, 55.05] while steps/(Nκ)² varied by 15.8×, directly measuring the improved O(exp(−K/(κN))) scaling rather than the prior O(exp(−K/(κ²N²))).

claims.claim: Theorem 3.14 extends the unified high-probability analysis to Markov sampling schemes beyond i.i.d. sub-sampling (Section 3, Theorem 3.14).
claims.evidence: Irreducible aperiodic lazy-refresh Markov chains replaced i.i.d. sampling on the full a9a-derived N=32, d=123 problem across three refresh probabilities (p=0.15, 0.30, 0.60) with 24 seeds × 80 epochs × 2 methods = 144 trajectories; all six combinations converged with strictly steeper q95 contraction and lower staleness as mixing time decreased, directly reproducing the mixing-time inflation mechanism.

SabaPivot/repro-a-short-and-unified-conv.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence on the full LIBSVM a9a dataset (32,561 rows, d=123) for all five claims, including 33,262 Lyapunov contraction checks with zero violations, 32-seed high-probability tail decay with zero bound violations, nonconvex stationarity certificates with verified negative curvature, a 9-cell IAG scaling census measuring exponent 1.004, and 144 Markov-chain trajectories showing mixing-time dependence. These are finite-consequence empirical audits of theorem guarantees on non-toy setups, not symbolic proof replications.

rcgp/repro-svd-as-a-fast-interpretabilit.paper_title: SVD as a Fast Interpretability Method for Transformers

claims.claim: Native Network Anatomy identifies dominant functional pathways with orders-of-magnitude efficiency gains over training-based interpretability baselines.
claims.evidence: The SVD computation time is measured (3.6s on GPT-2 Small MLP weights), but no actual training-based baseline (SAE, CLT) is run for comparison — the ~4000x speedup relies on literature estimates of ~4 hours for SAE training. Additionally, the claim that NaNA 'identifies dominant functional pathways' is not specifically tested; only raw SVD speed and memory are reported.

claims.claim: SVD-based decomposition of MLP weight matrices reveals Detector-Effector Units that provide interpretable rank-1 subspaces without auxiliary proxy models.
claims.evidence: Top 5 DEUs from Layer 10 of GPT-2 Small are extracted via SVD on W_in and W_out without any proxy model, and the table shows concrete token-cluster pairs (e.g., DEU #2: detector tokens n/N/m/E/e mapping to effector tokens ',/./:/"/!) demonstrating partial semantic interpretability of rank-1 subspaces on a non-toy model.

rcgp/repro-svd-as-a-fast-interpretabilit.overall: The logbook demonstrates that SVD on GPT-2 Small MLP weights is fast and training-free, and extracts DEUs with some interpretable token patterns. However, the efficiency comparison to training-based baselines relies on literature estimates rather than actual baseline runs, and the 'dominant functional pathways' aspect of Claim 1 is not directly tested.

SabaPivot/repro-randomized-feasibility-m.paper_title: Randomized Feasibility Methods for Constrained Optimization with Adaptive Step Sizes

claims.claim: Proposes Algorithm 2, a Gradient Method with Randomized Feasibility using an adaptive Polyak-type stepsize, and proves linear convergence in expectation to a prescribed tolerance ε for strongly convex, Lipschitz-smooth objectives, with iteration complexity O(log(1/ε)) (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: reproduce.py runs 8-seed QCQPs with 500 constraints and 10 dimensions using an adaptive Polyak stepsize eta=(f(x)-f*)/||g||^2; the fitted log-log merit slope is -1.066, consistent with linear convergence on a non-trivial constrained quadratic setup.

claims.claim: Introduces Algorithm 3, DoWS (Distance over Weighted Subgradients) with Randomized Feasibility, a parameter-free adaptive-stepsize method for convex possibly-nonsmooth objectives, proving an O(1/√T) worst-case convergence rate in expectation (Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: judge_extension.py runs DoWS on a 1000-constraint L1 nonsmooth problem with an independent LP certificate (f*=12.6655, residual 7.8e-16), 5 seeds, 5000 iterations; late merit slope is -0.537 (target -0.5) and sqrt(T)-scaled envelope spread is only 1.082x, empirically confirming the O(1/sqrt(T)) rate.

claims.claim: Introduces Algorithm 4, T-DoWS (Tamed DoWS), which removes the requirement that the constraint set Y be bounded, retaining an O(1/√T) rate up to logarithmic factors (Theorem 5.5).
claims.evidence: judge_extension.py runs T-DoWS on Y=R^10 with no radius projection; late slope -0.603, maximum iterate norm 1.065 vs 5.543 for untamed DoWS (5.2x separation), confirming taming removes bounded-Y requirement while retaining O(1/sqrt(T)) up to log factors.

claims.claim: Proves (Lemma 3.1) that infeasibility of iterates under the randomized feasibility update decreases geometrically almost surely with the number of feasibility updates, without requiring compactness of Y.
claims.evidence: reproduce.py runs 20 standalone randomized-feasibility trials (800 constraints, 10 dimensions, 4000 updates, deliberately infeasible starts at x=4.0); fitted log mean-square infeasibility decay is -0.01469 per update, confirming geometric log-linear decrease without compactness of Y.

claims.claim: Validates the theory on quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP) simulations under strongly convex and convex objectives with known/unknown optimal value f*, confirming predicted function-value decay and geometric infeasibility reduction (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: reproduce.py runs 24 QCQP method/seed cells (500 constraints, 10 dimensions, 2500 iterations) confirming objective-merit decay slopes (-1.07 Polyak, -0.32 DoWS/T-DoWS) and geometric infeasibility reduction; judge_extension adds 1000-constraint nonsmooth audit with LP-certified f* and improved slopes (-0.537, -0.603).

claims.claim: Evaluates Algorithms 3 and 4 against a primal-dual baseline on SVM classification with three real datasets (Banknote Authentication, Breast Cancer Wisconsin, MNIST 3-vs-5), comparing test misclassification error (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: judge_extension.py runs all three named real datasets—Banknote (1097/275×4), Breast Cancer (455/114×30), MNIST 3-vs-5 (11552/1902×784)—with DoWS, true T-DoWS (tamed formula), and a 3-fold cross-validated Arrow-Hurwicz primal-dual baseline; mean test errors are reported per dataset and method.

SabaPivot/repro-randomized-feasibility-m.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence from independent implementations supporting all six claims, including a judge-extension script that fixes initial weaknesses by adding an LP-certified nonsmooth rate experiment and running all three real SVM datasets with a cross-validated primal-dual baseline. The strongest results are the DoWS slope of -0.537 matching the predicted O(1/sqrt(T)) rate and the T-DoWS bounded-iterate separation on an unbounded ambient space.

algorise/repro-convergence-analysis-of-t.paper_title: Convergence Analysis of the Lion Optimizer in Centralized and Distributed Settings

claims.claim: Theorem 1 proves centralized Lion achieves a convergence rate of O(d^{1/2} T^{-1/4}) under standard smoothness, without requiring the coerciveness assumption used in prior analyses (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: T-sweep (d=30, T up to 100k, 10 seeds) gives slope -0.276 vs claimed -0.25 (R²=0.999); d-sweep (T=8000, d up to 1000) gives slope +0.393 vs claimed +0.5 (R²=0.966); combined data-collapse slope 0.84 (R²=0.915) across 110 runs on a non-trivial smooth nonconvex objective.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows that a variance-reduced Lion variant using STORM-based gradient estimators improves the rate to O(d^{1/2} T^{-1/3}) under an average smoothness assumption (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: T-sweep gives slope -0.293 vs claimed -0.333 (R²=0.999); VR beats plain Lion at all 6/6 matched (T, seed) points on identical data; d-slope +0.328 vs claimed +0.5 (R²=0.993); data-collapse R²=0.970 across 110 runs.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 establishes that distributed Lion across n heterogeneous nodes matches the centralized rate, converging as O(d^{1/2} (nT)^{-1/4}) (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: T-sweep (n=8, d=20, T up to 100k, 8 seeds) gives slope -0.234 vs claimed -0.25 (R²=0.9999); n-sweep (n up to 32) gives slope -0.311 vs claimed -0.25 (R²=0.997); combined data-collapse slope 0.988 (R²=0.925) across 88 runs with heterogeneous nodes.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 shows that adding variance reduction to distributed Lion improves the distributed rate to O(d^{1/2} (nT)^{-1/3}) (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: T-sweep gives slope -0.328 vs claimed -0.333 (R²=0.9999); VR beats plain distributed Lion at all 6/6 matched points; n-slope -0.384 vs claimed -0.333 (R²=0.994); data-collapse slope 1.013 (R²=0.977) across 88 runs.

claims.claim: Theorem 5 gives a communication-efficient Lion variant with unbiased sign compression achieving either O(d^{1/2} T^{-1/2} + d n^{-1/2}) or O(n^{1/2} T^{-1} + d n^{-1/2}) depending on the learning-rate choice (Theorem 5).
claims.evidence: The measured T-exponent (-0.283 to -0.300) does not match the claimed T^{-1/2} decay, and the measured n-exponent (-0.222) is far from the claimed n^{-1/2}; the floor-dominated regime was never reached at feasible T, so neither component of the claimed rate is cleanly confirmed.

claims.claim: Theorem 7 shows that combining bidirectional unbiased sign compression with variance reduction attains a communication-efficient rate of O(d^{1/4} T^{-1/4}), improving over the non-variance-reduced Theorem 6 rate (Theorem 7, Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: Theorem 7's own rate O(d^{1/4}T^{-1/4}) is approximately confirmed (T-slope -0.294 and -0.255 at two scales, R²>0.999), but the key improvement claim over Theorem 6 is not demonstrated: Thm 6 and Thm 7 are statistically indistinguishable at the main scale, and Thm 6 is empirically better at all 5 points in the small-scale discrimination probe.

algorise/repro-convergence-analysis-of-t.overall: The logbook provides strong empirical scaling-law evidence for Claims 1-4 (centralized and distributed Lion and their VR variants) with well-designed log-log sweeps, multiple seeds, and head-to-head comparisons on a non-trivial synthetic objective. Claims 5-6 are not convincingly reproduced: Claim 5's measured exponents deviate substantially from the theorem's rates and the asymptotic floor regime is never reached, while Claim 6's improvement of Theorem 7 over Theorem 6 is never observed and is contradicted at the small-scale probe.

ProCreations/repro-near-optimal-converge.paper_title: Near-Optimal Convergence of Accelerated Gradient Methods under Generalized and $(L_0,L_1)$-Smoothness

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 proves Algorithm 1 achieves oracle complexity of 5√ℓ(0)R̄/√ε + k(δ) gradient calls for functions with subquadratic or quadratic growth under generalized ℓ-smoothness (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements Algorithm 1 with GD warm-start counting as k(δ) across 9 cells with 5 ε values each, and reports that all targets are hit within the 5√ℓ(0)R̄/√ε + k(δ) bound (max calls/bound ratio 0.07595), with Lyapunov-certificate ratios below 0.12, providing concrete numerical evidence that the complexity bound holds on real algorithm runs.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.4 shows that optimizing over the free parameter δ yields complexity O(√ℓ(0)R/√ε), which is provably optimal in the small-ε regime (Corollary 3.4).
claims.evidence: 42 measured complexity runs on f(x)=exp(ax)-ax-1 across 6 cells and 7 accuracies (1e-1 to 1e-7) all stay within the certificate (max ratio 0.2126), and the lower-bound test on the worst-case tridiagonal instance (dimensions up to 1281, k up to 640) shows AGM maintains a stable 2.83–3.30x ratio to the lower bound while GD degrades from 3.46x to 39.46x, demonstrating the ε^{-1/2} optimal rate empirically.

claims.claim: For (L₀,L₁)-smooth functions (ℓ(s)=L₀+L₁s), the paper's bound reduces to O(√L₀R/√ε), removing the non-constant multiplicative factors present in prior results such as √(L₀+L₁‖∇f(x⁰)‖)R/√ε from Li et al. (2024a) and exp(L₁R)·√L₀R/√ε from Gorbunov et al. (2025) (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Sixty comparison cells evaluate the exact prior leading-factor expressions numerically: the smallest Li et al. factor relative to √L₀R/√ε is 2.117 and the smallest Gorbunov factor is 2.779, confirming both non-constant multipliers exceed 1 in every tested cell while the paper's bound has no such factor.

claims.claim: Algorithm 2 (Section 4) removes the initial gradient-descent phase required by Algorithm 1, giving a parameter-stable accelerated method without pre-running GD (Algorithm 2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 2 is implemented starting directly at x0 with adaptive step γ_k=1/ℓ(4ψ⁻¹(Γ_k R̄²)); all 48 cells (96,000 updates) report zero warm-start gradient calls, the max gap/certificate ratio is 0.758, and a destructive control forcing the unsafe 16/L₀ step breaks the certificate in all 9 control cells, confirming both the no-GD-pre-running and parameter-stability aspects.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 provides refined complexity bounds with improved non-dominant terms compared to prior accelerated methods under (L₀,L₁)-smoothness (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The exact Theorem 4.2 and 4.3 non-dominant expressions are evaluated side by side across 60 cells; the largest refined/previous ratio is 0.549, showing the refined term is consistently smaller while the leading √L₀R/√ε term is unchanged, and the logbook correctly notes the source does not claim uniform improvement over Vankov et al.

ProCreations/repro-near-optimal-converge.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence for all five claims through faithful algorithm implementations, systematic parameter sweeps, Lyapunov-certificate checks, a lower-bound optimality test, and destructive controls. The evidence ranges from algebraic expression evaluation (claims 3, 5) to full algorithm execution with gradient-oracle counting (claims 1, 2, 4), all at non-trivial scale.

ProCreations/repro-language-generation-w.paper_title: Language Generation with Replay: A Learning-Theoretic View of Model Collapse

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 proves that a hypothesis class is uniformly generatable with replay if and only if it is uniformly generatable in the standard no-replay setting, with identical sample complexity, showing replay is benign for the strongest notion of generation (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Lean 4.15.0 proof (code/claim1_uniform_replay.lean) checks the burn-in conversion for arbitrary type α, support predicate S, generator G, and threshold d, proving both directions with no sorry and sample_complexity_change = 0; 12,288 finite cells all reached threshold and remained fresh, but the Lean proof carries the universal quantifier.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 exhibits a countable hypothesis class that is non-uniformly generatable without replay but not non-uniformly generatable with replay, establishing a strict separation caused by replay (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Symbolic proof-carrying check proves the parameterized contradiction for arbitrary finite d: generation on h_infinity forces unbounded fresh naturals, the same sequence is valid for h_d via replay, and the finite intersection is exhausted by pigeonhole; 2,080 finite parameter pairs all confirm the contradiction.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 shows a computable algorithm using only membership queries can generate in the limit any countable hypothesis class even under replay conditions (Theorem 5.1).

vimarsh/repro-little-by-little-continual.paper_title: Little By Little: Continual Learning via Incremental Mixture of Rank-1 Associative Memory Experts
