agharsallah/n50ipdt5d5-logbook.paper_title: Revenue Guarantees of No-Swap-Regret Dynamics in First Price Auctions

claims.claim: For exact correlated equilibria in discrete first-price auctions with k discretization levels, expected revenue is at least v2 - 4/k, where v2 is the second-highest valuation (Theorem 2.5).
claims.evidence: Exact LP minimization of revenue over the full CE polytope across 30 instances (k=4–16, n=2,3, 5 valuation menus) shows min-CE revenue ≥ v2−4/k at every instance with minimum slack 0.125 (e.g., k=16, v2=1: min revenue 0.875 vs bound 0.75). This is a worst-case exact check, not a sample.

claims.claim: For ε-approximate correlated equilibria, expected revenue is at least v2 - 3/k - Θ(εk²) (Theorem 2.6).
claims.evidence: Exact LP minimization over the ε-CE polytope across 60 instances (k=4–12, ε=1e-4 to 5e-3, 3 valuation menus) shows min ε-CE revenue ≥ v2−3/k−2εk² at every instance with minimum slack 0.106 (e.g., k=8, ε=1e-3: revenue 0.724 vs bound 0.497). The Θ(εk²) term is instantiated with constant 2 from Lemma 3.8.

claims.claim: There exists an ε-approximate correlated equilibrium with revenue at most v2 - Θ(1/k) - Θ(ε), showing the ε-dependence in the revenue lower bound cannot be removed (Theorem 2.8).
claims.evidence: The LP-derived revenue-minimizing ε-CE serves as an explicit witness. For v1=v2=1, the gap v2−revenue equals exactly 2/k at ε=0 (k×gap0=2.000 constant across k=4–40) plus a monotonically growing ε-dependent term (e.g., k=8: extra gap 0.026/0.129/0.234 for ε=1e-3/5e-3/1e-2), demonstrating both Θ(1/k) and Θ(ε) components.

claims.claim: When bidders run no-swap-regret algorithms achieving swap regret O(√(kT)), the time-averaged revenue is at least v2 - 3/k - O(ε) after O(k^5/ε^2) rounds (Corollary 2.7).
claims.evidence: Actual Blum-Mansour no-swap-regret self-play (n=2, v1=v2=1, k=4,6,8, T up to 160k) yields time-averaged revenue exceeding v2−3/k−2ε_emp k² at all 27 configurations (e.g., k=8, T=160k: revenue 0.730 vs bound 0.263). Empirical swap regret scales as 0.53√(kT), confirming the O(√(kT)) rate. However, k is limited to ≤8 and all 3 seeds produce identical results, suggesting deterministic dynamics or unused seeds.

claims.claim: Time-averaged bidder behavior under no-swap-regret dynamics converges to an ε-approximate correlated equilibrium with probability 1-δ (Theorem 2.3).
claims.evidence: Time-averaged distribution from Blum-Mansour self-play (k=4,6, T=1k–50k) shows exact ε-CE violation decaying monotonically (k=4: 0.027→0.005 as T goes 1k→50k) and staying below 3√(k/T) at all 36 points. The ratio swap_regret/√(kT) is constant at ~0.43–0.53, confirming O(√(k/T)) convergence. Caveat: only k=4,6 tested, the probability 1−δ guarantee is not directly assessed, and all seeds yield identical results.

claims.claim: The revenue lower bounds are proved via a dual-fitting approach that uses a linear program and weak duality to bound revenue of approximate correlated equilibria (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The paper's explicit dual assignment (μ̂=v2−3/k, λ^{a,b}=1 iff a+1/k≤b≤v2−2/k) is checked for dual feasibility at every joint profile and weak duality across 12 configurations (k=4–10, ε=1e-4 to 1e-3). Dual constraints hold with minimum slack 0.10–0.25, and the dual objective lies below the primal LP optimum (weak duality gap 0.10–0.25) and at or above the closed form v2−3/k−2εk², directly realizing the dual-fitting proof numerically.

agharsallah/n50ipdt5d5-logbook.overall: All six claims are supported by concrete experimental evidence: Claims 1–3 and 6 use exact LP methods on the real CE/ε-CE polytopes providing worst-case verification, while Claims 4–5 run actual no-swap-regret dynamics confirming revenue guarantees and convergence. The main limitations are small k values (4–16 for LP, 4–8 for dynamics), identical results across all seeds in the dynamics experiments (suggesting deterministic dynamics or unused seed parameters), and the probability 1−δ aspect of Claim 5 not being directly tested.

ai-sherpa/sas-scheduling-thoughts-repro.paper_title: Scheduling Thoughts: Learning the Order of Thought in Diffusion Language Models

claims.claim: On Sudoku puzzle-solving with a 1B-parameter masked diffusion model, the learned Scheduling-Attention Schedule (SAS) order policy reaches 91.8% puzzle accuracy versus 82.0% for the best heuristic decoding schedule (Section 6.1, Table 1)
claims.evidence: On 5,000 held-out Sudoku puzzles with a denoiser matched to the paper's accuracy regime (Confidence Top-1 at 83.48% vs paper's 82.0%), the GRPO-trained SAS order policy scores 79.98% versus best heuristic (Margin) at 84.28% — a -4.30 pp gap, opposite in sign to the claimed +9.8 pp. Replicated on a stronger denoiser (SAS 95.28% vs 96.08%, -0.80 pp). Controls confirm the policy genuinely trained (untrained: 17.45%) and headroom exists (oracle: 99.80%).

claims.claim: Adding a second-stage fine-tuning step on top of SAS raises Sudoku puzzle accuracy further to 97.5%, and cell-level accuracy improves from 98.56% (Confidence heuristic) to 99.21% (SAS) (Section 6.1, Table 1)
claims.evidence: Second-stage fine-tuning along the frozen learned SAS order lowers puzzle accuracy from 79.98% to 75.06% (-4.92 pp), never approaching 97.5%. Cell accuracy shows SAS at 93.599% vs Confidence at 94.656% (-1.057 pp), opposite in sign to the claimed +0.65 pp improvement. The human-expert-order arm improves (+2.76 pp), confirming the fine-tuning machinery works but the SAS-order half fails.

claims.claim: On LLaMA/LLaDA-8B, SAS improves 5-shot GSM8K pass@1 from 64% (baseline schedule) to 76%, and MBPP pass@1 from 39.5% to 41% (Section 6.3, Figure 4)
claims.evidence: LLaDA-8B-Base was downloaded and the harness (5-shot prompting, block decoding, answer extraction) was verified to work, but the SAS order policy was not trained on LLaDA-8B due to measured compute cost (~6.7s per forward pass, ~14 min per GRPO iteration, ~166 GPU-hours per setting). No SAS checkpoint or code was released by the authors. The claim was not experimentally tested.

claims.claim: SAS maintains its advantage over heuristic schedules across generation lengths {128, 256, 512} and block sizes {1, 4, 8} (Section 6.3, Figure 4)
claims.evidence: The claim is specifically about LLaDA-8B on GSM8K/MBPP across lengths {128,256,512} and blocks {1,4,8}, which requires a trained SAS policy on LLaDA-8B that was not produced. A Sudoku block sweep (different task and backbone) was run as context only, showing SAS behind the best heuristic at every block size, but this does not test the claim.

claims.claim: In cross-domain transfer, a schedule policy trained on code and evaluated on math (256-256 setting) achieves a 0.713 pass rate, an 8.5-point improvement over heuristic schedules (Section 6.5, Table 4)
claims.evidence: Cross-domain transfer requires two separately GRPO-trained LLaDA-8B order policies (code and math) plus MBPP harness, estimated at ~1326 GPU-hours, which was beyond the session's budget. No policy checkpoints were released. The claim was not experimentally tested; only an internal arithmetic consistency check on the paper's numbers was performed.

claims.claim: Dense, self-aware reward shaping for the schedule policy is consistently comparable to or better than sparse 0/1 terminal rewards across generation configurations (Section 6.6, Figure 3)
claims.evidence: Both dense self-aware and sparse 0/1 terminal reward policies were trained from identical initialization on identical data with GRPO and compared across 11 decoding configurations (2 denoisers × block sizes 1/2/4/8, plus 3 difficulty buckets). Dense wins in 10/11 configurations by a mean of +2.98 pp and is never worse than sparse by more than 0.5 pp. Dense also wins on the self-aware objective (-1.1500 vs -1.6214). Caveat: tested on Sudoku, not the paper's GSM8K/LLaDA-8B setting from Figure 3.

ai-sherpa/sas-scheduling-thoughts-repro.overall: The logbook provides rigorous experimental evidence falsifying the two headline Sudoku accuracy claims (1 and 2) through a faithful re-implementation with appropriate controls, and verifies the reward-shaping claim (6) on the paper's own Sudoku task across 11 configurations. Claims 3–5 (LLaDA-8B results) remain genuinely untested due to quantified compute constraints and absent author-released checkpoints.

ai-sherpa/source-screening-repro.paper_title: On the Power of Source Screening for Learning Shared Feature Extractors

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows that training on an admissible subset of sources achieves the minimax-optimal statistical rate O(√(d/(Nλ_k))) for shared low-dimensional subspace estimation (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: On the paper's own synthetic setup (d=30, k=5, M=120, N up to 256K), the genie-balanced screened subset keeping 33% of sources achieves a fitted log||sinΘ||-vs-logN slope of -0.5282 (R²=0.9987) vs the theoretical -0.5, at 1.028× full-population error. The Eq.(6)/Eq.(5) improvement factor equals √κ to machine precision (4.4e-16) and the 2√-bound holds on 200/200 configs.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 establishes that a 'good' admissible source subpopulation exists whenever a spectral-norm condition on the source covariates holds (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Full-population κ=17.4286 matches the closed form β₁/βₖ=17.4286 exactly; the genie-balanced subset drives κ→1.0000 and a label-free empirical selector reaches κ=1.353. A positive control confirms the admissible subset exists with |S|=35=k·λ_min and κ=1.0000000, and downsampling the majority group lowers error 0.1653→0.1550 (-6.2%) on ~2.6× fewer samples.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 (genie-aided) and Algorithm 2 (empirical) for identifying informative source subsets are proven to output admissible subsets with high probability (Theorem 5, Algorithm 1, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: The constant c*=1.2188e-06 requires st.rank≥820,480 for non-empty output, but st.rank(A)≤k for A∈R^{k×M} (verified on 50 configs, k up to 4096). Algorithm 1 returns ∅ on 30/30 seeds on the paper's own Sec-5.1 population (k=5), giving Pr[admissible]=0 vs claimed ≥0.95. Even with the gate deleted, the algorithm collapses to uniform random draw with |S|=7 vs required 35 and κ=∞ on 30/30 seeds.

claims.claim: On real-world evaluations, training with a screened source subset yields 74.2% classification accuracy on ACSIncome and 90.5% on CelebA smile classification (Table 2).
claims.evidence: CelebA 90.5% is not reproduced: best accuracy across 18 cells is 82.44% (8.06 pp short), and a ceiling control shows a global logistic probe on full 192-d frozen ViT-Tiny features reaches only 85.27%, placing 90.5% beyond any frozen-feature pipeline. ACSIncome 74.21% matches the level but Ours−Full spans -0.91 to +0.95 pp (mean +0.05, positive in only 6/12 cells) vs the claimed monotone +0.6/+1.1/+1.4 pp, with screened κ staying at 126–18,345.

claims.claim: Figure 1 shows subspace reconstruction error is lower when training on a balanced, screened subset of sources than on the full heterogeneous source population (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: On the paper's synthetic setup (d=30, k=5, M=150), downsampling the majority group from 100% to 25% reduces subspace error from 0.1653 to 0.1550 (-6.2%) while using ~2.6× fewer total samples (45,000→17,400), with κ dropping from 17.43 to 4.29 — reproducing Figure 1's counter-intuitive result that balance beats volume.

ai-sherpa/source-screening-repro.overall: The logbook independently verifies the paper's core theoretical claims (minimax optimality of screened subsets, conditioning as the central mechanism, Figure 1's balance-beats-volume result) on the paper's own synthetic setup at full scale, but falsifies the algorithmic guarantee (Theorem 5: the stable-rank gate is provably unsatisfiable for all k<820,480) and the real-world effectiveness claims (CelebA 90.5% is above the frozen-feature ceiling; ACSIncome shows no screening-attributable gain).

gkalyanaraman3/XSpBSHzJAg.paper_title: A Perturbation Approach to Unconstrained Linear Bandits

claims.claim: The paper's perturbation-based algorithm, PABLO, reduces unconstrained Bandit Linear Optimization (uBLO) to a standard Online Linear Optimization (OLO) problem (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Exact numerical verification over 300 random configs confirms unbiasedness (max rel. err 3.25e-14), second-moment identity (1.00e-14), and tightness of both Cor 2.2 constants; end-to-end PABLO+KT implementation with d=8, T=2048, 400 seeds shows the reduction inequality holds (43.33 ≤ 6443.76) and martingale terms vanish within 1σ.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 gives an expected static-regret bound of the form E[R_T(u)] = O~(G*epsilon + d*kappa*E[||u||*sqrt(V_T log(...))]), with kappa=sqrt(d) in the norm-oblivious setting and kappa=1 in the norm-adaptive setting (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Empirical scaling confirms T^0.4837 (theory 0.5) across T∈[128,16384] and ‖u‖^0.9995 (theory 1) across ‖u‖∈[0.25,16] on a non-toy setup with scalar bandit feedback; the κ-dichotomy derivation is checked and Cor 2.2's E-branch (2d vs 4d²) is verified exactly, though d-dependence was not empirically confirmed due to a non-tight stochastic instance.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows PABLO attains the optimal sqrt(P_T) dynamic-regret dependence on the path-length P_T without requiring prior knowledge of P_T (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states 'Theorems 3.3, 4.3, 4.4 (dynamic regret, high-probability) were not checked — outside the board claims,' so Theorem 3.3's sqrt(P_T) dynamic-regret claim was never addressed.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 establishes a high-probability static-regret bound R_T(u) <= O~(dG(epsilon+||u||)log(T/delta) + G||u||sqrt(dT log(T/delta))) (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook states high-probability theorems 'were not checked,' and no experiments or derivations related to Theorem 4.2's high-probability static-regret bound appear anywhere in the logbook.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 proves the folklore Omega(sqrt(dT)) minimax lower bound for adversarial linear bandits on the unit Euclidean ball (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook identifies a concrete error in the Appendix F proof: per-round regret is computed in normalized units but the factor Δ√d is never restored, so the claimed R_T ≥ (1/6)·E[S_τ] should be (Δ√d/6)·E[S_τ]; an explicit counterexample (x_t≡0) violates the step for all tested (d,T), and a constant sweep shows the obstruction is structural (best achievable R/√(dT) scales like 1/d), meaning the proof as written yields Ω(√(T/d)) not Ω(√(dT)).

claims.claim: Conjecture 5.3 posits a minimax rate of R_T(u) = Theta(||u|| sqrt(T(d v log||u||))) for norm-oblivious comparators, left as an open problem (Conjecture 5.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook merely notes 'Conjecture 5.3 is explicitly left open by the paper' without any derivation, numerical check, or experimental evidence bearing on the conjectured minimax rate.

gkalyanaraman3/XSpBSHzJAg.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical and derivation-based evidence for the core reduction (Claim 1) and the T/‖u‖ scaling of Theorem 3.1 (Claim 2), while identifying a concrete, structurally significant error in the proof of Theorem 5.2 (Claim 5) that weakens its conclusion from Ω(√(dT)) to Ω(√(T/d)). Claims 3, 4, and 6 were never addressed.

ai-sherpa/magnitude-distance-repro.paper_title: Magnitude Distance: A Geometric Measure of Dataset Similarity

claims.claim: Magnitude distance is defined as d_Mag^t(X,Y) = 2·Mag_{X∪Y}(t) − Mag_X(t) − Mag_Y(t), with a tunable scale parameter t that governs sensitivity to global structure (small t) versus finer local structure (large t) (Section on Definition, Magnitude Distance).
claims.evidence: The definition d_Mag^t(X,Y)=2·Mag_{X∪Y}(t)−Mag_X(t)−Mag_Y(t) with Mag_X(t)=1ᵀK⁻¹1 and K_ij=exp(−t‖xᵢ−xⱼ‖) is implemented exactly in pure numpy (definitions page). The tunable-scale behavior is demonstrated on a two-ring construction where the fine/global sensitivity ratio rises monotonically from 0.213 (t=0.02) to 1.270 (t=20), a 5.97× swing across 10 log-spaced t values with 16 seeds.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 shows magnitude distance is symmetric and non-negative, satisfies identity of indiscernibles only up to magnitude equivalence, and does not satisfy the triangle inequality in R^D for D>1 (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Unit tests confirm symmetry (|d(X,Y)−d(Y,X)|≤4.4e-15 over 20 random pairs), non-negativity on samples, identity d_Mag(X,X)=0 exactly, and duplicate invariance. The triangle-inequality counterexample from the appendix (X={±eᵢ}_{i=1..500}, Z={0}, t=5) yields Mag(X∪Z)−Mag(X)=7.181597112, matching the paper's ~7.18 and confirming the triangle inequality fails in D>1.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.3 shows magnitude distance converges to 0 as t→0 and converges to the cardinality of the symmetric difference of the two datasets as t→∞ (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: For X={0,1,2,3}, Y={2,3,4,5} with |X△Y|=4, the logbook measures d_Mag^t→3.999999999 at t=30 (within 6.8e-10 of 4) and d_Mag^t→0.0200 at t=0.01, confirming convergence to |X△Y| as t→∞ and to 0 as t→0, matching Theorem 5.3's predictions on the paper's own construction.

claims.claim: Figure 2 shows magnitude distance remains discriminative in dimensions exceeding 1000, in settings where MMD's discriminative power collapses (Section on High-Dimensional Behavior, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: At D=2048 with t=1/√D, the paired mean-shift gap is +0.002639 (95% CI [0.002445, 0.002834], 20/20 wins, effect size 5.94), while fixed-bandwidth MMD (σ=1) collapses to gap 1.19e-16 (10/20 wins = chance) and Euclidean relative contrast collapses 1.82→0.12. The logbook honestly notes that dimension-scaled MMD (σ=√D) does not collapse, but the claim's specific setting (fixed-bandwidth MMD) is reproduced.

claims.claim: MagGN, a generative model trained with a multi-scale magnitude-distance loss, achieves an 11.97x training speedup over WGAN on MNIST while producing visually competitive samples (Table 1).
claims.evidence: A matched per-generator-step CPU timing at the paper's exact architecture (100→128→256→512→1024→784, batch 64, n_critic=5) yields 2.83–6.34× speedup (curriculum-average 4.00×), and an independent matched 500-epoch H200 GPU run yields 1.75× (MagGN 3935s vs WGAN 6876s) — both categorically below the claimed 11.97×. The structural argument (n_critic=5 caps achievable speedup near 6× before MagGN's own kernel-solve overhead) explains why 11.97× is not reproducible.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.5 proves magnitude distance has bounded outlier sensitivity, changing by only about 6-10% under significant outlier addition compared to a 17.6% change for Wasserstein distance in the same setting (Section 5, Theorem 5.5).
claims.evidence: On the paper's exact Figure-4 construction (B~N([0,0],1), Y~N([2,2],1), 4 outliers std 8, 30 pts/cluster, 24 seeds), magnitude relative change is 9.95% at t=5 and 6.76% at t=20 (paper: 10.29%/6.85%), versus 19.60% for Wasserstein (paper: 17.61%). The representative seed matches to <0.3 percentage points. The Figure-5 Huber radius sweep shows magnitude plateauing at 1.085× while sliced-Wasserstein grows 44.33× over a 50× radius increase.

ai-sherpa/magnitude-distance-repro.overall: This logbook independently verifies the core mathematical definition and properties of magnitude distance (claims 1–3, 6) with numerical evidence matching the paper's constructions to high precision, and verifies high-dimensional discrimination at D=2048 (claim 4). The 11.97× MagGN-over-WGAN speedup claim (claim 5) is falsified by both matched CPU per-step timing (2.8–6.3×) and an independent GPU 500-epoch run (1.75×).

Crusadersk/icml26-delayed-obs-rl-repro.paper_title: Minimax Optimal Strategy for Delayed Observations in Online Reinforcement Learning

claims.claim: For the unknown-delay-distribution setting, the algorithm achieves regret O~(H√((D_max∧B)SAK) + H√(Δ_maxSAK) + H(B+Δ_max)SA), extending the known-delay result (Theorem 2).

claims.claim: A matching lower bound of Ω(H√(D̃SAK/log D̃)) is established for constant-delay MDPs, where D̃ = min{D_max, H/4, B/2, S/4-1}, showing the upper bounds are optimal up to log factors (Theorem 3).

claims.evidence: The logbook directly verifies the new bound's exponents: H is linear (1.006, not H^{3/2}) and D_max scales as √ (0.494, not D_max^{5/2}) on the real MDP across a 64× delay range. Since the improvement factor H^{1/2}·D_max^2 is the algebraic ratio of the old and new bounds, verifying the new exponents suffices to confirm the claimed improvement over Chen et al. (2023).

claims.claim: The framework is generalized to MDPs with partially known dynamics, yielding regret O~(H√(K∑_{z∈Z_eff}(log|Y|)∧B(z)) + H∑B(z)) (Theorem 5, Section 8).
claims.evidence: The logbook contains no experiments involving partially known dynamics, no mention of Z_eff, Y, or B(z), and no test of the regret bound O~(H√(K∑_{z∈Z_eff}(log|Y|)∧B(z)) + H∑B(z)). The generalization to partially known dynamics (Theorem 5, Section 8) is never addressed.

Crusadersk/icml26-delayed-obs-rl-repro.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence on a genuine tabular episodic MDP (not a bandit proxy) supporting the upper bound scaling of Theorem 1, the matching lower bound of Theorem 3, and the improvement over Chen et al. (2023), with all five factors (D_max, S, A, K, H) independently swept and fit. However, Theorem 2 (unknown-delay-distribution) and Theorem 5 (partially known dynamics) are entirely unaddressed, and only a constant-delay model is tested rather than the stochastic inter-arrival of Assumption 1.

claims.claim: Lemma 4.1 establishes a calibration-sharpness decomposition showing expected error equals calibration error plus lack of sharpness plus irreducible aleatoric uncertainty, proving that improving proper scoring rules alone does not guarantee calibration (Lemma 4.1).
claims.evidence: This is a purely theoretical claim about Lemma 4.1's calibration-sharpness decomposition. The logbook contains no mathematical proof verification, derivation checking, or any analysis of the lemma itself; all experimental work addresses empirical claims only.

claims.claim: Proposition 5.2 proves that the proposed conditional kernel mean embedding (CKME) recalibration map achieves auto-calibration while provably preserving the sharpness of the original predictive distribution (Proposition 5.2, Definition 5.1).
claims.evidence: The claim is about what Proposition 5.2 proves mathematically (auto-calibration + sharpness preservation). The logbook never verifies the proof itself. Experimental evidence is mixed: U2 passes (CKME lowers SKCE on 7/10 fix-suite cells), but U1 fails (CKME acceptance 0.157 < Kuleshov 0.220), so the auto-calibration conclusion is not borne out empirically, yet this neither confirms nor refutes the proof's validity under its assumptions.

claims.claim: The novel Energy Distance Kernel (EDK), a characteristic kernel over probability distributions, can be evaluated in O(n log n) time for empirical distributions of size n, versus the O(n^2) cost of standard distributional kernels (Section 5, Energy Distance Kernel).

vissutagunawan/oBgLvd5YC6.paper_title: SimpleMem: Efficient Lifelong Memory for LLM Agents

sotayamashita/repro-row-stochastic-matri.paper_title: Row-Stochastic Matrices Can Provably Outperform Doubly Stochastic Matrices in Decentralized Learning

claims.claim: In the weighted Hilbert space L²(λ;R^d), the λ-induced row-stochastic mixing matrix W is self-adjoint whereas the doubly stochastic matrix W^ds is not, and this non-self-adjointness introduces additional multiplicative penalty terms (κ_λ > 1 and λ_max² > 1) that amplify consensus error under the doubly stochastic design (Section 5.2, Section 6.2).
claims.evidence: At 16-node, 10-seed scale, the row-stochastic matrix (Strategy II) has weighted adjoint residual 9.34e-17 (self-adjoint), while the doubly stochastic matrix (Strategy I) has residual 0.7684 (non-self-adjoint); the doubly stochastic weighted operator norm (0.8987) exceeds its spectral radius (0.8224), whereas the row-stochastic norm equals its spectral radius (0.6107), directly demonstrating the multiplicative penalty.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.5 gives O(1/T) convergence rates for both row-stochastic and doubly stochastic strategies, but the row-stochastic strategy achieves strictly smaller non-asymptotic consensus error and can converge faster even when its spectral gap is smaller than that of the doubly stochastic strategy (Theorem 6.5).
claims.evidence: At the paper's 16-node stochastic least-squares scale (dim 10, 300 iterations, 10 seeds, both weight vectors, three topologies), Strategy II has a smaller spectral gap in all six settings yet achieves lower median final weighted-gradient norm in all six and lower median distance to optimum in four of six; in the preregistered lambda_A exponential target, Strategy II wins on all three metrics (gradient 0.7641 ratio, distance 0.9495, consensus 0.9599) despite spectral gap 0.2479 vs 0.4000, directly supporting the claim that spectral gap alone does not determine convergence speed.

claims.claim: Theorem 7.1 derives a sufficient condition on the spectral gaps, 1 − ρ_Λ ≥ max{(1+η)κ_λ^(-1/3), λ_max^(-1/2)}(1 − ρ_J), under which the row-stochastic design provably converges strictly faster than the doubly stochastic design (Theorem 7.1).
claims.evidence: A concrete counterexample with lambda_max=5, kappa_lambda=2236.068, rho_J=0.98, and rho_Lambda=0.9910557 satisfies the stated max-formula condition at equality (factor 0.4472136), yet Appendix D.1 Equation (49a) fails with margin -1,257,806.31; the logbook also notes the current arXiv v3 uses a different min-formula that passes 23,987 parameter combinations with zero failures, indicating the claim as stated does not match the corrected theorem.

claims.claim: Corollary 7.3 and Algorithm 2 give topology construction guidelines showing that when node degrees scale proportionally with their assigned weights (d_i/d_j matching λ_i/λ_j within bounds set by R), the row-stochastic design outperforms the doubly stochastic design, satisfying a Loewner order condition on the graph Laplacians (Corollary 7.3, Remark 7.4, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: A 16-node graph with weights exactly proportional to degrees satisfies Equation 9 (margin 0.1583), yet the minimum eigenvalue of L(lambda) - R*L(1) is -0.0657, violating the full-space Loewner order; a structural argument shows that for heterogeneous weights, sqrt(lambda)^T [L(lambda)-R*L(1)] sqrt(lambda) < 0 for every R>0, providing a general counterexample to the claimed Loewner implication.

sotayamashita/repro-row-stochastic-matri.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence at the paper's 16-node scale reproducing the weighted self-adjointness property (Claim 1) and the convergence-speed advantage of row-stochastic matrices despite smaller spectral gaps (Claim 2), while furnishing explicit counterexamples that falsify the stated spectral sufficient condition (Claim 3) and the full-space Loewner order claim (Claim 4).

sotayamashita/repro-flat-minima-and-gene.paper_title: Flat Minima and Generalization: Insights from Stochastic Convex Optimization

claims.claim: In non-negative, beta-smooth stochastic convex optimization under a strong flatness condition, flat empirical minima can incur population risk of Omega(1) while sharp minima in the same setting generalize optimally (Theorem 1, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: A finite witness at n=8, d=257, rho=0.25 produced a flat minimizer with empirical risk 0 and population risk 0.140625, while the sharp minimizer had population risk 0 and empirical risk at delta=0.1 exactly equal to delta²/2=0.005, matching the theorem's construction and predictions.

claims.claim: SA-GD converges to a flat (rho-flat) empirical minimum at rate O(1/eta T) on the empirical risk, but its population risk lower bound is Omega(eta^2 (r-rho)^2 T), showing fast flat-minimum convergence does not guarantee generalization (Theorem 2 and Theorem 3, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The block-oracle recurrence was independently evaluated at T in {32,64,128,256} with final iterate norm 0.5 (inside unit ball), and the normalized population witness /(eta²r²T) remained positive and stable around 0.07 across all T values, confirming the predicted scaling.

claims.claim: SAM achieves the same empirical convergence rate as SA-GD, O(1/eta T + beta max{r-rho,0}^2), yet can converge to a sharp (non-flat) minimizer even when rho-flat minimizers exist, exhibiting a sharpness-empirical-risk gap of Omega(r^2) (Theorem 4 and Theorem 5, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: SAM satisfied the Theorem 5 empirical-risk upper bound in all 12 anisotropic quadratic runs across dimensions 16, 128, 512 with log-log slopes near -1.80, matched exact SA-GD on a radial control, and the sharp-minimum witness showed SAM remaining at zero with sharpness-aware gap exactly r²/2=0.03125.

claims.claim: Under realizability (rho=0), SAM's population risk has a lower bound of Omega(eta^2 r^2 T), matching stability-based upper bounds established via algorithmic stability (Theorem 6 and Theorem 8, Appendix A).
claims.evidence: The complete chained hard instance from Appendix C.3 was reconstructed at n=T in {6,7,8} (dimensions 385, 897, 2049), with the one-unseen-coordinate probability above the 1/3 threshold, no projection occurring, and population loss /(eta²r²T) at least {0.0347, 0.0400, 0.0444} across all suffix averages.

sotayamashita/repro-flat-minima-and-gene.overall: The logbook provides concrete finite instantiations of all four theoretical constructions from the paper, with numerical results matching the theorems' predictions at moderate dimensions (up to 2049) and multiple parameter settings. These are faithful finite witnesses of the paper's actual constructions rather than proxy tasks, though they do not constitute full proof verification.

sotayamashita/repro-robust-and-consisten.paper_title: Robust and Consistent Ski Rental with Distributional Advice

claims.claim: The Clamp Policy selects a threshold t̃ = min{max{t*_p̂, ceil(λb)}, floor(b/λ)} for a tunable robustness parameter λ in (0,1) (Definition 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: With b=50 and λ=1/3, inputs 1, 34, and 300 produced clamped outputs 17, 34, and 150, matching ceil(λb)=17 and floor(b/λ)=150 exactly; an independent check with distribution 0.8δ₁+0.2δ₅ and b=3 yielded optimum day 2 and expected cost 1.6.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 bounds the competitive ratio by min{1 + 1/λ - 1/b, [ρ_p̂(t̃) + bθ]/(1-θ)}, giving robustness independent of prediction error η and consistency approaching the optimal ratio as η approaches 0 (Theorem 4.4, Corollary 4.5).
claims.evidence: A discrete distribution pair with Wasserstein distance 0.5 (moving probability 0.1 from day 30 to day 35) produced an observed competitive ratio of 1.369863, which is below the theorem's computed bound of 1.971831, confirming the bound holds in a concrete non-trivial case.

claims.claim: The Water-Filling Algorithm's optimal randomized stopping distribution follows the geometric CDF F*(x) = min{(R-1)((1+1/(b-1))^x - 1), 1} for cost-monotone settings (Theorem 5.2, Section 5).
claims.evidence: At (b,R)=(50,1.7), the geometric CDF satisfied all active robustness inequalities with maximum error 5.33e-14, and its objective value 74.66528446748609 matched an independently solved SciPy HiGHS LP over 600 buying days to within 5.68e-14, confirming both feasibility and optimality.

claims.claim: A stopping distribution is R-robust if and only if μ(x) + (b-x)F(x) ≤ (R-1)x for all 1 ≤ x ≤ b-1 and μ(∞) ≤ (R-1)b (Lemma 5.1).
claims.evidence: Across five reconstructed distributions, all constraint slacks were at least -1.07e-14 (constraints satisfied to machine precision), and direct competitive-ratio enumeration over 600 horizons yielded worst-case ratio ≤1.7000000000000006, confirming that policies satisfying the Lemma 5.1 inequalities are R-robust.

claims.claim: Experiments show the Water-Filling Algorithm yields 5-20% consistency improvements over point-prediction baselines across diverse distributions, with the largest gains on bi-modal distributions (Table 2, Section 6).
claims.evidence: Direct arithmetic on the paper's own Table 2 shows uniform-distribution improvements of only 1.44%, 2.14% (unif100) and 1.19%, 2.29% (unif200), all below the claimed 5% lower bound; the largest gain on twopoint (16.33%, 16.99%) is consistent with the claim's second part but the 5–20% range is contradicted by the uniform results.

sotayamashita/repro-robust-and-consisten.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence—often at machine precision—supporting the four theoretical claims (clamp formula, competitive-ratio bound, geometric CDF optimality, and robustness characterization) through independent implementations and direct enumeration. Claim 5 is falsified by simple arithmetic on the paper's own Table 2, which shows uniform-distribution improvements of 1.19–2.29%, well below the stated 5% lower bound.

sotayamashita/repro-flatland-the-adventu.paper_title: Flatland: The Adventures of Gradient Descent with Large Step Sizes

claims.claim: Definition 2.3 formalizes 'large' step sizes using only local Lipschitz continuity of the gradient, requiring the step size to periodically exceed twice the local smoothness threshold, matching empirically observed edge-of-stability behavior (Definition 2.3).
claims.evidence: The definition was evaluated only on the scalar quadratic f(w)=Lw²/2 across seven curvatures (0.25–16), confirming the ηL and 2ηL thresholds are implemented without Hessian access, but this is a simplified toy objective rather than a non-trivial setup.

claims.claim: Proposition 2.5 establishes that the proposed equality line-search method (Algorithm 2) is Lipschitz-aware without requiring second-order information (Proposition 2.5).
claims.evidence: The lower bound ηL ≥ 2δ(1−c) was checked across seven quadratic curvatures with ηL ranging 1.800–1.967 against a bound of 1.782, but the logbook explicitly states this is 'an exact audit for quadratic objectives,' not a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.1 shows sharpness converges to its global minimum of 2/K, where K is the number of classes (Lemma 3.1, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: A concrete counterexample with K=10 and hidden activations {-2,-1,0,1,2} yields sharpness 0.4 > 0.2 = 2/K, demonstrating that Lemma 3.1/B.23 only proves a lower bound λmax(H) ≥ 2/K, not convergence to 2/K as the claim states.

claims.claim: Empirically, the loss decreases nonmonotonically while the product of step size and sharpness stays above the edge-of-stability threshold of 2 throughout training, with methods reaching edge-of-stability right from the start (Abstract, Figure 1).

claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states 'We did not run that experiment and did not substitute the quadratic audit for it. No paid compute was requested or used,' so no evidence was produced regarding NLS-ub's step-size cap, convergence, or test accuracy on SVHN with ResNet-34.

sotayamashita/repro-flatland-the-adventu.overall: The logbook provides toy-scale quadratic checks for Claims 1–2, a mathematical counterexample falsifying Claim 3's convergence assertion, and a partial real-image neural experiment (EMNIST, 200 updates) that falsifies Claim 4's strict 'throughout' wording while supporting the paper's softer 'very often' phrasing. Claim 5 was never addressed experimentally.

sotayamashita/repro-understanding-the-pe.paper_title: Understanding the Performance Gap in Preference Learning: A Dichotomy of RLHF and DPO

claims.claim: Under isomorphic mis-specification, where the reward model class equals the policy model class (ℱ = ℱ_Π), standard RLHF and standard offline DPO yield equal value: V_{r⋆}^{π_RLHF} = V_{r⋆}^{π_DPO} (Proposition 6, Section 3.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook runs a small finite-action construction from the paper and confirms the value gap between RLHF and DPO is 0 (root x=1.5126032554 shared by both solutions), but this is a simplified illustrative construction, not a general verification of Proposition 6.

claims.claim: Despite this equivalence between RLHF and offline DPO, online DPO can strictly outperform RLHF under the same isomorphic mis-specified model classes, i.e. V_{r⋆}^{π_RLHF} < V_{r⋆}^{π^online_DPO}, because online DPO leverages distributional information unavailable to the two-stage reward-modeling-then-policy-optimization pipeline (Proposition 7, Section 3.4).
claims.evidence: On the paper's specific construction with R=12 and x∈[-4,4], the online DPO value (20.336) exceeds the offline value (15.601) with maximum online gradient -0.0110116, supporting the claim but only on a small hand-crafted example, not a general or large-scale setup.

claims.claim: When the reward class is realizable but the policy class is weak, RLHF weakly dominates DPO (V_{r⋆}^{π_RLHF} ≥ V_{r⋆}^{π_DPO}), since DPO's implicit reward is bottlenecked by the policy class constraints (Proposition 3, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: A three-action construction yields RLHF value 1.8635 vs DPO value 1.3333 (gap 0.5301), consistent with the claim, but this is a minimal 3-action toy example from Appendix C.3 rather than a broader empirical demonstration.

claims.claim: For dual-token sparse prediction tasks, ℓ1-regularized reward model estimation achieves error Õ(√(k log d / n)), where k is the sparsity level and d the dimensionality, while policy-model estimation error under the same sparse ground-truth reward structure is lower-bounded by Ω(d/n), establishing a statistical separation showing RLHF needs asymptotically fewer samples than DPO to recover an effective reward/policy under sparse rewards (Theorem 10, Theorem 11, Section 4).
claims.evidence: 95 synthetic trials at small dimensions (d≤128, k=4) show reward errors normalized by √(k log d/n) stay below 1.213 while DPO errors normalized by d/n stay in [4.844, 6.475], with the gap growing with d, but the minimax lower bound is not proven and the paper's language-model experiments were not attempted.

sotayamashita/repro-understanding-the-pe.overall: The logbook provides real numerical runs on the paper's own small finite-action constructions for Propositions 3, 6, and 7, and a synthetic scaling study for the sparse-reward statistical separation, all of which produce numbers consistent with the claims. However, every setup is a simplified toy instance—small action spaces, low dimensions, synthetic data—and none constitute a full reproduction of the theoretical results or the paper's larger-scale experiments.

sotayamashita/repro-correct-looks-better.paper_title: Correct Looks Better: Pairwise Comparisons Reveal Accuracy Rankings

claims.claim: Elo-style rankings derived from pairwise comparisons achieve Spearman correlation above 0.9 (Pearson R greater than 0.87) with ground-truth accuracy rankings across five benchmarks: MMLU Pro, GPQA Diamond, SimpleQA, GSM8K, and BBH (Section on main results).
claims.evidence: A deterministic synthetic experiment with 10 synthetic models obtained rho=0.9879 and R=0.9918, but the actual five-benchmark result was never recomputed because 'original benchmark judgments are unavailable.' The published averages (rho=0.9019, R=0.8758) are merely restated from the paper, not independently verified.

claims.claim: On four of the five benchmarks, only 6-8.9% of model pairs require reordering (Kendall distance) between Bradley-Terry pairwise rankings and accuracy-based rankings (results section, Kendall distance analysis).
claims.evidence: The listed KD values (6.0%, 8.9%, 7.4%, 7.7%) are the paper's published numbers restated and converted via the identity tau = 1 - 2*KD; the logbook states 'raw matches are unavailable,' so no independent computation of Kendall distance from actual pairwise data was performed.

claims.claim: In the weak-judge regime on SimpleQA, Bradley-Terry pairwise ranking substantially outperforms direct evaluation, reducing ranking distance from 38.2% to 20% (SimpleQA weak judge experiment).
claims.evidence: An independent weak-judge simulation obtained pairwise KD 2.2% vs direct 59.1%, but this is on synthetic data, not the actual SimpleQA benchmark. The published values (20.0% vs 38.2%) are restated, not recomputed from real judgments.

claims.claim: Correcting pairwise comparisons for style and self-preference bias yields only modest ranking improvements, even though 58% of comparisons are non-discriminative pairs where both responses are equally correct or incorrect (bias correction analysis).
claims.evidence: A synthetic simulation showed tau changing from 0.9556 to 1.0000 (delta 0.0444) when removing a simulated style term, but the logbook explicitly states 'the empirical Figure 6 improvement cannot be recomputed without its source judgments,' so the actual bias-correction experiment was not reproduced.

claims.claim: Controlled interventions identify 'echo' (response repetition following the final answer) as a causal driver of judge preference on non-discriminative pairs, with an estimated contrast of -0.52 (95% CI [-0.57, -0.46]) (echo causal intervention experiment).
claims.evidence: The contrast of -0.52 and CI were recomputed arithmetically from the paper's published rates (0.29 and 0.81) using a two-proportion normal approximation, yielding [-0.573, -0.467]. No actual echo intervention experiment was conducted—this is a numerical consistency check of published inputs, not an independent experimental reproduction of the causal claim.

sotayamashita/repro-correct-looks-better.overall: The logbook does not independently reproduce any of the five claims on the actual benchmarks or with real model/judge inference. It provides synthetic simulations for some claims and arithmetic consistency checks of published aggregates for others, but no non-toy experimental evidence supporting or refuting the paper's claims.

sotayamashita/repro-a-sketch-and-project.paper_title: A Sketch-and-Project Analysis of Subsampled Natural Gradient Algorithms

claims.claim: For linear least-squares problems, subsampled natural gradient descent (SNGD) is shown to be directly equivalent to the regularized Kaczmarz method, and SPRING is equivalent to the Nesterov-accelerated regularized Kaczmarz (ARK) method (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The equivalence was checked on a four-row, three-parameter system with max absolute error 0.0, which is a minimal sanity check of an algebraic identity rather than a non-toy-scale experiment.

claims.claim: SNGD converges at rate (1-α)^t where α=λ_min(P̄), while SPRING converges at rate O((1-√(α/β))^t), giving up to a square-root improvement in iteration complexity over SNGD (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: On a 100×20 consistent linear least-squares system with all 4,950 row subsets enumerated, the theoretical SPRING-to-SNG rate-constant ratio was 2.515 and the empirical ratio across 32 held-out seeds was 1.735×, with median 800-step error at 0.00703× of SNG's, directly confirming acceleration on a non-trivial setup.

claims.claim: For general quadratic losses, SNGD requires the regularization parameter λ to exceed a threshold λ0 to guarantee convergence, and can diverge if regularization is insufficient (Proposition 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports that the accepted paper contains no Proposition 3, no parameter lambda_0, and no divergence-threshold theorem, so the claim as stated cannot be matched to any testable result in the paper.

claims.claim: Under an assumption that the regularized projector P̄ shares an eigenbasis with J^T J, SNGD provably outperforms SGD by a factor of k^β when the spectrum of the Jacobian decays polynomially (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Exact enumeration on 12-dimensional diagonal systems showed log-log slope 3.883 for i^-2 spectral decay versus 1.000 for flat spectrum, reproducing the superlinear scaling mechanism, but on a small system and without directly verifying the specific k^β outperformance factor over SGD.

claims.claim: A unified algorithm (Algorithm 1) captures both SNGD (momentum μ=0) and SPRING (μ∈(0,1)) as momentum-based updates using subsampled Jacobians, enabling single-minibatch convergence guarantees of any batch size.
claims.evidence: Setting momentum to zero in the unified update produced the SNG step with max absolute error 0.0, but this was verified only on the same small four-row, three-parameter system, making it a minimal algebraic sanity check.

claims.claim: Analysis of SPRING's convergence for general (non-least-squares) quadratic losses is left open as Conjecture 7, despite numerical experiments showing large empirical performance gains over SNGD.
claims.evidence: The logbook confirms by direct examination of the accepted paper that the accelerated sketch-and-project proof for general quadratic losses is explicitly left open (recorded as Conjecture 6.2) with Figure 5 providing numerical evidence, which matches the substance of the claim about the paper's content.

sotayamashita/repro-a-sketch-and-project.overall: The logbook provides a meaningful non-toy verification of SPRING acceleration over SNGD on a 100×20 system with exact subset enumeration and held-out testing, and confirms meta-claims about the paper's structure, but most other claims are checked only on minimal 3–12 dimensional toy systems or reference theorems absent from the accepted paper.

claims.claim: The paper formalizes randomized self-reduction learning and provides sample-complexity analysis under correlated sampling (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook checked only 4 boundary cases of the inequality k*epsilon<=rho and epsilon<=xi for k from 1 to 10, which the logbook itself acknowledges is 'not a theorem-prover certification' — a simplified spot-check of a theoretical claim, not a full verification.

claims.claim: RSR-Bench contains 80 benchmark functions for evaluating randomized self-reduction discovery (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Independent parsing of the benchmark data without the official aggregation script found exactly 80 rows and 80 unique function names, concretely confirming the benchmark size.

claims.claim: Vanilla Bitween discovers randomized self-reductions for 43 of 80 RSR-Bench functions, including the first known sigmoid reduction (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook freshly ran the official Vanilla Bitween pipeline on only the sigmoid function (1 of 43), discovering and symbolically proving a reduction with mean error 6.44e-05; the remaining 42 functions were only checked by aggregating the authors' canonical rows, and the 'first known' historical priority was not independently established.

claims.claim: Agentic Bitween discovers randomized self-reductions for 64 of 80 RSR-Bench functions by letting LLM agents propose query functions beyond the fixed prior query set (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook only performed independent aggregation of the authors' canonical rows to count 64/80 covered functions; no fresh LLM agent runs were executed, so the agentic discovery claim rests entirely on unverified author data.

claims.claim: On nonlinear invariant benchmarks, the regression backend outperforms the MILP backend in sample count and runtime (Table 2).
claims.evidence: A fresh paired run of both official backends on all 80 functions (Job 6a6370f47ef3c08464967823) showed MILP had lower reported sample complexity (26.360 vs 53.898), lower mean runtime (14.177s vs 15.074s), and more pairwise runtime wins (52 vs 28), directly contradicting the claim that regression outperforms MILP in both metrics.

sotayamashita/repro-learning-randomized-.overall: The logbook independently confirms the 80-function benchmark size and provides a fresh falsification of the regression-vs-MILP superiority claim across all 80 functions, but only offers toy-level evidence for the theoretical claim (4 boundary cases) and the vanilla Bitween claim (1 of 43 functions run), while the agentic Bitween claim lacks any fresh experimental evidence.

sotayamashita/repro-caos-conformal-aggre.paper_title: CAOS: Conformal Aggregation of One-Shot Predictors

claims.claim: CAOS aggregates nonconformity scores from multiple one-shot predictors by summing the k smallest scores (k=3 in experiments), reusing the same limited labeled data for both reference and calibration rather than splitting it (Equation 12).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides a concrete implementation audit with explicit per-round reference indices, one-shot scores, and k=3 selection: for calibration target index 2, references [0,1,3,4] yield scores [2,3,3,2], the three smallest [2,2,3] sum to 7, and prediction uses all five references. This directly demonstrates the sum-of-k-smallest aggregation with data reuse as described in the claim.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves CAOS achieves finite-sample marginal coverage Pr(Y_{n+1} in C_caos(X_{n+1})) >= 1-alpha despite violating classical exchangeability assumptions, via a monotonicity-based reduction to full conformal prediction (Theorem 4.1, Lemma 5.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook enumerates all 286 multisets of 10 examples over a 4-point binary domain with n=9, alpha=0.2, k=3, finding minimum coverage of exactly 0.8 and passing all 2,205 monotonicity checks. This is a real but clearly simplified finite-domain check, not a verification of the general theorem for arbitrary predictors or domains.

claims.claim: On the facial landmarking task at alpha=0.05, CAOS attains an average prediction set size of 16.14 +/- 0.58 with 0.955 coverage, versus the SCOS baseline's 36.07 +/- 0.94 set size at 0.976 coverage, a roughly 55% reduction in set size (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states the CelebA landmarking metrics (0.955 coverage, 16.14 set size vs. SCOS 36.07) were not independently rerun, and no DINOv3 features, 478 complete landmarking tasks, or 100-image test split were executed. No experimental evidence is provided for this claim.

claims.claim: On 9 RAFT text classification tasks using Llama2-7B at alpha=0.1, CAOS produces smaller prediction sets than SCOS on 8 of 9 tasks while maintaining target coverage in cases where SCOS fails to do so (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states the nine RAFT tasks using Llama2-7B were not rerun and that Llama2-7B was not run. No prediction set sizes or coverage figures were produced, so the claim of smaller sets on 8 of 9 tasks is not addressed experimentally.

claims.claim: The facial landmarking evaluation uses CelebA face crops at 178x218 resolution across 478 landmarking tasks on 100 test images, while the RAFT evaluation uses only 40 labeled examples per task across 9 real-world classification tasks (Section on Datasets).
claims.evidence: The logbook verified real CelebA data (202,599 rows, 24 images decoded at 178×218, 478 MediaPipe landmarks per face) and confirmed 11 RAFT tasks each have 50 labeled rows supporting a 40+10 split. However, only 24 images were sampled (not 100), and the exact 9-task subset could not be recovered, making this a partial verification on a reduced scope rather than a full reproduction of the stated setup.

sotayamashita/repro-caos-conformal-aggre.overall: The logbook provides a concrete implementation audit verifying the CAOS aggregation mechanism (k=3, data reuse) and a finite-domain enumeration check supporting the coverage theorem's conclusion on a small binary domain. The main application experiments (CelebA/DINOv3 landmarking and RAFT/Llama2-7B classification) were never run, and the dataset setup was only partially verified on a reduced sample.

rcgp/repro-unraveling-syntax-language-mo.paper_title: Unraveling Syntax: Language Modeling and the Substructure of Grammars

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 proves that language modeling KL-divergence decomposes recursively as a sum of conditioned KL-divergences over the constituent subgrammars of a probabilistic context-free grammar (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The numerical audit on a toy PCFG produced nonsensical results: negative KL values (subgrammar A = -1.637) and a large discrepancy between total KL (0.649) and the weighted sum (-1.146), with a difference of 1.795. The 'proof audit' is an assertion without any detailed verification of the theorem's steps.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows that any PCFG decomposes uniquely into inner subgrammars organized as a directed acyclic graph (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook contains no page or section addressing Theorem 4.1 (unique PCFG decomposition into inner subgrammars as a DAG). This claim is never mentioned or examined anywhere in the reproduction.

claims.claim: Unlike children who master simpler grammatical substructures before complex ones, small transformers reduce loss across all subgrammars roughly in parallel during training (Figure 1, Figure 2, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: No training experiments were run. The logbook only performed a code audit and theoretical analysis of the sufficient condition (Corollary 4.7), explicitly stating 'full empirical verification would require reproducing the complete training pipeline with per-subgrammar KL tracking, which exceeds the scope of this reproduction.'

claims.claim: Subgrammar-based pretraining lowers final loss for 2-layer transformers, but this benefit disappears for 4-layer transformers, while CKA analysis shows pretrained models have 8.9% to 21.7% higher attention-layer alignment than models trained from scratch (Figure 6, Table 1).
claims.evidence: No pretraining experiments were run and no CKA/RSA values were computed. The logbook states 'our reproduction didn't run the full pretraining experiments due to time constraints' and only audited the code in cka_analysis.py without executing it. The specific quantitative claims (8.9%-21.7% higher alignment, 2-layer vs 4-layer loss differences) are never tested.

claims.claim: On nested-parentheses generalization tests, prediction error grows approximately as an inverse logarithm of nesting depth, and ChatGPT-5-Instant solves 5/5 shallow arithmetic chains but only 2/5 deeply nested expressions (Figure 3, Section 6).
claims.evidence: No depth generalization experiments were run and no LLM (ChatGPT-5-Instant or otherwise) was tested. The logbook only performed a code audit and cited consistency with prior literature, stating 'this claim would be straightforward to reproduce with the provided code' but never actually running it.

rcgp/repro-unraveling-syntax-language-mo.overall: This logbook provides no substantive experimental evidence for any of the paper's five claims. The only numerical experiment attempted (KL decomposition audit) produced contradictory results with negative KL values, and all other claims were addressed solely through code inspection and theoretical plausibility arguments without executing any training or analysis pipelines.

Firemedic15/repro-single-rollout-hidden-.paper_title: Single-Rollout Hidden-State Dynamics for Training-Free RLVR Data Selection

claims.claim: On MATH-500 at a 2% data-selection budget, SHIFT achieves 62.67 Pass@1 versus 53.73 for random selection and 47.33 for CoreSet, and at a 4% budget SHIFT reaches 64.67 versus 54.53 for random (Section 4.2, Table 1).
claims.evidence: No GRPO RLVR training was performed and no Pass@1 numbers were produced; the logbook only reproduced the instance-selection step (which 7/14 instances SHIFT picks), not the downstream training and evaluation that the claim is about.

claims.claim: On MedQA at a 0.1% selection budget, SHIFT achieves 50.35 accuracy versus 45.28 for random selection, and on transfer to MedXpertQA-U, SHIFT reaches 12.22 versus 8.56 for random (Section 4.2, Table 2).
claims.evidence: No GRPO RLVR training on Qwen3-1.7B was performed, no MedQA or MedXpertQA-U accuracy numbers were produced, and the SHIFT selection mechanism was not even run on MedQA data.

claims.claim: The reasoning-induced representation shift (RIRS) utility score is defined as q(x) = ||Δ(x)||₂ where Δ(x) = e(x) − s(x) is the difference between end and start hidden-state anchor representations averaged across transformer layers, with a log transform q̃(x) = log(1+q(x)) applied before selection (Section 3.2, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook implemented Eqs. 1-3, 6, 7 exactly from the paper text and ran them on the paper's specified Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct model on real MATH-500 data (60 instances), producing non-degenerate q(x) values (mean 98.5, range [81.8, 122.0]) and log-transformed q̃(x) values (mean 4.60), confirming the formula is well-defined and produces a genuine per-instance signal on real model internals.

claims.claim: RIRS magnitude correlates strongly with downstream RLVR performance gain, with a Spearman correlation of ρ = 0.818 (p = 0.0038) across evaluated instances, while showing near-zero correlation (ρ = 0.064) with response length, indicating it is not simply a length proxy (Section 5, Table 4, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The primary sub-claim (Spearman ρ=0.818 with downstream RLVR performance gain) was never tested because it requires full RLVR training; the secondary sub-claim (ρ=0.064 with response length) was tested but yielded 0.218 on 60 instances with known token-truncation issues, a 3.4× discrepancy from the paper's value that neither cleanly confirms nor falsifies the length-independence claim.

claims.claim: An ablation shows that combining RIRS-based coverage (via quality-weighted farthest-first selection, Section 3.5) with the quality-weighting term q̃(x) yields complementary gains over using either component alone (Section 4.2, Table 3).
claims.evidence: The selection algorithm was implemented and run on real model features from 60 MATH-500 instances (vs. the paper's 350), comparing utility-only, coverage-only, and combined strategies on proxy metrics (mean utility and min pairwise diversity) rather than downstream RLVR accuracy; the combined strategy did not show clear complementary gains over coverage-only on these proxies (mean utility 4.649 vs. 4.654, diversity tied at 1.139), though the utility-only diversity collapse (0.173) was confirmed.

Firemedic15/repro-single-rollout-hidden-.overall: The logbook provides a genuine from-scratch implementation of the RIRS formula and SHIFT selection algorithm on the paper's real model and data, confirming the core computational mechanism (Claim 3), but the two flagship downstream-accuracy claims (Claims 1-2) and the main performance-gain correlation (Claim 4) were never tested due to the cost of GRPO training, and the ablation (Claim 5) was only evaluated on proxy metrics at reduced scale.

sotayamashita/repro-sharp-empirical-bern.paper_title: Sharp Empirical Bernstein Inequalities for the Variance of Bounded Random Variables

claims.claim: Under Assumption 1.1 (constant conditional mean mu and variance sigma^2 for X_t in [0,1], without independence or identical distribution), Theorem 4.1 constructs nonnegative supermartingales S_t+ and S_t- underlying a confidence sequence for the variance sigma^2 (Corollary 4.2).
claims.evidence: On a deliberately dependent non-iid stream (30,000 paths × 200 steps) with E[X_t|F_{t-1}]=0.5 and Var=0.04, both supermartingale terminal means stayed at or below 1 within Monte Carlo error (S+ = 0.9849 ± 0.0014, S- = 0.9920 ± 0.0014), and the confidence sequence achieved 100% time-uniform coverage across 1,000 paths × 300 stopping times against a 0.95 target.

claims.claim: Corollaries 4.3 and 4.4 give upper and lower empirical Bernstein inequalities for the variance that hold without assuming independence or identical distribution (Section 4, Corollaries 4.3-4.4).
claims.evidence: Coverage checks on four distributions including a dependent (non-iid) stream at n=1000 with 300 repetitions all showed 100% coverage with Wilson lower bounds above 0.987, and width comparisons demonstrated the sharp EB intervals are consistently narrower than Maurer-Pontil intervals across multiple sample sizes and distributions.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.8 shows that sqrt(n)(U_n - D_n) and sqrt(n)(L_n) converge almost surely to sqrt(2*Var[(X_i-mu)^2]*log(1/alpha)), matching the first-order term of the oracle Bernstein inequality under the additional constant-conditional-variance-of-squares Assumption 4.5, establishing asymptotic sharpness (Theorem 4.6, Theorem 4.7, Corollary 4.8).
claims.evidence: The corrected audit shows the upper scaled width converging to 1.008× the oracle constant at n=2,000,000 (strong evidence for the upper bound), but the lower scaled width remains at 1.253× the oracle constant at the same n, with a power-law fit (R²=0.999) suggesting but not demonstrating convergence. Since the claim requires both upper and lower to converge to the same constant, the lower bound's 25% gap at feasible sample sizes leaves the full claim unverified.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.10 extends the anytime-valid Bennett-type inequality to vector-valued random variables in a separable Hilbert space under a diameter-1 ball constraint (Assumption 4.9), with Corollary A.6 proving the same asymptotic sharpness result holds in this setting (Section 4.5, Appendix A, Theorem 4.10, Corollary A.6).
claims.evidence: The upper bound was checked in finite-dimensional R² (10,000 paths × 400 steps, 100% coverage) and R^5 (200 repetitions × n=1500, 100% coverage), which are proxy spaces for a general separable Hilbert space. The asymptotic sharpness component (Corollary A.6/A.8) was not verified—the upper ratio mean was 1.281 at n=1500, far from the oracle constant of 1, and no lower bound or larger-n asymptotic check was performed for the vector case.

sotayamashita/repro-sharp-empirical-bern.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence for the scalar supermartingale property and empirical Bernstein inequalities under dependence (Claims 1-2), partial evidence for asymptotic sharpness where the upper bound converges but the lower bound has not (Claim 3), and only finite-dimensional proxy evidence for the vector-valued extension without verifying asymptotic sharpness (Claim 4).

rahit/repro-high-accuracy-and-dimension-.paper_title: High-accuracy and dimension-free sampling with diffusions

claims.claim: The paper gives the first diffusion-based sampler with iteration complexity scaling polylogarithmically in 1/epsilon rather than polynomially, as established in the main result (Theorem 1.1 / Corollary 3.9).
claims.evidence: On the reverse probability-flow ODE of a Gaussian-mixture target, the collocation sampler's error decays geometrically in degree D (fit: 10^{-0.49D}, D=2→13 yielding 4.2e-2→1.1e-9) while Euler-Maruyama decays as N^{-0.999}; to reach ε=1e-8, collocation needs ~1.9×10³ vs Euler's ~4.0×10⁸ oracle calls, concretely demonstrating polylog vs polynomial scaling in 1/ε. The 'first' literature-priority qualifier is not tested, but the core scaling claim is supported by real runs.

claims.claim: The iteration complexity bound is O~((R/sigma)^2 * polylog(1/epsilon)), depending on the effective support radius R and noise scale sigma rather than explicitly on the ambient dimension d, under the 'bounded plus noise' assumption that the target is a compactly-supported distribution convolved with Gaussian noise (Assumption 1, Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: The exact Sec-2.2 Euler dimension barrier ‖x_h−x̂_h‖=√d(e^h−1−h) is reproduced to ≤2.6e-15 with fitted exponents 0.500 in d and 2.02 in h; collocation endpoint error stays flat (4e-11 to 7e-8) across d=1…400 at fixed budget; and the reverse-drift Lipschitz constant satisfies L̃/(R/σ)²≈1.000…0.944 with fit L̃~(R/σ)^1.977, confirming both dimension-freedom and the (R/σ)² law.

claims.claim: The proof relies on showing that higher-order time derivatives of the score function along the reverse process remain bounded and dimension-independent when initialized near (not exactly at) the true reverse trajectory (Lemma 3.3, Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: Higher-order time derivatives of the drift along the reverse process are measured as finite and bounded for k=1…4 (0.977, 1.55, 7.70, 79.5), the per-coordinate ‖·‖_{2,∞} norm is exactly d-independent by iid construction while the naive sup-norm grows only ~√log d (3.75→20.9 for d=1→10000), scaling with R/σ matches the (R/σ)^{2k} factor, and the destructive control shows σ→0 blow-up (1.56→255), confirming the noise floor is essential.

claims.claim: A collocation method using low-degree polynomial approximation of score derivatives, combined with Picard iteration, is shown to converge exponentially fast over small time windows (Lemma 3.2, Proposition 3.6).
claims.evidence: Chebyshev basis boundedness Σ|∫φ̃_j|=2.0000000000 exactly for all D∈{4,…,512}; spectral accuracy on ẋ=x shows geometric error decay (2.0e-4→5.3e-15 for D=2→8); Picard contraction ratio equals λρ(A) and is identical to 4 digits across d=1…1000, staying ≤½ when L̃γ_φh≤½ holds, with divergence at λ=90 (λρ=1.93, norm→6.1×10²⁰) confirming a real spectral contraction property.

claims.claim: For a Gaussian mixture with k components separated by Theta(sqrt(log k)), the resulting sampler achieves polylogarithmic scaling in both k and 1/epsilon, whereas prior diffusion-based samplers scaled polynomially in the ambient dimension d (Section 3, discussion following Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence: For k-component Gaussian mixtures with centers at √(log k)·e_i, the effective radius fits R~(log k)^0.500 (theory ½), the measured iteration driver L̃ grows only 0.33→1.07 as k goes 2→55 (sub-logarithmic, hence polylog(k)) while ambient d=k grows linearly, and sampler endpoint error at fixed polylog-size budget stays flat at 2.6e-12…4.7e-12 across k=2…55. The 'prior methods scale poly(d)' comparison is a literature statement not re-run.

rahit/repro-high-accuracy-and-dimension-.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous clean-room implementation of the paper's collocation/Picard diffusion sampler with concrete numerical evidence supporting all five claims: polylog(1/ε) convergence, dimension-freedom up to d=400, (R/σ)² scaling, bounded dimension-independent score derivatives, and polylog(k) complexity for separated mixtures. The main scope limitations are use of perfect scores (no score-estimation error), d=1 for the primary 1/ε test, k≤4 for derivative orders, and trajectory-measured rather than global-sup Lipschitz constants.

rahit/repro-compositional-transduction-w.paper_title: Compositional Transduction with Latent Analogies for Offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning

claims.claim: Compositional Transduction with Latent Analogies (CTA) achieves an average success rate of 56.3 across 8 OGBench manipulation tasks, roughly a 42% improvement over the strongest baseline HIQL-vee at 39.3 (Table 1, Section 6).
claims.evidence: The claim is about 56.3 avg success over 8 OGBench tasks with neural CTA vs HIQL-vee at 39.3, but no OGBench training or success-rate measurement was performed. Instead, the logbook verifies Proposition 4.4's closure and sufficiency lemmas on a 24-state, 2-action toy GCE-BCMP (closure spread 0/36 groups, sufficiency 480/480 pairs), which is a real but drastically simplified proxy.

claims.claim: On the Scene-play task, CTA reaches a direct out-of-combination (OOC) success rate of 73+/-9, versus a standard in-combination success rate of 94+/-4 (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is about neural CTA achieving 73±9 direct OOC and 94±4 standard success on Scene-play, but no OGBench training was run. The logbook instead verifies the analogy-transduction mechanism on a 24-state toy scene MDP, showing 360/360 OOC pairs solved optimally and naive retrieval failing 112/120 — real runs on a simplified setup, not the claimed benchmark result.

claims.claim: On Puzzle-4x4-play, CTA attains a direct OOC success rate of 80+/-8 versus a standard success rate of 100+/-1, outperforming HIQL-vee on direct OOC generalization (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The claim concerns Puzzle-4x4-play (16 buttons) with 80±8 / 100±1 rates, but the logbook uses a 2x3 puzzle (6 buttons, 384 states) instead. It verifies context-invariance (0.00e+00 deviation over 192 configs) and OOC transduction (192/192) exactly on this smaller puzzle, with a closed-form argument for extension to 16 buttons, but the actual 4x4 neural benchmark results are not reproduced.

claims.claim: The dual analogy representation alpha(s,g) = phi(g) - phi(s), derived from the temporal distance difference field (Proposition 4.4), formalizes transduction of analogies to unseen task combinations (Section 4, Section 5).
claims.evidence: The dual-analogy identity α(s,g)(x) = φ(x)^T(ψ(g)−ψ(s)) is verified to machine precision (max error 1.36e-13) over all 13,824 (s,g,x) triples on a concrete 24-state quasimetric MDP, with rank-15 factorization (reconstruction error 7.40e-14). Destructive controls confirm distinct encoders are necessary (symmetric-fit residual ≥1.0, random encoders error 20.47). This is a mathematical identity claim and the verification method is appropriate.

claims.claim: A t-SNE visualization of the learned analogy space shows task clustering consistent with the analogy representation remaining invariant to contextual variation (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is about a t-SNE visualization of 20,000 learned neural analogy features showing task clustering. The logbook instead computes exact context-invariance on a 24-state toy MDP (max deviation 0.00e+00 over 120 instances, 30 distinct field signatures vs 5 scalar values) and produces a PCA embedding — verifying the underlying property on a simplified setup without the actual neural t-SNE.

rahit/repro-compositional-transduction-w.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the paper's theoretical backbone (Proposition 4.4 and its lemmas) via exact computation on small finite MDPs with destructive controls, but none of the empirical OGBench results (Tables 1–2 success rates, Figure 4 neural t-SNE) are reproduced at the paper's actual scale. Claim 4's mathematical identity is genuinely verified; the remaining four claims are addressed only on toy proxies.

rahit/repro-learning-in-bayesian-stackel.paper_title: Learning in Bayesian Stackelberg Games With Unknown Follower's Types

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 proves that under action feedback alone (the leader observes only the follower's chosen action, not its type), any learning algorithm must incur regret that is exponential in the bit-complexity L of the follower's payoffs, specifically Omega(2^(2L)) (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive enumeration of the lower-bound instance family confirms |T_ε| = 2^(2B) exactly for B=1..10 (up to 1,048,576 instances), max vertex sharing = 6 over all vertices, and greedy-optimal coverage leaves R_T/2^(2B) → 0.031, providing concrete combinatorial evidence for the Ω(2^(2L)) lower bound. The oracle-informed destructive control collapses regret to O(1), confirming the barrier is action-feedback-specific.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.7 shows that under type feedback (the leader observes both the follower's action and revealed type), an algorithm achieves regret bounded by Otilde(K^2 log(1/delta) sqrt(T) + beta log^2(T)) against the optimal commitment baseline when the number of leader actions m is constant, holding with high probability (Section 4.4, Theorem 4.7).
claims.evidence: Simulation of the epoch schedule (ε_h = 2^(1−h)/K, T_h ≈ ⌈(1/2ε_h²)log(2K/δ)⌉) over T=10⁴…10⁹·⁵ recovers the √T regret exponent (regression slope 0.5027 vs predicted 0.5), verifies H ≤ log₄(5T) for all 7 horizon values, and confirms the K² prefactor is a valid upper bound (leading term scales ~K¹ ≤ K²). The constant-ε destructive control yields linear slope 1.0, confirming geometric refinement is essential.

claims.claim: Lemma 4.1's Find-Types procedure estimates the follower type distribution to within L-infinity error epsilon_h using Otilde(1/epsilon_h^2) rounds of interaction (Section 4.1, Lemma 4.1).
claims.evidence: Monte-Carlo with K=8 skewed types, 4000 trials per ε value, confirms ‖μ̂−μ‖∞ ≤ ε holds with failure probability ≪ δ=0.10 across all five ε configurations, and the sample-complexity rate exponent is recovered as 1.9995 vs predicted 2.0. The destructive control shows under-sampling to 0.25× breaks the guarantee (failure prob 0.174 > δ=0.10).

claims.claim: Lemma 4.3 bounds the oracle-query complexity of learning best-response polytope regions via the Find-Partition procedure at Otilde(K^(m+1) n^(2m+2)) (Section 4.2, Lemma 4.3).
claims.evidence: Exact LP-based verification over 30 random instances per configuration confirms all three structural bounds: vertices ≤ binom(n+m,m), facets ≤ Kn+m+K, and non-empty joint regions ≤ K^m n^(2m). The K-sweep (K=2..6) shows the ratio of non-empty regions to n^K decreasing from 0.556 to 0.036, directly demonstrating the polynomial collapse from n^K to polynomial growth that yields the K^(m+1) (not n^K) query bound.

claims.claim: The algorithm's positive result relies on iteratively refining the space of candidate leader commitments across epochs, tightening the precision parameter epsilon_h while using the Prune procedure (Lemma 4.4) to guarantee the optimal commitment is never discarded (Section 4.3, Lemma 4.4).
claims.evidence: Adversarial testing of the Prune procedure with μ̂ on the ε-sphere (worst-case Lemma 4.1 perturbation) across 480 tests shows 0/480 optimal commitments discarded, and max suboptimality of survivors ≤ 14Kε_h with linear ε-scaling (0.58→0.28→0.14 as ε halves). The destructive control removing safety margins (C₁=C₂=0) discards the optimum in up to 8/120 instances, confirming the margins are essential.

rahit/repro-learning-in-bayesian-stackel.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all five claims through clean-room reimplementations: exhaustive combinatorial enumeration for the lower bound, epoch-schedule simulation for the regret bound, Monte-Carlo for concentration guarantees, exact LP verification for structural bounds, and adversarial testing for the Prune procedure. Each claim includes a destructive control that fails exactly when expected, and honest scope notes appropriately delineate what is and isn't verified.

rahit/repro-bandit-social-leaning-dynami.paper_title: Bandit Social Leaning Dynamics with Exploration Episodes

claims.claim: In the Episodic Bandit Social Learning (EpiBSL) model with two-armed Bernoulli bandits and episode length m≥2, aggregate exploration fails with probability at least q_P^m > 0 for any symmetric utility aggregation function, even though each agent explores within its own episode (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive grid of 135 configurations (9 priors × {sum,max,min} × m∈{2,3,4,5,6}) confirms arm 2 abandoned with pulls ≤ N_P = 1+⌊(m−1)β₂/α₂⌋ with 0 exceptions; exact failure-tape probability Pr[Ev2]=(1−μ₂)^{N_P}>0 computed in rational arithmetic; log-slope of Pr[Ev2] vs m recovers −0.91629 matching theory (β₂/α₂)·ln(1−μ₂) exactly; m=1 control confirms within-episode exploration is the m≥2 mechanism.

claims.claim: When exploration failure occurs, Bayesian regret grows linearly in the time horizon T, satisfying BReg(T) ≥ c0(T − N0) for constants c0, N0 depending only on the prior (Corollary 4.5).
claims.evidence: Deterministic backbone Reg(T)≥(T−N)·G(μ) verified with 0 violations across 60,000 checks (200 realizations × T=300); on pure-failure realizations max|Reg(t)−t·G(μ)|=0.00e+00 (exactly linear, slope=G=1/2); mean regret 142.601 ≥ failfrac·T·G=142.500 confirms linear Bayesian regret via positive failure fraction; control with arm-1-truly-best gives Reg=0 (sublinear), confirming linearity is failure-specific.

claims.claim: For episode length m=2, learning failure occurs with positive probability even for non-symmetric per-episode utility aggregation functions, not just sum/min/max (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Appendix G.2 non-symmetric instance reproduced exactly: optimal value 1223/2000=0.6115, alternative values 0.6045 and 0.53, and optimal policy (arm2→skip/arm1) all match the paper verbatim; failure demonstrated for non-symmetric f at m=2 with Pr[abandoning tape]=2/5=0.400>0; control confirms γ₂<γ₁ yet arm 2 is optimally played first, showing the symmetric bad-start argument is insufficient.

claims.claim: For m=2 with symmetric utility functions, or for max/min aggregation at any episode length m, failure probability remains positive even without imposing exploration costs on agents (Theorem 4.7).
claims.evidence: Lemma 3.9 closed-form G-bounds verified over 1,320 grid configurations (660 for min, 660 for max) with 0 violations and exact tightness (residual 0.000e+00 at csel=0); failure without cost restriction confirmed for f=max and f=min at csel∈{0.01,0.5,1.0} and m∈{2,3,4} with arm 2 abandoned (pulls ≤ N_P=2) in all 18 cases, including maximal cost csel=1.

claims.claim: The stronger failure event StrongFail_{c,N} (at most N episodes ever try the good arm) occurs with probability at least 1/2 conditional on the base failure event FAIL_{c,N} (Lemma 3.4).
claims.evidence: Per-good-episode arm-2 pull probability ≥ c^m verified on 75-point belief×μ grid (min=1.0 ≥ 1/16); exhaustive enumeration of all 2^12=4096 good-episode sequences confirms Pr[Bridge]=0.9968≥1/2 and deterministic inclusion FAIL∩Bridge⇒StrongFail; paper's N'=6136 formula yields exact binomial tail 1.000000≥0.95; control with undersized N'=4 gives Pr[Bridge]=1.53e-05≪1/2, confirming the bound is non-vacuous.

rahit/repro-bandit-social-leaning-dynami.overall: All five theoretical claims are independently verified by a clean-room exact EpiBSL simulator using rational arithmetic, with exhaustive grids (135–1320 configurations), exact probability computations, and destructive controls on every claim. The reproduction faithfully addresses the paper's actual mathematical model at its real scale, not a proxy or simplified version.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 gives the first convergence bound for Federated DPO (FedDPO) under partial client participation, showing gradient-norm error scaling with local steps E, rounds R, sampled clients S, and gradient variance ζ²_g (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: The FedDPO partial-participation bound (Eq. 54) was tested on a 2D quadratic proxy (L_i=½||θ−c_i||²) across 60 configs with 60/60 holds and recovered the ζ²_g/S floor at R²=0.9999, but this is a simplified analytic instance, not actual DPO training on preference data.

claims.claim: Corollary 5.2 shows that under full participation (S=N) the 1/S variance-amplification term in the FedDPO bound vanishes, isolating the cost of partial participation (Corollary 5.2).
claims.evidence: Full-participation bound (Eq. 90) held 12/12 on the same 2D quadratic testbed, and client-sampling variance was exactly 0.000 at S=N vs 0.162 partial, but this verifies the mathematical structure on a proxy task rather than the actual FedDPO/DPO pipeline.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.4 introduces a staleness penalty term proportional to η·C_q·q_max, quantifying how delayed/asynchronous client updates degrade FedDPO convergence (Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: Staleness penalty was shown linear in q_max (slope 0.313, R²=0.996) and C_q ∝ (κ²+ζ²_g) (R²=0.998) on the quadratic testbed with a destructive control (C_q=0 when κ=ζ=0), but again on the 2D analytic proxy, not actual asynchronous DPO training.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.5 establishes a lower bound of Ω(Eκ²/S) showing that the dependence on client preference heterogeneity κ² and participation rate S cannot be removed by any FedDPO-style algorithm (Theorem 5.5).
