claims.claim: Theorem 3.8 gives the closed-form Local-Equivariant MMSE (LE-MMSE) estimator as a pixel-wise weighted sum over training patches, x̂_loc(y)[n'] = Σ_x Σ_n x[n]·w_{n',n}(x|y), with weights proportional to a Gaussian similarity N(Q_{n'}y; Q_n A x, σ² Q_n Q_n^T) between local patches (Theorem 3.8).
claims.evidence: The numerical audit checks the Theorem 3.8 formula on a 1D cyclic problem with 11 pixels, 7 training signals, and patch size 5; scalar and vectorized implementations agreed to 8.88e-16 and weights normalized to 1, but this is a clearly simplified setting far below the paper's 2D image scale.

claims.claim: The paper defines three hierarchical MMSE variants—MMSE (unconstrained), E-MMSE (translation-equivariant), and LE-MMSE (equivariant plus local)—showing LE-MMSE generalizes via patch recombination rather than memorizing the training set (Section 3, hierarchical MMSE variants).
claims.evidence: A separating example uses one length-12 1D signal with a single unit feature, showing LE-MMSE produces two peaks (sum=2) vs MMSE/E-MMSE (sum=1), demonstrating patch recombination; this is a minimal 1D toy construction, not a 2D image-scale reproduction.

claims.claim: Figure 5 shows strong agreement (PSNR ≳25 dB) between a trained UNet2D and the analytical LE-MMSE formula across denoising, inpainting, and deconvolution tasks on FFHQ, CIFAR-10, and FashionMNIST at 32x32 and 64x64 resolution (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: An A100 run using the authors' released patch-5 UNet2D checkpoints on 10,000 FashionMNIST training images evaluated the exact B=I Gaussian patch formula across 3 tasks and 3 noise levels, achieving 27.66–33.67 dB network-vs-formula PSNR in all 9/9 conditions, confirming the core ≥25 dB agreement claim on a non-toy setup with real checkpoints, though only one dataset/resolution and one test image per condition were used.

claims.claim: For inpainting, a physics-aware pre-inverse operator B=A⁺ reduces noise while preserving signal, whereas for deconvolution the pseudo-inverse can amplify noise enough that a regularized inverse is favored instead, a trade-off formalized via the terms Q_n^+ Δ_{n',n} and Tr(Cov_{n',n}) (Physics-Aware vs. Physics-Agnostic Trade-offs).
claims.evidence: A 1D audit with 32 pixels showed inpainting masking reduced noise gain from 32 to 24 and covariance trace from 5.0 to 2.81, while deconvolution pseudo-inverse noise gain was 4.41e7 vs 55.6 for a regularized inverse; this demonstrates the trade-off mechanism but on a simplified 1D proxy, not the paper's 2D setting.

claims.claim: Network-theory alignment with LE-MMSE degrades in low-density regions of the measurement distribution p(y), particularly at low noise levels when test samples fall outside high-probability training neighborhoods, explaining part of the train-test generalization gap (Measurement Density Effect).
claims.evidence: A 1D 6-component Gaussian-mixture surrogate with 21 parameters showed Spearman ρ=0.891 between -log p(y) and squared error, and six FashionMNIST checkpoint probes at σ=0.05 showed ρ=0.657 with 11.1× error ratio; both are small-scale proxy demonstrations rather than a full reproduction of the density effect on 2D images.

claims.claim: The trained network compresses roughly 3.1x10^7 training pixels into about 4x10^6 parameters while performing inference in about 4ms, roughly 175x faster than direct evaluation of the analytical LE-MMSE formula (~0.7s) (Computational Implications).
claims.evidence: The A100 run measured 4,646,817 trainable parameters in the released UNet2D (consistent with 'about 4M') and 4.281 ms median steady-state inference (consistent with 'about 4ms'); the exact formula took 0.309s yielding 72.2× speedup, confirming the direction and order of magnitude of the 175× claim on a non-toy setup, with the difference attributable to smaller 28×28 images vs the paper's 32×32 3-channel setup.

StochasticRhapsody/repro-an-analytic-the.overall: The logbook combines local 1D toy mechanism checks with one real A100 run using the authors' released FashionMNIST checkpoints, verifying the core network-formula agreement (≥25 dB in 9/9 conditions) and computational timing claims on a non-toy setup, while the remaining claims are only addressed on simplified 1D proxies.

Firemedic15/repro-multi-round-human-ai-c.paper_title: Multi-Round Human–AI Collaboration with User-Specified Requirements

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 gives finite-sample online control guarantees bounding the average counterfactual-harm violation rate by epsilon + (1+eta)/(eta*T) and the average complementarity violation rate by delta + (1+eta)/(eta*T), holding distribution-free with no assumptions on human behavior or problem distributions (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook implemented the exact threshold-update and prediction-set membership rules from scratch and ran T=2000 rounds across i.i.d., regime-switching, and fully adversarial (score=1 every round) scenarios; the realized average violation rate (0.109, 0.109, 0.110) stayed below the bound 0.1105 at every horizon, and an η-sweep confirmed the 1/(ηT) functional form.

claims.claim: The algorithm adapts two thresholds tau_t and lambda_t online via updates of the form tau_{t+1} = max{0, tau_t + eta(E_t^ch - epsilon)}, using nonconformity scores s(T_{t,r}, y) in [0,1] to construct prediction sets each round (Section on Algorithm & Theory).
claims.evidence: The update rule τ_{t+1}=max{0, τ_t+η(E_t^CH−ε)} was implemented verbatim and exercised through the Claim 1 audits; max τ_t reached 1.040 over 2000 rounds, confirming the threshold stays bounded near the score ceiling [0,1] as the proof's uniform-upper-bound step requires.

claims.claim: In LLM-simulated medical diagnosis experiments on the DDXPlus dataset (GPT-4o-mini as human, DeepSeek-Chat as AI), loosening the counterfactual-harm constraint increases the ground-truth loss rate (abandoning correct initial guesses) from 5.1% to 35.3% (Experimental Validation, DDXPlus experiment).
claims.evidence: No live LLM-simulated DDXPlus experiment was run (no GPT-4o-mini or DeepSeek-Chat API calls); only the dataset's existence was confirmed and a synthetic proxy showed the calibration mechanism. The specific 5.1%→35.3% numbers were not reproduced, and the logbook found they may be attributed to the crowdsourcing section rather than DDXPlus.

claims.claim: A crowdsourcing study with 50 participants and 1000 interactions on a collaborative shape-counting visual reasoning task shows that a looser counterfactual-harm threshold (epsilon_ch = 0.30, Algorithm B) produces a higher ground-truth loss rate than a tighter threshold (epsilon_ch = 0.05, Algorithm A) (Crowdsourcing Study).
claims.evidence: No crowdsourcing study was conducted and no human-subjects data was collected or released; the logbook only verified the underlying calibration mechanism (Claim 1's result) as a necessary precondition, which is insufficient to confirm the comparative claim about 50 participants and 1000 interactions.

claims.claim: The framework extends single-round conformal prediction guarantees (Theorem 3.1) to a multi-round setting where the AI's repeated interventions influence evolving human behavior, treating the human as a black box requiring no behavioral model (Theorem 3.1, Section on Technical Innovation).
claims.evidence: The structural argument (single-round offline calibration breaks under repeated interventions, necessitating online recalibration) was confirmed by close reading, and the key testable consequence—no behavioral model needed—was numerically confirmed by the adversarial worst-case audit in Claim 1 where the bound held with no assumption on the score sequence.

Firemedic15/repro-multi-round-human-ai-c.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the theoretical claims (1, 2, 5) via a from-scratch implementation with adversarial stress testing at T=2000, but the two empirical claims (3, 4) were not reproduced at all—no live LLM calls or human-subjects data—leaving them inconclusive.

GwendalTsang/repro-computationally-effic.paper_title: Computationally-efficient Graph Modeling with Refined Graph Random Features

claims.claim: The walk-stitching mechanism in GRFs++ combines multiple short random walks via 2l-level convolutions of the modulation function to produce an unbiased estimator equivalent to a longer walk, trading sequential walk sampling for parallel matrix-matrix multiplication (Lemma 2.1, Section 2.2.1).
claims.evidence: The 2l-level convolution identity was checked numerically for k=0..12 across l=1,2,4, yielding max error ~1e-17 (machine precision), and estimator bias was measured on 5 real paper graphs with 20 trials showing small bias (~0.002–0.005) consistent with unbiasedness; a control with wrong modulation confirmed bias, validating the lemma's core algebraic property.

claims.claim: Increasing the walk-stitching degree l (e.g., l=1,2,4) monotonically improves the mean squared error of the kernel estimator at no extra computational cost, as shown by the closed-form MSE expression for degree l=2 (Lemma 3.2, Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: MSE was computed on all 8 paper graphs (m=256, 15 trials) showing monotonic decrease from l=1→2→4 on every graph with ~2× drop per doubling, confirmed by a scaled HF Job run at m=512, 20 trials; raw CSV data is provided.

claims.claim: An efficient implementation variant achieves O(N) time complexity via a Johnson-Lindenstrauss Transform combined with matrix associativity, improving on the O(N^2) complexity of a sparse-matrix implementation (Section 3, Option II vs Option I).
claims.evidence: Matrix associativity was confirmed exact to ~6e-16; Option I scales as N^2.31 vs Option III at N^1.5 with 190× speedup at N=2048; JLT down-projection unbiasedness shown with bias decreasing monotonically in r and trials. The empirical N^1.5 (vs theoretical O(N)) is explained by dense factor matrices, but the mechanism and complexity gap are demonstrated.

claims.claim: On node clustering benchmarks, GRFs++ reduces error by roughly 13% on the dolphins dataset and roughly 15% on the eurosis dataset relative to standard GRFs (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Real ground-truth labels were unavailable for dolphins and eurosis; proxy reference partitions (exact-kernel spectral clustering) were used instead, yielding +33% for dolphins (not ~13%) and +8.3% for eurosis (not ~15%, though an earlier run gave 15.4%). The direction (GRFs++ beats GRFs) holds, but the specific claimed magnitudes cannot be verified with the proxy setup.

claims.claim: On mesh normal prediction, GRFs++ yields consistent gains of about 0.6-0.9% over regular GRFs (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Synthetic icospheres (not the paper's Thingi10K meshes) were used with known exact normals; the s2 icosphere showed +0.79% gain (within the 0.6–0.9% band) and direction matched on all meshes, but the data is a proxy substitute and larger meshes show gains shrinking to +0.08% due to cosine saturation.

claims.claim: On high-diameter graphs (diameter up to 159), GRFs++ shows improved kernel estimation accuracy for distant node pairs compared to baseline GRFs (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: Path graphs with diameter up to 159 (matching the paper's largest case) and a binary tree were tested with the faithful masked-kernel-error setup (m=64, 10 trials); GRFs++ showed 21–29% lower error for distant node pairs on all 4 graphs, confirmed by a scaled HF Job run.

GwendalTsang/repro-computationally-effic.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence for the theoretical claims (Lemma 2.1 convolution identity, MSE monotonicity, associativity/JLT mechanism) and the high-diameter graph claim, all on real or appropriately-matched setups. However, the node-clustering claim uses proxy reference labels that prevent verification of the specific 13%/15% magnitudes, and the mesh-normal claim uses synthetic icospheres rather than the paper's actual meshes.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 proves that the attention map converges uniformly over bounded regions of radius R at rate C(R)/√n, where C(R) grows exponentially with R (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: Non-toy setup (d=3, n up to 60k, 6 seeds, 48 query points) measuring sup attention-map error against the exact Gaussian limit. Fitted slopes are -0.500, -0.499, -0.499, -0.492 for R=1.0–2.5 (all within 0.01 of -1/2, r²≈0.99), and the prefactor C(R)=err·√n grows from 2.74 to 8.45 with a log-linear fit log C(R)=0.83+0.213R² (r²=0.996), confirming exponential growth in R² consistent with the e^{8R²H²} form.

claims.claim: Proposition 5.1 shows that in the hardmax regime, as the softmax temperature parameter tends to infinity, the convergence rate slows to 1/√(ln n) due to cancellation effects between opposite-signed extreme values (Proposition 5.1).
claims.evidence: Non-toy setup (scalar Gaussian, n up to 200k, 1600 replicates, 5 seeds) confirming the hardmax 1/√(ln n) rate: the Gumbel-scale constant std(Mn)·√(2ln n)/σ=1.302 matches π/√6=1.2825 to 1.5%, the fitted slope vs log(ln n) is -0.495 (theory -1/2), the n-slope is only -0.053 (9.4x shallower than parametric), and the softmax n-exponent collapses from 0.477 at τ=3 to 0.015 at τ=20, directly confirming the temperature-driven slowdown.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 establishes that for sub-Gaussian tokens, the transformed distribution converges at rate O(n^(-β)) with β = 1/(2(1+32Ψ)), where Ψ is the Attention-Reach Coupling defined via the spectral reach and attention horizon (Theorem 4.4, Definition 4.2).
claims.evidence: Non-toy setup (d=2, n up to 40k, 24 resamples, 400 queries, 4 seeds, Ψ swept over [0.64, 5.76]) measuring the transformed-distribution convergence exponent. Fitted β values are 0.441, 0.316, 0.244, 0.200, 0.158 — all strictly below 1/2 and monotonically decreasing in Ψ (r²≈0.99–1.00), confirming the sub-parametric rate and its qualitative dependence on the Attention-Reach Coupling as predicted by Theorem 4.4.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.5 shows the mean of the transformed distribution converges at rate O(n^(-1/(2(1+Ψ)))), exhibiting only polynomial (not exponential) dependence on the attention-reach coupling Ψ (Corollary 4.5).
claims.evidence: Non-toy setup (d=2, non-zero-mean Gaussian tokens, n up to 40k, 4 seeds, Ψ∈[1, 5.76]) comparing mean-functional and general Lipschitz exponents. β_mean ≥ β_gen in all 20 configurations (mean converges at least as fast as the general functional), and 1/(2β_mean) grows from 1.13 to 4.85 approximately linearly in Ψ, confirming polynomial (not exponential) dependence on the coupling as stated in Corollary 4.5.

claims.claim: Section 6 experiments on BERT using 1M and 20M Wikipedia tokens empirically confirm sub-parametric convergence with β < 1/2, contradicting the classical parametric 1/√n rate despite compactly supported token embeddings (Section 6).
claims.evidence: Real bert-base-uncased (110M) forward passes over real wikitext-103-raw-v1 text with a 503k-token pool (paper uses 1M/20M; the convergence exponent is a slope invariant to absolute pool size). The sup-error exponent β=0.337 (R²=0.977) and mean-error exponent β=0.414 (R²=0.993) are both clearly below the parametric 1/2, and the sup-error is slower than the mean-error, consistent with the paper's Section 6 finding of sub-parametric BERT attention convergence.

SabaPivot/repro-token-sample-complexity-.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from non-toy experiments supporting all five claims: Claims 1–4 are verified on synthetic Gaussian setups matching the paper's theoretical regimes with proper multi-seed methodology, and Claim 5 is verified on real BERT with real Wikipedia text at reduced but adequate scale for slope estimation.

Firemedic15/repro-de-linearizing-agent-t.paper_title: De-Linearizing Agent Traces: Bayesian Inference of Latent Partial Orders for Efficient Execution

claims.claim: On the Aliyun cloud-provisioning benchmark at full incomparable-pair coverage (IP-Cov=1.0), BPOP recovers dependency structure with Edge-F1 of 0.95, exceeding the best process-mining baseline (Heuristics Miner at 0.60) (Section 5.4, Figure 7).
claims.evidence: The official repo's own precomputed sweep on real ground-truth DAGs yields BPOP-family Edge-F1 of 0.83 (not 0.95) and HM 0.62 (close to paper's 0.60) at realized IP-Cov≥0.999; the qualitative ordering is supported but the specific 0.95 figure is not reproduced, and the toy proxy (0.77 vs 0.04) is a simplified method, not the paper's actual MCMC.

claims.claim: On WFCommons workflows, BPOP achieves Edge-F1 of 0.91 on SRASearch (22 nodes) and 0.79 on Epigenomics (41 nodes), versus 0.43 and 0.38 respectively for the best baseline (Heuristics Miner) (Section 5.3, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Node counts (22 for SRASearch, 41 for Epigenomics) are confirmed exactly from real WFCommons JSON, but the toy recovery proxy collapses to near-zero Edge-F1 (0.00/0.09) on these larger graphs and the paper's actual MCMC inference was never run, so the specific 0.91/0.79 vs 0.43/0.38 numbers are untested.

claims.claim: The compiled executor driven by BPOP-inferred graphs reaches 100% task completeness with zero fallback LLM calls and zero token usage once incomparable-pair coverage reaches 0.9-1.0, compared to 5.9 LLM calls and 32,208 tokens per task at IP-Cov=0.6 (Table 2, Section 5.4.2).
claims.evidence: Only a structural/logical argument ('IP-Cov=1.0 implies zero unresolved incomparable pairs by definition') is provided; the specific empirical numbers (5.9 LLM calls, 32,208 tokens at IP-Cov=0.6) were not independently reproduced because the full executor+LLM stack was not run.

claims.claim: Across 6 cloud provisioning scenarios, expert mode (SOP-only, using the inferred partial order) completes tasks in 34.4 seconds using 0 tokens but only 66.7% success, while hybrid mode (SOP plus LLM fallback) reaches 100% success in 225.2 seconds using 79,406 tokens, versus 1,319-2,580 seconds and 234k-382k tokens for a pure LLM explore mode (Table 3, Section 5.4.2).
claims.evidence: No experiments were run; the logbook only confirms that the released code implements the three-mode comparison design and that the 6 scenario names match, but explicitly states live LLM execution was out of scope.

claims.claim: BPOP models trace likelihood via a frontier-softmax formulation (Eq. 5) that avoids #P-complete enumeration of linear extensions, reducing likelihood computation to O(|≻h| + T|A|) time (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook implemented Eqs 4-6 from scratch and ran both frontier-softmax and brute-force enumeration on diamond posets |A|=4..12, showing frontier-softmax ops growing linearly (10→78) while brute-force grows factorially (24→479M, taking 57.4s at |A|=12 vs 0.24ms), concretely demonstrating the claimed O(|≻h|+T|A|) vs #P-hard contrast.

Firemedic15/repro-de-linearizing-agent-t.overall: This logbook provides a clean, exact verification of the algorithmic complexity claim (Claim 5) with concrete scaling numbers, but the empirical structure-recovery and execution-cost claims (1-4) are either only directionally supported via the authors' own precomputed artifacts or not tested at all due to not running the paper's MCMC inference or live LLM execution stack.

algorise/repro-distributionally-robust-m.paper_title: Distributionally Robust Markov Games with Average Reward

claims.claim: Under the irreducibility assumption on induced Markov chains for all deterministic policies and transition kernels in a compact, convex uncertainty set (Assumption 4.1), a stationary Nash equilibrium is proven to exist for average-reward distributionally robust Markov games, via a Kakutani fixed-point argument over the best-response correspondence (Theorem 5.8).
claims.evidence: 25 random DRMG instances with only 5 states and 3 actions per player show zero duality gap, consistent with Nash equilibrium existence, but this is a small-scale numerical sanity check of a general existence theorem, not a full reproduction.

claims.claim: The robust Bellman equation for the average-reward setting is shown to be solvable (Theorem 4.3), and the set of optimal robust policies is convex with the induced best-response correspondence upper semi-continuous (Theorems 5.6 and 5.7), which together underpin the equilibrium existence proof.
claims.evidence: Bellman residual is reported as exactly 0.000000e+00 across all 25 small (5-state, 3-action) instances, but the convexity of the optimal policy set is only described qualitatively without specific numerical evidence, and the scale is far below any realistic setting.

claims.claim: The proposed Robust Nash-Iteration algorithm (Algorithm 1), a value-iteration scheme maintaining per-agent value estimates updated via matrix-form stage games, is proven to converge to a Nash equilibrium given an equilibrium-selection oracle that returns globally optimal or saddle-point equilibria (Theorem 6.1, Assumption D.1).
claims.evidence: Convergence is demonstrated on 25 small instances with an empirical contraction rate of ~0.2232 and error at k=50 reported as exactly zero, but the 5-state, 3-action scale is toy and the suspiciously exact zero values raise concerns about numerical reliability.

claims.claim: As the discount factor approaches 1, discounted-reward Nash equilibria of the distributionally robust Markov game are shown to converge to average-reward Nash equilibria, linking the two reward criteria (Theorem 7.1).
claims.evidence: The log-log slope of -1.013 (CI [-1.037, -0.995]) and R² of 0.9996 numerically support the predicted O(1-gamma) convergence rate on small instances, but the contradictory 0/25 pass rate (despite aggregate statistics clearly satisfying the predicate) and inconsistent verdicts across pages undermine the reliability of the evidence.

algorise/repro-distributionally-robust-m.overall: The logbook provides small-scale numerical experiments (5 states, 3 actions per player) across 25 seeds that are broadly consistent with the paper's theoretical claims, but the scale is clearly toy and there are significant internal contradictions (notably Claim 4's 0/25 pass rate conflicting with its own reported statistics, and the conclusion claiming 6/6 predicates passed despite Claim 4 failing).

algorise/repro-near-optimal-regret-for-k.paper_title: Near-Optimal Regret for KL-Regularized Multi-Armed Bandits

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 establishes a high-probability regret upper bound of O~(ηK log^2 T) for KL-regularized multi-armed bandits in the high-regularization regime where η ≤ sqrt(T/K) (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The T-exponent at η=1 (0.1632, 95% CI [0.148, 0.177]) matches the predicted ~0.17 for a log²T law, and K-exponent (0.8893) and η-exponent (1.208) approximately match the predicted linear scaling, but at η=5 the T-exponent is 0.3312 (outside the [0.05, 0.3] accept band) and the composite ratio R_T/(ηK log²T) varies 4.89x across the grid, so the evidence is mixed rather than uniformly supporting or contradicting the bound.

claims.claim: In the low-regularization regime (η ≥ sqrt(T/K)), the same analysis yields a regret bound of O~(sqrt(KT log T)), which is η-independent (Theorem 4.2, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The sqrt(T) rate is confirmed (exponent 0.5151, 95% CI [0.506, 0.525]) and the η-free ceiling holds (max R_T/sqrt(KT log T) = 0.2408), but the K-exponent is not reproduced under any of three experimental designs (0.05, 0.71, 0.79 — none matching the predicted 0.5), and regret rises monotonically with η (slope 0.4818), so the claim is only partially supported.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.3 provides a lower bound of Ω(ηK log(T/(η^2 K))) in the high-regularization regime, establishing near-tightness with the upper bound in Theorem 4.2 (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: The lower bound is not violated by any algorithm tested (consistent with it being valid), but the functional form ηK log(T/(η²K)) fails to organize the data (R²=0.0021 against a 0.80 bar), the best algorithm achieves 3–9x less regret than the rate at unit constant, and the hard-instance construction from the proof could not be instantiated, leaving the claim without decisive experimental support or refutation.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 gives a lower bound of Ω(sqrt(KT)) in the low-regularization regime via a two-point construction method (Section 6.1, Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: The Bretagnolle-Huber certificate computed from measured quantities is valid in 25/25 configurations (measured regret exceeds certificate by 3.77–6.54x), the certificate itself scales as T^0.5007 (R²=0.9999), and the minimax proxy (min over 5 algorithms of sup-instance regret) scales as T^0.5328 with ratio to sqrt(KT) stable at 0.64–0.71 across a 16x range in T, providing concrete non-toy evidence supporting the Ω(sqrt(KT)) lower bound.

claims.claim: The KL-UCB algorithm uses an optimistic bonus term b_t(a) = sqrt(2 log(TK/delta) / (N_t(a) ∨ 1)) together with a novel peeling argument and Freedman's inequality to obtain tight high-probability bounds (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: The bonus formula is correctly implemented and coverage holds (0 violations in 120 runs), but the bonus is 2.8x looser than the data ever required (max normalized deviation 0.3598 vs. threshold 1.0), the bonus actively hurts in the high-regularization regime (52x regret increase across the bonus-constant range, with c=2 being 7.1x worse than c=0), and the peeling argument and Freedman's inequality are proof techniques with no separate empirical signature, so the 'tight' claim is not confirmed.

algorise/repro-near-optimal-regret-for-k.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous, large-scale reproduction (10,980 runs, 933M pulls, 30 seeds per config, pre-registered two-sided predicates) that verifies the Ω(sqrt(KT)) lower bound via a computed Bretagnolle-Huber certificate but finds mixed evidence for the upper-bound scaling and the tightness of the optimistic bonus, with the K-dependence of the low-regime bound and the functional form of the high-regime lower bound not reproducing.

vimarsh/repro-rmnp-row-momentum-normaliz.paper_title: RMNP: Row-Momentum Normalized Preconditioning for Scalable Matrix-Based Optimization

claims.claim: Replaces Muon's Newton-Schulz iteration with a row-wise (d_in) L2 normalization operation, motivated by empirically observed diagonal block structure in the Transformer layerwise Hessian (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Diagonal dominance ratios (r_avg≈4–5, r_min≈1–1.9) were measured on a char-level tiny-shakespeare GPT with d=256/4 layers, matching the paper's GPT-2 Small magnitudes (4.9/1.6), and a control isolates dominance as the driver of orthogonalization≈row-norm equivalence — but at a far smaller scale than the paper's d≥768 transformers.

claims.claim: Reduces per-iteration preconditioning complexity from O(mn*min(m,n)) for Muon to O(mn) for an m x n weight matrix (Section 3.1-3.2).
claims.evidence: Microbenchmark on square matrices up to 2048×2048 fitted Newton–Schulz scaling as m^2.42 and row-norm as m^0.92, confirming the claimed asymptotic separation of O(mn·min(m,n)) vs O(mn) with real timing data.

claims.claim: Measured preconditioning time over 100 steps drops from 2.98s to 0.20s (14.8x speedup) on GPT-2 125M and from 27.07s to 0.61s (44.3x speedup) on GPT-2 770M, relative to Muon (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: The reproduction ran on Apple MPS fp32 instead of the paper's RTX Pro 6000 with bf16/compile, yielding speedups of 56.7× (125M) and 86.1× (770M) vs the paper's 14.8× and 44.3×; the qualitative trend (speedup grows with scale) reproduces but the specific claimed numbers are not verified due to fundamental hardware divergence.

claims.claim: Achieves comparable or better perplexity than Muon on GPT-2/OpenWebText pretraining, improving by 0.04 (125M), 0.07 (355M), and 0.24 (770M) (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: A toy proxy (d=256, char-level tiny-shakespeare, 600 steps) shows RMNP trailing Muon by 1.9 ppl (6.43 vs 4.51), contradicting the paper's claim at this scale; the full GPT-2/OpenWebText pretraining at 125M–770M was never run.

claims.claim: On LLaMA models trained on C4, achieves perplexity improvements over Muon of 0.63 (60M) and 0.28 (135M), with negligible difference (0.02) at 350M (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: A toy LLaMA-style proxy (d=256, char-level tiny-shakespeare, 600 steps) shows RMNP trailing Muon by 0.29 ppl; the relative pattern (RMNP closer to Muon on LLaMA than GPT-2) reproduces qualitatively, but full C4 pretraining at 60M–350M was never run.

claims.claim: Establishes non-convex convergence guarantees (Theorems 5.5, 5.7, 5.9) under Frobenius and mixed-norm smoothness that match Muon's best-known minimax-optimal complexity (Section 5, Table 4).
claims.evidence: A numerical audit on a synthetic non-convex smooth objective fitted convergence exponents of −0.206 (RMNP) and −0.217 (Muon), both consistent with the predicted −0.25, with a non-smooth control flatlining — but this is a proxy objective, not the paper's actual training task, and does not constitute a proof verification.

vimarsh/repro-rmnp-row-momentum-normaliz.overall: The logbook provides real microbenchmark and mechanism evidence supporting RMNP's complexity advantage (Claim 2) and partial support for the diagonal-dominance motivation (Claim 1) and convergence rate (Claim 6) at toy/synthetic scale, but the two core perplexity claims (4–5) and the specific wall-clock speedup numbers (Claim 3) are not verified at the paper's scale due to lack of GPU resources.

algorise/repro-best-of-both-worlds-for-h.paper_title: Best-of-Both-Worlds for Heavy-Tailed Markov Decision Processes

claims.claim: For the known-transition setting, Algorithm 1 (HT-FTRL-OM), defined in Section 4.1, is proven in Theorem 4.1 to achieve regret of order poly(H,S,A)·σ(T^(1/α)+log T) in the adversarial regime (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: On a non-toy MDP (H=5, 25 states, 100 state-action pairs, T=20000, 20 seeds) with verified infinite-variance Lomax noise, the fitted regret exponents for α∈{1.2,1.4,1.6,1.8} are 0.921, 0.787, 0.714, 0.661 respectively—all within the pre-stated ±0.15 band of the predicted 1/α, with R²≥0.9846 and strictly decreasing in α, and the non-learning control shows 5× higher regret.

claims.claim: In the stochastic (self-bounding) regime, Theorem 4.1 shows HT-FTRL-OM attains an instance-dependent regret bound that reduces to order σ^(α/(α-1))ω_Δ(α) log T, i.e., logarithmic in T (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The increment ratios (1.22–1.65) are in the poly-logarithmic range but exceed both the log T reference (1.00) and the (log T)² reference (1.17) at some gap scales, and the instance-dependent gap-scaling slope is 0.202 versus the predicted 1.0 (R²=0.9995)—a 5× discrepancy that prevents confirmation of the specific log T rate or the correct ω_Δ dependence.

claims.claim: For the unknown-transition setting, Algorithm 2 (HT-FTRL-UOB), defined in Section 5.1, achieves adversarial-regime regret of order poly(H,S,A)·σ(T^(1/α) + √T log T + (log T)^2) per Theorem 5.1 (Section 5.1, Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: The fitted exponents for HT-FTRL-UOB are 1.058 (α=1.2) and 1.022 (α=1.8), both far outside the pre-stated acceptance windows [0.63,0.98] and [0.36,0.71] and near-linear rather than the predicted 1/α; while the qualitative ordering (unknown transitions cost more than known) is confirmed with paired CIs excluding zero, the quantitative scaling fails and the implementation replaces Comp-UOB with a looser bound that could inflate regret.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 further shows HT-FTRL-UOB attains an instance-dependent self-bounding-regime regret bound of order poly(H,S,A)·σ^(α/(α-1))ω_Δ(α)(log T)^2, matching a log-squared-T rate (Section 5.2, Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: The UOB increment ratios (4.63–5.12) exceed even the linear-growth reference (4.00), implying near-linear or super-linear regret rather than the predicted (log T)² rate (reference 1.17); all pre-stated predicates fail and the gap-dependence slope has the wrong sign (−0.396 vs +1.0), but the looser UOB approximation and frequent epoch restarts at T=20000 confound whether this reflects on the paper's exact algorithm.

claims.claim: Both algorithms assume losses have bounded α-moments for α∈(1,2] with unbounded variance, and rely on novel skipping loss estimators adapted to occupancy measures to control heavy-tailed feedback (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The heavy-tail assumption is cleanly verified: sample second moments diverge at the predicted rate 2/tail−1, Hill estimators recover the tail index, and E|l|^α ≤ σ^α holds for all configurations. However, the skipping estimator ablation shows skipping does not help at any constant tested (ratio OFF/ON = 0.894 at paper's C, 0.994 at C=1), the calibrated C=256 disables skipping entirely (skip rate ≈0), and misspecified α does not degrade performance, so the estimator's effectiveness is not confirmed.

algorise/repro-best-of-both-worlds-for-h.overall: This logbook provides a methodologically rigorous reproduction with verified infinite-variance noise, proper statistics, and pre-stated predicates, confirming the T^(1/α) adversarial scaling for the known-transition algorithm but failing to confirm the specific logarithmic rates, instance-dependent scaling, or skipping-estimator effectiveness for the remaining claims at T=20000.

algorise/repro-high-probability-converge.paper_title: High-Probability Convergence Guarantees of Decentralized SGD

claims.claim: Theorem 1 establishes that under assumptions (A1)-(A5), decentralized SGD achieves a high-probability convergence rate of O(sigma*sqrt(d)/sqrt(nT)) on the average squared gradient norm for non-convex costs, exhibiting linear speed-up in the number of nodes n (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: On a non-toy non-convex setup (d=10, n up to 64, 25 seeds), the complete graph topology shows no O(1/√n) speedup (log-log slope 0.0825, R²=0.4505), and the ring topology shows error increasing with n (slope 1.2484). Neither topology exhibits the claimed linear speedup in n.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 establishes that under assumptions (A1)-(A4) and (A6, mu-strong convexity), the last iterate of decentralized SGD achieves a high-probability rate of O(d*sigma^2*kappa/(n(T+t0))), also exhibiting linear speed-up without requiring a bounded-heterogeneity assumption (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The complete graph shows the O(1/n) rate (slope -1.0288, R²=0.998), but the results are identical to the no-communication (W=I) baseline, meaning the consensus mechanism is redundant for this mean-centered heterogeneity setup. The ring topology fails (slope -0.5336, R²=0.1918) and is also identical to W=I for n≥4, so the experiment neither properly tests nor falsifies the decentralized consensus mechanism.

claims.claim: Lemma 2 shows the averaged stochastic noise across nodes is O(sigma*sqrt(d)/sqrt(n))-sub-Gaussian, giving a high-probability analogue of the variance-reduction benefit of decentralized averaging (Lemma 2).
claims.evidence: Across n∈{1,...,64} with d=20, 25 seeds × 5000 samples, Var(ξ̄)·n/σ² = 0.9998 at n=64 with CIs containing 1.0 for all n, and the sub-Gaussian bound holds with ~99.95% empirical coverage. The negative control with Student-t(2) noise correctly fails (coverage drops to 0.0278 at n=64).

claims.claim: Compared to the prior high-probability analysis of Lu et al., this work removes the uniformly-bounded-gradient assumption and, for the strongly convex case, eliminates the requirement of asymptotically vanishing noise (Lemma 4, referencing Lu et al.).
claims.evidence: On a small setup (n=16, d=5, quartic objective), all 25 seeds converge despite unbounded gradients (max grad 388.17), supporting the claim that bounded-gradient assumptions can be removed. However, the negative control (fixed step size) also converges (0/25 diverge), indicating the test objective is too well-behaved to discriminate, and the vanishing-noise aspect of the claim is not tested.

algorise/repro-high-probability-converge.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous statistical evaluation with 25 seeds, bootstrap CIs, and negative controls, but the headline linear-speedup claims are not confirmed: Claim 1 is falsified by the complete graph showing no speedup, and Claim 2's O(1/n) result is trivialized by mean-centered heterogeneity making consensus redundant. Lemma 2 (sub-Gaussian noise averaging) is cleanly verified, while Lemma 4's test is too simplified to be conclusive.

algorise/repro-step-size-stability-in-st.paper_title: Step-Size Stability in Stochastic Optimization: A Theoretical Perspective

claims.claim: The paper introduces a stability index δ_t that quantifies how much a stochastic optimization step degrades progress as the step size grows, and links it directly to suboptimality bounds via average-iterate and last-iterate convergence theorems (Theorem 3, Theorem 4, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies the formula δ_0 = (α/2)||g_0||^2 on synthetic stochastic objectives with CV(delta_0/lr) = 3.2e-16, but this only confirms the arithmetic of a definition; the convergence theorems (Theorem 3, 4) linking δ_t to suboptimality bounds are not empirically tested on any real optimization task.

claims.claim: For SGD, the stability index is derived as δ_t^SGD = (α_t/2)‖g_t‖^2, which scales linearly (unboundedly) with the step size α_t (Section 4).
claims.evidence: On both linear and logistic regression tasks with 25 seeds, SGD's δ_0 scales with log-log slope = 1.000000 and R² = 1.000000, confirming exact linear scaling. On the linear task, SGD diverges 100% at lr ≥ 1.474, demonstrating unbounded growth causing instability.

claims.claim: For NGN, the stability index δ_t^NGN = (γ_t/2)‖g_t‖^2 ≤ δ_t^SGD, and it saturates rather than growing unboundedly for large step sizes, unlike SGD (Section 4).
claims.evidence: NGN achieves 0% divergence across all 22 step sizes (0.001–100) while SGD diverges at 8 of those, and the NGN/SGD mean_delta ratio is 0.1320 (well below 1.0). NGN's delta saturates at lr/2 for large step sizes (e.g., delta=50.0 at lr=100) due to gradient normalization, confirming bounded behavior unlike SGD.

claims.claim: For SPS, the stability index is bounded as δ_t^SPS ≤ min{α_t‖g_t‖^2, f(x_t,s_t) - C_t}, scaling sub-linearly with step size, in contrast to SGD's linear scaling (Section 4).
claims.evidence: On the linear regression task, SPS shows log-log slope = 0.176 [0.140, 0.214], clearly sub-linear, with delta saturating at ~0.1572 for lr ≥ 1.474. The bound δ ≤ f(x_t) holds at 100% of step sizes. On logistic regression, slope = 0.565 (still < 1.0) and the bound holds at all lrs, though the CI upper bound (0.625) exceeds the pre-stated 0.5 threshold.

claims.claim: Experiments on ResNet trained on CIFAR-10 and on linear/logistic regression tasks confirm that the theoretical stability-index bounds predict the empirically observed robustness ordering of SPS, NGN, and SPP over SGD across a range of step sizes (Section 5).
claims.evidence: No ResNet/CIFAR-10 experiments were conducted; only linear and logistic regression tasks were run. On linear regression, the ordering holds (SGD=14 stable lrs vs NGN=SPS=SPP=22), but on logistic regression all optimizers have identical 18/18 stable lrs, providing no differentiation. The key deep-learning experiment from the paper is entirely missing.

algorise/repro-step-size-stability-in-st.overall: The logbook provides solid empirical confirmation of the theoretical scaling properties of stability indices for SGD (linear), NGN (bounded), and SPS (sub-linear) on linear and logistic regression tasks with 25 seeds and bootstrap CIs. However, the ResNet/CIFAR-10 experiments central to the paper's empirical validation (Claim 5) were never conducted, and the stability index definition (Claim 1) was only checked arithmetically on synthetic data without testing the convergence theorems.

eamag/repro-training-ai-co-scientists-us.paper_title: Training AI Co-Scientists Using Rubric Rewards

claims.claim: Human experts prefer research plans generated by a Qwen3-30B-A3B model finetuned with rubric rewards over the initial (non-finetuned) model's plans in 70% of goals (p<0.0001), based on 225 hours of expert evaluation (Section 3.3, human study results).
claims.evidence: The script hardcodes wins=70, n_goals=100 from the paper and merely computes a binomial test p-value on those hardcoded numbers. No human evaluation was conducted and no model plans were generated or compared.

claims.claim: The finetuned model's plans satisfy automatically-extracted evaluation rubrics at 79.8±2.5%, compared to 73.8±2.9% for the baseline model's plans (Tables 1-2).
claims.evidence: The script hardcodes baseline=73.8% and finetuned=79.8% directly from the paper and computes a z-test on those hardcoded values. No model inference was run to generate plans, and no rubric satisfaction was actually measured.

claims.claim: Finetuning yields 12-22% relative improvements across domains, and training on the medical domain alone transfers with a 15% relative improvement on machine-learning research goals and 17.5% on ArXiv-paper-based goals, demonstrating cross-domain generalization (Section on cross-domain generalization results).
claims.evidence: All evaluation scores (e.g., Medical-Finetuned ML=7.66, ArXiv=8.03) are hardcoded from the paper and relative improvements are computed arithmetically. No model training or cross-domain evaluation was performed.

claims.claim: 84% of rubric items automatically extracted from source papers by the pipeline are approved as valid by human expert reviewers (Section 2.1, rubric generation validation).
claims.evidence: The script hardcodes the 84% approval rate and computes a CI, while only displaying sample rubrics loaded from the dataset. No human expert review of extracted rubrics was conducted.

claims.claim: Training uses Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a self-rewarding mechanism derived from the automatically extracted rubrics (Section 2.3).
claims.evidence: A GRPO loss module was implemented in PyTorch but tested only with a 16x16 dummy parameter matrix, random log-probabilities, and hardcoded rubric scores over 10 steps—no real model, real data, or actual training was involved.

claims.claim: Human experts rate the finetuned model's plans as matching or exceeding Grok-4-Thinking's plans for 59.6% of goals, while GPT-5-Thinking still outperforms all tested models including the finetuned one (Section 3.3 comparison to frontier baselines).
claims.evidence: All frontier model scores and the 59.6% match rate are hardcoded from the paper with no actual model inference or human expert comparison conducted.

eamag/repro-training-ai-co-scientists-us.overall: This logbook does not reproduce any claim experimentally; it merely re-derives statistics from the paper's own reported numbers and inspects dataset metadata. The only code touching real data loads parquet files to count rubric items, while all evaluation scores and win rates are hardcoded constants.

SabaPivot/repro-accurate-evaluation-of-q.paper_title: Accurate Evaluation of Quickest Changepoint Detectors via Non-parametric Survival Analysis

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 establishes that the finite-sample bias of the KM-ARL estimator decays exponentially with dataset size N.
claims.evidence: Across 20,000 Monte Carlo repetitions per sample size (N=2 to 64), every KM-ARL bias estimate fell within the numerically integrated Theorem 4.1 bounds (±4 MC-SE allowance), and the bound width contracted 24.28× from N=2 to N=64 (0.6446→0.02655), consistent with the exponential h^(N-1) structure of the theorem's integral form.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 establishes finite-sample bias bounds for the KM-ADD estimator under independent censoring.
claims.evidence: The same 20,000-repetition audit shows all KM-ADD bias estimates within the Theorem 4.2 lower/upper integrals, with bound width contracting 50.66× from N=2 to N=64 (0.6709→0.01324) and measured bias falling from 0.1513 to 6.05e-05.

claims.claim: Theorems 4.3 and 4.4 show that the truncation bias of KM-ARL and KM-ADD is smaller than that of conventional (non-censoring-aware) ARL/ADD estimators.
claims.evidence: Population-level numerical integration for exponential event times with bounded censoring confirms the Theorems 4.3–4.4 ordering: ARL LB bias −3.834 vs KM bias −2.247; ADD LB bias −2.474 vs KM bias −1.355, both satisfying B_TR(LB) ≤ B_TR(KM) ≤ 0. Only two parameter settings are tested, but the computation is exact (analytical integrals, no sampling noise).

claims.claim: KM-ARL and KM-ADD are shown to be asymptotically unbiased (Equation 11) whenever the support of the detection-point distribution does not exceed the censoring boundary, without requiring parametric assumptions (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The support audit with up to N=512 and 800–5000 repetitions shows bias vanishing when event support is covered (−0.00082±0.00055 at N=512) and at the equality boundary (0.000043±0.00073), while bias plateaus at −0.0998 when extrapolation is required. The logbook also identifies a formal inconsistency in the paper's stated condition t_F < t_H (since H is the CDF of min(event,censor), t_H ≤ t_F by construction), but the operational support-coverage claim is numerically confirmed.

claims.claim: On the WISDM Actitracker dataset (51,326 sequences ranging from length 1 to 54,401), KM-ARL/KM-ADD show substantially reduced variance versus LB-ARL/LB-ADD baselines (Figure 1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: On the full 51,326-sequence WISDM dataset (lengths 1–54,401, 1,369,349 rows, 61 no-change sequences—exactly matching paper statistics), the paper's analytical SE convention yields median LB/KM variance ratios of 176.18× for ARL and 3.09× for ADD, all exceeding 1. However, an independent nonparametric bootstrap (120 replicates) gives median ratios of 0.868 (ARL) and 0.023 (ADD), meaning the variance reduction is convention-dependent and does not hold universally for ADD under bootstrap.

claims.claim: Simulation experiments on Gaussian and Poisson process changepoint models show KM-ARL/KM-ADD remain accurate across censoring levels from 10% to 90% changepoint prevalence and irregular sequence lengths (Figures 2-4, Section 5).
claims.evidence: The full 36-scenario simulation (N=10,000 per scenario, ground truth N=20,000 with horizon 5,000) shows KM has a median relative error of 2.90% and wins 48/72 paired comparisons, but the worst-case KM-ARL relative error reaches 30.86% for Poisson at 90% prevalence with irregular lengths and threshold 3, directly contradicting the claim that KM 'remain accurate across' the full 10%–90% prevalence range.

SabaPivot/repro-accurate-evaluation-of-q.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence supporting the four theoretical claims (exponential bias decay, finite-sample bounds, truncation bias ordering, and asymptotic unbiasedness under support coverage) through well-designed Monte Carlo and numerical integration audits, and reproduces the WISDM Figure 1 variance reduction under the paper's own SE convention. However, the broad robustness claim for simulations is falsified by a 30.86% worst-case KM error at 90% prevalence, and the WISDM variance advantage is shown to be convention-dependent, not holding under nonparametric bootstrap for ADD.

eamag/repro-formalrx-rectify-and-examine.paper_title: FormalRx: Rectify and eXamine Semantic Failures in Autoformalization

claims.claim: FormalRX-8B achieves F1-scores of 0.88 for verdict and 0.71 for error categorization
claims.evidence: The script only validates the dataset schema (7030 samples) and performs arithmetic on hardcoded precision/recall values (0.932, 0.836) to confirm F1=0.881. No model inference was run on FormalRx-8B; the P/R values are constants in the script, not computed from actual predictions.

claims.claim: FormalRX-8B achieves accuracies of 0.75 for error localization and 0.73 for error correction
claims.evidence: The localization and correction accuracies are computed from hardcoded counts (ExMatch=4563, LLM=707, etc.) divided by 7030, not from actual model outputs. No inference was run to produce these counts; they are asserted constants.

claims.evidence: The baseline comparison table is presented with no evidence that any baseline (BLEU, LeanScorer, Qwen3, GPT-5, Claude, etc.) was actually evaluated. The numbers appear copied from the paper with no independent runs or artifacts.

eamag/repro-formalrx-rectify-and-examine.overall: This logbook does not constitute a reproduction: it validates the test dataset schema and performs arithmetic consistency checks on hardcoded numbers from the paper, but never runs the FormalRx-8B model or any baseline to generate predictions. All claimed metrics are asserted rather than independently measured.

Roman81/SCtGXNtk7Q.paper_title: Latent Reasoning in TRMs is Secretly a Policy Improvement Operator

claims.claim: Section 3.1 shows TRM's asymmetric readouts can be reinterpreted as classifier-free guidance, mixing an unconditional policy pi_u and a conditional policy pi_c via logit interpolation pi_w(a|s) proportional to pi_u(a|s)^(1-w) * pi_c(a|s)^w (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: This theoretical claim about reinterpreting TRM's asymmetric readouts as classifier-free guidance (logit interpolation between π_u and π_c) is never addressed in the logbook — no mathematical derivation, proof verification, or experimental test of the interpolation formula appears anywhere.

claims.claim: Section 3.2, Eq. 7 formalizes latent reasoning as controllable policy improvement, pi_w(y|s) proportional to pi_hat(y|s) * (pi_hat(y|s,o=1)/pi_hat(y|s))^w, acting as an advantage-like update without an explicit value function (Section 3.2, Eq. 7).
claims.evidence: This theoretical claim about Eq. 7 formalizing latent reasoning as controllable policy improvement via an advantage-like update is not addressed — the logbook contains no analysis or experimental validation of this equation or its policy-improvement interpretation.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 gives an Advantage Margin Condition under which latent reasoning improves performance, requiring the correct class's logit boost to exceed the expected boost under the mixed policy (Proposition 4.1).
claims.evidence: Proposition 4.1's Advantage Margin Condition is never verified — the logbook does not test, prove, or empirically validate this condition or its logit-boost requirement in any experiment.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.2 shows that minimizing the sequential Deep Improvement Supervision loss with strictly improving intermediate targets drives the expected Advantage Margin positive across all guidance scales (Proposition 4.2).
claims.evidence: Proposition 4.2's claim about the DIS loss driving the expected Advantage Margin positive is not addressed — no mathematical proof verification or margin-measurement experiments appear in the logbook.

claims.claim: On ARC-1, the compact 0.8M-parameter DIS model achieves 24% accuracy versus TRM's 12%, while the 7M-parameter medium model reaches 41.3% versus TRM's 40.4%, using 18x fewer forward-pass operations (T=1, n=2 vs. TRM's T=3, n=6) (Section 5.4).
claims.evidence: The 18x forward-pass reduction is verified by direct code instrumentation (336 vs 18 forward passes, 18.67x ratio), but the ARC-1 accuracy claims are only addressed at partial training: DIS-compact reached ~18.5% pass@2 at 52% of its schedule vs TRM-compact's 6.0% at 7.5% of its schedule on RTX 3090, not the paper's full 24% vs 12%. The 7M medium model (41.3% vs 40.4%) was never trained due to compute constraints.

claims.claim: DIS eliminates the learned Adaptive Computation Time halting mechanism in favor of fixed supervision steps, reducing training time from about 72 hours (TRM) to about 40 hours on identical 4xH100 hardware (Section 5.4, Training Efficiency).
claims.evidence: Code inspection confirms DIS eliminates the ACT halting mechanism (q_halt_loss computation is commented out in ACTLossHeadV4, fixed N_sup=6 schedule used instead of learned halting), and full-scale N-Queens runs on identical RTX 3090 hardware show DIS training in 4h40m vs TRM's 21h17m — a 4.6x wall-clock reduction, consistent with the paper's claimed training-time reduction direction, though the specific 72h→40h figures on 4xH100 for ARC-1 are not directly reproduced.

Roman81/SCtGXNtk7Q.overall: The logbook provides strong experimental evidence for the paper's efficiency claims (18x forward-pass reduction via code instrumentation, ACT elimination via code inspection, and wall-clock speedup via full-scale N-Queens runs) but only addresses ARC-1 accuracy at partial training scale and entirely omits the four theoretical/propositional claims (1–4).

algorise/repro-logarithmic-switching-reg.paper_title: Logarithmic Switching Regret for Online Convex Optimization

claims.claim: IRESET achieves logarithmic switching regret bounds for exponentially concave and strongly convex functions.
claims.evidence: At T=32,768, d=20, 12 seeds, IRESET per-segment regret fits a+b·lnL with R²=0.9982 (strongly convex) and R²=0.9951 (exp-concave) over a 128× range of segment lengths, with log-log power exponents 0.200 and 0.374 respectively—both well below the 0.5 sqrt(L) reference, and the log fit substantially outperforms the sqrt fit (R² 0.88/0.93). Baselines (plain OGD, oracle-restart) and horizon/dimension sweeps corroborate.

claims.claim: First work to establish optimal switching regret bounds for function classes beyond general convex functions.
claims.evidence: The rate separation is demonstrated concretely: plain OGD (general-convex baseline) shows power exponents 0.475/0.455 (near sqrt(L)=0.5) while IRESET shows 0.200/0.374, and at L=8192 OGD pays 5.5× IRESET's regret on strongly-convex losses. Total regret grows logarithmically in T (8× T increase yields only 1.39×/1.72× regret increase vs sqrt(8)=2.83). The 'first work' priority aspect is a bibliographic claim not testable by experiments, but the achievability and optimality of the bounds beyond general convexity are supported.

algorise/repro-logarithmic-switching-reg.overall: The logbook provides a non-toy experimental reproduction (T up to 65,536, d up to 40, 292 trials, 6–12 seeds with 95% CIs, two baselines, regression-based rate verification) demonstrating that IRESET achieves O(log L) per-segment switching regret for both strongly-convex and exp-concave losses, with clean separation from the general-convex sqrt(L) rate. The 'first work' bibliographic priority is not experimentally verifiable, but the core rate claims are well-supported by the data.

algorise/repro-zeroth-order-non-log-conc.paper_title: Zeroth-Order Non-Log-Concave Sampling with Variance Reduction and Applications to Inverse Problems

claims.claim: Theorem 1 establishes the first non-asymptotic convergence guarantee for variance-reduced zeroth-order Langevin sampling, bounding Fisher information FI(ν̄_{Nγ}||π) ≤ ε after O(d⁷L_m⁴/ε⁴) iterations using only O(1) function evaluations per iteration (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports FI increasing from 0.5465 to 1.9602, which does not demonstrate convergence to a small ε as the theorem claims; the O(1) per-iteration evaluation count (19.05) is weakly shown but the core convergence bound is not supported by the reported numbers.

claims.claim: The variance-reduced zeroth-order gradient estimator (Equation 8) combines a large-batch estimate (probability p, batch size b) with a small-batch recursive update (probability 1−p, batch size b′) that exploits correlation between consecutive iterates (Equation 8).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements the estimator with concrete parameters (b=40, p=0.1, b'=2) and reports observed per-step evaluations of 19.05, consistent with the recursive large-batch/small-batch design described in Equation 8.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 extends the Fisher-information convergence bound to posterior sampling with a black-box score-based generative model (SGM) prior via the ZO-APMC algorithm (Equation 12-13, Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides only a description of the ZO-APMC algorithm and asserts the bound holds, with no numerical results or experimental evidence demonstrating the Fisher-information convergence for posterior sampling with an SGM prior.

claims.claim: On 4x-accelerated radial-subsampled FastMRI brain reconstruction, ZO-APMC achieves 35.29 dB PSNR, the best among black-box methods (SCG, DPG, EnKG, Forward/Central-GSG) though slightly below the gradient-based APMC baseline at 36.55 dB (Section, Table 1).
claims.evidence: The reported PSNR of 35.29 dB exactly matches the paper's Table 1, but the total runtime of ~5 minutes on CPU for FastMRI reconstruction with SGM priors is implausibly fast for a full-scale reproduction, indicating a simplified setup.

claims.claim: On black-hole imaging with 100 GRMHD images from InverseBench, ZO-APMC attains 26.71 dB PSNR and χ²_cph of 5.42, the best result among evaluated black-box methods (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Measured PSNR of 26.69 dB and χ²_cph of 5.43 are close to the paper's 26.71 and 5.42, suggesting some real computation occurred, but processing 100 GRMHD images in ~5 minutes on CPU is clearly not full-scale.

claims.claim: Figure 2(b) validates the O(1) per-iteration batch complexity by showing multiple (p,b) parameter settings with fixed product pb=10 all converge to Fisher information below 0.01 (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The claim states all pb=10 configurations converge to Fisher information below 0.01, but the logbook's own table reports final FI values of 4.56, 4.33, 4.24, and 4.655—none below 0.01, directly contradicting the claim.

algorise/repro-zeroth-order-non-log-conc.overall: The logbook provides some concrete implementation details for the variance-reduced estimator (Claim 2) but fails to demonstrate the core convergence guarantees (Claims 1, 3) and directly contradicts the Fisher information threshold claimed in Claim 6. The FastMRI and black-hole imaging results (Claims 4, 5) appear to come from simplified setups given the implausibly short 5-minute CPU runtime.

algorise/repro-richer-bayesian-last-laye.paper_title: Richer Bayesian Last Layers with Subsampled NTK Features

claims.claim: Rich-BLL projects earlier-layer NTK gradient features onto the last-layer feature space and performs Bayesian linear regression in this transformed space, reducing posterior covariance computation to inverting an r×r matrix rather than an N×N or p×p matrix (Theorem 3.1, Section 3)
claims.evidence: Concrete Cholesky timing measurements on UCI concrete (p=17664, N=824, r=32) show r×r inversion at 0.143ms vs 4.807ms (N×N) and 38778ms (p×p), directly supporting the complexity reduction claim on real data.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 proves that using the approximated NTK features always yields predictive uncertainty greater than or equal to that of the standard Bayesian Last Layer, so the method provably never underestimates epistemic uncertainty relative to standard BLL (Theorem 3.3)
claims.evidence: On 5 UCI datasets × 10 seeds (~17790 test points), σ²_Rich ≥ σ²_BLL at 100% of test points with minimum differences always positive (e.g., 1.29e-04 on boston), empirically confirming the variance dominance on real data.

claims.claim: The subsampled variant of Rich-BLL requires only O(r) samples (independent of the full training set size N) to accurately approximate the posterior, per the concentration bound in Theorem 3.5 (Theorem 3.5)
claims.evidence: Measured log-log slope is -0.28 vs predicted -0.5, and N-independence is not clearly demonstrated: at S=512, N=500 error is 0.0029 while N=2000 error is 0.4009, suggesting the required subsample count may actually depend on N.

claims.claim: On UCI regression benchmarks (Boston, Concrete, Energy, Power, Wine), Rich-BLL achieves lower test negative log-likelihood than standard NNGP/BLL baselines (Table 2)
claims.evidence: Rich-BLL beats BLL on 4/5 UCI datasets but loses to NTK-GP on 4/5 (e.g., boston: Rich-BLL 3.035 vs NTK-GP 0.272; wine: 25.479 vs 3.069), contradicting the claim that Rich-BLL achieves lower NLL than NNGP/BLL baselines.

claims.claim: On CIFAR-10 to SVHN out-of-distribution detection, subsampled Rich-BLL achieves 0.56 NLL and 0.91 AUROC, compared to 0.58 NLL and 0.88 AUROC for the NNGP baseline (Table 5)
claims.evidence: CIFAR-10→SVHN was replaced with sklearn digits (classes 0-4 vs 5-9) due to CPU constraints; on this proxy, Rich-BLL AUROC (0.898) is slightly worse than BLL (0.905), opposite to the paper's claimed direction.

SabaPivot/repro-gradmem-learning-to-writ.paper_title: GradMem: Learning to Write Context into Memory with Test-Time Gradient Descent
