vimarsh/repro-why-linear-rnns-more-paral.paper_title: Why Are Linear RNNs More Parallelizable?

claims.claim: Any language recognized by a linear RNN (LRNN) over the rationals lies in PNC1, meaning LRNNs can be simulated by log-depth arithmetic circuits (Theorem 3, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides only a source audit of Theorem 3 with no independent proof verification or experimental evidence; reading the arXiv paper does not constitute verification of a complexity-class membership theorem.

claims.claim: LRNNs require only O(log n log* n) depth NC circuits, an O(log* n) overhead beyond the O(log n) depth of transformers/TC0 circuits (Corollary 5, Section 4).
claims.evidence: CUDA scan probes at n=1024 and n=2048 observed 10 and 11 balanced rounds, which the logbook itself states is 'not a proof of the complexity-class conversion'; this is a small-scale mechanistic probe, not verification of the O(log n log* n) depth bound.

claims.claim: Log-precision nonlinear RNNs can solve sorted deterministic graph connectivity, an L-complete problem, requiring Omega(log^2 n) depth and revealing a fundamental parallelization barrier absent in LRNNs (Theorem 2, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: A hand-designed explicit ReLU recurrence for sorted deterministic reachability matched a reference evaluator on 128/128 instances up to size 4096, verifying the construction mechanism on a simplified setup; however, L-completeness and the Omega(log^2 n) lower bound remain unverified mathematical claims.

claims.claim: Poly-precision nonlinear RNNs can express P-complete problems under FO reductions, implying no efficient parallel algorithm exists for them unless P=NC (Corollary 2, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: A hand-designed ReLU Boolean Circuit Value evaluator matched a reference on 128/128 instances up to 4096 gates, verifying the recurrent construction mechanism; P-completeness under FO reductions and the P!=NC consequence remain unverified theorems.

claims.claim: DPLR-based LRNN architectures such as RWKV-7 and DeltaNet can solve the PNC1-complete iterated 3x3 matrix multiplication problem using only 4 layers (Theorem 5, Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: A T4 CUDA job checked sequential and balanced 3x3 matrix products through length 2048 with max error 0.0, but the logbook does not clearly demonstrate that actual RWKV-7 or DeltaNet 4-layer architectures were used rather than generic matrix multiplication probes.

claims.claim: Experiments show nonlinear RNNs generalize on the L-complete graph connectivity task while transformers and Mamba fail to solve it, matching the theoretical complexity separation (Figure 2, Section 6).
claims.evidence: Figure 2 was source-verified but not retrained; a proxy experiment training GRU and Transformer classifiers for 1500 steps on a scaled-down parity-reachability task showed both at chance, which does not reproduce the paper's reported separation of RNN 96.50% vs Transformer 62.15% vs Mamba 50.95%.

vimarsh/repro-why-linear-rnns-more-paral.overall: The logbook provides small-scale CUDA mechanistic probes (balanced scans, matrix products, hand-designed ReLU recurrences) that check individual construction mechanisms but does not independently verify any complexity-theoretic theorem or reproduce the paper's main empirical result (Figure 2). Claims 1 and 6 lack any supporting experimental evidence, while Claims 2-5 are addressed only at toy scale with simplified proxies.

NaveenVenu/5nNNVY8NW4.paper_title: To Grok Grokking: Provable Grokking in Ridge Regression

claims.claim: The paper proves end-to-end grokking for zero-teacher ridge regression, including early training overfitting, delayed poor generalization, and eventual low generalization error (Theorem 4.1)
claims.evidence: Explicit GD on zero-teacher ridge regression (n=100, m=1000-2000, Gaussian features) checks all three Theorem 4.1 inequalities at every step across 24 runs (8 settings × 3 seeds × 4001 steps), with zero violations; grokking delay is observed (t1≈183, t2≈2250 at λ=1e-3).

claims.claim: The end-to-end grokking result is extended from the zero-teacher setting to realizable ridge regression with arbitrary realizable teacher functions (Theorem 4.2)
claims.evidence: Realizable-teacher GD trajectories (unit-norm teacher, λ∈{1e-3,…,3e-5}, m∈{1000,4000}, 3 seeds) confirm t1≤Eq.(6) upper bound, t2≥Eq.(7) lower bound, and eventual generalization (L_inf≤ε) in all 24 runs; t2 grows from 2,300 to 77,700 as λ shrinks 33× while t1 stays ~200.

claims.claim: Separate theorems decompose grokking into training-loss convergence, poor generalization during overfitting, and eventual generalization (Theorems 4.4-4.6)
claims.evidence: All three stage theorems checked numerically in 12 runs: Thm 4.4 (Ln≤ε past threshold), Thm 4.5 (L≥c below threshold), Thm 4.6 (ridge minimizer L≤2Ln+ε) all hold with zero violations; thresholds correctly bracket the grokking window (training fits by ~1.3k, generalization provably delayed until ~16k at λ=1e-4).

claims.claim: Decreasing weight decay and sample size can amplify grokking time in ridge-regression simulations, matching the paper's quantitative hyperparameter predictions (Figure 2)
claims.evidence: Full-scale reproduction of Figure 2 with exact spectral closed form (validated vs explicit GD to 1e-14): t2∝1/λ with log-log slope 1.0001, t1∝n (46→980 for n=25→400), m has negligible effect, t1/t2∝ln(ν²) with constant increments, all 60 measurements respect Eq.(8) bounds across 20 configs × 3 seeds.

claims.claim: Two-layer ReLU experiments qualitatively reproduce the predicted grokking-time dependence on hyperparameters beyond the linear setting (Figures 3 and 4)
claims.evidence: Figure 4 (both layers trained) does show grokking with test loss dropping below 1e-3 and t2 ratios of ~4× per 4× change in λ, but only 1 seed per config and one incomplete run (λ=0.0125 reached 1.34e-3 at 1M steps). Critically, Figure 3 (random features) shows NO grokking — test loss plateaus at ~0.19 and never drops below 0.01 in any configuration, contradicting the logbook's own narrative about 'drop times at 8.5k/86k/861k' which are unsupported by the raw output.

NaveenVenu/5nNNVY8NW4.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification of the paper's theoretical claims (Theorems 4.1, 4.2, 4.4-4.6) and a convincing full-scale reproduction of Figure 2's ridge regression simulations with quantitative matching. However, the Figure 3 reproduction fails to exhibit grokking (test loss plateaus far above threshold), and the logbook's narrative misrepresents this failure, while Figure 4 is only partially reproduced with a single seed per configuration.

geekwrestler/amemguard-consensus-repro.paper_title: A-MemGuard: A Proactive Defense Framework For LLM-Based Agent Memory

claims.claim: A-MemGuard reduces the direct memory-poisoning attack success rate on EHRAgent from 100% to 2.13% at the retrieval stage (Section on key results, direct poisoning).
claims.evidence: The ConsistencyChecker was run on 50–100 AgentPoison-style poisoned StrategyQA memory banks (not EHRAgent), showing ASR-r 100%→12–18% with Qwen judges. The end-to-end ReAct-StrategyQA run (N=40) showed ASR-r actually rising 0.593→0.688, though ASR-t dropped 0.343→0.256. The specific EHRAgent 100%→2.13% claim was never directly tested.

claims.claim: A-MemGuard reduces indirect prompt-injection attack success rates by over 60% across both tested LLM backbones, GPT-4o-mini and LLaMA-3.1-8B (Section on key results, indirect injection attacks).
claims.evidence: A scoped StrategyQA proxy (not MINJA/MMLU) showed a 66.7% mean reduction matching '>60%', but the undefended ASR stayed flat (0.10 or 0.167→0.133), meaning the self-reinforcing error cycle never ignited. The effect rests on a ~3-episode swing, and the actual mechanism (breaking a compounding cycle) was never tested.

claims.claim: In multi-agent system settings, A-MemGuard achieves a 0.950 task success rate compared to 0.800 for the baseline without defense (Section on key results, multi-agent systems).
claims.evidence: A 4-agent MISINFOTASK-style simulation on StrategyQA (N=30, not the paper's harness) yielded 0.967 defended task success (close to 0.950), but the undefended baseline was 0.467, far from the paper's 0.800. The defended value matches but the baseline dynamics differ substantially from the paper's setting.

claims.claim: A-MemGuard's consensus-based validation mechanism generates parallel reasoning paths from multiple retrieved memories and flags deviations from group consensus as anomalies, while its dual-memory structure stores detected failures as corrective lessons referenced before future actions (Section on technical approach).
claims.evidence: The consensus-based validation pillar was tested on proxy memory banks (detection 0.82–0.88), but the dual-memory lesson loop was tested (N=24) and added +0.000 marginal detection over consensus alone. Both pillars were evaluated only on simplified StrategyQA-derived setups, not the paper's full agent pipeline.

claims.claim: Knowledge graph analysis of reasoning paths reveals less than 1% structural overlap between benign and malicious reasoning paths, supporting the separability assumption behind consensus-based detection (Section on evidence of separability).
claims.evidence: KG triples were extracted from reasoning paths for N=50 banks and labeled-edge (head-relation-tail) overlap between benign and malicious paths was directly measured at 1.17%, closely matching the paper's <1% claim. The measurement methodology is sound and the result supports the separability assumption.

claims.claim: A-MemGuard maintains the highest accuracy on benign tasks compared to all other tested defense baselines, indicating minimal utility trade-off from its dual-memory and consensus mechanisms (Section on utility preservation).
claims.evidence: A-MemGuard was compared against only one defense baseline (isolated per-memory audit) on stealth poison (N=30): benign retention 0.889 vs 0.267, safe-and-useful 0.90 vs 0.53. The end-to-end ReAct-StrategyQA run showed ACC 0.657→0.744 (paper 0.630→0.767), supporting utility preservation, but the claim of 'highest among all tested defense baselines' was not fully tested.

geekwrestler/amemguard-consensus-repro.overall: This logbook provides mechanism-level evidence on StrategyQA-derived proxies that directionally supports most A-MemGuard claims, with the KG separability metric (Claim 5) directly verified at 1.17% overlap. However, no claim was tested on the paper's exact benchmarks (EHRAgent, MINJA/MMLU, MISINFOTASK) at full scale, the self-reinforcing error cycle never ignited, the dual-memory lesson loop showed zero marginal benefit, and the end-to-end ASR-r anomaly remains unexplained.

AceVikings/repro-18911-claim2.paper_title: Revisiting Neural Processes via Fourier Transform and Volterra Series

claims.claim: Continuous translation-equivariant operators are characterized via Volterra series expansions as an infinite sum of multilinear convolution operators, ρ_d[h] = C_0 + sum of higher-order convolution terms C_l[h] (Equation 3).
claims.evidence: A finite order-2 Volterra operator on a 64-point periodic domain was constructed and shown to be equivariant (max discrepancy 1.78e-15) and nonlinear, but this is a simplified discrete proxy for the general continuous-operator characterization claim, not a proof of the full theorem.

claims.claim: Set Fourier Convolutions (SFConvs) exploit the closed-form Fourier transform of the functional embedding to operate directly on irregularly sampled points without spatial discretization, achieving approximately global receptive fields with linear complexity O(|Xi|(|D_c|+|D_q|)) versus ConvCNP's grid-dependent cost (Equation 13).
claims.evidence: The authors' SetFourierConv was instantiated on irregular points, producing finite outputs and gradients with translation errors ~1e-6, and complexity scaling showed exact log-log slope 1.0 matching O(|Ξ|(|D_c|+|D_q|)); also confirmed on ZeroGPU in 1D/2D/3D.

claims.claim: SFVConvCNP integrates the Volterra series formulation with SFConv parameterization to give an interpretable operator decomposition as a sum of higher-order convolutions, distinguishing it from the standard-stacked SFConvCNP model (Section on proposed models).
claims.evidence: SetFourierVolterraConv with rank 2 was instantiated and independently reconstructed from its spectral blocks with zero discrepancy from the official forward output, confirming explicit first- and second-order convolution decomposition distinct from stacked SFConv; also ran on ZeroGPU in 1D/2D/3D.

claims.claim: On synthetic 1D sawtooth regression, SFConvCNP attains log-likelihood 1.19+/-0.01 and SFVConvCNP attains 1.18+/-0.01, both substantially outperforming attention-based baselines that collapse to -0.87 (Table 2).

claims.evidence: Only table provenance was checked and the SFConv layer was exercised on 2D irregular points, but the ~101M-parameter CIFAR-10 training was never rerun; the reported 1.74/0.03 values remain source-only with no independent reproduction.

claims.claim: On Kolmogorov flow, SFConvCNP achieves log-likelihood 1.89+/-0.01, surpassing ConvCNP's 1.73, and on ERA5 climate data it reaches 1.71+/-0.01 (West) and 1.89+/-0.01 (North) held-out regions, demonstrating spatial generalization via translation equivariance (Tables 5-6).
claims.evidence: Only table values were audited and 3D layer-level tests were run on ZeroGPU, but the Kolmogorov-flow and ERA5 training campaigns were never rerun; the reported log-likelihoods remain unverified source-only numbers.

AceVikings/repro-18911-claim2.overall: The logbook provides concrete implementation-level verification for the SFConv mechanism (Claim 2) and SFVConv decomposition (Claim 3), and a toy-scale check of Volterra equivariance (Claim 1), but all three benchmark performance claims (4–6) are backed only by table audits with no retraining or independent experimental runs.

The actual parameter count is 181.5M, not 300M as claimed, which is a notable discrepancy but does not falsify the core joint-prediction capability.

claims.claim: On APPS Leetcode memory-footprint prediction, the RLM attains a Spearman rank correlation of 0.930, and on Triton GPU kernel latency prediction it attains 0.516 (Table 3, Section 5).
claims.evidence: At n=512 with the released checkpoint and authors' eval recipe, APPS memory Spearman ρ=0.9268 (close to claimed 0.930, exceeds >0.9 threshold) and KBSS latency ρ=0.5353 (vs claimed 0.516, same ballpark). Both confirmed by Colab GPU run and local CPU validation with permutation and shuffled-target controls.

claims.claim: Across CodeNet's programming languages the unified RLM's Spearman-rho ranges as low as 0.647 (Python) up to 0.748 (C++), with C at 0.741 and Go at 0.670, averaged over 17 languages (Table 3, Section 5).
claims.evidence: Full GPU run at n=200/language across all 17 CodeNet languages yields mean per-language Spearman ρ=0.523 (independent local run: 0.523, Colab: 0.530), exceeding the >0.5 threshold with stratified bootstrap 95% CI [0.503, 0.554] and permutation p=0.0005. Specific per-language values differ from the paper's Table 3 (e.g., C++ 0.788 vs 0.748, Python 0.611 vs 0.647), but the overall claim of positive correlations across 17 languages is supported.

claims.claim: On NAS-Bench architecture ranking, the RLM attains an average Kendall-tau of 0.461, outperforming Arch2Vec (0.212) and CATE (0.238) and matching a GNN baseline (0.429) (Table 4, Section 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook evaluates NASBench101 accuracy prediction but reports Spearman ρ (0.407), not Kendall-tau as claimed (0.461). No comparison with Arch2Vec (0.212), CATE (0.238), or GNN baseline (0.429) was performed. The metric and baseline comparisons central to this claim are absent.

claims.claim: Ablations show the proposed decoder-head regression formulation reaches 0.800 Spearman-rho versus 0.717 for a normalized regression head and 0.478 for a standard regression head, and scaling from 300M to 600M T5Gemma parameters improves Spearman-rho from 0.744 to 0.782 (Table 5, Table 6, Section 6).
claims.evidence: No ablation experiments were conducted. The logbook does not compare decoder-head vs normalized regression head vs standard regression head (claimed 0.800 vs 0.717 vs 0.478), nor does it evaluate a 600M parameter model (claimed improvement from 0.744 to 0.782). Tables 5 and 6 are not reproduced.

Claims 4 and 5 are not addressed: no Kendall-tau metric or baseline comparisons were run for NAS-Bench, and no ablation or scaling experiments were performed.

claims.claim: In the zero-temperature (hardmax) limit of self-attention dynamics with negative-definite key-query interaction, token updates coincide with a Frank-Wolfe step on a quadratic objective over the convex hull of the tokens, and Theorem 3.1 gives a linear convergence rate bound J^t(x_i^{t+1}) ≤ (2/(t+1))·λ_max(B_0)·diam(K^0)^2 (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The hardmax=FW identity is confirmed bit-exact (diff=0.0) across 2250 comparisons over 200 configs with both PSD and NSD B, n∈{5,8,12,20}, d∈{2,3,5,8}, using an independent continuous LP solver (scipy HiGHS) for the FW oracle. However, the Theorem 3.1 convergence rate bound J^t ≤ (2/(t+1))·λ_max(B_0)·diam(K^0)^2 is explicitly listed as 'not attempted' in the failure-boundaries page, so that specific quantitative sub-claim remains unverified.

claims.claim: When the key-query matrix is positive definite, Theorem 4.2 shows super-exponential convergence of tokens to vertices, and Proposition 4.5 shows the induced cell structure coincides with B-norm Voronoi cells when vertices have equal norm (Section 4, Theorem 4.2, Proposition 4.5).
claims.evidence: With strictly positive-definite B (λ_min=1.7995), the hardmax dynamics are run and convergence order measured: constant γ=0.5 gives q=1.0 (exponential, log-slope -0.69314714 vs predicted -0.69314718, R²=1), accelerating γ^t=1-0.9^(2^t) gives q=2.0 (super-exponential, loglog slope 0.71698 vs log2=0.69315, R²=0.99974). Thm 4.2 product-form trajectory matches simulator to 4.4e-16. Prop 4.5 B-Voronoi identity holds at 100% over 40,000 samples; control breaking equal-norm gives 97.3% mismatch.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.8 establishes well-posedness of the singular ODE limit governing the hardmax dynamics (Section 4, Theorem 4.8, Equation 4.4).
claims.evidence: The singular ODE dx/dt=v_{σ(x)}-x is tested with d=4, B≻0, vertices on B-eigenvectors (strict cells). Analytic branch solves Eq. 4.4 with RHS residual 0.0; RK45 over 120 initial conditions matches analytic to 2.6e-11 (uniqueness); 0 cell changes, 0 blow-ups; δ=1e-6 perturbation yields trajectory shift 1.0e-6 (continuous dependence); Euler observed order 1.011 (R²=0.99998); boundary tie produces branch separation 3.67, confirming strict-cell hypothesis is necessary.

claims.claim: At finite inverse temperature β, Theorem 5.2 shows interior particles reach near-vertex configurations in O(1) steps with high probability, while Theorem 5.4 shows these metastable configurations persist for exponentially long times (on the order of e^β steps) before eventual collapse to a single cluster (Section 5, Theorem 5.2, Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: Finite-β softmax dynamics (B=I, d=5, orthonormal vertices, c0=1): T1=3 steps constant across β∈{20,25,30,40,50,60,80,100} (Thm 5.2: O(1), β-independent); T2={3,6,13,31,73,179,443,1104,2767} for β=3..11, with log(T2) vs β slope=0.8627, R²=0.99854 (Thm 5.4: e^{cβ}, c>0), tail slope 0.909 approaching c0=1. Deterministic dynamics used; the 'with high probability' aspect of Thm 5.2 is not separately tested via stochastic sampling.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 shows the argmax operation generically produces a singleton, and Lemma 2.2 shows the convex hull of tokens shrinks under step sizes γ^t ∈ (0,1), underpinning the Frank-Wolfe reformulation of hardmax attention (Section 2, Lemma 2.1, Lemma 2.2).
claims.evidence: Lemma 2.1: singleton fraction=1.0 over 100,000 random configs (0 ties, min gap 2.36e-5); tie-set normal B(v_i−v_j) has min norm 0.266>0 (measure-zero hyperplane); exact-rational audit of 90,000 systems yields 0 algebraic failures. Lemma 2.2: hull volume monotone non-increasing (max ratio 0.99999<1), containment residual 0.0; control γ=1.6 causes hull growth 18.58→39.05, confirming γ∈(0,1) is necessary.

ai-sherpa/attention-frank-wolfe-repro.overall: This logbook provides strong, independent numerical evidence for all five claims at the theorems' natural finite-n, finite-d scale, including exact-algebraic identity checks (claim 1), measured convergence orders matching predicted rates (claims 2, 4), ODE well-posedness via dual-method agreement and perturbation analysis (claim 3), and large-sample singleton/hull-shrinkage verification with controls (claim 5). The main gap is that Theorem 3.1's specific linear convergence rate bound (part of claim 1) is explicitly not tested, though the FW reformulation identity itself is verified bit-exactly.

kshitijthakkar/repro-rowstochastic-mixin.paper_title: Row-Stochastic Matrices Can Provably Outperform Doubly Stochastic Matrices in Decentralized Learning

claims.claim: In the weighted Hilbert space L²(λ;R^d), the λ-induced row-stochastic mixing matrix W is self-adjoint whereas the doubly stochastic matrix W^ds is not, and this non-self-adjointness introduces additional multiplicative penalty terms (κ_λ > 1 and λ_max² > 1) that amplify consensus error under the doubly stochastic design (Section 5.2, Section 6.2).
claims.evidence: E1 computes the weighted self-adjointness residual of the row-stochastic mixing matrix (paper Eq. 5, eps=0.3) on N=16 across 5 topologies, yielding residuals of 2.6e-17 to 3.3e-16 (machine precision), while the doubly-stochastic matrix's weighted penalty residual is nonzero on all 5 (0.347–1.219), with κ_λ=2.708>1 and λ_max²=4.84>1. This is an algebraic property of the matrix construction, independent of problem dimension, verified at the paper's node scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.5 gives O(1/T) convergence rates for both row-stochastic and doubly stochastic strategies, but the row-stochastic strategy achieves strictly smaller non-asymptotic consensus error and can converge faster even when its spectral gap is smaller than that of the doubly stochastic strategy (Theorem 6.5).
claims.evidence: The executable E2 code runs a synthetic quadratic gradient-tracking experiment at d=4, single seed, on 5 regular graphs; doubly-stochastic converges faster on 4/5 topologies and row wins only on complete by 5.9e-4 (a tie). The logbook describes an in-regime experiment (d=10, 10 seeds, degree-heterogeneous graphs) claiming 142 vs 344 iterations, but the code for this experiment (inregime.py) is not shown, so the setup cannot be independently verified.

claims.claim: Theorem 7.1 derives a sufficient condition on the spectral gaps, 1 − ρ_Λ ≥ max{(1+η)κ_λ^(-1/3), λ_max^(-1/2)}(1 − ρ_J), under which the row-stochastic design provably converges strictly faster than the doubly stochastic design (Theorem 7.1).
claims.evidence: E3 encodes Theorem 7.1's predicate exactly (R=0.7187) and computes it correctly as FALSE on all 5 topologies, agreeing with observed E2 outcomes on 4/5. However, the observed outcomes it is checked against come from the toy-scale E2 runs (d=4, single seed, synthetic quadratic), so the predictive validation is only at toy scale.

claims.claim: Corollary 7.3 and Algorithm 2 give topology construction guidelines showing that when node degrees scale proportionally with their assigned weights (d_i/d_j matching λ_i/λ_j within bounds set by R), the row-stochastic design outperforms the doubly stochastic design, satisfying a Loewner order condition on the graph Laplacians (Corollary 7.3, Remark 7.4, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook's in-regime section claims to follow Corollary 7.3/Algorithm 2 (degree proportional to λ) and verifies a Loewner order condition, but the code for this experiment is not shown anywhere in the logbook. No executable code verifies the Loewner order condition on graph Laplacians or the degree-proportionality construction guidelines.

kshitijthakkar/repro-rowstochastic-mixin.overall: The logbook provides a solid numerical verification of the self-adjointness mechanism (Claim 1) at the paper's node scale, but the convergence-rate and theorem-condition claims are only addressed on a toy-scale synthetic quadratic with d=4 and a single seed, and the in-regime results that would support Claims 2 and 4 lack shown executable code.

ProCreations/meteora-repro.paper_title: Ski Rental with Distributional Predictions of Unknown Quality

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows the algorithm achieves expected additive loss O(min(√b·max(EMD(p̂,p),1), b log b)), where EMD(p̂,p) is the Earth Mover's distance between the predicted and true distributions and b is the buy-ski-rental cost ratio (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Exact Fraction arithmetic on 54 prediction/truth pairs across b=2^4 to 2^20, with all 261 transported-tail Lemma 7 checks and all 54 truncation bounds passing, and maximum loss/min(√b·max(η,1), b log b) = 0.5. The code implements Algorithm 1 (compute K̂, find tail quantile U, return min(K̂+√b, U+√b)) exactly as described.

claims.claim: The algorithm attains consistency O(√b) when the prediction error (EMD) is 0 and robustness O(b log b) when the prediction is arbitrarily inaccurate, without needing to know the prediction error bound in advance (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: On the paper's two-phase geometric-tail hard family across 9 scales up to b=2^20, fitted consistency exponent is 0.50776 (target 0.5) and robustness exponent 0.99890 (target 1), with normalized ratios converging to 0.49854 and 0.25007 respectively. The no-error-bound property is confirmed by the function signature (prediction, buy_cost) producing identical threshold 1025 for 5 truths with EMD ranging from 0 to ~2.3×10^18 at b=2^20.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 proves a matching lower bound showing no algorithm can achieve additive loss o(b)·EMD(p̂,p), establishing that the √b factor in Theorem 1 is necessary (Theorem 4, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Exact Fraction enumeration of all thresholds K=0,...,b+3 plus infinity for 10 values of b (16 to 262144), with the two-truth midpoint construction showing randomized lower bound ratio bound/(b·EMD) approaching ~0.2, confirming no algorithm achieves o(b)·EMD. The construction uses δ=1/(8b), ε=1/(2b)+δ, and verifies positive lower bounds in all 10 rows.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a Pareto-optimal consistency-robustness tradeoff: any algorithm achieving O(√b) consistency must incur Ω(b log b) robustness (Theorem 6, Section 4)
claims.evidence: Reconstruction of the paper's two-phase prediction tail with exact Decimal arithmetic across 7 scales (b=2^8 to 2^20) and 3 consistency constants (C=0.5,1,2). The identity Δ(B)=c(A_B)-c(A_K)=(b/2)(r^B-r^K) is verified, and B0/2/(b log b) ratios are positive and increasing toward ~0.1, showing any O(√b)-consistent algorithm must incur Ω(b log b) robustness. A second regime with 8 non-power-of-two scales confirms with 48/48 exact Fraction identities.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 introduces a parameterized algorithm with expected cost c(ALG_p) ≤ min{(1+λ)(c(OPT_p)+B), (1+1/λ)c(OPT_p)}, allowing explicit interpolation between trusting the prediction and worst-case guarantees via λ ∈ [0,1] (Theorem 2, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: The Clamp Policy (Definition 4.1) is implemented and tested across 150 cells (25 true/predicted distribution pairs × 6 λ values) at b=100. The robustness bound 1+1/λ-1/b holds in all cells and is nearly tight at λ=0.9 (worst ECR 2.1 vs bound 2.101). The interpolation is demonstrated: λ=0.1 gives consistency 1.1986 but robustness 3.277, while λ=0.9 gives consistency 1.6215 but robustness 2.1, matching the claimed tradeoff dial.

ProCreations/meteora-repro.overall: This logbook provides strong concrete evidence for all five claims through exact arithmetic (Fraction/Decimal) implementations of the paper's algorithms and lower-bound constructions, spanning scales up to b=2^20 with hundreds of verified inequalities and identity checks. The reproduction is clean-room with no author code, and the evidence goes beyond assertions to show specific numerical ratios, exponent fits, and bound tightness.

ProCreations/icml2026-eeg-fm-bench-vGeNa.paper_title: Fine-Tuning Without Forgetting In-Context Learning: A Theoretical Analysis of Linear Attention Models

claims.claim: Corollary 4.4 shows that full fine-tuning of all attention parameters in a linear attention model drives zero-shot error to σ² while few-shot (in-context) error converges to σ² + θᵀΣθ, a substantially larger value, formalizing the degradation of in-context learning after full fine-tuning (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Three independently pretrained single-layer linear-attention models (d=5, σ²=0.1, 20-shot, 8000 pretrain + 4000 finetune steps) show full (V,Q) fine-tuning drives zero-shot MSE to 0.105 (within 5% of σ²=0.1) while 20-shot MSE rises from 0.355 to 1.337 (+277%), confirming the predicted ICL degradation pattern in 3/3 seeds.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 shows that restricting fine-tuning updates to the value matrix reduces zero-shot error to σ² + (2/(d+4))θ₀ᵀΣθ₀ while Corollary 4.8 shows the asymptotic few-shot error only rises to σ² + 1/(d+4)²θ₀ᵀΣθ₀, i.e. value-matrix-only fine-tuning improves zero-shot performance with far less degradation to in-context learning than full fine-tuning (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Freezing Q and tuning only V improves zero-shot MSE from 1.125 to 0.414 in all three seeds while 20-shot MSE changes only from 0.355 to 0.368 (+3.65%), versus full fine-tuning's 1.337; the absolute ICL disruption is 75.93× smaller than full tuning, confirming the qualitative prediction despite the zero-shot value landing 28.4% above the asymptotic formula (0.322).

claims.claim: Proposition 4.10 proves that tuning the auxiliary few-shot loss weight w to optimize few-shot performance on the fine-tuning task θ₀ necessarily reduces few-shot performance on other tasks θ ≠ θ₀, formalizing a trade-off between target-task adaptation and generalization to unseen tasks (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: Annealed auxiliary loss reduces target-task 20-shot MSE from 0.355 to 0.215 (−39.51%) in 3/3 seeds, while across eight task directions the cosine-similarity/error correlation is strongly negative (mean r=−0.875, R²=0.765) and the opposite task has +1.577 higher MSE than the target on average, directly demonstrating the target/OOD trade-off.

claims.claim: In synthetic linear-regression experiments (d=5, σ²=0.1, Σ=I₅, ‖θ₀‖₂²=1, m=n=20), Figure 4 confirms the theoretical zero-shot/few-shot error predictions across pretraining, full fine-tuning, and value-matrix fine-tuning regimes, and Figure 5 shows value-matrix fine-tuning attains the lowest error on the out-of-distribution task -θ₀ (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: At the exact paper settings (d=5, σ²=0.1, Σ=I₅, ‖θ₀‖²=1, m=n=20) with 200k MC samples, the regime ordering matches theory: full FT zero-shot 0.113≈σ² with 20-shot 1.31, value-only zero-shot 0.438 vs asymptote 0.322 with 20-shot 0.369; on OOD task −θ₀, value-only 20-shot MSE (0.410) is far below full FT (1.222) and near pretrained (0.393), confirming value-only attains the lowest error among fine-tuning methods.

claims.claim: On the MMLU benchmark using Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct fine-tuned on the Humanities category, full fine-tuning improves zero-shot accuracy but degrades 7-shot accuracy, whereas value-matrix-only fine-tuning preserves few-shot accuracy while still improving zero-shot performance (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: The paper's own Appendix B.2 Table 2 reports value-only V fine-tuning Humanities 7-shot accuracy at 67.75 versus base 70.13, a drop of 2.38 percentage points, directly contradicting the claim's assertion that value-only fine-tuning 'preserves few-shot accuracy'; value-only does improve zero-shot (+6.59 pp) and retains more 7-shot than full Q/K/V tuning (−2.38 vs −4.07 pp), but the unqualified 'preserves' clause is false per the paper's own data.

ProCreations/icml2026-eeg-fm-bench-vGeNa.overall: The logbook provides a faithful from-scratch reproduction of the synthetic linear-regression experiments (Claims 1–4) at the paper's exact settings, confirming the qualitative theoretical predictions about full fine-tuning degradation, value-only preservation, and the auxiliary-loss trade-off across three seeds with 30k–200k evaluation samples. Claim 5 is falsified by auditing the paper's own Table 2, which shows value-only fine-tuning drops 7-shot MMLU accuracy by 2.38 pp, contradicting the 'preserves' assertion.

ProCreations/vlm-robustbench-repro.paper_title: Dropout Universality: Scaling Laws and Optimal Scheduling at the Edge-of-Chaos

claims.claim: Dropout introduces a nonzero dropout field h that destroys the perfect-alignment fixed point c*=1 of the correlation map, so that even perfectly aligned inputs decorrelate after one layer, yielding a finite depth scale for information propagation even at critical initialization (Section 3, equations 14-16).
claims.evidence: Clean-room mean-field calculations iterate the published correlation map with 80-point Gauss-Hermite quadrature, showing zero-dropout gives c*=1 and ξ=∞ while all seven positive dropout rates (.0003–.2) yield c*<1 with finite ξ (e.g., p=.0003 gives c*=0.990, ξ=21.70; p=.1 gives c*=0.494, ξ=2.45), directly confirming the fixed-point destruction and finite depth scale.

claims.claim: Smooth activations (e.g., tanh, GELU) and kinked activations (e.g., ReLU-like) form two distinct universality classes with different critical exponents: smooth activations have (ν_t, β, δ, ν_ρ) = (1, 1, 2, 1/2) while kinked activations have (1, 2, 3/2, 1/3) (Section 3.1-3.2, Table 2).
claims.evidence: Five independently fitted critical exponents from clean-room mean-field recursions recover smooth tanh targets (ν_t=1.019, β=0.971, 1/δ=0.512, ν_ρ=0.482 vs. targets 1,1,1/2,1/2) and kinked ReLU targets (ν_t=1.019, β=1.965, 1/δ=0.666, ν_ρ=0.346 vs. targets 1,2,2/3,1/3), with all fits R²>0.99996, clearly distinguishing the two universality classes.

claims.claim: For smooth activations, rescaled order parameter and detuning variables collapse onto a universal function m̃ = sqrt(1+t̃^2) - t̃, confirming the predicted scaling form (Section 3.2, equations 30-31, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: 75 measured points across 5 dropout rates from the mean-field recursion collapse onto m̃=sqrt(1+t̃²)−t̃ with median absolute errors as low as 0.0023 at p=0.02 and t̃ spanning [−1.19, 3.99], directly testing the predicted universal scaling form rather than just fitting exponents.

claims.claim: A front-loaded (early, step-like) dropout schedule that concentrates dropout in the earliest layers under a fixed dropout budget reduces MLP test loss by 18-35% and improves accuracy by up to about 2 percentage points compared to constant dropout (Section 3.3, Table 3, Figures 6-9).
claims.evidence: A fresh 75-epoch CPU training run at the paper's MLP scale (width 256, depth 6, 5000/5000 CIFAR-10 subset, 5 paired seeds) shows 19.49% mean loss reduction (within the claimed 18–35% range), 5/5 paired wins (p=1.79e-5), and +0.696 pp accuracy improvement; a separate 20-seed 50-epoch run with an equal-budget late negative control confirms direction (20/20 wins, 10.2% loss reduction).

claims.claim: On a Vision Transformer trained on CIFAR-100 and CIFAR-10, front-loaded/step or linear-decreasing dropout schedules yield smaller but consistent gains of about 4-6% loss reduction and up to 0.66 percentage points accuracy improvement over constant dropout at a fixed budget (Section 3.3, Figures 10 and 12).
claims.evidence: A deterministic reaggregation of the authors' pinned official result arrays (with SHA-256 hash verification) confirms CIFAR-100 Linear (early) yields 4.15% loss reduction and +0.661 pp accuracy (10/10 paired wins) and CIFAR-10 Step (early) yields 6.32% loss reduction and +0.522 pp accuracy (5/5 paired wins), matching the claimed ~4–6% loss range and 0.66 pp accuracy bound; however, this is a reanalysis of official data rather than an independent ViT training run.

ProCreations/vlm-robustbench-repro.overall: The logbook provides strong independent evidence for the mean-field claims (1–3) via clean-room calculations with specific numerical results, and for the MLP schedule claim (4) via fresh training runs at the paper's scale. Claim 5 is confirmed by reanalysis of official result arrays rather than independent training, which is a weaker but still concrete form of verification.

ProCreations/repro-vlm-robustbench-audit.paper_title: On the Power of Source Screening for Learning Shared Feature Extractors

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows that training on an admissible subset of sources achieves the minimax-optimal statistical rate O(√(d/(Nλ_k))) for shared low-dimensional subspace estimation (Theorem 2).

The 31-percentage-point CelebA gap persists across the entire m×k sweep (max cell mean 61.14%), and random selection actually outperforms screening on CelebA.

claims.claim: Figure 1 shows subspace reconstruction error is lower when training on a balanced, screened subset of sources than on the full heterogeneous source population (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: At matched total budget on a synthetic heterogeneous setup (d=30, k=6, N=99, 8 replicates per cell), screened subsets achieve 4.6×–7.6× lower subspace error than the full population across all four budget levels. ProCreations/repro-vlm-robustbench-audit.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence at the paper's scale supporting the theoretical rate claims (Claims 1, 2, 5) and falsifies the real-world accuracy claim (Claim 4) with a dramatic 31-point CelebA gap. Claim 3 is falsified on textual grounds: the paper's Theorem 5 only covers Algorithm 1, not Algorithm 2, contradicting the claim that both are proven.

ProCreations/repro-convergence-of-two-ti.paper_title: Convergence of Two-Timescale Markovian Stochastic Approximations with Applications in Reinforcement Learning

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 establishes almost-sure stability (sup_n ||z_n|| < infinity) for two-timescale stochastic approximation iterates driven by Markovian noise, without requiring projection operators (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Eighteen unprojected 24-dimensional two-timescale SA paths across three Markov stickness regimes (0.15, 0.62, 0.90) and six seeds show bounded joint norms (max 6.17855) with zero projection/clipping calls, providing concrete empirical support for stability on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 proves that the fast-timescale iterate x_n converges to the equilibrium map lambda(y_n), i.e. lim_n ||x_n - lambda(y_n)|| = 0, with joint convergence to (lambda(y*), y*) (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: Analytically computed equilibrium maps across 18 paths yield tail/initial tracking-error ratios as low as 0.006410 and joint-equilibrium ratios of 0.004844, demonstrating convergence to the equilibrium map on a non-toy linear SA system.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.1 shows the fast-timescale iterate norm is controlled by the running maximum of the slow-timescale iterate, ||x_n|| <= K(1+||y_n^max||) almost surely, which is the key technical device enabling the stability proof (Lemma 3.1).
claims.evidence: Checkpointed prefix-maximum of ||y|| and empirically fitted constant K=1.803607 covers all 18 paths, with the full time-series audit confirming the bound ||x_n|| <= K(1+||y_n^max||) holds throughout each trajectory.

claims.claim: Theorem 7.2 gives the first almost-sure convergence proof for temporal difference learning with gradient correction and eligibility traces (TDC(lambda)) under off-policy, Markovian sampling conditions (Section 7, Theorem 7.2, Definition 7.1).
claims.evidence: Independent TDC(lambda) implementation on a 10-state, 2-action off-policy MDP with full-rank 6-feature matrix, 12 paths at lambda 0/0.45/0.8 for 260,000 updates each without projection, shows worst tail/initial residual ratio below 0.193 (0.045–0.058 at lambda 0.8), supporting convergence; however, the 'first proof' priority claim is not independently verified.

claims.claim: The convergence analysis relies on assumptions B.1-B.7 in the appendix, including a unique stationary distribution for the Markov noise chain (Assumption B.1) and learning-rate timescale separation lim_n beta(n)/alpha(n) = 0 (Assumption B.2) (Appendix B).
claims.evidence: All transition matrices verified irreducible with stationary residual below 1e-12 (B.1), step-size ratios beta/alpha reaching 0.02192 (B.2), plus destructive controls showing failure when assumptions are violated (no-separation control ends above 1.4815, reducible chain produces class-dependent endpoints separated by 0.49979).

ProCreations/repro-convergence-of-two-ti.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from non-toy setups (24-dimensional linear SA, 10-state off-policy TDC) across multiple seeds and parameter regimes, with destructive controls, supporting all five claims. The 'first proof' priority aspect of Claim 4 is acknowledged as not independently verified, but the convergence mechanism itself is empirically validated.

ProCreations/repro-toksuite-tokenizer-ch.paper_title: Why Self-Distillation Helps and Hurts: Denoising vs. Signal Forgetting

claims.claim: Deterministic-equivalent recursions for prediction risk in overparameterized linear self-training decompose error into a systematic 'signal forgetting' term that grows with the number of self-training iterations and a stochastic noise term that decays exponentially in iterations (Section on risk decomposition; Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: 96 finite-dimensional trajectories with fresh Gaussian designs at three aspect ratios (rho=1.5,2.0,2.5, n=240, p up to 600) yield 1,536 risk observations with median relative recursion error of 1.10% and bias/variance Spearman correlations of 1.000, confirming the deterministic-equivalent decomposition into growing systematic and decaying stochastic terms.

claims.claim: Test risk as a function of self-training iteration count follows a U-shaped curve, with an optimal early-stopping iteration set by the tradeoff between decaying stochastic error and accumulating systematic (signal-forgetting) error, occurring strictly under spectral anisotropy of the feature covariance (Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: 120 paired trajectories show empirical and theoretical optima matching exactly (5/5, 2/2, 1/1), all six 10,000-draw bootstrap CIs for improvement and degradation exclude zero, and the isotropic control (spike=1) removes the interior optimum while the anisotropic spike=25 restores it, confirming the U-shape requires spectral anisotropy.

claims.claim: In spiked covariance models, each self-training iteration acts as a direction-dependent spectral filter that preserves eigendirections aligned with strong signal (survival factor near 1) while suppressing weaker, noise-aligned eigendirections at a rate of approximately (1+τ)^(−t).
claims.evidence: 800 trajectories and 9,600 fresh-projection steps across five eigenvalues (1,2,5,25,100) show strictly ordered terminal retention (0.000270 to 0.887206) matching closed-form survival predictions within median absolute error 0.003324, with a 3,280x strong/bulk separation, each experiment isolating a single eigendirection to rule out cross-spike mixing.

claims.claim: An iterated Generalized Cross-Validation (iGCV) estimator is proposed that achieves uniform consistency for estimating risk along the self-training trajectory, enabling data-driven selection of the optimal early-stopping iteration without a held-out validation set.
claims.evidence: Following the paper's Appendix H spec exactly (overparameterized, power-law covariance, sparse signal, Eq 11-12 with M_t correction), fixed-lambda sup-gap slopes of -0.571 to -0.490 approximate the n^{-1/2} rate with R^2 0.881-0.996, argmin match is 1.00 at all n and rho at fixed lambda, and correctness gates pass (iGCV at t=0 reduces to classical GCV at 2.06e-16 relative error).

claims.claim: The theoretical denoising-forgetting risk tradeoff, derived for linear regression, is empirically confirmed to hold for deep networks, specifically ResNet-50 trained on CIFAR-10 under repeated self-distillation.
claims.evidence: No deep-network experiment was executed; the logbook only verifies that the paper's Appendix A reports specific numbers (47.7% to 43.6% at t=2 to 45.0%), explicitly stating it 'does not use author code, checkpoints, a training run, or any figure-only endpoint' — this confirms what the paper claims, not that the claim holds.

ProCreations/repro-toksuite-tokenizer-ch.overall: The logbook provides rigorous clean-room experimental verification of the four linear-theory claims (deterministic recursions, U-shaped early stopping, spectral filtering, and iGCV consistency) with proper controls, bootstrap inference, and correctness gates at non-trivial scale. The deep-network extension (Claim 5) was never independently run — only the paper's own reported numbers were checked against its source — leaving it unverified.

kshitijthakkar/repro-truthrl.paper_title: TruthRL: Incentivizing Truthful LLMs via Reinforcement Learning

claims.claim: On the CRAG benchmark with retrieval using Llama3.1-8B, TruthRL reduces hallucination rate from 43.5% (prompting baseline) to 19.4% and improves the truthfulness score from +5.3 to +37.2 (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This claim requires a converged Llama3.1-8B model evaluated on the CRAG test set. The logbook never ran evaluation on any test set; the only executed runs were 15-step toy GRPO training on Qwen2.5-3B with LoRA, and the specific hallucination (43.5%→19.4%) and truthfulness (+5.3→+37.2) numbers were never measured.

claims.claim: Averaged across four knowledge-intensive benchmarks with retrieval, TruthRL achieves a mean hallucination rate of 18.8% and truthfulness score of +25.6, versus 54.1% hallucination and -16.4 truthfulness for the prompting baseline (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This claim requires evaluation across four benchmarks (CRAG, NQ, HotpotQA, MuSiQue) with a converged model. The logbook audited all four datasets but never trained a converged model or ran any evaluation; the specific numbers (18.8%/+25.6 vs 54.1%/-16.4) were never measured.

claims.claim: Compared to vanilla accuracy-driven RL, TruthRL reduces hallucinations by 28.9 percentage points and improves truthfulness by 21.1 points (Section on hallucination reduction claims).
claims.evidence: The logbook ran a controlled ternary-vs-binary reward comparison on real GRPO training (960 live rollouts, 15 steps each arm), where the binary reward is a direct proxy for accuracy-driven RL. The reward mechanism was confirmed (abstain scores 0.0 vs -1.0), but no evaluation metrics were measured and the behavioral direction (28.9 pp hallucination reduction, 21.1 point truthfulness gain) was not observed at this scale.

claims.claim: An ablation shows the ternary reward formulation outperforms a binary reward on CRAG, achieving +37.2 truthfulness and 19.4% hallucination versus +20.8 and 39.5% for the binary variant (Table 3).
claims.evidence: Two real GRPO runs (ternary vs binary reward, Qwen2.5-3B + LoRA r=64, 15 steps, CRAG subset) confirmed the reward mechanism on 960 live rollouts: ternary pays abstention 0.0 (48/48 cases) and binary pays -1.0 (46/46 cases). claims.claim: On difficult CRAG questions, TruthRL attains a 15.5% hallucination rate versus near-100% for accuracy-optimized baselines, demonstrating improved knowledge-boundary recognition (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This claim requires evaluation on the difficult CRAG question subset with a converged model. The logbook never ran any test-set evaluation, never identified or evaluated on a difficult-question subset, and the specific numbers (15.5% hallucination vs near-100%) were never measured.

kshitijthakkar/repro-truthrl.overall: The logbook executed one controlled ternary-vs-binary reward comparison at toy scale (Qwen2.5-3B + LoRA, 15 GRPO steps, no test-set evaluation), confirming the reward mechanism on 960 live training rollouts but not observing the paper's claimed behavioral outcomes. The remaining five claims were never addressed because they require converged checkpoints or multi-model evaluation that the toy runs did not produce.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 proves that if the unconstrained network class universally approximates the target function class F, then CAffNet universally approximates the constrained target class {f_t in F | A(x) f_t <= b(x)}, with approximation error bound ||P* - f_t||_p < (3 + 3*sqrt(n_out))K (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides an independent KKT/metric-projection derivation yielding ||P*-f_target||_p <= (1+sqrt(n_out))||f_theta-f_target||_p, which is tighter than the paper's (3+3*sqrt(n_out))K bound and thus implies it; 30 independent SLSQP checks agree with the enumerated selector within 2.49e-14 with all bound ratios below 0.320, and a constructive ReLU-spline sequence reduces projected MSE by >1,000,000x with zero violations.

claims.claim: The CAffine layer's projection formula includes a trainable null-space component w_phi(x), P_gamma(x) = f_theta(x) - A_gamma^dagger(x)(A_gamma(x) f_theta(x) - b_gamma(x)) + (I - A_gamma^dagger(x) A_gamma(x)) w_phi(x), allowing joint optimization across multiple feasible projections rather than a fixed orthogonal projection (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The caffine_candidate function implements the exact formula P_gamma = f - A^dagger(Af-b) + (I-A^dagger A)w; a 500-step differentiable PyTorch run shows both theta and phi parameters have nonzero initial gradients (0.31075), MSE drops 11.11x with zero equality violation, and five distinct w_phi values produce five distinct feasible points on the same active face.

claims.claim: Unlike prior work (HardNet), CAffNet guarantees hard constraint satisfaction A(x)y <= b(x) without requiring A(x) to have full row rank, and handles arbitrary constraint cardinality via decomposition into sub-constraint combinations of at most min(m, n_out) constraints (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The stress grid of 540 systems across dimensions 2-4, three rank regimes (m<n, m=n, dependent m>n with 180 overcomplete systems), and continuous input variation shows 540/540 selected outputs feasible with max residual 5.66e-15; boundary controls show fixed-full pseudoinverse projection violates by 1.1667 and single-boundary projection by 1.8, while CAffNet's subset-enumeration selector achieves zero violation.

claims.claim: On the piecewise-constraint benchmark, CAffNet-TF (transformer variant) achieves a 73.33% MSE reduction relative to a soft-constrained neural network baseline while incurring zero constraint violations (Section on Experiments, piecewise constraints task).
claims.evidence: Five-seed CPU runs on the complete Appendix D.1 benchmark with published functions, 50 training points, 400 test points, and Adam at 1e-4 show CAffNet-TF achieving 94.1%-98.7% MSE reduction over the soft-constrained baseline with exactly zero violations across all seeds; the paper's 73.33% figure is independently confirmed as the exact arithmetic of its displayed table means (0.0045 vs 0.0012).

claims.claim: In the safety-critical control experiment, CAffNet successfully avoids obstacles whereas both HardNet and the soft-constrained baseline fail to do so (Section on Experiments, safety-critical control task).
claims.evidence: On 60 held-out initial states with the paper's unicycle dynamics, three obstacle polytopes, and 13-row CBF constraint system, CAffNet-FF records 0/60 collisions while HardNet has 32/60 (53.3%) and the soft-constrained NN has 27/60 (45.0%), directly reproducing the paper's Figure 6 finding; the logbook honestly notes reduced goal-reaching (30% arrival) due to smaller training budget but the obstacle-avoidance claim is fully supported.

ProCreations/dbfm-repro.overall: This logbook provides a thorough clean-room reproduction of all five claims with concrete numerical evidence: 540-system stress tests for hard constraints, differentiable joint optimization for the trainable null-space, independent SLSQP cross-checks for universal approximation, five-seed benchmark runs for the piecewise task, and 60-state evaluation for safety-critical control. The evidence consistently supports the paper's claims, with honest qualifications about reduced training budgets and architectural choices where the paper's specifications are incomplete.

SabaPivot/repro-hippo-zoo.paper_title: HiPPO Zoo: Explicit Memory Mechanisms for Interpretable State Space Models

claims.claim: HiPPO Zoo introduces five explicit polynomial-based extensions to classical HiPPO memory that individually replicate capabilities usually attributed to opaque learned SSMs like Mamba: Volterra, Salience, Associative Memory, Multiscale, and Forecasting HiPPO (Section 3).
claims.evidence: All five scripts execute end-to-end with concrete results: forecasting uses three coupled LegT systems (N=64) with H=4 and H=32 forecasts tracking the oracle GP posterior within ±1σ, and eigenfunctions of Q=TᵀT shifting from recent to longer lags.

claims.claim: Salience HiPPO implements adaptive, input-dependent memory allocation via a scalar measure-deformation mechanism (Equation 2) with a time-warping interpretation (Equation 3), demonstrated on a selective copying task with explicit history-measure visualizations (Section 3.2, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Selective-copying run with 3,000 TBPTT episodes, LegS N=256, T=30 achieves eval loss 1.0e-4 and cosine=1.0 on all 10 write-phase outputs; learned g(t) rises to ~4 on informative tokens and falls to ~0.2 otherwise, with measure concentrating at t=19,22,29.

claims.claim: Volterra HiPPO decomposes nonlinear dynamics into interpretable kernels parameterized in an orthogonal polynomial basis, validated by learning a quadratic Volterra system on the Wray-Green benchmark (Section 3.1, Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Five trials of 10^7 streaming steps on the official Wray-Green quadratic system (LegS N=64) show quadratic readout error plateauing while linear grows and MLP is much larger; decoded W2 kernel (50×50) visually matches the analytic 4e-3 μ⊗μ separable kernel.

claims.claim: Associative Memory HiPPO separates temporal encoding from content-addressable storage on a continuous address space, demonstrated via key-value associative recall with explicit visualization (Section 3.3, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: 3,500-episode run with fixed-ZOH LegT encoder (d_model=32, n_assoc=32) achieves eval loss 3.2e-6 and query-target cosine 1.0; 12 A-tokens receive distinct addresses on [0,1] with read/write diagonal and max pairwise kernel overlap 0.018 versus null overlaps near 1.0.

claims.claim: Multiscale HiPPO represents scale-dependent states as polynomial expansions (Equation 5) that support stable reconstruction across three orders of magnitude of timescale (Section 3.4, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: 64 OU-mixture trajectories (length 30,000, HiPPO order 16, scale dim 128) queried at lags 10–29,999; multiscale MSE excess over oracle is 0.041 vs 0.097 for best vanilla, with specific MSE values reported at lags 10/676/29,999 and raw mse_results.npz saved.

claims.claim: In the streaming/online training setups, the Salience model uses truncated backpropagation through time with fixed HiPPO parameters and only the neural readout learned online, while the Associative model uses chunk-wise gradient computation with state detachment between chunks (Section C.2-C.3).
claims.evidence: Source audit confirms Salience uses value_and_grad with stop_gradient(S_end) and fixed LegS A,b arrays (only Dense parameters optimized by AdamW 1e-3), while Associative detaches both S_end and C_end with fixed ZOH LegT encoder matching Appendix C.3; both converge to reported losses.

SabaPivot/repro-hippo-zoo.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence and specific experimental settings for all six claims using the authors' official code at paper scale, with artifacts and raw output files referenced. The reproduction is thorough, covering all five mechanisms plus the online-training appendix details.

ProCreations/repro-parameter-free-dynami.paper_title: Parameter-free Dynamic Regret: Time-varying Movement Costs, Delayed Feedback, and Memory

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 establishes an improved comparator-adaptive dynamic regret bound for unconstrained OCO with time-varying movement costs that replaces a quadratic dependence on lambda_t with a linear interaction term lambda_t*||g_t|| relative to the bound in Theorem 3.1 (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements the epoch rule and numerically verifies the key inequality across nine sequences, showing the quadratic ledger is 4.017x the first-order ledger and up to 299,999x in a destructive small-gradient sweep, directly testing the claimed replacement of lambda_t^2 with lambda_t*||g_t||.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 shows that for OCO with delayed feedback, the reduction to time-varying movement costs (via Lemma 5.1 and Algorithm 4) achieves regret depending on total delay d_tot rather than the worse max-delay times T (d_max*T) dependence of prior work, without requiring in-order feedback arrival (Section 5.1, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Twelve delay schedules including out-of-order arrivals verify the Lemma 5.1 reduction and show the missing-count bound of 2*d_tot, with a destructive one-long-delay control achieving d_max*T/d_tot = T = 512, directly contrasting total-delay vs max-delay dependence.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.7 gives a comparator-adaptive dynamic regret guarantee for OCO with time-varying memory (loss functions depending on the last H actions) by reducing memory-dependent losses to movement costs via the effective memory coupling coefficients xi_t (Section 5.2, Lemma 5.6, Theorem 5.7).
claims.evidence: Twelve settings with varying memory lengths through horizon 512 verify Lemma 5.6 holds, with xi_t <= B² and sum(xi_t)/sum(b_t²) <= 0.584, directly testing the memory-to-movement-cost reduction and the coupling coefficients used by Theorem 5.7.

claims.claim: Algorithm 2 is a dynamic parameter-free subroutine that maintains parallel learning-rate instances on an exponential grid, used within the Composite Mirror Descent scheme (Algorithm 1) to obtain comparator-adaptive guarantees (Section 3, Algorithms 1-2).
claims.evidence: The exact exponential grid eta_i = min(2^i/(L*sqrt(T)), 1/L) is instantiated at six horizons and three Lipschitz scales with independent CMD prox instances, and in 72 hindsight-tuning cells the closest grid rate is within 1.409x of the clipped optimum, below the factor-two guarantee.

claims.claim: Setting the movement-cost weights lambda_t=0 in the derived bounds recovers the standard optimal static and dynamic regret guarantees for classical OCO as a special case (Section 3, following Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: All 72 formula cells set lambda_t=0 and confirm byte-for-byte floating-point equality between the movement-augmented data term and the classical OCO gradient-variance term, with both g²+lambda² and g²+lambda|g| reducing exactly to g².

ProCreations/repro-parameter-free-dynami.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence across multiple test scenarios and destructive controls for all five theoretical claims, verifying key inequalities, reductions, and algorithmic properties at finite scale (up to T=512). While the scale is modest, the claims are theorem statements whose mathematical relationships are directly tested rather than merely asserted.

Crusadersk/icml26-pilot-grokking.paper_title: To Grok Grokking: Provable Grokking in Ridge Regression

claims.claim: The paper proves end-to-end grokking for zero-teacher ridge regression, including early training overfitting, delayed poor generalization, and eventual low generalization error (Theorem 4.1)

claims.claim: The end-to-end grokking result is extended from the zero-teacher setting to realizable ridge regression with arbitrary realizable teacher functions (Theorem 4.2)
claims.evidence: The extension to arbitrary realizable teacher functions (Theorem 4.2) is not empirically tested; the ridge simulation uses one specific realizable teacher, not a sweep over arbitrary teachers, and no formal proof verification is attempted.

claims.claim: Separate theorems decompose grokking into training-loss convergence, poor generalization during overfitting, and eventual generalization (Theorems 4.4-4.6)
