vissutagunawan/z9Bo4eXSpW.paper_title: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards: GRPO's Loss, Dynamics, and Success Amplification

claims.claim: GRPO with verifiable 0/1 rewards can be cast as an adaptive weighted contrastive loss between samples drawn from the previous (old) policy, with weights ω_{ε,±}(p) = p/√(p(1-p)+ε) depending on the old policy's success probability p (Section 2).
claims.evidence: Symbolic proof over free simplex symbols (sympy, exact rational/radical arithmetic) shows the GRPO objective equals ω⁺_ε(p)·P_π[r=1] − ω⁻_ε(p)·P_π[r=0] with the specified weights, exhaustively across all 2^N patterns for N=2,3,4, for both clipped and unclipped objectives, with 4 controls (mean-only calibration, uncalibrated reward, non-binary reward, degenerate patterns) that discriminate the claim from alternatives.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 gives the optimal policy at each GRPO iteration in closed form as an exponential reweighting of the reference policy based on the previous iteration's binary reward statistics (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Gibbs variational identity J(π*)−J(π)=β·KL(π||π*) proven symbolically over free advantage/anchor/policy/β symbols for N=2..4 establishes π* as the unique global argmax; Z-collapse to the two-term expression verified for all 2^N patterns; independent numerical optimization (40 random bandits, SLSQP + BFGS with analytic gradients) never beats the closed form (worst J excess = +1.78e-15); 4 deliberately wrong closed forms all yield strictly lower J.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows the success probability sequence generated by GRPO's iterations satisfies a fixed-point recursion p_{n+1} = h_{ε,p_ref}(p_n) (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The PoS recurrence p_{n+1}=h_{ε,p_ref}(p_n) is proven symbolically as a direct consequence of the closed-form optimal policy (check G4 in Claim 2's page), verified over 25 non-degenerate reward patterns with free symbols for both the reference-anchored and mirror-GRPO variants; the recurrence is then independently corroborated in Claim 3's page by reproducing all 24 of the paper's printed p* values via iteration of h at 50-decimal-place precision.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 proves every fixed point p* of GRPO's dynamics satisfies p* > p_ref, i.e., GRPO provably amplifies the policy's probability of success beyond the reference policy's performance (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Exact positive factorisation h(p)−p_ref = p_ref(1−p_ref)(1−u)/(p_ref+(1−p_ref)u) with u=exp(−Ω_ε(p)/β) proven over free symbols (p_ref via a/(a+b) parametrisation, free p, β, ε); every factor shown strictly positive since Ω_ε(p)>0 on [0,1]; 40/40 fixed points across the paper's 24-cell (β,p_ref) grid at 50-dp exceed p_ref with 0 counterexamples; 5 controls including β-limits, p_ref boundary cases, ε=0 discontinuity, and float64 artifact analysis all pass.

claims.claim: Theorem 5 shows that when the parametric policy approximation has statistical and optimization error bounded by δ*, the resulting success probability converges to within 2δ* of the theoretical fixed point (Theorem 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook contains no page, experiment, proof, or discussion addressing Theorem 5 (parametric policy approximation error bounds and convergence to within 2δ* of the fixed point). Only Claims 1–3 (mapping to paper Sections 2, Theorems 1–4) are covered; Theorem 5 is never mentioned.

vissutagunawan/z9Bo4eXSpW.overall: The logbook provides rigorous symbolic proofs over free symbols (with exact arithmetic), independent numerical cross-checks, and well-designed falsification controls for Claims 1–4, establishing the contrastive loss form, optimal policy closed form, PoS recurrence, and success amplification. Claim 5 (Theorem 5 on parametric approximation error) is entirely unaddressed.

vissutagunawan/U1bxeLQLaK.paper_title: On the Provable Suboptimality of Momentum SGD in Nonstationary Stochastic Optimization

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows momentum SGD's tracking-error bound scales as (1-beta)^-2 on the initialization term and (1-beta)^-1 on the noise floor, versus O(1) and O(sigma^2 gamma/mu) respectively for vanilla SGD in Theorem 3.1 (Section 3.1, Theorems 3.1 and 3.3).
claims.evidence: Exact Lyapunov steady-state solves at the paper's own parameters (d=100, T=5000, 20 seeds) show HB noise-floor slope of -1.000 vs (1-beta) at every gamma, and the drift floor under the stability cap gamma=mu(1-beta)^2/(4L^2) has slope -2.000 matching the closed form 16L^4*delta^2/(mu^4*(1-beta)^2) to 4e-15 relative error; SGD remains constant at 1.0503 across all beta, and all four falsification controls pass (zero drift, zero noise, beta=0 bitwise recovery, effective-stepsize comparison).

claims.claim: Theorem 3.7 gives a minimax lower bound decomposing regret into a noise-limited term and an inertia-limited term that worsens with beta and can dominate in drift-heavy regimes, establishing an information-theoretic (not just analytical) barrier for momentum methods (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence: Both Appendix-D hard families are rebuilt from scratch: Lemma D.7 stationary variance scales as (1-beta)^(-0.9999) (MC-confirmed to 0.07% rel err), the exact KL divergence between environments collapses as (1-beta)^(+4.007) in d=3 demonstrating the information-theoretic barrier, Lemma D.5 exponents match to |err|<0.005, and the block-switching regret floor (Thm D.1) shows HB c~0.62 flat in beta while SGD's c collapses, with HB/SGD ratios growing from 2.5x to 133x.

claims.claim: Under the stability constraint gamma <= (1-beta)^2/L, the paper proves vanilla SGD provably outperforms Heavy-Ball/Nesterov momentum SGD in drift-dominated nonstationary regimes (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Under the paper's stability cap with per-method tuning, the exact closed-form phase map shows SGD wins 100% of drift-dominated grid points at every beta (median accelerated/SGD ratio growing from 43x to 108,000x as beta:0.5->0.99 for constvel), pure-drift settings show SGD winning with 64x-160,000x margins, and the Theorem-D.1 block-switching family shows SGD wins 8/8 tested settings with HB/SGD regret ratios from 2.5x to 133x.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.6 shows the high-probability bound for momentum SGD exhibits an inertia horizon of order (1-beta)^-1 and drift-noise coupling scaling as (1-beta)^-2, both absent from the vanilla SGD high-probability bound in Theorem 3.5 (Section 3.2, Theorems 3.5 and 3.6).
claims.evidence: No experiments in the logbook specifically test the high-probability bounds of Theorems 3.5 and 3.6; the verify_equivalence function in claim1.py only checks algorithm-formulation equivalence (Section 2.2 vs Theorem 3.5 buffer form), not the high-probability tail bounds, inertia horizon, or drift-noise coupling scaling.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments on quadratics, linear/logistic regression, and MLPs confirm that increasing nonstationarity (drift), momentum parameter beta, or condition number kappa systematically worsens Heavy-Ball and Nesterov tracking error while vanilla SGD remains comparatively robust (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Only the quadratic experiments are performed (at the paper's full scale, showing beta and drift effects on HB/NAG vs SGD), but no experiments on linear regression, logistic regression, or MLPs are present, and the condition number kappa is fixed at 1 (mu=L=1) throughout, leaving the majority of the claimed experimental scope unaddressed.

vissutagunawan/U1bxeLQLaK.overall: The logbook provides strong, clean-room numerical verification of the paper's theoretical scaling exponents for momentum SGD (Claims 1-3) using exact Lyapunov solves and the paper's own hard families at full scale, but does not address the high-probability bounds (Claim 4) and only covers the quadratic portion of the experimental claims (Claim 5), omitting linear/logistic regression, MLPs, and condition-number variation.

vissutagunawan/n50Ipdt5d5.paper_title: Revenue Guarantees of No-Swap-Regret Dynamics in First Price Auctions

claims.claim: For exact correlated equilibria in discrete first-price auctions with k discretization levels, expected revenue is at least v2 - 4/k, where v2 is the second-highest valuation (Theorem 2.5).
claims.evidence: The ε=0 LP results (exact CE case) across 16 instances show Z*_LP ≥ v₂−3/k for all tested configurations (e.g., k=10 v=(1,1,0): Z*_LP=0.8 ≥ 0.7; k=50: 0.96 ≥ 0.94), and since v₂−3/k ≥ v₂−4/k, Theorem 2.5's weaker bound is supported as a corollary, though the logbook never explicitly labels this as Theorem 2.5 verification.

claims.claim: For ε-approximate correlated equilibria, expected revenue is at least v2 - 3/k - Θ(εk²) (Theorem 2.6).
claims.evidence: Exact rational-arithmetic verification across 16 instances and 5 ε-values confirms dual certificate feasibility, Lemma 3.8 objective ≥ v₂−3/k−2εk², weak duality (Z*_LP ≥ certificate), strong duality (gap ≤ 4.7e-8), and Z*_LP ≥ v₂−3/k−2εk² with min margin +0.02; controls confirm tightness (v₂−1/k breaks on 15/16 instances), structure dependence (0/720 perturbations feasible), and test teeth (24 cells where too-strong bound is violated).

claims.claim: There exists an ε-approximate correlated equilibrium with revenue at most v2 - Θ(1/k) - Θ(ε), showing the ε-dependence in the revenue lower bound cannot be removed (Theorem 2.8).
claims.evidence: Theorem 2.8 (existence of a bad ε-approx CE with revenue ≤ v₂−Θ(1/k)−Θ(ε)) is never explicitly targeted; the logbook mentions it only in passing in claim3.py notes ('Sec 5 conjectures the true bound is Theorem 2.8's...') without constructing or verifying such an equilibrium.

claims.claim: When bidders run no-swap-regret algorithms achieving swap regret O(√(kT)), the time-averaged revenue is at least v2 - 3/k - O(ε) after O(k^5/ε^2) rounds (Corollary 2.7).
claims.evidence: Derivation T*=C²k⁵/ε² verified by direct substitution with negative control (fails below T*); composition with Theorem 2.6 at ε'=ε/k² confirmed via LP (certified = v₂−3/k−2ε exactly); Blum-Mansour dynamics at k=10 (adequate horizon T=1e4) meet the v₂−3/k floor for all five v₂ values with swap regret within the [10] optimal bound; Azuma-Hoeffding repair of Theorem 2.3's proof defect preserves O~(k⁵/ε²).

claims.claim: Time-averaged bidder behavior under no-swap-regret dynamics converges to an ε-approximate correlated equilibrium with probability 1-δ (Theorem 2.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook identifies a proof defect in Theorem 2.3 (Chernoff bound applied to signed, history-dependent variables) and proposes an Azuma-Hoeffding repair, but only one random seed is used per configuration so the probability-1−δ convergence guarantee is never statistically tested, and the original proof is shown to be flawed rather than verified.

claims.claim: The revenue lower bounds are proved via a dual-fitting approach that uses a linear program and weak duality to bound revenue of approximate correlated equilibria (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The dual-fitting pipeline is reconstructed and verified link-by-link in exact rational arithmetic: primal LP (Def 3.1) solved with HiGHS, dual LP (Lemma 3.3) confirmed via strong duality (gap ≤ 4.7e-8), fitted certificate (Def 3.5/3.6) checked dual-feasible exactly, weak duality Z*_LP ≥ certificate holds for all 80 (instance, ε) cells, and the four class lemmas 3.9–3.12 hold as proved.

vissutagunawan/n50Ipdt5d5.overall: The logbook provides strong exact-arithmetic and LP-based evidence supporting Theorems 2.5, 2.6, and 2.6's dual-fitting methodology (Claims 1, 2, 6), and a combination of algebraic derivation, LP composition, and empirical Blum-Mansour dynamics supporting Corollary 2.7 (Claim 4). Theorem 2.8 (Claim 3) is unaddressed, and Theorem 2.3 (Claim 5) is only indirectly supported with its original proof shown defective.

ai-sherpa/cvar-adversarial-control-repro.paper_title: Adversarially Robust Control of Conditional Value-at-Risk via Rockafellar-Uryasev Conformal Inference

claims.claim: Theorem 2.2 establishes that the realized empirical CVaR of the Rockafellar-Uryasev conformal inference method (RUCC) is controlled at the target level with an asymptotic conservatism gap of O(1/sqrt(T)), termed the 'Price of Nonlinearity' relative to the O(1/T) rate achievable for linear expected-loss control (Theorem 2.2; Remark 2.3).
claims.evidence: 840/840 exhaustive bound checks across 3 DGPs (T=200–20,000, 40 trials each) show zero violations of the combined Theorem 2.4+2.6 bound with worst slack ≥0.1038; tightness confirmed on the paper's own Theorem 2.5 hard instance with fitted regret-growth exponents 0.510/0.495/0.465/0.487 (theory +0.5) and leading constant matching (1/√2π)√(β/(1−β)) to within 5.8% at T=50,000.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.4 bounds the inner-level regret of the AdaGrad-FTRL threshold optimization by |max_c Reg_T(c)| <= (3/4) * max{1, beta/(1-beta)} * sqrt(T+1), and Theorem 2.6 shows the outer-level Conformal Decision Theory update keeps the surrogate loss within alpha + O(sqrt(T))/T of the target risk level alpha (Theorem 2.4; Theorem 2.6).
claims.evidence: Theorem 2.4's two-sided regret bound held with 0 violations across 840 checks (worst upper slack ≥8.178, worst lower slack ≥6.682) and 60/60 unit tests (worst slack +6.369); Theorem 2.6's outer CDT bound verified via the combined explicit bound with constants C₁=13.6944, C₂=110.4444 at the paper's β=0.85/α=0.1/γ₀=0.05 config, also 0/840 violations.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 (Section 2.3) requires no assumptions on the data-generating process, combining an outer-level Conformal Decision Theory update for the risk-control parameter lambda_t with an inner-level AdaGrad-FTRL optimization over the threshold c_t (Section 2.3, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Algorithm structure confirmed as outer CDT update (unprojected, Rmk 2.7) plus inner AdaGrad-FTRL solved exactly via bisection; one fixed hyperparameter setting controlled CVaR to within [0.00019, 0.00067] across 7/7 structurally distinct DGPs including a no-mean Cauchy-like source and a λ-aware adversary, with zero retuning. The boundedness and feasibility stress tests confirm these are load-bearing technical conditions the paper itself states, but no process-level DGP assumption (i.i.d., stationarity, mixing, moments) is required.

claims.claim: On LLM toxicity control using RealToxicityPrompts and the Jigsaw Unintended Bias dataset with Llama 3.2-3B under uniform, adversarial tail-thickening, and adversarial-jump sampling regimes, RUCC maintains the target CVaR level across all regimes while a static lambda-hat baseline calibrated on the first 1000 samples becomes overly conservative or drifts above target (Section 3.1-3.2, Figure 2).

Cross-checked on 197,908 shipped Perspective-API scores (RUCC 107× tighter than static).

ai-sherpa/autoregressive-lm-secretly-ebm.paper_title: Autoregressive Language Models are Secretly Energy-Based Models: Insights into the Lookahead Capabilities of Next-Token Prediction

claims.claim: Proposition 3.2 establishes an exact bijection between autoregressive models (ARMs) and energy-based models (EBMs) in function space, via the mapping q(s_t,y_t) = r(s_t,y_t) for y_t=EOS and r(s_t,y_t)+V_q(s_t⊕y_t) otherwise, such that p^ebm_R(y|x) = p^arm_q(y|x) (Proposition 3.2).
claims.evidence: Over 8,000 random trials (V,T∈[2,7]) brute-forcing all V^T sequences, max abs probability residual |p_EBM−p_ARM|=1.33e-15 and log-partition residual 3.55e-15; bijectivity independently confirmed by round-trip r→q→r' with max diff 1.55e-15 over 500 trials, all at float64 machine precision in the theorem's native tabular domain.

claims.claim: Section 3.3 shows this ARM-EBM bijection corresponds to a special case of the soft Bellman equation from maximum-entropy reinforcement learning, with the soft value function V_q(s_t) capturing implicit lookahead over future tokens (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Over 5,000 trials, algebraic fixed-point residual |B(q*)−q*|=0.0 exactly; synchronous value iteration from two independent random inits converges to identical fixed point (max diff 0.0) in mean 3.92 sweeps; asynchronous random-order (Gauss-Seidel) updates also converge in 100% of trials with residual 0.0, confirming uniqueness despite γ=1.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 proves that minimizing negative log-likelihood over ARM functions and over EBM functions yields identical minima, showing teacher forcing is optimal in function space (Proposition 4.1).
claims.evidence: Over 400 random target distributions, closed-form ARM and EBM NLL minima agree to 1.78e-15, both equal H(p_data); independent gradient descent in each family converges to the same value (gaps ~8e-4); teacher-forcing optimum equals joint optimum to 1.78e-15; uniform/random controls show strictly positive excess NLL (≥0.0185/≥0.0533).

claims.claim: An error bound (Proposition 59) shows that distilling an EBM into an ARM yields KL(p^ebm_R, p^arm_q) ≤ 2T·max|q*(s,y)-q(s,y)|, bounding divergence by sequence length T times the maximum logit approximation error (Proposition 59).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive brute-force exact KL over 6,000 trials × 7 noise scales: 6000/6000 satisfy KL≤2T·max|q*−q| with min margin −1.94e-15 (machine-epsilon at zero, no real violations); independently corroborated by 80-point deterministic grid with 0 violations and worst ratio 0.133.

claims.claim: Converting an EBM to an equivalent ARM representation costs O(V^T) (exponential in sequence length), whereas converting an ARM to an EBM representation costs only O(VT) (linear) (Section on computational trade-offs).
claims.evidence: Instrumented op-counts over 30 configs (V∈{2,3,4,5,8}, T up to 12): EBM→ARM log(ops)-vs-T slope matches ln V within 0.020 (min R²=0.9994) with 0 cell-count mismatches; ARM→EBM cost is exactly (V+1)·T with 0 formula mismatch; ratio reaches 615× at V=3,T=8.

ai-sherpa/autoregressive-lm-secretly-ebm.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical verification of all five claims in the paper's own tabular function-space domain, with thousands of random trials and brute-force exact computations at machine precision. The reproduction is independent (pure NumPy, no official code used) and transparently scoped to the theorem's native setting rather than trained neural-network experiments.

claims.claim: The Most Influential Sets (MIS) problem for estimands with linear-fractional leave-set-out effects is reduced to a one-parameter sequence of top-k selections solved via Dinkelbach's method (Section 3.1, Algorithm 1)
claims.evidence: The logbook implements Dinkelbach's method with scores = w + η·c and verifies against exhaustive enumeration on 60 small instances (n=6,8,10; k=n/2) with 60/60 exact set matches and all objective values matching within 1e-10, confirming the reduction produces globally optimal solutions.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 costs O(n) per iteration and provably terminates in at most M+1 ratio updates, where M is the number of distinct achievable ratio values, returning a globally optimal set (Theorem 1)
claims.evidence: The implementation uses np.argpartition (O(n)) per iteration with vectorized operations; 150/150 small instances match exhaustive optima confirming global optimality; all 150 instances satisfy the M+1 iteration bound; empirical timing at n=1K–1M shows roughly linear scaling (10.5ms→99.5ms for 10× n increase at the upper end), though intermediate scaling ratios are noisy.

claims.claim: Under a uniform-denominator and generated-score-stability assumption, the empirical selection objective uniformly approximates the oracle orthogonal-score objective with o_p(1) error, yielding selection consistency given a separation condition on the ratio gap (Theorem 2)
claims.evidence: The consistency experiment uses a small synthetic setup (n=200, k=10) with a very strong signal (θ=0.3) and extremely low noise (std ≤ 0.02), showing 100% recovery. However, two earlier attempts with different injection methods showed 0% recovery at moderate separation gaps (1.0–2.0), and only gap=5.0 achieved 30/30. The asymptotic o_p(1) claim and the uniform-denominator assumption are not directly tested; this demonstrates the qualitative mechanism but not the theorem's conditions at scale.

claims.evidence: Multiple independent benchmark runs at n=1,000,000 and k=100,000 consistently report median wall-clock times of 39–94ms (well below the 200ms threshold) with 20/20 or 10/10 runs under 200ms. The median iteration count is 4 rather than the claimed 3, a minor discrepancy, but the primary runtime claim is strongly supported.

The warm-start mechanism is correctly implemented and traces MIS across k=1..K. lastmass/repro-mis-icml-2026.overall: The logbook provides concrete evidence supporting the core algorithmic claims: Dinkelbach reduction matches exhaustive search (Claims 1–2), the million-row runtime benchmark is well under 200ms (Claim 4), and the warm-start variant produces correct solutions (Claim 5). claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 shows that enforcing fairness metrics computed only on the accepted (selectively labeled) population is not a sufficient condition for true fairness over the full population (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides a concrete mathematical proof sketch showing that for equality of opportunity, both terms in the accepted-population disparity condition on A_t=1, making both expectations trivially 1 and thus Δ^{A=1}_t = 0 always, which directly supports Proposition 3.1's insufficiency claim.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 decomposes the observed disparity into the true disparity plus an error term depending on group-wise acceptance rates and prediction errors on rejected individuals, Δ̃ₜ = Δₜ + (r¹ₜε¹ₜ − r⁰ₜε⁰ₜ) (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook re-derives the decomposition Δ̃_t = Δ_t + (r¹_t ε¹_t − r⁰_t ε⁰_t) for qualification parity and provides the analogous forms for accuracy parity and equality of opportunity, with the key insight that the bias term involves the interaction of rejection rates and predictor errors on rejected individuals.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.6 gives inverse-propensity-weighting-based bounds that allow true fairness to be guaranteed from observable, selectively-labeled quantities (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides the IPW estimator formula, the generalization bound from Cortes et al. 2010 with Rényi divergence, and the final enforceable conditions (|Δ̃| ≤ ω/2 and ∑ᵢ rⁱ|ε̄ⁱ| ≤ ω/2), constituting a concrete mathematical re-derivation of Theorem 3.6's bounds.

claims.claim: The proposed SELLF algorithm (PPO with advantage regularization on observed disparity plus IPW-trained label predictor and Renyi divergence regularization) achieves 0.03 disparity in the lending environment versus 0.37-0.41 for baseline methods (Section 4, Table 1).
claims.evidence: SELLF was run for 50k steps (vs. paper's 500k) on synthetic data (vs. real FICO), achieving 0.0167 disparity vs. paper's 0.03 and PPO baseline 0.2957 vs. paper's 0.38 — the trend is confirmed but at clearly reduced scale and with proxy data.

claims.claim: In the crime recidivism environment (accuracy parity), SELLF achieves 0.05 disparity versus 0.06-0.13 for competing baselines (Section 5, Table 1).
claims.evidence: SELLF was run for 50k steps on synthetic COMPAS-like data, achieving 0.0209 disparity vs. paper's 0.05 and PPO 0.0946 vs. paper's 0.09 — trend confirmed but at reduced training scale and with synthetic data replacing the real COMPAS dataset.

claims.claim: In the school admission environment (qualification parity), SELLF attains 0.12 disparity, matching the POCAR Oracle baseline that has access to true labels (Section 5, Table 1, Figures 3-5).
claims.evidence: SELLF was run for 50k steps on synthetic ENEM-like data, achieving 0.0139 vs. paper's 0.12, but PPO also achieved very low disparity (0.0176 vs. paper's 0.15), suggesting the synthetic data lacks the group imbalance of the real dataset and weakens the comparison to the POCAR Oracle baseline.

amkkk/long-term-fairness-selective-label.overall: The logbook provides sound mathematical re-derivations of the three theoretical claims (Proposition 3.1, Theorem 3.2, Theorem 3.6), but all three empirical claims were tested only at toy scale (50k vs. 500k steps) with synthetic data replacing the real FICO, COMPAS, and ENEM datasets, confirming trends but not fully reproducing the paper's experimental results.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 establishes the scalar-identity case, showing SSMs with state matrices A_t = a_t I_N are equivalent to 1-semiseparable masked attention with a causal mask (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: 900 runs of scalar-identity SSM recurrence vs. masked attention show max error 1.07e-14 with zero failures across T∈{20,50,100} and multiple decay values; 200 random diagonal SSM cases (N=1..7, T=10..128) confirm recurrence≈attention to 7.1e-15 with off-diagonal cut rank exactly N in 200/200 cases; QK^T factorization verified to 1.78e-15 over 100 cases.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 gives a necessary and sufficient condition for an N-dimensional SSM to admit a 1-semiseparable masked-attention dual: its corresponding N-semiseparable matrix must have diagonal blocks each containing at most N new columns (Section 4.4, Definition 4.2).
claims.evidence: The first run's exhaustive 5×5 binary test showed the constructive dual succeeding in only 6/888 cases (N=1) and 6/8016 cases (N=2), indicating a broken or incomplete implementation of the biconditional construction. The second run abandoned the Theorem 4.1 condition entirely, only checking that diagonal SSM masks have semiseparable order ≤ N (which is Claim 1's extension, not the theorem's necessary-and-sufficient biconditional). The logbook itself discloses that the full biconditional was not reproduced.

claims.claim: General diagonal SSMs are shown to preserve the same O(NTd) training complexity as the scalar-identity case (Algorithm 1) while supporting richer, per-channel dynamics (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Exact FLOP count 4·N·T·d confirmed for three configurations; timing comparison shows recurrence scaling linearly (0.00037s→0.0097s for T=150→2400) while explicit attention scales quadratically (0.056s→45.5s), with ratio growing from 151x to 4674x; 200 random scalar-identity masks all have semiseparable order 1, and 200 random diagonal SSM masks have order up to N (N=1..5), confirming richer per-channel dynamics. Note: the witness matrix I4+E[3,1] test expected order 2 but measured order 1, an unexplained discrepancy, but the broader dynamics claim is supported by the 200-case sweep.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 proves the equivalence between N-semiseparable matrices and N-SSS (sequentially semiseparable) representable matrices (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: The Proposition 4.1 test generates matrices as M = L ∘ (QK^T) with Q,K ∈ ℝ^{T×N} and checks that semiseparable order ≤ N, which is trivially true by construction (rank of any submatrix of QK^T is at most N). This only checks one direction (N-SSS → N-SS) and is circular; the converse direction (N-SS → N-SSS representable) is never tested, and no SSS representation is actually constructed or verified.

claims.claim: Section 5 demonstrates a limitation: softmax attention is incompatible with the semiseparable-matrix duality framework due to rank explosion, and general (non-diagonal) SSMs may lack any attention dual despite having low state dimension (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The softmax rank explosion part is well-supported: causal softmax attention matrices are near-full-rank (97-100% of T) across T=5..100 and d_k=4..64, confirming incompatibility with low-rank semiseparable structure. However, the second part of the claim—that general non-diagonal SSMs may lack any attention dual despite low state dimension—is never addressed; no experiment with non-diagonal SSMs was conducted.

lastmass/repro-ssd-duality-icml-2026.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence for the scalar-identity and diagonal SSM-attention duality equivalences (Claims 1, 3) and the softmax rank explosion phenomenon, but fails to properly verify Theorem 4.1's biconditional condition (Claim 2), Proposition 4.1's two-way equivalence (Claim 4), or the non-diagonal SSM limitation (Claim 5), leaving three of five claims inconclusive.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 establishes the scalar-identity case, showing SSMs with state matrices A_t = a_t I_N are equivalent to 1-semiseparable masked attention with a causal mask (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Part A directly tests Proposition 3.1's scalar-identity equivalence: 9,000 runs (1,000 seeds × T∈{20,50,100} × a∈{0.5,0.8,0.95}) comparing the SSM recurrence x_t = a·x_{t-1} + b·u_t, y_t = c·x_t against 1-SS masked attention y = c·b·(M@u) with M[t,s]=a^(t−s), achieving max|error| = 5.77e-15 (machine precision, zero failures at 1e-12 threshold).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 gives a necessary and sufficient condition for an N-dimensional SSM to admit a 1-semiseparable masked-attention dual: its corresponding N-semiseparable matrix must have diagonal blocks each containing at most N new columns (Section 4.4, Definition 4.2).
claims.evidence: Both directions of Theorem 4.1 are tested at non-trivial scale: the necessary direction passes 60/60 cases (T up to 512, N up to 16, genuine dual constructions checked for block/new-column bounds), the sufficient direction passes 32/32 cases via independent implementation of Proposition 4.2's constructive proof (max reconstruction error 3.04e-10), and the impossibility direction confirms Proposition 5.1's counterexample has new-column count exactly T−1 at T from 8 to 512.

claims.claim: General diagonal SSMs are shown to preserve the same O(NTd) training complexity as the scalar-identity case (Algorithm 1) while supporting richer, per-channel dynamics (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Part A confirms Algorithm 1's operation count equals exactly 4·N·T·d at all four tested (N,T,d) configurations (e.g., (4,6,3)→288=288, (8,12,5)→1920=1920), and Part B's wall-clock timing sweep at T∈{150,…,2400}, N=4, d=16 yields log-log slopes 0.962 (recurrence, theory 1.0) vs 2.066 (attention, theory 2.0) with 82.98× speedup at T=2400, demonstrating O(NTd) vs O(T²) scaling.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 proves the equivalence between N-semiseparable matrices and N-SSS (sequentially semiseparable) representable matrices (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: No experiment in the logbook addresses Proposition 4.1's equivalence between N-semiseparable matrices and N-SSS (sequentially semiseparable) representable matrices; the logbook's Claim 3 page tests Theorem 4.1 and Propositions 4.2 and 5.1, but Proposition 4.1 specifically is never mentioned or tested.

claims.claim: Section 5 demonstrates a limitation: softmax attention is incompatible with the semiseparable-matrix duality framework due to rank explosion, and general (non-diagonal) SSMs may lack any attention dual despite having low state dimension (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The impossibility component is directly tested: Proposition 5.1's M = I_T + E_{T,1} (a 2-SS matrix from a 2-dimensional-state SSM) is confirmed to have new-column count exactly T−1 at every T from 8 to 512, certifying no bounded-width 1-SS dual exists when T−1 > N (32/35 (T,N) combinations). However, the softmax-attention rank-explosion incompatibility claim is not separately tested.

Crusadersk/icml26-structured-state-space.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical corroboration for Claims 1, 2, 3, and the impossibility half of Claim 5 via independent NumPy implementations with thousands of random instances and machine-precision agreement, at reasonable scale for algebraic identity verification. Claim 4 (Proposition 4.1, N-SSS equivalence) is entirely unaddressed, and the softmax-incompatibility half of Claim 5 lacks any experimental test.

Crusadersk/icml26-noisy-power-method-rep.paper_title: Improved Analysis of the Accelerated Noisy Power Method with Applications to Decentralized PCA

claims.claim: Theorem 2.2 establishes accelerated convergence for the Accelerated Noisy Power Method under a noise magnitude condition that scales as Δ_k·ε rather than the stricter Δ_k·ε^μ requirement of prior work (Xu, 2023) (Section 2, Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: On d=600, k=8 synthetic instances matching the paper's App. E.1 recipe, measured log-log slopes of iteration complexity are -0.518 for ANPM (theory -0.5, R²=0.998) and -1.009 for NPM (theory -1.0, R²=1.0); constant-magnitude adversarial noise at 215x-873x above Xu(2023)'s admissible decaying bound still achieves the accelerated rate; momentum sweep confirms monotonic improvement toward β* and complete failure at β_c.

claims.claim: Theorems 2.4 and 2.5 prove that the noise conditions on the orthogonal component ||U_-k^T Ξ_t||_2 and parallel component ||U_k^T Ξ_t||_2 (Equations 3-4) cannot be relaxed without breaking the accelerated convergence guarantee (Section 2, Theorems 2.4-2.5).
claims.evidence: Condition (3) tightness is demonstrated with a sharp convergence/failure transition at noise multiplier c≈1 (Part B), and worst-case optimality is supported by lower-bound scaling at -0.506 (R²=0.9999) matching the upper bound. However, the logbook's own construction for condition (4) tightness (Theorem 2.5) is provably incapable of exhibiting a failure mode and is explicitly disclosed as not reproduced, leaving one of the two theorems' tightness claims unaddressed.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 introduces ADePM, applying the improved ANPM analysis to decentralized PCA via an accelerated gossip protocol (Algorithm 1), achieving convergence rate O(sqrt(λ_k/(λ_k-λ_{k+1})) log(...)) with communication cost O(1/sqrt(γ_W) log(...)) comparable to non-accelerated decentralized methods (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: On a 10-agent synthetic decentralized PCA setup (d=50, ring+chord graph, γ_W=0.395), ADePM reaches the target in 17-19 outer iterations vs 54 for DePM at identical gossip rounds L across L∈{5,10,20,40,80}, yielding a stable 2.8-3.2x speedup and strictly lower total communication (comm ratio 0.315), directly supporting the accelerated rate at comparable communication cost.

claims.claim: Section 3.1 shows the accelerated gossip subroutine attains O~(1/sqrt(γ_W)) mixing versus the O~(1/γ_W) rate of standard (non-accelerated) gossip (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook tests ADePM on a single graph topology with γ_W=0.395 and does not vary the spectral gap to measure gossip mixing time scaling; no direct experimental evidence isolates the O~(1/√γ_W) vs O~(1/γ_W) mixing rate comparison for the accelerated gossip subroutine.

claims.claim: Section 4 experiments demonstrate that the optimal momentum parameter β* = λ_{k+1}^2/4 yields a square-root speedup over non-accelerated decentralized PCA methods, and that ADePM substantially outperforms DePM and DeEPCA baselines on real datasets (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The β*=λ_{k+1}²/4 optimality and square-root speedup are verified on synthetic data (momentum sweep: 53 iters at β* vs 518 at β=0; speedup growing 3x→29.5x as gap shrinks), and ADePM outperforms DePM 2.8-3.2x on synthetic data. However, the paper's real datasets (Digits, Ego-Facebook, Fed-Heart-Disease) are not used, and the DeEPCA comparison is mixed (DeEPCA is L-independent and achieves better accuracy at low L), so the full Section 4 claim is not reproduced at the paper's scale and data.

Crusadersk/icml26-noisy-power-method-rep.overall: The logbook provides strong, concrete numerical evidence for the core theoretical scaling claims (ANPM Δ_k^{-1/2} rate, milder noise conditions, decentralized accelerated convergence at comparable communication cost) on synthetic instances at reduced but non-trivial scale. However, the tightness of condition (4) is not reproduced, the gossip mixing-rate scaling is not directly tested, and the real-dataset experiments from Section 4 are entirely replaced by synthetic proxies.

lastmass/repro-tuf-q-learning-icml-2026.paper_title: The Role of Target Update Frequencies in Q-Learning

claims.claim: Periodic (target-network) Q-learning is formalized as a nested optimization with outer Bellman iterations and an inner SGD loop with decreasing step size α_n^(k) = 2/[ξ(k+s)] (Section 3, Theorem 4.5).
claims.evidence: The Theorem 4.5 Monte Carlo test (100 trajectories, K=50000) shows the bound holds at all checkpoints with decay slope -1.0032 vs theoretical -1.0, but the empirical MSE values are identical across γ∈{0.7,0.9,0.95} to 10 decimal places (e.g., 1.2916609758 at k=5 for all γ), strongly suggesting the simulation does not correctly vary γ. The formalization claim (nested optimization structure) is not independently verified.

claims.claim: With a constant target update frequency, the sample complexity to reach accuracy ε scales as O(log((1-γ)^-1 ε^-1)) / [ξ^2(1-γ)^4 ε^2 log(2(1+γ)^-1)], incurring an extra logarithmic factor in 1/ε (Theorem 1.1, Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: cost_formula_check.py evaluates the paper's own N(ε), K(ε) formulas and finds R²=0.997 for the ratio vs log(1/ε), but this is a circular check of the paper's own derived expressions, not an independent verification of Theorem 5.1. The GridWorld sweep data does not demonstrate the claimed scaling difference between schedules.

claims.claim: A geometrically increasing target update frequency schedule of order γ^{-2n/3} achieves sample complexity O(1) / [ξ^2(1-γ)^5 ε^2], removing the logarithmic dependence on ε present under constant schedules (Theorem 1.1, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: geometric_check.py confirms K_n = K0·γ^{-2n/3} grows at the predicted rate (R²=1.0), but this is tautological by construction. The cost formula comparison is circular (uses paper's own formulas). The sweep.json data shows both fixed and ICQL schedules produce nearly identical bias curves converging to zero after 7 outer loops, failing to demonstrate the claimed sample complexity advantage empirically.

claims.claim: GridWorld experiments show that small constant target update frequencies plateau at a high bias early in training while large constant frequencies converge slowly, whereas an increasing schedule avoids both failure modes (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The Claim 4 page is empty. The sweep.json data uses deterministic expected updates (explicitly disclosed: 'We use expected (deterministic) inner-loop updates'), not stochastic sampling. All K0 values (1000, 10000, 100000) and both schedules converge to zero bias after 7 outer loops, showing no evidence of the claimed failure modes (small frequencies plateauing, large frequencies converging slowly).

claims.claim: Lunar Lander and GridWorld experiments demonstrate that an increasing target update schedule stabilizes learning compared to constant-frequency baselines (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states 'LunarLander experiments (Figure 1) not reproduced.' The GridWorld experiments use deterministic updates and show no stabilization difference between schedules, as both fixed and ICQL converge identically.

lastmass/repro-tuf-q-learning-icml-2026.overall: The logbook primarily evaluates the paper's own derived formulas numerically (a circular sanity check) and runs limited GridWorld experiments using deterministic rather than stochastic updates, which cannot reproduce the claimed bias plateau and stabilization phenomena. No Lunar Lander experiments were run, and the key experimental figures (Figure 1, Figure 2) were not reproduced.

claims.claim: In the zero-temperature (hardmax) limit of self-attention dynamics with negative-definite key-query interaction, token updates coincide with a Frank-Wolfe step on a quadratic objective over the convex hull of the tokens, and Theorem 3.1 gives a linear convergence rate bound J^t(x_i^{t+1}) ≤ (2/(t+1))·λ_max(B_0)·diam(K^0)^2 (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Three independent code paths over 576 configurations (d∈{2,3,5,8}, n∈{6,8,10,12}) confirm the hardmax-argmax equals the FW LMO: exact 0.0 residual between sign-convention paths and 8.9e-16 residual against an independent scipy.linprog solve over the continuous convex hull; Theorem 3.1's rate bound holds with 0/4800 violations (worst ratio 0.0625).

claims.claim: When the key-query matrix is positive definite, Theorem 4.2 shows super-exponential convergence of tokens to vertices, and Proposition 4.5 shows the induced cell structure coincides with B-norm Voronoi cells when vertices have equal norm (Section 4, Theorem 4.2, Proposition 4.5).
claims.evidence: Proposition 4.5's dominance-cell = B-norm Voronoi-cell equivalence shows 0/5600 label mismatches across κ=3–10 and condition numbers 1–8; Theorem 4.2's constant-γ exponential rate matches log(1-γ) to 1.5e-5 relative error (R²=1.0, 12 configs) and the increasing-schedule super-exponential decay matches exp(-a·t(t+1)/2) to 9.6e-9 relative error with clear contrast against plain-exponential fit (R²≤0.939).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.8 establishes well-posedness of the singular ODE limit governing the hardmax dynamics (Section 4, Theorem 4.8, Equation 4.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook contains no experiment, simulation, or numerical check addressing Theorem 4.8 or the well-posedness of the singular ODE limit (Equation 4.4); this claim is never mentioned or tested anywhere in the reproduction.

claims.claim: At finite inverse temperature β, Theorem 5.2 shows interior particles reach near-vertex configurations in O(1) steps with high probability, while Theorem 5.4 shows these metastable configurations persist for exponentially long times (on the order of e^β steps) before eventual collapse to a single cluster (Section 5, Theorem 5.2, Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: Phase 1 clustering shows T₁ in 19–31 steps across β∈[16,128] (8× range), consistent with O(1) and matching the β≥β* threshold; Phase 2 trapping-time slopes match the theoretical gap 1-cos(2π/κ) to ≤2% error (R²>0.999) across κ=3,4,5,6, cross-validated against literal Monte-Carlo simulation of the categorical chain (worst 5% relative error, 6000 reps/config).

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 shows the argmax operation generically produces a singleton, and Lemma 2.2 shows the convex hull of tokens shrinks under step sizes γ^t ∈ (0,1), underpinning the Frank-Wolfe reformulation of hardmax attention (Section 2, Lemma 2.1, Lemma 2.2).
claims.evidence: While the LP check in Claim 1 indirectly shows the argmax always concentrates on a single vertex (0 mass off top vertex across 576 configs), and the FW dynamics implicitly rely on convex-hull invariance, the logbook never explicitly tests Lemma 2.1's generic-singleton property or Lemma 2.2's convex-hull shrinkage as standalone claims with dedicated measurements.

Crusadersk/icml26-frank-wolfe-attention-.overall: The logbook provides concrete, independently-cross-checked numerical evidence supporting Claims 1, 2, and 4 (Theorems 3.1, 4.2/4.5, 5.2/5.4) at small but mathematically sufficient scale, but does not address Claim 3 (Theorem 4.8) at all and only indirectly touches Claim 5 (Lemmas 2.1/2.2) without dedicated tests.

neonforestmist/randomized-feasibility-ad.paper_title: Randomized Feasibility Methods for Constrained Optimization with Adaptive Step Sizes

claims.claim: Proposes Algorithm 2, a Gradient Method with Randomized Feasibility using an adaptive Polyak-type stepsize, and proves linear convergence in expectation to a prescribed tolerance ε for strongly convex, Lipschitz-smooth objectives, with iteration complexity O(log(1/ε)) (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: The detailed page reports 30 independent trials on a QCQP (d=36, n=640) with 300 outer iterations and 192 feasibility updates, achieving final mean error 0.000367 (below prescribed tolerance 0.02) with log-linear slope -0.061 (R2=0.989); the negative control (Polyak denominator ×100) yields error 0.0633 above tolerance, confirming the algorithm-specific mechanism.

claims.claim: Introduces Algorithm 3, DoWS (Distance over Weighted Subgradients) with Randomized Feasibility, a parameter-free adaptive-stepsize method for convex possibly-nonsmooth objectives, proving an O(1/√T) worst-case convergence rate in expectation (Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: DoWS is executed on a genuinely nonsmooth L1 objective across horizons T=25–800, with log-log slope -0.691 (R2=0.994) and sqrt(T)×error bounded and decreasing (0.036→0.018); the mutation replacing sqrt(p_k) with p_k yields 1.6× larger error at T=800, confirming the prescribed denominator matters.

claims.claim: Introduces Algorithm 4, T-DoWS (Tamed DoWS), which removes the requirement that the constraint set Y be bounded, retaining an O(1/√T) rate up to logarithmic factors (Theorem 5.5).
claims.evidence: The only evidence page for Claim 3 reports 'clipped(c=2) final MSE 28.1015' versus baseline 0.1425, which does not demonstrate T-DoWS convergence on an unbounded constraint set or an O(1/√T) rate; no experiment isolating T-DoWS on unbounded Y is presented.

claims.claim: Proves (Lemma 3.1) that infeasibility of iterates under the randomized feasibility update decreases geometrically almost surely with the number of feasibility updates, without requiring compactness of Y.
claims.evidence: 120 independently seeded paths on a QCQP (n=10, m=1000) with 3000 feasibility updates show infeasibility decreasing from 3.199 to 1.19e-49, with log-linear slope -0.032 (R2=0.999) and 100% of paths below 1e-12; the beta=0 negative control shows exactly zero contraction (factor 1.0).

claims.claim: Validates the theory on quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP) simulations under strongly convex and convex objectives with known/unknown optimal value f*, confirming predicted function-value decay and geometric infeasibility reduction (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The Claim 5 evidence page reports a concentration bound proxy (max|S_t|/√t=2.776) and parameter error (0.0693), which do not address QCQP function-value decay or geometric infeasibility reduction as in Figure 1; while related evidence appears under Claims 1 and 4, no page demonstrates both strongly convex and convex QCQP cases with known/unknown f* together.

claims.claim: Evaluates Algorithms 3 and 4 against a primal-dual baseline on SVM classification with three real datasets (Banknote Authentication, Breast Cancer Wisconsin, MNIST 3-vs-5), comparing test misclassification error (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The Claim 6 evidence page reports least-squares MSE on synthetic data of sizes 64–512 and a pure-noise control, with no mention of SVM classification, the three real datasets (Banknote, Breast Cancer, MNIST 3-vs-5), Algorithms 3/4 versus a primal-dual baseline, or test misclassification error.

neonforestmist/randomized-feasibility-ad.overall: The logbook provides rigorous experimental evidence with proper negative controls for three theoretical claims (linear convergence of Algorithm 2, O(1/√T) rate of DoWS, and geometric infeasibility decrease of Lemma 3.1), but provides no relevant evidence for T-DoWS on unbounded sets (Claim 3), the Figure 1 QCQP validation (Claim 5), or the SVM experiments on real datasets (Claim 6).

amkkk/outcome-aware-spectral-feature-lea.paper_title: Outcome-Aware Spectral Feature Learning for Instrumental Variable Regression

claims.claim: The proposed augmented spectral feature learning loss (Eq. 4-5) modifies the standard SpecIV loss (Eq. 3) by incorporating an outcome-aware, augmented operator T_delta so that learned features are informed by the downstream causal outcome rather than only the instrument-treatment spectral structure (Section 3, Eq. 3-5).
claims.evidence: The augmented loss is implemented in speciv_core.py:63-115 and tested on a 1D synthetic IV setup (5000 samples, 5 seeds, d_feat=8, 3000 steps), but results are non-monotonic across delta values (delta=1.0 MSE 1.317 vs delta=0 MSE 0.331), only partially supporting the claim at toy scale.

claims.claim: Proposition 1 establishes a formal connection between the augmented loss and a low-rank approximation of the augmented operator, justifying why outcome-awareness corrects for spectral misalignment between the true causal function and the dominant singular functions of the un-augmented operator (Section 3, Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: Proposition 1 is restated but no independent mathematical verification or re-derivation is provided; the logbook merely asserts 'Theory verified' without checking the low-rank approximation connection numerically or algebraically.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 provides a non-asymptotic error bound for the resulting two-stage least squares (2SLS) estimator using the learned outcome-aware features (Section 4, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Theorem 1 is stated informally but the logbook explicitly notes the bound is 'not numerically computable from our toy experiments' and provides no independent proof verification; only an untrusted assertion of 'Theory verified' is given.

claims.claim: On synthetic data with controlled spectral misalignment, relative MSE is shown to improve as the balancing hyperparameter delta increases, illustrating the method's robustness to the target causal function being poorly represented by the top singular functions (Figure 2, Section 6.1).
claims.evidence: Two synthetic experiments at toy scale (5000 samples, 5 seeds, 1D) show mixed results: delta=0.5 improves median MSE in both setups, but delta=1.0 and delta=3.0 are worse than delta=0, contradicting the paper's claimed monotonic improvement with increasing delta.

claims.claim: The method is evaluated on the dSprites image-based IV benchmark using a newly introduced, more challenging structural function designed to induce spectral misalignment, comparing against the old and new structural functions (Figure 3, Section 6.2).
claims.evidence: The dSprites dataset pipeline was unavailable; a synthetic 64x64 proxy was used instead at 2000 samples with 3 seeds, showing 'high variance and no reliable advantage for delta>0' — the actual dSprites benchmark was never run.

claims.claim: The approach is additionally validated in an off-policy evaluation (OPE) reinforcement learning setting, demonstrating applicability beyond standard IV regression benchmarks (Section 6.3).
claims.evidence: The OPE reinforcement learning experiment (Section 6.3) is never mentioned or addressed anywhere in the logbook.

amkkk/outcome-aware-spectral-feature-lea.overall: This logbook provides a toy-scale implementation of the augmented spectral loss and runs small synthetic experiments with mixed, non-monotonic results that only partially support the paper's claims. The dSprites benchmark and OPE experiments were never reproduced, and the theoretical results (Proposition 1, Theorem 1) are only restated without independent verification.

amkkk/svrg-and-beyond-via-posterior-corr.paper_title: SVRG and Beyond via Posterior Correction

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows that applying posterior correction with an isotropic-Gaussian posterior family reduces exactly to the standard SVRG gradient update, and Theorem 2 proves SVRG is equivalent to VSGD-PoCo in the limit of zero sampling noise.
claims.evidence: An independent NumPy implementation compared SVRG (Alg. 1) against VSGD-PoCo with epsilon=0 (Alg. 3) step-by-step on 48 randomized finite-sum quadratic problems over 2112 trajectory steps, achieving max absolute error of 0.0, directly confirming exact algorithmic equivalence.

claims.claim: Using full-covariance Gaussian posteriors yields a Newton-like variance-reduced extension (VON-PoCo) with a novel Hessian correction term H̄_out\i(m_in − m_out) not present in prior variance-reduced Newton methods.
claims.evidence: Theorem 3 was audited against direct natural-parameter correction on deterministic quadratic problems with max mean abs error of 1.55e-15, and disabling the Hessian transport term produced a median gap of 0.075, confirming the term exists and materially changes the update; the official IVON-PoCoMo implementation matched an independent NumPy transcription with max param abs error of 0.0.

claims.claim: Using diagonal-covariance Gaussian posteriors with mega-batches and momentum yields an Adam-like extension (IVON-PoCoMo) suitable for transformer pretraining, which achieves 17.4 validation perplexity on GPT-2 125M pretrained on 50B tokens, versus 18.0 for IVON and 18.4 for AdamW (Section 4.3, Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: The key optimizer IVON-PoCoMo was never run at any scale due to an integration issue; the toy Shakespeare experiment (3.2M params, 200 steps) only ran AdamW and IVON, and the full GPT-2 125M / 50B-token experiment was not attempted, so the central empirical claim is unaddressed.

claims.claim: The variance-reduced methods show consistent gains in finetuning across ViT-B/32, Qwen2.5, and Llama-3.1 (Table 1) and in ResNet-50/ImageNet and ResNet-20/CIFAR-10 image classification, particularly when learning rates are not annealed to zero (Figures 4-5).

vissutagunawan/tn00ERVdgL.paper_title: Muon in Associative Memory Learning: Training Dynamics and Scaling Laws

claims.claim: In the noiseless setting, Muon achieves loss L(t) decaying exponentially as K·e^{-(1+o_K(1))t}, versus gradient descent's L(t) ≍ K/t, giving an exponential-vs-polynomial speedup (Theorem 4.1, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: At the paper's own K=100, M=C=10, eta=1 config, GD's t·L converges to 99.14 (predicted K=100) with log-log slope -1.004, while Muon's fitted decay rate is 1.00007 with L/(K·e^{-t})→0.985; time-to-eps over 7 orders of magnitude confirms GD needs ~1M steps vs Muon's 14 at eps=1e-4, and the K-sweep (100→10^6) shows the o_K(1) uniformity ratio vanishing to 1.00004.

claims.claim: Under label noise with power-law frequency decay p̃ᵢ ∝ i^{-β}, GD's excess loss is lower-bounded by Ω̃(log K / T^{1-1/β}) while Muon's is upper-bounded by Õ((log K/T)^2), yielding a steeper scaling-law exponent for Muon (Theorem 5.7, Theorem 5.8).
claims.evidence: GD's excess-risk exponent matches 1-1/β across β∈{1.25,1.5,2,3} (measured 0.218, 0.336, 0.500, 0.650 vs predicted 0.200, 0.333, 0.500, 0.667), grounded by the per-group mechanism (rate∝p_i, R=0.998); Muon's plateau exponent is ~1.94-1.96 and β-independent (predicted 2), confirming the steeper scaling-law exponent and its widening advantage as β→1.

claims.claim: Under label noise, Muon exhibits an Ω(C)-fold speedup over GD, where C is the size of each knowledge group in the associative memory model (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook does not directly test the Ω(C)-fold speedup claim under label noise as a function of group size C. Claim 1's speedup measurements are noiseless, and Claim 2's experiments measure scaling exponents rather than C-dependent speedup ratios in the noisy setting.

claims.claim: Muon is interpreted as an implicit matrix preconditioner arising from adaptive task alignment, distinguished from coordinate-wise SignGD by its exploitation of block-symmetric gradient structure; a Task-Representation-Aligned SignGD (TRA-SignGD) variant with oracle embedding access is shown to match Muon's performance (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Exact identities hold to machine precision: G_t = -(P-P̂_t) (0.0), msgn(G_t)=-msgn(P-P̂_t) (0.0); Prop 6.1 deviation ||msgn(P-P̂)-I||_max = 0.022 (bound 1.1) with K-sweep confirming o_K(1) decay ~1/C; Remark 6.2 contrast directions fixed to 2.6e-15; Thm 6.3 Muon@2η vs TRA-SignGD@η trajectories coincide (max|ΔL|=6.4e-4); vanilla SignGD control fails (task-space distance 11.2, loss 1.65 vs Muon's 0.80).

claims.claim: On imbalanced MNIST and LLaMA pre-training experiments, Muon shows a steeper power-law decay slope than SGD across multiple data budgets, empirically confirming the derived scaling laws (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states 'No LLaMA pre-training (Fig. 2)' and 'No imbalanced-MNIST MLP (Fig. 1c/d)' were run, as these require GPU-cluster resources. The empirical scaling-law confirmation on real datasets was never attempted.

vissutagunawan/tn00ERVdgL.overall: The logbook provides strong clean-room verification of the paper's theoretical claims (exponential vs polynomial convergence, noisy scaling-law exponents, and the preconditioner interpretation) at the associative-memory model's native scale with exact identities and fitted functional forms. However, the Ω(C)-fold noisy speedup claim and the empirical MNIST/LLaMA experiments were not addressed.

vissutagunawan/r3h23Jv26a.paper_title: Questioning the Coverage-Length Metric in Conformal Prediction: When Shorter Intervals Are Not Better

claims.claim: The Prejudicial Trick (Algorithm 1) constructs prediction intervals by returning a null (empty or minimal) interval with probability (1-p) and an adjusted conformal interval with probability p, provably preserving valid marginal coverage per Theorem 6 while shrinking average interval length (Section on Prejudicial Trick, Algorithm 1, Theorem 6)
claims.evidence: The logbook implements Algorithm 1 verbatim from the authors' code and shows on the paper's synthetic setup (bias=10, 5 seeds) that PT-VCP produces shorter intervals than VCP in 4/4 grid cells while marginal coverage stays ≥ 1-α (e.g., α=0.1, p=0.96: VCP len 22.894, PT len 22.418, PT coverage 0.905). VCP length matches the paper exactly to 6 significant figures, confirming pipeline fidelity.

claims.claim: On synthetic data, PT applied to Vanilla Conformal Prediction (PT-VCP) reduces average interval length from 22.894 to 22.614 at alpha=0.10 while preserving nominal coverage (Table 1)
claims.evidence: At α=0.10, p=0.96, the reproduction yields VCP length 22.894 (exact match to paper) and PT-VCP length 22.418 (vs paper's 22.614, a 0.196 gap attributable to PT's randomized nature and within the paper's reported PT std of 0.254). PT-VCP coverage is 0.905, preserving nominal 90% coverage. The length reduction direction is confirmed.

claims.claim: On real-world regression benchmarks (including MEPS and BIO), PT-VCP reduces interval length in 9 of 10 datasets while maintaining 90% marginal coverage (Table 2)
claims.evidence: The logbook never reproduces Table 2 (real-world interval length reduction across 10 datasets). It reproduces Tables 1 and 3 only. MEPS-19/20/21 are skipped entirely, and no length-reduction experiments on the 7 open real-world datasets are reported. The claim is not addressed.

claims.claim: Despite valid marginal coverage, the Prejudicial Trick yields highly unstable predictions: Proposition 2 proves its interval stability metric IS(C_PT) = p(1-p)(E(L))^2 > 0, meaning the same input can receive completely different interval outputs across repeated conformal calibration runs (Definition 1, Proposition 2)
claims.evidence: Part A matches the Proposition 4.2 closed form IS = p(1-p)·L_adj² to 0.13% relative error (empirical 25.666 vs closed-form 25.632 over 1000×200 draws), demonstrates the same input returning null intervals ~5% of runs vs wide intervals otherwise, and confirms VCP IS = 0 exactly. Part B reproduces Table 3 on 7 open datasets showing VCP IS = 0 and PT-VCP IS > 0 on all, with bias-consistent datasets matching to ~0.1%.

claims.claim: The proposed Interval Stability metric can flag methods, such as localized conformal prediction, that implicitly exploit PT-like randomness to shrink length, since Proposition 1 shows PT is a special case of localized CP when local scale estimators output extreme values (Definition 1, Proposition 1)
claims.evidence: Part A shows localized CP with a two-point scale estimator produces a length distribution bit-identical to PT (max diff = 0.0e+00 over 200k draws, IS variances equal at 25.697). Part B's blinded detector flags all 5 PT-like methods (including localized-CP with randomized scale and a shorter-average-length PT-in-disguise) with 0 false positives on 3 deterministic methods, achieving 100% detection accuracy.

vissutagunawan/r3h23Jv26a.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies 4 of 5 claims using the authors' verbatim code, with strong quantitative matches for the synthetic Table 1, the Proposition 4.2 closed form, Table 3 interval stability, and the Proposition 3.2 localized-CP↔PT equivalence plus a blinded detector test. Claim 3 (Table 2 real-world length reduction) is never addressed, as the logbook skips Table 2 entirely and omits MEPS datasets.

neonforestmist/mfvi-predictive-variance-.paper_title: Gaussian Mean Field Variational Inference can Overestimate Predictive Variance

claims.claim: MFVI underestimates posterior variance in parameter space but can overestimate predictive variance relative to the exact posterior, with Theorem 3.7 proving that for test points drawn from the training distribution's empirical covariance, MFVI's expected predictive variance exceeds that of the exact posterior (Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports only generic least-squares metrics (structured_mse=0.0026, rel_param_err=0.0088, n=200, d=4) with no computation of MFVI posterior variance, exact posterior variance, or predictive variance comparison as Theorem 3.7 requires. The reported quantities are unrelated to the claim's named concepts.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.6 shows a calibration constraint forcing MFVI to simultaneously underestimate variance in some directions while overestimating in others, with overestimation occurring specifically in directions where training data concentrates (Lemma 3.6).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides the same generic least-squares metrics (structured_mse=0.0027, rel_param_err=0.0073) with no directional variance analysis, no demonstration of simultaneous under/overestimation, and no connection to training data concentration directions as Lemma 3.6 requires.

claims.claim: In a pathological rank-1 training-data subspace scenario, as dimensionality increases the MFVI posterior's predictive variance converges to the prior variance, effectively discarding training information (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports structured_mse=0.0023 and rel_param_err=0.0277 at d=16, but provides no rank-1 subspace construction, no sweep over increasing dimensionality, and no measurement of predictive variance converging to prior variance. The experiment is unrelated to the pathological scenario described.

claims.claim: Temperature-scaled posteriors (cold posteriors, T<1) correct the predictive-variance overestimation and improve in-distribution predictions, while T>1 benefits out-of-distribution performance, offering a novel explanation for the Cold Posterior Effect.
claims.evidence: The logbook reports only structured_mse=0.0022 and rel_param_err=0.0313 with no temperature scaling experiments, no T<1 vs T>1 comparison, no in-distribution vs out-of-distribution evaluation, and no connection to the Cold Posterior Effect.

claims.claim: Experiments on basis function regression and UCI datasets show optimal temperatures below 1 for in-distribution test points and above 1 for out-of-distribution test points, consistent with the theoretical predictions (Section 6, UCI experiments).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports structured_mse=0.0025 and rel_param_err=0.0216 with no basis function regression, no UCI dataset experiments, and no measurement of optimal temperatures for in-distribution or out-of-distribution test points. None of the claim's experimental content is present.

neonforestmist/mfvi-predictive-variance-.overall: This logbook provides no actual evidence for any of the five claims. Every claim page reports identical generic least-squares metrics (structured_mse, rel_param_err) from small synthetic regression experiments that have no connection to MFVI, predictive variance, temperature scaling, UCI datasets, or any method or quantity named in the paper's claims.

amkkk/row-stochastic-matrices-outperform.paper_title: Row-Stochastic Matrices Can Provably Outperform Doubly Stochastic Matrices in Decentralized Learning

claims.claim: In the weighted Hilbert space L²(λ;R^d), the λ-induced row-stochastic mixing matrix W is self-adjoint whereas the doubly stochastic matrix W^ds is not, and this non-self-adjointness introduces additional multiplicative penalty terms (κ_λ > 1 and λ_max² > 1) that amplify consensus error under the doubly stochastic design (Section 5.2, Section 6.2).
claims.evidence: Across 9 configurations (n=10,20,50 × mild/moderate/high heterogeneity), RS matrix self-adjointness confirmed to machine precision (~1e-17) while DS fails (diff 0.038–0.252), with kappa_lambda growing from 1.36 to 3.05 with heterogeneity, directly supporting the penalty-term amplification claim.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.5 gives O(1/T) convergence rates for both row-stochastic and doubly stochastic strategies, but the row-stochastic strategy achieves strictly smaller non-asymptotic consensus error and can converge faster even when its spectral gap is smaller than that of the doubly stochastic strategy (Theorem 6.5).
claims.evidence: Decentralized gradient tracking on synthetic quadratic (n=20, d=10, T=200) shows Strategy II (row-stochastic) achieves 18–25x lower gradient norm and 2–3 orders lower consensus error across all weight configurations, including cases where rho_Lambda > rho_J (RS has smaller spectral gap) yet RS still converges faster.

claims.claim: Theorem 7.1 derives a sufficient condition on the spectral gaps, 1 − ρ_Λ ≥ max{(1+η)κ_λ^(-1/3), λ_max^(-1/2)}(1 − ρ_J), under which the row-stochastic design provably converges strictly faster than the doubly stochastic design (Theorem 7.1).
claims.evidence: 100 random graph/weight configurations (n in [10,30]) tested: the spectral condition was met in 28/100 cases, and in 16/88 cases where Strategy II had a smaller spectral gap (rho_Lambda > rho_J), the condition was still satisfied due to penalty terms, directly confirming the theorem's prediction.

claims.claim: Corollary 7.3 and Algorithm 2 give topology construction guidelines showing that when node degrees scale proportionally with their assigned weights (d_i/d_j matching λ_i/λ_j within bounds set by R), the row-stochastic design outperforms the doubly stochastic design, satisfying a Loewner order condition on the graph Laplacians (Corollary 7.3, Remark 7.4, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 2 pipeline (ScaleToDegrees → HavelHakimiConstruct → MakeConnected) implemented across 9 configurations (n=10–30), producing degree sequences proportional to lambda_i within target ranges, with spectral properties (rho_Lambda) computed for algorithm-constructed vs standard graphs, confirming the topology construction guidelines and degree-weight proportionality condition.

amkkk/row-stochastic-matrices-outperform.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all four theoretical claims through spectral analysis, algebraic verification, and convergence experiments on synthetic decentralized optimization problems with up to n=50 nodes. The reproduction is limited to synthetic quadratics and spectral analysis—no real-world ML training was completed due to a blocked CIFAR-10 experiment—but the evidence directly and consistently supports the paper's theoretical claims.

neonforestmist/two-layer-online-admissio.paper_title: A Two-Layer Framework for Joint Online Configuration Selection and Admission Control

claims.claim: The proposed SP-UCB--OLP algorithm, combining UCB-based exploration over surplus functions with an online-linear-programming admission rule, achieves Õ(√KT) regret for joint configuration selection and admission control over horizon T with K configurations (Theorem 9).

lastmass/repro-rucc-icml-2026.paper_title: Adversarially Robust Control of Conditional Value-at-Risk via Rockafellar-Uryasev Conformal Inference

claims.claim: Theorem 2.2 establishes that the realized empirical CVaR of the Rockafellar-Uryasev conformal inference method (RUCC) is controlled at the target level with an asymptotic conservatism gap of O(1/sqrt(T)), termed the 'Price of Nonlinearity' relative to the O(1/T) rate achievable for linear expected-loss control (Theorem 2.2; Remark 2.3).
claims.evidence: Three synthetic DGPs (adversarial oscillating, iid uniform, paper's hard instance) with T from 200 to 50,000 and 50 trials each (1,200 runs total) show CVaR_hat - alpha is always non-negative and decays with fitted exponents of -1.11, -1.04, and -1.01, all faster than the theoretical O(1/√T) upper bound, confirming the control guarantee.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.4 bounds the inner-level regret of the AdaGrad-FTRL threshold optimization by |max_c Reg_T(c)| <= (3/4) * max{1, beta/(1-beta)} * sqrt(T+1), and Theorem 2.6 shows the outer-level Conformal Decision Theory update keeps the surrogate loss within alpha + O(sqrt(T))/T of the target risk level alpha (Theorem 2.4; Theorem 2.6).
claims.evidence: The experiment tests downstream CVaR control across 5 DGPs at T=20000 but never directly measures the AdaGrad-FTRL regret |max_c Reg_T(c)| or the CDT surrogate loss bound alpha + O(√T)/T; the specific theorem bounds (Theorem 2.4 regret formula, Theorem 2.6 surrogate loss) are not verified by any numerical measurement.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 (Section 2.3) requires no assumptions on the data-generating process, combining an outer-level Conformal Decision Theory update for the risk-control parameter lambda_t with an inner-level AdaGrad-FTRL optimization over the threshold c_t (Section 2.3, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Paired comparison on identical loss sequences shows RUCC controls CVaR within 0.0004 of target under both benign and catastrophic-tail DGPs, while naive ACI (mean-targeting) fails with gaps of +0.721 and -0.098, directly demonstrating the no-assumptions property and the breakdown of linear methods for CVaR.

claims.claim: On LLM toxicity control using RealToxicityPrompts and the Jigsaw Unintended Bias dataset with Llama 3.2-3B under uniform, adversarial tail-thickening, and adversarial-jump sampling regimes, RUCC maintains the target CVaR level across all regimes while a static lambda-hat baseline calibrated on the first 1000 samples becomes overly conservative or drifts above target (Section 3.1-3.2, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly skips the LLM toxicity control experiment (RealToxicityPrompts, Jigsaw, Llama 3.2-3B) due to lack of GPU/dataset budget; no runs on the actual task were conducted.

claims.claim: On a portfolio-management task using S&P 500 and 10-Year Treasury data from 1991-2025 (via yfinance/FRED), evaluated separately on the 1991-2001 stable period, the 2009-2018 crisis-aftermath period, and the full 1991-2025 span, RUCC keeps realized CVaR near the target across multiple market shocks where the static baseline does not (Section 3.3-3.4, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Real S&P 500 data via yfinance is used across the three specified periods (T=2752, 2513, 8784) with CVaR gaps of -0.0071, -0.0038, -0.0022 (all controlled), but the setup is substantially simplified: ^TNX yield proxies the Treasury total-return index, loss scaling is arbitrary (×10 + 0.05), the static baseline comparison central to the claim is not run, and Figure 3 rolling-window visualizations are not reproduced.

lastmass/repro-rucc-icml-2026.overall: The logbook provides meaningful evidence for the core theoretical guarantee (Claim 1) and the distribution-free/no-assumptions property (Claim 3) through 1,450 synthetic runs, but does not directly measure the specific regret bounds of Theorems 2.4/2.6 (Claim 2), entirely skips the LLM toxicity experiment (Claim 4), and only partially addresses the portfolio claim with simplified proxies and no baseline comparison (Claim 5).

amkkk/is-spurious-correlation-removal-al.paper_title: Is Spurious Correlation Removal Always Learnable?

claims.claim: Under the Planted Clique hardness hypothesis (planted cliques of size k = m^(1/2−δ) in random graphs are not recoverable in polynomial time), there exist samplable multi-environment linear-Gaussian instances that are statistically learnable with polynomially many samples via exhaustive search but intractable for any polynomial-time algorithm (Hypothesis 3.1, Theorem 3.8).
claims.evidence: Proof verification is assertion-only (no detailed checking shown). Toy empirical results at d=10,20 actually show screening (polynomial-time) outperforming exhaustive search (1.000 vs 0.889 at d=10; 0.857 vs 0.762 at d=20), which does not support the claimed gap, though the theoretical claim is about existence under a hardness hypothesis and toy-scale results don't directly address it.

claims.claim: A phase transition in label-induced spurious correlation removal occurs at critical sample size n* ∝ k(d−k)/(|E|γ²), where k is the invariant subspace dimension, d the ambient dimension, |E| the number of environments, and γ the environment separation parameter; below n*/2 all estimators fail with constant error while above 2n* estimators achieve error O(k(d−k)/(n|E|γ²)) (Theorem 4.15).
claims.evidence: The table shows error dropping sharply from ~0.85-1.0 below n* to 0.0-0.333 above n* across gamma values 0.05-1.0, consistent with the predicted phase transition, but all experiments are at very small scale on synthetic linear-Gaussian data (n* as low as 16), with no specification of d, k, or |E| values used.

claims.claim: The predicted phase transition is validated empirically: exhaustive search reaches 75% accuracy using up to 27x fewer samples than polynomial-time methods on synthetic instances, and sharp transitions near the predicted critical sample size appear on both synthetic data and ColoredMNIST (Figure 1, Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: The 'ColoredMNIST' results are explicitly labeled as 'synthetic linear-Gaussian, not actual images,' so the real ColoredMNIST validation was never run. The 27x sample reduction claim is asserted but no comparative numbers between exhaustive search and polynomial-time methods are shown to demonstrate this ratio. Only the phase transition table from Claim 2 is reused.

claims.claim: Diversity across environments is necessary for removal to succeed: performance improves sharply once γ > 0, whereas low-diversity settings (γ ≈ 0) show persistent failure, and increasing diversity from 'low' to 'high' substantially improves worst-group accuracy on CelebA and Waterbirds and OOD performance on ColoredMNIST (Figure 2c, Table 2).
claims.evidence: Synthetic results show screening accuracy rising from 0.000 (gamma=0.00) to 1.000 (gamma>=0.50), supporting the diversity necessity pattern, but IRM results are erratic and no experiments on CelebA, Waterbirds, or actual ColoredMNIST were conducted—all datasets explicitly named in the claim were replaced by synthetic proxies.

amkkk/is-spurious-correlation-removal-al.overall: This logbook provides only toy-scale synthetic linear-Gaussian experiments on CPU, with no runs on the real datasets (CelebA, Waterbirds, ColoredMNIST) central to the paper's empirical claims. The phase transition pattern is weakly visible in synthetic data, but the computational gap and diversity claims are at best partially addressed at toy scale, and proof verification is assertion-only.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 proves that allocations produced by weighted empirical risk minimization are monotonically increasing in each user's individual bid, which enables construction of a truthful payment rule via Myerson's Lemma (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The '02-truthful-welfare' page reports 0 monotonicity violations across 38,000 truthful report checks on 80 instances with 10 users using binary 0-1 welfare, which directly tests the monotonicity property, but this is a clearly simplified finite-class setup far below the paper's scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 proves that for L2-regularized linear classifiers, the expected total payments collected by the accuracy auction are O(1), i.e., bounded by a constant independent of the number of samples m (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The '01-payer-scaling' page shows mean payer counts roughly constant (0.50–1.05) across m=100–1600 with fitted log-log exponent 0.005478, supporting O(1) scaling, but sample sizes are modest and payer count is a proxy for total payments rather than a direct measurement.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 proves that k-nearest-neighbor classifiers exhibit Ω(m) expected total payments under label noise, showing that the choice of learning algorithm materially affects auction revenue/payment scaling (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The '01-payer-scaling' page mentions a kNN label-noise control with exponent 0.998298, supporting Ω(m) scaling, but this is a single number mentioned in passing with no dedicated kNN experiment details, setup description, or multiple sample points shown.

claims.evidence: The '02-truthful-welfare' page reports 0 IR violations across 38,000 checks on 80 instances with 10 users, directly testing individual rationality, but on a small simplified finite-class setup rather than at the paper's experimental scale.

claims.claim: Experiments show the number of paying users plateaus quickly as sample size increases across different variance parameter settings, and higher model accuracy is associated with lower payment proportions (Section 7, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The '01-payer-scaling' page shows payer counts plateauing (0.50–1.05) and payer fraction declining from 0.0095 to 0.00044 across m=100–1600, addressing the plateau aspect, but the claim's requirements of varying variance parameters and the accuracy–payment-proportion relationship are not addressed.

claims.claim: Optimizing the accuracy-auction objective against a uniform-allocation baseline yields social welfare improvements of up to 23% with only modest accuracy tradeoffs (Section 7, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The '02-truthful-welfare' page reports 80/80 strict welfare improvements over uniform allocation on 80 instances with 10 users, showing the direction of the claim, but the specific 'up to 23%' quantification and the 'modest accuracy tradeoffs' measurement are entirely absent.

neonforestmist/accuracy-auctions-repro.overall: The logbook contains real but small-scale experimental evidence scattered across topic pages, with the claim pages themselves largely populated by irrelevant bandit/SGD experiments. None of the setups match the paper's experimental scale, and several claims are only partially addressed with key quantitative aspects missing.

Boopster/RgnoWsmYBM.paper_title: A Coin Flip for Safety: LLM Judges Fail to Reliably Measure Adversarial Robustness

claims.claim: Across an audit of 6,642 human-verified labels spanning 4 victim models (Gemma-3-1B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-27B, Qwen-3-32B) and 5 attack methods (Direct Prompting, GCG, GCG-REINFORCE, Best-of-N, PAIR), 4 safety judges (LlamaGuard-3, HarmBench, AegisGuard, JailJudge) are shown to perform only slightly better than random guessing on average (Section 3, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Using the full 6,642-row released dataset balanced to 2,746 rows across all 17 populated attack×model cells, the four-judge balanced mean accuracy is 0.551 (95% behavior CI 0.526–0.575), entirely below a 0.60 near-chance ceiling, with individual judges at 0.514–0.587, directly supporting 'slightly better than random guessing on average.'

claims.claim: ROC analysis shows JailJudge attains AUROC as low as 0.48 (worse than chance) on some attack-model pairs and no better than 0.64 on any attack, demonstrating near-chance discriminative ability under distribution shift (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: JailJudge AUROC on Llama-3.1 across five attacks spans 0.476–0.642 (GCG-R 0.476, GCG 0.642), closely matching the paper's reported floor of 0.48 and ceiling of 0.64, confirming near-chance discriminative ability on specific attack-model pairs.

claims.claim: Judge accuracy varies dramatically across attack-model combinations, with some judges scoring only 45% accuracy on specific attack-victim pairs, close to random guessing (Figure 3, Figure 4).
