michaldobiezynski/repro-a-sketch-and-pro.paper_title: A Sketch-and-Project Analysis of Subsampled Natural Gradient Algorithms

claims.claim: For linear least-squares problems, subsampled natural gradient descent (SNGD) is shown to be directly equivalent to the regularized Kaczmarz method, and SPRING is equivalent to the Nesterov-accelerated regularized Kaczmarz (ARK) method (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: On a non-toy setup (m=200, n=50, k=20, T=120), the logbook independently implements SNG/Kaczmarz and SPRING/ARK update formulas on identical subsample streams and measures max|SNG-Kaczmarz|=0.00e+00 and max|SPRING-ARK|=5.46e-14, confirming both algebraic identities to machine precision.

claims.claim: SNGD converges at rate (1-α)^t where α=λ_min(P̄), while SPRING converges at rate O((1-√(α/β))^t), giving up to a square-root improvement in iteration complexity over SNGD (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: On a controlled orthonormal construction where (1-α) is provably exact (m=8, k=1, α=1/8), the measured SNG per-step factor is 0.8716 vs the paper's 0.8750 (0.4% off). On a diagonal problem (α=0.01235, β=6.0), SPRING reaches 1e-6 in 130 iters vs SNG's 251 (1.9x reduction), with the rate-deficit ratio consistent with sqrt-type acceleration.

claims.claim: For general quadratic losses, SNGD requires the regularization parameter λ to exceed a threshold λ0 to guarantee convergence, and can diverge if regularization is insufficient (Proposition 3).
claims.evidence: The identity γ=1/(1+λ) (Prop 5.3) is reproduced to machine precision (1.1e-15) across multiple dimensions and λ values. On a coupled quadratic at n=60 with 8 seeds, the spectral radius ρ(I−η(F+λI)⁻¹H) decreases monotonically in λ, with divergence below and convergence above a threshold λ0~3e1 matching on 8/8 seeds.

claims.claim: Under an assumption that the regularized projector P̄ shares an eigenbasis with J^T J, SNGD provably outperforms SGD by a factor of k^β when the spectrum of the Jacobian decays polynomially (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: The SVS α formula (eq 29) is validated against brute-force enumeration (exact match: 3.153497e-2). Log-log slopes of α(k) are 1.98, 2.92, 3.91 for s=1,1.5,2, all superlinear and exceeding the eq-(27) lower-bound exponents (1, 2, 3). The SGD linear baseline is asserted from the paper rather than directly simulated, but the superlinear α-scaling mechanism is the core verifiable content.

claims.claim: A unified algorithm (Algorithm 1) captures both SNGD (momentum μ=0) and SPRING (μ∈(0,1)) as momentum-based updates using subsampled Jacobians, enabling single-minibatch convergence guarantees of any batch size.
claims.evidence: Setting μ=0 in the unified Algorithm 1 and comparing to SNG on identical sampling (m=120, n=40, k=15) yields max|diff|=0.00e+00 (exact identity). A batch-size sweep k=1..40 shows SNG converging at every batch size, with residuals descending from 2.3e-4 (k=1) to 1.7e-16 (k=40).

claims.claim: Analysis of SPRING's convergence for general (non-least-squares) quadratic losses is left open as Conjecture 7, despite numerical experiments showing large empirical performance gains over SNGD.
claims.evidence: The open status of Conjecture 6.2 is confirmed by verbatim paper text ('defer the resolution of this conjecture to future works'). Empirical gains are demonstrated two ways: exact SVS rate formulas predict ~1.65x SPRING speedup, and a direct SVS-SPRING vs SVS-SNG simulation at n=24 gives median speedups of 1.42-1.68x at small sample sizes, shrinking to 1.25x at k=8, matching Fig 5's trend.

michaldobiezynski/repro-a-sketch-and-pro.overall: The logbook provides concrete, non-circular numerical evidence supporting all six claims at non-toy scale (n=24-200), with several identities confirmed to machine precision and convergence behavior verified across multiple seeds. The main limitations are that some rate checks use controlled/simplified constructions and the SGD baseline in Claim 4 is asserted rather than directly simulated, but the core mechanisms are genuinely reproduced.

Srishti280992/repro-floating-point-netwo.paper_title: Floating-Point Networks with Automatic Differentiation Can Represent Almost All Floating-Point Functions and Their Gradients

claims.claim: Floating-point networks built from automatic differentiation can represent an arbitrary target floating-point function's values together with an arbitrary, independently chosen gradient on a bounded domain, using at least 9 layers (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Over 512 seeded float32 (z, target_value, target_grad) triples, the AD gradient matched the target bit-exactly in 512/512 cases and value+gradient were simultaneously bit-exact in 492/512; off-domain gradient was zero in 512/512. The 20 value misses arise from float32 rounding in the bias subtraction, but the core independent-gradient mechanism (the paper's novel contribution) is perfectly exact.

claims.claim: This representability result is established for the practical activation functions ReLU, ELU, GELU, Swish, Sigmoid, and tanh (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook only checks a sufficient condition (nonzero power-of-two derivative in [2^-23, 1]) at a single input point per activation for all six activations (6/6 pass), without constructing or testing the full representability network for each activation function. This is a proxy/witness check, not a full reproduction of Theorem 3.1 per activation.

claims.claim: A single floating-point network can produce a gradient that varies with the loss function's derivative, provided that derivative satisfies an antisymmetry condition g*(x,-y) = -g*(x,y) (Theorem 3.2, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Across 141 dyadic incoming derivatives, antisymmetry g*(x,-y)=-g*(x,y) held bit-exactly in 141/141 cases; the AD product differed from the classical chain-rule product in 71/141 cases due to underflow; forward identity was exact in 5/5 test inputs. This concretely demonstrates the decoupling mechanism on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.4 constructs networks that represent the correct function values while completely suppressing the computed gradient to zero (Lemma 3.4, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: ExactIndicator produced exact point-indicator values in 256/256 cases; TripleCancellation yielded exact zero AD gradient in 4096/4096 inputs over [-1000,1000] with max absolute gradient 0.0; the combined ZeroGradIndicator returned zero gradient in 256/256 cases. The destructive control (unsuppressed indicator gradient = 1048576) confirms the cancellation construction causes the suppression.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.5 constructs networks that output zero everywhere while still producing an arbitrary target gradient under automatic differentiation (Lemma 3.5, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: A clean-room scalar circuit (forward: x*2^-80*2^-80 underflows to signed zero before the large factor; reverse AD sees large factor first) produced exact zero forward output in 84/84 settings with exact target AD gradient in 84/84 cases (max_abs_output=0.0). Additionally, the released GradIndicator matched target gradients bit-exactly in 512/512 cases.

claims.claim: The construction exploits the non-associativity of floating-point arithmetic to decouple the computed gradient from the classical chain-rule proportionality that would hold under exact real arithmetic (Section 1.1).
claims.evidence: Over 200,000 random float32 triples, the two parenthesizations (a*b)*c vs a*(b*c) differed bitwise in 56,049 of 153,948 finite cases (36.4%); over 100,000 random incoming derivatives, the AD-style product (y*2^-100)*2^100 broke classical chain-rule proportionality in 43,827 cases (43.8%). Concrete hex witnesses are recorded in the CSV artifact.

Srishti280992/repro-floating-point-netwo.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence on non-toy float32 setups supporting five of six claims, with real PyTorch autograd runs, bit-exact comparisons, and destructive controls. Claim 2 is only addressed via a simplified single-point witness check of a sufficient derivative condition rather than full per-activation construction, making it a toy-level verification.

DineshAI/puNfWfBFNT.paper_title: Causal Representation Learning with Optimal Compression and  Complex Treatments

claims.claim: Lemma 3.2 derives a multi-treatment generalization bound decomposing individualized treatment effect (ITE) error into factual prediction error, representation-level imbalance across treatment arms, and model complexity (Lemma 3.2, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Step 1 of the proof is verified with a symbolic certificate (sympy) and numerically across 7 outcome families with 0 violations, plus extremal tightness at K=2. Steps 2-4 are tested on controlled simulations (held-out R²=0.808 with imbalance term vs -0.016 without) and 9 trained CFR representations (108/108 TV-IPM bounds hold, 54 fail when IPM deleted), but the constants C_F, C_B, C_C remain unidentified and the setup is not the paper's actual neural experiment.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 provides a finite-sample deviation bound on the optimal balancing weight, |α̂_S - α^bd(n)| <= r_S(n,δ,K)/κ_S, converting hyperparameter selection into a statistical estimation problem (Theorem 3.5, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: An explicitly constructed bounded profile (α₀=1, κ=0.5, compact range [0,2]) satisfies Assumption 3.4 and verifies |α̂−α₀|≤r/κ with 0 violations across 27 cells and 20,000 replicates, with a κ=0 control that correctly rejects. However, this is a deliberately constructed synthetic profile, not the paper's actual neural setup or a general proof.

claims.claim: Treatment Aggregation via the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) achieves O(1) computational complexity and a deviation term r_agg = O(sqrt(log(1/δ)/n)) independent of the number of treatments K, versus O(K^2) for pairwise balancing and O(K) for one-vs-all (Section 2).
claims.evidence: Operation counts are exact by construction (pair=K(K-1)/2, ova=K, agg=1), wall-clock timing shows flat aggregation at 0.007s across K=4,20,50 while pairwise grows to 0.51s, and concentration scaling shows agg variance decreasing as K^(-0.89). The O(1)-in-K claim is directly and concretely supported.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.8 shows the estimated balancing weight is asymptotically normal, with variance scaling as Θ(K^4/n) for pairwise balancing, Θ(K^2/n) for one-vs-all, and Θ(1/n) for the treatment aggregation strategy (Theorem 3.8, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: The same explicit bounded construction yields analytic variance limits (pair→0.25, ova→1, agg→4) matching Θ(K⁴/n), Θ(K²/n), Θ(1/n), with Monte Carlo at n=16M confirming within 1.5% and KS statistics ~0.005. A boundary control correctly produces non-normal mass. However, this is a specific constructed profile with fixed positive dependence ρ=0.25, not the paper's actual neural estimator.

claims.claim: At K=20 treatments, pairwise balancing becomes unstable (PEHE exceeding 1.3 under strong regularization) while the aggregation strategy maintains competitive accuracy of approximately 1.0 across regularization levels, empirically confirming its O(1) scalability (Section 4.2, Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: At K=20, N=1500, pair PEHE degrades 16.91→20.46 (+21%) while agg stays flat at 16.90 (<0.1% change), reproducing the qualitative pattern. However, absolute PEHE values are ~21× the paper's scale due to an outcome normalization difference, and no convention reproduces the paper's K=4 anchors within 15%, so the specific thresholds (pair>1.3, agg≈1.0) cannot be directly verified.

claims.claim: Multi-Treatment CausalEGM extends the discriminative framework to high-dimensional counterfactual generation and, via interpolation experiments, is shown to preserve the Wasserstein geodesic structure of the treatment manifold (Section 5.1, Section 5.2, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: On 784-dim Rotated MNIST with random init, latent-distance↔geodesic corr is 0.968 vs λ_geo=0 control at 0.123, tree midpoint lands at +0.015 vs control +0.145, and ADRF minimum recovers at T=4—strongly supporting the geodesic clause. However, counterfactual image generation MSE (0.0825) loses to a per-angle-mean baseline (0.0521), so the generation clause is not established, and the architecture is an MLP rather than the paper's full CausalEGM stack.

DineshAI/puNfWfBFNT.overall: The logbook provides concrete evidence supporting Claim 3 (O(1) complexity) at full fidelity and partial evidence for the other claims on constructed or simplified setups. Claims 1, 2, 4, 5, and 6 are addressed with real runs and numbers but on toy or controlled setups rather than the paper's actual experimental pipeline, with key gaps including unidentified constants (C1), synthetic profile constructions (C2, C4), scale mismatch (C5), and a failed generation sub-clause (C6).

Harshvardhan-Mestha/repro-efficient-trai.paper_title: Efficient Training-Free Multi-Token Prediction via Embedding-Space Probing

claims.claim: Lemma 3.1 proves that if the cosine similarity between a mask token's hidden state and the true next-token hidden state exceeds a threshold delta*, the correct token is guaranteed to appear in the Top-K predictions (Section 3, Lemma 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook empirically tested Lemma 3.1 on 200 random prompt/mask pairs using LLaMA3.2-3B-Instruct (a smaller model than the paper's 8B models), finding 0 violations. However, the claim is about a mathematical proof guaranteeing Top-K inclusion; empirical trials on a small model do not verify the proof itself, only provide proxy evidence on a simplified setup.

claims.claim: At block complexity (tree size) 60, the method achieves acceptance length tau of 1.71 on LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct and 1.66 on Qwen3-8B, compared to 1.62 and 1.56 respectively at block complexity 30 (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Only 10 general prompts of 256 tokens were used. The closest-to-greedy V5 results (temp=0.01) cover only LLaMA3.2-3B (τ=1.45–1.47 vs paper 1.56–1.63), not the 8B models in the claim. For LLaMA3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B, only V6 (temp=1.0) results exist (τ=2.00–3.69), which the logbook itself says overestimate due to diverse mask candidates. The specific claimed numbers (1.71, 1.66, 1.62, 1.56) were not reproduced.

claims.claim: The training-free method yields an approximately 12% improvement in acceptance length on LLaMA3 models and 8-12% on Qwen3 models relative to standard next-token decoding (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states this claim was not tested, as it requires SpecBench evaluation with standardized prompt sets and quality metrics, which were not available. No experiments were run for this claim.

claims.claim: The efficient implementation increases token throughput by up to 15-19%, including a 15% token-rate increase specifically measured on LLaMA3.1-8B, without modifying model weights or requiring auxiliary draft models (Table 3, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook's implementation was 80% slower than autoregressive decoding, but this implementation explicitly lacks KV cache, FlashAttention, optimized tree attention, and required CPU offloading for 8B models on a T4 GPU. Since the claim is specifically about an 'efficient implementation,' this unoptimized setup does not constitute a fair test of the claim.

claims.claim: Cosine similarity analysis across decoder layers shows accepted mask-token predictions reach approximately 0.45 similarity to the true next-token hidden state, versus approximately 0.35 for rejected predictions (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Results were collected on only 10 prompts and show inconsistent values across models: LLaMA3.2-3B at ~0.33–0.42 partially overlaps the paper's range, but Qwen3-8B shows ~0.84 and LLaMA3.1-8B shows ~0.27. Critically, the logbook does not clearly separate accepted vs. rejected predictions, which is the core of the claim (0.45 accepted vs 0.35 rejected).

Harshvardhan-Mestha/repro-efficient-trai.overall: The logbook provides only small-scale proxy evidence (10 prompts, 3B models, unoptimized implementation) for most claims, with two claims entirely unaddressed. No claim is verified at the paper's intended scale or with the paper's specific numerical results reproduced.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c00166.paper_title: Row-Stochastic Matrices Can Provably Outperform Doubly Stochastic Matrices in Decentralized Learning

claims.claim: In the weighted Hilbert space L²(λ;R^d), the λ-induced row-stochastic mixing matrix W is self-adjoint whereas the doubly stochastic matrix W^ds is not, and this non-self-adjointness introduces additional multiplicative penalty terms (κ_λ > 1 and λ_max² > 1) that amplify consensus error under the doubly stochastic design (Section 5.2, Section 6.2).
claims.evidence: On a 16-node graph with 10 seeds, the row-stochastic matrix had weighted adjoint residual 9.34e-17 (self-adjoint) while the doubly stochastic matrix had residual 0.7684 (not self-adjoint), and the doubly stochastic weighted operator norm (0.8987) exceeded its spectral radius (0.8224), demonstrating the multiplicative norm penalty, whereas the row-stochastic norm equaled its spectral radius (0.6107).

claims.claim: Theorem 6.5 gives O(1/T) convergence rates for both row-stochastic and doubly stochastic strategies, but the row-stochastic strategy achieves strictly smaller non-asymptotic consensus error and can converge faster even when its spectral gap is smaller than that of the doubly stochastic strategy (Theorem 6.5).
claims.evidence: On a 6-node graph with scalar deterministic quadratics, both strategies showed a 1/T rate (T×gradient constant within 1e-11 across T=250,500,1000) and row-stochastic had lower cumulative consensus error (0.00479 vs 0.09046), but the setup is simplified (scalar, deterministic, 6 nodes) and distance-to-optimum/consensus metrics were not uniformly better.

claims.claim: Theorem 7.1 derives a sufficient condition on the spectral gaps, 1 − ρ_Λ ≥ max{(1+η)κ_λ^(-1/3), λ_max^(-1/2)}(1 − ρ_J), under which the row-stochastic design provably converges strictly faster than the doubly stochastic design (Theorem 7.1).
claims.evidence: With 8 positive weights (lambda_max=5, kappa_lambda=2236.068, rho_J=0.98, rho_Lambda=0.9910557), the stated spectral-gap condition holds at equality, but Appendix D.1 Equation (49a) fails with margin -1,257,806.31, providing a concrete counterexample where the claimed sufficient condition does not guarantee the theorem's conclusion.

claims.claim: Corollary 7.3 and Algorithm 2 give topology construction guidelines showing that when node degrees scale proportionally with their assigned weights (d_i/d_j matching λ_i/λ_j within bounds set by R), the row-stochastic design outperforms the doubly stochastic design, satisfying a Loewner order condition on the graph Laplacians (Corollary 7.3, Remark 7.4, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: A 16-node graph with weights exactly proportional to degrees satisfies Equation 9 with minimum margin 0.1583, yet the minimum eigenvalue of L(lambda) - R*L(1) is -0.0657, violating the claimed full-space Loewner order. The obstruction is structural: L(lambda) annihilates sqrt(lambda) while L(1) annihilates 1, so the Loewner order cannot hold for heterogeneous weights.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c00166.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence verifying the weighted self-adjointness property of row-stochastic matrices (Claim 1) on a 16-node graph, and a toy-scale check of O(1/T) convergence and consensus error (Claim 2). It also presents explicit counterexamples with specific parameters and margins falsifying the spectral sufficient condition (Claim 3) and the full-space Loewner order claim (Claim 4).

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c14105.paper_title: Diffusion Bridge or Flow Matching? A Unifying Framework and Comparative Analysis

claims.claim: The paper frames Diffusion Bridge and Flow Matching in a shared stochastic optimal control/optimal transport framework (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook implemented both cost functionals from Equations 9–11 and showed the bridge/flow cost ratio approaches 1 (error 0.001249 at scale 20) across 80 scale values, numerically confirming that Flow Matching arises as the zero-drift limit of the Diffusion Bridge formulation.

claims.claim: Theoretical analysis shows the Diffusion Bridge cost function is lower than Flow Matching under the paper's formulation, implying more stable trajectories (Proposition 4.1; Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Independent numerical integration of the controller from Equation 20 compared against the closed-form cost in Equation 22 across dimensions 1, 4, 16, and 64 yielded a maximum bridge/flow cost ratio of 0.998750521 (never exceeding 1) with maximum relative disagreement of 4.12e-7, confirming the cost inequality; however, trajectory smoothness was not separately measured.

claims.claim: Under a shared Transformer architecture, Diffusion Bridge outperforms Flow Matching across image restoration and translation tasks (Table 1; Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The released repository contains no checkpoints or datasets and only ten tracked files; the Diffusion Bridge instructions reference absent train.py, test.py, and options/ files, so no matched Transformer training or evaluation was executed.

claims.claim: Diffusion Bridge remains stronger than Flow Matching as inpainting mask size increases, indicating better robustness under harder transformations (Table 2; Figure 3a).
claims.evidence: No experiments were run; the varying-mask inpainting comparison requires the same missing Diffusion Bridge training implementation, checkpoints, and datasets that were absent from the release.

claims.claim: Flow Matching degrades more steeply than Diffusion Bridge when training data size is reduced (Figure 3b; Table 7).
claims.evidence: Figure 3b and Table 7 require repeated matched training at several dataset sizes, but the public release provides no checkpoints, processed datasets, or complete Diffusion Bridge training code, so no runs were conducted.

claims.claim: Using the same network input conditions does not eliminate the performance gap between Flow Matching and Diffusion Bridge (Table 4).
claims.evidence: Table 4 depends on matched neural inputs and training, but the repository includes only partial Flow Matching scripts and omits the runnable Diffusion Bridge implementation and trained weights, preventing any controlled comparison.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c14105.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical verification of the two theoretical claims—the unifying framework (DB reduces to FM as drift vanishes) and the cost inequality (DB cost ≤ FM cost)—via CPU quadrature across multiple dimensions. The four empirical image-quality claims (3–6) are entirely unaddressed because the released repository lacks checkpoints, datasets, and a complete Diffusion Bridge training pipeline.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c00006.paper_title: Flat Minima and Generalization: Insights from Stochastic Convex Optimization

claims.claim: In non-negative, beta-smooth stochastic convex optimization under a strong flatness condition, flat empirical minima can incur population risk of Omega(1) while sharp minima in the same setting generalize optimally (Theorem 1, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: For n=8, d=257, rho=0.25, the flat witness had empirical risk 0 and population risk 0.140625 (>0.1), while the sharp witness had population risk 0 and empirical risk at delta=0.1 exactly equal to delta²/2=0.005, matching the theorem's finite construction across 1,000 deterministic trials.

claims.claim: SA-GD converges to a flat (rho-flat) empirical minimum at rate O(1/eta T) on the empirical risk, but its population risk lower bound is Omega(eta^2 (r-rho)^2 T), showing fast flat-minimum convergence does not guarantee generalization (Theorem 2 and Theorem 3, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: For T=16,64,256 with r=1/sqrt(T), the SA-GD block recurrence stayed within the unit ball and the normalized population witness (population risk divided by eta²r²T) remained positive with spread below 0.01 across all T values, confirming the predicted scaling of Omega(eta²(r-rho)²T) alongside the inverse-step empirical convergence.

claims.claim: SAM achieves the same empirical convergence rate as SA-GD, O(1/eta T + beta max{r-rho,0}^2), yet can converge to a sharp (non-flat) minimizer even when rho-flat minimizers exist, exhibiting a sharpness-empirical-risk gap of Omega(r^2) (Theorem 4 and Theorem 5, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: On f(w)=ReLU(w)²/2 with r=0.25, SAM initialized at zero remained exactly at zero after 100 steps, the sharpness-aware risk gap from the flat minimum at -1/2 was exactly r²/2=0.03125, and -1/2 remained a flat minimizer, confirming the one-dimensional counterexample.

claims.claim: Under realizability (rho=0), SAM's population risk has a lower bound of Omega(eta^2 r^2 T), matching stability-based upper bounds established via algorithmic stability (Theorem 6 and Theorem 8, Appendix A).
claims.evidence: The complete chained loss from Appendix C.3 was reconstructed at n=T={6,7,8} with dimensions {385,897,2049}; the probability of exactly one unseen coordinate exceeded the 1/3 threshold, no projection occurred (max norms 0.05-0.06), empirical loss was zero, and population loss/(eta²r²T) was at least {0.0347,0.0400,0.0444} across all suffix averages, confirming the Omega(eta²r²T) lower bound.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c00006.overall: The logbook independently implements all four explicit finite constructions from the paper and verifies their predicted numerical behavior: the flat-vs-sharp population risk gap, SA-GD's normalized population-risk scaling, SAM's convergence to a sharp minimum with exact r²/2 gap, and the realizable chained-loss lower bound with positive normalized constants across increasing n=T. These are faithful verifications of the paper's mathematical counterexamples at their intended construction scales, not reduced or proxy experiments.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c01695.paper_title: Robust and Consistent Ski Rental with Distributional Advice

claims.claim: The Clamp Policy selects a threshold t̃ = min{max{t*_p̂, ceil(λb)}, floor(b/λ)} for a tunable robustness parameter λ in (0,1) (Definition 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: With b=50 and λ=1/3, the logbook tests three cases (predicted thresholds 1, 34, 300) yielding clamped outputs 17, 34, 150, which exactly match min{max{t*, ceil(λb)}, floor(b/λ)} with ceil(50/3)=17 and floor(150)=150. An independent distribution example (0.8δ₁+0.2δ₅, b=3) also confirms the formula.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 bounds the competitive ratio by min{1 + 1/λ - 1/b, [ρ_p̂(t̃) + bθ]/(1-θ)}, giving robustness independent of prediction error η and consistency approaching the optimal ratio as η approaches 0 (Theorem 4.4, Corollary 4.5).
claims.evidence: On a concrete non-trivial instance (b=50, moving probability 0.1 from day 30 to 35, Wasserstein distance 0.5), the observed competitive ratio was 1.369863, which is below the theorem's computed bound of 1.971831, consistent with the claimed inequality. Evidence is limited to one test case but uses independent calculation of both the bound and the ratio.

claims.claim: The Water-Filling Algorithm's optimal randomized stopping distribution follows the geometric CDF F*(x) = min{(R-1)((1+1/(b-1))^x - 1), 1} for cost-monotone settings (Theorem 5.2, Section 5).
claims.evidence: At (b,R)=(50,1.7), the geometric CDF satisfies all active robustness constraints with maximum error 5.33e-14, and its objective value (74.6653) matches an independent SciPy HiGHS LP over 600 buying days to within 5.68e-14, confirming both feasibility and optimality of the geometric formula.

claims.claim: A stopping distribution is R-robust if and only if μ(x) + (b-x)F(x) ≤ (R-1)x for all 1 ≤ x ≤ b-1 and μ(∞) ≤ (R-1)b (Lemma 5.1).
claims.evidence: For all five reconstructed distributions, constraint slacks were at least -1.07e-14 (machine-feasible) and direct enumeration over 600 horizons gave worst-case ratio ≤1.7000000000000006, confirming that policies satisfying Lemma 5.1's inequalities achieve R-robustness. The converse direction of the 'if and only if' is not explicitly tested.

claims.claim: Experiments show the Water-Filling Algorithm yields 5-20% consistency improvements over point-prediction baselines across diverse distributions, with the largest gains on bi-modal distributions (Table 2, Section 6).
claims.evidence: Direct arithmetic on the paper's own Table 2 shows uniform-distribution improvements of only 1.44%, 2.14% (unif100) and 1.19%, 2.29% (unif200), all below the claimed 5% lower bound. The largest-gain-on-bi-modal sub-claim is supported (twopoint: 16.33%, 16.99%), but the '5–20% across diverse distributions' claim is contradicted by four data points.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c01695.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting Claims 1–4 through independent calculations, machine-precision constraint checks, and comparison with an independent LP solver on non-trivial instances (b=50, 600 horizons). Claim 5 is falsified by direct arithmetic on the paper's own Table 2, showing uniform-distribution improvements of 1.19–2.29%, well below the claimed 5% lower bound.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c06161.paper_title: Flatland: The Adventures of Gradient Descent with Large Step Sizes

claims.claim: Definition 2.3 formalizes 'large' step sizes using only local Lipschitz continuity of the gradient, requiring the step size to periodically exceed twice the local smoothness threshold, matching empirically observed edge-of-stability behavior (Definition 2.3).
claims.evidence: The definition was evaluated on a single-variable quadratic f(w)=Lw²/2 across seven curvatures, confirming that ηL and 2ηL thresholds can be computed without Hessian access. However, the claim's empirical component about 'matching edge-of-stability behavior' in real training was never tested on a neural network.

claims.claim: Proposition 2.5 establishes that the proposed equality line-search method (Algorithm 2) is Lipschitz-aware without requiring second-order information (Proposition 2.5).
claims.evidence: The lower bound η ≥ 2δ(1−c)/l(w,ηw) was checked on seven quadratic objectives where l(w,ηw)=L, with ηL ranging from 1.800 to 1.967 against a theoretical bound of 1.782. This is an exact audit but only on quadratic objectives, not on the non-quadratic objectives relevant to the paper's setting.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.1 shows sharpness converges to its global minimum of 2/K, where K is the number of classes (Lemma 3.1, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: For K=10 with hidden activations [-2,-1,0,1,2], the exact last-layer sub-Hessian yields sharpness 0.4, while 2/K=0.2. This concrete counterexample demonstrates that sharpness does not necessarily converge to 2/K, and the logbook identifies that Lemma 3.1/B.23 proves only a lower bound λmax(H) ≥ 2/K rather than convergence.

claims.claim: Empirically, the loss decreases nonmonotonically while the product of step size and sharpness stays above the edge-of-stability threshold of 2 throughout training, with methods reaching edge-of-stability right from the start (Abstract, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: No deep network training was conducted. The only experiment was a quadratic audit producing ηL between 1.800 and 1.967 (below 2), which the logbook itself acknowledges cannot address the claim about nonmonotone loss dynamics in neural networks.

claims.claim: Reaching the globally minimal sharpness too early in training slows convergence and generalization; the proposed NLS-ub variant, which caps step sizes below K, avoids this and achieves better practical performance (Section 3.2, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states: 'We did not run that experiment and did not substitute the quadratic audit for it. No paid compute was requested or used.' No experiment whatsoever was conducted for the NLS-ub comparison on SVHN with ResNet-34.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c06161.overall: The logbook provides toy-level checks of the definition and line-search proposition on quadratic objectives, and a concrete mathematical counterexample falsifying the claim that Lemma 3.1 proves convergence to 2/K. The two central empirical claims about deep network training (Claims 4 and 5) were never addressed, as no neural network experiments were run.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c08840.paper_title: Understanding the Performance Gap in Preference Learning: A Dichotomy of RLHF and DPO

claims.claim: Under isomorphic mis-specification, where the reward model class equals the policy model class (ℱ = ℱ_Π), standard RLHF and standard offline DPO yield equal value: V_{r⋆}^{π_RLHF} = V_{r⋆}^{π_DPO} (Proposition 6, Section 3.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook checks Proposition 3 on a three-action finite construction, reporting RLHF value 1.8634817 vs DPO 1.3333333. This is a real numerical check but on a clearly simplified synthetic setup, not a full-scale reproduction.

claims.claim: Despite this equivalence between RLHF and offline DPO, online DPO can strictly outperform RLHF under the same isomorphic mis-specified model classes, i.e. V_{r⋆}^{π_RLHF} < V_{r⋆}^{π^online_DPO}, because online DPO leverages distributional information unavailable to the two-stage reward-modeling-then-policy-optimization pipeline (Proposition 7, Section 3.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies value gap of 0 (within tolerance 1e-12) on a finite-action construction with shared root x=1.5126032554. This confirms the equivalence on a small synthetic example but does not constitute a full-scale reproduction.

claims.claim: When the reward class is realizable but the policy class is weak, RLHF weakly dominates DPO (V_{r⋆}^{π_RLHF} ≥ V_{r⋆}^{π_DPO}), since DPO's implicit reward is bottlenecked by the policy class constraints (Proposition 3, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports online DPO value 20.3364800 exceeding offline value 15.6014647 on a finite construction with R=12, x in [-4,4]. Real numbers on a simplified synthetic setup, not a full reproduction.

claims.claim: For dual-token sparse prediction tasks, ℓ1-regularized reward model estimation achieves error Õ(√(k log d / n)), where k is the sparsity level and d the dimensionality, while policy-model estimation error under the same sparse ground-truth reward structure is lower-bounded by Ω(d/n), establishing a statistical separation showing RLHF needs asymptotically fewer samples than DPO to recover an effective reward/policy under sparse rewards (Theorem 10, Theorem 11, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook runs 50 synthetic DTSP trials at d=128 with n from 128 to 2048, showing sparse reward estimation has lower error in all trials (ratios 2.4–3.0). This demonstrates the qualitative separation on synthetic data but, as the logbook itself notes, does not prove the asymptotic upper/lower bounds of Theorems 10–11.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c08840.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical checks of all four claims on simplified synthetic constructions (three-action examples and a d=128 sparse estimation simulation), demonstrating the qualitative predictions of the paper's propositions. However, none of these constitute full-scale reproductions—they are toy-scale verifications of theoretical results without formal proof checks or large-model experiments.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c34432.paper_title: Correct Looks Better: Pairwise Comparisons Reveal Accuracy Rankings

claims.claim: Elo-style rankings derived from pairwise comparisons achieve Spearman correlation above 0.9 (Pearson R greater than 0.87) with ground-truth accuracy rankings across five benchmarks: MMLU Pro, GPQA Diamond, SimpleQA, GSM8K, and BBH (Section on main results).
claims.evidence: The logbook ran a deterministic synthetic experiment with 10 synthetic models obtaining rho=0.9879, but explicitly states 'Original benchmark judgments are unavailable, so the empirical five-benchmark result was not recomputed.' No real benchmark data or model comparisons were used.

claims.claim: On four of the five benchmarks, only 6-8.9% of model pairs require reordering (Kendall distance) between Bradley-Terry pairwise rankings and accuracy-based rankings (results section, Kendall distance analysis).
claims.evidence: The logbook only applies the mathematical identity tau = 1 - 2*KD to the paper's own published KD values (6.0%, 8.9%, 7.4%, 7.7%) and states 'Raw matches are unavailable.' No independent recomputation of Kendall distance from actual pairwise comparison data was performed.

claims.claim: In the weak-judge regime on SimpleQA, Bradley-Terry pairwise ranking substantially outperforms direct evaluation, reducing ranking distance from 38.2% to 20% (SimpleQA weak judge experiment).
claims.evidence: An independent weak-judge simulation on synthetic data produced pairwise KD of 2.2% vs direct KD of 59.1%, showing the same directional pattern but with entirely different magnitudes than the paper's 20% vs 38.2% on actual SimpleQA. No real SimpleQA data was used.

claims.claim: Correcting pairwise comparisons for style and self-preference bias yields only modest ranking improvements, even though 58% of comparisons are non-discriminative pairs where both responses are equally correct or incorrect (bias correction analysis).
claims.evidence: A simulated style term was removed from synthetic data, changing tau from 0.9556 to 1.0000 (delta 0.0444), but the logbook states 'the empirical Figure 6 improvement cannot be recomputed without its source judgments.' The 58% non-discriminative rate is merely cited from the paper, not independently measured.

claims.claim: Controlled interventions identify 'echo' (response repetition following the final answer) as a causal driver of judge preference on non-discriminative pairs, with an estimated contrast of -0.52 (95% CI [-0.57, -0.46]) (echo causal intervention experiment).
claims.evidence: The logbook computed the contrast (-0.52) and CI ([-0.573, -0.467]) using a two-proportion normal approximation applied to the paper's published rates (0.29 and 0.81). This is arithmetic on published summary statistics, not an independent re-run of the echo intervention experiment with 500 pairs per condition.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c34432.overall: This logbook does not reproduce any of the five claims on the paper's actual benchmarks or experimental setup. It consists of synthetic simulations with 10 toy models, mathematical identity checks on the paper's own published numbers, and arithmetic recomputations from published summary statistics, with no access to original judgments or model outputs.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c10595.paper_title: A Sketch-and-Project Analysis of Subsampled Natural Gradient Algorithms

claims.claim: For linear least-squares problems, subsampled natural gradient descent (SNGD) is shown to be directly equivalent to the regularized Kaczmarz method, and SPRING is equivalent to the Nesterov-accelerated regularized Kaczmarz (ARK) method (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Independent implementation of SNG and regularized Kaczmarz updates on a 4×3 system yielded max absolute error 0.0 (within 1e-12), confirming algebraic equivalence; SPRING=ARK equivalence similarly identified via Theorem 6.1 in the accepted paper.

claims.claim: SNGD converges at rate (1-α)^t where α=λ_min(P̄), while SPRING converges at rate O((1-√(α/β))^t), giving up to a square-root improvement in iteration complexity over SNGD (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Exact enumeration on an 8-dimensional orthogonal system with one sampled row gives α=1/8 and contraction 0.875, matching the SNGD rate formula; however, the SPRING accelerated rate is only referenced via Equation 22 without an independent numerical run, and the system is small-scale.

claims.claim: For general quadratic losses, SNGD requires the regularization parameter λ to exceed a threshold λ0 to guarantee convergence, and can diverge if regularization is insufficient (Proposition 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports that the accepted arXiv version contains no Proposition 3, no λ₀ parameter, and no divergence theorem, so the claim's referenced content could not be located or tested.

claims.claim: Under an assumption that the regularized projector P̄ shares an eigenbasis with J^T J, SNGD provably outperforms SGD by a factor of k^β when the spectrum of the Jacobian decays polynomially (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Exact enumeration on 12-dimensional diagonal systems shows log-log slope 3.883 under i⁻² spectral decay vs 1.000 for flat spectrum, reproducing the superlinear scaling mechanism, but on a small system and without directly verifying the specific k^β outperformance factor over SGD.

claims.claim: A unified algorithm (Algorithm 1) captures both SNGD (momentum μ=0) and SPRING (μ∈(0,1)) as momentum-based updates using subsampled Jacobians, enabling single-minibatch convergence guarantees of any batch size.
claims.evidence: Setting momentum μ=0 in the unified update (Eq. 21) produced exactly the SNG step (Eq. 8) with max absolute error 0.0, and nonzero μ yields the SPRING recurrence, confirming the algebraic unification across tested row blocks and regularization values.

claims.claim: Analysis of SPRING's convergence for general (non-least-squares) quadratic losses is left open as Conjecture 7, despite numerical experiments showing large empirical performance gains over SNGD.
claims.evidence: The accepted paper explicitly states the accelerated sketch-and-project proof has not been extended to general quadratic loss due to unknown Lyapunov function, recorded as Conjecture 6.2, with Figure 5 providing numerical evidence; the logbook confirms this content exists in the paper.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c10595.overall: The logbook provides exact algebraic verification for the equivalence and unification claims (1, 5) and confirms the conjecture status (6), but convergence rate and spectral scaling claims (2, 4) are only checked on small 8–12 dimensional systems with exact enumeration, and Claim 3's referenced proposition was not found in the accepted paper.

claims.claim: The paper formalizes randomized self-reduction learning and provides sample-complexity analysis under correlated sampling (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook checked 4 boundary cases verifying that epsilon=min(rho/k, xi) satisfies k*epsilon<=rho and epsilon<=xi, which is tautologically true by definition of the minimum function. This does not constitute meaningful verification of the formalization or sample-complexity analysis.

claims.claim: RSR-Bench contains 80 benchmark functions for evaluating randomized self-reduction discovery (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Independent parsing of the benchmark without the official aggregation script found exactly 80 rows and 80 unique function names, directly confirming the benchmark size claim.

claims.claim: Vanilla Bitween discovers randomized self-reductions for 43 of 80 RSR-Bench functions, including the first known sigmoid reduction (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook ran the official Vanilla Bitween pipeline on only one function (sigmoid) with 30 training samples, discovering and symbolically proving one reduction. The 43/80 coverage figure was merely read from the authors' canonical rows, not independently reproduced, and the remaining 42 functions were not tested.

claims.claim: Agentic Bitween discovers randomized self-reductions for 64 of 80 RSR-Bench functions by letting LLM agents propose query functions beyond the fixed prior query set (Table 1).
claims.evidence: No LLM inference was run; the 64/80 count was obtained solely by aggregating the authors' canonical result rows. The logbook explicitly states 'the canonical authors result is the input data,' providing no independent experimental evidence.

claims.claim: On nonlinear invariant benchmarks, the regression backend outperforms the MILP backend in sample count and runtime (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Runtime was recomputed (LR: 4.791s vs MILP: 11.409s, favoring LR), but the logbook found no sample-count field in the available data. Since the claim requires both sample count and runtime to favor LR, the evidence is insufficient to verify or falsify the claim as stated.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c01650.overall: This logbook independently verifies only the benchmark size (Claim 2) and provides a limited single-function demonstration of the Vanilla Bitween pipeline (Claim 3, toy scope). Claims 1, 4, and 5 lack substantive independent experimental evidence: the theory check is tautological, the agentic results are merely read from canonical data, and the sample-count comparison is missing entirely.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c00321.paper_title: CAOS: Conformal Aggregation of One-Shot Predictors

claims.claim: CAOS aggregates nonconformity scores from multiple one-shot predictors by summing the k smallest scores (k=3 in experiments), reusing the same limited labeled data for both reference and calibration rather than splitting it (Equation 12).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements the k=3 aggregation with data reuse on a 5-example, 4-point binary domain, showing concrete per-round reference indices, scores, and aggregates (e.g., target index 2 uses references [0,1,3,4], scores [2,3,3,2], aggregate 7). This verifies the procedure's mechanics but on a clearly simplified setup far below the paper's scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves CAOS achieves finite-sample marginal coverage Pr(Y_{n+1} in C_caos(X_{n+1})) >= 1-alpha despite violating classical exchangeability assumptions, via a monotonicity-based reduction to full conformal prediction (Theorem 4.1, Lemma 5.2).
claims.evidence: An exhaustive enumeration over 286 multisets on a 4-point binary domain (n=9, alpha=0.2, k=3) found minimum coverage of exactly 0.8 and all 2,205 monotonicity checks passed. This is a real empirical check but on a tiny finite domain, not a verification of the general theorem or proof.

claims.claim: On the facial landmarking task at alpha=0.05, CAOS attains an average prediction set size of 16.14 +/- 0.58 with 0.955 coverage, versus the SCOS baseline's 36.07 +/- 0.94 set size at 0.976 coverage, a roughly 55% reduction in set size (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states the CelebA landmarking results (0.955 coverage, 16.14 set size vs. SCOS 36.07) 'were not independently rerun' and that required images, DINOv2 features, MediaPipe landmarks, and 478 tasks are outside the reproduction. No experiments were executed.

claims.claim: On 9 RAFT text classification tasks using Llama2-7B at alpha=0.1, CAOS produces smaller prediction sets than SCOS on 8 of 9 tasks while maintaining target coverage in cases where SCOS fails to do so (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook states 'The nine RAFT tasks using Llama2-7B were not rerun.' No experiments, data, or numerical results are presented for any RAFT task.

claims.claim: The facial landmarking evaluation uses CelebA face crops at 178x218 resolution across 478 landmarking tasks on 100 test images, while the RAFT evaluation uses only 40 labeled examples per task across 9 real-world classification tasks (Section on Datasets).
claims.evidence: The logbook only checked that the paper's text describes CelebA at 178×218, 478 tasks, 100 test images, and 40 labeled examples per RAFT task. No datasets were loaded, executed, or independently verified — this is a documentation check only.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c00321.overall: The logbook provides toy-scale empirical checks of the CAOS aggregation mechanism and finite-domain coverage on a 4-point binary domain, but none of the paper's application-level experiments (CelebA landmarking, RAFT classification) were attempted. The core empirical claims of the paper remain entirely unverified.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c34406.paper_title: Expected Return Causes Outcome-Level Mode Collapse in Reinforcement Learning and How to Fix It with Inverse Probability Scaling

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 shows that under gradient flow on expected return with softmax parameterization, the log-probability ratio between two outcomes i and j evolves as d/dt log(p_i/p_j) = p_i a_i - p_j a_j, causing exponential divergence independent of exploration, sampling noise, entropy bonuses, or KL regularization (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook independently derived the softmax logit gradient and confirmed Equation (2) matches finite differences to 1.36e-10 error. For unequal rewards (1.0, 0.8), integration from p=(0.505, 0.495) diverges to (0.986, 0.014), demonstrating the exponential divergence mechanism. The equal-rewards counterexample (zero gradient) is a degenerate case where all advantages vanish and does not meaningfully challenge the claim's core assertion about divergence under differential rewards.

claims.claim: Inverse Probability Scaling (IPS) reweights terminal rewards as r̃(o_g) = r(o_g)/max(p̂(o_g), ε) using empirical group frequencies, and under IPS gradient flow the stationary distribution satisfies p_i* = r(i)/Σ_k r(k), i.e., reward-proportional rather than collapsed (Theorem 4.1, Corollary 4.2).
claims.evidence: The IPS logit gradient was implemented independently and evaluated at the reward-proportional target p*=r/Σr for rewards (0.1, 0.5, 2.0, 0.5), yielding a maximum absolute gradient of 4.44e-16 (machine precision zero). Three substantially different initializations (skewed-first, skewed-last, uniform) all converged to the target with L1 errors below 1.76e-8.

claims.claim: On the HypoSpace benchmark, IPS-GRPO achieves substantially higher hypothesis-recovery rates than GRPO and FlowRL: 43.91% vs 16.02% and 12.82% on the Causal task, 90.00% vs 31.61% and 26.85% on 3D Voxel, and 60.74% vs 9.50% and 10.74% on Boolean (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook found the HypoSpace benchmark repository but no IPS-GRPO implementation, trained models, prompts, or training configuration. No experiments were run and no numerical evidence was produced for any of the three tasks.

claims.claim: On the discrete hyper-grid multimodal task, IPS-GRPO attains an ℓ₁ distance of 3.0×10⁻³ (n=2) and 3.7×10⁻⁴ (n=4) between the learned and target reward-proportional distributions, compared to 2.8×10⁻² and 5.2×10⁻⁴ for GRPO/FlowRL (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook constructed a 2D grid with 21 points per axis (441 outcomes) and compared exact deterministic gradient flows rather than the paper's GRPO training pipeline. IPS flow achieved L1=7.56e-12 and expected-return flow L1=1.565, neither matching the paper's reported values (3.0e-3 and 2.8e-2). Only n=2 was tested, not n=4. The setup is a simplified finite-outcome reduction, not the paper's full hyper-grid experiment.

claims.claim: On the SYNTH molecular generation task at a docking-score threshold of 0.80, IPS-GRPO achieves a yield of 7371±212 versus 5695±173 for REINVENT (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook found no author IPS-GRPO implementation, trained checkpoint, per-seed molecule lists, docking environment, or execution artifacts for the SYNTH task. No experiments were run and no numerical evidence was produced.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c34406.overall: The logbook provides clean numerical verification of the two theoretical claims (the expected-return log-ratio dynamics formula and the IPS reward-proportional stationarity), but does not reproduce any of the three empirical benchmark claims: HypoSpace and SYNTH were not run at all due to missing implementations, and the hyper-grid experiment was tested only on a simplified finite-outcome reduction with non-matching numbers.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c01847.paper_title: Rex: A Family of Reversible Exponential (Stochastic) Runge-Kutta Solvers

claims.claim: Rex converts explicit Runge-Kutta and stochastic Runge-Kutta schemes into algebraically reversible exponential solvers for diffusion ODEs and SDEs (Section 3).
claims.evidence: ODE round-trip errors of 6.66e-16–1.11e-15 for Euler/midpoint/RK4 and scalar SDE round-trip error of 1.47e-14 with same Brownian path (vs. 1.15 with different path) directly exercise the Lawson–Princeps Euler–Maruyama construction, but only on scalar ODE/SDE problems, not on diffusion-scale ODEs or SDEs as claimed.

claims.claim: The ODE Rex construction inherits arbitrary order of convergence and a non-zero linear stability region from the base McCallum-Foster method (Theorem A.1).
claims.evidence: Observed convergence orders of 1.018 (Euler), 2.021 (midpoint), and 4.023 (RK4) match expected base-method orders, and a non-zero stable interval [-0.001, 0] was found at zeta=0.999, confirming both inheritance of convergence order and a non-zero stability region using standard numerical-analysis methodology.

claims.claim: Rex achieves near-machine-precision reconstruction under exact inversion in image-generation inversion experiments (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: Near-machine-precision round-trip error of 4.44e-16 was demonstrated, but on a 16-dimensional analytic ODE rather than the image-generation inversion experiments referenced in Figure 7; Stable Diffusion inversion was explicitly not tested.

claims.claim: Rex improves or remains competitive on unconditional generation, text-conditioned generation, and image editing benchmarks versus prior reversible solvers (Figures 7-9).
claims.evidence: No image generation or editing quality experiments were run; the logbook states 'image quality is outside this CPU-only reproduction' and 'Stable Diffusion generation and editing quality were not tested,' so the benchmark competitiveness claim is unaddressed.

claims.claim: Rex enables accurate likelihood-based Boltzmann sampling on tri-alanine with flow models (Table 1).
claims.evidence: A 1D double-well energy toy check showed Rex round-trip error of 3.11e-15 and energy cycle error of 1.24e-14 versus Euler's 1.93e-2 and 7.61e-2, but the official Boltzmann implementation was unavailable and tri-alanine sampling with flow models was never attempted.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c01847.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the core algebraic reversibility mechanism and convergence/stability properties of Rex at scalar and small-scale ODE/SDE levels, but does not address the paper's principal application claims—image generation/editing quality and tri-alanine Boltzmann sampling—at their intended scale. Three of five claims are addressed only on toy problems, one application claim is entirely unaddressed, and only the convergence-order/stability claim is verified at an appropriate level.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c06034.paper_title: Success-Conditioning as Policy Improvement: The Optimization Problem Solved by Imitating Success

claims.claim: Success conditioning is proved to exactly solve a trust-region policy optimization problem with a chi-squared divergence constraint whose radius is determined by the data (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Across 32 random full-support two-step MDPs, the analytic success-conditioned policy was compared against an independent SLSQP constrained optimizer, yielding a maximum objective gap of 2.22e-13, constraint violation of 1.12e-12, and policy L-infinity gap of 1.16e-7 — all at floating-point tolerance.

claims.claim: At the optimum, relative policy improvement, chi-squared policy-change magnitude, and action-influence are shown to be exactly equal at every state (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: Across 256 random MDPs, all three quantities (relative advantage, chi-squared policy change, action influence) were computed independently from finite-MDP definitions, with maximum absolute errors of 6.66e-16 (statewise) and 4.44e-16 (occupancy-weighted), both at double-precision roundoff.

claims.claim: The analysis characterizes exact success conditioning as a conservative improvement operator that cannot degrade performance or induce dangerous distribution shift (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Across 256 random MDPs, minimum success gain was positive (0.003886) with statewise monotonicity margin at roundoff (-5.55e-16), and log-log regression of rare-action displacement vs. behavior probability yielded slope 0.49999, confirming the predicted square-root scaling under a fixed chi-squared radius of 0.25.

claims.claim: The paper analyzes return thresholding as an extension that can amplify improvement but can misalign the learned policy with the true objective (Section 5).
claims.evidence: A 100-arm Beta bandit with 300 thresholds showed a moderate threshold (0.834) achieving 2.57x the faithful-conditioning improvement (+0.00808 vs +0.00314), while an extreme threshold (0.969+) produced negative true-reward improvement (-0.00398), and the Proposition 7.1 proxy identity held to 2.49e-13 error.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c06034.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all four claims through independent computation and optimization on randomly generated finite MDPs and a 100-arm bandit. The mathematical identities are verified to machine precision across hundreds of random instances, and the thresholding experiment demonstrates both amplification and misalignment effects as claimed.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c02734.paper_title: CapBencher: Give Your LLM Benchmark a Built-in Alarm for Test-Set Overfitting

claims.claim: CapBencher caps Bayes accuracy by injecting randomness among logically correct answers, so above-cap performance can signal leakage or gaming (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The independent implementation of Theorem 2.1's capped_probability formula with K=4, L=2 yields a maximum capped accuracy of exactly 0.5 across all 21 grid points, and a 200,000-sample-per-point Monte Carlo simulation confirms the theoretical values with max absolute error 0.002182 (within the worst-case MC standard error of 0.001118). The cap is respected at every point.

claims.claim: Capped benchmark accuracy remains monotonically related to original benchmark accuracy for tracking and ranking LLM improvement (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The affine formula gives slope 1/3 > 0 for K=4, L=2, and the 21-point grid shows strictly increasing theoretical capped accuracy at every step; the 200,000-sample simulation per point follows the same line with max absolute error 0.002182, confirming monotonicity both analytically and numerically.

claims.claim: The paper uses exact binomial-test p-values rather than asymptotic approximations for contamination detection (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The code implements exact_one_sided_p_value using scipy.stats.binom.sf (exact binomial survival function), and a unit test compares SciPy's result against a direct finite-sum computation for n=20, k=15, alpha=0.5 with agreement; 5 tests pass. No normal or asymptotic approximation is used.

claims.claim: In a model-merge hacking simulation, the merged model's 56.52% accuracy is flagged as contaminated at the 5% significance level (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook only recomputes the binomial p-value from the paper's reported 56.52% accuracy and 1,319 examples (yielding p=1.39e-6 < 0.05), but explicitly states it did not rerun CMA-ES model merging or 7B-model inference to independently regenerate the 56.52% accuracy. The core experimental result was not reproduced—only the statistical decision on the reported number was checked.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c02734.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the mathematical foundations of CapBencher (the accuracy cap, monotonicity, and exact binomial test) through independent analytical derivation and large-scale Monte Carlo simulation. However, the model-merge detection claim is only checked on the paper's reported numbers without reproducing the actual model merging and inference pipeline.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c00039.paper_title: SVRG and Beyond via Posterior Correction

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows that applying posterior correction with an isotropic-Gaussian posterior family reduces exactly to the standard SVRG gradient update, and Theorem 2 proves SVRG is equivalent to VSGD-PoCo in the limit of zero sampling noise.
claims.evidence: The logbook checks algebraic equivalence between the isotropic PoCo direction and SVRG on four 2D positive-definite quadratic losses, finding max absolute error 0.0. This is a real numerical check but on a clearly simplified setup (2D, 4 examples, quadratic only), not a full mathematical proof or test on realistic problems.

claims.claim: Using full-covariance Gaussian posteriors yields a Newton-like variance-reduced extension (VON-PoCo) with a novel Hessian correction term H̄_out\i(m_in − m_out) not present in prior variance-reduced Newton methods.
claims.evidence: On the same 2D quadratic setup, the logbook confirms the Hessian correction term is nonzero (norm 1.847) and the SVRH formula matches to machine precision (error 4.4e-16). This verifies the algebraic construction on a toy instance but does not address the novelty claim relative to prior methods, nor test on realistic problems.

claims.claim: Using diagonal-covariance Gaussian posteriors with mega-batches and momentum yields an Adam-like extension (IVON-PoCoMo) suitable for transformer pretraining, which achieves 17.4 validation perplexity on GPT-2 125M pretrained on 50B tokens, versus 18.0 for IVON and 18.4 for AdamW (Section 4.3, Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states no experiment was executed for the GPT-2 125M / 50B-token pretraining claim; no perplexity numbers were independently produced.

claims.claim: The variance-reduced methods show consistent gains in finetuning across ViT-B/32, Qwen2.5, and Llama-3.1 (Table 1) and in ResNet-50/ImageNet and ResNet-20/CIFAR-10 image classification, particularly when learning rates are not annealed to zero (Figures 4-5).
claims.evidence: The logbook states the cross-model finetuning and image classification experiments were not rerun; no independent results on ViT, Qwen, Llama, ResNet-50/ImageNet, or ResNet-20/CIFAR-10 were produced.

sotayamashita/icml26-repro-c00039.overall: The logbook independently verifies the algebraic identities behind Claims 1 and 2 on tiny 2D quadratic instances, but does not execute any of the paper's empirical experiments for Claims 3 and 4. It establishes only a toy-scale sanity check of the analytical core, leaving all deep-learning benchmarks unaddressed.

ParetoOptimal/repro-4t8vevk79x.paper_title: Approximate Proportionality in Online Fair Division

claims.claim: Three natural greedy allocation rules (maximize relative item value, allocate to most unsatisfied agent, and minimize worst predicted dissatisfaction) each fail to guarantee any positive multiplicative approximation to PROP1 against an adaptive adversary (Section 3, Propositions 6-8).
claims.evidence: Exact rational (fractions.Fraction) certificates show Greedy 1 achieves R=4/(m+1) and Greedy 2 achieves R=4/m, both →0 as m grows to 1000. Greedy 3's full Appendix-A.1 adaptive construction is replayed for 40 rounds (234 goods), with 1/α^(t_k) verified to dominate the divergent harmonic lower bound at every checked round, confirming α→0.

claims.claim: Against a non-adaptive adversary, uniform random allocation achieves an Ω(1/log(n/δ)) approximation to PROP1 with probability at least 1-δ, specifically α = 27/(128·log(n/δ)), the first such multiplicative bound in the online setting without extra assumptions (Section 4, Theorem 9).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo with 4×10⁵ trials per row across a 12-row (n,δ) grid (n∈{2,3,5,10}, δ∈{0.1,0.05,0.01}) shows P[fail]=0≤δ for α=27/(128·ln(n/δ)) on equal small-goods instances, plus three non-uniform small-goods instance types (geometric, random, two-block) all passing. Near-PROP1 concentration as m grows is also demonstrated.

claims.claim: Given perfect maximum-item-value (MIV) predictions, Algorithm 1 guarantees a 1/n-PROP1 allocation (Section 5, Theorem 11).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 is implemented exactly from the paper's pseudocode (using the n²+n+1 potential from appendix Eq. 7) and tested on 6006 instances (structured adversarial + random n≤6, m≤15) with exact rational PROP1 checks; 0 failures, with the tightest observed R/(1/n)≈2.0.

claims.claim: Under one-sided MIV prediction error ε ∈ [0,1), the algorithm's approximation degrades gracefully to β = (1-ε)/(n-ε/n) (Section 5, Theorem 12).
claims.evidence: The Theorem-12 robustness wrapper is implemented exactly and tested across 18 (ε,n) combinations (ε∈{0,0.1,0.25,0.5,0.75,0.9}, n∈{2,3,5}) with 2500 instances each, including worst-case instances where every agent's max is exactly 1−ε. R_true≥β=(1−ε)/(n−ε/n) holds on every instance, and the degradation curve recovers 1/n at ε=0 and →0 as ε→1.

claims.claim: Even with perfect MIV predictions, no online algorithm can achieve any non-zero approximation to EF1, MMS, or PROPX (Section 5, Proposition 10).
claims.evidence: Proposition 10 (impossibility of non-zero EF1/MMS/PROPX approximation even with perfect MIV predictions) is never addressed in the logbook. No adversarial construction for EF1, MMS, or PROPX impossibility is implemented or tested.

ParetoOptimal/repro-4t8vevk79x.overall: The logbook provides strong, exact-rational verification for Claims 1–4 (greedy impossibility, random allocation bound, Algorithm 1's 1/n-PROP1 guarantee, and graceful degradation under prediction error) with concrete adversarial constructions and large-scale testing. kpshinnik/repro-lower-bounds-for-frank-w.paper_title: Lower Bounds for Frank-Wolfe on Strongly Convex Sets

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a constructive Omega(1/sqrt(epsilon)) lower bound on the number of iterations for Frank-Wolfe with short steps or exact line search when both the objective and the constraint set are smooth and strongly convex (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: The logbook independently checks the two key inequalities underpinning Theorem 6: eq (12) residual lower bound rₜ ≥ r₀/(1+(8/3)r₀t) holds with max violation 0.0e+00 along the reconstructed worst-case trajectory, and the Lemma 15 invariant cₜ∈[1,5/2] holds for 100% of r≤1/10 iterates (min 1.744, max 2.000). The empirical iteration complexity T~ε^{-0.509} matches the theoretical Ω(1/√ε) exponent of -0.5.

claims.claim: The lower-bound construction uses the specific instance of minimizing f(x) = ||x-p||_2^2 over the Euclidean unit ball B_1(0) with the unconstrained minimizer p on the boundary (||p||=1), showing this hard instance matches the known O(1/sqrt(epsilon)) upper bound of Garber et al. (2015) (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: The specific hard instance is confirmed: objective Hessian 2I gives µ=L=2, unit ball gives α=β=1 (smooth and strongly convex). Prop 3 upper bound rₜ²≤1/(t+1/r₀)² holds with max violation 1.7e-18. Boundary case (||p||=1) requires 744 iterations to reach gap 1e-6 vs 6 (interior) and 18 (exterior), and the worst-case rate gap~t^{-1.998} confirms tightness of the O(1/√ε) upper bound.

claims.claim: The lower bound is established via a 'backward reconstruction' technique that builds worst-case trajectories by working backward from terminal iterates, producing precise sequences over horizons of 10,000+ iterations (Section on Backward Reconstruction Strategy).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 was re-implemented in Python with mpmath at 60,000-bit precision, producing a 20,001-step worst-case trajectory (exceeding the 10,000+ claim). Forward re-simulation from the reconstructed initial condition matches the backward trajectory with max|Δr|=0.0e+00, confirming reversibility (Lemma 12). Precision sensitivity analysis (float64 fails at step 45, 100-digit fails at 321, full precision stable for 20,001 steps) yields ~0.31 digits/step, matching the paper's stated requirement.

claims.claim: The analysis reduces the dynamics to a two-dimensional invariant subspace parametrized by residual magnitude r and contraction factor s, revealing stable phases of monotonically increasing contraction followed by intermittent 'jumps' that explain the convergence stalling behavior (Section on Dynamical Analysis).
claims.evidence: Lemma 1 invariant subspace verified: max off-subspace component ~1e-13 across d=2,5,20,100. The g(r) phase partition correctly predicts sign of sₜ₊₁−sₜ on 100% of 2,000 sampled states. Stable-phase peak lengths grow with grid resolution ({2000:10, 20000:14, 200000:15}), supporting unboundedness. Prop 5 jump characterization holds on 415/415 sampled jumps.

claims.claim: The result shows strong convexity of the constraint set alone cannot yield convergence rates uniformly faster than O(1/sqrt(epsilon)), and this conclusion holds dimension-independently and extends to ellipsoidal constraints via affine invariance (Theorem 6, Implications).
claims.evidence: Dimension independence is bit-exact: identical gap trajectories across d=2,3,10,50,200 (max difference 0.0e+00). Ellipsoid affine invariance (Cor 17) verified: FW iterates commute with Φ=A^{1/2} to max error 5.3e-15, and gap identity gap_ell=(α/2)·gap_ball holds to 3.9e-16, confirming the ellipsoid inherits the ball's Ω(1/√ε) lower bound.

kpshinnik/repro-lower-bounds-for-frank-w.overall: The logbook provides concrete, high-precision numerical evidence supporting all five claims at the paper's full scale (20,001-iteration trajectories at 60,000-bit precision, dimensions up to 200, exact verification of key inequalities and invariants). The reproduction is a self-contained Python re-implementation cross-checked against the authors' Julia code, with all critical inequalities holding to machine or near-machine precision.

kpshinnik/repro-the-marginal-value-of-a-.paper_title: The (Marginal) Value of a Search Ad: An Online Causal Framework for Repeated Second-price Auctions

claims.claim: Under binary feedback, the proposed algorithm for repeated second-price auctions achieves regret O(√(dT) log³T + d log⁵T), where d is the feature dimension and T the horizon (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: At the paper's own Figure-2 scale (T=50000, d=5, 10 seeds), CausalUCB regret scales as T^0.567 (close to √T=0.5, excess attributable to log³T), while LinUCB grows linearly (exponent 0.93). Final regret 1337 vs LinUCB 4174, qualitatively matching the paper's Figure 2 separation. The d-scaling is weak (regret barely changes from d=2 to d=32), but the T-scaling evidence at non-toy scale supports the claimed rate.

claims.claim: A matching minimax lower bound of Ω(√(dT)) holds for T ≥ d², even when the bidder has perfect knowledge of the competing-bid CDF (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is a minimax lower bound (an impossibility result), which cannot be verified by running a single algorithm. The logbook only shows that their specific CausalUCB algorithm still exhibits √T regret (exponent 0.569) when G is known, but this does not constitute evidence that NO algorithm can beat Ω(√(dT))—it merely shows this particular algorithm doesn't benefit from knowing G. The logbook itself acknowledges the lower bound 'remains a theoretical result we do not (and cannot) reproduce by simulation.'

claims.claim: Under binary feedback, second-price auctions admit Õ(√(dT)) regret while first-price auctions are limited to Õ(T^(2/3)) regret, showing the payment rule strictly improves achievable regret (Section on regret comparison).
claims.evidence: HOB-CDF estimation error slopes measured over n=1000–128000 with 8 seeds: SPA binary slope −0.518 (≈n^{-1/2}, implying √T regret) vs FPA binary slope −0.304 (≈n^{-1/3}, implying T^{2/3} regret). The estimation rate separation is the mechanism driving the regret gap, and the slopes are in the right range for the claimed rates.

claims.claim: Under full-information feedback, both second-price and first-price auctions achieve the same Õ(√(dT)) regret rate, so the SPA advantage is specific to the binary-feedback setting (Section on regret comparison).
claims.evidence: Under full-information feedback, FPA estimation slope is −0.518, identical to SPA's −0.518, confirming both achieve the same n^{-1/2} rate. The identical slopes are expected since full information gives FPA the same HOB observations SPA already has under binary feedback.

claims.claim: Section 3 introduces an interval-splitting technique to estimate the highest-other-bid (HOB) directly from the observed payment in a won second-price auction (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The IntervalSplittingCDF estimator is implemented and tested on two HOB families (uniform and truncated-normal), recovering G to sup-error 0.022 and 0.007 respectively after 40000 rounds. The Figure-1 monotonicity property is reproduced (correlation between interval center and observation count = −1.0), and sup-error decreases with n (exponent −0.42).

kpshinnik/repro-the-marginal-value-of-a-.overall: The logbook provides a clean-room CPU simulation at the paper's own Figure-2 scale, with concrete numerical evidence supporting Claims 1, 3, 4, and 5 through regret scaling, estimation-rate separations, and interval-splitting recovery. Claim 2 (a minimax lower bound) is inherently theoretical and cannot be experimentally verified; the proxy check offered does not constitute evidence for an impossibility result.

claims.claim: The spiked cumulant model introduces two latent factors, one recoverable by PCA from the covariance and one appearing only in higher-order moments and invisible to PCA (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The spiked-cumulant model is implemented at d=800 with visible spike u* and hidden spike v*, and the logbook shows PCA/linear autoencoder cosine alignment theta_v stays at the random floor d^{-1/2}≈0.035 (0.042, 0.031 at k*=2; 0.015, 0.006 at k*=3), confirming v* is invisible to covariance-based methods.

claims.claim: For correlation exponent 2 ≤ k* < ∞, a minimal nonlinear autoencoder x̂ = (w/√d) σ(wᵀx/√d) with tied encoder-decoder weights provably recovers both latent spikes while PCA and linear autoencoders recover only the covariance-visible one (Section 2, Result 3.1).
claims.evidence: At k*=2, ReLU tied autoencoder achieves theta_v=0.134 (alpha=15) and 0.184 (alpha=30), well above the 0.035 floor, while linear/PCA remain at floor; at k*=3, tanh reaches 0.058 (~1.65x floor) while ReLU/linear collapse, consistent with the paper's own near-floor Fig. 7 regime. The activation-selective recovery phenomenon and PCA/linear failure are demonstrated with concrete numbers at non-toy scale.

claims.claim: Linear autoencoders achieve lower reconstruction (test) loss than nonlinear autoencoders yet fail to recover the hidden spike, demonstrating that self-supervised test loss misaligns with representation quality (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: At k*=2, linear AE has lower test reconstruction MSE (799.12 vs 800.11 for ReLU) yet worse downstream error on sign(x·v*) (0.497 vs 0.451) and no v* recovery (theta_v=0.031 vs 0.205), directly demonstrating test-loss/generalization misalignment with concrete numbers.

NaveenVenu/gvWsViQBYB.paper_title: Convergence Rate Analysis of the AdamW-Style Shampoo: Unifying One-Sided and Two-Sided Preconditioning

claims.claim: For AdamW-style Shampoo (Algorithm 1) with preconditioner exponents satisfying 1/p + 1/q = 1, Theorem 1 establishes the nonconvex convergence rate (1/K)Σ E[||∇f(X_k)||_*] ≤ O(√(m+n)·max{σ²L(f(X1)-f*)/K, √(L(f(X1)-f*)/K)}) for m×n matrix parameters over K iterations (Section 2, Theorem 1, Equation 9).
claims.evidence: Tested on a 4×4 synthetic quadratic with K∈{200,...,6400}; measured log-log slope was -0.102 versus the theoretical -0.25, less than half the predicted exponent. Real runs on a clearly simplified setup, but the rate is not actually confirmed at this scale.

claims.claim: This rate is shown to be analogous to the optimal SGD convergence rate O(σ²L(f(X1)-f*)/K) in the ideal case where ||∇f(X)||_* = Θ(√min{m,n})·||∇f(X)||_F and m, n are comparable, since ||∇f(X)||_F ≤ ||∇f(X)||_* ≤ √min{m,n}·||∇f(X)||_F (Section 1.1, Equations 2-3).
claims.evidence: The logbook does not test the SGD analogy or the nuclear-to-Frobenius norm ratio condition ||∇f||_* = Θ(√min{m,n})·||∇f||_F; only the √(m+n) prefactor was probed (Claim 3 in the logbook), which is a different sub-claim.

claims.claim: The analysis extends to preconditioning exponents satisfying 1/p+1/q = 2-ω for ω∈(0,2] without decoupled weight decay, yielding rate (1/K)Σ E[|||∇f(X_k)|^ω||_*] ≤ O((m+n)^(1-ω/2)/(ωK^(ω/4))), which reduces to the ω=1 rate at ω=1 and to the momentum-SGD rate at ω=2 (Section 1.1, Equation 4).
claims.evidence: Tested ω∈{0.5,1,2} on the same 4×4 synthetic quadratic; measured slopes were 73–78% of theoretical values (e.g., -0.367 vs -0.500 for ω=2). Correct ordering across ω but rates do not match theory at this scale, and the problem is toy-sized.

claims.claim: This is presented as the first convergence analysis of the two-sided (as opposed to only one-sided) preconditioned nonconvex Shampoo variant, unifying one-sided (p=1,q=∞ or vice versa) and two-sided (p,q<∞) preconditioning in a single Algorithm 1 framework (Section 1, Section 1.1).
claims.evidence: This is a novelty/priority claim about being the first two-sided nonconvex Shampoo analysis; the logbook provides no literature comparison or evidence to support or refute it, and it is not addressable by synthetic experiments alone.

agharsallah/omkg80xurl-logbook.paper_title: Bridging the Gap Between Average and Discounted TD Learning

claims.claim: Under i.i.d. sampling in the double-chain formulation, the algorithm converges to a unique, sample-independent fixed point of the projected Bellman equation with sample complexity Õ(ε^-1 η^-2) (Theorem 4.1).

claims.claim: Under Markovian sampling with constant stepsizes in the double-chain setting, the same Õ(ε^-1 η^-2) sample complexity is preserved (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Real Markov trajectories totaling 38.8B updates across 54 runs show T_ε(Markov)/T_ε(i.i.d.)=0.9996 median; fitted η exponent -2.0479 (95% CI [-2.1143, -1.9815]); Theorem 4.2's bound is never violated (worst ratio 0.0714); lag-1 autocorrelation 0.07–0.88 confirms genuine Markov correlation versus ≤0.0014 for i.i.d.

claims.claim: With decaying stepsizes, the method attains convergence guarantees with no explicit dimension-dependent terms (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Dimension swept 64× (d=4…256) at near-fixed η₁ (1.546× variation) on a 256-state MDP with 2.2B updates; convergence time varies only 2.173×; fitted dimension exponent -0.02680 (95% CI [-0.04513, -0.00847]), excluding linear (129 SEs) and quadratic (255 SEs) dimension dependence.

claims.claim: The paper reduces the condition-number dependence of average-reward TD learning from quartic (prior state of the art) to quadratic, matching the scaling known for discounted TD learning (Section 1, Table 1).
claims.evidence: On 54 shared instances (108 runs, 3.00 decades of η), the double-chain method's measured condition-number exponent is -1.9564 (95% CI [-1.9738, -1.9391]), the prior Õ(ε⁻¹η₂⁻⁴) bound evaluates to -4.0000, and discounted TD measures -1.9782 (95% CI [-2.0020, -1.9543]); the double-chain and prior CIs are disjoint by 2.044 exponent units.

claims.claim: A single-chain variant of the algorithm is also analyzed but only attains quartic sample complexity Õ(1/η^4 T) due to decorrelation requirements, contrasting with the double-chain method's quadratic rate (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: Theorem 4.4's explicitly instantiated bound on 81 cells (162 runs, 2.98 decades of η) yields η exponent -3.9805 (95% CI [-4.0055, -3.9555]) versus Theorem 4.2's -1.9484 (95% CI [-1.9871, -1.9097]) on the same instances; the CIs are disjoint by 2.0321 exponent units, with the single chain requiring up to 1.47e9× more samples.
