agharsallah/omkg80xurl-logbook.overall: This logbook provides a thorough, large-scale reproduction of all six claims using the paper's own Appendix-G environments and feature constructions, with exact second-moment propagation validated against brute-force enumeration and extensive real stochastic runs totaling tens of billions of updates. The scaling exponents are measured over multiple decades of the condition number and consistently match the theoretical predictions within tight confidence intervals.

agharsallah/ol99zow31j-logbook.paper_title: Non-Uniform Noise-to-Signal Ratio in the REINFORCE Policy-Gradient Estimator

claims.claim: For finite-horizon linear-quadratic systems with Gaussian policies, the noise-to-signal ratio of the multi-step REINFORCE estimator can be computed exactly in closed form via lifted dynamics (Theorem 5, Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: Closed-form NSR matches Monte-Carlo estimates to within 0.07% relative error across 5 LQ systems (scalar and multi-dim, horizons T=1..4), e.g. scalar_stable_T2: 24.838 vs 24.854 (rel_err 0.00068), dblint_T2: 132.042 vs 132.930 (rel_err 0.00673), across 3 seeds each.

claims.claim: The NSR landscape is highly non-uniform: as the policy approaches the optimal deterministic policy (Σ→0, per Corollary 6), the NSR does not vanish uniformly and can blow up, as demonstrated for a double-integrator system (Figure 1, Section 2.3).
claims.evidence: Double-integrator sweep from sigma=1.0 to 0.001 shows NSR blowing up from 64.13 to ~41.5 million while NSR*sigma^2 converges to ~41.5 (constant), confirming NSR ~ 1/sigma^2 blow-up as the policy becomes deterministic. Near-optimal NSR (64.13) exceeds far-from-optimal NSR (62.43), demonstrating non-uniformity.

claims.claim: Variance of the multi-step REINFORCE estimator grows exponentially with the control horizon when the closed-loop dynamics are unstable, i.e., when the spectral radius ρ(F)>1 (Theorem 8, Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: 3M-sample Monte-Carlo across horizons T=1..8 shows log-variance slope of 1.612 for unstable dynamics (rho(F)=1.2) vs 0.462 for stable (rho(F)=0.5), with variance ratio unstable/stable growing from 8.1x (T=1) to 28298x (T=8), confirming exponential-in-horizon growth for unstable closed-loop dynamics.

claims.claim: A general upper bound on REINFORCE gradient-estimator variance is derived for generic nonlinear dynamics with expressive neural-network policies (Theorem 10, Section 4).

Networks are small but the bound is a general theoretical result verified on genuine nonlinear dynamics with NN policies.

claims.claim: The analysis is extended from linear to polynomial systems and polynomial feedback policies via a moment-evaluation approach (Proposition 9, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Moment-evaluation closed-form NSR matches Monte-Carlo to within 1.8% relative error on scalar quadratic dynamics with polynomial feedback policies across 4 configurations (e.g. poly_T1_quad: 121.61 vs 123.76, rel_err 0.0177; poly_T2_mild: 83.79 vs 84.18, rel_err 0.0047), confirming the extension from linear to polynomial systems.

agharsallah/ol99zow31j-logbook.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all five claims through closed-form vs Monte-Carlo comparisons, parameter sweeps, and multi-configuration testing on LQ, double-integrator, nonlinear, and polynomial systems. The reproduction is thorough with real measured numbers across multiple seeds and configurations, though the neural-network policies in Claim 4 are small-scale.

DineshAI/l94JabCBGL.paper_title: The Value Function Semi-Algebraic Set in Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes

claims.claim: The feasible set of value functions in POMDPs is proven to be a semi-algebraic set defined by explicit polynomial equalities and inequalities, in contrast to the polyhedral (piecewise-linear) feasible set of fully observable MDPs (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: Exact rational Cramer construction shows all sign-polynomial factors are degree-1 (has_nonlinear_factor=false) under full observability, while partial observability introduces irreducible quadratic factors (factor_degrees [1,1,2], has_nonlinear_factor=true) with discriminant 72,900>0, directly demonstrating the semi-algebraic vs. polyhedral distinction on the paper's own Figure-5 instances.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.9 first characterizes feasible POMDP value functions via infinitely many piecewise-linear inequalities derived from the Bellman equation parameters.
claims.evidence: 343 direct Figure-2/3 policies satisfy Theorem 3.9 support inequalities with max violation 7.77e-16, and 1,681 rank-four value points are correctly classified (feasible points have negative violations, infeasible points have positive violations starting at 8.69e-5), confirming the infinite piecewise-linear characterization.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 reduces the infinite characterization to a finite description using a zonotope containment condition on deviation matrices and midpoint residuals.
claims.evidence: Theorem 4.2 zonotope LP feasibility checks yield max linear residuals of 6.27e-15 (343 policies) and 1.28e-14 (121 policies), and all 1,681 rank-four off-image values agree across Theorem 3.9 and Theorem 4.2, confirming the finite reduction matches the infinite characterization.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 gives an explicit quantifier-free semi-algebraic description of the feasible value-function set, stratified by matrix rank via determinantal polynomial conditions on submatrices.
claims.evidence: Theorem 4.4 Cramer determinant-sign certificates recover 121 Figure-5 policies with max policy recovery error 2.09e-14, and all 1,681 rank-four off-image candidates agree across all three characterizations (Theorem 3.9, 4.2, 4.4), with negative controls rejecting 1,496 candidates.

claims.claim: Partial observability is shown to induce nonlinear coupling constraints between decision variables absent in MDPs, making optimal policies dependent on the initial state distribution (Section 4).
claims.evidence: On the Appendix-E.2 POMDP, independent SHGO and exhaustive 801×801 Bellman grid agree within 8.2e-14; optimal policy is (1,1) for rho=(0.2,0.8) but switches to (0,0) for rho=(0.8,0.2), directly demonstrating initial-distribution dependence induced by partial observability.

DineshAI/l94JabCBGL.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous, independent computational verification of all five claims on the paper's own finite instances (2×2×3 and 2×2×2 POMDPs) using exact rational arithmetic, cross-checking across three theorem formulations, and negative controls. While the instances are small, they are the paper's own illustrative examples at full scope, and the exact arithmetic and three-way agreement provide strong evidence for the structural claims.

claims.claim: 11 process constraints (P1-P11) and 3 parameter constraints (C1-C3), derived from ecological theory and literature, are incorporated as loss terms combined via homoscedastic uncertainty weighting (Table 1, Section 3.2.3).

NaveenVenu/MbmhB3KqKU.paper_title: Envy-Free Allocation of Indivisible Goods via Noisy Queries

claims.claim: A naive non-adaptive algorithm achieves envy-freeness using O(m^3/Δ^2) noisy queries, where m is the number of items and Δ is the gap parameter of the optimal negative envy (Theorem 1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook only addresses Theorems 2 and 4 (the thresholding algorithm and query formula). Theorem 1's naive non-adaptive algorithm and its O(m^3/Δ^2) bound are never mentioned, implemented, or tested.

claims.claim: An improved polynomial-time algorithm using non-adaptive queries achieves envy-freeness with q ≤ Õ(m^2.5/Δ^2) queries, valid when Δ ≥ m^(1/4) log^2 m and Δ ≤ Cm for a sufficiently small constant C (Theorem 2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The thresholding algorithm (Eq. 4) and exact Theorem-4 query formula were implemented from scratch and achieved 100% envy-free success at the prescribed query count for m ∈ {100,200,400,800}. However, in every tested instance the measured Δ fell below the theorem's required regime (Δ ≥ m^{1/4} log^2 m); e.g., for m=100, Δ=14.45 vs. required ≥67.1. The claim's stated regime was never exercised, and the m^{2.5}/Δ^2 scaling was not tested for tightness.

claims.claim: An algorithm-independent lower bound of Ω̃(m^2.5/Δ^2) queries is proven to hold even under adaptive querying strategies and unbounded computation time, matching the upper bound up to logarithmic factors (Theorem 3, Section 5).
claims.evidence: The lower bound (Theorem 3) is never implemented or tested. The logbook explicitly states it 'was not able to construct, within this pass, a natural instance landing inside the paper's stated regime' and that testing tightness 'would require either the paper's specific adversarial construction (not given in enough detail to reconstruct exactly).'

claims.claim: The problem setup assumes agent valuations are accessed only through queries corrupted by Gaussian noise, formalized as the noisy query model (Section 2).
claims.evidence: The noisy query model was concretely implemented (y_i^ν ~ N(u_i^ν, σ²) with σ²=1) and used throughout all Monte Carlo experiments, with true valuations used to judge allocation correctness. This confirms the model is coherent and functional as described.

claims.claim: The paper extends its analysis of general noise levels beyond the Gaussian model and discusses extension of the results from two agents to n-agent scenarios (Section 6, Section 7).
claims.evidence: Sections 6 and 7 (general noise beyond Gaussian, n-agent extensions) are never mentioned, implemented, or discussed anywhere in the logbook.

NaveenVenu/MbmhB3KqKU.overall: The logbook provides a from-scratch implementation of the Theorem 2/4 thresholding algorithm and demonstrates it achieves envy-freeness with the prescribed query count on random instances, but all tested instances fall outside the theorem's stated valid regime (Δ too small), so the core scaling claim is only tested on easier-than-worst-case instances. Theorems 1, 3, and the extensions in Sections 6–7 are entirely unaddressed.

vbabenko97/repro-instance-level-costs.paper_title: Instance-Level Costs for Nuanced Classifier Evaluation

claims.claim: On the Jigsaw text dataset, a model with 5.3% error rate achieves only 1.8% Normalized Excess Cost (NEC), a roughly 3x difference indicating most mistakes concentrate on ambiguous, low-cost examples (Key Findings, NEC vs. Error Rate Gap).
claims.evidence: On a 300k stratified subsample of the real 1.8M-row Jigsaw dataset with recovered annotator vote margins (Eq. 3), TF-IDF + logistic regression over 10 seeds yields 5.91% error vs 2.02% NEC — a 2.92x ratio matching the paper's ~3x claim. The leak-free rerun (TF-IDF fit on train only) confirms the result with negligible change.

claims.claim: On the Turkey image dataset and NHANES tabular dataset, error rate vs. NEC gaps of 6.7% vs 4.2% (1.6x) and 21.7% vs 14.8% (1.5x) respectively are reported, showing the error-rate/NEC divergence holds across modalities (Key Findings, NEC vs. Error Rate Gap).
claims.evidence: Turkey reproduces closely: 6.70% error / 4.06% NEC (1.65x) vs paper's 6.7% / 4.2% (1.6x) using real Zenodo DCIC data with frozen ResNet-50 features. NHANES reproduces at 21.57% error / 15.70% NEC (1.37x) vs paper's 21.7% / 14.8% (1.5x) on real CDC data with N=7,457 — error rate matches well, NEC is somewhat higher but the qualitative divergence (NEC < error rate) holds across both modalities.

claims.claim: Costs are derived from three sources: multi-annotator vote-margin log-odds (Equation 3), threshold distance for continuous measurements (Equation 4), and direct annotator confidence ratings (Cost Derivation Methods section).
claims.evidence: All three cost-derivation transforms are implemented and validated: Eq. 3 (vote-margin log-odds) confirmed on real Jigsaw and Turkey votes (np.allclose assertion passes), Eq. 4 (threshold distance Δ=SBP−130) confirmed on real NHANES data, and the direct-rating transform (Δ=score−midpoint) demonstrated on synthetic data since iNaturalist's Gemini ratings were never released.

claims.claim: Table 2 reports fine-tuned model results including Jigsaw RoBERTa at 1.8% NEC / 4.7% error rate, Turkey ResNet at 2.3% NEC / 4.8% error rate, and iNaturalist ResNet at 9.3% NEC / 11.1% error rate (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Only a reduced-scope proxy was run: top-block (layer4+fc) fine-tuning of ResNet-50 on a 2,500-image Turkey subset, 3 seeds, on MPS (no GPU available — HF Jobs returned HTTP 402). Results (3.87% NEC / 6.67% error) show a negligible 0.06-point shift that is not statistically meaningful. Jigsaw RoBERTa-FT and iNaturalist ResNet-FT were not attempted.

claims.claim: Cost-weighted training produces inconsistent benefits: effects are negligible on Jigsaw and NHANES but counterproductive on iNaturalist, where cost-weighting increased NEC by 6.6% (The Cost-Weighting Paradox section).
claims.evidence: The broad 'inconsistency' claim is supported (different effects across datasets), but specific per-dataset results diverge: Jigsaw shows +11.4% NEC from cost-weighting (harmful, not 'negligible' as claimed), NHANES shows -1.9% (roughly matching 'negligible'), and iNaturalist (+6.6% counterproductive) is entirely blocked. The synthetic positive control also fails to reproduce the paper's reported benefit under any tested configuration.

claims.claim: Δ-regression training yields calibration information with mean absolute error of approximately 0.3 log-odds but provides no accuracy advantage over standard cross-entropy training (Performance Results / Training Strategies Evaluated section).
claims.evidence: Jigsaw Δ-regression MAE of 0.325 log-odds closely matches the paper's ~0.30. Regression NEC is slightly lower than standard CE on all three real datasets (Jigsaw: 1.96 vs 2.02, significant; Turkey: 3.80 vs 4.06, n.s.; NHANES: 15.40 vs 15.70, n.s.), but differences are practically negligible (≤0.3 NEC points), supporting the claim that regression provides calibration information without meaningful accuracy loss.

vbabenko97/repro-instance-level-costs.overall: The logbook convincingly reproduces the paper's central NEC-vs-error-rate divergence on real data across text (Jigsaw 2.92x), image (Turkey 1.65x), and tabular (NHANES 1.37x) modalities, and confirms the Δ-regression MAE. Fine-tuned Table 2 results are only toy-scale due to GPU unavailability, and the cost-weighting inconsistency claim has mixed evidence with iNaturalist blocked and Jigsaw diverging from the paper.

YMRohit/icml2026-27364-kernel-bounds-log.paper_title: On Uniform Error Bounds for Kernel Regression under Non-Gaussian Noise

claims.claim: Proposition 3.3 extends the uniform error bound to correlated (non-i.i.d.) sub-Gaussian noise, with Corollary 3.4 recovering the conditionally-independent sub-Gaussian case as a special case (Section 3.1, Proposition 3.3, Corollary 3.4)
claims.evidence: C2 experiment tests Prop 3.3 on 8 correlation structures (AR(1) phi up to 0.99, GP-correlated) x t in {10,50,200}: 0 invalid cells out of 168 (T2 core inequality, 80k draws/cell) and 0 out of 96 (T1 full uniform bound, 600 reps). At phi=0, Prop 3.3 and the i.i.d. bound produce identical violation rates, confirming Corollary 3.4 recovers the conditionally-independent case. The i.i.d. bound (Thm 3.2(a) misapplied) is invalid in 54/168 T2 cells and 12/96 T1 cells, with worst-case violation 241x nominal delta.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.5 derives a uniform bound for heavy-tailed (sub-exponential) noise via a truncation argument, achieving a 71.6% success rate at the final iteration in the sub-exponential (chi-squared, sigma_m=0.1) numerical experiment (Section 3.2, Section 5.3, Proposition 3.5)
claims.evidence: The C3 sub-exponential experiment (chi-squared, sigma_M=0.1) implements Prop 3.5 with truncation, but Prop 3.5 achieves 0% success at t=1000 (matching the paper's own target of '0% for t>50'). The 71.6% figure appears to belong to Thm 3.2(c), not Prop 3.5, based on the logbook's extracted paper targets (success_3_2c_at_t1000=0.716). The reproduction obtains 99.79% for Thm 3.2(c), not 71.6%; a 15-configuration sensitivity sweep yields 78.0%-99.9%, never reaching 71.6%. The specific numerical claim is not reproduced and appears misattributed.

claims.claim: In the safe control experiment with nominal dynamics f_nom(x_t,u_t)=0.5x_t+u_t-1 and unknown residual f(x_t)=exp(-x_t^2)sin(10x_t), the proposed uniform bounds yield higher feasibility and lower cost than baseline uncertainty quantification methods (Section 5.2, Figures 5-6)
claims.evidence: C3-T2 safe control experiment (bounded noise, f_nom=0.5x+u, f=exp(-x^2)sin(10x), t=1000): proposed bounds achieve 100% feasibility (Thm 3.2(a) and (b)) vs 99.4% (Abbasi-Yadkori) and 88.7% (Fiedler), with mean cost 0.627 vs 1.846 and 3.017 respectively (optimal=0.337). The proposed bounds dominate on both metrics across the full t-grid, with AY worst for t<=233.

claims.claim: In the uncertainty-region-size experiment sweeping noise bound m_bar in {0.01, 0.1, 1} and input dimension n_x in {1,2,3} with confidence parameter delta=0.001 over up to 1000 data points, the proposed bounds are consistently tighter than the Abbasi-Yadkori baseline (Section 5.1, Figures 3-4)
claims.evidence: C3-T1 tests 5 of 9 (n_x, m_bar) configurations (all three m values for n_x=1; all three n_x values for m=0.1) with delta=0.001, t up to 1000, 20-50 MC runs. Abbasi-Yadkori is never tighter than the proposed bound in any of 75 cells. AY/proposed ratio at t=1000 ranges from 1.85 to 8.31, growing with input dimension (2.33 at n_x=1, 3.24 at n_x=2, 8.31 at n_x=3 for m=0.1).

YMRohit/icml2026-27364-kernel-bounds-log.overall: The logbook provides strong, statistically rigorous evidence for Claims 1, 3, and 4: correlated-noise bounds are valid and separate from i.i.d. assumptions, safe-control feasibility/cost dominate baselines, and uncertainty regions are consistently tighter than Abbasi-Yadkori. Claim 2 is inconclusive because the 71.6% success rate is not reproduced (99.79% obtained, sensitivity sweep 78-99.9%) and appears misattributed to Prop 3.5 when the paper's own targets assign it to Thm 3.2(c).

Aza33/repro-beyond-text-to-sql-can-llms-.paper_title: Beyond Text-to-SQL: Can LLMs Really Debug Enterprise ETL SQL?

The benchmark and evaluation code are unavailable, blocking any real reproduction.

claims.claim: Persuasive Privacy (PP) is defined via a Stackelberg game in which a Sender commits to a mechanism M and a Bayes-rational Receiver updates beliefs, with privacy assessed by the tail bound inf_{S,x,Q} P_x[ΔS(Q,T,x) ≤ κ] ≥ 1-δ (Section 3, Definition 3).
claims.evidence: The source-conformance audit (verify_definition3_source.py) checks 12 required DOM nodes across Sections 2.2–2.5 and 3, rejects all 19 semantic mutants (inf-to-sup, drop S/x/Q, replace Q_T, data-dependent M, commitment-after-reveal), and an independent raw-source audit confirms the same. The operational instantiation in verify_pp.py computes the Bayes-rational posterior and (κ,δ) tail bound for concrete mechanisms M1 (κ=1.02, coverage 0.937≥0.9) and M2 (κ=0.70).

claims.claim: Proposition 6 shows a mechanism satisfies (ϵ,δ)-probabilistic differential privacy if and only if it satisfies (L,ℋ,ϵ,δ)-persuasive privacy, where L is the negative log-probability score, establishing full equivalence between the two frameworks (Section 4, Proposition 6).
claims.evidence: run_privacy_audit.py enumerates 9600 finite PDP/PP comparison cases across 48 kernels (including 2400 pure-DP δ=0 cases), computing PDP from likelihood ratios and PP from Bayes posteriors independently; max probability gap is 0.0 with zero pass/fail mismatches. The fixed-friendly-prior negative control falsely passes (1.0) while the worst-prior and PDP both fail (0.01), confirming the infimum is necessary.

claims.claim: Proposition 7 establishes that the deterministic empirical-average mechanism M(x,·)=δ_{x̄} satisfies (ℐ,𝒢_x^r,κ^r,0)-persuasive privacy with κ^r = r_1 + log r_2, giving privacy guarantees for a deterministic algorithm that standard differential privacy cannot certify (Section 5, Proposition 7).
claims.evidence: Across 72 positive-definite Gaussian priors verified to lie in G_x^r, every marginal deterministic-average relative score lies below the r_1+log(r_2) bound (worst slack −0.598), with two independent Gaussian-conditioning paths agreeing to 4.44e-16. The out-of-class negative control violates the bound (4.69 > 0.84) and ordinary-DP zero-support violation is confirmed, demonstrating standard DP cannot certify this release.

claims.claim: Proposition 4 shows persuasive privacy satisfies receiver post-processing (the receiver cannot amplify privacy loss via output transformation), while Proposition 5 shows it does not satisfy the sender post-processing inequality that differential privacy does (Section 3.2, Propositions 4-5).
claims.evidence: verify_postprocessing_exact.py proves receiver post-processing via exact rational Bayes identity Q(x|t,u)=Q(x|t) on 12 positive events, with an x-dependent kernel negative control changing posteriors on 6/6 events. For sender post-processing, an exact rational counterexample shows base mechanism bad masses [0, 1/5] become [0, 1/4] after coarsening (merging first two outputs), violating the δ=1/5 guarantee, confirmed by both directed PDP and direct PP calculation at Q(x')=1/10.

claims.claim: Proposition 3 shows that for conjugate prior families, composing two persuasive-privacy mechanisms with parameters (κ1,δ1) and (κ2,δ2) yields a mechanism satisfying (𝒮,𝒬_x,κ1+κ2,δ1+δ2)-PP (Section 3.1, Proposition 3).
claims.evidence: verify_composition_exact.py performs an exact rational audit over 9900 joint atoms with 39114 composition budget checks (10905 nontrivial), exercising adaptive second mechanisms and confirming Boole-Fréchet equality witnesses; all checks pass. An independent script (audit_composition_proof_chain.py, sharing no implementation) checks 20470 Boole-Fréchet cases and 2304 additive-score cases, with fail-sensitive controls showing max-κ, max-δ, averaged-conditional, and non-conjugate variants all break a required proof step.

DineshAI/OeY3gcvlvh.overall: The logbook provides strong computational verification of all five claims using exact rational arithmetic, exhaustive finite enumeration, independent verification scripts, and fail-sensitive negative controls. The main limitation is that finite-state checks cannot constitute complete proofs over arbitrary measurable spaces, but the scope is honestly stated and the evidence is as rigorous as computational verification allows.

imadreamerboy/repro-row-stochastic-matri.paper_title: Row-Stochastic Matrices Can Provably Outperform Doubly Stochastic Matrices in Decentralized Learning

claims.claim: In the weighted Hilbert space L²(λ;R^d), the λ-induced row-stochastic mixing matrix W is self-adjoint whereas the doubly stochastic matrix W^ds is not, and this non-self-adjointness introduces additional multiplicative penalty terms (κ_λ > 1 and λ_max² > 1) that amplify consensus error under the doubly stochastic design (Section 5.2, Section 6.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook numerically verifies self-adjointness on a single 16-node topology (weighted-similarity asymmetry 1.621e-16 for row-stochastic vs 7.982e-01 for doubly stochastic), but does not compute the penalty terms κ_λ or λ_max², nor test consensus error amplification — covering only one component of the claim on one finite instance.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.5 gives O(1/T) convergence rates for both row-stochastic and doubly stochastic strategies, but the row-stochastic strategy achieves strictly smaller non-asymptotic consensus error and can converge faster even when its spectral gap is smaller than that of the doubly stochastic strategy (Theorem 6.5).
claims.evidence: A deliberately small least-squares proxy (n=16, d=10, T=300, 5 seeds, proxy step size 0.004) shows a marginal tail-metric advantage of -0.000443407 for row-stochastic, but this does not verify the O(1/T) rates, the spectral gap condition, or non-asymptotic consensus error bounds from Theorem 6.5.

claims.claim: Theorem 7.1 derives a sufficient condition on the spectral gaps, 1 − ρ_Λ ≥ max{(1+η)κ_λ^(-1/3), λ_max^(-1/2)}(1 − ρ_J), under which the row-stochastic design provably converges strictly faster than the doubly stochastic design (Theorem 7.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states the sufficient condition was not evaluated ('Sufficient condition evaluated: false') because η is existential/unspecified and the graph edge list was not machine-readable, providing no numerical evidence for or against Theorem 7.1's condition.

claims.claim: Corollary 7.3 and Algorithm 2 give topology construction guidelines showing that when node degrees scale proportionally with their assigned weights (d_i/d_j matching λ_i/λ_j within bounds set by R), the row-stochastic design outperforms the doubly stochastic design, satisfying a Loewner order condition on the graph Laplacians (Corollary 7.3, Remark 7.4, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: The degree-weight proportionality check failed on the selected regular topology (equal degree 7, heterogeneous λ, L1 distance 46.2), but this only shows the tested topology does not satisfy the guidelines — it provides no evidence that satisfying the Corollary 7.3 conditions leads to outperformance.

imadreamerboy/repro-row-stochastic-matri.overall: The logbook provides a clean-room numerical check confirming self-adjointness of the row-stochastic construction versus non-self-adjointness of the doubly stochastic reference on one 16-node topology, plus a small proxy showing marginal row-stochastic advantage on a least-squares task. It does not evaluate the paper's theorems, penalty terms, sufficient conditions, or topology construction guidelines in any substantive way.

imadreamerboy/repro-to-grok-grokking-pro.paper_title: To Grok Grokking: Provable Grokking in Ridge Regression

claims.claim: The paper proves end-to-end grokking for zero-teacher ridge regression, including early training overfitting, delayed poor generalization, and eventual low generalization error (Theorem 4.1)
claims.evidence: Claim 1 concerns Theorem 4.1, a mathematical proof for the zero-teacher setting. The logbook's current evidence is a Section 5.1 simulation with a realizable teacher (not zero-teacher), and the earlier zero-teacher proxy was explicitly superseded. The logbook states it 'cannot establish the paper's asymptotic, high-probability, or arbitrarily-small-error statements' and does not verify the theorem proof.

claims.claim: The end-to-end grokking result is extended from the zero-teacher setting to realizable ridge regression with arbitrary realizable teacher functions (Theorem 4.2)
claims.evidence: Claim 2 concerns Theorem 4.2, a proof for arbitrary realizable teacher functions. The logbook runs simulations with one specific teacher (unit-norm isotropic direction), not arbitrary teachers, and does not verify the mathematical proof. No theorem verification is attempted.

claims.claim: Separate theorems decompose grokking into training-loss convergence, poor generalization during overfitting, and eventual generalization (Theorems 4.4-4.6)
claims.evidence: Claim 3 concerns Theorems 4.4–4.6, which are mathematical proofs decomposing grokking into stages. The logbook's simulations show a staged threshold-crossing pattern (train loss crosses before population loss), which is empirically consistent with the decomposition, but no theorem proof is verified and the logbook explicitly disclaims theorem verification.

claims.claim: Decreasing weight decay and sample size can amplify grokking time in ridge-regression simulations, matching the paper's quantitative hyperparameter predictions (Figure 2)
claims.evidence: The logbook reconstructs the Figure 2 weight-decay panel at the paper's scale (n=100, m=1000, 20 draws per condition), showing mean delay increasing from 75,087 at λ=2^-15 to 1,205,250 at λ=2^-19 — a clean ~2× delay per 2× decrease in λ. The sample-size sweep (n=10 to n=160) shows a directionally consistent but weak effect (delay 23,474 vs 22,140). Equation (8) diagnostics held in all evaluable rows, though hidden theorem constants were not fitted.

claims.claim: Two-layer ReLU experiments qualitatively reproduce the predicted grokking-time dependence on hyperparameters beyond the linear setting (Figures 3 and 4)
claims.evidence: The logbook contains no two-layer ReLU experiments. Figures 3 and 4 are never addressed; the reproduction covers only the linear ridge-regression simulations of Section 5.1.

imadreamerboy/repro-to-grok-grokking-pro.overall: The logbook provides a careful partial reconstruction of the Section 5.1 ridge-regression simulations at the paper's scale, with strong evidence for weight-decay-driven delay scaling and staged grokking in the linear setting. However, it does not verify any of the paper's theorems (Claims 1–3), does not address the two-layer ReLU experiments (Claim 5), and only partially reconstructs Figure 2 (Claim 4).

jomasego/repro-efficient-synthetic-netwo.paper_title: Efficient Synthetic Network Generation via Latent Embedding Reconstruction

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 decomposes the KL divergence between the true and synthetic network distributions into three error terms: sparsity parameter estimation error (E_ρ), embedding distribution approximation error (E_Φ), and generative model error in the latent space (E_gen) (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook only checked that E_ρ depends solely on ρ in a small n=200, r=2 setup; it did not numerically verify that the total KL equals E_ρ + E_Φ + E_gen, so the full three-term decomposition was never empirically confirmed.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 shows that the sparsity parameter estimation error E_ρ is O_p((log n / (w_n n))^{1/2}) under the sparse network regime (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: The verification is circular: it assumes the estimator rate ρ_err = O_p(√(log n/(w_n n))) and then shows E_ρ is proportional to it via a quadratic KL approximation; no independent estimation of E_ρ from data was performed, and the recovered constant (0.0386) does not match the theoretical value (0.0268).

claims.claim: On simulated sparse networks with n=1500 nodes and r=4 latent dimensions, the diffusion-based variant SyNG-D achieves a triangle density RMSE of 0.63×10^-4 and clustering coefficient RMSE of 4.58×10^-3, outperforming VGAE on both metrics (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The MLP DDPM variant (8000 CPU steps) was substituted for the paper's default ForestDiffusion variant, producing notably different quantitative values (Tri RMSE 1.13×10⁻⁴ vs paper 0.63×10⁻⁴; Clus RMSE 26.50×10⁻³ vs paper 4.58×10⁻³), and VGAE was not independently run—only paper-reported VGAE numbers were cited for comparison.

claims.claim: On real-world networks including PolBlogs, YouTube, DBLP, and Yelp, SyNG-D and SyNG-R achieve the best or competitive performance on triangle density, clustering coefficient, eigenvalue distribution, and degree centrality metrics (Tables 2-6).
claims.evidence: Only PolBlogs (n=1222) was evaluated out of the four claimed real-world datasets (PolBlogs, YouTube, DBLP, Yelp), and the MLP variant was used instead of the forest default; the claim covering all four datasets and multiple tables was not substantively reproduced.

claims.claim: SyNG-D requires the lowest equivalent FLOPs (e-FLOPs) among compared generators across network sizes, while GRAN and EDGE require substantially higher computational cost despite worse fidelity (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The e-FLOPs comparison is purely analytical with rough order-of-magnitude estimates (~6×10⁹, etc.) and no actual measured FLOPs from running the methods; moreover, the logbook's own table shows VGAE with lower e-FLOPs than SyNG-D at every network size, potentially contradicting the 'lowest among compared generators' claim.

claims.claim: On higher-order structural metrics such as 4-node graphlet counts and 4-cycle counts, SyNG variants outperform EDGE, GRAN, and CELL baselines (Table 7).
claims.evidence: Only the 4-cycle metric was computed on PolBlogs (the Orbit/graphlet metric was deferred due to ORCA compilation), using the MLP variant; the reproduced SyNG-R (0.23) and SyNG-D (0.47) 4-cycle errors are both worse than the paper-reported CELL baseline (0.20), so the claim of outperforming CELL is not supported by the reproduction.

jomasego/repro-efficient-synthetic-netwo.overall: This logbook provides only partial, reduced-scope reproductions: theoretical claims were verified through circular or incomplete numerical checks, empirical claims used an MLP substitute instead of the paper's forest diffusion default with mismatched quantitative values, only one of four real-world datasets was tested, and no independent baseline runs were conducted. The reproduction is insufficient to confirm the paper's claims at full scale.

NaveenVenu/P3Mnh7mF5a.paper_title: Provable Benefits of RLVR over SFT for Reasoning Models: Learning to Backtrack Efficiently

claims.claim: Theorem 2 proves that a model trained via SFT on shortest-path (optimal) trajectories converges to forward transition probabilities of 1 but keeps backward-pointing transition probabilities fixed at their pretrained values of L/(L+1) and 1/(L+1), i.e., it never learns to backtrack (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: No SFT training was performed. The logbook merely assumes the Theorem 2 converged probabilities (a_j,c_j→0.97; b_j,d_j fixed at L/(L+1) and 1/(L+1)) as simulation inputs, rather than independently verifying that SFT training produces them.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 proves that RLVR training drives all four transition probabilities (a_j, b_j, c_j, d_j) arbitrarily close to 1 in finite time by incorporating the model's own failed exploration trajectories during policy-gradient updates (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: No RLVR training was performed. The logbook uses 'all four probabilities → close to 1 (we use 0.97)' as a direct input assumption from Theorem 3, not an empirically measured outcome of policy-gradient training.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 establishes an exponential inference-time compute separation: RLVR-trained policies require Θ(WK) expected steps to reach the goal versus Θ(W·L^K) for SFT-trained policies, on a graph with W parallel branches, depth K, and L multi-edges per junction (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook simulates the paper's graph model and produces concrete numbers showing SFT cost growing exponentially (semi-log slope 1.897 vs expected log(5)=1.609) and RLVR linearly (log-log slope 1.21 vs ~1.0). However, this is a simplified setup: K only goes to 6 (not 15 as in the paper), only the return-journey subtask is simulated (not full hitting time to goal), and the transition probabilities are assumed from Theorems 2/3 rather than derived from actual training, making the verification partially circular.

claims.claim: Corollary 1 shows that even equipping the SFT policy with a duplicate-state-avoiding search agent only improves its complexity to Θ(WKL), still a factor of L worse than RLVR's Θ(WK) (Corollary 1).
claims.evidence: Corollary 1 (SFT + duplicate-state-avoiding search agent achieving Θ(WKL)) is never addressed in the logbook. No experiment involving a search agent was conducted.

claims.claim: Theorem 5 shows that distilling RLVR-generated reasoning traces via supervised fine-tuning recovers the efficient Θ(WK) complexity, and synthetic experiments with W=15, K=15, L=5 confirm hitting times converging to the predicted 4WK=900 (Theorem 5, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Theorem 5 (distillation recovering Θ(WK) complexity and synthetic experiments with W=15, K=15, L=5 converging to 4WK=900) is never addressed. No distillation experiment or Figure 3 reproduction was attempted.

NaveenVenu/P3Mnh7mF5a.overall: The logbook provides a single toy-scale Markov-chain simulation that numerically checks the exponential-separation consequence of Theorem 4 by plugging in the theoretically-derived probabilities from Theorems 2 and 3 as assumptions, at reduced depth (K≤6 vs 15) and only for the return-journey subtask. No actual SFT or RLVR training, no distillation experiments, and no reproduction of Theorems 2, 3, 5, or Corollary 1 were performed.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows that if a predictor gamma-hat satisfies weighted multicalibration with parameter alpha = epsilon/(2m), then running the standard optimal matching algorithm on gamma-hat's outputs achieves reward within additive error epsilon of the best decision rule in class C applied to the original predictor gamma (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The experiment runs 30 trials on n=4 bipartite graphs with a single identity decision rule in C, checking that the reward gap is within ε=0.35. Real runs and numbers, but n=4 with a trivial one-element decision class is a clearly simplified setup, not a meaningful test of the theorem.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 gives a sample complexity bound of O~(r n^6 log(r|C|/(epsilon delta)) / epsilon^4) samples to learn a multicalibrated predictor achieving precision epsilon and failure probability delta, where n is the number of agents/items and r is the mean-squared error of the initial predictor (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook merely evaluates the formula T = r·n^6·log(...)/ε^4 numerically and checks that the scaling exponents match (e.g., n^6 has exponent ~6). This is circular arithmetic—verifying that a formula has the exponents it was written with—rather than running any learning algorithm to empirically measure sample complexity.

claims.claim: In the worst case the sample complexity bound reduces to O~(n^8/epsilon^4), but the bound improves substantially when the initial predictor already has low MSE, reflecting realistic industrial-scale prediction settings (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Same as Claim 2: the logbook plugs r=n² into the formula and confirms the exponent is ~8, and shows T is smaller when r is smaller. This is trivially true from the formula itself and provides no independent evidence for the theorem or the 'realistic industrial-scale' claim.

claims.claim: A boosting-style multicalibration algorithm (Algorithm 1) iteratively updates the predictor by identifying and correcting miscalibration on 'edge e is chosen by decision rule c' subgroups, adapting fairness-style multicalibration techniques to the matching setting (Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The boosting algorithm is implemented and run on n=4 graphs over 10 trials, reporting convergence in avg 4 iterations. Real code and numbers, but the implementation corrects bias on individual edges rather than the paper's 'edge e chosen by decision rule c' subgroups, uses a trivial decision class, and operates at toy scale.

claims.claim: The multicalibration-for-matching guarantee is shown to generalize beyond bipartite matching to best-action selection, learning with rejection, and max-weight matroid basis selection, each attaining improved sample complexities based on problem structure (Section on extensions).
claims.evidence: Three extensions are tested on small synthetic instances (best-action n=5, rejection n=4, matroid n=5/k=3) with 20 trials each, all reporting 100% within ε. Real runs but clearly toy-scale with simplified implementations that don't exercise the full problem structure described in the paper.

Sor0ush/repro-multicalibration-yields-be.overall: The logbook runs small-scale synthetic experiments (n=4–6) that loosely exercise the paper's constructs, but for the sample complexity claims (2, 3) it only performs circular formula evaluation with no actual learning experiments. The experimental claims (1, 4, 5) are addressed on toy instances with trivial decision classes and simplified algorithms, providing weak evidence at best.

claims.claim: Jacobian Effective Rank (JER), a measure of input-output functional sensitivity, correlates strongly with compositional binding accuracy (r=0.65, p=0.001), and combined with a discriminability measure explains 74% of variance in binding accuracy (Correlation analysis / regression results).

SabaPivot/repro-spurious-correlation-rem.paper_title: Is Spurious Correlation Removal Always Learnable?

claims.claim: Under the Planted Clique hardness hypothesis (planted cliques of size k = m^(1/2−δ) in random graphs are not recoverable in polynomial time), there exist samplable multi-environment linear-Gaussian instances that are statistically learnable with polynomially many samples via exhaustive search but intractable for any polynomial-time algorithm (Hypothesis 3.1, Theorem 3.8).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides a concrete sign-invariant counterexample satisfying the stated fixed-radius margin of Hypothesis 3.2 while retaining two distinct maximizers, directly contradicting the exact-uniqueness step in Lemma 3.5/Theorem 3.8(a). Additionally, the source audit finds no reduction from Planted Clique Hypothesis 3.1 to the linear-Gaussian family; Theorem 3.8 relies on a separate black-box Hypothesis 3.2.

claims.claim: A phase transition in label-induced spurious correlation removal occurs at critical sample size n* ∝ k(d−k)/(|E|γ²), where k is the invariant subspace dimension, d the ambient dimension, |E| the number of environments, and γ the environment separation parameter; below n*/2 all estimators fail with constant error while above 2n* estimators achieve error O(k(d−k)/(n|E|γ²)) (Theorem 4.15).
claims.evidence: 110,592 independent fits with d=12, k=4, |E|=9 yield a supercritical projector-error slope of -0.9216 (R²=0.9989), closely matching the predicted -1 scaling. After normalizing by n|E|γ²/[k(d-k)], supercritical cells collapse to mean 1.8336 with CV 4.8%, confirming simultaneous inverse dependence on n, |E|, and γ². The directional-richness premise λ_min(F)/γ²=1.0000 is directly audited.

claims.claim: The predicted phase transition is validated empirically: exhaustive search reaches 75% accuracy using up to 27x fewer samples than polynomial-time methods on synthetic instances, and sharp transitions near the predicted critical sample size appear on both synthetic data and ColoredMNIST (Figure 1, Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: The 27x endpoint is source-supported (9000/330=27.27 at d=81), but the claim's sharp-transition-on-ColoredMNIST clause is contradicted: the manuscript itself describes ColoredMNIST improvement as 'smoother,' and the released supplement contains no ColoredMNIST implementation. Furthermore, above d=25 the code switches from exhaustive enumeration to guided random search, and the mean_gap=9.75x is right-censored, undermining the exhaustive-search framing.

claims.claim: Diversity across environments is necessary for removal to succeed: performance improves sharply once γ > 0, whereas low-diversity settings (γ ≈ 0) show persistent failure, and increasing diversity from 'low' to 'high' substantially improves worst-group accuracy on CelebA and Waterbirds and OOD performance on ColoredMNIST (Figure 2c, Table 2).
claims.evidence: The official synthetic suite shows selection accuracy rising from 0.0625 at zero/tiny diversity to 1.0 at medium/large diversity. A controlled ColoredMNIST study with 54 independently trained models (holding pooled flip probability fixed at 0.30) shows OOD accuracy gains of +34.5 points (N=1000) and +6.87 points (N=5000) when increasing only between-environment diversity. CelebA and Waterbirds were not reproduced due to missing executable protocols, but the core mechanism and ColoredMNIST claim are supported.

SabaPivot/repro-spurious-correlation-rem.overall: The logbook provides strong experimental evidence for the phase-transition scaling law (Claim 2) and the environment-diversity mechanism (Claim 4) through large-scale synthetic and ColoredMNIST experiments, while identifying genuine proof gaps and empirical contradictions in the hardness attribution (Claim 1) and the sharp-transition-on-ColoredMNIST conjunction (Claim 3).

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows the algorithm achieves expected additive loss O(min(√b·max(EMD(p̂,p),1), b log b)), where EMD(p̂,p) is the Earth Mover's distance between the predicted and true distributions and b is the buy-ski-rental cost ratio (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: The logbook ran a finite suite of 326,700 prediction/truth pairs on b ∈ {4, 9, 16} with 330 four-unit PMFs over eight days, checking tail-shift, U-tail, truncation, and scaled-truncation inequalities with 0 failures. This verifies the mechanism's arithmetic on small instances but cannot prove the asymptotic O(min(√b·max(EMD,1), b log b)) bound.

claims.claim: The algorithm attains consistency O(√b) when the prediction error (EMD) is 0 and robustness O(b log b) when the prediction is arbitrarily inaccurate, without needing to know the prediction error bound in advance (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Perfect-prediction gaps divided by √b were ≤1.0 for b ∈ {4, 9, 16} across 330 cases each, and the code confirms the algorithm accepts only p̂ and b (not the true distribution). However, these are finite checks on very small b values that cannot establish asymptotic O(√b) consistency or O(b log b) robustness.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 proves a matching lower bound showing no algorithm can achieve additive loss o(b)·EMD(p̂,p), establishing that the √b factor in Theorem 1 is necessary (Theorem 4, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: The logbook's source-level audit found that Theorem 4 proves the o(b)·EMD lower bound, while the distinct Theorem 5 proves the o(√b)·max(EMD,1) lower bound. The claim attributes the √b-necessity result to Theorem 4, but the source shows that result belongs to Theorem 5, making the claim's theorem attribution incorrect.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a Pareto-optimal consistency-robustness tradeoff: any algorithm achieving O(√b) consistency must incur Ω(b log b) robustness (Theorem 6, Section 4)
claims.evidence: The logbook ran a finite deterministic-threshold replay for b ∈ {16, 36, 64, 100} with C=1, finding thresholds {5, 18, 42, 78} with ratios to b log b of {0.113, 0.140, 0.158, 0.169}. This shows a finite pressure trend but explicitly does not prove Theorem 6's randomized asymptotic lower bound.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 introduces a parameterized algorithm with expected cost c(ALG_p) ≤ min{(1+λ)(c(OPT_p)+B), (1+1/λ)c(OPT_p)}, allowing explicit interpolation between trusting the prediction and worst-case guarantees via λ ∈ [0,1] (Theorem 2, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: On the exhaustive grid for b ∈ {4, 9, 16}, λ=0 matched Algorithm 1 in 108,900/108,900 cases, and positive λ values satisfied the reciprocal-branch inequality with 0 failures. However, the check cannot identify the theorem's unspecified big-O quantity B(p̂,p), leaving the full bound unverified on these small finite instances.

imadreamerboy/repro-ski-rental-distribut.overall: The logbook provides finite computational checks of the paper's algorithmic mechanisms on small instances (b ∈ {4, 9, 16}) and a source-level audit that correctly identifies a theorem misattribution in Claim 3. The finite checks verify proof-chain inequalities and interpolation behavior but are far too small to constitute verification of the paper's asymptotic theoretical results.

claims.claim: WIRE applies rotary position encodings to graphs by using Laplacian spectral coordinates to define graph-dependent rotation angles (Figure 1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: An independent NumPy implementation computes Laplacian eigenvectors as spectral coordinates, forms rotation angles via features @ frequencies.T, and applies block-diagonal 2D rotations on a 12-node graph; the rotation orthogonality error is 2.2e-16 and outputs are finite, directly demonstrating the WIRE construction as described.

claims.claim: The WIRE transformation is equivariant to node-order permutations up to sign flips and rotations in degenerate eigenspaces (Lemma 1).
claims.evidence: On a 14-node graph, sign-aligned spectral features after permutation differ by 1.3e-15 and WIRE outputs after frequency-gauge reparameterization differ by 1.2e-15; on a 4-cycle with repeated eigenvalue 2.0, the degenerate subspace has minimum principal cosine 1.0, confirming equivariance up to sign flips and degenerate-eigenspace rotations.

claims.claim: Regular RoPE is recovered as a special case of WIRE on grid graphs with appropriate learnable frequencies (Theorem 2, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: On a path graph of N=25, the second Laplacian eigenvector matches the normalized closed-form formula -cos((i+0.5)π/N) to 1.4e-14, and bijective coordinate recovery via arccos yields positions 0…24 with max error 4.9e-12 and strict monotonicity, confirming the 1D grid special case of Theorem 2.

claims.claim: WIRE asymptotically depends on graph effective resistance under the paper's spectral-feature assumptions (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The spectral resistance identity R(i,j)=||r_i−r_j||² holds to 2.2e-16 on a 10-node graph with resistance-weighted features; over 4096 Gaussian frequency draws (std=0.08), the MC mean rotated score (11.9539) matches the first-order prediction qᵀk(1−ω²R/2) (11.9540) with error 4.9e-5, well within the MC standard error of 4.2e-4.

claims.claim: Experiments report WIRE improvements on synthetic monochromatic-subgraph and shortest-path tasks, point-cloud transformers, and efficient graph transformer benchmarks (Table 1, Table 2, Table 3, Table 4).
claims.evidence: Only a scaled-down monochromatic-subgraph proxy was run: 1,600/400 graphs (vs 10k/1k), 80 epochs (vs 250), 2-layer 32d model (vs 4-layer), 2 seeds, showing a marginal −0.66% RMSE change; shortest-path, point-cloud, and GraphGPS benchmark experiments were not addressed at all.

Hrushi/repro-rotary-position-encodings-f.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, independent NumPy verification of all four theoretical claims (WIRE construction, permutation equivariance, RoPE recovery on grids, effective-resistance dependence) with machine-precision numerical agreement. The experimental claim is only weakly supported by a small proxy covering one of four benchmark types at greatly reduced scale.

jomasego/repro-understanding-dynamic-com.paper_title: Understanding Dynamic Compute Allocation in Recurrent Transformers

claims.claim: The ANIRA framework supports token-level variable-depth computation in recurrent transformers via two decision mechanisms, early allocation (ANIRA-E) and online halting (ANIRA-O), with a maximum recurrent depth of D=6 for most tasks and D=14 for the MANO task (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The only actual runs were 200-step trainings on Apple Silicon MPS with hidden=64: LANO (loss 1.183, expected depth 3.51) and MANO (6.4% accuracy, expected depth 2.94). MANO was run with D=6, not D=14 as the claim specifies, and the HF Jobs L4 run was cancelled. This confirms the code runs and produces variable-depth output, but at drastically reduced scale and without testing the D=14 MANO configuration.

claims.claim: On the LANO synthetic-language benchmark, Spearman correlations between expected computation depth and token-level complexity proxies range from +0.456 to +0.666 (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook only quotes Table 1 values from the paper (+0.456 to +0.666). No ANIRA model was trained to convergence on LANO, no incremental PCFG parser was run, and no Spearman correlations were independently computed. The 200-step toy LANO run did not produce any correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Both ANIRA-E and ANIRA-O show sharp accuracy drops when evaluated on unseen input sizes despite allocating additional computation to those inputs, indicating models learn size-specific rather than generalizable solutions (Section 6.2, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook describes Figure 3 and quotes Section 6.2 from the paper but reports no actual CLRS-Text training or per-size accuracy evaluation. No experiments were executed to verify accuracy drops on unseen input sizes.

claims.claim: ANIRA-E's compute allocation decisions are best explained by static hub-structure features (regression coefficient +0.134), whereas ANIRA-O's online halting decisions are dominated by algorithmic execution-state features such as DFS depth (+0.302) and newly enabled nodes (-0.286) (Section 6.4, Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook quotes Table 2 and Appendix A.8 values from the paper but performed no BREVO training, no feature extraction, and no regression analysis. No independent numerical results were produced.

claims.claim: Training exhibits a two-phase compute dynamic: an initial rapid increase in allocated depth while the task is being learned, followed by a phase of compute reduction with maintained task performance (Section 6.3, Figures 4-5).
claims.evidence: The logbook describes Figures 4-5 from the paper but did not train ANIRA-E/O on MANO or BREVO for 250k steps with per-step accuracy and depth logging. No training dynamics curves were independently generated.

claims.claim: On GSM-Symbolic math problems, neither ANIRA-E nor ANIRA-O allocates more computation to harder problem splits (P1, P2) than to the Main split, limiting the interpretability of the compute-allocation signal in natural language settings (Section 6.6, Table 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook quotes Table 3 values from the paper but did not finetune any model on Nemotron-CC-Math or evaluate on GSM-Symbolic splits. No independent depth-allocation measurements were produced.

jomasego/repro-understanding-dynamic-com.overall: This logbook is primarily a paper summary with quoted values and reproduction requirements, not an actual reproduction. The only executed experiments were 200-step toy-scale trainings on Apple Silicon MPS (hidden=64) that confirm the code runs but do not reproduce any of the paper's quantitative claims at scale.

kpshinnik/smart-repro.paper_title: Sample Margin-Aware Recalibration of Temperature Scaling

claims.claim: Proposition 3.2 (g-Boundedness) proves that the logit gap g tightly bounds the range of feasible optimal temperatures T for a target confidence level (Section 3.4, Proposition 3.2).

No real model logits were used.

claims.claim: The SMART temperature network is a single-hidden-layer MLP with hidden dimension 16 taking the normalized logit gap as input and producing a softplus-activated temperature, using only 49 parameters total (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook instantiated the SMART network in PyTorch and provided a concrete parameter breakdown: W1 (16,1)=16, b1 (16,)=16, W2 (1,16)=16, b2 (1,)=1, totaling 49, matching the formula 3*d+1=3*16+1=49. This is a straightforward architectural verification with actual code.

claims.claim: On CIFAR-100 with ResNet-50, SMART achieves 1.37% ECE at 15 bins versus 1.96% for PTS and 3.67% for CTS (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook simply restates the paper's Table 1 values (SMART 1.37%, PTS 1.96%, CTS 3.67%) without running any experiment on CIFAR-100 with ResNet-50. The script output explicitly labels these as 'Results from paper's Table 1' — no calibration was performed on any real dataset.

claims.evidence: The logbook merely copies the paper's Table 1 numbers (SMART 0.68%, Spline 5.61%) with no experiment run on ImageNet-C. The script output says 'Results from paper's Table 1' — no distribution shift experiment was conducted.

claims.evidence: The logbook lists approximate values 'from paper's Figure 1(c)' (50 samples → ~1.5% ECE) but performed no actual calibration experiment with 50 validation samples on ImageNet. No data efficiency experiment was run.

claims.evidence: The logbook restates the paper's Table 3 runtime values (SMART 23.03s, PTS 90.44s, CTS 5457.55s) without measuring any actual runtimes. No timing experiment was conducted.

SabaPivot/repro-adam-degenerate.paper_title: Towards Understanding Adam Convergence on Highly Degenerate Polynomials

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that on the degenerate polynomial loss L(x) = (1/k) x^k for k >= 4, Adam achieves local linear convergence when beta_1 < beta_2^(k/(2(k-2))), with asymptotic rate x_{t+1}/x_t -> beta_2^(1/(2(k-2))) (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: 200,000-step Adam trajectories for six (k,β₁,β₂) configurations across k=4,6,8 show measured contraction rates matching β₂^(1/(2(k−2)) to within 3.79×10⁻⁶ in the worst case (k=8, β₂=.999), with five of six configurations agreeing to ≤1.22×10⁻¹¹. Fitted loss slopes independently match k log(β₂)/(2(k−2)).

claims.claim: Gradient Descent and Heavy-Ball Momentum both exhibit only sublinear convergence of order Theta(t^{-1/(k-2)}) on the same degenerate polynomial objective, established in Theorems 5.1 and 5.3 respectively.
claims.evidence: Two-million-step GD and Heavy-Ball runs for k=4,6,8 yield tail log-log slopes of −0.499995/−0.499854, −0.249998/−0.249940, and −0.166666/−0.166622 respectively, all within 1.46×10⁻⁴ of the theoretical −1/(k−2) exponent.

claims.claim: Remark 5.8 quantifies the resulting complexity separation: Gradient Descent requires iteration complexity T_epsilon ~ epsilon^{-(k-2)} to reach accuracy epsilon, whereas Adam achieves T_epsilon ~ (k-2) ln(1/epsilon) (Remark 5.8).
claims.evidence: Six-million-step GD trajectories give log₁₀ T vs log₁₀(1/ε) slopes of 2.000089 (k=4) and 4.000041 (k=6), matching k−2. Adam hitting-time regressions yield slopes 398.016 (k=4) and 795.972 (k=6) vs predicted 2(k−2)/ln(1/β₂) = 397.998 and 795.997 for β₂=.99.

claims.claim: Lemma 5.4 shows the second moment estimate satisfies v_t/v_{t-1} -> beta_2 asymptotically, decoupling v_t from the instantaneous squared gradient g_t^2 and producing an effective learning rate that grows as beta_2^{-t/2} (Lemma 5.4).
claims.evidence: With β₁=0 and 150,000 steps, tail means of v_t/v_{t−1} equal 0.9900000000000001, 0.9499999999999998, 0.9299999999999998, and 0.9990000000000002 for target β₂=.99,.95,.93,.999 across k=4,6,8, with all errors below 2.23×10⁻¹⁶, confirming decoupling from g_t² which vanishes faster.

claims.claim: Section 6 identifies three convergence regimes governed by beta_1 relative to beta_2: stable exponential convergence, an intermediate regime with an initial exponential phase followed by loss spikes from fixed-point instability, and a SignGD-like oscillatory regime under tight v_t-g_t^2 coupling (Section 6, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Sixty-thousand-step traces at k=4, β₁=.9 with β₂=.91, .895, and .80 respectively exhibit monotone geometric decay, transient exponential decay followed by loss spikes, and persistent SignGD-like oscillation, matching the three predicted regimes with interior (non-boundary) parameter choices.

claims.claim: Figure 3 shows the empirical phase diagram of stability boundaries across different degeneracy orders k matches the theoretical predictions of Equations 8-9 (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: A 40×40 grid (β₁∈[0,.995], β₂∈[.60,.995]) with 25,000 Adam steps per cell for k=4 yields 92.69% agreement (1,483/1,600 cells) with the Equations 8–9 theoretical mask, with disagreement concentrated near finite-time transition boundaries. Only k=4 is tested in the dense grid, though Claims 1–4 cover k=4,6,8 separately.

SabaPivot/repro-adam-degenerate.overall: The logbook provides concrete, numerically rigorous evidence supporting all six claims on the exact analyzed objective L(x)=x^k/k, with runs up to 6 million steps and a 40×40 phase diagram totaling 40M Adam updates. The reproduction is independent (no official code existed), matches the paper's ε=0/no-bias-correction setting, and reports specific numerical errors that are consistently tiny across multiple degeneracy orders.

SabaPivot/repro-tau2-bench.paper_title: $\tau^2$-Bench: Evaluating Conversational Agents in a Dual-Control Environment

claims.claim: tau2-bench introduces a telecom dual-control environment where both the conversational agent and simulated user can act with tools in a shared dynamic state (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The script claim1_env.py parses the actual cloned repo source via AST, confirming 13 agent tools and 30 user tools with disjoint @is_tool-decorated functions, two separate databases (db.toml and user_db.toml), and a sync_tools() method in environment.py (L39-93) that couples agent-DB state into the user's device each turn, establishing the shared dynamic state.

claims.claim: The telecom domain is modeled with separate agent and user databases, 13 agent tools, 30 user tools, and 114 sampled tasks from a 2,285-task full set (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The script claim2_counts.py directly counts @is_tool-decorated functions (13 agent, 30 user), reads tasks.json (2285 tasks) and split_tasks.json['base'] (114 tasks), and verifies the intent balance (service 29, mobile_data 36, mms 49), with all assertions passing against the paper's Table 1.

claims.claim: The benchmark uses a compositional task generator that creates verifiable telecom tasks from intent and subtask components (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The script claim3_generator.py parses the source to confirm BaseTask has fields (init_funcs, fix_funcs, extra_env_assertions), identifies 15 SelectionSet groups across 3 intents (service 5, mobile_data 6, mms 4), verifies compose_tasks() cross-products these into 2285 full tasks, and confirms TaskManager.verify_task (L197-227) asserts pre/post-fix state and env assertions.

claims.claim: Agents show lower pass@1 in default dual-control telecom operation than in no-user and oracle-plan modes, isolating the cost of decentralized user coordination (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The script claim4_passat1.py recomputes pass@1 as mean binary reward over 456 simulations per cell (114 tasks × 4 trials) from shipped per-simulation reward_info.reward fields, yielding GPT-4.1: default 0.3421 < no-user 0.5154 < oracle-plan 0.7281 and o4-mini: default 0.4211 < no-user 0.6732 < oracle-plan 0.9627, with the ordering asserted and confirmed for both models.

claims.claim: Telecom performance declines as the number of required actions or distinct issues increases (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: The script claim5_decline.py bins shipped per-simulation rewards by #actions (len(evaluation_criteria.actions)) and #issues (|-separated subtasks in task id), showing clear downward trends across all four series (e.g., gpt-4.1/default by #actions: 0.542 at 2 actions → 0.0 at ≥9 actions; by #issues: 0.62 at 2 → 0.0 at 9), with trend checks confirming decline for all model/mode combinations.

SabaPivot/repro-tau2-bench.overall: The logbook provides concrete evidence for all five claims through AST-based source code analysis (claims 1-3) and recomputation of pass@1 statistics from raw per-simulation reward fields in shipped trajectory JSON files (claims 4-5), all at full benchmark scale (114 tasks, 456 sims per cell). The main limitation is that claims 4-5 rely on the authors' released trajectories rather than independently generated LLM runs, though the logbook recomputes aggregate statistics from raw per-simulation data rather than transcribing published numbers.

ParetoOptimal/repro-3kx1xu2bcc.paper_title: Lower Bounds for Frank-Wolfe on Strongly Convex Sets

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a constructive Omega(1/sqrt(epsilon)) lower bound on the number of iterations for Frank-Wolfe with short steps or exact line search when both the objective and the constraint set are smooth and strongly convex (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports reproducing all 7500 transitions from Equation 7 with maximum relative error 0.0, an independent exact-line-search implementation matching 1000 transitions with residual error ~1e-104, and a measured log iteration-vs-epsilon slope of -0.5038 against the claimed -0.5. This is concrete numerical evidence on the paper's own 2D construction at substantial scale.

claims.claim: The lower-bound construction uses the specific instance of minimizing f(x) = ||x-p||_2^2 over the Euclidean unit ball B_1(0) with the unconstrained minimizer p on the boundary (||p||=1), showing this hard instance matches the known O(1/sqrt(epsilon)) upper bound of Garber et al. (2015) (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports a measured log gap-vs-iteration slope of -1.9998 against the t^-2 prediction, with Proposition 3's upper bound showing 0 violations and max gap-to-bound ratio 1.0000000000000002 on the same orbit. The Claim 3 page also confirms the instance has Hessian 2I over the Euclidean unit ball with boundary optimizer, consistent with f(x)=||x-p||^2 over B_1(0).

claims.claim: The lower bound is established via a 'backward reconstruction' technique that builds worst-case trajectories by working backward from terminal iterates, producing precise sequences over horizons of 10,000+ iterations (Section on Backward Reconstruction Strategy).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports 7500 transitions reproduced, which falls short of the claimed 10,000+ iterations, and there is no dedicated page or explicit discussion of the backward reconstruction technique itself. No evidence addresses the method's mechanics or the 10,000+ horizon claim.

claims.claim: The analysis reduces the dynamics to a two-dimensional invariant subspace parametrized by residual magnitude r and contraction factor s, revealing stable phases of monotonically increasing contraction followed by intermittent 'jumps' that explain the convergence stalling behavior (Section on Dynamical Analysis).
claims.evidence: No page or evidence addresses the two-dimensional invariant subspace parametrized by residual magnitude r and contraction factor s, nor the stable phases of monotonically increasing contraction or intermittent jumps. The logbook mentions the witness is 2D but does not analyze the dynamical structure claimed.

claims.claim: The result shows strong convexity of the constraint set alone cannot yield convergence rates uniformly faster than O(1/sqrt(epsilon)), and this conclusion holds dimension-independently and extends to ellipsoidal constraints via affine invariance (Theorem 6, Implications).
claims.evidence: The logbook's Claim 3 page provides a counterexample with strongly convex objective (Hessian 2I) and strongly convex constraint set (Euclidean unit ball) with boundary optimizer, achieving measured complexity slope -0.5038, directly showing that even under stronger conditions (both objective and set strongly convex) the rate cannot beat O(1/sqrt(epsilon)). The dimension-independence and ellipsoidal extension are standard theoretical implications of the 2D construction.

ParetoOptimal/repro-3kx1xu2bcc.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence for the core lower-bound claim (Claim 1), tightness (Claim 2), and the impossibility of faster rates from strong convexity alone (Claim 5), with 7500 transitions reproduced at near-zero error and slopes matching theoretical predictions. However, Claims 3 and 4 regarding the backward reconstruction technique and dynamical analysis are not explicitly addressed, leaving those aspects unverified.

SabaPivot/repro-self-distillation-ridge.paper_title: Optimal Unconstrained Self-Distillation in Ridge Regression: Strict Improvements, Precise Asymptotics, and One-Shot Tuning

claims.claim: Theorem 2.2 proves that for any nonstationary ridge penalty λ (i.e., R'(λ) ≠ 0), the optimally mixed self-distilled student strictly improves on the teacher's squared prediction risk, with optimal mixing weight ξ*(λ) = -(λ/2)·R'(λ)/D(λ) obeying sign(ξ*(λ)) = -sign(R'(λ)) (Section 2.3, Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: On anisotropic Gaussian data (n=400, p=200, γ=0.5) with 200 λ values, two independently computed forms of ξ* agree to max absolute error 1.34e-12, sign(ξ*)=-sign(R') holds at every interior grid point, and R*_sd<R strictly away from the ridge optimum λ*=0.410266.

claims.claim: The optimal mixing weight ξ*(λ) can be negative, corresponding to a 'pro-learning' regime under over-regularization (λ > λ*), as opposed to the 'anti-learning' regime (ξ* > 1) identified in prior work by Das and Sanghavi (2023) (Section 2.3).
claims.evidence: In the same exact-risk sweep, ξ* ranges from -55.71 to 129.66, becomes negative whenever λ exceeds the empirical ridge optimum, and the unconstrained negative-ξ solution strictly beats the [0,1]-clipped solution throughout the over-regularized tail.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 derives exact deterministic equivalents for the optimal self-distillation risk R*_sd(λ) and mixing weight ξ*(λ) in the proportional asymptotics regime (n, p → ∞, p/n → γ) under general anisotropic covariance and deterministic signals (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: General anisotropic covariance with deterministic signals tested at three scales up to (n,p)=(1600,800) with 12–60 seeds; maximum absolute deviations of teacher and optimal-SD risks from Theorem 3.1 equivalents stay below 0.0167 across all settings.

claims.claim: In the isotropic-signal setting, Corollary 3.2 shows the optimal mixing weight changes sign exactly at λ* := γσ²/r², with ξ*(λ) < 0 for λ > λ* and ξ*(λ) > 0 for λ < λ* (Section 3.2, Corollary 3.2).
claims.evidence: Five isotropic configurations (γ∈{0.25,0.5,1}, r²∈{1,2,4}, p=250, 25 seeds, 200 λ values) all show ξ positive below λ* and negative above it; measured crossings match theory within 0.83%–7.44% relative error.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proposes a one-shot generalized cross-validation (GCV) estimator of the optimal mixing weight ξ* that is consistent in proportional asymptotics and avoids grid search, sample splitting, or refitting (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: At fixed λ=0.3, γ=0.5, mean |ξ_hat−ξ*| over 60 seeds decreases monotonically from 0.326 (n=200) to 0.138 (n=1600), consistent with root-n convergence, using only one fitted model and training data with no grid search, splitting, or refitting.

claims.claim: A curvature-based sufficient condition (Proposition 2.3, Eq. 10) predicts whether the self-distilled risk's global minimum over λ is strictly smaller than the teacher's; this test is verified exactly on all four real-data experiments (BlogFeedback, Communities and Crime, CIFAR10, Air Quality) in Table 2.
claims.evidence: The claim requires exact agreement on all four datasets, but the rerun finds Eq. 10 holds for Communities & Crime (curvature RHS=0.901<1) while the paper's Table 2 says it does not hold, and CIFAR10 was not rerun at all, so the asserted four-dataset exact agreement is not reproduced.

SabaPivot/repro-self-distillation-ridge.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence at non-trivial finite scale supporting claims 1–5, including exact-risk agreement to 1e-12, multi-scale deterministic-equivalent convergence, sign-change verification across five isotropic settings, and GCV consistency with root-n decay. Claim 6 is falsified because the curvature test disagrees with the paper on Communities & Crime and CIFAR10 was never rerun, breaking the 'all four datasets' requirement.

SabaPivot/repro-flow-matching-calibratio.paper_title: Flow Matching Calibration for Simulation-Based Inference under Model Misspecification

claims.claim: FMCPE refines a simulation-trained posterior estimator using a small set of real calibration samples via two sequential flow-matching stages: a data-space transport map T_X coupling real observations to simulator-space counterparts, and a parameter-space transport map T_Θ moving a simulation-informed source distribution toward the true posterior (Section on method).
claims.evidence: Code audit of paper-era posteriors.py confirms the cascaded inference order (y→T_X→proposal→T_Θ→corrected posterior) and trainers.py confirms both flow parameter sets in one optimizer with a single weighted loss, matching Equations 4–10 and Algorithms 1–2.

claims.claim: FMCPE is evaluated on two synthetic benchmarks (a 3-parameter/10-dimensional Gaussian task and a 2-parameter Pendulum task with friction-induced misspecification) and two real-world benchmarks (WindTunnel hatch-angle inference and LightTunnel RGB/polarizer-coefficient inference from 64x64x3 images) (Section on experiments).
claims.evidence: Source audit of icml2026.tex and four simulator implementations (pendulum.py, light_tunnel.py, wind_tunnel.py, Gaussian task) confirm all four benchmarks with matching parameter dimensions and observation types; only Pendulum was rerun, but the inventory claim is about the paper's evaluation scope.

claims.claim: FMCPE is tested across calibration set sizes N_cal in {10, 50, 200, 1000} with expanding nested construction over 5 independent runs, and is compared against NPE and MFNPE baselines using jjC2ST, Wasserstein distance (W2), and MSE metrics (Section on experimental setup).
claims.evidence: Executable nesting audit passed 15/15 subset relations for the paper-era prefix protocol across five seeds, source checks confirm all four N_cal sizes, five runs, nested construction, and jC2ST/W2/MSE metrics; the hosted T4 Job executed all four nested calibration sizes with 50,000 simulations (one seed rather than five).

claims.claim: In the Pendulum task, FMCPE correctly recovers the oscillation amplitude despite the omitted-friction misspecification, whereas NPE and MFNPE produce multimodal or biased posterior estimates even at N_cal=1000 (Section on Pendulum results).
claims.evidence: The hosted paper-era Pendulum run at N_cal=1000 across 500 observations shows FMCPE amplitude MAE of 2.4911 versus 0.5825 for NPE and 0.6215 for MFNPE, with paired 95% confidence intervals [1.737, 2.080] and [1.704, 2.036] excluding zero, and FMCPE has 24.8% multimodal posteriors versus 1.2% (NPE) and 2.6% (MFNPE)—directly contradicting the claim.

claims.claim: FMCPE achieves lower MSE than baselines particularly at small calibration sample sizes and produces better-calibrated, unimodal posteriors compared to MFNPE's overly sharp estimates (Section on results).
claims.evidence: The hosted run shows mixed MSE (FMCPE wins 5/8 pairwise comparisons but loses to NPE at N_cal=10 and to both baselines at N_cal=1000), worse coverage MAE at every calibration size (0.60–0.67 for FMCPE vs 0.03–0.46 for baselines), and more multimodal posteriors (24.8% vs 1.2%/2.6%), contradicting both the calibration and unimodality clauses.

SabaPivot/repro-flow-matching-calibratio.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the method structure, benchmark inventory, and experimental protocol through source/code audits and a hosted GPU run, but falsifies the two key empirical claims: FMCPE underperforms baselines on Pendulum amplitude recovery and posterior calibration in a single-seed run with 500 test observations and 600,000 posterior draw vectors.

ConductorAILabs/repro-sonicmaster.paper_title: SonicMaster: Towards Controllable All-in-One Music Restoration and Mastering

claims.claim: SonicMaster is trained on a purpose-built dataset of ~175k audio pairs derived from ~25k curated 30-second Jamendo segments, simulating 19 degradation effects across 5 categories (EQ, dynamics, reverb, amplitude, stereo) with paired text annotations (Section on Dataset).
claims.evidence: The logbook references a released dataset revision hash and mentions '19 functions' at the repository level, but provides no concrete evidence of inspecting the dataset to verify ~175k pairs from ~25k Jamendo segments, the 5 degradation categories, or paired text annotations. No dataset statistics or construction verification was performed.

claims.claim: The architecture combines multimodal DiT and DiT blocks operating in a Stable Audio Open VAE latent space, conditioned on FLAN-T5 Large text embeddings, trained with a rectified-flow velocity-prediction objective (Equations 1-5).
claims.evidence: The SonicMaster checkpoint (3.45 GB, SHA-256 d6af2075...) was downloaded and hashed, confirming the model exists, but no code inspection of DiT blocks, FLAN-T5 conditioning, or velocity-prediction objective is documented, and inference was blocked by the gated Stable Audio Open VAE returning HTTP 403.

claims.claim: SonicMaster Large achieves an FAD of 0.073, KL divergence of 0.888 (x1000), mel-spectrogram SSIM of 0.609, and a Production Quality score of 7.705 versus a 7.885 ground-truth reference (Table 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook computed custom metrics on 13 released gallery triplets (SSIM 0.3653, symmetric KL 0.01943) using a different metric implementation than the paper, on a small subset rather than the full evaluation split. FAD and PQ were not computed at all, and the SSIM/KL values do not match the paper's reported numbers (0.609, 0.888).

claims.claim: SonicMaster outperforms classical baselines Text2FX-EQ on EQ correction and WPE/HPSS on dereverberation and declipping tasks (Table 1, Table 2).
claims.evidence: No classical baselines (Text2FX-EQ, WPE, HPSS) were run or compared against. The 13-triplet evaluation only compares degraded inputs to released restorations, with no baseline comparison whatsoever.

claims.claim: Removing text conditioning (automatic mode) worsens KL divergence from 0.696 to 0.917 and degrades clipping (2.812) and stereo-width (0.1416) metrics relative to text-conditioned inference (ablation in Results section).
claims.evidence: The logbook attempted to run inference with targeted prompts and an empty-prompt automatic mode on an L40S, but the job terminated before any inference due to HTTP 403 on the gated Stable Audio Open VAE. No automatic-mode or text-conditioned outputs were produced.

claims.claim: In an 8-listener, 43-sample-pair subjective evaluation using 7-point Likert scores, SonicMaster shows statistically significant improvement over degraded inputs across all four attribute categories (amplitude, reverb, stereo, EQ), with text relevance scores ranging 5.11-6.19 (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states that a new human listening study was outside scope and was not conducted. No subjective evaluation data, Likert scores, or statistical significance tests were produced.

ConductorAILabs/repro-sonicmaster.overall: This logbook was largely blocked by an inaccessible gated VAE dependency, preventing any end-to-end inference. The only concrete experiment was a custom metric evaluation of 13 released gallery triplets, which used different metric implementations than the paper and did not match reported values, leaving all six claims without supporting evidence.

DineshAI/3NQSeJOfkz.paper_title: SVRG and Beyond via Posterior Correction

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows that applying posterior correction with an isotropic-Gaussian posterior family reduces exactly to the standard SVRG gradient update, and Theorem 2 proves SVRG is equivalent to VSGD-PoCo in the limit of zero sampling noise.
claims.evidence: Across 48 strongly-convex quadratic finite sums and 2,112 matched inner updates, the independent VSGD-PoCo recurrence and SVRG agree with max absolute error 0.0 (threshold 1e-12), using identical snapshots, schedules, and epsilon=0, which directly tests the Theorem 1/2 equivalence on a setup where Gaussian expected gradients are exact.

claims.claim: Using full-covariance Gaussian posteriors yields a Newton-like variance-reduced extension (VON-PoCo) with a novel Hessian correction term H̄_out\i(m_in − m_out) not present in prior variance-reduced Newton methods.
claims.evidence: Across 48 full-covariance trajectories (432 updates), an independent Gaussian natural-parameter update matches Theorem 3 to 1.55e-15 (mean) and 1.67e-16 (precision); deleting the Hessian transport term changes the update by median 0.075 (min 0.0025), and the pinned official IVON-PoCoMo code agrees with independent float64 equations to 0.0 error across 24 trials with transport-deletion gaps of median 0.151.
