claims.claim: Using diagonal-covariance Gaussian posteriors with mega-batches and momentum yields an Adam-like extension (IVON-PoCoMo) suitable for transformer pretraining, which achieves 17.4 validation perplexity on GPT-2 125M pretrained on 50B tokens, versus 18.0 for IVON and 18.4 for AdamW (Section 4.3, Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: The GPT-2 125M / 50B-token perplexity claim (17.4 vs 18.0 vs 18.4) was never measured: no GPU run was performed, no terminal metric or raw curve exists in the official repo, and the linked checkpoint belongs to a different experiment. The Algorithm-4 recurrence audit and a toy logistic regression experiment verify the optimizer's algebraic correctness but do not address the specific empirical perplexity claim.

claims.claim: The variance-reduced methods show consistent gains in finetuning across ViT-B/32, Qwen2.5, and Llama-3.1 (Table 1) and in ResNet-50/ImageNet and ResNet-20/CIFAR-10 image classification, particularly when learning rates are not annealed to zero (Figures 4-5).
claims.evidence: No actual finetuning or image-classification training experiments were run; Table 1 values were merely transcribed from the paper (not reproduced), and the released CIFAR launcher config differs materially from Appendix D.1 (epochs 20 vs 100, ESS 50k vs 500k, alpha 0.4 vs 0.1), preventing a faithful rerun. No direct measurements of ViT/Qwen/Llama finetuning or ResNet/ImageNet/CIFAR training were produced.

DineshAI/3NQSeJOfkz.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the two algorithmic/theoretical claims (Claims 1–2) via machine-precision numerical recurrence checks with appropriate negative controls, but provides no experimental evidence for the two large-scale empirical claims (Claims 3–4), which require GPU-scale training that was not attempted.

chupilka/repro-from-kepler-to-newton.paper_title: From Kepler to Newton: Inductive Biases Guide Learned World Models in Transformers

claims.claim: Standard tokenization of continuous planetary-motion data breaks spatial continuity, so that two physically close points falling into different bins are treated as unrelated; correcting this via reduced vocabulary size or continuous coordinates is needed for transformers to learn a coherent world model, and vocabulary size significantly affects when a spatial map emerges (Section 2, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: All 25 grid points (5 vocabulary sizes × 5 trajectory counts) completed with 20,001 updates on L4 GPUs; the reproduced scaling law 1−R²=0.8673·D_tokens^(−1.2082)·V^(1.3213) closely matches the paper's exponents (1.152, 1.328), and larger vocabulary worsens peak R² in 20/20 adjacent comparisons at the paper endpoint. The continuous-coordinate control was not run, but the vocabulary-size effect central to Figure 3 is concretely reproduced.

claims.claim: Without noisy-context training, autoregressive transformer predictions on continuous orbital variables accumulate error over rollouts; injecting Gaussian noise into the training context (optimal σ = 0.1) restores robustness to in-context perturbations at inference time (Section 3, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Six noise conditions (σ∈{0,0.01,0.03,0.1,0.3,1.0}) trained for 20,001 updates on T4 GPUs with 1,000 held-out trajectories; σ=0.1 beats σ=0 by 39.78% (bootstrap CI [35.55%,43.70%]) and σ=1 by 88.25% (CI [87.67%,88.80%]), confirming that noise injection restores robustness. The descriptive optimum is σ=0.03 rather than the paper's σ=0.1, a discrepancy at this single scale, but the core mechanism and the effectiveness of σ=0.1 are supported.

claims.claim: Context length controls which world model emerges: a short context length of 2 induces a Newtonian, force-based representation (R² ≈ 0.999), whereas a long context length of 100 induces a Keplerian, orbital-parameter representation (R² ≈ 0.998), demonstrating that temporal locality combined with spatial smoothness favors physically causal (Newtonian) over curve-fitting (Keplerian) world models (Section 4, Figure 6).
claims.evidence: The K3 page defines a confirmatory design (block sizes {1,2,5,10,20,50,100}, probing force and orbital parameters) but the conclusion explicitly states 'K3: not yet executed.' No runs, no probe results, no data exist for this claim.

claims.claim: Vafa et al.'s original transformer embeddings exhibit poor spatial locality (R² ≈ 0.86), motivating the paper's proposed inductive-bias corrections (Section 2, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The authenticated Vafa next_token checkpoint (archive SHA-256 56a92eed…, checkpoint SHA-256 c5c7f40c…) was loaded with weights_only=True and probed independently, yielding x R²=0.8592 and y R²=0.8587, matching the paper's reported ~0.86 to four decimal places. Held-out token-index probes (x R²=0.820, y R²=0.810) confirm the locality remains poor.

chupilka/repro-from-kepler-to-newton.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting Claims 1, 2, and 4 with sealed protocols, integrity checks, and independent replays, but Claim 3 was never executed. The reproduction is rigorous for completed claims but incomplete in coverage, notably missing the K3 context-length experiment and the K1 continuous-coordinate control.

vissutagunawan/UTiEfkfNQ2.paper_title: Improved Analysis of the Accelerated Noisy Power Method with Applications to Decentralized PCA

claims.claim: Theorem 2.2 establishes accelerated convergence for the Accelerated Noisy Power Method under a noise magnitude condition that scales as Δ_k·ε rather than the stricter Δ_k·ε^μ requirement of prior work (Xu, 2023) (Section 2, Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: At d=1000, k=10 (paper's scale), the logbook fits the iteration-complexity exponent over a decade of eigengaps: ANPM with β* yields T~Δ^{-0.519} (predicted -0.5) vs plain β=0 yielding T~Δ^{-1.018} (predicted -1.0), with empirical geometric factor ρ matching the closed-form Chebyshev rate to ≤3.1e-2. Under adversarial noise ξ=1e-4 at gap=1e-2, ANPM(β*) reaches sin θ_k=1e-2 in 56 iterations vs 549 for plain, confirming acceleration is preserved under perturbation.

claims.claim: Theorems 2.4 and 2.5 prove that the noise conditions on the orthogonal component ||U_-k^T Ξ_t||_2 and parallel component ||U_k^T Ξ_t||_2 (Equations 3-4) cannot be relaxed without breaking the accelerated convergence guarantee (Section 2, Theorems 2.4-2.5).
claims.evidence: The logbook's Claim 3 Part B demonstrates tightness of the orthogonal noise condition ||U_{-k}^T Ξ_t||_2 (Theorem 2.4): error floor scales exactly as coeff·ε with crossing at coeff=1.0, and 8× relaxation provably fails (floor 8e-4 ≫ ε=1e-4), plus a direction-control showing bulk noise is harmless. However, the parallel component condition ||U_k^T Ξ_t||_2 (Theorem 2.5, Eq. 4) is never experimentally addressed.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 introduces ADePM, applying the improved ANPM analysis to decentralized PCA via an accelerated gossip protocol (Algorithm 1), achieving convergence rate O(sqrt(λ_k/(λ_k-λ_{k+1})) log(...)) with communication cost O(1/sqrt(γ_W) log(...)) comparable to non-accelerated decentralized methods (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: On real datasets (Digits n=10 d=64, Ego-Facebook n=50 d=50) at identical per-iteration communication budget (L gossip rounds for every method), ADePM(β*) reaches sin θ_k=1e-2 in 2.6×–5.9× fewer iterations than DePM, with Ego-Facebook showing ADePM at 2.86e-9 vs DePM at 3.55e-3 for the same 8000 gossip rounds. Authors' reference CSVs reproduced to 2.03e-12 (Ego-Facebook) and 8.4e-14 (Digits-het).

claims.claim: Section 3.1 shows the accelerated gossip subroutine attains O~(1/sqrt(γ_W)) mixing versus the O~(1/γ_W) rate of standard (non-accelerated) gossip (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook uses accelerated gossip within ADePM but never isolates the gossip subroutine to measure its mixing rate as a function of the spectral gap γ_W. No sweep over graphs with varying γ_W is performed to verify the O~(1/√γ_W) vs O~(1/γ_W) scaling; only fixed graphs at fixed L values are tested.

claims.claim: Section 4 experiments demonstrate that the optimal momentum parameter β* = λ_{k+1}^2/4 yields a square-root speedup over non-accelerated decentralized PCA methods, and that ADePM substantially outperforms DePM and DeEPCA baselines on real datasets (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The synthetic rate experiment (Claim 1) confirms β*=λ_{k+1}²/4 yields the Δ^{-1/2} (square-root) rate vs Δ^{-1} for plain, and the decentralized experiments (Claim 2) show ADePM(β*) substantially outperforms DePM (2.6×–5.9× fewer iterations, six orders of magnitude lower final error on Ego-Facebook) and DeEPCA (which tracks DePM closely) on real datasets at equal communication budget.

vissutagunawan/UTiEfkfNQ2.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence at the paper's scale for the accelerated ANPM rate under perturbation (Claim 1), the decentralized ADePM speedup over baselines at equal communication cost (Claims 3, 5), and the tightness of the orthogonal noise condition (part of Claim 2). However, the parallel noise condition (Theorem 2.5) and the gossip mixing-rate scaling versus spectral gap (Claim 4) are never experimentally addressed.

ai-sherpa/fair-decisions-calibrated-scor.paper_title: Fair Decisions from Calibrated Scores: Achieving Optimal Classification While Satisfying Sufficiency

claims.claim: Even perfectly group-calibrated scores, including true class-conditional probabilities, provably violate predictive parity after thresholding, per Definitions 2.1 and 2.3 of sufficiency and predictive parity (Section 2, Definitions 2.1, 2.3).
claims.evidence: Real FICO data reproduces the paper's exact PPV/FOR/accuracy numbers (0.8819 accuracy, PPV 0.9101/0.7854, FOR 0.198/0.1289), and real COMPAS data shows PPV gap 0.0196 and FOR gap 0.0347; additionally, 818 independent synthetic Monte Carlo trials with perfectly calibrated scores show 100% predictive-parity violation rate, supporting the claim's universality assertion.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows that for a fixed selection rate, the optimal classifier applies a soft threshold to group-calibrated scores, with randomization needed at exactly one threshold boundary (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: The closed-form p*(μ)=s_{k*}+c_{k*}/μ was independently coded and cross-checked against a structure-agnostic LP oracle (scipy.optimize.linprog) across 4,500 random configurations (300 distributions × 15 selection rates, m=2–14), yielding max |p*_formula − p*_LP| = 3.33e-16 and realized selection rate matching target μ to 2.22e-16, confirming exact optimality of the soft-threshold rule.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 characterizes the boundary of the feasible region of achievable positive-predictive-value/false-omission-rate pairs as a continuous, piecewise curve composed of hyperbolic arcs and line segments (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: Independent boundary-tracing via root-finding on Theorem 3.3 reproduces the paper's Appendix I.1 FICO results exactly (max-acc (p,q)=(0.9116,0.2346), acc 0.8676; min-Δsep (p,q)=(0.9284,0.2607), Δsep=0.0702) and Appendix I.2 COMPAS results (max-acc (p,q)=(0.6446,0.3346), acc 0.6563; min-Δsep (p,q)=(0.6807,0.362), Δsep=0.1464); the Eq. (14) Δ_sep formula matches its exact raw-definition computation to 6.67e-09 across 25 random configurations.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 traces the intersection of group-specific feasible PPV/FOR regions to construct the optimal classifier satisfying sufficiency exactly (Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook independently implements intersection tracing of group-specific feasible PPV/FOR regions (C⁰∩C¹) via `intersection_curve` using grid search plus Brent refinement rather than Algorithm 1's exact quadratic-root tracing, yet reproduces the paper's exact optimal classifier parameters on both FICO and COMPAS to 4 decimals, confirming that intersection tracing constructs the correct optimal sufficiency-satisfying classifier.

claims.claim: A COMPAS case study demonstrates that optimal fair classifiers under sufficiency generally require group-specific decision thresholds rather than a single universal threshold (Section 7).
claims.evidence: The COMPAS case study is reproduced at full scale (n=5278), yielding the optimal sufficient classifier with group-specific boundaries intersected at (p,q)=(0.6446,0.3346) for max-accuracy and (0.6807,0.362) for min-Δsep; combined with Claim 1's finding that a single universal threshold (s≥0.5) produces PPV gap 0.0196 and FOR gap 0.0347 on the same COMPAS data, this demonstrates that group-specific thresholds are needed to satisfy sufficiency optimally.

ai-sherpa/fair-decisions-calibrated-scor.overall: The logbook provides strong independent verification of all five claims through real-data reproduction on FICO and COMPAS at the paper's own scale, LP-oracle cross-checks to machine precision for Theorem 3.3, exact raw-definition validation of the Δ_sep formula, and a large synthetic sweep confirming the predictive-parity violation phenomenon. The main limitation is that Algorithm 1's exact quadratic-root tracing is replaced by grid search plus Brent refinement, and the ACS Income experiment (Sec. 7.3) is not attempted.

ai-sherpa/momentum-sgd-suboptimality-rep.paper_title: On the Provable Suboptimality of Momentum SGD in Nonstationary Stochastic Optimization

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows momentum SGD's tracking-error bound scales as (1-beta)^-2 on the initialization term and (1-beta)^-1 on the noise floor, versus O(1) and O(sigma^2 gamma/mu) respectively for vanilla SGD in Theorem 3.1 (Section 3.1, Theorems 3.1 and 3.3).
claims.evidence: Exact discrete-Lyapunov stationary solution of the SGDM recursion shows HB noise floor scaling as (1-β)^-1.0000 (R²=1.0) at fixed γ=0.01, with SGD constant at 1.2314 (β-independent), directly confirming the Theorem 3.3 noise-floor exponent. The transient gain G(β)² measured in Claim 4 scales as (1-β)^-2.094 (R²=0.9999), confirming the initialization-term (1-β)^-2 scaling, and is absent for SGD (constant 0.951).

claims.claim: Theorem 3.7 gives a minimax lower bound decomposing regret into a noise-limited term and an inertia-limited term that worsens with beta and can dominate in drift-heavy regimes, establishing an information-theoretic (not just analytical) barrier for momentum methods (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence: Exact rational arithmetic evaluates the minimax exponent -2/(αq+2) at α=1,q=1 to exactly -2/3, matching the paper's upper-bound remark. The inertia window τ_β is measured directly at κ^1.064(1-β)^-0.990 (R²=0.9987), and a two-point Le Cam Bayes test shows momentum-limited discrimination error rising from 0.169 to 0.447 as β goes 0.5→0.99 while SGD stays near-perfect (4.8e-111). Though only the J=2 base case of the Fano packing is constructed, the exponent identity, inertia scaling, and information-barrier mechanism are all concretely demonstrated.

claims.claim: Under the stability constraint gamma <= (1-beta)^2/L, the paper proves vanilla SGD provably outperforms Heavy-Ball/Nesterov momentum SGD in drift-dominated nonstationary regimes (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Full reproduction of the paper's Table 1 at published scale (d=100, T=5000, 108 cells) via exact closed-form Lyapunov solution: 108/108 cells within 10% of printed values, winner agreement 34/36, SGD wins 31/36 settings matching the paper's 31/36. In the drift-dominated corner (β=0.99, γ=0.10, σ²=0.8), HB is 97.7× worse than SGD in the paper's own numbers, reproduced exactly.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.6 shows the high-probability bound for momentum SGD exhibits an inertia horizon of order (1-beta)^-1 and drift-noise coupling scaling as (1-beta)^-2, both absent from the vanilla SGD high-probability bound in Theorem 3.5 (Section 3.2, Theorems 3.5 and 3.6).
claims.evidence: Real deterministic recursions on κ=10 quadratic measure HB inertia horizon at exponent -0.998 (R²=0.9999991) vs SGD constant 273 iters (exponent 0.0), and transient gain G(β)² at exponent -2.094 (R²=0.9999) vs SGD constant 0.951. Stochastic 95th-percentile tail (500 seeds) rises monotonically with β for HB (0.843→3.778) while SGD is β-independent, confirming both Theorem 3.6 structures and their absence in Theorem 3.5.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments on quadratics, linear/logistic regression, and MLPs confirm that increasing nonstationarity (drift), momentum parameter beta, or condition number kappa systematically worsens Heavy-Ball and Nesterov tracking error while vanilla SGD remains comparatively robust (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Real online experiments on all four Section-4 task families (drifting quadratic, linear regression, logistic regression, backprop-trained 2-layer MLP) show SGD < HB(0.9) < HB(0.95) and SGD < NAG in every task. Drift, β, and κ sweeps are each strictly monotone increasing for Heavy-Ball. Scale is modest (3 seeds, synthetic data, small dimensions) but matches the paper's own synthetic experimental regime and covers all four task families and all three worsening axes.

ai-sherpa/momentum-sgd-suboptimality-rep.overall: This logbook provides strong independent verification of all five claims through exact algebraic computations, discrete-Lyapunov solutions at machine-precision accuracy, full-scale Table 1 reproduction (108/108 cells), and real online experiments across all four task families. Main limitations are the J=2 base case for the Fano argument, modest seed counts for Section 4 experiments, and synthetic data only, but the core quantitative claims are concretely supported.

ai-sherpa/mfvi-predictive-variance-repro.paper_title: Gaussian Mean Field Variational Inference can Overestimate Predictive Variance

claims.claim: MFVI underestimates posterior variance in parameter space but can overestimate predictive variance relative to the exact posterior, with Theorem 3.7 proving that for test points drawn from the training distribution's empirical covariance, MFVI's expected predictive variance exceeds that of the exact posterior (Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence: Closed-form MFVI covariance matches an independent from-scratch SciPy reverse-KL optimizer across 7 dimensions (P=2–64, max mean error 1.30e-07, max log-variance error 1.85e-05); every parameter coordinate shrinks (7/7, min shrink 2.99e-04) while the minimum-eigenvalue predictive direction overestimates (7/7, max gap +8.02e-04). Theorem 3.7 identity verified on 140 problems (max error 2.71e-08, 140/140 satisfy ≤0 bound) and 9 mpmath 90-digit re-solves (max residual 5.09e-90).

claims.claim: Lemma 3.6 shows a calibration constraint forcing MFVI to simultaneously underestimate variance in some directions while overestimating in others, with overestimation occurring specifically in directions where training data concentrates (Lemma 3.6).
claims.evidence: The calibration constraint Tr(Sigma^-1 S*)=P is verified to 8.21e-07 across 140 problems and in unit tests; the directional trade-off is demonstrated with first-PC overestimation (36/36 configs, min gap 3.26e-08) and last-PC reversal (36/36, min gap -0.1247), while all parameter coordinates shrink (7/7 dims). An adversarial anisotropic-prior falsifier correctly breaks the shared-eigenbasis assumption (36/36, median angle 89.3°), delineating the spherical-prior scope.

claims.claim: In a pathological rank-1 training-data subspace scenario, as dimensionality increases the MFVI posterior's predictive variance converges to the prior variance, effectively discarding training information (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: Rank-1 design (w=1/√P, S=133.7 fixed) measured P=2→1024: MFVI/prior ratio rises monotonically 0.0147→0.8845 while exact posterior stays flat at 7.42e-03 (119× ratio at P=1024), with Sherman-Morrison analytic cross-check agreeing to 1.21e-14. This directly demonstrates convergence to the prior variance as dimensionality grows.

claims.claim: Temperature-scaled posteriors (cold posteriors, T<1) correct the predictive-variance overestimation and improve in-distribution predictions, while T>1 benefits out-of-distribution performance, offering a novel explanation for the Cold Posterior Effect.
claims.evidence: Tempered S*(T)=T·S* tested across 15 configs (P=64–1024, 3 seeds): variance-matching gives T_ID=0.00839<1 and T_OOD=1.13057>1 (15/15 each), confirmed independently by exact-predictive NLL grids (T_ID=0.00423<1, T_OOD=1.14194>1, 15/15 each). Both metrics agree that cold T fixes ID overestimation and warm T fixes OOD underestimation.

claims.claim: Experiments on basis function regression and UCI datasets show optimal temperatures below 1 for in-distribution test points and above 1 for out-of-distribution test points, consistent with the theoretical predictions (Section 6, UCI experiments).
claims.evidence: RBF basis regression (Q=300) on 4 UCI datasets (kin8nm, energy, boston, airfoil) across 85 matched comparisons: ID optimum T<1 in 85/85, OOD optimum T>1 in 80/85 (100% on the paper's kin8nm benchmark, 40/40), OOD>ID in 80/85. The 5 energy failures are transparently attributed to its discrete feature 0 not creating genuine extrapolation. kin8nm ID range 0.596–0.728 and OOD range 1.740–2.275 match the paper's reported ranges.

ai-sherpa/mfvi-predictive-variance-repro.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all five claims at the paper's own scale and settings, with multiple independent cross-checks (closed form vs from-scratch optimizer, float64 vs 90-digit mpmath, matrix vs Sherman-Morrison). The reproduction is thorough across dimensions P=2–1024, 140+36+15+85 configurations, and four real UCI datasets, with honest reporting of the 5/85 energy OOD failures.

ai-sherpa/feature-resemblance-analogical.paper_title: Feature Resemblance: Towards a Theoretical Understanding of Analogical Reasoning in Transformers

claims.claim: Joint training on similarity premises (that A1 and A2 share a property) and attribution premises (that A2 has property C) provably yields perfect analogical reasoning via value-matrix feature alignment, with feature cosine similarity of 1-o(1) between aligned entities (Theorem 1, Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: Full-scale one-layer attention model (N=100, d=427, m=50, 5 seeds) with hand-derived numpy gradients: joint training yields 99.6% held-out analogical success and strongly positive feature similarity 0.7047±0.0086, confirming the mechanism of value-matrix feature alignment enabling analogical transfer.

claims.claim: Sequential (curriculum) training succeeds only when similarity structure is learned before attribution: the similarity-then-attribution order achieves 1-o(1) feature alignment (Theorem 2), while the reverse attribution-then-similarity order yields o(1) alignment and near-random test performance despite convergent training loss (Theorem 3, Proposition 3).
claims.evidence: Full-scale sequential training (5 seeds) shows decisive curriculum asymmetry: S→A order achieves 99.6% success with fsim 0.7551, while A→S order collapses to 0.40% success with fsim -0.0016, quantitatively reproducing the claimed necessity of similarity-before-attribution ordering.

claims.claim: Two-hop reasoning (A to B, B to C implies A to C) requires explicit identity-bridge examples (B to B) in training data to achieve perfect performance (Theorem 4); without identity bridges, two-hop reasoning fails completely with error rate 1-1/N despite successful learning of each individual hop (Theorem 5, Proposition 5).
claims.evidence: Full-scale two-hop experiment (5 seeds): with identity bridge, 99.6% success and fsim 0.7145; without bridge, 0.0% success and fsim 0.0021 despite both individual hops being learned to low loss, confirming the bridge is necessary for compositional transfer.

claims.claim: On synthetic data, GPT-2 with joint training reaches 0.995 +/- 6e-4 feature similarity and 100% task success, and two-hop reasoning with identity bridges reaches 0.9642 +/- 7e-4 similarity and 99.7% +/- 0.5% success, versus 0.016 +/- 6e-3 similarity and 0% success without identity bridges (Table 1).
claims.evidence: From-scratch GPT-2 decoder at paper's hyperparameters (N=100, 12 layers, 12 heads, T=500, AdamW, κ=3, 3 seeds): joint-training fsim 0.9896±0.0053 (paper 0.995), no-bridge fsim 0.0155±0.0293 (paper 0.016) with 0% success (paper 0%); at GPT-2-small width d=768, joint success 100% and two-hop+bridge success 100%, matching Table 1.

claims.claim: On natural-language experiments, Llama-3-1B under joint training reaches 0.8174 feature similarity and 73% success, and Qwen-2.5-1.5B reaches 0.8488 similarity and 85% success (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Full-parameter fine-tuning of Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen2.5-1.5B on the paper's premise set yields 4.3% and 5.0% held-out analogical success respectively, versus the claimed 73% and 85%; while the alignment-gap mechanism is directionally confirmed (positive only under joint training, destroyed by ablation), the specific quantitative results in the claim are contradicted by an order of magnitude.

claims.claim: Deep linear networks trained layer-by-layer show progressively increasing feature alignment with depth, reaching cosine similarity of at least 0.8 by the penultimate layer for same-label inputs (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: L=5 deep linear network (d=64, 5 seeds) trained layer-by-layer with hand-derived numpy gradients shows monotonically increasing same-label cosine alignment 0.630→0.922→0.958→0.962→0.963, with penultimate-layer alignment 0.962≥0.8, directly confirming Theorem 6's prediction.

ai-sherpa/feature-resemblance-analogical.overall: The logbook provides strong independent reproduction of claims 1-4 and 6 at full paper scale with from-scratch implementations, confirming the core theoretical mechanisms (joint-training alignment, curriculum necessity, identity-bridge necessity, depth-monotone alignment in deep linear nets). Claim 5 is falsified: real LLM fine-tuning experiments produce single-digit success rates versus the paper's claimed 73%/85%, though the mechanism direction is confirmed.

ai-sherpa/spurious-correlation-preferenc.paper_title: Spurious Correlation Learning in Preference Optimization: Mechanisms, Consequences, and Mitigation via Tie Training

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that mean spurious bias (asymmetric spurious-feature distributions across preference pairs) or causal-spurious correlation in the training distribution induces nonzero spurious parameters at the DPO population equilibrium (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Two algebraically independent solvers of Theorem 4.1's closed form agree to machine precision (1.3e-16–3.0e-16), the curvature-corrected prediction matches a real Newton-trained DPO fit to 4.2%–9.0% relative error across β, and a mechanism ablation isolates each channel (mean-bias-only → ‖θ_s*‖=1.789, correlation-only → 1.258, neither → 0.0 exactly) at full paper scale (d_c=d_s=5, n=10,000).

claims.claim: Theorem 5.3 decomposes deployment suboptimality under distribution shift into an irreducible shift term, driven by learned spurious parameters interacting with shifted spurious statistics, and a reducible estimation term that vanishes as sample size n approaches infinity (Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: SubOpt_Q plateaus at the shift floor 0.5641 across a 250× range of n (200→50,000: 0.667→0.568→0.562→0.567), while parameter estimation error decays with log-log slope -0.487 (theory: -0.5) and stays within a bounded 0.72×–0.87× multiple of the theorem's Γ_n bound at every n, with 20 seeds at full paper scale.

claims.claim: Tie training with equal-utility preference pairs shrinks spurious parameters while preserving causal learning, with an isotropic-case spurious-parameter reduction ratio of alpha*lambda_0 / (alpha*lambda_0 + (1-alpha)*sigma^2) (Theorem 6.2).
claims.evidence: Population-level tie-mixing ratio matches Corollary 6.3's closed form αλ_0/(αλ_0+(1-α)σ²) to ≤2.3% relative error across all α, finite-sample training (30 seeds) confirms the trend within ~1 std, and the causal decontamination check shows ‖θ_c,mix‖ stays within 6.1% of strict while relative distance to pure-causal decreases monotonically from 1.0 to 0.171.

claims.claim: In neural network experiments, strict (standard) training yields a spurious gap of about 0.70 and adversarial accuracy of about 0.25, whereas tie training at alpha=0.75 reduces the spurious gap to about 0.45 and raises adversarial accuracy to about 0.70 (Section on neural network experiments).
claims.evidence: Real CPU-trained MLPs at the paper's Appendix F.2 hyperparameters (5 seeds, 50K pairs) reproduce strict spurious gap 0.735 (paper ~0.70) and adversarial accuracy 0.231 (paper ~0.25), and tie training at α=0.75 raises adversarial accuracy to 0.678 (paper ~0.70) with a monotonic α-sweep matching Fig. 2 trends; the tie spurious gap of 0.259 is lower than the paper's ~0.45 but in the same direction and the paper labels this as qualitative persistence.

claims.claim: On the LLM synthetic Hotel Preferences benchmark, standard DPO achieves 92.25% in-distribution accuracy but drops to 74.00% under suppressed spurious correlation and 64.20% under adversarial spurious correlation, while informative tie training achieves 92.40% in-distribution, 82.85% suppressed, and 86.70% adversarial accuracy (Section on LLM synthetic benchmark, Hotel Preferences).
claims.evidence: 15 real DPO+LoRA fine-tuning runs of Llama-3.2-1B were executed, but the paper's headline +22.50-point adversarial gain from tie training did not appear (measured +1.82 ± 10.89, sign-flipping across seeds); however, the benchmark was reconstructed from prose with an unspecified training-time spurious correlation strength that governs the outcome, so the discrepancy cannot be attributed clearly to the claim being wrong versus the reconstruction differing from the paper's actual setup.

ai-sherpa/spurious-correlation-preferenc.overall: The logbook provides strong independent numerical evidence supporting the three log-linear theory claims (Theorems 4.1, 5.3, 6.2/Corollary 6.3) and the neural-network qualitative persistence experiment at the paper's own scale, while the LLM hotel benchmark was genuinely executed but yields inconclusive results due to an unspecified governing parameter in the paper's protocol.

NaveenVenu/ZXYcM3QuAR.paper_title: Density-Aware Translation of Spurious Correlations in Zero-Shot VLMs

claims.claim: Density-Aware Translation (DAT) achieves 83.33% worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds with CLIP ViT-L/14, surpassing prior methods by 4-14 percentage points and reducing the worst-group/average accuracy gap to 6.42% (Table 1).
claims.evidence: On the full Waterbirds dataset (4,795 train / 5,794 test) with CLIP ViT-L/14, the from-scratch DAT implementation achieves 80.06% worst-group accuracy (paper: 83.33%), a ~3-point gap, with the qualitative pattern—large WG improvement over zero-shot—holding across all three CLIP backbones tested.

claims.claim: On CelebA, DAT achieves 84.94% worst-group accuracy with only a 1.19% gap to average accuracy, and the label-free variant DAT* achieves comparable performance without spurious-attribute annotations (Table 2).
claims.evidence: CelebA was evaluated on a 6,000-image random subsample of the ~20K test partition (30% of full test set); on the headline ViT-L/14 backbone, DAT achieved only 52.94% WG (paper: 84.94%) and actually reduced WG accuracy relative to zero-shot, contradicting the claim for 2 of 3 backbones, though the reduced test scale makes this inconclusive rather than a definitive falsification.

claims.claim: DAT rescales image-text similarity scores by a density ratio computed via a Simplified Local Outlier Factor (SLOF), s-tilde_{y,a}(x) = s_{y,a}(x) / (D_{y,a}(z) + epsilon)^lambda, suppressing overconfident scores in sparse embedding regions (Method/Section on Key Technical Innovation).
claims.evidence: The SLOF density-translation formula was implemented from scratch and tested on a synthetic setup mirroring the paper's own diagnostic: SLOF correctly flagged atypical queries (mean SLOF 1.47 for wrong group vs 1.21 for true group), DAT reduced wrong-group preference from 13.0% to 7.7%, and error decreased monotonically with λ (13.0%→11.0%→8.0%→7.7%); the same formula is also exercised in the real Waterbirds experiment where it produces the claimed WG improvement.

claims.claim: On the COVID-19 medical imaging benchmark, DAT improves worst-group accuracy by over 20 percentage points to 65.22%, and on FMoW achieves 27.75% worst-group accuracy with a significant average-worst-group gap reduction (Medical & Multi-Label Domains results).
claims.evidence: Neither the COVID-19 benchmark nor FMoW was tested: COVID-19 was skipped due to unresolved dataset-construction ambiguity, and FMoW was skipped due to its ~70GB scale exceeding the compute budget. No experiments or results exist for this claim.

claims.claim: The authors prove that under a Kent (Fisher-Bingham) distribution assumption on CLIP's anisotropic embedding space, DAT reinstates anisotropy-sensitive log-likelihood terms that plain cosine similarity ignores, yielding Bayes-optimal alignment (Theoretical Contribution section).
claims.evidence: All three theoretical results were numerically verified: Proposition 3.1 (cosine ties with differing log-density) matched exactly; Theorem 3.3's margin decomposition identity and bounded remainder held across 2000 random parameter draws; Corollary 3.4's Kent expansion matched term-by-term across 500 random unit vectors with the anisotropy term vanishing at β=0.

claims.claim: DAT runs in approximately 150 seconds on an H100 GPU, versus 950+ seconds for the TIE baseline, while requiring no fine-tuning and generalizing across CLIP variants and other multimodal models such as ALIGN and AltCLIP (Practical Advantages section).
claims.evidence: TIE was not reimplemented; instead a naive k-NN proxy was used on 2,000 query images with A100 hardware (not H100). The density-only comparison showed 14–22x speedup (vs paper's ~5–6x), but the logbook itself acknowledges this proxy is not a like-for-like reproduction of the paper's specific 150s-vs-950s runtime figures, and generalization to ALIGN/AltCLIP was not tested.

NaveenVenu/ZXYcM3QuAR.overall: This logbook provides a solid from-scratch reproduction of DAT's core mechanism and theoretical foundations, with a close reproduction on Waterbirds (80.06% vs 83.33% WG) but significant gaps: CelebA was evaluated on a 30% test subsample with contradictory results for 2/3 backbones, COVID-19/FMoW were not tested at all, and the runtime claim used a proxy rather than a real TIE comparison.

arvkevi/tlm-illusion-repro.paper_title: The Illusion of Generalization in Tabular Language Models

claims.claim: Tabula-8B's binary classification achieves only a 2.5 percentage-point median lift over the majority-class baseline, while categorical classification shows a -0.3 point median lift, versus 32.6 points for quartile classification (Section 4.1.2, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: Full 165-dataset recomputation yields median lifts of binary 2.47 pp, categorical -0.33 pp, quartile 32.91 pp, closely matching the paper's 2.5, -0.3, and 32.6 points on the paper's actual evaluation scale.

claims.claim: 39.4% of evaluated datasets (65/165) show zero or negative lift over baseline for Tabula-8B, and 12 datasets show negative Cohen's Kappa, indicating worse-than-chance performance (Table 7, Table 6, Appendix C).
claims.evidence: Recomputation across all 165 datasets confirms exactly 65 at/below baseline (30 binary + 30 categorical + 5 quartile), yielding 39.4%, matching the claim. The 12 negative Cohen's Kappa sub-claim is not explicitly addressed, but the primary quantitative assertion is confirmed.

claims.claim: Instruction-tuning alone (Alpaca, no tabular exposure) reaches 58.6% accuracy versus Tabula-8B's 63.5% and a 47.7% base-Llama accuracy, recovering 92.2% of Tabula-8B's gain, with instruction-tuning contributing about 69% of the total gain versus 31% from tabular pretraining (Section 4.3.1, Table 4).
claims.evidence: Recomputed from all 119 binary/categorical datasets, the logbook reports 92.244% recovery of Tabula-8B's gain by Alpaca, matching the paper's 92.2%. The individual accuracy figures (58.6%, 63.5%, 47.7%) and the 69/31 split are not separately reported, but the key derived metric is confirmed.

claims.claim: On quartile classification, providing format examples alone (Alpaca+Q) achieves a 25.8-point lift versus Tabula-8B's 34.0-point lift, closing 71.3% of the 28.5-point gap, with the residual 8.2 points concentrated on contaminated stock/financial datasets (Section 4.3.2, Table 5).
claims.evidence: On all 26 held-out quartile datasets, Alpaca+Q closes 71.319% of the Alpaca-to-Tabula mean-accuracy gap, matching the paper's 71.3%. The specific lift values (25.8, 34.0, 28.5, 8.2) and the contamination-concentration claim are not separately reported.

claims.claim: All 753 evaluation rows of the us-womens-labor dataset are found verbatim in Tabula-8B's training corpus, and 844 matching date-day associations from unrelated T4 tables enable apparent memorization on the peloton-data task (Section 4.2.1, Section 4.2.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirms 753 unique rows in the original source and that 20/20 released T4 records match, plus Tabula's 750/753 accuracy and the 844 count from released data. However, it explicitly states no fresh raw-corpus sweep was performed (T4 corpus inaccessible), so the core claim that all 753 rows are verbatim in the training corpus is not independently verified—only 20 released records were checked, not all 753.

arvkevi/tlm-illusion-repro.overall: The logbook faithfully recomputes the paper's performance and ablation claims on the full 165-dataset artifact, with median lifts, failure counts, and recovery rates all closely matching reported values. The contamination claims are only partially supported: released evidence is cross-checked but the T4 training corpus was never independently swept, leaving the verbatim-contamination assertion unverified.

claims.claim: The paper presents an end-to-end framework for systematic rare-event analysis of probabilistic LLM outputs (Section 1).
claims.evidence: The framework components (TPS sampling, WHAM reweighting, diagnostics, mutation controls) are instantiated and run on both a synthetic 4-point distribution (TV 0.0163 vs truth) and TinyStories-8M, but the scaled run uses only 600 direct samples and 4×5×120 TPS steps—far below the paper's scale of millions of completions.

claims.claim: The implementation covers theory, efficient rare-completion generation strategies, probability estimation, and error analysis (Section 2).
claims.evidence: The code covers TPS rare-completion generation, WHAM probability estimation, and mutation-control error analysis, verified on a synthetic 4-state distribution (TV 0.0163) and a reduced-scale TinyStories-8M run; however, the 'theory' component is not separately tested and the real-model run is at drastically reduced sampling budget.

claims.claim: The paper analyzes rare completions in TinyStories models for ARI and log-probability observables (Section 4).
claims.evidence: A real run on roneneldan/TinyStories-8M with 32-token completions shows ARI biased means rising 3.10→9.78 and log-probability means rising -3.08→-0.68 with acceptance rates 0.732 and 0.507, but the total sample count (600 direct + 2400 TPS) is orders of magnitude below the paper's millions of completions.

claims.claim: The paper uses trajectory path sampling and MBAR-style reweighting to estimate rare-event probabilities and diagnose overlap between biased distributions (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: TPS and WHAM reweighting are implemented and run on TinyStories-8M: central TV is 0.102 (ARI) and 0.093 (log-probability), erased-bias mutation worsens log-probability TV to 0.435, and log-probability TPS reaches 6 new tail bins—but ARI reaches 0 new bins at this budget, so the joint tail-extension claim is only partially demonstrated at reduced scale.

MarxistLeninist/repro-rare-event-analysi.overall: The logbook demonstrates the core rare-event analysis mechanism (TPS + WHAM reweighting) working on both synthetic controls and TinyStories-8M, with directional bias response, low central TV, and effective mutation controls. However, all experiments run at drastically reduced scale (hundreds to thousands of samples vs millions in the paper), and the ARI tail-extension result fails at this budget, making every claim a toy-level rather than full reproduction.

alcray/repro-set-preserving-p2e-calibrat.paper_title: Set-Preserving Calibration from Conformal P-Values to E-Values

claims.claim: A calibrator is defined as set-preserving when converting conformal p-values at level alpha into e-values yields prediction sets identical to thresholding the e-values directly at 1/alpha (Section 2.1, Definition 2.2)
claims.evidence: Exhaustive attainable-rank enumeration across six theorem-valid grids (N=21, 50, 101, 1462) shows zero mismatches between p>alpha and log F(p)<-log(alpha) for every rank, with maximum mean-one normalization error of 3.27e-13. The raw CSV data confirms p_set_accepts and e_set_accepts agree in all listed cases.

claims.claim: Among left-continuous p-to-e calibrators, only the all-or-nothing calibrator can be exactly set-preserving, which motivates a new sigmoid-based P2E construction (Proposition 2.3, Theorem 2.6, Equation 9)
claims.evidence: The logbook provides an analytical proof audit tracing Proposition B.2's integral characterization through the forcing of f(alpha)=1/alpha and the collapse to F_AoN, plus independent finite-grid numerical confirmation that the (n,alpha)-dependent sigmoid construction escapes the impossibility by preserving every attainable rank.

claims.claim: The proposed sigmoid-based P2E calibrator is exact (expectation equal to 1), smooth, invertible, strictly positive, and strictly dominates the all-or-nothing calibrator in aggregation settings (Theorem 2.6)
claims.evidence: Mean-one normalization error ≤3.27e-13 across six grids; analytical calculus confirms strict monotonicity and invertibility of the logistic ratio; 500 predeclared seven-way rank tuples show P2E e-values never below AoN; all log e-values finite. The float64 underflow (1,333 zeros at n=1461) is a numerical representation issue, not a mathematical failure, as log-space evaluation preserves all orderings.

claims.claim: Applied to e-Cross-Conformal Prediction (ECCP), the P2E calibrator preserves exact 1-alpha coverage, whereas standard cross-conformal-prediction variants only guarantee approximate 1-2alpha coverage (Proposition 4.1)
claims.evidence: Exhaustive rank enumeration independently recovers 1-floor(alpha*N)/N, and 100-seed, 200-tree ECCP experiments on Abalone and Boston show direct true-response P2E coverage of 0.902147, 0.902170, and 0.902075 at nominal 0.90, all above 1-alpha. The faithful released-grid replay is within 0.005 of paper values.

claims.claim: Applied to Weighted Conformal Aggregation (WECA), data-dependent weighted merging of e-values across multiple models retains valid coverage (Proposition 4.2)
claims.evidence: Full four-task, 20-seed WECA protocol (1,120 rows) reproduces all 96 displayed coverage mean/SD entries at two-decimal precision, with P2E WECA mean coverages of 0.95183, 0.95398, 0.94968, and 0.96344 at nominal 0.95. However, 22/80 inference-stage P2E calls fall outside Theorem 2.6's noninteger domain, preventing literal Proposition 4.2 invocation for those runs; empirical coverage remains above nominal despite this.

claims.claim: Empirically, ECCP using the proposed P2E calibrator produces smaller prediction sets than baseline p-to-e conversion methods while maintaining valid coverage (Section 5)
claims.evidence: 100-seed paired comparison shows P2E shorter than all baselines (F1, F2, F3) on 100/100 seeds in both Abalone and Boston, with P2E lengths 6.695/9.765 vs F1 29.069/67.144, F2 10.213/53.734, F3 32.022/59.180, at valid coverage ~0.895. Exact analysis further shows 99,383 classical predictions are analytically unbounded but censored by the finite response grid, strengthening the efficiency conclusion.

alcray/repro-set-preserving-p2e-calibrat.overall: The logbook provides strong concrete evidence supporting all six claims: exhaustive rank-enumeration checks with near-zero numerical error for the core set-preservation mechanism, a detailed proof audit for the uniqueness result, and paper-scale 100-seed ECCP and 20-seed WECA experiments across multiple datasets confirming smaller P2E prediction sets with valid coverage. The main qualifications are float64 underflow in naive exponentiation (addressed by log-space evaluation), 22/80 WECA runs outside the theorem's stated domain, and the finding that published finite classical baseline lengths are grid-censored measurements of analytically unbounded sets.

imcypr/O88FCPAPAj.paper_title: Ranking Free RAG: Replacing Re-ranking with Selection in RAG for Sensitive Domains

claims.claim: METEORA replaces opaque re-ranking with rationale-driven evidence selection, adaptive cutoff detection, and rationale-based poisoned-evidence verification (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: A deterministic trace runs the METEORA pipeline on 4 short hand-crafted documents with an 8-term keyword encoder and a hardcoded string-matching verifier, confirming rationale pairing, elbow cutoff, expansion, and poison filtering operate on a miniature example — not a full-scale benchmark.

claims.claim: Across six datasets, METEORA reports 13.41% higher recall, 21.05% higher precision without expansion, 80% lower evidence volume, 33.34% higher answer accuracy, and 4.4x adversarial robustness improvement (Abstract).
claims.evidence: The Claim 2 page contains only a header with no experiments, runs, or numerical results for recall, precision, evidence volume, answer accuracy, or adversarial robustness.

claims.claim: Under the paper's latency setup, METEORA uses 12.23k input tokens and 2.91s total time, compared with 36.89k/4.04s for SBERT and 39.82k/4.61s for RankRAG (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The Claim 3 page describes a plan to record tokenizer revisions, chunking, warmup, and GPU timing but contains no executed runs or measured latency/token numbers.

claims.claim: The evaluation spans six legal, finance, and academic datasets with document counts and QA-pair counts listed for ContractNLI, CUAD, MAUD, PrivacyQA, FinQA, and QASPER (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The audit checked 4 of 6 datasets against the checksum-pinned LegalBench-RAG archive: document counts match for all four, question counts match for CUAD/MAUD/PrivacyQA but ContractNLI shows 977 vs 946, and FinQA and QASPER were never audited, leaving the six-dataset claim only partially addressed.

claims.claim: METEORA reports larger recall gains over the strongest baseline as document complexity increases, including +41.17% on MAUD (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The Claim 5 page contains only a header with no experiments, runs, or numerical results regarding recall gains scaling with document complexity or the +41.17% MAUD figure.

imcypr/O88FCPAPAj.overall: The logbook provides a toy-scale implementation audit of the METEORA pipeline (Claim 1) and a checksum-pinned data audit of 4 of 6 LegalBench-RAG datasets (partially relevant to Claim 4), but executes no benchmark runs for the aggregate retrieval, latency, or complexity-scaling claims. The most substantive finding — that Table 2's 'Avg. Tokens' column actually contains character counts — pertains to a bonus claim not in the judged set.

YMRohit/icml2026-64918-memorybench-logbo.paper_title: MemoryBench: A Benchmark for Memory and Continual Learning in LLM Systems

claims.claim: MemoryBench provides a three-module framework with a task provider, user simulator, and performance monitor for testing LLM-system continual learning from feedback logs (Figure 1)
claims.evidence: Static AST audit of the official code found all required symbols for all three modules: TaskProvider (16 symbols including load_memory_bench, 11 *_Dataset classes), UserSimulator (8 symbols including UserSimulator, FeedbackAgent, EvaluatorFactory), and PerformanceMonitor (6 symbols including evaluate_and_summary, summary_results), with 148 symbols catalogued in c1_symbols.csv.

claims.claim: MemoryBench covers 11 public datasets across three domains, four task-format categories, and two languages (Table 2)
claims.evidence: Exhaustive verification: each.json has 28 configs collapsing to exactly 11 source datasets; domain_tags match {Open-Domain, Legal, Academic&Knowledge}; task_tags match {Long-Short, Short-Long, Long-Long, Short-Short}; a full language census over all 4,063 rows via datasets-server confirms only en/zh with zh exactly where Table 2 places it; 4:1 train/test split verified on all 28 configs and spot-checked on 4 downloaded arrow files.

claims.claim: The benchmark includes both declarative/procedural memory and explicit/implicit feedback categories absent from prior memory benchmarks (Table 1)
claims.evidence: Released data confirmed to contain all four categories: declarative memory (13 corpus files, 103K chars in Locomo-0), procedural memory (dialog logs on all 200 train rows per corpus-free config), explicit feedback (multi-round critique turns: 198/200 WritingPrompts), and implicit feedback (satisfaction 1-10 + like/dislike/copy). Recomputed distributions match paper Tables 3/4: P(like|S>=8)=5.7% vs paper 5.8-8.4%, copy/like ratio 4.77 vs Eq.3 target 4.0, likes only at S>=7, dislikes only at S<=4. The 'absent from prior benchmarks' half is a literature claim assessed by inspection, not experimen

claims.claim: Off-policy results show that advanced memory systems such as A-Mem, Mem0, and MemoryOS do not consistently outperform simpler RAG baselines (Figure 2)
claims.evidence: Independent GPU runs (Qwen3-8B backbone, 200 train/50 test per dataset) show simple baselines win 2/3 corpus-free datasets (NFCats: BM25-S 5.00, WritingPrompts: Vanilla 0.2373) while A-Mem wins LexEval-Summarization by +0.013; on Locomo, Embed-S (0.5082) beats all memory systems but A-Mem (0.4797) and MemoryOS (0.4283) beat Vanilla (0.3433). This supports the weak-form claim 'not consistently outperform.' However, Mem0 was entirely invalid (401 errors), MemoryOS only ran on NFCats+Locomo for corpus-free, and only 3 of ~8 non-Locomo datasets were tested. The aggregation audit of the authors' ow

claims.claim: Efficiency measurements show large and inconsistent memory-operation and prediction-time costs for existing memory-based LLM systems (Figure 3)
claims.evidence: Independent timing measurements show memory-operation costs per case: MemoryOS 46.859s, A-Mem 0.056s, BM25-S 0.081s, Embed-S 0.044s — a 836.8x ratio between MemoryOS and A-Mem. Prediction times range from 0.376s (MemoryOS) to 2.814s (BM25-S). Mem0's 56s memory time is suspect due to integration failure (401 errors), but MemoryOS's extreme cost is real and confirms large, inconsistent costs across systems.

claims.claim: Comparisons with and without feedback show simulated user feedback can improve model performance on task-specific metrics (Table 11)
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states 'the C6 feedback experiment did not run: the account's HF credit balance was exhausted mid-job.' No experimental evidence was produced for this claim.

YMRohit/icml2026-64918-memorybench-logbo.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the structural and compositional claims (1-3) through code audits and exhaustive data analysis, and provides partial but real independent GPU-run evidence supporting the empirical claims about memory system performance (4) and efficiency costs (5), though with significant scope gaps (Mem0 integration failure, incomplete MemoryOS coverage, only 3 corpus-free datasets). Claim 6 was never addressed due to resource exhaustion.

claims.claim: In the zero-temperature (hardmax) limit of self-attention dynamics with negative-definite key-query interaction, token updates coincide with a Frank-Wolfe step on a quadratic objective over the convex hull of the tokens, and Theorem 3.1 gives a linear convergence rate bound J^t(x_i^{t+1}) ≤ (2/(t+1))·λ_max(B_0)·diam(K^0)^2 (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Across 32 configurations (dims 2–8, 8 seeds), the hardmax oracle and Frank-Wolfe linear minimization oracle agreed in 96/96 one-step comparisons with max update residual 0.0, and all 22,400 Theorem 3.1 rate checks passed (0 violations, worst objective-to-bound ratio 0.062).

claims.claim: When the key-query matrix is positive definite, Theorem 4.2 shows super-exponential convergence of tokens to vertices, and Proposition 4.5 shows the induced cell structure coincides with B-norm Voronoi cells when vertices have equal norm (Section 4, Theorem 4.2, Proposition 4.5).
claims.evidence: Across 12 positive-definite geometries (dims 2–8, conditions 1–8) and 7,200 points, B-Voronoi cell membership had 0 mismatches, equal-B-norm level residual was 7.2e-16, and both constant-rate and super-exponential formula residuals were below 1.2e-14; the official compute_cell_map smoke test also had 0 mismatches.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.8 establishes well-posedness of the singular ODE limit governing the hardmax dynamics (Section 4, Theorem 4.8, Equation 4.4).
claims.evidence: Euler refinements form a Cauchy sequence with median empirical order 0.91; discrete hardmax iteration converges to the ODE limit with median order 0.89 (worst gap 3.17e-3 at 1600 steps); median perturbation amplification stays below 1 across 300 trials, with honest reporting of non-Lipschitz behavior at switching surfaces (45/300 trials, worst absolute deviation 3.8e-3); 150 singular-set trials show branch spread ≤ 6.3e-3.

claims.claim: At finite inverse temperature β, Theorem 5.2 shows interior particles reach near-vertex configurations in O(1) steps with high probability, while Theorem 5.4 shows these metastable configurations persist for exponentially long times (on the order of e^β steps) before eventual collapse to a single cluster (Section 5, Theorem 5.2, Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: Early-phase clustering (Theorem 5.2) achieved ≥99.975% near-vertex success in 6 steps across β=8–16 with 2000 trials each; residence-time scaling (Theorem 5.4) via 20,000 exact geometric samples per β recovered exponential slopes 0.997 vs expected 1.0 (R²=0.9999) and 1.472 vs expected 1.5 (R²=0.9996).

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 shows the argmax operation generically produces a singleton, and Lemma 2.2 shows the convex hull of tokens shrinks under step sizes γ^t ∈ (0,1), underpinning the Frank-Wolfe reformulation of hardmax attention (Section 2, Lemma 2.1, Lemma 2.2).
claims.evidence: Lemma 2.1: 0 exact argmax ties in 42,000 rows over 6,000 configurations, min margin 9.09e-5, 95% upper bound on tie probability 7.13e-5, and 318/318 constructed ties resolved by 1e-9 perturbation. Lemma 2.2: 2016/2016 LP containment checks pass, 0 volume/diameter monotonicity violations, and negative controls at γ=1.5/−0.5 show 34–35 of 35 tokens escaping the hull.

Vassilbek/attention-frank-wolfe-icml2026.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all five claims through randomized geometry checks, exact algebraic identity verification, stochastic simulation with 20,000 replicates, LP-based containment testing, and Euler refinement studies, all on non-trivial dimensions (up to 8) with negative controls and official code smoke tests.

Yashp2003/bcN12UkftY.paper_title: FloorplanQA: A Benchmark for Spatial Reasoning in LLMs using Structured Representations

claims.claim: FloorplanQA (PlanQA) comprises 1,800 synthetic structured floor layouts (600 each for kitchens, living rooms, bedrooms) yielding 18,000 question-layout pairs across 11 cognitive/question categories, evaluated on 11 LLMs (Section 3.1, Table 1, Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook downloaded the real dataset and confirmed 600 layouts each for kitchen/living_room/bedroom (1,800 synthetic), but found 16,000 QA pairs (not 18,000), 8 tasks in 3 categories (not 11 categories), and 15 LLMs (not 11), attributing the mismatch to a paper version discrepancy.

claims.claim: Models achieve over 95% accuracy on metric-computation questions but fall below 50% accuracy on topology, rule-based validation, and geometric-planning questions, per the cognitive-target accuracy heatmap (Section 4.1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: DeepSeek-V4-Flash on only 21 questions (1 layout × 3 rooms × 7 tasks) showed Metric 100%, Topology 33.3%, Dynamic 0%, matching the claimed pattern, but this is a tiny fraction of the 16,000-question benchmark and cannot constitute a full reproduction.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 proves that a greedy allocation rule—repeatedly assigning one unit to the individual with the highest next marginal survival probability p_i(l)=Pr(X_i≥l)—optimally solves the single-round allocation problem for any realized frontier and budget (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports generic least-squares fitting metrics (structured_mse=0.0022, rel_param_err=0.0079, n=200, d=4) with no implementation of the greedy allocation rule, no comparison against brute-force optimal allocation, and no measurement of survival probabilities or frontier allocation outcomes. claims.evidence: The logbook reports structured_mse=0.0024 and rel_param_err=0.0168 from a generic regression experiment (n=200, d=6). claims.evidence: The logbook reports structured_mse=0.0022 and rel_param_err=0.0089 from a generic fitting experiment. There is no implementation of the surrogate value function computation, no runtime measurement across varying budget sizes b, and no memory profiling to verify O(b^5 log b) time or O(b^2) space complexity.

There is no use of ICPSR HIV transmission network data, no implementation of the adaptive surrogate policy or baseline policies (constant k∈{2,3,5,10}, fixed-fraction greedy), and no comparison of recruitment outcomes under model misspecification.

neonforestmist/exact-categorical-anova-r.paper_title: Exact Functional ANOVA Decomposition for Categorical Inputs Models

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 establishes that any function in L^2 over categorical inputs admits a Fourier expansion using basis functions phi_A^(z), defined via a signed inverse-likelihood construction, that automatically satisfy hierarchical orthogonality (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports a generic least-squares experiment (n=200, d=4, LS MSE=0.0024, rel-param err=0.0151) but does not test hierarchical orthogonality or the signed inverse-likelihood construction; the experiment does not verify the theorem's mathematical content.

claims.claim: When the empirical support equals the full hypergrid, the exact ANOVA decomposition is obtained by solving the linear system Gamma c(f) = mu(f) (Section on full-support decomposition).
claims.evidence: The experiment (n=200, d=16) does not use a full hypergrid support (which for d=16 binary variables would require 2^16=65536 points), so the linear system Gamma c(f) = mu(f) on the full hypergrid is never actually solved or tested.

claims.claim: For sparse empirical support of cardinality r much smaller than the full hypergrid size |E|, Algorithm 1 greedily selects basis elements to yield decomposition computation in O(r^3) rather than O(|E|^3) (Algorithm 1).

claims.claim: On the Mushrooms dataset (22 categorical variables, hypergrid size approximately 10^14), the method achieves near-perfect reconstruction (R^2 approximately 1, MSE approximately 10^-15) in 0.3 seconds (Experimental results section).
claims.evidence: The experiment uses a synthetic design (n=200, d=22) rather than the actual Mushrooms dataset, reports LS MSE=0.0021 (not the claimed ~10^-15), and provides no R^2 or timing measurements; none of the claim's specific metrics are reproduced.

claims.claim: On binarized MNIST (784 dimensions), the method achieves R^2 = 0.86 in 15 minutes using 10,000 basis elements (Experimental results section).
claims.evidence: The experiment uses d=16 (not 784), n=200, and reports only LS MSE=0.0022 and rel-param err=0.0244; there is no binarized MNIST data, no R^2=0.86 result, no 15-minute timing, and no 10,000 basis element count.

claims.claim: Equation (5) defines generalized SHAP values as shap_i(x) = sum over sets A containing i of f_A(x_A)/|A|, which exactly recovers standard SHAP values in the independent-features setting (Equation 5).
