amkkk/pinda-repro.paper_title: Data Augmentation of Contrastive Learning is Estimating Positive-incentive Noise

claims.claim: Standard predefined data augmentations in the contrastive learning framework are proven equivalent to a point estimate of positive-incentive (pi) noise (Section 3.4, Eq. 19).
claims.evidence: The logbook restates the paper's derivation steps (γ definition, auxiliary Gaussian, Dirac delta for fixed augmentations, conditional entropy formula, MI maximization equivalence) but does not show independent re-derivation or algebraic verification; it merely asserts 'the algebra is sound' without demonstrating the checking.

claims.claim: Task entropy is defined via auxiliary Gaussian distributions to bridge the contrastive loss with information-theoretic principles (Section 3.3, Eq. 9).
claims.evidence: The logbook lists the construction steps (γ mapping, auxiliary α|x~N(0,γ^{-1}), task entropy definition, conditional entropy integral) but these are restatements of the paper's equations rather than independent mathematical verification; no novel derivation or cross-check is shown.

claims.claim: The learned pi-noise generator (PiNDA) improves k-NN accuracy by about 5% and softmax regression accuracy by about 9% over a random-noise baseline on the Reuters dataset (Table II).
claims.evidence: Experiments used synthetic proxy data yielding ceiling accuracy (1.0000 for both baseline and PiNDA), making accuracy comparisons meaningless; the real Reuters dataset was never loaded because the official code lacks non-vision data handlers and a Reuters loader was not implemented.

claims.claim: PiNDA yields consistent accuracy gains when plugged into SimCLR, MoCo, BYOL, and SimSiam with ResNet18/ResNet50 backbones on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Fashion-MNIST, and STL-10 (Tables III and IV).
claims.evidence: Only SimCLR was tested (not MoCo, BYOL, or SimSiam) on synthetic CIFAR-10-like data with batch_size=64 and 10 epochs (vs paper's batch_size=256, 1000 epochs), with both baseline and PiNDA hitting 1.0000 ceiling accuracy; real CIFAR/STL datasets were not downloaded due to bandwidth constraints.

claims.claim: Visualizations of the learned pi-noise variance show the generator produces style-transfer-like augmentations that trace object outlines without supervision (Figures 1, 5, and 6).
claims.evidence: Variance maps were generated on synthetic uniform class-conditional Gaussian data where noise is spatially uniform and lacks semantic structure; the style-transfer-like patterns tracing object outlines require real image datasets which were never used.

claims.claim: The added computational cost of the pi-noise generator is modest: a DNN3 generator adds about 5s per epoch and 0.23GB memory on CIFAR-10, while a ResNet18 generator adds about 11s and 2.26GB memory (Table V).
claims.evidence: Only the ResNet18 generator was measured (DNN3 not tested) on synthetic data with batch_size=64, yielding +2.42s and +758.6MB overhead versus the paper's +11s and +2.26GB at batch_size=256; the absolute numbers differ substantially and only one of two generator architectures was benchmarked.

amkkk/pinda-repro.overall: This logbook provides no non-toy empirical evidence for any of the six claims: theoretical claims 1–2 are restated rather than independently verified, and empirical claims 3–6 were run exclusively on synthetic proxy data with ceiling accuracy or mismatched scale due to inability to download real datasets. The reproduction framework runs without errors but does not constitute a meaningful reproduction of the paper's results.

ProCreations/repro-on-the-computational-.paper_title: On the Computational Complexity of Performative Prediction

claims.claim: Theorem 1.2 (restated as Theorem 3.4) proves that computing an ε-performatively stable point is PPAD-complete even when ρ = Lβ/α ≤ 1 + O(ε), with the explicit constant ε′ = 0.088/6 ≈ 0.0147 (Section 1.1, Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: 1,728 reduction cells at dimensions 3–34 verify the exact affine map g(x)=x-(ε/ε')F(x) with identity error ≤5.55e-17, zero Lipschitz violations, and zero quadratic-argmin error; the sign-reversal destructive control fails all 1,728 cells, confirming the reduction mechanism is correctly constructed.

claims.claim: This PPAD-hardness persists in the simple setting where the loss is quadratic, ℓ(x;z) = ½||x−z||², and the distribution shift D(x) is given by an affine map g(x) (Section 3.1, Equation 2-3, Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The same 1,728 cells confirm zero quadratic-argmin error for ℓ(x;z)=½||x−z||² under affine g(x), and 16 direct RRM runs at dimensions 4–64 with ρ 0.2–0.97 all respect the exact contraction bound; the ρ=1 cycling control correctly exhibits the two-cycle, marking the phase boundary.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 shows a phase transition to tractability: when ρ ≤ 1 + O_ε(ε^4), an ε-performatively stable point can be computed in poly(d, log(1/ε)) time via an ellipsoid-method algorithm exploiting hypomonotonicity (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: An independently implemented central-cut ellipsoid solver completes 16 runs at dimensions 4–32 and tolerances 1e-2 to 1e-5, with all final residuals below tolerance (worst ratio 0.998) in ≤14,505 cuts; 1,024 hypomonotonicity cells satisfy the source bound with zero violation, and the ε^4→ε accuracy translation is verified across 5 parameter rows.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.7 establishes an unconditional information-theoretic lower bound: any algorithm requires 2^Ω(d) expected-risk-minimization (ERM) queries to find an ε-performatively stable point even when ρ ≤ 1 + O_ε(ε), and even for constant ε (Section 3.1, Corollary 3.7).
claims.evidence: 186 cells execute the Hirsch lower bound c((1/ε)-10)L)^(d-2) at dimensions 3–64 and three constant accuracies; the RRM-reveals-T identity has zero reconstruction error, and the minimum successive-dimension factor is 3.33>2, confirming exponential dimension dependence; the ε=0.1 control correctly collapses the base to zero.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.12 extends PPAD-hardness of performative stability from the hypercube constraint set to any well-bounded general convex constraint set (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.12, Definition 3.11).
claims.evidence: 28,672 support-function VI tests across 7 distinct well-bounded convex domains (disk, ellipse, rectangle, square, diamond, hexagon, octagon) yield zero confinement failures with minimum support witness 0.531; a 6-bit Sperner enumeration recovers 343 trichromatic triangles among 4,096 elementary triangles, and the thin-domain control correctly excludes all gadget vertices.

claims.claim: For the special case of strategic classification, Theorem 4.4 shows that computing a local optimum of the performative risk under single-label updates is PLS-hard, complementing prior NP-hardness results for global performative optimality (Abstract, Section 1.1, Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive enumeration of all 65,536 classifiers and 1,048,576 single-label neighbors on a 4-vertex, 6-edge weighted complete graph confirms the strategic-utility/cut-weight flip identity with zero error; induced strategic local optima exactly match direct local-max-cut masks [5,6,9,10], and the factor-two removal control breaks the correspondence on 12 masks.

ProCreations/repro-on-the-computational-.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical and combinatorial verification of the algebraic reduction mechanisms, solver implementations, and gadget constructions underlying all six complexity-theoretic claims, using exact arithmetic, destructive controls, and exhaustive enumeration where feasible. While universal PPAD/PLS-hardness statements inherently cannot be proven by finite computation, the logbook transparently verifies each theorem's constructive components on non-toy instances at meaningful scale.

rahit/repro-on-the-infinite-width-and-de.paper_title: On the Infinite Width and Depth Limits of Predictive Coding Networks

claims.claim: For linear residual networks with equilibrated activities, predictive coding (PC) and backpropagation (BP) share exactly the same set of width- and depth-stable feature-learning parameterizations, with scaling exponent alpha=1/2 (Theorem 2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Des4 (30 seeds, N=128) shows preactivation growth exponent collapses to +0.005 only at α≥1/2 (vs +0.69 at α=0, +0.10 at α=0.25), and Des5 (N=512) shows feature-update slope crosses zero uniquely at α=1/2 (+0.012, with sign flip from +3.65 below to negative above). The PC-specific gradient term shrinks with width (0.247→0.015 from N=64 to N=512), confirming PC shares BP's α=1/2.

claims.claim: For linear MLPs, Corollary 3.2 shows the equilibrated PC energy converges to the MSE loss as width N to infinity, so PC computes the same gradients as BP under any width-stable feature-learning parameterization (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Width sweep N=8..2048 (8 seeds each) shows s−1 scales as N^{-1.00275} (R²=0.998, theory −1), |F*/L−1| decays at the same rate, and cos(PC grad, BP grad) reaches 0.999996 at N=2048. The standard-parameterization control gives slope −0.003 (flat), confirming the convergence is specific to the stable parameterization.

claims.claim: For linear residual networks, the energy rescaling factor s(theta) = 1 + Theta(L/N), so PC gradients converge to BP gradients specifically in the regime where width N is much greater than depth L (Corollary 4.2, Equation 19).
claims.evidence: Grid of 1200 residual nets (N∈{16..256}×L∈{4..32}, 60 seeds) shows N-exponent of s−1 is −0.98 to −0.996 at every depth (theory −1), 2D fit gives logL coefficient 1.244 (theory +1, approaching asymptotically), and (s−1)N/L converges toward e−1=1.718 (reaching 1.577 at N=256, L=32). The α=0 control explodes with depth-slope 9.20 vs 1.25 for α=1/2.

claims.claim: Experiments on deep nonlinear residual networks with Tanh and ReLU activations show PC converges to BP gradients empirically as long as activity equilibrium is reached during the inference phase (Figure 4, Section 5).
claims.evidence: Real PC inference on Tanh/ReLU residual nets (N=512, L=8) shows cos(PC,BP) rising from ~0.22 to 0.9986 (Tanh) and 0.9952 (ReLU) as inference residual falls to ~1e-6, with corr(log-residual, 1−cos)=0.79. However, the setup uses synthetic Gaussian data, batch size 16, a single width/depth configuration, and only 2 seeds—clearly simplified relative to the paper's Figure 4 benchmarks.

claims.claim: The equilibrated energy for linear networks is derived in closed form as F*(theta) = (1/s(theta)) L(theta), where s(theta) = 1 + sum of squared norms of downstream weight products (Equations 5-6).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive grid of 4620 configurations (L∈{2..8}×N∈{2..12}×D∈{2..7}×5 seeds×{MLP,residual}) verifies F*=L/s to max abs error 4.44e-16 with inference stationarity at 7.5e-15. The L=2 special case s=1+‖w^L‖² is exact (err=0 over 2000 nets), and destructive controls (dropping a term of s: err 4.8e-2; forward-pass activities: gap 0.23) fail as expected.

rahit/repro-on-the-infinite-width-and-de.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, machine-precision verification of the paper's core theoretical results (closed-form equilibrated energy, width/depth scaling exponents, and the α=1/2 stability boundary) through exact computations with proper positive and negative controls. The nonlinear empirical claim (Claim 4) is demonstrated on a simplified synthetic setup rather than the paper's full-scale benchmarks.

rahit/repro-matroid-algorithms-under-siz.paper_title: Matroid Algorithms Under Size-Sensitive Independence Oracles

claims.claim: Under the size-sensitive independence-oracle cost model, any (possibly randomized) algorithm approximating matroid rank within a multiplicative factor of 1 ± 1/40 with probability at least 2/3 must incur Ω(n²) query cost in the worst case (Theorem 1.1.1).
claims.evidence: The witness lemma and witness-count bound are verified exhaustively over the complete 2^{3m} subset lattice (m=2,3,4) with 0 mismatches and 0 violations, the count bound is exactly tight (ratio 1.0000), and the exponential separation base T is computed exactly via rational arithmetic to m=320 yielding 1.128868 ≥ 1.128, establishing q=Ω(m) useful queries each of size Θ(n) ⇒ Ω(n²) cost.

claims.claim: For matroids whose maximum circuit size is at most c, a randomized algorithm finds a maximum-weight basis with expected query cost O(n^{2−1/c} log n), breaking the quadratic query-cost barrier (Theorem 1.1.1).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 is implemented verbatim and returns the exact max-weight basis on all 75 runs across c=2,3,4 and n up to 2560; the measured query-cost exponents after dividing out log n are 1.433/1.643/1.733 vs the predicted 1.5/1.667/1.75 (R²≥0.9998), all sub-quadratic, while the greedy control fits exponent 1.992≈2.0.

claims.claim: Distinguishing a partition matroid of part size 3 from one of part size 4 requires Ω(n²) query cost, matching the Õ(n²) upper bound for partition-size estimation (Theorem 1.1.2).
claims.evidence: The separation constant γ(3)=1.119930>1.1199 is computed exactly, the witness lemma holds with 0 mismatches over the full subset lattice, the exact multinomial ratio converges to γ(α) (verified to m=192), partition sizes of Q and Q' are verified as exactly 3 and 4 via backtracking min-cover, and the control γ(2)=0.866<1 correctly explains why the hard case is 3-vs-4.

claims.claim: For general non-decreasing query-cost functions f(|Q|), the paper proves an Ω(n·f(n/3)) lower bound using matroid unions of free and uniform matroids as hard instances (Section 6).
claims.evidence: The information threshold n/3 is verified exhaustively: all queries of size ≤m are independent for every S (m=2,3,4), the smallest informative query size is exactly m+1=n/3+1; greedy cost exponents match n·f(n) for f∈{1,√k,k,k²} with exponents {1.0,1.49,1.99,2.98}, and the partition threshold identity m/α=n/12 is verified exactly.

claims.claim: Linear-time size-sensitive oracle implementations are given for partition, graphic, bicircular, convex-transversal, and job-scheduling matroids (Section B).
claims.evidence: All five oracles (partition, graphic, bicircular, convex-transversal, job-scheduling) match independent reference implementations with 0 mismatches over the complete 2^{|E|} subset lattice, all matroid axioms hold exhaustively, and runtime scaling is measured as approximately linear (slopes 0.928, 1.011, 1.094) for three of the five oracles up to |I|=64000; the remaining two have correctness verified but runtime not benchmarked.

rahit/repro-matroid-algorithms-under-siz.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous clean-room reproduction of a pure-theory query-complexity paper, verifying the key combinatorial lemmas exhaustively on small instances, computing asymptotic separation constants exactly via rational arithmetic to large m, implementing the bounded-circumference algorithm with correct results and matching scaling exponents at n up to 2560, and confirming all five oracle implementations against independent references. The main limitations are inherently small exhaustive-check sizes and two unmeasured oracle runtimes, both honestly acknowledged.

rahit/repro-approximation-bounds-for-tra.paper_title: Approximation Bounds for Transformer Networks with Application to Regression

claims.claim: For d_x x n-dimensional sequence-to-sequence targets whose components are γ-Hölder continuous, a fixed-depth Transformer network with softmax attention achieves L^p approximation error ε (for any p in [1,∞)) using O(ε^{-d_x n/γ}) total parameters (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The reproduction verifies the piecewise-constant approximation bound eq.(2) at d_x=1, n=2 (slope -0.509 vs -0.5, R²=0.952), the ReLU step-layer identity (4.44e-16), and parameter count scaling, but no actual Transformer network is constructed—the self-attention contextual mapping (Step 3) is explicitly invoked from prior work, not re-derived or tested.

claims.claim: The same Hölder approximation result extends to the endpoint p=∞, the first explicit L^∞ bound established for standard softmax-attention Transformers, at the cost of parameter counts scaling with 3^{d_x n} (Theorem 1, case p=∞).
claims.evidence: The L^∞ rate is measured at small dimensions (slope -0.495 vs -0.5, R²=0.985), the trifling-region obstruction is demonstrated (deviation exactly 1/K), and the 3^{d_x n} multiplier is verified exactly across 6 configurations, but the median-of-shifts construction that actually achieves the L^∞ bound is invoked, not built or tested.

claims.claim: For target functions in the Sobolev class W^{1,p}, a depth-2 Transformer network achieves L^p approximation error ε using O(ε^{-d_x n}) parameters (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The Sobolev K^{-1} rate is confirmed at d_x=1, n=2 (slope -0.9987, R²=1.0) with p-independence shown via L¹/L² slopes, and parameter counts scale correctly, but no depth-2 Transformer is actually constructed—the self-attention token-mixing step is invoked from prior work.

claims.claim: Under nonparametric regression with dependent (β-mixing) observations, the excess risk of the Transformer-based empirical risk minimizer converges at rate m^{-γ/(γ+d_x n)} (up to log factors) for geometrically β-mixing data, and at rate m^{-rγ/((r+2)γ+(r+1)d_x n)} for algebraically β-mixing data with mixing parameter r (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The rate exponents are recovered algebraically by solving the bias-variance-dependence balancing equations (residuals 5.8e-6 for geometric, 1.4e-16 for algebraic across 24 configs each), but no actual β-mixing regression data is generated, no ERM is computed, and no finite-sample simulation is performed—only the exponent optimization from the proof is checked.

claims.claim: The proof technique shows that if the self-attention layer performs column averaging, the resulting network reduces to a generalized Transformer class that can approximate sequence-to-sequence Hölder functions, linking softmax and hardmax attention as special cases (Section 2.3).
claims.evidence: The column-averaging identity softmax(W^K=W^Q=O) = (1/n)Z11^T is verified to machine precision (3.55e-15 over 4000 random Z across 20 shapes), averaging-hardmax also equals column average (4.44e-16), softmax converges to hardmax as temperature→∞, and a destructive control confirms nonzero W^K,W^Q breaks the identity—this is an exact algebraic fact independent of scale.

rahit/repro-approximation-bounds-for-tra.overall: The logbook provides careful clean-room verification of the mathematical components underlying each theorem—approximation bounds, rate slopes, step-layer constructions, parameter count formulas, and the column-averaging attention identity—at small dimensions with appropriate destructive controls. However, no actual Transformer networks are constructed, the self-attention contextual mapping is invoked from prior work rather than verified, and no regression simulation is performed, making four of five claims addressed on simplified setups rather than fully reproduced.

rahit/repro-optimal-fair-aggregation-of-.paper_title: Optimal Fair Aggregation of Crowdsourced Noisy Labels using Demographic Parity Constraints

claims.claim: The demographic parity gap of majority-vote aggregated labels is bounded above by an exponentially decaying term in the number of annotators R, of the form sum over groups a of E[e^{-R K_phi(a,X)}] (Proposition 3.2).
claims.evidence: Exact Poisson-binomial and 2^R enumeration computations on the paper's own X=∅ regime show the Prop 3.2 bound holds across 15 exact configurations (max violation −3.33e-03, i.e., positive slack everywhere) and the Gao error bound holds across 800 grid configurations (max(err−bound)=−1.88e-05); destructive control with inflated exponent 2K fails 5/5, confirming the specific exponential form.

claims.claim: Under interpretable conditions on annotator skill, both Majority Vote and Bayesian aggregation are shown to achieve asymptotically unbiased fairness gaps relative to ground-truth labels as crowd size grows (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: Both MV and Bayes converge to Δ_DP(Y) in two setups (trivial limit 0 and non-trivial limit 0.2) to ~1e-5–1e-6, with the MV decay rate slope −0.1388/−0.1201 matching the predicted Gao exponent −K=−0.1453; the Bayes condition Σ(p−½)²=4.836 at R=60 is verified as diverging.

claims.claim: For majority voting with R annotators, the aggregated fairness gap is bounded by epsilon(R) times the sum of individual annotators' fairness gaps, showing majority voting can amplify rather than average out bias (Proposition 3.6).
claims.evidence: The Baillon constant η=0.4688223555 is computed exactly via two independent formula forms (agreement 1.67e-16, matching paper's 0.4688 to 2.24e-05); the Prop 3.6 bound holds across 8 exact configs (max violation −1.18e-02); systematic-bias amplification shows log-log slope 0.5000 confirming O(√R); destructive control with η'=1/√(2π) undershoots the exhaustive supremum 0.4215.

claims.claim: Convergence of the fairness gap to the ground-truth value requires a majority of annotators to have skill exceeding 0.5 plus a margin epsilon; without this, majority voting fails to converge (Section 3, following Proposition 3.6).
claims.evidence: At the no-signal point (all skills=½), Δ_DP(Ŷ^MV)=0 exactly for every R∈{3,10,40,100,200}, so the gap to Δ_DP(Y)=0.2 persists forever; the competent crowd (p=0.75) converges (gap 0.020→0.0000 from R=10 to 80); the low-signal band width shrinks with log-log slope −0.576≈−½, confirming ε~1/√R.

claims.claim: FairCrowd, a post-processing method, enforces a strict epsilon-fairness constraint on the output of any aggregation rule while provably bounding the resulting accuracy loss (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: FairCrowd's recipe enforces Δ_DP≈ε to ~1e-4 across 6 values of ε, and its risk matches an independently constructed LP optimum to 1e-6–1e-5 (exactly 2.8e-17 when constraint is slack at ε=0.30); control shows unconstrained Bayes has Δ_DP=0.2044 violating ε-fairness for ε<0.2044, confirming the β*-adjustment is necessary.

rahit/repro-optimal-fair-aggregation-of-.overall: The logbook provides exact computational verification of all five theoretical claims on the paper's own synthetic X=∅ regime using Poisson-binomial convolution, exhaustive 2^R enumeration, and an independent LP, with destructive controls confirming the specific mathematical forms. The main limitation is that the general case with continuous features X is not covered, but all tests use the paper's stated experimental setup with exact rather than approximate arithmetic.

rahit/repro-stability-and-generalization.paper_title: Stability and Generalization of Nonconvex Optimization with Heavy-Tailed Noise

claims.claim: Under Assumption 3.1 (bounded p-th centered moment, p-BCM, for p in (1,2]), Theorem 4.2 bounds the generalization gap between population and empirical gradients by 4ε + C_p σ_p n^{-(p-1)/p} using a truncation argument to handle heavy-tailed noise (Theorem 4.2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The closed-form constant C_p is verified exactly over a 200,001-point grid (min 1.0 at p=2, max 3.0 at p=1.2, matching the remark bounds), the truncation identity φ(τ*)=C_p σ_p n^{-(p-1)/p} holds to 4.35e-16 relative error over 120 configurations with τ* confirmed as the true minimizer via destructive scan, and Monte-Carlo with genuine Pareto heavy-tailed noise confirms the bound holds in 15/15 cells with the correct exponent recovered to 2e-16.

claims.claim: For Clipped SGD (Algorithm 1), Proposition 5.1 gives an on-average stability bound ε_c ≤ 2Lγ√(T/n) Σ η_t, and Theorem 5.2/Corollary 5.3 derive a resulting population gradient bound with rate O(n^{-(p-1)/(3(3p-2))}) (Section 5.1, Theorem 5.2, Corollary 5.3).
claims.evidence: Proposition 5.1 stability bound ε_c ≤ 2Lγ√(T/n)Ση_t is confirmed via genuine neighboring-dataset runs of Clipped SGD (12/12 configs, max ratio 0.030), with coupled ε decaying ~1/√n (0.184→0.040) while uncoupled stays flat (~0.99), and the Corollary 5.3 rate exponent -(p-1)/(3(3p-2)) is verified symbolically via sympy: all 4 balancing terms equal the target rational function for all p, with a destructive control showing mis-set T~n^{1/2} unbalances the rate.

claims.claim: For Mini-Batch Normalized SGD (Algorithm 2), Theorem 5.5 and Corollary 5.6 establish an improved generalization rate of O(n^{-(p-1)/(7p-6)}) compared to the clipped-SGD rate (Section 5.2, Theorem 5.5, Corollary 5.6).
claims.evidence: Proposition 5.4 stability bound for NSGD-B holds in 8/8 neighboring-dataset configurations (max ratio 0.018), coupled ε decays with n (0.221→0.025) while uncoupled stays flat (~0.37), and the Corollary 5.6 rate exponent -(p-1)/(7p-6) is verified symbolically: all 4 balancing terms of Theorem 5.5 equal the target for all p, with a destructive control confirming B=const breaks the rate.

claims.claim: For Normalized SGD with Momentum (Algorithm 3), Theorem 5.9 matches the O(n^{-(p-1)/(7p-6)}) rate of the normalized batch variant (Section 5.3, Theorem 5.9).
claims.evidence: Proposition 5.7 stability bound for NSGD-M holds in 8/8 configs (max ratio 0.086), coupled ε decays (0.154→0.034) while uncoupled stays flat (~1.44), and the Corollary 5.9 rate exponent -(p-1)/(7p-6) is verified symbolically: 4 balancing terms equal the target, the other 4 are strictly faster, and the rate is confirmed identical to NSGD-B's rational function (sympy simplify = 0).

claims.claim: The combined clipping-plus-momentum method (Algorithm 4) achieves the same stability bound as momentum alone (Proposition 5.12) and a matching rate of O(n^{-(p-1)/(7p-6)}) without dependence on the linear step-size term γ (Theorem 5.13, Section 5.4).
claims.evidence: Proposition 5.12 stability holds in 8/8 configs (max ratio 0.081); the γ-independence claim is directly demonstrated: ε_cm = 0.1594 flat across γ=0.25–2.0 (×1.00) while Clipped SGD grows ×6.1 over the same range, and momentum-alone ε_m equals NSGD-CM ε_cm(γ→∞) with rel diff 0.0e+00; symbolically, 5 balancing terms of Theorem 5.13 equal -(p-1)/(7p-6), γ appears only in the optimization-bias term 2G^pγ^{1-p}, and the stability term 2Lη/(1-β) is γ-free.

rahit/repro-stability-and-generalization.overall: The logbook provides rigorous computational verification of all five theoretical claims through exact symbolic algebra (sympy rational verification of rate exponents), numerical verification of stability bounds on genuine neighboring-dataset algorithm runs, and Monte-Carlo confirmation of the heavy-tailed generalization bound. Destructive controls (broken coupling, mis-set schedules, wrong constants) consistently fail as expected, isolating the mechanisms behind each result.

amkkk/repro-provably-data-driven-lagrang.paper_title: Provably Data-driven Lagrangian Relaxation for Mixed Integer Linear Programming

claims.claim: For learned Lagrangian Relaxation multipliers over s coupling constraints and N training samples, the expected excess risk of the ERM solution is upper bounded by O(s^1.5/√N) (Theorem 5.5).
claims.evidence: Synthetic concave dual functions (not actual MILP instances) with small s∈{2,4,8} and N∈{10,100}. For s=2 the log-log slope is -0.469 (close to -0.5), but for s=4 and s=8 the excess risk is nearly flat across N (e.g., s=4: 0.738→0.695 from N=10 to 100), showing no clear 1/√N decay, and the s-dependence does not cleanly match s^1.5.

claims.claim: A minimax lower bound of Ω(s/√N) is proven, showing linear dependence on the number of coupled constraints s is unavoidable for any learning algorithm (Theorem 5.6).
claims.evidence: The Fano lower bound computation returns 0.0 for every configuration (s=8,16,32; N=10..1000), providing no actual numerical evidence of the Ω(s/√N) bound. The 'predicted_omega_s_sqrtN' values are just the theoretical formula evaluated, not independently computed lower bounds.

claims.claim: Stochastic Gradient Ascent with iterate averaging is shown to achieve the matching O(s/√N) rate, closing the O(√s) gap between the ERM upper bound and the minimax lower bound and establishing minimax optimality (Theorem 5.12).
claims.evidence: All reported mean_excess_risk values are negative (e.g., s=4: -0.695 to -0.700), which is nonsensical for an excess risk metric measuring suboptimality. The values are nearly constant across N with no visible 1/√N decay, so the Θ(s/√N) rate is not demonstrated.

claims.claim: The framework is extended to learning-to-warm-start sub-gradient ascent for large-scale Mixed Integer Linear Programming, with an O(s/N) risk upper bound (Theorem 6.1) and matching Ω(s/N) minimax lower bound (Theorem 6.2).
claims.evidence: All mean_excess_risk values are negative (e.g., s=8: approximately -4.02 for all N) and essentially constant across N∈{10,20,50}, showing no 1/N decay. The negative and N-independent values do not constitute evidence for the Θ(s/N) rate.

claims.claim: The covering number of the dual multiplier class U is bounded as log N(δ,U,‖·‖₂,N) ≤ s·log(1+2Bπ_max s/δ), used to derive the Rademacher complexity bound R_N(U)=O(s^1.5/√N) (Lemma 5.3, Lemma 5.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook merely evaluates the paper's own formula log N(δ,U) ≤ s·log(1+2Bπ_max s/δ) for various s and δ, confirming arithmetic self-consistency. No actual covering numbers of the dual multiplier class U are computed independently, and the Rademacher complexity bound is asserted ('Dudley's integral directly yields') without numerical evaluation.

claims.claim: The dual function u(π,P) is shown to be concave in π with subgradient norm bounded by 2B√s under bounded constraint-violation assumptions on the MILP instance (Proposition 5.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Uses actual LP solving via HiGHS on random small MILP instances (s∈{2..32}). Concavity violations are at machine precision (≤2.3e-13), which is meaningful. However, the subgradient norm exceeds 2B√s for s=16 (ratio 1.061) and s=32 (ratio 1.039), indicating the bound is not strictly satisfied in these runs, possibly due to solver tolerances but not cleanly verified.

amkkk/repro-provably-data-driven-lagrang.overall: The logbook provides weak numerical evidence on simplified or synthetic setups. Several key computations produce nonsensical results—negative excess risk in Claims 3 and 4, and a Fano lower bound of exactly 0.0 in Claim 2—undermining the claimed verifications. Only Claim 6 uses actual MILP solving, and even there the subgradient bound is slightly exceeded at larger s.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 gives a bicriteria (1+κ, 1+1/κ) approximation via LP rounding: the returned subgraph K satisfies coverage loss W−e(K)≤(1+κ)·ε·W and size |K|≤(1+1/κ)·r (Theorem 1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: 48 random hypergraph instances with only n=5 vertices and edges from subsets of size 1–3; worst loss ratio 1.6 and size ratio 1.25 are within bounds, but the scale is far too small to constitute a non-toy verification of the theorem.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 proves a monotonicity/nestedness property (Kτ1⊆Kτ2 for τ1<τ2), derived from a connection to parametric minimum cuts, which is required for valid conformal calibration (Theorem 2, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: 32 random hypergraphs with n=6 vertices; nestedness confirmed on all instances, but n=6 is a clearly simplified/toy scale for verifying a structural theorem about parametric min-cuts.

claims.claim: Corollary 1 shows the entire nested sequence of subgraphs across thresholds can be computed in Õ(γ(m+n)²) time (Corollary 1, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Runtime measured only across n=6..20 (7 sizes, 3 runs each); log-log slope of 0.38 is sub-linear on tiny instances and does not empirically confirm the Õ(γ(m+n)²) asymptotic bound—the logbook itself admits 'the asymptotic bound is not empirically testable.'

claims.claim: Lemma 1 establishes a distribution-free marginal coverage guarantee ℙ(B*⊆Kτ*(A*))≥φ−δ under exchangeability, without requiring model probability estimates (Lemma 1).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive 40,320-permutation enumeration of 8 exchangeable scores confirms exact coverage=0.75 for φ=0.75, δ=0, but n=8 is a toy-scale instance for a distribution-free lemma that should hold for arbitrary n.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 proves NP-hardness of the conformal subgraph problem even for constant ε via reduction from clique detection, in Appendix B (Theorem 4, Appendix B).
claims.evidence: A single yes-instance (K3, achieves 31 induced edges) vs. no-instance (star, max 30) pair is tested via DP; this verifies the reduction separates one instance pair but is far from a general verification of NP-hardness.

claims.claim: On a synthetic 6x6 grid navigation experiment with 50 train/test routes, the LP-based method compresses the calibration set to 52 edges at φ=0.75 coverage and outperforms greedy baselines for φ≤0.8 (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The 6x6 grid with 50 train/test routes is the paper's own setup and 52 edges is achievable (seed=3, sorted, coverage 0.76), but the mean across 200 runs is 56.7 (not robust), and the claim that LP 'outperforms greedy baselines for φ≤0.8' is never directly addressed—the 4 strategies appear to be tie-breaking variants, not LP-vs-greedy comparisons.

amkkk/repro-compact-conformal-subgraphs.overall: The logbook provides toy-scale empirical tests of all five theoretical claims on very small instances (n=5–20, single reduction instance pair, n=8 exhaustive enumeration), and a partial reproduction of the 6x6 grid experiment that reproduces the 52-edge figure with a specific seed but does not address the greedy baseline comparison claimed in the paper.

claims.claim: In the zero-temperature (hardmax) limit of self-attention dynamics with negative-definite key-query interaction, token updates coincide with a Frank-Wolfe step on a quadratic objective over the convex hull of the tokens, and Theorem 3.1 gives a linear convergence rate bound J^t(x_i^{t+1}) ≤ (2/(t+1))·λ_max(B_0)·diam(K^0)^2 (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The Frank-Wolfe equivalence is confirmed (4,608,000/4,608,000 decisions match, 45/45 LP hull argmax checks), but the rate bound is contradicted: with B*=I, γ_t=2/(t+2), 0∈K^0 LP-certified in all 3 seeds, the origin leaves K^t at step 1, J^t plateaus at 0.146–0.177, and the stated bound is first violated at t=3769–4631, reaching 1.3–1.6× the bound by t=6000.

claims.claim: When the key-query matrix is positive definite, Theorem 4.2 shows super-exponential convergence of tokens to vertices, and Proposition 4.5 shows the induced cell structure coincides with B-norm Voronoi cells when vertices have equal norm (Section 4, Theorem 4.2, Proposition 4.5).
claims.evidence: At d=100, κ=20, n=120, 3 seeds, the Theorem 4.2 closed form matches simulation to 1.67e-16 under time-varying γ_t, vertices are exactly stationary (0.00 drift), the super-exponential branch follows 1/(t+1)! to 5.8e-07 relative error with diverging effective rate (0.90→1.99), and Proposition 4.5 matches on 4933/4933 test points.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.8 establishes well-posedness of the singular ODE limit governing the hardmax dynamics (Section 4, Theorem 4.8, Equation 4.4).
claims.evidence: At d=100, κ=10, n=30, the RHS discontinuity is quantified (jump 1.684), Euler iterates are Cauchy (7.76e-04→7.77e-05), Euler-vs-RK4 gap is 8.63e-06, the solution matches v+(x0-v)e^{-t} to 2.12e-15, continuity in initial data is linear in ε, invariance holds (0/12000 violations), and the discontinuous switching branch remains well-posed (switch time converges under h-refinement, integrators Cauchy through it).

claims.claim: At finite inverse temperature β, Theorem 5.2 shows interior particles reach near-vertex configurations in O(1) steps with high probability, while Theorem 5.4 shows these metastable configurations persist for exponentially long times (on the order of e^β steps) before eventual collapse to a single cluster (Section 5, Theorem 5.2, Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: On the paper's own SAP Markov chain with a 51-vertex regular simplex in R^50, Theorem 5.2's near-vertex event occurs at T1=10 (from the paper's formula, β-independent) in 800/800 runs vs guarantee 0.39–0.66, and Theorem 5.4's escape time T2 grows from 4 to 4422 steps with d(log T2)/dβ=0.997 over β∈[11,14], matching the claimed e^β scaling.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 shows the argmax operation generically produces a singleton, and Lemma 2.2 shows the convex hull of tokens shrinks under step sizes γ^t ∈ (0,1), underpinning the Frank-Wolfe reformulation of hardmax attention (Section 2, Lemma 2.1, Lemma 2.2).
claims.evidence: At d=100, n=256, Lemma 2.1 shows zero ties over 4000 random configurations (smallest margin 2.55e-05), the hull argmax solved as LP is a single token matching both the attention target and FW oracle in 60/60 cases, and Lemma 2.2 shows 0/200,000 support-function violations over 50 steps with mean width collapsing from 5.66 to 6.81e-14.

michaldobiezynski/repro-attention-s-forw.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence at non-toy scale (d=50–100, multiple seeds, LP-certified hull checks) supporting four of five claims, while producing an explicit counterexample to Theorem 3.1's rate bound under its own stated hypotheses. The reproduction is rigorous, using independent code paths, the paper's own formulas and definitions, and testing both claims and their necessity conditions.

amkkk/repro-magnitude-distance-a-geometr.paper_title: Magnitude Distance: A Geometric Measure of Dataset Similarity

claims.claim: Magnitude distance is defined as d_Mag^t(X,Y) = 2·Mag_{X∪Y}(t) − Mag_X(t) − Mag_Y(t), with a tunable scale parameter t that governs sensitivity to global structure (small t) versus finer local structure (large t) (Section on Definition, Magnitude Distance).
claims.evidence: The definition d = 2·Mag_{X∪Y}(t) − Mag_X(t) − Mag_Y(t) is numerically confirmed across t ∈ {0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0} with max error < 1e-15 on 2D Gaussian data (n_X=10, n_Y=12), and the tunability of t is indirectly supported by Claims 3 and 4 showing different behaviors at different scales.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 shows magnitude distance is symmetric and non-negative, satisfies identity of indiscernibles only up to magnitude equivalence, and does not satisfy the triangle inequality in R^D for D>1 (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Symmetry (error 6.22e-15) and non-negativity (d=0.5868≥0) are confirmed with concrete numbers, but the triangle inequality violation is only mentioned without actual violation values ('see find_triangle_violation.py' with no output shown), and identity of indiscernibles up to magnitude equivalence is never tested.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.3 shows magnitude distance converges to 0 as t→0 and converges to the cardinality of the symmetric difference of the two datasets as t→∞ (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: At t=1e-8, d=-5.96e-08≈0 confirming the t→0 limit, and at t=1e6, d=10.000=|XΔY|=10 confirming the t→∞ limit, both on disjoint 3D random point sets (n=6, n=4).

claims.claim: Figure 2 shows magnitude distance remains discriminative in dimensions exceeding 1000, in settings where MMD's discriminative power collapses (Section on High-Dimensional Behavior, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Across D ∈ {10,100,500,1000,2000} with 10 trials, magnitude distance increases from 0.165 to 0.965 while MMD stays flat/low (0.051→0.068), with the Mag/MMD ratio growing from 3.25x to 14.25x, demonstrating discriminability at D>1000 where MMD loses power.

claims.claim: MagGN, a generative model trained with a multi-scale magnitude-distance loss, achieves an 11.97x training speedup over WGAN on MNIST while producing visually competitive samples (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Only 30 of 500 epochs were run on RTX 5070 (vs L40S), no WGAN baseline was trained so the 11.97x speedup cannot be verified, no generated samples are shown so visual competitiveness is unassessed, and the loss actually increased from 0.0945 to 0.6449.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.5 proves magnitude distance has bounded outlier sensitivity, changing by only about 6-10% under significant outlier addition compared to a 17.6% change for Wasserstein distance in the same setting (Section 5, Theorem 5.5).
claims.evidence: The qualitative trend matches (magnitude more robust than Wasserstein), but the specific quantitative claims are not reproduced: magnitude changes 11.1% at t=20 (paper: ~6.85%) and 28.3% at t=5 (paper: ~10.29%), while Wasserstein shows 68.3% change vs the paper's 17.6%—likely because sliced Wasserstein was used instead of standard Wasserstein, a significant methodological difference.

amkkk/repro-magnitude-distance-a-geometr.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting the magnitude distance definition, its limiting behavior at extreme t values, and high-dimensional discriminability versus MMD. However, key parts of Theorem 5.2 (triangle inequality violation numbers, identity of indiscernibles) are missing, the MagGN speedup claim is only tested on a drastically reduced setup without a baseline, and the outlier robustness quantitative results diverge substantially from the paper due to a different Wasserstein variant.

michaldobiezynski/repro-a-tight-theory-o.paper_title: A Tight Theory of Error Feedback Algorithms in Distributed Optimization

claims.claim: EF21 achieves a tight convergence guarantee under contractive compression with optimal step size eta_star = (2/(L+mu)) * ((1-sqrt(epsilon))/(1+sqrt(epsilon))), and the resulting contraction rate rho_star is independent of the number of agents n (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook computes the largest generalized eigenvalue of the Lyapunov function V directly from eqs 7-8 without referencing the closed-form rho_star (eq 9), obtaining 0.884808 which matches the formula to 6 decimal places at kappa=10, eps=0.25; the rate spread over n={1,2,5,20,50} is 1.11e-16, confirming n-independence.

claims.claim: Under the statistical homogeneity (shared minimizer) assumption, classic Error Feedback (EF) matches EF21's optimal step size and contraction factor exactly, giving identical tight convergence rates (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: Both classic EF and EF21 converge at the identical realizable ||x||^2 rate of 0.873952 at the same eta_star=0.060606 on a homogeneous shared-minimizer instance; however, EF's own worst-case contraction via its distinct Lyapunov function (eq 10) was not independently computed—the equality is inferred from coinciding realizable rates plus EF21's worst-case matching rho_star.

claims.claim: Without the shared-minimizer assumption, classic EF can exhibit 2-periodic cycles under statistical heterogeneity and generally fails to converge in the multi-agent setting (Proposition 2.1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: Direct simulation of the paper's exact counterexample (n=2, 1D quadratics with mismatched minimizers ±1/mu, biased contractive compressor) shows classic EF in a period-2 orbit with |x_final|=0.5714 and oscillation amplitude 1.1429, while EF21 converges to |x_final|=5.55e-17 on the identical instance.

claims.claim: The worst-case multi-agent convergence rate proven in Theorem 3.1 exactly matches the known single-agent rate, showing the novel Lyapunov function recovers prior single-agent guarantees as a special case (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The generalized eigenvalue worst-case at n=1 equals 0.884808, exactly matching rho_star, with worst-case spread 1.11e-16 over n=1..50 confirming n-independence; however, the external cross-check against the Berg Thomsen et al. 2025 single-agent rate was explicitly not performed, so recovery of the prior external guarantee is unconfirmed.

claims.claim: For heterogeneous regularity parameters across agents, Corollary 3.2 extends the tight rates to deterministic, additive, positively homogeneous compressors using averaged parameters L-bar and mu-bar (Corollary 3.2).
claims.evidence: The claim page reports trajectory identity (max diff 4.44e-16 over 5000 steps), kappa(Hbar)=kSigma=4.5333, and worst-case contraction 0.782414=rho_star(kSigma), but the conclusion page reports different numbers (rho_star=0.787016, independent run=0.740033) and states the averaging rule was 'baked into the code rather than derived,' creating an unresolvable internal contradiction about both the methodology and the numerical results.

claims.claim: For the two-agent (n=2) heterogeneous case, an explicit cubic polynomial characterizes the empirically optimal convergence rate, and tuning the EControl algorithm's step size to its optimum yields eta=0, coinciding with EF21 (Law 4.3, Law 4.4, Section 4).
claims.evidence: EControl grid search over eta in [0, 0.140] finds argmin at eta=0 with rate 0.770349 exactly equal to EF21's rate on the same instance, directly verifying Law 4.4; the cubic's largest root 0.809242 (Law 4.3) is formula-only but self-consistent via homogeneous-limit reduction to rho_star=0.884808.

michaldobiezynski/repro-a-tight-theory-o.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical verification of the paper's central algebraic results—EF21's tight contraction rate, n-independence, the EF period-2 counterexample, and EControl's optimum at eta=0—through generalized eigenvalue computations and direct simulations at non-trivial conditioning (kappa=10). The main weakness is an unresolvable internal inconsistency in Claim 5's reporting (different numbers and contradictory methodology claims across pages) and formula-only verification of the cubic polynomial in Claim 6.

Sor0ush/repro-when-does-adaptation-win-s.paper_title: When Does Adaptation Win? Scaling Laws for Meta-Learning in Quantum Control

claims.claim: Theorem 4.8 derives a scaling law for the expected meta-learning adaptation gain, G_K ≥ A_∞(1 - e^{-βK}), where A_∞ = c·σ_τ^2 scales with task variance and β = η·μ_min depends on learning rate and landscape curvature, showing the gain saturates exponentially with gradient steps K (Theorem 4.8)
claims.evidence: The functional form G_K = A_∞(1-e^{-βK}) is empirically confirmed on classical LQR (R²=1.000, A_∞=0.0029, β=0.042) with variance scaling R²∈[0.97,0.99], and the component relationships (A_∞∝σ², β=η·μ_min) are supported by the LQR variance sweep and curvature measurement.

claims.claim: For the single-qubit X gate, the exponential saturation model fits with R^2 > 0.99 and adaptation rate β = 0.083, with negligible adaptation benefit when task variance σ_τ^2 < 0.002 (Section 4, or wherever the single-qubit results are reported)
claims.evidence: The exponential fit R²≈1.000 matches the paper's >0.99, but β≈1.23 does not match the paper's 0.083 (off by ~15x), and the run is explicitly a 300-iter CPU 'smoke' train with much smaller task variance than the paper's single-qubit suite.

claims.claim: On the two-qubit CZ gate under 10x the training noise level, meta-initialization achieves 54.2% fidelity while post-adaptation after K=10 gradient steps reaches 95.7% fidelity, a gain exceeding 40 percentage points, with R^2 = 0.986 and β = 0.333 for the exponential fit (Section 4)
claims.evidence: Mid-train checkpoints from a cancelled T4 job show Val Pre ≈54–56%, Val Post ≈97%, Gap ≈+42–43 pp, approximately matching the paper's 54.2%→95.7%, but the exponential-fit parameters R²=0.986 and β=0.333 are explicitly stated as pending, and no run completed.

claims.claim: Assumption 4.3 posits a Polyak-Łojasiewicz condition on the local loss landscape near optima, empirically validated with measured curvature μ ≈ 0.03 in the adaptation regime (Assumption 4.3, Figure 2a)
claims.evidence: The logbook text claims μ≈0.031 matching the paper, but the raw JSON output from the re-run shows μ=0.13424161554897968, a direct internal contradiction that prevents determining whether the paper's μ≈0.03 is confirmed.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.10 shows adaptation provides negligible benefit when task variance is small (homogeneous devices) or when the adaptation rate β is much less than the inverse of the gradient-step budget (Corollary 4.10)
claims.evidence: Low-variance eval from a smoke checkpoint shows K=10 gaps of 0.005–0.008 (negligible), but the diversity-scale sweep was broken—'upstream diversity_scale did not change compute_variance() in this codebase (all scales reported the same σ²)'—and the GPU job stalled, so the corollary is only partially tested at a single low-variance point.

claims.claim: A classical linear-quadratic regulator control task reproduces the same exponential saturation scaling law (R^2 = 0.99), indicating the scaling law arises from optimization geometry rather than quantum-specific physics (Section 4)
claims.evidence: The classical LQR meta-learning task produces an exponential saturation fit with R²=1.0000 (A_∞=0.0029, β=0.042) and variance scaling R²=0.9674–0.9860, matching the paper's R²≈0.99 claim on a real LQR task.

Sor0ush/repro-when-does-adaptation-win-s.overall: The logbook provides solid empirical support for the core scaling-law functional form on classical LQR (R²=1.000) and partial support for the two-qubit CZ fidelity jump, but several claims rest on incomplete runs, reduced-scale smoke tests, or contradictory raw data. The reproduction is a meaningful partial validation but falls short of fully reproducing the paper's quantum results at scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 proves that the attention map converges uniformly over bounded regions of radius R at rate C(R)/√n, where C(R) grows exponentially with R (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: On d=3 Gaussian tokens with n up to 60000, 48 sphere queries, and 6 seeds, the fitted log-log slopes of sup attention-map error vs n are -0.500, -0.499, -0.499, -0.492 for R=1.0,1.5,2.0,2.5 (r²≈0.99), confirming the 1/√n rate. The prefactor C(R)=err·√n grows from 2.74 to 8.45 with a log-linear fit log C(R)=0.83+0.213R² (r²=0.996), confirming exponential growth in R² consistent with the e^{8R²H²} form.

claims.claim: Proposition 5.1 shows that in the hardmax regime, as the softmax temperature parameter tends to infinity, the convergence rate slows to 1/√(ln n) due to cancellation effects between opposite-signed extreme values (Proposition 5.1).
claims.evidence: In the scalar-Gaussian hardmax regime with n up to 200000 and 1600 replicates, std(M_n)·√(2 ln n)/σ = 1.302 matches the Gumbel constant π/√6=1.2825 to 1.5%, the fitted slope of log std(M_n) vs log(ln n) is -0.495 (theory -1/2), and the softmax n-exponent collapses from 0.477 at τ=3 to 0.015 at τ=20, directly confirming the 1/√(ln n) slowdown as temperature→∞.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 establishes that for sub-Gaussian tokens, the transformed distribution converges at rate O(n^(-β)) with β = 1/(2(1+32Ψ)), where Ψ is the Attention-Reach Coupling defined via the spectral reach and attention horizon (Theorem 4.4, Definition 4.2).
claims.evidence: On d=2 Gaussian tokens with n up to 40000, 24 resamples, 400 queries, and 4 seeds, the fitted convergence exponent β = 0.441, 0.316, 0.244, 0.200, 0.158 at Ψ = 0.64, 1.44, 2.56, 4.00, 5.76 (r²=0.99–1.00), all strictly sub-parametric (β<1/2) and monotonically decreasing in Ψ, consistent with the theorem's qualitative structure (the constant 32 being a non-tight upper bound, so measured β exceeding the theoretical lower bound is expected).

claims.claim: Corollary 4.5 shows the mean of the transformed distribution converges at rate O(n^(-1/(2(1+Ψ)))), exhibiting only polynomial (not exponential) dependence on the attention-reach coupling Ψ (Corollary 4.5).
claims.evidence: On non-zero-mean Gaussian tokens (||m||=1.5) with n up to 40000 and 4 seeds, β_mean ≥ β_gen in all 20 configurations (mean converges at least as fast as the general Lipschitz functional), and 1/(2β_mean) grows 1.13→4.85 approximately linearly in Ψ∈[1,5.76], confirming polynomial (degree-1, not exponential) dependence on the attention-reach coupling as predicted by Corollary 4.5.

claims.claim: Section 6 experiments on BERT using 1M and 20M Wikipedia tokens empirically confirm sub-parametric convergence with β < 1/2, contradicting the classical parametric 1/√n rate despite compactly supported token embeddings (Section 6).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly did not run the real BERT experiment on 1M/20M Wikipedia tokens (transformers package and model download unavailable). Instead, it ran synthetic sub-Gaussian tokens showing β=0.316→0.136 < 1/2, which is essentially a re-run of the Claim 3 setup and does not address the BERT-specific or Wikipedia-data aspects central to Section 6.

agharsallah/k5blb595kx-logbook.overall: The logbook provides rigorous numerical verification of Claims 1–4 on non-toy synthetic Gaussian setups with proper statistical methodology (multiple seeds, resamples, log-log fitting, r² values), confirming the paper's theoretical rate predictions. Claim 5 is only addressed via a synthetic proxy, not the actual BERT-on-Wikipedia experiment that the claim describes.

claims.claim: In the population setting, Theorem 1 characterizes excess risk as a function of the magnitude and direction of the performative effect together with spurious features (Section 4, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook tests a simplified scalar risk R̃(λ)=b̄²−2λb̄+λ² (claim-performative-reg page) and verifies the exact risk identity Eq 6 via Monte Carlo vs trace (rel.err<0.012), but does not systematically vary the direction of the performative effect (parameter c) or spurious features to test Theorem 1's full characterization of excess risk as a function of magnitude, direction, and spurious features.

claims.claim: Corollary 2 shows the optimal regularization parameter in the population regime is proportional to the strength of the performative effect, with optimal risk remaining strictly positive (Section 4, Corollary 2).
claims.evidence: The closed-form λ*_pop = b̄·d/Tr((Σ⁻¹)₁₁) is exactly proportional to b̄ (slope 0.632), the exact-risk λ*_emp is monotonically increasing in b̄ with low-b̄ R²=0.96, and the optimal risk is strictly positive (R(λ*=0.296)=0.0795, and finite-sample opt risks 0.002–0.005), all in the population regime with non-trivial Toeplitz covariance.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 establishes a deterministic equivalent of the performative fixed point for over-parameterized ridge regression when the number of features exceeds the number of samples (Section 5, Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: In the over-parameterized regime (p>n, κ=p/n∈{1.5,2,3,4}), the performative fixed point is solved directly and three signatures of a deterministic equivalent are quantitatively confirmed: (A) CoV of risk decreases 0.276→0.075 as p grows 50→800 (log-log slope −0.468≈−½), (B) same-κ pairs converge to a common risk (1.9% spread shrinking with scale), and (C) the resolvent-trace edf matches the parameter-free self-consistent prediction to ≤0.07% relative error across five (κ,λ) settings.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 shows the optimal regularization moves in the same direction as the performative effect on predictive features under low noise, but in the opposite direction under high noise, in the over-parameterized regime (Section 5, Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Two independent methods—closed-form B1 from Eq (51) and direct minimization of the deterministic-equivalent risk from Eq (46)—agree to ≤6e-6 absolute error across six κ values (1.25–8), with B1 positive at σ=0.05 (low noise) and negative at σ=2.0 (high noise) for every κ, confirming the sign reversal predicted by Theorem 4.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments in Section 6 confirm that in the over-parameterized setting, performative effects can improve optimally-regularized risk when performativity reinforces existing trends, contrasting with the population-regime degradation (Section 6).
claims.evidence: No experiment in the logbook tests the specific Section 6 scenario of performative effects improving optimally-regularized risk when performativity reinforces existing trends in the over-parameterized setting, nor contrasts this with population-regime degradation; the conclusion page explicitly states real-data experiments are out of scope.
