However, no independent verification of the specific bounds, rates, or quantitative predictions of each individual theorem is provided — only the overall phenomenon is observed.

claims.claim: Decreasing weight decay and sample size can amplify grokking time in ridge-regression simulations, matching the paper's quantitative hyperparameter predictions (Figure 2)
claims.evidence: The lambda sweep shows grokking times of 132,827 / 1,295,175 / 12,629,026 for lambda=1e-2/1e-3/1e-4 (clean ~10x per 10x decrease, matching 1/lambda scaling), and the n-sweep shows monotone increase from 1,219,835 (n=50) to 1,550,282 (n=20) — both on the exact spectral GD dynamics with d=100.

claims.claim: Two-layer ReLU experiments qualitatively reproduce the predicted grokking-time dependence on hyperparameters beyond the linear setting (Figures 3 and 4)
claims.evidence: Two-layer ReLU experiments (d=50, n=50, m=1000, paper defaults, 3 seeds per config) show t2 ratios of 1:4.97:9.94 for lambda=0.5/0.1/0.05 vs theoretical 1:5:10 (<1% error), and t2 decreases monotonically with n (164,833→118,867 for n=30→120). Two small-lambda configs hit the 200k step cap, consistent with t2∝1/lambda extrapolating beyond the cap.

745H1N/grok-grokking-repro.overall: The logbook provides strong, concrete evidence for the core empirical claims: three-stage grokking in ridge regression (C1), the quantitative 1/lambda and n-dependence of grokking time (C4), and qualitative reproduction in two-layer ReLU networks (C5). However, the theorem-extension claims (C2, C3) are inadequately addressed — C2's supplementary code uses zero initialization (which prevents grokking) and shows no dynamics, while C3 relies on 'by construction' arguments without independent verification of the individual theorem bounds.

ai-sherpa/finetuning-without-forgetting-.paper_title: Fine-Tuning Without Forgetting In-Context Learning: A Theoretical Analysis of Linear Attention Models

claims.claim: Corollary 4.4 shows that full fine-tuning of all attention parameters in a linear attention model drives zero-shot error to σ² while few-shot (in-context) error converges to σ² + θᵀΣθ, a substantially larger value, formalizing the degradation of in-context learning after full fine-tuning (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Independently re-derived closed-form finite-n MSE for full fine-tuning matches Corollary 4.4 exactly: zero-shot error = 0.1 (=σ²) and 20-shot error = 1.4113, converging to 1.1 (=σ²+θ₀ᵀΣθ₀) as n→∞; cross-validated against literal token-by-token Monte-Carlo simulation of the model (within 6 SE) and confirmed across 145/145 (n,w,covariance) combinations including 4 covariance families up to d=20.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 shows that restricting fine-tuning updates to the value matrix reduces zero-shot error to σ² + (2/(d+4))θ₀ᵀΣθ₀ while Corollary 4.8 shows the asymptotic few-shot error only rises to σ² + 1/(d+4)²θ₀ᵀΣθ₀, i.e. value-matrix-only fine-tuning improves zero-shot performance with far less degradation to in-context learning than full fine-tuning (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Independently derived closed form gives value-matrix zero-shot error 0.3222 = σ²+2/(d+4)·θ₀ᵀΣθ₀ (matching Theorem 4.6) and asymptotic few-shot penalty 0.01235 = 1/(d+4)² (matching Corollary 4.8), which is 81× smaller than full fine-tuning's penalty of 1.0; cross-validated against Monte-Carlo simulation and robust across 4 covariance families.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.10 proves that tuning the auxiliary few-shot loss weight w to optimize few-shot performance on the fine-tuning task θ₀ necessarily reduces few-shot performance on other tasks θ ≠ θ₀, formalizing a trade-off between target-task adaptation and generalization to unseen tasks (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: Task-wise-optimal w*(20;θ₀)=0.654088 derived independently and verified against 200,001-point grid search (<2e-4); target-task 20-shot error strictly improves (gain 0.01593 > 0 in all 4 covariance settings), while Proposition 4.10's excess-error formula matches directly measured MSE differences to <1e-12 across 7 values of ρ, showing strictly positive, monotonically increasing degradation as task similarity ρ decreases from 1 to −1.

claims.claim: In synthetic linear-regression experiments (d=5, σ²=0.1, Σ=I₅, ‖θ₀‖₂²=1, m=n=20), Figure 4 confirms the theoretical zero-shot/few-shot error predictions across pretraining, full fine-tuning, and value-matrix fine-tuning regimes, and Figure 5 shows value-matrix fine-tuning attains the lowest error on the out-of-distribution task -θ₀ (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: Token-by-token Monte-Carlo simulation (40,000 prompts × 5 seeds) at the paper's exact setting (d=5, σ²=0.1, Σ=I₅, ‖θ₀‖²=1, m=n=20) recovers predicted zero-shot regime constants (pretrained 1.097≈1.1, full-FT 0.0998≈0.1, value-FT 0.3201≈0.3222) with per-regime curve RMSE ≤ 0.0042; on OOD task −θ₀ at 20 shots, value-matrix FT attains lowest error (0.3872) vs pretrained (0.3961) vs full-FT (1.2074).

claims.claim: On the MMLU benchmark using Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct fine-tuned on the Humanities category, full fine-tuning improves zero-shot accuracy but degrades 7-shot accuracy, whereas value-matrix-only fine-tuning preserves few-shot accuracy while still improving zero-shot performance (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: Real GPU experiment (19 LoRA fine-tuning runs of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct on 1,000 MMLU-Humanities items, r=128, 5 epochs, paper's LR grid) measured full-attention FT improving 7-shot Humanities by +4.80 pp (McNemar p=0.015/0.036/0.052) where the claim predicts degradation; value-only FT's 7-shot advantage over full-FT was only +0.27 pp (p=0.89/0.60/0.55, sign-inconsistent across seeds), and a matched-learning-rate control confirmed the absence of the predicted asymmetry.

ai-sherpa/finetuning-without-forgetting-.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, independently derived closed-form verifications of all four theoretical claims (1-4) at the paper's own scale, cross-validated against literal Monte-Carlo simulations of the linear attention model. Claim 5's real-LLM MMLU experiment was genuinely executed on GPU with 19 fine-tuning runs, but the measured 7-shot results directly contradict the claim's predicted degradation under full fine-tuning, constituting a falsification on a non-toy setup despite documented protocol deviations (no CoT rationales, deterministic scoring).

neonforestmist/pluralistic-curation-nonc.paper_title: Curated Synthetic Data Doesn’t Have to Collapse: A Theoretical Study of Generative Retraining with Pluralistic Preferences

claims.claim: Under a two-basin landscape assumption with cross-reward leakage gaps Δ1, Δ2 > 0 (Assumption 1, Section 2.1), Lemma 3 shows probability mass outside the union of ε-optimal basins decays geometrically under recursive curated retraining (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides a generic least-squares fitting exercise (n=200, d=16, MSE=0.0023) that uses claim-derived numbers as 'binding anchors' but never simulates a two-basin landscape, recursive curated retraining, or measures probability mass decay outside ε-optimal basins. No experiment related to Lemma 3's geometric decay claim is present.

claims.claim: Lemma 5 proves that under bounded leakage, basin mass remains bounded away from collapse, satisfying η ≤ a_t ≤ 1-η for the limiting basin weight a_t (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports a generic structural certificate (n=200, d=5, MSE=0.0026) with no simulation of bounded leakage dynamics, no measurement of basin weight a_t, and no verification that η ≤ a_t ≤ 1-η. The experiment is unrelated to Lemma 5's actual mathematical content.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 shows the limiting mixture preserves diversity: reward variance under a nontrivial two-component mixture has an explicit strictly positive lower bound proportional to (Δᵢ - 2ε)^2 (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook shows residuals decreasing with T=[100…1600] and a log-log slope of -0.518, but this is a generic 1/√T convergence rate demonstration, not a measurement of reward variance under a two-component mixture or verification of a lower bound proportional to (Δᵢ - 2ε)². The specific quantity in Theorem 6 is never computed.

claims.claim: Theorem 7 proves the limiting distribution from pluralistic curation coincides with the weighted Nash bargaining solution, maximizing (u1(p_α) - d1)^q (u2(p_α) - d2)^(1-q) at α* = q (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides a generic fitting exercise (n=200, d=7, MSE=0.0023) with no computation of Nash bargaining solutions, no evaluation of utility functions u1, u2, no comparison of pluralistic curation output against the Nash solution, and no verification that α* = q. The experiment is unrelated to Theorem 7.

claims.claim: CIFAR-10 flow-model retraining experiments (E3) show curation with balanced multi-reward preferences sustains higher entropy and diversity than single-reward curation across recursive retraining generations (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook claims 'CPU only' and reports a generic structural certificate (n=200, d=10, MSE=0.0027) with no actual CIFAR-10 flow-model training, no recursive retraining generations, no entropy or diversity measurements, and no comparison of multi-reward vs single-reward curation. No real CIFAR-10 experiment was conducted.

claims.claim: Text-domain experiments (E4) confirm that curation under two competing length-based reward preferences sustains entropy over recursive retraining, consistent with the two-basin theory (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports a generic fitting exercise (n=200, d=4, MSE=0.0023) with no text generation, no length-based reward preferences implemented, no recursive retraining, and no entropy measurements. The experiment bears no relationship to the claimed text-domain E4 experiment.

neonforestmist/pluralistic-curation-nonc.overall: This logbook does not reproduce or test any of the paper's claims. It uses a templated approach that extracts numbers and keywords from claim text, runs generic least-squares fitting exercises with those numbers as parameters, and reports MSE values that are unrelated to the actual mathematical or experimental content of the paper. No theoretical quantity (basin mass, reward variance, Nash solution) or experimental setup (CIFAR-10 flow models, text-domain retraining) is actually implemented or measured.

amkkk/optimal-bayesian-stopping-repro.paper_title: Optimal Bayesian Stopping for Efficient Inference of Consistent LLM Answers

claims.claim: The L-aggregated stopping policy with L=3 achieves asymptotic optimality for identifying the mode LLM answer (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Numerical verification of Theorem 3.2 rate formulas for 5 (p1,p2) configurations confirms the ordering E[n*,f] > E[n*,2] > E[n*,3] = E[n*,K], but this is formula plugging on simple 2-parameter examples, not a proof check or empirical stopping experiment at scale.

claims.claim: The coarse posterior approximation strictly dominates prior-free baselines in sample complexity while remaining fast to compute (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Same analytical rate comparison shows L>=3 < L=2 < prior-free for all 5 configurations, but runtime numbers (9.0–37.4ms) are explicitly labeled as 'paper, ms' and not independently measured; the 'fast to compute' portion is unverified.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 implements the L-aggregated stopping rule derived from the stopping condition in Equation 7 (Algorithm 1, Equation 7).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 implementation checked on a single K=8 example showing posterior values (0.283→0.951) and stopping at n=10 for 95% confidence, but no systematic validation across configurations or comparison to Equation 7's predicted rates.

claims.claim: Empirical query-count comparisons show the method identifies the mode LLM answer using fewer samples than exhaustive sampling across confidence levels (Table 1, Table 2).
claims.evidence: Table 1 reproduced with 10,000 synthetic trials showing L=3 using 18.07 vs ASC's 44.07 samples at 1-d=0.99 (59% reduction), but Table 2 (real-world LLM data on CommonsenseQA with Qwen/GPT-4o/LLaMA) was not attempted.

claims.claim: Experimental validation of sample-efficiency gains across confidence levels is presented in the experiments section (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Synthetic Table 1 trends show 39–59% sample reduction vs ASC across confidence levels, but the real-world validation on CommonsenseQA, GSM8K, and DisambiguationQA with actual LLMs (Section 5.3) was not attempted; only qualitative mention without numbers.

amkkk/optimal-bayesian-stopping-repro.overall: The logbook provides analytical formula verification and a 10,000-trial synthetic experiment confirming that L=3 matches the exact posterior's sample efficiency and uses up to 59% fewer samples than the ASC baseline. However, the real-world LLM experiments (Table 2, Section 5.3) are entirely unattempted, runtime figures are copied from the paper rather than measured, and the logbook is heavily contaminated with pages from unrelated papers (FOB, GCR-RL, GLBM-SCB).

90debasish/repro-jade-bridging-the-strat.paper_title: JADE: Bridging the Strategic-Operational Gap in Dynamic Agentic RAG

claims.claim: JADE jointly optimizes a Planner and seven Executor agentic roles via PPO under a Shared-Parameter Markov Decision Process formulation, achieving a 53.86 average F1 score across all evaluation datasets (Section 3.1, 3.4, Section 4, Table 2).
claims.evidence: No PPO training or evaluation was executed; the logbook only hardcodes the paper's Table 2 dataset scores and confirms their arithmetic mean is 53.857 (rounds to 53.86). A source-code read noted the shared-parameter architecture but found only 6 trainable executor roles (RA is frozen), not 7 as claimed. No independent experimental run produced this F1.

claims.claim: JADE improves average F1 by 8.29 points over the previous best baseline and by 12.64 points over MAO-ARAG (53.86 vs. 41.22), a decoupled planning-execution approach (Section 4, Table 2).
claims.evidence: No baselines were independently run; the logbook only recomputed arithmetic from hardcoded Table 2 values. The 12.64 MAO-ARAG gap is arithmetically consistent, but the claimed 8.29 best-baseline gap does not match Table 2 (RRR at 44.72 yields 9.14). This is a paper-internal arithmetic discrepancy, not experimental evidence from a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: An ablation shows the Document Selector module's contribution flips from harmful to helpful under joint training, moving its isolated F1 contribution from 41.13 to 58.24 once trained jointly with the rest of the system (Section 4, Table 3).
claims.evidence: No ablation training was performed; the logbook only confirms that the hardcoded Table 3 values show a sign flip (−0.61 frozen vs +1.14 trained). The values 41.13 and 58.24 are full-system scores under different training regimes, not an isolated DS module contribution. No actual ablation experiment was run.

claims.claim: JADE's 7B-parameter jointly-trained model (58.24 F1) outperforms a system using frozen GPT-4o executors (56.82 F1), indicating that co-adapted training of planner and executors matters more than raw executor model scale (Section 4, Table 4).
claims.evidence: No model training or evaluation was executed; the logbook only confirms 58.24 − 56.82 = 1.42 from hardcoded Table 4 values. The comparison confounds training status with model family (Qwen-7B vs GPT-4o), and no independent runs were conducted to verify either number.

claims.claim: A hyperparameter sensitivity analysis over the reward's alpha and beta penalty terms, and an analysis of multi-agent training dynamics, demonstrate co-adaptation where the planner learns to operate within executor capability boundaries while executors align to strategic intent (Section 4, Figures 3-4).
claims.evidence: No PPO training was run and no Figure 3/4 raw data was available. A synthetic reward sweep using made-up workflow values (f1=0.45/0.55, turns=1/3) trivially demonstrates that the reward formula penalizes longer workflows at high alpha/beta, but this does not address the actual claim about learned multi-agent co-adaptation dynamics. The HF Jobs canary failed with a 402 credit error, so no GPU experiment exists.

90debasish/repro-jade-bridging-the-strat.overall: This logbook is purely a numerical audit: it hardcodes the paper's own table values, checks arithmetic consistency, and reads the source code, but runs zero actual ML experiments (no training, no evaluation, no inference). All claims remain inconclusive because no independent experimental evidence on a non-toy setup was produced.

rahit/repro-evaluating-bivariate-causal-.paper_title: Evaluating Bivariate Causal Statements Based on Mutual Compatibility

claims.claim: For linear bivariate causal statements, any acyclic collection induces exactly one multivariate structural equation model whose pairwise marginals match the given statements (Lemma 2.3).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive enumeration of all 59,805 statement matrices (n=3,4,5 with entries in {-1,0,+1}) shows max marginal reconstruction error 4.4e-16; 600 continuous-coefficient models (n=6,8,10) show max error 2.6e-14; uniqueness tested destructively via 8,748 single-entry perturbations of Gamma with all producing marginal shifts; negative control (wrong Gamma construction) fails on 200/200 models.

claims.claim: The compatibility score defined via path-tracing decomposition of confounding (Definition 2.7) is proven to have positive expected value under a generic random causal model, supporting the paper's Confounding Postulate (Theorem 2.9).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive enumeration of 1,852 finite-support symmetric models (n=3,4,5) shows E[comp]>0 in all five classes (e.g., +6.677 at n=4 ternary), with the pivotal identity E[B*eps]=0 holding to 3e-15; decomposition verified at machine precision over 240 continuous models; destructive controls show biased supports break the identity (min E[comp]=-10.39 when unbiasedness dropped).

claims.claim: Empirical approximation of the compatibility score converges in polynomial sample complexity with respect to dimension, causal strength, and pathway contributions (Theorem 2.10).
claims.evidence: 3,200 runs verify the N^{-1/2} decay law (fitted slope -0.511 vs theory -0.5, R^2=0.979; destructive N^{-1} fit gives R^2=-1.91); a single constant C=5.37e-04 covers the n=4..10 dimension sweep with C_needed decreasing in n; sign-agreement operating point reproduced (93.4% at N=50, crossing 90% well under 100 samples as the paper states).

claims.claim: On synthetic linear models, compatibility scores decrease monotonically as injected error increases, and on LLM-generated causal statements higher-capacity models achieve higher compatibility scores, with some receiving negative (falsifying) scores (Section 2.7, Figures 2 and 4).
claims.evidence: No page for Claim 4 exists in the logbook; the Claim 6 page references a 'Claim 4 page' for the synthetic error-injection curves and LLM-generated causal statement results (Figures 2, 4), but that page was never created, so the empirical monotonicity and LLM-capacity claims were never addressed.

claims.claim: For graphical bivariate causal statements, computing the exact incompatibility score (minimum Hamming distance to a compatible statement graph) is proven NP-hard via reduction to transitive-closure editing (Section 3, NP-hardness result).
claims.evidence: The reduction is exhaustively verified on all 543 DAGs at n=4: incomp(D+all bidirected edges) equals exact ATE distance with 0 mismatches and identical histograms [219,324]; Lemma 3.4 holds as exact set equality (2,994=2,994) over all 46,656 statement graphs; destructive control (dropping transitive closure) changes results on 324/543 DAGs; n=5 shows GreedyTE suboptimal on 380/29,281 DAGs, consistent with search hardness.

claims.claim: A heuristic GreedyFAS+GreedyTE algorithm yields incompatibility scores that upper-bound the true incompatibility score and equal zero exactly when the true score is zero, and empirically increase monotonically with injected errors on synthetic graphs and on LLM outputs (Lemma 3.7, Sections 3.3-3.4, Figures 5-7).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive verification on all 216 (n=3) and 46,656 (n=4) statement graphs: Lemma 3.7(1) c>=incomp holds with 0 violations, Lemma 3.7(2) c=0<=>incomp=0 holds exactly (89 and 2,994 compatible graphs respectively); constructive certificates confirm heuristic output is compatible at distance c(G) for all 46,656 graphs; destructive control (corrupted compatible set) produces 11,189 violations. The empirical monotonicity part (Figures 5-7) is not addressed as the Claim 4 page is absent.

rahit/repro-evaluating-bivariate-causal-.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, exhaustive computational verification for five of six claims through complete domain enumeration, destructive controls, and clean-room implementations, but Claim 4 (empirical results on synthetic linear models and LLM-generated causal statements, Figures 2 and 4) was never addressed—its page does not exist. The theoretical and algorithmic claims are strongly supported; the empirical evaluation claims remain unverified.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-minimum-distance-sum.paper_title: Minimum Distance Summaries for Robust Neural Posterior Estimation

claims.claim: Minimum-distance summaries (MDS) adapt the query summary s* = arg min_s D(P_{x|s}, Q) at test time while keeping the pretrained neural posterior estimator fixed, preserving amortization (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Across 200 test-time adaptations, NPE and decoder parameters were checked for exact equality before and after every call (true in all cases), and MDS-adapted summaries achieved MSE 0.00463 vs. oracle vs. 2.606 for the naive contaminated summary, directly demonstrating the adapt-s*/keep-NPE-fixed mechanism.

claims.claim: MDS is implemented via a Maximum Mean Discrepancy objective using random Fourier feature approximations of the Gaussian kernel, with a decoder mean-embedding network trained offline via MSE and the summary optimized at test time by L-BFGS (Section 3.2, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: RFF approximation error shrinks monotonically with K (0.1216→0.0168 for K=32→2048), decoder training MSE matches OLS optimum within 0.001%, and L-BFGS decreased the MMD objective on 100% of queries with mean gradient norm 1.14e-6 at convergence.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that under Huber's ε-contamination model Q_ε = (1-ε)Q + εδ_y, the KL divergence between posteriors under MDS-adapted summaries for Q and Q_ε is O(ε), bounding robustness to small contamination (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: After fixing a Monte Carlo noise bug (switching to common random numbers, 60,000 reps), the fitted log-log exponent of KL vs. eps was p=2.225 (R²=0.991), and the direct KL/eps boundedness check showed the ratio shrinking (2.37e-05 near eps=0 vs. 5.09e-03 further out), consistent with the O(eps) upper bound; large-eps controls diverged as expected.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 shows that when the model is correctly specified, posterior consistency under the original summary statistics implies posterior consistency under MDS-adapted summaries (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: After replacing a noisy signed-bias endpoint check with RMSE-over-N (2000 reps/N, N from 25 to 1600), MDS-adapted posterior RMSE showed clean log-log slope -0.50 (R²=1.00, Spearman ρ=-1.00), matching the plain-summary slope, with near-nominal 90% coverage throughout—numerical evidence consistent with the consistency theorem's conclusion.

claims.claim: On the Gaussian model, MDS outperforms NPE, NNPE, and NPE-OR baselines across a range of contamination proportions, with degradation only appearing at contamination levels above 40% (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: At eps=0.20, MDS MSE was 0.0169 vs. NPE 2.65, NNPE 2.66, NPE-OR 0.0219; at eps=0.30, MDS 0.0194 vs. NPE 5.99, NNPE 6.01, NPE-OR 0.779; mean MDS MSE stayed at 0.177 up to eps=0.40 vs. 33.6 beyond, matching the claimed degradation threshold.

claims.claim: On a 1024-dimensional Cryo-EM inference task, MDS substantially improves robustness to Gaussian noise contamination while maintaining performance in the well-specified regime (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: No Cryo-EM simulator, GPU, or paper code was available; instead a 1024-dim diagonal Gaussian mean-estimation proxy was run (1024 independent copies of the Claim-5 mechanism), showing large MDS robustness gains at eps=0.1–0.3 and breakdown above 40%, but this does not test the actual tomographic/CTF/CNN Cryo-EM pipeline claimed in Figure 4.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-minimum-distance-sum.overall: The logbook provides concrete from-scratch numerical evidence supporting the paper's core mechanism (amortized test-time summary adaptation via RFF-MMD and L-BFGS), the O(eps) robustness bound, consistency preservation, and the Gaussian benchmark results, but the flagship 1024-dim Cryo-EM experiment is replaced by a clearly-labeled diagonal-Gaussian proxy that does not test the actual Cryo-EM task.

algorise/repro-multi-label-test-time-ada.paper_title: Multi-Label Test-Time Adaptation with Bayesian Conditional Priors

claims.claim: Bayesian Conditional Priors (BCP) reformulates multi-label test-time adaptation as an anchor-conditioned Bayesian update in logit space, adding a pointwise-mutual-information correction term PMI(ck, ca) computed from online first- and second-order co-occurrence statistics (Section on Method/Logit Space Implementation).
claims.evidence: E1 shows the logit-space update exactly equals the independent Bayes product form to 6.7e-16 deviation; E3 shows the online PMI estimator converges with power-law slope -0.379 (R² 0.992); E4 shows 98.6% sign agreement with the population limit at t=8192. These verify the mathematical formulation and estimator properties directly, independent of backbone.

claims.claim: With a ViT-B/16 CLIP backbone, BCP raises mean average precision from 62.61 (zero-shot CLIP) to 71.79 averaged across COCO2014, COCO2017, VOC2007, VOC2012 and NUS-WIDE, exceeding the BEM baseline's 64.80 mAP by 7.18 points (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Tested on 5 synthetic stream configs and OpenML yeast (14 labels), not CLIP ViT-B/16 on real benchmarks. Cross-config gain is +1.22 mAP vs the paper's +9.18; 1 of 5 configs is a wash; yeast is a wash (+0.06); BEM was not reimplemented. The paper's specific values (62.61, 71.79, 64.80) are never tested.

claims.claim: BCP's per-sample adaptation time is 0.112s versus roughly 0.24s for prior test-time adaptation baselines, i.e., about 2x faster, while requiring no backpropagation (Table 7).
claims.evidence: Zero backward passes verified structurally (0 in 8800 samples) and 5.34x speedup over TENT-style grad-TTA measured, but on an MLP encoder (~200k params) on CPU, not CLIP-RN50 on GPU. The paper's absolute timing values (0.112s, 0.24s) and the ~2x ratio are not tested on comparable hardware.

claims.claim: An anchor-correctness ablation shows mAP rises from 72.73 to 80.33 when the selected anchor label is a true positive (Anchor-Hit), but drops slightly (22.15 to 21.32) when the anchor is incorrect (Anchor-Miss), with anchors being correct in 85.38% of confident samples (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Hit/miss asymmetry pattern reproduces on synthetic streams and yeast (hit gain +3.47, miss gain -4.96, hit rate 91.4%; yeast: +2.80/-1.05), but magnitudes differ substantially from the paper (hit +7.60, miss -0.83) and the specific CLIP values (72.73, 80.33, 22.15, 21.32, 85.38%) are not tested.

claims.claim: BCP improves mAP across head, medium, and tail label frequency groups on COCO2014, e.g., head labels rise from 42.47 to 51.84 and tail labels from 57.93 to 69.22, showing gains are not concentrated only on frequent classes (Table 5).
claims.evidence: On the pre-designated COCO-like config (syn-coco80a), head gain is significantly negative (-0.29) and tail gain straddles zero (-0.03), failing the primary predicate. All-tier gains appear only on the 3 configs with material overall gains. The paper's specific COCO2014 values (42.47→51.84, 57.93→69.22) are not tested.

claims.claim: Using two anchor labels instead of one degrades performance (71.79 to 69.93 mAP on ViT-B/16), supporting the design choice of a single anchor for conditioning (Table 10).
claims.evidence: On synthetic streams, two anchors slightly HELP on average (paired drop -0.109, opposite sign to the paper's 71.79→69.93 degradation), with 1 anchor winning only on the 2 VOC-like configs where rank-2 anchor precision is lower. The paper's specific CLIP values and the monotone degradation claim are not tested on the real backbone.

algorise/repro-multi-label-test-time-ada.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous mechanism-level reproduction on synthetic streams and one small real dataset (yeast), verifying BCP's mathematical formulation (Claim 1) with exact identity checks and convergence analysis, but all benchmark-scale claims (Claims 2-6) are addressed only on simplified proxy setups without CLIP, yielding smaller magnitudes and one opposite-direction result (Claim 6).

claims.claim: Definition 1 introduces ℓ*-smoothness, bounding the Hessian via a general norm and its dual, ‖∇²f(x)h‖* ≤ ℓ(‖∇f(x)‖*)‖h‖, generalizing prior ℓ-smoothness beyond the Euclidean/ℓ2 setting (Section 3.1, Definition 1)
claims.evidence: The Definition-1 inequality ‖Hess f(x)h‖_∞ ≤ ℓ(‖∇f(x)‖_∞)‖h‖₁ held with 0/2000 violations on the quartic-on-simplex testbed (n=12), the closed-form ℓ(g)=Kg^(2/3) fitted log-log slope was 0.6667 (matching the predicted 2/3 exactly), and the control showed freezing ℓ at a small-gradient value violates the inequality at large gradient (LHS 145.64 > RHS 135.61) while the generalized ℓ*(g) bound holds (RHS 378.17).

claims.claim: Theorem 8 shows mirror descent under ℓ*-smoothness attains O(1/T) convergence for both average-iterate and last-iterate suboptimality with an appropriately chosen learning rate (Section 4, Theorem 8)
claims.evidence: Mirror descent with adaptive step size η_t ~ 1/ℓ(‖∇f(x_t)‖_*) was run for T∈{50,…,6400} on the quartic-on-simplex testbed (n=10); both average-iterate (fitted exponent -1.436) and last-iterate (fitted exponent -2.933) suboptimality decayed at least as fast as the predicted O(1/T) floor of -1.0, consistent with the theorem's upper bound.

claims.claim: Theorem 9 shows an accelerated mirror descent variant attains the optimal O(1/T^2) convergence rate under ℓ*-smoothness via a time-partition analysis technique (Section 4, Theorem 9)
claims.evidence: Accelerated mirror descent achieved a fitted log-log exponent of -2.082 (predicted -2.0) on the same testbed for T∈{20,…,2560}, closely matching the O(1/T²) rate, while a plain-MD control run in the same experiment decayed at -1.432 with the MD/AMD ratio growing from 6.55 to 163.95, confirming a genuine extra order of acceleration.

claims.claim: Theorem 10 and Theorem 11 extend the O(1/T) rate to optimistic mirror descent and mirror prox respectively, using a stability-tracking argument and a descent property for both update sequences (Section 4, Theorems 10-11)
claims.evidence: Both optimistic mirror descent and mirror prox were run for T∈{50,…,6400} on the quartic-on-simplex testbed; fitted exponents were OMD last -1.096, OMD avg -0.952, MP last -1.096, MP avg -0.952, all within 5-10% of the predicted -1.0, with monotonically decaying curves and no divergence.

claims.claim: Theorem 12 establishes an Õ(1/√t) anytime convergence rate for stochastic mirror descent under ℓ*-smoothness with a generalized bounded-noise assumption ‖ϵ_t‖* ≤ σ(‖∇f(x_t)‖*) (Section 5, Theorem 12)
claims.evidence: Stochastic mirror descent with generalized bounded noise σ(g)=σ₀(1+g) was run for T_max=6400 across 10 seeds with anytime step size η_t ~ 1/(ℓ·√t); the fitted log-log decay exponent of running-average suboptimality was -0.497 (predicted -0.5), with low cross-seed variance (1.5-2.2% of mean).

claims.claim: Proposition 4 shows that on the simplex, ℓ*-smoothness yields a constant smoothness parameter whereas standard ℓ-smoothness has an O(n) dimension dependence, illustrating the benefit of the generalized notion (Section 3.2, Proposition 4)
claims.evidence: For n∈{4,8,…,512}, the standard ℓ₂ smoothness constant matched the paper's closed form n-1 exactly (3,7,15,…,511; fitted log-log slope 1.049 vs predicted ~1.0) while the generalized ℓ* constant w.r.t. (‖·‖₁,‖·‖_∞) was exactly 1.0 at every n (relative spread 0.00), confirming dimension-independence.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-mirror-descent-under.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from from-scratch implementations of all mirror descent variants on a synthetic quartic-on-simplex testbed (n=10-12), with convergence rate exponents matching or exceeding the paper's predicted rates for all six claims and closed-form constants matching exactly. The main limitation is that all claims are tested on a single synthetic function rather than across the broader function classes the theorems cover, though the testbed is non-trivial (genuinely ℓ*-smooth, convex but not strongly convex).

DineshAI/RwiGcN2feP.paper_title: Unifying Low Dimensional Spectra in Deep Learning

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves the layer-wise Hessian in the L-deep linear unconstrained features model (UFM) has rank K^2 with all non-zero eigenvalues equal, analytically reproducing the bulk-outlier Hessian spectrum reported in prior empirical studies (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: At K=3, d=60, n=40, L=5, l=3 with a machine-precision DNC optimum (‖∇L‖∞=4.8e-16), the layer-wise Hessian has rank 9=K², max/min non-zero eigenvalue ratio 1.00, eigenvector alignment f_cc'=1.000, and the Kronecker-formula Hessian matches JAX autodiff Hessian to ≤1e-17 at an arbitrary point, independently certifying the Hessian code. Negative control at a random point shows f_cc'≪1 and unequal eigenvalues.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 decomposes the Gauss-Newton/Fisher Information component into three terms: G_within (rank 0), G_cross (rank K(K-1), producing the mini-bulk of eigenvalues), and G_class (rank K, producing the main outliers), mirroring Papyan's empirical knockout experiments (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: At the same K=3, d=60 optimum, the Gauss-Newton decomposition yields ranks 0/6/3 for G_within/G_cross/G_class matching K(K-1)=6 and K=3, with max/min non-zero eigenvalue ratios 1.00 for both G_class and G_cross, and max cosine between image(G_class) and image(G_cross) = 5.8e-18 (orthogonal). Negative control at a random point shows G_within≠0 and the clean split disappears.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 shows the aggregated gradient update is a sum over only K of the K^2 possible eigenvector directions, each with equal coefficient beta^(l+1)/K, explaining the observed gradient alignment with a low-dimensional subspace (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: JAX autodiff gradient projected onto the normalized natural basis gives exactly 3 non-zero coefficients (K=3), all equal to 0.33333 (1/K), with all off-diagonal coefficients exactly 0. Negative control at a random point shows coefficients spread across many directions and are unequal.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 proves the Gram matrix of the optimal weights, W_l*^T W_l*, has rank K with eigenvalues proportional to the squared norms of the class-mean features, giving a closed-form account of the low-rank weight structure (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: At the analytic optimum, rank(W_l^T W_l)=3=K with non-zero eigenvalues [1.8130, 1.8130, 1.8130] matching the closed-form (λ_H/λ_W)·n·‖μ_c‖² with relative error 0.0, and the recurrence λ_W W_l^T W_l = λ_W W_{l-1} W_{l-1}^T verified with relative error 0.0. Negative control at a random point gives rank d≫K.

claims.claim: For a deep linear UFM with K=3 classes, numerical experiments show K^2=9 Hessian outliers separating from the bulk and converging to equal eigenvalues over training, with eigenvector alignment metric f_cc' rising from about 0.2 to 1.0 (Figures 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: Full-batch GD training (K=3, d=60, n=40, L=5, lr=0.2, seed=20240406) over 30k epochs shows the top-9 eigenvalue ratio falling from 2.115 to 1.000, f_cc rising from 0.184 to 1.000, bulk collapsing to ~1e-16, and final loss 0.16484 matching the analytic optimum. The trajectory CSV documents the progressive equalization of 9 outliers separating from the bulk.

claims.claim: In the non-linear (ReLU) Deep UFM, K^2=9 Hessian outliers separate but do not fully converge to equal values, and the gradient has K non-zero coefficients that remain unequal, unlike the linear case (Figure 9, Table 2).
claims.evidence: ReLU deep UFM (K=3, d=65, L=5, l=4) trained 150k epochs shows 9 Hessian outliers separating from the bulk (bulk below 0.033) with max/min ratio 4.98 (vs linear 1.00), and gradient coefficients 0.894/0.057/0.029/... with top-K ratio 31.1 and nnz(>2%)=3=K, confirming unequal outliers and unequal coefficients. Training is 150k vs paper's 10⁶ epochs, but the qualitative inequality is consistent with the paper's own observation that ReLU outliers may never fully equalize.

DineshAI/RwiGcN2feP.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence at the paper's experimental scale (K=3, d=60-65, L=5) for all six claims, with independently certified Hessian code (Kronecker vs JAX autodiff), machine-precision global optima, negative controls at random points, and full training dynamics. The main concerns are contamination from an unrelated paper's content in some pages and reduced ReLU training epochs (150k vs 10⁶), but the substantive verification evidence is internally consistent and directly supports each claim.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows any online covering algorithm with competitive ratio rho(k, dot) can be converted into a learning-augmented algorithm with competitive ratio O(rho(eta, dot)), where eta is the prediction error defined as eta := min(|X|, |X symmetric-difference X-hat|) (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The generic conversion (lazy prediction-following + robustness combiner) is implemented and run on online set cover with exact ILP optima: at eta=0 the converted ratio is exactly 1.000 across three instance sizes (30/45, 45/70, 60/90), and at large eta the converted ratio equals the baseline to three decimals (1.141/1.141, 1.143/1.143, 1.179/1.179), demonstrating both consistency and robustness. Large-scale runs (400–5000 elements) with LP lower bounds confirm the converted algorithm stays below baseline and tracks eta rather than k.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows that given a polynomial-time (alpha, gamma)-decomposition, the ICE algorithm achieves competitive ratio O(alpha)*rho(eta, dot) + O(alpha * log^{-1}(gamma/(gamma-1)) * log k) (Theorem 2, Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: The decomposition oracle (greedy partial-cover with merging for Property B) and ICE algorithm are implemented and run on 12 cells with exact ILP optima (40–80 elements) and 12 cells with LP bounds (200–800 elements). Property (A) holds in 12/12 cells, Property (B) holds after merging in 12/12 cells, alpha is measured at 1.0–4.1, gamma at 1.04–1.53, and Theorem 2's bound holds in all 12 large-scale cells (ICE ratios 1.7–3.3 vs bounds 3.0–9.3).

claims.claim: For set cover and non-metric facility location, Theorem 5 gives a polynomial-time competitive ratio of O(log eta * log|S| + log k), improving on the classical O(log k) bound when prediction error eta is small, with a matching hardness lower bound ruling out O(log eta * log|S|) in polynomial time (Section 3.1, Theorem 5).
claims.evidence: Online set cover is implemented with exact ILP optima: the learning-augmented algorithm achieves ratio 1.000 at eta=0 (vs baseline 1.125–1.223), degrades monotonically with eta (1.025–1.068 at eta≈2, 1.096–1.159 at eta≈4), and matches baseline at eta≳7. Large-scale runs (200–800 elements, LP bounds) show ICE beats baseline at eta=0 (1.695 vs 2.169) and degrades gracefully. The hardness lower bound half is explicitly not addressed, as it is inherently unverifiable by finite experiments.

claims.claim: For metric facility location, Theorem 10 achieves competitive ratio O(log eta / log log eta), improving the classical O(log k / log log k) bound (Section 3.3, Theorem 10).
claims.evidence: Metric facility location is implemented with Meyerson's algorithm as baseline and exact ILP optima: at eta=0 the augmented ratio is 1.000 vs Meyerson's 1.330–1.493, and even at eta=8 it remains 13% better (1.221 vs 1.411). Large-scale runs (100–500 clients, LP bounds) show the augmented slope vs log(k) is 7.2x flatter than baseline at eta=0 (0.0035 vs 0.0252), closing to 1.5x at full corruption, demonstrating the eta-dependence over k-dependence.

claims.claim: For Steiner tree, Theorem 12 achieves competitive ratio O(log eta), and for group Steiner tree/forest the classical O(log^7 k log^5 |V|) bound becomes O(log^7 eta log^5 |V|) under the learning-augmented framework (Section 3.3/3.4, Theorem 12).
claims.evidence: Online Steiner tree is implemented with greedy baseline and MST reference: at eta=0 the augmented ratio is 1.000 across 12–30 terminals (vs baseline 1.257–1.378), and large-scale runs (100–800 terminals) show the augmented ratio is flat at 1.000 while the baseline grows (1.511→1.531). The group Steiner tree/forest half is tested on 7-node graphs with exact enumeration (48 cells, ratio 1.000 at perfect prediction), which is a toy-scale audit of the mechanism rather than a full verification of the asymptotic bound.

ProCreations/repro-learning-augmented-on.overall: The logbook implements and runs learning-augmented online algorithms for set cover, metric facility location, and Steiner tree with exact ILP optima (small scale) and LP lower bounds (larger scale), demonstrating the core properties of the generic conversion: exact consistency at eta=0, robustness at large eta, and competitive ratio tracking eta rather than k. The ICE algorithm and (alpha, gamma)-decomposition are also implemented with measured parameters confirming Theorem 2's bound, though the hardness lower bounds and group Steiner at scale remain only partially or minimally addressed.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-model-monotonicity-i.paper_title: Model Monotonicity in Autobidding Auctions: When Do Better Predictions Lead to Better Outcomes?

claims.claim: For target-CPA bidders without budget constraints using uniform bidding with multiplier mu=1 in first-price auctions, refining the prediction model (partitioning clusters into subclusters while preserving calibration) never decreases platform revenue, i.e., Rev(M_A) >= Rev(M_B) when M_A refines M_B (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: 500 random tCPA instances with 2-5 bidders, 16 base auctions, and depth-4 nested refinement chains yielded 0/2500 refinement-step violations of revenue monotonicity (worst decrease 0.0), providing concrete numerical support on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: The first-price auction revenue monotonicity proof for tCPA bidders relies on convexity of f(p) = max_i(t_i · p_i) via Jensen's inequality, since model refinement corresponds to a mean-preserving spread of this convex function (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: Direct convexity check of f(p)=max_i(t_i·p_i) passed 20,000/20,000 random trials, and the Jensen mechanism was isolated via a control: convex f=max satisfied the Jensen direction in 5000/5000 refinement trials while concave g=min satisfied it only 57.7% of the time, confirming convexity specifically drives the result.

claims.claim: Uniform bidding at multiplier mu=1 is simultaneously conversion-maximizing, revenue-maximizing among equilibria, and welfare-maximizing for tCPA bidders in first-price auctions (Theorem 5.2), and welfare monotonicity follows as a corollary when per-conversion values equal targets (Corollary 5.3).
claims.evidence: Grid-search perturbation of mu_i away from 1 across 200 instances (2490 checks) found 0 conversion/revenue/welfare violations, and a separate 500-instance/2500-step welfare-monotonicity sweep under v_i=t_i found 0 violations, supporting both Theorem 5.2 and Corollary 5.3.

claims.claim: There exist instances with tCPA bidders where second-price (VCG) auctions exhibit non-monotonicity in both revenue and welfare under model refinement, with a constructed counterexample showing a simultaneous 6.2% decrease in both metrics (Theorem 5.8).
claims.evidence: Revenue non-monotonicity in SPA reproduced robustly (-12.1% on the paper's instance, 62% of 20,000 random trials), but the simultaneous welfare decrease did NOT reproduce: welfare increased +2.2% on the paper's instance and 0/20,000 random trials showed simultaneous revenue+welfare decreases, because the simulator uses truthful mu=1 bidding rather than solving for SPA equilibrium multipliers that shift allocation.

claims.claim: Introducing budget constraints breaks revenue monotonicity even in first-price auctions, as optimal bidder multipliers shift under refinement and reduce competitive pressure, exemplified by a counterexample with a 16.8% revenue loss (Theorem 5.10).
claims.evidence: The paper's exact counterexample could not be reproduced: the logbook's own pacing solver converges to different multipliers (alpha=0.886 vs paper's 2.8565) and obtains the opposite sign (+11.1% vs -16.8%). While 364/3000 random budget-constrained instances showed a revenue decrease (worst -22.1%), the solver's convention mismatch means neither the specific counterexample nor the reported magnitude is confirmed, and the solver's correctness relative to the paper's model is unverified.

claims.claim: A centralized, non-strategic linear-programming benchmark allocation guarantees welfare monotonicity under budget constraints via a 'lifting' construction that preserves feasibility across refined partitions (Theorem 5.11), and the paper's overall characterization identifies exactly three settings where monotonicity holds (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Across 100 random budget-constrained instances, the lifted coarse LP allocation was feasible at the fine partition in 100/100 cases and the fine-level LP optimum was never below the coarse optimum (0 monotonicity violations, max gap 0.0), with the welfare-preservation identity also confirmed, supporting Theorem 5.11's lifting construction. The 'exactly three settings' characterization (Table 1) is a meta-summary indirectly supported by Claims 1, 3, and 6 but not independently tested.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-model-monotonicity-i.overall: The logbook provides solid numerical support for the four positive monotonicity claims (1, 2, 3, 6) via from-scratch simulators with thousands of random instances and zero violations, but the two non-monotonicity counterexample claims (4, 5) are not fully reproduced: the SPA welfare decrease never materializes under the logbook's truthful-bidding model, and the budget-constrained FPA counterexample yields the opposite sign due to an unrecovered bid-multiplier convention.

nstp/repro-breaking-the-computational-ba.paper_title: Breaking the Computational Barrier: Provably Efficient Actor–Critic for Low-Rank MDPs

claims.claim: The paper proposes Optimistic Actor-Critic (Opt-AC), presented in Algorithm 1, which avoids expensive planning oracles for low-rank MDPs by relying only on policy evaluation oracles (Section 4, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Opt-AC is implemented from scratch on a small chain MDP (H=6, |A|=4, d=12, 6 states), confirming the no-planning-oracle property (only tabular PE + Gram updates), optimism (V̂≥V* on 100% of iterations), and actor closed-form identity (KKT residual 1.5e-14), but at a clearly simplified scale far below the paper's setting.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 establishes a sample complexity of Õ(H⁵d³|A|²log|Θ|/ε²) for Opt-AC, improving on prior work by a factor of the rank d (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: The sample complexity bound Õ(H⁵d³|A|²log|Θ|/ε²) and the factor-d improvement are never tested; the logbook explicitly states 'We audit the algorithm's correctness and the optimism/no-planning mechanism the rate rests on, not the polynomial exponent.'

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 characterizes the computational (oracle-call) complexity of the algorithm as SL²K(1/K) supervised-learning oracle calls (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: The oracle structure (only tabular PE + Gram matrix per iteration, no planning oracle) is verified on the small chain MDP, which is consistent with the SL²K(1/K) characterization, but the specific complexity bound is not directly tested or counted.

claims.claim: The theoretical results are extended to approximately low-rank MDPs via conditional random Fourier features, with guarantees given for the misspecified setting (Section 6, Theorems 6.1 and 6.2).
claims.evidence: The cRFF error scaling is verified on a 1D density (D=1, Y=[-1,1], 5 contexts, 6 seeds) with exact Fourier coefficients: random-feature error slope -0.587 (theory -0.5), sampling error slope -0.514 (theory -0.5), d(ζ) slope 1.69 (theory 2), plus a degradation control showing A2 necessity (15.7× floor ratio), but this is a proxy for the full approximately low-rank MDP setting.

claims.claim: Opt-AC is validated empirically as cRFFSAC against a SAC baseline on six MuJoCo Gym environments: Ant, HalfCheetah, Hopper, Reacher, Pendulum, and InvertedPendulum (Section 7, Table 2).
claims.evidence: No MuJoCo experiments are run; the logbook explicitly states 'MuJoCo + multi-seed deep RL (GPU-hours), out of scope' and marks the claim as not audited.

nstp/repro-breaking-the-computational-ba.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous but small-scale independent audit of the algorithmic structure (Opt-AC's no-planning-oracle design and optimism mechanism) and the cRFF error scaling laws, both on toy/simplified setups, while leaving the sample complexity theorem, the full oracle-call complexity characterization, and all MuJoCo empirical validation completely unaddressed.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-efficient-privacy-lo.paper_title: Efficient privacy loss accounting for subsampling and random allocation

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 gives a closed-form reduction of the privacy loss distribution (PLD) of k-out-of-t random allocation to t-wise convolutions of exponentiated PLD terms (Section 4, Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: Two backends (GEOM, FFT) from the same vendored library agree to within 0.25% at t∈{5,…,100}, far below the paper's t∈{1000,10000}, and the single Monte-Carlo cross-check at (t,k)=(20,4) shows a 13% discrepancy (2.1575 vs 1.8762); this is an internal-consistency check at reduced scale, not an independent verification of the theorem.

claims.claim: The proposed algorithm computes an (α,β)-accurate approximation of the random allocation PLD in time O(log³(t)·log(t/β)/α²), using exponentiation-by-squaring with geometric-grid rounding (Section 4, Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: Wall-clock time plateaus at ~210s for t=3,000 through t=100,000, confounded by an apparent internal grid-size cap; the log^3(t) fit (R²=0.73) is actually worse than a plain log(t) fit (R²=0.84), so the specific O(log³(t)) scaling claim is neither confirmed nor refuted.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 introduces transformation rules φ_λ that apply Poisson subsampling directly to PLD realizations, allowing subsampling and random allocation to be composed within one unified PLD framework (Section 3, Theorem 3.3, Definition 3.1).
claims.evidence: The phi_lambda-based subsampled PLD from PLD_accounting agrees with Google's independently-developed dp_accounting native subsampled-Gaussian PLD to within <1% relative error for q≥0.01 across 16 configurations (sigma=4.0, q∈{0.001,…,0.1}, delta∈{1e-5,…,1e-8}), providing concrete cross-library evidence that the transform correctly captures Poisson subsampling.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments show the new random allocation privacy bounds are nearly identical to the Monte Carlo lower bounds of Chua et al. (2024a) and substantially tighter than RDP-based analytic bounds, for t ∈ {1000, 10000} and δ = 10⁻⁶ (Section 5, Figures 1-2).
claims.evidence: The 'PLD tighter than RDP' half is supported (3.82x–4.88x at t=1000 and t=10000, delta=1e-6), but the 'PLD nearly matches Monte Carlo lower bounds' half is untested: the from-scratch MC proxy simulates non-amplified k-fold composition (tracking RDP) rather than the true k-out-of-t random-allocation mechanism, so no valid MC lower bound was produced.

claims.claim: A toy Bernoulli mean-estimation experiment (n=10³, δ=10⁻¹⁰) shows random allocation requires strictly lower noise than Poisson subsampling for the same privacy level, demonstrating a genuine privacy (not just variance) advantage (Section 5, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: At the paper's stated parameters (n=1000, delta=1e-10, target epsilon=1.0), bisection over sigma shows random allocation requires 7.2–11.7% lower noise than Poisson subsampling across all four tested epoch counts (E∈{1,3,6,10}), directly supporting the claimed strict noise advantage.

claims.claim: Applied to a DP-SGD scenario with block-sparse coordinate sampling (n=6×10⁵, d=2²⁰, C=2¹⁵, E=10 epochs), the PLD accounting method improves privacy bounds over RDP composition even under heavy composition (Section 5, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: At the paper's stated scale (n=6×10⁵, d=2²⁰, C=2¹⁵, t=32 blocks, E=10 epochs, delta=1e-6), PLD accounting yields 2.55x–6.84x tighter epsilon than naive RDP composition across sigma∈{0.5,…,8}, with the gap persisting at heavy composition; however, the baseline is generic Mironov (2017) RDP rather than the paper's own refined RDP bounds.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-efficient-privacy-lo.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting claims 3, 5, and 6 at the paper's stated scales using independent cross-checks where possible, but claims 1 and 2 are tested only at reduced scale or with confounded measurements, and claim 4's critical Monte Carlo lower-bound comparison was never properly implemented.

ProCreations/repro-upper-linearizability.paper_title: Upper-Linearizability of Online Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization over Down-Closed Convex Sets

claims.claim: Theorem 1 proves that non-monotone DR-submodular functions over down-closed convex sets are 1/e-Upper-Linearizable via the exponential reparameterization h(x) = 1 - e^{-x} combined with a designed surrogate potential.
claims.evidence: 23,040 finite certificates across six nonseparable polynomial families (degree ≤4, dimensions 2–32) plus 576 additional cells at d=64 all pass, with destructive controls showing identity-mapping substitution yields 4 counterexamples and surrogate-zeroing yields 109 counterexamples, confirming the exponential reparameterization mechanism is necessary.

claims.claim: The BQND algorithm (Algorithm 1) reduces online non-monotone DR-submodular maximization to online linear optimization using a single gradient query per round.
claims.evidence: Across 589,824 total one-query rounds (dimensions 8/16/32, horizons 16,384 and 32,768, four seeds each), every round used exactly one oracle query via the exponential map 1-exp(-z*x), with max estimator error 1.848e-8 against 128-node quadrature and all norm bounds passing.

claims.claim: Proposition 1 shows BQND obtains O(T^{1/2}) static regret with only O(1) oracle queries per round, improving on prior work's O(T^{2/3}) regret for single queries or O(T^{1/2}) regret requiring T^{3/2} queries per round.
claims.evidence: 256 trajectories (T=128–16,384, dimensions 2–16, eight seeds) plus 24 extended trajectories (T=16,384–32,768, dimensions 8–32) yield fitted static-regret exponents of 0.491–0.501 across all dimensions, with exactly one query per round verified throughout; the prior-work comparison rates (T^{2/3} for single query, T^{3/2} queries for T^{1/2}) are registered but not independently reproduced as baselines.

claims.claim: Proposition 3 establishes a dynamic regret bound of Õ(T^{1/2}·√(1+P_T)) where P_T is the path length of the comparator sequence.
claims.evidence: 160 online cells (T=128–2,048, dimensions 4/8, four path regimes, four seeds) plus 24 extended cells (T=16,384–32,768, dimensions 4/8/16) show normalized regret R_T/sqrt(T(1+P_T)) bounded in [0.503, 0.649] across all regimes, with stationary paths yielding P_T=0 and slopes increasing with path complexity as expected.

claims.claim: In the bandit feedback model, the framework achieves O(T^{4/5}) regret (Proposition 6), and in the semi-bandit model O(T^{2/3}) regret (Proposition 4).
claims.evidence: 168 seeded horizon cells per protocol plus 24 extended cells (T=32,768–65,536, 12 seeds) yield fitted exponents of 0.664–0.674 for semi-bandit (close to 2/3) and 0.785–0.796 for bandit (close to 4/5), with concrete mean-regret endpoint values reported at both horizons.

ProCreations/repro-upper-linearizability.overall: The logbook provides substantial numerical evidence supporting all five claims through large-scale finite certificates, executed online trajectories, and destructive controls across multiple polynomial families, dimensions up to 64, and horizons up to 65,536. The main limitation is that experiments use specific DR-submodular function families rather than arbitrary ones, and prior-work comparisons rely on registered rates rather than independently reproduced baselines.

qy2100/repro-ballast-bayesian-active-lea.paper_title: BALLAST: Bayesian Active Learning with Look-ahead Amendment for Sea-drifter Trajectories under Spatio-Temporal Vector Fields

claims.claim: Proposition 1 shows that standard active-learning utility construction, which ignores the future trajectories of Lagrangian drifters, yields suboptimal observer placement decisions (Section 3.1, Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: A 36-configuration numerical sweep (12 seeds × 3 kernels, 2 candidate locations) shows 100% argmax disagreement between BALLAST and standard EIG for advecting drifters (mean gap 4.033 nats), with a proper control: 100% agreement and zero gap for inert drifters, confirming the proposition.

claims.claim: BALLAST's acquisition function uses an SPDE-based extended Gaussian process state f=[f, partial_t f]^T with Matern-3/2 temporal kernels to enable posterior sampling without the O(J*N_space^3*N_sampT^3) cost of naive sampling (Section 4.1, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Direct comparison of Kalman-filter/RTS-smoother (VaSE) posterior against dense Cholesky GP posterior on a 25×25 grid (N=625) with 50 time steps yields max absolute mean error of 1.9×10⁻¹⁵, confirming mathematical equivalence at machine precision on a non-trivial grid.

claims.claim: On synthetic Helmholtz ground-truth vector fields across 100 runs over 10 fields, BALLAST-aided sequential observer placement saves approximately 3 drifters (about 16% cost reduction) compared to uniform, Sobol, and expected-information-gain placement policies (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: After correcting a metric bug, the paper's own scripts show BALLAST winning all 3 tested fields (mean bias 1.511 vs EIG 6.868, UNIF 6.602), but savings overshoot to ~18 drifters (~90%) versus the claimed ~3 drifters (~16%), only 3 of 100 runs are covered, Sobol baseline is missing, and the specific 16% average cannot be estimated from 3 favorable fields.

claims.claim: On the high-fidelity SUNTANS ocean model over 100 independent runs, BALLAST achieves approximately 22% deployment cost savings relative to baseline placement policies (Section 5.3).
claims.evidence: Running the paper's own J=20 scripts on 3 SUNTANS seeds shows BALLAST winning all 3 (mean 2.318 < UNIF 2.680 < EIG 3.841) with crossover savings ~2.67 drifters, which is in the right ballpark of the claimed ~2 drifters (~22%), but only 3 of 100 runs and 2 of 4 baselines (Sobol, DIST-SEP missing) were tested, making the specific 22% figure unverifiable at this scale.

claims.claim: An ablation on the number of Monte Carlo vector-field samples J shows that J=20 achieves less than 1% utility gap regardless of decision time, balancing accuracy against computational cost (Section 5.1, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: At paper-scale N=25 with J_ref=100 (vs paper's J_ref=200), J=20 yields gaps of 2.26%, 2.02%, and 1.03% at t=3,5,7 respectively — all exceeding the 1% threshold — while J=50 passes all three; the different reference level (100 vs 200) means the result could change, and the paper's exact configuration was not run.

qy2100/repro-ballast-bayesian-active-lea.overall: The logbook provides strong machine-precision verification of the two theoretical claims (Proposition 1 suboptimality and VaSE posterior equivalence), but the empirical benchmark claims are only directionally confirmed on 3 seeds with missing baselines, and the J-ablation claim is not reproduced at the tested reference level.

algorise/repro-calibrated-test-time-guid.paper_title: Calibrated Test-Time Guidance for Bayesian Inference

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows the standard posterior-mean guidance approximation (Eq. 7) is biased for essentially all practical likelihoods unless the likelihood is constant (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Numerical experiments across d∈{2,10,50} and 9 noise levels with a quadratic observation model show non-zero Jensen gap (2.2→3198) and score MAE (5.6→264.7) scaling with dimension, confirming the bias predicted by Theorem 4.1 on non-trivial synthetic setups.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 shows Gaussian posterior approximations (Eq. 8) used in guidance are unbiased only under a standard normal prior and are otherwise systematically biased (Section 4, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: LGD error is machine-zero (~5.4e-7) for Gaussian prior + linear likelihood across d∈{2,5,10,20}, while MoG and Laplace-like priors show systematic bias growing from 14→63 (MoG) and 0.10→0.35 (Laplace-like) with dimension, confirming Theorem 4.2's conditions for unbiasedness.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 proves that rescaling the guidance scale cannot produce a properly tempered posterior for non-trivial likelihoods, since the tempered diffused likelihood cannot be obtained by exponentiation (Section 4, Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Tempering discrepancy Δ(γ)=0 only at γ=1 and is strictly non-zero for all 7 other γ values across d∈{2,10,50} and two likelihood families (quadratic and sinusoidal), with discrepancy scaling from 4.09 to 41.24 at γ=5, confirming Theorem 4.3.

claims.claim: The proposed gradient-free Calibrated Bayesian Guidance (CBG) estimator (Eq. 20) achieves an average C2ST score of 0.527 on the Bayesian inference benchmark, versus 0.803 for DPS and 0.750 for LGD (Section 6.1, Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements a simplified 2D Langevin setup without learned score networks or diffusion models; the resulting C2ST scores (CBG=0.520, DPS=0.482, LGD=0.527) do not match the paper's Table 1 values (0.527, 0.803, 0.750) and actually show DPS outperforming CBG, so the specific benchmark claim is not reproduced.

claims.claim: CBG improves monotonically with increased computational budget while competing guidance methods plateau, and on black-hole imaging attains a PSNR of 26.10 dB matching state-of-the-art reconstructions (Section 6.1; Section 6.2, Table 2).
claims.evidence: IW score error decreases monotonically (2.55→0.12 as K: 1→1024) on a simplified 2D quadratic-likelihood setup, partially addressing the budget-scaling claim; however, the black-hole imaging PSNR=26.10 dB claim is explicitly not computed due to resource constraints, leaving half the claim unaddressed.

algorise/repro-calibrated-test-time-guid.overall: The logbook provides reasonable numerical verification of the three theoretical claims (Theorems 4.1–4.3) on synthetic setups up to d=50, but the empirical claims (Table 1 C2ST scores and Table 2 black-hole PSNR) are only addressed on simplified 2D toy setups or not at all, failing to reproduce the paper's actual benchmark results.

algorise/repro-linear-bandits-beyond-inn.paper_title: Linear Bandits beyond Inner Product Spaces, the case of Bandit Optimal Transport

claims.claim: The EntUCB algorithm embeds transport plans into a Hilbert space via the Fourier isometry F on L²(ℝᵈ;ϱ), reducing the bandit optimal transport problem to linear bandit estimation in that space (Section 4.1, Equation 7).
claims.evidence: The Fourier isometry and cost linearity were tested on small discrete grids (up to 32×32), which are simplified discretizations of the continuous L²(ℝᵈ;ϱ) space; the near-machine-precision errors confirm a known mathematical identity but on a toy-scale approximation, not the full continuous setting.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 bounds the entropic regret as R_T^{H,ε}(A) ≤ σ√(2T log(2/δ)) + 2Cβ_T(δ)√(T log det(...)) with probability at least 1-δ (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: Twenty trials across T∈{200,500,1000,1500} checked that empirical regret falls below the theoretical upper bound, but this is a weak test (loose bounds are almost always satisfied) on small-scale problems with underspecified OT setup.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 shows that for Lipschitz costs with an entropy penalty decaying as ε_t = αt^{-α}, EntUCB achieves sublinear regret matching classical linear-bandit rates for the Kantorovich optimal transport problem (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Fitted log-log regret exponents γ∈{0.186,0.399,0.299} over the narrow range t∈[500,2000] are sublinear but do not clearly match the classical √T rate (γ=0.5) claimed; the setup is small-scale and the fitting window is too narrow to robustly establish the rate.

claims.claim: Corollary 5.3 establishes that in finite-dimensional/discrete settings with N basis coefficients, the algorithm attains Õ(√(NT)) regret, recovering the parametric OFUL-style rate (Corollary 5.3).
claims.evidence: Only 4 data points (N∈{4,16,36,64}) at T=1000 with normalized ratio standard deviation 0.0192 (~30% of mean) provide weak evidence for Õ(√(NT)) scaling on a small-scale discrete problem.

claims.claim: Corollary 5.4 shows that when basis coefficients decay at rate 1-n^{-q}, regret interpolates between Õ(√T) and Õ(T) depending on the decay exponent q (Corollary 5.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook only shows that regret at T=1000 decreases monotonically with q, but never tests the actual T-scaling behavior needed to verify interpolation between Õ(√T) and Õ(T); pointwise regret values at a single horizon cannot establish rate interpolation.

claims.claim: The confidence sets used by the algorithm are constructed via regularized least-squares in L²(ℝᵈ;ϱ), with width controlled by the log-determinant of the design operator, mirroring the classical OFUL confidence ellipsoid construction (Equations 11-12).
claims.evidence: A single run of 2000 iterations showing 100% coverage at δ=0.05 is expected for any valid confidence ellipsoid and does not test tightness; the setup is small-scale and the coverage result is a trivially satisfied necessary condition rather than a rigorous validation.

algorise/repro-linear-bandits-beyond-inn.overall: The logbook provides toy-scale numerical experiments on small discrete grids (up to 32×32) with short horizons (T≤2000) that only partially and weakly address the paper's theoretical claims. The tests are generally insufficient—checking empirical regret against loose bounds, fitting exponents over narrow ranges, and showing monotonicity without testing actual scaling rates—on underspecified OT problem setups.

ProCreations/repro-sampling-and-identity.paper_title: Sampling and Identity-Testing Without Approximate Tensorization of Entropy

claims.claim: Theorem 4 proves fast mixing of Glauber dynamics for mixtures of k distributions satisfying Approximate Tensorization of Entropy (ATE) when initialized from an empirical (data-based) distribution built from m = O(k/ε + log(1/δ)/ε) samples, reaching KL divergence at most ε in time t = c*n · O(log log(1/min μ(x)) + log(1/ε)) (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: The Glauber transition matrix is built exactly (not simulated) on 1,024–4,096 states and diagonalized via the reversible similarity transform, yielding exact TV-distance threshold crossings. The empirical-start mixing time collapses from 30,654 to 22 steps as rho_min falls from 0.5 to 0.005, while cold-start remains at 17,508—a 795.8× speedup that grows as rho_min shrinks, directly demonstrating the theorem's key qualitative prediction. The scale-up to n=12 (4,096 states) shows a 16,581× speedup, confirming the trend grows with state-space size.

claims.claim: The analysis avoids standard Chernoff-bound arguments in favor of moment generating function bounds on the KL divergence of empirical distributions, removing dependence on the minimum mixture weight (Section on Theorem 4, Lemma 21-22).
claims.evidence: Over 6,000 multinomial trials sweeping rho_min across four orders of magnitude (0.25 to 1e-4) at k∈{2,4,8}, the worst observed ratio KL(rho_hat||rho)/bound never exceeds 0.4614 and shows no trend in rho_min—exactly what the MGF bound predicts and the opposite of a 1/rho_min-dependent Chernoff argument, which would degrade by 3–4 orders of magnitude.

claims.claim: Theorem 5 gives an efficient identity-tester for mixtures of k ATE distributions in the coordinate-conditional sampling access model, resolving an open question posed by Blanca et al., with sample complexity O(c*n/ε)·log²(c*n/ε)·log(1/η)·log log(1/η)·|Σ| + O(√k·log(1/ρ*)/ε) (Theorem 5).
claims.evidence: The identity tester of Algorithm 1 is implemented in the coordinate-conditional sampling access model (oracle returns 8 noisy draws per query) and run on k=3, n=10 and scaled to k=5, n=20 (1,048,576 states). Type-I error is 0.067–0.10 against nominal 0.05, and power rises monotonically with sample size (100→300→1000) for every alternative, reaching 1.000 on large perturbations. The million-state scale-up with at most 1,000 samples confirms the guarantee comes from mixture structure and the conditional oracle, not state-space enumeration.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 combines a Local Testing step detecting large intra-component divergence via the coordinate oracle with a Posterior Weight Estimation step detecting mismatched mixture weights via a KL-test, both relying on the KL-Test subroutine of Theorem 24 (Section 4, Algorithm 1, Theorem 24).
claims.evidence: Both branches of Algorithm 1 are implemented and tested on alternatives designed so each is invisible to one branch: component-parameter shifts (caught by Local Testing at 0.983–1.000) leave mixture weights unchanged, while mixture-weight perturbations (caught by Posterior Weight Estimation at 0.983–1.000) leave components unchanged. The null is accepted at 0.067, directly demonstrating the two branches are complementary rather than redundant.

claims.claim: Lemma 11's chain rule for entropy decomposes the entropy of a mixture μ = Σₐ ρ(a)μₐ into an intra-component term Eₐ[Entμₐ[f]] and an inter-component term Ent_ρ[Eμₐ[f]], underlying the paper's use of Modified Log-Sobolev Inequalities in place of the Poincaré inequalities used in prior work by KLV24 and HMRW24 (Lemma 11, Remark 17).
claims.evidence: The chain-rule identity Ent_mu[f] = Σ_a ρ_a Ent_{μ_a}[f] + Ent_ρ[E_{μ_a}[f]] is verified by exact enumeration (no sampling) over 48 cells spanning n=8–14, k=3–10, and up to 16,384 states, with worst absolute error 8.882e-16—machine precision—with no growth in n or k. This confirms the algebraic decomposition underlying the paper's MLSI-based analysis.

ProCreations/repro-sampling-and-identity.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence for all five claims through exact computation (Glauber diagonalization, entropy chain rule) and Monte Carlo trials (MGF bound, identity tester). The main limitation is the small state-space scale for the Glauber chain experiments (n=10–12), but the exact computation and clear qualitative trends—particularly the growing speedup as rho_min shrinks—substantiate the paper's core predictions.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-understanding-behavi.paper_title: Understanding Behavior Cloning with Action Quantization

claims.claim: Behavior cloning with quantized actions and log-loss is proven to achieve sample complexity matching known lower bounds, up to the quantization error term (Theorem 2, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: d=3 linear dynamics with 20 seeds yields log-log slopes -0.496 (K=8, CI ±0.015, R²=0.999) and -0.499 (K=32, CI ±0.020, R²=0.997), matching the predicted -0.5 rate; a Le Cam two-point construction with beta sweep shows the phase transition bracketing exactly at beta=0.5 (error flat at 0.05-0.09 for beta=0.5, vanishing for beta=0.3, growing for beta=0.7), providing genuine lower-bound evidence.

claims.claim: Under Probabilistic Incremental Input-to-State Stability (P-IISS) of the dynamics and Relaxed Total Variation Continuity (RTVC) of the expert policy, the regret bound has only polynomial (not exponential) dependence on the horizon H with respect to quantization error epsilon_q (Theorem 3, Definition 3, Definition 4, Section 3.1-3.2).
claims.evidence: Fitted power-law exponent 1.81 (CI ±0.006, R²=0.99998) over H in {5,...,320} with 15 seeds and 600 trajectories/seed, with exponential fit rejected (R²=0.77); the smooth-policy negative control (RTVC-satisfying binning) collapses the exponent to 0.99, confirming the elevated exponent is attributable to RTVC violation and that polynomial—not exponential—growth holds. Limitation: P-IISS is not independently verified, only assumed via linear dynamics.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 shows that without a smoothness assumption on the quantizer, non-smooth quantizers can incur regret of order H*Omega(1) even though their in-distribution one-step error is only O(epsilon_q) (Theorem 6, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Deterministic case directly reproduces the paper's identity-policy/trap-quantizer construction: in-distribution error stays small (0.035-0.047) while per-step regret remains flat (0.067-0.095) across a 32x H range; conditional-on-trapped regret is pinned at ~4.00 across a 32x eps_q sweep (eps_q-independent), and the trap-free binning negative control's per-step regret is ~0.0008 (two orders of magnitude lower). The stochastic 1/|log eps_q| sub-case is not sharply distinguished from a plain eps_q fit (R²=0.986 vs 0.993), but the primary H*Omega(1) claim is supported by the deterministic evidenc

claims.claim: Theorem 7 proves that model-based data augmentation improves the horizon dependence to H*[sqrt(log|Pi|/n) + epsilon_q] without requiring the policy smoothness (RTVC) assumption (Theorem 7, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Model-based augmentation reduces the fitted horizon exponent from 1.81 (CI ±0.006) to 1.51 (CI ±0.030), non-overlapping CIs, with a 2.59x regret ratio at H=320; the smooth-policy negative control reverses the effect (ratio 0.007), confirming the benefit is specifically attributable to bypassing RTVC violation rather than a generic open-loop vs closed-loop artifact. Exponents do not exactly match the paper's H¹/H² formula constants but are directionally correct and clearly separated.

claims.claim: Information-theoretic lower bounds (Theorems 8-9) establish that regret must scale at least as H*(1/n + epsilon_q) for deterministic experts and H*(sqrt(1/n) + epsilon_q) for stochastic experts, matching the achievable upper bounds (Section 5, Theorems 8-9).
claims.evidence: Three genuine constructions: (1) Le Cam two-point with phase transition at beta=0.5 supporting the n^{-1/2} statistical rate; (2) needle-in-haystack with p=c/n showing risk flat across a 256x n-range (e.g., 0.605 to 0.607 for c=0.5), confirming Theorem 8's Theta(1/n) signature; (3) oracle rate-distortion floor with log-log slope -1.0008 (CI ±0.0016, R²=0.9999966) vs eps_q(K), confirmed n-independent over a 10,000x n-range. The earlier testing-hardness argument was correctly identified as wrong and replaced.

claims.claim: Empirically, binning quantizers are shown to preserve policy smoothness better than learned quantizers, while deterministic experts more often violate the RTVC requirement needed for the sharp regret bound (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: RTVC-violation rate ratio of ~17-21x (binning vs fine unstructured quantizer) across K in {4,...,128} with 30 seeds/point and non-overlapping CIs at every K, directly supporting the binning-vs-learned smoothness claim. However, the second part of the claim—deterministic experts more often violating RTVC than stochastic experts—is not addressed by any experiment in the logbook.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-understanding-behavi.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence across all six claims using multi-dimensional dynamics, genuine lower-bound constructions, fitted exponents with CIs, and destructive negative controls on most claims. The main gaps are: the deterministic-vs-stochastic expert comparison in Claim 6 is unaddressed, P-IISS is assumed rather than independently verified in Claim 2, and the stochastic sub-case of Theorem 6 is not sharply distinguished from simpler alternatives.

nstp/repro-shrinking-the-variance-shrink.paper_title: Shrinking the Variance: Shrinkage Baselines for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

claims.claim: The optimal James-Stein shrinkage coefficient for the baseline is derived in closed form as (n-1)/n times v2/(s2+v2), where v2 is the expected variance of leave-one-out estimates and s2 is the variability of true prompt-level values (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements the formula λ = (n-1)/n · v̂/(ŝ²+v̂) in code and tests it on toy Bernoulli reward data (n∈{10,100}, m∈{2,4,8,16}), showing MSE reductions consistent with the formula being beneficial, but does not verify the mathematical derivation/proof of optimality itself.

claims.claim: The shrinkage baseline reduces value-function mean-squared error by 13.4%-39.4% relative to RLOO across different rollout budgets, and reduces policy-gradient variance by 11.2%-67.1% (Section on empirical variance/MSE results).
claims.evidence: MSE reductions of 10.3%–50.9% and gradient-variance reductions of 0.5%–48.7% are measured on toy Bernoulli-reward simulations with synthetic mean-zero score functions (d=16, nbatch=3000); the direction matches the paper but the specific claimed ranges (13.4%–39.4% MSE, 11.2%–67.1% gradient variance) are not reproduced and the setup uses no real policy training or LLM checkpoints.

claims.claim: On mathematical reasoning benchmarks (MATH500, OlympiadBench, AMC23) with Qwen2.5-Math models, the shrinkage baseline yields 1.1%-4.3% accuracy gains over standard empirical-mean baselines (experiments section).
claims.evidence: No experiments involving MATH500, OlympiadBench, AMC23, Qwen2.5-Math models, or any LLM training/evaluation are present in the logbook; the claim is never addressed.

claims.claim: On Knights-and-Knaves logic puzzles, the method improves accuracy by 2.3%-15.2% across difficulty levels, with consistent gains also observed on Countdown and Maze tasks (experiments section).
claims.evidence: No experiments involving Knights-and-Knaves, Countdown, or Maze tasks are present in the logbook; the claim is never addressed.

claims.claim: On GSM8K, the James-Stein baseline achieves the highest test accuracy among RLOO, GRPO, ReMax, REINFORCE++, and BLOO baselines across 2, 4, and 8 generations per prompt (Table 1).
claims.evidence: No experiments involving GSM8K or comparisons against GRPO, ReMax, REINFORCE++, or BLOO baselines are present in the logbook; the claim is never addressed.

claims.claim: The shrinkage baseline requires no additional hyperparameters, remains unbiased via leave-one-out construction, and can be implemented as a drop-in replacement with about 10 lines of code (Section on implementation).
