claims.evidence: Markov curl ratio is 0.000 [0.000, 0.000] and non-Markov curl ratio is 0.6469 [0.6001, 0.6927] across 25 seeds on synthetic graphs of 8–52 nodes (0.1s wall time), demonstrating the topological integrability distinction but on a clearly simplified proxy setup rather than actual RL state-transition spaces.

claims.claim: HodgeFlow Policy Search achieves stability and sensitivity guarantees via Bellman-de Rham projection
claims.evidence: Max stability ratio 0.679 ≤ 1.0 and sensitivity gain 0.4459 [0.4158, 0.4758] across 25 seeds support non-expansiveness and sensitivity improvement, but experiments run in 0.1s on CPU on a synthetic setup far below the scale of real RL training.

claims.claim: HFPS significantly improves RL performance under non-Markovian dynamics
claims.evidence: HFPS vs TD difference is -0.000008 [-0.000263, 0.000238] across 30 seeds (not significant), with no scaling across non-Markov amplitudes (R²=0.0469), but the environment is a simplified proxy (3.6s CPU, returns near -0.11) rather than a standard RL benchmark, so this is a toy-scale result showing no advantage rather than a definitive falsification.

algorise/repro-hodgeflow-policy-search-b.overall: The logbook provides statistically rigorous but small-scale synthetic experiments: Claims 1 and 2 are supported on toy topological/gradient setups, while Claim 3 shows HFPS provides no measurable advantage over standard TD on a simplified environment. None of the experiments approach the scale of real RL benchmarks, so all three claims are addressed only at toy level.

SabaPivot/repro-autoregressive-language-.paper_title: Autoregressive Language Models are Secretly Energy-Based Models: Insights into the Lookahead Capabilities of Next-Token Prediction

claims.claim: Proposition 3.2 establishes an exact bijection between autoregressive models (ARMs) and energy-based models (EBMs) in function space, via the mapping q(s_t,y_t) = r(s_t,y_t) for y_t=EOS and r(s_t,y_t)+V_q(s_t⊕y_t) otherwise, such that p^ebm_R(y|x) = p^arm_q(y|x) (Proposition 3.2).
claims.evidence: Exact enumeration over 500 finite prefix trees (V=2-5, T=2-6, 183,950 responses) confirms ARM and EBM sequence distributions match to 5.33e-15 max log-prob error, with inverse roundtrip error 8.88e-16 and negative controls showing lookahead omission produces median TV 0.425.

claims.claim: Section 3.3 shows this ARM-EBM bijection corresponds to a special case of the soft Bellman equation from maximum-entropy reinforcement learning, with the soft value function V_q(s_t) capturing implicit lookahead over future tokens (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: 500 trials confirm the bijection is the unique soft-Bellman fixed point: max residual 0.0, convergence within T sweeps from two independent random starts (max difference 0.0), and wrong-discount (γ=0.9) negative control yields non-zero residual.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 proves that minimizing negative log-likelihood over ARM functions and over EBM functions yields identical minima, showing teacher forcing is optimal in function space (Proposition 4.1).
claims.evidence: 240 joint distributions with 720 context conditionals and 264,888 enumerated responses show EBM minimum, mapped ARM minimum, and teacher-forcing minimum all equal conditional entropy to 1.78e-15; random EBM and ARM both show positive excess risk.

claims.claim: An error bound (Proposition 59) shows that distilling an EBM into an ARM yields KL(p^ebm_R, p^arm_q) ≤ 2T·max|q*(s,y)-q(s,y)|, bounding divergence by sequence length T times the maximum logit approximation error (Proposition 59).
claims.evidence: 2,400 cells across 8 noise scales confirm both forward and reverse KL satisfy 2T·max|q*-q| with max ratio 0.159 and zero violations; horizon-factor control shows removing T (using 2ε) is violated (KL=4.22 > 4.0), confirming the T factor is necessary.

claims.claim: Converting an EBM to an equivalent ARM representation costs O(V^T) (exponential in sequence length), whereas converting an ARM to an EBM representation costs only O(VT) (linear) (Section on computational trade-offs).
claims.evidence: Exact operation census across V=2-6 and T up to 18 confirms ARM→EBM is linear in T (log-log slope exactly 1.0, R²>0.999) touching VT logits, while EBM→ARM is exponential (slope ratio 1.0025 vs expected log V, R²>0.999) touching geometric-sum edges; shortcut control confirms path-only conversion fails.

SabaPivot/repro-autoregressive-language-.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous, exhaustive finite-language verification of all five mathematical claims via exact enumeration over prefix trees with full code, predeclared gates, and negative controls. The small vocabulary and horizon sizes are appropriate because the claims are exact function-space propositions verified by complete enumeration rather than sampling.

Srishti280992/repro-linear-regression-wi.paper_title: Linear Regression with Unknown Truncation Beyond Gaussian Features

claims.claim: The paper gives the first polynomial-time, poly(d/ε), algorithm for truncated linear regression with an unknown survival set under sub-Gaussian (rather than Gaussian) feature distributions (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Official code at d=10 with 10 seeds shows learned-set PSGD error 1.04±0.19 vs OLS 9.85±0.26; clean-room runs at d=20,n=14000 for Gaussian/uniform/Rademacher features yield relerr 0.054/0.046/0.049; empirical scaling exponents (n^-0.38, d^0.79, d^0.41) support polynomial dependence. The word 'first' is bibliographic and not experimentally adjudicable, but the algorithmic content is concretely exercised on non-Gaussian sub-Gaussian features.

claims.claim: The algorithm assumes a known lower bound α on the truncation/survival probability, sub-Gaussian feature tails, and a well-conditioned observed covariance matrix (Section 3, three main assumptions).
claims.evidence: Numerical audits measure survival probability α≈0.435, covariance eigenvalues 0.64–0.66 for sub-Gaussian families, a Cauchy control with tail proxy 11.58 vs 1.1–1.2, and an anisotropic control collapsing eigenvalue to 0.0025, exercising all three assumptions with concrete metrics.

claims.claim: Phase I of the algorithm learns the unknown survival set as a union of k intervals via a novel positive-only PAC learning subroutine that runs in poly(k/ε) time (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: Exact normal-CDF testbed at k=5, N up to 32000, 8 reps shows symmetric-difference mass decaying with slopes -0.94 to -0.97 (near N^-1), output interval counts below theorem bounds, and a destructive no-gap-removal control at error 0.438 isolating the mechanism. Phase I is inherently 1D so this is the real task, not a toy proxy.

claims.claim: Phase II estimates the regression vector via projected stochastic gradient descent on a perturbed negative log-likelihood objective, after Phase I's set recovery (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Clean-room Phase II with uniform features shows analytic gradient matching finite differences at L2 error 1.5e-11, NLL decreasing monotonically with zero violations, and learned-set relerr 0.0493 matching oracle 0.0493; official 10-seed run confirms the two-phase design matters (learned 1.04 vs wrong-set 7.17).

claims.claim: Lemma 3.4 shows sub-Gaussianity implies smoothness of the auxiliary distributions used to construct reference distributions for learning from positive examples alone (Lemma 3.4).
claims.evidence: 58,320 exact interval-mass checks across 6 directions and 3 distances yield max ratio 1.00036 with zero violations under paper-style q constants, while a destructive q=1 control fails 1814 times with max ratio 1.531, demonstrating the smoothness slack is load-bearing.

claims.claim: This improves on prior work (LMZ24a) which required d^poly(k/ε) running time and was restricted to Gaussian features (Section on related work/Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Non-Gaussian end-to-end recovery (uniform relerr 0.046, Rademacher 0.049) and polynomial scaling evidence (d^0.79, d^0.41) concretely support the new method's sub-Gaussian and polynomial-time capabilities. LMZ24a was not benchmarked head-to-head, so the direct prior-work comparison remains textual, but the substantive improvement mechanisms are experimentally demonstrated.

Srishti280992/repro-linear-regression-wi.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence across official-code and clean-room implementations supporting all six claims: end-to-end recovery under Gaussian, uniform, and Rademacher features; exact-CDF Phase I interval learning with near-N^-1 scaling; finite-difference-verified Phase II gradients; and a 58k-check smoothness grid with destructive controls. The main gaps are the absence of a head-to-head LMZ24a benchmark and the inherent inability of experiments to prove theoretical polynomial-time or 'first' claims.

RyeCatcher/repro-scalora-optimally-scale.paper_title: ScaLoRA: Optimally Scaled Low-Rank Adaptation for Efficient High-Rank Fine-Tuning

claims.claim: Theorem 3 (Section 3.2) derives globally optimal closed-form scalar scaling factors for low-rank adapter increments based on the truncated-SVD optimality condition established in Theorem 1 (Section 3.1), avoiding its prohibitive computational cost (Theorem 1, Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The closed-form scalar scaling was confirmed to match the global optimum of the paper's scalar objective to max relative error 3.93e-16 over 200 random instances, cross-checked against independent L-BFGS and NNLS optima; the truncated-SVD optimality basis (Thm 1) was independently confirmed (L-BFGS reaches SVD value on 25/25 seeds, never beats it); cost avoidance was measured at 78x–1178x faster than rank-2r SVD up to m=n=1024.

claims.claim: Theorem 5 (Section 3.3) extends the scaling to a column-wise formulation solved via a 2r x 2r linear system, applicable when a non-negativity condition holds, which is empirically satisfied in about 80% of LoRA layers across iterations (Theorem 5, Figure 2d).
claims.evidence: The column-wise 2r×2r linear system was verified to machine precision (max relative error 3.87e-16, 200 seeds) with a non-vacuous non-negativity condition confirmed via adversarial control, but the empirical claim that the condition holds in ~80% of LoRA layers across iterations (Figure 2d) was explicitly scoped out and never tested on real training dynamics.

claims.claim: On GLUE with DeBERTaV3-base at rank r=4, ScaLoRA achieves 88.98% average accuracy versus 88.13% for standard LoRA (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: No GLUE fine-tuning runs were attempted; the claim was scoped out as GPU work with only a build runbook prepared, so there is no experimental evidence supporting or refuting the 88.98% vs 88.13% accuracy figures.

claims.claim: On commonsense reasoning benchmarks (BoolQ, PIQA, SIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-e, ARC-c, OBQA) at rank r=8, ScaLoRA achieves 74.51% average accuracy on LLaMA2-7B versus 73.63% for LoRA, with additional evaluation extending to LLaMA3-8B and Gemma-3-12B-pt on MetaMathQA, GSM8K, and MATH (Table 2, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: No commonsense reasoning or math benchmark runs were attempted; the claim was scoped out as GPU work, so there is no experimental evidence for the 74.51% vs 73.63% figures or the LLaMA3-8B/Gemma-3-12B extensions.

RyeCatcher/repro-scalora-optimally-scale.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the two mathematical theorem claims (Claims 1 and 2's theorem content) to machine precision via independent numerical cross-checks on synthetic instances, including cost measurements and adversarial controls. However, the empirical 80%-of-layers sub-claim and both accuracy benchmark claims (GLUE/DeBERTaV3 and commonsense/LLaMA2-7B) were never attempted, leaving half the paper's claims without any experimental evidence.

RyeCatcher/repro-scdataset-scalable-data.paper_title: scDataset: Scalable Data Loading for Deep Learning on Large-Scale Single-Cell Omics

claims.claim: On the Tahoe-100M dataset, scDataset achieves a 48x single-core throughput speed-up over AnnLoader true random sampling at block size 64 and fetch factor 64 (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: On the full Tahoe-100M corpus (100.6M cells x 62,710 genes), n=3 seeds, single-core with block=64/fetch=64, the measured ratio was 45.1x ± 1.6 (scDataset 1670.2 samples/sec vs AnnLoader 37.0), within ~6% of the claimed 48x on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: scDataset achieves a 27x single-core speed-up over HuggingFace Datasets at block size 64 (Figure 3), and an 18x speed-up over BioNeMo at block size 64 (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states this claim was scoped out and not attempted; no experiments were run against HuggingFace Datasets or BioNeMo baselines.

claims.claim: In multiprocessing mode (block_size=4, fetch_factor=16, num_workers=12), scDataset reaches roughly 2,593 samples/sec versus AnnLoader's 20 samples/sec in single-core mode, a 129x speed-up (Table 2).
claims.evidence: On the full corpus with block=4, fetch=16, 12 workers, n=3 seeds, the measured ratio was 121x ± 1 (scDataset 4386 samples/sec vs AnnLoader single-core 36.4), within ~6% of the claimed 129x on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: Despite the large throughput gains from block-based fetching, scDataset's optimal multiprocessing configuration maintains a plate-label sampling entropy of 3.59 versus 3.63 for true random sampling, indicating near-equivalent sample diversity (Table 2, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Base-2 plate-label entropy measured over n=3 seeds was 3.592 ± 0.001 for scDataset vs 3.631 ± 0.010 for true-random (gap 0.039), closely matching the paper's 3.59 vs 3.63 (gap 0.04) on the full corpus with the C3 multiprocessing configuration.

RyeCatcher/repro-scdataset-scalable-data.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence on the full Tahoe-100M corpus supporting claims 1, 3, and 4 with n=3 seeds and pre-registered ratio/entropy tolerances, all landing within ~6% of claimed values. Claim 2 was not attempted and remains unaddressed.

jomasego/repro-autocontrol-arena-synthes.paper_title: AutoControl Arena: Synthesizing Executable Test Environments for Frontier AI Risk Evaluation

claims.claim: The automated monitor achieves an F1 score of 92.8% for judging action outcomes and 89.4% for judging chain-of-thought reasoning (Section 4.5).

claims.claim: Average risk rate across evaluated models rises from 21.7% under baseline conditions (no stress, no temptation) to 54.5% under high-stress, high-temptation conditions, a roughly 2.5x increase (Section 5.2, Figure 8).

claims.claim: In the Episodic Bandit Social Learning (EpiBSL) model with two-armed Bernoulli bandits and episode length m≥2, aggregate exploration fails with probability at least q_P^m > 0 for any symmetric utility aggregation function, even though each agent explores within its own episode (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Exact m=2 EpiBSL simulation with Beta priors (arm 1 prior-good) over 135 FAIL-geometry instances shows P[FAIL_{c,3}] = 0.88 (sum), 0.94 (max), 0.78 (min), all clearly positive for three symmetric aggregation functions.

claims.claim: When exploration failure occurs, Bayesian regret grows linearly in the time horizon T, satisfying BReg(T) ≥ c0(T − N0) for constants c0, N0 depending only on the prior (Corollary 4.5).
claims.evidence: The deterministic bound Reg(T) ≥ (T−#consider)·G(μ) holds in 100% of strong-failure runs (119/119 sum, 127/127 max, 106/106 min), and regret trajectories on failed runs grow linearly tracking the (T−N)·G line while successful runs stay sublinear.

claims.claim: For episode length m=2, learning failure occurs with positive probability even for non-symmetric per-episode utility aggregation functions, not just sum/min/max (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Two genuinely non-symmetric aggregation functions (asym_late with f(1,0)=0.4≠f(0,1)=1.0, and asym_early with f(1,0)=1.0≠f(0,1)=0.3) both show positive P[FAIL] of 0.87 and 0.95 over 149 instances at m=2.

claims.claim: For m=2 with symmetric utility functions, or for max/min aggregation at any episode length m, failure probability remains positive even without imposing exploration costs on agents (Theorem 4.7).
claims.evidence: At zero exploration cost (c_expl=0), P[FAIL] remains 0.95 (sum), 0.94 (max), 0.91 (min) at m=2, essentially unchanged from costly settings, confirming failure is driven by myopic objective rather than exploration penalty.

claims.claim: The stronger failure event StrongFail_{c,N} (at most N episodes ever try the good arm) occurs with probability at least 1/2 conditional on the base failure event FAIL_{c,N} (Lemma 3.4).
claims.evidence: Among runs satisfying FAIL, the fraction also satisfying StrongFail (at most N episodes considering arm 2) is 1.00 for all three aggregations, exceeding the Lemma 3.4 guarantee of ≥1/2.

claims.claim: The proposed online Newton method using a sketch-and-project solver with Nesterov's acceleration (Algorithm 1, NASketch) matches the O(d^2) per-iteration time and memory complexity of first-order methods (Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: Wall-clock timing across d=64–1024 shows NASketch scaling slope 1.92 and first-order 2.10 (both ~O(d²)), versus exact Newton slope 2.69 (~O(d³)), with NASketch at ~9ms vs Newton ~120ms at d=1024.

claims.claim: The last iterate is proven asymptotically normal, with the limiting covariance characterized by a Lyapunov equation incorporating the sketching operator (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: M=8000 independent chains at d=4, T=5000 show KS statistic ~0.008, near-zero skew/kurtosis, and Lyapunov covariance Frobenius relative error 0.109, supporting asymptotic normality with the sketching-dependent covariance.

claims.claim: A fully online covariance estimator achieves convergence rate E[||Sigma_hat_t - Sigma*||] = O(1/sqrt(t*phi_t)) without requiring matrix inversion (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: Inversion-free online estimator over M=500 chains shows monotone error decay from 0.47 to 0.17, with fitted exponent -0.973 in sqrt(t·phi_t), satisfying the O(1/sqrt(t·phi_t)) upper bound.

claims.claim: Global convergence guarantees for the sketch-and-project Newton iterates are established (Theorem 3.8, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: All 30 seeds from far initializations (||x_0-x*||~8.5) at d=8, T=5000 converge to mean final error 0.083, tracking the sqrt(phi_T) consistency neighborhood without divergence.

claims.claim: A spectral radius recursion derived via the Cayley-Hamilton theorem proves contraction at rate 1 - sqrt(mu_t/nu_t) for the accelerated sketching operator (Lemma 3.6).
claims.evidence: Cayley-Hamilton recursion verified to machine precision (residual 0e+00, power-error 4.33e-15) and sup_z rho(G(z)) = 0.9550 exactly equals 1-sqrt(mu/nu), strictly below unaccelerated 1-mu=0.9873.

claims.claim: The framework recovers exact Newton behavior and the unaccelerated sketching case (gamma=1) as special cases, clarifying computational-statistical trade-offs (Proposition 4.4).
claims.evidence: All special-case identities hold to machine precision: gamma=1 NASketch matches vanilla sketch-and-project (0e+00), full sketch S=I recovers exact Newton (2.84e-15), Sigma*=0.5·Omega* (2.52e-17), and unaccelerated covariance match (5.58e-16).
