claims.claim: Domain randomization consistently decreases the rational risk gap versus baseline DQN, and increasing environment shift magnitude (0%-70% action randomization) correlates positively with the rational risk gap, matching the extrinsic-gap prediction (Figure 2b, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Fresh 5-seed runs robustly confirm the shift-magnitude prediction: Pearson r(shift, gap)=0.949 (p=0.014) on Taxi and r=0.991 (p=0.001) on CliffWalking across 0%–70% action randomization, closely matching bundled logs. Domain randomization reduces the gap on CliffWalking (−27.4% fresh) but only ties on Taxi, so the 'consistently decreases' sub-claim is only partially supported.

alphaXiv/repro-rationality-measurement-a.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical verification of the three theoretical claims (Lemma 2, Theorem 1, Theorem 2) on Taxi-v3, and fresh independent runs strongly reproduce the extrinsic-gap/shift-magnitude correlation. However, the Rademacher complexity in Theorem 2 is only proxied, and the regularisation claim (Claim 4) does not reproduce consistently in fresh runs, with some regularizers increasing the gap.

rdubwiley/on-the-power-of-source-screeni.paper_title: On the Power of Source Screening for Learning Shared Feature Extractors

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows that training on an admissible subset of sources achieves the minimax-optimal statistical rate O(√(d/(Nλ_k))) for shared low-dimensional subspace estimation (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The synthetic experiment (claim1_rate.py) on the paper's Section 5.1 model (M=100, d=30, k=6) with 30 seeds per point and N swept from 40k to 1.28M shows the screened subset achieves slope -0.524 (R²=0.999) vs the minimax-predicted -0.5, using only 42% of sources at 1.09× full-population error.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 establishes that a 'good' admissible source subpopulation exists whenever a spectral-norm condition on the source covariates holds (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The experiment (claim2_cond.py) demonstrates the conditioning mechanism: full-population κ=11.3 is reduced to 4.29 (balanced) and 4.40 (empirical, no oracle), matching the oracle, and the pooled estimator's error is minimized by discarding majority sources (0.390→0.377), confirming the spectral/conditioning mechanism underlying Theorem 3's existence claim.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 (genie-aided) and Algorithm 2 (empirical) for identifying informative source subsets are proven to output admissible subsets with high probability (Theorem 5, Algorithm 1, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: The algorithms were exercised on the paper's exact synthetic setup and real ACSIncome: the empirical selector correctly identifies well-conditioned subsets (κ 11→4.4, matching oracle), but at the paper's literal default n_i∈[10,30] no method recovers the subspace (err≈0.99), and on ACSIncome all methods tie at 77.6% with no reproduced improvement over full-population (reported +0.6–1.4% edge absent).

claims.claim: On real-world evaluations, training with a screened source subset yields 74.2% classification accuracy on ACSIncome and 90.5% on CelebA smile classification (Table 2).
claims.evidence: ACSIncome was run with a simplified FedRep (top-k SVD of per-state logistic weights, no alternating minimization) yielding 77.6% for all methods including screened, not the reported 74.2%; CelebA was not run at all, so half the claim is untested and the tested half uses a different methodology producing different numbers.

claims.claim: Figure 1 shows subspace reconstruction error is lower when training on a balanced, screened subset of sources than on the full heterogeneous source population (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The primary reproduction (claim1_rate.py) with the minimax-optimal split-averaging estimator shows screened-subset error is consistently 1.09× higher than full-population error (e.g., 0.092 vs 0.079 at N≈1.3M), directly contradicting the claim that reconstruction error is lower for the screened subset; a secondary experiment with a different pooled estimator shows only a marginal 3% reduction.

rdubwiley/on-the-power-of-source-screeni.overall: The logbook provides strong synthetic evidence for the theoretical rate claims (Theorems 2–3) but fails to reproduce the practical accuracy improvements on real-world data: ACSIncome shows no screening benefit under a simplified methodology and CelebA is untested, while the Figure 1 claim of lower reconstruction error for screened subsets is contradicted by the primary experiment.

rdubwiley/flow-matching-calibration-for-.paper_title: Flow Matching Calibration for Simulation-Based Inference under Model Misspecification

claims.claim: FMCPE refines a simulation-trained posterior estimator using a small set of real calibration samples via two sequential flow-matching stages: a data-space transport map T_X coupling real observations to simulator-space counterparts, and a parameter-space transport map T_Θ moving a simulation-informed source distribution toward the true posterior (Section on method).
claims.evidence: The from-scratch implementation trains two conditional flow-matching vector fields (u_X in data-space, u_Th in parameter-space) on the paper's Gaussian task (3-param, 10-dim) using only calibration pairs and the simulator; results show C2ST dropping from 1.00 (misspecified NPE) to 0.61 and W2 from 3.32 to 0.20 at Ncal=1000, demonstrating the two-stage correction mechanism with real runs and numbers.

claims.claim: FMCPE is evaluated on two synthetic benchmarks (a 3-parameter/10-dimensional Gaussian task and a 2-parameter Pendulum task with friction-induced misspecification) and two real-world benchmarks (WindTunnel hatch-angle inference and LightTunnel RGB/polarizer-coefficient inference from 64x64x3 images) (Section on experiments).
claims.evidence: Only the Gaussian synthetic benchmark was implemented and run; the Pendulum task, WindTunnel, and LightTunnel benchmarks were not addressed at all, covering 1 of 4 claimed evaluation settings.

claims.claim: FMCPE is tested across calibration set sizes N_cal in {10, 50, 200, 1000} with expanding nested construction over 5 independent runs, and is compared against NPE and MFNPE baselines using jjC2ST, Wasserstein distance (W2), and MSE metrics (Section on experimental setup).
claims.evidence: Calibration sizes {10,50,200,1000} with nested construction were run, but only 3 independent sets (not 5), no MFNPE baseline was implemented, and metrics used (C2ST, W2, MMD, SBC-KS) do not match the claimed jjC2ST and MSE, so the experimental protocol is only partially reproduced.

claims.claim: In the Pendulum task, FMCPE correctly recovers the oscillation amplitude despite the omitted-friction misspecification, whereas NPE and MFNPE produce multimodal or biased posterior estimates even at N_cal=1000 (Section on Pendulum results).
claims.evidence: The Pendulum task was never implemented or run; no experiments address oscillation amplitude recovery or multimodal/biased posterior behavior for NPE or MFNPE.

claims.claim: FMCPE achieves lower MSE than baselines particularly at small calibration sample sizes and produces better-calibrated, unimodal posteriors compared to MFNPE's overly sharp estimates (Section on results).
claims.evidence: No MSE metric was computed, no MFNPE baseline was implemented, and no Pendulum or real-world tasks were run; the Gaussian results show monotonic improvement with calibration size but do not test the specific claims about MSE superiority or MFNPE's overly sharp estimates.

rdubwiley/flow-matching-calibration-for-.overall: The logbook provides a credible from-scratch reproduction of FMCPE's two-flow correction mechanism on the paper's Gaussian synthetic task, with real metrics showing substantial improvement over misspecified NPE. However, only 1 of 4 benchmarks, 1 of 2 baselines, and none of the claimed MSE/jjC2ST metrics were reproduced, leaving most experimental claims unaddressed.

rdubwiley/bridging-the-gap-between-avera.paper_title: Bridging the Gap Between Average and Discounted TD Learning

claims.claim: Under i.i.d. sampling in the double-chain formulation, the algorithm converges to a unique, sample-independent fixed point of the projected Bellman equation with sample complexity Õ(ε^-1 η^-2) (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The claim1 experiment verifies the fixed point exists and is unique (eta1 > 0, min 0.0075; residual ||Abar theta* + b|| <= 1.46e-17 across 100 MDPs), and the algorithm converges to it (100/100 within 5% relative error). The claim2 experiment uses i.i.d. sampling (Theorem 4.1's setting) and shows 25/25 runs converge within the Õ(ε^-1 η^-2) bound with eps-sweep slope 1.39 matching the predicted ~1.40.

claims.claim: Under Markovian sampling with constant stepsizes in the double-chain setting, the same Õ(ε^-1 η^-2) sample complexity is preserved (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: No experiment tests Markovian sampling with constant stepsizes (Theorem 4.2's specific setting). The claim1 experiment uses Markovian sampling but with decaying stepsizes (Theorem 4.3); the claim2 experiment uses i.i.d. sampling with constant stepsizes. The constant-stepsize Markovian case is never directly run.

claims.claim: With decaying stepsizes, the method attains convergence guarantees with no explicit dimension-dependent terms (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The claim1 experiment uses decaying stepsizes (Theorem 4.3) with Markovian sampling and shows convergence (median rel err 0.0134). The claim3 experiment shows T*eta1^2/G is flat across d=8..64 (values 8.77, 6.26, 6.46, 6.16; spread 1.42x) while raw T grows 74x, supporting no explicit dimension-dependent terms. Though these two aspects are tested in separate experiments, together they address the claim.

claims.claim: The paper reduces the condition-number dependence of average-reward TD learning from quartic (prior state of the art) to quadratic, matching the scaling known for discounted TD learning (Section 1, Table 1).
claims.evidence: The claim2 experiment shows all 25 MDP configurations converge within the quadratic bound T <= ln(2/eps)/(2*alpha*eta1) (max ratio 0.798), with empirical eta1-scaling slope -1.33 (consistent with quadratic, far from quartic's -4) and eps-scaling slope 1.39 matching theory. The prior quartic algorithm was not re-implemented, but the positive quadratic claim is directly supported.

claims.claim: A single-chain variant of the algorithm is also analyzed but only attains quartic sample complexity Õ(1/η^4 T) due to decorrelation requirements, contrasting with the double-chain method's quadratic rate (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: No experiment implements or tests the single-chain variant of the algorithm. Theorem 4.4's quartic sample complexity claim for the single-chain method is never addressed in any experiment.

claims.claim: The condition number η1, defined via min over unit vectors of ||Φx||²_Dir + (μᵀΦx)², is shown to satisfy η1 >= (1/2)η3 relative to prior condition-number definitions (Equation 3, Lemma B.3).
claims.evidence: No experiment computes or compares eta1 against eta3 (prior condition-number definitions). The inequality eta1 >= (1/2)eta3 from Lemma B.3 is never tested numerically.

rdubwiley/bridging-the-gap-between-avera.overall: The logbook provides solid experimental evidence for convergence to the unique projected Bellman fixed point (Claim 1), quadratic condition-number scaling (Claim 4), and dimension-independence of the bound (Claim 3), using 100 MDPs with proper analytical cross-checks. However, Theorem 4.2's Markovian constant-stepsize setting, the single-chain variant (Theorem 4.4), and the eta1/eta3 relationship (Lemma B.3) are never tested.

rdubwiley/hedging-on-the-frontier-learni.paper_title: Hedging on the Frontier: Learning New Tasks with Few Samples

claims.claim: Weak monotonicity is formally defined as a preorder on hypotheses such that if model f dominates f' across all benchmark risks, then f also achieves lower risk on the new target task (Section 2.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook correctly implements the dominance preorder and computes moduli on the real LMArena table (33 models × 4 tasks), but this tests empirical consequences of the definition on a proxy dataset (not HELM/VHELM) rather than verifying the formal mathematical properties of the preorder itself.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 derives the limiting distribution of the Pareto covering number as the threshold t approaches 0, showing the density depends on normal vectors to the Pareto frontier and implicitly induces a natural prior over trade-offs (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Theorem 1's limiting distribution of the Pareto covering number is never addressed — no mathematical verification or numerical check of the density or its dependence on normal vectors to the Pareto frontier appears in the logbook.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 gives excess-risk upper bounds for Pareto ERM and Pareto Exponential Weights of the form ω̄_Q(t) + sqrt(2 log(2 N_Par(t,𝓕,𝐑)/δ)/n), while Corollary 1 shows this recovers the O(sqrt(K/n)) worst-case rate of prior work with adaptive, geometry-dependent constants (Theorem 2, Corollary 1).
claims.evidence: The excess-risk bounds of Theorem 2 and the O(sqrt(K/n)) recovery of Corollary 1 are not verified; the transfer simulation measures empirical excess risk but does not check the specific upper-bound forms or convergence rates claimed.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 shows model-selection aggregation over the Pareto frontier can achieve fast O(log K / n) rates without requiring strongly convex losses, provided the frontier satisfies a strongly concave gap condition (Assumption 2, Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Theorem 4's fast O(log K / n) aggregation rates under the strongly concave gap condition (Assumption 2) are never addressed — no experiment tests model-selection aggregation or the gap condition.

claims.claim: On HELM and VHELM benchmark data, empirical moduli of monotonicity violation are near zero, supporting approximate weak monotonicity in practice, and the adaptive margin-ERM estimator substantially outperforms unrestricted ERM at small target sample sizes (Figure 3, Figure 6).
claims.evidence: The logbook tests on LMArena data (not the paper's HELM/VHELM), finds varpi_Q(0)=+0.078 and omega_Q(0)=-0.078 matching the sign pattern, but uses ERM-Pareto as a proxy for the unreleased adaptive margin-ERM algorithm with simulated Bernoulli losses, showing only marginal improvement (0.00445 vs 0.00482 at n=8).

rdubwiley/hedging-on-the-frontier-learni.overall: The logbook provides real computational evidence for approximate weak monotonicity and Pareto-pruning on the LMArena table, but addresses only the empirical claims (1 and 5) on a proxy dataset with proxy algorithms, and entirely omits verification of the four theoretical claims (Theorems 1, 2, 4 and Corollary 1).

rdubwiley/on-the-coordination-of-value-m.paper_title: On the Coordination of Value-Maximizing Bidders

claims.claim: Under Assumption 1 (the coalition's top two bidders remain competitive against outside bids), the coordination mechanism guarantees each bidder in the coalition achieves higher value and lower Return-on-Spend constraint violations than independent bidding, with probability at least 1 - exp(-Δ²T/32B²N²) (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Monte-Carlo estimates of Δ match closed forms to ~5e-5 (0.16662 vs 1/6, 0.02493 vs 1/40), and the per-bidder utility bound E[(U^C−U^I)/T] ≥ Δ/N held in all three tested configurations (e.g., N=4: 0.0498 vs 0.0417). The overbid-family sweep confirmed coordination weakly helps in 10/10 cases.

claims.claim: The coordination mechanism in Algorithm 2 has only the coalition's highest-value bidder submit positive bids while all other coalition members bid zero against outside bidders.
claims.evidence: The coordination mechanism (Algorithm 2) is implemented in bidding.py and used across all experiments; the code structure and all simulation results are consistent with only the highest-value coalition bidder submitting positive bids while others bid zero.

claims.claim: When coalition members run a mirror-descent bidding algorithm, coordination yields strictly higher total coalition value than independent bidding in the limit as the number of rounds T approaches infinity (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Mirror-descent experiments (claim2.py) across 6 synthetic settings with T up to 20000 show value_C > value_I in all 6/6 cases (e.g., N=4: 0.800 vs 0.773, N=2: 0.666 vs 0.644), supporting the claim that coordination yields strictly higher total coalition value at large T.

claims.claim: On the real-world iPinYou dataset with N=4 bidders over 20,000 rounds, coordinated bidding raises average per-bidder value from 0.614±0.016 (independent) to 0.929 and utility from -0.040 to 0.156±0.012 (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The actual iPinYou dataset was not used; a log-normal proxy pool was substituted. The proxy shows coordination improves value (0.317→0.337) and utility (0.001→0.120) for N=4, but magnitudes are far from reported (0.620→0.928, −0.040→0.156), with value gain ~6.5% vs reported 49.7%.

claims.claim: On synthetic i.i.d. settings, coordination improves utility by roughly 0.23-0.30 and total value by 2-4% relative to independent bidding across N=2 and N=4 bidder configurations (Table 1).
claims.evidence: All synthetic i.i.d. Table 1 rows reproduced with max abs error 0.0014: N=2 utility −0.011→0.221 (gain 0.232) and value 0.644→0.666 (+3.4%); N=4 utility −0.077→0.301 (gain 0.378) and value 0.773→0.800 (+3.5%), matching the claimed utility and value improvement ranges.

claims.claim: The theoretical results extend to non-i.i.d. value distributions across bidders, where coordination is shown to improve total coalition utility by ΔT/2 (Theorem 5.1 and 5.2).
claims.evidence: Non-i.i.d. settings (rows 1b, 4a, 4b in claim2.py) with heterogeneous bidder distributions show coordination improves total utility in all 3 cases (e.g., 4a: −0.014→0.258, 4b: −0.062→0.619), supporting the extension to non-i.i.d. distributions, though the specific ΔT/2 bound from Theorems 5.1/5.2 is not numerically isolated.

rdubwiley/on-the-coordination-of-value-m.overall: The logbook provides strong reproduction of the paper's theoretical bounds (Δ closed forms, utility improvement) and all six synthetic Table 1 rows with max error 0.0014, but the real-world iPinYou claim is only addressed via a disclosed log-normal proxy that reproduces direction but not magnitude.

rdubwiley/on-the-accuracy-of-newton-step.paper_title: On the Accuracy of Newton Step and Influence Function Data Attributions

claims.claim: Theorem 1.5 bounds the Newton-step approximation error to the true leave-one-out retrained parameter using only local strong convexity in a neighborhood of the Newton step, rather than the global strong convexity assumed in prior analyses (Theorem 1.5, Section 3).
claims.evidence: An indirect proxy on a single (n=10000, d=10, k=2) configuration shows the global strong-convexity constant λ_min collapses from 0.238 to 2.0e-5 as probe radius increases, while local NS error stays bounded — suggestive of the theorem's mechanism but not a direct verification of the proof claim, and at toy scale.

claims.claim: For logistic regression with n samples, d-dimensional Gaussian features, and k removed points, the average-case Newton-step attribution error scales as Õ(kd/n²), while the average-case influence-function error scales as Õ((k^{3/2}d^{1/2}+k^{1/2}d^{3/2})/n²) (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: A 15-point grid (d∈{5,10,20,40}, n=100d², k∈{1,2,4,8}, 30 trials each) measuring exact leave-T-out retrain error yields log-log slopes of 1.09 (R²=0.997) for NS error vs kd/n² and 1.01 (R²=0.996) for NS-IF gap vs (k+d)√(kd)/n², confirmed on a second independent seed (1.01/0.97, R²≥0.99).

claims.claim: The derived upper bounds match corresponding lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors, showing the Newton step is provably more accurate than influence functions whenever d ≫ k (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: Across 15 grid configurations with two independent seeds, NS error is strictly less than IF error at 15/15 points (averaging ~4.4x more accurate), with the gap growing with d/k as predicted; the empirical scaling exponents ~1 for both rates are consistent with tight (matching) bounds, though the lower-bound matching itself is a proof claim not directly testable.

claims.claim: Rescaled and doubly-rescaled influence functions (RIF and DRIF) are shown to match the Newton step's Õ(kd/n²) average-case error rate while preserving the additivity property that plain influence functions have but the Newton step lacks (Theorem 1.6, Theorem 1.7).
claims.evidence: No experiments involving rescaled influence functions (RIF) or doubly-rescaled influence functions (DRIF) appear anywhere in the logbook; these methods are never mentioned or tested.

claims.claim: The paper's revised bounds remove the problematic 1/λ³ dependence on the regularization coefficient λ present in prior influence-function error analyses (Section 1, Discussion of prior bounds).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides only the indirect Claim-1 toy proxy showing global λ_min decaying, which is suggestive that 1/λ³-type bounds become vacuous, but no direct experiment tests whether the paper's revised bounds remove this dependence.

rdubwiley/on-the-accuracy-of-newton-step.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification of the core scaling-law claims (Claims 2 and 3) through a well-designed 15-point grid with independent seeds, but does not address RIF/DRIF (Claim 4) or directly test the 1/λ³ removal (Claim 5), and only offers a toy-scale indirect proxy for the local-vs-global convexity theorem (Claim 1).

binzhango/repro-beyond-text-to-sql-squir.paper_title: Beyond Text-to-SQL: Can LLMs Really Debug Enterprise ETL SQL?

claims.claim: SQLBench (Squirrel) comprises 469 syntax-error tasks (Squirrel-Syntax) and 516 semantic-error tasks (Squirrel-Semantic), built from over 1,000 seed SQL scripts spanning 26 business scenarios, with scripts averaging over 140 lines, AST width >11, and AST depth >8.7 (Benchmark Construction section).
claims.evidence: The logbook only confirms that the paper text contains the strings '469 Squirrel-Syntax', '516 Squirrel-Semantic', and '1,000+ SQL scripts spanning 26 business scenarios' via a PDF text-extraction script. No benchmark data or construction code was available, so the counts and structural statistics were never independently recomputed.

claims.claim: Claude-4-Sonnet achieves only 36.46% Graph Match score on Squirrel-Syntax debugging and 32.17% on Squirrel-Semantic debugging, the best performance among evaluated models (Main Results table).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies that the paper's Table 2 and Section 5.1 text contain '36.46' and '32.17' for Claude-4-Sonnet, but no model was run on the actual benchmark (which was unavailable). This is a paper-text audit, not experimental evidence supporting the claimed scores.

claims.claim: DeepSeek-V3 scores 30.28% (Graph Match) on Squirrel-Syntax and 21.32% on Squirrel-Semantic, while Qwen-2.5-Coder-32B scores 23.45% on Squirrel-Semantic, with most evaluated LLMs failing to exceed 20% success rate on enterprise SQL debugging (Main Results table).
claims.evidence: The script confirms the paper text contains DeepSeek-V3 scores of 30.28/21.32 and Qwen-2.5-Coder-32B semantic score of 23.45, and audits the below-20 pattern from the paper's own table (10/24 syntax, 15/24 semantic). No models were independently evaluated on the real benchmark, so these are transcribed paper values, not reproduced results.

claims.claim: SQLBench scripts contain on the order of 420+ tokens and 17.34-21.62 functions per script on average, reflecting enterprise-scale ETL SQL complexity rather than the short queries used in prior Text-to-SQL benchmarks (Benchmark Statistics section).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirms the paper text reports 496.90/425.93 tokens and 21.62/17.34 functions, but the official scripts were unavailable for recomputation. The toy proxy uses different tokenization (lexical vs LLM) and different AST tooling (sqlglot vs Calcite), yielding incomparable statistics (1005 tokens, 58 functions), so it does not verify the claim.

binzhango/repro-beyond-text-to-sql-squir.overall: This logbook is a paper-text audit that confirms the manuscript contains the reported numbers, but it provides no independent experimental evidence: the official Squirrel benchmark, model predictions, and evaluator were all unavailable. The only GPU run was on 12 synthetic toy tasks with a 7B model, which does not address any of the four claims about the real benchmark.

rdubwiley/sharp-empirical-bernstein-ineq.paper_title: Sharp Empirical Bernstein Inequalities for the Variance of Bounded Random Variables

claims.claim: Under Assumption 1.1 (constant conditional mean mu and variance sigma^2 for X_t in [0,1], without independence or identical distribution), Theorem 4.1 constructs nonnegative supermartingales S_t+ and S_t- underlying a confidence sequence for the variance sigma^2 (Corollary 4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook constructs a genuinely non-i.i.d. Markov chain (X_t's two-point support depends on X_{t-1}) satisfying Assumption 1.1 exactly (constant conditional mean 0.5, variance 0.04), and the ported confidence sequences achieve 100% simultaneous coverage (2000/2000 trajectories, ~1000 steps each) vs the 95% nominal target, directly confirming the supermartingale-based CS validity under Assumption 1.1 without independence or identical distribution.

claims.claim: Corollaries 4.3 and 4.4 give upper and lower empirical Bernstein inequalities for the variance that hold without assuming independence or identical distribution (Section 4, Corollaries 4.3-4.4).
claims.evidence: The same non-i.i.d. Markov-chain experiment tests the upper and lower empirical Bernstein confidence sequences (Corollaries 4.3/4.4) and measures 100% simultaneous coverage of the true variance across all time steps over 2000 trajectories, confirming the inequalities hold without independence or identical distribution assumptions.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.8 shows that sqrt(n)(U_n - D_n) and sqrt(n)(L_n) converge almost surely to sqrt(2*Var[(X_i-mu)^2]*log(1/alpha)), matching the first-order term of the oracle Bernstein inequality under the additional constant-conditional-variance-of-squares Assumption 4.5, establishing asymptotic sharpness (Theorem 4.6, Theorem 4.7, Corollary 4.8).
claims.evidence: At the paper's full scale (100 experiments, n=100..4900, three distributions), the measured sqrt(n)*(U_n - D_n) ratios to the oracle first-order term are 1.24x (Uniform), 1.49x (Beta(2,6)), and 1.56x (Beta(5,5)) at n=4900, with a clear decreasing trend from ~3.5x at n=100, and EB widths are 79-82% narrower than the Maurer-Pontil baseline, supporting asymptotic sharpness and finite-sample improvement.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.10 extends the anytime-valid Bennett-type inequality to vector-valued random variables in a separable Hilbert space under a diameter-1 ball constraint (Assumption 4.9), with Corollary A.6 proving the same asymptotic sharpness result holds in this setting (Section 4.5, Appendix A, Theorem 4.10, Corollary A.6).
claims.evidence: The Hilbert-space extension is tested only in R^50 (a finite-dimensional separable Hilbert space), with 30 experiments and n up to 150,000; coverage is 100% and the sharpness ratio decreases to 1.25x at n=150,000, but no infinite-dimensional or function-space instance (e.g., L^2) was tested, making this a reduced-scope check of the 'any separable Hilbert space' claim.

rdubwiley/sharp-empirical-bernstein-ineq.overall: The logbook provides strong experimental evidence for the scalar claims: non-i.i.d. validity is confirmed via a carefully constructed dependent Markov chain with 100% coverage over 2000 trajectories, and asymptotic sharpness is supported at the paper's full scale with convergence trends matching Corollary 4.8. The Hilbert-space extension is only checked on a finite-dimensional R^50 proxy, which is a disclosed toy-scale simplification.

claims.claim: The diffusion sampler attains delta-error in polylog(1/delta) steps given sufficiently accurate score estimates, improving the dependence on accuracy over prior high-accuracy samplers (Theorem 4.3)
claims.evidence: Experiments use exact OU sampler on 2D/10D Gaussians with known exact score s(x)=-x, demonstrating exponential convergence of the OU process to N(0,I) — a basic property unrelated to the paper's diffusion sampler with score estimates. The polylog scaling (exponent p=0.033, R²=0.899) reflects trivial geometric convergence, not the paper's theorem about approximate score diffusion samplers.

claims.claim: Under minimal data assumptions, the diffusion sampling complexity is stated as Õ(d polylog(1/delta)), where d is the data dimension (Theorem 4.3)
claims.evidence: Dimension scaling experiment on OU/Gaussian targets shows slope log(T) vs log(d) = 0.976, but errors at d=8 and d=12 exceed the target delta (W2²=1.03e-3 and 2.10e-3 vs delta=0.001), and the second version's numerical demo shows identical step counts (22) across all dimensions, failing to demonstrate O(d) scaling. The logbook itself notes 'The numerical demo does not clearly show O(d) scaling.'

claims.claim: When the data distribution has intrinsic dimension d*, the complexity reduces to Õ(d* polylog(1/delta)) (Corollary 4.4)
claims.evidence: The von Mises Langevin experiment completely failed to converge (flat MSE ~6.53, slope=0.008, R²=0.423). The second version's experiment shows constant 22 steps regardless of d* or ambient dimension, which trivially passes a 'stability check' but does not demonstrate d*-dependent scaling. No valid numerical evidence supports the claim.

claims.claim: Under a non-uniform Lipschitz condition, the diffusion sampling complexity is refined to Õ(sqrt(dL) polylog(1/delta)) (Theorem 4.9)
claims.evidence: The first experiment's uniform-Lipschitz case does not converge at all (slope=0.027, R²=0.447, flat errors ~0.28), making the 'nonuniform converges faster' comparison meaningless. The second experiment's steps/||J||_F ratio varies from 67 to 1.07 across configurations, showing no constant scaling with sqrt(dL), and the verdict is hardcoded to True unconditionally.

claims.claim: The same framework yields a polylog(1/delta)-accuracy sampler for log-concave and more general isoperimetric distributions using first-order gradient queries (Section 5)
claims.evidence: Experiments use analytical OU/proximal sampler on N(0,I) — the most trivial log-concave target — showing geometric convergence (exponent p=0.052, R²=0.938). This demonstrates well-known exponential mixing for strongly log-concave distributions, not the paper's specific framework involving RGO/FORS for general isoperimetric distributions. No non-trivial log-concave or isoperimetric target is tested.

nkapila6/71132.overall: All experiments are toy proxies using exact scores on Gaussian targets, demonstrating basic OU/geometric convergence rather than the paper's theoretical contributions about diffusion samplers with approximate scores. Several experiments fail to converge or produce meaningless results (C3, C4), and none test non-trivial distributions, actual score estimation, or the paper's specific algorithms at meaningful scale.

Sor0ush/repro-variational-adapter-for-cr.paper_title: Variational Adapter for Cross-modal Similarity Representation

claims.claim: VACSR models cross-modal similarity in a latent space using a variational adapter with Gaussian mixture modeling over a Hadamard-product similarity vector (Section 3.1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Structural checks on B=8, d=64 tensors confirm Hadamard product shape, 2-component GMM, and ELBO instantiation, but no real data or task-scale evaluation was performed.

claims.claim: On domain generalization to ImageNet variants (V2, Sketch, A, R), VACSR attains 74.3% accuracy on ImageNet and a 61.6% average across the out-of-distribution variants, the best among compared prompt- and adapter-based methods (Table 4).
claims.evidence: HF job on STL10 16-shot proxy failed; no numerical results for ImageNet or OOD variants were produced.

claims.claim: On base-to-novel generalization averaged across 11 datasets, VACSR reaches 85.74% accuracy on base classes and an 80.37% harmonic mean score (Table 5).
claims.evidence: Food101 base/novel proxy script was prepared but never completed; no accuracy or harmonic mean numbers were generated.

claims.claim: The distributional optimization loss L_sigma (Section 3.2) assigns lower predicted uncertainty to positive and hard-negative pairs and higher uncertainty to false-negative pairs.
claims.evidence: On synthetic data, sigma(positive)=0.44 < sigma(false_negative)=0.57 supports one ordering, but sigma(hard_negative)=0.68 > sigma(false_negative)=0.57 contradicts the claim's hard-negative prediction; all on a synthetic proxy setup.

claims.claim: Uncertainty estimates from the variational adapter show a strong negative correlation with R@1 retrieval accuracy, with correlation coefficients of -0.931 and -0.903 (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: On a synthetic COCO-like retrieval proxy, image-to-text binned Pearson r=-0.834 (paper -0.931) shows trend, but text-to-image correlation is NaN due to constant input; not at paper scale.

claims.claim: An ablation removing the Gaussian mixture prior causes the largest performance drop among tested components, indicating that modeling multi-modal similarity distribution complexity is the key driver of VACSR's gains (Table 6).
claims.evidence: On synthetic features, removing GMM (K=2→K=1) drops avg R@1 from 0.031 to 0.016, but only two configurations were compared (not all Table 6 ablation components) and absolute performance is near-random on a proxy task.

Sor0ush/repro-variational-adapter-for-cr.overall: This logbook verifies VACSR's architectural instantiation at toy scale and shows partial mechanistic trends on synthetic data, but all headline benchmark claims (Tables 4–5) remain unaddressed due to failed or incomplete runs. No claim is verified at the paper's real task and scale.

jrcrittenden/repro-distributionally-robu.paper_title: Distributionally Robust Markov Games with Average Reward

claims.claim: Under the irreducibility assumption on induced Markov chains for all deterministic policies and transition kernels in a compact, convex uncertainty set (Assumption 4.1), a stationary Nash equilibrium is proven to exist for average-reward distributionally robust Markov games, via a Kakutani fixed-point argument over the best-response correspondence (Theorem 5.8).
claims.evidence: On 30 team games (4-8 states, 3 actions, KL ball θ=0.01) with irreducibility verified, a stationary NE was found on 100% of instances with max NE-gap 1.67e-10. Zero-sum games found approximate NEs on all instances (max gap 1.78e-2), with the residual attributed to the minimax oracle only approximately satisfying Assumption D.1.

claims.claim: The robust Bellman equation for the average-reward setting is shown to be solvable (Theorem 4.3), and the set of optimal robust policies is convex with the induced best-response correspondence upper semi-continuous (Theorems 5.6 and 5.7), which together underpin the equilibrium existence proof.
claims.evidence: Max Bellman residual 7.88e-11 over 40 random DR-MDPs confirms solvability; convexity confirmed with max deviation 6.66e-16 across policy mixtures on a degenerate DR-MDP; USC supported by BR-value max jump decreasing linearly with grid refinement (0.119→0.086→0.050→0.025 for steps 0.20→0.025).

claims.claim: The proposed Robust Nash-Iteration algorithm (Algorithm 1), a value-iteration scheme maintaining per-agent value estimates updated via matrix-form stage games, is proven to converge to a Nash equilibrium given an equilibrium-selection oracle that returns globally optimal or saddle-point equilibria (Theorem 6.1, Assumption D.1).
claims.evidence: Span seminorm converged to ~1e-10 in 13-27 iterations on all 6 instances (3 team, 3 zero-sum, 6 states each); team games returned exact NE (gap=0.00e+00), zero-sum games returned approximate NE (gap ~1e-2) consistent with oracle limitations.

claims.claim: As the discount factor approaches 1, discounted-reward Nash equilibria of the distributionally robust Markov game are shown to converge to average-reward Nash equilibria, linking the two reward criteria (Theorem 7.1).
claims.evidence: Average-reward NE-gap of discounted equilibria decreased monotonically from 0.146 at γ=0.5 to 5.2e-12 at γ=0.99 on a 20-state structured trap environment; Figure 1 reproduction across 6 environments showed discounted worst-case avg reward converging to the average-reward baseline (gap 0.263 at γ=0.1 → 8.5e-5 at γ=0.99).

jrcrittenden/repro-distributionally-robu.overall: The logbook provides constructive numerical evidence supporting all four theoretical claims at the paper's own tabular scale (4-20 states, KL uncertainty ball θ=0.01), with from-scratch implementations of robust value iteration, Algorithm 1, and discounted-to-average-reward comparison. The main limitation is that zero-sum game results are only approximate (~1e-2 NE-gap) due to the minimax oracle not exactly satisfying Assumption D.1 in the robust setting, and convexity/USC tests are on single constructed instances.

rdubwiley/fine-tuning-without-forgetting.paper_title: Fine-Tuning Without Forgetting In-Context Learning: A Theoretical Analysis of Linear Attention Models

claims.claim: Corollary 4.4 shows that full fine-tuning of all attention parameters in a linear attention model drives zero-shot error to σ² while few-shot (in-context) error converges to σ² + θᵀΣθ, a substantially larger value, formalizing the degradation of in-context learning after full fine-tuning (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Synthetic experiment at the paper's exact setup (d=5, σ²=0.1, Σ=I₅, ‖θ₀‖²=1, n=20) shows full fine-tuning drives zero-shot error to 0.1036 vs predicted 0.1 (3.6% relative), while few-shot error rises from pretrained 0.357 to 1.286 vs predicted 1.1 (+260% degradation), confirming both the asymptotic predictions and the qualitative ICL degradation claim.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 shows that restricting fine-tuning updates to the value matrix reduces zero-shot error to σ² + (2/(d+4))θ₀ᵀΣθ₀ while Corollary 4.8 shows the asymptotic few-shot error only rises to σ² + 1/(d+4)²θ₀ᵀΣθ₀, i.e. value-matrix-only fine-tuning improves zero-shot performance with far less degradation to in-context learning than full fine-tuning (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Value-only fine-tuning in the synthetic experiment yields zero-shot error 0.369 (vs predicted 0.322, correctly worse than full-FT's 0.104 but better than pretrained 1.43) while few-shot error stays at 0.346 vs pretrained 0.357 (-3.2%), an >80x smaller ICL degradation than full-FT's +260%, confirming the theorem's key differential ordering even though the absolute few-shot value (0.346 vs predicted 0.112) has a large residual due to the pretrained model's own few-shot floor sitting above the asymptotic baseline.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.10 proves that tuning the auxiliary few-shot loss weight w to optimize few-shot performance on the fine-tuning task θ₀ necessarily reduces few-shot performance on other tasks θ ≠ θ₀, formalizing a trade-off between target-task adaptation and generalization to unseen tasks (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: Aux-loss fine-tuning in the synthetic experiment improves target-task few-shot error from 0.357 to 0.210 (-41%), while OOD few-shot error rises monotonically from 0.210 (cos=1.0) to 1.971 (cos=-1.0) with Pearson r=-0.925 (R²=0.856); the pretrained control model stays flat (0.349–0.375) across the same sweep, confirming the anisotropic degradation is induced by fine-tuning.

claims.claim: In synthetic linear-regression experiments (d=5, σ²=0.1, Σ=I₅, ‖θ₀‖₂²=1, m=n=20), Figure 4 confirms the theoretical zero-shot/few-shot error predictions across pretraining, full fine-tuning, and value-matrix fine-tuning regimes, and Figure 5 shows value-matrix fine-tuning attains the lowest error on the out-of-distribution task -θ₀ (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: The synthetic experiments confirm the Figure 4 predictions across pretraining, full-FT, and value-FT regimes with concrete numbers, but the Figure 5 claim that value-matrix fine-tuning attains the lowest error on the OOD task -θ₀ is never directly tested—no value_ft evaluation on -θ₀ was run; the OOD sweep was only performed for the aux_loss mode.

claims.claim: On the MMLU benchmark using Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct fine-tuned on the Humanities category, full fine-tuning improves zero-shot accuracy but degrades 7-shot accuracy, whereas value-matrix-only fine-tuning preserves few-shot accuracy while still improving zero-shot performance (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: The MMLU experiment used Qwen2.5-0.5B (6x smaller than paper's 3B), LoRA proxy instead of full parameter updates, only 150 training examples, and n=100 eval; full-attention FT showed directional consistency (0-shot +11%, 5-shot -4.8%) but within binomial noise, while value-only FT showed zero-shot accuracy decreasing (0.45→0.42), contradicting the paper's prediction, all at a scale too small to confirm or refute the claim.

rdubwiley/fine-tuning-without-forgetting.overall: The logbook provides strong independent synthetic verification of the paper's three core theoretical claims (Claims 1-3) using the paper's exact linear-attention model and hyperparameters, with correctly-signed and correctly-ordered effects and reasonable numerical agreement to asymptotic predictions. The MMLU real-data experiment is a disclosed toy-scale attempt (0.5B model, 150 examples) that is underpowered and partially inconsistent, and the Figure 5 sub-claim of Claim 4 is never addressed.

rdubwiley/theoretical-investigation-on-i.paper_title: Theoretical Investigation on Inductive Bias of Isolation Forest

claims.claim: Isolation Forest's expected depth function is derived in closed form by modeling the iTree growth process as a random walk with transition probabilities based on point spacing (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements the actual iTree growth process (uniform random split, recurse to isolation) and grows 480,000 trees across 60 configurations (n=5..80, 3 distributions, 4 seeds), comparing empirical Monte-Carlo average depth against the closed-form h_bar from Theorem 3.5. Max relative residual is 0.954%, mean Pearson correlation is 0.99989, confirming the closed-form formula matches the stochastic process it is derived from.

claims.claim: For marginal single anomalies, Isolation Forest's detection threshold scales as U·κ (data-dependent), while k-NN requires separation greater than U+(k-1)δ/2 (parameter-dependent on k), showing iForest has greater parameter adaptability (Theorems 4.3-4.5).
claims.evidence: The logbook does not contain any experiment addressing marginal single anomalies or Theorems 4.3-4.5. The parameter-adaptability experiment (Test B) is conducted only for central anomalies (Theorems 4.6-4.7), not the marginal case.

claims.claim: For central single anomalies, Isolation Forest's decision threshold is Θ(√(n₀κ)) versus k-NN's Θ(kδ), demonstrating iForest's lower sensitivity to centrally-located anomalies (Theorems 4.6-4.7, Table 2).
claims.evidence: Test A sweeps n0 from 10 to 640 and measures detection thresholds using the paper's exact closed-form Theorem 4.6 criterion: iForest threshold grows from 32.9 to 188.4 with log-log slope 0.427 (predicted 0.5 for Θ(√(n₀κ))), while k-NN threshold (k=5) is flat at 13.72 across all n0 with slope ≈0 (predicted 0 for Θ(kδ)). The asymmetry is quantitatively confirmed.

claims.claim: For marginal clustered anomalies of size n₁, Isolation Forest requires separation of order Θ(n₁²κ) while k-NN requires Θ(kδ) under the constraint ω(n₁)≤k≤o(n₀) (Theorems 4.8-4.9).
claims.evidence: The logbook contains no experiment addressing marginal clustered anomalies or Theorems 4.8-4.9. No clustered-anomaly construction or n₁-sweep is tested.

claims.claim: Empirical mean-squared error between empirical and theoretical expected depths decreases as the number of trees increases, confirming the concentration property of Proposition 3.1 (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The claim3 experiment uses a fixed 8,000 trees per configuration and reports overall residuals, but does not sweep the number of trees to demonstrate that MSE between empirical and theoretical depths decreases with more trees. The concentration property of Proposition 3.1 is not directly tested.

claims.claim: Across OpenML benchmark datasets, 930,738 of 930,751 tested dimensions satisfy the condition κ≥√(n+3) required for the theoretical analysis (Section 4, Assumption 4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook does not mention OpenML datasets, Assumption 4.2, or the condition κ≥√(n+3). No benchmark dataset analysis is performed.

rdubwiley/theoretical-investigation-on-i.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical validation for the closed-form expected depth formula (Claim 1) and the central-anomaly threshold scaling comparison between iForest and k-NN (Claim 3), both via from-scratch implementations on the paper's own 1D synthetic constructions. However, four of the six claims—marginal single anomalies, marginal clustered anomalies, the concentration property (MSE vs. number of trees), and the OpenML benchmark condition—are not addressed at all.

nkapila6/BhahZSDowo.paper_title: Benchmarking at the Edge of Comprehension

claims.claim: Critique-Resilient Benchmarking evaluates answers by treating an answer as correct unless an adversarial critique is upheld under bounded verification (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Loaded 179 real decisions from 8 evaluation files showing the critique-resilient pattern: 53 answerer wins (critique rejected) and 110 critique upheld, confirming answers are accepted unless an adversarial critique is upheld.

claims.claim: The protocol admits generated questions through feasibility gating that rejects questions whose self-answer is successfully critiqued or whose question is ill-posed (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: Artifact audit found 2 ill-posed question rejections, 16 ill-posedness debate transcripts, and 1439 self-answer critiques out of 2230 total, confirming both gates (ill-posedness and self-answer survival) operate in the real data.

claims.claim: The ranking model jointly estimates answerer, questioner, and item effects with an itemized bipartite Bradley-Terry model (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: Itemized BT model was fit on 2672 real game outcomes with 8 answerer effects (beta), 8 questioner effects (alpha), and 384 item effects (delta) estimated jointly via MAP, converging in 3053 iterations with training accuracy 0.9641.

claims.claim: Answerer Elo scores correlate more strongly with external benchmark means than a baserate predictor in the reported Spearman and Kendall analyses (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Spearman correlations show Elo beating baserate for AIME (0.929 vs 0.927) and BRUMO (0.881 vs 0.830) but losing for HMMT (0.850 vs 0.908); Kendall analysis was not performed, so the claim is only partially addressed with mixed results.

claims.claim: Train-set scores predict unseen question outcomes better than a baserate predictor in pooled log-loss and Brier score metrics (Table 2).
claims.evidence: 5-fold cross-validation by question key shows model log-loss 0.122 < baserate 0.156 and Brier 0.032 < baserate 0.035, confirming the two metrics specified in the claim; however, accuracy ties at 0.964 and the reproduction used a simpler model without item effects.

nkapila6/BhahZSDowo.overall: The logbook provides concrete evidence supporting claims 1-3 and 5 through artifact audits and independent computations on real repository data, though claim 4 yields mixed results with one of three benchmarks contradicting the claim and Kendall analysis missing. The reproduction is limited to existing repo data without full regeneration of the evaluation pipeline.

nkapila6/7pQIzVNctu.paper_title: Rex: A Family of Reversible Exponential (Stochastic) Runge-Kutta Solvers

claims.claim: Rex converts explicit Runge-Kutta and stochastic Runge-Kutta schemes into algebraically reversible exponential solvers for diffusion ODEs and SDEs (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Clean-room Rex implementation tested on dx/dt=-x/2 (scalar linear decay) achieves 5.33e-15 reconstruction error, but this is a trivial ODE far from the diffusion ODE/SDE setting the claim addresses.

claims.claim: The ODE Rex construction inherits arbitrary order of convergence and a non-zero linear stability region from the base McCallum-Foster method (Theorem A.1).
claims.evidence: Rex(Heun) fitted order 2.12 and Rex(RK4) fitted order 4.13 on dy/dt=-y+sin(t), with non-empty stability regions confirmed via stability function scan; however, only scalar test ODEs were used, not the diffusion setting, and only two orders were tested rather than 'arbitrary' order.

claims.claim: Rex achieves near-machine-precision reconstruction under exact inversion in image-generation inversion experiments (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: No code is shown for claim3.py; execution time of 0.02s is implausible for SD 1.5 model loading and inference on GPU, suggesting a stub rather than a real experiment.

claims.claim: Rex improves or remains competitive on unconditional generation, text-conditioned generation, and image editing benchmarks versus prior reversible solvers (Figures 7-9).
claims.evidence: No code is shown for claim4.py; execution time of 0.01s is impossible for SD 1.5 generation/editing on GPU, and the LPIPS comparison appears sourced from the paper rather than independently computed.

claims.claim: Rex enables accurate likelihood-based Boltzmann sampling on tri-alanine with flow models (Table 1).
claims.evidence: No code is shown for claim5.py; execution time of 0.01s is implausible for loading a pre-trained TarFlow model and generating 10k samples; metrics are self-described proxies (ESS proxy=6.97 vs paper ESS=0.104) that do not match the paper's actual evaluation.

nkapila6/7pQIzVNctu.overall: The logbook provides real (but toy-scale) numerical evidence for the algebraic reversibility and convergence-order properties of Rex on simple scalar ODEs, but the GPU-based claims (3-5) lack visible code and have implausibly short execution times, making them untrustworthy as evidence.

arthrod/repro-mmbert-annealed-multilingu.paper_title: mmBERT: A Modern Multilingual Encoder with Annealed Language Learning

claims.claim: mmBERT is pretrained on 3 trillion tokens split across three phases: 2.3T tokens pre-training, 600B tokens mid-training for context extension, and 100B tokens in a decay phase (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Script reads released language_counts.csv and configs: mid-training 600.8B and decay 114.2B tokens match paper's 600B/100B; pretrain shows ~1.99T unique tokens vs 2.3T claimed, with the discrepancy plausibly explained as tokens-seen vs unique-tokens counting. Three-phase structure and context extension (1024→8192) confirmed from configs.

claims.claim: Cascading Annealed Language Learning expands language coverage across training phases from 60 to 110 to 1,833 languages, with temperature sampling decreasing from 0.7 to 0.5 to 0.3 (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Language counts from released CSV: 61→110→1834 languages matching 60→110→1833. Additionally, MLM NLL measured across three checkpoints on a 16-language panel shows three distinct arrival tiers (high-resource at pretrain, mid-tier at ext, low-resource at decay), behaviorally confirming the cascade. Temperature schedule 0.7/0.5/0.3 not encoded in configs and remains unverified.

claims.claim: An inverse mask ratio schedule lowers the masking rate from 30% in pre-training to 15% in mid-training to 5% in the decay phase (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Configs read directly: mmBERT-small mlm_probability = 0.30/0.15/0.05 (exact match to 30/15/5%); mmBERT-base = 0.25/0.15/0.05 (base pretrain is 25%, not 30%). Mid and decay rates match exactly for both sizes; inverse direction confirmed. Discrepancy at base pretrain noted.

claims.claim: On GLUE, mmBERT Base scores 86.3 average versus 83.3 for XLM-R Base, and mmBERT Small scores 84.7 versus 78.3 for Multilingual MiniLM (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Ran 5 of 8 GLUE tasks (excluded MNLI/QQP/QNLI) with reduced 2-LR sweep, 3 epochs, maxlen=128 on 1x L4. Relative ordering reproduces (mmBERT-base 82.9 > XLM-R 76.3; mmBERT-small 79.6 > mMiniLM 67.6) but absolute numbers are 3-9 pts below paper's full-8 averages due to subset and reduced sweep.

claims.claim: On XTREME, mmBERT Base averages 72.8 versus 70.4 for XLM-R, and on MTEB Multilingual, mmBERT Base averages 54.1 versus 52.4 for XLM-R (Table 3, Table 5).
claims.evidence: XNLI cross-lingual transfer used as proxy for XTREME classification: 200k English NLI examples, 1 epoch, 9 languages, yielding mmBERT-base 73.98 vs XLM-R 71.52 (delta +2.46 vs paper's +2.5 XNLI gap). MTEB Multilingual embedding half (54.1 vs 52.4) was not reproduced at all. Reduced scale and partial coverage.

claims.claim: Adding low-resource languages during the decay phase yields a 68% relative increase (12.1 absolute F1 points) on Tigray despite only 100B decay-phase tokens (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Actual TiQuAD F1 (68% relative / 12.1 absolute) not reproduced. Instead, same-model MLM NLL ablation across released checkpoints shows Tigrinya drops sharply only at decay-all (1.07 nats small, 1.35 base) while controls move <0.07, confirming the decay-phase acquisition mechanism. Proxy metric, not the claimed F1 number.

arthrod/repro-mmbert-annealed-multilingu.overall: Claims 1-3 are confirmed from released training artifacts (configs and token CSV) with minor discrepancies noted. Claims 4-6 are addressed via scaled-down proxy experiments that reproduce relative orderings and mechanisms but not the paper's absolute numbers or full task suites.

prarabdhmisra/pZNo1YWT5x.paper_title: Balancing Understanding and Generation in Discrete Diffusion Models

claims.claim: XDLM unifies masked and uniform-noise discrete diffusion through a stationary noise kernel that recovers MDLM and UDLM as limiting cases (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: claim_kernel.py verifies in float64 that K is idempotent (max|K²−K| ≤ 1.78e-15), converges to MDLM's kernel at k=0 and UDLM's at k=1 with residual exactly 0.00e+00 and first-order convergence (slope 1.000001, R²=1.0), and induced posteriors match MDLM Eq.16/UDLM Eq.18 to ≤4.44e-16 exhaustively over all states for V≤512 and up to V=126464, with a negative control showing non-stationary kernels fail the semigroup identity by 2.14e-02.

claims.claim: An algebraic scalar reformulation of posterior and KL terms reduces memory and computation for large-vocabulary XDLM training (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: claim_scalar.py proves three implementations (matrix/vector/scalar) agree to 3.82e-13 relative error, then measures peak temporary memory exponents of 1.985/1.000/−0.00002 matching the algebraic 2/1/0 expectation, with 151× less memory at GPT-2's V=50257 and 999× vs the matrix form at V=4096; the logbook honestly notes the compute saving is a constant factor (1–4.3×) against a competent vector implementation, not asymptotic.

claims.claim: XDLM surpasses UDLM by 5.4 points on averaged zero-shot language benchmarks after OpenWebText training (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Running the authors' released ppl_eval with the released xdlm_k01_owt checkpoint on all 7 zero-shot benchmarks yields average PPL 54.110, matching the paper's 54.110 exactly (max per-dataset |Δ|=0.008), giving +5.46 vs the paper's UDLM baseline of 59.574; the XDLM side is independently measured on a full-scale L4 GPU run.

claims.claim: In few-step conditional image generation, XDLM reduces FID from MDLM's 80.8 to 54.1 at 4 steps (Table 3).
claims.evidence: Generating 50,000 class-conditional ImageNet images at 4 steps with the released xdlm_k01_imagenet_cond_vq16k checkpoint and computing FID via torch_fidelity yields 55.52, within ~1.4 points of the paper's 54.09 (attributed to a different ungated reference set) and far below MDLM's reported 80.75.

claims.claim: When applied to an 8B LLaDA model, LLaDA-XDLM reaches 15.0 MBPP at 32 sampling steps, more than doubling the base LLaDA score (Table 16).
claims.evidence: Running the authors' released OpenCompass eval with the released Mzero17/LLaDA-XDLM 8B checkpoint on the full 500-problem MBPP test set at 32 steps yields a score of 14.80 (74/500 pass@1, 0 timeouts), matching the paper's 15.0 within 1.3% and approximately doubling the reported 6.8 baseline.

prarabdhmisra/pZNo1YWT5x.overall: All five claims are supported by concrete experimental or numerical evidence: two mathematical claims verified via exact float64 linear algebra with machine-precision residuals and negative controls, and three empirical claims verified via full-scale evaluation with the authors' released checkpoints on GPUs. The reproduction is notably rigorous, publishing raw logs and honestly reporting a sign typo in the paper's Eq.19/89 and an unstated support condition in Eq.13.

Sor0ush/repro-gauge-equivariant-graph-ne.paper_title: Gauge-Equivariant Graph Networks via Self-Interference Cancellation

claims.claim: GESC introduces a Self-Interference Cancellation (SIC) module (Eq. 11) that replaces additive message aggregation with a rank-1 projection removing self-parallel components before attention, combined with U(1) gauge-equivariant transport of complex node embeddings (Eq. 9) (Section 5, Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements the rank-1 SIC projection (Eq. 11-12) and U(1) gauge transport (Eq. 9) and numerically confirms their core mathematical properties: self-parallel energy reduced from 2.85 to ~4.6e-7, projector idempotence within 1e-7, norm preservation under U(1) transport within 5e-7, and a finite GESCLayer forward pass. These are scale-independent structural/mathematical properties directly matching the claimed equations.

claims.claim: GESC outperforms the strongest prior baseline on Cora (84.9% vs 84.6% for DirGNN), Citeseer (72.1% vs 71.7% for TFE-GNN), Chameleon (65.0% vs 60.2% for TFE-GNN), and Texas (74.5% vs 70.3% for CGNN), ranking first on 5 of 9 benchmark datasets (Table 1).
claims.evidence: GPU runs on only 4 of 9 datasets (5 seeds each) yielded Cora 82.82±0.64% (paper 84.9%), Citeseer 70.66±1.48% (paper 72.1%), Texas 71.35±7.94% (paper 74.5%), and Chameleon failed in 4/5 runs. Results are 1.5–3pp below paper claims, 5 of 9 datasets were not tested, and the 'first on 5 of 9' ranking claim cannot be assessed.

claims.claim: On large-scale heterophilous graphs, GESC reaches 82.4% on Penn94 (vs 81.8% for GCNII) and 48.2% on arXiv-year (vs 47.6% for H2GCN), while H2GCN runs out of memory on snap-patents where GESC still achieves 48.1% (Table 4, Appendix D.1).
claims.evidence: No experiments were executed. The script merely documents paper-reported numbers and states that Penn94, arxiv-year, and snap-patents are absent from the public GESC repository. There is zero experimental evidence for any of the claimed large-scale results.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.8 proves a strictly reduced Lipschitz bound along self-parallel directions for GESC compared to standard message passing, and Theorem 5.5 establishes full gauge-equivariance of attention scores and gating decisions under local phase transformations (Theorem 5.5, Theorem 5.8).
claims.evidence: Numerical checks on small synthetic inputs (n=12, d=32) confirm gauge invariance of attention scores and gates under local U(1) rephasing (max error <2.4e-6) and show SIC reduces operator gain along self-parallel directions from 1.0 to ~1e-6. These are toy-scale numerical sanity checks of theorem consequences, not formal proof verification or evaluation on real graph data.

claims.claim: At 12 stacked layers, GESC maintains substantially higher accuracy than GCN and GAT, which both degrade sharply on homophilic and heterophilic graphs, demonstrating mitigation of oversmoothing (Figure 4, Section 6.4).
claims.evidence: GESC showed a small drop (81.4%→79.1%, −2.3pp) from depth 2→12 on Cora, but the inline GCN baseline was broken (~14% at both depths) and explicitly deemed 'not comparable to paper.' The claim's core comparison—GESC substantially outperforming GCN and GAT at 12 layers—was never successfully made.

claims.claim: Ablating the gauge-equivariant transport component causes up to a 3.8% accuracy drop, the largest degradation among the four ablated components (SIC, residual gating, transport, complex representations) tested in Table 2 (Table 2).
claims.evidence: A quick-mode ablation on a single dataset (Cora, 60 epochs, 1 seed) showed w/o SIC −4.6%, w/o GET −2.8%, w/o RG −1.0%, which contradicts the paper's ranking (GET largest at −3.8%). The script initially crashed with a NameError. This is a reduced-scope run that addresses the claim but does not reproduce the paper's finding; the component ranking differs.

Sor0ush/repro-gauge-equivariant-graph-ne.overall: The logbook provides solid numerical verification of GESC's core architectural and theoretical properties (SIC projection, U(1) transport, gauge invariance, Lipschitz reduction) but fails to reproduce the paper's benchmark accuracy claims: only 4 of 9 Table 1 datasets were tested with results 1.5–3pp below paper, Table 4 large-scale datasets were never run, the oversmoothing comparison lacked a working baseline, and the ablation ranking contradicted the paper on a single quick run.

Sor0ush/repro-lift-trajectory-augmentati.paper_title: Trajectory-Level Data Augmentation for Offline Reinforcement Learning

claims.claim: LIFT (Logging Improvement via Fine-Tuned Trajectories) identifies 'shortcut' actions satisfying γV^π(s',W) − V^π(s,W) ≥ ||s' − s_W|| and uses them to augment offline RL trajectories (Section 3, Theorem 3.6).
claims.evidence: The shortcut definition γV^π(s',W)−V^π(s,W) ≥ ||s'−s_W|| was checked on 62 pairs from a simple 2D coordinate-walk environment with a hand-crafted policy (PositionOnly, identity distortion), finding 58/62 satisfy the criterion. This is a toy proxy for the paper's positioning tasks, not the real experimental setup.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.3 proves that for linear dynamics f(s,a,W) = s + W·a, accumulated actions always constitute valid shortcuts regardless of the value function's properties (Proposition 3.3).
claims.evidence: Numerical verification across d=2,3,5 confirms zero placement error for accumulated actions under linear dynamics f(s,a,W)=s+W·a (331/331 pairs exact). This is a correct but toy-scale numerical check of a mathematical proposition; it confirms the algebraic identity but is not a full experimental reproduction.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.6 gives sufficient conditions—distance-improving policies, Lipschitz-continuous value functions, and linear placement-error (LPE) distortion—under which shortcuts can be safely identified via the bound γ·V^π(s_j,W) − V^π(s_i,W) − ||s_j−s_W|| ≥ (γ·L_V+1)·L_f·Σ||a_k|| (Theorem 3.6).
claims.evidence: The Theorem 3.6 bound was tested on coordinate-walk trajectories, but the estimated L_f is 0.0 for both 'movement' and 'regional_rotation' distortions, making the RHS always zero and the bound trivially satisfied. The test does not exercise the theorem's meaningful conditions (nonzero L_f), and the logbook's own interpretation contradicts its data (regional_rotation_higher_Lf=false).

claims.claim: LIFT-SC (trained with shortcut augmentation) consistently outperforms baseline CQL across positioning tasks with dimensionality ranging from d=2 to d=5 under partial observability, using direct-position, optical-image, and sensor-based observations (Experiments section).
claims.evidence: Only d=2 and d=3 were tested (not d=4,5), only direct-position observations (not optical-image or sensor-based), with 15 episodes and 200 CQL steps in quick mode. Results show CQL-SC wins at d=2 (median 0.60 vs 0.71) but loses at d=3 (median 0.86 vs 0.71), partially contradicting the 'consistently outperforms' claim at reduced scale.

claims.claim: LIFT-SC outperforms a warm-start SAC baseline specifically in 5-dimensional scenarios, but its shortcut-identification guarantee fails when contraction properties are violated, as in the f_regrot distortion setting (Experiments section).
claims.evidence: At d=5 with 15 episodes and 200 steps, LIFT-SC ties SAC under movement distortion (both median 1.118) and beats SAC under regional_rotation (0.975 vs 1.107). The claim states the shortcut guarantee fails under f_regrot, but the results show LIFT-SC performing better there, contradicting the claim's narrative. Reduced scale and mixed results.

claims.claim: The augmentation method is implemented as a single-line integration into the d3rlpy library, allowing it to be added to existing offline RL algorithms (Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The Shortcuts class is shown to implement d3rlpy's TransitionPickerProtocol, integration via transition_picker=Shortcuts() is demonstrated, and a functional check confirms the picker produces augmented transitions (action norm 0.1 vs 0.025 plain) with d3rlpy v2.8.1. This is a concrete implementation verification of a software-engineering claim.

Sor0ush/repro-lift-trajectory-augmentati.overall: The logbook provides toy-scale numerical checks of the theoretical claims (shortcut definition, Proposition 3.3, Theorem 3.6) on simple coordinate-walk environments and a concrete verification of the d3rlpy integration pattern. The empirical claims about LIFT-SC outperforming CQL and SAC across dimensions and observation types are only tested at drastically reduced scale with mixed or contradictory results, falling short of reproducing the paper's experimental findings.

Sor0ush/repro-luve-icml2026.paper_title: LUVE : Latent-Cascaded Ultra-High-Resolution Video Generation with Dual Frequency Experts

claims.claim: LUVE generates ultra-high-resolution video through a three-stage pipeline: Low-resolution Motion Generation (LMG) using a Wan2.1-1.3B backbone, Video Latent Upsampling (VLU), and High-resolution Content Refinement (HCR) with dual frequency experts (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The script only checks that VLUer source files exist and that hardcoded stage definitions match the paper's naming/order; no pipeline is executed and LMG/HCR code is unreleased, making this a static structural audit rather than a functional reproduction.

claims.claim: The Video Latent Upsampler (VLUer), a lightweight ~22M-parameter network combining an encoder, implicit neural representation module, and decoder, performs arbitrary-resolution upsampling directly in latent space (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: The released VLUer model with official checkpoint loaded was instantiated and parameter count measured at 22.11M (matching ~22M); on an A10G GPU, arbitrary-scale forward passes at 1.5× and 2.0× produced correct output shapes ([1,6,16,96,96] and [1,6,16,128,128]).

claims.claim: Dual frequency experts apply a low-frequency LoRA expert on attention modules during the high-noise diffusion stage and a high-frequency LoRA expert on feed-forward networks during the low-noise stage, with a switching timestep t_switch = 0.417 (Section 3.4).
claims.evidence: A minimal proxy DiT block (dim=64, 4 heads) was hand-implemented to verify the switching schedule and gradient isolation mechanism with t_switch=0.417; this is not the actual Wan2.1 model and no real LoRA experts or training was run, so it is a mechanism proxy only.

claims.claim: LUVE-2K achieves a VBench average score of 84.34 and LUVE-4K achieves 84.03, with FID_patch scores of 41.03 and 39.87 respectively (Table cited in results).
claims.evidence: The script only verifies that the paper's reported VBench averages are arithmetically consistent with sub-scores and runs a toy FID on synthetic Gaussian clouds; no videos were generated, no VBench evaluation was run, and no real FID_patch was computed.

claims.claim: In a human preference study with 20 participants evaluating 60 generated videos, LUVE achieved 63.5% preference for overall video quality over competing methods (Table 4).
claims.evidence: The script only checks that Table 4 percentages sum to ~100% and that 63.5% matches the paper; no human study was conducted and no generated videos were evaluated.

claims.claim: 4K video generation with LUVE takes 91 minutes of inference time and requires 39.32 GiB of memory (Table 8).
claims.evidence: The script confirms paper Table 8 numbers match the claim (91 min, 39.32 GiB) but the full 4K pipeline was never run; the only measurement is a VLUer component probe (0.46s, 4.42 GiB on A10G) which is a tiny fraction of the full pipeline and not comparable to the claimed end-to-end figures.

Sor0ush/repro-luve-icml2026.overall: This logbook provides concrete verification only for Claim 2 (VLUer parameter count and arbitrary-resolution upsampling on GPU). Claims 1 and 3 are addressed via structural audits or proxy implementations at toy scale, while Claims 4–6 are blocked by unreleased LMG/HCR checkpoints and consist solely of arithmetic checks of paper-reported numbers with no independent experimental evidence.

Sor0ush/repro-vacsr-variational-adapter-.paper_title: Variational Adapter for Cross-modal Similarity Representation

claims.claim: VACSR models cross-modal similarity in a latent space using a variational adapter with Gaussian mixture modeling over a Hadamard-product similarity vector (Section 3.1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: A from-scratch VACSRAdapter implementation produces Hadamard similarity (8×8×512), 2-component GMM posterior with mixture weights summing to 1.0, and ELBO losses, confirming the architecture exists and functions — but only on 8 synthetic feature vectors, not a real cross-modal retrieval setup.

claims.claim: On domain generalization to ImageNet variants (V2, Sketch, A, R), VACSR attains 74.3% accuracy on ImageNet and a 61.6% average across the out-of-distribution variants, the best among compared prompt- and adapter-based methods (Table 4).
claims.evidence: Real ImageNet evaluation returned null (no data available); the synthetic proxy with 100 classes yields near-random accuracy (~2% in-distribution, ~1.5% OOD average), far from the paper's 74.3%/61.6% and too small to constitute a meaningful reproduction.

claims.claim: On base-to-novel generalization averaged across 11 datasets, VACSR reaches 85.74% accuracy on base classes and an 80.37% harmonic mean score (Table 5).
claims.evidence: A 20-class synthetic base-to-novel split produces 10% base/novel/harmonic accuracy (essentially random for 10 classes), nowhere near the paper's 85.74%/80.37%; the 11-dataset benchmark was never run.

claims.claim: The distributional optimization loss L_sigma (Section 3.2) assigns lower predicted uncertainty to positive and hard-negative pairs and higher uncertainty to false-negative pairs.
claims.evidence: The theoretical derivation confirms σ* = ||y−μ||² yields the expected ordering (positive 0.05 < hard-neg 0.15 < false-neg 0.75), but the trained adapter on 6 synthetic samples shows ordering_matches_paper=false (false-negative σ=0.535 < hard-negative σ=0.539), so the empirical claim is not confirmed even at toy scale.

claims.claim: Uncertainty estimates from the variational adapter show a strong negative correlation with R@1 retrieval accuracy, with correlation coefficients of -0.931 and -0.903 (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: On 64 synthetic pairs, I→T correlation is -1.0 but this is degenerate — all 10 bins have R@1=0.0, making the correlation meaningless; T→I shows -0.73 with only one non-zero bin. The negative trend direction is weakly suggested but the setup is too small and the correlations too artifact-driven to verify the claimed coefficients.

claims.claim: An ablation removing the Gaussian mixture prior causes the largest performance drop among tested components, indicating that modeling multi-modal similarity distribution complexity is the key driver of VACSR's gains (Table 6).
claims.evidence: On 16 synthetic pairs, removing GMM drops avg R@1 by 9.375pp (15.6%→6.3%) while removing KL or L_sigma shows zero drop, matching the paper's trend that GMM is the largest contributor — but absolute accuracies are near-random and the setup is far below the paper's scale.

Sor0ush/repro-vacsr-variational-adapter-.overall: This logbook implements VACSR from scratch and validates the architecture and some qualitative trends (GMM importance, uncertainty-R@1 direction, L_sigma theory) on synthetic toy setups with 8–100 samples, but none of the paper's real benchmarks (ImageNet variants, 11-dataset base-to-novel, COCO retrieval) were reproduced. All quantitative results are near-random on tiny proxies and do not constitute a faithful reproduction of any performance claim.

nkapila6/iPjuUQbkfl.paper_title: A Random Matrix Perspective on the Consistency of Diffusion Models

claims.claim: Diffusion models trained on non-overlapping dataset splits generate visually similar samples from the same seed, and the similarity is predicted by a Gaussian linear theory baseline (Figure 1)
claims.evidence: Tested on synthetic Gaussian data with linear denoisers at d=50, n=500 (not actual diffusion models). Per-probe R^2=0.856 captures qualitative pattern, but median relative MSE error is 31.3x, indicating poor quantitative agreement. The diffusion-model visual-similarity portion of the claim was never addressed.

claims.claim: Finite-sample covariance effects renormalize the effective noise scale in the expected linear denoiser, causing overshrinkage of low-variance directions (Figure 2)
claims.evidence: At d=40, n=80, gamma=0.5: kappa=0.579 > sigma^2=0.500 confirmed, kappa-corrected shrinkage RMSE improved 87.2% over naive, and low-mode overshrinkage empirical=-0.0405 matches theory=-0.0366 within 10%, directly demonstrating the Silverstein renormalization effect.

claims.claim: The denoiser-variance theory predicts anisotropic, location-dependent cross-split deviations that decay with dataset size (Result 4.2)
claims.evidence: At d=128, rank=32, n=[300..2400]: median theory/empirical variance relative error=13.3%, empirical scaling exponent n^-1.10 close to theoretical 1/N, and anisotropy ratio=1.68 across eigenmodes, confirming anisotropic location-dependent variance decay.

claims.claim: The sampling-map analysis gives deterministic-equivalence formulas for expectation and variance over full diffusion trajectories (Results 5.1 and 5.2)
claims.evidence: At d=30, n=600: trajectory mean R^2=0.862 is moderate, but variance prediction R^2=0.002 is essentially zero—variance formula completely fails. The logbook attributes this to numerical integration issues and finite-n effects, but no improved or larger-scale experiment was attempted to resolve the discrepancy.

claims.claim: UNet and DiT experiments validate the theory's predictions about consistency, overshrinkage, and eigenmode-dependent deviations in the non-memorization regime (Figure 5)
claims.evidence: No UNet/DiT training or image-data experiments were performed. Only a text audit of the paper was conducted, extracting reported numbers (Spearman r=0.33) without any independent experimental evidence.

nkapila6/iPjuUQbkfl.overall: The logbook provides genuine independent verification of the core RMT theoretical predictions for linear denoisers on synthetic Gaussian data (Claims 2-3), with reasonable quantitative agreement. Claims 1 and 4 suffer from poor quantitative agreement or failed variance predictions at small dimensions, and Claim 5 (UNet/DiT validation on real images) was never attempted.

alphaXiv/repro-disempowerment-patterns.paper_title: Who’s in Charge? Disempowerment Patterns in Real-World LLM Usage

claims.claim: The study analyzes 1.5 million consumer Claude.ai interactions collected between December 12-19, 2025, using the privacy-preserving Clio analysis tool (Section 4.1, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Only quote verification from paper.txt was performed (confirming 1,499,397, Dec 12-19 2025, Clio appear in the paper). No experimental runs or data access; the proprietary dataset cannot be independently confirmed to exist or match the described collection parameters.

claims.claim: Severe reality-distortion potential is identified in 0.076% of conversations, consistent with the abstract's claim that severe disempowerment potential occurs in fewer than one in a thousand conversations (Section 4.2, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook verified internal arithmetic (0.076% = 1 in ~1316 < 1 in 1000) and reproduced Wilson-score CIs from reported point estimates, but the actual 0.076% rate was never measured on real data. The toy pipeline (660 synthetic conversations, inflated to 6.67% severe RD) does not address the specific quantitative claim.

claims.claim: Severe vulnerability-related disempowerment patterns occur in approximately one in 300 interactions (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Quote verification confirmed 'one in three hundred' appears in the paper, and the VULN classifier achieved 79.2% within-one agreement on the 660-conversation toy corpus, but the ~1-in-300 rate itself was never measured on real data and the toy rate (14.4%) is deliberately inflated and non-comparable.

claims.claim: Disempowerment rates vary sharply by domain: Relationships & Lifestyle shows the highest rate at approximately 8%, Society & Culture and Healthcare & Wellness show approximately 5% each, while Software Development shows rates below 1% (Section 4.2, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The official Clio pipeline (screener + per-schema classifier using official prompts, Llama-3.3-70B backend substitute) was run on a 660-conversation synthetic corpus across 11 domains. The qualitative ordering partially reproduced: Software Development lowest (1.67%), Relationships & Lifestyle highest (33.33%), but absolute rates are inflated 3-5x and Society & Culture (23.33% vs ~5%) and Healthcare (15% vs ~5%) deviate substantially from paper values.

claims.claim: A longitudinal analysis of over 500,000 randomly sampled interactions from Q4 2024 to Q4 2025 tracks historical trends in disempowerment patterns (Section 4.5, Figure 13).
claims.evidence: Only quote verification was performed (confirming '500K randomly sampled' and 'Q4 2024 to Q4 2025' appear in the paper). No temporal or longitudinal analysis was attempted; the cross-sectional toy pipeline does not address historical trends at all.

alphaXiv/repro-disempowerment-patterns.overall: The logbook is transparent that the paper's core empirical claims rest on proprietary Anthropic data that is inaccessible, making full reproduction impossible. The reproduction attempt is limited to quote verification, Wilson-CI arithmetic checks, and a toy 660-conversation synthetic pipeline that qualitatively reproduces the domain ordering (Claim 4) but cannot verify any of the specific quantitative rates.

claims.claim: The diffusion sampler attains delta-error in polylog(1/delta) steps given sufficiently accurate score estimates, improving the dependence on accuracy over prior high-accuracy samplers (Theorem 4.3)
claims.evidence: The full diffusion sampler (Algorithm 2) was tested end-to-end on a 1D 3-component Gaussian mixture with K≤32: KL decays as a power law K^(-2.72) (R²=0.9987 for power vs 0.9417 for geometric), not polylog(1/δ), and the improvement over the prior DDPM sampler is polynomial (exponent 1.99 vs 2.72), not exponential.
