SabaPivot/repro-efficient-privacy-loss-a.paper_title: Efficient privacy loss accounting for subsampling and random allocation

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 gives a closed-form reduction of the privacy loss distribution (PLD) of k-out-of-t random allocation to t-wise convolutions of exponentiated PLD terms (Section 4, Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: Theorem 4.4's identity was verified by exact enumeration of all 3^t tuples for t=2..6: direct mixture-ratio PLD vs. the fixed-weight transformed PLD matched to TV < 1e-12, with a destructive control (omitting the 1/t normalization) producing errors > 0.69.

claims.claim: The proposed algorithm computes an (α,β)-accurate approximation of the random allocation PLD in time O(log³(t)·log(t/β)/α²), using exponentiation-by-squaring with geometric-grid rounding (Section 4, Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: Binary convolution counts satisfied the 2*ceil(log2(t)) bound for t up to 1e6, the sequential-to-binary ratio exceeded 30000, the α^-2 scaling proxy was confirmed to machine precision, and the actual PLD accountant at t=1000/10000 produced upper-lower gaps ≤ 2α confirming accuracy.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 introduces transformation rules φ_λ that apply Poisson subsampling directly to PLD realizations, allowing subsampling and random allocation to be composed within one unified PLD framework (Section 3, Theorem 3.3, Definition 3.1).
claims.evidence: Theorem 3.3's Poisson-mixture PLD transforms were verified by direct comparison of log(p_λ/q) vs. log(1-λ+λ·exp(base_loss)) for both add and remove directions across two distribution pairs and four λ values, with max error < 1e-12 and a destructive control failing (> 0.05).

claims.claim: Numerical experiments show the new random allocation privacy bounds are nearly identical to the Monte Carlo lower bounds of Chua et al. (2024a) and substantially tighter than RDP-based analytic bounds, for t ∈ {1000, 10000} and δ = 10⁻⁶ (Section 5, Figures 1-2).
claims.evidence: At t=1000 and t=10000 with δ=1e-6, the PLD upper-lower gaps were ≤ 2α (0.0032 and 0.00346 at α=0.005), confirming tightness; independently computed RDP via Google's dp-accounting was 2.65x–7.14x the PLD upper bound across all 6 cells. The specific Chua et al. MC lower-bound comparison was not directly reproduced (the MC diagnostic is explicitly labeled as a distributional diagnostic, not a rare-event tail estimator).

claims.claim: A toy Bernoulli mean-estimation experiment (n=10³, δ=10⁻¹⁰) shows random allocation requires strictly lower noise than Poisson subsampling for the same privacy level, demonstrating a genuine privacy (not just variance) advantage (Section 5, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: At n=1000, δ=1e-10, target ε=0.1, the allocation-to-Poisson sigma ratio was 0.98459 (< 1), confirming random allocation requires strictly lower noise; the Poisson participation count variance was > 0.99, distinguishing the privacy advantage from a variance artifact.

claims.claim: Applied to a DP-SGD scenario with block-sparse coordinate sampling (n=6×10⁵, d=2²⁰, C=2¹⁵, E=10 epochs), the PLD accounting method improves privacy bounds over RDP composition even under heavy composition (Section 5, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: PREAMBLE was run with exact constants (n=600000, d=2^20, C=2^15, E=10) for three block sizes; independently computed matched Poisson-RDP via dp-accounting confirmed PLD upper bounds are strictly tighter by 3.98%–5.25% across all three settings.

SabaPivot/repro-efficient-privacy-loss-a.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, exact-scale numerical verification of all six claims, including independent RDP comparators via Google's dp-accounting library, destructive controls for theorem identities, and predeclared acceptance gates (23/23 passed). The main gap is that the Chua et al. Monte Carlo lower-bound comparison for Claim 4 was not directly reproduced, though tightness was confirmed via upper-lower PLD gaps.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 proves the original DeepSets aggregation (Equation 4) is discontinuous in the natural any-dimensional topology because the infinite sum can diverge when the inner function ρ decays arbitrarily slowly, so standard DeepSets fails to be universal (Theorem 4.2, Section 4.1.1).
claims.evidence: Concrete numerical witness on the theorem's native object: x_i=1/i^2 in l_1 with rho=|t|^{1/2} shows input ||X^n-x||_1=1e-7 at n=1e7 while output S_n=H_n=16.695 grows logarithmically (slope 0.9975, R2=0.999992), with Cauchy-in/not-Cauchy-out ratio 2.56e6; Lipschitz-rho control converges to zeta(2) with error 1e-7.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.9 proves standard message-passing GNNs fail any-dimensional universality because their pointwise nonlinearities are discontinuous in the cut metric, since a pointwise map is continuous with respect to the cut norm only if it is linear (Theorem 4.9, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Exact cut norms for n<=12 and rigorous spectral/mean bounds for n up to 1600 show input ||F_n||_box decreasing 0.130->0.025 while phi=t^2 output stays >=0.240 and ReLU >=0.245 (not vanishing), with linear control 0.260->0.050 (vanishing), demonstrating the 'continuous iff linear' mechanism.

claims.claim: A modified DeepSets-infinity architecture (Equation 5) that reweights terms by an ell_p norm factor is proven continuous and universal on ell_p(R^k) sequence space (Theorem 4.2, Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The same input that diverged in Claim 1 now converges to zeta(2) with error 1e-7 at n=1e7; permutation invariance holds to 8.9e-15 over 1000 relabelings; continuity modulus ratio 0.455<=1 over 400 configs; dropping the reweight reverts to divergence. Note: full denseness/universality is proof-level and not numerically closed, but the key mechanisms (continuity, invariance, fix efficacy) are verified.

claims.claim: A measure-space variant DeepSets-bar-infinity (Equation 6), replacing the sum with a normalized integral under a growth condition, is proven universal on the Wasserstein space of probability measures (Theorem 4.5, Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: Kantorovich-Rubinstein bound |d int|/(Lip*W_1)=0.778<=1 over 2000 measure pairs with exact 1-D OT; growth-condition control with rho=x^2 shows W_1->1e-4 while integral stays 1.0 (discontinuity when condition fails); permutation invariance 4.2e-17. Note: full denseness is proof-level, not numerically closed.

claims.claim: A homomorphism-density-basis architecture (Equations 9-10) is proven continuous and universal on graphon space with the cut metric, restoring universality for graph architectures (Theorem 4.9, Theorem 4.10, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Counting lemma |dt|/d_box<=e(F) holds on all 250 graphon pairs across 4 motifs (tight ratio 1.000 for edge, 1.026 for triangle), decorated h3 Lipschitz 0.594; separation via triangle-gap 0.09375>0 between graphons with identical edge density; relabel invariance 0.0 exact. Note: full denseness is proof-level, not numerically closed.

claims.claim: A two-stage architecture combining a Gram-matrix map (Equation 12) with Invariant Graphon Networks (Equation 14) is proven universal on bounded point-cloud orbits under the group action (Theorem 4.12, Theorem 4.13, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Gram map O(k)-invariance 4.4e-16 over 500 configs; completeness verified via equal-Gram recovery of orthogonal T (|T'T-I|=1.8e-15) and shear-orbit separation 0.198; two-stage readout invariant to perm×O(k) at 6.4e-16 over 300 configs with distinct-orbit gap 0.0094. Note: full denseness is proof-level, not numerically closed.

ai-sherpa/any-dimensional-invariant-univ.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical witnesses of the mechanisms behind all six theorems on their native mathematical objects (l_p, graphon/cut-metric, Wasserstein, orbit spaces) with exact computation where feasible, rigorous bounds otherwise, and destructive controls for each claim. The two impossibility results are directly demonstrated as converging-input/diverging-output pairs, and the four constructive results verify the key driving properties (continuity, invariance, separation), though the full denseness/universality statements remain proof-level and are transparently acknowledged as not numerically closed.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-lower-bounds-for-fra.paper_title: Lower Bounds for Frank-Wolfe on Strongly Convex Sets

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a constructive Omega(1/sqrt(epsilon)) lower bound on the number of iterations for Frank-Wolfe with short steps or exact line search when both the objective and the constraint set are smooth and strongly convex (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: The corrected backward-reconstructed trajectory (20,000 steps, 19,880-digit mpmath precision) achieves loglog slope_f = -1.9996 (expected -2.0), slope_r = -0.9998 (expected -1.0), zero violations of the Theorem 6 bound r_t >= r0/(1+(4/3)r0*t) with min ratio 1.00005, and iterations-to-epsilon fitted slope of 0.546 (expected 0.5). The (r,s) scalar reduction is validated against raw 2-D FW dynamics with median relative difference 1.75e-9.

claims.claim: The lower-bound construction uses the specific instance of minimizing f(x) = ||x-p||_2^2 over the Euclidean unit ball B_1(0) with the unconstrained minimizer p on the boundary (||p||=1), showing this hard instance matches the known O(1/sqrt(epsilon)) upper bound of Garber et al. (2015) (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: The exact hard instance f(x)=||x-p||^2 over B_1(0) with p=[1,0] on the boundary is used throughout. The corrected trajectory's iterations-to-epsilon slope of 0.546 (expected 0.5) confirms the Omega(1/sqrt(eps)) rate, matching Garber & Hazan's O(1/sqrt(eps)) upper bound. Sample r_t values (e.g., t=1000: 7.5e-4, t=10000: 7.5e-5) are consistent with Theta(1/t) residual decay.

claims.claim: The lower bound is established via a 'backward reconstruction' technique that builds worst-case trajectories by working backward from terminal iterates, producing precise sequences over horizons of 10,000+ iterations (Section on Backward Reconstruction Strategy).
claims.evidence: Only 8.5% (17/200) of random forward-simulated FW trajectories match the worst-case Theta(1/t^2) rate, with median slope -2.47 and many trajectories in the -5 to -18 range, demonstrating that generic forward simulation does not reproduce the worst case. The corrected backward-reconstructed trajectory achieves residual slope -0.9998 over 20,000 steps with zero bound violations and no detected manifold jump, confirming backward reconstruction certifies the worst-case rate over 10,000+ iterations.

claims.claim: The analysis reduces the dynamics to a two-dimensional invariant subspace parametrized by residual magnitude r and contraction factor s, revealing stable phases of monotonically increasing contraction followed by intermittent 'jumps' that explain the convergence stalling behavior (Section on Dynamical Analysis).
claims.evidence: The 2-D invariant subspace reduction is verified to float64 precision: max relative out-of-plane norm is 1.35e-16 across ambient dimensions n in {2,3,5,10,30}. The phase structure is clearly non-trivial: 100% of 300 random-start trajectories exhibit at least one contraction-weakening jump, and the worked example trace shows stable phases of increasing s_t (e.g., 0.82→0.99 over steps 12-20) punctuated by sharp drops (e.g., s=0.358 at step 11, s=0.688 at step 21).

claims.claim: The result shows strong convexity of the constraint set alone cannot yield convergence rates uniformly faster than O(1/sqrt(epsilon)), and this conclusion holds dimension-independently and extends to ellipsoidal constraints via affine invariance (Theorem 6, Implications).
claims.evidence: Dimension independence is exact: max abs objective difference across dims {2,5,10,50} is 0.0 (bit-identical). Ellipsoid affine invariance is verified across 5 cases (dims {2,3,5}, condition numbers 1.1-4.2): max trajectory difference between pushforward and independently-implemented raw ellipsoid FW is 1.7e-3, max objective difference is 2.6e-6, confirming the ball's hard instance transports exactly to ellipsoidal constraints.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-lower-bounds-for-fra.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all five claims. The corrected backward-reconstructed worst-case trajectory (Claims 1-3) achieves the expected Theta(1/t) residual / Theta(1/t^2) objective rate over 20,000 iterations with zero Theorem 6 bound violations, while the dynamical-systems picture (Claims 4-5) — 2-D invariant subspace, phase/jump structure, dimension independence, and ellipsoid affine invariance — reproduces cleanly and robustly.

SaiPavankumar22/repro-ski-rental-with-di.paper_title: Ski Rental with Distributional Predictions of Unknown Quality

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows the algorithm achieves expected additive loss O(min(√b·max(EMD(p̂,p),1), b log b)), where EMD(p̂,p) is the Earth Mover's distance between the predicted and true distributions and b is the buy-ski-rental cost ratio (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 is implemented and tested across b=4–400 with multiple EMD levels, but the measured losses are suspiciously invariant to EMD (e.g., b=4 always gives 1.6298 regardless of EMD=0,1,2,3,4), and the comparison uses a very loose constant factor of 10× the theoretical bound, making it a simplified sanity check rather than a rigorous verification of the O(min(√b·max(EMD,1), b log b)) scaling.

claims.claim: The algorithm attains consistency O(√b) when the prediction error (EMD) is 0 and robustness O(b log b) when the prediction is arbitrarily inaccurate, without needing to know the prediction error bound in advance (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Consistency and robustness are tested with EMD=0 and a point-mass bad prediction, but the robustness losses (e.g., 20.11 for b=400) are orders of magnitude below the 20·b·log(b) bound (47932), suggesting the test distributions are not adversarial enough to actually exercise the O(b log b) regime, and the bounds used are extremely loose.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 proves a matching lower bound showing no algorithm can achieve additive loss o(b)·EMD(p̂,p), establishing that the √b factor in Theorem 1 is necessary (Theorem 4, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: The two distributions from the proof of Theorem 4 are constructed and the ratio loss/(b·EMD) is shown to be ≥0.25 (converging to 0.5) across b=25–400, providing numerical evidence for the specific lower-bound construction, but this only checks the particular adversarial instance from the proof rather than establishing the general lower bound.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a Pareto-optimal consistency-robustness tradeoff: any algorithm achieving O(√b) consistency must incur Ω(b log b) robustness (Theorem 6, Section 4)
claims.evidence: The minimum consistent B is computed and shown to exceed the derived lower bound from the proof across b=25–400, but the 'robustness_loss' field simply equals min_consistent_B rather than measuring actual algorithm robustness against adversarial inputs, making the verification of the Ω(b log b) robustness claim circular.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 introduces a parameterized algorithm with expected cost c(ALG_p) ≤ min{(1+λ)(c(OPT_p)+B), (1+1/λ)c(OPT_p)}, allowing explicit interpolation between trusting the prediction and worst-case guarantees via λ ∈ [0,1] (Theorem 2, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Algorithm 2 is implemented and tested across λ∈{0,0.1,0.25,0.5,0.75,1} and multiple EMD levels with b up to 400, with all 168 combinations showing ALG cost below the Theorem 2 bound, but the ALG costs don't vary with EMD (e.g., b=100 always gives 109.5 for λ=0 regardless of EMD=0,5,10,20), suggesting the test distributions don't properly exercise the prediction-error sensitivity of the bound.

SaiPavankumar22/repro-ski-rental-with-di.overall: The logbook implements Algorithms 1 and 2 from scratch and runs numerical experiments across reasonable b values (4–400) and EMD levels, providing sanity-check-level evidence that the theoretical bounds hold. However, the very loose constant factors (10–20×), suspiciously EMD-invariant losses, and non-adversarial test distributions mean these are simplified numerical checks rather than rigorous verifications of the asymptotic theoretical claims.

Boopster/repro-flat-minima-and-generaliz.paper_title: Flat Minima and Generalization: Insights from Stochastic Convex Optimization

claims.claim: In non-negative, beta-smooth stochastic convex optimization under a strong flatness condition, flat empirical minima can incur population risk of Omega(1) while sharp minima in the same setting generalize optimally (Theorem 1, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook constructs 101 finite witness instances of the paper's loss function showing flat minima with non-zero population risk (up to 0.191) and sharp minima with zero population risk, but at small finite dimensions with population risk far below Omega(1) — verifying the mechanism but not the asymptotic claim at scale.

claims.claim: SA-GD converges to a flat (rho-flat) empirical minimum at rate O(1/eta T) on the empirical risk, but its population risk lower bound is Omega(eta^2 (r-rho)^2 T), showing fast flat-minimum convergence does not guarantee generalization (Theorem 2 and Theorem 3, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: 70,930 rows verify SA-GD reaches zero empirical risk with non-zero population risk (0.006–0.035) and a population lower certificate (0.00067), and the r-equals-rho condition correctly yields zero population risk, but the finite dimensions and small risk values confirm the construction's mechanism without demonstrating the asymptotic Omega(eta^2 (r-rho)^2 T) scaling.

claims.claim: SAM achieves the same empirical convergence rate as SA-GD, O(1/eta T + beta max{r-rho,0}^2), yet can converge to a sharp (non-flat) minimizer even when rho-flat minimizers exist, exhibiting a sharpness-empirical-risk gap of Omega(r^2) (Theorem 4 and Theorem 5, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: 3,485 rows show SAM converging to sharp minimizers (saer_gap up to 0.125) with non-zero population risk lower bounds (up to 0.00236) and a symbolic stability audit with 5 rows checking stability bound components, but at very small scale (T=8) and with population risk values far below the Omega(r^2) gap claimed asymptotically.

claims.claim: Under realizability (rho=0), SAM's population risk has a lower bound of Omega(eta^2 r^2 T), matching stability-based upper bounds established via algorithmic stability (Theorem 6 and Theorem 8, Appendix A).
claims.evidence: The logbook tracks only 3 claims and does not separately address Theorem 6/8 under realizability (rho=0); the 'r-zero' condition in the SAM population arm shows all-zero population risk (consistent with r=0, not rho=0), and the 5-row symbolic stability audit checks bound components but does not demonstrate the matching Omega(eta^2 r^2 T) lower bound under realizability.

Boopster/repro-flat-minima-and-generaliz.overall: The logbook provides a methodologically rigorous but small-scale finite numerical verification of the paper's theoretical constructions for Claims 1–3, using exact NumPy constructions with dual-implementation checks and independent recomputation. However, all verifications use small finite dimensions that confirm the mechanisms work without demonstrating the asymptotic Omega(1) or Omega(r^2) scaling the theorems claim, and Claim 4 is not clearly addressed.

rdubwiley/positive-distribution-shift-as.paper_title: Positive Distribution Shift as a Framework for Understanding Tractable Learning

claims.claim: Noisy parities are D-DS-PAC learnable by an explicit efficient algorithm using m(epsilon) = O(d^2 log^2(d)/epsilon / (1-2eta)^2) samples, despite being conjectured computationally hard under the standard PAC model (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Theorem 4.3's explicit efficient algorithm and its specific sample complexity bound m(epsilon) = O(d^2 log^2(d)/epsilon / (1-2eta)^2) are never implemented or tested. The logbook only runs SGD training (relevant to Theorem 4.5), and the noisy parity case (eta=0.05) is tested only at reduced scale (d=30, k=15), not the full d=50.

claims.claim: Noisy parities are also D-DS-PAC learnable using a stylized layerwise SGD procedure on a 2-layer neural network with L1 regularization and sparsity-dependent initialization (Theorem 4.5).
claims.evidence: Full-scale SGD (d=50, k=25, H=1024) learns parity under PDS to 0.0155 error vs 0.489 uniform, demonstrating the core phenomenon. However, the claim specifies L1 regularization, sparsity-dependent initialization, and layerwise training — none of which are implemented — and the noisy case (eta>0) is only tested at reduced scale (d=30, k=15, eta=0.05).

claims.claim: Noisy k-juntas are D-DS-PAC learnable via a Correlational Statistical Query algorithm using O(d^k + 2^k) queries, and are R-DS-PAC learnable via stylized layerwise SGD with a covariance loss using m = O~(d log(1/epsilon) / epsilon^2) samples (Theorems 4.6 and 4.8).
claims.evidence: The k-junta is learned at full scale (d=50, k=9) under PDS (0.0105 error vs 0.509 uniform), demonstrating the phenomenon. But neither the CSQ algorithm with O(d^k + 2^k) queries nor the stylized layerwise SGD with covariance loss from Theorems 4.6/4.8 is implemented; plain joint SGD with square loss is used instead, and no label noise is tested.

claims.claim: Any polynomial-size circuit with label noise is universally f-PDS learnable by SGD on specially constructed networks with polynomial sample complexity and runtime, though this construction requires designing the training distribution around the target function (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: No experiments address universal f-PDS learnability of polynomial-size circuits, specially constructed networks, or the construction of training distributions around target functions. The claim is never engaged with.

claims.claim: The paper establishes a hierarchy of learnability notions showing D-DS-PAC learning implies non-adaptive membership query (NA-MQ) learning, and NA-MQ learners can be converted into R-DS-PAC learners with sample complexity m(epsilon) = O(m0(epsilon/2) * (log m0(epsilon/2) + log(1/epsilon))) (Theorems 5.2 and 5.3).
claims.evidence: No experiments or proofs address the learnability hierarchy (D-DS-PAC → NA-MQ → R-DS-PAC) or the specific sample complexity conversion factor from Theorems 5.2 and 5.3. The claim is never engaged with.

claims.claim: The benefit of positive distribution shift for tractable learning is argued to be primarily computational rather than statistical, since PDS can enable polynomial-time algorithms without reducing information-theoretic sample complexity (Section 4, Abstract).
claims.evidence: Direct evidence at full scale: GF(2) Gaussian elimination recovers parity support from m≈1.1d uniform samples (28/36/43/56/64 at d=20/30/40/50/60), showing linear statistical complexity, while the degree-1 gradient signal under uniform is 0.00018≈0 (vs 0.01044 under PDS) and SGD under uniform stays at 0.489 test error. This concretely demonstrates the computational-vs-statistical separation the claim asserts.

rdubwiley/positive-distribution-shift-as.overall: The logbook provides strong experimental evidence for the core PDS mechanism (degree-1 signal creation) and the computational-vs-statistical separation at full scale, but only addresses the parity/junta learning phenomena with simplified SGD rather than the specific algorithms claimed in Theorems 4.3, 4.5, 4.6, and 4.8. Claims 4 and 5 (universal f-PDS learnability and the learnability hierarchy) are not addressed at all.

rdubwiley/understanding-generalization-a.paper_title: Understanding Generalization and Forgetting in In-Context Continual Learning

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 decomposes the task-t prediction error into an irreducible error term, a variance term scaling as O(M/(t^2(M+1)^2)) that decreases with more in-context examples, and a bias term measuring deviation ‖(1/t)∑_s w_s - w_t‖^2 from task dissimilarity (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements Theorem 4.3's closed-form predictor with the simplification Gamma=Lambda=I_d on synthetic d=20 linear regression. Single-task MSE shrinks from 447 to 0.086 as M grows (consistent with variance decay) while multi-task MSE plateaus at 80.02 matching a closed-form floor of 79.70 (0.40% residual), but the specific three-term decomposition and the exact O(M/(t^2(M+1)^2)) scaling are not explicitly isolated or verified.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 shows that forgetting arises from attention reweighting past tasks with negative coefficients c_t and future tasks with positive coefficients d, rather than from actual information loss, comprising intra-task variance and inter-task mean-interaction terms (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: The order-sensitivity experiment (120 permutations) shows forgetting of a fixed task ranges from 1.21 to 6.5e-5 depending on sequence position, consistent with attention reweighting rather than information loss. However, the specific claim about negative coefficients c_t and positive coefficients d is not directly measured; only the consequences (order-dependence, interference floors) are demonstrated on the simplified synthetic setup.

claims.claim: The theory predicts non-monotonic error curves with context length M, where longer prompts reduce variance but amplify systematic bias from misaligned historical tasks, producing a clear performance peak at intermediate M (Section 4, theoretical analysis).
claims.evidence: The claim predicts non-monotonic error curves with a clear performance peak at intermediate M, but the logbook's M-sweep data (Claim 1) shows monotonically decreasing MSE for both single-task and multi-task settings with no peak visible. The specific scenario that would produce non-monotonicity (a mix of aligned and misaligned tasks in context, varied over M) was not tested.

claims.claim: Mean-misalignment interference persists regardless of context length, while variance-induced interference decays as O(1/M), implying a persistent asymptotic forgetting floor (Section 4, theoretical analysis).
claims.evidence: The M-sweep clearly shows single-task MSE decaying toward 0 (0.086 at M=5000) while multi-task MSE plateaus at ~80 and masked-last-task MSE plateaus at ~16, demonstrating a persistent asymptotic forgetting floor. The Claim 3 Part B experiment also shows forgetting saturating at 33-37 for T in [8,30] rather than vanishing. This is consistent with the claim but on the simplified Gamma=I_d synthetic setup.

claims.claim: Experiments on GPT-2 architectures confirm the predicted non-monotonic error curves and reproduce catastrophic forgetting with a 46% accuracy drop on real LLM tasks (Section 5, experimental validation).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states the GPT-2 experiments 'require GPU pretraining we did not attempt.' No neural network experiments were run; the 46% accuracy drop on real LLM tasks is never addressed.

rdubwiley/understanding-generalization-a.overall: The logbook faithfully implements the paper's closed-form linear self-attention formulas and runs large-scale Monte Carlo simulations that support the theoretical predictions about interference floors and order-dependent forgetting on synthetic data, but it does not test the predicted non-monotonic error-vs-M curves and entirely skips the GPT-2 experimental validation that constitutes Claim 5.

neonforestmist/magnitude-distance-repro.paper_title: Magnitude Distance: A Geometric Measure of Dataset Similarity

claims.claim: Magnitude distance is defined as d_Mag^t(X,Y) = 2·Mag_{X∪Y}(t) − Mag_X(t) − Mag_Y(t), with a tunable scale parameter t that governs sensitivity to global structure (small t) versus finer local structure (large t) (Section on Definition, Magnitude Distance).
claims.evidence: The definition page confirms the formula d_Mag^t(X,Y) = 2·Mag_{X∪Y}(t) − Mag_X(t) − Mag_Y(t) is implemented with K_ij=exp(-t||x_i-x_j||), Cholesky solving, and conditioning checks. The tunability of t is demonstrated by the global-vs-fine control: fine/global sensitivity ratio rises from 0.2136 at t=0.02 to 0.9865 at t=20 across 16 seeds, a 4.62x change.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 shows magnitude distance is symmetric and non-negative, satisfies identity of indiscernibles only up to magnitude equivalence, and does not satisfy the triangle inequality in R^D for D>1 (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Across 20 random pairs, symmetry error is at most 8.88e-16 and all distances are positive (min 1.019869); equal sets yield exactly 0 and duplicate invariance holds. The D=500 triangle counterexample (X={±e_i}, Y=∅, Z={0}, t=5) reproduces the source's ~7.18 magnitude increment and shows the inequality fails by 12.363.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.3 shows magnitude distance converges to 0 as t→0 and converges to the cardinality of the symmetric difference of the two datasets as t→∞ (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: A single 1D instance with symmetric-difference cardinality 4 shows distance converging from 0.005 at t=0.01 to 3.999999999322 at t=30 (within 6.78e-10 of 4), with a monotone large-t tail. This is a simplified one-dimensional demonstration of both limits, not a comprehensive verification across dimensions or dataset configurations.

claims.claim: Figure 2 shows magnitude distance remains discriminative in dimensions exceeding 1000, in settings where MMD's discriminative power collapses (Section on High-Dimensional Behavior, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: An independent extension to D=2048 with 20 paired seeds shows magnitude distance at t=1/sqrt(D) has a positive paired gap of 0.000657 (95% CI [0.000607, 0.000708], 20/20 wins) while MMD with sigma=1 is exactly zero. The control shows MMD with sigma=sqrt(D) does not collapse (gap 0.01847), narrowing but not contradicting the claim about the paper's specific MMD bandwidth settings.

claims.claim: MagGN, a generative model trained with a multi-scale magnitude-distance loss, achieves an 11.97x training speedup over WGAN on MNIST while producing visually competitive samples (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The 11.97x speedup over WGAN is explicitly source-audited only and not rerun; no WGAN baseline is trained. The 12-epoch CPU MNIST run with the official architecture shows feasibility (proxy-FID 896.71→173.10) but does not reproduce the 500-epoch L40S timing or assess visual competitiveness, and the magnitude model's proxy-FID (173.10) is worse than the matched MMD control (91.63).

claims.claim: Theorem 5.5 proves magnitude distance has bounded outlier sensitivity, changing by only about 6-10% under significant outlier addition compared to a 17.6% change for Wasserstein distance in the same setting (Section 5, Theorem 5.5).
claims.evidence: The exact source-panel rerun (seeds 42/50/60, 30+30 points, 4 outliers from N([2,2],50I)) reproduces magnitude relative changes of 10.29% at t=5 and 6.85% at t=20, and Wasserstein change of 17.61%, matching the claimed 6-10% vs 17.6%. A 16-seed radius sweep in D=5 confirms all nonnegative weights satisfy the 2|X∪Y| bound and magnitude plateaus while sliced Wasserstein grows 10.65x.

neonforestmist/magnitude-distance-repro.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting claims 1, 2, 4, and 6 with real experiments at non-trivial scale (D=2048 discrimination, D=500 triangle counterexample, exact source-panel outlier reproduction). Claim 3 is demonstrated only on a single simplified 1D instance, and claim 5's specific 11.97x speedup and visual-competitiveness claims are not reproduced, though MNIST training feasibility is shown at reduced epochs.

nkapila6/5nNNVY8NW4.paper_title: To Grok Grokking: Provable Grokking in Ridge Regression

claims.claim: The paper proves end-to-end grokking for zero-teacher ridge regression, including early training overfitting, delayed poor generalization, and eventual low generalization error (Theorem 4.1)
claims.evidence: Source grep confirms Theorem 4.1 exists with three parts (training loss bound, generalization lower bound, norm convergence), and a numerical simulation with n=20, m=1000, lambda=1e-3, 5 seeds demonstrates all three grokking stages: train loss converges at ~200 steps, poor generalization sustained for ~3750 steps, then generalization at ~4700 steps across 5/5 seeds.

claims.claim: The end-to-end grokking result is extended from the zero-teacher setting to realizable ridge regression with arbitrary realizable teacher functions (Theorem 4.2)
claims.evidence: Only a source-level grep of the LaTeX confirms Theorem 4.2 exists with expected components (realizable teacher, t1/t2 definitions, conditions on n/m/lambda). No numerical simulation or proof verification was performed for this claim.

claims.claim: Separate theorems decompose grokking into training-loss convergence, poor generalization during overfitting, and eventual generalization (Theorems 4.4-4.6)
claims.evidence: Only a source-level grep confirms the three theorem labels (thm:training-performance-rf-realizable-case, thm:overfitting-rf-realizable-case, thm:generalization-rf-realizable-case) exist with appropriate titles. No numerical simulation or proof verification was performed.

claims.claim: Decreasing weight decay and sample size can amplify grokking time in ridge-regression simulations, matching the paper's quantitative hyperparameter predictions (Figure 2)
claims.evidence: Independent numpy reproduction with 10 seeds per config clearly shows t2 ~ 1/lambda scaling: lambda=1e-1→30 steps, 1e-2→239, 1e-3→2390, 1e-4→23900. The n trend (decreasing n increases grokking time) is present but very weak (~2% difference between n=20 and n=100), though consistently in the predicted direction.

claims.claim: Two-layer ReLU experiments qualitatively reproduce the predicted grokking-time dependence on hyperparameters beyond the linear setting (Figures 3 and 4)
claims.evidence: A 2-layer ReLU MLP (d=50, m=1000) was trained on MPS with 3 seeds, but 5 of 9 configurations did not grok within 100k steps. The 4 configurations that converged show the right qualitative trends (lambda=0.1: n=30→63333, n=50→57333, n=100→46667 steps), but the evidence is incomplete and limited in scope.

nkapila6/5nNNVY8NW4.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence for Claims 1 and 4 (zero-teacher grokking stages and t2~1/lambda scaling), but Claims 2 and 3 are only supported by source-level grep confirming theorem existence without proof verification or numerical demonstration. Claim 5 is a partial reproduction with many non-converging configurations, showing correct qualitative trends where results exist.

SabaPivot/repro-joint-learning-in-the-ga.paper_title: Joint Learning in the Gaussian Single Index Model

claims.claim: In the joint learning setting (as opposed to the planted-target-only model), gradient flow converges to the target direction even when the initial correlation m0 is negative, for first-nonzero-Hermite-coefficient index s≥2, with |1+m_t| decaying at rate Ce^{-c(t-τc)} after time τc ≥ Cd^{s-1} (Theorem 1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: The scaling experiment with d∈{8,...,256} and s∈{2,3} reproduces the d^{s-1} escape time (fitted exponents 0.94–1.03 for s=2, 1.94–1.97 for s=3, R²>0.99) and exponential |1+m_t| contraction (positive decay rates, min R²=0.981). The convergence to m=-1 for negative m0 is consistent with the paper's |1+m_t|→0 metric, and predictor recovery is confirmed (error ~1e-14).

claims.claim: This contrasts with the planted model, where a negative initial direction traps the gradient flow in a spurious basin; in joint learning the adaptively evolving link function f_t corrects for the early misalignment (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The planted-model ODE with negative m0 and s=3 remains trapped near m=0 (max |m|=0.0056), while the joint ODE converges to m=-1 with predictor error 1.13e-14, directly demonstrating the contrast: the adaptive link function in joint learning escapes the spurious basin that traps the planted model.

claims.claim: A dense reproducing kernel Hilbert space built from Hermite functions, K(x,y)=Σ_k c_k h_k(x) h_k(y), is constructed to adapt to the single-index structure for univariate function estimation (Proposition 2, Section 5).
claims.evidence: The Hermite kernel K(x,y)=Σ c_k h_k(x)h_k(y) with c_k=e^{-αk} is constructed and verified across 15 cells: direct kernel sums match weighted-feature inner products within 1.33e-15, minimum Gram eigenvalue is -3.16e-15 (numerical zero, confirming PSD), and truncation errors are monotonically nonincreasing with cutoff.

claims.claim: The joint gradient flow on Hermite coefficients and the index direction can be implemented in practice as a finite-dimensional ODE on ((a_k)_{k≤𝗄}, m), discretized via an Euler scheme (Section 5, Section 6).
claims.evidence: The finite-dimensional ODE on (a_k, m) is implemented and discretized via Euler with steps {0.08, 0.04, 0.02}; errors to the RK4 reference decrease monotonically with step refinement (max error 5.35e-5), all 9 stable cells remain bounded (|m|≤1.0), and all 3 destructive oversized-step controls correctly leave the stable region.

SabaPivot/repro-joint-learning-in-the-ga.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all four claims: Theorem 1's d^{s-1} scaling and exponential contraction are reproduced at d up to 256, the planted-vs-joint contrast is directly demonstrated, the Hermite RKHS construction is verified algebraically, and the Euler discretization is validated with convergence and destructive controls.

brettold/repro-from-token-to-token-pair-.paper_title: From Token to Token Pair: Efficient Prompt Compression for Large Language Models in Clinical Prediction

claims.claim: MedTPE combines token-pair encoding (TPE), dependency-aware token replacement of roughly 3% of least-common tokens, and self-supervised fine-tuning (SSFT) that updates only 0.5-1.0% of model parameters to align new token embeddings with the pretrained latent space (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Code audit of the official repo confirms all three components exist: tpe_vocabulary_modify_fn with dependency-aware heap-based replacement, SplitEmbedding SSFT with frozen non-new-token params and mean-embedding init (scale 0.5), and max_m=5000 default. Computed replacement fractions are 3.29% (Qwen) and 3.90% (Llama), and SSFT trainable fractions are 0.50% (Qwen) and 0.83% (Llama), matching the claimed ~3% and 0.5-1.0% ranges for the primary BPE models.

claims.claim: MedTPE reduces input token length by up to 31% and inference latency by 34-63%, with compression rates ranging 22.8-32.4% across datasets (Abstract; Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook only checks that Table 2 numbers are internally consistent (arithmetic on paper-reported values), not an independent re-run. The local compression proxy uses a simplified greedy pair-merge (not the actual TPE pipeline) and yields ~50% compression, which does not match the claimed 22.8-32.4% range; no independent latency measurements were made.

claims.claim: On MIMIC-IV ICU Mortality and Phenotyping (25 conditions) with Qwen2.5-1.5B, MedTPE maintains F1 on ICU Mortality (0.122 to 0.122) while improving Phenotyping F1 (0.201 to 0.218), alongside inference time dropping from 38.3 to 23.5 minutes (-38.6%) (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook extracts F1 and latency values from the paper's Table 2 and verifies arithmetic consistency, but no independent re-run on MIMIC-IV was performed (PhysioNet data unavailable, no GPU). There is no experimental evidence beyond restating the paper's own numbers.

claims.claim: MedTPE is evaluated across four clinical prediction tasks (ICU Mortality, Phenotyping, 30-day Hospital Readmission, 1-year Pancreatic Cancer prediction) and three LLM backbones spanning Qwen2.5, Llama3, and Gemma2 families, plus the clinically specialized Meditron3-8B (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Cross-referencing paper tables (Table 2, 6, 8, Appendix C.4) with the official repo confirms four clinical tasks (ICU Mortality, Phenotyping, Readmission, Pancreatic Cancer) and tokenizer branches for Qwen/Llama BPE and Gemma SentencePiece, plus Meditron3-8B references. The evaluation scope is documented and corroborated by code structure.

claims.claim: MedTPE's compression approach is additionally tested for generalization beyond clinical text, including scientific reasoning (ARC-Challenge), financial summarization (ECTSum), and Chinese medical QA (CMedQA2).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirms paper coverage of ARC-Challenge, ECTSum, and CMedQA2, and runs a simplified pair-merge compression proxy on ARC-Challenge questions, Chinese medical QA-like strings, and billsum financial text (not actual ECTSum). The proxy uses a toy greedy merge (not full TPE) on 48-sample subsets, and no actual Table 4 metrics (ROUGE/Acc/F1) were re-run.

brettold/repro-from-token-to-token-pair-.overall: The logbook provides a solid code-level audit confirming MedTPE's architecture and parameter fractions (Claims 1, 4), but does not independently reproduce any of the paper's quantitative results on MIMIC-IV, EHRSHOT, or cross-domain benchmarks due to lack of GPU and dataset access. Claims 2, 3 rely solely on paper arithmetic checks, and Claim 5 is addressed only with toy proxies.

SabaPivot/repro-high-probability-converg.paper_title: High-Probability Convergence Guarantees of Decentralized SGD

claims.claim: Theorem 1 establishes that under assumptions (A1)-(A5), decentralized SGD achieves a high-probability convergence rate of O(sigma*sqrt(d)/sqrt(nT)) on the average squared gradient norm for non-convex costs, exhibiting linear speed-up in the number of nodes n (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The nontrivial-network upgrade runs decentralized SGD (W≠J) on ring, torus, and sparse graphs with heterogeneous local objectives and independent node noise (d=50, 128 reps/cell, 3072 total repetitions). Observed q95 exponents are -0.5026 in T (ring), -0.5024 in T (torus), and -0.5031 in n (sparse), all R²≥0.99996, closely matching the claimed 1/√(nT) scaling. Network controls confirm nonzero consensus error (0.133–0.377) and ||W-J||_F=1.48–2.08, ruling out the centralized W=J special case.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 establishes that under assumptions (A1)-(A4) and (A6, mu-strong convexity), the last iterate of decentralized SGD achieves a high-probability rate of O(d*sigma^2*kappa/(n(T+t0))), also exhibiting linear speed-up without requiring a bounded-heterogeneity assumption (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The nontrivial-network upgrade on heterogeneous strongly convex quadratics (κ=3, persistent nonvanishing noise) yields torus T exponent -0.9688 (R²=0.9995) and sparse-graph n exponent -1.0307 (R²=0.9975), matching the claimed 1/(nT) last-iterate rate. The original reproduce.py independently gives -0.9799 in T and -1.0098 in n with q95·nT bounded between 99.94 and 109.49. The anomalous ring fit (-1.77) is acknowledged and retained rather than hidden.

claims.claim: Lemma 2 shows the averaged stochastic noise across nodes is O(sigma*sqrt(d)/sqrt(n))-sub-Gaussian, giving a high-probability analogue of the variance-reduction benefit of decentralized averaging (Lemma 2).
claims.evidence: The noise-averaging experiment draws 100,000 independent d=50 Gaussian samples per node count n∈{1,2,4,...,128}, averages across nodes, and measures projection-std exponent -0.49998 and RMS-norm exponent -0.49999, both matching 1/√n. The empirical MGF is at most 0.003741 of the theoretical bound, directly confirming the O(σ√d/√n)-sub-Gaussian tail property.

claims.claim: Compared to the prior high-probability analysis of Lu et al., this work removes the uniformly-bounded-gradient assumption and, for the strongly convex case, eliminates the requirement of asymptotically vanishing noise (Lemma 4, referencing Lu et al.).
claims.evidence: Assumption controls show gradient norms grow linearly with radius (fitted exponent 1.0, max norm 208,493) confirming unbounded gradients, late/early noise variance ratio 0.99869 confirming nonvanishing noise, no gradient clipping, and nonzero heterogeneity at the optimum. The convergence rates from Claims 1–2 are recovered under these relaxed conditions on nontrivial networks, providing concrete operational evidence that the paper's results hold without Lu et al.'s stronger assumptions.

SabaPivot/repro-high-probability-converg.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all four claims through clean-room implementations on nontrivial decentralized networks (ring, torus, sparse) with 3,072 total repetitions, real a9a data, and predeclared gates. The scaling exponents closely match the theoretical predictions (1/√(nT) for non-convex, 1/(nT) for strongly convex, 1/√n for noise averaging) under the paper's relaxed assumptions.

claims.claim: Proposition 5.1 establishes that Verbalized Bayesian Persuasion (VBP) returns an ε-approximate Bayes correlated equilibrium in static Bayesian persuasion settings and an ε-approximate Bayes-Nash equilibrium in multistage settings (Proposition 5.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies the operational content of Proposition 5.1 using exact numeric solvers (Stackelberg-commitment reproduces BCE, symmetric self-play converges to babbling) on the paper's three game scenarios, but does not verify the actual VBP system with LLMs or the proof itself — it uses analytic/numeric proxies rather than the Prompt-PSRO loop with an LLM best-response oracle.

claims.claim: Section 6.1.1 evaluates VBP on three dialogue scenarios: a Recommendation Letter (REL) task with a 1/3 vs 2/3 strong/weak student prior, a Courtroom (COR) task with a 30% guilt prior, and a Law Enforcement (LAE) patrol-allocation task (Section 6.1.1).
claims.evidence: All three scenarios (REL with 1/3-2/3 prior, COR with 30% guilt prior, LAE with patrol allocation) are implemented in bp_games.py with exact LP solutions cross-checked against both textbook values (COR sender reward 0.6, posterior 0.5; REL sender reward 2/3) and the paper's own Appendix B closed-form formulas, all matching exactly.

claims.claim: In the static, polarized-signal setting (S1), the sender's achieved reward matches the Bayes Correlated Equilibrium baseline, with honesty probability converging to approximately 100% for the strong/guilty/patrolled states and lying probability dropping to near 0% (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Reward matching BCE and honesty=100% are confirmed via analytic Stackelberg solvers on the real game setups, but the 'lying probability near 0%' part is explicitly contested (true BCE requires substantial lying: 50%/42.9%/66.7%) and attributed to LLM alignment behavior that was not reproduced — only a 0.5B CPU-only model was available for qualitative illustration, not the paper's Llama-3.1-8B.

claims.claim: Convergence experiments show exploitability decreasing to approximately 0.1 after 10 iterations, indicating proximity to equilibrium (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: The qualitative pattern of exploitability decreasing over ~10 iterations is reproduced using a noiseless numeric bisection search, but the floor is near-zero rather than ~0.1 because the actual LLM-driven best-response oracle (OPRO with Llama-3.1-8B) was not used — only a numeric analog was run.

claims.claim: In the multistage setting (S3), Algorithm 1 combines Prompt-PSRO with step-wise conditional prompt optimization via FunSearch, and performance in this setting declines relative to the static settings, with sender deception oscillating through bargaining dynamics before stabilizing (Section 5.3, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: The performance decline vs. static is confirmed quantitatively (sender reward 0.6667→0.5103, -23%) using a T=5 numeric grid-search extension, but the oscillating-deception dynamic is explicitly not observed (the logbook reports a flat fixed point), and the setup uses numeric solvers rather than the actual FunSearch-driven conditional prompt optimization with LLMs.

algorise/repro-verbalized-bayesian-persu.overall: The logbook faithfully reproduces the game-theoretic backbone (exact BCE solutions, commitment-vs-babbling distinction, multistage performance decline) using CPU-only numeric/analytic solvers cross-checked against textbook and paper formulas, but cannot reproduce the LLM-driven components of VBP (OPRO/FunSearch prompt optimization, alignment-driven honesty/oscillation dynamics) at the paper's scale due to compute constraints.

SabaPivot/repro-decision-tree-learning-o.paper_title: Decision Tree Learning on Product Spaces

claims.claim: For a function computable by an optimal decision tree with maximum depth D_opt and average depth Δ_opt over a product distribution, the greedy top-down heuristic constructs an ϵ-approximating tree of size at most max((e·Δ_opt/(ϵ·D_opt))^(Δ_opt·D_opt), e^(Δ_opt·D_opt)) (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: 72 exact greedy runs on product distributions (balanced depth-4 and chain depth-15 targets, ambient dimensions 20/40/80, biases 0.1/0.3/0.5/0.7, epsilons 0.10/0.15/0.25) all produce tree sizes within the literal Theorem 1.1 envelope, with maximum final error minus epsilon at 0.0 and 408 recorded split steps.

claims.claim: For balanced optimal trees where D_opt = Δ_opt = log s, the bound simplifies to a quasi-polynomial size s^(log(s)·log(e/ϵ)) (Theorem 1.1, balanced-tree corollary).
claims.evidence: Independent regression over balanced trees s=2^D for D=2..10 and four epsilon values yields log-log slope 2.0000 against ln(s), and raw_bound/[ln(s)^2·ln(e/epsilon)] is constant at 2.0814 across all 36 cells, confirming the quasi-polynomial simplification without circular algebra.

claims.claim: The paper gives the first practical parameter-free implementation of BuildTopDownDT that requires no prior knowledge of the optimal tree's size or depth, unlike the algorithm of Blanc et al. (2020) (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Across 72 configurations the greedy algorithm received only the target evaluator, ambient dimension, product bias, and epsilon—never s, D_opt, or Delta_opt—and terminated successfully, selecting zero irrelevant coordinates out of up to 80 searched, demonstrating practical parameter-free operation.

claims.claim: The size bound extends beyond the uniform-distribution setting analyzed by Blanc et al. (2020) to the strictly broader class of product distributions while remaining tighter for full binary trees (Section 1, comparison to prior work).
claims.evidence: 54 of 72 exact runs used non-uniform Bernoulli product biases (0.1, 0.3, 0.7) and all satisfied the theorem size bound, extending verification beyond the uniform setting; three correlated non-product controls were correctly excluded; the tighter full-tree bound is confirmed by the corollary scaling analysis.

SabaPivot/repro-decision-tree-learning-o.overall: The logbook provides exact, non-trivial empirical verification of all four claims through 72 greedy decision-tree runs on product distributions with ambient dimensions up to 80, predeclared gates, and destructive non-product controls. The 'first/tighter' priority aspects of claims 3-4 are source-backed assertions rather than experimentally provable, but the core technical content—parameter-free operation, product-distribution extension, and the size bounds—is concretely demonstrated.

kaustubh/repro-haloprobe-bayesian-detect.paper_title: HaloProbe: Bayesian Detection and Mitigation of Object Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models

claims.claim: Conditioning attention analysis on token position reveals hallucinated tokens receive higher attention than correct tokens, but this trend reverses when statistics are marginalized across positions, demonstrating Simpson's paradox in coarse-grained attention-based hallucination detection (Section 3.2, Figure 2a).
claims.evidence: Raw per-bin data shows hallucinated attention ≥ correct in 28/30 position bins, while marginal averages flip (correct 0.002873 > hallucinated 0.002656), demonstrating Simpson's paradox at full scale (36,753 tokens, 5000 images, LLaVA-1.5-7B).

claims.claim: Hallucinated objects appear less frequently than correct objects in the underlying data, and this class imbalance alone allows a trivial classifier to reach over 84% accuracy on hallucination detection without using genuine signal (Section 3.2, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: 85.41% of object tokens are correct (31,389/36,753), so a trivial all-correct classifier achieves 85.41% accuracy with AUROC 50.0, exceeding the claimed 84% floor, confirmed on both analysis and held-out test splits.

claims.claim: On LLaVA-1.5-7B, HaloProbe achieves 90.00% accuracy and 93.50 AUROC for hallucination detection, compared to 84.46% accuracy and 90.19 AUROC for the prior state-of-the-art method DIML (Table 1).
claims.evidence: HaloProbe reaches 89.84% accuracy / 92.82 AUROC (paper: 90.00 / 93.50) and beats the independently re-implemented DIML (85.98% / 89.66 AUROC vs paper's 84.46 / 90.19), with P/R/F1 of 93.1/95.1/94.1 closely matching the paper.

claims.claim: For hallucination mitigation with LLaVA-1.5 under greedy decoding, HaloProbe with post-processing reduces sentence-level hallucination (C_s) from a 51.6 baseline to 17.6, outperforming DIML's 25.0 (Table 2).
claims.evidence: HaloProbe+PP reaches C_s=22.2 (not 17.6), and DIML+PP achieves a lower C_s=18.4, inverting the claimed ordering that HaloProbe outperforms DIML (25.0); the mitigation mechanism reduces C_s substantially but the specific quantitative claim and comparative advantage are contradicted.

claims.claim: Ablating HaloProbe's external features and fine-grained attention components together drops detection accuracy from 90.0% to 84.4%, and ablating class-balanced training alone (using natural distribution) drops accuracy to 89.8% (Tables 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: Removing attention collapses AUROC from 92.82 to 65.55 (paper: 93.5→82.8), removing all features collapses AUROC to 50.71≈random (paper: 50.1), and natural-distribution training yields 90.25% accuracy (paper: 89.8%), confirming both ablation sub-claims with minor numerical offsets.

claims.claim: HaloProbe's hallucination-aware beam search mitigation uses a score function combining hallucinated/correct object counts and probabilities with beam width N_beam=5, threshold τ=0.5, and penalty β=0.1 (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The score function S=n_hal+p_hal−β(n_corr+p_corr) with N_beam=5 and β=0.1 matches the paper exactly; τ=0.5 is confirmed (though the claim mislabels it as 'threshold' vs paper's 'temperature'); empirical candidate-reranking demo shows C_s reduction from 50.7→34.7 with best F1 (78.1).

kaustubh/repro-haloprobe-bayesian-detect.overall: This logbook provides a thorough independent re-implementation at full paper scale (LLaVA-1.5-7B, 5000 COCO images, 36,753 tokens) that verifies the core scientific claims about Simpson's paradox, class imbalance, and the Bayesian detector's performance. claims.evidence: Box A on the same H=2, d=2 instance yields slope 0.860 (≤ 0.875) and correctly exceeds the simplified-model slope (0.860 > 0.698), reproducing the predicted ordering. claims.claim: Unlike the Nelson et al. (2022) analysis, the paper's bounds hold with high probability rather than in expectation, are model-free (independent of reward gaps), and do not require non-degeneracy coverage assumptions on the belief distribution (Section on comparison to Nelson et al. 2022).
claims.evidence: Qualitative probes on the H=2 instance show 90th-percentile regret slope 0.696 (sublinear), gap-shrunk slope 0.872 (barely sublinear), near-degenerate-design slope 0.651, and Plain LinUCB at 0.986 (linear). nmaher/repro-a-direct-approach-for-handl.overall: The logbook provides a methodologically sound numerical audit on a minimal H=2 HMM instance, with proper controls (oracle baseline, C-sensitivity sweep, alignment ablation) that reproduce all predicted orderings. SabaPivot/repro-the-relative-instability.paper_title: The Relative Instability of Model Comparison with Cross-validation

claims.claim: For soft-thresholded least squares with penalty lambda_n = o(n), single-algorithm assessment satisfies relative stability, with loss stability gamma decaying as 1/n^2 so that r(h) = Theta(1/n) -> 0 (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Across n=[90,...,90000] with 6 seeds and 4000 replications each, the fresh-seed audit measured gamma slope -2.0358 (target -2) and r(h) slope -1.0356 (target -1), confirming gamma=Theta(n^-2) and r(h)=Theta(n^-1)->0 for single soft-thresholding with lambda=sqrt(n).

claims.claim: When comparing two soft-thresholded least squares fits with tuning parameters lambda_n and lambda_n + delta_n where delta_n = Theta(1), relative stability fails: r(h) = Omega(sqrt(n)) does not vanish, invalidating the cross-validation central limit theorem needed for confidence intervals (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: With delta_n=1, the ST comparison r(h) slope is +0.3855 (positive, growing with n), confirming r(h) does not vanish; the Lasso comparison slope is +0.3837, independently corroborating the failure of relative stability for pairwise comparison with constant tuning gap.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments confirm that cross-validation confidence intervals remain valid for single soft-thresholding assessment across moderate sample sizes but fail for pairwise soft-thresholding comparisons even at very large sample sizes (Empirical Validation section).
claims.evidence: At n=90,000 with 2,500 CV replicates, nominal-95% coverage is 95.08% for single soft-thresholding but 65.16% for pairwise comparison; Lasso shows the same pattern (95.00% vs 64.04%), directly confirming valid single CIs and failed comparison CIs at large sample sizes.

claims.claim: Ridge regression is shown to satisfy relative stability for pairwise comparisons, in contrast to the Lasso and soft-thresholding, which exhibit relative instability even though each is individually (absolutely) stable (Critical Insight / Empirical Validation).
claims.evidence: Ridge comparison r(h) slope is -1.0808 (decreasing) with 94.96% coverage, while Lasso and ST each show individually stable single r(h) slopes (<-0.35) but positive comparison r(h) slopes (>0.10), confirming Ridge is comparison-stable whereas Lasso/ST are individually stable but comparison-unstable.

SabaPivot/repro-the-relative-instability.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous independent reproduction using exact Gaussian sufficient statistics at sample sizes up to 90,000 with thousands of replications, confirming all four claims with predeclared gates that all passed (18/18). The clean-room implementation faithfully captures the paper's theoretical predictions and empirical validation results.

algorise/repro-colorful-pinball-density-.paper_title: Colorful Pinball: Density-Weighted Quantile Regression for Conditional Guarantee of Conformal Prediction

claims.claim: Proposition 3.4 shows the optimal density weight for quantile regression equals the conditional density of the score evaluated at the true quantile, which for location-scale distributions is proportional to 1/sigma(x), capturing heteroscedastic structure ignored by standard pinball loss (Proposition 3.4).
claims.evidence: Synthetic heteroscedastic regression with known ground-truth weights shows density-weighted loss (0.0237) outperforms unweighted (0.0285), but this is a simplified proxy validating the theoretical proposition rather than a full-scale reproduction.

claims.claim: The proposed three-stage framework estimates joint quantiles at levels tau-delta, tau, tau+delta, computes density weights via the finite-difference w(x) = 2*delta / (q_hat_{tau+delta}(x) - q_hat_{tau-delta}(x)), then fine-tunes the central quantile with a weighted pinball loss before conformalization (Section 3, three-stage framework).

claims.evidence: 864 Gaussian Thompson-sampling paths across d∈{4,8}, prior scales {0.25,1,4}, horizons {64,128,256} show max regret-to-Theorem-1-bound ratio of 0.0780, confirming the reconstructed bound holds empirically.

claims.claim: Lemma 3, the generalized elliptical potential lemma, removes the standard requirement that the initial precision matrix V₀ ⪰ I_d and allows flexible exponents p∈[0,1], bounding the potential by 2^p T^(1-p)(log det V_T/det V₀)^p (Section 3, Lemma 3).
claims.evidence: The registered bound 2^p T^(1-p)(log det V_T/V₀)^p is violated by factor 36,191 in a direct counterexample (V₀=1e-6·I₁₂); the full Lemma 3 with trace correction holds (ratio 0.667), but the specific bound expression as claimed does not hold.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a matching lower bound showing the burn-in term dr√Tr(Σ₀) is unavoidable for non-pathological priors, via a bound of the form Reg^p(T) ≥ (r/π‖τ‖₂)Σᵢ₌₂^min{T,d}(i-1)τᵢ² (Section 4, Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: Algebraic evaluation on 36 spectra confirms the registered weaker sum is implied by the exact Theorem 6 formula, with lower-bound-to-burnin-scale ratios 0.066–0.157 for T≥d; a direct simulation of 3,888 Thompson-sampling paths across 81 cells shows all empirical means exceed the lower bound (min ratio 3.73).

claims.claim: Theorem 9 extends the additive regret decomposition beyond Gaussian priors and noise to strongly log-concave distributions, preserving the same additive structure between the minimax and burn-in terms (Section 5, Theorem 9).
claims.evidence: 216 1D grid-based and 432 multidimensional (d∈{2,4}) MALA-based Thompson-sampling paths with quartic-tilted strongly-log-concave prior and noise show positive curvature floors, sublinear regret slopes (max 0.692), and empirical regret within the additive structure (max ratio 1.048).

SabaPivot/repro-prior-diffusiveness-and-.overall: The logbook provides concrete simulation evidence supporting Claims 1, 2, 4, and 5 through hundreds to thousands of Thompson-sampling paths with reconstructed theoretical bounds, and falsifies Claim 3's specific bound expression (though the paper's full Lemma 3 with correction term is verified). The experiments are at modest dimensions (d≤8 for Gaussian, d≤4 for non-Gaussian) but directly test the claimed mathematical structures.

Deepakkambala/repro-revenue-guarantees-o.paper_title: Revenue Guarantees of No-Swap-Regret Dynamics in First Price Auctions

claims.claim: For exact correlated equilibria in discrete first-price auctions with k discretization levels, expected revenue is at least v2 - 4/k, where v2 is the second-highest valuation (Theorem 2.5).
claims.evidence: LP minimization over CE distributions (ε=0) on 5 small instances (k=5–15, 2–3 bidders) shows min revenue always exceeds v2−4/k with minimum margin 0.1333, but this is a numerical check on toy-scale discrete auctions, not a proof of the universal theorem.

claims.claim: For ε-approximate correlated equilibria, expected revenue is at least v2 - 3/k - Θ(εk²) (Theorem 2.6).
claims.evidence: Same LP with ε>0 on small instances shows revenue decreasing with ε and gap_over_eps_k2 values staying modest (max 0.239), consistent with Θ(εk²) scaling, but cannot certify the hidden constant and is limited to k≤15.

claims.claim: There exists an ε-approximate correlated equilibrium with revenue at most v2 - Θ(1/k) - Θ(ε), showing the ε-dependence in the revenue lower bound cannot be removed (Theorem 2.8).
claims.evidence: LP scan over 2-bidder instances (v1=v2=1, k=5–15) finds approximate equilibria with revenue below 1−1/k when ε>0 (e.g., k=10: revenue 0.4996 at ε=0.01), numerically supporting the existence claim at small scale.

claims.claim: When bidders run no-swap-regret algorithms achieving swap regret O(√(kT)), the time-averaged revenue is at least v2 - 3/k - O(ε) after O(k^5/ε^2) rounds (Corollary 2.7).
claims.evidence: The logbook only ran external-regret matching (explicitly weaker than swap regret), not the no-swap-regret algorithm the corollary requires; the algebraic derivation is asserted but not independently verified, and the dynamics control does not test the actual claim.

claims.claim: Time-averaged bidder behavior under no-swap-regret dynamics converges to an ε-approximate correlated equilibrium with probability 1-δ (Theorem 2.3).
claims.evidence: Empirical correlated-deviation gains were measured from external-regret matching (max 0.00015), but the actual no-swap-regret algorithm was never implemented, no δ-dependence was tested, and no high-probability convergence was demonstrated.

claims.claim: The revenue lower bounds are proved via a dual-fitting approach that uses a linear program and weak duality to bound revenue of approximate correlated equilibria (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The primal LP from Definition 3.1 was implemented and solved numerically on small instances, confirming optima are consistent with the claimed bound shape, but the dual-fitting assignment itself (the core of the claim) was not constructed or verified.

Deepakkambala/repro-revenue-guarantees-o.overall: The logbook provides toy-scale numerical LP audits on small discrete auctions (k≤15, 2–3 bidders) that are consistent with the revenue bound theorems but cannot verify the universal mathematical statements. Claims involving no-swap-regret dynamics (Claims 4–5) are largely unaddressed because only external-regret matching was implemented, not the swap-regret algorithms the theorems require.

Deepakkambala/repro-generalizing-stochas.paper_title: Generalizing Stochastic Smoothing for Differentiation and Gradient Estimation

claims.claim: Lemma 3 generalizes the stochastic-smoothing gradient identity to absolutely continuous but not necessarily differentiable densities, enabling smoothing with distributions such as Laplace and triangular that lack differentiable densities (Section 2, Lemma 3).
claims.evidence: A 1D step function was smoothed with Laplace and triangular perturbations and the score estimator was compared to finite differences (abs errors 0.0091 and 0.0323), confirming the identity on the two named nondifferentiable-density examples but at a simplified single-dimensional proxy scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 7 extends the smoothing framework to multivariate distributions with covariance matrices, allowing differentiation with respect to scale parameters (Section 2, Theorem 7).
claims.evidence: A 2D test with a non-diagonal 2×2 scale matrix L compared Theorem 7's score estimators for both input and scale-matrix derivatives against common-random finite differences (max abs errors 0.0195 and 0.0532), exercising the multivariate covariance feature but at a minimal 2D toy scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 8 derives estimators for the derivative of the output covariance matrix, enabling gradient-based uncertainty quantification (Section 2, Theorem 8).
claims.evidence: The output covariance derivative with respect to the input was estimated on the same 2D setup and compared to finite differences (max abs error 0.0299), but only the input-derivative entries were tested, not the full scale-matrix covariance derivative.

claims.claim: Section 4 benchmarks variance-reduction methods for stochastic-smoothing gradient estimation across 6 distributions (Gaussian, Logistic, Gumbel, Cauchy, Laplace, Triangular) and 24 combinations of sampling strategy (MC, Antithetic MC, Cartesian/Latin-Hypercube QMC and RQMC), covariate (None, f(x), Leave-One-Out) and antithetic pairing (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The script runs 6 distributions × 4 sampling modes × 3 covariates × 2 pairings = 144 rows, but omits two sampling modes (Cartesian QMC, Latin QMC), uses n=3 and s=64, making it a reduced proxy of the paper's full benchmark rather than a faithful reproduction.

claims.claim: Section 4 finds that Cartesian RQMC combined with the Leave-One-Out covariate, without antithetic pairing, achieves the lowest gradient-estimator variance among the tested combinations when feasible (Section 4).
claims.evidence: At the reduced proxy scale, Cartesian RQMC + LOO without pairing wins only for logistic and Cauchy; Gaussian, Gumbel, and Triangular are won by Latin RQMC + none, and Laplace by Cartesian RQMC + f(x) + pairing, so the claim is only partially supported and not uniformly reproduced at this scale.

claims.claim: Sections 4.2-4.5 demonstrate the framework on differentiable sorting/ranking (MNIST, n=5), Warcraft shortest-path prediction, differentiable rendering (Utah teapot pose estimation), and cryo-electron tomography simulation optimization (Section 4.2, Section 4.3, Section 4.4, Section 4.5).
claims.evidence: Only proxy/smoke tests were run: a synthetic hard-sorting gradient proxy and a 3×3 Dijkstra perturbation for Warcraft; the Utah teapot renderer and cryo-ET simulator were not executed at all due to unavailable assets, so the full four-application demonstration was not reproduced.

Deepakkambala/repro-generalizing-stochas.overall: The logbook provides toy-scale numerical checks supporting the core mathematical identities (Lemma 3, Theorems 7–8) and a reduced-structure variance benchmark proxy, but no experiment approaches the paper's actual scale or reproduces the real application pipelines.

Deepakkambala/repro-language-generation-.paper_title: Language Generation with Replay: A Learning-Theoretic View of Model Collapse

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 proves that a hypothesis class is uniformly generatable with replay if and only if it is uniformly generatable in the standard no-replay setting, with identical sample complexity, showing replay is benign for the strongest notion of generation (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: A finite audit on 6 tail-class targets with 14 rounds each (horizon 32) checks that post-burn-in outputs remain valid and fresh under replay, with sample complexity 1 in both settings. This instantiates the mechanism on a small finite prefix, not a full verification of the theorem.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 exhibits a countable hypothesis class that is non-uniformly generatable without replay but not non-uniformly generatable with replay, establishing a strict separation caused by replay (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: A finite-prefix simulation (horizon 32) shows replay forcing distinct inputs until a finite-budget target is exhausted at round 16, illustrating the obstruction mechanism but not the full countable-class construction.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 shows a computable algorithm using only membership queries can generate in the limit any countable hypothesis class even under replay conditions (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: A six-hypothesis truncation of a countable tail class with replay every third round checks the witness-protection filtering mechanism; the logbook itself labels it 'simplified' and 'not an exhaustive proof over all countable classes.'

claims.claim: Theorem 5.6 constructs an uncountable hypothesis class that is generatable in the limit without replay but becomes non-generatable in the limit once replay is permitted (Theorem 5.6).
claims.evidence: Finite prefixes of the branching construction show exponential ambiguity growth (2^20 = 1,048,576 replay-consistent branches at horizon 20), matching the uncountable separation intuition but not testing the actual uncountable construction.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.1 proves no deterministic generator using only membership queries can properly generate in the limit for all countable hypothesis classes (Theorem 6.1).
claims.evidence: The audit hardcodes `excluded_from_output = True` for every round, making the 'mistakes grow linearly' result tautological rather than an actual diagonalization test; no real adversarial logic is implemented.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.3 shows that even some finite hypothesis classes that are properly generatable in the limit without replay become impossible to properly generate once replay is introduced (Theorem 6.3).
claims.evidence: A 4-hypothesis finite class with horizon 32 checks that all first-output choices lead to replay obstruction where no hypothesis is a subset of both target supports, instantiating the mechanism on a small but real finite class.

Deepakkambala/repro-language-generation-.overall: The logbook provides small-scale finite numerical audits of the mechanisms behind six theoretical claims, but none constitute full verification of the infinite constructions. One audit (Claim 5) is tautological due to hardcoded results, while the others are legitimate but simplified toy instantiations.

Deepakkambala/repro-complexity-of-decent.paper_title: Complexity of Decentralized Optimization with Mixed Affine Constraints

claims.claim: For the smooth, strongly convex regime with mixed affine constraints, Theorem 4.1 gives an optimal communication complexity of O(√κ_f √κ̂_{C̃ᵀ} √κ_W log(1/ε)) that matches established lower complexity bounds (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The audit script computes condition-number proxies (√κ_f·√κ̂_{C̃ᵀ}·√κ_W) on small deterministic matrices (n=4–32, d=3) and path graphs, verifying algebraic scaling of the formula ingredients, but never implements or runs Algorithm 1/APAPC to confirm the actual convergence rate or optimality against lower bounds.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 provides a unified complexity bound O(√κ_f (√κ̃_{AC} + √κ̂_{C̃ᵀ}) √κ_W log(1/ε)) covering problems with simultaneously coupled (global) and local affine constraints (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: The same audit computes the mixed proxy √κ_f·(√κ̃_{AC}+√κ̂_{C̃ᵀ})·√κ_W and observes additive behavior (shared proxy 108.89 vs mixed proxy 4524.49 at n=32), but this only checks the formula's algebraic structure on toy-scale matrices without running any optimization algorithm.

claims.claim: The paper analyzes both smooth objectives (Theorem 2.4) and non-smooth objectives via a Gradient Sliding algorithm (Algorithm 2), each under mixed affine constraints (Section 2, Section 4, Algorithm 2).

claims.claim: The proposed framework is motivated by and applied to horizontal federated learning (consensus constraints), vertical federated learning (shared/global-variable constraints), and multi-task learning with node-specific local constraints (Section 1, Applications).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirms via paper inspection that Section 1 and Appendix B contain the FL and multi-task learning mappings, but provides no experimental or computational verification beyond reading the paper.

claims.evidence: APAPC (Algorithm 1) is identified in the paper and the audit verifies the complexity proxies it consumes, but APAPC itself is never implemented or run; the claim that it is the core building block for optimal rates is supported only by paper inspection.

Deepakkambala/repro-complexity-of-decent.overall: The logbook performs a small-scale numerical audit of condition-number quantities appearing in the complexity formulas on deterministic matrices up to n=32, confirming algebraic structure but never implementing or running any of the paper's algorithms.
