claims.evidence: Code implements latent_space_deviation as self(z)-z (ζ) and dphi via torch.func.jacrev (Dζ); tangent space orthogonality to ∇ζ and rank condition verified numerically on torus ground truth and learned projection.

claims.claim: Geodesic interpolation and the discrete exponential map are computed via augmented Lagrangian optimization with penalty terms enforcing the manifold constraint despite an inexact implicit representation (Section 3, Equations 6-11).
claims.evidence: AugLagrangeMinimize implements L-BFGS inner solve, Lagrange multiplier update, and penalty parameter increase matching Equations 7-11; constraint violation 2.8e-7 and gradient norm 2.1e-8 on torus ground truth; works on learned projection with 2.1e-2 constraint.

claims.claim: The implicit projection Π is learned by minimizing a denoising objective 𝒬(Π) = ∫∫ |z−Π(y)|² f_σ(z−y) dz dy, yielding a Gaussian-weighted barycenter projection with approximation error O(σ²) in the manifold interior (Section 4, Equation 12).
claims.evidence: Loss functional implementation verified in code and training pipeline runs, but the O(σ²) approximation error is only confirmed on a 1D circle manifold (exponent 2.014); on actual learned manifolds (VAE/point cloud) the measured exponent is 0.6-0.9 due to finite-sample variance, so the bound is not empirically confirmed on real latent manifolds.

claims.claim: The method is validated on five experimental settings: discrete shells with isometric autoencoders, motion capture data with a spherical VAE, image data with low-curvature autoencoders, extension to distance-function representations, and Pose-NDF neural distance functions, showing that geodesic interpolation avoids self-intersections better than linear interpolation (Sections 5.1-5.4, Appendix A.7, Figures 4-8).
claims.evidence: Only 2 of 5 paper settings run with real data (point cloud, cow/Klein bottle AE); Pose-NDF is run via a kNN proxy on VAE latent rather than actual Pose-NDF; SCAPE and MoCap not run at all. The self-intersection claim is measured via off-manifold latent distance (a proxy), not actual decoded-shape self-intersections; synthetic C-shape and figure-8 experiments are simplified proxies for the real-data claim.

PinoCookie/repro-geodesic-calculus-on-im.overall: The logbook provides solid verification of the core algorithmic components (Claims 1-3) through code audits and numerical experiments on ground-truth and learned manifolds. The O(σ²) error bound (Claim 4) and the full experimental validation (Claim 5) are only addressed on simplified or proxy setups, not at the paper's full scale.

Rajdeep/repro-symmetry-reveals-layerwise.paper_title: Symmetry Reveals Layerwise Dynamics: How Transformers Perform In-Context Classification

claims.claim: The transformer's forward pass for in-context linear classification is shown to implement a coupled mean-shift recursion, with attention matrix A_l = softmax(αX_lX_l^T + γY_lY_l^T) and update rules X_{l+1}=X_l+α'A_lX_l, Y_{l+1}=Y_l+γ'A_lY_l, given explicitly in equations (7)-(8) (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies algebraic equivalence between a structured transformer residual update and the coupled mean-shift recursion to floating-point precision (errors ~1e-16), but only on a tiny hand-constructed instance (9 tokens, 3 dimensions, 3 classes), not on actual trained transformer checkpoints.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that under a label-driven regime the geometric margin between classes grows exponentially with depth, Δ_l ≥ Δ_0(1+α')^l, and the label margin similarly diverges after a burn-in period (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: A deterministic simulation on a hand-crafted binary instance (8 context points, 2 classes) confirms the geometric margin lower bound holds at all layers, but the label margin lower bound fails after the computed burn-in layer (output: 'Label bound holds after burn-in: False'), indicating a possible discrepancy in the theorem's printed statement, all on a simplified toy setup.

claims.claim: Behavioral alignment between the symmetrized and original models is validated via three independent fingerprints (output probabilities, query Jacobians, and context-influence scores) all showing correlations above 0.95, confirming the extracted algorithm is not an artifact of the symmetrization procedure (Figure 3, Section 3).
claims.evidence: On released checkpoints with 128 held-out prompts, query-Jacobian Spearman is 0.9810 and true-class probability R² is 0.9883 (both above 0.95), but context-influence Spearman is only 0.6738, well below the claimed 'all above 0.95,' directly contradicting the claim as stated.

claims.claim: Retrained transformers given semi-supervised prompts (labeled plus unlabeled points) improve in-context classification accuracy from about 72% to over 85% as unlabeled context grows, demonstrating unlabeled points sharpen class geometry (Figure 8, Section 5).
claims.evidence: Evaluating the authors' released semi-supervised checkpoints on 1,000 newly sampled prompts shows accuracy rising from 0.7660 at 8 context examples to 0.8356 at 128 (unconstrained) and 0.7682 to 0.8372 (symmetrized), reproducing the claimed trend of unlabeled context improving in-context classification on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: The mean-shift mechanism remains robust when 30% of in-context labels are randomly flipped, since correctly labeled points reinforce each other while flipped labels contribute canceling noise (Appendix B.3, Figures 12-13).
claims.evidence: The logbook flips 30% of labels at evaluation time on clean-trained checkpoints (accuracy still improves with context, reaching 0.7716 at n=128), but explicitly notes the paper's experiment involved models trained with noisy labels and those checkpoints were not released, so the paper's actual experimental setup was not reproduced.

Rajdeep/repro-symmetry-reveals-layerwise.overall: The logbook provides a partial reproduction using released checkpoints and toy-level numerical checks: it verifies the semi-supervised accuracy trend (Claim 4) on real models, falsifies the 'all fingerprints above 0.95' claim (Claim 3) due to low context-influence correlation, and addresses Claims 1-2 only on simplified toy setups with a possible theorem discrepancy in the label bound. Claim 5 is not properly reproduced because the noisy-trained checkpoints are unavailable.

agharsallah/h8nydu966g-logbook.paper_title: Ski Rental with Distributional Predictions of Unknown Quality

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows the algorithm achieves expected additive loss O(min(√b·max(EMD(p̂,p),1), b log b)), where EMD(p̂,p) is the Earth Mover's distance between the predicted and true distributions and b is the buy-ski-rental cost ratio (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Exact closed-form implementation of Algorithm 1 tested across 5,280 grid points (b=16..8192, 6 distribution families, 11 EMD levels, 8 seeds); inequality loss ≤ C·min(√b·max(EMD,1), b·log(b)) holds with C=1.5 at 100% of points, with concrete raw data showing e.g. b=8192/EMD=409600 giving loss=91.0 vs bound=110,726 (b·log(b) cap active).

claims.claim: The algorithm attains consistency O(√b) when the prediction error (EMD) is 0 and robustness O(b log b) when the prediction is arbitrarily inaccurate, without needing to know the prediction error bound in advance (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Same Algorithm 1 implementation (code path confirmed to never read EMD or true distribution p) tested at EMD=0 (consistency: max loss/√b = 0.994 across 360 points) and at EMD up to 50b (robustness: max loss/(b·log b) = 0.518 across 360 points), both with 100% pass rate against C=1.5 bounds.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 proves a matching lower bound showing no algorithm can achieve additive loss o(b)·EMD(p̂,p), establishing that the √b factor in Theorem 1 is necessary (Theorem 4, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Paper's explicit two-point adversarial construction implemented with full enumeration of all deterministic threshold policies K∈{0..b+10, ∞}; min-over-K worst-case ratio stays 0.44–0.50 across b=16..8192 (50 points), converging to ~0.5 and never trending toward 0, confirming no algorithm achieves o(b)·EMD.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a Pareto-optimal consistency-robustness tradeoff: any algorithm achieving O(√b) consistency must incur Ω(b log b) robustness (Theorem 6, Section 4)
claims.evidence: Paper's hard-tail construction implemented; numeric argmin of cost sequence independently confirmed to match paper's K=⌈0.5b·log(b)⌉ at every b. Sweeping 21 candidate thresholds per b, the smallest B achieving √b-consistency yields robustness/(b·log b) converging to 0.25 (30 points, b=16..8192), never trending to 0.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 introduces a parameterized algorithm with expected cost c(ALG_p) ≤ min{(1+λ)(c(OPT_p)+B), (1+1/λ)c(OPT_p)}, allowing explicit interpolation between trusting the prediction and worst-case guarantees via λ ∈ [0,1] (Theorem 2, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Algorithm 2 (λ-robustification) tested across 15,840 points (6 λ values × Claim 1 grid); two-part bound holds at 100% with C=1.5. At λ=1, competitive ratio maxes at exactly 2.000 (e.g., b=64/uniform: alg_cost=128, OPT=64, ratio=2.000); at λ=0, output matches Algorithm 1 to full floating-point precision.

agharsallah/h8nydu966g-logbook.overall: This logbook provides strong numerical verification of all five theoretical claims through exact closed-form implementations of the paper's algorithms and adversarial constructions, tested across 22,220+ grid points spanning a 512× range of buy-cost b. The raw data is consistent with the claimed bounds, lower bounds, and Pareto tradeoffs, with no sampling noise or proxy approximations.

claims.claim: A weighted set is defined as a β-approximation preserving coreset (β-APC) if any α-approximate k-means solution computed on it yields an αβ-approximate solution on the full dataset (Definition 1.1).
claims.evidence: The verification checks the definition's semantics on a 3-point dataset (P=Ω={0,2,5}, k=1) with 6 candidate centers. This is a trivially small exhaustive check, not a non-toy experimental validation.

claims.claim: For Euclidean k-means, sensitivity sampling constructs a (1+ε)-APC of size Õ(kε^-3), improving on strong coreset size requirements (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: The numerical experiment runs Algorithm 2 on n=2000, d=8, k=4, ε=0.2 data, achieving median beta=1.0545 (within 1+ε) and coreset size 5992 matching the predicted Õ(kε^-3) bound of 5991. Real algorithm, non-trivial scale, concrete numbers.

claims.claim: For arbitrary metrics, an iterative downsampling approach constructs a (4+ε)-APC of size Õ(kε^-2) (Theorem 1.3).
claims.evidence: The arbitrary-metric experiment uses a 60-node random graph metric with k=4, producing a coreset of size 58 out of 60 points—barely a 3% reduction. This trivially small metric with a near-full-size coreset does not constitute a meaningful test of the Õ(kε^-2) size claim.

claims.claim: Sensitivity sampling with m = Cε^-2(k log(k/δ) + log N) points gives strong coreset concentration guarantees for a solution family of size N (Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: The falsification relies on a 2-point metric (P={0,1}, k=N=1) counterexample exploiting extreme δ values near 1. While mathematically interesting, this is a toy setup. The non-toy numerical experiment (n=2000, ε=0.2, δ=0.1) actually shows 100% success rate, supporting the claim at reasonable parameters.

claims.claim: For finite n-point metrics, sensitivity sampling yields strong coresets of size O(kε^-2 log n), matching known lower bounds without extra polylogarithmic factors (Corollary 2.3).
claims.evidence: The experiment runs sensitivity sampling on n=2000, k=4, ε=0.15 data with m=4053=O(kε^-2 log n), achieving median strong-coreset error of 0.0399 over 250 solutions (well within ε=0.15). Non-trivial scale with concrete supporting numbers.

claims.claim: A lower bound of Ω(log N / log log N) is proved showing that APC guarantees below β=4 are not achievable for the arbitrary-metric setting (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: The lower bound construction uses n=36 (r=6) for the main metric, with a 25-point witness metric in the proof certificate. While scaling checks extend to n=40000 for pigeonhole thresholds, the actual barrier and packing constructions are only verified at very small scale.

DineshAI/9YcP7zeO8h.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting Claims 2 and 5 on non-trivial data (n=2000), but Claims 1, 3, 4, and 6 are only addressed on toy-scale setups (3-point, 60-node, 2-point, and 36-point metrics respectively). The logbook's self-reported 6/6 verdict is overly optimistic; the proof-certificate approaches are mathematical checks rather than experimental evidence at scale.

snaykey/repro-newton-step-influence-func.paper_title: On the Accuracy of Newton Step and Influence Function Data Attributions

claims.claim: Theorem 1.5 bounds the Newton-step approximation error to the true leave-one-out retrained parameter using only local strong convexity in a neighborhood of the Newton step, rather than the global strong convexity assumed in prior analyses (Theorem 1.5, Section 3).
claims.evidence: On logistic regression (not globally strongly convex), the NS error scales as n⁻² (log-log slope −2.24, R²=0.999) across n=100–1600, confirming the O(kd/n²) rate predicted by the local-strong-convexity analysis holds without global strong convexity.

claims.claim: For logistic regression with n samples, d-dimensional Gaussian features, and k removed points, the average-case Newton-step attribution error scales as Õ(kd/n²), while the average-case influence-function error scales as Õ((k^{3/2}d^{1/2}+k^{1/2}d^{3/2})/n²) (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: Both IF and NS errors decay as n⁻² (exponents −1.995 and −2.012, R²≈0.998); NS k-exponent is 0.99 (matching linear-in-k), and IF d-exponent (1.29) exceeds NS d-exponent (0.73), consistent with the extra d^{3/2} term in the IF bound.

claims.claim: The derived upper bounds match corresponding lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors, showing the Newton step is provably more accurate than influence functions whenever d ≫ k (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: NS_err/(kd/n²) stays bounded in [1.0, 2.6] across n and d sweeps (supporting tight matching bounds), and IF/NS grows from 2.88× to 12.25× as d increases at fixed k=2, while shrinking toward ~4.5× as k→d—exactly the d≫k separation predicted.

claims.claim: Rescaled and doubly-rescaled influence functions (RIF and DRIF) are shown to match the Newton step's Õ(kd/n²) average-case error rate while preserving the additivity property that plain influence functions have but the Newton step lacks (Theorem 1.6, Theorem 1.7).
claims.evidence: RIF/DRIF errors stay within 1.0–2.8× of NS across k=1–32 (vs. 4.5–12.7× for plain IF), and additivity residuals are exactly 0.0 for IF and RIF at machine precision while NS residuals grow to 7.8e-5, confirming both the rate-matching and additivity properties.

claims.claim: The paper's revised bounds remove the problematic 1/λ³ dependence on the regularization coefficient λ present in prior influence-function error analyses (Section 1, Discussion of prior bounds).
claims.evidence: Sweeping λ from 10² to 10⁻⁴, the measured plain-IF error varies by only 2.73× while the prior-art k²d/(n²λ³) bound proxy explodes by 10¹⁸×, directly showing the empirical IF error lacks 1/λ³ dependence.

snaykey/repro-newton-step-influence-func.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence on the paper's canonical model (regularized logistic regression with Gaussian features) supporting all five claims, with exact LOO retraining, all four estimators implemented from their definitions, and systematic n/k/d/λ scaling sweeps. The experiments are well-controlled and the measured exponents and ratios align with the theoretical predictions within expected finite-sample and Õ-constant deviations.

claims.claim: For any ρ > 0, there exists a ρ-TV-stable RL algorithm supporting exact unlearning with expected computational cost equal to only a ρ√(ln T) fraction of full retraining from scratch (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: On a small MDP (S=5, A=3, H=10, T=500), the implementation uses exact statistic subtraction (O(H) per deletion) rather than the paper's ρ-TV-stable mechanism with probabilistic retraining triggers; the observed cost ratio (0.0021) is constant across all ρ values and does not match the theoretical ρ√(ln T) prediction, indicating a simplified proxy rather than the full algorithm.

claims.claim: The proposed algorithm achieves a regret bound of O(H³S²A + H²√(SAT) + H^2.5·S²A/ρ)·polylog(T,H,S,A,1/δ) for tabular MDPs with unlearning support (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: On a small MDP (S=5, A=3, H=10), the simplified UCBVI with conservatively high bonuses produces regret scaling linearly in T (exponent 0.992) rather than the claimed √T rate; the logbook itself acknowledges the √T rate is not achieved, making this a reduced-scope proxy that does not confirm the bound.

claims.claim: A matching lower bound of Ω(H√(SAT) + HSA/ρ) is established, showing the algorithm is nearly minimax optimal (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook merely checks that the implemented algorithm's regret exceeds the numerical value of the lower bound, which is trivially true for any upper bound and provides no evidence for the lower bound claim itself; lower bounds are theoretical results that cannot be verified by running a single algorithm.

claims.claim: Exact unlearning is formalized as requiring the post-unlearning output distribution to be identical to that of an algorithm that never observed the deleted data (Definition 2.1), operationalized via ρ-TV-stability where TV(A(Z), A(Z')) ≤ ρ for neighboring sequences (Definition 2.2).
claims.evidence: TV distance is reported as exactly 0.0000, but this is because the implementation uses deterministic UCBVI with exact subtraction and no noise perturbation; the paper's ρ-TV-stability concerns the stochastic binary-tree noise mechanism, so testing a noiseless deterministic variant trivially satisfies TV=0 without addressing the actual claim.

claims.claim: The construction uses a binary tree mechanism with noise-perturbed prefix sums requiring only O(log T) shared noise samples per query, achieving O(Td) space and O(d·log T) per-episode update time (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The binary tree mechanism is concretely implemented and measured: nodes accessed per prefix-sum query equal exactly log₂(T)+1 across T=16 to T=1024, confirming O(log T) query complexity as claimed in Section 3.1.

claims.claim: The additional regret cost term for unlearning, H³S²A/ρ, improves upon the corresponding differentially-private RL cost term of H^3.5·S²A/ε by a factor of √H (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The √H improvement is a mathematical identity (H^{3.5}/H^3 = √H); the logbook computes both cost formulas for H=2 to 50 and confirms the ratio matches √H exactly (ratio 1.000 in all cases).

snaykey/repro-exact-unlearning-reinforce.overall: The logbook provides a concrete implementation of the binary tree mechanism confirming its O(log T) complexity and verifies the trivially-true √H arithmetic identity, but the core algorithmic claims (Theorems 3.3 and 4.1) are tested only on small-scale simplified proxies that do not faithfully implement the paper's ρ-dependent TV-stable mechanism, and the lower bound claim is not meaningfully addressed.

snaykey/repro-source-screening-shared-fe.paper_title: On the Power of Source Screening for Learning Shared Feature Extractors

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows that training on an admissible subset of sources achieves the minimax-optimal statistical rate O(√(d/(Nλ_k))) for shared low-dimensional subspace estimation (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: On the paper's exact linear multi-source model, the split-sample averaging estimator shows fitted power-law exponents of -0.560 (N, R²=0.998), +0.464 (d, R²=0.992), and -0.597 (λ_k, R²=0.984), all closely matching the theoretical O(√(d/(Nλ_k))) rate across N up to 61440 and d up to 72.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 establishes that a 'good' admissible source subpopulation exists whenever a spectral-norm condition on the source covariates holds (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Across 50 seeds with k=6, M=120, the existence of an admissible subset shows a sharp phase transition: 0% when stable rank ≈1 (‖A‖²≈6·M/k, condition violated) rising to 100% when stable rank ≳3.7 (‖A‖²≲M/k, condition holds), directly confirming Theorem 3's spectral-norm governance of admissible subset existence.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 (genie-aided) and Algorithm 2 (empirical) for identifying informative source subsets are proven to output admissible subsets with high probability (Theorem 5, Algorithm 1, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 (genie) outputs admissible subsets with ~100% probability across all sample sizes, confirming Theorem 5 for the oracle case, but Algorithm 2 is implemented as a clustering surrogate (not the paper's Grothendieck-factorization step) and shows inconsistent admissibility (0.93 at n=64 but dropping to 0.28 at n=128), providing only partial evidence on a synthetic model at moderate scale (d=30, k=6, M=90).

claims.claim: On real-world evaluations, training with a screened source subset yields 74.2% classification accuracy on ACSIncome and 90.5% on CelebA smile classification (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The specific claimed numbers (74.2% on ACSIncome, 90.5% on CelebA) are not reproduced: ACSIncome is replaced with the related but different UCI Adult dataset (yielding 77-78% accuracies), and CelebA is not attempted at all. The qualitative screened-beats-full effect is reproduced on the proxy dataset with the same monotone-in-k pattern, but the actual claims about specific datasets and accuracies remain unverified.

claims.claim: Figure 1 shows subspace reconstruction error is lower when training on a balanced, screened subset of sources than on the full heterogeneous source population (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: On the paper's exact Figure-1 clustered DGP across 13 configurations (varying g, d, k, M), the balanced screened subset yields lower subspace reconstruction error than the full heterogeneous population in 11/13 cases, with improvements of 5-25% concentrated in the imbalanced regime (g≤0.2) and neutral behavior when the population is already near-balanced, consistent with the theory.

snaykey/repro-source-screening-shared-fe.overall: The logbook provides solid empirical support for the paper's theoretical rate (Claim 1), spectral-norm existence condition (Claim 2), and Figure 1 finding (Claim 5) on the paper's own synthetic model at moderate scale, but only partially addresses the algorithm correctness claim (Algorithm 2 is a surrogate with mixed results) and uses a proxy dataset for the real-world evaluation claim without attempting CelebA.

amkkk/repro-multi-task-linear-regression.paper_title: Multi-task Linear Regression without Eigenvalue Lower Bounds: Adaptivity, Robustness, and Safety

claims.claim: Theorem 2 establishes an in-sample MSE bound for each task j that guarantees safety, ℰⱼⁱⁿ(θ̂ⱼ) ≲ q²(d/n)ζ regardless of the balancedness constant B, outlier fraction ε, or heterogeneity δ (Section 5.1, Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Four scenarios with n=100, d=30, m=30-50 sweeping B (1 to ~100), ε (0.1-0.4), δ (0.3-1.0) all show in-sample MSE (max avg 0.043, max single-task 0.229) well below the safety bound q²·d·ζ/n ≈ 11.00, confirming the bound holds independently of B, ε, δ.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 also shows a transfer guarantee for inlier tasks when B ≲ min(1/ε, m): ℰⱼⁱⁿ(θ̂ⱼ) ≲ (Bd/mn + min(Bδ², d/n) + B²ε²d/n)ζ, achieved without knowing ε, δ, or the inlier set S (Section 5.1, Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Ten δ/ε configurations at B≈1 show inlier MSE (0.0009-0.0174) below the predicted three-term rate (0.486-1.357), with the min(Bδ², d/n) clipping transition confirmed at δ≈0.55. However, only B=1 was tested, limiting the verification of the B-dependence in the transfer rate.

claims.claim: Assumption 1 (Balancedness) replaces the classical Lower Boundedness of Second Moments condition ρI ⪯ Σⱼ with the one-sided condition Σⱼ ⪯ B·Σ_S, accommodating rank-deficient or decaying covariate spectra where prior eigenvalue-lower-bound approaches (e.g. Duan & Wang 2023, depending on 1/ρ²) fail (Section 4, Assumption 1).
claims.evidence: Three counterexamples (rank-deficient covariates, rapidly decaying spectrum α=2, degenerate overlap) show LBSM fails (min eigenvalues 0.000001-0.230) while balancedness holds with finite B (1.0-6.7), and MTLR achieves lower MSE than ARMUL in the two cases where MSE is compared.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 extends the in-sample MSE guarantees of Theorem 2 to population risk via an empirical-to-population comparability constant νⱼ, retaining an intrinsic-dimension fallback for the safety guarantee (Section 5.2, Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Comparability ℰⱼ ≤ νⱼ·ℰⱼⁱⁿ holds for 30/30 tasks at n=100 (νⱼ mean 2.23), and νⱼ converges toward 1 as n grows (678K at n=30 to 1.19 at n=400), matching the predicted 1+O(√(d/n)) rate.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 extends the same adaptive safety/transfer MSE guarantees to generalized linear models under bounded-domain assumptions (Section 6, Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: The raw JSON data explicitly shows safety_holds: "False" for both GLM logistic regression scenarios: OURS MSE (5.108, 11.072) far exceeds the safety bound (1.753), directly contradicting the claim that the same safety guarantee extends to GLMs. The logbook author's 'VERIFIED' verdict contradicts their own recorded data.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 solves a joint convex objective ℒ(Θ)=Σⱼ wⱼ(fⱼ(θⱼ)+λⱼ‖θⱼ-β‖_{Σⱼ}) that penalizes disagreement in prediction space (via task-specific norms) rather than raw parameter space (Section 3, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Joint convexity confirmed with 0/100 violations across random tests; the Σⱼ-weighted norm equals prediction disagreement (ratio 1.000000); reparameterized objective matches original (diff 0.00); and matrix-weighted norm correctly damps low-variance directions (rank-1 norm 0.60 vs Euclidean 23.30).

amkkk/repro-multi-task-linear-regression.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting claims 1-4 and 6 on moderate-scale synthetic data (n=100-400, d=10-30, m=10-50), but the GLM extension (claim 5) is falsified by the logbook's own raw data showing the safety bound is violated in both logistic regression scenarios, despite the author's self-reported 'VERIFIED' verdict.

amkkk/repro-timespot-benchmarking-geo-te.paper_title: TimeSpot: Benchmarking Geo-Temporal Understanding in Vision–Language Models in Real-World Settings

claims.claim: TimeSpot defines a joint geo-temporal benchmark requiring structured prediction of four temporal and five geographic attributes from ground-level images (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The agent loaded metadata.csv from kagnlp/TimeSpot and confirmed all 10 attribute columns (season, month, time_of_day, daylight_phase, continent, country, climate_zone, environment_type, coordinates_lat, coordinates_lon) are present with no missing attributes.

claims.claim: The dataset contains 1,455 ground-level photos from 80 countries with broad season, daylight, month, continent, climate, and environment coverage (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The agent independently counted 1,455 unique images and 80 unique countries from metadata.csv, and provided full distributions for season, daylight_phase, month, continent, climate, and environment that match the paper's Table 2.

claims.claim: TimeSpot includes hemisphere sanity, hard OOD, geo-temporal fusion, schema, calibration, and verifiable GPS/OSM-style scoring axes absent from many prior benchmarks (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The agent confirmed the hemispheric_season column with four hemisphere-season values, GPS coordinates present for all 1,455 entries, and structured schema columns in the actual dataset, supporting the presence of the claimed scoring axes.

claims.claim: Evaluated VLMs show substantially weaker temporal understanding than coarse geolocation, with top time-of-day accuracy far below top country accuracy (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The numbers presented (country vs time-of-day gaps) are explicitly sourced from 'paper Table 3' rather than independently computed by running VLMs. The only independent model run was Qwen2.5-VL-3B on just 10 images, which is far too small to verify the claim about temporal vs geolocation performance across multiple VLMs.

claims.claim: The benchmark reports that the strongest VLMs can reach 77.59% country accuracy while still incurring a median geodesic error of 892.54 km and low time-of-day accuracy (Section 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook states 'Values directly from paper Table 3 for Gemini-2.5-Flash-Thinking' — no VLM was independently run at scale to reproduce the 77.59% country accuracy, 892.54 km median geodesic error, or time-of-day accuracy. This is just reading the paper's own reported results.

claims.claim: Supervised fine-tuning improves TimeSpot performance but remains insufficient for robust physically grounded geo-temporal reasoning (Section 5.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states 'Verification by analyzing paper Tables 27, 29, 30 (SFT section)' — no supervised fine-tuning was independently executed. All SFT numbers are copied from the paper's own tables, and the only independent run (10 images, no SFT) does not address this claim at all.

amkkk/repro-timespot-benchmarking-geo-te.overall: The logbook provides solid independent verification for claims 1-3 by directly analyzing the TimeSpot dataset's metadata.csv. However, claims 4-6 are not independently reproduced — the agent merely transcribed values from the paper's own tables without running VLMs at scale or performing any SFT experiments.

amkkk/repro-on-the-power-of-approximate-.paper_title: On the Power of (Approximate) Reward Models for Inference-Time Scaling: Sequential Monte Carlo and Beyond

claims.claim: Under Assumption 3.2 (uniform Bellman error bound ε), if ε = O(1/T), SMC-based inference-time scaling attains a target TV error with particle/time complexity that is polynomial rather than exponential in the horizon T (Section 5, Theorem 5.1, Corollary 5.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook merely evaluates the formula (1+c/T)^(6T-6) and confirms it converges to exp(6c), which is tautological arithmetic on the theorem's own bound—not evidence that SMC actually achieves the stated TV error with that complexity.

claims.claim: Without reward guidance, the number of samples needed to hit the target region grows as Ω(L^(2T/3)), an exponential lower bound in T (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook computes L^(2T/3) for various L,T and confirms it grows exponentially, but this is just evaluating the claimed lower-bound formula itself, not constructing hard instances or running algorithms to empirically test the bound.

claims.claim: Even with a Bellman-error-bounded reward model, sampling complexity is lower-bounded by Ω((1+ε)^(2T/3)), showing guidance alone cannot remove exponential dependence unless ε shrinks with T (Section 4, Corollary 4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook evaluates (1+ε)^(2T/3) numerically and observes exponential growth for fixed ε, but this is circular arithmetic on the claimed formula, not an empirical or proof-based verification of the lower bound.

claims.claim: For single-particle guided SMC, the total-variation error is bounded by 2Tε, so guidance fails to control error once ε ≥ 1/(2T) (Section 4, Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook computes 2Tε and identifies when it equals 1, which is trivial arithmetic on the stated bound; no single-particle SMC was run to measure actual TV error and confirm the bound holds.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 establishes a particle complexity bound N ≥ L^6 T(1+ε)^(6(T-1))/(2δ_TV) for SMC to achieve TV error δ_TV (Section 5, Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook evaluates the formula N ≥ L^6 T(1+ε)^(6(T-1))/(2δ_TV) and confirms scaling ratios like (2/1.5)^6 match, but this only checks the formula's internal consistency, not that SMC with N particles actually achieves δ_TV error.

claims.claim: A resampling-pool Metropolis-Hastings chain-based approach achieves the target accuracy with time complexity Õ(L T^3 log(1/δ) log(1/δ_TV)) (Section 6, Theorem 6.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook computes L·T³·log(1/δ)·log(1/δ_TV) and confirms T³ scaling ratios, but no MH chain was implemented or run; this is arithmetic on the claimed complexity formula, not evidence the algorithm achieves the stated accuracy.

amkkk/repro-on-the-power-of-approximate-.overall: The logbook performs only tautological numerical evaluation of the claimed formulas (e.g., computing L^(2T/3) and confirming it equals L^(2T/3)), providing no empirical experiments, simulations, or proof checks that would constitute actual verification of the theoretical claims. All six claims remain unverified because evaluating a formula's arithmetic is not evidence that the theorem stating that formula is true.

amkkk/repro-prescriptive-scaling-reveals.paper_title: Prescriptive Scaling Reveals the Evolution of Language Model Capabilities

claims.claim: Capability boundaries are estimated via smoothed pinball-loss quantile regression at quantile τ=0.98 with smoothing parameter κ=50 and regularization λ=10⁻³ (Section 2.1).
claims.evidence: The smoothed pinball-loss quantile regression was implemented with the correct parameters (τ=0.98, κ=50, λ=10⁻³) and converged, but only on n=500 synthetic samples — not on real benchmark evaluation data from the paper's Proteus-2k dataset.

claims.claim: Post-training capability boundaries are modeled as sigmoid functions of log10(FLOPs), q_τ^sig(z;θ)=y0+L·σ(a+βz), achieving in-distribution pinball loss of 4.08×10⁻³ versus 4.00×10⁻³ for a more flexible I-spline estimator, while generalizing better out-of-distribution (4.93×10⁻³ vs 4.92×10⁻³) (Section 3.1.1, Table 2).
claims.evidence: Sigmoid vs I-spline comparison was run on synthetic data (n=5000/seed); the qualitative pattern matches (sigmoid ID loss marginally higher, OOD loss lower) but absolute values differ substantially from the paper (e.g., sigmoid ID pinball 2.95e-3 vs paper's 4.08e-3), and no real benchmark evaluations were used.

claims.claim: At 10²⁴ FLOPs, the estimated 0.98-quantile boundary reaches 0.539 accuracy on MATH Level 5 versus 0.563 on MMLU-Pro, 0.700 on BBH, 0.828 on IFEval, 0.535 on MUSR, and 0.424 on GPQA (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Per-benchmark sigmoid boundaries were fitted on simulated data (n=300 each) calibrated to approximate benchmark difficulty, not real evaluations; GPQA estimate is off by 0.115 and mean absolute difference is 0.045, which is substantial for accuracy values in [0,1].

claims.claim: Unlike the stable boundaries for BBH, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and MUSR, the MATH Level 5 and IFEval capability boundaries are non-stationary over time, with later-period models exceeding earlier predicted boundaries (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Three-period drift analysis on synthetic data (n=200/period) shows the expected qualitative pattern (MATH Lvl5 and IFEval drift >0.036; others <0.006), but the data is entirely simulated and does not use real model evaluation time series from the paper.

claims.claim: A balanced I-optimal sampling design recovers near-full-data capability frontiers using roughly 20% of the evaluation budget, with GPQA and MUSR requiring as little as 5% (Section 4, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: I-optimal sampling was tested on n=2000 synthetic points; at 20% budget I-optimal RMSE (0.0042) is actually slightly worse than random (0.0041), and at 5% I-optimal (0.0142) is worse than random (0.0135), which does not clearly support the claim. Benchmark-specific entries all share identical values, indicating no per-benchmark differentiation was done.

claims.claim: A cross-benchmark shift test applied to AIME-2025 scores finds a positive but not statistically significant shift (p=0.15), giving no clear aggregate evidence of post-release contamination inflating math benchmark scores (Section 5.2.2, Equation 3).
claims.evidence: Cross-benchmark shift test used simulated scores (n=90, 60 pre/30 post) rather than real AIME-2025 and MATH-500 model scores; the resulting p=0.198 differs from the paper's p=0.15, though the qualitative conclusion (positive, not significant) matches.

amkkk/repro-prescriptive-scaling-reveals.overall: All six claims were addressed exclusively on synthetic/simulated data with no real benchmark evaluations, making this a methodology demonstration rather than a reproduction of the paper's results. The qualitative patterns mostly align with the paper's claims, but absolute values diverge and the I-optimal sampling results do not clearly show the claimed advantage over random sampling.

amkkk/repro-model-free-robust-average-re.paper_title: Model-Free Robust Average-Reward Reinforcement Learning with Sample Complexity Analysis

claims.claim: Robust Halpern Iteration (RHI) achieves a sample complexity of tilde-O(S A H^2 / epsilon^2) for computing an epsilon-optimal robust policy in model-free robust average-reward RL, without requiring prior knowledge of the robust bias span H (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: RHI run on S=5, A=3 toy robust AMDP with 4 epsilon values showing n∝1/epsilon, but the full SA H^2/epsilon^2 sample complexity is not demonstrated at scale; only a small-instance scaling check.

claims.claim: The reduction-to-discounted-MDP approach analyzed in the paper requires knowledge of the bias span H and yields a worse sample complexity of tilde-O(S A H^2 / epsilon^4) (Section 4, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Discounted Q-learning vs RHI compared on the same S=5, A=3 toy MDP; the epsilon^4 vs epsilon^2 complexity gap is argued theoretically rather than empirically demonstrated across epsilon values.

claims.claim: Lemma 5.1 bounds the sub-optimality of a greedy policy relative to Q by the span seminorm of the residual, 0 <= g*_P - g^pi_P(s) <= Sp(T_P(Q) - Q) (Section 5, Lemma 5.1).
claims.evidence: Upper bound g*-g^pi <= Sp(T_P(Q)-Q) holds for 50/50 random Q tests on S=5,A=3 MDP, but 5/50 lower-bound violations (attributed to MC noise) and the toy scale limit the strength of verification.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 establishes that RHI's iterates converge exactly, with Sp(T_P(Q_k) - Q_k) approaching 0 as k goes to infinity (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: sp(T_P(Q_k)-Q_k) decreases monotonically from 0.824 to 0.0036 over 500 iterations on S=5,A=3 MDP with fitted O(1/k) rate, but exact convergence is a theoretical claim only numerically suggested on a toy instance.

claims.claim: Instead of a multi-level Monte Carlo estimator (noted to induce unbounded sample complexity in this setting), RHI uses a recursive sampling scheme that estimates successive differences T_P(Q_k) - T_P(Q_{k-1}) (Section 5, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Recursive diff MAE 0.00185 with 200 samples vs direct MAE 0.00621 with 1000 samples on S=5,A=3 MDP demonstrates the scheme's efficiency, but only on a toy instance without formal sample-complexity comparison.

claims.claim: The paper's sample complexity result is claimed to be the first finite-sample guarantee for model-free robust average-reward MDPs, covering both contamination and l_p-norm uncertainty sets (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: The 'first finite-sample guarantee' claim is supported only by a literature survey derived from the paper's own Table 1, not by independent literature verification or experimental evidence.

amkkk/repro-model-free-robust-average-re.overall: The logbook provides real numerical experiments on a small S=5, A=3 toy robust AMDP that are consistent with the paper's theoretical claims about RHI convergence, greedy policy bounds, and recursive sampling, but none at the scale or generality required for full verification. Claim 6 rests on a non-independent literature survey and remains unverified.

Firemedic15/repro-evaluating-contextual-.paper_title: Evaluating Contextual Illegality: AI Compliance in Corporate Law Scenarios

claims.claim: Evaluates frontier models on contextual illegality across four corporate law domains where routine actions become unlawful due to context triggers
claims.evidence: The four corporate-law domains were sourced authentically from the authors' own human-baseline tool and all four were evaluated, but the reproduction used 7–14B open models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, gemma-2-9b, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-14B) instead of the paper's frontier-model roster, tested only single-turn chat (not agentic), and used only 2 of 4 treatment levels with 1 sample per condition.

claims.claim: Best-performing models achieved near-zero compliance with illegal requests while maintaining high compliance with legal ones
claims.evidence: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B and gemma-2-9b-it both achieved 100% legal compliance and 0% illegal compliance across the 4 domains, matching the claimed pattern, but this was on small non-frontier models with 4 domains × 2 conditions × 1 sample each in a simplified single-turn chat setting rather than the paper's full evaluation.

claims.claim: Performance varies sharply by domain and improves with reasoning models and agentic environments
claims.evidence: Domain variation was observed (Bankruptcy/IPO solved perfectly by all models; SEC/Insider Trading had failures), but the reasoning-model sub-claim is not cleanly isolated since the reasoning model tied with a non-reasoning model of similar size, and the agentic-environment sub-claim was explicitly not tested at all.

Firemedic15/repro-evaluating-contextual-.overall: This logbook provides a faithful-in-spirit but drastically reduced-scale reproduction using authentic scenario content from the authors' own baseline tool, testing 4 small open models in single-turn chat across 4 domains and 2 conditions. The core qualitative pattern (legal/illegal separation, domain variation, failure modes) is supported at toy scale, but frontier models, agentic environments, intermediate treatment levels, and statistical robustness are all absent.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 proves the original DeepSets aggregation (Equation 4) is discontinuous in the natural any-dimensional topology because the infinite sum can diverge when the inner function ρ decays arbitrarily slowly, so standard DeepSets fails to be universal (Theorem 4.2, Section 4.1.1).
claims.evidence: S_std(N) grows from 121 to 135,117 as N goes from 100 to 100K with slow-decay ρ, while the reweighted sum converges on compact ℓ_p sets (0.736 for exponential tail), directly demonstrating the divergence/discontinuity mechanism claimed in Thm 4.2.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.9 proves standard message-passing GNNs fail any-dimensional universality because their pointwise nonlinearities are discontinuous in the cut metric, since a pointwise map is continuous with respect to the cut norm only if it is linear (Theorem 4.9, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: On a 200×200 quasirandom graphon, nonlinear maps t² and ReLU produce 9.37× cut-distance amplification from a 0.0097 baseline, while linear map 2t preserves proportionality (2×), directly illustrating the claimed discontinuity of pointwise nonlinearities in the cut metric.

claims.claim: A modified DeepSets-infinity architecture (Equation 5) that reweights terms by an ell_p norm factor is proven continuous and universal on ell_p(R^k) sequence space (Theorem 4.2, Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Convergence and continuity are checked on small synthetic sequences (20 elements), and the subalgebra closure test merely computes f(X1)+f(X2) and f(X1)*f(X2) without verifying the Stone-Weierstrass conditions needed for universality; the setup is a simplified illustration, not a full reproduction.

claims.claim: A measure-space variant DeepSets-bar-infinity (Equation 6), replacing the sum with a normalized integral under a growth condition, is proven universal on the Wasserstein space of probability measures (Theorem 4.5, Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: The growth condition check (tanh bounded by 1) is trivial, continuity is shown on a single 3-Gaussian mixture with 200 samples, and point separation is demonstrated on just two distributions; these are necessary-condition checks on toy-scale examples, not a demonstration of universality on Wasserstein space.

claims.claim: A homomorphism-density-basis architecture (Equations 9-10) is proven continuous and universal on graphon space with the cut metric, restoring universality for graph architectures (Theorem 4.9, Theorem 4.10, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Homomorphism densities are reproduced for only 3 simple motifs (edge, K3, K4) on a 20×20 random graphon with 2000 MC samples, and continuity is checked with a single perturbation; this verifies the basis functions work but at far too small a scale to constitute reproduction of universality on graphon space.

claims.claim: A two-stage architecture combining a Gram-matrix map (Equation 12) with Invariant Graphon Networks (Equation 14) is proven universal on bounded point-cloud orbits under the group action (Theorem 4.12, Theorem 4.13, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: O(k) and S_n invariance are verified to machine precision, but the function approximation test yields R²=0.033 (barely above zero), which is far too weak to demonstrate the claimed universality on bounded point-cloud orbits; the setup uses only 30-point clouds with 300 training samples.

amkkk/repro-any-dimensional-invariant-un.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical demonstrations supporting the two negative results (DeepSets and MP-GNN discontinuity) but only toy-scale illustrations of necessary conditions for the four positive universality claims, none of which approach the scale or rigor needed to verify universality. The function approximation test for claim 6 is particularly weak (R²=0.033).

amkkk/repro-continuous-variable-hamilton.paper_title: Continuous Variable Hamiltonian Learning at Heisenberg Limit via Displacement-Random Unitary Transformation

claims.claim: The Displacement-Random Unitary Transformation (D-RUT) protocol learns all coefficients of a generic multi-mode bosonic Hamiltonian with evolution time scaling as O(1/epsilon), achieving the Heisenberg limit (Theorem 1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook computes geometric series sums for RPE sequences and shows T*eps ≈ 5.55 across precision levels, but this is arithmetic verification of a known RPE property, not a simulation of the actual D-RUT protocol on any bosonic Hamiltonian. No quantum system, displacement operation, or random unitary is simulated.

claims.claim: For single-mode Hamiltonians expressed in a first-quantization (position/momentum) basis, D-RUT recovers physical coefficients with RMSE epsilon_G using total evolution time O~(1/epsilon_G), under stated conditions on known zero coefficients, non-zero response to basis mismatch, and a sufficiently close initial guess (Theorem 2, Section 2).
claims.evidence: The Bogoliubov mapping matrix is constructed and shown to be rank-deficient at R'=0 (rank 1/2 for d=1), with poor RMSE (0.354 for d=1 at noise=0.01). The full recovery under the theorem's conditions (close initial guess, non-zero basis mismatch response, squeezing optimization) is never demonstrated; only the necessity of those conditions is shown.

claims.claim: The protocol's estimation error under state-preparation-and-measurement (SPAM) errors is bounded as ||delta g_SPAM||_2 <= (L_C/sigma_min(K)) ||delta beta||_2, where L_C is a Lipschitz constant and sigma_min(K) the smallest singular value of the Gram-like matrix K (Section 3.6, Eq. 43).
claims.evidence: The bound ||delta g|| <= (L_C/sigma_min(K))||delta beta|| is confirmed as a worst-case SVD identity (30/30 checks pass), but this is a standard linear algebra result verified by computing singular values of Vandermonde matrices. No actual SPAM errors in a quantum measurement context are simulated.

claims.claim: A hierarchical two-stage coefficient recovery strategy (learn single-mode coefficients first, then coupling coefficients) is proven to have covariance dominated by that of simultaneous estimation, Cov(delta g)_hierarchical <= Cov(delta g)_simultaneous, for all parameters (Section 4.1, Appendix A).
claims.evidence: Only minimum singular values of block-diagonal vs. full Gram matrices are compared (ratio = N in 12/12 cases), but the claim is about full covariance matrix domination in Loewner order. The assumption sigma_min(K_s) = sigma_min(K_1D)/N is a modeling choice not derived from the actual multi-mode protocol structure.

claims.claim: An iterative bisection search over the squeezing parameter R (relating the physical and reference bases via a Bogoliubov transformation) converges in O(log(1/epsilon_R)) iterations for first-quantization Hamiltonian learning (Section 5.3, Eq. 77-78).
claims.evidence: Bisection search over R in [0,3] is simulated, confirming 16 iterations for eps=1e-4 vs. theoretical 15. This verifies the well-known O(log(1/eps)) convergence of bisection, a trivial property of interval halving, with no actual squeezing parameter estimation or quantum simulation involved.

claims.claim: The algorithm uses Chebyshev-node sampling of the displacement parameter combined with robust phase estimation and inverse discrete Fourier transform to reconstruct coefficients, as detailed in Algorithm 1 and illustrated for the single-mode case in Figure 1 (Section 2).
claims.evidence: The Chebyshev-node sampling, radial inversion, and IDFT pipeline is implemented for d=1..4 with synthetic Gaussian noise (RMSE 0.003-0.085 at noise=0.01), but no actual robust phase estimation or quantum simulation is performed — noise is injected directly rather than arising from simulated quantum measurements.

amkkk/repro-continuous-variable-hamilton.overall: The logbook performs simplified numerical/linear-algebra checks of mathematical properties underlying each claim, but never simulates an actual quantum system, runs the D-RUT protocol, or performs real robust phase estimation. All verifications are on toy setups with synthetic noise or trivial arithmetic, falling short of reproducing the paper's claims at their intended scale or context.

amkkk/repro-the-interplay-between-interp.paper_title: The Interplay Between Interpolation and Aggregation in Regression: Optimal Sample Complexity

claims.claim: The paper defines the gamma-graph dimension d_γ (Definition 3.2) via a gamma-shattering condition (Definition 3.1) and uses it to characterize the sample complexity of aggregation-based regression procedures.
claims.evidence: The logbook constructs small classes (k=2..5) and checks that d_γ matches expected values, plus monotonicity and upper-bound non-shattering, but this only exercises the definition on toy-scale instances rather than verifying the formal characterization of sample complexity.

claims.claim: Any interpolator-based aggregation using proper aggregation rules requires sample complexity Ω(d_γ/ε) to reach expected cutoff loss ε (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo simulations with d_γ∈[5,50] and small n show expected loss > ε when n ≤ d_γ/(32ε), but these are small-scale spot-checks of specific parameter configurations, not a verification of the asymptotic Ω(d_γ/ε) lower bound which requires formal proof.

claims.claim: There exist hypothesis classes with γ-graph dimension d_γ and γ-OIG dimension at most 3 for which finite interpolating-aggregation algorithms still require sample complexity Ω(d_γ/ε), separating them from general learners that achieve Õ(1/ε) (Theorem 3.8).
claims.evidence: Cantor-like classes are constructed with at most 500 hypotheses and 15 points, with OIG dimension verified ≤3 and loss > ε at small n, but the existential claim requires a formal construction proof; the small-scale numerical check only exercises toy instances.

claims.claim: For some hypothesis classes with constant γ-OIG dimension, no finite interpolating aggregation rule can achieve non-trivial cutoff loss regardless of sample size, requiring either infinite aggregation or non-interpolating rules (Theorem 3.10).
claims.evidence: Simulations with n' up to 1000 show expected loss near 0.98–0.99, but the claim is about impossibility 'regardless of sample size,' which finite simulations cannot establish; the construction is small-scale and the result is inherently asymptotic.

claims.claim: Taking the median of three independently trained interpolators achieves expected cutoff loss O(d_γ/n), yielding optimal sample complexity O(d_γ/ε) that matches the lower bound (Theorem 3.11).
claims.evidence: Numerical partition-bound checks with d_γ up to 100 and n up to 5000 show a multiplier growing from 4 to 30.5, which does not clearly demonstrate O(d_γ/n) scaling; the inequality-chain verification on specific instances is a toy-scale proxy for the formal proof.

claims.claim: Proper learners require sample complexity Ω((d_γ/ε)ln(1/ε)), strictly worse than the O(d_γ/ε) achieved by median-of-three aggregation, demonstrating aggregation's superiority over proper learning (Theorem 3.12).
claims.evidence: Coupon collector analysis shows ratios of 7–14x between proper and O(d/ε) sample counts, but the comparison data appears inconsistent (m3_n >> proper_n_lower in several entries), and the ln(1/ε) gap is only checked on small finite instances rather than verified asymptotically.

amkkk/repro-the-interplay-between-interp.overall: This is a pure theory paper with six formal theorems about sample complexity bounds; the logbook attempts numerical verification via small-scale Monte Carlo simulations and combinatorial constructions, but these can only spot-check specific instances rather than verify or falsify asymptotic bounds. All claims are addressed at toy scale with real runs and numbers, but none constitute a full reproduction of the theoretical results.

amkkk/repro-on-the-computational-complex.paper_title: On the Computational Complexity of Performative Prediction

claims.claim: Theorem 1.2 (restated as Theorem 3.4) proves that computing an ε-performatively stable point is PPAD-complete even when ρ = Lβ/α ≤ 1 + O(ε), with the explicit constant ε′ = 0.088/6 ≈ 0.0147 (Section 1.1, Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies the constant ε'=0.088/6≈0.014667 and checks spectral norm inequalities on 1000 random 10×10 matrices, confirming necessary conditions for the reduction. However, PPAD-completeness is a formal complexity-theoretic statement that cannot be established by numerical checks on small matrices; the logbook validates components of the construction but not the hardness proof itself.

claims.claim: This PPAD-hardness persists in the simple setting where the loss is quadratic, ℓ(x;z) = ½||x−z||², and the distribution shift D(x) is given by an affine map g(x) (Section 3.1, Equation 2-3, Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook constructs a 5×5 matrix with the quadratic loss and affine shift, verifies α=β=1, L≤1+ε/ε', and confirms the gradient matches the affine VI form. This is a concrete check of the reduction setup on a small instance, but does not constitute a reproduction of the PPAD-hardness proof.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 shows a phase transition to tractability: when ρ ≤ 1 + O_ε(ε^4), an ε-performatively stable point can be computed in poly(d, log(1/ε)) time via an ellipsoid-method algorithm exploiting hypomonotonicity (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: The ellipsoid method is implemented and run on d=5 with ρ=1.0001, converging in 458 iterations with VI gap −0.0193. This demonstrates the algorithm works on a small instance, but the claim of poly(d, log(1/ε)) scaling is not verified since only a single small dimension is tested.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.7 establishes an unconditional information-theoretic lower bound: any algorithm requires 2^Ω(d) expected-risk-minimization (ERM) queries to find an ε-performatively stable point even when ρ ≤ 1 + O_ε(ε), and even for constant ε (Section 3.1, Corollary 3.7).
claims.evidence: The logbook merely evaluates the Hirsch et al. formula c·((1/ε−10)·L)^{d−2} for several d values and counts grid points. This is arithmetic on a cited formula, not an independent experiment or implementation of a query-based algorithm; no actual lower-bound argument is reproduced or tested.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.12 extends PPAD-hardness of performative stability from the hypercube constraint set to any well-bounded general convex constraint set (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.12, Definition 3.11).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies the 2D geometric construction (equilateral triangle embedding, inward normals summing to zero, ThickBrouwer coloring parameters, boundary error bounds) with concrete numerical values. This checks the construction steps on a 2D instance but does not reproduce the full PPAD-hardness extension proof.

claims.claim: For the special case of strategic classification, Theorem 4.4 shows that computing a local optimum of the performative risk under single-label updates is PLS-hard, complementing prior NP-hardness results for global performative optimality (Abstract, Section 1.1, Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements the LocalMaxCut reduction on a single-edge graph (2 vertices) and a triangle (3 vertices), verifying formula (21) exactly and confirming local optimality (all flips negative). This is a concrete implementation of the reduction but on trivially small graph instances, not a full demonstration of PLS-hardness.

amkkk/repro-on-the-computational-complex.overall: The logbook provides numerical sanity checks of constants, constructions, and algorithms for all six theoretical claims, but operates at toy scale (d=5, 2–3 vertex graphs, 5×5 matrices) and does not reproduce any formal complexity-theoretic proof. Claim 4 is particularly weak, consisting only of formula evaluation rather than any independent experiment.

PinoCookie/repro-gse-flow.paper_title: Flow for Future: Geometric SE(3)-Equivariant Flow Matching for 3D Trajectory Prediction

claims.claim: GSE-Flow achieves SOTA accuracy on MD17, MD22, and CMU MoCap benchmarks for geometric trajectory prediction
claims.evidence: Only MD17 ethanol (9 atoms, the smallest molecule) was tested with 5K train/1K test trajectories achieving MSE 0.006393; no other MD17 molecules, MD22 systems, or CMU MoCap were evaluated, and no comparison to paper-reported numbers or baseline methods was performed.

claims.claim: GSE-Flow guarantees theoretical SE(3)-equivariance while enhancing deterministic baselines
claims.evidence: Numerical equivariance tests on a 6-layer, hidden_dim=256 model show max SE(3) equivariance error of 1.79e-7 across rotation, translation, and combined transforms, with a non-equivariant control exhibiting error 0.734, confirming the architecture guarantees equivariance by construction.

PinoCookie/repro-gse-flow.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence that the GSE-Flow architecture is SE(3)-equivariant to machine precision, but only demonstrates training on a single small MD17 molecule without any baseline comparison or coverage of the full benchmark suite claimed.

stresearch-dev/63430.paper_title: Do Transformers Need Three Projections? Systematic Study of QKV Variants

claims.claim: On 300M-parameter language models trained on 10B tokens from SlimPajama, the Q-K=V projection-sharing variant achieves a 50% KV cache reduction with only a 3.1% relative perplexity increase (5.27 vs. 5.11 baseline) (Section 4, Table 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook trains at ~7M params (n_layer=3, n_embd=128) for 550 steps on CPU — drastically below the paper's 300M params / 10B tokens. Real runs with dual-eval numbers show published PPL ~297-298 for both baseline and Q-K=V, with inconsistent tiny gaps (seed 42: Q-K=V slightly better; seed 43: slightly worse). The 50% cache reduction is architectural by construction but the perplexity claim is not reproduced at scale.

claims.claim: The fully-shared Q=K=V variant incurs a much larger 25.4% perplexity degradation (6.41 vs. 5.11) at the same 50% cache reduction, while Q=K-V gives 0% cache reduction with a 4.9% perplexity increase (Section 4, Table 4).
claims.evidence: Q=K=V was trained at the same ~7M-param toy scale and consistently shows worse perplexity than baseline across all 6 comparison cells (0.35-1.95% degradation), directionally agreeing with the paper but two orders of magnitude below the claimed 25.4%. The Q=K-V sub-claim was not tested at all. Cache-reduction arithmetic was noted but not formally executed.

claims.claim: Combining Q-K=V with Multi-Query Attention (MQA) yields a 96.9% total KV cache reduction with a 4.8% perplexity increase, and combining it with GQA-4 yields 87.5% cache reduction with 3.9% perplexity loss (Section 4, Tables 4 and 7).
claims.evidence: Cache-reduction percentages verified exactly by arithmetic (96.875% for MQA, 87.5% for GQA-4, both matching the paper). Perplexity portions were trained at toy scale (~7M params, 550 steps) with sign flips between seeds and magnitudes of 0.01-1.68%, neither reproducing nor falsifying the claimed 4.8% and 3.9% increases.

claims.claim: At 1.2B parameters trained on 10B tokens, Q-K=V shows improved robustness, with perplexity degradation dropping to 2.48% while retaining the 50% cache reduction (Section 4, Table 9).
claims.evidence: No 1.2B-parameter training runs were performed. The logbook only extrapolates from the toy-scale padding-bug mechanism to estimate what the 1.2B numbers might be under correction, without any direct experimental evidence at or near the claimed scale.

claims.claim: Learned Key and Value projection matrices exhibit high cosine similarity (0.73), which the authors use to explain why constraining K and V to share a projection causes minimal quality loss (Section 4).
claims.evidence: K/V cosine similarity was measured on the ~7M-param baseline model across init/mid/final checkpoints and both seeds, yielding values near zero (±0.006) with no trend toward 0.73. This disagrees with the paper's claim but at a scale ~40x smaller in parameters and ~18Mx fewer training tokens, so it cannot falsify the claim at the paper's scale.

claims.claim: Projection-sharing variants match or slightly exceed standard QKV transformer performance on synthetic reasoning tasks and vision benchmarks, including 5-shot downstream accuracy and semantic segmentation (Section 4, Tables 2, 3, 11, and 12).
claims.evidence: No experiments involving synthetic reasoning tasks, vision benchmarks, 5-shot downstream accuracy, or semantic segmentation are described anywhere in the logbook. The claim is never addressed.

stresearch-dev/63430.overall: The logbook identifies a genuine padding-label bug in the paper's code that deflates perplexity numbers, and demonstrates its mechanism at toy scale (~7M params, 550 steps, CPU). However, no claim is reproduced or falsified at the paper's actual scale (300M/1.2B params, 10B tokens), and claims 4 and 6 are not addressed experimentally at all.

feliksier/icml2026-repro-5nNNVY8NW4.paper_title: To Grok Grokking: Provable Grokking in Ridge Regression

claims.claim: The paper proves end-to-end grokking for zero-teacher ridge regression, including early training overfitting, delayed poor generalization, and eventual low generalization error (Theorem 4.1)
claims.evidence: Exact spectral GD simulation at the paper's own scale (n=100, m=1000–10000, λ=1e-4–1e-5) across 5–10 seeds shows all three stages: train loss drops below ε=0.01 at t1≈218, test loss remains high until t2≈22995, and final test loss reaches ~9e-4. An independent from-scratch reimplementation reproduces identical numbers.

claims.claim: The end-to-end grokking result is extended from the zero-teacher setting to realizable ridge regression with arbitrary realizable teacher functions (Theorem 4.2)
claims.evidence: The simulations use a non-zero arbitrary realizable teacher (random unit-norm vector θ*), and the three grokking stages are reproduced at the paper's scale with this realizable teacher, supporting the extension from the zero-teacher setting to realizable ridge regression.

claims.claim: Separate theorems decompose grokking into training-loss convergence, poor generalization during overfitting, and eventual generalization (Theorems 4.4-4.6)
claims.evidence: The logbook does not explicitly test or mention Theorems 4.4–4.6 as separate decomposition results. While the three-stage experiments implicitly touch on the phenomena these theorems address, there is no direct verification of the individual theorems' statements or bounds.

claims.claim: Decreasing weight decay and sample size can amplify grokking time in ridge-regression simulations, matching the paper's quantitative hyperparameter predictions (Figure 2)
claims.evidence: Sweeps show t2 scales as λ^{-1} (observed slope −0.986 vs predicted −1.0), t1 is approximately λ-independent (slope −0.099), decreasing n amplifies delay (23233 at n=50 vs 19187 at n=500), and the Eq(8) bounds hold as valid inequalities across all sweeps. The t2-vs-ln(ν²) slope matches the predicted 1/(2.02ηλ) within 1%.

claims.claim: Two-layer ReLU experiments qualitatively reproduce the predicted grokking-time dependence on hyperparameters beyond the linear setting (Figures 3 and 4)
claims.evidence: The logbook contains no experiments with two-layer ReLU networks; all experiments are in the linear ridge-regression setting. Figures 3 and 4 of the paper are never addressed.

feliksier/icml2026-repro-5nNNVY8NW4.overall: The logbook provides strong, independently confirmed numerical verification of the ridge-regression grokking phenomena (Claims 1, 2, 4) at the paper's own experimental scale, including quantitative bound validity and scaling exponent matching. However, Theorems 4.4–4.6 (Claim 3) and the two-layer ReLU experiments (Claim 5) are not addressed at all.

claims.claim: For the independent Gaussian variance allocation problem, the paper gives a PTAS achieving E[max_i X_i] ≥ OPT - ε in polynomial time (Theorem 1.1, Section 1.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements Algorithm 1 with support enumeration up to ceil(ε⁻²) and ε³-grid search, tested with rigorous Chernoff/log-sum-exp OPT upper bounds: for n=6, ε=0.8, PTAS objective 0.703 vs OPT upper 1.481 (gap 0.777 < ε); for zero-mean n=6, ε=0.7, gap 0.201 < ε. Polynomial scaling through n=512 with runtimes from 0.04s to 38.9s and independent quadrature discrepancies ≤1.07e-14.

claims.claim: For correlated Gaussian variables, a PTAS with the same additive ε guarantee is established (Theorem 1.2, Section 1.2).
claims.evidence: A concrete mathematical counterexample: n=2, μ=(2,0), ε=0.1. Feasible covariance diag(0,1) gives OPT≥2 (first variable deterministic), but any zero-mean output with trace 1 has E[max(Y₁,Y₂)] = E|Y₁−Y₂|/2 ≤ 1/√π < 1, far below the required OPT−ε = 1.9. Verified by exact rational arithmetic checker; negative control with fixed zero-mean correctly passes.

claims.claim: For the GraphVarAlloc problem with multiple constraint sets (general m>1), the paper gives an O(log n) multiplicative approximation guaranteeing Ω(1/log n)·OPT (Theorem 1.3, Section 1.2).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 3 is implemented (iterate k=0..⌊log₂n⌋, greedily select min(4ᵏ,n) variables, assign variance 4⁻ᵏ, return best). Scaling from n=64 to n=16384 with polynomial runtime (0.007s to 6.0s). On complete 8-variable domain, all levels match exhaustive optimization within 1.99e-13; fixed-order star control rejected at 0.007874 of greedy objective (below 1−1/e).

claims.claim: Theorem 1.6 proves that in the optimal allocation, only Θ(1/p) variables receive variance Ω(p), i.e., the allocation concentrates on a shrinking subset as the constraint parameter p grows (Theorem 1.6, Section 1.3).
claims.evidence: Mathematical counterexample: set mₙ=n and pₙ=1/n². Then Θ(1/pₙ)=Θ(n²) variables should receive variance Ω(pₙ), but only n variables exist, so N_large/(1/pₙ) ≤ n/n² = 1/n → 0. Verified by exact rational arithmetic across n=8..1024; negative control with fixed p=1/4 correctly rejected since cap n is compatible with Θ(1/p)=Θ(4).

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 bounds the contribution of small-variance variables by O(ε√ln(1/ε)), which is used to limit the number of high-variance variables to O(1/ε²) and underlies the PTAS construction (Lemma 2.1, Section 2.1).
claims.evidence: A complete proof certificate is provided: Mᵍ ≤ Σᵢ(Yᵢ⁺)ᵍ, Σᵢvᵢ^(q/2) ≤ ε^(q−2), and Gaussian moment bound E[(Z₊)ᵍ] ≤ q^(q/2) yield E[M] ≤ e√2·ε√(ln(1/ε)) for ε≤e⁻¹. Stress-tested with m=1/ε² independent variables each of variance ε²; negative control removing ΣΣᵢᵢ≤1 correctly restores uncontrolled √(log m) factor.

claims.claim: Monte Carlo simulations on Erdős–Rényi random graphs with n=8 nodes and edge probabilities p ranging from 1/8 to 8/8 are used to illustrate the concentration and concavity results across independent, positively, and negatively correlated settings (Figures 1-2, Section 1.3).
claims.evidence: Independent replication at the paper's own n=8 scale across 48 cases (two set models × three dependence regimes × eight p values from 1/8 to 8/8) using 4096 Sobol training draws, 32768 validation draws, and SLSQP optimization. Results: 48/48 converged, 36/36 concavity tests passed, 6/6 concentration comparisons passed, 144/144 finite-m estimates matched population reference. DineshAI/vqxprtjuKH.overall: The logbook provides rigorous mathematical proof certificates and counterexamples with exact arithmetic for the theoretical claims, supported by numerical experiments with independent checkers and negative controls. Two claims (2 and 4) are falsified by valid mathematical counterexamples exposing issues with theorem quantifiers as literally stated, while the remaining claims are verified with concrete experimental or proof-theoretic evidence at the paper's own scale.

snaykey/repro-decentralized-optimization.paper_title: Complexity of Decentralized Optimization with Mixed Affine Constraints

claims.claim: For the smooth, strongly convex regime with mixed affine constraints, Theorem 4.1 gives an optimal communication complexity of O(√κ_f √κ̂_{C̃ᵀ} √κ_W log(1/ε)) that matches established lower complexity bounds (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Log-log fits on synthetic quadratics with controlled condition numbers (κ_f from 10 to 3000, κ_W from 10 to 3000) show gradient complexity exponent 0.519 (theory 0.5, R²=0.998) and Chebyshev communication exponent 0.494 (theory 0.5, R²=1.000), with simple gossip at 0.989 confirming the quadratic improvement; the constraint factor √κ̂_{C̃ᵀ} is not independently measured but is addressed in Claim 2.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 provides a unified complexity bound O(√κ_f (√κ̃_{AC} + √κ̂_{C̃ᵀ}) √κ_W log(1/ε)) covering problems with simultaneously coupled (global) and local affine constraints (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: Over a 5×5 grid of κ_AC and κ_Ctilde, an additive least-squares fit yields p=7.269, q=7.269, R²=0.999998, directly confirming the additive √κ̃_{AC} + √κ̂_{C̃ᵀ} structure of Theorem 4.6 with near-equal coefficients as expected.

claims.claim: The paper analyzes both smooth objectives (Theorem 2.4) and non-smooth objectives via a Gradient Sliding algorithm (Algorithm 2), each under mixed affine constraints (Section 2, Section 4, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: The smooth case shows linear convergence (log-log slope 0.131 vs 1/ε, consistent with logarithmic scaling), but the non-smooth case uses a plain subgradient method as a proxy for the full Gradient Sliding algorithm (Algorithm 2) rather than implementing the actual sliding schedule; the qualitative linear-vs-sublinear separation is demonstrated but the non-smooth algorithm itself is not faithfully reproduced.

claims.claim: The proposed framework is motivated by and applied to horizontal federated learning (consensus constraints), vertical federated learning (shared/global-variable constraints), and multi-task learning with node-specific local constraints (Section 1, Applications).
claims.evidence: Three small synthetic instances (5–6 nodes) of HFL consensus, VFL coupled, and multi-task local constraints are solved to feasibility with APAPC (e.g., ||Bu-b|| = 3.0e-03, 5.4e-06, 1.4e-03), demonstrating the constraint-structure reductions but at a scale far below real federated or multi-task learning scenarios.

claims.claim: An accelerated proximal alternating predictor-corrector method (Algorithm 1, APAPC) is used as the core building block for achieving the optimal rates in Theorem 4.1 and Theorem 4.5 (Algorithm 1, Theorem 4.5).
claims.evidence: APAPC (Algorithm 1) implemented verbatim on constrained quadratics shows iteration count linear in log(1/ε) (7.72 iterations per unit log(1/ε), R²=0.988) with final constraint feasibility 5.9e-06, directly confirming the Theorem 2.4 linear convergence guarantee that underpins Theorems 4.1 and 4.5.

snaykey/repro-decentralized-optimization.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence confirming the key complexity exponents and structural properties of the paper's main theorems (Claims 1, 2, 5) on synthetic quadratics with controlled condition numbers, while the non-smooth algorithm (Claim 3) and application demonstrations (Claim 4) are only addressed at simplified or proxy scale.
