agharsallah/uhqdfvzbfi-logbook.paper_title: Characterization of Gaussian Universality Breakdown in High-Dimensional Empirical Risk Minimization

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 gives a min-max (deterministic-equivalent) formulation of the limiting asymptotics via an objective involving the Moreau envelope, enabling approximation of the mean and covariance of the high-dimensional ERM estimator θ̂ (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: At p=200-400, n=400-900 with 90 real ERM refits per config, the theory's alpha* matches empirical noise level to 0.1-1.7% relative error and mu* to 12.5-14.1%, while the kappa self-consistency residual is 4e-10 to 5e-9 across all 9 points, confirming the min-max saddle-point structure of Theorem 4.3 on a non-Gaussian mixture design.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 provides an explicit fixed-point system of four coupled equations, involving proximal operators and the loss function, that determines the asymptotic mean μ* and noise level α* of the ERM estimator (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: All four fixed-point equations of Theorem 4.4 are satisfied out-of-sample (500k fresh MC draws) with residuals ranging from 1e-8 (kappa) to 0.087 (nu), and the theory's mu*/alpha* match real logistic-regression ERM over 100 refits to 3-3.8% and 0.04-2.1% relative error respectively, at p=150-250, n=400-600.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.1 proves the projected test score x^Tθ̂ asymptotically equals x^Tμ* + α*z with z ~ N(0,1) independent of the data, i.e., a convolution of a (possibly non-Gaussian) distribution with an independent centered Gaussian variable (Theorem 6.1).
claims.evidence: Two-sample KS distance between the empirical test-score distribution (300 ERM refits × 15 test draws, p=200, n=400) and the theoretical convolution x^T mu* + alpha* z is 0.013-0.023 in both the Gaussian-engaging (phi=0) and non-Gaussian-engaging (phi=pi/2) configurations, confirming the convolution formula of Theorem 6.1.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows any twice-differentiable (C²) regularizer is asymptotically equivalent to an explicit quadratic surrogate defined via its gradient and Hessian at μ* (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: In paired real ERM runs (same X,y) with a genuinely non-quadratic pseudo-Huber regularizer vs its Theorem 3.3 quadratic surrogate at p=200-250, n=400-500, T=90, the relative difference in E[x^T theta_hat] is 0.25-4.6% (median 0.65%) and in E[(x^T theta_hat)^2] is 0.55-0.86%, confirming asymptotic equivalence.

claims.claim: The paper distinguishes three notions of Gaussian universality—performance, score, and minimizer universality—and characterizes precisely when each breaks down under non-Gaussian designs, validated on mixture models and MNIST (Section 7).
claims.evidence: On a bimodal-mixture elastic-loss sweep (p=150, n=350, T=200), the performance-universality gap grows ~3.5x from eta=0 (1.24% mean) to eta=1 (4.43% mean); on real MNIST digit images (p=400, n_train=1000, T=60), the decision score is clearly non-Gaussian (KS=0.102-0.108) while performance universality approximately holds, demonstrating the decoupling of score and performance universality as claimed in Section 7.

agharsallah/uhqdfvzbfi-logbook.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from real ERM refits and theory-solver comparisons at non-toy scales (p up to 400, n up to 900) for all five claims, using the authors' own code with non-Gaussian mixture designs and real MNIST data. All claims are supported by multiple seeds, out-of-sample verification, and CSV-level data showing small residuals and errors consistent with the paper's theoretical predictions.

agharsallah/9ylpoheked-logbook.paper_title: Magnitude Distance: A Geometric Measure of Dataset Similarity

claims.claim: Magnitude distance is defined as d_Mag^t(X,Y) = 2·Mag_{X∪Y}(t) − Mag_X(t) − Mag_Y(t), with a tunable scale parameter t that governs sensitivity to global structure (small t) versus finer local structure (large t) (Section on Definition, Magnitude Distance).
claims.evidence: Formula identity confirmed to machine precision (residual ≤1e-12) across 30 configs, and tunability experiment shows monotonic increase in fine/global ratio from 0.0012 to 0.4921 (425×) across t ∈ [0.02, 20], directly demonstrating t governs global-to-local sensitivity.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 shows magnitude distance is symmetric and non-negative, satisfies identity of indiscernibles only up to magnitude equivalence, and does not satisfy the triangle inequality in R^D for D>1 (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Symmetry (max error 4.2e-15, 60/60), non-negativity (min 1.16, 60/60), identity of indiscernibles (max 1.9e-11, 60/60), and triangle inequality violation at D=300 (violation 3.76) with triangle inequality holding at D=1 (margin ≥0.149) are all confirmed with concrete numerical runs.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.3 shows magnitude distance converges to 0 as t→0 and converges to the cardinality of the symmetric difference of the two datasets as t→∞ (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: Across 48 configs, d_Mag converges to 0.00013 at t=1e-4 (approaching 0) and to 5.999999999997 at t=1000 (matching |XΔY|=6), with monotonic increase confirmed across the full t range.

claims.claim: Figure 2 shows magnitude distance remains discriminative in dimensions exceeding 1000, in settings where MMD's discriminative power collapses (Section on High-Dimensional Behavior, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: At D ∈ {500, 1000, 2000} with n=64, magnitude distance (t=1/√D) shows positive discriminative gap (0.08–0.11) while Gaussian MMD²(σ=1) gap ≈ 0 at all dimensions, reproducing Figure 2's finding.

claims.claim: MagGN, a generative model trained with a multi-scale magnitude-distance loss, achieves an 11.97x training speedup over WGAN on MNIST while producing visually competitive samples (Table 1).
claims.evidence: CPU per-step timing microbenchmark (same architecture, batch 64, 5 seeds) yields 0.898× mean speedup (MagGN slower), and a cited independent H200 GPU full-train reproduction reports 1.747× — both far below the claimed 11.97×; the Table 1 arithmetic is correct but the base timings are not reproducible.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.5 proves magnitude distance has bounded outlier sensitivity, changing by only about 6-10% under significant outlier addition compared to a 17.6% change for Wasserstein distance in the same setting (Section 5, Theorem 5.5).
claims.evidence: With 4 outliers added to 30-point 2D clusters, magnitude distance changes 5.2–10.4% across t=5 and t=20 (10/10 configs), consistent with the paper's stated 6–10% range; however, the Wasserstein 17.6% comparison was not independently measured.

agharsallah/9ylpoheked-logbook.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence for all theoretical claims (1–4, 6) via clean-room magnitude implementations with machine-precision results and appropriate synthetic experiments. Claim 5's 11.97× speedup is falsified by both a CPU microbenchmark and a cited independent GPU full-train reproduction, both showing speedup well below 2×.

rahit/repro-a-formal-comparison-between-.paper_title: A Formal Comparison Between Chain of Thought and Latent Thought

claims.claim: Chain-of-thought (CoT) can evaluate directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) in a number of sequential decoding steps proportional to graph size, using attention as a scratchpad memory (Section 3, Theorem 3.5)
claims.evidence: Clean-room CoT construction evaluated 37 graph configurations with 1,343,440 exhaustively enumerated Boolean inputs, achieving exact-match accuracy 1.0 in all cases with steps = size(G) - n (max deviation 0). Destructive controls (truncated steps, flat attention, non-topological order, gate mutation) all degrade accuracy, confirming the mechanism.

claims.claim: Looped transformers implementing latent thought evaluate the same DAGs in a number of loop iterations proportional only to graph depth, performing parallel computation layer-by-layer for nodes at the same depth (Section 3, Theorem 3.7)
claims.evidence: Looped transformer construction evaluated 37 configurations with 557,008 enumerated inputs; accuracy is 1.0 at exactly r=depth(G) iterations in all 37 cases, and 26/37 fail at depth-1 (worst accuracy 0.0625). Chain family shows 1.0× speedup (no advantage, as predicted), while tree shows 3.75× and random 3.4×. Hidden width = size(G) vs 1 for CoT, matching the parameter trade-off.

claims.claim: Looped transformers with polylogarithmic iterations are shown to capture the parallel complexity classes AC^k and TC^k, and CoT with polylogarithmic steps is proven strictly weaker than looped models under standard complexity assumptions (Section 3, Theorem 3.13, Lemma 3.14, Theorems 3.15-3.16)
claims.evidence: STCON matrix-squaring construction is exhaustive over all 2^(n(n-1)) digraphs for n=4 (4,096) and n=5 (1,048,576), with first exact loop = ⌈log₂(n-1)⌉ in all cases; growth sweep to n=64 confirms logarithmic scaling (slope 1.005, R²=0.975). MAJORITY_n precision study under output rounding matches the closed-form ⌊log₂n⌋+1 bit requirement in 9/9 cases with exact binomial failure-set counts. The logbook honestly notes that the converse inclusion and strict separation rest on unproven assumptions and are not computationally checkable.

claims.claim: CoT with polynomially many steps can represent any fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme (FPRAS), giving it an approximate-counting capability that looped/latent-thought transformers cannot match under standard assumptions (Section 4, Theorem 4.7)
claims.evidence: Karp-Luby FPRAS for #DNF using the official repo's DNF generator: 10 configurations, 1,000 runs, 89,252,800 enumerated assignments for ground truth. Coverage is 1.000 in all configurations (target 0.95), worst p95 relative error 0.0197. On adversarial sparse instances (density ~3e-5), CoT achieves 0.0 relative error while naive MC returns zero in 96/100 runs. Positive control confirms agreement with official exact counter (max diff 0).

claims.claim: A pretrained CoT model augmented with an inference-time algorithm such as majority voting constitutes a fully polynomial almost uniform sampler (FPAUS), formalizing how stochastic decoding enables approximate counting (Section 4, Proposition 4.6)
claims.evidence: Using the official repo's coloring task with Glauber dynamics, 8 graphs with 978,940 enumerated colorings (largest state space 863,940). Exact TV via transition matrix shows T*(ε) linear in log(1/ε) with R²≥0.9994 in all cases, and T*(0.05) scales as n·log n (R²=0.993). Deterministic decoder TV = 1-1/|Ω| (0.983 to 0.9999988), confirming the predicted failure mode. No transformer is trained, but the sampler properties the theorem attributes to stochastic decoding are validated exactly.

claims.claim: Experiments on parallelizable tasks and DNF-counting-style approximation tasks empirically validate the predicted separation between CoT and latent/looped thought (Section 5.1-5.2)
claims.evidence: The paper's Table 1 trained-model experiments are explicitly not reproduced (GPU experiment not run). Instead, the theoretical loop-vs-step predictions are validated through constructive analysis at the paper's own input sizes (S5 n=64: 6 loops vs 63 steps; edit distance 32/16: 48 loops vs 561 steps; STCON n=32: 5 loops vs 1024 steps), with node functions exhaustively verified. This validates the predicted separation in principle but does not reproduce the paper's actual empirical experiments with trained models.

rahit/repro-a-formal-comparison-between-.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, mostly exhaustive verification of the paper's constructive theorems (Claims 1-5) through clean-room implementations with exact ground truth, but does not reproduce the paper's trained-model experiments (Claim 6), substituting constructive loop/step-count analysis instead.

agharsallah/n9nlcruiir-logbook.paper_title: Black-Box Assisted Regression: Phase Transitions and Minimax Optimality

claims.claim: The critical phase-transition threshold for black-box assisted regression is characterized as δc(n) ≍ n^(-β/(2β+d)), separating a prior-dominated regime from a sample-dominated regime (Section 5).
claims.evidence: 1D synthetic NW kernel sweep with β∈{1,2}: β=1 fitted slopes (-0.632 to -0.584) approximate the predicted -0.667, but β=2 fitted slopes (-0.05 to -0.28) are far from the predicted -0.800, explained away as bandwidth suboptimality rather than confirmed.

claims.claim: The proposed safe residual estimator achieves the minimax risk rate min{δ², n^(-2β/(2β+d))} up to a validation-selection cost, with the lower bound given in Theorem 5.4 and the matching upper bound in Theorem 5.5 (Theorem 5.4, Theorem 5.5).
claims.evidence: Same 1D synthetic setup; risk is stated to fall within 0.1× to 20× of the theoretical envelope min(δ², n^{-2β/(2β+d)}), a 200× ratio that only loosely confirms 'up to constant factors,' and the β=2 rate-suboptimality issue from Claim 1 undermines the upper-bound verification.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.7 provides an oracle inequality showing the validation-based selection between f0 and f0+r̂ performs nearly as well as the better of the two candidate predictors (Theorem 5.7).
claims.evidence: 1D synthetic setup (β=2, d=1) with a concrete table of oracle gaps across n∈{25–800} and δ∈{0.01–1.0}; gaps are always below the O(1/n_val) bound, but this is a simplified single-dimensional proxy for the general theorem.

claims.claim: In synthetic experiments at n=20 and δ=0.0, the safe residual estimator achieves risk 0.0027 compared to 0.1894 for learning from scratch (Tables 1-2).
claims.evidence: At n=20, δ=0.0 the logbook obtains Res(safe)=0.0002 and Scratch=0.0007, which differ substantially from the paper's claimed 0.0027 and 0.1894 (scratch MSE off by ~270×); the qualitative ordering is confirmed but the specific claimed numbers are not reproduced.

claims.claim: On CIFAR-100 with CLIP features at n=2000, the residual learning method achieves 66.7% accuracy versus 63.9% for a weighted-ensemble baseline, improving over the 59.4% zero-shot baseline (Section 6, CIFAR-100/CLIP experiments).
claims.evidence: The logbook's own GPU job is still running with no results reported; it cites two other teams' results (zero-shot ~61%, assisted ~70%) which show different absolute numbers than the claimed 59.4%/63.9%/66.7% and do not clearly report the weighted-ensemble baseline.

claims.claim: On AG News with Qwen3-8B at n=16, residual learning achieves 75.2% accuracy while the weighted-ensemble baseline exhibits negative transfer, dropping to 71.2% (Section 6, AG News/Qwen3-8B experiments).
claims.evidence: No own experimental results are presented — the table only restates the paper's numbers under 'Accuracy (paper)'; cited external reproductions report Res(safe)≈74.8–75.3% but do not report the weighted-ensemble 71.2% negative-transfer figure, so the specific claim is not independently verified by this logbook.

agharsallah/n9nlcruiir-logbook.overall: The logbook provides real but simplified 1D synthetic experiments that partially support the theoretical claims (1–3) and the qualitative mechanism of Claim 4, though specific numbers and β=2 rates do not match. Claims 5–6 are not independently reproduced: the logbook's own GPU experiments are incomplete and it relies on citing other teams' results with different absolute numbers.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 proves that all context-free languages can be recognized by looped transformers using O(log(n)) looping layers and O(n^6) padding tokens (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements Algorithm 1 & 2 as least fixpoints and checks recognition against an independent CYK oracle on 4,525 strings across 11 grammars with 0 mismatches and 536,533 slashed items verified against augmented-CYK with 0 false positives; Jordan-centroid depth is measured up to N=192 (fitted slope 1.046 in log₂ N, within the paper's bound), and the padding exponent converges to 5.993 at N=500–2000 with R²=1.000, confirming the O(n⁶) budget.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows unambiguous context-free languages can be recognized with fewer resources than the general case: O(log^2(n)) looping layers and O(n^3) padding tokens (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The marking algorithm is checked against CYK on 4,373 strings across 11 grammars with 0 mismatches; Fact 4.1 (path uniqueness) holds for all 8 unambiguous grammars (worst 1 path) and fails on 2 ambiguous controls (2 paths), confirming the hypothesis is load-bearing; depth decomposes as O(log n) outer iterations × O(log n) pebble rounds (11 rounds at N=44 vs raw chain of 21); padding exponent converges to 2.998 at N=500–2000 with R²=1.000.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 further reduces requirements for unambiguous linear context-free languages to O(log(n)) looping layers and O(n^2) padding tokens by exploiting the linearity constraint (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Proposition 4.1 (I₁=I*) is confirmed: all 4 linear grammars need exactly 1 productive pass while 4 non-linear unambiguous grammars need 3; recognition is correct (0/4,161 mismatches up to N=49); depth is a single O(log n) pebble-evaluated pass (12 rounds at N=60); padding exponent converges to 1.999 at N=500–2000 (R²=1.000), directly contrasted with 2.996 for the same grammar without linearity.

claims.claim: Lemma 4.1 shows that Boolean formula evaluation can be computed in O(log(n)) steps via a parallel pebbling argument, which underlies the padding-token constructions used in the main theorems (Section 4, Lemma 4.1).
claims.evidence: A RAKE+COMPRESS parallel tree contraction (the concrete realization of Rytter's pebble game) is compared against a recursive evaluator on 10,000 formulas across 4 shapes (random, balanced, left-deep, right-deep) with 0 wrong values; on adversarial left-deep chains up to 65,536 leaves (131,071 positions), only 18 rounds are needed (rounds/log₂n ≈ 1.06 and decreasing), confirming O(log n) depth and separating it from the Θ(n) naive pebbling.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.1 shows that Boolean Formula Value Problem (BFVP) recognition requires zero padding tokens while retaining logarithmic depth (Section 4, Corollary 4.1).
claims.evidence: Over 12,000 postfix formulas (balanced accept/reject, all tree shapes, up to 999 positions), the recognizer matches truth values with 0 errors and uses 0 padding symbols in every case (max_padding_symbols_used=0); round counts confirm O(log n) depth (18 rounds at 65,536 leaves); a fixed-depth control capped at 5 rounds fails from N=32 through N=8,192 while the log-depth recognizer succeeds, directly demonstrating the TC0≠NC1 point.

claims.claim: Table 1 summarizes the padding-versus-depth tradeoff across general, unambiguous, and linear-unambiguous context-free language classes, showing that grammatical restrictions systematically reduce required padding (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The reconstructed table reports measured padding exponents of 5.993, 2.998, and 1.999 (each with log–log fit R²=1.000 at N=500–2000), confirming the strict monotone reduction 6>3>2; the looping pattern is reproduced via measured productive outer iterations (general: single log pass, unambiguous: 3 passes giving log², linear: 1 pass giving log), matching Table 1's structure.

snaykey/repro-gp-thompson-sampling-regre.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous, independent re-implementation of the paper's algorithms with verification against from-scratch oracles (CYK, augmented-CYK, recursive Boolean evaluator) across 11 grammars, thousands of strings, and scaling to N=2000 for padding curves and 65,536 leaves for pebbling, with controls ruling out vacuous passes. All six theoretical claims receive concrete empirical support on a non-toy setup, though the transformer-realizability equivalence is taken as given rather than directly tested.

bsenst/repro-osf.paper_title: OSF: On Pre-training and Scaling of Sleep Foundation Models

claims.evidence: The logbook performs arithmetic on numbers extracted from the paper's own Appendix Tables 16-17 (21,482 recordings, 19,989k epochs → 166,575 hours), but no independent verification of actual NSRR dataset sizes was performed; this is restating paper claims, not reproducing them.

claims.claim: On MROS, OSF achieves 97.3 AUC for sleep staging and 92.8 AUC for arousal detection, outperforming SleepFM (96.4 and 90.3 AUC respectively) and a supervised ViT (96.9 and 88.4 AUC) (Table 2).

snaykey/repro-online-non-monotone-dr-sub.paper_title: Evaluating Bivariate Causal Statements Based on Mutual Compatibility

claims.claim: For linear bivariate causal statements, any acyclic collection induces exactly one multivariate structural equation model whose pairwise marginals match the given statements (Lemma 2.3).
claims.evidence: The A↔Γ=I−A⁻¹ bijection and pairwise-marginal identity were checked at machine precision (max round-trip error 7.49e-15, max pairwise-marginal error 1.49e-14) over 2000 random SEMs with n=3–8, plus a perturbation test confirming injectivity (marginal shifts by 0.5 when Γ is perturbed off the bijection).

claims.claim: The compatibility score defined via path-tracing decomposition of confounding (Definition 2.7) is proven to have positive expected value under a generic random causal model, supporting the paper's Confounding Postulate (Theorem 2.9).
claims.evidence: The compatibility score implementation is validated against the Figure 1 example (exact match: C^mult_23 = 0.015625, comp = −0.015625), and E[comp]>0 is confirmed via a closed-form anchor at n=3 (MC mean 1.024, CI [0.996, 1.053] bracketing the theoretical value 1.0) plus strictly positive CI lower bounds across n=5,7,10 under Gaussian, Laplace, and uniform coefficient laws with random SPD noise.

claims.claim: Empirical approximation of the compatibility score converges in polynomial sample complexity with respect to dimension, causal strength, and pathway contributions (Theorem 2.10).
claims.evidence: Empirical convergence rate is N^−0.61 (theory N^−0.5, R²=0.90), dimension growth is polynomial (~n^2.9 vs bound n^4), and the paper's specific >90% sign-agreement claim at <100 samples is reproduced (94.2% at N=80, 94.8% at N=99). The universal constant C is correctly noted as unidentifiable, and scaling rather than absolute constants is verified.

claims.claim: On synthetic linear models, compatibility scores decrease monotonically as injected error increases, and on LLM-generated causal statements higher-capacity models achieve higher compatibility scores, with some receiving negative (falsifying) scores (Section 2.7, Figures 2 and 4).
claims.evidence: The synthetic monotone-decrease claim (Figure 2) is fully reproduced on the paper's exact generator: % positive scores drop from 100% to 0.5% (Spearman ρ=−1.00) and mean score decreases (ρ=−0.98) over σ∈[0,1]. The falsification mechanism is demonstrated on real gapminder data (random baseline positive at +0.258, wrong statements negative at −0.161 and −2.117). The specific LLM model-ranking sub-claim is API-gated and not reproduced, which is honestly disclosed.

claims.claim: For graphical bivariate causal statements, computing the exact incompatibility score (minimum Hamming distance to a compatible statement graph) is proven NP-hard via reduction to transitive-closure editing (Section 3, NP-hardness result).
claims.evidence: The reduction equivalence incomp(D + all bidirected) = transitivity-editing(D) is verified exhaustively with zero mismatches across all 25 acyclic DAGs on n=3 and all 543 on n=4 (568 total), using two independent brute-force oracles. NP-hardness itself is correctly noted as inherited from the cited Weller et al. 2012 result.

claims.claim: A heuristic GreedyFAS+GreedyTE algorithm yields incompatibility scores that upper-bound the true incompatibility score and equal zero exactly when the true score is zero, and empirically increase monotonically with injected errors on synthetic graphs and on LLM outputs (Lemma 3.7, Sections 3.3-3.4, Figures 5-7).
claims.evidence: Lemma 3.7(1) and (2) are verified exhaustively over all 512 statement graphs at n=3 (0 violations of c(G)≥incomp(G) and c(G)=0⇔incomp(G)=0) and constructively at n=3–7 (600/600 cases where heuristic output G* is compatible and d(G,G*)≤c(G)). Synthetic monotonicity (Figure 5) is reproduced with Spearman ρ=1.00 (mean incompatibility rising from 0 to 5.58). The LLM-output ranking (Figures 6–7) is API-gated and not reproduced.

snaykey/repro-online-non-monotone-dr-sub.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, mostly exact verification of all six claims through machine-precision algebraic identity checks, Monte Carlo with confidence intervals, exhaustive combinatorial verification, and synthetic experiments matching the paper's own generators. The LLM-ranking components of claims 4 and 6 are API-gated and honestly disclosed as not reproduced, but the core scientific content (monotonicity, falsification mechanism, heuristic bounds) is verified on the paper's real tasks and data.

PinoCookie/repro-success-conditioning-as.paper_title: Success-Conditioning as Policy Improvement: The Optimization Problem Solved by Imitating Success

claims.claim: Success conditioning is proved to exactly solve a trust-region policy optimization problem with a chi-squared divergence constraint whose radius is determined by the data (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Across 500 random bandit/MDP environments (4-5 states, 8-10 actions), the logbook shows χ²(π⁺||π₀) = Γ to within |Δ| < 2.55e-15 and π⁺ matches the Lagrangian trust-region solution in 100% of trials, numerically confirming the trust-region equivalence theorem.

claims.claim: At the optimum, relative policy improvement, chi-squared policy-change magnitude, and action-influence are shown to be exactly equal at every state (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: Per-state equality of improvement (d·A/ρ), χ² divergence (d⁺·χ²), and action-influence (d⁺·I) is verified across 5000 state-trial pairs with max deviation 1.15e-15, and a parameter sweep over different state/action counts all show max|Δ| < 6e-15.

nmaher/repro-on-the-theory-of-continual-.paper_title: On the Theory of Continual Learning with Gradient Descent for Neural Networks

claims.claim: Theorem 1 gives a closed-form bound on train-time forgetting for task k after training on K-k subsequent tasks, of order O~(ηT√(K-k)/(d√n) + ηT√(K-k)/(d²polylog(d)) + η²T²K²/√m) (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: 195 closed-form runs and 120 full-GD runs measure the three-term structure of Theorem 1: finite-width remainder scales as m^(-0.499±0.071) vs predicted m^(-0.5), sampling term as n^(-0.449±0.047) vs predicted n^(-0.5), population term as d^(-1.960±0.177) vs predicted d^(-2.0). All exponents match or are conservative; the orthogonality control shows 2600× degradation when the structural assumption is broken.

claims.claim: The forgetting bounds hold under the parameter regime n = Θ~(d²K) samples, m = Ω~(d⁸K⁴) hidden-layer width, and ηT = Θ(d²) training iterations on a d-dimensional XOR cluster dataset with K tasks (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Along the prescribed path (n=d²K, ηT=0.15d², m=2×10⁴), forgetting decays as d^(-0.91±0.29) over d∈[12,64]. Breaking n=Θ̃(d²K) flattens the decay to d^(-0.02±0.19); breaking ηT=Θ(d²) by over-training reverses it to d^(+0.17). The width condition m=Ω̃(d⁸K⁴) is untestable (10¹⁶ at d=64) but m=300 reproduces the decay, and the ηT-consistency probe confirms the conditions are compatible (ηT_needed ∝ d^(1.82) m^(0.067), excluding incompatibility by 41σ).

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows that under the same width/sample/iteration conditions as Theorem 1, the misclassification error remains uniformly small across all K tasks with high probability after KT gradient descent iterations (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: 32 hinge-loss runs at d=50, K=6 across 8 configurations show zero misclassification error on all 6 tasks at the final iterate w_K, at both ηT=400 and ηT=1600. The noise control confirms this is not degenerate: error stays 0 at σ_c=0.1 but rises to ~0.49 at σ_c=1.0, showing the measurement instrument discriminates. The loss half requires ηT=Θ(d²): max train loss is 0.68 at ηT=400 but 0.007–0.019 at ηT=1600.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 bounds the delayed generalization gap by η T exp(ηT(K-k+1)/√m) / n for Lipschitz, smooth loss functions, showing the gap decays with sample size n (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The bound is never violated but is vacuous everywhere reachable: at the base point the RHS is ~10⁸²⁶ against a measured gap of 1.7×10⁻⁴. The 1/n direction is confirmed (measured slope -0.61 vs predicted -1.0), but the T-dependence is backwards (gap decreases at -0.73 while the bound increases linearly) and the m-dependence is backwards (gap increases with m while the bound decreases). A low-η probe makes the bounds finite but the network has not trained (loss 0.67–0.70 vs init 0.693).

claims.claim: Theorem 4 gives an improved generalization gap bound for self-bounded losses that scales poly-logarithmically rather than linearly in the number of iterations T, depending on the cumulative training loss of later tasks (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Over a 64× increase in T, Theorem 3's core ηT/n grows 64.0× while Theorem 4's core η/n Σ[t]F̂_k grows only 2.37× (slope +0.190 vs +1.000), confirming the poly-logarithmic improvement. Theorem 4 is tighter than Theorem 3 in all 24 low-η configurations by 0.23–1.75 decades, with best-case slack of a factor of 15. Both bounds hold in all 230 runs with zero violations.

claims.claim: Test-time forgetting is decomposed as the sum of train-time forgetting (Theorem 1) and the delayed generalization gap (Theorem 3/4), showing that network width, sample size, and later tasks' data jointly, not individually, control forgetting (Theorem 1, Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The decomposition's dropped term F_k(w_k)-F̂_k(w_k) measures +1.05×10⁻⁴±9.2×10⁻⁴ (t=+0.51), negative in 8/20 runs, and is the same order as the train-time forgetting being decomposed (4.29×10⁻⁴). A Monte-Carlo control (6.7× larger test set) reduced scatter only 1.28× instead of the expected 2.6×, ruling out test-set noise but not resolving the sign. The 4×4 grid shows n-slopes are all negative and steepen with m (-0.297→-0.453), but no m-slope is distinguishable from zero, supporting an asymmetric rather than symmetric 'joint control' interpretation.

nmaher/repro-on-the-theory-of-continual-.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous clean-room numerical audit of all four theorems via 959 runs, confirming the term structure of Theorem 1, the load-bearing nature of the n and ηT conditions, zero misclassification error for Theorem 2, and the poly-log improvement of Theorem 4 over Theorem 3. The generalization bounds (Theorems 3–4) are shown to be vacuous at all reachable scales, and the test-time decomposition (Claim 6) is unresolved because the dropped error term is the same order as the quantity being decomposed.

ai-sherpa/innovation-hallucination-chara.paper_title: Innovation: An Almost Characterization of Hallucination

claims.claim: The paper defines innovation (Definition 3.1) as a language model assigning nonzero probability mass to statements not present in the training data, and shows via Observation 3.2 that hallucinating with positive probability implies the model innovates (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The structural invariant H⊆U held in 100% of 160,000 trials across four regimes because O⊆F (corpus draws from p supported on F) deterministically forces H=Ω∖F to be disjoint from O, hence H⊆U. Both scatter and spike models never produced g(H)>0 without g(U)>0.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows that under K-Sparsity and Regular Facts assumptions, if the innovation mass g(U) > 0, the probability a model hallucinates is at least 1 - K/|U| (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: The spike model's empirical hallucination frequency exceeded the 1−K/|U| floor in all three regimes (0.9987≥0.9975, 0.9540≥0.9496, 0.8503≥0.8306) over 120,000 trials, and the exact posterior q=(K−|O|)/|U| never exceeded K/|U| in any trial.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.4 shows that a calibrated model with any positive missing probability mass necessarily innovates (Proposition 3.4).
claims.evidence: For the canonical calibrated coarsening Π={O singletons}∪{U-cell}, g(U)=p(U) to machine precision (diff 1.1e-16) in all 160,000 trials, with g(U)>0 whenever p(U)>0. The logbook transparently notes this tests the canonical witness from the proof, not all calibrated models exhaustively.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 gives a Markov-style bound showing the hallucination rate satisfies g(H) ≥ g(U)(1 - K/(δ|U|)) with probability at least 1-δ (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The empirical satisfied-fraction exceeded the 1−δ floor for every valid (regime, δ) pair (e.g., 0.999≥0.85 for easy/δ=0.15; 0.925≥0.70 for tight/δ=0.3), and the δ=0.15 case in the tight regime was correctly excluded since δ<K/|U|≈0.169, matching the theorem's domain.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 establishes a high-confidence bound where, with probability at least 1 - K/|U|, the hallucination rate satisfies g(H) ≥ g(U)/(K+1) (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Scatter satisfied the bound deterministically (1.000 in all regimes) via the pointwise argument |H|/|U|≥1−K/|U|≥1/(K+1), while spike's satisfaction frequency tracked the probabilistic floor (0.999/0.954/0.850 vs required 0.9975/0.9496/0.8306) across all three regimes.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.3 lower-bounds the innovation rate by g(U) ≥ p(U)/(K+1) minus a miscalibration distance term, linking missing probability mass to innovation (Proposition 4.3).
claims.evidence: The bound g(U) ≥ p(U)/(K+1) − TV-proxy held with positive slack (minimum 0.438) in all 480,000 model-evaluations across three model families and four regimes, using a conservative TV lower-bound proxy that understates true TV distance. The logbook acknowledges only one partition Π is tested, not all partitions as the universal statement requires.

ai-sherpa/innovation-hallucination-chara.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six theoretical claims by instantiating the paper's finite Kalai-Vempala framework at native scale (N up to 20,000, K up to 100, 160,000 corpora) and measuring each claimed inequality on executed runs of explicit model families. The main limitation is that universal claims (Props 3.4, 4.3) are verified on the canonical witness construction rather than exhaustively over all calibrated models or partitions, though the logbook is transparent about this scope.

claims.evidence: The selectivity score Δ was computed over all 4096 features for 60 matched emotion/neutral pairs per emotion; distributions are median-0 with positive skew (anger +0.55, happiness +0.30, sadness +0.11) and only ~1% of features have Δ>0.5, matching the paper's Figure 3 sparse-subset finding.

claims.claim: Feature-level steering induces target emotions with high fidelity while preserving intelligibility: anger induction reaches Emo-SIM of 0.912 with WER of 0.3, happiness induction reaches Emo-SIM of 0.885 with WER of 2.2, and sadness induction reaches Emo-SIM of 0.880 with WER of 1.5 (Table 1).

claims.claim: Steering along emotion-selective SAE features produces a significant mean F0 increase of +23.11 Hz (p=1.07×10⁻⁴) and RMS energy increase of +0.00435 (p=0.00769), with no significant change in duration (p=0.687) (Section 4.2.2).
claims.evidence: Paired acoustic analysis on 8 anger pairs shows F0 +15.6 Hz (p<0.001), RMS +0.0016 (p<0.001), duration p=0.29 (n.s.), reproducing the paper's sign and significance pattern (F0↑ sig, RMS↑ sig, duration n.s.) on real IndexTTS2 generations, though magnitudes are smaller due to reduced scale.

claims.claim: A blind listening study with 20 raters shows SAE-Emotion steering achieves an EMOS of 3.22 and NMOS of 3.49, outperforming both global steering and random-SAE-direction baselines (Table 2).

DineshAI/GMIHHrJ6Wp.paper_title: Model-Free Robust Average-Reward Reinforcement Learning with Sample Complexity Analysis

claims.claim: Robust Halpern Iteration (RHI) achieves a sample complexity of tilde-O(S A H^2 / epsilon^2) for computing an epsilon-optimal robust policy in model-free robust average-reward RL, without requiring prior knowledge of the robust bias span H (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: Model-free RHI on G(10,5) with ℓ₂ uncertainty across 5 ε-targets × 4 seeds (20 runs) all achieving ε-optimality, with log-log slope 2.36 consistent with Õ(ε⁻²); independent non-circularity check confirms estimation error ∝ n⁻⁰·⁴³ ≈ 1/√n. Limitations: SAH² dependence not directly tested, H used to set iteration count n=⌈H/ε⌉ though not in per-iteration updates.

claims.claim: The reduction-to-discounted-MDP approach analyzed in the paper requires knowledge of the bias span H and yields a worse sample complexity of tilde-O(S A H^2 / epsilon^4) (Section 4, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Reduction implemented with policy transfer verified on 4 ε values (all gaps within bound), γ=1−ε/H shown structurally undefined without H, and measured sample complexity slopes 3.06 (reduction) vs 2.40 (RHI) with growing budget ratio reaching 440× at smallest ε; algebra correctly reconstructs Õ(SAH²/ε⁴).

claims.claim: Lemma 5.1 bounds the sub-optimality of a greedy policy relative to Q by the span seminorm of the residual, 0 <= g*_P - g^pi_P(s) <= Sp(T_P(Q) - Q) (Section 5, Lemma 5.1).
claims.evidence: 300 randomized robust AMDPs across 5 uncertainty sets (contamination, ℓ₂, ℓ∞, ℓ₁) and 4 sizes with 0 violations of the two-sided inequality 0 ≤ g*−g^π ≤ Sp(𝒯_P(Q)−Q); non-greedy negative control violates the bound (gap ≈0.56 ≫ span ≈0.002), confirming non-vacuity and greedy-specificity.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 establishes that RHI's iterates converge exactly, with Sp(T_P(Q_k) - Q_k) approaching 0 as k goes to infinity (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Exact Halpern iteration on 9 instances including G(20,15) at paper scale shows span residual reduced >99% at k=3000 with O(1/k) log-slope ≈ −1 on all instances; non-expansion property directly verified with ratio ‖𝒯_P(Q₁)−𝒯_P(Q₂)‖_sp/‖Q₁−Q₂‖_sp reaching 1.0, confirming Banach–Picard inapplicability.

claims.claim: Instead of a multi-level Monte Carlo estimator (noted to induce unbounded sample complexity in this setting), RHI uses a recursive sampling scheme that estimates successive differences T_P(Q_k) - T_P(Q_{k-1}) (Section 5, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Model-free RHI with R-SAMPLE implemented with Q built from sampled T (estimation error genuinely nonzero), Proposition C.2 bounded accumulated error verified (max ‖T^k−𝒯_P(Q^k)‖∞ = 0.012 ≤ ε=0.15 across all 8 iterations), m_k shrinks from 48→4.3 as differences vanish, recursive budget 8,700 < single-level 18,000.

claims.claim: The paper's sample complexity result is claimed to be the first finite-sample guarantee for model-free robust average-reward MDPs, covering both contamination and l_p-norm uncertainty sets (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: Finite-sample regime verified at G(20,15) for all 3 uncertainty sets with concrete budgets and gaps: contamination (22,500 samples, gap 0.00178), TV/ℓ∞ (4,200 samples, gap 0.00022), ℓ₂ (127,500 samples, gap 0.00129), all well under ε=0.15. The 'first' novelty sub-claim is a literature positioning statement not experimentally provable, but the substantive finite-sample guarantee for both uncertainty families is verified.

DineshAI/GMIHHrJ6Wp.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all six claims through faithful from-scratch implementations of model-free RHI with R-SAMPLE, exact Halpern, and the reduction, each with negative controls, raw CSV/JSON data, and honest limitations. Key gaps include the smaller G(10,5) MDP for the scaling sweep (vs G(20,15) used elsewhere), untested SAH² dependence, and the inherently unverifiable 'first' novelty claim.

ai-sherpa/momentum-sharpness-stochastic-.paper_title: Momentum Further Constrains Sharpness at the Edge of Stochastic Stability

claims.claim: SGD with momentum (SGDM) exhibits an Edge of Stochastic Stability regime whose batch-size-dependent behavior cannot be explained by a single stability threshold, unlike vanilla SGD (Section 3).
claims.evidence: CIFAR-10 CNN (17k params, 3000 images) shows monotonically rising SGDM plateaus [9.45, 16.32, 24.51, 25.44] across batches [16, 64, 256, 512]; two-law fit SSE=26.1 vs single-threshold SSE=170.3 (6.5x reduction), with vanilla SGD control showing a qualitatively different, flatter batch-dependence pattern.

claims.claim: In the noise-dominated (small-batch) regime, SGDM's mean-square stability condition reduces to a spectral-radius condition rho(I - eta_eff K + eta_eff^2 G) < 1 with effective learning rate eta_eff = eta/(1-beta) (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: 60 scalar cases match the reduced-operator boundary to machine precision (residual ≤4.4e-16); 12 three-dimensional noncommuting PSD Hessian cases show full-vs-reduced spectral radius error shrinking from 3.2e-10 to 5.6e-05 as eta→0, confirming the O(eta^2) reduction; eta_eff/eta=2.0 for beta=0.5 confirmed; ||G-K⊗K||=131.6 confirms genuinely multiplicative noise.

claims.claim: Batch Sharpness converges to a plateau of approximately 2(1-beta)/eta at small batch sizes, indicating momentum drives SGD toward flatter regions than vanilla SGD in this regime (Section 4).
claims.evidence: CIFAR-10 CNN at b=16 measures Batch Sharpness plateau 9.45 vs predicted 2(1-beta)/eta=10.0 (5.5% relative error); SGDM/vanilla ratio=0.80 (below 1, direction consistent with law's 1-beta=0.5); MLP secondary cross-check matches at 5.14 vs 5.00 (2.8%).

claims.claim: Batch Sharpness converges to a plateau of approximately 2(1+beta)/eta for SGDM at large batch sizes, consistent with full-batch gradient descent dynamics and sharper minima (Section 4).
claims.evidence: CIFAR-10 CNN at b=512 measures plateau 25.44 vs predicted 2(1+beta)/eta=30.0 (15.2% error, attributed to model capacity ceiling); SGDM/vanilla ratio=1.32 (above 1, direction consistent with law's 1+beta=1.5); MLP secondary cross-check is tighter at 14.42 vs 15.00 (3.9%); the small-to-large-batch sign reversal (0.80x→1.32x) is confirmed.

claims.claim: Figure 3 empirically shows batch-size-dependent Batch Sharpness plateaus for MLP and CNN architectures on CIFAR-10, with SGD with Nesterov momentum (SGDN) reaching the deterministic plateau at smaller batch sizes than SGDM (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Both MLP (402k params) and CNN (17k params) trained on 8192 real CIFAR-10 images show batch-size-dependent plateaus rising to their deterministic boundaries; SGDN reaches 90% of its own deterministic boundary at b90=50 vs SGDM's 178 (MLP, 3.6x earlier) and b90=128 vs 603 (CNN, 4.7x earlier); deterministic boundaries independently verified by bisection (max rel err 4.6e-05).

claims.claim: Figure 6 shows intervention experiments in which increasing learning rate or momentum, or decreasing batch size, triggers sharp loss 'catapults' once Batch Sharpness exceeds its operating plateau (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: Three independent CNN seeds on CIFAR-10 show destabilizing interventions (lr-up 1.22x, mom-up 1.17x, batch-down 1.33x) all exceed control (1.05x) with no seed overlap between any destabilizing minimum and control maximum, while stabilizing moves stay at or below control; all branches recover (endpoint/peak <1); MLP secondary shows larger 2-4x catapults with same ordering.

ai-sherpa/momentum-sharpness-stochastic-.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence from real CIFAR-10 training runs with CNN and MLP architectures, exact Hessian-based Batch Sharpness measurements, and operator-level theorem verification, supporting all six claims at reduced scale (3000-8192 images, 17k-402k parameters, 450-3000 steps). The reproduction is rigorous in methodology—exact autograd HVP, multiple seeds for interventions, vanilla controls, independent boundary bisection—but operates at a fraction of the paper's full training budget and dataset size, with the large-batch plateau (Claim 4, 15.2% error) and CNN catapult magnitudes (Claim 6, 10-33%) being the loosest matches.

ai-sherpa/multivariate-distributional-rl.paper_title: Multivariate Distributional Reinforcement Learning Using Sliced Divergences

claims.claim: Theorem 1 proves that both uniform-sliced and max-sliced divergences retain the metric properties of the underlying base divergence when that base divergence is itself a metric on the reals (Section 4.1, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: All four metric axioms tested on 6 base×lift combinations over 40 random triples: identity exact (max d(X,X)=0), symmetry gap ≤8.9e-16, minimum triangle slack +0.305 (strictly positive), minimum positive distance 0.323. This is a finite-sample verification of a universal theorem, not a proof, but the evidence is concrete and consistent.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 proves the distributional Bellman operator is a contraction in the sup-sliced divergence metric under uniform slicing with shared scalar discounting γI_d, with contraction factor c(γ) (Section 4.2, Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Measured contraction ratios match base-specific c(γ) to machine precision: sliced-Wasserstein ratio = γ (max dev 2.2e-16), sliced-Cramér ratio = √γ (dev 4.4e-16), sliced-MMD ≤ √γ (0.9358 ≤ 0.9487 at γ=0.9). The Bellman operator was applied to real particle clouds with shared reward, isolating the γ-scaling factor.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 proves the max-slicing variant achieves a Bellman contraction under general dense per-state-action discount matrices Γ(s,a), resolving a previously open theoretical gap (Section 4.2, Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Paper's exact counterexample reproduced to 6 digits: uniform SW₁ 0.527393→0.567286 (ratio 1.076 > ‖A‖_op=0.9), showing uniform slicing expands. Over 60 random dense Γ, max-slicing had 0/60 violations (worst slack -0.040) while uniform had 1/60. The counterexample is decisive and matches the paper exactly.

claims.claim: Propositions 5 and 6 show uniform slicing preserves the unbiased-sample-gradient property needed for one-sample TD bootstrapping, while max-slicing and Wasserstein-based objectives violate this property (Section 4.4, Propositions 5-6).
claims.evidence: Monte-Carlo m=1 relative bias over 6000 draws: (U)-satisfying sliced-Cramér 2.1%, sliced-MMD 0.9%; (U)-violating sliced-Wasserstein 150.0%, max-sliced-Cramér 120.4%, max-sliced-Wasserstein 97.9%. Clean separation with the largest satisfying bias (2.1%) far below the smallest violating bias (97.9%). Analytic gradients validated against finite differences (rel-err < 1e-4).

claims.claim: SDRL supports sliced Wasserstein distance and sliced Cramér distance, each computable in O(Ln log n), as well as sliced Maximum Mean Discrepancy at O(Ln^2), as base divergences within the particle-based critic of Algorithm 1 (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Wall-clock timing over n∈{256,...,8192} with fitted exponents: sliced-Wasserstein p=1.00, sliced-Cramér p=0.97 (≈n log n), sliced-MMD p=2.34 (≈n²). At n=4096: 4.8ms / 20.4ms vs 5.24s (1097× gap), confirming the claimed complexity separation.

claims.claim: In the chain environment experiment, objectives satisfying the unbiased-gradient property (U) achieve a median Wasserstein distance of about 0.15-0.25 under standard TD updates, whereas objectives violating (U) degrade to roughly 0.4 or higher (Figure 2, Section 5).
claims.evidence: Chain MDP (K=10, γ=0.9) with genuine one-sample distributional TD over 50,000 updates × 3 seeds: (U)-satisfying sliced-Cramér median sliced W₂=0.164, sliced-MMD=0.169 (within stated 0.15–0.25 band); (U)-violating sliced-Wasserstein=0.516, max-sliced-Cramér=0.346 (degraded). Full-OT W₂ preserves the same ordering. Reduced particle count (N=64) but faithful task and regime.

ai-sherpa/multivariate-distributional-rl.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from real runs supporting all six claims: metric axioms hold on sampled triples, contraction factors match to machine precision, the dense-Γ counterexample reproduces to 6 digits, the unbiased-gradient dichotomy shows clean separation, complexity exponents match theory, and the chain experiment reproduces the (U)-separation with values in the paper's stated bands. The reproduction is independent (numpy/scipy from scratch, no paper code) and honest about the finite-sample nature of theorem verification.

ai-sherpa/diffusion-data-statistics-easy.paper_title: A theory of learning data statistics in diffusion models, from easy to hard

claims.claim: Diffusion denoisers trained on natural images exhibit a distributional simplicity bias: on CIFAR-10, a U-Net achieves nearly identical test loss on real images versus Gaussian clones matched in mean and covariance for roughly 10^3 training steps before performance diverges, indicating pair-wise statistics are learned first (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: Real CIFAR-10 grayscale (20k train/5k test) with a 3.5M-param DDPM U-Net on GPU: at lr 2e-5, real vs mean+cov-clone test losses are within 0.15% through step 300, diverging from step 750 to +20.2% by step 8000; mean-only clone stays flat at 0.1667, confirming the ordering mean >> mean+cov > real. The ~10^3 onset is shown to be optimizer-speed dependent (step 100 at lr 2e-4, step 750 at lr 2e-5), honestly reported.

claims.claim: For a k-th order cumulant target, the sample complexity threshold for weak recovery via projected gradient descent is n_hat(d,k) = omega(d^(k-1) log^2 d), with |v . w(n_hat)| approaching 1 as d approaches infinity after this many steps (Proposition 4.3).
claims.evidence: Measured escape-sample log-log slopes of n_hat vs d are 1.67, 2.02, 2.96 for k=2,3,4 (theory: 1,2,3), and the ratio n_hat/(d^(k-1) log^2 d) stays roughly constant per k across multiple d values. Above threshold (k=4, d=32, n=40000≈d^3), median |v.w|=0.997, approaching 1.

claims.claim: If the number of samples n(d) = o(n_hat(d,k*)), standard SGD provably fails to achieve weak recovery of the k*-th cumulant, establishing a sharp learnable/unlearnable sample-complexity separation (Proposition 4.4).
claims.evidence: For k=4, d=32 (d^3=32768), recovery rate sweeps from 0% (n=500) and 1% (n=1000, well below cubic) to 99.5% (n=40000, ~d^3), with a sharp transition between n=5000 (24%) and n=20000 (87%), demonstrating the learnable/unlearnable separation at the cubic threshold.

claims.claim: In a mixed-cumulant latent model, pair-wise statistics are recoverable with linear sample complexity n = Theta(d * polylog(d)), while recovering the fourth cumulant requires Omega(d^3) samples when latent variables are independent (Proposition 4.6).
claims.evidence: In the mixed-cumulant model with independent latents at linear budget n=1500 (<<d^3=32768), covariance overlap is 0.925 (100% recovery) while fourth-cumulant overlap is 0.057 (0% recovery); the cumulant only recovers at cubic budget n=40000 (overlap 0.997).

claims.claim: When latent variables underlying the pair-wise and higher-order statistics are positively correlated, the fourth-cumulant recovery sample complexity accelerates from cubic to linear in d (Proposition 4.6).
claims.evidence: Controlled single-variable intervention at the same linear budget n=1500: changing only latent alignment from independent (v_cum ⊥ v_cov) to correlated (v_cum = v_cov) flips fourth-cumulant overlap from 0.057 (0% recovery) to 0.919 (100% recovery), demonstrating cubic-to-linear acceleration.

claims.claim: Unconstrained SGD exhibits contraction dynamics toward w=0 for many activation functions, causing learning failure, whereas constraining updates to the unit sphere (spherical projection) preserves the ability to learn higher-order statistics (Proposition 4.7).
claims.evidence: For k=4 at d=12 and d=16, unconstrained SGD contracts ||w|| from 1.0 to ~0.39 with 100% of trials below 0.75 (overlap 0.61/0.48), while spherical projection maintains ||w||=1.0 with overlap 0.86/0.79, confirming that projection preserves higher-order learning where unconstrained SGD fails.

ai-sherpa/diffusion-data-statistics-easy.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from real runs supporting all six claims: Claims 2-6 on the paper's own online projected-SGD single-index/spiked-cumulant model at finite dimensions with clear scaling trends, and Claim 1 on real CIFAR-10 with a from-scratch DDPM U-Net on GPU. The main limitations—finite-d tests of asymptotic propositions and a grayscale 20k-image subset for Claim 1—are transparently reported and do not undermine the core phenomena demonstrated.

ai-sherpa/misspecified-embedding-dimensi.paper_title: On the Effect of Misspecifying the Embedding Dimension in Low-rank Network Models

claims.claim: Under the random dot product graph (RDPG) model where P = rho_n * X X^T for latent positions X in R^(n x r), Theorem 3.1 shows trailing eigenvectors associated with zero eigenvalues delocalize, with maximum entry magnitude bounded by r^2 (log n)^(4+6*gamma) / sqrt(n) (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Measured max entry of (r+1)-th eigenvector decays from 0.190 to 0.058 over n=250..4000 with log-log slope -0.423, consistent with n^{-1/2} delocalization up to polylog factors; all values below the stated bound at γ=0.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 shows that when the embedding dimension is over-specified (k>0 extra dimensions), consistent estimation of the latent positions still holds but only at the slower rate n^(-1/4), compared to the n^(-1/2) rate achieved under correct specification (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Correct-spec ASE 2→∞ error slope -0.495 (~n^{-1/2}) vs over-spec (d=7) slope -0.183, clearly separated and slower, consistent with the n^{-1/4} regime up to polylog prefactors; over-spec error still decreases, confirming consistency.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 also shows that when the embedding dimension is under-specified (k<0), there is a fundamental lower bound on estimation error of order sqrt(|k| * rho_n), which need not vanish as the network size grows, proving inconsistency (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Under-spec (d=3, |k|=2) error plateaus at [0.66, 0.65, 0.67, 0.70, 0.74] with slope +0.042, demonstrating non-vanishing error consistent with the sqrt(|k|ρ_n) lower bound up to an unspecified constant.

claims.claim: Under correct specification, the adjacency spectral embedding satisfies ||X_hat_{1:r} W - rho_n^{1/2} X_{1:r}||_{2,infty} <~ phi_n, typically achieving the n^{-1/2} rate; over-specification adds an error term of order sqrt(sigma^2 k) * r^2 (log n)^(5+6*gamma) / n^{1/4} (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Same measured runs show base term slope -0.495 (n^{-1/2}) and over-spec dominant term slope -0.183 (n^{-1/4} regime), reproducing the two-term polynomial rate structure; polylog exponent honestly disclosed as untestable at feasible n.

claims.claim: Section 3.1 states Conjecture 1, extending the over-/under-specification results from weighted networks to binary networks under relaxed variance conditions (Section 3.1, Conjecture 1).
claims.evidence: Binary Bernoulli RDPG runs reproduce all four behaviours: correct-spec slope -0.527, over-spec -0.189, under-spec +0.038 (flat floor), trailing delocalization -0.408, providing concrete numerical support for the unproven conjecture.

claims.claim: Section 4 presents simulation experiments across multiple noise distributions confirming the theoretical over- and under-specification rates (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Five noise laws (Gaussian, Laplace, Exp, Poisson, Bernoulli) yield correct-spec slopes near -1/2 (mean -0.541), over-spec in [-0.241, -0.159] (mean -0.213), and under-spec flat (|slope|<0.08), reproducing the Section 4 rate trichotomy universally.

ai-sherpa/misspecified-embedding-dimensi.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence from clean-room ASE runs on synthetic RDPGs (n up to 4000, rank 5, 5–8 reps) that reproduce the polynomial rate structure of all six claims, including the delocalization bound, the over/under-specification trichotomy, the binary conjecture, and multi-noise simulations. The main limitation is that polylog exponents and exact constants cannot be resolved at feasible n, which is honestly disclosed; the over-spec slope (-0.183) is somewhat shallower than the asymptotic -0.25 but is plausibly explained by polylog prefactors.

DineshAI/pRgUJfrFw9.paper_title: On the Anisotropy of Score-Based Generative Models

claims.claim: Score Anisotropy Directions (SADs) are defined as the ordered orthonormal eigenvectors of the average geometry matrix G_F = E[(F_θ(x_σ,σ))²], with ordering by eigenvalue magnitude conjectured to determine the network's generation preference (Definition 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook computes G_F at paper scale with one million networks on a real iDDPM U-Net (D=256), finding the leading eigenvector stable (cross-shard overlap 0.9977) but the smallest eigenvector unstable (overlap 0.199) and all audited interior directions failing identifiability gates, so the conjecture that eigenvalue ordering determines generation preference cannot be verified beyond the two endpoints.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows that under denoising score matching with linear architectures and rank-one data, convergence rate decays with the eigenvalues of the conditioning matrix, and this anisotropic effect is amplified further under SGD (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides a symbolic reconstruction of the convergence rate identity, confirmed by exact rational recurrence (error 0), population GD contraction (max error 2.35e-7), covariance trace vs eigenvalue (r=0.9999985), batch-one SGD across 96×4000×5 runs (r=0.9985), an independent finite-difference Hessian checker (error 1.27e-9), and a rejecting negative control—all on the exact linear/rank-one setting the theorem assumes.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 characterizes the orthogonal transformation that minimizes versus maximizes alignment α with the SADs, showing minimization corresponds to reversing the eigenvalue ordering (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook gives a symbolic exchange argument yielding (a-b)(x-y) that establishes the identity permutation as maximum and reversal as minimum over the full doubly-stochastic polytope, confirmed by exhaustive permutation enumeration over D=2–9 (409,112 permutations), a Haar-orthogonal sweep (384/384 within bounds), an independent optimizer (errors <6e-14), and a rejecting negative control.

claims.claim: For an iDDPM U-Net, generation performance degrades monotonically as the eigenvalue associated with the aligned data direction increases, with the model performing best on data aligned with small-eigenvalue SAD eigenvectors (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: Five paired paper-scale iDDPM endpoint runs consistently show lower SW2 for the smallest-eigenvalue SAD direction versus the largest (mean difference 3.89, 95% CI [2.74, 5.28]), but only two endpoints are tested; the monotonic degradation across intermediate eigenvalues cannot be assessed because all audited interior SADs fail the cross-shard identifiability gate.

claims.claim: On MNIST, CelebA-HQ, and CIFAR-10, minimizing alignment α with the SADs substantially improves Sliced Wasserstein-2 distances relative to the default natural alignment, whereas maximizing alignment induces mode collapse (Figure 8, Figure 9).
claims.evidence: No actual training, generation, or SW2 evaluation was performed on any of the three datasets; the four routes consist of a single timed CPU update (resource estimate only), an unsuccessful artifact search, an audit of the published figure image, and a failed falsification search, none of which constitute independent experimental evidence.

claims.claim: Closed-form average geometry expressions are derived per architecture: MLPs yield G_F = αI + β·11ᵀ, CNNs yield a block-diagonal Kronecker structure reflecting spatial organization, and Transformers yield at most T distinct eigenvalues where T is the number of tokens (Section on architecture-specific results).
claims.evidence: Conditional moment derivations yield the three claimed matrix families exactly, confirmed by actual executable MLP (36K networks, residual 0.025), CNN (24K networks, residual 0.031), and Transformer (32K networks, residual 0.030, exactly 7 eigenvalue groups for T=7) experiments, an independent exhaustive Rademacher-domain checker with max error 0 for all three, and controls that reject broken assumptions.

DineshAI/pRgUJfrFw9.overall: The logbook provides rigorous symbolic and numerical verification for the three theorem/proposition claims (2, 3, 6) with independent checkers and negative controls, but the empirical generation claims (1, 4, 5) remain incomplete: Claims 1 and 4 are limited by unstable interior SAD identifiability at paper scale, and Claim 5 has no actual training or generation runs on any real-image dataset.

ai-sherpa/bandit-optimal-transport-repro.paper_title: Linear Bandits beyond Inner Product Spaces, the case of Bandit Optimal Transport

claims.claim: The EntUCB algorithm embeds transport plans into a Hilbert space via the Fourier isometry F on L²(ℝᵈ;ϱ), reducing the bandit optimal transport problem to linear bandit estimation in that space (Section 4.1, Equation 7).
claims.evidence: On Uniform{0,1} marginals with ϱ on integer lattice points, e^{−2πi⟨x,ξ⟩}=1 identically, so F collapses to the ϱ-mean: a unit-norm zero-mean function f=(1,−1,−1,1)/2 has ‖f‖=1.0 but ‖Ff‖=0.0 (verified on 100 random zero-mean vectors, all ≤2.5e-16). Eq (7) gives LHS=0.0 vs RHS=0.5 on the admissible diagonal coupling.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 bounds the entropic regret as R_T^{H,ε}(A) ≤ σ√(2T log(2/δ)) + 2Cβ_T(δ)√(T log det(...)) with probability at least 1-δ (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: A real EntUCB run on the paper's Fourier map (off-lattice 6×6 support, D=16 frequencies, transport value exactly linear in features with error 1.78e-15), T=2500, 12 seeds, RLS confidence sets: measured entropic regret mean 160.4 (max 190.3) stays below the full Theorem 5.1 RHS (mean 23366, min 15978) in 12/12 seeds, giving coverage 1.0 ≥ 1−δ=0.95.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 shows that for Lipschitz costs with an entropy penalty decaying as ε_t = αt^{-α}, EntUCB achieves sublinear regret matching classical linear-bandit rates for the Kantorovich optimal transport problem (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Real EntUCB run with ε_t=0.5·t^{−0.5} over T∈{500,…,4000}, 12 seeds: cumulative Kantorovich regret grows as T^0.491 (R²=0.996), matching the classical √T rate, while a uniform-random policy on the same instances grows as T^1.000 (R²=1.0). Entropic bias Σε_t·H=43.1 is sublinear.

claims.claim: Corollary 5.3 establishes that in finite-dimensional/discrete settings with N basis coefficients, the algorithm attains Õ(√(NT)) regret, recovering the parametric OFUL-style rate (Corollary 5.3).
claims.evidence: On a 3×3 uniform OT instance, Assumption 3 holds with ζ(n)=1_{n≥2} (top-2 coefficient partial sum 4.0 ≥ ‖c*‖=3.873) yet γ₃=2.0≠0. Truncating to N=2 dimensions yields a fixed per-round gap of 1.0 (true optimum 0.0 vs played cost 1.0), giving regret 4096 = 45.25·√(NT) at T=4096 — linear, not Õ(√(NT)).

claims.claim: Corollary 5.4 shows that when basis coefficients decay at rate 1-n^{-q}, regret interpolates between Õ(√T) and Õ(T) depending on the decay exponent q (Corollary 5.4).
claims.evidence: The sequence γ_i=1/i is in L² (‖c*‖₂=1.2825, finite) and satisfies Assumption 3 for all q>0 (partial sums H_n ≥ H_2=1.5 ≥ ‖c*‖₂ for n≥2), yet its ℓ¹ tail diverges (partial sum grows 7.49 at n=10³ to 15.09 at n=2×10⁶). The q=4 witness shows actual tail 0.1717 vs derivable bound 1.6e-7.

claims.claim: The confidence sets used by the algorithm are constructed via regularized least-squares in L²(ℝᵈ;ϱ), with width controlled by the log-determinant of the design operator, mirroring the classical OFUL confidence ellipsoid construction (Equations 11-12).
claims.evidence: On Uniform{0,1} marginals, all 50 random couplings map to the identical feature (1,1,1,1) (deviation ≤2.5e-16), while the diagonal coupling has cost 0.0 and the anti-diagonal has cost 1.0 — no linear predictor can separate them, making the RLS problem rank-degenerate. Additionally, Eq (12) requires adding a 4×4 operator DΛ to a 3×3 Gram matrix M_tM_t*, which is dimensionally undefined.

ai-sherpa/bosonic-hamiltonian-d-rut-repr.paper_title: Continuous Variable Hamiltonian Learning at Heisenberg Limit via Displacement-Random Unitary Transformation

claims.claim: The Displacement-Random Unitary Transformation (D-RUT) protocol learns all coefficients of a generic multi-mode bosonic Hamiltonian with evolution time scaling as O(1/epsilon), achieving the Heisenberg limit (Theorem 1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: Six random Hamiltonians × 8 time budgets yield measured RMSE-vs-T log-log slope mean -0.9922 (range [-1.0247, -0.9480]), with a destructive SQL control (fixed κ=1) collapsing to slope -0.4968, demonstrating the Heisenberg 1/T scaling from real RPE-sampled runs.

claims.claim: For single-mode Hamiltonians expressed in a first-quantization (position/momentum) basis, D-RUT recovers physical coefficients with RMSE epsilon_G using total evolution time O~(1/epsilon_G), under stated conditions on known zero coefficients, non-zero response to basis mismatch, and a sufficiently close initial guess (Theorem 2, Section 2).
claims.evidence: With Bogoliubov basis correction, coefficient-error slope mean -0.9986 across 6 seeds; omitting the correction produces a non-decaying bias floor (~2.6e-2), confirming the correction is necessary and the Õ(1/ε_G) scaling holds.

claims.claim: The protocol's estimation error under state-preparation-and-measurement (SPAM) errors is bounded as ||delta g_SPAM||_2 <= (L_C/sigma_min(K)) ||delta beta||_2, where L_C is a Lipschitz constant and sigma_min(K) the smallest singular value of the Gram-like matrix K (Section 3.6, Eq. 43).
claims.evidence: L_C=1.1086428947 computed from the actual response gradient/Hessian on disk r=0.70, σ_min(K)=0.1853732 from the Algorithm-1 design, and 48/48 displacement-perturbation cases satisfy ‖δg‖ ≤ (L_C/σ_min(K))‖δβ‖ with max ratio 0.30423.

claims.claim: A hierarchical two-stage coefficient recovery strategy (learn single-mode coefficients first, then coupling coefficients) is proven to have covariance dominated by that of simultaneous estimation, Cov(delta g)_hierarchical <= Cov(delta g)_simultaneous, for all parameters (Section 4.1, Appendix A).
claims.evidence: Closed-form Schur-complement algebra shows Cov_sim − Cov_hier is PSD in 40/40 random full-column-rank designs (min eigenvalue 2.57e-13), corroborated by Monte-Carlo with 12,000 draws/trial confirming the ordering in 40/40 trials.

claims.claim: An iterative bisection search over the squeezing parameter R (relating the physical and reference bases via a Bogoliubov transformation) converges in O(log(1/epsilon_R)) iterations for first-quantization Hamiltonian learning (Section 5.3, Eq. 77-78).
claims.evidence: 90/90 bisection searches over the squeezing parameter converge within tolerance and under the ⌈log₂(W/2ε)⌉ ceiling, with measured iteration-count slope 1.4332 ≈ 1/ln2 matching the O(log(1/ε_R)) law.

claims.claim: The algorithm uses Chebyshev-node sampling of the displacement parameter combined with robust phase estimation and inverse discrete Fourier transform to reconstruct coefficients, as detailed in Algorithm 1 and illustrated for the single-mode case in Figure 1 (Section 2).
claims.evidence: 60 exact reconstructions (orders 2–6, 1920 response cells) using the full Chebyshev-radial + angular + inverse-DFT pipeline achieve max coefficient error 1.08e-15, with wrong-sign angular inversion control breaking recovery (error 0.5257).

ai-sherpa/bosonic-hamiltonian-d-rut-repr.overall: This logbook provides a faithful independent CPU reproduction of all six claims of the D-RUT paper at the paper's native experimental scale (degree-2 bosonic Hamiltonians, finite-Fock simulation), with measured scaling laws, algebraic certificates, and destructive controls throughout. The evidence is concrete and numerical rather than proof-level, but the mechanism is genuinely implemented and the results consistently support the paper's claims.

ai-sherpa/capacity-multihead-attention-r.paper_title: A Capacity-Based Rationale for Multi-Head Attention

claims.claim: Recovering a graph with m' relations in d_model-dimensional embeddings requires total key dimension D_K = Θ(m' log m' / d_model), established as a lower bound (Section 7) and matched by a constructive upper bound (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Exact log₂ C(m(m-1), m') computed via lgamma stays within ratio 1.14–1.62 of the surrogate m'log₂(m²/m') across m up to 1024 and sparse→dense m', confirming the Θ lower bound; Construction II separation margins measured at m=2048/4096 grow monotonically with C (e.g., m=4096: -24→338) at budget D_K=Θ(m log m/d_model), confirming the matching upper bound.

claims.claim: For permutation graphs (m' = m), the capacity requirement simplifies to D_K = Θ(m log m / d_model) (Section 4/Section 7).
claims.evidence: The m'=m specialization is confirmed by exact bit-counts: log₂ C(m(m-1), m) tracks m·log₂ m with ratios 1.224→1.143 (m=64→1024), monotonically decreasing toward 1, confirming the log m (not log m²) collapse; the constructive upper bound and trained model (Claim 4) realize this rate.

claims.claim: Multi-head attention's advantage arises because splitting into heads reduces the effective block size B, shrinking the noise term N3(B) ≍ (B/d_model)√(d_k log m) that governs interference from superposition (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Directly measured superposition noise N_3(B) at m=4096, d_model=256, d_k=64 fits N_3=0.119·B with R²=0.988; signal is block-size-independent (CV=0.026); single-head noise N_3(B=m)=477 vs multi-head N_3(B=d_model)=48 yields a 9.9× ratio, confirming the mechanism.

claims.claim: Empirical scaling of the optimal total key dimension matches theory: D_K* ≈ 1.19·(m log m/d_model) with R²=0.944 (R²=0.992 after excluding three outlier points), and the optimal head count scales as h* ≈ 1.65(m/d_model) − 6.64 with per-head widths d_k* in [5,24] (median 11) (Section 6).
claims.evidence: Trained max-attention models on the paper's 12-cell grid (m∈{64,128,256,512}×d_model∈{16,32,64}) yield D_K*=0.84·(m log m/d_model) with R²=0.943 (Pearson 0.982), matching the paper's R²=0.944; the same three (d_model=16, m>64) outliers are identified (R²=0.975 excl.); head-count law h*=0.51(m/d_model)-0.64 (R²=0.967) and d_k*∈[4,12] (median 8) reproduce the qualitative structure, though absolute constants differ due to 1-seed/≤500-step vs 10-seed/≤200k-step compute budget.

claims.claim: The multi-head capacity advantage persists in a fuller Transformer setting with softmax normalization, value routing, and frozen GPT-2 embeddings, since the analysis establishes capacity is purely key-query driven (Appendix C).
claims.evidence: The multi-head advantage is tested with genuine softmax attention, value routing, and correlated non-orthogonal embeddings (mean|cos|=0.29) at m≤512, d_model≤64, showing single-head collapse (acc 0.57, relMSE 0.37–0.61) vs multi-head success (acc 1.0, relMSE 0.000–0.006); however, the paper's headline setting uses frozen GPT-2 embeddings at m=6144, d_model=768, which is ~12× larger in both dimensions and not reproduced.

claims.claim: Capacity requirements are largely insensitive to context length, tested over sequence lengths ℓ ∈ {16,32}, with only modest degradation when evaluating at longer lengths than training (Section 6.1, Appendix A.3).
claims.evidence: Context-window retrieval trained at ℓ∈{16,32} for m∈{128,256} shows near-identical plateau accuracy across settings: at threshold D_K, m=256 gives t16e16=0.969, t32e32=0.932, t16e32=0.943 (max gap 0.036), and m=128 gives max gap 0.086, confirming insensitivity to context length and modest long-eval degradation as claimed.
