SabaPivot/repro-floating-point-networks-.overall: The logbook provides a from-scratch binary32 reverse-mode AD tape with bit-exact verification of all six claims through constructive gadget tests, activation witnesses, antisymmetry sweeps, and exhaustive non-associativity certificates, all with appropriate destructive controls. The evidence strongly supports the paper's mechanisms on representative domain points, though finite grids cannot replace the universal proofs.

SabaPivot/repro-discovering-scaling-expo.paper_title: Discovering Scaling Exponents with Physics-Informed Müntz-Szász Networks

claims.claim: MSN-PINN models targets as sums of power-law terms u_theta(x) = sum_k c_k x^{mu_k}, treating both coefficients {c_k} and exponents {mu_k} as trainable parameters optimized via a two-timescale scheme with exponent learning rate eta_mu set to roughly 0.5 times the coefficient learning rate eta_c (Equation 1, Section 3.1, Algorithm 1, Section 3.5).
claims.evidence: The reproduction implements u_theta(x)=sum_k c_k x^{mu_k} with separate Adam groups at eta_c=0.01 and eta_mu=0.005 (exactly 0.5x), and three 10,000-epoch runs recover the planted spectrum with max exponent error 0.070143%, while frozen-exponent controls show 6.77% median error and finite-difference gradient checks match to 8.43e-12.

claims.claim: For the 2D Laplace equation corner singularity with a 270-degree wedge angle, MSN-PINN recovers the exponent as mu=0.6667 against the true classical Kondrat'ev value of 2/3, a 0.009% error (Table 2).
claims.evidence: A full 2D polar wedge model (K=4, 15,000 epochs, 200 arc points, 100 edge points, 3 seeds) recovers the 270° DD corner exponent with 0.008625% mean error in the independent CPU replay (paper: 0.009%), and an independent finite-difference Laplacian check confirms harmonicity with max residual 1.96e-7.

claims.claim: On a 40-configuration wedge benchmark spanning 5 angles and 4 boundary condition types, the constraint-aware MSN-PINN achieves 100% success rate with 0.022% mean exponent error, versus only 55% success and 5.96% mean error for the naive MSN-PINN without the constraint term, a roughly 270-fold improvement in accuracy (Section I.8, Table 11).
claims.evidence: 40 real wedge optimizations (5 angles × 4 BCs × 2 methods) confirm 100% success for constraint-aware training with ~0.013% mean error, versus 45% success and ~1.67% error for the naive package; the qualitative finding and constraint-aware numbers match, though the exact naive baseline (55%/5.96%) and 270-fold ratio are not numerically reproduced by the clean-room implementation.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.5 shows the exponent recovery error scales as O(sigma / (c_min * Delta^2 * sqrt(N))), where Delta is the minimum separation between exponents, implying degraded conditioning as exponents become closely spaced, analogous to an optical resolution limit (Theorem 4.5, Remark 4.6).
claims.evidence: The Delta^-2 conditioning is supported (small-separation slope of -1.948), but a bounded structured perturbation refit from N=200 to N=3200 yields an error ratio of 0.9999991 instead of the claimed 0.25, contradicting the N^{-1/2} factor in the stated O(sigma/(c_min*Delta^2*sqrt(N))) scaling under bounded noise.

claims.claim: Adding a constraint-aware loss term of the form sum_k |c_k| sin^2(mu_k * omega) to steer critical points toward physically valid exponents improves accuracy on the corner-singularity example from 14.6% error to 0.009% error (Theorem 4.8, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The constrained endpoint (~0.009% error) is reproduced, but 33 naive runs across 11 source-supported protocols yield protocol means ranging from 0.00000017% to 66.1%, with none within two percentage points of the claimed 14.6% naive baseline; the primary three-seed naive protocol already achieves 0.000115% error without the constraint term.

claims.claim: Two exponents become distinguishable (resolvable) only when their separation Delta is at least 0.1; below this threshold they merge into an intermediate value, termed the Rayleigh limit for exponent resolution (Table 10, Section I.6, Remark I.1).
claims.evidence: A Table-10-style grid of 50 optimizer runs (5 separations × 10 Adam approaches) shows resolved rates of exactly 0.0 for Delta=0.02 and 0.05, and 1.0 for Delta=0.10, 0.20, and 0.30, confirming the practical resolution threshold at Delta=0.1.

SabaPivot/repro-discovering-scaling-expo.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous clean-room reproduction with full-scale 2D wedge models, 40 real optimization runs, 620 nonlinear recovery fits, and 500 resolution trials, confirming the core method (Claims 1, 2, 3, 6) while falsifying two specific numerical/theoretical claims (Claims 4, 5) with concrete counterexamples.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows a symmetric smoothing operator with positive coefficients can be rescaled by a diagonal matrix (via a symmetric Sinkhorn iteration) into a diffusion operator that is self-adjoint with respect to a mass-weighted inner product (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: A 512-point irregular closed curve with nonuniform masses (103.46× max/min ratio) directly tests the mass-weighted self-adjointness property: constant-preservation error 8.27e-13, mass-weighted self-adjointness error ‖diag(m)Q−Qᵀdiag(m)‖∞ = 2.17e-19, strictly positive minimum entry, and 6 iterations to 0.1% tolerance.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 proves that for Gaussian and exponential kernels, the Sinkhorn-normalized operators converge uniformly on bounded domains to continuous diffusion operators as sampling resolution increases (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: A resolution sweep on [0,1] with n={65,129,257,513,1025} and trapezoidal masses for both Gaussian and exponential kernels shows monotonically decreasing error against the 1025-point reference, with measured log-log convergence rates of 2.1273 (Gaussian) and 2.1100 (exponential), directly demonstrating continuum convergence on a bounded domain.

claims.claim: The symmetric Sinkhorn algorithm empirically requires only 5 to 10 iterations to reduce normalization error below 0.1% (Section 4/5, empirical convergence results).
claims.evidence: Across 13 independent test cells (five resolutions × two kernel families, a 512-point nonuniform curve, a 2048-point two-ring cloud, and a 1176-voxel sparse domain), iterations to 0.1% row-sum error range from 6 to 8 (median 8), all falling within the paper's stated 5–10 range.

claims.claim: The normalized operators simultaneously satisfy symmetry, mass conservation, entrywise positivity, and spectral damping (eigenvalues in [0,1]), properties not jointly satisfied by standard row- or symmetric-normalization schemes (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: On a strongly nonuniform two-cluster cloud, row normalization shows symmetry error ≥0.02637, standard symmetric normalization shows constant-preservation error ≥0.37858, while Sinkhorn achieves constant error ≤7.02e-13, symmetry ≤1.39e-17, positive entries, and eigenvalues in [−7.81e-17, 1.0000000000000004], demonstrating that only Sinkhorn jointly satisfies all four properties.

claims.claim: The method is demonstrated on point clouds, sparse voxel grids (jaw bone geometry), and Gaussian mixture models with covariance-aware kernels, showing Laplacian-like smoothing on each irregular data type (Section 5, experiments).
claims.evidence: All three named modalities are tested with concrete runs: a 2048-point cloud (variance reduction 0.6319→0.3826), a 1176-voxel sparse domain (88.47% roughness reduction), and a 220-component full-covariance GMM on the 172,974-vertex Stanford Armadillo with Mahalanobis distance using fitted 3×3 covariances (99.85% Dirichlet energy reduction). The specific jaw-bone geometry is substituted with other 3D domains, but all three irregular data types are demonstrated.

claims.claim: Shape analysis experiments on the Armadillo mesh show spectral distributions remain consistent across sampling modalities, with eigenvalue divergence appearing only at scales matching sampling resolution, validating the Theorem 4.2 convergence guarantee (Section 5).
claims.evidence: On the 172,974-vertex Stanford Armadillo, 32 diffusion-generator eigenvalues are computed from point, voxel, and GMM representations; modes 2–10 mean relative errors are 10.91% (voxel) and 6.20% (GMM) against the point reference, and a nested resolution sweep shows error decreasing monotonically from 35.58% (n=250) to 11.39% (n=800), directly demonstrating spectral consistency across modalities and resolution-dependent divergence.

SabaPivot/repro-sinkhorn-normalization-o.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims through multi-resolution kernel sweeps, normalization baseline comparisons, and real Stanford Armadillo geometry experiments across point, voxel, and GMM modalities. Some setups are simplified (1D interval for convergence, jaw-bone geometry substituted), but the core mathematical and empirical claims are directly tested with real runs and measured quantities.

claims.claim: RDNGD achieves iteration and oracle complexity of O(d·ε⁻²) for smooth nonconvex problems and O(d·ε⁻¹) for smooth convex problems using only a pairwise comparison oracle on Riemannian manifolds (Table 1).
claims.evidence: 108 nonconvex runs (Rayleigh quotient on spheres, d=5/10/20, ε=0.4/0.3/0.2, 12 seeds) all succeed within ceil(12d/ε²) iterations, and 108 convex runs (smooth quadratic, same dimensions, ε=0.1/0.05/0.025) all succeed within ceil(10d/ε) iterations, with exactly two comparison queries per iteration and no value/gradient access.

claims.claim: The recurrent variant RRDNGD attains linear convergence for strongly convex objectives, requiring O(d log(1/ε)) oracle calls (Table 1).
claims.evidence: RRDNGD on strongly convex quadratic at d=5/10/20 with 12 seeds and 8 recurrent phases shows log₂-error-vs-phase slopes of −1.033, −1.000, and −1.018, demonstrating approximately one bit of error reduction per phase with 80d pairwise evaluations per phase, consistent with O(d log(1/ε)) oracle cost.

claims.claim: RDFW, a projection-free Riemannian dueling Frank-Wolfe method, achieves O(ε⁻¹) iteration complexity with O(d·ε⁻²) oracle calls for smooth convex problems using only a linear minimization oracle (Table 1).
claims.evidence: RDFW on smooth convex objective over probability simplex (d=5/10/20, 144 runs) uses zero projections, one LMO call per iteration, and M_k ∝ d(k+3) comparison directions; query-vs-iteration log-log slopes of 1.905–1.908 match dT² scaling, and error-vs-iteration slopes of −1.92 to −2.21 are at least as fast as O(1/T).

claims.claim: Lemma 3.1 and Lemma 3.2 show the comparison-based gradient direction estimator is unbiased for the normalized gradient with improved constants over prior Euclidean dueling optimization work (Section 3, Lemma 3.1, Lemma 3.2).
claims.evidence: 200,000 sphere directions at d=2/5/10/50 confirm the ideal estimator is unbiased (agreement ≤0.002191 with exact expectation) and improved constants hold (C_hat=0.80–0.90 vs 1/√(2π)=0.399), but the practical finite-ν estimator at ν=0.5 shows 6.27–7.50% sign disagreement and 0.0277–0.1492 orthogonal bias, contradicting the unqualified claim that 'the comparison-based gradient direction estimator is unbiased.'

claims.claim: The framework is applied to a black-box adversarial attack on DNNs with sphere-constrained perturbations and to horizon leveling via SO(2) image rotation, both using only pairwise comparison feedback (Section on real-world applications).
claims.evidence: Horizon leveling on SO(2) with 19 tilts using only paired misalignment preferences achieves loss <1e-5 in 19/19 cases; black-box adversarial attack on pretrained CIFAR-10 VGG11-BN with 1000 steps and 10 comparison directions per step succeeds on 3/4 images, moving margin from +9.32 to −4.90 with ℓ2=0.5 sphere constraint (max radius error 3.58e-7), using only pairwise sign feedback.

claims.claim: The method covers Hadamard manifolds and bounded-sectional-curvature spaces, with demonstrated applications including Rayleigh quotient maximization on the unit sphere and Karcher mean computation on SPD matrices (Section on synthetic applications).
claims.evidence: Rayleigh quotient on S⁹ (bounded positive curvature) succeeds 12/12 at ε=0.2 with median gradient norm 0.01468; Karcher mean on 16 noncommuting 8×8 dense SPD matrices under affine-invariant metric (min commutator norm 0.429) converges from 1.411 to 1.334, within 1.36e-5 relative gap and 0.0059 affine-invariant distance of independently computed Karcher mean (reference residual 2.53e-13), using only comparison signs.

SabaPivot/repro-riemannian-dueling-optim.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting five of six claims through executed runs on real Riemannian manifolds, real DNN adversarial attacks, and Monte Carlo estimator analysis, with multiple seeds and dimensions. Claim 4 is falsified because the practical finite-ν comparison estimator exhibits measurable bias at larger perturbation scales, contradicting the unqualified unbiasedness assertion, even though the ideal estimator and improved constants are confirmed.

SabaPivot/repro-quantifying-the-noise-se.paper_title: Quantifying the noise sensitivity of the Wasserstein metric for images

claims.claim: Theorem 2 bounds the expected signed 1-Wasserstein distance between a clean n-pixel image and its Gaussian-noise-perturbed counterpart by (2/√π)σn log2(n) + (1/(2√π))σn, i.e., growth roughly linear in n with a log factor, for zero-sum noise of standard deviation σ (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Finite Monte Carlo audit at n∈{8,16,32} with 80 zero-sum Gaussian noise pairs per resolution using exact POT transport: all one-noise and two-noise bound checks passed (largest ratio 0.141), and fitted resolution slope 1.157 is consistent with the predicted n·log(n) growth.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 shows that for p-Wasserstein distances with integer p>1, the expected p-th power error is bounded by (4/√π) n σ, so the per-image error scales as (nσ)^(1/p), improving (becoming more noise-robust) as p increases, in contrast to the Euclidean (L2) metric's linear scaling in σ (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: 54 bound cells across p∈{2,3,4}, n∈{8,16,32}, and six noise levels all passed E[W_p^p] upper-bound checks; fitted σ-slopes at n=32 are 0.511, 0.345, 0.262 against predicted 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, and L2 exponent measured at 1.001, confirming the stated contrast.

claims.claim: Theorems 4 and 5 extend the noise-sensitivity bounds to the deviation between the true and noisy Wasserstein distances computed between two distinct images, rather than a single noisy image against its clean version (Theorems 4-5).
claims.evidence: Two distinct Hsp90 projections compared on the 32×32 torus across 7 noise levels with 30 pairs per level using exact W1/W2/W3 transport: all 21/21 two-image deviation inequalities held, with largest observed/bound ratios of 0.0604 (W1), 0.2017 (W2), and 0.1133 (W3).

claims.claim: On cryo-electron microscopy projection images of the hsp90 protein with noise level σ=0.01, the squared-Wasserstein (W2) distance matrix preserves the ground-truth diagonal similarity structure across viewing angles, while the L2 distance matrix degrades to an unstructured/random pattern (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Full 20-projection Hsp90 dataset with 190 pairs and 12 noise trials at σ=0.01 using exact OT: W2 clean/noisy Spearman correlation is 0.987 and standardized matrix similarity 0.874, both far above L2's 0.834 and 0.528, confirming W2 preserves diagonal viewing-angle structure while L2 degrades.

claims.claim: Figure 2 empirically confirms that the W2 distance error follows the predicted (nσ)^(1/2) scaling law as noise increases, while the L2 distance error grows linearly in σ (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Nine-level noise sweep from 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻² at 32×32 with 40 trials per level and exact transport yields L2 log-log slope 1.0006 (claimed 1.0) and W2 slope 0.5021 (claimed 0.5), directly reproducing the square-root vs. linear scaling distinction.

claims.claim: Section 4.4 reports a counterintuitive phenomenon in which Wasserstein distance between sparse images can decrease as noise increases, because added noise bridges transport gaps between distant mass concentrations (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: Two unit masses at (8,8) and (24,24) on the 32×32 torus across 7 noise levels with 35 trials show W2 decreasing 60.4%, W3 72.1%, W4 76.0% while W1 increases; the optimal-plan audit confirms direct source-to-target flow drops from 1.0 to 0.0 at the W2 minimum, demonstrating the noise-bridge mechanism.

SabaPivot/repro-quantifying-the-noise-se.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims on non-toy setups: exact optimal transport on 32×32 toroidal grids, the authors' released Hsp90 cryo-EM data, and multiple noise levels and transport orders. The main limitation is reduced trial counts (12–80 vs. the paper's ~100), but the experimental design, data, solver, and geometry faithfully match the paper's methodology.

SabaPivot/repro-optimal-design-for-multi.paper_title: Optimal Design for Multinomial Logit Model with Applications to Best Assortment Identification

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 gives a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) reformulation of the linear maximization oracle (LMO) needed for optimal design in the multinomial logit (MNL) model (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: 12 independent seeded instances (N=7–10, d=3, K=3–5) implemented the full Charnes–Cooper MILP from Eq. (B.7) and compared against exhaustive enumeration; all 12 matched with 0.0 objective error and 0.0 MIP gap, confirming the MILP reformulation equivalence.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 establishes a stopping/approximation guarantee for a lifted Frank-Wolfe algorithm that solves the MNL optimal design problem without requiring exact LMO calls (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: 8 seeds with N=10, d=3, K=4 (375 assortments) ran lifted Frank–Wolfe with exact line search; Dinkelbach LMO matched exhaustive LMO on every iteration, all 8 stopped within the theorem bound (largest g/bound=0.927), and a negative control shrinking ε_lift to 80% broke PSD dominance 8/8.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 shows the proposed best assortment identification algorithm achieves sample complexity O~(d log(N/δ)(1/Δmin² + 1/(κΔmin)) + T0), where d is the feature dimension, N is the number of arms/assortments, and Δmin is the minimum reward gap (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: Binary search over 18 gap values on the full C.5 stopping certificate recovered slopes -2.0378 (R²=0.99999973) for Δ⁻² and -1.0259 (R²=0.99999997) for (κΔ)⁻¹, with a 108-cell (N,d,κ,Δ) grid confirming the rate formula up to polylog factors.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.5 shows that using the lifted G-optimal design in place of the MILP-based design multiplies the sample complexity by a factor of only (1+ε_lift), while remaining computationally tractable (Corollary 4.5).
claims.evidence: Measured ε_lift via generalized eigenvalue condition on 8 instances (all PSD premises hold, 80% control breaks 8/8), then propagated each factor through the C.5 certificate at 4 gaps (32 comparisons); normalized stopping-time multiplier fell in [1.0328, 1.0726], consistent with (1+ε_lift) up to polylog excess.

claims.claim: Table 1 reports average LMO runtime comparisons across methods (MILP vs. lifted surrogate) for varying problem sizes (Table 1).
claims.evidence: All 12 Table-1 configurations were transcribed from the PDF and cross-checked; 120 fresh Dinkelbach lifted-LMO calls were run across all (N,K) pairs, and v2 independently ran the compact MILP, reproducing the paper's pattern of nearly-flat lifted scaling versus combinatorial oracle growth.

claims.claim: Figure 1 reports the average stopping time τ of the best assortment identification algorithm as N (number of arms) is varied over {30, 50, 100, 200} and K (assortment size) over {3, 4, 5}, using feature dimension d=5 and failure probability δ=0.05 (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The primary PDF shows Figure 1 uses N={10,20,30,40,50} and K={2,3,4,5}, whereas the registered claim specifies N={30,50,100,200} and K={3,4,5}—a grid that exactly matches Table 1, not Figure 1.

SabaPivot/repro-optimal-design-for-multi.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting claims 1–5 through independent implementations, exact solver comparisons, negative controls, and certificate-based rate verification on non-trivial instances. Claim 6 is falsified because the registered parameter grid does not match Figure 1's actual experimental settings in the paper.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 proves the original DeepSets aggregation (Equation 4) is discontinuous in the natural any-dimensional topology because the infinite sum can diverge when the inner function ρ decays arbitrarily slowly, so standard DeepSets fails to be universal (Theorem 4.2, Section 4.1.1).
claims.evidence: Concrete construction on ℓ_1 with x_i=1/i² (valid ℓ_1 point, norm ζ(2)) and ρ(t)=|t|^{1/2} shows input converging at 1e-7 while DeepSets output H_n diverges to 16.70 with logarithmic slope 0.998; Cauchy-in-input/non-Cauchy-in-output ratio 2.56e6 directly witnesses discontinuity. Lipschitz-ρ control converges to ζ(2), isolating the slow-decay mechanism.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.9 proves standard message-passing GNNs fail any-dimensional universality because their pointwise nonlinearities are discontinuous in the cut metric, since a pointwise map is continuous with respect to the cut norm only if it is linear (Theorem 4.9, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Exact cut norms for n≤12 and spectral bounds for n up to 1600 show input cut-distance →0 (0.130→0.025) while nonlinear φ=t² and ReLU outputs stay bounded at ≈0.250; linear φ=2t+3 output →0.050, exhibiting the 'continuous iff linear' dichotomy at native graphon generality with Rademacher constructions.

claims.claim: A modified DeepSets-infinity architecture (Equation 5) that reweights terms by an ell_p norm factor is proven continuous and universal on ell_p(R^k) sequence space (Theorem 4.2, Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: On the exact input that broke original DeepSets (x_i=1/i², ℓ_1), the reweighted DeepSets-∞ converges to ζ(2) at 1e-7 error; permutation invariance holds at 8.9e-15 over 1000 relabelings; continuity modulus ratio ≤0.455 over 400 configs. Dropping the reweight reverts to divergence (control). Universality/denseness is evidenced via separation and invariance ingredients rather than a full density proof.

claims.claim: A measure-space variant DeepSets-bar-infinity (Equation 6), replacing the sum with a normalized integral under a growth condition, is proven universal on the Wasserstein space of probability measures (Theorem 4.5, Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: Kantorovich-Rubinstein bound |Δ∫ρ|/(Lip·W₁) ≤ 0.778 over 2000 empirical measure pairs with exact 1-D OT confirms Lipschitz continuity; growth-condition control with ρ=x² shows W₁→1e-4 while ∫x²dμ=1 (discontinuity when condition fails); permutation invariance at 4.2e-17. Full Wasserstein-space denseness is not separately proven but key mechanism is verified.

claims.claim: A homomorphism-density-basis architecture (Equations 9-10) is proven continuous and universal on graphon space with the cut metric, restoring universality for graph architectures (Theorem 4.9, Theorem 4.10, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Counting-lemma bound |Δt(F)|/d_□ ≤ e(F) verified exactly on 250 graphon pairs for edge (tight at 1.000), path3 (1.104≤2), triangle (0.916≤3), 3-star (0.978≤3); Eq-9 decorated density h_3 has finite Lipschitz constant 0.529; separation shown (triangle+iso vs P4: same edge density 0.375, triangle gap 0.094); relabel invariance exact at 0.0.

claims.claim: A two-stage architecture combining a Gram-matrix map (Equation 12) with Invariant Graphon Networks (Equation 14) is proven universal on bounded point-cloud orbits under the group action (Theorem 4.12, Theorem 4.13, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: O(k) invariance of Gram map at 4.4e-16 over 500 configs; completeness verified via same-orbit Gram equality (2.2e-16) with recovered orthogonal transform (|T'T-I|=1.1e-15) and distinct-orbit separation (shear gap 0.198); two-stage readout invariant to combined permutation×O(k) at 6.4e-16 over 300 configs with distinct-orbit gap 0.0094.

SabaPivot/repro-any-dimensional-invarian.overall: All six claims are addressed with clean-room numerical implementations at native mathematical generality (ℓ_p spaces, graphon cut metric, Wasserstein space, orbit spaces), using exact computations where feasible and rigorous bounds otherwise, each with a destructive control isolating the claimed mechanism. The two impossibility results are witnessed by concrete diverging examples, and the four constructive results verify continuity, invariance, and separation properties, though full denseness proofs for universality are not reproduced.

SabaPivot/repro-certificate-guided-pruni.paper_title: Certificate-Guided Pruning for Stochastic Lipschitz Optimization

claims.claim: Certificate-Guided Pruning (CGP) maintains an explicit active set A_t of candidate optima using confidence-adjusted Lipschitz envelopes, certifying with high probability that any point outside A_t is suboptimal (Section 3, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: 12,120,300 exhaustive membership checks across 40,401 grid points and 300 snapshots show 0 violations of Lemmas 4.2/4.3, 0 pruned-but-optimal points, and x* never eliminated, with a strictly positive pruning margin of +0.027688; the L/4 destructive control breaks the envelope in 280/300 snapshots and prunes x* in 87/300.

claims.claim: Under a margin condition with near-optimality dimension α (Assumption 2.3), the Shrinkage Theorem bounds the active set volume as Vol(A_t) ≤ C·(2(β_t + Lη_t) + γ_t)^(d−α) (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: Vol(A_t) ≤ C·(2(β_t+Lη_t)+γ_t)^(d−α) holds in 135/135 snapshots (max ratio 0.662), the margin exponent d−α is independently measured by exhaustive lattice counting up to 4.17M sites matching to ≤9.6e-04, and the C/10 control fails in 80/135 snapshots.

claims.claim: CGP achieves ε-optimality with probability at least 1−δ using T = Õ(L^d ε^{-(2+α)} log(1/δ)) samples, improving on the worst-case Õ(ε^{-(2+d)}) rate whenever α < d (Theorem 4.8).
claims.evidence: 108 exact covering-number computations (N_cover up to 743M) recover the ε-exponent as 2+α to within 0.0045, the L-exponent as d (0.986/1.984/2.999), and the log(1/δ) factor as affine (R²=0.999998); the margin-blind control correctly yields exponent 2+d.

claims.claim: A matching lower bound shows any algorithm requires Ω(ε^{-(2+α)}) samples under the same margin condition, establishing CGP's minimax sample-complexity optimality (Theorem 4.9).

SabaPivot/repro-fast-estimation-for-fore.paper_title: Fast Estimation for Forest Matrix of Signed Graphs

claims.claim: GSCF (Generalized Spanning Converging Forest) generates spanning converging forests for signed graphs using loop-erased random walks in expected O(n) time, per Theorem 5.2 (Section 5.1, Algorithm 1, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Independent from-scratch implementation of Algorithm 1 timed across n=1,000 to 2,000,000 (7 repeats/size, median) yields OLS linear fit R²=0.9838 with slope 166 ns/node and near-zero intercept, plus power-law exponent p=1.150 — empirically confirming O(n) scaling across 3 orders of magnitude on non-trivial synthetic signed graphs.

claims.claim: FMDE estimates the diagonal of the forest matrix via sampling in O(ln) time, where l is the number of samples (Section 6.2, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: FMDE/FMDE+ implemented from Algorithm 2 pseudocode and validated against exact dense matrix inversion on real Bitcoinotc (5,881 nodes) and Gnutella08* (6,301 nodes) datasets downloaded from SNAP; errors decrease monotonically with l, and independent OLS fits give R²=0.9994 (time vs l) and R²=0.9905 (time vs n), confirming O(ln) complexity.

claims.claim: FMDE+ incorporates additional network information to achieve the same O(ln) time complexity as FMDE but with lower variance, and Theorem 6.3 proves its superior performance on balanced signed graphs (Section 6.2, Theorem 6.3).
claims.evidence: On real Bitcoinotc data, FMDE+ average relative error is 11.5×–11.8× lower than FMDE at matched l; on Gnutella08* the gap is 942×; unit tests directly confirm Theorem 6.3 with MSE(FMDE)=0.1878 ≥ MSE(FMDE+)=0.0051 on a balanced signed graph at l=1, and FMDE+ runs at the same O(ln) complexity as FMDE.

claims.evidence: On the real SlashdotZoo network (n=79,116, m=515,397), sparse-LU factorization of (I+L) took 961.9s single-threaded (same order as the paper's 991.5s on 72 cores), while FMDE+ completed in 1.32s single-threaded (close to the paper's <1.1s on 72 cores); the ~10³× ratio between exact and estimator is independently confirmed, with small numerical differences attributable to hardware.

claims.claim: The methods scale to the FullUSA network with roughly 2.3×10^7 (over twenty million) nodes, where exact computation fails but FMDE+ completes within one hour (Table 3).
claims.evidence: GSCF, FMDE, and FMDE+ each completed 5/5 trials directly at n=23,947,300 (m=115,417,200, avg out-degree 4.82) with the Lemma 4.4 invariant 0≤q_ii≤1 holding across all 23.9M nodes, both estimators agreeing on q̄≈0.2058, and peak RSS of 5,144 MB — demonstrating the method runs at the paper's literal 20M+ scale where exact inversion is infeasible.

claims.claim: FMDE+ achieves roughly ten times lower average relative error than FMDE across tested networks (Figure 2).

SabaPivot/repro-accuracy-first-r-nyi-dif.paper_title: Accuracy-First Rényi Differential Privacy and Post-Processing Immunity

claims.claim: The paper reformulates mechanisms as returning pairs (y, ε) rather than separate output and privacy-loss functions, resolving prior notational obstacles to defining post-processing immunity for accuracy-first privacy (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: 1000 random finite mechanisms (output spaces size 2–6) show identical output mass and privacy loss (max error 0e+00) between the pair (y,ε) and the old representation, with exact round-trip and post-processing carry of ε (0/1000 failures).

claims.claim: Pure ex-post privacy (δ=0) satisfies post-processing immunity, but δ-probabilistic ex-post privacy with δ>0 does not, even though the latter is shown equivalent to (ε,δ)-probabilistic differential privacy for constant ε (Theorem 3.2, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Pure ex-post PPI: 0/1000 violations across random finite mechanisms with random post-processings. δ-probabilistic PPI fails on an exact 4-output witness (P=[0.2,0.3,0.25,0.25], Q=[0.001,0.11,0.4445,0.4445], ε₀=ln3, δ=0.2) where violating P-mass rises from 0.2=δ to 0.5>δ after deterministic post-processing, with post-merge loss 1.505>ε₀=1.099. Constant-ε ↔ (ε,δ)-probabilistic-DP equivalence: 0/1000 failures.

claims.claim: The paper introduces α-ex-post Rényi differential privacy (Section 4), proves it satisfies post-processing immunity (Theorem 4), and proves it composes adaptively with total privacy loss ε* = Σε_i (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: Rényi divergence D_α contracts under 1000 random coarse-grainings (0/1000 PPI violations, max violation 0e+00). Two-step adaptive composition yields ε*=ε₁+ε₂ exactly (0/1000 failures, max error 1.3e-15, machine precision).

claims.claim: The sequential precision-weighted Gaussian mechanism (Algorithm 2, Appendix C.4) is shown to achieve α-ex-post RDP equivalent to the original Brownian mechanism (Theorem 5, Section 5).
claims.evidence: 250,000 simulation paths over 7 cumulative privacy levels show the precision-weighted Gaussian matches the Brownian target (Var=tᵢ, Cov=min(tᵢ,tⱼ)) with max variance error 0.271% and max covariance error 0.223%; the covariance identity is additionally verified analytically.

claims.claim: Table 1 summarizes that pure ex-post privacy has post-processing immunity but the Brownian mechanism does not satisfy it, whereas α-ex-post RDP satisfies both post-processing immunity and compatibility with the Brownian mechanism (Table 1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: All three operative Table 1 rows independently checked: pure ex-post (PPI✓ via 0/1000, BM✗ via Gaussian failure probability 0.001350>0 at ε_T=3.5), δ-probabilistic (PPI✗ via exact witness from Claim 2, BM✓), α-ex-post RDP (PPI✓ via 0/1000, BM✓ via Brownian equivalence from Claim 4).

claims.claim: On the Adult dataset, a data-dependent stopping rule (Algorithm 1) using a private validation set generates synthetic data while minimizing privacy budget over ε ∈ [0.01, 1] subject to maintaining classifier accuracy thresholds (Figure 1, Section 6).
claims.evidence: Full 45,222-row UCI Adult dataset, 30 runs, 20/40/40 split with disjoint private validation, 7 log-spaced ε∈[0.01,1]: median accepted ε=0.0464, mean val/test accuracy 0.810/0.809 (baseline 0.752), query RMSE strictly decreasing across all releases — confirming the accuracy-first stopping phenomenon.

SabaPivot/repro-accuracy-first-r-nyi-dif.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all six claims through finite-mechanism Monte Carlo tests (Claims 1–3, 5), a 250k-path Brownian equivalence simulation (Claim 4), and a full-scale Adult dataset experiment with 30 runs (Claim 6), all from an independent from-scratch numpy/scipy/sklearn implementation. The evidence includes exact algebraic counterexamples, machine-precision composition checks, and honest scope limitations regarding Monte Carlo vs formal proof.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 gives a bicriteria (1+κ, 1+1/κ) approximation via LP rounding: the returned subgraph K satisfies coverage loss W−e(K)≤(1+κ)·ε·W and size |K|≤(1+1/κ)·r (Theorem 1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: LP + (1+κ,1+1/κ) rounding on random planted-optimum hypergraphs (n up to 100, eps in {0.05,0.1,0.2}, kappa in {0.5,1,2}) shows coverage-loss ratios 0.27–0.53 (all ≤1) and size ratios 0.33 (all ≤1), satisfying both bicriteria bounds with real measured CSV data.

claims.evidence: Lagrangian max-weight-closure implemented as min-cut, swept over 30 thresholds per graph (gamma in {3,5}, n in {20–55}), yields 0 nestedness violations and 0 coverage-monotonicity violations across all 32 configurations in the raw data.

claims.claim: Corollary 1 shows the entire nested sequence of subgraphs across thresholds can be computed in Õ(γ(m+n)²) time (Corollary 1, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Parametric lambda sweep measures ≤n distinct breakpoints and runtime scaling with fitted exponents 1.99 (gamma=2) and 1.57 (gamma=4) across N up to 720; sizes are modest but the quadratic trend and breakpoint bound are concretely demonstrated.

claims.evidence: Split-conformal experiment with 6000 trials per config across phi in {0.7,0.95}, delta in {0.05,0.1}, n_cal in {50,200}, and four distributions (uniform, beta, expon, bimodal) shows empirical coverage ≥ phi−delta at every configuration (e.g., 0.686≥0.65, 0.855≥0.85).

claims.claim: Theorem 4 proves NP-hardness of the conformal subgraph problem even for constant ε via reduction from clique detection, in Appendix B (Theorem 4, Appendix B).
claims.evidence: Clique-to-conformal-subgraph reduction tested on graphs with 8–12 vertices across c in {0.2,0.3}, k in {3,4} shows 1.0 yes/no agreement rate with epsilon pinned to the target constant, confirming reduction faithfulness with 36 configurations in the raw data.

claims.claim: On a synthetic 6x6 grid navigation experiment with 50 train/test routes, the LP-based method compresses the calibration set to 52 edges at φ=0.75 coverage and outperforms greedy baselines for φ≤0.8 (Section 5).
claims.evidence: 6x6 grid with 50 routes reproduces the paper's setup; LP produces 37–55 edges (paper reports ~52 at phi=0.75; logbook gets 44–50 at phi=0.75) and beats forward-greedy in 15/20 seed/phi combinations with lower average objective at every phi level.

SabaPivot/repro-compact-conformal-subgra.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims through real algorithm implementations—LP rounding, min-cut nestedness, parametric sweeps, split-conformal calibration, NP-hardness reduction verification, and the grid benchmark—with measured results across multiple parameter settings, seeds, and distributions. The main limitation is modest problem sizes in several experiments, but the setups are non-toy and the measured numbers directly address each claim.

SabaPivot/repro-causal-modeling-of-selec.paper_title: Causal Modeling of Selection in Evolution

claims.claim: Definition 1 formalizes an evolutionary selection model as a DAG G^(T) over trait variables X^(0)...X^(T), heritable factors epsilon^(0)...epsilon^(T), and reproduction/selection indicators S^(0)...S^(T-1), distinguishing it from one-shot static selection models (Section 2, Definition 1).
claims.evidence: 60 independently generated models across d∈{6,8,10,15,20} and T∈{1,2,3,5} were all acyclic with 0 node-count and edge-count errors against Definition 1 formulas, covering 3,475 within-trait, 462 selection, 2,655 factor-to-trait, and 1,947 inheritance edges.

claims.claim: Lemma 1 shows that repeated evolutionary selection induces conditional dependencies among variables that are absent under static selection models, so applying static-selection graphical models to evolutionary data can yield false causal discoveries (Section 2, Lemma 1).
claims.evidence: 40,800 exact d-separation queries found 985 strict witnesses where the static graph asserted separation but the repeated-selection graph remained connected, with witnesses at every tested T (164, 193, 414, 214 at T=1,2,3,5), and 0 cases where evolutionary separation implied static separation failed.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 proves that the clique-augmented DAG G^+ (Definition 2) fully captures all d-separation/conditional-independence constraints implied by the evolutionary selection model, without needing to explicitly model the selection variables (Section 3, Definition 2, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Across 40,800 pair-and-conditioning-set queries, d-separation in the independently constructed G+ matched the evolutionary-selection graph with 0 mismatches, and a destructive control omitting the selection clique disagreed 5,543 times, confirming the result is non-vacuous.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 establishes that applying standard constraint-based algorithms such as PC or GES (Algorithm 1) to G^+ is sound and complete: oriented edges correspond to true causal relations, while unoriented edges may reflect the presence of selection (Section 3, Theorem 2, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: On 150 oracle CPDAGs, all 3,843 adjacency checks and 573 compelled directions were sound with 0 errors, and 2,775 selection-clique edges correctly remained unoriented; however, finite-sample PC/GES runs at N=5,000 showed no directed-edge precision advantage (gain −0.0113 for PC, −0.0002 for GES), which does not falsify the asymptotic theorem but fails to reproduce its practical benefit.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 shows that combining heterogeneous data from multiple environments/domains via the CDNOD-based procedure (Algorithm 2) improves identifiability of the evolutionary selection model compared to single-environment data (Section 4, Theorem 4, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: On 145 heterogeneous oracle graph configurations, adding the domain index ζ yielded 252 additional sound trait orientations with 0 lost single-domain orientations and 0 soundness errors; withholding ζ directions removed exactly those 252 gains, but finite-sample CD-NOD on 24 runs produced 0.0 orientation-count gain over pooled PC.

claims.claim: The proposed identification procedure is validated on synthetic graphs of varying size and on seven real-world datasets spanning biology, agriculture, and social science (Section 5).
claims.evidence: 75 PC and 75 GES synthetic runs at N=5,000 showed directed-edge adjacency precision below all-edge precision (PC 0.7195 vs 0.7309; GES 0.6085 vs 0.6087), contradicting the paper's reliability claim; only 1 of 7 real-world datasets (California PUMS, 155,618 rows) was executed, without ground truth, leaving the real-data validation largely unaddressed.

SabaPivot/repro-causal-modeling-of-selec.overall: The logbook provides strong computational verification of the paper's oracle-level graphical theorems (Definitions 1–2, Lemmas 1, Theorems 1–2, Theorem 4) via extensive d-separation audits and CPDAG checks, but the finite-sample empirical claims are not reproduced: PC/GES directed-edge precision showed no advantage and CD-NOD added no orientations, while only 1 of 7 real-world datasets was partially executed.

SabaPivot/repro-accurate-large-sample-un.paper_title: Accurate Large-sample Uncertainty Quantification using Stochastic Gradient Markov Chain Monte Carlo

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 bounds the relative error between the true stationary covariance Σ_θ and the discrete-time proxy covariance Σ_ψ as ‖Σ_θ − Σ_ψ‖/‖Σ_θ‖ ≤ C_v λ^(1/2), scaling with the step size λ (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: On the authors' German Credit data (N=800, d=21) with nonlinear Poisson SGD, 24 coupled chains across 6 step sizes and 4 seeds (2.88M updates) all remained finite, and a single constant C_v=0.043805 upper-bounded every measured covariance error by C_v·sqrt(λ) over a 16× step-size range, supporting the theorem's upper envelope.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 derives an explicit formula for the minibatch noise covariance without assuming constant noise, enabling exact rather than approximate stationary covariance solutions (Theorem 4.3, Section 4).
claims.evidence: A numerical audit on a heterogeneous 5D quadratic model (N=240, B=24, 240,000 stationary samples) tested Theorem 4.3's equation (16) including location-dependent Hessian terms; the formula matched empirical noise covariance to 0.61% (with replacement) and 0.53% (without replacement) Frobenius relative error, directly verifying the non-constant-noise formula.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.5 and Corollary 4.6 provide non-asymptotic 2-Wasserstein distance bounds between the true and proxy algorithm distributions, giving W₂(π_θ,π_ψ) ≤ Aλ/B for SGD (Theorem 4.5, Corollary 4.6).

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 gives a two-stage tuning procedure: offline sandwich covariance estimation from a subsample, followed by solving coupled equations for preconditioned step sizes (Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The full released German Credit pipeline was executed at its original configuration (500 epochs, 30 repetitions, 2 batch sizes, 3 tuning rules, 180 method paths, 2.7M updates), producing sandwich covariance estimates and preconditioned chains; independently, the Boston audit solved the coupled equations to residuals 7.2e-15 (B=16) and 1.5e-14 (B=50), confirming the two-stage construction works when correctly implemented.

claims.claim: On the Boston housing dataset under strong model misspecification, the proposed DQ+exact method maintains accurate covariance estimates while competing continuous-time and constant-noise methods diverge (Table 3).
claims.evidence: Table 3's own reported values show CT (continuous-time) is finite everywhere (0.247–3.126) and is more accurate than EX in 2 of 4 comparisons; only LR+WS diverges. A reduced-budget official-code run (80 epochs, 3 reps) on full Boston data also failed to reproduce EX superiority at B=16 (CT/EX = 4.030/5.989), contradicting the claim that competing continuous-time methods diverge.

claims.claim: Proposition B.1 extends the covariance and error-bound results to SGLD with momentum, recovering the non-momentum results as the momentum parameter κ→0 (Proposition B.1, Appendix B).
claims.evidence: While the SGD specialization (β=∞) was verified to residuals ≤1.84e-13 on the 21D German Credit Hessian, the finite-temperature SGLD case (β=N=800) showed proposition residuals growing to 0.54470 at κ=0.5; an independent scalar 2×2 counterexample confirmed the discrepancy (Proposition B.1 miss of 0.05003) with a 2M-step simulation matching the exact Lyapunov variance within 0.62%, falsifying the extension to SGLD with momentum as stated.

SabaPivot/repro-a-perturbation-approach-.paper_title: A Perturbation Approach to Unconstrained Linear Bandits

claims.claim: The paper's perturbation-based algorithm, PABLO, reduces unconstrained Bandit Linear Optimization (uBLO) to a standard Online Linear Optimization (OLO) problem (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Exact enumeration over all 2d perturbation atoms (no Monte-Carlo error) confirms unbiasedness E[ℓ̃]=ℓ to rel err 7.06e-15 and the second-moment identity to 7.96e-15 across 300 configs with d∈[1,16]; Cor 2.2 constants attained exactly (ratio=1.000000); end-to-end PABLO+KT reduction tested at d=8, T=2048, 800 seeds with martingale corrections within ~2σ of zero and reduction inequality 44.0≤4031 holding.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 gives an expected static-regret bound of the form E[R_T(u)] = O~(G*epsilon + d*kappa*E[||u||*sqrt(V_T log(...))]), with kappa=sqrt(d) in the norm-oblivious setting and kappa=1 in the norm-adaptive setting (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: PABLO+KT static regret fitted exponent in T is 0.4994 (theory 0.5) across T∈[128,16384] and linear in ‖u‖ with exponent 1.0001 (theory 1) across a 64× range of ‖u‖; the κ=√d vs κ=1 dimension separation is not stressed end-to-end (oblivious i.i.d. instance), but its ingredient Cor 2.2 E‖ℓ̃‖²≤2d‖ℓ‖² is verified exactly tight.

claims.evidence: Dynamic regret against a moving comparator scales as √(P_T) with fitted exponent 0.5125 (theory 0.5) and D_T/√(P_T) flat (~28–30) across a 43× range of P_T at d=8, T=4096; a parameter-free learner with no knowledge of P_T reproduces the same rate up to a looser constant (exponent 0.625).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 establishes a high-probability static-regret bound R_T(u) <= O~(dG(epsilon+||u||)log(T/delta) + G||u||sqrt(dT log(T/delta))) (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: The two Theorem 4.2 terms are derived exactly from Freedman's inequality applied to the Cor 2.2 constants (verified tight in Claim 1): B_worst=2dG(ε+‖u‖), V_worst=2dG²(ε+‖u‖)²T; empirically the bound holds w.p.≥1−δ across 600 seeds on fixed losses (exceedance never exceeds δ, C≤0.12), with measured V∝‖u‖² (2.002), B∝‖u‖ (1.000), V∝T (0.996), and sub-Gaussian tail R²=0.9956.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 proves the folklore Omega(sqrt(dT)) minimax lower bound for adversarial linear bandits on the unit Euclidean ball (Theorem 5.2).
