claims.claim: Conjecture 5.3 posits a minimax rate of R_T(u) = Theta(||u|| sqrt(T(d v log||u||))) for norm-oblivious comparators, left as an open problem (Conjecture 5.3).
claims.evidence: Both arms of the ∨ (max) are corroborated: dimension arm Θ(‖u‖√(dT)) via Le Cam lower bound (fitted exponent in d=0.5000) and PABLO+KT achievability (upper/lower ratio bounded [9.8,11.0]); norm arm Θ(‖u‖√(T log‖u‖)) via d=1 KT minimax-optimal closed-form (exponent→0.5); the max (not product) join structure fits with R²=1.000, c=1.00, with arms crossing exactly at log‖u‖=d.

SabaPivot/repro-a-perturbation-approach-.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, independently re-implemented evidence (exact 2d-atom enumeration, multi-seed end-to-end runs, explicit counterexamples) confirming the perturbation reduction, comparator-adaptive √T/‖u‖ rates, optimal √(P_T) dynamic regret, high-probability Freedman bound, and Conjecture 5.3's two-arm max structure, while identifying a concrete load-bearing proof error in Theorem 5.2's Appendix-F argument that weakens it by a factor of d.

SabaPivot/repro-semi-knockoffs-a-model-a.paper_title: Semi-knockoffs: a model-agnostic conditional independence testing method with finite-sample guarantees

claims.claim: Semi-knockoffs avoids the train-test data split required by prior conditional-independence testing methods such as HRT while still yielding valid p-values, via nonparametric paired tests requiring only conditional expectations ν_j and ρ_j rather than exact knockoff construction (Theorem 3.3, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Seed-51 reruns through the pinned Semi_KO class reproduced RF/NN p-values to ≤1.1×10⁻¹⁶, confirming the method fits conditional models and computes paired Wilcoxon p-values on the full sample without train-test split; GB showed minor drift (0.016–0.017) but followed the same algorithmic path.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 establishes that the Semi-knockoffs procedure controls the false discovery rate at level q, i.e. FDR(S_SKO) ≤ q (Theorem 3.4, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Oracle Gaussian experiment with known ν and ρ: 120 datasets at q=0.20 yielded mean FDP 0.183 (below 0.20) and power 1.00, empirically corroborating Theorem 3.4's FDR control under its stated oracle assumptions; the estimated-conditional case (FDP 0.463) is explicitly outside the theorem's scope.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows that for null (non-relevant) features, regularized empirical risk minimizers trained with and without the feature remain close, with an ‖θ̃^j − θ̂‖₂ ≤ O_P(√(log(1/δ)/n)) bound, giving optimization stability guarantees for regularized models (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: 80-repeat Ridge experiment across n∈{100,200,400,800,1600} produced a log parameter-gap/log n slope of −0.503, closely matching the theoretical −1/2 rate from Theorem 4.1, confirming the O_P(√(log(1/δ)/n)) bound empirically.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 provides a double-robustness property: the loss difference between imputed feature distributions decays at a compound rate O_P(a_n b_n) even when both the predictive model and the sampler have estimation error (Theorem 4.3, Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: 60-repeat 2×2 factorial at n∈{200,400,800,1600} showed both-nuisances-learned loss-gap slope −0.993 (matching n⁻¹), single-fixed slopes ~−0.49 (matching n⁻¹ᐟ²), both-fixed slope 0.005, and learned-gap vs measured a_n·b_n slope 0.996, directly confirming the compound rate.

claims.claim: On simulated data with adjacent-feature support, Semi-knockoffs maintains type-I error control while achieving higher power than HRT, and derandomization with 5 permutations under masked correlation further increases power (Figure 4, Figure 5, Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: 50-seed aggregation shows Semi p5 power of 1/1/1 (adjacent) and .940/.720/.780 (masked) vs HRT .793/.998/.840 and .240/.360/.160, with type-I rates .054/.042/.056 (adjacent) and .074/.057/.074 (masked)—power gain is clear and type-I is approximately controlled, modestly exceeding 0.05 in some masked cases.

claims.claim: On the Wisconsin Breast Cancer real dataset, Semi-knockoffs is applied across Random Forest, Neural Network, and Gradient Boosting models to demonstrate model-agnostic feature selection (Figure 6, Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: The method was executed across RF, NN, and GB on WDBC with 50 seeds each, producing discovery counts (p1 means 1.98/1.94/1.60, p5 means 3.56/4.16/2.02) and pooled artificial-null rate 3.3%, demonstrating model-agnostic feature selection with null control; however, true feature relevance is unknown so power is unidentifiable.

SabaPivot/repro-semi-knockoffs-a-model-a.overall: The logbook provides substantial empirical evidence supporting Claims 1–5 through independent reruns, oracle FDR experiments, rate-fitting regression experiments, and 50-seed synthetic power/type-I aggregations. Claim 6's model-agnostic application is demonstrated but the logbook correctly notes that without ground-truth feature relevance on WDBC, power claims are unidentifiable and discovery counts show wide seed variability.

bsenst/repro-meda-medical-oriented-activ.paper_title: MEDA: Medical-Oriented Activation Editing for Hallucination Mitigation in Medical Large Vision-Language Model

claims.claim: MEDA improves response factuality with up to 10.2% gain on IU-Xray benchmark
claims.evidence: The logbook describes a GPT-2 activation steering proxy demo but reports no numerical results, uses no medical LVLM, and runs no experiments on IU-Xray. No concrete evidence supports or refutes the 10.2% gain claim.

claims.claim: MEDA exhibits strong generalization and few-shot robustness across six benchmarks and six medical LVLMs
claims.evidence: The logbook only proposes a validation approach and lists inferred benchmarks/models but executes no experiments across any benchmarks or LVLMs. No data is presented to assess generalization or few-shot robustness.

bsenst/repro-meda-medical-oriented-activ.overall: This logbook provides no experimental results whatsoever—it is a methodology description and reproduction plan only. Neither claim is addressed with any real runs or numbers on a non-toy setup.

divaspoudel/repro-finite-and-corruption-.paper_title: Finite and Corruption-Robust Regret Bounds in Online Inverse Linear Optimization under M-Convex Action Sets

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 achieves an uncorrupted regret bound of O(d^2) for online inverse linear optimization over M-convex feasible action sets (Theorem 3.1, Section 3)
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 was implemented on uniform matroids (a subclass of M-convex sets) with d up to 15, but every instance produced exactly 1 mistake, yielding near-constant regret (3.18–5.19) that never approaches the d² scaling, so the experiments confirm consistency but do not stress-test the bound.

claims.claim: With center-of-gravity-based prediction, Algorithm 1 improves the regret bound to O(d log d), covering M-convex sets including matroids (Theorem 4.2, Section 4)
claims.evidence: Center-of-gravity prediction was tested via Monte Carlo (30k samples) on uniform matroids with d up to 15, again yielding only 1 mistake per instance and near-constant regret (1.09–3.33), which is consistent with but does not meaningfully exercise the O(d log d) bound.

claims.claim: Algorithm 2 attains a corruption-robust regret bound of O((C+1) d log d) against adversarially corrupted feedback, without requiring prior knowledge of the corruption count C (Theorem 5.3, Section 5)
claims.evidence: Algorithm 2 was tested only at d=8, T=500 with C∈{0,5,10,20}; restarts match C and regret grows somewhat with C (3.52→44.13), but the single small dimension and non-monotone regret jump from C=10 to C=20 make this a limited proxy test.

claims.claim: A matching lower bound of Omega(d) is proved to hold even for M-convex instances, establishing near-tightness of the upper bounds (Theorem 6.1, Section 6)
claims.evidence: The logbook itself acknowledges the worst-case lower bound cannot be empirically verified; the numerical test of Algorithm 1 on random instances shows small non-growing regret, which is irrelevant to the lower bound, and the theoretical proof is only restated, not independently checked.

claims.claim: The volume-contraction lemma shows that whenever the algorithm's prediction errs, the feasible volume fraction shrinks by at least a factor of 1 - 1/e, underlying the O(d log d) regret proof (Lemma 4.1, Section 4)
claims.evidence: The logbook restates the Grünbaum-based proof sketch and claims the contraction factor 1−1/e was 'verified to hold in all test cases' but provides no concrete volume measurements or numerical evidence of contraction; this is an assertion, not demonstrated evidence.

divaspoudel/repro-finite-and-corruption-.overall: The logbook runs minimal numerical experiments on uniform matroids (a subclass of M-convex sets) at small dimensions (d≤15) where the algorithms make only 1 mistake per instance, producing near-constant regret that is consistent with but does not meaningfully exercise the claimed bounds. Theoretical claims (lower bound, volume contraction) are restated rather than independently verified, and no concrete volume-contraction measurements are provided.

ai-sherpa/prescriptive-scaling-llm-capab.paper_title: Prescriptive Scaling Reveals the Evolution of Language Model Capabilities

claims.claim: Capability boundaries are estimated via smoothed pinball-loss quantile regression at quantile τ=0.98 with smoothing parameter κ=50 and regularization λ=10⁻³ (Section 2.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook independently reimplements the smoothed pinball loss rho_tau^kappa, confirms code defaults of tau=0.98, kappa=50, lambda=1e-3, and validates via unit tests (gradient match to 4e-6, check-loss convergence to 1.4e-4). Coverage MAE of 1.78% in-sample and 2.18% out-of-sample on full six-task data confirms the estimator works as described.

claims.claim: Post-training capability boundaries are modeled as sigmoid functions of log10(FLOPs), q_τ^sig(z;θ)=y0+L·σ(a+βz), achieving in-distribution pinball loss of 4.08×10⁻³ versus 4.00×10⁻³ for a more flexible I-spline estimator, while generalizing better out-of-distribution (4.93×10⁻³ vs 4.92×10⁻³) (Section 3.1.1, Table 2).
claims.evidence: From-scratch no-split pinball loss measured as sigmoid 0.00460 vs I-spline 0.00447, reproducing the near-equality and ordering; under the paper's period-split protocol these become 4.08e-3 vs 4.00e-3 (ID) and 4.93e-3 vs 4.92e-3 (OOD), matching Table 2. OOD calibration error 0.0221 < 0.0241 confirms the sigmoid's generalization advantage.

claims.claim: At 10²⁴ FLOPs, the estimated 0.98-quantile boundary reaches 0.539 accuracy on MATH Level 5 versus 0.563 on MMLU-Pro, 0.700 on BBH, 0.828 on IFEval, 0.535 on MUSR, and 0.424 on GPQA (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Independent from-scratch sigmoid fit on ~3663 real models per task yields boundaries at 10^24 FLOPs within 0.012 of Table 1 for all six tasks (e.g., MATH 0.544 vs 0.539, GPQA 0.425 vs 0.424); the released fitter matches all six to within 0.001.

claims.claim: Unlike the stable boundaries for BBH, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and MUSR, the MATH Level 5 and IFEval capability boundaries are non-stationary over time, with later-period models exceeding earlier predicted boundaries (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Per-period OOS coverage MAE cleanly separates stable tasks (BBH 0.0143, GPQA 0.0188, MMLU-Pro 0.0167, MUSR 0.0186, all <2%) from non-stationary ones (MATH 0.0294 with per-period 0.0325/0.0179/0.0379; IFEval 0.0292 with 0.0480 declining to 0.0194), confirming later-period models exceed earlier-predicted boundaries for MATH and IFEval.

claims.claim: A balanced I-optimal sampling design recovers near-full-data capability frontiers using roughly 20% of the evaluation budget, with GPQA and MUSR requiring as little as 5% (Section 4, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: I-optimal alpha sweep reproduces OOS macro MAE of 0.1098/0.0690/0.0517 at 5/10/20% budgets (paper: 0.110/0.069/0.052), showing flattening past 20%. GPQA@5% reaches 0.0236 (1.26x full-data) and MUSR@5% reaches 0.0297 (1.59x full-data), confirming near-full-data recovery from 5% budget for these tasks.

claims.claim: A cross-benchmark shift test applied to AIME-2025 scores finds a positive but not statistically significant shift (p=0.15), giving no clear aggregate evidence of post-release contamination inflating math benchmark scores (Section 5.2.2, Equation 3).
claims.evidence: From-scratch logit-logit group-shift test on n=90 models yields gamma=0.5757 (paper 0.576) and one-sided permutation p=0.1484 (paper 0.15), not significant at 0.05; the released reference implementation returns identical values, confirming no clear contamination evidence.

ai-sherpa/prescriptive-scaling-llm-capab.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims through independent from-scratch implementations and cross-checks against the authors' released code on the paper's full-scale released data (thousands of real model checkpoints). The reproduction is CPU-only but appropriate since the paper's claims concern analysis methodology applied to existing benchmark measurements rather than new model training.

rahit/repro-beyond-structural-symmetries.paper_title: Beyond Structural Symmetries: Linear Mode Connectivity via Neuron Identifiability

claims.claim: Effective symmetry breaking is defined as breaking parameter symmetries in a way that changes the realized input-output function on the data support, not merely the structural parameter space, formalized via effective function classes (Section 4, Proposition 4.2).
claims.evidence: Closed-form realization cost matches independent min-norm least-squares solve to 7.994e-15 over 200 trials; exhaustive enumeration of all 40,320 permutations of S_8 shows every permutation costs machine-zero (2.24e-30) when F projects to zero on the data support despite all structural symmetries being broken, versus min non-identity cost of 0.197 when F lies in the support; destructive tilt control shows monotonic increase from ~0 to 0.199.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 shows the projected center gap between neurons scales as γ^out = Θ(σ_F√k · m^{-2/k}), linking symmetry-breaking effectiveness to intrinsic data dimension k and neuron count m.
claims.evidence: σ_F homogeneity exact to 2.4e-15; m-exponent slopes recovered as -1.018/-0.509/-0.267 vs predicted -1/-0.5/-0.25 for k=2/4/8 with R²>0.998; ratio γ/RHS₀ bounded in [1.767, 2.611] (max/min=1.478) across all 35 (m,k) cells spanning 64× in m and 16× in k; destructive rank-1 control collapses exponent to ≈-2 as predicted.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 bounds the chord deviation of ReLU networks along the linear interpolation path between two independently trained, effectively symmetry-broken solutions, and Proposition 5.2 uses this bound to establish a linear-mode-connectivity (LMC) barrier bound.
claims.evidence: Exact arc-cosine L² evaluation (validated vs Monte Carlo at 1e-4 relative error) recovers β^{3/2} exponent as 1.49888 vs 1.5 with R²=0.999999 over 90,045 exact evaluations and 3.5 decades of β; Prop 5.2 inequality holds with 0 violations in 420 checks and tightness instance achieves equality to 6.68e-12; destructive controls confirm exponent 1.0 or 2.0 are 1.56e5× worse and regime violation (β≥1) breaks the law.

claims.claim: Neuron identifiability, enabled by effective symmetry breaking, permits merging representations from independently trained networks without any prior activation alignment step (Section 4, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: At σ_F=16 (center-dominated regime), L^act(I)=L^act(P*) with 64/64 fixed points of the exact Hungarian optimum over all 64! permutations across 3 independent training pairs; exhaustive enumeration at m=8 confirms identity is rank 1 of 40,320 with zero gap to optimum; destructive control with different F for run B collapses ratio to 0.084 and fixed points to 0, isolating shared F as the mechanism.

claims.claim: Section 4.5 identifies a tradeoff whereby strong symmetry breaking that improves identifiability comes at the cost of reduced feature-learning capability.
claims.evidence: On the canonical random-feature-hard target y=relu(v'x), identifiability rises 0.111→1.000 (Spearman 0.95) while MSE/Var rises 0.0012→0.4963 (426× worse, Spearman 1.0) across the same σ_F sweep; feature movement falls monotonically 2.205→0.035 and MSE/RF-floor climbs to 0.79, showing convergence to random-feature baseline; exact realization cost scales as σ_F^0.99626 (predicted 1), confirming the quantitative tradeoff.

claims.claim: Experimental validation across activation matching, LMC barrier measurements, and neuron swap costs under varying subspace coherence ν(𝒰) is reported in Figures 3-6, consistent with the spectral concentration result of Theorem 4.4.
claims.evidence: Theorem 4.4 spectral concentration is verified: bound holds 7/7 coherence levels with C=1, √ν slope 0.507 vs 0.5 over 21,000 Gram matrices, and corollary transitions from 0/3000 to 3000/3000. However, the Sec. 6 Q4 coherence experiment at native scale (d=20, k=2) produced barriers approximately flat in ν(U) (0.269–0.305 under one reading) rather than the paper's reported trend of low barrier at high coherence and high barrier at low coherence; Figs. 3-5 on MNIST/CIFAR-10 were not attempted.

rahit/repro-beyond-structural-symmetries.overall: Five of six claims are verified with machine-precision exact computations, recovered scaling exponents, exhaustive permutation enumeration, and destructive controls on non-trivial setups. Claim 6's experimental component (the Q4 coherence experiment) did not reproduce the paper's reported trend, leaving that claim inconclusive despite the underlying Theorem 4.4 being verified.

divaspoudel/repro-on-the-interaction-of-.paper_title: On the Interaction of Batch Noise, Adaptivity, and Compression, under $(L_0,L_1)$-Smoothness: An SDE Approach

claims.claim: Under (L0,L1)-smoothness with unbounded-variance gradient noise, distributed SGD (DSGD) requires a stepsize satisfying η·ηt < 2ε/[(L0+L1·E[‖∇f(Xt)‖])(1+dσ1̄²/N)+dNσ0̄²L1], i.e., an adaptive rate that scales inversely with the gradient norm to guarantee convergence (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Numerical audit on synthetic quartic f(x)=Σx_j⁴/4 (d=1000, N=8) shows stepsizes ≤0.05 converge and ≥0.10 diverge, consistent with the theoretical bound η≈0.099, but this is a simplified synthetic objective, not a real ML task at the paper's scale.

claims.claim: For distributed compressed SGD (DCSGD) with unbiased compression of rate ω̄, the derived SDE analysis shows compression is asymptotically equivalent to DSGD with an inflated noise parameter σ1²=ω̄/d, meaning stronger adaptivity is required as the compression rate increases (Theorem 4.2, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Random sparsification tested on the same synthetic quartic shows divergence without normalization and convergence with it for ω∈{4,8,16}, but the experiment does not directly verify the asymptotic noise-inflation equivalence σ₁²_eff=ω̄/d; it only observes a divergence/normalization pattern on a toy objective.

claims.claim: Gradient update normalization emerges from the SDE analysis as a necessary stability condition whenever L1·σ1̄²>0, i.e., when gradient noise variance grows with the gradient norm under (L0,L1)-smoothness (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Quadratic objective (d=30) with aggressive η=1.0 shows normalization prevents divergence, but divergence also occurs at σ₁²=0, so the experiment does not cleanly isolate the L₁·σ₁²>0 condition as the specific driver; the setup is a small synthetic problem.

claims.claim: DSignSGD is proven to converge under heavy-tailed noise modeled as Student-t distributed with degrees of freedom ν=1 (unbounded expectation), without requiring a Robbins-Monro-style decaying learning rate schedule, unlike DSGD/DCSGD (Theorem 4.4, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: DSignSGD tested on a 1D function f(x)=x⁴/4 with Student-t(ν=1) noise converges, but the experiment uses a decaying schedule η_t=1/√(t+1), which appears to contradict the claim that DSignSGD does not require a Robbins-Monro-style decaying schedule; the 1D scale is extremely simplified.

claims.claim: Empirical validation on MLPs, ResNets, and Vision Transformers shows DSGD diverges as noise variance σ increases unless adaptive scheduling or normalization is applied, while DCSGD exhibits the same instability under random sparsification with compression rates ω∈{4,8,16} (Figure 1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Only a tiny MLP (20→32→1) on regression is tested; no ResNet or Vision Transformer experiments are attempted despite the claim explicitly naming them. DCSGD adaptive results show increasing loss with higher ω (0.338→4.259), which does not clearly demonstrate the claimed instability pattern.

divaspoudel/repro-on-the-interaction-of-.overall: The logbook provides numerical experiments on synthetic objectives (quartic, quadratic, 1D) and a tiny MLP that are broadly consistent with the paper's theoretical claims, but all experiments are at toy scale far below the paper's stated empirical scope (ResNets, ViTs). The reproduction validates qualitative trends but does not constitute a full or faithful reproduction of any claim at the paper's intended scale.

rahit/repro-decentralized-online-convex-.paper_title: Decentralized Online Convex Optimization with Efficient Communication: Improved Algorithm and Lower Bounds

claims.claim: Top-DOGD achieves O(ω^{-1/2}ρ^{-1}n√T) regret for convex loss functions under compressed communication, improving on prior bounds (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Clean-room Top-DOGD on real a9a data (n≤64, T≤1.2M) satisfies the explicit bound (19.5n+16)DG√(LT) in all 7 configurations (ratios 5.25e-3–5.46e-3); 738/738 blocks pass all three proof inequalities; fitted T-exponent +0.511 (R²=0.997) and L-exponent +0.505 (R²=0.990) match the predicted √T and √L scaling.

claims.claim: Top-DOGD achieves O(ω^{-1}ρ^{-2}n ln T) regret for strongly convex loss functions (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: 5 configurations on a9a with μ=0.1 strong convexity satisfy the explicit Thm 3.2 bound (0 violations); 479/479 blocks pass intermediate inequalities; regret fits R=1.9061·ln(T+8)+14088.28 (R²=0.9995) with power exponent +0.000135, confirming logarithmic growth; destructive control swapping in convex step size yields √T growth (p=+0.486).

claims.claim: The paper reduces dependence on compression quality ω from the previously known O(ω^{-2}ρ^{-4}n^{1/2}√T) (convex) and O(ω^{-2}ρ^{-4}n^{1/2} ln T) (strongly convex) bounds down to O(ω^{-1/2}ρ^{-1}n√T) and O(ω^{-1}ρ^{-2}n ln T) respectively, cutting the exponent on ω^{-1} from quadratic/quartic to square-root/linear (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Grid evaluation of L(ω,ρ,n) over 2,912 cells gives d log L/d log ω = -1.013 (claimed -1) and sqrt(L) ω-exponent -0.507 (claimed -1/2); measured gossip rounds yield ω-exponent -1.023 and ρ-exponent -1.919; head-to-head on a9a shows Top-DOGD 1.29x–2.56x lower regret than DC-DOGD, and the bound gap widens by ~10^7 as ω shrinks from 1 to 0.01.

claims.claim: First lower bounds for decentralized online convex optimization with compressed communication are established: Ω(ω^{-1/2}ρ^{-1/4}n√T) for convex functions and Ω(ω^{-1}ρ^{-1/2}n ln T) for strongly convex functions (Theorems 3.3 and 3.4).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive verification of the lower-bound construction: 300 cycle graphs (0 spectral-gap violations), 300 BFS families (0 mismatches), 262,144 Rademacher sign patterns (min ratio 1.111, 0 failures); 120/120 grid cells satisfy the full chain; 15 executed games show measured regret exceeding the theorem's RHS by 4.25x–4.41x; fitted exponents match ω^{-1/2}, √T, and ρ^{-1/4} for the convex bound.

claims.claim: The algorithm combines a two-level blocking update framework with an online compressed gossip strategy and a projection error compensation scheme to jointly control consensus, compression, and projection error (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive verification of all three components: 2,097,144 compressor paths (deviation identically 0 in exact rationals), 1,062,864 int64 top-k checks (0 violations), 80 gossip runs (0 exceed Lemma 3.3, mean conserved to ~1e-15); ablation shows removing L₂ compensation makes tracking error grow as n^{+0.9994} vs n^{-5.51}, and removing L₁ gossip makes consensus error 3.7e11–1.2e16 times larger.

claims.claim: Bandit-feedback extensions are provided: one-point feedback achieves O(ω^{-1/4}ρ^{-1/2}d^{1/2}n(ln n)^{1/4}T^{3/4}) regret (Theorem 4.1) and two-point feedback achieves O(ω^{-1/2}ρ^{-1}dn ln n√T) regret (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Gradient estimator identities verified (4M draws, errors ~1e-3) and explicit bounds hold in 0/10 cells with correct exponent composition (+0.75/+0.50 at R²=1.0), but measured regret T-exponents are +0.998 (one-point) and +0.943 (two-point), far from the claimed +0.75 and +0.50; the prescribed step sizes are too small for affordable horizons, so the asymptotic rates are not observed as executed regret curves.

rahit/repro-decentralized-online-convex-.overall: The logbook provides strong experimental support for Claims 1–5 through clean-room implementations on real data, exhaustive finite-domain enumerations, and destructive controls, confirming the regret bounds, exponent reductions, lower-bound construction, and algorithmic mechanism. Claim 6's bandit regret rates remain unconfirmed: the bounds hold but the measured T-scaling exponents (+0.998/+0.943) do not match the claimed T^{3/4}/T^{1/2} rates at affordable horizons.

divaspoudel/repro-best-of-both-worlds-fo.paper_title: Best-of-Both-Worlds for Heavy-Tailed Markov Decision Processes

claims.claim: For the known-transition setting, Algorithm 1 (HT-FTRL-OM), defined in Section 4.1, is proven in Theorem 4.1 to achieve regret of order poly(H,S,A)·σ(T^(1/α)+log T) in the adversarial regime (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Implemented on a tiny MDP (S=2, A=3, H=2) with T≤1000; regret/T^{1/α} ratio ranges 2.02–3.63, roughly but not cleanly constant, on a clearly simplified setup far below the paper's intended scale.

claims.claim: In the stochastic (self-bounding) regime, Theorem 4.1 shows HT-FTRL-OM attains an instance-dependent regret bound that reduces to order σ^(α/(α-1))ω_Δ(α) log T, i.e., logarithmic in T (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: On the same tiny MDP, regret/log(T) ratio grows from 26.2 to 173.1 across T=100–1000, with regret values (120.7, 240.2, 598.8, 1195.9) tracking near-linear rather than logarithmic growth; the toy setup and possible implementation issues prevent definitive falsification of the theoretical claim.

claims.claim: For the unknown-transition setting, Algorithm 2 (HT-FTRL-UOB), defined in Section 5.1, achieves adversarial-regime regret of order poly(H,S,A)·σ(T^(1/α) + √T log T + (log T)^2) per Theorem 5.1 (Section 5.1, Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: Implemented HT-FTRL-UOB on the same small MDP with T≤500; regret/(T^{1/α}+√T) ratio increases from 1.40 to 2.38, only roughly consistent with the claimed scaling on a clearly simplified setup.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 further shows HT-FTRL-UOB attains an instance-dependent self-bounding-regime regret bound of order poly(H,S,A)·σ^(α/(α-1))ω_Δ(α)(log T)^2, matching a log-squared-T rate (Section 5.2, Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: On the tiny MDP with T≤500, regret/(log T)^2 ratio grows from 5.9 to 11.2, not cleanly constant; the simplified setup is insufficient to confirm or refute the log-squared-T rate.

claims.claim: Both algorithms assume losses have bounded α-moments for α∈(1,2] with unbounded variance, and rely on novel skipping loss estimators adapted to occupancy measures to control heavy-tailed feedback (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Verified that a Pareto distribution satisfies E[|X|^α]=σ^α and truncative nonnegativity via 1M samples, and noted 0% skip fraction at T=100–1000 meaning the skipping estimator is never actually exercised; this is a basic distribution-property check on a toy setup, not a demonstration of the estimator's heavy-tail control in practice.

divaspoudel/repro-best-of-both-worlds-fo.overall: This logbook provides only toy-level numerical audits on a minimal MDP (S=2, A=3, H=2, T≤1000) with simplified FTRL implementations; the adversarial-regime claims show rough scaling consistency while the stochastic-regime claims show regret growth inconsistent with the predicted logarithmic rates, and the skipping estimator is never triggered. No claim is verified at a scale or rigor sufficient to constitute reproduction of the paper's theoretical guarantees.

divaspoudel/repro-trees-to-flows-and-bac.paper_title: Trees to Flows and Back: Unifying Decision Trees and Diffusion Models

claims.claim: TreeFlow establishes a formal correspondence showing decision trees arise as discrete approximations of continuous diffusion flows, with equivalence conditions proved as Theorems 2.1-2.10 (Section 2, Theorems 2.1-2.10).
claims.evidence: Numerical audits on 2D synthetic data (make_moons, 4-cluster) check smoothness, moment trends, velocity determinism, and ultrametric inequality for only 4 of 10 theorems; these are sanity checks on toy data, not verification of formal equivalence proofs.

claims.claim: DSmTree (Discretized Score Matching for Trees) distills tree structure from a trained diffusion model by matching score functions at tree nodes, enabling efficient inference while preserving distributional properties, achieving competitive quality relative to the diffusion teacher (Experiment 3, DSM-Tree Implementation).
claims.evidence: DSmTree implemented on 3 small UCI datasets with a DecisionTree as teacher (not a diffusion teacher as the paper describes), a 2-layer MLP student, and CPU-only training; 2/3 datasets within 2% gap but setup is a simplified proxy of the paper's actual pipeline.

claims.claim: Implicit tree structures are shown to emerge naturally from flow dynamics without explicit tree-building, demonstrated via an information decay analysis along tree paths (Experiment 1 and Experiment 2).
claims.evidence: Trained a 3-layer MLP score network on 2D synthetic datasets (4-corners, moons, 800 samples) and found valid dendrograms via agglomerative clustering with r=0.99 information decay correlation on Moons; clearly reduced-scale proxy demonstration.

claims.claim: TreeFlow supports bidirectional conversion between flow and tree representations, validated through a dedicated flow-to-tree instantiation experiment on tabular data (Experiment 4, TreeFlow Instantiation).
claims.evidence: TreeFlow tested on 3 small UCI datasets with a 128-unit MLP, CPU-only, 400 epochs; average TSTR accuracy of 44% and ARI of 0.38 indicate the model is far below the paper's scale, and the logbook itself notes generation quality is limited by model capacity.

claims.claim: Sample complexity bounds are derived for learning tree-structured flows, extending the main theoretical results with additional convergence analyses (Appendices C-H).
claims.evidence: Numerical checks of power-law convergence, bias-variance, concentration, and GTSM convergence on make_moons with depth-4 trees and ≤2000 samples; these are empirical sanity checks on synthetic data, not verification of formal sample complexity bounds derived in appendices.

divaspoudel/repro-trees-to-flows-and-bac.overall: All five claims are addressed only at toy scale: small 2D synthetic datasets or small UCI datasets with reduced model capacity on CPU, without baseline comparisons or GPU-scale training. The logbook provides preliminary empirical signals consistent with the paper's claims but does not constitute a faithful reproduction at the paper's intended scale.

rahit/repro-maximin-relative-improvement.paper_title: Maximin Relative Improvement: Fair Learning as a Bargaining Problem

claims.claim: Relative improvement is defined as the ratio of actual risk reduction to the maximum possible reduction from a baseline predictor, per Equation 1: ρ_P(f) = [R_P(f0) − R_P(f)] / [R_P(f0) − R_P(f*_P)] (Section 2, Equation 1).
claims.evidence: Clean-room reimplementation on full ACS 2018 PUMS (n=1,036,126, 400 configurations) reproduces all 40 entries of Appendix Table 2 exactly (8/8 cells, 5/5 entries each), confirms endpoint identities ρ_g(f_g*)=1 with max error 0.000 and ρ_g(f_0)=0, and verifies the closed-form expression against Eq.(1) with max discrepancy 1.917e-10 over 8M cells, plus a destructive control that breaks all 8 cells when the baseline is mis-specified.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves a no-harm guarantee: when the baseline predictor f0 is in the feasible class F, the maximin relative improvement solution f_RI satisfies R_g(f_RI) ≤ R_g(f0) for every group g (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: On 400 configurations (800 group-checks), MMRI never raises any group's risk above baseline (0/400 harmed, min slack 5.13e-04, 0 negatives). Destructive controls confirm the property is criterion-specific (MMR harms 34/400, GDRO 213/400) and hypothesis-dependent (removing f_0∈F by offsetting the intercept flips 0/400 to 165/167 harmed), with grid-resolution control showing at most 1.166e-04 improvement from continuous optimization.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.2 shows that, for two groups (m=2), relative improvement uniquely satisfies Pareto optimality, symmetry, scale invariance, and individual monotonicity simultaneously, and recovers the Kalai-Smorodinsky bargaining solution (Proposition 4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook does not address Proposition 4.2 at all — no experiments test Pareto optimality, symmetry, scale invariance, individual monotonicity, or the Kalai-Smorodinsky recovery for the two-group case.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.4 extends the axiomatic guarantees to more than two groups (m>2) via a leximin refinement that preserves scale invariance and a modified individual monotonicity property (Proposition 4.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook does not address Proposition 4.4 — no experiments test the leximin refinement, scale invariance, or modified individual monotonicity for m>2 groups.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.4 establishes that the empirical maximin relative improvement estimator converges to the population solution at rate O(1/√n) under standard regularity conditions (Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook does not address Theorem 5.4 — no convergence-rate experiments or finite-sample analysis of the empirical estimator are presented.

agharsallah/qitzdbvct0-logbook.paper_title: Full-Batch Gradient Descent Outperforms One-Pass SGD: Sample Complexity Separation in Single-Index Learning

claims.claim: For quadratic activation σ(z) = z², when the sample size n = o(d log d), spherical gradient flow fails to achieve weak recovery, showing full-batch updates offer no statistical advantage over one-pass SGD in this regime (Theorem 3.1).

claims.claim: With a truncated quadratic activation, full-batch spherical gradient flow achieves weak recovery with only n ≳ d samples, compared to the n ≳ d log d samples required by one-pass SGD, establishing a sample complexity separation (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports δ* growing from 3.13 (d=32) to 9.99 (d=128) for truncated quadratic, which actually shows the sample-to-dimension ratio increasing substantially with d, potentially contradicting the claimed O(d) scaling; however, at such small dimensions this cannot reliably confirm or refute the asymptotic claim.

divaspoudel/repro-fine-tuning-without-fo.paper_title: Fine-Tuning Without Forgetting In-Context Learning: A Theoretical Analysis of Linear Attention Models

claims.claim: Corollary 4.4 shows that full fine-tuning of all attention parameters in a linear attention model drives zero-shot error to σ² while few-shot (in-context) error converges to σ² + θᵀΣθ, a substantially larger value, formalizing the degradation of in-context learning after full fine-tuning (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo audit (100K samples, d=5) of closed-form expressions confirms zero-shot error matches theory (0.0995 vs 0.1000) and few-shot error exceeds zero-shot (1.409 vs 0.100), but this is a small-scale numerical check of theoretical formulas, not a proof or full-scale demonstration.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 shows that restricting fine-tuning updates to the value matrix reduces zero-shot error to σ² + (2/(d+4))θ₀ᵀΣθ₀ while Corollary 4.8 shows the asymptotic few-shot error only rises to σ² + 1/(d+4)²θ₀ᵀΣθ₀, i.e. value-matrix-only fine-tuning improves zero-shot performance with far less degradation to in-context learning than full fine-tuning (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Numerical audit at d=5 confirms value-matrix FT zero-shot error matches theory (0.3207 vs 0.3222) and few-shot error is much lower than full FT (0.4714 vs 1.4087), but finite-n deviations from asymptotic predictions and small scale make this a toy-scale consistency check.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.10 proves that tuning the auxiliary few-shot loss weight w to optimize few-shot performance on the fine-tuning task θ₀ necessarily reduces few-shot performance on other tasks θ ≠ θ₀, formalizing a trade-off between target-task adaptation and generalization to unseen tasks (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: Numerical computation at d=5, n=20 shows task-optimal weights differ (w*(θ₀)=0.654 vs w*(-θ₀)=0.931) with excess error 0.093 when using the wrong task's optimal w, confirming the trade-off qualitatively at toy scale.

claims.claim: In synthetic linear-regression experiments (d=5, σ²=0.1, Σ=I₅, ‖θ₀‖₂²=1, m=n=20), Figure 4 confirms the theoretical zero-shot/few-shot error predictions across pretraining, full fine-tuning, and value-matrix fine-tuning regimes, and Figure 5 shows value-matrix fine-tuning attains the lowest error on the out-of-distribution task -θ₀ (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: Actual training of 1-layer, 1-head linear attention model (d=5, 2000 pretrain + 500 FT iterations, 3 seeds) shows qualitative trends matching Figures 4-5 (ICL forgetting under full FT, preservation under value-FT, value-FT lowest on -θ₀), but quantitative deviations from theory are substantial (e.g., pretrained ZS 0.939 vs theory 1.100) and the setup is small-scale synthetic.

claims.evidence: No MMLU experiments were run; the logbook states GPU compute was unavailable (HF Jobs 402, no local GPU), so there is zero experimental evidence for this claim.

agharsallah/2xmljj67yy-logbook.paper_title: Keep Everyone Happy: Online Fair Division of Numerous Items with Few Copies

claims.claim: The OFD-UCB algorithm models agent utility as an unknown linear function of item-agent features, using a contextual-bandit upper-confidence-bound estimator with round-robin initialization for the first N rounds to learn from limited observed utilities (Section on Algorithms).
claims.evidence: 120 runs across horizons 256–2048, 5–10 agents, dims 8–16 confirm exact round-robin permutations in the first N rounds, with ablation controls showing UCB bonus removal worse in 116/120 and learning disabled worse in 119/120 runs, directly verifying the algorithm's structural properties.

claims.claim: For linear utility functions, OFD-UCB achieves regret in T>0 rounds bounded by 2*alpha_T*w_max*sqrt(2dT*log(lambda+TL/d)) with probability at least 1-delta (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: 120 synthetic stochastic trials check the Theorem 1 regret certificate numerically (max regret/bound ratio 0.022, slope 0.513), but this is a numerical proxy for a formal proof on synthetic instances with trivial CPU compute, not a full-scale experimental reproduction.

claims.claim: A generalized regret bound extends the result to arbitrary compatible bandit algorithms 𝔄, bounding the regret of OFD-𝔄 in T rounds by 2*w_max*sqrt(T)*sqrt(sum_{t=1}^T [h(m_t,n_t,O_t)]^2) (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: 120 compatible estimators (constant, inverse-sqrt, elliptical) pass the per-round inequality and Cauchy-Schwarz bound (max ratio 0.047) with a halved-envelope destructive control rejecting 12,960 cells, but this is numerical verification of a theoretical bound on synthetic instances, not a formal proof or real-world evaluation.

claims.claim: An alternative bound (Theorem 3) applies to goodness functions that are locally monotonically non-decreasing and Lipschitz continuous, replacing w_max with c_max in the same sqrt(T) regret structure.
claims.evidence: 100 synthetic instances of log-Nash and square-root welfare functions pass monotonicity, Lipschitz, and c_max checks with max ratio 0.047, and a sinusoidal nonmonotone control is rejected, but this numerically checks Theorem 3's conditions on synthetic instances rather than providing a formal proof.

claims.claim: The fairness-efficiency tradeoff is controlled via a weighted Gini social-evaluation function with parameter rho in (0,1], interpolating between Egalitarian Social Welfare and Utilitarian Social Welfare.
claims.evidence: Across 4,096 utility vectors, rho=1 matches utilitarian welfare and rho→0 closure matches min utility to 2.84e-14; 352 allocation sweeps show mean utility rising by 704.5 and Gini rising by 0.87 from fair to utilitarian endpoint, with reversed-weight controls separating in all 4,096 cases, directly verifying the interpolation property.

agharsallah/2xmljj67yy-logbook.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from synthetic instances supporting all five claims, with proper ablation and destructive controls. DineshAI/iSD2q5Tius.paper_title: Innovation: An Almost Characterization of Hallucination

claims.claim: The paper defines innovation (Definition 3.1) as a language model assigning nonzero probability mass to statements not present in the training data, and shows via Observation 3.2 that hallucinating with positive probability implies the model innovates (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The set-inclusion proof (O⊆F ⟹ H⊆U ⟹ g(H)≤g(U)) is mathematically correct and trivially verifiable; the executable truth-table certificate checks all premise/conclusion rows, and 160,000 native corpora at |Ω|=20,000 corroborate with a negative control (removing O⊆F yields g(H)=1, g(U)=0) that fails as expected.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows that under K-Sparsity and Regular Facts assumptions, if the innovation mass g(U) > 0, the probability a model hallucinates is at least 1 - K/|U| (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: The proof certificate correctly derives q≤K/|U| from K-sparsity and then Pr[g(H)>0|X]≥1−q≥1−K/|U| via a positive-mass unseen witness; native spike rates (0.998225, 0.958075, 0.845875) exceed the theoretical floors (0.997498, 0.949648, 0.830621) across all three regimes with 40,000 corpora each, and the non-Regular-Facts negative control yields 0 vs required 0.99.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.4 shows that a calibrated model with any positive missing probability mass necessarily innovates (Proposition 3.4).
claims.evidence: The witness proof (p(U)>0 ⟹ ∃y*∈U with p(y*)>0 ⟹ p(B*)>0 ⟹ g(y*)=p^Π(y*)>0) is correct and exhaustively checked over 56,105 complete partition models through |Ω|=6; native calibrated runs show |g(U)−p(U)|=0 in all 160,000 corpora, and removing calibration permits g(U)=0 as expected.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 gives a Markov-style bound showing the hallucination rate satisfies g(H) ≥ g(U)(1 - K/(δ|U|)) with probability at least 1-δ (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The Markov inequality derivation (E[Z|X]=q·g(U)≤K·g(U)/|U|, then Pr[Z>K·g(U)/(δ|U|)]≤δ) is correct; the executable certificate checks 2,359 exact substitutions with strictly positive factors over the correct strict domain δ∈(K/|U|,1), and native runs pass all admissible regime/δ pairs with the Regular-Facts-removed control failing (0 vs 0.9).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 establishes a high-confidence bound where, with probability at least 1 - K/|U|, the hallucination rate satisfies g(H) ≥ g(U)/(K+1) (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: The two-case proof (m≤a: deterministic g(H)≥a; m>a: probabilistic via Regular Facts) is correct and exhaustive; native scatter models satisfy 1.000000 in all regimes and spike models exceed floors (0.998225, 0.958075, 0.845875 vs 0.997498, 0.949648, 0.830621), with a sharpness certificate at equality and a negative control (denominator K instead of K+1) that correctly fails.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.3 lower-bounds the innovation rate by g(U) ≥ p(U)/(K+1) minus a miscalibration distance term, linking missing probability mass to innovation (Proposition 4.3).
claims.evidence: The cellwise coarsening lemma (|B|≤(K+1)|U∩B| ⟹ p^Π(U∩B)≥p(U∩B)/(K+1)) combined with the TV variational inequality is correct; 480,000 native model evaluations across calibrated, scatter, and spike families exercise nonzero TV in 320,000 cases with minimum slack 0.588235, and removing K-sparsity yields g(U)=1/5<1/4 as expected.

DineshAI/iSD2q5Tius.overall: The logbook independently reconstructs correct mathematical proofs for all six theoretical claims about innovation and hallucination in abstract language models, corroborated by native-scale Monte Carlo experiments (N up to 20,000, 40,000 corpora per regime, 480,000 model evaluations) with appropriate negative controls. For an algebraic identity theorem, exact verification on any instance is sufficient.

claims.claim: SNGD converges at rate (1-α)^t where α=λ_min(P̄), while SPRING converges at rate O((1-√(α/β))^t), giving up to a square-root improvement in iteration complexity over SNGD (Theorem 1).

The negative control (noncommuting H) showed 0/200 violations, meaning the instrument failed to discriminate, leaving the core comparison claim unaddressed.

claims.claim: A unified algorithm (Algorithm 1) captures both SNGD (momentum μ=0) and SPRING (μ∈(0,1)) as momentum-based updates using subsampled Jacobians, enabling single-minibatch convergence guarantees of any batch size.

nstp/repro-gradient-descent-as-a-percept.paper_title: Gradient Descent as a Perceptron Algorithm: Understanding Dynamics and Implicit Acceleration

claims.claim: Theorem 1.1 (Section 1.2) shows that for logistic regression with a linear model as the margin γ→∞, gradient descent reduces to the batch perceptron algorithm, requiring at most O(nR²/ω²) iterations.
claims.evidence: The logbook's 'Claim 1' addresses Theorem 2.1 (nonlinear convolutional model → Quadratic Perceptron), not Theorem 1.1 (linear logistic regression → batch perceptron with O(nR²/ω²) complexity). No experiment tests the linear-model reduction or its iteration bound.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.1 (Section 2) shows that gradient descent on a nonlinear convolutional model with kernel size k=2 and large ‖w₀‖ reduces to a 'Quadratic Perceptron Algorithm' with iteration complexity Õ(√d/μ).
claims.evidence: GD and QPA prediction signs match exactly (mismatch 0.0e+00) at ‖w₀‖=10⁶ across 2 seeds with d=10, n=20, while the control at ‖w₀‖=1 yields mismatch 0.31/0.10, confirming the asymptotic reduction. claims.evidence: On the paper's two-sample dataset (5), QPA steps scale as d^0.513 (R²=0.997) and batch perceptron steps scale as d^0.997 (R²=1.000) over d∈{10,25,50,100,200,400}, directly exhibiting the √d acceleration gap. Falsification controls (disabled option-2, orthogonal data) collapse the respective rates.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 (Section 4) establishes spectral bounds on the eigenstructure of matrices induced by the convolutional reparameterization, underpinning the accelerated convergence result.
claims.evidence: All four eigenvalue cases of A(a) match closed-form expressions to ≤3.6e-15, the operator-norm sandwich ‖a‖≤‖A‖≤√2‖a‖ holds in every case, and the explicit eigenvector formula residual is 9.4e-16. Perturbing A breaks the spectrum (error 2.25e+00), confirming the structure is diagnostic.

claims.claim: Section 6 extends the acceleration results to larger convolution kernels and two-layer models, showing the largest allowable step size decreases as kernel size increases.
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states Section 6 (kernel sizes k>2, two-layer models, step-size decrease with kernel size) was not tested: 'Not tested: kernel sizes k>2 (Sec 6, Prop 6.1).' No experiments address this claim.

nstp/repro-gradient-descent-as-a-percept.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence for the core theoretical results (Theorem 2.1 reduction, Proposition 4.1 eigenstructure, Theorems 5.1/5.2 rate separation) via from-scratch NumPy implementations with falsification controls, but does not address Theorem 1.1 (linear case) or Section 6 (larger kernels).

nstp/repro-near-optimal-dynamic-matching.paper_title: Near-Optimal Dynamic Matching via Coarsening with Application to Heart Transplantation

claims.evidence: From-scratch SM_b implementation with LP-guided matching at b=100 (α(100)=0.650) measures ratio 0.952±0.034 over 20 seeds, exceeding the bound; breaking the LP mechanism collapses the ratio to 0.475 (below the bound), confirming the mechanism is load-bearing.

claims.claim: In simulations on real UNOS heart transplant data from January-June 2019, the proposed clustered policy achieves a competitive ratio of 0.91, compared to 0.63 for non-capacitated stochastic matching (b=1) and 0.51 for the US status quo post-2018 allocation policy.
claims.evidence: From-scratch CSM on 4 clusters of size b=100 (400 offline nodes) with Assumption 2 enforced exactly at δ=0.1 measures ratio 0.943±0.029 vs bound 0.520; violating Assumption 2 drops the ratio to 0.580, confirming the bounded-variance hypothesis matters.

claims.claim: The proposed framework is estimated to deliver approximately 150 additional successful heart transplants per month compared to the current U.S. status quo policy, based on the real-data simulation.
claims.evidence: CSM with η=0.1 estimation error (given weights perturbed within Assumption 4 band) measures 0.946±0.025 vs bound 0.416; adversarial anti-correlated estimates collapse the ratio to 0.203, confirming the bounded-error hypothesis is load-bearing.

claims.claim: The base stochastic b-matching result relied upon (Brubach et al., 2016) guarantees a competitive ratio of at least 1 - b^(-1/2+epsilon) - e^(-b^2*epsilon/3) for any epsilon > 0 (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: CSM with 3 good clusters and 1 bad cluster (measured ρ=0.031) achieves ratio 0.918±0.030 vs bound 0.504; scaling the bad cluster to ρ≈0.44 drops the ratio to 0.531, confirming the good/bad-cluster guarantee degrades as predicted.

claims.claim: The framework extends to settings with estimation error in cluster weights (Theorem 5) and to cluster-dependent error rates (Theorem 7).
claims.evidence: UNOS data is proprietary, so a synthetic proxy (200 patients, 40 donor types, 5-dim features) is used; coarsening achieves 0.667 vs 0.372 (1.79×) matching the paper's 1.78× relative improvement, but absolute values 0.91/0.51 are not reproduced on real data.

nstp/repro-near-optimal-dynamic-matching.overall: The logbook provides from-scratch implementations of SM_b and CSM with numerical verification that all four theoretical competitive-ratio bounds (Theorems 1, 3, 5, 7) hold on non-trivial synthetic instances (b=100) satisfying the stated hypotheses, each with a falsification control confirming the relevant assumption is load-bearing. The UNOS empirical claim (0.91 vs 0.51) is only tested on a synthetic proxy reproducing the relative improvement factor but not the absolute numbers.

DineshAI/b3EvCd8sYE.paper_title: Evaluating Bivariate Causal Statements Based on Mutual Compatibility

claims.claim: For linear bivariate causal statements, any acyclic collection induces exactly one multivariate structural equation model whose pairwise marginals match the given statements (Lemma 2.3).
claims.evidence: Symbolic verification via SymPy over generic free-symbol matrices for n=2..6 confirms all algebraic identities (pairwise marginal equality, strict lower-triangularity of Gamma, unit lower-triangularity of A, and both round-trip bijections) as exact rational-function identities, with negative controls showing incorrect constructions fail.

claims.claim: The compatibility score defined via path-tracing decomposition of confounding (Definition 2.7) is proven to have positive expected value under a generic random causal model, supporting the paper's Confounding Postulate (Theorem 2.9).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive path-configuration enumeration for n=3..9 (5.4M summands, 0 failures) confirms every summand of eq.(6) has a degree-one Gamma entry; exact polynomial identities for n=3..6 verify comp=sum(B²+2B·eps) and E[sum B·eps]=0 symbolically using only Assumption 2.8; the strict-positivity witness E[B_23²]=E[Σ_N,11²]·Var(Γ_21)·Var(Γ_31) is derived in closed form. Monte Carlo over 60 gating configurations shows 58/60 CIs strictly above zero (2 underpowered, none contradicting).

claims.claim: Empirical approximation of the compatibility score converges in polynomial sample complexity with respect to dimension, causal strength, and pathway contributions (Theorem 2.10).
claims.evidence: Independently measured minimum sample sizes N* across sweeps of n, a+b, V, eps, and delta yield joint-fit exponents (+2.59, +0.75, +3.77, +1.82) all below the theorem's caps (4, 4, 4, 2); a reconstructed derivation from measured sensitivity (L exponents 2.21, 1.70, 1.00 matching predictions 2, 2, 1) and verified 1/√N concentration rate composes to exponents (4.41, 3.40, 4.00, 2.00, 1.00) matching the theorem's (4, 4, 4, 2, 1); large-deviation rate is linear in N (R²>0.995) confirming delta exponent 1, with t(3) negative control collapsing the rate.

claims.claim: On synthetic linear models, compatibility scores decrease monotonically as injected error increases, and on LLM-generated causal statements higher-capacity models achieve higher compatibility scores, with some receiving negative (falsifying) scores (Section 2.7, Figures 2 and 4).
claims.evidence: Figure 2 reproduced at full scale (1000 lists/point, 12 parameter curves): fraction of positive scores strictly decreases with injected error in all 12 curves, with mean 0.960 at zero error. LLM transcripts (165/195 completed) show systematic cross-model differences (Kruskal-Wallis p=1.98e-7), multiple models with negative scores, and a suggestive capacity trend (Spearman ρ=0.501, p=0.097 on 12-model extended ladder), though only 6/9 paper models were reachable and the paper's own subset is underpowered (p=0.468).

claims.claim: For graphical bivariate causal statements, computing the exact incompatibility score (minimum Hamming distance to a compatible statement graph) is proven NP-hard via reduction to transitive-closure editing (Section 3, NP-hardness result).
claims.evidence: The paper's reduction (incomp(G+) = ACYCLIC TRANSITIVITY EDITING optimum) is verified exhaustively for all 25 acyclic digraphs on 3 vertices and all 543 on 4 vertices, plus 300 sampled at n=5, with negative controls confirming the acyclicity hypothesis is load-bearing and the agreement is non-trivial. The external NP-hardness premise (Weller et al. 2012) is explicitly assumed, not reproduced.

claims.claim: A heuristic GreedyFAS+GreedyTE algorithm yields incompatibility scores that upper-bound the true incompatibility score and equal zero exactly when the true score is zero, and empirically increase monotonically with injected errors on synthetic graphs and on LLM outputs (Lemma 3.7, Sections 3.3-3.4, Figures 5-7).
claims.evidence: Lemma 3.7(1) c(G)≥incomp(G) and 3.7(2) c(G)=0⟺incomp(G)=0 verified exhaustively over all 512 statement graphs on 3 vertices and all 262,144 on 4 vertices, plus 400 sampled at n=5. Figure 5 shows positive monotone increase in all 12 curves (slopes 0.52–0.91, Bonferroni-corrected CIs excluding zero, 0/96 significant inversions). LLM capacity correlation (Figure 7) is weak (ρ=−0.464, p=0.294 on 7 models) but the density confound is reproduced (ρ=−0.361, p=6.4e-5).

DineshAI/b3EvCd8sYE.overall: This logbook provides strong evidence for all six claims through symbolic verification of mathematical lemmas/theorems (Claims 1, 2, 5), empirically validated sample-complexity bounds with reconstructed derivations (Claim 3), and full-scale synthetic experiments with committed LLM transcripts (Claims 4, 6). The main limitations are incomplete LLM model coverage (6/9 reachable) and consequently underpowered capacity-correlation tests, but the core quantitative claims—monotonicity, negative scores, systematic differences, and exhaustive lemma verification—are well-supported.

DineshAI/sW8U2TYDMp.paper_title: Probabilistic Modeling of Latent Agentic Substructures in Deep Neural Networks

claims.claim: Agents are formalized as probability distributions with epistemic utility of an outcome o defined as the logarithmic score U(o) = log P(o) (Section 2).
claims.evidence: Numerical check on P=(0.3,0.5,0.2) confirms U(o)=log P(o) pointwise with error 0.0 and E_P[log P]=-H(P) with error 0.0; destructive control detecting P[o] instead of log(P[o]) passes.

claims.claim: Theorem 10 proves that strict unanimity (every agent strictly benefiting) is impossible under linear pooling for outcome spaces of any size, because linear pooling behaves as a random dictatorship (Section 3.1, Theorem 10).
claims.evidence: Symbolic proof certificate shows weighted sum of welfare gaps equals -Σβ_i[KL(P_i||P)+KL(P||P_i)]<0 via Gibbs' inequality; four numerical fixtures (2–4 agents, 2–5 outcomes) confirm with residual ~1e-16, and 70-digit Decimal checker gives residual 1E-70.

claims.claim: Theorem 9 shows strict unanimity is achievable under logarithmic pooling once the outcome space has at least three outcomes, contrasting with the impossibility results for two outcomes (Theorem 8) and linear pooling (Theorem 10) (Section 3.1, Theorems 8-10).
claims.evidence: Predeclared construction with ε=1e-5 yields strictly positive minimum gaps (~0.000115) for 2–4 agents under log pooling; independent 70-digit checker reproduces gaps; linear-pool control gives negative gaps and binary grid finds 0 strict cases among 24,255, confirming Theorem 8 contrast.

claims.claim: Theorem 19 formalizes the 'Waluigi effect,' proving that manifesting a benevolent persona in a language model necessarily strengthens the weight of an antagonistic counterpart component under compositional stability constraints (Section 5, Theorem 19).
claims.evidence: Counterexample with identical aligned duplicate H=A=(1,-1,0) and antagonist W=(-1,1,0): perturbation Δβ=(+0.05,-0.05,0) increases benevolent weight but leaves Waluigi weight unchanged (0.0) because pool shift is exactly zero, while Theorem 19's conditional inequality holds at equality—contradicting the claim's 'necessarily strengthens' universal.

claims.claim: Theorem 21 proves that a 'manifest-then-suppress' strategy ('Waluigi shattering') achieves strictly greater suppression of misalignment than directly reinforcing pure benevolence (Section 5.1, Theorem 21).
claims.evidence: Projection geometry on 4-outcome uniform P yields pure-benevolence first-order reduction 0.05 vs elicited-span reduction 0.0866 (strict gain 0.0366); 70-digit checker confirms; two controls (inside-span, event-orthogonal) reduce gain to exactly zero; finite exponential tilts converge toward first-order prediction.

claims.claim: Theorem 14 shows that a compositional benefit enjoyed by a parent agent does not necessarily propagate to its child subagents under recursive decomposition (Section 4.1, Theorem 14).
claims.evidence: Construction with P1=(0.6,0.3,0.1), t=1.5, α=0.4 shows parent gap +0.129 while child-one gap becomes negative at λ=2 (-0.062) and decreases to -4.348; parent reconstruction error ~1e-16 and global-pool shift ~5.6e-17 confirm invariants; clone control stays positive and incompatible tilt breaks invariants.

DineshAI/sW8U2TYDMp.overall: The logbook provides theorem-level verification through symbolic derivations, predeclared constructions, numerical fixtures, independent 70-digit Decimal checkers, and negative controls for all six claims. Claim 4's broad 'necessarily strengthens' wording is falsified by a valid counterexample where the antagonist weight remains unchanged while the theorem's conditional inequality still holds.

nstp/repro-convergence-of-steepest-desce.paper_title: Convergence of Steepest Descent and Adam under Non-Uniform Smoothness

claims.evidence: RMSProp (linear, slope=-0.044) vs AdaGrad (sublinear, loglog slope=-0.85), AMSGrad (-0.48), and heavy-ball (~-1.0) are compared on a 1D logistic loss, confirming the qualitative ordering but only on a toy scalar problem.

claims.evidence: The logbook contains no experiments involving stochastic gradients or any stochastic setting; the extension from deterministic to stochastic is never addressed.

nstp/repro-convergence-of-steepest-desce.overall: The logbook provides empirical support for the paper's theoretical results on toy-scale problems (d=2, n=20, or 1D scalar losses), confirming that NS/NL bounds hold and that sign GD/RMSProp/Adam exhibit linear convergence while GD/AdaGrad/AMSGrad are sublinear. However, the stochastic extension (Claim 5) is entirely unaddressed, and the two-layer neural network claim (Claim 3) is only tested on a 1D proxy.

DineshAI/QRtzkKrbJi.paper_title: Gradient Flow Sampler-based Distributionally Robust Optimization

claims.evidence: All six algorithms (1–6) were implemented and their defining transitions independently checked on an 8-dimensional smooth conformance fixture: WGF transition error 0, SVGD error 8.67e-19, WFR weight-sum error 0 with 72 birth-death events, RGO acceptance rate 0.756, and 6/6 injected defects rejected by the negative control.

The theta=1 negative control correctly yields first-hit time 0.401 for tolerance 0.1.

claims.evidence: An exact 1D entropy-Wasserstein DRO instance with Phi(theta)=theta², L_Phi=2, exact inner sampler, and unit-variance stochastic gradients yields minimum iteration counts 48, 231, 1076, 7973, 35635 for eps=0.2,0.1,0.05,0.02,0.01. The normalized quantity S*eps²/log(1/eps) stays between 0.774 and 1.193, certifying Omega(eps^-2 log(1/eps)) rather than O(eps^-2). The antithetic zero-variance control reaches eps=0.01 in 8 iterations, confirming stochastic variance as the mechanism.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 bounds the total computational complexity of the WGF-based DRO algorithm (Algorithm 3) as Õ(L_Φ L²_U L²_f d² / (λ³_U ε⁴_opt)) (Section 5, Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Four routes were explored: proof dependency reconstruction (old 2+2=4 composition broken by Claim 3 but a flawed proof is not a counterexample), version comparison (v3 changes to eps^-6 but correction is not a lower bound), primary source audit (no direct-product embedding theorem found), and a dedicated Gaussian ULA falsification attempt whose work-to-eps^-4 ratios decrease from 0.046 to 0.0007, remaining within the bound. Neither a valid proof nor a valid counterexample was established.

Across all 120 nonzero comparisons, WFR has 29 and WGF has 20 strict-dominance violations. The dominance-satisfying synthetic control correctly produces zero violations.

claims.claim: Table 1 summarizes the dimension-dependence improvements across gradient-variation, gradient-variance, and small-loss metrics for linear, convex, and strongly convex function classes relative to prior best-known results (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Direct transcription check confirmed all 'Ours' cells in Table 1 match Theorems 1–4, and the relative-ranking check showed linear-mode d-exponent (-0.14) is not spuriously better than convex-mode (-0.97), confirming the qualitative consistency the table asserts.

RyeCatcher/repro-improved-dimension-depe.overall: The logbook provides a from-scratch CPU implementation of Algorithms 1–2 with 200 seeds per config, exact closed-form constructions for V_T/W_T/F_T, and cross-validation against scipy, but all regret-bound claims (C1–C5) are tested at scales (d≤30, T≤4000) where large algorithm-internal constants dominate the environment signal, preventing confirmation of the claimed polynomial exponents. Only the Table 1 transcription/consistency check (C6) is fully verified; the rest are toy-scale experiments where bounds were never clearly violated (except a 9% overshoot in C4 at d=5) but claimed rates could not be confirmed.

RyeCatcher/repro-revisiting-the-bertrand.paper_title: Revisiting the Bertrand Paradox via Equilibrium Analysis of No-regret Learners

claims.claim: For symmetric-cost Bertrand competition with any non-increasing demand function, Theorem 2.1 shows two no-external-regret learners can sustain high prices while guaranteeing each firm's utility is at least 1/(4e^2) of the monopoly profit (Theorem 2.1).
claims.evidence: 220 seeds with random non-increasing step functions (k in [8,60]): worst-case closed-form utility/monopoly = 0.033973 vs bound 0.033834 (margin +0.00014), CCE validity margin = 0.0, and independent LP-max CCE utility = 0.250306 — concrete numerical evidence that the construction clears the stated bound and is a valid CCE.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.2 shows that when both learners use no-swap-regret algorithms, prices converge toward marginal cost, with expected utility bounded above by f(c+1/k)/k, demonstrating strong competitive pressure (Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: 210 seeds (k in [6,26]) solving LP-max over the full CE polytope: bound-minus-achieved margin = +4.65e-4 (never violated), worst achieved/bound ratio = 0.50; negative controls (deterministic collusion and increasing demand) both fired, confirming the bound is load-bearing.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.3 shows an asymmetric setting—one no-external-regret learner paired with one no-swap-regret learner—can still sustain high, collusive-like prices under certain demand structures such as constant demand (Theorem 2.3).
claims.evidence: The Φ-CE construction was verified as valid (obedience margins ≥ 0) across 150 instances with k up to 1.5M, and the utility ratio was shown not to decay with k. However, the worst observed ratio is 9.5e-5 — extremely small — and the paper provides no numeric λ0 to match, so the 'high, collusive-like prices' aspect is only qualitatively supported, not quantitatively confirmed.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.5 shows that as the number of firms n grows, the total utility attainable under no-external-regret dynamics decays exponentially, as e^(1-n/2) (Theorem 2.5).
claims.evidence: 200 seeds (n in [2,12], k in [6,40]) over the diagonal CCE subclass: worst-case (bound − achieved) margin = +9.46e-4, never violated; negative control (all-play-monopoly) overshoots the bound by 6.4x at n=15, confirming the bound is non-trivial.

claims.claim: Under asymmetric costs, Theorem 2.6 shows high-utility coarse correlated equilibria exist for broad demand classes (including linear and exponential demand) under no-external-regret learning, while Theorem 2.7 shows that under no-swap-regret learning the higher-cost firm's utility converges to zero regardless of the demand function (Theorems 2.6 and 2.7).
claims.evidence: Theorem 2.7 is verified: LP-max E[u_2] over the full asymmetric CE polytope = exact zero across 120 seeds. Theorem 2.6 is only partially addressed: existence of high-utility CCEs confirmed qualitatively on four named demand families (worst min-ratio = 0.327), but the formal regularity conditions on λ1/λ2 from Appendix A.2 were not reconstructed or checked numerically, so the full theorem statement is not verified.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments across multiple demand functions show utilities converging toward 1/e ≈ 0.368 of the monopoly utility under no-external-regret dynamics (Numerical results section).
claims.evidence: 200 points (50 log-spaced k-values from 10 to 3000 × 4 demand functions) using independent LP: at large k (≥500), worst |ratio − 1/e| = 7.7e-6 across all four demand families, monotonically improving with k, directly replicating the paper's stated experimental design.

RyeCatcher/repro-revisiting-the-bertrand.overall: The logbook provides concrete LP-based numerical verification for Claims 1, 2, 4, and 6, and for Theorem 2.7 within Claim 5, with 200+ seeds, worst-case reporting, and negative controls throughout. Claims 3 and Theorem 2.6 are only partially verified due to missing numeric constants in the paper and unchecked formal regularity conditions, respectively.

RyeCatcher/repro-doubly-exponential-lowe.paper_title: (Doubly) Exponential Lower Bounds for Follow the Regularized Leader in Potential Games

claims.claim: Theorem 1.2 proves that in two-player m×m potential games, Follow the Regularized Leader (FTRL) can require 2^Ω(m log m) iterations to reach an ε-Nash equilibrium for ε = 1/poly(m), for any permutation-invariant regularizer and any learning rate schedule η^(t) = 1/t^α with α ∈ [0,1) (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: FTRL was run on the adversarial construction for m=3..13 showing T growth from 270 to 827,640, but the negative control (random games) failed to discriminate—random games also hit the 200k cap at m_B≥8 with only 4.1× ratio, meaning the slowdown cannot be attributed specifically to the paper's construction. The power-law fit (R²=0.9985) actually fits better than the exponential model at this small scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 1.3 shows there exists an n-player binary-action potential game in which fictitious play requires 2^Ω(2^n) iterations to reach an ε-Nash equilibrium for ε = 1/2^n, a doubly exponential lower bound (Theorem 1.3).
claims.evidence: Lemma 5.3's factorial bound T_k≥(k−1)! was checked exactly for k=1..60 with 0 violations; real FP simulation matches the recursion order-of-magnitude (k=9: 45,725 vs 69,028); the negative control (non-snake path) converges instantly (T≤18), cleanly isolating the snake property as necessary.

claims.claim: Theorem 1.1 establishes a matching-type positive result: alternating ε-lazy no-regret dynamics converge to an ε-Nash equilibrium in any potential game after at most exp(O_ε(1/ε^2)) iterations (Theorem 1.1, restated as Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: 1,000 runs (200 seeds × 5 ε values) with zero censoring, all converging well within exp(O(1/ε²)); the negative control on the same hard instance shows alternating+lazy converges in T=23 vs simultaneous+non-lazy T=92,338 (~4,015× gap), confirming both hypotheses are load-bearing.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.2 shows that for FTRL with learning rate η ≤ 1/L (L the smoothness constant of the potential), the potential function value is non-decreasing across iterations, without requiring alternation or laziness (Proposition 3.2).
claims.evidence: The inequality Φ(x^(t+1))−Φ(x^(t)) ≥ (1/2η)‖x^(t+1)−x^(t))‖² was checked across 300,000 steps with worst slack of −2.220e-16 (floating-point noise), confirming the bound holds essentially exactly. The negative control at η=5/L was inconclusive but does not undermine the positive verification.

claims.claim: Example 3.3 constructs a 'spurious fixed point' showing FTRL can maintain a highly suboptimal strategy (error proportional to 1/t) indefinitely relative to the observed utility sequence, illustrating why FTRL, unlike gradient descent under Legendre regularizers, need not reach an O_ε(ε)-Nash equilibrium (Example 3.3).
claims.evidence: The bound x₂(t) ≤ R/(ηt) held across 200 seeds and post-flip suboptimality persisted (rising to 1.000 by t=200), confirming the spurious fixed point. However, the negative control (OMD contrast, central to the 'unlike gradient descent' part of the claim) failed due to a floating-point underflow artifact from seeding OMD at FTRL's degenerate starting point rather than running its own trajectory.

claims.claim: The two-player exponential lower bound construction uses a payoff matrix A of odd dimension m with maximum entry 2m−1, dividing the FTRL trajectory into 2m−1 'transition periods' governed by Property 4.3 (period consistency) and Lemma 4.1 bounding action probability by R/(η^(t)γ) (Section 4, Definition 4.2, Property 4.3, Lemma 4.1, Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: Lemma 4.1 bound held with 0 violations across 80,000 checks; Property 4.3 showed 0 skips and 0 non-monotone transitions on 94.7% of classified rounds; matrix dimension (odd m) and max entry (2m−1) matched exactly across all 5 tested sizes. Both negative controls fired cleanly: non-FTRL points violated Lemma 4.1 (42/688 violations) and random games yielded 0/1999 classified periods.

RyeCatcher/repro-doubly-exponential-lowe.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification for Claims 2, 3, 4, and 6, with exact arithmetic checks, clean negative controls, and adequate seed counts. Claims 1 and 5 are only partially supported: Claim 1's negative control failed to discriminate adversarial from random instances at reachable scale, and Claim 5's OMD contrast was invalidated by a floating-point underflow design flaw.

qy2100/repro-discovering-scaling-exponen.paper_title: Discovering Scaling Exponents with Physics-Informed Müntz-Szász Networks

claims.claim: MSN-PINN models targets as sums of power-law terms u_theta(x) = sum_k c_k x^{mu_k}, treating both coefficients {c_k} and exponents {mu_k} as trainable parameters optimized via a two-timescale scheme with exponent learning rate eta_mu set to roughly 0.5 times the coefficient learning rate eta_c (Equation 1, Section 3.1, Algorithm 1, Section 3.5).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements the MSN-PINN ansatz u(x)=Σ c_k x^{μ_k} with both coefficients and exponents trainable, using a two-timescale Adam optimizer with η_c=0.01 and η_μ=0.005 (ratio 0.5), across 21 runs (7 seeds × 3 configs). The method is numerically stable (0/21 diverged) and achieves accurate single-exponent recovery (0.016%–0.272% error for x^{2/3}), confirming the described method works as stated.

claims.claim: For the 2D Laplace equation corner singularity with a 270-degree wedge angle, MSN-PINN recovers the exponent as mu=0.6667 against the true classical Kondrat'ev value of 2/3, a 0.009% error (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The reproduction recovers μ̂=0.6667 with ≈0.009% relative error against the true Kondrat'ev value 2/3, and a second harmonic at ≈1.3335 vs analytic 4/3, matching Table 2's reported values. The logbook author's 'boundary leakage' critique is a methodological objection to the paper's experimental design, not evidence that the numerical result fails to reproduce.

claims.claim: On a 40-configuration wedge benchmark spanning 5 angles and 4 boundary condition types, the constraint-aware MSN-PINN achieves 100% success rate with 0.022% mean exponent error, versus only 55% success and 5.96% mean error for the naive MSN-PINN without the constraint term, a roughly 270-fold improvement in accuracy (Section I.8, Table 11).
claims.evidence: The exact Table 11 magnitudes (constraint 100%/0.022% vs naive 55%/5.96%) were not reproduced under any single setup tested. Under the eigenfunction arc: constraint 100%/0.0101% vs naive 63%/24.18%; under the non-leaking constant arc: constraint 83%/17.1% vs naive 4%/174%. Only 20 of 40 configurations were tested, and no setup yielded the paper's specific numbers.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.5 shows the exponent recovery error scales as O(sigma / (c_min * Delta^2 * sqrt(N))), where Delta is the minimum separation between exponents, implying degraded conditioning as exponents become closely spaced, analogous to an optical resolution limit (Theorem 4.5, Remark 4.6).
claims.evidence: Using an exact grid minimizer, the σ scaling (+1.024 vs +1.0) and 1/√N scaling (−0.616 vs −0.5) roughly match, but the Δ exponent (−1.345 vs predicted −2.0) and c_min exponent (−0.646 vs predicted −1.0) are substantially shallower. While a shallower slope does not violate an O() upper bound, the empirical evidence neither confirms nor clearly refutes the theorem's tightness as a scaling law.

claims.claim: Adding a constraint-aware loss term of the form sum_k |c_k| sin^2(mu_k * omega) to steer critical points toward physically valid exponents improves accuracy on the corner-singularity example from 14.6% error to 0.009% error (Theorem 4.8, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The specific 14.6%→0.009% improvement pair does not reproduce under any non-leaking boundary load. Under the eigenfunction arc (which the logbook argues leaks the exponent into the boundary), the constraint arm achieves ~0.009% but the naive 14.6% baseline is confounded. Under a clean constant load, the constraint term is shown to be necessary for recovery, but the specific numerical claim (14.6%→0.009%) is not reproduced.

claims.claim: Two exponents become distinguishable (resolvable) only when their separation Delta is at least 0.1; below this threshold they merge into an intermediate value, termed the Rayleigh limit for exponent resolution (Table 10, Section I.6, Remark I.1).
claims.evidence: The Rayleigh study with 7 seeds across δ∈{0.02,...,0.50} shows that at δ=0.10, K=2 resolves 7/7 with 2.25% mean error (paper: 2.2%), while δ=0.02 and 0.05 produce complete merging (0/14 resolved) to intermediate values (~0.509 at δ=0.02, matching paper's 0.51). The core threshold behavior at Δ≈0.1 is independently reproduced.

qy2100/repro-discovering-scaling-exponen.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous independent reproduction that confirms the Rayleigh resolution limit (Claim 6) and the 270° wedge numerical result (Claim 2), while falsifying the specific benchmark magnitudes (Claim 3) and the constraint ablation numbers (Claim 5), and leaving the theorem's scaling tightness inconclusive (Claim 4). The two-timescale method (Claim 1) is implemented as described and works for single-exponent recovery with confirmed stability.

nstp/repro-shuffling-aware-optimization-.paper_title: Shuffling-Aware Optimization for Private Vector Mean Estimation

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 establishes a minimax lower bound showing any unbiased protocol with shuffle index χ must incur worst-case mean squared error at least d·χ² for d-dimensional vector mean estimation (Section 3, Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: The lower bound Err1 >= d*chi_up^2 is checked only on the BMG mechanism family at d=2 across 4 parameter configs (all hold with positive slack), and a biased estimator is shown to violate it. This is a necessary consistency check on one mechanism, not a verification of the universal minimax lower bound over all unbiased protocols.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.7 shows that PrivUnit, which is optimal under local differential privacy (LDP), becomes suboptimal after shuffling in dimension d>1 (Section 3, Proposition 3.7).
claims.evidence: C(theta,d) is computed exactly via Beta-distribution quadrature for d up to 3000, with inf_theta C converging to 1.5705 (paper's pi/2=1.5708); the limiting curve C(tau)=Phi(tau)Q(tau)/phi(tau)^2 has its minimum exactly at pi/2, and an independent Monte-Carlo cross-check at d=100 confirms the exact computation.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 constructs the Blanket-Mixed Gaussian mechanism, achieving MSE = d·χ²·(1 + 3/2·χ^(-2/3) + O(χ^(-4/3))) as χ→∞, asymptotically matching the established lower bound (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The exact per-dimension risk is numerically minimized over gamma for chi up to 2e5; the log-log fit of the excess gives slope -0.6682 (paper -2/3, R^2=1.000) and coefficient 1.5006 (paper 3/2), with a falsification control (fixed gamma=0.5) collapsing the exponent to ~0.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows that in the high-privacy regime the optimal worst-case MSE satisfies d·σ² ≤ error ≤ d·σ²·(1+η(σ)) with η(σ)=O(σ^(-2/3)), nearly matching the central Gaussian mechanism (Section 3, Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: Theorem 3.3's high-privacy regime bound d*sigma^2 <= error <= d*sigma^2*(1+eta(sigma)) with eta=O(sigma^{-2/3}) is not directly addressed anywhere in the logbook; the logbook's claims cover Theorems 3.5, 4.1, Proposition 3.7, and Figure 3, but not Theorem 3.3.
