claims.claim: Numerical evaluations compare the proposed shuffle-index-based mechanisms against baseline shuffle-model mechanisms in terms of empirical MSE (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook compares shuffled-BMG RMSE against the central-Gaussian baseline at a single calibration point (n=1000, delta=1e-5, gap 3.72%) using theoretical privacy profiles rather than empirical MSE from actual shuffled protocols, and does not include other baseline shuffle-model mechanisms as the paper's Section 5 describes.

nstp/repro-shuffling-aware-optimization-.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification for Proposition 3.7 (pi/2 constant) and Theorem 4.1 (asymptotic exponent and coefficient), partial consistency checks for Theorem 3.5 on the BMG family only, and a simplified single-point numerical comparison for Section 5. Theorem 3.3 is not addressed at all.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 shows that small logit distance implies high linear representational similarity, yielding an explicit lower bound on mean Canonical Correlation Analysis (mCCA) between two models' representation spaces (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Numerical audit with 4000 samples confirms m_CCA ≥ 1 − d²_logit/(m μ_m) holds with 0/7 violations across a noise sweep (min slack +5×10⁻⁴), and a shuffle control breaks the bound (m_CCA drops 0.996→0.008 < 0.969), confirming the inequality genuinely certifies the paired linear relationship.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.9 shows logit distance upper-bounds the linear identifiability dissimilarity measure d_rep (defined in Definition 3.7), and Corollary 3.8 shows logit distance is zero if and only if this dissimilarity vanishes (Section 3.3-3.4).
claims.evidence: Exact Definition-3.7 d_rep computation (all pivots × subsets) confirms d_rep ≤ C·d_logit/σ_min with 0/6 violations (min slack +1.85); unit test shows d_rep=0 for linearly-equivalent models (d_logit=0), and shuffle control breaks the bound (d_rep jumps 0.011→1.98 > 0.294). The Corollary 3.8 'zero iff' direction is only implicitly supported via the bound and unit tests, not explicitly tested.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows KL divergence also bounds logit distance under a τ-lower-boundedness assumption, but the bound scales as τ^-1 and becomes practically vacuous for typical models (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Both inequalities of Theorem 3.3 hold with 0/4000 violations at τ=0.1 (lower bound tight, min slack +0.007); dropping the τ-assumption breaks the upper bound with 288/4000 violations and worst ratio 119,021, confirming the τ⁻¹ scaling makes the bound practically vacuous as stated.

claims.claim: On the Synth, CIFAR, and SUB distillation benchmarks, students trained with an L1/L2 logit-distance loss reduce d_rep by one to three orders of magnitude versus KL-distilled students, and improve mCCA by 0.42 on Synth, 0.25 on CIFAR, and 0.20 on SUB (Table 1, Table 2).
claims.evidence: Only the Synth benchmark is addressed, using a from-scratch spiral proxy with a small MLP (not the paper's pipeline). L1 d_rep=1.60 vs KL d_rep=7.03 shows ~4.4× reduction (not 1–3 orders of magnitude), and mCCA improvement is 0.017 (not 0.42). CIFAR and SUB benchmarks are entirely unaddressed.

claims.claim: On the SUB dataset, L1-logit-distilled students achieve 75% concept classification accuracy versus 6% for KL-distilled students (Section 5.1-5.2).
claims.evidence: The SUB dataset concept classification accuracy experiment (75% L1 vs 6% KL) is never addressed; the logbook explicitly states CIFAR/SUB are out of scope.

claims.claim: On a synthetic embedding visualization, the L1-distilled student preserves teacher geometry (d_rep≈1.3, mCCA≈0.99) while the KL-distilled student loses class structure (d_rep≈6.9, mCCA≈0.62) (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: On a from-scratch spiral proxy (small MLP, 3 seeds), L1 student d_rep=1.60/mCCA=0.997 approximates the paper's ~1.3/~0.99, and KL d_rep=7.03 approximates ~6.9, but KL mCCA=0.980 is far from the paper's ~0.62. Qualitative ordering (L1 preserves geometry better) holds robustly across all seeds, but key magnitudes and the full pipeline are not reproduced.

nstp/repro-logit-distance-bounds-represe.overall: The logbook provides rigorous numerical verification of the paper's three theoretical claims (Theorems 3.3, 3.4, 3.9) with exact computations, falsification controls, and 0 violations, but the empirical claims are only partially addressed: the Synth benchmark is run on a toy proxy with mismatched magnitudes, and CIFAR/SUB benchmarks and concept accuracy experiments are entirely missing.

bsenst/repro-evidential-reasoning-advanc.paper_title: Evidential Reasoning Advances Interpretable Real-World Disease Screening

claims.claim: EviScreen constructs dual knowledge banks from historical cases and retrieves regional evidence for retrospection-style interpretability during disease screening (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook only inspects code structure (FAISS indices, PatchCore-style retrieval) but never actually constructs or runs the dual knowledge banks. No experimental evidence is provided.

claims.claim: On the JSIEC dataset, EviScreen achieves an AUROC of 91.32% along with specificity of 72.92% at 95% recall (Spe@95%R) and 59.39% at 99% recall (Spe@99%R) (Table 1).
claims.evidence: No evaluation was run on JSIEC. The logbook confirms the evaluation script exists and metrics are implemented, but reports no numerical results whatsoever. The claimed AUROC of 91.32% is not confirmed or refuted.

claims.claim: EviScreen is evaluated across four disease-screening datasets (JSIEC, RIADD, CheXpert, and Derm12345) using AUROC, AP, Spe@95%R, Spe@99%R, Spe@100%R, and CSR metrics (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Only JSIEC and RIADD are present in the evaluation code; CheXpert and Derm12345 are noted as not supported. No evaluation was actually executed on any dataset. This is code inspection only.

claims.claim: A training-free variant uses contrastive retrieval to generate abnormality maps that provide localization interpretability without additional training (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook describes the training-free variant code in the reproduce_directly/ directory but never runs it. No abnormality maps were generated or evaluated. Code inspection only.

claims.claim: An ablation study isolates the contribution of the evidential reasoning components (evidence retrieval and evidence-aware reasoning) to overall screening performance (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook notes the framework supports separate Stage 1 and Stage 1+2 evaluation, but no ablation experiment was actually run. No comparison numbers are reported.

claims.claim: Performance scaling of the dual knowledge banks with respect to bank size is analyzed separately from the main results (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook states the scaling analysis was not reproduced and no experiments with varying bank sizes were conducted. No results.

bsenst/repro-evidential-reasoning-advanc.overall: This logbook is entirely a code inspection exercise with zero experimental runs, no datasets downloaded, no models trained, and no numerical results produced. It confirms the codebase structure exists but provides no experimental evidence for any claim.

nstp/repro-towards-fully-parameter-free-.paper_title: Towards Fully Parameter-Free Stochastic Optimization: Grid Search with Self-Bounding Analysis

claims.claim: Theorem 2 (Section 4) shows GRASP-NC achieves a near-optimal non-convex stochastic optimization convergence rate up to logarithmic factors, fully agnostic to smoothness, gap, and noise parameters (Theorem 2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Grasp-NC was reimplemented from scratch on a non-convex smooth objective (d=8, bounded noise Δ=0.5) with self-bounding step-size ranges derived from observable quantities only. Measured ||grad||² vs T log-log slope is -0.789 (R²=0.977) over T∈[2k,64k], satisfying the guaranteed O(T^{-1/2}) upper bound. The falsification control (single huge fixed step, no grid) yields slope -0.000, confirming the self-bounding grid mechanism is essential.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 and Theorem 4 (Section 5) show GRASP-C attains accelerated convergence combined with an ensemble error term in the convex smooth case (Option-I) and maintains universality for Holder-smooth convex objectives without requiring a lower-bound assumption on problem parameters (Option-II), unlike the prior state-of-the-art U-DoG method (Theorems 3-4, Table 1b).
claims.evidence: The Theorem 3 (Option-I) part is verified on a non-toy setup: deterministic regime slope -1.601 (near T^{-2} with log overhead) and noisy regime slope -0.368 (near T^{-1/2}), with a tiny-domain control showing no convergence. However, Theorem 4 (Option-II Hölder universality) is only tested on low-dimensional radial proxy objectives where ν=1 matches -2 but ν<1 instances converge faster than the worst-case exponent -(1+3ν)/2, so the exponent is not pinned. The 'unlike U-DoG' comparison is not addressed at all.

claims.claim: Self-bounding analysis (Section 3.1) derives parameter search ranges by comparing target convergence rates against trivial benchmark rates, guaranteeing non-vacuous bounds without any knowledge of smoothness, initial distance, or noise level.
claims.evidence: The self-bounding mechanism is embedded in the reimplemented algorithms (e.g., grasp_nc derives step-size ranges from g0, T, and user ε's without knowing true L, d0, or noise), and the algorithms converge, providing indirect support. However, the specific analytical claim about deriving parameter search ranges by comparing target convergence rates against trivial benchmark rates is not directly or separately tested — no experiment isolates the self-bounding analysis itself or verifies non-vacuity of the derived ranges as a standalone result.

claims.claim: Table 2 (Section 5.1) shows the ensemble/model-averaging guarantee achieves gap-dependent variance reduction of the form sqrt(V0/sqrt(M)) + (sigma_l+V1) log(N/delta)/M, improving over the uniform-averaging rate of sigma_l/sqrt(M).
claims.evidence: A Monte Carlo simulation with 40,000 trials directly tests the gap-dependent ensemble bound (Lemma 1): N=20 candidates, heteroscedastic bounded noise satisfying Var≤V0+V1·gap and |noise|≤σ, with δ=0.1. Empirical violation rate is 0.0000 (≤δ), minimum slack +0.60. The falsification control (dropping concentration terms) yields 10.9% violations, confirming the concentration terms are necessary and correctly sized.

claims.claim: Experiments (Tables 3-5, Section 6) show GRASP achieves a relative performance gap rho in [0.08, 0.23] compared to optimally hyperparameter-tuned baselines, while remaining robust to a reduced number of initial sampling rounds.
claims.evidence: The logbook uses synthetic logistic regression proxies instead of the paper's ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 setup. Convex proxy gives ρ=0.01 (paper: [0.08,0.16]); non-convex proxy gives ρ=0.70–1.65 (paper: [0.08,0.23]), far outside the claimed range. The real neural network experiment is not run, and robustness to reduced initial sampling rounds is not tested.

nstp/repro-towards-fully-parameter-free-.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous from-scratch NumPy reimplementation of the GRASP algorithms with falsification controls, verifying the non-convex convergence rate (Theorem 2) and the gap-dependent ensemble bound (Lemma 1/Table 2) on non-toy setups. The convex smooth Theorem 3 rate is also verified, but the Hölder universality (Theorem 4), the U-DoG comparison, the self-bounding analysis as a standalone claim, and the ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 experiments remain only partially addressed or toy.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 proves the original DeepSets aggregation (Equation 4) is discontinuous in the natural any-dimensional topology because the infinite sum can diverge when the inner function ρ decays arbitrarily slowly, so standard DeepSets fails to be universal (Theorem 4.2, Section 4.1.1).
claims.evidence: Single (X, ρ) pair with X_i = i^-0.8 demonstrates the divergence mechanism (raw partial sum grows 3.40 over 2nd half of N=4000 vs Eq.5 growth of 1.06e-5), but this is one concrete instance, not a general proof of discontinuity.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.9 proves standard message-passing GNNs fail any-dimensional universality because their pointwise nonlinearities are discontinuous in the cut metric, since a pointwise map is continuous with respect to the cut norm only if it is linear (Theorem 4.9, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Exact brute-force cut norm on Rademacher matrices at n∈{8,10,12,14}: linear map ψ(x)=2x scales ‖·‖_□ by exactly 2 (to 1e-9) confirming continuity, while nonlinear φ(x)=x² yields ‖φ(A_n)‖_□ = 1−1/n exactly at all n (0.875, 0.9, 0.9167, 0.9286), confirming discontinuity independent of ‖A_n‖_□. Closed-form matches are exact, not statistical.

claims.claim: A modified DeepSets-infinity architecture (Equation 5) that reweights terms by an ell_p norm factor is proven continuous and universal on ell_p(R^k) sequence space (Theorem 4.2, Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Zero-padding compatibility is exact (compat_error=0.0) and single-instance convergence on X_i=2^-i (k=2) reaches double precision by N=20, but only one compact-set instance is tested — not a general continuity or universality proof.

claims.claim: A measure-space variant DeepSets-bar-infinity (Equation 6), replacing the sum with a normalized integral under a growth condition, is proven universal on the Wasserstein space of probability measures (Theorem 4.5, Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo convergence of empirical measures with single ρ=(x², tanh(x)) shows error decreasing from 0.0759 to 0.00240 over n=200–200000, consistent with O(1/√n) scaling, but this is a statistical demonstration on one instance, not a proof of universality on Wasserstein space.

claims.claim: A homomorphism-density-basis architecture (Equations 9-10) is proven continuous and universal on graphon space with the cut metric, restoring universality for graph architectures (Theorem 4.9, Theorem 4.10, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Homomorphism-density expansion at m=3 on n=6 random graphon matches independent manual expansion to 1.33e-15 (machine precision), confirming the core algebraic identity the theorem relies on; i<j vs i≠j ambiguity resolved decisively (1.372 vs 2.114). The exact identity is the load-bearing mechanism, though only m=3 is tested.

claims.claim: A two-stage architecture combining a Gram-matrix map (Equation 12) with Invariant Graphon Networks (Equation 14) is proven universal on bounded point-cloud orbits under the group action (Theorem 4.12, Theorem 4.13, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Gram map invariance under O(k) holds to 2.22e-16, equivariance under S_n holds exactly (0.0), and boundary-case limit is exact; Lipschitz ratios stay bounded (0.198–0.259) as ε→0. The novel Gram-map component is verified exactly; IGN universality (Thm 4.13) is cited from prior work [46] and not independently re-derived.

RyeCatcher/repro-any-dimensional-invaria.overall: The logbook provides exact numerical verification of key algebraic mechanisms for Claims 2, 5, and 6 (closed-form matches at machine precision), while Claims 1, 3, and 4 are demonstrated on single small instances without general proofs. The reproduction is self-contained and honest about limitations but operates at small scale throughout.

RyeCatcher/repro-convergence-analysis-of.paper_title: Convergence Analysis of the Lion Optimizer in Centralized and Distributed Settings

claims.claim: Theorem 1 proves centralized Lion achieves a convergence rate of O(d^{1/2} T^{-1/4}) under standard smoothness, without requiring the coerciveness assumption used in prior analyses (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: On a synthetic NumPy objective, T-exponent measured -0.272 vs claimed -0.25 (within tolerance), but d-exponent measured 0.749 vs claimed 0.50 (failed). Negative control (smoothness violated) correctly flipped T-exponent to +0.50. Real runs on a simplified setup, partial confirmation only.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows that a variance-reduced Lion variant using STORM-based gradient estimators improves the rate to O(d^{1/2} T^{-1/3}) under an average smoothness assumption (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: T-exponent measured -0.288 vs claimed -0.333 (within tolerance) and correctly steeper than Claim 1, but d-exponent measured 0.869 vs claimed 0.50 (failed). Negative control showed degradation when average smoothness violated. Simplified synthetic setup, partial confirmation.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 establishes that distributed Lion across n heterogeneous nodes matches the centralized rate, converging as O(d^{1/2} (nT)^{-1/4}) (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: T-exponent measured -0.288 vs claimed -0.25 (within tolerance), but n-exponent measured -1.624 vs claimed -0.25 (badly failed) and d-exponent 0.739 vs 0.50 (failed). Cross-check at n=1 matched centralized to 4 decimals, but identified node-spacing confound invalidates n-scaling. Simplified setup, partial confirmation.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 shows that adding variance reduction to distributed Lion improves the distributed rate to O(d^{1/2} (nT)^{-1/3}) (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: T-exponent measured -0.301 vs claimed -0.333 (within tolerance), but n-exponent -1.024 vs -0.333 (failed) and d-exponent 0.899 vs 0.50 (failed). Cross-check at n=1 matched centralized VR to 4 decimals. Same node-spacing confound. Simplified setup, partial confirmation.

claims.claim: Theorem 5 gives a communication-efficient Lion variant with unbiased sign compression achieving either O(d^{1/2} T^{-1/2} + d n^{-1/2}) or O(n^{1/2} T^{-1} + d n^{-1/2}) depending on the learning-rate choice (Theorem 5).
claims.evidence: All three exponents failed: T-exponent -0.182 vs -0.50, n-exponent -1.953 vs -0.50, d-exponent 0.662 vs 1.00. No component of the claimed rate was confirmed, but acknowledged confounds (node-spacing, untuned chained min/max hyperparameter formulas) prevent calling this a falsification. Simplified setup, no confirmation.

claims.claim: Theorem 7 shows that combining bidirectional unbiased sign compression with variance reduction attains a communication-efficient rate of O(d^{1/4} T^{-1/4}), improving over the non-variance-reduced Theorem 6 rate (Theorem 7, Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: All exponents failed (T: -0.129 vs -0.25, d: 0.561 vs 0.25, n: -2.288 vs 0). Head-to-head comparison at T=6400 showed Thm7 (0.1149) did NOT beat Thm6 (0.1029), contradicting the paper's improvement claim, but on a toy setup with acknowledged confounds (untuned constants, node-spacing). Simplified setup, no confirmation and a contradicting head-to-head result.

RyeCatcher/repro-convergence-analysis-of.overall: The logbook runs real NumPy experiments on synthetic non-convex objectives with negative controls and cross-checks, confirming T-exponents for Claims 1-4 but failing to reproduce d-exponents and n-exponents across all claims, and failing all exponents for Claims 5-6. All experiments are on clearly simplified synthetic setups (CPU, <1 min, small controlled instances), so no claim reaches full verification or falsification at non-toy scale.

RyeCatcher/repro-ski-rental-with-distrib.paper_title: Ski Rental with Distributional Predictions of Unknown Quality

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows the algorithm achieves expected additive loss O(min(√b·max(EMD(p̂,p),1), b log b)), where EMD(p̂,p) is the Earth Mover's distance between the predicted and true distributions and b is the buy-ski-rental cost ratio (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: The logbook tests loss/min(√b·max(EMD,1), b log b) across b=16–4096 with 20 random trials per b, finding ratios ≤1.0 that do not grow with b (mildly falling from 1.0 to 0.956), directly supporting the O(min(√b·max(EMD,1), b log b)) scaling claim.

claims.claim: The algorithm attains consistency O(√b) when the prediction error (EMD) is 0 and robustness O(b log b) when the prediction is arbitrarily inaccurate, without needing to know the prediction error bound in advance (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Consistency ratio loss/√b at EMD=0 is ≈1.00 flat across b=16–4096; robustness ratio loss/(b log b) at large EMD falls from 0.090 to 0.0019 (bounded, shrinking); and inspect.signature confirms the algorithm takes only (phat, b) with no EMD or p parameter, addressing all three sub-claims.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 proves a matching lower bound showing no algorithm can achieve additive loss o(b)·EMD(p̂,p), establishing that the √b factor in Theorem 1 is necessary (Theorem 4, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: The paper's explicit two-instance adversarial construction from Appendix B was replicated exactly: min cost differences above 0.05 floor (0.219–0.254) stable across b=16–4096, and EMD(p₁,p₂) tracks 1/b closely (e.g., 0.000246 vs 1/b=0.000244 at b=4096), confirming the construction's properties that establish the lower bound.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a Pareto-optimal consistency-robustness tradeoff: any algorithm achieving O(√b) consistency must incur Ω(b log b) robustness (Theorem 6, Section 4)
claims.evidence: Reconstructing the Section-4 instance with a documented OCR transcription fix (T=100b instead of b/100), B/(b log b) stays in range 0.034–0.142 across b=64–4096 with shrinking increments (2.58×, 1.37×, 1.18×), consistent with Θ(b log b) rather than a faster trend, and robust loss equals B which is Ω(b log b) and non-vanishing.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 introduces a parameterized algorithm with expected cost c(ALG_p) ≤ min{(1+λ)(c(OPT_p)+B), (1+1/λ)c(OPT_p)}, allowing explicit interpolation between trusting the prediction and worst-case guarantees via λ ∈ [0,1] (Theorem 2, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Algorithm 2 was implemented from explicit pseudocode and tested across 75 (b, λ, trial) combinations with 0 violations of alg_cost ≤ min{(1+λ)(OPT+B), (1+1/λ)OPT}; λ=0 matches Algorithm 1 exactly and λ=1 with concentrated p̂ clamps to K+1=b recovering the classical buy-at-day-b policy.

RyeCatcher/repro-ski-rental-with-distrib.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all five theoretical claims through exact-arithmetic implementations of the paper's algorithms and proof constructions, tested across b=16–4096 with appropriate scaling checks. While these are theoretical claims that numerical experiments can only support rather than prove, the scaling tests, zero bound violations, and replication of the paper's own adversarial constructions constitute faithful non-toy verification.

RyeCatcher/repro-non-uniform-noise-to-si.paper_title: Non-Uniform Noise-to-Signal Ratio in the REINFORCE Policy-Gradient Estimator

claims.claim: For finite-horizon linear-quadratic systems with Gaussian policies, the noise-to-signal ratio of the multi-step REINFORCE estimator can be computed exactly in closed form via lifted dynamics (Theorem 5, Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: Lifting algebra and mean-gradient recursion verified to machine precision (rel err 0.0 and 7.9e-10), but the full second-moment/NSR closed-form decomposition (the core of Theorem 5) was never transcribed; NSR was only checked via MC consistency on a small scalar system.

claims.claim: The NSR landscape is highly non-uniform: as the policy approaches the optimal deterministic policy (Σ→0, per Corollary 6), the NSR does not vanish uniformly and can blow up, as demonstrated for a double-integrator system (Figure 1, Section 2.3).
claims.evidence: Theorem 3's exact closed-form second moments independently implemented and matched MC to 0.46%; blow-up sweep on the paper's double-integrator showed NSR rising 4656→4.04e7 with fitted log-log slope -1.9984 (theory -2); negative control (σ₀→0 at fixed σ) correctly showed monotone decrease, confirming directional prediction.

claims.claim: Variance of the multi-step REINFORCE estimator grows exponentially with the control horizon when the closed-loop dynamics are unstable, i.e., when the spectral radius ρ(F)>1 (Theorem 8, Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: Theorem 9 sandwich held exactly (15/15 cases) and MC variance growth ratios showed correct ordering (12.4x/1197x/117363x for stable/marginal/unstable), but only scalar n=m=1 systems were tested and Theorem 8's exact bound formula was not transcribed.

claims.claim: A general upper bound on REINFORCE gradient-estimator variance is derived for generic nonlinear dynamics with expressive neural-network policies (Theorem 10, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Bound held with comfortable margin on 3 configs (LHS/RHS ratio 0.083–0.096), but the policy was a 2-parameter toy (not an expressive neural network) and both sides were MC estimates of heavy-tailed 4th moments rather than exact computations.

claims.claim: The analysis is extended from linear to polynomial systems and polynomial feedback policies via a moment-evaluation approach (Proposition 9, Section 3).
claims.evidence: REINFORCE score-function unbiasedness confirmed on the paper's polynomial system (4.5% max relative error vs CRN finite-difference), but the exact symbolic moment-evaluation approach—the actual novelty of Proposition 9—was never implemented.

RyeCatcher/repro-non-uniform-noise-to-si.overall: The logbook provides a strong independent verification of Claim 2's NSR blow-up phenomenon on the paper's own double-integrator example, including a correctly-firing negative control. The remaining four claims were addressed only partially on simplified scalar or small-scale setups, with the core closed-form or exact-moment components left unimplemented.

RyeCatcher/repro-model-free-robust-avera.paper_title: Model-Free Robust Average-Reward Reinforcement Learning with Sample Complexity Analysis

claims.claim: Robust Halpern Iteration (RHI) achieves a sample complexity of tilde-O(S A H^2 / epsilon^2) for computing an epsilon-optimal robust policy in model-free robust average-reward RL, without requiring prior knowledge of the robust bias span H (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: RHI was tested on S=3 tabular MDPs with only 3 epsilon values; sub-optimality was trivially 0.0 at every epsilon (optimal policy found immediately), and H was replaced by a fixed constant H_hat=2.0. Fitted exponent 2.31 from 3 data points is too weak to confirm the claimed O(1/epsilon^2) scaling on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: The reduction-to-discounted-MDP approach analyzed in the paper requires knowledge of the bias span H and yields a worse sample complexity of tilde-O(S A H^2 / epsilon^4) (Section 4, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook found no 'epsilon^-4' string in any arXiv version and the paper's own Table 1 lists the reduction baseline at O(SAH^2/epsilon^2), but the logbook explicitly acknowledges it could not access the camera-ready (which the claims are numbered against), so it cannot exclude that the camera-ready contains a derivation the arXiv versions omit.

claims.claim: Lemma 5.1 bounds the sub-optimality of a greedy policy relative to Q by the span seminorm of the residual, 0 <= g*_P - g^pi_P(s) <= Sp(T_P(Q) - Q) (Section 5, Lemma 5.1).
claims.evidence: The span-seminorm bound held on all 20 seeds with worst-case RHS-LHS margin 1.49 (never violated), and the negative control—breaking irreducibility with a disconnected 2-state MDP—produced a visible failure (residual span 0.10 after 20k iterations vs <1e-11 on well-posed instances), confirming the test is meaningful.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 establishes that RHI's iterates converge exactly, with Sp(T_P(Q_k) - Q_k) approaching 0 as k goes to infinity (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: On S=3 instances, residual span only reached 0.0090 after 200 iterations (not near zero), sub-optimality was trivially 0.0 from k=1 onward, and the negative control (beta_k=1, no anchoring) also converged even faster (3e-14), meaning the test did not discriminate Halpern anchoring from plain fixed-point iteration.

claims.claim: Instead of a multi-level Monte Carlo estimator (noted to induce unbounded sample complexity in this setting), RHI uses a recursive sampling scheme that estimates successive differences T_P(Q_k) - T_P(Q_{k-1}) (Section 5, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Direct arithmetic shows standard MLMC expected cost grows linearly with level cap ({258, 500, 1000, 2000, 4000} for caps {5,10,20,40,80}), confirming unboundedness, and inspection of Algorithm 1 confirms RHI's m_k is a deterministic closed-form function of (k, span(d_k), epsilon) with no random stopping rule.

claims.claim: The paper's sample complexity result is claimed to be the first finite-sample guarantee for model-free robust average-reward MDPs, covering both contamination and l_p-norm uncertainty sets (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: Both contamination and TV uncertainty-set families reached sub-optimality 0.0 at epsilon in {0.2, 0.1} on small S=3 instances, but the 'first finite-sample guarantee' novelty/priority claim is inherently unverifiable by code, and the scale is too small to constitute a non-toy reproduction.

RyeCatcher/repro-model-free-robust-avera.overall: The logbook provides meaningful numerical verification of the span-seminorm sub-optimality bound (Claim 3) with a firing negative control, and confirms the structural MLMC-vs-recursive-sampling claim (Claim 5) by direct calculation. However, most experimental checks run on trivially small S=3 instances where the optimal policy is found immediately, limiting their ability to test complexity scaling or convergence behavior, and the camera-ready version referenced by the claims was never obtained.

RyeCatcher/repro-gradient-flow-through-d.paper_title: Gradient Flow Through Diagram Expansions: Learning Regimes and Explicit Solutions

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 shows that for targets expressible as polynomials in parameters and Kronecker deltas, the coefficients of the formal power series expansion of the loss's time derivatives are themselves polynomials in the width H, the parameterization exponent p, and the initialization variance sigma^2 (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Only s=0 and s=1 terms tested (not all s), on small H∈{4..32} with ASYM model f=UV^T; s=0 exact-vs-MC error 0.39% and s=1 polynomial-fit residual 0.55% are real checks of polynomial structure but at drastically reduced scope.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 characterizes the leading and Pareto-optimal terms of the loss expansion for identity-tensor targets, organizing gradient-flow learning regimes into a polygon structure defined by scaling conditions on H, p, and sigma^2 (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Only one polygon vertex (point A) and one algebraic edge-count identity checked; edge-count identity matched exactly over 2000 trials and tail slope -1.4993 vs predicted -1.5, but the full Pareto polygon classification was not tested.

claims.claim: An NTK-like regime, in which features do not evolve during training, appears only at points/edges B-C of the Pareto polygon in the asymmetric parameterization case, while Proposition 8.2 proves the NTK kernel stays static throughout training in the symmetric matrix case (nu=2), explaining the absence of an NTK limit there (Section 4, Proposition 8.2).
claims.evidence: SYM nu=2 joint-motion correlation 0.99999 and ASYM diagonal stabilization tested, but only one direction of the Prop 8.2 IFF was checked, on a 27×27 matrix with a corrected formula exponent; partial coverage of a compound claim.

claims.claim: Mean-field, feature-evolving regimes require the initialization variance to scale as sigma^2 proportional to 1/H (symmetric case) or sigma^2 proportional to 1/H^(2/nu) (asymmetric case), corresponding to edges B-E and C-D of the Pareto polygon respectively (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Symmetric case (sigma^2=c/H) well-tested with negative control: correct exponent converges to 15.58 vs target 15.0 (3.9% gap), wrong exponent diverges 42.8×, but the asymmetric case (sigma^2~1/H^(2/nu)) was never tested, so only half the compound claim is addressed.

claims.claim: For the canonical polyadic (symmetric, nu=2) identity-tensor target, Section 9 derives a complete closed-form solution to the gradient flow (Equations 19-20), valid across all parameter scalings.
claims.evidence: t=0 relative error 2.86% (p=30) and long-time limits match exactly for H=96,48,24, but intermediate-time values are off by ~2× at H=96 and the formula required algebraic rewriting due to cancellation; partial validation of a 'complete' closed-form claim.

claims.claim: For the nu=4 symmetric case, Section 10 derives a gradient-ascent solution identifying convergent low-noise and divergent high-noise regimes separated by an explicit threshold given in Equation 23.
claims.evidence: Tested at p=H=6 with only 3 seeds per regime; low-noise 0/3 blew up and high-noise 3/3 blew up, but the threshold formula required dropping a sign (flagged as ambiguous transcription), and the scale is far below any meaningful reproduction.

RyeCatcher/repro-gradient-flow-through-d.overall: This logbook provides small-scale numerical sanity checks for all six theoretical claims using CPU-only NumPy/SciPy computations, with honest reporting of limitations and a useful negative control on Claim 4. However, every claim is tested at substantially reduced scope—partial polynomial orders, single polygon vertices, one direction of equivalences, only the symmetric case of compound claims, or tiny model sizes—so none achieves full verification.

RyeCatcher/repro-online-packet-schedulin.paper_title: Online Packet Scheduling with Deadlines and Learning

claims.claim: For the deterministic algorithm EDF_Φ^L in 2- and 3-bounded K-OPSD, the Φ-regret upper bound is Õ(√(KT)), matching sleeping-bandit-style rates (Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: Small-scale setup (K=3, T≤2000, 20 seeds) with stochastic arrivals; alpha=1 regret slope 0.599 is sub-linear, but the claimed Φ-regret was trivially negative at this scale, so the actual claimed quantity was not meaningfully tested.

claims.claim: The deterministic algorithm ALG^θ achieves competitive ratio θ_K in [√2, Φ) for finite K packet types, breaking the classical golden-ratio Φ = (1+√5)/2 competitive-ratio barrier for 2-bounded deadline instances (Proposition 4.1).
claims.evidence: Adversarial search via differential_evolution over 2-bounded instances with exact offline_opt ground truth, K∈{2,3,4,5}; no instance exceeded θ_K, and K=2 search found ratio 1.4134 vs θ_2=1.41421 (within 0.06%), directly testing the worst-case competitive ratio claim.

claims.claim: The learning variant ALG^θ,U attains a θ_K-regret upper bound of Õ(√(KT)), which is shown to be nearly tight against a matching Ω(√T) lower bound (Theorem 4.2, Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Small-scale setup (K=3, T≤2000) showed sub-linear alpha=1 regret (slope 0.355) with a working negative control (random policy slope 1.172), but θ_K-regret was trivially negative and the Ω(√T) lower bound (Thm 4.3) was not assessed at all.

claims.claim: The randomized algorithm ALG^R2 for 2-bounded instances achieves a 5/4-regret bound of Õ(√(KT)) (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: Small-scale setup (T≤2000) measured alpha=1 regret slope 1.061, which exceeds the sub-linear pass criterion and appears closer to linear; the logbook attributes this to burn-in dominating the budget, but the result neither confirms nor cleanly falsifies the Õ(√(KT)) claim at this scale.

claims.claim: The randomized algorithm ALG^Rs for s-bounded (unbounded slackness) instances achieves an e/(e-1)-regret bound of Õ(√(KT)) (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Small-scale setup (K=3, T≤2000, 20 seeds) measured alpha=1 regret slope 0.549, close to √T, but the scale is too small to confirm the asymptotic e/(e-1)-regret bound and the claimed quantity itself was not directly tested.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 establishes that sleeping bandits are a special case of 1-bounded K-OPSD, formally connecting the packet scheduling model to the multi-armed bandit framework (Section 2.2, Lemma 2.1).
claims.evidence: Exact identity check with two independently-coded execution paths (K-OPSD engine vs sleeping-bandit engine), same RNG stream and UCB policy, K=5, T=500, 5 seeds, produced bit-identical scheduled-type sequences (max_gain_diff=0.0), confirming the formal reduction.

RyeCatcher/repro-online-packet-schedulin.overall: The logbook provides a genuine self-contained implementation with exact offline computation and negative controls, but the scale is very small (T≤2000, K≤5, 20 seeds) which limits its ability to test asymptotic regret claims. Two structural claims (competitive ratio bound and sleeping-bandit reduction) are verified via exact computation and identity checks, while the four regret-rate claims are only toy-level due to small scale and trivially-satisfied claimed quantities.

RyeCatcher/repro-the-implicit-bias-of-ad.paper_title: The Implicit Bias of Adam and Muon on Smooth Homogeneous Neural Networks

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 proves that any limit point of the normalized parameter trajectory θₜ/‖θₜ‖ under normalized steepest descent is the direction of a KKT point of the corresponding max-margin problem (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Tested only the l2-norm instance of a general-norm theorem on linear (L=1) synthetic data at finite T; measured cos=0.99754 and kkt_rel=0.00000, which is a clean but simplified proxy for the asymptotic KKT-convergence claim.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 extends the margin-maximization convergence result to momentum steepest descent under decaying learning rates, using an Approximate Steepest Descent framework introduced in Definition 5.1 (Theorem 3.3, Definition 5.1).
claims.evidence: Same simplified setup as Claim 1 (l2 instance, linear data, finite T) with momentum c1=1.0; measured cos=0.99904, kkt_rel=0.00000, r_tail_mean=1.0000, but this is a small-scale proxy for an asymptotic limit-point theorem.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.4 shows Muon, applied simultaneously across weight matrices, is a special case of normalized momentum steepest descent with respect to the matrix spectral norm ‖·‖_msp (Corollary 3.4).
claims.evidence: The Muon SVD orthogonalization step was shown to equal argmin over the spectral-norm ball to machine precision (max relative error 0.00000 across 20 random 3x6 momentum matrices), directly confirming the algebraic identity the claim asserts.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.5 shows Muon-Signum hybrid algorithms exhibit margin maximization with respect to the max of the spectral norm and the ℓ∞ norm (Corollary 3.5).
claims.evidence: Duality gap was exactly zero (8.88e-16) and KKT residual was 0.01557 on a converged point, but the claim asserts asymptotic margin maximization and the experiment uses linear data at finite T—a simplified proxy.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.6 shows Adam without a stability constant exhibits implicit bias toward ℓ∞-margin maximization under a decaying learning rate regime when c₁ ≥ c₂ (Theorem 3.6).
claims.evidence: Adam trajectory on linear (L=1) synthetic data at finite T with c1=1.0/c2=0.5 yielded cos=0.99853 and kkt_rel=0.00000, but this is a small-scale finite-T proxy for an asymptotic implicit-bias theorem.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes that under normalized steepest descent with a learning rate schedule satisfying ∫₀^∞ η(t)dt = ∞, the soft margin γ̃(θₜ) increases monotonically (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Soft margin was computed at 398 checkpoints on the l2-NSD linear-data trajectory with worst single-step drop of -3.9e-5 (consistent with Euler noise), but the setup is a simplified L=1 linear instance rather than a general smooth homogeneous network.

RyeCatcher/repro-the-implicit-bias-of-ad.overall: The logbook provides clean numerical evidence on small linear (L=1) synthetic setups for all six theoretical claims, with one exact algebraic identity (Claim 3) verified at machine precision. The remaining five claims are tested on simplified proxy setups that, while producing results consistent with the theorems, do not constitute full reproductions at the paper's intended scope.

RyeCatcher/repro-lower-bounds-for-frank-.paper_title: Lower Bounds for Frank-Wolfe on Strongly Convex Sets

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a constructive Omega(1/sqrt(epsilon)) lower bound on the number of iterations for Frank-Wolfe with short steps or exact line search when both the objective and the constraint set are smooth and strongly convex (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: A 747-step backward-constructed trajectory shows strictly monotone s_t (0 breaks), zero eq-(12) violations, zero Prop-3 upper-bound violations, and a log-log slope of -0.982 (within [-1.15,-0.85]), confirming r_t=Theta(1/t); a negative control with 6 generic starting points breaks monotonicity within 0-3 steps.

claims.claim: The lower-bound construction uses the specific instance of minimizing f(x) = ||x-p||_2^2 over the Euclidean unit ball B_1(0) with the unconstrained minimizer p on the boundary (||p||=1), showing this hard instance matches the known O(1/sqrt(epsilon)) upper bound of Garber et al. (2015) (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: Upper-bound constant (1.0) and lower-bound constant (8/3) yield a ratio range [1.285, 2.656] with max/min=2.07<5 over the full horizon, confirming both bounds share the same Theta(1/t) asymptotic order.

claims.claim: The lower bound is established via a 'backward reconstruction' technique that builds worst-case trajectories by working backward from terminal iterates, producing precise sequences over horizons of 10,000+ iterations (Section on Backward Reconstruction Strategy).
claims.evidence: Round-trip accuracy (2.79e-13) and graded precision-sensitivity (break at steps 44/482/747 for float64/150-digit/400-digit) confirm the backward-reconstruction mechanism, but the horizon is ~750, not the claimed 10,000+; the logbook itself acknowledges this is a 'toy-scale substitute' for the specific 10,000-iteration figure.

claims.claim: The analysis reduces the dynamics to a two-dimensional invariant subspace parametrized by residual magnitude r and contraction factor s, revealing stable phases of monotonically increasing contraction followed by intermittent 'jumps' that explain the convergence stalling behavior (Section on Dynamical Analysis).
claims.evidence: The (r,s) forward map matches ground-truth full-vector FW simulation to 5.17e-11 relative error over 20 seeds, and Proposition 5's jump-characterization inequalities hold with 0 failures across 35 and 31 triggering instances.

claims.claim: The result shows strong convexity of the constraint set alone cannot yield convergence rates uniformly faster than O(1/sqrt(epsilon)), and this conclusion holds dimension-independently and extends to ellipsoidal constraints via affine invariance (Theorem 6, Implications).
claims.evidence: Dimension independence confirmed by embedding the same state into R^5 and R^20 (max abs error 1.91e-12); ellipsoid affine invariance confirmed with a fixed 2x2 matrix A showing y_t=Ax_t to 1.55e-11 and matching primal gap to 6.29e-14.

RyeCatcher/repro-lower-bounds-for-frank-.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting the core mathematical claims—rate verification, bound matching, 2D reduction, and affine invariance—using a self-contained NumPy/SciPy instrument with negative controls. The main limitation is that horizons are ~750 rather than the paper's 10,000+, making Claim 3's specific scale assertion only toy-verified.

RyeCatcher/repro-on-the-computational-co.paper_title: On the Computational Complexity of Performative Prediction

claims.claim: Theorem 1.2 (restated as Theorem 3.4) proves that computing an ε-performatively stable point is PPAD-complete even when ρ = Lβ/α ≤ 1 + O(ε), with the explicit constant ε′ = 0.088/6 ≈ 0.0147 (Section 1.1, Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies the algebraic identity (residual 7.2e-16) and Lipschitz bound ρ ≤ 1+ε/ε' on 20 small random/deterministic instances with a working negative control, but explicitly states it does NOT reproduce PPAD-completeness itself, which rests on cited external results (Deligkas et al. 2024). Only proof-component bookkeeping is checked, not the hardness claim.

claims.claim: This PPAD-hardness persists in the simple setting where the loss is quadratic, ℓ(x;z) = ½||x−z||², and the distribution shift D(x) is given by an affine map g(x) (Section 3.1, Equation 2-3, Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirms the quadratic loss has identical gradients to the canonical form (residual 0.0) and α=β=1 exactly, but this is a small-scale algebraic equivalence check; the PPAD-hardness claim itself is inherited from Claim 1 and not independently reproduced.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 shows a phase transition to tractability: when ρ ≤ 1 + O_ε(ε^4), an ε-performatively stable point can be computed in poly(d, log(1/ε)) time via an ellipsoid-method algorithm exploiting hypomonotonicity (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: A simplified single-run ellipsoid method (not the full EVI-averaging algorithm) is tested on dimensions d=2–32, showing polynomial scaling (slope ~1.91) and linear-in-log(1/tol) behavior, but the ε^{1/4}-precision mechanism is explicitly untested and d=32 hit the iteration cap before convergence.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.7 establishes an unconditional information-theoretic lower bound: any algorithm requires 2^Ω(d) expected-risk-minimization (ERM) queries to find an ε-performatively stable point even when ρ ≤ 1 + O_ε(ε), and even for constant ε (Section 3.1, Corollary 3.7).
claims.evidence: The logbook uses a simplified 'hidden needle in m^d-cell grid' adversary (not the paper's Hirsch et al. 1989 Sperner-triangulation construction), with a different exponent (d vs d−2), tested only for d=2–6. The Prop. 3.2 bookkeeping identity is verified exactly, but the core lower-bound construction is not the paper's own.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.12 extends PPAD-hardness of performative stability from the hypercube constraint set to any well-bounded general convex constraint set (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.12, Definition 3.11).
claims.evidence: Only the outer bookkeeping reduction (Corollary 3.13) is verified with a generic affine F stand-in (identity residual 1.1e-15); the actual PPAD-hardness content of Theorem 3.12 — the 2D-Sperner arithmetic circuit construction — is explicitly stated as out of scope and not reconstructed.

claims.claim: For the special case of strategic classification, Theorem 4.4 shows that computing a local optimum of the performative risk under single-label updates is PLS-hard, complementing prior NP-hardness results for global performative optimality (Abstract, Section 1.1, Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: The full LocalMaxCut→strategic-classification reduction gadget is implemented exactly (population, distribution weights, symmetric metric, exact best-response, single-flip local search), and bidirectional solution correspondence is verified against an independent graph-only local-max-cut computation on 20 random graphs (20/20 both directions), with a bug caught and fixed during the audit and a working negative control.

RyeCatcher/repro-on-the-computational-co.overall: The logbook provides careful, transparent component-level verification of theoretical proof steps (algebraic identities, Lipschitz bounds, reduction gadgets) with negative controls, but for 5 of 6 claims the core complexity-theoretic hardness/lower-bound content is either taken from cited external results or replaced by simplified proxy constructions. Only Claim 6 implements the paper's actual reduction construction and verifies bidirectional solution correspondence with independent ground truth.

RyeCatcher/repro-unifying-low-dimensiona.paper_title: Unifying Low Dimensional Spectra in Deep Learning

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves the layer-wise Hessian in the L-deep linear unconstrained features model (UFM) has rank K^2 with all non-zero eigenvalues equal, analytically reproducing the bulk-outlier Hessian spectrum reported in prior empirical studies (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Finite-difference Hessian on 20 random (K,L,d,n,λ) architectures shows relative eigenvalue spread 3.2e-10 and rank K² correct in 20/20, with negative control at a random point showing spread 3.55 — concrete numerical verification of the theorem's structural prediction.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 decomposes the Gauss-Newton/Fisher Information component into three terms: G_within (rank 0), G_cross (rank K(K-1), producing the mini-bulk of eigenvalues), and G_class (rank K, producing the main outliers), mirroring Papyan's empirical knockout experiments (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Decomposition built from raw definitions (not assuming DNC) on 20 seeds shows ||G_within||=9.7e-33, rank(G_class)=K and rank(G_cross)=K(K-1) in 20/20, self-consistency error 9.5e-16, and G_l matching finite-diff Hessian to 2.0e-10; negative control shows ||G_within||=0.456.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 shows the aggregated gradient update is a sum over only K of the K^2 possible eigenvector directions, each with equal coefficient beta^(l+1)/K, explaining the observed gradient alignment with a low-dimensional subspace (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Finite-diff data-loss gradient projected onto K² basis across 20 seeds shows diagonal coefficient spread 3.0e-10, off-diagonal/diagonal ratio 1.5e-10, and residual fraction 1.8e-8; however, the negative control was not numerically measured, only inferred.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 proves the Gram matrix of the optimal weights, W_l*^T W_l*, has rank K with eigenvalues proportional to the squared norms of the class-mean features, giving a closed-form account of the low-rank weight structure (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: Gram matrix rank K confirmed in 20/20 seeds with eigenvalue spread 5.6e-12; negative control with random W_l shows rank 4 and spread 0.94, providing clear discrimination.

claims.claim: For a deep linear UFM with K=3 classes, numerical experiments show K^2=9 Hessian outliers separating from the bulk and converging to equal eigenvalues over training, with eigenvector alignment metric f_cc' rising from about 0.2 to 1.0 (Figures 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: Very small-scale setup (K=3, L=3, d=3, n=4) shows eigenvalue CV decreasing from 2.46 to 0.00037 and f_align rising from 0.806 to 1.0, but the starting alignment (0.806) does not match the claimed ~0.2, and the scale is far below typical UFM experiments.

claims.claim: In the non-linear (ReLU) Deep UFM, K^2=9 Hessian outliers separate but do not fully converge to equal values, and the gradient has K non-zero coefficients that remain unequal, unlike the linear case (Figure 9, Table 2).
claims.evidence: At the same small scale (K=3, d=3, 8000 steps), only 2 of the claimed 9 outliers separate from the bulk rather than all 9, directly contradicting the specific 'K²=9 Hessian outliers separate' sub-claim; the qualitative contrast with the linear case (eig_cv=4.50 vs 0.002) is confirmed but the specific 9-outlier structure is not reproduced.

RyeCatcher/repro-unifying-low-dimensiona.overall: The logbook provides rigorous numerical verification of the four analytical theorem claims (4.1–4.4) using finite-difference Hessians, multiple seeds, and negative controls on small UFM instances. The two experimental claims (5–6) are addressed only at very small scale (d=3, n=4), with claim 6 partially contradicting the paper's specific 9-outlier prediction.

RyeCatcher/repro-understanding-behavior-.paper_title: Understanding Behavior Cloning with Action Quantization

claims.claim: Behavior cloning with quantized actions and log-loss is proven to achieve sample complexity matching known lower bounds, up to the quantization error term (Theorem 2, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Closed-form comparison of transcribed Theorem 2/3 and Theorem 8/9 formulas over 200 randomized draws shows statistical n-exponents match to 2.2e-16 error, and the quantization H-exponent asymmetry (Thm2/3 ~1.963 vs lower bounds 1.0) is confirmed numerically, with a negative control (wrong n^-1/4 exponent) correctly rejected.

claims.claim: Under Probabilistic Incremental Input-to-State Stability (P-IISS) of the dynamics and Relaxed Total Variation Continuity (RTVC) of the expert policy, the regret bound has only polynomial (not exponential) dependence on the horizon H with respect to quantization error epsilon_q (Theorem 3, Definition 3, Definition 4, Section 3.1-3.2).
claims.evidence: Direct numerical evaluation of the transcribed Theorem 3 formula across 200 random linear-modulus draws yields worst-case log-log slope 1.98 (R^2 0.993), confirming polynomial (degree ~2) H-dependence, while exponential fit R^2 is only 0.786; negative control with synthetic 2^H correctly flagged as exponential.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 shows that without a smoothness assumption on the quantizer, non-smooth quantizers can incur regret of order H*Omega(1) even though their in-distribution one-step error is only O(epsilon_q) (Theorem 6, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Monte-Carlo simulation of the paper's own worked example (A=0.2, B=0.3, k=1, d=0.6, arctan expert, H=40, 4000 trajectories/cell, 10 seeds) shows in-distribution quant error shrinking (slope 0.55, R^2 0.946) while deployed regret stays flat at [11.3, 12.8] (shrink ratio 0.916); binning negative control shrinks correctly (ratio 0.036).

claims.claim: Theorem 7 proves that model-based data augmentation improves the horizon dependence to H*[sqrt(log|Pi|/n) + epsilon_q] without requiring the policy smoothness (RTVC) assumption (Theorem 7, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Only the idealized n→∞ realizable limit of Algorithm 1 was implemented on the trap instance (augmented regret ratio 0.187 vs naive 0.943); finite-sample MLE training of pihat and the transition model (the sqrt(log|Pi|/n) piece) was explicitly not implemented, making this a reduced-scope demonstration.

claims.claim: Information-theoretic lower bounds (Theorems 8-9) establish that regret must scale at least as H*(1/n + epsilon_q) for deterministic experts and H*(sqrt(1/n) + epsilon_q) for stochastic experts, matching the achievable upper bounds (Section 5, Theorems 8-9).
claims.evidence: The paper's specific tabular MDP constructions for Theorems 8-9 were not reconstructible from the text; instead, the underlying classical mechanisms (exact Le Cam two-point minimax risk showing n-independence at boundary gap, and exact Lipschitz-quantization floor ratio 0.5) were verified on abstract instances, not the paper's own constructions.

claims.claim: Empirically, binning quantizers are shown to preserve policy smoothness better than learned quantizers, while deterministic experts more often violate the RTVC requirement needed for the sharp regret bound (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: No empirical section exists in the paper to reproduce against; the logbook constructed synthetic Lipschitz experts and a synthetic 'learned' quantizer (binning + one O(eps_q)-width trap), showing binning O(1)-jump rate 0% vs learned-trap 100% and deterministic TVC violation 100% vs Gaussian-smoothed 0% across 200 seeds — a qualitative demonstration on proxy instances.

RyeCatcher/repro-understanding-behavior-.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical and simulation-based checks for all six claims, with negative controls and honest reporting of protocol deltas. Three claims (1, 2, 3) are verified with direct formula evaluation or simulation of the paper's own examples, while three claims (4, 5, 6) are addressed only on simplified or proxy setups due to missing finite-sample training, unreconstructible constructions, or absence of an empirical section.

Srishti280992/repro-softjax-softtorch-em.paper_title: SoftJAX & SoftTorch: Empowering Automatic Differentiation Libraries with Informative Gradients

claims.claim: SoftJAX and SoftTorch provide differentiable soft surrogates for hard primitives including thresholding (sign, abs, round, ReLU, clip via Heaviside relaxations), Boolean/fuzzy logic operators, discrete indexing (SoftIndex), and sorting/ranking (Sections 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: A local audit exercised sign, abs, round, heaviside, relu, clip, logical_and/or/xor/any/all, sj.argmax, sj.dynamic_index_in_dim, and six sort/rank methods, confirming finite gradients on the soft path and zero/undefined gradients on the hard path across all operator groups.

claims.claim: The libraries identify an 'STE pitfall' where applying straight-through estimation separately to each factor of a multiplicative composite operation causes gradients to vanish, and show this is avoided by applying STE to the composite function as a whole (Section 2, Equation 1).
claims.evidence: A scaled audit over 8 multiplicative composites with 5,000 scalar points each (40,000 gradient evaluations) showed naive per-factor STE has 15.625% exact zero-gradient regions while composite STE wrapper has 0% zero-gradient regions, directly demonstrating the pitfall and its remedy.

claims.claim: Four families of differentiable sort/rank operators are implemented: optimal-transport-based, unit-simplex-projection-based (SoftSort, NeuralSort), permutahedron-projection-based (FastSoftSort, and a novel entropy-regularized SmoothSort variant), and sorting-network-based (Sections 4.1-4.4).
claims.evidence: Six concrete methods were exercised and differentiated: ot (optimal transport), softsort and neuralsort (unit simplex projection), fast_soft_sort and smooth_sort (permutahedron projection), and sorting_network, all producing monotone sorted outputs with finite gradients, directly mapping to the four claimed families including the novel smooth_sort variant.

claims.claim: FastSoftSort achieves the lowest memory footprint (~420KB) among benchmarked soft-sorting methods at n=4096, while the sorting-network approach is fastest at ~1.0ms (3.8x the hard baseline), versus ~16ms for SoftSort and ~37ms for NeuralSort (Section 5, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: The paper's own benchmark.py was rerun on an H200 GPU at n=4096: fast_soft_sort had the lowest smooth-method memory at 436.1 KB (close to the claimed ~420 KB), sorting_network had the fastest smooth gradient at 0.371 ms (3.19x hard vs claimed 3.8x), and the ordering sorting_network < softsort < neuralsort was preserved, with absolute timings differing due to hardware.

claims.claim: A case study applies SoftJAX operators (sj.argmax, sj.dynamic_index_in_dim) to soften the manifold-point-selection step of MuJoCo XLA's collision detection pipeline, enabling gradient flow through a previously non-differentiable physics operation (Appendix B).
claims.evidence: A real mujoco-mjx box-on-plane model was built and mjx.forward() produced 4 penetrating contacts; the installed hard MJX _manifold_points selector yielded gradient norm 0.0 while the SoftJAX relaxation using sj.argmax and sj.dynamic_index_in_dim yielded gradient norm 216.52 with finite gradients distributed to non-selected vertices, demonstrating the Appendix B mechanism on real MJX contact geometry.

Srishti280992/repro-softjax-softtorch-em.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all five claims: operator coverage and gradient checks across all primitive families, a 40,000-point STE pitfall demonstration, six sort/rank methods across four families, an H200 benchmark confirming memory and speed ordering, and a real MJX box-plane contact showing gradient flow through the softened manifold-point selector. The reproduction is thorough with only minor hardware-dependent deviations in absolute benchmark timings.

RyeCatcher/repro-the-interplay-between-i.paper_title: The Interplay Between Interpolation and Aggregation in Regression: Optimal Sample Complexity

claims.claim: The paper defines the gamma-graph dimension d_γ (Definition 3.2) via a gamma-shattering condition (Definition 3.1) and uses it to characterize the sample complexity of aggregation-based regression procedures.
claims.evidence: Brute-force exhaustive shattering search recovers exact dimensions for bit-vector family (dim=d, d=1..5) and unique-tail family (dim=r for multiple (k,r) pairs), with a firing negative control (singleton class → dim=0) and exact step-function reproduction (dim=4 for γ<0.5, dim=0 for γ≥0.5).

claims.claim: Any interpolator-based aggregation using proper aggregation rules requires sample complexity Ω(d_γ/ε) to reach expected cutoff loss ε (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: Using the paper's own Theorem C.1 construction at d=20, ε=0.05, n=12: single-interpolator loss 0.176 (analytic) / 0.177 (MC), both >ε; 3-fold median worst-case loss 1.0 >ε; negative control at n=20000 yields loss 0.0 <ε. Closed-form and Monte Carlo agree within 1%.

claims.claim: There exist hypothesis classes with γ-graph dimension d_γ and γ-OIG dimension at most 3 for which finite interpolating-aggregation algorithms still require sample complexity Ω(d_γ/ε), separating them from general learners that achieve Õ(1/ε) (Theorem 3.8).
claims.evidence: The bit-vector construction with mean rule shows loss 1.0 >ε at n=3, but the logbook itself documents that mean and median coincide algebraically in this construction (unanimous wrong values), so the key separation mechanism is not probed. The γ-OIG dimension ≤3 check was unreliable and not completed, and the general-learner Õ(1/ε) comparison was not tested.

claims.claim: For some hypothesis classes with constant γ-OIG dimension, no finite interpolating aggregation rule can achieve non-trivial cutoff loss regardless of sample size, requiring either infinite aggregation or non-interpolating rules (Theorem 3.10).
claims.evidence: Unique-tail family at k=8000, r=89 shows worst-case loss 0.890 ≥0.85, with a firing negative control at k=9 (loss 0.690 <0.85). However, a single domain layer replaces the paper's countable-union construction, and the constant γ-OIG dimension is not independently verified.

claims.claim: Taking the median of three independently trained interpolators achieves expected cutoff loss O(d_γ/n), yielding optimal sample complexity O(d_γ/ε) that matches the lower bound (Theorem 3.11).
claims.evidence: A single matched-n comparison at n=150 (chosen post hoc after n=12 was found to be a regime where median hurts) shows median-of-3 loss 0.0219 vs single-S loss 0.0414 (~1.9x better). This is directional evidence only; the O(d_γ/n) rate is not demonstrated via scaling, and the comparison point was selected after observing failures.

claims.claim: Proper learners require sample complexity Ω((d_γ/ε)ln(1/ε)), strictly worse than the O(d_γ/ε) achieved by median-of-three aggregation, demonstrating aggregation's superiority over proper learning (Theorem 3.12).
claims.evidence: A self-derived coupon-collector construction (not the paper's Theorem C.5 constants) shows a flat-then-cliff shape: proper-learner loss 0.0505 at n=30 vs 0.0 at n=1842, with median-of-3 ahead at n=30 (0.0084). The ln(1/ε) factor is not directly isolated; the construction uses the authors' own constants and is explicitly labeled as targeting qualitative mechanism only.

RyeCatcher/repro-the-interplay-between-i.overall: The logbook provides solid computational verification of the gamma-graph dimension definition (Claim 1) and the Theorem 3.5 lower bound (Claim 2) via brute-force and Monte-Carlo methods on the paper's own constructions. The remaining four claims are addressed only on simplified or post-hoc-selected instances that do not fully probe the theorems' separation mechanisms or scaling rates.

digantodebbarma/repro-complexmcp-evaluat.paper_title: ComplexMCP: Evaluation of LLM Agents in Dynamic, Interdependent, and Large-Scale Tool Sandbox

claims.claim: ComplexMCP provides a benchmark with over 300 tools spanning 7 stateful sandboxes for evaluating LLM agents on interdependent tool use (Section on core contributions).
claims.evidence: An AST and configuration audit of the official repository at commit 570c75b finds 314 model-visible server tools across 15 servers (7 stateful, 8 stateless) and 47 tasks in the bundled parquet (SHA-256 verified), confirming the 'over 300 tools / 7 stateful sandboxes' claim; the 315-vs-314 discrepancy is explained as a client-side retrieve_tools pseudo-tool.

claims.claim: On the 47-task benchmark, human performance reaches 93.61% success rate while top LLMs trail substantially: Gemini-3-Flash 55.31%, Claude-opus-4 41.84%, and GPT-5.1 19.14% (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook only extracts Table 2 values from the paper PDF and confirms they are integer-consistent with plausible success counts, plus smoke-tests the released judge; no independent model or human rerun was performed (explicitly stated: independent_model_and_human_rerun=False).

claims.claim: Tool retrieval performance degrades as the action space expands beyond 300 tools, a bottleneck termed 'tool retrieval saturation' (Section 4.2, Figure 6).
claims.evidence: A MiniLM embedding-retrieval proxy on the real 314-tool catalog shows Recall@30 dropping from 0.998 to 0.483 as distractors increase, but this is a retrieval proxy, not the end-to-end agent-success experiment of Figure 6; the logbook itself acknowledges 'figure6_end_to_end_agent_rerun: False' and that the paper's claim is not universal across models.

claims.claim: Models exhibit a 'clean-slate' bias and over-confidence, assuming empty environments and skipping verification steps, leading to unintended consequences (Section 4.2, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies that the benchmark has nonempty initial cart states (6 of 7 seeds) and that 22 ground-truth trajectories require cart inspection before checkout, but no model trajectories were evaluated, so the claim that models actually exhibit clean-slate bias and over-confidence is never tested.

claims.claim: Agents display 'strategic defeatism,' rationalizing failure rather than pursuing recovery strategies, a pattern particularly evident in GPT-5.1 (Section 4.2, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirms 13 ground-truth tasks contain error-recovery-retry sequences and that the Jeremy Moments case matches the paper's appendix, but the GPT-5.1 evaluated trajectories and Figure 5 labels are absent from the release, so the prevalence (33.7%) and GPT-5.1 prominence claims are not independently testable.

digantodebbarma/repro-complexmcp-evaluat.overall: The logbook rigorously audits the released repository and benchmark data, confirming the benchmark's scale and structural mechanisms, but does not independently reproduce any model evaluation results. Claims requiring model trajectories or human evaluation remain unverified because the release omits evaluated trajectories, model snapshots, and annotation labels.

claims.claim: AOEB covers five essential capabilities for retrieval in LLM agents: code, tool, reasoning, and memory retrieval.
claims.evidence: The logbook performed a structural audit of the official codebase, finding 40 tasks registered across code (10), tool (3), reasoning (22), memory (5), and multimodal (8 cross-cutting) categories, plus a smoke test using BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 on 3 synthetic code queries against 5 documents achieving NDCG@5 = 0.9437. However, the actual AOEB datasets are unavailable, so the smoke test used proxy data rather than the benchmark's real tasks, and no full-scale evaluation was conducted.

claims.claim: AOEB provides Multi-Modal evaluation with both textual and visual data for each task category in agent-centric retrieval.
claims.evidence: The logbook analyzed 11 custom AOEB-NG task config files and reported that all define multimodal modalities (IMAGE, MIXED, or SEQ), but no multimodal retrieval was actually run—the smoke test used a text-only model on synthetic code data. Since the AOEB datasets are not publicly available, there is no experimental evidence that the task configs reference real, populated visual data; the claim is supported only by structural inspection of JSON configs, not by any runs or numbers.

erobinson/repro-aoeb-benchmarking-agent-.overall: The logbook establishes through structural code analysis that AOEB's codebase defines 40 tasks spanning code, tool, reasoning, memory, and multimodal categories, with multimodal modalities specified in task config files. However, full verification is blocked by the unavailability of AOEB datasets, and the only experimental evidence is a toy-scale smoke test on synthetic data with a text-only embedding model, which does not address the multimodal claim.

rakshi-the-neural-nexus/repro-from-obser.paper_title: From Observations to States: Latent Time Series Forecasting

claims.claim: LatentTSF reduces latent chaos: for iTransformer on the Electricity dataset, the mean Euclidean distance between adjacent-timestep latent embeddings drops from 94.03 (standard iTransformer) toward the raw-observation baseline of 12.94 (Section 5.4, Figure 1/5).
claims.evidence: The logbook contains no experiment measuring Euclidean distance between adjacent-timestep latent embeddings; the latent chaos metric (94.03 → 12.94) from Section 5.4/Figure 1/5 is never addressed.

claims.claim: On the Electricity dataset with iTransformer, LatentTSF improves average MAE across horizons from 0.375 to 0.299 (Section 5.2, Table 1).
claims.evidence: On Electricity × iTransformer, the reproduction measured LatentTSF avg MAE = 0.303 (paper 0.299) and MSE = 0.194 (exact match), beating the observation-space baseline (0.347 MAE, 0.239 MSE) on all four horizons. The LatentTSF endpoint closely matches; the baseline is stronger than the paper's reported 0.375, so the improvement magnitude is smaller but the direction and LatentTSF result are confirmed.

claims.claim: The theoretical analysis shows the prediction loss (ℒPred) and alignment loss (ℒAlign) each implicitly maximize a mutual information objective between predicted and ground-truth latent states (Section 4.1-4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook does not address the theoretical mutual information analysis of ℒPred and ℒAlign from Sections 4.1–4.2; no derivation, proof check, or empirical MI estimation is present.

claims.claim: LatentTSF's gains are more pronounced at long forecasting horizons (T=720) than at shorter horizons, and particularly strong on high-dimensional datasets like Traffic (Section 5.2, Table 1/6).
claims.evidence: On Traffic (862 series) × iTransformer, LatentTSF beats the baseline on every horizon with MAE gaps 0.048/0.041/0.044/0.137, showing the largest gain at T=720. The baseline matches the paper closely (0.801 vs 0.798 MSE; 0.536 vs 0.526 MAE) and LatentTSF MAE matches (0.469 vs 0.464), confirming both the high-dimensional and long-horizon aspects.

claims.claim: Default loss weights are set to 10 for the prediction term and 15 for the alignment term across the two-stage latent state-space construction and forecasting pipeline (Section 3.5, Table 4-5).
claims.evidence: All LatentTSF runs use --mse_weight 10.0 and --cosine_weight 15.0, confirmed in the raw CSV columns (mse_weight=10.0, cosine_weight=15.0 on all four latent rows), matching the paper's stated defaults of α=10 and β=15.

rakshi-the-neural-nexus/repro-from-obser.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting Claims 2, 4, and 5 through real runs on Electricity and Traffic with iTransformer, but does not address the latent chaos measurement (Claim 1) or the theoretical mutual information analysis (Claim 3). The Traffic reproduction is particularly strong with near-exact baseline matching, while the Electricity baseline is stronger than the paper's, slightly shrinking the reported improvement magnitude.

Srishti280992/repro-accurate-sgmcmc-uq.paper_title: Accurate Large-sample Uncertainty Quantification using Stochastic Gradient Markov Chain Monte Carlo

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 bounds the relative error between the true stationary covariance Σ_θ and the discrete-time proxy covariance Σ_ψ as ‖Σ_θ − Σ_ψ‖/‖Σ_θ‖ ≤ C_v λ^(1/2), scaling with the step size λ (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: On paper-scale German Credit (N=1000, D=20), the logbook solved the exact discrete Lyapunov equation across a 7-point step-size sweep and reported a log-log slope of 1.0009 with the relative error bounded by approximately 1.69e-2·√λ, consistent with the claimed O(√λ) upper bound (the actual scaling being tighter at O(λ) still satisfies the upper bound).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 derives an explicit formula for the minibatch noise covariance without assuming constant noise, enabling exact rather than approximate stationary covariance solutions (Theorem 4.3, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook exhaustively enumerated 429,344 minibatches across seven batch-size configurations on a D=20 German Credit subsample and found a maximum absolute residual of 2.22e-16 (machine precision) between the Theorem 4.3 formula and brute-force computation, directly confirming the explicit noise covariance formula.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.5 and Corollary 4.6 provide non-asymptotic 2-Wasserstein distance bounds between the true and proxy algorithm distributions, giving W₂(π_θ,π_ψ) ≤ Aλ/B for SGD (Theorem 4.5, Corollary 4.6).
claims.evidence: On Poisson N=2000, D=50 with 48 scaling cells and German Credit with 11,999 iterates, the logbook fitted scaling exponents of (1.105, -1.101) and (1.092, -1.082) for well-specified and misspecified settings (R²>0.9999), closely matching the claimed λ/B behavior, and the iterate-wise Theorem 4.5 bound check had 0 violations with 82,400x minimum slack.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 gives a two-stage tuning procedure: offline sandwich covariance estimation from a subsample, followed by solving coupled equations for preconditioned step sizes (Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: On German Credit at native scale (N=1000, D=20), the logbook reproduced the two-stage procedure with subsample-based J_hat and V_hat estimation, showing the relative gap to the full-data target decreasing from 13.23 (M=100) to 1.14 (M=500) to 0.29 (M=800), confirming the offline estimation stage converges as expected.

claims.claim: On the Boston housing dataset under strong model misspecification, the proposed DQ+exact method maintains accurate covariance estimates while competing continuous-time and constant-noise methods diverge (Table 3).
claims.evidence: On Boston housing at native scale (N=506, D=12) with 540 SGD chains (6 batch sizes × 3 tuning rules × 30 repetitions × 500 epochs), DQ+exact stayed flat (0.244→0.298, 1.22x change) while CT degraded (0.130→0.775, 12.53x) and LR+WS remained unusable (0.971–0.974), matching the claimed qualitative divergence pattern.

claims.claim: Proposition B.1 extends the covariance and error-bound results to SGLD with momentum, recovering the non-momentum results as the momentum parameter κ→0 (Proposition B.1, Appendix B).
claims.evidence: The logbook solved the full 2-state momentum covariance equation at D=20 (vectorized as a 1600×1600 linear system) and found the κ=0 residual to be 5.36e-16 (machine precision), confirming that Proposition B.1's momentum extension exactly recovers the non-momentum formulas in the κ→0 limit.

Srishti280992/repro-accurate-sgmcmc-uq.overall: The logbook provides concrete native-scale numerical evidence for all six claims, using exact linear algebra, exhaustive minibatch enumeration, Wasserstein scaling audits, and 540-chain Boston housing experiments on the official codebase. The reproduction is rigorous, with machine-precision residuals confirming theoretical formulas and empirical scaling exponents closely matching predicted bounds.

agharsallah/j0y3snbo9g-logbook.paper_title: Theoretical Investigation on Inductive Bias of Isolation Forest

claims.claim: Isolation Forest's expected depth function is derived in closed form by modeling the iTree growth process as a random walk with transition probabilities based on point spacing (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: No experimental setup, runs, or numerical results are present; the page only restates the claim and references absent 'Result + figure cells'.

claims.evidence: No experiments or data are provided; the page merely repeats the claim statement with no supporting artifacts.

claims.claim: For central single anomalies, Isolation Forest's decision threshold is Θ(√(n₀κ)) versus k-NN's Θ(kδ), demonstrating iForest's lower sensitivity to centrally-located anomalies (Theorems 4.6-4.7, Table 2).
claims.evidence: No runs, tables, or figures are included; the page only restates the claim and points to missing result cells.

claims.evidence: No experimental evidence or numerical results appear anywhere on the page; only the claim statement is repeated.

claims.claim: Empirical mean-squared error between empirical and theoretical expected depths decreases as the number of trees increases, confirming the concentration property of Proposition 3.1 (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: No MSE values, tree-count sweeps, or figures are present; the page contains only the claim text and a placeholder reference to absent result cells.

agharsallah/j0y3snbo9g-logbook.overall: This logbook contains no actual experimental evidence — every claim page merely restates the claim and references result cells that do not exist. No runs, numbers, figures, or artifacts are provided for any of the six claims.

tomyimkc/repro-on-regret-bounds-of-thomp.paper_title: On Regret Bounds of Thompson Sampling for Bayesian Optimization

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 constructs a two-armed instance showing GP-TS incurs Ω(1/δ^c) cumulative regret with probability at least δ, establishing a high-probability regret lower bound with polynomial dependence on 1/δ (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The exact Theorem 3.1 two-armed construction was implemented with 200k MC trials; Pr(R_T>=T/2) decays polynomially (fitted exponent 2.24, not exponential), and the GP-UCB control decays faster at every checkpoint, matching the theorem's mechanism.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 bounds the second moment of cumulative regret as E[R_T²] = O(T γ_T log T), yielding a high-probability regret upper bound of O(√(T γ_T log T/δ)) that improves the dependence on δ by a factor of 1/√δ over prior results (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: On the theorem's own finite-domain setting (30-point grid, SE kernel, 20k trials, T up to 1600), the ratio E[R_T²]/(T·γ_T·log T) decreases monotonically (0.818→0.049, log-log slope -0.678), consistent with the O(.) bound, while the greedy-mean control's ratio grows (slope +0.392).

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 derives expected lenient-regret bounds that are polylogarithmic in the time horizon T, matching GP-UCB's high-probability bounds asymptotically (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: For each fixed Δ>0, E[|T(Δ)|] grows sublinearly (log-log slopes 0.15–0.37 vs T), consistent with polylog-in-T bounds; the Δ→0 control shows much steeper growth (slope 0.78), confirming the positive-tolerance precondition matters. The Δ-scaling exponent (1.35 vs predicted ~2) undershoots but direction is correct.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 proves an improved cumulative regret upper bound of O(√T log T) for the squared exponential kernel and Õ(√T) for Matérn kernels with smoothness ν > 2, matching GP-UCB rates while relaxing prior smoothness requirements (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: All kernels including the ν=1.5 control (violating ν>2) show similar exponents (~0.41–0.42), so the general √T-type growth holds but the paper's specific smoothness-relaxation claim is not confirmed; the 25–50 point discretized domain saturates information gain before smoothness effects differentiate kernels, as acknowledged by the logbook.

tomyimkc/repro-on-regret-bounds-of-thomp.overall: Claims 1–3 are verified on the paper's own named settings with large-scale Monte Carlo and theorem-faithful controls that degrade as predicted.
