michaldobiezynski/repro-outcome-aware-sp.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification of the three theoretical claims (augmented loss, Proposition 4.1, Theorem 5.1) on the paper's own instance with disjoint code paths and genuine resampling up to n=1e7, and confirms the dSprites misalignment claim on real images at paper scale. The synthetic MSE claim is only validated under oracle features (toy), and the OPE claim is untestable due to a harness failure that affects baseline and method identically.

michaldobiezynski/repro-online-conformal.paper_title: Online Conformal Prediction via Universal Portfolio Algorithms

claims.claim: UP-OCP is a parameter-free online conformal prediction method requiring no stepsize tuning, whose regret analysis is built on universal portfolio algorithms (Section 4.2, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The closed-form betting fraction lambda_t=(N+1/2)/t matches the Cover-Ordentlich universal-portfolio integral to 1.110e-16 over all 2669 rounds on real AXP Prophet scores, the coin-betting wealth/regret duality closes to 1.563e-12, and coverage drifts only 2.136e-02 across a 1e9-fold score rescaling versus 9.494e-01 for the tuned SF-OGD baseline.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 shows UP-OCP achieves linearized regret of order O(√(T ln T)) in the worst case, improving to O(ln T) as the miscoverage target α→1 (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: An exact worst-case dynamic program (validated to 2.66e-15 against exhaustive 2^T enumeration) shows the regret stays at ≤0.4843 of the printed bound F_T out to T=1e8, with per-decade log-log slopes 0.5689→0.5359 tracking sqrt(T ln T)'s own slopes 0.5869→0.5290; at α=1-1e-8 the slope collapses to 0.1293 fitting R*=0.060 ln T+0.291.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 establishes a finite-time miscoverage bound of the form MisCov_T ≤ ε_T + √(2α(1-α)ε_T), where ε_T grows only logarithmically in T (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: Fitting T·eps_T = a ln T + b recovers a=1.5000/2.5000/3.5000 against theory's q+3/2 with residuals down to 1.3e-6, and the exact worst-case miscoverage via reachability DP peaks at 0.7692 of the bound with all real runs ≤0.8149; the disclosed knife-edge S_t=0 violation is a degenerate boundary case that does not undermine the bound's form or logarithmic growth for admissible non-degenerate sequences.

claims.claim: On the AXP dataset at α=0.05, UP-OCP achieves 0.932 marginal coverage with an average prediction set size of 14.8 and a longest error streak of 4 days, versus 0.920 coverage, 16.9 average set size, and a 15-day longest error streak for the Kalman/KT baseline (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Coverage reproduces closely (UP-OCP 0.932 vs 0.932, KT 0.923 vs 0.920) but average sizes land ~10% low (13.3 vs 14.8, 15.2 vs 16.9) and streaks are 3 days short, because the paper cites a 5-year Kaggle file for a stated 2008-2018 horizon with a log-scale specification inconsistent with the reported set sizes, making the exact score stream unmatchable.

claims.claim: Across miscoverage rates from 0.05 to 0.25, UP-OCP empirically achieves the best Pareto trade-off between coverage and set size compared to the parameter-free KT baseline (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: On the same AXP Prophet score stream across 50 alphas in [0.05, 0.25], UP-OCP produces a smaller average set size at 50/50 targets and Pareto-dominates 50/50 KT frontier points, with a mean size gap of 1.2801 (10.17%); the comparative nature of the claim means the data-source mismatch affecting Claim 4 does not apply.

claims.claim: On a synthetic sinusoidal nonconformity-score sequence, UP-OCP tracks periodic volatility—expanding prediction sets during high-noise phases and shrinking them afterward—matching the best hyperparameter-tuned P-Control baseline without any tuning (Figures 3-4).
claims.evidence: Using the paper's exact sinusoid generator (P=200, S_mag=10, S_min=2, sigma=0.3, T=3000, 10 trials), UP-OCP's interval width correlates 0.9767 with the noise-free envelope (KT 0.7471), swings 3.348x between high/low phases (KT 1.353x), lags only 3 steps (KT 18), and achieves average size 19.079 vs the ex-post-best tuned P-Control's 19.292 (ratio 0.9890); the measured UP/KT size ratio 0.7897 independently matches the paper's Table-7 ratio of 0.784.

michaldobiezynski/repro-online-conformal.overall: The logbook provides strong, independently validated evidence for five of six claims, including machine-precision verification of the universal-portfolio identity, exact worst-case dynamic programs for both theorems validated against brute-force enumeration, and faithful reproductions of the empirical comparisons on real and synthetic data. Claim 4 is inconclusive due to an unresolvable data-provenance mismatch in the paper itself (citing a 5-year Kaggle file for an 11-year horizon with inconsistent log-scale specification), though qualitative orderings from Table 1 do reproduce.

michaldobiezynski/repro-model-monotonici.paper_title: Model Monotonicity in Autobidding Auctions: When Do Better Predictions Lead to Better Outcomes?

claims.claim: For target-CPA bidders without budget constraints using uniform bidding with multiplier mu=1 in first-price auctions, refining the prediction model (partitioning clusters into subclusters while preserving calibration) never decreases platform revenue, i.e., Rev(M_A) >= Rev(M_B) when M_A refines M_B (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: 360 refinement comparisons across 60 random instances (20,000 users, 60 advertisers, 8→1536 clusters) show 0 revenue monotonicity violations, with the only negative gap at -2.31e-14 relative (machine round-off) and the smallest genuine gap at +0.066; revenue is computed from explicit winner-determination code, not substituted from the closed form.

claims.claim: The first-price auction revenue monotonicity proof for tCPA bidders relies on convexity of f(p) = max_i(t_i · p_i) via Jensen's inequality, since model refinement corresponds to a mean-preserving spread of this convex function (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: The Jensen decomposition residual is 1.47e-15, showing the total revenue increase is accounted for term-by-term by per-cluster Jensen gaps; calibration holds at 8.67e-18 as an emergent property; and a concave-min control (replacing max_i with min_i) breaks monotonicity in 60/60 instances on the identical generator, isolating convexity as the operative ingredient.

claims.claim: Uniform bidding at multiplier mu=1 is simultaneously conversion-maximizing, revenue-maximizing among equilibria, and welfare-maximizing for tCPA bidders in first-price auctions (Theorem 5.2), and welfare monotonicity follows as a corollary when per-conversion values equal targets (Corollary 5.3).
claims.evidence: CPA identity holds to 1.78e-15 with 0/60 conversion-monotonicity violations and 149 infeasible observations at mu>1; revenue and welfare excess over mu=1 are +0.000 across 2,300 feasible profiles; welfare monotonicity shows 0/360 violations. Caveat: the revenue-maximality test uses a superset of equilibria rather than a characterized equilibrium set, and some +0.000 excesses reflect no-op deviations, but a violation would have refuted the claim.

claims.claim: There exist instances with tCPA bidders where second-price (VCG) auctions exhibit non-monotonicity in both revenue and welfare under model refinement, with a constructed counterexample showing a simultaneous 6.2% decrease in both metrics (Theorem 5.8).
claims.evidence: Solving the binding-CPA fixed point from g=[1,1] independently recovers multipliers [36.5, 6.578947]→[14.714286, 25.0], yielding Rev 3.2300→3.0300 and Welfare 3.2300→3.0300 (-6.19%, matching the paper's 6.2%); a 6,000-point BR grid scan confirms the profile is a genuine Nash equilibrium. Equilibrium multiplicity (30 distinct equilibria) is noted but does not affect this existence claim.

claims.claim: Introducing budget constraints breaks revenue monotonicity even in first-price auctions, as optimal bidder multipliers shift under refinement and reduce competitive pressure, exemplified by a counterexample with a 16.8% revenue loss (Theorem 5.10).
claims.evidence: Exact breakpoint enumeration of the spend step function independently recovers alpha_1 = 2.856502→1.952790, yielding Rev 5.5268→4.5977 (-16.81%, matching the paper's 16.8%); the mechanism is directly observable (multiplier down 31.6%, constrained bidder's wins up 2→3); genericity scans show 14/347 and 3/47 revenue violations at small and large scale respectively.

claims.claim: A centralized, non-strategic linear-programming benchmark allocation guarantees welfare monotonicity under budget constraints via a 'lifting' construction that preserves feasibility across refined partitions (Theorem 5.11), and the paper's overall characterization identifies exactly three settings where monotonicity holds (Table 1).
claims.evidence: At 9,600 LP variables with binding budgets, 0/36 welfare-monotonicity violations with min gap +4.552%; the lifting construction x^A_{i,C'} := x^B_{i,C} is explicitly built and verified feasible to 1.11e-15 and objective-preserving to 1.97e-15, with the refined optimum dominating it in 12/12 instances. Table 1 audit finds exactly 3 monotone settings and confirms 7/7 non-monotone rows, with appendix counterexamples B.3 (41.67%) and B.4 (66.176%/0.0921%) reproduced.

michaldobiezynski/repro-model-monotonici.overall: All six claims are supported by concrete experimental evidence at non-toy scale (20,000 users, 60 advertisers, up to 1536 clusters, 9,600-variable LPs), with counterexample multipliers independently solved rather than copied from the paper. The reproduction is rigorous, featuring control experiments, genericity scans, and honestly stated caveats that do not undermine any claim.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 gives a bicriteria (1+κ, 1+1/κ) approximation via LP rounding: the returned subgraph K satisfies coverage loss W−e(K)≤(1+κ)·ε·W and size |K|≤(1+1/κ)·r (Theorem 1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: 0/221 violations of either bicriteria bound across 13 instances (n up to 304, m up to 300) with 6 kappa and 3 eps values, where the size bound is checked against MILP-exact optima r (mip_rel_gap 0) for all 39 (instance, eps) pairs; coverage bound driven to 93.3% of allowance confirming non-vacuity.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 proves a monotonicity/nestedness property (Kτ1⊆Kτ2 for τ1<τ2), derived from a connection to parametric minimum cuts, which is required for valid conformal calibration (Theorem 2, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: 0/37920 nestedness violations for the parametric-min-cut family Khat_tau across 4 instances × 3 kappa × 80 tau values, plus 0/7080 for an independent Lagrangian grid; Example 1 reproduced exactly (tau=0.6 selects {0,1,2,3}, tau=0.7 selects {0,1,4,5,6}, non-nested). The disclosed deviation—that the literal identity K_tau=Khat_tau fails in 239/960 cases due to min-cut ties—does not affect the calibration-relevant nestedness, which is the property the claim states.

claims.claim: Corollary 1 shows the entire nested sequence of subgraphs across thresholds can be computed in Õ(γ(m+n)²) time (Corollary 1, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: k≤n on 19/19 instances at n up to 4656, max-flow calls all ≤2k+3, and T/Q ratio decreasing from 1.1e-08 to 4.8e-10 across 4.6 decades with log-log slopes 0.71/0.77 (<1). The disclosed substitution of O(k) separate max-flow calls for the single GGT parametric flow is a conservative (slower) test that still fits within the Õ(γ(m+n)²) budget.

claims.claim: Lemma 1 establishes a distribution-free marginal coverage guarantee ℙ(B*⊆Kτ*(A*))≥φ−δ under exchangeability, without requiring model probability estimates (Lemma 1).
claims.evidence: Empirical coverage of 0.6133/0.7049/0.8129/0.9120 against bounds 0.55/0.65/0.75/0.85 over 12000 samples per phi level on a 10×10 grid with 180 edges, |D1|=|D2|=100, delta=0.05; mean |K| is only 40–61% of context edges (non-trivial), and a deliberately mistuned quantile control falls below the bound at every phi, discriminating valid from invalid calibration.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 proves NP-hardness of the conformal subgraph problem even for constant ε via reduction from clique detection, in Appendix B (Theorem 4, Appendix B).
claims.evidence: 36/36 reductions (eps in {0.3,0.5,0.7}, r in {3,4,5}, |V'| up to 452) decided correctly by MILP against brute-force max-clique ground truth, with construction invariants P1, P2, P3 holding on every instance and razor-thin single-edge separation margins. The disclosed deviation (c=1 with s derived, vs. paper's polynomially large c) preserves all three properties the proof depends on; reduction correctness is size-independent so small instances are not a proxy.

claims.claim: On a synthetic 6x6 grid navigation experiment with 50 train/test routes, the LP-based method compresses the calibration set to 52 edges at φ=0.75 coverage and outperforms greedy baselines for φ≤0.8 (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Across 10 runs matching Appendix G.1's exact specification, LP edges at phi=0.75 have median 52.5 (modal 52 in 4/10 runs, paper reports 52); the 20-edge bypass is omitted in 7/10 runs matching the paper's description; LP is strictly smaller than both greedy baselines at 11/11 grid points with phi≤0.8 (e.g., 57.5 vs 70.1/69.3 at phi=0.75) while the advantage vanishes at phi≥0.85, matching the paper's qualifier.

michaldobiezynski/repro-compact-conforma.overall: The logbook provides concrete, non-toy experimental evidence supporting all six claims: bicriteria bounds verified against MILP-exact optima, nestedness verified with the paper's own counterexample reproduced, timing consistent with the theoretical bound at n up to 4656, conformal coverage verified via 12000-sample Monte Carlo with a discriminating control, reduction correctness verified on 36 instances, and the grid experiment faithfully reproduced with honest disclosure of a bimodal distribution. Three deviations are transparently disclosed but do not undermine any claim's core assertion.

michaldobiezynski/repro-semi-knockoffs-a.paper_title: Semi-knockoffs: a model-agnostic conditional independence testing method with finite-sample guarantees

claims.claim: Semi-knockoffs avoids the train-test data split required by prior conditional-independence testing methods such as HRT while still yielding valid p-values, via nonparametric paired tests requiring only conditional expectations ν_j and ρ_j rather than exact knockoff construction (Theorem 3.3, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: On the paper's Fig.4 DGP (n=300, p=50, GradientBoostingRegressor, 50 reps), SKO with no train-test split yields type-I error 0.0532 (oracle ν_j/ρ_j) and 0.0505 (estimated ridge imputers) at nominal 0.05, while a naive no-split HRT-style statistic on the same data blows up to 0.9363, confirming validity comes from the semi-knockoff construction. R2 tracks the paper (0.903 no-split vs 0.851 split vs paper's 0.910/0.886).

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 establishes that the Semi-knockoffs procedure controls the false discovery rate at level q, i.e. FDR(S_SKO) ≤ q (Theorem 3.4, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 3 with oracle ν_j/ρ_j at q=0.2 over 200 independent repetitions yields FDR = 0.1808 ± 0.0111, which is below the q=0.2 bound, with power 1.000. The estimated-imputer variant (outside the theorem's scope) gives 0.2032 ± 0.0116, consistent with the theorem applying only to the oracle case.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows that for null (non-relevant) features, regularized empirical risk minimizers trained with and without the feature remain close, with an ‖θ̃^j − θ̂‖₂ ≤ O_P(√(log(1/δ)/n)) bound, giving optimization stability guarantees for regularized models (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Closed-form ridge ERM tested over n=1e3 to 1e6: log-log slope of ‖θ̃^j − θ̂‖₂ vs n is −0.498 overall (theory −0.500), stable at −0.533/−0.476 on disjoint windows. The δ-dependence at n=2000 over 4000 seeds shows q(δ)/√(log(1/δ)) monotonically decreasing with max/min ratio 1.81 and linear fit R²=0.9984, confirming the upper bound holds.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 provides a double-robustness property: the loss difference between imputed feature distributions decays at a compound rate O_P(a_n b_n) even when both the predictive model and the sampler have estimation error (Theorem 4.3, Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: RMS(double-robust loss difference)/(a_n·b_n) stays flat at 2.74–2.84 across n=1e3 to 2e5 (2.3 decades), directly testing O_P(a_n b_n). Log-log slopes: a_n −0.513, b_n −0.497, compound loss difference −1.013 (theory −1), while single-decay comparator is −0.504. Complex-learner Fig.3 reproduction gives concentration ratios 3.51×/6.57×/3.07× for RF/NN/GB.

claims.claim: On simulated data with adjacent-feature support, Semi-knockoffs maintains type-I error control while achieving higher power than HRT, and derandomization with 5 permutations under masked correlation further increases power (Figure 4, Figure 5, Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: The adjacent-support conjunct is well-supported: SKO power 0.983 vs HRT 0.850 at type-I 0.0505 vs 0.0974, with derandomization lifting power to 1.000. However, the masked-correlation derandomization gain cannot be tested because all three methods (SKO, SKO-p5, HRT) saturate at power 1.000 in the reproduction, and the substitute metric (median p-value) is confounded by p5's inflated type-I (0.0718).

claims.claim: On the Wisconsin Breast Cancer real dataset, Semi-knockoffs is applied across Random Forest, Neural Network, and Gradient Boosting models to demonstrate model-agnostic feature selection (Figure 6, Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: The identical SKO procedure runs unchanged on real sklearn RandomForestRegressor, MLPRegressor, and GradientBoostingRegressor on the genuine WDBC dataset (n=569, p=30, 50 reps each), making non-zero discoveries (1.9/2.6/1.8 of 30) with single-permutation type-I at 0.04/0.04/0.00, closely matching the paper's 0.04/0.06/0.00.

michaldobiezynski/repro-semi-knockoffs-a.overall: The logbook provides strong from-scratch experimental evidence supporting five of six claims, including finite-sample p-value validity, FDR control, and two asymptotic rate verifications, all on non-toy setups with real sklearn models and datasets. The one gap is Claim 5's masked-correlation derandomization gain, which is untestable due to power saturation in the reproduction.

michaldobiezynski/repro-near-optimal-and.paper_title: Near-Optimal and Efficient First-Order Algorithm for Multi-Task Learning with Shared Linear Representation

claims.claim: TPGD (Algorithm 1) is a two-phase first-order gradient-descent method for jointly estimating a shared linear representation and task-specific parameters in multi-task learning (Section 4, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Finite-difference gradient audit confirms Phase I and Phase II updates match the stated losses to 1.30e-05 and 1.16e-06 respectively, no SVD/QR calls exist inside the iteration loop (matching Table 1's AC="-"), and joint (B,W) estimation reaches err=0.041327 on the paper's d=200, k=20, T=200, N=1000 configuration.

claims.claim: Phase I performs K1/2 iterations of unregularized gradient descent as a warm start, and Phase II performs the remaining K1/2 iterations of regularized gradient descent with penalty term ||B^T B − WW^T||_F^2 (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Switch point confirmed at tau=300=K1/2; Phase-II gradient matches the penalized objective Lhat+(1/8)||B^TB-WW^T||_F^2 to 1.16e-06; the penalty drives ||B^TB-WW^T||_F from 0.03278 to 2.814e-15 while all-Phase-I GD leaves it unchanged at 0.03278; Theorem A.1 warm-start criterion met at N=1e5 (0.152 <= 0.3144).

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 and Corollary 5.3 prove the method attains a near-optimal population estimation error of order Õ(dk/(NT)), improving over existing likelihood-based methods by a factor of k, where d is input dimension, k is representation dimension, T is the number of tasks, and N is per-task sample size (Section 5.1, Theorem 5.1, Corollary 5.3).
claims.evidence: Log-log slopes measured at -1.0267/-1.0037/-1.0002 in N (theory -1) and +0.9738/+0.9532 in k (theory +1 for dk/(NT), +2 for prior dk^2/(NT)), with err/(sigma^2 dk/(NT)) stable in [1.910, 2.062] across configurations including the paper's Figure-1 settings; d and T exponents match the paper's max{d,T}k/(NT) form.

claims.claim: The algorithm achieves Õ(1) iteration complexity, i.e., convergence in a number of iterations independent of the problem dimensions up to logarithmic factors (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: Iterations to reach 1.1x final error stay in [31, 42] (ratio 1.35) across a 16x sweep in d (flat: 33.5, 31.0, 31.5, 33.5, 32.0), 8x in T, 8x in k, and 1000x in N; no monotone growth in d is visible, which rules out poly(d) iteration scaling over the tested range.

claims.claim: The estimation-error guarantee requires a per-task sample size of N ≳ σ²(d+T)kκ⁴/σ_k²(Σ*) (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: Only 3 configurations tested, all with kappa=1, so the kappa^4 factor—a key component of the stated condition—is never exercised; the onset N* is read from a coarse 11-point grid with an arbitrary 1.25 ratio threshold; while sufficiency is shown in tested cases, the full form sigma^2(d+T)k kappa^4/sigma_k^2(Sigma*) is only partially validated.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.4 establishes excess-risk bounds for transferring the learned representation to a new task, decomposing the risk into representation approximation error and task-specific optimization error (Section 5.2, Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: The 1/K2 optimization term coefficient fits to 19.39-22.99 against the theory's sigma^2 k=20 across isotropic and anisotropic H; the representation term decays as N^-1.00 to N^-1.01 matching the predicted 1/N; all 24 measured (H,N,K2) excess risks lie below the Theorem 5.4 bound (max ratio 0.477), confirming the two-term decomposition.

michaldobiezynski/repro-near-optimal-and.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence from a from-scratch numpy implementation supporting 5 of 6 claims, with the rate claim (Claim 3) most decisively verified through log-log slope measurements showing k^1 rather than k^2 scaling. Claim 5 is inconclusive because the kappa^4 dependence in the sample-size condition is never tested (kappa=1 throughout), and the onset detection uses a coarse grid with an arbitrary threshold.

michaldobiezynski/repro-continuous-varia.paper_title: Continuous Variable Hamiltonian Learning at Heisenberg Limit via Displacement-Random Unitary Transformation

claims.claim: The Displacement-Random Unitary Transformation (D-RUT) protocol learns all coefficients of a generic multi-mode bosonic Hamiltonian with evolution time scaling as O(1/epsilon), achieving the Heisenberg limit (Theorem 1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: A 4-decade sweep of total evolution time on five systems (Kerr, generic single-mode order-4, Bose-Hubbard dimer at 69 and 6 parameters, generic 2-mode order-4) yields tail log-log slopes of -0.9901, -0.9794, -0.9746, -0.9714, -0.9757, all within 3% of the claimed -1, while a SQL control through the identical estimator returns -0.5012 against theoretical -0.5, confirming the harness discriminates Heisenberg from standard-quantum-limit scaling. Trotter-density dependence reproduces the paper's qualifier (slopes floor at -0.12/-0.05 at density 0.5 and recover to -0.99/-0.98 at density 8), and a S

claims.claim: For single-mode Hamiltonians expressed in a first-quantization (position/momentum) basis, D-RUT recovers physical coefficients with RMSE epsilon_G using total evolution time O~(1/epsilon_G), under stated conditions on known zero coefficients, non-zero response to basis mismatch, and a sufficiently close initial guess (Theorem 2, Section 2).
claims.evidence: On the paper's own Section 8.1 systems (harmonic G=[5.0,2.5,0] and anharmonic G=[5.0,2.5,0.1]), full Algorithm 2 implementation yields RMSE(G)-vs-T tail slopes of -0.9766 and -0.9554, within 5% of the claimed -1, with the mapping matrix M reproducing the paper's closed-form entries (1.250000, 7.500000, 3.750000) to six decimals and cond(M)=7.222 confirming well-posed inversion. Seed re-run gives -1.0126 and -0.9647.

claims.claim: The protocol's estimation error under state-preparation-and-measurement (SPAM) errors is bounded as ||delta g_SPAM||_2 <= (L_C/sigma_min(K)) ||delta beta||_2, where L_C is a Lipschitz constant and sigma_min(K) the smallest singular value of the Gram-like matrix K (Section 3.6, Eq. 43).
claims.evidence: The log-log slope of RMSE(g) vs sigma_beta is +0.9878 (and +1.1114 end-to-end through the full pipeline), matching the paper's Fig. 3 linear scaling prediction of +1. The bound with numerically evaluated L_C=28.2048 and sigma_min(K)=0.01404 holds in all 80 draws, though the logbook itself acknowledges this half is partly definitional; the discriminating evidence is the confirmed linearity, which is the empirical content of the claim.

claims.claim: A hierarchical two-stage coefficient recovery strategy (learn single-mode coefficients first, then coupling coefficients) is proven to have covariance dominated by that of simultaneous estimation, Cov(delta g)_hierarchical <= Cov(delta g)_simultaneous, for all parameters (Section 4.1, Appendix A).
claims.evidence: On the D-RUT protocol's own design matrix (N=4 modes, order 4, 494 simultaneous coefficients, 69 shared targets, equal 1976-probe budget), covariance domination holds for only 51/69 parameters with min eig(Cov_sim - Cov_hie) = -5.4061 < 0, so Loewner ordering fails. Under v1's own same-data block design on the Bose-Hubbard dimer (260 probes, Fock ncut=20), the ordering reverses for all 69 parameters (eig in [-1.1066e+04, +3.18e-12]), cross-checked by 3000 Monte-Carlo draws within 4.4%. The proof gap is identified: v1 Eq. 108 reproduces only after replacing A with A_1 (the stage-1 Gram), with m

claims.claim: An iterative bisection search over the squeezing parameter R (relating the physical and reference bases via a Bogoliubov transformation) converges in O(log(1/epsilon_R)) iterations for first-quantization Hamiltonian learning (Section 5.3, Eq. 77-78).
claims.evidence: With every f(R) evaluation driven through the full D-RUT + RPE pipeline (48 shots/stage, 50 probes, Fock dimension 60), the attained eps_R tracks eps_g'/K with log-log slope +1.0369 over 1.79 decades (Eq. 78 predicts +1), with ratios in [0.519, 1.125] across 6 budgets. Above the floor, iteration count is n_iter = 1.2492 log2(1/eps_R) - 2.060, confirming O(log(1/eps_R)); below the floor, targets are unreachable by iteration alone (eps_R=1e-4 succeeds in 1/16 repeats at K=24). Attained eps_R vs evolution time gives slope -1.0678, matching Eq. 79's total cost.

claims.claim: The algorithm uses Chebyshev-node sampling of the displacement parameter combined with robust phase estimation and inverse discrete Fourier transform to reconstruct coefficients, as detailed in Algorithm 1 and illustrated for the single-mode case in Figure 1 (Section 2).
claims.evidence: Noiseless Algorithm 1 (Chebyshev radial fit + Eq. 12 inverse DFT) recovers all 14 coefficients of a generic order-4 Hamiltonian to max |g_hat - g| = 3.186e-13. The RUT-average identity is cross-checked against a projector matrix power (agreement to 3.1e-13) and brute-force random-theta Trotter Monte Carlo (agreement to 4.8e-03, within MC s.e. ~0.013), and Trotter convergence gives slope -1.996 matching second-order Trotter. The structural claim about the algorithm's components is confirmed; the paper's secondary conditioning rationale for Chebyshev nodes is separately falsified at d=4 but is n

michaldobiezynski/repro-continuous-varia.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous from-scratch reimplementation of the D-RUT protocol with full truncated-Fock simulation, real binomial shot noise, SQL controls, and seed-robustness checks, verifying five of six claims including the central Heisenberg-limit scaling result. Claim 4 is falsified: the covariance domination statement fails for 18/69 parameters on the protocol's own design matrix and reverses entirely under same-data block design, with the proof gap precisely localized to a substitution of A for A_1 in v1 Eq. 108.

michaldobiezynski/repro-gradient-flow-th.paper_title: Gradient Flow Through Diagram Expansions: Learning Regimes and Explicit Solutions

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 shows that for targets expressible as polynomials in parameters and Kronecker deltas, the coefficients of the formal power series expansion of the loss's time derivatives are themselves polynomials in the width H, the parameterization exponent p, and the initialization variance sigma^2 (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Exact-arithmetic ODE Taylor coefficients match a closed algebraic form to rel.err 6.20e-16, and brute-force Wick enumeration of E[tr(M0^d)] over all perfect matchings (d<=6) is cross-checked against independent Monte Carlo (max rel.dev 5.88e-03, within 2.1 s.e.) at non-trivial sizes (H=256, p=128 for SYM; H=48, p=24 for ASYM).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 characterizes the leading and Pareto-optimal terms of the loss expansion for identity-tensor targets, organizing gradient-flow learning regimes into a polygon structure defined by scaling conditions on H, p, and sigma^2 (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Exact Pareto-set enumeration for SYM nu=2 (s<=3) yields no monomial above the predicted polygon (empty discrepancy set), and measured H-scaling exponents 1.989/2.967/3.935 (SYM) and 0.991/1.978/2.949 (ASYM) match predicted integers 2/3/4 and 1/2/3 within 2.1%, with ASYM nu=3 p-exponents 3.000 and 4.895 against predicted 3 and 5.

claims.claim: An NTK-like regime, in which features do not evolve during training, appears only at points/edges B-C of the Pareto polygon in the asymmetric parameterization case, while Proposition 8.2 proves the NTK kernel stays static throughout training in the symmetric matrix case (nu=2), explaining the absence of an NTK limit there (Section 4, Proposition 8.2).
claims.evidence: The f→Theta map is verified as injective on Sym(p) (sigma_min=7.4833, sigma_max=10.5830), confirming Proposition 8.2's equivalence; ASYM B-C scaling shows NTK drift falling to 0.0289 at H=16384 with f(t) matching (1−e^{-2t})I to 5e-4, versus drift 0.407 at the C-D edge and 0.634 in SYM. The registry's 'stays static' wording is a misparaphrase—the paper states an equivalence, and the 63% kernel motion in SYM confirms the paper's actual claim.

claims.claim: Mean-field, feature-evolving regimes require the initialization variance to scale as sigma^2 proportional to 1/H (symmetric case) or sigma^2 proportional to 1/H^(2/nu) (asymmetric case), corresponding to edges B-E and C-D of the Pareto polygon respectively (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Measured symmetric mean-field exponents are a*=0.485 [0.479,0.492] (nu=4, p=16), 0.492 [0.486,0.498] (nu=4, p=8), and 0.305 [0.292,0.315] (nu=6, p=8), matching 2/nu rather than the registered 1/H; bootstrap intervals exclude a=1 by >50 half-widths, and residual H-drift at a=1 is −0.228 to −1.514 per decade versus −0.042 to −0.238 at a=2/nu. The asymmetric 2/nu scaling is confirmed (a*=0.595 approaching 0.667).

claims.claim: For the canonical polyadic (symmetric, nu=2) identity-tensor target, Section 9 derives a complete closed-form solution to the gradient flow (Equations 19-20), valid across all parameter scalings.
claims.evidence: An independently coded theory curve from eqs. (19)-(20) matches exact gradient flow (itself validated against RK4 on the full parameter ODE to rel.err 1.13e-08) with max_t abs(E[L]−theory)/(p/2) ≤ 0.0005 across six configurations including the paper's Fig. 5 setup (p=512, H=1024/512/256), at the Monte Carlo noise floor; long-time limits hit exactly 128.0000 and 0.0000 against max((p−H)/2, 0).

claims.claim: For the nu=4 symmetric case, Section 10 derives a gradient-ascent solution identifying convergent low-noise and divergent high-noise regimes separated by an explicit threshold given in Equation 23.
claims.evidence: The dichotomy reproduces (L→31.9998 below threshold vs blow-up to 6.33e12 above), the blow-up exponent is 1.335 vs predicted 4/3=1.3333, and over the paper's own theta axis (10^0–10^2) the boundary follows 1/theta with window-wise exponents converging −0.778→−0.833→−0.999 (p=8) and −0.778→−0.927 (p=16), with rho_c/rho* climbing monotonically to 0.815; robustness confirmed by 200x stricter divergence criterion and 4x finer step leaving brackets unchanged.

michaldobiezynski/repro-gradient-flow-th.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, from-scratch numerical verification of five of six claims with exact-arithmetic checks, Monte Carlo cross-validation, and non-trivial model sizes (H up to 16384, p up to 512), all on CPU with deterministic reproducibility. Claim 4 is falsified as registered: the symmetric mean-field exponent is measured as 2/nu (not 1/H) for nu>2, matching the paper's Appendix E rather than its Section 5 shorthand.

sotayamashita/repro-beyond-first-order-a.paper_title: Beyond First-order Asymptotics in Sequential Mean Testing

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 establishes a central limit theorem for the empirical KL_inf statistic, showing sqrt(n)(KL_inf(q_hat_n, m_o) - KL_inf(q, m_o)) converges in distribution to N(0, sigma^2(q, m_o)) (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: On Bernoulli(0.6) with m0=0.2 and 20,000 samples per n, the standardized variance is 1.012 at n=100, 1.002 at n=500, and 1.015 at n=2000, with KS distance to N(0,1) decreasing from 0.053 to 0.012 across n∈{100,250,500,1000,2000}, providing concrete numerical support for the CLT on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 extends this result to the stopping time tau_alpha, proving sqrt(log(1/alpha))(tau_alpha/log(1/alpha) - 1/KL_inf(q,m_o)) converges to a Gaussian limit N(0, sigma^2_bd(q,m_o)) as alpha to 0 (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: With 20,000 paths per alpha over {10^-4,…,10^-128}, the constant-boundary standardized variance stays in 0.99–1.02 and KS distance decreases from 0.091 at 10^-4 to 0.018 at 10^-128, demonstrating the asymptotic Gaussian convergence of the stopping time as alpha→0.

claims.claim: The proof decomposes the normalized KL_inf statistic into a term from the dual optimization (shown to vanish in probability) and a standard empirical-mean term that converges to Gaussian, combined with verification of Anscombe's condition to transfer the CLT to the stopping time (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The RMS of the root-n-scaled difference between optimized empirical KL-inf and the objective at the population dual maximizer (λ*=-2.5) decreases monotonically from 0.087 (n=100) to 0.039 (n=500) to 0.020 (n=2000), supporting the vanishing optimization term in the decomposition; however, the Anscombe condition itself is not independently tested.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.5 constructs asymptotically valid confidence intervals for the stopping time using only a single simulation run, without requiring multiple independent replicates (Proposition 4.5).
claims.evidence: Single-path plug-in intervals show coverage increasing from 0.803 at alpha=10^-4 to 0.945 at alpha=10^-128 across 20,000 independent paths, approaching the 0.95 asymptotic target as alpha decreases, with each interval constructed from only its own stopping path.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments on synthetic Beta and Bernoulli distributions and on real crop-yield data show empirical stopping-time distributions converging to the theoretical Gaussian limit, with stronger agreement at smaller significance levels alpha (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Only Bernoulli(0.6) experiments were run (KS distance 0.053→0.012 for fixed-sample, 0.091→0.018 for stopping-time); the Beta(3,2) synthetic experiments and DSSAT crop-yield real-data experiments explicitly were not reproduced, covering only a subset of the distributions claimed in Section 5.

sotayamashita/repro-beyond-first-order-a.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence on a non-toy Bernoulli(0.6) setup with 20,000 samples/paths supporting the fixed-sample CLT (Theorem 4.2), stopping-time CLT (Theorem 4.4), decomposition vanishing term, and single-path interval coverage (Proposition 4.5). The broader Section 5 numerical claim is only partially addressed, as Beta and DSSAT crop-yield experiments are entirely missing.

michaldobiezynski/repro-full-batch-gradi.paper_title: Full-Batch Gradient Descent Outperforms One-Pass SGD: Sample Complexity Separation in Single-Index Learning

claims.claim: For quadratic activation σ(z) = z², when the sample size n = o(d log d), spherical gradient flow fails to achieve weak recovery, showing full-batch updates offer no statistical advantage over one-pass SGD in this regime (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: At fixed δ=n/d=3 (which is o(d log d)), the squared-overlap decays monotonically with d from 0.370 (d=50) to 0.152 (d=800), with slope vs log d = −0.084 (R²=0.956), and the empirical threshold δ* grows from [3,3,4,4] across d=[50,100,200,400] with slope 0.577 (R²=0.80). This is finite-d directional evidence on a non-toy setup (d≤800, 16 seeds, paper's own Fig-1 hyperparameters) consistent with the asymptotic failure claim.

claims.claim: With a truncated quadratic activation, full-batch spherical gradient flow achieves weak recovery with only n ≳ d samples, compared to the n ≳ d log d samples required by one-pass SGD, establishing a sample complexity separation (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: At δ=8, the truncated-activation squared-overlap is essentially flat across d: [0.77,0.78,0.72,0.77,0.77] with slope −0.001, while plain quadratic decays (slope −0.032). At matched n (δ=3, d=100), full-batch truncated gives 0.34 vs one-pass SGD 0.04. The d-independent plateau directly supports n≳d for truncated full-batch; the SGD gap supports the separation directionally.

claims.claim: Using the truncated activation on squared loss with small initialization (r₀ = d^-15), full-batch gradient descent achieves strong recovery in T ≳ log d gradient steps given n ≥ CM⁴d samples (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: T_strong (steps to overlap>0.99) at δ=10, M=8, η=0.1/M², init 1/d² is [1341,1532,1703,1837,2001] for d=50…800, with a clean linear fit vs log d: slope=234.6, R²=0.996. The init substitution (1/d² instead of d^-15, which underflows float64) uses the paper's own Fig-2 figure init and is documented.

claims.claim: The trajectory of full-batch gradient descent decomposes into an initial angle-reduction phase lasting O(log d/η) steps followed by geometric convergence during a refinement phase (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Phase-1 length (steps to overlap≥0.5) grows with log d: [343,477,487,546,672] for d=50…800, slope=104.7 (R²=0.93), consistent with O(log d/η). Phase-2 (overlap≥0.9 to strong recovery) shows log ‖θ_t−θ*‖² linear in t with mean R²=0.999 across d, confirming geometric convergence.

claims.claim: Full-batch methods with truncated activation match the information-theoretic sample lower bound of n ≳ d, removing the extra log d factor that is unavoidable for one-pass SGD under quadratic activation (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: The quadratic threshold δ* grows with log d (slope 0.577, values [3,3,4,4]) while the truncated threshold stays roughly flat (slope 0.216, values [2.5,3,3,3]). Corroborated by fixed-δ curves: at δ=8 the truncated overlap slope is −0.001 (flat) vs quadratic −0.032 (decaying). The evidence is directional and rests on a coarse grid (R²=0.60 for truncated threshold), but the combined picture supports the claimed log-d removal.

michaldobiezynski/repro-full-batch-gradi.overall: The logbook provides concrete finite-d numerical evidence on a non-toy setup (d up to 800, paper's own hyperparameters, multiple seeds) that directionally supports all five claims: the strongest results are the clean T~log d scaling for strong recovery (R²=0.996) and the two-phase trajectory with geometric convergence (R²=0.999), while the asymptotic threshold claims (1 and 5) are supported only directionally via finite-d trends with moderate R² values.

michaldobiezynski/repro-gradient-flow-sa.paper_title: Gradient Flow Sampler-based Distributionally Robust Optimization

claims.claim: The paper introduces a unified PDE gradient flow framework for distributionally robust optimization (DRO) with six concrete algorithms, including Wasserstein Gradient Flow (Algorithm 3) and Wasserstein Fisher-Rao flow (Algorithm 4) variants for entropy-regularized Wasserstein DRO (Section 4, Algorithms 3-4).
claims.evidence: At d=50 on a nonconvex sigmoid Sinkhorn-DRO problem with a 250k-sample SNIS reference, WGF (Alg 3), WFR (Alg 4), and RGO (Alg 6) all produce DRO gradient estimates within 2.1% relative error of the reference worst-case conditional, while SVG (Alg 5) fails at 7.95% exactly as the paper predicts; the ε→0 reduction to WRM closes linearly (0.499→0.039) and RGO's τ-limitation is confirmed by acceptance-rate collapse (0.264→0.00042).

claims.claim: Proposition 1 shows the Wasserstein gradient flow sampler must run for time at least on the order of O((1/λ) log(L/√(λε))) to produce an ε-accurate gradient estimate (Section 4, Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: On the real d=50 WGF inner flow across an 8× range of λ and 6.7× range of L, the measured first-passage-time coefficient scales as λ^(−1.089) (R²=0.943) against the stated 1/λ prefactor, and the log(1/ε) dependence is confirmed with λ·dT/dlog(1/ε) flat at 0.536±0.117 across all λ values.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 proves the outer loop of the gradient-flow-sampler-based DRO algorithm requires O(1/ε²_opt) iterations to reach an ε-stationary point (Section 5, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Running the actual two-loop Algorithm 3 on the d=50 nonconvex Sinkhorn-DRO objective with measured L_Φ=0.0522 and constant step r=1/L_Φ over 3 seeds, the log-log slope of outer iterations S vs 1/ε_opt is 2.161 (R²=0.9975), stable across windows (2.009/2.305), and S·ε²_opt stays bounded within 1.5× over 1.06 decades.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 bounds the total computational complexity of the WGF-based DRO algorithm (Algorithm 3) as Õ(L_Φ L²_U L²_f d² / (λ³_U ε⁴_opt)) (Section 5, Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Running full Algorithm 3 with d swept 25→200 (8×) and L_U²/α_U³ swept 50×, the measured dimension exponent is 0.745 (vs bound's 2) and geometry exponent 0.212 (vs bound's 1); the measured-cost/bound ratio is ≤1 and monotonically decreasing on both sweeps, confirming the upper bound holds conservatively.

claims.claim: On CIFAR-10 adversarial training under PGD attacks, the WFR- and WGF-based DRO methods achieve consistently higher robust accuracy across all perturbation settings compared to baseline DRO methods (Section 6.3).
claims.evidence: Real CIFAR-10 with PGD-7 attacks is used, but at drastically reduced scale: 5000/50000 training images, 3 epochs, and a 33k-parameter CNN achieving ~38% clean accuracy (barely above 10% random), with margins of only 0.9–1.5 points over 2 seeds; WGF beats baselines at 3/3 budgets and WFR at η_w=0.004 also does, but WFR at η_w=0.10 only wins 1/3, showing the result is fragile to hyperparameter choice at this scale.

claims.claim: Lemma 1 establishes that the entropy-regularized DRO problem is equivalent to a Schrödinger half-bridge problem, enabling sampling from the conditional worst-case distribution (Section 3.1, Lemma 1).
claims.evidence: At d=50 with N=16 data points and K=2500 support points on a nonconvex sigmoid loss, the first-order optimality residual of the DRO problem evaluated at the Schrödinger half-bridge solution is 4.55×10⁻¹⁵ (signal scale 0.9986), and an independent mirror-ascent route solving the two-marginal entropic-OT problem via Sinkhorn lands at TV 0.0094 from the half-bridge route with objective gap 2.74×10⁻⁴.

michaldobiezynski/repro-gradient-flow-sa.overall: The logbook provides strong quantitative evidence for claims 1–4 and 6 on a non-trivial d=50 nonconvex Sinkhorn-DRO setup with real algorithm implementations, measured scaling exponents, and independent verification routes. Claim 5 is addressed on real CIFAR-10 with PGD attacks but at severely reduced scale (10% data, tiny model, 3 epochs) with small and somewhat fragile margins, making it a toy-scale reproduction rather than a full verification.

michaldobiezynski/repro-near-optimal-reg.paper_title: Near-Optimal Regret for KL-Regularized Multi-Armed Bandits

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 establishes a high-probability regret upper bound of O~(ηK log^2 T) for KL-regularized multi-armed bandits in the high-regularization regime where η ≤ sqrt(T/K) (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: On a non-toy K=10 Bernoulli bandit with T up to 3×10^5 and 40 seeds, the log-log power-of-T fit gives slope 0.336 (ruling out polynomial-in-T growth), the (log T)² model fits far better than log T (RMSE 6.52 vs 29.90), and regret/η (CV 0.107) and regret/K (CV 0.036) are near-constant, supporting all three prongs of O~(ηK log² T). The fitted exponent 2.27 is close to 2, and the linearity checks use only 3 data points each, but the overall scaling evidence is substantive.

claims.claim: In the low-regularization regime (η ≥ sqrt(T/K)), the same analysis yields a regret bound of O~(sqrt(KT log T)), which is η-independent (Theorem 4.2, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: On minimax-gap Bernoulli instances (K=10, gap ~√(K/T)), the log-log slope of regret vs T is 0.507 (target 0.5), regret/√(KT) is constant at ≈0.95 with CV 0.010, and worst-case regret across η∈{200,500,2000} has CV 0.067, confirming both the √T rate and η-independence. The √(log T) sub-factor inside O~(√(KT log T)) is not separately isolated but is subdominant and plausibly absorbed by O~.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.3 provides a lower bound of Ω(ηK log(T/(η^2 K))) in the high-regularization regime, establishing near-tightness with the upper bound in Theorem 4.2 (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook reconstructs the Section 6.2 hard-instance family at real dimensions (K∈{50,100,200}, A=K/2 informative arms) and verifies the key proof step: min over all policies of the summed suboptimality between maximally-separated instances equals (0.249±0.001)·ηK/t with dimension-independent constant (CV 0.0039). The KL normalization equals exactly 2 and the time-summation ratio equals 1.000, assembling the stated Ω(ηK log(T/(η²K))) order including the Ω(K) dependence.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 gives a lower bound of Ω(sqrt(KT)) in the low-regularization regime via a two-point construction method (Section 6.1, Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook runs only KL-UCB (a single near-optimal algorithm) on the Section 6.1 hard instance (K=16) and shows it achieves Θ(√(KT)) regret (slope 1.033, ratio CV 0.017). This demonstrates achievability on the hard instance, not that no algorithm can beat √(KT), so it does not verify the lower bound claim. No proof-step reconstruction (unlike Claim 3) or multi-algorithm lower-bound verification is performed.

claims.claim: The KL-UCB algorithm uses an optimistic bonus term b_t(a) = sqrt(2 log(TK/delta) / (N_t(a) ∨ 1)) together with a novel peeling argument and Freedman's inequality to obtain tight high-probability bounds (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: The bonus b_t(a)=√(2 log(TK/δ)/(N_t(a)∨1)) is implemented exactly as specified, and over 2000 runs (K=10, T=20000, δ=0.05) the good event E(δ) is never violated (empirical P(fail)=0.0000), which is strong evidence for Lemma 4.1's coverage guarantee. The peeling and Freedman components are proof techniques not directly testable, but their algorithmic consequence (coverage) and the resulting tight bounds (verified in Claims 1–2) are empirically supported.

michaldobiezynski/repro-near-optimal-reg.overall: The logbook provides substantive empirical evidence for 4 of 5 claims through scaling checks, proof-step reconstruction at real dimensions, and coverage tests on non-toy bandit setups. Claim 4 (lower bound Ω(√(KT))) is left inconclusive because the logbook only demonstrates achievability by one algorithm on the hard instance rather than verifying the lower-bound argument over all algorithms.

sotayamashita/repro-foundations-of-equiv.paper_title: Foundations of Equivariant Deep Learning: Unifying Graph and Sheaf Neural Networks

claims.claim: The arXiv paper introduces sheaf neural networks by replacing graph Laplacian diffusion with sheaf-Laplacian diffusion that can encode asymmetric, signed, and varying-dimensional relations (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The reproduction independently constructed L_F = δᵀδ and passed six focused tests including orientation invariance, positive semidefiniteness, constant-sheaf equivalence to the graph Laplacian, and signed-edge preservation, confirming the sheaf-Laplacian diffusion operator encodes the claimed structural properties.

claims.claim: The sheaf diffusion operator is presented as a drop-in generalization of the diffusion operation used in graph convolutional networks (Section 2.1).
claims.evidence: A single train_network implementation accepts either D_F = I - L_F/d_max or the unsigned graph operator without operator-specific branching, with matched depth/width/seed across SheafNN-16/GCN-16 and SheafNN-32/GCN-32, and the constant-sheaf test recovers the ordinary graph Laplacian, demonstrating drop-in generalization.

claims.claim: On synthetic semi-supervised node-classification tasks over signed graphs, sheaf neural networks outperform Kipf-Welling GCN variants across feature and edge-noise regimes (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: Real experiments were run with 5 trials across 2×3×3 conditions showing SheafNN winning 36/36 matched comparisons (mean margin +0.18185), but at drastically reduced scale: 240 nodes vs 5000, 120 epochs vs 1000, and a 3×3 noise grid vs 5×5. A scaled attempt (600 nodes, 240 epochs) failed to produce metrics.

claims.claim: The experiments average results over five random graph trials and report standard-deviation error bars for SheafNN and GCN comparisons (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The results CSV contains 360 trial records (72 conditions × 5 trials), and summary.json shows all 72 architecture/condition summaries have trial_count = 5 and a finite sample_std_accuracy, confirming five-trial averaging with standard-deviation reporting.

sotayamashita/repro-foundations-of-equiv.overall: The logbook provides solid implementation-level verification for the structural and methodological claims (1, 2, 4) through focused unit tests and a five-trial experimental design with standard deviations. The central empirical claim (3) is supported only at substantially reduced scale (240 vs 5000 nodes, 120 vs 1000 epochs, smaller noise grid), with a scaled attempt having failed to produce usable metrics.

sotayamashita/repro-a-random-matrix-pers.paper_title: A Random Matrix Perspective on the Consistency of Diffusion Models

claims.claim: Diffusion models trained on non-overlapping dataset splits generate visually similar samples from the same seed, and the similarity is predicted by a Gaussian linear theory baseline (Figure 1)
claims.evidence: The agent tested only the Gaussian linear baseline on synthetic data (dimension 48), explicitly stating 'The neural image models and Figure 1 images were not rerun.' The MSE ratio and map RMSE results validate the linear mechanism but not the claim about trained diffusion models generating visually similar samples.

claims.claim: Finite-sample covariance effects renormalize the effective noise scale in the expected linear denoiser, causing overshrinkage of low-variance directions (Figure 2)
claims.evidence: The Silverstein fixed point was solved by bisection, yielding kappa=0.530 vs noise variance 0.4 at n=96. The RMT-renormalized denoiser RMSE was 0.00515 versus 0.0884 for the raw-population predictor, with correction correlation 0.989 and 100% of eigenmodes showing overshrinkage across all four sample sizes.

claims.claim: The denoiser-variance theory predicts anisotropic, location-dependent cross-split deviations that decay with dataset size (Result 4.2)
claims.evidence: Across n=96–768, anisotropy Pearson correlations ranged 0.901–0.922, location Spearman correlations 0.906–0.955, and the fitted variance scaling slope was -1.087, consistent with the predicted inverse-n decay. All three factorization components of Result 4.2 were directly tested.

claims.claim: The sampling-map analysis gives deterministic-equivalence formulas for expectation and variance over full diffusion trajectories (Results 5.1 and 5.2)
claims.evidence: Full-trajectory integration via Gauss-Legendre quadrature yielded mean-map relative RMSE of 0.0015–0.0089, empirical/theory variance ratios of 0.817–1.184, and a cross-split scaling slope of -0.980, all passing predeclared thresholds at every sample size.

claims.claim: UNet and DiT experiments validate the theory's predictions about consistency, overshrinkage, and eigenmode-dependent deviations in the non-memorization regime (Figure 5)
claims.evidence: The agent explicitly states 'The paper-scale neural experiment requires image datasets and 50,000-step training runs across non-overlapping splits; it was not rerun.' No UNet or DiT experiments were conducted, so the claim about neural-network validation remains unaddressed.

sotayamashita/repro-a-random-matrix-pers.overall: The logbook provides solid numerical evidence for the paper's theoretical RMT claims (Claims 2–4) through synthetic Gaussian experiments at dimension 48 with appropriate methods (Silverstein fixed point, Monte Carlo, quadrature). However, the diffusion-model-specific claims (Claims 1 and 5) were not substantiated: Claim 1 was only tested on the linear baseline without trained models, and Claim 5's UNet/DiT experiments were never run.

michaldobiezynski/repro-solving-stochast.paper_title: Solving Stochastic Variational Inequalities without the Bounded Variance Assumption

claims.claim: All three proposed methods replace the standard bounded-variance assumption with the relaxed condition E||G̃(z)-G(z)||^2 ≤ B^2||z-z0||^2 + σ^2, allowing variance to grow with distance from a reference point z0 (Section 1).
claims.evidence: On a d=100 VI with a constructed growing-variance oracle (B=0.15, σ=0.05), the logbook empirically measures E||G̃-G||² = 1.374 against the bound value 1.375 over 20,000 oracle draws and 5 seeds, confirming the relaxed variance condition holds. The bounded-variance baseline (SGDA) diverges to ~9.4e4 while the paper's FBF converges to 0.003, demonstrating practical relevance of the relaxed assumption.

claims.claim: The mini-batching forward-backward-forward algorithm achieves Õ(ε^-4) oracle complexity for the weak-Minty nonmonotonicity parameter ρ < 1/(12L) (Section 2).
claims.evidence: At d=100, 5 seeds, 200k iterations, mini-batch FBF achieves complexity exponents of 3.72 (linear weak-MVI at 96% of 1/(12L) threshold) and 3.54 (nonlinear weak-MVI at 88% of threshold), with final ε-window exponents rising to 3.78 and 3.81, converging to 4 from below. N(ε)·ε⁴ is bounded and non-increasing across ~2 decades of ε, directly confirming the Õ(ε⁻⁴) upper bound on instances sitting hard against the ρ threshold.

claims.claim: The multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) method achieves the same Õ(ε^-4) complexity while tolerating the widest nonmonotonicity range ρ < 1/L, the strongest of the three theoretical results (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Inside the MLMC-only band (1/(12L) < ρ < 1/L), MLMC achieves exponent 3.67 (stable across windows: 3.64→3.68) at ρ=0.2752 (3.4× the FBF threshold) and 3.05 at ρ=0.2752 on a nonlinear operator (5.7× its FBF threshold). A 12-point ρ-tolerance sweep directly measures boundaries: FBF and VR stop at 0.119/L, MLMC continues to 0.447/L (3.8× wider), confirming both the same complexity and the widest nonmonotonicity range.

claims.claim: The variance-reduced single-loop algorithm uses only 3 stochastic oracle samples per iteration and incorporates Halpern anchoring for stability, under an added expected-Lipschitzness assumption (Section 4).
claims.evidence: A runtime oracle counter confirms exactly 3 stochastic samples per iteration across all 4000 iterations and 5 seeds on a d=100 weak-MVI instance, with the algorithm structure being one evaluation at z plus two at the half-step. Halpern anchoring β_k = 1/(k+1) = Θ(1/k) is implemented and the anchored iterate reaches residual 0.1926 (down from ~1.4), confirming both structural properties of the claim.

claims.claim: All three algorithms match the best-known Õ(ε^-4) complexity for driving the expected residual norm below ε on monotone and structured nonmonotone (weak-MVI) VIs, while applying to unbounded-domain bilinear min-max problems that violate the classical bounded-variance assumption (Section 1).
claims.evidence: All three algorithms are tested at d=100, 5 seeds, on both a monotone unbounded bilinear min-max (κ=30, ρ=0) and a weak-MVI operator (ρ at 96% of 1/(12L)), all under the growing-variance oracle that violates bounded variance. Every run reaches 1.4e-4 to 6.4e-4 residual with N(ε)·ε⁴ bounded and non-increasing; mini-batch FBF and MLMC attain exponents 3.69 and 3.37 (final windows 3.81, 3.71) on the weak-MVI instance, while VR single-loop runs inside the bound (exponent 1.78), all consistent with Õ(ε⁻⁴).

michaldobiezynski/repro-solving-stochast.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence at d=100 with 5 seeds across linear, bilinear, and nonlinear weak-MVI instances, measuring complexity exponents in the asymptotic regime, confirming ρ-threshold orderings via sweep, and verifying the 3-samples/iter budget via runtime counters. All five claims are supported by non-toy experimental runs with proper methodology, though the exact algorithm constants are standard instantiations rather than paper-specified values and the upper MLMC range (0.45/L to 1/L) is not tested.

michaldobiezynski/repro-finite-time-conv.paper_title: Finite-time Convergence Analysis of Actor-Critic with Evolving Reward

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 establishes finite-time bounds for single-timescale actor-critic with evolving rewards, with actor error G_T and critic error W_T each bounded by O(1/√T) + O(F_T·√T) + O(√(F_T/T)) + O(ε), where F_T measures cumulative reward-parameter variation over T iterations (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: On a 300-state, 20-action MDP with a 150-dim critic over 4 seeds and T=80K, the theorem's RHS is never violated (measured/bound ratio 7.24e-05→8.23e-06), and the distinctive F_T mechanism is demonstrated: actor-error decay shifts from -0.519 (F_T→0) to -0.209 (F_T=Θ(1)), with the gap growing 1.26×→2.39× as T increases, matching the O(F_T·√T) prediction.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.7 shows that when the reward parameter is updated via gradient-based steps with step size η^φ_t = c_φ/t and bounded gradients, F_T = O(1/T), so the bounds reduce to G_T = O(1/√T) + O(ε) and W_T = O(1/√T) + O(ε), matching the best-known rate for static-reward actor-critic (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: With η^φ_t = c_φ/t, F_T decays at log-log slope -2.001 (stable at -1.998 over last two decades), satisfying O(1/T); actor and critic errors decay at slopes -0.519 and -1.155 (both ≤ -0.5), and the evolving/static error ratio stays ≤1.40 across the full T grid, versus 3.35 for non-decaying reward variation.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.8 bounds the distribution mismatch under Markovian sampling without dependence on the mixing time, improving prior convergence rates by a factor of log²T in the static-reward case (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: The exactly-propagated distribution mismatch stays ≤0.177·η^θ_t/(1−γ) across a 50× mixing-time range (t_mix 18→901), with the multiplicative constant moving only 1.90× while t_mix moves 50×; mismatch·√t contracts 0.42–0.74× across the last two decades where log²T would require 3.13× growth, confirming no log²T inflation.

claims.claim: Assumption 4.1 (sufficient exploration) requires the matrix A_θ to be negative definite with singular values bounded above by -λ, underpinning the actor-critic convergence analysis (Section 4, Assumption 4.1).
claims.evidence: Across 300 (MDP, policy) constructions at S=400, d=200, A_θ is negative definite in every case (worst eigenvalue -3.5e-05); the implied λ upper-bounds the observed critic contraction in all 60 mean-path runs (correlation 0.992), and off-policy re-weighting breaks negative definiteness in 100/100 constructions (eigenvalues up to +0.0261), showing the assumption is non-vacuous.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 defines a single-timescale actor-critic scheme with step sizes η^θ_t = c_θ/√t and η^ω_t = c_ω/√t for policy and critic updates, alongside an arbitrary update rule for the evolving reward parameter φ_t (Section 3.3, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 implemented from scratch at S=500, A=20, d=200, d_θ=200 over 5 seeds × 120K iterations: all seeds keep iterates finite and raise the discounted return (e.g., 5.065→6.207), with G_T and W_T decaying at slopes -0.544 and -1.186; ablation shows c/√t beats c/t (23× worse actor error) and two-timescale (35× worse actor error) on identical problems and seeds.

michaldobiezynski/repro-finite-time-conv.overall: The logbook provides a from-scratch numpy implementation of the paper's Algorithm 1 with linear function approximation, tested on MDPs with 200–500 states, 10–20 actions, and 100–200 dimensional critics over up to 120K iterations with multiple seeds. All five claims are supported by concrete numerical evidence including closed-form computation of the paper's own error quantities, appropriate ablations, and honest reporting of limitations.

Edd16/icml2026-aaFfUg013C-repro.paper_title: EPSVec: Efficient and Private Synthetic Data Generation via Dataset Vectors

claims.claim: Dataset vectors are computed and privatized once and incur no additional privacy cost for generating arbitrarily many subsequent synthetic samples, decoupling privacy budget from generation volume (Section 4, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: A numpy simulation (HF Job 6a5c7e4a) perturbs a single vector with Gaussian noise calibrated to (ε=1.0, δ=1e-5) and shows identical RDP bounds (0.1704) and DP epsilon (1.815) for 1 vs. 1000 post-processed samples. This validates the post-processing principle on a simplified vector, not on real embeddings or LLM-scale generation.

claims.claim: At privacy budget epsilon=5, EPSVec++ achieves MAUVE scores of 72.3±2.7 on IMDb and 62.2±0.2 on BioRxiv, versus 14.9±2.2 and 1.9±0.1 respectively for the PP++ baseline, though PP++ scores higher on Yelp (69.8±3.0 vs. 62.9±4.0) (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The 'claim-1-fix' page performs no MAUVE computation, no text generation, and uses no real datasets; it simply restates the paper's exact numbers (72.3±2.7, 62.2±0.2, 14.9±2.2, 1.9±0.1) as a 'local computation' with no HF job or GPU. No Yelp results are addressed at all.

claims.claim: A BERT classifier trained on EPSVec-generated synthetic data and evaluated on real data reaches 86.9% accuracy on IMDb, exceeding the 86.0% achieved when training directly on real data (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The 'claim-2-fix' page performs no BERT training, no synthetic data generation, and no classification; it merely restates the paper's numbers (86.9% vs 86.0%) as a 'local computation' with no HF job or GPU.

claims.claim: Ablation on IMDb shows dataset-vector injection alone improves MAUVE from 48.2 to 67.8, and pretrained (non-instruction-tuned) base models outperform instruction-tuned models, improving from 28.6 to 67.8 MAUVE with the full pipeline (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The 'claim-3-fix' page performs no ablation and computes no MAUVE scores; it just restates the paper's numbers (48.2→67.8) and does not address the pretrained-vs-instruction-tuned comparison (28.6→67.8) at all.

claims.claim: Generation occurs at standard inference cost without the batch-size dependencies of prompting-based private baselines (PP/PP++), requiring the fewest private in-context samples among compared methods (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: The 'claim-4-fix' page presents a purely conceptual cost model with assumed numbers (standard cost = batch size exactly) and no real inference timing; the 'claim-3' page offers a trivial operation count (1 vs 1000 by construction). Neither measures actual inference cost, and the 'fewest private in-context samples' claim (Figure 5) is never addressed.

Edd16/icml2026-aaFfUg013C-repro.overall: This logbook provides only one real (toy) experiment — a numpy RDP simulation for Claim 1 — while all other claims are addressed by either restating the paper's numbers without computation or presenting trivial conceptual arguments. No real text generation, MAUVE evaluation, BERT training, or inference timing was performed.

Edd16/icml2026-SDyesowNUa-repro.paper_title: Private Learning with Public Feature Conditioning

claims.claim: Cond-DP replaces the standard public embedding Θ^pub x^pub with a conditioned version Θ^pub C x^pub, where C is derived from the structure of public features, then applies DPSGD to the resulting loss (Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: HF job 6a5dd366bee6ee1cf4ed2185 runs a proxy experiment on synthetic public feature covariance with M = Phi_public^{-1/2}, reporting condition number improvement (2500→1.0) and gradient variance reduction (66%). This demonstrates the preconditioning concept but does not implement Algorithm 1's specific Θ^pub C x^pub formulation on real data.

claims.claim: Cond-DP satisfies (ε,δ)-differential privacy with noise variance σ² = Õ(M²T/ε²n²), incurring no additional privacy cost relative to standard DPSGD (Theorem 4.3).

claims.claim: Proposition 3.5 bounds the average consensus error of the decision, tracking, and auxiliary variables at O((ab)^-n K^-1) under the strongly-connected time-varying directed graph assumption (Section 3, Proposition 3.5, Assumption 3.1).

claims.claim: FAB is empirically validated on distributed hyperparameter tuning, distributed data hyper-cleaning on Fashion-MNIST and BERT/IMDB, and distributed policy evaluation for reinforcement learning, with an ablation over network size, mixing-matrix weights, and model size (Section 4.1-4.3, Figures 1-8).

sabaridsnfuji/repro-on-the-epistemic-unc.paper_title: On the Epistemic Uncertainty of Overparametrized Neural Networks

claims.claim: Overparametrized one-hidden-layer ReLU networks (M>M* neurons) exhibit continuous non-identifiability through weight-splitting, where redundant neurons split a true neuron's contribution via coefficients constrained to a simplex, in addition to the discrete permutation symmetries present in exactly-specified models (Section 3.1, Section 3.2, Corollary 2).
claims.evidence: The corrected experiment (t16_claim1_v2.py) builds M=4 genuine per-neuron ReLU units with weights w_j = lambda_j * a_true, each passed through its own ReLU, and confirms sum_j ReLU(w_j·x) = ReLU(a_true·x) with max error 3.553e-15 across 20 Dirichlet splits × 200 random inputs. Off-simplex coefficients (negative, non-normalized) correctly break the identity, confirming the simplex constraint is necessary and matching Corollary 2.

claims.claim: Because standard information-theoretic uncertainty measures fail on these non-identifiable parameters, epistemic uncertainty is instead defined via the trace of the posterior weight covariance, EU(y|x) := tr(Cov_P(w|·)), enabling a variance-based decomposition into discrete (permutation) and continuous (splitting) sources of residual uncertainty (Section 2.1, Section 2.2, Example 1).
claims.evidence: The corrected experiment (eu_c2_v2.py) on a small network (p=3, M*=2, M=5) confirms both discrete and continuous EU sources are genuine non-trivial contributors (EU_disc=2.82, EU_cont=0.61, EU_full=3.20), but exact additivity does not hold (7.1% gap between EU_full and EU_disc+EU_cont). The paper does not claim strict additivity, so the qualitative decomposition is supported but the quantitative decomposition is only demonstrated on a toy-scale network.

claims.claim: For one-hidden-layer ReLU networks, Theorem 1 characterizes the induced posterior over splitting coefficients as following symmetric Dirichlet distributions with concentration parameter alpha=(p+1)/2 (Lemma 4), with posterior means of individual redundant neurons scaling as O(M^-1/2) and within-neuron covariance remaining constant while cross-neuron covariance decays as O(M^-1) (Theorem 1, Corollary 1, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Real importance-resampling posterior sampling across M=5–80 confirms posterior-mean-norm scaling exponent -0.508 (theory -0.5), but the Dirichlet concentration alpha=(p+1)/2 is only confirmed as a generative mechanism (Gaussian weights → chi² norms → Dirichlet, fitted alpha within 0.6% of theory at k=3,5,8) rather than from actual posterior inference (which recovers the sampling prior alpha≈1 due to flat likelihood). The cross/within-covariance-ratio exponent -1.365 deviates 36% from theory -1.0, and within-neuron covariance constancy is not clearly confirmed.

claims.claim: The posterior over splitting coordinates remains non-degenerate even as the number of training samples n approaches infinity, showing that substantial parameter-space uncertainty persists despite the underlying function being fully identified (Section 3.2, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The corrected experiment (t16_claim4_v2.py) generates real synthetic data for n=10–10000 and confirms std(loglik) across Dirichlet splittings stays at machine precision (~4e-16 to ~5e-13) for all n, while std(loglik) across true-weight perturbations grows from 0.045 to 24.4. Empirical posterior over splitting coefficients via rejection sampling stays within 0.008 of the prior mean with stable entropy proxy (~2.86–2.89) across all n, confirming no concentration as n grows.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-on-the-epistemic-unc.overall: The logbook provides genuine numerical verification of the structural mathematical claims about weight-splitting non-identifiability (Claim 1) and non-degenerate posterior as n→∞ (Claim 4) on small but appropriate one-hidden-layer ReLU network setups. The EU decomposition (Claim 2) and Dirichlet concentration/scaling claims (Claim 3) are only partially confirmed on toy-scale networks, with notable gaps including non-additivity of EU sources and the Dirichlet concentration being confirmed only as a generative mechanism rather than from actual posterior inference.

claims.claim: For any ρ > 0, there exists a ρ-TV-stable RL algorithm supporting exact unlearning with expected computational cost equal to only a ρ√(ln T) fraction of full retraining from scratch (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: Measured unlearning cost as a fraction of full retraining across T up to 65,536 and ρ from 0.02 to 0.40 with 6,000 deletions per cell; regression yields fraction ~ ρ^0.926 (ln T)^0.517 (R²=0.994), closely matching the predicted ρ^1 (ln T)^0.5 scaling.

claims.claim: The proposed algorithm achieves a regret bound of O(H³S²A + H²√(SAT) + H^2.5·S²A/ρ)·polylog(T,H,S,A,1/δ) for tabular MDPs with unlearning support (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Regret measured on tabular MDPs (S=5,A=3,H=5, 4 seeds) shows T-exponent of 0.561 at low noise matching √T, and excess regret scaling as ρ^-0.938 vs predicted ρ^-1; a 180-cell scope expansion up to (16,6,10) confirms regret stays below the three-term bound in all configurations.

claims.claim: A matching lower bound of Ω(H√(SAT) + HSA/ρ) is established, showing the algorithm is nearly minimax optimal (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: Exact Bayes regret computed with Fraction arithmetic on the paper's adversarial hard MDP family (3S states, Bernoulli absorbing) across 11 cells (A=2,3,4; n=2–16), all yielding positive normalized regret consistent with H√(SAT); exact TV-stability calibration across 9 cells confirms HSA/ρ floor with coupling budget 4t_a·ρ·Δ=1/4.

claims.claim: Exact unlearning is formalized as requiring the post-unlearning output distribution to be identical to that of an algorithm that never observed the deleted data (Definition 2.1), operationalized via ρ-TV-stability where TV(A(Z), A(Z')) ≤ ρ for neighboring sequences (Definition 2.2).
claims.evidence: Exact replacement checks on 2,326,848 finite sequences (dimensions 1–3, horizons 4–8) and 1,269,504 additional cells (dimensions 1–4, horizons 9–31) all show byte-exact identity between edited prefix vectors and fresh rebuilds, confirming the sufficient-statistic edit mechanics and maximal-coupling distributional correctness underlying the TV-stability definition.

claims.claim: The construction uses a binary tree mechanism with noise-perturbed prefix sums requiring only O(log T) shared noise samples per query, achieving O(Td) space and O(d·log T) per-episode update time (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Directly counted ancestor updates per episode equal exactly log2(T)+1 at T=256,1024,4096,16384; allocated nodes equal exactly 2T−1 (2.00 per leaf); nodes touched per deletion remain 2.2–2.9 independent of T; 411 additional non-power-of-two cases all pass dyadic decomposition checks.

claims.claim: The additional regret cost term for unlearning, H³S²A/ρ, improves upon the corresponding differentially-private RL cost term of H^3.5·S²A/ε by a factor of √H (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Exact Fraction arithmetic over 405 cells confirms the √H ratio holds, but the specific exponents in the claim (H³S²A/ρ and H^3.5·S²A/ε) do not match the pinned source, which states H^2.5·S²A/ρ and H³·S²A/ε; the registered/source squared-rate ratio is exactly H in every cell, confirming the exponent mismatch is systematic.

ProCreations/repro-exact-unlearning-in-r.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental and exact-arithmetic evidence supporting claims 1–5, including measured cost scaling, regret bounds, lower-bound constructions, definition mechanics, and binary-tree complexity. Claim 6 is falsified because the specific exponents stated in the claim differ from the pinned source, even though the qualitative √H improvement factor is correct.

Edd16/icml2026-UstfBHsp6p-repro.paper_title: Tuning the Implicit Regularizer of Masked Diffusion Language Models: Enhancing Generalization via Insights from $k$-Parity
