sotayamashita/repro-physics-from-video.paper_title: Physics from Video: Identifiability of Time-Invariant Second-Order ODEs under Minimal Trajectory Conditions

claims.claim: The level-set slope-coverage condition (Definition 4.1) requires that each state level of the latent trajectory be attained at least three times with distinct instantaneous velocities, which guarantees the learned latent space is locally affine to the true physical state and enables exact recovery of the ODE parameters.
claims.evidence: The logbook describes exact SymPy symbolic verification of the chain-rule reduction to a quadratic Q(u,v)=A(u)v²+B(u)v+C(u), the three-root Vandermonde determinant (v₁-v₂)(v₁-v₃)(v₂-v₃)≠0 forcing f''=0 and parameter recovery, plus a two-slope adverse control showing the quadratic remains nonzero. These are correct algebraic arguments at full theorem scope with machine-readable certificates referenced.

claims.claim: For strictly underdamped second-order ODEs, a single video clip of length at least twice the oscillation period suffices to identify the physical parameters (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides the exact argument that zero crossings spaced by P/2 yield three interior crossings in any 2P window with pairwise-distinct velocities v, -qv, q²v (q∈(0,1)), plus a 100-phase numerical scan confirming all cases had ≥3 interior crossings, and a zero-damping adverse control where q=1 causes velocity coincidence. This covers the full theorem scope.

claims.claim: In critically damped, overdamped, and undamped regimes, a single trajectory lacks sufficient slope diversity to satisfy the coverage condition, so parameters are not identifiable from one clip alone (Theorem 4.5).
claims.evidence: The logbook covers all four characteristic-root branches with exact certificates: distinct real roots (derivative has at most one zero), repeated real root (degree-one factor), constant solution (one state, zero speed), and undamped (v²=ω²(A²-u²) giving at most two velocities). Each branch correctly shows coverage fails, matching the theorem's non-identifiability conclusion.

claims.claim: Three trajectories with diverse velocities at each shared state level can substitute for temporal coverage within a single clip, restoring identifiability of the shared physics parameters across regimes (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: The logbook applies the same trajectory-agnostic chain-rule quadratic from Claim 1 across three trajectories, showing one root per trajectory yields the same nonzero Vandermonde determinant forcing all coefficients to vanish, with a two-trajectory adverse control where (v-v₁)(v-v₂) remains nonzero. The algebraic argument is correct at full theorem scope.

claims.claim: On a real wheel-mounted phone pendulum, the encoder-only method recovers a damping parameter gamma0 = 8.998 +/- 0.009 compared to the physics-based estimate of 8.26, and a variance-floor regularizer outperforms a KL-divergence regularizer, particularly in non-oscillatory regimes (Experimental Validation section).
claims.evidence: The resource audit documents that all required evidence is absent from the official repository: no wheel-phone source video, no processed real-video input, no five trial outputs, and no variance-floor vs KL comparison outputs. A synthetic CPU smoke run at seed 0 and 10 steps was completed but does not test the real-video claim.

sotayamashita/repro-physics-from-video.overall: The logbook provides mathematically sound exact symbolic verification for the four theoretical claims (chain-rule reduction, Vandermonde elimination, characteristic-root branch coverage, and multi-trajectory extension) with appropriate adverse controls. The real wheel-phone experimental claim remains unaddressed because the official repository lacks the source video, processed inputs, and trial outputs needed to reproduce it.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 proves that mean-shift-induced spiked eigenvalues (set Λ_A) are spectrally separable from the covariance-induced spikes (set Λ_P) in high dimensions, using tools from Random Matrix Theory under the additive low-rank perturbation model (Section 3, Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: At d=800 with one-spike Gaussian covariance and one mean-shift cluster at d/n=1, median absolute errors from the predicted spike value 4.5 are 0.1211 (covariance spike) and 0.1078 (mean-shift spike), providing finite-size evidence for two spectral sources but only under a single Gaussian family, not the theorem's general finite-fourth-moment assumptions.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.11 (Eigenspace Invariance) shows that the eigenspace of the uncontaminated sample covariance matrix remains asymptotically invariant under mean-shift mixture contamination, regardless of the mixture weight π (Section 3, Theorem 3.11).
claims.evidence: Across d=100,200,400,800 with one Gaussian family and one contamination proportion, the median invariance residual has log-log slope -0.526 reaching 0.2376 at d=800, showing convergence trends but not covering the theorem's general compactly supported spectral distributions or all mixture weights π.

claims.claim: The proposed two-stage Mean-Shift PCA (MS-PCA, Algorithm 1) deliberately injects an artificial knockoff mean-shift perturbation A'_n = m'γ'^T with mixture weight π' (e.g., π'=0.5 or π'=1) and threshold ϵ=Cn^(-1/2) to identify and remove the mean-shift eigenvalues while leaving covariance-induced eigenvalues invariant (Section 2, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: At d=800, d/n=1, π'=1, C=1, Algorithm 1 returned a stable spiked component in only 16 of 25 trials (64%); a concrete counterexample at d=400, seed=4402800 shows original spikes [4.842, 4.475] and perturbed spikes [7.248, 4.731, 4.411] with no match within ε=0.05, and dense/iterative eigenvalues agree within 1.33e-14 ruling out numerical error.

claims.claim: Both mean-shift-induced spikes and covariance-induced spikes fluctuate at order O(n^-1/2), except the largest eigenvalue at the spectral edge which fluctuates at order O(n^-2/3), as used to set the matching threshold in the algorithm (Section 2, citing Theorem 2.19/2.16/2.15 of prior RMT results).
claims.evidence: Using 25 trials at four sizes, the spectral-edge eigenvalue standard deviation has log-log slope -0.658 (close to -2/3) while the covariance-associated spike has slope -0.340 (vs expected -1/2), but four finite Gaussian sizes cannot establish the cited general asymptotic RMT fluctuation orders.

claims.claim: Section 4 numerical experiments show that existing Robust PCA methods fail to recover the true principal component even with only 5% outlier proportion when the aspect ratio d/n does not vanish (e.g., d/n=1), whereas MS-PCA consistently recovers it (Figure 2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Under the paper's stated conditions (5% contamination, d/n=1, d=800, 25 trials), MS-PCA returned no stable spiked component in 9 of 25 trials, making its first quartile alignment 0 despite a median alignment of 0.798, directly contradicting the claim that MS-PCA 'consistently recovers' the true principal component.

Claims 1, 2, and 4 receive only toy-level evidence from single-Gaussian-family experiments that cannot establish the general asymptotic theorems.

claims.claim: RACO directly applies conflict-averse gradient descent to objective-specific pairwise preference losses instead of relying on explicit reward models (Section 3).
claims.evidence: A closed-form pairwise DPO loss was implemented and gradient correctness confirmed via finite differences on 135 synthetic cases (max error 2.86e-10), but no actual RACO training, CAGrad application, or LLM alignment was performed; the logbook itself notes reward-model fitting, stochastic minibatches, and transformer training were not tested.

claims.evidence: No large-model training or evaluation was performed; the logbook explicitly states that multi-GPU training across Qwen 3, Llama 3, and Gemma 3, summarization/safety scoring, and baseline comparisons were entirely absent.

sotayamashita/repro-reward-free-alignmen.overall: The logbook provides rigorous numerical verification of the paper's theoretical contributions (Theorems 3.1–3.2) and mathematical formulations on synthetic test cases, but completely omits the large-scale empirical experiments that constitute the paper's main experimental claim. Claims 1–2 are confirmed only at the level of abstract mathematical properties on synthetic geometries, Claims 3–4 are numerically verified on smooth test functions, and Claim 5 is entirely unaddressed.

DineshAI/28nj9x9hLa.paper_title: A Fine-Grained Understanding of Uniform Convergence for Halfspaces

claims.claim: For inhomogeneous halfspaces in R^d with d>=2, Theorem 1.2 constructs distributions in the realizable case where consistent hypotheses incur population error Theta(d*ln(n/d)/n), matching the first-order VC bound and showing it is essentially tight (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: Monte-Carlo on the exact X_{d/2,k} construction across d∈{2,4,8,16} and n∈{4000,16000,64000} yields a stable ratio er_D/(d·ln(n/d)/n)=0.125, with P(er≥(1/144)·rate)=1.00 exceeding the proof's required 1/15. Symbolic exhaustive verification of Lemma 3.1 over d∈{2,4}, k∈{2,3,4,5} reports 0 failures, and the constant chain reconstructs c=1/144. Negative control on isotropic-sphere data gives ratio 0, confirming construction specificity.

claims.claim: Theorem 1.3 establishes an agnostic-case lower bound for inhomogeneous halfspaces showing the excess-error deviation scales as sqrt(tau*ln(1/tau)) where tau is the true error, again matching general VC theory (Theorem 1.3).
claims.evidence: Monte-Carlo on the exact X_{d/2,k} construction with d=64 and n up to ~613k shows deviation/√(er_S·d·ln(e/er_S)/n) stable at 0.73–0.84 across k∈{4,8,16,32,64}, with witnesses found in 400/400 trials and P(τ/2≤er_S≤2τ)=1.00. Lemma 3.2 (Klein–Young anti-concentration) is independently verified by exact binomial CDF over a grid with non-negative slack everywhere.

claims.claim: For homogeneous halfspaces in R^2, Theorem 1.4 shows every consistent hypothesis in the realizable case has population error at most ln(2/delta)/n, an O(1/n) rate improving on the standard VC bound by a logarithmic factor (Theorem 1.4).
claims.evidence: Exact version-space computation across uniform, boundary, and lopsided distributions at n∈{1000,4000,16000} gives q_0.95(er_D·n)∈[3.58,3.88]≈ln(2/0.05)=3.689, with empirical tail tracking 2(1−ε)^n. The δ-dependence is pinned: the (1−δ)-quantile of er_D·n equals ln(2/δ). Negative control with inhomogeneous R² halfspaces yields er_D·n/ln(n)≈1 (ln(n)/n rate), confirming the homogeneous hypothesis is essential.

claims.claim: Theorem 1.7 proves a matching lower bound showing the ln ln n overhead identified in Corollary 1.6 when combining dyadic risk bands is unavoidable, giving the first known separation between single-band and multi-band uniform convergence guarantees for R^2 homogeneous halfspaces (Corollary 1.6, Theorem 1.7).
claims.evidence: The exact §3.3 construction (k=2B^L circle points, nested C_i, disjoint shells) at L=4..9 with n up to ~4.83M shows multi-band normalized gap gap_mb constant (0.42–0.47) while single-band normalized gap gap_sb grows (0.656–0.689), with ratio gap_sb/gap_mb matching √(ln ln n) (1.45→1.65). Witness probability is 0.72–0.85, demonstrating the ln ln n overhead is unavoidable and the single-vs-multi-band separation.

claims.claim: The critical-wedge localization argument in Lemma 2.2 is the key technical tool used to derive the sharp dimensional threshold separating d=2 homogeneous halfspaces from general d>=2 behavior (Lemma 2.2).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive verification of Lemma 2.2's two obligations over 160 random atomic measures × 5 ε-values × shift grid yields 11200 shift checks with 0 violations; minimum measure slack ε−μ(G_ε°)≥0 and minimum shift slack er_D(h_α)−(ε−er_D(h_0))=0.0194>0. The dependency chain Lemma 2.2→Lemma 2.3→Theorem 1.5→Corollary 1.6 is documented, establishing the lemma's role in the dimensional threshold result.

DineshAI/28nj9x9hLa.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence on the paper's exact adversarial constructions at non-toy scale for all five claims, including stable rate ratios across multiple dimensions and sample sizes, negative controls confirming specificity, and symbolic verification of core lemmas. The main limitation is that lower-bound claims are corroborated on the specific construction rather than proven universally, and raw output from the new verification runs is not shown (only the superseded toy baseline output is displayed).

ProCreations/repro-on-the-role-of-batch-.paper_title: On the Role of Batch Size in Stochastic Conditional Gradient Methods

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 establishes in-expectation convergence for momentum stochastic conditional gradient (SCG) methods under a μ-KL condition, with stepsize β=O(1/K), learning rate η=Õ(1/μ), and momentum α=min{1,O((εμ)²/(ρσ)²)} (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 was run with Theorem 4.1's prescribed parameters on both a synthetic mu-KL quadratic (d=20) and MNIST multinomial logistic regression (d=7850, L and mu measured from data). On MNIST, K ranged 172-3489 (20x span) and achieved/eps stayed within 1.59x under one global constant, confirming the form of K(eps) and sufficiency of the parameter prescription on a real problem.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.1 derives a critical effective batch size BS ≍ (Tμρσ⋆/L)^(2/3), beyond which increasing batch size under a fixed token budget yields diminishing and eventually negative returns, splitting the error into noise-dominated, intermediate (scaling as T^(-1/3)), and iteration-starved regimes (Section 4, Corollary 4.1).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 was run on both synthetic (d=20) and MNIST (d=7850) setups across 5 token budgets each. U-shaped error curves in BS were observed in 5/5 budgets on both: error rises at small BS (noise-dominated) and large BS (iteration-starved), with a flat intermediate basin, directly observing the three-regime structure on real data.

claims.claim: The batch-size-times-sequence-length (BST) scaling rule predicts the optimal product BS scales as T^(2/3) with stepsize β∼1/K and constant momentum α (Equation 6, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The crossover BS was empirically located at 5 token budgets on synthetic quadratics, yielding exponents 0.664-0.765 against the predicted 0.667. A symbolic certificate with exact Fraction arithmetic verified BS~T^(2/3) for all positive parameters. Real regression experiments on 3/4 sklearn datasets bracketed 2/3 (0.56-0.71), with one outlier (iris, 1.02) honestly reported.

claims.claim: On a 124M-parameter NanoGPT model under a 1.3B-token training budget, the optimal configuration found empirically is batch size B=256, sequence length S=1024, and stepsize β=3.6×10^(-4) (Table 1-2, Section 6.3).
claims.evidence: Exact Fraction arithmetic on the paper's own Table 1 shows beta=2.4e-4 yields mean 3.3706 while the claimed optimal beta=3.6e-4 yields 3.3717, a difference of 11/10000 > 0. The claimed 'optimal' stepsize is not the strict argmin of the paper's own table, though the difference is within one standard deviation.

claims.claim: Increasing the batch size beyond the predicted optimum (e.g., to 2048 or 4096 for a 1B-parameter model) degrades validation loss by 0.005-0.04, consistent with the theoretical saturation-then-degradation prediction (Figures 3-4, Section 6.5-6.6).
claims.evidence: No independent NanoGPT or 1B-parameter training was run. The logbook only performed pixel-level extraction of the paper's own figure, confirming the reported degradation ranges (2048: +0.005-0.008, 4096: +0.028-0.039). This verifies the figure's content but provides no independent experimental evidence for the claim.

claims.claim: An adaptive restarting strategy that increases batch size and sequence length during training, following the derived scaling law, outperforms fixed schedules while preserving the theoretical convergence guarantees of Theorem 4.1 (Section 6.5-6.6).
claims.evidence: The paper's own text states restarted and fixed large-batch variants 'match in performance at the end of the training,' contradicting the unqualified 'outperforms.' Independent MNIST experiments (d=7850) confirmed the growing>shrinking direction (6/6) but the adaptive schedule beat a tuned fixed baseline in only 1/6 comparisons, failing to reproduce outperformance.

ProCreations/repro-on-the-role-of-batch-.overall: The logbook provides solid experimental verification of the theoretical claims (Claims 1-3) through synthetic and MNIST-scale experiments with measured problem constants, and falsifies Claims 4 and 6 using the paper's own data plus independent MNIST runs. Claim 5 remains unverified because no independent large-model training was conducted—only the paper's own figure was parsed.

Lumasik2006/repro-theoretical-limitation.paper_title: On the Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-based Link Prediction

claims.evidence: The script claim1_rank.py numerically confirms rank(H·Eᵀ)=d exactly for d∈{50,100,200} on 3000×800 matrices, and confirms the MoS log-probability matrix has rank exactly d+1 at K=1 (201 for d=200, 1001 for d=1000) on 3000×2000 matrices, matching Table 7. claims.claim: In the isotropic-signal setting, Corollary 3.2 shows the optimal mixing weight changes sign exactly at λ* := γσ²/r², with ξ*(λ) < 0 for λ > λ* and ξ*(λ) > 0 for λ < λ* (Section 3.2, Corollary 3.2).
claims.evidence: With sigma=1, r=2, gamma=1/2, the predicted lambda*=0.125 matches the numerical scan: nearest zero crossing at 0.1279, largest positive-xi lambda at 0.1206, smallest negative-xi lambda at 0.1279, confirming the sign flip pattern xi*>0 below lambda* and xi*<0 above.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proposes a one-shot generalized cross-validation (GCV) estimator of the optimal mixing weight ξ* that is consistent in proportional asymptotics and avoids grid search, sample splitting, or refitting (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Across 288 one-shot fits (p=50–400, 24 seeds, lambda in {0.1,0.5,2.0}) using only the training split with no refitting or grid search, median weight error at lambda=0.1 shrinks 2.94x from p=50 to p=400 (0.5691→0.1937), and sign accuracy is 100% for lambda=0.1 and 2.0 at p=400; near-zero oracle weights at lambda=0.5 cause sign instability but magnitude still improves.

claims.claim: A curvature-based sufficient condition (Proposition 2.3, Eq. 10) predicts whether the self-distilled risk's global minimum over λ is strictly smaller than the teacher's; this test is verified exactly on all four real-data experiments (BlogFeedback, Communities and Crime, CIFAR10, Air Quality) in Table 2.
claims.evidence: On Communities and Crime (n=99, p=99, lambda*=1.414), the reproduced curvature condition Eq. 10 holds (D/RHS=0.738<1) with a measured global gain of +1.95%, contradicting the paper's Table 2 entry of no-test/no-gain for that dataset; additionally, CIFAR10 was not rerun, so the 'all four' claim cannot be confirmed.

Srishti280992/repro-self-distillation-ri.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence for the paper's core theoretical results (Claims 1–5) through synthetic experiments at reasonable scale with tight precision and convergence behavior. Claim 6 is falsified because the curvature test on Communities and Crime yields results contradicting the paper's Table 2 entry, and CIFAR10 was not checked.

tomyimkc/repro-exploration-free-algorith.paper_title: Exploration-free Algorithms for Multi-group Mean Estimation

claims.claim: Multi-group mean estimation is formulated as allocating a sampling budget of T across K groups to minimize the p-norm objective R_p(n) = ||{sigma_k^2/n_k}_{k=1}^K||_p (Section 2).
claims.evidence: 960 convex optimization instances (K up to 50, p in {1,2,4,10}) solved via independent entropic mirror descent all reached interior solutions with KKT marginal spreads at ~1e-15 and zero multi-start disagreement; the linear-cost control collapsed to a vertex in 240/240 instances, confirming the p-norm objective has the structurally distinct interior-allocation property the formulation claims.

claims.claim: Proposition 2.1 shows the optimal allocation requires n_k* = Theta(T) samples per group, which justifies an exploration-free (non-adaptive) sampling strategy (Section 2).
claims.evidence: Proposition 2.1's closed-form n_k*(T) was confirmed as the true minimizer across 540 instances (K up to 100, p including infinity) with KKT spreads ~1e-15 and direct-vs-closed-form objective gaps ~1e-15; the allocation fraction n_k*/T was T-independent to ~1e-17 across T from 100 to 10^7, and the sublinear-schedule control's optimality ratio diverged from 3.92 to 112122.60, confirming Theta(T) allocation is necessary.

claims.claim: The non-adaptive Algorithm 1, which assumes a variance lower bound, achieves regret E[R_infinity(n) - R_infinity(n*)] <= 4*sqrt(2)*sigma^2*F_Alg1,infinity*T^(-3/2)*sqrt(log T) for p=infinity, and O(T^-2 log T) for p<infinity, improving prior bounds by a factor of log T (Theorem 3.1, Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 was implemented from pseudocode and tested across 6400 Monte Carlo trials (400 seeds × 16 (p,T) settings, T up to 20000) with zero bound violations against Theorems 3.1/3.2's exact displayed constants; the invalid-sigma_bar control showed 14.08x regret degradation and 214/400 bound violations at the most severe misspecification, confirming the precondition's necessity. The 'improves prior bounds by log T' comparison to Aznag et al. (2023) was not independently replicated.

claims.claim: Algorithm 2 removes the variance lower-bound requirement using adaptive elimination via lower/upper confidence bounds, and Theorem 4.1 shows it matches Algorithm 1's convergence rate without prior variance knowledge (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 2 was implemented without any variance lower bound and tested across 3200 trials (200 seeds × 16 settings, T up to 20000) with zero violations against Theorem 4.1's exact constants; the convergence rates match Algorithm 1's (T^{-3/2}√log T for p=∞, T^{-2}log T for p<∞), and the control showed Algorithm 2's relative gap shrank 229x from T=1000 to T=64000 while naive uniform allocation's gap stayed fixed at 0.0688.

claims.claim: Section 5 extends the framework to linear contextual bandits with Algorithm 3, and Theorem 5.5 bounds regret by (80*d*sigma^2)/(lambda_min^C) * T^-2 * log T for p=1 (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 3 was implemented with OLS residual-variance estimation and tested across 400 trials (100 seeds × 4 T values up to 24000) with zero violations against Theorem 5.5's exact constant (80·d·σ²/λ_min^C · T^{-2}·log T); the context-aware control showed 1.30x worse β̂ estimation error, confirming the decide-then-observe structural requirement matters, though only at the smallest (K=5, d=4) of the paper's settings.

tomyimkc/repro-exploration-free-algorith.overall: All five claims are supported by concrete, non-toy experimental evidence: formulation and closed-form claims verified to floating-point precision across hundreds of instances, and all three algorithm-vs-theorem claims (Theorems 3.1/3.2, 4.1, 5.5) held with zero bound violations across thousands of Monte Carlo trials at T up to 64000, each with an informative control isolating the claim's specific mechanism. The main unaddressed gap is the 'improves prior bounds by log T' comparison in claim 3, which would require independently re-implementing Aznag et al. (2023).

tomyimkc/repro-convergence-analysis-of-t.paper_title: Convergence Analysis of the Lion Optimizer in Centralized and Distributed Settings

claims.claim: Theorem 1 proves centralized Lion achieves a convergence rate of O(d^{1/2} T^{-1/4}) under standard smoothness, without requiring the coerciveness assumption used in prior analyses (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: On the noisy quadratic (L=1 smooth, bounded variance, f*=0) at theorem hyperparameters with 8 seeds, the fitted T-exponent is -0.2356 (claim -0.25) and d-exponent is 0.4749 (claim +0.5), with ratio to bound d^{1/2}T^{-1/4} stable in [1.008, 1.049] across a 16x T-range and [1.025, 1.108] across a 16x d-range. The control (inflating init scale to violate ||x1||_inf<=eta) causes the ratio to blow up to 23694, confirming the test is non-vacuous.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows that a variance-reduced Lion variant using STORM-based gradient estimators improves the rate to O(d^{1/2} T^{-1/3}) under an average smoothness assumption (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Lion-VR with STORM on the same quadratic at theorem hyperparameters gives fitted T-exponent -0.3252 (claim -0.333) and d-exponent 0.4695 (claim +0.5), with ratio to bound stable in [1.035, 1.057]. VR beats non-VR Lion by 1.93x to 2.51x with non-VR T-exponent only -0.1954, and the heavy-noise control degrades the exponent to -0.2733, confirming average-smoothness is what VR exploits.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 establishes that distributed Lion across n heterogeneous nodes matches the centralized rate, converging as O(d^{1/2} (nT)^{-1/4}) (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Distributed Lion on heterogeneous nodes (mean-zero biases) at theorem hyperparameters with T>=n shows fitted n-exponent -0.2108 (claim -0.25) and T-exponent -0.2326 (claim -0.25), with ratio to bound d^{1/2}(nT)^{-1/4} in [0.979, 1.117]. Speedup vs n=1 grows to 1.79x at n=16, approaching the predicted n^{1/4}=2.0.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 shows that adding variance reduction to distributed Lion improves the distributed rate to O(d^{1/2} (nT)^{-1/3}) (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Dis-Lion-VR at theorem hyperparameters with T>=n^2 gives fitted T-exponent -0.3356 (claim -0.333) with ratio to bound stable in [1.112, 1.124]. VR beats non-VR Dis-Lion by 1.90x to 2.50x with non-VR T-exponent -0.2065 (Theorem 3 territory). The n-exponent is -0.2498 vs claim -0.333, somewhat off but limited by the small n-range (1-8).

claims.claim: Theorem 5 gives a communication-efficient Lion variant with unbiased sign compression achieving either O(d^{1/2} T^{-1/2} + d n^{-1/2}) or O(n^{1/2} T^{-1} + d n^{-1/2}) depending on the learning-rate choice (Theorem 5).
claims.evidence: The upper bound holds (ratios 0.04-0.40, well below 1) but is too loose to test the specific rate: in regime 1 the measured values actually increase with T (0.42 to 0.82), opposite to the T^{-1/2} term, and the n-sweep does not monotonically follow the floor d/n^{1/2}. The biased-double-sign control is consistently worse (2.95-6.23 vs 0.42-0.82), confirming the unbiased sign matters, but the rate scaling itself is not demonstrated.

claims.claim: Theorem 7 shows that combining bidirectional unbiased sign compression with variance reduction attains a communication-efficient rate of O(d^{1/4} T^{-1/4}), improving over the non-variance-reduced Theorem 6 rate (Theorem 7, Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: The T-exponent is roughly consistent (-0.2186 vs claim -0.25), but the d-exponent is 0.7315 vs claim +0.25—a major discrepancy attributed to tanh gradient saturation. VR improvement over non-VR is marginal (1.03-1.09x) with nearly identical T-exponents (-0.2186 vs -0.2129), and the biased control is not consistently worse. The load-bearing d^{1/4} factor and decisive VR gap could not be demonstrated on any constructible instance satisfying both average-smoothness and bounded-gradient assumptions.

tomyimkc/repro-convergence-analysis-of-t.overall: The logbook empirically verifies the convergence rate exponents for Theorems 1-4 on a noisy quadratic satisfying all stated assumptions, with proper controls confirming non-vacuity and VR improvements. Theorems 5 and 7 are only partially addressed: Theorem 5's loose upper bound holds but its specific scaling is not demonstrated, and Theorem 7's d^{1/4} factor and VR gap are not observable on feasible test instances.

erobinson/repro-ppd-transformer-uq-2026.paper_title: Transformers Can Learn Posterior Predictive Distributions In-Context

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 shows self-attention can implement an iterative solver for the posterior predictive mean and variance, with error decaying exponentially in attention depth L as exp(-(1-ρ)L) (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The claim-1 page only describes a plan ('We will implement the constrained theory parameterization and verify...') with no experimental results, tables, or figures. The conclusion mentions 'mu_MSE decreases from 0.78 (L=2) to 0.01 (L=32)' but provides no experimental setup, no data, and no visible artifact supporting these numbers.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 bounds the total variation distance between the transformer's output distribution and the true posterior predictive distribution as TV(p_n,q_θ) ≲ e^{-(1-ρ)L} + δ_MLP + 1/C + ε_tail, tying error to depth L and bin count C (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The claim-2 page only states an approach ('We will train models across L ∈ {2,4,8,16,32} and C ∈ {16,32,64,128,256}...') with no actual results. The conclusion cites 'TV distance decreases from 0.59 (L=4,C=16) to 0.18 (L=32,C=128)' but no experiment details, training setup, or data are provided anywhere to back this.

claims.claim: Theorems 5.1-5.3 show that row-stochastic (Jacobi-preconditioned) attention normalization is necessary for generalization beyond the pretraining sample-size range, since the condition number grows as Θ(n) and requires depth L ≳ n·log(1/ε) for fixed accuracy ε (Theorem 5.1-5.3).
claims.evidence: The claim-3 page only describes the theorems and states 'We will verify the step size scaling with n and the condition number growth.' No experimental results, plots, or data tables are shown. The conclusion's mention of 'slope -0.83' is an unbacked assertion with no visible methodology.

claims.claim: Unnormalized attention models diverge when evaluated outside the pretraining context-size range, whereas normalized attention with row-stochastic scaling remains stable across context sizes (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: An actual experiment was run (RBF kernel, d=8, L=16, C=128, 5000 steps on RTX 3070) showing unnormalized TV spiking from ~0.29 to ~0.91 outside the pretraining range while normalized degrades gradually from ~0.46 to ~0.52. However, parameters are significantly reduced from the paper (L=16 vs 32, C=128 vs 256, 5K vs 100K steps), and the normalized model's TV is monotonically increasing and high (0.35–0.52), not clearly 'stable' as claimed.

claims.claim: Empirical results confirm that increasing attention depth and bin resolution improves posterior predictive distribution approximation, consistent with the theoretical bounds (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The experiment shown uses a single fixed configuration (L=4, C=16) and varies context size n' instead of varying attention depth L or bin count C. The claim is specifically about depth and bin resolution improving approximation, but neither L nor C is varied in the experiment, so the claim is not actually addressed.

erobinson/repro-ppd-transformer-uq-2026.overall: This logbook is largely incomplete: three of five claims have only plans with no visible results, and the Claim 5 experiment tests the wrong variables (context size instead of depth L and bin count C). Only Claim 4 has a real experiment, but at significantly reduced scale with results that only partially match the paper's claims. The logbook also confusingly interleaves content from an unrelated paper (AOEB benchmark).

ProCreations/repro-inference-aware-meta-.paper_title: Inference-Aware Meta-Alignment of LLMs via Non-Linear GRPO

claims.claim: IAMA optimizes the objective ℛ[π] = g(R1[π],...,Rm[π]) − β·KL[π||πref], where each Ri measures reward under an inference-time transformation such as Best-of-N sampling, allowing a single trained base policy π to adapt to multiple alignment criteria at inference time (Section 3, Equation 1).
claims.evidence: Exact rational-arithmetic certificates verify the Best-of-N objective polynomial and KL term across dimensions up to 2048 with multiple reward transformations and aggregations; real CPU inference on Qwen2.5-1.5B and DistilGPT2 demonstrates Best-of-N selection raising the multi-reward aggregate on a frozen base policy with two conflicting reward criteria; full-support deterministic policy training (120 cells) shows the objective strictly increases.

claims.claim: Non-linear GRPO (Algorithm 1) replaces the standard scalar reward with an approximated functional derivative ∂R/∂π evaluated at the current policy's empirical distribution, requiring only a drop-in reward function on top of standard GRPO (Section 4, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Exact derivative identity is verified coordinate-by-coordinate in 700 exhaustive coordinates using Fraction arithmetic (grouped CDF formula vs. ordered-outcome differentiation); finite-difference checks at dimensions up to 2048 show max error 6.62e-13; wrong-sign control confirms correct-sign updates improve the objective; full-support update using the functional derivative as drop-in signal shows positive objective change in all 60 cells.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 proves linear convergence of exact non-linear GRPO updates to the optimal policy, with excess loss bounded by β·KL[π*||π0] / ((L+β)/L)^T − 1 under a step size η=1/L (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Symbolic proof certificate verifies the telescoping algebra with exact Fraction values: interior KL coefficients are identically zero, initial coefficient is L+β, terminal coefficient is negative for 45 rational (L,β,T) cells; geometric denominator reduces to the registered β·KL/(ρ^T−1) expression; numerical check on 80 finite-policy iterates at dimensions 32–512 shows max gap-minus-bound of −0.029 (bound holds).

claims.claim: Theorem 5.3 shows that with approximation error ε and optimization residual δ, inexact non-linear GRPO updates converge to a neighborhood of the optimum with an additive bias term of 2(ε+δ)/β (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: Symbolic certificate verifies α=β/4, μ=L+β/2, Young inequality terms combine to 2/beta, and interior KL coefficients cancel exactly for 45 rational cells; 40 perturbed finite-policy trajectories at dimensions 32–512 with injected ε and δ show max weighted-gap-minus-bound of −0.038 (bound holds) and budget excess below 1e-16.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 shows that naive weighted-sum training collapses to a degenerate policy outputting only a single medium value (δ0.5), whereas IAMA with Best-of-N yields a bimodal optimal policy π*(y) ∝ y^(α−1)(1−y)^(α−1)/(y^α+(1−y)^α)^2 with α=1/(N−1) (Section 3, Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: Exact rational-arithmetic certificate verifies the change of variables, stationarity (first-order condition exactly zero in 11,253 rows), strict convexity, and density chain rule for N=2…1024; boundary density exceeds center value with minimum ratio 1.389; exact 2,016-point rational grid confirms naive weighted sum has unique maximum at y=1/2 with value 3/4, verifying the δ0.5 collapse.

claims.claim: On the HH-RLHF task with Alpaca-7B, IAMA trained with Best-of-N sampling (N=4) pushes the helpfulness-harmlessness Pareto front forward relative to standard alignment, while without Best-of-N sampling IAMA performs equivalently to standard alignment (Section 6.2).
claims.evidence: No independent Alpaca-7B training or HH-RLHF evaluation was executed (large_model_rerun=false); the logbook only verifies SHA-256 hashes of the paper's source files and checks that the text contains the claimed anchors, which is source provenance checking, not experimental reproduction.

ProCreations/repro-inference-aware-meta-.overall: The logbook provides rigorous exact algebraic and symbolic verification of the paper's mathematical claims (objective formulation, functional derivative, convergence theorems, and bimodal proposition) but completely lacks independent experimental reproduction of the central empirical result on HH-RLHF with Alpaca-7B, offering only source-hash verification for that claim.

claims.claim: Frictional Q-Learning uses a contrastive variational autoencoder (cVAE) to generate candidate actions aligned with replay-buffer-supported actions while separating salient features from irrelevant variation (Section on Architecture Components).
claims.evidence: The logbook trains a neural cVAE with PyTorch on real Gymnasium MuJoCo replay trajectories (HalfCheetah, Hopper, Ant, Walker2d) across 12 cells with 3 seeds each, achieving target reconstruction MSE ≤0.0027 and selected-candidate cosine ≥0.9975 with replay actions, demonstrating the candidate-generation and salient/irrelevant separation mechanism on non-toy data.

claims.claim: Theorems 1-4 establish convergence guarantees for BCQ-style constraints under coherent replay buffers in deterministic MDPs, while Theorem 5 addresses error convergence when orthogonal actions diverge from true dynamics (Theorem 1-4, Theorem 5).
claims.evidence: An exact two-state counterexample (code/exact_theorem5_zero_reward_counterexample.py) with transition mismatch p_0=(0,1) vs p_theta=(1,0) and zero reward yields Bellman fixed point Q=(0,0) under both kernels, giving extrapolation error exactly (0,0) despite the mismatch—contradicting Theorem 5's claimed non-zero fixed point for all reward functions. Theorems 1-4 are supported by 192 exact Fraction-arithmetic cells with zero Bellman residual, but the compound claim is falsified by the Theorem 5 counterexample.

claims.claim: Lemma 2 shows that orthonormal vectors of rank k>=2 always exist in continuous action spaces, underpinning the method's use of orthogonal 'anti-support' directions (Lemma 2).
claims.evidence: Exact rational Householder constructions (code/orthogonal_scope_exact.py and code/exact_fql_theorem_certificate.py) verify orthonormal complement vectors across dimensions 2–4096 and ranks 2–64, with 220+960+3840+11520 rows all showing exactly zero pairwise and action-complement dot products in Fraction arithmetic, plus a rank-1 destructive control correctly producing no complement.

claims.claim: On Humanoid-v4, FQL achieves a return of 6,713.75 +/- 103.89, outperforming SAC (6,463.46) and TD3 (6,524.20) with narrower standard deviation (Table 3).
claims.evidence: Independent reaggregation from released TensorBoard event streams using the paper's 'Seed' metric (mean of per-seed max Test/return) produces FQL 6713.753±103.893, SAC 6463.458±322.067, TD3 6524.199±401.628, matching Table 3 exactly; a destructive final-checkpoint control fails to reproduce, confirming the metric definition matters.

claims.claim: An ablation over the friction coefficient beta shows task-dependent optimal values, with HalfCheetah-v4 exhibiting instability at suboptimal beta settings (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Reaggregation of released raw runs across β∈{0.0,1.0,2.0,5.0} and 5 MuJoCo tasks (5 seeds each) shows different optimal β per task (HalfCheetah β=2.0, Hopper β=5.0, Ant β=0.0, etc.), and HalfCheetah suboptimal settings exhibit larger mean peak-to-later drawdowns (8190.88 at β=0.0 vs 3125.99 at β=2.0).

claims.claim: A comparison of incorporating orthogonal actions via the critic versus via data augmentation shows the critic-based approach outperforms augmentation across most MuJoCo environments (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Matched-beta comparison from released raw runs across 5 environments (5 seeds per route) shows critic-based orthogonal action incorporation has higher final mean return in 4/5 environments (Hopper, Walker2d, Ant, Humanoid), with augmentation higher only in HalfCheetah-v4, consistent with 'across most MuJoCo environments.'

ProCreations/repro-frictional-q-learning.overall: The logbook provides rigorous evidence for 5 of 6 claims through exact arithmetic constructions, neural cVAE training on real MuJoCo replay data, and independent reaggregation from released raw TensorBoard streams. However, it also provides an exact counterexample that falsifies Theorem 5's universal non-zero-fixed-point claim under zero-reward transition mismatch, making Claim 2 falsified despite Theorems 1-4 being supported.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 proves that under the coupling σ = β^{-(1+η)/4}, the fSGLD invariant measure converges in KL divergence and Wasserstein-2 distance to the Hessian-trace regularized target distribution as β→∞ (Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook constructs an exact counterexample using u(θ)=|θ|³ (piecewise, C¹˒¹ with 6-Lipschitz gradient, dissipative) satisfying the paper's stated assumptions, and shows via exact rational arithmetic that the target Laplace width scales as Θ(β⁻³ᐟ⁸) while the smoothed invariant Gaussian width scales as Θ(β⁻¹¹ᐟ³²), giving a width ratio Θ(β¹ᐟ³²)→∞ and hence KL divergence growing rather than vanishing under σ=β⁻⁽¹⁺η⁾ᐟ⁴.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 establishes a non-asymptotic Wasserstein-1 convergence bound for fSGLD to the flatness-biased stationary distribution, with corollary 3.3 giving a Wasserstein-2 rate of O(λ^{1/4}) (Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook's exact counterexample identifies a C¹˒¹ objective (piecewise |θ|³/quadratic) satisfying the paper's stated Lipschitz and dissipativity assumptions, but whose second derivative jumps from 6 to 1 at θ=1, making the Hessian—and thus the theorem's target v(θ)=u(θ)+(σ²/2)tr(H(θ))—undefined at that point, contradicting the theorem's universal quantifier over admissible objectives.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 derives excess risk bounds for the Hessian-trace regularized objective, showing convergence toward global flat minima (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: The logbook constructs a C^∞ objective with u″(x)=1+(1/4)sin(2πx³), Hessian bounded in [3/4,5/4], satisfying dissipativity with A=1/2, b=1, but whose fourth derivative u⁗(−n)/π=−3n→−∞, making the theorem's constant containing inf_θ Σ∂⁴u/(∂θ_i∂θ_j∂θ_k∂θ_l) equal to −∞, so the claimed O(β⁻⁽¹⁺η⁾) excess-risk bound is not finite under the paper's own stated assumptions.

claims.claim: Training ResNet-34 from scratch, fSGLD with the theoretically prescribed β-σ coupling reaches 62.02±0.29% accuracy on CIFAR-100N versus 59.18±0.33% for SAM, while running at ~23.7 s/iter versus SAM's 41.3 s/iter (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The independent CPU run trains on only 2,048 of 50,000 images for 1 epoch (vs. the paper's 150 epochs on A100), yielding near-chance accuracies (fSGLD 1.27–1.53%, SAM 0.97–1.22% on 100 classes); while fSGLD is faster and slightly higher in this pilot, the setup is far below the paper's scale and cannot confirm or refute the claimed 62.02% vs 59.18%.

claims.claim: Fine-tuning ViT-B/16, fSGLD with β-σ coupling attains 75.18% on CIFAR-100N versus 74.66% for SAM (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The independent CPU fine-tuning run uses only 512 of 50,000 CIFAR-100N images for 1 epoch (vs. the paper's 75 epochs on A100), producing near-chance accuracies (fSGLD 0.92–1.10%, SAM 1.72–5.57%); the reversed ordering at this drastically reduced scale cannot falsify or verify the claimed 75.18% vs 74.66%.

claims.claim: An ablation in Section 4.3 shows the theoretically prescribed β-σ coupling substantially outperforms fixed-β heuristics across all benchmarks, and Figure 3 shows fSGLD converges to solutions with lower Hessian maximum eigenvalues and trace than SGD, matching or exceeding SAM's flatness at lower cost (Section 4.3, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook's source audit of all ten coupled-vs-fixed cells in the paper's own tables finds exactly one exception—ResNet-34 WV-5: 89.86 coupled vs 90.63 fixed—directly contradicting the claim's 'across all benchmarks' wording; the paper itself acknowledges 'with the single exception,' making the universal quantifier in the claim false.

ProCreations/repro-flatness-aware-stocha.overall: The logbook provides mathematically rigorous exact-arithmetic counterexamples that falsify the three theoretical claims (Proposition 3.1, Theorem 3.2, Theorem 3.5) by identifying objectives satisfying the paper's stated assumptions but violating the theorems' conclusions or well-posedness. The empirical claims (4–5) are addressed only by drastically reduced CPU pilots (≤2,048 images, 1 epoch) that are toy-scale and cannot confirm the paper's headline numbers, while Claim 6's universal ablation wording is falsified by the paper's own tabulated exception.

claims.claim: RMCTS matches or exceeds AlphaZero's MCTS-UCB quality in tiny fraction of the time
claims.evidence: The head-to-head quality test used only 10 games and showed RMCTS losing 3-5 (40% win rate), which does not support 'matches or exceeds.' The speedup was measured only on CPU (3.17x average), not the ~40x GPU/TensorRT claim that constitutes the paper's headline 'tiny fraction of the time' result, so neither component of the claim was adequately tested at the paper's scale.

claims.claim: Recursively re-estimates action values using regularized optimal posterior policies from Monte-Carlo tree search
claims.evidence: The regularized posterior policy formula (pi*(a) = c0 * pi0(a) / (Q_max - Q(a) + delta)) is implemented in the actual C codebase (RMCTS.c:111) and numerically verified: posterior correctly favors high-Q actions (65.3% weight on best action), regularization behaves as expected across T values, and the Newton solver converges with max error 2.59e-08.

claims.claim: Generates search tree using prior policies then recursively processes from leaves to root
claims.evidence: Code paths in RMCTS.c confirm BFS tree expansion via assign_simulations proportional to prior policy (line 478) and leaf-to-root recursive propagation in reverse order via MCTS_propagate_all (line 563), with a 128-simulation run producing 128 tree nodes, informative prior (KL=2.802 vs uniform), and search policy (KL=2.780) consistent with the described two-stage algorithm.

erobinson/repro-recursive-monte-carlo-tr.overall: The logbook provides solid verification of the algorithmic claims (regularized posterior formula and BFS-plus-recursive-propagation architecture) through code inspection and numerical tests on the real Othello setup. However, the headline speed-and-quality claim is inadequately tested: only 10 head-to-head games were run (RMCTS lost 3-5), and the GPU/TensorRT speedup that drives the 'tiny fraction of the time' claim was never measured.

Srishti280992/repro-model-monotonicity-a.paper_title: Model Monotonicity in Autobidding Auctions: When Do Better Predictions Lead to Better Outcomes?

claims.claim: For target-CPA bidders without budget constraints using uniform bidding with multiplier mu=1 in first-price auctions, refining the prediction model (partitioning clusters into subclusters while preserving calibration) never decreases platform revenue, i.e., Rev(M_A) >= Rev(M_B) when M_A refines M_B (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: Across 360 refinement comparisons from 60 random instances (20,000 users, 60 bidders, up to 1,536 fine clusters), revenue_monotonicity_violations = 0 with min revenue gap +0.2445. The concave min-control produced 348/360 violations, confirming the max-operator is the active mechanism. Calibration error was 6.11e-16.

claims.claim: The first-price auction revenue monotonicity proof for tCPA bidders relies on convexity of f(p) = max_i(t_i · p_i) via Jensen's inequality, since model refinement corresponds to a mean-preserving spread of this convex function (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: 60,000 random convexity checks of f(p)=max_i(t_i·p_i) found 0 violations with positive slack up to 2.746. The cluster-by-cluster Jensen decomposition matched the actual revenue gap with max absolute residual 1.55e-15, directly confirming the mean-preserving-spread + convexity mechanism.

claims.claim: Uniform bidding at multiplier mu=1 is simultaneously conversion-maximizing, revenue-maximizing among equilibria, and welfare-maximizing for tCPA bidders in first-price auctions (Theorem 5.2), and welfare monotonicity follows as a corollary when per-conversion values equal targets (Corollary 5.3).

Edd16/icml2026-IbRm6gwmew-repro.paper_title: Lookahead Sample Reward Guidance for Test-Time Scaling of Diffusion Models

ProCreations/repro-benign-overfitting-in.paper_title: Benign Overfitting in Adversarial Training for Vision Transformers

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 gives the first theoretical analysis showing adversarially trained Vision Transformers achieve robust training loss at most ε together with clean test error and robust test error both bounded by exp(−C·d·SNR²)-type terms under the sample/SNR condition N·SNR²=Ω(1) (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence on synthetic (d=200) and MNIST 0-vs-1 (d=784) data showing clean test error decreasing exponentially with d·SNR² (regression slopes -0.358, R²=0.806 and -0.150, R²=0.919), and tracks the (1-τ/||μ||)² factor in robust error across a radius sweep, confirming the theorem's predicted bound forms on non-toy setups.

claims.claim: Under Condition 4.1's overparameterization requirement d=Ω̃(ε⁻²N²d_h), the analysis identifies two regimes depending on the adversarial perturbation radius τ relative to the signal norm ‖μ‖₂: attention heads remain trainable when τ≤O(‖μ‖₂/log d_h), while the ViT degenerates to an effectively linear model when ω(‖μ‖₂/log d_h)≤τ≤O(‖μ‖₂) (Theorem 4.2, Condition 4.1).
claims.evidence: The radius sweep at N=200, SNR=0.5 shows two distinct regimes: below τ/||μ||≈0.1 the model trains (entropy drops from 1.609 to 1.329, clean/robust errors near zero), while at τ/||μ||=0.5 the model fails (robust error=1.0, entropy stuck at 1.605=uniform), with the transition occurring well below ||μ||, consistent with the predicted ||μ||/log d_h boundary scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 shows that once the perturbation radius satisfies τ≥‖μ‖₂, the robust test error is bounded below by 0.25, establishing a sharp failure threshold for adversarial robustness (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: At τ/||μ||=1.0 and 1.5, the measured robust test error is 1.000 on adversarially trained models, satisfying the ≥0.25 lower bound of Theorem 4.3, with the collapse being sharp (robust accuracy drops from 0.997 at τ/||μ||=0.1 to 0.000 at 0.5).

claims.claim: The proof technique introduces a scalarized V-matrix decomposition and vectorized Q&K matrix formulation, with Lemma 5.3 establishing softmax robustness under small perturbations and Lemma 5.4 establishing attention-map uniformity under moderate perturbations (Section 5.1-5.2, Lemma 5.3, Lemma 5.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies the scalarized-V and vectorized-QK structural identities with exact Fraction arithmetic across 560 dimension cells (all zero residual), and checks Lemma 5.3's softmax robustness bound (26 cells, rational Taylor bounds) and Lemma 5.4's uniform-attention envelope (39 cells) with exact rational arithmetic, all passing.

claims.claim: Synthetic and real-data experiments (MNIST, CIFAR-10, Tiny-ImageNet) empirically confirm a phase transition in benign overfitting at the predicted boundary N·SNR²=Ω(1), matching the theory's two-regime prediction (Figure 1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The phase transition at N·SNR²=Ω(1) is clearly confirmed on synthetic data (d=200) and MNIST 0-vs-1 (binary subset), but CIFAR-10 was only partially run (18 cells, 'phase trend not cleanly resolved') and Tiny-ImageNet was never executed, leaving two of the three claimed real-data datasets without proper coverage.

claims.claim: Ablations over the ratio τ/‖μ‖₂ (0.02, 0.1, 0.5) show attention entropy decreasing with benign overfitting at the smallest ratio, persistent high entropy with linear collapse at 0.1, and non-convergence at 0.5 (Figure 3, Appendix B.1).
claims.evidence: While entropy decrease at τ/||μ||=0.02 (0.6931→0.4183) and non-convergence at 0.5 (loss≈log 2) reproduce, the specific prediction of 'persistent high entropy' at 0.1 is contradicted: entropy at 0.1 is 0.4170, statistically indistinguishable from 0.4183 at 0.02, not elevated—confirmed robust across a 25× noise-scale sweep.

ProCreations/repro-benign-overfitting-in.overall: The logbook provides strong empirical support for the theoretical predictions (Claims 1-4) through non-toy experiments on synthetic and MNIST data plus exact arithmetic verification of proof techniques, but only partially covers the real-data experiments (Claim 5) and falsifies one specific sub-claim about attention entropy behavior (Claim 6).

gchauhan/repro-autobidding-monotonicity.paper_title: Model Monotonicity in Autobidding Auctions: When Do Better Predictions Lead to Better Outcomes?

claims.claim: For target-CPA bidders without budget constraints using uniform bidding with multiplier mu=1 in first-price auctions, refining the prediction model (partitioning clusters into subclusters while preserving calibration) never decreases platform revenue, i.e., Rev(M_A) >= Rev(M_B) when M_A refines M_B (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: 500 random instances (20 users, 3 advertisers) with random cluster refinements all confirm Rev(M_A) >= Rev(M_B), and the paper example matches exactly (coarse=0.8075, fine=0.8250). The revenue computation correctly uses cluster-averaged predictions and weights.

claims.claim: The first-price auction revenue monotonicity proof for tCPA bidders relies on convexity of f(p) = max_i(t_i · p_i) via Jensen's inequality, since model refinement corresponds to a mean-preserving spread of this convex function (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: Convexity of f(p)=max_i(t_i*p_i) verified with 10,000 random draws in R^4 showing f(E[X]) <= E[f(X)], calibration preservation (w_coarse*p_coarse = sum(w_sub*p_sub)) confirmed, and Jensen's inequality applied directly to refined partitions showing weighted sum of sub-cluster f-values >= coarse f-value.

claims.claim: Uniform bidding at multiplier mu=1 is simultaneously conversion-maximizing, revenue-maximizing among equilibria, and welfare-maximizing for tCPA bidders in first-price auctions (Theorem 5.2), and welfare monotonicity follows as a corollary when per-conversion values equal targets (Corollary 5.3).
claims.evidence: Tests confirm mu=1 is the maximum feasible multiplier (CPA = mu*t_i <= t_i), revenue increases monotonically with mu, revenue equals welfare when v_i=t_i (diff=0.0), and welfare monotonicity follows from revenue monotonicity. Tests are basic but correct on the actual FPA/tCPA setup.

claims.claim: There exist instances with tCPA bidders where second-price (VCG) auctions exhibit non-monotonicity in both revenue and welfare under model refinement, with a constructed counterexample showing a simultaneous 6.2% decrease in both metrics (Theorem 5.8).
claims.evidence: Exact counterexample reproduction with matching numbers: coarse model revenue=3.23, fine model revenue=3.03, both revenue and welfare decrease by 6.2%. Equilibrium multipliers (gA=36.5, gB=6.579 coarse; gA=14.714, gB=25.0 fine) and per-auction payments all match the paper.

claims.claim: Introducing budget constraints breaks revenue monotonicity even in first-price auctions, as optimal bidder multipliers shift under refinement and reduce competitive pressure, exemplified by a counterexample with a 16.8% revenue loss (Theorem 5.10).
claims.evidence: Counterexample with same parameters as paper shows revenue decrease under refinement with budget constraints (coarse=6.07, fine=4.60, -24.3%). The logbook's percentage differs from the paper's 16.8% because the coarse-model revenue computation incorrectly uses individual predictions instead of cluster-averaged predictions; using cluster averages yields 5.53, matching the paper's 16.8%. The non-monotonicity phenomenon is confirmed regardless.

claims.claim: A centralized, non-strategic linear-programming benchmark allocation guarantees welfare monotonicity under budget constraints via a 'lifting' construction that preserves feasibility across refined partitions (Theorem 5.11), and the paper's overall characterization identifies exactly three settings where monotonicity holds (Table 1).
claims.evidence: 100 random LP instances (3 advertisers, 10 users, with budgets) all show LP welfare non-decreasing under partition refinement. The LP is correctly formulated with budget and supply constraints. The three monotonicity settings from Table 1 are listed, though only settings 1 and 3 are directly tested in this logbook.

gchauhan/repro-autobidding-monotonicity.overall: The logbook provides numerical verification of all six claims through random testing (500+ instances for Claims 1-2, 100 for Claim 6) and exact counterexample reproductions (Claims 4-5). The strongest evidence is the precise matching of the VCG non-monotonicity counterexample (Claim 4), while Claim 5 has a computational bug in coarse-model revenue that inflates the percentage but still confirms the direction of the effect.

ProCreations/repro-doubly-regularized-ma.paper_title: Doubly Regularized Markov Decision Processes for Robust Reinforcement Learning

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 bounds the average sub-optimality of the proposed DR-RPO algorithm by AveSubopt(K) ≤ c·d²H²/(α√K)·log(3dHK·vol(A)/p), matching the sample complexity of existing greedy value-iteration methods for robust MDPs while enabling direct policy optimization (Theorem 5.2, Section 5).
claims.evidence: DR-RPO was fully implemented and run on the paper's off-dynamics linear MDP (d=4, H=3, 16 actions); measured AveSubopt was below the Theorem 5.2 bound in all 15 cells (rho×K×5 seeds), with worst ratio 0.0384, and empirical decay rates of K^-0.662, K^-0.652, K^-0.592 are at least as fast as the promised 1/√K.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.4 shows that under linear MDP assumptions the robust Q-function is linear in the feature map, admitting a closed-form ridge-regression solution (Eq. 4.3) for tractable function approximation (Proposition 4.4).
claims.evidence: Normal equations for the Proposition 4.4 ridge solution were solved on 112 cells (d=2–64, n=16–4096) plus 16 protection cells (d=96–128, n=8192–16384); largest residual |Az−Φᵀy|∞ was 4.97e-14, and ν was monotone non-increasing in ρ in every cell.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.6 extends the linearity result to regularized robust MDPs (RRMDPs) using truncated value functions (Eq. 4.5), enabling the same closed-form approach under a different regularization scheme (Proposition 4.6).
claims.evidence: RRMDP truncated ridge normal equations were solved on 112 cells (d=2–64, n=16–4096) plus 16 protection cells (d=96–128); largest residual 3.55e-14, truncation was active and differed from the untruncated control in all 128 cells, with coefficient gaps 0.24–2.10 and active-target fractions 0.33–0.92.

claims.claim: DR-RPO's exploration relies on an upper-confidence-bound bonus term Γ_h^k(s,a)=β·Σ_iφ_i(s,a)√(1_i^T(Λ_h^k)^{-1}1_i), used in Algorithm 1 (Line 15) to drive optimistic exploration in large state-action spaces (Algorithm 1, Line 15).
claims.evidence: The UCB bonus was computed from explicit Gram matrices on 36 cells (d=2–64, n=4–4096) plus 6 protection cells (d=96–128, n up to 32768); bonus was strictly positive and monotonically decreasing in every cell, with fitted shrinkage exponents in [−0.499, −0.304], bracketing the theoretical 1/√n rate.

claims.claim: In the off-dynamics linear MDP experiment, DR-RPO outperforms LSVI-UCB, OPPO, and Optimistic NPG in robustness across perturbation levels ρ∈{0.1,0.3,0.5} (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: A 100-seed rerun of the Appendix A.1 environment with exact finite-state DP evaluation found DR-RPO beaten by Optimistic NPG in 4 of 9 high-shift cells (e.g., ρ=0.3, q=0.6: NPG 1.0896 vs DR-RPO 1.0711; ρ=0.3, q=1.0: NPG 0.6516 vs DR-RPO 0.6513), directly contradicting the claim that DR-RPO outperforms Optimistic NPG across the perturbation grid.

claims.evidence: CPU reproduction with exact finite-horizon DP evaluation (d=8, 10 seeds, 15 target probabilities) showed DR-RPO retention V(p)/V(0.5) at p=0.85 exceeding both non-robust baselines (LSVI-UCB 0.239, OPPO 0.240) in all six DR/RR settings (DR-RPO 0.247–0.270), and remaining within 0.017 retention of DR-LSVI-UCB throughout.

ProCreations/repro-doubly-regularized-ma.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting Claims 1–4 and 6 through executed implementations with exact DP evaluation, multi-seed runs, and high-dimensional protection sweeps, while falsifying Claim 5 via a 100-seed counterexample showing DR-RPO does not consistently outperform Optimistic NPG.

amkkk/algebraic-view-expressivity-rnn-re.paper_title: An Algebraic View of the Expressivity of Recurrent Language Models

claims.claim: The paper develops an algebraic framework in which a recurrent language model's expressivity reduces to whether its syntactic monoid divides the wreath product of the transition monoids of its layers, formalized via algebraic cores, cascade juxtaposition, and the ambient wreath product (Section 3, Definitions 3.4-3.8).
claims.evidence: Three small transducers (2-3 states, 2-symbol alphabets) with exhaustive word enumeration up to length 3 confirm transition monoid finiteness and a division relation (mod-2 monoid divides flip-flop monoid), but this only demonstrates the framework's mechanism on tiny instances rather than verifying the universal algebraic reduction theorem.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.20 (the cascade juxtaposition identity) shows the realized wreath product of two cascaded algebraic RNNs equals the wreath product of their individual realized wreath products, up to canonical isomorphism, formalizing how expressivity composes across recurrent layers (Section 3.6.3, Proposition 3.20).
claims.evidence: Two cascade architectures (mod-2+identity giving monoid size 2, full 2x2 giving monoid size 8) are enumerated and the cascade monoid cardinality matches the wreath product, but only 2-state transducers with 15 words are checked, far from verifying the universal isomorphism stated in Proposition 3.20.

claims.claim: As a case study on diagonal state-space models (SSMs) such as Mamba-style linear recurrences, the same architecture cannot implement an even-modulus counter under floating-point arithmetic with nonnegative recurrence multipliers, yet can realize every even-modulus counter under unsigned-integer quantization (Section 4, Abstract).
claims.evidence: Float32 simulations with three alpha values (0.5, 0.9, 0.99) show convergence to fixed points and no parity capability, while unsigned-integer recurrences yield exact period-M cycles for M=2,4,6,8; however, only a single scalar recurrence is tested over T=300 steps with three alpha values, which is a simplified numerical demonstration rather than a full-scale SSM evaluation or formal proof.

claims.claim: The framework's Krohn-Rhodes-based decomposition (Appendix, Section 3.6.3) shows that algebraic impossibility results (a required factor of the syntactic monoid cannot be realized by any layer monoid in a given architecture family) rule out recognition of a target language, while observational realization constructs an explicit acceptor when the factor is realizable (Section 3.6.3, Corollary 3.21).
claims.evidence: Submonoid lattices are enumerated for monoids of size 2-4 (C2, C3, flip-flop, T2), showing group/aperiodic classification and a T2 decomposition, but this only checks tiny instances and does not verify the universal Krohn-Rhodes decomposition or the impossibility/realization dichotomy of Corollary 3.21.

amkkk/algebraic-view-expressivity-rnn-re.overall: All four claims are addressed with real Python implementations and concrete numerical results, but exclusively on small finite-state or scalar-recurrence instances (2-4 states, T=300, 3 parameter values) that demonstrate the paper's mechanisms without verifying the universal theorems. The logbook is transparent about its toy-scale scope throughout.

Edd16/icml2026-KSF8Q492oV-repro.paper_title: TimeGuard: Channel-wise Pool Training for Backdoor Defense in Time Series Forecasting

claims.claim: TimeGuard uses a two-stage channel-wise reliable pool training paradigm: Stage I time-aware pool initialization via Reverse-Consistency Filtering (RCF) and Neighborhood Diversity Filtering (NDF), and Stage II Distance-Regularized Loss Selection (DRLS) for progressive pool expansion (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Proxy numpy experiments on synthetic data (HF job Edd16/6a5cbef2bee6ee1cf4ed10ad, cpu-basic) demonstrate channel-wise pooling preserves per-channel info 5.54x better than flatten and time-aware selection reduces forgetting by 37.67%, but the actual RCF, NDF, and DRLS components are not implemented—only simplified analogues (mean+std pooling, recency weighting, anchor-based selection) on 3 synthetic tasks with 12 channels.

Edd16/icml2026-oKizUOP7E4-repro.paper_title: PrivGate: Steering Contextual Integrity in LLMs via Latent Space Geometry

claims.claim: Discovers Privacy Manifold where models linearly encode privacy sensitivity within residual streams.
claims.evidence: The experiment uses synthetic hidden states h = y·s·v + ε with a planted privacy direction v (D=128), not residual streams from any real LLM. Linear probe AUROC 0.9981 and PCA alignment cos(PC1,v)=0.94 are trivially expected when the direction is planted by construction; no real transformer residual streams were examined.

claims.claim: Achieves out-of-distribution AUROC of 0.97 in risk identification on real-world PrivacyLens benchmark.
claims.evidence: The HF job's 0.9783 OOD AUROC was on synthetic covariate-shifted data, not PrivacyLens. The local run loaded real PrivacyLens (493 rows) but used synthetic neutral paragraphs as negatives (PrivacyLens has no negative class), yielding a 1.0 AUROC that the logbook itself admits is an easy-separation upper bound, not a calibrated benchmark score. Neither evaluation reproduces the paper's PrivacyLens benchmark result.

claims.claim: Achieves 70% reduction in privacy leakage with less than 5% computational overhead.
claims.evidence: Leakage reduction was measured on synthetic residual streams where projecting out the planted direction v trivially removes the signal (100% reduction by construction; 95.86% excess-AUROC). Overhead was measured on a simulated MLP block (4096×128 GEMM), not a real transformer deployment. No real model or real privacy leakage scenario was tested.

Edd16/icml2026-oKizUOP7E4-repro.overall: This logbook provides only toy-scale evidence: all experiments use synthetic residual streams with planted privacy directions rather than real LLM residual streams, and the one real dataset (PrivacyLens) was evaluated with synthetic negatives in a trivially separable setup. None of the three claims were reproduced at the paper's actual scale or with the paper's actual methodology.

Edd16/icml2026-ebRDSATK4K-repro.paper_title: Signal Strength Estimation in Logistic Regression Using Data Splitting

claims.claim: Utilizes data-splitting strategy to efficiently estimate signal strength in logistic regression.
claims.evidence: A real experiment was run (d=50, n=800, 15 trials) comparing naive vs data-splitting estimators, but the split estimator MSE (4.10) was actually worse than the naive MSE (0.34), and the split ||beta|| estimate (0.97) was far from the true value (3.0) while naive was closer (3.55). The setup is clearly toy-scale and the results contradict the claimed direction, but since it is not a full-scale reproduction it cannot be classified as falsified.

claims.claim: Analyzes exact asymptotics of M-estimator with data-driven, non-decomposable regularizer adapting to true covariance structure.
claims.evidence: A real experiment compared adaptive vs fixed-lambda ridge under isotropic and anisotropic covariances (d=50, n=800, 15 trials), finding variance reduction but increased bias and instability (adaptive lambda collapsed to zero in the anisotropic regime). No theoretical asymptotic analysis was reproduced, and the setup is toy-scale with mixed results that do not clearly validate the claimed covariance-adaptive advantage.

claims.claim: Validates method through theoretical analysis and numerical experiments addressing issues from separable data.
claims.evidence: A real separable-data experiment (signal scaled 8x, n=800, d=50) showed unregularized MLE diverging (||beta_hat||=122.68) while split-ridge (3.73) and adaptive-ridge (2.00) remained bounded, which is directionally consistent with the claim. However, no theoretical analysis was reproduced and the setup is toy-scale, so this is not a full validation.

Edd16/icml2026-ebRDSATK4K-repro.overall: The logbook runs a single small-scale experiment (d=50, n=800, 15 trials) that touches on all three claims with real numerical outputs, but at toy scale and with mixed-to-contradictory results: the data-splitting estimator underperformed the naive baseline, the adaptive regularizer showed bias-variance tradeoffs rather than dominance, and only the separable-data stability result was directionally supportive. No theoretical analysis was reproduced for any claim.

Edd16/icml2026-ucbH88BgIk-repro.paper_title: Local Redundancy: An Information-Theoretic Measure of Plasticity from Synthetic Memorization

claims.claim: Introduces local redundancy as information-theoretic measure of plasticity derived from universal compression theory.
claims.evidence: A numpy/cpu-basic proxy computed a 'local-redundancy score' as mean pairwise distance (not the information-theoretic measure from compression theory) and found a moderate correlation of +0.317 with a plasticity proxy, on a simplified synthetic setup rather than the paper's actual formulation and scale.

claims.claim: Expected squared gradient norm on synthetic memorization task provides efficiently computable lower bound on local redundancy.
claims.evidence: On a toy numpy setup, memorized samples showed LOWER squared gradient norm (0.948) than normal samples (1.248), contradicting the expected direction, but the actual lower-bound relationship between gradient norm and local redundancy was never directly tested and the setup is too simplified to constitute falsification.

claims.claim: Local redundancy predicts downstream performance better than existing measures (effective rank, dead neuron fraction, weight norm).
claims.evidence: On a toy numpy setup, local redundancy's |corr| with a downstream proxy (0.265) was worse than a 'representation norm' baseline (0.422), contradicting the claim, but the baseline used does not match the paper's specified baselines (effective rank, dead neuron fraction, weight norm) and the setup is a simplified proxy.

Edd16/icml2026-ucbH88BgIk-repro.overall: The logbook runs a single simplified numpy/cpu-basic proxy experiment that loosely relates to all three claims but does not faithfully implement the paper's information-theoretic local redundancy measure, its gradient-norm lower bound, or the specified baselines. Results at toy scale are mixed-to-negative: claim 1 shows only moderate correlation, and claims 2–3 produce results opposite to the paper's predictions.

HamsterSashka/repro-stochastic-linear-ba.paper_title: Stochastic Linear Bandits with Parameter Noise

claims.claim: For stochastic linear bandits with parameter noise on general action sets of size K and dimension d, the paper proves a regret upper bound of tilde-O(sqrt(dT log(K/delta)) * sigma_max^2) over horizon T (Section on main results / regret upper bound theorem).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements phased elimination with G-optimal design and sweeps T (4000–400000), σ²_max (0.02–0.32), log K (K=8–2500), and d (3–8) with 200 seeds. Measured exponents T:0.500, σ²_max:0.501, log K:0.598 broadly match the claimed √(dT·log(K/δ)·σ²_max) rate. The Gaussian-law simulation of θ_hat is a simplification but faithfully represents the theoretical estimator distribution for rate verification.

claims.claim: A matching regret lower bound of tilde-Omega(d sqrt(T) * sigma_max^2) is established, tight up to logarithmic factors when log(K) is approximately d (lower bound theorem).
claims.evidence: The 'lower-bound consistency' check merely sets K=e^d and confirms the upper-bound formula yields d-exponent 1.039—this is algebraic substitution into the upper bound, not a lower-bound experiment. No hard instance construction, adversarial argument, or proof that no algorithm can beat d√T is provided. The lower bound claim is unaddressed.

claims.claim: For l_p unit ball action sets with p<=2 (dual norm q), the minimax regret is characterized as Theta-tilde(sqrt(dT) * sigma_q^2), substantially better than the d*sqrt(T) regret of the classic additive noise model (minimax regret theorem, l_p unit ball case).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements VALEE on the ℓ₂ ball with both parameter noise and an additive-noise control. Parameter-noise regret fits T^0.506·d^0.534 (claim √(dT): 0.5/0.5); additive control fits T^0.536·d^1.008 (claim d√T: 0.5/1.0). The dimension-exponent gap of 0.474≈0.5 directly confirms the √d separation. Dimensions up to d=96 and T up to 500000 with 300 seeds constitute a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: The paper shows that a simple explore-then-exploit algorithm achieves the optimal regret bounds up to logarithmic factors under the parameter noise model (algorithmic contribution section).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements simplified algorithm cores: VASE uses Gaussian-law simulation of θ_hat instead of actual bandit rewards, and VALEE uses oracle-tuned exploration length (grid search over n) rather than a data-dependent stopping rule. Neither implements median-of-means or robust estimation. While the rate-determining structure is present and rates match, these simplifications fall short of reproducing the actual algorithm.

HamsterSashka/repro-stochastic-linear-ba.overall: The logbook provides meaningful numerical evidence for the upper-bound scaling (Claim 1) and the ℓ₂-ball minimax separation from additive noise (Claim 3), with well-matched exponents on non-trivial setups. However, the lower bound (Claim 2) is not actually addressed—only an upper-bound substitution is performed—and the algorithmic contribution (Claim 4) is verified only on simplified cores with oracle tuning and Gaussian simulation rather than full algorithm runs.

hameefy/repro-convergence-of-steepest-de.paper_title: Convergence of Steepest Descent and Adam under Non-Uniform Smoothness

claims.claim: The paper introduces a non-uniform smoothness assumption (Assumption 1) in which curvature is an affine function of the objective value, generalizing standard L-smoothness (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The audit checks ||∇²f(θ)||_{p→q} ≤ H₀ + H₁f(θ) across all five example families and three dual pairs with 579 Hessian evaluations and 0 violations; the control setting H₁=0 shows the required uniform L grows by up to 6.8×10¹⁶ on exponential loss while the affine bound stays valid; and the special case H₁=0 with (p,q)=(2,2) recovers L-smoothness with max ||H||₂/H₀ = 1.00000000 for logistic regression.

claims.claim: Under this assumption, steepest descent (sign GD) is shown to converge linearly on logistic regression with separable data and is provably faster than standard gradient descent (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: On n=15, D=8 separable logistic regression with the exact Theorem-2 step size, sign GD achieves linear convergence (R²=1.0000000, rate 7.254e-4) with the Phase-2 bound holding iterate-by-iterate (max actual/bound=1.000000), while GD fits t^{-0.997} (Θ(1/t)); at n=200, D=40 the T(ε) log-log slope is 0.097 for sign GD vs 1.029 for GD, and the non-separable control plateaus at f≈0.40.

claims.claim: Adam is shown to converge at a linear rate with a constant step size on certain two-layer neural networks under the non-uniform smoothness assumption (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: On a two-layer network (n=60, D=12, m=8, smoothed leaky ReLU, exponential loss) with constant η=9.685e-4 and δ=0, Adam drives f from 0.991 to 6.36e-24 with linear rate R²=1.0000000 and T(ε) slope 0.085; GD stays sublinear (slope 1.07); linearity holds across 8 (β₁,β₂) settings and widths m∈{4,8,16,32,64}; contradictory-duplicate control (f*>0) plateaus at 0.4615.

claims.claim: RMSProp-type adaptive methods are analyzed and shown to be provably faster than AdaGrad, AMSGrad, and heavy-ball momentum under non-uniform smoothness (Section 6).
claims.evidence: Theorem 6's Ω(1/T) lower bound holds in all 12 (method, η, β) configurations for GD/HB/AdaGrad/AMSGrad over T up to 10⁶, all 10 intermediate inequalities of the Appendix-G proof chain pass, the four slow methods are empirically Θ(1/T) while RMSProp/Adam are linear, and forcing non-increasing effective steps on RMSProp/Adam restores Ω(1/T).

claims.claim: The convergence analysis is extended from the deterministic steepest descent setting (Section 4) to the stochastic setting (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The Claim 5 page is listed in the index but its content is not present in the truncated logbook; no experimental evidence regarding the stochastic extension (Section 5) is visible.

hameefy/repro-convergence-of-steepest-de.overall: The logbook provides a thorough numerical audit of a theory paper, verifying Claims 1–4 with autodiff Hessians, exact operator norms, iterate-by-iterate bound checks, appropriate controls, and robustness sweeps. Claim 5 cannot be assessed because its page is absent from the truncated logbook.

HamsterSashka/repro-clasp-online-convex-.paper_title: CLASP: Online learning algorithms for Convex Losses And Squared Penalties

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows that for convex losses with step size eta_t = 1/t^beta, CLASP achieves regret O(T^max{beta,1-beta}) and cumulative squared constraint violation O(T^(1-beta)) simultaneously for any beta in (0,1) (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook runs CLASP on adversarial online-linear instances with T up to 20000 across β∈{0.3,0.5,0.7}, measuring log-log growth slopes. Regret slopes (0.701, 0.505, 0.320) match or fall below the claimed max{β,1−β} exponents (0.700, 0.500, 0.700), and CCV slopes (0.694, 0.428, 0.151) are all at or below the claimed 1−β. Constant-step-size controls yield slopes ~0.77–0.99, confirming the setup is meaningful.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows that for strongly convex losses with step size eta_t = 1/(mt), CLASP achieves the first simultaneous logarithmic bounds O(log T) on both regret and cumulative squared constraint violation (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: On strongly convex losses (m=1, n=8, T up to 40000) with η_t=1/(mt), regret log-log slope is 0.095≈0 with a bounded, flat Regret/log(T) ratio (~0.45→0.40), and CCV log-log slope is 0.030≈0 with CCV fitting ~1.14·log T. The 1/√t control yields slopes ~0.47–0.51, confirming the logarithmic improvement stems from strong convexity.

claims.claim: CLASP (Algorithm 1) performs a gradient step followed by projection onto the intersection of a static constraint set and a time-varying dynamic constraint set, with the analysis relying on firm non-expansiveness of the projection operator (Algorithm 1, Lemmas 1-3).
claims.evidence: The code implements x_{t+1}=P_{K∩C_t}(x_t−η_t∇f_t(x_t)) via proj_box_halfspace, which is consistent with the described algorithm structure (gradient step + projection onto static box ∩ dynamic halfspace). However, the claim about the analysis relying on firm non-expansiveness of the projection operator (Lemmas 1–3) is never explicitly addressed or tested.

claims.claim: Section 7 empirically compares CLASP against AdaGrad, RECOO, and Switch on online linear regression and online support vector machine tasks, showing competitive cumulative squared constraint violation with reduced memory overhead relative to Switch (Section 7).
