claims.evidence: The logbook contains no comparison against AdaGrad, RECOO, or Switch, no online linear regression or online SVM tasks, and no measurement of memory overhead. This claim is entirely unaddressed.

HamsterSashka/repro-clasp-online-convex-.overall: The logbook provides solid numerical evidence supporting the theoretical growth-rate bounds for both the convex (Claim 1) and strongly convex (Claim 2) regimes through well-designed adversarial setups with appropriate controls. However, the algorithm-structure claim (Claim 3) is only implicitly supported by the implementation without addressing the firm non-expansiveness lemmas, and the empirical comparison claim (Claim 4) is not addressed at all.

ai-sherpa/certificate-guided-pruning-rep.paper_title: Certificate-Guided Pruning for Stochastic Lipschitz Optimization

claims.claim: Certificate-Guided Pruning (CGP) maintains an explicit active set A_t of candidate optima using confidence-adjusted Lipschitz envelopes, certifying with high probability that any point outside A_t is suboptimal (Section 3, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: 150 snapshots across 3 objectives × 5 seeds × 10 checkpoints with 6,060,150 exhaustive grid membership checks under real sub-Gaussian noise (σ=0.1): Lemma 4.2 max residual -0.0102 ≤ 0 (150/150), Lemma 4.3 max residual -0.1742 ≤ 0 (150/150), 0 x* eliminations; destructive L/4 control breaks it (138/150 violations, 51 x* eliminations).

claims.claim: Under a margin condition with near-optimality dimension α (Assumption 2.3), the Shrinkage Theorem bounds the active set volume as Vol(A_t) ≤ C·(2(β_t + Lη_t) + γ_t)^(d−α) (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: Volume bound Vol(A_t) ≤ C·w_t^(d−α) holds 180/180 snapshots (d∈{1,2,3} × 3 objectives × 5 seeds) with max ratio 0.755; exponent d−α=d/p recovered by exhaustive lattice counting across 9 configurations to max |err|=1.5e-2 (R²≥0.999); C/10 control fails 124/180.

claims.claim: CGP achieves ε-optimality with probability at least 1−δ using T = Õ(L^d ε^{-(2+α)} log(1/δ)) samples, improving on the worst-case Õ(ε^{-(2+d)}) rate whenever α < d (Theorem 4.8).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive covering counts up to 70,074,033 sites recover ε-exponent 2+α to max |err|=0.0369, L-exponent d to max |err|=0.0043, and log(1/δ) linearity R²=0.999998 across 9 (d,p) configurations; margin-blind control recovers 2+d instead, confirming the α<d improvement. Caveat: verifies the covering-number components of the theorem rather than an end-to-end CGP run to ε-optimality.

claims.claim: A matching lower bound shows any algorithm requires Ω(ε^{-(2+α)}) samples under the same margin condition, establishing CGP's minimax sample-complexity optimality (Theorem 4.9).
claims.evidence: Hard instance verified exactly L-Lipschitz over 31,996,000 chords (deviation 0.0), near-optimal set matches ball with 0 mismatches, KL=ε²/2σ² matches MC to 9.5e-4, Le Cam n*·ε²/σ² constant to rel-spread 1.7e-16, T_LB exponent 2+α recovered to max |err|=0.0386; M-ary needle test collapses from 0.94 to 0.56 below T_LB budget.

claims.claim: CGP-Adaptive learns the Lipschitz constant L online via a doubling scheme, adding only an O(log T) multiplicative overhead to the sample complexity (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: Doubling count K=⌈log₂(L*/L₀)⌉ exact 36/36 configurations, final L̂∈[L*,2L*) 36/36; safety flips exactly at L* (x* excluded while L̂<L*, 0 exclusions once L̂≥L*); overhead normalized by log₂(ratio) bounded at 2.00/1.33/1.17/1.20; frozen L*/4 control excludes x* 30/30.

claims.claim: CGP-TR, a trust-region variant, scales to dimension d > 50 via certified restarts that provably never falsely eliminate the region containing the true optimizer x* (Theorem 6.1, Section 6).
claims.evidence: At native d=60 and d=100: 0/200 false eliminations at both dimensions with min slack +0.5004; L*/8 control falsely eliminates x*'s region 67/200 (d=60) and 80/200 (d=100); allocation N_j scaling exponent 1.985 vs predicted 2 (R²=0.99995). Objective is p=1 cone rather than paper's Rover-60/Ant-100 simulators, but the restart guarantee tested is dimension-free.

ai-sherpa/certificate-guided-pruning-rep.overall: The logbook provides a thorough independent numpy reimplementation verifying all six theoretical claims through exhaustive lattice counting (up to 70M sites), real CGP runs with sub-Gaussian noise, and destructive controls that fail in predicted directions. Main limitations are the use of p-cone objectives rather than the paper's Section-7 simulator benchmarks and verification of theorem components (covering numbers, hard instances) rather than end-to-end ε-optimality runs for the sample-complexity claims.

ProCreations/repro-coverage-improvement-.paper_title: Coverage Improvement and Fast Convergence of On-policy Preference Learning

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 shows on-policy DPO converges exponentially (linearly per round) in the number of iterations K once the per-round batch size exceeds a generalized coverage threshold C*_p(R), with total sample complexity O~(R^2/ε^2 ∨ (ln R/ε)·C*_p(R)) (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Finite Bradley–Terry bandit experiments at multiple scales (up to 128 actions, 48 parameters, 8 rounds, 8 seeds) show on-policy KL contraction per round (log-KL slopes of -0.445 to -0.532), coverage improvement (up to 1318x eigenvalue gain), and on-policy/fixed-policy KL ratios as low as 0.021. An exact Fraction-arithmetic audit of 3,840 cells verifies the affine recurrence r_{k+1}=q(1+a·r_k), its fixed point, and contraction envelope, directly checking the theorem's mathematical structure.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.2 proves any offline learner sampling from a fixed base policy π0 requires Ω(1/ε^2 · C*_p(R)) samples to reach error ε, a quadratic-in-1/ε separation from the on-policy rate (Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: 320 matched two-round fits show on-policy KL scales as n^{-1.061} and is 3.38x lower than fixed-offline at 600 pairs; 128 stress trials varying base-policy skew show coverage collapse and 27.36x KL rise; expanded (96,32) and (128,48) families show on-policy/fixed-policy KL ratios of 0.021 and 0.025. An exact 129×129 grid verifies the logistic curvature inequality KL(Ber(σ(z1))||Ber(σ(z2))) ≤ (z1-z2)²/8 used in the lower-bound argument.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 shows a hybrid sampler using preferential G-optimal experimental design (via Kiefer-Wolfowitz equivalence with centered features) achieves ‖θ̂_2 − θ*‖ ≤ ε in just two rounds with sample complexity O~(dR^2/ε^2 · log(1/δ)), removing dependence on the coverage constant (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook's exact source-text audit against the pinned main.tex (SHA-256 9dca675...) finds that Theorem 4.4 concludes ||θ̂_2 − θ*||_{V(π*)} ≤ ε (weighted norm), not the Euclidean ||θ̂_2 − θ*|| ≤ ε stated in the claim. An exact rational counterexample with V=diag(1,1/16), e=(0,2), ε=1 shows e^T V e = 1/4 ≤ 1 but e^T e = 4 > 1, demonstrating the two norms are not equivalent without a lower eigenvalue bound on V(π*).

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 shows on-policy reward-distillation methods that learn reward differences rather than preferences converge at rate O(n^-1 ∨ e^{-Ω(K)}), faster than preference-based on-policy DPO but inheriting reward-model error ε_RM (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: 512 realizable threshold trials show n^{-1.031} disagreement slope for exact reward differences; 336 softmax trials show direct differences recover reward at machine precision (1.66e-15 MAD) while Bernoulli preference labels give n^{-0.538} MAD; 128 perturbation trials confirm ε_RM transfers one-for-one. An exact Fraction-arithmetic certificate over 13,725 cells verifies the contraction recurrence max(2ε_RM, ξ·C_F(r_k)) stays within the envelope max(2ε_RM, 2ξ/η, R·η^k), and 2,520 rate cells verify the n^{-1} normalization.

claims.claim: On the general-chat UltraFeedback benchmark, the proposed on-policy distillation approach achieves a 45.44% AlpacaEval win-rate versus 41.26% for the offline baseline, while naive REBEL-style distillation degrades performance unless calibrated (RDRC) (Section on experimental validation).
claims.evidence: Source table extraction from the pinned main.tex (cross-checked by an independent parser) shows 45.44 is the AlpacaEval win-rate for on-policy DPO iteration 3, not for on-policy distillation. The distillation methods report different values: PDFR 43.99, REBEL 43.81 (iter 3) / 42.90 (iter 5), and RDRC 44.07. The claim's attribution of 45.44 to 'on-policy distillation' is contradicted by the paper's own table.

ProCreations/repro-coverage-improvement-.overall: The logbook provides rigorous finite-scale experimental evidence and exact Fraction-arithmetic proof-structure verification supporting the convergence mechanisms in Claims 1, 2, and 4, while falsifying Claims 3 and 5 by identifying a norm mismatch in the theorem statement and a method misattribution in the experimental table, respectively.

ihsanandrinal/navi-repro-2026.paper_title: Segment-driven Structural Induction and Semantic Alignment for Heterogeneous Tabular Representation

claims.claim: The proposed NAVI framework combines Masked Segment Modeling (MSM) and Entropy-driven Segment Alignment (ESA) to model heterogeneous tabular data at the header-value segment level (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook only provides a static code inspection of the NAVI repository (identifying NaviForMaskedLM, GlobalHeaderEncoder, SegmentProjection classes by line number), but no experimental run was ever executed to verify the architecture functions as described. Code reading alone is an assertion, not concrete experimental evidence.

claims.claim: On the generative header prediction task, NAVI achieves 0.9995 accuracy on the Product domain and 0.9998 on the Movie domain, versus HAETAE's 0.9260 and 0.8982 respectively (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Multiple attempts to run the HAETAE baseline on a 20-table Product subset all failed due to infrastructure issues (encoding errors, .json vs .jsonl file extension bug, hardcoded pretrained model paths). The final patched run started training but timed out at ~30 minutes (exit 1, 1784.9s) after reaching only ~19/1643 batches. No accuracy numbers were ever produced, and no NAVI model training was attempted at all.

claims.claim: On value imputation, NAVI scores 0.7933 (Product) and 0.7077 (Movie), compared to HAETAE's 0.7785 and 0.6911 (Table 1).
claims.evidence: No page or experiment exists for value imputation. The logbook index lists only Claim 1, data preparation, Claim 2, conclusion, and executive summary — value imputation was never addressed.

claims.claim: Under column-permutation robustness testing, NAVI's performance drops by only 0.02% on the Product domain versus a 6.92% drop for HAETAE (Table 2).
claims.evidence: No page or experiment exists for column-permutation robustness testing. This claim was never addressed in the logbook.

claims.claim: NAVI attains header-clustering NMI scores of 0.9005 (Product) and 0.9144 (Movie), exceeding HAETAE's 0.8742 and 0.8864 (Table 3).
claims.evidence: No page or experiment exists for header-clustering NMI scores. This claim was never addressed in the logbook.

claims.claim: Ablations show that removing the context-free attribute embedding (CAE) or the MSM objective substantially degrades reconstruction and downstream classification performance, and entropy-based routing outperforms random routing on value imputation (0.7933 vs. 0.7903) (Table 5).
claims.evidence: No page or experiment exists for ablation studies (CAE removal, MSM removal, entropy-based vs random routing). This claim was never addressed in the logbook.

ihsanandrinal/navi-repro-2026.overall: This logbook failed to produce any experimental results. The only completed work was a static code review of the NAVI architecture (Claim 1) and repeated failed attempts to launch the HAETAE baseline on a 20-table Product subset, with the sole partially-started run timing out before producing any metrics. Claims 2–6 remain entirely unverified.

HamsterSashka/repro-optimal-sample-compl.paper_title: The Optimal Sample Complexity of Linear Contracts

claims.claim: Theorem 1.1 establishes uniform convergence: for sample size s ≥ 3456 ln(4/δ)/ε², with probability at least 1−δ, the empirical and expected utility of every linear contract differ by at most ε (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook's Claim 2 page measures uniform error sup_α|u_p(S,α)−u_p(D,α)| on a 40000-population proxy with 400 trials: fitted decay rate p=−0.498 (matching 1/√s), n-independence confirmed (sup-err flat at 0.007–0.009 across n=2..200), and δ-dependence linear (s=23.7·ln(1/δ)−3.0). The ε-scaling exponent of −1.718 vs claimed −2.0 is somewhat off but consistent with the bound being a non-tight upper bound for the tested instance.

claims.claim: Corollary 1.2 shows the Empirical Utility Maximization algorithm achieves an ε-approximation of the optimal linear contract using s ≥ 6912 ln(4/δ)/ε² samples and O(1/ε) oracle queries (Corollary 1.2).
claims.evidence: EUM suboptimality decays (p=−0.605) and is n-independent, but the sample-complexity scaling experiment (Part B) yields an exponent of q=−0.563 instead of −2.0 because the generic instance is too easy (s_needed=10–23 for ε=0.01–0.04). The hard instance showing q≈2.3 is mentioned in the summary text but has no corresponding code or output. The O(1/ε) oracle query complexity is never tested.

claims.claim: The O(ln(1/δ)/ε²) sample complexity matches the lower bound of Dütting et al. (2025) up to constant factors, and is independent of the action space size n and the number of outcomes m (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: n-independence is confirmed in both experimental pages (flat suboptimality and flat uniform error across n=2..200), but m is fixed at 5 throughout with no sweep, and the lower-bound matching against Dütting et al. (2025) is referenced only as a hard-instance result (q≈2.3) that lacks documented code or output.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 shows the expected reward of a linear contract is non-decreasing in the contract parameter α, a structural property exploited to build fine-grained covering arguments where general pseudo-dimension bounds fail (Lemma 2.1).
claims.evidence: No experiment in the logbook tests whether the expected reward of a linear contract is non-decreasing in α, nor is this structural property explicitly verified or used in any covering argument.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.2 constructs an L2 cover of the reward function class of size O(1/ν²), obtained by discretizing empirical rewards into ν-intervals, taking pullbacks to parameter space, and combining with grid discretization of the outcome axis (Lemma 2.2).
claims.evidence: No experiment constructs or evaluates an L2 cover of the reward function class; the discretization, pullback, and grid-combination procedure described in Lemma 2.2 is not implemented or tested.

HamsterSashka/repro-optimal-sample-compl.overall: The logbook provides solid numerical evidence for Theorem 1.1's uniform convergence rate, n-independence, and δ-dependence, but does not properly verify Corollary 1.2's 1/ε² sample complexity (the generic instance is too easy and the hard-instance experiment is undocumented), and Lemmas 2.1–2.2, m-independence, and lower-bound tightness are not addressed.

HamsterSashka/repro-robust-mean-estimati.paper_title: Sample Complexity Bounds for Robust Mean Estimation with Mean-Shift Contamination

claims.claim: Under a frequency-witness (spectral) condition on the contaminating distribution, Algorithm 1 estimates the mean of a mean-shift-contaminated distribution to error ϵ with probability at least 2/3 using O(d·log(...)/((1-α)A-2α)δ)²) samples (Theorem 3.2, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The Laplace d=1 sub-experiment shows log(n_req) scaling with slope 1.818 on log(1/δ) (R²=0.905), approximately matching the predicted exponent of 2, but the Gaussian sub-experiment is degenerate (n saturates at grid floor 100 for all ε, exponent ≈0, R²<0). Only one of two distribution families is established, and only d=1 is tested rather than general d.

claims.claim: The main upper bound states that under mild technical assumptions characterized by a Fourier-based parameter δ, an algorithm exists using Õ_α(d/δ²) samples to estimate the contaminated mean (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: Same d=1 Laplace experiment supports the Õ(d/δ²) scaling with measured exponent 1.818 ≈ 2, but this is only one dimension and one distribution family; the Gaussian case fails to produce meaningful scaling data due to experimental design issues (grid floor too high).

claims.claim: A matching one-dimensional lower bound shows any algorithm requires Ω(1/(δσ)^(1/3)) samples to achieve error ϵ under specific L2 Fourier-transform and tail-decay conditions, and more generally 1/δ^Ω(1) samples are required even in one dimension, qualitatively matching the upper bound (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: A convex-LP relaxation of the two-point lower-bound construction on a spatial grid (dx=0.15) for Laplace d=1 yields n_LB ~ (1/δ)^1.371 (R²=0.999) and ||Q1-Q2||_1 ~ δ^0.764, showing qualitative polynomial matching with the upper bound. However, this is a relaxed numerical approximation rather than the exact Section 4 construction, tested only for Laplace in d=1, and does not verify the specific Ω(1/(δσ)^{1/3}) form claimed.

HamsterSashka/repro-robust-mean-estimati.overall: The logbook provides partial numerical evidence for the δ-scaling relationships in the paper, but only in d=1 and primarily for the Laplace distribution. The upper-bound scaling (Claim 1/2) is supported for Laplace but degenerate for Gaussian, and the lower-bound construction uses a convex relaxation rather than the exact method.

gchauhan/repro-grpo-rlvr.paper_title: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards: GRPO's Loss, Dynamics, and Success Amplification

claims.claim: GRPO with verifiable 0/1 rewards can be cast as an adaptive weighted contrastive loss between samples drawn from the previous (old) policy, with weights ω_{ε,±}(p) = p/√(p(1-p)+ε) depending on the old policy's success probability p (Section 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies the algebraic identity A(q,o) = (r-p)/√(p(1-p)+ε) for 10 values of p, confirming ω⁺=(1-p)/√(p(1-p)+ε) for r=1 and ω⁻=p/√(p(1-p)+ε) for r=0, and checks the contrastive weighting direction (ω⁻/ω⁺ > 1 when p>0.5). This is a direct numerical verification of the stated mathematical identity.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 gives the optimal policy at each GRPO iteration in closed form as an exponential reweighting of the reference policy based on the previous iteration's binary reward statistics (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook evaluates the GRPO objective at 100 random perturbations around the closed-form solution and confirms all give strictly lower values, verifies the closed-form matches h() to machine precision, and tests three β regimes (0.1, 0.5, 2.0) showing correct regularization behavior. The first-order optimality condition derivation is standard and correct.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows the success probability sequence generated by GRPO's iterations satisfies a fixed-point recursion p_{n+1} = h_{ε,p_ref}(p_n) (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements h_{ε,p_ref}(p) in both sigmoid and logit forms, verifies they are identical for 6 values of p, demonstrates convergence to a fixed point (p*=1.0, residual 0.00e+00) in 4 iterations with β=0.5, p_ref=0.2, and tests 8 configurations. The ε=0 numerical instability is also confirmed.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 proves every fixed point p* of GRPO's dynamics satisfies p* > p_ref, i.e., GRPO provably amplifies the policy's probability of success beyond the reference policy's performance (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies the proof logic (exp(-1/(β√(p(1-p)+ε))) < 1 implies h(p) > p_ref for all p) and tests 14 configurations spanning β ∈ {0.01,0.1,0.5,1.0} and p_ref ∈ {0.05,...,0.9}, all showing p* > p_ref. The condition h(p_ref) > p_ref is directly verified for multiple (β, p_ref) pairs.

claims.claim: Theorem 5 shows that when the parametric policy approximation has statistical and optimization error bounded by δ*, the resulting success probability converges to within 2δ* of the theoretical fixed point (Theorem 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook simulates 101 steps of parametric GRPO with bounded error (uniform in [-δ*, δ*]) for δ* ∈ {0.005,0.01,0.02,0.05}, confirming all steps stay within 2δ* of the theoretical fixed point p*=1.0. The TV distance bound |p̃_n - p_n| ≤ 2·TV is verified, and the δ*=0 case correctly shows exact convergence.

gchauhan/repro-grpo-rlvr.overall: The logbook provides correct numerical verification of all five theoretical claims through direct implementation of the paper's equations, testing across multiple parameter configurations. However, the verifications are purely numerical checks of mathematical identities and recursions on scalar Bernoulli examples, and the paper's GSM8K experimental validation was explicitly not reproduced.

MarxistLeninist/repro-fourier-learning-d.paper_title: A Fourier perspective on the learning dynamics of neural networks: from sample complexities to mechanistic insights

claims.claim: Theorem 3 proves that for translation-invariant, isotropic inputs, online SGD requires sample complexity n ≫ N³ log²(N) to extract phase information, because phase modifications are encoded only in fourth-order cumulants corresponding to an information exponent k*=4 (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies the information exponent k*=4 via a Monte Carlo moment audit at N=64 (120k samples × 10 reps), showing SNR<3 at degrees 1–3 and SNR=84 at degree 4, with strong controls (amplitude signal at degree 2, mutation collapsing to degree 1). However, the direct SGD recovery experiment did not converge within ~70·N³ samples at N≤48, so the actual sample-complexity scaling n≫N³log²N was never empirically demonstrated, and the log²N factor was not addressed.

claims.claim: For non-isotropic inputs with power-law Fourier amplitude spectra, the dominant principal subspace has eigenvalue λ_{k0} ≈ √N, raising the effective signal-to-noise ratio to λ_{k0}² ≈ N and reducing the required sample complexity for phase learning to quasi-linear in N (Section on power-law spectrum effect).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies the λ_{k0}² signal-scaling law at N=64: at dominant k0=2, measured amplification 22.27× matches predicted 22.49×, and at non-dominant k0=8, de-amplification 0.28× matches predicted 0.28×. However, the specific quantitative claims λ_{k0}≈√N (4.74≠8 at N=64), λ_{k0}²≈N (22.27≠64), and quasi-linear sample complexity were not tested, and no SGD experiment demonstrated accelerated learning under power-law spectra.

claims.claim: Two-layer networks trained on ALOT texture images (cotton vs. lace) first rely on amplitude-based features before subsequently exploiting phase information to distinguish classes (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The amplitude-before-phase ordering is demonstrated in the synthetic Fourier model with single online-SGD neurons: amplitude cue (exponent 2) recovered at n≈158k, phase cue (exponent 4) not recovered within 7.7M samples. However, the claim specifically concerns two-layer networks trained on ALOT texture images (cotton vs. lace), which were not used—no real images or two-layer architectures were tested.

claims.claim: Flattening the Fourier amplitude spectrum of training images causes a dramatic slowdown in learning, while replacing per-image amplitudes with class-averaged amplitudes (removing amplitude-based discriminative signal) instead produces a significant speedup in learning (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: No experiment addresses flattening the Fourier amplitude spectrum of training images or replacing per-image amplitudes with class-averaged amplitudes. The logbook's C3 page tests signal-strength scaling in the synthetic model, not the image-level spectral manipulations described in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The sequential amplitude-then-phase learning behavior is confirmed across multiple architectures (ResNet18, fully connected networks) and datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR-100) and across different optimizers (Section on experimental validation).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states 'The paper's image-scale experiments (ImageNet/CIFAR CNNs, Fig. 1/3e) are not reproduced.' No experiments use ResNet18, fully connected networks, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, or multiple optimizers; only the synthetic Fourier model with single neurons was tested.

MarxistLeninist/repro-fourier-learning-d.overall: The logbook provides a careful numerical audit of the paper's core mathematical mechanisms—information exponent 4 for phase signals and λ² signal amplification under power-law spectra—in the synthetic Fourier model at small scale (N≤64) with well-designed controls. However, it does not reproduce any of the paper's image-scale experiments (ALOT, ImageNet, CIFAR-100), does not directly demonstrate the predicted N³ sample-complexity scaling via SGD recovery, and leaves claims 4 and 5 entirely unaddressed.

sotayamashita/repro-joint-model-data-spa.paper_title: Joint Model and Data Sparsification via the Marginal Likelihood

claims.claim: Joint ARD extends standard Automatic Relevance Determination by introducing per-sample noise variances λ_i as primary parameters (rather than a single shared scalar), yielding a heteroscedastic marginal-likelihood objective that jointly sparsifies features and down-weights outlying samples (Section 3).
claims.evidence: A ten-seed synthetic run at the paper's n=500, d=50 scale reports weight-support recall 0.970, outlier recall 0.838, and outlier/inlier learned-noise ratio 116.42 with objective decrease across all seeds, demonstrating that per-sample noise variances separate outliers while retaining feature sparsity.

claims.claim: The heteroscedastic objective admits closed-form updates across multiple sparse Bayesian learning optimization schemes, including EM, MacKay-style updates, and ℓ1/ℓ2-IRLS variants (Section 3), preserving the conjugacy of standard ARD.
claims.evidence: Independent numerical checks show EM vs. MacKay noise update agreement to 0.0 error, MacKay vs. ℓ2-IRLS agreement to 1.41e-12, and a 30-solve ℓ1-IRLS audit with primal residual ≤6.05e-8, dual residual ≤5.00e-7, Fenchel tightness ≤2.85e-13, map-back stationarity ≤2.22e-16, and exhaustive-grid agreement to 3.48e-12, with a 10% perturbation control raising residual to 0.250.

claims.claim: On tabular benchmarks with 10% injected outlier contamination, joint ARD reduces RMSE relative to the homoscedastic baseline by 32.07% (Energy, EM), 69.91% (Carbon, EM), and 45.12% (Protein, MacKay) (Table 3), while the learned effective support size for samples (~91%) tracks the true contamination rate and feature-level sparsity is maintained (ESS(θ) ≈ 5-40%).
claims.evidence: A reduced protocol (2 seeds, 64 random Fourier features, ≤500 rows, EM for all datasets) yielded RMSE changes of −2.6% (Energy), +10.4% (Carbon), and −6.6% (Protein) versus the paper's claimed 32.07%, 69.91%, and 45.12%, but the setup differs from the paper's unspecified kernel parameters and preprocessing, and Protein used MacKay rather than EM, so the mismatch cannot be attributed to the claim itself.

claims.claim: Joint ARD achieves competitive robustness relative to Student-t and Huber robust baselines in RVM kernel regression across a range of contamination levels (Figure 4), with the largest gains over homoscedastic modeling occurring for sparse signals under low contamination (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: A single-seed, single-contamination-level Boston run reports Joint ARD RMSE 7.527 versus Student-t 6.890, Huber 7.575, and homoscedastic 7.810, and a synthetic grid (3 support fractions × 3 contamination levels × 5 seeds) probes the sparse-regime component, but neither covers the full range of contamination levels or the RVM kernel-regression setting at paper scale.

sotayamashita/repro-joint-model-data-spa.overall: The logbook provides rigorous numerical and synthetic-scale verification for the methodological claims (Claims 1–2) but cannot substantiate the empirical benchmark claims (Claims 3–4) at paper scale due to missing experimental details and absent author code.

gchauhan/repro-theoretical-perspectives-.paper_title: Theoretical Perspectives on Data Quality and Synergistic Effects in Pre- and Post-Training Reasoning Models

claims.claim: Balanced pretraining data distributions prevent instability (exponential growth in Hessian curvature) during subsequent post-training optimization, inducing latent capabilities later activated by post-training (Section 7).
claims.evidence: Spectral radius computation directly confirms the stability condition (ρ=10 for imbalanced vs ρ=0.1 for broad pretraining), and LSA training experiments show Hessian growth is 2.6x smaller with balanced pretraining (2.69x vs 7.08x) with 15.7% better test loss, further corroborated by transformer experiments showing 5.8% better MSE.

claims.claim: Insight 2 argues SFT datasets should be curated to be small in volume and high in quality, since excessively large SFT datasets dilute informative pretraining signal (Section 5, Insight 2).
claims.evidence: LSA model (d=100) shows a turning point (optimal at B=200, degradation at B=500), but effect sizes are small (5.7% improvement range) and the simplified linear model does not reproduce the paper's GPT-2 scale experiments that provide the main empirical support.

claims.claim: Insight 1 shows selecting SFT examples that are hard for the pretrained model optimizes post-training data selection, formalized via the test-error formula in Proposition 5.1 (Section 5, Proposition 5.1, Insight 1).
claims.evidence: While the Proposition 5.1 formula is numerically verified (1.7% relative error), actual training experiments in both LSA (hard=167.40, easy=119.75, random=104.96) and transformer (hard=127.82, easy=109.43, random=119.41) show hard examples perform WORST, directly contradicting the claim that hard examples optimize post-training data selection.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 characterizes the SFT loss minimizer in closed form via a pseudo-inverse formulation, and Theorem 4.2 proves gradient descent converges to it at an explicit rate (Section 4, Theorem 4.1, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Theorem 4.1 is verified with relative error 0.000485 between the pseudo-inverse analytical minimizer and empirical GD solution, and Theorem 4.2 is supported by monotonic error reduction (0.6768 to 0.1595 over 200 steps) with empirical convergence rate α=0.937 within the theoretical bound.

claims.claim: Outcome-supervision (OS/RL) training is shown to be most effective for incremental adaptation on tasks that are already partially learned during pretraining, per Insight 4, while exhibiting high sensitivity to sample variation near stability boundaries per Insight 3 (Section 6, Insight 3, Insight 4).
claims.evidence: Spectral radius computation confirms the stability condition (ρ=0.1 for incremental vs ρ=10 for new task), but LSA training contradicts the effectiveness claim (new task test loss 146.46 vs incremental 183.25) while transformer training supports it (incremental 122.40 vs new task 230.36), and the sensitivity-to-sample-variation claim (Insight 3) is never directly tested.

claims.claim: Experiments on linear self-attention models and GPT-2 architectures in Section 8 empirically confirm that SFT benefits from smaller curated datasets while OS/RL benefits from larger ones (Section 8).
claims.evidence: LSA experiments show both SFT and OS have turning points (SFT optimal at B=200, OS optimal at B=100), partially supporting SFT degradation but contradicting the claim that OS benefits from larger datasets; the GPT-2 architecture experiments are not reproduced, and the small continuous transformer substitute yields noisy, inconclusive results.

gchauhan/repro-theoretical-perspectives-.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification of the paper's formal theorems (4.1, 4.2, 5.1) and the spectral stability conditions at LSA scale, but actual training experiments contradict the hard-examples claim (Claim 3) and give mixed results for OS effectiveness (Claim 5) and SFT/OS scaling (Claim 6), with no GPT-2 scale reproduction.

snaykey/repro-kl-zerosum-games.paper_title: Two-Layer Linear Auto-Regressive Models Estimate Latent States

claims.claim: The informal main result states that the hidden representation learned by a two-layer linear autoregressive model trained on a partially observed linear dynamical system coincides, up to a similarity transformation S, with the state estimates of the optimal Kalman filter (Theorem 1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: On the paper's system (n=4, p=2, m=3, T=32000, L=16, H=5), the logbook directly measures coordinate-wise R² between S·Ĝ₁z̄ₜ and Kalman states x̂ₜ, obtaining [0.9993, 0.9992, 0.9997, 0.9998] (mean 0.9995, MSE 0.0113), demonstrating the similarity-transform equivalence holds at high precision.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 (Section 4.4) formalizes this latent-state-recovery result, giving explicit finite-sample error bounds between the learned representation and the Kalman filter estimate up to the similarity transformation.
claims.evidence: Across T=3000→32000 (8 trials each), recovery MSE decreases monotonically from 0.0642 to 0.0094 with log-log slope -0.82, and mean R² rises from 0.9981 to 0.9997, confirming finite-sample decay behavior consistent with Theorem 4's bounds (the slightly shallower slope is plausibly explained by the ‖z̄ₜ‖² factor under marginal stability).

claims.claim: Theorem 2 (Section 4.3) bounds the in-sample prediction error at global optima of the empirical risk at a rate of O(H/T), where H is history length and T is trajectory length.
claims.evidence: The in-sample prediction error (1/T)Σ‖(Ĝ₂Ĝ₁−OC)z̄ₜ‖² decays from 1.102 to 0.0813 across T=3000→32000 with log-log slope -1.098, closely matching the predicted 1/T rate (target -1) at the ERM global optimum.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 (Section 4.3) gives a finite-sample bound on parameter estimation error in Frobenius norm for the learned autoregressive weights.
claims.evidence: The Frobenius-norm parameter error ‖Ĝ₂Ĝ₁−OC‖²_F decays from 8.36 to 0.7426 across T=3000→32000 with log-log slope -1.012, nearly exactly matching the predicted 1/T rate.

claims.claim: Proposition 1 (Section 4.1) shows the Kalman filter is well-approximated by a finite-history autoregressive model, with truncation error decaying exponentially in history length L.
claims.evidence: Truncation error ‖x̂ₜ−C_L z̄ₜ‖² collapses from 1161.0 (L=1) to 3.29e-09 (L=20) with fitted per-L decay base 0.24837, matching the theoretical ρ(Ā)²=0.24843 to within 0.02%, directly confirming the exponential decay rate predicted by Proposition 1.

claims.claim: In numerical experiments, a grid search over hidden dimension h identifies h=4 as optimal, matching the true latent state dimension n=4 (Section 5.2, Table 1), and learned activations achieve mean R-squared >= 0.979 alignment with Kalman filter state estimates (Section 5.3, Figure 2, Table 2).
claims.evidence: Mean R² of 0.9980 (H=1) and 0.9996 (H=5) both exceed the claimed 0.979 threshold; grid-search training loss shows a clear elbow at h=4 (0.486) with plateau for h≥4 (successive changes <1%), though the strict argmin lands at h=10 (0.474) within the noise-dominated flat region — the elbow at the true dimension n=4 is reproduced.

snaykey/repro-kl-zerosum-games.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence from an independent from-scratch NumPy/SciPy implementation on the paper's own system model (n=4, p=2, m=3), directly measuring each theorem's quantities across T and L sweeps with 8 trials. All six claims are supported by real numerical results, with the only notable caveat being that the grid-search strict argmin falls at h=10 rather than h=4, though the loss elbow correctly coincides with the true dimension n=4.

snaykey/repro-spa-binary-feedback.paper_title: The (Marginal) Value of a Search Ad: An Online Causal Framework for Repeated Second-price Auctions

claims.claim: Under binary feedback, the proposed algorithm for repeated second-price auctions achieves regret O(√(dT) log³T + d log⁵T), where d is the feature dimension and T the horizon (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook runs the paper's IPW value estimator (eq.5) with interval-splitting Ĝ on d-dimensional linear Gaussian contexts with Beta(5,7) HOB, measuring T-exponent 0.541 (R²=0.988) and d-exponent 0.494 (R²=0.994) with regret/√(dT) CV of 7.1%, confirming the leading √(dT) rate of Theorem 1 on a non-toy setup, though polylog factors are not resolved.

claims.claim: A matching minimax lower bound of Ω(√(dT)) holds for T ≥ d², even when the bidder has perfect knowledge of the competing-bid CDF (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook constructs the exact Le Cam two-point family from Appendix J with known atom-bearing CDF G, measures the Bayes-optimal policy's regret at T-exponent 0.523 (R²=0.999) with strictly positive constant ≥0.0565, and shows d-embedding scales linearly (exponent 0.962), providing concrete evidence for the Ω(√(dT)) lower bound even with perfect CDF knowledge.

claims.claim: Under binary feedback, second-price auctions admit Õ(√(dT)) regret while first-price auctions are limited to Õ(T^(2/3)) regret, showing the payment rule strictly improves achievable regret (Section on regret comparison).
claims.evidence: On matched Beta(5,7) HOB instances at d=4 with binary feedback, SPA achieves exponent 0.490 (R²=0.9998) while FPA achieves exponent 0.688 (R²=0.999, within 0.022 of 2/3), with the FPA/SPA regret ratio widening to 95.8× at T=64000, confirming the strict order separation.

claims.claim: Under full-information feedback, both second-price and first-price auctions achieve the same Õ(√(dT)) regret rate, so the SPA advantage is specific to the binary-feedback setting (Section on regret comparison).
claims.evidence: Under full-information feedback on matched Beta(5,7) instances at d=4, both SPA (exponent 0.489, R²=0.9998) and FPA (exponent 0.496, R²=0.9998) land at √T with a gap of only 0.007, confirming that the SPA advantage vanishes under full information.

claims.claim: Section 3 introduces an interval-splitting technique to estimate the highest-other-bid (HOB) directly from the observed payment in a won second-price auction (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements the eq.(4) interval-split ĝ_t with Lemma-1 Bernstein confidence width, measuring sup-norm error decay at n^{-0.450} (R²=0.995) on Beta(5,7) and n^{-0.423} (R²=0.996) on a point-mass distribution, with 100% Bernstein-width coverage across all grid cells and seeds.

snaykey/repro-spa-binary-feedback.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all five claims using the paper's actual causal mechanisms (IPW estimator, interval-splitting HOB estimator, Le Cam construction) on non-trivial parameter ranges with multiple seeds and high-quality log-log fits. The main limitations are the use of an explore-then-commit variant instead of the full Algorithm 3 and the focus on leading polynomial rates rather than polylog factors, but these do not undermine the core rate verifications.

snaykey/repro-linbandit-param-noise.paper_title: Stochastic Linear Bandits with Parameter Noise

claims.claim: For stochastic linear bandits with parameter noise on general action sets of size K and dimension d, the paper proves a regret upper bound of tilde-O(sqrt(dT log(K/delta)) * sigma_max^2) over horizon T (Section on main results / regret upper bound theorem).
claims.evidence: VASE (Algorithm 2) with median-of-means variance estimation (Algorithm 1) was implemented at d=10, K=25, 30 seeds, with T swept from 4k to 512k. The measured tail log-log slope in T is 0.490 (theory: 0.5), the K-dependence over K:5→1280 is only 1.24× (vs 16× for √K) with log(K/δ)-exponent 0.25, the sigma-exponent is 0.85 (near-linear, consistent with sigma_max² inside the square root), and the ratio regret/(√(dT log(K/δ))·σ) is bounded at ≈2.5. These concrete scaling signatures on a non-toy setup support the upper bound claim.

claims.claim: A matching regret lower bound of tilde-Omega(d sqrt(T) * sigma_max^2) is established, tight up to logarithmic factors when log(K) is approximately d (lower bound theorem).
claims.evidence: The hard hypercube instance {-1,+1}^d/√d (with log K = d·log 2 ≈ d, the tightness regime) was constructed and the Le Cam/Assouad information limit was Monte-Carlo measured across d=4→20 and T=4k→128k. The measured floor scales as d^1.006 · T^0.502, the optimal Neyman-Pearson sign estimator's success probability matches the analytic Le Cam value Φ(z)=0.6915 to <0.5% and never exceeds the power cap, and a real batched phased-elimination algorithm sits above the floor within a log factor (ratio 3.2–4.6). This is concrete evidence on a non-toy setup supporting the lower bound.

claims.claim: For l_p unit ball action sets with p<=2 (dual norm q), the minimax regret is characterized as Theta-tilde(sqrt(dT) * sigma_q^2), substantially better than the d*sqrt(T) regret of the classic additive noise model (minimax regret theorem, l_p unit ball case).
claims.evidence: VALEE (Algorithm 3) was run on the ℓ2-ball with σ_q² held constant at 0.50 across d=4→16 (T=40000, 30 seeds), yielding a parameter-noise d-exponent of 0.563 (theory: 0.5 for √d) with a nearly flat normalized ratio regret/(√(dT)·σ_q²) of 33.9→37.2 (+10% drift over 4× change in d). The additive-noise baseline (OFUL/LinUCB) shows d-exponent 1.325, demonstrating the √d-vs-d separation central to the claim.

claims.claim: The paper shows that a simple explore-then-exploit algorithm achieves the optimal regret bounds up to logarithmic factors under the parameter noise model (algorithmic contribution section).
claims.evidence: VALEE's exact explore-then-commit rule (basis exploration + median-of-means + adaptive doubling + commit â_i = sign(θ̂_i)|θ̂_i|^{q-1}/||θ̂||_q^{q-1}) was implemented at d=8, σ_q²=0.50, T swept 4k→256k, 30 seeds. The measured tail log-log slope in T is 0.500 (optimal √T rate) with a flat normalized ratio regret/√(dT·σ_q²) ≈ 25.8. The naive fixed-budget explore-then-commit baseline shows slope 0.639 (close to the sub-optimal 2/3 rate), confirming the separation the paper predicts.

snaykey/repro-linbandit-param-noise.overall: The logbook implements the paper's actual algorithms (VASE with Algorithm 1 variance estimation, VALEE with exact commit rule) and constructs a measured Le Cam lower bound, all on non-toy setups (d=8–10, T up to 512k, K up to 1280, 30–40 seeds). The measured scaling exponents in T, d, K, and σ closely match the theoretical predictions across all four claims, providing concrete empirical support for the paper's upper bound, lower bound, ℓp-ball separation, and explore-then-exploit optimality results.

snaykey/repro-autobidding-monotonicity.paper_title: Model Monotonicity in Autobidding Auctions: When Do Better Predictions Lead to Better Outcomes?

claims.claim: For target-CPA bidders without budget constraints using uniform bidding with multiplier mu=1 in first-price auctions, refining the prediction model (partitioning clusters into subclusters while preserving calibration) never decreases platform revenue, i.e., Rev(M_A) >= Rev(M_B) when M_A refines M_B (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: 3000 random FPA instances (2-5 bidders, 4-11 subclusters) with random calibration-preserving refinement chains yielded 0 violations of Rev(M_A) >= Rev(M_B), with 56.8% showing strict increases and mean gap +0.3931.

claims.claim: The first-price auction revenue monotonicity proof for tCPA bidders relies on convexity of f(p) = max_i(t_i · p_i) via Jensen's inequality, since model refinement corresponds to a mean-preserving spread of this convex function (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: 200,000 random convexity checks of f(p)=max_i(t_i·p_i) found 0 violations (worst Jensen slack 8.9e-16), and 5,000 mean-preserving-spread split checks found 0 violations with mean E[f] gain +0.1216, directly confirming both ingredients of the proof mechanism.

claims.claim: Uniform bidding at multiplier mu=1 is simultaneously conversion-maximizing, revenue-maximizing among equilibria, and welfare-maximizing for tCPA bidders in first-price auctions (Theorem 5.2), and welfare monotonicity follows as a corollary when per-conversion values equal targets (Corollary 5.3).
claims.evidence: Across 300 random FPA instances, feasibility held iff mu<=1 (0 mismatches), best-response dynamics placed all winning bidders at mu*=1 (0/300 deviations), and revenue/conversions/welfare were each maximal at mu=1 over the feasible sweep (0/300 failures for each metric).

claims.claim: There exist instances with tCPA bidders where second-price (VCG) auctions exhibit non-monotonicity in both revenue and welfare under model refinement, with a constructed counterexample showing a simultaneous 6.2% decrease in both metrics (Theorem 5.8).
claims.evidence: The paper's §B.1 counterexample was recomputed exactly: coarse model yields Rev=Welfare=3.23, fine model yields 3.03, a 6.19% simultaneous drop, with winners [A,A,B,B]→[A,B,B,B] matching the paper. An independent scan of 3000 random SPA instances found 189 with simultaneous revenue+welfare drops.

claims.claim: Introducing budget constraints breaks revenue monotonicity even in first-price auctions, as optimal bidder multipliers shift under refinement and reduce competitive pressure, exemplified by a counterexample with a 16.8% revenue loss (Theorem 5.10).
claims.evidence: The paper's §B.2 counterexample was recomputed exactly: revenue 5.5268→4.5977 (16.81% drop), Advertiser 1's spend equals budget 3.185 in both models (budget_binds_exactly=True), liquid welfare 5.53→4.60, with all bids and allocations matching. An independent scan found 458/3000 random budgeted-FPA instances with strict revenue losses.

claims.claim: A centralized, non-strategic linear-programming benchmark allocation guarantees welfare monotonicity under budget constraints via a 'lifting' construction that preserves feasibility across refined partitions (Theorem 5.11), and the paper's overall characterization identifies exactly three settings where monotonicity holds (Table 1).
claims.evidence: 400 random budgeted instances solved via cluster-granularity LP (scipy/HiGHS) with lifting check yielded 0 welfare-monotonicity violations (mean gain +0.0346); a negative control with buggy subcluster-level variables failed 319/400, confirming the lifting construction is load-bearing. The Table 1 three-setting characterization is supported by the combination of C1/C3/C6 (monotone) and C4/C5 (non-monotone) results, though not independently enumerated.

snaykey/repro-autobidding-monotonicity.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence for all six claims: exact reproduction of the paper's counterexamples (C4: 3.23→3.03, C5: 5.5268→4.5977) and Monte Carlo verification of positive results across thousands of random instances (C1/C2/C3/C6) with zero violations. The setup faithfully implements the paper's model (tCPA bidders, calibrated predictions, uniform bidding, FPA/VCG/LP) at reasonable scale with documented robustness checks and a negative control.

snaykey/repro-online-bilateral-trade-gbb.paper_title: A Stronger Benchmark for Online Bilateral Trade: From Fixed Prices to Distributions

claims.claim: Under a bounded-density assumption on buyer/seller valuation distributions, the proposed algorithm achieves Õ(T^{3/4}) regret against the best fixed price distribution satisfying Global Budget Balance (GBB) (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: A comparable 3-phase ETC algorithm on bounded-density instances (Uniform[0,1] and Beta(2,4)/Beta(4,2)) with T up to 64000 and 24 seeds yields fitted regret exponents of 0.769 and 0.740, bracketing the claimed 3/4, with median budget ≈ 0 confirming GBB feasibility.

claims.claim: Without the bounded-density assumption, any algorithm suffers Ω(T) linear regret against the GBB benchmark, shown via a needle-in-the-haystack construction proving discretization is impossible (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The needle construction with atoms (K=8, K=32) shows grid-based learners suffer exactly linear regret (exponent 1.000, grid GBB value 0 vs OPT=δ), but this only tests grid learners on a simplified 2-point atom construction, not the universal 'any algorithm' quantifier of Theorem 3.1.

claims.claim: Bounded density lets the learner restrict to a uniform K×K price grid with discretization error O(log(T)/K), showing no separation between one-dimensional SBB learning and two-dimensional GBB distribution learning (Lemma 5.1, Lemma 5.2).
claims.evidence: Exact numeric-integration computation on asymmetric Beta instances shows discretization gaps decaying as K^{-1.1} to K^{-1.8} (within the O(log(K)/K) envelope) and 1-D SBB gaps identical to 2-D GBB gaps at every K, directly supporting both the error bound and the no-separation claim.

claims.claim: In the profit-collection phase, regret is bounded by Õ(β + T/K + √(KT)) where β is the accumulated budget (Lemma 7.1, Lemma 7.2).
claims.evidence: Across 9 (T,K) cells with 16 seeds, the ratio of phase regret to (β + T/K + √(KT)) stays constant in [0.17, 0.22], flat over a 16× horizon range and 4× K range, confirming the Õ(β + T/K + √(KT)) scaling of Lemma 7.1/7.2.

claims.claim: The pure-exploration phase estimates all K² price-pair outcomes using only 2K exploration samples via sample reuse across the observable/non-observable GFT decomposition (Lemma 8.1, Lemma 8.2).
claims.evidence: The GFT decomposition identity matches direct Monte-Carlo to 7.5e-4 (MC noise floor) across all 256 pairs, and estimation error from 2K empirical CDF samples contracts as m^{-0.493} ≈ m^{-1/2} over 40 seeds, confirming the K²→2K sample-reuse compression.

claims.claim: The UCB-based constrained-bandit optimization phase achieves Õ(K√T) regret while preserving GBB feasibility, combining with the other phases to yield the overall Õ(T^{3/4}) rate (Lemma 9.1, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: At fixed K=8, the constrained UCB bandit phase yields a fitted regret exponent of 0.570 (≈ 1/2 up to log factors) over T up to 30000 with 16 seeds, while the worst budget dip (−45) remains under 10% of the granted buffer β₀≈490, confirming both the Õ(K√T) rate and GBB feasibility.

snaykey/repro-online-bilateral-trade-gbb.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting five of six claims on non-toy setups with real distributions, proper GBB benchmark computation, and adequate seed counts; the Ω(T) lower bound (Claim 2) is demonstrated only at the mechanism level for grid learners on a simplified needle construction, not as the universal impossibility result stated in Theorem 3.1.

snaykey/repro-dal-prior-free-piecewise-s.paper_title: DAL: A Practical Prior-Free Black-Box Framework for Piecewise Stationary Bandits

claims.claim: DAL (Detection Augmented bandit) is presented as Algorithm 1 (Section 3), a black-box framework that pairs any stationary bandit algorithm with a change detector to handle piecewise stationary environments.
claims.evidence: The same DAL wrapper (base + detector + restart) is run with two structurally different bases on non-toy setups: UCB1 on a switching Bernoulli MAB (K=5, T=20000) and LinUCB on a piecewise-stationary linear bandit (K=15, d=6, T=20000), with the LinUCB result showing a 25.9x regret reduction (852.6 vs 22059.8) when detection is enabled.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 (Section 4) proves DAL achieves an order-optimal O~(sqrt(N_T * T)) regret bound, where N_T is the number of change-points over horizon T.
claims.evidence: A 4x4 grid sweep over N_T∈{2,4,8,16} and T∈{4000,...,32000} with 6 seeds yields fitted exponents of 0.514 for N_T and 0.428 for T (R²=0.969), and a combined (N_T*T) exponent of 0.471 (R²=0.961), both close to the predicted 0.5 on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: Table 1 (Section 4) shows DAL combined with LinUCB matches the state-of-the-art d*sqrt(N_T*T) regret bound for piecewise-stationary linear bandits, and DAL with GLM-UCB attains the same rate for generalized linear bandits.
claims.evidence: The sqrt(N_T*T) scaling is supported (exponents 0.552 and 0.386), but the dimension exponent is 0.352 versus the claimed d^1, and GLM-UCB is not implemented or tested at all, leaving half the claim (generalized linear bandits) entirely unaddressed.

claims.claim: For piecewise-stationary self-concordant bandits, DAL improves the regret bound from the prior d^(2/3) T^(2/3) N_T^(1/3) rate to d*sqrt(N_T*T) (Table 1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Self-concordant bandits are proxied by a linear bandit (explicitly acknowledged), and the measured horizon exponent (0.341) is below the claimed 0.5; while the logbook argues it is closer to 0.5 than to the prior 2/3, the actual self-concordant setting is never tested.

claims.claim: DAL is empirically compared against MASTER (Wei & Luo, 2021), ADA-OPKB (Hong et al., 2023), and WeightUCB (Wang et al., 2023) in piecewise-stationary environments (Section 5.1, Figures 1-3) and drifting environments (Section 5.2, Figures 4-5).
claims.evidence: Only 2 of 3 named baselines are run, and both are simplified stand-ins (SW-UCB for WeightUCB, scheduled-restart for MASTER) rather than the actual algorithms; ADA-OPKB is not implemented at all, and drifting environments (Section 5.2) are not tested.

claims.claim: The regret analysis in Appendix A.1 decomposes total regret into false-alarm cost, detection latency, the base stationary algorithm's regret, and forced-exploration cost.
claims.evidence: Every time-step's instantaneous regret is assigned to exactly one of four buckets (false-alarm, detection-latency, base, forced-exploration) on a non-toy setup (K=5, T=24000, N_T=10, 6 seeds), with the four terms summing to total regret to floating-point precision (residual ~1e-12) under both a calibrated and an over-sensitive detector.

snaykey/repro-dal-prior-free-piecewise-s.overall: The logbook provides concrete empirical evidence for the black-box framework property (Claim 1), the sqrt(N_T*T) regret scaling (Claim 2), and the four-way regret decomposition (Claim 6) on non-toy setups. However, Claims 3–5 are substantially incomplete: the d^1 dimension factor and GLM-UCB are not verified, self-concordant bandits are proxied by linear bandits, one of three baselines is missing, and drifting environments are untested.

sotayamashita/repro-lower-bounds-for-fra.paper_title: Lower Bounds for Frank-Wolfe on Strongly Convex Sets

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a constructive Omega(1/sqrt(epsilon)) lower bound on the number of iterations for Frank-Wolfe with short steps or exact line search when both the objective and the constraint set are smooth and strongly convex (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: The logbook independently implements the backward construction (G map) and forward recurrence (F map) for the quadratic-over-ball instance, testing horizons T=16–256 with 120–768 decimal digits of precision. Forward-backward consistency errors are below 1e-100, all iterates remain feasible, and the explicit gap bound f(x_t)-f(x*) ≥ 9μD²/(30752t²) is confirmed numerically with terminal_gap×t² values all positive and above 0.25.

claims.claim: The lower-bound construction uses the specific instance of minimizing f(x) = ||x-p||_2^2 over the Euclidean unit ball B_1(0) with the unconstrained minimizer p on the boundary (||p||=1), showing this hard instance matches the known O(1/sqrt(epsilon)) upper bound of Garber et al. (2015) (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: The reproduction uses exactly f(x)=||x-p||² over the unit ball with ||p||=1, and the terminal_gap_times_t_squared column (0.259–0.531) confirms the Ω(1/t²) rate, which converts to Ω(1/√ε). The logbook explicitly cross-references Garber and Hazan (ICML 2015) for the matching O(1/t²) upper bound under the same algorithm and geometry assumptions.

claims.claim: The lower bound is established via a 'backward reconstruction' technique that builds worst-case trajectories by working backward from terminal iterates, producing precise sequences over horizons of 10,000+ iterations (Section on Backward Reconstruction Strategy).
claims.evidence: The backward reconstruction technique is implemented and verified (G run backward, F replayed forward with errors below 1e-100), but the maximum horizon tested is T=256 with 512 backward steps—far short of the claimed 10,000+ iterations. The technique is demonstrated at reduced scale rather than at the claimed horizon.

claims.claim: The analysis reduces the dynamics to a two-dimensional invariant subspace parametrized by residual magnitude r and contraction factor s, revealing stable phases of monotonically increasing contraction followed by intermittent 'jumps' that explain the convergence stalling behavior (Section on Dynamical Analysis).
claims.evidence: The 2D (r,s) dynamics are implemented via the F and G maps and numerically verified, but the logbook provides no visible analysis or data demonstrating 'stable phases of monotonically increasing contraction' or intermittent 'jumps.' The figures that might show this behavior are omitted from the text, leaving the phenomenological claims unsupported by concrete evidence.

claims.claim: The result shows strong convexity of the constraint set alone cannot yield convergence rates uniformly faster than O(1/sqrt(epsilon)), and this conclusion holds dimension-independently and extends to ellipsoidal constraints via affine invariance (Theorem 6, Implications).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides algebraic witnesses showing that any polynomial rate Kε^{-q} with q<1/2 is exceeded by the lower bound Aε^{-1/2} for sufficiently small ε (tested for q=0, 0.25, 0.49 with K=1,10), and argues dimension-independence via zero-coordinate embedding of the 2D trajectory. The ellipsoidal extension via affine invariance is not explicitly tested but follows as a standard mathematical corollary from the ball case.

sotayamashita/repro-lower-bounds-for-fra.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous independent numerical verification of the backward construction and gap bounds for the paper's hard instance at moderate horizons (up to 256), confirming the Ω(1/√ε) lower bound and its tightness against the Garber-Hazan upper bound. However, it does not reach the claimed 10,000+ iteration horizons, and the dynamical phase/jump analysis is not evidenced in the visible logbook content.

snaykey/repro-adaptive-bandits-contextua.paper_title: Why Agentic Theorem Prover Works: A Statistical Provability Theory of Mathematical Reasoning Models

claims.claim: Theorem 1 establishes that the space of finite measures with bounded mass forms a compact metric space under the bounded Lipschitz metric, providing the topological foundation for the measure-valued goal encoding of the reachability MDP (Theorem 1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook instantiates a finite K (nK=7) where compactness of M_{<=W}(K) is trivially true (closed bounded subset of R^n), though it does verify dBL metric axioms via exact LP and Lemma 7 (weak-convergence metrization) with real numerical checks. The essential analytic difficulty (Arzelà-Ascoli, Prokhorov for infinite compact K) is absent.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 proves that under mild Feller-type continuity conditions on the transition kernel, optimal deterministic Markov policies exist for the finite-horizon time-bounded reachability MDP (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: On a finite MDP (S=6, A=4, B=5), existence of an optimal deterministic Markov policy is trivially guaranteed by compactness of finite state/action spaces; the logbook does verify optimality via backward induction and a Feller-necessity control with a discontinuous utility, but the main existence claim is vacuously easy on this setup.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 shows that sequences of functions satisfying Bellman sub-/super-solution inequalities yield provability certificates (upper and lower bounds on the optimal value function) without requiring the full MDP to be solved, with the certificate gap defined as UB(x0) - LB(x0) (Theorem 3, Definition 5, Section 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook checks 200 random valid sub-/super-solution constructions that bracket V*_b at every state and depth on a finite reachability MDP (S=6, A=4, B=6) with exact Bellman operator computation, confirms the score-certificate gap saturates 2*eps, and demonstrates that violating the Bellman inequality breaks the bound (U_B < V*_B by 0.034). The bracketing property is non-trivial even on finite MDPs.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 bounds the worst-case regret of score-guided planning under uniform score-approximation error εb as 0 ≤ V*_B(x0) - V^{πh}_B(x0) ≤ 2∑_{b=1}^{B} εb, showing performance degrades linearly with accumulated approximation error (Theorem 4, Section 6).
claims.evidence: Across 2000 trials on a concrete MDP (S=7, A=5, B=6) with uniform score noise, regret always lies in [0, 2*sum(eps_b)] with zero violations; a minimal adversarial B=1 MDP achieves regret/bound ratio of 0.9995, demonstrating the constant 2 and linear form are tight.

claims.claim: Theorem 5 shows that under a margin condition on action-value separation, the expected regret improves to O(Bε^{β+1}) for β>0, i.e., faster than the worst-case linear-in-B rate of Theorem 4 (Theorem 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook computes exact per-state regret expectations under the margin law P(Delta<=t)=(t/t0)^beta with 4e6 sampled gaps, fitting log-log exponents of 1.500, 2.001, 3.008, 4.011 against theory beta+1 for beta in {0.5,1,2,3}, and confirms linearity in horizon B (slope 1.00). The two-action setup captures the essential margin mechanism.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 derives a high-probability estimation-error bound of order O(L H d_D/(d_D+2) (log(n/δ)/n)^{1/(d_D+2)}) under a doubling-dimension assumption on the relevant problem domain, formalizing how statistical complexity of a biased real-world problem distribution governs sample efficiency (Theorem 6, Section 7).
claims.evidence: The finite-sample bound (eq. 2) holds with empirical coverage 1.000 >= 0.90 across 300 trials on [0,1]^2 with McShane Lipschitz-extension estimator; the sup-error rate exponent matches 1/(d_D+2) for d_D in {1,2,3} (0.325, 0.261, 0.199), and the L_H power fits d_D/(d_D+2)=0.503 vs theory 0.500.

snaykey/repro-adaptive-bandits-contextua.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence for all six theorems by instantiating the underlying measure-theoretic, MDP, and statistical objects with exact computations, but Claims 1-2 are checked on finite setups where the theorems' conclusions are trivially true, while Claims 3-6 are verified on setups that capture the essential mathematical structure with tightness and necessity controls.

snaykey/repro-decentralized-oco-compress.paper_title: Decentralized Online Convex Optimization with Efficient Communication: Improved Algorithm and Lower Bounds

claims.claim: Top-DOGD achieves O(ω^{-1/2}ρ^{-1}n√T) regret for convex loss functions under compressed communication, improving on prior bounds (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: On a non-toy setup (n=12 agents, d=10, ring-lattice graph, Top-k compression, T up to 8000, 12 seeds), the logbook measures network regret scaling as n^{1.000} (R²=1.000) and T^{0.535} (R²=0.999), consistent with the claimed O(n√T) rate. The ω/ρ dependence is not directly tested in regret here but is addressed separately in Claim 3.

claims.claim: Top-DOGD achieves O(ω^{-1}ρ^{-2}n ln T) regret for strongly convex loss functions (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: On the same non-toy setup with strongly convex quadratic losses (σ=1, n=12, d=10, 8 seeds), regret grows logarithmically: fit 0.80·ln(T)+17.15 with R²=0.99993, and the power-law exponent collapses to 0.034, confirming the O(n ln T) rate of Theorem 3.2.

claims.claim: The paper reduces dependence on compression quality ω from the previously known O(ω^{-2}ρ^{-4}n^{1/2}√T) (convex) and O(ω^{-2}ρ^{-4}n^{1/2} ln T) (strongly convex) bounds down to O(ω^{-1/2}ρ^{-1}n√T) and O(ω^{-1}ρ^{-2}n ln T) respectively, cutting the exponent on ω^{-1} from quadratic/quartic to square-root/linear (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The ω and ρ dependence is measured on a proxy quantity — gossip consensus rounds, not regret itself. The measured exponents (ω^{-0.95}, ρ^{-1.05}) are in the improved regime and rule out prior ω^{-2}ρ^{-4}, but the mapping from consensus-round exponents to regret-bound exponents is assumed, not verified, making this a proxy-task assessment rather than a direct regret measurement.

claims.claim: First lower bounds for decentralized online convex optimization with compressed communication are established: Ω(ω^{-1/2}ρ^{-1/4}n√T) for convex functions and Ω(ω^{-1}ρ^{-1/2}n ln T) for strongly convex functions (Theorems 3.3 and 3.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook measures a regret floor of T^{0.502}·n^{1.000} on a Rademacher hard instance, but this is an upper bound on optimal regret (one algorithm's performance), not a certified lower bound. The novel ω/ρ dependence in the lower bound is not verified — the ω sweep yields a near-flat ω^{-0.006}, contradicting the claimed ω^{-1/2}. Information-theoretic lower bounds cannot be certified by simulation, as the logbook itself acknowledges.

claims.claim: The algorithm combines a two-level blocking update framework with an online compressed gossip strategy and a projection error compensation scheme to jointly control consensus, compression, and projection error (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: All three components are implemented in the codebase. Ablations on a non-toy setup (n=12, d=10, T=4000, 20 seeds) show projection-error compensation reduces regret by 7.4% when enabled (313.5 vs 336.7) and compressed gossip reduces consensus error by 25x (3.81e-2 vs 9.54e-1). The two-level blocking update is implemented but only tested in degenerate mode (block=1), which is a partial limitation.

claims.claim: Bandit-feedback extensions are provided: one-point feedback achieves O(ω^{-1/4}ρ^{-1/2}d^{1/2}n(ln n)^{1/4}T^{3/4}) regret (Theorem 4.1) and two-point feedback achieves O(ω^{-1/2}ρ^{-1}dn ln n√T) regret (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: On a non-toy bandit setup (n=12, d=6, k=3, 6 seeds), one-point feedback regret scales as T^{0.753} (R²=0.99991), matching the claimed T^{3/4} rate, and two-point feedback scales as T^{0.467} (R²=0.99991), matching √T. The T-exponent separation (0.753 vs 0.467) reproduces the claimed feedback-model improvement. The ω/ρ/d/n dependencies are not tested.

snaykey/repro-decentralized-oco-compress.overall: The logbook provides a genuine from-scratch NumPy implementation of Top-DOGD and verifies the core regret rate scaling (n√T for convex, n ln T for strongly convex, T^{3/4}/√T bandit separation) on non-toy setups with good fits. However, the ω/ρ dependence is only tested via a consensus-cost proxy (not regret), and the lower-bound claim is fundamentally unverifiable by simulation with its novel ω dependence actually contradicted by the data.

sotayamashita/repro-on-densest-k-subgrap.paper_title: On Densest $k$-Subgraph Mining and Diagonal Loading: Optimization Landscape and Finite-Step Exact Convergence Analysis

claims.claim: Theorem 4 extends the Motzkin-Straus theorem to show the relaxed problem's maximum value equals 1+λ-1/ω, where ω is the largest clique size, establishing that diagonal loading parameter λ≥1 is the minimal value ensuring tightness of the penalty-based relaxation.
claims.evidence: On K2 with ω=2 and λ=1/2, exact rational arithmetic gives the maximum of xᵀ(A+λI)x as 3/4 at x=(1/2,1/2), while the claimed formula 1+λ-1/ω yields 1. The logbook also notes arXiv v3 uses the corrected formula 1+(λ-1)/ω=3/4, confirming the literal claim formula is wrong.

claims.claim: Corollary 1 proves that when λ≥1 there always exists a global maximizer of the relaxed objective that is integral, so the relaxed and combinatorial problems share the same optimal value.
claims.evidence: A general algebraic exchange construction shows that for any non-integral feasible point with λ≥1, moving mass from a lower-gradient fractional coordinate to a higher-gradient one yields nonnegative objective gain (2δ(grad_i−grad_j)+2(λ−a_ij)δ²≥0) and terminates at an integral point. This is backed by an exhaustive exact-arithmetic audit of 1,098 graphs (2–5 vertices) and 376,434 graph-point-λ cases with zero failures.

claims.claim: Lemma 1 shows that for λ>1 there does not exist a non-integral local maximizer, establishing the strict dichotomy that all integral stationary points are local maximizers while non-integral stationary points are strict saddles.
claims.evidence: On the three-vertex star with center 2, k=2, λ=2 (satisfying λ>1), the integral point (1,1,0) is stationary but the feasible point (9/10,1,1/10) increases the objective by exactly 1/50, disproving that all integral stationary points are local maximizers. The first component (no non-integral local maximizer for λ>1) is verified algebraically, but the composite claim as stated is falsified by this counterexample.

claims.claim: Theorem 5 shows that increasing the diagonal loading parameter beyond λ=1 introduces additional spurious local maxima, implying λ=1 optimally trades off relaxation tightness against optimization difficulty.
claims.evidence: An algebraic argument shows increasing λ raises only the selected-side gradient term in the local-maximum condition, so existing local maxima are never removed. Exhaustive checks over 31,668 integral supports (graphs with 2–5 vertices, λ from 1.5 to 3) found zero violations. A direct witness on the three-vertex star shows selecting two leaves is not a local maximum at λ=1.5 but becomes a strict (spurious) local maximum at λ=3, with the center-plus-leaf solution being better by exactly 2.

claims.claim: The saddle-escaping Frank-Wolfe algorithm (Section 3.1) has per-iteration complexity O(m+k log n) and is shown to converge in a finite number of steps to an integral local maximizer of the densest k-subgraph relaxation.
claims.evidence: Version inspection reveals the claim combines v3's complexity O(m+k log n) with v4's saddle-escaping algorithm (which actually reports O(m+n)). A concrete counterexample on the empty 4-vertex graph with k=2, λ=1.5, and uniform initialization shows standard Frank-Wolfe (v3) has zero gradient gap and remains stuck at a non-integral saddle, contradicting finite-step convergence to an integral maximizer for the v3 algorithm referenced in the claim's complexity.

claims.claim: Experiments show the Frank-Wolfe algorithm achieves denser subgraphs than competing methods LRBO, L-ADMM, and EXPP while incurring lower computational cost on real-world graphs with millions of vertices (Section 4).
claims.evidence: No experiments were run. The pinned official repository lacks million-vertex input graphs and implementations of LRBO and EXPP comparators, making it impossible to test the empirical claim. The logbook correctly declines to promote any synthetic proxy as evidence.

sotayamashita/repro-on-densest-k-subgrap.overall: The logbook provides rigorous exact-arithmetic counterexamples that falsify Claims 1, 3, and 5 as literally stated, and supplies algebraic certificates plus exhaustive small-graph audits that verify Claims 2 and 4. Claim 6 is unaddressed due to missing datasets and comparator implementations in the official repository.

harveechen/repro-information-geometry-lo.paper_title: Information Geometry Loss for Time Series Forecasting

claims.claim: InfoGeo Loss achieves average improvements of 6.8% in MSE and 5.3% in MAE on seven datasets with five architectures
claims.evidence: The official-backbone experiment (paper's 5 architectures from TSLib with official hyperparameters and full schedules on ETTh1, ETTm2, Weather) shows mean Δ MSE −20.5% with InfoGeo winning only 2/15 cells, including 0/5 on ETTh1 (−16% to −39%) and 0/5 on Weather (−15% to −49%), where the paper reports +3 to +8% on every cell. The compact 210-run grid (all 7 datasets × 5 architectures × 3 seeds) also shows negative mean Δ MSE (−8.4%), and the MSE baselines match the paper's own baseline column within a few percent, confirming the pipeline is faithful.

claims.claim: The approach proves statistical consistency and establishes convergence guarantees
claims.evidence: The theoretical properties were audited on a simplified 2-parameter Gaussian model (not the full forecasting setup). Consistency is numerically supported: the M-estimator converges at log-log slope −0.51 (theory: −0.5) while a Cauchy control violating regularity does not converge. However, the convergence guarantee (Thm 4.3) has an identified assumption gap: the un-squared Fisher distance d_F has a kink at the optimum, violating L-smoothness, causing fixed-step GD/NGD to plateau at O(η) (0.042 at η=0.05 → 0.0016 at η=0.002); squaring d_F restores machine-precision convergence (7.7e-32).

claims.claim: Fisher information metric quantifies intrinsic distributional distance on statistical manifolds
claims.evidence: Rigorous numerical audit on the Gaussian manifold confirms: (A) local KL expansion matches ½ε²vᵀIv to ratio 0.999996 at ε=1e-4; (B) closed-form Fisher-Rao distance matches independent numerical shortest-path computation to ≤6.9e-4 relative error; (C) reparameterization invariance holds to ≤6.5e-4 gap where Euclidean distance shifts 7.6%; (D) metric axioms hold with 0 violations in 2000 random trials while KL controls fail symmetry 2000/2000 and √KL fails triangle inequality 189/2000.

harveechen/repro-information-geometry-lo.overall: The logbook provides strong evidence that the paper's headline empirical claim (Claim 1) is falsified: InfoGeo degrades performance on both a 210-run compact grid and a 15-cell official-backbone experiment using the paper's own architectures with official hyperparameters, with baselines matching the paper's. The theoretical claims are partially supported on simplified setups: the Fisher metric properties (Claim 3) are rigorously confirmed, while statistical consistency (Claim 2) holds numerically but the convergence guarantee has an identified assumption gap.

ProCreations/repro-on-the-convergence-ra.paper_title: On the Convergence Rate of LoRA Gradient Descent

claims.claim: LoRA gradient descent converges to a stationary point at rate O(1/log T) in the general case without assuming Lipschitz smoothness of the reparameterized objective (Theorem 3, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The explicit non-asymptotic bound min_t ||grad J(V_t)||^2 <= 5(J(V_0)-L*)/log(1+T/K) was evaluated at 31,586 checkpoint cells across 1,655 runs (112M steps), 11 loss families, shapes up to 512x512, ranks 1-128, and horizons up to T=200,000, with 0 violations and max ratio 0.01685. A dedicated probe drove the reparameterized objective's gradient-Lipschitz constant to 2.011e6 times the original L without any bound failing, directly testing the 'without Lipschitz smoothness of J' clause.

claims.claim: When adapter norms are bounded, the same LoRA gradient descent algorithm converges at the faster rate O(1/T) (Theorem 3, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The conditional O(1/T) bound 5(J(V_0)-L*)/(eta_bar*T) was evaluated at all 31,586 checkpoint cells using the measured max adapter norm C per path, with 0 violations and max ratio 0.07081. The adapter norm stayed bounded on all 1,655 paths (max 82.95, median post-1000-step growth only 1.149x), confirming the hypothesis holds under the paper's own step rule without projection or clipping.

claims.claim: The analysis relies only on Assumption 1 (Lipschitz smoothness of the original, non-reparameterized loss) and Assumption 2 (the loss is lower bounded), avoiding artificially imposed smoothness on the LoRA-reparameterized objective (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: A dedicated probe (reparam_smoothness_probe.py) drove ||V_0||_F from 1 to 3000 across 432 cells, measuring the gradient-Lipschitz constant of J growing from 33.57 to 4.011e6 (5.1 orders of magnitude, up to 2.011e6x the original L), while Lemma 1, Lemma 2, and all Theorem-3 bounds held with 0 failures. The executed pipeline uses only L (Assumption 1), L* (Assumption 2), J(V_0), ||V_t||, and ||grad L|| — no reparameterized-smoothness constant appears in any formula.

claims.claim: The proof derives a Lipschitz-like descent lemma (Lemma 1) accounting for higher-order terms from the bilinear BA^T reparameterization, paired with an adaptive step-size rule ηt = min{1/(5√2 L(‖Vt‖^2+‖∇L(·)‖)), 1} (Lemma 2, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The six-term Lemma 1 inequality and the Lemma 2 descent guarantee J(V_{t+1}) <= J(V_t) - (eta_t/5)||grad J(V_t)||^2 were evaluated at every one of 112,120,000 executed steps with 0 violations beyond float64 round-off (worst Lemma-1 slack -9.095e-13, worst Lemma-2 residual 9.538e-13). The step rule eta_t = min{1/(5*sqrt(2)*L*(||V_t||^2+||grad L||)), 1} was used exactly as stated. Exact Fraction arithmetic cross-checks on 1,152 cells and destructive controls (step inflation breaking descent at 50x) confirm the test has power.

claims.claim: The paper shows the derived convergence rate is independent of the chosen LoRA rank, since gradient descent on the low-rank factors operates dimension-free (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: A controlled rank sweep with ||V_0||_F held identical across ranks 1-128 (383 runs, 7.1M steps) showed the Theorem-3 bound varying by median 1.0027x and worst 1.0913x over a 64-fold rank change across 54 matched groups. The rank symbol r is absent from all executed formulas. A real distilgpt2 transformer (82M params) run with 200 full-batch updates per rank at ranks 1-32 (1,200 total updates) showed C_log varying by 2.71x while trainable params varied 32x, with 0 Lemma-2 violations.

ProCreations/repro-on-the-convergence-ra.overall: This logbook provides substantial experimental evidence supporting all five claims by executing the paper's exact algorithm (112M steps, 1,655 runs) and evaluating the paper's own explicit inequalities at every checkpoint and every step, across 11 certified loss families, matrix shapes up to 512x512, ranks 1-128, horizons up to 200K, plus a real distilgpt2 transformer. The methodology is rigorous: it controls for confounds (e.g., normalizing ||V_0|| across ranks), includes destructive controls showing the guarantees break when the step rule is violated, provides exact rational arithmetic cross-checks, and independently verifies gradient identities.

sotayamashita/repro-softmax-as-linear-at.paper_title: Softmax as Linear Attention in the Large-Prompt Regime: a Measure-based Perspective

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 establishes non-asymptotic concentration bounds of order σ⁶ln(L)/L^(c₂/σ²) showing finite-prompt softmax attention outputs converge to their infinite-prompt counterparts as prompt length L grows, for i.i.d. Gaussian inputs (Section 3, Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: Numerical audit on small dimensions (d=2,5) with two covariance types and prompt lengths up to L=512, showing log-log slopes of -0.958 to -0.999 and L=512/L=8 error ratios of 0.0147–0.0172 with separated 95% intervals, but this is a reduced-scale test of a general concentration theorem.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.4 extends the concentration result to gradients, giving comparable convergence rates for gradient stability along the training trajectory (Section 3, Proposition 3.4).
