However, the headline performance claims (Claims 1 and 2) were not meaningfully tested: downstream evaluation used random labels on synthetic data with no baseline comparisons, and no real MIMIC-IV experiments were conducted.

ai-sherpa/robust-ski-rental-distribution.paper_title: Robust and Consistent Ski Rental with Distributional Advice

claims.claim: The Clamp Policy selects a threshold t̃ = min{max{t*_p̂, ceil(λb)}, floor(b/λ)} for a tunable robustness parameter λ in (0,1) (Definition 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: 3800/3800 instances over b ∈ {10,20,50,100,200} × 19 λ values × 5 prediction families satisfy the clamp identity t̃ = min{max{t*_p̂, ⌈λb⌉}, ⌊b/λ⌋}, with the clamp binding in 53.4% of cases. Algorithm 1 returns a true minimizer in 600/600 instances (max gap 2.27e-13), and removing the clamp lets adversarial predictions drive the worst-case ratio to 200.0 at b=200 versus 4.3167 with the clamp.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 bounds the competitive ratio by min{1 + 1/λ - 1/b, [ρ_p̂(t̃) + bθ]/(1-θ)}, giving robustness independent of prediction error η and consistency approaching the optimal ratio as η approaches 0 (Theorem 4.4, Corollary 4.5).
claims.evidence: Exact adversary search (point mass δ_x is worst case for linear-fractional CR) over a 7×19 (b,λ) grid shows sup CR ≤ 1+1/λ−1/b in 133/133 cells, with the bound attained exactly (slack 0.0) at b=5,λ=0.05 and b=50,λ=0.5. Consistent branch: 263/263 (p̂,p) pairs respect the min-of-two bound while measured CR rises monotonically 1.3321→1.9125 as η goes 0→16, never breaching the ceiling 3.48. At η=0, CR equals ρ_p̂(t̃) exactly (diff 0.0), with |CR−ρ| = 0.0305·η (R²=0.80).

claims.claim: The Water-Filling Algorithm's optimal randomized stopping distribution follows the geometric CDF F*(x) = min{(R-1)((1+1/(b-1))^x - 1), 1} for cost-monotone settings (Theorem 5.2, Section 5).
claims.evidence: For 35/35 (b,R) cells, the paper's own optimization problem solved as an LP via SciPy HiGHS (never shown the geometric formula) returns a CDF matching F* to 2.73e-14 in sup-norm with relative objective gaps below 1e-9. Theorem 5.3's threshold (92.92 at b=50,R=1.7) is recovered to the integer: F* optimal for every y≥93, strictly suboptimal for every y≤92 (excess up to 26.19%). 72/72 upward perturbations of F* break measured robustness, confirming maximality.

claims.claim: A stopping distribution is R-robust if and only if μ(x) + (b-x)F(x) ≤ (R-1)x for all 1 ≤ x ≤ b-1 and μ(∞) ≤ (R-1)b (Lemma 5.1).

rahit/repro-the-implicit-bias-of-steepes.paper_title: The Implicit Bias of Steepest Descent with Mini-batch Stochastic Gradient

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows that without momentum, mini-batch steepest descent converges to an approximate max-margin solution only when batch size exceeds the threshold b > 4Rn/(γ+4R), with the margin gap shrinking as batch size increases (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive enumeration of 2,886,348 (n,b,γ/R) triples across 136 independently solved datasets shows 0 admit b<n, confirming the threshold collapses to b=n. 60 native-scale runs (n=200, all 12 divisors of 200, 5 seeds) show margin rising monotonically from -0.052 at b=1 to 0.054 at b=200, with rel err falling 1.81→0.16. The 737,280-run exhaustive Prop 4.2 counterexample (0/737,280 classify both, invariant residual 3.55e-15) and its destructive control (16384/16384 after label fix) further confirm the mechanism.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 shows that adding momentum allows convergence to the max-margin solution even with small batch sizes, provided β₁→1, revealing a batch-momentum tradeoff (Theorem 4.3, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: 216 native-scale runs (12 batch sizes × 6 momenta × 3 seeds) show the batch-momentum tradeoff: at b=20, rel err drops 0.857→0.261→0.167 as β₁ goes 0→0.9→0.99, landing within 0.007 of full-batch. The critical-momentum scaling exponent measures 0.33288 vs predicted 1/3 (error 4.6e-4 over 9 decades). The m=1 consistency check gives exactly zero residual, and the destructive control (gradient permutation) moves b=20/β₁=0.99 from 0.167 to 8.90.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.5 shows the momentum-enabled convergence rate is slowed by a factor of m/(1-β₁) relative to the momentum-free large-batch case (Corollary 4.5, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: At full batch (m=1, isolating the 1/(1-β₁) leg), 21 runs at T=200,000 show the gap is non-decreasing in β₁ across all 7 values, growing 9.39× from β₁=0 to β₁=0.99999, with excess ~Q^1.27 (at least linear). The m-leg via VR runs shows gap increasing from 0.00288 to 0.00397 as m goes 1→200. The one-sided bound holds: 0/20 cells exceed the calibrated ceiling, and the estimator control returns -0.50000000 on synthetic t^-0.5.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 proves that variance reduction recovers the exact full-batch implicit bias for any batch size, eliminating the batch-size dependence of the margin, though Corollary 4.7 shows this comes at a convergence rate slowed by a factor of m^(2+a) (Theorem 4.6, Corollary 4.7, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: 360 runs at T=20,000 across all 12 admissible batch sizes show VR spread of 0.282 (vs plain 1.653); extended to T=1,000,000 the spread collapses to 0.0173 across all 12 batch sizes (min 0.0192, max 0.0365). Three destructive controls on the control variate (drop full-grad, sign-flip, frozen snapshot) each destroy recovery (1.00/1.29/1.00 vs 0.16 intact). Time-to-threshold scales as m^0.40 vs Cor 4.7's m^2.5, confirming direction as an upper bound.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.9 constructs an orthogonal, scale-skewed data example on which per-sample (batch-size-one) steepest descent converges to a fundamentally different implicit bias than the full-batch solution (Theorem 4.9, Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: On the constructed orthogonal scale-skewed dataset (K=10, imbalanced counts, α spanning 4 decades), per-sample Normalized-SGD reaches cos(W_t, W̄)=0.999994 while cos(W_t, W*)=0.933, and SignSGD reaches cos(W_t, W̄)=0.999994 while cos(W_t, W*)=0.560. Scale-independence is exact (identical cosine 0.99998881 across 8 decades of α, W̄ deviation 0.0). Class-frequency control shows W̄ and W* separating from 0.950 (balanced) to 0.749 (extreme). Closed-form W̄ checked to 1.07e-14.

claims.claim: Synthetic multi-class linear classification experiments with normalized-SGD under the ℓ₂ norm, varying batch size (b∈{20,200}) and momentum (β∈{0,0.5,0.99}), empirically confirm that momentum or variance reduction restores full-batch-like convergence in small-batch regimes (Section 5, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: 135 runs at the paper's exact configuration (n=200, d=5, K=10, T=20,000, 5 seeds) reproduce all nine Figure 1 panels under l2: full-batch rel err 0.1599 vs b=20/β=0 at 0.8574 (5.36× worse), β=0.5 at b=20 partially recovers to 0.5918, β=0.99 at b=20 reaches 0.1658, and three VR cells at b=20 span only 0.00053. Same ordering holds under l_inf and spectral norms. Destructive control (permuted labels) yields negative margin -0.317 with 164/200 misclassified.

MarxistLeninist/repro-tdc-2timescale-mar.paper_title: Convergence of Two-Timescale Markovian Stochastic Approximations with Applications in Reinforcement Learning

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 establishes almost-sure stability (sup_n ||z_n|| < infinity) for two-timescale stochastic approximation iterates driven by Markovian noise, without requiring projection operators (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook runs TDC on a small MDP (|S|=8, |A|=2, K=4) with Markovian sampling for 150,000 steps and 5 seeds, reporting finite max ||theta_n - theta*|| = 3.78 without projection. This provides real numerical evidence of boundedness, but on a clearly simplified setup with finite N that cannot establish the asymptotic almost-sure stability statement of Theorem 3.2.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 proves that the fast-timescale iterate x_n converges to the equilibrium map lambda(y_n), i.e. lim_n ||x_n - lambda(y_n)|| = 0, with joint convergence to (lambda(y*), y*) (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook measures slow-iterate convergence (||theta_n - theta*||, rel. error ~0.104) but never measures ||x_n - lambda(y_n)|| for the fast iterate, which is the specific quantity Theorem 3.3 concerns. Joint convergence to (lambda(y*), y*) is not directly tested.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.1 shows the fast-timescale iterate norm is controlled by the running maximum of the slow-timescale iterate, ||x_n|| <= K(1+||y_n^max||) almost surely, which is the key technical device enabling the stability proof (Lemma 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook does not measure ||x_n|| against the running maximum of the slow iterate ||y_n^max||, nor does it check the bound ||x_n|| <= K(1+||y_n^max||). This specific technical lemma is not addressed by any experiment.

claims.claim: Theorem 7.2 gives the first almost-sure convergence proof for temporal difference learning with gradient correction and eligibility traces (TDC(lambda)) under off-policy, Markovian sampling conditions (Section 7, Theorem 7.2, Definition 7.1).
claims.evidence: On Baird's 7-state counterexample (5 seeds, N=20,000, lambda in {0.0, 0.4, 0.8}), TDC stays bounded (max||theta|| ~2.81) while naive TD diverges, providing real numerical evidence of TDC stability under Markovian off-policy sampling. However, the experiment shows boundedness rather than convergence to a fixed point (norms plateau at ~2.8), the problem is small-scale, and the 'first' priority claim cannot be verified numerically.

claims.claim: The convergence analysis relies on assumptions B.1-B.7 in the appendix, including a unique stationary distribution for the Markov noise chain (Assumption B.1) and learning-rate timescale separation lim_n beta(n)/alpha(n) = 0 (Assumption B.2) (Appendix B).
claims.evidence: The stepsize schedule satisfies beta/alpha = n^{-0.1} -> 0 (Assumption B.2) and the behavior chain has a stationary distribution by construction (consistent with B.1), but the logbook does not systematically verify all assumptions B.1-B.7, and the claim is about what the paper's proofs rely on rather than an experimentally testable statement.

MarxistLeninist/repro-tdc-2timescale-mar.overall: The logbook provides a well-structured numerical audit with real experiments on small MDPs (|S|<=8) and Baird's counterexample, showing boundedness of TDC without projection under Markovian sampling and divergence of naive TD. However, it operates on toy-scale problems with finite horizons, does not directly measure fast-iterate convergence to the equilibrium map or the key Lemma 3.1 bound, and cannot verify asymptotic almost-sure claims or priority claims.

algorise/repro-near-optimal-convergence-.paper_title: Near-Optimal Convergence of Accelerated Gradient Methods under Generalized and $(L_0,L_1)$-Smoothness

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 proves Algorithm 1 achieves oracle complexity of 5√ℓ(0)R̄/√ε + k(δ) gradient calls for functions with subquadratic or quadratic growth under generalized ℓ-smoothness (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: The exact bound holds as an inequality in 100% of 70000 configs and the L0 exponent matches (0.53 vs 0.5), but the fitted 1/ε exponent is 0.25 vs the theory's 0.5 — a substantial discrepancy the logbook attributes to the additive k(δ) term not being negligible, but did not resolve by pushing ε further.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.4 shows that optimizing over the free parameter δ yields complexity O(√ℓ(0)R/√ε), which is provably optimal in the small-ε regime (Corollary 3.4).
claims.evidence: The prescribed ε-independent δ is within 0.2% of optimal at the two smallest ε values (10⁻⁸, 10⁻⁹), supporting the small-ε claim, but the ratio is non-monotone across the ε range (up to 3.1x at 10⁻⁵–10⁻⁶) with no explanation, and U-shape structure was not confirmed at all ε values.

claims.claim: For (L₀,L₁)-smooth functions (ℓ(s)=L₀+L₁s), the paper's bound reduces to O(√L₀R/√ε), removing the non-constant multiplicative factors present in prior results such as √(L₀+L₁‖∇f(x⁰)‖)R/√ε from Li et al. (2024a) and exp(L₁R)·√L₀R/√ε from Gorbunov et al. (2025) (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Total complexity stays within a factor of 1.22x across a 640x range of L1 (0.1 to 32.0), directly contradicting the exp(L1R) multiplicative factor from Gorbunov et al. (2025) which would predict astronomical growth; the specific L1²R² polynomial form was not confirmed, but the core qualitative claim of no exponential blowup is directly supported.

claims.claim: Algorithm 2 (Section 4) removes the initial gradient-descent phase required by Algorithm 1, giving a parameter-stable accelerated method without pre-running GD (Algorithm 2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 2 never calls a GD warm-start phase at any configuration, and achieves 100% convergence across a 10,000x range of Γ0 mis-specification (0.01x to 100x), with a graded iteration-count penalty (298 to 604 iterations) rather than failure — directly confirming both the warm-start removal and parameter stability claims.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 provides refined complexity bounds with improved non-dominant terms compared to prior accelerated methods under (L₀,L₁)-smoothness (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The 3-term model improves R² from 0.027 to 0.832 over leading-term-only, showing the refinement matters, but 17% of variance remains unexplained and the fitted coefficients (0.01, 13.41, -252.47) have implausible signs/scale for the theorem's stated O(·) constants, suggesting collinearity rather than clean confirmation of the specific functional form.

algorise/repro-near-optimal-convergence-.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental support for the structural/qualitative claims (no exponential L1R blowup, Algorithm 2's warm-start-free design and parameter stability) but does not cleanly verify the quantitative complexity scaling claims, with the ε-exponent discrepancy in Claim 1 and non-monotone δ-optimality in Claim 2 being the most significant unresolved gaps. All experiments use an approximate (not exact) (L0,L1)-smooth test family at dim=30, which is a legitimate but non-trivial limitation.

algorise/repro-can-adaptive-gradient-met.paper_title: Can Adaptive Gradient Methods Converge under Heavy-Tailed Noise? A Case Study of AdaGrad

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 gives the first convergence guarantee for AdaGrad under heavy-tailed noise with tail index p in (4/3, 2], showing a convergence rate of tilde-O(1/T^((3p-4)/(4p))) (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: AdaGrad passes a four-conjunct convergence predicate at all six p in (4/3, 2] (R² 0.997–0.9997, slope CIs strictly negative, error reductions 156x–1496x), while constant-step SGD on identical noise streams fails at all nine p; the accumulator-growth test matches t^(2/p) within 0.092 at all nine p (Spearman ρ=1.00), confirming the p-dependent mechanism.

claims.claim: This convergence rate is achieved without prior knowledge of the tail index p or the noise level, with AdaGrad adapting automatically to both (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: A single (γ=0.1, λ=1.0) setting converges across all nine tail indices, a 25x learning-rate sweep (6/6 cells pass), and a 25x noise-scale sweep (3/3 cells pass), while SGD fails in all six learning-rate cells with negative slopes; the paired AdaGrad/SGD final-error ratio reaches 0.0002.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 provides an algorithm-dependent lower bound for the one-dimensional case of AdaGrad, implying the minimax-optimal rate for heavy-tailed stochastic optimization is not attainable by AdaGrad (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: The arithmetic gap (3p-4)/(4p) < (p-1)/(3p-2) is verified at 10,000 grid points and an informed clipped-SGD beats AdaGrad in 6/6 cells with advantage collapsing monotonically (ρ=-1.00), but a lower bound is a universal statement over all instances that finite simulation cannot verify; the experiments are consistent with but do not establish the lower bound.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 shows that a normalized AdaGrad-Norm variant achieves a faster rate of O(1/T^((p-1)/(2p))) under a bounded-objective assumption, valid for all p in (1, 2] (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: AdaGrad-Norm has a statistically resolved negative slope at all nine p including below 4/3 (supporting the range extension), but it is 4.8x–39x slower than plain AdaGrad at every p on this instance, providing no empirical support for 'faster'; additionally, the bounded-objective assumption required by Theorem 4.2 is not enforced since f(x)=0.5‖x‖² is unbounded.

claims.claim: The authors identify the regime p in (1, 4/3] as unresolved and a primary limitation of their analysis (Section 5, Limitations).
claims.evidence: The documentary content is confirmed by inspection: Theorem 3.1 covers p∈(4/3,2] and Section 5 lists p∈(1,4/3] as the primary unresolved limitation; the boundary probe shows final error degrades 26.9x [23.1, 34.1] from p=1.95 to p=1.10 monotonically (ρ=-1.00), with no discontinuity at 4/3, consistent with the paper's 'unresolved' framing.

algorise/repro-can-adaptive-gradient-met.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, pre-registered empirical evidence on a non-toy setup (d=20, T=100k, 40 seeds, unclipped Student-t noise, MoM with bootstrap CIs, negative controls) supporting AdaGrad's convergence and adaptivity under heavy-tailed noise (Claims 1, 2, 5), but cannot verify the algorithm-dependent lower bound (Claim 3) or the 'faster' rate claim for AdaGrad-Norm (Claim 4) due to the fundamental gap between finite simulation on a benign instance and worst-case theoretical guarantees.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.7 extends PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds to non-compact symmetry groups (e.g., translations) by evaluating empirical risk only on a set of orbit representatives rather than the full dataset (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence: The experiment measures the gap between representative risk and orbit-averaged risk on translations with only 3000 training samples and 15 epochs on CPU, showing the gap collapses from 0.623 to 0.088 with orbit-aware training. This is a proxy measurement (gap between two risk estimates) rather than a direct verification of the PAC-Bayes bound on orbit representatives, and the scale is clearly reduced.

claims.claim: Assumption 3.1 relaxes the requirement of an invariant data distribution, allowing the target function to be equivariant with noise-dependent variation rather than requiring strict distributional invariance (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The experiment sweeps a symmetry-violation parameter η∈[0,0.30] with 12 seeds and reports 100% coverage with non-vacuous bounds (0.763–0.917), directly testing bound validity under approximate invariance. However, the setup uses only 3000 training samples and 15 epochs, which is a clearly reduced scale compared to the paper's likely full MNIST experiments.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.5 shows that averaging hypotheses to their equivariant counterparts strictly reduces the KL divergence term in the PAC-Bayes bound, yielding a tighter generalization guarantee (Section 2, Theorem 2.5).
claims.evidence: The paired 20-seed experiment shows KL reduction from 1224.81 to 1141.54 (18/20 seeds, p≈0.0004), supporting the KL-reduction part of the claim. However, the 'yielding a tighter generalization guarantee' part is not supported—Claim 4's results show the bound is not tighter—and the scale (3000 samples, 15 epochs) is clearly reduced.

claims.claim: On rotated MNIST restricted to rotations between -90 and 90 degrees (violating the uniform rotation distribution assumption of prior work), equivariant CNNs achieve both higher empirical accuracy and a strictly smaller, tighter PAC-Bayes generalization bound than the non-equivariant baseline (Section 4, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The 20-seed paired experiment directly contradicts the claim: equivariant model accuracy is significantly worse (-0.0157, CI [-0.0264, -0.0050]) and the bound is not tighter (+0.0033, CI [-0.0115, 0.0181]). However, the setup uses translations instead of the claimed rotations on MNIST, with only 3000 samples and 15 epochs, making it a simplified setup rather than a full falsification.

algorise/repro-symmetries-in-pac-bayesia.overall: The logbook provides real experimental runs with rigorous paired designs and confidence intervals at a clearly reduced scale (3000 samples, 15 epochs, CPU), finding support for the theoretical machinery (KL reduction, orbit representatives, approximate invariance) but a negative result for the empirical benefit claim. All four claims are addressed only at toy scale, with Claim 4 additionally using a different symmetry group (translations vs. rotations) than specified in the claim.

algorise/repro-sharp-inequalities-betwee.paper_title: Sharp Inequalities between Total Variation and Hellinger Distances for Gaussian Mixtures

claims.claim: Theorem 2.1 bounds the chi-squared divergence between two Gaussian location mixtures by a quantity of the form (C0 v TV^{-alpha(TV)}) * TV, with alpha(t) = (2+delta)/log(log(1/t) v e) (Theorem 2.1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: 400 Gaussian-mixture pairs with deterministic adaptive quadrature spanning TV from 7.3e-10 to 4.19e-01 (373/400 in the loglog-activation regime), C0 calibrated out-of-sample on 200 pairs and tested on the held-out 200, yielding 0 violations at every δ∈{0.5,1.0,2.0} — concrete numerical evidence on a non-toy setup supporting the bound.

claims.claim: Corollary 2.4 derives that the Hellinger distance between two Gaussian location mixtures is bounded by TV raised to the power 1-o(1), where the o(1) term decays as 1/log log(1/TV) (Corollary 2.4).
claims.evidence: Same 400-pair sweep with held-out testing confirms 0/200 Hellinger-bound violations at every δ, directly checking H ≤ max(C0, TV^{-α(TV)})·TV on the same non-toy setup as Claim 1.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 and Lemma 3.2 show this exponent is sharp by an explicit construction using Chebyshev polynomial zeros satisfying Hn >= TVn^{1-alpha*(TVn)} with alpha*(t)=0.33/log log(1/t), proving the 1-o(1) factor cannot be improved (Theorem 3.1, Lemma 3.2, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The literal Chebyshev-Vandermonde construction is implemented at 60-digit precision (26 configurations, n=11–61), and the inequality form holds at 22/26 points, but the empirical sharpness exponent plateaus at ~0.103 versus the claimed 0.33 — a factor of 3.3 short with no trend toward the target, and 4/26 failures at both small and large n remain unexplained, so the key quantitative claim is neither confirmed nor refuted.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 uses the sharp TV-Hellinger inequality together with a metric-entropy argument to characterize the minimax rate for learning Gaussian location mixtures in total variation distance, resolving an open problem posed by Jia et al. (2023) (Theorem 4.3, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Two parametric sub-classes (single Gaussian, 2-atom mixture) with real estimators yield fitted rates n^{-0.97} (R²=0.997) and n^{-1.037} (R²=0.987), matching the n^{-1} prediction, but these are finite-dimensional cases where the parametric rate is classically known and do not exercise the theorem's novel nonparametric metric-entropy argument over the general compact class.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.5 shows the inequality yields a Hellinger-distance error rate of epsilon^{2(1-o(1))} for robust estimation of Gaussian mixtures under Huber contamination, with Theorem 4.6 establishing a matching lower bound (Theorem 4.5, Theorem 4.6, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The paper's Yatracos estimator is implemented, but the experimental design couples n=max(500,20/ε²) to ε, confounding the contamination rate with the sample-size rate; the fitted exponent of 6.87 is far from the predicted range [1.34,1.57] and limiting value 2.0, but the logbook itself identifies this as a design artifact and did not rerun with n decoupled, leaving the claim untested.

algorise/repro-sharp-inequalities-betwee.overall: The logbook provides solid numerical evidence for the core TV-Hellinger inequality (Claims 1–2) via deterministic quadrature with out-of-sample validation across six decades of TV, but the sharpness constant (Claim 3), the nonparametric minimax rate (Claim 4, tested only on parametric sub-classes), and the robust estimation rate (Claim 5, confounded experimental design) are not convincingly reproduced.

algorise/repro-practical-and-scalable-ha.paper_title: Practical and Scalable Hamiltonian Monte Carlo Without the Metropolis Test

claims.claim: For Gaussian targets, the asymptotic bias of unadjusted Hamiltonian/Langevin samplers is upper bounded by the energy error variance per dimension (EEVPD), independent of dimensionality (Section 3, Equation 20).
claims.evidence: 57 Gaussian runs across d=10–100 with step-size sweeps all mixed well (worst R-hat 1.0046, ESS 49k–200k). EEVPD is stable across dimension (~0.01 at ε=0.05 for all d) and monotone in ε, while b_cov² generally stays below or within a small constant factor of EEVPD, supporting the claim that EEVPD upper-bounds bias independently of dimensionality. Some d=100 runs at the smallest ε show b_cov² slightly exceeding EEVPD, attributable to finite-sample noise when both quantities are tiny.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 provides an automatic step-size tuning scheme using log-normal weighting with a forgetting factor that preferentially weights recent samples during burn-in, targeting a user-specified bias tolerance (Section 4, Equation 25).
claims.evidence: The tuning loop converges monotonically from ε₀=0.5 to ε≈0.008–0.009 across d=10–100, targeting EEVPD=3e-4, with no oscillation or overshoot and dimension-adaptive final step sizes — directly demonstrating Algorithm 1's automatic step-size tuning without Metropolis accept/reject.

claims.claim: Lemma 5.1 bounds the microcanonical dimensionality factor Delta(H) between 0.37 d^(-1/4) and 3.1 for MCHMC and MCLMC (Section 5, Lemma 5.1, Equation 29).
claims.evidence: Measured ΔH grows monotonically with d (1.01 at d=10, 3.07 at d=100, 4.68 at d=200), exceeding the claimed upper bound of 3.1 at d=200. The violation is not marginal (4.68 vs 3.1) and ΔH increases consistently, providing concrete evidence that the Lemma 5.1 upper bound does not hold at d=200.

claims.claim: Across six benchmark problems (32-101 dimensions, including ill-conditioned Gaussians, Rosenbrock, Brownian motion, German credit logistic regression, and Neal's funnel), the Gaussian EEVPD-bias bound holds approximately even for non-Gaussian targets, except Brownian motion inference where bias is overestimated by about 1.5x (Section 6, Figure 2, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Only 6 of 18 sampler-benchmark configurations achieved R-hat < 1.05, and all 6 converging configurations are the two Gaussian targets. The four non-Gaussian benchmarks (Rosenbrock, Brownian motion, German credit, Neal's funnel) all failed to mix (R-hat up to 13.2, ESS as low as 0.13/5000), making any bias statistics from those chains uninformative about the target distribution.

claims.claim: MCHMC achieves an efficiency gain over standard HMC of about (9/4)^(1/8) ≈ 1.11 for a fixed covariance error under matched step-size scaling (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: The measured MCHMC-vs-HMC efficiency ratio is 2.36x vs the predicted 1.11x, but the HMC baseline has R-hat=1.537 (above the 1.05 mixing threshold), making its b_cov²=15.19 unreliable as the denominator. The MCHMC-vs-Langevin comparison (both mixed) shows ratio ~1.0, but that does not test the claim about HMC. The key comparison is compromised by the HMC baseline's failure to converge.

algorise/repro-practical-and-scalable-ha.overall: The logbook provides solid experimental evidence supporting the Gaussian theory (Claims 1–2) with proper convergence diagnostics, and identifies a concrete violation of the ΔH upper bound at d=200 (Claim 3). However, the non-Gaussian benchmark suite (Claim 4) and the HMC efficiency comparison (Claim 5) are both compromised by chain mixing failures, leaving those claims unevaluated.

algorise/repro-solving-stochastic-variat.paper_title: Solving Stochastic Variational Inequalities without the Bounded Variance Assumption

claims.claim: All three proposed methods replace the standard bounded-variance assumption with the relaxed condition E||G̃(z)-G(z)||^2 ≤ B^2||z-z0||^2 + σ^2, allowing variance to grow with distance from a reference point z0 (Section 1).
claims.evidence: The noise model sanity check confirms the relaxed variance condition E||ξ||^2 = B^2||z-z_ref||^2 + σ^2 with fitted exponent 1.9998 (R^2=1.0), and FBF-MB converges at all tested dimensions (decay exponents 0.244-0.257, 100% convergence) while the bounded-variance SEG comparator degrades up to 10^12x more as B grows.

claims.claim: The mini-batching forward-backward-forward algorithm achieves Õ(ε^-4) oracle complexity for the weak-Minty nonmonotonicity parameter ρ < 1/(12L) (Section 2).
claims.evidence: All 5 swept points with ρ* < 1/(12L) converge with 100% rate and positive decay CIs, the deterministic stability boundary is at 3.258x the paper's threshold, and oracle complexity exponents (2.673-2.830) are consistent with the claimed Õ(ε^-4) upper bound.

claims.claim: The multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) method achieves the same Õ(ε^-4) complexity while tolerating the widest nonmonotonicity range ρ < 1/L, the strongest of the three theoretical results (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The coupled MLMC estimator achieves 17.2x smaller bias than fixed-batch at matched cost (slope -3.645 vs -0.997), the stability boundary is at 0.990x the paper's 1/L threshold, and convergence holds inside the ρ*L ≤ 0.85 band (10/10 points ≥90% converged) while failing outside. The linear-operator negative control confirms the effect is specific to biased nonlinear cases.

claims.claim: The variance-reduced single-loop algorithm uses only 3 stochastic oracle samples per iteration and incorporates Halpern anchoring for stability, under an added expected-Lipschitzness assumption (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Oracle call counting confirms exactly 3.000 samples per iteration, convergence occurs at all 4 swept gamma values (100%), and the paired ablation shows Halpern anchoring has a statistically significant effect at 3/4 gamma settings (CIs exclude zero for gamma=0.2, 0.1, 0.05).

claims.claim: All three algorithms match the best-known Õ(ε^-4) complexity for driving the expected residual norm below ε on monotone and structured nonmonotone (weak-MVI) VIs, while applying to unbounded-domain bilinear min-max problems that violate the classical bounded-variance assumption (Section 1).
claims.evidence: At matched oracle budget N_ref=48000, all three algorithms reduce residual below 0.5x initial (FBF-MB: 0.165, MLMC-FBF: 0.309, VR-FBF-Halpern: 0.025), with empirically measured complexity exponents (1.216-2.609) all within a plausible range of the claimed Õ(ε^-4) bound, on bilinear min-max problems with state-dependent unbounded variance.

algorise/repro-solving-stochastic-variat.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence with 24 seeds, 95% CIs, negative controls, and ablations supporting all five claims on bilinear min-max problems with state-dependent unbounded variance. The reproduction is limited to synthetic problem families at moderate scale (d≤160, T≤16000) rather than large-scale real-world instances.

algorise/repro-accelerating-langevin-mon.paper_title: Accelerating Langevin Monte Carlo via Efficient Stochastic Runge-Kutta Methods beyond Log-Concavity

claims.claim: The proposed stochastic Runge-Kutta LMC algorithm achieves a uniform-in-time convergence rate of O(d^1.5 h^1.5) in non-log-concave settings (Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: The h-exponent is verified on a non-toy non-log-concave GMM (d=10, 30 seeds, 3000 paths): RKLMC-2G measures 1.482 [1.428, 1.537] vs claimed 1.5, with Euler control at 1.010. However, the d-exponent measures 0.053 [0.002, 0.103] over d=4..64, far below the claimed 1.5, and uniformity-in-time is not tested (only T=2). The d-exponent does not falsify the theorem (it is an upper bound) but also does not support it, leaving the combined rate claim only partially evidenced.

claims.claim: The algorithm requires only two gradient evaluations per iteration, compared to three required by the prior stochastic Runge-Kutta scheme of Li et al. (2019) (Section 1).
claims.evidence: An instrumented gradient counter (CountingGrad) measures exactly 2.000000 calls/step for RKLMC-2G across 4 targets and multiple step sizes, with the 2/3 cost ratio exact. The scheme's coefficients satisfy order conditions (12)-(14) in exact rational arithmetic, and the uniqueness derivation (alpha=2/3, b1=3/2, a11=3/4) matches eq. (15)-(16).

claims.claim: Higher-order Runge-Kutta variants of the method are shown to achieve improved complexity bounds under additional smoothness assumptions (Theorems 2.5-2.7).
claims.evidence: Both 3-gradient schemes attain the claimed order (RKLMC-3G: 1.477, RKLMC-3G(b): 1.502), but the paired difference RKLMC-3G minus RKLMC-2G at h=2^-9 is -2.77e-07 with p=0.80, showing no measurable accuracy improvement. The 'improved complexity' aspect is not demonstrated, and the theorems themselves are not independently verified.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments compare the proposed Runge-Kutta LMC methods against baseline Euler-based ULA schemes on synthetic and real datasets (Section 4, Figures 3-5).
claims.evidence: The strong-error comparison is reproduced on a non-toy setup: RKLMC-2G is 33x more accurate than LMC at h=2^-9 and 12x at equal gradient budget, with rates 1.482 vs 1.010. The 8-mode GMM structure is captured by all methods (0 modes missed). The logbook correctly notes the paper uses only synthetic data (no real datasets), and sampling-quality metrics sit at the Monte-Carlo floor, but the core numerical comparison is reproduced.

claims.claim: A complexity comparison table contrasts the proposed method against competing algorithms, including those of Li et al. and Sabanis (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The proposed method's complexity exponent is verified: measured 0.681 [0.657, 0.705] vs theoretical 2/3, and the gradient count (2 vs 3) is exact. However, the logbook explicitly states it did not re-derive or verify rows for Sabanis & Zhang or Li et al., and the d-linearity component does not reproduce, so the comparison aspect of the table is unaddressed.

algorise/repro-accelerating-langevin-mon.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, non-toy evidence verifying the h-exponent convergence rate (1.482 vs 1.5) and the two-gradient-per-iteration claim, with strong experimental controls (30 seeds, common Brownian paths, pre-registered intervals). However, the d^1.5 dimension scaling is not reproduced (measured ~0.05), the higher-order improvement is not demonstrated, and the complexity comparison with competing algorithms is not addressed, leaving three claims inconclusive.

algorise/repro-convergence-of-steepest-d.paper_title: Convergence of Steepest Descent and Adam under Non-Uniform Smoothness

claims.claim: The paper introduces a non-uniform smoothness assumption (Assumption 1) in which curvature is an affine function of the objective value, generalizing standard L-smoothness (Section 3).
claims.evidence: 40,000 random trials (D up to 50, n up to 200) using Proposition 2's exact closed-form constants (H0=0, H1=max_i||x_i||^2) show the Hessian bound holds in 100% of trials with max ratio 0.066, confirming the non-uniform smoothness assumption is non-vacuous on logistic regression.

claims.claim: Under this assumption, steepest descent (sign GD) is shown to converge linearly on logistic regression with separable data and is provably faster than standard gradient descent (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Across 15 seeds and 8 target losses (1e-2 to 1e-9) on exponential loss with separable data, GD fits a power law with slope 1.072 (theory ~1, sublinear) while NSD fits log-linear with R²=0.9994, and NSD beats GD in 100% of seeds, directly supporting the linear-vs-sublinear separation claim.

claims.claim: Adam is shown to converge at a linear rate with a constant step size on certain two-layer neural networks under the non-uniform smoothness assumption (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Small two-layer network (D=6, width=12, n=80, 8 seeds) with tanh activation that does not satisfy Proposition 4's requirement of derivative bounded away from zero; RMSProp shows clean linear fit (R²=0.964) but Adam's fit is noisy (R²=0.783) and both plateau at nonzero floor loss, so the linear-rate claim for Adam is not established on a setup matching the paper's conditions.

claims.claim: RMSProp-type adaptive methods are analyzed and shown to be provably faster than AdaGrad, AMSGrad, and heavy-ball momentum under non-uniform smoothness (Section 6).
claims.evidence: 1D logistic loss example (the paper's own construction): 4/4 sublinear-predicted methods (GD, heavy-ball, AdaGrad, AMSGrad) confirmed with slopes ≈ -1.0 and R²>0.999998, but RMSProp and Adam underflow float64 (reaching 0.0 and 4e-296) making their rate fits invalid artifacts; the quantitative linear rate for adaptive methods is not measured, though the qualitative separation is enormous.

claims.claim: The convergence analysis is extended from the deterministic steepest descent setting (Section 4) to the stochastic setting (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook's examination of the paper's section structure shows Section 5 is 'Convergence of RMSProp & Adam' (deterministic), not a stochastic extension of Section 4, and the Conclusion explicitly lists stochastic generalization as future work — directly contradicting the claim that the paper extends analysis to the stochastic setting.

algorise/repro-convergence-of-steepest-d.overall: The logbook provides solid numerical evidence for Claims 1 and 2 (non-uniform smoothness bound holds; sign-GD linear vs GD sublinear separation), partial evidence on simplified setups for Claims 3 and 4 (small networks and 1D examples with measurement defects), and correctly identifies Claim 5 as not matching the paper's actual content.

claims.claim: The HJ-Prox estimator's approximation error is uniformly bounded by sup_x ||prox^δ_{tf}(x) - prox_{tf}(x)|| ≤ sqrt(n t δ) (Theorem 3.2, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The bound is violated in 6/18 configurations (e.g., n=50, δ=0.02: sup error 0.3117 vs bound 0.2236; n=100, δ=0.05: 0.5487 vs 0.5000), but all violations occur at small δ where Monte-Carlo estimation noise in the prox itself dominates, and the logbook cannot separate MC noise from the theoretical approximation error. The bound holds for δ≥0.05 across all dimensions, but the scaling fit (R²=0.066) does not confirm the √(ntδ) shape.

claims.claim: Replacing exact proximal steps with HJ-Prox in the proximal point method and proximal gradient descent preserves almost-sure convergence under mild assumptions (Theorem 3.5, Theorem 3.6, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: PPM on a quadratic (n=40, 15 seeds) reproduces cleanly with mean relative iterate distance 0.000829, but PGD on LASSO (A∈R^{120×60}, 15 seeds) fails with mean relative distance 0.232 and 0% of seeds below 0.15 tolerance, as the HJ objective plateaus at ~777 vs exact PGD's 62.7. The claim covers both methods; one succeeds and one fails at the achievable sample budget, and the asymptotic convergence guarantee cannot be definitively confirmed or refuted with finite-N experiments.

claims.claim: The HJ-Prox substitution extends convergence guarantees to Douglas-Rachford splitting and Davis-Yin splitting for composite objectives f+g+h with h L-smooth (Theorem 3.8, Theorem 3.9, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: DRS (n=40, 15 seeds) reproduces with mean relative distance 0.1295 and 100% of seeds below 0.25 tolerance, but DYS with L-smooth h (n=40, 15 seeds) is borderline at 0.2748 with only 46.7% of seeds in tolerance and CI [0.2500, 0.2996] straddling the threshold. DYS with an indicator constraint at n=8 fails outright (0.7824, 0% in tolerance), but that supplementary panel is at toy scale. The claim covers both DRS and DYS; one is confirmed and the other is marginal.

claims.claim: HJ-Prox is also applied within the primal-dual hybrid gradient algorithm via conjugate operator approximations (Theorem 3.10, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: PDHG with HJ-Prox (A∈R^{30×40}, 12 seeds, 300 iterations) achieves mean relative iterate distance 0.1355 with 95% CI [0.1177, 0.1533], all 12 seeds within 0.25 tolerance, and worst seed 0.1821. This is concrete evidence on a non-toy setup that HJ-Prox substitution in PDHG converges to the exact-prox solution.

claims.claim: Splitting reduces the effective Lipschitz constant relative to non-split approaches, and hybrid exact/approximate strategies outperform fully approximate proximal methods in experiments (Section 3.3, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: At n=8 with 10 seeds, the split hybrid PGD map has empirical Lipschitz constant 0.9274 [0.9235, 0.9313] vs non-split PPM at 1.0256 [1.0227, 1.0286] with non-overlapping CIs, confirming the contraction mechanism, and the hybrid variant (objective 1.1879) outperforms the fully-HJ variant (1.2212). However, the non-splitting method reaches a lower objective (1.1623) than either splitting variant, contradicting the practical benefit, and n=8 is clearly toy scale.

algorise/repro-operator-splitting-with-h.overall: The logbook provides concrete multi-seed experiments with confidence intervals that verify PDHG convergence (Claim 4) and partially support several other claims, but cannot definitively confirm or refute the theoretical bounds and asymptotic convergence guarantees due to Monte-Carlo noise confounding at finite sample counts and toy-scale testing for the Lipschitz claim. Only 1 of 5 claims has clean, non-toy evidence fully supporting it.

algorise/repro-lower-bounds-for-frank-wo.paper_title: Lower Bounds for Frank-Wolfe on Strongly Convex Sets

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a constructive Omega(1/sqrt(epsilon)) lower bound on the number of iterations for Frank-Wolfe with short steps or exact line search when both the objective and the constraint set are smooth and strongly convex (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: On the deepest certified trajectory (T=75000, gap spanning 8+ decades), the slope of log N(eps) vs log(1/eps_gap) is 0.5024 with 95% CI [0.5013, 0.5033] and R^2=0.99999, closely matching the theoretical 1/2; cross-instance slope across 7 reconstructions is 0.5014 [0.5001, 0.5031]; the gap-curve exponent is 2.0001 with R^2=0.9999999999; and the benign contrast (p=(2,0)) converges 4743x faster, confirming the slowness is attributable to the construction.

claims.claim: The lower-bound construction uses the specific instance of minimizing f(x) = ||x-p||_2^2 over the Euclidean unit ball B_1(0) with the unconstrained minimizer p on the boundary (||p||=1), showing this hard instance matches the known O(1/sqrt(epsilon)) upper bound of Garber et al. (2015) (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: An explicit initial point x0*=(0.2149.., 0.5677..) inside the unit ball is identified, from which 600-digit exact-line-search FW tracks the certified reduced trajectory for 750 steps with max relative deviation 10^-350 and gap exponent 2.006 [2.006, 2.006]; a precision ladder (float64 breakaway at step 66, dps=100 at step 343, scaling 3.25 steps/digit) explains why double precision cannot observe the worst case; and 500 random seeds all stay below the worst-case envelope (sup t^2*gap max=0.112 vs worst-case 0.5625).

claims.claim: The lower bound is established via a 'backward reconstruction' technique that builds worst-case trajectories by working backward from terminal iterates, producing precise sequences over horizons of 10,000+ iterations (Section on Backward Reconstruction Strategy).
claims.evidence: Nine backward-reconstructed trajectories span horizons up to T=75,000 (eps=1e-5) and T=25,000 (eps=3e-5), both exceeding 10,000; every consecutive pair satisfies the forward map (Prop. 4) with max residual 2.08e-56 across all 111,103 total steps; the forward/backward Lyapunov rates are +0.2936 and -0.2936 digits/step respectively; and full-horizon forward replay at 600 digits yields terminal relative error 10^-378, consistent with the measured amplification.

claims.claim: The analysis reduces the dynamics to a two-dimensional invariant subspace parametrized by residual magnitude r and contraction factor s, revealing stable phases of monotonically increasing contraction followed by intermittent 'jumps' that explain the convergence stalling behavior (Section on Dynamical Analysis).
claims.evidence: The Prop. 4 (r,s) recursion holds with max residual 1.5e-36 on 100 random x-space FW trajectories; iterates stay in span(p,x0) with max deviation 1.7e-16 across dimensions 5-100; on all 9 certified worst-case trajectories s_t is non-decreasing on exactly 100% of steps with r<=0.5 with zero jumps for r<=0.3; and perturbed runs show escape time increasing monotonically with perturbation smallness (6/6 ordered pairs), with every escape ending via a Prop. 5 jump.

claims.claim: The result shows strong convexity of the constraint set alone cannot yield convergence rates uniformly faster than O(1/sqrt(epsilon)), and this conclusion holds dimension-independently and extends to ellipsoidal constraints via affine invariance (Theorem 6, Implications).
claims.evidence: Gap sequences are bit-identical (deviation 0.0) across d=2..100 with 150 seeds and T=3000; the affinely mapped 750-step worst-case trajectory satisfies the ellipsoid FW one-step map at scale 10 with residual 5.9e-121 (negative control with buggy formula fails at 3.62); and float64 paired exponent differences across scales 1-10 have max 0.151 with all CIs straddling 0, while v3's spurious departure at scale 10 is reproduced exactly as three implementation bugs.

algorise/repro-lower-bounds-for-frank-wo.overall: This logbook provides rigorous, concrete numerical evidence supporting all five claims through certified backward-reconstructed FW trajectories up to 75,000 steps, high-precision (up to 600-digit) arithmetic, per-step forward-map certificates with residuals below 1e-55, pre-registered falsifiable predicates, negative controls, and systematic root-cause analysis of prior failed attempts. The evidence is non-toy in scale and scope, spanning multiple decades of accuracy, dimensions, and ellipsoid eccentricities.

algorise/repro-to-grok-grokking-provable.paper_title: To Grok Grokking: Provable Grokking in Ridge Regression

claims.claim: The paper proves end-to-end grokking for zero-teacher ridge regression, including early training overfitting, delayed poor generalization, and eventual low generalization error (Theorem 4.1)
claims.evidence: Exact closed-form GD trajectory (validated to 1.6e-15 vs iterative GD) checked at 246 time points across 10 seeds at paper scale (n=100, m=1000): 0/7380 bound violations across all three theorem items, with median t1=206 and t2=22414 showing the predicted ~109x generalization delay and test loss <= 2.5e-261 at 3M steps.

claims.claim: The end-to-end grokking result is extended from the zero-teacher setting to realizable ridge regression with arbitrary realizable teacher functions (Theorem 4.2)
claims.evidence: With unit-norm random teacher at paper defaults (n=100, m=1000, 10 seeds), empirical t1 <= Eq.(6) bound holds 10/10 (e.g., 207 <= 1370), empirical t2 >= Eq.(7) bound holds 10/10 (e.g., 22483 >= 8143), and eventual generalization L(theta_t) <= 2.6e-3*eps at t=3M on every seed.

claims.claim: Separate theorems decompose grokking into training-loss convergence, poor generalization during overfitting, and eventual generalization (Theorems 4.4-4.6)
claims.evidence: Thm 4.4 (train loss <= eps for all t >= T44=1328): 0 violations across 500 time points, 10/10 seeds; Thm 4.5 (test loss >= c for all t <= T45=16285): 0 violations, 10/10 seeds; Thm 4.6 (GD converges to theta*_lambda, generalization inequality): 10/10 seeds with relative distance 0.0 to fixed point. The bracketing T44 << T45 confirms the decomposition captures the grokking mechanism.

claims.claim: Decreasing weight decay and sample size can amplify grokking time in ridge-regression simulations, matching the paper's quantitative hyperparameter predictions (Figure 2)
claims.evidence: Log-log slope of empirical t2 vs lambda is -1.0001 (theory -1, R^2=1.000000) across 7 lambda values; t1 strictly increasing in n (46 to 996 for n=25..400); t2 varies only 1.4% across m=500..4000; t1 and t2 linear in ln(nu^2) with R^2=0.9967 and 1.00000 — all matching Figure 2's quantitative predictions at paper scale with 5 seeds.

claims.claim: Two-layer ReLU experiments qualitatively reproduce the predicted grokking-time dependence on hyperparameters beyond the linear setting (Figures 3 and 4)
claims.evidence: Random ReLU features (d=100, n=100, m=10000): t2_rel scales x10.6/x9.8 per 10x lambda decrease, t1 increases with n, m has no monotone effect, nu^2 widens overfitting gap. Full two-layer net (d=50, n=50, m=1000, explicit float64 GD to 1.5M steps): t2 = 283000/142000/71000 for lambda=0.025/0.05/0.1 (exact 1/lambda halving), t1 nondecreasing in n, m varies t2 by 7%, t2 increases with nu^2 — all qualitatively matching Figures 3-4.

algorise/repro-to-grok-grokking-provable.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all five claims at the paper's own experimental scale, using exact spectral GD solutions for the quadratic (ridge) cases and explicit float64 full-batch GD for the non-linear two-layer ReLU network. The reproduction is rigorous: multiple seeds, comprehensive bound-checking at hundreds of time points, quantitative slope/R^2 analysis for hyperparameter scaling, and validation of the closed-form solver against iterative GD.

algorise/repro-steady-state-behavior-of-.paper_title: Steady-State Behavior of Constant-Stepsize Stochastic Approximation: Gaussian Approximation and Tail Bounds

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 (i.i.d. noise) and Theorem 4.1 (Markovian noise) bound the Wasserstein distance between the centered-scaled steady state Y^(α) = (X^(α) − x*)/√α and its Gaussian limit N(0, Σ_Y) by U√α log(1/α) (Theorems 3.1 and 4.1).
claims.evidence: Across four SA settings (SGD iid, linear SA, contractive SA, Markovian SGD), the empirical W_1 slopes (0.51–0.75) exceed 0.5 and the normalized ratio W_1/(√α log(1/α)) is monotonically decreasing in α on a 7-point grid down to α=1/320 with N=400K chains, consistent with the U√α log(1/α) upper bound.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 establishes an explicit non-asymptotic Wasserstein bound of order O(α^{1/2} log(1/α)) for constant-stepsize SGD on smooth, strongly convex objectives (Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: 1-D SGD on f(x)=x²/2 with exact W_1 computation yields slope 0.533 (R²=0.998) and Σ_Y=0.16667 matching theory (1/6) to 4 decimal places, directly confirming the O(√α log(1/α)) rate for smooth strongly convex SGD.

claims.claim: Propositions 3.2 and 3.3 extend the same O(α^{1/2} log(1/α)) Wasserstein bound to linear stochastic approximation with a Hurwitz matrix and to contractive nonlinear stochastic approximation, respectively (Propositions 3.2 and 3.3, Section 3.2.2, Section 3.2.3).
claims.evidence: 2-D linear SA with a non-normal Hurwitz matrix gives W_1 slope 0.561 (R²=0.996) and contractive nonlinear SA gives slope 0.512 (R²=0.999), with empirical covariance matching the Lyapunov equation to 3 decimal places in both cases.

claims.claim: For one-dimensional projections, the paper derives a non-uniform Berry-Esseen-type tail bound |P(⟨Y^(α),ζ⟩ > a) − P(Z_ζ > a)| ≤ C_d α^{1/4} log^{1/2}(1/α) / a, which improves as the deviation level a grows (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Using N=1.6M chains for linear-SA projections, sup_a a|Δ(a)| decays with slope 0.583 (R²=0.999), which is faster than the predicted α^{1/4}log^{1/2}(1/α) rate, consistent with the upper bound; uniformity in a is confirmed by no blow-up across a∈{0.5,…,3}.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 extends the Gaussian approximation and tail bounds for SGD, linear SA, and contractive nonlinear SA from i.i.d. noise to Markovian noise (Proposition 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Markovian SGD with a two-state skew-exponential noise shows W_1 vanishing (slope 0.749) against the correct long-run covariance (Σ_Y=0.1667) while flooring at ~0.09 against the naive marginal covariance (Σ_Y=0.0833), directly confirming that the long-run covariance correction is essential.

claims.claim: Proposition 5.1 shows a different convergence rate of order α^{1/h} for constant-stepsize SA applied to general convex objectives with Gibbs-type limiting distributions (Proposition 5.1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: For f(x)=|x|^h/h, E|X| scales as α^{0.513} (h=2, theory 0.5, R²=0.9998) and α^{0.249} (h=4, theory 0.25, R²=0.99999); for h=4, W_1 to the Gibbs target is 0.0012 vs 0.0483 to the best Gaussian, and kurtosis is 2.19 matching the Gibbs law rather than 3 for Gaussian.

algorise/repro-steady-state-behavior-of-.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from CPU simulations (400K–1.6M chains, 7-point stepsize grids) supporting all six claims across SGD, linear SA, contractive SA, Markovian noise, and Gibbs-limit settings. The setups are low-dimensional (1-D and 2-D) with simple objectives, but the SA instances are non-trivial and the measured rates and covariances match the theoretical predictions.

algorise/repro-learning-rate-annealing-i.paper_title: Learning Rate Annealing Improves Tuning Robustness in Stochastic Optimization

claims.claim: For SGD with a polynomial decay-of-degree-p annealing schedule under multiplicative stepsize misspecification factor ρ ≥ 1, the convergence rate is O(ρ^(1/(2p+1))/√T) in the convex Lipschitz setting (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Exact Theorem-1 numerics via scipy.integrate.quad yield bound exponents 0.3333/0.2000/0.1111 for p=1/2/4 (R²=1.000000), matching 1/(2p+1). Empirical projected-SGD worst-case over a 9-instance family at T=20,000 with 1,500 seeds gives slopes 0.334/0.174/0.093, and 0/120 bound violations confirm the upper bound is respected.

claims.claim: Fixed (non-annealed) stepsize schedules incur a convergence rate of O(ρ/√T), i.e. linear dependence on the misspecification factor ρ, compared to the sublinear dependence achieved by annealed schedules (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: On the same worst-case instance family (T=20,000, 1,500 seeds), log-log slopes vs ρ are 0.975 for fixed (R²=0.9997) and 0.948 for inv-sqrt (R²=0.996), confirming near-linear dependence, while annealed schedules on identical instances show sublinear slopes (0.334/0.174/0.093/0.200).

claims.claim: For cosine annealing schedules, h(u) = ½(1+cos(πu)), the convergence rate scales as O(ρ^0.2) times the baseline rate, derived via tail-behavior analysis of the schedule (Corollary 3).
claims.evidence: Exact Theorem-1 numerics for cosine yield a coefficient of 4.06–4.60 × ρ^0.2 over ρ∈[1,50] (matching the paper's stated 4–5 band) with asymptotic exponent 0.2022 (R²=0.99994); empirical worst-case SGD slope is 0.200 (R²=0.975), and 0/30 bound violations.

claims.claim: Robustness guarantees for annealed learning-rate schedules extend from the convex Lipschitz case to the convex smooth setting under stepsize stability constraints (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Projected SGD on a d=10 convex quadratic (β=1, T=20,000, 600 seeds) shows fixed-schedule slope 0.998 (R²=0.9997) vs annealed slopes 0.510/0.333/0.344 for poly1/poly2/cosine, confirming sublinear-vs-linear separation in the smooth setting. The stepsize-stability condition η_t ≤ 1/(2β) is satisfied at all ρ (max violation fraction 0.00).

claims.claim: Experiments on synthetic logistic regression and CIFAR-10 with WideResNet confirm that annealing schedules are more robust to coarse learning-rate grid search than fixed stepsizes, with the performance gap widening as grid resolution becomes coarser (Section on experimental validation).
claims.evidence: The synthetic logistic regression part (n=4,000, d=20, T=6,000) is reproduced at the paper's scale, showing the fixed/cosine excess-loss ratio growing monotonically to ~60x at γ=64. However, the CIFAR-10/WideResNet experiment was replaced by a 64→64→10 MLP on 1,797 sklearn digits images (T=3,000), which did not reproduce the finding due to divergence-cliff dominance at this reduced scale.

algorise/repro-learning-rate-annealing-i.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical and empirical verification of the four theoretical claims (1–4) through exact Theorem-1 coefficient computation, worst-case SGD simulations with thousands of seeds, and bound checks on appropriate convex instances. Claim 5 is only partially reproduced: the synthetic logistic regression experiment confirms the widening robustness gap, but the CIFAR-10/WideResNet experiment is replaced by a clearly reduced-scale MLP-on-digits substitute that fails to reproduce the paper's finding.

algorise/repro-revenue-guarantees-of-no-.paper_title: Revenue Guarantees of No-Swap-Regret Dynamics in First Price Auctions

claims.claim: For exact correlated equilibria in discrete first-price auctions with k discretization levels, expected revenue is at least v2 - 4/k, where v2 is the second-highest valuation (Theorem 2.5).
claims.evidence: The LP computes exact minimum revenue over CE constraints (scipy linprog/HiGHS) for 7 configurations (k up to 40, 2-3 bidders, multiple valuations). All satisfy Z* ≥ v₂ − 4/k, with concrete numbers showing gaps from 0.1 to 0.4.

claims.claim: For ε-approximate correlated equilibria, expected revenue is at least v2 - 3/k - Θ(εk²) (Theorem 2.6).
claims.evidence: The ε-CE LP sweep over ε ∈ {0, 1e-3, 2e-3, 4e-3} at k ∈ {10,20,40} shows Z*(ε) ≥ v₂ − 3/k − 2εk² on all grid points, with fitted degradation slopes (22.73, 31.35, 37.42) well within 2k² bounds, confirming the O(εk²) rate.

claims.claim: There exists an ε-approximate correlated equilibrium with revenue at most v2 - Θ(1/k) - Θ(ε), showing the ε-dependence in the revenue lower bound cannot be removed (Theorem 2.8).
claims.evidence: The LP minimum Z*(ε) < v₂ for all ε > 0 (e.g., k=10, ε=0.001: Z*=0.4773, gap=0.0227; k=40, ε=0.004: Z*=0.2871, gap=0.2129), confirming existence of an ε-CE with revenue below v₂. The gap includes both 1/k and ε dependence (e.g., gap ≥ 0.2/k + ε holds across configs).

claims.claim: When bidders run no-swap-regret algorithms achieving swap regret O(√(kT)), the time-averaged revenue is at least v2 - 3/k - O(ε) after O(k^5/ε^2) rounds (Corollary 2.7).
claims.evidence: Blum-Mansour dynamics (n=2, k=10, T=1e5) yield time-averaged revenue 0.4942 with realized swap regret rate ε̂=0.00854, satisfying the Corollary 2.7 bound (0.4942 ≥ v₂−3/k−2k²ε̂ = −1.508). However, the bound is trivially negative and only one configuration is tested; the O(k^5/ε^2) round complexity is not independently verified.

claims.claim: Time-averaged bidder behavior under no-swap-regret dynamics converges to an ε-approximate correlated equilibrium with probability 1-δ (Theorem 2.3).
claims.evidence: Realized swap regret rate ε̂(t) ≤ 2.82·√(k/t) at all checkpoints confirms O(√(kT)) swap regret. Concentration across 5 seeds (std 1.20e-04) is tight, though 5 seeds is insufficient to rigorously verify the 1−δ high-probability guarantee.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 shows that in the diagonal perturbation case, the KL divergence of the proximal posterior scales as ε²d_y + ε²Σᵢσ²/sᵢ², which is substantially smaller (often by orders of magnitude) than the KL divergence of the Approx-IMH posterior (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.2).
