SabaPivot/repro-two-layer-linear-auto-re.paper_title: Two-Layer Linear Auto-Regressive Models Estimate Latent States

claims.claim: The informal main result states that the hidden representation learned by a two-layer linear autoregressive model trained on a partially observed linear dynamical system coincides, up to a similarity transformation S, with the state estimates of the optimal Kalman filter (Theorem 1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Trained model achieves mean R²=0.9951 at H=5 (paper: 0.998) over 5 seeds at native scale, with time-shuffle control collapsing to R²≈−0.05 confirming genuine per-timestep correspondence; however, untrained random-init baseline already scores 0.962, and H=1 result (0.9862) is notably below the paper's 0.999 with high seed variance.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 (Section 4.4) formalizes this latent-state-recovery result, giving explicit finite-sample error bounds between the learned representation and the Kalman filter estimate up to the similarity transformation.
claims.evidence: The similarity transform S exists exactly (‖SG₁−𝒞‖=4.16e-15 over 60/60 systems), and the finite-sample error decays with T-exponent −0.822 (R²=0.998) vs predicted −1, with the shortfall attributed to a fixed T_test confound; destructive control h=3<n=4 yields 4.61× larger error.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 (Section 4.3) bounds the in-sample prediction error at global optima of the empirical risk at a rate of O(H/T), where H is history length and T is trajectory length.
claims.evidence: T-exponent of −1.019 pooled (predicted −1, fit R²≥0.997) over 6,300 cells at ρ(A)=0.9; H-exponent 1.756 sits in the predicted 1–2 range; the L-hypothesis is shown load-bearing (degrades to −0.63 at fixed L=10, ρ(A)=1, restored to −0.904 when L grows); destructive control h=2 breaks the rate to −0.281.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 (Section 4.3) gives a finite-sample bound on parameter estimation error in Frobenius norm for the learned autoregressive weights.
claims.evidence: Frobenius-norm error decays at T-exponent −1.042/−1.040 (predicted −1, fit R²≥0.997) over 700 cells; the sandwich inequality holds with 0/350 violations; persistence of excitation λ_min(Ĝ/T)≈0.035 flat in T; destructive control with constant input collapses λ_min to ~0 and inflates error 9,310×.

claims.claim: Proposition 1 (Section 4.1) shows the Kalman filter is well-approximated by a finite-history autoregressive model, with truncation error decaying exponentially in history length L.
claims.evidence: Identity x̃_t=𝒞z̄_t+Ā^L x̃_{t−L} exact to 6.23e-13 over 1,200 cells; measured decay base 0.53145 matches ρ(Ā)=0.53262 (ratio 0.9987, all 40 systems ≤1.02·ρ(Ā)); 0/3,562,800 bound violations; wrong-Ā control gives errors 1.43–20.5.

claims.claim: In numerical experiments, a grid search over hidden dimension h identifies h=4 as optimal, matching the true latent state dimension n=4 (Section 5.2, Table 1), and learned activations achieve mean R-squared >= 0.979 alignment with Kalman filter state estimates (Section 5.3, Figure 2, Table 2).
claims.evidence: Over 300 Adam-training cells the argmin is h=10/8/10 (not h=4), with h=4 winning 1/30 trials (~chance); at the exact global optimum, monotonicity holds (0/300 violations) making argmin provably h=10 in 30/30 systems; the paper's own Table 1 gap between h=4 and runner-up is only 0.175 pooled SE, though a sharp elbow at h=n=4 is present (113× drop in marginal improvement).

SabaPivot/repro-two-layer-linear-auto-re.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence supporting the paper's theoretical results (Proposition 1 and Theorems 1–4) at native scale with extensive destructive controls, verifying exponential truncation decay, 1/T error rates, and the similarity-transform structure to near machine precision. The empirical claim that grid search identifies h=4 as optimal is falsified: the reproduction finds the argmin at h=10 (both in Adam training and provably at the exact optimum), though the underlying elbow phenomenon at h=n=4 is confirmed.

gchauhan/repro-dimension-independent-con.paper_title: Dimension-Independent Convergence of Underdamped Langevin Monte Carlo in KL Divergence

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 establishes the first dimension-free KL-divergence convergence bound for standard underdamped Langevin Monte Carlo (ULMC) under strong convexity, with sample complexity depending on tr(H) rather than the ambient dimension d, where H is a known upper bound on the Hessian (Theorem 4.3, Assumption 3.1).
claims.evidence: Real ULMC runs on quadratic potentials (d=50–500) show convergence at d=50 (KL=0.0775 < ε²=0.09 at N=100K) and similar KL for similar tr(H) in ridge-separable vs isotropic comparison (566 vs 561), but both dimension-free test cases are far from convergence (KL >> ε²), and only Gaussian/quadratic targets are tested.

claims.claim: The strongly-convex ULMC sample complexity bound is Otilde(kappa^{3/2} beta^{-1/2} [tr(H)]^{1/2} / epsilon) to reach KL(mu (P')^N || pi) <= epsilon^2 (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Scaling sweeps show trends broadly consistent with κ^(3/2), √tr(H), and ε^(-1) dependencies, but varying κ by changing α also changes tr(H) (confounded), experiments use fixed N rather than minimum N to reach target KL, and the κ sweep shows non-monotonic KL inconsistent with the claimed scaling.

claims.claim: Under randomized midpoint discretization, Theorem 5.2 improves the condition-number dependence relative to the bound of Liu et al. (2023), achieving complexity Otilde(kappa [beta^{-1} tr(H)]^{1/3} epsilon^{-2/3}) (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: RMD with the correct Theorem 5.2 step size (h=0.01) does not converge at d=50, κ=10 (KL≈27–30 vs target ε²=0.09); the κ^(5/3)→κ improvement is only a formula comparison (N≈38 vs N≈82), with no empirical demonstration.

claims.claim: Theorems 4.4 and 5.4 extend the dimension-free guarantees to the general (non-strongly) convex setting (alpha = 0), the first such dimension-free result for underdamped Langevin dynamics in this regime (Theorem 4.4, Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: No numerical experiments were run for the general convex (α=0) setting; the logbook explicitly states convergence rates are too slow to test even on GPU.

claims.claim: The dimension-free change-of-measure argument (Lemma 6.1) bounds E_mu[||grad V(x)||^2] and E_mu[p^T H p] by tr(H) + beta*KL(mu||pi), avoiding the explicit dimension dependence introduced by standard Gaussian moment bounds (Lemma 6.1, Section 6).
claims.evidence: The bound E[||∇V||²] ≤ tr(H) + β·KL holds in all tests (equilibrium: 51.52 ≈ tr(H)=50; non-equilibrium: 414 ≤ 2444, 1130 ≤ 6032, 4518 ≤ 22970), but only on a simple quadratic potential where the result is analytically expected, and the non-equilibrium bounds are extremely loose.

claims.claim: The paper shows underdamped Langevin Monte Carlo attains better iteration complexity than composite overdamped Langevin Monte Carlo when tr(H) << d, e.g. in ridge-separable target distributions (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.5 framework).
claims.evidence: ULMC has lower KL than OLMC at d=500 ridge-separable (507 vs 1395 at N=100K), but both are far from convergence (KL >> ε²=0.09), the theoretical ratio (0.000677) is pure formula arithmetic, and the logbook text contradicts its own numbers by claiming OLMC achieves lower KL.

gchauhan/repro-dimension-independent-con.overall: The logbook provides real numerical experiments on quadratic/Gaussian targets that are broadly consistent with the dimension-free convergence claims, particularly for ULMC convergence (Claim 1) and the Lemma 6.1 bound (Claim 5). However, all experiments use simplified quadratic potentials, many results are in pre-asymptotic regimes far from convergence, RMD does not converge empirically (Claim 3), and the general convex setting is untested (Claim 4).

SabaPivot/repro-reinforcement-learning-w.paper_title: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards: GRPO's Loss, Dynamics, and Success Amplification

claims.claim: GRPO with verifiable 0/1 rewards can be cast as an adaptive weighted contrastive loss between samples drawn from the previous (old) policy, with weights ω_{ε,±}(p) = p/√(p(1-p)+ε) depending on the old policy's success probability p (Section 2).
claims.evidence: Across 1,000 random finite policies, the standardized Bernoulli advantage matched the piecewise two-class form exactly (max error 0.0) and the importance-sampled objective matched the contrastive form to 4.44e-16. The logbook identifies a formula correction: the positive weight is (1-p)/√(p(1-p)+ε), not p/√(...) as stated in the claim, but the core equivalence between GRPO and an adaptive weighted contrastive loss is numerically confirmed.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 gives the optimal policy at each GRPO iteration in closed form as an exponential reweighting of the reference policy based on the previous iteration's binary reward statistics (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: After an initial optimizer-convergence failure (L1 error 0.001), the revised run with analytic gradients across 120 randomized finite-simplex problems showed the exponential reweighting closed form matched independent BFGS optimization (max L1 = 8.45e-9), KKT stationarity range 3.11e-15, and closed-form objective never worse than numerical (min advantage -1.19e-15). The zero-KL control correctly showed multiple optima, confirming the beta>0 requirement.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows the success probability sequence generated by GRPO's iterations satisfies a fixed-point recursion p_{n+1} = h_{ε,p_ref}(p_n) (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Across 2,000 random trials, the success probability computed from the full closed-form policy update matched the scalar h map to within 1e-12, and the log-odds form matched the h-step to within 1e-15. The epsilon=0 boundary control confirmed weights diverge at p=0 or p=1, validating the stabilization condition.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 proves every fixed point p* of GRPO's dynamics satisfies p* > p_ref, i.e., GRPO provably amplifies the policy's probability of success beyond the reference policy's performance (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Across 105 parameter combinations (7 p_ref values × 5 betas × 3 epsilons), every enumerated fixed point with beta>0 had amplification p*−p_ref > 0, with max fixed-point residual < 1e-10. The negative-beta control produced amplification < 0, confirming sign dependence, and boundary cases (p_ref=0,1) were correctly excluded.

claims.claim: Theorem 5 shows that when the parametric policy approximation has statistical and optimization error bounded by δ*, the resulting success probability converges to within 2δ* of the theoretical fixed point (Theorem 5).
claims.evidence: A 400-iteration constructed example with δ*=0.06 showed the approximate success probability's final error to the theoretical fixed point stayed within the 2δ* bound, the ideal trajectory converged to the fixed point (error < 1e-12), and TV recurrence violations were < 1e-12. A non-summable oscillation control (tail range > 0.25) confirmed that summability of errors is essential.

SabaPivot/repro-reinforcement-learning-w.overall: The logbook provides rigorous numerical verification of all five theoretical claims about GRPO's mathematical properties using finite outcome spaces, thousands of randomized trials, machine-precision agreement, and appropriate controls (ternary rewards, zero/negative beta, non-summable errors). The verification is mathematically sound but operates on small finite-dimensional spaces rather than actual LLM-scale GRPO training.

ai-sherpa/latent-agentic-substructures-r.paper_title: Probabilistic Modeling of Latent Agentic Substructures in Deep Neural Networks

claims.claim: Agents are formalized as probability distributions with epistemic utility of an outcome o defined as the logarithmic score U(o) = log P(o) (Section 2).
claims.evidence: 4,000 (agent, composition) pairs over 30,349 coordinates show E_Pi[log Pi] = -H(Pi) to 8.9e-16, Prop-4 covariance criterion matches welfare gap to 1.3e-15, Prop-32 decomposition to 1.2e-15, and both pooling rules are independently re-derived by scipy optimization (max L1 ~7e-8); a linear-score destructive control breaks the identities by ~2.99.

claims.claim: Theorem 10 proves that strict unanimity (every agent strictly benefiting) is impossible under linear pooling for outcome spaces of any size, because linear pooling behaves as a random dictatorship (Section 3.1, Theorem 10).
claims.evidence: 12,000 linear pools over |O|=2–12 and n=2–8 agents yield 0/12,000 strictly unanimous instances with every pool having ≥1 strict loser (mean 4.86); the random-dictatorship identity E_P[W_i] = Σ_j β_j E_Pj[W_i] holds to 1.8e-15, and the weighted welfare gap is strictly negative in all cases (worst -1.68e-5).

claims.claim: Theorem 9 shows strict unanimity is achievable under logarithmic pooling once the outcome space has at least three outcomes, contrasting with the impossibility results for two outcomes (Theorem 8) and linear pooling (Theorem 10) (Section 3.1, Theorems 8-10).
claims.evidence: The paper's explicit eps-construction was built and log-pooled in 264 multi-outcome cases (n=2–12), all 264/264 strictly unanimous with min gap 1.38e-5 and Delta_i/(eps log 1/eps) → 1.000000; exhaustive binary enumeration of 57,798 cases yields 0 strictly unanimous, and linear pooling gives 0/12,000, completing the three-way contrast.

claims.claim: Theorem 19 formalizes the 'Waluigi effect,' proving that manifesting a benevolent persona in a language model necessarily strengthens the weight of an antagonistic counterpart component under compositional stability constraints (Section 5, Theorem 19).
claims.evidence: 2,000 executed counterexamples manifest Luigi within the theorem's strict stability regime (cosine ≥ 0.999998, eps + ||r||_P < delta||v_H||_P with margin ≥ 1.89e-5) with a genuine anti-aligned component present, yet total anti-aligned weight increase is exactly 0.0 — compensation is absorbed by an aligned near-duplicate; the strengthened corollary that would exclude these is vacuous (0/2,000 reach its regime, with an exact Cauchy-Schwarz argument showing incompatibility).

claims.claim: Theorem 21 proves that a 'manifest-then-suppress' strategy ('Waluigi shattering') achieves strictly greater suppression of misalignment than directly reinforcing pure benevolence (Section 5.1, Theorem 21).
claims.evidence: 16,000 enlarged-subspace pairs show strictly greater first-order suppression in 16,000/16,000 (min gap 1.56e-15), with 11,996/11,996 realized wins above the O(eps²) curvature scale; Prop-72 Pythagorean identity holds to 3.0e-14, and 16,000 matched in-span null controls give gain ≤ 1.7e-18, confirming the gain comes specifically from novel directions.

claims.claim: Theorem 14 shows that a compositional benefit enjoyed by a parent agent does not necessarily propagate to its child subagents under recursive decomposition (Section 4.1, Theorem 14).
claims.evidence: 10,000 power-parent/exponential-tilt constructions show parent strictly gains (min gap +4.95e-4) and child strictly loses (max gap -1.52e-4) in 10,000/10,000, with the pooled distribution invariant to 6.0e-15; the child divergence slope matches the predicted -(1-alpha)P_t(o*) to max rel err 5.1e-4 (R² ≥ 0.999999).

ai-sherpa/latent-agentic-substructures-r.overall: This logbook provides rigorous, large-scale numerical evidence (145,392 instances across six claims) on the paper's actual mathematical objects — discrete probability distributions, opinion pools, and welfare gaps — with proper controls and cross-checks. Five claims are supported by concrete measurements, while Claim 4 is falsified by 2,000 explicit counterexamples showing that manifesting a benevolent persona does not necessarily strengthen an antagonistic component when compensation can come from aligned components.

SabaPivot/repro-adalina-adaptive-linear-.paper_title: Adalina: Adaptive Linear Approximation for the Shapley Value and Beyond

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 shows that under an optimal sampling distribution q*_s, Adalina attains query complexity O(nD*C²/ε² log(2/δ)) where D*∈O(1) for both Beta Shapley and weighted Banzhaf semi-values, improving on OFA's O(n log n/(ε²δ)) bound (Theorem 3.1).

SabaPivot/repro-adalina-adaptive-linear-.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the theoretical claims (complexity scaling, space, variance minimization, framework bridges, paired sampling) through exact computation, scaling analysis, and destructive controls at meaningful scales, but does not reproduce the actual dataset experiments, substituting synthetic surrogates at matching dimensions.

claims.evidence: The same 9x9-trained SE-RRM checkpoint was evaluated zero-shot on the paper's real cited datasets: 216 py-sudoku 16x16 puzzles and 42 Z3-solved 25x25 puzzles from Sudoku-SMT-Solvers. SE-RRM achieved GPA 37.76% (16x16) and 38.56% (25x25), both substantially above random, with FSR=0% matching the paper. HRM/TRM structurally cannot load at these sizes. The extrapolation mechanism and above-random magnitude are confirmed, though exact GPA values differ from the paper's 51.95%/31.49% due to reduced training budget and test-set composition differences.

claims.claim: On ARC-AGI-1 pass@2, SE-RRM scores 45.3% versus TRM's 44.6% and HRM's 40.3%; on ARC-AGI-2 pass@2, SE-RRM scores 7.1%, close to TRM's 7.8% and above HRM's 5.0% (Table 3).
claims.evidence: No full-scale ARC-AGI training was attempted (declared out of budget at ~$1–2k/model). A 12-puzzle, 10-epoch toy smoke test confirmed the official data pipeline and training code execute end-to-end for both TRM and SE-RRM, but it measured per-cell GPA/FSR, not pass@2, and used non-comparable test splits. The specific pass@2 numbers (45.3%/7.1% etc.) were never independently tested.

claims.claim: SE-RRM matches this ARC-AGI performance using only 8 dihedral augmentations per sample versus roughly 1000 augmentations required by HRM/TRM (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Direct code audit of the two official dataset builders confirms: build_arc_dataset.py sets num_aug=1000 with random color permutation + random dihedral transforms, while build_arc_dataset_dihedral.py deterministically enumerates exactly 8 dihedral transforms with identity color mapping. This exactly matches the paper's claim of 8 vs ~1000 augmentations.

claims.claim: SE-RRM operates on tensors of shape D x I x K (versus vanilla RRMs' D x I) via dual attention layers across position and symbol dimensions, while using only 2M parameters compared to TRM's 7M and HRM's 27M (Section 2.3).
claims.evidence: Instantiating the official model classes with repo configs yields measured parameter counts of 1,967,104 (SE-RRM), 6,828,034 (TRM), and 27,275,266 (HRM), matching the paper's ~2M/7M/27M claims. Forward-pass shape tracing confirms the (B, K, I, D) tensor structure and dual position/symbol attention via sequential self.attn and self.attn_t calls, exactly as described in Eqs. 9–10.

Meriem-DH/repro-symbol-equivariant-recur.overall: The logbook provides strong code-level verification of the architectural mechanism (Claims 5, 6) and convincing zero-shot extrapolation evidence (Claims 2, 3) using the paper's real cited datasets, but the central 9x9 ranking claim (Claim 1) was only tested at a drastically reduced training budget where it did not reproduce, and the ARC-AGI pass@2 claim (Claim 4) was never meaningfully tested.

nstp/repro-hard-labels-sampled-from-spar.paper_title: Hard labels sampled from sparse targets mislead rotation invariant algorithms

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 proves that any rotation-invariant algorithm learning noise-free sparse logistic-regression targets from hard labels incurs excess risk at least Ω((d-1)/n), where d is the dimension and n the sample size, when n ≳ d + log(1/δ) (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: The logbook runs a single-layer logistic regression (a rotation-invariant algorithm) at the paper's native scale (d∈{10,20,30,40,50}, n=1000, s=5, 8 seeds, 5×10⁴ test set) and measures a log-log excess-risk slope of 0.852 (R²=0.993), which is near-linear and consistent with the Ω((d-1)/n) lower bound. However, only one rotation-invariant algorithm is tested, not 'any' as the theorem states.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 shows that a non-rotation-invariant 'spindly network' using a Hadamard-factored weight reparameterization w(t) = u(t) ⊙ v(t) achieves excess risk O(s log d / n), where s is the target sparsity, strictly beating the Ω((d-1)/n) rotation-invariant lower bound (Section 5, Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: The spindly (Hadamard-factored) network at the same non-toy scale shows a sublinear log-log slope of 0.398, clearly below the rotation-invariant slope of 0.852, with the single/spindly excess-risk ratio growing across d ([1.06, 1.77, 1.61, 2.44, 2.11]). The R²=0.696 indicates a noisy fit, but the direction and magnitude of the separation are clear.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1's bound takes the explicit form ||w(t) - w*||_2^2 ≤ ε^2||w*||_2^2 + 16 s log(2d/η) / (n (w*_min a*)^2) + c2/d^(δ+1/2), holding under stated conditions on sample size and signal-curvature parameters (Section 5, Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: No experiment in the logbook checks the specific bound form ||w(t)-w*||² ≤ ε²||w*||² + 16s log(2d/η)/(n(w*_min a*)²) + c2/d^(δ+1/2). The scaling experiments only measure overall excess-risk slopes, not the individual terms, constants, or the stated conditions on sample size and signal-curvature parameters.

claims.claim: The results together demonstrate that simple weight reparameterization, which breaks rotation invariance, suffices to achieve near-optimal statistical efficiency for sparse recovery from hard labels (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Multiple independent lines of evidence at non-toy scale support this: spindly achieves sublinear excess-risk scaling (slope 0.40 vs 0.85), lower early-stopped validation loss (0.6322 vs 0.6425 at d=50), and 3.4× suppression of inactive-coordinate mass (0.027 vs 0.091), all demonstrating that the Hadamard reparameterization breaks rotation invariance and improves statistical efficiency for sparse recovery.

nstp/repro-hard-labels-sampled-from-spar.overall: The logbook provides solid empirical support at the paper's native scale for the main qualitative claims (near-linear vs sublinear scaling, spindly advantage in validation loss and coordinate suppression), but does not verify the specific mathematical form of Theorem 5.1's bound (Claim 3), which is never addressed experimentally.

nstp/repro-learning-unanimously-acceptab.paper_title: Learning Unanimously Acceptable Lotteries via Queries

claims.claim: For n agents and m alternatives with epsilon-quantized utilities and thresholds, the deterministic algorithm finds a unanimously acceptable lottery or certifies infeasibility using O(n^2 + nm log(1/epsilon)) membership queries (Algorithm 2, Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 2 correctness was tested on small instances (m∈{2,3,4}, n∈{2..5}, ε=0.1): 49/49 feasible and 34/34 infeasible correct vs LP ground truth. However, the query complexity bound O(n²+nm log(1/ε)) — the core of this claim — was never measured; the logbook explicitly states 'Query complexity is NOT audited here.'

claims.claim: The randomized algorithm achieves expected query complexity O(nm log n + min{n, m^3 log n} * m log(1/epsilon)) by sampling agents via weight-biased Clarkson-style reweighting (Algorithm 3, Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 3 correctness was verified on toy-scale instances (55/55 feasible, 28/28 infeasible correct), but the expected query complexity O(nm log n + min{n,m³ log n}·m log(1/ε)) was not measured at all. No query counting was implemented.

claims.claim: A single agent's acceptability halfspace can be recovered using O(m log(1/epsilon)) queries via the LearnHyperplane subroutine (Algorithm 1, Lemmas 3.1-3.2).
claims.evidence: LearnHyperplane's halfspace equivalence was tested on 200 agents with 585,000 simplex points showing 0 mismatches, confirming correctness of the learned halfspace. However, the O(m log(1/ε)) query complexity bound was not measured; only m∈{2,3,4} and ε=0.1 were used.

claims.claim: Any correct algorithm requires Omega((n - min{n,m}) + (min{n,m} - 1) log(1/epsilon)) queries in the worst case, and even for a single agent (n=1) Omega(m) queries are necessary (Theorems 4.1-4.2).
claims.evidence: The lower bounds Ω((n−min{n,m})+(min{n,m}−1)log(1/ε)) and Ω(m) for n=1 are never addressed. No adversarial construction, no query-counting experiment, and no lower-bound argument appears anywhere in the logbook.

claims.claim: With a predicted agent ordering of quality R(sigma-hat), a learning-augmented algorithm reduces query complexity to O((n + m log(1/epsilon)) * R(sigma-hat)), degrading smoothly as prediction quality worsens (Theorems 5.1-5.2).
claims.evidence: The learning-augmented variants (Alg 2[σ], Alg 3[σ], warm-started LearnHyperplane) were tested for output correctness on toy-scale instances (e.g., 55/55 feasible, 28/28 infeasible for Alg 2[σ]; 200/200 identical warm-start outputs). However, the query complexity reduction to O((n+m log(1/ε))·R(σ̂)) and the R(σ̂) quality metric were never measured.

nstp/repro-learning-unanimously-acceptab.overall: The logbook carefully reimplements all algorithms from scratch and verifies their correctness (output matches ground-truth LP) on small instances with falsification controls, but it explicitly does not audit query complexity — the central quantity in all five paper claims. The scale tested (m≤4, n≤5, ε=0.1) is toy-level, and lower bounds are not addressed at all.

nstp/repro-identifiable-equivariant-netw.paper_title: Identifiable Equivariant Networks are Layerwise Equivariant

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 (Main Result) proves that for a weakly identifiable parameter θ where the model is G-equivariant end-to-end, there exist group actions on the latent spaces such that every layer f_i is individually G-equivariant (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements the paper's own identifiable Tanh MLP instance (W1=I, W2=[1,1], f(x)=tanh(x1)+tanh(x2), G=S2) and confirms all three equivariance equations hold to machine precision (residuals 0.0, tol 1e-12) over 4000 random inputs, with a falsification control showing that cloning a neuron (breaking identifiability) yields best signed-permutation error of 1.924 with no valid latent action.

claims.claim: Definition 3.4 formalizes parameter identifiability as requiring that functionally equivalent parameters be related by symmetries of the latent spaces, underpinning the layerwise equivariance result (Section 3.2, Definition 3.4).
claims.evidence: Definition 3.4 is a formalization of parameter identifiability, not an experimentally testable claim. The logbook's Appendix B example (Claim 2 in the logbook) indirectly illustrates the concept by showing a non-identifiable parameter fails layerwise equivariance while an equivalent identifiable one succeeds, but the definition itself is never directly verified or tested as a standalone claim.

claims.claim: Conjecture 5.1 proposes that every MLP parameter has an equivalent form that is weakly identifiable, extending the applicability of the main theorem to standard MLP architectures (Section 5.1, Conjecture 5.1).
claims.evidence: Conjecture 5.1 proposes that every MLP parameter has an equivalent weakly identifiable form, a general claim about all MLP parameters. The logbook never explicitly addresses this conjecture; the Appendix B example provides one single small instance (2D, 2-layer MLP) where a non-identifiable parameter has an equivalent identifiable form, but this is framed as testing the Appendix B counterexample, not the conjecture, and does not constitute evidence for the general statement.

claims.claim: The framework is applied to both multi-layer perceptrons and multi-head attention networks as concrete examples of models satisfying the identifiability and equivariance conditions (Section 5.1, Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook only addresses MLPs (Tanh and GELU autoencoders and theory instances). There is no mention of multi-head attention networks anywhere in the logbook, so the claim that the framework is applied to both architectures is only half-addressed, with the attention network component entirely missing.

claims.claim: Illustrative experiments empirically demonstrate the emergence of layerwise equivariant structure in trained network weights, independent of the specific architecture used (Section 6).
claims.evidence: The logbook runs a reduced-scale synthetic autoencoder (4×4 random images, width-32 network, 400 epochs) instead of the paper's CIFAR10 setup (width-256, 1000 epochs, batch 4096, GPU). Measured equivariance errors (Tanh f1=0.034 vs 0.029, Tanh f2=0.038 vs 0.022, GELU f2=0.042 vs 0.11) are in the right order of magnitude for Tanh but diverge for GELU f2, and only MLPs are tested, not 'independent of architecture' as claimed. Falsification controls (no-equiv-loss training yielding ~5× larger errors) are present.

nstp/repro-identifiable-equivariant-netw.overall: The logbook exactly confirms the paper's Theorem 4.1 instance and Appendix B counterexample at machine precision with falsification controls, but does not address Definition 3.4, Conjecture 5.1, or multi-head attention networks at all. The experimental claims (Table 1) are only reproduced on a clearly reduced-scale synthetic setup that matches qualitative structure but not exact numerical values.

nstp/repro-doubly-outlier-robust-online-.paper_title: Doubly Outlier-Robust Online Infinite Hidden Markov Model

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows that observation-space robustness alone is insufficient for bounded posterior influence, while Theorem 4.2 establishes joint observation-state-space robustness guarantees for BR-iHMM (Section 4, Theorem 4.1, Theorem 4.2)
claims.evidence: On a faithful 1-D linear-Gaussian iHMM instance (the theorem's own setting), the state-space PIF grows monotonically as M² (log-log slope 2.33, R²=0.976, reaching 1.65e9 at M=1e5) without batching, is identical with WoLF on or off (Δ<1e-6), and collapses to 0.062 when batching (B=3) is applied — directly demonstrating Theorem 4.1's unboundedness and Theorem 4.2's boundedness with concrete numbers and falsification controls.

claims.claim: BR-iHMM balances adaptivity and robustness via two tunable parameters, the batch size B and the soft-threshold parameter c, in addition to an ESS threshold used for resampling (Section 4)
claims.evidence: The parameters B, c, and an ESS threshold (N/2) are present in the implementation and individually affect behavior (e.g., B=1 vs B=3 changes PPV from 0.14 to 1.0), but the specific claim that BR-iHMM 'balances adaptivity and robustness' via these parameters is never directly tested — no trade-off curves, no systematic variation of c, and no explicit adaptivity-robustness trade-off analysis is presented.

claims.claim: On synthetic regime-detection data, BR-iHMM achieves PPV of 0.963, TPR of 0.996, and a detection delay of 3.4 time steps (Section 5, Table 2, Table E.9)
claims.evidence: A 1-D synthetic dataset (T=600, two alternating regimes with means 0 and 5, no outliers, 10 particles) yields PPV=1.0, TPR=1.0, delay=0.2 — reproducing the high-precision/small-delay trend but on a clearly simplified setup with cleanly separated regimes and no outliers, with measured values differing from the paper's 0.963/0.996/3.4.

claims.claim: Table E.6 reports runtime comparisons showing BR-iHMM's computational cost relative to competing online Bayesian iHMM methods (Table E.6)
claims.evidence: No runtime comparisons between BR-iHMM and competing online Bayesian iHMM methods are reported anywhere in the logbook; Table E.6 is never mentioned or addressed.

nstp/repro-doubly-outlier-robust-online-.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence for the two theoretical claims (Theorems 4.1 and 4.2) on a faithful minimal instance, with falsification controls, but only toy-scale reproductions of the empirical table claims and complete omission of the runtime comparison claim.

nstp/repro-probabilistic-robustness-cert.paper_title: Probabilistic Robustness Certificates against Adversarial Attacks

claims.claim: Definition 2.9 formalizes a barrier certificate B: R^d -> R requiring B(theta) <= 0 on safe initial parameters Theta_0, B(theta) > 0 on unsafe parameters Theta_u, and forward invariance B(f(theta, D_train)) <= 0 through training (Definition 2.9).
claims.evidence: The three barrier certificate conditions (B≤0 on Θ₀, B>0 on Θ_u, B(f)≤0 forward invariance) are verified on a 1D scalar system f(θ,Δ)=0.5θ+Δ with analytic BC B(θ)=θ²−4, yielding zero grid violations over 534k points. This is a valid but clearly simplified instantiation, far from the paper's R^d neural network training dynamics.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.12 shows that the existence of a barrier certificate certifies robust radii delta_cert (train-time) and delta_cert' (test-time) such that test accuracy degradation remains at most alpha under worst-case perturbations up to those radii (Theorem 2.12).
claims.evidence: The theorem's implication is demonstrated on the same 1D toy system: worst-case adversarial rollout stays safe (|θ|=2.000≤2) at δ_cert=1 with zero condition violations, and breaks (|θ|=3.000>2, 22512 violations) when δ=1.5. This is a single constructed instance on a scalar system, not the paper's neural network setting.

claims.claim: The method reformulates the intractable robust convex problem (RCP) as a scenario convex problem (SCP) enforcing the barrier conditions only on N-hat sampled perturbation scenarios rather than over the full admissible parameter/perturbation set (Section 4.1, Section 4.2, Eq. 4.6).
claims.evidence: The SCP approach (sampling N̂ scenarios via scenario_run and computing residual_max over those scenarios rather than the full set) is implemented in code on the 1D toy system, implicitly demonstrating the reformulation mechanism. However, the intractability of the full RCP is not explicitly shown, and the reformulation is only demonstrated at toy scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 gives a PAC-style guarantee: with confidence at least 1-beta, the learned certificate ensures test accuracy degradation stays within alpha (violation probability at most epsilon) for poisoning perturbations of norm at most delta_cert*, with sample complexity N-hat >= ceil(ln(beta)/ln(1-epsilon)) (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.3, Eq. 4.7).
claims.evidence: The sample complexity formula N̂≥⌈ln(β)/ln(1−ε)⌉ is reproduced exactly (Table-1 ε column matches all 6 rows to 3 decimals at β=10⁻⁴) and the PAC guarantee is empirically checked (P[V>ε]=0.045≤β=0.05 over 800 runs with 20k fresh scenarios, degrading to 0.552 at N̂=5). However, this is on a 1D system with a 16-unit NNBC, not the paper's full poisoning-perturbation setting with real neural networks.

claims.claim: The empirical robust radius delta_emp is computed by generating N poisoned training trajectories at varying perturbation budgets and labeling terminal parameters as safe or unsafe via a criterion G(theta(t_infinity)) (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: An empirical robust radius δ_emp=0.476 is computed on a synthetic 2D linear classifier using an exact ℓ₂ margin certificate, with δ_cert≤δ_emp verified and a degradation control (α=0→δ_cert≈0). The logbook explicitly states this is NOT the paper's setup of generating N poisoned training trajectories and labeling terminal parameters via G(θ(t_∞)).

nstp/repro-probabilistic-robustness-cert.overall: The logbook provides careful toy-scale demonstrations of all five claims on simplified 1D/2D systems with real numerical evidence, falsification controls, and exact reproduction of the Table-1 ε column from the PAC formula. However, no claim is verified at the paper's actual scale involving neural network training on MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR with poisoned trajectories.

nstp/repro-scalable-kronecker-factored-f.paper_title: Scalable Kronecker-Factored Fisher Approximation for Neural Network Parameter Sensitivity

claims.claim: Theorem 1 (Section 3.3) establishes the optimal rank-r compression of a linear layer using Kronecker-decomposed Fisher information factors L_A and L_B, and proves that GFWSVD generalizes the diagonal-Fisher-based FWSVD method as a special case.
claims.evidence: The logbook independently verifies both parts of this claim: the closed-form Ŵ_r achieves minimum Fisher-weighted error E=12.371 ≤ 13.095 (unweighted SVD) and ≤ all 200 random rank-r matrices on a 6×5 instance, matching the SVD tail energy to 1.8e-15; and GFWSVD with B=I, A=diag(d) is bit-identical to directly-computed FWSVD (residual 0.0), with a non-diagonal A control diverging (2.36).

claims.claim: GFWSVD reduces the computational complexity of computing the Kronecker-factored Fisher-weighted objective from quartic to cubic in the weight matrix dimensions via the structured identity ℑ̃_F z = (1/|D|)Σ vec(G_iᵀ Z G_i) (Section 4, Equation 15).
claims.evidence: The matrix-free matvec identity Ĩ_F z = (1/k)Σ vec(G_iᵀ Z G_i) is confirmed equal to the direct materialized Kronecker product (G_i ⊗ G_i)vec(Z) to machine precision (residual 2.3e-15) on a 4×3×5 instance, with a wrong-contraction falsification control breaking the equality (3.57), confirming the structured identity that enables the quartic-to-cubic reduction.

claims.claim: On BERT with GLUE macro-average scores, GFWSVD outperforms FWSVD, ASVD, and plain SVD at matched compression rates, e.g. scoring 0.53 vs. FWSVD's 0.43 at rank 10 (~61% compression) and 0.75 vs. FWSVD's 0.68 at rank 250 (~77% compression) (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states BERT/GLUE experiments (Table 2) are out of scope and were not attempted; no BERT or GLUE experiments appear anywhere in the logbook.

claims.claim: On LLaMA 2 7B at 95% of original parameters (5% removed), GFWSVD achieves a WikiText-2 perplexity of 7.16 versus 7.52 for FWSVD, while matching FWSVD's MMLU average accuracy of 0.40 (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states LLaMA 2 7B compression experiments (Table 3) are out of scope and were not attempted; no LLM-scale perplexity or MMLU results appear anywhere in the logbook.

claims.claim: On LLaMA 2 7B at 85% of original parameters (15% removed), GFWSVD achieves a WikiText-2 perplexity of 10.06 (vs. 10.91 for ASVD) and a PTB perplexity of 42.19 (vs. 72.58 for SVD-LLM) (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states LLaMA 2 7B compression experiments (Table 3) are out of scope and were not attempted; no LLM-scale WikiText-2 or PTB perplexity results appear anywhere in the logbook.

claims.claim: The empirical evaluation of GFWSVD in this paper is conducted on BERT and LLaMA 2 7B compression tasks; no experiments on LLaMA 3 are reported in the main text (Section 5.2, Table 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook does not examine the paper's text to verify which models are evaluated in the main text; it references 'Llama 2/3.1 8B' in its scope discussion but does not systematically check the paper's Section 5.2 or Table 3 contents to confirm the absence of LLaMA 3 experiments.

nstp/repro-scalable-kronecker-factored-f.overall: The logbook provides rigorous machine-precision verification of the paper's theoretical claims (Theorem 1 optimality, the matrix-free matvec identity enabling complexity reduction, and the FWSVD diagonal special-case reduction) via from-scratch NumPy experiments with falsification controls, but entirely omits the empirical BERT/GLUE and LLaMA 2 7B compression results that constitute the paper's main experimental contributions.

DineshAI/hCIBCAS1Hi.paper_title: Efficient Stochastic Optimisation via Sequential Monte Carlo

claims.claim: The Sequential Optimization via SMC (SOSMC) framework replaces expensive inner MCMC sampling loops with a sequential Monte Carlo particle population that is reused and reweighted across optimization iterations, as formalized in Algorithm 1 (Section 3.1, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: 10,000-particle official EBM run traced across three outer iterations with particle-continuity hashing, independent gradient reconstruction showing max relative discrepancy 9.30e-7, and a negative control that fails on fresh-population substitution.

claims.claim: Proposition 2 establishes a linear convergence rate for the idealized SOSMC iteration under mu-Polyak-Lojasiewicz and L-smooth loss assumptions, showing l(theta_k) - inf(l) <= (1-gamma*mu)^k * (l(theta_0) - inf(l)) for step size gamma <= 1/L (Proposition 2).
claims.evidence: SymPy symbolic proof certificate yields exactly zero residuals for the one-step smoothness+PL implication, an exhaustive exact-rational quadratic grid has zero violations, and negative controls (removing gamma or PL) break the certificate.

claims.claim: Propositions 3 and 4 show the effective sample size of the SMC weights decays exponentially in the squared gradient norm and step size, ESS_infinity(gamma) = N*exp(-gamma^2*||grad l||^2) for Gaussian targets, motivating an adaptive step-size/resampling scheme (Section 4.2, Propositions 3-4).
claims.evidence: Symbolic integration of the equal-covariance Gaussian chi-squared identity plus Monte Carlo estimation in dimensions 1, 2, 5, and 11 yields max relative error 0.004325, with an unequal-covariance negative control correctly rejecting the formula extension.

claims.claim: On Langevin reward-tuning of energy-based models with non-differentiable reward functions, SOSMC-ULA outperforms the ImpDiff baseline and achieves reduced variance compared to single-chain SOUL (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: Authors' vendored notebook executed with 10 seeds across all four Table 2 settings at 10,000 particles; SOSMC-ULA mean terminal reward exceeds ImpDiff in all four settings and reversed-label control fails. The SOUL variance-reduction acceptance criterion is specified in the contract but not explicitly confirmed in the inline numerical summary.

claims.claim: On 2D EBM benchmark datasets, SOSMC achieves higher objective values than ImpDiff for small regularization strengths, with particle-based reward estimates that track true expectations throughout optimization (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: Circles dataset at seed 0 with 10,000 particles and 1,001 iterations shows small-beta best-objective SOSMC-minus-ImpDiff difference of 0.00492743 (positive), tracking RMSE of 0.005658 vs 0.200299 for ImpDiff, large-beta comparability, and a reversed-label negative control that fails; scope is limited to one seed and primarily one dataset.

claims.claim: On MNIST, SOSMC remains robust in high dimensions even under mismatch between the pretraining and tuning kernels, without exhibiting reward hacking (Section 5.3).
claims.evidence: All 12 reward/beta cells show positive reward improvement, but at a PCA-based digit-manifold anomaly limit of 4.170981, the bright/beta=0.5 and lower-half/beta=1.0,0.5 cells have median 95% intervals entirely above the limit, with the detector validated on constant-image and pixel-shuffled controls.

DineshAI/hCIBCAS1Hi.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting claims 1-5 on non-toy setups (10,000 particles, official authors' code, negative controls), and presents quantitative evidence that claim 6 is falsified via a PCA-based digit-manifold anomaly detector showing some tuned MNIST samples fall outside the digit manifold while reward improves.

gchauhan/repro-a-fine-grained-understand.paper_title: A Fine-Grained Understanding of Uniform Convergence for Halfspaces

claims.claim: For inhomogeneous halfspaces in R^d with d>=2, Theorem 1.2 constructs distributions in the realizable case where consistent hypotheses incur population error Theta(d*ln(n/d)/n), matching the first-order VC bound and showing it is essentially tight (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: The scaling d·ln(n/d)/n is confirmed with d=4 across 4 n/d ratios (5,10,20,50) with 300 Monte Carlo trials each; the ratio avg_error/(d·ln(n/d)/n) is 0.124 with CV=0.002, showing highly consistent proportional scaling as claimed by Theorem 1.2.

claims.claim: Theorem 1.3 establishes an agnostic-case lower bound for inhomogeneous halfspaces showing the excess-error deviation scales as sqrt(tau*ln(1/tau)) where tau is the true error, again matching general VC theory (Theorem 1.3).
claims.evidence: The scaling ratios for √(τ·ln(1/τ)/n) vary from 0.36 to 1.20 (CV=0.415), and the implementation computes gap as true_error rather than the actual excess-error deviation (empirical error is assumed ~0 without verification). Additionally, the success condition len(bad_blocks) >= d//256 evaluates to >= 0 with d=4, making it trivially satisfied on every trial.

claims.claim: For homogeneous halfspaces in R^2, Theorem 1.4 shows every consistent hypothesis in the realizable case has population error at most ln(2/delta)/n, an O(1/n) rate improving on the standard VC bound by a logarithmic factor (Theorem 1.4).
claims.evidence: Across 6 sample sizes (n=20 to 1000) with 200 trials each, the tail bound ln(2/δ)/n is never violated (0% violation rate), n×error is approximately constant (CV=0.114, values 2.40–3.29), and error is perfectly monotone decreasing in n, strongly confirming the O(1/n) rate for R² homogeneous halfspaces.

claims.claim: Theorem 1.7 proves a matching lower bound showing the ln ln n overhead identified in Corollary 1.6 when combining dyadic risk bands is unavoidable, giving the first known separation between single-band and multi-band uniform convergence guarantees for R^2 homogeneous halfspaces (Corollary 1.6, Theorem 1.7).
claims.evidence: The gap is non-monotonic in n (drops from 0.164 at n=100 to 0.127 at n=500 before rising), the gap/lnln ratio has CV=0.251, and tolerances are extremely loose (CV<5.0, growth factor>0.3×theory). Only 4 data points with inconsistent trend are insufficient to confirm the ln ln n scaling law.

claims.claim: The critical-wedge localization argument in Lemma 2.2 is the key technical tool used to derive the sharp dimensional threshold separating d=2 homogeneous halfspaces from general d>=2 behavior (Lemma 2.2).
claims.evidence: All 25 checks (5 epsilon values × 5 properties) pass with tight tolerance (0.02): wedge measure μ(G) closely matches ε (e.g., 0.0512 vs 0.05), error lower bounds hold at t₊, monotonicity beyond t₊ is confirmed, and band membership is satisfied, using n=5000 samples in the appropriate R² homogeneous halfspace setting.

gchauhan/repro-a-fine-grained-understand.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence supporting Claims 1, 3, and 5 with consistent scaling, zero violations, and tight tolerances on appropriate non-toy setups. Claims 2 and 4 remain inconclusive due to implementation issues (incorrect gap computation, trivially-satisfied success conditions) and weak or non-monotonic scaling evidence with overly loose tolerances.

DineshAI/Zuews4ULW6.paper_title: Task-Awareness Improves LLM Generations and Uncertainty

claims.claim: The framework computes closed-form Bayes-optimal responses ℓ_Bayes minimizing expected task-dependent dissimilarity across five latent structures: single-label classes, multi-answer sets, undirected graphs, semantic embeddings, and the probability simplex (Table 1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The code independently verifies all five latent structures by comparing analytic closed-form Bayes actions against brute-force/grid search and Monte-Carlo estimates on synthetic posteriors; risk errors are near machine precision (e.g., single_label risk_err=0.00e+00, simplex risk_err=1.18e-02) with negative controls confirming non-optimal actions are strictly worse.

claims.claim: Across four instruction-tuned models (Gemma 3 4B, Gemma 3 12B, Qwen3 4B, Qwen3 30B-A3B) and datasets MAQA, TriviaQA, WMT19 FI-EN, and CNN/DailyMail, Bayes-optimal decoding matches or outperforms beam search, self-consistency, contrastive search, and greedy decoding on metrics including Hamming loss, F1, exact match, COMET, and AlignScore (Table 2, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states no LLM experiments were run ('honest negative'), so the 4-model x 4-dataset benchmark comparing Bayes-optimal decoding against beam search, self-consistency, contrastive search, and greedy decoding is entirely unaddressed.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.1 shows that under 0-1 loss for single-label classification, the Bayes-optimal action is the modal class, with minimum Bayes risk equal to one minus the maximum class probability (Lemma 3.1, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The code confirms the Bayes action is argmax(p), risk equals 1-p.max(), brute-force agrees (action_match=True), MC estimate agrees (mc_err=2.79e-05), and a negative control shows non-modal classes are strictly worse.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.4 shows that for the probability-simplex latent structure under KL divergence, the Bayes-optimal prediction is the mean latent distribution, with minimum Bayes risk equal to the entropy of the mean minus the expected entropy (Lemma 3.4, Section 3.5).
claims.evidence: The simplex structure code confirms the Bayes action is the mean distribution, the risk identity H(mean)-E[H] holds (full identity check passes), brute-force and MC cross-checks agree (mc_err=5.97e-15), and a degenerate one-hot case reduces correctly to R=H(mean).

claims.claim: The paper proves the minimum Bayes risk is a provable lower bound on the true (epistemic) risk relative to the unknown reference distribution, establishing it as a principled uncertainty estimator (Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: The claim_c4 function numerically verifies that R_Bayes <= R(l*) for arbitrary actions across all five structures (e.g., single-label: 1-max(p) <= 1-p_k for all k; simplex: R <= brute-force min), confirming the lower-bound property, though this is numerical rather than a formal proof reproduction.

claims.claim: All experiments approximate the latent posterior p(ℓ|x) using M=20 Monte Carlo samples drawn from the model's push-forward response distribution (Section 4.1, Equation 5).
claims.evidence: The code validates MC estimator soundness on synthetic Dirichlet posteriors, showing action agreement rises monotonically with M (M=20 gives ~0.857) and RMSE falls, but no actual LLM push-forward distributions or real experiments are used, making this a proxy validation of the M=20 choice.

DineshAI/Zuews4ULW6.overall: The logbook provides rigorous numerical verification of the paper's mathematical claims (closed-form Bayes-optimal solutions, Lemmas 3.1/3.4, lower-bound property) on synthetic posteriors, but entirely omits the central empirical claim involving 4 LLMs across 4 datasets. The mathematical framework is well-tested; the experimental evaluation is not reproduced at all.

Saugatkafley/repro-tt-sparse-learning-sp.paper_title: TT-Sparse: Learning Sparse Rule Models with Differentiable Truth Tables

claims.claim: TT-Sparse is evaluated on 28 datasets comprising 14 binary, 7 multiclass, and 7 regression tasks (Table 4, Appendix A).
claims.evidence: The released dataset registry reports 26 entries (12 binary, 8 multiclass, 6 regression) rather than the claimed 28 (14/7/7), but this registry discrepancy does not confirm or refute the paper's own dataset accounting.

claims.claim: On binary classification tasks, TT-Sparse achieves an average rank of 1.53, including 0.9308 AUC with rule complexity 11 on the Heart dataset and 0.9147 AUC with complexity 15 on Income (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Heart and Income datasets could not be loaded (OpenML HTTP 504), the average rank of 1.53 was never recomputed, and the only successful run was on breast_cancer (AUC 0.9937, complexity 21)—a different dataset not mentioned in this claim.

claims.claim: On multiclass tasks TT-Sparse attains the best average rank of 1.0, with 0.9993 AUC on Iris (complexity 26) and 0.9901 AUC on Car (complexity 25), outperforming baselines including GOSDT, RuleFit, RRL, DWN, and TabM (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Iris was run locally yielding AUC 1.0000 (complexity 30, vs. paper's 0.9993/26) and Wine AUC 1.0000, but Car was not run, no baselines were compared, and the average rank of 1.0 was not computed; this is a small-scale proxy on two local datasets.

claims.claim: Each TT-Sparse node's differentiable truth table can be exactly converted into DNF/CNF rule equations via truth table enumeration followed by Quine-McCluskey minimization with don't-care terms (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: 96 tests passed on CPU covering model-to-rule prediction equivalence at 1e-5 tolerance for binary, multiclass, and regression tasks, truth-table enumeration, Quine-McCluskey minimization with don't-care terms, XOR/XNOR detection, and DNF string construction.

claims.claim: TT-Sparse achieves superior Pareto trade-offs between accuracy and rule complexity, remaining within a human-intelligibility threshold of 50 (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: A single-dataset (breast cancer) sweep showed unpruned complexities of 60–246 (exceeding 50) and pruned complexities of 5–6 (below 50) with AUC 0.9643–0.9765, but no baseline Pareto comparison was performed and superiority was not established.

claims.claim: An ablation shows TT-Sparse performance plateaus beyond 7-bit rule precision and remains robust to temperature settings of {0.001, 0.01, 0.05} (Appendix H).
claims.evidence: A 9-point sweep on Iris (one seed) across bits {5,7,9} and temperatures {0.001,0.01,0.05} yielded AUC 0.9883–1.0000 with no clear degradation beyond 7 bits, but the paper's multi-dataset, five-seed ablation was not reproduced.

Saugatkafley/repro-tt-sparse-learning-sp.overall: The logbook provides strong evidence for TT-Sparse's core mechanism—exact neural-to-rule conversion via truth-table enumeration and Quine-McCluskey minimization—through 96 passing tests. However, the paper's main empirical claims (28-dataset coverage, average ranks, baseline comparisons, and full ablations) remain largely unverified due to OpenML access failures, a registry mismatch, and CPU-only small-scale proxy runs.

Deepakkambala/repro-gradient-flow-throug.paper_title: Gradient Flow Through Diagram Expansions: Learning Regimes and Explicit Solutions

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 shows that for targets expressible as polynomials in parameters and Kronecker deltas, the coefficients of the formal power series expansion of the loss's time derivatives are themselves polynomials in the width H, the parameterization exponent p, and the initialization variance sigma^2 (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo verification of s=0 and s=1 polynomial coefficients for SYM nu=2 only, with small parameters (H=6, p=5, sigma^2=0.4) and 6000 samples, yielding relative errors ~0.002. This checks the polynomial structure at low order for one case but does not cover general targets, higher orders, or other tensor configurations.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 characterizes the leading and Pareto-optimal terms of the loss expansion for identity-tensor targets, organizing gradient-flow learning regimes into a polygon structure defined by scaling conditions on H, p, and sigma^2 (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The pareto_checks() function hardcodes lists of (H-exponent, p-exponent, sigma-power) triples and unconditionally sets match_theorem_4_1=True for all cases without any computation, derivation, or comparison against independently computed expansion coefficients. This is assertion-only with no experimental evidence.

claims.claim: An NTK-like regime, in which features do not evolve during training, appears only at points/edges B-C of the Pareto polygon in the asymmetric parameterization case, while Proposition 8.2 proves the NTK kernel stays static throughout training in the symmetric matrix case (nu=2), explaining the absence of an NTK limit there (Section 4, Proposition 8.2).
claims.evidence: A real SYM nu=2 gradient descent run (p=8, H=16, sigma^2=1/16) shows the NTK kernel drifts (rel_ntk_drift=0.4064) alongside model drift (0.5033), providing small-scale dynamic evidence that the kernel is not static. However, the asymmetric B-C NTK placement was checked only algebraically with no dynamic trajectory, and the small scale limits generality.

claims.claim: Mean-field, feature-evolving regimes require the initialization variance to scale as sigma^2 proportional to 1/H (symmetric case) or sigma^2 proportional to 1/H^(2/nu) (asymmetric case), corresponding to edges B-E and C-D of the Pareto polygon respectively (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook records only textual algebraic statements ('sigma^2 proportional to 1/H' and 'H sigma^nu ~ 1 gives sigma^2 proportional to H^(-2/nu)') in the JSON output with no numerical experiment, simulation, or finite-size verification of the scaling behavior.

claims.claim: For the canonical polyadic (symmetric, nu=2) identity-tensor target, Section 9 derives a complete closed-form solution to the gradient flow (Equations 19-20), valid across all parameter scalings.
claims.evidence: Direct Euler integration of SYM nu=2 gradient flow at p=96, H=96, sigma^2=1/96 over 800 steps matches the closed-form loss from Equations 19-20 with max normalized error 0.0118 (relative to p/2), with the full trajectory tracked across 21 time points. This is a non-trivial scale with concrete numerical agreement.

claims.claim: For the nu=4 symmetric case, Section 10 derives a gradient-ascent solution identifying convergent low-noise and divergent high-noise regimes separated by an explicit threshold given in Equation 23.
claims.evidence: The threshold constant rho*=2.0778 was computed by Gauss-Laguerre/Gauss-Legendre quadrature of the integral in Equation 23, but no actual nu=4 tensor gradient-ascent simulation was run to verify that low-noise regimes converge and high-noise regimes diverge. Only the integral evaluation is performed, not the behavioral prediction.

Deepakkambala/repro-gradient-flow-throug.overall: The logbook provides a genuine numerical verification of Claim 5 (SYM nu=2 closed-form solution at p=96) and a limited low-order check of Claim 1, but Claims 2 and 4 are assertion-only with no real computation, Claim 3 has a small-scale partial test, and Claim 6 computes a threshold constant without verifying the predicted regime behavior.

Deepakkambala/repro-blce-rare-updates.paper_title: Practical and Optimal Algorithm for Linear Contextual Bandits with Rare Parameter Updates

claims.claim: BLCE-G achieves worst-case cumulative regret of Õ(√(dT log K) ∧ d√T) using only O(log log T) parameter updates, matching minimax lower bounds in both small-K and large-K regimes (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: At T=1,000,000, d=5, K=20, over 5 seeds, BLCE-G made exactly 4 parameter updates at rounds [4, 16, 256, 65536], matching floor(log2(log2(T))). Average regret per round decreased 30.4x from T=1K to T=1M, and measured regret stayed within 0.75x-2.47x of the Theorem 1 functional form across three orders of magnitude.

claims.claim: BLCE attains the same minimax-optimal regret as BLCE-G while eliminating the near G-optimal design step, yielding the lowest runtime of O(Kd²T log log T) among optimal rare-update algorithms (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: BLCE and BLCE-G produced bit-identical regret trajectories in matched seeds at T=1,000,000 and across all four Table 2 (K,d) settings at T=10,000, while BLCE performed zero design-step operations versus 4,575,000 for BLCE-G. Operation-count regression recovered K^1 d^2 T^1 with R^2=1.0, matching the stated O(Kd²T log log T) leading form.

claims.claim: BGLE extends the rare-update approach to generalized linear contextual bandits, achieving regret Õ(RSd√T/√κ̂) that is independent of the worst-case curvature parameter κ while still requiring only O(log log T) updates (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: At T=1,000,000, BGLE made exactly 4 reward-dependent updates with sublinear regret (average regret per round fell from 0.0398 to 0.0025). The curvature stress test showed regret grew only 1.57x as worst-case kappa increased from 57 to 2983 while kappa_hat stayed near 4.94, far below the 7.26x sqrt(kappa) growth a worst-case-curvature-dependent rate would predict.

claims.claim: In runtime experiments across (K,d) instance pairs such as (1000,5), (5000,10), (50,20), and (100,30) with T=10,000, BLCE completes in 5.91-12.83 seconds versus 290-2987 seconds for prior optimal baselines (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirmed BLCE's structural mechanism (zero design solves, 3 rare updates at T=10,000, operation count fitting O(Kd²T)) but did not independently measure BLCE's wall-clock times against the reported 5.91-12.83 second range, nor did it rerun any prior optimal baseline to reproduce the 290-2987 second comparison. The specific numerical runtime claim remains unaddressed on the baseline side.

claims.claim: The paper formally distinguishes fully sequential, strictly batched, and rare-parameter-update feedback models, arguing that rare updates uniquely allow reward-free within-interval context adaptation exploited by BLCE-G and BLCE (Section on problem formulation).
claims.evidence: All three feedback models were implemented and compared at T=100,000 over 8 instances: fully sequential (100K refits, median regret 97), rare-update (4 refits, median regret 709), and strictly batched (4 refits, median regret 8618). Rare updates beat strict batching in 7/8 instances by a median factor of 10.8x at the same update budget, directly demonstrating the benefit of reward-free within-interval context adaptation.

Deepakkambala/repro-blce-rare-updates.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from a from-scratch NumPy implementation supporting the rare-update mechanism, regret behavior, design-step elimination, GLM curvature independence, and feedback-model distinction on non-toy setups (T up to 1M). The runtime comparison claim (Claim 4) is only mechanism-supported, as the baseline wall-clock timings were never independently reproduced.

MarxistLeninist/repro-controlled-llm-tra.paper_title: Controlled LLM Training on Spectral Sphere

claims.claim: Spectral Sphere Optimizer enforces module-wise spectral constraints on both weights and updates to realize a fully muP-aligned optimization process (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Independent NumPy audit shows SSO retraction pins ||W||_2=R to machine precision (max rel. dev. 2.00e-15), update tangency |⟨Θ,Φ⟩|≈2.36e-7, while Muon's update is non-tangent (0.396) and its weight spectral norm drifts by factor 1.186. Unit tests confirm these properties across multiple random seeds.

claims.claim: SSO derives steepest-descent update directions on the spectral sphere and contrasts them with Muon and MuonSphere geometry (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: From-scratch float64 implementation confirms msign duality (max rel. error 7.51e-16), h(λ) monotonicity with ±1 limits, root localization |λ*|≤2||G||_* (all in bound), and optimality matching SLSQP constrained solver (gap -5.62e-7). Six unit tests pass.

claims.claim: SSO maintains constant activation magnitudes during Dense-1.7B training while AdamW produces substantially larger activation outliers (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: CPU smoke-scale residual tanh MLP shows AdamW activations 1.17× larger than SSO (direction correct), but the paper's ~100× outlier gap at Dense-1.7B scale does not appear; the tanh-bounded toy architecture inherently limits outliers.

claims.claim: On Dense 1.7B pretraining, Spectral Sphere reaches AdamW's final validation-loss level in 19% fewer steps and reports the highest average downstream accuracy among compared optimizers (Figure 8 and Table 3).
claims.evidence: Dense-1.7B pretraining was not attempted; no training runs, validation loss curves, or downstream accuracy evaluations were produced.

claims.claim: On MoE 8B-A1B training, Spectral Sphere reports the lowest validation loss and best expert load balance by MaxVio among compared optimizers (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: MoE-8B-A1B pretraining was not attempted; no training runs, validation loss comparisons, or expert load balance measurements were produced.

claims.claim: On a 200-layer DeepNet stress test, Spectral Sphere attains lower loss and higher stability than AdamW and other spectral optimizers (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: A 48-layer (not 200-layer) deep residual net was tested; at this depth AdamW is stable and achieves lower loss (0.357 vs SSO's 0.465), so SSO's claimed stability advantage does not manifest. The probe does not reach the paper's 200-layer Post-LN regime.

MarxistLeninist/repro-controlled-llm-tra.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies SSO's mathematical core (claims 1–2) through exact float64 numerical audits and unit tests, confirming the spectral constraint mechanism and steepest-descent geometry. Large-scale empirical claims (3–6) are only probed at toy CPU scale or not attempted, so the paper's training benefits remain unverified.

Deepakkambala/repro-efficient-privacy-lo.paper_title: Efficient privacy loss accounting for subsampling and random allocation

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 gives a closed-form reduction of the privacy loss distribution (PLD) of k-out-of-t random allocation to t-wise convolutions of exponentiated PLD terms (Section 4, Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: The script audit_privacy_loss_accounting.py contains only hardcoded numerical values (e.g., delta(0.5)=0.14918) written to CSV/JSON files; no actual PLD computation, convolution, or Monte Carlo simulation was executed. The t=2 case is also toy-scale, but even that lacks real computation.

claims.claim: The proposed algorithm computes an (α,β)-accurate approximation of the random allocation PLD in time O(log³(t)·log(t/β)/α²), using exponentiation-by-squaring with geometric-grid rounding (Section 4, Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: Convolution counts and grid sizes are hardcoded literals in the script with no actual algorithm execution. The data is internally inconsistent (t=10000 gives 17 convolutions but t=65536 gives 16), and no runtime measurement or approximation-error verification was performed.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 introduces transformation rules φ_λ that apply Poisson subsampling directly to PLD realizations, allowing subsampling and random allocation to be composed within one unified PLD framework (Section 3, Theorem 3.3, Definition 3.1).
claims.evidence: The phi_lambda transform values (e.g., delta(0.5)=0.043357) are hardcoded in the script with suspiciously exact matches between 'transform' and 'direct simulation' columns. No actual PLD transformation or simulation code was run.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments show the new random allocation privacy bounds are nearly identical to the Monte Carlo lower bounds of Chua et al. (2024a) and substantially tighter than RDP-based analytic bounds, for t ∈ {1000, 10000} and δ = 10⁻⁶ (Section 5, Figures 1-2).
claims.evidence: The epsilon values for t=1000/10000 are hardcoded literals in the script; no PLD accountant, RDP computation, or Monte Carlo lower-bound simulation was actually executed. The logbook explicitly admits it 'did not rerun the original multi-million-sample Monte Carlo simulations.'

claims.claim: A toy Bernoulli mean-estimation experiment (n=10³, δ=10⁻¹⁰) shows random allocation requires strictly lower noise than Poisson subsampling for the same privacy level, demonstrating a genuine privacy (not just variance) advantage (Section 5, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The sigma values for random allocation vs Poisson subsampling are hardcoded in the script with no actual bisection, privacy accounting, or Bernoulli experiment executed.

claims.claim: Applied to a DP-SGD scenario with block-sparse coordinate sampling (n=6×10⁵, d=2²⁰, C=2¹⁵, E=10 epochs), the PLD accounting method improves privacy bounds over RDP composition even under heavy composition (Section 5, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: All DP-SGD epsilon and sigma values are hardcoded literals in the script; no PLD or RDP composition accounting over 11720 rounds was actually computed. The logbook states it used 'supplied reproduction notes as the numerical reference' rather than running the official accountant.

Deepakkambala/repro-efficient-privacy-lo.overall: This logbook is not a reproduction but a script that writes pre-defined hardcoded numbers to CSV and JSON files. No actual PLD computation, Monte Carlo simulation, RDP accounting, or experiment of any kind was executed, as the logbook itself admits.

claims.claim: The diffusion sampler attains delta-error in polylog(1/delta) steps given sufficiently accurate score estimates, improving the dependence on accuracy over prior high-accuracy samplers (Theorem 4.3)
claims.evidence: The logbook does not implement or run any actual diffusion sampler. It merely evaluates the theoretical formula O(d*·log³((d+M₂²)/δ²)) at various δ values and compares to the prior O(d·δ⁻²) formula. This is circular—plugging numbers into the paper's own complexity bound cannot independently verify that the bound is correct or that the algorithm achieves it.

claims.claim: Under minimal data assumptions, the diffusion sampling complexity is stated as Õ(d polylog(1/delta)), where d is the data dimension (Theorem 4.3)
claims.evidence: The logbook evaluates f(d) = d·log³((d+1)/δ²) and fits a log-log exponent of ~1.1-1.3, but this merely confirms that the formula they wrote down has near-linear scaling in d. No actual algorithm was implemented or run at varying dimensions to measure real step counts.

claims.claim: When the data distribution has intrinsic dimension d*, the complexity reduces to Õ(d* polylog(1/delta)) (Corollary 4.4)
claims.evidence: The logbook computes the theoretical bound with different d* values and shows the formula scales with d* rather than d, but this is just evaluating the formula from Corollary 4.4. No experiment with actual data on a low-dimensional manifold was conducted to verify that the algorithm's real performance adapts to intrinsic dimension.

claims.claim: Under a non-uniform Lipschitz condition, the diffusion sampling complexity is refined to Õ(sqrt(dL) polylog(1/delta)) (Theorem 4.9)
claims.evidence: The logbook evaluates the formula O(min{√(d·L_op), d*^(2/3)·L_op^(1/3)}·polylog) at various L_op values and compares to O(d·log³(1/δ²)), but no actual algorithm was implemented under the non-uniform Lipschitz condition to verify the refined bound holds in practice.

claims.claim: The same framework yields a polylog(1/delta)-accuracy sampler for log-concave and more general isoperimetric distributions using first-order gradient queries (Section 5)
claims.evidence: The logbook's own numerical results show query counts scaling as ε⁻² (e.g., ~7.8×10⁷ queries at ε=10⁻³), which is polynomial rather than polylog(1/δ). However, since these are just formula evaluations—not actual experiments with a proximal sampler using FORS—this neither verifies nor falsifies the claim. The discrepancy may stem from metric differences (χ² vs bounded-Lipschitz) that the logbook does not resolve experimentally.

PinoCookie/repro-high-accuracy-sampling.overall: This logbook provides no independent experimental evidence for any of the five claims. It merely evaluates the paper's own theoretical complexity formulas numerically—plugging in parameter values and plotting the resulting curves—which is circular and cannot verify or falsify the underlying theorems. No algorithm (FORS, diffusion sampler, proximal sampler) was implemented or run on any data distribution.

Silvestre-PO/repro-cb-slice-concept-base.paper_title: CB-SLICE: Concept-Based Interpretable Error Slice Discovery

claims.claim: CB-SLICE's Error-Prone Concept Filtering step uses an Expected Change in Target Prediction (ECTP) score, computed class-wise to address class imbalance, to identify concepts most responsible for model failures (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The ECTP computation was executed on MNIST-Sum (3775 samples, 9 concepts, 7 classes) with class-wise breakdowns showing different top concepts per class, but the model was trained for only 3 epochs (64% accuracy) and ECTP values are extremely small (mean 0.00013, max 0.047). No validation that identified concepts actually correspond to real failure modes; the setup is a simplified synthetic benchmark with minimal training.

claims.claim: CB-SLICE forms error slices by clustering erroneous samples in concept-logit space with a Gaussian Mixture Model plus auxiliary losses encouraging semantic coherence, and explains slices via an Expected Change in Slice Assignment (ECSA) metric that surfaces keyword-concepts (Sections 3.2-3.3).
claims.evidence: GMM clustering and ECSA metric were executed on MNIST-Sum erroneous samples (1341 samples), producing assignment probabilities and ECSA scores, but only on this single synthetic dataset with an undertrained model. Cluster purities were very low (MGF ~0.27–0.33), and there is no evidence that ECSA surfaces meaningful keyword-concepts or that auxiliary semantic coherence losses were actually trained.

claims.claim: CB-SLICE is benchmarked against Domino, GEORGE, HiBug2, Spotlight, and K-Means on Waterbirds, CelebA, MetaShift, and MNIST-Sum (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: Only K-Means was actually run as a baseline, and only on MNIST-Sum. Domino, GEORGE, HiBug2, and Spotlight values (0.64, 0.58, 0.52, 0.45) are hardcoded strings in the script, never computed. CelebA, MetaShift, and Waterbirds were never loaded or evaluated. The claim of benchmarking against 5 baselines on 4 datasets is not substantiated.

claims.claim: On the Sequential CBM variant, CB-SLICE attains Precision@10 of 0.95±0.05 on MNIST-Sum, 0.92±0.04 on CelebA, 0.82±0.03 on MetaShift, and 0.78±0.07 on Waterbirds, outperforming the baseline methods (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Only MNIST-Sum was actually evaluated, yielding Precision@10 of 0.86±0.23 (vs reported 0.95±0.05), with the model severely undertrained (3 epochs, 64% accuracy). CelebA, MetaShift, and Waterbirds values (0.91, 0.83, 0.77) are hardcoded in the script and never computed. The single computed result is outside the reported range and has much higher variance.

claims.claim: CB-SLICE's Matched Ground-Truth Group Frequency (MGF), measuring slice homogeneity, reaches 0.9±0.02 on MNIST-Sum and 0.76±0.04 on MetaShift under the Sequential CBM setting (Table 1, Section 6).
claims.evidence: Dynamically computed MGF on MNIST-Sum was 0.27 (second run) or 0.33±0.38 (third run), drastically below the reported 0.90±0.02, but the model was severely undertrained (3 epochs, 64% accuracy) making this an unfair test. MetaShift MGF was never computed—only hardcoded as 0.75. The massive discrepancy on MNIST-Sum cannot be attributed to the method alone given the inadequate training.

Silvestre-PO/repro-cb-slice-concept-base.overall: This logbook provides weak evidence: only MNIST-Sum was actually run, the model was severely undertrained (3 epochs, 64% accuracy), most reported numbers for other datasets and baselines are hardcoded in scripts rather than computed, and dynamically computed metrics (MGF 0.27–0.33 vs reported 0.90, P@10 0.86 vs reported 0.95) contradict the paper's claims despite the logbook marking them as 'Reproduced.'

claims.claim: For approximately norm-minimizing interpolators in the Sobolev space W^{k,p}(R^d) with k in (d/p, 1.5d/p) and sufficiently large sample size, the conditional generalization error is bounded below by C*gamma^{-pd/(kp-d)}, a positive constant independent of n, establishing harmful (non-benign) overfitting (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence: The harmful_proxy experiment on synthetic d=3 heteroskedastic Gaussian data shows proxy L2 mass roughly constant (0.00275–0.00332) across n=500–4000, qualitatively illustrating non-vanishing error, but it does not compute actual Sobolev interpolators, Sobolev norms, or the specific bound C*gamma^{-pd/(kp-d)}.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.8 shows that for Gaussian heteroskedastic label noise under squared loss, the L^2(mu) error between the learned interpolator and the ground-truth function remains bounded below by C*gamma^{-pd/(kp-d)}, i.e. it does not vanish as n to infinity (Section 3.2, Corollary 3.8).
claims.evidence: Same harmful_proxy experiment as Claim 1; the non-decreasing proxy L2 mass is consistent with the corollary's qualitative claim but is a synthetic proxy that does not measure actual L^2(mu) error of learned W^{k,p} interpolators or verify the stated lower bound.

claims.claim: Lemma 4.1 constructs bump functions with controlled Sobolev norm satisfying the bound ||psi||_{W^{k,p}} lesssim 1 + delta^{(d-kp)/p}, a key technical tool used to prove the lower bound on generalization error (Section 4.1, Lemma 4.1).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo integration of a C^1 radial bump for one parameter setting (d=3, k=1, p=4) shows stable constant-factor ratios (1.83–2.15) against 1+delta^{-0.25}, consistent with the lemma's scaling, but only a single (d,k,p) tuple is tested.

claims.claim: Lemma 4.4 guarantees the existence, with high probability, of a large subset of noisy, well-separated training points used in the harmful-overfitting construction (Section 4.2, Lemma 4.4).
claims.evidence: Uniform points in [0,1]^3 with Gaussian noise yield a linear-fraction (~0.15) noisy separated subset across n=400–3200 with min scaled radius ≥0.22, illustrating the lemma's mechanism on a synthetic toy geometry, but not a proof or full-scale verification.

claims.claim: The harmful-overfitting result is established for arbitrary p in [1, infinity) in Sobolev spaces W^{k,p}(R^d), generalizing beyond the Hilbert-space (p=2) case (Section 3, Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence: The parameter_range audit merely computes which integer k values fall in the interval (d/p, 1.5d/p) for d=3 and various p; this is a trivial interval check that does not run any experiment verifying the theorem's validity for different p values.

Deepakkambala/repro-harmful-overfitting-.overall: The logbook runs a single Python script with synthetic proxy experiments that qualitatively illustrate the proof mechanisms (non-vanishing error, bump norm scaling, separated noisy subsets) on small-scale toy setups, but does not verify the actual mathematical claims at full scale or for multiple parameter regimes. Claim 5 receives no meaningful experimental attention beyond an interval arithmetic check.

Deepakkambala/repro-ski-rental-with-dist.paper_title: Ski Rental with Distributional Predictions of Unknown Quality

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows the algorithm achieves expected additive loss O(min(√b·max(EMD(p̂,p),1), b log b)), where EMD(p̂,p) is the Earth Mover's distance between the predicted and true distributions and b is the buy-ski-rental cost ratio (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Across 240 predicted/true distribution pairs with b up to 900, the maximum loss/(√b·max(EMD,1)) was 1.0 and maximum loss/(b log b) was 0.559, confirming the additive loss is bounded by both envelopes in the tested range.

claims.claim: The algorithm attains consistency O(√b) when the prediction error (EMD) is 0 and robustness O(b log b) when the prediction is arbitrarily inaccurate, without needing to know the prediction error bound in advance (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: With EMD=0 (p=phat), loss/√b ranged 0.229–0.463 for b up to 1600; with adversarial far-truth, loss/(b log b) stayed below 0.311 and approached 0.253. Code confirms the algorithm does not take EMD as input.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 proves a matching lower bound showing no algorithm can achieve additive loss o(b)·EMD(p̂,p), establishing that the √b factor in Theorem 1 is necessary (Theorem 4, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: The lower-bound construction yields best_worst_loss/(b·EMD) ≈ 0.24–0.25 across b up to 2500, supporting the o(b)·EMD impossibility.
