claims.claim: The OFD-UCB algorithm models agent utility as an unknown linear function of item-agent features, using a contextual-bandit upper-confidence-bound estimator with round-robin initialization for the first N rounds to learn from limited observed utilities (Section on Algorithms).
claims.evidence: Round-robin allocates every agent exactly once in first N=6 rounds (counts=[1,1,1,1,1,1]); UCB selection matches independently recomputed argmax on 19994/19994 post-warm-up rounds; linear-truth held-out RMSE shrinks 19x (0.0153→0.00079) while nonlinear-control RMSE stays flat at ~0.20 across 12 seeds and T=20000.

claims.claim: For linear utility functions, OFD-UCB achieves regret in T>0 rounds bounded by 2*alpha_T*w_max*sqrt(2dT*log(lambda+TL/d)) with probability at least 1-delta (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Across 60 seeds at T=3000 with all constants enforced as hard bounds, 0/60 violations of the Theorem 1 bound (max regret 27.72 vs bound 1924.89); biased-noise control (300x R mean) produces 5/60 violations with max regret 2781.8 exceeding the bound, confirming the test is non-vacuous.

claims.claim: A generalized regret bound extends the result to arbitrary compatible bandit algorithms 𝔄, bounding the regret of OFD-𝔄 in T rounds by 2*w_max*sqrt(T)*sqrt(sum_{t=1}^T [h(m_t,n_t,O_t)]^2) (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Two structurally distinct OFD-compatible algorithms (per-round ridge and K=25-batched ridge) both yield 0/60 violations of the Theorem 2 bound across 60 seeds; h'=0 control (breaking Definition 1 compatibility) yields 60/60 violations with bound exactly 0 and positive realized regret, confirming non-vacuity.

claims.claim: An alternative bound (Theorem 3) applies to goodness functions that are locally monotonically non-decreasing and Lipschitz continuous, replacing w_max with c_max in the same sqrt(T) regret structure.
claims.evidence: Using log-NSW as the locally-monotone-Lipschitz goodness function, 0/60 violations with honest full-trajectory c_max (mean regret 0.43 vs mean bound 474.7); stale-c_max control (last 1% of rounds only) yields 7/60 violations (rate 0.117 > delta=0.05), confirming the Lipschitz constant must cover the full realized domain.

claims.claim: The fairness-efficiency tradeoff is controlled via a weighted Gini social-evaluation function with parameter rho in (0,1], interpolating between Egalitarian Social Welfare and Utilitarian Social Welfare.
claims.evidence: At 500 agents and 1,200,000 evaluated (draw,rho) pairs, G_rho matches USW at rho=1 to 4.73e-11 max absolute error, converges to ESW at rho=1e-6 with max absolute error 3e-6, and is monotonically non-decreasing in rho for 100% of 1,197,000 adjacent pairs; reversed-weight control converges to max(U) instead of min(U), confirming the non-increasing ordering is load-bearing.

tomyimkc/repro-keep-everyone-happy-onlin.overall: This logbook provides independent from-scratch implementations with real runs, multiple seeds (12-60), and non-vacuous controls for all five claims, including structural verification of the OFD-UCB mechanism, empirical regret bound checks for Theorems 1-3, and large-scale verification of the weighted-Gini interpolation identity. All claims are supported by concrete numerical evidence on non-toy setups.

claims.claim: The optimal collaborative prediction set C*(x) has a two-threshold form: it augments the human-proposed set H(x) with labels whose score exceeds threshold a*, and prunes labels within H(x) whose score exceeds threshold b* (Theorem 2.1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: Exact ILP HACO optimum vs. exact kink-based two-threshold search on smooth Gaussian-mixture populations shows relative gap shrinking monotonically from 0.0219 (L=30) to 0.0020 (L=150), approaching the continuous-population limit the theorem addresses, while a corrupted-score positive control stays flat at ~1.24, confirming the test discriminates.

claims.claim: The counterfactual harm principle requires P(Y not in C(X) | Y in H(X)) < epsilon, i.e., the AI must not remove correct labels the human already proposed (Section 1).
claims.evidence: CUP-Offline pruning threshold b-hat fit on calibration sets up to 100K yields mean exchangeable harm rate 0.072–0.085, below eps=0.1, across 8 seeds with 20K test points; label-shift control degrades to 0.10–0.12, confirming the guarantee rests on exchangeability.

claims.claim: The complementarity principle requires P(Y in C(X) | Y not in H(X)) >= 1-delta, i.e., the AI must recover correct labels the human missed (Section 1).
claims.evidence: CUP-Offline augmentation threshold a-hat yields mean exchangeable complementarity coverage 0.83–0.85, exceeding target 1-delta=0.80, with 100% of runs at largest n_cal satisfying coverage >= 0.80; label-shift control drops below target at intermediate n_cal.

claims.claim: The offline calibration procedure gives distribution-free finite-sample coverage guarantees whose bounds depend on the sizes of the calibration sets used to fit a* and b* (Proposition 4.1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Continuous CQR-style score with 2000 seeds per n_cal shows upper bounds hold 5/5 for both in-H and out-H, slack 1/(n1+1) shrinks monotonically from 0.018 to 0.00018 as n_cal grows 200→20000, and shifted-test control breaks lower bounds (coverage drops to 0.853 and 0.767). One in-H lower-bound bin dips to 0.876 vs target 0.90, attributable to finite-seed sampling noise on the conditional subset.

claims.claim: The CUP-Online algorithm updates thresholds a_t and b_t via stochastic approximation steps (a_{t+1}=a_t+eta(1{s(x_t,y_t)>a_t}-delta), and analogously for b_t) to track target error rates under arbitrary distribution shift, including shifts caused by humans adapting their behavior to the AI (Section 4.2, Proposition 4.2).
claims.evidence: CUP-Online SA updates on T=30000 streams track in-error rate to 0.107–0.110 (target 0.10) and out-error rate to 0.205–0.207 (target 0.20) under no-shift, score-shift, and human-adaptation shifts, all within Proposition 4.2 bounds (10/10 seeds); warm-started fixed baseline deviates by 0.013–0.033 under shift.

tomyimkc/repro-human-ai-collaborative-un.overall: All five claims are supported by rigorous independent implementations on synthetic data with known conditionals, including exact ILP optimization, calibration up to 100K samples, and online streams of 30K steps with proper controls that break preconditions. The reproduction does not cover the paper's real-world application datasets (ImageNet-16H, DDXPlus, Communities-and-Crime), but the theoretical claims are directly and faithfully tested at non-trivial scale.

claims.claim: LatentMAS replaces text-mediated multi-agent communication with auto-regressive latent thought generation and a shared latent working memory (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Latent thoughts (0 decoded tokens) and KV-cache working memory transfer (max|Δ|=2.2e-16) were implemented on a small self-contained transformer (d48–d96, L4–L8), not on the paper's Qwen3 models; the mechanism is demonstrated but at toy scale.

claims.claim: The paper proves latent thoughts can be more expressive than equivalent text reasoning under a linear representation hypothesis (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Independent derivation reproduces the Ω(d_h·m/log|V|) bound with exact arithmetic; Qwen3 efficiency constants 235.7/377.2/471.4 match the paper to within 0.06, and the ternary-alphabet control confirms the constant's origin.

claims.claim: Latent working memory preserves information equivalently to directly inputting preceding agents' outputs under the paper's formal setup (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: KV-memory vs direct-input equivalence holds at machine precision (max|Δlogit| ≤ 5.6e-17) across three causal transformer configs, with the non-causal control correctly breaking (0.16–0.64); this is an architectural property faithfully tested on controlled transformers.

claims.claim: LatentMAS reports higher accuracy, lower output token usage, and faster inference than single-agent and text-based MAS baselines across six general tasks in the sequential MAS setting (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The efficiency/complexity half (Theorem 3.4) is verified symbolically and via FLOP scaling, but the accuracy comparison across six general tasks (Table 1) was never run—no large-LLM benchmark experiments were executed.

claims.claim: On AIME, GPQA-Diamond, and other reasoning-intensive tasks, LatentMAS is evaluated under both sequential and hierarchical MAS settings with accuracy, token, and speed metrics (Table 2).
claims.evidence: No AIME, GPQA-Diamond, or other reasoning-intensive benchmark experiments were run; the logbook explicitly states this requires multi-GB model downloads and GPU inference beyond budget.

claims.claim: Input-output alignment improves downstream accuracy by 2.3% to 5.3% across three analyzed benchmarks (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: The alignment mechanism (closed-form least-squares W_a) is noted but the +2.3–5.3% accuracy gain was never measured; no benchmark experiments with/without alignment were executed.

MarxistLeninist/repro-latent-collaborati.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the paper's three theoretical theorems (expressiveness bound, lossless KV-memory equivalence, complexity advantage) via exact arithmetic and controlled transformer experiments, and demonstrates the core mechanisms at toy scale. claims.claim: NGIF's parameterization allows selection criteria for the inferred vector field beyond minimal kinetic energy, generalizing the standard gradient-flow (optimal-transport) approach used by prior baselines (Section 3, subsections 3.1-3.4).
claims.evidence: On tracer particles in turbulence (65,536 particles, 3 seeds), the divergence gauge cuts divergence energy ~8× and the curl gauge cuts curl energy ~14× relative to other gauges while TV stays in a 0.136–0.171 band; the curl gauge recovers gradient-flow behavior (curl energy 0.005 on Gigli σ=0.06); λ sweep over four orders of magnitude shows ≤1.2× spread in accuracy.

claims.claim: Experiments on low- and high-dimensional physics problems show NGIF improves distributional accuracy over gradient-restricted baselines (Section 4).
claims.evidence: On Vlasov-Poisson (3 seeds), NGIF gauges (0.182–0.189) are statistically tied with the gradient parameterization (0.1820±0.0075); on tracer particles NGIF-Curl beats gradient param by only 2.4% relative; on high-dim turbulence NGIF-Kin has 2× better enstrophy spread but worse mean enstrophy error. Results are mixed at reduced scale (8K test functions vs 50K, 40K iterations vs 500K).

claims.claim: Table 5 gives a comparative summary showing NGIF better captures non-potential transport than gradient-flow baselines across the tested settings (Table 5).
claims.evidence: Four of six baselines (CFM, NCSM, HOAM, DICE) were not implemented; the NGIF-vs-AM ordering reproduces (3.3× gap) but the NGIF-vs-weak-form-gradient comparison ties (0.182 vs 0.182–0.189); absolute errors are ~3× the paper's. claims.claim: Figures 1-4 visually compare NGIF's inferred trajectories/densities against gradient-restricted baselines across the experimental settings (Section 4, Figures 1-4).
claims.evidence: All four figures were redrawn from actual experimental runs with backing quantitative data: Fig. 3 shows vortex roll-up in all weak-form models but flat beams for AM; Fig. 4 shows NGIF-Kin tracking enstrophy spread to 21% vs 44% for gradient param; Fig. 1 reproduces the analytic minimal-KE potential shape; Fig. 2 reproduces density ordering matching measured TV.

vimarsh/repro-leveraging-gauge-freedom-f.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the mathematical foundation of NGIF (gauge freedom, weak-form invariance, regularizer selection) to machine precision and reproduces the visual comparisons from real runs, but the headline accuracy claim over gradient-restricted baselines yields mixed results at reduced scale—NGIF ties the gradient parameterization on Vlasov-Poisson and shows only marginal gains on tracer particles, though it does improve enstrophy-distribution tracking in high dimensions.

Srishti280992/repro-model-free-robust-av.paper_title: Model-Free Robust Average-Reward Reinforcement Learning with Sample Complexity Analysis

claims.claim: Robust Halpern Iteration (RHI) achieves a sample complexity of tilde-O(S A H^2 / epsilon^2) for computing an epsilon-optimal robust policy in model-free robust average-reward RL, without requiring prior knowledge of the robust bias span H (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: Model-free RHI runs on Garnet robust AMDPs sweep epsilon (5 values, 20 runs all epsilon-optimal, log-log slope 2.48≈2), S*A (6 configurations, normalized slope 1.07≈1 after dividing by H²/ε²), and H (reward rescaling, budget slope 2.48≈2), directly testing the full SAH²/ε² structure with actual transition-sample counts.

claims.claim: The reduction-to-discounted-MDP approach analyzed in the paper requires knowledge of the bias span H and yields a worse sample complexity of tilde-O(S A H^2 / epsilon^4) (Section 4, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: The reduction-to-discounted approach is implemented with exact policy transfer; H-dependence is demonstrated (γ=1−ε/H becomes −1.54 when H is underestimated to H/10, invalidating the discount), and the configured reduction budget slope is 3.995≈4 versus RHI's measured 2.45≈2 on the same epsilon grid.

claims.claim: Lemma 5.1 bounds the sub-optimality of a greedy policy relative to Q by the span seminorm of the residual, 0 <= g*_P - g^pi_P(s) <= Sp(T_P(Q) - Q) (Section 5, Lemma 5.1).
claims.evidence: The bound 0 ≤ g*_P − g^π_P(s) ≤ Sp(T_P(Q)−Q) is checked on 300 randomized robust AMDPs across contamination, l2, l-infinity, and l1 uncertainty sets with sizes up to (10,5), yielding 0 left-side and 0 right-side violations, plus a negative control where a non-greedy policy violates the bound.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 establishes that RHI's iterates converge exactly, with Sp(T_P(Q_k) - Q_k) approaching 0 as k goes to infinity (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Exact model-known Halpern iteration on 9 robust AMDP instances (3 uncertainty sets × 3 sizes, largest G(20,15)) reduces Sp(T_P(Q_k)−Q_k) by more than 99% over 3000 iterations in all 9/9 cases, and the non-expansion ratio max‖T(Q1)−T(Q2)‖_sp/‖Q1−Q2‖_sp reaches 1.0, consistent with the Halpern (non-contractive) convergence mechanism.

claims.claim: Instead of a multi-level Monte Carlo estimator (noted to induce unbounded sample complexity in this setting), RHI uses a recursive sampling scheme that estimates successive differences T_P(Q_k) - T_P(Q_{k-1}) (Section 5, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1's R-SAMPLE is implemented and audited across 18 configurations (G(10,5) and G(20,15) × contamination/TV/l-infinity/l2 × ε=0.20/0.15/0.10): all 18 keep accumulated sampled-operator error below ε (worst ratio 0.142), all 18 use genuinely sampled T estimates with nonzero error, and all 18 show decreasing m_k; recursive budget 8,700 samples beats single-level 18,000.

claims.claim: The paper's sample complexity result is claimed to be the first finite-sample guarantee for model-free robust average-reward MDPs, covering both contamination and l_p-norm uncertainty sets (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: Finite-sample model-free RHI runs at G(20,15) produce epsilon-optimal robust policies for contamination (gap 0.00178 at 22,500 samples), TV/l-infinity (gap 0.00022 at 4,200 samples), and l2 (gap 0.00129 at 127,500 samples), all below ε=0.15, covering both uncertainty families; the 'first' historical-priority sub-claim is correctly noted as non-experimentally provable.

Srishti280992/repro-model-free-robust-av.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims through systematic model-free RHI experiments with exact RRVI ground-truth evaluation, including epsilon/S*A/H scaling sweeps, 300-instance lemma stress tests, 9-instance convergence checks, 18-case R-SAMPLE audits, and finite-sample runs across uncertainty families. The main limitation is modest Garnet-MDP scale (S≤30, A≤15), but the experiments directly test the claimed theoretical dependencies with measured slopes matching predictions.

claims.claim: SOMG (Algorithm 2) for finite-horizon Markov games achieves a regularization-dependent regret bound of O(β⁻¹d³H⁷log²(dT/δ)), logarithmic in T, versus a regularization-independent bound of O(d³ᐟ²H³√T log(dT/δ)) (Theorem 3.1, Section 3.3).

claims.evidence: On a valid Model-2 covariance (d=100, s=10, gap γ=0.1) where on-support diagonal=0.190 < off-support diagonal=0.900, DiagThresh yields sin²=1 at population level and recovers 0/10 support coords in 100% of 200 finite-sample draws (n=5000), while the Model-1 control recovers 10/10.

claims.claim: Covariance thresholding fails analogously, returning an estimate 𝐮 with sin²∠(𝐮,𝐯)=1 with probability at least 1/2 despite sufficient samples (Lemma 3, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Using the paper's exact near-Ramanujan graph construction (s=10, u=401, d=411), CovThresh returns sin²=1 on all 12 population graph seeds and 100% of 20 draws at n=20000, with pre-threshold sin²≈4.4e-16 confirming v was the true top eigenvector before thresholding.

claims.claim: Greedy correlation-based selection recovers at most one true support coordinate under Model 2, even when seeded with a correct coordinate (Lemma 4, Section 3).
claims.evidence: With the exact Lemma-12 Householder construction (s=20, d=39, n=10^6), GreedyCorr seeded at a true coordinate recovers exactly 1 support coord at population level (sin²=0.974 ≥ 1−1/s=0.95) and max=1 across all 100 finite-sample seeds.

claims.claim: The proposed Restarted Truncated Power Method (RTPM) achieves ⟨𝐯,𝐮⟩² ≥ 9/10 with probability ≥ 1-δ under Model 2 using n = Ω(s² log(s) log(d/δ)) samples and O(nd²) runtime (Theorem 1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: RTPM's cos² transitions from 0.215 to 0.992 as n increases; fitted n_scale ∝ s^{2.23} (R²=0.99, theory s²) across s=3..8; n_scale decreases monotonically with gap γ and relaxed target error; RTPM recovers v (cos²≈0.97) on the counterexample instances. Runtime scaling is inconclusive (d≤300 constant-overhead regime) but the recovery and sample-complexity claims are supported by real runs.

claims.claim: Sparse k-PCA cannot be solved by deflation-based self-reduction to the single-component case, since deflated covariance matrices can have fully dense top eigenvectors (Lemma 11, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: In all 60 deterministic configurations (d∈{4,6,10,50,200} × Δ∈{0.3,0.1,0.01,10⁻³} × γ∈{0.5,0.1,0.01}), the deflated covariance PΣP has a fully dense top eigenvector (nnz=d) despite Σ having a 2-sparse leading pair and u being 3-sparse with ⟨u,v₁⟩²=1−Δ.

snaykey/repro-combinatorial-sparse-pca.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence for all five claims by constructing the paper's own Model-2 counterexamples, running the named algorithms, and measuring the predicted failure modes, recovery metrics, and eigenvector densities across multiple seeds and parameter sweeps. The constructions are non-toy (d up to 411, up to 200 seeds) and include positive controls and ablations.

snaykey/repro-kstep-lookahead-rl.paper_title: Fast Non-Episodic Finite-Horizon RL with K-Step Lookahead Thresholding

claims.claim: For K=1, Algorithm 1 (LG1T) achieves regret min{O(SA/Δ_+), O(√(SAT))}, matching the minimax constant-regret lower bound for non-episodic finite-horizon MDPs (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: LG1T regret plateaus at 818.1 for T≥8000 with fixed gap (tail slope 0.029≈0, constant in T), and in the hard regime Δ_+=2/√T the regret slope vs T is 0.496≈0.5 matching √(SAT). The Le Cam two-point construction yields an algorithm-independent lower bound with indistinguishability radius slope -0.497≈-0.5, confirming minimax Ω(√(SAT)).

claims.claim: For general K≥2, Algorithm 2 achieves regret max{O((K-1)√(SAT)), O(C_{K-1}√(SAT) log T)}, which is sublinear whenever max(K, C_{K-1}√(SA)) = o(√T) (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: LG2T regret is sublinear in T (slope 0.627, consistent with the √(T log T) factor of Corollary 4.5; per-step regret → 0; regret/T = 0.00040). The SA dependence exponent (0.758) is noisy but the sublinearity and K-ordering (LG2T slower than LG1T) are confirmed on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: Under stochastic dominance assumptions, the K-step lookahead greedy policy equals the optimal policy in binary-state MDPs for any K≥1, while for general state spaces with K<T there exists an MDP instance where the K-step lookahead policy incurs Θ(T) optimality gap (Theorem 3.3, Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: Exact DP on 500 random binary-state stochastic-dominance MDPs shows K-greedy = optimal for 100% of instances (K=1,2,3). The explicit App. B.2 hard instance yields gap = T−K exactly (max error 0.00, linear slope 1.000) across T from 20 to 3200 and K from 1 to 5, confirming Θ(T) optimality gap.

claims.claim: On synthetic MDPs with 10 states/5 actions, the one-step greedy policy π¹ attains a 0.75 competitive ratio versus 0.96 for the two-step greedy policy π², and on 100-state/25-action MDPs the ratios are 0.80 versus 0.94 (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: On 1000 random MDPs per size with exact DP, π¹ ratios are 0.799/0.822 (paper: 0.75/0.80) and π² ratios are 0.956/0.944 (paper: 0.96/0.94). The ordering π²>π¹ with both <1 holds, and finite-horizon validation confirms the gain-ratio proxy is faithful. Magnitudes are in the correct band.

claims.claim: On JumpRiverSwim with 5, 8, and 15 states over 20,000 steps, the proposed LG1T, LG2T, LG1-2T, and LG1T-RL methods consistently exceed cumulative reward of all tabular RL baselines, with LG1T-RL matching PMEVI-KLUCRL after switching at 10,000 steps (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: LG1T/LG2T/LG1-2T exceed all tested baselines (UCRL2, Optimistic-Q, Q-learning) on JumpRiverSwim at 5/8/15 states over T=20000. However, LG1T-RL (switching to UCRL2 at step 10000) performs poorly (1972 vs 3944 for best baseline) and PMEVI-KLUCRL was not implemented, so the 'LG1T-RL matching PMEVI-KLUCRL' sub-claim is not tested; the core dominance finding holds on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: On FrozenLake (4x4 grid) and AnyTrading over 20,000 steps, LG1T/LG2T and LG2T/LG1-2T respectively achieve the highest cumulative reward among all benchmarked methods (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: FrozenLake 4×4 is verified: best LG (LG2T) achieves 4050.12 vs best baseline 3652.52. However, the AnyTrading half of the claim was not run at all due to missing external market-data feed, so only one of two claimed environments is addressed.

snaykey/repro-kstep-lookahead-rl.overall: The logbook provides strong evidence for the theoretical claims (1-3) via exact DP constructions and rate-level empirical verification, and reasonable support for the synthetic MDP competitive ratios (4). The empirical dominance claims (5-6) are partially verified on non-toy setups but with incomplete baseline subsets and one entirely missing environment (AnyTrading).

snaykey/repro-gaussian-dam.paper_title: Dense associative memory for Gaussian distributions

claims.claim: The Wasserstein LSE energy functional E(xi) := -1/beta * log(sum_i exp(-beta * W_2^2(X_i, xi))) generalizes classical dense associative memory energy to Gaussian densities on Bures-Wasserstein space (Section 2).
claims.evidence: Closed-form W_2^2 validated against Monte-Carlo OT (rel-err 1.3e-3), BW energy converges to classical DAM energy as covariances vanish (diff 0.0 at eps=1e-4), and stored patterns are Phi fixed points (W_2 err 1.7e-8) — three independent numerical checks on non-toy setups.

claims.claim: Storage capacity N = Omega(exp(d*alpha^2/16)) is achievable with high probability on Wasserstein spheres, extending exponential vectorial storage capacity results to Gaussian distributions (Theorem 1, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Log-linear fit of N_max vs d yields slope 1.843 with R²=0.978 over d=2..6, demonstrating exponential-in-d storage capacity via the Algorithm-2 construction with >=90% storage rate; dimensions are modest but the core exponential scaling claim is supported by real runs.

claims.claim: Retrieval error decays exponentially in dimension under Wasserstein perturbations, per convergence bounds established for the update rule (Theorems 2-3, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Geometric per-iteration contraction L=0.226 (R²=0.996) over 20 trajectories verifies Theorem 2; one-step error decays exponentially in d (gamma_emp=1.219, R²=0.965 over d=4..20, 8 orders of magnitude) respecting the theoretical upper bound, with exponent scaling linearly in beta, verifying Theorem 3.

claims.claim: Synthetic experiments with N=10,000 Gaussian measures in d=50 dimensions show retrieval convergence at temperature beta=1 but failure at beta=0.1, validating the theoretical separation/temperature conditions (Section 4.1, Figures 3 and 6).
claims.evidence: At N=10000, d=50, retrieval accuracy is 1.000 at beta=1 and 0.000 at beta=0.1 across 200 probes, exactly matching the claimed temperature-driven phase transition at the stated scale.

claims.claim: Gaussian word embeddings derived from the Text8 corpus exhibit a sharp phase transition in retrieval success around beta approximately 15, confirming that sharp energy basins yield robust memory (Section 4.1.1, Figures 4-5).
claims.evidence: The text8/Word2Gauss corpus experiment was not reproduced; instead a synthetic surrogate of N=2000 diagonal Gaussians was used, showing a sharp phase transition (0.0 to 1.0) but at a different beta location and without the real corpus, embeddings, or the specific beta≈15 value.

claims.claim: Extended tests with non-commuting covariances (N=1000, d=10) still maintain one-step convergence under suitable beta, despite higher variance (Section 6.2.3, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: N=1000, d=10 with genuinely non-commuting covariances (mean ||[Σi,Σj]||_F=1.911) achieves one-step retrieval accuracy 1.000 with W_2 error ~1e-8; the 'higher variance' sub-clause is honestly reported as not separable from numerical noise, but the primary one-step convergence claim holds.

snaykey/repro-gaussian-dam.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence verifying five of six claims, including the Wasserstein LSE energy identity, exponential storage capacity, retrieval error decay, synthetic phase transition, and non-commuting covariance convergence. Claim 5 (Text8 word embeddings) is only addressed with a synthetic surrogate, not the real corpus experiment, making it a toy reproduction.

MarxistLeninist/repro-normuon-making-muo.paper_title: NorMuon: Making Muon more efficient and scalable

claims.claim: NorMuon combines Muon's orthogonalized updates with neuron-wise adaptive normalization based on second-order momentum statistics (Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Unit tests confirm the numpy implementation matches Algorithm 1 line-by-line to 1e-10, including momentum, NS5 orthogonalization, per-row second-moment normalization, RMS-matched scaling, and decoupled weight decay; 7/7 tests pass.

claims.claim: The optimizer analysis shows Muon lowers update condition numbers but leaves high variance in per-neuron update norms, while NorMuon normalizes neuron contributions (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The Figure-1 geometry pattern (Muon: low condition number/high per-neuron CV; NorMuon: low condition number/low CV; AdamW: high condition number/low CV) is reproduced over 5 seeds, but using gradients from a tiny 2-layer MLP rather than the paper's actual transformer training setting.

claims.claim: NorMuon achieves 21.74% better step efficiency than Adam and 11.31% improvement over Muon on the 1.1B pretraining setting (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The 1.1B pretraining comparison was not run; the logbook only confirms internal arithmetic consistency of the reported percentages, not the underlying training results.

claims.claim: NorMuon also improves validation-loss trajectories over Muon and AdamW at the 5.4B scale (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The 5.4B-scale validation-loss trajectory comparison was not reproduced; no experiments were run at this scale.

claims.claim: On 5.4B training, NorMuon keeps optimizer-state memory close to Muon and below AdamW, with about 2.9% total training-step time overhead over AdamW (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Memory accounting is exactly verified (NorMuon = Muon + m scalars ≈ 1.0002× Muon, exactly 0.5× AdamW), but the 2.9% step-time overhead was not measured at any representative scale; the logbook explicitly states the time figure is out of scope.

claims.claim: NorMuon outperforms Muon in Modded-NanoGPT pretraining at 124M and 350M parameter scales (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Modded-NanoGPT pretraining at 124M and 350M was not run; no experiments were executed for this claim.

MarxistLeninist/repro-normuon-making-muo.overall: The logbook provides a solid verification of NorMuon's algorithmic mechanism (Claim 1) and exact memory accounting, plus a toy-scale reproduction of the Figure-1 optimization geometry (Claim 2) using a tiny MLP proxy. The headline large-scale training claims (3, 4, 6) and the step-time overhead portion of Claim 5 were not reproduced due to compute constraints.

Srishti280992/repro-the-implicit-bias-of.paper_title: The Implicit Bias of Steepest Descent with Mini-batch Stochastic Gradient

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows that without momentum, mini-batch steepest descent converges to an approximate max-margin solution only when batch size exceeds the threshold b > 4Rn/(γ+4R), with the margin gap shrinking as batch size increases (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook computes gamma=0.36108, R=4.28457 on the native Section 5 setup, yielding threshold b*=195.87, and verifies the admissibility condition rho>0 holds only for b=200 among tested batch sizes. An exhaustive algebra sweep over 5,182,400 (n,b,gamma,R) cells found 0 mismatches between rho>0 and b>b*, and the Section 5 runs show b=200 has lower relative margin error (0.078) than b=20 (0.112), confirming the margin-gap trend.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 shows that adding momentum allows convergence to the max-margin solution even with small batch sizes, provided β₁→1, revealing a batch-momentum tradeoff (Theorem 4.3, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The effective-margin condition rho=gamma-2(1-beta)m(m^2-1)R was evaluated for the native b=20 instance, requiring beta>0.999957, consistent with the beta->1 tradeoff. Empirically, at b=20 the relative margin error decreased monotonically with momentum: 0.1116 (beta=0), 0.0768 (beta=0.5), 0.0521 (beta=0.99), with the best small-batch result surpassing the full-batch no-momentum error of 0.0780.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.5 shows the momentum-enabled convergence rate is slowed by a factor of m/(1-β₁) relative to the momentum-free large-batch case (Corollary 4.5, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: A 200,000-step rate audit with 3 seeds and 18 settings shows steps-to-cosine>=0.95 growing monotonically with 1/(1-beta) at full batch (100→200→500→6000→30000→41000 for beta 0→0.9→0.99→0.999→0.9999→0.99999). A Corollary-4.5 envelope C*m/(1-beta)*(n+log t)/sqrt(t), calibrated only on the full-batch beta=0 trace, had 0 violations across all audited settings after t>=1000, confirming the bound holds empirically.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 proves that variance reduction recovers the exact full-batch implicit bias for any batch size, eliminating the batch-size dependence of the margin, though Corollary 4.7 shows this comes at a convergence rate slowed by a factor of m^(2+a) (Theorem 4.6, Corollary 4.7, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: An SVRG-style estimator (grad_b(W)-grad_b(snapshot)+grad_full(snapshot)) was implemented and run at b=20 on the native Section 5 setup. VR without momentum achieved relative margin error 0.0611, better than the full-batch b=200 no-momentum result of 0.0780, supporting recovery of full-batch-like margin behavior. The Corollary 4.7 slowdown factor m^(2+a) was computed arithmetically (1, 5.66, 55.90, 316.23 for m=1,2,5,10) but not empirically tested for rate.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.9 constructs an orthogonal, scale-skewed data example on which per-sample (batch-size-one) steepest descent converges to a fundamentally different implicit bias than the full-batch solution (Theorem 4.9, Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: The orthogonal scale-skewed construction (n=500, k=10, imbalanced classes min 6/max 158, scales 0.42–5.59) shows per-sample normalized-SGD converges to the theorem-predicted bias with cosine 0.99961 but has cosine only 0.36549 to the L2 max-margin solution. Per-sample SignSGD similarly shows cosine 0.99950 to the theorem bias and 0.22073 to max-margin, confirming a fundamentally different implicit bias direction.

claims.claim: Synthetic multi-class linear classification experiments with normalized-SGD under the ℓ₂ norm, varying batch size (b∈{20,200}) and momentum (β∈{0,0.5,0.99}), empirically confirm that momentum or variance reduction restores full-batch-like convergence in small-batch regimes (Section 5, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The Section 5 synthetic setup (n=200, k=10, d=5, 20000 steps, 5 seeds) was run with b∈{20,200}, beta∈{0,0.5,0.99}, and VR. At b=20, momentum (beta=0.99) reduced relative margin error to 0.0521 and VR reduced it to 0.0611, both below the full-batch b=200 no-momentum baseline of 0.0780, confirming that momentum or VR restores full-batch-like convergence in small-batch regimes.

Srishti280992/repro-the-implicit-bias-of.overall: The logbook provides a thorough reproduction of all six claims on the paper's native synthetic setup, combining algebraic verification of theorem conditions with empirical training runs across multiple seeds and settings. The main gap is that some corollary slowdown factors (Claims 3 and 4) are verified primarily through bound-respect checks rather than direct rate-matching, and the VR slowdown factor is only checked arithmetically.

Lu032145/repro-cocoreviewbench-completen.paper_title: CoCoReviewBench: A Completeness- and Correctness-Oriented Benchmark for AI Reviewers

claims.claim: CoCoReviewBench curates 3,900 papers from ICLR (2017-2025) and NeurIPS (2021-2024), building category-specific benchmark subsets across a two-level taxonomy of 23 subcategories under 5 top-level categories (Quality, Clarity, Significance, Originality, Policy) (Section 3, Section 3.1, Appendix A).
claims.evidence: All 13 annual JSONL files were parsed, confirming 3,900 unique paper IDs across 9 ICLR files (2017–2025) and 4 NeurIPS files (2021–2024), with 23 non-N/A subcategories and 5 top-level categories verified from official source code; category-specific subsets were deterministically reconstructed from released atomic-opinion labels.

claims.claim: A single human reviewer covers on average only 3.03 of 5 top-level categories and 5.10 of 23 subcategories per paper; aggregating all reviewers for a paper raises coverage to 3.98 top-level categories and 9.23 of 23 subcategories (an 81% relative improvement in subcategory coverage over a single reviewer), yet aggregated subcategory coverage is still only about 40% (Section 3.1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Full-data aggregation over all 3,900 papers reproduced single-reviewer means of 3.031 top-level and 5.099 subcategory coverage, and all-reviewer means of 3.980 and 9.234, yielding 81.11% relative improvement and 40.15% aggregate coverage—all matching reported values at paper precision.

claims.claim: Treating reviewer-author and inter-reviewer discussions plus the meta-review as expert adjudication signals, incorrectness is identified via inter-reviewer conflicts in 22.13% of papers (7.63% of reviews) and via reviewer-author conflicts in 75.72% of papers (36.76% of reviews); over 13% of submissions show a score gap of 4 or more between the highest and lowest overall reviewer scores (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The score-gap component was reproduced (526/3,900 = 13.49%, supporting 'over 13%'), but paper-level conflict rates from released annotations yielded 23.15% and 77.97% versus reported 22.13% and 75.72%, and no source-supported denominator reproduced the review-level rates of 7.63% or 36.76%; the exact author statistics pipeline is unavailable, preventing determination of whether discrepancies stem from methodology differences.

claims.claim: CoCoReviewBench is the only benchmark among compared peer-review resources (PeerRead, MReD, NLPeer, SEA, ReviewMT, Re2, Aspects, RottenReviews, GRE-bench, RevUtil) to simultaneously support atomic opinions, fine-grained labels, category-level evaluation, rebuttal signal, meta signal, conflict detection, and incorrect annotation (Table 1).
claims.evidence: CoCoReviewBench's seven capabilities were confirmed from released schema and code, and no prior resource supports all seven under either strict (70/77 exact cells) or lenient (74/77) scoring; although one matrix cell is contradicted (SEA meta-signal audited as ✓ vs reported ✗), SEA still supports only 1 of 7 capabilities, so the uniqueness conclusion survives.

claims.claim: Analysis on CoCoReviewBench shows AI reviewers remain limited in correctness and thoroughness relative to humans, are prone to hallucinations, and that reasoning models are more effective reviewers than non-reasoning approaches because they better substantiate their critiques (Abstract, Section 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook contains no experiments evaluating AI reviewers, comparing reasoning versus non-reasoning models, or assessing hallucination rates; Claim 5 was never addressed in the reproduction.

Lu032145/repro-cocoreviewbench-completen.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, deterministic CPU-only audits of Claims 1–4 using the full released benchmark with pinned commits and sensitivity analyses, verifying the corpus/taxonomy structure, reviewer-coverage statistics, and Table 1 uniqueness, while revealing discrepancies in conflict-rate statistics and leaving the AI-reviewer analysis (Claim 5) entirely unaddressed.

claims.claim: The HJ-Prox estimator's approximation error is uniformly bounded by sup_x ||prox^δ_{tf}(x) - prox_{tf}(x)|| ≤ sqrt(n t δ) (Theorem 3.2, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: exp01 ran a full grid (n∈{1,2,5,10,50,200} × t∈{.01,.1,1,10} × δ∈{1e-4…1}, 6 functions, 720 cells) with large-N/exact-quadrature reference; the bound held with max ratio 0.798 and zero violations across 640 trustworthy cells (80 ℓ₂ cells excluded due to MC noise limitations, self-flagged).

claims.claim: Replacing exact proximal steps with HJ-Prox in the proximal point method and proximal gradient descent preserves almost-sure convergence under mild assumptions (Theorem 3.5, Theorem 3.6, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: exp03 (600 runs, 25–50 seeds, K=20k–40k) confirmed PPM almost-sure convergence (all seeds to rel-err 2e-6, negative control stalls at 0.50) and perturbation bounds hold exactly (max violation 0.0); however PGD's theory arm diverged at practical N (rel-err 174) because required N_k is unaffordable, and 'mild assumptions' is contradicted (N_min up to 5.78e88).

claims.claim: The HJ-Prox substitution extends convergence guarantees to Douglas-Rachford splitting and Davis-Yin splitting for composite objectives f+g+h with h L-smooth (Theorem 3.8, Theorem 3.9, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: exp03 shows DRS converges to a bias floor (5.7e-3) and DYS to 1.1e-2 with fixed-point residuals dropping (DYS ~230×, DRS ~8×), perturbation bounds exact across all cells; exp04-T2 confirms DYS on sparse-group-LASSO with HJ obj 3.989 vs exact 3.893 (+2.5%) and coefficient correlation 0.9997.

claims.claim: HJ-Prox is also applied within the primal-dual hybrid gradient algorithm via conjugate operator approximations (Theorem 3.10, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Direct HJ-Prox on the conjugate g* (an indicator for ℓ1/ℓ2 penalties) produces all-NaN across all 150 runs (mean_ess=0), violating Thm 3.10's L-Lipschitz assumption; only a Moreau-decomposition reformulation (prox_{g*}=I−prox_g) runs, converging to a 4.2e-2 floor, but this route is not what the paper's 'conjugate operator approximations' phrasing describes.

claims.claim: Splitting reduces the effective Lipschitz constant relative to non-split approaches, and hybrid exact/approximate strategies outperform fully approximate proximal methods in experiments (Section 3.3, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: The arithmetic mechanism (CHK-19: J_{f+g} ≥ J_f + J_g, log-ratio up to 5.31) is confirmed, but the empirical splitting-beats-PPM result (Fig 3) did NOT reproduce at reduced K≈200 (opposite ordering observed: PPM 7.64 < PGD 8.92); hybrid ordering (CHK-21) holds on all 3 seeds but is not statistically significant (p=0.25), and all experiments ran at 50–1000× reduced iterations vs the paper.

JG1310/repro-operator-splitting-with-ham.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous numerical audit confirming the paper's core theoretical bounds (Thms 3.2/3.3) and almost-sure convergence for PPM, DRS, and DYS at full scale, but the flagship GSE2034 real-data experiment failed (importance-weight collapse, obj 122 vs 11) and the empirical splitting/hybrid advantages were tested only at heavily reduced scale with the key Fig-3 result inverted.

Srishti280992/repro-steady-state-behavio.paper_title: Steady-State Behavior of Constant-Stepsize Stochastic Approximation: Gaussian Approximation and Tail Bounds

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 (i.i.d. noise) and Theorem 4.1 (Markovian noise) bound the Wasserstein distance between the centered-scaled steady state Y^(α) = (X^(α) − x*)/√α and its Gaussian limit N(0, Σ_Y) by U√α log(1/α) (Theorems 3.1 and 4.1).
claims.evidence: Four SA families (1-D SGD, 2-D linear SA, 2-D contractive nonlinear SA, 1-D Markov SGD) with 7 step sizes and N=120K chains show fitted W1-vs-α power-law slopes of 0.725, 0.834, 0.634, and 0.797—all exceeding 0.5, meaning W1 decays faster than √α, consistent with the U√α log(1/α) bound. The normalized ratios W1/(√α log(1/α)) remain bounded across the grid.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 establishes an explicit non-asymptotic Wasserstein bound of order O(α^{1/2} log(1/α)) for constant-stepsize SGD on smooth, strongly convex objectives (Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: 1-D quadratic SGD with i.i.d. uniform noise shows W1 slope 0.725 (R²=0.946), empirical variance converging to target 1/6 (0.1673 vs 0.1667 at smallest α), and max bound ratio 0.0146, directly supporting the O(α^{1/2} log(1/α)) Wasserstein bound for constant-stepsize SGD.

claims.claim: Propositions 3.2 and 3.3 extend the same O(α^{1/2} log(1/α)) Wasserstein bound to linear stochastic approximation with a Hurwitz matrix and to contractive nonlinear stochastic approximation, respectively (Propositions 3.2 and 3.3, Section 3.2.2, Section 3.2.3).
claims.evidence: 2-D linear SA with Hurwitz matrix A=[[-1.05,0.85],[-0.55,-0.9]] shows W1 slope 0.834 (R²=0.944) with covariance converging to Lyapunov target; 2-D contractive nonlinear SA with tanh³ perturbation shows slope 0.634 (R²=0.835) with covariance errors shrinking to ~0.001 Frobenius norm at smallest α.

claims.claim: For one-dimensional projections, the paper derives a non-uniform Berry-Esseen-type tail bound |P(⟨Y^(α),ζ⟩ > a) − P(Z_ζ > a)| ≤ C_d α^{1/4} log^{1/2}(1/α) / a, which improves as the deviation level a grows (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Linear SA projections onto ζ=(1,1)/√2 with N=320K chains show sup_a a|Δ(a)| fitting slope 0.883 (R²=0.880), faster than the theoretical α^{1/4} rate, with max scaled error 0.0113. Tail errors decrease with α and the 1/a scaling prevents high-a terms from dominating, consistent with the non-uniform Berry-Esseen bound.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 extends the Gaussian approximation and tail bounds for SGD, linear SA, and contractive nonlinear SA from i.i.d. noise to Markovian noise (Proposition 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Markov-noise SGD with ρ=1/3 shows W1 to the correct long-run covariance target decaying with slope 0.797 (R²=0.965) to 0.0016, while W1 to the naive marginal-covariance target stays flat at 0.095–0.099 (59× larger at smallest α), confirming the long-run covariance correction is essential for the Markovian extension.

claims.claim: Proposition 5.1 shows a different convergence rate of order α^{1/h} for constant-stepsize SA applied to general convex objectives with Gibbs-type limiting distributions (Proposition 5.1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: 1-D SGD on f_h(x)=|x|^h/h for h=2 and h=4 shows E|X| scaling as α^0.512 (theory 0.5, R²=0.998) and α^0.242 (theory 0.25, R²=0.994) respectively; h=4 scaled kurtosis is 2.138 vs Gibbs target 2.185 and Gaussian 3, supporting the α^{1/h} rate and non-Gaussian Gibbs limiting distribution.

Srishti280992/repro-steady-state-behavio.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims through well-designed experiments on synthetic SA instances satisfying the theorem assumptions, including a falsification control for Markovian covariance. The experiments use adequate sample sizes (120K–320K) and step-size grids spanning an order of magnitude, though they are limited to low dimensions (1-D and 2-D) and do not attempt proof verification.

jaytau/repro-the-crowded-embedding-space.paper_title: The Crowded Embedding Space: A Mean-Field Mechanism for Emergent Marginalization in Retrieval-Augmented Agents

claims.claim: Phase transition occurs where minority user goals suffer catastrophic collapse in performance as majority goal density increases in dense retrieval

jaytau/repro-the-crowded-embedding-space.overall: This logbook provides strong, multi-faceted evidence for Claim 1: a numerical audit of Theorem 2.2, synthetic Monte Carlo replication, reproduction across four real datasets with two pretrained encoders, and a novel causal control isolating density from index size. The reproduction is rigorous, with raw data tables, confidence intervals, and point-by-point comparison against the paper's own published coordinates extracted from arXiv LaTeX source.

michaldobiezynski/repro-ski-rental-with-.paper_title: Ski Rental with Distributional Predictions of Unknown Quality

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows the algorithm achieves expected additive loss O(min(√b·max(EMD(p̂,p),1), b log b)), where EMD(p̂,p) is the Earth Mover's distance between the predicted and true distributions and b is the buy-ski-rental cost ratio (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Across 12,500 random + 125 adversarially hill-climbed instances spanning b=10²–10⁶, the worst loss/bound ratio is 1.5733 with log-log slope −0.0390 (flat-to-decreasing), and both branches of the min are exercised (45.6–53.0% of instances bind the b log b branch); primitives brute-force validated to 7e−15.

claims.claim: The algorithm attains consistency O(√b) when the prediction error (EMD) is 0 and robustness O(b log b) when the prediction is arbitrarily inaccurate, without needing to know the prediction error bound in advance (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Over b=10²–10⁸, consistency loss/√b converges to 0.4999 (slope +0.5185 vs theory 0.5) and robustness loss/(b ln b) converges to 0.2500 (slope +0.9963 vs theory 1.0); the algorithm's code signature confirms no η/EMD input parameter.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 proves a matching lower bound showing no algorithm can achieve additive loss o(b)·EMD(p̂,p), establishing that the √b factor in Theorem 1 is necessary (Theorem 4, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Exact minimax over the complete algorithm class (all A_K and mixtures) yields 0.2222·b with log-log slope +1.0017, confirming a Θ(b) multiplier that negates o(b); brute-force over all K at b=100 matches the reduced candidate set to the last digit (21.6655).

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a Pareto-optimal consistency-robustness tradeoff: any algorithm achieving O(√b) consistency must incur Ω(b log b) robustness (Theorem 6, Section 4)
claims.evidence: Exact Pareto frontier over all randomized algorithms gives minimum robustness 0.2249·b ln b at consistency budget 1.0·√b (slope +1.0268 vs theory 1.0), with Algorithm 1 at 0.2693·b ln b (1.11× gap at b=10⁶); the two-point mixture restriction is provably lossless for a single-constraint LP.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 introduces a parameterized algorithm with expected cost c(ALG_p) ≤ min{(1+λ)(c(OPT_p)+B), (1+1/λ)c(OPT_p)}, allowing explicit interpolation between trusting the prediction and worst-case guarantees via λ ∈ [0,1] (Theorem 2, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Across 15,000 instances over b=10²–10⁶ and λ∈{0.05,…,1.0}, the worst-case c(ALG)/((1+1/λ)c(OPT)) is 0.9999998571 with 0 violations, λ=1 reproduces ratio 2.00000 exactly, and the first branch holds with b-independent constant 0.78786.

michaldobiezynski/repro-ski-rental-with-.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all five theorem-based claims through a self-contained reimplementation of the paper's model, algorithms, and lower-bound constructions, spanning multiple decades of b with adversarial search and brute-force validation of primitives. The two lower-bound claims are checked via exact minimax/Pareto computations over the complete algorithm class, while the three upper-bound claims are sampled checks that did not falsify and reached near-tight corners of the parameter space.

Srishti280992/repro-innovation-an-almost.paper_title: Innovation: An Almost Characterization of Hallucination

claims.claim: The paper defines innovation (Definition 3.1) as a language model assigning nonzero probability mass to statements not present in the training data, and shows via Observation 3.2 that hallucinating with positive probability implies the model innovates (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook constructs finite universes (N up to 20,000) with corpora drawn from p supported on F, confirming H⊂U with frequency 1.000 across 40,000 trials per regime, so g(H)>0 implies g(U)>0 structurally. A negative control where the corpus assumption is violated correctly produces g(H)=1, g(U)=0, demonstrating the assumption's necessity.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows that under K-Sparsity and Regular Facts assumptions, if the innovation mass g(U) > 0, the probability a model hallucinates is at least 1 - K/|U| (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: Exact posterior q=(K-|O|)/|U| is computed and 1-q ≥ 1-K/|U| holds with min slack ≥ 0.000550 across all regimes; empirical spike hallucination frequencies (e.g., 0.998175, 0.955900, 0.845325) match the exact probabilities. Negative control removing Regular Facts yields hallucination probability 0, below the 0.889 floor.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.4 shows that a calibrated model with any positive missing probability mass necessarily innovates (Proposition 3.4).
claims.evidence: Using the canonical partition (observed singletons plus one U-cell), g(U)=p(U) exactly with max error 2.22e-16 across all regimes; whenever p(U)>0 (frequency 1.000), g(U)>0. Negative control with an uncalibrated model placing all mass on observed statements shows g(U)=0 despite p(U)=0.8.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 gives a Markov-style bound showing the hallucination rate satisfies g(H) ≥ g(U)(1 - K/(δ|U|)) with probability at least 1-δ (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Scatter model satisfies g(H) ≥ g(U)(1-K/(δ|U|)) deterministically (100% across all valid δ/regime combinations); spike model satisfies at rates exceeding 1-δ (e.g., 0.998 ≥ 0.85). Tight regimes correctly exclude δ=0.15 when K/|U|≈0.169 > δ, respecting the theorem's domain.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 establishes a high-confidence bound where, with probability at least 1 - K/|U|, the hallucination rate satisfies g(H) ≥ g(U)/(K+1) (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Scatter satisfies g(H) ≥ g(U)/(K+1) in 100% of trials; spike satisfies at rates (0.998175, 0.955900, 0.845325, 0.844625) all exceeding the required 1-K/|U| thresholds (0.997498, 0.949648, 0.830620, 0.830620). Non-Regular-Facts control fails as expected.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.3 lower-bounds the innovation rate by g(U) ≥ p(U)/(K+1) minus a miscalibration distance term, linking missing probability mass to innovation (Proposition 4.3).
claims.evidence: Exact TV distances computed for calibrated, scatter, and spike models over 120,000 evaluations per regime; all slacks g(U) - [p(U)/(K+1) - TV] are positive with minimum 0.588235. Negative control without K-Sparsity (K=2, 99 observed + 1 unseen in one cell) yields g(U)=0.01 < RHS=0.1667, confirming the bound fails without the assumption.

Srishti280992/repro-innovation-an-almost.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous numerical audit of all six theoretical claims by constructing finite probability distributions at non-trivial scale (N up to 20,000, K up to 100, 160,000 total corpora) with multiple model families, exact formula unit tests, and assumption-violating negative controls. All claimed inequalities are confirmed to hold under the stated assumptions and to fail when assumptions are removed.

Srishti280992/repro-lbw-gaussian-cbo-vi.paper_title: Variational inference via Gaussian interacting particles in the Bures-Wasserstein geometry

claims.claim: The Linearized Bures-Wasserstein (LBW) parametrization identifies each non-degenerate Gaussian with its optimal transport map from a reference measure, yielding a closed-form weighted barycenter (Eq. 3.3, Section 3) that avoids the fixed-point iteration required in standard Bures-Wasserstein geometry.
claims.evidence: 240 random SPD trials through d=50 show max reconstruction/OT/distance errors all ~1e-13; 16M-sample Monte Carlo pushforward identity matches closed form (z-score -1.24); closed-form LBW barycenter objective matches Frechet optimizer to 5.91e-08 while standard BW barycenters required 6-199 fixed-point iterations vs zero for LBW.

claims.claim: The proposed Gaussian consensus-based optimization (CBO) particle system drives N Gaussian particles toward consensus via stochastic exploration plus deterministic drift toward exponentially-weighted barycenters omega(mu) = exp(-alpha*E(mu)) (Eq. 4.2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Vectorized vs per-particle loop recurrence matched exactly (max diff 0.0e+00), consensus point equaled direct weighted LBW barycenter (max diff 0.0e+00), multiplicative noise vanished at consensus (0.0e+00) with linear state dependence (slope 1.02, corr 0.97), and measured drift rates matched the Euler formula to machine precision across lambda/dt combinations.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves convergence of the Gaussian CBO dynamics to global minimizers at an exponential rate under smoothness conditions on the energy functional (Theorem 4.1, Eq. 4.10).
claims.evidence: On a smooth Gaussian-kernel MMD energy with finite positive theorem constants (C1=1.280, C2=0.429), 8 runs of 2000 particles showed exponential variance collapse (median rate 1.883) but the consensus limit energy (median 0.2185) was ~6.68x the global minimum (0.0327), with median excess 0.186 — concrete evidence that the dynamics do not converge to global minimizers as claimed.

claims.claim: Lemma 4.1 establishes well-posedness of the particle dynamics under local Lipschitz continuity of the energy functional E (Lemma 4.1, Eq. 4.3).
claims.evidence: The C-infinity function E(z)=(1+||z||^2)^2 is locally Lipschitz on every bounded set yet its growth-weighted ratio rises from 2.67 to 20000 (log-log slope 0.986), showing local Lipschitz continuity alone is insufficient for the well-posedness proof's required global growth bound; KL near singular covariances exhibits the same divergence.

claims.claim: On 2D Gaussian mixture targets A-D, Gaussian CBO outperforms Bures-Wasserstein Gradient Flow on non-convex, non-log-concave problems, with gradient flow becoming trapped on bimodal targets where CBO finds superior solutions (Section 5.1, Table 1, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: 100 paired seeds per target A-D using the released optimizer protocol and independent 80x80 Gauss-Hermite KL scoring show CBO beats BWGF on all four targets (median diffs -0.104, -0.015, -0.018, -0.033) with all bootstrap 95% CIs excluding zero and CBO win rates of 63-81%.

claims.claim: An extended exponential map defined on all of Sym_d (rather than only Sym_d++ - I) automatically preserves positive semi-definiteness of covariances at no added computational cost, enabling exploration of singular Gaussians (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Across 100,000 random symmetric tangents in d=2..20 (including 20,000/20,000 outside the OT cone at d=10,20), zero negative covariances were produced with min eigenvalue staying positive; a 200,000-step Brownian path spent 95.97% of steps outside the cone yet Sigma_T remained PSD every step; exact singular construction yielded eigenvalues [0.0, 2.25].

Srishti280992/repro-lbw-gaussian-cbo-vi.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence verifying the LBW geometry/barycenter (Claim 1), CBO dynamics mechanics (Claim 2), mixture-target superiority (Claim 5), and PSD-preserving extended exponential map (Claim 6), while presenting constructive counterexamples falsifying the convergence-to-global-minimizers theorem (Claim 3) and the local-Lipschitz-only well-posedness lemma (Claim 4).

Papajams/repro-to-grok-grokking-ridge-re.paper_title: To Grok Grokking: Provable Grokking in Ridge Regression

claims.claim: The paper proves end-to-end grokking for zero-teacher ridge regression, including early training overfitting, delayed poor generalization, and eventual low generalization error (Theorem 4.1)
claims.evidence: Numerical audit on n=100, m=1000 Gaussian-feature setup over 8000 GD steps checks all three Theorem 4.1 bounds (train-loss upper, test-loss lower, parameter-norm upper) with zero substantive violations; empirical grokking time of 7792 steps confirms the three-stage phenomenon with concrete trace data.

claims.claim: The end-to-end grokking result is extended from the zero-teacher setting to realizable ridge regression with arbitrary realizable teacher functions (Theorem 4.2)
claims.evidence: Same audit setup with a random unit-norm realizable teacher yields t1=204, t2=8000, grokking time=7796, with all per-step envelopes holding (zero substantive violations) and empirical times within the theoretical bounds (t1_theory=1467, t2_theory=11982).

claims.claim: Separate theorems decompose grokking into training-loss convergence, poor generalization during overfitting, and eventual generalization (Theorems 4.4-4.6)
claims.evidence: The C1 audit explicitly decomposes into the three theorem checks: Theorem 4.4 (train-loss envelope, zero violations of part i), Theorem 4.5 (test-loss lower bound during overfitting, zero violations of part ii), and Theorem 4.6 (parameter-norm bound and eventual test-loss convergence to c=0.01, zero violations of part iii).

claims.claim: Decreasing weight decay and sample size can amplify grokking time in ridge-regression simulations, matching the paper's quantitative hyperparameter predictions (Figure 2)
claims.evidence: Hyperparameter sweep over λ (1e-7 to 1e-2), n (50 to 350), m (200 to 2000), and ν² (0.25 to 4) with concrete t1/t2 measurements confirms all four predicted trends: t2∝1/λ (t2·λ≈2.25 for uncapped points), n↑→t1↑ (100→870), m has minor effect (~200–330), ν²↑→t1↑ (130→310); empirical t1 consistently below theoretical upper bounds.

claims.claim: Two-layer ReLU experiments qualitatively reproduce the predicted grokking-time dependence on hyperparameters beyond the linear setting (Figures 3 and 4)
claims.evidence: Full two-layer ReLU network (d=50, n=50, m=1000, manual backprop) shows clear grokking (t1=2000, t2=57600) and confirms t2∝1/λ (t2·λ≈5475 across λ=0.5,0.2,0.1), n↓→t1↓ (n=10→400, n=200→10000), m minor effect, and ν²↑→t2↑; random-features ReLU (d=100, m=10000) confirms n↑→t1↑ and m minor, though t2 not reached due to approximation error.

Papajams/repro-to-grok-grokking-ridge-re.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all five claims on non-toy setups matching the paper's experimental scale, including per-step bound verification for Theorems 4.1–4.6, hyperparameter sweeps confirming predicted trends, and two-layer ReLU experiments demonstrating qualitative transfer of grokking-time dependencies to the nonlinear setting. An additional falsification experiment shows the simplified Eq. 8 bounds fail under spike-and-slab features while the general distribution-free theorem holds.

michaldobiezynski/repro-robust-stochasti.paper_title: Robust Stochastic Gradient Posterior Sampling with Lattice Based Discretisation

claims.claim: SGLRW replaces the Gaussian noise injection of SGLD with bounded binary/ternary lattice updates, so that stochastic noise enters only through the off-diagonal elements of the discretisation covariance matrix (Section on lattice construction; Lemma 4.3).
claims.evidence: A genuine K=2e6 Monte-Carlo run on d=50 Bayesian linear regression with real B=8 minibatches measured the diagonal mass of the minibatch second-moment error matrix at 0.000 for SGLRW vs 0.227 for SGLD (analytic: 0.000 vs 0.225), directly confirming that stochastic noise enters SGLRW only off-diagonal.

claims.claim: Under α-stable heavy-tailed gradient noise with α=1.5, where second moments do not exist, SGLD becomes unstable while SGLRW remains stable across increasing noise scales (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: On a d=50 four-mode Gaussian mixture with 60 chains × 3000 iterations across 6 noise scales using paired α-stable(α=1.5) noise, SGLD diverges in 40% of chains at scale 50 with occupancy 0.000 from scale 20 onward, while SGLRW has 0% divergence and 0.999 occupancy at scale 20, directly supporting the instability vs stability claim.

claims.claim: On Bayesian linear regression with N=1000, d=20, at batch size B=8 and step size δ_t=10⁻³, SGLRW attains KL divergence 6.060 versus 19.889 for SGLD (Table 1).
claims.evidence: On the exact conjugate posterior (N=1000, d=20, B=8), measured KLs of SGLRW=6.206, SGLD=19.840, Clipped=18.485 all fall within 3% of Table 1's 6.060/19.889/18.184, reproducing the ordering and ratio (3.20 vs 3.28); however, the reproduction required delta_base=1e-2 rather than the paper's stated 1e-3, a 10x deviation from the claimed hyperparameter.

claims.claim: Lemma 4.3 shows the second-moment discretisation error of SGLRW equals the off-diagonal part of SGLD's error matrix, M_SGLRW = offdiag(M_SGLD), eliminating the diagonal noise inflation that afflicts SGLD (Lemma 4.3).
claims.evidence: An independent K=2e6 Monte-Carlo run executing both samplers on real B=8 minibatches in d=50 measured M_SGLRW = offdiag(M_SGLD) to a relative Frobenius error of 0.006, confirming the identity numerically within sampling tolerance; the separately reported analytic id-relerr=0.00 is correctly identified as a tautology and not relied upon.

claims.claim: On UCI logistic regression benchmarks, SGLRW achieves consistent KL-divergence improvements over both SGLD and Clipped-SGLD across a range of learning rates (Table 2).
claims.evidence: On the full UCI breast-cancer dataset (N=569, d=31) with a from-scratch NUTS gold standard (max split-R̂=1.0006), sweeping 5 learning rates × 2 batch sizes × 2 seeds, SGLRW has lower KL than Clipped-SGLD in 10/10 cells and is best of three in 7/10; it loses to plain SGLD only at the smallest step sizes (δ≤3e-3) where all samplers are already near NUTS, which is a partial but not complete exception to 'consistent over both.'

claims.claim: On an LLM sentiment classification task, SGLRW consistently outperforms Clipped-SGLD in predictive quality across varying batch sizes and dataset scales (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: On real IMDB reviews with frozen facebook/opt-350m embeddings (8225-parameter Bayesian head, 2 seeds, 2000 iterations), SGLRW beats Clipped-SGLD in only 4/9 batch×scale cells with a mean NLL gap of +0.0021 in Clipped-SGLD's favor against a seed-to-seed spread of 0.0026, making the two samplers statistically indistinguishable and directly contradicting 'consistently outperforms'; even at larger learning rates where clipping is active (up to 53% of coordinates), SGLRW loses all three additional cells.

michaldobiezynski/repro-robust-stochasti.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting five of six claims through genuine Monte-Carlo runs, full-scale Bayesian regression, a from-scratch NUTS reference on UCI data, and real OPT-350m IMDB experiments, while falsifying the LLM sentiment claim by showing SGLRW and Clipped-SGLD are indistinguishable on that task. The reproduction is notably rigorous in flagging its own integrity issues, including a 10x step-size deviation in Claim 3 and a tautological analytic check in Claims 1/4.

michaldobiezynski/repro-follow-the-pertu.paper_title: Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader for Decoupled Bandits: Best-of-Both-Worlds and Practicality

claims.claim: In the adversarial regime, the proposed FTPL policy for decoupled bandits achieves O(sqrt(KT)) regret, matching the lower bound of Avner et al. 2012 (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Log-log slope of regret vs T = 0.448 (target ~0.5) at K=8 over 120 seeds, and regret/sqrt(KT) bounded in [0.201, 0.251] across K in {2,4,8,16} at T=8000, providing concrete evidence for O(sqrt(KT)) scaling in both T and K.

claims.claim: In the stochastic (SCA) regime, with perturbation parameter alpha in (1,3], the FTPL policy achieves a time-independent regret bound of O(K/Delta_min), improving on the standard MAB O(sum log T/Delta_i) bound (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: FTPL alpha=3 regret slope vs T = 0.104 (flat/saturating) compared to coupled UCB1 slope 0.338 (growing), with plateau 68.5 within ratio 1.37 of K/Delta_min=50 on K=5, T up to 1e5, supporting time-independent O(K/Delta_min) behavior.

claims.claim: Setting alpha=3 yields a near-optimal best-of-both-worlds regret bound of O(sqrt((K/Delta_min) * sum(1/Delta_i)) + K/Delta_min) (Corollary 3).
claims.evidence: The same unchanged alpha=3 policy yields adversarial slope 0.532 (~sqrt(T)) and stochastic slope 0.104 (~constant) simultaneously, with measured stochastic plateau 68.5 matching the Corollary-3 formula value 82.3 to ratio 0.83 (order-1 constant).

claims.claim: The exploration probabilities q_{t,i} are computed via a closed-form approximation requiring only O(K log K) time per round through sorting, avoiding convex optimization or geometric resampling used by prior FTRL/FTPL decoupled-bandit methods (Equation 7, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Per-round wall-clock time-vs-K log-log slope = 0.899 (near-linear, decisively not the 2.0 of O(K^2)), implemented via a single sort with no convex optimization or resampling; closed-form distribution matches Monte-Carlo leader distribution at Pearson corr 0.972, though TV=0.140 indicates a loose approximation.

claims.claim: In adversarial-regime experiments, the proposed method runs approximately 2020 times faster than the Decoupled-Tsallis-INF baseline while achieving comparable regret.
claims.evidence: On the paper's own timing protocol (K in {2,...,512}, 100 repetitions), FTPL speedup over FTRL-with-convex-solver crosses x2020 between K=16 (x977) and K=32 (x5321), with comparable regret (140.72±5.04 vs 119.73±4.93 over 500 runs at T=10000); the logbook also documents that the factor drops to x3-x66 if FTRL is reduced to a scalar root-find, clarifying the claim's scope.

claims.claim: In stochastic-regime experiments, the method outperforms both the EB-TC pure-exploration policy and naive mixed exploration/exploitation policies.
claims.evidence: On the paper's exact stochastic instance (K=5, Delta_min=0.05, T=10000, 1000 runs), FTPL (66.92±1.78) beats the mixed policies (3525±8.71 and 3588±8.81) by x53 but loses to EB-TC (15.00±0.66) by x4.5, contradicting the conjunctive claim that FTPL outperforms both EB-TC and naive mixed policies.

michaldobiezynski/repro-follow-the-pertu.overall: A thorough from-scratch numpy reproduction with 120-1000 seeds verifies the adversarial O(sqrt(KT)) regret, stochastic time-independent O(K/Delta_min) regret, best-of-both-worlds combination, O(K log K) closed-form complexity, and the ~2020x speedup claim. Claim 6 is falsified because EB-TC outperforms FTPL on the paper's own stochastic instance, breaking the conjunctive claim.

michaldobiezynski/repro-minimizing-upper.paper_title: Minimizing Upper Confidence Bounds: A Data-Driven Framework for Stochastic Programming

claims.claim: The Average Percentile Upper Bound (APUB) is defined as U^apub[μ|P̂_n] := (1/α)∫₀^α U^efron[μ|P̂_n] dτ, integrating Efron's percentile upper bound over confidence level τ from 0 to α (Definition 2.2, Section 2)
claims.evidence: The two equivalent representations of APUB (trapezoid integral and closed-form CVaR) agree to a max relative gap of 7.34e-04 across multiple alpha values, and the ordering APUB >= Efron endpoint > sample mean holds for all tested alpha at n=500, M=4000 bootstrap.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.7 proves APUB converges almost surely to the true population mean as sample size n approaches infinity, for every confidence level in (0,1] (Theorem 2.7)
claims.evidence: At n=20000 with R=100 trials, bias is <= 0.026 for all alpha levels tested, and std-vs-n log-log slopes are -0.52, -0.51, -0.51, -0.49 (theoretical -0.5), demonstrating the expected finite-sample signature of a.s. convergence at faithful scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows the APUB-embedded stochastic optimization model achieves first-order asymptotic correctness, with coverage probability exceeding the nominal confidence level up to an O(N^{-1/2}) term (Theorem 3.3)
claims.evidence: On a 1-D newsvendor instance with nominal 0.90, empirical coverage is at or above 0.90 for all N>=100 (0.93-0.96), with N=50 at 0.87 within Monte-Carlo tolerance. The O(N^{-1/2}) rate is not cleanly isolated (excess slope +1.28), but the substantive coverage guarantee holds.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 establishes that both the optimal values and optimal solution sets of the APUB-based optimization problem converge almost surely to their true counterparts as sample size increases (Theorem 3.5)
claims.evidence: On the 1-D newsvendor, MSE of the optimal solution decreases from 0.209 to 0.00478 (slope -1.02) and optimal value error from 0.534 to 0.088 (slope -0.50), both converging to the closed-form truth x*=2.693, v*=1.963 at expected rates over R=200 replications.

claims.claim: On a Gamma(2,1) numerical example with nominal level α=0.05 and sample sizes ranging from 80 to 10,000, APUB's coverage probability approaches the 0.95 nominal level faster than Efron's percentile bound and standard large-sample approximations (Figure 1, Example 2.5)
claims.evidence: APUB mean coverage is 0.979 (always >= 0.95, over-covering) while Efron and normal approximation means are both 0.949, already hugging the 0.95 nominal level. APUB is consistently further from 0.95 than the alternatives, directly contradicting the claim that it approaches 0.95 faster.

claims.claim: The framework is validated on two-stage product mix and multi-product newsvendor problems, showing APUB balances robustness and practicality compared to Sample Average Approximation (SAA) and Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) (Section 5)
claims.evidence: The SAA < APUB < DRO ordering reproduces on a 3-product newsvendor with N_train=60 and a CVaR surrogate for DRO, but this is heavily reduced from the paper's 20-product x 8-department copula-dependent instance with true Wasserstein DRO.

michaldobiezynski/repro-minimizing-upper.overall: The logbook provides faithful numerical verification of the paper's definition (Claim 1) and three asymptotic theorems (Claims 2-4) on legitimate instances at adequate scale, while honestly reporting that the comparative coverage-speed claim (Claim 5) is contradicted by the data and the Section 5 validation (Claim 6) is only demonstrated at toy scale.

michaldobiezynski/repro-lower-bounds-for.paper_title: Lower Bounds for Frank-Wolfe on Strongly Convex Sets

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a constructive Omega(1/sqrt(epsilon)) lower bound on the number of iterations for Frank-Wolfe with short steps or exact line search when both the objective and the constraint set are smooth and strongly convex (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: Short-step FW on the paper's hard instance (f(x)=||x-p||^2 over B_1(0), ||p||=1) yields a log-log gap-decay slope of -2.0006 over iterations 200–20000 with g[1000]=1.001e-6 vs predicted 1.0e-6, concretely confirming the Theta(1/t^2) gap decay and hence the Omega(1/sqrt(epsilon)) iteration lower bound for the short-step disjunct. The exact-line-search disjunct is not forward-reproduced (forward simulation shows slope -3.2772, escaping the stall), but the claim is disjunctive and the short-step half is tightly verified.

claims.claim: The lower-bound construction uses the specific instance of minimizing f(x) = ||x-p||_2^2 over the Euclidean unit ball B_1(0) with the unconstrained minimizer p on the boundary (||p||=1), showing this hard instance matches the known O(1/sqrt(epsilon)) upper bound of Garber et al. (2015) (Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: Iterations-to-gap pairs (epsilon, T) = (1e-2, 13), (1e-4, 103), (1e-6, 1002), (1e-8, 10004) yield fitted exponent alpha=0.4823 with 100x-ratios approaching sqrt(100)=10 (9.7 then 9.98), concretely demonstrating 1/sqrt(epsilon) scaling on the paper's exact hard instance, matching the Garber et al. (2015) upper bound exponent.

claims.claim: The lower bound is established via a 'backward reconstruction' technique that builds worst-case trajectories by working backward from terminal iterates, producing precise sequences over horizons of 10,000+ iterations (Section on Backward Reconstruction Strategy).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements backward reconstruction at d=100, T=30,000 with reconstruction error 4.67e-07, but only inverts the deterministic short-step FW dynamics—not the exact-line-search worst-case trajectories that the paper's backward reconstruction technique targets. Inverting a known deterministic forward trajectory is a simplified proxy for the paper's constructive adversarial backward method, which is the novel contribution.

claims.claim: The analysis reduces the dynamics to a two-dimensional invariant subspace parametrized by residual magnitude r and contraction factor s, revealing stable phases of monotonically increasing contraction followed by intermittent 'jumps' that explain the convergence stalling behavior (Section on Dynamical Analysis).
claims.evidence: The 2D invariance (off-plane coordinate = 0.00e+00) is a symmetry artifact guaranteed by the choice p=e_0, x_0=e_1 (all LMO outputs stay in span{e_0,e_1} by construction), not a deep confirmation. The 257 contraction-worsening jumps are a qualitative observation on a simplified setup rather than a rigorous dynamical analysis.

claims.claim: The result shows strong convexity of the constraint set alone cannot yield convergence rates uniformly faster than O(1/sqrt(epsilon)), and this conclusion holds dimension-independently and extends to ellipsoidal constraints via affine invariance (Theorem 6, Implications).
claims.evidence: The ellipsoid affine-invariance test (diag(3,1) transform) preserves alpha=0.482, a non-trivial check that the rate extends to ellipsoidal constraints. The dimension-independence test (alpha=0.482 for d=2,5,20,100) is degenerate since the trajectory is the same 2D dynamics embedded in each ambient dimension, but the ellipsoid result is a genuine confirmation of the affine-invariance implication.

michaldobiezynski/repro-lower-bounds-for.overall: The logbook concretely verifies the short-step core of the paper's Omega(1/sqrt(epsilon)) lower bound on the paper's own hard instance, with gap-decay slopes and iteration counts matching theoretical predictions to high precision. However, the novel exact-line-search disjunct is not reproduced, the backward reconstruction only inverts deterministic short-step dynamics rather than constructing adversarial exact-LS trajectories, and several checks (2D invariance, dimension-independence) are symmetry artifacts of the specific initialization.

michaldobiezynski/repro-convergence-of-s.paper_title: Convergence of Steepest Descent and Adam under Non-Uniform Smoothness

claims.claim: The paper introduces a non-uniform smoothness assumption (Assumption 1) in which curvature is an affine function of the objective value, generalizing standard L-smoothness (Section 3).
claims.evidence: On separable logistic regression (n=200, d=10), the log-log slope of Hessian spectral norm vs loss is 0.916 (R²=0.994), consistent with proportional curvature (H0=0), and the bound ||H|| ≤ 24.83·f holds at 100% of sampled points.

claims.claim: Under this assumption, steepest descent (sign GD) is shown to converge linearly on logistic regression with separable data and is provably faster than standard gradient descent (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Sign-GD shows geometric decay (semilog slope -4.93e-3, R²=0.9994) reaching f<1e-6 at t=2379, while GD shows ~1/t sublinear decay (log-log slope -0.96, semilog R²=0.78) and never reaches 1e-6, on separable logistic regression with T=20000.

claims.claim: Adam is shown to converge at a linear rate with a constant step size on certain two-layer neural networks under the non-uniform smoothness assumption (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: On the paper's Prop-4 two-layer network (D=50, n=500, width m=50, 2500 trained parameters), constant-step Adam achieves semilog slope -4.53e-3 (R²=0.9946) with final loss 1.02e-10, vs GD plateauing at 2.05e-2, demonstrating linear convergence.

claims.claim: RMSProp-type adaptive methods are analyzed and shown to be provably faster than AdaGrad, AMSGrad, and heavy-ball momentum under non-uniform smoothness (Section 6).
claims.evidence: On the paper's exact 1-D logistic loss example from Section 6, RMSProp (4.5e-14) and Adam (7.5e-14) show linear decay (semilog R²=0.999) while GD, heavy-ball, AdaGrad, and AMSGrad plateau at ~1e-4 with log-log slopes ~-1, matching the Omega(1/T) lower bound.

claims.claim: The convergence analysis is extended from the deterministic steepest descent setting (Section 4) to the stochastic setting (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Direct source check of paper.txt confirms Section 5 is titled 'Convergence of RMSProp & Adam' (deterministic), and Section 7 explicitly defers the stochastic setting to future work; the registry claim that Section 5 extends analysis to the stochastic setting contradicts the paper's actual structure.

michaldobiezynski/repro-convergence-of-s.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting claims 1–4 on the paper's own problem setups at reasonable scale, and correctly identifies claim 5 as a mischaracterization of the paper's structure by checking the source text. The reproduction is a self-contained numpy harness with no external dependencies, running the paper's exact constructions.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 proves the original DeepSets aggregation (Equation 4) is discontinuous in the natural any-dimensional topology because the infinite sum can diverge when the inner function ρ decays arbitrarily slowly, so standard DeepSets fails to be universal (Theorem 4.2, Section 4.1.1).
claims.evidence: The sum ‖Σρ(X_i:)‖ grows from 0.779 (n=10) to 3.420 (n=1e6) with stable log-log slope ~0.24 across two disjoint decade windows, replicated across 200/200 random output layers, while the Eq.5 control converges to 0.482 with Cauchy tail 1.22e-11 on the identical sequence — concretely demonstrating the divergence mechanism on ℓ₂(ℝ⁶⁴) with k=64.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.9 proves standard message-passing GNNs fail any-dimensional universality because their pointwise nonlinearities are discontinuous in the cut metric, since a pointwise map is continuous with respect to the cut norm only if it is linear (Theorem 4.9, Section 4.2).
