claims.evidence: Eight nonlinear pointwise maps maintain frozen cut-norm gaps matching their closed-form Jensen gaps to 3 d.p. (slopes within ±0.03 of zero) up to n=2048, while two linear maps decay to a rigorous upper bound ≤0.035 — directly confirming the 'continuous iff linear' mechanism. The MPNN sub-experiment is tautological by construction (both graphs 96-regular with constant features) and carries no independent weight.

claims.claim: A modified DeepSets-infinity architecture (Equation 5) that reweights terms by an ell_p norm factor is proven continuous and universal on ell_p(R^k) sequence space (Theorem 4.2, Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Continuity is well-supported (modulus ~ε^0.986 over four decades, S_∞ invariance 3.3e-16), but the universality sweep plateaus at 10–19% relative error and is non-monotone for 2/3 targets, failing to demonstrate density. The setup truncates ℓ₂ to 512 terms with k=16, a finite-dimensional proxy for the infinite-dimensional theorem.

claims.claim: A measure-space variant DeepSets-bar-infinity (Equation 6), replacing the sum with a normalized integral under a growth condition, is proven universal on the Wasserstein space of probability measures (Theorem 4.5, Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: Continuity is strong (exact Hungarian W₂, four-decade modulus collapse, growth-condition blow-up to 2e19 when violated), but universality plateaus at 23–29% relative error and increases at the largest width. The setup uses 256-atom empirical measures with k=8, a proxy for the full Wasserstein space.

claims.claim: A homomorphism-density-basis architecture (Equations 9-10) is proven continuous and universal on graphon space with the cut metric, restoring universality for graph architectures (Theorem 4.9, Theorem 4.10, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Machine-precision verification (4.44e-16) that Eq.9 expands into exactly the 64 simple 4-node graph motifs with no non-simple motifs appearing — a proof-level algebraic check of the continuity mechanism. Continuity decay slope −1.024 vs frozen pointwise-IGN gap ~0.092, and universality fit reaches 0.46% relative RMSE at 22 features, though on a single target with 130/40 train/test graphons.

claims.claim: A two-stage architecture combining a Gram-matrix map (Equation 12) with Invariant Graphon Networks (Equation 14) is proven universal on bounded point-cloud orbits under the group action (Theorem 4.12, Theorem 4.13, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Exact group invariance (2.2e-16) for both Gram-map and IGN stages, Lipschitz constant stable at ~0.1078 across four decades of perturbation, all 20 distinct-orbit pairs have certified positive δ₂ separation, and universality RMSE converges from 79% to 0.53% at M=64 features — though on a single target functional with a random-feature first stage.

michaldobiezynski/repro-any-dimensional-.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical instantiations of six pure-theory claims from a paper with no original experiments. Continuity/discontinuity mechanisms (Claims 1, 2, 5, 6) are decisively demonstrated on non-trivial setups, while the universality/density halves of Claims 3 and 4 plateau well short of zero error on finite-dimensional proxies, warranting toy status.

michaldobiezynski/repro-adaptive-persona.paper_title: Adaptive Personalized Federated Learning via Multi-task Averaging of Kernel Mean Embeddings

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 establishes finite-sample guarantees for a Q-aggregation estimator of kernel mean embeddings, with a bound that trades off bias governed by the maximum distributional distance ΔV against variance controlled by the combined sample size nV (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: At d=100, B=60 agents, n_k=250 (15,000 samples), 8 seeds, the measured E[MMD²] of Algorithm 1 tracks the theorem's leading bias/variance trade-off within ratios [0.63, 2.21] across two decades of Δ, converging to 0.988 at n_k=2000, with fitted rate n^(−1.006) matching the predicted n^(−1); the uniform-weight baseline exceeds the same bound by up to 29×, confirming the test discriminates.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.6 bounds the excess risk of the personalized model by 2RΘ·E[MMD(P̂(ω̂), P₁)], where RΘ controls the RKHS norm of the loss class, linking the KME estimation error directly to downstream task risk (Corollary 4.6).
claims.evidence: On the paper's own Example 4.2/5.1 instance (d=50, B=200, n_k=150, 20 seeds) with closed-form R_Θ=57.2 and exact constrained minimizer, the bound 2R_Θ·E[MMD] holds with 0 violations across 900 adversarial (weight, instance) points including single-agent vertices reaching excess risk 66.6 (within 23× of their bound), and tracks excess risk with correlation 0.990 along a τ-sweep.

claims.claim: Per Example 4.5, the learned collaboration weights automatically shift toward local-only learning (ω₁ ≈ 1) recovering the naive O(n₁^{-1/2}) rate when no beneficial collaborators exist, and toward pooling when other agents share similar distributions, without prior knowledge of heterogeneity (Example 4.5).
claims.evidence: With 200 dissimilar agents (MMD=1.0), learned w₁=1.0000 at all n₁ and measured MMD follows n₁^(−0.4994)/n₁^(−0.5116) with MMD/√(TrΣ₁/n₁) in [0.988,1.034], confirming the naive O(n₁^(−1/2)) rate and constant; with 30 identical + 29 dissimilar agents, 100% of collaborative mass routes to the identical group unaided, yielding a 5.43× gain over local.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 quantifies the communication-statistical efficiency tradeoff when the method is implemented with D-dimensional random Fourier features, adding an approximation error term of order C√(log B/D) (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: The RFF perturbation of MMD² geometry decays as D^(−0.545)/D^(−0.518) across D=4…4096 (theory D^(−1/2)) with implied constant C=0.0716 flat to 1.43×, and grows 1.242× per decade of B up to B=1000 against √(log B)=1.225× predicted; end-to-end, Algorithm 2's excess over its D→∞ limit is resolvable at 9/9 D values and stays below the theorem's term.

claims.claim: On a synthetic concept-shift experiment with 100 agents and 10 samples each, the method's adaptive weighting correctly improves performance once intra-group similarity crosses the transition point σc² = 0.5 (Section 6.1).
claims.evidence: Using the paper's exact Table-1 configuration (B=100, n_k=10, d=20, σ_Y²=2), the Oracle MSE crosses Local MSE at σ_c²=0.314, not 0.5; sweeping the unstated ridge parameter λ moves the crossing only within [0.198, 0.314], never reaching 0.5, and this crossing is solver-independent since it depends solely on Oracle-vs-Local MSE.

claims.claim: On the FEMNIST handwriting benchmark with 192 agents, the adaptive weighting scheme consistently outperforms a uniform-weighting baseline using fixed, untuned hyperparameters (Section 6.3).
claims.evidence: On the real LEAF FEMNIST partition with 192 writers and the paper's exact architecture/budget, Q-aggregation (mean accuracy 0.3847) beats GrandMean (0.3320) on only 58.3% of agents at matched budget—not 'consistently'—and beats Local (0.4873) on only 26.6% of agents, directly contradicting the paper's claim of 'always better than local training'; the paper's stated ordering (GrandMean generally superior to Local) is also reversed.

michaldobiezynski/repro-adaptive-persona.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence verifying the four theoretical claims (Theorems 4.4 and 5.2, Corollary 4.6, Example 4.5) on non-trivial setups with measured rates and bounds matching predictions, while falsifying both empirical claims: the Section 6.1 transition point is measured at σ_c²=0.314 rather than 0.5, and the Section 6.3 FEMNIST experiment shows the method does not consistently outperform baselines on 192 real writers.

michaldobiezynski/repro-dynamic-programm.paper_title: Dynamic Programming for Epistemic Uncertainty in Markov Decision Processes

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 establishes that when the proposed dynamic programming conditions hold for an ambiguity-averse MDP, a stationary optimal policy exists among the class of transition-uncertain MDPs considered (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: On an sa-rectangular M_c instance (|S|=200, |A|=8, K=5, γ=0.95), the saddle gap V*(P_w) - V^{ν,essinf} measures 3.553e-15, the empirical contraction modulus is 0.950000 vs γ=0.95, and a DP-free cross-check (exact linear solve + nature coordinate descent) agrees to 1.780e-12; a control removing product structure yields residual 0.1562, confirming the zeros are discriminating.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.2 shows value iteration and policy iteration converge under the ambiguity-averse framework, with error bounds of 2γ^n/(1-γ) for value iteration and γ^n for policy iteration after n steps (Proposition 4.2).
claims.evidence: On |S|=100, |A|=5, K=4, γ=0.9, VI error/bound ratio ≤ 0.0500 at every n=0..220, PI is monotone (min increment +2.508e-08) with max ratio 0.1754 for n≥1, and the fitted per-iteration VI contraction factor is 0.900000 vs γ=0.9, all matching the claimed bounds.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 proves that, among monotone law-invariant risk measures, only the essential infimum and essential supremum satisfy the dynamic programming conditions for static (non-resampled) transition kernels, while expectation becomes additionally admissible once kernels are resampled at each step (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: On |S|=30, |A|=4, K=3, γ=0.95, Condition-1 residuals show essinf/esssup at 3.6e-15/7.1e-15 under both kernel models, E at 5.3e-15 for resampled but 8.873e-03 (22.2σ) for static, and VaR/CVaR/ERM at 1.4e-02 to 9.2e-02 (14–163σ); the paper's Example 3.8 counterexample is independently reproduced (1.386294 vs 1.346574).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.5 shows that under an added Wasserstein-1 continuity assumption, expectation is the unique risk measure compatible with dynamic programming for resampled kernels, and no such measure exists for static kernels (Theorem 4.5).
claims.evidence: The LLN sweep shows ρ(avg_n X_i) converging to E(X)=10.43337 for all measures, but DP compatibility requires ρ(X)=ρ(avg_n) for all n, which fails for CVaR by 0.31201; essinf satisfies the averaging identity but is measured as not W1-continuous (perturbation ratio 6026.92 vs E's 1.00); E is compatible for resampled (5.3e-15) but incompatible for static (8.873e-03, 22.2σ).

claims.claim: The characterization implies that risk measures such as CVaR, Value-at-Risk, and entropic risk are incompatible with exact dynamic programming under this framework, explaining their lack of tractable recursive solutions (Section 4, following Theorem 4.4/4.5).
claims.evidence: ERM violates positive homogeneity by -0.2861, CVaR and VaR violate independent additivity by +0.1831 and +0.1346, and all three carry Bellman residuals of 1.4e-02 to 9.2e-02 (14–163σ) under both kernel models, while compatible measures sit at machine precision on the identical code path.

michaldobiezynski/repro-dynamic-programm.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence on non-toy MDP instances (up to |S|=200, |A|=8) supporting all five claims, with non-circular computations, bootstrap standard errors, and discriminating controls. The universally quantified positive directions of the theorems cannot be proven by single instances, but the falsifiable refutation content is measured at high statistical significance and the compatible measures are confirmed at machine precision.

michaldobiezynski/repro-asymptotic-theor.paper_title: Asymptotic Theory of Iterated Empirical Risk Minimization, with Applications to Active Learning

claims.claim: The paper derives sharp asymptotic characterizations of test error for a two-stage iterated empirical risk minimization procedure, in which a first linear estimator's predictions enter as an argument in the loss function of a second ERM trained on the same Gaussian-mixture dataset, in the high-dimensional proportional regime (abstract only).
claims.evidence: State evolution from Theorem 2.1 compared to finite-d simulation at d=2000, n=16000, alpha=8, square loss, indicator policy: mean |theory-sim|=0.00081 (0.68% of test error), 12/15 grid points within 2 s.e.m., with degenerate psi=gamma limit collapsing to single-stage closed form to 2e-16 and independent re-simulation confirming agreement. Caveat: only zero-mean, square-loss instantiation tested.

claims.claim: The analysis addresses the statistical dependency introduced by reusing the same data across both ERM stages and by the prediction-dependent loss of the second stage, unlike classical single-stage ERM analyses (abstract only).
claims.evidence: Ablation setting chi=0 (treating stages as independent) inflates mean |theory-sim| from 0.00081 to 0.00473 (5.83x), with 12/15 grid points outside 2 s.e.m. and max deviation 0.01121 (24 s.e.m.), while the full theory including chi stays within noise. The chi term is O(1) and sign-changing, confirmed by independent re-simulation.

claims.claim: Applying the theory to pool-based active learning removes oracle and sample-splitting assumptions required by prior active learning analyses (abstract only).
claims.evidence: Three-pipeline comparison at d=2000, gamma=0.5: theory tracks the no-oracle, no-splitting re-use pipeline to within 0.00046, while sample splitting costs +0.04656 (+40.3%) and oracle base classifier gives 0.04436 vs 0.10541 budget-constrained. Caveat: reproduction uses gamma=0.5 while paper's held-out inset is at gamma=0.7, and part of the claim is a literature statement verified by reading rather than measurement.

claims.claim: The theory uncovers a fundamental tradeoff in how a fixed labeling budget should be allocated across the two active learning stages (abstract only).
claims.evidence: Interior optimum psi* found at all four budgets gamma=0.2/0.3/0.5/0.7 with paired gains over passive selection of 6.2-19.6% at 5.75-19.3 s.e.m.; both failure modes (too-small psi giving weak base classifier, too-large psi leaving no active-selection budget) are visible in the non-monotone curves, and theory independently reproduces the same shape.

claims.claim: The paper demonstrates a double-descent behavior in test error that is driven by the data selection mechanism itself, rather than by model complexity or sample size alone (abstract only).
claims.evidence: Fine psi scan at fixed d=2000 and |S|=8000 shows interpolation peak at psi=0.12 (predicted 1/alpha=0.125) with prominence +0.01122 (13.2 s.e.m.) and +0.02601 (27.7 s.e.m.) above flanking minima; base-classifier error peaks at same psi, confirming the overfitting-driven selection mechanism. Independent re-simulation reproduces the peak at 0.13252.

michaldobiezynski/repro-asymptotic-theor.overall: This logbook provides strong numerical evidence for all five claims at non-toy scale (d=2000, n=16000), with theory-simulation agreement at the Monte-Carlo noise floor, a critical chi-ablation isolating the cross-stage dependency term, paired statistics for active-learning phenomena, and independent re-simulations. The main limitations are that only the zero-mean square-loss case is tested and the Otilde(n^-1/4) convergence rate is unmeasurable.

michaldobiezynski/repro-no-free-lunch-no.paper_title: No Free Lunch: Non-Asymptotic Analysis of Prediction-Powered Inference

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 gives an exact non-asymptotic characterization of when PPI++ has lower estimation error (mean squared error) than using gold-standard labels alone, as a function of the correlation between pseudo-labels and gold-standard labels and the number of labeled samples n (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: 35 (population x n) configurations across 5 joint laws including real AlphaFold and galaxies populations at n=6..400 with up to 3e6 MC replicates show Theorem 4.1 matching measured MSE to max |MC/theory - 1| = 1.118% (max |z|=2.75), while the asymptotic formula errs by up to 85.8%; sign agreement in all 35 rows, cross-checked by two independent simulators.

claims.claim: For Gaussian data, PPI++ outperforms the gold-standard-only estimator if and only if the correlation between pseudo- and gold-standard labels is at least 1/sqrt(n-2), a finite-sample threshold that vanishes only as n grows (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Measured zero-crossing rho* of MSE(PPI++)-MSE(classical) matches 1/sqrt(n-2) to 0.2-0.9% for n=6..400, with log-log slope -0.5418 on [12,100] converging to -0.4886 on [400,1e4] against the -0.5 asymptote, confirmed by two independent simulators (raw draws and exact sufficient statistics).

claims.claim: The paper derives exact non-asymptotic variance expressions for PPI++ under sample splitting, in contrast to prior asymptotic 'free lunch' results claiming PPI++ variance is always at most that of gold-standard-only estimation (Section 4, Propositions 4.1-4.6).
claims.evidence: All six propositions reproduce within MC error (max |z|=2.75, Prop 4.6 holds in 100% of draws with algebraic residual 3.64e-14), and the asymptotic free lunch is measurably false: Var(CF)/Var(classical) = 1.51679 at n=6 down to 1.00506 at n=400 on a non-Gaussian population with rho=0, exceeding 1 by 15.7-65.7 MC sigma at every n.

claims.claim: Corollaries 4.1-4.2 extend the main finite-sample no-free-lunch result to derived estimation settings beyond the basic mean-estimation case (Section 4, Corollaries 4.1-4.2).
claims.evidence: Cor 4.1 cross-fit branch matches to 0.334% for n=12..1000 and single-sample to 0.48-0.93% for n<=400; Cor 4.2's premise held in 22 configurations with 0 violations of its conclusion (margins +18.5 to +524.9 sigma); Prop 4.2 finite-N threshold matches all five (n,N) settings at ~4% tolerance. The logbook notes the corollaries extend across estimator variants and sampling regimes within mean estimation, not beyond it.

claims.claim: Experiments on real-world datasets illustrate that the theoretical finite-sample threshold on correlation predicts when PPI++ underperforms gold-standard-only estimation in practice (Section 5).
claims.evidence: On real AlphaFold (10,802 proteins, corr 0.815) measured CF tipping point n*=18 matches Theorem 4.1 prediction of 18 and SS n*=10 matches paper's 10; on galaxies (16,743 objects, corr 0.741) CF n*=10 and SS n*=6 match theory and paper; pseudo-label degradation shifts tipping point 18->28->>40->never (measured) vs 18->26->46->never (predicted). A coverage sub-result (87% at n=20) does not reproduce (measured 0.581) but is disclosed and does not bear on the threshold claim.

michaldobiezynski/repro-no-free-lunch-no.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous from-scratch reproduction of all five claims using pure numpy/scipy with no authors' code, testing on both synthetic and the paper's two real datasets with up to 4e6 MC replicates and independent cross-checks. All claims are supported by concrete numerical evidence on non-toy setups, with one disclosed non-reproducing sub-result (coverage magnitude) that does not affect any registered claim.

michaldobiezynski/repro-on-the-sharp-inp.paper_title: On the Sharp Input-Output Analysis of Nonlinear Systems under Adversarial Attacks

claims.claim: The paper analyzes an ℓ1-norm (least-absolute-deviation) estimator and proves it achieves an estimation error bound of Θ(ρ^τ), where ρ is the system's contraction factor and τ is the input memory length (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Real LP solutions of the ℓ1 estimator on n=100/m=5/r=10 systems with the paper's Appendix-F adversary show geometric decay with fitted base 0.5287–0.5639 vs ρ=0.5 and 0.2739–0.2904 vs ρ=0.25 across 4–6 decades, on a non-toy setup. Significant caveat: the linear instance with exact basis makes the ρ^τ decay partly tautological (error tracks ||A^τ||_2), and T=1200 is far below the theorem's certified horizon, but the bound's predicted rate is observed.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1's guarantee requires the adversarial attack probability to satisfy p < 1/(2τ), which ensures the probability (1-p)^τ of an attack-free observation window exceeds one half (Assumption 2.8, Remark 2.9).
claims.evidence: Closed-form computation shows min of (1−1/(2τ))^τ = 0.500000 only at the excluded boundary τ=1, monotone increasing to e^{−1/2}; Monte-Carlo over 4e5 steps confirms empirical clean-window frequency matches (1−p)^τ and exceeds 1/2; the n=100 LP estimator degrades by three orders of magnitude once (1−p)^τ crosses below 1/2.

claims.claim: A matching lower bound of order Θ(ρ^τ L r/λ) is established, proving the upper bound of Theorem 3.1 is order-optimal and that no estimator can improve on this rate under probabilistic adversarial attacks (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The Appendix-E construction implemented verbatim produces bit-identical observation trajectories in 12/12 instances (ρ×τ configurations), the map gap equals Lρ^τc to 1e-12 in 10/12, λ satisfies the paper's lower bound in 12/12, and the ratio error/(ρ^τ L√r/λ) is τ-independent at 0.056–0.143 across three ρ values, confirming order-optimality on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: The estimation error is shown to decay exponentially with the input memory length τ through the contraction factor ρ ∈ (0,1) (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The same n=100 LP sweeps show 4.76–5.49 decades of geometric decay with fitted base matching ρ to 6–12%, and err/||A^τ||_2 confined to [1.85, 7.38] across the full sweep, confirming the contraction-driven exponential mechanism of Section 3.2. However, the paper's own Section 4 / Figure 1 nonlinear experiment (tanh, M=25) does not reproduce: τ trend in 1/4 settings, ρ trend in 2/4, and l1 loses to LS in 0/8.

claims.claim: Section 3.2 first derives sufficient conditions for exact recovery in the case without past-state effects (Theorem 3.3, Section 3.2.1), then extends the analysis to the general case with nonzero past-state terms (Section 3.2.2).
claims.evidence: With past-state removed (Section 3.2.1 setting), the LP recovers G* at machine precision (1.3e-12 relative) and the sign flip of condition (15) coincides exactly with the LP recovery onset at T=300 for τ=10; restoring nonzero past-state (Section 3.2.2) yields strictly positive error (0.48 at τ=5, 0.015 at τ=10), confirming the two-stage structure on a non-toy n=100 setup.

michaldobiezynski/repro-on-the-sharp-inp.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from deterministic CPU runs supporting all five claims on non-toy n=100 setups, including LP-exact ℓ1 estimation showing ρ^τ decay, verification of the p<1/(2τ) threshold, bit-identical trajectories confirming the lower-bound construction, and machine-precision exact recovery when past-state terms are removed. The main weakness is that Claims 1 and 4 reproduce only on the linear member of the assumption class where the decay is partly instance-driven, and the paper's own nonlinear Figure 1 experiment fails to reproduce.

michaldobiezynski/repro-optimal-conversi.paper_title: Optimal conversion from Rényi Differential Privacy to $f$-Differential Privacy

claims.claim: The intersection-based conversion rule, defined as f_ρ(·)(α) = sup_{τ≥0.5} f_{τ,ρ(τ)}(α), is proven to be the pointwise tightest possible black-box conversion from an RDP profile to a valid hypothesis-testing trade-off function (Theorem 4.4, Section 4).
claims.evidence: A Bernoulli witness is certified to satisfy the full RDP profile (max divergence violation +5.329e-15 on a 131K-point independent audit grid) while attaining the bound to 5.551e-17, and 207 mechanisms yield min slack +1.737e-12 with no violation; the bound is computed by bisection independent of the witness, and a naive fixed-grid contrast fails by +1.324e-02, confirming the test is non-circular and informative.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 establishes that the boundary of the single-order RDP privacy region is optimally tight for any individual (τ, ρ) Rényi-DP guarantee considered in isolation.
claims.evidence: Over 14 orders × 1999 Type-I levels, the computed boundary lies on the level set D_τ=ρ to ≤4.159e-11, the RR witness attains its boundary point to 5.551e-17 with full trade-off inside the region (min slack −5.551e-17 = machine epsilon), and 180 random mechanisms never violate the bound (min slack +2.248e-10); the paper's Fig. 1 anchor D_1.5=0.73396918 is independently confirmed.

claims.claim: Lemma 4.2 shows that intersecting all τ-order single-order regions yields a valid universal lower bound on the trade-off functions attainable by any mechanism satisfying the given RDP profile.
claims.evidence: The sup-of-boundaries formula matches an independently computed 2-D occupancy scan of the intersection at error/step ratio 1.00 across an 8× refinement (error tracking grid resolution, not plateauing), and 207+ mechanisms including Laplace, subsampled Gaussian, and 200 random 256-outcome mechanisms all satisfy T_M ≥ f_ρ with min slack +1.737e-12; Monte-Carlo mechanisms (100-dim Gaussian, DP-SGD) show deficits within their DKW bands.

claims.claim: Symmetric Randomized Response mechanisms (instances of Bernoulli-based witness mechanisms) are constructed to achieve exact recovery under the intersection conversion, saturating the optimal bound at various Type I error levels (Proposition 4.5).
claims.evidence: For p∈{0.6,0.75,0.9,0.99}, R_DP(ε,0) is contained in every single-order region to +1.776e-15 over 2e5 orders up to τ=1e14, the finite-τ_max gap decays as τ_max^{-1.00} (fitted slopes −1.0007/−0.9999), the closed-form τ→∞ member gives sup|f_ρ−f_{ε,0}|=4.441e-16 (machine epsilon), and RR witnesses saturate the bound at 10 Type-I levels to worst error 6.994e-14.

claims.claim: No other black-box conversion rule can uniformly Blackwell-dominate the intersection rule, establishing the fundamental limit of what can be inferred about a mechanism's f-DP guarantee from its RDP profile alone (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: All 5 candidate rules exceeding f_ρ are refuted at 100% of alphas by a certified RR witness in S_ρ (true Gaussian trade-off by 9.925e-02, even f_ρ+1e-8 by 1.000e-08), while every admissible alternative (integer orders, τ>1 only, orders≤100, classical RDP→(ε,δ)→f-DP) stays pointwise ≤f_ρ, with the classical route giving up 0.4765 in beta at its worst point.

michaldobiezynski/repro-optimal-conversi.overall: A 747-line from-scratch NumPy/SciPy audit provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all five claims of this theory paper, using independent computation methods (occupancy scans, certified witnesses on offset grids, Monte-Carlo mechanisms) at scale exceeding the paper's own Appendix C setup. The evidence is transparent about limitations (finite τ truncation, α-restriction for precision-sensitive tests, inability to replace universal proofs) but the numerical identities and inequalities hold to machine precision across 207 mechanisms, 1999 Type-I levels, and orders up to 1e14.

michaldobiezynski/repro-gradient-descent.paper_title: Gradient Descent with Large Step Size Restores Symmetry in Deep Linear Networks with Multi-Pathway

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 shows equal distribution of target singular values across H parallel pathways reduces sharpness by a factor of H^(2/L-1) relative to single-pathway (winner-takes-all) solutions, where L is network depth (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Full-parameter Hessian top eigenvalues measured via complex-step HVPs on d=100 networks across a 12-point (L,H) grid match the H^(2/L-1) sharpness-reduction factor to max relative error 2.94e-12, with WTA sharpness independently landing on L*sigma*_1^(2-2/L) to eight digits.

claims.claim: Below the stability threshold (learning rate eta < 2/S_1), gradient descent reproduces gradient-flow symmetry-breaking into a winner-takes-all pathway, while eta > 2/S_1 triggers edge-of-stability oscillations that re-balance singular values across pathways (Section 5.1, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: Real GD on d=100, L=20, H=2 for 3000 steps shows WTA endpoint (0.99882, 0.00118) with lambda_max=19.9554≈S_1=20 below threshold, and re-balanced endpoint (0.48639, 0.50127) with lambda_max=10.8273≈2/eta=10.7177 above threshold, including an intermediate partial-balance regime and observed two-phase symmetry-breaking dynamics.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.2 establishes a depth-dependent worst-case-return learning-rate ceiling eta_WCR, with the tolerance ratio gamma_WCR(L) scaling as Theta(log L), so deeper networks tolerate a wider range of large step sizes during re-balancing (Section 6, Theorem 6.2, Proposition 6.3).
claims.evidence: Two independent computations—root of the paper's boundary equation (matching Table 82 to 3.42e-04) and from-scratch bisection of Definition 6.1 through the simulated chain map (agreeing to 5.08e-09)—confirm gamma_WCR(L)>2 with Theta(log L) scaling verified over L=10 to 1e7, with slopes matching Eq. (87) to 0.9985.

claims.claim: With heterogeneous pathway depths (e.g., L_1, L_2 in {3,5,7}^2), large-step gradient descent still converges to the theoretically predicted equilibrium that equalizes marginal sharpness 2(L_h-1)sigma_hi^(1-2/L_h) across pathways, overriding the architectural depth asymmetry (Section 5.3, Proposition 5.1, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Real d=100 networks across all 9 depth pairs in {3,5,7}^2 trained 4000 GD steps at eta=2/lambda_1^min converge to the Eq. (18) marginal-sharpness equilibrium with max relative deviation 0.0252 and marginal-sharpness spread ≤0.0479, while a small-eta control collapses to shallow-path WTA (0.99823, 0.00177).

claims.claim: Nonlinear MLPs with Tanh activations and multi-pathway structure exhibit an analogous large-step re-balancing phenomenon to the deep linear network case (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: All 7 seeds of a d=100 two-pathway Tanh MLP re-balance at the large step size (balance 0.8960-0.9999), with lambda_max≈2/eta* under the asymmetric variant; the logbook honestly reports that the companion small-eta WTA regime does not appear under the paper's literal MLP init, but the claim concerns the re-balancing phenomenon, which holds.

michaldobiezynski/repro-gradient-descent.overall: This logbook provides rigorous, non-toy experimental evidence supporting all five claims, using d=100 networks with sharpness measured from full-parameter Hessians via complex-step differentiation rather than read off the paper's formulas. The reproduction is notably thorough in its independent validation paths (e.g., two separate methods for gamma_WCR, independent equilibrium solving before training for Claim 4) and honestly reports caveats such as the MLP WTA regime being initialization-dependent.

michaldobiezynski/repro-generalized-boun.paper_title: Generalized Boundary FDR Control under Arbitrary Dependence: An Approach on Closure Principle

claims.claim: The Domino procedure controls the k-boundary FDR (k-bFDR) - defined as the probability that the k least-significant discoveries in the rejection set are all false - under arbitrary dependence among p-values or e-values, without structural assumptions (Section 2, Definition 2.2; Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: 106 cells (7 Domino variants × 8 dependence structures × {pi1=0.2, global null}) at m=100 with 2000–20000 reps show max k-bFDR = 0.0485 ≤ alpha = 0.05, with 0 cells significantly above alpha; same-harness controls (BH bFDR=0.178, Algorithm-3-as-printed=0.503) confirm the metric detects inflation.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 proves that the rejection set R produced by the Domino algorithm satisfies k-bFDR(R) <= alpha under arbitrary dependence (Section 3, Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: Over the same 106 cells, max(k-bFDR/alpha) = 0.970 with 0 significant exceedances; the tightest cell (phi1_Bonf, independent global null) measures 0.0485 against the exact closed form 1-(1-alpha/m)^m = 0.04878, a gap of 0.18 MC SE, showing the bound holds and is non-vacuous.

claims.claim: Proposition 2.3 shows k-bFDR reduces to k-FWER under the global null and is otherwise upper bounded by k-FWER, situating k-bFDR between per-comparison and family-wise error control (Section 2, Proposition 2.3).
claims.evidence: 0/108000 pathwise indicator mismatches under the global null and 0/108000 violations of k-bFDP ≤ 1{|H0∩R|≥k} at pi1=0.2, with the inequality strictly slack in 7 of 27 cells (e.g., BH k=1: 0.1618 vs 0.4185); the logbook honestly notes the equality is definitional, but the non-vacuity evidence confirms the substantive ordering claim.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 establishes equivalence between the Domino procedure and the e-value closure principle when using an appropriate local test, connecting Domino to existing multiple-testing paradigms (Section 4, Proposition 4.1).
claims.evidence: Fully exhaustive enumeration at m=9 (50048 subsets, every S, W, T) yields 40/40 identical rejection sets; at m=100, 3000/3000 identical across 2263984 subset-level tests with 0 converse violations; 22123 subsets satisfying (9) but failing standalone (6) confirm the two sides are genuinely different functions, making the agreement non-circular.

claims.claim: Algorithms 3 and 4 reduce the computational complexity of implementing the closure-based procedure from exponential O(2^m) to polynomial O(m^2) for Bonferroni and harmonic-mean-based local tests (Section 3, Algorithms 3-4).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 4 matches exhaustive 2^{m-k} ground truth with 0/51 mismatches at wall-time log-log slope 1.69 ≤ 2; corrected Bonferroni scan matches exhaustive ground truth with 0/102 mismatches at slope 0.63; 15996x speedup at m=20. Algorithm 3 as printed is falsified (60/102 mismatches, k-bFDR 0.9970), but the paper's own Table 1 matches the corrected factor (m-l+k)/k, confirming the complexity-reduction result is valid with a write-up erratum.

michaldobiezynski/repro-generalized-boun.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, non-toy experimental evidence at the paper's own m=100 scale across 106 cells with 20–200× replication counts, confirming k-bFDR control, theorem tightness, pathwise proposition validity, e-closure equivalence, and polynomial complexity reduction. A substantive erratum is identified: Algorithm 3 as printed contains an incorrect factor that breaks the closure procedure, but the corrected version (which the authors' own results implicitly use) validates the complexity claim.

michaldobiezynski/repro-calibrating-deci.paper_title: Calibrating Decision Robustness via Inverse Conformal Risk Control

claims.claim: Theorem 1 establishes that the CREME estimator α̂_ℓ(λ) satisfies E[α̂_ℓ(λ)] ≥ E[ℓ_λ(X_{n+1}, Y_{n+1})], yielding distribution-free, finite-sample upper bounds on both miscoverage and regret simultaneously (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: 640 validity tests across 8 decision problems with 20,000 resampled calibration sets each show 0 violations beyond 3 SE; specific numerical examples (e.g., newsvendor λ=0.524, n=10: miscoverage gap +0.04719 vs theory 0.04785, regret gap +0.16507) and exact eq. (6) gap ≥0 in all configurations confirm the inequality for both miscoverage and regret losses.

claims.claim: Proposition 2 shows the estimator's error decays at the parametric O(n^{-1/2}) rate in the calibration sample size n, giving a finite-sample guarantee rather than only an asymptotic one (Proposition 2).
claims.evidence: Measured log-log slope of RMS estimation error is -0.5025 on [1e3,1e5] and -0.4964 on [1e4,1e6], close to theoretical -0.5; rms*sqrt(n) is flat across five decades (0.46948 to 0.50354), and eq. (8) coverage ≥0.9867 at δ=0.1, confirming the parametric rate empirically.

claims.claim: Proposition 3 proves that, under majorant consistency, miscoverage weakly decreases and regret weakly increases as the robustness parameter λ increases, characterizing a true, certified miscoverage-regret Pareto frontier (Proposition 3).
claims.evidence: Miscoverage weakly decreasing in 8/8 problems (max increment -1.65e-02 ≤ 0); Assumption 3.6 holds in 7/8 problems with 0 counterexamples and 0 dominated frontier points in those 7; the closed-form newsvendor counterexample where Assumption 3.6 fails is independently derivable and exhibits the predicted failure mode. The logbook honestly discloses that the regret monotonicity test is tautological under degenerate X, but the miscoverage monotonicity, strict-domination counts, and counterexample are genuine independent evidence.

claims.claim: The CREME (Conformal REgret Miscoverage Estimate) algorithm is empirically validated across four distinct decision-making paradigms: linear programming, the newsvendor problem, portfolio selection, and shortest-path optimization (Experiments section).
claims.evidence: All four paradigms (LP, newsvendor, portfolio, shortest-path) were re-implemented from Appendix G.1 and run through Algorithm 1; Gap decreases with n in all four paradigms and mean absolute difference to Table 1 is 0.041. Significant caveats exist: shortest-path Gap is ~2x off (0.245/0.142/0.130 vs 0.11/0.06/0.06) due to reconstructed network spec, and the 2-asset portfolio is degenerate (λ cannot move the decision), but the qualitative claim of validation across four paradigms is supported.

claims.claim: Across all four experimental settings, CREME maintains strong performance on both validity (coverage) and accuracy simultaneously, whereas competing calibration methods sacrifice one criterion to achieve the other (Experiments section).
claims.evidence: Under the paper's Fig. 3 protocol, CREME validity is 0.957 (min 0.843) vs Monte Carlo 0.322 (min 0.180), a 3x gain, while accuracy converges (-2.967→-0.116). Fig. 4 shows baselines buy miscoverage 0.056 at regret 0.624 vs CREME's 0.354/0.403. The logbook discloses that under unit weights the Fig. 4 ranking reverses (CREME worse than all baselines), but the primary Fig. 3 validity-accuracy trade-off reproduces decisively and the qualitative Fig. 4 direction holds under any weighting.

michaldobiezynski/repro-calibrating-deci.overall: The logbook provides concrete, non-toy experimental evidence supporting all five claims through a from-scratch implementation spanning 8 decision problems (d=1 to d=1121), 20,000 trials, and n up to 1e6, with specific numerical results for each claim. Notable caveats include a degenerate portfolio instance, a reconstructed shortest-path network with ~2x Gap discrepancy, tautological regret monotonicity under degenerate X, and weight-dependent Fig. 4 rankings, but these do not overturn the core claims.

michaldobiezynski/repro-combinatorial-sp.paper_title: Combinatorial Sparse PCA Beyond the Spiked Identity Model

claims.claim: Diagonal thresholding provably fails on the general-covariance model (Model 2), failing to detect any true support element with probability at least 1/2 even with a Θ(1) eigenvalue gap (Lemma 1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: On a numerically certified Model-2 instance (d=1000, s=9, lam2/lam1=0.5≤0.9, v1(Sigma)=v verified at runtime), diagonal thresholding returned sin²=1.0 on 65/65 runs across n=400–50000 with 0/9 support coordinates recovered, while a spiked-identity control recovered 9/9 with sin²=0.00066.

claims.claim: Covariance thresholding fails analogously, returning an estimate 𝐮 with sin²∠(𝐮,𝐯)=1 with probability at least 1/2 despite sufficient samples (Lemma 3, Section 3).
claims.evidence: On a Model-2 instance constructed from the proof (d=211, s=10, 50-regular graph, lam2/lam1=0.787≤0.9), covariance thresholding returned sin²=1.0 on 23/23 runs at n=5e4–1e6 with zero output mass on supp(v), and sin²=1.0 for all 5 rebuilt Sigma(tau) instances; spiked control gave sin²=0.000121.

claims.claim: Greedy correlation-based selection recovers at most one true support coordinate under Model 2, even when seeded with a correct coordinate (Lemma 4, Section 3).
claims.evidence: On a Model-2 instance (s=100, d=199, lam2/lam1=0.9, verified at runtime), greedy correlation seeded at a true support coordinate recovered only 1/100 support coordinates with sin²=0.994975≥1−1/s=0.99 on 100% of seeds at n=2e5; population bounds (max 0.00595≤1/s on true support, min 0.04050≥0.4/√s on decoys) independently match the proof; spiked control recovered 10/10.

claims.claim: The proposed Restarted Truncated Power Method (RTPM) achieves ⟨𝐯,𝐮⟩² ≥ 9/10 with probability ≥ 1-δ under Model 2 using n = Ω(s² log(s) log(d/δ)) samples and O(nd²) runtime (Theorem 1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: RTPM achieved ⟨v,u⟩²≥9/10 on all 40 runs across 4 Model-2 instances (mean 0.9411, worst 0.9149) at δ=0.1, exceeding 1−δ=0.90, including the three instances where baselines failed totally; however, the sample-complexity constant was fitted rather than tested, r=5s was used instead of the theorem's r=Ω(s²), and the O(nd²) runtime exponent was unconfirmed (measured 1.75–2.17).

claims.claim: Sparse k-PCA cannot be solved by deflation-based self-reduction to the single-component case, since deflated covariance matrices can have fully dense top eigenvectors (Lemma 11, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: On the paper's exact construction (54 configurations, d=4–2000, Δ and γ over two orders of magnitude), the deflated top eigenvector had |supp|=d exactly in 54/54 cases with min |entry|/max=5.297e-3, and running the second deflation iteration showed the barrier bites (best 4-sparse Rayleigh quotient 1.4051 vs λ1=1.5680).

michaldobiezynski/repro-combinatorial-sp.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all five claims on non-toy setups, with each construction transcribed from the paper's proofs, numerically certified to satisfy Model-2 hypotheses at runtime, and paired with spiked-model controls ruling out implementation bugs. The main weakness is Claim 4, where the sample-complexity constant is fitted rather than tested, the parameter regime (r=5s vs Ω(s²)) does not match the theorem, and the runtime exponent is noise-dominated, though the headline accuracy guarantee is properly confirmed.

michaldobiezynski/repro-accelerating-lan.paper_title: Accelerating Langevin Monte Carlo via Efficient Stochastic Runge-Kutta Methods beyond Log-Concavity

claims.claim: The proposed stochastic Runge-Kutta LMC algorithm achieves a uniform-in-time convergence rate of O(d^1.5 h^1.5) in non-log-concave settings (Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: Measured strong-error h-exponents of 1.602/1.466/1.472 at d=10/100/200 on a non-log-concave GMM (LMC control 0.99), flat window error across t0=4–32 (max/min 1.23), and stationary bias 0.0399±0.0735 unresolved from zero vs LMC's 1.5531±0.0741. The d^{1.5} prefactor is satisfied but loose (measured d-exponent ~0), consistent with an upper bound.

claims.claim: The algorithm requires only two gradient evaluations per iteration, compared to three required by the prior stochastic Runge-Kutta scheme of Li et al. (2019) (Section 1).
claims.evidence: Instrumented gradient oracle counts exactly 2.00 grad-U per iteration for RKLMC-2G vs 3.00 for SRK-LD (Li et al. 2019 eq. 9), with order conditions (12)-(14) confirmed to machine precision. Accuracy-equalized comparison shows 5.867e+02 vs 7.425e+02 gradient evaluations at eps=1e-3.

claims.claim: Higher-order Runge-Kutta variants of the method are shown to achieve improved complexity bounds under additional smoothness assumptions (Theorems 2.5-2.7).
claims.evidence: All order-1.5 family members measure h-exponents 1.466/1.468/1.463/1.443/1.457 vs Euler's 0.993; inverted complexity exponents eps^-0.682 (theory -2/3) vs eps^-1.007 for LMC, yielding 16.9x smaller gradient budget at eps=1e-3. Order conditions verified to machine precision.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments compare the proposed Runge-Kutta LMC methods against baseline Euler-based ULA schemes on synthetic and real datasets (Section 4, Figures 3-5).
claims.evidence: GMM slopes LMC 0.997 vs RKLMC-2G 1.602; synthetic BLR slopes 1.005 vs 1.650; Figure 3 histogram reproduced (L1=0.0397 vs i.i.d. floor 0.0345); Figure 4 reproduced (8/8 modes, occupancy TV 0.0088). The logbook documents that the paper uses synthetic data only and has Figures 1-4, not 3-5, but the substantive comparison against Euler ULA reproduces.

claims.claim: A complexity comparison table contrasts the proposed method against competing algorithms, including those of Li et al. and Sabanis (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Table 1's N-G column reproduced exactly (2/3/1+higher-derivative oracles), H-D column reproduced (TELMC requires Hessian-vector and grad-Laplacian), and measured mixing-time eps-exponents -0.682/-0.693/-0.686 match the tabulated -2/3 with Euler control at -1.007.

michaldobiezynski/repro-accelerating-lan.overall: A rigorous from-scratch numpy reproduction with proper controls (Euler order-1 baseline, machine-precision order conditions, independent reference path) that confirms the h^{1.5} rate, two-vs-three gradient count, improved complexity, experimental comparisons, and Table 1 entries, while honestly documenting that the d^{1.5} scaling is loose and that the paper uses synthetic data only with Figures 1-4.

michaldobiezynski/repro-gaussian-mean-fi.paper_title: Gaussian Mean Field Variational Inference can Overestimate Predictive Variance

claims.claim: MFVI underestimates posterior variance in parameter space but can overestimate predictive variance relative to the exact posterior, with Theorem 3.7 proving that for test points drawn from the training distribution's empirical covariance, MFVI's expected predictive variance exceeds that of the exact posterior (Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence:
360 generic BLR instances (P up to 500, Haar-rotated covariances, both N

P) show predictive-variance ratio E_phat[x'S*x]/E_phat[x'Sigma x] above 1 in 360/360 (min 1.000437, median 1.5246) and parameter trace ratio Tr(S*)/Tr(Sigma) below 1 in 360/360 (max 0.0734); proof identity (58) reproduced to 5.9e-12 and S* independently re-derived via L-BFGS to 1e-7 agreement with the closed form.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.6 shows a calibration constraint forcing MFVI to simultaneously underestimate variance in some directions while overestimating in others, with overestimation occurring specifically in directions where training data concentrates (Lemma 3.6).
claims.evidence: On the same 360 instances, the calibration identity (1/P)sum R(v_q)=1 holds to 2.345e-10; only 18.70% of eigendirections are overestimated (median max R=19.90), R>1 at the data's first principal component in 360/360 instances (min 7.2968), and Spearman correlation between data concentration and overestimation has median 0.9564, confirming the directional claim empirically rather than just algebraically.

claims.claim: In a pathological rank-1 training-data subspace scenario, as dimensionality increases the MFVI posterior's predictive variance converges to the prior variance, effectively discarding training information (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: Dense P×P posterior inversion to P=2048 shows MFVI/prior predictive variance reaching 0.9902, with a validated closed form (agreement to 2e-16 at P=512) extending to 0.999986 at P=1,048,576; gap decay log-log slope -0.9994 matches theoretical P^{-1}; exact posterior remains at 4.866e-02 of prior at P=1024, confirming the 20x overestimation. The disclosed post-hoc kappa choice affects only the finite-P figure match, not the config-independent asymptotic claim.

claims.claim: Temperature-scaled posteriors (cold posteriors, T<1) correct the predictive-variance overestimation and improve in-distribution predictions, while T>1 benefits out-of-distribution performance, offering a novel explanation for the Cold Posterior Effect.
claims.evidence: In the paper's rank-1 setting, NLL over 10,000 repetitions shows ID optimal T dropping from 0.5248 (P=2) to 0.05248 (P=1024) with a 0.555-nat gain, OOD optimal T = 10.96 (P=2) and ~1.000 (P=1024); additionally, a hyperparameter-free variance-matching statistic is below 1 for ID in 360/360 generic instances and above 1 for OOD in 360/360, confirming both directions config-independently.

claims.claim: Experiments on basis function regression and UCI datasets show optimal temperatures below 1 for in-distribution test points and above 1 for out-of-distribution test points, consistent with the theoretical predictions (Section 6, UCI experiments).
claims.evidence: On real UCI data with the paper's Appendix-B protocol (6 datasets, 10 splits, Q=500 RBF features, 2000 Adam steps), Train and ID T*<1 in 30/30 marginal and 30/30 joint cases, and T*_OOD > T*_ID in 30/30 and 30/30; the sinc experiment shows 7x amplification of ID variance inflation from Q=16 to Q=1024 with ID T* falling 0.3162→0.0079. The unhedged 'above 1 for OOD' holds in only 16/30 marginal cases, but the paper's own hedged wording and the unconditional ordering reproduce fully; disclosed shrinkage (10 vs 15 splits, 6 vs 9 datasets) reduces power without substituting a proxy.

michaldobiezynski/repro-gaussian-mean-fi.overall: This logbook provides rigorous numerical verification of all five claims through dense linear algebra on 360 generic BLR instances (P up to 500), rank-1 constructions to P=2048, and real UCI experiments with the paper's own protocol, all from a single seeded script with bit-identical re-runs. The main limitations are disclosed post-hoc hyperparameter choices for the rank-1 figure match, grid censoring in UCI OOD temperatures, and reduced splits/datasets in UCI experiments—none of which overturn the core qualitative predictions.

claims.claim: Retrofitting single-system deterministic simulators (Walrus, Lola, Poseidon) with the CRPS-based noise-injection method yields 20-54% reductions in rollout CRPS across datasets (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: A small CNN (~48 hidden channels, 4 blocks) on a synthetic 48×48 2D Navier-Stokes system shows 73.9% CRPS reduction, confirming direction but on a drastically simplified setup with magnitude outside the paper's 20-54% range.

claims.claim: The same single-system retrofitting produces VRMSE gains of up to 21.5% on Rayleigh-Benard, 29.6% on Euler, and 10.1% on Shear Flow (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: Same toy setup reports 76.0% VRMSE improvement on one synthetic system; the paper's per-dataset numbers (21.5% RB, 29.6% Euler, 10.1% Shear Flow) are not individually addressed and the magnitude far exceeds the claimed range.

claims.claim: Retrofitting the HalfWalrus foundation model yields 34-40% improvements in CRPS and over 13% improvement in VRMSE on multi-system adaptation (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: A 2-system-pretrained small CNN adapted to a third synthetic system yields 44.2% CRPS / 35.2% VRMSE improvement, but this is explicitly a toy analog of the protocol, not the 640M-parameter HalfWalrus foundation model.

claims.claim: The method injects noise via conditional layer normalization and trains with a CRPS scoring-rule loss (Algorithm 1) to convert a pretrained deterministic checkpoint into a probabilistic one without retraining from scratch (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 is implemented verbatim from the paper (zero-init AdaLN heads, noise MLP, fair CRPS loss with M=4, differential learning rates, backbone loaded from deterministic checkpoint) and demonstrated to correctly convert a deterministic checkpoint into a working stochastic ensemble without retraining from scratch.

claims.claim: CRPS retrofitting requires under 2 days of training per system on a single H100 GPU, compared to weeks needed for the original deterministic pre-training (Section 5, Table 5).
claims.evidence: Relative overhead of +20% is measured on the toy setup (49.4s vs 41.2s), directionally consistent with the paper's +1% to +25% range, but the absolute 'under 2 days on H100' claim is not testable since the entire experiment runs in minutes on an A10G.

Firemedic15/repro-probabilistic-retrofit.overall: The logbook faithfully implements the paper's Algorithm 1 (conditional layer norm noise injection + fair CRPS loss) and demonstrates it works on a small synthetic 2D turbulence system with a tiny CNN, confirming the method's directionality. However, all numerical claims are tested only at toy scale (48×48 grid, ~48-channel CNN, minutes of compute), far below the paper's 222M-640M parameter models on The Well datasets, so specific magnitudes and per-dataset results remain unverified.

Storm1t/repro-a-tight-theory-of-error-fe.paper_title: A Tight Theory of Error Feedback Algorithms in Distributed Optimization

claims.claim: EF21 achieves a tight convergence guarantee under contractive compression with optimal step size eta_star = (2/(L+mu)) * ((1-sqrt(epsilon))/(1+sqrt(epsilon))), and the resulting contraction rate rho_star is independent of the number of agents n (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: 15 parameter combinations (L, μ, ε) confirm ρ* ∈ (0,1), independence from n (tested n=1,3,10), monotonicity in ε, and the κ→1 edge case (ρ=0.707107 vs √0.5=0.707107). However, the logbook explicitly states it did not run the full PEP/SDP pipeline, so the 'tight' aspect of the guarantee is not independently verified.

claims.claim: Under the statistical homogeneity (shared minimizer) assumption, classic Error Feedback (EF) matches EF21's optimal step size and contraction factor exactly, giving identical tight convergence rates (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: 40 parameter combinations across L ∈ {1,5,50}, μ ∈ {0.1,0.5,1.0}, ε ∈ {0.05,...,0.95} confirm EF and EF21 share identical η* and ρ* from the closed-form formulas, directly supporting the matching claim.

claims.claim: Without the shared-minimizer assumption, classic EF can exhibit 2-periodic cycles under statistical heterogeneity and generally fails to converge in the multi-agent setting (Proposition 2.1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: 9 parameter combinations (μ ∈ {0.5,1.0,2.0}, ε ∈ {0.1,0.5,0.9}) confirm the adversarial counterexample construction yields x₁ = -x₀ to machine precision, demonstrating the 2-cycle failure mode.

claims.claim: The worst-case multi-agent convergence rate proven in Theorem 3.1 exactly matches the known single-agent rate, showing the novel Lyapunov function recovers prior single-agent guarantees as a special case (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: 60 parameter combinations across n ∈ {1,2,5,20,100} confirm ρ* is identical for all n (100% match rate), directly verifying the single-agent rate recovery and n-independence.

claims.claim: For heterogeneous regularity parameters across agents, Corollary 3.2 extends the tight rates to deterministic, additive, positively homogeneous compressors using averaged parameters L-bar and mu-bar (Corollary 3.2).
claims.evidence: 12 heterogeneous configurations (including 3-agent and extreme heterogeneity cases) confirm that averaged parameters L̄, μ̄ yield rates at least as good as worst-case homogeneous rates. The scope is limited to verifying the formula properties, not the full tightness proof.

claims.claim: For the two-agent (n=2) heterogeneous case, an explicit cubic polynomial characterizes the empirically optimal convergence rate, and tuning the EControl algorithm's step size to its optimum yields eta=0, coinciding with EF21 (Law 4.3, Law 4.4, Section 4).

Storm1t/repro-row-stochastic-matrices-ca.paper_title: Row-Stochastic Matrices Can Provably Outperform Doubly Stochastic Matrices in Decentralized Learning

claims.claim: In the weighted Hilbert space L²(λ;R^d), the λ-induced row-stochastic mixing matrix W is self-adjoint whereas the doubly stochastic matrix W^ds is not, and this non-self-adjointness introduces additional multiplicative penalty terms (κ_λ > 1 and λ_max² > 1) that amplify consensus error under the doubly stochastic design (Section 5.2, Section 6.2).
claims.evidence: 14 heterogeneous graph cases (path, star, ring, sizes 3-12) numerically confirm row-stochastic self-adjointness (similarity asymmetry ~1e-16) and DS non-self-adjointness (weighted adjoint residual = 0.135), with all 14/14 cases showing DS incurs κ_λ penalty.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.5 gives O(1/T) convergence rates for both row-stochastic and doubly stochastic strategies, but the row-stochastic strategy achieves strictly smaller non-asymptotic consensus error and can converge faster even when its spectral gap is smaller than that of the doubly stochastic strategy (Theorem 6.5).
claims.evidence: 576-cell grid over λ_max, ρ_J, and gap ratios shows strictly positive A-slack (0.562) and B-slack (1.152), min leading coefficient ratio 1.0002 > 1.0, and 576/576 cells where row-stochastic has smaller spectral gap yet tighter bounds.

claims.claim: Theorem 7.1 derives a sufficient condition on the spectral gaps, 1 − ρ_Λ ≥ max{(1+η)κ_λ^(-1/3), λ_max^(-1/2)}(1 − ρ_J), under which the row-stochastic design provably converges strictly faster than the doubly stochastic design (Theorem 7.1).
claims.evidence: Concrete counterexample with λ_max=16, κ_λ=4×10^6, ρ_J=0.536, ρ_Λ=0.878 shows the stated max-based condition with κ_λ^{-1/3} holds while the source theorem's min-based condition with λ_max^{-1/2} does not, demonstrating the claim's formula diverges from the paper's actual theorem.

claims.claim: Corollary 7.3 and Algorithm 2 give topology construction guidelines showing that when node degrees scale proportionally with their assigned weights (d_i/d_j matching λ_i/λ_j within bounds set by R), the row-stochastic design outperforms the doubly stochastic design, satisfying a Loewner order condition on the graph Laplacians (Corollary 7.3, Remark 7.4, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: Five independent counterexamples: 120/120 test vectors reject the source Laplacian quadratic form, Loewner order fails (min eigenvalue = -0.051 < 0 on a 3-node path with degree-proportional weights), and degree-proportional weights are not gap maximizers (alternative weights give 13.1% better gap on a 4-node paw graph).

Storm1t/repro-row-stochastic-matrices-ca.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence verifying the self-adjointness and convergence bound advantages of row-stochastic matrices (Claims 1-2) on multiple small-to-mid graph configurations, while falsifying Claims 3-4 with specific counterexamples showing the stated spectral condition formula and topology construction guidelines do not hold as written.
