claims.evidence: The logbook implements a genuine deconvolution learner on the fixed-variance Gaussian family N(0,1) with known Gaussian noise, running Monte Carlo trials (up to n=12800) confirming l2 error decays at slope -0.505 (CLT predicts -0.5), error inflation matches e^{(σ α)²/2} (slope 0.88, R²=0.9998), and the log(1+σ r) enumeration sub-term is confirmed logarithmic (Part D).

claims.claim: Corollary 2.14 specializes this bound to Gaussian and Laplace noise models, e.g. for N(0, sigma^2 I_d) noise the extra sample cost scales as O~(d*tau(epsilon)/epsilon^2) * log(1+sigma*r) (Section 2, Corollary 2.14).
claims.evidence: Part B of the Claim 1 audit confirms the Gaussian noise error inflation factor e^{(σ α)²/2} (slope 0.88, R²=0.9998), Part D confirms the log(1+σ r) term is logarithmic, and the Claim 2 audit confirms the eps^{-2} scaling (exponent -1.934 vs predicted -2). The Laplace noise model is not tested, but the primary Gaussian example is confirmed.

claims.claim: Claim 2.5 shows unrestricted Gaussian families {N(mu, sigma^2) : sigma > 0} violate the Local Lipschitz Decodability condition (Assumption 2.1) and are therefore not learnable under this noise model, establishing necessity of the assumption (Section 2, Claim 2.5, Assumption 2.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook never addresses Claim 2.5, the unrestricted Gaussian family {N(μ,σ²): σ>0}, or the Local Lipschitz Decodability condition (Assumption 2.1). No experiment tests whether this family violates the assumption or is unlearnable.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 establishes a sample complexity bound for total-variation learnability under adversarial corruption of s samples with l-infinity budget C, without requiring the Low-Frequency Property (Assumption 2.9) needed in the additive-noise setting (Section 3, Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook contains no experiments related to Theorem 3.2, adversarial corruption, total-variation learnability, or the Low-Frequency Property (Assumption 2.9). This claim is never addressed.

claims.claim: Section 4 derives the first sample complexity bounds for learning k-mixtures of uniform distributions (k-UMMs) under both additive noise and adversarial corruption, and for k-component Gaussian mixture models under adversarial corruption with n >= O~(s*k*d^2/epsilon^2)*log(1/delta) + O~(d*s^2/epsilon^2)*log(1+C/delta) (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook contains no experiments on k-mixtures of uniform distributions, Gaussian mixture models, or the specific sample complexity bound n >= Õ(s·k·d²/ε²)·log(1/δ) + Õ(d·s²/ε²)·log(1+C/δ). Section 4 results are never tested.

HamsterSashka/repro-provable-bounds-for-.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting the additive-noise learnability mechanism (Theorem 2.13/Cor 2.14) on a 1-D Gaussian instance—confirming learnability, error inflation, and the logarithmic enumeration term—and verifies the eps^{-2} rate of the minimum-distance engine. However, three of the five claims (necessity of the decodability assumption, adversarial-corruption bounds, and mixture-model results) are entirely unaddressed.

HamsterSashka/repro-decentralized-online.paper_title: Decentralized Online Convex Optimization with Efficient Communication: Improved Algorithm and Lower Bounds

claims.claim: Top-DOGD achieves O(ω^{-1/2}ρ^{-1}n√T) regret for convex loss functions under compressed communication, improving on prior bounds (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: End-to-end Top-DOGD regret on a synthetic convex D-OCO instance (n=6, d=8, 2-nearest ring, T≈92K) yields an omega-exponent of -0.602 vs claimed -0.50, with a DC-DOGD control at -1.133; the scaling direction is supported but the setup is clearly reduced in scale (small n, small d, synthetic linear losses).

claims.claim: Top-DOGD achieves O(ω^{-1}ρ^{-2}n ln T) regret for strongly convex loss functions (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: No experiment in the logbook addresses the strongly convex regret bound; all runs use convex (linear) losses only.

claims.claim: The paper reduces dependence on compression quality ω from the previously known O(ω^{-2}ρ^{-4}n^{1/2}√T) (convex) and O(ω^{-2}ρ^{-4}n^{1/2} ln T) (strongly convex) bounds down to O(ω^{-1/2}ρ^{-1}n√T) and O(ω^{-1}ρ^{-2}n ln T) respectively, cutting the exponent on ω^{-1} from quadratic/quartic to square-root/linear (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The convex reduction is tested at small scale: Top-DOGD exponent -0.602 vs DC-DOGD control -1.133 supports the claimed square-root-vs-steeper improvement in omega-dependence, but the strongly convex reduction (omega^-2 to omega^-1) is never tested and the setup is n=6, d=8 synthetic.

claims.claim: First lower bounds for decentralized online convex optimization with compressed communication are established: Ω(ω^{-1/2}ρ^{-1/4}n√T) for convex functions and Ω(ω^{-1}ρ^{-1/2}n ln T) for strongly convex functions (Theorems 3.3 and 3.4).
claims.evidence: Construction primitives verified exactly (E[wait]=1/omega, exponent -0.998; cycle delay=dist/omega, exponent -0.994) and forced epoch-adversary regret scales omega^-0.491*sqrt(T) vs claimed omega^-0.50, but only on a small synthetic construction (n=8 cycle), only the convex case, and a universal lower bound cannot be proven by simulating one algorithm.

claims.claim: The algorithm combines a two-level blocking update framework with an online compressed gossip strategy and a projection error compensation scheme to jointly control consensus, compression, and projection error (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The Top-DOGD implementation does combine two-level blocking (L=L1+L2), online compressed gossip (CHOCO with error feedback), and projection error compensation, with a control showing naive biased gossip stalls at 8.5e-2 while error-feedback CHOCO reaches 2e-3; however all demonstrations are at n=6-8, d=8-20 scale.

claims.claim: Bandit-feedback extensions are provided: one-point feedback achieves O(ω^{-1/4}ρ^{-1/2}d^{1/2}n(ln n)^{1/4}T^{3/4}) regret (Theorem 4.1) and two-point feedback achieves O(ω^{-1/2}ρ^{-1}dn ln n√T) regret (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: No experiments in the logbook address the bandit-feedback extensions (one-point or two-point feedback); the reproduction only covers the full-information convex and lower-bound claims.

HamsterSashka/repro-decentralized-online.overall: The logbook provides small-scale synthetic numerical evidence supporting the omega-scaling of the convex regret bound and the lower-bound construction primitives, but does not address the strongly convex bound or bandit-feedback extensions at all. All experiments are at reduced scale (n≤8, d≤20) on synthetic instances, making this a mechanism-level audit rather than a full reproduction.

HamsterSashka/repro-pca-of-probability-m.paper_title: PCA of Probability Measures: Sparse and Dense Sampling Regimes

claims.claim: The empirical covariance operator error is bounded as E||Σ−Σ̂||_HS ≤ R^{1/2} n^{-1/2} + 2R^{1/4} r_m(Φ), combining a parametric n^{-1/2} inter-measure term with an intra-measure approximation term r_m(Φ) (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: Dense n-sweep (m=2000 fixed) yields covariance HS error slope -0.490 (R²=0.998) matching n^{-1/2}, and direct per-measure embedding error r_m(KME) yields slope -0.501 (R²=1.000) matching m^{-1/2}; the degraded control scales worse at -0.264. The additive two-term fit (C2) is weaker (R²=0.83) but the individual rate components are well-confirmed on a non-toy setup (100 anchors, up to 1280 measures, 20 trials).

claims.claim: The dense-regime n^{-1/2} rate for empirical covariance operator estimation is proven minimax optimal (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: Le Cam two-point construction in D=8 Gaussian feature space shows n-sample KL stays flat (0.110→0.112) under n^{-1/2} separation while diverging under n^{-1/4} (0.43→28.58), MC optimal test error remains ~0.42, and the empirical upper-bound slope is -0.501, confirming matching upper and lower rates.

claims.claim: The PCA excess risk satisfies E_q^PCA ≲ n^{-1/2} + √q·m^{-α}, with the √q factor depending on the number of retained components (Theorem 3.7, Equation 5).
claims.evidence: PCA excess risk is only measured at q=1 (slope -0.967, R²=0.996); the √q factor dependence on the number of retained components is never tested, and the m^{-α} term in the PCA excess risk itself is not directly measured (only the building-block r_m is measured).

claims.claim: A sparse-to-dense transition occurs at sampling threshold m ≍ n^{1/(2α)}, separating regimes dominated by the m^{-α} versus n^{-1/2} terms (Section 3).
claims.evidence: No 2D (n,m) sweep is performed to identify the transition threshold m ≍ n^{1/(2α)}; the experiments fix one variable and sweep the other separately, so the sparse-to-dense crossover is never directly observed or tested.

claims.claim: Under practical embeddings, KME and sliced-Wasserstein (SW) require m ≳ n samples per measure while linear optimal transport (LOT) requires m ≳ n^{d/2} to reach the dense regime (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Only the KME embedding is tested; sliced-Wasserstein (SW) and linear optimal transport (LOT) embeddings are never implemented or measured, so the claimed sample complexity thresholds m ≳ n for SW and m ≳ n^{d/2} for LOT are not addressed at all.

HamsterSashka/repro-pca-of-probability-m.overall: The logbook provides solid numerical evidence for the covariance error rate decomposition (Claim 1) and the minimax optimality of the n^{-1/2} rate via a Le Cam construction (Claim 2), both on non-toy setups. Claims 3–5 are not substantively addressed: the √q PCA factor, the sparse-to-dense transition threshold, and the SW/LOT embedding comparisons are all missing.

HamsterSashka/repro-error-analysis-of-di.paper_title: Error Analysis of Discrete Flow with Generator Matching

claims.claim: Unlike discrete diffusion models, discrete flow models trained with generator matching and sampled via uniformization incur no truncation error from truncating the noising time horizon and no discretization error, so the analysis focuses on transition-rate estimation error and early-stopping error (Section 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirms flow initialization error is exactly 0.0e+00 across small settings (K=8, D≤10) and diffusion init error is strictly positive decaying as exp(-1.000*T), but this is a training-free numerical check of a mathematical identity on a small state space, and it only addresses truncation/initialization error while the claim also asserts zero discretization error, which is never tested.

claims.claim: The paper derives a novel Girsanov-type theorem for continuous-time Markov chains (Theorem 1, Change of Measure) that yields a bound on the KL divergence between path measures of two CTMCs with different transition rates, expressed via a Bregman divergence of the transition rates (Theorem 2, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: No experiment in the logbook addresses the Girsanov-type theorem (Theorem 1), the KL divergence bound between CTMC path measures, or the Bregman divergence expression (Theorem 2); these claims are never engaged with.

claims.claim: The stochastic estimation error is decomposed into stochastic error and approximation error, balanced against early-stopping error by choice of the early-stopping parameter, with the resulting stochastic error bound matching the state-of-the-art rate for continuous flow matching and the early-stopping bound matching the most recent discrete diffusion result (Section 1).
claims.evidence: The early-stopping error is verified exactly (tau-exponent 1.000, linear in D with exponent 0.996), but the estimation error is checked via a Nadaraya-Watson kernel surrogate on small dimensions (d=1–3, n≤4000) rather than an end-to-end trained flow, with measured exponents steeper than Stone's theory (-0.63 vs -0.50 at d=2); the reconstructed overall rate n^-0.111 vs claimed n^-0.100 is close but derived from surrogate components.

claims.claim: The framework provides, per the authors, the first non-asymptotic error analysis for discrete flow models, extending the analysis to neural network function classes with ReLU activations under an explicit assumption (Assumption 2, Section 5).
claims.evidence: No experiment addresses the claim of providing the first non-asymptotic error analysis for discrete flow models, nor the extension to neural network function classes with ReLU activations under Assumption 2; these aspects are never tested.

HamsterSashka/repro-error-analysis-of-di.overall: The logbook provides careful but limited training-free numerical checks of two of the four claims: it confirms the zero initialization error property of discrete flow (Claim 1) and verifies component-level rate exponents for the early-stopping and estimation error decomposition (Claim 3) using small-scale surrogates. Claims 2 and 4 are entirely unaddressed, and no actual flow model is trained or evaluated.

HamsterSashka/repro-corrected-samplers-f.paper_title: Corrected Samplers for Discrete Flow Models

claims.claim: Establishes non-asymptotic discretization error bounds for samplers of discrete flow models without imposing boundedness restrictions on transition rates or source distributions (abstract only).
claims.evidence: The audit on a 27-state DFM (D=3, S=2) with exact propagation confirms the Theorem-1 RHS upper-bounds measured Euler TV for all K (8–512) and across shrinking δ (sup-rate up to 200), with the vanishing term scaling K^-0.52 matching the predicted K^-1/2. However, the bound is numerically vacuous (RHS ~33–70 >> 1) at this scale, and the rate-agnostic control bound unexpectedly also held, weakening the 'no boundedness' demonstration.

claims.claim: Derives the discretization error bound by analyzing a one-step lower bound for the Euler sampler, which evaluates transition rates only at the initial state within each time interval (abstract only).
claims.evidence: The logbook tests the final Theorem-1 bound but does not address the specific methodological claim that the bound is derived via a one-step lower bound analysis of the Euler sampler evaluating transition rates at the initial state. No experiment isolates or verifies this derivation approach.

claims.claim: Introduces two corrected samplers, a time-corrected sampler and a location-corrected sampler, that reduce discretization error relative to standard tau-leaping and Euler solvers with minimal added computational overhead (abstract only).
claims.evidence: Both corrected samplers are implemented and tested on the same 27-state toy DFM: time-corrected achieves TV~K^-1.0 vs Euler's K^-0.97 (marginal), and location-corrected achieves TV~K^-2.0 (substantial), with NFE 66.85 vs 64.00 showing minimal overhead. However, no real-scale or text-to-image experiments are conducted.

claims.claim: The location-corrected sampler has lower complexity than existing parallel samplers for discrete flow models (abstract only).
claims.evidence: On the 27-state setup, location-corrected converges at TV~K^-2.0 vs Euler's K^-0.97, requiring ~12 vs ~2175 steps to reach TV≤1e-3 at nearly identical NFE (66.85 vs 64.00), strongly supporting lower complexity in direction and magnitude. But this is a simplified exact-propagation toy setup, not a full-scale parallel sampling benchmark.

claims.claim: Experiments on simulated discrete-state data and text-to-image generation show the corrected samplers achieve improved generation quality and faster inference time than baseline samplers (abstract only).
claims.evidence: The logbook includes only toy-scale simulated discrete-state experiments (27 states, D=3, S=2); the text-to-image generation component of the claim is entirely absent, and no real-scale experiments or baseline quality comparisons are provided.

HamsterSashka/repro-corrected-samplers-f.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous but narrow training-free numerical audit on a 27-state toy DFM with exact propagation, confirming the direction of the theoretical bounds and the dramatic advantage of the location-corrected sampler (K^-2.0 vs K^-1.0 scaling). However, it addresses only 2 of 5 claims at toy scale, omits the text-to-image experiments entirely, and does not test the one-step lower bound derivation methodology.

HamsterSashka/repro-the-implicit-bias-of.paper_title: The Implicit Bias of Steepest Descent with Mini-batch Stochastic Gradient

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows that without momentum, mini-batch steepest descent converges to an approximate max-margin solution only when batch size exceeds the threshold b > 4Rn/(γ+4R), with the margin gap shrinking as batch size increases (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: On a small synthetic setup (n=24, k=3, d=4), the logbook confirms the threshold condition (only m=1 qualifies since m < 1+γ/(4R)=1.037) and shows uphill-loss-step fraction increasing monotonically from 0.000 (full batch) to 0.332 (b=1), but uses proxy metrics rather than directly measuring the margin gap claimed in Theorem 4.1.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 shows that adding momentum allows convergence to the max-margin solution even with small batch sizes, provided β₁→1, revealing a batch-momentum tradeoff (Theorem 4.3, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook contains no experiments with momentum (β₁); all runs use SignSGD without momentum, so Theorem 4.3's batch-momentum tradeoff is never addressed.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.5 shows the momentum-enabled convergence rate is slowed by a factor of m/(1-β₁) relative to the momentum-free large-batch case (Corollary 4.5, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: No momentum experiments are present in the logbook, so the m/(1-β₁) slowdown factor from Corollary 4.5 is never tested.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 proves that variance reduction recovers the exact full-batch implicit bias for any batch size, eliminating the batch-size dependence of the margin, though Corollary 4.7 shows this comes at a convergence rate slowed by a factor of m^(2+a) (Theorem 4.6, Corollary 4.7, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: On a small synthetic setup (n=24), VR peak cosine-to-full-batch direction reaches ~1.000 for all batch sizes (min 0.9996 at b=1) vs plain 0.772, confirming directional recovery; however, the measured iteration slowdown (slope 0.01 vs predicted m^{2+a}=m^{2.5}) is far below the theoretical bound, providing only qualitative rate confirmation.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.9 constructs an orthogonal, scale-skewed data example on which per-sample (batch-size-one) steepest descent converges to a fundamentally different implicit bias than the full-batch solution (Theorem 4.9, Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook constructs orthogonal scale-skewed data (x_i = α_i e_{y_i}, n=8, K=4) matching Theorem 4.9's setup and shows per-sample SignSGD aligns with the predicted Wbar bias (cos=0.9981) while diverging from the full-batch direction (cos=0.9457), with full-batch itself differing from Wbar (cos=0.9428), directly confirming the fundamentally different implicit bias.

claims.claim: Synthetic multi-class linear classification experiments with normalized-SGD under the ℓ₂ norm, varying batch size (b∈{20,200}) and momentum (β∈{0,0.5,0.99}), empirically confirm that momentum or variance reduction restores full-batch-like convergence in small-batch regimes (Section 5, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook uses inf-norm SignSGD instead of ℓ₂-normalized SGD, does not test any momentum values (β∈{0,0.5,0.99}), and uses batch sizes 1–24 instead of {20,200}, so the specific Section 5 experimental setup is not reproduced.

HamsterSashka/repro-the-implicit-bias-of.overall: The logbook provides real numerical evidence on small synthetic setups for three of six claims: the no-momentum batch threshold (Claim 1, via proxy metrics), VR directional recovery (Claim 4), and the orthogonal scale-skewed different-bias example (Claim 5, directly verified). It entirely omits momentum-related claims (2, 3) and does not reproduce the paper's Section 5 experimental setup (Claim 6), using a different norm and no momentum.

HamsterSashka/repro-instance-dependent-c.paper_title: Instance-Dependent Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning via Maximum Likelihood Estimation

claims.claim: CT-MLE estimates the state marginal density directly to guide exploration in continuous-time RL, rather than explicitly estimating drift and diffusion functions of the underlying SDE (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook never implements CT-MLE or any density estimation procedure; it only runs training-free numerical audits of variance and fluctuation scaling on a synthetic OU process. No evidence bears on whether CT-MLE estimates state marginal density directly versus drift/diffusion.

claims.claim: The main regret bound (Theorem 5.10) scales with the eluder dimension of the squared Hellinger distance and the cumulative policy variance term sum of Var^u_n, rather than depending explicitly on the planning horizon (Theorem 5.10).
claims.evidence: The logbook audits component quantities (Var^u scaling as G^1.889 vs predicted G^2, per-interval fluctuation as Delta^3.118 vs predicted ~3) on a synthetic 1D OU process, but explicitly states the full eluder-dimension regret bound was not simulated. No regret was measured, no eluder dimension computed, and the claim about independence from planning horizon was never tested.

claims.claim: Corollary 5.13 shows that when observation frequency (measurement gaps Delta_n,k) adapts to problem complexity, the regret bound becomes nearly independent of the specific measurement schedule chosen (Corollary 5.13).
claims.evidence: A training-free proxy (trapezoid return-reconstruction MSE) on a synthetic 1D OU process shows placement spread of 28% across permutations and 98.5% cross-strategy spread at matched sum-Delta^2, while MSE tracks sum Delta^3 (R^2=0.99) better than the paper's sum Delta^2 (R^2=0.78). This is a proxy task on a simplified setup, not actual regret, and the results partially contradict the paper's specific aggregate.

claims.claim: Proposition 5.9 shows the eluder dimension used in the analysis remains low under a quadratic density model, giving a concrete instantiation of the general instance-dependent bound (Proposition 5.9).
claims.evidence: Proposition 5.9, eluder dimension under a quadratic density model, and any concrete instantiation of the bound are never mentioned or tested anywhere in the logbook.

claims.claim: Algorithm 2 introduces a Monte Carlo-style randomized measurement strategy that samples timepoints within fixed intervals to obtain unbiased reward estimates without substantially increasing measurement cost (Algorithm 2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 2, randomized measurement strategies, unbiasedness of reward estimates, and measurement cost are never implemented or discussed in the logbook.

HamsterSashka/repro-instance-dependent-c.overall: The logbook provides training-free numerical audits of two structural quantities (reward-variance scaling and measurement-resolution fluctuations) on a synthetic 1D OU process, partially supporting component scaling laws but never implementing CT-MLE, measuring regret, computing eluder dimension, or testing Algorithm 2. Three of five claims are entirely unaddressed, and the two examined are at toy scale with proxy metrics.

HamsterSashka/repro-stochastic-gradient-.paper_title: Stochastic Gradient Methods under Heavy-Tailed Noises in Weakly Convex Optimization

claims.claim: Theorem 1 establishes high-probability convergence of projected stochastic subgradient descent (SsGD) for weakly convex functions under sub-Weibull(theta) noise, on a bounded constrained domain (Section 4.1, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook never tests sub-Weibull(theta) noise or Theorem 1's projected (unclipped) SsGD high-probability guarantee on a bounded domain; both logbook pages use Pareto/p-BCM noise only.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows mini-batch clipped-SsGD converges with high probability under p-BCM (p in (1,2]) gradient noise on an unbounded domain, with O(log(T/delta)) dependence on the failure probability delta (Section 4.2, Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The 'Claim 2' page tests clipped-SsGD delta-dependence on an unbounded domain with p-BCM noise at a single fixed T=1000 and without mini-batching, showing log-fit R2=0.98–0.999 and flat quantile ratios (1.3–1.6x) versus heavy-tailed unclipped controls (38–174x blow-up); however, the O(log(T/delta)) T-dependence and the mini-batch mechanism central to Theorem 2 are not exercised.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 gives a fixed-time-horizon variant of the clipped-SsGD result that removes the log T factor, achieving O(log(1/delta)) dependence on delta instead (Section 4.2, Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The 'Claim 2' page uses Thm-3 fixed-horizon tuning (constant lambda, eta) and confirms logarithmic delta-dependence (log-fit R2 up to 0.999), but T is held fixed at 1000 so the distinguishing claim—removal of the log T factor relative to Theorem 2—is never directly tested by varying T.

claims.claim: The resulting sample complexity for clipped-SsGD under p-BCM noise is O~(epsilon^{-2p/(p-1)}) (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: No experiment computes or verifies the sample complexity O~(epsilon^{-2p/(p-1)}); the logbook measures rate exponents in T but never converts to epsilon-accuracy sample counts or tests the complexity bound.

claims.claim: Theorems 4 and 5 provide in-expectation convergence guarantees for clipped-SsGD under p-BCM noise, with Theorem 5 removing the logarithmic dependence on the time horizon when the horizon is fixed (Section 4.2, Theorems 4-5).
claims.evidence: The 'Claim 1' page tests projected clipped-SsGD under p-BCM noise on a bounded domain with Thm-5 fixed-horizon tuning, measuring log-log slopes of -0.240/-0.341/-0.422 for p=1.3/1.5/1.7 (R2=1.000) against predicted (1-p)/p = -0.231/-0.333/-0.412 (within ~4%), with a p-BCM-violating control showing degraded slopes, directly supporting the in-expectation rate claim.

HamsterSashka/repro-stochastic-gradient-.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence for the in-expectation convergence rate of Theorems 4/5 (Claim 5) via precise exponent matching on a genuinely weakly-convex problem with infinite-variance noise, and partial evidence for the poly-log delta-dependence of Theorems 2/3 (Claims 2/3) at fixed horizon without mini-batching. Theorems 1 (sub-Weibull) and the sample complexity claim (Claim 4) are not addressed at all.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-two-layer-linear-aut.paper_title: Two-Layer Linear Auto-Regressive Models Estimate Latent States

claims.claim: The informal main result states that the hidden representation learned by a two-layer linear autoregressive model trained on a partially observed linear dynamical system coincides, up to a similarity transformation S, with the state estimates of the optimal Kalman filter (Theorem 1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: At T=10000 with 5 seeds and n_obs=6>=n_state=4, the learned two-layer linear AR hidden state (global optimum via reduced-rank regression) achieves mean R²=0.9921 with the Kalman filter state after ridge alignment, and a time-shuffle negative control collapses to R²=0.0003, confirming genuine structure recovery on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 (Section 4.4) formalizes this latent-state-recovery result, giving explicit finite-sample error bounds between the learned representation and the Kalman filter estimate up to the similarity transformation.
claims.evidence: The logbook measures relative Frobenius-norm recovery error decreasing with T (0.49→0.15 over T=1000..16000, fitted exponent -0.422), but explicitly states the exact Theorem 4 bound expression is unavailable and cannot be verified; the experiment only shows generic error decrease, not the specific finite-sample bound claimed.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 (Section 4.3) bounds the in-sample prediction error at global optima of the empirical risk at a rate of O(H/T), where H is history length and T is trajectory length.
claims.evidence: With T=3000 and H varied over {2,4,8,16,32,64}, the generalization gap (test MSE - train MSE) correlates with H/T at r=0.993, supporting the O(H/T) rate claim of Theorem 2 on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 (Section 4.3) gives a finite-sample bound on parameter estimation error in Frobenius norm for the learned autoregressive weights.
claims.evidence: Using a fixed ground-truth LDS system with a T=40000 proxy ground-truth weight matrix, the Frobenius-norm parameter estimation error decays with fitted exponent -0.513 across T={500..8000} over 5 seeds, closely matching the theoretical O(1/√T) rate of -0.5.

claims.claim: Proposition 1 (Section 4.1) shows the Kalman filter is well-approximated by a finite-history autoregressive model, with truncation error decaying exponentially in history length L.
claims.evidence: The exact closed-form identity x̂_t - C_ext·z̄_t = Ā^L·x̂_{t-L} holds to machine precision (max error 6.52e-16), and the truncation error decays over 15 orders of magnitude with per-seed fitted decay rate matching the true spectral radius ρ(Ā) to 1.6% median relative error across 5 seeds.

claims.claim: In numerical experiments, a grid search over hidden dimension h identifies h=4 as optimal, matching the true latent state dimension n=4 (Section 5.2, Table 1), and learned activations achieve mean R-squared >= 0.979 alignment with Kalman filter state estimates (Section 5.3, Figure 2, Table 2).
claims.evidence: Training loss is mathematically guaranteed non-increasing in d_hidden for nested reduced-rank regression (confirmed empirically: monotone, minimum at d≥6), so pure loss minimization cannot select h=4; validation-based selection yields majority h=3 (votes [3,4,4,3,3,3,4,5]); while R²=0.9921 at d=4 with T=10000 meets the 0.979 threshold, the grid-search-identifies-h=4-optimal part of the claim is contradicted.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-two-layer-linear-aut.overall: The logbook provides strong experimental support for the theoretical claims (Theorems 1-3, Proposition 1) on independently constructed synthetic LDS systems, with proper global-optimum fitting, negative controls, and scaling experiments. Theorem 4's specific bound remains unverifiable without the theorem statement, and the grid-search claim is falsified by both mathematical argument and empirical evidence, though the R² alignment threshold is met in a separate high-T experiment.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-no-free-lunch-non-as.paper_title: No Free Lunch: Non-Asymptotic Analysis of Prediction-Powered Inference

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 gives an exact non-asymptotic characterization of when PPI++ has lower estimation error (mean squared error) than using gold-standard labels alone, as a function of the correlation between pseudo-labels and gold-standard labels and the number of labeled samples n (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo simulation with 1500 trials per config, correct PPI++ estimator (theta_ppi = mean(Y_lab) + lambda_hat*(mean(Yhat_unlab)-mean(Yhat_lab))), n in {20,50,100,200,500}, and sweep of rho around 1/sqrt(n-2) shows threshold behavior consistent with Theorem 4.1: far from threshold, PPI++ MSE is clearly higher below and lower above, with disagreements only near the boundary (MSE ratio 0.97-1.01).

claims.claim: For Gaussian data, PPI++ outperforms the gold-standard-only estimator if and only if the correlation between pseudo- and gold-standard labels is at least 1/sqrt(n-2), a finite-sample threshold that vanishes only as n grows (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Same simulation confirms the formula rho*(n)=1/sqrt(n-2) arithmetically and tests the iff-condition empirically: 34/45 rho-points across n={20,50,100,200,500} show PPI++ win/loss matching the threshold prediction, with remaining disagreements confined to within 10-15% of the boundary where MSE ratios are near 1.0.

claims.claim: The paper derives exact non-asymptotic variance expressions for PPI++ under sample splitting, in contrast to prior asymptotic 'free lunch' results claiming PPI++ variance is always at most that of gold-standard-only estimation (Section 4, Propositions 4.1-4.6).
claims.evidence: Simulation with corrected PPI++ estimator found 5 explicit configurations (e.g., n=30 rho=0.0945, n=100 rho=0.0505, n=300 rho=0.0290) where PPI++ MSE exceeds classical MSE despite rho>0, providing concrete finite-sample counterexamples to the asymptotic 'free lunch' claim that PPI++ variance is always <= classical variance.

claims.claim: Corollaries 4.1-4.2 extend the main finite-sample no-free-lunch result to derived estimation settings beyond the basic mean-estimation case (Section 4, Corollaries 4.1-4.2).
claims.evidence: Extended corrected PPI++ to OLS slope estimation (derived estimand), sweeping rho around threshold for n in {30,100,300}: 9/12 configurations show the same threshold-like behavior as mean estimation, with 2 mismatches near the boundary, providing concrete evidence that the no-free-lunch phenomenon extends beyond basic mean estimation.

claims.claim: Experiments on real-world datasets illustrate that the theoretical finite-sample threshold on correlation predicts when PPI++ underperforms gold-standard-only estimation in practice (Section 5).
claims.evidence: On the paper's actual AlphaFold (rho=0.815) and Galaxies (rho=0.741) datasets with 2000 trials, only 11/18 configurations are consistent with theory — systematic failures occur at n=4-8 where theory predicts PPI++ should outperform but it doesn't, and the reproduction does not replicate the paper's Section 5 experimental methodology (varying n rather than varying predictor quality as the paper likely did).

sabaridsnfuji/repro-no-free-lunch-non-as.overall: The logbook provides solid simulation-based evidence for Claims 1-4 using a corrected PPI++ estimator, confirming the finite-sample no-free-lunch threshold phenomenon for mean estimation, the Gaussian threshold formula, counterexamples to asymptotic free lunch, and qualitative extension to OLS slope. Claim 5 remains inconclusive: while the paper's actual AlphaFold and Galaxies datasets were obtained and tested, only 61% of configurations match theory and the experimental approach (sweeping n with fixed high-correlation data) differs from the paper's likely methodology of varying predictor quality.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-quantifying-llm-atte.paper_title: Quantifying LLM Attention-Head Stability: Implications for Circuit Universality

claims.claim: Middle-layer attention heads show the lowest cross-refit stability, e.g., layer 5 drops to ≈0.70 stability versus ≈1.0 in layer 1, quantified via a layer-wise mean stability measure (Equation 5, Section 4.1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: A 6-layer GPT2-architecture model (4 heads, 64-dim, random init, toy data, 3 seeds, 25 epochs) was genuinely trained and per-head cosine-similarity stability computed, yielding layer stabilities [0.496, 0.496, 0.506, 0.503, 0.502, 0.508] — all at chance level with no middle-layer dip, but the setup is far below the paper's pretrained-LLM scale.

claims.claim: Middle layers also exhibit broader, less sharply defined off-diagonal head-to-head matching patterns across refits compared to early/late layers (Section 4.2, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Off-diagonal head-to-head cosine-similarity matrices were computed on the same 6-layer toy model, yielding per-layer off-diagonal std [0.027, 0.027, 0.032, 0.028, 0.027, 0.031] with no layer-dependent pattern, but the random-init toy setup is too small to reproduce the paper's pretrained-model phenomenon.

claims.claim: In deeper architectures (8- and 12-layer models), the least-stable layer occurs at a relative depth r≈0.4–0.8, showing stronger mid-depth divergence than shallower models (Section 4.6.2, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: Models at depths 6, 8, and 12 were trained (3 seeds each) and least-stable-layer relative depths computed (0.20, 0.57, 0.36), but all per-layer stabilities sit at ~0.5 chance level, making the 'least stable layer' location noise-driven rather than a structural signal at this toy scale.

claims.claim: Using AdamW (weight decay) yields a clear increase in attention-head seed-stability for deeper MLP models (8- and 12-layer) without degrading task performance (Section 4.5, Figure 6).
claims.evidence: An 8-layer model was trained under AdamW (weight_decay=0.05) vs plain SGD with 3 seeds each, yielding mean stabilities AdamW=0.5012 vs SGD=0.5034 (delta=-0.0022), but both are at chance level so no optimizer effect is detectable at this toy random-init scale.

claims.claim: Higher query-weight norms correlate with lower head stability, suggesting weight-norm control as a mechanistic driver of the weight-decay stability effect (Section 4.4.1).
claims.evidence: Per-layer query-weight norms and stability were computed on the 6-layer toy model, yielding Pearson r=+0.093 (weak, wrong sign vs paper's predicted negative), but with only 6 data points the correlation estimate has extremely high variance and the setup is toy-scale.

claims.claim: The residual stream is consistently more stable across refits than the corresponding attention heads, across all tested architectures and optimizers, as measured via Centered Kernel Alignment (Section 4.7, Figure 9, Appendix A.7).
claims.evidence: Linear CKA was implemented from scratch and applied to a 6-layer trained model, yielding residual CKA mean=0.783 vs attention-output CKA mean=0.903 — a decisive opposite-direction result (attention more stable than residual at every layer), but at toy scale with random-init briefly-trained models rather than the paper's real pretrained LLMs.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-quantifying-llm-atte.overall: All six claims were addressed with genuine gradient-based training and real numerical measurements, but exclusively at toy scale (6–12 layer, 64-dim, random-init GPT2-architecture models on tiny text data, ~3 min total compute), where most signals sit at chance level and Claim 6's CKA result runs opposite to the paper. The reproduction is honest about its limitations but does not approach the paper's pretrained-LLM scale, so no claim is verified or falsified at full scale.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-on-the-accuracy-of-n.paper_title: On the Accuracy of Newton Step and Influence Function Data Attributions

claims.claim: Theorem 1.5 bounds the Newton-step approximation error to the true leave-one-out retrained parameter using only local strong convexity in a neighborhood of the Newton step, rather than the global strong convexity assumed in prior analyses (Theorem 1.5, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Measured Hessian min-eigenvalue collapsing 3400x along a ray from θ_hat (confirming global strong convexity fails) while local μ_local=0.1489 holds, with NS-error vs n slope -2.057 (predicted -2, R²=0.973) on n up to 16000; ridge-regularized negative control does not collapse, confirming the effect is genuine.

claims.claim: For logistic regression with n samples, d-dimensional Gaussian features, and k removed points, the average-case Newton-step attribution error scales as Õ(kd/n²), while the average-case influence-function error scales as Õ((k^{3/2}d^{1/2}+k^{1/2}d^{3/2})/n²) (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: Joint log-log regression across a 20-point (n,d) grid gives NS d-slope 0.985 (predicted 1) and IF d-slope 1.709 (predicted ~1.5 at k=1), with R²=0.975; n-slopes of ~-1.56 (predicted -2) show a notable discrepancy likely attributable to finite-size effects, but the d-exponent match and high R² support the claimed scaling. Only k=1 is tested, so k-dependence is unverified.

claims.claim: The derived upper bounds match corresponding lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors, showing the Newton step is provably more accurate than influence functions whenever d ≫ k (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: Across d in {5,10,20,40,80} with k=1 and 15 paired trials per d (75 total), NS beat IF in 75/75 trials (binomial p=2.65e-23), with median IF/NS error ratio growing monotonically from 3.49x to 21.13x as d increases, directly demonstrating the d≫k advantage.

claims.claim: Rescaled and doubly-rescaled influence functions (RIF and DRIF) are shown to match the Newton step's Õ(kd/n²) average-case error rate while preserving the additivity property that plain influence functions have but the Newton step lacks (Theorem 1.6, Theorem 1.7).
claims.evidence: RIF additivity residual is 9.67e-16 (machine precision) vs NS's 9.13e-04, with a broken-joint-Hessian negative control reproducing NS's large residual; DRIF and RIF errors at n=8000 (3.51e-4 and 4.51e-4) are close to NS (3.05e-4) and much better than IF (1.72e-3), though only 4 n-values are tested without an exponent fit.

claims.claim: The paper's revised bounds remove the problematic 1/λ³ dependence on the regularization coefficient λ present in prior influence-function error analyses (Section 1, Discussion of prior bounds).
claims.evidence: Lambda sweep across {2.0,...,0.0625} shows 1/μ_local essentially flat (slope -0.001, ranging 6.57–6.60) while 1/λ³ explodes 34000x (0.12 to 4096), directly demonstrating that the local-convexity constant used by the revised bound is independent of λ, removing the cubic dependence.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-on-the-accuracy-of-n.overall: The logbook provides a from-scratch reproduction with concrete numerical evidence on the paper's exact synthetic setup (Gaussian-feature logistic regression with exact leave-T-out retrain as ground truth), including negative controls and parameter sweeps. Key limitations are that only k=1 is tested (leaving k-dependence unverified for the scaling laws), the n-exponent in Claim 2 deviates notably from -2, and RIF/DRIF scaling is checked at only 4 points without an exponent fit.

tomyimkc/repro-learning-the-best-under-c.paper_title: Learning the Best Under Constraints: A Duality-Based Framework

claims.claim: Establishes instance-dependent lower bound on sample complexity as multi-level optimization problem.
claims.evidence: The experiment used a hand-derived simplified bound (max of unconstrained/constraint terms) rather than the paper's multi-level optimization formulation, and a naive track-and-stop algorithm rather than the paper's duality-based method, on a 2-arm single-covariate fixed instance. Real runs produced ratios of 30–41, but these do not test the actual claim about multi-level optimization.

claims.claim: Duality-based decomposition algorithm achieves computationally efficient updates with convergence to relaxed bound.
claims.evidence: The paper's duality-based algorithm with online λ updates was never implemented, and the measurement apparatus is demonstrably broken: the main-run ratio of 0.165 (<1) is mathematically impossible for a valid lower bound, and the positive control failed to stop early despite an expected bound of 13.6, indicating a stopping-rule/bound mismatch that invalidates all measurements.

tomyimkc/repro-learning-the-best-under-c.overall: Neither claim was verified or falsified. Claim 1 was tested only on a simplified proxy (non-paper bound and algorithm) yielding toy-level evidence, while Claim 2's experiment had fundamental measurement bugs (impossible ratio <1, failed positive control) and omitted the core duality-based algorithm, making all results uninterpretable.

tomyimkc/repro-decentralized-bandits-wit.paper_title: Decentralized Bandits without Global Clock for Dynamic Matching Market

claims.claim: Way-SE achieves O(K²logT/Δ_min²) regret in one-sided learning with uncoordinated player arrivals
claims.evidence: The normalized constant C = regret·Δ_min²/(K²·log T) grows from ~0.65 at T=2500 to ~7.20 at T=20000 (seed 0), a ~11× increase over an 8× increase in T, consistently across both seeds, indicating regret grows substantially faster than O(K² log T / Δ_min²). The setup is non-toy (K=5, T up to 20000, dynamic player arrivals/departures with p_arrive=0.05, p_departure=0.0001).

claims.claim: Way-SE-2S achieves O(T^((K-1)/K)logT) sublinear regret in fully decentralized two-sided setting without global signals
claims.evidence: Log-log regression of regret vs T in the dynamic two-sided setting (K=2, departures) yields an exponent of 1.39 avg (range 1.02–1.77 across 2 seeds), far exceeding the claimed (K-1)/K = 0.5. Even the minimum observed exponent (1.02) is more than double the claimed value. The static positive control yields exponent 0.39, below 0.5, suggesting the implementation can achieve sublinear regret when departures are absent.

tomyimkc/repro-decentralized-bandits-wit.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence that both regret bounds are violated: Claim 1's normalized constant grows unboundedly with T, and Claim 2's dynamic regret exponent far exceeds the claimed sublinear rate. However, both falsifications rest on small-scale setups (K=5 and K=2 respectively, only 2 seeds each) and implementations that may not faithfully capture the paper's exact algorithms, particularly the 'Way' exploration strategy.

claims.claim: MaxRL defines a compute-indexed family of sample-based objectives that interpolates between standard RL and exact maximum likelihood as sampling compute increases (Abstract).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides a numerical audit of the Maclaurin expansion showing gradient weights W_T = (1-q^T)/p interpolating monotonically from 1.0 at T=1 (standard RL) to 1/p at T→∞ (exact ML), with concrete tables across multiple success rates (p=0.01 to 0.50) and truncation orders (T=1,4,16,64), confirming the compute-indexed interpolation property.

claims.claim: The MaxRL objectives admit a simple unbiased policy-gradient estimator for non-differentiable sampling settings (Abstract).
claims.evidence: The logbook derives the advantage estimator adv_i = (r_i - mean_r)/(mean_r + epsilon), shows its correspondence to the truncated ML gradient weight, and provides a Monte Carlo verification (10,000 trials, N=8, p=0.25) yielding 0.6523 vs theoretical 0.7500 (13% relative error). The mathematical derivation is sound and the numerical check is approximately consistent, though the 13% gap leaves some uncertainty about finite-sample behavior.

claims.claim: The paper claims MaxRL converges to maximum-likelihood optimization in the infinite-compute limit (Abstract).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides numerical tables showing L_T(p) = -sum_{k=1}^{T} q^k/k converging to exact log(p) as T increases, with geometric convergence rate (1-p)^T. For p=0.1, relative error drops from 0.609 at T=1 to 0.0001 at T=64, confirming convergence to maximum-likelihood optimization in the infinite-compute limit.

claims.claim: Empirically, MaxRL Pareto-dominates tested existing methods across all evaluated models and tasks (Abstract).
claims.evidence: The only empirical test was a toy binary denoising task with an 8-parameter 2-layer linear policy and 200 problems, yielding pass@1 of 0.010 for both methods (tie) and pass@32 of 0.165 (MaxRL) vs 0.155 (GRPO), a marginal 1.06x difference. This does not reproduce the paper's claimed Pareto dominance across multiple models and tasks at scale.

claims.claim: MaxRL reports up to 20x test-time scaling efficiency gains compared with a GRPO-trained counterpart (Abstract).
claims.evidence: The toy experiment achieved only a 1.06x efficiency ratio (0.165/0.155), far from the claimed 20x. The full-scale Qwen3-4B experiment requiring 4×8 H200 GPUs was not conducted due to compute constraints, so the 20x scaling efficiency claim was only addressed on a drastically simplified 8-parameter setup.

erobinson/repro-maximum-likelihood-reinf.overall: The logbook provides solid numerical verification of the three theoretical claims (compute-indexed interpolation, unbiased estimator, and convergence to ML) through mathematical derivation and numerical audit. The two empirical claims were only tested on a toy 8-parameter binary denoising task showing marginal 1.06x gains, with no large-scale reproduction attempted due to compute limitations.

tomyimkc/repro-statistical-consistency-a.paper_title: Statistical Consistency and Generalization of Contrastive Representation Learning

claims.claim: A minimizer of the contrastive loss ℒ(s) is proven to be a maximizer of the ranking-based retrieval objective ℰ(s), establishing Fisher consistency between the contrastive training objective and downstream retrieval performance (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Exact finite-discrete computation (d_x=10, d_y=200) of population L and E with 7200 perturbations and 7800 exhaustive column swaps yielding zero violations in both L-minimality and E-maximality, plus a mismatched-negative control showing L_gap=0.409 and E_gap=0.099 (both positive), directly testing the theorem's mathematical content on a non-trivial instantiation.

claims.claim: A calibration-style inequality bounds the downstream retrieval suboptimality by the square root of the excess contrastive risk, ℰ*−ℰ(s) ≤ √(2/τ·(ℒ(s)−ℒ*)), quantitatively linking upstream loss gaps to downstream ranking gaps (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: Exact computation of E*-E(s) ≤ √(2/τ·(L(s)-L*)) across 12,177 candidate scorers in 3 worlds with different τ and sizes, yielding zero violations (worst LHS-RHS=0.0), with an adversarial homotopy reaching ratio 0.4997 showing the bound is non-vacuous, and a reverse-direction control falsified by 11 scalar multiples having zero downstream gap but upstream excess up to 109.4.

claims.claim: For supervised contrastive representation learning (SCRL), the generalization bound scales as O(1/m + 1/√n) in the number of negatives m and number of anchors n (Theorem 4.5).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo measurement of generalization gap at a single scorer (population optimum s*) in a finite discrete world (d_x=15, d_y=150) shows inner-error log-log slope -0.884 vs theory -1 and outer-error slope -0.499 vs theory -0.5, but the setup tests only one point rather than the sup over a function class W that the theorem states, making it a proxy for the full uniform bound.

claims.claim: For self-supervised contrastive representation learning (SSCRL) with shared negative samples, the generalization bound scales as O(1/√m + 1/√n), a slower rate in m than the supervised case (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: Same simplified single-scorer finite-discrete setup as Claim 3, measuring shared-negative RMS gap slope -0.460 vs theory -0.5, a flooring n-sweep (tail slope 0.004), and floor-vs-m slope -0.442, with an independent-negative control slope -0.678; results are qualitatively consistent but on a proxy setup rather than the full function-class uniform bound.

claims.claim: The generalization analysis decomposes error into an inner error term from negative sampling and an outer error term from anchor point sampling, explaining why increasing the number of negatives improves rather than degrades generalization, contradicting prior O(log m/√n) bounds (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Inner error monotonically decreasing across m (slope -0.906, opposite to deteriorating log m bounds) and outer error level ratio 0.952 between m=10 and m=200 under independent negatives vs 3.805 under shared negatives, demonstrating separability on the same simplified single-scorer finite-discrete proxy setup rather than a full reproduction of the decomposition over a function class.

claims.claim: Empirical validation on CLIP models shows generalization behavior consistent with the derived bounds as negative sample size is scaled (Section 5).
claims.evidence: No real CLIP model, no DFN/ImageNet/MSCOCO data, no GPU; instead a synthetic finite-discrete world (d_x=15, d_y=150) with n up to 16000 (vs paper's 6-14M) using a plug-in frequency estimator as a stand-in for trained CLIP, showing monotone-then-saturating E_hat curves at the paper's m/n ratios with a mismatched-negative control that breaks the effect.

tomyimkc/repro-statistical-consistency-a.overall: The logbook provides exact-computation verification of the two pointwise theoretical claims (Fisher consistency and calibration inequality) on non-trivial finite-discrete instantiations with thorough controls, and demonstrates the generalization-rate scaling claims (3-5) and the CLIP empirical claim (6) on clearly simplified proxy setups with real but approximate Monte Carlo numbers.

RyeCatcher/repro-balancing-learning-rate.paper_title: Balancing Learning Rates Across Layers: Exact Two-Step Dynamics and Optimal Scaling in Linear Neural Networks

claims.claim: For two-layer linear networks trained on single-index targets, Theorem 5.3 gives exact closed-form test-loss expressions after one and two gradient steps, with the one-step loss containing linear signal-alignment terms plus quadratic/interaction over-updating terms, and the two-step loss exhibiting higher-order dependence on the product η₁η₂ of the two layers' learning rates.
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo validation of the closed-form two-step loss at small widths h∈{50,100,200} shows gaps shrinking with h (e.g., L2 gap 0.00098→0.00006→0.00005), confirming asymptotic-order consistency but not an exact algebraic re-derivation or evaluation at scale.

claims.claim: Corollary 5.4 shows that for a learning-rate budget η₁+η₂=2h^α with 1<α≤3/2, symmetric learning rates η₁=η₂=h^α are suboptimal after one gradient step but become locally optimal after two steps in sufficiently wide two-layer networks.
claims.evidence: Finite-difference curvature tests at α∈{0.5,1.0,1.25,1.5} confirm d²L₁/dt²<0 (suboptimal after one step) and d²L₂/dt²>0 at h=4·max(h*,256) for α∈{1.25,1.5} (locally optimal after two steps), with an analytic fallback resolving a float64 underflow case.

claims.claim: For three-layer linear networks, Theorem 5.5 derives analogous one- and two-step test-loss formulas under a critical learning-rate scaling η₁,η₂≤O(h), a stricter regime than the O(h√h) scaling used for two-layer networks.
claims.evidence: Three-layer closed-form validation at h∈{50,100,200} shows tight 1-step matches but loose 2-step gaps (0.0379→0.0215→0.0130), confirming qualitative shrinking trend without precise numerical agreement at these small widths.

claims.claim: Corollary 5.6 demonstrates a similar transition from asymmetric to balanced optimal learning rates in three-layer networks for 0<α≤2/3.
claims.evidence: Curvature sign tests at α∈{0.3,0.5} confirm the asymmetric-to-balanced transition (d²L₁/dt²<0, d²L₂/dt²>0 at h=4h*), matching the corollary's interior predictions; the α=2/3 boundary is flagged as potentially inconsistent with the paper's h*-equation but this appears to be an asymptotic-approximation artifact rather than a refutation of the transition claim.

claims.claim: Proposition 5.1 decomposes each layer's gradient as G_ℓ^t = B_ℓ^t - A_ℓ^t, where A terms capture data-aligned components and B terms capture self-interaction effects that are suppressed by a factor of 1/(√h - 1) below the critical learning-rate threshold.
claims.evidence: Algebraic identity G=B−A holds exactly (max error 0.0); the suppression claim ||B||/||G||≤1/(√h−1) holds at every h∈{50,100,200,400} for both two- and three-layer cases with fitted decay exponents −0.46 and −0.50 (theory: −0.5), and a negative control shows the OCR-literal ||G−A||/||G|| is flat near 2, confirming it is a transcription artifact.

RyeCatcher/repro-balancing-learning-rate.overall: The logbook provides careful numerical validation of the paper's theoretical claims at small widths (h≤1024), with direct curvature-sign tests confirming the optimality transitions (Claims 2, 4) and exact algebraic identity plus scaling checks confirming the gradient decomposition (Claim 5), while the closed-form loss expressions (Claims 1, 3) are validated only as asymptotic-order matches via Monte Carlo rather than full-scale verifications.

RyeCatcher/repro-gaussian-mean-field-var.paper_title: Gaussian Mean Field Variational Inference can Overestimate Predictive Variance

claims.claim: MFVI underestimates posterior variance in parameter space but can overestimate predictive variance relative to the exact posterior, with Theorem 3.7 proving that for test points drawn from the training distribution's empirical covariance, MFVI's expected predictive variance exceeds that of the exact posterior (Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence: At N=20, P=5 with spherical prior, the measured difference E[exact_var − MFVI_var] = −2.04e−05 against variances of ~0.0248 is a 0.08% relative gap at the numerical noise floor; the setup is too small and too symmetric for the diagonal approximation to be meaningfully wrong, so the instrument cannot discriminate the theorem's predicted direction.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.6 shows a calibration constraint forcing MFVI to simultaneously underestimate variance in some directions while overestimating in others, with overestimation occurring specifically in directions where training data concentrates (Lemma 3.6).
claims.evidence: The test uses an arbitrary random PSD covariance with a diagonal approximation and no training data, yielding avg_R=11.30 instead of 1.0; this purely algebraic proxy does not instantiate data-calibrated MFVI via KL minimization, so it does not test the actual conditions of Lemma 3.6.

claims.claim: In a pathological rank-1 training-data subspace scenario, as dimensionality increases the MFVI posterior's predictive variance converges to the prior variance, effectively discarding training information (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: Rank-1 setup with only P∈{2,4,8,16} and N=10 produced ratios of 0.07–0.14 (not converging to 1.0 as predicted), but the dimensions are far too small for an asymptotic claim and the setup uses exact rather than data-driven MFVI, so it cannot confirm or refute the pathological effect.

claims.claim: Temperature-scaled posteriors (cold posteriors, T<1) correct the predictive-variance overestimation and improve in-distribution predictions, while T>1 benefits out-of-distribution performance, offering a novel explanation for the Cold Posterior Effect.
claims.evidence: The experiment merely verifies that var_{T=0.5} = 0.5 × var_{T=1.0}, which is definitional and cannot fail; the substantive claims—that cold posteriors correct overestimation, improve in-distribution predictions, and that T>1 helps OOD—were never tested.

claims.claim: Experiments on basis function regression and UCI datasets show optimal temperatures below 1 for in-distribution test points and above 1 for out-of-distribution test points, consistent with the theoretical predictions (Section 6, UCI experiments).
claims.evidence: No real UCI data or basis function regression was used; a purely synthetic NLL proxy yielded opt_T_id=0.3 (matching) but opt_T_ood=0.3 (contradicting the expected >1), so the OOD prediction is not confirmed and the setup is a simplified proxy rather than the paper's actual experiments.

RyeCatcher/repro-gaussian-mean-field-var.overall: This logbook consists entirely of small-scale synthetic NumPy/SciPy experiments (N≤20, P≤16, no real datasets, no actual MFVI training) that are too simplified to meaningfully verify or falsify any of the five claims. The only non-toy attempt (Claim 1) produced a noise-level difference that the setup itself cannot discriminate, rendering it inconclusive.

RyeCatcher/repro-stochastic-gradient-met.paper_title: Stochastic Gradient Methods under Heavy-Tailed Noises in Weakly Convex Optimization

claims.claim: Theorem 1 establishes high-probability convergence of projected stochastic subgradient descent (SsGD) for weakly convex functions under sub-Weibull(theta) noise, on a bounded constrained domain (Section 4.1, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook only evaluates the formula O(σ² log(1/δ) max_t(η_t)) at δ=0.01 and checks the asymptotic order as θ→1/2. No actual SsGD algorithm was implemented or run on any weakly convex problem with sub-Weibull noise; the 'verification' is just confirming the theorem's formula structure, not testing whether the bound holds empirically or verifying the proof.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows mini-batch clipped-SsGD converges with high probability under p-BCM (p in (1,2]) gradient noise on an unbounded domain, with O(log(T/delta)) dependence on the failure probability delta (Section 4.2, Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook computes log(T)≈6.91 and log(1/δ)≈3.00 for T=1000, δ=0.05 and confirms the formula contains both terms. No clipped-SsGD was run on any unbounded-domain problem with p-BCM noise; this is arithmetic evaluation of a formula, not experimental evidence that the convergence bound holds.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 gives a fixed-time-horizon variant of the clipped-SsGD result that removes the log T factor, achieving O(log(1/delta)) dependence on delta instead (Section 4.2, Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook evaluates bounds [7.60, 9.90, 12.21] for Theorem 2 and [3.00, 3.00, 3.00] for Theorem 3 at T=100,1000,10000, showing T3 is constant. This only confirms the formula structures differ as claimed; no algorithm was run to test whether the fixed-horizon bound actually holds in practice.

claims.claim: The resulting sample complexity for clipped-SsGD under p-BCM noise is O~(epsilon^{-2p/(p-1)}) (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook plugs p=1.1, 1.5, 2.0 into the exponent formula -2p/(p-1) getting -22.0, -6.0, -4.0. This is just evaluating the claimed formula at sample points, not deriving or empirically validating the sample complexity through any optimization experiment.

claims.claim: Theorems 4 and 5 provide in-expectation convergence guarantees for clipped-SsGD under p-BCM noise, with Theorem 5 removing the logarithmic dependence on the time horizon when the horizon is fixed (Section 4.2, Theorems 4-5).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirms Theorem 4's bound contains log(eT)≈7.91 for T=1000 while Theorem 5's does not. This is a structural comparison of formula text, not an experimental test of in-expectation convergence behavior of clipped-SsGD under p-BCM noise.

RyeCatcher/repro-stochastic-gradient-met.overall: The logbook performs only arithmetic evaluations of theorem formulas at specific parameter values, confirming that the mathematical expressions have the claimed structure. No optimization algorithms were implemented or run on any problem, no convergence behavior was tested, and no proofs were verified, making the evidence insufficient to confirm or refute any of the five theoretical claims.

RyeCatcher/repro-a-fine-grained-understa.paper_title: A Fine-Grained Understanding of Uniform Convergence for Halfspaces

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes a public-state baseline privacy bound via standard composition, epsilon = O(sqrt(Delta^2 log(1/delta) T/(n^2 sigma^2))) when the noise-blending parameter beta_t = 0, against which the hidden-state analysis (Theorem 3.2) is compared (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: An RDP-composition accountant reproduced sqrt(T) scaling (slopes 0.501 and 0.502) and the sqrt(d/K) ratio (within 1%), but the logbook explicitly flags a discrepancy: the paper attributes the no-d/K formula to beta_t=1 and the d/K-scaled formula to beta_t=0, the opposite of the claim. The check is described as a standard-composition sanity check, not an independent derivation.

RyeCatcher/repro-privacy-amplification-i.overall: The logbook provides formula evaluations and small-scale numerical checks that partially support the paper's theoretical claims, but most are conducted at simplified scales (dim=5, single parameter settings, proxy theorems) rather than full reproductions. Only Claim 2's direct closed-form evaluation with a discriminating negative control reaches a verified bar; the rest are toy-scale spot checks.

RyeCatcher/repro-softmax-as-linear-atten.paper_title: Softmax as Linear Attention in the Large-Prompt Regime: a Measure-based Perspective

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 establishes non-asymptotic concentration bounds of order σ⁶ln(L)/L^(c₂/σ²) showing finite-prompt softmax attention outputs converge to their infinite-prompt counterparts as prompt length L grows, for i.i.d. Gaussian inputs (Section 3, Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: Small-dimensional CPU-only setup testing only qualitative shape (monotone decrease in L, increase in σ) rather than the actual σ⁶ln(L)/L^(c₂/σ²) bound; constants c₁,c₂ undetermined, and the pre-registered negative control (log-power fit gain margin 0.0077) failed to clear the 0.02 threshold, so the ln(L) correction term is not statistically distinguished from a pure power law.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.4 extends the concentration result to gradients, giving comparable convergence rates for gradient stability along the training trajectory (Section 3, Proposition 3.4).
claims.evidence: grad_V leg is explicitly an analytic reduction of Claim 1's quantity (not an independent simulation), grad_U uses finite differences (ε=1e-3) without autodiff, no negative control, and only qualitative monotonicity and ordering are checked on a small setup (L up to 1000, unspecified small d).

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 shows that under Gaussian input measures, the infinite-prompt softmax attention operator reduces to an affine map T^(U,V)[μ](z) = Vm + VΓK^⊤Qz, i.e., structurally equivalent to linear attention (Section 2, Lemma 2.1).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo estimate (400k samples, d=4) of the exact Gaussian integral matches the closed-form affine map to 0.37% relative error, and the Γ→0 limit collapses to Vm at 6.8e-9 relative error — a tight numerical confirmation of an exact, dimension-independent identity.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 proves that the asymptotic training risk of finite-prompt softmax attention under gradient flow is bounded by the infinite-prompt linear-attention risk plus an error term ε, allowing optimization analyses to transfer from linear to softmax attention (Section 4, Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: d=2 setup with gradient flow replaced by ~60 steps of L-BFGS-B on MC-sampled risk (n_mc=150); the gap shrinks (0.267→0.139→0.024) qualitatively but the optimizer and scale are far from the paper's asymptotic gradient-flow regime.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 shows that in the large-prompt regime, softmax attention achieves Bayes-optimal risk for in-context linear regression with anisotropic Gaussian covariates, extending prior results restricted to the isotropic case (Section 5, Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: Anisotropic Σ=diag(3.0,0.3) at d=2 with the same L-BFGS-B approximation as Claim 4; gap shrinks (0.475→0.138→0.040) but the setup is small-scale with an approximate optimizer, not a faithful test of Bayes-optimality in the large-prompt regime.

RyeCatcher/repro-softmax-as-linear-atten.overall: The logbook numerically confirms Lemma 2.1's exact Gaussian-integral identity (Claim 3) with tight Monte Carlo agreement, but the remaining four claims are tested only on small-dimensional setups with approximate optimizers and qualitative shape checks rather than quantitative bound verification.

RyeCatcher/repro-convergence-rate-of-the.paper_title: Convergence Rate of the Last Iterate of Stochastic Proximal Algorithms

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes an Õ(1/√T) convergence rate for the last iterate of proximal SGD under componentwise convexity and L-smoothness of each fi (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Proximal SGD was implemented per the paper's formula on N=200 componentwise-convex L-smooth quadratics with exact optimum, swept over T∈{100,…,30000} with 192 seeds reporting worst-case error; fitted log-log slope of −0.512±0.042 falls within the pre-registered ±0.1 tolerance of −0.5, and a negative control (mismatched L on 20% of components) produced 600–2500× larger errors at every horizon.

claims.claim: The analysis replaces the standard bounded-variance assumption with the weaker requirement of a finite second moment of the gradient at the solution, E||∇fi(x*)||² = σ*² < ∞ (Section 2, Assumption 1).
claims.evidence: The exact formula E||∇f_i(x*)||² = σ*² < ∞ was found verbatim in the SHA-pinned arXiv LaTeX source at line 310 within the assumptions block, confirming the paper uses finite second moment at the solution rather than bounded variance.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 extends the Õ(1/√T) last-iterate rate to a randomized incremental proximal method when the regularizer decomposes additively and each component gj is Lipschitz continuous (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: RIPM was implemented on a 1D instance with m=5 Lipschitz regularizer components and 192 seeds across six horizons, but the fitted worst-case slope of −0.640±0.073 missed the pre-registered ±0.1 tolerance of −0.5 by 0.14, and the negative control (non-Lipschitz g_j) shifted the slope only to −0.390, short of the 0.2 threshold needed to fire.

claims.claim: Section 4.4 applies the framework to a BlockProx algorithm for graph-guided regularizers used in multi-task and federated learning, proving last-iterate convergence without assuming bounded gradients (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: BlockProx was tested on a 4-node ring graph with network-Lasso regularizers across T=200–100,000; the printed constant step τ=1/(3L) produced a flat gap (~0.15–0.19) while a decreasing-step control decayed as expected, and a textual inconsistency was found between the theorem statement (no √T) and its proof (T-dependent τ), but the anchored claim does not mention step size so the defect sits outside the claim's scope.

claims.claim: The obtained Õ(1/√T) rate matches, up to logarithmic factors, the last-iterate guarantees for unconstrained SGD under bounded variance from Garrigos et al. (2025) (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Four independent passages in the SHA-pinned LaTeX source (lines 227–229, 395, 411, 733) state that Garrigos et al. (2025) achieve their last-iterate guarantee 'without bounded variance' or that bounded variance 'can be avoided,' directly contradicting the claim's attribution of 'under bounded variance' to that work; the mechanism is a sentence-boundary error at line 447 where the qualifier belongs to a different citation (jain2019making).

RyeCatcher/repro-convergence-rate-of-the.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous empirical and textual audit with pre-registered criteria, negative controls, 192-seed worst-case statistics, SHA-pinned source verification, and independent replication. It verifies the main rate claim (C1) and assumption claim (C2), falsifies the Garrigos attribution (C5) with strong textual evidence, and honestly reports toy-grade results for C3 and C4 where the simplified setups could not fully confirm the claims.

RyeCatcher/repro-the-implicit-bias-of-st.paper_title: The Implicit Bias of Steepest Descent with Mini-batch Stochastic Gradient

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows that without momentum, mini-batch steepest descent converges to an approximate max-margin solution only when batch size exceeds the threshold b > 4Rn/(γ+4R), with the margin gap shrinking as batch size increases (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Exact algebraic computation of the threshold (n=20, R=4.7087, γ=2.3589, b*=17.774) showing only b=n satisfies it among divisors, plus exact replication of Prop 4.2's counterexample (ε=0.3, 200 order/stepsize draws, 0/200 reached both-correct) — this is the paper's own construction, not a proxy.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 shows that adding momentum allows convergence to the max-margin solution even with small batch sizes, provided β₁→1, revealing a batch-momentum tradeoff (Theorem 4.3, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Tested on the smallest possible instance (m=2, b=1): negative control β1=0 fails (margin=-0.3808), β1∈{0.5,0.99} succeeds (margin≈56–74), but β1=0.5 succeeds far below the theoretical threshold 0.9605, and the general condition across (m,β1) was not swept.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.5 shows the momentum-enabled convergence rate is slowed by a factor of m/(1-β₁) relative to the momentum-free large-batch case (Corollary 4.5, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The epochs-to-first-success proxy saturated (values {1,1,2,3,1,1} across 6 settings) and the monotonicity check in m/(1-β1) returned False; the only other evidence is transcription of the rate formula from the paper text, which is not independent verification.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 proves that variance reduction recovers the exact full-batch implicit bias for any batch size, eliminating the batch-size dependence of the margin, though Corollary 4.7 shows this comes at a convergence rate slowed by a factor of m^(2+a) (Theorem 4.6, Corollary 4.7, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: On n=20 data, VR gap=0.0437 matches full-batch gap=0.0443, but the intended negative control (plain small-batch gap=0.0401) did not fail, so the batch-size-dependence elimination is not cleanly demonstrated — only the VR-equals-full-batch agreement is shown at small scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.9 constructs an orthogonal, scale-skewed data example on which per-sample (batch-size-one) steepest descent converges to a fundamentally different implicit bias than the full-batch solution (Theorem 4.9, Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: On a very small instance (K=3, n=9), per-sample SignSGD matches the closed-form W̄ (cos=0.9995), but cos(per-sample, full-batch)=0.9570 fails the <0.9 bar, so the 'fundamentally different implicit bias' half is not separated at this scale.

claims.claim: Synthetic multi-class linear classification experiments with normalized-SGD under the ℓ₂ norm, varying batch size (b∈{20,200}) and momentum (β∈{0,0.5,0.99}), empirically confirm that momentum or variance reduction restores full-batch-like convergence in small-batch regimes (Section 5, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: Reduced from K=10/n=200/T=20000 to K=4/n=20/T=150 with b∈{5,20} instead of {20,200}: VR restores margin (0.4108 > 0.3444 baseline) but β1=0.99 does not (0.3387 < 0.3444), only β1=0.5 does — partial, non-monotone confirmation at reduced scale.

RyeCatcher/repro-the-implicit-bias-of-st.overall: The logbook provides exact algebraic verification and counterexample replication for Claim 1, but all other claims are tested on very small instances (n≤20, CPU-only, <1 min total) where proxy metrics often saturate or negative controls fail to discriminate. The reproduction is honest about limitations but lacks the scale needed to fully confirm or falsify the rate-scaling and implicit-bias-divergence claims.

RyeCatcher/repro-on-the-sharp-input-outp.paper_title: On the Sharp Input-Output Analysis of Nonlinear Systems under Adversarial Attacks

claims.claim: The paper analyzes an ℓ1-norm (least-absolute-deviation) estimator and proves it achieves an estimation error bound of Θ(ρ^τ), where ρ is the system's contraction factor and τ is the input memory length (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook found that Theorem 3.1 (lines 929-950) in their copy names an ℓ2-norm estimator, not ℓ1/LAD, and that the ℓ1 estimator appears only as a baseline in experiments (lines 6095-6114). However, the logbook also identifies a version mismatch — the claims reference a Theorem 3.4 that does not exist in their copy (which has 3.1, 3.3, 3.5) — so this finding may not apply to the version the claims were anchored against.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1's guarantee requires the adversarial attack probability to satisfy p < 1/(2τ), which ensures the probability (1-p)^τ of an attack-free observation window exceeds one half (Assumption 2.8, Remark 2.9).
claims.evidence: A numerical sweep over τ=1..20000 confirmed that p = 1/(2τ) - 1e-9 yields (1-p)^τ > 0.5 for all τ, with the asymptotic value approaching exp(-1/2) ≈ 0.6065, and that p slightly above 1/(2τ) can violate the inequality, confirming the threshold is non-vacuous.

claims.claim: A matching lower bound of order Θ(ρ^τ L r/λ) is established, proving the upper bound of Theorem 3.1 is order-optimal and that no estimator can improve on this rate under probabilistic adversarial attacks (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook found no Theorem 3.4 in their copy; the lower bound is Theorem 3.5 at Ω(ρ^τ·L/λ) with no factor of r, and the paper explicitly states the bound is independent of r (lines 1324-1325). However, the same version mismatch (claims reference a nonexistent Theorem 3.4) means this discrepancy may stem from checking the wrong revision rather than a genuine falsification.

claims.claim: The estimation error is shown to decay exponentially with the input memory length τ through the contraction factor ρ ∈ (0,1) (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Fitting log(bound) vs τ (τ=35..60) on the closed-form eq (14) at ρ=0.5 recovered a slope of -0.66158 vs expected -0.69315 (abs error 0.0316, under the 0.05 threshold), and a wrong-ρ'=0.8 negative control produced RMSE 21.08 vs 0.0167 for the true-ρ fit, confirming the exponential decay rate matches log(ρ).

claims.claim: Section 3.2 first derives sufficient conditions for exact recovery in the case without past-state effects (Theorem 3.3, Section 3.2.1), then extends the analysis to the general case with nonzero past-state terms (Section 3.2.2).
claims.evidence: Theorem 3.3 (lines 1040-1050) is stated under the hypothesis x_t^(τ)=0 and eps_t=0 (no past-state, no approximation error) for exact recovery, and Section 3.2.2's title (line 1122) is 'BEYOND THE ZERO PAST STATE AND APPROXIMATION EFFECT' with line 1136 explicitly extending 3.2.1's analysis to general basis functions, matching the claim's two-stage structure.

RyeCatcher/repro-on-the-sharp-input-outp.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical and textual verification for the attack-probability threshold (Claim 2), exponential decay rate (Claim 4), and section structure (Claim 5), but Claims 1 and 3 are undermined by a version mismatch where the claims reference a Theorem 3.4 absent from the logbook's copy of the paper, making those findings inconclusive rather than definitive falsifications.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-optimal-unconstraine.paper_title: Optimal Unconstrained Self-Distillation in Ridge Regression: Strict Improvements, Precise Asymptotics, and One-Shot Tuning

claims.claim: Theorem 2.2 proves that for any nonstationary ridge penalty λ (i.e., R'(λ) ≠ 0), the optimally mixed self-distilled student strictly improves on the teacher's squared prediction risk, with optimal mixing weight ξ*(λ) = -(λ/2)·R'(λ)/D(λ) obeying sign(ξ*(λ)) = -sign(R'(λ)) (Section 2.3, Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: On synthetic ridge (n=500, p=250, 20 λ values), strict improvement was observed at every λ (avg 11.56%, min 0.02%), and the sign relationship sign(ξ*(λ)) = -sign(R'(λ)) was explicitly checked via numerical differentiation at all 20 points with 100% match rate.

claims.claim: The optimal mixing weight ξ*(λ) can be negative, corresponding to a 'pro-learning' regime under over-regularization (λ > λ*), as opposed to the 'anti-learning' regime (ξ* > 1) identified in prior work by Das and Sanghavi (2023) (Section 2.3).
claims.evidence: On the same synthetic setup, 7 of 20 λ values yielded negative optimal mixing weights (min ξ* ≈ -5.0), directly confirming the existence of the pro-learning regime with ξ* < 0 under over-regularization.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 derives exact deterministic equivalents for the optimal self-distillation risk R*_sd(λ) and mixing weight ξ*(λ) in the proportional asymptotics regime (n, p → ∞, p/n → γ) under general anisotropic covariance and deterministic signals (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The actual Theorem 3.1 fixed-point kappa formula with resolvent traces was implemented for anisotropic AR(1) covariance (ρ=0.6) and deterministic signal; relative error for R(λ) shrank from 6.62% (n=100) to 0.22% (n=6400), and a misspecified-covariance negative control gave 10.5% error as expected.

claims.claim: In the isotropic-signal setting, Corollary 3.2 shows the optimal mixing weight changes sign exactly at λ* := γσ²/r², with ξ*(λ) < 0 for λ > λ* and ξ*(λ) > 0 for λ < λ* (Section 3.2, Corollary 3.2).
