claims.evidence: A sign change in ξ*(λ) was detected (1 sign change across 30 λ values on synthetic n=500, p=250 data), but the code only checks that any sign change exists—it never verifies that the sign change occurs at the predicted λ* = γσ²/r² nor that ξ* < 0 for λ > λ* and ξ* > 0 for λ < λ*.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proposes a one-shot generalized cross-validation (GCV) estimator of the optimal mixing weight ξ* that is consistent in proportional asymptotics and avoids grid search, sample splitting, or refitting (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The real Theorem 4.1 GCV estimator (exact df=tr(hat matrix), Eqs 17-20) was implemented at n up to 6400/p up to 3200 with correct sign and ~8x error reduction over a naive baseline, but the mean absolute error plateaus at ~0.11-0.13 rather than vanishing, so asymptotic consistency is not demonstrated at accessible compute scale.

claims.claim: A curvature-based sufficient condition (Proposition 2.3, Eq. 10) predicts whether the self-distilled risk's global minimum over λ is strictly smaller than the teacher's; this test is verified exactly on all four real-data experiments (BlogFeedback, Communities and Crime, CIFAR10, Air Quality) in Table 2.
claims.evidence: The Eq (10) curvature test was run on only 3 of the 4 required real datasets (CIFAR10 missing), and on Air Quality the test predicted no gain but a real above-noise-floor 3.27% gain was observed—a mismatch—so the claim of exact verification on all four datasets is not supported.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-optimal-unconstraine.overall: The logbook provides solid experimental support for Claims 1-3 (strict improvement, negative mixing weights, and deterministic-equivalent convergence) with real formula implementations and negative controls, but Claims 4-6 are only partially addressed: the sign-change location is not verified, GCV consistency is not demonstrated at accessible scale, and one of four real datasets is missing with a counterexample on another.

RyeCatcher/repro-hallucination-is-a-cons.paper_title: Hallucination is a Consequence of Space-Optimality: A Rate-Distortion Theorem for Membership Testing

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 (Rate-Distortion Lower Bound) proves that the minimum per-key memory budget for membership testing in the sparse regime satisfies liminf B(M_j)/n_j >= min KL(mu_K || mu_N) over output distributions meeting the specified error constraints (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook tests that the RHS minimization is well-posed (grid-resolution spread 3.19e-04, KKT residual 6.66e-03 on a novel quadratic-cost instance), but never constructs a membership tester, never measures a per-key memory budget B(M_j)/n_j, and never tests the actual inequality. The KKT stationarity check is nearly self-certifying since a converged solver satisfies its own optimality conditions regardless of the theorem's truth.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 shows that when the KL-divergence minimizer is unique, any asymptotically memory-optimal membership tester's query output distributions must converge in Wasserstein-1 distance to the theoretical optimizers (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Uniqueness is genuinely tested (15 random starts converge to a single basin, spread 1.20e-14 on C4-type and 4.51e-04 on C3-type; negative control moves L1 0.2000 to the true optimum in one KKT step), but the W1 convergence is tested along a straight-line interpolation (1-t)*feasible + t*optimum where both the objective gap and W1 distance reach zero together by construction, so the convergence half cannot fail regardless of the theorem.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that under log-loss constraints the unique optimal probability-estimation solution assigns all facts to a single high-confidence score x* = e^{-epsilon_K}, while non-facts are distributed as mu_N* = (1-q*)delta_0 + q*delta_{x*}, so a fraction q* of non-facts receive the same score as facts — an unavoidable 'hallucination channel' (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: An independent grid solver blind to the closed form recovers the log-loss optimal solution in 80/80 random instances (worst relerr 1.644e-03, structural match 80/80, resolution-stable), and the swapped-parameter negative control has strictly worse KL in all 16 feasible cases out of 27 tested, with 11 infeasible — a clean discrimination.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 shows that for FNR/FPR-constrained binary membership classifiers, the optimal score distributions are mu_K* = Bernoulli(1-epsilon_K) and mu_N* = Bernoulli(epsilon_N), formalizing hallucination in the binary-decision setting (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: An independent solver blind to the Bernoulli answer recovers it in 80/80 random instances (worst relerr 5.97e-04, median ~3.98e-10, resolution-independent at ~1.6e-10 across grid sizes 21–121), with structural match 80/80. The negative control is weak (swapped Bernoulli is infeasible in all logged instances, so no objective comparison is possible), but the forward evidence of blind recovery to near-machine precision is strong.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 derives a finite-support correction to the memory lower bound involving the chi-squared divergence between the optimal fact/non-fact score distributions, applicable to testers restricted to finite output supports (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: Mutual information F_p = I(X;Xhat)/p computed from its own definition (not the paper's formula) on two 2-atom supports yields fitted slopes matching the predicted -chi2/(2 ln 2) coefficient to relative error 4.08e-06 (C4 support) and 1.21e-05 (C3 support), while the swapped-chi2 negative control is off by 32%. The instrument caught and fixed its own bug (a stray factor causing divergence), demonstrating it can fail.

RyeCatcher/repro-hallucination-is-a-cons.overall: The logbook provides genuine numerical verification for three claims (Theorems 4.1, 4.3, 3.3) via an independent optimization solver and mutual-information computation with discriminating negative controls, while the remaining two (Theorems 3.1, 3.2) are only tested on proxy aspects — optimization well-posedness and uniqueness — rather than the actual claims about memory bounds and Wasserstein convergence.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-asymptotically-optim.paper_title: Asymptotically Optimal Sequential Testing with Markovian Data

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 gives a non-asymptotic instance-dependent lower bound on the expected stopping time, E_Q[tau_alpha] ≥ (log(1/alpha)/D_M^inf(Q,P) − 2C_Q/min_i pi_i)^+, where D_M^inf(Q,P) is a stationary-weighted projection distance and C_Q bounds a Poisson-equation solution (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: The concrete output JSON shows the lower bound violated at all tested alphas (fraction_holding=0.0, mean_tau 30-148 vs lower_bound 391-2680). A prose fix note describes retuning the test-bed (grid-searched for pi_star=0.181) and extending to alpha=1e-25 where the bound becomes non-trivial (lower_bound=14.9, mean_tau=161.1), but no output JSON is shown for this fixed run, and the bound is non-trivial at only one extreme alpha with a specifically tuned 5-state chain.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 bounds the Poisson-equation solution constant C_Q via the pseudo-spectral gap of the underlying Markov chain (Section 3, Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: The concrete output JSON shows C_Q computed via an ad-hoc mixing_time/min_pi proxy on the wrong kernel P (C_Q=8.24). A prose fix note describes implementing the exact Proposition 3.1 formula via pseudo-spectral gap on the correct kernel Q (gamma_ps=0.519, C_Q=15.64), but no output JSON is shown for this corrected computation, and the code merely evaluates the bound formula without verifying it against the actual Poisson-equation solution constant.

claims.claim: The proposed Sequential Markov Chain Test (Algorithm 1) builds an empirical transition kernel and a martingale statistic L_t accumulating row-wise KL divergences from the null class, stopping when L_t exceeds an adaptive boundary beta_t (Section 4, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The SequentialMarkovTest class implements an empirical kernel and martingale statistic, but the fixed version uses per-transition log-likelihood ratios rather than the paper's 'row-wise KL divergences,' and the Round-3 fix replaces the boundary with a KT-mixture predictive at beta_t=log(1/alpha), which the logbook itself acknowledges is 'still not the paper's literal Algorithm 1 boundary.'

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves the proposed test is alpha-correct and asymptotically optimal, with limsup_{alpha->0} E_Q[tau_alpha]/log(1/alpha) ≤ 1/D_M^inf(Q,P), matching the Theorem 3.3 lower bound (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: For alpha-correctness, the concrete output initially shows a meaningless 0.01 (due to an outer-loop break bug), then 100% false positives after the bug is removed; a Round-3 fix table self-reports 4/100 false positives at alpha=0.05 after switching to a KT-mixture predictive. For asymptotic optimality, the concrete output JSON shows ratio 0.049 (far from 1); a prose fix note describes retuning the test-bed to D_M=0.3025 yielding ratio 0.846, but no output JSON is shown for this retuned run.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 extends the one-sided asymptotic optimality result to the two-sided testing setting (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: The verify_claim_5 function creates a second alternative kernel Q2 but never uses it in the test; it simply runs the same one-sided SequentialMarkovTest under Q and reports a stop time. No two-sided testing procedure (combining evidence against both Q1 and Q2, or testing H0 against a composite alternative) is implemented.

claims.claim: The framework is applied to detect MCMC transition-kernel misspecification (Section 5.1, Corollary 5.1) and to validate linear transition dynamics in MDPs (Section 5.2, Corollary 5.3).
claims.evidence: The MCMC misspecification part runs the generic one-sided sequential test on a random 4-state chain (not a real MCMC kernel like Metropolis-Hastings) and reports detection. The MDP linear transition dynamics validation part (Corollary 5.3) is not addressed at all—no code or experiment for MDP validation exists.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-asymptotically-optim.overall: The logbook attempts to reproduce the paper's theoretical claims on small 4-5 state Markov chains but the concrete output JSONs show failures for the lower bound and asymptotic optimality claims, with described fixes relying on specifically grid-searched test-beds and prose-reported results without corresponding output artifacts. The two-sided testing claim was never actually implemented, and the MDP application was not addressed.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-proximal-imh-proxima.paper_title: Proximal-IMH: Proximal Posterior Proposals for Independent Metropolis–Hastings with Approximate Operators

claims.claim: Proximal-IMH's proposal admits a closed-form linear correction x = K x̃ where K = (AᵀA+βI)⁻¹(AᵀÃ+βI), derived by solving a regularized least-squares problem around the approximate posterior sample x̃ (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: 20 random trials with varying dimensions (d∈[3,12]) and β values compared the direct least-squares correction formula against the closed-form Kx̃, yielding max absolute difference of 1.1e-14 across all trials — floating-point-exact confirmation of the algebraic identity.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 shows that in the diagonal perturbation case, the KL divergence of the proximal posterior scales as ε²d_y + ε²Σᵢσ²/sᵢ², which is substantially smaller (often by orders of magnitude) than the KL divergence of the Approx-IMH posterior (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Using the paper's exact Equation 10 formulas in the theorem's stated high-SNR regime (diagonal forward operators, d up to 50, σ∈[0.05,0.2]), D_p was smaller than D_a by 2–4 orders of magnitude in all 5 configurations (e.g., 546.2 vs 0.150, 601.6 vs 0.833).

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows the mixing-time constant of Proximal-IMH depends only on ‖I−K⁻¹‖, which is provably no larger than the corresponding quantity ‖I−F̃⁻¹F‖ for Latent-IMH, with equality only when F̃=F (Section 3.3, Equation 16).
claims.evidence: After fixing the F definition and enforcing β=σ², the ordering ‖I−K⁻¹‖ ≤ ‖I−F̃⁻¹F‖ held in all 5 diagonal-structured configurations (e.g., 0.09312 vs 0.09325, 0.38958 vs 0.39059), with small margins consistent with modest perturbations and the theorem's equality condition.

claims.claim: On the bimodal Bayesian inverse problem experiment with three perturbation types (multiplicative spectral, additive low-rank, and low-rank approximation), Proximal-IMH achieves substantially higher acceptance rates and convergence comparable to NUTS, versus Approx-IMH and Latent-IMH (Section 4.1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: A 2D problem with a 4×2 forward matrix and 5000 samples showed only ~0.5% acceptance improvements on 2/3 perturbation types and degradation on the third; no NUTS or Latent-IMH baselines were run, and the gains are far from 'substantially higher' as claimed.

claims.claim: On the MNIST VAE-decoder inverse problem (d_z=128, d_x=784, d_y=100) with spectral perturbations (condition number ≈60) and linearized Helmholtz operators (condition number ≈420), Proximal-IMH shows lower error, faster convergence, and reduced trial-to-trial variance than Approx-IMH, and is robust to the choice of β (variance <0.4% across tests) (Section 4.2, Figures 6-7).
claims.evidence: No experiments were executed; the logbook only lists infrastructure requirements and recommendations, explicitly stating 'Not Verifiable — No Compute.'

claims.claim: On the nonlinear acoustic-scattering Helmholtz inverse problem with 44 source terms on a 32×32 medium grid, Proximal-IMH converges to accuracy comparable to NUTS while retaining the computational advantages of an independence proposal (Section 4.3, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: No experiments were executed; the logbook only lists infrastructure requirements and recommendations, explicitly stating 'Not Verifiable — No Compute.'

sabaridsnfuji/repro-proximal-imh-proxima.overall: The logbook provides solid numerical verification of the three theoretical claims (closed-form K, KL divergence scaling, mixing-time ordering) using the paper's exact formulas in appropriate regimes, but the empirical claims are largely unaddressed: Claim 4 is tested only on a 2D toy without key baselines, and Claims 5–6 were not attempted at all.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-ski-rental-with-dist.paper_title: Ski Rental with Distributional Predictions of Unknown Quality

claims.claim: Theorem 1 shows the algorithm achieves expected additive loss O(min(√b·max(EMD(p̂,p),1), b log b)), where EMD(p̂,p) is the Earth Mover's distance between the predicted and true distributions and b is the buy-ski-rental cost ratio (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: 64 (b, EMD) points with b up to 1000 and EMD up to 1852 show loss/bound ratios ranging 0.0033–0.80 with zero bound violations, exercising both the EMD<1 and EMD>1 regimes of min(√b·max(EMD,1), b log b).

claims.claim: The algorithm attains consistency O(√b) when the prediction error (EMD) is 0 and robustness O(b log b) when the prediction is arbitrarily inaccurate, without needing to know the prediction error bound in advance (Theorem 1, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Using the same algorithm_main, consistency loss/√b ratio maxes at 1.06 across b∈{8..1000} with perfect prediction (EMD=0), and robustness loss/(b log b) ratio maxes at 0.17 under adversarial Dirac prediction, both well within the claimed O(√b) and O(b log b) bounds.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 proves a matching lower bound showing no algorithm can achieve additive loss o(b)·EMD(p̂,p), establishing that the √b factor in Theorem 1 is necessary (Theorem 4, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: The log-log fit of loss vs b·EMD across 3 adversarial families yields slope 0.43 (R²=0.63), which is sub-linear and does not demonstrate the claimed Ω(b·EMD) rate; moreover, Theorem 4 is an existential lower bound over all algorithms that a single-algorithm experiment can only partially probe.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a Pareto-optimal consistency-robustness tradeoff: any algorithm achieving O(√b) consistency must incur Ω(b log b) robustness (Theorem 6, Section 4)
claims.evidence: The per-b adversarial search over only 5 candidate predictions shows robustness ratio not shrinking to zero (slope 0.77 vs b log b), consistent with the tradeoff, but this tests one algorithm rather than proving the impossibility result over all algorithms, and the sub-1.0 slope suggests the worst case may not be fully found.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 introduces a parameterized algorithm with expected cost c(ALG_p) ≤ min{(1+λ)(c(OPT_p)+B), (1+1/λ)c(OPT_p)}, allowing explicit interpolation between trusting the prediction and worst-case guarantees via λ ∈ [0,1] (Theorem 2, Section 2.2)
claims.evidence: Across 180 (scenario × b × λ) points, both bound1=(1+λ)(OPT+B) and bound2=(1+1/λ)OPT hold with zero violations, while the deliberately broken negative control violates bound2 in 60/180 cases, demonstrating the check has discriminating power.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-ski-rental-with-dist.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting the upper-bound claims (Theorems 1 and 2) across non-trivial parameter ranges, but the lower-bound and impossibility results (Theorems 4 and 6) are only partially probed via single-algorithm experiments that cannot verify existential claims over all algorithms.

RyeCatcher/repro-prior-diffusiveness-and.paper_title: Prior Diffusiveness and Regret in the Linear-Gaussian Bandit

claims.claim: Theorem 1 bounds the Bayesian regret of Thompson sampling in the linear-Gaussian bandit by dσ√T·C₂(d,T,σ,r,Σ₀) + 3rd√Tr(Σ₀^(1/2))·C₁(d,T) + √(2r²Tr(Σ₀)) (Section 2, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo simulation at d=4, T=300, Σ0=0.5·I_4 with 20 seeds yielded mean regret 61.0 and max 110.0 against RHS bound 1213.8 — the bound holds but at a clearly small scale far from the paper's asymptotic regime, with a very loose margin.

claims.claim: Corollary 2 simplifies this to an additive decomposition Reg(T)=Õ(σd√T + dr√Tr(Σ₀)), separating a minimax term σd√T from a prior-dependent burn-in term dr√Tr(Σ₀) that does not multiply the √T factor, improving on the Kalkanli and Özgür (2020) bound where the burn-in term scaled as dr√(Tr(Σ₀))√T (Section 2, Corollary 2).
claims.evidence: The key Cauchy-Schwarz step Tr(Σ0^(1/2)) ≤ sqrt(d·Tr(Σ0)) was tested on 200 random PSD matrices (d=2..11), always yielding ratio ≤1 with isotropic-limit gap at machine precision (1.8e-15), and a negative control (d-dropped false bound) correctly failed on 0/200 trials; the external Kalkanli-Özgür comparison was not independently re-derived.

claims.claim: Lemma 3, the generalized elliptical potential lemma, removes the standard requirement that the initial precision matrix V₀ ⪰ I_d and allows flexible exponents p∈[0,1], bounding the potential by 2^p T^(1-p)(log det V_T/det V₀)^p (Section 3, Lemma 3).
claims.evidence: The bound was numerically checked on 60 random (d,p,V0) trials with T=40 steps, with worst-case slack 6.07 (always non-negative) and p→0 limit gap 4.7e-4, but T=40 and small dimensions constitute a clearly simplified setup for this finite-horizon lemma.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 proves a matching lower bound showing the burn-in term dr√Tr(Σ₀) is unavoidable for non-pathological priors, via a bound of the form Reg^p(T) ≥ (r/π‖τ‖₂)Σᵢ₌₂^min{T,d}(i-1)τᵢ² (Section 4, Theorem 6).
claims.evidence: Only algebraic self-consistency of Theorem 6 against Corollary 7 was checked (implied_c converging to 1/(2π) across d∈{5,...,3000}, matching closed form to 2.8e-17), not the actual minimax lower-bound argument against real bandit policies, which the logbook explicitly states is out of scope.

claims.claim: Theorem 9 extends the additive regret decomposition beyond Gaussian priors and noise to strongly log-concave distributions, preserving the same additive structure between the minimax and burn-in terms (Section 5, Theorem 9).
claims.evidence: A structural/closed-form comparison of transcribed formulas showed the burn-in term grows by factor 1.185 from T to 50T (vs √50≈7.07 for a √T-scaled term), confirming no hidden √T factor, but the strongly-log-concave proof machinery justifying the extension was not touched.

RyeCatcher/repro-prior-diffusiveness-and.overall: The logbook provides small-scale numerical checks of five theoretical claims, with one (Claim 2) receiving a reasonably rigorous algebraic verification including negative controls, and the rest tested at clearly reduced scale or via proxy checks (algebraic consistency, structural comparison) rather than full reproduction. The reproduction is honest about limitations but uniformly operates well below the paper's intended regime.

claims.claim: RDNGD achieves iteration and oracle complexity of O(d·ε⁻²) for smooth nonconvex problems and O(d·ε⁻¹) for smooth convex problems using only a pairwise comparison oracle on Riemannian manifolds (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Real runs on small dimensions (d=5–50) with a Rayleigh quotient objective, but the nonconvex case fails to converge at eps=1e-3 for d=20 and d=50 (final gaps 0.0086 and 0.021, both above target), and fitted log-log exponents [(5,0.42),(10,1.63),(20,1.1)] do not match the claimed O(d·ε⁻²) rate of 2.0; the convex case was initially absent and later showed inconsistent exponents including negative values at small d.

claims.claim: The recurrent variant RRDNGD attains linear convergence for strongly convex objectives, requiring O(d log(1/ε)) oracle calls (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Linear convergence (rates < 1.0) is observed on a squared-geodesic-distance objective at d=5,10,20, but oracle call counts far exceed the predicted O(d·log(1/ε)) scaling — e.g., d=20, eps=0.01 requires 30120 oracle calls vs. predicted 92.1 (a 327× overshoot), and d=10, eps=0.01 requires 9660 vs. predicted 46.1 — so the complexity bound is not reproduced at this small scale.

claims.claim: RDFW, a projection-free Riemannian dueling Frank-Wolfe method, achieves O(ε⁻¹) iteration complexity with O(d·ε⁻²) oracle calls for smooth convex problems using only a linear minimization oracle (Table 1).
claims.evidence: RDFW is run on a linear objective at d=5,10,20 with 4 eps values, but fitted exponents (0.14–0.35) are far below the claimed O(ε⁻¹)=1.0 for iterations and O(d·ε⁻²)=2.0 for oracle calls; the method converges in 2–19 iterations, much faster than the worst-case bound on this easy instance, so the claimed rates are neither matched nor falsified.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.1 and Lemma 3.2 show the comparison-based gradient direction estimator is unbiased for the normalized gradient with improved constants over prior Euclidean dueling optimization work (Section 3, Lemma 3.1, Lemma 3.2).
claims.evidence: After the 2026-07-31 fix, the unbiasedness test uses the real finite-difference comparison oracle (tangent-projected Gaussian sampling, exponential map perturbations, actual objective evaluations) on a random quadratic Rayleigh quotient, yielding cosine similarities of 0.999, 0.993, and 0.975 at d=10, 20, 50 respectively across 2000 trials, directly supporting the Lemma 3.1/3.2 unbiasedness-of-direction claim.

claims.claim: The framework is applied to a black-box adversarial attack on DNNs with sphere-constrained perturbations and to horizon leveling via SO(2) image rotation, both using only pairwise comparison feedback (Section on real-world applications).
claims.evidence: The claim page was initially empty; the original code only contains a toy 2D linear-classifier demo (`sphere_constrained_attack_demo`) that was never called from main, and the 2026-07-31 fix text is truncated mid-sentence so no concrete results for either the DNN adversarial attack or the SO(2) rotation experiment are visible.

claims.claim: The method covers Hadamard manifolds and bounded-sectional-curvature spaces, with demonstrated applications including Rayleigh quotient maximization on the unit sphere and Karcher mean computation on SPD matrices (Section on synthetic applications).
claims.evidence: Rayleigh quotient optimization is run at d=20 and Karcher mean on 5×5 SPD matrices with only 5 input matrices, but the SPD manifold implementation uses a simplified retraction (X+V) and a crude logarithmic map approximation (M−mean instead of the matrix logarithm), so the manifold geometry is not faithfully represented despite producing real numerical outputs.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-riemannian-dueling-o.overall: The logbook provides concrete evidence supporting the gradient estimator unbiasedness claim (Claim 4) via the real comparison oracle, but the complexity-scaling claims (1–3) are only tested at toy scale with small dimensions and simple objectives where fitted exponents do not match the theoretical rates, and the real-world applications claim (5) has no visible results due to page truncation.

RyeCatcher/repro-why-are-linear-rnns-mor.paper_title: Why Are Linear RNNs More Parallelizable?

claims.claim: Any language recognized by a linear RNN (LRNN) over the rationals lies in PNC1, meaning LRNNs can be simulated by log-depth arithmetic circuits (Theorem 3, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook ran 20 seeded bounded-dimension LRNN-style convolutional instances comparing balanced-tree vs. direct sequential evaluation (worst error 0, max symbolic depth 7), but this is a small-scale proxy of the proof mechanism, not a theorem-level verification that all LRNN languages lie in PNC1.

claims.claim: LRNNs require only O(log n log* n) depth NC circuits, an O(log* n) overhead beyond the O(log n) depth of transformers/TC0 circuits (Corollary 5, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook merely computed log* n for n up to 1,000,000 (finding overhead factors of 4–5), which is a numerical sanity check of the iterated-log function's magnitude, not a construction or test of actual NC circuits at the claimed depth.

claims.claim: Log-precision nonlinear RNNs can solve sorted deterministic graph connectivity, an L-complete problem, requiring Omega(log^2 n) depth and revealing a fundamental parallelization barrier absent in LRNNs (Theorem 2, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: A one-pass reachability update for sorted deterministic graphs was tested on 20 seeded instances (20/20 correct) with a working negative control on unsorted edges, but the Omega(log^2 n) depth lower bound was explicitly not addressed, so only the constructive half was tested at small scale.

claims.claim: Poly-precision nonlinear RNNs can express P-complete problems under FO reductions, implying no efficient parallel algorithm exists for them unless P=NC (Corollary 2, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook verified a scalar stack encoding (push/pop/top semantics) on 20 seeded toy traces with 20/20 exact matches and max bit length 14, but this only witnesses the encoding mechanism; the FO reduction and P-completeness claim were not reproduced.

claims.claim: DPLR-based LRNN architectures such as RWKV-7 and DeltaNet can solve the PNC1-complete iterated 3x3 matrix multiplication problem using only 4 layers (Theorem 5, Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: The vectorized 3x3 matrix recurrence was verified against direct multiplication on 20 seeded chains (worst error 0, sign agreement 20/20), but the actual RWKV-7 and DeltaNet 4-layer architectures were never implemented or tested, so the core claim about specific architectures remains unaddressed.

claims.claim: Experiments show nonlinear RNNs generalize on the L-complete graph connectivity task while transformers and Mamba fail to solve it, matching the theoretical complexity separation (Figure 2, Section 6).
claims.evidence: No training experiments were rerun; the logbook only extracted plotted coordinates from the paper's own LaTeX source (RNN=96.50%, Mamba=50.95%, Transformer=62.15%) and checked them against a pass criterion, which is a transcription of the paper's own results, not independent experimental evidence.

RyeCatcher/repro-why-are-linear-rnns-mor.overall: The logbook provides small-scale NumPy/SciPy sanity checks for the theoretical mechanisms behind claims 1–5 (all toy scope), but does not independently reproduce any theorem, architectural construction, or training experiment. Claim 6 has no independent experimental evidence whatsoever, as only the paper's own figure coordinates were read back.

claims.claim: EDEN computes an adaptive branching factor B_t = max(1, floor(B_max · H̄_t(y_{1:t}))) that scales monotonically with normalized output entropy at each decoding step (Section 3.1.2, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The formula B_t = max(1, floor(B_max · H̄_t)) was audited over 10,001 dense grid points per B_max value and 83,900 real decoding nodes, yielding zero formula violations and zero monotonicity violations under both full-vocabulary and Top-p entropy definitions.

claims.claim: A regret bound shows entropy-adaptive branching achieves lower expected cumulative regret than fixed-width branching policies (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The paper releases no code or parameters for the regret bound, so the logbook used assumed parameters (T=100, M=6000, A(H)=1+3H, etc.) in a 5,000-trial Monte Carlo simulation; the theorem-aligned proxy improves at low variance but the empirical Bernoulli-gap control shows entropy allocation has worse regret at Var(H)=0.06 and 0.08, yielding mixed rather than conclusive evidence on a simplified proxy setup.

claims.claim: On MATH 500, EDEN reaches 32.8% accuracy using only 840 expansions versus 29.2% accuracy for width-3 beam search using 1200 expansions (Section 4.1, Table 1).
claims.evidence: On the full MATH-500 split with Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Beam-3 achieved 47.0% accuracy [42.6, 51.4] while EDEN full (B_max=5) achieved 42.8% [38.6, 47.0] and EDEN Top-p achieved 44.8% [40.4, 49.2], directly contradicting the paper's claim that EDEN (32.8%) beats Beam-3 (29.2%); EDEN full collapsed to B_t=1 at all 131,669 nodes, making it identical to greedy.

claims.claim: On HumanEval, EDEN attains 31.3% accuracy with 965 expansions compared to beam search's 28.8% with 1200 expansions, and on SciBench, EDEN reaches 7.4% versus beam search's 6.9% (Table 1).
claims.evidence: On HumanEval (164 problems), Beam-3 scored 52.4% vs EDEN full's 51.2% (identical to greedy, all 18,773 nodes chose B=1), contradicting the paper's claimed EDEN advantage; on SciBench (580 examples), EDEN full scored 9.14% vs Beam-3's 8.45% (a 0.69-point directional match) but with heavily overlapping CIs [6.90, 11.55] vs [6.21, 10.69], insufficient to confirm the claim.

claims.claim: EDEN is reported to have a 75% posterior probability of being the best-performing method overall across the evaluated benchmarks (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Using a transparent binomial hierarchical logistic model with 200,000 posterior draws across three prior settings, P(EDEN best) was 0/200,000 in every case (<0.0005%), far from the claimed 75%; Majority-5 was best in 98.23% of draws, and EDEN's mean Friedman rank was 6.5 out of 10 methods.

claims.claim: Entropy estimation used for branching remains accurate under sublinear sampling, allowing EDEN to work with closed/black-box APIs that expose only sampled tokens (Section 4.3, Figure 6).
claims.evidence: Entropy RMSE does decay at N^{-1/2}-like rates (slopes -0.51 to -0.52) across 42,000 estimates, and Top-k EDEN improves over baselines on 1,319 GSM8K examples, but the branch-agreement test is degenerate (all 400 true first-token decisions are B=1, so accuracy at actual branching boundaries is untested) and the paper's actual estimator is unavailable, replaced by a Chao-Shen proxy.

jiawei2ch/repro-entropy-informed-decodin.overall: The logbook confirms EDEN's branching formula and monotonicity but demonstrates that with Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, full-vocabulary entropy normalization collapses EDEN to width-1 (greedy) at >99.99% of nodes, causing it to lose to Beam Search on MATH500 and HumanEval and yielding near-zero posterior probability of being best. The regret bound is only tested via an assumed-parameter numerical proxy with mixed results, and the black-box entropy claim is tested in a degenerate regime where no actual branching decisions occur.

gchauhan/repro-reward-shaping-for-infere.paper_title: Reward Shaping for (Inference-Time) Alignment: A Stackelberg Game Perspective

claims.claim: Theorem 1 (Section 4.2) shows the optimal shaped reward has a threshold structure: responses are assigned reward B if their true utility exceeds a prompt-dependent threshold m*(x), and 0 otherwise.
claims.evidence: A 5-response numerical example (r_U=[1,2,3,4,5], B=5, β=1) confirms the threshold structure with rewards [0,0,0,0,5] and self-consistency m*=4.783=E[r_U], but this is a small-scale illustration of a theorem, not a proof or large-scale test.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 (Section 4.3) proves the helper function F_x(m) is continuous and strictly decreasing with a unique root at m*(x), enabling the threshold to be computed via bisection.
claims.evidence: On the same 5-response example, F_x(m) was checked for continuity (max jump 2.38e-6), strict monotonicity (10,000 grid points), and unique root (bisection to m*=4.783, F≈-1.78e-15), but this is a numerical illustration on a tiny discrete setup, not a general proof.

claims.claim: In GPT-4 evaluation across HH-RLHF and SHP with Qwen and Llama backbones, the proposed SRS reward-shaping method achieves average Win-Tie rates of 66.83%, 69.6%, and 66.65% against vanilla, Minmax, and Meanstd baselines respectively (Table 3, Section 6.4).
claims.evidence: Only 10 prompts were evaluated using a reward model (Skywork-Reward-V2-Qwen3-8B) as judge instead of GPT-4, with proxy baselines (post-hoc sample selection rather than ARGS-style token-level shaping). SRS vs MinMax yielded 20% win-tie (paper: 69.6%), contradicting the claim, while the average 70.0% vs 67.7% is coincidental given offsetting errors.

claims.claim: A motivating example in Section 3.2 shows that shaping rewards (r̃(left)=0, r̃(neutral)=3) instead of using true utilities yields expected utility of 1.69 versus 1.23 under direct optimization on a model biased toward P(left)=0.9, P(neutral)=0.1.
claims.evidence: Independent numerical implementation of the KL-regularized objective with P(left)=0.9, P(neutral)=0.1, r_U(left)=1, r_U(neutral)=2 exactly reproduces the paper's values: direct optimization yields 1.2320 utility, shaped reward (0,3) yields 1.6906, matching the claimed 1.23 vs 1.69.

claims.claim: Table 2 (Section 6.3) reports SRS integrated into Controlled Decoding and ARGS achieves the highest reward across four evaluation settings while maintaining comparable response diversity and coherence to baselines.
claims.evidence: On 5 prompts with Qwen3-8B (K=3, greedy decoding, 1 seed), SRS mean reward is 2.50 while MinMax achieves 3.17 — SRS does NOT achieve the highest reward as claimed. The setup is far below the paper's scale (1,000 prompts, K=10, 3 seeds, nucleus sampling), making this a simplified but non-supportive test.

claims.claim: Ablation results in Table 4 (Section 7.1) show SRS's threshold-based shaping outperforms both direct reward-capping and mean-based thresholding baselines.
claims.evidence: On synthetic data (1,000 prompts), SRS (3.40) outperforms CAP (3.04) and MeanStd (2.95) as claimed, and on 5 real-model prompts SRS (2.50) > CAP (2.03) and MeanStd (2.04). However, the synthetic setup is a proxy task and the real-model test uses only 5 prompts, far below the paper's scale.

gchauhan/repro-reward-shaping-for-infere.overall: The logbook exactly reproduces the motivating example (Claim 4) and provides small-scale numerical illustrations of Theorems 1 and 2, but the empirical claims (3, 5, 6) are tested on drastically reduced setups (5–10 prompts, proxy baselines, reward-model judge instead of GPT-4) with some results contradicting the paper. The theoretical claims are illustrated but not proven, and the empirical claims lack the scale needed for verification.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-linear-regression-wi.paper_title: Linear Regression with Unknown Truncation Beyond Gaussian Features

claims.claim: The paper gives the first polynomial-time, poly(d/ε), algorithm for truncated linear regression with an unknown survival set under sub-Gaussian (rather than Gaussian) feature distributions (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Wall-clock vs n log-log slope of 0.94 across d∈{4,8,16,32,64} with n=8d·log(d)/ε² is consistent with polynomial runtime, but d≤64, synthetic data, and estimation error grows from 0.24 to 1.66 across d, indicating the setup is too small to confirm the full poly(d/ε) guarantee; the 'first' novelty claim is not experimentally verifiable.

claims.claim: The algorithm assumes a known lower bound α on the truncation/survival probability, sub-Gaussian feature tails, and a well-conditioned observed covariance matrix (Section 3, three main assumptions).
claims.evidence: Assumptions are verified by construction in the implementation, and a 10-seed alpha sweep at d=6, n=500 shows error decreasing roughly monotonically (0.469→0.353) as survival probability rises from 0.15 to 0.98, but this is a small synthetic setup, not a full-scale test of all three assumptions.

claims.claim: Phase I of the algorithm learns the unknown survival set as a union of k intervals via a novel positive-only PAC learning subroutine that runs in poly(k/ε) time (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: Phase I runtime is flat (~39μs) across k∈{1,2,4,8,16} and Jaccard accuracy stays high (0.95–0.99) when n scales as 60k·log(k)/ε, but the implementation is a simple sort+merge on synthetic data with d=6, not the full PAC learning subroutine at scale.

claims.claim: Phase II estimates the regression vector via projected stochastic gradient descent on a perturbed negative log-likelihood objective, after Phase I's set recovery (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Projected SGD beats naive OLS across 3 feature families × 5 seeds (e.g., 0.414 vs 0.673 for Gaussian) and error decreases with epochs (0.168→0.064 initially), but at d=8, n=800 with absolute errors remaining high (0.41–0.48), this is a small-scale qualitative confirmation only.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.4 shows sub-Gaussianity implies smoothness of the auxiliary distributions used to construct reference distributions for learning from positive examples alone (Lemma 3.4).
claims.evidence: A KDE-based smoothness proxy at d=5 averaged over 20 projections gives finite, same-order-of-magnitude bounds for uniform (0.24), mixture (0.22), and Rademacher (1.53) features, consistent with Lemma 3.4, but this is a low-dimensional numerical proxy, not a formal verification of the lemma.

claims.claim: This improves on prior work (LMZ24a) which required d^poly(k/ε) running time and was restricted to Gaussian features (Section on related work/Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: No LMZ24a code was found or run; the comparison relies entirely on quoting the paper's own textual claim about LMZ24a's d^poly(k/ε) rate and Gaussian-only restriction, with no independent experimental evidence about LMZ24a's actual runtime or feature limitations.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-linear-regression-wi.overall: This logbook provides toy-scale numerical evidence (d≤64, synthetic data, own implementation) consistent with the paper's qualitative predictions for Claims 1–5, including polynomial runtime scaling, graceful alpha degradation, interval recovery with scaled samples, SGD convergence beating OLS, and finite smoothness under sub-Gaussian features. Claim 6's improvement over LMZ24a remains unverified since no baseline code was run.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-innovation-an-almost.paper_title: Innovation: An Almost Characterization of Hallucination

claims.claim: The paper defines innovation (Definition 3.1) as a language model assigning nonzero probability mass to statements not present in the training data, and shows via Observation 3.2 that hallucinating with positive probability implies the model innovates (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook checks g(H) <= g(U) across 2,400 synthetic trials with 0 violations, but this is a set-containment tautology by construction — the code defines g(H) as mass on a subset of the event underlying g(U), so violations are impossible unless there is a bug. The logbook itself acknowledges it is 'close to a tautology given the definitions.'

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows that under K-Sparsity and Regular Facts assumptions, if the innovation mass g(U) > 0, the probability a model hallucinates is at least 1 - K/|U| (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: 960 in-scope and 720 out-of-scope trials show 0 violations of P(hallucinate|innovate) >= 1-K/|U|, but the construction enforces T <= K deterministically, so the bound is never tested near tightness. The logbook admits the bound 'only gets easier to satisfy as d grows' in their construction, meaning the numerical check does not stress-test the theorem's content.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.4 shows that a calibrated model with any positive missing probability mass necessarily innovates (Proposition 3.4).
claims.evidence: 1,447 trials with 0 violations, but the test is near-definitional: the code sets g_U_calibrated = max(0, p_U - eps) with eps < p_U sampled by construction, so g(U) > 0 follows algebraically whenever p(U) > 0. The logbook acknowledges this is 'close to definitional given how we constructed calibrated.'

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 gives a Markov-style bound showing the hallucination rate satisfies g(H) ≥ g(U)(1 - K/(δ|U|)) with probability at least 1-δ (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: 9,600 trials across five delta values show 0% empirical violation rate, but the deterministic T <= K construction means the Markov bound is never approached near its violation boundary. The logbook explicitly states 'a 0% empirical violation rate is consistent with, but does not sharply confirm, the claimed at most delta ceiling since we never observed values close to it.'

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 establishes a high-confidence bound where, with probability at least 1 - K/|U|, the hallucination rate satisfies g(H) ≥ g(U)/(K+1) (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: 3,360 trials across 16 (n,K) configurations show empirical P(E) = 1.0 everywhere, but the failure branch (probability <= K/|U| that E fails) is never observed. The logbook admits 'we never actually observed the failure branch of this high-confidence bound,' so the probability claim is not genuinely tested.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.3 lower-bounds the innovation rate by g(U) ≥ p(U)/(K+1) minus a miscalibration distance term, linking missing probability mass to innovation (Proposition 4.3).
claims.evidence: 1,800 trials with 0 violations, but the logbook itself flags this as 'close to tautological': with calibration_distance defined as exact |g(U)-p(U)|, the inequality reduces to g(U) >= p(U) - calib_dist >= p(U)/(K+1) - calib_dist, which holds for any K>=0 by algebra. The logbook states it is 'a consistency/sanity check, not an independent stress test.'

sabaridsnfuji/repro-innovation-an-almost.overall: The logbook provides a systematic synthetic numerical audit of all six theory claims with 0 violations across 20,287 trials, but the constructions are non-adversarial, several checks are near-tautological by design, and the interesting boundary/tightness cases of the theorems are never probed. This constitutes a consistency check under the paper's own assumptions rather than a genuine verification or falsification of the mathematical claims.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-on-the-computational.paper_title: On the Computational Complexity of Performative Prediction

claims.claim: Theorem 1.2 (restated as Theorem 3.4) proves that computing an ε-performatively stable point is PPAD-complete even when ρ = Lβ/α ≤ 1 + O(ε), with the explicit constant ε′ = 0.088/6 ≈ 0.0147 (Section 1.1, Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook constructs its own hidden-permutation successor-path instance over 2^d hypercube vertices requiring exactly 2^d-1 RRM iterations (d=2..14, slope=1.0, R²=1.0), but explicitly states this is not the paper's PPAD reduction and uses piecewise-constant g rather than the paper's affine reduction map. The corrected-threshold probe using the paper's actual affine map with random (A,b) found no hardness signal.

claims.claim: This PPAD-hardness persists in the simple setting where the loss is quadratic, ℓ(x;z) = ½||x−z||², and the distribution shift D(x) is given by an affine map g(x) (Section 3.1, Equation 2-3, Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The hidden-path construction uses quadratic loss but piecewise-constant (not affine) distribution shift, so it does not match the claim's specific affine-shift setting. The experiment that does use the paper's exact affine reduction map (g(x)=(I-Ā)x-b̄) with random (A,b) converges in every trial, providing no hardness signal in the claim's actual setting.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 shows a phase transition to tractability: when ρ ≤ 1 + O_ε(ε^4), an ε-performatively stable point can be computed in poly(d, log(1/ε)) time via an ellipsoid-method algorithm exploiting hypomonotonicity (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: GD-on-residual solver on quadratic-loss/affine-shift instances (d up to 320, ε down to 0.001, ρ=0.7) shows iterations scaling linearly in log(1/ε) with R²=0.999 and essentially flat in d (d^0.27). All 14 returned points independently confirmed ε-stable. The logbook transparently notes it did not pin down the precise ε⁴ threshold constant.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.7 establishes an unconditional information-theoretic lower bound: any algorithm requires 2^Ω(d) expected-risk-minimization (ERM) queries to find an ε-performatively stable point even when ρ ≤ 1 + O_ε(ε), and even for constant ε (Section 3.1, Corollary 3.7).
claims.evidence: A generic END-OF-LINE-style hidden-path oracle requires exactly 2^d-1 queries for the follow-the-path algorithm (d=4..16, slope=1.0, R²=1.0), but this is a self-constructed generic gadget, not the paper's specific reduction from performative ERM. Running one algorithm on one instance family cannot establish a lower bound over all algorithms.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.12 extends PPAD-hardness of performative stability from the hypercube constraint set to any well-bounded general convex constraint set (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.12, Definition 3.11).
claims.evidence: The same hidden-path construction re-run under a random affine transformation to a non-axis-aligned convex polytope shows the same 2^d-1 RRM iteration requirement (d=2..12, slope=1.0, R²=1.0), but this is the logbook's own construction, not the paper's Theorem 3.12 reduction, and the persistence under affine transformation is structurally trivial.

claims.claim: For the special case of strategic classification, Theorem 4.4 shows that computing a local optimum of the performative risk under single-label updates is PLS-hard, complementing prior NP-hardness results for global performative optimality (Abstract, Section 1.1, Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: A Gray-code tightness check computationally confirms that a natural single-bit-flip local-search potential is not tight at scale (tightness drops from 50% at n=3 to ~1% at n=10), ruling out the naive approach. An abstract single-label-update oracle shows 2^n-1 step counts (n=4..16, slope=1.0), but this is a generic hidden-path gadget, not the paper's PLS reduction from strategic classification.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-on-the-computational.overall: The logbook provides a genuine numerical audit of Claim 3's tractability scaling (poly(d, log(1/ε)) with R²=0.999 and independently verified ε-stability), but for the five complexity-theoretic claims it only constructs self-made proxy instances exhibiting exponential scaling patterns, explicitly disclaiming any verification of the paper's actual PPAD/PLS reductions or information-theoretic lower bounds.

gchauhan/repro-hippo-zoo-explicit-memory.paper_title: HiPPO Zoo: Explicit Memory Mechanisms for Interpretable State Space Models

claims.claim: HiPPO Zoo introduces five explicit polynomial-based extensions to classical HiPPO memory that individually replicate capabilities usually attributed to opaque learned SSMs like Mamba: Volterra, Salience, Associative Memory, Multiscale, and Forecasting HiPPO (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Codebase inspection confirms all five extensions exist with distinct formulations: VanillaHiPPO, MLPHiPPO, SalienceHiPPO, AssocMemHiPPO as nn.Module classes, plus MultiscaleHiPPO and ForecastingHiPPO as standalone scripts with Kronecker product constructions. This is a structural/definitional claim appropriately verified by code inspection.

claims.claim: Salience HiPPO implements adaptive, input-dependent memory allocation via a scalar measure-deformation mechanism (Equation 2) with a time-warping interpretation (Equation 3), demonstrated on a selective copying task with explicit history-measure visualizations (Section 3.2, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Reference script run_salience.py executed with n=256, d_model=64 for 3000 steps achieving final loss 0.00014; salience gate shows adaptive behavior (write phase mean 4.34 vs filler phase mean 2.26, 1.93× higher) with write-phase cosine similarity 0.9985, and HiPPO A,b confirmed fixed as module attributes. Visualizations generated with 6 panels including memory snapshots and gate activations.

claims.claim: Volterra HiPPO decomposes nonlinear dynamics into interpretable kernels parameterized in an orthogonal polynomial basis, validated by learning a quadratic Volterra system on the Wray-Green benchmark (Section 3.1, Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Quadratic reader achieved 30.8% improvement over linear (0.531 vs 0.768) on Wray-Green, but the logbook explicitly states it used 'simplified linear/quadratic readers rather than the full Volterra kernel fitting pipeline,' did not recover explicit kernel functions or visualize kernel weights, and used signal length 20,000 vs the paper's 100,000. The core claim of interpretable kernels in an orthogonal polynomial basis was not directly validated.

claims.claim: Associative Memory HiPPO separates temporal encoding from content-addressable storage on a continuous address space, demonstrated via key-value associative recall with explicit visualization (Section 3.3, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Full reference script run_assoc.py executed with n_hippo=32, n_assoc=32, d_model=32 for 3500 steps achieving final loss 0.000004 (1475× reduction), demonstrating key-value associative recall. Orthogonality of Legendre basis verified with proper quadrature (error <0.005 at order 8, <0.155 at order 32). Write/read gates and OP basis mechanism confirmed through training convergence and visualizations.

claims.claim: Multiscale HiPPO represents scale-dependent states as polynomial expansions (Equation 5) that support stable reconstruction across three orders of magnitude of timescale (Section 3.4, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Multiscale setup tested across 3 orders of magnitude (α=0.1 to 100) with 4 scales × 32 per scale = 128 state dimensions; multiscale concatenated reader achieved 0.062 loss vs single-scale 0.574 (9.2× improvement). Per-scale readers show clear timescale specialization (α=1.0: 0.508 → α=16.0: 0.129 test loss).

claims.claim: In the streaming/online training setups, the Salience model uses truncated backpropagation through time with fixed HiPPO parameters and only the neural readout learned online, while the Associative model uses chunk-wise gradient computation with state detachment between chunks (Section C.2-C.3).
claims.evidence: Source code verification confirms SalienceHiPPO has A,b as fixed module attributes (not in param tree) with only 13 trainable neural network parameter arrays, and both models use jax.lax.stop_gradient at chunk boundaries with state carrying across chunks. Training runs confirm stable convergence for both Salience (35× loss reduction) and AssocMem (1475× loss reduction) models.

gchauhan/repro-hippo-zoo-explicit-memory.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting claims 1, 2, 4, 5, and 6 through reference script executions on GPU with real training runs and numerical results. Claim 3 (Volterra HiPPO) is only partially addressed with a simplified setup that explicitly does not recover or visualize the interpretable kernels central to the claim, making it a toy-level reproduction.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-beyond-relu-bifurcat.paper_title: Beyond ReLU: Bifurcation, Oversmoothing, and Topological Priors

claims.claim: Proves a supercritical pitchfork bifurcation condition α·w·λ_k = 1 under which odd C^3 activation functions destabilize the homogeneous fixed point and create stable non-homogeneous patterns in GNN dynamics (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Across 25 graph/seed configs (5 families × 5 seeds, N=64), subcritical mean amplitude is exactly 0.0 and supercritical mean amplitude is 0.0189, with 214/225 supercritical branches confirmed Jacobian-stable (max real eigenvalue negative), directly supporting the pitchfork bifurcation condition α·w·λ_k=1.

claims.claim: Derives a √μ scaling law for the amplitude of emergent patterns near the bifurcation point, where μ measures distance from criticality, and validates this scaling empirically (Theorem 3.2, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Pooled log-log regression across 25 configs yields a fitted amplitude scaling exponent of 0.5079 versus the theoretical 0.5 (1.6% deviation), confirming the √μ scaling law near criticality.

claims.claim: Shows Dirichlet energy stays at zero in the subcritical regime and grows linearly in the supercritical regime, quantifying departure from oversmoothing (Corollary 3.4).
claims.evidence: Subcritical Dirichlet energy is exactly 0.0 across all 25 configs, and supercritical energy grows with μ with an independently fitted linear R²=0.69; the qualitative regime split is cleanly confirmed, though the linear fit quality is moderate as honestly disclosed.

claims.claim: Proves that near the bifurcation point the NTK becomes asymptotically rank-one, dominated by the bifurcating eigenmode, explaining emergent topological learning priors (Corollary 4.1).
claims.evidence: The direct empirical NTK of a static one-shot map shows no rank-one concentration (top-1 ratio 0.220 near critical vs 0.189 far), contradicting the claim; a different object (susceptibility operator R=(I-αwL)^{-1}) does show a 1/μ pole and top-1 ratio of 0.996, but its equivalence to the NTK is asserted, not demonstrated.

claims.claim: Extends the scalar analysis to realistic multidimensional GNNs, proving emergent patterns are rank-one separable states aligned with graph and feature eigenmodes (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: Rank-one separable patterns emerge from generic random initial conditions (rank-1 ratio 0.9996 mean across 9 configs with 3 graph families × 3 feature dims), but the setup uses small graphs (N=20, d=4–16) which the logbook itself acknowledges is 'toy scale' and not the 'realistic multidimensional GNN' the theorem addresses.

claims.claim: Demonstrates that substituting bifurcation-inducing activations (e.g., sine) for standard monotone ones maintains performance in 64-layer GNNs on Cora, avoiding representational collapse under depth (Figure 5, Section 6).
claims.evidence: On real Cora at the full 64-layer depth, sine's Dirichlet energy is 65,460× larger than ReLU's (3.07 vs 4.69e-5) and effective rank is 32 vs 2.67, but the network is untrained (random Xavier weights) and only representational statistics—not the claimed downstream classification accuracy—are evaluated, making this a proxy-task assessment of the 'maintains performance' claim.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-beyond-relu-bifurcat.overall: The logbook provides solid numerical evidence for the paper's core dynamical-systems theorems (bifurcation condition, √μ scaling, Dirichlet energy regimes) across multiple small graph families, but the NTK rank-one claim has contradictory evidence from the direct NTK computation, and the empirical Cora claim is evaluated only via proxy metrics on an untrained network rather than the claimed task performance.

claims.claim: For resettable streams with Inc(x,Δ) and Reset(P) operations, the paper constructs sketches robust to adaptive adversaries while maintaining prefix-max error |F̂ₜ - Fₜ| ≤ ε·max_{t'≤t} F_{t'} (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook implemented the paper's actual Algorithm 2 (rate-halving driven by DP-noised BTM view of sample size) and tested it against a genuinely adaptive adversary over 100 trials at T=500, eps=0.15, delta=0.05, achieving a 1% violation rate within the 5% budget — concrete evidence on the real task.

claims.claim: The robust cardinality sketch uses O(ε⁻² log^{3/2}(T) · log(T/δ)) bits of space, avoiding the Ω(n) space lower bound that applies to relative-error non-robust variants (Theorem 2.4).
claims.evidence: A properly union-bound-calibrated Binary Tree Mechanism was implemented and measured across T in {64, 256, 1024, 4096, 16384}, yielding a fitted log(T) exponent of 1.68 (theory: 1.5) with R2=0.999, closely matching the claimed log^{3/2}(T) scaling.

claims.claim: The robust sum sketch achieves O(ε⁻² log^{11/2}(T) · log²(1/δ)) bits of space under adaptive adversarial updates (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The experiment used a naive geometric-bucket-weighting scheme (per-bucket weight 2^b) rather than the paper's actual threshold-truncation construction (F_t = D_t + P_t), yielding a fitted exponent of 7.94 vs theory's 5.5 — a real but simplified construction that does not replicate the paper's mechanism, so the result neither confirms nor refutes the theorem.

claims.claim: Robustness for Bernstein statistics is achieved with poly(ε⁻¹, log(T/δ)) space, i.e., polylogarithmic in the stream length T (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Using the same naive bucketed-BTM construction as Claim 3 (not the paper's threshold-truncation mechanism), error grew by ~36,600x over a 4096x T range — clearly not polylogarithmic, but on a simplified construction that does not match the paper's actual approach, so this is a toy-level attempt, not a reproduction.

claims.claim: The robustification technique adapts the Binary Tree Mechanism from differential privacy under continual observation, giving an exponential space improvement over prior polynomial-space wrapper techniques for adaptive robustness (Section 2, building on Theorem 2.4).
claims.evidence: The validated BTM-based cardinality sketch (polylog space, from Claim 2) was compared against a naive O(T)-space baseline across T up to 262144, showing a space ratio growing to thousands — a concrete demonstration of the polylog-vs-linear (exponential) separation the claim asserts.

claims.claim: Two concrete adaptive attacks are demonstrated against standard (non-robust) sketches: a re-insertion attack that reduces effective sampling probability from p to p², and a sample-and-delete attack that empties the sample while the active set stays large (Section 1, motivating the vulnerabilities).
claims.evidence: The paper's actual Algorithm 1 (Bernoulli sampling with deletions) was implemented and both attacks were tested: re-insertion over 20,000 trials at p=0.2 yielded a both-checkpoint rate matching p^2=0.04, and the sample-and-delete attack emptied the sample to 0 while the active set stayed large — both quantitative predictions reproduced.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-adaptively-robust-re.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting 4 of 6 claims using the paper's actual algorithms (Algorithm 1, Algorithm 2, calibrated BTM), while Claims 3 and 4 were addressed only via a simplified bucketing construction that explicitly does not replicate the paper's threshold-truncation mechanism, yielding results that contradict the theorems but on the wrong construction.

RyeCatcher/repro-robust-linear-dueling-b.paper_title: Robust Linear Dueling Bandits with Post-serving Context under Unknown Delays and Adversarial Corruptions

claims.claim: The proposed RCDP-UCB algorithm for linear dueling bandits with post-serving context achieves a cumulative regret upper bound of Õ(d(√T + C + D)), where d is the feature dimension, T the horizon, C the corruption budget, and D the delay complexity (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Small-scale simulation (T≤1200, 20 seeds, CPU/NumPy) with qualitative order checks: √T growth ratio median 1.68× (below 2.0× linear benchmark), monotone regret increase across C and Λ sweeps, and a negative control (full-blind-phase flat per-round regret ratio 0.996 vs. shrinking baseline 0.730). These are real runs but at toy scale with trend-level checks, not a full-scale reproduction of the Õ(d(√T+C+D)) bound.

claims.claim: Delay complexity D is defined as max(Λ^{1/2}, μ_τ), unifying stochastic and adversarial delay regimes into a single regret term without requiring the algorithm to know which regime it faces (Assumption 4.5).
claims.evidence: The adversarial check computes D_t from the paper's own combinatorial construction and confirms tightness to √(2Λ) (ratios 0.89→0.995), and the stochastic check confirms worst-of-20 pending counts within 5× of the Õ bound. However, these test auxiliary lemma bounds, not the core unification claim; the formula D=max(Λ^{1/2},μ_τ) is confirmed as a textual match at four source sites, and the 'without knowing the regime' property is not directly experimentally tested.

claims.claim: The adaptive weighting mechanism sets weights ω_s = min(1, α/‖Δz_s‖_{Ṽ_{s-1}^{-1}}) with α = √d/(C+D) to down-weight potentially corrupted or stale observations (Equation 4).
claims.evidence: Criterion (a) checks ω·‖Δz‖≤α where ω=min(1,α/‖Δz‖), which reduces to min(‖Δz‖,α)≤α — a tautology true by definition of min for all inputs; 5000 trials at 4.4e-16 residual measure floating-point arithmetic, not the paper. Criterion (b) confirms mean weight monotonically decreases as C+D grows (1.0→0.57→0.58→0.23), a qualitative trend. Formula transcription is confirmed but not falsifiably tested.

claims.claim: A matching lower bound of Ω(d√T + dC + D') is established, showing the algorithm's regret is optimal up to a √d factor under adversarial delays (Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: The algebraic gap check computes the ratio of d·D (upper bound) to D' (lower bound) and confirms it equals √d in the adversarial regime and 1 in the stochastic regime across d∈{4,9,16,25} — a closed-form identity from the paper's own formulas, not experimental evidence. The illustrative simulation of the hard instance shows qualitative linear-in-M scaling (ratios 2.13 vs 2.08) but is explicitly labeled as unable to verify the universal minimax statement. Neither constitutes full verification of the lower bound theorem.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 maintains a replay buffer of post-serving contexts and updates both a learned context estimator φ̂_t and the parameter estimate Θ_t via weighted maximum likelihood estimation with clipping (Section 3, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Replay buffer confirmed by construction (running sums in code), φ̂_t ridge-regression error decay slope of -0.67 over t∈[50,1500] passes an order-of-magnitude check (criterion: slope < -0.2), and weighted logistic MLE with clipping confirmed in implementation with weights ≤1 and clipping occurring. Structural/descriptive confirmation at small scale with one order-of-growth sub-check.

RyeCatcher/repro-robust-linear-dueling-b.overall: All five claims were addressed with real code and runs, but exclusively on small controlled CPU instances (T≤2400, ≤20 seeds) using qualitative trend checks, tautological identity tests, or closed-form algebraic computations — none at a scale or rigor level that constitutes full verification or falsification of the paper's theoretical claims. The logbook is methodologically careful (pre-registered criteria, negative controls, honest self-downgrades) but the experimental scope is uniformly toy-scale.

Srishti280992/repro-optimal-design-mnl-b.paper_title: Optimal Design for Multinomial Logit Model with Applications to Best Assortment Identification

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 gives a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) reformulation of the linear maximization oracle (LMO) needed for optimal design in the multinomial logit (MNL) model (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: The MILP formulation (binary x, Charnes-Cooper alpha, McCormick relaxation with S0/S1/U0/U1, normalization 1^T U1=1, big-M bounds) was implemented and tested on 24 seeded instances (N=7-9, d=3, K=3-4), achieving 24/24 exact matches to brute-force enumeration with max QFIP objective error 0.0. Destructive controls confirm sensitivity: removing Fisher centering changed 22/24 oracle choices and wrong denominator changed 23/24.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 establishes a stopping/approximation guarantee for a lifted Frank-Wolfe algorithm that solves the MNL optimal design problem without requiring exact LMO calls (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: Sixteen lifted Frank-Wolfe runs using the (d+1)-dimensional lifted information matrix and Dinkelbach ratio oracle all reached the stopping criterion g_tilde <= (1+0.1)(d+1), and all satisfied the Theorem 3.5 true-G bound (max true_g/bound = 0.373). Dinkelbach vs brute-force ratio oracle agreed with max value error 0.0, and shrinking the PSD lift factor by 20% failed the dominance check in 10/16 instances.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 shows the proposed best assortment identification algorithm achieves sample complexity O~(d log(N/δ)(1/Δmin² + 1/(κΔmin)) + T0), where d is the feature dimension, N is the number of arms/assortments, and Δmin is the minimum reward gap (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: 132 BSI trajectories with actual MNL feedback, regularized MLE, Frank-Wolfe G-optimal design sampling, and gradient-based CI stopping achieved 132/132 correct best-assortment identification and 132/132 CI-separation stops. The fixed-geometry gap sweep (N=50, d=5, delta=0.05) shows log(tau) vs log(1/Delta^2) slope 1.083 with R^2=0.901, confirming the dominant 1/Delta_min^2 scaling. Full predictor regression gives slope 1.032.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.5 shows that using the lifted G-optimal design in place of the MILP-based design multiplies the sample complexity by a factor of only (1+ε_lift), while remaining computationally tractable (Corollary 4.5).
claims.evidence: Twelve paired exact-vs-lifted G-design BSI runs on common instances show all 24/24 trajectories correctly identify the best assortment and stop by CI separation. The median lifted/exact stopping-time ratio is 1.000, below the median measured (1+epsilon_lift)=1.028. Per-pair ratios fall below the measured factor in 11/12 cases, consistent with a high-probability sample-complexity statement.

claims.claim: Table 1 reports average LMO runtime comparisons across methods (MILP vs. lifted surrogate) for varying problem sizes (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Independent timing on the Table 1 grid (N in {30,50,100,200}, K in {3,4,5}, d=5, 5 seeds per cell) shows lifted Dinkelbach oracle mean runtime at most 1.009 ms, with minimum speedup 577x and median speedup 1490x over the MILP LMO (capped at 0.25s). Large-cell MILP calls frequently fail to report finite optimality gaps under the cap, consistent with the paper's tractability argument.

claims.claim: Figure 1 reports the average stopping time τ of the best assortment identification algorithm as N (number of arms) is varied over {30, 50, 100, 200} and K (assortment size) over {3, 4, 5}, using feature dimension d=5 and failure probability δ=0.05 (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: 120 actual BSI trajectories on the Figure 1 grid (N in {30,50,100,200}, K in {3,4,5}, d=5, delta=0.05, 10 seeds per cell) with computed lifted G-optimal design, MNL feedback, and CI-based stopping achieve 120/120 correct best-assortment identification and 120/120 CI-separation stops with 0 cap hits. Stopping times are empirically measured and aggregated by (N,K) cell.

Srishti280992/repro-optimal-design-mnl-b.overall: The logbook provides a thorough multi-iteration reproduction of all six claims, with exact MILP-brute-force equivalence checks, lifted FW convergence verification with negative controls, 132 stochastic BSI trajectories confirming 1/Delta^2 sample complexity scaling, paired exact-vs-lifted design comparisons, independent runtime measurements, and full Figure 1 grid experiments. The main limitations are small instance sizes for the algebraic claims (1-2) and a custom self-normalized confidence rule for the BSI experiments, but the core mechanisms and scaling relationships are numerically confirmed.

gchauhan/repro-when-shared-knowledge-hur.paper_title: When Shared Knowledge Hurts: Spectral Over-Accumulation in Model Merging

claims.claim: Singular Value Calibration (SVC) is a training-free, data-free post-processing method that computes the SVD of the merged task matrix, measures subspace-wise task overlap via projection coefficients s_i^r, and rescales inflated singular values as σ̃^r = γ^r · σ^r while preserving spectral directions (Method/Algorithm section).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides concrete code inspection of the official repository (merge_func.py lines 85-150) showing SVD computation via torch.linalg.svd, projection coefficient calculation via einsum operations, singular value rescaling via Sm_NEW / s_list, and spectral direction preservation by reconstructing with original Um and Vm — all matching the paper's algorithm description.

claims.claim: On 8 vision datasets with ViT-B/32, adding SVC to Task Arithmetic improves accuracy from 68.9% to 81.9%, a +13.0% gain, with additional gains on TIES (+7.4%) and DARE (+14.9%) (Table results, vision benchmarks).
claims.evidence: Only 5 of 8 vision datasets were tested (Cars, RESISC45, SUN397 unavailable). On this subset, TA+SVC improved from 79.01% to 91.31% (+12.31% vs paper's +13.0%), DARE improved +14.93% (vs +14.9%), and TIES improved +7.83% (vs +7.4%) — directionally consistent but on a reduced dataset subset, not a full reproduction.

claims.claim: On a 14-dataset vision benchmark, Task Arithmetic + SVC reaches 76.7% accuracy versus a 57.7% baseline, a +19.0% improvement (Table results, 14-dataset vision).
claims.evidence: The 14-dataset benchmark was never attempted — ViT-L/14 checkpoints were unavailable due to Google Drive rate limiting, and the additional datasets were not downloaded. No experimental results exist for this claim.

claims.claim: SVC also improves NLP merging results, including a +4.8% gain for T0 with TA+SVC on classification tasks and a 12.1% gain on T5-based benchmarks (NLP experiments section).
claims.evidence: NLP experiments were not addressed at all. The logbook states T0 and T5 models, NLP datasets, and evaluation scripts were not available in the SVC repository, and no NLP runs were executed.

claims.claim: Cross-task spectral overlap is shown to concentrate in the top singular-value subspaces (Figure 3), and the singular-value inflation gap persists across different merging methods (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: No spectral analysis was performed. The logbook explicitly states this claim was not addressed — no projection coefficients s_i^r were analyzed for subspace concentration, and Figures 3 and 4 were not reproduced.

claims.claim: SVC's computational cost is 5.1 seconds for ViT-B/32 and 517.2 seconds for LLaMA2-7B, requiring no gradient computation, making it far cheaper than training-based merging alternatives (Computational cost section).
claims.evidence: Partial timing was measured (~13 seconds for ViT-B/32 vs paper's 5.1 seconds, attributed to GPU differences), but LLaMA2-7B timing was never tested. The 'no gradient computation' aspect is confirmed, but the specific runtime claims are not substantiated.

gchauhan/repro-when-shared-knowledge-hur.overall: The logbook provides a meaningful partial reproduction: the SVC algorithm implementation was verified through code inspection, and 5 of 8 vision datasets showed improvements consistent with the paper's claims on ViT-B/32. However, three major claims (14-dataset benchmark, NLP results, spectral analysis figures) were never addressed, and computational cost was only partially measured.

Srishti280992/repro-stronger-benchmark-b.paper_title: A Stronger Benchmark for Online Bilateral Trade: From Fixed Prices to Distributions

claims.claim: Under a bounded-density assumption on buyer/seller valuation distributions, the proposed algorithm achieves Õ(T^{3/4}) regret against the best fixed price distribution satisfying Global Budget Balance (GBB) (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The budget-repaired ETC audit runs real sampled trades on Beta(2,4)/Beta(4,2) at T=4,000..64,000 with regret exponent 0.714 and nonnegative prefix budgets, but uses a simplified ETC scaffold with an ad-hoc budget repair rule rather than the paper's full Algorithm 1, and the earlier real-phase run showed budget violations without the repair.

claims.claim: Without the bounded-density assumption, any algorithm suffers Ω(T) linear regret against the GBB benchmark, shown via a needle-in-the-haystack construction proving discretization is impossible (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The Yao-style needle certificate constructs M=16T disjoint hidden cells with indistinguishable off-needle transcripts, giving an algorithm-independent hit probability bound of T/M=0.0625 and certified regret 0.075T with fitted slope 1.000 across T=512..32,768, directly demonstrating the linear lower bound mechanism.

claims.claim: Bounded density lets the learner restrict to a uniform K×K price grid with discretization error O(log(T)/K), showing no separation between one-dimensional SBB learning and two-dimensional GBB distribution learning (Lemma 5.1, Lemma 5.2).
claims.evidence: Exact LP and numerical integration on two bounded-density Beta-product instances show GBB grid discretization gaps with slopes -2.150 and -2.160 (well within O(log T/K)) for K=4..96, and the SBB-gap to GBB-gap ratio is exactly 1.0 at every K, directly testing the no-separation claim.

claims.claim: In the profit-collection phase, regret is bounded by Õ(β + T/K + √(KT)) where β is the accumulated budget (Lemma 7.1, Lemma 7.2).
claims.evidence: Real Exp3 profit-collection runs over nonnegative-profit grid arms with stochastic sampled trades across 9 (T,K) cells and 16 seeds each show all 144 runs stop before T, with regret ratio to β+T/K+√(KT) ranging from 0.075 to 0.393 (mean 0.191), consistently below the claimed bound.

claims.claim: The pure-exploration phase estimates all K² price-pair outcomes using only 2K exploration samples via sample reuse across the observable/non-observable GFT decomposition (Lemma 8.1, Lemma 8.2).
claims.evidence: Simultaneous exploration at K=16 estimates all 256 price-pair L/R terms using 2KN samples (reuse factor 8.0×), the identity GFT=L+R+PRO closes to 2.22e-16, and mean estimation error contracts with slope -0.505 matching N^{-1/2} across N=64..2048 with 40 seeds.

claims.claim: The UCB-based constrained-bandit optimization phase achieves Õ(K√T) regret while preserving GBB feasibility, combining with the other phases to yield the overall Õ(T^{3/4}) rate (Lemma 9.1, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The active constrained-UCB audit runs on all K²=64 arms with real stochastic GFT/profit from sampled valuations and active subsidizing-arm selections; across T=2,000..30,000 and 16 seeds, fitted regret exponent is 0.623, max regret/(K√T log T) is 0.130, budget dip is bounded at 45.0, and every run uses at least 346 subsidizing rounds across 28 distinct arms.

Srishti280992/repro-stronger-benchmark-b.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims through exact LP benchmarks, stochastic trade simulations, and construction-level lower bounds, with Claims 2-6 verified at non-trivial scale. Claim 1 remains at toy level because the end-to-end regret audit uses a simplified ETC scaffold with an ad-hoc budget repair rather than the paper's full Algorithm 1.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-tau-2-bench-evaluati.paper_title: $\tau^2$-Bench: Evaluating Conversational Agents in a Dual-Control Environment

claims.claim: tau2-bench introduces a telecom dual-control environment where both the conversational agent and simulated user can act with tools in a shared dynamic state (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: Direct inspection of the cloned repo confirmed agent-side TelecomTools in tools.py and user-side TelecomUserTools in user_tools.py, both operating over shared environment state in environment.py, data_model.py, and user_data_model.py — concrete code-level evidence of the dual-control design.

claims.claim: The telecom domain is modeled with separate agent and user databases, 13 agent tools, 30 user tools, and 114 sampled tasks from a 2,285-task full set (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Grep commands on the live repo produced exact counts: 13 @is_tool decorators in tools.py, 30 in user_tools.py, len(tasks_full.json)=2285, and len(split_tasks.json['base'])=114, all matching Table 1; separate db.toml and user_db.toml files confirmed distinct databases.

claims.claim: The benchmark uses a compositional task generator that creates verifiable telecom tasks from intent and subtask components (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Inspection of create_tasks.py showed it combines three per-issue-type task managers (mobile_data, service, mms), with task IDs as pipe-separated subtask compositions and explicit intent tags plus derived personas, directly confirming the compositional generator design.

claims.claim: Agents show lower pass@1 in default dual-control telecom operation than in no-user and oracle-plan modes, isolating the cost of decentralized user coordination (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: No LLM API credentials or local model runtime were available, so no agent conversations were run and no pass@1 numbers were produced across the three control modes; the claim was never experimentally addressed.

claims.claim: Telecom performance declines as the number of required actions or distinct issues increases (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Same lack of LLM backend as Claim 4 means no per-task pass/fail outcomes were generated; while task complexity metadata exists, no performance-vs-complexity analysis was actually run.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-tau-2-bench-evaluati.overall: The logbook provides rigorous static code and data inspection that fully verifies the three structural/design claims (dual-control architecture, exact tool/task counts, compositional generator) with concrete commands and exact numeric matches. The two empirical performance claims were not addressed at all due to absence of any LLM backend, with no attempt to substitute open-source models.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-unveiling-the-struct.paper_title: Unveiling the Structure of Do-Calculus Reasoning via Derivation Graphs

claims.claim: For a graph with no edges, the derivation graph decomposes into 2^|V|-1 connected components, one per distinct outcome variable (Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: Directly built derivation graphs for every nonempty outcome subset Y on edgeless DAGs with n=2..5, summing connected components to exactly 3, 7, 15, 31 = 2^n-1 in all cases.

claims.claim: The number of causally equivalent expressions reachable via do-calculus derivations is upper bounded by 3^|V\Y|, where Y is the set of outcome variables (Proposition 2).
claims.evidence: On 6 random 5-node DAGs, reachable-state counts (54, 36, 36, 37, 24, 81) were all ≤ 3^4=81, with the bound saturated only on the sparsest graph; edgeless-graph tests confirmed the bound is tight (component size = 3^(n-|Y|) exactly).
