claims.claim: Looped transformers with polylogarithmic iterations are shown to capture the parallel complexity classes AC^k and TC^k, and CoT with polylogarithmic steps is proven strictly weaker than looped models under standard complexity assumptions (Section 3, Theorem 3.13, Lemma 3.14, Theorems 3.15-3.16)
claims.evidence: STCON exhaustively verified for n=4 (4,096 graphs) and n=5 (1,048,576 graphs) with ceil(log2(n-1)) iterations, and MAJORITY precision studied. The strict separation between polylog-step CoT and looped models relies on explicitly unproven complexity assumptions (P≠NP, AC⁰≠TC⁰, etc.) that are non-computational. The verifiable parts are at toy scale only.

claims.claim: CoT with polynomially many steps can represent any fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme (FPRAS), giving it an approximate-counting capability that looped/latent-thought transformers cannot match under standard assumptions (Section 4, Theorem 4.7)
claims.evidence: Unbiased Karp-Luby #DNF FPRAS implemented on 11 standard configs (n_vars 4-12) and 6 sparse adversarial configs (n_vars 14-24) with mean relative error 0.0059 and bitset exact enumeration as ground truth. No actual CoT transformer model was used; this is an algorithmic implementation at reduced scale.

claims.claim: A pretrained CoT model augmented with an inference-time algorithm such as majority voting constitutes a fully polynomial almost uniform sampler (FPAUS), formalizing how stochastic decoding enables approximate counting (Section 4, Proposition 4.6)
claims.evidence: Exact Glauber transition matrix analysis on 6 very small graph configurations (up to 5 vertices, 48 proper colorings) shows rapid mixing for the single irreducible case (path5-3colors, T*(0.1)=78) and correctly identifies reducible chains as negative controls. No pretrained CoT model with majority voting was actually evaluated.

claims.claim: Experiments on parallelizable tasks and DNF-counting-style approximation tasks empirically validate the predicted separation between CoT and latent/looped thought (Section 5.1-5.2)
claims.evidence: 14 parallel task configs (n_bits ≤ 64) and 5 DNF counting configs (n_vars ≤ 6) demonstrate the predicted speedup pattern algorithmically, but the logbook itself states no transformer was trained and this does not reproduce the paper's Section 5 trained-model experiments.

amkkk/repro-a-formal-comparison-between-.overall: This logbook provides algorithmic simulations that verify the formal constructions and algorithmic predictions of the paper at small scale (graphs with ≤64 nodes, DNF with ≤24 variables, coloring on ≤5-vertex graphs), but no actual transformer models were trained or evaluated. All six claims are addressed with real runs and numbers on clearly simplified setups, constituting toy-scale evidence rather than full reproductions.

ai-sherpa/differentiable-coherent-factua.paper_title: Differentiable Conformal Training for LLM Reasoning Factuality

claims.claim: Differentiable Coherent Factuality (DCF) achieves up to a 141% improvement in claim retention over frequency-based baselines on the MATH dataset at reliability level α=0.03 (1.76 vs. 0.73 claims retained) (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: The retention numbers (1.76 vs 0.73, recomputed gain 141.10%) match the paper's Table 7 exactly, but the paper's own table reports DCF coverage of 96.55% against the 97.00% target implied by 'at reliability level α=0.03' (marked 'No*' by the authors). The independent re-run on 100 real released MATH problems confirms the mechanism produces large gains at nearby α (e.g., +186.5% at α=0.05 with coverage met), but at α=0.03 with coverage satisfied, retention drops to 0.070 claims/problem—far from 1.76. The composite claim as stated is not attainable.

claims.claim: DCF achieves up to a 61% improvement in claim retention over frequency-based baselines on the FELM dataset at α=0.01 (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Source verification confirms 61.26% gain (rounds to 61%) with coverage 99.15% ≥ 99.00% target. An independent end-to-end re-run on 711 real FELM problems (using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct locally for frequency scoring, 20-fold CV, 60 test evaluations per α) shows DCF retains 0.3072 claims/problem at 99.53% coverage while the frequency baseline retains 0.0000—exceeding the claim. The α-shape (DCF advantage concentrated at strict reliability, evaporating as α relaxes) reproduces across 8 reliability levels.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 (Calibration Convergence) shows that as temperature parameters approach their limits, DCF's soft nonconformity scores converge to the hard Coherent Factuality algorithm's scores, recovering its conformal quantile properties (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: On 50 synthetic graphs matching the paper's reported MATH/FELM statistics, running the full Algorithm-1 pipeline at 10 temperatures (T=1.0→0.001) shows mean absolute soft-vs-hard nonconformity error contracting from 1.3804 to 4.97e-06 (277861× reduction), with 48/50 graphs recovering the hard score within 1e-10 and 15/15 conformal quantiles recovering to within 1e-6. Destructive controls (fixed β=8: error 0.3196; violation term removed: error 0.9714) confirm mechanism dependence.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 (Prediction Convergence) shows DCF's soft retention probabilities converge to the original Coherent Factuality prediction set, preserving test-time coverage guarantees (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: On 25 calibration + 25 held-out synthetic graphs at α=0.05 (τ̂α=0.9695), running the gated soft argmax pipeline (Algorithm 2) at 10 temperatures shows node-level agreement with the hard CF prediction set rising from 85.6% to 100.0% and holding at 100.0% for all T≤0.01 (four consecutive temperatures), with mean |soft−hard| falling to 0.0361.

claims.claim: DCF's soft relaxations achieve 90-100% agreement with hard Coherent Factuality predictions across α∈[0.01, 0.10], validating the smooth approximation (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Source verification of the paper's Table 2 (64,335 predictions) confirms min=90.2%, max=100.0%, n-weighted mean=95.17%—all within [90,100]%. An independent re-run on 27 real released MATH problems (227 claims, 20-fold CV) gives 100.0% agreement under protocol A (prediction relaxation) and 93.0–93.8% under protocol B (end-to-end), both within the claimed band. A 200-threshold stress test (45,400 comparisons) shows worst-case 82.38% at non-conformal boundary thresholds, but 100% at conformally selected thresholds.

claims.claim: DCF jointly relaxes claim scoring together with logical-ancestor coherence enforcement and constrained argmax selection, rather than treating these graph operations independently (Section 3.2-3.4).
claims.evidence: A central finite-difference gradient (h=1e-3) of the retention loss through the full coupled pipeline (filter→ancestor-coherence→violation→soft-supremum→gated argmax) on 40 synthetic graphs shows all 5/5 scorer parameters carry nonzero mean gradients (L2 norm 0.01867). An ancestor-removal ablation (q_v,τ=p_v,τ) changes soft retention probabilities by total L1=2.0558 over 214 nodes, affecting 29/40 graphs, confirming the graph structure is not decorative.

ai-sherpa/differentiable-coherent-factua.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous independent reproduction: claims 2–6 are verified with concrete experimental evidence on real released data (claims 2, 5) or synthetic graphs matching paper statistics with destructive controls (claims 3, 4, 6), while claim 1 is falsified because the paper's own Table 7 shows coverage of 96.55% falls short of the 97% reliability target that the claim's 'at reliability level α=0.03' qualifier requires.

nstp/repro-provably-efficient-policy-rew.paper_title: Provably Efficient Policy-Reward Co-Pretraining for Adversarial Imitation Learning

claims.claim: CoPT-AIL jointly pretrains a policy and a reward function prior to adversarial imitation learning, in contrast to standard adversarial imitation learning (AIL) pipelines that train policy and reward purely online (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements the CoPT-AIL mechanism (π¹=π^BC for policy pretraining, r¹=log π^BC for reward pretraining) versus standard AIL (random initialization) on a tabular MDP with |S|=2, |A|=2, H=2, exercising the distinction but at a clearly simplified scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 establishes a provable imitation-gap bound for CoPT-AIL showing improvement over the bound for standard AIL as a function of pretraining quality (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Theorem 1 Eqs. (7) and (8) are numerically checked on a small tabular MDP: reward error 0.003 ≤ RHS 18.15 with 1/N decay slope −1.33, and imitation gap −0.048 ≤ RHS 26.89. The bounds hold but are extremely loose (RHS ≫ LHS) on this |S|=2, H=2 instance, confirming direction and scaling but not tightness at a toy scale.

claims.claim: Proposition 1 and Proposition 2 characterize structural properties of the co-pretraining objective that underlie the Theorem 1 guarantee, including how pretraining error propagates into the final imitation gap (Propositions 1-2).
claims.evidence: Proposition 1 (Eq. 4) holds with LHS −0.043 ≤ RHS 4.79 on the tabular instance, and the policy-error term correctly inflates 9× when pretraining is removed. Proposition 2 (Eq. 6) achieves exact equality to machine precision (residual 3.3e−16) with a working falsification control. Both are verified on a |S|=2, H=2 toy MDP, not a general proof.

claims.claim: The paper claims to give the first theoretical guarantee showing that pretraining (of both policy and reward) provably reduces the imitation gap in adversarial imitation learning, distinguishing it from prior AIL theory that does not model pretraining benefits (Section 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies that the theoretical bounds hold and the mechanism functions, but the claim of being the 'first' theoretical guarantee of this type requires surveying prior AIL literature, which the logbook does not address.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 specifies the core CoPT-AIL co-pretraining procedure, with Algorithms 2 and 3 given as implementation variants/complementary methods (Algorithms 1-3).
claims.evidence: The AIL loop is implemented with two initialization modes corresponding to Algorithm 1 (random r¹) and Algorithm 2 (r¹=log π^BC) on a tabular MDP, but Algorithm 3 is never mentioned or implemented, leaving the claim only partially addressed at toy scale.

nstp/repro-provably-efficient-policy-rew.overall: The logbook provides a careful from-scratch numerical audit of the paper's theoretical results (Propositions 1–2, Theorem 1) on small tabular MDPs, with exact computations, unit tests, falsification controls, and confirmed 1/N reward-error scaling, but all at a simplified scale far below the paper's deep-RL experiments. The novelty positioning claim (Claim 4) is unaddressed, and Algorithm 3 is not implemented.

nstp/repro-a-2sg-adaptive-and-asymmetric.paper_title: A$^2$SG: Adaptive and Asymmetric Surrogate Gradients for Training Deep Spiking Neural Networks

claims.claim: A2SG's asymmetric surrogate gradient (Eq. 10) allocates larger gradients to higher membrane potentials and achieves 96.74% accuracy on CIFAR10 with ResNet19, versus 95.17% for the LSG baseline (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook never addresses Table 1 with ResNet19 or the LSG baseline. Its toy SNN experiment (Claim 6) targets a different table (Table 2: VGG16, A2SG vs BOX) on synthetic data, and even there A2SG accuracy (0.915) is marginally below BOX (0.922), not reproducing the paper's reported advantage.

claims.claim: On CIFAR100 with ResNet19, A2SG reaches 81.05% accuracy compared to 76.85% for LSG (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook never addresses Table 1 with ResNet19 or the LSG baseline on CIFAR100. Its toy proxy (Claim 7) targets a different table (Table 7: VGG16, A2SG vs BOX) on synthetic 10-class data, where A2SG (0.546) does not exceed BOX (0.550).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 proves that asymmetric surrogate gradients achieve lower coefficient-of-variation (CV) than symmetric variants when L·κ > σ² (Section 4.3, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Using the paper's own f_asy, f_sym, and CV formula with true Gaussian weight, the logbook computes CV_asy > CV_sym in all 6 configurations where Lκ > σ² (e.g., Lκ=0.5: CV_asy=3.098 vs CV_sym=2.872). The ASY closed form matches direct integration to 10⁻¹¹, and the logbook identifies a concrete algebra error in the paper's SYM triangle moments (paper CV_sym=0.422 vs faithful integration=1.420).

claims.claim: Section 4.1 establishes a direct connection between the local gradient variation coefficient and Fisher Information Matrix eigenvalues, showing reduced CV corresponds to a flatter loss landscape (Section 4.1, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook reproduces Eq.7 (the FIM largest-eigenvalue bound) at non-toy scale across 5 FC-layer configurations (n×m up to 8×7, 200K MC samples): λmax(F) ≤ μ²λmax(E[(a⊗1)(a⊗1)ᵀ]) + cμ²CV(δ) holds with recovered c≈1.01, the Weyl backbone is exact, and degradation with c=0.1 correctly violates the bound. This verifies the mathematical connection between CV and FIM eigenvalues, though the Figure 1 visualization itself is not directly tested.

claims.claim: On ImageNet, E-SpikeFormer combined with A2SG achieves 85.43% accuracy at 35.64 mJ energy consumption (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook does not address ImageNet, E-SpikeFormer, or energy consumption measurements at all. No experiment related to Table 3 was conducted.

claims.claim: On CIFAR10-DVS, A2SG reaches 82.36% accuracy with the VGGSNN architecture (Table 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook does not address CIFAR10-DVS or the VGGSNN architecture. No experiment related to Table 4 was conducted.

nstp/repro-a-2sg-adaptive-and-asymmetric.overall: The logbook provides rigorous numerical falsification of Theorem 4.2 (Claim 3) with concrete counterexamples and an identified algebra error, and verifies the FIM eigenvalue bound (Claim 4) at non-toy scale. However, the paper's main empirical claims (CIFAR10/100 with ResNet19 vs LSG, ImageNet with E-SpikeFormer, CIFAR10-DVS with VGGSNN) are never addressed at the correct architecture, dataset, or baseline — only toy proxies on different tables (Tables 2/7 with VGG16 vs BOX) are provided, and those do not reproduce the reported accuracy gains.

SabaPivot/repro-optimal-fair-aggregation.paper_title: Optimal Fair Aggregation of Crowdsourced Noisy Labels using Demographic Parity Constraints

claims.claim: The demographic parity gap of majority-vote aggregated labels is bounded above by an exponentially decaying term in the number of annotators R, of the form sum over groups a of E[e^{-R K_phi(a,X)}] (Proposition 3.2).
claims.evidence: The Prop 3.2 bound was checked exactly (Poisson-binomial, no Monte Carlo) across 15 configurations with max violation −3.33e-03 (never violated), and the underlying Gao error bound held across 800 configurations with max(err−bound)=−1.88e-05; the destructive control replacing the exponent with 2K produced 5/5 violations, confirming the specific exponential form.

claims.claim: Under interpretable conditions on annotator skill, both Majority Vote and Bayesian aggregation are shown to achieve asymptotically unbiased fairness gaps relative to ground-truth labels as crowd size grows (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: Both MV and Bayes aggregators converge to Δ_DP(Y) to ~1e-5–1e-6 in two setups (trivial target 0 and non-trivial target 0.2), with the MV decay rate slope −0.14 matching the predicted Gao exponent −K=−0.145, and the Bayes condition Σ(p−½)²=4.836 at R=60 confirmed as diverging.

claims.claim: For majority voting with R annotators, the aggregated fairness gap is bounded by epsilon(R) times the sum of individual annotators' fairness gaps, showing majority voting can amplify rather than average out bias (Proposition 3.6).
claims.evidence: The Baillon constant η=0.4688223555 was computed via two independent formula forms agreeing to 1.67e-16 (matching paper's 0.4688), the Prop 3.6 inequality held across 8 exact configs (max violation −1.18e-02), and the systematic-bias amplification showed log-log slope exactly 0.5000 confirming O(√R) growth; the destructive control with η'=1/√(2π) undershot the exhaustive supremum 0.4215, confirming the larger constant is necessary.

claims.claim: Convergence of the fairness gap to the ground-truth value requires a majority of annotators to have skill exceeding 0.5 plus a margin epsilon; without this, majority voting fails to converge (Section 3, following Proposition 3.6).
claims.evidence: At the no-signal point (all skills p=½), Δ_DP(Ŷ^MV)=0 exactly for every R from 3 to 200, keeping the gap to Δ_DP(Y)=0.2 permanently, while the competent crowd (p=0.75) converges (gap 0.020 at R=10 → 0.0000 at R=80); the tolerated skill band width shrinks with log-log slope −0.576≈−½, matching ε~1/√R.

claims.claim: FairCrowd, a post-processing method, enforces a strict epsilon-fairness constraint on the output of any aggregation rule while provably bounding the resulting accuracy loss (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: FairCrowd's recipe achieved Δ_DP equal to target ε to ~1e-4 across 6 ε values while its risk matched an independently constructed linear-programming optimum to 1e-6–1e-5 (exactly 2.8e-17 when the constraint is slack at ε=0.30); the control confirmed unconstrained Bayes violates ε-fairness (Δ_DP=0.2044) for any ε<0.2044, showing the β*-adjustment is necessary.

SabaPivot/repro-optimal-fair-aggregation.overall: All five theoretical claims are supported by exact, clean-room computations on the paper's own synthetic model (X=∅), with Poisson-binomial convolution and exhaustive 2^R enumeration replacing Monte Carlo, plus destructive controls and an independent LP verification for FairCrowd optimality. The main limitation is that real-dataset benchmarks and multiclass generalization are not covered, but the core theoretical propositions are rigorously verified at the paper's own scale.

SabaPivot/repro-innovation-an-almost-cha.paper_title: Innovation: An Almost Characterization of Hallucination

claims.claim: The paper defines innovation (Definition 3.1) as a language model assigning nonzero probability mass to statements not present in the training data, and shows via Observation 3.2 that hallucinating with positive probability implies the model innovates (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The scaled audit performed 3,450,000 exact mass checks across regimes up to |Ω|=1,000,000 confirming g(H)≤g(U) (hence g(H)>0⇒g(U)>0), with minimum margin 0 indicating tight cases were exercised. The destructive control relaxing observed factuality produced g(H)=1, g(U)=0, confirming the assumption's necessity.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows that under K-Sparsity and Regular Facts assumptions, if the innovation mass g(U) > 0, the probability a model hallucinates is at least 1 - K/|U| (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: Exact hypergeometric posterior probabilities were computed across 5 regimes (up to |U|=1,000,000, K=5,000) and 5 support families; all 23 exact event rows satisfy Pr[g(H)>0]≥1−K/|U| with 0 failures. Two regimes (million ultra-sparse and tight-20%) attain the bound exactly (0.999900 and 0.800000), demonstrating tightness. The Regular-Facts-relaxed control yields event probability 0 vs required 0.9.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.4 shows that a calibrated model with any positive missing probability mass necessarily innovates (Proposition 3.4).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive Bell(7) enumeration (877 partitions) with exact Fraction arithmetic yielded 263,100 checks confirming g(U)>0 whenever g=p^Π and p(U)>0, with 0 failures. An additional 4,000 large random partition configurations up to |Ω|=1,000,000 all passed. The uncalibrated control shows p(U)=0.5 coexisting with g(U)=0.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 gives a Markov-style bound showing the hallucination rate satisfies g(H) ≥ g(U)(1 - K/(δ|U|)) with probability at least 1-δ (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Exact hypergeometric event probabilities were computed for 161 model-regime-δ combinations across 5 regimes and 7 admissible δ values per regime, with 0 failures and minimum margin 9.999×10⁻⁵ near the theorem's domain boundary. The Regular-Facts-relaxed control at δ=0.5 gives hallucination mass 0 vs threshold 0.8 and event probability 0 vs required 0.5.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 establishes a high-confidence bound where, with probability at least 1 - K/|U|, the hallucination rate satisfies g(H) ≥ g(U)/(K+1) (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: All 23 exact event rows across 5 regimes and 5 support families satisfy Pr[g(H)≥g(U)/(K+1)]≥1−K/|U| with 0 failures. Spike profiles attain the confidence floor exactly in two regimes (0.9999 and 0.8), exercising both proof branches. The destructive control yields event probability 0 vs required 0.9.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.3 lower-bounds the innovation rate by g(U) ≥ p(U)/(K+1) minus a miscalibration distance term, linking missing probability mass to innovation (Proposition 4.3).
claims.evidence: Bell(7) exhaustive enumeration provides 263,100 exact coarsening-lemma checks and 771,760 full-inequality checks (g(U)≥p(U)/(K+1)−TV(g,p^Π)) with 0 failures and minimum margin 0. An asymptotic tightness sequence through K=10,000 shows the ratio p^Π(U)/[p(U)/(K+1)] approaching 1.0001, and the K-sparsity-relaxed control violates the bound (0.333<0.495).

SabaPivot/repro-innovation-an-almost-cha.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous numerical audit of all six theorem/proposition claims using exact rational arithmetic, exact hypergeometric posterior probabilities, exhaustive Bell(7) partition enumeration, and scaled regimes up to |Ω|=1,000,000 with K up to 5,000. All checks pass with tightness demonstrated and destructive controls confirming each assumption's necessity, though the audit explicitly notes it is not a formal proof replacement.

SabaPivot/repro-minimax-learning-of-inte.paper_title: MiniMax Learning of Interpretable Factored Stochastic Policies from Conjoint Data, with Uncertainty Quantification

claims.claim: Formulates optimal treatment selection from conjoint data as finding a stochastic policy over combinatorial profiles that maximizes expected outcome Q(π), rather than a single best profile (Section 2.2, Equation 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements the product-policy expectation and baseline-eliminated quadratic objective in repro/policy.py, with unit fixtures confirming that degenerate marginals reproduce single-profile decisions and interior probabilities genuinely mix profiles, matching Eq. 1's formulation.

claims.claim: Uses the Delta method to propagate parameter uncertainty from the fitted outcome model into asymptotically valid variance-covariance estimates for the estimated optimal policy and its value (Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: The analytic implicit Jacobian agrees with central finite differences to max error 7.73e-11, 80-decimal re-solves change the policy by at most 1.11e-16, and conditional-design synthetic policy coverage ranges 0.94–0.9625 across 12 cells, supporting asymptotic validity of the Delta method covariance.

claims.claim: Models strategic settings (e.g., two competing candidates) as a zero-sum minimax game max_πA min_πB Q(πA, πB), invoking von Neumann's minimax theorem to guarantee equilibrium existence (Section 2.3, Equation 3).
claims.evidence: While the full-simplex LP oracle verifies zero duality gap on matching pennies and a 3x3 fixture, a concrete two-binary-factor counterexample shows the restricted factored policy class has a duality gap of 0.8375 (restricted max-min −0.59125 vs. restricted min-max 0.24625), meaning von Neumann's theorem does not guarantee equilibrium existence for the paper's actual factored policy class.

claims.claim: Derives a closed-form average-case optimal policy π^{a*} = C^{-1}B under pairwise (two-way) interaction effects, using an L2-regularization term λn·||π^a − p||² that shrinks the solution toward the empirical profile distribution p (Section 2.2, Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: Independent derivation confirms the C matrix structure (diagonal −4λ, within-factor off-diagonal −2λ, cross-factor entries from interactions) and B vector; binary and multilevel fixtures show KKT residuals below 1e-12 and match exhaustive grid maximization, with the noted scope condition that C^{-1}B requires an interior concave solution.

claims.claim: Simulation studies show RMSE convergence with sample size across 5–20 factors (variance dominating bias) and confidence interval coverage approaching the nominal 95% level for n ≥ 5000 in the adversarial setting (Section 3.2, Section 3.4).
claims.evidence: Full 200-replication reruns across K={5,10,20} and n={500,1500,3500,10000} show RMSE decreasing at every sample-size step in all 12 series (e.g., K=5: 0.0127→0.0029), variance exceeding squared bias in every cell, policy coverage 0.941–0.959, and adversarial coverage 0.9275–0.9825 across 3,000 datasets with 12,000/12,000 converged GLM fits.

claims.claim: Applies the minimax framework to 2016 U.S. presidential election conjoint data, finding that adversarial equilibrium predictions align more closely with actual electoral outcomes than non-strategic (single-optimizer) predictions (Section 4).
claims.evidence: An independent Python rerun on frozen processed Ono conjoint data (5,230 pairs, 490 features) produces adversarial Democratic share 0.4990 (distance 0.0121 to actual Clinton share 0.5111) vs. average comparator 0.6141 (distance 0.1029), reproducing the claim's direction that adversarial equilibrium predictions align more closely with actual electoral outcomes, approximately 8.5× closer.

SabaPivot/repro-minimax-learning-of-inte.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical and algebraic evidence supporting five of six claims, including full-scale simulations with 200 replications and a real-data election rerun, while falsifying Claim 3 by demonstrating a duality gap in the restricted factored policy class that invalidates the von Neumann equilibrium guarantee as worded.

SabaPivot/repro-rotation-invariant-spher.paper_title: Rotation-Invariant Spherical Watermarking via Third-Order SO(3) Representation Coupling

claims.claim: The method (TRIAD) constructs a third-order spherical bispectrum by coupling three irreducible SO(3) representations via tensor products and projecting onto the trivial representation using Clebsch-Gordan coefficients, yielding a rotation-invariant scalar that preserves phase information (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The third-order contraction I = sum C^0_0 c(l1,m1)c(l2,m2)c(l3,m3) is implemented with exact SymPy Wigner-3j coefficients, and a control experiment shows replacing the CG coupling with a random tensor changes the statistic by 88.3 under rotation while a single coefficient changes by only 1.08, demonstrating the invariance is carried by the Clebsch-Gordan contraction.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves the third-order bispectrum invariant is strictly invariant under arbitrary SO(3) rotations, with perturbations to higher-order harmonic coefficients producing detectable changes in the invariant (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Rotating SH coefficients with Wigner-D matrices and recomputing the bispectrum yields max absolute error 2.3e-14 over four independent rotations, and a phase-twisted signal preserves the power spectrum within 1.8e-15 yet changes the bispectrum by 12.4, numerically confirming both strict rotation invariance and perturbation detectability.

claims.claim: Watermarks are embedded into spherical harmonic coefficients at degrees 6, 8, and 14 via SO(3)-equivariant operations to avoid perceptible artifacts in low-frequency (coarse) content (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The verify_watermark.py script embeds bits [1,0,1] into the per-degree power spectrum at degrees [6, 8, 14] and recovers them exactly, with the power spectrum showing max rotation deviation of 2.84e-14; the PSNR/SSIM results on 72 SUN360 panoramas (Claim 5) further support the perceptibility claim.

claims.claim: Under arbitrary 3D rotations, TRIAD maintains near-100% bit accuracy while baseline watermarking methods (with or without rotation augmentation) collapse in performance (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Over 200 rotation trials, TRIAD achieves 1.0 bit accuracy while a raw-coefficient baseline collapses to 0.505; the SUN360 benchmark independently confirms 0.9975 rotation accuracy across 2,304 rotation cases on 72 real panoramas, though only a simple coordinate-dependent baseline (without rotation augmentation) was tested.

claims.claim: Watermarked panoramic images retain high visual fidelity, with PSNR of 39.22 dB and SSIM of 0.9946 (Section 5).
claims.evidence: On 72 real SUN360 panoramas at native 1024×512 resolution with 32-bit payload, the reproduction reports mean PSNR 46.75 dB (min 41.15) and mean SSIM 0.9987 (min 0.9832), both exceeding the paper's reported 39.22 dB and 0.9946, with an independent verifier recomputing all aggregates from raw per-image records.

claims.claim: TRIAD also achieves 100% bit accuracy under JPEG compression, Gaussian blur, Gaussian noise, and resizing, though embedding capacity is constrained to roughly 32-64 bits because harmonics above degree 16 are vulnerable to lossy compression and aliasing (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The SUN360 distortion benchmark achieves 2304/2304 (100%) correct bits under JPEG Q=50, Gaussian blur, Gaussian noise, and resize on 72 real panoramas; a synthetic experiment confirms 32-bit and 64-bit payloads survive in degrees ≤16 (min 99.2% and 99.6% respectively) while degrees >16 collapse under JPEG (71.7%) and resize (51.0%), directly demonstrating the capacity ceiling mechanism.

SabaPivot/repro-rotation-invariant-spher.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous clean-room reproduction implementing the paper's exact Wigner-3j bispectrum contraction, testing rotation invariance and watermark robustness on 72 real SUN360 panoramas at native resolution with proper baselines and negative controls. The main limitation is that the authors' neural model and code are unavailable (repository contains only a README), so this is a faithful algorithmic reproduction rather than a direct rerun of the original trained system.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 proves that all context-free languages can be recognized by looped transformers using O(log(n)) looping layers and O(n^6) padding tokens (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Clean-room implementation of Algorithms 1/2 on the inherently ambiguous CFL {a^i b^j c^k : i=j or j=k}, exhaustively checking all 9,840 strings (n=1..8) with zero disagreements against independent CKY on 1,200 items and 67,200 slashed items; exact polynomial degree computation confirms O(n^6) padding (degree 6 for GAP configurations), and alternation depth stays within 2*ceil(log2(2n)) up to n=120.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows unambiguous context-free languages can be recognized with fewer resources than the general case: O(log^2(n)) looping layers and O(n^3) padding tokens (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Chytil marking algorithm implemented on unambiguous Dyck-1 with all 8,190 strings (L=1..12) checked exhaustively: 3.3M item-realizability checks with zero CKY disagreements, Fact 4.1 path uniqueness confirmed (max 1 directed path vs 14 for ambiguous control), and exact polynomial degree 3 for total padding allocation matching O(n^3).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 further reduces requirements for unambiguous linear context-free languages to O(log(n)) looping layers and O(n^2) padding tokens by exploiting the linearity constraint (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Two linear-unambiguous grammars (a^n b^n and w w^R) tested exhaustively over 32,766 strings each with zero CKY disagreements; Proposition 4.1 (I_1=I_*) holds on all 65,532 linear-grammar strings (0 mismatches) while the non-linear Dyck-1 control fails on 12,864 strings; exact edge-padding polynomial degree is 2 for linear grammars and 3 for the non-linear control.

claims.claim: Lemma 4.1 shows that Boolean formula evaluation can be computed in O(log(n)) steps via a parallel pebbling argument, which underlies the padding-token constructions used in the main theorems (Section 4, Lemma 4.1).
claims.evidence: Pebble game blocks B_activate/B_square/B_pebble implemented and tested on 93,898 formulas exhaustively (1-6 leaves, all shapes/assignments) with zero errors; right-deep caterpillar chains up to 2048 leaves show iters=log2(leaves) within ceil(log2 V)+1 bound in 'activate-once' mode. The logbook honestly reports that the literal 'refresh' reading of Appendix C yields linear iterations, attributing this to under-specification of the activation condition rather than falsifying the lemma.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.1 shows that Boolean Formula Value Problem (BFVP) recognition requires zero padding tokens while retaining logarithmic depth (Section 4, Corollary 4.1).
claims.evidence: C-RASP program (Lemma B.2) and pebble game (Lemma C.2) implemented clean-room; all 12,207,030 strings over {T,F,~,&,|} (L=1..10) enumerated with zero well-formedness mismatches, 165,588 formulas decided with zero BFVP errors, zero padding symbols used (postfix bijection confirmed), all runs within ceil(log2 V)+1 depth bound, and three destructive controls fail exactly where expected.

claims.claim: Table 1 summarizes the padding-versus-depth tradeoff across general, unambiguous, and linear-unambiguous context-free language classes, showing that grammatical restrictions systematically reduce required padding (Table 1).
claims.evidence: All six Table 1 languages tested (566,612 strings total) with grammar classes certified by exhaustive parse-tree counting; exact padding polynomial degrees are 6 (general), 3 (unambiguous), 2 (linear-unambiguous) for every language, with reduction factors of 646x-3023x at n=16. The logbook explicitly acknowledges it does not reproduce the training accuracy cells of Table 1 but verifies the structural padding-depth tradeoff the table supports.

SabaPivot/repro-context-free-recognition.overall: This logbook provides strong empirical support for all six claims through faithful clean-room implementations of the paper's algorithms, verified exhaustively on non-trivial CFLs with independent ground truth, destructive controls, and exact polynomial-degree computation. The principal limitation is that finite experiments cannot prove universal asymptotic theorems, but the evidence consistently confirms the claimed mechanisms and resource bounds.

SabaPivot/repro-provably-data-driven-lag.paper_title: Provably Data-driven Lagrangian Relaxation for Mixed Integer Linear Programming

claims.claim: For learned Lagrangian Relaxation multipliers over s coupling constraints and N training samples, the expected excess risk of the ERM solution is upper bounded by O(s^1.5/√N) (Theorem 5.5).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo Rademacher supremum on a 3×5 (s,N) grid with s up to 128 and N up to 512 shows s_slope≈1.499 and N_slope≈-0.500, directly matching the O(s^1.5/√N) rate; the hard-family ERM with exact median computation shows s^1.0/√N, safely below the upper bound.

claims.claim: A minimax lower bound of Ω(s/√N) is proven, showing linear dependence on the number of coupled constraints s is unavoidable for any learning algorithm (Theorem 5.6).
claims.evidence: Using Theorem 5.6's exact Bernoulli distribution with ε=0.5/√N, exact empirical MILP-dual solving across 100,000 trials yields s^1.0003 N^-0.5007 scaling; binary packing experiments show log2_size_per_dimension=0.125 for s=16,32,64, confirming the Fano construction's information-theoretic structure.

claims.claim: Stochastic Gradient Ascent with iterate averaging is shown to achieve the matching O(s/√N) rate, closing the O(√s) gap between the ERM upper bound and the minimax lower bound and establishing minimax optimality (Theorem 5.12).
claims.evidence: Literal Algorithm-1 SGA with 3,047,424 exact binary Lagrangian subproblem solves across 20 (s,N) cells and 768 trials shows s_slope≈0.991 and N_slope≈-0.497, closely matching the claimed O(s/√N) rate; all cells satisfy the finite upper bound; negative control with fixed learning rate shows non-decaying error floor.

claims.claim: The framework is extended to learning-to-warm-start sub-gradient ascent for large-scale Mixed Integer Linear Programming, with an O(s/N) risk upper bound (Theorem 6.1) and matching Ω(s/N) minimax lower bound (Theorem 6.2).
claims.evidence: Warm-start ERM as sample mean of exact per-instance dual optima (π*=c) across 150,000 trials and 30 (s,N) cells shows s^1.0002 N^-0.9998 scaling with max 0.91% relative error from the exact variance formula sσ²p(1-p)/N, matching O(s/N); negative control with absolute error recovers the slower √N rate.

claims.claim: The covering number of the dual multiplier class U is bounded as log N(δ,U,‖·‖₂,N) ≤ s·log(1+2Bπ_max s/δ), used to derive the Rademacher complexity bound R_N(U)=O(s^1.5/√N) (Lemma 5.3, Lemma 5.4).
claims.evidence: Empirical covering nets for s=4,8,16,32 with N=256 and three radii show all 18,000 dual function evaluations within requested δ and all net cardinalities below (1+2Bπ_max s/δ)^s; Dudley entropy integral with √s radius weighting yields dimension slope≈1.048, supporting the O(s^1.5/√N) Rademacher complexity.

claims.claim: The dual function u(π,P) is shown to be concave in π with subgradient norm bounded by 2B√s under bounded constraint-violation assumptions on the MILP instance (Proposition 5.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: 240 generic binary MILPs with 8 variables and s=2,4,8, solved by full enumeration of 256 states, checked across 9,600 random multiplier pairs: zero concavity violations (max residual 7.1e-15), zero supergradient-inequality violations, max subgradient norm 9.23 ≤ bound 11.78; negative control replacing min by max produces violation 5.35.

SabaPivot/repro-provably-data-driven-lag.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence for all six theoretical claims through scaling experiments and structural checks on the paper's own binary MILP constructions, with exact subproblem solves, millions of stochastic iterations, negative controls, and deterministic reproducibility. The experiments verify the key rate mechanisms (s^1.5/√N, s/√N, s/N) and structural properties (concavity, subgradient bounds, covering numbers) rather than re-running a full MILP benchmark suite.

SabaPivot/repro-budget-feasible-mechanis.paper_title: Budget-Feasible Mechanisms for Submodular Welfare Maximization in Procurement Auctions

claims.claim: BFM-SWM is the first budget-feasible mechanism with provable approximation guarantees for submodular welfare maximization in procurement auctions, achieving an approximation ratio of 0.0328 for general submodular functions (Theorem 4.8).
claims.evidence: Exact symbolic reconstruction in Q(√6) arithmetic independently derives 1/C = 3/(4(13+4√6)) = 0.03289768…, matching the paper's constant. Empirically, BFM-SWM was run on 32 non-monotone directed-cut instances (n=14) with brute-force OPT, all 32 satisfying the exact inequality (min ratio 0.212 ≫ 0.0328), with a negative control (empty-set) failing 8/8 stressed instances.

claims.claim: BFM-SWM attains an improved approximation ratio of 0.0877 for monotone submodular welfare functions and runs in O(n log(OPT/ε)) time (Theorem 4.10, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Exact symbolic reconstruction in Q(√6) derives 2/(13+4√6) = 0.08772715…, matching the paper. 32 monotone coverage instances (n=16) all satisfy the inequality (min ratio 0.274). Runtime query-complexity scaling over n=32–512 yields log-log slope 0.918, consistent with O(n log(OPT/ε)).

claims.claim: BFM-VM achieves a deterministic approximation ratio of 1/(12+4√3) ≈ 0.0528, substantially improving the prior best-known ratio of 1/64 ≈ 0.0156 due to Balkanski et al. 2022 (Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: Exact symbolic reconstruction in Q(√3) derives 1/(12+4√3) = 0.05283121…, matching the paper. BFM-VM was run on 32 coverage instances (n=16) with brute-force OPT, all satisfying v(S) ≥ v(O)/(12+4√3) (min ratio 0.308). The 3.38× improvement over 1/64 ≈ 0.0156 is direct arithmetic.

claims.claim: BFM-VM reduces running time from O(n²logn) to O(nlogn) relative to prior budget-feasible mechanisms (Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: Query-complexity measured over n=32–512: BFM-VM log-log slope 0.989 (consistent with Θ(n log n)) vs naive-greedy-VM slope 1.983 (consistent with Θ(n²)). The quadratic baseline is a structural proxy for the O(n²log n) prior mechanisms, with 5 data points showing clear asymptotic separation.

claims.claim: BFM-SWM satisfies obvious strategyproofness, individual rationality, non-negative auctioneer surplus, and budget feasibility (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Direct arithmetic checks on 24 mechanism outputs confirm budget feasibility (p(S)≤B, 0 violations), individual rationality (p(u)≥c(u), 0 violations), and non-negative surplus (v(S)−p(S)≥0, 0 violations). Strategyproofness tested via 1152 cost-deviation tests (24 instances × ~48 sellers × 7 deviation levels) with 0 profitable deviations found.

claims.claim: On influence-maximization experiments, BFM-SWM achieves between 1.22x and 26.41x improvement over baselines, with an average improvement factor of 4.49x (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: Authors' own C++ code run on SNAP Slashdot (77,360 nodes, 905,468 edges) across 10 budgets: BFM-SWM wins 10/10, average improvement 4.56× closely matching paper's 4.49×. Observed range 2.97×–6.36× falls within the claimed 1.22×–26.41× range; extremes not reproduced because only one of three datasets was run at full scale, but results are consistent with the claim.

SabaPivot/repro-budget-feasible-mechanis.overall: The logbook implements both BFM-SWM and BFM-VM mechanisms from scratch, reconstructs all three approximation constants in exact algebraic arithmetic (Q(√6), Q(√3)), validates them on 32 real submodular function instances each with brute-force OPT, measures runtime scaling confirming O(n log n) vs O(n²), checks economic properties with 1152 deviation tests, and runs the authors' own C++ code on full-scale SNAP Slashdot for influence maximization. Negative controls throughout confirm the checks have teeth.

SabaPivot/repro-unifying-low-dimensional.paper_title: Unifying Low Dimensional Spectra in Deep Learning

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves the layer-wise Hessian in the L-deep linear unconstrained features model (UFM) has rank K^2 with all non-zero eigenvalues equal, analytically reproducing the bulk-outlier Hessian spectrum reported in prior empirical studies (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Across 160 constructed balanced optima (K∈{2,3,4,6}, depths 2–5), all Hessian ranks are exactly K² with max nonzero-eigenvalue CV of 1.91e-15 and max relative error from the closed form of 4.47e-15, confirming the theorem's rank and equal-eigenvalue predictions at machine precision.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 decomposes the Gauss-Newton/Fisher Information component into three terms: G_within (rank 0), G_cross (rank K(K-1), producing the mini-bulk of eigenvalues), and G_class (rank K, producing the main outliers), mirroring Papyan's empirical knockout experiments (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Across all 160 configurations, G_within rank is 0, G_cross rank is K(K-1), G_class rank is K, with max Frobenius reconstruction residual 2.34e-15 and max class/cross Frobenius cosine 3.35e-17, confirming both the rank decomposition and orthogonality.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 shows the aggregated gradient update is a sum over only K of the K^2 possible eigenvector directions, each with equal coefficient beta^(l+1)/K, explaining the observed gradient alignment with a low-dimensional subspace (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Projection of the layer gradient onto all K² normalized feature-mean tensors across 160 configurations yields only K nonzero diagonal coefficients (off-diagonal < 7.14e-17), with diagonal CV 8.91e-16 and closed-form coefficient match within 1.73e-15 relative error.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 proves the Gram matrix of the optimal weights, W_l*^T W_l*, has rank K with eigenvalues proportional to the squared norms of the class-mean features, giving a closed-form account of the low-rank weight structure (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: All 160 layer configurations have weight rank exactly K, nonzero singular value CV of 4.35e-16, and Theorem 3.4 scale (including dependence on n, depth, C, λ) matching within 1.08e-15 relative error.

claims.claim: For a deep linear UFM with K=3 classes, numerical experiments show K^2=9 Hessian outliers separating from the bulk and converging to equal eigenvalues over training, with eigenvector alignment metric f_cc' rising from about 0.2 to 1.0 (Figures 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: Three independent linear-UFM training runs from random initialization (K=4, depth=4, 4000 Adam steps) show K²-to-bulk ratio growing from ~1.98 to >4.15e7, top-K² eigenvalue CV falling below 0.096, and eigenvector alignment rising from 0.282 to >0.993, reproducing the claimed separation, equalization, and alignment phenomena (though with K=4 rather than the paper's K=3).

claims.claim: In the non-linear (ReLU) Deep UFM, K^2=9 Hessian outliers separate but do not fully converge to equal values, and the gradient has K non-zero coefficients that remain unequal, unlike the linear case (Figure 9, Table 2).
claims.evidence: Three ReLU-UFM training runs (10000 Adam steps, final loss <2.31e-7) show K²-to-bulk separation >2.376 but top-K² eigenvalue CV remaining >0.767 and diagonal-gradient coefficient CV remaining >0.291, contrasting with the linear runs' CV <0.096 and <0.0047 respectively, reproducing the claimed unequal finite-training structure.

SabaPivot/repro-unifying-low-dimensional.overall: The logbook provides machine-precision numerical verification of Theorems 4.1–4.4 across 160 constructed optima and reproduces the qualitative training dynamics (outlier separation, equalization vs. non-equalization) from random initialization in both linear and ReLU UFMs. The main limitation is that claims 5–6 use K=4 instead of the paper's K=3 and at small scale (width 8, depth 4), but the phenomena tested are parameter-general and the model class matches the paper's UFM exactly.

SabaPivot/repro-continuous-variable-hami.paper_title: Continuous Variable Hamiltonian Learning at Heisenberg Limit via Displacement-Random Unitary Transformation

claims.claim: The Displacement-Random Unitary Transformation (D-RUT) protocol learns all coefficients of a generic multi-mode bosonic Hamiltonian with evolution time scaling as O(1/epsilon), achieving the Heisenberg limit (Theorem 1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: 16 degree/seed cases with 96 inverse-time sweeps show log-log coefficient error slopes of -1.0000, supporting O(1/ε) Heisenberg scaling; a destructive control replacing 1/T with 1/√T reportedly destroys the slope, indicating the scaling is specific to the protocol.

claims.claim: For single-mode Hamiltonians expressed in a first-quantization (position/momentum) basis, D-RUT recovers physical coefficients with RMSE epsilon_G using total evolution time O~(1/epsilon_G), under stated conditions on known zero coefficients, non-zero response to basis mismatch, and a sufficiently close initial guess (Theorem 2, Section 2).
claims.evidence: 24 reference-frame/basis cases across 120 total-time cells show coefficient-error slopes of -1.0000, supporting O~(1/ε_G) recovery; omitting basis correction serves as a destructive control.

claims.claim: The protocol's estimation error under state-preparation-and-measurement (SPAM) errors is bounded as ||delta g_SPAM||_2 <= (L_C/sigma_min(K)) ||delta beta||_2, where L_C is a Lipschitz constant and sigma_min(K) the smallest singular value of the Gram-like matrix K (Section 3.6, Eq. 43).
claims.evidence: 48 displacement-perturbation cases directly solve the recovery error and verify ||δg|| ≤ (L_C/σ_min(K))||δβ|| with maximum observed error-to-bound ratio of 0.11756, providing concrete numerical confirmation of the SPAM bound.

claims.claim: A hierarchical two-stage coefficient recovery strategy (learn single-mode coefficients first, then coupling coefficients) is proven to have covariance dominated by that of simultaneous estimation, Cov(delta g)_hierarchical <= Cov(delta g)_simultaneous, for all parameters (Section 4.1, Appendix A).
claims.evidence: 10 multi-mode information-matrix cases verify that Cov_sim − Cov_hier is positive semidefinite and every hierarchical marginal variance is no larger than the simultaneous one, with worst-case amplification ratio strictly greater than one.

claims.claim: An iterative bisection search over the squeezing parameter R (relating the physical and reference bases via a Bogoliubov transformation) converges in O(log(1/epsilon_R)) iterations for first-quantization Hamiltonian learning (Section 5.3, Eq. 77-78).
claims.evidence: 90 squeezing searches across tolerances from 1e-2 to 1e-6 confirm root error ≤ ε_R and iteration counts within the logarithmic ceiling O(log(1/ε_R)), directly testing the bisection convergence claim.

claims.claim: The algorithm uses Chebyshev-node sampling of the displacement parameter combined with robust phase estimation and inverse discrete Fourier transform to reconstruct coefficients, as detailed in Algorithm 1 and illustrated for the single-mode case in Figure 1 (Section 2).
claims.evidence: 60 exact coefficient reconstructions across polynomial orders 2–6 with 3,540 response cells yield maximum coefficient error 1.106e-11; uniform radial nodes and wrong-sign angular inversion are executed as destructive controls.

SabaPivot/repro-continuous-variable-hami.overall: The logbook provides numerical evidence from a CPU-only simulation of the classical reconstruction layer supporting all six theoretical claims, with multiple test cases and destructive controls per claim. The evidence is concrete and non-trivial in coverage, but is limited to finite polynomial orders and simulated (not physical quantum) measurements, and the uniformly perfect scaling slopes of -1.0000 across all cases raise questions about whether the setup tests emergent properties or trivially-true-by-construction relationships.

SabaPivot/repro-beyond-theorem-proving-f.paper_title: Beyond Theorem Proving: Formulation, Framework and Benchmark for Formal Problem-Solving

claims.claim: The paper formulates formal problem-solving as a deterministic Markov decision process and implements FPS inside formal theorem proving environments (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook inspected the official Lean 4 repository confirming ProblemSol stores Answer+Proof, FPS.problem builds a proof predicate, and FPS.solve applies ProblemSol.mk. An independent Lean mirror proves transition single-valuedness and execution uniqueness axiom-free under Lean 4.15.0, supplemented by a 128-transition finite audit with mutant killing.

claims.claim: Deductive Formal Problem-Solving decouples forward answer construction from optional backward proof validation for find-all problems (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The official PropSolvingServer creates separate Forward, Backward, and Answer goals using refine @Iff.intro, confirming code-level decoupling. A finite audit of 21,845 predicate-pair cases found 3,025 forward-only complete-but-unsound cases, demonstrating backward validation is observably distinct from forward-only solving.

claims.claim: FPS soundness is proved: any direct answer produced by FPS satisfies the formal problem predicate (Theorem 3.6).
claims.evidence: The Lean mirror proves fps_soundness {P} (s : ProblemSol P) : P s.Answer := s.Proof axiom-free under Lean 4.15.0, directly matching Theorem 3.6. A finite certificate enumerated 18,434 answer/predicate combinations with 9,217 true accepted and 9,217 false injections rejected, and a proof-field mutant was killed.

claims.claim: D-FPS completeness and soundness for find-all problems are stated as formal theorems under the paper's conditions (Theorems 3.8 and 3.9).
claims.evidence: The Lean mirror proves dfps_complete (h : truth <-> answer) : truth -> answer := h.mp and dfps_sound : answer -> truth := h.mpr, both axiom-free, matching Theorems 3.8 and 3.9. The official implementation packages the target as Iff and splits with Iff.intro. Finite audit of 21,845 cases included 255 full-iff cases and 3,025 forward-only controls.

claims.claim: The benchmark suite consists of FormalMath500, MiniF2F-Solving, and PutnamBench-Solving, constructed from informal and theorem-proving math benchmarks (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Local audit counted 387 records for FormalMath500, 375 for MiniF2F-Solving, and 324 for PutnamBench-Solving (1,086 total), all with nine core schema fields and no duplicates. export_fps_benchmark.py regenerated all 1,086 Lean files byte-for-byte against the official data tree.

claims.claim: The strongest evaluated baselines solve at most 23.77% of FormalMath500, 27.47% of MiniF2F-Solving, and 0.31% of PutnamBench-Solving (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Using the initial-release commit 39489d1f with 18 solving JSONLs, rescoring with solved iff submission nonempty and eq_proof not null yields maxima of 92/387=23.77%, 103/375=27.47%, and 1/324=0.31% across 6,516 method-problem slots, exactly matching Table 1.

SabaPivot/repro-beyond-theorem-proving-f.overall: The logbook provides concrete evidence for all six claims through Lean formal proofs, finite-instance audits with mutant killing, full-dataset record verification, and exact rescoring of baseline results from the original release commit. The evidence is specific with checkable certificates, file paths, and numerical results rather than mere assertions.

SabaPivot/repro-learning-augmented-onlin.paper_title: Learning-Augmented Online Minimization with Dual Predictions

claims.claim: For laminar set cover, the proposed dual-prediction algorithm achieves E[ALG] = (1+epsilon)*OPT + O(R*eta/epsilon) for any constant epsilon>0, where eta measures dual prediction error (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 is implemented on dyadic parking-permit laminar trees (K=3–6, random costs, α=0.5) with exact HiGHS LP solves (duality gap 1.42e-14); the master bound ALG ≤ OPT/α + ‖(ŷ−y*)₊‖₁/α + R‖(y*−ŷ)₊‖₁/(1−α) passes on 1960/1960 instances with minimum slack 0.0204, and 490/490 perfect-prediction tests confirm consistency.

claims.claim: For metrical task systems, the dual-prediction algorithm (Algorithm 3, an A*-style search minimizing d(s_{t-1},s)+c_t(s)+w_hat_t(s)) achieves a (1+eta/OPT)-competitive ratio driven by the span seminorm of Bellman-operator discrepancies (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 3 is tested on 45 Euclidean MTS instances up to 100 states and T=250 with exact DP optima; the bound ALG ≤ OPT + η (Bellman span-norm residual) passes on 45/45 instances with zero violations and minimum slack 154.99, while exact-dual control gives ALG=OPT on 45/45.

claims.claim: Optimal dual solutions are stable under instance perturbations, satisfying ||y1* - y2*||_1 = O(|X1 Delta X2|), whereas optimal primal solutions can change arbitrarily under a single-element perturbation (Lemma A.1).
claims.evidence: On 400/400 perturbation pairs over dyadic laminar trees (K=4–7, β=1), the dual Lipschitz bound ‖y*(X)−y*(X')‖₁ ≤ 2β|X△X'| holds with worst normalized dual change 2.0000000000000027, while the optimal primal cover changes up to 6×|X△X'|, demonstrating the stated contrast.

claims.claim: Event predictions for caching are similarly shown to be unstable, since a single prediction error can cause the competitive ratio to collapse (Lemma A.3).
claims.evidence: The paper's three-stage caching witness is executed with a single event replacement (last event of Stage 1 changed from k to 2); for k=8,16,32,64 the predicted-policy-to-OPT fault ratios are 146×, 273×, 528×, 1040× respectively, confirming that one event-prediction error collapses performance.

claims.claim: On the parking permit problem, the learning-augmented dual-prediction algorithm achieves 1.8x to 4.4x better competitive ratios than classical algorithms at K=9 permit types, and it outperforms baselines on the k-server problem using real bike-sharing data (Experiments section).
claims.evidence: Parking permit: 153 years of GHCN Central Park data, K=9, leave-one-out learned dual ratio 1.142857 vs classical 2.080/5.030, yielding 1.82×/4.401× improvement matching paper targets 1.8×/4.4×. k-server: full Citi Bike Manhattan data (731 train days 2023–24, 365 test days 2025), learned dual beats WFA and DC for all k=2–9.

claims.claim: For general (non-laminar) set cover, even perfect dual predictions cannot beat the classical H_m competitive ratio under the standard LP formulation, showing laminar structure is necessary for the improvement (Lemma A.4).
claims.evidence: Exact rational certificates for m=4,8,…,128 show online cost equals H_m exactly (e.g., H_128=5.433147) with perfect dual (dual=1, primal=1, prediction error=0), confirming that even perfect standard-LP dual predictions cannot beat H_m for non-laminar set cover.

SabaPivot/repro-learning-augmented-onlin.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence across all six claims, including exact LP-based verification of the laminar set-cover bound on 1960 instances, exact-DP verification of the MTS bound on 45 instances, stability/instability witnesses on 400 perturbation pairs, caching instability constructions, full-scale real-data experiments on 153 years of weather and 1096 days of Citi Bike data, and exact rational certificates for the non-laminar H_m barrier up to m=128.

bsenst/repro-beyond-accuracy-latent-pert.paper_title: Beyond Accuracy: Latent Perturbations for Cognitive-Aware Diagnosis

claims.claim: The approach outperforms standard machine learning classifiers in detecting rare conditions while maintaining strong performance on common diagnoses across four public and three private rare-disease datasets.
claims.evidence: All seven datasets are synthetic proxies generated from known symptom-disease mappings, not the real public or private clinical datasets referenced in the paper. On these proxies, DMAE accuracy (~89%) is consistently lower than all baselines (~96-97%), and rare-disease F1 is generally not superior, but since the setup is synthetic rather than the paper's real data, this neither reproduces nor falsifies the original claim.

claims.claim: Using denoising masked autoencoders to generate counterfactual reasoning, the method addresses cognitive anchoring bias by proactively suggesting cognitively neglected but plausible rare diseases.
claims.evidence: Counterfactual generation was implemented and run on synthetic proxy datasets, showing positive but small cognitive gaps (0.003-0.035) and high faithfulness (94-99%), but rare disease suggestion rates are only 0-2%, which does not meaningfully demonstrate 'proactively suggesting cognitively neglected but plausible rare diseases' as claimed. No clinical validation was performed.

bsenst/repro-beyond-accuracy-latent-pert.overall: The logbook implements the DMAE architecture and runs experiments on synthetic proxy datasets for all seven claimed datasets, but the use of synthetic data rather than real clinical datasets means neither claim is verified or falsified at the paper's intended scale. The results on toy data actually contradict Claim 1 and only weakly support the mechanism in Claim 2.

ai-sherpa/hippo-zoo-explicit-memory-repr.paper_title: HiPPO Zoo: Explicit Memory Mechanisms for Interpretable State Space Models

claims.claim: HiPPO Zoo introduces five explicit polynomial-based extensions to classical HiPPO memory that individually replicate capabilities usually attributed to opaque learned SSMs like Mamba: Volterra, Salience, Associative Memory, Multiscale, and Forecasting HiPPO (Section 3).
claims.evidence: All five mechanisms execute at native architectural scale with concrete measured observables: Volterra quadratic error 5,121 vs linear 6,741,608 with kernel Pearson 0.975; Salience gate range [3.78, 4.78] with 0.902× phase ratio; Associative recall cosine 0.9996 vs 0.4537 distractor; Multiscale MSE at/below best single-timescale HiPPO across 3.48 orders of magnitude; Forecasting rank-12 explains 97.5%/65.6% variance at short/long horizons.

claims.claim: Salience HiPPO implements adaptive, input-dependent memory allocation via a scalar measure-deformation mechanism (Equation 2) with a time-warping interpretation (Equation 3), demonstrated on a selective copying task with explicit history-measure visualizations (Section 3.2, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Salience HiPPO trained on the official selective-copying task at native n=256, d_model=64 (1200/3000 episodes); the learned gate g(t) is non-constant ranging [3.779, 4.784], differs between memorize and output phases (0.902× ratio), and the induced history measure concentrates 54–62% of mass in the recent quarter at snapshots [19, 22, 29], demonstrating input-dependent measure deformation with eval loss 0.003508 and output-phase cosine 0.8486.

claims.claim: Volterra HiPPO decomposes nonlinear dynamics into interpretable kernels parameterized in an orthogonal polynomial basis, validated by learning a quadratic Volterra system on the Wray-Green benchmark (Section 3.1, Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Volterra HiPPO run on the native 10,000,000-step Wray-Green signal at n=64 (3/5 trials): quadratic readout cumulative error 5,121 vs linear 6,741,608 (1317× lower), and the decoded Legendre-basis kernel matches the true bilinear Volterra kernel at Pearson correlation 0.9750 with relative L2 error 0.2229.

claims.claim: Associative Memory HiPPO separates temporal encoding from content-addressable storage on a continuous address space, demonstrated via key-value associative recall with explicit visualization (Section 3.3, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Associative Memory HiPPO trained at full official 3500-episode schedule (native n_hippo=32, n_assoc=32): eval loss 2.91e-06, recall cosine 0.9999/0.9998 at query slots, written-token cosine 0.9996 vs best distractor 0.4537 with argmax correct, and 12 content-derived write addresses are near-orthogonal (max pairwise kernel overlap 0.0165 vs null 95th percentile 0.9997).

claims.claim: Multiscale HiPPO represents scale-dependent states as polynomial expansions (Equation 5) that support stable reconstruction across three orders of magnitude of timescale (Section 3.4, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Multiscale HiPPO at native n=16, m=128, T=30,000 (4/64 MC trials): reconstruction MSE [0.0247, 0.2523, 0.7553] at lags [10, 676, 29999] spanning 3.48 orders of magnitude, at or below the best single-fixed-timescale HiPPO MSE [0.0247, 0.2971, 0.8041] at every probed lag and within 1.17× of the oracle projection floor.

claims.claim: In the streaming/online training setups, the Salience model uses truncated backpropagation through time with fixed HiPPO parameters and only the neural readout learned online, while the Associative model uses chunk-wise gradient computation with state detachment between chunks (Section C.2-C.3).
claims.evidence: Both official scripts call jax.lax.stop_gradient on carried state at TBPTT chunk boundaries; an independent jax.grad unit test on a 2-chunk rollout shows gradient d(loss_chunk2)/d(state_chunk1) = 0.000 with detachment vs 0.206 without, and the Salience parameter pytree contains only readout/gate weights (no A/b leaves), confirming fixed HiPPO parameters with online-learned readout only.

ai-sherpa/hippo-zoo-explicit-memory-repr.overall: This logbook executes the official hippo-zoo mechanism code end-to-end at native architectural scale (HiPPO orders, signal lengths, model widths all unchanged) with only repetition counts reduced for CPU budget, producing concrete numerical evidence for all six claims. The reproduction includes independent unit tests validating HiPPO discretization and TBPTT gradient isolation, and honestly discloses reduced trial/episode counts without overclaiming convergence.

bsenst/repro-structured-multi-modal-grap.paper_title: Structured Multi-modal Graph Disentanglement for Psychiatric Diagnosis

claims.claim: SMGD achieves improved in-domain diagnosis and more reliable cross-dataset generalization under modality gap
claims.evidence: Experiments on synthetic multi-site data (300 train / 150 test subjects) show both SMGD and baseline achieving 100% in-domain accuracy (no improvement), and SMGD actually underperforming the baseline on cross-dataset generalization (44.7% vs 54.7% accuracy, 0.470 vs 0.583 AUC). The synthetic setup is a simplified proxy, not real neuroimaging data, so this neither reproduces nor definitively falsifies the claim.

claims.claim: Achieves this without expert-crafted features
claims.evidence: On synthetic data, SMGD with raw 32-dim features achieved 54% cross-dataset accuracy vs 52% with simulated 16-dim expert features, showing comparable performance. However, the expert features were simulated rather than real biomarkers, and the entire setup uses synthetic data, making this a toy-scale demonstration rather than a full reproduction.

bsenst/repro-structured-multi-modal-grap.overall: This logbook only tests SMGD on synthetic multi-site neuroimaging data with a from-scratch implementation, finding that cross-dataset generalization actually favors the baseline and that raw vs. expert feature comparison is based on simulated features. No real datasets (ABIDE, ADHD-200, etc.) were used, so neither claim is reproduced at the paper's intended scale.

SabaPivot/repro-prescriptive-scaling-rev.paper_title: Prescriptive Scaling Reveals the Evolution of Language Model Capabilities

claims.claim: Capability boundaries are estimated via smoothed pinball-loss quantile regression at quantile τ=0.98 with smoothing parameter κ=50 and regularization λ=10⁻³ (Section 2.1).
claims.evidence: Source-hash audit of official commit 5bdca776 confirms constants tau=0.98, kappa=50, lambda=0.001 present in the implementation; negative control (tau=0.95) correctly fails the contract.

claims.claim: Post-training capability boundaries are modeled as sigmoid functions of log10(FLOPs), q_τ^sig(z;θ)=y0+L·σ(a+βz), achieving in-distribution pinball loss of 4.08×10⁻³ versus 4.00×10⁻³ for a more flexible I-spline estimator, while generalizing better out-of-distribution (4.93×10⁻³ vs 4.92×10⁻³) (Section 3.1.1, Table 2).
claims.evidence: Rerun of official sigmoid_pinball_baselines.py over 18 task-fold combinations yields mean train pinball loss sigmoid=4.083e-3 vs ispline=4.003e-3 and mean validation sigmoid=4.930e-3 vs ispline=4.918e-3, closely matching the claimed 4.08/4.00 and 4.93/4.92 values.

claims.claim: At 10²⁴ FLOPs, the estimated 0.98-quantile boundary reaches 0.539 accuracy on MATH Level 5 versus 0.563 on MMLU-Pro, 0.700 on BBH, 0.828 on IFEval, 0.535 on MUSR, and 0.424 on GPQA (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Sigmoid model evaluated at 1e+24 FLOPs produces boundaries MATH Level 5=0.5395, MMLU-Pro=0.5626, BBH=0.6996, IFEval=0.8278, MUSR=0.5352, GPQA=0.4245, all matching Table 1 values to 3 decimal places; negative control confirms values change at a different FLOPs target.

claims.claim: Unlike the stable boundaries for BBH, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, and MUSR, the MATH Level 5 and IFEval capability boundaries are non-stationary over time, with later-period models exceeding earlier predicted boundaries (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Period-held-out OOS MAE shows MATH Level 5 (0.0294) and IFEval (0.0292) substantially higher than BBH (0.0143), GPQA (0.0188), MMLU-Pro (0.0167), MUSR (0.0186); unstable-pair mean 0.0293 exceeds stable-four mean 0.0171, with positive share shift of 0.025.

claims.claim: A balanced I-optimal sampling design recovers near-full-data capability frontiers using roughly 20% of the evaluation budget, with GPQA and MUSR requiring as little as 5% (Section 4, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Recomputed error ratios from Figure 5 channels show 20% budget macro ratio=1.81 (<2 threshold), 5% GPQA ratio=1.24 (<1.3), and 5% MUSR ratio=1.51 (<1.6), supporting near-full frontier recovery at reduced budgets.

claims.claim: A cross-benchmark shift test applied to AIME-2025 scores finds a positive but not statistically significant shift (p=0.15), giving no clear aggregate evidence of post-release contamination inflating math benchmark scores (Section 5.2.2, Equation 3).
claims.evidence: Rerun of official AIME-vs-MATH permutation test with 2000 permutations yields positive shift gamma=0.576 and p-value=0.148, matching the claimed positive-but-not-significant result at p≈0.15.

SabaPivot/repro-prescriptive-scaling-rev.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence matching all six claimed values through reruns of official scripts, code audits, and recomputations from result channels. The reproduction relies on the paper's own code and bundled data rather than independent reimplementation, but the specific numbers are consistently corroborated.

claims.claim: The HJ-Prox estimator's approximation error is uniformly bounded by sup_x ||prox^δ_{tf}(x) - prox_{tf}(x)|| ≤ sqrt(n t δ) (Theorem 3.2, Section 3.1).

claims.claim: Lemma 3.1 shows the fast-timescale iterate norm is controlled by the running maximum of the slow-timescale iterate, ||x_n|| <= K(1+||y_n^max||) almost surely, which is the key technical device enabling the stability proof (Lemma 3.1).

nstp/repro-efficiently-learning-drifting.paper_title: Efficiently Learning Drifting Halfspaces with Massart Noise

claims.claim: The paper's polynomial-time algorithm learns margin-separable halfspaces under distribution drift with Massart noise achieving error eta + O~(Delta^{1/3}/gamma), where eta bounds the Massart noise rate, Delta is the drift rate, and gamma is the margin parameter (Theorem 1.1, Section 1.1).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1+2 is implemented from scratch and run on non-toy instances (d=10, multiple Delta/gamma/eta). The trajectory-average excess error at W=2*Delta^{-2/3} has measured Delta-slope ~+0.33 across gamma values (matching +1/3), the constant A*gamma/Delta^{1/3} stays below 1, the 9/10 probability statement is checked over 30 independent runs, and the bound assembled from Fact 3.1 + Lemma 3.1 + Lemma 3.2 at the paper's own W yields Delta-exponent 1/3 to machine precision. Falsification controls confirm the margin and Massart hypotheses are load-bearing.

claims.claim: Under the low-degree polynomial hardness conjecture, any efficient algorithm for this drifting halfspace problem must incur excess error Omega(Delta^{1/3}), matching the algorithm's guarantee and establishing an information-computation gap (Theorem 1.2, Section 1.1).
claims.evidence: The low-degree hardness construction (Def 4.3) is implemented with exact Rademacher-tail computations. The critical trajectory length m* scales as Delta^{-0.6727} (paper: -2/3) and d^{+0.1458} (paper: +1/6), and the induced excess-error threshold Delta*m* scales as Delta^{+0.3273} (paper: +1/3). The closed-form I_j is cross-checked against brute-force 2^15 enumeration (residual 2e-12). A realisability caveat exists (hypercube tail atom is Theta(1/sqrt(d)) not 2^{-O(d)}), but the scaling evidence is unaffected.

claims.claim: For general VC-dimension-d hypothesis classes under Massart noise, the statistically optimal (possibly inefficient) error rate is O~(sqrt(d*Delta)), better than the Theta((d*Delta)^{1/3}) rate achievable under adversarial noise (Theorem 2.1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: ERM (Algorithm 3) is implemented and run on the Theorem-2.2 family across d in {64,256,1024} and multiple Delta values. The excess/sqrt(d*Delta/(1-2eta)) ratio is constant in [0.0244, 0.0257], slopes in Delta (+0.499) and d (+0.497) match +1/2, and ERM/Bayes ratio is [0.97, 1.02], confirming Theta-tilde optimality. The 4x-drift control yields ratio ~2.0, validating the sqrt law.

claims.claim: A matching information-theoretic lower bound of Omega(sqrt(d*Delta)) is proved for halfspaces under random classification noise (RCN), establishing optimality at Theta~(sqrt(d*Delta)) (Theorem 2.2, Section 2).
claims.evidence: The exact Bayes risk on the Theorem-2.2 family is computed (not estimated) via Poisson-binomial distributions. Over 15 configs, excess/sqrt(d*Delta/(1-2eta)) is constant in [0.0246, 0.0251]. Measured slopes: +0.4963 in Delta, +0.5004 in d, -0.4999 in (1-2eta), all matching the paper's +1/2, +1/2, -1/2. The sampling-relaxation control confirms the bound is sampling-limited as the proof claims.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 formally shows that no polynomial of degree less than O(gamma^{-c/4}) can distinguish the null from alternative hypothesis in the associated trajectory-testing problem, giving the formal low-degree hardness evidence for the Delta^{1/3} scaling (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The degree-k advantage^2 is computed exactly. At the paper's m=1648 with d=2001, degree-1 gives advantage^2=0.781 (<1, no distinguisher) while degree-2 gives 1.086 (>1), consistent with the degree limit gamma^{-c/4}≈1.61. The m*(k) values for k=1..8 are stable (1783 down to 1584), and the m* vs Delta slope (-0.6727) matches the paper's -2/3.

claims.claim: In the realizable setting, the algorithm's error improves to O~(Delta*gamma^{-3/2}), surpassing the prior best known bound of O~(Delta*gamma^{-2}) (Theorem 3.2, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The realizable Algorithm 5+6 is run at W=(gamma*Delta)^{-1/2} with mu=gamma. The Delta-exponent is +0.47 to +0.50 (matching sqrt(Delta)), and the head-to-head vs [HL94] shows the paper's rule yields lower error at every gamma, with the gain ratio scaling as gamma^{-1/2} (predicted from gamma^{-3/2} vs gamma^{-2}). ai-sherpa/truncated-policy-gradient-repr.paper_title: Estimation of Treatment Effects Under Nonstationarity via the Truncated Policy Gradient Estimator

Srishti280992/repro-the-interplay-betwee.paper_title: The Interplay Between Interpolation and Aggregation in Regression: Optimal Sample Complexity

claims.claim: The paper defines the gamma-graph dimension d_γ (Definition 3.2) via a gamma-shattering condition (Definition 3.1) and uses it to characterize the sample complexity of aggregation-based regression procedures.
claims.evidence: The logbook computes d_γ exactly for the sparse-zero class H_{γ,d} at d=2..8 (all d-sets shattered, all (d+1)-sets obstructed) and performs sampled boundary checks at d=16..1024 with 1024 random trials per dimension, achieving pass/fail rates of 1.000 throughout. Monte Carlo with 2048-4096 trials matches within 1.93e-4, and the benign zero-control yields loss 0, confirming the lower bound is tied to the proper-aggregation condition.

claims.evidence: The repair script builds exact one-inclusion hypergraphs on H_{γ,d} restrictions (d=3..7, up to 6435 vertices) with the proof's orientation-to-smallest-value rule, finding max oriented out-degree exactly 1 (certifying γ-OIG ≤ 3). The finite aggregation separation is checked at d_γ ∈ {64,128,256} with m ∈ {1,3,7,15} hypotheses: hard supports outside all finite zero unions yield selector loss exactly 1.0 in all 24 cells, while the non-interpolating zero oracle achieves loss 0.0.

claims.evidence: The repair script directly evaluates Eq. (30) of Theorem 3.10 with k_u=s² for n' ∈ {128,512,2048,8192,16384} and m ∈ {1,4,16,128,1024} at ε=0.05.
