The paper's claim concerns LLM generation iterations reduced by knowledge retrieval; without an LLM, it is unclear how 'iterations to convergence' were measured or whether this metric corresponds to the paper's concept.

bsenst/repro-agentic-framework-for-epide.overall: The logbook provides toy-scale evidence that the pipeline mechanics (graph verification, PyTorch compilation, constraint checking) function as described, but the core agentic component—LLM-based graph generation—is entirely absent, with fixed hand-crafted graphs used instead. Most claims are only partially addressed at simplified scale, and the FAISS retrieval claim is inconclusive because the key iteration metric cannot be meaningfully measured without an LLM.

amkkk/repro-discoformer-plug-in-density-.paper_title: DiScoFormer: Plug-In Density and Score Estimation with Transformers

claims.claim: Proposition 3.2 proves that, under normalized data with Q=K=X/h and V=I_n, self-attention recovers the exact normalized Gaussian kernel density estimator formula, establishing attention as a functional generalization of KDE (Proposition 3.2).
claims.evidence: Independent numerical verification of the algebraic identity at machine precision: polarization identity diff < 1e-10, attention=reweighted KDE diff=6.29e-08, constant-norm exact KDE diff=3.07e-08, and score formula matching -0.412143=-0.412143. This is a mathematical proposition and the numerical checks are appropriate and rigorous.

claims.claim: The transformer density/score estimator achieves substantially lower MSE than KDE across dimensions 1-10 and generalizes to Gaussian mixture models with up to 19 modes despite being trained only on 1-10 modes (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Only 300 training steps on standard normal data (vs paper's 150k steps on GMM mixtures on GPU), and the single measured result at d=2 shows Transformer MSE=17.75 vs KDE MSE=15.48 (Transformer worse). The ~500x training budget gap and wrong data distribution make this neither a valid verification nor falsification.

claims.claim: On a 2D Laplace distribution at sample size n=2048, the transformer achieves MSE of 0.2756 versus 0.2990 for KDE (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Transformer MSE ~1.0 (near-constant predictions) and KDE MSE ~0.66 at n=2048, both far from paper values (0.2756 and 0.2990). The model was trained only 300 steps and the KDE bandwidth (Scott rule) differs from the paper's, so neither value matches the paper's protocol.

claims.claim: The transformer exhibits sub-quadratic runtime scaling and remains tractable at n=32,768 samples, a regime where KDE runs out of GPU memory (Figure 11).
claims.evidence: Sub-quadratic scaling O(n^1.28) confirmed on CPU with query set capped at min(n,500), but the exponent differs substantially from the paper's O(n^0.59) on GPU, and the KDE OOM claim could not be tested (scipy KDE did not OOM on CPU). The capped query set and CPU-only setup constitute a reduced-scope benchmark.

claims.claim: The learned score function is used to construct score-debiased KDE (SD-KDE), reducing bias from O(h²) to O(h⁴), and to compute plug-in entropy/Fisher information estimates via equations (10)-(11) (Section 4/Applications).
claims.evidence: SD-KDE showed no bias reduction (-2.0%, MSE identical to KDE at 0.0038), Transformer entropy=6.48 vs true 2.84, and Fisher info=6.3e-5 vs true 2.0. These results reflect a 300-step undertrained model with near-zero score signal, not a meaningful test of the claim.

claims.claim: A single pre-trained model, without retraining, is applied to solve Fokker-Planck-type PDEs for a Landau equation plasma simulation, matching the analytical covariance evolution (Applications section).
claims.evidence: Simulation diverged with final covariance 7.61 vs analytical 1.05 (MSE=19.36) using a 300-step undertrained model whose Fisher information was ~6.3e-5. The score estimates are too inaccurate to test whether a properly trained model could solve the PDE.

amkkk/repro-discoformer-plug-in-density-.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the theoretical Proposition 3.2 (self-attention=KDE) via machine-precision numerical checks, and partially confirms sub-quadratic runtime scaling on a reduced CPU setup. All four empirical claims requiring trained models are inconclusive because the agent trained for only 300 steps (vs the paper's 150k) on CPU without GPU access, producing near-constant predictions that cannot meaningfully test the paper's claims.

Storm1t/repro-no-free-lunch-non-asymptot.paper_title: No Free Lunch: Non-Asymptotic Analysis of Prediction-Powered Inference

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 gives an exact non-asymptotic characterization of when PPI++ has lower estimation error (mean squared error) than using gold-standard labels alone, as a function of the correlation between pseudo-labels and gold-standard labels and the number of labeled samples n (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo simulation (100,000 trials) across 7 Gaussian configurations (n ∈ {10,20,30,50,100}, ρ ∈ {0.0–0.9}) shows empirical variance of Cross-fit PPI++ matches the Theorem 4.1 formula to within 1.2% relative error, confirming the exact non-asymptotic characterization.

claims.claim: For Gaussian data, PPI++ outperforms the gold-standard-only estimator if and only if the correlation between pseudo- and gold-standard labels is at least 1/sqrt(n-2), a finite-sample threshold that vanishes only as n grows (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Across 76 configurations (n ∈ {10,20,50,100} × 19 ρ values), the threshold ρ > 1/√(n-2) correctly predicts whether PPI++ outperforms classical in 100% of cases for both single-sample and cross-fit variants, with 100,000 MC trials per configuration.

claims.claim: The paper derives exact non-asymptotic variance expressions for PPI++ under sample splitting, in contrast to prior asymptotic 'free lunch' results claiming PPI++ variance is always at most that of gold-standard-only estimation (Section 4, Propositions 4.1-4.6).
claims.evidence: Five of six propositions (4.1, 4.3, 4.4, 4.5, 4.6) are numerically verified with small relative errors (max 0.79%) and unbiasedness confirmed within 3σ; Proposition 4.2 is not mentioned in the logbook, but the core claim of exact non-asymptotic variance expressions is supported by the majority of propositions being confirmed.

claims.claim: Corollaries 4.1-4.2 extend the main finite-sample no-free-lunch result to derived estimation settings beyond the basic mean-estimation case (Section 4, Corollaries 4.1-4.2).
claims.evidence: Corollary 4.1's condition (covariance estimation error > |σ_fy| implies CF-PPI++ underperforms classical) is confirmed across 12 configurations with matching threshold predictions; Corollary 4.2's specific numerical predictions (e.g., ρ=0, n=10: CF-PPI++ MSE 0.125 vs Classical 0.100, 25% worse) are confirmed.

claims.claim: Experiments on real-world datasets illustrate that the theoretical finite-sample threshold on correlation predicts when PPI++ underperforms gold-standard-only estimation in practice (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook uses simulated binary data from a latent Gaussian model rather than the actual AlphaFold/Galaxies datasets, with the logbook itself acknowledging 'exact numerical values would differ from the original AlphaFold/Galaxies results'; the qualitative crossover pattern matches but the real-world dataset experiments are not reproduced.

Storm1t/repro-no-free-lunch-non-asymptot.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification of the paper's core theoretical results (Theorem 4.1, Gaussian threshold, and most propositions) via rigorous Monte Carlo simulation with 100,000 trials per configuration and small relative errors. However, the real-world experiment claim (Claim 5) is only addressed on simulated proxy data, not the actual AlphaFold dataset, making it a toy reproduction of that specific claim.

MarxistLeninist/repro-sharp-local-minima.paper_title: Sharp description of local minima in the loss landscape of high-dimensional two-layer ReLU neural networks

claims.claim: Stationary points of the two-layer ReLU teacher-student loss admit an exact reduced description via order-parameter matrices (Q, R, T) satisfying the coupled equations ℱ_R(Q,R)=0 and ℱ_Q(Q,R)=0 (Section 2, Result 1).
claims.evidence: The ReLU Gaussian integrals I₂ and I₃ match an independent quadrature derivation to 4.4e-16 and 2.2e-16 over 60 random covariance matrices; the order-parameter loss matches Monte Carlo at four (d,K,M) configurations (d up to 3200) within noise (z-scores ≤1.65); and the flow field F_Q, F_R matches the Monte-Carlo weight-space gradient pushed through the chain rule to MC accuracy (relative errors 2–5e-3).

claims.claim: Local minima organize into distinct families classified by k₁, the number of anti-aligned student units, with a block-symmetric ansatz applied to the order parameters (Section 2-3.1, Result 2, Equation 8).
claims.evidence: 97 roots found at M=17 by projecting the general stationarity field onto the block ansatz all satisfy the general (not reduced) equations to ≤9.8e-11; gradient flow from 500 random initializations at d=1000 produces discrete loss clusters whose dominant level matches the predicted k₁=1 fixed point to 1.4e-08; at M=8, 1000 trajectories produce a single spurious level matching the predicted k₁=1 minimum to 1e-06.

claims.claim: In the well-specified regime (K=M), spurious minima persist via a compensation mechanism where aligned neurons offset anti-aligned units, but the k₁=1 minima family is eliminated under overparameterization while higher-order families merge into connected manifolds, as verified using the string method (Section 3.1, Figures 1 and 3).
claims.evidence: Perturbative stability tests show K=M spurious fixed points (k₁=1,2) survive weight perturbation up to σ=0.3 but escape to global minimum at K>M (escape fraction 1.0); Jacobian spectra confirm exactly one positive eigenvalue per added neuron for k₁=1,2 and 17 zero modes at K=M+2; reachability rises 87.8%→99.8%→100% at M=8 and 14.4%→68% at M=17. The string method was not used, but alternative probes confirm the mechanism.

claims.claim: When the SGD learning rate satisfies η = o_d(1), one-pass SGD trajectories converge to gradient-flow dynamics, making local minima attractive fixed points of the SGD dynamics in summary-statistics space (Section 3.2, Result 3).
claims.evidence: One-pass SGD at η=1 diverges (all 72 runs nan) due to the η² I₄ term; at η≤0.3 the dynamics are stable and track the order-parameter ODE integrated from the same initial (Q,R) at d=392, M=8. The specific asymptotic scaling η=o_d(1) is not tested, but the qualitative convergence to gradient flow at small η is confirmed.

claims.claim: Training dynamics exhibit discrete loss plateaus corresponding to the distinct spurious-minima families predicted by the theory, confirmed empirically in simulations (Section 3.2, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Gradient flow from 500 random initializations at M=17, d=1000 produces a sharply quantized final-loss distribution with clusters at 0.012796, 0.024766, 0.036175, etc., each matching a predicted k₁-family fixed point. The discrete loss levels corresponding to spurious-minima families are confirmed, though explicit training-curve plateau dynamics are not shown.

claims.claim: Convergence behavior is compared across normalized GD, orthonormalized GD, and two-layer GD variants in addition to standard SGD (Section 3.2, Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states in its limitations section that 'the normalised/orthonormalised gradient-descent variants (Appendix F) were not attempted,' so no experiments comparing nGD, onGD, or two-layer GD variants were run.

MarxistLeninist/repro-sharp-local-minima.overall: The logbook provides strong, independently derived numerical evidence supporting the paper's core theoretical framework: exact ReLU integrals verified to machine precision, fixed-point families validated against general stationarity equations, and the overparameterization destabilization mechanism confirmed by two independent probes. Claims 4–5 receive more limited support at smaller scale, and Claim 6 (optimizer comparison) was not addressed at all.

DineshAI/QYA0Q28ssf.paper_title: Quantifying Error Propagation and Model Collapse in Diffusion Models

claims.claim: Under finite drift energy assumptions, the intra-generation KL divergence between the generated distribution and the training target is bounded above by (1/2)ε̂ᵢ², the learned-path score error energy (Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: A machine-checked derivation reconstructs the Girsanov path-KL identity and data-processing inequality yielding KL ≤ ε̂²/2, and a 10D five-component GMM calibration (500 reverse steps, 20,000 trajectories, 5 seeds) shows exact path KL = ε̂²/2 with endpoint estimators not contradicting the bound; mutation controls (0.49 coefficient, 0.1× budget) are correctly rejected.

claims.claim: A matching lower bound on the chi-squared divergence, χ²(p̂^(i+1) ∥ qᵢ) ≥ (1/4)ηᵢε²⋆,ᵢ − C·ε⁴⋆,ᵢ, holds for small score errors (ε²⋆,ᵢ ≤ 1), where ηᵢ ∈ [0,1] is the observability coefficient (Proposition 3.3, Definition 3.2).
claims.evidence: The certificate reconstructs the conditional Girsanov projection, Taylor remainder, and observability transfer producing the exact 1/4 leading coefficient, and numerical calibration on both Gaussian and non-Gaussian two-component mixture endpoints with tunable η (0 to 0.9626) shows χ²/(ηε²) = 1.00005–1.01725 for positive η, with quadrature disagreement 6.94e-18 and mutation controls rejecting a 0.24 coefficient.

claims.claim: Combining the upper and lower bounds yields a two-sided equivalence χ²(p̂^(i+1) ∥ qᵢ) ≍ ε²⋆,ᵢ in the perturbative regime (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The same certificate derives the upper bound coefficient 4 via square bound and Jensen/Itô control, and the calibration confirms two-sided scaling χ²/(ηε²) ≈ 1 for positive η across Gaussian and non-Gaussian endpoints, with eta-zero rows as explicit edge controls and mutation controls (3.9 coefficient, 0.50× upper) correctly rejected.

claims.claim: When the score-error series ∑ᵢ ε²⋆,ᵢ diverges, the accumulated divergence across generations cannot vanish and has a non-zero floor limsup Dᵢ ≥ αη̄ε̄ / [16(1+(1-α)²)] (Proposition 4.1).
claims.evidence: The checker reconstructs the chi-squared refresh contraction, innovation lower bound, summed recurrence, and Cesàro/limsup floor, verifying the exact floor constant αη̄ε̄/[16(1+(1-α)²)] for multiple α values; a control with ε²ᵢ=1/(i+1) correctly shows that divergence alone does not force a pointwise floor, and the checker separately requires the eventual pointwise floor assumption before accepting the displayed bound.

claims.claim: When ∑ᵢ ε²⋆,ᵢ converges, accumulated divergence across generations satisfies D_{N+1} + C_bias ≍ Σᵢ(1-α)^{2(N-i)}ε²⋆,ᵢ + (1-α)^{2(N+1-i₀)}D_{i₀}, decaying geometrically at rate (1-α)² per generation, where α is the fraction of fresh data mixed in each round (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: The certificate checks that under summability of ε²⋆,ᵢ, both RHS terms (discounted energy and decayed initial) vanish to zero, while the LHS D_{N+1}+C_bias ≥ C_bias > 0, making a fixed multiplicative equivalence impossible; numerical computation shows the required upper asymptotic constant diverges (26.8 at N=10, 1.4e15 at N=160), and controls confirm that setting C_bias=0 or moving it to the RHS removes the contradiction.

claims.claim: The α-dependent tradeoff between drift and stability is empirically confirmed on a 10D Gaussian mixture and on Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10, with low α producing collapse-driven drift and high α maintaining stability (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The 10D GMM route shows the expected alpha ordering (+108% at α=0.1 vs +14% at α=0.9) but uses a population-endpoint substitute for the literal KDE solver, and the Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 experiments are entirely missing due to incomplete protocol specifications (11+ missing fields for Fashion-MNIST, 20 absent fields for CIFAR-10); no trained image diffusion models were run.

DineshAI/QYA0Q28ssf.overall: The logbook provides rigorous verification of the four theoretical propositions (C1–C4) through machine-checked derivations and non-toy 10D numerical calibrations with mutation controls, and presents a mathematically sound falsification of Theorem 4.2's multiplicative equivalence (C5) due to the C_bias placement. The empirical claim (C6) remains unaddressed on images and only partially supported on GMM with a substituted solver.

bsenst/repro-seizure-semiology-suite-s-3.paper_title: Seizure-Semiology-Suite($S^3$): A Clinically Multimodal Dataset, Benchmark, and Models for Seizure Semiology Understanding

claims.claim: S3 comprises 438 seizure videos from 116 patients (300 epileptic, 138 non-epileptic seizures), with over 35,000 dense annotations covering 20 ILAE-defined semiological features (Table 5, Appendix A.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook directly inspected ground-truth CSVs and confirmed 438 total videos, 116 unique patients, 20 ILAE-defined semiological features, and a 300/138 ES/NES split from task7_annotation.csv. The 35,000 annotation count is only weakly supported (1,900 'yes' labels found, with 35K inferred from multi-field counts), but the core structural statistics are concretely verified from data files.

claims.claim: Trained annotators agree strongly with epileptologists, with Pearson correlation r=0.893 for epileptic seizures and r=0.782 for non-epileptic seizures (Table 5, Appendix A.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirms the Pearson r values are reported in the paper's Table 5 but states the raw inter-annotator comparison data is not included in the GitHub repo, making independent reproduction impossible. No re-annotation or alternative verification was performed.

claims.claim: The two-stage neuro-symbolic framework for epileptic-versus-non-epileptic seizure classification (Task 7) achieves F1=0.96, and report-augmented diagnosis yields an average F1 improvement of 21.12% over baseline (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Baseline Task 7 metrics (with/without report) were confirmed from released CSVs, but the F1=0.96 two-stage result requires the unreleased seizure_omni_sft model and no Random Forest script was found in the repo. The logbook's own calculation of report-augmented improvement from available baseline data yields ~4.9%, not the claimed 21.12%, and no independent experiments were run.

claims.claim: General MLLMs perform weakly on fine-grained tasks: the best model reaches only F1=0.32 for spatial/laterality reasoning (Qwen2.5-VL-32B, Task 3) and 8.19s/12.72s onset/offset MAE for temporal localization (Task 4), while Lingshu-32B exceeds 50s MAE on the same task (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Repo CSVs show directional consistency (Qwen2.5-VL-32B best for temporal, Lingshu-32B worst) but specific numbers do not match: repo shows Head F1=0.55 vs paper's 0.32 for Qwen2.5-VL-32B, onset MAE=10.14s vs 8.19s, and Lingshu onset MAE=43.76s which does not exceed 50s as claimed. No independent inference was run; only pre-computed CSVs were compared to paper values.

claims.claim: Seizure-specific fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-Omni raises Task 1 feature-recognition F1 from 0.38 to 0.47 via SFT and Task 4 temporal MAE from 25.50s to 20.02s via GRPO, yielding average relative improvements of 12% (SFT) and 15% (GRPO) across tasks (Table 3).
claims.evidence: Base model Task 1 F1 was partially confirmed (repo 0.372 vs paper 0.38), but the fine-tuned models (seizure_omni_sft, seizure_omni_grpo) are not publicly released and no training or inference experiments were run. The claimed improvements (F1 0.38→0.47, MAE to 20.02s, 12%/15% averages) remain unverified.

bsenst/repro-seizure-semiology-suite-s-3.overall: The logbook provides a useful data audit confirming dataset structural statistics (Claim 1) from released CSVs, but cannot independently verify any model performance claim because seizure videos are DUA-gated, fine-tuned model checkpoints are unreleased, and no GPU experiments were run. Claims 2–5 lack independent experimental evidence.

claims.claim: Feature Activation Coverage measures post-training data diversity in an interpretable LLM feature space rather than using only text-level diversity metrics (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The FAC metric formula (Eq. 4–6) is correctly implemented on the official released SAE checkpoint (k=65536, TopK=20, tied weights confirmed), and the theory (Pinsker, chain rule, Theorem 4.1) is verified numerically. However, the metric is tested on synthetic activations constructed from W_dec columns rather than real LLM forward passes on real data, making the monotonicity sweep largely tautological by construction.

claims.claim: FAC Synthesis uses sparse autoencoders to identify missing features in a seed dataset and generate synthetic samples that activate those features (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The two-step synthesis pipeline structure is reproduced using official repo prompts and the exact paper generator (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct via HF Inference Providers), but the hosted generator refused all toxic synthesis requests (span coverage 0/0/0 for all features), and the 'identify missing features' step requires backbone forward passes that were never performed. The pipeline was exercised but did not functionally produce samples activating target features.

claims.claim: The paper reports consistent diversity and downstream-performance improvements on instruction following, toxicity detection, reward modeling, and behavior steering (Section 5).
claims.evidence: No FAC diversity gain was measured (proxy signal shows 0→0 due to generator refusals), and no downstream task evaluations (ToxicChat AUPRC, RewardBench, behavior steering, AlpacaEval) were run. The claim of consistent improvements across four tasks was never empirically addressed.

claims.claim: Using 100% of selected missing features outperforms lower selected-feature ratios across the four downstream tasks in the reported ablation (Table 7).
claims.evidence: The ablation over selected-feature ratios (Table 7) is never mentioned or attempted in the logbook; no experiment varying the feature-selection ratio was run.

claims.claim: The paper identifies a shared interpretable feature space across LLaMA, Mistral, and Qwen that enables cross-model knowledge transfer (Section 6).
claims.evidence: All three family SAE checkpoints (LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen) were loaded and verified to share k=65536 and TopK=20, confirming structural comparability. However, the actual cross-model knowledge transfer experiment (Table 3, 3×3×3 design) and semantic feature-overlap analysis were not performed, so the claim of a shared interpretable feature space enabling transfer remains untested beyond checkpoint-level existence.

Small-Hackathon/repro-less-is-enough-sta.overall: The logbook reproduces the FAC metric definition and SAE architecture on official checkpoints, and verifies the supporting theory, but all core empirical claims—diversity gains, downstream improvements, ablations, and cross-model transfer—remain untested because the 8B backbone forward passes and fine-tuning experiments require GPU resources that were unavailable. The synthesis pipeline was structurally exercised but failed to produce intended outputs due to hosted safety refusals.

bsenst/repro-asymmetric-contrastive-obje.paper_title: Asymmetric Contrastive Objectives for Efficient Phenotypic Screening

claims.claim: Asymmetric contrastive objectives outperform prior methods on BBBC021 and RxRx3-core for phenotype grouping and drug-target interaction inference.
claims.evidence: The logbook only tests on a synthetic BBBC021 proxy (150 treatments, 30 MoA classes) with a 25K-parameter CNN, not the real BBBC021 dataset or RxRx3-core. SPC achieves mAP 0.093 vs WSL 0.082 on this proxy, but the paper's actual metrics (NSC=97%, NSCB=95%) and datasets (BBBC021, RxRx3-core) were never evaluated; RxRx3-core was not tested at all.

claims.claim: The method maintains improved performance compared to models 10x larger in parameter count, suitable for settings with limited data or compute.
claims.evidence: No experiments were run comparing SPC with ResNet18 against larger models (ViT/B DINOv2, Phenom-1, etc.). The logbook only provides a parameter-count table and restates the paper's findings ('The paper demonstrates that...') without any independent experimental evidence on HaCaT or any other dataset.

bsenst/repro-asymmetric-contrastive-obje.overall: This logbook provides only a toy-scale synthetic proxy experiment for Claim 1 and no actual experiments for Claim 2. Neither the real BBBC021, RxRx3-core, nor HaCaT datasets were used, and the model tested (25K params) is orders of magnitude smaller than the paper's ResNet18.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 proves that under the nonlinear mixture model and domain variability assumptions, content is identifiable via an invertible mapping, and when differential independence holds with a full-rank style Jacobian, style is also identifiable via an invertible mapping (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook tested Theorem 3.4 on a synthetic linear mixing model g(c,s)=A_c c + A_s s, not the nonlinear mixture model the theorem addresses; the nonlinear test was only at random initialization (orthogonality loss 0.0916, untrained), so the full nonlinear identifiability claim was not tested.

claims.claim: Content-Style Differential Independence (Assumption 3.1) requires that content-induced and style-induced tangent subspaces on the data manifold be orthogonal, i.e., R(J_c g) ⊥ R(J_s^(n) g), rather than requiring statistical independence or a sparse Jacobian (Assumption 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook constructed synthetic subspaces showing orthogonal Jacobian column spaces (||J_c^T J_s||_F = 1.55e-07) coexisting with statistical dependence (cross-correlation 0.4126), demonstrating the point on a simplified synthetic setup rather than the paper's full data manifold.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.6 shows that when orthogonality is only approximate (violated by an angle up to π/2 − ξ), content remains fully identifiable while the learned style representation retains a content-dependence bounded by a term scaling with sin(ξ) (Theorem 3.6).
claims.evidence: The logbook constructed synthetic subspaces with controlled angles for xi ∈ {0°–45°}, showing content recovery error up to 0.5687 and style dependence growing to 0.5906 at xi=45°, but this is a simplified synthetic verification rather than a test on the paper's actual nonlinear model and data.

claims.claim: On counterfactual generation, CSDI-GAN achieves FID scores of 4.4 on AFHQ and 4.3 on CelebA-HQ, outperforming I-StyleGAN and Block Independence GAN baselines (Table 1a).
claims.evidence: The logbook states full-scale AFHQ/CelebA-HQ training was infeasible and only mentions verifying the architecture at MNIST scale, but reports no actual FID scores from any experiment — only the paper's own table values are reproduced, providing no independent experimental evidence.

claims.claim: On domain translation, CSDI-GAN achieves FID scores of 7.1 on AFHQ (33 domains) and 12.9 on CelebA-HQ (2 domains) (Table 1b).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports only the paper's table values for domain translation FID and states full-scale training was not attempted; no actual FID scores from any scale of experiment are provided as independent evidence.

claims.claim: CSDI-GAN enforces Jacobian orthogonality via a stochastic regularizer computed with Hutchinson's trace estimator, avoiding explicit storage of the d×d_c and d×d_s Jacobian matrices for high-dimensional images (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook independently implemented the Hutchinson trace estimator, compared it to exact Jacobian computation (error ~0.028 for K=50 probes), and demonstrated 236x memory reduction on realistic 256x256x3 images (d=196608), with implementation details matching the paper's Section 4 approach.

jomasego/repro-content-style-identificat.overall: The logbook provides toy-scale numerical audits supporting the three theoretical claims on simplified synthetic setups, and concretely verifies the Hutchinson trace estimator methodology on realistic image dimensions. The two empirical FID claims (Claims 4–5) were never actually tested at any scale — no independent FID scores were produced — leaving them inconclusive.

bsenst/repro-sedras-wz-llm-claims.paper_title: SEDRAS: Symbolically Evaluated Deep Research And Science

claims.claim: SEDRAS achieves 34% proof success rate on LCI-Test with 100 classical combinatorial identities, outperforming DeepSeek-V3 and Goedel-Prover-V2
claims.evidence: The logbook ran numerical verification of 10 well-known combinatorial identities (n=0..15) and verified 2 WZ certificates using sympy, but never ran the WZ-LLM pipeline, the LCI-Test benchmark, Lean 4 proofs, or any baseline (DeepSeek-V3, Goedel-Prover-V2). No evidence about the 34% success rate was produced; the experiments verify mathematical prerequisites, not the system's proving performance.

claims.claim: WZ-LLM framework proves 5 identities on LCI-Test on which symbolic-only baseline fails
claims.evidence: The logbook provides no independent experimental evidence for this claim. It merely restates the paper's Table 1 decomposition (29 sketch-guided + 5 direct = 34 total) and asserts consistency. No symbolic-only baseline was run, no WZ-Prover was run, and no specific identities were identified or tested.

bsenst/repro-sedras-wz-llm-claims.overall: This logbook performs a mathematical sanity check (verifying that classical combinatorial identities are true and that WZ certificates are valid for 2 examples) but does not address either claim about the WZ-LLM system's end-to-end performance on LCI-Test. The actual system was never run due to unreleased code and lack of GPU resources, so neither the 34% success rate nor the 5-identity complementary coverage claim was tested.

Srishti280992/repro-a-geometric-analysis.paper_title: A Geometric Analysis of Small-sized Language Model Hallucinations

claims.claim: Across a dataset of 300,000 responses (150 responses per prompt for 200 time-sensitive prompts, across 10 small LLMs of 7B-32B parameters), genuine responses show tighter intra-class clustering than hallucinated responses, with the ratio of inter-class to intra-class embedding distance averaging 1.13 in raw embedding space (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Full structural replay on SOCRATES-300K (297,795 rows, MD5 bc4765491d74c007052470006aaed08f) across 1,777 valid-geometry model-prompt pairs yielded raw_sep_mean=1.1324, matching the claimed 1.13, with per-model values shown for all 10 models.

claims.claim: Fisher Discriminant Analysis projection amplifies the separability ratio between genuine and hallucinated response clusters from 1.13× to an average of 7.26× across the 10 evaluated models, with a shared optimal regularization value of λ≈1.2 across architectures (Table 1, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Same structural run at λ=1.2 (from config best_lambda) produced fisher_sep_mean=7.2613, matching the claimed 7.26×, with per-model Fisher separability values shown for all 10 models. The amplification from 1.13 to 7.26 is directly confirmed.

claims.claim: A label-propagation classifier built on the Fisher-projected embedding space achieves average accuracy of 87.2% and average F1-score of 90.7% for hallucination classification, with per-model F1 ranging from 84.0% to 95.3% (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Full label-propagation run across 31,080 evaluations (20 splits, 1/3 test fraction, all 10 models) yielded accuracy_avg=0.8722, f1_avg=0.9071, f1_min=0.8397, f1_max=0.9530, matching claimed 87.2% accuracy, 90.7% F1, and 84.0%-95.3% range.

claims.claim: Label-propagation F1 performance saturates once 30-50 labeled training responses are available, demonstrating label-efficient hallucination classification (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Training-size sensitivity replay across 364,520 evaluations and 1,554 eligible pairs shows F1 of 87.95%, 89.18%, 89.80%, 90.35%, 90.55% at ~29, 39, 49, 74, 99 labels respectively; gain from ~49 labels to endpoint is only 0.75pp, confirming saturation in the 30-50 label range.

claims.claim: Observed Wasserstein distances between genuine and hallucinated response distributions exceed the null-hypothesis (random label permutation) baseline for 87.6% of prompts on average, with per-model rates ranging from 81.5% to 94.5%, indicating genuine geometric structure rather than sampling artifacts (Table 5, Figures 3 and 6).
claims.evidence: Structural run with 100 permutations yielded above_null_avg=0.8764 (87.6%), above_null_min=0.8148 (81.5%), above_null_max=0.9450 (94.5%), matching all claimed values for Wasserstein distance exceeding the random-permutation null baseline.

Srishti280992/repro-beyond-relu-bifurcat.paper_title: Beyond ReLU: Bifurcation, Oversmoothing, and Topological Priors

claims.claim: Proves a supercritical pitchfork bifurcation condition α·w·λ_k = 1 under which odd C^3 activation functions destabilize the homogeneous fixed point and create stable non-homogeneous patterns in GNN dynamics (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Across 25 configurations on 5 graph families (N=64), subcritical fixed points collapsed to max ||x*||=3.18e-12 while supercritical ones had min ||x*||=0.2848 with mean eigenmode alignment 0.9951 and stable Jacobian radii (max 0.9941), directly confirming the pitchfork bifurcation at w·λ_k=1.

claims.claim: Derives a √μ scaling law for the amplitude of emergent patterns near the bifurcation point, where μ measures distance from criticality, and validates this scaling empirically (Theorem 3.2, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Log-log slope of amplitude vs μ averaged 0.49997±0.00129 across 5 graph families and 9 μ-values, with measured/predicted ratio 1.0038 and a wrong μ¹ model fitting 4.47e4× worse by log-RSS, quantitatively confirming the √μ scaling law.

claims.claim: Shows Dirichlet energy stays at zero in the subcritical regime and grows linearly in the supercritical regime, quantifying departure from oversmoothing (Corollary 3.4).
claims.evidence: Subcritical Dirichlet energy was at most 8.23e-24 (numerical zero) across all graph families, while supercritical energy grew linearly with measured/predicted slope ratio 1.008±0.012 using E_D≈(1−λ_k)a(μ)², with raw CSV data confirming the transition.

claims.claim: Proves that near the bifurcation point the NTK becomes asymptotically rank-one, dominated by the bifurcating eigenmode, explaining emergent topological learning priors (Corollary 4.1).
claims.evidence: On N=160 BA/ER/WS graphs, eig2/eig1≤4.73e-16 for the scalar NTK K_w=d_w x* d_w x*^T, top eigenvector aligned with bifurcating mode (min cosine 0.9949), finite-difference and implicit-function derivatives agreed to 4.98e-5, and top_eig×μ converged to graph-specific constants confirming 1/μ divergence; subcritical participation ratios dropped toward rank-one as w/w_k→1.

claims.claim: Extends the scalar analysis to realistic multidimensional GNNs, proving emergent patterns are rank-one separable states aligned with graph and feature eigenmodes (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: In 27 configurations with symmetric W and d∈{4,8,16}, subcritical states collapsed to ||X*||≤1.87e-9 while supercritical states were rank-one separable (max s2/s1=0.00371) with left alignment 0.99905 and right alignment 0.99999, though feature dimensions are smaller than practical GNN widths.

claims.claim: Demonstrates that substituting bifurcation-inducing activations (e.g., sine) for standard monotone ones maintains performance in 64-layer GNNs on Cora, avoiding representational collapse under depth (Figure 5, Section 6).
claims.evidence: On full real Cora (2708 nodes, 1433 features, 7 classes) with bifurcation-aware dense W at 64 layers, sine maintained E_D/d=2.852 while ReLU collapsed to 1.72e-15 (ratio 1.65e15), directly demonstrating representational collapse avoidance; however, no classification accuracy was reported to confirm the 'maintains performance' aspect.

Srishti280992/repro-beyond-relu-bifurcat.overall: The logbook provides strong clean-room numerical evidence for the theoretical bifurcation claims (1–5) via closed-form predictions, cross-validated derivative computations, and multiple graph families, and demonstrates collapse avoidance on full-scale Cora for claim 6. The main gaps are small feature dimensions in claim 5 and the absence of accuracy metrics for claim 6's 'maintains performance' assertion.

claims.evidence: The logbook provides an MSE trajectory [8.3148→0.5739] over 700 SGD steps on a d=32, n=500 synthetic problem, but this does not demonstrate that the specific closed-form dual update nu_t = nu_{t-1} + log(1+alpha_t e^{s(w_t;zeta_t)}) - log(1+alpha_t e^{nu_{t-1}}) was implemented or that numerical stability against exponential-average baselines was tested.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.6 proves SCENT achieves an O(1/sqrt(T)) convergence rate for convex compositional entropic risk minimization objectives of the form log(E[exp(s(w;zeta))]), improving on SCGD's O(1/T^{1/4}) rate (Section 3, Theorem 3.6).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports eigenvalues and a condition number (cond=2.669) of some matrix, which has no connection to measuring or verifying an O(1/sqrt(T)) convergence rate versus SCGD's O(1/T^{1/4}) rate.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.3 proves the dual iterates nu_{i,t} remain bounded within an interval [c0, c1] across all iterations, preventing numerical overflow in the exponential terms (Section 3, Lemma 3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports the same MSE trajectory as Claim 1 (init=8.3148, final=0.5739), with no tracking of dual iterates nu_{i,t}, no interval bounds [c0, c1], and no evidence of boundedness or overflow prevention.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 shows that for fixed w, SPMD's convergence is characterized by the second-order moment ratio kappa = E[z^2]/E[z]^2, and is provably faster than standard SGD by a factor proportional to 1/e^{(nu*-c0)} (Section 4, Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides five final MSE values (mean=1.3734, std=0.4231) from multi-seed runs, but there is no measurement of kappa = E[z^2]/E[z]^2, no comparison with standard SGD, and no verification of the speedup factor proportional to 1/e^{(nu*-c0)}.

claims.claim: On extreme classification benchmarks Glint360K and TreeOfLife-10M, SCENT consistently outperforms the SOX, U-max, and BSGD baselines on both training and validation convergence (Section 5, extreme classification experiments).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports a 'concentration proxy' max|S_t|/√t=1.4953 on a tiny synthetic setup, with no experiments on Glint360K or TreeOfLife-10M, no classification metrics, and no comparison against SOX, U-max, or BSGD baselines.

neonforestmist/repro-geometry-aware-effi.overall: This logbook provides no meaningful evidence for any of the six claims. Every claim is supported by generic numerical outputs from small synthetic optimization experiments that bear no relationship to the paper's actual theoretical results or empirical benchmarks.

claims.claim: Non-linear GRPO (Algorithm 1) replaces the standard scalar reward with an approximated functional derivative ∂R/∂π evaluated at the current policy's empirical distribution, requiring only a drop-in reward function on top of standard GRPO (Section 4, Algorithm 1).

claims.claim: PANDA (Penalty-Augmented Nikaido–Isoda Descent–Ascent) is a first-order stochastic policy-gradient algorithm for bilevel optimization where the lower level is a regularized min-max zero-sum Markov game (Section on algorithm structure).

claims.evidence: The logbook reuses the same MSE trajectory from Claim 1 (97.7% relative drop) but never computes the Nikaido-Isoda function, its gradient norm, or verifies the PL inequality ½‖∇g‖² ≥ μ·g for any μ depending on regularization or state/action probabilities.

claims.claim: Under Assumptions 1-3, PANDA reaches an ε-stationary point of the bilevel objective in Õ(ε^{-1}) outer iterations with total sample complexity Õ(ε^{-3}), matching the best-known rates for bilevel RL without restrictive convexity assumptions (Theorem 1).

wrice/repro-graph-pruning.paper_title: Selecting Samples on Graphs: A Unified Dataset Pruning Framework for Lossless Training Acceleration

claims.claim: The paper casts dataset pruning as a graph problem with node weights for intrinsic importance and edge weights for extrinsic diversity/interaction, yielding a Maximum Weight Clique formulation (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook's exact rational audit found the literal samplewise formulation double-counts symmetric pair interactions: the MWCP value is 1/1 while the literal samplewise value is 2/1, and the objective-equivalence check is classified as contradicted, indicating the formulation as stated does not correctly reduce to MWCP.

claims.claim: Under mild conditions, the unified objective becomes submodular and admits a greedy approximation guarantee (Section 3.6; Appendix F).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides a concrete witness where the marginal sequence is 1/1 then 3/1, directly violating the diminishing-returns property required for submodularity; the diminishing-returns and greedy-premise checks are both classified as contradicted under exact rational arithmetic.

claims.claim: UGIES outperforms state-of-the-art dataset pruning methods on CIFAR-10/100 with ResNet-18 (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states it does not present paper-reported benchmark values as reproduced measurements, and no CIFAR-10/100 experiments with ResNet-18 were executed.

ai-sherpa/decentralized-mixed-affine-con.paper_title: Complexity of Decentralized Optimization with Mixed Affine Constraints

claims.claim: For the smooth, strongly convex regime with mixed affine constraints, Theorem 4.1 gives an optimal communication complexity of O(√κ_f √κ̂_{C̃ᵀ} √κ_W log(1/ε)) that matches established lower complexity bounds (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook cites the paper's own Section 4.1 showing Theorem 4.1 applies to problem (S) (shared-variable constraints only), while the general mixed problem (P) is addressed by Theorem 4.6 in Section 4.3. The claim attributes Theorem 4.1 to 'mixed affine constraints,' which is a scope misattribution. The rate formula itself is numerically confirmed (log-log slope 0.476 for κ_f, linear Chebyshev degree growth with slope 1.000), but the theorem's stated scope does not cover the full mixed problem.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 provides a unified complexity bound O(√κ_f (√κ̃_{AC} + √κ̂_{C̃ᵀ}) √κ_W log(1/ε)) covering problems with simultaneously coupled (global) and local affine constraints (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: The logbook builds the block-diagonal K=diag(B,B̃) reformulation of problem (13) and runs APAPC across 6 configurations of (κ_AC, κ_Chat). Mixed outer iterations remain at 82 across all configs (independent of κ_AC, κ_Chat), while per-iteration communication is structurally additive: degree_AC + degree_Chat raw matvecs per iteration (e.g., 37+9=46 at κ_AC=36, κ_Chat=9, yielding 3772 total), confirming the additive bound O(√κ_f (√κ̃_AC + √κ̂_{C̃ᵀ}) √κ_W log(1/ε)).

claims.claim: The paper analyzes both smooth objectives (Theorem 2.4) and non-smooth objectives via a Gradient Sliding algorithm (Algorithm 2), each under mixed affine constraints (Section 2, Section 4, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: Smooth: Algorithm 1 (APAPC) solves a mixed-constraint strongly-convex quadratic (κ_f=32) in 3428 iterations to relative error 9.92e-09 and feasibility 2.25e-11. Nonsmooth: Algorithm 2 (Gradient Sliding) on an L1-penalized objective with mixed-affine-constraint matrix B converges from 166.4 to 1.5070, matching an independent 20,000-iteration FISTA reference (1.5003, 0.45% relative gap) with 1035 closed-form inner subproblems solved to first-order optimality residual ≤2.46e-12.

claims.claim: The proposed framework is motivated by and applied to horizontal federated learning (consensus constraints), vertical federated learning (shared/global-variable constraints), and multi-task learning with node-specific local constraints (Section 1, Applications).
claims.evidence: HFL: path-incidence Kronecker consensus matrix with rank 15/15 and exact nullspace containment of the all-equal vector, solved by APAPC in 95 iterations (rel. err 9.2e-08). VFL: feature-partitioned aggregation with shared-top-model consensus, rank 14/14, solved in 785 iterations (9.9e-08). Multi-task: distinct non-identical per-node local constraint blocks, rank 9/9, solved in 1404 iterations (9.9e-08). All three are real constraint constructions solved end-to-end against independent KKT ground truth.

claims.claim: An accelerated proximal alternating predictor-corrector method (Algorithm 1, APAPC) is used as the core building block for achieving the optimal rates in Theorem 4.1 and Theorem 4.5 (Algorithm 1, Theorem 4.5).
claims.evidence: Corrector ablation: removing Algorithm 1's corrector step causes 1.416× (κ_f=64) and 1.419× (κ_f=256) slowdown at aggressive step sizes. Chebyshev spectral compression: degree-⌈√κ_W⌉ Chebyshev acceleration on path/cycle/star/random graphs up to n=64 compresses worst-case condition number from 1659.4 to 1.7115 (969.6× compression), confirming the mechanism behind √κ_W entering the rate.

ai-sherpa/decentralized-mixed-affine-con.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence—real APAPC and Gradient Sliding implementations run to measured convergence, Chebyshev spectral computations on real graphs up to n=64, and literal HFL/VFL/multi-task constraint constructions—confirming four of five claims. Claim 1 is falsified on scope: the paper's own text restricts Theorem 4.1 to the shared-variable-only problem (S), not the general mixed problem (P), even though the rate formula itself is numerically confirmed.

Srishti280992/repro-a-capacity-based-rat.paper_title: A Capacity-Based Rationale for Multi-Head Attention

claims.claim: Recovering a graph with m' relations in d_model-dimensional embeddings requires total key dimension D_K = Θ(m' log m' / d_model), established as a lower bound (Section 7) and matched by a constructive upper bound (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Exact combinatorial counting of log2 C(m(m-1),m') vs m'log2(m²/m') yields ratios in 1.13–1.20 across m up to 2048 and various m', supporting the lower bound; explicit constructed QK matrices (W_Q=X_src^T R, W_K=X_tgt^T R) achieve positive separation margins up to m=4096, supporting the upper bound.

claims.claim: For permutation graphs (m' = m), the capacity requirement simplifies to D_K = Θ(m log m / d_model) (Section 4/Section 7).
claims.evidence: The m'=m rows of the exact counting table show log2 C(m(m-1),m) / (m log2 m) ratios decreasing from 1.20 to 1.13 for m=128–2048, and the same explicit QK construction with h∝m/d_model and d_k∝log m yields D_K=Θ(m log m/d_model) with positive margins.

claims.claim: Multi-head attention's advantage arises because splitting into heads reduces the effective block size B, shrinking the noise term N3(B) ≍ (B/d_model)√(d_k log m) that governs interference from superposition (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Direct measurement of max off-target attention scores from constructed QK matrices at m=4096, d_model=256, d_k=64 shows N3(B) increasing from 18.8 (B=16) to 482.0 (B=4096) with through-origin linear fit R²=0.989, and signal/noise crossover beginning at B=128, directly demonstrating that reducing B via more heads shrinks superposition noise.

claims.claim: Empirical scaling of the optimal total key dimension matches theory: D_K* ≈ 1.19·(m log m/d_model) with R²=0.944 (R²=0.992 after excluding three outlier points), and the optimal head count scales as h* ≈ 1.65(m/d_model) − 6.64 with per-head widths d_k* in [5,24] (median 11) (Section 6).
claims.evidence: A 381-record, 3-seed, 40k-step RGR sweep over m∈{64,128,256,512} and d_model∈{16,32,64} confirms D_K* scales linearly in m log(m)/d_model (R²=0.944 excluding the same three d_model=16 outliers), h* grows linearly with m/d_model (slope 1.99, R²=0.872), and per-head widths stay small (median 8); however, the measured constant is 1.60 vs the paper's 1.19 and R²=0.992 is not achieved, so the scaling form is confirmed but exact constants are not matched.

claims.claim: The multi-head capacity advantage persists in a fuller Transformer setting with softmax normalization, value routing, and frozen GPT-2 embeddings, since the analysis establishes capacity is purely key-query driven (Appendix C).
claims.evidence: A full pre-LN Transformer block with frozen GPT-2 embeddings, softmax attention, residual stream, and GELU MLP at m=6144 shows single-head accuracy collapsing to 0.000 at D_K=64,128,512 (only 0.267 at D_K=256) while multi-head variants reach 0.90–0.97; separate softmax RGR and value-routing experiments show the same pattern.

claims.claim: Capacity requirements are largely insensitive to context length, tested over sequence lengths ℓ ∈ {16,32}, with only modest degradation when evaluating at longer lengths than training (Section 6.1, Appendix A.3).
claims.evidence: Twelve train/eval configurations at m=256, d_model=32, h=4 with D_K∈{32,48,64} and ℓ_train,ℓ_eval∈{16,32} (3 seeds each) show F1≥0.9995 for D_K≥48 across all length combinations, and the below-threshold D_K=32 shows only 0.0167 absolute F1 drop when evaluating at ℓ=32 after training at ℓ=16.

Srishti280992/repro-a-capacity-based-rat.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence—exact combinatorial counting, explicit QK matrix constructions, direct noise measurements, a 381-record capacity sweep, a full GPT-2 Transformer block, and context-length experiments—supporting all six claims at reduced but non-trivial scale. The qualitative scaling relationships reproduce faithfully, though the Claim 4 capacity constant (1.60 vs 1.19) and some R²/head-count parameters differ from the paper, attributable to fewer seeds and shorter optimization.

claims.evidence: The logbook only confirms that the head pruning scripts run and produce the expected output format, but reports no actual pruning results, overlap statistics, or non-overlap percentages from their own runs; the 73.58% figure cited is from the paper, not reproduced.
