claims.claim: Theorem 1 establishes that the space of finite measures with bounded mass forms a compact metric space under the bounded Lipschitz metric, providing the topological foundation for the measure-valued goal encoding of the reachability MDP (Theorem 1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Constructive epsilon-net verification on continuous cubes [0,1]^d for d=1,2,3 with mass bounds W=1,2,4 and epsilons 1/2,1/4,1/8 (27 cells) using exact rational arithmetic, all satisfying the BL error budget; plus a noncompact control on N showing Dirac sequences fail to have Cauchy subsequences, demonstrating compactness is necessary.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 proves that under mild Feller-type continuity conditions on the transition kernel, optimal deterministic Markov policies exist for the finite-horizon time-bounded reachability MDP (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Continuous Feller kernel p(target|x,a)=1-max_i|x_i-a_i|/2 checked on compact X=A=[0,1]^d for d=1,2,3, horizons 1,2,4,8 (48 cells) with exact compact-action maximizer a=x attaining value with deterministic policy error 0; noncompact control on (0,1]^d shows strictly positive gaps (min 1/48) that vanish when compact limit is restored.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 shows that sequences of functions satisfying Bellman sub-/super-solution inequalities yield provability certificates (upper and lower bounds on the optimal value function) without requiring the full MDP to be solved, with the certificate gap defined as UB(x0) - LB(x0) (Theorem 3, Definition 5, Section 5).
claims.evidence: Exact Fraction arithmetic verification of Bellman sub-/super-solution inequalities on [0,1] across 45 cells (horizons 1,2,4,8,16; states x=j/8), all with zero lower/upper inequality violations and L_H(x)<=V_H(x)<=U_H(x); broken-certificate controls show bracket failures rising from 8/9 to 9/9 as perturbation increases, confirming the inequalities are the active ingredient.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 bounds the worst-case regret of score-guided planning under uniform score-approximation error εb as 0 ≤ V*_B(x0) - V^{πh}_B(x0) ≤ 2∑_{b=1}^{B} εb, showing performance degrades linearly with accumulated approximation error (Theorem 4, Section 6).
claims.evidence: Z3 SMT solver returns 'unsat' for the one-step violation query Q*(a*)-Q*(a_h)>2eps under uniform score error assumptions, symbolically confirming the core inequality; tightness witness with eps=1/4, Q*(a*)=1/2, Q*(a_h)=0 achieves loss=2eps, showing the factor 2 is tight; finite-horizon bound follows by standard Bellman telescoping.

claims.claim: Theorem 5 shows that under a margin condition on action-value separation, the expected regret improves to O(Bε^{β+1}) for β>0, i.e., faster than the worst-case linear-in-B rate of Theorem 4 (Theorem 5).
claims.evidence: Exact Fraction arithmetic over 75 cells with occupancy law P(Delta<=u)=u^beta for beta=1,2,3,4,8, horizons 1,8,16, and epsilons 1/64 to 1/4; fitted log-log exponents are exactly 2,3,4,5,9 matching beta+1, with max regret/theorem-bound ratio 0.5 confirming all cells are within the bound.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 derives a high-probability estimation-error bound of order O(L H d_D/(d_D+2) (log(n/δ)/n)^{1/(d_D+2)}) under a doubling-dimension assumption on the relevant problem domain, formalizing how statistical complexity of a biased real-world problem distribution governs sample efficiency (Theorem 6, Section 7).
claims.evidence: k-NN estimation on [0,1]^{d_D} embedded in R^20 (ambient dim fixed at 20) for d_D in {1,2,3,4,6} with n up to 64000 and Gaussian noise; all fitted MAE exponents are more negative than the predicted -1/(d_D+2) upper-bound exponents, and exponent regression yields slope 0.9618 with R^2=0.9662, supporting that the rate tracks intrinsic rather than ambient dimension.

Srishti280992/repro-why-agentic-theorem-.overall: The logbook provides concrete computational evidence for all six theorem claims using continuous domains, exact rational arithmetic, Z3 symbolic verification, exact margin-law checks, and k-NN numerical experiments with control experiments. The evidence is on non-toy setups (continuous cubes, embedded manifolds in R^20, n up to 64000) and is consistent with all claims, though verification is limited to specific instances of general theorems rather than full proof mechanization.

amkkk/repro-certificate-guided-pruning-f.paper_title: Certificate-Guided Pruning for Stochastic Lipschitz Optimization

claims.claim: Certificate-Guided Pruning (CGP) maintains an explicit active set A_t of candidate optima using confidence-adjusted Lipschitz envelopes, certifying with high probability that any point outside A_t is suboptimal (Section 3, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Active set maintenance was tested only on 1-2D synthetic objectives (quadratic, sinusoidal) with 5 seeds each — dimensions far below the paper's intended setting, and the objectives are simple controlled functions rather than realistic optimization tasks.

claims.claim: Under a margin condition with near-optimality dimension α (Assumption 2.3), the Shrinkage Theorem bounds the active set volume as Vol(A_t) ≤ C·(2(β_t + Lη_t) + γ_t)^(d−α) (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: Volume bound was verified only at d=1,2,3 on synthetic objectives with manually constructed margin structure; while the bound held 9/9 and the C/10 control failed, the dimensions are far below any practical scale and the objectives are by construction designed to satisfy the margin condition.

claims.claim: CGP achieves ε-optimality with probability at least 1−δ using T = Õ(L^d ε^{-(2+α)} log(1/δ)) samples, improving on the worst-case Õ(ε^{-(2+d)}) rate whenever α < d (Theorem 4.8).
claims.evidence: The logbook computes covering number exponents (recovering d) rather than directly measuring CGP's end-to-end sample complexity T; the ε-exponent verified is the covering number exponent d, not the claimed sample complexity exponent (2+α), and all errors are suspiciously exactly 0.0000 across d=1,2,3 only.

claims.claim: A matching lower bound shows any algorithm requires Ω(ε^{-(2+α)}) samples under the same margin condition, establishing CGP's minimax sample-complexity optimality (Theorem 4.9).
claims.evidence: The lower bound is verified only for a single margin parameter (α=1, giving exponent 3.0) on a constructed hard instance, with Lipschitz deviation reported as exactly 0.0 — this is a single-case component check rather than a demonstration across the range of α values the theorem addresses.

claims.claim: CGP-Adaptive learns the Lipschitz constant L online via a doubling scheme, adding only an O(log T) multiplicative overhead to the sample complexity (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: The doubling scheme is verified to converge L_hat to [L*, 2L*) across 18 configs, but the 'mean overhead ratio 1.00' does not directly measure the claimed O(log T) multiplicative sample complexity overhead — it appears to track doubling counts rather than actual sample complexity, and no end-to-end overhead measurement is reported.

claims.claim: CGP-TR, a trust-region variant, scales to dimension d > 50 via certified restarts that provably never falsely eliminate the region containing the true optimizer x* (Theorem 6.1, Section 6).
claims.evidence: While dimensions d=60,100 exceed the d>50 threshold and 0/600 false eliminations with an L*/8 control is notable, the experiments use synthetic objectives with known x* location and the 0/600 result is suspiciously perfect, suggesting the test may be too easy rather than a faithful stress test of the trust-region guarantee.

amkkk/repro-certificate-guided-pruning-f.overall: The logbook provides component-level numerical checks of CGP's theoretical properties on small-scale synthetic objectives (d=1-3 for most claims), with destructive controls and multiple seeds, but does not attempt end-to-end runs or realistic-scale experiments. The suspiciously perfect results (0.0000 errors, 0/600 failures) and proxy computations (covering numbers instead of actual sample complexity) indicate simplified toy setups rather than faithful reproductions.

Srishti280992/repro-mash-modeling-absten.paper_title: MASH: Modeling Abstention via Selective Help-Seeking

claims.claim: On HotPotQA, MASH improves answer accuracy by 7.6 percentage points over the baseline OTC selective help-seeking approach (55.42% vs. 44.76%) (Section 4.1, Table 1).
claims.evidence: Released artifacts reproduce the endpoint accuracies exactly (MASH 55.4186%→55.42%, OTC 44.7637%→44.76%), but the computed delta is 10.655 pp, not the claimed 7.6 pp — the paper's own endpoints contradict its stated improvement magnitude.

claims.claim: On 2WikiMultihopQA, MASH improves accuracy by 6.64 percentage points over baseline OTC (45.99% vs. 39.59%) (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Released artifacts reproduce the endpoints (MASH 45.9948%→45.99%, OTC 39.5873%→39.59%), but the computed delta is 6.408 pp, not the claimed 6.64 pp.

claims.claim: MASH improves average Tool Productivity by 3.83 points across evaluated datasets compared to baseline OTC (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Recomputed mean Tool Productivity gains across NQ, HotPotQA, and 2Wiki are +2.77 (OTC), +4.46 (Exp-Dec), and +5.62 (OTC-Strict) — none of the three named variants matches the claimed +3.83 average improvement.

claims.claim: On the subset of HotPotQA questions requiring exactly one search, MASH achieves 56.4% accuracy versus 40.0% for baseline OTC (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Filtering HotPotQA predictions to exactly-one-search questions yields 56.366% for MASH OTC-Strict and 40.019% for baseline OTC, matching the claimed 56.4% and 40.0% from Table 2.

claims.claim: In the abstention inference mode, MASH with OTC-Strict reaches 59.9% precision on HotPotQA versus 53.1% for a DPO-based abstention baseline, and achieves 91.2% on the Abs(0) abstention classification metric on HotPotQA (Section 4.2, Table 3).
claims.evidence: Recomputed abstention metrics from released artifacts give MASH OTC-Strict precision 59.886%→59.9%, DPO precision 53.137%→53.1%, and Abs(0) 91.215%→91.2%, all matching the claimed Table 3 values.

claims.claim: MASH is trained via a two-step pipeline of warm-start supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning with three reward formulations (Exponential Decay, OTC, OTC-Strict) that balance accuracy against search-call penalties (Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: Code-path audit confirms the two-step pipeline: warm-start SFT scripts (generate_warm_start_data.sh, train_warm_start_model.sh) followed by RL training (mash_training.sh) with retrieval_penalty_type={exp,otc,otc_strict}, and reward_functions.py/reward_manager.py implement all three penalty formulations; released warm-start checkpoints are also available.

Srishti280992/repro-mash-modeling-absten.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous metric audit of released MASH prediction artifacts on full-scale test sets, verifying endpoint accuracies and Claims 4–6, but falsifying the three headline improvement-magnitude claims (Claims 1–3) because the paper's own reported endpoints yield deltas that contradict the stated improvement figures.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows a symmetric smoothing operator with positive coefficients can be rescaled by a diagonal matrix (via a symmetric Sinkhorn iteration) into a diffusion operator that is self-adjoint with respect to a mass-weighted inner product (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: From-scratch implementation of symmetric Sinkhorn on Gaussian and exponential kernels with n=200-500 in 3D with non-uniform mass yields self-adjointness error <1e-16 and mass conservation error <5e-11, confirmed across 10 random test vector pairs per configuration with uniqueness checks.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 proves that for Gaussian and exponential kernels, the Sinkhorn-normalized operators converge uniformly on bounded domains to continuous diffusion operators as sampling resolution increases (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Convergence is tested only on a 1D domain [0,1] at a single resolution N=800, comparing eigenvalues to analytical heat kernel values. The conclusion mentions a resolution sweep N=100→3200 but no such data appears on the claim page, so convergence-as-N-increases is not actually demonstrated with shown numbers.

claims.claim: The symmetric Sinkhorn algorithm empirically requires only 5 to 10 iterations to reduce normalization error below 0.1% (Section 4/5, empirical convergence results).
claims.evidence: Iteration counts range from 2 to 108 across bandwidths; only sigma≥0.4 (Gaussian) and sigma≥0.25 (Exponential) fall within 5-10, while moderate bandwidths like sigma=0.30 require 17 iterations. Additionally, the logbook uses a Gauss-Seidel (alternating) variant that converges faster than the paper's symmetric Sinkhorn, creating a methodological mismatch that makes comparison unreliable.

claims.claim: The normalized operators simultaneously satisfy symmetry, mass conservation, entrywise positivity, and spectral damping (eigenvalues in [0,1]), properties not jointly satisfied by standard row- or symmetric-normalization schemes (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Head-to-head comparison on identical n=1500 kernel matrices shows Sinkhorn Q satisfies all four properties (symmetry err 1.2e-16, mass err 3.1e-11, all positive, spectrum in [0,1]), while row-normalization fails symmetry (err 0.031) and classical symmetric normalization fails mass conservation (err 0.28), tested across sigma=0.05, 0.1, 0.2.

claims.claim: The method is demonstrated on point clouds, sparse voxel grids (jaw bone geometry), and Gaussian mixture models with covariance-aware kernels, showing Laplacian-like smoothing on each irregular data type (Section 5, experiments).
claims.evidence: All three modalities are tested with synthetic data: randomly generated 5000-point cloud, a small 16^3 synthetic voxel grid (~205 occupied, not real jaw bone geometry), and a synthetic 200-component GMM. The method is demonstrated to produce valid operators with monotone Dirichlet energy decay, but the real jaw bone voxel geometry is not used.

claims.claim: Shape analysis experiments on the Armadillo mesh show spectral distributions remain consistent across sampling modalities, with eigenvalue divergence appearing only at scales matching sampling resolution, validating the Theorem 4.2 convergence guarantee (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Spectral consistency is tested on a sphere geometry proxy rather than the Stanford Armadillo mesh (49,990 vertices) referenced in the claim. Low-mode agreement (err 0.12-0.18) and high-mode divergence (err 0.3-0.6) are shown across 4 sampling modalities on the sphere, demonstrating the expected pattern but on drastically simplified geometry.

amkkk/repro-sinkhorn-normalization-diffu.overall: The logbook provides credible numerical verification for the core algebraic properties (Claims 1 and 4) with from-scratch implementations and head-to-head baseline comparisons, but uses simplified or synthetic setups for the convergence theorem (1D only), data modality demonstrations (synthetic data, no jaw bone), and shape analysis (sphere proxy instead of Armadillo mesh). Claim 3 yields mixed results across bandwidths with a different algorithm variant than the paper describes.

Srishti280992/repro-efficiently-learning.paper_title: Efficiently Learning Drifting Halfspaces with Massart Noise

claims.claim: The paper's polynomial-time algorithm learns margin-separable halfspaces under distribution drift with Massart noise achieving error eta + O~(Delta^{1/3}/gamma), where eta bounds the Massart noise rate, Delta is the drift rate, and gamma is the margin parameter (Theorem 1.1, Section 1.1).
claims.evidence: The script implements a drifted Massart perceptron (Algorithm 2 style) on actual drifting gamma-margin halfspace trajectories in d=10 with window sizes up to W=276310, across four (Delta, gamma, eta) configurations. All runs achieved success probability 1.0 with worst excess/bound ratio of 5.16e-4. The proof-budget assembly independently confirms Delta^{1/3} scaling (slope 0.3375 after removing log factor, R^2=0.999997).

claims.claim: Under the low-degree polynomial hardness conjecture, any efficient algorithm for this drifting halfspace problem must incur excess error Omega(Delta^{1/3}), matching the algorithm's guarantee and establishing an information-computation gap (Theorem 1.2, Section 1.1).
claims.evidence: For d=2001, the critical trajectory length m* has measured Delta-slope of -0.667 (matching -2/3), and the induced hard excess Delta*m* has slope +0.333 (matching +1/3), both with R^2>0.9999. A brute-force hypercube tail cross-check at d=15 exactly matches the convolution calculation (residual 0.0), validating the implementation.

claims.claim: For general VC-dimension-d hypothesis classes under Massart noise, the statistically optimal (possibly inefficient) error rate is O~(sqrt(d*Delta)), better than the Theta((d*Delta)^{1/3}) rate achievable under adversarial noise (Theorem 2.1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: Exact Poisson/binomial Bayes-ERM excess computations on the paper's lower-bound family across d in {64,256,1024} and Delta in {1e-3,3e-4,1e-4} show the normalized ratio to sqrt(d*Delta/(1-2*eta)) stays constant in [0.0242, 0.0249], confirming the sqrt(d*Delta) statistical rate.

claims.claim: A matching information-theoretic lower bound of Omega(sqrt(d*Delta)) is proved for halfspaces under random classification noise (RCN), establishing optimality at Theta~(sqrt(d*Delta)) (Theorem 2.2, Section 2).
claims.evidence: Exact Bayes risk computations under the RCN condition (1-2*eta)^3 > d*Delta show Delta-slope +0.497, d-slope +0.503, and gap-slope -0.498, all matching the theoretical 1/2, 1/2, -1/2 exponents with R^2>0.9999. The normalized ratio to sqrt(d*Delta/(1-2*eta)) stays in [0.0232, 0.0249].

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 formally shows that no polynomial of degree less than O(gamma^{-c/4}) can distinguish the null from alternative hypothesis in the associated trajectory-testing problem, giving the formal low-degree hardness evidence for the Delta^{1/3} scaling (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: At d=2001, Delta=1e-4, c=0.25, the degree-1 likelihood advantage-squared at the paper's m=d^{1/6}*Delta^{-2/3} is 0.781 < 1 (not distinguishable), while the 3m control gives 21.07 > 1 (distinguishable), confirming the threshold is load-bearing. The degree limit proxy is 1.608, consistent with O(gamma^{-c/4}).

claims.claim: In the realizable setting, the algorithm's error improves to O~(Delta*gamma^{-3/2}), surpassing the prior best known bound of O~(Delta*gamma^{-2}) (Theorem 3.2, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The claim states the realizable error rate as O~(Delta*gamma^{-3/2}), but the measured proof-budget Delta-slope is exactly +0.5 (i.e., sqrt(Delta)), not +1.0 (i.e., Delta). The logbook itself identifies this discrepancy, noting the paper's Theorem 3.2 uses sqrt(Delta)*gamma^{-3/2}, not Delta*gamma^{-3/2}. The evidence contradicts the claim as stated.

Srishti280992/repro-efficiently-learning.overall: The logbook provides a thorough numerical reproduction implementing the paper's algorithms and exact constructions, verifying the Delta^{1/3} algorithmic rate, the low-degree hardness scaling, and the sqrt(d*Delta) statistical rates. Claim 6 is falsified as stated because the evidence shows sqrt(Delta) scaling rather than the claimed Delta scaling.

bsenst/repro-auditing-sybil-explaining-d.paper_title: Auditing Sybil: Explaining Deep Lung Cancer Risk Prediction Through Generative Interventional Attributions

claims.claim: S(H)NAP is presented as the first interventional audit framework for the Sybil lung cancer risk prediction model, using generative interventional attributions validated by expert radiologists (abstract only).
claims.evidence: The 'first' novelty claim cannot be verified by reproduction, expert radiologist validation was never performed, and the simplified LMPI approximation test on synthetic 64³ volumes produced inconsistent R² values (0.989, -0.784, -15.70), with no diffusion bridge implementation.

claims.claim: Sybil often exhibits behavior akin to an expert radiologist in differentiating malignant pulmonary nodules from benign ones, according to the interventional audit (abstract only).
claims.evidence: Real runs on synthetic 64³ voxel volumes showed directional differentiation between malignant (+0.026 logit) and benign (-0.036 logit) nodules, but used simplified spherical nodules without real CT scans, diffusion-bridge removal, or expert-annotated data.

claims.claim: Despite extensive prior clinical validation, Sybil shows sensitivity to clinically unjustified artifacts in CT scans (abstract only).
claims.evidence: Artifact sensitivity was tested on synthetic 64³ volumes with simple high-intensity blobs, yielding a non-significant effect (-0.019 logit, p=0.343), which neither supports nor falsifies the claim given the simplified proxy artifacts far from real ECG leads or gown snaps.

claims.claim: Sybil exhibits an unexplained directional (radial) bias in its decision-making process, uncovered through interventional analysis (abstract only).
claims.evidence: Radial bias was probed on synthetic data by inserting nodules at varying distances from lung center, yielding a non-significant result (slope=0.0015, R²=0.186, p=0.161) in the opposite direction to the paper, on a setup without real CT data or pleura-based distance measurement.

claims.claim: The work argues for shifting evaluation of such clinical risk-prediction models from purely statistical validation toward causal analysis before clinical deployment (abstract only).
claims.evidence: The distinction between statistical and causal validation was illustrated on synthetic data, but the artifact contribution was negligible (+0.004 probability units) with predictions nearly identical (correlation ≈ 1.0), providing only a toy demonstration of the advocacy argument.

bsenst/repro-auditing-sybil-explaining-d.overall: The logbook loaded the pre-trained Sybil model and ran experiments on synthetic 64³ voxel CT volumes with simplified nodules and artifacts on CPU in ~5 minutes, but lacked the diffusion bridge, real CT data, expert radiologist validation, and large-scale insertions central to the paper. Most results were non-significant or inconsistent, establishing only a toy-level directional nodule differentiation signal.

amkkk/repro-steady-state-constant-stepsi.paper_title: Steady-State Behavior of Constant-Stepsize Stochastic Approximation: Gaussian Approximation and Tail Bounds

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 (i.i.d. noise) and Theorem 4.1 (Markovian noise) bound the Wasserstein distance between the centered-scaled steady state Y^(α) = (X^(α) − x*)/√α and its Gaussian limit N(0, Σ_Y) by U√α log(1/α) (Theorems 3.1 and 4.1).
claims.evidence: Four SA families (1D SGD, 2D linear SA, 2D contractive SA, 1D Markov SGD) were simulated at 6 stepsizes with 200K steps each, yielding W1 slopes (0.244–0.819) and bounded W1/(√α·log(1/α)) ratios (max 0.296). However, all systems are 1D or 2D with simple drift functions, far below the general d-dimensional setting of Theorems 3.1 and 4.1.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 establishes an explicit non-asymptotic Wasserstein bound of order O(α^{1/2} log(1/α)) for constant-stepsize SGD on smooth, strongly convex objectives (Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: 1D SGD on a quadratic f(x)=βx²/2 with β=3 was simulated at 6 stepsizes, yielding W1 slope 0.833 and variance ratios 1.01–1.23 against the Lyapunov target. This is a single 1D quadratic objective, a clear simplification of the smooth strongly convex setting in Proposition 3.1.

claims.claim: Propositions 3.2 and 3.3 extend the same O(α^{1/2} log(1/α)) Wasserstein bound to linear stochastic approximation with a Hurwitz matrix and to contractive nonlinear stochastic approximation, respectively (Propositions 3.2 and 3.3, Section 3.2.2, Section 3.2.3).
claims.evidence: Two 2D systems (linear SA with Hurwitz matrix A=[[-1,2],[0,-2]] and contractive SA with γ=0.55) were simulated with sliced-W1 slopes of 0.192 and 0.417. These are low-dimensional specific instances, not a full test of the general Hurwitz/contractive settings.

claims.claim: For one-dimensional projections, the paper derives a non-uniform Berry-Esseen-type tail bound |P(⟨Y^(α),ζ⟩ > a) − P(Z_ζ > a)| ≤ C_d α^{1/4} log^{1/2}(1/α) / a, which improves as the deviation level a grows (Section 4).
claims.evidence: A 2D linear SA system was used to compute tail errors |Δ(a)| for a∈{0.5,…,3.0} at 6 stepsizes, showing monotonic decrease with a. However, many entries are exactly 0 (likely no samples exceeded the threshold, not true zero error), and the α^{1/4}log^{1/2}(1/α) scaling is not quantitatively verified—only the 1/a improvement is demonstrated on a 2D system.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 extends the Gaussian approximation and tail bounds for SGD, linear SA, and contractive nonlinear SA from i.i.d. noise to Markovian noise (Proposition 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: 1D SGD with a simplified two-state Markov chain (ρ=0.70) was simulated, showing W1 slope 0.489 against the correct long-run covariance versus systematically higher W1 against naive marginal covariance. The logbook itself acknowledges this is a 'simplified two-state Markov chain (not general Markov noise),' and it is only 1D.

claims.claim: Proposition 5.1 shows a different convergence rate of order α^{1/h} for constant-stepsize SA applied to general convex objectives with Gibbs-type limiting distributions (Proposition 5.1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: 1D SA on f(x)=|x|^h/h with h=4 yielded E|X| scaling slope 0.235 (vs. predicted 0.25), kurtosis 2.06–2.29 (vs. theoretical 2.188), and W1 to gennorm smaller than to Gaussian. This is a single 1D instance confirming the rate and distributional shape, but not a full test of the general convex setting.

amkkk/repro-steady-state-constant-stepsi.overall: The logbook provides real Monte Carlo simulations with concrete numbers across all six claims, but every experiment uses 1D or 2D systems with simplified drift and noise models, which are clear reductions from the general d-dimensional settings of the theorems and propositions. All claims are addressed with supportive evidence at toy scale, but none are verified at the full scope of the paper's theoretical results.

Srishti280992/repro-amortized-variationa.paper_title: Amortized Variational Inference for Partial-Label Learning: A Probabilistic Approach to Label Disambiguation

claims.claim: ViPll models the posterior P(Y|X,S) over true labels using a Dirichlet variational distribution whose parameters are output by an amortized inference network, factorizing the generative process as P(Y)P(X|Y)P(S|X,Y) instead of the standard discriminative formulation (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: The audit script executed the released Dirichlet/candidate-mask code on all 33,649 real-world rows, confirming `alpha = 1 + softplus(logits)`, `Dirichlet(alpha)` with `rsample`, and P(Y)/P(X|Y)/P(S|X,Y) loss terms; masked posterior simplex error was 1.19e-7 with zero outside-candidate mass vs. 0.684 unmasked leakage.

claims.claim: ViPll incorporates a conditional variational autoencoder to model P(X|Y) (Section 4.2) and a maximum-entropy prior satisfying candidate-label-set constraints (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: The max-entropy prior summed to 1.0 and satisfied singleton/candidate frequency bounds on 5/5 real-world datasets, and a paired CVAE control with zeroed label-conditioning produced nonzero reconstruction deltas on 5/5 datasets, confirming both components are functional.

claims.claim: Training proceeds in three phases: initialization, a 500-epoch CVAE warm-up, and a 1000-epoch main training loop using Monte Carlo sampling (Section 4.5).
claims.evidence: AST analysis of the released code confirmed the three-phase structure (initialization, CVAE warm-up with `range(501)`, main loop with `num_epoch=1001` and Monte Carlo `rsample` calls); a GPU canary run on Bird-song confirmed warm-up diagnostics and main-loop mechanics. The epoch counts are off by one (501/1001 vs. claimed 500/1000), a negligible implementation discrepancy.

claims.claim: On 5 real-world partial-label datasets, ViPll attains 76.15% (+/-1.56) accuracy on Bird-song and 78.52% (+/-2.27) on Lost, outperforming 9 baselines including PlKnn, Proden, PiCO, and CroSel on the majority of settings (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Independent reduction of the committed five-fold CSV files yields Bird-song 76.150% (±1.558) and Lost 78.516% (±2.266), matching the claimed 76.15 (±1.56) and 78.52 (±2.27); ViPll wins 42/45 method-dataset comparisons against the 9 baselines.

claims.claim: On synthetic partial-label benchmarks, ViPll reaches 96.64% (+/-3.92) accuracy on CIFAR-10 and 77.76% (+/-0.51) on CIFAR-100 (Table 3).
claims.evidence: Independent reduction of the committed synthetic benchmark CSVs yields CIFAR-10 96.642% (±3.917) and CIFAR-100 77.764% (±0.507), matching the claimed 96.64 (±3.92) and 77.76 (±0.51).

claims.claim: An ablation removing the modeling of Markov equivalence in the generative structure causes significant accuracy degradation, validating the choice of generative modeling (Section 4, ablation study).
claims.evidence: Matched fold comparisons show full ViPll beats the ablation (which omits the CVAE and max-entropy prior) on 10/10 datasets, with paired t-tests significant at p<0.05 on 9/10; the largest gaps are CIFAR-100 +32.02, MNIST +27.88, and KMNIST +18.37 points.

Srishti280992/repro-amortized-variationa.overall: The logbook provides concrete execution-based evidence for all six claims through mechanism audits on 33,649 real-world rows, independent CSV reduction matching paper numbers exactly, ablation statistics with paired t-tests, and a GPU canary run. However, no full independent retraining of all datasets and baselines was attempted; results are verified against the authors' committed output files rather than freshly generated runs.

claims.claim: For the independent Gaussian variance allocation problem, the paper gives a PTAS achieving E[max_i X_i] ≥ OPT - ε in polynomial time (Theorem 1.1, Section 1.2).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 (support enumeration on eps^3 grid) was implemented and tested across n=3..24 with eps in {0.1,0.05,0.025}, achieving max additive gap 0.0208 against a 0.005 reference mesh, with exhaustive enumeration confirming exact recovery in 36/36 cases at n=3,4.

claims.claim: For correlated Gaussian variables, a PTAS with the same additive ε guarantee is established (Theorem 1.2, Section 1.2).
claims.evidence: Only a one-factor covariance model was tested (not general correlation matrices) at n=2..8 over 50 cells; while the worst gap of 0.33% of eps supports the additive guarantee for this restricted correlation structure, the setup is a simplified proxy for the general correlated Gaussian claim.

claims.claim: For the GraphVarAlloc problem with multiple constraint sets (general m>1), the paper gives an O(log n) multiplicative approximation guaranteeing Ω(1/log n)·OPT (Theorem 1.3, Section 1.2).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 3 (greedy multi-level selection) was implemented and tested at n=4..256 across 35 cells with up to 1024 constraint sets, showing conservative ratio stable in [0.276, 0.339] with ratio*ln n rising from 0.43 to 1.88, while control baselines decay as expected.
