claims.evidence: On the real LRGB Peptides-functional graph (N=434, diameter=159, matching Table 3 exactly), relative Frobenius error on 185,772 distant-pair entries reduced 31.1% (0.5216→0.3596, paired SE 0.0043) over 10 paired seeds; 5 of 6 graphs run matched Table 3 exactly on (diameter, N), with GRF++ reducing error by 31-63% on every graph.

michaldobiezynski/repro-computationally-.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence on non-toy setups supporting all six claims, using real datasets (eurosis, Peptides LRGB, Thingi10K meshes), proper statistical controls (paired seeds, negative controls, z-scores), and scaling measurements up to N=128,000. Notable caveats include Lemma 3.2's literal closed form being numerically falsified (though the symmetry-free variant holds and the monotonicity headline is confirmed), the registry's 13%/15% figures understating actual clustering gains, and 2 of 8 Table-3 graphs not being run.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.7 establishes an excess risk bound under sample-only performativity, and Theorem 3.10 establishes a performative excess risk bound under full (sample-and-population) performativity (Theorem 3.7, Theorem 3.10).
claims.evidence: Bound-holding checked across 900 Thm 3.7 and 900 Thm 3.10 evaluations over L2-regularized logistic RERM trajectories (d up to 28, n up to 1e5, 200k population, 5 seeds), with the T-regime dichotomy (bounded/linear/exponential in T depending on εκ) reproducing exactly to 2-4 decimals and asymptotic log-log slopes matching theory within 0.03. Though bound-holding slack is wide (~280x), the discriminating rate-structure evidence is data-driven and non-toy.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.16 gives a cumulative performative excess risk bound whose convergence to zero as n→∞ requires either m=o(n) with εκ/γ<1, or a slower rate m=o(n·(εκ/γ)^{-Tp}) when εκ/γ≥1, a weaker stability requirement than prior work's εκ/γ<1 condition (Theorem 3.16).
claims.evidence: Cumulative bound held in 72/72 evaluations across 36 population roll-outs (d=28, n up to 60147, 200k population) under two sensitivity settings. The rate-dichotomy is confirmed by a genuine quantitative prediction: log-log slope sign flip exactly at the theory-derived threshold exponent a*=0.7501, with all five swept exponents' measured slopes within 0.0136 of predicted values, including correct divergence above the threshold.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.11 shows the counterintuitive result that retraining on performatively distorted samples can tighten generalization bounds by improving estimation of the transition map, rather than degrading them (Corollary 3.11).
claims.evidence: On 150 real RERM retraining trajectories (n=40000, d=28, T=8 rounds, 200k population, partial take-up with observed m_t), the deployable Thm 3.10 bound for θ₀ falls monotonically from 23.4338 to 23.2854 nats, lower at T=8 than T=1 in 142/150 trajectories. The named mechanism is measured directly: transition-map sensitivity estimation error |U_T − s*| falls with log-log slope −0.5021 vs Wald theory −0.5, and the tightening scales correctly as 1/√(nT) (4.32% at n=2000 vs 1.17% at n=40000). Part II's pooled interval is tighter in 100% of trajectories without losing coverage.

claims.claim: The empirical case study on German Federal Employment Agency data (over 60 million rows, 1975-2017) computes a sample-performativity excess risk bound of 0.302 nats (logistic loss) at 95% confidence on n=60,147 jobseekers with m=1,816 affected by the intervention (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The Corollary 3.8 bound arithmetic reproduces to six decimals (0.017512 + 0.289601 = 0.307112 nats) at the paper's exact operating point (n=60147, m=1816, 30 seeds), with all constants (D_Z, D_X, L_ell, L_a) re-derived from a pipeline built to App. C.1.1 specifications and found conservative. The registry's 0.302 is explained as v1 arithmetic. Realised gap of −0.00071 nats is inside the bound in 30/30 seeds. Caveat: actual IAB data is access-restricted, so a 200k synthetic population at identical scale is used, but the bound is a closed-form function of n, m, and certified constants that does

claims.claim: Under full performativity, a semi-simulated scenario varying treatment rates ξ ∈ {0.01,...,0.5} demonstrates a trade-off where the generalization gap increases with treatment intensity, decomposed into sampling, complexity, and performative terms (Section 4, Figure 1.3).
claims.evidence: The App. C.3 form of the Thm 3.13 bound rises strictly from 7.9402 to 41.4329 across all 50 treatment rates (ξ=0.01..0.50), with the performative term accounting for 101.5% of the rise. The realised gap is measured at −0.00032 to +0.04450 nats (32 seeds, Spearman +0.978, s.e.m. ≤1e-4) and replicated with the authors' own released transition map (−0.00033 to +0.03928, 16 seeds, Spearman +0.997, 0/50 violations). Same synthetic-data caveat as Claim 4 applies; the literal Thm 3.13 expression is U-shaped (min at ξ=0.03) while only the plotted App. C.3 form is monotone across the full sweep.

michaldobiezynski/repro-performative-lea.overall: All five claims are supported by concrete experimental evidence on non-toy setups (d up to 28, n up to 1e5, 200k populations, 30-150 seeds, deterministic re-runs). The strongest evidence includes exact reproduction of the T-regime dichotomy (Claim 1), a quantitative slope-sign-flip prediction at the theory-derived threshold a*=0.7501 (Claim 2), direct measurement of the estimation-error mechanism with correct 1/√(nT) scaling (Claim 3), six-decimal reproduction of the bound arithmetic with re-derived constants (Claim 4), and a measured realised-gap trade-off replicated with the authors' own transition map (Claim 5). The main limitation is that access-restricted German IAB data is replaced by synthetic populations at identical scale for Claims 4-5, though the bound computations are closed-form and do not depend on specific data values.

michaldobiezynski/repro-dimension-free-m.paper_title: Dimension-Free Multimodal Sampling via Preconditioned Annealed Langevin Dynamics

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes a dimension-uniform bound on the KL divergence between the target Gaussian-mixture measure and the annealed Langevin dynamics (ALD) output under a prescribed annealing horizon T^d = ε^{-1} K_d, provided the sufficient spectral condition sum_i w_i sum_{j>=1} (lambda_j/gamma_j) log(1+lambda_j/sigma_ij) < infinity holds, linking smoothing eigenvalues lambda_j, preconditioner eigenvalues gamma_j, and mixture component variances sigma_ij (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook exactly recomputes Theorem 3.1's constant K_d, showing sup_d K_d = 15.55 (converged from d=1 to d=2000) for the prescribed spectra versus 58165 and still growing for the flat spectra, and runs the paper's ALD protocol (N=20000, dt=9e-3, n=m=2500, 3 seeds) showing the empirical KL tracks the K_d/T envelope with a noise-corrected ratio plateauing at ~1.0-1.2 rather than growing with d, though the estimator noise floor is comparable to the bound itself.

claims.claim: Section 3 gives an alternate sufficient spectral condition, sum_i w_i sum_{j>=1} lambda_j^2/(gamma_j sigma_ij) < infinity, for dimension-uniform stability of the annealed process (Section 3, Equation 8).
claims.evidence: The logbook evaluates S6_d = sum_i w_i sum_j lambda_j^2/(gamma_j sigma_ij) termwise to d=2000, showing convergence to 1547.19 for the prescribed spectra (tail ratio 1.00002 from d=400 to d=2000) versus divergence to 1.43e10 for the flat spectra, with the implication 16 K_d <= S6_d holding at all nine audited dimensions for both configurations.

claims.claim: Section 4 decomposes the total sampling error into an initialization term (Proposition 4.3), a score-approximation term (Proposition 4.4) requiring a preconditioner spectrum decaying at rate at least j^{-3.5}, and an annealing-induced bias term from Theorem 3.1 (Section 4, Propositions 4.3-4.4).
claims.evidence: While the three-term decomposition structure recomputes correctly (E_init=18.17, E_score=0.0054, E_bias=0.252) and the Prop-4.1 inequality holds at every audited d, the test is vacuous (bound 18.43 vs measured KL 0.58, 32x slack), the end-to-end Figure-4 prediction does not reproduce (admissible j^-3.5 KL grows 40x from 0.0146 to 0.5832 rather than staying uniformly controlled, and the inadmissible j^-1 is better at d<=30), and the logbook's own summability computation shows the Prop-4.4 summand converges to 0.0025, collapsing the condition to sum_j gamma_j < inf rather than requiring j^-3.5.

claims.claim: Assumption 2.1 requires trace-class covariances for the infinite-dimensional Gaussian mixture target, ensuring the measures are well-posed on Hilbert space as dimension d grows (Section 2, Assumption 2.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook samples the target mixture at d up to 1600 with 20000 samples per point, showing that for the trace-class spectrum j^-1.25 the partial trace converges (5.548 towards 6.43), E||X^d||^2 saturates at 30.422, and the d..2d tail energy decays 0.4752->0.1406 (Cauchy in L2), while for the non-trace-class j^-0.75 all diagnostics reverse (sum=30.602, E||X^d||^2=55.216 growing, tail energy growing to 6.6915).

claims.claim: Numerical experiments in Section 5 show that with diagonal preconditioner Gamma = Diag(j^{-1.5}) and smoothing covariance C = Diag(40*j^{-2.7}), the empirical KL divergence between the true mixture and the ALD output stays uniformly bounded for dimensions d in {1,...,75}, whereas a flat-spectrum preconditioner fails to maintain this bound (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Using the paper's Appendix D protocol verbatim (N=20000, dt=9e-3, S=20, n=m=2500, kNN k=20, 3 seeds, 48 runs), the prescribed spectra (Gamma=Diag(j^-1.5), C=Diag(40j^-2.7)) yield max KL 0.1804 across d in {1,...,75} sitting inside a same-distribution null-control band reaching 0.0780, while the flat-spectrum choice climbs monotonically to 6.0554 at d=75, a 34x separation.

michaldobiezynski/repro-dimension-free-m.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous from-scratch reproduction of the paper's Appendix D protocol at non-trivial scale (d up to 75 for ALD runs, d up to 2000 for spectral sums, d up to 1600 for trace-class diagnostics), confirming the dimension-uniform KL bound (Claim 1), the alternate spectral condition (Claim 2), the trace-class well-posedness (Claim 4), and the headline Figure-3 dichotomy (Claim 5), while the Section 4 error decomposition (Claim 3) remains inconclusive due to a vacuous bound test, a non-reproducing end-to-end prediction, and a mischaracterized rate requirement.

michaldobiezynski/repro-large-scale-unce.paper_title: Large-scale Uncertainty Quantification for Latent Variable Models Using Subsampling Markov Chain Monte Carlo

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes a joint scaling limit for SGLD-Gibbs in which global parameters converge to an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck diffusion process while latent variables converge to independent jump processes under polynomial hyperparameter scaling (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: At the paper's own scale (N=30,000, dim=96, 64 chains × 80,000 iterations), the stationary-covariance trace ratio is 1.0042 with deviation shrinking across n=7,500/30,000/120,000 (1.0020/1.0042/1.0015), OU drift is 0.5734 vs c_h=0.5774, latent holding times match Exp(c_b) at KS p=0.686, and a discriminating control dropping the Jensen term moves the trace ratio to 1.3967, confirming the match is specific to the theorem's diffusion matrix.

claims.claim: The latent-involved Fisher information matrix decomposes as the true Fisher information plus an algorithm-induced 'Jensen gap' term M_star arising from single-sample Gibbs updates, which quantifies extra posterior uncertainty from latent variable estimation (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Although the headline rel-Fro of 5.830e-03 is admittedly circular (M defined as (Icond-I)/N in code), two non-circular checks support the decomposition: a disjoint-half estimator with actually sampled latents lands at 7.359e-03 from the exact closed form, and the running sampler's minibatch gradient noise satisfies b·Cov(G)=I_n+M_n to a trace ratio of 1.0009 over 120,000 minibatches; M_star is confirmed PSD with eigenvalues in [4.52e-15, 0.291].

claims.claim: Using S>1 conditional Gibbs draws per iteration shrinks the Jensen gap to M_star/S, so algorithm-induced variability vanishes as S goes to infinity, improving calibration at added computational cost (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: The 1/S law is measured two independent ways: a paired common-random-number estimator over 120,000 minibatches gives a log-log slope of -0.9996 (theory -1) across S=1..20 with per-S ratios in [0.9976, 1.0019], and end-to-end in the sampler the base-free algorithm-induced covariance difference between S=1 and S=10 is 506.18 vs a prediction of 505.77 (ratio 1.0008).

claims.claim: Two hyperparameter tuning strategies are given: a Bernstein-von Mises strategy setting Gamma to the inverse latent-involved Fisher information, and a bagged-posterior strategy setting Gamma to the inverse observed information J_star, each yielding distinct stationary covariance targets (Section 3.4, Table 2).
claims.evidence: Five independent runs at N=30,000 each match their own Table-2 covariance target (trace ratios 0.9997–1.0055) while missing the other tuning's target by 28–40% (cross-scores 0.7207 and 1.4009), with all 96 per-coordinate variance ratios in [0.957, 1.076]; the BvM target is confirmed S-invariant while the bagged target's S-dependent term shrinks as predicted.

claims.claim: On real flow cytometry data, SGLD-Gibbs attains ARI/AMI of 0.80/0.82 compared to 0.47/0.68 for stochastic variational inference, and on 20 Newsgroups SGRLD-Gibbs achieves perplexity 2052 versus 2402 for SVI (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: The flow-cytometry ARI/AMI half was never measured because the paper does not name the dataset; on 20 Newsgroups, SGRLD-Gibbs beats SVI at all three vocabulary sizes (direction reproduces) but no configuration matches the paper's absolute perplexities (closest: 2681/2444 at V=10,000 vs paper's 2402/2052, off by 11.6%/19.1%), with vocabulary size selected post hoc.

michaldobiezynski/repro-large-scale-unce.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence at the paper's own experimental scale for the four theoretical claims (Theorem 3.1 scaling limit, Fisher information decomposition, 1/S Jensen gap shrinkage, and distinct Table-2 covariance targets), including discriminating controls that rule out vacuous matches. The real-data claim is inconclusive because half the experiment was never run and the 20 Newsgroups absolute perplexities do not reproduce at any tested configuration.

michaldobiezynski/repro-foam-frequency-a.paper_title: FOAM: Frequency and Operator-Error Based Adaptive Damping Method for Reducing Staleness-Oriented Error for Shampoo

claims.claim: FOAM's operator-gap staleness error bound shows the damping term epsilon scales as 1/(p·epsilon_0^((p+1)/p)), while the eigendecomposition-refresh error grows as (1-beta^f)·R_SG^2 with refresh period f (Section 5.1, Lemma 5.2).
claims.evidence: On inverse-p-th roots of real Shampoo L-factor snapshots from a live 2000-step run, the damping exponent matches theory to five decimals at p=2,3,4 (-1.50000, -1.33333, -1.25000), the prefactor probe converges to 1.000000, and the Lipschitz inequality holds on 70/70 probes with chain ratio ≤1 at every eps_0 tested. This is a scale-free matrix-analysis fact, so the 128×128 factor substrate is adequate.

claims.claim: FOAM's regret staleness error is bounded by the term eta/(1-beta)·{r(1-beta^f)R_SG^4/epsilon_0^2}, exposing a trade-off where increasing the damping factor epsilon suppresses staleness error but inflates preconditioning cost (Section 5.2, Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: On the theorem's own convex online setting (4000-param multiclass logistic regression vs L-BFGS global optimum), the staleness bound holds in 18/18 grid cells and the trade-off reproduces in both directions: staleness gap falls monotonically with eps_0 while fresh regret is U-shaped with minimum at eps_0=1e-5 then 3.5× inflation. The corrected eps_0 exponent of -1.07 is in the safe direction relative to the bound's -2.

claims.claim: FOAM's three-phase algorithm (sensing, adapting, frequency control) updates the damping factor multiplicatively via epsilon_t <- max(epsilon_0, epsilon_{t-1}·h_t/tau) using an error proxy h_t = alpha(epsilon_{t-1})/p · RC(epsilon_{t-1}), capped by a maximum threshold epsilon_max (Section 6, Algorithms 1-3).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 3 implemented verbatim from pseudocode and instrumented over 594 live FOAM updates at the paper's own hyperparameters: branch logic correct 594/594, containment in [eps_0, eps_max] 594/594, non-degenerate adaptation (218 up/68 down), and the sensing proxy h_t upper-bounds the true relative operator gap on 80/80 independent probes with rho=0.9968.

claims.claim: On ViT trained on ImageNet-1K and Conformer trained on LibriSpeech, FOAM reaches equal or better accuracy/WER than standard (stale) Shampoo baselines in substantially less wall-clock time (Section 7, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: Tested on a 1.81M-param ViT on CIFAR-100 (not ImageNet-1K) with 3 paired seeds × 300 steps; Conformer/LibriSpeech not attempted at all. Quality half confirmed (paired +0.07pp accuracy), but the wall-clock advantage is contradicted (FOAM 26% slower in 3/3 seeds) because EVD is only 20% of CPU step cost at this scale.

claims.claim: FOAM's adaptive frequency control reduces eigendecomposition (EVD) calls to approximately 10% for the L factor and 5% for the R factor relative to a fixed per-step refresh schedule on ViT (Section 7, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: On a 1.81M-param ViT/CIFAR-100 at the paper's own config, the selective-refresh mechanism works (38–59% EVD reduction, L>R ordering in 4/6 cells) but the specific magnitudes are far off: L=47.22% and R=43.33% at 200 steps vs the paper's ~10% and ~5%. Full-scale ViT/ImageNet-1K experiment not attempted.

claims.claim: An ablation isolating adaptive damping alone (without selective EVD refresh) achieves lower training loss but significantly higher wall-clock time than full FOAM, showing both mechanisms are needed to balance loss and computational overhead (Section 7.3, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: On the same ViT/CIFAR-100 setup with 3 paired seeds, the compute mechanism is confirmed (540 vs 198 EVD calls, 2.7×, deterministic in 3/3 seeds) but the loss direction is reversed: damping-only loss is higher by +0.0271±0.0193 in 3/3 paired seeds rather than lower as the paper claims. Full-scale experiment not attempted.

michaldobiezynski/repro-foam-frequency-a.overall: The three theory/algorithm claims (1–3) are rigorously verified with real Shampoo factor snapshots, the theorem's own convex setting, and live FOAM updates at the paper's hyperparameters. The three systems claims (4–6) are addressed only on a 1.81M-param ViT/CIFAR-100 proxy that confirms the selective-refresh mechanism but contradicts the headline wall-clock and loss-ordering magnitudes, with the paper's actual ImageNet-1K and LibriSpeech experiments never attempted.

michaldobiezynski/repro-data-reconstruct.paper_title: Data Reconstruction: Identifiability and Optimization with Sample Splitting

claims.claim: For two-layer networks with polynomial activation of degree >=3, training samples are exactly recoverable from the KKT stationarity conditions under an interpolation rank condition, whereas linear activations recover only aggregate quantities and quadratic activations recover only second-order moment matrices (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: At d=n=64, alpha=3, m=2254 neurons with rank(K)=2080=N, the Theorem-4.1 pipeline recovers 64/64 samples from (a,W) alone to max error 3.853e-10; rank-deficient controls (m=N/2 and d=48) recover 0/48; explicit alpha=1 and alpha=2 alternative-data constructions are exact KKT points (residuals 8.40e-16 and 6.00e-14) that the cubic system rejects with 100% residual (1.673).

claims.claim: The exact-recoverability proof shows the KKT conditions determine a symmetric order-alpha tensor that admits a unique orthogonal decomposition for almost all cases satisfying the interpolation condition (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The kernelised interpolation recovers f to 1.354e-11 and T to 1.562e-11 with emergent symmetry (asymmetry 2.19e-11), versus 1.302e-01 in the rank-deficient control; whitening via Df(v) with lambda_min=1.683e-03 yields a power-method-with-deflation that returns all 64/64 components to 3.853e-10 sample error, though uniqueness of the decomposition is supported indirectly rather than proven exhaustively.

claims.claim: The proposed sample-splitting algorithm alternates first-order gradient descent with splitting of candidate reconstructions along negative-curvature directions of a proxy matrix S(x_i), avoiding explicit Hessian computation (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Lemma B.2's proxy bound holds 8/8 iterates on both synthetic (d=64) and the paper's 784-1000-1000-1 MNIST architecture (-1.8320e-03 >= -1.9549e-03); 20-step Lanczos on HVPs matches exact lambda_min(S) to 1.33e-15 using 235x fewer HVPs; 8/8 splits strictly decrease loss at 98-99% of the second-order prediction; ReLU yields ||S||_F=0, confirming smooth-activation requirement.

claims.claim: The sample-splitting algorithm provably reaches an epsilon-second-order stationary point in O(epsilon^-2) total iterations, comprising O(epsilon^-1/2) splitting steps and O(epsilon^-2) gradient-descent iterations (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: 21/21 runs (5 eps values x 3 seeds at d=64, repeated at d=128 and d=192) terminate on the eps-2SOSP criterion with total iterations inside the explicit Appendix-B.3 bound at every point (worst ratio 6.0e-02); log-log growth exponents 0.88 and 0.80 over the last decade are below the theoretical 2; 0 descent-rule violations in 2,212,623 gradient steps; 284/287 splits meet the guaranteed decrease.

claims.claim: On MNIST and CIFAR-10 reconstruction from fully-connected d-1000-1000-1 networks, sample splitting improves reconstruction quality on 21 of 25 top samples (84%) when layered atop the Haim et al. (2022), Buzaglo et al. (2024), and Loo et al. (2024) baselines (Section 6).
claims.evidence: At the paper's stated protocol (60,000 Adam iterations, splitting every 20,000, 50% batch cap, step cap 0.01) on a 784-1000-1000-1 GELU network with 100 MNIST images, splitting improved only 9/25 (k=2n=200) and 1/25 (k=60) top samples versus the claimed 21/25 (84%), with mean top-25 L2 degrading in both settings (3.4168->3.5510 and 2.5476->3.2127); the paper's curvature threshold lambda_*=-0.1 is never reached (deepest curvature -7.3e-04 vs threshold -3.17e-03), so the literal algorithm would split nothing.

michaldobiezynski/repro-data-reconstruct.overall: The logbook provides strong non-toy numerical evidence supporting the paper's theoretical claims (identifiability boundary, tensor decomposition, algorithm mechanism, and complexity bound) at d=64-192 with machine-precision recovery and 21 controlled optimization runs, but the headline empirical claim of 21/25 improved reconstructions is contradicted by the MNIST/Loo baseline measurement showing only 9/25 and 1/25 with quality degradation.

claims.claim: Lemma 4.1 establishes a calibration-sharpness decomposition showing expected error equals calibration error plus lack of sharpness plus irreducible aleatoric uncertainty, proving that improving proper scoring rules alone does not guarantee calibration (Lemma 4.1).
claims.evidence: On an exact enumerable joint law (d=64, N=4000 atoms, 400-point Y-grid), the Lemma 4.1 decomposition closes to relative residual 3.83e-16 across four fitted tree-GDN models (e.g., 0.5803058 = 0.0046193 + 0.2184122 + 0.3572742), and the negative example is measured: K=8→K=128 improves expected CRPS 0.6975→0.5803 while calibration error worsens 0.000418→0.004619.

claims.claim: Proposition 5.2 proves that the proposed conditional kernel mean embedding (CKME) recalibration map achieves auto-calibration while provably preserving the sharpness of the original predictive distribution (Proposition 5.2, Definition 5.1).
claims.evidence: On the same exact joint law, max_g TV(Q̃_g, P_{Y|Q̃=g}) = 0.000e+00, calibration error drops 6.519e-03→0, and sharpness I(Y;X|Q) = I(Y;X|Q̃) = 0.22168188; an adversarial probe with a corrupted map drives max TV to 9.833e-01, confirming the check is falsifiable. Caveat: the Q→Q̃ map was injective, so the non-trivial pooling case for sharpness preservation was not exercised.

claims.claim: The novel Energy Distance Kernel (EDK), a characteristic kernel over probability distributions, can be evaluated in O(n log n) time for empirical distributions of size n, versus the O(n^2) cost of standard distributional kernels (Section 5, Energy Distance Kernel).
claims.evidence: Sort-based EDK log-log timing slope measures 1.019–1.068 across two independent runs and two decades (theory 1.062 for n log n), while the naive pairwise form measures 1.836–2.053 (theory 2.0); the two implementations agree to 2.090e-14 relative error, with 634x–763x speedup at n=31623 and n=1e7 evaluated in 1.8–3.7s.

claims.claim: On the UCI regression benchmark (9 datasets, 20 predefined train/validation/test splits), CKME recalibration improves CRPS over the uncalibrated baseline, e.g. reducing normalized CRPS to 0.560±0.016 for a Distributional Random Forest on the Naval dataset and 0.594±0.178 for a Mixture Density Network on the Energy dataset, versus 1.000 for the uncalibrated model (Table 1).
claims.evidence: On the full Table-1 grid (9 datasets × 4 base models × 5 recalibrators, 550 splits), CKME reduces relative CRPS to 0.632±0.019 (naval/DRF) and 0.622±0.157 (energy/MDN) versus 1.000 uncalibrated; the energy/MDN cell falls within the paper's own sd, and across 16 well-powered cells the CKME column matches Table 1 at Pearson r=0.995 with mean absolute deviation 0.035. The naval/DRF value is 13% short of the paper's 0.560±0.016, but the improvement direction and overall pattern reproduce.

claims.claim: CKME recalibration achieves auto-calibration acceptance across datasets and base models (Distributional Random Forests, Mixture Density Networks, Bayesian Neural Networks, Gaussian Density Networks), outperforming PIT recalibration (Kuleshov et al., 2018) and the parametric GPBeta approach (Song et al., 2019) (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: Over the complete 36-cell Figure-1 grid, SKCE acceptance at α=5% is 0.439 for CKME versus 0.486 for PIT, 0.510 for uncalibrated, and 0.431 for GPBETA; on the 16 well-powered cells it is 0.294 for CKME versus 0.394 for PIT and 0.375 for uncalibrated. CKME is strictly the best method in only 10/36 cells and strictly worse than the best baseline in 24/36, contradicting the claim that CKME outperforms PIT and GPBETA. The test shows 0/5 false rejections under a null-by-construction check, and the same cells reproduce the paper's CRPS numbers at r=0.995, ruling out a broken test or weak CKME as expl

michaldobiezynski/repro-nonparametric-di.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence verifying Claims 1–4 on non-trivial setups (exact joint laws, full UCI benchmark grid with 550 splits, timing over 5 decades of n), while Claim 5 is falsified by measured SKCE acceptance rates showing CKME below PIT and the uncalibrated model across the grid. The reproduction is rigorous in scope—reimplementing all methods from scratch with adversarial probes and type-I error checks—but relies on reimplementations rather than author code, introducing unknown fidelity gaps.

michaldobiezynski/repro-stable-localized.paper_title: Stable Localized Conformal Prediction via Transduction

claims.claim: Stable (localized) Conformal Prediction (StCP/SLCP) uses a conditional CDF estimator trained on labeled source-task data plus an empirical marginal distribution estimated from unlabeled target data, calibrated via a regularized optimization with parameter λ (Equation 7, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 was implemented on the paper's LogAbs DGP (d=5, n=30, m=500, 150 repeats) and both lambda endpoints were reproduced: lambda=0 returns the conformal quantile to MAE 4.294e-04 (GLCP) / 4.726e-03 (CQR), and lambda=1e12 returns the source plug-in to 2.48e-13 (CQR arm, substantive). Both data streams were shown to be active (threshold sensitivity to resampling U_m and L_n separately).

claims.claim: StCP's coverage error is bounded by O(min(ε + λ^{1/2} + n^{-1}, δ_S + λ^{-1/2} + n^{-1})), establishing robustness of marginal coverage to the choice of λ (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Across 32 cells (8 lambda values × 2 score families × 2 n values, 250 repeats each, exact closed-form coverage), the bound holds in every cell with C=0.55, and coverage moves only from 0.90342 to 0.93618 across seven decades of lambda, directly supporting the robustness-to-lambda part of the claim. The bound itself cannot be falsified due to the free constant C, but the measured ingredients (eps, delta_S) and the narrow coverage band provide concrete support.

claims.claim: Standard conformal prediction has set-size variance of order O(n^{-1}), while StCP achieves O(m^{-1} + {n(1+λ)²}^{-1}), yielding substantial stability gains when the unlabeled target sample size m greatly exceeds the calibration size n (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: All four predicted exponents were measured by log-log regression over two successive windows: standard conformal Var(L) vs n gives slopes -1.008/-0.994 (theory -1), StCP Var(L) vs (1+lambda) gives -2.000/-1.999 (theory -2), StCP Var(L) vs n at lambda=100 gives -0.935/-0.991 (theory -1), and the m^{-1} term gives -1.018/-1.129 (theory -1). The Beta order-statistic computation was cross-checked against direct simulation.

claims.claim: On real data across five datasets, StCP/SLCP reduces prediction-set-size standard deviation by 20-48% when built on GLCP and by 6-29% when built on CQR, while maintaining marginal coverage near the nominal 90% level (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Only 3 of 5 datasets were run (DERMA and TISSUE, both MedMNIST image-classification tasks with discrete conformal scores, were not implemented). Of the 3 run, coverage-matched oracle-adjusted reductions were GLCP 65.1%/25.6%/20.6% and CQR 41.0%/14.5%/22.9% — 4 of 6 cells fall inside the paper's ranges but 2 BIO cells exceed them, and pipeline differences (different feature selection, response scaling, and conditional-CDF learner) are acknowledged.

claims.claim: On synthetic data, the largest stability gains occur at a small calibration size of n=30, with standard deviation reductions of 31.2% (GLCP-based) and 16.3% (CQR-based) (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The structural ordering (largest gain at n=30, monotone decrease to n=500) reproduces at the paper-matched operating point, but the specific magnitudes do not: at the calibrated Std(DP)/Std(base) ratio, the reproduction measures 45.1% (GLCP) and 42.0% (CQR) versus the paper's 31.2% and 16.3% — a 1.5x and 2.7x discrepancy attributed to a structurally different CQR score implementation.

claims.claim: A data-driven procedure for selecting λ maintains empirical coverage within the interval [1-α-α_tol, 1-α+α_tol+(n+1)^{-1}] (Theorem 4.7).
claims.evidence: Across 6 configurations (2 score families × 3 source-estimator corruption levels, 300 repeats each, exact coverage), the data-driven lambda selection maintained coverage in [0.89738, 0.90705], all inside the guaranteed interval [0.8800, 0.9523). The guarantee was shown non-vacuous: under the same corrupted estimators, the unregularised plug-in reached coverage 0.5401 and 1.0000.

michaldobiezynski/repro-stable-localized.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the four theoretical claims (1, 2, 3, 6) on the paper's own LogAbs synthetic DGP using exact closed-form computations, careful multi-window exponent fitting, and cross-checks, but the two empirical-table claims (4, 5) remain inconclusive due to 2 of 5 real datasets not being implemented and systematic magnitude mismatches (1.5x–2.7x) stemming from a different conditional-CDF learner and CQR score construction.

michaldobiezynski/repro-simple-algorithm.paper_title: Simple Algorithms for Bad Triangle Transversals with Applications to Correlation Clustering

claims.claim: A pivot procedure (Algorithm 4) transforms bad triangle transversal covers into clusterings with at most (3/2)|X| mistakes for correlation clustering on complete signed graphs, improving on the prior factor-of-2 bound (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive case analysis over all 50 feasible triplet sign/F-pattern combinations yields max (d-sum)/(b-sum) = 1.500000 exactly, cross-checked entry-by-entry against the paper's Table 1 and Table 2 (all 30 non-dash entries reproduce to 3 dp). Empirical pivot runs on 60 (instance, cover) pairs at n=100-200 give max E[mistakes]/|F| = 1.3123, never exceeding 1.5, and exact ILP on 5 complete graphs gives OPT_CC/OPT_BTT = 1.0000.

claims.claim: Three novel, simpler and faster 2-approximation algorithms are given for the Bad Triangle Transversal problem on general graphs: a folklore O(m)-LP-solve approach (Algorithm 1), a deterministic complementary-slackness method (Algorithm 2), and a randomized rounding algorithm for weighted variants (Algorithm 3).
claims.evidence: All three algorithms tested on 10 signed graphs (n=60-250, m up to 19900, up to 23389 bad triangles) achieve worst cost/LP_Delta = 2.0000 exactly on the paper's hexagram graph (LP=OPT=66, all return 132), with all covers verified feasible. Algorithm 1 required 2-3 LP solves vs single solves for Algorithms 2 and 3, confirming the relative efficiency claim. The logbook correctly notes the paper itself does not claim Algorithm 1 as novel (it is attributed to Krivelevich 1995).

claims.claim: For complete signed graphs, a randomized (2+epsilon)-approximation algorithm runs in tilde-O(epsilon^-7 m^1.5) time, matching the runtime of finding a maximal edge-disjoint bad-triangle packing and improving on the standard 3-approximation baseline (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The approximation factor is verified: 24/24 runs satisfy E|C| <= (2+2eps)LP_Delta with worst E|C|/OPT_BTT = 1.4939 against exact ILP. However, the runtime claim is not reproduced: Cao et al. 2024b's solver was replaced by a substitute MWU solver, and the measured m^1.5 slope of 1.54 is confounded because bad-triangle enumeration on complete graphs is itself Theta(m^1.5), so the timing cannot discriminate between efficient and inefficient solvers. The eps^-7 exponent is untestable at this scale (measured 2.14, far below 7).

claims.claim: Bad Triangle Transversal on general graphs is shown to be as hard to approximate as vertex cover, implying Unique-Games-Conjecture hardness for any approximation ratio better than 2-epsilon (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: On 9 random graphs (n=60-200), exact ILP gives OPT_BTT(H) = OPT_VC(G) with exact equality on 9/9 instances (e.g., 36=36, 70=70, 86=86, 119=119). The paper's Algorithm 2 cover on H maps back to a valid vertex cover of G on 9/9 instances, and the approximation ratio transfers with zero loss (1.7093 -> 1.7093 on every instance). The UGC-hardness implication is inherited from Khot & Regev 2008 and is not computable, but the reduction machinery that is the paper's contribution reproduces exactly.

claims.claim: On complete signed graphs, it is NP-hard to approximate Bad Triangle Transversal (and correlation clustering, cluster deletion, and minimum strong triadic closure) better than a 2137/2136 ratio, via a gap-preserving reduction from minimum 2CNF deletion using hexagram gadgets (Theorem 6, Theorem 7).
claims.evidence: The crux identity OPT_BTT(G) = 11n + OPT_MD holds exactly on 20/20 instances (n=3-12 variables, 14 with non-trivial OPT_MD), verified by exact ILP against brute-force 2^n Minimum 2CNF Deletion. LP_Delta is strictly below OPT on those 14 instances, confirming integrality does real work. The lone hexagram optimum is 9.0 by exact ILP, OPT_CC = OPT_BTT on 3/3 instances, and the gap constant (11+3/194)/(11+2/194) = 2137/2136 is derived in exact rational arithmetic. Scale is limited to 168 nodes by the double exponential cost of exact ILP plus brute-force deletion, but the construction is the paper'

michaldobiezynski/repro-simple-algorithm.overall: The logbook provides strong from-scratch experimental evidence supporting four of five claims: exhaustive case analysis for the 3/2 pivot bound, exact 2-approximation ratios for all three algorithms, exact equality in the vertex-cover reduction, and exact verification of the hexagram reduction identity and gap constant. Claim 3 is inconclusive because the approximation factor is verified but the runtime half uses a substitute solver with confounded timing measurements.

michaldobiezynski/repro-robust-and-consi.paper_title: Robust and Consistent Ski Rental with Distributional Advice

claims.claim: The Clamp Policy selects a threshold t̃ = min{max{t*_p̂, ceil(λb)}, floor(b/λ)} for a tunable robustness parameter λ in (0,1) (Definition 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Across 4000 random predicted distributions the clamp formula holds with the clamp genuinely binding (2647 lower, 429 upper), and on 20 (b, λ) cells the clamp endpoints exactly match the maximal Lemma-4.3-safe threshold set; the clamped policy's realized CR reaches 0.999895 of the 1+1/λ−1/b bound while the unclamped policy degrades to CR=b.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 bounds the competitive ratio by min{1 + 1/λ - 1/b, [ρ_p̂(t̃) + bθ]/(1-θ)}, giving robustness independent of prediction error η and consistency approaching the optimal ratio as η approaches 0 (Theorem 4.4, Corollary 4.5).
claims.evidence: Zero bound violations across 1920 (p, p̂) pairs spanning b∈{50,100,200,500}×λ∈{1/3,0.5,0.7,0.9}; the η-free robust term saturates at 0.9999 under adversarial predictions, and the consistency gap decays monotonically from 0.056348 to 0.000000 as η→0 with the bound collapsing to exactly CR(p) at η=0.

claims.claim: The Water-Filling Algorithm's optimal randomized stopping distribution follows the geometric CDF F*(x) = min{(R-1)((1+1/(b-1))^x - 1), 1} for cost-monotone settings (Theorem 5.2, Section 5).
claims.evidence: An exact HiGHS LP over the paper's own Lemma-5.1 polytope (32 cells, up to 2500 variables) matches objective(F*) to a worst relative gap of 1.379e-14, and the LP's optimal CDF coincides pointwise with F* to 8.504e-14; the Thm 5.3 threshold regime also reproduces with F* optimal above the threshold and suboptimal below it.

claims.claim: A stopping distribution is R-robust if and only if μ(x) + (b-x)F(x) ≤ (R-1)x for all 1 ≤ x ≤ b-1 and μ(∞) ≤ (R-1)b (Lemma 5.1).
claims.evidence: Brute-force robustness R_direct computed from the raw cost definition C_z(x) matches the lemma's two-condition R_lemma to 1.643e-13 across 2000 random stopping distributions spanning four shape families, supports to 2000 days, and b to 500; agreement also holds exactly on F* and Purohit outputs.

claims.claim: Experiments show the Water-Filling Algorithm yields 5-20% consistency improvements over point-prediction baselines across diverse distributions, with the largest gains on bi-modal distributions (Table 2, Section 6).
claims.evidence: The Table-2 grid reproduces closely (10/10 baseline cells exact, 13/15 within 1e-4) and the largest gain is on bi-modal at 16.99% matching the paper, but only 3/5 families reach the claimed 5% threshold—the two uniform families yield 1.2–2.3%, a shortfall also visible in the paper's own published table, making the '5-20% across diverse distributions' characterization an overstatement rather than a clean reproduction or falsification.

michaldobiezynski/repro-robust-and-consi.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, independently-constructed numerical evidence from a single CPU-only NumPy/SciPy script that verifies all four theoretical claims (clamp formula, CR bounds, optimal CDF, robustness characterization) at near-machine precision across non-trivial scales, while the experimental claim (Claim 5) reproduces the table numerically but reveals that the '5-20% across diverse distributions' magnitude is overstated even in the paper's own data.

michaldobiezynski/repro-multi-level-stra.paper_title: Multi-Level Strategic Classification: Incentivizing Improvement through Promotion and Relegation Dynamics

claims.claim: Proposition 2.1 shows that in the two-level (single promotion) sequential setting, improvement becomes infeasible only when (1-beta*gamma)*c+ > c-, an impossibility region strictly smaller than in the one-shot strategic classification setting (Proposition 2.1).
claims.evidence: On a 230-point (c+, c-) grid, 0/86 in-region points show improvement and 144/144 wedge points are incentivizable; empirical impossibility area 0.3739 vs theory 0.3600 vs one-shot 1.0000. An independent raw-form solver (raw_control.py) that never encodes (1-beta*gamma) recovers the boundary sharply, with improvement absent at 0.99x and present at 1.01x of (1-beta*gamma)c+.

claims.claim: Theorems 3.1-3.2 characterize optimal long-run agent behavior across threshold ranges, showing a 'leg-up region' where mu < delta/(1-gamma) permits mixtures of gaming and genuine improvement rather than pure strategies (Theorems 3.1-3.2).
claims.evidence: Over 240 thresholds × ~4000 attribute points, mixtures (a+*>0 and a-*>0) occur at 32/32 in-region thresholds where x_circ>0, 0/8 where x_circ=0, and 0/200 outside the leg-up region. Measured x_circ matches theory max{0, s_(K-1)} to 9.3e-04 (sub-grid-step), and Theorem 3.2 case boundaries land within one mu-grid step of theoretical values 14.5536 and 16.7857.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that without a leg-up mechanism, reaching a target attribute level M is infeasible whenever M >= r / [(1-beta)(1-gamma)^2 * c+], establishing a fundamental limit on achievable improvement absent promotion incentives (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Across 4 instances with 511 candidate designs each, 0/769 candidates with mu_L >= B were feasible, but max M/B = 0.234 and max absorbing mu_L/B = 0.172 — the search never approaches the bound. An alternative bound r/[(1-beta)(1-gamma)c+] with a different exponent is equally unviolated by the same data, so the experiment cannot discriminate the paper's specific functional form.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 gives sufficient conditions under which a leg-up mechanism permits agents to reach arbitrarily high levels, and proposes the threshold sequence mu_l = delta*l/(1-gamma), setting each level's threshold at the dynamical steady-state attribute value (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Using the steady-state threshold mu_l = delta(l-1)/(1-gamma), 5/5 targets (M in {2.5, 5, 10, 20, 40}, L up to 17) are feasible with max gaming 7.1e-15 and liminf x+ = M exactly; bisected r_crit = 0.40000 matches theoretical r_min = 0.40000 to 5 dp. The printed formula mu_l = delta*l/(1-gamma) fails at M=2.5 and M=5 (off-by-one), but the claim's substantive assertion about steady-state thresholds reaching arbitrarily high levels is confirmed.

claims.claim: The reduction in effective unit cost of improvement from c+ to (1-beta*gamma)*c+ under the sequential multi-level formulation is identified as the mechanism that strictly expands the incentivizable region relative to one-shot strategic classification (Section 2, Proposition 2.1).
claims.evidence: Bisection over 12 (beta, gamma) pairs at c+=0.8 gives c-*/c+ matching 1-beta*gamma to max 0.001% relative error across a 4x range (0.19 to 0.75), while the one-shot prediction of 1.0 is off by 25-81% on every pair. An independent raw-form solver that never encodes (1-beta*gamma) recovers c-*/c+ to within 0.006%, ruling out circularity.

michaldobiezynski/repro-multi-level-stra.overall: The logbook provides strong, non-circular experimental support for four of five claims through Bellman fixed-point solutions, grid sweeps, bisections, and an independent raw-form control solver, with Theorem 4.1 remaining inconclusive due to insufficient discriminating power in the finite design search. An off-by-one error in the printed Theorem 4.2 formula is identified but the underlying steady-state result reproduces cleanly.

michaldobiezynski/repro-on-the-existence.paper_title: On the Existence of Consistent Adversarial Attacks in High-Dimensional Linear Classification

claims.claim: Proposition 1 gives the geometric existence condition for a consistent (label-preserving) adversarial attack: ε·d*_q*(ŵ_⊥) ≥ |⟨ŵ,x⟩|, where ŵ_⊥ is the component of the classifier orthogonal to the ground-truth direction (Section 3.1, Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: An exact HiGHS primal LP solving the constrained supremum without invoking the paper's duality identity matches eps·d*_{q*}(ŵ_⊥) to relative gap 1.645e-15 at d=1000 on a real trained ERM predictor, with 0/72000 iff counterexamples across q∈{2,3,∞} and Corollary 2 matching 400k-sample MC frequencies within 0.0008.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 shows that, for the well-specified Gaussian model, the consistent robust-error and consistent boundary-error metrics concentrate to closed-form integrals depending on √(q-m²), in contrast to the standard (inconsistent) robust error which depends on √q, formally explaining why consistent attacks are less effective at fixed perturbation budget (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: At d=2000 with a real ERM predictor, closed-form Theorem-3.1 integrals match measured consistent error metrics to max deviation 0.0040, and a decisive discrimination test shows substituting √q for √(q−m²) mis-predicts E_rob^cns by up to 0.2684 (~50× the residual), confirming the specific functional form; the eq.-26 constant also converges to 5.24e-04 at d=2000 independently.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 characterizes the asymptotic robust-ERM performance in a latent-space (misspecified) linear classification model via a system of self-consistent equations in the proportional limit n,p,d→∞, distinguishing underparameterized (γ≤1) from overparameterized (γ>1) regimes (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The replica self-consistent fixed-point system (eqs. 37/39/40) was never implemented or solved; only proxy measurements of self-averaging (std ~ d^{-0.44}) and proportional-limit drift (≤1.05% at γ=0.5) were performed at full scale, which any proportional-limit theory would satisfy, and the q_f/q vs γ curve shows no visible kink distinguishing the two regimes.

claims.claim: Section 4.3 shows overparameterization has a dual effect: the consistent boundary error E_bnd^cns increases with overparameterization (greater vulnerability to label-preserving attacks), while the aggregate consistent robust error E_rob^cns decreases because overparameterization improves clean generalization (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: At d=500 with real ERM on the paper's exact latent model, E_bnd^cns increases with ψ at all α (+0.1420/+0.0576/+0.0213), E_rob^cns decreases in the large-ψ regime (−0.0074/−0.0324/−0.0333) with the correct α-ordering, and the decomposition E_rob^cns = E_clean + E_bnd^cns closes to 1e-16, directly confirming the clean-generalization mechanism; levels differ from the paper due to using r=0 ERM instead of robust training, but the qualitative dual effect is reproduced.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 gives the exact asymptotic characterization of the consistent error metrics (E_rob^cns and E_bnd^cns) for the latent-variable classification model under misspecification (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: The 0.0009 max deviation between measured and 'theory' columns equals exactly the MC noise floor √(0.25/3×10^5), and the comparison is circular: the 'theory' side reuses the empirically measured threshold from the same trained θ_hat rather than evaluating eq. 45's closed form from (α,ψ,λ,r), so Theorem 4.2's predictive content—that (m,q,A) are predicted via Theorem 4.1 without training—is never tested; only Proposition 2 and concentration of A are verified as proxies.

michaldobiezynski/repro-on-the-existence.overall: The logbook provides strong, non-circular verification for Claims 1 and 2 via exact LP certificates and decisive discrimination tests at d=1000–2000, and phenomenological verification for Claim 4's dual-effect trend at d=500. Claims 3 and 5 are honestly labelled as proxy measurements: the Theorem 4.1 fixed-point system was never implemented, and the Theorem 4.2 comparison was circular, with its residual matching the MC noise floor exactly.

michaldobiezynski/repro-on-the-accuracy-.paper_title: On the Accuracy of Newton Step and Influence Function Data Attributions

claims.claim: Theorem 1.5 bounds the Newton-step approximation error to the true leave-one-out retrained parameter using only local strong convexity in a neighborhood of the Newton step, rather than the global strong convexity assumed in prior analyses (Theorem 1.5, Section 3).
claims.evidence: On n=65536, d=64, k=32 with 5 random drop-sets and independent full Newton retrains (residuals 5.3e-13..1e-11), the local bound C_h·C_op holds in 5/5 cases at ~2.00x tightness with local C_op≈1.001, while the global constant is unavailable (lambda_min(H_theta)/n decays from 0.235 to 1.612e-04 as ||theta||→20, making C_op^global=∞). The self-consistent ball radius setting is a legitimate but disclosed circularity; the substantive evidence is that C_op stays ~1.0 over the local ball.

claims.claim: For logistic regression with n samples, d-dimensional Gaussian features, and k removed points, the average-case Newton-step attribution error scales as Õ(kd/n²), while the average-case influence-function error scales as Õ((k^{3/2}d^{1/2}+k^{1/2}d^{3/2})/n²) (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: Over a 29-point (n,d,k) grid (n=8192..524288, d=16..128, k=2..512, ~1650 full Newton retrains), measured log-log slopes match predictions: NS error +1.045/+0.984/+0.934/−1.941 vs predicted +1/+1/+1/−2, and IF−NS gap +0.679/+1.408/+1.335/+1.464/−1.978 vs predicted forms. Composite-ratio spreads are 1.47x (NS) and 1.28x (IF−NS) vs 3.66x for the wrong kd/n² alternative, discriminating the claimed (k^{3/2}d^{1/2}+k^{1/2}d^{3/2})/n² form.

claims.claim: The derived upper bounds match corresponding lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors, showing the Newton step is provably more accurate than influence functions whenever d ≫ k (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: Empirical two-sided tightness holds across the 29-point grid (measured/rate 0.97..1.42 for NS, 2.12..2.71 for IF−NS gap, near-constant prefactors), and the IF/NS error ratio reaches 17.15x at d/k=64 with log-log slope +0.395 in d/k (predicted +0.5, explained by V-shaped contamination from the other term, fit within 1.27x). The lower-bound proofs themselves cannot be numerically verified, but the empirical tightness and the directly measured sqrt(d/k) advantage are concrete evidence supporting the claim.

claims.claim: Rescaled and doubly-rescaled influence functions (RIF and DRIF) are shown to match the Newton step's Õ(kd/n²) average-case error rate while preserving the additivity property that plain influence functions have but the Newton step lacks (Theorem 1.6, Theorem 1.7).
claims.evidence: DRIF matches the NS rate (k-slope +1.004, d-slope +0.985, 1.85x spread) and RIF is additive to float precision (8.571e-14), but RIF's average-case error does NOT match kd/n² (k-slope +1.430, 8.76x spread, reaching 10.59x the NS error at k=512). The adversarial max_T bound (Thm 1.12) that could rescue RIF was never tested—only uniform random drop-sets were used—and the paper's own Thm 1.13 separates RIF from DRIF, suggesting the registry claim may be misstated.

claims.claim: The paper's revised bounds remove the problematic 1/λ³ dependence on the regularization coefficient λ present in prior influence-function error analyses (Section 1, Discussion of prior bounds).
claims.evidence: Over lambda from 1e-1 to 1e-4 (n=65536, d=64, k=32), the prior bound's log-log slope in lambda is −3.033 (growing to 1.813e+06, 1.79e6×||theta_hat||), while the new bound C_h·C_op has slope −0.209 tracking the true NS error's −0.208 at constant ~2.03x. The analytic substitution C_op^global:=1/(n*lambda) is empirically validated by lambda_min(H_theta)/n bottoming out at exactly the regularizer floor (1.002e-04 at lambda=1e-4), addressing the disclosed partial circularity.

michaldobiezynski/repro-on-the-accuracy-.overall: This logbook provides strong, reproducible experimental evidence for claims 1, 2, 3, and 5 through ~1650 independent full Newton leave-k-out retrains on synthetic Gaussian logistic regression at non-trivial scale (n up to 524288, d up to 128), with scaling analyses that discriminate the paper's predicted rates from alternatives. Claim 4 is genuinely inconclusive: DRIF and additivity are verified, but RIF's average-case error is empirically contradicted and the adversarial bound that might rescue it was never tested.

MarxistLeninist/O88FCPAPAj.paper_title: Ranking Free RAG: Replacing Re-ranking with Selection in RAG for Sensitive Domains

claims.claim: METEORA replaces opaque re-ranking with rationale-driven evidence selection, adaptive cutoff detection, and rationale-based poisoned-evidence verification (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook implemented the ECSE adaptive cutoff detection algorithm on SQuAD (67 samples) with query embedding substituted for DPO-tuned rationale generation and no Verifier LLM for poisoned-evidence verification, so only one of the three claimed components was partially exercised on a simplified proxy setup.

claims.claim: Across six datasets, METEORA reports 13.41% higher recall, 21.05% higher precision without expansion, 80% lower evidence volume, 33.34% higher answer accuracy, and 4.4x adversarial robustness improvement (Abstract).
claims.evidence: Real runs on SQuAD proxy (n=67) showed +25.9% precision and 58-61% volume reduction vs fixed top-k baselines, but none of the six domain-specific datasets were used, downstream accuracy was not evaluated, and adversarial robustness was not tested, so the multi-dataset, multi-metric claim was only partially addressed on a proxy task.

claims.claim: Under the paper's latency setup, METEORA uses 12.23k input tokens and 2.91s total time, compared with 36.89k/4.04s for SBERT and 39.82k/4.61s for RankRAG (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook contains no latency measurements, input token counts, or timing comparisons against SBERT or RankRAG; the efficiency claim from Table 1 was never addressed.

claims.claim: The evaluation spans six legal, finance, and academic datasets with document counts and QA-pair counts listed for ContractNLI, CUAD, MAUD, PrivacyQA, FinQA, and QASPER (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly used SQuAD as a proxy instead of any of the six domain-specific datasets (ContractNLI, CUAD, MAUD, PrivacyQA, FinQA, QASPER), so the claim about evaluation spanning those specific datasets was not addressed.

claims.claim: METEORA reports larger recall gains over the strongest baseline as document complexity increases, including +41.17% on MAUD (Section 5).
claims.evidence: No experiments on MAUD or any domain-specific dataset were conducted, and no analysis of recall gains as a function of document complexity was performed; the claim was never addressed.

MarxistLeninist/O88FCPAPAj.overall: This logbook provides only a toy-scale proxy reproduction of METEORA's core ECSE selection algorithm on 67 SQuAD samples with query embeddings replacing rationale generation, showing directional improvements in precision and volume reduction. Three of five claims were never addressed (latency, six-dataset evaluation, complexity-scaling recall), and the remaining two were tested only on a simplified proxy setup far from the paper's scale and domain.

Edd16/icml2026-Sh3rKEAxlW-repro.paper_title: MDN: Parallelizing Stepwise Momentum for Delta Linear Attention

claims.claim: The stepwise momentum rule is analyzed as a second-order dynamical system that admits complex conjugate eigenvalues, and stability is enforced via a quadrant-based constraint β_t ≤ 1−α_t with μ_t ∈ (e⁻¹, 1) (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements a hand-picked second-order recurrence (a1=0.8, a2=-0.2) and confirms complex-conjugate roots exist, but never tests the actual quadrant-based stability constraint β_t ≤ 1−α_t with μ_t ∈ (e⁻¹, 1), and explicitly notes full-scale MDN projection matrices require validation.

claims.claim: MDN is evaluated at 1.3B parameters trained on 100B tokens against Transformers, Mamba2, and GDN, reporting perplexity, commonsense reasoning, and in-context retrieval metrics (Section 4.2, Table 2).
claims.evidence: Instead of 1.3B/100B training, the logbook runs a synthetic next-token prediction task (seq_len=40, 32 features, 60-way vocab, 1200 sequences) where MDN does not even beat baselines (mdn_beats_mamba=False, mdn_beats_transformer=False); the logbook itself states no real Mamba2/GDN scales were run.

claims.claim: MDN achieves the highest average score on LongBench at 16K sequence length among the compared architectures (Section 4.2, Table 3).
claims.evidence: LongBench at 16K sequence length is never mentioned anywhere in the logbook; no retrieval benchmark results are reported.

claims.claim: On the synthetic MQAR associative-recall task, MDN outperforms competing linear attention variants across varying sequence lengths (Section 4.1, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The MQAR associative-recall task is never mentioned in the logbook; the only synthetic task is a next-token prediction proxy unrelated to MQAR.

claims.claim: An ablation on the 400M-parameter model isolates the contribution of the momentum components and the stability constraint to overall performance (Section 4.3, Table 4).
claims.evidence: No ablation study isolating momentum components versus the stability constraint is described; the 400M-parameter model is never mentioned.

claims.claim: Decoding latency and training throughput comparisons show MDN attains competitive throughput relative to other linear attention models while retaining causal parallelizability (Section 4.3, Figure 6).
claims.evidence: The logbook computes only FLOP-count proxies at seq_len=64, d_model=128, n_layers=2 comparing linear recurrence vs dense attention, not actual throughput or latency against other linear attention models; the logbook notes execution-throughput was not measured.

Edd16/icml2026-Sh3rKEAxlW-repro.overall: This logbook addresses only 3 of 6 claims, all via tiny synthetic proxies (seq_len 40–64, d_model 128) far below the paper's scale, and 3 claims are entirely unaddressed. The eigenvalue demonstration confirms a mathematical concept but not the specific stability constraint, and the downstream-performance proxy actually shows MDN failing to beat baselines.

Edd16/icml2026-rVcYqFCgY9-repro.paper_title: Rethinking 3D Shape Generation: Diffusion over Superquadrics

claims.claim: Diffusion over Superquadrics (DoSs) represents each 3D shape with 128x15 tokens (~7KB) versus 2,048x3 points (24KB) for point clouds or 32^3x3 voxels (384KB) for dense voxel grids, drastically reducing diffusion-state dimensionality (Introduction, Section 3, Methodology).
claims.evidence: The logbook models each shape as a 12-D parameter vector (48 bytes), not the paper's 128×15 token representation (~7KB), and explicitly states the 7KB figure 'includes un-modeled learned code.' The comparison uses 1k-point clouds instead of the paper's 2,048×3 or 32³ voxel grid, so the actual diffusion-state dimensionality claim is only addressed via a simplified proxy.

claims.claim: On ShapeNet, DoSs attains 1-NNA@CD scores of 53.80 (Chair), 61.92 (Airplane), and 57.50 (Car), reported as competitive against baselines including DPM, PVD, TIGER, LION, MeshDiffusion, and DiT-3D (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook never runs the full diffusion model on ShapeNet, reports no 1-NNA@CD scores, and makes no comparison to DPM, PVD, TIGER, LION, MeshDiffusion, or DiT-3D. The overview explicitly states 'distributional metrics are out of scope.'

claims.claim: DoSs generates a shape in approximately 0.6 seconds at batch size 1 on an RTX 3090, with about 2 hours of training time per category (Section 4, Experiments).
claims.evidence: Only primitive decode wall-clock (~0.74 ms on CPU) was measured; the logbook itself notes 'the 0.6s figure includes diffusion sampling + network forward passes, which dominate' and those were not measured. No RTX 3090 runs and no training-time measurement at all.

JG1310/repro-sharp-inequalities-between-.paper_title: Sharp Inequalities between Total Variation and Hellinger Distances for Gaussian Mixtures

claims.claim: Theorem 2.1 bounds the chi-squared divergence between two Gaussian location mixtures by a quantity of the form (C0 v TV^{-alpha(TV)}) * TV, with alpha(t) = (2+delta)/log(log(1/t) v e) (Theorem 2.1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: exp02 checks Corollary 2.4 on 6000 random Gaussian location mixture pairs with 0 violations and fitted sub-polynomial slope 0.0042 (vs 0.5 for trivial bound); exp01 reproduces the Chebyshev sharp construction over 96 grid points (n=11..201, TV down to ~6e-280) with identities matching to ~1e-121 and gap·loglog(1/TV) staying in [0.16, 0.66], confirming the Θ(1)/loglog correction is genuinely present. 91/96 points satisfy the asymptotic 0.33 threshold; the 5 pre-asymptotic undershoots are consistent with the TV↓0 nature of the theorem.

claims.claim: Corollary 2.4 derives that the Hellinger distance between two Gaussian location mixtures is bounded by TV raised to the power 1-o(1), where the o(1) term decays as 1/log log(1/TV) (Corollary 2.4).
claims.evidence: Theorem 4.3's entropic bracket is a direct consequence of Corollary 2.4 (verified in exp02 with 0/6000 violations) and the nonzero exponent gap (verified in exp01). The D12 exponent diagnostic numerically confirms the TV-risk bracket [ε^{2(1+α)}, ε²] collapses to ε² as ε→0, with the (2+δ)/loglog correction vanishing monotonically across ε=1e-2..1e-12.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 and Lemma 3.2 show this exponent is sharp by an explicit construction using Chebyshev polynomial zeros satisfying Hn >= TVn^{1-alpha*(TVn)} with alpha*(t)=0.33/log log(1/t), proving the 1-o(1) factor cannot be improved (Theorem 3.1, Lemma 3.2, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The upper rate ε^{2(1-(2+δ)/loglog)} follows from Cor 2.4 (exp02, 0/6000 violations) applied to the Yatracos TV guarantee; the matching lower rate ε^{2(1-0.33/loglog)} follows from the Theorem 3.1 construction (exp01, reproduced to ~1e-121). The D12 diagnostic confirms both exponents converge monotonically to 2 as ε↓0, certifying rate-optimality on the contamination term.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 uses the sharp TV-Hellinger inequality together with a metric-entropy argument to characterize the minimax rate for learning Gaussian location mixtures in total variation distance, resolving an open problem posed by Jia et al. (2023) (Theorem 4.3, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Claim 4 is the same as Claim 2 (Theorem 4.3): the entropic characterization of the minimax TV learning rate is supported by exp02 (Cor 2.4 holds universally) and exp01 (sharpness construction), with D12 exponent bookkeeping confirming the bracket structure.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.5 shows the inequality yields a Hellinger-distance error rate of epsilon^{2(1-o(1))} for robust estimation of Gaussian mixtures under Huber contamination, with Theorem 4.6 establishing a matching lower bound (Theorem 4.5, Theorem 4.6, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Claim 5 is the same as Claim 3 (Theorems 4.5/4.6): the matching upper/lower Hellinger robust rates are certified by reuse of exp02 (upper bound via Cor 2.4) and exp01 (lower bound via Theorem 3.1 construction), with D12 confirming exponent convergence to the optimal ε² rate.

JG1310/repro-sharp-inequalities-between-.overall: This logbook provides a serious CPU-only numerical audit of a pure-theory paper, checking the main inequality (Corollary 2.4) on 6000 random mixture pairs with 0 violations and reproducing the sharp Chebyshev construction over 96 grid points spanning ~250 decades of TV with high-precision arithmetic. The corollary claims (Theorems 4.3, 4.5, 4.6) are verified by reuse of these experiments plus exponent diagnostics, which is appropriate given they are mathematical consequences of the verified inequalities.

claims.evidence: The numerical audit on Tesla T4 implements the bisection method on f_q'(lambda) and verifies the Lagrangian-dual solution with concrete numbers: for rewards [1,0,0,0] with delta=0.001, lambda*=9.84, mu*=-9.58, and the key property that higher reward variance yields larger lambda* (more conservative updates) is confirmed with specific values across multiple reward distributions.

claims.claim: The QUATRO objective (Theorem 3.3, Eq. 14) combines a query-specific advantage term Aqi = (R(o(i)|q) − μq⋆)/λq⋆ − 1 with a log-ratio stabilizer term that prevents policy overestimation without clipping (Eq. 15).
claims.evidence: The numerical audit confirms the advantage formula A_q^i = (R - mu*)/lambda* - 1 produces correct sign behavior, and the log-ratio stabilizer term changes the loss by -0.097 (13x difference vs no-stabilizer: -0.1046 vs -0.0080), with high-advantage samples showing bounded loss with stabilizer (-8.77) vs unbounded without (-10.45).

JG1310/repro-fixed-budget-is-no-harder-t.paper_title: Fixed Budget is No Harder Than Fixed Confidence in Best-Arm Identification up to Logarithmic Factors

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 establishes that the FC2FB meta-algorithm converts a fixed-confidence algorithm into a fixed-budget algorithm whose error probability decays exponentially in the budget (Section 3, Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Numerical audit checks C3–C6 verify each inequality step of the Theorem 3.2 proof chain to double precision on a parameter grid (A∈{50,300}, Q∈{1,5}, δ0∈{1/e,0.5}, B∈{2e3,1e4,5e4}), confirming the geometric-sum bound, exponent lower bound, and final bound relaxation. claims.claim: When the fixed-confidence sample complexity is T*_delta = A*ln(1/delta) + C, FC2FB yields a fixed-budget sample complexity of O(A*ln(1/delta)*ln(A*ln(1/delta)/Q) + C), matching the fixed-confidence complexity up to logarithmic factors (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Check C7 numerically solves the Theorem 3.2 bound for B_FB(δ) by bisection and computes the FB/FC ratio T_FB(δ)/(A·ln(1/δ)+C), yielding ratios [91.9, 82.1, 79.7, 78.9, 78.8] across δ∈{1e-1,…,1e-6} with log-log slope −0.0114 (≪0.15), confirming the overhead is bounded and sub-polynomial rather than a polynomial gap.

claims.claim: FCW2S (Algorithm 4) converts a weak fixed-confidence algorithm (Definition 4.1) into a strong one (Definition 3.1) via parallel execution and majority voting (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Check C8 verifies the amplification bound (4e·δ0)^{L/4} ≤ δ to double precision for δ0∈{1/(8e), 1/(4e)−ε} and δ∈{1e-2,1e-4}. claims.claim: FC2AT (Algorithm 6) is an anytime variant of the meta-algorithm using a doubling trick that requires no prior knowledge of the budget (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Checks C11–C12 verify the doubling budget floor (T_{I_f} ≥ T/4 for Q∈{1,4}, T∈{2e3,…,2e5}) and the constant-4 identity relating the anytime bound to the Theorem 3.2 bound. ProCreations/repro-a-fully-first-order-l.paper_title: A Fully First-Order Layer for Differentiable Optimization

claims.claim: FFOLayer computes an ε-approximate hypergradient using an active-set Lagrangian oracle that requires no Hessian evaluations, achieving Õ(1) first-order oracle calls per hypergradient estimate (Section 4.2, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: 14 measurements across 7 scales (1/ε from 10 to 1000) all satisfy error ≤2ε, and gradient-oracle calls fit log(1/ε) with slope 7.16 and R²=0.9995, directly demonstrating polylogarithmic scaling. claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that the 'ghost bilevel optimization' reformulation, which treats active constraints as equalities, preserves the accuracy of the hypergradient computed at the original constrained-optimization solution (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Analytic ghost vs. implicit derivatives match to 3.39×10⁻¹¹ at regular points on a 2D strongly-convex QP, with a boundary control at x=0 correctly showing left/right derivative separation where differentiability fails. Nine released-layer executions on box/budget/SOC QPs cross-check with worst relative error 1.35×10⁻⁴ against independent finite differences.

claims.claim: For constrained bilevel optimization, the method achieves an oracle complexity of Õ(δ⁻¹ε⁻³), matching best-known rates for non-smooth non-convex optimization, while extending prior guarantees from linear to general convex constraints (Section 4, complexity analysis).
claims.evidence: 48 native trials on a released general-convex SOC program (4 ε × 4 δ × 3 seeds) all converge with finite gradients; measured log-log exponents (0.225 vs 1/ε, 0.257 vs 1/δ) are below the paper's Õ(δ⁻¹ε⁻³) upper bound, consistent with it being a worst-case bound. Removing strong convexity causes unbounded failure, confirming the theorem's assumptions are necessary.

claims.claim: On synthetic decision-focused-learning QP tasks and 9×9 Sudoku constraint-learning tasks formulated as linear programs, FFOLayer matches the convergence of exact differentiable-optimization solvers CvxpyLayer and qpth while using a substantially faster backward pass (Experiments section, synthetic QP and Sudoku benchmarks).
claims.evidence: At d_y=800 with matched seed and data, FFOLayer and qpth convergence matches (test loss gap 1.03×10⁻⁴), but qpth's backward pass takes 45.76s versus FFOLayer's 51.74s—qpth is 1.13× faster backward, directly contradicting the claim's 'substantially faster backward pass.' FFOLayer is faster in total time (5.25×) only because qpth's forward is much slower.

claims.claim: FFOLayer's PyTorch implementation is objective-agnostic, exposing task-loss influence via a single detached gradient coefficient c := detach(dF/dy*), allowing users to substitute it for CvxpyLayer with minimal code changes (Section on practical implementation).
claims.evidence: The same unmodified released layer runs on 3 convex programs (box QP, nonnegative-budget QP, SOC QP) × 3 upper objectives (linear, quadratic, log-sum-exp), all 9/9 finite with worst relative error 1.35×10⁻⁴ and min cosine 0.9999999966 against independent finite differences, demonstrating objective-agnosticism via the detached gradient coefficient.

claims.claim: FFOLayer outperforms the gradient-unrolling baseline LPGD in the reported experiments while eliminating the cubic-complexity Hessian inversion required by standard implicit differentiation (Experiments section, comparison with LPGD).
claims.evidence: The released LPGD Sudoku command fails immediately (0/1125 batches, 'Unsupported mode lpgd'), and an official-fork dimension sweep shows LPGD is faster at d_y=16,32,64 (ratios 0.28–0.63), contradicting unconditional 'outperforms LPGD.' The Hessian-elimination sub-claim is supported by AST audit (zero Hessian/inverse calls), but the conjunctive claim fails on the LPGD-outperformance component.

ProCreations/repro-a-fully-first-order-l.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, paper-scale experimental evidence verifying claims 1, 2, 3, and 5 through released-code execution, independent finite-difference oracles, and destructive controls, while falsifying claims 4 and 6 with concrete counterexamples: qpth's backward pass is 1.13× faster than FFOLayer's at d_y=800, and the released LPGD mode is non-functional with mixed outperformance results across dimensions.

ProCreations/repro-addressing-instrument.paper_title: Efficient Neural Controlled Differential Equations via Attentive Kernel Smoothing

claims.evidence: Five-seed runs on the authors' own code measure MVC-GP NFE at 37.8±2.7, cubic at 224.2±4.8, and linear at 309.4±20.8, all roughly 40–50% of the claimed 95.17, 595.91, and 633.11 respectively—discrepancies far exceeding the reported standard deviations, though the ordering (GP < cubic < linear) is preserved.

claims.claim: On SpokenArabicDigits, MVC-CDE with GP smoothing requires 95.40 ± 0.89 NFE versus 2237.40 ± 20.02 for linear spline and 1003.80 ± 24.19 for cubic spline, corresponding to total training times of 7.32 ± 0.15s versus 106.15 ± 3.76s and 57.90 ± 1.73s respectively (Table 1, Section C.1).

claims.claim: On UWaveGestureLibrary, MVC-CDE with GP achieves 218.60 ± 10.04 NFE and 12.29 ± 0.27s training time, versus 4340.60 ± 216.07 NFE / 176.19 ± 5.13s for linear spline and 1076.60 ± 33.57 NFE / 53.22 ± 2.25s for cubic spline (Table 1, Section C.1).
claims.evidence: Five-seed UWaveGestureLibrary runs measure MVC-GP NFE at 168.6±3.3 (vs 218.60), cubic at 1011.0±90.3 (vs 1076.60, close), and linear at 2001.0±133.3 (vs 4340.60, far off); the linear-spline NFE and MVC-GP NFE deviate well beyond their standard deviations from the claimed values.

claims.claim: MVC-GP demonstrates a speedup ranging from 4.3× to 14.5× compared to standard spline-based neural CDE methods across the evaluated datasets (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Measured training-time speedups span 4.15× to 17.01× across three datasets, versus the claimed 4.3×–14.5×; while 4 of 6 individual comparisons fall within the claimed band, the measured range is wider at both ends, with the upper bound (17.01×) substantially exceeding 14.5×.

claims.evidence: A standard LTE derivation independently recovers the L_{1/(p+1)} quasi-norm functional for NFE, and a 504-cell closed-form audit using X_h(t)=a·sin(t/h) with 60-digit arithmetic confirms h^{-1} scaling (max ratio error <10^{-59}) and δ^{-1/(p+1)} tolerance dependence across 7 solver orders, 3 tolerances, 3 amplitudes, and 8 scales.

claims.claim: Figure 4 shows that under additive noise, smoothing-based methods (kernel/GP) maintain almost constant NFE, while interpolation-based (linear/cubic spline) methods show a drastic increase in both NFE and error rate (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: A 120-cell noise sweep (3 methods × 5 seeds × 8 noise levels) on the authors' code shows MVC-GP NFE changes by 0.0 with only 2.40 accuracy points lost at noise 0.7, while cubic adds 183.6 NFE and loses 50.38 points and linear adds 2116.8 NFE and loses 39.93 points, directly supporting the claim that smoothing maintains near-constant NFE while splines degrade drastically.
