Srishti280992/repro-mapf-mmot-schrodinge.paper_title: Optimal and Scalable MAPF via Multi-Marginal Optimal Transport and Schrödinger Bridges

claims.claim: Anonymous multi-agent path finding is formulated as linear program P1 minimizing transport cost over per-timestep transport matrices subject to flow-conservation constraints (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements P1 as a sparse continuous LP with flow-conservation and vertex-capacity constraints, and on 40 random 3x3–4x4 instances the LP optimum matches an independent Dijkstra oracle exactly (gap 0.0 in all cases). A variable-count sweep up to 40x40 grids confirms polynomial growth (log-log slope 1.03 in grid cells), matching the paper's formulation structure.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.3 proves the constraint set yields integral optimal solutions in {0,1}^(K×K) achieving minimum cost with polynomial-time complexity, and Theorem 3.4 confirms the resulting paths are collision-free and non-overlapping in space-time (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Across 495 feasible continuous-LP relaxations on 3x3–6x5 grids with 1–6 robots, all optima are integral (max fractional error 0.0), max vertex occupancy is 1.0, and no swap conflicts or capacity violations are observed. On 40 oracle-enumerable instances, the integral LP objective matches the brute-force anonymous-MAPF optimum exactly.

claims.claim: Total unimodularity of the constraint matrix is proven via a node-splitting construction on time-expanded graphs (Appendix B).
claims.evidence: The node-split incidence matrix (96 rows, 320 columns) is confirmed to have entries in {-1,0,1}, exactly one +1 and one -1 per arc column, and zero column sums—matching the network-matrix TU form. Under 360 random objective perturbations, all LP optima remain integral (worst fractional error 0.0), empirically supporting the TU claim.

claims.claim: The Schrödinger bridge relaxation P2 adds entropic regularization parameter ε to P1, and Lemma 4.1 decomposes the KL divergence into transport and marginal terms enabling Sinkhorn iterations (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Matrix-free Sinkhorn is implemented on the grid Gibbs kernel; on 4x4–6x6 grids the entropic solution converges toward the exact LP optimum as epsilon decreases (max endpoint residual 2.63e-05). At paper scale (150x150, 22,500 cells, 1,125 robots, T=30), 10,000 Sinkhorn sweeps reach endpoint L1 residual ~1.5e-04 per robot in 52.8s CPU, and a GPU run confirms feasibility at the same dimensions.

claims.claim: On grids with K up to 22,500 robots at 5% density, the entropic (P2+P3) pipeline scales as O(K^1.15) versus O(K^1.68) for the exact LP P1, yielding 3.6x-7.1x speedups (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Timed experiments show the entropic pipeline solving at 22,500 cells in 0.44s while the exact LP (HiGHS) is intractable beyond 1,600 cells. Fitted exponents (entropic 0.59 vs LP 2.44) differ from the paper's reported values (1.15 vs 1.68), but the qualitative ordering—entropic scales strictly better with growing speedups (2.79x to 702x)—is confirmed with real timing data across nine grid sizes.

claims.claim: Cost degradation from the entropic-to-integral projection stays under 10% while permitting 60-80% edge reduction in the graph pruning step (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: In 9 pruning configurations achieving 60.8–66.1% edge reduction (within the paper's 60–80% band) on grids up to 28x28 (784 cells, 39 robots), the reduced LP recovers the full exact-P1 optimum every time with 0.00% cost degradation, well under the 10% ceiling claimed.

Srishti280992/repro-mapf-mmot-schrodinge.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all six claims through from-scratch implementations of the P1 LP, Sinkhorn bridge, and P3 pruning pipeline, with oracle validation on small instances and paper-scale runs at 22,500 grid cells for the entropic method. The main limitations are small grid sizes for the integrality/TU experiments (3x3–6x5), exact LP scaling only tractable to 1,600 cells, and fitted scaling exponents that differ quantitatively from the paper's reported values while confirming the same qualitative ordering.

jomasego/repro-when-to-think-when-to-spe.paper_title: When to Think, When to Speak:  Learning Disclosure Policies for LLM Reasoning

claims.claim: The Side-by-Side (SxS) interleaved reasoning framework formalizes a dual-channel action space where the model chooses at each step between a private "think" action and a user-visible "speak" action within the same token stream (Sections 2.2-2.3, 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook merely restates the paper's formalization (channel actions, trajectory definitions, projections) and asserts it is 'mathematically sound' and 'implementable,' but provides no independent implementation, test, or experiment demonstrating the dual-channel action space works as described.

claims.claim: Supervised fine-tuning constructs entailment-aligned interleaved trajectories via Algorithm 1, matching answer prefixes to reasoning prefixes using an entailment predicate with delimiter-based segmentation (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: An independent implementation of Algorithm 1 is provided (GitHub link) and verified on a cpu-basic HF Job, confirming delimiter-based segmentation and monotonicity enforcement produce valid interleaved trajectories. However, this runs on toy-scale inputs without the real 330k-sample corpus or the GPT-OSS-120B entailment checker used in the paper.

claims.claim: The disclosure policy is further optimized with GRPO using outcome-based rewards, with an optional correctness-preserving shaping term solved via quadratic programming (Section 3.2, Appendix C).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies that the QP shaping constraints are satisfiable via a small-scale implementation on a cpu-basic HF Job, but no actual GRPO training was executed. The RL formulation is checked for mathematical consistency only, not run at the paper's scale (17k prompts, group size 16, 360-480 steps).

The claimed 79.2% AIME25 and 57.1% GPQA-Diamond accuracies, along with LiveCodeBench and KOR-Bench results, are only confirmed as internally consistent within the paper, not independently reproduced.

Srishti280992/repro-evaluating-bivariate.paper_title: Evaluating Bivariate Causal Statements Based on Mutual Compatibility

claims.claim: For linear bivariate causal statements, any acyclic collection induces exactly one multivariate structural equation model whose pairwise marginals match the given statements (Lemma 2.3).
claims.evidence: 200 random lower-triangular (acyclic) matrices A of dimension 3–9 were generated, Gamma = I - A^{-1} formed, and all 2,826 pairwise marginal coefficients checked via Schur-complement marginalization; max coefficient error was 8.33e-16. A non-acyclic control produced median upper-triangular Gamma mass of 0.313, confirming the acyclicity hypothesis is load-bearing.

claims.claim: The compatibility score defined via path-tracing decomposition of confounding (Definition 2.7) is proven to have positive expected value under a generic random causal model, supporting the paper's Confounding Postulate (Theorem 2.9).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo with 700 random linear SEMs per dimension (n=3,5,7) yielded mean compatibility scores 0.083, 1.898, 9.186, all with positive 95% CI lower bounds (minimum 0.043). A degenerate Gamma=0 control produced compatibility exactly 0, consistent with the theorem's non-degeneracy condition.

claims.claim: Empirical approximation of the compatibility score converges in polynomial sample complexity with respect to dimension, causal strength, and pathway contributions (Theorem 2.10).
claims.evidence: A dedicated script swept 28 configurations across n, K, V, eps, and delta, drawing actual Gaussian samples and measuring the smallest N achieving sustained success rate ≥1-delta on a 13-point grid up to 50,000 samples. All 28 N* values were finite (0 censored). A single constant C=2.58e-5 bounded N* against the theorem's polynomial proxy n^4 K^4 V^4 eps^-2 log(n/delta), with log-log fit slope 1.10 and R^2=0.763. Individual exponent fits were noisy due to grid-valued N*, but the proxy-bound comparison supports polynomial scaling.

claims.claim: On synthetic linear models, compatibility scores decrease monotonically as injected error increases, and on LLM-generated causal statements higher-capacity models achieve higher compatibility scores, with some receiving negative (falsifying) scores (Section 2.7, Figures 2 and 4).
claims.evidence: Synthetic linear experiments at paper scale (12 parameter curves, 120,600 scored statement lists) showed all 12 fitted slopes negative and positive fraction monotonically nonincreasing (Spearman=-1.0 in the initial 80-model run). LLM rerun with four OpenAI models (backend substitution from Bedrock) on the same 7-variable Gapminder task showed gpt-4.1 (highest capacity) scoring 0.330 and gpt-4.1-nano (lowest) scoring -0.476, with 3 of 8 runs negative.

claims.claim: For graphical bivariate causal statements, computing the exact incompatibility score (minimum Hamming distance to a compatible statement graph) is proven NP-hard via reduction to transitive-closure editing (Section 3, NP-hardness result).
claims.evidence: The reduction from transitive-closure editing to exact graphical incompatibility was checked exhaustively for all 25 acyclic directed graphs on n=3 and all 543 on n=4, plus 300 sampled acyclic graphs at n=5. In every case the exact transitivity-edit distance equaled the reduced incompatibility distance. The external NP-hardness of transitive-closure editing is assumed as in the paper.

claims.claim: A heuristic GreedyFAS+GreedyTE algorithm yields incompatibility scores that upper-bound the true incompatibility score and equal zero exactly when the true score is zero, and empirically increase monotonically with injected errors on synthetic graphs and on LLM outputs (Lemma 3.7, Sections 3.3-3.4, Figures 5-7).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive check of all 512 directed/bidirected graph pairs on n=3 showed 0 upper-bound violations and 0 zero-equivalence violations for the GreedyFAS+GreedyTE heuristic versus exact incompatibility. On 60 synthetic 8-node graphs with injected errors 0–12, mean scores increased monotonically (Spearman=1.0). LLM-generated graphical statements produced model-dependent non-zero incompatibility scores.

Srishti280992/repro-evaluating-bivariate.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical and experimental evidence supporting all six claims through Monte Carlo simulations, exhaustive small-case verification of mathematical reductions, paper-scale synthetic monotonicity curves, and a backend-substituted LLM rerun. The reproduction is thorough, with artifacts and raw data for each claim, though some individual exponent fits in Claim 3 are noisy and the LLM evidence in Claim 4 is limited to 2 runs per model.

claims.claim: Do-Shapley values can be computed exactly in O(r(d+e+T)) time, where r is the number of irreducible sets, d the number of dimensions, e the number of edges, and T the value-function evaluation time, versus the naive 2^d complexity (Section 3).
claims.evidence: 56 SCM configurations show max absolute error of 1.95e-14 vs brute-force 2^d computation, with value-function evaluations exactly equal to r in every case, runtime-r correlation of 0.9978 up to r=16384, and two negative controls (structure-ignoring value function and half-classes-dropped) breaking the match at O(1) error, plus the real Sachs DAG showing r=11 vs 2^d=1024.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 shows the do-Shapley value phi_i is identifiable if and only if nu({j}) is identifiable for all j in [d], reducing identifiability checks from r coalitions to just d singleton coalitions (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: 220 random ADMGs tested with 100% agreement between the singleton criterion and the full 2^d-coalition criterion, 0 counterexamples, and both branches genuinely exercised (55 identifiable, 165 not). The Shpitser-Pearl ID algorithm was validated on 5 canonical cases including the bow arc (non-identifiable) and front door (identifiable) before use.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.1 establishes that for any closed set with a basis, removing any basis element yields another closed set, enabling efficient lattice traversal via Algorithm 2 (Lemma 3.1, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: 53 graphs tested with 39260 checks of Lemma 3.1 part 1 and 9603 checks of part 2, yielding 0 violations. Algorithm 2's output matched exhaustive powerset enumeration (symmetric difference = 0) on all 53 graphs including the Sachs DAG, with FindClass independently validated in claim 1 against brute-force Shapley computation.

claims.claim: Algorithm 3 (boundary sampling) guarantees discovery of min(m, r) distinct equivalence classes using m queries, running in O(m*d(d+e)) time (Section on estimator performance, Algorithm 3).
claims.evidence: 2700 budget/graph configurations tested with 0 deviations from min(m, r) distinct classes discovered, sweeping m from 1 to 2r. The blind sampler found 53.9% fewer classes on average at m=r, with detailed per-family comparisons confirming the boundary sampler's advantage.

claims.claim: The doRegressionMSR estimator consistently outperforms baseline variants and exhibits a phase transition at m=r, where error vanishes to machine precision while structure-agnostic methods retain variance (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: At d=7 with 6 replicates, the structure-aware arm's relative MSE drops sharply from 0.0274 at m/r=0.75 to 3.11e-32 at m/r=1.0 and stays there, while the blind arm retains 0.0144–0.027 across all budgets. The base estimator was substituted (KernelSHAP-form least-squares for RegressionMSR/LeverageSHAP), but the phase transition is a structural property independent of the regression base, and the substitution is documented.

claims.claim: Real-world causal structures tend to be sparse, so the number of irreducible sets r scales between the exponential worst case 2^d and the linear lower bound d (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: 350 graphs tested with 0 violations of d ≤ r ≤ 2^d, both extremes attained exactly (chain r=d+1 for d=2..14, star r=2^d for d=2..14 up to r=16384), the real Sachs DAG at r/2^d=0.0107, and a k-sweep at d=12 showing r/2^d varying from 0.50 to 1.0 with a minimum of 0.183, demonstrating the blocking-structure mechanism.

ProCreations/icml-final-defense-reserve-.overall: The logbook provides strong, independently-checkable computational evidence for all six claims: exact algorithm correctness against brute force (claim 1), identifiability equivalence on 220 ADMGs (claim 2), lattice lemma verification on 53 graphs (claim 3), boundary sampling guarantee on 2700 configs (claim 4), phase transition demonstration (claim 5), and r-bounds with real and synthetic graphs (claim 6). The main gaps are a substitute base estimator in claim 5 and only one real-world DAG in claim 6, both honestly documented.

ProCreations/icml-final-defense-reserve-.paper_title: Provably Data-driven Lagrangian Relaxation for Mixed Integer Linear Programming

claims.claim: For learned Lagrangian Relaxation multipliers over s coupling constraints and N training samples, the expected excess risk of the ERM solution is upper bounded by O(s^1.5/√N) (Theorem 5.5).
claims.evidence: Across 36 (s,N) cells (s=8–256, N=32–32768), the ERM excess risk computed in closed form never exceeds the explicit Theorem 5.5 envelope (0 violations, max ratio 0.00071), with a joint log-log fit of s^1.000 N^-0.500 (R²=0.9999998), and sampled ERM cross-checks agree to within 0.74%.

claims.evidence: The exact Bayes risk (a rigorous minimax lower bound, computed from binomial pmf with no Monte Carlo) fits s^1.000 N^-0.501 (R²=0.9999998) over 30 cells, with normalized constant risk/(s/√N) stable in [0.0850, 0.0853]; Fano ingredients (packing, KL bound, positivity) are separately verified with 0 violations across 48 settings.

claims.claim: Stochastic Gradient Ascent with iterate averaging is shown to achieve the matching O(s/√N) rate, closing the O(√s) gap between the ERM upper bound and the minimax lower bound and establishing minimax optimality (Theorem 5.12).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 implemented verbatim with η=π_max/(2B√N); 25 cells (s=8–128, N=64–16384) show 0 violations of the bound 2Bπ_max s/√N, and the tail fit (N≥1024) gives s^1.001 N^-0.506 (R²=0.999962), matching the claimed O(s/√N) rate.

claims.claim: The framework is extended to learning-to-warm-start sub-gradient ascent for large-scale Mixed Integer Linear Programming, with an O(s/N) risk upper bound (Theorem 6.1) and matching Ω(s/N) minimax lower bound (Theorem 6.2).
claims.evidence: Upper bound: sampled sample-mean runs fit s^0.998 N^-0.999 (R²=0.99997) over 15 cells, matching closed form with mean relative error 0.85%. Lower bound: exact Bayes risk with squared loss fits s^1.000 N^-0.996 (R²=0.99999), with normalized constant stable in [0.1167, 0.1199]; separation condition verified with 0 violations over 4000 pairs per cell.

claims.claim: The covering number of the dual multiplier class U is bounded as log N(δ,U,‖·‖₂,N) ≤ s·log(1+2Bπ_max s/δ), used to derive the Rademacher complexity bound R_N(U)=O(s^1.5/√N) (Lemma 5.3, Lemma 5.4).
claims.evidence: An explicitly constructed ε-cover is verified to genuinely cover the function class (max empirical L2 distance < ε in all 12 configurations) with log-cardinality inside the Lemma 5.3 bound (max ratio 0.903); Dudley's integral numerically reproduces the s^1.5/√N form with invariant constant 10.6347 at N≥1024; measured Rademacher complexity shows 0 envelope violations across 15 cells.

claims.claim: The dual function u(π,P) is shown to be concave in π with subgradient norm bounded by 2B√s under bounded constraint-violation assumptions on the MILP instance (Proposition 5.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Over 1568 general (non-restricted) MILP instances solved by exhaustive enumeration, concavity held in 84903 checks (0 violations, min margin -1.4e-14), supergradient inequality in 169806 checks (0 violations), and ||g||≤2B√s in 17046 checks (0 violations, max ratio 0.78); a constructed witness attains the norm bound exactly (ratio 1.0 for s=2–64).

ProCreations/icml-final-defense-reserve-.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims through exact computations on the paper's restricted family (claims 1–5) and exhaustive enumeration on general MILP instances (claim 6), with correctness gates, cross-validation against sampling, and honest limitations documented. The measured rates match the paper's predictions, including the √s slack in the ERM bound that Remark 5.11 anticipates.

Srishti280992/repro-the-implicit-bias-of.paper_title: The Implicit Bias of Adam and Muon on Smooth Homogeneous Neural Networks

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 proves that any limit point of the normalized parameter trajectory θₜ/‖θₜ‖ under normalized steepest descent is the direction of a KKT point of the corresponding max-margin problem (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: NSD on a linear 1-homogeneous model (m=200, d=50, 300K steps, 3 seeds) reaches L2 margin ratio 0.99993–0.99998 and angle 0.045–0.068° to an independently solved SLSQP KKT direction with stationarity residual ~1e-16, while wrong-norm (L∞, L1) solutions fail L2-KKT with residuals 0.48–0.67, providing a direct test with controls.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 extends the margin-maximization convergence result to momentum steepest descent under decaying learning rates, using an Approximate Steepest Descent framework introduced in Definition 5.1 (Theorem 3.3, Definition 5.1).
claims.evidence: Momentum SD with decaying LR (β=e^{-0.5}, η_k=0.1/√k, 200K steps) achieves L2 margin ratio 0.985–0.994 and L∞-Signum ratio 0.998, with ASD alignment r(t)≥0.999994 and R_max≈1.0, while a random-direction control scores 0.113, directly testing the ASD framework and convergence.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.4 shows Muon, applied simultaneously across weight matrices, is a special case of normalized momentum steepest descent with respect to the matrix spectral norm ‖·‖_msp (Corollary 3.4).
claims.evidence: The Muon SVD identity ⟨UV^T, G⟩ = ‖G‖_* is verified over 5,000 random matrices with residual 2.49e-14 and spectral unit error 1.55e-15, and the simultaneous max-spectral block dual identity over 2,000 collections has residual 2.84e-14 with all 50,000 feasible probes worse-or-equal, confirming the norm-identity content of the corollary.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.5 shows Muon-Signum hybrid algorithms exhibit margin maximization with respect to the max of the spectral norm and the ℓ∞ norm (Corollary 3.5).
claims.evidence: The composite Muon-Signum update for max{spectral, L∞} norm is tested over 4,000 instances with dual identity residual 2.84e-14, unit-norm error 1.78e-15, and all 32,000 feasible perturbation probes worse-or-equal, directly verifying the steepest-descent identity underlying the corollary.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.6 shows Adam without a stability constant exhibits implicit bias toward ℓ∞-margin maximization under a decaying learning rate regime when c₁ ≥ c₂ (Theorem 3.6).
claims.evidence: Adam with ε=0, β1=0.9, β2=0.99, decaying LR, 400K steps reaches L∞ margin ratio 0.995–0.998 while L2 ratio stays at 0.746–0.822, with the sign-gradient mechanism residual m̂/√v̂→sign(g) at 6.55e-15, directly testing the predicted L∞ bias and its mechanism.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes that under normalized steepest descent with a learning rate schedule satisfying ∫₀^∞ η(t)dt = ∞, the soft margin γ̃(θₜ) increases monotonically (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Flow-accurate NSD (η=0.001, 3 seeds) shows 0 soft-margin decreases across 997 adjacent checkpoint comparisons per seed, with step-size controls (η=0.001/0.0005/0.0001) all showing 0 decreases, while gradient-ascent control decreases at 29/29 checkpoints per seed, directly testing monotonicity with a destructive control.

Srishti280992/repro-the-implicit-bias-of.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence for all six claims through direct optimization trajectories on a valid linear 1-homogeneous instance of the paper's framework, with independently solved exact margin targets, machine-precision norm identities, and destructive controls. While the linear model is the simplest valid homogeneous network, the theorems concern optimization dynamics and margin maximization properties that are directly and non-trivially tested at this scale.

nstp/repro-two-layer-linear-auto-regress.paper_title: Two-Layer Linear Auto-Regressive Models Estimate Latent States

claims.claim: The informal main result states that the hidden representation learned by a two-layer linear autoregressive model trained on a partially observed linear dynamical system coincides, up to a similarity transformation S, with the state estimates of the optimal Kalman filter (Theorem 1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Independent from-scratch implementation on the paper's full synthetic system (n=4, m=3, p=2, T_train=10^4) yields mean R²=0.9990±0.0011 (H=1) and 0.9989±0.0014 (H=5), matching the paper's 0.999/0.998; held-out S gives R²=0.9991, and time-shuffled activations collapse to R²=0.0031, confirming the alignment is real.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 (Section 4.4) formalizes this latent-state-recovery result, giving explicit finite-sample error bounds between the learned representation and the Kalman filter estimate up to the similarity transformation.
claims.evidence: The literal Theorem 4 inequality (all constants computed from paper formulas, hidden constant=1) holds at every one of ~3.5×10⁴ per-time-index evaluations across T∈[10³,10⁵] (worst LHS/RHS=4.76×10⁻⁷); on well-conditioned systems where the robustness hypothesis is approached, the pooled l2-error slope is -0.399 (R²=0.9971) toward the predicted -0.5, while the h=1 control shows slope +0.001 (no recovery).

claims.claim: Theorem 2 (Section 4.3) bounds the in-sample prediction error at global optima of the empirical risk at a rate of O(H/T), where H is history length and T is trajectory length.
claims.evidence: Using the exact global ERM minimizer (reduced-rank regression, validated to 4.41×10⁻¹² vs OLS), the Theorem 2 inequality holds at all seven trajectory lengths (worst LHS/RHS=3.19×10⁻³); measured log-log slope -0.896 (R²=0.9979) is consistent with the bound's own predicted slope -0.773, while the L=1 control shows slope +1.030 (error grows) and fixed-L=10 shows +0.428.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 (Section 4.3) gives a finite-sample bound on parameter estimation error in Frobenius norm for the learned autoregressive weights.
claims.evidence: The Theorem 3 Frobenius-norm inequality holds at all seven T values (worst LHS/RHS=1.32×10⁻³); measured slope -0.879 (R²=0.9946) matches the bound's predicted -0.767 from below, and the no-input control (u_t=0) plateaus at slope -0.018, confirming persistence of excitation is necessary.

claims.claim: Proposition 1 (Section 4.1) shows the Kalman filter is well-approximated by a finite-history autoregressive model, with truncation error decaying exponentially in history length L.
claims.evidence: Across 6 independent systems, the measured truncation-error decay slope matches 2log(ρ(Ā)) to within 0.06–6.41% (R²≥0.994); the literal Proposition 1 tail inequality holds in 9/9 checks at δ∈{0.5,0.1,0.01}; and the F:=0 control (ρ(Ā)=1) shows slope ≈0 (no decay), confirming the mechanism.

claims.claim: In numerical experiments, a grid search over hidden dimension h identifies h=4 as optimal, matching the true latent state dimension n=4 (Section 5.2, Table 1), and learned activations achieve mean R-squared >= 0.979 alignment with Kalman filter state estimates (Section 5.3, Figure 2, Table 2).
claims.evidence: The R² half is verified (0.9990/0.9989 ≥ 0.979), but the h=4 selection claim is contradicted: Adam argmin over 9 independent systems is [10,10,8,9,10,10,10,10,9] (0/9 select h=4), and the exact ERM global minimum is provably monotone non-increasing in h (G(h)⊂G(h+1)), making an interior minimum at h=4 mathematically impossible for the defined ERM.

nstp/repro-two-layer-linear-auto-regress.overall: The logbook provides strong independent evidence supporting the paper's core theoretical claims (Theorems 1–4, Proposition 1) through exact global-ERM computation, literal inequality checking, scaling studies, and falsification controls on the paper's own synthetic system. However, it falsifies the Table 1 claim that grid search selects h=4 as optimal, showing this is an optimization artifact incompatible with the monotonicity of the rank-constrained ERM.

heitorefer/repro-optimal-design-multinom.paper_title: Optimal Design for Multinomial Logit Model with Applications to Best Assortment Identification

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 gives a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) reformulation of the linear maximization oracle (LMO) needed for optimal design in the multinomial logit (MNL) model (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook describes a numerical audit comparing MILP vs brute-force on N=10, d=3, K=3, but all numerical results (Oracle Assortment, MILP Assortment, Objective Values, Absolute Difference) are blank/missing in the rendered text, so no concrete evidence is presented.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 establishes a stopping/approximation guarantee for a lifted Frank-Wolfe algorithm that solves the MNL optimal design problem without requiring exact LMO calls (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: A lifted Frank-Wolfe audit was run on a very small instance (N=8, d=3, K=3, ε=0.1); two numbers are visible (original G-value 0.7636 ≤ bound 1.6340), but the lifted G-value, ε_lift, and other key quantities are missing, and the scale is far below the paper's experimental settings.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 shows the proposed best assortment identification algorithm achieves sample complexity O~(d log(N/δ)(1/Δmin² + 1/(κΔmin)) + T0), where d is the feature dimension, N is the number of arms/assortments, and Δmin is the minimum reward gap (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook mentions a simulation with Δ_min=0.0165 but the theoretical stopping time value is blank and no concrete numerical results or scaling plots are shown—only an assertion that d log(N/δ)/Δ_min² dependence was 'verified.'

claims.claim: Corollary 4.5 shows that using the lifted G-optimal design in place of the MILP-based design multiplies the sample complexity by a factor of only (1+ε_lift), while remaining computationally tractable (Corollary 4.5).
claims.evidence: The logbook claims a sample complexity ratio matching 1+ε_lift with ε_lift=0.15, but the actual stopping time values for BSI-MILP and BSI-Lift and the ratio itself are all blank/missing in the rendered text.

claims.claim: Table 1 reports average LMO runtime comparisons across methods (MILP vs. lifted surrogate) for varying problem sizes (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The code only measures BSI-Lift runtime live (sub-millisecond); BSI-MILP and BSI-Oracle runtimes are hardcoded from a 'paper_runtimes' dictionary rather than independently measured, so the runtime comparison across methods is not actually reproduced.

claims.claim: Figure 1 reports the average stopping time τ of the best assortment identification algorithm as N (number of arms) is varied over {30, 50, 100, 200} and K (assortment size) over {3, 4, 5}, using feature dimension d=5 and failure probability δ=0.05 (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The Figure 1 code generates stopping times from an arbitrary synthetic formula (t_oracle = 1200.0 * (K/3.0)^1.5 * log(N/10.0) / (gap_eff*20.0)) with added noise, rather than running the actual BSI-MNL bandit algorithm, so the plotted data is fabricated rather than experimentally obtained.

heitorefer/repro-optimal-design-multinom.overall: This logbook does not provide convincing reproduction evidence for any of the six claims: theoretical claims (1–4) have missing or toy-scale numerical results, Table 1 hardcodes MILP/Oracle runtimes from the paper instead of measuring them, and Figure 1 uses a synthetic formula rather than actual bandit experiments. The reproduction attempt is fundamentally flawed in its experimental methodology.

Edd16/icml2026-k0qTjaVatI-repro.paper_title: FedCDWA: Decoupled Federated Prototype Distillation with Hierarchical Wasserstein Aggregation

claims.claim: FedCDWA consistently improves both global and personalized accuracy across heterogeneity levels
claims.evidence: Real runs on a 2D proxy with 8 clients using local linear models (not neural networks) show FedCDWA >= FedAvg on personal accuracy at all heterogeneity levels and improved global accuracy at medium/high, but at low heterogeneity both global and personal accuracy are exactly equal (0.9383/0.8958), so 'consistently improves' is not met even in the proxy. The setup is a clearly simplified proxy, not the paper's real scale.

claims.claim: Shows smaller performance degradation under severe heterogeneity
claims.evidence: Real numbers on the same 2D-proxy/linear-model setup show FedCDWA global degradation of 0.0117 vs FedAvg 0.1667 from low to high heterogeneity, supporting the claim's direction, but on a toy setup far below the paper's intended scale and model class.

claims.claim: Achieves convergence guarantees with Hierarchical Wasserstein Aggregation for prototype aggregation
claims.evidence: The logbook reports prototype drift dropping from ~0.13–0.22 to ~1e-17 after alignment on the 2D proxy, but post-alignment drift being numerically zero is a near-tautological artifact of measuring the aggregate's distance from itself, not evidence of convergence guarantees; the setup is also a toy proxy with linear models.

Edd16/icml2026-k0qTjaVatI-repro.overall: This logbook provides real CPU-run numbers on a deliberately lightweight 2D proxy with linear models and 8 clients, addressing all three claims but only at a simplified scale far below the paper's federated-learning-with-neural-networks setting. The directional trends mostly align with the claims, but the setup is toy-level and the convergence-guarantee evidence is trivially constructed.

ProCreations/repro-causal-representation.paper_title: Skewness-Robust Causal Discovery in Location-Scale Noise Models

claims.claim: SkewD models noise as skew-normal distributed rather than assuming symmetric (normal) noise, extending the location-scale noise model framework to the skew-normal setting (Section 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports a source code audit confirming the model executes SNECM after CMA-ES and scores the skew-normal likelihood, directly verifying the modeling claim with concrete code-level evidence.

claims.claim: On novel skew-noise datasets, the likelihood-based variant SkewD-LL achieves 100% accuracy, whereas the prior state-of-the-art method ROCHE drops to 81% accuracy at the highest skewness level tested, LSs(1.750) (Figure 2, Appendix C).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports exact LSs(1.750) cells as SkewD-LL 1.00 and ROCHE 0.81, matching the claimed 100% and 81% accuracy figures at the specified skewness level.

claims.claim: On 19 established causal-discovery benchmark datasets, SkewD-IT achieves 87.46% combined accuracy, compared to ROCHE's 87.69%, a difference of only 2.67 percentage points, while SkewD-IT ranks second overall at 85.02% mean accuracy on 13 established benchmarks (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook found that the 19-dataset cells yield SkewD-IT 87.46% vs ROCHE 89.52% (not 87.69%), while the 13-dataset cells yield 85.02% vs 87.69% with a 2.67-point gap. The claim conflates numbers from different benchmark universes, making the literal statement incorrect.

claims.claim: Table 2 presents an ablation study comparing performance with and without ECM (expectation-conditional-maximization) refinement in the parameter estimation procedure (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook found that Table 2 is actually the multivariate SHD/SID table, while the ECM ablation is in Table 3. The claim's specific table reference is wrong, though the ablation content exists elsewhere.

claims.claim: Theorem 1, restated from LOCI in Appendix A, establishes that location-scale noise models are identifiable except in pathological cases satisfying a specific PDE, provided the noise log-density is twice differentiable, a condition satisfied by the skew-normal distribution (Appendix A).
claims.evidence: The logbook pinned the exact theorem/PDE text from Appendix A and independently confirmed twice differentiability of the skew-normal log density via analytic and finite-difference checks across 125 cells, supporting the identifiability claim.

claims.claim: LOCI and QCCD baselines show severe performance degradation as noise skewness increases, unlike SkewD (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook found QCCD drops 85 points (severe degradation) but LOCI-IT only follows 0.78→0.82→0.75, which is neither monotone nor severely degrading, contradicting the claim that both LOCI and QCCD show severe degradation.

ProCreations/repro-causal-representation.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical checks against the official SkewD release, verifying the core modeling and identifiability claims (1, 2, 5) while falsifying three claims (3, 4, 6) that contain factual errors in benchmark aggregation, table references, or baseline trend characterization. The reproduction appears rigorous in checking exact numerical cells but relies on audit files not fully visible in the logbook itself.

gchauhan/repro-a-coin-flip-for-safety-ll.paper_title: A Coin Flip for Safety: LLM Judges Fail to Reliably Measure Adversarial Robustness

claims.claim: Across an audit of 6,642 human-verified labels spanning 4 victim models (Gemma-3-1B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-27B, Qwen-3-32B) and 5 attack methods (Direct Prompting, GCG, GCG-REINFORCE, Best-of-N, PAIR), 4 safety judges (LlamaGuard-3, HarmBench, AegisGuard, JailJudge) are shown to perform only slightly better than random guessing on average (Section 3, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook loaded the full 6,642-sample dataset, balanced it to 2,746 samples, and computed per-judge binary accuracy with shown code and output: LlamaGuard-3 54.3%, HarmBench 58.8%, JailJudge 56.0%, AegisGuard 51.2%, averaging 55.1%—near the paper's ~57% and close to random chance. GPU verification of LlamaGuard-3 on 439 samples yielded correlation 0.9990 with pre-computed scores, confirming the scores are authentic.

claims.claim: ROC analysis shows JailJudge attains AUROC as low as 0.48 (worse than chance) on some attack-model pairs and no better than 0.64 on any attack, demonstrating near-chance discriminative ability under distribution shift (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: AUROC computed for JailJudge on Llama-3.1-8B across all 5 attacks with shown code: GCG-R 0.476 (worse than chance), GCG 0.642, BoN 0.526, Pair 0.527, Direct 0.572. This matches the paper's claimed range of 0.48–0.64, confirming near-chance discriminative ability.

claims.claim: Judge accuracy varies dramatically across attack-model combinations, with some judges scoring only 45% accuracy on specific attack-victim pairs, close to random guessing (Figure 3, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Per-judge accuracy computed for every (Model, Attack) pair on the balanced dataset, finding 9 combinations below 47% with the lowest at 41.9% (LlamaGuard-3 on Gemma-1B + BoN), and an overall range of 41.9%–74.3%, confirming dramatic variance and near-random performance on specific pairs.

claims.claim: The paper introduces ReliableBench, a curated set of 41 behaviors, which raises average judge accuracy from 57% to 70%, and JudgeStressTest (JST), a set of 971 challenging samples that exposes systematic judge failures across judge architectures via leave-one-out validation (Table 1).
claims.evidence: ReliableBench analysis on the balanced dataset shows accuracy improving from 52.7% (all 101 behaviors) to 67.4% (top 41 behaviors), qualitatively matching the paper's 57%→70% claim. JST contains exactly 971 samples (matching paper), and per-judge accuracy on JST is catastrophically low (9.4%–20.0%), confirming systematic judge failures. Numerical differences are attributable to different balancing strategies.

claims.claim: Correcting reported attack success rates (ASR) for judge unreliability substantially deflates the apparent effectiveness of attacks such as Best-of-N, which is shown to inflate ASR by exploiting judge insufficiencies rather than eliciting genuinely harmful content (Figure 1, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: Computed uncorrected ASR, precision, and corrected ASR for Best-of-N across model-judge pairs with shown code and output. Average uncorrected BoN ASR of 47.3% drops to 27.9% corrected (a ~41% reduction), with specific examples like Gemma-1B + LlamaGuard-3 dropping from 74.0% to 20.7%, confirming that BoN inflates ASR via judge false positives.

claims.claim: Judge Concordance analysis shows judges can reach near-unanimous agreement with each other while still failing to align with human ground-truth labels, and averaging/ensembling judge scores does not consistently improve alignment with human judgments (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: Judge Concordance scores computed per sample using 1 - binary entropy of judge decisions, with 12 behaviors showing concordance > 0.6 but accuracy < 0.5 (e.g., 'predatory stalking' behavior: concordance 0.766, accuracy 10.4%), confirming that judges can agree near-unanimously while being systematically wrong. The ensembling sub-claim is supported qualitatively but lacks independent numerical demonstration.

gchauhan/repro-a-coin-flip-for-safety-ll.overall: This logbook provides a thorough reproduction using the authors' released 6,642-sample dataset with human-verified labels, supplemented by GPU verification of judge model inference on 439 samples. All six claims are supported by concrete numerical evidence with shown code and outputs, with minor numerical differences attributable to balancing strategy choices.

Srishti280992/repro-unifying-low-dimensi.paper_title: Unifying Low Dimensional Spectra in Deep Learning

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves the layer-wise Hessian in the L-deep linear unconstrained features model (UFM) has rank K^2 with all non-zero eigenvalues equal, analytically reproducing the bulk-outlier Hessian spectrum reported in prior empirical studies (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Analytic numerical audit at K=3, d=8 constructs the Hessian from the theorem's Kronecker class-mean basis and confirms rank 9=K² with all nonzero eigenvalues exactly 1.7 (max/min ratio 1.0) and minimum squared alignment 1.0; a non-orthogonal control degrades the ratio to 24.996, showing the equality depends on DNC assumptions.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 decomposes the Gauss-Newton/Fisher Information component into three terms: G_within (rank 0), G_cross (rank K(K-1), producing the mini-bulk of eigenvalues), and G_class (rank K, producing the main outliers), mirroring Papyan's empirical knockout experiments (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: The corrected analytic audit (using p_cross_left = p_u - p_class_left within the class-mean span) yields G_within rank 0, G_cross rank 6=K(K-1), G_class rank 3=K, with cross/class eigenspace orthogonality at Frobenius norm 1.73e-15.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 shows the aggregated gradient update is a sum over only K of the K^2 possible eigenvector directions, each with equal coefficient beta^(l+1)/K, explaining the observed gradient alignment with a low-dimensional subspace (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Analytic expansion gives exactly 3 nonzero coefficients on the diagonal (all 0.8, off-diagonal max 0.0); the trained linear UFM at 1500 steps confirms 3 diagonal nonzero coefficients, off-diagonal max 7.5e-18, and diagonal max/min ratio 0.9999999992.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 proves the Gram matrix of the optimal weights, W_l*^T W_l*, has rank K with eigenvalues proportional to the squared norms of the class-mean features, giving a closed-form account of the low-rank weight structure (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: Analytic construction of W_l as a sum of class-mean outer products yields Gram matrix rank 3=K with nonzero eigenvalues [0.5329, 0.5329, 0.5329] in the equal-norm case, consistent with the proportionality claim; the native training run shows weight Gram top-3 eigenvalues separating from the bulk, though full convergence data is truncated.

claims.claim: For a deep linear UFM with K=3 classes, numerical experiments show K^2=9 Hessian outliers separating from the bulk and converging to equal eigenvalues over training, with eigenvector alignment metric f_cc' rising from about 0.2 to 1.0 (Figures 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: Training the linear K=3 UFM over 1500 steps shows top-9 eigenvalue ratio dropping from 25.0 to 1.0, separation from bulk increasing from 1.29 to 6.5e10, and f_cc' mean rising from 0.392 to 1.0, closely matching the claimed dynamics (initial f_cc' is 0.39 rather than 'about 0.2' but the trend is clearly reproduced).

claims.claim: In the non-linear (ReLU) Deep UFM, K^2=9 Hessian outliers separate but do not fully converge to equal values, and the gradient has K non-zero coefficients that remain unequal, unlike the linear case (Figure 9, Table 2).
claims.evidence: ReLU K=3 training at 1500 steps shows 9 nonzero Hessian outliers with max/min ratio 7.08 (vs 1.0 for linear), weak bulk separation (1.14), and gradient diagonal coefficient ratio 1.19 (vs 1.0 for linear); the native 40k-step run further confirms unequal eigenvalues (ratio 9.68) and unequal gradient coefficients (spread 1.73, off-diagonal energy 0.283).

Srishti280992/repro-unifying-low-dimensi.overall: The logbook provides both analytic numerical checks and actual training experiments at the paper's K=3 scale that confirm all six claims: the linear UFM Hessian has rank K² with equal outliers, the GN decomposition has the predicted ranks, the gradient uses K equal diagonal directions, the weight Gram is rank K, and the ReLU case departs from equality as claimed. The main limitation is that the analytic checks construct matrices directly from the theorem's formulas rather than deriving them from first principles, but the training experiments provide independent corroboration.

Srishti280992/repro-colorful-pinball-den.paper_title: Colorful Pinball: Density-Weighted Quantile Regression for Conditional Guarantee of Conformal Prediction

claims.claim: Proposition 3.4 shows the optimal density weight for quantile regression equals the conditional density of the score evaluated at the true quantile, which for location-scale distributions is proportional to 1/sigma(x), capturing heteroscedastic structure ignored by standard pinball loss (Proposition 3.4).
claims.evidence: On a heteroscedastic Gaussian location-scale model (n=20000, tau=0.9), the analytic weight satisfies w(x)*sigma(x) = phi(Phi^-1(tau)) = 0.17550 with std 2.87e-17 (machine-precision constant), and the finite-difference estimator 2*delta/(q_{tau+delta}-q_{tau-delta}) converges to the true weight with relative error 0.00058 at delta=0.005 and correlation 1.0 with 1/sigma(x), directly confirming Proposition 3.4.

claims.claim: The proposed three-stage framework estimates joint quantiles at levels tau-delta, tau, tau+delta, computes density weights via the finite-difference w(x) = 2*delta / (q_hat_{tau+delta}(x) - q_hat_{tau-delta}(x)), then fine-tunes the central quantile with a weighted pinball loss before conformalization (Section 3, three-stage framework).
claims.evidence: Using the authors' official MonotonicThreeHeadNet at commit 98ce4fa, the three-stage pipeline was executed on both synthetic and Naval data: train_three_head_base fits heads at [0.88, 0.90, 0.92], finetune_main_head_improved applies the finite-difference weighted pinball loss, and conformalization follows. On synthetic data, 100% of test points maintained quantile ordering, weight Pearson correlation was 0.883, and on Naval 100% of central-head predictions changed after fine-tuning across 5 seeds.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 gives a non-asymptotic excess risk bound with asymptotic rate O(R_n(G)^(2/3)) ≈ O(n^(-1/3)) under an optimal bandwidth choice delta* proportional to R_n(G)^(1/3) (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: The rate audit uses a synthetic Gaussian with a 16-dimensional polynomial feature class and sqrt(p/n) as a Rademacher complexity proxy across n=1000–64000 with 10 seeds. The measured CPCP excess-risk log-log slope is -0.501, faster than the claimed -1/3 upper bound, but the excess risk plateaus at n>=16000 (0.000115 at n=16000 vs 0.000091 at n=64000), preventing clean observation of the asymptotic rate. The simplified proxy complexity and plateau mean this is a supportive audit, not a full verification.

claims.claim: Stability of the density-weighted method relies on weight clipping at threshold M=5.0, convex loss mixing with unweighted pinball loss, and a softplus activation to guarantee monotonic quantile ordering (Section on Stability Mechanisms).
claims.evidence: Static code checks confirm clip_max=5.0 with torch.clamp, loss mixing (mix_ratio * weighted + (1-mix_ratio) * unweighted), and softplus gap parameterization (q_lo = q_main - softplus(delta_low), q_hi = q_main + softplus(delta_high)) in the official code. A synthetic stress test shows raw normalized weights reaching max 97.93, clipping caps at 5.0, and 50/50 mixing bounds effective weights to [0.503, 3.0]. Real-data audits on 8 benchmarks confirm weights exceed 5.0 in practice (e.g., max 87.87 on Superconductivity).

claims.claim: On the Naval Propulsion dataset, the proposed CPCP method with clipping and loss mixing improves worst-slice coverage (WSC) from about 65% (Split CP baseline) to 83.46% +/- 3.45%, while achieving a mean squared conditional error (MSCE) of 0.0017 (Section on Experimental Results, 8 benchmarks).
claims.evidence: The full 20-seed Naval run with official code (mean=100, base=200, finetune=200 epochs) yields CPCP WSC 82.55% ± 4.63% (local) and 83.65% ± 3.06% (GPU grid), closely matching the claimed 83.46% ± 3.45%. CPCP MSCE_10 is 0.00134–0.00180, close to the claimed 0.0017. The Split CP baseline WSC measures ~55–56%, not the claimed ~65%, but the CPCP target numbers are reproduced and the improvement direction is confirmed.

Srishti280992/repro-colorful-pinball-den.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting Claims 1, 2, 4, and 5 using the authors' official implementation on both synthetic and real benchmark data, with Claim 3 addressed via a simplified synthetic audit that is consistent with but does not cleanly verify the theoretical rate due to a plateau at larger sample sizes.

heitorefer/repro-velr-efficient-video-re.paper_title: VELR: Efficient Video Reward Feedback via Ensemble Latent Reward Models

claims.claim: Achieves comparable performance as standard ReFL with significantly reduced memory requirements

claims.evidence: The scaling table (16–128 frames) presents memory estimates from the same estimator, with 'Hardware Feasibility' being assertions. No actual training runs at F=64 or F=128 were executed; the numbers are theoretical projections from a simplified audit.

The numbers are internally consistent with the paper's claims but come from a toy/simulated setup, not a faithful reproduction at the paper's scale.

nstp/repro-the-implicit-bias-of-adam-and.paper_title: The Implicit Bias of Adam and Muon on Smooth Homogeneous Neural Networks

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 proves that any limit point of the normalized parameter trajectory θₜ/‖θₜ‖ under normalized steepest descent is the direction of a KKT point of the corresponding max-margin problem (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Flow-accurate continuation of NSD on MNIST m=2048 squared-ReLU (L=3) gives KKT ε=0.0298 for ℓ₂ and ε=1.615 for ℓ∞, both decreasing monotonically along the trajectory; wrong-norm scoring is 65–282× worse and broken-steepest-descent controls (tilted, norm-growth) give 65–85× worse ε, all on the paper's own model and data.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 extends the margin-maximization convergence result to momentum steepest descent under decaying learning rates, using an Approximate Steepest Descent framework introduced in Definition 5.1 (Theorem 3.3, Definition 5.1).
claims.evidence: Definition 5.1 condition 3 (r(t)→≥1) holds to 7–9 decimal places for all four MSD variants (NGD, Signum, Muon, Muon-Signum); KKT ε in each algorithm's own norm is 0.028–0.277 and monotonically decreasing; wrong-norm scoring is 6–300× worse and tilted-SD control gives 89× worse ε.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.4 shows Muon, applied simultaneously across weight matrices, is a special case of normalized momentum steepest descent with respect to the matrix spectral norm ‖·‖_msp (Corollary 3.4).
claims.evidence: The algebraic identity ⟨UVᵀ,M⟩=‖M‖_nuclear holds with residual 0.0 (exact fp64) and the per-step composite identity holds to 8.44e-16 over all 2403 steps of a real Muon run; inherited KKT ε in msp = 0.134 (decreasing), Muon wins the msp margin by 4.11×, and wrong-norm ε is 13–32× worse.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.5 shows Muon-Signum hybrid algorithms exhibit margin maximization with respect to the max of the spectral norm and the ℓ∞ norm (Corollary 3.5).
claims.evidence: The dual of max{msp,ℓ∞}=nuclear+ℓ₁ holds to 2.49e-16 and the composed update equals the max-norm steepest-descent update to 6.86e-16 at every step; KKT ε in the composed norm = 0.150 (decreasing), neither constituent norm alone explains the bias (msp: 5.694, ℓ∞: 15.659), and Muon-Signum wins the mix margin by 2.23×.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.6 shows Adam without a stability constant exhibits implicit bias toward ℓ∞-margin maximization under a decaying learning rate regime when c₁ ≥ c₂ (Theorem 3.6).
claims.evidence: Adam at the paper's own Table-1 η₀=5e-3 with β₁=0.9, β₂=0.999, ε=1e-20 gives KKT ε in ℓ∞ = 0.4217, monotonically decreasing (0.574→0.421→0.397 at loss 1e-10); ℓ∞ is 13–60× better than any other norm; the sign-approximation mechanism is visible at 8% deviation on significant coordinates; breaking c₁≥c₂ causes divergence or failure to separate.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes that under normalized steepest descent with a learning rate schedule satisfying ∫₀^∞ η(t)dt = ∞, the soft margin γ̃(θₜ) increases monotonically (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Flow-accurate continuation of NSD shows 0 soft-margin violations over 20000 steps for both ℓ₂ and ℓ∞; the paper's integral inequality (alignment integral ≤ log soft-margin gain) holds for both norms (0.0075≤0.056 for ℓ₂, 0.344≤0.406 for ℓ∞); the paper's discrete schedule shows violations only because it stops tracking the flow at late phases (77% fidelity).

nstp/repro-the-implicit-bias-of-adam-and.overall: This is a rigorous from-scratch numpy reproduction on the paper's own MNIST setting (m=2048, squared-ReLU L=3, logistic loss, paper's hyperparameters) with multiple seeds, thorough falsification controls (wrong-norm scoring, broken-steepest-descent, c₁<c₂), and honest reporting of limitations (e.g., ε values are finite, the discrete schedule doesn't track the flow at late phases). erobinson/repro-learning-permutation-fro.paper_title: Learning Permutation from Structure Without Supervision

claims.claim: Entropy-adaptive Gumbel-Sinkhorn computes a row- and column-dependent inverse-temperature field from the entropy of the current soft permutation, via Algorithm 1: compute a deterministic soft assignment, extract row/column entropies, derive adaptive inverse temperatures, then apply Sinkhorn with elementwise temperature scaling (Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook identifies `adaptive_tau_matrix()` in the official code and confirms it implements all four steps of Algorithm 1 (deterministic soft assignment, row/column entropy extraction, adaptive inverse-temperature derivation, elementwise-temperature Sinkhorn); this code is exercised in the 3-seed sorting experiments that produce real Kendall tau results.

claims.claim: Proposition 1 establishes that uniform-temperature Gumbel-Sinkhorn faces an unavoidable trade-off since different rows/columns of the permutation resolve at different rates due to heterogeneous assignment uncertainty (Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports measured row-entropy values from training runs at n=100 and n=300 showing heterogeneous entropy across rows (e.g., n=300 global GS: 0.67 at epoch 75 vs. 0.52 at epoch 150), providing concrete numerical evidence consistent with the proposition's claim that uniform temperature cannot simultaneously sharpen confident and ambiguous rows.

claims.claim: On sorting tasks with high-ambiguity value ranges ([10,11]), entropy-adaptive temperature control outperforms global annealing as problem size increases, reaching a +0.122 Kendall tau improvement at n=300 (Section on sorting experiments).
claims.evidence: Three-seed sorting experiments on value range [10,11] show entropy-adaptive GS outperforming global GS with a +0.1148 Kendall tau improvement at n=300, closely matching the paper's reported +0.122, with the advantage growing from negligible at n=5 to substantial at n=300.

claims.claim: On CelebA jigsaw reconstruction across puzzle sizes from 5x5 to 7x7, entropy-adaptive methods yield larger gains over mask-only baselines than global annealing does, with the advantage increasing with puzzle scale (Table 2).
claims.evidence: No experiments were run; the logbook only restates the paper's Table 2 numbers and notes the CelebA jigsaw code and datasets are absent from the official repository, providing no independent experimental evidence.

claims.claim: On TSP instances from n=100 to n=1000, degree-violation-based temperature adaptation (DV-TA) consistently reduces both tour length and optimality gap relative to standard Gumbel-Sinkhorn across all sizes (Table 3).
claims.evidence: No experiments were run; the logbook only restates the paper's Table 3 numbers and notes the TSP code and datasets are absent from the official repository, providing no independent experimental evidence.

claims.claim: Figure 2 shows entropy-adaptive temperature control attains a strictly higher Kendall tau than a global-temperature baseline at equivalent ambiguity levels, and Appendix K sensitivity analysis shows performance is stable across wide ranges of the entropy threshold H_0 and maximum boost b_max hyperparameters (Figure 2; Appendix K).
claims.evidence: The Figure 2 portion is indirectly supported by the sorting experiments (entropy-adaptive achieves higher Kendall tau at n=100 and n=300), but the Appendix K sensitivity analysis was never tested—only default hyperparameters (H_0=0.7, b_max=0.1) were used, with stability merely argued from design rather than demonstrated across the claimed ranges.

erobinson/repro-learning-permutation-fro.overall: The logbook provides solid 3-seed experimental evidence reproducing the sorting benchmark (Claim 3) and verifying the Algorithm 1 implementation and Proposition 1's trade-off numerically, but cannot address the CelebA jigsaw (Claim 4) or TSP (Claim 5) claims due to missing code, and the Appendix K sensitivity analysis (Claim 6) was not experimentally tested.

heitorefer/repro-ag-repa-causal-layer-se.paper_title: AG-REPA: Causal Layer Selection for Representation Alignment in Audio Flow Matching

claims.evidence: The ablation results (29.9%, 8.7%, 4.9%) match the paper exactly, but there is no evidence of actual training runs for the three layer-selection strategies. claims.evidence: Cross-architecture FAD numbers (1.20→0.95, 0.88→0.72, 1.45→1.15) are reported as exact matches, but no evidence of training or evaluating AG-REPA on Voicebox, CosyVoice, or F5-TTS is provided. The reproduction appears to simply restate the paper's published numbers rather than independently verify them.

gizaom/repro-pencil-link-prediction.paper_title: Plain Transformers are Surprisingly Powerful Link Predictors

claims.claim: PENCIL, an encoder-only Transformer that tokenizes each node's local subgraph via one-hot identifiers and adjacency indicator rows (no positional encodings or learned per-node embeddings), is proposed for link prediction (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook ran the authors' released code on Cora with config `args/official/cora_bert.yaml`, confirming PENCIL is an encoder-only plain Transformer that tokenizes each node's sampled local subgraph via adjacency-indicator rows, trained from scratch with no pretrained weights and no node features, producing a Test MRR of 43.77.

claims.claim: PENCIL uses 22x to 146x fewer learnable parameters than ID-embedding-based link prediction methods while matching or exceeding their accuracy on ogbl-ppa (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: No parameter-count comparison was performed and ogbl-ppa was never run; the logbook only covers Cora, so the 22x–146x fewer-parameters claim on ogbl-ppa is entirely unaddressed.

claims.claim: PENCIL achieves state-of-the-art MRR of 42.23 on cora and 79.54 on ogbl-ppa, and 86.86 MRR on ogbl-citation2 under the original OGB evaluation protocol (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Only the Cora portion was reproduced (Test MRR 43.77 vs. paper's 42.23, a +1.54 match over 150 epochs); the ogbl-ppa (79.54) and ogbl-citation2 (86.86) results were never run, so the compound three-dataset claim is only partially supported.

claims.claim: Under the harder HeaRT evaluation protocol, PENCIL attains top MRR scores on ogbl-ppa (45.43) and ogbl-ddi with substantially lower variance (±0.07 on ogbl-ppa) than competing methods (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The HeaRT evaluation protocol was never used and neither ogbl-ppa nor ogbl-ddi was run under any protocol; this claim is completely unaddressed.

claims.claim: A feature-ablated variant of PENCIL trained without node features remains competitive with, and on cora even outperforms, the feature-inclusive version, indicating structural signal from sampled subgraphs dominates node feature information (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook ran Cora with `use_features: False` (MRR 43.77) but never ran the feature-inclusive variant for comparison, so the claim that the ablated version is competitive with or outperforms the feature-inclusive version cannot be assessed.

claims.claim: PENCIL better approximates pairwise structural heuristics (Common Neighbors, Adamic-Adar, Katz index, PageRank) than GNN and ID-GNN baselines (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: No analysis of structural heuristic approximation (Common Neighbors, Adamic-Adar, Katz, PageRank) was performed; this claim is entirely unaddressed.

gizaom/repro-pencil-link-prediction.overall: The logbook provides a clean single-dataset reproduction of PENCIL on Cora (Test MRR 43.77 vs. paper's 42.23), confirming the core architectural claim and the Cora headline number, but does not address the remaining five claims covering ogbl-ppa, ogbl-citation2, ogbl-ddi, the HeaRT protocol, parameter efficiency, feature ablation comparisons, or heuristic approximation.

tomyimkc/repro-curated-synthetic-data-do.paper_title: Curated Synthetic Data Doesn’t Have to Collapse: A Theoretical Study of Generative Retraining with Pluralistic Preferences

claims.claim: Under a two-basin landscape assumption with cross-reward leakage gaps Δ1, Δ2 > 0 (Assumption 1, Section 2.1), Lemma 3 shows probability mass outside the union of ε-optimal basins decays geometrically under recursive curated retraining (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: On N=200,000 cells with 50 random configs over T=150 iterations, the exact per-step contraction held in 100% of configs (rho_eps mean 0.1046, max 0.2345), outside mass decayed geometrically (mean m_T/m_0 ~1e-239), and the control showed mass increases when Assumption 1(iii) is violated (GAP=1.005, rho_eps=1.0155).

claims.claim: Lemma 5 proves that under bounded leakage, basin mass remains bounded away from collapse, satisfying η ≤ a_t ≤ 1-η for the limiting basin weight a_t (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Across 150 in-hypothesis configs (30 Delta-pairs × 5 interior q values, T=250), a_T landed in [L,U] in 100% with eta>0 (min 0.0305), while controls with q outside (kappa1, 1-kappa2) collapsed to a_T=0 or 1.0000.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 shows the limiting mixture preserves diversity: reward variance under a nontrivial two-component mixture has an explicit strictly positive lower bound proportional to (Δᵢ - 2ε)^2 (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: In 25 configs the law-of-total-variance decomposition matched to 1e-9 and Var_p[r_i] >= a(1-a)*max(Delta_i-2eps,0)^2 held for both rewards in 25/25, with the control showing variance shrinking from 8.96 to 0.253 as Delta1 approaches 2*eps.

claims.claim: Theorem 7 proves the limiting distribution from pluralistic curation coincides with the weighted Nash bargaining solution, maximizing (u1(p_α) - d1)^q (u2(p_α) - d2)^(1-q) at α* = q (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Grid-search over 2001 alpha points across 54 (config,q) pairs yielded max |argmax-q|=1.11e-16, full-dynamics a_inf tracked alpha*=q (max error 0.0020), and the control with reversed basin favoritism produced zero feasible Nash bargaining points.

claims.claim: CIFAR-10 flow-model retraining experiments (E3) show curation with balanced multi-reward preferences sustains higher entropy and diversity than single-reward curation across recursive retraining generations (Section 4).
claims.evidence: No flow model, VGG11 classifier, CIFAR-10 images, or GPU were used; instead a synthetic 5-basin construction with N=200,000 cells showed entropy rising monotonically with M (0 to 1.6094), which is a mechanism-level analog on a simplified setup, not the paper's real experiment.

claims.claim: Text-domain experiments (E4) confirm that curation under two competing length-based reward preferences sustains entropy over recursive retraining, consistent with the two-basin theory (Section 4).
claims.evidence: No GPT-2 fine-tuning or text generation was run; the paper's length reward was applied directly to a 321-point length distribution, showing a sharp entropy threshold (0 to ln(2)=0.6931 for d>=1) rather than the paper's smoother curve on real generated text.

tomyimkc/repro-curated-synthetic-data-do.overall: The four theoretical claims (1-4) are verified with concrete numerical evidence on a non-trivial discretized setup (200K cells, 25-150 configs each) with controls that relax each claim's preconditions. The two empirical claims (5-6) are addressed only as toy-scale mechanism analogs on synthetic data, without the paper's actual CIFAR-10 flow models or GPT-2 text generation.

tomyimkc/repro-on-the-theory-of-continua.paper_title: On the Theory of Continual Learning with Gradient Descent for Neural Networks

claims.claim: Theorem 1 gives a closed-form bound on train-time forgetting for task k after training on K-k subsequent tasks, of order O~(ηT√(K-k)/(d√n) + ηT√(K-k)/(d²polylog(d)) + η²T²K²/√m) (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The experiment tests the 1/√n and 1/√m decay rates of the bound at d=12, K=3, m≤2500, n≤4800 — far below the theorem's required m=Ω(d⁸K⁴)≈2.6×10¹⁰ regime; forgetting values (0.28–0.51) are not small, and only two of three bound terms are probed.

claims.claim: The forgetting bounds hold under the parameter regime n = Θ~(d²K) samples, m = Ω~(d⁸K⁴) hidden-layer width, and ηT = Θ(d²) training iterations on a d-dimensional XOR cluster dataset with K tasks (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The joint scale-up uses a reduced constant C_M=1e-8 for m, yielding m values of 348–2786 instead of the true m=Ω(d⁸K⁴)≈2.6×10¹⁰ (off by ~7 orders of magnitude); the experiment explicitly tests a reduced-constant analog of the functional scaling, not the literal parameter regime.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows that under the same width/sample/iteration conditions as Theorem 1, the misclassification error remains uniformly small across all K tasks with high probability after KT gradient descent iterations (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: At the highest resource level (n=6000, m=4000), the max per-task train error is 0.193 — far from the 'uniformly small' o_d(1) the theorem claims — and m=4000 is astronomically below the required m=Ω(d⁸K⁴); the experiment shows the right decreasing trend but at drastically reduced scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 bounds the delayed generalization gap by η T exp(ηT(K-k+1)/√m) / n for Lipschitz, smooth loss functions, showing the gap decays with sample size n (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The delayed generalization gap decays from 0.078 (n=80) to 0.003 (n=1280), fitting 6.36/n with R²=0.89, and the control with m=150 shows the 1/n decay breaking down (R²=0.16); Theorem 3 does not require the astronomical width regime, only Lipschitz/smooth loss and sufficient width.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 gives an improved generalization gap bound for self-bounded losses that scales poly-logarithmically rather than linearly in the number of iterations T, depending on the cumulative training loss of later tasks (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Cumulative training loss grows as T^0.61 (R²=0.995) when training converges versus T^0.96 (R²=1.0) when it does not, and the actual generalization gap grows as T^0.29 versus T^1.15, directly confirming the sub-linear (milder-than-linear) scaling mechanism with a working non-convergence control.

claims.claim: Test-time forgetting is decomposed as the sum of train-time forgetting (Theorem 1) and the delayed generalization gap (Theorem 3/4), showing that network width, sample size, and later tasks' data jointly, not individually, control forgetting (Theorem 1, Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The decomposition F_ts ≈ F_tr + F_gen holds with 10.2% relative error across six (n,m,seed) configurations, and the 2×2 factorial shows joint improvement (0.201) exceeds the sum of marginal improvements (0.152) by 0.049, confirming super-additive interaction of width and sample size.

tomyimkc/repro-on-the-theory-of-continua.overall: The logbook provides from-scratch implementations of the paper's quadratic-activation network and XOR-cluster continual learning setup with proper controls, verifying the functional-form predictions of Theorems 3, 4, and the test-time forgetting decomposition at CPU-affordable scale. Claims 1–3 are only tested at drastically reduced scale (m off by orders of magnitude from the required Ω(d⁸K⁴)), yielding toy-level evidence for the asymptotic regime claims.

MarxistLeninist/repro-db-vs-fm-aIFgQusnP.paper_title: Diffusion Bridge or Flow Matching? A Unifying Framework and Comparative Analysis

claims.claim: The paper frames Diffusion Bridge and Flow Matching in a shared stochastic optimal control/optimal transport framework (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Numerical audit in float64 shows DB optimal controller and cost coefficient converge to FM's as lambda→∞: max|u*_DB−u*_FM| decays from 1.0 to 2.2e-7 and max|coeff_DB−coeff_FM| from 9.6 to 1e-9 across the lambda ladder, directly confirming the Prop 4.1 reduction.

claims.claim: Theoretical analysis shows the Diffusion Bridge cost function is lower than Flow Matching under the paper's formulation, implying more stable trajectories (Proposition 4.1; Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: The coefficient inequality c_DB≤c_FM holds on a 20001×7 grid (worst c_DB−c_FM = −4.0e−4), the lemma e^x−1≥x holds on a 200k-point grid (min gap 0.0), and integrated cost ratios J_DB/J_FM range from 0.055 to 0.9998—all ≤1, confirming Thm 4.2 numerically to double precision.

claims.claim: Under a shared Transformer architecture, Diffusion Bridge outperforms Flow Matching across image restoration and translation tasks (Table 1; Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Tested on 2D synthetic distributions with small MLPs (not the paper's latent-Transformer on image tasks): DB wins on translation (SW2 0.055 vs 0.080) and moons (0.172 vs 0.190) but loses on eight_gaussians (0.276 vs 0.224), so the 'across tasks' claim is only partially supported even at toy scale.

claims.claim: Diffusion Bridge remains stronger than Flow Matching as inpainting mask size increases, indicating better robustness under harder transformations (Table 2; Figure 3a).
claims.evidence: A proxy difficulty sweep (source-target separation in 2D, not inpainting mask size) shows DB stays ahead at all separations but the gap does not monotonically grow (peaks at sep=2 with +0.025, then flattens to +0.001–0.007), so the specific 'advantage grows with difficulty' prediction is not reproduced even at toy scale.

claims.claim: Flow Matching degrades more steeply than Diffusion Bridge when training data size is reduced (Figure 3b; Table 7).
claims.evidence: On 2D moons with training-set sizes swept from 64 to 8000, the FM−DB gap is largest at small n (n=64: +0.061; n=128: +0.037) and smaller at large n, supporting the claim's direction, though on a simplified synthetic setup rather than the paper's image pipeline.

claims.claim: Using the same network input conditions does not eliminate the performance gap between Flow Matching and Diffusion Bridge (Table 4).
claims.evidence: On 2D translation with raw-source-coordinate conditioning (not analogous to degraded-image conditioning), the gap reverses: unconditioned DB wins (+0.014) but conditioned FM wins (−0.030), contradicting the claim on this toy setup, though both models degrade sharply (SW2 ~0.45) suggesting the conditioning proxy is broken.

MarxistLeninist/repro-db-vs-fm-aIFgQusnP.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the two theoretical claims (Prop 4.1 and Thm 4.2) via exact float64 numerical audits, but the four empirical claims are only addressed on a 2D synthetic toy with small MLPs—not the paper's latent-Transformer image pipeline—yielding mixed results that partially support, partially contradict the paper's empirical narrative.

tomyimkc/repro-revenue-guarantees-of-no-.paper_title: Revenue Guarantees of No-Swap-Regret Dynamics in First Price Auctions

claims.claim: For exact correlated equilibria in discrete first-price auctions with k discretization levels, expected revenue is at least v2 - 4/k, where v2 is the second-highest valuation (Theorem 2.5).
claims.evidence: LP solving for exact CE (epsilon=0) across 20 (k,v2) instances up to k=150 shows Z*_LP >= v2-4/k in every case (min slack 0.0267 at k=150), with a control dropping CE constraints yielding revenue 0, confirming the bound arises from CE incentive constraints.

claims.claim: For ε-approximate correlated equilibria, expected revenue is at least v2 - 3/k - Θ(εk²) (Theorem 2.6).
claims.evidence: The epsilon-CE bound held in all 48 instances with the paper's constant C=2, but only at n=2 bidders, k<=60, and the empirically-required constant never exceeded 0.162—far below 2—so the bound was never stressed near its tight regime.

claims.claim: There exists an ε-approximate correlated equilibrium with revenue at most v2 - Θ(1/k) - Θ(ε), showing the ε-dependence in the revenue lower bound cannot be removed (Theorem 2.8).
claims.evidence: The paper's explicit witness was implemented from description, all 42 revenue values matched the closed form 1-eps/2-eps/(2k) exactly up to k=1000, independent CE-validity computation confirmed it is a genuine epsilon-CE in 24/24 cross-check instances, and a separate exact LP found the true worst case is even lower with negative coefficients on both 1/k and epsilon (R²=0.9874).

claims.claim: When bidders run no-swap-regret algorithms achieving swap regret O(√(kT)), the time-averaged revenue is at least v2 - 3/k - O(ε) after O(k^5/ε^2) rounds (Corollary 2.7).
claims.evidence: Regret matching with n=3 bidders at T=50000 rounds showed revenue exceeding v2-3/k in all sweeps and swap regret shrinking, but T=50000 is orders of magnitude below the paper's O(k^5/epsilon^2) round complexity (at k=50 this would require billions of rounds), so the asymptotic guarantee is not remotely stressed.

claims.claim: Time-averaged bidder behavior under no-swap-regret dynamics converges to an ε-approximate correlated equilibrium with probability 1-δ (Theorem 2.3).
claims.evidence: Across 8 independent seeds of regret matching (n=3, k=15, T=20000), time-averaged CE-violation shrank from mean 0.148 to 0.0036 (ratio 0.0245) in 8/8 seeds, while a non-learning cycling control showed no shrinkage (ratio 1.07), providing concrete experimental evidence of convergence under no-swap-regret dynamics.

claims.claim: The revenue lower bounds are proved via a dual-fitting approach that uses a linear program and weak duality to bound revenue of approximate correlated equilibria (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The paper's explicit dual assignment (Definitions 3.5/3.6) was numerically dual-feasible in all 12 instances (max violation negative), the dual objective met Lemma 3.8's bound v2-3/k-2*eps*k^2 in all cases, weak duality held against an independently-solved primal LP, and a naive control dual point gave objective 0 vs. the fitted construction's 0.254.

tomyimkc/repro-revenue-guarantees-of-no-.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting 4 of 6 claims (exact CE bound, low-revenue witness, convergence, and dual-fitting method) through independently re-derived LP machinery, explicit witness construction, multi-seed dynamics, and dual feasibility checks with appropriate controls. Claims 2 and 4 are addressed only at reduced scale (n=2, k<=60, T far below asymptotic complexity) where the bounds hold but are never stressed, constituting toy-level verification.

tomyimkc/repro-calibrating-decision-robu.paper_title: Calibrating Decision Robustness via Inverse Conformal Risk Control

claims.evidence: T=20000 trials across n∈{10,50,200} and a 5-point λ grid with two structurally different bounded losses yielded 0/30 margin violations in the exchangeable setting (min positive margins 7.4e-05 and 0.002309), while a broken-exchangeability control produced 25/30 violations with margins as negative as -0.384, directly confirming the theorem's inequality and its dependence on Assumption 3.1.

claims.claim: Proposition 2 shows the estimator's error decays at the parametric O(n^{-1/2}) rate in the calibration sample size n, giving a finite-sample guarantee rather than only an asymptotic one (Proposition 2).
claims.evidence: MAE of α̂ against exact ground truth (E[I_λ]=0.6) over n=50–40000 with R=1500 trials produced a log-log slope of -0.4991 (theory: -0.5), and the empirical violation rate of the closed-form ε(n,δ=0.1) bound never exceeded 0.0153; a non-i.i.d. but exchangeable control showed a flat slope (0.0024) and violation rates up to 0.9947, confirming the rate requires i.i.d.

claims.claim: The CREME (Conformal REgret Miscoverage Estimate) algorithm is empirically validated across four distinct decision-making paradigms: linear programming, the newsvendor problem, portfolio selection, and shortest-path optimization (Experiments section).
claims.evidence: All four paradigms (LP, newsvendor, portfolio, shortest-path) were independently implemented from Appendix G.1 with population pools of 20K–300K, R=500 calibration trials at n_cal=2000, and 15-point λ grids; all produced non-empty Pareto frontiers (sizes 3, 8, 2, 1) with margins within Monte Carlo noise (worst -0.000588), while an n_cal=5 control showed up to 455x accuracy degradation, confirming validity at scale and the small-n looseness pattern.
