sotayamashita/repro-simulcost-release-au.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, complete enumeration evidence falsifying the solver count (12 vs 13) and task counts (2,916/2,577 vs 2,947/1,931) in the pinned public release, partially verifies SimulCost's own cost-tracking properties without auditing other benchmarks, and leaves the frontier-model performance claim entirely unaddressed due to lack of paid API access.

michaldobiezynski/repro-accelerated-and-.paper_title: Accelerated and Stable Convergence with Anchored Generalized Optimistic Method

claims.claim: Theorem 1 proves that with fixed step size η* ∈ (0, 1/(2√3 L)) and anchoring coefficient βk = 2/(k+6), GOMA achieves ‖G(x_k)‖² ≤ 264L²/(k+6)² ‖x0−x*‖², an O(1/k²) accelerated last-iterate convergence rate for monotone Lipschitz operators (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: GOMA Case I was run on a dim=40 monotone Lipschitz bilinear saddle operator (L=1.7658) for 5000 iterations with the prescribed β_k=2/(k+6) and η*=0.99/(2√3 L), yielding a log-log slope of −1.990 (target −2) and max residual ratio 52.844 ≤ 264, with confirmation that the full-range max equals the asymptotic-window max.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 establishes the same O(1/k²) accelerated last-iterate rate under an alternative fixed exploration step size γ* ∈ (0, (1/3L)√(5/26)) (Section 4.1, Case II).
claims.evidence: GOMA Case II on the same dim=40 bilinear saddle with γ*=0.99·(1/(3L))√(5/26) over 5000 iterations produced a log-log slope of −1.971 (target −2) and max residual ratio 206.093 ≤ 780.8, with the constant 780.8 independently confirmed as (16/γ*²+32L²)/L².

claims.claim: Theorem 4 shows that under state-dependent stochastic noise (E‖Ĝ(x,ξ)‖² ≤ σ² + κ‖G(x)‖²), a simplified variant of GOMA with γ_k=0 achieves E‖G(x_N)‖² ≤ 1570L²κ‖x0−x*‖²/√(N+1) + 8σ²/(κ√(N+1)), an O(1/√k) last-iterate rate (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: The γ_k=0 simplified stochastic GOMA with additive Gaussian noise (σ=0.5, κ=1) averaged over 120 seeds at N∈{200,500,1000,2000,5000} on the dim=40 bilinear saddle yielded a log-log slope of −0.464 (target −0.5) with monotonically decreasing E‖G(x_N)‖²=[5.21,3.43,2.49,1.79,1.17], all under the Theorem-4 envelope; the rate match is the discriminating test since the envelope carries three orders of magnitude of slack.

claims.claim: The stochastic O(1/√k) last-iterate guarantee is obtained using linearly increasing minibatch sizes without requiring variance reduction techniques, and the paper claims it as the first such guarantee for stochastic monotone Lipschitz variational inequalities (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: A standalone dim=200, 200-seed run of γ_k=0 GOMA with linearly increasing minibatch b_k=k+1 (no variance reduction) at N∈{200,500,1000,2000,5000} produced a log-log slope of −0.441 (target −0.5) with E‖G(x_N)‖²=[29.53,19.85,14.72,10.82,7.13] under the envelope, explicitly spending Σ_k b_k up to 12.5M oracle calls to exercise the growing-batch mechanism; the bibliographic 'first such guarantee' sub-clause is acknowledged as non-numerically-testable.

michaldobiezynski/repro-accelerated-and-.overall: All four claims are supported by concrete numerical experiments on monotone Lipschitz bilinear saddle operators at moderate scale (dim=40–200, up to 5000 iterations, 120–200 seeds for stochastic claims), with measured log-log rate slopes closely matching the theoretical predictions of −2, −2, and −0.5. The primary evidence is rate-based since the theorem constants are very loose upper bounds (measured values are 4–2000× below the stated bounds), and all experiments use a single operator family (bilinear saddle) rather than multiple diverse monotone operators.

DineshAI/r6wfuAKmVb.paper_title: Leaderboard Incentives: Model Rankings under Strategic Post-Training

claims.claim: The paper proves that current leaderboard benchmarks induce a Stackelberg ranking game in which no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium generally exists among competing model developers (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Z3 symbolic verification constructs a concrete continuous-domain witness game (capabilities (1, 1/2), v=1-exp(-(θ+e)), c(e)=e, rewards (1,0)) and proves profitable deviation in all five boundary/interior cases (all unsat), with a negative control showing PNE exists when reward gap drops to 1/4. Numerical best-response dynamics across 4 reward gaps also show non-convergence.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.3 shows that whenever a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium does exist, the resulting equilibrium ranking preserves the latent capability ordering of the models (Section 4, Proposition 4.3).
claims.evidence: A Z3-verified counterexample uses paper-admissible flat cost c(e)=max(e-1,0)^2 (nonnegative, non-decreasing, convex, zero at zero, divergent per Assumption 4.1) with equal rewards (1,1) and efforts (0, 3/4): both players achieve maximum utility 1 (no profitable deviation), yet the lower-capability player has strictly higher score (1/2+3/4 > 1+0), violating capability ordering. Negative control with strict linear cost removes the inversion.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 identifies 'just-overtake' incentives as the failure mode: if there exists a rank r such that the cost of the required effort to overtake is less than the reward gap between ranks r-1 and r, the follower game admits no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium (Section 4, Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: A Z3-verified counterexample with the same admissible flat cost, rewards (0.1, 0), and efforts (1,1) shows a PNE exists: the high-capability player wins at zero cost, and the lower player cannot profitably overtake (cost 0.25 > reward 0.1). Yet at the all-zero profile, the catch-up effort infimum is 1/2 with zero cost (strictly below the 0.1 reward gap), so Theorem 4.6's antecedent holds while its conclusion fails.

claims.claim: The tune-before-test (TbT) protocol is proven to induce a benchmark game with a unique Nash equilibrium that ranks models by latent quality, with monotone stabilizing effects as the TbT level increases (Section 5, Proposition 5.3).
claims.evidence: A Z3-verified counterexample with admissible flat cost shows both (1,0) and (1,1) are PNE for every TbT level Δ≥0 (the common TbT baseline cancels from score comparisons), demonstrating non-uniqueness. The all-zero profile is not a PNE (lower player can overtake for free), but two distinct nonzero equilibria persist at all TbT levels, contradicting the uniqueness claim.

claims.claim: Under power-law capability scaling, the TbT threshold needed to stabilize rankings grows only polynomially in the reward gaps between adjacent ranks (Section 5, Proposition 5.6).
claims.evidence: A counterexample family v(θ,e)=1-1/(2+e+θ) satisfies the displayed generalized-logit conditions (C1–C3 verified by direct derivatives) with c(e)=e, capabilities 1 and 0, and reward gap 2. The lower model's catch-up-effort infimum is exactly 1 for every TbT baseline, so its cost never reaches the reward gap, meaning no finite stabilizing threshold exists—contradicting Proposition 5.6's polynomial growth claim.

claims.claim: An empirical demonstration on Winogrande shows that after applying TbT with 3,000 training steps, at least 384,668 additional training steps would be required to change the induced model ranking (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: No independent empirical reproduction was performed. The logbook only reconstructs Figure 1's red curve from the hashed PDF source (calibrating to 384,668) and checks text anchors in LaTeX sources, but the arXiv bundle contains no raw per-checkpoint Winogrande measurements, fit parameters, training code, or checkpoints, making the underlying empirical claim unverifiable.

DineshAI/r6wfuAKmVb.overall: The logbook provides rigorous Z3-verified symbolic counterexamples that falsify claims 2–5 by exploiting a flat cost region permitted by the paper's own Assumption 4.1, while verifying claim 1's existential no-PNE result with a concrete witness. Claim 6's empirical Winogrande result remains unreproduced due to missing raw data and training artifacts.

Edd16/icml2026-p1GwEz0pix-repro.paper_title: Frequentist Consistency of Prior-Data Fitted Networks for Causal Inference

claims.claim: Existing PFN-based causal estimators (evaluated across TabPFN, Do-PFN, CausalPFN, and CausalFM) exhibit a prior-induced confounding bias because their implicit priors concentrate on nearly unconfounded data-generating processes, which prevents frequentist consistency of the resulting ATE estimates (Table 1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: A numpy/scipy proxy script on cpu-basic HF infrastructure uses a hand-crafted prior bias on synthetic data (True ATE=2.0, PFN estimate=3.23, bias=1.23), but no actual PFN models (TabPFN, Do-PFN, CausalPFN, CausalFM) were trained or evaluated, so the claim about existing PFN-based estimators is only addressed on a simplified proxy.

claims.claim: The one-step posterior correction (OSPC) procedure uses the efficient influence function to calibrate PFN-based ATE posteriors without retraining the underlying network, restoring frequentist consistency (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The same proxy script applies a 'simplified linear correction' reducing bias from ~1.23 to ~0.41 on synthetic data, but this is not the actual OSPC procedure using efficient influence functions on real PFN posteriors — it is a toy-scale demonstration of the debiasing mechanism.

claims.claim: Under L2 convergence conditions on nuisance estimates, the MP-OSPC posterior satisfies a semi-parametric Bernstein-von Mises theorem, becoming asymptotically equivalent to the classical augmented inverse-propensity-weighted (A-IPTW) estimator (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Two proxy Monte Carlo runs show estimates near the true ATE with decreasing SEs, but one run (claim-3 page) shows empirical coverage collapsing to 0–15% at all sample sizes, contradicting proper BvM calibration. Neither run uses the actual MP-OSPC estimator; both are numpy/scipy proxies.

claims.claim: MP-OSPC combines martingale posteriors with copulas to produce smooth functional posteriors over nuisance functions, which is a prerequisite for the OSPC calibration to apply in practice (Section 4, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The claim-3-fix page provides only a textual restatement of the MP-OSPC architecture (martingale posteriors + copulas → smooth functional posteriors → OSPC) with no HF job, no code, no implementation, and no numerical results demonstrating the copula construction or smoothness of functional posteriors.

claims.claim: On the ACIC 2016 benchmark, the calibrated MP-OSPC estimator is empirically compared against uncalibrated PFN baselines for coverage and bias (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The claim-4-fix page reports 'accuracy' numbers (MP-OSPC 89%, TabPFN 82%, etc.) from a local numpy simulation with no HF job and no actual ACIC 2016 data; the metrics reported (accuracy) do not match the paper's coverage and bias metrics, and no real benchmark comparison was conducted.

claims.claim: L2-convergence of nuisance estimates as a function of dataset size is validated empirically, supporting the conditions required for the Bernstein-von Mises result (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The claim-5-fix page runs OLS on synthetic linear data (y=2x+1+noise) and finds a log-log slope of -0.4924, but this merely verifies the well-known parametric convergence rate of OLS on trivial data, not the L2 convergence of the paper's actual nuisance estimators in the PFN/MP-OSPC framework.

Edd16/icml2026-p1GwEz0pix-repro.overall: This logbook provides only toy-scale numpy/scipy proxy simulations with no actual PFN models trained, no real datasets (e.g., ACIC 2016) used, and no genuine implementation of OSPC or MP-OSPC. Several claims lack any HF job entirely and rely on local computations with fabricated-looking numbers or textual descriptions, making the overall reproduction attempt low quality.

DineshAI/rHndxbqWyh.paper_title: Nonparametric LLM Evaluation from Preference Data

claims.claim: DMLRank defines Generalized Average Ranking Scores (GARS) as θ=E[F(μ(X))], a unifying functional that recovers Borda scores, Bradley-Terry log-odds projections, and Rank Centrality stationary-distribution scores as special cases (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Independent reconstruction of BT (constrained least-squares residual 4.441e-16), RC (stationarity residual 8.327e-17), and Borda identities at machine precision, with a wrong-symmetrization control correctly failing at 0.249, confirms all three GARS special-case recoveries.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 derives a debiased efficient-influence-function estimator for GARS that is asymptotically normal, √n(θ̂_EIF−θ)→N_d(0,Σ), and achieves the semiparametric efficiency bound under cross-fitted nuisance estimation (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: A saturated finite-state MAR model checks the EIF mean-zero property (0.0) and pathwise derivative identity (2.776e-17) at machine precision, with an omitted-IPW control correctly failing (0.051), verifying the core algebraic content of Theorem 5.1; continuous-context asymptotic rate conditions remain untested assumptions.

claims.claim: On synthetic data with n=1000, the debiased Borda estimator has error 0.15±0.03 with 0.94±0.06 coverage, versus the plugin estimator's 0.38±0.08 error and only 0.17±0.09 coverage, showing plugin confidence intervals are invalid while debiased ones are not (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Four clean-room routes show the correct qualitative direction (debiased lower error, higher coverage) but fail to match the paper's specific numbers (e.g., plugin error 0.023 vs claimed 0.38, debiased 0.015 vs 0.15); the exact DGP seed, error metric, and p-value are undisclosed and the author archive returned HTTP 410.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.2 characterizes the A-optimal preference-labeling policy under a budget constraint as π*_jk(x)=clip_[α,1]√(tr(J_jkV_jkJ_jkᵀ)/(λ_A c_jk)), balancing informativeness, influence on the target functional, and per-comparison cost (Theorem 6.2).
claims.evidence: The A-optimal policy formula is confirmed by budget satisfaction (4.441e-16 error), agreement with independent multi-start SLSQP (5.855e-8), KKT conditions at machine precision (1.332e-15), and an inverted-informativeness control showing a positive objective gap (12.38).

claims.claim: Under a fixed budget of β=2000 comparisons, the A-optimal labeling policy achieves lower MSE than random data collection for all three GARS types tested: Borda (0.108±0.041 vs 0.133±0.060), Bradley-Terry (2.565±1.046 vs 2.910±1.143), and Rank Centrality (0.010±0.008 vs 0.017±0.007) (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Three allocation routes yield inconsistent directions (Route 1 oracle shows A-optimal better for all three, but Routes 2–3 show BT and RC reversals with crossing confidence intervals), and none match the paper's specific MSE values; the author v1 seed, coefficient draws, and exact configuration are unavailable.

claims.claim: The framework is applied to real Chatbot Arena preference data with n=32,980 prompts and K=20 models, using toxicity score and TF-IDF prompt embeddings as covariates, where plugin estimators yield near-zero-width (invalid) confidence intervals while debiased estimators retain interpretable uncertainty (Section 7, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Full-scale run on n=32,980 prompts and K=20 models with toxicity and TF-IDF covariates shows plugin median widths are 1.4–4.0% of debiased EIF widths across all three GARS types, directly supporting the claim that plugin intervals collapse while debiased intervals retain interpretable uncertainty; data sourced from a public mirror of the gated official dataset.

DineshAI/rHndxbqWyh.overall: The logbook provides strong machine-precision verification of the paper's theoretical claims (GARS special cases, EIF algebra, A-optimal policy KKT) and a faithful full-scale Chatbot Arena run supporting the interval-collapse claim. The two simulation-table claims (3, 5) remain inconclusive because the exact author experimental configurations are unavailable and clean-room numbers do not match the reported values.

jomasego/repro-siamesenorm-breaking-the-.paper_title: SiameseNorm: Breaking the Barrier to Reconciling Pre/Post-Norm

claims.claim: SiameseNorm is a two-stream residual architecture with shared parameters that couples Pre-Norm-like and Post-Norm-like streams to decouple their optimization dynamics while retaining both paradigms' distinct characteristics (Section 3).
claims.evidence: A code audit of the official implementation confirms the two-stream design (x and y inputs to OLMoSequentialBlock.forward), shared parameters across streams (single set of attention/FFN projections), stream-specific LayerNorm positioning (pre-attn norm on y, scaled residual on x), and the scaling factor c=((layer_id+1)*2)**0.5. A standalone smoke test confirmed streams diverge under identical inputs.

claims.claim: On 1.3B-parameter OLMo-based models (16 layers, 2048 hidden size, 16 heads) trained on 100B tokens of FineWeb-Edu at learning rate 2e-3, SiameseNorm attains average perplexity 10.48 versus 10.89 for Pre-Norm, while standard Post-Norm and HybridNorm diverge under this setting (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Experiments were run on a 20M-parameter model (8 layers, d_model=384) on synthetic random-token data (vocab=8192) for 5000 steps on Mac MPS, not the 1.3B model on 100B tokens of FineWeb-Edu. Results showed SiameseNorm diverging at step 15 (gn=83.9) and Post-Norm/HybridNorm remaining stable, but the setup lacks warmup, proper initialization, and real language data, making it a proxy task rather than a test of the actual claim.

claims.claim: At the same 2e-3 learning rate / 100B-token setting, SiameseNorm reaches 39.6% arithmetic-task accuracy versus 28.1% for Pre-Norm, a 40.9% relative gain, and an average downstream score of 55.63 versus 52.94 (Table 1).
claims.evidence: No experiments were run for this claim. The logbook states downstream task evaluation requires a trained 1.3B checkpoint, which was never produced. No proxy or partial evaluation was attempted.

claims.claim: At a lower learning rate of 1e-3 (100B tokens), SiameseNorm still improves over Pre-Norm, achieving 10.43 average perplexity and 53.53 average score versus 10.84 and 51.91 for Pre-Norm (Table 1).
claims.evidence: A 20M-parameter model on synthetic random-token data was trained at lr=1e-3: Pre-Norm converged (PPL 1.0005) while SiameseNorm diverged (gn=1254 at step 24). However, the setup uses default PyTorch initialization, no warmup, and random tokens rather than FineWeb-Edu, making it a clearly simplified proxy rather than a test of the 1.3B/100B-token claim.

claims.claim: During training, SiameseNorm keeps gradient norms below 0.5, matching Pre-Norm's stability and avoiding the gradient explosions observed with Post-Norm variants (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: Gradient norms were measured on a 20M-parameter model on synthetic random-token data: SiameseNorm reached max GN of 83.9 (lr=2e-3) and 1254.5 (lr=1e-3), contradicting the paper's <0.5 claim. However, the setup lacks the paper's initialization schemes (mitchell/full_megatron), warmup, real data, and 1.3B scale, so it is a toy proxy rather than a faithful test of the stability claim.

jomasego/repro-siamesenorm-breaking-the-.overall: The logbook verifies the architectural design of SiameseNorm through a thorough code audit of the official implementation, confirming the two-stream shared-parameter structure. However, all performance and stability claims were only tested on a 20M-parameter synthetic random-token task without proper initialization or warmup, which is too far removed from the paper's 1.3B/FineWeb-Edu setting to constitute reproduction or falsification.

DineshAI/Ir6N7U5Kea.paper_title: Causal Matrix Completion under Multiple Treatments via Mixed Synthetic Nearest Neighbors

claims.claim: MSNN provably preserves Synthetic Nearest Neighbors' entry-wise finite-sample error bound (Theorem 4.5) and asymptotic normality with convergence rate scaling as K_MSNN^(-1/2) (Theorem 4.6) (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: A rank-one counterexample satisfying the paper's stated assumptions shows error converging to -1 (not 0) and standardized mean diverging (-5.67, -6.91, -8.00 at N=16,81,256) across 72 repetitions, because MSNN Assumption 4.3 drops the signal-energy lower bound required by the cited SNN Assumption 6.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.10 shows the expected number of usable data subgroups under MCAR grows by a multiplicative factor of [∑_d' (p_d'/p_d)^(r+1)]^c for MSNN relative to standard SNN, formalizing the effective-sample-size gain from mixed anchor sets (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: An exact symbolic certificate derives E[K_MSNN(d)]/E[K_SNN(d)] = (1+o(1))·[∑_d'(p_d'/p_d)^(r+1)]^c by dividing Theorem 4.8's leading terms and canceling common factors, confirmed by an independent checker that exits nonzero when an exponent is mutated.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.11 shows the relative efficiency gap between data-sparse and data-rich treatment levels is reduced from quadratic to linear order under MSNN (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Exact algebraic division of Theorem 4.8 terms yields sparse-to-rich exponents of rc+r+c for SNN versus r for MSNN, confirming the dominant term changes from quadratic (rc) to linear (r), verified by an independent checker with a mutation control that fails correctly.

claims.claim: On MCAR-generated data at a low treatment probability p(d)=0.01, MSNN achieves a 4.69% feasible rate and mean relative error of 3.91e-2, versus a 0.03% feasible rate and 0.806 MRE for standard SNN (Table 1).
claims.evidence: A 10-seed run at paper scale (300×100, rank 3, p=0.01) reproduces the MSNN feasible rate (4.689% vs 4.69%) and the number 0.0391 under the released code's normalized MAE, but the paper's own MRE definition (mean |prediction-truth|/|truth|) gives 0.252±0.116, contradicting the reported 3.91e-2.

claims.claim: Under MNAR data, MSNN consistently attains 3-26% feasible imputation rates versus under 5% for SNN, with 2-3x error reductions across treatment levels (Tables 2-3).
claims.evidence: The paper's own Tables 2-3 show MSNN feasible rates ranging 3.13–54.16% (not 3–26%), SNN rates up to 22.66% (not under 5%), and three of six error-reduction ratios exceeding 3x (up to 3.42x), directly contradicting the claimed ranges.

claims.claim: Mixed anchor rows/columns are constructed via bipartite cliques spanning multiple treatment levels while preserving the target row's same-treatment data, relying on the shared latent row factor assumption (Assumption 2.5) (Section 3.2-3.3, Algorithms 2-3).
claims.evidence: At paper scale (300×100, rank 3, noise 0.001, p=0.01, 10 seeds), 382/382 selected mixed-anchor cliques pass all treatment-preservation invariants, 382/382 corrupted-edge controls are rejected, and Assumption-2.5-violating estimates show 638x higher error (2.23 vs 0.0035).

DineshAI/Ir6N7U5Kea.overall: The logbook provides concrete evidence for all six claims: exact symbolic certificates verify Corollaries 4.10 and 4.11, a full-scale noisy test verifies the mixed-anchor construction, and counterexamples or metric/range contradictions falsify the theorem transfer, Table 1 MRE, and Tables 2-3 range claims.

sotayamashita/repro-adalina-adaptive-lin.paper_title: Adalina: Adaptive Linear Approximation for the Shapley Value and Beyond

claims.claim: Adalina (Algorithm 1) is a randomized adaptive linear-approximation algorithm achieving O(n/ε² log(1/δ)) utility-query complexity while using only Θ(n) space (Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Concrete scaling experiments show n log-log slope of 1.000000, ε slope of -2.000000, δ spread of 0, and linear-memory slope of 0.9667 (with quadratic control at 2.0000) across n=8...1024, directly supporting the O(n/ε² log(1/δ)) complexity and Θ(n) space claims.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 shows that under an optimal sampling distribution q*_s, Adalina attains query complexity O(nD*C²/ε² log(2/δ)) where D*∈O(1) for both Beta Shapley and weighted Banzhaf semi-values, improving on OFA's O(n log n/(ε²δ)) bound (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The optimal law q*_s is computed for Shapley, weighted Banzhaf (w=0.3), and Beta-Shapley (2,3) over n=8...4096; D* stays below 25 for weighted-Banzhaf and Beta-Shapley, and all 128 alternative Dirichlet laws yield D(q)/D* ≥ 1.8248, confirming optimality and bounded D*.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 proves that paired sampling reduces the estimation problem to approximating (U−U^c)/2 and provably lowers MSE whenever E[U(S)·U([n]\S)] > 0 (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Exact enumeration of all 2^8-2 subsets confirms z_{S^c} = -z_S with zero error; paired/unpaired MSE ratio is 0.00614 when E[U(S)U(S^c)] = +3.99 (pairing helps) and 2.00000 when the product is negative (pairing hurts), directly confirming the conditional claim of Theorem 3.2.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows Adalina achieves improved mean-square error approaching the optimal E[‖ϕ̂^γ*−ϕ‖²₂] while preserving O(n/ε² log(1/δ)) query complexity for symmetric semi-values, and the paper shows SHAP-IQ does not minimize query complexity under this framework (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Exact variance quadratic has grid minimum at γ*=0.8355414701 (oracle variance 0.72955 vs 23.3018 at γ=0); Algorithm 1 with 64 seeds at budgets 256–4096 yields adaptive/oracle MSE ratios 0.995–1.005 and adaptive/uncentered ratios 0.026–0.033, and SHAP-IQ's query driver is strictly larger than q* at every tested size.

claims.claim: Experiments on spambase (n=57), FOTP (n=51), MinibooNE (n=50), and philippine (n=308) datasets, using 1000 queries per player averaged over 10 seeds, empirically validate the theoretical complexity/variance predictions (Figures 1-4).
claims.evidence: The four dataset dimensions (n=57, 51, 50, 308), 1000 queries/player, and 10 seeds are covered, but analytic-ground-truth utilities replace the actual named OpenML datasets, trained gradient-boosting tree models, author preprocessing, and paper comparators, making this a proxy setup rather than a full reproduction.

algorise/repro-the-catastrophic-failure-.paper_title: The Catastrophic Failure of *the* k-Means Algorithm in High Dimensions, and How Hartigan's Algorithm Avoids It

claims.claim: In the high-noise, high-dimensional regime where σ² > n, Lloyd's k-means algorithm fails catastrophically: essentially every partition of the data becomes a fixed point of the algorithm (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: Real experiments show Lloyd's fixed-point rate rising from 0% to 34.08% over d=2..200 (Spearman ρ=0.873, p=0.0047), but 34% is far from 'essentially every partition' and the 2^n·n prefactor makes the asymptotic bound vacuous at n=50; the trend direction is confirmed but the claim's magnitude is not reached at CPU-tractable scale.

claims.claim: In the same high-noise regime, Hartigan's k-means algorithm avoids this pathology, having no incorrect fixed points with high probability (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: Hartigan's fixed-point rate is exactly 0/10,000 across all dimensions tested, a clean contrast with Lloyd's, but the experiment uses uniformly-random partitions as a proxy for 'incorrect' partitions rather than directly testing the claim's formal statement, and the scale (n=50, d≤200) is below the asymptotic regime.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.8 bounds the probability that any q-approximately balanced partition is not a fixed point of Lloyd's algorithm by 2^n · n · ρ_q^(d/4) (Corollary 3.8).
claims.evidence: Fixed-point rate climbs from 0% to 75.4% (ρ=0.941, p=0.0051), showing the corollary's implied direction, but the actual 2^30·30·ρ_q^(d/4) bound saturates at 1.0 at every tested d, so the bound itself is neither verified nor falsified—only the qualitative trend is observed at reduced scale.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.12 bounds the probability that any incorrect partition is a fixed point of Hartigan's algorithm by 2^n · ρ_h^(d/4), a substantially tighter bound than Lloyd's case (Corollary 3.12).
claims.evidence: Hartigan's fixed-point rate is 0/6,000 trials vs Lloyd's 75.4%, and ρ_h < ρ_q is confirmed algebraically, but the 2^n·ρ_h^(d/4) bound is vacuous (saturates at 1.0) at n=30, and 'incorrect partition' formalism is tested via random-partition proxy rather than directly.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 shows Lloyd's single-sample reassignment step persists misclassification errors once the noise level exceeds σ > (2c̄τ(c−1))/√(c(c+c̄)) (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: With correctly computed threshold σ_thresh=2/√6≈0.8165, all 14 tested σ values ≥2× threshold yield classification accuracy in [0.5234, 0.5392] (within chance band [0.35, 0.65]) across 25 seeds, directly corroborating Theorem 3.4's prediction that misclassification errors persist above the noise threshold.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments empirically demonstrate the divergence between Lloyd's catastrophic-failure behavior and Hartigan's robustness as dimension grows, corroborating the theoretical bounds (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The pre-registered accuracy-based predicate failed (Spearman ρ=0.119, p=0.78 for |Δ accuracy| vs d), with both algorithms plateauing at ~0.52–0.54 at σ²=n; while the fixed-point-rate metric in Claims 1–4 does show divergence, the specific experiment designed for Claim 6 did not demonstrate it.

algorise/repro-the-catastrophic-failure-.overall: The logbook provides real experimental evidence for the qualitative Lloyd-vs-Hartigan contrast (fixed-point rates diverge with dimension) and cleanly verifies Theorem 3.4's noise threshold, but the asymptotic probability bounds (Claims 1–4) cannot be numerically verified at the CPU-tractable scales tested (n=30–50, d≤200) where the 2^n prefactor renders them vacuous, and the accuracy-based divergence test (Claim 6) explicitly failed.

algorise/repro-online-learning-with-rece.paper_title: Online Learning with Recency: Algorithms for Sliding-window Streaming Multi-armed Bandits

claims.claim: Any algorithm that finds the exact best arm at any step with probability at least 1/2+Omega(1) in the sliding-window streaming multi-armed bandits model requires Omega(W) arm memory, even with unlimited arm pulls (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The paper's hard instance (μ_i = 1-i/(3W), n=2W, descending means) is implemented directly at W∈{32,64,128,256} with 25 seeds; the oracle envelope matches the (M+1)/(W+1) information ceiling exactly (0.00000 deviation, 36 cells), the memory threshold for success≥0.75 scales as M*=0.7500W-0.25 (R²=1.0), and at M=W/4 success is 0.25-0.27 while at M=W it is 1.000, directly demonstrating that 1/2+Ω(1) success forces M=Ω(W).

claims.claim: An epsilon-best arm can be found with probability at least 1-delta at any step using only O(1/epsilon) arm memory and O((n/epsilon^2) log(W/delta)) arm pulls, independent of the total stream length n (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The paper's bucket algorithm (B=ceil(2/ε) buckets, keep latest arm per bucket) is implemented at n=100,000, W=1,000, 25 seeds across ε∈[0.05,0.40]: zero failures vs δ=0.05, peak memory scales as 1.993/ε (R²=0.99957), memory is flat at 20.00 arms across n∈{20k,50k,100k} and W∈{200,1k,5k} (spread 0.00), pulls scale as 1/ε^1.99964 (R²≈1.0), and an ablation at m/256 pulls produces failure rate 0.065>δ, confirming the test is failable.

claims.claim: For regret minimization under the paper's new epoch-wise regret notion, any single-pass algorithm achieving o(T/W^2) regret requires Omega(W) arm memory, establishing a sharp memory-regret trade-off with a transition around Theta(W) arm memory (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The transition location scales linearly as M*=0.3666W (R²=0.99994) and regret decreases ~32% from M=W/8 to M=W with disjoint CIs, but the growth-rate separation central to the claim is not observed: log-log regret-vs-T slopes are 0.8962 (starved) vs 0.9002 (full), difference -0.004 vs the required ≥0.20, on both descending and random-order instances. The lower bound over all single-pass algorithms cannot be verified by simulating three heuristics, and the separation regime requires T~1.8e50, far beyond simulatable scale.

claims.claim: The sliding-window streaming MAB model separates data arrival (window movement) from arm sampling, distinguishing it from non-stationary and mortal bandit models where the environment changes only as a result of arm pulls (Section 1).
claims.evidence: The pull-rate response experiment at T=20,000, 25 seeds cleanly separates the models: sliding-window change rate is pull-independent (slope +0.000182, CI [-0.000164,+0.000528] contains 0) and nonzero at p=0 (0.0197), while rested-drift (slope +0.016901, CI strictly positive) and mortal-budget (slope +0.001904, CI strictly positive) are both exactly 0 at p=0 and increase with pull rate. The passive change rate matches the theoretical 2/W with log-log slope -0.9909 (R²=0.99999).

algorise/repro-online-learning-with-rece.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence verifying Claims 1, 2, and 4 at non-toy scale with pre-stated two-sided predicates, honest failure reporting, and ablations confirming tests are failable. Claim 3 is honestly reported as unsettled: the linear transition scaling is confirmed but the growth-rate separation and the universal lower bound over all algorithms are not demonstrated, with a quantified explanation of why simulation cannot reach the relevant regime.

algorise/repro-solving-imperfect-recall-.paper_title: Solving Imperfect-Recall Games via Sum-of-Squares Optimization

claims.claim: For single-player imperfect-recall extensive-form games (IREFGs), the Sum-of-Squares/moment hierarchy converges to the optimal utility u* as the relaxation degree d goes to infinity, i.e. lim_{d→∞} u^d_sos = lim_{d→∞} u^d_mom = u* (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook tests a complete Sherali-Adams/RLT LP moment relaxation as a 'CPU-friendly proxy' for the paper's SDP-based Moment-SOS hierarchy, explicitly noting no SDP solver was available. While 31 instances (5 hand-built + 26 random, up to 8 info sets) converge to exhaustively-verified true optima with real numbers, the LP hierarchy is a different, weaker mathematical object than the SDP-based SOS hierarchy the paper's Theorem 4.1 actually concerns.

claims.claim: Under a genericity assumption on the utility function u, the SOS hierarchy for single-player IREFGs achieves finite convergence at some finite degree d ≥ d0, rather than only asymptotic convergence (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Finite convergence is observed on all 31 tested instances via the LP proxy (first-exact degrees d0 ≤ 3 on hand-built games, finite d0 ≤ l on random games), but this tests the Sherali-Adams LP hierarchy's finite convergence, not the SDP-based SOS hierarchy's. The SOS hierarchy is tighter, so LP convergence is suggestive but not a direct verification of the paper's specific claim.

claims.claim: For single-player non-absentminded IREFGs, the degree-(ℓ+1) SOS relaxation is exact, i.e. a single semidefinite program at that level solves the game exactly (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: 26/26 non-absentminded random instances reach LP-hierarchy exactness at degree ≤ l+1 (pre-registered predicate P1, Wilson CI [87.1%, 100%]), with real runs and verified optima. However, the exactness-at-degree-(l+1) property is verified for the LP relaxation, not the SDP-based SOS hierarchy; the logbook explicitly states 'feasibility of the true SDP relaxation was not separately checked.'

claims.claim: A Select-Verify-Cut framework extends the KKT-based moment-SOS hierarchy to multi-player IREFGs, yielding analogous finite-convergence and single-level-solvability guarantees under genericity and non-absentmindedness (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states this claim was NOT TESTED: the code implements only single-player IREFGs with no multi-player verify/cut loop, no Select-Verify-Cut framework, and no second player. No experiments or artifacts address this claim.

claims.claim: Strictly concave/monotone single-player IREFGs are shown to admit finite SOS convergence, while SOS-concave/SOS-monotone IREFGs converge already at the first hierarchy level (Theorem 6.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states this claim was NOT TESTED: no game was constructed to satisfy the paper's SOS-concavity or SOS-monotonicity definitions, and no SOS certificate of concavity/monotonicity was computed. An earlier 'PARTIAL' rating was retracted after being identified as an artifact of a bugged relaxation.

claims.claim: In the empirical comparison of Table 1 (Section 7), the SOS approach consistently recovers certified global optima across tested instances, whereas projected gradient descent only succeeds probabilistically, with reported success rates in the 70-89% range.
claims.evidence: The PGD degradation pattern is directly reproduced at scale: success rates fall from 100% (l=2-3) to 56-63% (l=7-8), slope -7.44, R²=0.877, crossing the paper's 70-89% band. However, the 'SOS approach' side is tested via the LP proxy, not the actual SDP-based SOS hierarchy, so the certified-optima recovery is demonstrated for a different relaxation hierarchy than the paper's.

algorise/repro-solving-imperfect-recall-.overall: This logbook provides real experimental evidence on 31 single-player IREFG instances using an LP-based Sherali-Adams relaxation as a proxy for the paper's SDP-based SOS/moment hierarchy, reproducing convergence patterns and the PGD degradation effect from Table 1. However, the core method (SDP-based SOS hierarchy) is never directly tested, and three claims (multi-player SVC, SOS-concave subclasses, vertex-restricted extensions) are not addressed at all.

algorise/repro-adversarially-robust-cont.paper_title: Adversarially Robust Control of Conditional Value-at-Risk via Rockafellar-Uryasev Conformal Inference

claims.claim: Theorem 2.2 establishes that the realized empirical CVaR of the Rockafellar-Uryasev conformal inference method (RUCC) is controlled at the target level with an asymptotic conservatism gap of O(1/sqrt(T)), termed the 'Price of Nonlinearity' relative to the O(1/T) rate achievable for linear expected-loss control (Theorem 2.2; Remark 2.3).
claims.evidence: The experiment measures CDT quantile convergence on synthetic Beta distributions (T=8000, 20 seeds), finding a log-log slope of -1.1488 which is actually steeper than the theoretical -0.5. This is consistent with the O(1/sqrt(T)) upper bound but does not compare against the O(1/T) linear case as the claim requires, and the synthetic setup is a simplified proxy for the theorem's setting.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.4 bounds the inner-level regret of the AdaGrad-FTRL threshold optimization by |max_c Reg_T(c)| <= (3/4) * max{1, beta/(1-beta)} * sqrt(T+1), and Theorem 2.6 shows the outer-level Conformal Decision Theory update keeps the surrogate loss within alpha + O(sqrt(T))/T of the target risk level alpha (Theorem 2.4; Theorem 2.6).
claims.evidence: The reported mean regret is 0.00 ± 0.00 across 20 seeds, which trivially satisfies the theoretical bound of 477.34 but is suspiciously exact and does not meaningfully stress-test the regret bound. The surrogate excess of -0.1215 at T=5000 is much larger than the claimed O(sqrt(T))/T ≈ 0.014 scale, raising questions about whether Theorem 2.6's rate is actually confirmed.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 (Section 2.3) requires no assumptions on the data-generating process, combining an outer-level Conformal Decision Theory update for the risk-control parameter lambda_t with an inner-level AdaGrad-FTRL optimization over the threshold c_t (Section 2.3, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The CDT outer loop is tested on 4 synthetic Beta distributions (T=5000) with violation gaps of 0.0005–0.0017, showing distribution-free convergence. However, only the outer CDT quantile tracker is tested; the full Algorithm 1 with the inner AdaGrad-FTRL threshold optimization is not exercised as an integrated system, and all distributions are synthetic.

claims.claim: On LLM toxicity control using RealToxicityPrompts and the Jigsaw Unintended Bias dataset with Llama 3.2-3B under uniform, adversarial tail-thickening, and adversarial-jump sampling regimes, RUCC maintains the target CVaR level across all regimes while a static lambda-hat baseline calibrated on the first 1000 samples becomes overly conservative or drifts above target (Section 3.1-3.2, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states 'SYNTHETIC APPROXIMATION -- no LLM available for inference' and generates toxicity scores synthetically rather than using RealToxicityPrompts, the Jigsaw dataset, or Llama 3.2-3B. The five regimes tested (uniform_iid, heavy_tailed, adversarial_shift, gradual_shift, jump_return) do not match the paper's three specified sampling regimes, making this a proxy task rather than a reproduction.

claims.claim: On a portfolio-management task using S&P 500 and 10-Year Treasury data from 1991-2025 (via yfinance/FRED), evaluated separately on the 1991-2001 stable period, the 2009-2018 crisis-aftermath period, and the full 1991-2025 span, RUCC keeps realized CVaR near the target across multiple market shocks where the static baseline does not (Section 3.3-3.4, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Real S&P 500 data from yfinance is used across three periods, but all standard deviations are reported as 0.0000 across 10 seeds, which is implausible for a stochastic online algorithm and suggests a measurement issue. The claim mentions both S&P 500 and 10-Year Treasury data via yfinance/FRED, but only yfinance is cited, and the reported 'Surrogate RA' values do not clearly correspond to realized CVaR.

algorise/repro-adversarially-robust-cont.overall: The logbook provides only toy-scale or synthetic-proxy experiments for all five claims: synthetic Beta distributions for the theoretical claims, synthetic toxicity scores instead of real LLM datasets for Claim 4, and suspicious zero-variance results with incomplete data sources for Claim 5. No claim is reproduced at the paper's actual experimental scale or with the paper's real datasets and models.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.1 establishes a sample complexity bound for estimating a discrete distribution under the ℓ∞ norm (Theorem 2.1).
claims.evidence: OLS log-log slopes of -0.4994 to -0.5076 with R² ≥ 0.9998 across 5 alphabet sizes (k∈{10,20,50,100,200}), 11 sample sizes up to n=200,000, and 5000 seeds per point confirm the 1/√n ℓ∞ concentration scaling predicted by Theorem 2.1.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.2 gives a refined bound that improves upon prior ℓ∞ estimation analyses, including the results of Blanchard et al. (2023) (Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: The experiment tests a proxy (Laplace-smoothed vs naive empirical estimator) rather than the actual bound improvement of Theorem 2.2 over Blanchard et al. (2023); the proxy results are mixed—refined better in 20/36 cells, no significant difference in 15/36, and significantly worse in 1/36 (geometric, n=100)—with effect sizes ≤1e-5 for n≥500, which neither clearly supports nor refutes the theoretical bound claim.

claims.claim: Theorems 2.5 and 2.6 extend the estimation bounds to more general settings and parameter regimes beyond the basic case covered in Theorem 2.1 (Theorem 2.5, Theorem 2.6).
claims.evidence: Pearson correlation between Shannon entropy and mean ℓ∞ error across 36 configurations (k∈{20,...,1000} × 3 distributions × 2 n-regimes, 5000 seeds each) is r=-0.598, p=0.000117, confirming the predicted negative entropy-error dependence; geometric's k-invariant error correctly reflects effective support size rather than nominal alphabet size.

claims.claim: The paper's improved bounds connect to information-theoretic quantities such as KL divergence, drawing on techniques related to Garivier (2011) (Section 2).
claims.evidence: Pooled log-log Pearson correlation between ℓ∞ error and KL divergence over N=45,000 individual (seed, n) points is r=0.9608 (p≈0), with OLS slope 0.494 and R²=0.923, confirming the ℓ∞-error ∝ √KL relationship consistent with Pinsker-type information-theoretic links.

claims.claim: Appendix results Theorem A.1 through Theorem A.8, particularly A.2, A.3, and A.6, provide the auxiliary lemmas underlying the main sample complexity proofs (Appendix A).
claims.evidence: Zero violations (0/180) of Hoeffding ≥ Bernstein ≥ Bennett ≥ empirical tail probability ordering across 2 n-regimes × 3 distributions × 30 thresholds with 100,000 Monte Carlo trials each (1.8×10⁷ total simulated samples), confirming the concentration inequalities underlying the auxiliary lemmas hold at every tested grid point.

algorise/repro-improved-distribution-est.overall: The logbook provides strong, well-powered numerical evidence (5000 seeds, n up to 200,000, pre-stated predicates, proper statistical tests) confirming the core scaling behaviors and qualitative predictions of Theorems 2.1, 2.5-2.6, the KL-divergence connection, and the appendix concentration bounds on non-toy setups. The test of Theorem 2.2's claimed improvement uses a proxy estimator comparison with mixed results (including one reversal), which does not directly verify or falsify the theoretical bound improvement over prior work.

codemaivanngu/icml2026-repro-fa-opd.paper_title: Adversarial Dual On-Policy Distillation from Expressive Teacher

claims.claim: FA-OPD trains a student MLP policy using a Flow Matching teacher via two channels: reward distillation (an FM-enhanced discriminator scoring state-action pairs for PPO optimization) and action distillation (FM-generated target actions regressed via MSE) (Section 3.2-3.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook shows FA-OPD running on maze2d-medium-v2 for 5M steps with --action-input true and --reward-type airl, and code traces reveal flow_matching.py and an MLP student policy (DistActorCritic with MLPBasic), but there is no explicit verification that the FM-enhanced discriminator scores state-action pairs for PPO rewards or that FM-generated target actions are regressed via MSE — the dual-channel mechanism is only indirectly inferred from command-line flags and traceback paths, not from loss breakdowns or architectural analysis.

claims.claim: On the Walker2d environment with suboptimal expert demonstrations (dataset IDs 2-5), FA-OPD significantly surpasses Diffusion Policy and Flow-Matching Policy baselines, in some cases exceeding the expert's own performance (Section 4.3, Table 1).
claims.evidence: No Walker2d experiments were run; the logbook only tests maze2d-medium-v2. No Diffusion Policy or Flow-Matching Policy baselines were executed, so the claim about FA-OPD surpassing these baselines on Walker2d with suboptimal demonstrations (dataset IDs 2-5) is entirely unaddressed.

claims.claim: Under increasing observation noise (up to 1.5x), FA-OPD maintains greater than 0.95 success rate on the Hand-rotate task while Diffusion Policy drops to approximately 0.82 (Section 4.2, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: No Hand-rotate task experiments and no observation-noise robustness experiments were conducted anywhere in the logbook. The claim about maintaining >0.95 success rate under 1.5x noise while Diffusion Policy drops to ~0.82 is completely unaddressed.

claims.claim: FA-OPD achieves best or near-best final performance across 6 benchmark environments, including near-100% success on Hand-rotate and Fetch-pick tasks, converging faster than GAIL-family baselines (Figure 2, Table 3, Appendix F.1).
claims.evidence: Only 1 of 6 benchmark environments (maze2d-medium-v2) was tested, and the key environments Hand-rotate and Fetch-pick were not run. FA-OPD achieved ~0.81–0.87 success on maze2d while the AIRL baseline achieved ~0.90, which does not support the claim of best/near-best performance or faster convergence than GAIL-family baselines on this environment.

claims.claim: Ablations show that neither a reward-distillation-only configuration (beta=0) nor an action-distillation-dominated configuration matches the performance of the full dual-distillation configuration (Appendix F.2).
claims.evidence: No ablation experiments were run — there is no beta=0 (reward-only) configuration, no action-distillation-dominated configuration, and no comparison to the full dual-distillation configuration. The ablation claim is entirely unaddressed.

codemaivanngu/icml2026-repro-fa-opd.overall: The logbook only reproduces FA-OPD and an AIRL baseline on a single environment (maze2d-medium-v2) at 5M steps, leaving the paper's core claims about Walker2d, noise robustness on Hand-rotate, multi-environment benchmarks, and ablations completely unaddressed. The single environment tested actually shows AIRL outperforming FA-OPD, providing no support for the paper's performance claims.

JG1310/repro-on-the-theory-of-continual-.paper_title: On the Theory of Continual Learning with Gradient Descent for Neural Networks

claims.claim: Theorem 1 gives a closed-form bound on train-time forgetting for task k after training on K-k subsequent tasks, of order O~(ηT√(K-k)/(d√n) + ηT√(K-k)/(d²polylog(d)) + η²T²K²/√m) (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Pre-registered exponent bands for each term of the bound all hit (width init -0.498±0.001, width dyn -1.008±0.003, sampling n -0.494±0.076, lag +0.498±0.003), exact solver validated against real hinge-GD to 4.0e-13 over 16 paired runs, bound audit 0 violations in 306 certified runs, and rotation control confirming ρ².02 failure law when orthogonality is broken.

claims.claim: The forgetting bounds hold under the parameter regime n = Θ~(d²K) samples, m = Ω~(d⁸K⁴) hidden-layer width, and ηT = Θ(d²) training iterations on a d-dimensional XOR cluster dataset with K tasks (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Co-scaled walk at m=d³K² over d=16–128 hits all pre-registered bands (margins flat 0.243–0.254, signed forgetting slope -1.08±0.06, drift plateau, width share ≤0.28% and decreasing), real 295k-neuron networks match solver to 10⁻¹³, paper-scale m=d⁸K⁴ endpoint computed via validated width parameterization, and all three broken-condition arms (frozen-n, overtrain, small-m) fail in predicted directions.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows that under the same width/sample/iteration conditions as Theorem 1, the misclassification error remains uniformly small across all K tasks with high probability after KT gradient descent iterations (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: At adequate horizon (ηT=3d²), max train and test error exactly 0.0000 across all 22 runs × 6 tasks × d∈{24,32,48}; solver K×K harvest at d=96 confirms 0.0 error; loss curve landmarks match predictions (ramp slope 1.113, knee spread 1.92, creep 4.3e-4); o_d(1) loss clause verified with ×6.6 monotone decrease on hypothesis path and flat control off it; noise ladder transitions at predicted σ_c window.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 bounds the delayed generalization gap by η T exp(ηT(K-k+1)/√m) / n for Lipschitz, smooth loss functions, showing the gap decays with sample size n (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Gap identity verified to 2–5% across 12 of 13 configurations (one disclosed 18% at n=500 in predicted second-order regime), 1/n scaling confirmed for logistic loss (slope -0.98±0.04), propagation growth 1.0000–1.0038 under orthogonality, norm-tracked bound holds with 0 violations at ~365× tightness, and duplication (×r law) and saturation (rise-stall-fall at margin-1) controls match predictions.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 gives an improved generalization gap bound for self-bounded losses that scales poly-logarithmically rather than linearly in the number of iterations T, depending on the cumulative training loss of later tasks (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Visible content shows setup with T=10⁵ logistic traces and K=3 continual gaps over 32× T-range; overview reports B.1-vs-linear tightness ladder growing 1.9×→8×10⁷ with both bounds held, non-monotone gap(T) confirmed, and label-noise mechanism break producing predicted linear C(T); pre-registered zero-parameter constant 1/ηs=2d²/η used throughout.

claims.claim: Test-time forgetting is decomposed as the sum of train-time forgetting (Theorem 1) and the delayed generalization gap (Theorem 3/4), showing that network width, sample size, and later tasks' data jointly, not individually, control forgetting (Theorem 1, Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Appendix notes describe star experiments at one (d,K) with n_later-ray following 1/√n over three decades, all star families certified, and joint-vs-alone comparison confirming the decomposition; the decomposition itself is a structural consequence of the individually verified train-time forgetting bound (claim 1) and delayed generalization gap (claims 4–5).

JG1310/repro-on-the-theory-of-continual-.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous, multi-pronged reproduction of all six claims using an exact solver validated against real gradient descent to floating-point precision, pre-registered acceptance bands, blind re-derivations, assumption-breaking controls, and bound audits with zero violations across hundreds of runs at non-trivial scale (d≤128, m up to 10⁷ explicitly and 10¹⁸ via parameterization, K≤16).

wrice/repro-conditional-dpo-rlhf.paper_title: Conditional Equivalence of DPO and RLHF: Assumptions, Failure Modes, and Provable Alignment

claims.claim: The paper proves DPO-RLHF equivalence is conditional on the RLHF-optimal policy preferring human-preferred responses (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Audited 112 finite preference configurations confirming the population stationary point Δ_rlhf = Δ_ref + r/β matches the finite RLHF optimum, supporting the conditional equivalence relationship. The sample-level loss having no finite minimizer is a separate observation that does not contradict the population-level proof claim.

claims.claim: When the equivalence assumption fails, DPO optimizes relative advantage over the reference policy rather than absolute human-preference alignment (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Across 75 preference shift cases, the logbook confirmed DPO loss reduction monotonically improves relative log-likelihood advantage Δ > Δ_ref without guaranteeing absolute alignment Δ > 0 when Δ_ref < 0, directly supporting the claim.

claims.claim: The paper characterizes undesirable solution spaces in which policies reduce DPO loss while preferring dispreferred responses (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Concrete witness pairs (Δ_ref < Δ < 0) were emitted where DPO loss decreases while p(y_w|x) < 0.5, demonstrating policies that reduce DPO loss while preferring dispreferred responses.

claims.claim: Constrained Preference Optimization augments RLHF with constraints and derives a stationary DPO-like loss with an adaptive reference-based margin (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook found that for all 135 positive-γ cases the exact constrained RLHF objective is unbounded as Δ→+∞, contradicting the claim of a well-formed constrained optimization, while the reference-margin approximation does yield a stationary DPO-like loss, producing both supporting and contradicting evidence.

claims.claim: The paper gives a soft-margin ranking interpretation showing DPO can implement margin ranking with potentially negative targets (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Across 150 cases, scaled DPO loss β⁻¹ softplus(−β(Δ−Δ_ref)) was shown to converge monotonically to hinge loss max(0, Δ_ref−Δ) as β→256, including with negative target margins, directly supporting the soft-margin ranking interpretation.

claims.claim: Experiments on standard benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance for CPO (Section 6).
claims.evidence: No language model was trained or evaluated; the author repository was unavailable and GPU constraints prevented any benchmark experiments, so the SOTA claim was never addressed.

wrice/repro-conditional-dpo-rlhf.overall: The logbook provides numerical verification of the paper's theoretical claims (1, 2, 3, 5) through systematic grid searches over synthetic preference configurations, and reveals a potential issue with CPO's exact constrained objective being unbounded for positive γ (claim 4). The empirical SOTA claim (6) was not reproduced at all due to missing code and compute.

JG1310/repro-chebyshev-policies-and-the-.paper_title: Chebyshev Policies and the Mountain Car Problem: Reinforcement Learning for Low-Dimensional Control Tasks

claims.claim: Theorem 2.4 gives the first closed-form optimal control solution for Mountain Car, α(t)=C·ẋ(t), a policy depending only on velocity, closing a 36-year-old open problem (Section 2, Theorem 2.4).
claims.evidence: A from-scratch reimplementation of π_ana on exact MountainCarContinuous-v0 dynamics achieves R̄=99.368 (paper: 99.39) with 100/100 goal-reaching and min-max 99.174–99.495 (paper: 99.15–99.52), and all six derivation checks (D1–D6) pass numerically, confirming the velocity-only policy α(t)=C·ẋ(t).

claims.claim: The derived analytical worst-case policy achieves returns of 99.15-99.52 on Mountain Car, versus 96.67 for ARS (regret 2.72), 93.91 for PPO (regret 5.48), and 94.61 for SAC (regret 4.78) (Section 2).
claims.evidence: The analytical policy's return band (99.15–99.52) is reproduced (99.174–99.495), but the specific baseline returns (ARS 96.67, PPO 93.91, SAC 94.61) and regret numbers (2.72, 5.48, 4.78) come from pretrained RL-Baselines3-Zoo agents that were not available; from-scratch MLP-ARS achieves regret 0.71 instead of 2.72, so the comparison numbers cannot be verified or falsified.

claims.claim: The degree-3 Chebyshev policy CH-3-ARS attains regret 0.65 on Mountain Car, a 4.18x improvement over neural ARS, using only 16 parameters versus 4,355 for a 2x64x64x1 MLP -- a 277x reduction in parameter count (Section 4, Section 5).
claims.evidence: The parameter-count identity (16 vs 4355, ratio 272×) is verified exactly, but the regret factor of 4.18× is not reproduced: the assigned number does not appear in the paper (which says 6.18×), and under controlled from-scratch comparison the Chebyshev policy fails at shared hyperparameters (0/100 goal) while the MLP succeeds; with policy-matched exploration noise=0.3, CH-3-ARS reaches R=98.26 (regret ~1.11), not the claimed 0.65.

claims.claim: CH-3-PPO attains regret 1.29 on Mountain Car, a 4.24x improvement over standard PPO, and CH-3-REINFORCE attains regret 0.77, a 3.53x improvement over standard ARS (Section 5).
claims.evidence: CH-3-PPO achieves regret 1.97 (not the claimed 1.29) and the 4.24× factor depends on unavailable pretrained-Zoo baselines; CH-3-REINFORCE fails entirely (0/100 goal) under shared hyperparameters, inverting the paper's claim that REINFORCE succeeds with Chebyshev but fails with neural policies—though the logbook attributes this to exploration-scale mismatch rather than a fundamental falsification.

claims.claim: Table 2 shows Chebyshev policies generalize beyond Mountain Car: CH-ARS reaches -150.8 vs ARS's -218.3 on Pendulum, and on real-world Aero 2 hardware CH-PPO reaches -55.8 vs PPO's -182.0, indicating improved sim-to-real transfer (Table 2).
claims.evidence: On Pendulum, Chebyshev beats MLP (CH-ARS −291.8 vs MLP −647.0), reproducing the qualitative ordering but not the paper's specific numbers (−150.8 vs −218.3); the Aero 2 real-world hardware experiment is entirely blocked and unreproduced, so the sim-to-real transfer claim is unaddressed.

JG1310/repro-chebyshev-policies-and-the-.overall: The logbook provides strong concrete evidence for the analytical Mountain Car controller (Claim 1) and the parameter-count identity, but the regret-reduction factors and baseline comparisons (Claims 2–4) are not reproducible without pretrained RL-Zoo baselines, and the Pendulum absolute numbers and Aero 2 hardware results (Claim 5) are not reproduced.

HamsterSashka/repro-finite-and-corruptio.paper_title: Finite and Corruption-Robust Regret Bounds in Online Inverse Linear Optimization under M-Convex Action Sets

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 achieves an uncorrupted regret bound of O(d^2) for online inverse linear optimization over M-convex feasible action sets (Theorem 3.1, Section 3)
claims.evidence: Across 316 runs on 4 M-convex families (d=4–12, T=5000) plus an adaptive worst-case adversary (d=4–16), #mistakes never exceeded C(d,2) (0 violations), fitted exponent p=1.82≤2, regret flat in T; non-M-convex control shows linear T-growth and bound violations.

claims.claim: With center-of-gravity-based prediction, Algorithm 1 improves the regret bound to O(d log d), covering M-convex sets including matroids (Theorem 4.2, Section 4)
claims.evidence: Exact center-of-gravity (via linear-extension DP) on 4 M-convex families and adaptive adversary (d=4–12, T=3000) yielded 0 violations of #mistakes ≤ log_{e/(e-1)}(d!) with max ratio 0.577; cog beats topo (24 vs 39 mistakes at d=12); non-M-convex control exceeds bound (142–242 mistakes vs 14–23).

claims.claim: Algorithm 2 attains a corruption-robust regret bound of O((C+1) d log d) against adversarially corrupted feedback, without requiring prior knowledge of the corruption count C (Theorem 5.3, Section 5)
claims.evidence: 63 configurations (d=6,8,10; C=0–16; 3 corruption patterns, T=3000) showed 0 violations of #mistakes ≤ (C+1)log_{e/(e-1)}(d!) and restarts ≤ C; measured C-slopes 8.0/12.5/18.0 below bound's 14.3/23.1/32.9; algorithm never reads C; control without restart grows linearly in T (regret 113–769 at T=3000).

claims.claim: A matching lower bound of Omega(d) is proved to hold even for M-convex instances, establishing near-tightness of the upper bounds (Theorem 6.1, Section 6)
claims.evidence: Reduction verified by brute force: 80 segments not M-convex in Z^m, 80 embeddings M-convex in Z^{m+1}, objective identity 0.0e+00, 0/1600 argmax mismatches; transcript invariance 0/300 mismatches across 5 learners; measured E[R_T] slopes 0.471–0.479 per dimension vs proof's ~0.475; oracle learner scores 0.000.

claims.claim: The volume-contraction lemma shows that whenever the algorithm's prediction errs, the feasible volume fraction shrinks by at least a factor of 1 - 1/e, underlying the O(d log d) regret proof (Lemma 4.1, Section 4)
claims.evidence: 355 exact rational volume ratios (linear-extension DP, not sampling) at every mistake round: 0 violations of Vol(P_{t+1})/Vol(P_t) ≤ 1−1/e, worst ratio 0.5333 vs threshold 0.6321; Gruenbaum intermediate step Vol(P\H)/Vol(P) ≥ 1/e held with worst 0.4667 vs 0.3679; control with topological-order point violates in up to 55.3% of rounds.

HamsterSashka/repro-finite-and-corruptio.overall: All five claims are supported by concrete numerical experiments with exact computation (linear-extension DP for volumes and centroids, brute-force M-convexity checks), multiple M-convex families, adaptive adversaries, and matched controls that break when hypotheses are relaxed. The reproduction is rigorous and directly tests the non-asymptotic bounds from each proof.

claims.claim: Reasoning collapse (template collapse) is diagnosed via two axes -- within-input diversity H(Z|X) and cross-input dependence I(X;Z) -- using mutual-information proxies (Retrieval-Acc and MI-ZScore-EMA) that correlate with performance (+0.39 Spearman) while entropy correlates negatively (-0.11 to -0.14) (Section 2, Table 1).
claims.evidence: A local numpy simulation with 200 synthetic sequences (vocab 1000, length 20) shows H(Z|X) drops from 7.45 to 0.24 bits and cross-input MI from 7.25 to 0.0015 bits in artificially collapsed vs. normal generation. claims.claim: The task gradient norm is upper-bounded by the square root of within-prompt reward variance, ||g_task|| <= sqrt(RV(x)), so when reward variance is low, input-agnostic regularization gradients dominate and reasoning collapses toward generic templates (Section 3, Figure 3, Table 2).
claims.evidence: A numpy toy simulation (200 inputs × 32 dims, no real LM gradients) swept reward variance from 1e-4 to 2.0 and found weak/negative correlations: gradient specificity vs log variance r=-0.0599, collapse fraction vs log variance r=-0.1064, with collapse fractions staying near zero (0.01–0.075). The mathematical bound ||g_task|| <= sqrt(RV(x)) was not formally verified, and the toy results actually fail to reproduce the claimed mechanism.

claims.claim: A quartile ablation on reward variance shows performance degrades monotonically from the highest-variance quartile (Q1) to the lowest (Q4), providing causal evidence for the reward-variance-to-collapse mechanism (Section 3, Table 6).
claims.evidence: A local numpy simulation of 10,000 synthetic tokens binned into quartiles by reward variance shows degradation when removing Q2 (0.006923) exceeds degradation when removing the highest-variance quartile (0.006613), which is non-monotonic and contradicts the claim. Additionally, per-quartile mean rewards are non-monotonic (Q2=0.0186 vs highest-var=-0.0220). This is a purely synthetic setup with no real RL training.

claims.claim: Reward-variance-aware (SNR-aware) top-p filtering, which retains only the highest-reward-variance prompts before each policy update, yields an average +6.9% improvement over the PPO baseline across seven environments (Sokoban, FrozenLake, MetaMathQA, Countdown, SearchQA, WebShop, DeepCoder), four algorithms (PPO, DAPO, GRPO, Dr. GRPO), multiple model scales (Qwen2.5 0.5B-7B, Llama3.2-3B), and both text and vision-language modalities (Qwen2.5-VL) (Section 4, Table 3, Table 4).
claims.evidence: A numpy toy proxy simulating four modalities and three scale regimes yields mean_delta_perf=+0.0038 (0.38%), far below the claimed +6.9%, with mean_delta_spec=-0.0007 (negative, contradicting improved input dependence). No real environments (Sokoban, FrozenLake, etc.), no real algorithms (PPO, DAPO, GRPO, Dr. GRPO), and no real models (Qwen2.5, Llama3.2) were used.

claims.claim: Reward-variance computation adds less than 0.1% overhead, and filtering with rho=0.9 reduces per-step training time by 26-41% while matching or exceeding unfiltered performance (Table 5).
claims.evidence: A local operation-count analysis estimates variance tracking overhead at 0.004% (below 0.1%), but this is an analytical estimate, not a runtime measurement. The ρ=0.9 filtering computation reduction is estimated at 10%, well below the claimed 26-41%, and the claim that filtered performance matches or exceeds unfiltered performance was not tested at all.

claims.claim: The RCB algorithm achieves an O(sqrt(KdT)) regret bound, where K is the number of arms, d the feature dimension, and T the time horizon (Section 4.3, Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Confound-controlled fixed-gap environment measurements show horizon exponents of 0.5161 (K=5) and 0.5148 (K=20) and dimension exponent 0.5475 against theory 0.5; the K-exponent of 0.7027 is explained by the (K−1)/√K factor from IPGS (best-fit power law 0.7020 over K∈{2..40}), and the derived closed form R=(σ/2)·((K−1)/√K)·√(dW) fits all 20 configurations with R²=0.9974 and 2.4% mean error. A proof audit found a constant error (151σ→≥176σ) but it is T/K/d-independent, leaving the Õ order intact.

claims.claim: RCB simultaneously satisfies an epsilon-Dynamic Bayesian Incentive Compatibility (epsilon-DBIC) constraint, requiring a minimum cold-start sample size N(epsilon) that scales cubically with the number of arms K and linearly with dimension d (Section 4.2, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Running the real mechanism shows ε-DBIC is violated in 5.6% of cold-start rounds at K=10 (worst gain −1.83 vs budget 0.05), with violation rate growing with K; additionally, N(ε)'s effective d-exponent is 0.0453 at the paper's own d∈{2,3,5,10,70} (not linear), and Theorem 1's N(ε) is infeasible at every horizon tested (up to 46,346× the warfarin cohort).

claims.claim: The two-stage mechanism separates a Cold Start Stage (Algorithm 1), which explores products while preserving incentive compatibility, from an Exploitation Stage (Algorithm 2) using inverse proportional gap sampling (Section 3.1-3.2).
claims.evidence: All 5 structural checks pass on a real run (K=5, d=5, T=30000): both stages reached, all 4 phases exercised, 0 miscounted organic rounds of 1537, every arm saturates before transition; the specific cold-start rule keeps ε-DBIC gain ≥ −ε in 95.1% of rounds vs 28.5% for a uniform-random baseline, isolating the design's incentive-protecting effect.

claims.claim: The analysis reveals a tradeoff in which larger incentive budgets epsilon reduce required cold-start sample sizes but affect the regret guarantee (Section 4, Theorem 1 and Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: N(ε) is strictly monotonically decreasing in ε (closed form confirmed numerically), and running the real mechanism confirms operationally: measured T_cold falls from 196,520 → 2,453 and total regret falls from 47,550 → 628 as ε rises from 0.02 to 0.12, demonstrating the tradeoff in lock-step.

claims.claim: In warfarin-dosing simulations using real data, RCB achieves a weighted risk score of approximately 0.29 compared to a physician baseline of 0.20, with error rates around 35% (Section 5.2, Table 1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: On the real 5,528-patient IWPC cohort, the physician baseline (error 0.3882, risk score 0.2236) closely matches the paper (≈0.388, 0.20), but RCB's measured weighted risk score is 0.2599–0.2636 across ε∈{0.025,0.035,0.045}, well short of the claimed ≈0.291; a full-information oracle ceiling of 0.3734 confirms 0.29 is achievable but RCB run online does not reach it.

ai-sherpa/rcb-two-stage-incentivized-exp.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous from-scratch reproduction with confound-controlled regret measurements, a proof audit, unit-tested formula verification, and real-data warfarin simulations. ai-sherpa/dimension-free-diffusion-sampl.paper_title: High-accuracy and dimension-free sampling with diffusions

claims.claim: Global convergence guarantees for the sketch-and-project Newton iterates are established (Theorem 3.8, Section 3.2).

claims.claim: A spectral radius recursion derived via the Cayley-Hamilton theorem proves contraction at rate 1 - sqrt(mu_t/nu_t) for the accelerated sketching operator (Lemma 3.6).
claims.evidence: The Cayley-Hamilton recursion p_tau = Tr·p_{tau-1} − Det·p_{tau-2} is verified to machine precision (max error 3.11e-15), the supremum spectral radius equals the bound 1−sqrt(mu/nu) = 0.9258, and the accelerated per-step rate (0.912) beats the unaccelerated rate (0.933).

sotayamashita/repro-saqnn-universal-appr.paper_title: SAQNN: Spectral Adaptive Quantum Neural Network as a Universal Approximator

ai-sherpa/boundary-fdr-domino-repro.paper_title: Generalized Boundary FDR Control under Arbitrary Dependence: An Approach on Closure Principle

claims.claim: The Domino procedure controls the k-boundary FDR (k-bFDR) - defined as the probability that the k least-significant discoveries in the rejection set are all false - under arbitrary dependence among p-values or e-values, without structural assumptions (Section 2, Definition 2.2; Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: 48 Monte Carlo cells (8 adversarial dependence structures including near-comonotone, boundary-negative equicorrelation, AR(1), block, and t-copula at m=100) show max measured k-bFDR = 0.0495 ≤ alpha=0.05, while uncontrolled comparators (naive: 0.9972, BH: 0.1907) blow through alpha under identical dependence, confirming the metric detects violations.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 proves that the rejection set R produced by the Domino algorithm satisfies k-bFDR(R) <= alpha under arbitrary dependence (Section 3, Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: Across all 48 cells, max k-bFDR/alpha ratio = 0.989 (never violated); tightness confirmed at the independent global-null k=1 instance where measured 0.0475 matches exact closed form 1-(1-alpha/m)^m = 0.04878 within 0.85 MC SE, and BH reaches 0.1907 under the same DGP showing the bound is informative.

claims.claim: Proposition 2.3 shows k-bFDR reduces to k-FWER under the global null and is otherwise upper bounded by k-FWER, situating k-bFDR between per-comparison and family-wise error control (Section 2, Proposition 2.3).
claims.evidence: 0/150,635 pathwise mismatches between k-bFDR and k-FWER indicators across all replications; non-vacuous slack demonstrated in 18/24 pi1=0.3 cells (e.g., equicorr_rho_neg_boundary k=1: bFDR 0.0137 vs k-FWER 0.0443, a 3.2× gap). The logbook honestly notes the equality under global null is near-definitional, but the measured slack under signal is a genuine quantitative result.

claims.evidence: The closed-form e-closure rule (eq. 9) matches literal exhaustive 2^(m-1)-superset brute force with 0/2000 mismatches across 5 dependence structures at m=9, and Domino-E (configured with this local test) achieves max k-bFDR 0.0051 ≤ 0.05 over 16 adversarial m=100 cells. The logbook transparently notes it does not re-verify the algebraic identity proof itself, but the tractable content—exhaustive agreement and control validity—is concretely demonstrated.

claims.claim: Algorithms 3 and 4 reduce the computational complexity of implementing the closure-based procedure from exponential O(2^m) to polynomial O(m^2) for Bonferroni and harmonic-mean-based local tests (Section 3, Algorithms 3-4).
claims.evidence: Corrected polynomial scan matches exhaustive O(2^(m-k))-superset ground truth 0/420 mismatches (m∈{8,10,12,14}, k∈{1,2}); wall-time log-log slope 0.45 ≤ 2 confirms sub-quadratic scaling; 37273× measured speedup at m=20. However, Algorithm 4 (harmonic-mean local test) is explicitly not re-implemented, and Algorithm 3 as printed is falsified (214/240 exhaustive mismatches, k-bFDR inflated to 19.9× alpha)—the corrected factor (m-l+k)/k is what achieves the reduction.

ai-sherpa/boundary-fdr-domino-repro.overall: This logbook provides strong, independently re-implemented Monte Carlo and exhaustive-brute-force evidence supporting all five claims at the paper's own m=100 scale across genuinely adversarial dependence structures, with uncontrolled comparators confirming the metrics detect violations.
