The resulting cost proxy SA*H_eff^2/eps^2 scales as eps^-4.0 across all sizes in the sweep, confirming both the H-dependence and the worse eps^-4 rate.

claims.claim: Lemma 5.1 bounds the sub-optimality of a greedy policy relative to Q by the span seminorm of the residual, 0 <= g*_P - g^pi_P(s) <= Sp(T_P(Q) - Q) (Section 5, Lemma 5.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook tests 6000 random Q vectors on the base MDP and 12200 total across the size sweep, computing greedy policies, their true robust average reward via RRVI, and the residual span. Zero violations of 0 <= g*-g^pi <= sp(T_P(Q)-Q) are found across all instances and sizes.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 establishes that RHI's iterates converge exactly, with Sp(T_P(Q_k) - Q_k) approaching 0 as k goes to infinity (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Exact RHI run for 3000 iterations shows residual span decreasing from 2.113621 to 2.337e-03 with a log-log decay slope of -0.999 (theory O(1/k)), and final sub-optimality g*-g^pi = 0.0e+00. The O(1/k) decay is stable across the size sweep with slopes in [-0.998, -0.998].

claims.claim: Instead of a multi-level Monte Carlo estimator (noted to induce unbounded sample complexity in this setting), RHI uses a recursive sampling scheme that estimates successive differences T_P(Q_k) - T_P(Q_{k-1}) (Section 5, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The successive-difference oracle estimate (-0.085634 +/- 0.004513) is within noise of the true difference (-0.076349). The K-order MLMC bias decreases from 8.40e-02 (K=0) to 9.39e-04 (K=4), while the single-level estimator at matched budget only reaches 0.0269, confirming the recursive scheme's bias reduction advantage across all tested sizes.

claims.claim: The paper's sample complexity result is claimed to be the first finite-sample guarantee for model-free robust average-reward MDPs, covering both contamination and l_p-norm uncertainty sets (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: RHI converges at O(1/k) rate on both contamination (residual to 2.33e-03) and l_2 uncertainty sets (residual to 2.41e-03), with convergence stable across the size sweep. The 'first guarantee' priority claim is correctly disclosed as not computationally verifiable; the checkable coverage content is confirmed.

snaykey/repro-robust-avg-reward-rl.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all six claims through from-scratch NumPy implementations of robust Bellman operators, RRVI ground truth, exact and data-driven RHI, and the K-order MLMC oracle, with scaling laws verified across a size sweep up to SA=1000. The reproduction is rigorous and transparent about limitations such as variable hit rates at small epsilon and the non-verifiability of the priority claim.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows a symmetric smoothing operator with positive coefficients can be rescaled by a diagonal matrix (via a symmetric Sinkhorn iteration) into a diffusion operator that is self-adjoint with respect to a mass-weighted inner product (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: On a 120-point Gaussian kernel with non-uniform mass, the logbook measures M-self-adjointness residual 2.78e-17, mass conservation 3.58e-09, entrywise positivity (min 1.99e-13), spectrum [0,1], and uniqueness via 7 random initializations converging to the same Q (deviation 8.87e-10).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 proves that for Gaussian and exponential kernels, the Sinkhorn-normalized operators converge uniformly on bounded domains to continuous diffusion operators as sampling resolution increases (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: On [0,1]^2 with fixed sigma=0.15, resolutions N=64–2048, both Gaussian and exponential kernels, sup-norm error to a 4096-point reference decreases from ~0.047 to 0.010 and ~0.041 to 0.0087 respectively, with monotonically decreasing successive differences, demonstrating uniform convergence behavior.

claims.claim: The symmetric Sinkhorn algorithm empirically requires only 5 to 10 iterations to reduce normalization error below 0.1% (Section 4/5, empirical convergence results).
claims.evidence: The Eq.(34) normalization error metric was implemented and measured across 5 independent settings (point clouds, GMM, voxel sphere shell, varying kernels and N), yielding iteration counts {5, 6, 6, 6, 7} to reach E < 0.1%, all within the claimed 5–10 window.

claims.claim: The normalized operators simultaneously satisfy symmetry, mass conservation, entrywise positivity, and spectral damping (eigenvalues in [0,1]), properties not jointly satisfied by standard row- or symmetric-normalization schemes (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: On a shared 100-point Gaussian kernel with non-uniform mass, all four diffusion properties were measured for Sinkhorn Q (all pass), row-normalization (fails M-symmetry, residual 0.13), and symmetric-normalization (fails mass conservation, error 0.30), directly confirming the joint-property claim.

claims.claim: The method is demonstrated on point clouds, sparse voxel grids (jaw bone geometry), and Gaussian mixture models with covariance-aware kernels, showing Laplacian-like smoothing on each irregular data type (Section 5, experiments).
claims.evidence: Laplacian-like smoothing was demonstrated on synthetic proxy instances of each modality class (300-point sphere, 568-voxel torus, 60-component random GMM) rather than the paper's real datasets such as jaw-bone geometry; energy decay and mass conservation were measured but at reduced scope and scale.

claims.claim: Shape analysis experiments on the Armadillo mesh show spectral distributions remain consistent across sampling modalities, with eigenvalue divergence appearing only at scales matching sampling resolution, validating the Theorem 4.2 convergence guarantee (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Cross-modality spectral consistency was reproduced on a unit sphere proxy (with analytic LB spectrum as ground truth) rather than the Stanford Armadillo mesh specified in the claim; the 1-3-5-7 degeneracy pattern and 12.6–27.4% cross-modality agreement were measured, but on simplified geometry at moderate point counts.

snaykey/repro-sinkhorn-diffusion.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification of the paper's core theoretical claims (Theorems 4.1/4.2, algorithmic convergence, joint diffusion properties) on constructed kernels at moderate scale, but the experimental/phenomenological claims (5, 6) are addressed only on synthetic proxy data rather than the paper's real datasets and geometries.

claims.claim: Do-Shapley values can be computed exactly in O(r(d+e+T)) time, where r is the number of irreducible sets, d the number of dimensions, e the number of edges, and T the value-function evaluation time, versus the naive 2^d complexity (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Over 60 random SCMs (d=4..10), the class-based exact algorithm matches brute-force 2^d Shapley values to max abs error 2.93e-14 and issues exactly r value-function queries per trial (vs 2^d for brute force), directly confirming the O(r(d+e+T)) complexity claim with concrete numerical evidence.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 shows the do-Shapley value phi_i is identifiable if and only if nu({j}) is identifiable for all j in [d], reducing identifiability checks from r coalitions to just d singleton coalitions (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: An identifiability oracle validated on 4 textbook graphs (bow-arc, front-door, chain, front-door set form) was applied to 400 random ADMGs with latent confounders; the iff (all singletons identifiable <=> all classes identifiable) held in 400/400 cases, and the check count reduced from mean r=35.3 to d≈5 singletons. The caveat is that the oracle is a district-based approximation rather than the full Shpitser-Pearl ID procedure, but the core theorem's logical structure is empirically confirmed.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.1 establishes that for any closed set with a basis, removing any basis element yields another closed set, enabling efficient lattice traversal via Algorithm 2 (Lemma 3.1, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive brute-force verification over 23,333 closed sets from 400 random DAGs (d=3..8) found zero violations of either part of Lemma 3.1 (basis-element removal yields closed set; non-full closed set has valid extension). Cross-confirmed by C1's machine-precision agreement where Algorithm 2's traversal must reach all r classes.

claims.claim: Algorithm 3 (boundary sampling) guarantees discovery of min(m, r) distinct equivalence classes using m queries, running in O(m*d(d+e)) time (Section on estimator performance, Algorithm 3).
claims.evidence: The boundary sampler returned exactly min(m,r) distinct classes in 400/400 cases across budgets m=r/3..2r, with every accepted query being a new class, while the naive random sampler found only ~61 of ~105 classes at m=r. The per-query work is O(d(d+e)) via FindClass calls, matching the stated O(m*d(d+e)) runtime.

claims.claim: The doRegressionMSR estimator consistently outperforms baseline variants and exhibits a phase transition at m=r, where error vanishes to machine precision while structure-agnostic methods retain variance (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: The phase transition mechanism is demonstrated on 40 synthetic linear-Gaussian SCMs (d=5..10) with a simplified structure-aware estimator (truncated class weights) vs a permutation Monte-Carlo baseline, not the paper's doRegressionMSR on TALENT-benchmark learned graphs. The aware estimator reaches 1.53e-30 relative MSE at m>=r while the agnostic baseline retains ~1.7e-2, reproducing the qualitative phase transition but on a proxy setup rather than the paper's actual estimator and data.

claims.claim: Real-world causal structures tend to be sparse, so the number of irreducible sets r scales between the exponential worst case 2^d and the linear lower bound d (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The two extremal families (chain r=d+1, independent r=2^d) are verified exactly for d=3..12, and 120 random sparse DAGs all satisfy d<=r<=2^d with mean r/2^d=0.69. However, the claim is specifically about 'real-world causal structures' and the paper's Figure 4 uses TALENT-learned graphs; synthetic random DAGs are a proxy for real-world structures, not the actual data the claim references.

snaykey/repro-do-shapley.overall: The logbook provides strong, concrete evidence for the four structural/algorithmic claims (C1-C4) through exact computation against brute-force ground truth with thousands of test cases. The two empirical claims (C5-C6) are addressed on synthetic proxy setups that reproduce the qualitative mechanisms but do not use the paper's actual TALENT-benchmark data or the doRegressionMSR estimator.

sotayamashita/repro-budgeted-active-expe.paper_title: Budgeted Active Experimentation for Treatment Effect Estimation from Observational and Randomized Data

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 implements a budgeted active experimentation procedure combining observational logs and an unlabeled candidate pool via a multi-criteria acquisition function (Equation 7) balancing epistemic uncertainty, domain discrepancy, and overlap deficit (Section 3, Algorithm 1, Equation 7).
claims.evidence: Independent implementation of Algorithm 1 on a 48-candidate, 8-type pool with budget 16 correctly computes all three rank-normalized acquisition terms with weights (0.5,1.0,0.7), selects top-4 per round across 4 rounds, and ablations setting each weight to zero change the first-round selection, confirming all three components are active.

claims.claim: Lemma 4.4 establishes that pseudo-outcomes remain unbiased under adaptive sampling because randomization protects unbiasedness regardless of how covariates are selected (Lemma 4.4).
claims.evidence: Exact enumeration across dimensions {2,4,8,16} and assignment probabilities {0.25,0.40,0.50,0.70,0.75} yields maximum conditional-expectation error 1.11e-16; 640 independent 512-query adaptive sequences all have zero inside 95% CIs; a destructive control selecting covariates after seeing treatment produces bias 1.0420, confirming the timing assumption matters.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.5 provides finite-sample self-normalized concentration bounds, controlling the error ||θ^λ - θ*||_{Vλ} for adaptively collected data (Theorem 4.5).
claims.evidence: 1,920 adaptive experiments across 48 conditions (dimensions {2,4,8,16} × budgets {64,128,256,512} × confidence {0.20,0.10,0.05}, 40 repetitions each) all show empirical simultaneous coverage at least nominal and every left/right ratio ≤ 1 for the self-normalized bound.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.8 proves asymptotic normality via a martingale central limit theorem, showing sqrt(B)(θ^0 - θ*) converges to N(0, Σπ⁻¹ΩπΣπ⁻¹) (Theorem 4.8).
claims.evidence: 160 independent adaptive sequences per budget level {64,128,256,512,1024,2048} for a 4-dimensional effect yield RMSE budget slope -0.48267 (close to -0.5), scaled covariance coefficient of variation 0.01741, and marginal 95% coverage 0.931–0.975, consistent with martingale CLT predictions.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.9 establishes a minimax lower bound showing the sqrt(d/B) estimation rate cannot be beaten, with Corollary 4.10 confirming the estimator achieves minimax optimality up to logarithmic factors (Theorem 4.9, Corollary 4.10).
claims.evidence: Upper-bound grid over dimensions {2,4,8,16} × budgets {256,512,1024,2048} with 80 repetitions gives dimension exponent +0.57391 and budget exponent -0.50521; separate lower-bound certificate over d∈{2,4,8,16,32} shows KL upper bound 0.0512 independent of d and B with PEHE separation proportional to sqrt(d/B).

claims.claim: On ride-hailing data, the budgeted active experimentation framework reduces RCT labeling cost by approximately 80% compared to a random sampling baseline at comparable estimation performance (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The proprietary ride-hailing data (4.5M/6.5M observational rows, 1.2M candidate pool, 1.3M test set) is unavailable with no public download or implementation; the logbook preserves hyperparameters but does not execute any experiment on real or substitute data.

sotayamashita/repro-budgeted-active-expe.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from independent implementations supporting all five theoretical/algorithmic claims (Algorithm 1 mechanics, Lemma 4.4 unbiasedness, Theorem 4.5 finite-sample bounds, Theorem 4.8 asymptotic normality, Theorem 4.9/Corollary 4.10 minimax rate) via exact enumeration, Monte Carlo simulations, ablations, and destructive controls at moderate scale. The industrial ride-hailing claim remains unaddressed because the proprietary data is unavailable and no substitute experiment was run.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 establishes the scalar-identity case, showing SSMs with state matrices A_t = a_t I_N are equivalent to 1-semiseparable masked attention with a causal mask (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Both the scalar-identity SSM recurrence and the 1-SS masked-attention form were implemented independently and compared over 30 random configurations (T up to 24, N up to 6, d up to 5) in float64, yielding max error 1.78e-15 — machine-precision agreement confirming the identity.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 gives a necessary and sufficient condition for an N-dimensional SSM to admit a 1-semiseparable masked-attention dual: its corresponding N-semiseparable matrix must have diagonal blocks each containing at most N new columns (Section 4.4, Definition 4.2).
claims.evidence: A from-scratch new-column counter (Definition 4.2) was tested on positive cases (12 random fine 1-SS matrices, all #new-cols ≤ N), the Remark 4.1 example (3 new columns > N=2), and negative cases (I+E_{T,1} with #new-cols = T−1 = 11 at T=12), confirming both directions of the iff.

claims.claim: General diagonal SSMs are shown to preserve the same O(NTd) training complexity as the scalar-identity case (Algorithm 1) while supporting richer, per-channel dynamics (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 was compared against both the direct recurrence and explicit kernel to 8.9e-16 over 20 random cases; exact flop count measured as 8192 = 4·4·64·8 matching 4NTd; empirical log-log scaling slopes of 1.00 (recurrence) vs 2.12 (attention) confirm O(T) vs O(T²).

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 proves the equivalence between N-semiseparable matrices and N-SSS (sequentially semiseparable) representable matrices (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: Both implications tested: N-SSS ⇒ N-SS (sep_rank ≤ N over 20 random diagonal time-varying SSMs) and N-SS ⇒ N-SSS (reconstruction error 1.78e-15 over 20 random general semiseparable matrices); the B.3 rank table (1,2,1,3) including duplicated-decay rank collapse reproduced exactly.

claims.claim: Section 5 demonstrates a limitation: softmax attention is incompatible with the semiseparable-matrix duality framework due to rank explosion, and general (non-diagonal) SSMs may lack any attention dual despite having low state dimension (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Softmax rank explosion confirmed: rank(V)=1 → rank(softmax(V))=T at T=6 exactly, plus random causal softmax near-full rank sweep (gap T−rank = 2–14 for T up to 320); the 2-SS matrix I+E_{T,1} shown to have no 1-SS dual (new-cols 11 ≫ N=2, ALS fit residual 1.02 vs 6.6e-15 for a control matrix).

snaykey/repro-ssm-duality.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical verification of all five theorem-level claims by independently implementing the SSM recurrences, attention duals, and structural counters from the paper's definitions, checking identities to float64 machine precision and structural counts exactly on small but non-trivial instances. These are mathematical identity and structural characterization claims, so the small-scale numerical verification is appropriate and faithful rather than toy.

claims.claim: In the zero-temperature (hardmax) limit of self-attention dynamics with negative-definite key-query interaction, token updates coincide with a Frank-Wolfe step on a quadratic objective over the convex hull of the tokens, and Theorem 3.1 gives a linear convergence rate bound J^t(x_i^{t+1}) ≤ (2/(t+1))·λ_max(B_0)·diam(K^0)^2 (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Direct numerical comparison shows hardmax step equals Frank-Wolfe step to 3.331e-16, softmax converges to hardmax at β=5000 (error 4.312e-07), and the Theorem 3.1 bound is never violated across 2400 checks (worst ratio 0.6014) over 40 random instances.

claims.claim: When the key-query matrix is positive definite, Theorem 4.2 shows super-exponential convergence of tokens to vertices, and Proposition 4.5 shows the induced cell structure coincides with B-norm Voronoi cells when vertices have equal norm (Section 4, Theorem 4.2, Proposition 4.5).
claims.evidence: Closed-form trajectory matches simulation to 1.665e-16, vertices stationary to 5.551e-17, and B-norm Voronoi cell agreement is 100% with equal-norm vertices but fails (4819 disagreements) when norms differ, confirming both Theorem 4.2 and Proposition 4.5.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.8 establishes well-posedness of the singular ODE limit governing the hardmax dynamics (Section 4, Theorem 4.8, Equation 4.4).
claims.evidence: Under the theorem's genericity conditions, the singular ODE reduces to a linear ODE whose analytic residual is 1.110e-16; an independent RK4 integrator of the discontinuous field agrees to 4.176e-12, continuous-dependence Lipschitz ratio is 0.0498, and solutions stay in K — numerically witnessing all four well-posedness properties.

claims.claim: At finite inverse temperature β, Theorem 5.2 shows interior particles reach near-vertex configurations in O(1) steps with high probability, while Theorem 5.4 shows these metastable configurations persist for exponentially long times (on the order of e^β steps) before eventual collapse to a single cluster (Section 5, Theorem 5.2, Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: Monte-Carlo of the finite-β Gumbel Markov chain shows median hitting time T1=1 (O(1)) across β=3..8, and median residence time T2 grows exponentially in β (log-linear slope 0.507, correlation 0.963), matching the predicted e^β scaling signature.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 shows the argmax operation generically produces a singleton, and Lemma 2.2 shows the convex hull of tokens shrinks under step sizes γ^t ∈ (0,1), underpinning the Frank-Wolfe reformulation of hardmax attention (Section 2, Lemma 2.1, Lemma 2.2).
claims.evidence: 20000 random configurations yield 0 argmax ties (100% singleton) with a constructible measure-zero tie case, and hull containment holds with max LP slack 1.566e-7 with non-increasing diameter over 200 trajectories × 25 steps.

snaykey/repro-attention-frank-wolfe.overall: The logbook provides concrete, independent numerical evidence supporting all five claims through direct implementation of the paper's operators and Monte-Carlo simulations. The reproduction is CPU-only at modest scale but faithfully tests the paper's identities, rates, and scaling predictions with real runs and numbers.

snaykey/repro-multitask-linreg.paper_title: Multi-task Linear Regression without Eigenvalue Lower Bounds: Adaptivity, Robustness, and Safety

claims.claim: Theorem 2 establishes an in-sample MSE bound for each task j that guarantees safety, ℰⱼⁱⁿ(θ̂ⱼ) ≲ q²(d/n)ζ regardless of the balancedness constant B, outlier fraction ε, or heterogeneity δ (Section 5.1, Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Direct numerical check of the safety inequality across 4 adversarial regimes (d=30, n=100, m=30): max in-sample MSE ratios to (d/n)ζ are 0.09–0.22, all well below 1, while DP blows up to 9.96 under 40% outliers of radius 50, confirming safety independent of B, ε, δ.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 also shows a transfer guarantee for inlier tasks when B ≲ min(1/ε, m): ℰⱼⁱⁿ(θ̂ⱼ) ≲ (Bd/mn + min(Bδ², d/n) + B²ε²d/n)ζ, achieved without knowing ε, δ, or the inlier set S (Section 5.1, Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Independent rerun of δ- and ε-sweeps (12 MC reps, 5-fold CV) shows MTLR all-task MSE 0.019–0.035 (δ-sweep) and 0.014–0.066 (ε-sweep), matching the paper's reported ranges in order of magnitude and monotonicity; MTLR beats ITL by ~20× and DP throughout, with q selected by CV blind to ε, δ, S.

claims.claim: Assumption 1 (Balancedness) replaces the classical Lower Boundedness of Second Moments condition ρI ⪯ Σⱼ with the one-sided condition Σⱼ ⪯ B·Σ_S, accommodating rank-deficient or decaying covariate spectra where prior eigenvalue-lower-bound approaches (e.g. Duan & Wang 2023, depending on 1/ρ²) fail (Section 4, Assumption 1).
claims.evidence: Direct computation of both constants: for rank-deficient Example 3, ρ_min≈0 so 1/ρ²=∞ (vacuous) while B_emp=1.2500 exactly matches the paper's closed form |S|/|S∩I|=10/8; under eigendecay α=0→2, 1/ρ² explodes from 4.7e3 to 3.8e13 while B_emp stays flat at ~2.0–2.1.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 extends the in-sample MSE guarantees of Theorem 2 to population risk via an empirical-to-population comparability constant νⱼ, retaining an intrinsic-dimension fallback for the safety guarantee (Section 5.2, Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: ν_j computed as n grows shows monotonic decrease 8.48→1.27 (n:40→1280), and the comparability bound E_j ≤ ν_j E^in_j holds for 100% (30/30) of tasks with E^in=0.0235, E_pop=0.0244, ν̄=1.91 on a fitted MTLR model.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 extends the same adaptive safety/transfer MSE guarantees to generalized linear models under bounded-domain assumptions (Section 6, Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Logistic MTL (d=20, m=30, n=150) with matrix-weighted penalty shows transfer: related-task E^in=0.033 vs ITL 0.174 (5.3× improvement) in the favorable regime, and safety: bounded error (mean 0.35, max 0.90) under δ=3, ε=0.3 contamination, tracking ITL rather than collapsing.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 solves a joint convex objective ℒ(Θ)=Σⱼ wⱼ(fⱼ(θⱼ)+λⱼ‖θⱼ-β‖_{Σⱼ}) that penalizes disagreement in prediction space (via task-specific norms) rather than raw parameter space (Section 3, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Prediction-space identity ‖v‖_Σj = (1/√n)‖X_j v‖ confirmed to machine precision (max error 1.11e-16), and joint convexity confirmed with 0 chord violations over 400 random segments on m=8, d=12, n=60 tasks.

snaykey/repro-multitask-linreg.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all 6 claims through an independent from-scratch NumPy/SciPy implementation on non-trivial synthetic setups (d=20–30, m=30, n=100–200). Structural theorem claims are verified by direct bound/constant computation, while empirical transfer claims are reproduced via the paper's own sweeps with results landing in reported ranges.

claims.claim: RACO is an offline, reward-free preference-alignment method that accepts user-specified objective weights and explicitly handles conflicting objectives (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The pairwise logistic loss formula is verified against closed-form (residual < 1e-12) and a 3-parameter model pipeline computes two objective-specific losses with non-colinear gradients and applies CAGrad-Clip, but this is a toy model, not a real LLM setup as implied by Table 1.

claims.claim: The method uses CAGrad-Clip to limit correction gradients so updates better respect preferred objective trade-offs (Figure 1, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: CAGrad-Clip solver is verified on synthetic gradient witnesses (e.g., g1=[1,-4], g2=[-1,1]) finding interior α≈0.356 with scale invariance across 10^-8 to 10^8, and Theorem 3.2 shows Γ improvement of 0.2091, but only on synthetic 2D gradient examples, not real LLM training.

claims.claim: On TL;DR summarization, RACO achieves better Pareto frontiers for conciseness-quality and faithfulness-quality trade-offs than AMoPO and weighted-loss DPO baselines (Figure 2, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states TL;DR fine-tuning was not re-executed; the CPU Pareto proxy uses a 56-parameter synthetic model with linear scalarization as baseline, not TL;DR data or the AMoPO/weighted-loss DPO baselines, and RACO does not strictly dominate in any of 5 weight settings (hypervolume 0.7398 vs 0.7487).

claims.claim: On BeaverTails safety alignment, RACO improves harmlessness-helpfulness Pareto trade-offs across Qwen3 and Gemma3 setups (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: BeaverTails safety alignment with Qwen3/Gemma3 was not re-executed; the proxy experiment does not use BeaverTails data, does not involve Qwen3 or Gemma3 models, and does not measure harmlessness-helpfulness trade-offs.

claims.claim: Ablations show clipping and the correction-radius constant affect validation margins and Pareto frontiers (Figure 5, Figure 6).
claims.evidence: A clip-radius ablation on the 56-parameter synthetic proxy (c ∈ {0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9}) shows measurable shifts in converged operating point and final losses, consistent with the paper's ablation direction, but at toy scale with small effect sizes and no reproduction of Figure 5-6 magnitudes.

wrice/repro-raco.overall: The logbook provides rigorous mathematical and algorithmic verification of RACO's core components (loss formulation, CAGrad-Clip solver, Theorems 3.1-3.2) on synthetic toy setups, but does not reproduce any of the paper's empirical LLM results on TL;DR or BeaverTails. Claims 3 and 4 are entirely unaddressed at the paper's scale, while Claims 1, 2, and 5 are verified only on simplified proxy models.

ParetoOptimal/repro-ga20h0vr6f.paper_title: Reinforcement Learning for Reachability: Guaranteeing Asymptotic Optimality

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes a PAC guarantee that, for a sufficiently small guessed minimum transition probability p_k, there exists a number of simulations N_k such that the learned policy is ε_k-optimal with probability at least 1-δ_k (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: At stage k=4 (p_k=1/16 ≤ p_min=1/D), 100% of learned policies are eps_k-optimal (eps_k=0.0625) across 300 MDPs, exceeding the required 1-delta_k=93.75%, providing concrete empirical support for the PAC guarantee.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 shows that once the approximation error ε_k falls below a threshold ε_diff—the minimum value gap between optimal and suboptimal memoryless deterministic policies—any ε_k-optimal policy is guaranteed to be exactly optimal, not merely near-optimal (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive enumeration of all memoryless deterministic policies on 199 MDPs with genuine optimality gaps confirms that every eps_diff-optimal policy is exactly optimal, with zero exceptions, directly testing the theorem's implication.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 proves that using a summable failure schedule δ_k = 1/2^k, the Borel-Cantelli lemma guarantees only finitely many stages fail, so the algorithm's policy is exactly optimal from some finite stage onward with probability 1 (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: Per-stage failure rate decreases sharply from 30% toward zero and all runs stabilize at the optimal policy from a finite stage onward; the logbook transparently notes the residual floor is a finite-compute artifact of capping N_k, consistent with the asymptotic theory.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 bounds ε_diff via transition-complexity parameter D, showing ‖v_π − v_π'‖_1 ≥ (2D)^(-2|A|·|S|) 2^(-2|S|) for any two distinct memoryless deterministic policies, giving an explicit MDP-structure-dependent characterization of when exact optimality is reached (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive enumeration of all policy pairs on 200 rational-transition MDPs (D=6) shows every nonzero L1 value gap (minimum observed 0.00226) exceeds the Theorem 4.1 bound of 2.55e-25, with no gap falling strictly between 0 and the bound.

claims.claim: Empirical evaluation on standardized benchmarks shows the algorithm's policy becomes exactly optimal at a median stage k=2, far earlier than the stage (k≈16) at which the theoretical worst-case value-bound guarantees convergence (empirical validation section).
claims.evidence: Optimal policy emerges at median stage 1 (mean 1.85), close to the paper's reported median 2 (mean 2.3), and far below the worst-case bound stage of ~16, reproducing the early-emergence finding; however, the logbook does not clearly identify 'standardized benchmarks' and the median differs slightly from the paper.

ParetoOptimal/repro-ga20h0vr6f.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence across 200-300 generated tabular MDPs supporting all five claims, including exhaustive policy enumeration for the theoretical bounds and staged-simulation results for convergence behavior. However, only a validation script reading cached JSON is shown—the actual MDP generation and simulation code is absent, and the benchmarks used are not clearly identified as the paper's 'standardized benchmarks.'

DineshAI/ZVyd4r9Xl5.paper_title: Beyond Majority Voting: LLM Aggregation by Leveraging Higher-Order Information

claims.claim: The Optimal Weight (OW) algorithm assigns each LLM a weight ω_i = σ_k^{-1}(x_i) based on its accuracy x_i, and Theorem 1 proves OW is Bayes-optimal among all aggregators with access to the same first-order accuracy information (Algorithm 1, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Symbolic likelihood factorization certificate shows OW argmax equals MAP under stated assumptions; independent exact-rational checker over 418 profiles across 5 (K,N) configurations yields 0 mismatches; negative control confirms conditional independence is load-bearing.

claims.claim: The Inverse Surprisingly Popular (ISP) algorithm uses only second-order information (pairwise prediction correlations, no ground-truth labels) to compute a counterfactual advantage score per label, and Theorem 2 proves the ordering E[Adv_ISP(s*)] ≥ E[Adv_MV(s*)] ≥ E[Adv_SP(s*)], i.e., ISP dominates majority voting which dominates the classical Surprisingly Popular algorithm (Algorithm 2, Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Exact sparse polynomial identities for E[Adv_ISP−Adv_MV] and E[Adv_MV−Adv_SP] derived symbolically with all terms nonnegative when x_i≥1/K; independent Fraction checker over 55 profiles passes; scope control shows reversal when premise violated.

claims.claim: In simulated experiments with N=4 agents and M=10,000 questions, ISP achieves 90.48% accuracy versus 85.13% for majority voting at K=2 answer options, and 94.45% versus 92.64% at K=4 options, with the gap shrinking at rate Θ(1/K) (simulation results section).
claims.evidence: 89 independent full-scale runs (N=4, M=10000) at K=2,4,6,8,10 show paper values within 95% predictive intervals (K=2: ISP 90.16% vs paper 90.48%, MV 85.00% vs 85.13%; K=4: ISP 94.41% vs 94.45%, MV 92.38% vs 92.64%); exact closed-form slope on extended K grid is −0.983, consistent with Θ(1/K).

claims.claim: On real-world datasets, OW-L attains 73.66% accuracy on UltraFeedback, 90.37% on MMLU, and 85.78% on ARMMAN, each exceeding majority voting's 72.21%, 89.32%, and 85.24% respectively (Table 3).
claims.evidence: Four verification routes all failed: no author code or prediction cache found, exact retained row IDs and shuffle maps unavailable, ARMMAN records inaccessible, Azure provenance absent; no faithful rerun or falsification was possible.

claims.claim: Across 16 model ensembles, OW-L outperforms majority voting in 97.92% of cases, with absolute accuracy improvements ranging from 0.54% to 14.20% (Section on real-world experiments).
claims.evidence: All 48 appendix rows reconstructed and arithmetically checked: 47/48 OW-L wins over MV (97.92%), best-lift range 0.54–14.20 pp confirmed; independent integer checker and quantifier controls pass. Note this verifies the paper's published aggregate arithmetic, not independently regenerated predictions.

claims.claim: Corollary 1 connects the optimal aggregation weights to the Bradley-Terry model, showing that in the binary setting the optimal weights are proportional to the inverse logistic function of each model's accuracy (Corollary 1).
claims.evidence: Algebraic derivation shows σ_2^{-1}(x)=log(x/(1-x))=logit(x) and BT probability yields identical score difference; exact rational composition and 60-digit Decimal checks agree; controls reject wrong transforms, finite endpoints, and negative scaling.

DineshAI/ZVyd4r9Xl5.overall: The logbook provides strong mathematical and simulation-based evidence for the theoretical claims (1, 2, 6) and the synthetic experiments (3), plus an arithmetic audit of the published ensemble tables (5). The real-data claim (4) remains genuinely inaccessible due to unavailable prediction caches, proprietary model provenance, and restricted datasets.

ParetoOptimal/repro-wpfvujddqc.paper_title: Approximation of Log-Partition Function in Policy Mirror Descent Induces Implicit Regularization for LLM Post-Training

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 derives, via a Lambert-W closed-form solution, that PMD-mean's normalization constant λ scales inversely with the KL weight τ as τ→0, so a mixed KL–χ² regularizer remains active even when the nominal KL weight vanishes (Theorem 3.1, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: KKT stationarity of the Lambert-W solution verified to 3.40e-16 across 144 configs up to A=32768 with continuous rewards; Eq(6) bounds 0/144 violations; the general small-τ scaling law λ/τ → E_π[(Δ)₊] confirmed with end-ratio error 0.0023 and log-log slope error 0.0121, showing the χ² weight stays active as τ→0.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.2 shows PMD-mean implicitly solves a policy-improvement objective regularized by both KL(π‖πt) and an adaptive χ²(π‖πt) term whose coefficient depends on reward statistics under finite-sample estimation error (Proposition 3.2, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The mixed KL-χ² subproblem (Eq 12) reproduces the PMD-mean update to 6.22e-15 across 96 configs up to A=32768 via KKT root-find, confirmed by an independent exponentiated-gradient solver (1.25e-16) and a 200/200 global perturbation certificate; finite-sample equivalence holds at 7.82e-14.

claims.claim: Section 4.2.2 shows the χ² regularization weight adapts dynamically to the mean reward, intensifying regularization and producing more conservative policy updates when expected rewards are low (Section 4.2.2, Propositions 4.9–4.10).
claims.evidence: χ² gap between PMD-part and PMD-mean updates is monotone-decreasing in expected reward on 105/105 configs up to A=8192 (gap 60.47→0.0000 binary) and on continuous Beta rewards (272.8→1.270); suppression-rate law slope −p (mean) vs −1 (part) verified at A=1024 with error 0.0021.

claims.claim: On AIME24/AIME25 math reasoning benchmarks, PMD-mean improves a 30B model from 36.56/27.92 (GRPO) to 50.83/37.19, and a 7B model from 17.08/10.52 (GRPO) to 19.69/19.48 (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The AIME24/25 absolute scores (30B: 36.56/27.92→50.83/37.19; 7B: 17.08/10.52→19.69/19.48) are explicitly stated as 'reported, not reproduced' with no GPU training conducted; the logbook's GRPO comparison runs only on proxy tabular/function-approximation tasks, not on AIME benchmarks.

claims.claim: PMD-mean achieves a 4.6x throughput speedup over on-policy gradient training (staleness=1) by amortizing over larger batches while maintaining comparable or superior accuracy (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The amortization mechanism is measured on a real PyTorch transformer pipeline (1.33x speedup on 2 CPU threads, generation share 85.9% vs paper's 90.0%), and the Table-2 arithmetic is verified (4.52x), but the claimed 4.6x magnitude is explicitly not reproduced (magnitude_4p6x_reproduced: false); the measured speedup is on CPU, far below the GPU-cluster result.

claims.claim: Figure 4 shows PMD-mean remains stable throughout training while an alternative variant, PMD-part, is highly unstable, empirically validating the implicit regularization mechanism (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Multi-seed training (16 seeds, 400 steps) with a linear-softmax policy (d=64, A=4096) reproduces the Figure 4 phenomenon — PMD-part collapses in 7/16 seeds (final 0.562±0.496) while PMD-mean reaches 1.000 with 0/16 collapses — but on a synthetic sparse-reward task with a linear model, not the actual LLM training (Qwen on math reasoning) depicted in the paper's Figure 4.

ParetoOptimal/repro-wpfvujddqc.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification of the paper's three theoretical claims (Theorem 3.1, Proposition 3.2, and the adaptive χ² conservatism mechanism) at action-space scales up to 32768 with multiple independent solvers. The empirical LLM claims (AIME scores, 4.6x throughput, Figure 4 stability) are addressed only through proxy experiments on simplified setups, with the AIME benchmark results entirely unreproduced.

ai-sherpa/robust-async-q-corruption-repr.paper_title: Corruption-Tolerant Asynchronous Q-Learning with Near-Optimal Rates

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows Robust Async-Q achieves a finite-time convergence rate of O(1/√T), matching classical asynchronous Q-learning, plus an additive O(√ε) term where ε∈[0,1/2) is the fraction of adversarially corrupted rewards (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Real runs on an independently generated MDP (|S|=3, |A|=2, γ=0.9) with T up to 64k and 8 seeds measure a log-log convergence slope of -0.586 (R²=0.970) at ε=0, close to the theoretical -0.5. The corruption floor grows with ε (1.83× from ε=0 to 0.4) and is magnitude-independent (robust flat ratio 1.52× vs vanilla Q-learning's 276× growth across attack magnitudes 1→1000). The exact √ε exponent is not cleanly pinned (slope 0.549, R²=0.731) but the qualitative behavior and the worst-case construction in Claim 2 jointly support the claim.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 gives an information-theoretic lower bound of Ω(√ε), proving the additive corruption term in the upper bound is unavoidable (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The Appendix-D two-MDP construction (Eq. 74-78) is reproduced exactly: contaminated pmfs are bit-identical (max diff 0.0, KL=0), the Q*-gap of 0.7215 exceeds the target 0.5σ̄√ε/(1-γ)=0.7071, and a real two-point hypothesis test (T=500, 3000 trials) yields max testing error 0.566 ≥ 1/4, confirming the lower bound's indistinguishability argument empirically.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 extends the guarantee to a reward-agnostic setting where the algorithm needs no prior knowledge of the reward distribution's bounds (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: Robust Async-RAQ without knowledge of reward bounds achieves a convergence slope of -0.586 (R²=0.949) at ε=0, matching the known-statistics variant's order (ratio 1.000). The rate evidence is solid; however, the p-robustness test yields floors identical to 16 significant figures across p∈{1,2,4}, which is suspicious and suggests the p parameter may not meaningfully affect the computation at this configuration, though it does not undermine the primary reward-agnostic claim.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 extends the near-optimal finite-time rate to single-trajectory Markovian sampling with time-correlated data, with the bound inflated by the chain's mixing time (Section 6).
claims.evidence: A genuine single-trajectory Markov chain (not resampled) with measured mixing time τ̄=4, confirmed geometric decay, and lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.772 decaying to 0.024 by lag 16. Robust Async-RAQ-M converges on this correlated data (error 8.33→0.247), and the mixing-time inflation slope of 0.422 (R²=0.966) is consistent with the theoretical √τ scaling.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 (Robust Async-Q) combines a trimmed-mean reward estimator with an adaptive threshold G_t to filter corrupted rewards before the standard Q-learning update, requiring only knowledge of the corruption fraction ε and minimum state-action visitation probability λ_min (Algorithm 1, Assumption 1).
claims.evidence: The TRIM estimator's magnitude independence is directly demonstrated (flat ratio 1.14× vs naive mean's 464× growth over attack magnitudes 1→2000), the Theorem-1 concentration bound holds empirically (fail-rate 0.000 ≤ δ=0.1), λ_min dependence is confirmed by monotone increases in both burn-in T̄ and error as λ_min decreases, and the threshold mechanism correctly keeps in-range and rejects out-of-range estimates.

ai-sherpa/robust-async-q-corruption-repr.overall: This logbook provides concrete experimental evidence from independent from-scratch implementations supporting all five claims, with real runs measuring convergence rates, lower-bound constructions, reward-agnostic variants, Markovian sampling, and algorithmic mechanisms on a small but sufficient MDP with T up to 200k iterations. The main limitations—imperfect √ε exponent pinning, suspiciously identical p-variant floors in Claim 3, and a reduced burn-in constant—are honestly disclosed and do not undermine the core rate/order and mechanism claims.

snaykey/repro-stability-bounded-diff.paper_title: Stability beyond Bounded Differences: Sharp Generalization Bounds under Finite $L_p$ Moments

claims.claim: Theorem 2.2 establishes a concentration inequality for functions of independent random variables under finite Lp moment conditions exhibiting a two-regime bound combining polynomial and sub-Gaussian terms (Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: Monte-Carlo with n=20, ν=2.5, N=800k draws: far-tail exponent α=2.749≈ν=2.5 (R²=0.991), tail-ratio plateau 2.475 vs predicted C0^ν=2.756, and sub-Gaussian surrogate underestimates true tail by 5.09e10×, confirming the two-regime structure.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.6 extends the concentration results to the heavy-tailed regime p ∈ (1,2), yielding bounds unavailable to prior uniform-boundedness-based approaches (Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: Monte-Carlo with ν=1.5 (p∈(1,2)), N=300k: far-tail exponent α=1.556≈1.5 (R²=0.9992), plateau 1.81 vs C0^ν=1.837, and two independent variance estimates differing by 4.4× confirming infinite variance where bounded-difference tools fail.

claims.claim: Assumption 3.1 defines (Lp,β)-Lipschitz stability, requiring only that the replace-one stability increment have finite p-th moments for some p≥2, replacing deterministic uniform stability (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Ridge regression with B=20,000 triples: ‖H‖_2=0.0265 and ‖H‖_3=0.0683 are finite while sup H climbs across draws ([0.45, 0.48, 1.34]) and is 50.7× larger than ‖H‖_2, demonstrating finite Lp moments coexist with unbounded uniform stability.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 provides a high-probability generalization bound for empirical risk minimization under (Lp,β)-Lipschitz stability (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Paper's Section-4 protocol replicated: ridge ERM, m∈{500,1000}, ν∈{2.2,4.4}, N=50k. Tail-ratio plateaus match C0^{ν/2} within 0.3–2.3% for ν=2.2 and 7.7–12.2% for ν=4.4; far-tail exponents recover ν/2 (1.02–1.03 and 2.04–2.17).

claims.claim: Theorems 3.9 and 3.10 extend the concentration framework to sampling without replacement and derive generalization bounds R(h)−R̂(h) for transductive regression under (Lp,β)-Lipschitz stability (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: WoR variance ratio 0.501 matches finite-population correction 0.5013 to 4 sig-figs (N=400, m=200, K=60k); transductive gap plateau 1.846 vs C0^{ν/2}=1.837 (0.5% error) with far-tail exponent 1.441≈ν/2=1.5 over 30k partitions.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.14 establishes high-probability generalization bounds for meta-learning algorithms under Assumption 3.12, which decomposes stability into meta-stability across tasks, within-task stability, and test-sample stability (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Three-level stability decomposition is demonstrated (all increments have tail exponents >2: 2.03/2.73/2.07), but the key tail-ratio plateau (11.273) does not match the predicted C0^{ν/2}=3.375 (off by 3.3×), and the far-tail exponent 3.352 is 12% above ν/2=3.0; the primary quantitative diagnostic fails at finite N.

snaykey/repro-stability-bounded-diff.overall: The logbook provides genuine, independently generated Monte-Carlo evidence supporting the two-regime concentration predictions of Theorems 2.2, 2.6, 3.4, and 3.9/3.10, with tail exponents and ratio plateaus closely matching theoretical predictions. The meta-learning claim (Theorem 3.14) is only partially supported: the three-level decomposition is shown but the primary quantitative diagnostic (tail-ratio plateau) fails to converge at the available sample size.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 gives a bicriteria (1+κ, 1+1/κ) approximation via LP rounding: the returned subgraph K satisfies coverage loss W−e(K)≤(1+κ)·ε·W and size |K|≤(1+1/κ)·r (Theorem 1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: 288 rows of LP-rounding results on small hypergraphs (n=7..10) with exhaustive optimal computation show both inequalities satisfied (e.g., lost_weight=4.174 vs bound=4.194), but the instance sizes are clearly toy-scale and the theorem is a mathematical guarantee that empirical testing can only probe on finite instances.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 proves a monotonicity/nestedness property (Kτ1⊆Kτ2 for τ1<τ2), derived from a connection to parametric minimum cuts, which is required for valid conformal calibration (Theorem 2, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: 30 weighted hypergraphs with exhaustive vertex-subset enumeration confirm nested chains with at most n+1 sets, but 'enumerate every vertex subset' implies very small instances, making this a toy-scale structural check of the monotonicity theorem.

claims.claim: Corollary 1 shows the entire nested sequence of subgraphs across thresholds can be computed in Õ(γ(m+n)²) time (Corollary 1, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Structural audit on 30 small instances counts flow-network nodes/arcs and nested-set cardinalities matching the parametric-cut bound's components, but does not implement or time the actual parametric min-cut algorithm, and instances are small enough for exhaustive enumeration.

claims.claim: Lemma 1 establishes a distribution-free marginal coverage guarantee ℙ(B*⊆Kτ*(A*))≥φ−δ under exchangeability, without requiring model probability estimates (Lemma 1).
claims.evidence: 20,000 independent Monte Carlo repetitions per setting across n∈{19,49,99} and φ∈{0.60,0.75,0.90} (180,000 total) confirm coverage intervals compatible with ⌈(n+1)φ⌉/(n+1)≥φ, with an exchangeability-violation control showing diagnostic sensitivity, at a reasonable simulation scale for conformal prediction.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 proves NP-hardness of the conformal subgraph problem even for constant ε via reduction from clique detection, in Appendix B (Theorem 4, Appendix B).
claims.evidence: Finite enumeration of all graphs through 5 vertices plus a deterministic sample at 6 vertices verifies the CLIQUE-to-densest-subgraph reduction core with no counterexample, but this is inherently a toy-scale check of a theoretical NP-hardness proof, not a proof itself.

claims.claim: On a synthetic 6x6 grid navigation experiment with 50 train/test routes, the LP-based method compresses the calibration set to 52 edges at φ=0.75 coverage and outperforms greedy baselines for φ≤0.8 (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Ten independent repetitions of the 6×6 grid navigation with 50 train/test routes reproduce the LP advantage: mean edge counts at φ=0.75 are 50.8 (LP) vs 57.8 (forward-greedy) vs 62.0 (reverse-greedy), with LP lowest at every target from 0.60–0.80, matching the paper's setup and qualitative claims despite the unavailable author seed.

sotayamashita/repro-compact-conformal-su.overall: The logbook provides real numerical evidence for all six claims, with the theoretical claims (1–3, 5) verified on small toy-scale instances via exhaustive search or structural audit, and the empirical claims (4, 6) reproduced at reasonable simulation or paper-matching scale. The reproduction is methodologically sound but limited by small instance sizes for the theoretical results and an unavailable random seed for the exact 52-edge point in Claim 6.

sotayamashita/repro-conditional-conforma.paper_title: Testing For Distribution Shifts with Conditional Conformal Test Martingales

claims.claim: The conditional conformal test martingale (CTM) uses a fixed reference dataset D0 rather than an ever-growing reference set, avoiding test-time contamination that dilutes evidence of distribution shift in standard CTMs (Section 3).
claims.evidence: 100 paired streams with n=1000 show fixed-reference CTM p-values are further from 0.5 (0.763 vs 0.624), demonstrating that the growing reference dilutes shift evidence by 0.139 toward 0.5.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes finite-sample, anytime-valid type-I error control, bounding the probability of falsely rejecting the null by alpha with probability at least 1-delta over the randomness of the reference set (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: A Dirac point-mass null P yields ECDF p_hat=1 always, causing Algorithm 1 to deterministically reject at step 10—a finite counterexample within the theorem's universal 'any null P' scope, with 1000-stream randomized tie-breaking control confirming the issue.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows the method achieves asymptotic power one whenever the effective signal strength Delta_k is positive, with expected stopping time bounded by O(1/Delta_0^2 * ln(1/(alpha*Delta_0)) + 1/Delta_0^2) (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: 900 runs across 6 Gaussian alternatives all achieve power 1.0, with median stopping time decreasing from 126 to 18 as signal proxy increases, and fitted log-log slope of -1.510 consistent with the inverse-square upper bound.

claims.claim: The betting function (Eq. 8) subtracts a Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz-based estimation-error correction term from the standard betting score to remove spurious wealth gains from estimation uncertainty (Section 3, Equation 8).
claims.evidence: 600 null streams with DKW correction yield 0/600 false rejections (0%) vs 224/600 (37.3%) without correction, directly demonstrating the correction term removes spurious wealth gains under the null.

claims.claim: On synthetic experiments with immediate, delayed, and gradual distribution shifts, the conditional CTM detects shifts faster than the standard (invalid) CTM while maintaining type-I error control at alpha=0.05 (Figure 2, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Full synthetic grid with 100 trials per setting shows conditional CTM is faster in only 5/9 settings; all three gradual-shift rates (0.001, 0.002, 0.004) show the growing-reference CTM detecting faster, contradicting the blanket speed claim.

claims.claim: On ImageNet-C corruption benchmarks, detection performance improves with reference set size n >= 500, with detection ratio exceeding 1 for corruption groups involving larger distributional shifts (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The ImageNet-C entropy arrays are unavailable from the official repository and the experiment was not executed; no proxy or substitute was run.

sotayamashita/repro-conditional-conforma.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting claims 1, 3, and 4, and concrete counterexamples falsifying claims 2 and 5, while claim 6 remains unaddressed due to missing data. The reproduction is rigorous with proper ablations, multiple trials, and mathematically valid counterexamples.

ParetoOptimal/repro-6veqdkmfkh.paper_title: Efficient Diffusion Models under Nonconvex Equality and Inequality constraints via Landing

claims.claim: The paper introduces a landing-based mechanism that replaces explicit projections for constrained diffusion on generic nonconvex feasible sets, yielding overdamped (OLLA) and underdamped (ULLA) Langevin variants that enforce equality and inequality constraints throughout the diffusion process (Section 4.1, Lemma 1).
claims.evidence: Both OLLA and ULLA were implemented on three genuinely nonconvex sets (torus, two-sphere intersection, sphere_cap) with actual trained MLP score networks and no projections, yielding violations of 2e-4 to 1e-8. However, the setup is clearly reduced in scale: R^3 manifolds, 3000 training points, small MLPs with KDE-score regression instead of the paper's CWPM objective, and a simplified Gaussian conditional momentum model for ULLA.

claims.claim: Lemma 1 proves the landing property dJ(X_t) = -alpha*sigma(t)^2*J(X_t)dt, giving exponential decay of equality-constraint violations and finite-time feasibility (within time tau_{j,epsilon}) for inequality constraints (Section 4.1, Lemma 1).
claims.evidence: Across 60 equality configurations (4 manifolds including 2 nonconvex, 5 alphas, 3 sigma schedules, 512 particles each) the fitted exponential decay rate matches -alpha to max 4.36% relative error (mean 0.63%, R^2 >= 0.997685), with dt-convergence confirming the residual floor is a discretization artifact. Across 45 inequality configurations, decay of g+eps matches -alpha to max 4.13% error, all particles reach feasibility, and first-feasibility time agrees with tau_{j,eps} (median error 7.8e-4 for the affine constraint).

claims.claim: ULLA achieves up to 47x faster sampling than RDDPM on mesh-constrained data while maintaining competitive Jensen-Shannon Distance scores against RFM and RDDPM baselines (Table 1, Table 2).
claims.evidence: RDDPM and RFM were not run, so the specific '47x vs RDDPM' cannot be measured. On a simplified sphere-constrained 3D task, ULLA-30 achieves 7.4x wall-clock speedup and 55.8x fewer gradient evaluations over a projected DDPM-400, but ULLA's JSD (0.430378) is not competitive, while OLLA-80 matches the projection baseline (0.169738 vs 0.17018) at 5.7x speedup. The speed mechanism is demonstrated but the specific claim is not verified.

claims.claim: On the Earth-surface constrained task, the landing method maintains an average equality-constraint violation of about |h| ≈ 3.9e-9, reported as mean ± standard error over five independent runs (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The Earth-surface protocol was replicated on real USGS earthquake data (8690 epicenters) with five independent seeded runs, trained score model, and backward OLLA landing with no projections. Measured mean avg |norm(x)-1| = 1.1221e-8 ± 4.73e-11 (SE), within a factor of ~2.9 of the paper's 3.9e-9, same order of magnitude. The constraint violation is determined by the landing dynamics rather than score quality, so the simplified MLP does not undermine the core measurement.

claims.claim: On mixed-constraint tasks including 7-DOF robot trajectories and molecular conformations, ULLA sustains constraint violations of roughly |h| ≈ 1e-5 and |g+| ≈ 1e-9 while achieving superior JSD scores compared to baselines that diverge or fail in high dimensions (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The 7-DOF Franka Panda robot task was executed at the paper's exact dimensions (d=140, 280, 420, 560) with real FK equality and joint-limit inequalities, yielding |h| ~ 1.4e-16 and g+ = 0.0 (better than claimed 1e-5/1e-9) with JSD comparable to the projection baseline. However, the molecular conformation half was not run, the 'superior JSD over failing baselines' was not verified (projected baseline converged, JSD was comparable not superior), and the sampler is a direct MCMC-like chain using the cheap ULLA variant without curvature corrections rather than a trained diffusion model.

claims.claim: The proposed discretization scheme achieves roughly 2x memory efficiency during training by collapsing momentum into approximated vectors, compared to projection-based approaches (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Both momentum-collapsed and explicit-momentum discretizations were implemented and memory measured directly: retained buffer byte ratio is exactly 2.0 at all three sizes (100x2000, 200x4000, 400x8000), tracemalloc peak ratio climbs toward 2 (1.74 to 1.92), reconstructed momentum matches true momentum (median relative error 5.5e-5, cosine 0.999981), and the collapsed chain reproduces the explicit chain's terminal law within the finite-sample floor.

ParetoOptimal/repro-6veqdkmfkh.overall: The logbook provides a thorough from-scratch numpy reproduction with strong numerical verification of Lemma 1's decay and finite-time feasibility (claim 2), faithful replication of the Earth-surface constraint violation with real data (claim 4), and direct measurement of the 2x memory claim (claim 6). Key gaps include missing RDDPM/RFM baselines and mesh-constrained data for claim 3, missing molecular conformation experiments for claim 5, and simplified score training (KDE regression instead of CWPM) throughout claims 1, 3, and 4.

SabaPivot/repro-steady-state-constant-st.paper_title: Steady-State Behavior of Constant-Stepsize Stochastic Approximation: Gaussian Approximation and Tail Bounds

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 (i.i.d. noise) and Theorem 4.1 (Markovian noise) bound the Wasserstein distance between the centered-scaled steady state Y^(α) = (X^(α) − x*)/√α and its Gaussian limit N(0, Σ_Y) by U√α log(1/α) (Theorems 3.1 and 4.1).
claims.evidence: W_1 distances for SGD (iid), linear SA, contractive SA, and SGD (Markov) decay with empirical power-law slopes 0.512–0.749 across a 7-point stepsize grid (down to α=1/320) with 400K samples each, and the normalized ratio W_1/(√α log(1/α)) is monotonically decreasing in all four settings, consistent with the asserted upper bound.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 establishes an explicit non-asymptotic Wasserstein bound of order O(α^{1/2} log(1/α)) for constant-stepsize SGD on smooth, strongly convex objectives (Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: 1-D SGD on f(x)=x²/2 with N=400K stationary iterates and exact 1-D W_1 computation shows decay slope 0.533 (R²=0.9982) and rescaled variance matching the theoretical Σ_Y=1/6 to 4 decimal places.

claims.claim: Propositions 3.2 and 3.3 extend the same O(α^{1/2} log(1/α)) Wasserstein bound to linear stochastic approximation with a Hurwitz matrix and to contractive nonlinear stochastic approximation, respectively (Propositions 3.2 and 3.3, Section 3.2.2, Section 3.2.3).
claims.evidence: 2-D linear SA (Hurwitz, non-normal A) and contractive nonlinear SA show W_1 decay slopes 0.561 and 0.512 (R²>0.996) via 256-direction sliced-W_1, with empirical covariance matching the Lyapunov equation to 3 decimal places.

claims.claim: For one-dimensional projections, the paper derives a non-uniform Berry-Esseen-type tail bound |P(⟨Y^(α),ζ⟩ > a) − P(Z_ζ > a)| ≤ C_d α^{1/4} log^{1/2}(1/α) / a, which improves as the deviation level a grows (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Scaled tail error a|Δ(a)| for linear-SA projections (N=1.6M chains) decays with slope 0.583 (R²=0.9988) across deviation levels a∈{0.5,…,3}, confirming the 1/a factor and that the bound holds; the actual decay is faster than the predicted α^{1/4} rate, which is consistent with the bound being an upper bound.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 extends the Gaussian approximation and tail bounds for SGD, linear SA, and contractive nonlinear SA from i.i.d. noise to Markovian noise (Proposition 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Markov SGD with the correct long-run covariance shows W_1 decaying (slope 0.749), while using the naive marginal covariance floors at ~0.09 and never shrinks, directly confirming that the covariance correction in Proposition 4.1 is essential.

claims.claim: Proposition 5.1 shows a different convergence rate of order α^{1/h} for constant-stepsize SA applied to general convex objectives with Gibbs-type limiting distributions (Proposition 5.1, Section 5).
