SabaPivot/repro-laplacian-connectivity-r.paper_title: Impact of Connectivity on Laplacian Representations in Reinforcement Learning

claims.claim: The approximation error of a rank-k learned Laplacian representation used for linear value function approximation is upper-bounded by ‖v−v̂_k‖_Φ ≤ ‖r̄‖_Φ√(1/(λ₂λ_{k+1})) + ‖v‖_Φ√(2ε/(λ_{k+1}−λ_k)), decomposing into truncation error and feature-estimation error (Theorem 3.3, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: 1000 random MDPs (476 gridworld + 524 fully-random asymmetric) with exact computation of the Laplacian eigenbasis, value function, and eps from Assumption 3.1's own residual; 0/1000 violations of the Theorem 3.3 bound with min slack 1.64e-06, and the truncation sub-bound also 0/1000 violations with machine-precision tightness (min slack^2 = 1.14e-12).

claims.claim: The truncation error term is bounded by ‖v−v_k‖²_Φ ≤ ‖r̄‖²_Φ/(λ₂λ_{k+1}), showing the bound scales inversely with the algebraic connectivity λ₂ of the state-transition graph, so poorly-connected MDPs induce larger approximation error (Lemma 3.4, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Full reproduction of Table 1 at native scale (15x15 gridworld, k=20, eta-sweep, 5 seeds): analytical error matches paper to max 0.22% relative error across all 10 eta values, lambda2 matches to max 0.24%, and Spearman(lambda2, error) = -1.000 confirms the claimed perfectly monotonic inverse scaling with algebraic connectivity.

claims.claim: The Graph Drawing Objective's feature-estimation error is bounded by ‖Π_Ψ−Π_Ψ̃‖₂ < √(2ε/(λ_{k+1}−λ_k)), depending on the spectral gap between the k-th and (k+1)-th eigenvalues (Lemma 3.5, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: 1000 trials across 4 non-uniform/asymmetric policy families with 0/1000 symmetric kernels (min asymmetry 0.093, median 0.650); Phi-self-adjointness residual max |Phi L - (Phi L)^T| = 2.78e-17 (machine precision) across all trials, and Theorem 3.3 holds with 0/1000 violations on this exclusively-asymmetric population.

claims.claim: The analysis defines a Φ-self-adjoint Laplacian L = I − (P+Φ⁻¹PᵀΦ)/2 (Equation 6, Section 3) and applies without assuming symmetry of the induced transition kernel, i.e., it holds for general non-uniform behavior policies (Lemma 3.6, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Lemma 3.5's projection bound isolated and tested on 1530 trials (867 RL Laplacians, 633 generic p.s.d. matrices, 30 actual NumPy-trained GDO feature sets): 0/1530 violations with min slack 0.233, and in the informative regime (RHS<1) 0/38 violations; Davis-Kahan gap-scaling confirmed with Spearman(LHS, sqrt(2*eps/gap)) = 0.590.

claims.claim: Propositions 4.1 and 4.2 establish that this matrix-based Laplacian formulation is equivalent to the operator-theoretic Laplacian representation formulation of Wu et al. (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Operator-theoretic route built independently from matrix route across 1000 random MDPs: Prop 4.1 identities (adjoint, inner product, operator identity, L~==L) hold to <=1.8e-15; Prop 4.2 eigenvalue equivalence to 5.2e-11, representation projector equivalence median 3.4e-15, trace-min optimum to 2.8e-15, and GDO re-derivation to 1.6e-14.

SabaPivot/repro-laplacian-connectivity-r.overall: This logbook provides rigorous independent numerical verification of all five theoretical claims through large-scale Monte Carlo audits (1000-1530 trials each) with exact computation of every quantity in pure NumPy, plus a full native-scale reproduction of the paper's Table 1. All bounds, identities, and scaling relationships hold with zero violations and machine-precision residuals across diverse MDP families including asymmetric non-grid cases.

claims.claim: Persuasive Privacy (PP) is defined via a Stackelberg game in which a Sender commits to a mechanism M and a Bayes-rational Receiver updates beliefs, with privacy assessed by the tail bound inf_{S,x,Q} P_x[ΔS(Q,T,x) ≤ κ] ≥ 1-δ (Section 3, Definition 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook instantiates Definition 3 exactly on finite stochastic mechanisms M1, M2, computing the (κ,δ)-PP parameter as the max over x of the exact (1−δ)-quantile of Δ_S under T~M(·|x) with no Monte Carlo, confirming Δ_S = log(M(T|x)/P(T)) and obtaining M1 κ=0.8083-PP (coverage 1.0000) and M2 κ=0.6757-PP (coverage 1.0000).

claims.claim: Proposition 6 shows a mechanism satisfies (ϵ,δ)-probabilistic differential privacy if and only if it satisfies (L,ℋ,ϵ,δ)-persuasive privacy, where L is the negative log-probability score, establishing full equivalence between the two frameworks (Section 4, Proposition 6).
claims.evidence: Exact finite audit over 48 kernels and 2880 comparison cases (kernel × pair × ε × δ) computes PDP probability from likelihood ratios and PP probability independently from Bayes posteriors, yielding max |PP-endpoint prob − PDP prob| = 0.00e+00 and 0 pass/fail mismatches; a negative control confirms the worst-case prior is essential.

claims.claim: Proposition 7 establishes that the deterministic empirical-average mechanism M(x,·)=δ_{x̄} satisfies (ℐ,𝒢_x^r,κ^r,0)-persuasive privacy with κ^r = r_1 + log r_2, giving privacy guarantees for a deterministic algorithm that standard differential privacy cannot certify (Section 5, Proposition 7).
claims.evidence: 72 in-class Gaussian priors from 𝒢ₓʳ (n=5, r₁=1.0, r₂=3.0) yield max relative DSS score 0.9379 ≤ κʳ = r₁+log r₂ = 2.0986, with closed-form vs literal DSS agreement to 6.7e-16; an out-of-class prior violates the bound (6.4770 > 2.0986) and ordinary DP gives infinite likelihood ratio, confirming the class restriction is load-bearing.

claims.claim: Proposition 4 shows persuasive privacy satisfies receiver post-processing (the receiver cannot amplify privacy loss via output transformation), while Proposition 5 shows it does not satisfy the sender post-processing inequality that differential privacy does (Section 3.2, Propositions 4-5).
claims.evidence: Receiver post-processing: max ΔS unchanged (0.8083 → 0.8083) with coverage preserved at 1.0000; sender post-processing: exact counterexample where a (ln 2, 0.1)-PDP mechanism with P_a=[0.41,0.50,0.09], P_b=[0.7199,0.28,0.0001] has δ jump to 0.59 after merging t2,t3, breaking the guarantee.

claims.claim: Proposition 3 shows that for conjugate prior families, composing two persuasive-privacy mechanisms with parameters (κ1,δ1) and (κ2,δ2) yields a mechanism satisfying (𝒮,𝒬_x,κ1+κ2,δ1+δ2)-PP (Section 3.1, Proposition 3).
claims.evidence: Exact product-channel computation on finite space: M1 (κ1=0.8083, δ1=0.1) ⊗ M2 (κ2=0.6757, δ2=0.1) gives composed coverage 1.0000 ≥ 0.80 at (κ1+κ2=1.4840, δ1+δ2=0.2), with actual composed κ=0.8514 ≤ 1.4840 confirming the additive budget is a valid upper bound.

SabaPivot/repro-persuasive-privacy.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all five claims through exact finite computation (no Monte Carlo), independent verification paths (closed-form vs literal), negative controls, and 7/7 unit tests. The reproduction is rigorous with machine-precision agreement between computation methods and transparent acknowledgment that universal quantifiers over continuous classes are checked on finite samples supplemented by algebraic verification.

SabaPivot/repro-provable-benefits-of-rlv.paper_title: Provable Benefits of RLVR over SFT for Reasoning Models: Learning to Backtrack Efficiently

claims.claim: Theorem 2 proves that a model trained via SFT on shortest-path (optimal) trajectories converges to forward transition probabilities of 1 but keeps backward-pointing transition probabilities fixed at their pretrained values of L/(L+1) and 1/(L+1), i.e., it never learns to backtrack (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: After 100,000 cross-entropy updates on golden-path transitions at W=15, K=15, L=5, forward probabilities reached a=0.99995 and c=0.99995 while backward probabilities stayed exactly at pretrained b=5/6=0.83333 and d=1/6=0.16667 to floating-point precision; a control supervising all four rows with RLVR traces drove all above 0.9999, confirming the mechanism.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 proves that RLVR training drives all four transition probabilities (a_j, b_j, c_j, d_j) arbitrarily close to 1 in finite time by incorporating the model's own failed exploration trajectories during policy-gradient updates (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Exact sign-gradient RLVR updates at W=15, K=15, L=5 drove the minimum over all 60 transition probabilities from 1/6 to 0.99999 in 650 finite iterations, with expected hitting time falling from 50,142 to 900.16 versus the perfect-policy limit of 900.00; adjoint gradient finite-difference checks achieved 1.5e-7 relative error.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 establishes an exponential inference-time compute separation: RLVR-trained policies require Θ(WK) expected steps to reach the goal versus Θ(W·L^K) for SFT-trained policies, on a graph with W parallel branches, depth K, and L multi-edges per junction (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Exact Bellman solutions over K=1..9 and L=2,3,4,5 confirm RLVR hitting time is linear in WK (ratio approaching 4) and SFT grows exponentially in K. However, fitted log-slopes (1.51, 1.68, 1.84, 1.98) match log((L+1)^2/L) rather than log(L), indicating the actual SFT rate is Theta(W((L+1)^2/L)^K), not Theta(WL^K) as stated; the exponential separation itself is confirmed.

claims.claim: Corollary 1 shows that even equipping the SFT policy with a duplicate-state-avoiding search agent only improves its complexity to Θ(WKL), still a factor of L worse than RLVR's Θ(WK) (Corollary 1).
claims.evidence: The analytical proposal-count proxy gives SFT-search cost WK(2+1/b+1/d)=WK(L+3+1/L)=Theta(WKL) versus RLVR at 4WK; over L=2..10 the SFT/RLVR ratio grows linearly (log-log slope 0.975), and ratio/L converges toward a constant, confirming the factor-L gap.

claims.claim: Theorem 5 shows that distilling RLVR-generated reasoning traces via supervised fine-tuning recovers the efficient Θ(WK) complexity, and synthetic experiments with W=15, K=15, L=5 confirm hitting times converging to the predicted 4WK=900 (Theorem 5, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: SFT on converged RLVR teacher traces (all four transition types supervised) at W=15, K=15, L=5 drove all probabilities above 0.9999 and reached expected hitting time 901.35, within 0.15% of the predicted 4WK=900; the exact all-one policy gives 900.00 under the same counting convention.

SabaPivot/repro-provable-benefits-of-rlv.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous clean-room numerical reproduction of all five claims on the paper's full synthetic Markov chain model at W=15, K=15, L=5, using exact Bellman solves rather than noisy simulation. The exponential separation (Claim 3) is confirmed qualitatively, but the evidence indicates the actual SFT growth base is (L+1)^2/L rather than L, suggesting the stated Theta(WL^K) rate may be an underestimate of the true exponential rate.

SabaPivot/repro-mash-selective-help-seek.paper_title: MASH: Modeling Abstention via Selective Help-Seeking

claims.claim: On HotPotQA, MASH improves answer accuracy by 7.6 percentage points over the baseline OTC selective help-seeking approach (55.42% vs. 44.76%) (Section 4.1, Table 1).
claims.evidence: Released artifacts confirm endpoint accuracies (MASH=55.42%, OTC=44.76%) but the computed improvement is 10.65 pp, not the claimed 7.6 pp — the stated magnitude is contradicted by the paper's own released data.

claims.claim: On 2WikiMultihopQA, MASH improves accuracy by 6.64 percentage points over baseline OTC (45.99% vs. 39.59%) (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Released artifacts confirm endpoints (MASH=45.99%, OTC=39.59%) but the computed improvement is 6.41 pp, not the claimed 6.64 pp.

claims.claim: MASH improves average Tool Productivity by 3.83 points across evaluated datasets compared to baseline OTC (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Recomputed Tool Productivity improvements for the three reward variants are 2.77, 4.46, and 5.62 pp — none equals the claimed 3.83-point average improvement.

claims.claim: On the subset of HotPotQA questions requiring exactly one search, MASH achieves 56.4% accuracy versus 40.0% for baseline OTC (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Released HotPotQA one-search subset accuracies are 56.3656% (MASH) and 40.0194% (OTC), which round exactly to the claimed 56.4% and 40.0%.

claims.claim: In the abstention inference mode, MASH with OTC-Strict reaches 59.9% precision on HotPotQA versus 53.1% for a DPO-based abstention baseline, and achieves 91.2% on the Abs(0) abstention classification metric on HotPotQA (Section 4.2, Table 3).
claims.evidence: Released abstention outputs yield MASH precision 59.8856→59.9%, DPO precision 53.1374→53.1%, and Abs(0) 91.2153→91.2%, all matching the claimed values.

claims.claim: MASH is trained via a two-step pipeline of warm-start supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning with three reward formulations (Exponential Decay, OTC, OTC-Strict) that balance accuracy against search-call penalties (Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: A code-path audit at the cited repository commit confirms the two-stage pipeline (warm-start SFT → RL) and three reward formulations (exponential_decay, otc, otc_strict) are implemented as described, though no full retraining was executed.

SabaPivot/repro-mash-selective-help-seek.overall: The logbook performs arithmetic verification on released evaluation artifacts and a code-structure audit, confirming endpoint values for claims 4–6 but falsifying the specific improvement magnitudes claimed in claims 1–3. No independent model training or evaluation runs were conducted; all evidence derives from recomputing metrics on the authors' released data.

SabaPivot/repro-calibrated-preference-le.paper_title: Calibrated Preference Learning: The Case of Label Ranking

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 proves that full-rank calibration implies both sub-k calibration and top-k calibration, but Table 1 gives a counterexample showing sub-k calibration does not imply full-rank calibration (Section 4, Theorem 4.2, Table 1).
claims.evidence: 200 random full-rank-calibrated constructions satisfied all sub-k and top-k marginal identities with max error 0, and Table 1's exact fractions were reproduced (sub-2 error 0, top-1 error 1/6, full-rank L1 error 2/3), confirming both the implication and the strict converse failure.

claims.claim: Table 2 provides a counterexample showing top-k calibration does not imply full-rank calibration, and that sub-k and top-k calibration are mutually incomparable notions (Section 4, Table 2).
claims.evidence: Exact rational checks found a top-1-calibrated-but-not-full-rank witness (top-1 error 0, sub-2 error 1/6, full-rank L1 error 1) in Table 3 of the current source, plus a rankwise-calibrated distribution in Table 2 that is neither sub-2 nor top-1 calibrated; together with Table 1 these witness mutual incomparability. The table-number attribution differs from the claim but the mathematical content is confirmed.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 shows sub-k calibration implies rankwise sub-k calibration and top-k calibration implies rankwise top-k calibration, establishing a strict hierarchy of calibration notions defined in Definitions 1-7 (Section 4, Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Summing coordinate-marginal identities over ranks in exact rational constructions reproduced the rankwise identities with zero numerical error, and Tables 1–3 supply strictness witnesses, matching the implication graph of Theorem 4.3.

claims.claim: On RewardBench2, Plackett-Luce and Mallows-Model reward models are found to be generally poorly calibrated (measured via top-1 Expected Calibration Error), while RPC achieves the strongest calibration for pairwise rankings (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: On RewardBench2, recomputation over 60 models × 1,865 examples yielded median top-1 ECE 0.4687 (best 0.1348), confirming poor calibration of BT reward models. RPC's strongest pairwise calibration was confirmed on three label-ranking datasets (e.g., political ECE 0.1161 vs PL 0.3354 / Mallows 0.4162), though this belongs to §5.1 rather than §5.2 as the claim implies.

claims.claim: Top-1 ECE correlates strongly with reward-model accuracy in the Focus and Safety categories of RewardBench2 but only weakly in the Math and Precise-IF categories, showing calibration is an imperfect proxy for benchmark accuracy (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: Kendall tau between lower ECE and higher accuracy across 60 RewardBench2 models was 0.6984 (Focus), 0.6750 (Safety), 0.5312 (Precise-IF), and 0.4956 (Math), with a 500-permutation destructive control centered near zero, confirming the relative ordering though the Math/Precise-IF correlations (0.50–0.53) are moderate rather than strictly 'weak.'

SabaPivot/repro-calibrated-preference-le.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence for all five claims: exact rational audits of the calibration hierarchy counterexamples and implications, and a full recomputation over 60 RewardBench2 models for the empirical claims. Two claims required scope/attribution corrections (Table 2→3 for Claim 2, and RPC belonging to §5.1 for Claim 4), but the substantive content of each claim is supported by real runs and numbers.

ai-sherpa/dp-zeroth-order-hidden-state-p.paper_title: Privacy Amplification in Differentially Private Zeroth-Order Optimization with Hidden States

claims.claim: For the hidden-state threat model, Theorem 3.2 establishes a Rényi differential privacy bound for zeroth-order optimization that improves with the number of coordinate-update directions K, in contrast to standard composition-based bounds (Theorem 3.2, Section 3).
claims.evidence: 18 d×K×T settings instantiate the Theorem-3.2 shifted-RDP objective with feasible schedules (all feasible=true); best public/hidden RDP ratio of 1.2103 confirms the hidden bound is tighter than composition, and K-doubling in the saturated regime yields exactly sqrt(2) improvement, confirming the 1/sqrt(K) law emerges from the mechanism rather than being refit.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.3 gives a closed-form DP guarantee for strongly convex losses, epsilon = O(sqrt(Delta^2 log(1/delta)/(n^2 sigma^2) * min(T, M*R*n*sqrt(d)/(K*Delta)))), showing privacy loss saturates rather than growing with the number of iterations T (Corollary 3.3, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The Corollary-3.3 formula is evaluated over 120 cells; 32 cells beyond the saturation threshold T* show constant epsilon as T grows, and destructive controls (removing the outer min or the K denominator) restore divergence and eliminate the K-benefit respectively, confirming both properties are load-bearing.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.7 shows the zeroth-order update map has a (c1, c2)-generalized Lipschitz property, and Lemma 3.8 derives high-probability concentration bounds using a Beta(K/2, (d-K)/2) distribution to control the anisotropic noise introduced by directional perturbations (Lemma 3.7, Lemma 3.8, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Across 6 (d,K) settings with 2500 Haar-Stiefel draws each, squared projection mass matches Beta(K/2,(d-K)/2) with max mean error 0.001287, max relative variance error 0.056404, and all KS p-values > 0.2275; the c1 high-probability bound holds in all settings, and a non-orthogonal control exposes why the Stiefel premise is necessary.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.9 bounds the forward Wasserstein-infinity distance between adjacent privacy processes as W_infinity(w_t, w_t') <= min(2R, 2*eta*Delta*t/sqrt(K)), which underlies the shifted-divergence argument used to prove convergent (non-diverging) privacy loss over iterations (Lemma 3.9, Section 3).
claims.evidence: 480 measured Wasserstein-infinity distances across 4 (d,K) pairs, 2 step sizes, and 5 checkpoints all satisfy min(2R, 2·eta·Delta·t/sqrt(K)) with max normalized ratio 1.0 (tight); a destructive control omitting 1/K averaging violates the envelope 722 times, confirming the scaling depends on the directional averaging mechanism.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes a public-state baseline privacy bound via standard composition, epsilon = O(sqrt(Delta^2 log(1/delta) T/(n^2 sigma^2))) when the noise-blending parameter beta_t = 0, against which the hidden-state analysis (Theorem 3.2) is compared (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Source-text parsing of Theorem 3.1 detects that the no-d/K formula sqrt(Delta²·log(1/delta)·T/(n²·sigma²)) is assigned to beta_t=1 in the paper, not beta_t=0 as the claim states; beta_t=0 instead carries a d/K factor. Both actual source formulas are numerically verified over 120 cells, but the claim's parameter label contradicts the cited theorem.

ai-sherpa/dp-zeroth-order-hidden-state-p.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence—feasible RDP schedules, formula grids, Haar-Stiefel distributional tests, and Wasserstein couplings with destructive controls—at the paper's own parameter scale, independently verifying the K-improvement, saturation, Beta concentration, and W-infinity envelope claims. Claim 5 is falsified as literally registered due to a beta_t parameter-label mismatch with the source theorem, though both actual baseline formulas are numerically confirmed.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 derives a dual representation showing the optimal controlled transition rates for the Generalized Schrodinger Bridge on graphs, and Proposition 3.4 establishes the corresponding Hopf-Cole transformation on graphs (Section 3, Theorem 3.1, Proposition 3.4).
claims.evidence: On an 8-node, 37-edge directed graph with random rates and running cost, the continuity equation, HJB equation (Theorem 3.1), and Hopf-Cole system (Proposition 3.4) residuals all measure below 1.3e-9; boundary conditions hold to machine precision; u* is exactly zero on non-edges and column-sums to ~3.8e-15; 40000-particle Monte Carlo Feynman-Kac and 60000-particle controlled simulations agree within sampling noise; 400 random feasible perturbations are all strictly worse in KL divergence.

claims.claim: On a 9,559-node supply chain subgraph, GSBoG achieves a Terminal Variation of 0.03 versus 0.27 for baseline methods, with mean congestion of 21.13 versus 84.09-178.19 for alternatives (Table 2, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The paper's LEMON subgraph and trained gIPF network are unavailable, so a synthetic 9559-node layered network with the same degree bound was generated and solved with exact dynamic IPF instead of the learned solver. GSBoG achieves lower congestion than baselines (11.3 vs 43.7–47.4) and near-exact terminal matching, qualitatively matching the paper's structure, but the specific claimed numbers (0.03 TV, 21.13 congestion, 84.09–178.19 baselines) are not reproduced.

claims.claim: On the bipartite assignment task, GSBoG attains 100% accuracy for problem sizes n≤10 and 90% accuracy for n=20, with 85% of the learned coupling mass placed on optimal edges (Table 3, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The paper's own graph construction (Appendix C.1) is used at the paper's sizes (n=6,8,10,20), but the bridge is solved exactly via dynamic IPF rather than the paper's learned gIPF network. Accuracy is reproduced and exceeded (1.0 at all n, vs paper's 100%/100%/100%/90%), but the mass-on-optimal-edges claim is not fully reproduced: n=8 yields 79.8% and n=20 yields 80.9%, both below the claimed 85%.

claims.claim: On a 500-state Markov state model of Chignolin protein folding, GSBoG-controlled trajectories achieve a 99.7% folding rate versus 0.55% for uncontrolled dynamics and 71.69% for a committor-guided baseline (Table 4, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: The chignolin MSM is not public, so a synthetic 500-state analogue with two 240-state basins joined by a 20-state channel was constructed. The uncontrolled fold rate reproduces closely (0.56% vs 0.55%) and GSBoG achieves 100% (vs 99.7%), but the baseline comparison is not reproduced: committor-guided reaches 98.8% (vs paper's 71.69%) and attraction flow reaches 100% (vs 62.08%), so the claimed ordering over baselines fails.

claims.claim: The GSBoG-controlled folding pathway has an energy barrier of 1.39 kB·T_sim under a running-cost objective, compared to 6.94 kB·T_sim for uncontrolled dynamics (Table 4).
claims.evidence: On the same 500-state analogue MSM, using the paper's barrier definition, the ordering reproduces (uncontrolled 5.94 > GSBoG f=0 5.57 > GSBoG with cost 3.30 kBT) and the effect is monotone in cost weight, but the magnitude is far smaller than claimed (factor 1.8 vs the paper's factor ~5; specific values 1.39 and 6.94 are not reproduced).

ParetoOptimal/repro-b7bjkrfnjw.overall: The logbook provides rigorous numerical verification of the paper's theoretical contributions (Theorem 3.1 and Proposition 3.4) with multiple independent cross-checks at 1e-9 precision, but the experimental claims are only partially addressed on proxy instances due to the paper's lack of public code and data, reproducing qualitative structure and trends without matching the specific reported numbers.

GAMI000/repro-beyond-rational-illusion-b.paper_title: Beyond Rational Illusion: Behaviorally Realistic Strategic Classification

claims.claim: Pro-SF models strategic agents' feature manipulation via a prospect-guided utility function combining loss aversion, probability distortion, and reference-point bias (Equation 12).
claims.evidence: The logbook independently implements equation_12_utility combining probability distortion (weight_probability from Eq. 10), loss aversion (kappa=2.25, alpha/beta curvature), and reference-point bias (quantized reference via K=5), using the paper's stated defaults. The code runs successfully on real Adult/Spam data and the Equation 10 probe confirms the probability weighting function produces sensible values (p=0.05→0.134, p=0.8→0.599).

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 shows that training a classifier under a rational-agent assumption while agents actually exhibit psychological biases creates irreducible deployment error, manifesting as over-defense or under-defense failure modes (Section 4, Proposition 4.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook's analysis is primarily a theoretical audit noting that Proposition 4.1 explicitly assumes nonzero near-boundary error rather than deriving irreducibility from distribution mismatch alone. The independent runs show directional error patterns (rational baseline has under-defense error 0.184 on Adult under prospect deployment; Pro-SF trades to mixed over/under-defense), but this is only weakly consistent with the claim's mechanism and does not formally verify or falsify the proposition.

claims.claim: Under fully non-rational agent behavior, Pro-SF substantially outperforms a rational-baseline classifier, e.g., 81.50% vs 72.42% accuracy on Adult and 82.41% vs 69.54% on Credit (Table 1, Section 6).
claims.evidence: The independent 3-seed run on Adult (12k rows) reproduces the direction: Pro-SF 83.95% vs Rational 78.64% (+5.31), and Spam 93.24% vs 84.84% (+8.40). However, Credit—one of the two specifically claimed datasets—was not tested, exact values differ from the paper (81.50/72.42 and 82.41/69.54), and the setup uses a simplified 25-point grid action set rather than the paper's undisclosed candidate sets.

claims.claim: Under a mixed population of rational and non-rational agents, Pro-SF still outperforms the rational baseline, e.g., 78.68% vs 74.31% on Adult and 86.71% vs 78.16% on Spam (Table 1, Section 6).
claims.evidence: The independent 3-seed mixed-population run (20% rational) reproduces the direction on both datasets: Adult 72.21% vs 67.94% (+4.27) and Spam 86.02% vs 78.40% (+7.63), compared to the paper's 78.68/74.31 and 86.71/78.16. The setup uses reduced data, an independently specified action grid, and only 2 of 6 datasets, so exact values are not reproduced.

claims.claim: An ablation on synthetic data shows all three prospect-theory components contribute, with removing probability distortion causing the largest drop, from 78.92% to 73.50% accuracy (Table 2).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 establishes that message passing neural networks (MPNNs) are Lipschitz (Holder) continuous with respect to an action metric d_M on bofop-signals: ||H(A_1,f_1) - H(A_2,f_2)||_2 <= C'_{D,r} d_M((A_1,f_1),(A_2,f_2)) (Theorem 4.1).

claims.claim: The privacy cost enters through the multiplicative factor c(epsilon) = (e^epsilon + 1)/(e^epsilon - 1), which the paper shows is optimal (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook shows c(ε)=1/(2q-1)=(e^ε+1)/(e^ε-1)=1/tanh(ε/2) exactly, proves the unbiased estimator c·mean(z) attains the Cramér-Rao variance (c²-μ²)/n, and constructs a Le Cam two-point lower bound (Bernoulli(33/64) vs Bernoulli(31/64)) giving minimax MSE Ω(c²/n), establishing optimality of the privacy factor.

claims.claim: Two orderings of corruption and privacy are analyzed: Corruption-then-LDP (CTL), yielding a corruption term of alpha, and LDP-then-Corruption (LTC), yielding a corruption term of c(epsilon)*alpha (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Exact expectation calculations show CTL bias |F-h|=α|b-h|≤2α and LTC bias |F-h|=α|cb-h|≤α(c+1)≤2cα, with endpoint adversaries (h,b)=(1,-1) and (h,b)=(-1,1) attaining 2α and (c+1)α respectively, verified over 1,600 exact Fraction-arithmetic cases.

claims.claim: The paper introduces PrivXPO and SquareXPO as the first online algorithms for private and robust alignment from preference labels, with PrivXPO achieving suboptimality O(c(epsilon)*sqrt(log|Pi|*T)/T) (Section 4, Algorithms PrivXPO and SquareXPO).
claims.evidence: While the PrivXPO rate O(c(ε)√(log|Π|T/T)) is supported by an implementation with c² scaling and the XPO meta theorem, the 'first online algorithm' claim is contradicted by arXiv:2510.13512 (published 2025-10-15, before the target's 2025-12-29 date), which presents an online KL-regularized RLHF protocol with ε-local randomized response on preference labels and a theorem-level online regret guarantee, meeting all five scope-matching criteria.

claims.claim: Offline algorithms Priv-chi-PO and Square-chi-PO achieve suboptimality gaps of O(c(epsilon)*sqrt(log|Pi|/n)) and O(c(epsilon)*sqrt(log|Pi|/n) + alpha) respectively under the CTL corruption model (Section 3, Offline Settings).
claims.evidence: Finite-policy implementations match Algorithms 1 and 3 (PrivChiPO selects A_high with scores -0.671 vs -2.510; SquareChiPO selects A_low with losses 16.36 vs 2.60), and the rate algebra correctly instantiates √(c²log/n)=c√(log/n) and √(c²log/n+α²)≤c√(log/n)+α via the offline meta theorem, with an independent checker verifying monomial exponents.

DineshAI/r3PKGNlKET.overall: The logbook provides rigorous mathematical derivations with exact-arithmetic numerical cross-checks, independent checkers, and negative controls for the theoretical claims (1-4, 6), all of which are supported. Claim 5 is falsified because the 'first online algorithm' novelty assertion is contradicted by a concrete, dated, scope-matched prior work (arXiv:2510.13512), even though the PrivXPO rate itself is correctly derived.

Srishti280992/repro-alignment-sensitive-.paper_title: Alignment-Sensitive Minimax Rates for Spectral Algorithms with Learned Kernels

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 establishes that over signal classes with Effective Span Dimension (ESD) at most K, the minimax excess risk is asymptotically equivalent to K·σ², holding without classical eigenvalue-decay or source-condition assumptions (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: At d=1000 across K={4,8,16,32,64,128}, the logbook computes a constructive PC upper bound of 1.98·K·σ² (below the theorem's 2K·σ²) and an executable Assouad-hypercube lower bound of 0.4793·K·σ² via Gauss-Hermite quadrature, bracketing the claimed K·σ² rate from both sides.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 shows the principal-component (PC) estimator's risk is sandwiched as (d†−1)σ² ≤ Risk ≤ 2d†σ², where d† is the Effective Span Dimension defined as the smallest number of leading eigenfunctions whose remaining tail signal energy no longer exceeds the noise level σ² (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: 400 randomized trials at d=1000 with log-normal permuted spectra and σ²=1e-3 all satisfy (d†−1)σ² ≤ R*_PC ≤ 2d†σ², with observed ratios R*/(d†σ²) ranging 1.00–1.31 including deliberately non-monotone orderings.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 gives convergence rates for a quota sequence {K_n}: the minimax risk over populations satisfying d†(σ0²/n; θ*, λ) ≤ K_n scales as Θ(K_n σ0²/n) (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Across n={200,…,12800} with K_n=⌈n^0.35⌉, the oracle-PC upper ratio is consistently 1.90·K_n·σ0²/n and the embedded hypercube Bayes lower bound is 0.4793·K_n·σ0²/n, bracketing Θ(K_n·σ0²/n) at multiple sample sizes.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 proves that overparameterized gradient flow (OP-GF) can reduce the Effective Span Dimension over training time by assigning larger adapted eigenvalues to strong signal directions with initially small eigenvalues, moving the problem into a lower minimax-risk complexity class (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Using the paper's Section 6 construction (d=5000, n=10000, J=15, λ_j=j⁻¹, θ_{⌊j^q⌋}=j⁻¹·⁷⁵) with Equation (12) OP-GF dynamics, ESD reductions are {0,3,6,55} for q={1,1.5,2,3}, showing larger reductions under worse initial alignment with q=3 dropping from 88 to 33.

claims.claim: Section 7 and Section 8 extend the Effective Span Dimension framework to linear regression (via SVD, minimax rate Θ(σ0²K/n)) and RKHS regression (rate Θ(σ̄²K_n/n) with effective noise σ̄² = (σ0² + ||f*||²_∞)/n) (Section 7, Section 8).
claims.evidence: Linear regression (n=300, p=400, 11 SVD stretches) and RKHS (800 Mercer coordinates, 10000-point grid, σ̄²=(1+‖f*‖²∞)/n≈0.0111, 16 perturbations) both satisfy the ESD sandwich at non-trivial scale, implying rates Θ(σ0²K/n) and Θ(σ̄²K_n/n) respectively, though no explicit lower-bound audit is provided for these extensions.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments show that span profiles decrease during OP-GF training—with larger improvements when initial signal-spectrum alignment is worse—and that deeper models attain lower Effective Span Dimension than shallow variants given sufficient training iterations (Numerical Validation).
claims.evidence: Span-profile decrease and alignment-dependence are shown in Claim 4 data (q=3: 88→33 vs q=1: 10→10); the 20-replication depth study yields mean final ESD D=0:33.2 > D=1:32.45 > D=3:31.7 with strict ordering, though the effect size is modest and deeper models receive 3× more training steps.

Srishti280992/repro-alignment-sensitive-.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims, including both upper and lower finite-dimensional bounds for the minimax-rate claims (1,3), exhaustive sandwich checks for the PC risk inequality (2), and paper-scale OP-GF simulations using the Section 6 construction for the ESD-reduction and depth claims (4,6). The main limitations are the absence of explicit lower-bound audits for the linear/RKHS extensions (5) and the modest, confound-prone depth effect in Claim 6.

Srishti280992/repro-haloprobe-bayesian-d.paper_title: HaloProbe: Bayesian Detection and Mitigation of Object Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models

claims.claim: Conditioning attention analysis on token position reveals hallucinated tokens receive higher attention than correct tokens, but this trend reverses when statistics are marginalized across positions, demonstrating Simpson's paradox in coarse-grained attention-based hallucination detection (Section 3.2, Figure 2a).
claims.evidence: On 36,753 labeled object tokens from 5000 COCO images with LLaVA-1.5-7B, the raw per-bin data shows hallucinated tokens have higher image attention than correct tokens in 28/30 position bins, yet after marginalization correct tokens have higher attention (0.002873 vs 0.002656), concretely demonstrating Simpson's paradox at full paper scale.

claims.claim: Hallucinated objects appear less frequently than correct objects in the underlying data, and this class imbalance alone allows a trivial classifier to reach over 84% accuracy on hallucination detection without using genuine signal (Section 3.2, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Across 36,753 CHAIR-labeled tokens, 31,389 are correct and 5,364 hallucinated, yielding an 85.41% correct-token base rate; an always-correct classifier achieves 85.41% accuracy (85.35% on the held-out test split) with AUROC exactly 50.0, confirming the trivial classifier exceeds 84% with no genuine signal.

claims.claim: On LLaVA-1.5-7B, HaloProbe achieves 90.00% accuracy and 93.50 AUROC for hallucination detection, compared to 84.46% accuracy and 90.19 AUROC for the prior state-of-the-art method DIML (Table 1).
claims.evidence: On a 2500-train/500-test COCO split with LLaVA-1.5-7B, HaloProbe achieves 89.84% accuracy and 92.82 AUROC vs the paper's 90.00/93.50, while the DIML reimplementation reaches 85.98% accuracy and 89.66 AUROC vs the paper's 84.46/90.19; HaloProbe's superiority over DIML is preserved on both metrics.

claims.claim: For hallucination mitigation with LLaVA-1.5 under greedy decoding, HaloProbe with post-processing reduces sentence-level hallucination (C_s) from a 51.6 baseline to 17.6, outperforming DIML's 25.0 (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The baseline C_s of 51.0 closely matches the paper's 51.6, validating the pipeline, but HaloProbe+post-processing reaches C_s=22.2 rather than the claimed 17.6, and DIML+post-processing achieves a lower C_s of 18.4, inverting the claimed HaloProbe-over-DIML ordering on the decisive sentence-level hallucination metric.

claims.claim: Ablating HaloProbe's external features and fine-grained attention components together drops detection accuracy from 90.0% to 84.4%, and ablating class-balanced training alone (using natural distribution) drops accuracy to 89.8% (Tables 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: Ablating attention features drops accuracy from 89.84% to 82.36% (paper: 90.0→84.4), confirming attention is load-bearing; ablating all genuine features collapses AUROC to 50.71 (paper: 50.1); and natural-distribution training yields 90.25% accuracy (paper: 89.8%), all on the same 2500/500 split with three-seed averaging.

claims.claim: HaloProbe's hallucination-aware beam search mitigation uses a score function combining hallucinated/correct object counts and probabilities with beam width N_beam=5, threshold τ=0.5, and penalty β=0.1 (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The score function S(b_j) = n_hal + p_hal - β(n_corr + p_corr) with N_beam=5, β=0.1, and τ=0.5 is confirmed from Section 4.2, and an empirical demonstration on 150 COCO images shows the argmin-S selection reduces C_s from 50.7 to 34.7, validating the score function's behavior at the specified hyperparameters.

Srishti280992/repro-haloprobe-bayesian-d.overall: This is a full-scale independent reimplementation of HaloProbe on LLaVA-1.5-7B with 5000 MS COCO images and 36,753 labeled tokens, with no official runnable code available. Five of six claims are supported by concrete evidence at paper scale, while Claim 4 is falsified because HaloProbe's post-processing C_s of 22.2 misses the claimed 17.6 and DIML outperforms HaloProbe, inverting the reported ordering.

ai-sherpa/known-delay-distribution-onlin.paper_title: Minimax Optimal Strategy for Delayed Observations in Online Reinforcement Learning

claims.claim: For the known-delay-distribution setting, the proposed algorithm achieves regret O~(H√((D_max∧B)SAK) + HBSA) for tabular MDPs with delayed observations, where D_max is the maximum delay and B is the branching factor (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: On the paper's hard-instance family, the (D_max∧B) capping is clearly demonstrated: at B=4 regret is flat (2.9% spread) across a 24× D_max range, at B=8 it plateaus near D_max≈8, and a joint fit over 36 (D_max,B) points yields R²=0.808 with the min versus 0.437 without. The K-exponent measures 0.472 (R²=0.998) up to 12.8M episodes, and the bound holds in 36/36 random-MDP configurations.

claims.claim: For the unknown-delay-distribution setting, the algorithm achieves regret O~(H√((D_max∧B)SAK) + H√(Δ_maxSAK) + H(B+Δ_max)SA), extending the known-delay result (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The unknown-delay agent uses the paper's exact augmented planner with the paper's own hazard estimator and optimism over it (no proxy multiplier). The full three-term bound is satisfied in 36/36 configurations (worst ratio 0.0075), the Δ_max term stays within its allowance in 5/5 settings, and the shared (D_max∧B) term inherits Claim 1's evidence. The Δ_max term is not saturated on these instances, but the bound holds and the mechanism is correctly implemented.

claims.claim: A matching lower bound of Ω(H√(D̃SAK/log D̃)) is established for constant-delay MDPs, where D̃ = min{D_max, H/4, B/2, S/4-1}, showing the upper bounds are optimal up to log factors (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: On the real CodeMDP+tree hard instance, R(D̃=24)/R(D̃=2) measures 1.652 for Algorithm 1 (1.645 for UCB, 1.714 for Thompson) versus 1.618 predicted with the log penalty and 3.464 without; shape fit gives R²=0.960 with √(D̃/log D̃) versus -0.435 without. The moment-matching LP recovers Bernstein's constant 0.279296 vs 0.280169 (0.31% error), and a Bayes likelihood-ratio test stays at chance on the √(m/λ) frontier.

claims.claim: The result improves on the prior bound of Chen et al. (2023) by a factor of H^(1/2) D_max^2, tightening O~(H^{3/2}D_max^{5/2}√(SAK)) down to O~(H√(D_maxSAK)) (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Two single-line ablations isolate the two mechanisms: variance-dependent vs Hoeffding bonus gives a ratio H-exponent of 0.518 (claimed 0.5, R²=0.730), and pooled vs per-augmented-pair counts gives a ratio D_max-exponent of 2.216 over D_max≤4 (claimed 2.0), with honest reporting of turnover past D_max=4 due to saturation. Measured regret is inside this paper's bound in all configurations while sitting orders of magnitude below Chen et al.'s bound.

claims.claim: The framework is generalized to MDPs with partially known dynamics, yielding regret O~(H√(K∑_{z∈Z_eff}(log|Y|)∧B(z)) + H∑B(z)) (Theorem 5, Section 8).
claims.evidence: The (log|Y|)∧B(z) min is measured on the delayed instantiation with |Y| up to 2.3×10¹⁵: joint fit R²=0.808 with the min vs 0.437 without, identical to Claim 1's evidence since the delayed MDP is a special case of Theorem 5. Algorithm 3 on an explicit non-delayed Assumption-2 instance cuts regret 3–5× versus a flat per-(x,y,a) learner, confirming the qualitative benefit of Z_eff structure, though the |Z_eff| exponent is not resolved on that abstract family.

ai-sherpa/known-delay-distribution-onlin.overall: This logbook provides substantial experimental evidence supporting all five claims, primarily through exact augmented-MDP computation on the paper's own hard-instance family at scales up to 12.8M episodes. The key structural predictions—the (D_max∧B) capping, the log D̃ penalty in the lower bound, and the two-mechanism improvement over Chen et al.—are each isolated and measured with honest reporting of where instances saturate or exponents overshoot.

claims.claim: The optimal collaborative prediction set C*(x) has a two-threshold form: it augments the human-proposed set H(x) with labels whose score exceeds threshold a*, and prunes labels within H(x) whose score exceeds threshold b* (Theorem 2.1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: Exact two-threshold search vs ILP optimum over all 0/1 sets shows relative gap shrinking 0.0105→0.0041 as label grid refines (L=40→200), while a shuffled-score positive control stays flat at 1.4–1.7×, confirming the near-zero gap reflects the theorem's structure rather than a vacuous test.

claims.claim: The counterfactual harm principle requires P(Y not in C(X) | Y in H(X)) < epsilon, i.e., the AI must not remove correct labels the human already proposed (Section 1).
claims.evidence: CUP-Offline's split-conformal pruning threshold controls realized harm to 0.063 (target ε=0.08) at n_cal=80,000 with 90% of seeds ≤ ε, while a model-drift control (frozen threshold, drifted test scorer) breaks the guarantee (harm=0.377, 100% violation).

claims.claim: The complementarity principle requires P(Y in C(X) | Y not in H(X)) >= 1-delta, i.e., the AI must recover correct labels the human missed (Section 1).
claims.evidence: CUP-Offline's augmentation threshold yields mean complementarity coverage 0.7821 vs target 0.78 at n_cal=80,000, with model-drift control collapsing to 0.516 (100% below target), confirming the mechanism enforces the principle; the 60% per-seed clearance rate is consistent with the marginal nature of conformal guarantees.

claims.claim: The offline calibration procedure gives distribution-free finite-sample coverage guarantees whose bounds depend on the sizes of the calibration sets used to fit a* and b* (Proposition 4.1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Two-sided finite-sample bounds hold (lower bounds 100%/100%, upper bounds 80%/100% of n_cal settings) with the 1/(n1+1) slack shrinking monotonically 0.0198→0.00020 as n_cal grows 150→15,000, and a noise-inflation control breaks the lower bounds (out-H coverage drops to 0.658 vs target 0.82).

claims.claim: The CUP-Online algorithm updates thresholds a_t and b_t via stochastic approximation steps (a_{t+1}=a_t+eta(1{s(x_t,y_t)>a_t}-delta), and analogously for b_t) to track target error rates under arbitrary distribution shift, including shifts caused by humans adapting their behavior to the AI (Section 4.2, Proposition 4.2).
claims.evidence: SA recursion implemented exactly as specified tracks both targets within the Proposition 4.2 bound 12/12 seeds under all three shift regimes (none, context-drift, human-sharpens), with the human-adaptation shift yielding |out-δ|=0.0036 for CUP vs 0.0450 for a warm-started-then-frozen baseline (12× worse).

ai-sherpa/human-ai-collaborative-uq-repr.overall: This logbook provides from-scratch numpy/scipy implementations of all five theoretical claims at non-trivial scale (label grids to 200, calibration sets to 80k, online streams to 22k steps) with appropriate positive and negative controls, verifying the two-threshold structure, harm/complementarity guarantees, finite-sample bounds, and online SA tracking. All experiments use synthetic data rather than the paper's real application datasets, but the claims being tested are primarily theorems and propositions whose validity is checkable on designed data-generating processes.

ai-sherpa/unfolded-laplacian-spectral-em.paper_title: Unfolded Laplacian Spectral Embedding: A Theoretically Grounded Approach to Dynamic Network Representation

claims.claim: Theorem 1 (Section 3.2) establishes that ULSE-n1 satisfies cross-sectional stability (identical latent positions Bzi:(t)=Bzj:(t) imply identical embeddings Yi:(t)=Yj:(t)) and longitudinal stability (identical latent positions and degree heterogeneity across times t,u imply identical embeddings across those times) (Theorem 1, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Finite-sample cross-sectional and longitudinal deviations shrink monotonically from 0.0627→0.0087 and 0.0488→0.0074 as n grows 80→1280 on a 3-community dynamic SBM, tracking the O(1/√(ρn)) reference; the degree-premise control is honestly reported as finite-n-limited but cleanly demonstrated at population level in claim 3.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 proves ULSE-n1 embeddings converge almost surely to their noise-free counterparts at rate O(1/(ρ^{1/2} n^{1/2})) (Theorem 2, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Measured log-log decay slopes of -0.926 (ρ=0.5) and -0.935 (ρ=0.8) over n=60→960 with 8 trials each, both steeper than the claimed -0.5 upper-bound rate; error·√(ρn) shrinks monotonically (0.502→0.156), confirming the bound holds across a 16× range of n.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 shows the noise-free ULSE-n1 embeddings themselves satisfy both cross-sectional and longitudinal stability properties, forming the basis for Theorem 1 (Theorem 3, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Using the exact population probability matrix (zero sampling noise), cross-sectional deviation ≤5.5e-15 and eligible longitudinal deviation ≤2.4e-15 at n up to 1200, while a destructive control breaking the D̃(t)=D̃(u) premise produces a real drift of 0.0009–0.0043 (3.87e11× larger), directly demonstrating both the stability and the necessity of the premise.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 extends the stability results to ULSE-n2 under the requirement that the embedding dimension equals the number of communities (d=K), relaxing the degree-uniformity assumption needed for ULSE-n1 (Theorem 4, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: ULSE-n2 at d=K=3 stays at machine precision (≤2.9e-14) on the identical B_A↔B_B snapshot pair that broke ULSE-n1's longitudinal premise (0.0009 drift in claim 3), directly exercising the relaxation; finite-sample results up to n=1280 show deviations shrinking with n for both eligible and relaxed pairs.

claims.claim: Proposition 1 establishes a dynamic Cheeger-type inequality bounding the k-way conductance φk(𝒢) of the dynamic network in terms of the singular values σk of the unfolded normalized Laplacian (Proposition 1, Section 3.4).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive partition enumeration (n=7,8,9; 4 graph families; up to 21,147 partitions per graph) confirms the lower bound in 84/84 cells (45/45 non-trivial); a calibrated spectral upper bound extends the check to n=20/50/100 (84/84 pass), with the heuristic matching the exact optimum in 168/168 comparable cells and the poly(k) constant measured as order-1 (≤1.28, flat in k).

ai-sherpa/unfolded-laplacian-spectral-em.overall: This logbook provides concrete, from-scratch experimental evidence supporting all five theoretical claims of the paper, with dynamic SBMs at n up to 1280 for stability/convergence theorems and exhaustive partition enumeration plus scaled checks for the Cheeger bound. The reproduction is independent (no author code used), includes unit tests and destructive controls, and honestly reports limitations such as finite-sample noise obscuring the degree-premise control and the small-graph scope of exact conductance enumeration.

ai-sherpa/branch-and-cut-learning-repro.paper_title: Theoretical Challenges in Learning for Branch-and-Cut

claims.claim: Selecting cuts by LP bound improvement, a common supervision signal for learned cut selection, can produce branch-and-cut trees that are 2^Omega(n) times larger than trees produced by selecting cuts via a simpler efficacy proxy score (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Exact rational LP computations show LP-bound improvement ranks C2 (23/20) over C1 (3/20) while efficacy ranks C1 (0.1746) over C2 (0.1646); running strong-branching B&B on the paper's 2D cut gadget yields C1 tree=55 vs C2 tree=1821 at m=27, with the gap growing exponentially across all measured m values.

claims.claim: Arbitrarily small perturbations (epsilon) to the right-hand sides of cuts can change the minimum achievable branch-and-cut tree size from a single node to 2^Omega(n) nodes (Theorem 3.3, Section 3).
claims.evidence: On the disjoint-triangle stable set construction, the tight clique cut yields a measured minimum tree of 1 node (integral root LP) while the perturbed cut with eps'=1/8000 yields exactly 511=2^9-1 nodes at m=8, with the two root LPs differing by only m*eps'<=eps.

claims.claim: A learned branching policy whose per-node scores differ from strong branching by at most an arbitrarily small epsilon for any epsilon>0 can still produce a search tree of at least 2^(n+1)-1 nodes, versus at most 2n+1 nodes for strong branching itself (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: On the 5-variable packing block with alpha-scaling making all strong-branching scores equal, the learned scorer differs by at most eps/2=5e-13; measured B&B trees at n=14 are 29 (=2n+1) for strong branching vs 367727 (>=2^15-1=32767) for the learned policy.

claims.claim: Merely k deviations from the strong branching trajectory can inflate the resulting tree size by a factor of 2^Omega(k) (Theorem 4.4, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Measured tree sizes grow from 25 (k=0) to 71077 (k=12) on the packing instance at n=12, with every k satisfying the lower bound 2^k*2n/7 and a fitted log2(tree)-vs-k slope of 0.950, confirming 2^Omega(k) growth.

claims.claim: Even branching policies that assign identical scores to candidate variables can produce exponentially different tree sizes depending solely on the tie-breaking rule used (Proposition 2).
claims.evidence: Using the same clamped scoring function min(Score_SB, 9) where b and y1 both score 9, two tie-breaking rules yield measured trees of 25 (=2n+1) vs 81007 (>=2^13-1=8191) at n=12, a 3240x gap from tie-breaking alone.

ai-sherpa/branch-and-cut-learning-repro.overall: The logbook independently re-implements all five worst-case constructions from the paper using exact rational arithmetic and a from-scratch best-bound branch-and-bound engine, then measures actual tree sizes rather than transcribing formulas. All five exponential separations are demonstrated with concrete counted node totals on the paper's own gadgets, cross-validated against HiGHS with exact agreement.

claims.claim: In the population setting, Theorem 1 characterizes excess risk as a function of the magnitude and direction of the performative effect together with spurious features (Section 4, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements the literal RRM iteration (eq 4) to convergence (1e-14 tolerance) at d=100, p=200, and the measured fixed-point risk matches the exact eq(6) formula to ≤0.70% across 6 instances, with the iterate matching the closed-form fixed point to 1.8e-16. Dependence on magnitude, direction, and spurious features is numerically demonstrated.

claims.claim: Corollary 2 shows the optimal regularization parameter in the population regime is proportional to the strength of the performative effect, with optimal risk remaining strictly positive (Section 4, Corollary 2).
claims.evidence: Numeric argmin of the exact eq(6) risk yields λ*-vs-b̄ slopes of 1.0000, 0.8358, 0.3777 for ρ=0, 0.4, 0.8, matching the predicted (1−ρ²) = 1.000, 0.840, 0.360. Optimal risk is strictly positive (0.0073 = Var(b)) for variable b, vanishing only in the degenerate constant-b/Σ=I case.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 establishes a deterministic equivalent of the performative fixed point for over-parameterized ridge regression when the number of features exceeds the number of samples (Section 5, Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The base D=0 deterministic equivalent matches finite-sample ridge to ≤1.3% across n=60/120/240 with convergence. The D≠0 performative fixed-point DE matches 5-step RRM to ≤6.1%, within the theorem's O(‖D‖²) tolerance, with correct risk ordering and initialization independence (0.58% gap). The DE was independently derived and validated against real ridge fits rather than the paper's eq(14) due to a PDF extraction issue.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 shows the optimal regularization moves in the same direction as the performative effect on predictive features under low noise, but in the opposite direction under high noise, in the over-parameterized regime (Section 5, Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Using continuous common-random-number optimization directly on the real 5-step RRM mechanism at κ=1.1, d=200, p=400, n=364: low noise (σ=0.2 < σ_B1≈0.383) gives Δλ*=+0.0210 (same direction), high noise (σ=0.9 > σ_B1) gives Δλ*=−0.0306 (opposite direction), confirming the sign flip.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments in Section 6 confirm that in the over-parameterized setting, performative effects can improve optimally-regularized risk when performativity reinforces existing trends, contrasting with the population-regime degradation (Section 6).
claims.evidence: Over-parameterized optimal risk falls monotonically from 0.232 to 0.067 as b̄ increases from 0 to 0.3 (validated DE), with a direct finite-sample CRN-optimized anchor confirming improvement (0.2179 on < 0.2199 off). Population optimal risk remains strictly positive (0.00075–0.00095) at every b̄ tested, demonstrating the regime contrast.

ai-sherpa/optimal-reg-performative-repro.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from independent numpy/scipy implementations at the paper's own scale (d=100–200, p=200–400, κ=1.1–2.0) supporting all five claims, with unit tests, common-random-number optimization, and honest disclosure of a transcription bug and a PDF extraction limitation. The reproduction is thorough and the evidence is non-toy, matching the paper's synthetic-Gaussian experimental regime.

Edd16/icml2026-06Nk3dJDMq-repro.paper_title: Steer Like the LLM: Activation Steering that Mimics Prompting

claims.claim: The paper derives prompt steering interventions by subtracting unsteered activations from prompt-steered activations and trains PSR models to approximate successful prompt interventions (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: A toy linear model (d=32, n=400) demonstrates that subtracting unsteered mean activations from steered mean activations yields a usable steering direction (agreement 0.905 vs 0.955 baseline), but no PSR model training was attempted and the setup is far below the paper's LLM scale.

claims.claim: Prompt steering applies highly token-dependent intervention strengths, motivating token-specific activation steering rather than constant coefficients (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: No experiment analyzes token-dependent intervention strengths or reproduces Figure 2; the logbook only contains a single toy mechanism demonstration.

claims.claim: PSR models estimate token-specific steering coefficients from activations and are trained with log-likelihood or MSE objectives to imitate prompt steering (Sections 3.4 and 3.5).

ai-sherpa/tight-margin-voting-bounds-rep.paper_title: Tight Margin-Based Generalization Bounds for Voting Classifiers over Finite Hypothesis Sets

claims.claim: Theorem 1 proves a margin-based generalization bound for voting classifiers over finite hypothesis sets that is asymptotically tight in the joint tradeoff between hypothesis-set size |H|, margin θ, empirical margin loss, sample size n, and failure probability δ (Section 1, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Real AdaBoost voting classifiers over explicit finite stump hypothesis sets on 6 real datasets; Theorem 1 dominates the measured sup_{f∈C(H)}(L_D−L_S^θ) in 18/18 configurations with c=1 (max required c=0.5661), and the Theorem-1 excess matches the GKL20 lower-bound excess term-for-term over 27,648 parameter configurations (max|ratio−1|=0.0) while the previous best bound is loose by up to 22.98×. The n-sweep shows the bound's decay slope (−0.4498) tracks the measured empirical process (−0.4610, R²=0.989).

claims.claim: The bound closes a gap left open since Schapire et al.'s original margin bound and Breiman's improvement for the zero empirical-margin-loss case, eliminating the remaining √(ln(n)/ln(e/L_S^θ(f))) factor that persisted through Germain et al.'s interpolating bound (Section 1).
claims.evidence: The dominant-term ratio gz13/Theorem-1 equals √(ln n/ln(e/L)) to 4.44e-16 at the measured empirical margin losses of real AdaBoost ensembles (36 rows), with real magnitude 1.36–2.65×. 24/36 real AdaBoost runs achieve L_S^θ=0 at a valid θ inside the theorem's range, where Breiman's leading term is 2.25–3.58× worse than Theorem 1's. The interpolation endpoint control confirms gz13 degenerates to Breiman at L=0.

claims.claim: Lemma 6 bounds the Rademacher complexity term used in the proof, with the bound proved via the technique in Section 5 (Section 3.2, Lemma 6).
claims.evidence: Convex-hull identity verified over 560M (σ,f) checks (max violation 1.78e-15); exact empirical Rademacher complexity by exhaustive 2^n enumeration (up to 2^20=1,048,576 sign vectors) satisfies Massart's bound 5/5 (max ratio 0.7262); the contraction step R̂_{φ,F} ≤ (L_φ/n)·R̂_H holds 4/4 with exact L_φ; ‖φ‖_∞ tail holds 15/15; the lemma's conclusion dominates the measured empirical process 5/5 (max ratio 0.0040). Destructive controls (Massart without ln|H|, non-Lipschitz φ) fail as predicted.

claims.claim: Lemma 5 establishes a half-margin generalization bound, proved in Section 6 (Section 3.2, Lemma 5).
claims.evidence: The decomposition identity holds to 1.18e-16 over 240 real configurations; the binomial engine Pr[g~Q_f] is confirmed by 20,000 real MC draws (max|diff|=0.00589, 24/24 within 3 SE) and exact enumeration (8.9e-16); the inner bound holds 18/18 (min slack +0.137); the n^{−1/2} rate is recovered as slope −0.4907 vs theory −1/2 (R²=0.9985); the Hoeffding discretisation bound holds 6/6 with a 121× out-of-regime destructive control.

claims.claim: Lemma 7 bounds the Lipschitz constants of auxiliary functions used to construct the tight bound, building on Rademacher complexity and contraction-inequality techniques adapted from Larsen and Schalburg (Section 5.1, Lemma 7).
claims.evidence: The analytic derivative matches finite differences to 1.27e-07; exact L_φ and L_ρ satisfy the closed-form bound exp(−Nθ²/8)(Nθ+1/θ) on 15/15 in-regime pairs (max ratios 0.1132/0.1547); the −1/8 decay exponent is recovered from measured data (slope −0.13163, R²=0.9994); the constants dominate all 4,841,118 difference quotients at real measured margins; the out-of-regime destructive control shows exponential smallness vanishes. An intermediate-display indexing slip is transparently reported but the lemma's conclusion is verified directly against exact constants.

ai-sherpa/tight-margin-voting-bounds-rep.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous, non-toy reproduction of all five claims: real AdaBoost voting classifiers over explicit finite hypothesis sets on 6 real datasets, exhaustive 2^n Rademacher enumeration (up to 2^20), destructive controls on every claim, and transparent reporting of limitations including a minor intermediate-display slip. The evidence independently supports the validity, tightness, and lemma-level proof machinery of the paper's bounds.

tomyimkc/repro-loss-aware-distributional.paper_title: Loss-Aware Distributionally Robust Optimization via Trainable Optimal Transport Ambiguity Sets

claims.claim: The paper formulates learning the ambiguity set for OT-DRO as a bilevel problem in which the upper level tunes the ambiguity-set geometry parameter theta and the lower level solves a standard OT-DRO problem (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: On the paper's own Eq. 43 closed-form construction, the lower level was convex in 1200/1200 random w-triples, the upper-level value function was nonconvex in 4/25 theta-direction checks, and the naive non-nested loop's final objective (10.89) was 42.54% worse than the proper bilevel loop (7.64), with re-solving at the naive theta recovering 7.62 — isolating that degradation comes from not solving the lower level to convergence.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 establishes that the proposed hypergradient descent procedure converges to a critical point of the bilevel problem under mild conditions, including square-summable step sizes (Section 5.1, Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: On the same Eq. 43 instance, the not-summable schedule (c/(i+1)^0.75) reached tail-mean ||hypergrad|| of 0.047 while the summable control (c/(i+1)^1.5) plateaued at 0.123 (2.6x higher) over 400 iterations, and constant step sizes showed monotonically shrinking tail gnorm (0.0405→0.0392→0.0389) — both matching Theorem 5.1's two statements.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 computes hypergradients through the nonsmooth conservative implicit function theorem, allowing differentiation through conic (OT-DRO) programs without assuming the solution map is continuously differentiable (Section 5, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: A genuine kink was located with left/right derivative gap 0.543 (959.8x the baseline median 0.000566), the active data-point index switched (7→6) across it, both one-sided derivatives yielded descent (3.279→3.189 and 3.279→3.128), and the naive wide-step symmetric estimate (-0.892) matched neither true slope (errors 0.136, 0.892) — directly demonstrating differentiation through a nonsmooth solution map without assuming continuous differentiability.

claims.claim: In portfolio optimization experiments with k=2, J=30, n_b=20, gamma=0.05, beta=0.1, the relative improvement of the learned ambiguity set over a fixed Wasserstein ball increases as sample size decreases (Section 6.1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The experiment substitutes a type-1 Mahalanobis cost for the paper's type-2 (squared) cost, a deliberate scope reduction; within that reduced scope the worst-case relative improvement is perfectly monotone across J (0.0802 at J=10 down to ~0 at J=40, fraction 1.0 concordant pairs), but the out-of-sample metric showed no clean trend at 12 trials per J.

claims.claim: Figure 3 shows the learned ambiguity set still enforces the coverage constraint, containing the true data-generating distribution with the specified high probability despite being shaped to reduce loss (Section 6.1, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Same type-1 cost substitution; bootstrap coverage held at 0.86 after learning (near the 0.9 target) and degraded to 0.7378 under the lambda_p=0 ablation, but the stricter fresh-sample diagnostic showed coverage of genuinely independent draws was only 0.0147 even before learning — a bootstrap-proxy limitation at J=30 rather than a test of the paper's type-2 cost setting.

claims.claim: Across 10 independent linear regression trials, the learned decision-focused ambiguity set consistently yields less conservative (lower average loss) decisions than baseline OT-DRO ambiguity sets (Section 6.2, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: On the paper's exact Eq. 43 construction (no cost substitution), the learned set beat the baseline on 10/10 headline trials and 26/30 full trials (mean relative OOS improvement 0.0387), while a loss-uninformed random-direction control improved in only 0.2 of trials with mean change -0.0783, and bootstrap coverage stayed at 0.878 (above the 0.85 target).

tomyimkc/repro-loss-aware-distributional.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence with explicit controls supporting four of six claims on the paper's own closed-form construction, with the bilevel structure, convergence theorem, nonsmooth differentiation mechanism, and regression consistency all verified. The two portfolio-CVaR claims are tested only under a type-1 cost substitution (vs the paper's type-2), making them toy-scale demonstrations of the same mechanism rather than full reproductions.

vimarsh/repro-stochastic-sparse-attentio.paper_title: Stochastic Sparse Attention for Memory-Bound Inference

claims.claim: S²ANTA-prop achieves a 1.50x decode-step attention kernel speedup over FlashInfer at 32k-token contexts on an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada GPU, while matching baseline accuracy (Section 3.4, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: On an RTX 4000 Ada with synthetic bf16 tensors at exact Llama-3.1-8B attention shapes (H=32, KVH=8, D=128, GQA-4) and full 32k context, S²ANTA-prop at S=128 measured 1.517× vs FlashInfer (420.9 µs → 277.5 µs), within 1% of the claimed 1.50×, with 200 CUDA-event-timed iterations and tight IQR spread.

claims.claim: S²ANTA-flash achieves a 1.51x speedup over FlashDecoding at matched accuracy operating points, using S=128 (prop) or S=2048 (flash) sampled value-cache rows (Section 3.4, Figure 4).

claims.claim: On 32k-token RULER tasks, S²ANTA-prop with S=128 scores 95.40±1.10 on FWE and 98.25±0.62 on NIAH, within confidence intervals of the baseline SDPA implementation (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states Claim 4 was removed because Llama-3.1-8B at 32k context does not fit the 20 GB card; no experiment, proxy, or substitute was run, so the RULER FWE/NIAH accuracy claim was never addressed.

claims.evidence: An explicit χ² test on 8192 independent estimates per scheme yielded χ²=59.9/63.1/65.4 (expected 64 dof) confirming unbiasedness for all three estimators, and the 1/S variance law was confirmed with a log-log slope of −1.000 (R²=1.0000) from both closed-form and independent Monte-Carlo methods on 2048 real attention head-instances from Llama-3.2-1B.

vimarsh/repro-stochastic-sparse-attentio.overall: The logbook provides strong evidence for the kernel-level speedup claim (1.517× vs 1.50×) and the mathematical unbiasedness/variance claims (χ² test and slope −1.000), but the end-to-end system claim and the GSM8K accuracy claim were only tested at substantially reduced scale or on synthetic proxies, and the RULER accuracy claim was not addressed at all.
