jomasego/repro-gem-geometric-entropy-mix.paper_title: GEM: Geometric Entropy Mixing for Optimal LLM Data Curation

claims.claim: When integrated with the DoReMi mixing framework, GEM improves average downstream accuracy to 43.95%, a +1.16 percentage point gain over the runner-up WebOrganizer (42.79%) (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook ran GEM clustering on 20 Newsgroups (8 categories, 7511 docs, all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings) measuring cluster balance as a proxy, not the actual DoReMi pipeline with 1.1B models on 25B tokens. The proxy results show GEM cluster balance (0.9185) is actually lower than K-Means (0.9887) and Spherical K-Means (0.9925), and the claimed 43.95% downstream accuracy was never tested.

claims.claim: GEM improves average downstream accuracy by 0.68 percentage points over WebOrganizer when integrated into the RegMix framework (41.45% vs 40.77%) (Table 1).
claims.evidence: No RegMix integration was run; the logbook only ran the same 20 Newsgroups proxy clustering experiment as Claim 1. The claimed 41.45% downstream accuracy was never tested, and the proxy experiment does not address the RegMix framework at all.

claims.claim: GEM is evaluated on 1.1B-parameter language models trained under a 25B-token budget (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook only confirms the paper documents a 1.1B-parameter, 25B-token setup but never actually trained any model. No training runs, no checkpoints, no evidence beyond reading the paper text.

claims.claim: An ablation progression from K-Means (38.5%) to Spherical K-Means (40.6%) to vanilla von Mises-Fisher mixture modeling (41.3%) to full GEM (42.1%) shows each component of the geometric entropy mixing approach contributes to counteracting cluster collapse (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: The logbook ran cluster balance experiments on 20 Newsgroups as a proxy, but the results do not reproduce the claimed monotonic accuracy progression: K-Means (0.9887) and Spherical K-Means (0.9925) have higher balance than GEM (0.9185), and vanilla vMF (0.7697) is lowest. The actual accuracy progression (38.5%→40.6%→41.3%→42.1%) was never tested.

claims.claim: The Geometric Influence Score (GIS) selection criterion achieves 84.17% versus 80.41% for random selection in the corresponding ablation (Table 4, Appendix B.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook ran a real experiment on 20 Newsgroups (5 prototypes per cluster, 24 clusters) but GIS (69.41%) actually underperformed random selection (72.90%), contradicting the paper's claim. However, this is a toy setup (8-class classification vs. LLM taxonomy generation) so it cannot definitively falsify the full-scale claim.

claims.claim: A sensitivity analysis over the number of clusters K finds performance peaks at K=36 (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook ran cluster balance vs. K experiments on 20 Newsgroups, but cluster balance decreases monotonically with K and does not peak at K=36. The actual claim about downstream accuracy peaking at K=36 (41.21%) was never tested; the proxy metric (cluster balance) is a different quantity entirely.

jomasego/repro-gem-geometric-entropy-mix.overall: The logbook ran only proxy experiments on the 20 Newsgroups dataset with small embeddings, never attempting the actual 1.1B-parameter, 25B-token training pipeline that is central to all claims. The proxy results do not clearly support the paper's claims—in fact, GIS underperformed random selection and GEM showed lower cluster balance than K-Means baselines on the toy task.

745H1N/repro-mossp.paper_title: MoSSP: A Momentum-Based Single-Loop Stochastic Penalty Method for Nonconvex Constrained DC-regularized Optimization

claims.claim: MoSSP-P, a single-loop stochastic penalty method using Polyak momentum, attains an oracle complexity of O(epsilon^-4) for finding a stochastic epsilon-KKT point of the nonconvex constrained DC-regularized problem, under an approximately feasible initialization ||c(x_0)||^2 = O(K^-1/4) (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: A synthetic constrained DC-regularized least-squares problem with d=15, N=300, batch size 8, and 4000 iterations was run, yielding a fitted KKT convergence exponent of -0.0483 versus the theoretical -0.25, which is far off and on a clearly simplified setup.

claims.claim: MoSSP-R, which replaces Polyak momentum with recursive (variance-reduced) momentum and uses initial batch size b_0 = O(K^1/3), improves the oracle complexity to O(epsilon^-3) under a mean-squared smoothness assumption (Theorem 3.2, Assumption 3.1).
claims.evidence: On the same small synthetic problem (d=15, N=300), MoSSP-R achieved a fitted exponent of -0.2856 versus the expected -0.33; while directionally consistent, this is a toy-scale proxy, not the paper's real experimental setting.

claims.claim: These are presented as the first complexity results for single-loop methods on nonconvex DC-regularized optimization with nonlinear constraints, in contrast to prior double-loop approaches (Section 3, Corollaries 3.1-3.2).
claims.evidence: No evidence is provided regarding whether these are the first complexity results for single-loop methods on nonconvex DC-regularized optimization with nonlinear constraints; the logbook contains no literature comparison or novelty analysis.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments on binary classification with DC regularization on LIBSVM datasets (a9a, phishing, australian) show MoSSP-P and MoSSP-R reduce constraint violation faster than the double-loop baselines SPDC and SALM (Section 4.1-4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook does not use LIBSVM datasets (a9a, phishing, australian), does not perform binary classification, and does not compare against SPDC or SALM baselines; instead it uses a small synthetic regression problem with only an SGD baseline, so the claim is never addressed.

745H1N/repro-mossp.overall: The logbook runs MoSSP-P and MoSSP-R on a tiny synthetic problem (d=15, N=300) and fits convergence exponents that are far from theoretical predictions, especially for MoSSP-P. Claims 3 and 4 are not addressed at all: there is no novelty analysis and no experiments on the paper's actual LIBSVM binary classification tasks with SPDC/SALM baselines.

ParetoOptimal/repro-9ylpohekod.paper_title: Magnitude Distance: A Geometric Measure of Dataset Similarity

claims.claim: Magnitude distance is defined as d_Mag^t(X,Y) = 2·Mag_{X∪Y}(t) − Mag_X(t) − Mag_Y(t), with a tunable scale parameter t that governs sensitivity to global structure (small t) versus finer local structure (large t) (Section on Definition, Magnitude Distance).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements Mag_X(t) = 1^T Z^{-1} 1 with Z = exp(-t*D) and the distance formula d = 2·Mag_{X∪Y}(t) − Mag_X(t) − Mag_Y(t), computing a finite value of 0.901325 on two 12-point 3D sets at t=0.5, directly confirming the definition is correctly implemented and computable.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 shows magnitude distance is symmetric and non-negative, satisfies identity of indiscernibles only up to magnitude equivalence, and does not satisfy the triangle inequality in R^D for D>1 (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: On a single 12-point 3D example, the logbook checks symmetry (d(X,Y)=d(Y,X)), non-negativity (0.901325≥0), and identity (d(X,X)=0.0), but these are trivially satisfied properties; the non-trivial part of Theorem 5.2—failure of the triangle inequality in R^D for D>1—is never tested, and 'identity up to magnitude equivalence' is only partially checked (d(X,X)=0 but no test of distinct sets yielding d=0).

claims.claim: Theorem 5.3 shows magnitude distance converges to 0 as t→0 and converges to the cardinality of the symmetric difference of the two datasets as t→∞ (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: Using two point sets with symmetric-difference cardinality 14, the logbook computes d_Mag = 0.0036 at t=1e-3 (converging to 0) and d_Mag = 14.0 at t=30 (matching symmetric-difference cardinality exactly), directly reproducing both limits of Theorem 5.3.

claims.claim: Figure 2 shows magnitude distance remains discriminative in dimensions exceeding 1000, in settings where MMD's discriminative power collapses (Section on High-Dimensional Behavior, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook compares MMD (Gaussian kernel, sigma=1) vs normalized magnitude distance (t=1/sqrt(D)) across dimensions {10,100,500,1000,1500} on two shifted Gaussians: MMD collapses to 0.0 by dimension 100 while magnitude distance remains stable at ~0.66 through dimension 1500, directly testing the claimed high-dimensional discrimination.

claims.claim: MagGN, a generative model trained with a multi-scale magnitude-distance loss, achieves an 11.97x training speedup over WGAN on MNIST while producing visually competitive samples (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states this claim was not run: 'GAN training beyond the scope of this offline theory reproduction.' No MagGN or WGAN training was executed, so the 11.97x speedup claim is entirely unaddressed.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.5 proves magnitude distance has bounded outlier sensitivity, changing by only about 6-10% under significant outlier addition compared to a 17.6% change for Wasserstein distance in the same setting (Section 5, Theorem 5.5).
claims.evidence: The logbook contaminates one point at increasing outlier radii and shows normalized magnitude distance plateauing at ~0.42 while a 'Wasserstein-like distance (mean displacement)' grows unboundedly; however, the specific quantitative claims (6-10% change for magnitude vs 17.6% for Wasserstein) are not verified, and the Wasserstein comparison uses a proxy rather than actual Wasserstein distance, on a small synthetic setup.

ParetoOptimal/repro-9ylpohekod.overall: The logbook provides direct computational verification of the magnitude distance definition, its scale-parameter limits (Theorem 5.3), and high-dimensional discrimination versus MMD, but only partially and superficially addresses metric properties (Theorem 5.2) and outlier sensitivity (Theorem 5.5) on small toy examples, and entirely skips the MagGN training speedup claim.

jomasego/repro-agenthijack-icml2026.paper_title: AgentHijack: Benchmarking Computer Use Agent Robustness to Common Environment Corruptions

claims.claim: AgentHijack constructs 3,321 corrupted tasks by applying nine configurable corruption types to the 369 original tasks from OSWorld (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook audited the actual task definition file (test_all.json) and confirmed 369 tasks across 10 domains, listed 9 corruption implementations in noise.py with specific function names, and verified the arithmetic 9 × 369 = 3,321. This is a concrete code-audit verification of a structural claim.

claims.claim: The nine corruptions are grouped into visual disruptors (pop-ups, resolution changes, desktop marks, subtitles, multiple applications), unexpected operations (accidental touches, app minimization), and environmental errors (network failures, verification requirements) (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook inspected noise.py and config/default.yaml, listing all 9 corruption types with specific function names and line numbers, and confirmed the three-group taxonomy (5 visual disruptors, 2 unexpected operations, 2 environmental errors) matches the paper's description.

claims.claim: UI-TARS-1.5-7B achieves 24.21% success on clean OSWorld tasks but only 18.74% average success under AgentHijack corruptions, demonstrating substantial performance degradation (Table 2).
claims.evidence: No experiments were run. The logbook explicitly states 'The paper's reported numbers are taken as ground truth' and 'Full reproduction of all 3,321 tasks × 1 agent would require ~50+ GPU-hours.' The per-corruption breakdown uses approximate values (~19%, ~20%) rather than independently obtained results.

claims.claim: AgentHijack-Agent, which combines an enhanced action generator trained with Data-Augmented Group Relative Policy Optimization (DA-GRPO) and an onlooker validation module, raises average success under corruption to 22.89% (from 18.74% for UI-TARS-1.5-7B), a 4.15-point improvement (Table 2, Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: No evaluation runs were performed. The logbook states 'The paper's reported 22.89% is taken as ground truth.' While the model and code are confirmed to be publicly available, no independent experimental results were produced to verify the 22.89% or the 4.15-point improvement.

claims.claim: AgentHijack-Agent yields corruption-specific gains of +11.23% on pop-up disruptors and +9.67% on verification-requirement errors relative to the baseline agent (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: No experiments were run to independently verify the +11.23% pop-up gain or +9.67% verification gain. The logbook only cites the paper's Section 5.2 numbers and provides qualitative explanations for why these gains might occur, without producing any actual experimental data.

claims.claim: An ablation isolating the onlooker module versus the enhanced action generator shows both components are individually necessary for robustness gains (Figure 6, Section 5.3).
claims.evidence: No ablation experiments were executed. The logbook merely describes Figure 6 from the paper ('Figure 6 in the paper shows that...') without running any of the ablation variants (without RL, without onlooker) to independently confirm that both components are individually necessary.

jomasego/repro-agenthijack-icml2026.overall: The logbook provides a thorough code audit that verifies the benchmark's structural claims (369 tasks, 9 corruption types, 3,321 total, three-group taxonomy) but performs zero experimental runs for any of the four numerical performance claims (Claims 3-6), explicitly taking the paper's published numbers as ground truth. This is a code-and-paper review, not a reproduction of experimental results.

745H1N/repro-decision-tree.paper_title: Decision Tree Learning on Product Spaces

claims.claim: For a function computable by an optimal decision tree with maximum depth D_opt and average depth Δ_opt over a product distribution, the greedy top-down heuristic constructs an ϵ-approximating tree of size at most max((e·Δ_opt/(ϵ·D_opt))^(Δ_opt·D_opt), e^(Δ_opt·D_opt)) (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook tests the bound exp(Δ_opt·D_opt·log(e/ε)) on only majority functions with s=3,7,15 (depths 2-4) and 3000 samples; the tested bound is a simplified version of the actual claim's max((e·Δ/(ε·D))^(Δ·D), e^(Δ·D)), and the bounds are astronomically loose (10^5 to 10^34) vs actual tree sizes of 1-71, making satisfaction trivial. The influence computation also appears buggy, using a global CURRENT_RELEVANT_VARS that doesn't update after splits.

claims.claim: For balanced optimal trees where D_opt = Δ_opt = log s, the bound simplifies to a quasi-polynomial size s^(log(s)·log(e/ϵ)) (Theorem 1.1, balanced-tree corollary).
claims.evidence: The quasi-polynomial bound s^(log(s)·log(e/ε)) is computed and checked for s=3,7,15 only, with the same tiny majority-function setup; the bound values are so enormous (e.g., 10^34 for s=15) that the trivially small greedy trees (size 39-71) satisfy them vacuously, providing no meaningful test of the bound's tightness or correctness at scale.

claims.claim: The paper gives the first practical parameter-free implementation of BuildTopDownDT that requires no prior knowledge of the optimal tree's size or depth, unlike the algorithm of Blanc et al. (2020) (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook's greedy_build function uses max_depth=tree_depth_opt*3+5, which requires knowledge of D_opt, directly contradicting the 'parameter-free' claim; no comparison with Blanc et al.'s algorithm is performed, and no evidence is presented that the implementation requires no prior knowledge of optimal tree size or depth.

claims.claim: The size bound extends beyond the uniform-distribution setting analyzed by Blanc et al. (2020) to the strictly broader class of product distributions while remaining tighter for full binary trees (Section 1, comparison to prior work).
claims.evidence: A minimal uniform-vs-product distribution comparison is shown for s=3,7,15 at a single ε=0.1, and the Blanc et al. bound is computed analytically but not via running their algorithm; the 'tighter for full binary trees' aspect is not meaningfully demonstrated since both bounds are astronomically larger than actual tree sizes at this scale.

745H1N/repro-decision-tree.overall: The logbook implements a small-scale greedy decision tree learner on majority functions with s≤15 and 3000 samples, finding that trivially small trees satisfy extremely loose theoretical bounds. The reproduction is too small and simplified to constitute a meaningful verification of any of the four claims, and the implementation contradicts the parameter-free claim by using D_opt-dependent parameters.

bsenst/repro-idrbench-understanding-the-.paper_title: IDRBench: Understanding the Capability of Large Language Models on Interdisciplinary Research

claims.claim: IDRBench evaluates 10 LLMs, including GPT-4o-mini, o1-mini, o3-mini, Gemini 1.5-pro, Gemini 2.0-flash, Llama-3.1-70B, Llama-3.3-70B, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, DeepSeek-v3, and DeepSeek-r1, on three progressive interdisciplinary-research tasks (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirmed all 10 model names and 3 task names (IPI, I3, I2R) from the paper text and verified the dataset structure on HuggingFace with 5 JSON files covering all tasks and sample counts.

claims.claim: On the IDR Paper Identification (IPI) task, which uses a 1:10 positive-to-negative sampling ratio (120 positive vs. 1,200 negative papers), the best zero-shot model (Llama-3.1-70B) reaches only 0.416 F1 versus a 0.176 random baseline (Section 3.2.1, Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook could not run Llama-3.1-70B; instead it ran Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on 100 samples achieving F1=0.057. The random baseline calculation yielded 0.399 (uniform) rather than the claimed 0.176, and the specific 0.416 result was never tested at the paper's scale.

claims.claim: On the IDR Idea Integration (I3) task, zero-shot average F1 falls from 0.550 at difficulty Level 1 to a 58.8% relative drop at the harder Level 2 (Section 3.2.2, Table 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook ran Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on 55 samples per I3 subset, finding F1=0.730 and 0.747 (no drop, slight increase), which contradicts the claimed 58.8% drop. However, the logbook notes the 1.5B model guesses 'Yes' for everything, making this a toy setup that cannot meaningfully confirm or falsify the claim about larger models.

claims.claim: On the IDR Idea Recommendation (I2R) task, scored by Swiss-tournament Mean Reciprocal Rank, Gemini 1.5-pro is the top performer at both difficulty levels (0.703 at Level 1, 0.662 at Level 2) (Section 3.2.3, Table 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook only verified the I2R data structure (690 samples, ~28 candidates each) but ran no model evaluations and computed no MRR scores. No experiments were conducted to test whether Gemini 1.5-pro is the top performer.

claims.claim: Generated IDR ideas show high semantic similarity to ground truth (avg. 0.756 for integration reasoning, 0.812 for abstracts) but very low lexical overlap (BLEU 0.010-0.018), indicating models grasp conceptual links but cannot generate detailed methodological content (Section 5.2, Table 6).
claims.evidence: The logbook computed only a random-pair BLEU baseline of 0.006 for context but did not generate any model outputs, compute SciBERT semantic similarity, or compute BLEU on actual model generations. The core metrics (0.756/0.812 similarity, 0.010-0.018 BLEU) were never measured.

claims.claim: Positive IDR samples disproportionately combine Computer Science with Physics or Quantitative Biology (50%) compared to the general arXiv distribution (23%) (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook analyzed the full positive dataset and found CS+Physics (18.5%) and CS+QB (24.2%) together comprise 42.7% of positive samples, confirming the overrepresentation claim. The 23% ArXiv baseline was not independently verified as it requires the full ArXiv corpus, but the direction and approximate magnitude of the claim are supported.

bsenst/repro-idrbench-understanding-the-.overall: The logbook primarily verifies dataset structure and one data-distribution claim through direct analysis, while model evaluation claims (2-5) are either unaddressed or tested only with a 1.5B toy model on small subsets, which is far below the paper's model class and scale. No claim involving actual LLM performance numbers was reproduced at the paper's scale.

745H1N/repro-spurious-correlation.paper_title: Is Spurious Correlation Removal Always Learnable?

claims.claim: Under the Planted Clique hardness hypothesis (planted cliques of size k = m^(1/2−δ) in random graphs are not recoverable in polynomial time), there exist samplable multi-environment linear-Gaussian instances that are statistically learnable with polynomially many samples via exhaustive search but intractable for any polynomial-time algorithm (Hypothesis 3.1, Theorem 3.8).
claims.evidence: The logbook runs a small synthetic experiment (d=12, k=1) measuring minimax risk scaling (MSE ~ n^{-0.60}), but this tests statistical estimation error, not computational intractability. There is no comparison between exhaustive search and polynomial-time algorithms, no connection to planted clique hardness, and no demonstration that any instance is learnable via exhaustive search but intractable for polynomial-time methods.

claims.claim: A phase transition in label-induced spurious correlation removal occurs at critical sample size n* ∝ k(d−k)/(|E|γ²), where k is the invariant subspace dimension, d the ambient dimension, |E| the number of environments, and γ the environment separation parameter; below n*/2 all estimators fail with constant error while above 2n* estimators achieve error O(k(d−k)/(n|E|γ²)) (Theorem 4.15).
claims.evidence: The experiment on a small synthetic setup (d=10, k=1, 12 environments) does show a phase transition in sample size and finds n_emp ~ gamma^{-2.77} (expected gamma^{-2}), confirming the direction of the gamma dependence. However, it only varies gamma and does not independently vary k, d, or |E| to verify the full formula n* ∝ k(d-k)/(|E|γ²), nor does it test the specific n*/2 and 2n* error bounds.

claims.claim: The predicted phase transition is validated empirically: exhaustive search reaches 75% accuracy using up to 27x fewer samples than polynomial-time methods on synthetic instances, and sharp transitions near the predicted critical sample size appear on both synthetic data and ColoredMNIST (Figure 1, Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: The logbook contains no experiment comparing exhaustive search to polynomial-time methods, no measurement of 75% accuracy or 27x sample efficiency, and no experiments on ColoredMNIST. The claim's specific empirical predictions are entirely unaddressed.

claims.claim: Diversity across environments is necessary for removal to succeed: performance improves sharply once γ > 0, whereas low-diversity settings (γ ≈ 0) show persistent failure, and increasing diversity from 'low' to 'high' substantially improves worst-group accuracy on CelebA and Waterbirds and OOD performance on ColoredMNIST (Figure 2c, Table 2).
claims.evidence: Experiment 3 on a small synthetic setup (d=10, k=1) shows estimation error decreasing as gamma increases, partially supporting the diversity-necessity claim. However, all real-dataset experiments mentioned in the claim (CelebA, Waterbirds, ColoredMNIST worst-group/OOD accuracy) are completely absent.

745H1N/repro-spurious-correlation.overall: The logbook provides only a small-scale synthetic numerical check of minimax risk scaling and gamma-dependent phase transition behavior, without addressing the core complexity-theoretic claim or any of the real-dataset empirical validations. Most claims remain unverified or only weakly supported on toy setups.

mykoname/repro-building-social-world-mod.paper_title: Building Social World Model with Large Language Models

claims.claim: Social World Model learns state-transition functions for social beliefs from temporal patterns without explicit human annotations.
claims.evidence: A Qwen3-0.6B LoRA model trained on only 1,024 rows with 8 news items and length-512 sequences (vs the paper's 8B full fine-tuning on full data with 30 news items and length-1,024) showed the deployable prior reducing RMSE by 36.93% vs a matched all-news comparator on 855 validation rows. This is real scaled mechanism evidence, but the model is ~13x smaller, training data ~8x smaller, and the architecture is LoRA rather than full fine-tuning—clearly a reduced-scale setup.

claims.claim: Outperforms time-series foundation models with RMSE reductions of 8.4% on Polymarket and 11.2% on Kalshi.
claims.evidence: The historical TimeLLM comparator, original SWM checkpoint, predictions, seeds, and data manifest are unavailable, so the specific 8.4%/11.2% RMSE reductions cannot be reconstructed. The CPU proxy showed degradation on Polymarket (-4.56%) and improvement on Kalshi (+3.56%); the GPU A100 scaled run beat a matched all-news Qwen3-0.6B comparator but lost to last-value persistence on every platform/subset, and did not test against any time-series foundation model.

claims.claim: SWM-Bench includes 10,000+ datapoints spanning diverse domains including politics, sports, cryptocurrency, and elections.
claims.evidence: The dataset audit confirmed 12,789 unique transition rows (8,546 train + 760 Kalshi test + 3,483 Polymarket test) with zero duplicate keys, zero train/test transition-key overlap, and valid attributions/timestamps. Categories include Politics, Election/Elections, and Crypto; however, no released split contains an explicit 'Sports' label, which is a minor discrepancy in the compound domain listing but does not undermine the core 10,000+ datapoints and diversity claim.

mykoname/repro-building-social-world-mod.overall: The logbook provides a thorough but reduced-scale reproduction: Claim 1 is supported only at toy scale (Qwen3-0.6B LoRA, 1,024 rows), Claim 2 cannot be verified because the historical TimeLLM comparison artifacts are unavailable and proxy results are mixed, and Claim 3's size and most domain components are directly confirmed by a rigorous data audit.

745H1N/repro-fairness-aggregation.paper_title: Fairness in Aggregation: Optimal Top-$k$ and Improved Full Ranking

claims.claim: A polynomial-time algorithm computes an optimal (alpha-bar, beta-bar)-k-fair top-k aggregate ranking under the Spearman footrule (L1) distance, solved via the ellipsoid method after showing the ILP constraint matrix is totally unimodular (Theorem 3.1, Lemma 3.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook uses brute-force enumeration of all C(d,k) subsets on d=8 items with 5 rankings, not the polynomial-time ellipsoid method described in the paper. Total unimodularity of the ILP constraint matrix is never verified, and the actual algorithm is not implemented; only the trivial fact that optimal top-k can be found by exhaustive search on a tiny instance is demonstrated.

claims.claim: A polynomial-time algorithm achieves a 2-approximation for the fair full ranking problem on d candidates, improving on the previous best 3-approximation, by first computing an optimal fair top-k list and then extending it to a full ranking via minimum-cost perfect matching (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements a simple greedy heuristic (iteratively pick item minimizing max positional deviation) on d=8, not the paper's algorithm of computing optimal fair top-k then extending via minimum-cost perfect matching. The observed ratio of 1.44 vs optimal is for a different algorithm on a toy instance, not the paper's 2-approximation algorithm.

claims.claim: The full ranking algorithm runs in O(nd^2 + d^3) time, where n is the number of input rankings and d is the number of candidates, with the final matching step costing O(d^3) (Section 4, Complexity analysis).
claims.evidence: No timing measurements, complexity analysis, or implementation of the matching step are present in the logbook. The O(nd^2 + d^3) runtime claim is never addressed.

claims.claim: Empirical evaluation shows the proposed algorithms achieve solutions within 1-3% of optimal, substantially outperforming baseline fair aggregation methods across multiple distance metrics (Section on empirical performance).
claims.evidence: The logbook tests on d=8 with 5 rankings using brute-force and greedy methods (not the paper's algorithms), reports a 44% gap from optimal for full ranking (contradicting the claimed 1-3%), does not compare against any baseline fair aggregation methods, and uses only Spearman footrule distance. The paper's empirical claims are not meaningfully addressed.

745H1N/repro-fairness-aggregation.overall: The logbook runs trivial brute-force and greedy heuristics on a tiny 8-item instance, never implementing the paper's actual algorithms (ellipsoid method with TU, minimum-cost perfect matching extension) or verifying their theoretical properties. None of the four claims are substantively reproduced; the experiments are too small and use different methods than the paper describes.

745H1N/repro-gradient-stabilizer.paper_title: GradientStabilizer: Fix the Norm, Not the Gradient

claims.claim: GradientStabilizer replaces the update magnitude of a gradient with a statistically stabilized estimate while preserving the instantaneous gradient direction, and provides a theoretical bound showing the stabilized magnitude stays bounded during gradient-norm spikes regardless of spike size (Theorem 3.2, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Direction preservation is confirmed via cosine similarity = 1.0 in 5 random 10-dimensional tests, but this is trivially true by construction (scaling a vector by a positive scalar preserves direction). The theoretical bound (Theorem 3.2) on stabilized magnitude staying bounded during spikes is never addressed, and the setup is a tiny linear regression, not a realistic scale.

claims.claim: GradientStabilizer widens the range of learning rates over which training remains stable compared to standard gradient clipping baselines (Section 4).
claims.evidence: On the toy linear regression setup, the stabilizer is stable in 6/7 learning rates while gradient clipping is stable in 7/7, which actually contradicts the claim that GradientStabilizer widens the stable LR range compared to clipping. However, this is a simplified convex problem, not the deep-network setting the paper targets, so it cannot constitute a full falsification.

claims.claim: GradientStabilizer is evaluated for reducing training divergence across five domains: LLM pre-training in FP16, quantization-aware LLM pre-training in FP4, ImageNet image classification, reinforcement learning (MuJoCo environments), and time-series forecasting with PatchTST (Section 4, Appendix B).
claims.evidence: None of the five claimed domains (LLM FP16, FP4 quantization, ImageNet, MuJoCo RL, PatchTST time-series) are addressed. The logbook only runs a 10-dimensional linear regression experiment.

claims.claim: The method is shown to reduce Adam's sensitivity to weight-decay configuration in addition to improving control over optimizer state evolution (Section 3-4).
claims.evidence: The logbook does not use Adam, does not test weight-decay configurations, and does not examine optimizer state evolution. This claim is entirely unaddressed.

745H1N/repro-gradient-stabilizer.overall: The logbook runs only a minimal 10-dimensional linear regression experiment that trivially confirms direction preservation and actually shows the stabilizer performing worse than clipping on this toy problem. None of the paper's five evaluation domains, theoretical bounds, or Adam-specific claims are addressed.

bsenst/repro-innoeval.paper_title: InnoEval: On Research Idea Evaluation as a Knowledge-Grounded, Multi-Perspective Reasoning Problem

claims.claim: InnoEval is compared against six baselines (CoT, RAG, GraphEval, ResearchAgent, InternAgent, ScholarEval) across point-wise, pair-wise, and group-wise research idea evaluation tasks (Table 1, Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook verified dataset sizes from GitHub (217 point-wise, 172 groups, 372 pairs) and confirmed Table 1 lists the six named baselines, but no baselines or InnoEval were actually run. This is a check of the paper's own table and repo, not an experimental reproduction of the comparison.

claims.claim: In point-wise classification InnoEval reaches 75.58% accuracy / 75.74% F1 on the binary setting and 73.73% accuracy / 74.56% F1 on the three-class setting, outperforming the strongest baseline ScholarEval by 16.18 F1 points (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook checked internal numerical consistency of Table 1 (16.18 F1 gap matches) but explicitly states 'Could not independently run the models to verify these numbers.' 745H1N/repro-pruning-graphon.paper_title: Pruning at Initialisation through the lens of Graphon Limit: Convergence, Expressivity, and Generalisation

claims.claim: Theorem 4.7 proves that pruning masks generated by factorised saliency scores (encompassing SNIP, GraSP, magnitude, and random pruning) converge in cut-norm metric to deterministic limit bipartite graphons as network width grows (Section 4.3, Theorem 4.7).
claims.evidence: The experiment measures mask density (trivially 0.5000 by construction when pruning 50% of weights per row) rather than cut-norm convergence to a deterministic limit graphon. It only tests magnitude and random pruning (not SNIP or GraSP), and the density result is tautological, providing no evidence for or against cut-norm convergence.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.7 establishes a universal approximation result showing sparse networks retain universal approximation capability for target functions depending only on a fixed k-dimensional active coordinate subspace, provided the limiting graphon contains an 'active rectangle' with uniformly lower-bounded edge probabilities (Section 5.2, Theorem 5.7, Assumption 5.2).
claims.evidence: The experiment measures relative output error between pruned and unpruned networks on a single linear regression task (d=10, width=200), not universal approximation. It does not test the active rectangle condition (Assumption 5.2), does not vary the k-dimensional active coordinate subspace, and errors are large (51% at 50% sparsity), so it cannot support or refute the universal approximation theorem.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.1 derives an infinite-width graphon-NTK generalisation bound in which the complexity term depends on y^T K_W^{-1} y / m, where K_W is the graphon-modulated kernel (Section 6.2, Theorem 6.1).
claims.evidence: No experiment in the logbook computes a graphon-NTK kernel K_W, evaluates y^T K_W^{-1} y / m, or tests any generalisation bound. The claim is never addressed.

claims.claim: Proposition 6.3 shows the graphon-NTK Gram matrix incorporates a path-density proxy that weights input coordinates, explaining why data-driven (structured) pruning improves feature alignment relative to uniform pruning (Section 6.3, Proposition 6.3).
claims.evidence: No experiment computes a graphon-NTK Gram matrix, a path-density proxy, or compares data-driven vs. uniform pruning in terms of feature alignment. The claim is never addressed.

745H1N/repro-pruning-graphon.overall: The logbook runs only two trivial experiments: one showing mask density is 0.5 when pruning 50% (tautological), and one measuring relative output error on a single linear task with a tiny network. None of the four theoretical claims about cut-norm convergence, universal approximation, graphon-NTK generalisation bounds, or path-density proxies are actually tested.

bsenst/repro-intentrl-training-proactive.paper_title: IntentRL: Training Proactive User-intent Agents for Open-ended Deep Research via Reinforcement Learning

claims.evidence: The logbook ran intent evaluation on the real DeepResearch Bench (50 queries, same embedding model) but used oracle criteria-informed heuristics instead of the actual RL-trained IntentRL model, yielding 89.93% precision (vs paper's 36.44%) and baseline scores of 1.60%/0.50% (vs paper's 21.11%/18.00%). 745H1N/repro-kernel-density.paper_title: Even Faster Kernel Matrix Linear Algebra via Density Estimation

claims.claim: The paper improves on the algorithm of Backurs, Indyk, Musco, and Wagner (2021) for kernel matrix linear algebra tasks -- matrix-vector products, matrix-matrix products, spectral norm, and entry sums -- to (1+ε) relative error (abstract only).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements standard Random Fourier Features (not the paper's KDE-based algorithm) on a toy scale (n=200, d=10) and shows decreasing relative error for approximate matvec/matmat, but never compares to the BIMW 2021 algorithm or implements the paper's actual method, so the core claim of improvement over prior work is not tested.

claims.evidence: No comparison of ε-dependence between the paper's algorithm and prior kernel matrix algorithms is performed; the logbook only shows RFF error decreasing with feature count D, which does not address the claim about reduced polynomial dependence on 1/ε.

claims.evidence: No experiments or analysis related to conditional lower bounds or quadratic-time hardness are present in the logbook; this claim is never addressed.

745H1N/repro-kernel-density.overall: The logbook implements a standard Random Fourier Features approximation on toy-scale data (n=200, d=10) rather than the paper's KDE-query-based algorithms, and does not compare against the BIMW 2021 baseline or address lower bounds. None of the four claims are substantively verified or falsified by the experiments presented.

jomasego/repro-the-entropic-signature-of.paper_title: The Entropic Signature of Class Speciation in Diffusion Models

claims.claim: For variance-preserving diffusion SDEs, entropy production concentrates on a logarithmic timescale ts = (1/2) log d + O(1), matching previously identified class-speciation times (Section 4.2, Equation 16).
claims.evidence: Numerical audit on Gaussian mixture (d=8 to 128, 20K samples, 100 time steps) shows VP t_s values (0.31, 0.67, 1.02, 1.27, 1.82) tracking 0.5 log(d) with an approximately constant offset of ~-0.7, consistent with t_s = 0.5 log d + O(1). This is the appropriate test bed for the theoretical SDE claim.

claims.claim: VP and EDM/VE diffusion processes show divergent entropy-transition behavior: VP exhibits sharp transitions in rescaled time while EDM/VE exhibits broader mixing regions that scale with the square root of dimension d (Section 4.3, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Same Gaussian mixture setup shows VP t_s increasing monotonically with d while VE t_s values (0.11, 0.31, 0.21, 0.21, 0.92) are erratic and non-monotonic, demonstrating divergent transition behavior. However, the specific √d scaling claim for VE/EDM transition width is not clearly demonstrated by the tabulated peak-time data alone.

claims.claim: On EDM2-XS, partitioned class-conditional entropy tracking isolates the noise regimes where individual classes commit to their semantic identity, with different classes (e.g., tiger shark vs. paintbrush) peaking at different noise levels (Section 5.2, Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: No EDM2-XS experiments were conducted. The logbook explicitly states 'Scaled reproduction (local proxy)' and only references the Gaussian mixture from Claims 1-2. The specific claim about tiger shark vs. paintbrush peaking at different noise levels in a trained model was never addressed.

claims.claim: On Stable Diffusion 1.5, low-frequency attributes such as color and global structure show early entropy decay while high-frequency localized object details collapse later, corresponding to the sequence of visual feature emergence (Section 5.3, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: No Stable Diffusion 1.5 experiments were conducted. The logbook states 'Scaled reproduction (local proxy)' and only offers a theoretical argument from the Gaussian mixture. The specific claim about low-frequency vs high-frequency attribute entropy decay in SD 1.5 was never tested.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 estimates class-conditional entropy via local likelihood increments from conditional versus unconditional denoisers, enabling tracking of semantic speciation in trained models without closed-form posteriors (Section 5, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 was implemented and tested on a synthetic two-component Gaussian mixture with an oracle denoiser, showing entropy decay from H=1 to H=0. However, the claim specifically concerns tracking semantic speciation 'in trained models without closed-form posteriors,' and the oracle denoiser setup has closed-form posteriors, making this a simplified proxy rather than a full validation.

claims.claim: Optimal classifier-free guidance intervals differ depending on the target metric, with FID-optimized guidance range [0.27, 1.50] versus FDDINOv2-optimized range [0.93, 5.28] (Appendix C, Table 1-2).
claims.evidence: No guidance sweep experiments were run. The logbook states 'Literature reproduction' and reports the table values (FID [0.27, 1.50], FDDINOv2 [0.93, 5.28]) directly from the paper's Appendix C without any independent experimental verification.

jomasego/repro-the-entropic-signature-of.overall: The logbook provides genuine numerical verification for the two theoretical SDE claims (Claims 1-2) on a Gaussian mixture setup and a toy validation of Algorithm 1 on synthetic data. However, the three model-based claims (EDM2-XS, SD 1.5, CFG intervals) were not experimentally addressed at all, relying on proxies or direct citation of the paper's own tables.

jomasego/repro-ef-lic.paper_title: Efficient Learned Image Compression without Entropy Coding

claims.claim: EF-LIC eliminates entropy coding from learned image compression by using unconstrained vector quantization, showing that VQ index sequences exhibit minimal statistical redundancy and approach maximum entropy under distortion-optimal conditions (Section on Statistical Redundancy Removal).
claims.evidence: Code audit confirms no entropy coding module exists and indices are packed as fixed-length bitstrings, but the core scientific claim—that VQ index sequences exhibit minimal statistical redundancy and approach maximum entropy—was never empirically tested; no entropy measurements were taken on actual VQ indices.

claims.claim: EF-LIC removes correlation redundancy via representation-domain latent decorrelation using context-conditioned autoregressive affine transforms that directly reparameterize latents instead of predicting conditional probability distributions, making the method GPU-friendly and parallelizable (Section on Correlation Redundancy Removal).
claims.evidence: Code audit confirms the affine reparameterization architecture (quadtree partitioning, mean/scale context, subtract-mean/divide-scale before VQ) matches the paper, but 'GPU-friendly and parallelizable' was not tested (all runs were on CPU), and no measurements of correlation reduction were performed.

claims.claim: On the Kodak dataset with LPIPS distortion, EF-LIC achieves a 67.86% BD-rate (bitrate) reduction compared to the MS-ILLM baseline (Experimental Results, Kodak).
claims.evidence: EF-LIC RD curve was measured on Kodak (24 images, 5 rate points: LPIPS 0.272 at 0.036 BPP to 0.152 at 0.178 BPP), but the MS-ILLM baseline was never run, so the 67.86% BD-rate reduction cannot be computed or verified.

claims.claim: EF-LIC encodes in 17.62ms and decodes in 13.72ms per image versus 165.38ms and 147.79ms for MS-ILLM, corresponding to roughly 3x faster encoding and 5x faster decoding while matching compression performance of entropy-coding-based variants (Table of computational efficiency results).
claims.evidence: CPU timings (~150ms encode / ~250ms decode on Apple M3) are on completely different hardware from the paper's GPU measurements and cannot verify the specific 17.62ms/13.72ms claims; MS-ILLM latency was not measured at all; repo README numbers are cited but not independently reproduced.

claims.claim: Beyond Kodak, EF-LIC achieves consistent BD-rate reductions on Tecnick (-55.46%), DIV2K (-62.33%), and CLIC 2020 (-63.22%) relative to MS-ILLM (Benchmark Performance results).
claims.evidence: No experiments were run on Tecnick, DIV2K, or CLIC 2020; the logbook explicitly states these evaluations were not performed due to compute constraints.

claims.claim: A lightweight variant, EF-LIC-s, further reduces computation to 9.94ms encoding and 6.26ms decoding per image (Computational Efficiency results).
claims.evidence: The EF-LIC-s variant is not present in the official repository (only the full 35.9M-parameter model exists), and no experiments were run to verify the 9.94ms/6.26ms latency claims.

jomasego/repro-ef-lic.overall: The logbook confirms via code audit that the EF-LIC architecture matches the paper's description (VQ without entropy coding, affine latent reparameterization) and provides EF-LIC RD numbers on Kodak via CPU inference, but none of the six quantitative claims are independently verified. No MS-ILLM baseline was run, no GPU experiments were conducted, no entropy measurements were taken, and three of six datasets/variants were never evaluated.

745H1N/repro-embedding-collapse.paper_title: Provable Accuracy Collapse of Embedding-Based Representations under Dimensionality Mismatch

claims.claim: For every integer D ≥ 240 and ε > 0, there exists a triplet constraint collection that is realizable in dimension D but for which any embedding in at most c·D dimensions satisfies at most a 1/2+ε fraction of the triplets (Theorem 1.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook runs a simplified experiment with random Gaussian points (n_items=min(D,100)) and PCA projection to 2D, showing accuracy ~0.59 for D=240. However, the theorem is an existential worst-case statement about ANY embedding; the experiment only evaluates PCA (not optimal low-dim embedding), uses random (not adversarially constructed) instances, and the observed accuracy 0.59 is above the 1/2+ε bound the theorem claims.

claims.claim: The proof of accuracy collapse proceeds by constructing random average-case triplet instances shown to be satisfiable in D dimensions via Lemma 2.3 and Lemma 2.5, then bounding the achievable accuracy in reduced dimension d ≈ ε²D using a VC-dimension argument (Lemma 2.6, Section 2.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook does not verify any component of the proof structure—Lemma 2.3, Lemma 2.5, the VC-dimension argument in Lemma 2.6, or Section 2.3 are never referenced or checked. Only a loose empirical experiment is run with no connection to the proof machinery.

claims.claim: Under the Unique Games Conjecture, distinguishing triplet instances with (1−ε)-fraction satisfiability from instances with only 1/2+ε-fraction satisfiability is NP-hard regardless of the embedding dimension used, via a gap reduction from Maximum Acyclic Subgraph (Theorem 1.4, Theorem 3.1, Theorem 3.2, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook contains no experiments, discussion, or analysis related to the NP-hardness result, the Unique Games Conjecture, the gap reduction from Maximum Acyclic Subgraph, or any of Theorems 1.4/3.1/3.2. This claim is entirely unaddressed.

claims.claim: Experiments with ground-truth Euclidean embeddings and uniformly random triplets empirically confirm the predicted sharp accuracy collapse as embedding dimension falls below the ground-truth dimension D (Figure 1, Figure 2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook does run experiments with ground-truth Euclidean embeddings (Gaussian points) and random triplets, showing accuracy decreasing from 1.0 at full dimension to ~0.59-0.69 at 2D. However, the setup is significantly simplified: only n_items=min(D,100) points are used, only PCA projection (not optimal embedding) is evaluated, and the 'sharp' collapse transition is not clearly demonstrated across a fine grid of target dimensions as the paper's figures likely show.

745H1N/repro-embedding-collapse.overall: The logbook provides a basic empirical illustration of accuracy degradation under PCA dimensionality reduction for random triplet instances, but does not verify the paper's main theoretical claims (Theorem 1.3, proof structure, or NP-hardness) and only loosely approximates the paper's experimental claims with a small-scale, simplified setup.

745H1N/repro-special-federated.paper_title: Server-Proximal Aggregation for Federated Domain-Incremental Learning under Partial Participation: Task-Uniform Convergence and Backward Transfer

claims.claim: SPECIAL (Server-Proximal Efficient Continual Aggregation for Learning) modifies FedAvg only at the server by blending the aggregated model with the previous task's final parameters via a closed-form proximal update theta^{t+1} = (1/(1+lambda))*theta_bar^{t+1} + (lambda/(1+lambda))*theta^{i-1} (Algorithm 3, Equation 6).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements special_aggregate as (1-alpha)*avg + alpha*prev_global, which matches the server-side blending form, but only on a d=10 synthetic vector toy with no real federated training, clients, or tasks.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 proves a backward knowledge transfer (BKT) bound showing that after training on task K, the loss on any earlier task increases by at most a drift-controlled correction term that vanishes at rate O(1/(t*E*M*N*L*B^2)), shrinking with more communication rounds, local epochs, and participating clients (Section 4.2, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: BKT is measured as average squared distance to synthetic task optima (2.29 vs 2.35 at task 5), but the specific O(1/(t*E*M*N*L*B^2)) rate is never tested—no scaling analysis with communication rounds, local epochs, or client count is performed, and the setup is d=10 synthetic vectors.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 and Corollary 1 give a task-uniform, non-convex convergence rate of O(sqrt(E/(N*T))) in expected gradient norm for federated domain-incremental learning (FDIL) under partial participation, matching single-task FedAvg rates while holding simultaneously across all tasks (Section 4.3, Theorem 2, Corollary 1).
claims.evidence: No convergence rate analysis is present in the logbook; gradient norms are never measured, and the O(sqrt(E/(N*T))) rate is never compared to single-task FedAvg rates.

claims.claim: The FDIL problem setup assumes K sequential tasks share a fixed label space Y while input domains differ across tasks, with M heterogeneous clients and only N < M clients sampled without replacement per round to model partial participation (Section 2.1).
claims.evidence: The toy experiment uses 5 synthetic tasks but does not model heterogeneous clients, partial participation with N<M sampling, or domain-differing inputs with shared label space in any meaningful way.

745H1N/repro-special-federated.overall: The logbook provides only a toy synthetic demonstration (d=10 vectors, no real data, clients, or federated training) showing SPECIAL has marginally lower BKT than FedAvg. It does not address convergence rates (Claim 3) or the FDIL problem setup (Claim 4) in any substantive way.

ParetoOptimal/repro-vqt4w3lelx.paper_title: On Densest $k$-Subgraph Mining and Diagonal Loading: Optimization Landscape and Finite-Step Exact Convergence Analysis

claims.claim: Theorem 4 extends the Motzkin-Straus theorem to show the relaxed problem's maximum value equals 1+λ-1/ω, where ω is the largest clique size, establishing that diagonal loading parameter λ≥1 is the minimal value ensuring tightness of the penalty-based relaxation.
claims.evidence: On 4 planted-clique graphs (n up to 200, ω verified by Bron-Kerbosch), the normalized relaxed value matches the formula 1+(λ-1)/ω to 1e-9 for all λ<1 tested, tightness holds with gap 0.0 vs exact ILP for all λ≥1, and tightness fails for every λ<1 — directly confirming both the value formula and minimality of λ=1.

claims.claim: Corollary 1 proves that when λ≥1 there always exists a global maximizer of the relaxed objective that is integral, so the relaxed and combinatorial problems share the same optimal value.
claims.evidence: Across 30 graphs (n=20..200) × 3 values of λ≥1 (90 combos), exact ILP optima were computed via HiGHS; zero tightness violations occurred (relaxed optimum never exceeds combinatorial optimum) and the best relaxed value was always attained by an integral point (best_solution_non_integral_count=0), directly exhibiting integral global maximizers.

claims.claim: Lemma 1 shows that for λ>1 there does not exist a non-integral local maximizer, establishing the strict dichotomy that all integral stationary points are local maximizers while non-integral stationary points are strict saddles.
claims.evidence: 3600 FW runs across 12 graphs (n=20..200) at λ∈{1.5,2.5,5.0} found 16 non-integral stationary points, all certified as strict saddles via explicit curvature certificates (d^T(A+λI)d = 2λ-2A_ij > 0, min 3.0) with zero first-order term, and all escaped to integral points; zero non-integral local maximizers were found, plus a constructed two-clique saddle verified analytically.

claims.claim: Theorem 5 shows that increasing the diagonal loading parameter beyond λ=1 introduces additional spurious local maxima, implying λ=1 optimally trades off relaxation tightness against optimization difficulty.
claims.evidence: On 6 graphs with 200 shared random starts across λ∈{1.5,...,50}, the count of distinct local maxima grows monotonically with λ on every graph, 1660/1660 set-inclusion certificates confirm existing maximizers persist as λ grows, and 1198 new spurious maxima appear at λ=50 that fail the local-optimality certificate at λ=1.5, with solution quality degrading monotonically.

claims.claim: The saddle-escaping Frank-Wolfe algorithm (Section 3.1) has per-iteration complexity O(m+k log n) and is shown to converge in a finite number of steps to an integral local maximizer of the densest k-subgraph relaxation.
claims.evidence: Deterministic operation counts on sparse graphs up to 1M vertices / 5M edges show per-iteration cost scaling linearly with m+n (log-log slope 0.991, r=0.999987), and FW converges to integral points in ≤5 steps at every scale including 1M vertices, confirming both the complexity bound and finite-step exact convergence.

claims.claim: Experiments show the Frank-Wolfe algorithm achieves denser subgraphs than competing methods LRBO, L-ADMM, and EXPP while incurring lower computational cost on real-world graphs with millions of vertices (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Real SNAP graphs (ego-Facebook 4k vertices, ca-GrQc 5k vertices) show FW matching or beating greedy-peeling and top-k-degree baselines, but the named baselines LRBO/L-ADMM/EXPP were not implemented and million-vertex real graphs were not tested, so the specific comparison in the claim remains unaddressed.

ParetoOptimal/repro-vqt4w3lelx.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification of the paper's theoretical claims (Theorems 4-5, Corollary 1, Lemma 1) using exact ILP and Bron-Kerbosch verification on graphs up to n=200, plus deterministic complexity measurements up to 1M vertices. The empirical comparison claim (Claim 6) is only partially addressed: real-graph runs use smaller graphs and substitute simpler baselines for the named LRBO/L-ADMM/EXPP methods.

745H1N/repro-rnn-expressivity.paper_title: An Algebraic View of the Expressivity of Recurrent Language Models

claims.claim: The paper develops an algebraic framework in which a recurrent language model's expressivity reduces to whether its syntactic monoid divides the wreath product of the transition monoids of its layers, formalized via algebraic cores, cascade juxtaposition, and the ambient wreath product (Section 3, Definitions 3.4-3.8).
claims.evidence: The logbook runs a simple numerical RNN (d=5, tanh) with random weights and checks output stability, but never engages with the algebraic framework: no syntactic monoid computation, no wreath product division test, no algebraic cores or cascade juxtaposition definitions are implemented or verified.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.20 (the cascade juxtaposition identity) shows the realized wreath product of two cascaded algebraic RNNs equals the wreath product of their individual realized wreath products, up to canonical isomorphism, formalizing how expressivity composes across recurrent layers (Section 3.6.3, Proposition 3.20).
claims.evidence: The experiment cascades two small RNNs and reports output norms at lengths 3-20, but does not compute or compare realized wreath products of individual layers vs. the cascade, nor verify any isomorphism. Running a neural network forward pass is not a test of the algebraic identity in Proposition 3.20.

claims.claim: As a case study on diagonal state-space models (SSMs) such as Mamba-style linear recurrences, the same architecture cannot implement an even-modulus counter under floating-point arithmetic with nonnegative recurrence multipliers, yet can realize every even-modulus counter under unsigned-integer quantization (Section 4, Abstract).
claims.evidence: The claim concerns diagonal SSMs (Mamba-style), even-modulus counters, floating-point vs. unsigned-integer quantization. The logbook never implements an SSM, a counter, or any quantization scheme — it only runs a generic tanh RNN and checks finite-precision output differences.

claims.claim: The framework's Krohn-Rhodes-based decomposition (Appendix, Section 3.6.3) shows that algebraic impossibility results (a required factor of the syntactic monoid cannot be realized by any layer monoid in a given architecture family) rule out recognition of a target language, while observational realization constructs an explicit acceptor when the factor is realizable (Section 3.6.3, Corollary 3.21).
claims.evidence: Krohn-Rhodes decomposition, algebraic impossibility results, and observational realization of acceptors are never mentioned or implemented in the logbook. The experiments bear no relation to this claim.

745H1N/repro-rnn-expressivity.overall: The logbook runs a generic numerical RNN forward-pass experiment that is fundamentally mismatched with the paper's algebraic automata theory content; none of the four claims about syntactic monoids, wreath products, SSM counters, or Krohn-Rhodes decomposition are meaningfully tested. The reproduction attempt does not engage with the actual mathematical framework of the paper.

bsenst/repro-seg-research-segmentation-w.paper_title: Seg-ReSearch: Segmentation with Interleaved Reasoning and External Search

claims.evidence: The +4.7% and +3.5% figures were taken directly from the paper's Table 5; the code audit confirms the reward formulas exist but no training ablations were run to independently reproduce these deltas.

claims.evidence: The +7.4 point difference (50.0 - 42.6) was computed from the paper's Table 7 values; no experiments varying max search turns were conducted to independently confirm this improvement.

bsenst/repro-seg-research-segmentation-w.overall: This logbook performed no experimental runs whatsoever—it explicitly states 'analytical verification only' and that all claims were verified via 'code analysis and paper data extraction.' Every numerical result cited is simply copied from the paper's own tables, and the 8B model weights are noted as unreleased, making independent inference impossible. This constitutes a code audit and literature review, not a reproduction.

Srishti280992/repro-continuous-variable-.paper_title: Continuous Variable Hamiltonian Learning at Heisenberg Limit via Displacement-Random Unitary Transformation

claims.claim: The Displacement-Random Unitary Transformation (D-RUT) protocol learns all coefficients of a generic multi-mode bosonic Hamiltonian with evolution time scaling as O(1/epsilon), achieving the Heisenberg limit (Theorem 1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: A genuine two-mode finite-Fock setup (per-mode truncation 12, Hilbert dim 144) with 14 learned coefficients including 4 cross-mode coupling terms, 64 displacement settings, sampled RPE with binomial noise across 6 random Hamiltonians and 8 time budgets yields Heisenberg slope -0.9746 (range [-1.06, -0.92]) vs SQL control slope -0.5027, with coupling-only slope -1.0286, directly demonstrating O(1/ε) scaling for multi-mode coefficient recovery.

claims.claim: For single-mode Hamiltonians expressed in a first-quantization (position/momentum) basis, D-RUT recovers physical coefficients with RMSE epsilon_G using total evolution time O~(1/epsilon_G), under stated conditions on known zero coefficients, non-zero response to basis mismatch, and a sufficiently close initial guess (Theorem 2, Section 2).
claims.evidence: Single-mode finite-Fock D-RUT (dim 24) with explicit Bogoliubov inverse (R₀=0.15) recovers physical coefficients with corrected RMSE slope -1.0431 across 6 seeds and 8 budgets, while the omit-basis control leaves a non-decaying floor of 3.71e-3, confirming both the O~(1/ε_G) scaling and the necessity of basis correction.

claims.claim: The protocol's estimation error under state-preparation-and-measurement (SPAM) errors is bounded as ||delta g_SPAM||_2 <= (L_C/sigma_min(K)) ||delta beta||_2, where L_C is a Lipschitz constant and sigma_min(K) the smallest singular value of the Gram-like matrix K (Section 3.6, Eq. 43).
claims.evidence: Using the analytic degree-2 response with L_C=1.1086 and σ_min(K)=0.2201 on the Algorithm-1 disk, all 48/48 displacement-perturbation cases satisfy ||δg||₂ ≤ (L_C/σ_min(K))||δβ||₂ with max ratio 0.1435, directly confirming the SPAM perturbation bound of Eq. 43.

claims.claim: A hierarchical two-stage coefficient recovery strategy (learn single-mode coefficients first, then coupling coefficients) is proven to have covariance dominated by that of simultaneous estimation, Cov(delta g)_hierarchical <= Cov(delta g)_simultaneous, for all parameters (Section 4.1, Appendix A).
claims.evidence: Exact covariance matrices computed from 40 D-RUT feature design matrices show Cov_sim − Cov_hier is PSD in 40/40 cases (min eigenvalue 9.96e-9), with Monte Carlo samples (12000 draws) corroborating the ordering, providing concrete numerical evidence for the hierarchical covariance dominance claim.

claims.claim: An iterative bisection search over the squeezing parameter R (relating the physical and reference bases via a Bogoliubov transformation) converges in O(log(1/epsilon_R)) iterations for first-quantization Hamiltonian learning (Section 5.3, Eq. 77-78).
claims.evidence: Actual bisection loops over the squeezing signal g'(ΔR)=0.5·sinh(2ΔR) with true root √3/10 across 3 brackets and 10 tolerances (1e-2 to 5e-7) show 90/90 searches within the logarithmic ceiling, with iterations-vs-ln(1/ε_R) slope 1.4321 matching 1/ln(2)=1.4427.

claims.claim: The algorithm uses Chebyshev-node sampling of the displacement parameter combined with robust phase estimation and inverse discrete Fourier transform to reconstruct coefficients, as detailed in Algorithm 1 and illustrated for the single-mode case in Figure 1 (Section 2).
claims.evidence: Chebyshev radial sampling combined with angular inverse-DFT reconstruction achieves max coefficient error 3.61e-12 across 60 reconstructions (degrees 2–6, 5160 response cells), while the wrong-sign angular inversion control fails with max error 1.66, and a finite-Fock U(1) twirl certificate yields off-diagonal residual 1.09e-15.

Srishti280992/repro-continuous-variable-.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims of the D-RUT paper, using finite-Fock bosonic operators, physical displacement matrices, U(1) twirls, sampled robust phase estimation with binomial noise, and destructive controls (SQL, wrong-sign, omit-basis) across multiple random seeds and parameter regimes. The reproduction is simulation-based at moderate Fock dimensions (12–24 per mode) rather than physical hardware, but directly tests the algorithmic mechanisms and scaling laws claimed in the paper.

snaykey/repro-near-optimal-first-order.paper_title: Near-Optimal and Efficient First-Order Algorithm for Multi-Task Learning with Shared Linear Representation

claims.claim: TPGD (Algorithm 1) is a two-phase first-order gradient-descent method for jointly estimating a shared linear representation and task-specific parameters in multi-task learning (Section 4, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements TPGD from scratch with analytic gradients on the paper's Eq. 4 generative model (d=60, k=3, T=40, N=1500), showing estimation error dropping from 7.50e-2 to 3.90e-4 (1.44× the dk/(NT) floor) with subspace distance 0.096, confirming joint first-order estimation of B and W without SVD or method-of-moments steps.

claims.claim: Phase I performs K1/2 iterations of unregularized gradient descent as a warm start, and Phase II performs the remaining K1/2 iterations of regularized gradient descent with penalty term ||B^T B − WW^T||_F^2 (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The implementation explicitly splits K1=300 iterations into 150 unregularized GD steps (Phase I) and 150 steps with the (1/8)||B^T B - WW^T||_F^2 penalty (Phase II), measuring the coupling ||B^T B - WW^T||_F dropping from 1.42e-2 to 1.16e-16 across the phase boundary, directly confirming the regularizer enforces balancedness.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 and Corollary 5.3 prove the method attains a near-optimal population estimation error of order Õ(dk/(NT)), improving over existing likelihood-based methods by a factor of k, where d is input dimension, k is representation dimension, T is the number of tasks, and N is per-task sample size (Section 5.1, Theorem 5.1, Corollary 5.3).
claims.evidence: Log-log slopes from real TPGD runs show k-exponent +0.94 (R²=0.997, decisively +1 not +2), N-slope -1.05, d-slope +0.84, T-slope -0.87, with the general max{d,T}·k/(NT) bound holding across six (d,T) shapes at ratios 1.13–1.41. The k-sweep raw errors (k=1→9.4e-5 through k=6→5.1e-4) show near-linear scaling, directly confirming the factor-k improvement over dk²/(NT).

claims.claim: The algorithm achieves Õ(1) iteration complexity, i.e., convergence in a number of iterations independent of the problem dimensions up to logarithmic factors (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: With fixed step size η=0.30 held constant across d∈{40,80,160,320} (8× range), iterations to reach 3× the statistical floor remain in the band 24–29 (ratio 1.21), showing no polynomial-in-d blow-up, consistent with Õ(1) iteration complexity.

claims.claim: The estimation-error guarantee requires a per-task sample size of N ≳ σ²(d+T)kκ⁴/σ_k²(Σ*) (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: Recovery phase transitions measured over 4 seeds show threshold N* increasing from 120 to 240 as (d+T)k grows from 240 to 360–480, with N*/((d+T)k) in a narrow 0.5–0.67 band and sharp failure below threshold, confirming the (d+T)k scaling of the sample requirement (with σ, κ, σ_k held fixed).

claims.claim: Theorem 5.4 establishes excess-risk bounds for transferring the learned representation to a new task, decomposing the risk into representation approximation error and task-specific optimization error (Section 5.2, Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: Transfer SGD with decaying step over K2∈{50,200,800,3200} fits excess = A + B/K2 for both learned B̂ (A=1.34e-3, B=0.92) and exact B* control (A=1.10e-4, B=1.13), with the representation-approximation floor A being 12× larger for the learned representation and the 1/K2 optimization term present in both, directly demonstrating the two-term decomposition of Theorem 5.4.

snaykey/repro-near-optimal-first-order.overall: The logbook provides concrete computational evidence on the paper's own generative model (Eq. 4) with non-trivial dimensions (d up to 320, T up to 300, N up to 3000) for all six claims, including systematic log-log slope fits, phase-transition measurements, and control experiments. The reproduction is faithful to the algorithm specification and directly measures the theorems' stated quantities, though it is limited to synthetic instances with fixed conditioning (κ=1, σ_k=1) and does not audit proofs.

snaykey/repro-kmeans-hd-failure.paper_title: The Catastrophic Failure of *the* k-Means Algorithm in High Dimensions, and How Hartigan's Algorithm Avoids It

claims.claim: In the high-noise, high-dimensional regime where σ² > n, Lloyd's k-means algorithm fails catastrophically: essentially every partition of the data becomes a fixed point of the algorithm (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo simulation of Model 2.1 (n=20, σ²=40>n) with 300 GMM draws per dimension shows the fraction of random balanced partitions that are Lloyd fixed points climbs from 0.28 at d=50 to 1.00 at d=1600, while the control (σ²=2.50<n) stays below 0.66, directly demonstrating the σ²>n threshold drives the catastrophe.

claims.claim: In the same high-noise regime, Hartigan's k-means algorithm avoids this pathology, having no incorrect fixed points with high probability (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: Across 200 GMM draws per dimension in the same σ²=40>n regime, zero incorrect balanced partitions are Hartigan fixed points at any d (0.000 throughout), while Lloyd's incorrect-fixed rate climbs to 1.000; Hartigan's mean NMI rises to 0.735 at d=1600 versus Lloyd's 0.038.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.8 bounds the probability that any q-approximately balanced partition is not a fixed point of Lloyd's algorithm by 2^n · n · ρ_q^(d/4) (Corollary 3.8).
claims.evidence: The paper's closed-form ρ_q (Eq. 18) evaluates to 0.998613 ∈ [0,1), and the per-partition mechanism is empirically confirmed: the fraction of q-balanced partitions that are not Lloyd fixed points drops from 0.688 at d=50 to 0 by d=800. The assembled 2^n·n·ρ_q^(d/4) bound is vacuous at finite n, which is consistent with the paper's own statement that d≳n³ is needed.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.12 bounds the probability that any incorrect partition is a fixed point of Hartigan's algorithm by 2^n · ρ_h^(d/4), a substantially tighter bound than Lloyd's case (Corollary 3.12).
claims.evidence: ρ_h (Eq. 27) evaluates to 0.629572, far below ρ_q=0.998613, confirming ρ_h<ρ_q. The assembled 2^n·ρ_h^(d/4) crosses below 1 at d=200 (9.4e-05) and decays to 0, while Lloyd's bound stays at 10^6–10^7, directly demonstrating the 'substantially tighter' claim.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 shows Lloyd's single-sample reassignment step persists misclassification errors once the noise level exceeds σ > (2c̄τ(c−1))/√(c(c+c̄)) (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: With a one-misclassified-sample partition (n=20, c=11, c̄=9) and σ=13.730 (1.60× the Eq. 13 threshold of 8.581), 500 GMM draws per dimension show P(repair) collapses from 0.064 at d=50 to 0.000 by d=400, confirming persistence. The logbook honestly discloses that the Eq. 15 base ρ evaluates outside [0,1) at these parameters, but the theorem's conclusion is directly verified by simulation.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments empirically demonstrate the divergence between Lloyd's catastrophic-failure behavior and Hartigan's robustness as dimension grows, corroborating the theoretical bounds (Section 4).
claims.evidence: A full NMI grid (n=40, 50 trials per cell, d∈{50,200,800,2000}, σ²∈{5,20,80,200}) shows Hartigan's NMI climbing toward 1.00 with increasing d at every noise level while Lloyd's stays flat and low (e.g., σ²=20: Hartigan 0.11→1.00 vs Lloyd ≈0.02), reproducing the Figure 1 divergence pattern.

snaykey/repro-kmeans-hd-failure.overall: The logbook provides concrete Monte Carlo evidence across all six claims using the paper's Model 2.1 GMM with from-scratch Lloyd and Hartigan implementations, proper control conditions, and 200–500 independent trials per cell. The central dichotomy—Lloyd's catastrophic fixed-point abundance versus Hartigan's zero incorrect fixed points in the σ²>n regime—is directly measured and corroborated by the ρ-constant evaluations and the NMI divergence grid, with limitations (vacuous union bounds at finite n, Eq. 15 constant mismatch) honestly disclosed.

claims.claim: For the independent Gaussian variance allocation problem, the paper gives a PTAS achieving E[max_i X_i] ≥ OPT - ε in polynomial time (Theorem 1.1, Section 1.2).
claims.evidence: The PTAS is implemented from scratch and tested at n∈{50,100,200} with support k=⌈1/ε²⌉ as small as k/n=0.02, exercising the support-restriction mechanism. The additive gap E[max]−OPT is measured against a projected-gradient OPT on a shared 80k CRN bank, with worst gap 0.0033 across all (n,ε) cells—well within the smallest ε=0.3.

claims.claim: For correlated Gaussian variables, a PTAS with the same additive ε guarantee is established (Theorem 1.2, Section 1.2).
claims.evidence: The correlated PTAS is tested only at n∈{4,5,6} with general PSD covariance, and in most configurations k=⌈1/ε²⌉≥n (e.g., k=7 for n=4,5,6 at ε=0.4), so the support-restriction mechanism that defines the PTAS is not meaningfully exercised. Real runs with general covariance exist, but the scale is far below the independent case's n=200.

claims.claim: For the GraphVarAlloc problem with multiple constraint sets (general m>1), the paper gives an O(log n) multiplicative approximation guaranteeing Ω(1/log n)·OPT (Theorem 1.3, Section 1.2).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 3 is implemented exactly (level sweep + submodular greedy) and tested on constructed adversarial multi-scale instances (geometric, nested, laminar) at n up to 64. The minimum adversarial ratio ALG3/OPT is 0.900, well above the 1/log n floor (~0.24 at n=64), and adversarial ratios are below random-instance ratios, confirming the instances stress the algorithm.

claims.claim: Theorem 1.6 proves that in the optimal allocation, only Θ(1/p) variables receive variance Ω(p), i.e., the allocation concentrates on a shrinking subset as the constraint parameter p grows (Theorem 1.6, Section 1.3).
claims.evidence: The count of OPT variables with variance ≥½p is directly measured at n∈{32,64} across p∈{1/16,…,1/2}. The product count·p stays bounded in [0.33,0.67], confirming Θ(1/p) scaling. Achievability (construction reaches 0.83–0.92 of OPT) and necessity (fewer-support allocations strictly worse) are also checked.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 bounds the contribution of small-variance variables by O(ε√ln(1/ε)), which is used to limit the number of high-variance variables to O(1/ε²) and underlies the PTAS construction (Lemma 2.1, Section 2.1).
claims.evidence: The lemma's left-hand side E[max(0,max Y_i)] is estimated via 400k Monte Carlo samples on the maximal small-variance configuration (⌊1/ε²⌋ variables at variance ε²), with ε down to 0.08 (156 variables). The ratio to ε√ln(1/ε) stays bounded in [1.26,1.68] and converges toward 2, confirming the O(ε√ln(1/ε)) bound.

claims.claim: Monte Carlo simulations on Erdős–Rényi random graphs with n=8 nodes and edge probabilities p ranging from 1/8 to 8/8 are used to illustrate the concentration and concavity results across independent, positively, and negatively correlated settings (Figures 1-2, Section 1.3).
claims.evidence: The ER Monte Carlo is rerun at n up to 100 (scaled from the paper's n=8 to make the asymptotic concentration trend visible). Effective support N_eff shrinks from ~8.3 to ~3.9 as p grows at n=100, and OPT/m shows concavity (67–83% of discrete second differences ≤0) across independent, positive, and negative correlation settings, with the expected ordering negative ≥ independent ≥ positive.

snaykey/repro-variance-allocation.overall: The logbook provides a thorough from-scratch reproduction of five of the paper's six claims at reasonable scale with real numerical evidence, including adversarial instances for the O(log n) guarantee and direct measurement of the Θ(1/p) concentration phenomenon. The correlated PTAS (Claim 2) is tested only at very small scale (n≤6) where the PTAS support-restriction mechanism is not binding in most configurations, making it a toy-level verification.

Srishti280992/repro-doubly-exponential-f.paper_title: (Doubly) Exponential Lower Bounds for Follow the Regularized Leader in Potential Games

claims.claim: Theorem 1.2 proves that in two-player m×m potential games, Follow the Regularized Leader (FTRL) can require 2^Ω(m log m) iterations to reach an ε-Nash equilibrium for ε = 1/poly(m), for any permutation-invariant regularizer and any learning rate schedule η^(t) = 1/t^α with α ∈ [0,1) (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: Direct FTRL simulations across 4 regularizer families and 4 alpha schedules reach 65.6M rounds at m≤9 (m=9 hitting 63M cap without ε-NE), while the exact S/P recurrence audit through m=256 verifies 816 cells with all S_k=P_{k-1} and P_k=(k-1)P_{k-1} equalities holding, matching the factorial oracle at every dimension and yielding log2(T) vs m·log2(m) slope 0.819, confirming 2^Ω(m log m) scaling.

claims.claim: Theorem 1.3 shows there exists an n-player binary-action potential game in which fictitious play requires 2^Ω(2^n) iterations to reach an ε-Nash equilibrium for ε = 1/2^n, a doubly exponential lower bound (Theorem 1.3).
claims.evidence: Constructed hypercube-path games run through n=9 (192 vertices, log2(total)=1178.16, 0 shortcuts, unique improver at every vertex), and the exact signed recurrence through k=100 yields 99 cells all positive with T_k≥(k-1)! and 0 violations, with log2(log2(total)) vs n slope 1.28 confirming doubly exponential growth.

claims.claim: Theorem 1.1 establishes a matching-type positive result: alternating ε-lazy no-regret dynamics converge to an ε-Nash equilibrium in any potential game after at most exp(O_ε(1/ε^2)) iterations (Theorem 1.1, restated as Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: 512 sampled alternating ε-lazy MWU configurations (3–8 actions, ε∈{0.1,0.05,0.02,0.01}) all reach 2ε-NE (latest at round 4,898) with K≤range(Φ)/ε satisfied in all cases; exhaustive enumeration of 1,497 complete finite-family games (4,491 dynamics, 6.7M rounds) all converge with 0 potential decreases; destructive ε/100-threshold controls fail the K bound in 80/80 cases.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.2 shows that for FTRL with learning rate η ≤ 1/L (L the smoothness constant of the potential), the potential function value is non-decreasing across iterations, without requiring alternation or laziness (Proposition 3.2).
claims.evidence: 80,000 simultaneous Euclidean-FTRL steps across 80 random identical-interest games at ηL∈{0.1,0.3,0.7,1.0} produce zero violations of Φ(x_next)−Φ(x)≥‖x_next−x‖²/(2η), while the destructive control at ηL=5 produces 29 potential decreases, confirming the step-size condition is active.

claims.claim: Example 3.3 constructs a 'spurious fixed point' showing FTRL can maintain a highly suboptimal strategy (error proportional to 1/t) indefinitely relative to the observed utility sequence, illustrating why FTRL, unlike gradient descent under Legendre regularizers, need not reach an O_ε(ε)-Nash equilibrium (Example 3.3).
claims.evidence: The explicit two-action construction with utility sequence (1,0)^t followed by (0,1) yields a log-log slope of −0.994528 for residual bad-action mass (matching 1/t scaling), with strategy remaining 0.999998 suboptimal and only 2e-12 L1 movement after the shock at t=10^6; the reset-history control moves immediately to suboptimality −0.236, confirming inertia is the mechanism.

claims.claim: The two-player exponential lower bound construction uses a payoff matrix A of odd dimension m with maximum entry 2m−1, dividing the FTRL trajectory into 2m−1 'transition periods' governed by Property 4.3 (period consistency) and Lemma 4.1 bounding action probability by R/(η^(t)γ) (Section 4, Definition 4.2, Property 4.3, Lemma 4.1, Figure 2b).
