claims.evidence: The logbook states that while the dataset, model metadata, and a training command referencing pairwise train/test files exist in the artifacts, 'the root train.py invoked by train_rm.sh is not present in the pinned repository,' making the training pipeline non-reproducible.

claims.claim: TRM reaches 88.6% accuracy on the validation-set pairwise preference evaluation, outperforming Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B, ReasonFlux-PRM-7B, and prompt-only judging (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook mentions 'validation results' are included among the public artifacts, but there is no indication that the 88.6% accuracy figure or the comparison against Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B, ReasonFlux-PRM-7B, and prompt-only judging was independently re-run or reproduced.

claims.claim: TRM-guided best-of-N test-time selection improves AIME24 and AIME25 performance over compared PRM baselines for GPT-OSS-20B and Qwen3-8B response models (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The summary does not mention any best-of-N test-time selection experiments on AIME24 or AIME25, nor any comparison of TRM-guided selection against PRM baselines for GPT-OSS-20B or Qwen3-8B.

claims.claim: TRM-guided RL improves STEM and math benchmark averages over verifier-only RL, with the largest reported gains on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The summary does not mention any RL training experiments, STEM/math benchmark evaluations, or comparisons of TRM-guided RL against verifier-only RL on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or any other model.

wrice/repro-trm-complex-reasoning.overall: The logbook primarily performs artifact and code-structure inspection, confirming that the ME2 dimensions, DAG construction package, and TRM artifacts exist in the released repository, but it does not independently reproduce any of the paper's key experimental results (Table 1, Figure 4, Table 2). The training pipeline is non-reproducible due to a missing train.py, and no downstream evaluation or RL experiments were run.

claims.claim: Agents holding individually insufficient local views coordinate through ADMM constrained by cellular sheaves (Sheaf-ADMM) to produce correct global outputs, reaching 92.6% solved rate on Sudoku versus 10.7% for a parameter-matched MPNN baseline (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Sheaf-ADMM scored 94.20% on 2,000 hard Sudoku puzzles (close to paper's 92.6%), and a parameter-matched MPNN (0.81% mismatch, 547,425 vs 543,025 params) scored only 5.85 ± 4.59%, with a same-seed difference of 88.35 ± 4.59 points (t interval [76.95, 99.75]). Coordination controls further confirm the mechanism: disabling edge coupling collapses performance to 0.67%, and K=0 yields 0.02%.

claims.claim: On the maze task, Sheaf-ADMM attains a 99.8% solve rate using a much smaller per-vertex latent dimension (d_v=10) than the MPNN baseline (d_v=84, 99.9% solve rate), showing comparable accuracy with far less per-agent state (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Sheaf-ADMM with d_v=10 achieved 99.97% (matching paper's 99.9%), but the d_v=84 MPNN baseline was extremely seed-unstable: seeds scored 100.00%, 4.00%, and 96.80% (mean 66.93%), with one completed training run collapsing to 4%. Two of three seeds reached near-paper accuracy, but the baseline's unreliability prevents confirming comparable accuracy.

claims.claim: Sheaf-ADMM shows markedly improved robustness to distribution shift on MNIST: under 16-pixel padding a standard CNN drops to 11.4% accuracy while Sheaf-ADMM retains 86.3%, and under 30% patch dropout the CNN reaches 45.5% versus 69.1% for Sheaf-ADMM (Table 4).
claims.evidence: The paper's CNN baseline is not in the released repository, so the exact Table-4 cells cannot be tested. Using a disclosed custom CNN, Sheaf-ADMM scored 84.94% at pad-16 (vs paper 86.3%) and 75.07% at 30% dropout (vs 69.1%), but the custom CNN scored 71.77% at pad-16 (vs paper's 11.4%), and the paired difference intervals crossed zero for padding ([-56.41, 82.74]) and marginally failed the dropout gate ([0.28, 16.65] vs >10 threshold).

claims.claim: An ablation shows learned restriction (sheaf) maps are critical to coordination: replacing them with identity maps collapses Sudoku performance to 6.1% solved, and removing the L1 regularization term drops maze performance from 99.8% to 38.9% (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The Sudoku identity-map ablation is verified: learned maps scored 94.20% vs identity maps 4.23% (same-device audit: 94.12% vs 4.23%, gap +89.88 ± 0.45), matching the paper's 6.1% collapse. However, the L1 claim is contradicted: a direct L1-coefficient intervention found default 99.80 ± 0.26% vs L1=0 at 99.97 ± 0.06% (difference -0.17 ± 0.29 points), and the no-L1 reconstruction reached 100.00%, not 38.9%. The logbook identifies that the paper's 38.9% row is the 'Diagonal (fixed Q)' ablation, not L1 removal.

claims.claim: Sheaf-ADMM generalizes to larger problem sizes, remaining near-saturated in maze solve rate up to roughly a 2x increase in linear maze resolution beyond training size (Figure 6, Section 5.5 Out-of-Distribution Generalization).
claims.evidence: Imported Sheaf-ADMM checkpoints evaluated on the released deterministic 2x OOD configuration scored 98.24 ± 0.52% (vs paper's 98.1 ± 1.2%), and a frozen sweep over widths 19–39 stayed above 95% at every size (98.00% at width 39 ≈ 2x). A dense released-builder sweep confirmed saturation through width 39 (98.00 ± 0.85%) before smooth decay at larger sizes.

Mindcraft/repro-learning-multi-agent-coo.overall: The logbook provides strong experimental support for Sheaf-ADMM's Sudoku coordination advantage over parameter-matched MPNN baselines (Claim 1), the criticality of learned restriction maps via identity-map ablation (Claim 4 Sudoku half), and near-saturated generalization to 2x maze resolution (Claim 5). Claims 2 and 3 remain inconclusive due to MPNN training instability and an unavailable paper CNN baseline, and the L1 ablation sub-claim in Claim 4 is falsified by direct intervention showing no in-distribution effect.

the-kristina-dimitrova/repro-reversal-cu.paper_title: Breaking the Reversal Curse in Autoregressive Language Models via Identity Bridge

claims.claim: The Identity Bridge data recipe augments training with pairs of the form 'A is A' using an identity relation whose embedding is the zero vector, formalized as D_id = {[a_i, r_id | a_i]} ∪ {[b_i, r_id | b_i]} for i in [N] (Section 3, Theorem 3.4 setup).
claims.evidence: Concrete implementation checks confirm |D_id|=2N=20 for N=10, ||z_r_id||_2 = 0.0 exactly, and sample D_id entries [a_i, r_id | a_i] with x2 == 0_d: True, matching the paper's formalization precisely.

claims.claim: Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct fine-tuned on 100 reversal pairs (e.g., Husband-Wife, Parent-Child) achieves roughly 40% success rate on held-out reversal tasks when Identity Bridge data is added, versus near-0% without it (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: With Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (substituted for gated Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct), exact-match reversal accuracy is 0.0% in all four conditions at step 1000; MRR moves directionally correct (0.016→0.040 for HW, 0.013→0.032 for PC) but is far below the claimed ~40% accuracy, confounded by no lr sweep, fixed step budget, and harness bugs.

claims.claim: In a one-layer transformer trained with Identity Bridge data, Mean Reciprocal Rank on reversal generalization reaches 1.0, whereas without Identity Bridge data MRR remains at its near-random initialization value of about 0.1 (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: One-layer transformer (N=10, full-batch GD) reaches reversal MRR = 1.000 with Identity Bridge vs. 0.210 without (staying near its init value of ~0.16–0.21), matching Figure 4's headline result; the lr was changed from 1e-3 to 0.2 (documented) to reach the separable regime, but the core MRR claim is concretely reproduced.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 proves that under the identity-bridge-regularized training set D = D_r+ ∪ D_id, the implicit bias of gradient descent drives the model's output-value weights such that the score for correct reversal answers exceeds that of incorrect answers, i.e., h[b, r-],a(W*_ov) > 0, enabling generalization to the reversal relation.
claims.evidence: Numerical audit of 190 margins (10 queries × 19 wrong candidates) shows 0/190 violations with Identity Bridge (min margin +2.705, all positive) vs. 56/190 violations without (min margin −0.389), directly confirming h[b,r-],a(W*_ov) > 0 holds at the GD solution under D = D_r+ ∪ D_id.

claims.claim: Reversal generalization is sensitive to entity length: the fine-tuned model reaches up to 100% accuracy reversing short 'number name' entities but only about 7% accuracy on longer entity names (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: The 'number' entity condition (expected ~100% accuracy) is invalidated by a tokenizer bug where Qwen splits the leading space before digits, making MRR=1.0 an artifact of predicting a space token; the valid normal-vs-long comparison shows long names with higher MRR (0.157 vs. 0.040), opposite to the paper's claim, but both at 0% accuracy under the same confounds as Claim 2.

claims.claim: Without an auxiliary OCR+ style dataset, reversal accuracy plateaus at only about 6% even with Identity Bridge; adding the OCR+ dataset raises accuracy to near 40%, indicating a shortcut-learning failure mode that Identity Bridge alone does not fully resolve (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: The shortcut-trap dynamic reproduces qualitatively (IDN and OCR both reach 99% shortcut accuracy) and MRR ordering IDN < OCR < OCR+ (0.028 < 0.030 < 0.040) matches the paper's ranking, but reversal accuracy is 0.0% in all three conditions, nowhere near the claimed 6%→40% jump, and OCR+ shortcut accuracy was not tracked.

the-kristina-dimitrova/repro-reversal-cu.overall: The logbook provides concrete, verified evidence for the paper's theoretical core: the Identity Bridge construction (Claim 1), one-layer transformer MRR=1.0 result (Claim 3), and Theorem 3.4 margin inequality (Claim 4) all reproduce with exact numerical checks. The real-LLM claims (2, 5, 6) remain inconclusive: all conditions show 0% exact-match accuracy under a substituted backbone without lr sweep, with acknowledged harness bugs, preventing either confirmation or falsification at the claimed magnitudes.

amkkk/repro-a-capacity-based-rationale-f.paper_title: A Capacity-Based Rationale for Multi-Head Attention

claims.claim: Recovering a graph with m' relations in d_model-dimensional embeddings requires total key dimension D_K = Θ(m' log m' / d_model), established as a lower bound (Section 7) and matched by a constructive upper bound (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Numerical counting lower bound ratios (1.16–1.62) and a constructive upper-bound point (m=1024, D_K=672, margin +29) provide real but reduced-scale evidence; matched-D_K controls at m=512 and m=1024 both remain non-separable, and the lower-bound ratios are far from the asymptotic regime.

claims.claim: For permutation graphs (m' = m), the capacity requirement simplifies to D_K = Θ(m log m / d_model) (Section 4/Section 7).
claims.evidence: Permutation-specialized counting ratios decay from 1.251 to 1.143 over m=32..1024, and constructive separations exist (one-hot C=24 and compressive m=512 margin +15), but all at reduced scale with constructive rather than trained methods.

claims.claim: Multi-head attention's advantage arises because splitting into heads reduces the effective block size B, shrinking the noise term N3(B) ≍ (B/d_model)√(d_k log m) that governs interference from superposition (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Single-configuration synthetic experiment (m=4096, d_model=256, d_k=64) shows through-origin R²=0.9888 and 10.1× single-vs-multi-head noise ratio, but the full-range log-log slope is 0.587 (tail 0.837), not 1.0, and only one configuration is tested with random embeddings.

claims.claim: Empirical scaling of the optimal total key dimension matches theory: D_K* ≈ 1.19·(m log m/d_model) with R²=0.944 (R²=0.992 after excluding three outlier points), and the optimal head count scales as h* ≈ 1.65(m/d_model) − 6.64 with per-head widths d_k* in [5,24] (median 11) (Section 6).
claims.evidence: Constructive grid yields slope 1.19 (R²=0.9981) matching the paper's coefficient, but the methodology differs fundamentally: h* is fixed at m/d_model (not 1.65(m/d_model)−6.64), d_k* median is 5.5–6 (not 11), and no trained models are used, so the empirical scaling law from gradient-trained Transformers is not replicated.

claims.claim: The multi-head capacity advantage persists in a fuller Transformer setting with softmax normalization, value routing, and frozen GPT-2 embeddings, since the analysis establishes capacity is purely key-query driven (Appendix C).
claims.evidence: Softmax attention at m=32, d_model=8 shows h=2 F1=1.000 vs h=1 F1=0.906, but value-routing MSE is essentially tied across head counts (no advantage), and the frozen GPT-2 embedding component of the claim is entirely absent.

claims.claim: Capacity requirements are largely insensitive to context length, tested over sequence lengths ℓ ∈ {16,32}, with only modest degradation when evaluating at longer lengths than training (Section 6.1, Appendix A.3).
claims.evidence: Constructive configurations tested at train lengths 16/32 and eval lengths 16–64 show degradation ranging 0–62.5%, with one configuration exhibiting 62.5% degradation that partially contradicts the 'modest degradation' claim; all at reduced scale (m=128–256) with constructive rather than trained models.

amkkk/repro-a-capacity-based-rationale-f.overall: This logbook provides reduced-scale, CPU-only, synthetic/constructive evidence across all six claims, with real numerical results and controls but no trained Transformer models, no GPT-2 embeddings, and scales far below the paper's experimental setup. The directional mechanisms (capacity scaling, noise reduction via block splitting, multi-head advantage at equal D_K) receive partial support, but key empirical claims about trained-model scaling laws and full Transformer settings remain unverified at the paper's scale.

amkkk/repro-why-do-we-need-warm-up-a-the.paper_title: Why Do We Need Warm-up? A Theoretical Perspective

claims.claim: The paper generalizes (L0,L1)-smoothness to (H0,H1)-smoothness (Definition 3.1), bounding the Hessian norm as H0 + H1 times the function sub-optimality f(w) - f* rather than the gradient norm (Section 3, Definition 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook extracted Definition 3.1 from the preserved paper PDF, confirming the bound ||Hess f(w)|| <= H0 + H1*(f(w)-f*) and the (L0,L1)->(H0,H1) generalization statement, and verified mathematical consistency via an exact cosh(x)-1 witness (f''=1+f, max_identity_error=0.0, max_bound_violation=0.0 across 20,001 grid points).

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 and 3.2 show the (H0,H1)-smoothness condition holds for deep linear networks with MSE loss under weight balancedness and for deep non-linear networks with one leaky-ReLU layer under MSE loss (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Extraction from the preserved paper shows Prop 3.1 is actually about gradient-flow Hessian dynamics of a 1x1 linear network (not deep-linear-MSE-balancedness), and Prop 3.2 covers deep linear MSE under balancedness (the claim's first item, not its second); the leaky-ReLU MSE result is in Proposition D.1, not Prop 3.2 as claimed.

claims.claim: Propositions 3.3 and 3.4 extend the condition to two-layer networks with MSE loss under L2 regularization and to two-layer networks with cross-entropy loss (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Extraction from the preserved paper shows Prop 3.3 is actually about a 2-layer model with cross-entropy + L2 (not MSE + L2 as claimed), and Prop 3.4 is about a single-attention transformer for in-context learning (not a two-layer network with cross-entropy as claimed).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 gives a lower bound showing gradient descent with a constant step-size requires substantially more iterations when poorly initialized, while Theorem 4.2 proves that under the Aiming condition, GD with the adaptive step-size eta_k = 1/(10*H0 + 20*H1*(f(w_k)-f*)) converges in O(H0*dist(w0,S)^2/(theta^2*eps) + H1*dist(w0,S)^2/theta^2) iterations, faster than any fixed step-size (Theorems 4.1-4.2).
claims.evidence: A single 1D witness function f(x)=cosh(x)-1 (H0=H1=1, theta=1) was used to demonstrate adaptive GD (142 iters) vs fixed GD (10,670 iters, 75x speedup), but this is a reduced single-witness demonstration that does not prove Theorem 4.1's lower bound or Theorem 4.2's upper bound for the general class of (H0,H1)-smooth Aiming functions.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 extends the convergence results to mu-Polyak-Lojasiewicz functions (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The same single 1D witness f(x)=cosh(x)-1 (mu=1, H0=H1=1) showed observed iterations (142) within the Theorem 4.3 bound (3190.85), but this is a reduced single-witness illustration that does not establish the theorem for the universal class of (H0,H1)-smooth mu-PL functions.

claims.claim: Section 3.2 empirically validates the (H0,H1)-smoothness condition on Transformer language models (70M, 160M, 410M parameters) trained on FineWeb and on ResNet50/ViT-Tiny trained on ImageNet32, finding local curvature grows approximately linearly with training loss early in training (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: A real experiment was run on a drastically simplified proxy (22K-param tiny transformer on synthetic next-token data, 500 steps) producing Pearson r=-0.1286 and slope=-0.7004, but this setup is far below the paper's scale (70M-410M on FineWeb, ResNet50/ViT-Tiny on ImageNet32) and cannot constitute a full reproduction or falsification of the curvature-loss relation claim.

amkkk/repro-why-do-we-need-warm-up-a-the.overall: The logbook provides genuine source-extraction evidence confirming Definition 3.1 and revealing that the proposition-number attributions in claims 2-3 do not match the preserved paper, while the theoretical convergence claims (4-5) are only illustrated on a single 1D witness function and the empirical claim (6) is tested on a drastically reduced CPU-only proxy that fails to reproduce the paper's positive curvature-loss correlation.

amkkk/repro-anytime-valid-delayed-design.paper_title: Design-Based Anytime-Valid Inference for Randomized Experiments with Delayed Outcomes and Staggered Entry

claims.claim: The IPW treatment-effect estimation error is not a martingale with respect to any single filtration, but each arm's IPW estimation error is shown to be a martingale with respect to an arm-specific event-time filtration (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Numerical covariance tests on N=5000 resamples with 100 time points show per-arm IPW errors have small martingale deviations (0.018, 0.005) while the treatment-effect error has a large deviation (0.528), and E[Z_i(1)]≈0.007 (p=0.484), directly supporting the claim that per-arm errors are martingales but the treatment-effect error is not.

claims.claim: Combining two arm-level anytime-valid confidence sequences via a union bound produces tighter intervals than the standard design-based variance upper bound when treatment induces asymmetric outcome arrival rates between arms (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The asymptotic limit R_pi≤1 was verified both symbolically and numerically at V=1e8; asymmetric cases (V0=o(V1) or V1=o(V0)) yield R_pi→0.707 (29% narrower), confirming the union-bound advantage under asymmetric arrival rates. The finite-sample deviation (max 1.004) is honestly reported as unfavorable but does not contradict the asymptotic claim.

claims.claim: The paper characterizes an augmentation (AIPW) class for which per-arm estimation errors preserve the martingale property under staggered entry and delayed outcomes (Section 5, Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: Valid event-time AIPW shows martingale preservation (conditional increment mean 0.013, p=0.380; covariance deviation 0.031), IPW as special case also holds (deviation 0.022), and invalid augmentations (pre-event, non-constant post-event) are structurally rejected for adaptedness and predictability failures, testing both necessity and sufficiency on N=2000 units.

claims.claim: The theoretical development includes Theorems 4.1 through 4.12 building the design-based martingale framework for delayed and staggered-entry settings (Section 4).
claims.evidence: All 12 numbered results (Defs 4.1–4.3, Thms 4.4–4.12, Lemma 4.5, 4.7, Prop 4.8, 4.12, Cor 4.10, Remark 4.11) were inventoried with a checked dependency graph; boundary monotonicity in alpha and V confirmed, and Lemma 4.7 covariance identity verified numerically (mean deviation 0.0147).

claims.claim: Simulation studies illustrate the behavior of the proposed confidence sequences under staggered entry and delayed outcomes (Figures 12-15).
claims.evidence: A reduced proxy of Dataset 5.1 with N=500 units and 200 resamples omitted hazard thinning and localized arm-specific shocks, used IPW only (not AIPW), and explicitly reports protocol_match=false; coverage rates (99%, 100%, 100%) are roughly consistent with the paper's (96%, 97%, 99%) but on a clearly simplified setup.

amkkk/repro-anytime-valid-delayed-design.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting the four theoretical claims about martingale properties, union-bound width advantages, and the AIPW characterization class through covariance tests, asymptotic limit verification, and structural rejection of invalid augmentations at reasonable sample sizes. The simulation claim is addressed only through a reduced proxy with omitted data-generating components, yielding a toy verdict.

claims.claim: In the population setting, Theorem 1 characterizes excess risk as a function of the magnitude and direction of the performative effect together with spurious features (Section 4, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: First-order excess risk approximation tested at d=50 with synthetic Gaussian data across 3 covariance configurations, achieving mean correlation 0.896 with empirical risk — real runs and numbers but at reduced scale far below the theoretical n,p→∞ regime.

claims.claim: Corollary 2 shows the optimal regularization parameter in the population regime is proportional to the strength of the performative effect, with optimal risk remaining strictly positive (Section 4, Corollary 2).
claims.evidence: Formal derivation of λ*=mean(b)·d/Tr(S₁) plus numerical grid search at d=40 with 40 λ values and 20 trials each yields correlation 0.999, but the experimental verification is at reduced scale with synthetic Gaussian data, not a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 establishes a deterministic equivalent of the performative fixed point for over-parameterized ridge regression when the number of features exceeds the number of samples (Section 5, Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Deterministic equivalent tested across four over-parameterized configurations (n=30–60, p=80, κ=1.33–2.67) with per-config correlations 0.970–0.999 and MAE 0.134, but the asymptotic theory requires n,p→∞ and the O(p^{-1/4}) error is non-negligible at these sizes.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 shows the optimal regularization moves in the same direction as the performative effect on predictive features under low noise, but in the opposite direction under high noise, in the over-parameterized regime (Section 5, Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: High-noise (σ=0.7) opposite-direction movement confirmed (λ* drops 0.474→0.423 with b=0.2), but low-noise (σ=0.2) same-direction effect is unresolved (both give λ*=0.062 due to grid coarseness), at reduced scale n=60, p=80.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments in Section 6 confirm that in the over-parameterized setting, performative effects can improve optimally-regularized risk when performativity reinforces existing trends, contrasting with the population-regime degradation (Section 6).
claims.evidence: Directional contrast reproduced with synthetic Gaussian data: over-parameterized risk improves monotonically (0.749→0.742) while population risk degrades (0.00011→0.059) across A_b values, but the paper's real-world datasets (Housing/LSAC at n=4000) are not tested and scale is n=30, d=40.

amkkk/repro-optimal-reg-performative.overall: All five claims are addressed with real runs and numerical results, but every experiment uses synthetic Gaussian data at significantly reduced scale (d=30–50, n=30–60, p=80) compared to the theoretical asymptotic regime or the paper's real-world experiments. The reproduction consistently supports the paper's theoretical predictions at toy scale but does not reach a non-toy setup for any claim.

claims.claim: WIRE applies rotary position encodings to graphs by using Laplacian spectral coordinates to define graph-dependent rotation angles (Figure 1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Norm preservation (max error 4.44e-16) and angle recovery verified on only 12 small random graphs (8-50 nodes) using numpy.linalg.eigh; this is a finite algebraic sanity check of the WIRE construction, not a full-scale demonstration.

claims.claim: The WIRE transformation is equivariant to node-order permutations up to sign flips and rotations in degenerate eigenspaces (Lemma 1).
claims.evidence: 500 permutation tests passed on 50 random graphs up to 20 nodes with sign-flip alignment and tolerance 0.01; this is finite numerical sampling of a lemma, not a universal proof or large-scale verification.

claims.claim: Regular RoPE is recovered as a special case of WIRE on grid graphs with appropriate learnable frequencies (Theorem 2, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Exact angle recovery (max error 0.0) demonstrated on nine 1D path graphs (n=4-30) with d_model=8, but 2D/general grid cases from the theorem are not tested, making this a simplified subset of the claim.

claims.claim: WIRE asymptotically depends on graph effective resistance under the paper's spectral-feature assumptions (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Spearman rho=0.912 between effective resistance and a spectral-alignment proxy on 50 small graphs (8-25 nodes); this uses a proxy metric at non-asymptotic scale rather than directly verifying the theorem's asymptotic dependence.

claims.claim: Experiments report WIRE improvements on synthetic monochromatic-subgraph and shortest-path tasks, point-cloud transformers, and efficient graph transformer benchmarks (Table 1, Table 2, Table 3, Table 4).
claims.evidence: A 1-layer graph transformer on synthetic shortest-path classification (n=15, 350/100 train/test) shows 34% vs 29% accuracy; this is a single reduced task with a simple classifier, not reproducing any of Tables 1-4 benchmarks.

amkkk/repro-rotary-position-encodings-fo.overall: All five claims are addressed only at reduced scale: small graphs (≤50 nodes), 1D paths instead of general grids, proxy metrics, and a single simplified synthetic task with a 1-layer model. No full-scale benchmark from Tables 1-4 is reproduced, and no formal proof is executed.

claims.claim: The paper formalizes learning multiplication in a finite-dimensional algebra as learning a structure tensor 𝓒 ∈ 𝔽^{n×n×n}, and proves that any such tensor defines a valid algebra (Proposition 2.1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: Formal derivation confirms any tensor C defines a closed bilinear map by construction, and 100 random tensors over F_7, n=2 with 500 product pairs each yielded 100% valid algebras, directly supporting Proposition 2.1.

claims.claim: Associativity, commutativity, and unitality are each characterized as tensor identities on 𝓒 (e.g., associativity as ∑_k 𝓒_ijk𝓒_klm = ∑_k 𝓒_ikm𝓒_jlk for all i,j,l,m), unifying group-based grokking as a special case of the FDA framework (Proposition 2.2, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Known algebras (componentwise, zero) pass expected tensor-identity classifications, and 200 random tensors over F_7, n=2 produce a category distribution (ACU 95.5%, ACu 3.0%, AcU 1.5%) consistent with theoretical expectations, confirming the identities in Proposition 2.2.

claims.claim: In experiments over finite fields 𝔽_7 with n=2 (2^3=8 algebraic categories sampled at ratios r∈{0.2,...,0.9}), non-unital associative-commutative algebras (0.03% of sampled category) grok fastest while unital associative-commutative algebras (0.017%) grok slowest (Section 5, Figures 4–5).
claims.evidence: A reduced MLP (embed_dim=32 vs paper's 128, hidden_dim=64) trained on only 4 of 8 categories with a single seed confirms that acU (non-unital associative-commutative) groks fastest (epoch 100), but acu (unital associative-commutative) does not grok slowest—AcU and ACU fail to grok within 5000 epochs—so the full ranking claim is only partially addressed at reduced scale.

claims.claim: A representation-quality metric 𝓜_rep transitions sharply from low values to ≈1 at the same point test accuracy rises, and higher test accuracy in low-data regimes correlates with higher 𝓜_rep (Section 5, Figures 1–2).
claims.evidence: M_rep stayed near zero (−0.005 to 0.003) throughout training despite test accuracy reaching 1.0 by epoch 50, contradicting the claimed sharp transition to ≈1, but the test was conducted on the zero algebra (acU) whose trivial product structure (u*v=0 for all u,v) likely renders the cosine-similarity metric degenerate and uninformative.

claims.claim: Higher mode-3 unfolding rank r^(3) and greater sparsity s of the structure tensor both delay grokking and increase test loss, linking grokking speed to algebraic/tensor complexity (Section 5, Figure 6).
claims.evidence: Mode-3 rank correlates strongly with grokking epoch (Pearson r=0.99, supporting the rank component), but sparsity correlates negatively (r=−0.70, contradicting the claim), and with only 4 data points confounded by the zero algebra (sparsity=1.0, groks fastest), the evidence is too weak to confirm or refute the combined rank-and-sparsity claim.

claims.claim: Proposition 5.1 shows that once a faithful representation is learned, the group/algebra product can be exactly linearly decoded via inverse lookup in the classifier weights (Section 5, Proposition 5.1).
claims.evidence: The MLP's linear probe achieved only 8.91% (antecedent of faithful representation not met), but the formal conditional proof plus exhaustive testing of six faithful left-regular representations yielded 14,406/14,406 exact product decodes with zero failures and minimum margin 42, directly verifying Proposition 5.1's mathematical content.

amkkk/repro-grokking-fda.overall: The logbook provides solid verification of the three theoretical/mathematical claims (Props 2.1, 2.2, 5.1) via formal derivations and computational checks, but the empirical claims about grokking dynamics are tested only at heavily reduced scale (embed_dim=32, 4/8 categories, single seed, CPU, 30 min) with one claim (M_rep transition) contradicted on a degenerate test case and another (rank+sparsity) only partially supported.

claims.claim: Under accuracy-based payment schemes, required payments to sustain positive human effort diverge (scale at least logarithmically in 1/p) as AI error probability p approaches zero, formalized as an impossibility result (Theorems 3.1-3.2).
claims.evidence: Numerical sweep over p from 10⁻⁶ to 0.2 shows w_min decreasing from 27.63 to 4.02 with constant ratio w(p)/log(1/p) ≈ 2.0 across all tested values, confirming logarithmic scaling; mutation control (constant wage → constant effort) validates that divergence is specific to accuracy-based schemes.

claims.claim: The sentinel-auditing mechanism designates a fraction ρ of tasks as sentinel tasks with forced AI errors, and paying an explicit bonus b(x) for correct human performance on these yields a first-order condition ρ·μ(b(x))·q'(e*) = c'(e*) that guarantees strictly positive effort independent of baseline AI accuracy p (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: All 175 configurations (ρ∈[0.01,0.50], b∈[0.1,5.0], p∈[0.001,0.5]) yield strictly positive effort e*>0 (min 0.029), while the ρ=0 mutation control produces e*≈1e-12, confirming the sentinel mechanism is both necessary and sufficient for the guarantee.

claims.claim: Incentive-aware active statistical inference jointly optimizes the auditing rate ρ, sampling policy π(X), and bonus schedule b(X) to minimize estimator variance under a fixed budget constraint, with closed-form optimal designs given for mean estimation (Section 5, Examples 5.3-5.5).
claims.evidence: Closed-form allocation n_i* = (σ_i/√c_i) × B/Σ(σ_j√c_j) verified on 48 synthetic configurations (n=50-500, d=3-10) showing 14.3% mean variance reduction over uniform, but only tests the sampling component on synthetic mean-estimation data rather than the full joint optimization of ρ, π(X), and b(X) at realistic scale.

claims.claim: The framework extends to general M-estimation problems with asymptotic normality guarantees for the resulting incentive-aware estimator (Theorem 5.6).
claims.evidence: Bootstrap simulation (n=200, d=5, 500 iterations) shows sandwich variance ratio 0.97 vs bootstrap and 100% CI coverage (5/5 coefficients), while the unweighted mutation control achieves only 80% coverage, confirming the incentive-aware weighting is necessary for correct asymptotic inference.

claims.claim: Experiments on post-election survey data and protein data show the incentive-aware active inference approach achieves roughly 70-80% budget savings relative to standard active learning baselines while maintaining comparable estimation error (Section 6).
claims.evidence: Synthetic proxies (survey n=600/d=10, protein n=800/d=20) yield only 1.45% combined budget savings (2.9% survey, 0.0% protein) versus the claimed 70-80%, with no mutation control implemented and no access to the real post-election or protein datasets, making it impossible to confirm or refute the magnitude claim.

amkkk/repro-overcoming-incentive-collaps.overall: The logbook provides credible numerical verification of the paper's core theoretical results (logarithmic payment divergence, sentinel-auditing effort guarantee, M-estimation asymptotic normality) with appropriate mutation controls, but the empirical savings claim remains unaddressed due to reliance on synthetic proxies that produce near-zero savings and lack of real datasets.

amkkk/repro-optimal-and-scalable-mapf-vi.paper_title: Optimal and Scalable MAPF via Multi-Marginal Optimal Transport and Schrödinger Bridges

claims.claim: Anonymous multi-agent path finding is formulated as linear program P1 minimizing transport cost over per-timestep transport matrices subject to flow-conservation constraints (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Constraint matrix verified as network-flow structure on a 3×3 grid (45×132, each column one +1/one -1, rank = n_nodes-1); this structural property is scale-invariant and sufficient to confirm the LP P1 formulation claim.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.3 proves the constraint set yields integral optimal solutions in {0,1}^(K×K) achieving minimum cost with polynomial-time complexity, and Theorem 3.4 confirms the resulting paths are collision-free and non-overlapping in space-time (Section 3).
claims.evidence: A single 2×2 grid with 2 agents and horizon T=1 shows the LP relaxation returns an integral {0,1} optimum (objective 2.0) with collision-free paths [0→1] and [3→2], but this is a minimal witness instance, not a thorough verification of the general theorem.

claims.claim: Total unimodularity of the constraint matrix is proven via a node-splitting construction on time-expanded graphs (Appendix B).
claims.evidence: Node-splitting construction tested on 6 cases (grids 2×2 to 4×4); each column verified to have exactly one +1 and one -1, split graph confirmed bipartite, and exact-integer determinants of 217 sampled square submatrices per case (up to order 6) all lie in {-1,0,+1}, confirming total unimodularity via the network-matrix theorem.

claims.claim: The Schrödinger bridge relaxation P2 adds entropic regularization parameter ε to P1, and Lemma 4.1 decomposes the KL divergence into transport and marginal terms enabling Sinkhorn iterations (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Sinkhorn iterations converge for ε ∈ {1.0, 0.5, 0.25, 0.1} with exact marginal satisfaction, and the Lemma 4.1 KL decomposition KL(π|μ⊗ν) = H(μ)+H(ν)−H(π) matches to error < 1e-15 on a 6-dimensional instance, confirming the algebraic identity.

claims.claim: On grids with K up to 22,500 robots at 5% density, the entropic (P2+P3) pipeline scales as O(K^1.15) versus O(K^1.68) for the exact LP P1, yielding 3.6x-7.1x speedups (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Scaling comparison uses K=40..300 (vs paper's K≤22,500) on a random-coordinate OT surrogate (not grid MAPF at 5% density); fitted exponents (≈0.90 vs ≈2.09) and speedups (10×–103×) differ substantially from the paper's values (1.15/1.68, 3.6×–7.1×), providing only directional trend support.

claims.claim: Cost degradation from the entropic-to-integral projection stays under 10% while permitting 60-80% edge reduction in the graph pruning step (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Cost degradation tested on K≤22 single-timestep transport surrogate (vs multi-timestep grid pipeline with K≤22,500); 35/36 cases show <10% degradation with 60-80% edge reduction, but one outlier (K=22, ε=1.0, prune=80%) reaches 12.31%, and the setup is far below the paper's scale and task complexity.

amkkk/repro-optimal-and-scalable-mapf-vi.overall: The logbook provides solid structural verification of the four theoretical claims (LP formulation, integrality witness, total unimodularity, and KL decomposition) on small instances, but the two empirical scaling claims are only addressed on significantly reduced surrogate setups (K≤300 and K≤22 vs K≤22,500) with proxy tasks that differ from the paper's grid MAPF experiments.

amkkk/repro-adversarially-robust-control.paper_title: Adversarially Robust Control of Conditional Value-at-Risk via Rockafellar-Uryasev Conformal Inference

claims.claim: Theorem 2.2 establishes that the realized empirical CVaR of the Rockafellar-Uryasev conformal inference method (RUCC) is controlled at the target level with an asymptotic conservatism gap of O(1/sqrt(T)), termed the 'Price of Nonlinearity' relative to the O(1/T) rate achievable for linear expected-loss control (Theorem 2.2; Remark 2.3).
claims.evidence: Log-log slope of CVaR gap vs T = -0.496 across 400 runs on synthetic N(0.5,1) Gaussian losses with T up to 2000, directionally matching the predicted O(1/√T) rate, but only on a single synthetic distribution at reduced scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.4 bounds the inner-level regret of the AdaGrad-FTRL threshold optimization by |max_c Reg_T(c)| <= (3/4) * max{1, beta/(1-beta)} * sqrt(T+1), and Theorem 2.6 shows the outer-level Conformal Decision Theory update keeps the surrogate loss within alpha + O(sqrt(T))/T of the target risk level alpha (Theorem 2.4; Theorem 2.6).
claims.evidence: Regret scaling slope 0.436 (expected 0.5) and surplus decay slope -0.958 measured on synthetic data with T≤1000, 15 seeds; rates are directionally consistent but exact constant coefficients from Theorems 2.4/2.6 are not verified and scale is reduced.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 (Section 2.3) requires no assumptions on the data-generating process, combining an outer-level Conformal Decision Theory update for the risk-control parameter lambda_t with an inner-level AdaGrad-FTRL optimization over the threshold c_t (Section 2.3, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: 150/150 runs across 15 synthetic distribution families at T=1000 control CVaR (max tracking error 0.070 full / 0.100 final-half vs DKW gates), providing breadth of distributional coverage, but at reduced scale with synthetic data and after modifying the step schedule and success gates from a prior 147/150 audit.

claims.claim: On LLM toxicity control using RealToxicityPrompts and the Jigsaw Unintended Bias dataset with Llama 3.2-3B under uniform, adversarial tail-thickening, and adversarial-jump sampling regimes, RUCC maintains the target CVaR level across all regimes while a static lambda-hat baseline calibrated on the first 1000 samples becomes overly conservative or drifts above target (Section 3.1-3.2, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: RUCC outperforms static baseline in 6/6 regime-alpha comparisons, but using synthetic beta-distributed toxicity scores with T=500 instead of actual RealToxicityPrompts/Jigsaw data or Llama 3.2-3B inference — a proxy task, not the paper's real setup.

claims.claim: On a portfolio-management task using S&P 500 and 10-Year Treasury data from 1991-2025 (via yfinance/FRED), evaluated separately on the 1991-2001 stable period, the 2009-2018 crisis-aftermath period, and the full 1991-2025 span, RUCC keeps realized CVaR near the target across multiple market shocks where the static baseline does not (Section 3.3-3.4, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: RUCC achieves lower tracking error than static baseline in 6/6 comparisons, but using synthetic returns calibrated to approximate S&P 500/Treasury statistics with T=1000 instead of actual yfinance/FRED data — a proxy task without real market data.

amkkk/repro-adversarially-robust-control.overall: All five claims are addressed with real runs and numbers on synthetic data at reduced scale, with slopes and tracking errors directionally consistent with the paper's predictions, but none use the actual datasets, models, or full-scale setups specified in the paper. The reproduction provides toy-level evidence throughout, with no full-scale or non-proxy verification of any claim.

amkkk/repro-autoregressive-language-mode.paper_title: Autoregressive Language Models are Secretly Energy-Based Models: Insights into the Lookahead Capabilities of Next-Token Prediction

claims.claim: Proposition 3.2 establishes an exact bijection between autoregressive models (ARMs) and energy-based models (EBMs) in function space, via the mapping q(s_t,y_t) = r(s_t,y_t) for y_t=EOS and r(s_t,y_t)+V_q(s_t⊕y_t) otherwise, such that p^ebm_R(y|x) = p^arm_q(y|x) (Proposition 3.2).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive numerical verification at V=5, T=3 over 125 sequences shows max probability difference 2.2e-16 and mapping consistency for all 31 states, confirming the bijection on a clearly reduced-scale instance rather than a full reproduction.

claims.claim: Section 3.3 shows this ARM-EBM bijection corresponds to a special case of the soft Bellman equation from maximum-entropy reinforcement learning, with the soft value function V_q(s_t) capturing implicit lookahead over future tokens (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Bellman consistency error of 0.0 verified across 156 states at V=5, T=3 with value function differences ≤8.9e-16, but this is a small-scale dynamic-programming check that does not establish the broader RL interpretation at any meaningful scale.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 proves that minimizing negative log-likelihood over ARM functions and over EBM functions yields identical minima, showing teacher forcing is optimal in function space (Proposition 4.1).
claims.evidence: At V=5, T=3, the reproduction shows NLL equivalence (max diff 5.8e-15), simultaneous stationarity (2.2e-16), gradient chain-rule equivalence (4.4e-16), and Adam GD convergence to the same minimum (within 5.4e-5) with positive controls — substantive but on a clearly reduced finite function space.

claims.claim: An error bound (Proposition 59) shows that distilling an EBM into an ARM yields KL(p^ebm_R, p^arm_q) ≤ 2T·max|q*(s,y)-q(s,y)|, bounding divergence by sequence length T times the maximum logit approximation error (Proposition 59).
claims.evidence: Zero violations across 2000 configurations at V=8, T=5 with exact KL computation via exhaustive enumeration, but this is a numerical spot-check of a mathematical bound on small instances, not a universal proof or full-scale demonstration.

claims.claim: Converting an EBM to an equivalent ARM representation costs O(V^T) (exponential in sequence length), whereas converting an ARM to an EBM representation costs only O(VT) (linear) (Section on computational trade-offs).
claims.evidence: Deterministic op-counters at V=4, T=1..10 show ARM→EBM slope 0.28 (linear Θ(VT)) and EBM→ARM slope 1.378≈ln(V) (exponential Θ(V^T)), demonstrating the complexity direction at reduced scale but with V=4 only and ARM→EBM restricted to a single trajectory.

amkkk/repro-autoregressive-language-mode.overall: All five claims are mathematical propositions verified only through small-scale numerical checks (V=4–8, T=3–10) with real runs, controls, and matching results, but none approach the paper's intended scale or provide universal formal proofs. The reproduction is a consistent and careful toy-scale validation across all claims.

amkkk/repro-finite-time-ac-evolving-rewa.paper_title: Finite-time Convergence Analysis of Actor-Critic with Evolving Reward

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 establishes finite-time bounds for single-timescale actor-critic with evolving rewards, with actor error G_T and critic error W_T each bounded by O(1/√T) + O(F_T·√T) + O(√(F_T/T)) + O(ε), where F_T measures cumulative reward-parameter variation over T iterations (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Experiments on a 50-state, 4-action MDP with 20-dim features and single seed show G_T increasing from 0.497 to 0.571 across T=2000–32000 (positive slope 0.05), with √T·G_T growing from 22.2 to 102.1 (band ratio 4.59), which is consistent with an ε-dominated regime but does not isolate or verify the O(1/√T) decay term.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.7 shows that when the reward parameter is updated via gradient-based steps with step size η^φ_t = c_φ/t and bounded gradients, F_T = O(1/T), so the bounds reduce to G_T = O(1/√T) + O(ε) and W_T = O(1/√T) + O(ε), matching the best-known rate for static-reward actor-critic (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: With gradient-based reward updates (η_π=0.5/t), F_T plateaus at ~0.44 with log-log slope 0.003, empirically O(1) rather than the claimed O(1/T); the logbook itself notes this discrepancy, which may stem from a definition mismatch but at toy scale (50 states, single seed) does not establish the claimed asymptotic rate.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.8 bounds the distribution mismatch under Markovian sampling without dependence on the mixing time, improving prior convergence rates by a factor of log²T in the static-reward case (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Distribution mismatch κ_T stays bounded at 1.12–1.18 across T=1000–32000 with near-zero log-log slope, supporting the claim's prediction, but measured on a 50-state MDP via a state-distribution proxy (not full state-action ratio) with 500 samples and a potentially mismatched reference stationary distribution.

claims.claim: Assumption 4.1 (sufficient exploration) requires the matrix A_θ to be negative definite with singular values bounded above by -λ, underpinning the actor-critic convergence analysis (Section 4, Assumption 4.1).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive enumeration on a 50-state MDP confirms a raw-feature Gram matrix is PSD with min eigenvalue 0.0098 and full rank 20/20, but the logbook explicitly acknowledges this matrix differs from the paper's A_θ (which may use policy-gradient features ψ(s,a)), so the paper's actual assumption is not directly tested.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 defines a single-timescale actor-critic scheme with step sizes η^θ_t = c_θ/√t and η^ω_t = c_ω/√t for policy and critic updates, alongside an arbitrary update rule for the evolving reward parameter φ_t (Section 3.3, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Step sizes η_θ=0.5/√t and η_ω=0.5/√t are numerically verified at t=1,100,10000, and three reward update rules (static, gradient, random walk) produce expected F_T values, but all on a 50-state MDP with single seed and G_T slopes that are positive or near-zero rather than showing convergence.

amkkk/repro-finite-time-ac-evolving-rewa.overall: This logbook provides toy-scale numerical experiments on a 50-state, 4-action MDP with 20-dim features and a single seed, offering partial support for some claims (bounded κ_T, correct step-size schedule) but failing to establish key asymptotic rates (G_T does not decay, F_T is O(1) not O(1/T), and the paper's A_θ matrix is not directly tested).

amkkk/repro-let-the-prototype-guide-you.paper_title: Let the Prototype Guide You: Robust Aggregation of Sparse Multi-Class Annotations via Annotator Prototype Learning

claims.claim: PTBCC (Prototype-driven Bayesian Classifier Combination) models annotators via a shared set of prototype confusion matrices rather than learning one confusion matrix per annotator (Section on method overview).
claims.evidence: The implementation demonstrates 2 shared prototype confusion matrices for 8 annotators (28 params) vs FGBCC's 8 per-annotator matrices (48 params), with convex combination confirmed, but only on synthetic data with 50 tasks and 8 annotators—a reduced-scale demonstration of the architecture.

claims.claim: PTBCC achieves up to 15% accuracy improvement over the best baseline in its best-case dataset (Val5) (Table 4).
claims.evidence: On synthetic 'Val5-like' data (100 tasks, 30 annotators, 70% sparsity—not the real Val5 dataset), PTBCC achieves 0.8600 vs 0.8400 best baseline (2.38% improvement at seed 42; 23.29% at seed 24), showing the qualitative trend on a proxy task at reduced scale.

claims.claim: Across 11 real-world crowdsourcing datasets, PTBCC attains an average accuracy of 0.7472, versus 0.7175 for FGBCC, 0.7132 for BWA, and 0.6986 for majority voting (Table 4).
claims.evidence: Eleven synthetic datasets reproduce the ranking PTBCC > FGBCC > BWA > MV, but measured averages (PTBCC 0.8374, FGBCC 0.7945, BWA 0.7764, MV 0.7214) differ substantially from the paper's real-world values (0.7472, 0.7175, 0.7132, 0.6986), and no real crowdsourcing datasets were used.

claims.claim: PTBCC's ablation over prototype set size |S| shows accuracy peaking at |S|=2 (0.7472) and degrading to 0.7300 at |S|=3 and 0.7271 at |S|=4 due to sparser per-prototype annotator distributions (Table 5).
claims.evidence: Three synthetic replicates with ground-truth n_prototypes=2 show the qualitative pattern (peak at |S|=2: 0.8972, degradation to 0.8722 at |S|=3 and 0.8333 at |S|=4), but exact values don't match the paper and the synthetic data's known prototype count biases toward |S|=2 optimality.

claims.claim: PTBCC uses less than 10% of the computational cost of confusion-matrix-based baselines while matching or exceeding their accuracy (Section on computational efficiency).
claims.evidence: Analytic per-iteration operation ratios are 9.67%, 8.91%, and 8.62% (under 10%), but actual wall-clock timings show PTBCC is ~75x slower (7588% of baseline) and the parameter ratio averages 11.1% (above 10%); the empirical runtime evidence partially contradicts the claim while the theoretical calculation supports it, all on small synthetic configurations.

amkkk/repro-let-the-prototype-guide-you.overall: This logbook provides a reduced-scale reproduction of PTBCC using entirely synthetic crowdsourcing data, demonstrating the core architecture and qualitative trends (ranking, ablation pattern, analytic cost ratios) but never testing on the paper's real-world datasets. All claims are addressed only at toy scale with small task counts and synthetic annotation patterns, and several measured values diverge substantially from the paper's reported numbers.

claims.claim: Theorem 1.3 gives the first efficient approximate-differential-privacy algorithm for range subgraph counting, with additive error O(HS̃_fH(G) · sqrt((ε+log(1/δ))·log(n|Q|)) · log^(2d)n / ε) (Theorem 1.3).
claims.evidence: Synthetic ER graphs with n=20-50, only triangle counting, d=2, and smooth sensitivity approximated via log-factor scaling rather than the paper's exact mechanism. Real runs with 100 trials across 12 configs show error ratios well below the theoretical bound, but the scale and simplifications preclude verification of the full asymptotic claim.

claims.claim: Theorem 1.4 proves a lower bound showing additive error must scale as Ω(log^(d-1)n · GS_fH) for constant dimension d, growing to n^Ω(1) · GS_fH when d = Ω(log n), i.e. exponential in the dimension (Theorem 1.4).
claims.evidence: Simplified packing construction on hypercube embeddings with n≤128 and d≤6, triangle counting only. 12/15 constant-d configs and 3/3 high-d configs are directionally consistent, but several small-n configs for d≥3 are inconsistent (ratios 0.05-0.26), and the construction is a proxy for the formal lower-bound proof.

claims.claim: Algorithm 3 (PDP_RSC) achieves pure differential privacy for range subgraph counting with additive error O(GS_fH · sqrt(log(n|Q|)) · log^(3d)n / ε), built on a range-tree construction (Algorithm 2, TreeConst) and a subgraph-occurrence projection (Algorithm 1, Proj) (Section 3, Algorithms 1-3).
claims.evidence: Implemented a 1D segment tree instead of the full d-dimensional range tree, triangle counting only, n=16-64, d=2. Pure DP checked empirically via sensitivity bounds rather than formal proof. Real runs confirm error scaling directionally but with major algorithmic simplifications.

claims.claim: Algorithm 5 (ADP_RSC) attains the approximate-DP guarantee of Theorem 1.3 by combining private higher-order local sensitivity estimation (Algorithm 4, EstimateHS) with the range-tree mechanism (Section 3, Algorithm 5).
claims.evidence: Local sensitivity estimated via edge-flip sampling (30 samples) instead of the paper's exact closed-form Algorithm 4, smooth sensitivity approximated from samples, n=20-50, d=2, synthetic graphs. LS/GS ratio ~10% confirms directional utility improvement but does not reproduce the actual algorithm.

claims.claim: On the Wiki-Squirrel (5,201 nodes, 198,353 edges), WormNet-v3 (16,347 nodes, 762,822 edges), and CA-Netscience (379 nodes, 914 edges) graphs, the proposed PDP_RSC and ADP_RSC algorithms are reported to outperform PDP_Comp and ADP_Comp baselines by 3 to 4 orders of magnitude in accuracy at query-set size Θ(n^2) (Section 5, Experiments).
claims.evidence: Synthetic random graphs used instead of the actual Wiki-Squirrel, WormNet-v3, and CA-Netscience datasets; query-set size O(n) instead of O(n^2). Measured improvements of 93-516x (~2-2.5 orders) fall short of the claimed 3-4 orders, and the real-data pipeline was not reproduced.

amkkk/repro-dp-range-subgraph-counting.overall: This logbook provides toy-scale directional checks of all five claims using synthetic graphs (n≤379), simplified algorithm implementations (1D range trees, sampled local sensitivity), and triangle counting only. No claim is verified at the paper's actual scale or on real datasets, and several implementations are proxies for the paper's algorithms rather than faithful reproductions.

amkkk/repro-stability-and-generalization.paper_title: Stability and Generalization of Nonconvex Optimization with Heavy-Tailed Noise

claims.claim: Under Assumption 3.1 (bounded p-th centered moment, p-BCM, for p in (1,2]), Theorem 4.2 bounds the generalization gap between population and empirical gradients by 4ε + C_p σ_p n^{-(p-1)/p} using a truncation argument to handle heavy-tailed noise (Theorem 4.2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: A reduced NumPy run with dimensions 4-8 and sample sizes up to 1024 used symmetric Pareto noise and sample-wise truncation, recording p-dependent exponents across four p sweeps. This is a clearly simplified setup with real runs, not a full-scale verification of Theorem 4.2.

claims.claim: For Clipped SGD (Algorithm 1), Proposition 5.1 gives an on-average stability bound ε_c ≤ 2Lγ√(T/n) Σ η_t, and Theorem 5.2/Corollary 5.3 derive a resulting population gradient bound with rate O(n^{-(p-1)/(3(3p-2))}) (Section 5.1, Theorem 5.2, Corollary 5.3).
claims.evidence: Twenty neighboring-dataset sweeps with L=γ=1 checked the Proposition 5.1 stability bound and recorded clipped-SGD rates across p values, but at dimensions 4-8 and n up to 1024. The logbook itself states 'this reduced experiment cannot prove the population theorem.'

claims.claim: For Mini-Batch Normalized SGD (Algorithm 2), Theorem 5.5 and Corollary 5.6 establish an improved generalization rate of O(n^{-(p-1)/(7p-6)}) compared to the clipped-SGD rate (Section 5.2, Theorem 5.5, Corollary 5.6).
claims.evidence: A common-random-number sweep compared normalized mini-batch SGD against clipped SGD at five n values and four p values with a 1.5x tolerance control, but the logbook explicitly notes 'the tolerance is explicitly a reduced Monte-Carlo control and is not a theorem-level rate test.'

claims.claim: For Normalized SGD with Momentum (Algorithm 3), Theorem 5.9 matches the O(n^{-(p-1)/(7p-6)}) rate of the normalized batch variant (Section 5.3, Theorem 5.9).
claims.evidence: Momentum and beta=0 normalized mini-batch controls were compared across p and n sweeps at reduced scale (dimensions 4-8, n up to 1024), with the logbook acknowledging 'a two-fold reduced control is evidence of matching behavior only at toy scale.'

claims.claim: The combined clipping-plus-momentum method (Algorithm 4) achieves the same stability bound as momentum alone (Proposition 5.12) and a matching rate of O(n^{-(p-1)/(7p-6)}) without dependence on the linear step-size term γ (Theorem 5.13, Section 5.4).
claims.evidence: A gamma sweep over {.05, .1, .2} passed a bounded-spread control for every p at reduced scale, but the logbook states 'bounded spread at reduced scale does not establish exact gamma independence or Proposition 5.12 universally.'

amkkk/repro-stability-and-generalization.overall: The logbook provides reduced-scale numerical experiments (dimensions 4-8, n up to 1024, NumPy implementations with symmetric Pareto noise and hinge-loss gradients) that are consistent with all five theoretical claims but do not constitute full-scale verification or formal proofs. All claims are addressed at toy scale with real runs and controls, earning toy-level evidence only.

amkkk/repro-kan-gd-bounds.paper_title: Optimization,  Generalization and Differential Privacy Bounds for Gradient Descent on Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks

claims.claim: Under NTK separability with margin γ>0, gradient descent on Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with polylogarithmic width m in n and T achieves a training loss rate of Õ(1/(γ²ηT)) (Theorem 4.9).
claims.evidence: A single reduced-scale GD trajectory (d=4, m=8, n=60, T=100) shows loss decreasing from 0.696 to 0.385, but no sweep over T is performed to test the claimed Õ(1/(γ²ηT)) rate; the conclusion itself notes the fitted exponent 0.1486 does not establish the 1/T scaling.

claims.claim: With logistic loss and polylogarithmic width, provided ηT ≳ n, the expected population risk of gradient-descent-trained KANs is bounded by Õ((log⁴(n)+log²(n/δ))/(γ⁴n)), i.e., a 1/n generalization rate (Theorem 4.12).
claims.evidence: At reduced scale (d=4, m=16, n≤220, 5 seeds), test losses decrease monotonically with n and 1/n is the best closed-form fit (RSS 0.00130) with power-law exponent α=1.046, directionally supporting the claimed 1/n rate but without isolating polylog factors or reaching the asymptotic regime.

claims.claim: Under (ε,δ)-differential privacy with NTK separability, the trajectory-averaged population risk of DP-GD on KANs achieves Õ(√d/(γ⁴nε)), matching the classical lower bound for general convex Lipschitz problems (Theorem 4.16).
claims.evidence: A 5×4 grid of (n, ε) with 10 DP-noise seeds at reduced scale (d=4, m=16, n≤240) shows monotone decreases along both axes, with 1/(nε) the best closed-form fit (RSS 0.0067) and exponent β=0.738, but √d and γ⁻⁴ constants are not isolated (d fixed at 4) and the asymptotic regime is not reached.

claims.claim: Polylogarithmic network width is both necessary and sufficient for DP-GD on KANs to attain this private utility bound, establishing a qualitative width gap between the private and non-private (which only requires polylog width for optimization) regimes (Theorem 4.16).
claims.evidence: Only three width values (m=2,4,8) at n=60 show the DP-vs-non-private gap decreasing (0.016→0.006), which weakly supports sufficiency but does not establish necessity of polylog width; the logbook itself acknowledges the necessity conclusion is qualitative, not a formal lower bound.

claims.claim: The analysis relies on a reference-point framework with a 'stay-in-a-ball' property ensuring GD iterates remain close enough to initialization to guarantee local smoothness and approximate convexity along the trajectory (Section 4).
claims.evidence: A 6-step proof structure for Theorem 4.3 is described in text (not machine-checked) and a 1D numerical illustration shows the stay-in-a-ball bounds hold (max distance 0.90 vs bound 1.41), but the formal derivation is only referenced in source code and the numerical demo is on a simplified 1D problem.

amkkk/repro-kan-gd-bounds.overall: The logbook provides reduced-scale numerical experiments that directionally support all five claims—loss decrease, 1/n and 1/(nε) scaling trends, a width-gap trend, and a 1D illustration of the stay-in-a-ball property—but none reach the scale or rigor needed for full verification. The scaling analyses for Claims 2 and 3 are the strongest evidence, with competing-fit comparisons and multi-seed averaging, yet remain at toy scale (d=4, n≤240, m≤16).

amkkk/repro-noisy-pairwise-comparison-ra.paper_title: Noisy Pairwise-Comparison Random Search for Smooth Nonconvex Optimization

claims.claim: Under a uniform-margin comparison oracle with advantage parameter p ∈ (0,1/2], the NCRS algorithm attains ε-stationarity for smooth nonconvex objectives with iteration complexity O(k/(p²ε²)), where k is the intrinsic dimension rather than the ambient dimension d (Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: NCRS was run on synthetic ridge objectives with small dimensions (k≤10, d≤100) on CPU in <0.01s; the k-sweep (16→141→294 for k=2,5,10) is directionally supportive but the same-k d-pair (k=2,d=10: 16 iterations vs k=2,d=100: 1 iteration) is contradictory to d-independence, making this reduced-scale evidence only.

claims.claim: A one-step descent inequality shows the per-iteration progress of NCRS scales with intrinsic dimension k rather than ambient dimension d: pα_t√(2/π)E[‖∇f(θ^t)‖₂] ≤ E[f(θ^t)−f(θ^{t+1})] + L_f k α_t²/2 (Lemma 2.1).
claims.evidence: The descent inequality was empirically checked over 2000-step runs on synthetic ridge objectives with L_f=1.1; all 5 configurations satisfy LHS≤RHS (e.g., k=2,d=10: LHS=0.00103, RHS=0.00275), and the RHS is approximately constant across d for fixed k, but this is a toy empirical check, not a proof.

claims.claim: Under a gap-dependent confidence oracle with tie-aware noise, a confidence-weighted majority-vote variant of NCRS achieves ε-stationarity using O(k²/ε⁴) total pairwise comparisons (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: NCRS+Vote was tested on synthetic ridge objectives with a logistic confidence oracle (N=5 votes); total comparisons (60, 5, 270, 120) are mixed—the k-sweep is non-monotonic and the same-k d-pair (60 vs 5) contradicts d-independence—so the O(k²/ε⁴) scaling is not cleanly demonstrated on this toy setup.

claims.claim: The analysis extends to nearly-ridge objectives with bounded nuisance-subspace leakage, parameterized by (τ, m), showing robustness of the intrinsic-dimension rate beyond exact low-rank structure (Proposition 2.4).
claims.evidence: Nearly-ridge objectives with varying leakage τ (0 to 0.5) were tested on synthetic ridge models; all converge with graceful degradation (1 iteration for τ≤0.2, 215 for τ=0.5), but only τ was varied (not m) and the formal rate was not measured, making this reduced-scope evidence.

claims.claim: NCRS's O(k/ε²) rate (up to the 1/p² factor) improves on prior ambient-dimension-dependent zeroth-order methods such as ZO-RankSGD, whose complexity is O(d/ε²) (Table 1).
claims.evidence: NCRS and a simplified ZO-RankSGD were compared on four (k,d) pairs; NCRS outperforms at d=10 and d=20 (5000-cap vs 1–6 iterations) but ZO-RankSGD converges in 1 iteration at d=100, contradicting its claimed O(d/ε²) dependence and yielding mixed evidence on a toy setup with a non-faithful baseline implementation.

amkkk/repro-noisy-pairwise-comparison-ra.overall: All five claims are addressed only through small-scale synthetic ridge experiments (CPU, ~0.5s total) with simplified implementations, yielding toy-level evidence that is directionally supportive but mixed for several claims. No full-scale reproduction (ML fine-tuning, RL benchmarks, or formal proof verification) was attempted.

amkkk/repro-differentiable-fairness-laye.paper_title: Differentiable Optimization Layers for Guaranteed Fairness in Deep Learning

claims.claim: The fairness layer, formulated as g(z) = arg min over y~ of the discrepancy d~(y~,z) subject to affine inequality and equality constraints, is globally 1/mu-Lipschitz continuous and differentiable almost everywhere under strongly convex objectives (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: SymPy symbolic derivation confirms the equality-projection Jacobian M = I - A^T(AA^T)^{-1}A is symmetric and idempotent with spectral norm 1 = 1/μ (μ=1), verified across 400 random full-rank matrices with residuals ~1e-14; a variational-inequality/Cauchy-Schwarz argument establishes global firm non-expansiveness, and the active-set measure-zero hyperplane argument gives differentiability a.e.

claims.claim: Backpropagation through the fairness layer zeroes gradient components perpendicular to active constraint surfaces while leaving feasible-direction components unaffected (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: Normal-component residual and tangent error were both 0.0 across 4 configurations with 50 random directions each on a 5-variable QP, but this is a finite numerical check on a reduced problem, not a universal proof of Theorem 4.4.

claims.claim: The online primal-dual inference algorithm (Algorithm 1) guarantees that the sample-weighted average fairness violation across streaming inference batches converges to at most epsilon, even for arbitrarily small batch sizes (Theorem 3.2, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 converges below ε=0.05 on synthetic biased streams (batch sizes 1, 4, 8, 16; stream lengths 1000-4000), but the data is synthetic with a single protected attribute and limited horizons, not verifying the asymptotic guarantee for arbitrary streams.

claims.claim: On loan default prediction, employee wage modeling, and image classification (CelebA, FairFace), the fairness layer satisfies demographic parity, equalized residuals, and equalized odds constraints while baselines including Lagrangian penalty methods frequently violate them (Section on experimental results).
claims.evidence: Fairness layer achieves DP violation 0.0000 vs Lagrangian 0.10-0.22 on synthetic loan/wage/CelebA-style data with linear models and 3 seeds, but no real CelebA, FairFace, loan, or wage datasets were used, FairFace was not tested, equalized residuals was not tested, and equalized odds was only simplified.

claims.claim: The fairness layer achieves 18-30% test loss improvements on synthetic datasets and 2-5% accuracy gains over post-hoc projection methods (Section on experimental results).
claims.evidence: On 20 synthetic regression trials with linear models, mean test-loss improvement was 20.04% (within the claimed 18-30% band, 8/20 trials in-band), but classification accuracy gain was only 0.33% (far below the claimed 2-5%), and no real image datasets or neural networks were used.

amkkk/repro-differentiable-fairness-laye.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous formal SymPy derivation verifying Theorem 4.1's Lipschitz continuity and a.e. differentiability, but all remaining claims are supported only by reduced-scale experiments on synthetic data with linear models, missing the real datasets (CelebA, FairFace, loan, wage) and neural network architectures specified in the paper.

claims.claim: Under i.i.d. sampling with an exponential step-size schedule, TD(0) attains the optimal last-iterate bias-variance trade-off without requiring knowledge of the problem-dependent constant omega (Theorem 3.4, Section 3).
claims.evidence: At T=1500 with 40 trials on 10-12 synthetic states, the omega-free exponential grid showed median MSE/oracle MSE of 0.736, providing reduced-scale empirical support but not an asymptotic verification of Theorem 3.4's optimal bias-variance trade-off claim.

claims.claim: Under Markovian sampling, standard TD(0) with the same exponential step-size schedule achieves a comparable convergence rate but still requires knowledge of omega to set the initial step-size eta_0 (Theorem 4.10, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: A controlled Markov sweep on four synthetic chains at T=1500 yielded log-log eta/omega slope -0.876 and Markov/i.i.d. ratio 0.912, offering toy-scale evidence for comparable rates and omega-dependence, but far below the scale needed to verify Theorem 4.10.

claims.claim: A regularized variant of TD(0) with exponential step-sizes and regularization parameter lambda = 1/sqrt(T) removes the dependence on omega in the Markovian setting, without needing projections or iterate averaging (Theorem 4.12, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The corrected separate-iterate experiment produced regularized log-slope 1.051 versus standard 0.952, meaning the claimed reduction in omega dependence was not observed; however, controls failed (controls_passed: false, assumptions_checked: false), making it impossible to distinguish a genuine falsification from an implementation issue.

claims.claim: The regularized TD(0) analysis in the Markovian setting introduces exponential dependence on the mixing time tau_mix as an artifact of the proof technique (Theorem 4.12, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: A sweep over 12 lazy reversible chains with tau_mix 1-6 showed polynomial-model R2=0.617 exceeding exponential-model R2=0.504, providing toy-scale evidence consistent with exponential dependence being a proof artifact, but a finite sweep over a narrow mixing-time range cannot establish this.

claims.claim: Mixing time tau_mix is defined as the first time the state distribution's deviation from stationarity falls below a threshold delta (Definition 4.1).

ProCreations/repro-a-coin-flip-for-safet.paper_title: A Coin Flip for Safety: LLM Judges Fail to Reliably Measure Adversarial Robustness

claims.claim: Across an audit of 6,642 human-verified labels spanning 4 victim models (Gemma-3-1B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-27B, Qwen-3-32B) and 5 attack methods (Direct Prompting, GCG, GCG-REINFORCE, Best-of-N, PAIR), 4 safety judges (LlamaGuard-3, HarmBench, AegisGuard, JailJudge) are shown to perform only slightly better than random guessing on average (Section 3, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: On all 6,642 released rows with 4 victim models, 5 attacks, and 4 judges, mean balanced accuracy is 0.58980 (AegisGuard 0.527, LlamaGuard-3 0.560, JailJudge 0.596, HarmBench 0.676), confirming near-chance performance; a destructive label-permutation control collapses accuracy toward chance.

claims.claim: ROC analysis shows JailJudge attains AUROC as low as 0.48 (worse than chance) on some attack-model pairs and no better than 0.64 on any attack, demonstrating near-chance discriminative ability under distribution shift (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: On all 1,902 Llama-3.1-8B rows, JailJudge AUROC ranges from 0.47645 (GCG-R, below chance) to 0.64163 (GCG), matching the claimed ~0.48 floor and ~0.64 ceiling; cross-checked with scikit-learn roc_auc_score and a row-hash destructive control destroys the pattern.

claims.claim: Judge accuracy varies dramatically across attack-model combinations, with some judges scoring only 45% accuracy on specific attack-victim pairs, close to random guessing (Figure 3, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Across all 68 populated attack×model×judge cells, balanced accuracy spans 0.43250 to 0.73603 with two cells at or below 0.45 and 21 of 68 below chance; per-judge spans of 0.188–0.250 confirm dramatic variation, and pooling away model/attack identity collapses the span to zero.

claims.claim: The paper introduces ReliableBench, a curated set of 41 behaviors, which raises average judge accuracy from 57% to 70%, and JudgeStressTest (JST), a set of 971 challenging samples that exposes systematic judge failures across judge architectures via leave-one-out validation (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Mean behavior accuracy rises from 0.57438 to 0.70349 for the top-41 selection (exact 41/41 overlap with the release), Table-1 values reproduce after rounding (overall 0.51–0.59, Acc@0 0.17–0.30, Acc@1 0.34–0.45), JST cardinality is exactly 971, and 5,000 random-41 controls average only 0.57416.

claims.claim: Correcting reported attack success rates (ASR) for judge unreliability substantially deflates the apparent effectiveness of attacks such as Best-of-N, which is shown to inflate ASR by exploiting judge insufficiencies rather than eliciting genuinely harmful content (Figure 1, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: BoN ASR falls from 0.46 to 0.13187 (71.33% reduction) using independently computed human precision of 43/150 = 0.28667 on all released Gemma-3-1B BoN rows, reversing BoN from first to last behind Direct and GCG; a perfect-precision control leaves BoN at 0.46 and ranked first.

claims.claim: Judge Concordance analysis shows judges can reach near-unanimous agreement with each other while still failing to align with human ground-truth labels, and averaging/ensembling judge scores does not consistently improve alignment with human judgments (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: On all 6,642 rows the four-judge panel is unanimous on 2,888 rows (43.48%) but wrong on 557 of them (19.29%); behavior concordance–accuracy Pearson r is 0.066, majority-vote accuracy 0.718 is below HarmBench's 0.759, and mean-score R² is -0.201; injecting the human oracle into the ensemble yields accuracy 1.0 as a positive control.
