ai-sherpa/brain-alignment-convergent-evo.paper_title: Alignment between Brains and AI: Evidence for Convergent Evolution across Modalities, Scales and Training Trajectories

claims.claim: Brain alignment correlates with task performance more strongly for language models (Pearson r=0.89, p<7.5×10⁻¹³, on LLM Leaderboard 2 performance) than for vision models (Pearson r=0.53, p<2.0×10⁻⁴⁴, on ImageNet accuracy) (Figure 1d-e, Table 1).
claims.evidence: Independent computation on 36 language and 594 vision models from released parquets yields language r=0.8743 (p=3.25e-12) vs vision r=0.5305 (p=2.03e-44), confirming the qualitative claim that language alignment correlates far more strongly with performance than vision; the 0.016 gap from the paper's 0.89 is transparently acknowledged and the vision r matches to 4 decimal places, with a permutation control collapsing both to near-zero.

claims.claim: For language models, a logarithmic fit between brain alignment and performance (R²=0.80) outperforms a linear fit (R²=0.78), with individual benchmark correlations ranging r=0.66–0.84 (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Independent curve fitting on 36 language models yields log R²=0.8004 (paper: 0.80) exceeding linear R²=0.7645 (paper: 0.78), with six component benchmark correlations ranging r=0.684–0.816 (paper: 0.66–0.84), and permutation control collapsing R² to 0.022.

claims.claim: Layer-wise analysis shows vision models exhibit progressively increasing brain alignment with network depth, whereas language models peak in brain alignment at middle layers (3/8 to 5/8 normalized depth), with deeper vision layers converging toward language-model-like organization (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Vision per-bin median alignment rises monotonically across all 8 depth bins (Spearman ρ=1.0 in all 4 subjects, peak at deepest bin); language peaks at bin 3/8 (0-indexed) for all 4 subjects, within the claimed 3/8–5/8 window; cross-modal deep-vs-shallow vision-to-language-middle contrast is positive in all 4 subjects (0.0007–0.008), small but directionally universal.

claims.claim: Across Pythia model checkpoints, brain alignment stabilizes by approximately 10% of training tokens for language models, while vision models show a sharp early increase in alignment reaching about 85% of maximum by 20% of training samples, indicating alignment emerges before performance gains (Figure 3, Pythia correlations r=0.73–0.95).
claims.evidence: At 11.2% of training, all 8 Pythia alignment trajectories are 0.933–1.090× their later median (CV≤0.073) while performance gain fraction is only 0.764 median; vision early alignment reaches 0.950 of eventual max; Pythia alignment-performance r range for the paper's 6-model Figure-3 set is 0.7345–0.9505, matching the claimed 0.73–0.95, with transparent reporting that 6.9b/12b models fall outside this range.

claims.claim: Kernel-size (spatial scale) analysis shows brain alignment decreases at larger scales in primary visual areas V1, V2, V3 (Δ=−5.30, −2.81, −1.05) while increasing in limbic regions such as orbitofrontal cortex (Δ=+1.56), with sign consistency of 0.83 across subjects (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Independent computation from the official 11-kernel CSV yields V1=−5.228, V2=−2.839, V3=−1.097, OFC=+1.549 (paper: −5.30, −2.81, −1.05, +1.56), all signs matching and all within 0.5 of stated values; mean sign consistency across 180 regions is 0.8125 (paper: 0.83); multi-scale slopes confirm directional divergence.

claims.claim: Inter-subject consistency of alignment scores is very high for both language models (r=0.997–1.000) and vision models (r=0.970–0.999), supporting a shared, near-universal organizational principle underlying brain-model correspondence (Tables 2–3).
claims.evidence: Pairwise Pearson correlations of per-model whole-brain alignment vectors across all 6 subject pairs yield language r=0.9997–0.9999 and vision r=0.9975–0.9998, both within the paper's stated ranges (0.997–1.000 and 0.970–0.999 respectively), with permutation control collapsing max |r| to 0.257.

ai-sherpa/brain-alignment-convergent-evo.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous independent statistical reproduction of all six claims from the paper's own released precomputed alignment data (90M+ rows), with SHA-256-verified source files, genuine from-scratch numpy/scipy computations, unit tests of statistical primitives, and destructive controls. While it does not regenerate model activations or rerun the GPU alignment pipeline, the claims being verified are statistical claims about correlations, fits, and patterns in the released data, and the measured numbers land within a few percent of the paper's stated values in every case.

AITrailblazer/repro-cocoreviewbench-comp.paper_title: CoCoReviewBench: A Completeness- and Correctness-Oriented Benchmark for AI Reviewers

claims.claim: CoCoReviewBench curates 3,900 papers from ICLR (2017-2025) and NeurIPS (2021-2024), building category-specific benchmark subsets across a two-level taxonomy of 23 subcategories under 5 top-level categories (Quality, Clarity, Significance, Originality, Policy) (Section 3, Section 3.1, Appendix A).
claims.evidence: The logbook independently inspected 13 frozen venue/year JSONL files (ICLR 2017–2025, NeurIPS 2021–2024), each containing exactly 300 records, totaling 3,900 unique paper IDs, and found exactly 23 non-N/A subcategories under 5 top-level category prefixes, directly matching the paper's stated scale and taxonomy.

claims.claim: A single human reviewer covers on average only 3.03 of 5 top-level categories and 5.10 of 23 subcategories per paper; aggregating all reviewers for a paper raises coverage to 3.98 top-level categories and 9.23 of 23 subcategories (an 81% relative improvement in subcategory coverage over a single reviewer), yet aggregated subcategory coverage is still only about 40% (Section 3.1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Using a paper-consistent denominator of 14,098 reviews, the logbook recomputes single-reviewer coverage as 3.0311 top-level / 5.0987 subcategory and aggregate coverage as 3.9800 / 9.2341, yielding an 81.11% relative improvement and 40.15% absolute subcategory coverage, matching the paper's 3.03, 5.10, 3.98, 9.23, 81%, and 40% figures.

claims.claim: Treating reviewer-author and inter-reviewer discussions plus the meta-review as expert adjudication signals, incorrectness is identified via inter-reviewer conflicts in 22.13% of papers (7.63% of reviews) and via reviewer-author conflicts in 75.72% of papers (36.76% of reviews); over 13% of submissions show a score gap of 4 or more between the highest and lowest overall reviewer scores (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook recomputes from released annotations: inter-reviewer conflicts in 863/3,900 papers (22.13%) and 1,075/14,098 reviews (7.63%), reviewer-author conflicts in 2,953/3,900 papers (75.72%) and 5,182/14,098 reviews (36.76%), and 526/3,900 papers (13.49%) with a reviewer score gap ≥4, all matching the paper's stated percentages.

claims.claim: CoCoReviewBench is the only benchmark among compared peer-review resources (PeerRead, MReD, NLPeer, SEA, ReviewMT, Re2, Aspects, RottenReviews, GRE-bench, RevUtil) to simultaneously support atomic opinions, fine-grained labels, category-level evaluation, rebuttal signal, meta signal, conflict detection, and incorrect annotation (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook performed an independent feature audit of 11 hash-pinned primary sources against 7 predeclared explicit-support definitions, reconstructing the full 11×7 Boolean matrix with all 77/77 cells matching the paper's Table 1; CoCoReviewBench scores 7/7 while no comparator exceeds 3/7, confirming the exclusivity claim.

claims.claim: Analysis on CoCoReviewBench shows AI reviewers remain limited in correctness and thoroughness relative to humans, are prone to hallucinations, and that reasoning models are more effective reviewers than non-reasoning approaches because they better substantiate their critiques (Abstract, Section 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states no model call, GPU run, or paid inference was performed for the AI-reviewer comparison, and C5 remains entirely unevaluated with no experimental evidence presented.

AITrailblazer/repro-cocoreviewbench-comp.overall: The logbook provides rigorous deterministic verification of claims C1–C4 by independently recomputing benchmark statistics from released data files and auditing primary sources with hash-pinning, but claim C5 (AI reviewer evaluation) is entirely unaddressed because no model-based experiments were run.

snaykey/repro-behavior-cloning-aq.paper_title: Understanding Behavior Cloning with Action Quantization

claims.claim: Behavior cloning with quantized actions and log-loss is proven to achieve sample complexity matching known lower bounds, up to the quantization error term (Theorem 2, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: On a scalar MDP with stochastic softmax expert, the logbook measures squared Hellinger decay with log-log slope -0.915 (target -1) and TV slope -0.509 (target -0.5) across n=50–3200, with n·D_H² roughly constant (4.1→5.9), confirming the √(log|Π|/n) rate that matches the known lower bound, and regret stays under the Theorem 2 bound at every n.

claims.claim: Under Probabilistic Incremental Input-to-State Stability (P-IISS) of the dynamics and Relaxed Total Variation Continuity (RTVC) of the expert policy, the regret bound has only polynomial (not exponential) dependence on the horizon H with respect to quantization error epsilon_q (Theorem 3, Definition 3, Definition 4, Section 3.1-3.2).
claims.evidence: Sweeping H∈{2..64}, the stable system (λ=0.6, P-IISS) shows polynomial regret (log-log slope 1.177, tail exponential rate 0.02242≈0) while the unstable system (λ=1.5) shows exponential compounding (tail rate 0.4055 = log 1.5 exactly, with regret 7×10^10 at H=64), directly demonstrating the Theorem 3 dichotomy.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 shows that without a smoothness assumption on the quantizer, non-smooth quantizers can incur regret of order H*Omega(1) even though their in-distribution one-step error is only O(epsilon_q) (Theorem 6, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Implementing the paper's exact arctan construction (A=0.2, B=0.3, H=200, 20000 MC trajectories), the in-distribution error stays at 3.668·ε_q (flat across ε_q=0.02–0.08) while deployment regret/H is 0.48–0.66 (bounded away from 0), and regret/(H·ε_q) grows from 6.0 to 33.0 as ε_q shrinks, confirming H·Ω(1) regret despite O(ε_q) one-step error.

claims.claim: Theorem 7 proves that model-based data augmentation improves the horizon dependence to H*[sqrt(log|Pi|/n) + epsilon_q] without requiring the policy smoothness (RTVC) assumption (Theorem 7, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: On the same non-smooth arctan instance where plain BC gives regret 58.72 (H·Ω(1)), Algorithm 1's model-based augmentation yields regret 9.4582 (≈H·ε_q floor of 4.0, ratio 2.365), a 6.2× improvement, with the statistical term flat at the ε_q floor as n grows, all without any RTVC assumption.

claims.claim: Information-theoretic lower bounds (Theorems 8-9) establish that regret must scale at least as H*(1/n + epsilon_q) for deterministic experts and H*(sqrt(1/n) + epsilon_q) for stochastic experts, matching the achievable upper bounds (Section 5, Theorems 8-9).
claims.evidence: Constructed Le Cam two-point instances yield minimax lower bound log-log slopes of -1.0 (deterministic, H/n rate) and -0.497 (stochastic, H/√n rate) across n=30–3000, and the coupled instances produce identical quantized data (quant_data_indistinguishable=True), forcing the additive H·ε_q term regardless of n.

claims.claim: Empirically, binning quantizers are shown to preserve policy smoothness better than learned quantizers, while deterministic experts more often violate the RTVC requirement needed for the sharp regret bound (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Across 60k state pairs at scales 0.05 down to 0.0008, the binning quantizer has RTVC violation rate 0.0 and sup jump 0.1 ≤ ε'=0.15, while the learned quantizer has a persistent sup jump of 0.7 ≫ ε' at every scale, and the raw deterministic expert has transport cost 1.0 at scale 10⁻⁶, confirming binning preserves RTVC while learned quantizers and deterministic experts violate it.

snaykey/repro-behavior-cloning-aq.overall: The logbook constructs the paper's own theorem instances (scalar arctan MDPs, Le Cam two-point lower bound constructions, binning vs. learned quantizers) and numerically measures the exact quantities each theorem predicts, with rates matching targets closely (e.g., slopes -0.915 vs -1, -1.0 vs -1, -0.497 vs -0.5) and key contrasts clearly demonstrated (polynomial vs exponential, O(ε_q) vs H·Ω(1), binning vs learned). All six claims are supported by concrete experimental evidence on non-toy setups appropriate for a theory paper.

snaykey/repro-amortized-vi-pll.paper_title: Amortized Variational Inference for Partial-Label Learning: A Probabilistic Approach to Label Disambiguation

claims.claim: ViPll models the posterior P(Y|X,S) over true labels using a Dirichlet variational distribution whose parameters are output by an amortized inference network, factorizing the generative process as P(Y)P(X|Y)P(S|X,Y) instead of the standard discriminative formulation (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook independently implements the amortized Dirichlet posterior q(y|x,s)=Dir(alpha) with alpha=softplus(f_phi(x,s))+1, the generative factorization P(Y)P(X|Y)P(S|X,Y), and the reverse-KL/beta-ELBO objective, with numerical evidence showing the objective L=-beta-ELBO decreases from 88.65 to 81.98 on sklearn digits, confirming the structural claim about the model formulation.

claims.claim: ViPll incorporates a conditional variational autoencoder to model P(X|Y) (Section 4.2) and a maximum-entropy prior satisfying candidate-label-set constraints (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: The CVAE for P(X|Y) is implemented with Gaussian encoder/decoder and closed-form KL, with reconstruction loss decreasing from 59.89 to 24.39 and closed-form KL matching a 2000-sample MC estimate to 0.9% relative error; the max-entropy prior achieves entropy ratio 1.000 and satisfies both lower- and upper-bound candidate-set constraints.

claims.claim: Training proceeds in three phases: initialization, a 500-epoch CVAE warm-up, and a 1000-epoch main training loop using Monte Carlo sampling (Section 4.5).
claims.evidence: All three training phases (initialization, CVAE warm-up, main MC loop) are implemented with correct structure and MC samples b=b'=10 matching the paper, but epoch counts are scaled down 10x from 500/1000 to 50/100, so the specific epoch counts asserted in the claim are not reproduced.

claims.claim: On 5 real-world partial-label datasets, ViPll attains 76.15% (+/-1.56) accuracy on Bird-song and 78.52% (+/-2.27) on Lost, outperforming 9 baselines including PlKnn, Proden, PiCO, and CroSel on the majority of settings (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The 5 real-world datasets (Bird-song, Lost, etc.) with BLIP2 features were not used; sklearn digits served as a proxy. ViPll peak accuracy was 0.907, below PRODEN-lite (0.939) and PL-KNN (0.933), so the ranking claim was not reproduced and the specific accuracy figures (76.15%, 78.52%) were never tested.

claims.claim: On synthetic partial-label benchmarks, ViPll reaches 96.64% (+/-3.92) accuracy on CIFAR-10 and 77.76% (+/-0.51) on CIFAR-100 (Table 3).
claims.evidence: CIFAR-10/100 with BLIP2 features were not used; separable Gaussian blobs served as a proxy for CIFAR-10 where ViPll reached 100% accuracy, and CIFAR-100 was not attempted at all. The specific claimed numbers (96.64%, 77.76%) were never directly tested.

claims.claim: An ablation removing the modeling of Markov equivalence in the generative structure causes significant accuracy degradation, validating the choice of generative modeling (Section 4, ablation study).
claims.evidence: A controlled ablation was run on sklearn digits comparing generative ViPll (0.772) vs discriminative ablation (0.885), finding the ablation is 11.3 points better—the opposite of the paper's claim—but this is on a simplified proxy dataset with reduced training, not the paper's actual experimental setup, so it cannot constitute a full falsification.

snaykey/repro-amortized-vi-pll.overall: The logbook provides a faithful independent re-implementation of ViPll's core architectural components (Dirichlet posterior, CVAE, max-entropy prior, three-phase training structure), verifying the structural claims 1-2, but all performance and ranking claims (4-6) are tested only on small proxy datasets (sklearn digits, Gaussian blobs) with 10x-reduced training epochs, where ViPll fails to outperform baselines and the ablation result contradicts the paper.

snaykey/repro-magnitude-distance.paper_title: Magnitude Distance: A Geometric Measure of Dataset Similarity

claims.claim: Magnitude distance is defined as d_Mag^t(X,Y) = 2·Mag_{X∪Y}(t) − Mag_X(t) − Mag_Y(t), with a tunable scale parameter t that governs sensitivity to global structure (small t) versus finer local structure (large t) (Section on Definition, Magnitude Distance).
claims.evidence: The definition is implemented directly from Def 3.1-3.2/4.2 with two independent algebraic forms agreeing to 3.02e-14; Fig 1 protocol (D=100, n=200, N(0,I) vs N(μ,I)) shows monotone increase in mean shift and normalized distance converging to 1 (0.967 at μ=2), with small-t/global vs large-t/local behavior confirmed by concrete numbers.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 shows magnitude distance is symmetric and non-negative, satisfies identity of indiscernibles only up to magnitude equivalence, and does not satisfy the triangle inequality in R^D for D>1 (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Symmetry confirmed to 3.55e-15 over 300 random pairs, non-negativity (min 0.0886≥0), self-distance 2.99e-12≈0, and a deterministic triangle-inequality counterexample in D>1 with positive slack up to +8.02 (D=500), while the D=1 control holds (worst slack −2.23e-3≤0 over 4000 triples).

claims.claim: Theorem 5.3 shows magnitude distance converges to 0 as t→0 and converges to the cardinality of the symmetric difference of the two datasets as t→∞ (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: Constructed sets with |X∆Y|=9 yield d(t=1e-4)=1.33e-3→0 and d(t=60)=9.0000 exactly matching the symmetric difference cardinality, with monotone convergence across the full t-grid from 1e-4 to 60.

claims.claim: Figure 2 shows magnitude distance remains discriminative in dimensions exceeding 1000, in settings where MMD's discriminative power collapses (Section on High-Dimensional Behavior, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: MMD (Gaussian σ=1) collapses to identically 0 by D≈50 (SNR 24.1→0.0) while magnitude distance with adaptive t=1/√D remains strictly positive and shift-ordered through D=1000 (shifted 0.0467 > null 0.0457, SNR=0.44). The core contrast—MMD degenerate, magnitude still discriminative—is reproduced, though the logbook honestly notes magnitude SNR also decays at extreme D.

claims.claim: MagGN, a generative model trained with a multi-scale magnitude-distance loss, achieves an 11.97x training speedup over WGAN on MNIST while producing visually competitive samples (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Only 30 generator updates on CPU (vs 500 epochs on L40S GPU), measured 2.64× speedup (not 11.97×), against WGAN-GP rather than vanilla WGAN, and 'visually competitive samples' explicitly not verified. The critic-free mechanism is demonstrated on real MNIST but at drastically reduced scale and scope.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.5 proves magnitude distance has bounded outlier sensitivity, changing by only about 6-10% under significant outlier addition compared to a 17.6% change for Wasserstein distance in the same setting (Section 5, Theorem 5.5).
claims.evidence: The bound 0≤d≤2|X∪Y| holds (max ratio 0.50<1 over 120 pairs), and on the Fig 4 outlier protocol magnitude distance changes by 1.90%/5.46% (t=20/t=5) vs 21.4% for Wasserstein, reproducing the claimed ordering (mag≪Wasserstein, decreasing in t) though absolute magnitude percentages are below the paper's 6.85%/10.29% due to a different outlier configuration.

snaykey/repro-magnitude-distance.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous clean-room reproduction of the mathematical definitions, theorems, and discriminability experiments with concrete numerical evidence for five of six claims. The MagGN speedup claim (Claim 5) is only addressed at drastically reduced CPU scale with a different baseline, yielding 2.64× instead of 11.97× and no sample-quality evaluation.

claims.claim: The paper defines a Safe KL divergence with a bounded-density constraint (Definition 2.1, Equations 3-4) whose induced approximation to LogSumExp satisfies F_ρ − O(ρ) ≤ F ≤ F_ρ (Proposition 2.4, Section 2).
claims.evidence: On 35 configurations (5 random 200-dim instances × 7 ρ values), the logbook measured F_ρ ≤ F with gap F − F_ρ ≤ ρ on every config (gap/ρ ∈ [0.057, 0.191], linear slope 0.112), and confirmed the bounded-density constraint max_i dν*/dµ < 1/ρ on every instance.

claims.claim: The rescaled SoftPlus-based conjugate of the Safe KL function is proven to be ρ-strongly convex, with its own conjugate being (1/ρ)-smooth (Lemma 2.7, Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: Finite-difference second derivatives measured min f_ρ'' = 4ρ ≥ ρ (confirming ρ-strong convexity) and max f*_ρ'' = 1/(4ρ) ≤ 1/ρ (confirming (1/ρ)-smoothness) across ρ ∈ {0.5, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001}, with Legendre conjugacy error < 3e-4.

claims.claim: The approximation family is shown to bound and connect to the CVaR functional, recovering CVaR and LogSumExp as limiting cases (Proposition 2.6, Section 2.1).
claims.evidence: On 4000 samples, F_ρ → LogSumExp as ρ → 0 (error decreasing monotonically from 0.115 to 1e-5) and λF_ρ(φ/λ) → CVaR_ρ as λ → 0 (relative error < 5% at λ=0.01), with the gap shrinking linearly in λ (slope 0.788).

claims.claim: In continuous entropy-regularized optimal transport experiments with regularization ε=0.01, the proposed semi-dual formulation (Equations 14-15) avoids the numerical overflow issues of the baseline and reaches a converged objective in roughly 10^4 iterations (Figure 2, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Overflow thresholds reproduced exactly (float64: z≥7.10, float32: z≥0.89); on a 4096-sample 2-D OT problem with ε=0.01 and the paper's MLP architecture, the baseline raw-exp semi-dual overflows to NaN at iteration 126 while the SoftPlus surrogate converges by iteration 1500 within the 10^4-iteration budget.

claims.claim: In KL-regularized distributionally robust optimization on California Housing, the proposed method converges with a stepsize of η=10⁻⁴ across batch sizes of 10, 100, and 1000, whereas the baseline requires a much smaller η=10⁻⁶ at batch size 10 (Figure 3, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: On the real California Housing dataset with the paper's objective, the proposed method diverges at η=1e-4 for batch size 10 (contradicting the specific claim), while the general direction is supported at batch sizes 100 and 1000 (100× stepsize gap at |D|=100, objective 8.30 vs 25.9 at |D|=1000); the specific batch-size-10 claim is not reproduced.

claims.claim: In unbalanced optimal-transport-based DRO on MNIST with label noise, the proposed approach (Equation 22) converges faster than the baseline (Equation 21) using η=10⁻⁴ versus the baseline's required η=10⁻⁵ (Figure 4, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Using sklearn load_digits (1797 8×8 images) as a proxy for MNIST, the proposed SoftPlus method is stable at η=1e-2 while the baseline raw-exp overflows at η≥1e-4 (max stable η=1e-7), and accuracy rises from 0.099 to 0.905 under 25% label noise; however, the dataset is a scaled-down proxy rather than MNIST at the paper's scale.

snaykey/repro-logsumexp-opt.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence verifying the three theoretical claims (Safe-KL bound, strong convexity/smoothness, CVaR connection) on non-trivial instances, and reproduces the overflow mechanism and convergence behavior for the eOT experiment. The two DRO experiments use reduced-scale setups (real dataset but partial claim failure for CalHousing; 8×8 digit proxy for MNIST), yielding partial reproductions of the stepsize-advantage claims.

snaykey/repro-multinomial-logit-design.paper_title: Optimal Design for Multinomial Logit Model with Applications to Best Assortment Identification

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 gives a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) reformulation of the linear maximization oracle (LMO) needed for optimal design in the multinomial logit (MNL) model (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: On 20 random instances (N∈[6,9], K=3, d=5), the Charnes-Cooper reformulation objective matched brute-force enumeration exactly (to 1e-8) on all instances, and a valid relaxation upper bound bracketed the optimum on every instance, confirming the exact compact MILP reformulation.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 establishes a stopping/approximation guarantee for a lifted Frank-Wolfe algorithm that solves the MNL optimal design problem without requiring exact LMO calls (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: On 6 random instances, the lifted FW design's G-optimality g(π̂) (4.1–5.1) stayed below the certified bound 2(1+ε_lift)(1+ε)d (25–41) on all 6, and the Kiefer-Wolfowitz equivalence g(π*)≈d=5 was confirmed (values 5.3–5.5), numerically supporting Theorem 3.5's guarantee.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 shows the proposed best assortment identification algorithm achieves sample complexity O~(d log(N/δ)(1/Δmin² + 1/(κΔmin)) + T0), where d is the feature dimension, N is the number of arms/assortments, and Δmin is the minimum reward gap (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: The full BSI-MNL algorithm was implemented and returned the correct assortment in 93.8% of 32 runs (near the 1−δ=0.95 target), and stopping time qualitatively grew with N and shrinking Δmin, but heavy right-censoring at a 3000-sample cap prevented any quantitative verification of the O~(d log(N/δ)(1/Δmin² + 1/(κΔmin)) + T0) rate.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.5 shows that using the lifted G-optimal design in place of the MILP-based design multiplies the sample complexity by a factor of only (1+ε_lift), while remaining computationally tractable (Corollary 4.5).
claims.evidence: Paired comparison of lifted vs. exact-oracle design on N=10, K=3 instances yielded only 2 uncensored pairs (ratios 1.00 and 1.76, mean 1.38), with 6 of 8 pairs censored at the sample cap—too few data points to quantitatively confirm the (1+ε_lift) multiplier, though directionally consistent.

claims.claim: Table 1 reports average LMO runtime comparisons across methods (MILP vs. lifted surrogate) for varying problem sizes (Table 1).
claims.evidence: All 12 combinatorial size entries C(N,K) were reproduced with zero error (up to C(200,5)=2.5B), the lifted LMO runtime was near-constant (~0.1–0.3 ms across all sizes), and brute-force oracle runtime grew with C(N,K) until infeasible, reproducing Table 1's qualitative structure; the MILP column was substituted with brute-force due to lack of Gurobi.

claims.claim: Figure 1 reports the average stopping time τ of the best assortment identification algorithm as N (number of arms) is varied over {30, 50, 100, 200} and K (assortment size) over {3, 4, 5}, using feature dimension d=5 and failure probability δ=0.05 (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The BSI-MNL stopping time was measured on a scaled-down grid (N∈{8,10,12,15}, K=3 only) versus the paper's N∈{30,50,100,200}, K∈{3,4,5}; τ increased with N (1658→~2700), reproducing the qualitative trend, but 6/8 runs were censored at the 3000 cap for N≥10, making absolute values non-comparable to the paper's Figure 1.

snaykey/repro-multinomial-logit-design.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical verification for the design-side theoretical claims (Theorems 3.3, 3.5, and Table 1) with exact matching and bound-checking on real instances, while the bandit-side claims (Theorem 4.4, Corollary 4.5, Figure 1) are only addressed at toy scale due to sample-cap censoring and significantly reduced problem sizes.

ai-sherpa/sosmc-particle-optimisation-re.paper_title: Efficient Stochastic Optimisation via Sequential Monte Carlo

claims.claim: The Sequential Optimization via SMC (SOSMC) framework replaces expensive inner MCMC sampling loops with a sequential Monte Carlo particle population that is reused and reweighted across optimization iterations, as formalized in Algorithm 1 (Section 3.1, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: 10,000-particle from-scratch implementation of Algorithm 1 with independent gradient reconstruction via central finite differences yielding L2-relative error 1.97e-10; negative control (fresh uncorrelated population) breaks the estimate by 56.8%, confirming particle continuity is load-bearing.

claims.claim: Proposition 2 establishes a linear convergence rate for the idealized SOSMC iteration under mu-Polyak-Lojasiewicz and L-smooth loss assumptions, showing l(theta_k) - inf(l) <= (1-gamma*mu)^k * (l(theta_0) - inf(l)) for step size gamma <= 1/L (Proposition 2).
claims.evidence: SymPy machine-checked one-step descent+PL certificate with symbolic residual exactly 0; exhaustive rational grid of 1,728 instances with 0 violations; negative controls (γ>1/L and μ=0) correctly break the guarantee as predicted.

claims.claim: Propositions 3 and 4 show the effective sample size of the SMC weights decays exponentially in the squared gradient norm and step size, ESS_infinity(gamma) = N*exp(-gamma^2*||grad l||^2) for Gaussian targets, motivating an adaptive step-size/resampling scheme (Section 4.2, Propositions 3-4).
claims.evidence: SymPy-derived chi² identity from direct Gaussian integral matching Eq. 19 exactly; Monte Carlo verification across dims 1/2/5/11 with 400K samples each yields max 1.68% relative error; unequal-covariance negative control rejected with 82–98% error, confirming scope limitation.

claims.claim: On Langevin reward-tuning of energy-based models with non-differentiable reward functions, SOSMC-ULA outperforms the ImpDiff baseline and achieves reduced variance compared to single-chain SOUL (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: 10,000 particles, 10 seeds, 4 settings (including non-differentiable indicator rewards and 10-D state): SOSMC-ULA exceeds ImpDiff mean terminal reward in 4/4 settings (Welch t=87–236) and has lower run-to-run std than single-chain SOUL in 4/4 settings (1.1×–140×); terminal quality scored by independent 400K-sample oracle.

claims.claim: On 2D EBM benchmark datasets, SOSMC achieves higher objective values than ImpDiff for small regularization strengths, with particle-based reward estimates that track true expectations throughout optimization (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: 10,000 particles, 500 iterations, 5 seeds across 3 real 2D benchmarks × 4 small-β values: SOSMC higher best-attained objective in 11/12 cells (12th a tie inside seed noise), better exact-expectation tracking in 12/12 (1.8×–49× lower RMSE), and large-β objectives comparable in all 6 contrast cells; disclosed weakness that final-iterate metric favors SOSMC in only 5/12 cells is transparently reported.

claims.claim: On MNIST, SOSMC remains robust in high dimensions even under mismatch between the pretraining and tuning kernels, without exhibiting reward hacking (Section 5.3).
claims.evidence: Neural EBM trained on real MNIST via PCD (2,000 updates), 128-dimensional parameter tuned under quantified kernel mismatch (condition number 8.0): all 12 reward×β cells stable (ESS ≥ 94/2,000, zero non-finite weights, reward improved in 12/12); calibrated anomaly detector (limit 3.031, validated on 4 adversarial controls scoring 15–121) places every cell's 95% CI below the limit; per-step gradient noise (3–4× above MCMC floor) honestly disclosed but loop remains stable.

ai-sherpa/sosmc-particle-optimisation-re.overall: This logbook provides concrete, numerically reported experimental evidence for all six claims through from-scratch implementations with independent cross-checks (finite differences, SymPy, Monte Carlo) and negative controls throughout. The main simplification is claim 6's MLP-over-code-space architecture rather than the paper's pixel-space convolutional EBM, but the key mechanisms—high-dimensional tuning, kernel mismatch, and reward-hacking detection—are genuinely exercised on real MNIST at non-trivial scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 gives a bicriteria (1+κ, 1+1/κ) approximation via LP rounding: the returned subgraph K satisfies coverage loss W−e(K)≤(1+κ)·ε·W and size |K|≤(1+1/κ)·r (Theorem 1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: 360 independent checks across 24 random planted weighted hypergraphs with ε∈{0.05,0.1,0.2} and κ∈{0.25,0.5,1.0,2.0,4.0}: both bicriteria inequalities hold in 100% of trials (max coverage ratio 0.875, max size ratio 0.97), directly confirming Theorem 1's bounds via exact LP solving with HiGHS.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 proves a monotonicity/nestedness property (Kτ1⊆Kτ2 for τ1<τ2), derived from a connection to parametric minimum cuts, which is required for valid conformal calibration (Theorem 2, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Nestedness of the parametric-min-cut subgraph family confirmed in 16/16 random hypergraph instances; LP-rounding matches parametric-min-cut selection in 73/80 τ-checks (91%); the paper's Example 1 counterexample is reproduced showing optimal solution is non-monotone while the algorithm remains nested.

claims.claim: Corollary 1 shows the entire nested sequence of subgraphs across thresholds can be computed in Õ(γ(m+n)²) time (Corollary 1, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Breakpoint count k≤n holds across all tested sizes (m+n=20 to 120, k stays 3–6); wall-clock runtime log-log slope of 1.03 is within the O((m+n)²) envelope, empirically confirming the structural and scaling properties underlying the Õ(γ(m+n)²) bound.

claims.claim: Lemma 1 establishes a distribution-free marginal coverage guarantee ℙ(B*⊆Kτ*(A*))≥φ−δ under exchangeability, without requiring model probability estimates (Lemma 1).
claims.evidence: The two-stage split-conformal procedure is correctly implemented and tested over 400 trials with empirical coverage exceeding φ−δ at all three levels, but the setup is a 3×4 grid with only 17 edges where mean K size is ~16.94/17—nearly the entire graph—making the coverage test trivially easy to pass and not a meaningful test of the guarantee under real compression.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 proves NP-hardness of the conformal subgraph problem even for constant ε via reduction from clique detection, in Appendix B (Theorem 4, Appendix B).
claims.evidence: The Appendix B clique-to-conformal-subgraph reduction is constructively verified on 4 CLIQUE instances (2 YES, 2 NO) with constant ε=0.3: the coverage threshold (1−ε)W correctly separates YES cases (solution meets threshold) from NO cases (falls short), confirming the reduction's key equivalence and gap properties.

claims.claim: On a synthetic 6x6 grid navigation experiment with 50 train/test routes, the LP-based method compresses the calibration set to 52 edges at φ=0.75 coverage and outperforms greedy baselines for φ≤0.8 (Section 5).
claims.evidence: On the 6×6 grid with 50 train/test routes averaged over 10 runs, LP uses 59.9±11.8 edges at φ=0.75 (paper reports 52, within 1σ) and LP edge count is ≤ both forward- and reverse-greedy baselines for all φ≤0.8, reproducing the paper's qualitative finding and landing within statistical error of the reported number.

snaykey/repro-compact-conformal-subgraph.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting 5 of 6 claims through from-scratch implementations (LP solving, parametric min-cut, conformal calibration, clique reduction, grid experiment), with the coverage guarantee (Claim 4) tested only on a trivially small setup where K covers nearly all edges. The reproduction is rigorous in methodology and provides specific numerical evidence, though some theoretical claims are checked on modest-scale synthetic instances.

snaykey/repro-maximin-relative-improveme.paper_title: Maximin Relative Improvement: Fair Learning as a Bargaining Problem

claims.claim: Relative improvement is defined as the ratio of actual risk reduction to the maximum possible reduction from a baseline predictor, per Equation 1: ρ_P(f) = [R_P(f0) − R_P(f)] / [R_P(f0) − R_P(f*_P)] (Section 2, Equation 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook downloads official 2018 ACS PUMS data, applies the paper's exact filters (2780 records), and recomputes Equation 1 with maximum absolute error 0.00e+00; the oracle-gap ratio (0.101), MMRI RI values (56.92%/56.90% vs paper's 57%/57%), and MMR RI values (-73.61%/82.46% vs paper's -74%/82%) all closely match the paper on real census data.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves a no-harm guarantee: when the baseline predictor f0 is in the feasible class F, the maximin relative improvement solution f_RI satisfies R_g(f_RI) ≤ R_g(f0) for every group g (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: On the real ACS data, both groups show non-positive risk differences versus baseline (-0.004308, -0.042618), and 250 seeded convex quadratic stress tests with feasible baselines produced 0/250 violations of the no-harm inequality.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.2 shows that, for two groups (m=2), relative improvement uniquely satisfies Pareto optimality, symmetry, scale invariance, and individual monotonicity simultaneously, and recovers the Kalai-Smorodinsky bargaining solution (Proposition 4.2).
claims.evidence: On the real ACS frontier, Pareto optimality, symmetry (label-swap invariance), and scale invariance (affine-transform invariance) all pass for the MMRI solution, and the two group relative improvements differ by only 2.387e-04, corroborating the KS equal-RI mechanism; individual monotonicity is additionally tested on a nested-class construction.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.4 extends the axiomatic guarantees to more than two groups (m>2) via a leximin refinement that preserves scale invariance and a modified individual monotonicity property (Proposition 4.4).
claims.evidence: The evidence is a single small constructed 3-group example with 4-5 risk profiles, verifying leximin selection, Pareto optimality, scale invariance, and modified individual monotonicity on that specific construction, but not on real data or at any meaningful scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.4 establishes that the empirical maximin relative improvement estimator converges to the population solution at rate O(1/√n) under standard regularity conditions (Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: A Monte Carlo experiment with 160 repetitions across 6 sample sizes in a simplified 1D Gaussian linear-regression setting yields a log-log slope of -0.550 and roughly constant sqrt(n)-scaled gaps (0.92–1.22), consistent with O(1/√n), but the setup is a clearly simplified parametric case that does not cover the theorem's full regularity conditions.

claims.claim: Table 1 shows relative improvement is the only compared fairness criterion (versus Group DRO, minimax regret, Nash bargaining, and explained variance) that jointly satisfies Pareto optimality, scale invariance, and individual monotonicity (Table 1, Section 3.1-3.3).
claims.evidence: Across 5,000 seeded two-group finite feasible sets, concrete scale-invariance counterexamples were found for Group DRO, minimax regret, and explained variance, and an individual-monotonicity counterexample was found for Nash bargaining, while relative improvement passed all three axiom tests with zero violations, supporting the claim that RI alone jointly satisfies PO, SI, and IM.

snaykey/repro-maximin-relative-improveme.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence on real ACS census data supporting the relative improvement definition, no-harm guarantee, two-group axioms, and the axiomatic comparison table, with close quantitative matches to the paper's reported figures. The multigroup leximin and convergence-rate claims are addressed only on small constructed or simplified parametric setups, which are useful corroboration but fall short of full-scale reproduction.

ProCreations/repro-who-said-neural-netwo.paper_title: Who Said Neural Networks Aren't Linear?

claims.claim: A Linearizer is defined as f(x) = g_y^{-1}(A g_x(x)) for invertible neural networks g_x, g_y and linear operator A, making f linear under induced vector-space operations (Section 2.1-2.2).
claims.evidence: The released Linearizer class was tested with distinct analytic nonlinear bijections and a full-rank non-diagonal core in dimension 24 over 256 pairs, yielding induced-space linearity error 1.751e-15 and round-trip error 1.332e-15, with a Euclidean control error of 0.086482 confirming non-linearity under ordinary operations.

claims.claim: The composition of two Linearizers with compatible spaces is itself a Linearizer, with the composed operator obtained by matrix multiplication of the underlying cores (Proposition 2.5).
claims.evidence: Two official Linearizer objects with dense noncommuting full-rank cores in dimension 28 over 192 vectors were composed and compared to a third Linearizer with core A2·A1, yielding composition error 9.869e-16, with reversed-order control error 1.411884 and commutator norm 8.061610 confirming noncommutativity.

claims.claim: A Linearizer f is idempotent, i.e. f(f(x)) = f(x), if and only if its core matrix A is an idempotent matrix (A^2 = A), enabling architectural (rather than optimization-based) enforcement of idempotent generative networks (Lemma 4.2, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: A rank-13 orthogonal projector placed inside the released Linearizer class over 256 vectors in dimension 32 (including off-subspace inputs) yielded core residual ||A²−A|| = 1.500e-15 and network idempotence error 7.155e-16, while adding 0.2I to break core idempotence produced control error 0.265376.

claims.claim: In the one-step flow-matching application, the product of per-step update operators over hundreds of integration steps collapses into a single operator, enabling one-step diffusion sampling without retraining (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: The released FlowMatcher.sample and sample_one_step methods were run with the authors' time-dependent LoRA core for 10, 50, and 200 Euler steps on 16 samples in a 64-dimensional latent space, yielding worst iterative-versus-collapsed error 3.169e-15, with reversed-order product control error ≥0.006103.

claims.claim: Modular style transfer is achieved by fixing the shared encoders g_x, g_y while swapping only the style-specific core matrix A_style, allowing algebraic interpolation between styles from a single trained network (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The released LinearKernel style core was tested at three style indices with one shared encoder over 8 RGB tensors (432 values each), yielding worst core-linearity error 1.624e-16, operator interpolation error 0.0, and style-swap output change 0.085949, with a nonlinear tanh-core control showing error 0.208488.

ProCreations/repro-who-said-neural-netwo.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from the exact released architecture at commit adfca2c3 for all five claims, with machine-precision errors for the main results and non-trivial destructive controls (Euclidean non-linearity, reversed-order products, broken projectors, nonlinear cores) confirming each property is non-vacuous. The scale is moderate (dimensions 24–64) but sufficient for testing dimension-independent structural identities, and all tests use the authors' actual code rather than proxy implementations.

kondratevakate/repro-optimal-decision-ma.paper_title: Optimal Decision-Making Based on Prediction Sets

claims.claim: The paper proposes a decision-theoretic framework that minimizes expected loss (risk) against a worst-case distribution consistent with a prediction set's coverage guarantee, characterizing the minimax-optimal policy for a fixed prediction set (abstract only).
claims.evidence: An independent LP solver exhaustively checks the complete 2-label/2-action integer-loss family plus 120 random 3-label cases across five alpha values, with all 28,950 comparisons matching the closed-form robust risk to 1.42e-14, and a destructive control confirms the out-of-set penalty changes the policy as predicted.

claims.claim: Building on the minimax-optimal policy, the authors derive an optimal prediction-set construction that minimizes robust risk subject to a coverage constraint (abstract only).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states this claim was not attempted; no experiments address the non-atomic feature-space assumption, Fenchel-Rockafellar duality, randomized-kernel relaxation, or derandomization of Proposition 3.1 and Theorem 3.3.

claims.claim: Risk-Optimal Conformal Prediction (ROCP) is introduced as a practical algorithm that targets these risk-minimizing sets while maintaining finite-sample, distribution-free marginal coverage (abstract only).
claims.evidence: A literal implementation of Algorithm 1 passes 14,850 exhaustive exchangeability orbit/alpha checks with worst coverage matching the finite-sample bound to 1.11e-16, and fresh empirical runs on 20 COVID seeds and 20 BDD splits show mean miscoverage within 0.00244 of alpha across seven alpha values.

claims.claim: Empirical evaluations on medical diagnosis and safety-critical decision-making tasks show ROCP reduces critical mistakes compared to baselines, with the largest gains when out-of-set errors are costly (abstract only).
claims.evidence: Using official cached probabilities evaluated from scratch, ROCP reduces critical-mistake rates below RAC on COVID (e.g., 1.19% vs 1.54% for Pneumonia at alpha=0.05 under Lambda0) and achieves zero critical mistakes under the high-cost Lambda1 while RAC remains nonzero; on BDD, ROCP realized loss is 2.320±0.019 vs RAC 2.981±0.075 with reduced collision rates across hazard states.

kondratevakate/repro-optimal-decision-ma.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical and experimental evidence supporting Claims 1, 3, and 4 through independent LP audits, exhaustive exchangeability checks, and fresh empirical runs on real COVID and BDD datasets. Claim 2 was explicitly not attempted, leaving the optimal prediction-set construction theory unverified.

snaykey/repro-conditional-coverage-diagn.paper_title: Conditional Coverage Diagnostics for Conformal Prediction

claims.claim: The paper introduces a family of Excess Risk of the Target Coverage (ERT) metrics—L1-ERT, L2-ERT, and KL-ERT—for evaluating conditional coverage in conformal prediction, built on the principle that no classifier can outperform a constant 1-alpha predictor under perfect conditional coverage (Table 1, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The reproduction implements L1-, L2-, and KL-ERT risk differences on the paper's exact 8-dimensional heteroskedastic Gaussian DGP and validates them against direct population-distance calculations on 200,000 samples, with maximum Monte Carlo discrepancy of 0.001480 across all three metrics.

claims.claim: Using LightGBM as the underlying classifier for L1-ERT achieves 68.4% relative statistical power (relative to maximum), compared to only 38.3% for the PartitionWise classifier underlying CovGap (Table 2, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: LightGBM and PartitionWise were never used; instead a five-fold polynomial logistic classifier and a ten-cluster partition estimator were substituted on synthetic data only, and the TabArena datasets were not tested. The specific power numbers (68.4%/38.3%) were not reproduced—the logbook itself notes v2 reports different values (68.9%/33.7%).

claims.claim: In synthetic experiments, group-based metrics like CovGap remain unreliable and unaligned with their theoretical values even at 5,000 test points, whereas ERT metrics such as L1-ERT converge with far fewer samples (Figure 4, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: On the paper's exact synthetic DGP with n=500, 1500, 5000, five-fold ERT estimates converge toward truth (0.0767→0.0835→0.0922 vs true 0.0943), while the partition estimator diverges (0.0313→0.0259→0.0155), directly demonstrating the claimed sample-efficiency gap.

claims.claim: The metrics decompose conditional coverage error into asymmetric components ell_plus-ERT and ell_minus-ERT, separating unnecessary conservatism (over-coverage) from excessive aggressiveness (under-coverage) (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: The reproduction computes KL-ERT decomposition on synthetic coverage profiles, finding KL-total 0.068428, KL-plus 0.039661, KL-minus 0.028767 with additive identity error of 3.469e-18, and confirms that conservative and aggressive controls activate opposite components.

claims.claim: Classification experiments report divergent KL_plus-ERT and KL_minus-ERT values across conformal prediction methods, demonstrating the over/under-coverage decomposition in practice (Table 4, Section 4.3.2).
claims.evidence: The actual classification experiments (MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100) were not run; the logbook only transcribed Table J.1 values from the PDF and exercised the KL-plus/KL-minus formulas on synthetic Bernoulli profiles (conservative 0.0371, aggressive 0.4118), which is a proxy for the claimed classification-experiment result.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 estimates the ERT metrics from finite samples using k-fold cross-validation to avoid overfitting the classifier used in the estimation (Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: On oracle-conditionally-covered data where true L1-ERT is 0, an in-sample memorizer falsely reports 0.1880 while five-fold cross-validated evaluation reports 0.0054, directly demonstrating that Algorithm 1's k-fold mechanism prevents classifier overfitting in ERT estimation.

snaykey/repro-conditional-coverage-diagn.overall: The logbook provides solid executable verification of the ERT metric identities, sample efficiency, asymmetric decomposition, and cross-validation safeguard on the paper's synthetic DGP, but does not reproduce the real-data benchmarks—LightGBM/TabArena power comparisons and image classification experiments were not run.

RyeCatcher/repro-capacitated-fair-range-.paper_title: Capacitated Fair-Range Clustering: Hardness and Approximation Algorithms

claims.claim: For capacitated fair-range clustering with a constant number of demographic groups, the paper gives a polynomial-time O(log k)-approximation algorithm for k-median and O(log^2 k)-approximation for k-means running in (nk^t)^O(1) time (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook only performed text-level source matching (checking that tokens 'O(log k)', 'O(log^2 k)', and '(nk^t)^O(1)' appear in the theorem statement) and explicitly states 'I did not replay the approximation algorithm.' No algorithm was implemented, no approximation ratios were tested on any instance, and no runtime was measured.

claims.claim: For any epsilon>0, a randomized (3+epsilon)-approximation algorithm exists for capacitated fair-range k-median with running time (O(2^t k epsilon^-1 log n))^O(k)*n^O(1), and a corresponding (9+epsilon)-approximation for k-means, matching the best known guarantees for capacitated clustering without fair-range constraints (Theorem 5.5).
claims.evidence: The logbook only verified theorem-text presence of '(3+epsilon)' and '(9+epsilon)' tokens and computed trivial arithmetic (2^3=8, 2^20=1048576) as a 'negative control.' No FPT algorithm was implemented or tested; the logbook explicitly states 'I did not replay the FPT algorithm.'

claims.claim: No polynomial-time algorithm can approximate capacitated fair-range k-median or k-means to any polynomial factor unless P=NP, and this hardness holds even on tree metrics and even when fair-range feasibility is trivially satisfiable (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook states 'I did not replay the reduction.' It only checked that the theorem text contains 'any polynomial factor' and 'tree metrics' phrases, and verified the trivial observation that fair-range and capacitated fair-range coincide when capacities are unlimited. This does not test the hardness claim itself.

claims.claim: Under P≠NP, no polynomial-time algorithm can approximate the problem to a factor better than (Delta-2)/16 on tree metrics, where Delta is the distance aspect ratio (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook only confirmed the formula '(Delta-2)/16' appears in the source and plugged in a few values (Delta=18→1.0, etc.), which is trivial arithmetic on the stated formula. No hardness reduction was implemented or tested; the logbook states 'no hardness proof replay.'

claims.claim: Assuming Gap-ETH, no f(k)*n^o(k)-time algorithm, for any computable function f, can approximate capacitated fair-range k-median to any polynomial factor, ruling out algorithms with running time subexponential in k (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook only matched theorem text for the Gap-ETH clause and f(k)n^{o(k)} runtime token, and checked the same trivial unlimited-capacity equivalence as Claim 3. It explicitly states 'I did not replay the Gap-ETH reduction.' No reduction was implemented or tested.

RyeCatcher/repro-capacitated-fair-range-.overall: This logbook performs only text-matching of theorem statements and trivial arithmetic on stated formulas; no algorithm is implemented, no approximation ratio is empirically tested, and no hardness reduction is replayed. It provides no experimental evidence that supports or refutes any of the five theoretical claims.

RyeCatcher/repro-high-accuracy-and-dimen.paper_title: High-accuracy and dimension-free sampling with diffusions

claims.claim: The paper gives the first diffusion-based sampler with iteration complexity scaling polylogarithmically in 1/epsilon rather than polynomially, as established in the main result (Theorem 1.1 / Corollary 3.9).
claims.evidence: The logbook only checked that the LaTeX source contains the polylogarithmic headline and 'first diffusion-based sampler' prose, and evaluated the trivial expression log^2(1/epsilon)/(1/epsilon) on a grid. No diffusion sampler was implemented or run; this is a source-text audit, not experimental evidence.

claims.claim: The iteration complexity bound is O~((R/sigma)^2 * polylog(1/epsilon)), depending on the effective support radius R and noise scale sigma rather than explicitly on the ambient dimension d, under the 'bounded plus noise' assumption that the target is a compactly-supported distribution convolved with Gaussian noise (Assumption 1, Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirmed line numbers where the assumption, theorem, and radius explanation appear in the LaTeX, and noted no explicit dimension symbol on the theorem line. No experiment was conducted—this is purely a source-text presence check with no runs or numerical evidence.

claims.claim: The proof relies on showing that higher-order time derivatives of the score function along the reverse process remain bounded and dimension-independent when initialized near (not exactly at) the true reverse trajectory (Lemma 3.3, Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: The logbook evaluated the paper's own near-trajectory bound formula on a d-grid and found it increases with d (164687 to 951864), noting an explicit log(d) term. This is a formula evaluation from the paper's text, not an independent verification of the derivative boundedness proof, and it actually suggests the claim's 'dimension-independent' wording may be stronger than what the source supports.

claims.claim: A collocation method using low-degree polynomial approximation of score derivatives, combined with Picard iteration, is shown to converge exponentially fast over small time windows (Lemma 3.2, Proposition 3.6).
claims.evidence: The logbook ran a scalar affine Picard map x_{m+1}=1+q*x_m with q=0.4, showing geometric error decay at ratio ~0.4, and a negative control with q=1.1 showing divergence. This is a real computation but on a trivially simplified scalar toy unrelated to the paper's actual collocation method for score derivatives.

claims.claim: For a Gaussian mixture with k components separated by Theta(sqrt(log k)), the resulting sampler achieves polylogarithmic scaling in both k and 1/epsilon, whereas prior diffusion-based samplers scaled polynomially in the ambient dimension d (Section 3, discussion following Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence: The logbook substituted R=Theta(sqrt(log k)) and sigma=1 into a proxy complexity formula from the paper and found proxy/log k constant across k values. This is algebraic substitution into the paper's own formula, not an experiment with an actual Gaussian mixture sampler.

RyeCatcher/repro-high-accuracy-and-dimen.overall: This logbook is essentially a source-text audit with trivial formula evaluations; no diffusion sampler was implemented, no sampling experiments were run, and no proofs were independently checked. The only actual computation (Claim 4's scalar Picard iteration) is on a toy unrelated to the paper's method, and the rest are line-number checks or algebraic substitutions.

RyeCatcher/repro-transformers-learn-the-.paper_title: Transformers Learn the Optimal DDPM Denoiser for Multi-Token GMMs

claims.claim: Theorem 1 gives the first convergence analysis for gradient-descent training of a transformer under the population DDPM objective on multi-token Gaussian mixture (MTGM) data, showing the training loss converges to within O(epsilon) of the Bayes-optimal risk (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook only verified that the paper's LaTeX source contains the convergence statement (line-number matching) and evaluated a tautological proxy (gap/ε = 1.0 for all ε values, which is trivially true when gap is defined as ε). No transformer was trained, no MTGM data was generated, and no actual convergence behavior was measured.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows the trained transformer yields a score network whose score-matching error is bounded by epsilon times (SNR+1) (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook checked that the source contains the theorem bound line and evaluated the formula ε(SNR+1) at SNR values [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 5.0] with ε=0.02, which is just arithmetic on the bound's own expression. No trained score network was evaluated and no actual score-matching error was measured against the bound.

claims.claim: Corollary 3 establishes a 'mean denoising mechanism': the self-attention layer's weights concentrate uniformly across tokens sharing the same underlying pattern, so the model approximates the Bayes-optimal MMSE estimator by averaging same-pattern tokens (Section 4.2, Corollary 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook verified source lines for concentration/uniformity statements and ran a toy weight-vector computation showing deviations from the exact same-pattern mean shrink from 1.58 to 0.05 as ε decreases from 1e-1 to 1e-4, testing the concentration mechanism's mathematical form on a simplified setup without training a real transformer.

claims.claim: Proposition 1 shows the trained transformer converges to the oracle MMSE estimator for the multi-token Gaussian mixture denoising problem (Section 4.1, Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook matched proposition ingredients by source line number and ran a toy witness computation (ᾱ=0.64, ρ=1.5) showing identity gap of 0.0 with the correct oracle target and 0.44 with a wrong global-mean negative control, testing the oracle MMSE formula on a single simplified instance rather than reproducing the full approximation result.

claims.claim: Corollary 4 shows the learned mean-denoising mechanism generalizes to test data with a distribution shift from the training mixture (Section 4, Corollary 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook verified the shifted-mixture corollary exists in the source and ran a toy same-pattern averaging computation showing the estimate stays 2.0 when mixture counts change from 3 to 6, testing the invariance property on a simplified setup without training or evaluating on actual distribution-shifted data.

claims.claim: Single-head softmax attention parameters can be exactly recovered using O(d^2) value queries via a two-phase algorithm that first recovers the output projection vector v with length-1 queries, then recovers the attention matrix W column-by-column with length-2 queries (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Numerical replay on very small instances (d=3–6) shows machine-precision recovery (W error 4.66e-15, v error 0.0) with query counts matching d+d^2, but this is a bounded finite-instance check of a universal theorem, not a proof or full-scale reproduction.

claims.claim: When rank(W) <= r << d, the attention matrix can instead be recovered with only O(rd) queries using rank-one projections and nuclear norm minimization from compressed sensing (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: The rank-one measurement identity was confirmed (error 5.33e-13) on small instances (d=6, r=1,2), but the recovery backend was a factorized least-squares solver rather than the nuclear-norm minimization the claim specifically relies on, so the core compressed-sensing component was not exercised.

claims.claim: Under norm bounds and margin conditions on the parameters, epsilon-accurate approximate recovery is achievable with O(d^2) queries tolerating additive noise tau = O(min{mu, epsilon_v/sqrt(d), mu*epsilon_w/(W^2 d)}) (Theorem 6.2).
claims.evidence: Robust recovery was tested on small instances with only the all-coordinates-nonzero branch exercised, using a smaller explicit constant in tau; measured errors (2.67e-5 for v, 0.0096 for W) stayed below targets, but coverage of the theorem's conditions is partial and scale is limited.

claims.claim: Multi-head attention parameters are non-identifiable from queries: distinct parameter sets can produce identical input-output maps, ruling out exact parameter extraction without further structural assumptions (Proposition 7.1).
claims.evidence: The paper's own witness family was instantiated to produce two parameter sets with gap 2.588 that yield identical input-output maps (max function gap 1.78e-15), directly verifying this existential non-identifiability claim.

claims.claim: Length-2 queries reduce the softmax attention weight to a sigmoid, alpha = sigma(s1 - s2), enabling inversion via sigma^-1 into linear equations in the unknown parameters (Section preceding Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Both algebraic identities were directly tested on random two-row probes: sigmoid-identity error 2.22e-16 and logit-linearization error 1.49e-12, confirming the exact reduction to machine precision.

ProCreations/repro-nonlinear-autoencoder.paper_title: A Solvable High-Dimensional Model Where Nonlinear Autoencoders Learn Structure Invisible to PCA While Test Loss Misaligns With Generalization

claims.claim: The spiked cumulant model introduces two latent factors, one recoverable by PCA from the covariance and one appearing only in higher-order moments and invisible to PCA (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Quadrature confirms E[λν]=0 but E[λ²ν]=0.817, and S-whitened PCA at d=256 recovers u (overlap 0.846) but not v (0.026); removing the S-whitening control makes v covariance-visible (0.975), directly demonstrating the higher-order-only structure.

claims.claim: For correlation exponent 2 ≤ k* < ∞, a minimal nonlinear autoencoder x̂ = (w/√d) σ(wᵀx/√d) with tied encoder-decoder weights provably recovers both latent spikes while PCA and linear autoencoders recover only the covariance-visible one (Section 2, Result 3.1).
claims.evidence: At α=8, d=256, the tied nonlinear autoencoder achieves v-overlap 0.1865 versus PCA's 0.0250, with the nonlinear hidden advantage ≥0.052 across all α≥6 runs; the linear/PCA baseline recovers u but stays near-random on v on the same datasets.

claims.claim: Approximate Message Passing weakly recovers both spikes once the sample-to-dimension ratio α exceeds a threshold α_weak^AMP determined by the moments of the coupling coefficients (Result 3.2).
claims.evidence: AMP recovery at d=256 grows from v=0.066 at α=1 to v=0.412 at α=5, with the independent-latent control collapsing to v=0.054, demonstrating threshold-dependent recovery driven by mixed moments; scale is smaller than the paper's d=10,000 figure but uses the same released AMP code and channel.

claims.claim: Under conditions C2 < 0 and C3 ≠ 0, spherical gradient flow on the nonlinear autoencoder achieves weak recovery of the hidden spike in logarithmic time Θ(log d) (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Quadrature yields C2=-0.160 and C3=-0.011 (satisfying the theorem's conditions), the independent-latent control drives C3 to ~5e-15, and hitting-time across d=4,096 to 4,194,304 fits log(d) with R²=0.9945 versus sqrt(d) R²=0.771, directly supporting Θ(log d) scaling.

claims.claim: Linear autoencoders achieve lower reconstruction (test) loss than nonlinear autoencoders yet fail to recover the hidden spike, demonstrating that self-supervised test loss misaligns with representation quality (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Across three seeds at α=6, d=256, the linear autoencoder has consistently lower reconstruction loss (mean 127.64 vs 128.13) yet lower hidden-spike overlap (mean 0.026 vs 0.078), with only the activation differing between the two otherwise identical models.

ProCreations/repro-nonlinear-autoencoder.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence for all five claims using the authors' released code at a pinned commit, with destructive controls for each claim (whitening removal, independent latents, wrong-rate fitting, activation swap). The main limitation is that most experiments run at d=256 rather than the paper's larger figures, but the mechanisms and qualitative predictions are clearly demonstrated at this scale.

michaldobiezynski/repro-learning-high-di.paper_title: Learning High-Dimensional Parity Functions with Product Networks using Gradient Descent

claims.claim: Product networks trained with gradient descent under controlled stochastic data sparsity are shown to learn high-dimensional parity functions, with the problem formalized in Section 3 and main theoretical results developed in Section 4.
claims.evidence: At p_e=1/N, the product node converges (|W-W_true|<0.05) for N=50,100,200,500 with final L1 errors 0.0496/0.0443/0.0495/0.0494, while the dense control at p_e=7/N never converges (L1~0.73-0.75), demonstrating sparsity-gated learnability with a proper failing control.

claims.claim: Theorems F.5-F.7 in Appendix F establish core convergence guarantees for the product-network learning dynamics on parity functions (Theorem F.5-F.7, Appendix F).
claims.evidence: At N=100000, M=1000, alpha=10, the per-step variance contraction factor measures 0.999609 against the derived theorem constant m^2=(1-2*alpha*p_e)^2=0.999600 (0.001% gap), stable across windows, and tracks the predicted constant to within 0.05% over an 8x alpha sweep with no free parameters.

claims.claim: Theorems F.10-F.12 give polynomial scaling laws relating required network width to input dimension N under the sparsity conditions studied (Theorem F.10-F.12, Appendix F).
claims.evidence: Required layer width P*(N)=1 (exponent 0) for N=1600 to 25600 with 64/64 nodes converging, and the stability law alpha_lim=0.39*N^1.045 (R2=0.9995) over a 128x width range, both polynomial exponents as the theorems assert.

claims.claim: Theorems F.14-F.16 provide sample complexity bounds for learning parity functions with the product-network architecture (Theorem F.14-F.16, Appendix F).
claims.evidence: Sample complexity measures 161.3*N^1.002 (R2=1.0000) over N=1600 to 102400 with 3 seeds each and zero censored points, samples/N flat at 162-166 across the full 64x range, directly confirming the O(N) bound.

claims.claim: Section 5 reports experimental validation of the theoretical predictions across varying input dimensions and network configurations, complementing the initialization analysis in Theorems H.1-H.9 (Section 5, Appendix H).
claims.evidence: At N=100000 the node converges at step 16520 (L1=8.79e-3); optimal sparsity p_e*=2.00/N is identical across N=5000/20000/50000 (CV 0.000); and symmetric N(1/2,1/4) init preserves mu0=1-mu1 to 0.0022 vs 0.5828 for off-centre init (263x difference, 2 seeds).

michaldobiezynski/repro-learning-high-di.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from a from-scratch numpy reproduction supporting all five claims, with four claims tested at the paper's headline scale N=100000 and one at N up to 102400. Rate constants are independently derived from the paper's update rule rather than transcribed, and two independent training engines cross-validate on N=200 dynamics.

ProCreations/repro-a-theory-of-learning-.paper_title: A theory of learning data statistics in diffusion models, from easy to hard

claims.claim: Diffusion denoisers trained on natural images exhibit a distributional simplicity bias: on CIFAR-10, a U-Net achieves nearly identical test loss on real images versus Gaussian clones matched in mean and covariance for roughly 10^3 training steps before performance diverges, indicating pair-wise statistics are learned first (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook loads the authors' released CIFAR-10 checkpoint loss arrays at steps 1, 6, 32, 178, and 1000 and independently recomputes the real-vs-matched-clone gap, finding a maximum gap of 0.003652 through step 1000, with a mean-only-clone control increasing the gap to 0.421843. This is the real CIFAR-10 U-Net scale, though it uses released checkpoint outputs rather than a new training run.

claims.claim: For a k-th order cumulant target, the sample complexity threshold for weak recovery via projected gradient descent is n_hat(d,k) = omega(d^(k-1) log^2 d), with |v . w(n_hat)| approaching 1 as d approaches infinity after this many steps (Proposition 4.3).
claims.evidence: Spherical SGD with k*=4 at dimensions 8, 12, 16, 24 (48 trajectories each) with n=30*d^3 samples achieves minimum final overlap 0.9336 and weak-recovery rate 0.917, with a Gaussian-spike control dropping to 0.1973. The measured scaling slope of 3.0 is consistent with d^(k-1), though dimensions are small.

claims.claim: If the number of samples n(d) = o(n_hat(d,k*)), standard SGD provably fails to achieve weak recovery of the k*-th cumulant, establishing a sharp learnable/unlearnable sample-complexity separation (Proposition 4.4).
claims.evidence: The same spherical-SGD system stopped at n=floor(0.02*d^3) across dimensions 8-24 (48 trajectories each) shows maximum best overlap of only 0.2963 and weak-recovery rate 0.021, while increasing to 30*d^3 raises overlap by at least 0.6459, directly demonstrating the below-threshold failure regime.

claims.claim: In a mixed-cumulant latent model, pair-wise statistics are recoverable with linear sample complexity n = Theta(d * polylog(d)), while recovering the fourth cumulant requires Omega(d^3) samples when latent variables are independent (Proposition 4.6).
claims.evidence: The released mixed-cumulant generator at dimensions 24-128 with n=40*d samples and 12 datasets per dimension shows pair-wise u overlap ≥0.9969 while fourth-cumulant v score overlap ≤0.1691 under independent latents, directly demonstrating the linear-vs-cubic separation at linear sample budget.

claims.claim: When latent variables underlying the pair-wise and higher-order statistics are positively correlated, the fourth-cumulant recovery sample complexity accelerates from cubic to linear in d (Proposition 4.6).
claims.evidence: With the correlated-latent switch (a0=sign(a1)) at n=40*d across dimensions 24-128, every correlated run achieves v overlap ≥0.7832, while the matched independent-latent control stays ≤0.1691, yielding a gain of at least 0.6892 and demonstrating linear-sample fourth-cumulant recovery under positive correlation.

claims.claim: Unconstrained SGD exhibits contraction dynamics toward w=0 for many activation functions, causing learning failure, whereas constraining updates to the unit sphere (spherical projection) preserves the ability to learn higher-order statistics (Proposition 4.7).
claims.evidence: 128 paired d=16 trajectories with 50,000 samples each show projected SGD preserves norm (deviation 2.2e-16) with crossing rate 0.820, while unconstrained SGD contracts to norm 0.1861 with crossing rate 0.062. Only one activation is tested, but the contraction-vs-projection mechanism is directly demonstrated.

ProCreations/repro-a-theory-of-learning-.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence for all six claims using the paper's released code with appropriate controls, multiple dimensions, and multiple independent trajectories. The main limitations are that Claim 1 uses released checkpoint outputs rather than a new training run, Claims 2-3 use small dimensions (d=8-24), and Claim 6 tests only one activation function.

DineshAI/repro-a-sketch-and-project-anal.paper_title: A Sketch-and-Project Analysis of Subsampled Natural Gradient Algorithms

claims.claim: For linear least-squares problems, subsampled natural gradient descent (SNGD) is shown to be directly equivalent to the regularized Kaczmarz method, and SPRING is equivalent to the Nesterov-accelerated regularized Kaczmarz (ARK) method (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Independent implementations of SNGD and regularized Kaczmarz from identical state and sampled row block yield update residual exactly 0; SPRING and ARK transformed states differ by 2.60e-15 and 5.33e-15, confirming the algebraic equivalence to machine precision.

claims.claim: SNGD converges at rate (1-α)^t where α=λ_min(P̄), while SPRING converges at rate O((1-√(α/β))^t), giving up to a square-root improvement in iteration complexity over SNGD (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Across 5 independent least-squares problems with 72 paired sample streams and 360 steps, SPRING has a lower fitted convergence factor than SNGD on 5/5 problems (observed SNGD ~0.97 vs SPRING ~0.92), with median speedup to 0.1% relative error of 2.18×, consistent with a square-root improvement.

claims.claim: For general quadratic losses, SNGD requires the regularization parameter λ to exceed a threshold λ0 to guarantee convergence, and can diverge if regularization is insufficient (Proposition 3).
claims.evidence: On a fixed 4×2 general quadratic, the expected update map spectral radius is 1.04701 at weak regularization (λ=1e-8, indicating divergence) and 0.99904 at λ=10 (indicating convergence), with the stability statistic ξ changing sign near λ≈1.778, directly demonstrating the threshold behavior.

claims.claim: Under an assumption that the regularized projector P̄ shares an eigenbasis with J^T J, SNGD provably outperforms SGD by a factor of k^β when the spectrum of the Jacobian decays polynomially (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: With shared eigenbasis enforced by construction and target β=2, the SNGD rate proxy fits exponent 1.838 across k=1,2,4,8 (close to k^β=k^2), while a flat-spectrum negative control fits exponent 1.031 (close to linear k^1); the SNGD/SGD ratio grows from 1.78× to 10.24×.

claims.claim: A unified algorithm (Algorithm 1) captures both SNGD (momentum μ=0) and SPRING (μ∈(0,1)) as momentum-based updates using subsampled Jacobians, enabling single-minibatch convergence guarantees of any batch size.

kineticdrive/made-repro.paper_title: MADE: Benchmark Environments for Closed-Loop Materials Discovery

claims.claim: MADE evaluates closed-loop materials discovery on ternary, quaternary, and quinary intermetallic compound systems (3-5 elements), with 10 randomly sampled systems per complexity level (Section on benchmark design).
claims.evidence: Three system manifest files at `MADE/data/systems_10_mp_20/` were programmatically verified to each contain exactly 10 systems with uniform element cardinality (3, 4, 5 for ternary/quaternary/quinary respectively), with sha256 hashes recorded; 150 baseline + 150 Chemeleon+MLIP episodes were run across all 30 systems (5 episodes each), confirmed in `verification/c3-overall-result.json` and `verification/lane-timing-ledger.json`.

claims.evidence: Config `MADE/configs/oracle/orb.yaml` specifies `model_name: orb-v3-conservative-inf-omat`, `optimizer: fire`, `steps: 500`; a loader canary confirmed checkpoint sha256 `0a41ef11...` (102,097,517 bytes) byte-identical to the official Orbital Materials release (`verification/identity-canary-receipt.json`, `verification/paper-provenance-crosscheck.json`); budget 50 was trajectory-confirmed across 50 episode files with 2,500 entries and zero deviations (`verification/runtime-identity.json`).

claims.claim: On simple (ternary) systems, a Chemeleon-generator-plus-MLIP-ranking pipeline achieves an acceleration factor (AF) of 6.4 versus a random baseline of 1.00, the strongest result among tested policies (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Using the paper's own `DiscoveryCurveMetrics.acceleration_factor` estimator (after fixing a shipped API-drift bug), ternary-only AF measured 3.41 ± 0.37 (SEM) across 50 episodes on 10 systems, which is ~8 standard errors below the claimed 6.4 and outside the pre-registered tolerance of 1.24 (`verification/c3-componentN-result.json`); the all-sizes AF of 7.08 ± 0.64 is compatible with 6.4, but the claim as stated specifies 'simple (ternary) systems'; the 'strongest among tested policies' clause was never tested because comparator policies were not run.

claims.claim: An LLM-orchestrated ReAct-style agentic pipeline achieves AF=5.4 and EF=6.0, competitive with the best modular pipeline while improving structural diversity of discovered candidates (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The Qwen3.6-27B orchestrator arm was withdrawn as an invalid experiment due to a destructive re-selection bug in the shipped agent harness; a gpt-5.6 substituted-LLM arm on a 5-system ternary subset measured AF=1.67 vs the paper's 5.4 and EF=1.301 vs 6.0 (`verification/c4-diversity-result.json`), a contrary result but at reduced scope; diversity metrics from the withdrawn arm point in opposite directions (space groups 2.28× toward the claim, compositions 0.36× and mSUN 0.50× against it) and cannot adjudicate the claim.

claims.claim: Tightening the stability threshold from ε=0.1 eV/atom to 0.01 eV/atom degrades the effectiveness of MLIP-ranking policies due to surrogate model errors, while the relative importance of planning increases as system complexity grows from ternary to quinary (Section on results).
claims.evidence: A pre-registered single-system pilot ran 20 real episodes at both ε=0.1 and ε=0.01 eV/atom with budget 50; at ε=0.01 both MLIP-ranking and random found zero qualifying discoveries in all 10 episodes, making the degradation comparison unformable on that system, while at ε=0.1 the MLIP arm reached AF=10.0 (`verification/c5-pilot-eps010-result.json`, `c5-pilot-eps001-result.json`); the full matched-arm, both-epsilon, all-arity experiment was not attempted (~155+ GPU-hours), so no planning-by-arity trend was tested.

kineticdrive/made-repro.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous full-scale reproduction of the MADE benchmark's structural design (30 systems, 300 episodes) and oracle configuration, confirming the benchmark composition and oracle setup claims, while falsifying the ternary-specific AF=6.4 claim (ternary AF=3.41) despite the all-sizes average being compatible, and producing only toy-scale or incomplete evidence for the LLM-orchestrator and threshold-sensitivity claims.

ProCreations/repro-how-to-correctly-repo.paper_title: How to Correctly Report LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluations
