AITrailblazer/repro-ppi-no-free-lunch.overall: The logbook provides computational verification of the three core theoretical claims (Theorem 4.1, Gaussian threshold, exact variance expressions) via exact arithmetic and grid enumeration with negative controls, but entirely omits Claim 4 (corollaries) and Claim 5 (real-world experiments). Srishti280992/repro-ptbcc-prototype-aggr.paper_title: Let the Prototype Guide You: Robust Aggregation of Sparse Multi-Class Annotations via Annotator Prototype Learning

claims.claim: PTBCC (Prototype-driven Bayesian Classifier Combination) models annotators via a shared set of prototype confusion matrices rather than learning one confusion matrix per annotator (Section on method overview).
claims.evidence: The code in run_real_ptbcc.py implements PTBCC with shared prototype confusion matrices v[s,k,l] (shape s_count×k×k) and annotator-specific Dirichlet mixture weights pi[j,s] (shape n_workers×s_count), with variational updates maintaining eta[j,s] and mu[s,k,l], concretely demonstrating the shared-prototype parameterization rather than per-annotator confusion matrices.

claims.claim: PTBCC achieves up to 15% accuracy improvement over the best baseline in its best-case dataset (Val5) (Table 4).

claims.claim: Across 11 real-world crowdsourcing datasets, PTBCC attains an average accuracy of 0.7472, versus 0.7175 for FGBCC, 0.7132 for BWA, and 0.6986 for majority voting (Table 4).
claims.evidence: On 10 of 11 datasets (Aircr unavailable), the reproduction yields PTBCC macro average 0.7246, not the claimed 0.7472; BWA averages 0.7010 (vs claimed 0.7132) and MV 0.6937 (vs claimed 0.6986); FGBCC was not reproduced at all. The missing Aircr would need ~0.97 accuracy to reconcile the gap, which is implausible.

Srishti280992/repro-graphop-sparse-gnn.paper_title: A Graphop Analysis of Graph Neural Networks on Sparse Graphs: Generalization and Universal Approximation

claims.claim: Graphops are introduced as self-adjoint, positivity-preserving operators over probability spaces, unifying dense graphons and sparse graphs as a single class of limit objects (Definition 3.1).
claims.evidence: Finite exact certificates verify self-adjointness and positivity preservation for dense block graphons (n=4–4096) and sparse cycle operators (n=4–4096), with asymmetric and negative-edge controls correctly rejected; a proof certificate derives graphop status for arbitrary probability spaces from Fubini, coordinate swap, and positive-integral monotonicity, validated by an independent premise-graph checker with deletion controls.

claims.claim: A restricted subclass called bounded-fiber operators (bofops) is defined via fiber measures nu_x satisfying ess sup_{x in Omega} nu_x(Omega) < infinity, capturing sparse connectivity patterns within the graphop framework (Definition 3.1).
claims.evidence: Fiber-mass/norm identity (||A||_{∞→∞} = ess sup_x ν_x(Ω)) is verified across 34 dense/sparse/nonuniform families up to 16,384 vertices; sparse cycles maintain fiber mass 2 while an unbounded diagonal family (masses 1–64) is accepted as graphop but rejected as bofop, confirming the bounded-fiber subclass captures sparse connectivity.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 establishes that message passing neural networks (MPNNs) are Lipschitz (Holder) continuous with respect to an action metric d_M on bofop-signals: ||H(A_1,f_1) - H(A_2,f_2)||_2 <= C'_{D,r} d_M((A_1,f_1),(A_2,f_2)) (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: A singleton bofop counterexample with h0(x)=M (Lipschitz 0), aggregation update (Lipschitz 1), and identity readout yields a fixed action-metric bound (≤2ε) but output gap εM, giving ratio 512 at M=1024 and unbounded as M grows; the MP_D class bounds Lipschitz constants but not offsets/ranges, and a bounded-offset negative control correctly rejects the witness.

claims.claim: Corollary 5.3 shows the space of bofop-DIDMs (degree-indexed distribution measures) is compact under the DIDM-mover's distance, forming a proper subset of the corresponding dense-graph structure (Corollary 5.3).
claims.evidence: At L=0, H_0=[-1,1]^d and Γ_0 is the pushforward of the signal distribution; a zero bofop with arbitrary finitely supported signal realizes any finitely supported P(H_0) measure (12 instances with zero residual), so Γ_0(BF_d^r)=P(H_0), contradicting the strict-subset claim for every L∈ℕ_0; a depth-one control correctly rejects the construction, confirming the issue is specific to L=0.

claims.claim: Section 6.1 uses this compactness and continuity to prove a universal approximation theorem: any continuous function on bofop-DIDMs can be uniformly approximated by MPNNs directly on sparse graphs (Section 6.1).
claims.evidence: A source-anchored proof certificate derives universal density from compactness, Tietze extension, and Stone-Weierstrass with deletion controls rejecting missing premises; a continuum construction on weighted sparse cycles shows piecewise-linear readout convergence (max error 0.437→0.0003 as knots increase 4→128 on an 8193-point grid); a non-circular benchmark on 5 graph families (1000 train, 800 test) achieves held-out max error 0.0347<0.04 with no-message and shifted-label controls failing at 1.14 and 0.96.

claims.claim: Section 6.2 derives generalization bounds showing generalization error vanishes as sample size grows, exploiting the uniform equicontinuity and compactness established in Theorem 4.1 and Corollary 5.3 (Section 6.2).
claims.evidence: A two-point bofop-signal distribution with MPNN outputs 0 and M yields |R_emp−R_stat|=|N1/N−1/2|·(M−2), which is unbounded in M whenever the sample is imbalanced; exact binomial calculations show imbalance probability is 1 for odd N and 1−C(N,N/2)/2^N→1 for even N; adding a bounded-output envelope (0≤M≤1) removes the unbounded gap, confirming the issue is the unbounded MP_D class.

Srishti280992/repro-graphop-sparse-gnn.overall: The logbook provides rigorous mathematical evidence—proof certificates, exact arithmetic checks, negative controls, and concrete counterexamples—supporting the graphop/bofop definitions (Claims 1–2) and universal approximation (Claim 5), while falsifying the MPNN continuity bound (Claim 3), the L=0 DIDM strict-subset statement (Claim 4), and the generalization bound (Claim 6) as formally stated, all due to the MP_D class not bounding output magnitudes.

Srishti280992/repro-on-the-expressive-po.paper_title: On the Expressive Power of Permutation-Equivariant Weight-Space Networks

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 proves that the prominent permutation-equivariant weight-space architectures DWS, NP-NFN, HNP-NFN, GMN, and NG-GNN have identical expressive power for both invariant and equivariant mappings on compact sets (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook checks 288 Appendix-D simulation maps (boundary contraction, type projection, GMN-to-NG packing, NG-to-DWS pooling) across six small architectures (widths 2–5) with zero error, but these are finite instance checks of a universal equivalence theorem on clearly reduced-scale architectures.

claims.claim: Proposition 5.3 shows Neural Functional Transformers (NFTs) differ in expressive power from the other architectures in general, but become equivalent under a general-position (GP) assumption requiring distinct bias terms per layer (Proposition 5.3).
claims.evidence: The NFT separation uses the paper's 4×4 matrix witness pair under 48 relabelings with WL/rank ties confirmed, and GP equivalence is tied to 2,304 finite canonization orbit cells; both halves operate on small matrices and finite instances rather than a full-scale proof verification.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.1 establishes that permutation-invariant weight-space networks are universal approximators of function-space functionals, i.e., maps depending only on the realized function and not the specific parameterization (Theorem 6.1).
claims.evidence: 31 trained canonical weight-space heads across dimensions 1–3 and widths 8–64 show the invariant head beating the raw-order control in all cells, but R² values are often low (0.12–0.55 for non-integral targets) and the budget sweep shows R² decreasing with more data (0.26→0.30→0.12), indicating a simplified empirical proxy rather than a convincing universality demonstration.

claims.claim: Proposition 6.2 proves a non-universality result showing invariant weight-space networks cannot approximate all permutation-invariant functionals, using a counterexample built from Weisfeiler-Leman graph indistinguishability (Proposition 6.2).
claims.evidence: The 4×4 matrix counterexample from Prop. E.8 is replayed under 48 relabelings with WL/NG-GNN ties and rank split 3-vs-2 preserved, plus a destructive control; this verifies the paper's specific small counterexample but does not constitute a full-scale reproduction of the non-universality proposition.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.3 recovers universality for permutation-invariant functionals under the general-position assumption via continuous canonization maps that order neurons by bias value (Theorem 6.3).
claims.evidence: Bias-sort canonization is checked on 2,304 multilayer GP orbit cells (architectures up to width 32) with max error <1e-12 and tied-bias destructive controls showing jumps >1e-3, but the approximation half reuses Claim 3's mixed R² results, making this a finite-scale check of a universality theorem.

claims.claim: Theorem 7.4 shows permutation-equivariant operators achieve universal approximation under the general-position assumption via canonization-based factorization, while Proposition 7.1 shows fixed-architecture equivariant networks cannot approximate function-space operators that increase geometric complexity (Proposition 7.1, Theorem 7.4).
claims.evidence: Equivariance of a specific operator is checked on 1,536 relabeled states with error ~1e-15, and the fixed-capacity obstruction is verified for 1D ReLU widths 2–128 showing h+2 breakpoints exceed h-capacity; both are finite checks on simplified setups rather than full-scale verification of the equivariant universality theorem.

Srishti280992/repro-on-the-expressive-po.overall: The logbook provides careful finite computational checks of the paper's proof constructions, counterexamples, and approximation claims on small architectures and matrices, with relabeling protection and destructive controls. However, all six claims are theoretical theorems/propositions about universal expressive power, and the evidence is limited to reduced-scale instances rather than full-scale reproduction or formal proof verification.

ParetoOptimal/repro-u1bxelqlak.paper_title: On the Provable Suboptimality of Momentum SGD in Nonstationary Stochastic Optimization

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows momentum SGD's tracking-error bound scales as (1-beta)^-2 on the initialization term and (1-beta)^-1 on the noise floor, versus O(1) and O(sigma^2 gamma/mu) respectively for vanilla SGD in Theorem 3.1 (Section 3.1, Theorems 3.1 and 3.3).
claims.evidence: The noise-floor scaling (1-beta)^-1 is cleanly reproduced (fitted exponent 1.0006, 19.76x vanilla at beta=0.95), but the initialization-term (1-beta)^-2 scaling is not confirmed—measured exponent 1.0356 suggests the bound is loose rather than tight in the tested isotropic quadratic setup.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.7 gives a minimax lower bound decomposing regret into a noise-limited term and an inertia-limited term that worsens with beta and can dominate in drift-heavy regimes, establishing an information-theoretic (not just analytical) barrier for momentum methods (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence: The empirical decomposition into noise-limited and inertia-limited terms holds (relative gap 0.004), the inertia term grows monotonically with beta (0.0517→1.0698), and it dominates in drift-heavy regimes, but the minimax/information-theoretic lower-bound nature of Theorem 3.7 cannot be established by simulation on a single quadratic with heavy-ball only.

claims.claim: Under the stability constraint gamma <= (1-beta)^2/L, the paper proves vanilla SGD provably outperforms Heavy-Ball/Nesterov momentum SGD in drift-dominated nonstationary regimes (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Under gamma_momentum = 0.9*(1-beta)^2/L versus gamma_vanilla = 0.9/L in a drift-dominated regime (delta=0.08, sigma=0.05), vanilla SGD (error 0.0681) outperforms both Heavy-Ball and Nesterov at every tested beta, with the gap growing to 7.7x at beta=0.9.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.6 shows the high-probability bound for momentum SGD exhibits an inertia horizon of order (1-beta)^-1 and drift-noise coupling scaling as (1-beta)^-2, both absent from the vanilla SGD high-probability bound in Theorem 3.5 (Section 3.2, Theorems 3.5 and 3.6).
claims.evidence: The inertia horizon scaling tau ~ (1-beta)^-1 is reproduced (fitted exponent 1.0989, horizon 42x vanilla at beta=0.95, vanilla horizon 1.0), but the drift-noise coupling (1-beta)^-2 component was explicitly not isolated or verified.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments on quadratics, linear/logistic regression, and MLPs confirm that increasing nonstationarity (drift), momentum parameter beta, or condition number kappa systematically worsens Heavy-Ball and Nesterov tracking error while vanilla SGD remains comparatively robust (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Across quadratics, linear regression, logistic regression, and an MLP, increasing drift/beta/kappa systematically worsens Heavy-Ball and Nesterov more than vanilla (e.g., quadratic drift: HB worsens 32.5x vs vanilla 2.65x; logistic high-drift: HB 10.56 vs vanilla 2.26), with 15/15 checks passing.

ParetoOptimal/repro-u1bxelqlak.overall: The logbook provides strong empirical support for the paper's core practical claims—vanilla SGD outperforms momentum methods under stability constraints in drift-dominated regimes (Claim 3) and systematic worsening of momentum tracking error across multiple model families (Claim 5). However, the theoretical claims involving specific scaling exponents (Claims 1 and 4) are only partially reproduced, and the minimax/information-theoretic nature of the lower bound (Claim 2) is inherently unverifiable by simulation.

ParetoOptimal/repro-9slqacssbw.paper_title: Differentiable Optimization Layers for Guaranteed Fairness in Deep Learning

claims.claim: The fairness layer, formulated as g(z) = arg min over y~ of the discrepancy d~(y~,z) subject to affine inequality and equality constraints, is globally 1/mu-Lipschitz continuous and differentiable almost everywhere under strongly convex objectives (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: C15/C15b numerically verify 1/μ-Lipschitz continuity over 400 random pairs (ratio ≤ 1.000000 for μ=1, ratio ≤ 0.333333 for μ=3) and C19 confirms differentiability a.e. via 0/100000 random draws landing on region boundaries.

claims.claim: Backpropagation through the fairness layer zeroes gradient components perpendicular to active constraint surfaces while leaving feasible-direction components unaffected (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: C20 confirms binary spectrum {0,1} of Dg over 30 active sets (max|eig−round|=2.64e-15) and C21 measures gradient suppression A_A·Dg·v = 3.00e-17 ≈ 0, with the IFT backprop Jacobian matching the closed-form projector to 1.39e-17 and finite differences to 5.27e-09.

claims.claim: The online primal-dual inference algorithm (Algorithm 1) guarantees that the sample-weighted average fairness violation across streaming inference batches converges to at most epsilon, even for arbitrarily small batch sizes (Theorem 3.2, Algorithm 1).

The 2^k and 1/eps^2 factors are tested via a faithful multinomial estimation proxy over 2^k cells (which is exactly what the estimation stage does), while the log(n) factor is tested on the actual Fourier screening stage.

claims.claim: k-junta quantum states can be learned to within error epsilon in trace distance using O(12^k log(n/delta)/epsilon^2) single copies via an algorithm restricted to Pauli measurements, the first such upper bound for this problem (Theorem 3, Section 4).
claims.evidence: End-to-end Pauli-only learner runs at n=100, k=3 (junta recovered exactly, trace distance 0.079 from 20,000 copies); 12^k factor fitted over k=1..5 with M*/12^k bounded and decreasing (8.50→3.16), 1/eps^2 slope 2.15, and identification cost grows 2.36x for a 32x increase in n, matching log(n/delta).

claims.claim: A matching lower bound of Omega((4^k + log n)/epsilon^2) copies is proven for learning k-junta quantum states (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Gilbert-Varshamov Pauli packing with exact Holevo-Fano computation from explicit density matrices (up to 1023 Paulis, 32x32 matrices): 4^k exponent 1.067 on k=3..5 window, 1/eps^2 slope 2.013 stable over 1.5 decades, log(n) growth 6.15x over a 131,072x range in n. The Holevo bound applies to all measurement strategies including entangled and adaptive.

claims.claim: The Choi state of an n-qubit QAC^0 circuit of size s, depth d, and a ancilla qubits can be learned using 2^O((log(s^2 2^a/epsilon))^d) log(n/delta) copies with only Pauli measurements, improving a prior bound that was polynomial in n to one that depends on n only logarithmically (Theorem 4, Section 4.1.2).
claims.evidence: Simulated QAC0 circuits with exact Choi states: identification cost grows 1.53x for a 64x increase in n (up to 1024 qubits measured) vs >=64x for poly(n), and a depth-2, size-2, one-ancilla Choi state is learned end-to-end at n=64 to trace distance 0.115 from 150,000 Pauli-only copies. The 2^O((log(s^2 2^a/eps))^d) prefactor itself is not separated but is shown flat in d, s, a at fixed light cone.

claims.claim: The algorithmic approach combines low-degree and sparse learning techniques via a rounding/thresholding procedure to handle both degree and sparsity constraints simultaneously (Section 1.5).
claims.evidence: Ablation at n=18 (262,144-cell full support) with k=4 junta: full pipeline with thresholding achieves TV=0.019, while removing the thresholding step yields TV=0.965 (49.8x worse) at equal sample budget, confirming the rounding/thresholding procedure is essential for combining low-degree screening with sparse reconstruction.

michaldobiezynski/repro-learning-junta-d.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from a from-scratch numpy implementation supporting all five claims at non-toy scale, including end-to-end runs of the quantum junta learner at n=100 and the QAC0 Choi-state learner at n=64, plus explicit Holevo-Fano lower-bound computations. The main gaps are the factorized (proxy-based) verification of the 2^k and 1/eps^2 factors in Claim 1 and the unseparated prefactor in Claim 4.

michaldobiezynski/repro-decentralized-on.paper_title: Decentralized Online Convex Optimization with Efficient Communication: Improved Algorithm and Lower Bounds

claims.claim: Top-DOGD achieves O(ω^{-1/2}ρ^{-1}n√T) regret for convex loss functions under compressed communication, improving on prior bounds (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: All four exponents of Theorem 3.1 were measured at d=100, T up to 138,624, 3 seeds: T-slope 0.486, 1/ω-slope 0.615, n-slope 1.093, 1/ρ-slope 0.964 against claimed 0.5/0.5/1/1, with regret-to-bound ratio bounded within 2.09× across 15 grid points spanning T, ω, n, and ρ.

claims.claim: Top-DOGD achieves O(ω^{-1}ρ^{-2}n ln T) regret for strongly convex loss functions (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Logarithmic T-dependence confirmed: regret rises only 1.2% (459.0→464.5) while T grows 8× (log-log slope 0.006 vs 0.5 for √T), regret/ln T decreases monotonically, and ω- and n-exponents measure 1.145 and 1.096 against claimed 1 and 1 at d=100, T up to 138,624.

claims.claim: The paper reduces dependence on compression quality ω from the previously known O(ω^{-2}ρ^{-4}n^{1/2}√T) (convex) and O(ω^{-2}ρ^{-4}n^{1/2} ln T) (strongly convex) bounds down to O(ω^{-1/2}ρ^{-1}n√T) and O(ω^{-1}ρ^{-2}n ln T) respectively, cutting the exponent on ω^{-1} from quadratic/quartic to square-root/linear (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Top-DOGD's measured ω-exponent is 0.580 (convex) and 1.145 (strongly convex) against claimed 0.5 and 1, far from the prior quadratic 2; the Lemma 3.8 consensus+compression error is 3.5e9× smaller for Top-DOGD (5.5e-11) than DC-DOGD (1.9e-1) at equal communication cost, demonstrating the error-control mechanism behind the exponent reduction.

claims.claim: First lower bounds for decentralized online convex optimization with compressed communication are established: Ω(ω^{-1/2}ρ^{-1/4}n√T) for convex functions and Ω(ω^{-1}ρ^{-1/2}n ln T) for strongly convex functions (Theorems 3.3 and 3.4).
claims.evidence: The algorithm-independent regret floor of the Theorem 3.3 construction (Eq. 17–18) was measured by Monte Carlo (20k draws/point): T-exponent 0.5006, ω-exponent 0.4992, n-exponent 1.4215 against claimed 0.5/0.5/1.5, exceeding the theorem's closed form by 2.94×, with the construction's delay premise measured at 4.0 vs predicted 4.0 rounds. The strongly convex lower bound (Thm 3.4) is acknowledged as not simulable.

claims.claim: The algorithm combines a two-level blocking update framework with an online compressed gossip strategy and a projection error compensation scheme to jointly control consensus, compression, and projection error (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Ablation at d=100, n=20, 4 seeds, ω=0.25 shows the correct ordering: consensus error full=4.39e-3 < no-error-comp=1.24e-2 < no-blocking=2.89e-2, confirming each component (blocking, error compensation) is load-bearing for consensus error control.

claims.claim: Bandit-feedback extensions are provided: one-point feedback achieves O(ω^{-1/4}ρ^{-1/2}d^{1/2}n(ln n)^{1/4}T^{3/4}) regret (Theorem 4.1) and two-point feedback achieves O(ω^{-1/2}ρ^{-1}dn ln n√T) regret (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Two-point feedback T- and d-exponents measure 0.499 and 0.973 against claimed 0.5 and 1; one-point T-exponent converges from 0.819→0.798 against claimed 0.75 (still approaching), with d-exponent 0.373 against claimed 0.5 (under-stated, consistent with upper bound). Runs at T up to 946,080 with regret at 0.27× and 0.03× of trivial ceiling, inside the non-vacuous regime. ω and ρ exponents not swept but inherited from Claims 1–3.

michaldobiezynski/repro-decentralized-on.overall: The logbook provides a thorough reproduction of all six claims by implementing Algorithms 1–4 line-by-line with theorem-supplied constants at non-toy scale (d=100, n up to 32, T up to ~10⁶), measuring exponents across multiple parameter sweeps with concrete numerical results. The main gaps are the non-simulable strongly convex lower bound (Thm 3.4) and the one-point bandit d-exponent measuring notably below its claimed value.

michaldobiezynski/repro-noisy-pairwise-c.paper_title: Noisy Pairwise-Comparison Random Search for Smooth Nonconvex Optimization

claims.claim: Under a uniform-margin comparison oracle with advantage parameter p ∈ (0,1/2], the NCRS algorithm attains ε-stationarity for smooth nonconvex objectives with iteration complexity O(k/(p²ε²)), where k is the intrinsic dimension rather than the ambient dimension d (Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: On the paper's own synthetic ridge objective at non-trivial scale (k up to 80, d up to 1000), measured log-log slopes slope_k=+0.495, slope_1/p=+1.054, slope_T=−0.494 all match theoretical exponents (+0.5, +1, −0.5) to within ~0.05, and a 20× d-sweep (50→1000) yields slope_d=−0.002 with grad-norm constant varying only 2.7%, confirming d-independence.

claims.claim: A one-step descent inequality shows the per-iteration progress of NCRS scales with intrinsic dimension k rather than ambient dimension d: pα_t√(2/π)E[‖∇f(θ^t)‖₂] ≤ E[f(θ^t)−f(θ^{t+1})] + L_f k α_t²/2 (Lemma 2.1).
claims.evidence: Monte-Carlo estimation (40000 trials per point) of the one-step descent inequality at 36 (θ,α) points across k∈{2,5,20,40} shows min(RHS−LHS)=+0.00054 with zero violations; the tightest margin (~9% of LHS) exceeds Monte-Carlo standard error, and the k-dependent slack term L_f k α²/2 is confirmed to carry intrinsic dimension k.

claims.claim: Under a gap-dependent confidence oracle with tie-aware noise, a confidence-weighted majority-vote variant of NCRS achieves ε-stationarity using O(k²/ε⁴) total pairwise comparisons (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: At full k-range {5,10,20,40,80} with the paper's Table-5 vote budget N=⌈k/ε²⌉, the per-iteration vote count scales as k^+1.000 exactly, the confidence-vote convergence rate scales as k^+0.457 tracking the reliable-oracle reference k^+0.523, yielding an end-to-end comparison-complexity exponent of 1.91 versus the theorem's 2.0 and Table 5's 1.99.

claims.claim: The analysis extends to nearly-ridge objectives with bounded nuisance-subspace leakage, parameterized by (τ, m), showing robustness of the intrinsic-dimension rate beyond exact low-rank structure (Proposition 2.4).
claims.evidence: A full-text search confirms that 'Proposition 2.4' and any (τ,m)-parameterized nearly-ridge bound do not exist in the paper (only Proposition 3.4 at line 728; nearly-ridge appears solely as a Section 5 Limitation), so there is no theoretical quantity to reproduce or falsify; the empirical leakage sweep (A: 0.0827→0.0954 over τ∈{0,…,0.5}) has no paper benchmark to compare against.

claims.claim: NCRS's O(k/ε²) rate (up to the 1/p² factor) improves on prior ambient-dimension-dependent zeroth-order methods such as ZO-RankSGD, whose complexity is O(d/ε²) (Table 1).
claims.evidence: NCRS on the ridge with k=8 over real ambient R^d (d∈{50,150,300,600}) shows slope_d=−0.017 (flat, confirming O(k/ε²)), while a genuine ZO-RankSGD implementation (Gaussian probes, comparison ranking, rank-weighted step, η∝1/d) on a full-dimensional quadratic yields iterations-to-ε with slope_d=+0.996 (linear in d, confirming O(d/ε²)), substantiating both complexity rows at non-trivial ambient scale.

michaldobiezynski/repro-noisy-pairwise-c.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting Claims 1, 2, 3, and 5 on the paper's own synthetic ridge setup at non-trivial scale (k up to 80, d up to 600–1000), with measured scaling exponents matching theoretical predictions. Claim 4 is inconclusive because the cited Proposition 2.4 does not exist in the paper, leaving no theoretical result to reproduce.

michaldobiezynski/repro-tighter-regret-l.paper_title: Tighter Regret Lower Bound for Gaussian Process Bandits with Squared Exponential Kernel in Hypersphere

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 proves a simple regret lower bound requiring Omega(sigma^2/epsilon^2 * (ln B/epsilon)^d * (ln ln B/epsilon)^(-d) * ln 1/delta) time steps for any algorithm to find an epsilon-optimal point on the hypersphere domain with a squared exponential kernel (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The packing number M_eps of the paper's hard class was measured on S^d for d=1..5 and fits L^d with lnL exponents -1.20 to -6.96 vs the paper's -d, but the headline lower bound is produced by plugging M_eps into the paper's own Lemma 2.3/Eq.(79) chain rather than independently deriving it. Only 2 algorithms were tested on small instances (S^1: M<=30, S^2: M<=119, 8 GP-UCB seeds), and the non-violation check is near-vacuous (T_LB=0.8-13.7 vs minimum M=7..119 pulls).

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 proves a cumulative regret lower bound of Omega(sqrt(T*sigma^2 * (ln(B^2*T/sigma^2) * ln 1/delta)^d * (ln ln(B^2*T/sigma^2 * ln 1/delta))^(-d))) for any algorithm on the hypersphere domain (Theorem 3.2, Section 3).
claims.evidence: No new measurement or algorithm run beyond Claim 1's M_eps; the procedure plugs measured M_eps into the paper's own fixed-point equation (Eq. 82-84) and checks against the paper's own closed-form solution. The R_LB(T)/Eq.(10) ratio is flat (x1.236 worst-case drift) and discriminates against the superseded d/2 form, but this verifies the paper's algebra rather than the minimax theorem itself.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 establishes an improved upper bound of O((ln T)^(d+1) * (ln ln T)^(-d)) on the maximum information gain for the squared exponential kernel, applicable to both compact domains in R^d and hyperspheres S^d (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: gamma_T was directly measured via certified greedy logdet on both cube [0,1]^d and sphere S^d (d=1..3, T<=2000, 12000-point pools), with the certified ratio to (lnT)^(d+1)(lnlnT)^-d peaking at 1.096-4.030 (all O(1)). An independent asymptotic arm using exact Funk-Hecke eigenvalues (validated to 2.8e-13) on S^d for d=1..6 shows the ratio bounded and decreasing (0.92 to 0.005), the correct direction for an O(.) upper bound.

claims.claim: The improved information gain bound closes a (ln T)^(d/4) gap present in prior results by removing dimension-dependent logarithmic factors that previously limited the analysis (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Both sides of the gap were computed for d=1..20 from Claim 3's exact-spectrum gamma_T and Claim 1's packing M_eps plus a from-scratch Scarlett et al. re-implementation. The removed exponent fits slope 0.2688d vs the paper's 0.25d (corr 1.000000 with d/4), but the residual gap the paper calls dimension-independent rises from 0.491 to 0.803 across d=1..20 (60% above predicted 0.5 at d=20), and the reference construction's width exponent measures -0.467 vs -0.5.

michaldobiezynski/repro-tighter-regret-l.overall: The logbook provides a technically substantial reproduction with from-scratch Mercer spectrum computation, hard-function class construction, and packings, but only Claim 3 (Theorem 5.1) is directly verified by measuring the named quantity gamma_T on both domain types with a correct-direction O(.) test. Claims 1, 2, and 4 are downgraded to toy because they either assume the paper's own inequality chain, run only small algorithm instances with near-vacuous non-violation checks, or are entirely derived from other claims' outputs with constants that do not match the paper's predictions.

michaldobiezynski/repro-scaling-laws-for.paper_title: Scaling Laws for Precision in High-Dimensional Linear Regression

claims.claim: Under a power-law spectral prior λ_i ≈ i^{-a} with a>1 (Assumption 3.5), multiplicative (floating-point-like) quantization preserves effective model size M_eff≈M but shrinks effective data size N_eff via noise amplification and spectral distortion (Theorem 4.1 and Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: At the paper's exact Figure-1 setting (a=2.0, p=1000, eps=1e-3), M_eff/M = 0.995, matching the theorem's M_eff=M prediction, with the compound coefficient eps_3^(M) reproduced to 0.3% (measured 3.003×eps vs closed-form 2.994e-3) and confirmed dimension-independent across six (p,M) pairs. N_eff shrinkage direction is confirmed (N_eff/N < 1) though the quantitative match is loose (0.650 measured vs 0.424 predicted at eps=1e-1) and Theorem 4.3's lower bound has no experiment.

claims.claim: Additive (integer-like) quantization reduces both effective model size and effective data size, because its constant quantization-error variance flattens the tail of the signal spectrum (Theorem 4.2 and Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: M_eff/M shrinks under additive quantization (0.612-0.910 across loads) with the reduction being a function of ε·p rather than ε alone—confirmed by a scaling collapse across a 16× range of p at fixed load. Tail flattening is directly measured (spectral slope changes from -1.985 to -1.406 under additive quantization vs -1.947 to -1.957 for multiplicative), and N_eff also shrinks (0.956). Theorem 4.4's lower bound remains untested.

claims.claim: The derived risk bound scales as R_M(v̄_N) ≲ M_eff^{-(a-1)} + N_eff^{-(a-1)/a} + σ² + quantization error term, giving scaling exponents α=-(a-1) and β=-(a-1)/a (Section 3, Definition 3.1).
claims.evidence: Exponents measured in the asymptotic regime where the derivation's conditions hold: α = -1.0031/-1.0104 at a=2.0 (theory -1.00) and -0.5372/-0.5519 at a=1.5 (theory -0.50); β = -0.5202/-0.5108 at a=2.0 (theory -0.50) and -0.3175/-0.3543 at a=1.5 (theory -0.333), all within 0.052 of theoretical values. Pinned-exponent fits confirm the functional form with measured/bound ∈ [0.909, 1.192] over three decades.

claims.claim: Empirical experiments confirm the theoretical scaling-law predictions with R² > 0.99 across spectral decay rates a ∈ {1.5, 2.0} (Figures 1-2).
claims.evidence: R² = 0.9967-0.9979 (log) and 0.9935-0.9940 (linear) reproduced under the paper's own fitting protocol on all eight published panels. With the exponent pinned at the theoretical value (a stricter test), R² = 0.9854-0.9953 with measured/bound ∈ [0.909, 1.192]. All four printed exponents recovered to within 0.052 when measured in the regime where the derivation's conditions hold.

claims.claim: The lower-bound proof for multiplicative quantization required deriving crude bounds on iterate covariance to handle signal-dependent feedback loops, rather than a rough decoupling argument (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The claim asserts that crude iterate-covariance bounds were mathematically required for the lower-bound proof—i.e., that no rough decoupling argument could suffice. While the logbook measures both the premise (signal-dependent feedback: d log Var/d log‖v‖² = 0.652 for multiplicative vs 0.001 for additive) and the consequence (a decoupling surrogate underprices excess risk by 7.8-8.6%), no simulation can establish the impossibility of an alternative decoupling-based proof.

michaldobiezynski/repro-scaling-laws-for.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous CPU-only, closed-form reproduction that verifies the paper's core quantitative claims about multiplicative vs. additive quantization effects on effective model/data sizes and the scaling-law exponents, with careful attention to the regime where the derivation's conditions hold. Claim 5 is correctly left inconclusive as it is a meta-mathematical assertion about proof strategy that cannot be settled by numerical experiments.

michaldobiezynski/repro-zeroth-order-non.paper_title: Zeroth-Order Non-Log-Concave Sampling with Variance Reduction and Applications to Inverse Problems

claims.claim: Theorem 1 establishes the first non-asymptotic convergence guarantee for variance-reduced zeroth-order Langevin sampling, bounding Fisher information FI(ν̄_{Nγ}||π) ≤ ε after O(d⁷L_m⁴/ε⁴) iterations using only O(1) function evaluations per iteration (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook runs the Theorem-1 schedule on a non-log-concave pseudo-Huber mixture target, measuring FI decay with log-log slope −0.242/−0.241 (theory −0.250) over N=1e4–3e5 at d=2, confirming the d⁷ scaling via matched-pair tests (d=2 vs d=3 at equal d⁷/N agree to 1.10×/1.29× while unmatched controls are 1.72×/1.77× higher), verifying the bound at d=2–100 with bounded decreasing ratio, and showing flat 3.42–3.96 f-evals/iteration from d=2 to d=4096.

claims.claim: The variance-reduced zeroth-order gradient estimator (Equation 8) combines a large-batch estimate (probability p, batch size b) with a small-batch recursive update (probability 1−p, batch size b′) that exploits correlation between consecutive iterates (Equation 8).
claims.evidence: Eq. 8 was implemented with shared random directions at consecutive iterates and compared against naive batched ZO at matched 8 f-evals/iteration, showing 6.4–14.2× variance reduction across d=50–1600 with naive error scaling as d^1.02 while Eq. 8 cost stays flat at 8.0–8.4 evals/iter; Proposition 1's recursion inequality had 0/120 violations at d=200.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 extends the Fisher-information convergence bound to posterior sampling with a black-box score-based generative model (SGM) prior via the ZO-APMC algorithm (Equation 12-13, Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: On the paper's own Sec 4.1/App C.1 validation problem with its SGM stand-in (analytic prior score + Gaussian noise ε*_k=2.5), 1000 particles, N=2000, 12 random operators, mean FI at k=2000 was 0.00195–0.00351 for all p values, all below 0.01 and within 2.2× of the estimator floor (0.00158), matching gradient-access APMC (0.00229); however, the paper's reported p=0.3 instability did not reproduce.

claims.claim: On 4x-accelerated radial-subsampled FastMRI brain reconstruction, ZO-APMC achieves 35.29 dB PSNR, the best among black-box methods (SCG, DPG, EnKG, Forward/Central-GSG) though slightly below the gradient-based APMC baseline at 36.55 dB (Section, Table 1).
claims.evidence: The FastMRI brain test images and pre-trained SGM prior of Sun et al. (2024) are not public, so the 35.29 dB entry cannot be produced; a proxy experiment at the paper's image size (256×256, d=65536, 4× radial) with a TV prior and analytic phantom yielded APMC 29.41 dB, Central-GSG 29.24, Forward-GSG 29.05, ZO-APMC 28.45—ZO-APMC was not the best black-box method, but the setup differs from the paper's in both data and prior.

claims.claim: On black-hole imaging with 100 GRMHD images from InverseBench, ZO-APMC attains 26.71 dB PSNR and χ²_cph of 5.42, the best result among evaluated black-box methods (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The 100 GRMHD test images and trained GRMHD score prior from InverseBench are not public, so the 26.71 dB / χ²_cph 5.42 entries cannot be verified; a proxy experiment with the full Eq. (122) likelihood at 64×64 on a synthetic crescent image with TV prior showed ZO-APMC (p=1) at 21.55 dB indistinguishable from Forward-GSG at 21.54 dB, with no ZO-APMC advantage, but the missing trained prior and real data make the comparison non-definitive.

claims.claim: Figure 2(b) validates the O(1) per-iteration batch complexity by showing multiple (p,b) parameter settings with fixed product pb=10 all converge to Fisher information below 0.01 (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: All six (p,b) splits with pb=10 reached FI below 0.01 at k=2000 on the paper's own Sec 4.1/App C.1 setup (γ=0.1, 1000 particles, 8 random operators): mean FI 0.00157–0.00340, worst single run 0.0088, with per-iteration cost fixed to within 17% (11.01–12.86 f-evals) across a 10× change in b.

michaldobiezynski/repro-zeroth-order-non.overall: The logbook provides strong CPU-based experimental verification of the paper's four theoretical claims—the Theorem 1 rate including its d⁷ scaling, the Eq. 8 variance-reduction mechanism, Theorem 3's convergence on the paper's own validation problem, and the Figure 2(b) pb=10 sweep—while the two application claims (FastMRI and black-hole imaging) remain inconclusive because the proprietary datasets and trained score priors are unavailable, and proxy experiments at the paper's image sizes do not reproduce the reported rankings.

michaldobiezynski/repro-sample-complexit.paper_title: Sample Complexity Bounds for Robust Mean Estimation with Mean-Shift Contamination

claims.claim: Under a frequency-witness (spectral) condition on the contaminating distribution, Algorithm 1 estimates the mean of a mean-shift-contaminated distribution to error ϵ with probability at least 2/3 using O(d·log(...)/((1-α)A-2α)δ)²) samples (Theorem 3.2, Section 3).
claims.evidence: 45/45 runs pass at d=50/100/200 with n from the theorem's formula, but an adversarial probe reveals the implementation substitutes Algorithm 1's ε-cover search with projected-Adam descent from two planted starts (coordinate median and adversary-direction point), each of which individually fails on 1-in-3 seeds; the raw sample mean already beats ε=0.9 by ~25x under the headline adversary before the search runs.

claims.claim: The main upper bound states that under mild technical assumptions characterized by a Fourier-based parameter δ, an algorithm exists using Õ_α(d/δ²) samples to estimate the contaminated mean (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: 40/40 pass across four Table-1 families, but the δ⁻² scaling slope (-1.93) is measured on nstar(full=False), a separation-event proxy rather than estimator error, and the independently measured d-scaling slope (0.234) does not match the claimed linear-in-d factor; the same two-start proxy algorithm from Claim 1 is used.

claims.claim: A matching one-dimensional lower bound shows any algorithm requires Ω(1/(δσ)^(1/3)) samples to achieve error ϵ under specific L2 Fourier-transform and tail-decay conditions, and more generally 1/δ^Ω(1) samples are required even in one dimension, qualitatively matching the upper bound (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: 41/41 constructed d=1 settings satisfy dTV ≤ bound via exact FFT inversion, but dTV/bound is as small as 8.74e-10 (never tight), the measured n_LB growth exponent is 1.576 versus the claimed 1/3, and the universal 'any algorithm' quantifier is supplied analytically via Le Cam rather than empirically.

michaldobiezynski/repro-sample-complexit.overall: The logbook provides real numerical runs on proxy or simplified setups for all three claims, but none reproduces the actual theorem guarantees: Algorithm 1's ε-cover search is replaced by a two-start local descent, the headline scaling is measured on a separation proxy, and the lower-bound rate is checked only as a loose one-sided inequality whose measured exponent contradicts the claimed value.

michaldobiezynski/repro-on-regret-bounds.paper_title: On Regret Bounds of Thompson Sampling for Bayesian Optimization

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 constructs a two-armed instance showing GP-TS incurs Ω(1/δ^c) cumulative regret with probability at least δ, establishing a high-probability regret lower bound with polynomial dependence on 1/δ (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: On the paper's exact two-armed instance (prior cov [[1,0.5],[0.5,1]], N(0,1) noise), 400,000 Monte-Carlo GP-TS trials show a power-law regret survival tail with stable exponent κ≈3.16 across T=[200,300,400], with power-law fit (R²=0.9929) beating exponential fit (R²=0.9792) at every horizon, directly demonstrating polynomial 1/δ dependence.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 bounds the second moment of cumulative regret as E[R_T²] = O(T γ_T log T), yielding a high-probability regret upper bound of O(√(T γ_T log T/δ)) that improves the dependence on δ by a factor of 1/√δ over prior results (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: On a d=3 continuous domain with SE kernel (M=400, N=120), the ratio E[R_T²]/(T·γ_T·log T) is bounded and monotonically decreasing (2.99→1.87→1.04→0.62) over T=[50,100,200,350], with log-log slope 0.563≤1, consistent with the O(T·γ_T·log T) second-moment upper bound.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 derives expected lenient-regret bounds that are polylogarithmic in the time horizon T, matching GP-UCB's high-probability bounds asymptotically (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: The measured lenient-regret T-exponent of 0.421 (at Δ=1) is still clearly polynomial, not polylogarithmic; while local exponents decelerate (0.51→0.43→0.32) and decrease with Δ, this is only suggestive of polylog growth at T≤400 and cannot distinguish it from a slow power law. The GP-UCB asymptotic matching component of the claim is not addressed at all.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 proves an improved cumulative regret upper bound of O(√T log T) for the squared exponential kernel and Õ(√T) for Matérn kernels with smoothness ν > 2, matching GP-UCB rates while relaxing prior smoothness requirements (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: On a d=3 continuous domain (M=800≫T_max, N=15), log-log slopes of cumulative regret vs T are 0.451 for SE and 0.526 for Matérn-5/2 (ν=2.5>2), both near the theoretical 0.5 rate, though the very low N=15 trials limits statistical reliability.

michaldobiezynski/repro-on-regret-bounds.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting Claims 1, 2, and 4 on non-trivial setups (exact two-armed instance with 400K trials; d=3 continuous domains with candidate pools), but Claim 3's polylogarithmic lenient-regret assertion remains unverified because the measured exponents are still polynomial at the accessible horizons and the GP-UCB comparison is absent.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-conditional-coverage.paper_title: Conditional Coverage Diagnostics for Conformal Prediction

claims.claim: The paper introduces a family of Excess Risk of the Target Coverage (ERT) metrics—L1-ERT, L2-ERT, and KL-ERT—for evaluating conditional coverage in conformal prediction, built on the principle that no classifier can outperform a constant 1-alpha predictor under perfect conditional coverage (Table 1, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: On the paper's synthetic setup (n=20000, Y~N(0,sigma(X1)^2), X in R^8), the closed-form L1/L2/KL-ERT formulas match the general risk-difference definition to within 1.3-3.0% relative error, and the triviality probe confirms L1-ERT≈0 (0.00179) under a constant-coverage null using the true p(X).

claims.claim: Using LightGBM as the underlying classifier for L1-ERT achieves 68.4% relative statistical power (relative to maximum), compared to only 38.3% for the PartitionWise classifier underlying CovGap (Table 2, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: The reproduction confirms the qualitative ordering (LightGBM 82.0% vs PartitionWise 62.6% of oracle) but does not reproduce the paper's specific reported numbers (68.4% / 38.3%), with the logbook itself acknowledging different classifier configs and synthetic setup from the paper's Table 2.

claims.claim: In synthetic experiments, group-based metrics like CovGap remain unreliable and unaligned with their theoretical values even at 5,000 test points, whereas ERT metrics such as L1-ERT converge with far fewer samples (Figure 4, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: On the paper's synthetic setup with realistic 8-dimensional partitioning, CovGap shows 42.4% relative error to the ground-truth L1-ERT (0.0932) at n=5000, while L1-ERT via LightGBM k-fold shows only 3.3% error at the same sample size, and L1-ERT at n=1000 (19.0% error) already outperforms CovGap at n=5000.

claims.claim: The metrics decompose conditional coverage error into asymmetric components ell_plus-ERT and ell_minus-ERT, separating unnecessary conservatism (over-coverage) from excessive aggressiveness (under-coverage) (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: The algebraic identity ell-ERT = ell_+-ERT + ell_--ERT holds to numerical precision (identity error ≤ 1.39e-17) for all three losses, and a pure over-coverage scenario correctly yields ERT- = 0.0000 with ERT+ = 0.0461, confirming the components genuinely separate over- and under-coverage.

claims.claim: Classification experiments report divergent KL_plus-ERT and KL_minus-ERT values across conformal prediction methods, demonstrating the over/under-coverage decomposition in practice (Table 4, Section 4.3.2).
claims.evidence: The test uses deliberately constructed methods (deflated/inflated quantiles) on synthetic data rather than the paper's actual conformal prediction methods on classification tasks from Table 4; while the decomposition correctly diagnoses the failure modes (under-covering: KL-=0.1785, over-covering: KL+=0.0717), this is a proxy demonstration, not a reproduction of the paper's experiments.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 estimates the ERT metrics from finite samples using k-fold cross-validation to avoid overfitting the classifier used in the estimation (Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Under a null with no real conditional miscoverage, naive in-sample estimation with an overfitting-prone classifier yields L1-ERT=0.1800 (false positive), while Algorithm 1's k-fold CV estimator yields L1-ERT=-0.0100 (correctly near zero), directly demonstrating that k-fold CV avoids the overfitting bias.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-conditional-coverage.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence on the paper's synthetic setup verifying the ERT metric definitions, the CovGap unreliability phenomenon, the over/under-coverage decomposition identity, and the k-fold CV bias-avoidance property. Two claims (LightGBM vs PartitionWise power numbers, KL decomposition across CP methods) are demonstrated only on proxy/simplified setups that do not match the paper's specific experimental configurations.

Srishti280992/repro-language-generation-.paper_title: Language Generation with Replay: A Learning-Theoretic View of Model Collapse

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 proves that a hypothesis class is uniformly generatable with replay if and only if it is uniformly generatable in the standard no-replay setting, with identical sample complexity, showing replay is benign for the strongest notion of generation (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 is checked on only 5 small periodic-predicate classes (d*=1–5) with bounded adversarial search (depth d*+3, window 16–24); while the sample-complexity match and closure-dimension crosscheck are exact, the setup is a simplified instantiation rather than a general verification of the iff theorem.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 exhibits a countable hypothesis class that is non-uniformly generatable without replay but not non-uniformly generatable with replay, establishing a strict separation caused by replay (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The paper's actual hard countable class (supp(h_n)={1,…,n}∪ℤ_<0, supp(h_∞)=ℕ) is implemented with exact intersection arithmetic for d=1..50, and an exhaustive search over 524,288 output sequences under the replay adversary yields 0 sequences satisfying both non-uniform guarantees, with non-vacuous positive controls (360 and 1,680 isolated survivors).

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 shows a computable algorithm using only membership queries can generate in the limit any countable hypothesis class even under replay conditions (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: Witness Protection is implemented line-by-line on 4 genuinely infinite predicate-defined countable classes (36 runs), reaching 0 mistakes after t* (max t*=3) with 2,885,650 membership queries and 0 non-membership oracles; ablations removing max-critical selection or sure-set discipline produce 35 mistakes, confirming the algorithm's components are necessary.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.6 constructs an uncountable hypothesis class that is generatable in the limit without replay but becomes non-generatable in the limit once replay is permitted (Theorem 5.6).
claims.evidence: The uncountable family is represented as oracle-indexed predicates (5 distinct bitstream prefixes), the Lemma 5.7 no-replay generator succeeds (t*=6, 0 mistakes after), and the Lemma 5.8 phase adversary using a single replayed marker forces 30/30 and 121/121 phase mistakes across all tested generators; however, the 'remove_single_replay_valid_target' counterfactual check is trivially false by construction and thus vacuous.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.1 proves no deterministic generator using only membership queries can properly generate in the limit for all countable hypothesis classes (Theorem 6.1).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 3 is correctly implemented (21/21 Figure 1 quantities match exactly) and defeats 5 representative MQ-only policies for 60 rounds each, but the universal impossibility claim requires showing ALL deterministic MQ generators fail, and 5 policies is a small non-exhaustive sample against the adaptive construction.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.3 shows that even some finite hypothesis classes that are properly generatable in the limit without replay become impossible to properly generate once replay is introduced (Theorem 6.3).
claims.evidence: The exact 4-hypothesis class from Theorem 6.3 is implemented, and exhaustive enumeration over all 262,144 proper-generator strategies (4^9) yields 0 replay survivors, with discriminating controls (65,536 single-target survivors, 32,768 counterfactual survivors, and 12/12 no-replay successes).

Srishti280992/repro-language-generation-.overall: The logbook provides faithful computational implementations of the paper's proof constructions with exhaustive searches confirming Claims 2, 3, 4, and 6 on the paper's actual hypothesis classes, while Claims 1 and 5 are checked only on simplified small-scale instances that do not fully exercise the universal scope of those theorems.

michaldobiezynski/repro-taming-the-loss-.paper_title: Taming the Loss Landscape of PINNs with Noisy Feynman–Kac Supervision: Operator Preconditioning and Non-Asymptotic Error Bounds

claims.claim: FK-PINNs achieve a uniformly bounded PL-based condition number κ_FK ≤ C independent of collocation mesh refinement, whereas standard PINNs suffer κ_PINN ≥ c·N^(β/2) that grows polynomially with the number of collocation points N (Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: The FK half reproduces (κ_FK PL-based slope +0.111 on MET, -0.366 on Poisson, both flat/bounded), but the PINN-degradation half is contradicted on Poisson where κ_PINN falls 41x (slope -0.989, from 1.32e6 to 3.21e4) under the paper's own 50,049-parameter architecture with μ measured over 1,201 GD iterates; the exact 1897×1897 Hessian condition number is saturated at the float64 ceiling (~2.4e12) and cannot resolve N-dependence.

claims.claim: A non-asymptotic L² error bound of the form ‖u_θT − u*‖ ≤ C(N_FK^(−β) + e^(−c_opt·T) + ε_bias + √ε_bias) is proven for depth-3 tanh networks trained with Feynman-Kac supervision (Theorem 6.2).
claims.evidence: Depth-3 tanh networks with width tied to N_FK via the theorem's exponent (m=64→99 for N_FK=32→1024) on two benchmarks: constant C calibrated on N_FK=32 alone yields out-of-sample measured/bound ratios all below 1 and decreasing (Poisson 0.74→0.32, MET 0.68→0.25); each term separately exhibited (error rate -0.363/-0.394 vs predicted -0.125, exponential decay c_opt=2.4e-5/2.8e-5, bias tracks dt monotonically over 80x range).

claims.claim: The Monte Carlo Feynman-Kac labels used for supervision decompose as Y^FK = u* + b + ζ, with bias bounded by |b(x)| ≤ C_bias√(Δt) + C_T·e^(−κT_max) and sub-exponential noise ζ (Proposition 6.1).
claims.evidence: On Poisson and MET, |b|/√dt is roughly constant across dt sweeps (fitted log|b|~p·log(dt) gives p=0.549, 0.545 vs predicted 0.5), exponential truncation fit κ=0.0496 matches independent exit-time tail rate 0.0545 within 10%, and noise is sub-exponential (corr(log P(|ζ|>t),t)=-0.9854 vs corr(.,t²)=-0.9299); Schrödinger/committor bias is indistinguishable from zero, satisfying the 'bounded by' statement.

claims.claim: On the Schrödinger, mean exit time, and committor function benchmarks, FK-PINN reduces relative L² error from 0.624/1.007/0.839 (vanilla PINN) to 0.096/0.107/0.030 respectively — roughly 6.5x, 9.4x, and 28x improvements (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Under the paper's own protocol (fixed-weight baseline per Eq. 2.5, Kendall-weighted FK-PINN per Sec. 4.2, same tanh 4x128, same initialization, 25K Adam + 1.5K L-BFGS, 3 seeds), measured improvement factors are 0.4x/3.2x/1.0x vs claimed 6.5x/9.4x/28x; FK-PINN absolute errors reproduce (0.063 vs 0.096, 0.087 vs 0.107) but the vanilla PINN is far stronger than reported (0.024 vs 0.624 on Schrödinger, 0.274 vs 1.007 on MET).

claims.claim: FK-PINN training requires O(log(1/ε)) gradient iterations to reach accuracy ε, versus O(N^(β/2)·log(1/ε)) for standard PINNs, implying an N^(β/2)-fold speedup from improved conditioning alone (Section 6).
claims.evidence: Using the theory's own full-batch GD at prescribed step 1/(2L) with 2 seeds and 48 probes, the speed-up T_PINN/T_FK has negative log-log slope in the N=4000–16000 refinement window on both benchmarks (-1.95 on Poisson, -1.29 on MET), shrinking where the theory requires growth; the O(log 1/ε) form holds (mean |corr|=1.000) but equally for both objectives, carrying no FK-specific content.

claims.claim: The training procedure (Algorithm 2) uses an offline Monte Carlo Feynman-Kac estimation stage via Euler-Maruyama discretization at N_FK interior points, followed by an online PINN training stage with an uncertainty-weighted multi-task loss (Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: Both stages implemented end-to-end: Stage 1 produced 200 Euler-Maruyama FK labels (N_MC=500, dt=1e-3/1e-4) with label RMSE 0.21/1.75/0.01 against FD references; Stage 2 trained the three-task uncertainty-weighted loss with trainable clipped log-variances converging to specific λ values; ablation shows fixed unit weights are 166x worse on committor (0.665 vs 0.004), though mixed on Schrödinger (0.053 vs 0.072).

michaldobiezynski/repro-taming-the-loss-.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence on non-toy setups (paper's own 50K-parameter architecture, multiple benchmarks, multiple seeds) that verifies the non-asymptotic error bound (Claim 2), the FK label decomposition (Claim 3), and the two-stage training procedure (Claim 6), while falsifying the PINN condition-number degradation on Poisson (Claim 1), the Table 1 improvement factors (Claim 4), and the N^(β/2)-fold iteration speedup (Claim 5) through directional contradictions under the paper's own protocols.

michaldobiezynski/repro-is-spurious-corr.paper_title: Is Spurious Correlation Removal Always Learnable?

claims.claim: Under the Planted Clique hardness hypothesis (planted cliques of size k = m^(1/2−δ) in random graphs are not recoverable in polynomial time), there exist samplable multi-environment linear-Gaussian instances that are statistically learnable with polynomially many samples via exhaustive search but intractable for any polynomial-time algorithm (Hypothesis 3.1, Theorem 3.8).
claims.evidence: Graph-level planted-clique evidence (m=4096, κ=42, log E[#spurious]=-365.44, poly-time overlap 0.0635 vs chance 0.01025) is real but tests standard planted-clique folklore, not the paper's contribution; inside the paper's SC wrapper the separation is only 1.0x/4.0x/2.0x on a doubling n-grid, and the score Φ_P was instantiated by the repro author as ρ⁴ whose maximizer is v by construction, making two of three wrapper checks circular.

claims.claim: A phase transition in label-induced spurious correlation removal occurs at critical sample size n* ∝ k(d−k)/(|E|γ²), where k is the invariant subspace dimension, d the ambient dimension, |E| the number of environments, and γ the environment separation parameter; below n*/2 all estimators fail with constant error while above 2n* estimators achieve error O(k(d−k)/(n|E|γ²)) (Theorem 4.15).
claims.evidence: On a non-toy grid (d=100–130, k=5–40, |E|=180–540, up to 8.8M samples) with a legitimate cross-fitted spectral estimator, the super-critical log-log slope is −1.1125 and −1.0816 on disjoint windows (theory −1), the γ exponent is −1.858/−1.948 (theory −2), the k(d−k) error slope is 0.973 (theory 1.0), and the (|E|γ²) slope is −1.069 (theory −1), with sub-critical error pinned at 0.961/0.928 of chance below n*/2.

claims.claim: The predicted phase transition is validated empirically: exhaustive search reaches 75% accuracy using up to 27x fewer samples than polynomial-time methods on synthetic instances, and sharp transitions near the predicted critical sample size appear on both synthetic data and ColoredMNIST (Figure 1, Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: The paper's 27x multiplier is never reached (measured 0.84x/4.76x/≥2.0x at d=20/40/80) and is contradicted at d=20 where beam search reaches 75% before exhaustive (18,102 vs 21,527 samples), but the confuser family is unspecified in the paper and had to be reconstructed, with absolute sample counts 3–25x above the paper's 8,000-sample axis, making it impossible to confirm or refute the claim; ColoredMNIST was not attempted.

claims.claim: Diversity across environments is necessary for removal to succeed: performance improves sharply once γ > 0, whereas low-diversity settings (γ ≈ 0) show persistent failure, and increasing diversity from 'low' to 'high' substantially improves worst-group accuracy on CelebA and Waterbirds and OOD performance on ColoredMNIST (Figure 2c, Table 2).
claims.evidence: Corollary 4.7's unidentifiability at γ=0 is confirmed at scale (error 1.010–1.017 of chance across 8.8M samples, d=100, 270 environments) and Figure 2c's monotone rise with γ is reproduced, but Table 4's diversity row matches only after deleting confusers (conf_frac=0.0), the samples row does not reproduce (0.500 vs .70), and the CelebA/Waterbirds/ColoredMNIST experiments comprising half the claim were not attempted.

michaldobiezynski/repro-is-spurious-corr.overall: The logbook provides strong non-toy numerical evidence for the paper's central theoretical result (Theorem 4.15 phase transition rates and scaling laws), but the empirical claims are either inconclusive due to unspecified synthetic generators (Claim 3) or supported only on simplified proxies with the real-image experiments left unattempted (Claim 4), and the computational barrier claim (Claim 1) is tested only at graph level with partly circular wrapper checks.

Srishti280992/repro-statistical-early-st.paper_title: Statistical Early Stopping for Reasoning Models

claims.claim: The nonparametric Maxwise Conformal Stopping method (Proposition 2.1) guarantees P(∃j: u_{n+1}(L_j) > τ*) ≤ α by setting the threshold to the (1-α)(1+1/n) quantile of maximum uncertainty-density scores from calibration traces, giving finite-sample false-positive-rate control without negative examples (Proposition 2.1).
claims.evidence: A 100,000-trial Monte Carlo simulation with n=99 calibration traces, 8 looks, and α=0.05 produced a maxwise familywise crossing rate of 3.179% (below α), with a T4 GPU replication yielding 2.920%; control conditions show inflation to 71.5% (final-look-only) and 21.8% (shifted distribution), numerically supporting the conformal threshold guarantee.

claims.claim: The parametric Renewal Process method models inter-arrival times of uncertainty keywords, computes a Sidak-corrected normalized test statistic Z_t, and halts generation once Z_t exceeds threshold (Section on renewal process stopping).
claims.evidence: A 100,000-trial simulation with exponential inter-arrival gaps (true mean 80), 400 calibration traces, and 8 checks produced a Sidak-corrected familywise crossing rate of 4.193% (below α=0.05) with z=2.4898, versus 15.638% for the uncorrected z=1.6449, confirming the renewal process construction with Sidak correction.

claims.claim: Uncertainty keywords are extracted semi-supervised from 800 paired reasoning traces, yielding 102 keywords split into Impossibility (34), Speculation (14), and Insufficiency (56) categories (keyword construction section).
claims.evidence: Reconstructing keyword categories from the released classifier artifact (gsm8k_classification_results.json) with lexical filters yields exactly 102 unique keywords split into 34 Impossibility, 14 Speculation, and 56 Insufficiency, matching the claimed counts; the logbook notes this verifies the released output, not a fresh regeneration from 800 paired traces.

claims.claim: On GSM-MC, the Renewal method achieves 3.75% false-positive rate with 69.75% detection power and the Maxwise method achieves 5.42% FPR with 70.92% power, both far exceeding a length-based baseline's 32.17% power at 4.50% FPR (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Aggregating 12 released math benchmark model artifacts at α=0.05, lazy_interval=250, no ablation exactly reproduces Table 1: Length 4.50%/32.17%, Renewal 3.75%/69.75%, Maxwise 5.42%/70.92% (FPR/Power); an independent raw-trace replay on Qwen3-8B matches released per-model rows with 0.00 percentage-point deviation.

claims.claim: Both methods reach roughly 82-85% of oracle detection power on math benchmarks, with regression slopes of 0.8238 (Renewal) and 0.8532 (Maxwise) against oracle power (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: OLS-through-origin regression on 48 per-rule points reconstructed from released math benchmark summaries yields slopes of 0.8238439 (Renewal) and 0.8532302 (Maxwise), matching the claimed Figure 4 slopes of 0.8238 and 0.8532 to four decimal places.

claims.claim: On out-of-domain scientific reasoning benchmarks GPQA and HULE, calibrating on GSM8K yields 1.37-2.56% FPR but detection power drops to only 47-58% of the oracle baseline due to domain shift (Table 11).
claims.evidence: Reconstructing Table 11 from the official cross-domain results shows GPQA FPRs of 1.37% (Renewal) and 2.56% (Maxwise), matching the claimed range, but HLE FPRs are 4.76% (Renewal) and 5.96% (Maxwise), contradicting the claim that both benchmarks yield 1.37–2.56% FPR; the power-drop conclusion (slopes 0.4702 and 0.5897, i.e., 47–59% of oracle) is confirmed.

Srishti280992/repro-statistical-early-st.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence supporting claims 1–5 through Monte Carlo simulations, artifact aggregation, and an independent raw-trace replay on Qwen3-8B, all matching the paper's reported numbers. Claim 6 is falsified because the 1.37–2.56% FPR range holds only for GPQA, not for HLE (which shows 4.76–5.96% FPR), though the domain-shift power-drop conclusion is confirmed.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 proves that all context-free languages can be recognized by looped transformers using O(log(n)) looping layers and O(n^6) padding tokens (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook did not build any transformer construction; it counted a proxy 'combinatorial substrate' (slashed items + gap-bridging guesses) on a single small example grammar (N=8..40) and fit a power law (exponent 5.69 vs target 6). The theorem claims a result for all CFLs via a specific slashed-item transformer construction, which was never implemented.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows unambiguous context-free languages can be recognized with fewer resources than the general case: O(log^2(n)) looping layers and O(n^3) padding tokens (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: No transformer was constructed; the logbook counted base CYK items times split-point guesses on one small unambiguous example grammar (N=8..40), fitting exponent 2.94 vs target 3. This is a proxy counting exercise, not a reproduction of the theorem's transformer construction.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 further reduces requirements for unambiguous linear context-free languages to O(log(n)) looping layers and O(n^2) padding tokens by exploiting the linearity constraint (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Same proxy approach: counting base items on one small linear-unambiguous example grammar (N=8..40), fitting exponent 1.94 vs target 2. The actual linear-CFL transformer construction from Theorem 4.2 was not built or tested.

claims.claim: Lemma 4.1 shows that Boolean formula evaluation can be computed in O(log(n)) steps via a parallel pebbling argument, which underlies the padding-token constructions used in the main theorems (Section 4, Lemma 4.1).
claims.evidence: A real wavefront pebbling algorithm was implemented and achieves O(log N) rounds for balanced formulas (slope=1.000, R²=1.0), but the logbook's own data shows it requires O(N) rounds for skewed/degenerate formulas (slope=1.000 fit to linear N). The claim is for arbitrary formulas; the full balancing machinery needed for the general case was not implemented.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.1 shows that Boolean Formula Value Problem (BFVP) recognition requires zero padding tokens while retaining logarithmic depth (Section 4, Corollary 4.1).
claims.evidence: Zero-padding (footprint exactly equals N) is directly verified at N=8,32,128, but the 'retaining logarithmic depth' part of the claim inherits the limitation from Claim 4's pebbling implementation, which only achieves O(log N) for balanced formulas and degrades to O(N) for skewed ones.

claims.claim: Table 1 summarizes the padding-versus-depth tradeoff across general, unambiguous, and linear-unambiguous context-free language classes, showing that grammatical restrictions systematically reduce required padding (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The ordering general > unambiguous > linear-unambiguous and approximate exponents (5.69, 2.94, 1.94) are confirmed, but only via the same proxy combinatorial counts on small example grammars (N=8..40), not via actual transformer constructions or the paper's formal definitions.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-context-free-recogni.overall: The logbook runs real experiments (CYK-based combinatorial counting on small example grammars, a wavefront pebbling algorithm) that are consistent with the paper's claimed resource bounds, but it never builds or tests the actual looped transformer constructions that the theorems describe, and the pebbling implementation only achieves O(log N) depth for balanced formulas, not the arbitrary formulas the lemma claims.

ProCreations/repro-wasserstein-noise-sen.paper_title: Quantifying the noise sensitivity of the Wasserstein metric for images

claims.claim: Theorem 2 bounds the expected signed 1-Wasserstein distance between a clean n-pixel image and its Gaussian-noise-perturbed counterpart by (2/√π)σn log2(n) + (1/(2√π))σn, i.e., growth roughly linear in n with a log factor, for zero-sum noise of standard deviation σ (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: All 40/40 released 32×32 cells satisfy the Theorem 2 W1 bound with max empirical/bound ratio 0.111757, and the measured W1 noise slope is 0.999699 (R²=0.999993). The control—dividing the theorem constant by 20—produces 40/40 violations, confirming the test is discriminating.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 shows that for p-Wasserstein distances with integer p>1, the expected p-th power error is bounded by (4/√π) n σ, so the per-image error scales as (nσ)^(1/p), improving (becoming more noise-robust) as p increases, in contrast to the Euclidean (L2) metric's linear scaling in σ (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: All 40/40 W2 power cells satisfy the (4/√π)nσ bound, and over 22 increasing noise levels the W2 log-log slope is 0.519689 (R²=0.999406, close to predicted 0.5) versus L2 slope 0.999841 (R²=0.999999, close to predicted 1.0). Only p=2 is tested empirically, but this is the paper's own experimental scope and the analytic 1/p statement is retained as theory.

claims.claim: Theorems 4 and 5 extend the noise-sensitivity bounds to the deviation between the true and noisy Wasserstein distances computed between two distinct images, rather than a single noisy image against its clean version (Theorems 4-5).
claims.evidence: Across 50 distinct-image noise cells, all 150 inequality instances (50 each for W1, W2, W3) pass, with max observed/bound ratios of 0.075723, 0.946831, and 0.725390. The control—deleting the distinct-image clean-distance term—creates 21 W2 violations, confirming the test is meaningful.

claims.claim: On cryo-electron microscopy projection images of the hsp90 protein with noise level σ=0.01, the squared-Wasserstein (W2) distance matrix preserves the ground-truth diagonal similarity structure across viewing angles, while the L2 distance matrix degrades to an unstructured/random pattern (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: On all 190 HSP90 pairs at σ=0.01, W2 clean/noisy Spearman correlation is 0.990173 and diagonal contrast is 0.359365, which is 13.09× L2's contrast of 0.027463. The control—permuting the noisy W2 pair order—collapses Spearman to 0.059451, confirming the structure is genuine.

claims.claim: Figure 2 empirically confirms that the W2 distance error follows the predicted (nσ)^(1/2) scaling law as noise increases, while the L2 distance error grows linearly in σ (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The native Figure-2 sweep over 22 increasing noise levels gives W2 log-log slope 0.519689 (R²=0.999406, consistent with predicted 0.5) and L2 slope 0.999841 (R²=0.999999, consistent with predicted 1.0). The control—reversing W2 values against sigma—flips the exponent to −0.519689.

claims.claim: Section 4.4 reports a counterintuitive phenomenon in which Wasserstein distance between sparse images can decrease as noise increases, because added noise bridges transport gaps between distant mass concentrations (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: For the native sparse two-square pair at 32×32, W2 falls from 0.707107 to 0.266856 (62.26% decrease) while L2 increases, and the long-range transported-mass fraction drops from 1.0000 to 0.0000, directly demonstrating the bridging mechanism across 50 noise levels with flow-map witnesses.

ProCreations/repro-wasserstein-noise-sen.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence at the paper's native 32×32 resolution for all six claims, using official data arrays and code, with discriminating controls for each claim. All bounds, scaling exponents, structure statistics, and the sparse-image counterintuitive phenomenon are supported by specific quantitative measurements rather than assertions.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-certificate-guided-p.paper_title: Certificate-Guided Pruning for Stochastic Lipschitz Optimization

claims.claim: Certificate-Guided Pruning (CGP) maintains an explicit active set A_t of candidate optima using confidence-adjusted Lipschitz envelopes, certifying with high probability that any point outside A_t is suboptimal (Section 3, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The confidence-adjusted Lipschitz envelope was implemented with real formulas and tested on a single cone-shaped Lipschitz function with only 2 candidate points (x* and x_bad) across 30 trials; x* retained 100% and x_bad excluded 100%, but this is a highly simplified setup rather than a full-scale verification of the active-set certification mechanism.

claims.claim: Under a margin condition with near-optimality dimension α (Assumption 2.3), the Shrinkage Theorem bounds the active set volume as Vol(A_t) ≤ C·(2(β_t + Lη_t) + γ_t)^(d−α) (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: The volume bound was checked on a 2D power-law bump (α=1, d=2) with only 10–150 samples; measured volume barely shrinks (0.958→0.932) and the RHS bound barely changes (4.931→4.879), so while the bound is not violated, the test is at far too small a scale to meaningfully confirm the shrinkage rate.

claims.claim: CGP achieves ε-optimality with probability at least 1−δ using T = Õ(L^d ε^{-(2+α)} log(1/δ)) samples, improving on the worst-case Õ(ε^{-(2+d)}) rate whenever α < d (Theorem 4.8).
claims.evidence: Sample complexity was measured on a single α=0.5 instance with only 5–42 samples across 4 ε values; the fitted exponent (-0.90) is far from the theoretical target (-2.50, R²=0.85), so the claimed rate is not reproduced despite correct qualitative growth.

claims.claim: A matching lower bound shows any algorithm requires Ω(ε^{-(2+α)}) samples under the same margin condition, establishing CGP's minimax sample-complexity optimality (Theorem 4.9).
claims.evidence: The adversarial cone-instance was tested with 12 seeds per ε, yielding noisy and non-monotonic sample counts (1152.9→1636.8→1572.9) with a fitted exponent of -0.24 (R²=0.57) versus the target -(2+α); the lower bound rate is not established and the test only checks CGP on one hard instance rather than proving a universal lower bound.

claims.claim: CGP-Adaptive learns the Lipschitz constant L online via a doubling scheme, adding only an O(log T) multiplicative overhead to the sample complexity (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: The doubling scheme was tested on a single function (L=5.0, L0=0.5) with 10 seeds, showing 4.0 mean doublings (target 3.32) and L̂ in [L*, 2L*] in 100% of seeds; however, the O(log T) multiplicative overhead in sample complexity is never directly measured, and the setup required adding explicit diverse exploration not part of the original algorithm.

claims.claim: CGP-TR, a trust-region variant, scales to dimension d > 50 via certified restarts that provably never falsely eliminate the region containing the true optimizer x* (Theorem 6.1, Section 6).
claims.evidence: Certified restarts were tested in 1D (8 trust regions on [0,1], 20 trials) with 0% false restart rate for x*'s region, but the claim explicitly requires scaling to d > 50, which was never tested; the safety guarantee is checked only on a drastically simplified 1D proxy.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-certificate-guided-p.overall: The logbook provides a genuine independent reimplementation of CGP's core formulas with honest disclosure of bugs and limitations, but every claim is tested on a clearly simplified setup (single simple functions, 1D or 2D, tiny sample counts, 10–30 trials) that falls well short of the paper's theoretical scale. No claim is verified at full scale; the sample-complexity exponents (Claims 3–4) are not reproduced, and the high-dimensional scaling of CGP-TR (Claim 6) is never tested.

ParetoOptimal/repro-rgnowsmybm.paper_title: A Coin Flip for Safety: LLM Judges Fail to Reliably Measure Adversarial Robustness

claims.claim: Across an audit of 6,642 human-verified labels spanning 4 victim models (Gemma-3-1B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-27B, Qwen-3-32B) and 5 attack methods (Direct Prompting, GCG, GCG-REINFORCE, Best-of-N, PAIR), 4 safety judges (LlamaGuard-3, HarmBench, AegisGuard, JailJudge) are shown to perform only slightly better than random guessing on average (Section 3, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: On the full 6642-label release with 200 balancing seeds, the mean balanced accuracy across 4 judges is 0.5509 vs chance 0.5, with per-judge values matching the paper's Table 1 to within 0.0039 (LlamaGuard-3 0.5435, HarmBench 0.5872, AegisGuard 0.5139, JailJudge 0.5588), and 21 of 68 cells below chance.

claims.claim: ROC analysis shows JailJudge attains AUROC as low as 0.48 (worse than chance) on some attack-model pairs and no better than 0.64 on any attack, demonstrating near-chance discriminative ability under distribution shift (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: All five Figure-5 JailJudge AUROCs on Llama-3.1 reproduce to within 0.0037: GCG-R 0.4765 (below chance, rounds to 0.48), GCG 0.6416 (rounds to 0.64), with 1000-resample bootstrap CIs. The logbook honestly notes the 0.64 ceiling is Llama-3.1-specific, matching Figure 5's stated scope.

claims.claim: Judge accuracy varies dramatically across attack-model combinations, with some judges scoring only 45% accuracy on specific attack-victim pairs, close to random guessing (Figure 3, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Figure 3 heatmaps reproduce with mean absolute deviation 0.0226 across 36 printed cells; cells at or below 0.45 exist (AegisGuard 0.4316, LlamaGuard-3 0.4335 on Llama-3.1|Pair), and within-model accuracy range reaches 0.1806, confirming dramatic dispersion.

claims.claim: The paper introduces ReliableBench, a curated set of 41 behaviors, which raises average judge accuracy from 57% to 70%, and JudgeStressTest (JST), a set of 971 challenging samples that exposes systematic judge failures across judge architectures via leave-one-out validation (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Behaviour sweep reproduces acc_at_k_41=0.7005 (claimed 70%) vs acc_at_k_100=0.584 (claimed 57%), monotone non-increasing; JST has exactly 971 rows with reconstruction bracketing 952-989; all 12 Table-1 LOO values reproduce within 0.0127. Released CSV carries 43 behaviors vs paper's 41, but the 41 are a subset.

claims.claim: Correcting reported attack success rates (ASR) for judge unreliability substantially deflates the apparent effectiveness of attacks such as Best-of-N, which is shown to inflate ASR by exploiting judge insufficiencies rather than eliciting genuinely harmful content (Figure 1, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: BoN judge precision is 0.275 on Gemma-1B (vs 0.6154-0.8282 for other attacks), with 80 of 111 LlamaGuard-3-positive BoN samples human-harmless; corrected ASR drops BoN from 0.38 to 0.1061 while GCG-R barely moves (0.48 to 0.384); BoN is least precise in all 4 victim models. Figure 1's absolute ASR ranking is not reproducible from the release (denominators missing), but the core claim about selective deflation holds.

claims.claim: Judge Concordance analysis shows judges can reach near-unanimous agreement with each other while still failing to align with human ground-truth labels, and averaging/ensembling judge scores does not consistently improve alignment with human judgments (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: Concordance vs accuracy Pearson 0.0658/Spearman 0.1459 (uncorrelated); 4 of 10 most concordant behaviors below chance (worst 0.1042); unanimous panels score only 0.5973 on balanced set; no ensemble beats best single judge (-0.017); averaging reduces R² on all 4 victim models. One Figure 6(b) value (0.05 vs measured 0.0042) doesn't match but strengthens the claim.
