ParetoOptimal/repro-rgnowsmybm.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous, full-scale reproduction from the authors' own sha256-pinned data release, reimplementing every protocol from scratch with 200 balancing seeds and matching the paper's headline numbers to within ~0.01-0.04 across all six claims. The main gaps are Figure 1's absolute ASR levels (denominators not released) and minor release-vs-text discrepancies (43 vs 41 behaviors), neither of which undermines the core findings.

michaldobiezynski/repro-can-microcanonic.paper_title: Can Microcanonical Langevin Dynamics Leverage Mini-Batch Gradient Noise?

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 proves that when mini-batch gradient noise is anisotropic across dimensions, the stationary distribution of microcanonical Langevin dynamics (if it exists) deviates from the true target posterior due to non-vanishing noise-induced drift, in contrast to the isotropic-noise case covered by Proposition 1 (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: A from-scratch numpy implementation of the paper's exact isokinetic velocity map, averaging 2,000,000 antithetic draws, measured anisotropic drift matching the closed-form -(eps^2/2(d-1)^2)PVu to within 0.3% (ratio 0.9970-1.0012, cos +1.0000) at d=10 and within 0.2% at d=200, while isotropic drift fell to 2.03e-08 (d=10) and 9.5e-11 (d=200), 2473x/460x below the smallest anisotropic value and at the Monte-Carlo noise floor — directly confirming the Theorem 3.1 / Proposition 1 dichotomy.

claims.claim: A diagonal gradient-noise preconditioner (pSMILE-naive), built from moving averages of per-dimension gradient standard deviations to enforce local isotropy, reduces the empirically measured bias by roughly 5-10x relative to unpreconditioned mini-batch MCLMC across anisotropic-noise benchmarks (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Running App. C's 15-point step-size refinement at the reported 10-chain × 10^6-sample budget on all 12 Table-1 cells at d=10, the geometric-mean bias reduction was 1.63x over 9 anisotropic cells and 2.57x over 6 Diagonal+Correlated cells (paper: 5.31x / 10.18x), with 4 of 9 cells showing no reduction or a bias increase; the pSMILE-naive column reproduced the paper's (ICG diag 0.0370 vs 0.038) but the SMILE-naive baseline did not (0.0790 vs 0.245), collapsing the claimed ratio.

claims.claim: An energy-variance-based adaptive tuner that fits a Gamma distribution to the energy error ΔE dynamically sets step-size guardrails, letting epoch-wise mini-batch sampling with pSMILE-naive match the accuracy of full-batch MCLMC (Algorithm 1, Table 2).
claims.evidence: On all 3 Table-2 datasets (Airfoil, Bikesharing, Energy) at 10 chains and 3 splits, Algorithm 1 driving the step size produced worse LPPD than the fixed η=1e-3 that App. E.1 prescribes for Table 2 (+0.254 vs +0.375, +0.132 vs +0.164, +1.770 vs +1.769); Eq. 6's asymmetric update gives log-η a built-in drift of -6.9e-04/step analytically (-1.7e-03 to -2.9e-03 measured), collapsing η from 1e-3 to ~2e-18 within one epoch-wise run, and the paper's own App. E.1 fixes η=0.001 so Table 2 never ran Algorithm 1.

claims.claim: On larger-scale Bayesian neural network posteriors (ResNet-18 with 11.2M parameters and a ViT with 22M parameters), pSMILE achieves uncertainty quantification competitive with state-of-the-art methods while using mini-batch gradients (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The claim names ResNet-18 (11.2M) and ViT (22M) on CIFAR-10/Imagenette, but the reproduction ran LeNet-5 with 61,706 parameters on Fashion-MNIST (~180x smaller model, simpler dataset); at that reduced scale pSMILE with Algorithm 1 beat the deep-ensemble baseline (+0.0127 LPPD) and matched SGHMC (+0.0027 LPPD, -0.0070 Acc) using mini-batch gradients, but the 11.2M/22M posteriors the claim specifies were never measured.

michaldobiezynski/repro-can-microcanonic.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, from-scratch numerical evidence confirming the paper's theoretical core (Theorem 3.1's anisotropic noise-induced drift) while falsifying two empirical magnitude/mechanism claims (Claims 2 and 3) at the paper's own scale and chain counts. Claim 4 was addressed only at a ~180x-reduced scale (62k-parameter LeNet vs 11.2M/22M networks), yielding supportive but non-definitive results.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 proves the original DeepSets aggregation (Equation 4) is discontinuous in the natural any-dimensional topology because the infinite sum can diverge when the inner function ρ decays arbitrarily slowly, so standard DeepSets fails to be universal (Theorem 4.2, Section 4.1.1).
claims.evidence: The fix provides a rigorous numerical witness: x_i=1/i² (ℓ₁-Cauchy, tail→5e-7 at n=1e6) with ρ(t)=√|t| (Hölder-1/2) produces an output sum growing as log(n) (fitted slope 0.9995, R²=0.9999998), while the destructive control with Lipschitz ρ=identity converges to ζ(2)=π²/6 to 1e-6 precision—concretely demonstrating Cauchy-in/not-Cauchy-out with proper attribution to ρ's slow growth.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.9 proves standard message-passing GNNs fail any-dimensional universality because their pointwise nonlinearities are discontinuous in the cut metric, since a pointwise map is continuous with respect to the cut norm only if it is linear (Theorem 4.9, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The fix's exact brute-force cut/box norm computation across a 6-point eps-sweep shows the linear control's output is consistently smaller than nonlinear outputs, but the nonlinear outputs also shrink roughly proportionally with eps (e.g., input 0.000853 → nonlinear 0.001265 at eps=0.01), failing to demonstrate the key discontinuity signature of non-vanishing output as input vanishes. The logbook itself acknowledges 'a cleaner asymptotic separation was not achieved.'

claims.claim: A modified DeepSets-infinity architecture (Equation 5) that reweights terms by an ell_p norm factor is proven continuous and universal on ell_p(R^k) sequence space (Theorem 4.2, Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The reweighted sum converges to 1.341487256584251 at n=1e6, matching the n=1e7 reference to 8 significant figures, while the destructive control (removing reweighting) reproduces Claim 1's divergent value of 14.39—concretely confirming the ell_p reweighting restores summability. Permutation invariance verified to 6.7e-16 over 200 relabelings. Universality remains proof-level as disclosed.

claims.claim: A measure-space variant DeepSets-bar-infinity (Equation 6), replacing the sum with a normalized integral under a growth condition, is proven universal on the Wasserstein space of probability measures (Theorem 4.5, Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: The KR bound is tested on 500 1D measure pairs using sorted order statistics (simplified from general ℝ^k Wasserstein space), with 99% satisfaction and max ratio 1.023 slightly exceeding the theoretical bound. Only the continuity/Lipschitz component is tested, not universality on the full Wasserstein space.

claims.claim: A homomorphism-density-basis architecture (Equations 9-10) is proven continuous and universal on graphon space with the cut metric, restoring universality for graph architectures (Theorem 4.9, Theorem 4.10, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The counting lemma is verified on 80 random pairs of n=7 graphons (very small) with only 3 motifs (edge/wedge/triangle), achieving 100% satisfaction. The separation test uses graphons with substantially different edge densities (0.505 vs 0.674), not a close pair. Universality (denseness of the homomorphism-density basis) is not addressed.

claims.claim: A two-stage architecture combining a Gram-matrix map (Equation 12) with Invariant Graphon Networks (Equation 14) is proven universal on bounded point-cloud orbits under the group action (Theorem 4.12, Theorem 4.13, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: O(3)-invariance of the Gram matrix is verified to machine precision (max error 1.24e-14) over 500 configs with completeness and shear-separation tests, but only k=3 with 20-point clouds and 3 motifs are used—a simplified proxy of the full architecture. Universality on bounded point-cloud orbits is not tested.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-any-dimensional-inva.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification of the core divergence/convergence mechanisms behind Claims 1 and 3 (large scale, destructive controls, known-asymptotic matching), but Claim 2 is inconclusive (nonlinear outputs shrink with eps rather than staying bounded away), and Claims 4–6 are tested only on simplified setups (1D measures, n=7 graphons, k=3 point clouds) without addressing universality.

ParetoOptimal/repro-anvg7nnupp.paper_title: Demystifying LLM-as-a-Judge: Analytically Tractable Model for Inference-Time Scaling

claims.claim: Result 3 (best-of-k limit) shows that when the reward weight vector equals the teacher's (w_R = w_T) and temperature T→0, the generalization error decays as δ(x) = (π/k²)·s²(x)·exp(ΔT(x)²/s²(x)), i.e. a Θ(1/k²) power-law rate governed by extreme value theory (Result 3).
claims.evidence: Exact quadrature (no Monte-Carlo) over k=3..1,000,000 and six values of a=ΔT/s shows the ratio δ·k²/(πs²exp(a²))→1 (reaching 0.999997 at k=10⁶) and local log-log slopes converge to -2 (worst deviation 5.814e-06 at k=300k–1M), confirming both the Θ(1/k²) rate and the EVT leading constant; cross-checked against Monte-Carlo (max|z|=2.65), Remark 5 x-averages (max rel diff 0.00114), and the authors' own BLR_zero_T.py code.

claims.claim: Result 2's high-temperature expansion δ(x) = ΔT(x)² + s²(x) + Σ C_l(x)/t(x)^l + O(t(x)^-4) shows generalization error decreases monotonically with more inference-time samples k when the reward is close to the teacher (Result 2).
claims.evidence: Exact coefficient extraction shows the l=1 and l=2 terms match Result 2 to 7.26e-08 and 3.52e-05 relative, but the l=3 term is contradicted: its (1-1/k)(1-2/k)(1-3/k) factor forces it to zero at k=2,3 yet the measured 1/t³ coefficient is as large as 85.52 (smallest 0.387 vs predicted 0.0), and the fitted remainder slope is -2.99 to -3.25 (O(t⁻³), not the stated O(t⁻⁴)); the monotonicity conclusion itself is separately verified across 48 well-aligned configurations.

claims.claim: Remark 3 identifies a threshold t < 3C₂(x)/C₁(x) under substantial reward misspecification below which the generalization error becomes non-monotonic in k, with an optimal finite k* ≈ 2t*/(t*-t) beyond which further sampling increases error (Remark 3).
claims.evidence: Minimizing the paper's own l≤2 truncation gives k*=(4/3)t*/(t*-t), confirmed numerically to 2.47e-08 relative over 35 cells, while the claimed k*≈2t*/(t*-t) is larger by exactly 1.5× in every cell—a fixed discrepancy, not an approximation; the threshold t*=3C₂/C₁ and the existence of non-monotonicity below it are separately verified (measured threshold tracks t* with constant offset, relative accuracy reaching 0.966 at c=100).

claims.claim: Remark 4 derives an optimal reward-sampling temperature t(x) = 2(1-2/k)·C₂(x)/C₁(x) for fixed k>2 that balances selection sharpness against reward misalignment (Remark 4).
claims.evidence: The formula t=2(1-2/k)C₂/C₁ is confirmed as the exact stationary point of the l≤2 series to machine precision (max relative error 2.15e-16 over 42 cells), the exact error has an interior optimal temperature in every swept configuration, and the formula converges to the exact optimum (ratio 0.958 at c=100) consistent with its stated t>>1 validity regime.

claims.claim: Remark 6 shows inference-time scaling outperforms training-data scaling when reward-teacher alignment is strong, quantified by ∂log(δ)/∂log(k) = -2 versus a much smaller magnitude for ∂log(δ)/∂log(n) (Remark 6).
claims.evidence: From the Remark 5 closed form, ∂log δ/∂log k = -2 to 1e-10 absolute, confirmed independently by exact quadrature slopes converging to -2; ∂log δ/∂log n ranges from -0.078 to -0.00073 across n=10⁴..10⁵, giving a magnitude ratio |∂log k|/|∂log n| of 25.5 to 2759; Remark 6 eq (24) matches the numerically differentiated n-exponent to 3.88e-06 relative, and the advantage shrinks with task difficulty as the paper asserts.

ParetoOptimal/repro-anvg7nnupp.overall: The logbook provides rigorous exact-arithmetic verification of Claims 1, 4, and 5, and exact-arithmetic falsification of the specific equations in Claims 2 and 3 (wrong l=3 term and remainder order in Result 2; wrong 1.5× coefficient in Remark 3's k* formula), while confirming the qualitative conclusions (monotonicity, threshold existence, non-monotonicity) those claims also assert.

heitorefer/repro-how-good-is-post-hoc-wa.paper_title: How Good is Post-Hoc Watermarking With Language Model Rephrasing?

claims.claim: The simplest Gumbel-max post-hoc watermarking scheme dominates the Pareto frontier of quality-versus-detectability tradeoffs under nucleus sampling, outperforming more recent alternatives such as DiPMark and MorphMark (Section 4.2, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The table provides concrete -log10 p values (Gumbel-max 8.74 vs Green-Red 0.54-2.26, DiPMark 1.15, SynthID 1.82), but MorphMark is entirely absent from the comparison despite being named in the claim, quality metrics for non-Gumbel-max schemes are only qualitative ('Moderate'), and the executive summary indicates execution was 'Local CPU (SmolLM2-360M audit)' at ~$0 cost, suggesting a small-scale setup.

claims.claim: Larger language models preserve semantic fidelity better during post-hoc rephrasing but struggle to reach low detection p-values due to lower output entropy, whereas smaller models more effectively hide strong watermark signals (Section 4.3, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The table shows a clear inverse trend in -log10 p across model scales (SmolLM2-135M: 10.42 → Llama-3.1-8B: 1.95), supporting the detection part of the claim, but quality is reported only qualitatively ('Low/Variable', 'Moderate', 'High', 'Superior') without actual BERTScore or cross-entropy numbers, making the 'larger models preserve semantic fidelity better' assertion unverified quantitatively.

claims.claim: Beam search decoding, especially with biased scoring, consistently improves the quality-detectability Pareto frontier relative to standard sampling across watermarking schemes (Section 4.4, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Concrete numbers show beam search with biased scoring improves both detectability and quality for Green-Red (0.54→1.84, +0.06 BERTScore) and SynthID (1.82→3.41, +0.04 BERTScore), but only 2 of the 3 mentioned schemes have results (DiPMark is listed in the method but absent from the table), and no sample sizes or statistical significance are reported.

claims.claim: Entropy-aware detection filtering yields only modest gains, never exceeding 20%, with most watermarking configurations retaining just 30-40 successful detection settings (Section 4.5, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: No experimental results table is provided — only a code snippet of the entropy filtering implementation and qualitative assertions that gains are '<15%'. The claim's specific quantitative predictions ('never exceeding 20%', '30-40 successful detection settings') are not backed by any reported numbers or configuration-by-configuration breakdown.

claims.claim: On verifiable code text (HumanEval/MBPP), all post-hoc watermarking methods face a heavily constrained tradeoff between pass@1 functional correctness and detectability, with Gumbel-max still achieving the best Pareto frontier and smaller models again outperforming larger ones (Section 4.6, Figures 6-7, Table 3).
claims.evidence: Only 5 HumanEval problems were tested with SmolLM2-360M (Pass@1=0.60 at T=0.7, 0.40 at T=1.0), MBPP is not tested at all, and the Llama-3.1-8B rows are explicitly labeled '(Paper)' rather than reproduced. The claim about 'smaller models again outperforming larger ones' is not supported by the data shown, as the smaller model has lower Pass@1 than the paper's larger model results.

claims.claim: Non-English languages exhibit a steeper quality-detectability tradeoff than English under post-hoc watermarking, as shown in the multilingual robustness evaluation (Section 4.7, Table 4).
claims.evidence: Only approximate BERTScore values are reported per language (en ~0.89, es ~0.84, fr ~0.83, ru ~0.79) with no paired detection p-values per language, making it impossible to verify the 'steeper quality-detectability tradeoff' claim which requires both quality and detectability metrics at matched detection levels. The method description conflates 'codebase audit' with evaluation, and the ~$0 compute cost raises doubts about whether Llama-3.1-8B was actually run.

heitorefer/repro-how-good-is-post-hoc-wa.overall: This logbook provides limited experimental evidence, mostly consisting of small-scale CPU runs with SmolLM2-360M and code auditing rather than full reproduction at the paper's scale. Several claims lack key comparisons (MorphMark missing, MBPP untested, no per-language detection metrics), and quality metrics are frequently qualitative rather than quantitative.

michaldobiezynski/repro-efficient-bayesi.paper_title: Efficient Bayesian Inference from Noisy Pairwise Comparisons

claims.claim: BBQ's EM algorithm has closed-form updates that guarantee monotonic improvement of the likelihood and convergence to a stationary point, in contrast to gradient-based methods like Crowd-BT which lack such convergence guarantees (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Over 48,413 EM iterations on 4 real datasets, the log-posterior never decreased beyond -6.821e-13 (round-off), the EM fixed point matched an independent L-BFGS-B optimum to 3.48e-10 nats with max|grad|=1.489e-05, and Crowd-BT's objective decreased on 39 of 100 outer iterations on IHQ-unscreened, empirically confirming the claimed contrast.

claims.claim: BBQ converges within seconds on all tested datasets, whereas Crowd-BT takes approximately 15 minutes on the HUMAINE dataset (105,220 comparisons) despite BBQ using an unoptimized plain NumPy implementation (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: On 105,220 real HUMAINE votes, BBQ converged in 0.278 s while Crowd-BT took 66.3 s (to the paper's stopping rule) or 170.9 s (100 outer iterations that never self-terminate), confirming the seconds-vs-minutes ordering; the absolute 900 s was not matched but the logbook explains this is due to vectorized NumPy vs scalar C++ implementation.

claims.claim: On the unscreened IHQ dataset, BBQ achieves 61.92% top-1 agreement with final rankings, compared to 33.15% for Crowd-BT and 24.32% for Bayes-BT (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Over 10,000 rater bootstraps on the released IHQ-unscreened split, BBQ measured 40.34±0.96%, Crowd-BT 52.00%, and Bayes-BT 60.08±0.96% — the claimed 61.92/33.15/24.32 is missed by 21.6 points with inverted ordering, while the same pipeline reproduces the other three IHQ/MT-Bench columns to within 0.1 points.

claims.claim: BBQ ranks first in Kendall's Tau agreement on 5 of 8 evaluated datasets and second on the remaining three, and achieves 100% top-1 agreement on the MT-Bench, WD, and HiFiC datasets (Table 1).
claims.evidence: On all 4 reconstructible datasets BBQ ranked first or second in Kendall's tau, and MT-Bench top-1 was exactly 100.00% over 10,000 resamples; the paper's own Table 1 was independently checked to contain 5 firsts and 3 seconds with 100% top-1 on MT-Bench/WD/HiFiC, though WD, HiFiC, and ConHa could not be re-measured due to unreleased data.

claims.claim: At the 99% confidence level, BBQ and Crowd-BT both show well-calibrated Type I error rates of about 1%, while Bayes-BT is overly conservative at about 0.1% (Appendix G, Figure 6).
claims.evidence: Across 88,760 H0 trials, Crowd-BT (0.713%) and Bayes-BT (0.025%) reproduced the paper's values, but BBQ measured 0.048% — at Bayes-BT's conservative level, not ~1%; under all four interval constructions tested, BBQ and Bayes-BT rates were within a factor of two, and the one construction reaching ~1% (scale-pinned: 0.854%) put Bayes-BT at the same rate (0.855%).

claims.claim: BBQ's rater-quality parameter (mixture weight q_r modeling whether a rater follows Bradley-Terry or guesses randomly) correlates with Pearson r=0.724 with rater agreement to final rankings on the unscreened IHQ data, enabling identification of unreliable crowdsourced raters without a separate screening procedure (Figure 2, Equation 2).
claims.evidence: Measured r = +0.8550 (p = 6.8e-18) between q_r and rater agreement on unscreened IHQ, exceeding the claimed 0.724 in the same direction, with the unscreened correlation exceeding the screened correlation (+0.7555) under all nine definitions of agreement tested, and the operational claim verified by BBQ recovering the hand-screened consensus (tau 0.8519) better than Bayes-BT (0.8307).

michaldobiezynski/repro-efficient-bayesi.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous from-scratch NumPy reproduction at the paper's own scale (10,000 bootstraps, 10,000 H0 trials, 105,220 real HUMAINE votes), confirming the EM convergence, runtime, ranking, and rater-quality claims while falsifying the specific IHQ-unscreened top-1 numbers and BBQ's Type I error calibration with concrete counter-evidence.

jomasego/repro-lfq-logit-aware-final-blo.paper_title: LFQ: Logit-aware Final-block Quantization for Boosting the Generation Quality of Low-Bit Quantized LLMs

claims.claim: Optimizes the final transformer block of a quantized LLM using a cross-entropy loss between full-precision and quantized logits (integrating the LM head into the objective), rather than the MSE loss used for earlier blocks (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The LFQ method (CE loss on final block logits through LM head) was implemented and run on Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct at W4, a much smaller model than the paper's 7B+ scale. The only result shows LFQ PPL (55.72) is worse than the baseline block-wise PTQ (47.70), which does not support the method's effectiveness even at this scale.

claims.claim: Can be layered on top of existing block-wise post-training quantization methods, including FlexRound, OmniQuant, and Block-AP (Section 3, Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook states three quantizer classes (FlexRound, OmniQuant, Block-AP) were implemented in code, but provides no executed runs, results, or evidence that any of them were actually used with LFQ. Code existence alone is not experimental evidence.

claims.claim: Improves IFEval and MATH500 accuracy for quantized Qwen2.5 models while maintaining WikiText2 perplexity and MMLU accuracy comparable to the underlying PTQ baselines (Table 1).
claims.evidence: IFEval and MATH500 were never run. The only experiment (WikiText2 PPL on 0.5B) shows LFQ at 55.72 vs baseline PTQ at 47.70, which contradicts the claim that LFQ maintains WikiText2 perplexity comparable to baselines. Key generation benchmarks are entirely missing.

claims.claim: On L1-Qwen-7B-Max, LFQ improves AIME'24 greedy accuracy from 30% to 43.33% and recovers pass@8 to within 0.5 percentage points of the full-precision baseline (Table 2).
claims.evidence: No experiments were run for this claim. The logbook explicitly states it requires GPU compute not available and only reproduces the paper's Table 2 numbers without any independent execution.

claims.claim: Ablation on Llama 3.1 8B shows both integrating the LM head and using the cross-entropy loss (rather than MSE) are necessary to obtain generation-quality gains (Table 4).
claims.evidence: The ablation was run on Qwen2.5-0.5B (not Llama 3.1 8B as claimed) using WikiText2 PPL (not IFEval/MATH500 as in the claim). All three LFQ variants report identical PPL of 55.72, which is suspicious and does not demonstrate that either component is necessary. The actual claim about generation-quality gains was never tested.

claims.claim: Optimizing beyond the single final block (k=1) yields diminishing returns in generation quality (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: No experiments were run for this claim. The logbook only describes the paper's Figure 2 results without any independent execution of k=1, k=2, k=3 comparisons.

jomasego/repro-lfq-logit-aware-final-blo.overall: This logbook only ran experiments on a 0.5B model with WikiText2 PPL, and the results actually show LFQ performing worse than the baseline PTQ (55.72 vs 47.70 PPL). Most claims were not addressed due to CPU-only compute constraints, and the one ablation attempted has suspiciously identical results across all variants and uses the wrong model and metric.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-an-odd-estimator-for.paper_title: An Odd Estimator for Shapley Values

claims.claim: Observation 3.1 proves that Shapley values depend exclusively on the odd component of the coalition set function, so the even component can be discarded without loss (Section 3).
claims.evidence: 15 random coalition-value functions at d=8 with substantial even-degree Fourier energy (6.81 vs odd 10.61) were decomposed; reconstructing from odd-only components yielded brute-force Shapley values matching the full function to max absolute difference 1.24e-14, directly confirming that discarding the even component leaves Shapley values unchanged.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 proves that paired sampling orthogonalizes the regression, provably separating the odd and even objectives and giving the first general theoretical justification for this widely used sampling heuristic (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: 3000 sampled pairs at d=8 showed paired mean odd-even cross-term of exactly 0.00e+00 vs -0.0031 unpaired, with the algebraic cancellation mechanism chi_T(-x)=(-1)^|T|chi_T(x) verified numerically, confirming exact orthogonalization under paired sampling.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 shows that Fourier basis regression exactly recovers Shapley values, which forms the theoretical basis of the OddSHAP algorithm (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: 25 random functions at d=9 were tested by computing Shapley values from the exact Möbius/Fourier-basis closed form and comparing to brute-force ground truth, yielding max absolute error 9.06e-14, confirming exact recovery in the noiseless full-information limit.

claims.claim: In Table 1, across eight estimators and eight benchmarks (with sample budget m≈100d), OddSHAP attains the lowest average rank (1.50), beating the prior best method RegressionMSR (rank 2.25) (Section 5, Table 1).
claims.evidence: Only 3 estimators (not 8) were compared on 2 dimensions with random games (not 8 benchmarks); after fixing implementation bugs, OddSHAP's avg rank was 2.5 vs KernelSHAP-unpaired's 1.625, so it did not attain the lowest rank, but the setup is too different from the paper's to constitute a proper falsification.

claims.claim: OddSHAP reduces estimation error by 6–62x relative to LeverageSHAP on tabular data benchmarks (Section 5, Table 1).
claims.evidence: LeverageSHAP was never available or tested — the shapiq package resolved it to None — so no comparison was made and the 6–62x improvement claim could not be addressed at all.

claims.claim: Figure 2 shows OddSHAP's advantage over baselines is largest for moderate-to-high dimensional problems (d≥30) when given sufficient sampling budget (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Only d∈{8,10} was tested, never reaching the d≥30 regime the claim concerns; at d=10 budget=1000 OddSHAP's MSE (0.375) was worse than both KernelSHAP variants (0.029/0.046), showing no growing advantage, but the tested dimensions are far below the claim's scope.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-an-odd-estimator-for.overall: The logbook provides solid numerical verification of the three foundational theoretical claims (Observation 3.1, Theorem 3.2, Theorem 3.5) via brute-force ground-truth comparisons at small scale. The empirical claims (Table 1 ranking, LeverageSHAP improvement, dimension-dependent advantage) remain unaddressed due to missing official implementations, insufficient estimator/benchmark coverage, and dimensions far below the paper's regime.

gauravmishra9/repro-think-twice-before-y.paper_title: Think Twice Before You Act: Protecting LLM Agents Against Tool Description Poisoning via Isolated Planning

claims.claim: Tool-Guard defends LLM agents against cross-tool description poisoning—where a poisoned tool's description can bias agent behavior even when that tool is never invoked—via isolated planning that dynamically partitions tools and validates actions before execution (Section 4, Figure 3)
claims.evidence: On 3 of 4 AgentDojo suites with gpt-4o (228 scored passes, 0 errored), undefended ASR was 70.18% (paper: 70.17%) and Tool-Guard reduced it to 0.00% (paper: 1.75%). A custom trajectory check (repro/mechanism_check.py) confirmed the cross-tool pathway: 1 of 7 successful attacks invoked none of the poisoned tools. Benign no-defense utility matched exactly (82.46), localizing divergences to the defense path; utility shortfalls are reported but do not undermine the security claim.

claims.claim: On adaptive/semantic attacks, Tool-Guard keeps attack success rate near 0%, compared to non-negligible ASR for competing defenses (Table 4)
claims.evidence: Only the non-adaptive 'Original' row ran (ASR with defense 0.00% on banking+slack). All adaptive variants (Align-Evade, Susp-Evade, Combined, PAIR, TAP) were never executed due to API quota exhaustion. The claim is specifically about adaptive attacks, so no evidence addresses it.

claims.claim: Across stability tests, Tool-Guard maintains attack success rates between 0.40% and 1.54% (Table 3)
claims.evidence: The stability node was launched but produced only one contaminated repeat (19 of 64 passes rate-limited) and was cancelled. No clean 5-repeat run was ever completed. Two incidental data points (ASR 0.00–6.25%) from other runs are explicitly described as anecdotal, not a variance estimate.

claims.claim: Tool-Guard incurs 1.22M-2.24M tokens of overhead versus 0.84M-1.61M tokens for the no-defense baseline, roughly 1.45x token overhead (Table 1)
claims.evidence: The no-defense baseline reproduced within 10% across all 4 suites (benign 0.79M vs 0.84M; attack 1.77M vs 1.61M), but Tool-Guard's own token row never ran because the split_replan driver does not instrument tokens. The headline 1.45× ratio requires the numerator, which is entirely missing.

claims.claim: Tool-Guard's isolation mechanism is shown to be necessary via an ablation study, and it is evaluated against five existing defenses on the AgentDojo and ASB benchmarks (Section 5, Figure 2, Table 6)
claims.evidence: No usable experimental results: 1 of 12 five-defense jobs completed (only the 'none' baseline); both ablation runs (Val-Only, Val+Mask) were 83–99% rate-limited and excluded; ASB was never in scope. The ablation code was implemented and validated in a one-task debug run, but no scored results exist.

gauravmishra9/repro-think-twice-before-y.overall: This logbook provides strong, concrete evidence for the paper's central claim (Claim 1): cross-tool poisoning is demonstrated and Tool-Guard suppresses ASR to 0.00% on a non-toy setup with careful controls. Claims 2, 3, and 5 were never substantively attempted due to API quota exhaustion, and Claim 4 verified only the baseline denominator while the Tool-Guard numerator is missing.

claims.claim: For the independent Gaussian variance allocation problem, the paper gives a PTAS achieving E[max_i X_i] ≥ OPT - ε in polynomial time (Theorem 1.1, Section 1.2).
claims.evidence: Exact quadrature with exhaustive mesh-search OPT for n=3,4 (very small) and proxy grid reference for n=8,16; gaps within eps, but the tested algorithm is a simplified restricted-support heuristic, not the paper's full PTAS, and exact-OPT cases are limited to n≤4.

claims.claim: For correlated Gaussian variables, a PTAS with the same additive ε guarantee is established (Theorem 1.2, Section 1.2).
claims.evidence: Only n=2 (bivariate correlated normals) tested with exact closed-form E[max] and 400-point grid OPT across rho∈{-0.5,0,0.5,0.8}; all gaps within eps, but a single bivariate case is far too small to verify a PTAS for general correlated Gaussians.

claims.claim: For the GraphVarAlloc problem with multiple constraint sets (general m>1), the paper gives an O(log n) multiplicative approximation guaranteeing Ω(1/log n)·OPT (Theorem 1.3, Section 1.2).
claims.evidence: Cycle-graph instances only (n=8,16,32) with exact quadrature and a loose single-variable upper bound on OPT; ratio·ln(n) stays bounded (1.82→2.34), consistent with the claim, but only one graph structure and a non-tight upper bound are tested.

claims.claim: Theorem 1.6 proves that in the optimal allocation, only Θ(1/p) variables receive variance Ω(p), i.e., the allocation concentrates on a shrinking subset as the constraint parameter p grows (Theorem 1.6, Section 1.3).
claims.evidence: Original n=8 test showed a decreasing high-variance count (4→4→0→0), but the wider-p fix experiment on a simplified reformulation found k* stuck at 5 across p∈{10,…,5000} (p·k* growing, not constant), failing to confirm Θ(1/p) scaling due to missing constrained-optimization structure.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 bounds the contribution of small-variance variables by O(ε√ln(1/ε)), which is used to limit the number of high-variance variables to O(1/ε²) and underlies the PTAS construction (Lemma 2.1, Section 2.1).
claims.evidence: Exact quadrature E[max] for n=1/ε² variables each with variance ε² across ε from 0.5 to 0.0005 (1000× range, up to n=4000); ratio measured/(ε√ln(1/ε)) stays bounded in [1.24, 1.71], directly confirming the O(ε√ln(1/ε)) functional form.

claims.claim: Monte Carlo simulations on Erdős–Rényi random graphs with n=8 nodes and edge probabilities p ranging from 1/8 to 8/8 are used to illustrate the concentration and concavity results across independent, positively, and negatively correlated settings (Figures 1-2, Section 1.3).
claims.evidence: At n=8 matching the paper's scale, the concentration trend runs the wrong direction (high-variance count increases with edge probability p in independent and positive-correlation regimes: 4→6→8→8), while concavity is only weakly supported from the original coarse-discretization run; the logbook attributes the failure to possible parameter conflation but does not resolve it.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-allocating-variance-.overall: The logbook provides a solid exact-quadrature verification of Lemma 2.1's small-variance bound (Claim 5) across a wide parameter range, but the PTAS claims (1–2) are tested only on very small instances (n≤4 with exact OPT, n=2 for correlated), the graph claims (3–4) are limited to cycle graphs or simplified reformulations, and the Erdős–Rényi concentration trend (Claim 6) is not reproduced.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-alignment-sensitive-.paper_title: Alignment-Sensitive Minimax Rates for Spectral Algorithms with Learned Kernels

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 establishes that over signal classes with Effective Span Dimension (ESD) at most K, the minimax excess risk is asymptotically equivalent to K·σ², holding without classical eigenvalue-decay or source-condition assumptions (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: 60 random configurations at d=40, σ²=0.3; regression of exact PC-estimator risk vs K=d† yields slope 0.3087 (2.9% relative error vs σ²=0.3). R²=0.442 reflects expected scatter from the bias term but the linear scaling with correct constant is confirmed on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 shows the principal-component (PC) estimator's risk is sandwiched as (d†−1)σ² ≤ Risk ≤ 2d†σ², where d† is the Effective Span Dimension defined as the smallest number of leading eigenfunctions whose remaining tail signal energy no longer exceeds the noise level σ² (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: 40 random configurations at d=40; exact closed-form PC-estimator risk computed at true d†, and all 40 instances satisfy (d†−1)σ² ≤ Risk ≤ 2d†σ². A real implementation bug (wrong denominator in tail-energy threshold) was found, disclosed, and fixed before the bounds held.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 gives convergence rates for a quota sequence {K_n}: the minimax risk over populations satisfying d†(σ0²/n; θ*, λ) ≤ K_n scales as Θ(K_n σ0²/n) (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Table across n=20–320 (d=60, σ0²=2.0, K_n=round(√n)) shows risk/(K_n·σ0²/n) ratios of 0.976–1.000, confirming the Θ(K_n·σ0²/n) rate across a 16× range of n with exact closed-form risk computation.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 proves that overparameterized gradient flow (OP-GF) can reduce the Effective Span Dimension over training time by assigning larger adapted eigenvalues to strong signal directions with initially small eigenvalues, moving the problem into a lower minimax-risk complexity class (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: ODE simulation of OP-GF dynamics (Eq 12) at d=20 with a strong signal (θ=3.0) placed at a poorly aligned coordinate; comparing ESD under static vs OP-GF-adapted eigenvalues at the same trained θ shows reduction from 16 to 1, directly confirming the claimed mechanism on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: Section 7 and Section 8 extend the Effective Span Dimension framework to linear regression (via SVD, minimax rate Θ(σ0²K/n)) and RKHS regression (rate Θ(σ̄²K_n/n) with effective noise σ̄² = (σ0² + ||f*||²_∞)/n) (Section 7, Section 8).
claims.evidence: Only the linear regression extension (Section 7) is tested, on a single random Gaussian design (n=200, d=30) where d†=30=d (trivial case: all coordinates retained, no dimensionality reduction demonstrated). The RKHS regression extension (Section 8, rate Θ(σ̄²K_n/n)) is not tested at all.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments show that span profiles decrease during OP-GF training—with larger improvements when initial signal-spectrum alignment is worse—and that deeper models attain lower Effective Span Dimension than shallow variants given sufficient training iterations (Numerical Validation).
claims.evidence: Using the paper's exact parameterization, span-profile reduction grows with misalignment q (1.0 at q=1.0, 2.5 at q=2.0) and depth comparison shows monotonic ESD decrease (D=0→9, D=1→3, D=3→1). A real baseline bug (trivial zero-initialization comparison) was found and corrected to the proper static-vs-adapted comparison.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-alignment-sensitive-.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting 5 of 6 claims through exact closed-form computations and ODE simulations at moderate scale (d=20–60), with two genuine bugs found and fixed during development. The main gap is Claim 5, where only the linear regression extension is tested in a trivial case (d†=d) and the RKHS extension is entirely unaddressed.

ProCreations/repro-fast-estimation-fores.paper_title: Fast Estimation for Forest Matrix of Signed Graphs

claims.claim: GSCF (Generalized Spanning Converging Forest) generates spanning converging forests for signed graphs using loop-erased random walks in expected O(n) time, per Theorem 5.2 (Section 5.1, Algorithm 1, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Seven graph sizes from 1,000 to 2,000,000 nodes yield an executed-transition exponent of 0.999697 (R²=1.000000), directly supporting O(n) scaling; correctness is validated against exact sparse (I+L) inverses on two real networks, with controls exercising both positive loop erasure and negative-unicycle retention.

claims.claim: FMDE estimates the diagonal of the forest matrix via sampling in O(ln) time, where l is the number of samples (Section 6.2, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: A 4×3 n-by-l work grid produces an executed-operation exponent of 0.999744 (R²=0.999999) with both n and l independently varied, confirming O(ln) scaling; accuracy is cross-checked against sparse LU factorization of I+L for 256 nodes on BitcoinOTC and Gnutella08.

claims.claim: FMDE+ incorporates additional network information to achieve the same O(ln) time complexity as FMDE but with lower variance, and Theorem 6.3 proves its superior performance on balanced signed graphs (Section 6.2, Theorem 6.3).
claims.evidence: On the 6,301-node Gnutella08 topology with balanced node-switch signing, 48 paired repetitions of 64 forests yield Var(FMDE+)/Var(FMDE)=0.00001414 with FMDE+ no larger on 100% of nodes, using a paired design that holds sampled forests fixed to isolate the variance-reduction effect.

claims.claim: On the SlashdotZoo network, exact diagonal computation via direct matrix inversion takes 991.5 seconds while FMDE+ completes in under 1.1 seconds (Table 1).
claims.evidence: An independent 623-sample run processes all 79,116 KONECT SlashdotZoo nodes with 99,325,244 executed operations and 100% finite outputs; the specific timing values (991.5s exact vs. 0.487–1.033s FMDE+) are cited from the paper's Table 1 rather than independently measured, but the full-scale run on the real network confirms the algorithm completes rapidly.

claims.claim: The methods scale to the FullUSA network with roughly 2.3×10^7 (over twenty million) nodes, where exact computation fails but FMDE+ completes within one hour (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The official DIMACS FullUSA graph (23,947,347 nodes, 58,333,344 arcs, verified by SHA-256) is processed end-to-end with five complete paired samples and 100% finite outputs; exact computation is shown infeasible by the 4.588 PB dense-inverse memory requirement, and the paper's reported FMDE+ times (1,204–3,598s) are all within one hour.

claims.claim: FMDE+ achieves roughly ten times lower average relative error than FMDE across tested networks (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: At matched l=4,674 with exact sparse-LU diagonal references, FMDE+ lowers average relative error by 13.45× on BitcoinOTC and 486.57× on Gnutella08, both exceeding the claimed roughly tenfold improvement, with BitcoinOTC remaining above tenfold at every tested sample budget.

ProCreations/repro-fast-estimation-fores.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence on real networks (BitcoinOTC, Gnutella08, SlashdotZoo, FullUSA) at full scale for all six claims, including independent scaling exponents, exact-inverse accuracy validation, and paired variance comparisons. The main weakness is that wall-clock timing for Claims 4 and 5 relies on paper-reported values rather than independent measurement, though the algorithms were executed on the actual networks at full scale.

ParetoOptimal/repro-bi9moh3uzw.paper_title: High-Dimensional Learning Dynamics of Quantized Models with Straight-Through Estimator

claims.claim: In the high-dimensional limit, the microscopic dynamics of straight-through estimator (STE) training converge to a stochastic differential equation governed by Eq. (15) (Section IV, Theorem IV.3).
claims.evidence: The SDE drift and diffusion coefficients match the one-step conditional moments of the finite-d STE chain (worst level-grouped t-statistic 1.09, worst relative error 0.005, second-moment ratio within 0.006 of 1 across d up to 8000), and the 1-Wasserstein distance between the empirical coordinate measure and the SDE law decays with fitted exponent -0.455 (close to d^{-1/2}) with W1*sqrt(d) roughly constant across a 16-fold range of d.

claims.claim: The macroscopic summary statistics of STE training concentrate onto a deterministic ODE trajectory (Eqs. (24)-(25)) with concentration rate O_d(d^{-1/2}) as dimension d grows (Section V-B, Theorem V.3).
claims.evidence: The q-component deviation from the ODE trajectory is flat in d (0.043 at d=200 vs 0.041 at d=3200), not decaying at d^{-1/2}; the cause is directly measured—Assumption V.1 fails with the marginal's excess kurtosis reaching 12.5 in the exact d→∞ limit, producing a closure error on q_psi of ~0.05 that persists from finite d to the limit, while the input-only control (which needs no closure) does concentrate properly.

claims.claim: STE training exhibits an extended plateau followed by a sharp drop in generalization error across bit-widths b in {2,3,4,5}, with the plateau length depending on the quantization range ω (Section VI-A1/VI-A2, Figures 2-3).
claims.evidence: Plateaus exist at all bit widths (96, 93, 144, 75 tau for b=2,3,4,5) and plateau length depends on omega (0–330 tau range), but the post-plateau sharpness ratio drops from 102.8 (b=2) and 27.8 (b=3) to only 2.89 (b=4) and 0.65 (b=5), meaning the descent after the shelf is slower than the shelf itself at b=5, contradicting 'sharp drop across b in {2,3,4,5}'.

claims.claim: For input-only quantization, a closed-form stable fixed point exists under the learning-rate condition 0 < η < 2(σ_ψ^2 + λ)/σ_ψ^4 (Section VI-C1, Proposition VI.1).
claims.evidence: Across 24 configurations and 4 learning rates, the closed-form fixed point is an exact ODE zero (worst relative |dq/dtau| = 1.4e-16), Jacobian eigenvalues match analytics to 4.3e-14, RK4 converges to it to 5.7e-14, and the stability threshold 2(σ_ψ²+λ)/σ_ψ⁴ is recovered by bisection to relative 4.7e-16 with convergence at 0.95η* and divergence at 1.05η* in every configuration.

claims.claim: The asymptotic deviation of the STE-trained quantized model from the unquantized linear model is characterized across three regimes, with a leading-order correction term of size O_Δ(Δ^2) depending on the fractional quantization level position (Section VI-C2, Theorem VI.3).
claims.evidence: All three regimes are confirmed: the interior correction σ_ψ²Δ²p(1-p) matches the solved fixed point to 6.5e-13 over 70 Figure-6 points with the underlying identity exact to 4.5e-15, the O_Δ(Δ²) scaling fits exponent 1.9999999999999942 with amplitude correct to 9.5e-15, the saturated regime matches to 1.1e-16, and the p∈{0,1} regime respects its o(1/√log(1/η)) bound.

ParetoOptimal/repro-bi9moh3uzw.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous from-scratch reproduction that verifies the SDE limit (Claim 1), the fixed-point theorem (Claim 4), and the three-regime characterization (Claim 5) with high-precision numerical evidence, while falsifying the ODE concentration claim (Claim 2) by directly measuring that Assumption V.1 fails in the d→∞ limit, and falsifying the 'sharp drop across all bit-widths' claim (Claim 3) by showing the drop is not sharp at b=4,5.

claims.claim: A weighted set is defined as a β-approximation preserving coreset (β-APC) if any α-approximate k-means solution computed on it yields an αβ-approximate solution on the full dataset (Definition 1.1).
claims.evidence: The APC definition was operationally exercised on a Gaussian mixture at n=18000, d=10, k=10 with 12 candidate solutions spanning coreset α from 1.0076 to 58.1016; the realized β max was 1.0166, well below the 1+ε=1.2 bound, demonstrating the α→αβ lifting behavior at non-trivial scale.

claims.claim: For Euclidean k-means, sensitivity sampling constructs a (1+ε)-APC of size Õ(kε^-3), improving on strong coreset size requirements (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: Sensitivity sampling with m=ceil(kε⁻³) was tested on synthetic Gaussian (n=18000) and sklearn digits (n=1797, d=64); all max cost ratios stayed below 1+ε (e.g., 1.0109 at ε=0.2 on synthetic, 1.0225 on digits), and the ε⁻³ size scaling was confirmed across ε=0.4, 0.2, 0.1.

claims.claim: For arbitrary metrics, an iterative downsampling approach constructs a (4+ε)-APC of size Õ(kε^-2) (Theorem 1.3).
claims.evidence: Three-stage iterative metric downsampling on Euclidean (n=2200) and line (n=2600) metrics produced final coreset sizes 30 and 51 with full-data cost ratios 1.2083 and 1.4741, both below the 4+ε=4.5 bound; the nearest-coreset-point lifting lemma was stress-tested on 15000 random cases per metric with worst ratios 1.6614 and 2.0564.

claims.claim: Sensitivity sampling with m = Cε^-2(k log(k/δ) + log N) points gives strong coreset concentration guarantees for a solution family of size N (Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: The formula m=Cε⁻²(k log(k/δ)+log N) was directly tested at n=7000, k=10, N=1000, ε=0.2, δ=0.1, C=1.3 (m=1722); over 220 independent coreset samples, simultaneous preservation of all N solutions succeeded at rate 1.0000 versus the 1−δ=0.9 target, and the ε-sweep confirmed ε⁻² scaling.

claims.claim: For finite n-point metrics, sensitivity sampling yields strong coresets of size O(kε^-2 log n), matching known lower bounds without extra polylogarithmic factors (Corollary 2.3).
claims.evidence: With C=1.5, k=5, ε=0.25, sample sizes grew logarithmically with n (749, 832, 915, 999 for n=512–4096) with success rates ≥0.967, and m·ε² stayed nearly constant (57.19–57.25) across ε values, confirming the O(kε⁻² log n) upper bound; the matching-lower-bound clause is literature-attributed and not independently verified.

claims.claim: A lower bound of Ω(log N / log log N) is proved showing that APC guarantees below β=4 are not achievable for the arbitrary-metric setting (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: The (1,2)-distance lower-bound family was constructed at n=1024, 4096, 16384 with r=√n; greedy packing produced 200 r-subsets with max intersections below τ·r caps, exact hypergeometric tails were 1.48e-07 to 8.12e-42, and the best shared-output β barriers were 3.875, 3.9375, 3.9688, approaching 4 from below as predicted.

Srishti280992/repro-approximation-preser.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence at non-trivial scale (n up to 18000, coreset sizes up to 10000, lower-bound constructions up to n=16384) supporting all six claims through independent implementations of sensitivity sampling, iterative downsampling, concentration testing, and the lower-bound construction. These are finite-scale audits of asymptotic theoretical results rather than formal proof verification, and some constructions use simplified approximations of the paper's algorithms.

Srishti280992/repro-generalizing-stochas.paper_title: Generalizing Stochastic Smoothing for Differentiation and Gradient Estimation

claims.claim: Lemma 3 generalizes the stochastic-smoothing gradient identity to absolutely continuous but not necessarily differentiable densities, enabling smoothing with distributions such as Laplace and triangular that lack differentiable densities (Section 2, Lemma 3).
claims.evidence: 65,536-sample Sobol estimates of the Heaviside gradient match analytic values across all six distributions, with Laplace (nondifferentiable density) error 2.2e-06 and Triangular (nondifferentiable, compactly supported) error 0.00151, directly exercising the relaxed density assumptions of Lemma 3.

claims.claim: Theorem 7 extends the smoothing framework to multivariate distributions with covariance matrices, allowing differentiation with respect to scale parameters (Section 2, Theorem 7).
claims.evidence: Bivariate Gaussian with non-diagonal scale matrix L=[[0.82,0],[0.28,1.08]] and two halfspace outputs: 65,536-sample Sobol estimates yield Frobenius errors 7.04e-05 for the input Jacobian and 4.19e-04 for the full 2×2×2 scale-derivative tensor against closed-form analytic derivatives.

claims.claim: Theorem 8 derives estimators for the derivative of the output covariance matrix, enabling gradient-based uncertainty quantification (Section 2, Theorem 8).
claims.evidence: Three independent binary threshold outputs with closed-form covariance derivatives: 65,536-sample Sobol estimates give Frobenius errors 2.41e-04 for input-covariance derivatives and 4.59e-04 for scale-covariance derivatives, with near-zero off-diagonal covariance residuals confirming the mean-correction terms.

claims.claim: Section 4 benchmarks variance-reduction methods for stochastic-smoothing gradient estimation across 6 distributions (Gaussian, Logistic, Gumbel, Cauchy, Laplace, Triangular) and 24 combinations of sampling strategy (MC, Antithetic MC, Cartesian/Latin-Hypercube QMC and RQMC), covariate (None, f(x), Leave-One-Out) and antithetic pairing (Section 4).
claims.evidence: A complete 144-cell factorial census (6 distributions × 4 sampling strategies × 3 covariates × 2 antithetic settings) was executed with real estimator runs on hard n=3 sorting/ranking, producing CSV artifacts with mean oracle errors, standard deviations, and within-distribution ranks for every cell.

claims.claim: Section 4 finds that Cartesian RQMC combined with the Leave-One-Out covariate, without antithetic pairing, achieves the lowest gradient-estimator variance among the tested combinations when feasible (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The executed code shown in the logbook produces target ranks [18,18,21,3,15,20] (mean rank 15.8) for Cartesian RQMC + Leave-One-Out + no antithetic, directly contradicting the claim; the logbook attributes this to an incorrect Cartesian RQMC implementation and reports corrected runs with ranks [1,1,1,1,3,1], but the corrected code and its output are not shown in the logbook.

claims.claim: Sections 4.2-4.5 demonstrate the framework on differentiable sorting/ranking (MNIST, n=5), Warcraft shortest-path prediction, differentiable rendering (Utah teapot pose estimation), and cryo-electron tomography simulation optimization (Section 4.2, Section 4.3, Section 4.4, Section 4.5).
claims.evidence: All four application classes are exercised with real gradient-based optimization runs showing improvement, but each uses a clearly simplified setup: MNIST uses centroid-similarity features instead of a CNN, Warcraft uses direct 12×12 cost-map optimization instead of CNN from RGB terrain, teapot rendering is single-angle instead of 4-DoF, and cryo-ET uses a local 64×64 phantom instead of the external TEM simulator.

Srishti280992/repro-generalizing-stochas.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical verification of the paper's core theoretical results (Lemma 3, Theorems 7–8) via analytic comparisons on non-trivial sample sizes, and runs a complete 144-cell variance-benchmark census. However, the shown code output for Claim 5 contradicts the paper's best-configuration finding, the claimed corrected runs are not evidenced in the logbook, and the four application demonstrations are reduced proxies rather than full reproductions.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-continuous-variable-.paper_title: Continuous Variable Hamiltonian Learning at Heisenberg Limit via Displacement-Random Unitary Transformation

claims.claim: The Displacement-Random Unitary Transformation (D-RUT) protocol learns all coefficients of a generic multi-mode bosonic Hamiltonian with evolution time scaling as O(1/epsilon), achieving the Heisenberg limit (Theorem 1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: The test uses a single-mode (d=3) Hamiltonian rather than the 'generic multi-mode' setting claimed, and assumes a Heisenberg-limited measurement noise model (std ~ 1/T) rather than deriving it from the quantum protocol; the fitted 1.0 decay rate confirms the linear reconstruction pipeline preserves the assumed input precision, but does not verify the D-RUT protocol itself achieves Heisenberg scaling.

claims.claim: For single-mode Hamiltonians expressed in a first-quantization (position/momentum) basis, D-RUT recovers physical coefficients with RMSE epsilon_G using total evolution time O~(1/epsilon_G), under stated conditions on known zero coefficients, non-zero response to basis mismatch, and a sufficiently close initial guess (Theorem 2, Section 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states this is 'the mathematically identical polynomial/inverse-DFT reduction as Claim 1, under a linear relabeling of operators' — the same single-mode d=3 setup with assumed Heisenberg noise, adding only a basis relabeling without testing the first-quantization-specific conditions (known zero coefficients, non-zero response to basis mismatch, close initial guess) stated in Theorem 2.

claims.claim: The protocol's estimation error under state-preparation-and-measurement (SPAM) errors is bounded as ||delta g_SPAM||_2 <= (L_C/sigma_min(K)) ||delta beta||_2, where L_C is a Lipschitz constant and sigma_min(K) the smallest singular value of the Gram-like matrix K (Section 3.6, Eq. 43).
claims.evidence: Concrete numerical test on d=2, M=12 measurements with 15 random perturbation trials at scales 10^-4 to 10^-2: all trials satisfy the specific bound ||δg|| ≤ (L_C/σ_min(K))||δβ|| with max ratio 0.657, verifying the exact proportionality constant of the inequality, not just qualitative behavior.

claims.claim: A hierarchical two-stage coefficient recovery strategy (learn single-mode coefficients first, then coupling coefficients) is proven to have covariance dominated by that of simultaneous estimation, Cov(delta g)_hierarchical <= Cov(delta g)_simultaneous, for all parameters (Section 4.1, Appendix A).
claims.evidence: Simplified to a 2-mode model with d=1 per mode (disclosed), and the covariance comparison is reported only for the shared mode-A coefficient rather than 'all parameters' as claimed; while both Monte Carlo (8.359e-07 vs 1.079e-06) and exact OLS theory (9.329e-07 vs 1.224e-06) confirm dominance, the scope is substantially reduced from the general multi-mode claim.

claims.claim: An iterative bisection search over the squeezing parameter R (relating the physical and reference bases via a Bogoliubov transformation) converges in O(log(1/epsilon_R)) iterations for first-quantization Hamiltonian learning (Section 5.3, Eq. 77-78).
claims.evidence: The logbook honestly discloses that the paper's exact Eq. 77-78 bisection-search description was not found in the accessible text; the tested bisection over a condition-number objective converges in log2(1/ε) iterations, but this is a generic property of any bisection algorithm and does not verify the paper's specific derivation or algorithm.

claims.claim: The algorithm uses Chebyshev-node sampling of the displacement parameter combined with robust phase estimation and inverse discrete Fourier transform to reconstruct coefficients, as detailed in Algorithm 1 and illustrated for the single-mode case in Figure 1 (Section 2).
claims.evidence: Full end-to-end single-mode pipeline demonstrated at d=2, T=2000: Chebyshev radial nodes, per-degree angle sets, RPE-style noisy measurement of C(β), Vandermonde polynomial fit, and inverse-DFT extraction via Eq. 12, recovering all five coefficients with RMSE 0.00476 — matching the paper's own single-mode Figure 1 illustration scope.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-continuous-variable-.overall: The logbook implements the D-RUT reconstruction pipeline classically via an exact reduction to coherent-state expectation values, providing concrete numerical verification of the SPAM error bound (Claim 3) and the end-to-end Algorithm 1 illustration (Claim 6). However, the Heisenberg scaling (Claims 1-2) and hierarchical covariance (Claim 4) are tested only on simplified single-mode or low-dimensional setups with assumed noise models, and the paper's specific bisection algorithm (Claim 5) was not located in the source text.

MunchProductionz/repro-beyond-text-to-sq.paper_title: Beyond Text-to-SQL: Can LLMs Really Debug Enterprise ETL SQL?

claims.claim: SQLBench (Squirrel) comprises 469 syntax-error tasks (Squirrel-Syntax) and 516 semantic-error tasks (Squirrel-Semantic), built from over 1,000 seed SQL scripts spanning 26 business scenarios, with scripts averaging over 140 lines, AST width >11, and AST depth >8.7 (Benchmark Construction section).
claims.evidence: The logbook constructed synthetic proxies (75–150 tasks) and a public-ETL proxy (150 mutations of 79 Mozilla BigQuery scripts across 26 namespace strata), demonstrating a construction pattern at reduced scale, but never verified the actual 469/516 task counts, 1,000+ seed scripts, or specific complexity metrics on the real Squirrel benchmark.

claims.claim: Claude-4-Sonnet achieves only 36.46% Graph Match score on Squirrel-Syntax debugging and 32.17% on Squirrel-Semantic debugging, the best performance among evaluated models (Main Results table).
claims.evidence: Provider-routed Claude Sonnet 4 was run on synthetic proxy tasks (50.7% syntax, 11.4% semantic on v4; 28.0% syntax, 27.3% semantic on v5 Proxy AST Match), but the data, metric (Proxy AST Match vs. Graph Match), and model environment all differ from the paper, making the specific 36.46%/32.17% numbers and 'best model' ranking unverifiable.

claims.claim: DeepSeek-V3 scores 30.28% (Graph Match) on Squirrel-Syntax and 21.32% on Squirrel-Semantic, while Qwen-2.5-Coder-32B scores 23.45% on Squirrel-Semantic, with most evaluated LLMs failing to exceed 20% success rate on enterprise SQL debugging (Main Results table).
claims.evidence: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B was run on proxy data (22.8% semantic Proxy AST Match on v4, 0% on v5 with 24 empty-provider errors), but DeepSeek-V3 was never run, the metric differs (Proxy AST Match vs. Graph Match), and the 'most LLMs < 20%' claim was not tested on the actual benchmark.

claims.claim: SQLBench scripts contain on the order of 420+ tokens and 17.34-21.62 functions per script on average, reflecting enterprise-scale ETL SQL complexity rather than the short queries used in prior Text-to-SQL benchmarks (Benchmark Statistics section).
claims.evidence: The v5 public-ETL proxy averages 161.21 lines, 791.63 tokens, 42.33 functions, depth 12.85, and width 89.07, which is in the enterprise complexity range for some measures but differs substantially for others (tokens, functions, width) and uses different data and measurement tools than the paper.

MunchProductionz/repro-beyond-text-to-sq.overall: The logbook establishes a well-documented toy-scale proxy reproduction using synthetic and public Mozilla BigQuery ETL data with real API-based model runs (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, Claude Sonnet 4, and three calibration models), but it never had access to the private Squirrel benchmark, the Calcite Graph Match evaluator, or the historical model environments, so none of the paper's specific quantitative claims are verified or falsified at scale.

ParetoOptimal/repro-uxzfldxrbj.paper_title: Quantifying LLM Attention-Head Stability: Implications for Circuit Universality

claims.claim: Middle-layer attention heads show the lowest cross-refit stability, e.g., layer 5 drops to ≈0.70 stability versus ≈1.0 in layer 1, quantified via a layer-wise mean stability measure (Equation 5, Section 4.1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: On the paper's own released 8-layer 8-head MLP refits (20 anchors, 1.6M head-to-head comparisons), layer-wise stability S_l bottoms at layer 5 with S=0.648 (seed 1) and 0.721 (20-anchor mean) versus S=0.970 at layer 1, matching the paper's ≈0.70 vs ≈1.0 claim; the U-shape holds for 17/20 anchors.

claims.claim: Middle layers also exhibit broader, less sharply defined off-diagonal head-to-head matching patterns across refits compared to early/late layers (Section 4.2, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Off-diagonal alignment mass for late layers 7-8 (0.674) exceeds that of middle layers 4-5 (0.636), and row kurtosis—the paper's own 'flatter = lower kurtosis' statistic—is lowest at layers 7-8 (1.83, 1.36) rather than at middle layers (2.87, 3.01), contradicting the claim that middle layers are broader than both early and late layers.

claims.claim: In deeper architectures (8- and 12-layer models), the least-stable layer occurs at a relative depth r≈0.4–0.8, showing stronger mid-depth divergence than shallower models (Section 4.6.2, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: The 8-layer component is verified exactly (r_l_min=0.625, inside [0.4, 0.8] for 16/20 Adam anchors), but the 12-layer model and the 'stronger mid-depth divergence than shallower models' comparison could not be tested because no weights for 2-, 4-, or 12-layer architectures were released.

claims.claim: Using AdamW (weight decay) yields a clear increase in attention-head seed-stability for deeper MLP models (8- and 12-layer) without degrading task performance (Section 4.5, Figure 6).
claims.evidence: Stability increases from 0.836 (Adam) to 0.867 (AdamW) with zero overlap across 20 refits each, but wikitext-2 test perplexity degrades from 70.8 to 91.5 (p<1e-6, every AdamW refit worse than every Adam refit), and in-distribution C4 perplexity also worsens (31.0→33.1, p<1e-29), directly contradicting 'without degrading task performance.'

claims.claim: Higher query-weight norms correlate with lower head stability, suggesting weight-norm control as a mechanistic driver of the weight-decay stability effect (Section 4.4.1).
claims.evidence: Pearson correlation between per-layer query-weight Frobenius norm and layer-wise stability is negative in all 40/40 released refits (mean r=-0.69 for Adam, -0.83 for AdamW; pooled -0.68 and -0.81), and query norms peak at layers 4-5 where stability is lowest, with AdamW reducing mean query norm from 33.0 to 24.6 alongside the stability gain.

claims.claim: The residual stream is consistently more stable across refits than the corresponding attention heads, across all tested architectures and optimizers, as measured via Centered Kernel Alignment (Section 4.7, Figure 9, Appendix A.7).
claims.evidence: Under a matched RBF-CKA metric applied to both residual and head-z activations, residual CKA exceeds head CKA in 8/8 layers for both Adam (mean 0.870 vs 0.445, min margin 0.167) and AdamW (mean 0.880 vs 0.481, min margin 0.201); the claim holds for the 2 released architectures, though only 2 of the paper's 26 architectures had available weights.

ParetoOptimal/repro-uxzfldxrbj.overall: The logbook provides strong concrete evidence reproducing the core mid-layer instability dip (claim 1), the query-norm/stability correlation (claim 5), and residual-stream superiority under CKA (claim 6) on the paper's own released 8-layer checkpoints, while falsifying the off-diagonal breadth claim (claim 2) and the 'no performance cost' part of the AdamW claim (claim 4) with rigorous counter-evidence; claims requiring 12-layer or shallower-model comparisons remain unaddressed due to missing released weights.

ParetoOptimal/repro-lq8fnvme8v.paper_title: Minimum Distance Summaries for Robust Neural Posterior Estimation

claims.claim: Minimum-distance summaries (MDS) adapt the query summary s* = arg min_s D(P_{x|s}, Q) at test time while keeping the pretrained neural posterior estimator fixed, preserving amortization (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: SHA256 of the NPE state dict is bit-identical before and after 1300 test-time adaptations (ab4d0fcb... both times), with a single offline decoder fit serving the entire 13-level sweep on a 50000-dataset training setup, directly confirming the frozen-NPE amortization claim.

claims.claim: MDS is implemented via a Maximum Mean Discrepancy objective using random Fourier feature approximations of the Gaussian kernel, with a decoder mean-embedding network trained offline via MSE and the summary optimized at test time by L-BFGS (Section 3.2, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: RFF-MMD vs exact Gaussian MMD² correlation 0.9993, decoder MSE trained offline to holdout R² 0.994, and L-BFGS reduces the objective in 98.5% of 1300 runs averaging 8 evaluations—all measured on the 50000-dataset Gaussian benchmark with the paper's stated hyperparameters.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that under Huber's ε-contamination model Q_ε = (1-ε)Q + εδ_y, the KL divergence between posteriors under MDS-adapted summaries for Q and Q_ε is O(ε), bounding robustness to small contamination (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: In an exact conjugate-Gaussian instance, the influence function matches closed form to 4.2e-10 relative error, sup_y||IF|| is finite across 9 cells, the gradient bound holds at all 1503 points, and sup_y KL decays with log-log slope 2.01 (O(ε²), satisfying O(ε)), with a forward-KL counterexample confirming the MMD's necessity.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 shows that when the model is correctly specified, posterior consistency under the original summary statistics implies posterior consistency under MDS-adapted summaries (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: In the exact conjugate-Gaussian setting, a 3-decade N sweep (10–10000, 40 seeds) shows both original-summary and MDS-summary posteriors concentrating at the same N^{-1/2} rate (slopes -0.478 vs -0.483), with max error ratio 1.11 and a vanishing summary gap (slope -0.475).

claims.claim: On the Gaussian model, MDS outperforms NPE, NNPE, and NPE-OR baselines across a range of contamination proportions, with degradation only appearing at contamination levels above 40% (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: On the full-scale Gaussian benchmark (50000 training datasets, 100 test datasets per level), NPE-OR is the best arm at 6 of 7 contaminated levels (e.g., posterior MMD 0.86 vs MDS 1.31 at eps 0.2; 2.11 vs 6.91 at eps 0.7), and NNPE beats MDS on posterior MMD from eps 0.3 onward, contradicting the 'outperforms NPE, NNPE, and NPE-OR' conjunct.

claims.claim: On a 1024-dimensional Cryo-EM inference task, MDS substantially improves robustness to Gaussian noise contamination while maintaining performance in the well-specified regime (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The 1024-dimensional task uses reduced scale (n_train 4000 vs 15000, rff_dim 512 vs 1024, n_test 50 vs 100) and a substituted molecular ensemble; the robustness gain reproduces (RMSE 30.4→5.4 at eps 0.5) but well-specified performance fails (MDS 5.04 vs NPE 1.53 at eps 0.0), with the failure attributed to a weak decoder (R² 0.13) plausibly caused by the halved rff_dim and reduced training data.

ParetoOptimal/repro-lq8fnvme8v.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the structural/architectural claims (1–2) and the theoretical claims (3–4) with exact analytic computations and full-scale Gaussian experiments, but falsifies the Gaussian benchmark claim (5) by showing NPE-OR outperforms MDS at most contamination levels, and only partially addresses the cryo-EM claim (6) on a reduced-scale setup where the well-specified regime breaks down.

ParetoOptimal/repro-jl2f2y3iuc.paper_title: Fine-Tuning Without Forgetting In-Context Learning: A Theoretical Analysis of Linear Attention Models

claims.claim: Corollary 4.4 shows that full fine-tuning of all attention parameters in a linear attention model drives zero-shot error to σ² while few-shot (in-context) error converges to σ² + θᵀΣθ, a substantially larger value, formalizing the degradation of in-context learning after full fine-tuning (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: An independently derived exact closed form for the n-shot test error, cross-validated against Monte-Carlo (24 configs, 400k prompts each, max |z|=1.78) and the authors' released code (max abs gap 0.0024), confirms across 120 swept cells that zero-shot error equals σ² exactly (gap 0.0) and asymptotic few-shot error equals σ²+θᵀΣθ exactly (gap 0.0 analytically, 2.2e-11 numerically), with few-shot strictly worse than zero-shot in every cell.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.6 shows that restricting fine-tuning updates to the value matrix reduces zero-shot error to σ² + (2/(d+4))θ₀ᵀΣθ₀ while Corollary 4.8 shows the asymptotic few-shot error only rises to σ² + 1/(d+4)²θ₀ᵀΣθ₀, i.e. value-matrix-only fine-tuning improves zero-shot performance with far less degradation to in-context learning than full fine-tuning (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Across 20 zero-shot cells, 100 w*(n) cells, and 40 asymptotic-limit cells, the argmin v21 equals θ₀/(d+4) exactly (gap 0.0), the minimum zero-shot loss equals σ²+2/(d+4)θ₀ᵀΣθ₀ (gap 4e-15), Corollary 4.8 w*(n) is the exact argmin (gap 0.0), and the asymptotic few-shot error equals σ²+1/(d+4)²θ₀ᵀΣθ₀ (gap 0.0), with the degradation ratio matching (d+4)² exactly at d=5,10,20,40,80.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.10 proves that tuning the auxiliary few-shot loss weight w to optimize few-shot performance on the fine-tuning task θ₀ necessarily reduces few-shot performance on other tasks θ ≠ θ₀, formalizing a trade-off between target-task adaptation and generalization to unseen tasks (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: Proposition 4.10's excess-error formula reproduces to machine precision (gap 2e-15 over 256 cells), the rho-parameterized form matches (gap 1e-15 over 128 cells), excess error is non-negative in all cells, and the (1-ρ)² dependence is confirmed; however, a constructed counterexample (θ=−0.0819·θ₀, distance 1.08 from θ₀) yields excess error exactly 0.0, contradicting the word 'necessarily' in the claim's paraphrase, though the paper's own proposition statement is consistent with this edge case.

claims.claim: In synthetic linear-regression experiments (d=5, σ²=0.1, Σ=I₅, ‖θ₀‖₂²=1, m=n=20), Figure 4 confirms the theoretical zero-shot/few-shot error predictions across pretraining, full fine-tuning, and value-matrix fine-tuning regimes, and Figure 5 shows value-matrix fine-tuning attains the lowest error on the out-of-distribution task -θ₀ (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: Using the authors' released code at exact paper settings (d=5, σ²=0.1, Σ=I₅, ‖θ₀‖²=1, m=n=20) over 3 seeds, trained curves match theory with max relative deviation 0.014–0.063 across all regimes, and value-matrix fine-tuning (ZS V) achieves the lowest 20-shot error on −θ₀ in all 3 seeds (0.392 vs 1.251 for full fine-tuning), reproducing both Figure 4 and Figure 5 conclusions.

claims.claim: On the MMLU benchmark using Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct fine-tuned on the Humanities category, full fine-tuning improves zero-shot accuracy but degrades 7-shot accuracy, whereas value-matrix-only fine-tuning preserves few-shot accuracy while still improving zero-shot performance (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: Four MMLU experiment attempts were launched but none completed: the 3B model exceeded GPU budget, and the 0.5B substitution's fine-tuning arms collapsed to chance-level accuracy (24.6%) under answer-only supervision, producing no fine-tuned model that improved zero-shot accuracy, so no evidence supports or contradicts the claim.

ParetoOptimal/repro-jl2f2y3iuc.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, machine-precision verification of all four theoretical claims (Claims 1–4) through an independently derived closed form cross-validated against Monte-Carlo and the authors' own code, plus a 3-seed reproduction of the synthetic experiments using the authors' released pipeline. The MMLU experiment (Claim 5) was never completed due to GPU constraints and a collapsed substitution, leaving it entirely unaddressed.

DineshAI/repro-the-catastrophic-failure-.paper_title: The Catastrophic Failure of *the* k-Means Algorithm in High Dimensions, and How Hartigan's Algorithm Avoids It

claims.claim: In the high-noise, high-dimensional regime where σ² > n, Lloyd's k-means algorithm fails catastrophically: essentially every partition of the data becomes a fixed point of the algorithm (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive enumeration of all 456 q-balanced binary partitions for n=10, σ²=22.03>10, across 24 datasets shows lloyd_all_q_fixed_rate=1.0 and lloyd_q_fixed_fraction=1.0 at every d≥512 (up to d=32768), while the low-noise control (σ²=1) yields 0/24 all-fixed trials and only ~25% partition-level fixed fraction, directly supporting the high-noise pathology claim.

claims.claim: In the same high-noise regime, Hartigan's k-means algorithm avoids this pathology, having no incorrect fixed points with high probability (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive testing of all 510 nontrivial incorrect binary partitions across 24 datasets shows hartigan_incorrect_fixed_fraction decreasing from 0.00678 at d=128 to exactly 0.0 at d=8192 and d=32768, with hartigan_no_incorrect_fixed_rate=1.0 (24/24) at both largest dimensions, directly confirming Hartigan avoids incorrect fixed points in the high-noise regime.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.8 bounds the probability that any q-approximately balanced partition is not a fixed point of Lloyd's algorithm by 2^n · n · ρ_q^(d/4) (Corollary 3.8).
claims.evidence: The closed-form bound 2^n·n·ρ_q^(d/4) was independently transcribed and evaluated in float64 with ρ_q=0.9903∈(0,1), yielding bound values 0.482 at d=4096, 5.03e-14 at d=16384, and 5.94e-66 at d=65536, with empirical exhaustive enumeration agreeing (all 456 q-balanced partitions fixed by d=8192).

claims.claim: Corollary 3.12 bounds the probability that any incorrect partition is a fixed point of Hartigan's algorithm by 2^n · ρ_h^(d/4), a substantially tighter bound than Lloyd's case (Corollary 3.12).
claims.evidence: The formula 2^n·ρ_h^(d/4) was reproduced with ρ_h=0.99998∈(0,1), and the structural improvement (removing the factor n from the prefactor) is confirmed; however, for this parameter slice ρ_h>ρ_q, so the Hartigan bound is not numerically smaller than Lloyd's at finite d—the 'substantially tighter' characterization is supported only structurally, not numerically.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 shows Lloyd's single-sample reassignment step persists misclassification errors once the noise level exceeds σ > (2c̄τ(c−1))/√(c(c+c̄)) (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: At 1.1× the noise threshold (σ²=19.855, threshold σ²≈18.05), Lloyd stay-rate rises from 0.724 at d=64 to 1.000 at d=4096 with 1024 trials/point, while the 0.5× control shows Lloyd stay-rate falling from 0.448 to 0.034, confirming regime-dependent persistence as predicted by Theorem 3.4.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments empirically demonstrate the divergence between Lloyd's catastrophic-failure behavior and Hartigan's robustness as dimension grows, corroborating the theoretical bounds (Section 4).
claims.evidence: At σ²=80 with d up to 65536 and 32 trials/point, Lloyd achieves mean NMI 0.0143 with 100% unchanged rate while Hartigan achieves NMI 1.0 with 32/32 exact recoveries at d=16384 and 65536; the divergence is consistent across multiple noise levels (σ²=10,20,40,80), though at reduced scope (K=2, one initialization, 32 vs 100 trials) compared to the paper.

DineshAI/repro-the-catastrophic-failure-.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all six claims through exhaustive partition enumeration (claims 1–2), float64 formula audits with empirical agreement (claims 3–4), threshold-controlled single-sample experiments (claim 5), and dimension-sweep GMM experiments (claim 6). The main qualification is that claim 4's 'substantially tighter' characterization is only structurally confirmed (smaller prefactor) but not numerically for the tested parameter slice where ρ_h>ρ_q.

ProCreations/repro-beyond-relu-bifurcati.paper_title: Beyond ReLU: Bifurcation, Oversmoothing, and Topological Priors

claims.claim: Proves a supercritical pitchfork bifurcation condition α·w·λ_k = 1 under which odd C^3 activation functions destabilize the homogeneous fixed point and create stable non-homogeneous patterns in GNN dynamics (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Across five 56-node graph families, subcritical origins have spectral radius <1 while supercritical branches (αwλ_k=1.003) are nonzero, stable under the full iteration Jacobian, and align ≥0.999803 with the critical eigenmode, directly testing both sides of the bifurcation threshold.

claims.claim: Derives a √μ scaling law for the amplitude of emergent patterns near the bifurcation point, where μ measures distance from criticality, and validates this scaling empirically (Theorem 3.2, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Fifty Newton solves of the full nonlinear recurrence across 10 μ values × 5 graph families yield log-log slopes 0.4996–0.5013, and a deliberately wrong linear-in-μ model has ≥4285× worse residual, confirming the √μ scaling law with an unfitted exponent.

claims.claim: Shows Dirichlet energy stays at zero in the subcritical regime and grows linearly in the supercritical regime, quantifying departure from oversmoothing (Corollary 3.4).
claims.evidence: Direct computation of the Dirichlet energy xᵀ(I−A)x on converged fixed points gives exactly zero in all subcritical cases and supercritical energy-vs-μ fits with R²≥0.99997, with an independent spectral identity oracle matching within 7.79e-5.

claims.claim: Proves that near the bifurcation point the NTK becomes asymptotically rank-one, dominated by the bifurcating eigenmode, explaining emergent topological learning priors (Corollary 4.1).
