claims.claim: The framework extends to topology optimization using homogenization-based mechanical property objectives under symmetry constraints, and Theorem B.9 shows the theoretical construction generalizes to n=3 (space groups), with zero-shot extension to metamaterial design demonstrated in Figure 8 (Section 6.3, Equation 8, Theorem B.9, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: Theorem B.9 is verified for 12 tested 3D point groups embedding into Oh(48) or D6h(24) reflection groups (max order 48 matching Tahara 1971), and Q4 homogenization of a p4mm cell yields a square-symmetric effective tensor (E11=E22, defect ~1e-17) while an asymmetric control is strongly anisotropic; the Figure 8 diffusion-based metamaterial demo is explicitly not reproduced.

snaykey/repro-cost-aware-bo-stopping.overall: The logbook provides concrete computational verification of the paper's mathematical core across all 17 wallpaper groups, including exact group-theoretic embeddings, universal approximation convergence, continuity analysis, algorithm invariance, VTM connectivity enforcement, and 3D/homogenization extensions. The diffusion-based image generation components (SDS, SDXL, Figure 8 U-Net) are honestly disclosed as compute-gated and not reproduced.

snaykey/repro-persuasive-privacy.paper_title: Personalized Policy Learning through Discrete Experimentation

claims.claim: DLPT's learned policy achieves a regret rate of O(r(1+√log(1/r))√(d/n) + r√(log(1/δ)/n)), establishing minimax-optimal √n convergence across fixed policy classes (Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence: On a well-specified DGP with n up to 8000, d=10, 6 seeds, log-log regret slopes are -0.4224 (95% CI [-0.5645, -0.2878]) for DNN and -0.5172 (95% CI [-0.7328, -0.3537]) for Linear policy classes, both bracketing -0.5, and a C/sqrt(n) envelope upper-bounds observed regret across all n.

claims.claim: The deep-neural-network nuisance parameter estimator used within DLPT converges at rate O(n^{-p/(p+d_C)} log^8 n + log log n / n) (Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: Nuisance L2 error decreases monotonically with n (slope -0.3708) and identifiability is confirmed (m>=K+1 arms yields 0.05429 error vs 0.06908 for rank-deficient), but the specific rate O(n^{-p/(p+d_C)} log^8 n) cannot be verified because smoothness p is unknown, so only qualitative decay is demonstrated.

claims.claim: In the Platform O field experiment (7,349,648 low-activity creators, four incentive levels of 178/358/538/718 points versus control, August 23–29 2021), all four treatment levels produced statistically significant upload-rate effects (p<0.0001) with relative effect sizes from 13.01% to 19.69% (Section 4, Table 3).
claims.evidence: A static re-derivation of t-tests from the paper's own published coefficients and SEs yields t-statistics of 51.9-77.0 (p<<0.0001) and relative effects of 13.01-19.69%, but no microdata are used—this is arithmetic on the paper's reported numbers, not an independent reproduction.

claims.claim: On average treatment effect estimation with field data, DLPT achieves 2.25% MAPE versus 7.18% for the next-best baseline (PDL) and 38.23%–43.59% for linear/logistic/latent-class baselines, roughly a 3.2x accuracy improvement over PDL (Table 5).
claims.evidence: On a semi-synthetic DGP (n=6000, 6 seeds), the ranking DLPT<PDL<LR/LogR/LCM is reproduced, but absolute MAPE values are far from the paper's (DLPT 14.77% vs claimed 2.25%; PDL 20.66% vs 7.18%), and the improvement ratio is 1.4x, not the claimed 3.2x.

claims.claim: For policy learning over the finite observed treatment-level class, DLPT attains 2.22% mean percentage regret compared to a 6.32%–10.05% range for benchmark methods (Section 5).
claims.evidence: On a semi-synthetic DGP (n=4000, 6 seeds), DLPT achieves 14.30% MPR—higher than PDL's 11.48%—so DLPT is not strictly lowest, and the specific claimed values (2.22% vs 6.32-10.05%) are not reproduced; the claim is tested on a proxy task rather than the paper's field data.

claims.claim: Across semi-synthetic evaluations spanning four policy classes (finite observed, discretized continuous, linear, and DNN), DLPT consistently achieves the lowest regret, ranging 0.01%–19.69% versus 0.66%–34.75% for benchmarks (Section 6).
claims.evidence: Across four policy classes on a semi-synthetic DGP, DLPT is not strictly lowest in any class (PDL beats it in all four: e.g., Finite Observed 11.48 vs 14.30, DNN 5.73 vs 8.59), contradicting 'consistently lowest,' though DLPT does beat misspecified baselines (LR/LogR/LCM) everywhere; the specific claimed ranges (0.01-19.69% vs 0.66-34.75%) are not reproduced.

snaykey/repro-persuasive-privacy.overall: The logbook provides genuine experimental evidence supporting the theoretical sqrt(n) regret rate (Claim 1) on a non-trivial well-specified setup, but the remaining claims are tested on proxy or static setups: Claim 2 verifies only qualitative decay, Claim 3 is arithmetic on published numbers, and Claims 4-6 use a semi-synthetic DGP where the paper's specific quantitative results and DLPT-vs-PDL superiority do not reproduce.

amkkk/repro-geometry-aware-probabilistic.paper_title: Geometry-Aware Probabilistic Circuits via Voronoi Tessellations

claims.claim: Proposition 3.2 proves that a single Voronoi-gated node breaks tractability of probabilistic circuits even with fully factorized experts, because oblique Voronoi cell boundaries prevent the partition-function integral from factorizing (Proposition 3.2).
claims.evidence: Symbolic derivation correctly shows sigmoid(a1*x1+a2*x2+c) cannot factorize into h1(x1)*h2(x2) for nonzero a1,a2, and numerical 2D integration confirms non-factorization (ratio 2.80 ≠ 1).

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 shows that when Voronoi gating regions are geometrically aligned with the circuit's variable partition (Hierarchical Factorized Voronoi, or HFV, construction), the partition function decomposes and exact tractable inference is restored, with Theorem 3.14 giving inference time O(|C|K^m) for m-way factorizations with K cells per factor (Theorem 3.5, Theorem 3.14).
claims.evidence: Symbolic derivation correctly shows axis-aligned HFV gates allow sum-product commutativity yielding Z=prod_j Z_j, and numerical 4-variable 2-factor example confirms factorization error = 0 with O(|C|K^m) complexity argument.

claims.claim: For the non-factorized Voronoi-gated PCs, Algorithm 1 provides an anytime refinement procedure yielding certified lower and upper bounds on partition functions, marginals, and conditionals that tighten monotonically at a rate of O(2^{-t/d}) after t refinement steps (Algorithm 1, Theorem 3.9).
claims.evidence: Symbolic derivation shows bisection refinement gives gap(t) ≤ L·sqrt(d)·S/2^{floor(t/d)} = O(2^{-t/d}) for Lipschitz densities, and numerical table over 8 refinement steps shows monotonic tightening with gap*2^{t/2} strictly decreasing from 0.683 to 0.054.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.16 proves exponential convergence of the soft-to-hard Voronoi gate during temperature annealing: 1 minus the max soft gate weight is bounded by (K-1)exp(-alpha*gamma(u)) (Theorem 3.16).
claims.evidence: Symbolic proof correctly derives 1-max_k w_k ≤ (K-1)exp(-beta*gamma(u)) from softmax properties, and numerical verification across 8 beta values with 225 test points shows 0 bound violations.

claims.claim: On eight synthetic 2D/3D benchmarks (including CheckerBoard, Pinwheel, Spiral, and TwistedEight) compared against EinsumNet and HCLT baselines, VT-gated circuits attain certified lower bounds that often exceed baseline exact log-likelihoods, while HFV circuits match baseline performance with exact tractability preserved (Figure 1, experimental comparison).
claims.evidence: Only 2 of 8 benchmarks tested at reduced scale (N=500, 2D only) with simplified GMM baseline instead of EinsumNet/HCLT; VT is worse than baseline on both, but setup is too reduced to confirm or falsify the full claim.

amkkk/repro-geometry-aware-probabilistic.overall: The logbook provides sound symbolic re-derivations with supporting numerical examples for all four theoretical claims (Proposition 3.2, Theorems 3.5/3.14, Algorithm 1/Theorem 3.9, Theorem 3.16), constituting genuine verification. The experimental claim was addressed only on a reduced 2-of-8-dataset toy setup with simplified baselines, yielding counter-directional but insufficient evidence.

snaykey/repro-lora-gd-v2.paper_title: Asymptotic Optimality of the High-Dimensional Gaussian Mechanism and Improved Low-Dimensional Mechanisms for Differential Privacy

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 proves that as dimension T→∞, the Gaussian mechanism achieves the best privacy-utility tradeoff among all additive-noise mechanisms in the high-privacy regime δ ≤ δ⋆ (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies the tailored-Jensen inequality E[g(R²/T)] ≥ g(u0) = δ_Gauss for 5 competitor shapes (p ∈ {0.5,1,1.5,3,4}) across T=2..10000 with minimum gap +1.1e-6 ≥ 0, shows exact competitor δ converging to δ_Gauss as T grows, and provides two controls demonstrating necessity of both the δ≤δ⋆ and T→∞ hypotheses.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.3 shows that Haar symmetrization of arbitrary additive noise preserves mean squared error while improving privacy, establishing that spherically symmetric noise distributions are optimal (Lemma 3.3).
claims.evidence: MSE preservation is confirmed as an exact identity (max deviation 5.1e-13 over T∈{2,3,5,10,50}), and privacy improvement δ'≤δ is directly computed via 2-D quadrature in T=2 across 12 anisotropic-Gaussian settings (e.g., δ'=0.042 ≤ δ=0.238), with the convexity bracket δ'≤B≤δ verified for T=3,5,10.

claims.claim: The paper introduces the Spherical Generalized Gamma (SGG) family, a three-parameter family with radial density f(r) = pβ^((α+1)/p)/Γ((α+1)/p) · r^α · exp(-βr^p) that includes the Gaussian and ℓ2 mechanisms as special cases (Definition 4.1-4.2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The radial density is implemented exactly as written and verified to be a valid density (normalization error 1.8e-15), with the Gaussian special case (p=2, α=T−1, β=1/(2σ²)) matching N(0,σ²I_T) to 7.5e-15 relative error and the ℓ2-Laplace special case (p=1, α=T−1, β=1/θ) matching c·exp(−‖x‖/θ) to 2.2e-15, across T=2..10.

claims.claim: Figure 2 shows that in low dimensions (T=2 to 5) at ε=0.1, certain SGG mechanisms reduce MSE by up to 15% relative to the Gaussian and ℓ2 mechanisms, with the improvement shrinking as dimension increases (Figure 2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Reproducing the paper's SGG search at ε=0.1, the logbook finds max MSE reductions of 14.84%, 11.92%, 10.00%, and 8.63% over the better of Gaussian/ℓ2 baselines at T=2,3,4,5 respectively—monotonically shrinking with dimension, with optimal p*=4.0 far from both Gaussian (p=2) and ℓ2 (p=1), confirmed at 8000-node resolution.

claims.claim: Table 2 reports empirical lower bounds on the threshold δ⋆ above which Gaussian optimality holds, e.g. δ⋆ ≥ 0.737 at ε=0.25 and δ⋆ ≥ 0.198 at ε=16.0 (Table 2).
claims.evidence: All 7 δ⋆ thresholds are recomputed from the closed-form Gaussian privacy function g and its analytic derivatives via bisection on the supporting-line property, matching the paper's Table 2 to a maximum absolute error of 7.8e-7 (e.g., 0.736671 vs 0.736670 at ε=0.25; 0.197615 vs 0.197615 at ε=16.0).

claims.claim: The paper resolves an open question from Joseph et al. (2025) by providing a tight composition analysis for the ℓ2 mechanism via the unified SGG framework and an FFT-based composition algorithm (Section 4.4, Algorithm 7).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 7 is implemented with single-step PRV CDF via radial integral, FFT convolution for k-fold composition, and validated against exact Lemma 4.1 (2.4e-3 error) and analytic √k-GDP Gaussian composition (1.4e-4 error across k=2..64); the same code path handles Gaussian (p=2) and ℓ2 (p=1), and the ℓ2 accountant is 70×–3e5× tighter than basic composition.

snaykey/repro-lora-gd-v2.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims through deterministic CPU-only computations: exact algebraic identities verified to machine precision (claims 3, 5), the Jensen inequality underlying the asymptotic optimality proof verified across multiple dimensions and competitor shapes with convergence and controls (claim 1), direct quadrature and convexity-bracket verification of Haar symmetrization (claim 2), reproduced low-dimensional SGG advantage matching the paper's ~15% magnitude and shrinking trend (claim 4), and a validated FFT composition algorithm demonstrating tight ℓ2 accounting (claim 6).

amkkk/repro-non-euclidean-gradient-desce.paper_title: Non-Euclidean Gradient Descent Operates at the Edge of Stability

claims.claim: Directional smoothness D is defined so that, for non-Euclidean gradient descent with step size eta, the loss decreases if and only if D <= 2/eta (Definition 2.1).
claims.evidence: Numerical verification on a 5-dimensional random PSD quadratic using only the l2 norm pairing, with 26 step sizes confirming the directional smoothness condition. Small dimension and single norm make this a simplified check of a mathematical definition that applies to arbitrary norms.

claims.claim: Generalized sharpness S is defined as the maximum of d^T times the Hessian of the loss times d subject to the norm of d being at most 1 under an arbitrary norm, generalizing the largest-eigenvalue sharpness used for vanilla gradient descent (Definition 2.2).
claims.evidence: Generalized sharpness computed for l2, l1, and linf norms on 6×6 matrices with exact enumeration for linf (64 vertices). Multiple norms tested, but dimensions are very small (n=6) and the setup is a simplified numerical check rather than a full-scale demonstration.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 proves non-Euclidean gradient descent on quadratic objectives converges linearly when the step size eta < 2/S, where S is the generalized sharpness (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: Linear convergence verified on 5 random quadratic objectives (n=8) with 6 step sizes each, but only using the l2 norm. The theorem applies to arbitrary norms; testing only l2 on small dimensions is a simplified numerical check.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 proves divergence occurs from some initialization when eta > 2/S for non-Euclidean gradient descent on quadratics (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Divergence confirmed for η>2/S on 5 small quadratics (n≤8) initialized along the top eigenvector, but only with l2 norm pairing. Small scale and single norm limit this to a toy-level numerical check of the theorem.

claims.claim: Experiments show l-infinity-descent on CIFAR-10 and Tiny Shakespeare exhibits generalized sharpness stabilizing slightly above the 2/eta threshold, unlike vanilla GD which stabilizes at 2/eta (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Experiment uses synthetic 200-sample data with a 2-layer network (10→32→3) instead of CIFAR-10/Tiny Shakespeare with deep architectures. Sharpness values are reported but at drastically reduced scale, and l-infinity descent is approximated via sign gradient.

claims.claim: SignGD and Muon (without momentum) are shown to exhibit normalized sharpness converging near the 2/eta edge-of-stability threshold, extending the phenomenon to optimizers used in practice (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: SignGD and a simplified Muon (without Newton preconditioning) tested on synthetic 200-sample data with a tiny 2-layer network. The claim is about practical optimizers at scale (Figure 5), but the reproduction uses a proxy Muon implementation and no real datasets.

amkkk/repro-non-euclidean-gradient-desce.overall: All six claims are addressed only at toy scale: theoretical claims 1-4 are numerically checked on small-dimensional quadratics (mostly l2 norm only), and experimental claims 5-6 use synthetic data with tiny networks instead of CIFAR-10/Tiny Shakespeare. No claim is verified at the paper's actual scale or with the full generality claimed.

amkkk/repro-beyond-first-order-asymptoti.paper_title: Beyond First-order Asymptotics in Sequential Mean Testing

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 establishes a central limit theorem for the empirical KL_inf statistic, showing sqrt(n)(KL_inf(q_hat_n, m_o) - KL_inf(q, m_o)) converges in distribution to N(0, sigma^2(q, m_o)) (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Empirical variance of sqrt(n)(KL_hat - KL) = 0.039715 vs theoretical 0.039866 (ratio 0.9962) with n=1000 and 5000 repetitions on Bernoulli(0.45), m_o=0.55, providing concrete numerical support for the CLT on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 extends this result to the stopping time tau_alpha, proving sqrt(log(1/alpha))(tau_alpha/log(1/alpha) - 1/KL_inf(q,m_o)) converges to a Gaussian limit N(0, sigma^2_bd(q,m_o)) as alpha to 0 (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: Variance ratios are 0.69, 0.70, 0.95, 1.04, 1.26 across alpha levels 0.1 to 0.001; the ratio approaches 1 at alpha=0.005 but then overshoots to 1.26 at alpha=0.001, breaking the convergence trend with only 2000 repetitions providing noisy estimates.

claims.claim: The proof decomposes the normalized KL_inf statistic into a term from the dual optimization (shown to vanish in probability) and a standard empirical-mean term that converges to Gaussian, combined with verification of Anscombe's condition to transfer the CLT to the stopping time (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Remainder |R_n| decreases from 0.0102 (n=50) to 0.00024 (n=2000) supporting vanishing; empirical-mean CLT variance ratio 1.016 with normality p=0.92; Anscombe condition std=31.17 vs bound=249.16 — all three components independently confirmed with concrete numbers.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.5 constructs asymptotically valid confidence intervals for the stopping time using only a single simulation run, without requiring multiple independent replicates (Proposition 4.5).
claims.evidence: Coverage rates of 30.4%, 34.6%, 32.6% vs nominal 95% across alpha=0.1, 0.05, 0.01 show no trend toward the nominal level as alpha decreases, directly contradicting the asymptotic validity claim with concrete evidence.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments on synthetic Beta and Bernoulli distributions and on real crop-yield data show empirical stopping-time distributions converging to the theoretical Gaussian limit, with stronger agreement at smaller significance levels alpha (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Reduced-scale runs (alpha only to 0.01, max_n=20000) on synthetic distributions show Beta ratio 0.96-0.98 but Bernoulli ratio stuck at 0.41-0.43 with no convergence trend; 'real crop-yield data' is actually a Gaussian simulation, and no normality test of the stopping-time distribution is reported.

amkkk/repro-beyond-first-order-asymptoti.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical support for the theoretical claims (Theorem 4.2 CLT, proof decomposition) on non-toy Bernoulli setups, but the stopping-time CLT shows mixed convergence, the single-run CI coverage dramatically fails at 30-35% vs 95% nominal with no improvement trend, and the numerical experiments use simulated rather than real crop-yield data with Bernoulli results not converging.

amkkk/repro-the-optimal-sample-complexit.paper_title: The Optimal Sample Complexity of Linear Contracts

claims.claim: Theorem 1.1 establishes uniform convergence: for sample size s ≥ 3456 ln(4/δ)/ε², with probability at least 1−δ, the empirical and expected utility of every linear contract differ by at most ε (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: Step-by-step formal derivation from covering number O(1/ε²), Hoeffding's inequality, and union bound yields s ≥ 3456·ln(4/δ)/ε²; numerical checks across 5 (ε,δ) pairs confirm the bound holds, and the derivation is mathematically sound.

claims.claim: Corollary 1.2 shows the Empirical Utility Maximization algorithm achieves an ε-approximation of the optimal linear contract using s ≥ 6912 ln(4/δ)/ε² samples and O(1/ε) oracle queries (Corollary 1.2).
claims.evidence: EUM algorithm run on synthetic data with only n=5 actions, m=4 outcomes, ε=0.5, δ=0.2 across 5 trials; this is a reduced-scale demonstration, not a full reproduction, though it does use the paper's sample size and achieves the ε-approximation.

claims.claim: The O(ln(1/δ)/ε²) sample complexity matches the lower bound of Dütting et al. (2025) up to constant factors, and is independent of the action space size n and the number of outcomes m (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: Formal analysis confirms both upper bound (O(ln(1/δ)/ε²), constant 3456) and lower bound (Ω(ln(1/δ)/ε²)) share the same rate, and the 1D covering argument shows independence from n and m across 25 configurations.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 shows the expected reward of a linear contract is non-decreasing in the contract parameter α, a structural property exploited to build fine-grained covering arguments where general pseudo-dimension bounds fail (Lemma 2.1).
claims.evidence: Direct analytical proof: R(α,a)=α·E[y|a]+β, so dR/dα=E[y|a]≥0 for non-negative outcomes; numerical verification across 20 actions × 101 α values yields 0 monotonicity violations.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.2 constructs an L2 cover of the reward function class of size O(1/ν²), obtained by discretizing empirical rewards into ν-intervals, taking pullbacks to parameter space, and combining with grid discretization of the outcome axis (Lemma 2.2).
claims.evidence: Grid-based L2 cover constructed for single-parameter (α only, β fixed) linear contracts with simplified discretization rather than the paper's pullback construction; scaling ratio (24.5) does not cleanly match expected O(1/ν²) ratio (100), indicating a reduced approximation.

amkkk/repro-the-optimal-sample-complexit.overall: The logbook provides formal mathematical derivations supporting the theoretical claims (Theorem 1.1, lower bound comparison, Lemma 2.1) and reduced-scale synthetic experiments for the algorithmic and constructive claims (Corollary 1.2, Lemma 2.2). It is a reasonable reproduction for a theory paper but the experimental claims are only validated on toy setups.

amkkk/repro-black-box-assisted-regressio.paper_title: Black-Box Assisted Regression: Phase Transitions and Minimax Optimality

claims.claim: The critical phase-transition threshold for black-box assisted regression is characterized as δc(n) ≍ n^(-β/(2β+d)), separating a prior-dominated regime from a sample-dominated regime (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The threshold δc(n) = n^(-β/(2β+d)) is correctly derived by equating prior error δ² with sampling error n^(-2β/(2β+d)), and numerical verification across 12 configurations (n=20–200, δ at 0.1×, 1×, 10× δc) shows the expected regime separation with sample-dominated risks matching n^(-2β/(2β+d)) closely.

claims.claim: The proposed safe residual estimator achieves the minimax risk rate min{δ², n^(-2β/(2β+d))} up to a validation-selection cost, with the lower bound given in Theorem 5.4 and the matching upper bound in Theorem 5.5 (Theorem 5.4, Theorem 5.5).
claims.evidence: Proof sketches for Theorems 5.4–5.5 are provided but incomplete, and numerical verification on a simplified kernel estimator shows 5 of 15 configurations failing the 2× bound check (e.g., n=20, δ/δc=2.0: risk 0.2253 vs bound 0.1357), indicating the simplified implementation does not reliably achieve the claimed rate.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.7 provides an oracle inequality showing the validation-based selection between f0 and f0+r̂ performs nearly as well as the better of the two candidate predictors (Theorem 5.7).
claims.evidence: A proof sketch for the oracle inequality is given and a numerical simulation (n=100, d=2, 500 trials) shows a selected-to-oracle risk ratio of 1.003, but the setup uses a simplified kernel regression rather than the paper's procedure, so it is a proxy demonstration rather than a full reproduction.

claims.claim: In synthetic experiments at n=20 and δ=0.0, the safe residual estimator achieves risk 0.0027 compared to 0.1894 for learning from scratch (Tables 1-2).
claims.evidence: Real Monte Carlo runs at n=20, δ=0.0 with 2000 trials show residual risk 0.0008 vs scratch risk 0.2661, matching the paper's directional finding (residual ≪ scratch), but absolute values differ substantially from the paper's 0.0027 vs 0.1894 due to a simplified kernel estimator and different bandwidth.

claims.claim: On CIFAR-100 with CLIP features at n=2000, the residual learning method achieves 66.7% accuracy versus 63.9% for a weighted-ensemble baseline, improving over the 59.4% zero-shot baseline (Section 6, CIFAR-100/CLIP experiments).
claims.evidence: The experiment uses 20-class synthetic 32-dimensional features at n=1000 instead of real CIFAR-100 images with CLIP features at n=2000; the directional hierarchy (residual 52.2% > ensemble 48.8% > zero-shot 44.6%) matches the paper's pattern but absolute accuracies are far below the claimed 66.7%/63.9%/59.4%.

claims.claim: On AG News with Qwen3-8B at n=16, residual learning achieves 75.2% accuracy while the weighted-ensemble baseline exhibits negative transfer, dropping to 71.2% (Section 6, AG News/Qwen3-8B experiments).
claims.evidence: The experiment uses 4-class synthetic 20-dimensional features at n=16 instead of real AG News text with Qwen3-8B; the directional pattern matches (residual 69.0% > prior 68.2% > ensemble 66.6% with negative transfer), but absolute values differ substantially from the paper's 75.2%/71.2%.

amkkk/repro-black-box-assisted-regressio.overall: The logbook provides correct derivations and simplified numerical verifications for the three theoretical claims, and proxy experiments for the three empirical claims that match directional predictions but use synthetic data at reduced scale rather than the paper's real datasets and models. No claim is fully reproduced at the paper's original scale and setup.

amkkk/repro-hallucination-rate-distortio.paper_title: Hallucination is a Consequence of Space-Optimality: A Rate-Distortion Theorem for Membership Testing

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 (Rate-Distortion Lower Bound) proves that the minimum per-key memory budget for membership testing in the sparse regime satisfies liminf B(M_j)/n_j >= min KL(mu_K || mu_N) over output distributions meeting the specified error constraints (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook computes KL divergence for Bernoulli distributions across four error configurations, confirming non-negativity and monotonicity, but only addresses the binary/Bernoulli special case while Theorem 3.1 covers general output distributions via the data-processing inequality.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 shows that when the KL-divergence minimizer is unique, any asymptotically memory-optimal membership tester's query output distributions must converge in Wasserstein-1 distance to the theoretical optimizers (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook constructs artificial sub-optimal Bernoulli distributions with decreasing perturbation deltas and shows W1 distance shrinks proportionally—this is trivially true by construction and does not test convergence of actual asymptotically memory-optimal testers.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that under log-loss constraints the unique optimal probability-estimation solution assigns all facts to a single high-confidence score x* = e^{-epsilon_K}, while non-facts are distributed as mu_N* = (1-q*)delta_0 + q*delta_{x*}, so a fraction q* of non-facts receive the same score as facts — an unavoidable 'hallucination channel' (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook numerically verifies x* = exp(-eps_K) and q* = eps_N/x* for four parameter settings and checks constraint satisfaction, but this is formula plug-in verification for the Bernoulli-adjacent special case rather than a proof or empirical test of the full log-loss theorem over continuous score spaces.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 shows that for FNR/FPR-constrained binary membership classifiers, the optimal score distributions are mu_K* = Bernoulli(1-epsilon_K) and mu_N* = Bernoulli(epsilon_N), formalizing hallucination in the binary-decision setting (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook computes Bernoulli(1-eps_K) and Bernoulli(eps_N) and performs local perturbation analysis showing nearby feasible points have higher KL, but explicitly acknowledges this 'does not constitute a global optimization proof,' leaving the global optimality claim unverified.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 derives a finite-support correction to the memory lower bound involving the chi-squared divergence between the optimal fact/non-fact score distributions, applicable to testers restricted to finite output supports (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook discretizes Bernoulli distributions to uniform bins and checks the chi-squared correction term decreases with bin count, but the observed scaling (1.778→0.356 for 2→10 bins) does not match the predicted 1/num_bins halving pattern, and only uniform binning of the two-point distribution is tested.

amkkk/repro-hallucination-rate-distortio.overall: The logbook provides numerical sanity checks of the theorems' formulas in the Bernoulli/binary special case across several error parameter configurations, but does not constitute formal proofs or empirical tests on actual membership-testing data. All five claims are addressed only on simplified special cases with no global optimality verification or general-distribution analysis.

amkkk/repro-quantifying-the-noise-sensit.paper_title: Quantifying the noise sensitivity of the Wasserstein metric for images

claims.claim: Theorem 2 bounds the expected signed 1-Wasserstein distance between a clean n-pixel image and its Gaussian-noise-perturbed counterpart by (2/√π)σn log2(n) + (1/(2√π))σn, i.e., growth roughly linear in n with a log factor, for zero-sum noise of standard deviation σ (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Symbolic derivation with sympy confirms the bound constant 2/√π ≈ 1.1284 and formula E[W₁] ≤ (2/√π)σn log₂(n) + (1/(2√π))σn; Monte Carlo (n=100, σ=0.1, 2000 trials) empirically confirms the bound holds (mean W₁=0.0265 ≤ bound=77.79).

claims.claim: Theorem 3 shows that for p-Wasserstein distances with integer p>1, the expected p-th power error is bounded by (4/√π) n σ, so the per-image error scales as (nσ)^(1/p), improving (becoming more noise-robust) as p increases, in contrast to the Euclidean (L2) metric's linear scaling in σ (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Symbolic derivation confirms bound constant 4/√π ≈ 2.2568 and formula E[W_p^p] ≤ (4/√π)nσ; empirical tests for p=2 and p=3 confirm the bound holds and that W₂ error < L₂ error, supporting sub-linear scaling.

claims.claim: Theorems 4 and 5 extend the noise-sensitivity bounds to the deviation between the true and noisy Wasserstein distances computed between two distinct images, rather than a single noisy image against its clean version (Theorems 4-5).
claims.evidence: Triangle inequality derivation E[|W_p(X,Y)−W_p(X+Z₁,Y+Z₂)|] ≤ E[W_p(X,X+Z₁)] + E[W_p(Y,Y+Z₂)] is sound; empirical test (n=150, σ=0.08, 500 trials) confirms deviation bound holds (mean deviation=0.0049 ≤ bound=202.53).

claims.claim: On cryo-electron microscopy projection images of the hsp90 protein with noise level σ=0.01, the squared-Wasserstein (W2) distance matrix preserves the ground-truth diagonal similarity structure across viewing angles, while the L2 distance matrix degrades to an unstructured/random pattern (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Used synthetic 1D projections (64 bins, 20 angles) rather than actual 2D cryo-EM images of hsp90; the proxy actually contradicts the claim (L2 preserves angular structure better than W2), but the setup is too dissimilar from the paper's conditions to constitute falsification.

claims.claim: Figure 2 empirically confirms that the W2 distance error follows the predicted (nσ)^(1/2) scaling law as noise increases, while the L2 distance error grows linearly in σ (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: On a 1D proxy (n=100), the W2 scaling exponent was 1.199 vs predicted 0.5, failing to reproduce the claimed (nσ)^(1/2) scaling; L2 linear scaling (exponent 1.003) was confirmed, but the 1D sorted Wasserstein proxy is too different from 2D OT to decisively evaluate the claim.

claims.claim: Section 4.4 reports a counterintuitive phenomenon in which Wasserstein distance between sparse images can decrease as noise increases, because added noise bridges transport gaps between distant mass concentrations (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: On 1D sparse distributions (256 bins, <5% nonzero), W₁ decreased by 96.71% as σ increased from 0 to 0.5, clearly demonstrating the counterintuitive noise-bridging phenomenon, but on a simplified 1D setup rather than 2D sparse images.

amkkk/repro-quantifying-the-noise-sensit.overall: The logbook provides sound formal derivations confirming the theoretical bounds in Theorems 2–5, with empirical Monte Carlo checks that the bounds hold. The empirical claims (cryo-EM comparison, Figure 2 scaling, counterintuitive decrease) were tested only on 1D synthetic proxies, with the cryo-EM and scaling-law results failing to reproduce the claimed phenomena on these proxies, leaving those claims inconclusive except for the noise-bridging effect which was demonstrated at toy scale.

amkkk/repro-near-optimal-mtl-shared-repr.paper_title: Near-Optimal and Efficient First-Order Algorithm for Multi-Task Learning with Shared Linear Representation

claims.claim: TPGD (Algorithm 1) is a two-phase first-order gradient-descent method for jointly estimating a shared linear representation and task-specific parameters in multi-task learning (Section 4, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Small-scale synthetic implementation (d=10, k=3, T=5, N=100) confirms two-phase GD structure with joint B/W estimation and loss decreasing 3.33→2.46, but at toy scale with no comparison to paper baselines.

claims.claim: Phase I performs K1/2 iterations of unregularized gradient descent as a warm start, and Phase II performs the remaining K1/2 iterations of regularized gradient descent with penalty term ||B^T B − WW^T||_F^2 (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Two-phase split (30+30 iterations) is confirmed, but the implemented penalty is ||B^T B - I_k||_F^2 + ||W||_F^2/T, a surrogate for the paper's ||B^T B - WW^T||_F^2, so the specific regularization claim is not faithfully reproduced.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 and Corollary 5.3 prove the method attains a near-optimal population estimation error of order Õ(dk/(NT)), improving over existing likelihood-based methods by a factor of k, where d is input dimension, k is representation dimension, T is the number of tasks, and N is per-task sample size (Section 5.1, Theorem 5.1, Corollary 5.3).
claims.evidence: The Õ(dk/(NT)) bound is restated and values plugged in, but numerical scaling is negligible (error 1.807→1.800 when doubling N, 1.807→1.806 when doubling T), far from convincingly demonstrating the claimed rate; no actual theorem proof or meaningful empirical validation at scale.

claims.claim: The algorithm achieves Õ(1) iteration complexity, i.e., convergence in a number of iterations independent of the problem dimensions up to logarithmic factors (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: All four configurations (d=6–30, k=2–5, T=3–10) hit the K=120 iteration cap without converging, providing no evidence for or against Õ(1) iteration complexity.

claims.claim: The estimation-error guarantee requires a per-task sample size of N ≳ σ²(d+T)kκ⁴/σ_k²(Σ*) (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: The formula N ≳ σ²(d+T)kκ⁴/σ_k²(Σ*) is structurally restated with isotropic assumptions (κ=1, σ_k²=1), and scaling of min_N with d and T is shown, but empirical convergence experiments at reduced scale show only noisy trends.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.4 establishes excess-risk bounds for transferring the learned representation to a new task, decomposing the risk into representation approximation error and task-specific optimization error (Section 5.2, Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: The excess-risk decomposition ExcessRisk = RepApproxError + TaskOptError is verified as an algebraic identity at toy scale (d=10, k=3, T=5), but the task-opt error is negative (-2.824) and transfer scaling across T_train shows no clear monotonic trend, providing weak evidence.

amkkk/repro-near-optimal-mtl-shared-repr.overall: This logbook implements TPGD at small synthetic scale and restates theoretical formulas, but provides no convincing empirical or formal verification of the paper's main theoretical claims at meaningful scale. The penalty term in Phase II deviates from the paper, iteration complexity is untested, and numerical scaling results are too weak to confirm the claimed rates.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.7 establishes an excess risk bound under sample-only performativity, and Theorem 3.10 establishes a performative excess risk bound under full (sample-and-population) performativity (Theorem 3.7, Theorem 3.10).
claims.evidence: Symbolic bound structures for Theorems 3.7 and 3.10 are presented with all conditions (3.1–3.3) checked; the expressions match the paper's stated forms and asymptotic analysis confirms convergence behavior.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.16 gives a cumulative performative excess risk bound whose convergence to zero as n→∞ requires either m=o(n) with εκ/γ<1, or a slower rate m=o(n·(εκ/γ)^{-Tp}) when εκ/γ≥1, a weaker stability requirement than prior work's εκ/γ<1 condition (Theorem 3.16).
claims.evidence: The cumulative bound structure for Theorem 3.16 is presented with two convergence regimes confirmed: m=o(n) when εκ/γ<1 and the slower rate m=o(n·(εκ/γ)^{-Tp}) when εκ/γ≥1, matching the claimed relaxation of prior stability requirements.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.11 shows the counterintuitive result that retraining on performatively distorted samples can tighten generalization bounds by improving estimation of the transition map, rather than degrading them (Corollary 3.11).
claims.evidence: A reduced-scale simulation (T=5, n=2000) shows cumulative M_T yields tighter bounds (0.087 vs 0.105) and θ₀ gives the tightest bound, demonstrating the counterintuitive result but at clearly reduced scale.

claims.claim: The empirical case study on German Federal Employment Agency data (over 60 million rows, 1975-2017) computes a sample-performativity excess risk bound of 0.302 nats (logistic loss) at 95% confidence on n=60,147 jobseekers with m=1,816 affected by the intervention (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The proprietary German Federal Employment Agency data was not accessible; the logbook only evaluates the bound formula using the paper's own reported constants (getting 0.307 vs claimed 0.302), which is not an independent reproduction.

claims.claim: Under full performativity, a semi-simulated scenario varying treatment rates ξ ∈ {0.01,...,0.5} demonstrates a trade-off where the generalization gap increases with treatment intensity, decomposed into sampling, complexity, and performative terms (Section 4, Figure 1.3).
claims.evidence: A reduced-scale semi-simulation (n=10,000) varying ξ from 0.01 to 0.50 shows the generalization gap increasing monotonically (from -0.020 to 0.928), confirming the claimed trade-off direction but at reduced scale.

amkkk/repro-performative-learning-theory.overall: The logbook provides symbolic verification of the three theoretical claims and reduced-scale simulations supporting the two applied claims, but cannot independently reproduce the empirical case study due to proprietary data access. The theoretical verification evidence is somewhat shallow—final expressions are shown but derivation steps and sympy code are not—yet the structures and convergence analyses are consistent with the paper's claims.

amkkk/repro-provable-bounds-sample-compr.paper_title: Provable Bounds for the Learnability of Sample-Compressible Families from Noisy Samples

claims.claim: Theorem 2.13 gives a sample complexity bound for learning a sample-compressible family f* from samples corrupted by additive independent noise (e.g., f*⊗G), requiring n >= N^Clean_{tau,t,m}(6*epsilon, delta/2) + O~(d*tau(epsilon)/epsilon^2 * log(...)) samples for l2 error epsilon (Section 2, Theorem 2.13).
claims.evidence: The logbook evaluates a self-constructed proxy formula (using (d+log(1/delta))/epsilon^2 for N^Clean) and checks that it exhibits the claimed 1/epsilon^2, linear-d, and log(1/delta) scaling. This is circular: the formula was designed to have these properties, so verifying them proves nothing about the theorem itself.

claims.claim: Corollary 2.14 specializes this bound to Gaussian and Laplace noise models, e.g. for N(0, sigma^2 I_d) noise the extra sample cost scales as O~(d*tau(epsilon)/epsilon^2) * log(1+sigma*r) (Section 2, Corollary 2.14).
claims.evidence: The logbook writes down a formula of the form O~(d*tau/epsilon^2)*log(1+sigma*r) and confirms it scales as log(1+sigma*r) and linearly in d. The 'exact' matching is trivially guaranteed because the evaluated formula was constructed to match the claimed form; no derivation from Theorem 2.13 is reproduced.

claims.claim: Claim 2.5 shows unrestricted Gaussian families {N(mu, sigma^2) : sigma > 0} violate the Local Lipschitz Decodability condition (Assumption 2.1) and are therefore not learnable under this noise model, establishing necessity of the assumption (Section 2, Claim 2.5, Assumption 2.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides a correct mathematical argument: for same-mean Gaussians, H^2 = 1 - sqrt(2*sigma1*sigma2/(sigma1^2+sigma2^2)), TV <= sqrt(2)*H, and as sigma2->infty, |sigma1-sigma2|->infty while TV remains bounded, so no finite Lipschitz constant L satisfies the LLD condition. Numerical table confirms the ratio |sigma1-sigma2|/TV diverges. This is a sound proof of the claim.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 establishes a sample complexity bound for total-variation learnability under adversarial corruption of s samples with l-infinity budget C, without requiring the Low-Frequency Property (Assumption 2.9) needed in the additive-noise setting (Section 3, Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook evaluates a self-constructed formula that omits LFP terms and then confirms LFP terms are absent. This is circular — the 'no LFP required' conclusion follows from the formula's design, not from any derivation of Theorem 3.2. The monotonic scaling checks on a proxy formula do not verify the theorem.

claims.claim: Section 4 derives the first sample complexity bounds for learning k-mixtures of uniform distributions (k-UMMs) under both additive noise and adversarial corruption, and for k-component Gaussian mixture models under adversarial corruption with n >= O~(s*k*d^2/epsilon^2)*log(1/delta) + O~(d*s^2/epsilon^2)*log(1+C/delta) (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook evaluates self-constructed formulas for k-UMM and k-GMM bounds and checks their scaling in k, d, s, C. The formulas were written to match the claimed asymptotic forms, so the scaling checks are tautological. The 'first bounds' historical claim is explicitly acknowledged as unverifiable numerically.

amkkk/repro-provable-bounds-sample-compr.overall: The logbook provides a legitimate mathematical proof for Claim 3 (unrestricted Gaussian families violate LLD), but for the other four claims it merely evaluates self-constructed proxy formulas and confirms they have the claimed scaling — a circular exercise that does not verify the underlying theorems. The reproduction is formula evaluation, not theorem verification or empirical learning experiments.

amkkk/repro-a-direct-second-order-method.paper_title: A Direct Second-Order Method for Solving Two-Player Zero-Sum Games

claims.claim: Theorem 1 establishes a correspondence between fixed points of the Douglas-Rachford (DR) operator and Nash equilibria via the lifting transform z = ẑ − γF(ẑ) (Theorem 1, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Numerical verification on a single 4x6 game confirms the forward direction (Nash → DR fixed point) at machine precision, but this is a small-scale check of a theorem, not a formal proof or full-scale demonstration.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 proves local quadratic convergence of the hybrid semi-smooth Newton method, with residual bound ‖R^γ_DRS(z_{k+1})‖ ≤ C‖R^γ_DRS(z_k)‖² (Theorem 4, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: SSN residual sequence on a 4x5 game (1.45e-02 → 6.58e-03 → 1.43e-08 → 3.20e-14 → 1.24e-22) shows quadratic convergence pattern, but only on a small instance and not a formal proof of Theorem 4.

claims.claim: Lemma 1 shows the DRS residual operator is monotone and 1-Lipschitz continuous, which is the key property enabling application of a semi-smooth Newton (SSN) solver (Lemma 1).
claims.evidence: Numerical tests on 10 small game instances show 1-Lipschitz at 100% but monotonicity only at 99.3-99.7% for some gamma values; the asserted formal derivation is not explicitly shown, and the scale is small.

claims.claim: On 400x800 random zero-sum games, the hybrid PSSN methods reach a duality gap of 1e-12 in about 4.3-4.4 seconds versus 21.97 seconds for PRM+, an order-of-magnitude speedup in the high-precision regime (numerical results table, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Runs at 20x40 and 30x60 (not 400x800) show directional speedup of 5.9-9.5x, but final duality gaps (1.37e-02, 7.35e-02) are far from the claimed 1e-12, so the specific precision and timing claims are not reproduced.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 performs a one-time switch from the first-order Predictive Regret Matching+ (PRM+) method to the Douglas-Rachford semi-smooth Newton (DRSSN) subroutine of Algorithm 2, combining global efficiency with local superlinear convergence (Algorithms 1-2).
claims.evidence: The one-time switch mechanism is demonstrated on 15x30-50x100 games, but PRM+ stalls at duality gap 0.1-0.3 (switch threshold 1e-3 not reached) and DRSSN does not converge (final dgap 0.01-0.24), so the claimed combined convergence is not realized.

amkkk/repro-a-direct-second-order-method.overall: The logbook provides reduced-scale numerical demonstrations supporting the directional validity of the paper's theoretical and empirical claims, but none at the paper's full 400x800 scale or with formal proofs. All five claims are addressed only on toy-sized instances with incomplete convergence, making this a partial reproduction with limited evidentiary weight.

amkkk/repro-equivalence-of-context-and-p.paper_title: Equivalence of Context and Parameter Updates in Modern Transformer Blocks

claims.claim: In Gemma-style transformer blocks, the entire effect of prepending context can be exactly reproduced by rank-1 patches ΔWgate = Wgate(zC−z)zT/‖z‖² and ΔWup = Wup(zC−z)zT/‖z‖² applied to the MLP gate and up-projection weight matrices, plus a patch Δm to the RMSNorm scale (Theorem 1, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Algebraic identity verified at machine precision (max diff 5.7e-13) across 5 random seeds at d_model=64, d_ff=256, confirming the rank-1 patch formula reproduces the context-conditioned MLP output exactly as Theorem 1 states.

claims.claim: The rank-1-plus-RMSNorm-patch construction extends inductively from a single block to full L-layer transformers, yielding a perfect implicit weight patch for the whole network (Theorem 2, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Inductive extension confirmed at machine precision across L=2,4,6,8,12 layers (max diff <1e-11), with context-conditioned and patched models matching exactly, confirming Theorem 2's algebraic construction.

claims.claim: A perfect implicit weight patch exists whenever the block's inner function is input-controllable (Definition 3) and its outer function is output-controllable (Definition 4), a sufficient condition proved in general form (Theorem 5, Section 5).
claims.evidence: Controllability conditions checked numerically at d_model=16, d_ff=64 with 30 random trials; all satisfied conditions and patches worked at machine precision, but this is reduced-scale numerical evidence for a general theorem rather than a formal proof or full-scale demonstration.

claims.claim: In float32 precision, the implicit weight-patched model matches the context-conditioned model's output logits almost exactly, achieving 100% token-prediction agreement, whereas standard bfloat16 implementation only reaches 87.5% agreement (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Tested at d_model=24 with random weights and simulated bf16 (no actual mantissa truncation), yielding f32=100% and bf16=100%; the paper's specific 87.5% bf16 figure was not reproduced due to the simplified setup and lack of real bf16 arithmetic.

claims.claim: Using a numerically stable RMSNorm inversion in bfloat16 raises token-prediction agreement between the patched and context-conditioned models from 87.5% to 98% (Section 4).
claims.evidence: At d_model=16 with random weights, both naive and stable RMSNorm inversion yield 100% agreement, failing to reproduce the paper's 87.5%→98% improvement; the reduced scale makes precision effects negligible and the specific quantitative claim untestable.

claims.claim: The rank-1 patch derivation is shown to generalize across Gemma, Llama, Mistral, Mixtral, GPT-2, GPT-J, and mixture-of-experts architectures (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Algebraic identity verified at machine precision for 5 of 7 architectures (Gemma, Llama, Mistral, GPT-2, GPT-J) at d_model=32, but Mixtral and MoE were not tested and the scale is far below real models.

amkkk/repro-equivalence-of-context-and-p.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical confirmation of the paper's core algebraic theorems (Theorems 1 and 2) at machine precision, but the precision-related empirical claims (Section 4) and cross-architecture generalization are only addressed at toy scale with random weights, failing to reproduce the paper's specific quantitative results.

amkkk/repro-step-size-stability-in-stoch.paper_title: Step-Size Stability in Stochastic Optimization: A Theoretical Perspective

claims.claim: The paper introduces a stability index δ_t that quantifies how much a stochastic optimization step degrades progress as the step size grows, and links it directly to suboptimality bounds via average-iterate and last-iterate convergence theorems (Theorem 3, Theorem 4, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies the average-iterate suboptimality bound (Theorem 3) on a small synthetic quadratic (d=10, 500 steps, no stochastic gradients), confirming 7.17 ≤ 16.36, but Theorem 4 (last-iterate) was not tested and the setup is clearly reduced-scale.

claims.claim: For SGD, the stability index is derived as δ_t^SGD = (α_t/2)‖g_t‖^2, which scales linearly (unboundedly) with the step size α_t (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirms δ^SGD = (α/2)‖g‖² to machine precision over 50 step sizes (0.0001–1000) and 2000 random gradient checks, with R²=1.0 and slope exactly 0.5, demonstrating linear unbounded scaling as claimed.

claims.claim: For NGN, the stability index δ_t^NGN = (γ_t/2)‖g_t‖^2 ≤ δ_t^SGD, and it saturates rather than growing unboundedly for large step sizes, unlike SGD (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook demonstrates δ_NGN ≤ δ_SGD across 50 step sizes and shows NGN saturating at a ceiling (0.2733) while SGD grows to 779.4 at α=1000, confirming the saturation property and the inequality on a concrete numerical setup.

claims.claim: For SPS, the stability index is bounded as δ_t^SPS ≤ min{α_t‖g_t‖^2, f(x_t,s_t) - C_t}, scaling sub-linearly with step size, in contrast to SGD's linear scaling (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies δ_SPS ≤ min{α‖g‖², f−C} across 60 step sizes and shows SPS saturating at 1.0587 for α≥9.25 while SGD grows linearly to 396.8, confirming the sub-linear scaling bound numerically.

claims.claim: Experiments on ResNet trained on CIFAR-10 and on linear/logistic regression tasks confirm that the theoretical stability-index bounds predict the empirically observed robustness ordering of SPS, NGN, and SPP over SGD across a range of step sizes (Section 5).
claims.evidence: ResNet/CIFAR-10 experiments were not reproduced at all; synthetic regression (n=200, d=20) shows mixed results where SPS underperforms SGD on logistic regression (9/20 vs 20/20), partially contradicting the claimed robustness ordering, and the main experimental evidence is missing.

amkkk/repro-step-size-stability-in-stoch.overall: The logbook numerically confirms the algebraic stability-index formulas and their scaling properties for SGD, NGN, and SPS (claims 2–4), and provides a toy verification of the suboptimality bound structure (claim 1). However, the key empirical claim (claim 5) is inconclusive because ResNet/CIFAR-10 experiments were not run and synthetic results partially contradict the claimed robustness ordering.

amkkk/repro-optimal-transport-group-fair.paper_title: Optimal Transport under Group Fairness Constraints

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 (FairSinkhorn) modifies the Sinkhorn algorithm with an additional group-level projection step to compute exact F-fair transport plans as defined in Definition 3.3 (Section 4, Algorithm 1, Definition 3.3).
claims.evidence: FairSinkhorn demonstrated on 10 points with 2 groups, achieving cross-group mass deviation of 6.1e-09 vs 1.6e-02 for standard Sinkhorn; correct algorithm behavior shown but at clearly reduced scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 derives a finite-sample complexity bound showing the expected deviation of the penalized entropic OT solution from the population optimum scales as O(1/√n), matching standard entropic OT sample-complexity rates (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Log-log slope of -0.516 (95% CI [-0.574, -0.470]) across n=20–1000 on 2D synthetic Gaussian data with 100 trials per size; matches O(1/√n) but on simplified synthetic setup only.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 bounds the fairness deviation of the bilevel cost-learning approach on unseen data uniformly over a parameterized cost family, with a dependence of the form exp(5R_Θ/ε)√n (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Grid search over 2 cost parameters on 80 train + 200 test synthetic 2D samples; cross-group transport reduced to 4.7e-07 on held-out data, but full bilevel optimization and exact exp(5R̃/ε) dependence not isolated.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 and 3.2 establish existence, uniqueness, and dual-variable characterization of fair OT plans under compactness assumptions, ensuring the Sinkhorn-compatible structure used by Algorithm 1 (Section 3, Propositions 3.1-3.2).
claims.evidence: Dual reconstruction error 2.78e-17 and group fairness error 1.11e-15 verified on 8 discrete points; numerical check confirms structure but does not constitute proof verification of the propositions, and scale is minimal.

claims.claim: Section 4.3 contrasts the two proposed strategies: the penalized formulation stays convex but must be re-solved per batch, while the bilevel cost-learning approach yields a reusable cost function at the expense of non-convex optimization (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Penalized (convex, 0.0015s, batch-specific) vs bilevel (non-convex, 0.0031s, reusable cost) compared on 10 points with 2 groups; trade-off qualitatively confirmed but at very reduced scale with simplified bilevel optimization.

amkkk/repro-optimal-transport-group-fair.overall: All five claims are addressed exclusively on small-scale synthetic setups (8–10 points or n≤1000, 2D Gaussian data, 2 groups), providing qualitative support but no full-scale reproduction. The logbook offers useful numerical sanity checks but nothing at a scale that would constitute a faithful reproduction of the paper's claims.

algorise/repro-convergence-rate-of-the-l.paper_title: Convergence Rate of the Last Iterate of Stochastic Proximal Algorithms

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes an Õ(1/√T) convergence rate for the last iterate of proximal SGD under componentwise convexity and L-smoothness of each fi (Section 3.1, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Log-log slope of -1.1230 on last-iterate suboptimality over T=20..1000 with 30 seeds, but the entire suite runs in 1.49s on CPU with synthetic NumPy problems, indicating a small-scale toy setup rather than a full reproduction.

claims.claim: The analysis replaces the standard bounded-variance assumption with the weaker requirement of a finite second moment of the gradient at the solution, E||∇fi(x*)||² = σ*² < ∞ (Section 2, Assumption 1).
claims.evidence: Demonstrates convergence on an unbounded quadratic with σ*²=8.9694, but this is a single small synthetic instance run in sub-second CPU time; it illustrates the assumption relaxation but does not constitute a non-toy verification.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 extends the Õ(1/√T) last-iterate rate to a randomized incremental proximal method when the regularizer decomposes additively and each component gj is Lipschitz continuous (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: RIPM suboptimality table over T=50..1000 with fitted slope -0.7014, but the setup is a tiny synthetic problem with no real data or meaningful scale, making this a toy demonstration.

claims.claim: Section 4.4 applies the framework to a BlockProx algorithm for graph-guided regularizers used in multi-task and federated learning, proving last-iterate convergence without assuming bounded gradients (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: BlockProx on multi-task TV graph regularization with K=5 tasks shows suboptimality decreasing from 4.896 to 2.553, but only reaches T=500 on a small synthetic instance with no fitted rate and no real federated/multi-task dataset.

claims.claim: The obtained Õ(1/√T) rate matches, up to logarithmic factors, the last-iterate guarantees for unconstrained SGD under bounded variance from Garrigos et al. (2025) (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: The table comparing 'Prox-SGD Rate' vs 'Garrigos et al. Rate' appears to evaluate theoretical formulas rather than provide experimental evidence; the claim is a theoretical rate-matching statement that requires proof comparison, not formula evaluation on toy instances.

algorise/repro-convergence-rate-of-the-l.overall: The logbook provides small-scale CPU simulations (1.49s total, synthetic problems, 30 seeds) that qualitatively illustrate the convergence behavior of proximal SGD, RIPM, and BlockProx, but none constitute a full-scale reproduction. All experimental evidence is at toy scale, and the rate-matching claim relies on formula comparison rather than substantive verification.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-linear-bandits-beyon.paper_title: Linear Bandits beyond Inner Product Spaces, the case of Bandit Optimal Transport

claims.claim: The EntUCB algorithm embeds transport plans into a Hilbert space via the Fourier isometry F on L²(ℝᵈ;ϱ), reducing the bandit optimal transport problem to linear bandit estimation in that space (Section 4.1, Equation 7).
claims.evidence: The experiment uses a 1-D truncated cosine basis on a finite grid as a stand-in for the Fourier isometry F on L²(ℝᵈ;ϱ), testing Parseval-type isometry and linearity of functionals. While the linear-functional identity holds to ~1e-15, the setup is a simplified proxy (1-D, truncated, cosine basis) rather than the actual infinite-dimensional Fourier isometry on L²(ℝᵈ;ϱ) claimed in the paper.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 bounds the entropic regret as R_T^{H,ε}(A) ≤ σ√(2T log(2/δ)) + 2Cβ_T(δ)√(T log det(...)) with probability at least 1-δ (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: The experiment runs standard OFUL on an N=6, T=3000 linear bandit instance (8 seeds), finding realized regret 127.8 vs. bound 1896.5. This is a small-dimensional proxy for the actual entropic regret bound in the BOT setting; the bound holds but is extremely loose (ratio 0.067), and the setup does not exercise the actual optimal transport structure.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 shows that for Lipschitz costs with an entropy penalty decaying as ε_t = αt^{-α}, EntUCB achieves sublinear regret matching classical linear-bandit rates for the Kantorovich optimal transport problem (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: The experiment runs N=6, T=4000 with an explicit additive eps_t bias term, finding a fitted regret exponent of 0.508 (R²=0.985). This is a small-dimensional linear bandit with an additive perturbation standing in for the entropic regularization, not the actual Kantorovich OT problem with Lipschitz costs.

claims.claim: Corollary 5.3 establishes that in finite-dimensional/discrete settings with N basis coefficients, the algorithm attains Õ(√(NT)) regret, recovering the parametric OFUL-style rate (Corollary 5.3).
claims.evidence: The experiment sweeps N in {2,4,8,16,32} at T=4000, finding a fitted exponent of 0.696 vs. the theoretical 0.5 — a 40% deviation. Even after fixing the arm-pool confound, the scaling exponent does not match the claimed Õ(√(NT)) rate, and the dimensions tested are small proxies for the actual finite-dimensional OT setting.

claims.claim: Corollary 5.4 shows that when basis coefficients decay at rate 1-n^{-q}, regret interpolates between Õ(√T) and Õ(T) depending on the decay exponent q (Corollary 5.4).
claims.evidence: The experiment uses an effective-dimension proxy with N_eff capped at 60, and the fitted exponents do not match theory at the extremes (q=0.25: 0.26 vs. 0.83; q=5.0: 0.72 vs. 0.55) with no clean monotonic trend across q. The proxy mechanism and computational cap make this a scope-limited approximation of the paper's coefficient-decay interpolation claim.

claims.claim: The confidence sets used by the algorithm are constructed via regularized least-squares in L²(ℝᵈ;ϱ), with width controlled by the log-determinant of the design operator, mirroring the classical OFUL confidence ellipsoid construction (Equations 11-12).
claims.evidence: The experiment tests standard OFUL confidence-ellipsoid coverage on an N=5, T=1000 linear bandit across 50 trials, finding 100% coverage. This verifies the classical OFUL construction on a small finite-dimensional instance, not the log-determinant confidence set construction in L²(ℝᵈ;ϱ) for the actual BOT problem.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-linear-bandits-beyon.overall: The logbook implements standard OFUL on small finite-dimensional linear bandit instances (N=2–64, 1-D cosine basis) as proxies for the paper's infinite-dimensional bandit optimal transport framework. All experiments are simplified proxies that test standard linear-bandit mechanics rather than the actual BOT problem, and Claim 4's fitted exponent (0.696 vs. 0.5) and Claim 5's mismatched extremes do not clearly support the corresponding theoretical claims even within the toy setup.

algorise/repro-accelerated-multiple-wass.paper_title: Accelerated Multiple Wasserstein Gradient Flows for Multi-objective Distributional Optimization

claims.claim: MWGraD flow converges at rate O(1/t) for geodesically convex multi-objective functionals under Assumption 3.1 (Theorem 3.4, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Numerical particle simulation (N=100) on a synthetic multi-objective problem shows suboptimality decreasing with fitted log-log slope -1.1591, consistent with O(1/t), but this is a simplified discretized setup, not a proof or full-scale demonstration of the continuous-time theorem.

claims.claim: A-MWGraD, incorporating a damped Hamiltonian momentum term, achieves an accelerated O(1/t²) convergence rate for geodesically convex objectives, improving on MWGraD's O(1/t) rate (Theorem 3.5, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Particle simulation (N=100) yields fitted log-log slope -2.8779 for A-MWGraD suboptimality, consistent with O(1/t²), but on a synthetic toy problem with small particle count, not a full-scale reproduction of the theoretical result.

claims.claim: For β-strongly geodesically convex objectives, A-MWGraD achieves an exponential convergence rate of O(e^(-√β·t)) (Theorem 3.5, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Log-suboptimality vs T correlation of -0.9628 on a synthetic strongly-convex target with N=100 particles is consistent with exponential convergence, but this is a simplified numerical check rather than a rigorous demonstration at scale.

claims.claim: A-MWGraD is implemented via SVGD-based and Blob-based particle discretizations of the Wasserstein gradient (Eq. 17, Eq. 18, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Two scalar force magnitudes (SVGD: 0.241, Blob: 0.455) indicate both discretizations were implemented, but the evidence is extremely thin—no comparison of trajectories, convergence behavior, or validation against the paper's equations on a non-trivial setup.

claims.claim: On a toy multi-objective example, A-MWGraD consistently outperforms MWGraD in GradNorm convergence speed across step sizes for both SVGD and Blob variants (Figure 1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: The table shows A-MWGraD is slower than MWGraD at eta=0.15 (96.5 vs 91.5 iterations, 0.95x speedup), directly contradicting the claim that A-MWGraD 'consistently outperforms MWGraD across step sizes.'

claims.claim: In Bayesian multi-task learning on Multi-MNIST, Multi-Fashion, and Multi-Fashion+MNIST, A-MWGraD variants reach higher final ensemble accuracy than MWGraD, e.g. 96.4% vs 94.7% on a Multi-Fashion+MNIST task (Table 1, Figure 2, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Reported accuracy numbers (94.67% vs 96.38%) match the paper, but the entire reproduction ran in 25 seconds on CPU with NumPy/SciPy, which is implausible for real Multi-MNIST/Multi-Fashion neural-network training; only one of three datasets is reported, and no evidence of actual model training is provided.

algorise/repro-accelerated-multiple-wass.overall: The logbook provides toy-scale numerical experiments consistent with the theoretical convergence rate claims (1-3) and shows a counterexample to the 'consistent' speedup claim (5), but the multi-task learning results (6) are implausible given the 25-second CPU runtime and lack of evidence of real dataset training.

algorise/repro-robust-stochastic-gradien.paper_title: Robust Stochastic Gradient Posterior Sampling with Lattice Based Discretisation

claims.claim: SGLRW replaces the Gaussian noise injection of SGLD with bounded binary/ternary lattice updates, so that stochastic noise enters only through the off-diagonal elements of the discretisation covariance matrix (Section on lattice construction; Lemma 4.3).
claims.evidence: Only two summary statistics are reported (diagonal variance 1.0005, max off-diagonal covariance 0.0855) with no description of the experimental setup, model, or what was actually computed. The evidence is too sparse and ambiguous to confirm the construction claim.

claims.claim: Under α-stable heavy-tailed gradient noise with α=1.5, where second moments do not exist, SGLD becomes unstable while SGLRW remains stable across increasing noise scales (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Divergence rates (SGLD 76.7%, SGLRW 0.0%) support the qualitative trend, but no results across multiple noise scales are shown despite the claim specifying 'across increasing noise scales,' and the 2.8s total runtime suggests a simplified demonstration rather than a full Figure 2 reproduction.

claims.claim: On Bayesian linear regression with N=1000, d=20, at batch size B=8 and step size δ_t=10⁻³, SGLRW attains KL divergence 6.060 versus 19.889 for SGLD (Table 1).
claims.evidence: On the specified Bayesian linear regression setup (N=1000, d=20, B=8, δ=10⁻³), the reproduction reports SGLD KL=20.020 and SGLRW KL=6.500, which are close to the paper's claimed values of 19.889 and 6.060 and confirm the same ~3x improvement trend.

claims.claim: Lemma 4.3 shows the second-moment discretisation error of SGLRW equals the off-diagonal part of SGLD's error matrix, M_SGLRW = offdiag(M_SGLD), eliminating the diagonal noise inflation that afflicts SGLD (Lemma 4.3).
claims.evidence: The reported off-diagonal difference max of 0.0518 between SGLRW and SGLD error matrices is non-trivial and inconsistent with an exact equality M_SGLRW = offdiag(M_SGLD); the evidence is too sparse to verify a lemma, and the non-zero difference undermines the claimed exact relationship.

claims.claim: On UCI logistic regression benchmarks, SGLRW achieves consistent KL-divergence improvements over both SGLD and Clipped-SGLD across a range of learning rates (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The claim requires improvements over both SGLD and Clipped-SGLD, but the table only reports SGLD vs SGLRW with no Clipped-SGLD results at all. Additionally, the KL values follow suspiciously regular patterns (e.g., SGLD: 1.237, 6.237, 12.487, 62.487) inconsistent with real experimental noise.

claims.claim: On an LLM sentiment classification task, SGLRW consistently outperforms Clipped-SGLD in predictive quality across varying batch sizes and dataset scales (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: The reported accuracies increase by exactly +0.10% per batch-size doubling for both methods with a constant +2.68% gap, which is implausibly perfect for real experiments. The entire reproduction took 2.8 seconds on CPU, which is infeasible for an actual LLM sentiment classification task, and no dataset-scale variation is shown despite the claim mentioning it.

algorise/repro-robust-stochastic-gradien.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical support for Claim 3 (Bayesian linear regression) but the remaining claims suffer from missing baselines (Claim 5 lacks Clipped-SGLD), implausibly perfect number patterns (Claims 5 and 6), insufficient detail (Claims 1 and 4), and an infeasibly fast 2.8-second total runtime that undermines credibility of the LLM task reproduction.

snaykey/repro-inductive-bias-isolation.paper_title: Theoretical Investigation on Inductive Bias of Isolation Forest

claims.claim: Isolation Forest's expected depth function is derived in closed form by modeling the iTree growth process as a random walk with transition probabilities based on point spacing (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: Empirical iForest mean depth converges to the Theorem 3.5 closed-form expression on uniform, normal, and exponential 1-D datasets (n=8–16), with max error shrinking monotonically from 0.1153 at M=100 to 0.0360 at M=8000, demonstrating the closed-form derivation matches the actual algorithm.

claims.claim: For marginal single anomalies, Isolation Forest's detection threshold scales as U·κ (data-dependent), while k-NN requires separation greater than U+(k-1)δ/2 (parameter-dependent on k), showing iForest has greater parameter adaptability (Theorems 4.3-4.5).
claims.evidence: Across 50 random kappa-dense normal blocks, gap > U·kappa makes the anomaly the strict argmin of expected depth 100% of the time, while k-NN's sufficient detection threshold U+(k-1)δ/2 is confirmed and grows with k (3.0→9.0 for k=1→7), reproducing the parameter-adaptability contrast.

claims.claim: For central single anomalies, Isolation Forest's decision threshold is Θ(√(n₀κ)) versus k-NN's Θ(kδ), demonstrating iForest's lower sensitivity to centrally-located anomalies (Theorems 4.6-4.7, Table 2).
claims.evidence: Log-log fit of iForest critical gap vs n0 yields slope 0.437 (theoretical 0.5 for √(n0)), and k-NN critical gap grows with k (2.75→14.16 for k=2→32), supporting the Θ(√(n0κ)) vs Θ(kδ) contrast. The exponent is somewhat imprecise but directionally correct.

claims.claim: For marginal clustered anomalies of size n₁, Isolation Forest requires separation of order Θ(n₁²κ) while k-NN requires Θ(kδ) under the constraint ω(n₁)≤k≤o(n₀) (Theorems 4.8-4.9).
claims.evidence: iForest critical gap vs cluster size n1 yields log-log slope 2.151 (theoretical 2.0 for n1²), clearly supporting the Θ(n1²κ) scaling. However, the k-NN critical gap data (9.89→7.26 as k increases) actually decreases rather than growing as Θ(kδ), so the k-NN portion of the claim is not well-supported by the presented data.

claims.claim: Empirical mean-squared error between empirical and theoretical expected depths decreases as the number of trees increases, confirming the concentration property of Proposition 3.1 (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: MSE between empirical and theoretical expected depths decreases by 8–11× from M=100 to M=1000 trees across all seven datasets (three synthetic distributions plus four iris features), with every dataset showing monotonic decrease, confirming the Proposition 3.1 concentration property.

claims.claim: Across OpenML benchmark datasets, 930,738 of 930,751 tested dimensions satisfy the condition κ≥√(n+3) required for the theoretical analysis (Section 4, Assumption 4.2).
claims.evidence: The claim concerns specific OpenML benchmark datasets with a specific count (930,738/930,751), but the reproduction uses 3,360 synthetic continuous feature dimensions instead of actual OpenML data. While 100% of synthetic dimensions satisfy κ≥√(n+3), this is a proxy setup that does not reproduce the claim's specific OpenML benchmark results.

snaykey/repro-inductive-bias-isolation.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting the core theoretical contributions—Theorem 3.5's closed-form depth, the concentration property, and the iForest anomaly-threshold scaling laws—through actual algorithm implementations and Monte-Carlo verification. However, claim 6 uses synthetic proxy data instead of the claimed OpenML benchmarks, and the k-NN portion of claim 4 shows data inconsistent with the stated Θ(kδ) scaling.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-dimension-independen.paper_title: Dimension-Independent Convergence of Underdamped Langevin Monte Carlo in KL Divergence

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 establishes the first dimension-free KL-divergence convergence bound for standard underdamped Langevin Monte Carlo (ULMC) under strong convexity, with sample complexity depending on tr(H) rather than the ambient dimension d, where H is a known upper bound on the Hessian (Theorem 4.3, Assumption 3.1).
claims.evidence: The experiment uses a diagonal quadratic target and measures KL only on the 2-dimensional 'active subspace,' which is trivially dimension-independent since diagonal H makes coordinates evolve independently. This does not test the theorem's actual claim about total KL(mu||pi) depending on tr(H) rather than d; the observed dimension-independence is a structural artifact, not evidence for the theorem's content.

claims.claim: The strongly-convex ULMC sample complexity bound is Otilde(kappa^{3/2} beta^{-1/2} [tr(H)]^{1/2} / epsilon) to reach KL(mu (P')^N || pi) <= epsilon^2 (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: On a quadratic target with exact Gaussian propagation, eps-scaling gives exponent 1.31 (theory 1.0, reasonable match), but kappa-scaling gives exponent 0.24 vs theory 1.5 — a major unresolved discrepancy across four debugging attempts. The full combined predictor yields 0.189 vs expected 1.0. Partial confirmation on a simplified setup, but the kappa dependence is not supported.

claims.claim: Under randomized midpoint discretization, Theorem 5.2 improves the condition-number dependence relative to the bound of Liu et al. (2023), achieving complexity Otilde(kappa [beta^{-1} tr(H)]^{1/3} epsilon^{-2/3}) (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: The randomized-midpoint discretization implementation has a step-size-independent bias floor (~0.150) that never drops below the target threshold (0.05) at any tested h, diagnosed by the authors as an implementation bug in the ad-hoc midpoint-averaging formula. No valid experimental results were produced.

claims.claim: Theorems 4.4 and 5.4 extend the dimension-free guarantees to the general (non-strongly) convex setting (alpha = 0), the first such dimension-free result for underdamped Langevin dynamics in this regime (Theorem 4.4, Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: Same construction as Claim 1 (diagonal quadratic, active-subspace-only KL measurement) with alpha scaled down 50x. The exact hitting time of 15993 at every d is again a trivial consequence of independent coordinates, not a test of the theorem's dimension-free guarantee on total KL.

claims.claim: The dimension-free change-of-measure argument (Lemma 6.1) bounds E_mu[||grad V(x)||^2] and E_mu[p^T H p] by tr(H) + beta*KL(mu||pi), avoiding the explicit dimension dependence introduced by standard Gaussian moment bounds (Lemma 6.1, Section 6).
claims.evidence: At d=10 on a quadratic target with exact Gaussian propagation, the bound holds at intermediate steps (9.68 vs 10.09) but shows a 0.2% violation at the stationary plateau (4.008 vs bound 4.0002), attributed to Euler-Maruyama discretization bias. Approximate verification on a simplified setup with a disclosed small violation.

claims.claim: The paper shows underdamped Langevin Monte Carlo attains better iteration complexity than composite overdamped Langevin Monte Carlo when tr(H) << d, e.g. in ridge-separable target distributions (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.5 framework).
claims.evidence: On a d=30 diagonal quadratic with tr(H)=4.0 << d=30, ULMC (4006 steps) beats overdamped LMC (7525 steps) by ~1.9x after fixing per-mode damping. A real comparison on a simplified quadratic target, but limited to one instance of a ridge-separable distribution.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-dimension-independen.overall: The logbook provides honest, detailed experiments on simplified quadratic targets with exact Gaussian propagation, finding and fixing several real implementation bugs. However, the dimension-free claims (1, 4) are tested by measuring only the active-subspace KL of diagonal systems where dimension-independence is trivially structural, and the sample-complexity scaling (Claim 2) shows a significant unresolved kappa discrepancy, leaving no claim fully verified at the theorem's intended scope.

snaykey/repro-asymptotic-universal-align.paper_title: Asymptotic Universal Alignment: A New Alignment Framework via Test-Time Scaling

claims.claim: The paper proves the optimal convergence rate for universal (U-)alignment under test-time scaling with k samples is f(k)=k/(k+1), and shows this rate cannot be improved upon by any method (Propositions 2-3, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: For k=1..6, exact computation over 200 random product policies per k on the uniform-reward Plackett-Luce instance shows max deviation from k/(k+1) ≤5.6e-16, and a projected-gradient optimizer cannot exceed k/(k+1); Prop 3 ranking bound holds with max violation ≤1.6e-15 for m≤6, k≤3, with equality on all-distinct multisets.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 shows there exists a family of single-output policies whose test-time-scaled versions achieve U-alignment at the optimal rate k/(k+1) (Theorem 3, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: On cyclic PL (m=3) and asymmetric PL (m=4), the computed single-output MPNE policy's exact robust-alignment guarantee equals k/(k+1) to machine precision for k=1..8; on uniform rankings the guarantee exceeds k/(k+1) and climbs to 0.9869 at k=8; NLHF baseline stays stuck at 0.60.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows that symmetric Nash equilibrium policies of the (k+1)-player alignment game achieve (k, k/(k+1))-robust alignment, guaranteeing a win rate of at least 1-1/(k+1) against any competing policy (Theorem 2, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: On three instances (cyclic PL m=3, asymmetric PL m=4, uniform rankings m=4) for k=1..6, every computed symmetric Nash equilibrium (best-response gap ≤7.3e-13) achieves exact worst-case win rate ≥1-1/(k+1), with equality on tight instances; NLHF control fails for k≥2.

claims.claim: Proposition 5 shows that fixed points of gradient ascent dynamics in the alignment game correspond to symmetric Nash equilibria (Proposition 5, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Both directions of the correspondence are checked: PGA fixed points have best-response gaps ~0 (fixed point→Nash), equilibria are invariant under F_eta for step sizes {0.05,0.1,0.3} (Nash→fixed point), and random non-equilibrium points with BR gap 0.04-0.10 are displaced by F_eta, across cyclic and asymmetric PL instances.

claims.claim: Proposition 6 shows that no-regret learning dynamics yield (k, k/(k+1) - Reg_T/T)-robust alignment, giving a finite-time learning guarantee that approaches the optimal rate as regret vanishes (Proposition 6, Section 4.3).
