claims.evidence: Hedge self-play on asymmetric PL (m=4) for k=2,3 and T up to 3200 shows guarantee ≥ k/(k+1) - Reg_T/T in all cases, with Reg_T/T shrinking from 0.054 to 0.021 as T grows; on cyclic PL (m=3) Reg_T=0 and guarantee equals k/(k+1) exactly; mode-collapsed control stays below optimal.

snaykey/repro-asymptotic-universal-align.overall: The logbook provides exact numerical certifications of all five theoretical claims on concrete, deliberately-tight preference instances (Condorcet cycles, uniform reward, uniform rankings) using closed-form win-rate computation and full enumeration, with adversarial controls. These are instance-level verifications confirming the stated inequalities hold with equality where tight, not universal re-proofs.

snaykey/repro-scaling-exponents-pinn.paper_title: Discovering Scaling Exponents with Physics-Informed Müntz-Szász Networks

claims.claim: MSN-PINN models targets as sums of power-law terms u_theta(x) = sum_k c_k x^{mu_k}, treating both coefficients {c_k} and exponents {mu_k} as trainable parameters optimized via a two-timescale scheme with exponent learning rate eta_mu set to roughly 0.5 times the coefficient learning rate eta_c (Equation 1, Section 3.1, Algorithm 1, Section 3.5).
claims.evidence: The ansatz u=sum_k c_k x^{mu_k} with both c_k and mu_k trainable is implemented with two-timescale optimization (eta_mu=0.5*eta_c); single-exponent recovery achieves mu=0.500000 with 9.8e-13% relative error, and Prop 3.2 exact K=1 representation gives 0 error.

claims.claim: For the 2D Laplace equation corner singularity with a 270-degree wedge angle, MSN-PINN recovers the exponent as mu=0.6667 against the true classical Kondrat'ev value of 2/3, a 0.009% error (Table 2).
claims.evidence: On the 270-degree Laplace corner (omega=3pi/2), constraint-aware MSN-PINN recovers mu=0.66666 vs Kondrat'ev 2/3, with 0.0004% relative error (paper: 0.009%), averaged 0.0011% over 5 seeds, using the paper's App I.8 hyperparameters.

claims.claim: On a 40-configuration wedge benchmark spanning 5 angles and 4 boundary condition types, the constraint-aware MSN-PINN achieves 100% success rate with 0.022% mean exponent error, versus only 55% success and 5.96% mean error for the naive MSN-PINN without the constraint term, a roughly 270-fold improvement in accuracy (Section I.8, Table 11).
claims.evidence: Across 40 configurations (5 angles x 4 BC types x 2 methods), constraint-aware MSN-PINN achieves 100% success with 0.0059% mean error, matching the paper's 100%/0.022%; the naive baseline (5%/14.99%) is stricter than the paper's 55%/5.96% but confirms the claimed direction and magnitude of improvement.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.5 shows the exponent recovery error scales as O(sigma / (c_min * Delta^2 * sqrt(N))), where Delta is the minimum separation between exponents, implying degraded conditioning as exponents become closely spaced, analogous to an optical resolution limit (Theorem 4.5, Remark 4.6).
claims.evidence: Four independent log-log scaling fits recover the Theorem 4.5 exponents: sigma slope 1.06 (target +1), N slope -0.50 (target -0.5), Delta slope -1.75 in the resolvable regime (target -2), c_min slope -1.01 (target -1), each from 40-trial M-estimation runs.

claims.claim: Adding a constraint-aware loss term of the form sum_k |c_k| sin^2(mu_k * omega) to steer critical points toward physically valid exponents improves accuracy on the corner-singularity example from 14.6% error to 0.009% error (Theorem 4.8, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Ablation on the 270-degree corner shows naive (no L_con) worst-of-5 error 14.14% (paper 14.6%) dropping to 0.0004% with the constraint-aware loss (paper 0.009%), a >1000x improvement matching the paper's 'three orders of magnitude' claim.

claims.claim: Two exponents become distinguishable (resolvable) only when their separation Delta is at least 0.1; below this threshold they merge into an intermediate value, termed the Rayleigh limit for exponent resolution (Table 10, Section I.6, Remark I.1).
claims.evidence: Direct two-exponent recovery shows merged fraction dropping from 62% (Delta=0.02) and 38% (Delta=0.05) to 0% at Delta=0.10 and above, and the Gram matrix condition number explodes from 102 (Delta=0.5) to 41007 (Delta=0.02), confirming the Delta>=0.1 Rayleigh threshold.

snaykey/repro-scaling-exponents-pinn.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from real PDE and scaling experiments (pure NumPy/SciPy on CPU) supporting all six claims, with multiple seeds, ablations, and log-log fits. The constraint-aware results match the paper closely; the naive baseline is stricter than the paper's but confirms the claimed improvement direction.

ProCreations/repro-laplacian-connectivit.paper_title: Impact of Connectivity on Laplacian Representations in Reinforcement Learning

claims.claim: The approximation error of a rank-k learned Laplacian representation used for linear value function approximation is upper-bounded by ‖v−v̂_k‖_Φ ≤ ‖r̄‖_Φ√(1/(λ₂λ_{k+1})) + ‖v‖_Φ√(2ε/(λ_{k+1}−λ_k)), decomposing into truncation error and feature-estimation error (Theorem 3.3, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: 512 randomly generated 10-state asymmetric Markov kernels all satisfy the full Theorem 3.3 inequality with minimum slack 0.365641, and a destructive control that deletes the feature-estimation term fails on all 512 trials, confirming both terms are necessary.

claims.claim: The truncation error term is bounded by ‖v−v_k‖²_Φ ≤ ‖r̄‖²_Φ/(λ₂λ_{k+1}), showing the bound scales inversely with the algebraic connectivity λ₂ of the state-transition graph, so poorly-connected MDPs induce larger approximation error (Lemma 3.4, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: All 512 truncation inequalities pass with minimum squared slack 0.294861, and a 7-point bottleneck sweep from λ₂=0.02 to 1.0 shows the bound falls monotonically with correlation corr(λ₂,bound)=-0.977, directly confirming the inverse-connectivity scaling claim.

claims.claim: The Graph Drawing Objective's feature-estimation error is bounded by ‖Π_Ψ−Π_Ψ̃‖₂ < √(2ε/(λ_{k+1}−λ_k)), depending on the spectral gap between the k-th and (k+1)-th eigenvalues (Lemma 3.5, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: All 512 projector-distance inequalities pass with minimum slack 0.012517, and a destructive control understating the bound by 4× fails on all 512 trials, confirming the spectral-gap dependence is correctly calibrated.

claims.claim: The analysis defines a Φ-self-adjoint Laplacian L = I − (P+Φ⁻¹PᵀΦ)/2 (Equation 6, Section 3) and applies without assuming symmetry of the induced transition kernel, i.e., it holds for general non-uniform behavior policies (Lemma 3.6, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: On 512 asymmetric kernels (minimum asymmetry 0.904), the Φ-self-adjointness residual max ‖ΦL−(ΦL)^T‖ is 1.388e-17; additionally, exact rational arithmetic on 24 non-reversible kernels up to 128 states yields exact zero residual for the self-adjointness identity, confirming the construction works without transition-kernel symmetry.

claims.claim: Propositions 4.1 and 4.2 establish that this matrix-based Laplacian formulation is equivalent to the operator-theoretic Laplacian representation formulation of Wu et al. (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Across 512 kernels, operator/matrix residual is exactly 0.0 with adjoint and energy residuals at most 2.22e-16 and GDO residual at most 1.55e-15; exact Fraction arithmetic on 24 kernels through 128 states confirms exact zero residual for operator action, inner-product identities, and Dirichlet energy, providing algebraic (not merely numerical) confirmation of equivalence.

ProCreations/repro-laplacian-connectivit.overall: The logbook provides rigorous numerical and exact-arithmetic verification of all five theoretical claims on randomly generated asymmetric finite-state MDPs, with well-designed destructive controls that fail when bounds are violated. The exact rational arithmetic expansion to 128 states for claims 4 and 5 elevates those from numerical agreement to algebraic identity checks.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-learning-augmented-o.paper_title: Learning-Augmented Online Minimization with Dual Predictions

claims.claim: For laminar set cover, the proposed dual-prediction algorithm achieves E[ALG] = (1+epsilon)*OPT + O(R*eta/epsilon) for any constant epsilon>0, where eta measures dual prediction error (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: On a K=9 parking permit instance (a laminar set-cover special case), the experiment uses genuine offline-optimal DP as the prediction baseline and shows ALG within 1.7% of OPT at zero error, with excess cost growing monotonically from 0.54 to 4.63 as error_prob increases from 0 to 0.7 (fitted exponent 0.57, R²=0.80), confirming the theorem's qualitative structure of near-optimality with perfect prediction and linear-in-eta degradation.

claims.claim: For metrical task systems, the dual-prediction algorithm (Algorithm 3, an A*-style search minimizing d(s_{t-1},s)+c_t(s)+w_hat_t(s)) achieves a (1+eta/OPT)-competitive ratio driven by the span seminorm of Bellman-operator discrepancies (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: A 25-state, T=250 path-metric MTS instance with exact backward-DP Bellman ground truth implements Algorithm 3's A*-style decision rule directly; at eta=0 the ratio is 1.025 (near-optimal) and grows monotonically to 3.05x as eta increases to 4.0, confirming the (1+eta/OPT)-competitive structure on a non-trivial instance.

claims.claim: Optimal dual solutions are stable under instance perturbations, satisfying ||y1* - y2*||_1 = O(|X1 Delta X2|), whereas optimal primal solutions can change arbitrarily under a single-element perturbation (Lemma A.1).
claims.evidence: Using scipy.optimize.linprog on a constructed 4-5 element laminar set-cover LP, the round-2 instance shows primal support flipping from {Z} to {X,Y} (fully disjoint) under a single-element perturbation, while the dual shift on common elements is 0.0—directly demonstrating both dual stability (||y1*-y2*||_1 = O(1)) and primal instability as claimed.

claims.claim: Event predictions for caching are similarly shown to be unstable, since a single prediction error can cause the competitive ratio to collapse (Lemma A.3).
claims.evidence: The round-2 implementation adds the paper's adversarial Stage 3 to the Lemma A.3 construction (k=8, cache size 7); sweeping Stage 3 cycles from 4 to 400 shows CR_single_error climbing from 1.27x to 2.54x trending toward LRU's 5.1x-6.88x, while perfect-prediction stays near-optimal—demonstrating that a single misprediction causes unbounded-trending competitive-ratio degradation.

claims.claim: On the parking permit problem, the learning-augmented dual-prediction algorithm achieves 1.8x to 4.4x better competitive ratios than classical algorithms at K=9 permit types, and it outperforms baselines on the k-server problem using real bike-sharing data (Experiments section).
claims.evidence: The parking permit half is addressed with genuine O(K)-deterministic and O(log K)-randomized baselines at K=9, f=1.5 (dual-prediction CR=1.00 vs classical CRs of 5.83 and 10.23), but the k-server/bike-sharing experiment using real data—explicitly part of this claim—was never attempted, leaving a major component of the claim entirely unaddressed.

claims.claim: For general (non-laminar) set cover, even perfect dual predictions cannot beat the classical H_m competitive ratio under the standard LP formulation, showing laminar structure is necessary for the improvement (Lemma A.4).
claims.evidence: Exact LP solving via scipy.optimize.linprog on the classic worst-case non-laminar set-cover instance (m=4 to 16) shows the fractional LP optimum fixed at 1.0 while H_m grows from 2.08 to 3.38, confirming that the structural gap between the LP relaxation (which any dual prediction targets) and the classical online ratio is independent of prediction quality and grows with m.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-learning-augmented-o.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting claims 1-4 and 6 through real implementations on non-toy setups (parking permit K=9, 25-state MTS, exact LP-based set-cover constructions, and the paper's own caching worst-case), with genuine bug-finding and fixing across two rounds. Claim 5 remains inconclusive because the k-server/bike-sharing half of the experiments was never attempted, though the parking permit half was substantively verified.

DineshAI/29sn1uqWn3.paper_title: Why Are Linear RNNs More Parallelizable?

claims.claim: Any language recognized by a linear RNN (LRNN) over the rationals lies in PNC1, meaning LRNNs can be simulated by log-depth arithmetic circuits (Theorem 3, Section 4).
claims.evidence: A machine-checkable certificate validates the universal affine-monoid associativity identity (A,b)∘(C,d)=(AC,bC+d) symbolically and checks the balanced-tree depth recurrence D(n)=ceil(log2 n) on boundary cases up to 1,048,577, with 256 independent exact-integer cases and a negative control (reversed bias) correctly rejected.

claims.claim: LRNNs require only O(log n log* n) depth NC circuits, an O(log* n) overhead beyond the O(log n) depth of transformers/TC0 circuits (Corollary 5, Section 4).
claims.evidence: A compositional depth certificate checks the derivation chain (Claim 1 depth → Q-to-Z lift → Jung 1985 → O(log n log* n)) symbolically, validates exact rational gate substitution on 3,025 pairs, audits log-star boundaries to 65,537 bits, and correctly rejects the paper's printed rational-addition typo as a negative control.

claims.claim: Log-precision nonlinear RNNs can solve sorted deterministic graph connectivity, an L-complete problem, requiring Omega(log^2 n) depth and revealing a fundamental parallelization barrier absent in LRNNs (Theorem 2, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The complete sorted-DGC domain through 6 vertices (29,367 instances) is exhaustively checked: the counter-machine scan, integer-exact ReLU RNN, and reference reachability agree everywhere; the ReLU zero mask is audited on 8,193 integers; the conditional lower-bound qualifier is retained; and removing the nonzero-index guard produces 636 errors.

claims.claim: Poly-precision nonlinear RNNs can express P-complete problems under FO reductions, implying no efficient parallel algorithm exists for them unless P=NC (Corollary 2, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The paper's base-2 stack encoding is correctly identified as defective (vanishing margin) and rejected; a corrected base-4 gapped encoding with fixed 1/4 separation is validated exhaustively on 32,767 stacks through depth 14, 29,524 strings, and 1,568 monotone-CVP assignments, with the NC≠P conditional assumption retained.

claims.claim: DPLR-based LRNN architectures such as RWKV-7 and DeltaNet can solve the PNC1-complete iterated 3x3 matrix multiplication problem using only 4 layers (Theorem 5, Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: RWKV-7 arithmetic is verified on 280 products with an explicit BOS-repair, but the DeltaNet router is obstructed: a rational 2×2 matrix cannot have a primitive 1,404th root (φ(1404)=432>2), invalidating the published proof; no alternative four-layer DeltaNet construction is established, so the existential claim remains unresolved.

claims.claim: Experiments show nonlinear RNNs generalize on the L-complete graph connectivity task while transformers and Mamba fail to solve it, matching the theoretical complexity separation (Figure 2, Section 6).
claims.evidence: Audits of the released artifacts found the sole checkpoint is a self-attention model (not RNN) diverging 11–43 points from Figure 2, and the generator contains a bug creating a perfect endpoint shortcut; however, no faithful five-model training run was executed, and identity requirements for falsification were not met.

DineshAI/29sn1uqWn3.overall: The logbook provides rigorous machine-checkable certificates and exhaustive finite-domain validations supporting Claims 1–4, while correctly identifying that Claims 5 and 6 remain unresolved due to a genuine mathematical obstruction in the DeltaNet router and the absence of a faithful five-model training reproduction, respectively.

DineshAI/Iww9TICvKj.paper_title: Convergence of Two-Timescale Markovian Stochastic Approximations with Applications in Reinforcement Learning

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 establishes almost-sure stability (sup_n ||z_n|| < infinity) for two-timescale stochastic approximation iterates driven by Markovian noise, without requiring projection operators (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Numerical simulation of two-timescale SA on specific instances (historical: d=3 linear, 25k steps; current: nonlinear d≤64, up to 400k steps) shows bounded iterates, but finite-horizon runs on constructed families cannot establish the almost-sure infinite-horizon stability claimed by Theorem 3.2.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 proves that the fast-timescale iterate x_n converges to the equilibrium map lambda(y_n), i.e. lim_n ||x_n - lambda(y_n)|| = 0, with joint convergence to (lambda(y*), y*) (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: Tracking errors and joint convergence ratios were measured on specific nonlinear families (d=8/32/64, up to 400k steps) with real runs and numbers, but finite-horizon numerical convergence on constructed instances cannot establish the almost-sure limit claimed by Theorem 3.3.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.1 shows the fast-timescale iterate norm is controlled by the running maximum of the slow-timescale iterate, ||x_n|| <= K(1+||y_n^max||) almost surely, which is the key technical device enabling the stability proof (Lemma 3.1).
claims.evidence: Empirical K values were measured on finite paths (historical: d=3, K≤0.84; current: nonlinear family with analytic certificates, adversarial K≤28.8), but as the logbook itself notes, a measured running maximum is tautologically finite at finite horizon and cannot establish one finite K for all n on almost every path.

claims.claim: Theorem 7.2 gives the first almost-sure convergence proof for temporal difference learning with gradient correction and eligibility traces (TDC(lambda)) under off-policy, Markovian sampling conditions (Section 7, Theorem 7.2, Definition 7.1).
claims.evidence: TDC(λ) was simulated on small MDPs (historical: nS=5, d=3, λ=0 with no eligibility traces; current: nS=20, d=10, λ up to 0.97, up to 240k steps) showing residual reduction, but finite-horizon runs on small MDPs cannot prove almost-sure convergence, and the 'first such proof' priority claim is unaddressed by simulation.

claims.claim: The convergence analysis relies on assumptions B.1-B.7 in the appendix, including a unique stationary distribution for the Markov noise chain (Assumption B.1) and learning-rate timescale separation lim_n beta(n)/alpha(n) = 0 (Assumption B.2) (Appendix B).
claims.evidence: A source audit reads the hash-pinned arXiv TeX and exhaustively checks all six labeled assumption environments, confirming B.1 contains 'unique invariant probability measure', B.2 contains the β/α→0 limit, and that Theorem 3.3 and the TDC proof reference all six labels; destructive controls (removing B.2, changing B.3 type) correctly fail.

DineshAI/Iww9TICvKj.overall: The logbook provides real numerical runs on simplified instances for claims 1-4 (finite-horizon simulations of mathematical theorems about almost-sure properties) and a legitimate exhaustive source audit for claim 5. Claims 1-4 are addressed at toy scale only; claim 5 is verified as a factual statement about the paper's dependency structure.

claims.claim: RDNGD achieves iteration and oracle complexity of O(d·ε⁻²) for smooth nonconvex problems and O(d·ε⁻¹) for smooth convex problems using only a pairwise comparison oracle on Riemannian manifolds (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The empirical RDNGD sweep uses very small dimensions (d=4,8,16) with large epsilon values (0.35,0.25,0.18), and the schedule_checks in verify.py merely compute d/ε² and d/ε ratios that are trivially true by algebra (4x and 2x doubling). The symbolic certificate is referenced but not shown in the logbook.

claims.claim: The recurrent variant RRDNGD attains linear convergence for strongly convex objectives, requiring O(d log(1/ε)) oracle calls (Table 1).
claims.evidence: RRDNGD slopes near -1 per phase are demonstrated only at d=4,8,16 on f(x)=||x||²/2, and the schedule check in verify.py computes d·log(1/ε) which is trivially logarithmic by construction. The finding that Algorithm 2's printed schedule is defective is interesting but the counterexample uses d=1.

claims.claim: RDFW, a projection-free Riemannian dueling Frank-Wolfe method, achieves O(ε⁻¹) iteration complexity with O(d·ε⁻²) oracle calls for smooth convex problems using only a linear minimization oracle (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The RDFW oracle sum (3,280,000 = 8.2·d·T²) is an exact arithmetic computation of the batch schedule, not an experiment. The empirical sweep uses small dimensions (d=3,7,15) with only two T values (10 and 80), making the slope estimate weak.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.1 and Lemma 3.2 show the comparison-based gradient direction estimator is unbiased for the normalized gradient with improved constants over prior Euclidean dueling optimization work (Section 3, Lemma 3.1, Lemma 3.2).
claims.evidence: Lemma 3.2 is confirmed by both closed-form Gamma-function evaluation at d=2,3,5,25,100,1000 (all C_hat in [0.3989,1]) and Monte Carlo at d=5,25,100 with 80k samples. Lemma 3.1 is tested on a 13-cell non-vacuous sweep (2M directions each) on a specifically constructed worst-case L-smooth function, confirming the bound's scaling in all four arguments (d,nu,L,||grad f||). Negative controls (tightened bound violated 13/13, sign-blind oracle at 0.5) are meaningful.

claims.claim: The framework is applied to a black-box adversarial attack on DNNs with sphere-constrained perturbations and to horizon leveling via SO(2) image rotation, both using only pairwise comparison feedback (Section on real-world applications).
claims.evidence: The attack uses a different VGG checkpoint than the paper, only 4 test inputs, and the paper's exact hyperparameters (nu=eta=1e-6) fail to change any labels (0/2). The successful route uses different settings (nu=.01, eta=.04, radius=.5). The SO(2) route substitutes deterministic tilt angles for the HLW dataset's human annotations. Real runs exist but on a clearly simplified/proxy setup.

claims.claim: The method covers Hadamard manifolds and bounded-sectional-curvature spaces, with demonstrated applications including Rayleigh quotient maximization on the unit sphere and Karcher mean computation on SPD matrices (Section on synthetic applications).
claims.evidence: Rayleigh quotient optimization runs at the paper's dimensions (d=100,150) with 50,000 duels across 3 held-out seeds each, achieving gaps ~4e-6 to ~7.6e-6 with zero unit-norm error. Dense noncommuting SPD Karcher mean experiments use n=5,10, m=50 with relative reference gaps below 3e-5. Negative controls (reversed comparison signs) show no progress in both cases, confirming the oracle is the sole signal.

DineshAI/nDfDnsyllY.overall: The logbook provides strong evidence for Claims 4 and 6 at the paper's scale with meaningful negative controls, but Claims 1-3 rely on small-dimension sweeps and trivially-true algebraic schedule checks, and Claim 5 uses a proxy setup where the paper's exact attack hyperparameters fail. The reproduction is transparent about limitations but only partially reaches the paper's intended scale.

DineshAI/TBSyYj4VV6.paper_title: Accelerating Regression Tasks with Quantum Algorithms

claims.claim: The proposed quantum algorithm constructs epsilon-approximate GLM sparsifiers in time O~(r*sqrt(mn)/epsilon + poly(n))*log(s_max/s_min), giving a quadratic speedup in sample count m over the classical O~(mr) algorithm (Theorem 10).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence across 11 parameter cells (n=2, m=16, r=1) showing Algorithm 2 sets M=Θ(n/ε²) and passes it to MultiSample, which requires M≤m; for all tested ε values M>m (e.g., ε=0.25 gives M=32>16), violating the sampler's stated domain. Additionally, the explicit Ω(ε⁻²) processing loop contradicts the claimed O~(ε⁻¹) runtime. A negative control at ε=√(n/m) shows the contradiction disappears, confirming the issue is a missing precondition rather than an unconditional rejection.

claims.claim: For linear regression, the quantum algorithm runs in O~(r*sqrt(mn)/epsilon + n^3) time versus O~(mr + n^3) classically (Corollary 23).
claims.evidence: The logbook ran finite classical leverage-score sampling and regression solves (m=2048, n=8, k=256, objective ratio 1.0000041750) and 20-seed first-hit sweeps, but no quantum algorithm was executed or certified. The logbook itself acknowledges 'a universal complexity theorem cannot be verified from finite scaling,' and no proof certificate or counterexample was found.

claims.claim: The paper gives the first quantum algorithm for Lasso regression, running in O~(r*sqrt(mn)/epsilon + poly(n,1/epsilon)) time versus O~(mn^2 + n^3) classically (Corollary 26).
claims.evidence: The logbook found an exact rational counterexample to the displayed inequality (A=[1], b=[1], λ=100, ε=1/10: left side ≥1 vs right bound 33/40) showing a missing λ in the printed minimand, but this is a display-level typo, not evidence about the existence or runtime of the quantum Lasso algorithm. No quantum implementation, proof certificate, or prior-art exhaustiveness check was available.

claims.claim: Ridge regression is solved in O~(r*sqrt(mn)/epsilon + n^3) quantum time versus O~(mr + poly(n,1/epsilon)) classically (Corollary 25).
claims.evidence: The logbook verified the ridge augmentation identity [A; √λ I],[b;0] preserves the objective exactly (max error <1e-12) and ran finite sampled solves (λ=0.5, m=2048, k=256, ratio 1.0002072182), but the quantum runtime claim O~(r√(mn)/ε+n³) was not executed or certified. The reduction is correct but the inherited quantum complexity guarantee remains unverified.

claims.claim: Huber regression is handled via a gamma_p-loss framework in O~(r*sqrt(mn)/epsilon + poly(n,1/epsilon)) quantum time (Corollary 12).
claims.evidence: The logbook verified that γ₁ equals the Huber loss exactly on a 7-point grid (error <1e-12) and is continuous at |x|=1, and ran a finite Huber coreset solve (ratio 1.0020256149), but the quantum runtime claim O~(r√(mn)/ε+poly(n,1/ε)) was not executed or certified. No quantum subroutine was implemented.

claims.claim: For l_p regression with p in (0,2], the algorithm achieves quadratic speedup in the sample parameter m, which the authors note dominates runtime when m >> n (Corollary 11).
claims.evidence: The logbook verified the p-homogeneity identity for p∈{0.25,0.5,1,1.5,2} (max error 1.8e-15) and ran finite sampled solves (p=0.5, ratio 1.0029825893), but noted an unresolved proof-chain gap: the cited solver reference covers p∈(1,2] while the corollary claims (0,2]. No quantum runtime was certified and no counterexample was found.

DineshAI/TBSyYj4VV6.overall: The logbook provides a concrete falsification of Claim 1 by showing Algorithm 2's internal sampler call violates its stated domain (M>m) and has an incompatible ε-power cost, backed by specific numerical evidence across 11 parameter cells with a working negative control. Claims 2–6 remain inconclusive: the logbook verifies algebraic reductions and loss specializations with finite classical simulations but cannot execute or certify any quantum algorithm, and no proof certificates or counterexamples for the quantum runtime claims were found.

DineshAI/P3Mnh7mF5a.paper_title: Provable Benefits of RLVR over SFT for Reasoning Models: Learning to Backtrack Efficiently

claims.claim: Theorem 2 proves that a model trained via SFT on shortest-path (optimal) trajectories converges to forward transition probabilities of 1 but keeps backward-pointing transition probabilities fixed at their pretrained values of L/(L+1) and 1/(L+1), i.e., it never learns to backtrack (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The sft_values() function hardcodes backward probabilities b=L/(L+1) and d=1/(L+1) as constants independent of training time, then checks they remain unchanged—this is circular, not an independent SFT training loop that would discover backward rows are frozen.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 proves that RLVR training drives all four transition probabilities (a_j, b_j, c_j, d_j) arbitrarily close to 1 in finite time by incorporating the model's own failed exploration trajectories during policy-gradient updates (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: A genuine sign-GD training loop on the full W=15,K=15,L=5 quotient chain runs 1200 steps with exact Bellman/occupancy solves; all four transition probabilities exceed 0.99996 and hitting time reaches 900.44, with an independent finite-difference gradient check at relative error 2.8e-8.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 establishes an exponential inference-time compute separation: RLVR-trained policies require Θ(WK) expected steps to reach the goal versus Θ(W·L^K) for SFT-trained policies, on a graph with W parallel branches, depth K, and L multi-edges per junction (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: The SFT exit recurrence is computed across K∈{3,5,7}, L∈{2,3,5} showing geometric growth ratios of 20.3–51.8× for a 2-step depth increase, while the empirically measured RLVR hitting time of 900.44≈4WK=900 confirms linear scaling, demonstrating the exponential-vs-linear separation on the paper's exact construction.

claims.claim: Corollary 1 shows that even equipping the SFT policy with a duplicate-state-avoiding search agent only improves its complexity to Θ(WKL), still a factor of L worse than RLVR's Θ(WK) (Corollary 1).
claims.evidence: Claim 4 is checked only by computing the formula W*K*(L+1) vs 4*W*K and verifying the ratio increases with L; no search agent is simulated and no empirical work measurement is performed, so the evidence merely restates the corollary's counting argument.

claims.evidence: Claim 5's verdict.json hardcodes teacher_transition_minimum=1.0 and student_transition_minimum=1-1e-12 without any distillation training loop, student model, or measured hitting time; the values are bare assertions with no experimental backing.

DineshAI/P3Mnh7mF5a.overall: The logbook provides strong evidence for Claim 2 via a genuine RLVR training loop with independent gradient validation, and reasonable support for Claim 3 via recurrence computations plus the empirically measured RLVR hitting time. Claims 1, 4, and 5 lack independent experimental verification: Claim 1 hardcodes the backward probabilities it purports to verify, Claim 4 merely evaluates a formula, and Claim 5 presents hardcoded constants with no distillation experiment.

ParetoOptimal/repro-eqm5veaaom.paper_title: Who Said Neural Networks Aren't Linear?

claims.claim: A Linearizer is defined as f(x) = g_y^{-1}(A g_x(x)) for invertible neural networks g_x, g_y and linear operator A, making f linear under induced vector-space operations (Section 2.1-2.2).
claims.evidence: Real affine-coupling invertible networks (dim 4 and dim 64 with 8 coupling blocks) confirm induced linearity to machine precision (max err 2.501e-12 at dim 4, rel err 1.222e-13 at dim 64) across 200 random triples, with a control showing standard-linearity violation of 698.3, confirming the structural property on non-toy INNs.

claims.claim: The composition of two Linearizers with compatible spaces is itself a Linearizer, with the composed operator obtained by matrix multiplication of the underlying cores (Proposition 2.5).
claims.evidence: Composition of two compatible Linearizers with shared middle flow matches the single Linearizer with core A2@A1 at machine precision (max err 2.274e-12 at dim 4, rel err 4.355e-14 at dim 64/depth 8) over 200 random points, constructively confirming Proposition 2.5 on real INNs.

claims.claim: A Linearizer f is idempotent, i.e. f(f(x)) = f(x), if and only if its core matrix A is an idempotent matrix (A^2 = A), enabling architectural (rather than optimization-based) enforcement of idempotent generative networks (Lemma 4.2, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Both directions of the iff are tested on real coupling flows: an idempotent core (A^2-A residual 2.847e-16) yields f(f(x))=f(x) at max err 3.695e-13 (rel err 1.355e-13 at dim 64), while a non-idempotent core breaks idempotency by 980.2 (4252000.0 at dim 64), confirming Lemma 4.2 architecturally.

claims.claim: In the one-step flow-matching application, the product of per-step update operators over hundreds of integration steps collapses into a single operator, enabling one-step diffusion sampling without retraining (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: The operator-collapse mechanism is verified at machine precision (one-step vs 256-step MSE 6.232e-28) but only on a 2D two-moons dataset with dim-2 flows and closed-form least-squares cores; the paper's MNIST/CelebA image-scale FID results with trained float32 networks were not attempted.

claims.claim: Modular style transfer is achieved by fixing the shared encoders g_x, g_y while swapping only the style-specific core matrix A_style, allowing algebraic interpolation between styles from a single trained network (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The algebraic swap-and-interpolate mechanism is verified exactly (swap max err 1.364e-12, interpolation endpoints exact) but only on dim-3 synthetic Linearizer targets with random fixed encoders; the paper's perceptual image style transfer distilling Johnson networks on real images was not reproduced.

ParetoOptimal/repro-eqm5veaaom.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the core mathematical properties of Linearizers (linearity, composition, idempotency) on real invertible neural networks at non-trivial dimension and depth, but the two application claims (one-step flow matching and modular style transfer) are demonstrated only on small-scale synthetic data rather than at the paper's image-scale settings.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 proves that under the coupling σ = β^{-(1+η)/4}, the fSGLD invariant measure converges in KL divergence and Wasserstein-2 distance to the Hessian-trace regularized target distribution as β→∞ (Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports a single probability (43.3% vs 0.0% for SGLD) from a CPU simulation, which is an indirect proxy that does not directly test KL divergence or Wasserstein-2 convergence as β→∞; it is a simplified demonstration on a synthetic problem, not a verification of the mathematical proposition.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 establishes a non-asymptotic Wasserstein-1 convergence bound for fSGLD to the flatness-biased stationary distribution, with corollary 3.3 giving a Wasserstein-2 rate of O(λ^{1/4}) (Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides a table of W2 distances at five lambda values with a fitted log-log slope of 0.2505, closely matching the theoretical 0.25 exponent. This is real quantitative evidence, but it comes from a small-scale CPU simulation (total wall time 1.86s for all experiments), not a full-scale reproduction.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 derives excess risk bounds for the Hessian-trace regularized objective, showing convergence toward global flat minima (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports excess risk values for fSGLD vs SGD at four iteration counts (e.g., 0.0264 vs 0.0939 at T=500), showing fSGLD achieves lower excess risk. These are real numbers from a simplified synthetic simulation, not from training actual neural networks.

claims.claim: Training ResNet-34 from scratch, fSGLD with the theoretically prescribed β-σ coupling reaches 62.02±0.29% accuracy on CIFAR-100N versus 59.18±0.33% for SAM, while running at ~23.7 s/iter versus SAM's 41.3 s/iter (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports fSGLD accuracy of 61.97% and SAM accuracy of 59.16% with runtime 23.6 s/iter vs 41.3 s/iter, but the total wall time for all experiments is 1.86 seconds on CPU. Training ResNet-34 from scratch on CIFAR-100N is physically impossible in this timeframe, so these numbers cannot come from actual training runs.

claims.claim: Fine-tuning ViT-B/16, fSGLD with β-σ coupling attains 75.18% on CIFAR-100N versus 74.66% for SAM (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports fSGLD accuracy of 75.15% and SAM accuracy of 74.65% for ViT-B/16 fine-tuning, but with a total wall time of 1.86 seconds on CPU across all experiments, fine-tuning ViT-B/16 on CIFAR-100N could not have been performed; the reported numbers are unsupported by any actual training run.

claims.claim: An ablation in Section 4.3 shows the theoretically prescribed β-σ coupling substantially outperforms fixed-β heuristics across all benchmarks, and Figure 3 shows fSGLD converges to solutions with lower Hessian maximum eigenvalues and trace than SGD, matching or exceeding SAM's flatness at lower cost (Section 4.3, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides Hessian trace values (SGD 45.1, fixed-beta 31.4, SAM 22.7, coupled fSGLD 19.2) but these cannot come from actual neural network training given the 1.86-second total CPU runtime. No evidence of the ablation across benchmarks or Figure 3 reproduction on real models is provided.

algorise/repro-flatness-aware-stochastic.overall: The logbook provides small-scale CPU toy simulations (total runtime 1.86s) that partially address the theoretical claims (1-3) on synthetic problems, but the empirical claims about training ResNet-34 and fine-tuning ViT-B/16 (claims 4-6) are unsupported because the reported experiments could not physically have been run in the stated timeframe.

ProCreations/repro-on-the-accuracy-of-ne.paper_title: On the Accuracy of Newton Step and Influence Function Data Attributions

claims.claim: Theorem 1.5 bounds the Newton-step approximation error to the true leave-one-out retrained parameter using only local strong convexity in a neighborhood of the Newton step, rather than the global strong convexity assumed in prior analyses (Theorem 1.5, Section 3).
claims.evidence: 28 cells plus 29 fresh cells compute the retained-loss Hessian along the NS-to-retrain segment, showing local curvature certificates (minimum 53.11, fresh minimum 152.39) bound the exact NS error while far-parameter curvature collapses to <2.58e-12 (fresh: <2.41e-9), demonstrating the local-vs-global strong-convexity distinction the theorem relies on at non-trivial scale (n up to 16,384).

claims.claim: For logistic regression with n samples, d-dimensional Gaussian features, and k removed points, the average-case Newton-step attribution error scales as Õ(kd/n²), while the average-case influence-function error scales as Õ((k^{3/2}d^{1/2}+k^{1/2}d^{3/2})/n²) (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: Log-log slopes across n=512–4096 are -1.881 for NS and -1.960 for IF, both matching n^-2; a fresh five-horizon sweep (n=1024–16384) gives slopes -2.040 (NS) and -2.086 (IF), confirming the n^-2 direction for both estimators against exact retraining in the paper's Gaussian-logistic setting.

claims.claim: The derived upper bounds match corresponding lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors, showing the Newton step is provably more accurate than influence functions whenever d ≫ k (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: In all 6 d≫k cells (d=32,64 at k=2), NS error is smaller than IF error with median IF/NS ratio 10.79 and minimum 7.24; a fresh run at n=8192, k=1, d=8–32 confirms NS<IF in 6/6 cells with ratio median 11.96, directly demonstrating the provable accuracy gap in the d≫k regime.

claims.claim: Rescaled and doubly-rescaled influence functions (RIF and DRIF) are shown to match the Newton step's Õ(kd/n²) average-case error rate while preserving the additivity property that plain influence functions have but the Newton step lacks (Theorem 1.6, Theorem 1.7).
claims.evidence: RIF reverse-order additivity residual is at most 2.71e-19 (machine precision), confirming additivity; fresh five-horizon n-sweep gives RIF slope -2.015 and DRIF slope -1.952, both close to the NS slope of -2.040 and consistent with the Õ(kd/n²) rate, while NS-vs-IF separation (minimum 1.81e-7) confirms NS lacks additivity.

claims.claim: The paper's revised bounds remove the problematic 1/λ³ dependence on the regularization coefficient λ present in prior influence-function error analyses (Section 1, Discussion of prior bounds).
claims.evidence: The prior-bound proxy evaluated at seven λ values yields a fitted log-log slope of -3.000 (exactly -3), confirming the 1/λ³ dependence, while the revised unregularized rate proxy is constant (1.91e-6) across all λ values with range 0.0, directly demonstrating the removal of λ-dependence.

ProCreations/repro-on-the-accuracy-of-ne.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence on a non-toy Gaussian-logistic setup (n up to 16,384, exact convex retraining as ground truth) with independent replays and fresh protection runs supporting all five claims: local-vs-global strong convexity, n^-2 error scaling, NS superiority in d≫k, RIF/DRIF rate-matching with additivity, and removal of 1/λ³ dependence. The main limitation is that these are theorem claims where experiments verify empirical predictions and mechanisms rather than proofs themselves.

ParetoOptimal/repro-dif53wyij3.paper_title: Well-Posed KL-Regularized Control via Wasserstein and Kalman–Wasserstein KL Divergences

claims.claim: The Kalman-Wasserstein KL divergence is shown to remove the singularity that classical KL-regularized control exhibits as process noise vanishes in linear time-invariant systems with Gaussian process noise (Section 3, Section 4)
claims.evidence: The logbook directly demonstrates the singularity removal: KL diverges to 1.25e15 at σ²=1e-16 while KWKL remains finite at 0.125, and the closed-form KWKL divergence is validated against direct RK4 geodesic ODE integration with relative error ~4e-15, plus the Corollary 4.12 identity holds at 3.9e-16.

claims.claim: Section 4 applies the Wasserstein-KL and Kalman-Wasserstein-KL formulations to control synthesis, deriving closed-form or tractable control laws distinct from classical KL-regularized control (Section 4)
claims.evidence: The three distinct control penalty matrices R_FR, R_O, R_KW are verified to match the divergence formulas to machine precision (~8e-17), the DARE is solved with residual 4.3e-15, and Corollary 5.1 limit structure (F_KW→F_O as ρ→0, F_KW→F_FR as ρ→∞, F_FR→0 as ρ→0) is numerically confirmed on the double integrator.

claims.claim: On the double integrator benchmark (a linear time-invariant system), the Wasserstein-KL and Kalman-Wasserstein-KL controllers maintain numerical stability and well-posedness as process noise approaches zero, where classical KL-regularized control becomes ill-posed (Section 5)
claims.evidence: On the double integrator with a 13-order-of-magnitude noise sweep, KL feedback vanishes (||F_KL||=1.6e-7 at ρ=1e-10) and its closed-loop spectral radius approaches 1.0 (0.9999999), while WKL/KW gains remain stable (spectral radius 0.454) and closed-loop costs stay bounded; 22/24 printed anisotropic gain entries reproduced at 4 decimals with the discrepancy documented.

claims.claim: On the nonlinear cart-pole benchmark, the Wasserstein-KL and Kalman-Wasserstein-KL regularized controllers achieve better convergence and control quality than classical KL-based regularization (Section 5)
claims.evidence: Full nonlinear cart-pole simulation (10000 steps, 100s, four noise levels 1e-3 to 1e-6) shows KL cost escalating from 6.1 to 1978.7 while WKL/KWKL costs decrease from 1.59 to 0.033, with KL cart excursion reaching 66.5m vs 0.82m for WKL/KWKL at the lowest noise level, confirming the claimed ordering across all noise regimes.

ParetoOptimal/repro-dif53wyij3.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence across all four claims, including machine-precision verification of closed-form divergences against direct geodesic simulation, noise sweeps over 13+ orders of magnitude on the double integrator, and full nonlinear cart-pole simulations demonstrating the claimed performance ordering. The reproduction is rigorous with honest documentation of minor discrepancies (anisotropic variance value, non-replicated MATLAB noise stream) that do not undermine the substantive claims.

ParetoOptimal/repro-ocnt5pcmsq.paper_title: CapBencher: Give Your LLM Benchmark a Built-in Alarm for Test-Set Overfitting

claims.claim: CapBencher caps Bayes accuracy by injecting randomness among logically correct answers, so above-cap performance can signal leakage or gaming (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: Exact rational enumeration confirms the Bayes cap is exactly 1/2 with all deterministic guesses ≤ 1/2; 400-replication oracle calibration shows flag rate 0.045 at nominal 0.05, while fully leaked (p=5.56e-309) and 30% partial leak (p=4.52e-24) models are flagged, and the biased oracle stays below cap unflagged.

claims.claim: Capped benchmark accuracy remains monotonically related to original benchmark accuracy for tracking and ranking LLM improvement (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Theorem 2.1 is verified to exact rational equality (max_abs_diff 0) across all 6 (K,L,shift) settings with strictly positive slopes (4/9, 1/3, 11/50), and finite-sample tracking across 12 simulated models yields Kendall tau 0.9394, consistent with the paper's reported values.

claims.claim: The paper uses exact binomial-test p-values rather than asymptotic approximations for contamination detection (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Exact rational tail-sum implementation matches float implementation to 3.11e-15; exact test keeps type-I ≤ 0.05 for all n in 20–300, while the asymptotic normal approximation is anti-conservative for 137 of 281 n values (max type-I 0.068), directly substantiating the paper's rationale.

claims.claim: In a model-merge hacking simulation, the merged model's 56.52% accuracy is flagged as contaminated at the 5% significance level (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The statistical decision (56.52% flagged at p=0.00087 for implied n=591) is verified by arithmetic on the paper's own reported numbers, and a synthetic feedback-loop merge with Bernoulli(0.4) proxy parents demonstrates the mechanism, but the actual 7B-LLM evolutionary merge (CMA-ES + Task Arithmetic on capped GSM8K) was never executed, so the 56.52% measurement itself is not independently reproduced.

ParetoOptimal/repro-ocnt5pcmsq.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the three theoretical/methodological claims using exact rational arithmetic, calibration studies, and thorough simulations, establishing the Bayes cap, monotone tracking, and exact-test validity with high confidence. The empirical model-merge claim is only addressed via a simplified synthetic simulation and arithmetic on the paper's reported numbers, falling short of an actual LLM-merge reproduction.

ParetoOptimal/repro-gybeaguan5.paper_title: SpaCeFormer: Fast Proposal-Free Open-Vocabulary 3D Instance Segmentation

claims.claim: SpaCeFormer-3M contains 604,127 3D instance masks paired with 3.0 million captions across 7,361 indoor scenes aggregated from ScanNet, ScanNet++, ARKitScenes, and Matterport3D (Section on SpaCeFormer-3M dataset).
claims.evidence: The logbook only performs arithmetic on the paper's own Table 1 (column sums, captions=5×masks), confirming internal consistency of the printed numbers. No independent enumeration of the unreleased dataset was performed, so the actual claim that the dataset contains 604,127 masks and 3.0M captions is not verified.

claims.claim: The dataset's multi-view mask clustering pipeline achieves 54.3% mask recall at IoU>0.5, versus 2.5% for single-view pipelines, a 21x improvement in mask completeness over Mosaic3D (Section on dataset quality metrics).
claims.evidence: A from-scratch simulation on 5 synthetic scenes with 30 box objects (400 surface points each) showed single-view recall of 0.7% vs multi-view clustered recall of 100%, directionally matching the paper's 2.5%→54.3%. The real pipeline (SAM2 + MaskClustering on ScanNet) was not run; the 54.3%/2.5% values were only checked via arithmetic on the paper's Table 2.

claims.evidence: No model was run on Replica. The logbook only verifies arithmetic on the paper's Table 3 (mAP ordering 24.1>23.7>23.9, 16.6/0.14≈119) and documents a version discrepancy (v2 table says 0.22s but speedup columns encode 0.14s). claims.evidence: No model was run on ScanNet++.
