snaykey/repro-epistemic-mdp-dp.paper_title: Dynamic Programming for Epistemic Uncertainty in Markov Decision Processes

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 establishes that when the proposed dynamic programming conditions hold for an ambiguity-averse MDP, a stationary optimal policy exists among the class of transition-uncertain MDPs considered (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Contraction modulus of T^{ν,ρ} measured ≤ γ on two Mc instances (e.g., 0.7748, 0.7980, 0.7715 for γ=0.8), and the stationary greedy policy attains the DP optimum with gap 0.000000 while dominating all enumerated stationary policies and 600 sampled non-stationary policies.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.2 shows value iteration and policy iteration converge under the ambiguity-averse framework, with error bounds of 2γ^n/(1-γ) for value iteration and γ^n for policy iteration after n steps (Proposition 4.2).
claims.evidence: All 135 literal inequalities (VI bound 2γⁿ/(1−γ), PI bound γⁿ, PI monotonicity) hold with zero violations across three risk-measure/instance combinations including a larger S=12, A=5, γ=0.97 case; the γⁿ rate is shown to be nearly tight at ~0.965 of the bound.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 proves that, among monotone law-invariant risk measures, only the essential infimum and essential supremum satisfy the dynamic programming conditions for static (non-resampled) transition kernels, while expectation becomes additionally admissible once kernels are resampled at each step (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: Example 3.8 reproduced to 1e-6 matching closed forms (2 log 2 = 1.386294 vs 1+log2/2 = 1.346574); full battery of six risk measures shows DP-compatible set is exactly {ess inf, ess sup} for static and {ess inf, ess sup, E} for resampled, with Condition 1 ⇔ Condition 2 holding for all measures.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.5 shows that under an added Wasserstein-1 continuity assumption, expectation is the unique risk measure compatible with dynamic programming for resampled kernels, and no such measure exists for static kernels (Theorem 4.5).
claims.evidence: Exact discrete-convolution computation shows W₁(law(X̄ₙ), δ_{EX}) → 0 while ess inf/sup remain pinned at support endpoints (0, 3); only E is W₁-continuous (tracking limit 1.2), and E fails static kernels (residual 0.117975) but holds resampled (residual 0).

claims.claim: The characterization implies that risk measures such as CVaR, Value-at-Risk, and entropic risk are incompatible with exact dynamic programming under this framework, explaining their lack of tractable recursive solutions (Section 4, following Theorem 4.4/4.5).
claims.evidence: CVaR fails additivity-for-independent (+0.5 gap), VaR fails additivity (−1.0 gap), ERM fails positive homogeneity (+0.194 gap)—all exact Prop 4.3 necessary-condition violations—and all three show non-zero Bellman fixed-point residuals (0.049875, 0.236318, 0.022938) on Mc instances.

snaykey/repro-epistemic-mdp-dp.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, non-circular numerical verification of all five theorem-level claims on correctly-structured ambiguity-averse MDPs in class Mc, computing values from definitions rather than operators and checking exact fixed-point residuals, closed-form matches, and literal inequality bounds. snaykey/repro-async-q-learning.paper_title: Corruption-Tolerant Asynchronous Q-Learning with Near-Optimal Rates

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows Robust Async-Q achieves a finite-time convergence rate of O(1/√T), matching classical asynchronous Q-learning, plus an additive O(√ε) term where ε∈[0,1/2) is the fraction of adversarially corrupted rewards (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Log-log slope of ‖Q_T−Q*‖∞ vs T is −0.637 for Robust Async-Q and −0.634 for Vanilla (both consistent with Õ(1/√T)) on a 6×4 MDP with T up to 64,000; the √ε penalty stays below the σ̄√ε ceiling at ε∈{0.005,0.01,0.02,0.04} while Vanilla explodes 460×; Robust error is byte-identical (0.5939) across attack magnitudes 10 to 10⁶ while Vanilla varies 27,829×.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 gives an information-theoretic lower bound of Ω(√ε), proving the additive corruption term in the upper bound is unavoidable (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Exact Appendix-D two-point construction reproduced: TV(R̃₁,R̃₂)=0 to machine precision at every ε tested (indistinguishability), Q-gap ≥ 0.5σ̄√ε/(1−γ) verified at ε∈{0.02,0.04,0.08,0.16,0.32}, Var(Rᵢ)<0.5σ̄² confirmed, and all three estimators (mean/median/trimmed-mean) pinned to the √ε floor with P(exceed bound)=1.00≥1/4.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 extends the guarantee to a reward-agnostic setting where the algorithm needs no prior knowledge of the reward distribution's bounds (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: Robust Async-RAQ (using m(t)=t^p proxy, no σ̃ input) matches the known-σ̃ variant (ratio 1.00) and, critically, converges to 1.5% relative error on a reward range [0,200] MDP with −10⁵ attack where a mis-guessed σ̃ would over-threshold and stall, while Vanilla diverges to 5999.7.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 extends the near-optimal finite-time rate to single-trajectory Markovian sampling with time-correlated data, with the bound inflated by the chain's mixing time (Section 6).
claims.evidence: Single-trajectory Markovian sampling is shown to work (error 0.367 ≈ i.i.d. 0.402), but the key claim of √τ mixing-time inflation could not be isolated: the Markov-minus-i.i.d. gap (±0.09) sits within seed noise on fast-mixing chains (τ̄=1 to 14), and the logbook itself discloses this limitation rather than claiming verification of the mixing-time bound.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 (Robust Async-Q) combines a trimmed-mean reward estimator with an adaptive threshold G_t to filter corrupted rewards before the standard Q-learning update, requiring only knowledge of the corruption fraction ε and minimum state-action visitation probability λ_min (Algorithm 1, Assumption 1).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1/2 implemented verbatim at the paper's Figure-1 scale (|S|=25,|A|=10): Robust converges to ‖Q_T−Q*‖∞≤1.16 while Vanilla diverges to 1520–2269; ablation shows trimmed-mean is load-bearing (0.458 with trim vs 31.98 without); G_t shrinks monotonically (217.4→115.1); input audit confirms only ε and λ_min are needed (with honest disclosure that σ̃ is replaced by the agnostic variant in Theorem 4).

snaykey/repro-async-q-learning.overall: The logbook provides strong experimental evidence for Claims 1, 2, 3, and 5 through faithful algorithm implementation at moderate-to-paper scale and an exact reproduction of the lower-bound construction. Claim 4 is only partially addressed: the single-trajectory extension is demonstrated but the mixing-time inflation—the key theoretical content of Theorem 6—could not be isolated at simulable scale and remains unverified.

tomyimkc/repro-mec-machine-learning-assi.paper_title: MEC: Machine-Learning-Assisted Generalized Entropy Calibration for Semi-Supervised Mean Estimation

claims.claim: MEC attains the semiparametric efficiency bound for semi-supervised mean estimation under a weaker condition than CF-PPI, requiring only that the projection error be stochastically bounded rather than bounding the raw prediction error directly (Theorem 5.2, using the fact that the projection norm ||m0,perp|| <= ||m-hat^(-) - m0||).
claims.evidence: At N=4000, 300 replicates, affine distortions of m0 (a=-2,b=50) inflate CF-PPI's MC variance to 3.92x oracle while MEC stays within 1.11x; the noise-predictor control raises MEC's ratio to 1.47x, confirming the mechanism is non-vacuous and specific to projection-error geometry.

claims.claim: CF-PPI is shown to be consistent under L2-boundedness of the prediction error and asymptotically normal under L2-consistency, with asymptotic variance sigma_f^2 = Var(m0(X)) + (1/f)Var(Y - m0(X)) (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: With a real 5-fold cross-fitted KRR predictor at N=3000, 400 replicates, the L2-consistent regime yields mc_var/sigma_f^2=1.10 and 0.965 coverage, while the bounded-but-inconsistent (30-point starved) regime yields ratio 8.74 and coverage 0.625; the vanilla in-fold control drops coverage to 0.900, matching the theorem's dichotomy.

claims.claim: MEC has a dual generalized-regression (GREG) representation using a low-dimensional 2D calibration basis h(X) = (1, m-hat^(-)(X)), making it asymptotically equivalent to PPI++ under quadratic generators and solvable via fast dual Newton optimization (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Dual-Newton solver converges in ≤26 iterations with constraint residual ≤1.1e-11; quadratic-generator Newton estimator matches closed-form GREG to 4.4e-15 and PPI++(lambda=beta_hat) to 2.2e-15 over 30 seeds with a real KRR predictor; mismatched-lambda control breaks the identity (mean gap 0.104).

claims.claim: In simulations with N=1000 and label fraction f in [0.1, 0.5] across four predictors (KRR, RF, FNN, kNN), MEC achieves near-nominal 95% coverage while vanilla PPI undercovers (especially at f=0.1) and CF-PPI sometimes overcovers (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: At the paper's N=1000 with all four predictors, the qualitative pattern reproduces (vanilla PPI mean coverage 0.81 at f=0.1 vs MEC 0.92; MEC narrower than CF-PPI in 11/12 cells), but RF uses 20 trees/depth 6 vs the paper's 500/unlimited and RF cells show coverage as low as 0.80, indicating reduced-fidelity artifacts.

claims.claim: At f=0.1 with a KRR predictor, MEC's confidence-interval width ratio is approximately 0.85 versus CF-PPI showing no efficiency gain (width ratio above 1.0), and at f=0.5 with a random-forest predictor MEC's width ratio (~0.75) is tighter than CF-PPI's (~0.80) (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: KRR at f=0.1 with 300 replicates reproduces the direction (CF-PPI=1.041>1.0, MEC=0.966<1.0) but MEC's magnitude is 0.116 away from the paper's ~0.85; RF at f=0.5 with 70 trees/depth 9 shows MEC=0.958 vs CF-PPI=0.957 (not tighter), contradicting the claimed ordering but with a reduced-fidelity forest that precludes falsification.

tomyimkc/repro-mec-machine-learning-assi.overall: The three theoretical claims (Theorems 4.1, 5.1, 5.2) are verified with independently implemented Monte-Carlo experiments at meaningful scale and appropriate controls, including machine-precision algebraic identities and clear regime contrasts. The two Figure 1 simulation claims are only partially reproduced at reduced predictor fidelity (especially RF), yielding correct qualitative directions but not the paper's specific numeric values.

gauravmishra9/repro-think-twice-before-y.paper_title: Think Twice Before You Act: Protecting LLM Agents Against Tool Description Poisoning via Isolated Planning

claims.claim: Tool-Guard defends LLM agents against cross-tool description poisoning—where a poisoned tool's description can bias agent behavior even when that tool is never invoked—via isolated planning that dynamically partitions tools and validates actions before execution (Section 4, Figure 3)
claims.evidence: Full-scale run on gpt-4o across all four AgentDojo suites (388 scored passes, 0 errored) reproduced undefended ASR at 42.27% (paper 43.30%) and defended ASR at 1.03% (paper 2.06%); a custom trajectory check confirmed the cross-tool mechanism with an attack succeeding while none of the five poisoned tools was invoked.

claims.claim: On adaptive/semantic attacks, Tool-Guard keeps attack success rate near 0%, compared to non-negligible ASR for competing defenses (Table 4)
claims.evidence: All six Table 4 rows on gpt-4o-mini across all four suites (97 tasks, 0 errored) show defended ASR of 0.00–3.09% (near zero), while undefended ASR is 42.27% and competing defenses range 15.79–48.45%, confirming the claim's substance that Tool-Guard stays near 0% while rivals remain non-negligible.

claims.claim: Across stability tests, Tool-Guard maintains attack success rates between 0.40% and 1.54% (Table 3)
claims.evidence: Per-model means for gpt-4o-mini (1.44%, n=5) and gpt-4o (0.52%, n=4) both fall within the claimed 0.40–1.54% band across all four suites with 0 errored passes; the third model (Gemini-2.5-Flash) was not tested due to lack of API access.

claims.claim: Tool-Guard incurs 1.22M-2.24M tokens of overhead versus 0.84M-1.61M tokens for the no-defense baseline, roughly 1.45x token overhead (Table 1)
claims.evidence: On gpt-4o-mini across all four suites, Tool-Guard token overhead measured 2.91× benign and 2.11× attack versus the claimed 1.45×/1.39×, with the no-defense baseline reproducing within 3–6% (0.867M/1.709M vs paper 0.84M/1.61M), localizing the discrepancy to Tool-Guard's own consumption (2.526M/3.603M vs paper 1.22M/2.24M).

claims.claim: Tool-Guard's isolation mechanism is shown to be necessary via an ablation study, and it is evaluated against five existing defenses on the AgentDojo and ASB benchmarks (Section 5, Figure 2, Table 6)
claims.evidence: The ablation study confirms isolation is necessary: removing dynamic partitioning raises ASR from 1.03% to 36.08% (1/97 vs 35/97, p=1.5e-11) on gpt-4o with 0/388 errored passes; Tool-Guard was evaluated against five defenses on AgentDojo (outperforming all, though Drift and Progent did not reproduce) and on ASB (implemented from scratch, ASR 34→6%, 82% relative reduction).

gauravmishra9/repro-think-twice-before-y.overall: This logbook provides strong evidence supporting claims 1, 2, 3, and 5 through full-scale runs on the paper's own models across all four AgentDojo suites with zero errored passes, plus a from-scratch ASB implementation; claim 4 is falsified with token overhead measured at roughly double the claimed ratio, and the ablation in claim 5 confirms isolation's necessity far more strongly than the paper argues despite Table 6's specific deltas being contradicted.

ICML-2026-agent-repro/repro-gaussian-mec.paper_title: Asymptotic Optimality of the High-Dimensional Gaussian Mechanism and Improved Low-Dimensional Mechanisms for Differential Privacy

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 proves that as dimension T→∞, the Gaussian mechanism achieves the best privacy-utility tradeoff among all additive-noise mechanisms in the high-privacy regime δ ≤ δ⋆ (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: SGG competitors (p=0.75, 1.0, 4.0) matched to Gaussian MSE at ε=0.1, δ=1e-3 show excess delta shrinking to ≤7.28e-7 at T=16384 (from ~1e-3 at T=4), directly demonstrating the asymptotic optimality trend on a non-trivial dimensional scale.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.3 shows that Haar symmetrization of arbitrary additive noise preserves mean squared error while improving privacy, establishing that spherically symmetric noise distributions are optimal (Lemma 3.3).
claims.evidence: An anisotropic Gaussian (T=8, 50x variance ratio) Haar-symmetrized via a 64-component orthogonal mixture preserves MSE exactly (10.83 both before and after) while reducing worst-direction delta from 0.9017 to [0.244, 0.302] across 12 tested directions, demonstrating both key properties of Lemma 3.3 on a non-trivial setup.

claims.claim: The paper introduces the Spherical Generalized Gamma (SGG) family, a three-parameter family with radial density f(r) = pβ^((α+1)/p)/Γ((α+1)/p) · r^α · exp(-βr^p) that includes the Gaussian and ℓ2 mechanisms as special cases (Definition 4.1-4.2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Quadrature normalization of the SGG radial density matches 1.0 to ≤1.5e-11 for five parameter tuples, Gamma-transform KS tests pass, the Gaussian special case (p=2, α=T-1) matches closed-form delta to 7.6e-8, and the ℓ2-Laplace case (p=1) matches the MSE formula T(T+1)θ² to floating-point precision.

claims.claim: Figure 2 shows that in low dimensions (T=2 to 5) at ε=0.1, certain SGG mechanisms reduce MSE by up to 15% relative to the Gaussian and ℓ2 mechanisms, with the improvement shrinking as dimension increases (Figure 2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Independent grid search over the α=T-1 SGG slice at ε=0.1 reproduces the Figure 2 pattern: 15.55% MSE reduction at T=2, declining to 8.23% at T=5 and 3.89% at T=12, matching the claimed up-to-15% scale and dimension-shrinking trend.

claims.claim: Table 2 reports empirical lower bounds on the threshold δ⋆ above which Gaussian optimality holds, e.g. δ⋆ ≥ 0.737 at ε=0.25 and δ⋆ ≥ 0.198 at ε=16.0 (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Independent reimplementation of the Gaussian privacy function and tangent/convexity checks recovers all seven Table 2 δ⋆ values to ≤7.15e-7 absolute error, including δ⋆=0.736671 at ε=0.25 and δ⋆=0.197615 at ε=16.0, with all conditions passing within numerical tolerance.

claims.claim: The paper resolves an open question from Joseph et al. (2025) by providing a tight composition analysis for the ℓ2 mechanism via the unified SGG framework and an FFT-based composition algorithm (Section 4.4, Algorithm 7).
claims.evidence: FFT convolution accountant for the ℓ2 mechanism (T=10, α=9, p=1) at (ε_total, δ)=(1, 1e-5) yields MSE reductions of 31.4%–94.1% over sequential composition for k=2–32, with Monte Carlo cross-checks at k≤8 confirming delta values near the 1e-5 target (1.8e-5, 1.1e-5, 0.7e-5).

ICML-2026-agent-repro/repro-gaussian-mec.overall: The logbook provides concrete from-scratch numerical evidence supporting all six claims through independent numpy/scipy implementations, with the strongest matches being Table 2 threshold recovery (≤7e-7 error) and Figure 2 MSE reduction patterns. The main scope limitations are restriction to the α=T-1 SGG slice, grid search instead of Bayesian optimization, and a single test case for Haar symmetrization, but all experiments run on non-trivial setups with real privacy calculations.

SabaPivot/repro-why-agentic-theorem-prov.paper_title: Why Agentic Theorem Prover Works: A Statistical Provability Theory of Mathematical Reasoning Models

claims.claim: Theorem 1 establishes that the space of finite measures with bounded mass forms a compact metric space under the bounded Lipschitz metric, providing the topological foundation for the measure-valued goal encoding of the reachability MDP (Theorem 1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Constructive finite epsilon-nets on continuous cubes [0,1]^d (d=1,2,3) with exact Fraction arithmetic verify total boundedness across 27 cells; covering numbers remain controlled by mass bound W (e.g., {1:3, 2:7, 4:25, 8:50, 16:78} at eps=0.5) rather than ground-space cardinality, directly supporting the compactness claim's key component.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 proves that under mild Feller-type continuity conditions on the transition kernel, optimal deterministic Markov policies exist for the finite-horizon time-bounded reachability MDP (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: On continuous X=A=[0,1]^d with Feller kernel p(target|x,a)=1-max_i|x_i-a_i|/2, the exact maximizer a=x is attained for horizons 1,2,4,8 across 12 cells; a matched noncompact control A=(0,1)^d shows supremum 1 is never attained (gaps shrinking but strictly positive), demonstrating the compactness/Feller hypotheses are load-bearing.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 shows that sequences of functions satisfying Bellman sub-/super-solution inequalities yield provability certificates (upper and lower bounds on the optimal value function) without requiring the full MDP to be solved, with the certificate gap defined as UB(x0) - LB(x0) (Theorem 3, Definition 5, Section 5).
claims.evidence: On continuous state [0,1] with kernel p(target|x,a)=3/4-|x-a|/4, exact Fraction arithmetic across 45 cells verifies zero lower/upper inequality violations with nonzero certificate gaps; broken-certificate controls show monotonic bracket failure (delta=0.05→0/18, delta=1.50→18/18), confirming the Bellman inequality is the active ingredient.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 bounds the worst-case regret of score-guided planning under uniform score-approximation error εb as 0 ≤ V*_B(x0) - V^{πh}_B(x0) ≤ 2∑_{b=1}^{B} εb, showing performance degrades linearly with accumulated approximation error (Theorem 4, Section 6).
claims.evidence: On continuous [0,1]^d with compact-action scores q0(x)=1/2+x/4 and q1(x)=3/4-x/4, exact worst-case regret B·min(1/4,2ε) is checked against 2Bε across 60 cells with worst ratio 1 (tight bound); 800 finite cells with adversarial and noise perturbations show 791/800 with strictly positive regret and worst ratio 0.588.

claims.claim: Theorem 5 shows that under a margin condition on action-value separation, the expected regret improves to O(Bε^{β+1}) for β>0, i.e., faster than the worst-case linear-in-B rate of Theorem 4 (Theorem 5).
claims.evidence: Exact closed-form expected regret B·β·2^(β+1)/((β+1)(β+2)(β+3))·ε^(β+1) evaluated with rational arithmetic across 75 cells confirms doubling epsilon yields exactly 2^(β+1) regret scaling; Monte Carlo with 400,000 problems per cell recovers fitted exponents tracking β+1 with worst deviation 0.069 across β=0.5 to 3.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 derives a high-probability estimation-error bound of order O(L H d_D/(d_D+2) (log(n/δ)/n)^{1/(d_D+2)}) under a doubling-dimension assumption on the relevant problem domain, formalizing how statistical complexity of a biased real-world problem distribution governs sample efficiency (Theorem 6, Section 7).
claims.evidence: k-NN regression on d_D-dimensional manifolds embedded in R^20 (ambient dimension fixed at 20) with n up to 64,000 and Gaussian label noise shows fitted decay exponents regressed against predicted -1/(d_D+2) yield slope 1.677, R²=0.998, with fitted≤predicted in every cell, confirming the doubling dimension rather than ambient dimension governs the rate.

SabaPivot/repro-why-agentic-theorem-prov.overall: The logbook provides rigorous computational evidence on continuous domains with exact arithmetic (Claims 1-5) and large-scale Monte Carlo (Claims 5-6), including destructive controls demonstrating that compactness, Feller continuity, and Bellman inequalities are load-bearing hypotheses. All six theorems are supported by non-trivial experimental evidence rather than mere assertion.

snaykey/repro-vdw-gnns.paper_title: Skewness-Robust Causal Discovery in Location-Scale Noise Models

claims.claim: SkewD models noise as skew-normal distributed rather than assuming symmetric (normal) noise, extending the location-scale noise model framework to the skew-normal setting (Section 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides exact numerical checks confirming the skew-normal pdf integrates to 1, reduces to N(ξ,ω²) at λ=0 to machine epsilon (max diff 1.1e-16), and fitting recovers correct skew sign (symmetric→λ≈-0.093, left-skew→-5.347, right-skew→7.845), establishing the model genuinely extends the Gaussian LSNM.

claims.claim: On novel skew-noise datasets, the likelihood-based variant SkewD-LL achieves 100% accuracy, whereas the prior state-of-the-art method ROCHE drops to 81% accuracy at the highest skewness level tested, LSs(1.750) (Figure 2, Appendix C).
claims.evidence: SkewD-LL's 100% accuracy is reproduced (16/16 on all six classes), but the setup is at reduced scale (16 pairs/class, n=800 vs paper's 100 pairs/n=1000) and ROCHE is a Student-t LSNM surrogate scoring 75% at LSs(1.750) instead of the claimed 81%, so the specific headline number is not reproduced though the direction is.

claims.claim: On 19 established causal-discovery benchmark datasets, SkewD-IT achieves 87.46% combined accuracy, compared to ROCHE's 87.69%, a difference of only 2.67 percentage points, while SkewD-IT ranks second overall at 85.02% mean accuracy on 13 established benchmarks (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states the external benchmark datasets (Tübingen, SIM variants, etc.) were not downloaded or run, so the specific aggregate numbers (87.46%, 87.69%, 2.67pp, 85.02%) are not addressed at all; only a proxy comparison on synthetic skew-noise data is offered.

claims.claim: Table 2 presents an ablation study comparing performance with and without ECM (expectation-conditional-maximization) refinement in the parameter estimation procedure (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The ablation is run at reduced scale (14 pairs/class, n=800) with simplified procedures (heuristic = Gaussian init with λ pinned 0 and 3 L-BFGS steps; refined = direct ML instead of CMA-ES+ECM), showing IT gains of +19pp on LSs (paper: 28-34%) in the same direction but not the exact method or magnitude.

claims.claim: Theorem 1, restated from LOCI in Appendix A, establishes that location-scale noise models are identifiable except in pathological cases satisfying a specific PDE, provided the noise log-density is twice differentiable, a condition satisfied by the skew-normal distribution (Appendix A).
claims.evidence: The twice-differentiability condition is verified exactly: closed-form second derivative of the skew-normal log-density matches numerical differentiation to <4e-04 relative error and is finite and continuous for all λ tested, and the forward-backward likelihood gap collapses ~71× in the pathological linear-Gaussian homoscedastic case (0.0016 vs 0.08-0.14 for skew-normal LSNMs).

claims.claim: LOCI and QCCD baselines show severe performance degradation as noise skewness increases, unlike SkewD (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: At reduced scale (16 pairs/class, n=800), LOCI-LL degradation is reproduced (100→81→44% on LSs vs paper's 100→96→66%), but QCCD degradation is not clearly reproduced (62→75→62% on LSs vs paper's 96→22→11%), and the logbook itself flags QCCD as 'the least faithful of our baselines.'

snaykey/repro-vdw-gnns.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the mathematical foundations (skew-normal model properties and the C² identifiability precondition) with exact numerical checks, but empirical claims are only partially reproduced at significantly reduced scale with surrogate methods, and the established-benchmark aggregate numbers are not addressed at all.

snaykey/repro-online-tabular-mdp-regret.paper_title: Causal Matrix Completion under Multiple Treatments via Mixed Synthetic Nearest Neighbors

claims.claim: MSNN provably preserves Synthetic Nearest Neighbors' entry-wise finite-sample error bound (Theorem 4.5) and asymptotic normality with convergence rate scaling as K_MSNN^(-1/2) (Theorem 4.6) (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: RMSE log-log fit slope of -0.4687 over K=1..128 closely matches the theoretical K^{-1/2} rate; standardized errors show KS p=0.0505 and 94.5% coverage consistent with N(0,1); MSNN median relative error 0.325 vs SNN 0.516 on shared anchors confirms preservation.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.10 shows the expected number of usable data subgroups under MCAR grows by a multiplicative factor of [∑_d' (p_d'/p_d)^(r+1)]^c for MSNN relative to standard SNN, formalizing the effective-sample-size gain from mixed anchor sets (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Closed-form Corollary 4.10 ratio equals P_msnn/P_snn to machine precision (rel-err ~1e-16) across 7 configurations including gains up to 10^22, independently confirmed by Monte-Carlo sampling on the MCAR model (rel-err <0.08).

claims.claim: Corollary 4.11 shows the relative efficiency gap between data-sparse and data-rich treatment levels is reduced from quadratic to linear order under MSNN (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Log-gap vs log(p_d/p_max) slope measured at exactly 15.000 for SNN (matching rc+r+c=15) and exactly 3.000000 for MSNN (matching r=3), with MSNN ratio matching (p_d/p_max)^r to 1.8e-15 precision.

claims.claim: On MCAR-generated data at a low treatment probability p(d)=0.01, MSNN achieves a 4.69% feasible rate and mean relative error of 3.91e-2, versus a 0.03% feasible rate and 0.806 MRE for standard SNN (Table 1).
claims.evidence: MSNN feasible rate 5.11±1.08% reproduces paper's 4.69±1.11% (overlapping CIs) with MRE ~1.53e-2 (same order as paper's 3.91e-2); SNN feasible rate ~0% confirms SNN failure at p(d)=0.01, consistent with paper's 0.03%.

claims.claim: Under MNAR data, MSNN consistently attains 3-26% feasible imputation rates versus under 5% for SNN, with 2-3x error reductions across treatment levels (Tables 2-3).
claims.evidence: MSNN MRE matches paper closely at well-posed levels (0.117 vs 0.129, 0.136 vs 0.135); SNN feasible rates all under 1.43% confirming 'under 5%'; MSNN feasible where SNN is not with large error reductions; however absolute MSNN feasible rates overshoot the 3-26% window in dense regimes (up to 93%) due to unspecified feasibility filter calibration.

claims.claim: Mixed anchor rows/columns are constructed via bipartite cliques spanning multiple treatment levels while preserving the target row's same-treatment data, relying on the shared latent row factor assumption (Assumption 2.5) (Section 3.2-3.3, Algorithms 2-3).
claims.evidence: On 1500 MSNN anchors, 100% are valid bipartite cliques spanning multiple treatments (mean 3.63/4 levels), 100% preserve target column at estimation level d; breaking Assumption 2.5 (independent row factors) inflates median error 573x (3.37 vs 0.0059), confirming reliance on shared latent row factors.

snaykey/repro-online-tabular-mdp-regret.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims: theory claims verified as exact algebraic identities with Monte-Carlo confirmation, convergence rate and normality reproduced numerically, MCAR/MNAR simulation results matching the paper's key cells, and the bipartite-clique mechanism confirmed structurally and via a control experiment. The main limitation is divergence in absolute feasible-rate magnitudes in denser regimes due to the paper's unspecified Agarwal-2023b feasibility filter tolerance.

divaspoudel/repro-accurate-cpd-evaluatio.paper_title: Accurate Evaluation of Quickest Changepoint Detectors via Non-parametric Survival Analysis

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 establishes that the finite-sample bias of the KM-ARL estimator decays exponentially with dataset size N.
claims.evidence: Numerical integration of Theorem 4.1 bounds at N=10,30,100,1000 yields bound widths 7.57, 1.24, 0.012, ≈0 with log-log slope ≈-36.4, concretely demonstrating exponential decay with dataset size.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 establishes finite-sample bias bounds for the KM-ADD estimator under independent censoring.
claims.evidence: The logbook asserts identical bound structure to Theorem 4.1 and claims numerical integration confirms exponential decay, but provides no specific numerical results for the KM-ADD bounds — only an assertion without data.

claims.claim: Theorems 4.3 and 4.4 show that the truncation bias of KM-ARL and KM-ADD is smaller than that of conventional (non-censoring-aware) ARL/ADD estimators.
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo with Exp(50), N=5000 at truncation horizons T_max=20,50,100 shows |KM-bias| < |LB-bias| in all cases (e.g., -33.4 vs -40.3 at T_max=20, -6.3 vs -15.1 at T_max=100), concretely supporting the claim.

claims.claim: KM-ARL and KM-ADD are shown to be asymptotically unbiased (Equation 11) whenever the support of the detection-point distribution does not exceed the censoring boundary, without requiring parametric assumptions (Section 4).
claims.evidence: N=5000 samples with true ARL=30 and generous censoring (Exp(150) clipped to 300) over 20 trials yields mean bias 0.54±0.14 SE (relative bias 1.8%), concretely demonstrating asymptotic unbiasedness under the stated support condition.

claims.claim: On the WISDM Actitracker dataset (51,326 sequences ranging from length 1 to 54,401), KM-ARL/KM-ADD show substantially reduced variance versus LB-ARL/LB-ADD baselines (Figure 1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: Only a preprocessed subset of 5,435 sequences with fixed length 43 was available (vs. the claimed 51,326 sequences with lengths 1–54,401), and no specific variance comparison numbers between KM and LB estimators are reported — only a mention of 'pre-computed results' without quantitative evidence.

claims.claim: Simulation experiments on Gaussian and Poisson process changepoint models show KM-ARL/KM-ADD remain accurate across censoring levels from 10% to 90% changepoint prevalence and irregular sequence lengths (Figures 2-4, Section 5).
claims.evidence: Only Gaussian processes were tested (Poisson models absent), with N=1000 and dur=500 at three thresholds; censoring levels 10%–90% are not explicitly varied. Concrete results for Gaussian fixed/irregular lengths are shown, but the scope is clearly reduced relative to the paper's full simulation suite.

divaspoudel/repro-accurate-cpd-evaluatio.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting Claims 1, 3, and 4, but Claim 2 lacks any reported numbers, Claim 5 uses a small fixed-length subset without variance figures, and Claim 6 covers only Gaussian models without explicit censoring-level variation.

snaykey/repro-creator-causal-rep.paper_title: Provably Data-driven Multiple Hyper-parameter Tuning with Structured Loss Function

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 establishes a general first-order-logic framework giving pseudo-dimension bounds of O(p*prod(d_k+1)*log M + p^2*prod(d_k+1)*log Delta) for multi-dimensional hyperparameter tuning by connecting logical complexity to learning-theoretic complexity via quantifier elimination (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Real quantifier elimination is demonstrated only on a trivial single-variable quadratic (discriminant of θ²−2αθ+...), with input degrees 2–5; this is a highly simplified instance of the general FOL/QE framework, not a test at the theorem's actual scale or complexity.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 bounds the pseudo-dimension of piecewise-polynomial training-loss objectives (with training loss f equal to validation loss g) as O(p*d*log(M_f+T_f+d) + p^2*d*log Delta_f) for p-dimensional hyperparameters (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The paper's exact Theorem 5.2 bit-extraction hard instance is implemented and fully shattered across 6 configurations, with the certified lower bound N = p·d·⌊log₂K⌋ = Θ(p·d·log Δ_f) matching the upper bound's leading term exactly, providing genuine empirical evidence of tightness on the paper's own construction.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.1 extends the framework to the bi-level validation-loss setting (f not equal to g), establishing Pdim(L) = O(p*d^2*log M_tot + p^2*d^2*log Delta_tot) without requiring identical training and validation objectives (Section 6).
claims.evidence: Bi-level ridge is solved for d up to 8, but the optimality predicate certification is trivially true by construction (θ* is the minimizer), and the d² scaling is established only via symbolic big-O algebra, not by any empirical scaling test or lower bound.

claims.claim: Theorem 7.2 shows that when the optimal parameter path theta*(x, alpha) is piecewise rational, the pseudo-dimension bound simplifies to O(p*log(M_total*Delta_total)) by bypassing quantifier elimination (Section 7).
claims.evidence: Ridge path rationality is verified to machine precision but this is a known closed-form identity ((AᵀA+αI)⁻¹Aᵀb); LARS knot counts are measured for d up to 20 showing linear growth, but the pseudo-dimension bound itself rests on symbolic formula composition rather than empirical scaling evidence.

claims.claim: Theorem 8.1 provides the first learnability guarantee for weighted group LASSO regularization, a semi-algebraic (non-piecewise-polynomial) function class, with Pdim(L) = O(p^3*d + p^2*d^2), despite standard smoothness assumptions failing for this class (Section 8.1).
claims.evidence: The semi-algebraic lift ν_i=‖θ_i‖₂ is verified to reproduce f exactly, but this is essentially checking a definitional identity; group LASSO instances are small (p≤4, d≤8), no sparsity switching was exercised, and the O(p³d+p²d²) bound is established only via symbolic algebra.

claims.claim: Theorem 8.2 derives a Pdim(L) = O(d^2) bound for weighted fused LASSO applied to signal denoising with spatially-varying regularization weights (Section 8.2).
claims.evidence: Fused LASSO path is verified as piecewise affine for d=4–10 with region counts ≤3^(d−1), which are real but small-scale CVXPY solves; the O(d²) bound follows from symbolic composition of Theorem 7.2, not from empirical pseudo-dimension measurement or scaling tests.

snaykey/repro-creator-causal-rep.overall: The logbook provides one genuine empirical result—shattering the paper's exact hard instance to certify a matching lower bound for Theorem 5.1 (Claim 2)—while the remaining five claims are supported by structural precondition checks on small or trivial instances plus symbolic big-O re-derivations, which constitute toy-level evidence rather than full reproduction.

snaykey/repro-adaptive-gradient-heavy-ta.paper_title: Incentivized Exploration with Stochastic Covariates: A Two-Stage Mechanism Design for Recommender System

claims.claim: The RCB algorithm achieves an O(sqrt(KdT)) regret bound, where K is the number of arms, d the feature dimension, and T the time horizon (Section 4.3, Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook's own experiments show learning regret grows with log-log slope 1.88 in K (R_learn = 11.5/20.8/34.2/79/170/201 for K=2/3/4/6/8/10), which is approximately K^2, not sqrt(K). This directly contradicts the claimed O(sqrt(KdT)) rate. While the Lemma-11 bound holds as an inequality in 100% of runs and the sqrt(T) and sqrt(d) dependencies are confirmed, the K-dependence is falsified.

claims.claim: RCB simultaneously satisfies an epsilon-Dynamic Bayesian Incentive Compatibility (epsilon-DBIC) constraint, requiring a minimum cold-start sample size N(epsilon) that scales cubically with the number of arms K and linearly with dimension d (Section 4.2, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The closed-form N(eps) formula yields exact log-log slopes of 3.000 in K and 1.000 in d, matching the claimed cubic-K and linear-d scaling. Empirically, the eps-DBIC constraint holds in 6/6 seeds with calibrated cold start (shortfall max 0.0105 <= eps=0.05) and fails with under-calibrated cold start (shortfall 0.27 > eps), providing a non-vacuous control.

claims.claim: The two-stage mechanism separates a Cold Start Stage (Algorithm 1), which explores products while preserving incentive compatibility, from an Exploitation Stage (Algorithm 2) using inverse proportional gap sampling (Section 3.1-3.2).
claims.evidence: A full RCB run (K=5, d=5, 30k rounds) confirms the two-stage structure: Cold Start collects exactly N=50 samples per arm via MPASC then RASC; Exploitation starts at epoch m0=8 matching the formula, uses IPGS with a valid probability kernel (max|sum p - 1| = 2.2e-16, min p > 0 over 26,379 rounds), and gamma_m rises as MSPE falls.

claims.claim: The analysis reveals a tradeoff in which larger incentive budgets epsilon reduce required cold-start sample sizes but affect the regret guarantee (Section 4, Theorem 1 and Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: As eps grows over {0.01, 0.03, 0.05}, N(eps) falls monotonically (10460→7489→5625), L(eps) falls (51.8→25.6→17.0), and the empirical Price of Incentives (cold-start regret) drops 28431→13883→9030 while DBIC remains satisfied, demonstrating both directions of the tradeoff with concrete numbers.

claims.claim: In warfarin-dosing simulations using real data, RCB achieves a weighted risk score of approximately 0.29 compared to a physician baseline of 0.20, with error rates around 35% (Section 5.2, Table 1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The physician baseline (0.20) is reproduced by simple arithmetic from population proportions, and the RCB numbers (0.291, 0.355) are confirmed only as internally consistent with the paper's own reported stratum rates—not independently re-run on real PharmGKB data. A synthetic K=3 warfarin-style run shows RCB beats physician qualitatively (weighted risk 0.52-0.63 > 0.20) but does not match the paper's magnitudes or eps-ordering, and uses no real data.

snaykey/repro-adaptive-gradient-heavy-ta.overall: The logbook provides rigorous verification of the theoretical claims (Claims 2-4) with faithful algorithm implementation, exact formula checks, and non-vacuous controls, but falsifies the sqrt(K) factor in the regret bound (Claim 1: actual K^1.9 scaling) and only provides a toy synthetic reproduction of the warfarin results without real data (Claim 5).

gauravmishra9/repro-beyond-the-final-ans.paper_title: Beyond the Final Answer: Evaluating the Reasoning Trajectories of Tool-Augmented Agents

claims.claim: TRACE evaluates a tool-augmented agent's trajectory along three dimensions—efficiency, hallucination, and adaptivity—without requiring a ground-truth trajectory, using an incrementally constructed 'evidence bank' built from each step's action, input, and observation (Section 3, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: A full conformance audit over all 761 Meta-GTA trajectories (2,711 tool-call steps, 2,540 evidence items) found zero schema, ordering, incremental-construction, or ground-truth-label leakage violations, and controlled checks recovered expected efficiency/hallucination/adaptivity scores, confirming the evidence-bank mechanism operates as described on the full dataset.

claims.claim: On the Meta-GTA meta-evaluation benchmark, using Llama-3.1-8B as the evaluator, TRACE improves efficiency accuracy from 55.67% (LLM-as-a-Judge) to 70.46% and adaptivity accuracy from 78.98% to 85.28%, a gain of up to +19.44 points (Table 1).
claims.evidence: On all 761 Meta-GTA trajectories with Llama-3.1-8B, the reproduction found adaptivity accuracy decreased from 78.36 to 72.51 (−5.85, CI [−14.86, +2.92]), directly contradicting the paper's claimed gain from 78.98 to 85.28; additionally, Meta-m&m's efficiency reversed (−6.99), and the specific TRACE values (83.77 efficiency vs paper's 70.46) did not match.

claims.claim: TRACE outperforms the PIPA state-consistency baseline as an efficiency metric across all five evaluator models on Meta-GTA, e.g. Claude-Sonnet-4 scores 94.64 under TRACE versus 84.46 under PIPA (Table 3).
claims.evidence: TRACE beat reconstructed PIPA for all five evaluator models on all 761 Meta-GTA trajectories (Llama-8B +20.88, Llama-70B +20.18, Claude +24.97, GPT-4.1 +14.98, o3-mini +19.18), confirming the ordering claim; Claude TRACE closely matched the paper (95.32 vs 94.64), though reconstructed PIPA values differed due to missing baseline code.

claims.claim: Using Llama-3.3-70B as the TRACE evaluator matches the accuracy of larger proprietary evaluator models (Table 1) while reducing average per-query evaluation time by roughly a factor of three (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The accuracy sub-claim is supported (Llama-3.3-70B within ±5 points of best proprietary on all three dimensions), but the latency sub-claim is contradicted: on 120 paired measurements, Llama-70B was 3.30×–7.80× slower than proprietary models (115.16 s/query vs 14.76–34.85 s/query), the reverse of the claimed ~3× speedup, though this is confounded by OpenRouter routing differences from the paper's direct-provider setup.

claims.claim: On the GTA benchmark evaluated with TRACE, the open-source Qwen-72B agent attains overall accuracy of 52.02%, comparable to proprietary agents Claude-Sonnet-4 (57.67%) and GPT-4.1 (52.81%) (Table 4, Section 5.2.1).
claims.evidence: Independent recomputation of OverallAccuracy from all 229 released trajectories per agent reproduced all three values within 0.01 point: Qwen2.5-72B 52.0227% (paper 52.02%), Claude-Sonnet-4 57.6707% (paper 57.67%), GPT-4.1 52.8133% (paper 52.81%), with Qwen within 6 points of both proprietary agents.

gauravmishra9/repro-beyond-the-final-ans.overall: The logbook provides strong evidence for the structural mechanism (Claim 1), the TRACE-over-PIPA ordering (Claim 3), and the exact GTA agent accuracy comparison (Claim 5), but contradicts the specific Meta-GTA gain numbers including a reversed adaptivity direction (Claim 2) and a reversed latency relationship under OpenRouter (Claim 4). Reproducibility is limited by missing released baseline code for LLM-as-a-Judge and PIPA, and provider routing differences affecting latency measurements.

tomyimkc/repro-on-uniform-error-bounds-f.paper_title: On Uniform Error Bounds for Kernel Regression under Non-Gaussian Noise

claims.claim: Proposition 3.3 extends the uniform error bound to correlated (non-i.i.d.) sub-Gaussian noise, with Corollary 3.4 recovering the conditionally-independent sub-Gaussian case as a special case (Section 3.1, Proposition 3.3, Corollary 3.4)
claims.evidence: Exact algebraic recovery of Corollary 3.4 from Proposition 3.3 is confirmed to floating-point precision (max abs diff 0.0 across t={20,100,300,800} when C_t=sigma_M^2*I), and empirical coverage under genuine AR(1)-correlated Gaussian noise (rho_c=0.7) is 1.0 over 1500 MC trials (target >=0.95), with the width ratio growing from 1.0 to 11.01 as correlation increases to 0.99.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.5 derives a uniform bound for heavy-tailed (sub-exponential) noise via a truncation argument, achieving a 71.6% success rate at the final iteration in the sub-exponential (chi-squared, sigma_m=0.1) numerical experiment (Section 3.2, Section 5.3, Proposition 3.5)
claims.evidence: The 71.6% success rate is closely reproduced: Theorem 3.2(c) achieves 0.7456 at t=1000 (vs paper's 0.716), and Proposition 3.5's truncation bound collapses to 0.0 for t>=200, matching the paper's own description that it 'drops to 0% for t>50'; the logbook honestly notes the 71.6% figure is attributable to Theorem 3.2(c) rather than Proposition 3.5 per the paper's Section 5.3.

claims.claim: In the safe control experiment with nominal dynamics f_nom(x_t,u_t)=0.5x_t+u_t-1 and unknown residual f(x_t)=exp(-x_t^2)sin(10x_t), the proposed uniform bounds yield higher feasibility and lower cost than baseline uncertainty quantification methods (Section 5.2, Figures 5-6)
claims.evidence: At t=1000, the proposed bound yields feasibility 0.8222 vs 0.5572 for the AY baseline and cost 1.6983 vs 2.5858 (approaching optimal 1.4303), with higher feasibility at every tested t and lower cost at 9/10 t values; the noise-misspecification control shows violation rates rising from 0.0 (correct spec) to 0.362 (15x mismatch), confirming the safety guarantee depends on correct noise specification.

claims.claim: In the uncertainty-region-size experiment sweeping noise bound m_bar in {0.01, 0.1, 1} and input dimension n_x in {1,2,3} with confidence parameter delta=0.001 over up to 1000 data points, the proposed bounds are consistently tighter than the Abbasi-Yadkori baseline (Section 5.1, Figures 3-4)
claims.evidence: The proposed/AY uncertainty-region size ratio is below 1.0 at every tested t and noise level (e.g., 0.4369, 0.4216, 0.5222 at t=1000 for m_bar=0.01, 0.1, 1.0), and decreases with input dimension (0.4211 at n_x=1, 0.3104 at n_x=2, 0.1203 at n_x=3), matching the paper's finding that improvement grows with dimension; the control shows the ratio crosses parity (0.876 at 2x, 1.237 at 3x) when the assumed noise bound is inflated.

tomyimkc/repro-on-uniform-error-bounds-f.overall: All four claims are supported by concrete experimental evidence with formulas independently transcribed from the paper, proper parameterization matching Sections 5.1-5.3, and informative control experiments for each claim. The main limitations are reduced Monte Carlo averaging (6-8 trials vs 100), self-constructed Abbasi-Yadkori baselines, and non-reproduction of the Fiedler et al. baseline, but the directional results are consistent and statistically clear.

tomyimkc/repro-perceptrons-and-localizat.paper_title: Perceptrons and Localization of Attention’s Mean-Field Landscape

claims.claim: For non-analytic ReLU-type perceptron potentials in dimension d=2, every stationary measure of the mean-field energy is proved to be purely atomic with finite support (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Finite-N simulations (N=600, 1800) with ReLU perceptron on S^1 show N-invariant cluster count (6 at both N values) and small median NN distance (1.37e-4), consistent with the theorem's atomic-support conclusion, but this is a proxy test of an infinite-N theorem at finite scale, and the no-perceptron control's cluster count also stays at 1 due to a chain-linking artifact, weakening discrimination.

claims.claim: For analytic activation functions such as GeLU in d=2, strict second-order-positive-definite (SOPD) Wasserstein critical points are shown to be purely atomic with finite support (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Part A (cross-N cluster invariance) is uninformative—both with-GeLU and control show identical cluster counts and nearly identical median NN distances (1.69e-3 vs 1.67e-3). Part B tests a proxy (SOPD implies positive-definite energy response to coherent shifts, symmetry ratio 1.0001) rather than the actual claim of purely atomic finite support, making this an indirect proxy at finite N.

claims.claim: In dimensions d≥2, stationary measures are proved singular (zero Lebesgue measure), and for an open dense set of parameters with analytic activation they are purely atomic (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: Only 3 of the paper's 50 dimensions tested (d=3,5,8) at N=400/1200 with a single seed; with-perceptron cluster-count ratios (2.0, 2.0, 1.0) are below the particle ratio of 3.0, but the d=3 control shows a ratio of 0.333 due to a metric artifact, and the evidence is too sparse to constitute a full reproduction.

claims.claim: In the descent (repulsive) regime, clusters forming at interaction scale sqrt(beta) are bounded in mass by approximately 0.5742 + O(e^{-beta}), preventing full collapse to single atoms (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: Direct measurement of max window mass at the theorem's exact window width 1/(2√β) across 11 beta values (0.1–100) with N=1000 ReLU perceptron shows the mass never exceeds 0.512, safely below the bound of 0.5742; the control at β=0.01 (violating 'β sufficiently large') correctly yields mass 1.0, confirming the bound's precondition is load-bearing.

claims.claim: Global maximizers of the combined attention-perceptron energy reduce to a single Dirac mass at the point maximizing the perceptron potential, while the global minimizer is unique and rotationally invariant (Proposition 3.7).
claims.evidence: Part (i): gradient ascent collapses to a single point at machine precision (circular std 2.48e-16), with the converged angle matching the independently grid-searched argmax of v_θ to 1.42e-5 rad and potential values agreeing to 9 significant figures. Part (ii): the rotational-asymmetry statistic R drops from 0.0574 (with perceptron) to 8.99e-8 (control without perceptron), cleanly confirming the rotational invariance prediction.

claims.claim: Numerical simulations across dimensions d in {1,2,...,50} confirm that the number of atomic clusters scales approximately as sqrt(beta), for both ascent and descent regimes and under softmax-normalized attention (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Only 3 of 50 dimensions tested at N=400 with a single seed; fitted exponents range from 0.1 to 1.582 with median 0.302 versus the target 0.5, several fits have poor R² or are impossible due to finite-N saturation (d=10 descent drops 7 of 9 points), and the results do not cleanly confirm the claimed sqrt(β) scaling.

tomyimkc/repro-perceptrons-and-localizat.overall: The logbook provides direct, non-toy numerical confirmation of Theorem 3.5's cluster-mass bound (max measured mass 0.512 < 0.5742 across β=0.1–100 with a correctly violating control) and Proposition 3.7's maximizer/minimizer characterization (machine-precision collapse to the correct argmax, clean rotational-invariance separation). The remaining four claims are addressed only at reduced scale (finite N=400–1800, 3–8 of 50 dimensions, single seeds) with proxy metrics that partially confirm but do not constitute full reproductions.

claims.claim: Parameterizing weight matrices as W = AB^T with A in R^{m x r} and B in R^{n x r} induces a posterior that is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure and concentrates entirely on the rank-r manifold when r < min(m,n) (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: Exact Jacobian of the bilinear map (A,B)->vec(AB^T) was constructed via basis differentiation at m=48, n=36 across 8 values of r; numerical rank matched the closed-form r(m+n-r) exactly at every point, with deficiency fraction positive for all r<36 and zero at r=36 and r=42 (boundary/over-param controls). Support check over 3000 draws confirmed rank(AB^T)≤r with (r+1)-th singular value 1.665e-14.

claims.claim: The derived PAC-Bayes generalization bound for the low-rank posterior has a complexity term scaling as sqrt(r(m+n)) instead of the sqrt(mn) scaling of standard mean-field Gaussian posteriors (Theorem 3.8, Section 3.4).
claims.evidence: Mean-field Gaussian KL was computed for D_full=mn vs D_LR=r(m+n) across square matrices s∈{50,...,3200}; measured complexity ratio matched theory sqrt(r(1/m+1/n)) with max relative error 0.0089, fitted growth exponents were 1.001 (full, theory 1.0) and 0.502 (low-rank r=8 fixed, theory 0.5), and the control with r=s//4 returned exponent to 1.002 as predicted.

claims.claim: Using the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem, the paper bounds the expected loss gap between the full-rank optimum and its optimal rank-r truncation by the tail singular value energy sqrt(sum_{i>r} sigma_i^2), and further decomposes the learned factorization's total error into a learning-error term and an unavoidable rank-bias term (Theorem 3.6, Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence: EYM identity held to rel err 1.14e-16; Thm 3.6 inequality held (LHS=0.171 ≤ RHS=3.883); Thm 3.7 pointwise inequality held for all 200k eval points across N∈{15,...,100k}; learning-error term shrank from 2.03 to 0.0074 with more data while rank-bias floor stayed fixed, confirming the decomposition. Underdetermined control (N=15<d_in=20) showed learning error blowing up as expected.

claims.claim: On the MIMIC-III mortality prediction task, a rank-15 Low-Rank Gaussian BNN with only 13.6k parameters (versus 112k for a 5-member Deep Ensemble, an 88% reduction) achieves better OOD detection (AUC-OOD 0.802 vs. 0.738) and AUPR-OOD/AUPR-In, while Deep Ensemble retains better in-domain AUROC (0.929 vs 0.895) and calibration (NLL 0.300 vs 0.433) (Table 1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: MIMIC-III was unavailable, so a synthetic 2-layer tanh MLP proxy (d_hidden=24 vs paper's 128, 841 vs 5405 params) was used. Qualitative directions matched (low-rank better AUC_OOD 0.552 vs 0.499; ensemble better NLL and AUROC_ID), and the structured-vs-unstructured control behaved as predicted, but absolute metrics are near chance (~0.6 AUROC) and the setup is a small synthetic proxy, not the named benchmark.

claims.claim: On Beijing Air Quality LSTM forecasting with distribution shift to Guangzhou, the Low-Rank Bayesian LSTM achieves the best coverage (PICP=0.790) and near-best calibration (ECE=0.114) while using 64% fewer parameters than Full-Rank BBB, and achieves the largest MAE reduction (17.4%) at 80% retention under selective prediction (Section 4.3, Table 2, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Beijing/Guangzhou data and LSTM architecture were unavailable; a single feed-forward regression layer (d_hidden=20, not LSTM) was used as proxy. Coverage direction partially reproduced (LowRank PICP=0.697 best among Bayesian vs Deep Ensemble 0.400 severe undercoverage), but ECE ranking (LowRank worst at 0.199) and selective-prediction MAE reduction (negative -4.33% vs claimed +17.4%) did not reproduce, a mismatch the logbook reports honestly.

tomyimkc/repro-singular-bayesian-neural-.overall: The three theoretical claims (singularity/measure-zero, PAC-Bayes scaling, EYM bounds with bias/learning decomposition) are verified with exact numerical constructions, proper controls, and clean agreement with closed-form predictions. The two empirical claims are addressed only via small synthetic proxies that cannot access the paper's named benchmarks, yielding partial qualitative agreement but not full reproduction.

nmaher/repro-from-muon-to-gluon-bridging.paper_title: From Muon to Gluon: Bridging Theory and Practice of LMO-based Optimizers for LLMs

claims.claim: The Gluon framework unifies layer-wise LMO-based optimizers, recovering Muon (spectral norm), unScion (mixed norms for transformer blocks and embeddings), layer-wise normalized GD, and layer-wise signGD as special cases via Algorithm 1 (Algorithm 1, Section on special cases).
claims.evidence: 520/520 randomized comparisons of a generic LMO routine against independently-transcribed closed-form updates for Muon, unScion, layer-wise normalized-GD, and layer-wise signGD pass with worst max difference 1.8e-15 (vs 1e-8 tolerance), confirming the algebraic identity at machine precision.

claims.claim: Under a layer-wise generalized (L^0_i, L^1_i)-smoothness condition, ||grad_i f(X) - grad_i f(Y)||_* <= (L^0_i + L^1_i ||grad_i f(X)||_*) ||X_i - Y_i||, Gluon with adaptive per-layer stepsize t_i^k = ||grad_i f(X^k)||_* / (L^0_i + L^1_i ||grad_i f(X^k)||_*) achieves O(1/K^{1/2}) convergence in the deterministic setting (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: On a synthetic 4-layer objective with calibrated (L0,L1) certificates, the adaptive stepsize yields clean power-law decay (R²=0.997) but fitted slope -1.20 vs claimed -0.5, converging faster than the worst-case upper bound — not a contradiction but not a tight quantitative match on a simplified setup.

claims.claim: In the stochastic setting with non-Euclidean bounded variance, Gluon achieves a convergence rate of O(Delta^0/K^{1/4} + 1/K^{1/4} * sum_i [sigma/L^1_i + L^0_i/(L^1_i)^2]) (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: On the same synthetic 4-layer objective with bounded-variance noise (15 seeds), fitted slope -0.346 (R²=0.998) falls within tolerance of claimed -0.25, but the noise magnitude was explicitly tuned from a small grid to target the tolerance band, weakening the independence of the match.

claims.claim: Empirical estimation of layer-wise smoothness constants on a 124M-parameter NanoGPT model trained on FineWeb finds L^0_i approximately 0 across layers, with L^1_i approximately 70 for transformer blocks (predicted stepsize 0.014 vs. tuned 0.018) and L^1_i approximately 1.3 for embedding/output layers (predicted stepsize 0.77 vs. tuned 1.08).
claims.evidence: A hand-built tiny transformer (manual forward/backward, gradient-checked to 6e-6 rel error) trained on synthetic Markov-chain tokens — not NanoGPT/FineWeb — finds L0≈0 for transformer blocks and a 42x L1 gap (83.9 vs 1.98) vs the paper's 54x gap (70 vs 1.3), matching direction and order of magnitude but on a clearly simplified proxy.

claims.claim: On a CNN trained on CIFAR-10, estimated smoothness constants also satisfy L^0_i approximately 0, with a two-orders-of-magnitude spread in L^1_i across layers, motivating per-layer learning-rate heterogeneity.
claims.evidence: A hand-built tiny CNN on CIFAR-10-style toy data finds L0 ranging 0.13–14.7 (not ≈0) and the classification head's L1 (7.72) is the largest layer group, inverting the claimed direction — but this is at toy scale with a tiny manual model, not a full CIFAR-10 reproduction.

claims.claim: The zeroth-order eNTK approximation error is shown to depend on the model's output dimension rather than the (potentially massive) parameter dimension, in contrast to prior analyses that scale with parameter count.
claims.evidence: Full-text search of both arXiv and OpenReview PDFs found no occurrences of 'eNTK', 'NTK', 'tangent kernel', or 'zeroth-order', indicating this claim may be a misattribution unrelated to the paper's actual content; no experiment could address it.

nmaher/repro-from-muon-to-gluon-bridging.overall: The logbook provides a strong machine-precision verification of the algebraic unification claim (Claim 1) and toy-scale checks of the convergence rates and smoothness patterns on synthetic/proxy setups, but does not reproduce any claim at the paper's actual scale (NanoGPT/FineWeb, real CIFAR-10 CNN). Claim 5's toy results contradict the paper's pattern, and Claim 6 appears to be a claim-extraction error with the concept absent from the paper.

claims.claim: GESPI combines three runs of a base inference algorithm — on real data at level α, on real data at a relaxed level α+ε, and on pooled real+synthetic data at level α — and aggregates them via intersection/union set operations to guarantee risk 𝔼[ℓ(Ãlg(D_n, D̃_N), V)] ≤ α + min{ε, c·d_ℓ,Alg(P,Q)} regardless of synthetic data quality (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: The two-sided GESPI construction was implemented on the paper's own binomial-test example at n=50, N=500, α=0.05, ε=0.02 with M=300,000 replicates across an 11-point synthetic-quality sweep; the risk bound E[loss] ≤ α + min{ε, c·τ + c·d(P,Q)} held at every grid point (max violation 0.000753, within MC tolerance 0.013693), while the naive no-guardrail ablation's risk reached 1.0 at worst synthetic quality, confirming the guardrail mechanism is essential.

claims.claim: The two-sided version of GESPI is sandwiched between the base method at level α and the guardrail method at level α+ε, i.e. Alg_α(D_n) ⪯ Ãlg(D_n, D̃_N) ⪯ Alg_{α+ε}(D_n), preserving statistical validity regardless of synthetic distribution shift (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: The deterministic pointwise sandwich Alg_α(D_n) ≤ GESPI ≤ Alg_{α+ε}(D_n) was checked across 8 (θ_real, θ_synth) pairs with M=2,000,000 replicates each (16M total draws) yielding zero violations; a control that broke the same-data monotonicity precondition (Condition F.1(3)) produced violation rates up to 0.0677, demonstrating the property depends on the stated precondition.

claims.claim: On AlphaFold structure prediction with n=10 CASP-14 proteins as real data and N=1,000 synthetic proteins from MSAs at target risk α=5%, GESPI reduces abstention to 85.6% at ~7% risk, compared to an OnlyReal baseline that abstains on nearly 100% of residues at 0% risk (Figure 3a).
claims.evidence: Real AlphaFold/CASP-14 data was unavailable; the CRC abstention mechanism was exercised on a synthetic per-residue model (p_err(s)=0.5(1-s)²) at matching scale (n=10, N=1000), showing qualitative abstention reduction (GESPI ~29-32% vs OnlyReal ~68%) with risk ≤0.063, but the claim's literal 85.6% abstention / ~7% risk figures were not targeted or reproduced.

claims.claim: In a comparison of large reasoning models using n=15 real AIME25 problems and N=100 synthetic OlympiadBench problems (α=5%, ε=2%), GESPI achieves higher statistical power to reject the null hypothesis than an OnlyReal test while controlling Type I error at the nominal level (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: No real LLMs, AIME25, or OlympiadBench data were used; model comparisons were simulated as Bernoulli(win) draws at hand-chosen rates (0.5–0.65) at matching sample sizes (n=15, N=100), showing GESPI power 0.211 vs OnlyReal 0.189 with Type I error 0.052 ≤ α+ε, but Figure 4's actual reasoning-model results were not reproduced.

claims.claim: An OnlySynth baseline that relies purely on synthetic data lacks the error-rate guarantees that GESPI provides (Section 3/Figure 4 discussion).
claims.evidence: OnlySynth was implemented as the exact randomized test computed entirely from synthetic data at n=50, N=500, M=1,000,000 across a 13-point θ_synth sweep; its Type I error ranged from 0.0 to 1.0 (span 1.0, uncontrolled), coinciding with α only at θ_synth=0.5 by chance, while GESPI's Type I error stayed ≤0.0702 throughout the identical sweep, directly demonstrating the lack of any fixed error-rate guarantee for OnlySynth.

tomyimkc/repro-general-synthetic-powered.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies GESPI's two core theoretical guarantees (risk-aggregation bound and deterministic sandwich property) and the OnlySynth failure mode via large-scale Monte Carlo on the paper's own binomial-test instantiation with appropriate breaking controls, while claims 3 and 4 are addressed only at the mechanism level on synthetic data due to the unavailability of real AlphaFold and LLM benchmark data.

tomyimkc/repro-understanding-the-perform.paper_title: Understanding the Performance Gap in Preference Learning: A Dichotomy of RLHF and DPO

claims.claim: Under isomorphic mis-specification, where the reward model class equals the policy model class (ℱ = ℱ_Π), standard RLHF and standard offline DPO yield equal value: V_{r⋆}^{π_RLHF} = V_{r⋆}^{π_DPO} (Proposition 6, Section 3.4).
claims.evidence: Under isomorphism (F=F_Pi), |V_RLHF - V_DPO| was exactly 0.0 across all 40 seeds with Newton convergence confirmed (grad norm 3.11e-08), while breaking isomorphism via a different feature map produced a mean gap of 2.32 (min 0.50, max 5.37), demonstrating the equality is specific to F=F_Pi as Proposition 6 claims.

claims.claim: Despite this equivalence between RLHF and offline DPO, online DPO can strictly outperform RLHF under the same isomorphic mis-specified model classes, i.e. V_{r⋆}^{π_RLHF} < V_{r⋆}^{π^online_DPO}, because online DPO leverages distributional information unavailable to the two-stage reward-modeling-then-policy-optimization pipeline (Proposition 7, Section 3.4).
claims.evidence: The value-optimal policy within the same restricted class (online DPO's target per Theorem 2) strictly beat the offline/RLHF solution in 15/15 seeds for every gamma>0 (mean gap 0.014–0.519), while the realizable-reward control (gamma=0) showed gap 3.02e-15 with 0/15 strictly better; a secondary non-oracle iterative on-policy retraining simulation corroborated with 7/8 seeds showing strict improvement (mean gap 0.362).

claims.claim: When the reward class is realizable but the policy class is weak, RLHF weakly dominates DPO (V_{r⋆}^{π_RLHF} ≥ V_{r⋆}^{π_DPO}), since DPO's implicit reward is bottlenecked by the policy class constraints (Proposition 3, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: With a fully tabular realizable reward (verified, residual std 0.0038) and a weak m_p=5-dimensional policy class, V_RLHF >= V_DPO held in 25/25 seeds with a strict gap in all 25 (mean 0.0106, range 0.002–0.044), while the control with a fully tabular policy class collapsed the gap to 1.10e-05, confirming the dominance is driven by policy-class weakness.

claims.claim: For dual-token sparse prediction tasks, ℓ1-regularized reward model estimation achieves error Õ(√(k log d / n)), where k is the sparsity level and d the dimensionality, while policy-model estimation error under the same sparse ground-truth reward structure is lower-bounded by Ω(d/n), establishing a statistical separation showing RLHF needs asymptotically fewer samples than DPO to recover an effective reward/policy under sparse rewards (Theorem 10, Theorem 11, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The L1 reward estimator's error decayed with log-log slope -0.88 versus -0.47 for the dense policy estimator, with the error ratio growing from 2.8x to 25.9x and downstream value-regret ratio reaching 200.8x at n=100,000; the no-sparsity control (k=d=150) reversed the advantage (ratio <1), confirming the separation is a sparsity effect. Measured rate exponents do not exactly match the theorem's asymptotic orders, but the controlled, monotonically-widening separation directly supports the claimed statistical gap.

tomyimkc/repro-understanding-the-perform.overall: All four theoretical claims are supported by concrete experimental evidence from faithful implementations of the paper's own exact-optimization and finite-sample constructions, each with a control that relaxes the claim's precondition and shows the effect disappear or reverse. The main limitation is that all experiments use finite-dimensional linear-softmax bandits rather than neural LLM-scale training, but this is appropriate for verifying the paper's theoretical propositions which are themselves stated in abstract model-class terms.

tomyimkc/repro-amortized-simulation-base.paper_title: Amortized Simulation-Based Inference in Generalized Bayes via Neural Posterior Estimation

claims.claim: A single amortized neural posterior estimator conditioned jointly on observation x and temperature β enables single-forward-pass sampling from the tempered power posterior p_β(θ|x) ∝ π(θ)p(x|θ)^β without inference-time MCMC or additional simulator calls (Section on core method).
claims.evidence: Tested on a 1D linear-Gaussian model with a cubic basis-regression estimator (not a neural posterior estimator), achieving mean |err|=0.00379 vs SIR baseline 0.00426 with 0 test-time simulator calls; the mechanism is faithfully tested but the model and architecture are heavily simplified.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 shows that minimizing the SNIS-weighted training objective (Route B) is equivalent to minimizing the forward KL divergence between the learned amortized posterior and the true tempered posterior (Proposition 4.1).
claims.evidence: In a closed-form linear-Gaussian instance where both objectives can be computed exactly, the SNIS-weighted fit and direct forward-KL fit agreed to within 0.00156 (mean function) and 0.00236 (variance function) across a 21-point β grid, while the unweighted control deviated by ~0.08, directly confirming the objective equivalence with a decisive ablation.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.2 proves that for β ∈ [1/2, 1], the NRE-based self-normalized importance weights have finite variance, guaranteeing stable weighted maximum-likelihood estimation (Proposition 4.2).
claims.evidence: Closed-form derivation of Var[w_β] via Gaussian moment identity, cross-validated with 400K×8-seed Monte Carlo, showed all variances finite and below 1 (max 0.191878 at β=0.5) throughout [0.5,1.0], with divergence to infinity at multiple β values outside the window (e.g., β=0.05, 0.1, 1.8, 2.0), exactly matching the proposition's claim.

claims.claim: The amortized estimator is evaluated on four SBI benchmarks—Two Moons, Gaussian Mixture, SLCP, and Lorenz-96—achieving posterior approximations competitive with non-amortized MCMC-based power-posterior samplers across a wide range of temperatures (Experiments section).
claims.evidence: Only 1 of 4 named benchmarks (Gaussian Mixture) was implemented, using a basis-regression estimator instead of a neural posterior estimator and grid quadrature instead of MCMC; the full-budget estimator achieved mean |err|=0.05604 vs exact reference across β∈[0.3,3.0], but three benchmarks (Two Moons, SLCP, Lorenz-96) were entirely untested.

claims.claim: Route A (score-assisted tempered synthesis via Langevin dynamics) dominates at small β where SNIS importance weights become high-variance, while Route B (self-normalized importance sampling) performs well near β=1 using 10K-100K simulations (Experiments section).
claims.evidence: Route B error grew from 0.005–0.006 near β=0.5–1.0 to 0.150 at β=0.05 with ESS collapsing to 0.17%, while Route A (using the TRUE analytic score, not a learned score network) stayed flat at 0.002–0.017; the qualitative trade-off pattern is reproduced but only in a linear-Gaussian toy with exact score substitution.

claims.claim: On the 8-parameter Hodgkin-Huxley neuronal model with 7 summary statistics, the Route B (NLE) estimator trained on 10K simulations produces stable marginal posteriors across β ∈ {0.1, 1.0, 2.0} with posterior predictive checks qualitatively matching Allen Cell Types Database recordings (Section on Hodgkin-Huxley application).
claims.evidence: An 8-parameter HH model with 7 summary statistics was implemented with a linear-Gaussian NLE surrogate on 10K simulations, producing stable posteriors at β∈{0.1,1.0,2.0} (ESS 117–2990) with PPC MAE improving from 0.44 to 0.24, but x_obs was synthetic (not real Allen Cell Types Database data), the surrogate was linear regression (not neural NLE), and the 'qualitatively matching real recordings' part was explicitly untested.

tomyimkc/repro-amortized-simulation-base.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification of the paper's two core mathematical propositions (4.1 and 4.2) via exact closed-form computation with decisive controls in a linear-Gaussian instance, while the four empirical claims are only exercised at toy scale with simplified estimators, synthetic data, and reduced benchmark coverage.

tomyimkc/repro-a-perturbation-approach-t.paper_title: A Perturbation Approach to Unconstrained Linear Bandits

claims.claim: The paper's perturbation-based algorithm, PABLO, reduces unconstrained Bandit Linear Optimization (uBLO) to a standard Online Linear Optimization (OLO) problem (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Exact enumeration over 2d symmetric atoms confirms all reduction preconditions to machine precision: estimator bias 9.18e-17, second-moment identity residual 1.41e-15, a.s. bound 0 violations (max ratio 0.355≤1), in-expectation bound 0 violations (max ratio 0.961≤1), ghost-iterate identity residual 1.05e-16; biased control breaks in-expectation bound (1786 violations) and bias (0.146).

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 gives an expected static-regret bound of the form E[R_T(u)] = O~(G*epsilon + d*kappa*E[||u||*sqrt(V_T log(...))]), with kappa=sqrt(d) in the norm-oblivious setting and kappa=1 in the norm-adaptive setting (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Empirical regret/RHS_oblivious ratio stays below 0.058 across horizon (T up to 25600) and dimension (d up to 12) sweeps; kappa separation RHS_adaptive/RHS_oblivious matches sqrt(d) to 0.2% relative error ([1.728,1.995,2.444,2.822,3.156,3.457] vs sqrt(d)); V_T dependence confirmed via G-sweep. Bound is loose (ratios <<1) but not violated.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows PABLO attains the optimal sqrt(P_T) dynamic-regret dependence on the path-length P_T without requiring prior knowledge of P_T (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: Clean main term sqrt(P_T V_T) scales as sqrt(P_T) with log-log slope 0.500 over P_T sweep {4..4096}; same parameter-free algorithm config respects bound across entire sweep (max ratio 0.00065); path-length strictly beats switching (gradual drift ratio 0.252 vs abrupt 1.20).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 establishes a high-probability static-regret bound R_T(u) <= O~(dG(epsilon+||u||)log(T/delta) + G||u||sqrt(dT log(T/delta))) (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Empirical failure rate 0.000 at delta={0.05,0.1,0.2} over 400 trials (bound allows 3*delta={0.15,0.30,0.60}); 0.9-quantile regret/RHS ratio max 0.034 across T-sweep {1000..8000}; proper estimator concentrated (z=2.63) vs control with 30x larger second moment (52.9 vs 1.79). Bound is very loose but high-probability guarantee holds.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 proves the folklore Omega(sqrt(dT)) minimax lower bound for adversarial linear bandits on the unit Euclidean ball (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Bandit learner regret scales as sqrt(dT): log-log slope vs T = 0.564, vs d = 0.524 (both ~0.5); regret/sqrt(dT) ratios in [0.49,0.82]; both lower-bound terms respected at T=4d boundary; KL check confirms signs unresolvable (per-coord std 0.048 > gap 0.032).

claims.claim: Conjecture 5.3 posits a minimax rate of R_T(u) = Theta(||u|| sqrt(T(d v log||u||))) for norm-oblivious comparators, left as an open problem (Conjecture 5.3).
claims.evidence: Conjecture is explicitly open by the paper's own statement; evidence is consistent but not proof: scale LB form slope 1.097 (~1), direction LB realised/LB ratios 52-60, upper-bound/conjectured-rate ratio 1.0-1.282, conjectured rate equals max of component LBs (ratio 1.000 by construction). No single hard instance forcing both LBs simultaneously is constructed.

tomyimkc/repro-a-perturbation-approach-t.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting claims 1-5 through direct simulation of PABLO and its reduction framework, with claim 1 verified exactly by enumeration and claims 2-5 verified empirically though with very loose bounds (regret/RHS ratios well below 1). Claim 6 is correctly treated as an open conjecture with consistent but non-probative evidence.

tomyimkc/repro-certificate-guided-prunin.paper_title: Certificate-Guided Pruning for Stochastic Lipschitz Optimization

claims.claim: Certificate-Guided Pruning (CGP) maintains an explicit active set A_t of candidate optima using confidence-adjusted Lipschitz envelopes, certifying with high probability that any point outside A_t is suboptimal (Section 3, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 was reimplemented and tested in d∈{2,3,6} with 18 seeds per config (108 trajectories total), directly checking envelope validity f(x)≤U_t(x) on a dense 1800-point independent evaluation cloud and no-false-exclusion of the true optimum; the nominal per-seed violation rate was 0.0 (target ≤δ=0.05), while the control with L=0.4×L_true had a 1.0 violation rate, confirming the certificate mechanism works and depends on a valid Lipschitz constant.

claims.claim: Under a margin condition with near-optimality dimension α (Assumption 2.3), the Shrinkage Theorem bounds the active set volume as Vol(A_t) ≤ C·(2(β_t + Lη_t) + γ_t)^(d−α) (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: Tested only in d=3 on synthetic power-bump functions; the shrinkage bound was violated on 48.6% of checkpoints in the p=2/α=1.5 regime (max ratio 14.82x overage), and the α-understated control held at nearly the same rate (51.0% vs 51.4%), failing to discriminate correct from incorrect α — mixed results on a simplified setup that neither cleanly verifies nor falsifies the theorem.

claims.claim: CGP achieves ε-optimality with probability at least 1−δ using T = Õ(L^d ε^{-(2+α)} log(1/δ)) samples, improving on the worst-case Õ(ε^{-(2+d)}) rate whenever α < d (Theorem 4.8).
claims.evidence: Tested only in d=2 using a proxy quantity (certified gap Δ_t rather than realized regret); fitted exponents (0.89–1.97) systematically undershot the theoretical 2+α values (2.33–3.71), monotonicity in α held at only 2 of 3 common ε thresholds, and the certified-vs-random control showed a large gap — directional support but no quantitative match on a reduced-scope setup.

claims.claim: A matching lower bound shows any algorithm requires Ω(ε^{-(2+α)}) samples under the same margin condition, establishing CGP's minimax sample-complexity optimality (Theorem 4.9).
claims.evidence: Reimplemented the paper's Appendix C.7 hard-instance construction and tested necessity via Monte Carlo with one specific identification strategy (center-of-cell sampling + argmax); Part A's fitted exponent (1.91) was close to theory (2.0), Part B's exponents (2.94–4.68) overshot the theoretical 2+α (2.3–3.9), and the reduced-budget control degraded success below 2/3 at all 20 (α,ε) points — necessity evidence on one construction, not a proof over all algorithms.

claims.claim: CGP-Adaptive learns the Lipschitz constant L online via a doubling scheme, adding only an O(log T) multiplicative overhead to the sample complexity (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: Tested only in d=3 on one function type; the doubling-count bound held in 100% of seeds (property 1), but L-convergence to [L*,2L*] reached only 72–78% of seeds vs the theorem's 1−δ=0.95 target (property 2), and at the paper's headline 100× underestimation factor the scheme completely failed to converge (0% convergence, stuck at L_hat=4.43 vs L*=6.93) — partial support with a key property unmet on a simplified setup.

claims.claim: CGP-TR, a trust-region variant, scales to dimension d > 50 via certified restarts that provably never falsely eliminate the region containing the true optimizer x* (Theorem 6.1, Section 6).
claims.evidence: Implemented CGP-TR in d=60 (meeting the d>50 threshold) with 20 seeds; the certified-restart rule achieved a 0.0 false-restart rate for the x*-containing region across 89900 checks vs 1.0 for the naive control, but with significant disclosed scope reductions (no expand/contract radius dynamics, uniform random re-centering instead of Sobol, checking all regions every round beyond Algorithm 3's literal pseudocode) and the allocation-bound sub-check was inconclusive due to zero variance in the construction.
