tomyimkc/repro-certificate-guided-prunin.overall: The logbook provides clean verification of Claim 1 (active-set certificate validity with strong controls) but only toy-level evidence for Claims 2–6, each of which was exercised on a simplified setup (low dimensions, synthetic functions, proxy quantities, or reduced algorithm dynamics) with mixed or partial numerical results that do not cleanly confirm the paper's theoretical guarantees.

tomyimkc/repro-steady-state-behavior-of-.paper_title: Steady-State Behavior of Constant-Stepsize Stochastic Approximation: Gaussian Approximation and Tail Bounds

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 (i.i.d. noise) and Theorem 4.1 (Markovian noise) bound the Wasserstein distance between the centered-scaled steady state Y^(α) = (X^(α) − x*)/√α and its Gaussian limit N(0, Σ_Y) by U√α log(1/α) (Theorems 3.1 and 4.1).
claims.evidence: 1-d quadratic with h=2.0 and a 2-state Markov chain (flip p=0.3); 600k samples across 5 stepsizes. Ratios W1/(√α log(1/α)) stay bounded (max 0.087 i.i.d., 0.170 Markovian), consistent with the bound, but the setup is a single 1-dimensional quadratic with the simplest possible 2-state chain—far below the general d-dimensional, general-drift, general-noise setting of Theorems 3.1/4.1.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 establishes an explicit non-asymptotic Wasserstein bound of order O(α^{1/2} log(1/α)) for constant-stepsize SGD on smooth, strongly convex objectives (Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: 2-d objective f(x)=0.5(x−x*)ᵀH(x−x*)+0.25‖x−x*‖⁴ with 5 seeds and 120k samples; sliced W1 ratios max 0.164, log-log slope 0.443≈0.5. The nonlinear quartic term is a genuine improvement over pure quadratic, but it is still a single 2-d objective family—clearly simplified relative to the general smooth strongly-convex setting of Proposition 3.1.

claims.claim: Propositions 3.2 and 3.3 extend the same O(α^{1/2} log(1/α)) Wasserstein bound to linear stochastic approximation with a Hurwitz matrix and to contractive nonlinear stochastic approximation, respectively (Propositions 3.2 and 3.3, Section 3.2.2, Section 3.2.3).
claims.evidence: 2-d linear SA with one specific Hurwitz matrix A=[[1.6,0.4],[−0.2,1.2]] and one contractive rotation map (ρ=0.7); 300k samples. Ratios are bounded (max 0.028 linear, 0.043 contractive), but the contractive arm's W1 is nearly flat across α (slope −0.050), suggesting measurement noise domination, and both instances are single 2-d cases far below the general setting.

claims.claim: For one-dimensional projections, the paper derives a non-uniform Berry-Esseen-type tail bound |P(⟨Y^(α),ζ⟩ > a) − P(Z_ζ > a)| ≤ C_d α^{1/4} log^{1/2}(1/α) / a, which improves as the deviation level a grows (Section 4).
claims.evidence: 1-d SGD chain with 2M samples across 5 deviation levels and 4 stepsizes; smallest C_d=0.022, 1/a improvement confirmed (32× error drop vs 5× for 1/a). The tail bound is well-tested with good statistical power, but the setup is a 1-d chain (the projection is trivially the identity), a simplified special case of the d-dimensional projection bound.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 extends the Gaussian approximation and tail bounds for SGD, linear SA, and contractive nonlinear SA from i.i.d. noise to Markovian noise (Proposition 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: 2-d linear and contractive SA driven by a 2-state Markov chain (flip p=0.5); 200k samples. Poisson-equation covariance error shrinks with α (0.032→0.005), W1 ratios bounded (max 0.025/0.037), tail C_d=0.005. However, the 2-state chain produces a rank-deficient S_eff=[[0.5,−0.5],[−0.5,0.5]] and the setup is a single 2-d instance, well below the general Markov-chain setting of Proposition 4.1.

claims.claim: Proposition 5.1 shows a different convergence rate of order α^{1/h} for constant-stepsize SA applied to general convex objectives with Gibbs-type limiting distributions (Proposition 5.1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: 1-d objective f(x)=|x|^h/h for h∈{2,3,4,6} with 200k samples; log-log slopes of median|X| vs α are 0.505/0.357/0.230/0.110 vs expected 1/h=0.500/0.333/0.250/0.167. The h=2 control correctly recovers 0.5 and the ratio diagnostic (constant /α^{1/h} vs growing /√α) supports the scaling, but h=6 is significantly off (0.110 vs 0.167) due to inadequate burnin, and the setup is 1-d.

tomyimkc/repro-steady-state-behavior-of-.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from 1-2 dimensional constant-stepsize SA simulations that is consistent with all six claims, with thoughtful controls (weak drift, non-Hurwitz, expansive maps, slow-mixing chains) confirming preconditions are load-bearing. However, every experiment runs on clearly simplified toy instances—1-2 dimensions, specific simple objectives, 2-state Markov chains—far below the paper's general d-dimensional regime, so these are sanity checks rather than full reproductions.

tomyimkc/repro-efficiently-learning-drif.paper_title: Efficiently Learning Drifting Halfspaces with Massart Noise

claims.claim: The paper's polynomial-time algorithm learns margin-separable halfspaces under distribution drift with Massart noise achieving error eta + O~(Delta^{1/3}/gamma), where eta bounds the Massart noise rate, Delta is the drift rate, and gamma is the margin parameter (Theorem 1.1, Section 1.1).
claims.evidence: The actual DriftedMassart/DriftPerceptron algorithm is implemented faithfully (correct epoch length W=2*floor(Delta^{-2/3}*log(1/Delta)), step size mu=gamma/sqrt(W), Massart-weighted gradient, held-out trajectory selection) on margin-separable drifting halfspaces with RCN noise. The measured excess error scales as Delta^{0.287} (theory: Delta^{1/3}=0.333, abs diff 0.046) across 5 Delta values with 8 seeds, and the frozen-hypothesis control is 2.56x worse at all 5 deltas, confirming the re-estimation mechanism is load-bearing.

claims.claim: Under the low-degree polynomial hardness conjecture, any efficient algorithm for this drifting halfspace problem must incur excess error Omega(Delta^{1/3}), matching the algorithm's guarantee and establishing an information-computation gap (Theorem 1.2, Section 1.1).
claims.evidence: The experiment uses a window-length resource budget as a proxy for low-degree polynomial restriction (60-round vs 300-round detector), not the actual low-degree polynomial framework. The gap ratio of 2.0x is measured on the agent's own trajectory-testing construction, not the paper's Def 4.1/4.3, and targets only the qualitative information-computation gap, not the precise Delta^{1/3} exponent.

claims.claim: For general VC-dimension-d hypothesis classes under Massart noise, the statistically optimal (possibly inefficient) error rate is O~(sqrt(d*Delta)), better than the Theta((d*Delta)^{1/3}) rate achievable under adversarial noise (Theorem 2.1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: Exact ERM via dynamic programming on k-interval classes (d=2,4,8) is a real experiment, but the specific class exhibits near-parametric convergence rather than the worst-case VC rates the theorem describes. Massart excess is <= adversarial excess at only 14/18 points, and the claimed sqrt(d*Delta) vs (d*Delta)^{1/3} exponents are not recovered.

claims.claim: A matching information-theoretic lower bound of Omega(sqrt(d*Delta)) is proved for halfspaces under random classification noise (RCN), establishing optimality at Theta~(sqrt(d*Delta)) (Theorem 2.2, Section 2).
claims.evidence: A Le Cam-style detectability test on the agent's own RCN trajectory-testing construction shows a genuine phase transition (AUC 0.499 to 0.992), but the d*Delta matching control is loose (max AUC gap 0.187 between d=8 and d=16 at matched d*Delta, and d*Delta at AUC>=0.9 differs by 2x). This is supportive evidence for a detectability threshold, not a reproduction of the lower bound proof.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 formally shows that no polynomial of degree less than O(gamma^{-c/4}) can distinguish the null from alternative hypothesis in the associated trajectory-testing problem, giving the formal low-degree hardness evidence for the Delta^{1/3} scaling (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Dimension d is used as a stand-in for the margin parameter gamma, and window length as a proxy for polynomial degree. The resource-scaling exponent of 0.500 is estimated from only 2 data points (d=16 vs d=64) and is explicitly not claimed to match the paper's O(gamma^{-c/4}) bound. The paper's actual Def 4.1/4.3 construction was not accessible.

claims.claim: In the realizable setting, the algorithm's error improves to O~(Delta*gamma^{-3/2}), surpassing the prior best known bound of O~(Delta*gamma^{-2}) (Theorem 3.2, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The experiment uses a continual-tracking scaffold instead of the paper's discrete-epoch ERM-selection algorithm. The new update's fitted gamma-exponent (-1.330) is somewhat close to the claimed -1.5, but the prior update's exponent (-1.403) falls far short of the claimed -2.0. The new update beats the prior at all 7 gammas, supporting the qualitative direction but not the precise magnitudes.

tomyimkc/repro-efficiently-learning-drif.overall: The logbook provides a faithful empirical reproduction of Claim 1's main algorithmic result (Theorem 1.1), confirming the Delta^{1/3} drift-rate scaling with a meaningful frozen-hypothesis control. The remaining five claims are addressed with real but simplified proxy experiments at small scale that capture qualitative directions without recovering the paper's precise theoretical rates or constructions.

tomyimkc/repro-all-erms-can-fail-in-stoc.paper_title: All ERMs Can Fail in Stochastic Convex Optimization Lower Bounds in Linear Dimension

claims.claim: In dimension d = 6m, there exists a stochastic convex optimization instance where every ε-ERM solution with ε = Θ(m^{-3/2}) incurs constant excess risk and fails to generalize (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: At m=6..10 (d=36..60), the closed-form ERM w_S* is verified as the empirical minimizer (beats 0 and 8 random feasible points, 100% of checks) with median population excess risk 0.0445–0.0582 that is positive for 100% of samples and does not decay with m (log-log slope -0.211), consistent with Ω(1). The control relaxing ε to Θ(m^{-1/2}) drives the Lemma-5 bound negative, confirming the ε=Θ(m^{-3/2}) precondition is necessary.

claims.claim: For λ-strongly convex losses with m^{-3/2} ≤ λ ≤ m^{-1/2}, any ε-ERM solution w_S satisfies F(w_S) − min F(w) ≥ Ω(1/(λ m^{3/2})) (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: At m=10, sweeping λ across [m^{-3/2}, m^{-1/2}], the Lemma-5 lower bound scales with log-log slope 1.000 against the rate 1/(λ m^{1.5}), is positive for all λ, and the realized excess exceeds the bound everywhere (excess_meets_lemma5_bound_all=True). The control below the admissible range confirms the min{...} cap binds as predicted.

claims.claim: When ηT = Ω(m^{3/2}), gradient descent incurs constant generalization error with high probability, as a corollary of the ERM lower bound (Corollary 3).
claims.evidence: Projected subgradient descent at m=8 converges to the bad ERM: final GD median excess (0.0445) equals the bad-ERM excess (0.0445), and the analytical optimization-error rate 1/(ηT) crosses m^{-3/2} exactly at ηT=m^{1.5} (rate_threshold_factor=1.0), confirming GD becomes an O(m^{-3/2})-ERM and inherits constant excess via Theorem 1.

claims.claim: Gradient descent's excess risk is lower-bounded by F(w_S^{GD}) − min F(w) = Ω(min{√(ηT/m^{3/2}), 1}) (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Using the closed-form GD trajectory from Lemma 7 at m=8, the load-bearing h_D gap grows with log-log slope 0.56 against ηT (matching the predicted √ rate) and slope 1.12 against √(ηT/m^{1.5}), is monotonically increasing, and the Lemma-7 proven lower bound is positive for all ηT. The control confirms the √(ηT/m^{1.5}) form would exceed the known upper bound ηT/m below ηT=√m, validating the precondition.

claims.claim: This new generalization lower bound of Ω(ηT + √(ηT/m^{3/2})) for constrained gradient descent narrows the previously exponential gap to the best known upper bound of O(ηT + ηT/m) (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Analytical comparison across the overfitting curve confirms the new lower bound Ω(η√T + √(ηT/m^{1.5})) never exceeds the upper bound O(η√T + ηT/m) (new_lower_le_upper_all=True), the gap ratio grows polynomially (log-log slope 0.378), and the horizon needed to witness overfitting drops from 2^m to m^{3/2}/η with asymptotic reduction slope 0.977 approaching 1, confirming exponential narrowing.

claims.claim: The construction uses Feldman's asymptotically good binary code combined with a novel 'link function' mapping sample information to bad ERM solutions while preserving convexity, giving the first proof that all approximate ERMs fail in linear dimension (Section on technical construction / proof of Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The code is asymptotically good (ρ=0.125–0.167, separation holds at k=12,16,20), the link function uniquely identifies the sample (v_S^s is the unique maximizer for 100% of samples, p>0 always), the loss is convex (400 midpoint tests, worst violation 0.0), and the critical ablation setting γ_c=0 collapses the h_D overfitting gap to exactly 0, demonstrating the link function is the mechanism driving ERM failure.

tomyimkc/repro-all-erms-can-fail-in-stoc.overall: The logbook faithfully instantiates the paper's explicit SCO construction (Feldman code, link function, closed-form ERM and GD trajectories) at m=6–10 (d=36–60) with real numerical computations, controls, and ablations, providing concrete evidence supporting all six claims including constant excess risk for approximate ERMs, the curvature-refined rate, GD overfitting, the √-rate GD lower bound, polynomial gap narrowing, and the structural necessity of the link function. The main limitation is small m due to the 2^{2m} codeword materialization, but the construction is the paper's own at the paper's scale, not a simplified proxy.

tomyimkc/repro-gaavi-global-asymptotic-a.paper_title: GAAVI: Global Asymptotic Anytime Valid Inference for the Conditional Mean Function

claims.claim: GAAVI achieves approximately uniform (asymptotically anytime-valid) type-I error control at level alpha for all times t greater than or equal to a burn-in time t0, under boundedness assumptions on the outcome (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: R=3000 repeats, T=3000 steps under the global null show empirical type-I error of 0.0227 (adaptive) and 0.0197 (oscillating) at alpha=0.10, both below nominal; a control dropping the l>0 variance floor inflates error to 0.1217 (3.6 SE above alpha), confirming the guarantee and its load-bearing condition.

claims.claim: Under L2(P_X) convergence of sequential regressors and a positive covariance condition, GAAVI rejects a false global null with probability one in finite time, i.e. achieves power one (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: With a consistent regressor satisfying the positive-covariance condition, rejection probability ramps from 0.014 (T=250) to 1.0 (T=4000) across R=1500 repeats; a reflected-control regressor engineered to violate the covariance condition produces zero rejections at all horizons through T=8000.

claims.claim: Under nuisance consistency (Assumption 4.5), the expected sample complexity N_f(alpha) satisfies limsup_{alpha->0} E[N_f(alpha)]/log(1/alpha) <= Gamma^{-1}(tau,f), matching the optimal sample complexity of parametric Gaussian location testing (Theorem 4.7).
claims.evidence: The ratio E[N_f]/log(1/alpha) decreases monotonically from 79.6 to 28.4 across alpha from 0.1 to 1e-30, approaching but remaining 18.1% above the reference Gamma^{-1}=24.0; the asymptotic inequality is never numerically satisfied at any tested alpha, and the setup uses a simplified constant-shift DGP with a scalar running-mean regressor.

claims.claim: GAAVI is formulated for two data-generating processes: testing a generic conditional mean function global null (DGP1) and testing a conditional average treatment effect global null with binary treatment under a positivity assumption on propensity scores (Section 2, Assumption 2.3).
claims.evidence: Both DGP1 (phi=Y) and DGP2 (augmented-IPW phi_CATE) are implemented from the paper's equations; at n=300,000 with 10 seeds, max per-bin bias is 0.00214 for DGP1 and 0.0065–0.033 for DGP2 (oracle and misspecified g), and sweeping kappa from 5 to 1000 inflates Var(phi_CATE) 3.47x while bias stays flat, confirming the positivity assumption's role.

claims.claim: The test is constructed via a predictable weighted martingale whose confidence-sequence inversion yields function-valued asymptotic confidence sequences for the CMF/CATE, evaluated on synthetic data and the French jobs real-world dataset (Section 3, Section 5).
claims.evidence: CS inversion is demonstrated on synthetic data only: coverage of the true c=0 is 0.9993 at T=3000 (vs nominal 0.90) and CS width shrinks 177x, but the function-valued aspect is reduced to a 21-point grid of constant candidates, and the French jobs real-world evaluation is entirely missing due to no network access.

tomyimkc/repro-gaavi-global-asymptotic-a.overall: The logbook provides non-trivial Monte Carlo evidence (R=1500–3000, T=3000–8000) with mechanism-isolating controls verifying type-I error control (Theorem 4.2), power one (Theorem 4.4), and the two-DGP formulation (Section 2), while the asymptotic sample-complexity bound (Theorem 4.7) and the full confidence-sequence claim (including the French jobs evaluation) are only partially addressed on simplified setups.

tomyimkc/repro-achieving-logarithmic-reg.paper_title: Achieving Logarithmic Regret in KL-Regularized Zero-Sum Markov Games

claims.claim: OMG (Algorithm 1) for two-player zero-sum matrix games achieves a regularization-dependent regret bound of O(β⁻¹d²(1+σ²log(T/δ))log(T/d)), logarithmic in T, alongside a regularization-independent bound of O((1+σ)d√T log(T/δ)) (Theorem 2.1, Section 2.3).
claims.evidence: At 10×10 actions, d=8, T=3000, 10 seeds, the beta=0 control yields growth exponent 0.489 (matching √T≈0.5) while regularized betas (0.3, 1.0, 3.0) yield exponents 0.053, 0.040, 0.044 (near-zero, consistent with logarithmic), with NE solver validated to 2.66e-15 dual-gap residual and regret-to-bound ratios not growing with T.

claims.claim: SOMG (Algorithm 2) for finite-horizon Markov games achieves a regularization-dependent regret bound of O(β⁻¹d³H⁷log²(dT/δ)), logarithmic in T, versus a regularization-independent bound of O(d³ᐟ²H³√T log(dT/δ)) (Theorem 3.1, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: At 4 states, 3×3 actions, H=3, d=4, T≤600, 6 seeds, the regularized exponents (0.20–0.22) are clearly below the beta=0 control (0.489) but do not reach the near-zero regime expected for logarithmic regret, and the instance is far below the paper's asymptotic scale.

claims.claim: OMG attains sample complexity min{Õ(d²/ε²), Õ(β⁻¹d²/ε)} for matrix games, and SOMG attains min{Õ(d³H⁶/ε²), Õ(β⁻¹d³H⁷/ε)} for Markov games, both improving over prior O(β⁻¹... ) and O̅(d√T) bounds from Yang et al. 2025a (VMG) (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Sample-complexity exponents from regret-to-PAC conversion at small scale show OMG regularized p=-1.061 (close to -1) and control p=-1.640, but SOMG regularized p=-1.331 (between -1 and -2, not cleanly matching -1), and the comparison against Yang et al. 2025a (VMG) was not implemented.

claims.claim: The Markov-game regret analysis uses superoptimistic bonuses satisfying 2|Q⁺−Q̄| ≥ |Q⁺−Q^μ|, combined with three maintained Q/V-function estimates, to eliminate the √T dependence via squared rather than linear bonus terms (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: In a synthetic single-stage ridge-regression setup matching the paper's bonus construction (d=10, 2000 trials), the superoptimistic-gap property 2|Q⁺−Q̄|≥|Q⁺−Q^μ| holds with coverage 1.0 at full margin, degrading monotonically to 0.7315 with no bonus, directly confirming the algebraic mechanism and its necessity.

claims.claim: Both OMG and SOMG recover the standard Õ(√T) regret bound when the KL regularization strength β = 0, showing the logarithmic-regret improvement is specific to regularized play (Section 2.3, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Beta sweeps show beta=0 exponents of 0.381 (OMG) and 0.488 (SOMG), near but not tightly at 0.5, with an anomalous non-monotonic point at OMG beta=0.05 (p=0.887), at modest scale (T≤1500 for OMG, T≤350 for SOMG).

tomyimkc/repro-achieving-logarithmic-reg.overall: The logbook provides strong, decisive evidence for Claim 1 (OMG matrix-game logarithmic vs √T regret) and Claim 4 (superoptimistic-gap algebraic property) at non-trivial scale with exact NE solves and proper controls. Claims 2, 3, and 5 are only directionally supported at small Markov-game scale (4 states, H=3, T in the hundreds) where the logarithmic regime is not fully reached and the VMG comparison is absent.

tomyimkc/repro-balancing-learning-rates-.paper_title: Balancing Learning Rates Across Layers: Exact Two-Step Dynamics and Optimal Scaling in Linear Neural Networks

claims.claim: For two-layer linear networks trained on single-index targets, Theorem 5.3 gives exact closed-form test-loss expressions after one and two gradient steps, with the one-step loss containing linear signal-alignment terms plus quadratic/interaction over-updating terms, and the two-step loss exhibiting higher-order dependence on the product η₁η₂ of the two layers' learning rates.
claims.evidence: At h=1000 with 8 seeds, the one-step closed form matches independent GD to 0.0026 relative error and the two-step form to 0.00078 in the small-lr regime; the two-step leading log-log slope in η₁η₂ is 3.99 (confirming degree-4 vs degree-2 for one step), and the control with non-orthogonal X breaks the match (rel error 5.3e7 vs 3.6e-4).

claims.claim: Corollary 5.4 shows that for a learning-rate budget η₁+η₂=2h^α with 1<α≤3/2, symmetric learning rates η₁=η₂=h^α are suboptimal after one gradient step but become locally optimal after two steps in sufficiently wide two-layer networks.
claims.evidence: At h=1000, for all tested α∈{1.1,1.25,1.5}, the one-step symmetric curvature is negative (suboptimal, e.g. -8.6e-7 at α=1.5 with gain 0.001 from asymmetry) while the two-step curvature is positive (locally optimal, +5.4e-5 with global minimizer at 0.5); empirical GD cross-check confirms step-1 minimizer at 0.1 and step-2 at 0.5; control at α=1.6 flips step-2 curvature to -0.0013.

claims.claim: For three-layer linear networks, Theorem 5.5 derives analogous one- and two-step test-loss formulas under a critical learning-rate scaling η₁,η₂≤O(h), a stricter regime than the O(h√h) scaling used for two-layer networks.
claims.evidence: The 3-NN one-step formula's dominant signal term is -2η/h (natural scale O(h)), confirmed structurally and quantitatively (3.9% max relative error vs GD at h=1000); the 3-NN two-step divergence onset is lr≈190 (onset/h=0.19) vs 2-NN onset lr=100000 (onset/h=100), confirming O(h) is stricter than O(h√h); control at lr=h gives loss 1.7e7 vs 0.10 at lr=0.05h.

claims.claim: Corollary 5.6 demonstrates a similar transition from asymmetric to balanced optimal learning rates in three-layer networks for 0<α≤2/3.
claims.evidence: The asymmetric-to-balanced transition is confirmed for α∈{0.2,0.3,0.4,0.5} at h=1000: one-step symmetric curvature negative (suboptimal) and two-step curvature positive (locally optimal, minimizer at 0.5), with empirical GD cross-check at α=0.5 confirming step-1 minimizer at 0.1 and step-2 at 0.5; however, at the α=2/3 boundary the step-2 curvature turns negative (-0.012) because the budget reaches the surrogate's O(h) regime limit, so the full claimed range is not fully covered.

claims.claim: Proposition 5.1 decomposes each layer's gradient as G_ℓ^t = B_ℓ^t - A_ℓ^t, where A terms capture data-aligned components and B terms capture self-interaction effects that are suppressed by a factor of 1/(√h - 1) below the critical learning-rate threshold.
claims.evidence: The decomposition G_l = B_l - A_l is exact to 1.3e-18 across both layers and h∈{50,100,200,500,1000}; the ratio ||B||/||A|| equals 1/√h exactly (0.0316 at h=1000, within the stated bound 1/(√h-1)=0.0327) with log-log slope -0.50; the control scaling W2 by 10× raises the ratio to 0.316, confirming suppression disappears above the critical threshold.

tomyimkc/repro-balancing-learning-rates-.overall: All five claims are supported by concrete experimental evidence at the paper's scale (h=1000) using independent numpy implementations with GD cross-checks and controls that break when preconditions are violated. The main caveat is Claim 4, where the transition is verified for α≤0.5 but breaks at the α=2/3 boundary due to the surrogate's validity regime, leaving the upper end of the claimed range unconfirmed.

tomyimkc/repro-multiple-choice-learning-.paper_title: Multiple Choice Learning of Low-Rank Adapters for Language Modeling

claims.claim: On the TextCaps image-captioning task with 3 candidate hypotheses, LoRA-MCL attains a SPIDEr score of 0.955 versus 0.915 for a LoRA-MLE baseline with diverse beam search (Section 5, Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly did not run real TextCaps, a real vision-language model, or compute SPIDEr. Instead it used a 12-token vocabulary synthetic Markov-chain mixture with a proxy 'expected positional match' metric (0.204 vs 0.330), which is not comparable to the claimed 0.955 vs 0.915 SPIDEr scores.

claims.claim: On a synthetic bilingual English-French TextCaps captioning task, LoRA-MCL reaches 0.464 SPIDEr on French generations versus 0.411 for the baseline (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Same synthetic Markov-chain analog as Claim 1 with K=2 modes, using a proxy metric (0.196 vs 0.265) instead of SPIDEr on real bilingual TextCaps data. No real bilingual captions, no real captioning model, and the proxy scores are not comparable to the claimed 0.464 vs 0.411.

claims.claim: Under Assumption 2 (data generated from a mixture of latent processes), Proposition 1 shows the Winner-Takes-All loss acts as a conditional form of hard-EM, with min_θ ℒ(θ) − log K ≤ min_θ ℒ_WTA(θ) ≤ ℋ(x|c,z) ≤ min_θ ℒ(θ) (Section 4.1, Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook directly implemented Assumption 2 (K=6 categorical mixture, 60-symbol vocabulary, 500K samples) and verified all three inequalities both analytically and via an actual WTA hard-EM optimizer: H(x)-logK=2.124 ≤ WTA=2.164 ≤ H(x|z)=2.124 ≤ H(x)=3.916, with a leaky-support control confirming the Assumption-4 tightness dependence (gap shifts from +0.041 to -1.001).

claims.claim: For Markov chain data, Corollary 1 proves standard MLE converges to a weighted average of transition matrices, whereas LoRA-MCL recovers the individual modes (Section 4.2-4.3, Corollary 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook implemented Corollary 1's Markov-chain mixture construction (K=3 chains, 6-state vocabulary, 50K sequences of length 100) and confirmed MLE converges to the theoretical weighted-average transition matrix (max error 0.006) while being far from individual modes (error 0.776), whereas WTA hard-EM recovers individual chains (error 0.0018, 100% recovery accuracy), with a near-identical-chains control degrading recovery to chance level (0.362 vs 1/3).

claims.claim: On AudioCaps audio captioning with 5 candidate hypotheses, LoRA-MCL's test loss decreases monotonically from 2.152 at K=1 to 1.927 at K=5 (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook did not run real AudioCaps or a real audio-captioning model. It used a synthetic 5-component categorical mixture (vocab 100, 300K samples) with proxy NLL values (4.409 to 2.861) that are not comparable to the claimed 2.152 to 1.927, though the qualitative monotonic decrease pattern was observed with a flat-control confirming the mechanism.

tomyimkc/repro-multiple-choice-learning-.overall: The logbook provides genuine verification of the two theoretical claims (Proposition 1's inequality chain and Corollary 1's MLE-averages-vs-WTA-recovers-modes dichotomy) through direct implementation at scale with appropriate controls. The three empirical benchmark claims (TextCaps, bilingual TextCaps, AudioCaps) are only addressed through synthetic Markov-chain or categorical-mixture analogs with proxy metrics, not on the real datasets or models, so their specific numerical claims remain unreproduced.

MarxistLeninist/icml2026-repro-Kk5UZgkWF.paper_title: Combinatorial Sparse PCA Beyond the Spiked Identity Model

claims.claim: Diagonal thresholding provably fails on the general-covariance model (Model 2), failing to detect any true support element with probability at least 1/2 even with a Θ(1) eigenvalue gap (Lemma 1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: An independent Model-2 counterexample with flat diagonal and a decoy block shows DiagThresh yields median sin^2=1.0 over 41 seeds (missing true support entirely), with a proper Model-1 positive control (sin^2=0.07) and RTPM recovery control (sin^2=0.0006). The construction is independent rather than the exact paper matrix, but concretely demonstrates the failure mechanism.

claims.claim: Covariance thresholding fails analogously, returning an estimate 𝐮 with sin²∠(𝐮,𝐯)=1 with probability at least 1/2 despite sufficient samples (Lemma 3, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The explicit r-regular-graph block construction from Lemma 3 (s=16, u=9, tau=0.05) is implemented; population-level thresholding flips to the U-block (sin^2=1.0), finite-sample CovThresh with n=12000 gives median sin^2=1.0, and the eigenratio condition lambda1/lambda2=1.58>=4/3 is verified, with Model-1 control at sin^2=0.004.

claims.claim: Greedy correlation-based selection recovers at most one true support coordinate under Model 2, even when seeded with a correct coordinate (Lemma 4, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The Hadamard g_r construction from Lemma 4 (s=8) is implemented; inequality (7) holds on the population matrix and empirically with probability 1.0 over 41 seeds. GreedyCorr seeded at a correct coordinate i*=0 yields median sin^2=0.93, close to the theoretical lower bound 1-1/s=0.875, confirming recovery of at most one coordinate.

claims.claim: The proposed Restarted Truncated Power Method (RTPM) achieves ⟨𝐯,𝐮⟩² ≥ 9/10 with probability ≥ 1-δ under Model 2 using n = Ω(s² log(s) log(d/δ)) samples and O(nd²) runtime (Theorem 1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: RTPM achieves sin^2<=0.12 on all three counterexample Sigmas (0.0006, 0.004, 0.11), and the C5 scaling experiment shows n=12s^2 log d yields recovery probability>=0.95 for all tested s while linear budget n=30s yields probability 0.0, supporting the s^2 sample complexity. The log-log slope (~1.00) is noisy at small scales but the sufficiency and negative controls provide concrete support for the theorem's mechanism.

claims.claim: Sparse k-PCA cannot be solved by deflation-based self-reduction to the single-component case, since deflated covariance matrices can have fully dense top eigenvectors (Lemma 11, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: No experiment in the logbook addresses Lemma 11 or deflation-based self-reduction for sparse k-PCA; the pages cover only C1-C6 (baseline failures, RTPM success, scaling, and sample-splitting), with no construction or test of deflated covariance matrices having dense top eigenvectors.

MarxistLeninist/icml2026-repro-Kk5UZgkWF.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting Claims 1-4 by implementing explicit counterexample constructions from the paper's lemmas, running 41+ seeds with proper Model-1 positive controls and RTPM recovery controls, and demonstrating that all three baselines fail while RTPM succeeds on Model 2. Claim 5 (deflation impossibility) is never addressed, and the sample-complexity scaling evidence is directionally supportive but noisy at small scales.

Srishti280992/repro-codetaste-can-llms-g.paper_title: CodeTaste: Can LLMs Generate Human-Level Code Refactorings?

claims.claim: CodeTaste comprises 100 refactoring instances mined from 87 GitHub repositories across 6 programming languages, with an average of 91.52 files and 2,605.39 lines changed per task (Section 3.5, Table 1).
claims.evidence: The independent audit script parsed all 100 golden.diff files from the released v1.0.0 artifact, yielding instances=100, unique_repositories=87, languages=6, and golden means of files_changed=91.52 and lines_edited=2605.39, all matching the claim exactly.

claims.claim: On the Instructed Track, GPT-5.2 achieves a 69.6% alignment score and 76.0% functional-correctness (Pass) rate, versus 32.4% alignment and 47.0% Pass for Claude Sonnet 4.5, and 11.8% alignment for Qwen3 (Section 4.2, Table 3).
claims.evidence: Recomputed metrics from 2000 released evaluation results show GPT-5.2 at 69.6% alignment and 76.0% PASS (matching), but Claude Sonnet 4.5 at 32.1% alignment and 43.0% PASS (claim says 32.4% and 47.0%) and Qwen3 at 10.7% alignment (claim says 11.8%), contradicting the specific values in the claim.

claims.claim: On the Open Track, where agents see only a high-level focus area instead of a detailed specification, the best alignment score collapses to 7.7% (GPT-5.2, Direct mode) (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: GPT-5.2 Open Direct alignment from released outputs is 7.93% (rounded to 7.9%), not the claimed 7.7%; while the qualitative collapse below 8% is supported, the specific numerical value is contradicted.

claims.claim: A propose-then-implement (Plan mode) decomposition raises GPT-5.2's Open Track alignment from 7.7% to 14.1%, and Oracle multiplan selection raises it further to 19.4% (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Released outputs show GPT-5.2 Open Track alignment of 7.9% (direct) → 15.1% (plan) → 20.6% (multiplan), whereas the claim asserts 7.7% → 14.1% → 19.4%; the directional improvement is confirmed but all three specific values are contradicted.

claims.claim: Static-rule evaluation uses an average of 93.07 additive/reductive OpenGrep rules per task (30 additive, 63 reductive) to measure Instruction Following Rate alongside test-suite Pass rate (Section 3.4, Table 1).
claims.evidence: Counting YAML rule objects across all 100 instances gives 17.94 additive, 63.41 reductive, and 81.35 total rules per task on average, contradicting the claimed 30 additive, 63 reductive, and 93.07 total; the reductive count is close but additive and total are substantially off.

claims.claim: GPT-5.2's superior alignment comes at roughly $5.17 per task in agent inference cost, compared to $3.46 for Claude Sonnet 4.5 and $0.59 for GPT-5.1 Codex Mini (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: Released Instructed Direct metadata gives cost_mean of $5.1747 for GPT-5.2, $3.4634 for Claude Sonnet 4.5, and $0.5943 for GPT-5.1 Codex Mini, matching the claimed $5.17, $3.46, and $0.59 per task.

Srishti280992/repro-codetaste-can-llms-g.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous full-scale audit of the CodeTaste v1.0.0 release artifacts using independent code over 100 instances and 2000 evaluation results, verifying the benchmark composition and inference-cost claims exactly. However, it falsifies several specific numerical values in the performance-leaderboard, Open-Track, and rule-count claims, with released outputs differing from the claimed values for Claude Sonnet 4.5, Qwen3, Open Track alignment, Plan/Multiplan gains, and additive/total rule counts.

Srishti280992/repro-gaussian-mechanism-s.paper_title: Asymptotic Optimality of the High-Dimensional Gaussian Mechanism and Improved Low-Dimensional Mechanisms for Differential Privacy

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 proves that as dimension T→∞, the Gaussian mechanism achieves the best privacy-utility tradeoff among all additive-noise mechanisms in the high-privacy regime δ ≤ δ⋆ (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: At T=16384 with ε=0.1 and δ=1e-3, three non-Gaussian SGG competitors (p=0.75, 1.0, 4.0) matched to Gaussian MSE show absolute excess delta ≤ 7.28e-7, with the trend of convergence visible from T=4 (excess up to 0.0016) through T=16384, supporting the asymptotic optimality claim on a non-trivial scale.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.3 shows that Haar symmetrization of arbitrary additive noise preserves mean squared error while improving privacy, establishing that spherically symmetric noise distributions are optimal (Lemma 3.3).
claims.evidence: An anisotropic T=8 Gaussian mixture with 50x variance ratio was Haar-symmetrized via a 64-component random-orthogonal mixture; MSE was preserved exactly (10.83 both before and after), and worst-direction delta dropped from 0.9017 to [0.244, 0.302] across 12 tested directions, concretely demonstrating both signatures of Lemma 3.3.

claims.claim: The paper introduces the Spherical Generalized Gamma (SGG) family, a three-parameter family with radial density f(r) = pβ^((α+1)/p)/Γ((α+1)/p) · r^α · exp(-βr^p) that includes the Gaussian and ℓ2 mechanisms as special cases (Definition 4.1-4.2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: For five spread-out (T,α,β,p) tuples, the SGG radial density normalized to 1.0 within 1.5e-11, and the transform z=βr^p passed Gamma(k,1) KS tests; the p=2 Gaussian special case matched closed-form delta to 7.6e-8, and the p=1 l2-Laplace case matched the analytic MSE formula T(T+1)θ² to floating-point precision.

claims.claim: Figure 2 shows that in low dimensions (T=2 to 5) at ε=0.1, certain SGG mechanisms reduce MSE by up to 15% relative to the Gaussian and ℓ2 mechanisms, with the improvement shrinking as dimension increases (Figure 2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Grid search over the α=T-1 SGG slice at ε=0.1 found MSE reductions of 15.55% at T=2, 11.60% at T=3, 9.60% at T=4, 8.23% at T=5, declining to 4.54% at T=10 and 3.89% at T=12, reproducing both the up-to-15% magnitude and the shrinking-with-dimension trend from Figure 2.

claims.claim: Table 2 reports empirical lower bounds on the threshold δ⋆ above which Gaussian optimality holds, e.g. δ⋆ ≥ 0.737 at ε=0.25 and δ⋆ ≥ 0.198 at ε=16.0 (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Reimplemented Gaussian privacy function derivatives and tangent-support/convexity checks recovered all seven Table 2 δ⋆ thresholds to within 7.15e-7 absolute error (e.g., ε=0.25: 0.736671 vs 0.736670; ε=16.0: 0.197615 vs 0.197615), with all conditions holding within numerical tolerance.

claims.claim: The paper resolves an open question from Joseph et al. (2025) by providing a tight composition analysis for the ℓ2 mechanism via the unified SGG framework and an FFT-based composition algorithm (Section 4.4, Algorithm 7).
claims.evidence: FFT convolution accountant for l2 mechanism (T=10, p=1, α=9) at (ε_total,δ)=(1,1e-5) yielded MSE reductions of 31.4%–94.1% over sequential composition for k=2–32, with Monte Carlo cross-checks at k≤8 confirming composed delta near the 1e-5 target (1.8e-5, 1.1e-5, 0.7e-5), supporting the tight-composition claim.

Srishti280992/repro-gaussian-mechanism-s.overall: This logbook provides concrete from-scratch numerical evidence (numpy/scipy only) supporting all six claims: high-dimensional Gaussian convergence, Haar symmetrization, SGG normalization and special cases, low-dimensional MSE reductions, Table 2 threshold recovery, and FFT composition gains for the l2 mechanism. The evidence is a numerical audit of a theory paper rather than a proof reconstruction, with some scope limitations (SGG subset only for Claim 1, grid search instead of Bayesian optimizer for Claim 4).

ProCreations/repro-faircrowd-demographic.paper_title: Optimal Fair Aggregation of Crowdsourced Noisy Labels using Demographic Parity Constraints

claims.claim: The demographic parity gap of majority-vote aggregated labels is bounded above by an exponentially decaying term in the number of annotators R, of the form sum over groups a of E[e^{-R K_phi(a,X)}] (Proposition 3.2).
claims.evidence: Exact enumeration of a one-coin Bernoulli aggregation model at seven crowd sizes (R=5 to 257) checks the Proposition 3.2 DP-gap upper bound; all inequalities pass with the exponential term decreasing by a factor of 6.293e+07 (slope -0.0707), and a destructive control omitting one group term breaks the bound at 4 horizons, confirming the bound's structure.

claims.claim: Under interpretable conditions on annotator skill, both Majority Vote and Bayesian aggregation are shown to achieve asymptotically unbiased fairness gaps relative to ground-truth labels as crowd size grows (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: Exact majority-vote and Bayesian likelihood-ratio rules evaluated at seven increasing crowd sizes show DP-gap errors converging to 3.598e-08 (MV) and 4.567e-09 (Bayes) at R=257, while a destructive control with skill 0.47 (violating the condition) retains error 0.370506, directly supporting the asymptotic unbiasedness claim.

claims.claim: For majority voting with R annotators, the aggregated fairness gap is bounded by epsilon(R) times the sum of individual annotators' fairness gaps, showing majority voting can amplify rather than average out bias (Proposition 3.6).
claims.evidence: Exact Poisson-binomial majority probability computed for heterogeneous annotators at six crowd sizes confirms all Proposition 3.6 inequalities hold with eta=0.4688, and the measured amplification of the mean individual gap by up to 5.37x demonstrates bias amplification; replacing eta with 0.20 invalidates the bound at all six sizes.

claims.claim: Convergence of the fairness gap to the ground-truth value requires a majority of annotators to have skill exceeding 0.5 plus a margin epsilon; without this, majority voting fails to converge (Section 3, following Proposition 3.6).
claims.evidence: Exact heterogeneous crowds built on both sides of the skill condition show correctness reaching 0.99993 when the condition is satisfied versus falling to 2e-12 when violated, with a destructive control (flipping adversarial annotators to skill 0.90) restoring correctness to 1, directly demonstrating the necessity of the skill threshold for convergence.

claims.claim: FairCrowd, a post-processing method, enforces a strict epsilon-fairness constraint on the output of any aggregation rule while provably bounding the resulting accuracy loss (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The FairCrowd LP solved on a finite-support instance enforces DP gap at 0.05 with risk 0.2605, confirmed by an independent 746-vertex exhaustive enumeration oracle matching the same optimum; removing the fairness constraint yields the unconstrained Bayes classifier with DP gap 0.25, exceeding epsilon by 0.20.

ProCreations/repro-faircrowd-demographic.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence for all five claims through exact finite enumeration of standard crowdsourcing models (one-coin Bernoulli, Poisson-binomial) and finite-support LP optimization, with independent oracle verification and destructive controls at each step. The setup is appropriate for verifying theoretical propositions, using exact computation at reasonable crowd sizes (up to 257) rather than sampling, though all results are limited to specific finite instances rather than general proofs.

MarxistLeninist/repro-no-swap-regret-fir.paper_title: Revenue Guarantees of No-Swap-Regret Dynamics in First Price Auctions

claims.claim: For exact correlated equilibria in discrete first-price auctions with k discretization levels, expected revenue is at least v2 - 4/k, where v2 is the second-highest valuation (Theorem 2.5).
claims.evidence: The paper's Definition 3.1 LP was rebuilt from scratch and solved exactly with scipy HiGHS for n=2 bidders across k∈{5,10,20,40} and v₂∈{0,0.2,0.5,0.8,1}; the LP minimum revenue satisfies v₂−4/k in every case (e.g., k=10, v₂=1 gives LP_min=0.800 vs bound 0.600), with the actual gap being exactly 2/k.

claims.claim: For ε-approximate correlated equilibria, expected revenue is at least v2 - 3/k - Θ(εk²) (Theorem 2.6).
claims.evidence: The Definition 3.1 LP was solved exactly over k∈{6,8,10,14,20,28,40} and ε∈{0,1e-4,1e-3,5e-3,1e-2,5e-2}; raw data shows gap(ε=0)·k=2.0 exactly for all k (confirming Θ(1/k)) and the log-log slope of the ε-dependence vs k is 2.14≈2 (confirming Θ(εk²)), with the full data table provided.

claims.claim: There exists an ε-approximate correlated equilibrium with revenue at most v2 - Θ(1/k) - Θ(ε), showing the ε-dependence in the revenue lower bound cannot be removed (Theorem 2.8).
claims.evidence: The true ε-CE minimum revenue was computed via an exact LP with auxiliary swap-gain variables; for k=10, revenue drops from 0.800 (ε=0) to 0.709 (ε=0.01) to 0.455 (ε=0.05), showing Θ(1/k)+Θ(ε) dependence (not Θ(εk²)), and the ordering per-pair-LP-min ≤ true-ε-CE-min holds at every grid point.

claims.claim: When bidders run no-swap-regret algorithms achieving swap regret O(√(kT)), the time-averaged revenue is at least v2 - 3/k - O(ε) after O(k^5/ε^2) rounds (Corollary 2.7).
claims.evidence: Regret-matching dynamics were simulated for k=10 with v₂∈{0,0.2,0.5,0.8,1} and for v₁=v₂=1 with k∈{10,30,50}; time-averaged revenue converges to v₂−2/k (e.g., k=10→0.80, k=30→0.933, k=50→0.959), satisfying the v₂−3/k guarantee in all cases, though the specific O(k^5/ε²) round complexity was not directly verified.

claims.claim: Time-averaged bidder behavior under no-swap-regret dynamics converges to an ε-approximate correlated equilibrium with probability 1-δ (Theorem 2.3).
claims.evidence: During regret-matching dynamics (k=10, v₁=v₂=1), the maximum per-pair swap-deviation of the empirical distribution μ̂ was tracked and converges to ≈0.100=1/k, demonstrating convergence to an O(1/k)-approximate correlated equilibrium, consistent with Theorem 2.3; only one setting was tested and the exact convergence rate was not verified.

claims.claim: The revenue lower bounds are proved via a dual-fitting approach that uses a linear program and weak duality to bound revenue of approximate correlated equilibria (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The Definition 3.1 linear program (the core of the dual-fitting approach) was independently reconstructed from the paper and solved exactly, confirming that its optimum lower-bounds the revenue of all ε-approximate correlated equilibria across the tested grid; the LP construction and its bounding property are directly verified through the exact numerical results of Claims 1–3.

MarxistLeninist/repro-no-swap-regret-fir.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous reproduction of the paper's core revenue guarantees by independently rebuilding and exactly solving the paper's LP (Definition 3.1) across a grid of k and ε values, confirming the Θ(1/k) and Θ(εk²) functional forms, verifying the matching upper bound, and demonstrating the revenue guarantee and convergence through no-swap-regret dynamics simulations. The main limitations are the restriction to n=2 bidders, finite k≤40 for the LP audits, and the use of regret matching rather than the paper's specific algorithm for dynamics.

prarabdhmisra/4CwO8At8Hw.paper_title: The Catastrophic Failure of *the* k-Means Algorithm in High Dimensions, and How Hartigan's Algorithm Avoids It

claims.claim: In the high-noise, high-dimensional regime where σ² > n, Lloyd's k-means algorithm fails catastrophically: essentially every partition of the data becomes a fixed point of the algorithm (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive enumeration of all 2047 bipartitions at n=12, σ²=2n=24>n, 40 trials shows fraction of Lloyd fixed points = 1.000000 at d≥256, with Lloyd converging in exactly 1.00 iteration and output error matching input error (0.4111 vs 0.4111). Large-n scaling (n=50,100,200) confirms Lloyd FP fraction reaches 1.000000 at d=4096 for n=50,100.

claims.claim: In the same high-noise regime, Hartigan's k-means algorithm avoids this pathology, having no incorrect fixed points with high probability (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: Same exhaustive setup shows 0 of 2034 incorrect partitions survive as Hartigan fixed points at d=16384 (P(exists)=0.000 on all 40 seeds), while all 2034 are Lloyd fixed points — a 3438x separation. Hartigan error from random init drops to 0.0000 at d≥4096. Large-n scaling confirms Hartigan FP fraction = 0.000000 at every (n,d) cell for n=50,100,200.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.8 bounds the probability that any q-approximately balanced partition is not a fixed point of Lloyd's algorithm by 2^n · n · ρ_q^(d/4) (Corollary 3.8).
claims.evidence: Corollary 3.8 inequality (LHS ≤ 2^n·n·ρ_q^(d/4)) holds at every d tested (16 to 65536) with 1969 q-balanced partitions enumerated exhaustively over 30 trials. The per-partition Eq.(17) bound also holds at every d. Large-n scaling confirms Eq.(17) holds at all (n,d) for n=50,100,200.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.12 bounds the probability that any incorrect partition is a fixed point of Hartigan's algorithm by 2^n · ρ_h^(d/4), a substantially tighter bound than Lloyd's case (Corollary 3.12).
claims.evidence: The Corollary 3.12 inequality itself holds at every d tested (verified separately), but the claim's characterization 'substantially tighter than Lloyd's case' is contradicted: Hartigan's bound needs d>1.92e6 to fall below 1 vs Lloyd's d>1.37e4 (140x worse), because ρ_h=0.99998 is far closer to 1 than ρ_q=0.99686. A sigma sweep shows this degrades monotonically to 193,773x worse at σ²=400.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 shows Lloyd's single-sample reassignment step persists misclassification errors once the noise level exceeds σ > (2c̄τ(c−1))/√(c(c+c̄)) (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: Lemmas 3.1/3.2 match scaled chi-square distributions (KS p=0.77, 0.89). Eq.(14) bound holds at every d (4 to 4096) with σ=6>threshold 2.0702, and P(misclassification persists)=1.000000 at d≥1024. Sigma sweep shows the bound holds at every σ above the Eq.(13) threshold and fails below it, with ρ hitting exactly 1.000000 at the threshold — confirming it is sharp.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments empirically demonstrate the divergence between Lloyd's catastrophic-failure behavior and Hartigan's robustness as dimension grows, corroborating the theoretical bounds (Section 4).
claims.evidence: At σ²=18.05 (paper's F.5 value), n=40, 100 reps: NMI diverges from 0.0446 vs 0.0427 (d=2) to 0.0193 vs 1.0000 (d=2048) for Lloyd vs Hartigan. Lloyd converges in 1.00 iteration at d=2048. Hartigan achieves lower k-means loss in 100% of runs for d≥128. The divergence is specific to the high-noise intermediate regime (absent at σ²=1 and σ²=200).

prarabdhmisra/4CwO8At8Hw.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous, independent reproduction from paper text only, using exhaustive partition enumeration at n=12 (exact, not sampled), large-n scaling to n=200, analytic bound verification, and KS distributional tests. Five of six claims are verified with concrete numerical evidence; Claim 4's 'substantially tighter' characterization is falsified by showing Hartigan's bound requires 140x higher dimension than Lloyd's to become non-vacuous.

Auenchanters/repro-conservation-laws-for.paper_title: Conservation Laws for Modern Neural Architectures

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that for feedforward layers with GELU or SiLU activations, all conservation laws are constant functions of the parameters, unlike the layer-wise rescaling laws known for ReLU/linear networks (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Exact rank computation on float64 models (D=24, 3 seeds) confirms 0 non-trivial conservation laws for both ffn-gelu and ffn-silu (rank=24=D, bound=0=predicted, residual=0.0e+00, tight), matching Theorem 4.1's prediction that all conservation laws are constant functions.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 characterizes the conservation laws of SwiGLU-activated layers via the invariants ||A_{:,i}||^2 - ||C_{i,:}||^2 across matched columns/rows of the gating and value projection matrices (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: SwiGLU model (D=36, 3 seeds) shows exact count: rank=32, bound=4, closure=4, predicted=4, tight, with residuals at float64 floor (2.97e-15 to 5.06e-15), confirming the ||A_{:,i}||^2 - ||C_{i,:}||^2 invariants are conserved and the characterization is complete.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 shows standard multihead attention conserves Q_i^T Q_i - K_i^T K_i and V_i^T V_i - O_i^T O_i per head, while Theorem 4.4 extends this characterization to attention with rotary positional encoding (RoPE) (Theorems 4.3-4.4, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: One-head MHA (D=24) and MHA+RoPE (D=24) close the sandwich: partial Lie closure brings the upper bound from 8→6 (MHA) and 6→4 (RoPE), matching the predicted counts, while the predicted invariants are verified conserved at residuals ≤1.1e-15 across 3 seeds each. Two-head cases (D=64) have verified invariants but inconclusive counts due to incomplete closure.

claims.claim: Theorems 4.5-4.7 derive conservation laws for dense softmax-gated Mixture-of-Experts, sparse (top-k) MoE, and sigmoid-gated MoE variants (Theorems 4.5-4.7, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Softmax-gated MoE (dense and top-2) are verified with exact counts (7/7 and 9/9, tight, residuals ≤1.3e-14), but sigmoid-gated MoE is falsified: the predicted gating invariant sum_i W^(i) has relative residual 1.00 (entirely non-conserved) across all seeds and shapes, with the law count short by exactly d=3. Corroborated independently by gradient flow (drift 1.397e-02, not responding to tolerance) and discrete SGD (slope_tau=0.891, first-order like a non-law).

claims.claim: Predicted conservation laws are empirically validated by measuring how the conservation error scales with learning rate during training of Qwen-3-style RoPE/MoE models and Vision Transformers on WikiText-103, Penn Treebank, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet-1K (Figure 2, Section 6).
claims.evidence: The tau^2 conservation-error scaling is measured under SGD on tiny synthetic models (D=24–63, random teacher-student data, 3 seeds), confirming slopes 1.981–1.990 against the predicted 2, but none of the specific models (Qwen-3-style RoPE/MoE, Vision Transformers) or datasets (WikiText-103, Penn Treebank, CIFAR-10, ImageNet-1K) mentioned in the claim are used.

Auenchanters/repro-conservation-laws-for.overall: The logbook provides exact numerical verification of conservation law characterizations for GELU/SiLU FFN, SwiGLU, MHA, and MHA+RoPE (claims 1–3), and falsifies the sigmoid-gated MoE theorem (claim 4) with three independent code paths agreeing that sum_i W^(i) is not conserved. The empirical scaling validation (claim 5) is addressed only on small synthetic models, not on the real architectures and datasets named in the paper.

ParetoOptimal/repro-jnv4sl4yzh.paper_title: Set-Preserving Calibration from Conformal P-Values to E-Values

claims.claim: A calibrator is defined as set-preserving when converting conformal p-values at level alpha into e-values yields prediction sets identical to thresholding the e-values directly at 1/alpha (Section 2.1, Definition 2.2)
claims.evidence: 1200 split-conformal instances (60×20 test points, 6 calibration sizes, 3 score distributions, 1201-point grid) show P2E and AoN yield identical_sets_fraction=1.0 with 0 grid disagreements, while F1/F2/F3 yield 0.0 identical fraction with 6-7× set inflation.

claims.claim: Among left-continuous p-to-e calibrators, only the all-or-nothing calibrator can be exactly set-preserving, which motivates a new sigmoid-based P2E construction (Proposition 2.3, Theorem 2.6, Equation 9)
claims.evidence: Exhaustive sweep of 40,360,599 two-level calibrators finds exactly 1 set-preserving survivor matching AoN [10.0, 0.0, 0.1]; constrained-minimum computation over 2000-bin grid gives minimum integral 1.0 at L1 distance 0.0 from AoN; 200,000 random decreasing step calibrators yield 0 set-preserving; P2E evades the proposition legitimately with Lebesgue integral 1.19846 > 1.

claims.claim: The proposed sigmoid-based P2E calibrator is exact (expectation equal to 1), smooth, invertible, strictly positive, and strictly dominates the all-or-nothing calibrator in aggregation settings (Theorem 2.6)
claims.evidence: Across 24 configurations, exactness holds to 4.44e-16, F(alpha)=1/alpha error is exactly 0.0, inverse round-trip error 1.43e-13, derivative matches central differences to 2.51e-09 with max derivative -129.0, strict positivity confirmed (min log F = -11825, all finite), domination gap over AoN is 0.000185 ≥ 0 below alpha, and aggregation shows 0 subset violations with strict size ratio 0.993694.

claims.claim: Applied to e-Cross-Conformal Prediction (ECCP), the P2E calibrator preserves exact 1-alpha coverage, whereas standard cross-conformal-prediction variants only guarantee approximate 1-2alpha coverage (Proposition 4.1)
claims.evidence: ECCP coverage measured at 0.9008 against 0.9 guarantee; merged e-variable exact to error 0.0; UR-MI rejection rates 0.101092/0.097848/0.099118 under independent/comonotone/two-block dependence over 400,000 null draws (all within MC noise of alpha=0.1); CCP's Eq. 13 floor computed at 0.768235 on the same configuration.

claims.claim: Applied to Weighted Conformal Aggregation (WECA), data-dependent weighted merging of e-values across multiple models retains valid coverage (Proposition 4.2)
claims.evidence: WECA covers at 0.952361 and UR-WECA at 0.951528 against 0.95 target with weights selected on a strictly disjoint tuning split over 200 simplex candidates; weighted merge exact to 2.22e-16; data-dependent weights are non-trivial (mean 0.333, 0.25, 0.133, 0.033, 0.25, 0, 0); classical calibrators F1/F2 collapse to coverage 1.0 with length 25.95.

claims.claim: Empirically, ECCP using the proposed P2E calibrator produces smaller prediction sets than baseline p-to-e conversion methods while maintaining valid coverage (Section 5)
claims.evidence: On synthetic data and the 442-point diabetes dataset over 100 trials each, ECCP(P2E) produces the smallest sets (5.141 and 186.77) versus AoN (5.166, 194.63) and classical calibrators F1/F2/F3 (16.29/12.96/19.57 and 583.04/503.43/684.26), with valid coverage (0.9008, 0.9047) and 0 containment violations of P2E ⊆ AoN.

ParetoOptimal/repro-jnv4sl4yzh.overall: This logbook provides concrete, from-scratch numerical evidence across all six claims, including exhaustive calibrator sweeps, machine-precision property checks, null Monte-Carlo of UR-MI under multiple dependence structures, and full conformal prediction pipelines on both synthetic and real (diabetes) data. The reproduction faithfully implements the paper's equations and demonstrates the claimed set-preservation, coverage validity, and efficiency properties, though using different datasets and base learners than the paper's original OpenML benchmarks.

Srishti280992/repro-efficient-stochastic.paper_title: Efficient Stochastic Optimisation via Sequential Monte Carlo

claims.claim: The Sequential Optimization via SMC (SOSMC) framework replaces expensive inner MCMC sampling loops with a sequential Monte Carlo particle population that is reused and reweighted across optimization iterations, as formalized in Algorithm 1 (Section 3.1, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The high-rigor audit implements Algorithm 1 mechanics (ULA forward kernel, reverse-ULA backward kernel, incremental reweighting, ESS-based resampling) on a 2D MLP energy with 10,000 particles over only 5 steps. The finite-difference gradient check (max L2 error 6.6e-12) and fresh-population negative control (break ratio 1.04) confirm the mechanics work, but the setup is a small-scale 2D toy problem, not the paper's actual application scale.

claims.claim: Proposition 2 establishes a linear convergence rate for the idealized SOSMC iteration under mu-Polyak-Lojasiewicz and L-smooth loss assumptions, showing l(theta_k) - inf(l) <= (1-gamma*mu)^k * (l(theta_0) - inf(l)) for step size gamma <= 1/L (Proposition 2).
claims.evidence: The audit exhaustively checks 38,400 iterate-level inequalities for quadratic losses with eigenvalues in [μ, L] and step size γ=1/L, finding zero violations of l(θ_k) - inf(l) ≤ (1-γμ)^k(l(θ_0) - inf(l)) across dimensions 1-8, multiple μ/L ratios, and 8 random initializations per configuration. This is a thorough numerical verification of Proposition 2 on the canonical PL-smooth function class.

claims.claim: Propositions 3 and 4 show the effective sample size of the SMC weights decays exponentially in the squared gradient norm and step size, ESS_infinity(gamma) = N*exp(-gamma^2*||grad l||^2) for Gaussian targets, motivating an adaptive step-size/resampling scheme (Section 4.2, Propositions 3-4).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo simulation with 120,000-400,000 samples per setting directly confirms ESS_∞(γ)/N = exp(-γ²||∇l||²) for Gaussian targets across dimensions {1,2,5,11,32} and step sizes {0.05,0.1,0.2,0.35,0.5}, with max relative error 0.46-1.2% between empirical ESS fractions and the closed-form formula. An unequal-covariance negative control column confirms the formula is scoped to matched-covariance Gaussians.

claims.claim: On Langevin reward-tuning of energy-based models with non-differentiable reward functions, SOSMC-ULA outperforms the ImpDiff baseline and achieves reduced variance compared to single-chain SOUL (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: The high-rigor audit runs 10,000 particles, 10 seeds, and 4 settings with independent oracle evaluation (400K samples), showing SOSMC-ULA beats ImpDiff 40/40 and has lower std than SOUL 4/4. However, the comparison uses different learning rates per method (SOSMC: 0.42, ImpDiff: 0.16, SOUL: 0.22) and SOUL uses only ~125 samples vs 10,000 particles, making the baseline comparison fundamentally unfair rather than a faithful reproduction.

claims.claim: On 2D EBM benchmark datasets, SOSMC achieves higher objective values than ImpDiff for small regularization strengths, with particle-based reward estimates that track true expectations throughout optimization (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: The high-rigor audit fits GMM EBMs to moons/circles/blobs and runs 10,000 particles for 500 iterations, showing SOSMC-ULA wins 12/12 small-β cells and tracks true reward with lower RMSE. However, SOSMC-ULA uses lr=0.18 while ImpDiff uses lr=0.010 (18× difference) with only 1% particle refresh probability, heavily handicapping the baseline and undermining the objective-value comparison. The particle tracking result for SOSMC-ULA itself is credible but the head-to-head comparison is not.

claims.claim: On MNIST, SOSMC remains robust in high dimensions even under mismatch between the pretraining and tuning kernels, without exhibiting reward hacking (Section 5.3).
claims.evidence: The high-rigor audit trains a neural EBM via PCD on 12,000 MNIST images reduced to 64 PCA dimensions with 128 energy parameters, tests kernel mismatch (condition number 8), and uses a Mahalanobis anomaly detector as a reward-hacking proxy. All 12 reward×β cells show improvement, stable ESS, and no hacking. However, the setup is substantially simplified (64-dim PCA vs full 784-dim images, 128 parameters, mild mismatch, proxy detection) compared to the paper's full-scale MNIST experiments.

Srishti280992/repro-efficient-stochastic.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification for the two theoretical claims (PL convergence inequality and Gaussian ESS decay formula) through exhaustive audits with thousands of instances and tight error margins. The experimental claims (4-6) are addressed at moderate particle scale but with handicapped baselines using different learning rates and reduced sample budgets, making those comparisons proxy-level rather than faithful reproductions.

Srishti280992/repro-on-the-theory-of-con.paper_title: On the Theory of Continual Learning with Gradient Descent for Neural Networks

claims.claim: Theorem 1 gives a closed-form bound on train-time forgetting for task k after training on K-k subsequent tasks, of order O~(ηT√(K-k)/(d√n) + ηT√(K-k)/(d²polylog(d)) + η²T²K²/√m) (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The visible experiments use train_sequence_linear_closed_form (a linearized proxy), not actual gradient descent on a two-layer neural network as Theorem 1 describes. The sampling term exponent is -0.676 (vs. predicted -0.5) over n=[250,8000] and the finite-width remainder exponent is -0.499 over m=[100,10000], with orthogonality control showing a 2486x increase. The referenced 'strengthened' 195-run/120-GD-run evidence is described in text but its numerical results are not shown in the logbook.

claims.claim: The forgetting bounds hold under the parameter regime n = Θ~(d²K) samples, m = Ω~(d⁸K⁴) hidden-layer width, and ηT = Θ(d²) training iterations on a d-dimensional XOR cluster dataset with K tasks (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The width condition m=Ω~(d⁸K⁴) is explicitly acknowledged as unreachable (2.28e16 units at d=64,K=3) and replaced with m=max(600,3d²), far below the theorem's requirement. The n=1.5d²K and ηT=0.70d² scaling directions are tested with the linearized closed-form proxy, showing d^{-1.223} decay on the prescribed path vs. d^{-0.246} with fixed n, but neither the full width regime nor actual GD dynamics are tested.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows that under the same width/sample/iteration conditions as Theorem 1, the misclassification error remains uniformly small across all K tasks with high probability after KT gradient descent iterations (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The visible evidence uses train_sequence_linear_closed_form with closed-form linear-loss dynamics, not actual gradient descent. All 8 seeds show 0.0 misclassification across 6 tasks at d=50,K=6,n=1600,m=1200,ηT=1600, and the under-resourced control shows 0.615 mean error. However, zero error under linearized dynamics may be an artifact of the proxy rather than a test of Theorem 2's GD-based guarantee. The referenced 32 hinge-GD runs are described but their data is not shown.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 bounds the delayed generalization gap by η T exp(ηT(K-k+1)/√m) / n for Lipschitz, smooth loss functions, showing the gap decays with sample size n (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Uses actual gradient descent (train_sequence_gd) with logistic loss (1-Lipschitz, 1/4-smooth, matching theorem requirements) at d=20,K=6,η=30,T=160. The absolute delayed generalization gap fits A/n+B with R²=0.970 at m=5000, decaying 4.43x from n=80 to n=1280, while the m=150 width control degrades to R²=0.239, confirming both the 1/n prediction and the width dependence. The bound is noted as vacuous (RHS≈1e826 vs. measured gap≈1.7e-4) but never violated.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 gives an improved generalization gap bound for self-bounded losses that scales poly-logarithmically rather than linearly in the number of iterations T, depending on the cumulative training loss of later tasks (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: The visible code uses a single-task setup (K=1) via sample_tasks(d,1,n,seed), not the multi-task continual learning scenario Theorem 4 addresses. The self-boundedness check |f'|≤f passes for logistic loss, and cumulative loss grows only 2.37x vs. 64x for T across checkpoints [50,1600], but this is measured in a simplified single-task proxy rather than the K-task setting the theorem describes.

claims.claim: Test-time forgetting is decomposed as the sum of train-time forgetting (Theorem 1) and the delayed generalization gap (Theorem 3/4), showing that network width, sample size, and later tasks' data jointly, not individually, control forgetting (Theorem 1, Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: The decomposition F_ts = F_tr + F_gen is tested using train_sequence_linear_closed_form (linearized proxy) at d=50,K=3,n=3000,m=2000 with rho=0.25, and the 2×2 joint-control grid (n,m)∈{100,1000}² uses the same proxy. The decomposition error and joint-control pattern are measured, but not with actual GD dynamics on neural networks as the theorems assume.

Srishti280992/repro-on-the-theory-of-con.overall: The logbook provides concrete evidence confirming the 1/n decay prediction of Theorem 3 using actual gradient descent with logistic loss, but the remaining five claims are tested primarily on a linearized closed-form proxy rather than the GD-on-neural-networks dynamics the theorems describe, and the critical width condition m=Ω~(d⁸K⁴) is acknowledged as infeasible and left untested.

Srishti280992/repro-mira-a-score-for-con.paper_title: MIRA: A Score for Conditional Distribution Accuracy and Model Comparison

claims.claim: MIRA's Uniform Mass Property (Proposition 3.1) establishes that the probability mass lambda_n assigned to randomly constructed regions follows a Uniform[0,1] distribution when the candidate matches the true conditional distribution.
claims.evidence: Across 24 matched Gaussian configurations spanning dimensions 1–32 and multiple sigma values, KS statistics against Uniform[0,1] were ≤0.000478 with p-values of 1.0, while shifted-mass negative controls showed KS ≥0.0758 with p≈0, confirming the uniform mass property numerically.

claims.claim: Under the null hypothesis of a correctly specified candidate distribution, the Mira statistic reduces to Laplace's rule of succession, p(k|n) = (n+1)/(N+2) for k=1 and (N-n+1)/(N+2) for k=0 (Proposition 3.2).
claims.evidence: Exact beta-integral identity matched Laplace's formula to within 6.85e-12 for N up to 2000, and a 600,000-trial simulation for N=8 and N=64 recovered p(k=1|n)=(n+1)/(N+2) with max empirical bin error 0.0123.

claims.claim: As N approaches infinity under correct model specification, the expected Mira score converges to 2/3 with theoretical variance converging to 1/18 (Corollary 3.4).
claims.evidence: Exact finite-N moments computed by enumeration show convergence: at N=8192 the mean is 0.666626 (within 4.07e-05 of 2/3) and variance is 0.0555488 (within 6.78e-06 of 1/18), with the finite-N mean matching (2N+3)/(3(N+2)).

claims.claim: Proposition 3.5 proves a lower bound that any candidate model achieves a Mira score mu_Mira(M) >= 1/2.
claims.evidence: Over 207 monotone radial-CDF maps, all (2u-1)T(u) integrals were non-negative with minimum asymptotic score 0.528865, and 300,000-trial Gaussian misspecification simulations at N=128 yielded minimum raw Mira score 0.504964, both above the 1/2 bound.

claims.claim: In a Bayesian model comparison experiment on four strong gravitational lensing forward models in 13 dimensions, MIRA correctly ranks the true model (EPL plus 3 Sersic sources) as the best fit (Section 5.3, Bayesian Model Comparison).
claims.evidence: A differentiable 24×24 strong-lensing forward model with 13 parameters and MALA posterior draws (N=1280, L=100) ranked EPL+3 Sersic first at 0.7228, followed by SIE+3 (0.6011), EPL+1 (0.5544), SIE+1 (0.5426), with bootstrap SEs ≤0.0043 and a GPU rerun reproducing the ranking; residual RMS audits confirm the fit ordering.

claims.claim: In a high-dimensional robustness test on 64x64x3 galaxy images, MIRA detects prior and noise-model misspecification using as few as L=16 true fiducial samples (Section 5.3).
claims.evidence: Using real Galaxy10/DECaLS 64×64×3 images (12,288D) with rank-64 PCA priors and exact posterior draws at L=16, N=64, the correct spiral-prior sigma=2 model scored 0.6653 (closest to 2/3), misspecified sigma=0.5 scored 0.5294, and wrong smooth-galaxy priors collapsed to ~0.504, demonstrating detection of both noise and prior misspecification.

Srishti280992/repro-mira-a-score-for-con.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical and experimental evidence supporting all six claims: Claims 1–4 via exact theorem audits with negative controls, and Claims 5–6 via real forward-model and real-image experiments at the paper's stated dimensionalities and sample sizes. The main caveat is that the empirical claims use independently constructed posterior generators rather than the paper's unreleased original artifacts, but the MIRA scoring methodology is tested at full scale on non-toy setups.

Jaycee766/repro-an-interactive-paradigm-.paper_title: An Interactive Paradigm for Deep Research

claims.claim: The interruption decision rule triggers PauseAsk when the expected value gain ΔEV(n*) exceeds the pause cost C(n*) = C0·(1 + pauses_j/Tol_j), otherwise the system proceeds autonomously (Section 2.4).
claims.evidence: The decision rule C(n*)=C0·(1+pauses_j/Tol_j) with strict > inequality was implemented and exhaustively tested on 24,400 grid cases (25 C0 × 16 pauses × 61 ΔEV), all matching, plus algebraic identity checks (C(0)=C0, monotonicity, strict inequality at equality) and a worked example at C0=0.7 yielding C=1.166667.
