ParetoOptimal/repro-fagn04tvzq.paper_title: Belief Propagation Converges to Gaussian Distributions in Sparsely-Connected Factor Graphs

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that variables in pairwise chain factor graphs develop increasingly Gaussian-distributed beliefs as topological distance from prior factors increases, driven by repeated convolution via the Central Limit Theorem (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The cumulant-dilution law (Eq. 5) is confirmed to machine precision (max abs error 3.48e-15 over 64 convolutions), and on the paper's 13-variable chain with 51 seeds the KL drops monotonically from 0.345366 at the prior to 0.00567333 at hop 2, crossing the 0.02 threshold; a 64-hop chain shows |κ̂₃| shrinking by factor 22.66 and KL falling to 9.44e-06, with Edgeworth prediction matching to 2.5% relative error.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 extends the Gaussian convergence result to tree-topology factor graphs, provided the message non-Gaussianity ε satisfies ε² ≪ ε with increasing distance from the nearest prior factor (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: The Lemma 4.3 multiplication correction is bounded by 0.542 × ε² and 0.00908 × ε across a 47-fold range of ε (m=4 to 512), directly measuring the ε²≪ε condition; on the paper's 127-variable binary tree with 64 leaf priors and 51 seeds, KL drops from 0.259257 at prior-bearing leaves to 0.0170923 one hop away and 0.00210879 two hops away.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.5 uses computation-tree equivalence to show loopy factor graphs exhibit the same Gaussian convergence mechanism as tree graphs under identical assumptions (Theorem 4.5).
claims.evidence: Computation-tree equivalence is verified to machine precision (max abs belief difference 1.11e-16) on a 3×3 grid unwrapped to depth 5 (69 variable copies), with the unwrapped tree and loopy BP sharing no code path; the paper's 4×4 loopy grid with one prior shows KL dropping from 0.206512 to 0.00859309 one hop away, below the 0.02 threshold.

claims.claim: Lemma 4.2 identifies an 'exclusion zone' in which non-Gaussian prior factors prevent Gaussian convergence when the prior-to-pairwise variance ratio R is less than or equal to approximately 6 (Lemma 4.2).
claims.evidence: Bisection recovers the critical u=0.49916 and R=6.01685 (residual 4.44e-16), the steady-state variance relation (Eq. 14) holds to 6.1e-15 relative error in simulation, and the empirical BP sweep crosses the 0.02 KL threshold at R=5.45 (zero-mean kernels) and R=5.95 (random-noise kernels), both within ~10% of the claimed R≈6.

claims.claim: Figure 4 shows all tested topologies reach a KL divergence below 0.02 within 3 hops from prior factors, and that higher node degree increases non-Gaussianity in star graphs while weaker priors enable faster Gaussian emergence (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: All three topologies are below KL 0.02 within 3 hops (chain at hop 2, tree and grid at hop 1; worst KL at hop 3 is 0.00180539); star-graph center KL rises from 0.0846 to 0.1572 as degree goes 3→11 (Pearson r=0.912); and the prior-strength sweep drives KL monotonically from 0.154813 to 0.0153179 as R increases from 0.19 to 208.

claims.claim: Figure 5 applies the theory to stereo depth estimation belief propagation, showing Gaussian convergence in textureless image regions while non-Gaussian beliefs persist at high-contrast edges (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: On the real Middlebury Cones pair at 30000 variables and 32 disparity levels, BP reduces MSE from 21.78 to 6.04 and mean KL from 0.268 to 0.059; textureless pixels reach median KL 0.01277 with 79.0% below the 0.02 threshold, while high-contrast edge pixels stay at mean KL 0.260 with only 19.2% below it—an 11.9-fold split in the predicted direction.

ParetoOptimal/repro-fagn04tvzq.overall: This logbook provides a thorough from-scratch reproduction of all six claims using the paper's own parameters and scales, including a real stereo depth experiment on the Middlebury Cones dataset at 30000 variables. Every claim is backed by concrete numerical evidence—machine-precision checks of the underlying mechanisms (cumulant dilution, computation-tree equivalence, steady-state variance), multi-seed empirical runs on the paper's specified topologies, and measured thresholds consistent with the paper's predictions.

Srishti280992/repro-fluxnet-learning-cap.paper_title: FluxNet: Learning Capacity-Constrained Local Transport Operators for Conservative and Bounded PDE Surrogates

claims.claim: Proposition 1 shows that under periodic boundary conditions with symmetric stencils, FluxNet's flux-based update rule (the same flux serves as outflow for the sender cell and inflow for the receiver cell) exactly preserves the global sum of the transported quantity, yielding conservation errors at the machine-precision level (~1e-7 to 1e-8) (Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: Independent NumPy audit of 400 random 1D periodic transport cases across stencil radii 1–8 yielded max absolute mass drift of 1.42e-14, with an open-boundary control correctly detecting a 0.25 mass loss, directly confirming the algebraic cancellation mechanism at machine precision.

claims.claim: The L-Head and U-Head mechanisms parameterize outflow as a fraction of the cell's available capacity above a lower bound (or below an upper bound), and Propositions 2 and 3 prove that this construction guarantees the next state stays within the prescribed bounds without any post-hoc clipping or projection (Propositions 2 and 3).
claims.evidence: Independent reimplementation of L-Head and U-Head updates tested over 300 random cases showed L-Head minimum of 0.0137 (above lower bound 0) and U-Head maximum of 0.989 (below upper bound 1), with boundary cases (all-zero, all-one) yielding 0.0 error, confirming the capacity-fraction construction guarantees bounds without clipping.

claims.claim: On the shallow-water equations rollout task at horizon T=2, FluxNet-LAP achieves a depth MAE of 3.12e-3 versus 6.74e-3 for the best baseline (a post-hoc projection method), while also reducing conservation error from 3.3e-7 (baseline) to 3.3e-8 (Table 3).
claims.evidence: Fresh shallow-water corpus (64×64 grid, 40 train/26 test trajectories) trained with official harness: FluxNet-LAP achieved h MAE 6.535e-3 vs 1.306e-2 for projection baseline, with conservation drift 2.905e-8 vs 2.255e-7, confirming the claim's direction, ranking, and conservation scale on a non-toy PDE task, though absolute MAE values are ~2× higher than the paper's specific numbers.

claims.claim: On the traffic flow benchmark at horizon T=2, FluxNet-D attains an MAE of 3.48e-3 compared to 15.9e-3 for a CNN-AR baseline, and reduces conservation error from 2.1e-2 to 7.7e-8, though FluxNet-D shows slightly higher upper-bound violation rates on some settings (1.87% vs 3.20% for CNN-AR) (Table 4).
claims.evidence: Official traffic corpus (Nx=256, 100 train/100 test, 3 seeds, 60 epochs) trained with official harness: FluxNet-D achieved MAE 5.789e-3 vs 1.574e-2 for CNN-AR, conservation drift 9.435e-8 vs 2.439e-2, confirming FluxNet-D beats CNN-AR and reduces conservation by ~5 orders of magnitude on a non-toy setup, though absolute MAE and exact violation rates differ from paper values.

claims.claim: On the spinodal decomposition experiment, a FluxNet model trained to take steps of 1000*dt achieves a 17.3x rollout speedup relative to the base timestep while preserving two-point correlation statistics of the simulated microstructure (Table 5).
claims.evidence: Spinodal reproduction on 128×128 grid with 1000dt FluxNet-D model trained 30 epochs measured 50.67× rollout speedup (vs paper's 17.3×) with final two-point error 9.80e-4 comparable to phase-field seed-spread of 7.10e-4 (ratio 1.38×), confirming the mechanism of large speedup with preserved microstructure statistics on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: The D-Head (dual bounds) variant enforces upper and lower capacity constraints via a dual consistency loss (DCL) rather than a strict architectural guarantee, achieving empirically near-zero bound violations rather than the exact guarantees proven for the single-bound L-Head and U-Head cases (Section on Bound Enforcement / D-Head).
claims.evidence: Source inspection confirms D-Head averages branches (combined_change = (outflow_change + inflow_change)/2) and DCL is MSE between outflow/inflow guarded by positive weight; independent counterexamples show averaged D-Head updates can violate upper bound by 0.499 and lower bound by 0.499 while preserving mass (drift 0.0), confirming dual-bound satisfaction is empirical via DCL, not a strict architectural guarantee.

Srishti280992/repro-fluxnet-learning-cap.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all six claims: structural properties (conservation to 1e-14, single-bound guarantees, D-Head limitation) are verified through independent audits with controls, and empirical benchmarks (shallow-water, traffic, spinodal) are confirmed in direction and mechanism through real model training on non-toy PDE tasks at reduced scale, though absolute numbers differ from the paper's specific table values.

MarxistLeninist/repro-agd-l0l1-smoothnes.paper_title: Near-Optimal Convergence of Accelerated Gradient Methods under Generalized and $(L_0,L_1)$-Smoothness

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 proves Algorithm 1 achieves oracle complexity of 5√ℓ(0)R̄/√ε + k(δ) gradient calls for functions with subquadratic or quadratic growth under generalized ℓ-smoothness (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook never implements Algorithm 1 or references Theorem 3.3; it only implements Algorithm 2 (Theorems 4.1/4.2). The oracle complexity 5√ℓ(0)R̄/√ε + k(δ) for Algorithm 1 under generalized ℓ-smoothness is not addressed.

claims.claim: Corollary 3.4 shows that optimizing over the free parameter δ yields complexity O(√ℓ(0)R/√ε), which is provably optimal in the small-ε regime (Corollary 3.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies O(√L0·R/√ε) complexity with constant 2.00≤5 and √L0 scaling, but attributes this to Theorem 4.2 (Algorithm 2), not Corollary 3.4 (Algorithm 1). The free parameter δ and its optimization are never mentioned.

claims.claim: For (L₀,L₁)-smooth functions (ℓ(s)=L₀+L₁s), the paper's bound reduces to O(√L₀R/√ε), removing the non-constant multiplicative factors present in prior results such as √(L₀+L₁‖∇f(x⁰)‖)R/√ε from Li et al. (2024a) and exp(L₁R)·√L₀R/√ε from Gorbunov et al. (2025) (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook demonstrates L1-independence of the leading complexity term: a 64× change in L1 (0.25→16) moves N_cert by <2% (447315→455112 at ε=1e-9), and the naive global-L method using L_eff=L0+L1·‖∇f(x⁰)‖=217 is 2× slower than Algorithm 2 on the quartic, concretely showing the initial-gradient penalty is removed.

claims.evidence: The logbook implements Algorithm 2 from pseudocode and shows it converges from iteration 0 with the certificate f(yᵏ)−f* ≤ ΓₖR² holding immediately (0 violations across 3000 iterations on 3 functions), with no GD warmup phase. However, parameter stability is not explicitly tested and Algorithm 1 is not implemented for contrast.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 provides refined complexity bounds with improved non-dominant terms compared to prior accelerated methods under (L₀,L₁)-smoothness (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook does not mention Theorem 4.3 or any refined complexity bounds with improved non-dominant terms. Only Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 are addressed.

MarxistLeninist/repro-agd-l0l1-smoothnes.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous float64 numerical audit of Algorithm 2 (Theorems 4.1 and 4.2) and Appendix A, verifying the per-iteration certificate, the O(√L0·R/√ε) complexity with L1-independent leading term, and acceleration over GD and naive global-L baselines. However, it does not address Theorem 3.3, Corollary 3.4, or Theorem 4.3, leaving three of the five claims entirely unexamined.

Srishti280992/repro-efficient-preference.paper_title: Efficient Preference Poisoning Attack on Offline RLHF

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 shows that flipping a single preference label shifts the DPO gradient by a vector o_i·β·Δψ_i that is independent of the current policy parameter θ, enabling reformulation of preference poisoning as a binary sparse approximation problem in gradient space (Section 3, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: 20,000 random trials at d=768 with two independent θ values per trial confirm the gradient-shift identity to machine precision (max identity error 5.02e-15, max θ-dependence error 8.87e-15), directly validating that the flip-induced shift equals o_i·β·Δψ_i and is independent of θ.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 establishes a lower bound on the number of required label flips, |ℱ| ≥ ||g†||_2/(2β), showing flip requirements scale linearly with the target gradient norm (Section 3, Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: Collinear sharp constructions at β=1 for K∈{1,2,4,8,16,32} attain the lower bound ||g†||₂/(2β) exactly (gap 0.00 in all cases), confirming the bound is tight and scales linearly with target gradient norm; orthogonal cases show the bound is a valid lower bound.

claims.claim: The Binary-Aware Lattice Attack (BAL-A) uses a penalty parameter M ≥ M_0(B,R,K*) so that the shortest lattice vector has coefficients constrained to {-1,0,1}^n, and under a separation condition ρ_k² > M²(K*-k), recovers the true K*-flip attack pattern exactly (Section 4.1, Lemma 4.1, Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Audited on small planted dictionaries (d=18, n=12, K=4) with exhaustive search rather than the actual LLL/Babai lattice algorithm; the ternary-coefficient property (Lemma 4.1) and the separation/recovery condition (Theorem 4.3) were verified separately at different M values rather than jointly at M≥M₀, and no full BAL-A implementation was tested.

claims.claim: The Binary Matching Pursuit Attack (BMP-A) recovers the exact flip support within K* iterations when the gradient dictionary's coherence satisfies μ(V) < b/((2K*-1)B) (Section 5.2, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: On a non-orthogonal Gaussian dictionary (d=256, n=64, μ=0.2032), BMP-A achieved 100% exact support recovery across 2000 trials per K for K=1–5, including in the theorem-certified region (K≤2 where μ<b/((2K-1)B)) and beyond, confirming the coherence sufficient condition is valid and conservative.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.4 provides impossibility certificates against K-flip attacks under a spectral norm condition ||g†||_2 - ε > √K·||V||_2 and a coherence condition (||g†||_2 - ε)² > B²(K + μ(V)K(K-1)) (Section 5, Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: Across 240 random small dictionaries with K≤4, whenever either the spectral or coherence certificate fired (120 and 121 times respectively), exhaustive brute-force over all binary supports up to budget K found zero false certificates, confirming both impossibility conditions are sound.

claims.claim: On the SHP dataset, the crafted attack shifts the trained policy far closer to the intended target than clean training does (||π_θ†-π_θ̂||_1 ≈ 0.012 vs ||π_clean-π_θ̂||_1 ≈ 0.224), and BMP-A runs roughly four orders of magnitude faster than BAL-A (1.37×10⁻⁴s vs 0.6865s) on the same data subset (Section 6.2.3).
claims.evidence: Real SHP data and DistilBERT features were used, but the attack subset was reduced to n=20 (vs paper's n=50), BAL-A was replaced by exhaustive brute-force search rather than the actual lattice algorithm, and the reported policy L1 distances (0.0042 vs 0.066) do not match the paper's claimed values (0.012 vs 0.224); the qualitative direction and ~7862× speedup are reproduced but at reduced scale and scope.

Srishti280992/repro-efficient-preference.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification of the paper's core theoretical results (gradient-shift identity, flip lower bound, BMP-A coherence recovery, and impossibility certificates) through independent implementations with exhaustive controls. The BAL-A lattice guarantee and SHP real-data diagnostic are only partially addressed at reduced scale without the actual lattice algorithm or paper-scale subset sizes.

Srishti280992/repro-unfolding-generative.paper_title: Unfolding Generative Flows with Koopman Operators: Trajectory-Preserving Linearization

claims.claim: The method formulates Conditional Flow Matching dynamics via a Koopman generator that lifts nonlinear vector-field dynamics into a linear evolution over observables, using the identity L g(x_t) = ∇_x g(x_t)·v(x_t) (Section 4, Eq. 8).
claims.evidence: The Koopman generator identity L g(x) = ∇_x g(x)·v(x) was numerically verified on a 4D nonlinear vector field with 6 nonlinear observables over 100,000 states, achieving max absolute error 2.42e-08 (CPU) and 1.92e-08 (T4 GPU) against centered finite-difference directional derivatives; the identity also appears in both v1 (Eq. 8) and v3 (Eq. 4) of the paper.

claims.claim: A decoder-free parametrization concatenates the raw state with learned observables, g̃(x) = [x, g_θ(x)], avoiding reconstruction error from a separate decoder (Section 4, Eq. 14).
claims.evidence: The released official code implements KoopmanEncoder, KoopmanDecoder, and KoopmanAutoencoder (not decoder-free [x, g_θ(x)]), and the released MNIST checkpoint loads into KoopmanAutoencoderSong with both autoencoder.encoder and autoencoder.decoder modules present and zero missing/unexpected keys, directly contradicting the decoder-free parametrization claim for the final artifact.

claims.claim: Training combines a Generator loss enforcing Koopman consistency with a Target Consistency loss aligning the exponentiated generator trajectory to the terminal state (Section 4.3, Eqs. 15-16).
claims.evidence: The official code defines 7 loss classes (ReconstructionLoss, ConsistencyLoss, TargetLoss, TargetPhaseLoss, FiniteDifferenceLoss, BoundaryConsistencyLoss, DiscriminatorLoss), and the released MNIST checkpoint's loss_config enables consistency, target, target_phase, reconstruction, and lpips simultaneously, contradicting the claim that training combines only a Generator loss and a Target Consistency loss.

claims.claim: On MNIST, one-step (one-shot) generation with the Koopman linearization attains FID 60.6 versus FID 190 for a CFM baseline under the same one-step budget (Section 5, Table 4).
claims.evidence: While v1 Table 4 reports Koopman FID 60.6 and CFM FID 190, the camera-ready v3 Table 7 reports Koopman with consistency FID 7.1 and OT-CFM FID 181.0, and the released checkpoint filename indicates FID 4.801—all substantially different from the claimed 60.6/190 values.

claims.claim: On 2D toy datasets (Swiss Roll, Eight Gaussians, Two Moons), the method achieves MMD scores within about 0.02 of the CFM baseline while enabling full-trajectory linearization (Section 5, Table 1, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The source audit confirms all 11 released v1 MMD pairs have abs_gap ≤ 0.02 (max 0.0161), but this is only table arithmetic, not reproduction. The independent 2D toy experiment using a simplified hand-crafted Koopman lift and basic CFM MLP found 2 of 3 datasets exceeded the 0.02 threshold (eight_gaussians gap 0.021, two_moons gap 0.037), with much higher MMD values than the paper, indicating the simplified implementation does not reproduce the paper's results.

claims.claim: An ablation shows the decoder-free architecture outperforms an encoder-decoder variant, and the combined Generator+Consistency loss reaches FID 20 on MNIST versus worse scores for either loss alone (Section 5, Table 3, Figures 9-10).
claims.evidence: V3 Table 5 reports FID 143.5 for recon+phase, 6.43 for recon+phase+target, and 7.1 for recon+phase+0.01target+consistency—adding consistency slightly worsens FID, contradicting the claim that combined loss reaches FID 20 and outperforms either loss alone. Additionally, the released checkpoint uses KoopmanAutoencoderSong (encoder-decoder), not the claimed decoder-free architecture.

Srishti280992/repro-unfolding-generative.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical verification of the Koopman generator identity (Claim 1) and thorough code/checkpoint audits that falsify Claims 2, 3, 4, and 6 by showing the camera-ready v3 and official artifacts differ substantially from the v1-based claims. The only independent experimental reproduction attempt (Claim 5) uses a simplified implementation on 2D toy data and partially contradicts the paper's MMD results, yielding a toy-level assessment rather than full verification or falsification.

Srishti280992/repro-stable-simulation-re.paper_title: STABLE: Simulation-Ready Tabletop Layout Generation via a Semantics–Physics Dual System

claims.claim: STABLE achieves 0 object collisions (0 OC metric) on task-driven tabletop layout generation, compared to non-zero collision counts for baseline methods (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The reproduction runs exact OBB and PyBullet collision detection on 72 scenes, achieving 0.000 collision pairs and 0.00% OC for the 'physics_corrector_full' method. claims.evidence: The paper's own Table 1 (recorded in PAPER_TABLES) lists AvgGPT as 9.2 (STABLE) vs 8.8 (MesaTask) on a 1-10 scale, while 99.0 and 81.5 are the AwS column values. Srishti280992/repro-stable-simulation-re.overall: This logbook provides internally consistent experimental results on a simplified proxy of STABLE's physics-correction concept, using synthetic fallback layouts and a hand-crafted torch optimizer rather than the paper's learned model on real model-generated scenes. Srishti280992/repro-convex-distance-oper.paper_title: Convex Distance Operator Transport: A Convex and Geometry-Preserving Formulation

claims.claim: CDOT formulates cross-domain distribution alignment as a convex quadratic program over transport polytopes, with Theorem 3.4 establishing existence of an optimal coupling and convexity of the objective (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook computed the exact Kronecker Hessian A.T @ A for 36 finite transport-polytope panels (n=3,4,5), finding minimum eigenvalue 1.345e-07 (positive semidefinite) and nonnegative Jensen gaps, with a destructive control (negating the squared structural term) producing 34 convexity violations.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 proves the CDOT discrepancy is a valid pseudometric on attributed compact metric-measure spaces, while Theorem 3.7 derives a 'dispersion gap' relating CDOT to Gromov-Wasserstein via ℛ_GW,2(π) − ℛ(π) = 𝒱(π) (Theorem 3.5, Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence: Exact SLSQP minima were computed on eight random three-point metric-measure spaces with 512 ordered triples showing zero pseudometric failures, and the dispersion gap identity R_GW,2(P) - R(P) = V(P) held on 64 random four-point couplings to maximum absolute error 3.89e-16 (machine precision).

claims.claim: On synthetic 2D clustered point clouds with n=500 samples, CDOT achieves a matching MSE of 0.0016±0.00, lower than both FGW (0.0034±0.00) and IsoRank (0.0033±0.00) (Table 2).
claims.evidence: At paper scale (4 clusters × 500 points, N=2000, alpha=0.5, T=200, 100 PCG64 trials), the reproduction yielded CDOT 0.00169, FGW 0.00351, IsoRank 0.00338, closely matching the paper's 0.0016/0.0034/0.0033 with paired CIs for CDOT-minus-baseline wholly below zero.

claims.evidence: The public OASIS-3 archive audit found one 168-node session among 975 (contradicting '170-node networks'), and the first-100-subject 4,950-pair panel produced diffusion accuracies of CDOT 0.7186 vs FGW 0.1540 (paper: 0.6136 vs 0.1853), failing to reproduce the claimed specific numeric values.

claims.claim: On TUDataset graph classification benchmarks, CDOT outperforms FGW on MUTAG (0.8617±0.07 vs 0.8249±0.08) and ENZYMES (0.5133±0.04 vs 0.4450±0.03) using an RBF-kernel SVM with 10-fold cross-validation (Table 4).

claims.claim: Theorem 5.6 gives a non-asymptotic risk bound decomposing into an O(1/T) optimization error and a statistical error term, with Corollary 5.7 establishing asymptotic consistency under Frank-Wolfe optimization (Theorem 5.6, Corollary 5.7).
claims.evidence: A Lean 4.32 certificate formally verified the theorem skeleton (risk decomposition into optimization and statistical errors, FW schedule composition, consistency) with exit code 0, a destructive bad-schedule control was rejected with exit code 1, and six finite FW panels (T=2..32) showed zero optimization-envelope violations with max gap/bound ratio 0.00074.

Srishti280992/repro-convex-distance-oper.overall: The logbook provides concrete mathematical and experimental evidence supporting the paper's theoretical claims (convexity, pseudometric, dispersion gap, risk bound) via exact computations, Lean formal verification, and destructive controls, and reproduces the synthetic Table 2 ordering. The OASIS-3 dataset description and diffusion accuracy values are contradicted by the public archive, and the ENZYMES graph-classification superiority claim is consistently reversed across three seeds.

claims.claim: In the population setting, Theorem 1 characterizes excess risk as a function of the magnitude and direction of the performative effect together with spurious features (Section 4, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Twelve block-covariance cells varying performative magnitude, direction, and spurious coordinates show the displayed leading risk tracking the exact fixed point with maximum absolute residual 0.000991884, providing concrete numerical support for Theorem 1's excess-risk characterization on a non-trivial setup (p=88, n=80).

claims.claim: Corollary 2 shows the optimal regularization parameter in the population regime is proportional to the strength of the performative effect, with optimal risk remaining strictly positive (Section 4, Corollary 2).
claims.evidence: At Sigma=I, constant nonzero b=0.2 and lambda*=b, the exact fixed-point risk is 0.0 and the displayed leading risk is 6.939e-18, contradicting the claim that optimal risk remains strictly positive; a nonuniform-b control at the same mean yields positive risk (0.0132), confirming the zero is a genuine counterexample rather than an implementation artifact.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 establishes a deterministic equivalent of the performative fixed point for over-parameterized ridge regression when the number of features exceeds the number of samples (Section 5, Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: For p=88>n=80, 40 two-deployment Gaussian runs give mean excess risk 0.336192 versus the deterministic equivalent 0.328403, with the gap 0.007789 below one empirical SE (0.010002), providing concrete evidence that Theorem 3's deterministic equivalent matches finite-sample behavior in the over-parameterized regime.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 shows the optimal regularization moves in the same direction as the performative effect on predictive features under low noise, but in the opposite direction under high noise, in the over-parameterized regime (Section 5, Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Exact deterministic-equivalent optimization moves lambda by +0.000692 at noise 0.2 (same direction as performative effect) but by -0.002341 and -0.006853 at noise 0.7 and 1.0 (opposite direction), concretely reproducing the low/high-noise sign reversal claimed in Theorem 4.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments in Section 6 confirm that in the over-parameterized setting, performative effects can improve optimally-regularized risk when performativity reinforces existing trends, contrasting with the population-regime degradation (Section 6).
claims.evidence: Sixteen paired released-mechanism runs over twelve lambdas with identical seeds show that reinforcing performativity (b=0.2) moves the optimal lambda from 0.05 to 0.07 and reduces optimal risk from 0.274612 to 0.268981 (improvement of 0.005630), with the b=0 control confirming the improvement is attributable to performativity.

ProCreations/repro-optimal-regularizatio.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting four of the five claims through direct evaluation of the paper's formulas and mechanisms on a non-trivial over-parameterized setup (p=88, n=80), with independent replay paths and paired controls. Claim 2 is falsified by a specific counterexample (Sigma=I, constant b) where optimal risk is exactly zero, contradicting the strict-positivity assertion, though this appears to be a boundary case that may or may not fall within the corollary's intended scope.

Srishti280992/repro-dal-a-practical-prio.paper_title: DAL: A Practical Prior-Free Black-Box Framework for Piecewise Stationary Bandits

claims.claim: DAL (Detection Augmented bandit) is presented as Algorithm 1 (Section 3), a black-box framework that pairs any stationary bandit algorithm with a change detector to handle piecewise stationary environments.
claims.evidence: 69 native DAL execution paths (33 linear, 18 GLM, 18 SCB) with d=4–16, T up to 65536, N_T=1–7 all produce finite regret with 100% change detection and 0 false alarms, exercising the black-box wrapper (forced exploration, two-window detector, base reset) on a non-toy bandit task.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 (Section 4) proves DAL achieves an order-optimal O~(sqrt(N_T * T)) regret bound, where N_T is the number of change-points over horizon T.
claims.evidence: 11/11 proof anchors found in SHA-pinned LaTeX/HTML source; 1,520,640 condition-grid cells with 196,308 admissible cells passing all 12 proof-step conditions; 6/6 negative controls fail at expected assumptions; rate-scheduled DAL paths show T slopes of 0.508–0.515, consistent with the claimed sqrt(T) factor.

claims.claim: Table 1 (Section 4) shows DAL combined with LinUCB matches the state-of-the-art d*sqrt(N_T*T) regret bound for piecewise-stationary linear bandits, and DAL with GLM-UCB attains the same rate for generalized linear bandits.
claims.evidence: 10 table rows extracted from pinned arXiv v1/v5 sources confirming DAL+LinUCB and DAL+GLM-UCB rows contain d*sqrt(N_T*T) rates; 72 rate-scheduled paths show T slopes 0.508 (linear) and 0.515 (GLM) close to the 0.5 target, though d and N_T slopes for linear are negative, indicating incomplete scaling verification.

claims.claim: For piecewise-stationary self-concordant bandits, DAL improves the regret bound from the prior d^(2/3) T^(2/3) N_T^(1/3) rate to d*sqrt(N_T*T) (Table 1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Extracted table rows show prior SCB rate d^(2/3)T^(2/3)N_T^(1/3) and DAL SCB rate d*sqrt(N_T*T); 196,608-cell exact regime audit shows strict improvement whenever T>d^2*N_T with 0 worse cells; SCB rate fits show T slope 0.515 and minimum old/new bound ratio 1.665.

claims.claim: DAL is empirically compared against MASTER (Wei & Luo, 2021), ADA-OPKB (Hong et al., 2023), and WeightUCB (Wang et al., 2023) in piecewise-stationary environments (Section 5.1, Figures 1-3) and drifting environments (Section 5.2, Figures 4-5).
claims.evidence: Paper-native figure inventory confirms all 5 arXiv v1 figure anchors (ps-lbs, ps-glbs, ps-scbs, drift-pbs, final_reg_vs_delta_drift) with 1.72MB of existing PDFs and all 3 competitors (MASTER, ADA-OPKB, WeightUCB) named in the experiment sections; v5 contains 7.02MB of consolidated figure PDFs with the same baselines.

claims.claim: The regret analysis in Appendix A.1 decomposes total regret into false-alarm cost, detection latency, the base stationary algorithm's regret, and forced-exploration cost.
claims.evidence: 140-cell exact rational ledger over d=1–64, N_T=1–31, T=10^4–10^10 with five decomposition terms (false-alarm, late-detection, latency, base, forced-exploration) all positive and reconstructing the exact total; 69 native DAL paths partition realized regret with max residual 1.68e-08; proof inventory finds corresponding anchors in source.

Srishti280992/repro-dal-a-practical-prio.overall: The logbook provides concrete evidence for all six claims through source auditing, 69 native DAL execution paths, 72 rate-scheduled scaling fits, exact ledgers, and a paper-native figure inventory, though it relies on reimplementations rather than the authors' original code and some empirical d/N_T scaling fits are inconsistent with claimed rates.

claims.claim: LatentMAS replaces text-mediated multi-agent communication with auto-regressive latent thought generation and a shared latent working memory (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: A static audit of the official LatentMAS codebase (commit 9a9e4d3) confirmed the Figure 3 mechanism: reasoners call generate_latent_batch, update a shared past_kv, emit empty outputs, and the Judger alone decodes text via generate_text_batch with past_for_decoding=past_kv when latent_steps>0; models.py shows latent vectors derived from last hidden states fed back through inputs_embeds with past_key_values passed through.

claims.claim: The paper proves latent thoughts can be more expressive than equivalent text reasoning under a linear representation hypothesis (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: A numerical counting audit confirmed |H|=3^d_h for d_h=1..12, |H^m|=3^(d_h*m) on enumerated grids, and exact minimum text length matched ceil(d_h*m*log3/log|V|) on all 72 grid points; at Qwen vocabulary size 151,936, reproduced paper-scale ratios of 235.7/377.1/471.4 tokens per latent step for d_h=2560/4096/5120, matching the paper's constants.

claims.claim: Latent working memory preserves information equivalently to directly inputting preceding agents' outputs under the paper's formal setup (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: A real-model KV-cache audit on SmolLM2-135M-Instruct, Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, and Qwen3-0.6B across 36 comparisons showed max cached-vs-full relative logit L2 of 5.59e-06, 100% top-1 agreement, and an omit-prefix control with minimum relative L2 of 0.293, confirming the formal cache identity that underpins Theorem 3.3 on real pretrained transformers.

claims.claim: LatentMAS reports higher accuracy, lower output token usage, and faster inference than single-agent and text-based MAS baselines across six general tasks in the sequential MAS setting (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Running the official code with Qwen3-4B at N=40 across all six Table 1 tasks, LatentMAS accuracy was below TextMAS on 6/6 tasks (mean -25.8 pp: e.g., GSM8K 57.5% vs 85.0%, ARC-Challenge 57.5% vs 87.5%, MBPP+ 22.5% vs 55.0%), contradicting the conjunctive claim of higher accuracy than both baselines, though token reduction (74.6% mean) and speedup (3.71x mean) were directionally reproduced.

claims.claim: On AIME, GPQA-Diamond, and other reasoning-intensive tasks, LatentMAS is evaluated under both sequential and hierarchical MAS settings with accuracy, token, and speed metrics (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Qwen3-8B was run on AIME24, AIME25, and GPQA-Diamond under both sequential and hierarchical MAS settings emitting accuracy/token/speed metrics, but at N=5 with a 512-token cap all accuracies were 0/5 (0.0%) for all methods, which is far below the paper's N=30 and 8192-20000 token caps, making the evaluation structurally present but informatively vacuous.

claims.claim: Input-output alignment improves downstream accuracy by 2.3% to 5.3% across three analyzed benchmarks (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: A direct audit of the alignment matrix W_a from Qwen3-4B/8B/14B embedding shards showed W_a is identity to numerical precision for tied Qwen3-4B (||W_a-I||/||I||=1.54e-06, so no accuracy change is possible) and near-orthogonal with ~90% least-squares residual for untied Qwen3-8B/14B (mean cos(v,vW_a)=0.009/0.004), contradicting the claimed 2.3%-5.3% downstream accuracy improvement.

Srishti280992/repro-latent-collaboration.overall: The logbook provides strong verification of the architectural and theoretical claims (Claims 1-3) through static code audit, numerical theorem verification, and real-model KV-cache experiments, but falsifies the empirical accuracy claims (Claims 4 and 6) with concrete runs showing LatentMAS underperforming TextMAS and W_a being ineffective. Claim 5 was addressed only at toy scale (N=5, 512 tokens, all-zero accuracy).

ChefThomas/repro-towards-understanding-c.paper_title: Towards Understanding Continual Factual Knowledge Acquisition of Language Models: From Theory to Algorithm

claims.claim: Theorem 1 characterizes the training dynamics of a single-layer Transformer during continual factual knowledge acquisition, showing parameter convergence to the optimal Bayesian prediction with oscillation around the convergence point (Section 2, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: A 3-category categorical SGD model (target [0.7,0.2,0.1], z=1.4, eta=0.04, 15000 steps, 3 seeds) shows convergence (mean L1=0.027, early/late error ratio 1.146) with bounded tail oscillation (std=0.096, 99.92% bounded), and full-gradient control removes oscillation (tail std=1.58e-30). This is a reduced mathematical model, not a single-layer Transformer, so it tests the theorem's qualitative predictions on a toy setup.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows attention allocation during factual knowledge acquisition is governed by a 'Diversity Index' measuring the breadth of token-object associations (Section 2, Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Integration of the Appendix E.2 ODE on 3 distributions (broad/medium/narrow) shows the proof invariant is conserved (drift 3.01e-5) and attention is perfectly anti-correlated with diversity (Spearman=-1.0), but the printed theorem invariant drifts 3.896 when learning rates differ, indicating an equation-level discrepancy. This is a simplified ODE audit, not a Transformer experiment.

claims.claim: The analysis demonstrates regularization-based continual learning methods only adjust the convergence rate of parameters without altering the underlying forgetting tendency, whereas data replay methods shift the convergence dynamics itself (Section 3).
claims.evidence: A single-parameter logistic continual-learning model shows replay shifts the convergence target (replay alpha=0.8 endpoint=0.260 matches target 0.26), but positive L2 regularization also shifts the endpoint (0.522 vs naive 0.100), partially contradicting the broad claim. Only zero-importance regularization shares the naive endpoint. This is a toy scalar model, not a full continual-learning experiment.

claims.claim: STOC (Selecting Tokens via attentiOn Contribution) selects fixed-length text snippets for generative replay by aggregating token-level attention scores across layers and heads and applying a sliding window, optionally followed by MinHash deduplication (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Source code audit at commit 75ba0ee confirms layer/head attention aggregation (attn.mean(dim=(0,1))), fixed-length sliding-window scoring, and correct window selection on a unit test (high-contribution window at position 4 selected). MinHash/deduplication code was not found in the repository, but the claim describes it as optional, and the core algorithm mechanism is confirmed in the released implementation.

claims.claim: On the synthetic 120,000-individual biography dataset with five relational attributes, STOC outperforms random-selection and LAMOL replay baselines across data mixing ratios from 0.5 to 0.9 (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook only confirms that transcribed Table 2 values match the camera-ready LaTeX source (all 12 comparisons found, STOC wins all 12). No experiments were run: the 120,000-person biography dataset is missing from the release, no GPU jobs were created (HTTP 403/402), and no independent training or evaluation was performed.

claims.claim: On real-world KnowEdit benchmarks, STOC improves Pythia-160M's ZSRE continual-knowledge accuracy to about 27.56% versus a 24.42% naive baseline, and improves Qwen2.5-0.5B to about 37.47% versus 34.58% (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirms Table 3 values (Pythia-160M 24.42→27.56, Qwen2.5-0.5B 34.58→37.47) match the camera-ready source and downloaded 1,301 KnowEdit ZSRE examples, but no model training or evaluation was performed due to GPU access failure (HTTP 403/402, $0 billed). No independent empirical results were generated.

ChefThomas/repro-towards-understanding-c.overall: The logbook provides toy-scale numerical audits supporting the qualitative predictions of Theorems 1-3 on simplified mathematical models, and verifies the STOC algorithm's core mechanism via source code inspection, but fails to independently reproduce either empirical table (Claims 5-6) because no GPU compute was available and key released artifacts (dataset, checkpoints) are missing.

Srishti280992/repro-riemannian-networks-.paper_title: Riemannian Networks over Full-Rank Correlation Matrices

claims.claim: CorNets extend Multinomial Logistic Regression (MLR), Fully Connected (FC), and convolutional layers to the full-rank correlation manifold Cor+(n) under five Riemannian geometries: ECM, LECM, OLM, LSM, and PHCM (Section 2, Table 1).
claims.evidence: The audit tests MLR and FC layer constructions for all five geometries on 5×5 correlation matrices with 4096 trials, confirming valid outputs and machine-precision oracle checks, but does not test convolutional layers (one of the three claimed layer types) and involves no network training, making it a small-scale numerical construction check rather than a full reproduction.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 gives closed-form expressions for Log-Euclidean correlation FC layers under ECM, LECM, OLM, and LSM, e.g. the ECM-FC output is Y = Cor∘Chol^{-1}(V^EC + I_m) (Theorem 3.5, Equations 10-13).
claims.evidence: The closed-form FC expressions for ECM, LECM, OLM, and LSM were verified by round-trip reconstruction to machine precision (max errors 3.3e-16 to 1.0e-13) across 4096 trials; since these are deterministic mathematical formulas, scale does not affect correctness.

claims.claim: On the NTU120 dataset, CorNet-ECM/CorNet-LECM achieve accuracy of 65.04±0.14 / 65.03±0.10, outperforming the classic SPDNet (57.59±0.22) by 7.76%/7.75% and the best Grassmannian baseline GyroGr-Scaling (43.90±0.23) by over 21 points (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The table audit found that the paper's Table 2 reports SPDNet NTU120 = 51.25±0.36, not 57.59±0.22 as claimed; 57.59±0.22 is GrNet's value, and GyroGr-Scaling (43.90) is the weakest Grassmannian method, not the best baseline.

claims.claim: On the Radar dataset, CorNet-ECM reaches 97.71±0.61 accuracy, surpassing SPDNet (93.25±1.10) by 5.15%, and CorNets outperform SPDNet across all four datasets (HDM05, FPHA, NTU120) by margins of 17.69%, 6.58%, and 13.84% respectively (Table 2, Section 5).
claims.evidence: The Radar point margin for CorNet-ECM over SPDNet is 4.46 (relative 4.78%), not 5.15; the 5.15 margin belongs to CorNet-LECM (98.40), and the NTU120 best-CorNet margin is 13.79, not the claimed 13.84.

claims.claim: Ablation on mixed geometries (Table 3) shows that using consistent (diagonal) metrics for both the convolutional and MLR layers yields the best accuracy overall, e.g. ECM-ECM achieves 81.35±1.27 on HDM05, the top result in that row/column comparison.
claims.evidence: While ECM-ECM=81.35 is indeed the best in its HDM05 row, exhaustive enumeration of Table 3 shows diagonal metrics win only 8/10 rows; HDM05 LECM-OLM (79.21) beats LECM-LECM (78.05), and FPHA OLM-LECM (92.27) is the global maximum, beating diagonal OLM-OLM (91.63).

claims.claim: Replacing SPDNet's covariance input with correlation input on HDM05 improves accuracy from 64.57±0.61 to 66.81±0.83, while it degrades performance on Radar (93.25±1.10 to 89.49±0.67) and FPHA (85.59±0.72 to 83.37±0.40), illustrating dataset-dependent benefits of correlation embeddings (Table 4).
claims.evidence: The direction-of-effect claims are correct (HDM05 +2.24, Radar −3.76, FPHA −2.22), but the HDM05 correlation standard deviation is 0.73 in Table 4, not 0.83 as stated in the claim.

Srishti280992/repro-riemannian-networks-.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous small-scale numerical audit verifying the mathematical layer constructions (Claims 1–2) and a systematic table-level audit that falsifies the empirical benchmark claims (Claims 3–6) by finding concrete attribution and arithmetic errors against the paper's own tables. No actual model training was attempted, so the empirical accuracy claims are checked only against the paper's published tables, not independently reproduced.

ProCreations/repro-procedural-generation.paper_title: Procedural Generation Of Algorithm Discovery Tasks in Machine Learning

claims.claim: DiscoGen procedurally generates over 400 million distinct algorithm discovery tasks via a combinatorial formula N_tasks = 2*3*b*(2^m-1)*(3^d-2^(d+1)+1) depending on the number of modules m, datasets d, and backends b (Section 4.2, Equation 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook recomputes all ten Table-1 domain rows using the formula and independently enumerates Cartesian states for four finite domains, both yielding a sum of 493,355,172 (>400M); a destructive control removing the train/test nonemptiness correction changes the m=3,d=4,b=2 count, confirming the formula is genuinely exercised.

claims.claim: Including additional domains beyond the main evaluation set, DiscoGen's total task space reaches approximately 99 billion tasks (Appendix C).
claims.evidence: Fourteen Appendix-C domain rows sum exactly to 99,299,115,384 (≈99 billion), independently confirmed by inventorying 14 domain configurations in the official repository; removing On-Policy MARL collapses the total below 2 billion as a destructive control.

claims.claim: Across the 10 domains used in the main evaluation, per-domain task counts range from 900 (Greenhouse Gas Prediction) to 426,043,800 (On-Policy RL), with a median of 59,622 tasks per domain (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The executed table has 10 domains with minimum 900 (Greenhouse Gas Prediction), maximum 426,043,800 (On-Policy RL), and median 59,622, recomputed via independent Python order statistics from all ten parsed rows rather than accepting printed summary lines.

claims.claim: DiscoBench provides a fixed evaluation subset built from DiscoGen, comprising, for each domain, m single-module tasks (DiscoBench Single) plus one comprehensive all-modules-active task (DiscoBench All) (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: All 74 released m+1 DiscoBench configurations pass schema validation with zero failures, and four official builder runs materialize 82 code/description files at a pinned tree digest; a destructive control confirming that activating a second module in a single-module config is rejected validates the m-single-plus-one-all structure.

claims.claim: As the number of editable modules increases in DiscoBench tasks, agent success rates consistently decline while the achievable performance ceiling rises (Appendix G).
claims.evidence: Success-rate means by module count [51.4, 28.7, 5.533, 0.0] are monotonically nonincreasing across all three models from 1 to 4 editable modules, and the mean four-environment ceiling rises from 99.3475 to 108.3300 (+8.9825); however, these numbers are parsed from the paper's Appendix G table rather than independently produced by running agents.

ProCreations/repro-procedural-generation.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence for all five claims through formula recomputation, exhaustive state enumeration, configuration validation, and builder execution with independent oracles and destructive controls. Claims 1–4 are rigorously verified through genuine computation on the official codebase; Claim 5 is supported by concrete numbers but relies on parsing the paper's reported Appendix-G results rather than independently running agent experiments.

Jaycee766/repro-effective-reasoning-chai.paper_title: Effective Reasoning Chains Reduce Intrinsic Dimensionality

claims.claim: On Gemma-3 4B across 14 CoT reasoning strategies on GSM8K, intrinsic dimensionality achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.93 (p<0.01) with overall accuracy (geometric mean across in-distribution GSM8K test and 5 OOD stress sets), outperforming token perplexity (0.82), length (0.31), and KL divergence (-0.17) as predictors (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook only recomputes Spearman correlations from the paper's own printed Table 1 values (data/table1_gemma4b.csv), yielding 0.9303 vs 0.93. No independent LoRA fine-tuning, intrinsic-dimension computation, or accuracy evaluation was performed; this verifies table arithmetic, not the claim.

claims.claim: On the smaller Gemma-3 1B model, intrinsic dimensionality still correlates at 0.75 with overall generalization performance, again beating token perplexity (0.63), length (0.24), and KL divergence (-0.18), showing the metric's predictive power holds across model scale (Table 2, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Recomputation from the paper's rounded Table 2 yields 0.7217, not the claimed 0.75, and no independent experiment was run—only table arithmetic was checked. The discrepancy is attributed to rounding but cannot be resolved without full-precision data.

claims.claim: Intrinsic dimension is computed as the parameter count at which a LoRA-rank Pareto frontier of training accuracy versus trainable parameters first crosses a fixed accuracy threshold (e.g., 63.0% for Gemma-3 4B), visualized via the accuracy-vs-parameters curves for each reasoning strategy (Figure 2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The Pareto-frontier threshold-crossing algorithm was implemented and unit-tested, but only on a synthetic 4-row example with parameters [1,2,4,8] and fabricated accuracies. The logbook explicitly states that reconstructing Figure 2's empirical curves is not possible from the paper alone.

claims.claim: The correlation between intrinsic dimensionality and generalization performance is robust to threshold choice, remaining between 0.72 and 0.94 across 1B and 4B models when using 70%, 80%, or 90% of epoch-1 training accuracy or 90% of validation accuracy as the threshold (Table 3, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook only checks that the eight coefficients in Table 3 fall within the reported 0.72–0.94 range (internal consistency of the paper's own table). No independent recomputation of any threshold-sensitivity correlation was performed, as the underlying LoRA accuracy curves were unavailable.

Jaycee766/repro-effective-reasoning-chai.overall: This logbook is a CPU-only arithmetic audit of the paper's printed tables, with no model training, no independent metric computation, and no evaluation runs. It confirms the paper's table arithmetic is largely self-consistent but provides no independent experimental evidence for any of the four claims.

MarxistLeninist/repro-all-erms-fail-sco.paper_title: All ERMs Can Fail in Stochastic Convex Optimization Lower Bounds in Linear Dimension

claims.claim: In dimension d = 6m, there exists a stochastic convex optimization instance where every ε-ERM solution with ε = Θ(m^{-3/2}) incurs constant excess risk and fails to generalize (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook tests the closed-form ERM at d=6m² (not the claimed d=6m), with only m∈{2,3}. It verifies that the unique exact minimizer w★ overfits by Ω(1)≈0.235–0.267, but does not test the 'every ε-ERM' claim at ε=Θ(m^{-3/2}) nor the linear-dimension setting.

claims.claim: For λ-strongly convex losses with m^{-3/2} ≤ λ ≤ m^{-1/2}, any ε-ERM solution w_S satisfies F(w_S) − min F(w) ≥ Ω(1/(λ m^{3/2})) (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: The robustness section shows a qualitative trend (excess risk decreases from 0.187 to 0.081 as λ goes from 0 to 0.8), but never checks the specific bound Ω(1/(λm^{3/2})) quantitatively, and only tests at m=2 or 3 without verifying the stated λ range or the exact scaling.

claims.claim: When ηT = Ω(m^{3/2}), gradient descent incurs constant generalization error with high probability, as a corollary of the ERM lower bound (Corollary 3).
claims.evidence: The GD experiment at m=2 shows the population gap rising and saturating at ≈0.21 as ηT grows, qualitatively matching constant generalization error, but the 'high probability' aspect is unaddressed and the scale (m=2) is far too small to verify the ηT=Ω(m^{3/2}) threshold.

claims.claim: Gradient descent's excess risk is lower-bounded by F(w_S^{GD}) − min F(w) = Ω(min{√(ηT/m^{3/2}), 1}) (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: At m∈{2,3}, the logbook shows the GD gap grows and saturates, and the ratio gap/min(√(ηT/m^{1.5}),1) stays ≥0.041, but the measured log-log slope is ≈0.71 rather than the predicted 0.5, so the exact Ω(min{√(ηT/m^{3/2}),1}) functional form is not cleanly isolated at this scale.

claims.claim: This new generalization lower bound of Ω(ηT + √(ηT/m^{3/2})) for constrained gradient descent narrows the previously exponential gap to the best known upper bound of O(ηT + ηT/m) (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: No experiment in the logbook directly compares the lower bound Ω(ηT + √(ηT/m^{3/2})) against the upper bound O(ηT + ηT/m) or addresses whether the previously exponential gap is narrowed; the GD experiments only test the lower-bound side at toy scale.

claims.claim: The construction uses Feldman's asymptotically good binary code combined with a novel 'link function' mapping sample information to bad ERM solutions while preserving convexity, giving the first proof that all approximate ERMs fail in linear dimension (Section on technical construction / proof of Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The Feldman building-block gap (ρ/4) is verified at m∈{2,3,4,6,8} and the link-ablation control confirms the link term is necessary (removing it restores w=0 as a good ERM), but the construction is tested at d=6m² not the claimed linear d=6m, and the 'all approximate ERMs fail' property is only checked via uniqueness of the exact minimizer, not for ε-ERMs.

MarxistLeninist/repro-all-erms-fail-sco.overall: The logbook provides genuine numerical evidence that the paper's explicit construction (at d=6m², m∈{2,3}) produces a unique overfitting ERM with constant excess risk, and that GD overfits qualitatively. However, the headline linear-dimension (d=6m) result, the 'every ε-ERM' claim, the strong-convexity quantitative bound, and the gap-narrowing comparison are not substantiated at the claimed scale or specificity.

Srishti280992/repro-off-policy-large-act.paper_title: Off-Policy Learning in Large Action Spaces: Optimization Matters More Than Estimation

claims.claim: Proposition 2.1 shows gradient descent on OPE-based objectives (e.g., IPS, Clipped IPS, Doubly Robust, MIPS, OffCEM, POTEC) can be trapped in suboptimal regions for O(K) iterations, where K is the number of actions (Section 2, Proposition 2.1).
claims.evidence: The numerical simulation directly tests the O(K) plateau claim: gradient ascent escape time to pi_target>=0.1 scales linearly with K (slope 2.0044 iters/action, R²=0.99999856) across K=5 to K=5000, with K=5000 requiring 10007 iterations.

claims.claim: Proposition 2.2 proves the optimization landscape of OPE-based objectives contains exponentially many local maxima in K (Section 2, Proposition 2.2).
claims.evidence: The tiled-widget construction certifies 2^t strict local maxima for K=5t actions: exhaustive Hessian checks confirm all 4096/4096 signed maxima are strict (negative eigenvalue) up to t=12, with log2(count) vs K slope exactly 0.20000 (R²=1.0), confirming 2^(K/5) scaling.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 proves that weighted log-likelihood (PWLL) objectives combined with L2-regularized softmax policies are strongly concave, guaranteeing a unique global maximum (Section 3, Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: Across 300 randomized feature embeddings, the analytically-computed L2-regularized PWLL Hessian has max eigenvalue <= -0.049 in 300/300 cases (worst -0.0500), while IPS is non-concave in 300/300 cases (mean max eigenvalue 0.4007), directly confirming the strong concavity property.

claims.claim: Figure 2 shows that low mean-squared error of the off-policy value estimator does not correlate with high reward from the learned policy, i.e., good OPE performance does not predict good OPL performance (Section 4, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The high-rigor run trains actual IPS/CIPS/SNIPS/DR/PWLL policies on a controlled 200-context, 500-action bandit with known ground truth, showing CIPS has lowest OPE MSE (0.137) but IPS achieves highest reward (1.0) while SNIPS has low MSE (0.182) but poor reward (0.438). However, this is a simplified proxy setup, not the paper's Figure 2 scale or datasets.

claims.claim: Figure 1 shows OPE-based objectives are highly sensitive to batch size and learning rate, whereas PWLL objectives (including LPI, cLPI, and RegKL variants) remain robust across these hyperparameter configurations (Section 3, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The high-rigor run trains actual IPS and PWLL on a 200-context, 500-action bandit across a 4×5 batch-size×learning-rate grid, showing IPS CV=1.294 (range 0.002–0.019) vs PWLL CV=0.0032 (range 0.986–1.0). However, only IPS and PWLL are tested—not the LPI, cLPI, and RegKL variants specified in the claim—and the setup is much smaller than the paper's Figure 1.

claims.claim: On large-action-space benchmarks including MovieLens (K=60K), Twitch (K=200K), and GoodReads (K=1M actions), PWLL-based policies outperform estimator-aware methods such as POTEC (Section 4, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The synthetic native-K benchmark (second attempt) actually contradicts the claim: PWLL loses to POTEC on MovieLens (0.928 vs 0.943) and Twitch (0.929 vs 0.982), winning only on GoodReads (0.930 vs 0.915).
