claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 gives three convergence-rate regimes for the effective sample size n_eff = gamma*n: polynomial spectral decay yields rate O~((n_eff)^(-2l/(1+2l))), exponential decay yields O~(1/n_eff), and finite rank yields O~(D/n_eff) (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Log-log slopes of optimal bound MISE vs n (up to n=128000) match theory: poly ℓ=1 slope −0.676 (theory −0.667), poly ℓ=2 slope −0.790 (theory −0.800), finite rank D=8 slope −1.000 with MISE·n→8.01≈D, and exponential decay shows the (log n)/n signature (n·MISE grows 2.13×).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 shows the fully data-driven model-selection procedure achieves minimax-optimal convergence rates without requiring prior knowledge of spectral decay or the overlap parameter (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Hold-out CV selecting λ without knowledge of ℓ or γ achieves slope −0.725 vs oracle −0.708 (theory −0.667), with max CV/oracle ratio 1.27 across n up to 128000, demonstrating adaptive rate-matching.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 establishes a matching minimax lower bound of order (n_eff)^(-2beta/(1+2beta)) over Sobolev spaces, confirming the adaptivity result of Theorem 4.2 is rate-optimal (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Fano packing construction on critical band j₀=n^{1/(1+2ℓ)} yields pairwise L2² separation slope −0.667 matching the upper-bound rate, with non-vacuous bracket floor 0.22, confirming rate-optimality.

claims.claim: The method is validated empirically on both synthetic and semi-real data (Section 5.1, Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: Only a single Monte-Carlo consistency check (rel=0.003) with a negative control is provided; no semi-real data experiments are conducted, and the synthetic check merely verifies that simulation matches exact spectral computation rather than reproducing the paper's Section 5 empirical validation on synthetic and semi-real datasets.

DineshAI/ziqS4yXFQX.overall: The logbook provides solid numerical spectral verification of the three theoretical claims (Theorems 4.1–4.3) with well-designed rate checks, bound domination tests, and negative controls on a non-toy finite-dimensional RKHS setup. However, the empirical validation claim (Section 5) is essentially unaddressed: no semi-real data experiments are run, and the sole synthetic check is a trivial simulation-vs-exact-computation consistency test rather than the paper's actual empirical experiments.

Shibashish/repro-protein-design-with-age.paper_title: Protein Design with Agent Rosetta: A Case Study for Specialized Scientific Agents

claims.claim: Using simplified action syntax raises Agent Rosetta's composition-penalty generation success rate from about 70% (GPT-5 without the simplification) to at least 98.88% across all tested LLMs (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: 900 real LLM generations (5 models × 9 prompts × 10 reps × 2 syntaxes) through Hugging Face Inference Providers, graded with a verifier validated against all 5 of the paper's adjudicated examples. All 5 models scored 100.00% (450/450) on simplified syntax, clearing the 98.88% floor; original syntax ranged 4.44–57.78%, consistent with the paper's ~70% GPT-5 ceiling. The ~70% GPT-5 figure itself was not directly tested (closed API), but the core claim about simplified syntax is directly confirmed at the paper's own scale.

claims.claim: On fixed-backbone sequence design across 8 test protein structures (74-125 residues), Agent Rosetta's action success rate is at least 86% across all LLMs, and its median RMSD matches ProteinMPNN within 0.20 Å tolerance while outperforming baselines on 5 of 8 conformations (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The paper's own Table 5 reports Qwen3 30B Instruct at 25% action success, directly contradicting 'at least 86% across all LLMs.' The RMSD-within-0.20-Å sub-claim (worst gap 0.105 Å) and the 5-of-8-conformations sub-claim are confirmed by arithmetic audit of the paper's tables, and ProteinMPNN was independently re-run (256 designs, 50.2% recovery vs ~52.4% published), but Agent Rosetta itself was not independently executed (requires licensed Rosetta build with ≥130 MPI processes).

claims.claim: Gemini 2.5 Flash and Qwen3 Instruct achieve the best cost-performance tradeoff among LLM backbones tested for backbone-stabilization design, using 30 LLM queries per trajectory and 128 candidate designs per step (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Protocol constants (30 queries, 128 designs) were confirmed from released config files, and Pareto analysis of the paper's own Table 5 correctly places both named models on the cost-performance frontier (exactly those two after filtering by ≥80% action success). However, no independent experiments were run—both the cost figures and RMSD numbers are taken directly from the paper's tables without re-measurement.

claims.claim: For designing a single non-canonical formyl-tryptophan (TRF) residue into the protein core across 4 de novo folds (40-153 residues), GPT-5 achieves the highest TRF inclusion success rate, about 14.5%, on the most challenging structure (PDB 8UZL) (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook independently re-implemented Rosetta's LayerSelector burial algorithm and applied it to all 4 NCAA targets downloaded from RCSB, confirming 8UZL has 0 core-layer residues (vs 3–6 for others), supporting the paper's stated mechanism for why 8UZL is hardest. However, the actual claim—GPT-5 achieving ~14.5% TRF inclusion success on 8UZL—was never tested, as it requires the full Rosetta + AF3 pipeline.

claims.claim: Agent Rosetta outperforms the human expert baseline on AF3 RMSD and pLDDT metrics for non-canonical amino acid design, evaluated over 16 independent trajectories per method with 1,000 bootstrap samples (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: Arithmetic audit of the paper's Tables 7–8 shows the claim holds for 2 of 4 backbones (GPT-5: 855 mÅ/82.3 pLDDT; Gemini: 1137 mÅ/79.2 pLDDT vs human 2789 mÅ/78.6 pLDDT) but Qwen3 235B is worse than human on both metrics (3133 mÅ/66.8 pLDDT). The averaging is asymmetric (human over 3 PDBs, agents over 4). No independent experiments were run; all values are from the paper's own tables.

Shibashish/repro-protein-design-with-age.overall: The logbook provides a strong full-scale reproduction of Claim 1 (900 generations, validated grader, 100% simplified syntax across all models) and a solid independent re-run of the ProteinMPNN baseline (256 designs), but Claims 2–5 were only arithmetically audited against the paper's own tables or tested via proxy experiments, because the Rosetta C++ build, ESMFold, and AlphaFold 3 were all unavailable. The audits are thorough and surface real discrepancies (Qwen3 30B's 25% action success falsifies Claim 2 as stated; Claim 5's averaging is not like-for-like), but these are not independent experimental verifications.

prarabdhmisra/J0y3sNbo9G.paper_title: Theoretical Investigation on Inductive Bias of Isolation Forest

claims.claim: Isolation Forest's expected depth function is derived in closed form by modeling the iTree growth process as a random walk with transition probabilities based on point spacing (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: The Theorem 3.5 closed form matches an exact DP solution of the Theorem 3.2 random walk to 5.81e-16 relative error over 11,880 (dataset, point) pairs (n=3..24) and 4.24e-16 over 1.65M states at n up to 256 with no error growth; real iTrees match within Monte Carlo error (worst mean rel. err. 0.0037 at n≤200, 0.011 at n≤1000), and the full depth distribution of the rightmost point passes chi-square goodness-of-fit in 0/9 rejections.

claims.claim: For marginal single anomalies, Isolation Forest's detection threshold scales as U·κ (data-dependent), while k-NN requires separation greater than U+(k-1)δ/2 (parameter-dependent on k), showing iForest has greater parameter adaptability (Theorems 4.3-4.5).
claims.evidence: The k-NN formula U+(k-1)δ/2 is reproduced to 9.77e-10 (R²=1.0) and parameter adaptability is demonstrated, but the iForest threshold 'scales as U·κ' is contradicted: worst-case critical separation over κ-dense blocks yields log-log slopes of +0.009/+0.000/+0.021 on κ (n=10/20/50) vs predicted +1.0, with the threshold staying 1.07–1.31·U regardless of κ (up to 43× below U·κ).

claims.claim: For central single anomalies, Isolation Forest's decision threshold is Θ(√(n₀κ)) versus k-NN's Θ(kδ), demonstrating iForest's lower sensitivity to centrally-located anomalies (Theorems 4.6-4.7, Table 2).
claims.evidence: The n₀ exponent (+0.42±0.01) is close to the predicted +0.5, but the κ exponent is +0.005±0.016 vs predicted +0.5 (raising κ from 2 to 80 moves the threshold by −0.18%), and the k-NN Θ(kδ) summary is contradicted at δ=0 where the measured threshold is (k+4)U/4 = 1.5/2/3/5/9/17 for k=2..64, not 0 as Θ(k·0) implies.

claims.claim: For marginal clustered anomalies of size n₁, Isolation Forest requires separation of order Θ(n₁²κ) while k-NN requires Θ(kδ) under the constraint ω(n₁)≤k≤o(n₀) (Theorems 4.8-4.9).
claims.evidence: The n₁² exponent is confirmed (+2.118, 95% CI +2.085..+2.151, R²=0.99975 on the paper's own construction) and the ω(n₁)≤k constraint is verified (k-NN never flags all anomalies for k≤n₁), but the κ exponent is +0.186±0.095 vs predicted +1.0, and Θ(kδ) at δ=0 yields a measured threshold of 5.0 (not 0) at every k.

claims.claim: Empirical mean-squared error between empirical and theoretical expected depths decreases as the number of trees increases, confirming the concentration property of Proposition 3.1 (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Over 70 (configuration, M) cells with n=50..800 and M=100..1000, the pooled MSE-vs-M exponent is −1.0091±0.0329 (0.28σ from predicted −1), MSE falls 7.7–12.5× from M=100 to M=1000, three negative controls (h̄+0.5, shuffled h̄, Liu's c(n)) are flat with |slope|≤0.133, and the RMS deviation exponent is −0.573 (95% CI containing −0.5).

claims.claim: Across OpenML benchmark datasets, 930,738 of 930,751 tested dimensions satisfy the condition κ≥√(n+3) required for the theoretical analysis (Section 4, Assumption 4.2).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive measurement on 8,609 numeric dimensions of 43 OpenML datasets finds only 64.93% satisfy κ≥√(n+3) vs the claimed 99.99860% (a 56.8σ shortfall); the mechanism is proven exhaustively (arithmetic-progressions yield κ=1 exactly in 5,997/5,997 cases), and a paired control with uniform surrogates at identical n gives 98.96% satisfaction, isolating the failure to real data structure.

prarabdhmisra/J0y3sNbo9G.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the core theoretical machinery (Theorem 3.5's closed form is exact to machine precision, and the concentration property of Proposition 3.1 holds at rate 1/M) but falsifies the κ-scaling factors in the anomaly-detection thresholds of Theorems 4.3–4.9 (κ exponents near 0 instead of +0.5 or +1.0) and the empirical OpenML claim (64.9% vs 99.998%).

prarabdhmisra/uYWVGk1Qt0.paper_title: Towards Understanding Adam Convergence on Highly Degenerate Polynomials

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that on the degenerate polynomial loss L(x) = (1/k) x^k for k >= 4, Adam achieves local linear convergence when beta_1 < beta_2^(k/(2(k-2))), with asymptotic rate x_{t+1}/x_t -> beta_2^(1/(2(k-2))) (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive 400×400 grid over (beta1,beta2) for k=4,6,8,10,12 shows r(J)<1 matches Eq.(8)+(9) at ≥99.9994% (100% off-boundary); measured x_{t+1}/x_t matches beta2^{1/(2(k-2))} to worst relative error 1.76e-09 over 200 seeded runs; sharpness sweep shows convergence destroyed immediately past the threshold; eps=1e-8 negative control recovers the Thm 5.1 power law within 3%.

claims.claim: Gradient Descent and Heavy-Ball Momentum both exhibit only sublinear convergence of order Theta(t^{-1/(k-2)}) on the same degenerate polynomial objective, established in Theorems 5.1 and 5.3 respectively.
claims.evidence: GD asymptotic slope at T=600k matches -1/(k-2) to worst error 3.64e-04 (R²=1.0000000); continuous-time HB matches to 5.03e-04 for beta1≤0.9; closed-form ODE validated to machine precision. The discrete HB divergence at beta1=0.99 is a step-size artifact outside the continuous-time theorems' scope, transparently reported.

claims.claim: Remark 5.8 quantifies the resulting complexity separation: Gradient Descent requires iteration complexity T_epsilon ~ epsilon^{-(k-2)} to reach accuracy epsilon, whereas Adam achieves T_epsilon ~ (k-2) ln(1/epsilon) (Remark 5.8).
claims.evidence: GD hitting-time exponent matches k-2 with measured T_eps agreeing to exact closed-form inversion within 0.2%; Adam T_eps is exactly linear in ln(1/eps) (min R²=0.99999993) with prefactor regressed on (k-2) at R²=1.0000000 and intercept ≈0.005; separation of 317 orders of magnitude measured at k=12, eps=1e-32.

claims.claim: Lemma 5.4 shows the second moment estimate satisfies v_t/v_{t-1} -> beta_2 asymptotically, decoupling v_t from the instantaneous squared gradient g_t^2 and producing an effective learning rate that grows as beta_2^{-t/2} (Lemma 5.4).
claims.evidence: v_t/v_{t-1} matches beta2 to worst |error| 6.81e-13 over 40 converging configs (k=4–12 × beta2=0.8–0.99); d ln(eta_eff)/dt matches -0.5 ln(beta2) to 6.27e-12; decoupling rate d ln R/dt matches -ln(beta2)/(k-2) to 7.48e-12; Regime-III negative control deviates by 0.2–0.5, confirming the convergence hypothesis is load-bearing.

claims.claim: Section 6 identifies three convergence regimes governed by beta_1 relative to beta_2: stable exponential convergence, an intermediate regime with an initial exponential phase followed by loss spikes from fixed-point instability, and a SignGD-like oscillatory regime under tight v_t-g_t^2 coupling (Section 6, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Fig. 6's three configurations measured: Regime I (0 spikes, final -4061.68, max omega*lambda=27.31 vs 2/eta=2000), Regime II (29858 spikes, max spike 58.7 decades, omega*lambda exceeds threshold by 2.4e14), Regime III (final R_t=0.06, tight v_t-g_t^2 coupling); Regime-I slope -0.0943106795 matches paper's -0.0943 to 6.0e-13; exhaustive 51×51 grid agrees at 99.86–100% off-boundary; Eq.(6) violation separates Regime I from II/III with zero errors on 4603 points.

claims.claim: Figure 3 shows the empirical phase diagram of stability boundaries across different degeneracy orders k matches the theoretical predictions of Equations 8-9 (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Fig. 3(b) heatmap reproduces at 99.376% (k=4) and 99.584% (k=6), 100% off-boundary; boundary located quantitatively with median ratio of measured error to independently predicted finite-T resolution limit = 0.977; error scales as 1/T (11x reduction for 16x T increase); Eq.(9) lower-left corner matches to 2.0e-05–2.4e-04 in all 10 binding cases; eta-independence confirmed (2.8e-04 change for 10x eta change).

prarabdhmisra/uYWVGk1Qt0.overall: This logbook provides rigorous numerical verification of all six claims through exhaustive grid searches, multi-k testing, log-space integration validated against float64 Adam, and quantitative boundary location with finite-run resolution analysis. The reproduction is at the paper's actual theoretical scale (degenerate polynomial optimization), with careful negative controls and transparent reporting of limitations.

ProCreations/repro-softjax-softtorch-inf.paper_title: SoftJAX & SoftTorch: Empowering Automatic Differentiation Libraries with Informative Gradients

claims.claim: SoftJAX and SoftTorch provide differentiable soft surrogates for hard primitives including thresholding (sign, abs, round, ReLU, clip via Heaviside relaxations), Boolean/fuzzy logic operators, discrete indexing (SoftIndex), and sorting/ranking (Sections 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: Both released libraries execute five threshold operators with max value disagreement 5.551e-17 and max gradient disagreement 3.331e-16; fuzzy logic, SoftIndex, discrete indexing, sort and rank all produce finite gradients; destructive control shows hard mode yields exactly zero gradient norms versus 3.097231 and 2.909352 in soft mode.

claims.claim: The libraries identify an 'STE pitfall' where applying straight-through estimation separately to each factor of a multiplicative composite operation causes gradients to vanish, and show this is avoided by applying STE to the composite function as a whole (Section 2, Equation 1).
claims.evidence: At x=(-0.5,-0.25), separate STE factors produce gradient norm exactly 0.0 while composite STE produces norm 0.005191866, with both SoftJAX and SoftTorch agreeing to machine precision and hard forward values remaining zero — directly demonstrating the pitfall and its fix.

claims.claim: Four families of differentiable sort/rank operators are implemented: optimal-transport-based, unit-simplex-projection-based (SoftSort, NeuralSort), permutahedron-projection-based (FastSoftSort, and a novel entropy-regularized SmoothSort variant), and sorting-network-based (Sections 4.1-4.4).
claims.evidence: All four families (OT, SoftSort/NeuralSort, FastSoftSort/SmoothSort, sorting network) execute with finite gradients; six SoftJAX methods and five SoftTorch methods agree with max cross-library sorted-value disagreement of 1.113e-08; destructive control of deleting permutahedron implementations reduces coverage from four to three families.

claims.claim: FastSoftSort achieves the lowest memory footprint (~420KB) among benchmarked soft-sorting methods at n=4096, while the sorting-network approach is fastest at ~1.0ms (3.8x the hard baseline), versus ~16ms for SoftSort and ~37ms for NeuralSort (Section 5, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: At n=4096 using the authors' benchmark driver, FastSoftSort uses 336.992 KiB (memory winner), sorting network is fastest at 0.667ms, SoftSort is 17.55ms, NeuralSort is 33.51ms — all qualitatively matching the paper's reported ordering and approximate magnitudes, with destructive control showing SoftSort substitution worsens memory by 24.7x and latency by 26.3x.

claims.claim: A case study applies SoftJAX operators (sj.argmax, sj.dynamic_index_in_dim) to soften the manifold-point-selection step of MuJoCo XLA's collision detection pipeline, enabling gradient flow through a previously non-differentiable physics operation (Appendix B).
claims.evidence: On the paper's n=5 manifold case, hard MuJoCo-XLA selection leaves one of five vertices with zero gradient while sj.argmax plus sj.dynamic_index_in_dim yields nonzero gradients at all 5/5 vertices, with hard mode exactly matching original indices; destructive control replacing SoftJAX operators with jnp.argmax restores the zero-gradient vertex.

ProCreations/repro-softjax-softtorch-inf.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence for all five claims through direct execution of the released SoftJAX and SoftTorch libraries, cross-library agreement checks, and destructive controls. While the benchmark numbers in Claim 4 differ somewhat in absolute value from the paper's reported figures, the qualitative ordering and approximate scales match, and all other claims are supported at their native scale with specific quantitative results.

tomyimkc/repro-posterior-sampling-reinfo.paper_title: Posterior Sampling Reinforcement Learning with Gaussian Processes for Continuous Control: Sublinear Regret Bounds for Unbounded State Spaces

claims.claim: Theorem 4.11 establishes a Bayesian regret bound for GP-PSRL of order R_T = O(H^{3/2} sqrt((d_s+d_a) gamma_N(sigma^2, R̃) T log T)), giving tight sqrt(gamma_T) dependence on the maximum information gain rather than a linear dependence (Theorem 4.11).
claims.evidence: The log-log slope of median regret vs mean gamma_T across 7 RBF lengthscales (35 seeds each, T=1600) was 0.4685 (R²=0.7961), only 0.0315 from the predicted sqrt exponent of 0.5 and 0.5315 from the linear alternative of 1.0; the diagonal-belief control showed 3.6x regret vs the well-specified fit at matched gamma_T, confirming the kernel-induced generalization mechanism drives the rate.

claims.claim: Lemma 4.7 uses a recursive application of the Borell-Tsirelson-Ibragimov-Sudakov inequality to show that states visited by the algorithm remain within a ball of near-constant radius with high probability, enabling analysis without assuming bounded state spaces (Lemma 4.7).
claims.evidence: As T grew 16x (200→3200), empirical mean max|state| grew only 1.1629x (2.225→2.5875), closely matching the theoretical R growth ratio of 1.1675x; P(max>R)=0.0 across all settings (within the claimed ≤2/T bound); the unstable-dynamics control grew by a factor of 1.32e9 over the same range, confirming the BTIS mechanism is load-bearing.

claims.claim: The analysis requires only Holder continuity of the GP kernel with parameters L>0 and alpha in (0,1] (Assumption 3.4), removing prior requirements of four-times-differentiable kernels (Section 3, Assumption 3.4).
claims.evidence: The experiment numerically confirmed that Matérn-1/2 has a genuine first-order kink (f'(0+)=-0.999999) while all four tested kernels have finite Hölder(α=1) constants, and the α=2 ratio diverged by 99991x as gap shrank while α=1 stayed flat — but this tests kernel properties numerically rather than verifying the proof's validity, and only checks order-1 differentiability as a witness against 4x-differentiability.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.13 specializes the general regret bound to Matérn kernels, giving concrete polynomial-in-T rates for this standard kernel family (Corollary 4.13).
claims.evidence: Fitted T-exponents for Matérn-0.5/1.5/2.5 were 0.313/0.239/0.221 vs theoretical 0.833/0.700/0.643 (mean absolute error 0.468), correctly ordered by smoothness but undershooting by roughly half due to finite-grid saturation at T≤800 on a 325-cell grid with d=2.

claims.claim: The regret analysis assumes a bounded action space (Assumption 3.1) and a deterministic, uniformly bounded reward function (Assumption 3.2), while state spaces remain unbounded (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Part A showed 1.46x growth in max|state| over a 128x R_a sweep (vs theoretical 1.004x) with states reaching only 19.9% of grid half-width; Part B showed a rising-then-plateau regret-vs-R_max pattern (slope 0.766 rising, 0.0003 plateau) — qualitatively consistent with the assumptions' mechanistic roles but at d=2, T≤1200, without tight quantitative matches.

tomyimkc/repro-posterior-sampling-reinfo.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting the two core theoretical predictions (sqrt(gamma_T) regret dependence and near-constant-radius state bounds) with well-designed controls, while the remaining three claims receive only toy-scale qualitative confirmation due to reduced dimensionality, small grids, or the inherently proof-technique nature of the claim.

tomyimkc/repro-efficient-online-variatio.paper_title: Efficient Online Variational Estimation via Monte Carlo Sampling

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 gives recursive formulas for computing the evidence lower bound and its gradient online in state-space models using intermediate functions h_t, u_t, v_t that satisfy state-dependent recursions, avoiding costly regression steps (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The exact h_t/v_t recursion was cross-checked against independent 200,000-path ancestral Monte Carlo across 5 seeds (T=250, d_x=4), yielding max z-scores of 1.72 (ELBO) and 1.37 (gradient)—within MC noise—while a broken-recursion control that drops the h_{t-1} carry-over produced errors 4000–9000x larger, confirming the specific recursive structure of Prop. 4.1.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.5 establishes geometric ergodicity of the extended Markov chain combining states, observations, and functional approximations under Assumptions 4.2-4.4, justifying the proposed contrast lower bound on log-likelihood (COLBO) (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The Dobrushin contraction mechanism underlying Theorem 4.5 was tested on a discretized 81-point state space with a directly-parameterized two-region potential, verifying Lemma C.8's bound and forgetting behavior across 5 epsilon settings, but this is a simplified sub-mechanism rather than the full extended Markov chain on continuous state space with neural-network potentials that the theorem covers.

claims.claim: Algorithm 2 (RMCVI) samples N i.i.d. particles from the filtering distributions q_t^phi and uses self-normalized importance sampling weights (Equation 16) to approximate expectations on finite support instead of via regression (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 2's literal SNIS equations (13, 16, 17) were implemented and shown to converge monotonically to the exact ELBO as N grows (RMSE 30.1→5.4 from N=3 to N=1000), while a no-importance-weights control plateaued (only 1.18x improvement vs 4.98x), directly confirming that the self-normalized IS construction—not mere particle averaging—is what makes the algorithm correct.

claims.claim: On the chaotic RNN state-space model, RMCVI achieves 1-step smoothing RMSE of 8.9(+/-0.2)x10^-2 and filtering RMSE of 10.3(+/-0.2)x10^-2 in 1 ms per step, matching the accuracy of the regression-based approach of Campbell et al. 2021 (9.2x10^-2 smoothing RMSE, 4.8 ms per step) while being about 55 times faster (Table 1, Section 6).
claims.evidence: The paper's actual chaotic RNN generative model and metric formulas (Eq. 61/62) were used, but the trained MLP variational family was replaced by a closed-form EKF/RTS construction, yielding smoothing RMSE ~0.126 vs the paper's reported 8.9×10⁻², and wall-clock timing was replaced by regression-fit counts (0 vs 150), so the specific numerical and speed claims are not reproduced.

claims.claim: On an air-quality dataset with sensor failures, the method recovers smoothed state estimates during the failure period, demonstrating robustness of the online variational approach (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: A synthetic 8-dimensional observation / 5-dimensional latent state proxy with a 40-step missing-observation gap was used with a closed-form Kalman/RTS smoother (not RMCVI), showing smoothing reduces gap-period MSE by 1.40x over filtering (collapsing to 1.0x in the F=0 control), but the real UCI Air Quality dataset and the paper's learned online variational method were not used.

tomyimkc/repro-efficient-online-variatio.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, controlled verification of the paper's core mathematical machinery (Prop. 4.1's recursive formulas and Algorithm 2's SNIS mechanism) via exact computation cross-checked against large-sample Monte Carlo, and a toy-level test of the geometric-ergodicity proof mechanism on a discretized state space. The two empirical benchmark claims (chaotic-RNN Table 1 and air-quality recovery) are addressed only at toy level due to substitution of closed-form estimators for trained neural networks and synthetic for real data.

ProCreations/repro-efficient-stochastic-.paper_title: Efficient Stochastic Optimisation via Sequential Monte Carlo

claims.claim: The Sequential Optimization via SMC (SOSMC) framework replaces expensive inner MCMC sampling loops with a sequential Monte Carlo particle population that is reused and reweighted across optimization iterations, as formalized in Algorithm 1 (Section 3.1, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: A 4,096-particle population is run through 12 optimization iterations of Algorithm 1, retaining 1563 original ancestors after adaptive resampling with nonzero path-reweighting increments; a destructive control replacing particles with fresh IDs yields zero ancestry overlap, concretely demonstrating particle reuse and reweighting.

claims.claim: Proposition 2 establishes a linear convergence rate for the idealized SOSMC iteration under mu-Polyak-Lojasiewicz and L-smooth loss assumptions, showing l(theta_k) - inf(l) <= (1-gamma*mu)^k * (l(theta_0) - inf(l)) for step size gamma <= 1/L (Proposition 2).
claims.evidence: On a 6-dimensional PL quadratic (μ=0.4, L=5.0, γ=1/L, 60 steps), all 61 losses satisfy Proposition 2's bound with max loss/bound ratio 1.000000 and final loss 3.612101e-05; a destructive control at γ=2.05/L causes the L-eigenmode to grow 44.954x, confirming the bound's sensitivity to step size.

claims.claim: Propositions 3 and 4 show the effective sample size of the SMC weights decays exponentially in the squared gradient norm and step size, ESS_infinity(gamma) = N*exp(-gamma^2*||grad l||^2) for Gaussian targets, motivating an adaptive step-size/resampling scheme (Section 4.2, Propositions 3-4).
claims.evidence: With 1,000,000 particles, Monte Carlo ESS ratios match the closed form N·exp(-γ²||∇l||²) over γ=0..0.5 with max absolute ratio error 0.002238; the destructive control confirms that holding γ=0.5 instead of 0.1 loses 772,275.6 effective particles, consistent with exponential decay.

claims.claim: On Langevin reward-tuning of energy-based models with non-differentiable reward functions, SOSMC-ULA outperforms the ImpDiff baseline and achieves reduced variance compared to single-chain SOUL (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: Executing the released JAX notebook for 5 seeds yields SOSMC-ULA mean final reward 0.601177 vs ImpDiff 0.542338, and SOUL/SOSMC variance ratio of 5906.8x; collapsing to a single chain (destructive control) produces 2/5 failed seeds and variance 0.119076, supporting both the performance and variance-reduction claims.

claims.claim: On 2D EBM benchmark datasets, SOSMC achieves higher objective values than ImpDiff for small regularization strengths, with particle-based reward estimates that track true expectations throughout optimization (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: On both 5,001-step, 10,000-particle runs at β=0.1 and β=0.25, SOSMC final fresh rewards (0.998586, 0.995783) exceed ImpDiff (0.994957, 0.968917), and weighted tracking error improves 4.17x/5.55x; discarding SOSMC weights (destructive control) increases tracking error by more than 4x in both runs.

claims.claim: On MNIST, SOSMC remains robust in high dimensions even under mismatch between the pretraining and tuning kernels, without exhibiting reward hacking (Section 5.3).
claims.evidence: At the 784-dimensional MNIST model, the released checkpoint executes the clipped/jittered pretraining kernel followed by the unclamped ULA tuning kernel, retaining diversity at 1.004702x with finite-energy particles; the all-white destructive control has zero diversity and 100% saturation, confirming the absence of reward hacking.

ProCreations/repro-efficient-stochastic-.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence for all six claims through native-scale executions: persistent particle reuse (4096 particles), convergence bound verification on a PL quadratic, million-particle ESS law validation, five-seed Langevin reward comparisons, full 5001-step 2D EBM runs, and 784-dimensional MNIST checkpoint evaluation. Each claim is supported by specific numerical results and a destructive control, with byte-identical reproducibility across three runs.

tomyimkc/repro-provably-data-driven-lagr.paper_title: Provably Data-driven Lagrangian Relaxation for Mixed Integer Linear Programming

claims.claim: For learned Lagrangian Relaxation multipliers over s coupling constraints and N training samples, the expected excess risk of the ERM solution is upper bounded by O(s^1.5/√N) (Theorem 5.5).
claims.evidence: Empirical Rademacher complexity of U on the paper's restricted construction scales with log-log slope -0.515 vs N (expect -0.5) and 1.237 vs s (expect +1.5), and is bounded by 12×s^1.5/√N in all 18 configs; excess risk is non-negative and below the envelope in all configs including the hard construction with eps~1/√N.

claims.claim: A minimax lower bound of Ω(s/√N) is proven, showing linear dependence on the number of coupled constraints s is unavoidable for any learning algorithm (Theorem 5.6).
claims.evidence: Worst-case excess risk over a Varshamov-Gilbert packing set tracks Ω(s/√N) with slope -0.510 vs N and 1.039 vs s, minimum ratio 0.0806 across all configs; all three Fano proof lemmas (5.7 geometric separation, 5.8 KL bound, 5.9 risk-distance reduction) verified numerically; constant-eps control collapses risk to 0 and s=1 control gives classical 1/√N rate.

claims.claim: Stochastic Gradient Ascent with iterate averaging is shown to achieve the matching O(s/√N) rate, closing the O(√s) gap between the ERM upper bound and the minimax lower bound and establishing minimax optimality (Theorem 5.12).
claims.evidence: SGA with iterate averaging and step size η=π_max/(2B√N) yields risk bounded by the paper's explicit bound 2Bπ_max·s/√N in all 15 configs, with log-log slope -0.488 vs N (expect -0.5) and 0.9999 vs s (expect +1); 10× larger step size degrades risk by ~2.4×, confirming the step-size condition is load-bearing.

claims.claim: The framework is extended to learning-to-warm-start sub-gradient ascent for large-scale Mixed Integer Linear Programming, with an O(s/N) risk upper bound (Theorem 6.1) and matching Ω(s/N) minimax lower bound (Theorem 6.2).
claims.evidence: Warm-start upper bound holds: risk ≤ Popoviciu envelope s/(4N) in all 18 configs with slope -1.010 vs N and 0.918 vs s; lower bound holds: worst-case packing risk ratio ≥ 0.236 with slope -1.019 vs N. Note: the degenerate-distribution control failed (eps=0 still samples a two-point distribution), but this is a control-design bug that does not affect the bound verification.

claims.claim: The covering number of the dual multiplier class U is bounded as log N(δ,U,‖·‖₂,N) ≤ s·log(1+2Bπ_max s/δ), used to derive the Rademacher complexity bound R_N(U)=O(s^1.5/√N) (Lemma 5.3, Lemma 5.4).
claims.evidence: Lemma 5.3 covering number bound holds: log(measured net size) ≤ s·log(1+2Bπ_max·s/δ) across the full δ-sweep; both the numerical Dudley integral bound and Monte-Carlo Rademacher estimate are ≤ 14×s^1.5/√N in all 18 configs with N-slope -0.455 (expect -0.5). The empirical s-slope of 1.015 (below 1.5) is consistent with the upper bound not being tight on this construction.

claims.claim: The dual function u(π,P) is shown to be concave in π with subgradient norm bounded by 2B√s under bounded constraint-violation assumptions on the MILP instance (Proposition 5.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: Concavity, subgradient inequality, and ‖g‖≤2B√s all hold on 200 separable instances per s (up to s=64) and 40 dense instances per s (up to s=6 with exact 2^s enumeration); worst norm ratio 0.564; all three controls break correctly (convex function fails concavity, negated subgradient violates inequality 240/240, assumption-violating instance breaks norm bound 200/200).

tomyimkc/repro-provably-data-driven-lagr.overall: All six theoretical claims are supported by experiments on the paper's own restricted MILP construction at non-trivial scale (s up to 64, N up to 50000, 24-40 seeds), with measured scaling exponents matching theory and controls that break when preconditions are violated. The verification is limited to the closed-form restricted instance family rather than general MILP instances or real applications, and one control in Claim 4 had an implementation bug, but the core bound verifications are sound.

tomyimkc/repro-server-proximal-aggregati.paper_title: Server-Proximal Aggregation for Federated Domain-Incremental Learning under Partial Participation: Task-Uniform Convergence and Backward Transfer

claims.claim: SPECIAL (Server-Proximal Efficient Continual Aggregation for Learning) modifies FedAvg only at the server by blending the aggregated model with the previous task's final parameters via a closed-form proximal update theta^{t+1} = (1/(1+lambda))*theta_bar^{t+1} + (lambda/(1+lambda))*theta^{i-1} (Algorithm 3, Equation 6).
claims.evidence: The closed-form update was checked against an independent 60-step gradient-descent minimizer across 20000 random configurations (d up to 100, lambda spanning 1e-3 to 1e2), yielding max residual 2.544e-15; lambda=0 reduces exactly to FedAvg (diff 0.0 over 4000 configs), and communication cost is identical (ratio 1.000).

claims.claim: Theorem 1 proves a backward knowledge transfer (BKT) bound showing that after training on task K, the loss on any earlier task increases by at most a drift-controlled correction term that vanishes at rate O(1/(t*E*M*N*L*B^2)), shrinking with more communication rounds, local epochs, and participating clients (Section 4.2, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The BKT bound was tested on an isotropic-quadratic convex loss (L=1 by construction) with only K=2 tasks and d=30, where alignment was artificially constructed by placing client optima; the bound held (0/1920 violations) and the correction-term slope vs t was -1.000, but this is a clearly simplified proxy for the general smooth possibly non-convex losses and general K the theorem addresses.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 and Corollary 1 give a task-uniform, non-convex convergence rate of O(sqrt(E/(N*T))) in expected gradient norm for federated domain-incremental learning (FDIL) under partial participation, matching single-task FedAvg rates while holding simultaneously across all tasks (Section 4.3, Theorem 2, Corollary 1).
claims.evidence: A genuinely non-convex synthetic loss (28.1% negative Hessian entries) was used at d=16, K=4, M=64 with stochastic gradients; the min-gradient-norm decreased with T and N (correct direction) but with log-log slopes of -2.049 and -1.933 versus the theorem's -0.5, the E-slope (-2.062) went opposite to the theorem's worst-case direction, and the headline ratio of measured-to-reference rate was 39.25x, so the quantitative O(sqrt(E/(N*T))) rate was not reproduced.

claims.claim: The FDIL problem setup assumes K sequential tasks share a fixed label space Y while input domains differ across tasks, with M heterogeneous clients and only N < M clients sampled without replacement per round to model partial participation (Section 2.1).
claims.evidence: A synthetic FDIL generator with K=6 tasks, M=200 clients, C=10 labels confirmed all structural properties: all tasks share the same label set Y, between-task domain shift (20.0) vastly exceeds within-task split-half noise (0.073, ratio 274x), client heterogeneity exceeds bootstrap control (ratio 78.5x), and without-replacement sampling over 20000 rounds produced zero duplicates with chi-square p=0.9735 and pairwise co-selection matching the hypergeometric value.

tomyimkc/repro-server-proximal-aggregati.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence verifying the algebraic correctness of SPECIAL's closed-form server update (Claim 1) and the structural fidelity of the FDIL problem setup (Claim 4), while offering only toy-scale evidence for the BKT bound (Claim 2) and convergence rate (Claim 3) on simplified synthetic losses where the quantitative rate exponents were not matched.

gizaom/repro-structure-centric-graph-fou.paper_title: Structure-Centric Graph Foundation Model via Geometric Bases

claims.claim: SCGFM models graphs as metric measure spaces and learns geometric bases B_k in [0,1]^(M x M) that define a shared structural coordinate system, aligning input graphs to these bases via Sliced Gromov-Wasserstein distance (Section 3, Eq. 7).
claims.evidence: The logbook runs the released SCGFM pipeline end-to-end but never inspects the code or verifies the architectural claims (metric measure spaces, geometric bases B_k in [0,1]^(M×M), Sliced Gromov-Wasserstein alignment). No evidence is provided about the model's internal design or mathematical formulation.

claims.claim: In 5-shot graph classification across COX2, NCI1, BZR, COLLAB, IMDB-BINARY, COLORS-3, and PROTEINS, SCGFM attains a 51.70% mean in-domain accuracy and reaches 26.31-26.97% on the cross-domain COLORS-3 transfer task versus near-chance (<=15%) for baseline GFMs (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook reproduces 8 of 10 Table 1 columns with strong agreement (mean Δ −0.76, all within reported std), but the COLORS-3 transfer results (26.31–26.97%), the baseline GFM comparison (≤15%), and PROTEINS are not tested. The logbook also disputes the '51.70% mean in-domain accuracy' figure, stating it is the overall average including COLORS-3, not an in-domain mean.

claims.claim: In 5-shot node classification across Cora, CiteSeer, PubMed, Photo, Computers, and Reddit, SCGFM achieves a 65.90% average accuracy and maintains approximately 84.17% on Reddit regardless of pre-training source domain (Table 2, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Five of six node datasets are reproduced with excellent agreement (mean Δ −0.52 over Photo, Computers, Cora, CiteSeer, PubMed), but Reddit (84.17%) is explicitly not covered—absent from the released build config and outside compute budget—so the 65.90% six-dataset average and the Reddit domain-independence claim cannot be verified.

claims.claim: An ablation removing the structure-aware projected-feature component drops Cora accuracy from 70.54% to 29.49%, while the same ablation on PROTEINS yields a negligible change (68.70% to 68.86%), showing dataset-dependent reliance on topology versus features (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: No ablation experiments are mentioned anywhere in the logbook. The structure-aware projected-feature ablation, the Cora 70.54→29.49 drop, and the PROTEINS 68.70→68.86 negligible change (Figure 5) are never addressed.

claims.claim: SCGFM is the only method able to complete extreme scalability stress tests, processing graphs of 5x10^6 nodes with about 12GB peak memory while competing baselines encounter out-of-memory errors (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: No scalability experiments are mentioned. The 5×10^6 node stress test, 12GB peak memory measurement, and baseline out-of-memory comparisons (Figure 6) are never addressed.

claims.claim: Performance saturates around K=12 geometric bases and M in [8,16] base nodes, with larger bases (M=32) adding unnecessary complexity without accuracy gains (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: No hyperparameter sweep over K (number of bases) or M (base nodes) is mentioned. The saturation around K=12 and M∈[8,16] versus M=32 (Figure 7) is never addressed.

gizaom/repro-structure-centric-graph-fou.overall: The logbook rigorously reproduces substantial portions of the paper's two main few-shot classification tables (8/10 graph columns, 5/6 node datasets) at full protocol scale with strong numerical agreement, but four of six claims are entirely unaddressed and the two partially covered claims have significant gaps (COLORS-3, Reddit, baselines, ablations, scalability, and hyperparameter sweeps are all missing).

speak2arpit/repro-vectorworld-efficient-.paper_title: VectorWorld: Efficient Streaming World Model via Diffusion Flow on Vector Graphs

claims.claim: VectorWorld reduces nuPlan endpoint distance from 0.250m to 0.078m and collision rate from 9.30% to 3.01% compared to prior methods (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook verified that baseline rows match the Scenario Dreamer source paper and validated the EPD/collision metric protocol on released GT tiles (GT EPD=0.25m, 0% collisions), but VectorWorld's own claimed numbers (0.078m, 3.01%) were never independently regenerated—no generated scenes were evaluated because the sampling code is unreleased.

claims.claim: VectorWorld achieves the lowest Fréchet distance (0.94) among non-privileged methods on Waymo Open Motion (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirmed the table arithmetic (0.94 < 1.38 < 1.61) and that baseline rows match the Scenario Dreamer paper, but the Fréchet distance of 0.94 was never independently computed—no generation runs were executed due to lack of GPU credits and Waymo license restrictions (only 17 sample tiles available).

claims.claim: VectorWorld generates a 64m×64m vector-graph tile in approximately 6 ms, enabling real-time closed-loop rollouts exceeding 1 kilometer for autonomous driving simulation (Section on closed-loop performance, Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook benchmarked the exact released architecture on Apple M3 Pro, measuring 104–315ms for 1-NFE MeanFlow (not 6ms), and confirmed the 1-NFE vs multi-NFE speedup mechanism (33–102×). However, the specific 6ms claim relies only on a roofline projection to H20 hardware, and the 1km+ closed-loop rollout was never tested because the simulator is unreleased.

claims.claim: Motion-aware gated VAE warm-start initialization reduces jerk from 16.6 to 9.6 and increases closed-loop success rate from 42% to 78% versus history-free initialization (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirmed the motion-aware gated VAE exists in released checkpoints and ran an IDM proxy on 15 real tiles showing cold-start ego jerk 1.5–1.6× higher than warm-start (directionally matching the paper's 1.73× ratio), but this used a rule-based IDM driver instead of the full simulator, only 15 tiles, did not measure success rate at all, and absolute jerk values (0.79 vs 1.16 m/s³) are far from the paper's 9.6 vs 16.6.

claims.claim: Retraining the driving policy inside the VectorWorld simulator raises stress-test success rate from 25.0% to 56.0% (Table 2).
claims.evidence: No experiment was run—the logbook only audited that the machinery (RTG-FiLM heads, anchor+residual actions, K-disks vocab, DeltaSim data) exists in released checkpoints. The 25.0%→56.0% stress-test success numbers were never measured because the PPO training loop and simulator are unreleased.

claims.claim: VectorWorld is benchmarked against the SLEDGE and ScenDream generative world-model baselines on Waymo Open Motion and nuPlan (Section on evaluation datasets).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirmed both SLEDGE (ECCV 2024, autonomousvision/sledge) and ScenDream/Scenario Dreamer (CVPR 2025, princeton-computational-imaging/scenario-dreamer) are real public projects with code, and that VectorWorld's Table 1 uses both as baselines, with the minor nuance that SLEDGE appears only in nuPlan rows (not Waymo).

speak2arpit/repro-vectorworld-efficient-.overall: The logbook provides thorough structural audits—confirming baseline provenance, metric protocol validity on GT tiles, architecture diffs against Scenario Dreamer, and component existence in released checkpoints—but cannot independently verify any of VectorWorld's own reported performance numbers because the sampling/simulator code is unreleased and no GPU was available for generation runs. Only Claim 6 (baseline existence) is fully verified; Claims 1–3 and 5 are inconclusive, and Claim 4 is addressed only via a simplified IDM proxy on 15 tiles.

sotayamashita/repro-zeroth-order-optimiz.paper_title: Zeroth-Order Optimization at the Edge of Stability

claims.claim: For ZO-GD, the mean-square critical step size satisfies 2/(Tr(H) + 2*lambda_max(H)) <= eta_ms* <= 2/Tr(H), showing dependence on the full Hessian spectrum rather than just the top eigenvalue (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: 13 spectra (dimensions 2–32, condition numbers 1–1000, varied shapes) show operator/root agreement to 1.37e-13 relative error, bounds contain the root in 13/13 cases, 0.9η* stable and 1.1η* unstable in 13/13 cases, and a matched-trace/matched-top-eigenvalue pair with different intermediate spectra yields a 2.51% root difference, directly demonstrating full-spectrum dependence.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 extends the mean-square stability bound to ZO-GD with momentum (ZO-GDM), showing the critical step size is adjusted by the momentum parameter beta (Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: 12 joint position/momentum operator cases across β=0,0.3,0.6,0.9 show operator/root agreement to 2.09e-12, bounds containment 12/12, and the ZO critical step size decreases (0.5866→0.0771) as β increases while the first-order threshold moves oppositely (2.0→3.8), a discriminating control confirmed by 200,000-sample Monte Carlo (relative error 0.00155).

claims.claim: For frozen ZO-Adam, the mean-square stability threshold depends on the spectrum of the preconditioned Hessian P^{-1}H rather than the raw Hessian (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: 36 commuting preconditioner cases show operator/root agreement to 1.59e-12 and preconditioned bounds contain the root in 36/36; changing P causes 24/36 raw-H bracket failures and a 6.41× threshold range, directly showing dependence on P⁻¹H rather than H; the noncommuting case is measured (15.15% mismatch) and appropriately excluded.

claims.claim: Empirically, ZO-GD, ZO-GDM, and ZO-Adam all stabilize their trace/curvature statistics near the theoretically predicted mean-square edge-of-stability thresholds when trained on a CNN on CIFAR-10, ResNet20, and a Vision Transformer (Section 5, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: No CNN, ResNet20, or Vision Transformer training on CIFAR-10 was executed; the logbook explicitly states no architecture training, author plots, or cached numbers are presented as direct evidence.

claims.claim: Practical stability tracking during training requires only the trace and top eigenvalue of the Hessian, not the full spectrum, via the bounds given in Equations 23-25 (Section 5, Equations 23-25).
claims.evidence: 49 unique spectra (dimensions 4–256) show trace/top-eigenvalue brackets containing the root in 49/49 cases; matrix-free Hutchinson trace and power-iteration top-eigenvalue estimates achieve 94.4% coverage versus 33.3% for the low-budget negative control, and top-only relative error grows from 2.59 at d=4 to 83.87 at d=256.

claims.claim: Catapult-like dynamics appear when the step size is increased past the mean-square stability threshold in the empirical experiments (Section 5, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: A 3-dimensional fixed quadratic with 20,000 replicas shows a 1.62× loss spike when stepping from 0.75η* to 1.30η* versus 0.812× without the step increase, but the setup lacks an evolving Hessian and cannot reproduce the paper's neural-network curvature drop and re-equilibration dynamics.

sotayamashita/repro-zeroth-order-optimiz.overall: The logbook provides rigorous numerical verification of the three theoretical claims (Theorems 1–3) and the two-statistic tracking bounds via independently materialized covariance operators, full-spectrum roots, Monte Carlo checks, and discriminating controls across varied spectra. The empirical neural-network training claim is honestly left unexecuted, and the catapult dynamics claim is limited to a 3D quadratic toy that captures only the instability-spike mechanism.

heitorefer/repro-crisp-spectral-mts-fore.paper_title: Crisp: A Spectral-Based Interaction Strategy for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting

claims.claim: Outperforms 20+ baselines in multivariate time series forecasting
claims.evidence: A from-scratch Crisp-lite was compared against only 4 baselines (not 20+) on a 6,000-row subset of ETTh1 with 96→24 forecasting, 100 epochs, CPU-only. Crisp-lite beat full-attention (0.484 vs 0.871 MSE) but did NOT beat a simple channel-independent linear baseline (0.484 vs 0.444 MSE), so the claim's direction is only partially supported at drastically reduced scale.

claims.claim: Forces attention weights for spectrally inconsistent neighbors to exactly zero via strictly sparse blocking mechanism
claims.evidence: A numerical audit of the masked-softmax spectral-blocking mechanism on 16 synthetic channels across 5 seeds shows 100% exact-zero fraction for all mechanism-flagged spectrally-inconsistent pairs (max/mean/min blocked weight = 0.0 in every seed), with a relaxed soft-gate control confirming the exactness specifically comes from the -inf pre-softmax masking design (control leaves mean 0.048, max 0.288 positive weights on the same pairs).

heitorefer/repro-crisp-spectral-mts-fore.overall: The logbook verifies the mechanism-design claim (exact-zero sparsity via masked-softmax) with a clean numerical audit and control, but only provides a toy-scale proxy for the benchmark-magnitude claim, where Crisp-lite fails to outperform a simple linear baseline at reduced scale.

ProCreations/repro-generalized-boundary-.paper_title: Generalized Boundary FDR Control under Arbitrary Dependence: An Approach on Closure Principle

claims.claim: The Domino procedure controls the k-boundary FDR (k-bFDR) - defined as the probability that the k least-significant discoveries in the rejection set are all false - under arbitrary dependence among p-values or e-values, without structural assumptions (Section 2, Definition 2.2; Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: 26 p-value and 26 e-value extremal LPs over arbitrary joint dependence for m=4 hypotheses attain maximum k-bFDR of exactly 0.1 at alpha=0.1, never exceeding it, providing concrete optimization-based evidence of FDR control under worst-case dependence.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.4 proves that the rejection set R produced by the Domino algorithm satisfies k-bFDR(R) <= alpha under arbitrary dependence (Section 3, Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: 2,420,538 exhaustive closure-event checks across all k values, null configurations, and rejection-boundary placements produce 0 violations of the set-theoretic event inclusion underlying Theorem 3.4, verified by an independent event oracle.

claims.claim: Proposition 2.3 shows k-bFDR reduces to k-FWER under the global null and is otherwise upper bounded by k-FWER, situating k-bFDR between per-comparison and family-wise error control (Section 2, Proposition 2.3).
claims.evidence: 1,538 global-null events show 0 equality violations between k-bFDR and k-FWER, and 386,896 general events show 0 cases where k-bFDR's boundary event exceeds k-FWER's event, confirming both the equality-under-global-null and upper-bound properties.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 establishes equivalence between the Domino procedure and the e-value closure principle when using an appropriate local test, connecting Domino to existing multiple-testing paradigms (Section 4, Proposition 4.1).
claims.evidence: All 32,768 local-test threshold patterns for m=4 and k=[1,2] yield 327,680 Domino vs. e-value-closure comparisons with 0 discrepancies, including nonmonotone patterns that would expose accidental equivalence assumptions.

claims.claim: Algorithms 3 and 4 reduce the computational complexity of implementing the closure-based procedure from exponential O(2^m) to polynomial O(m^2) for Bonferroni and harmonic-mean-based local tests (Section 3, Algorithms 3-4).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 4 produces 357 mismatches across 6,427 cases versus exhaustive harmonic closure, with a concrete counterexample at p=[0.07, 0.07], alpha=0.1 where Algorithm 4 rejects 2 hypotheses but exhaustive closure rejects 0 (joint statistic 0.1319 > 0.1); Algorithm 3 has 0 mismatches across 8,967 cases.

ProCreations/repro-generalized-boundary-.overall: The logbook provides concrete computational evidence—LP optimization over arbitrary dependence, exhaustive event enumeration, and direct algorithm execution—supporting Claims 1–4 and falsifying Claim 5 via a specific Algorithm 4 counterexample. The methodology is appropriate for verifying finite instances of mathematical theorems, though all verifications are limited to small m (primarily m=4).

ProCreations/repro-questioning-coverage-.paper_title: Questioning the Coverage-Length Metric in Conformal Prediction: When Shorter Intervals Are Not Better

claims.claim: The Prejudicial Trick (Algorithm 1) constructs prediction intervals by returning a null (empty or minimal) interval with probability (1-p) and an adjusted conformal interval with probability p, provably preserving valid marginal coverage per Theorem 6 while shrinking average interval length (Section on Prejudicial Trick, Algorithm 1, Theorem 6)
claims.evidence: All 16 admissible (alpha,p) cells preserve marginal coverage to maximum error 1.110e-16 and strictly reduce mean length (smallest gain 0.009771), confirmed by an independent closed-form inverse-CDF oracle and byte-identical across three warning-strict runs.

claims.claim: On synthetic data, PT applied to Vanilla Conformal Prediction (PT-VCP) reduces average interval length from 22.894 to 22.614 at alpha=0.10 while preserving nominal coverage (Table 1)
claims.evidence: The released script's bias=20 configuration yields VCP/PT lengths 43.565801/42.439739, not 22.894/22.614; correcting to bias=10 recovers VCP=22.893815 but gives PT=22.514392, not 22.614, so the specific registered numbers are not reproduced.

claims.claim: On real-world regression benchmarks (including MEPS and BIO), PT-VCP reduces interval length in 9 of 10 datasets while maintaining 90% marginal coverage (Table 2)
claims.evidence: Across 50 runs on all ten named public benchmark families, 10/10 show shorter PT-VCP intervals (exceeding the claimed 9/10), with mean VCP/PT coverage 0.899679/0.898356 near nominal 90%, and the zero-bias control reverses to 0/10 wins.

claims.claim: Despite valid marginal coverage, the Prejudicial Trick yields highly unstable predictions: Proposition 2 proves its interval stability metric IS(C_PT) = p(1-p)(E(L))^2 > 0, meaning the same input can receive completely different interval outputs across repeated conformal calibration runs (Definition 1, Proposition 2)
claims.evidence: With nonconstant lengths [1,2,5,10], Definition 1 gives IS = p(1-p)E[L²] = 5.200000, while the claimed formula p(1-p)(E[L])² = 3.240000 differs by 1.96; the qualitative conclusion IS > 0 holds, but the specific formula as registered is contradicted.

claims.claim: The proposed Interval Stability metric can flag methods, such as localized conformal prediction, that implicitly exploit PT-like randomness to shrink length, since Proposition 1 shows PT is a special case of localized CP when local scale estimators output extreme values (Definition 1, Proposition 1)
claims.evidence: Proposition 1's extreme-scale construction is verified (radius error 0.0), but a localized-scale counterexample with scales 0.5/1.5 at equal probability has Interval Stability 4.0 with exactly zero expected-length shrinkage across four amplitudes (slope 0.0), contradicting the claim that nonzero IS flags length-shrinking exploitation.

ProCreations/repro-questioning-coverage-.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, independently oracle-verified evidence confirming the PT mechanism's coverage validity and length reduction (Claims 1, 3) while falsifying three specific quantitative or implicational claims (Claims 2, 4, 5) through exact counterexamples and configuration-mismatch demonstrations.

sotayamashita/repro-lec-selection-condit.paper_title: LEC: Linear Expectation Constraints for Selection-Conditioned Risk Control in Selective Prediction and Routing Systems

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 proves that thresholding on a calibrated statistic derived from a linear expectation constraint yields a finite-sample marginal FDR guarantee, Pr(err=1 | u ≤ threshold) ≤ α, for a new exchangeable test sample using only calibration data (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive enumeration of all 2^9 × 9 = 4,608 binary error vectors and held-out roles shows selected error = 0.500 at α=0.25 (bound 0.250) and 0.500 at α=0.40 (bound 0.400), both strict violations of the claimed Pr(err=1 | u≤threshold) ≤ α, with zero row-order mismatches confirming permutation invariance.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 extends this guarantee to two-model routing systems, showing that jointly calibrated thresholds for both models maintain system-level FDR control over routed predictions (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Running the two-model calibrator (Equation 11) with identical model outputs over the same 4,608-case enumeration yields identical violations: selected error 0.500 at α=0.25 and α=0.40, exceeding both bounds, providing a concrete special-case counterexample to the routing theorem.

claims.claim: On CommonsenseQA with LLaMA-3.2-3B at target FDR level α=0.05, LEC achieves power of 0.1959 compared to 0.1191 for COIN-CP, an improvement of roughly 8 percentage points at the same nominal FDR level (Table 1, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: No experiments were executed on CommonsenseQA with LLaMA-3.2-3B; the logbook explicitly states 'Executed evidence: None' and only references source-table transcription, so the power comparison of 0.1959 vs 0.1191 is neither reproduced nor refuted.

claims.claim: LEC's calibration procedure relies only on exchangeable calibration data (no distributional assumptions beyond exchangeability) to compute the FDR-constrained, retention-maximizing threshold (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The calibration procedure was confirmed to be row-order invariant (zero mismatches across 13,824 cases), verifying it uses only exchangeable calibration data, yet the same enumeration shows selected error = 0.500 exceeding bounds at α=0.25 and α=0.40, demonstrating exchangeability alone is insufficient for the claimed guarantee.

claims.claim: The two-model routing evaluation (Section 4.3) shows a weaker model combined with a stronger one via LEC's joint threshold calibration accepts more correct predictions than either model used alone at the same FDR budget (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: No two-model CommonsenseQA routing evaluation was executed; the logbook states 'Executed evidence: None' and clarifies the identical-output construction was a theorem counterexample audit, not a reproduction of the empirical routing benefit.

sotayamashita/repro-lec-selection-condit.overall: The logbook provides exhaustive finite-case counterexamples (4,608 enumerated cases with specific numerical violations at α=0.25 and α=0.40) that challenge the paper's distribution-free FDR guarantees in Theorems 3.1 and 3.2, but completely omits the empirical CommonsenseQA evaluations for Claims 3 and 5, leaving those unaddressed.

ai-sherpa/koopman-generator-linearizatio.paper_title: Unfolding Generative Flows with Koopman Operators: Trajectory-Preserving Linearization

claims.claim: The method formulates Conditional Flow Matching dynamics via a Koopman generator that lifts nonlinear vector-field dynamics into a linear evolution over observables, using the identity L g(x_t) = ∇_x g(x_t)·v(x_t) (Section 4, Eq. 8).
claims.evidence: A from-scratch nonlinear time-varying 3-state system with an exact 5-dim Koopman-invariant dictionary confirms Eq. 8 (Lg=∇g·v) to 6.2e-12 max residual across 100k states via independent finite-difference oracle, and Eq. 12 (g(x_t)=exp(tL)g(x_0)) to 2.6e-13 max relative error across 600 trials via independent adaptive ODE solver, with a negative control breaking to 0.66 error (>10^5x worse).

claims.claim: A decoder-free parametrization concatenates the raw state with learned observables, g̃(x) = [x, g_θ(x)], avoiding reconstruction error from a separate decoder (Section 4, Eq. 14).
claims.evidence: Byte-pinned PDF text extraction shows v1 explicitly describes a decoder-free architecture ('we concatenate the state itself'), while v3 (current camera-ready) Section 6.1 explicitly defines 'an encoder (gϕ) and decoder (gψ⁻¹), both using a SongUNet architecture' mapping to/from a 1024-d latent—mutually exclusive designs.

claims.claim: Training combines a Generator loss enforcing Koopman consistency with a Target Consistency loss aligning the exponentiated generator trajectory to the terminal state (Section 4.3, Eqs. 15-16).
claims.evidence: v1 Section 4.3 defines exactly two loss terms (Generator loss Eq. 15 + optional Target Consistency loss Eq. 16), while v3 replaces this with an explicit four-term weighted sum L_train = λ_phase·L_phase + λ_target·L_target + λ_recon·L_recon + λ_cons·L_cons (Eqs. 8-11), confirmed in v3's training-loop pseudocode.

claims.claim: On MNIST, one-step (one-shot) generation with the Koopman linearization attains FID 60.6 versus FID 190 for a CFM baseline under the same one-step budget (Section 5, Table 4).
claims.evidence: v1 Table 4 reports Koopman 1-step MNIST FID 60.6 and CFM 1-step FID 190, but v3 Table 7 reports Koopman NFE=1 MNIST FID 7.1 and OT-CFM NFE=1 FID 181—both numbers changed between versions, with the Koopman FID shifting by nearly an order of magnitude.

claims.claim: On 2D toy datasets (Swiss Roll, Eight Gaussians, Two Moons), the method achieves MMD scores within about 0.02 of the CFM baseline while enabling full-trajectory linearization (Section 5, Table 1, Figure 4).

claims.claim: A Linearizer f is idempotent, i.e. f(f(x)) = f(x), if and only if its core matrix A is an idempotent matrix (A^2 = A), enabling architectural (rather than optimization-based) enforcement of idempotent generative networks (Lemma 4.2, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Idempotent projector A (A²=A, err 2.2e-16) yields f∘f=f to 1.5e-10, while a non-idempotent control A separates by 1025; N-fold composition L^N = L{g,g,A^N} verified for N∈{5,25,100} (max err 8.4e-9). The mathematical iff is rigorously confirmed with proper controls.

claims.claim: In the one-step flow-matching application, the product of per-step update operators over hundreds of integration steps collapses into a single operator, enabling one-step diffusion sampling without retraining (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: The operator collapse identity (200 Euler steps, sequential vs collapsed err 3.7e-13, B=product err 0.0) is verified on N=4 with random matrices, but no actual flow-matching model or diffusion sampling on real data is demonstrated—the 'enabling one-step diffusion sampling without retraining' application aspect is unaddressed.

claims.claim: Modular style transfer is achieved by fixing the shared encoders g_x, g_y while swapping only the style-specific core matrix A_style, allowing algebraic interpolation between styles from a single trained network (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Core interpolation equals induced-space output interpolation to 1.5e-11 across α∈{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0} with exact endpoints, but this is verified on N=4 synthetic random matrices with no trained network, no real images, and no actual style transfer—the 'modular style transfer is achieved from a single trained network' application claim is not demonstrated.

DineshAI/Eqm5VEaAom.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the core mathematical theorems of the Linearizer framework (linearity, composition, idempotency) to machine precision with negative controls on a small synthetic setup. The flow-matching collapse and style-transfer algebraic identities are also confirmed numerically, but the corresponding application claims (actual diffusion sampling, style transfer on images) are not addressed, leaving those claims at toy-level evidence.

CHI 2021 controlled study (998 real participants, 9,980 decisions, randomized CLEAR vs BB conditions), yielding a measured treatment effect of -0.779 MAPE pp (95% CI [-1.651, 0.093]) with a placebo control (permuted labels: -0.042 pp, CI [-0.776, 0.693]) confirming the estimator does not manufacture effects.

claims.evidence: The logbook provides exact verification: Part A checks partition identity for all 64 garblings on |X|=3,|Ŷ|=2,|Z|=2 with symbolic p,u; Part B confirms R_XYZ == R_XY == R_X on 500/500 random decision problems using exact rational arithmetic; Part C shows a non-garbling pseudo-explanation strictly increases R (1/2 → 1); the Ames empirical arm shows no significant positive gain of Z over X+Ŷ (-1.21%, CI [-1.52, -0.91]).

claims.claim: In the Ames Iowa housing case study using three features (year built, bedrooms, building material) and SHAP explanations, the theoretic value of explanation is a 24.2% MAPE improvement (95% CI [22.4, 26.1]), while the potential human-complementary value is only 9% MAPE improvement (95% CI [8.1, 9.9]) (Section B).
claims.evidence: The full Ames pipeline (2,930 homes, XGBoost, SHAP TreeExplainer, synthetic human via OLS Eq. 10, utility u=-|s-a|/s, 100 splits) reproduces both headline numbers: TVE 25.68% vs paper 24.2% [22.4, 26.1] and PHCV 8.81% vs paper 9% [8.1, 9.9], with the Figure-1 signal ordering (theoretic > complementary for all signals; explanations add nothing over features) also matching.

DineshAI/fVso2kGVrF.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence on non-toy setups for all six claims: the Ames housing case study (2,930 real homes, 100 splits) reproduces both headline numbers within the paper's CIs, Proposition 4 is verified via exact rational arithmetic over 500 random problems plus exhaustive garbling checks, Definition 8 is instantiated on a real 998-participant controlled study, and both worked examples are reproduced with exact arithmetic and real data respectively.

DineshAI/7UEBX1KU1y.paper_title: Conditional Equivalence of DPO and RLHF: Assumptions, Failure Modes, and Provable Alignment

claims.claim: The paper proves DPO-RLHF equivalence is conditional on the RLHF-optimal policy preferring human-preferred responses (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides a concrete numerical counterexample: with beta=1, reward_gap=1, delta_ref=0, the boundary condition holds (0 > -1), RLHF optimum is delta*=1, but the DPO loss derivative at delta=1 is -0.269 (negative, not stationary) and DPO loss is strictly lower at delta=2 (0.127 vs 0.313), showing the DPO and RLHF optima do not coincide even when the stated condition is satisfied.

claims.claim: When the equivalence assumption fails, DPO optimizes relative advantage over the reference policy rather than absolute human-preference alignment (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook proves via exact-real arithmetic that L_DPO = -log σ(β(δ−δ_ref)) is shift-invariant in (δ−δ_ref) with strictly negative derivative at every finite δ, confirming DPO optimizes relative advantage; additionally, 9 real-data DPO runs (3 seeds × 3 corrupted references, 384 train + 128 held-out pairs) all lowered the objective with at least one misaligned reference on held-out pairs.

claims.claim: The paper characterizes undesirable solution spaces in which policies reduce DPO loss while preferring dispreferred responses (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides an exact witness: when delta_ref < -reward_gap/beta, delta_ref/2 lies in U={delta_ref < delta < 0}, which prefers the rejected response yet has lower DPO loss than the reference; monotonicity and boundary controls pass, and all 9 real-data DPO trajectories lowered loss with at least one entering U (max U fractions 0.198–0.495).

claims.claim: Constrained Preference Optimization augments RLHF with constraints and derives a stationary DPO-like loss with an adaptive reference-based margin (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Direct differentiation of the constrained-RLHF objective recovers the paper's adaptive margin with analytic first-order residual 0.0 and finite-difference residual 2.78e-11; controls confirm that omitting the margin breaks stationarity, reference-probability substitution restores it, and gamma=0 recovers DPO.
