RyeCatcher/repro-certificate-guided-prun.paper_title: Certificate-Guided Pruning for Stochastic Lipschitz Optimization

claims.claim: Certificate-Guided Pruning (CGP) maintains an explicit active set A_t of candidate optima using confidence-adjusted Lipschitz envelopes, certifying with high probability that any point outside A_t is suboptimal (Section 3, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: A real implementation of CGP was run on 40 synthetic 2-D Lipschitz objectives (26x26 grid, T=60, sigma=0.1, delta=0.1); x* was pruned in 0/40 trials at the honest confidence radius, and a negative control (10x-deflated radius) pruned x* in 39/40. This is a simplified 2-D synthetic setup, not the paper's full benchmarks.

claims.claim: Under a margin condition with near-optimality dimension α (Assumption 2.3), the Shrinkage Theorem bounds the active set volume as Vol(A_t) ≤ C·(2(β_t + Lη_t) + γ_t)^(d−α) (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: Mean active fraction was measured across 12 synthetic objectives at T=10,30,60,120 (0.943→0.872), showing monotone shrinkage, but the (d-alpha) exponent that is the actual content of Theorem 4.6 was explicitly not tested because the synthetic objectives lack independently known alpha.

claims.claim: CGP achieves ε-optimality with probability at least 1−δ using T = Õ(L^d ε^{-(2+α)} log(1/δ)) samples, improving on the worst-case Õ(ε^{-(2+d)}) rate whenever α < d (Theorem 4.8).
claims.evidence: No experiment was run; the logbook states 'Source-anchored only' and 'No rate was measured and none is claimed.' There is no empirical evidence supporting the sample complexity rate.

claims.claim: A matching lower bound shows any algorithm requires Ω(ε^{-(2+α)}) samples under the same margin condition, establishing CGP's minimax sample-complexity optimality (Theorem 4.9).
claims.evidence: No experiment was run; the logbook states this is 'a source-presence check and nothing more' and that 'a lower bound over all algorithms is not reachable by simulation.' No empirical evidence is provided.

claims.claim: CGP-Adaptive learns the Lipschitz constant L online via a doubling scheme, adding only an O(log T) multiplicative overhead to the sample complexity (Theorem 5.1, Section 5).
claims.evidence: The adaptive variant was not implemented; the logbook states 'Source-anchored only' with no experiments or measurements related to the doubling scheme or O(log T) overhead.

claims.claim: CGP-TR, a trust-region variant, scales to dimension d > 50 via certified restarts that provably never falsely eliminate the region containing the true optimizer x* (Theorem 6.1, Section 6).
claims.evidence: CGP-TR was not implemented and no d>50 run was performed; the logbook explicitly states 'CGP-TR was not implemented, so its restart guarantee is untested here.' No empirical evidence exists.

RyeCatcher/repro-certificate-guided-prun.overall: This logbook provides one small-scale synthetic experiment (Claim 1, 2-D, 40 trials) and one partial measurement (Claim 2, volume shrinkage without testing the exponent), while four claims have no experiments at all and are merely source-presence checks. The reproduction is a thin audit that does not substantively verify any of the paper's theoretical claims at scale.

RyeCatcher/repro-bregman-meets-l-vy-stoc.paper_title: Bregman meets Lévy: Stochastic Mirror Descent with Heavy-Tailed Noise in Continuous and Discrete Time

claims.claim: Under the Lévy Mirror Flow model with centered Lévy noise having finite p-th moments (1<p≤2), time-averaged orbits achieve ε-optimality within Õ(ε^(-p/(p-1))) time for convex objectives (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: No experiment was run; the logbook explicitly states 'no time-complexity was measured' and only performed a source-presence check for Theorem 1.

claims.claim: For strongly convex objectives, the process converges geometrically to an uncertainty ball whose radius scales as O(ησ²_tame + η^(p-1)σ^p_heavy), despite jump discontinuities of arbitrary magnitude (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: A real experiment was run (quadratic objective, p=1.7, 60 seeds, 4000 steps) showing mean squared distance increasing monotonically with η (0.0090→0.0363), but this only tests that the radius grows with η and does not separate the two-term structure O(ησ²_tame + η^(p-1)σ^p_heavy) that is the actual content of Theorem 4.

claims.claim: The first-passage (hitting) time to within δ of the optimum for strongly convex objectives is Õ(δ^(-2p/(p-1))) (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: No experiment was run; the logbook states that a discrete proxy 'would measure the integrator rather than the flow' and only performed a source-presence check.

claims.claim: The discrete-time Stochastic Dual Averaging analogue achieves an O(T^(-(p-1)/p)) ergodic convergence rate on convex functions, matching the continuous-time rate (Theorem 5).
claims.evidence: SDA was implemented with Pareto noise at three p-values (200-400 seeds, T up to 16000), but the fitted exponents (-0.2475, -0.6480, -0.6040) are non-monotone where the prediction is monotone, and the measurement error at p=1.7 (0.236) exceeds the entire predicted span (0.214), making the results too noisy to confirm or refute the O(T^{-(p-1)/p}) rate on this simplified 1-D Euclidean setup.

claims.claim: For strongly convex functions, the discrete-time method requires Ω((σ^p/ε)^(1/(p-1)) log(1/ε)) iterations to reach ε-accuracy (Corollary 1).
claims.evidence: No experiment was run; the logbook correctly notes that a lower bound over all schedules cannot be established by simulation and states 'Not attempted.'

claims.claim: A novel 'weak Itô formula' for Lipschitz-smooth convex functions under Lévy integrators is proved to enable the analysis despite discontinuous sample paths and potentially infinite noise variance when p<2 (Section 2).
claims.evidence: No experiment was run; the logbook states 'A proof of a stochastic-calculus lemma is not something this audit verifies' and only checked source presence.

RyeCatcher/repro-bregman-meets-l-vy-stoc.overall: This logbook provides real experimental evidence for only 2 of 6 claims (Claims 2 and 4), both on simplified 1-D setups with results too weak to confirm or refute the paper's theorems; the remaining 4 claims received no experimental treatment beyond source-presence checks.

RyeCatcher/repro-asymptotically-optimal-.paper_title: Asymptotically Optimal Sequential Testing with Markovian Data

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 gives a non-asymptotic instance-dependent lower bound on the expected stopping time, E_Q[tau_alpha] ≥ (log(1/alpha)/D_M^inf(Q,P) − 2C_Q/min_i pi_i)^+, where D_M^inf(Q,P) is a stationary-weighted projection distance and C_Q bounds a Poisson-equation solution (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: A single 2-state chain pair (Q=[[0.7,0.3],[0.7,0.3]], P=[[0.85,0.15],[0.2,0.8]]) was tested with 20 seeds at four alpha values; the lower-bound RHS is 0 for three of four alphas, making the check trivially satisfied, and only one alpha yields a nontrivial RHS of 4.04 vs. observed mean 53.10.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 bounds the Poisson-equation solution constant C_Q via the pseudo-spectral gap of the underlying Markov chain (Section 3, Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: On a 2-state chain (P=[[0.8,0.2],[0.1,0.9]]), the source constant C_P=11.62 dominates the exact max ratio 4.44 over sign functions, and a negative control on a slow-mixing chain shows a wrong constant (2.0) fails (25.0>2.0), but this is only a 2-state exhaustive enumeration, not a general proof.

claims.claim: The proposed Sequential Markov Chain Test (Algorithm 1) builds an empirical transition kernel and a martingale statistic L_t accumulating row-wise KL divergences from the null class, stopping when L_t exceeds an adaptive boundary beta_t (Section 4, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: An exact replay of Algorithm 1 on a fixed 6-step path [0,1,1,0,1,1] computes the empirical transition kernel, L_t=3.94 (row-wise KL accumulations), and adaptive boundary beta_t=7.48 from the source formulas, confirming the algorithm's procedural construction as described.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves the proposed test is alpha-correct and asymptotically optimal, with limsup_{alpha->0} E_Q[tau_alpha]/log(1/alpha) ≤ 1/D_M^inf(Q,P), matching the Theorem 3.3 lower bound (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: On the same 2-state pair with 20 seeds, the ratio mean_tau/log(1/alpha) decreases from 25.4 to 13.6 as alpha shrinks, but remains far above the asymptotic target 1/D=4.44; null false-rejection is 0 within a 12k-step horizon, but the finite-alpha regime is nowhere near asymptotic.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 extends the one-sided asymptotic optimality result to the two-sided testing setting (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: A parallel two-sided test on singleton {P} vs {Q} with alpha=beta=0.05 and 20 seeds shows zero wrong-decisions, but mean_tau/log(1/alpha)=14.05 vs target 4.44 and 11.57 vs target 3.79, far from the asymptotic constants.

claims.claim: The framework is applied to detect MCMC transition-kernel misspecification (Section 5.1, Corollary 5.1) and to validate linear transition dynamics in MDPs (Section 5.2, Corollary 5.3).
claims.evidence: Tiny structural checks only: a 2-state MCMC stationarity residual distinguishes good (5.5e-17) from bad (0.08) kernels, and a small linear-MDP least-squares residual distinguishes representable (1.1e-16) from non-representable (0.43) kernels, without actually running the sequential test to detect misspecification.

RyeCatcher/repro-asymptotically-optimal-.overall: The logbook provides small-scale toy checks (2-state chains, 20 seeds, 6-step paths) for five of six claims and one exact procedural replay of Algorithm 1's construction. No claim is tested at the scale or generality the paper intends; the asymptotic optimality claims in particular are far from their limiting regime in the experiments.

RyeCatcher/repro-bridging-the-gap-betwee.paper_title: Bridging the Gap Between Average and Discounted TD Learning

claims.claim: Under i.i.d. sampling in the double-chain formulation, the algorithm converges to a unique, sample-independent fixed point of the projected Bellman equation with sample complexity Õ(ε^-1 η^-2) (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states 'I did not run the stochastic TD recursion.' Instead, it checked uniqueness of the projected Bellman linear system on 20 small stationary toy instances (min eigenvalue 0.08956, solver disagreement 6.22e-15) and fit a rate proxy, but never executed the actual TD algorithm on a real MDP.

claims.claim: Under Markovian sampling with constant stepsizes in the double-chain setting, the same Õ(ε^-1 η^-2) sample complexity is preserved (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: No paper-specific MDP was instantiated; only a toy proxy model τ_mix = ceil(log(1/α)) was used to fit the bound shape (T exponent -0.8876, η exponent -1.8808), which is an algebraic check of the theorem's rate rather than a simulation of Markovian TD learning.

claims.claim: With decaying stepsizes, the method attains convergence guarantees with no explicit dimension-dependent terms (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The only 'experiment' was counting standalone 'd' tokens in theorem text (0 in theorem block, 2 in prose). No computation, simulation, or numerical verification of any kind was performed—this is a text audit, not an experimental reproduction.

claims.claim: The paper reduces the condition-number dependence of average-reward TD learning from quartic (prior state of the art) to quadratic, matching the scaling known for discounted TD learning (Section 1, Table 1).
claims.evidence: The quartic-to-quadratic exponents (4,4,4 prior; 2 two-chain; 2 discounted) were read from Table 1 in the paper, not experimentally derived. The only computation was checking η1/η3 ratios on 20 small stationary toy instances (min 1.0461), which supports same-order comparison but does not benchmark prior algorithms or replay finite-sample proofs.

claims.claim: A single-chain variant of the algorithm is also analyzed but only attains quartic sample complexity Õ(1/η^4 T) due to decorrelation requirements, contrasting with the double-chain method's quadratic rate (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: No single-chain TD algorithm was run. The logbook only performed algebraic fits of the bound shape: conditional quartic fit (η exponent -4 when η'=Θ(η)) and a negative control (η exponent -3 when η' held constant). These are arithmetic checks of the theorem's formula, not algorithmic experiments.

claims.claim: The condition number η1, defined via min over unit vectors of ||Φx||²_Dir + (μᵀΦx)², is shown to satisfy η1 >= (1/2)η3 relative to prior condition-number definitions (Equation 3, Lemma B.3).
claims.evidence: The inequality η1 ≥ (1/2)η3 was checked numerically on 20 small stationary reversible toy instances (min ratio 1.0461, max 2.0022), providing concrete but limited-scale numerical evidence rather than a symbolic proof or full-scale verification.

RyeCatcher/repro-bridging-the-gap-betwee.overall: This logbook provides no actual simulation of the TD learning algorithms described in the paper; all evidence consists of text audits, small linear-algebra checks on toy stationary instances, or algebraic fits of bound shapes. The claims are theoretical and the reproduction attempts only proxy-level verification on simplified setups, with Claim 3 lacking any experimental content whatsoever.

RyeCatcher/repro-anytime-detection-of-st.paper_title: Anytime Detection of Strategic Deviations in Multi-Agent Systems

claims.claim: For normal-form games, the framework defines a per-round e-value E_{i,t}(a_i')(lambda) = 1 - lambda*X_{i,t}(a_i') requiring only observed payoff evaluations, not knowledge of the equilibrium strategies themselves (Section 2, Lemma 2.2).
claims.evidence: A one-step arithmetic instantiation (observed payoff 0.40, deviation payoff 0.70, λ=0.60, E=1.18) confirms the formula's dependence on payoff evaluations, but no sequential game was replayed and the protocol delta explicitly states 'I did not replay a sequential game instance.'

claims.claim: Theorem 2.6 shows family-wise error rate (FWER) is controlled at level alpha when the accumulated test supermartingale threshold reaches sum_i |A_i| / alpha, where A_i is agent i's action set (Section 2, Theorem 2.6).
claims.evidence: Source line hits confirm the threshold formula Σ|A_i|/α appears in the paper, and a trivial arithmetic instantiation (action sizes [2,3,4], α=0.1, threshold=90.0) is computed, but no simulation of false positive rates or empirical FWER verification was performed.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.7 bounds the expected detection time of an equilibrium deviation at O(log(sum_i |A_i| / alpha) / eta^2), where eta is the deviation's payoff-improvement magnitude (Section 2, Theorem 2.7).
claims.evidence: An algebraic comparison of the source's exact bound 12(log b + log(4/η) + log(3/2))/η² against a simplified surrogate shows the dropped log(1/η) term grows materially as η shrinks (ratio 1.83→2.60), but this is formula arithmetic, not an empirical detection-time experiment.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.8 adapts a Benjamini-Hochberg procedure to the sequential e-value setting for false discovery rate (FDR) control, and the paper shows empirically in a 2x2 game that this FDR procedure detects deviations faster than the conservative FWER-controlling baseline (Section 2, Theorem 2.8).
claims.evidence: Source lines confirm the FDR theorem and earlier-than-FWER proposition, and visual inspection of a pre-packaged figure (fig_renders/fwer_vs_fdr_comparison.png) shows FDR mean stopping time 1546 vs FWER 1765, but the 300-game experiment was never rerun — only pre-existing assets were inspected.

claims.claim: For stochastic games, Theorem 3.4 bounds detection time by (log b + C_i) / KL-bar_i(mu), where KL-bar_i(mu) is a state-averaged Kullback-Leibler divergence, and Remark 3.5 extends this via mixture martingales to handle deviations of unknown magnitude (Section 3, Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: Source line hits confirm the stationary bound and mixture remark, and an algebraic scaling comparison (b=20, C_i=0.7, w=0.2) shows constant ratio 1.4355 across KL values preserving 1/KL̄ scaling, but no stochastic game or likelihood-ratio martingale was replayed on trajectories.

claims.claim: Empirical validation on Grid Soccer and Predator-Prey environments shows detection times matching the theoretical O(1/epsilon^2) scaling, including under the mixture-martingale extension for unknown deviation magnitude (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Visual inspection of pre-packaged figures (martingale_scaling.png, prey_predator_scaling.png) shows blue empirical curves tracking green theoretical references, and a toy KL probe on synthetic distributions P=[0.55,0.30,0.15], Q=[0.10,0.25,0.65] yields log-log slope -1.9117, but Grid Soccer and Predator-Prey experiments were never rerun.

RyeCatcher/repro-anytime-detection-of-st.overall: This logbook is a source-code audit and formula-instantiation exercise: it confirms that the paper's theorems and formulas exist in the source text and performs small arithmetic/algebraic checks, but no actual experiments (sequential games, stochastic games, Grid Soccer, or Predator-Prey) were ever run. All six claims are addressed only at toy level with pre-packaged figure inspection and synthetic one-step computations.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows a symmetric smoothing operator with positive coefficients can be rescaled by a diagonal matrix (via a symmetric Sinkhorn iteration) into a diffusion operator that is self-adjoint with respect to a mass-weighted inner product (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: A 9-point Gaussian-kernel smoothing matrix with nonuniform masses was tested, yielding max|Q1-1|=5.86e-13, weighted self-adjointness error=8.33e-17, spectrum in [2.25e-4, 1.00], and convergence to the same diagonal scaling from two initializations (diff=3.17e-13). This is a single tiny instantiation, not a general verification of the theorem.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 proves that for Gaussian and exponential kernels, the Sinkhorn-normalized operators converge uniformly on bounded domains to continuous diffusion operators as sampling resolution increases (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: A bounded weighted circle in R^2 was used as a proxy domain with a dense n=2048 reference operator. Gaussian-kernel error drops to a ~5.5e-5 floor by n=64, and exponential-kernel error decreases monotonically from 1.163e-1 (n=32) to 5.147e-4 (n=512). This is a simplified 1D-circle surrogate, not a full convergence proof replay.

claims.claim: The symmetric Sinkhorn algorithm empirically requires only 5 to 10 iterations to reduce normalization error below 0.1% (Section 4/5, empirical convergence results).
claims.evidence: Three small deterministic proxies (point-cloud Gaussian, Erdős–Rényi, geometric-graph) reached mean abs error <1e-3 in 7, 8, and 7 iterations respectively, matching the 5–10 iteration claim. However, these are explicitly described as small proxies, not the paper's original staged assets.

claims.claim: The normalized operators simultaneously satisfy symmetry, mass conservation, entrywise positivity, and spectral damping (eigenvalues in [0,1]), properties not jointly satisfied by standard row- or symmetric-normalization schemes (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: On one toy family, Sinkhorn satisfied all four properties (max|Q1-1|=5.86e-13, self-adjointness error=8.33e-17, min entry=9.03e-4, eigenvalues in [2.25e-4, 1.00]), while row normalization broke weighted symmetry (error=1.20e-1) and symmetric normalization broke constant preservation (max|Q1-1|=2.45e-1). This is a crisp but single small-scale demonstration.

claims.claim: The method is demonstrated on point clouds, sparse voxel grids (jaw bone geometry), and Gaussian mixture models with covariance-aware kernels, showing Laplacian-like smoothing on each irregular data type (Section 5, experiments).
claims.evidence: Only a source-text fragment audit was performed (confirming the paper mentions 3/3 modalities and Gaussian-mixture covariances at lines 124, 299, 435, 441), but no experiments were run on any data type. The claim is about experimental demonstration of Laplacian-like smoothing, which was never addressed computationally.

claims.claim: Shape analysis experiments on the Armadillo mesh show spectral distributions remain consistent across sampling modalities, with eigenvalue divergence appearing only at scales matching sampling resolution, validating the Theorem 4.2 convergence guarantee (Section 5).
claims.evidence: A 1D interval proxy was used instead of the Armadillo mesh, showing low-mode spectral distortion (modes 2-5: 6.07e-4 at n=64 down to 8.92e-6 at n=512) is markedly smaller than high-mode distortion (modes 11-20: 1.08e-2 at n=64 down to 1.55e-4 at n=512), reproducing the claimed low-frequency-stable/high-frequency-resolution-limited pattern on a simplified surrogate.

RyeCatcher/repro-sinkhorn-normalization-.overall: The logbook provides small-scale numerical probes (9-point matrices, 1D circle/interval proxies, small random graphs) that are consistent with the paper's theoretical claims but do not constitute full reproductions at the paper's experimental scale. Claim 5 was never experimentally addressed—only a text audit was performed—making it inconclusive.

Real runs but on small instances, not a theorem-level verification.

claims.evidence: A 4-vertex weighted-path Lagrangian witness with 17 sampled λ values showed nested optimal sets ([], [0,1,2], [0,1,2,3]) with nestedness check true. Real computation but on a tiny instance, without implementing the parametric min-cut algorithm itself.

claims.claim: Corollary 1 shows the entire nested sequence of subgraphs across thresholds can be computed in Õ(γ(m+n)²) time (Corollary 1, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Only a source text audit was performed: the runtime token appears 3 times and content is at lines 255–263, but the active 'Corollary 1' anchor was found missing (commented out at lines 275–279). No runtime reimplementation or timing experiment was conducted, so there is no experimental evidence addressing the complexity claim.

claims.claim: Lemma 1 establishes a distribution-free marginal coverage guarantee ℙ(B*⊆Kτ*(A*))≥φ−δ under exchangeability, without requiring model probability estimates (Lemma 1).
claims.evidence: A tiny binary toy model (scores {0.4, 0.8}, calibration size 3, φ=0.75, δ=0) achieved exact finite coverage 0.8971 via exhaustive enumeration without any probability-estimation module. Real computation but on a heavily compressed instance, not the full general lemma.

claims.evidence: A tiny reduction-style witness (ε=0.25, r=3, W=23) separated a yes-3-clique case (best induced edges=18, above threshold 17.25) from a no-clique control (17, below threshold) via exact DP. Faithful to the reduction shape but not a full hardness proof.

claims.evidence: The experiment was never rerun. Only source text (lines 652–658) and presence of figure assets were checked. No raw curve values were extracted and no LP-vs-greedy comparison was executed, so there is no experimental evidence supporting or contradicting the empirical claim.

RyeCatcher/repro-compact-conformal-subgr.overall: The logbook provides real but small-scale toy computations for claims 1, 2, 4, and 5 (LP rounding checks, nestedness witness, coverage enumeration, and reduction witness), while claims 3 and 6 received only source-text audits with no experiments run at all. No claim was verified or falsified at full scale; the toy instances are directionally consistent but far below the paper's theorem-level or experimental-scale claims.

RyeCatcher/repro-maximin-relative-improv.paper_title: Maximin Relative Improvement: Fair Learning as a Bargaining Problem

claims.claim: Relative improvement is defined as the ratio of actual risk reduction to the maximum possible reduction from a baseline predictor, per Equation 1: ρ_P(f) = [R_P(f0) − R_P(f)] / [R_P(f0) − R_P(f*_P)] (Section 2, Equation 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook confirms the source contains Equation 1 and checks ratio arithmetic on a made-up triple (10,7,4)→0.5, but this is a source-presence check with trivial arithmetic, not a reproduction of a definition.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves a no-harm guarantee: when the baseline predictor f0 is in the feasible class F, the maximin relative improvement solution f_RI satisfies R_g(f_RI) ≤ R_g(f0) for every group g (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: A finite-set probe with only 4 candidate points and baseline risks (10,8) tests no-harm on a tiny made-up instance, plus a negative control removing f0 from F; real numbers but far below any meaningful scale.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.2 shows that, for two groups (m=2), relative improvement uniquely satisfies Pareto optimality, symmetry, scale invariance, and individual monotonicity simultaneously, and recovers the Kalai-Smorodinsky bargaining solution (Proposition 4.2).
claims.evidence: A 4-point toy frontier with baseline (10,10) and optima (4,2) shows the RI-selected point coincides with the KS point at equal relative improvement (0.5,0.5) and survives an affine rescaling, but this is a bounded illustration, not a proof replay.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.4 extends the axiomatic guarantees to more than two groups (m>2) via a leximin refinement that preserves scale invariance and a modified individual monotonicity property (Proposition 4.4).
claims.evidence: A three-group toy with a handful of candidate points tests leximin selection and a modified monotonicity direction on made-up data; real numbers but a trivially small finite instance with no theorem verification.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.4 establishes that the empirical maximin relative improvement estimator converges to the population solution at rate O(1/√n) under standard regularity conditions (Theorem 5.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook evaluates a proxy function 1/√n + √(log(2m/δ)/n) at four values of n and confirms it scales as 1/√n rather than 1/n, which is tautological arithmetic, not an empirical convergence test of the actual estimator.

claims.claim: Table 1 shows relative improvement is the only compared fairness criterion (versus Group DRO, minimax regret, Nash bargaining, and explained variance) that jointly satisfies Pareto optimality, scale invariance, and individual monotonicity (Table 1, Section 3.1-3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook parses Table 1 entries from the source and reports that only the RI row has PO+SI+IM all satisfied, but this merely reads the paper's own table rather than independently verifying the axiomatic properties of each criterion.

RyeCatcher/repro-maximin-relative-improv.overall: The logbook provides toy-scale numerical illustrations and source-text audits for all six theoretical claims, using tiny made-up finite examples (3-4 candidate points) and trivial arithmetic checks. No claim is independently verified at meaningful scale or via formal proof replay; the experiments merely confirm that the paper's formulas are internally consistent and that small hand-crafted instances behave as the theorems predict.

RyeCatcher/repro-alignment-sensitive-min.paper_title: Alignment-Sensitive Minimax Rates for Spectral Algorithms with Learned Kernels

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 establishes that over signal classes with Effective Span Dimension (ESD) at most K, the minimax excess risk is asymptotically equivalent to K·σ², holding without classical eigenvalue-decay or source-condition assumptions (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: The agent computed oracle PC risk on toy witness instances with K=1..4, obtaining ratios [2.0, 1.5, 1.333, 1.25] consistent with K·σ² scaling, but explicitly did not replay the minimax lower-bound proof and used only small finite instances.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 shows the principal-component (PC) estimator's risk is sandwiched as (d†−1)σ² ≤ Risk ≤ 2d†σ², where d† is the Effective Span Dimension defined as the smallest number of leading eigenfunctions whose remaining tail signal energy no longer exceeds the noise level σ² (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: A single 4-dimensional toy instance (θ=(0,0,0,1), λ=(4,3,2,1), σ²=0.5) was checked: d†=2, oracle PC risk=1.5 falls within [0.5, 2.0], and a negative control with wrong constant fails, but this is one tiny instance, not a general verification.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 gives convergence rates for a quota sequence {K_n}: the minimax risk over populations satisfying d†(σ0²/n; θ*, λ) ≤ K_n scales as Θ(K_n σ0²/n) (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: Rate-shape probe on small instances (n=16..128) with σ₀²=1 and K_n=ceil(log n) yields ratios converging toward ~1.2, but the agent explicitly did not replay the lower-bound proof and only checked scaling on toy finite witnesses.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 proves that overparameterized gradient flow (OP-GF) can reduce the Effective Span Dimension over training time by assigning larger adapted eigenvalues to strong signal directions with initially small eigenvalues, moving the problem into a lower minimax-risk complexity class (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: The agent manually swapped the spectrum from λ=(6,5,4,3,2,1) to λ'=(1,0.9,0.8,7,6,0.7) on a 6-dimensional toy signal, showing d† drops from 4 to 2, but explicitly did not run the OP-GF ODE—this is a hand-constructed spectrum shift, not gradient flow.

claims.claim: Section 7 and Section 8 extend the Effective Span Dimension framework to linear regression (via SVD, minimax rate Θ(σ0²K/n)) and RKHS regression (rate Θ(σ̄²K_n/n) with effective noise σ̄² = (σ0² + ||f*||²_∞)/n) (Section 7, Section 8).
claims.evidence: Linear regression part verified risk equivalence on a tiny 3×2 design matrix (difference 4.16e-17); RKHS part was only a notation audit with no computation, and the agent found the anchored formula σ̄²=(σ₀²+||f*||²_∞)/n does not match the theorem source's σ̄²=σ₀²(1+C₀²).

claims.claim: Numerical experiments show that span profiles decrease during OP-GF training—with larger improvements when initial signal-spectrum alignment is worse—and that deeper models attain lower Effective Span Dimension than shallow variants given sufficient training iterations (Numerical Validation).
claims.evidence: No experiments were rerun; the agent only rendered the paper's pre-packaged PDF figures to PNGs and visually inspected them, which provides no independent experimental evidence supporting or contradicting the claim.
