claims.evidence: Independent NumPy/Torch implementations of canonical, class-wise, and top-label soft-binning ECL variants produce finite losses with autograd-vs-finite-difference gradient agreement at ~1e-11 max error for all three variants, confirming differentiability and correctness of the formulas as specified in the paper's appendices.

claims.claim: On MNIST-to-SVHN top-label calibration with LeNet-5, ECL reduces ECE to 21.5% versus 61.9% for the uncalibrated baseline; with ResNet20, ECL achieves 36.8% ECE versus 48.2% for PseudoCal; with DenseNet40, ECL achieves 38.4% ECE versus 80.8% uncalibrated (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The paper's Table 2 is headed 'Digit → SVHN' and its setup explicitly states non-target domains are merged into the source (MNIST+USPS), so the six cited ECE values correspond to a composite-source experiment, not the MNIST-only-to-SVHN scope asserted by the claim; the numbers are transcribed accurately but the claimed dataset scope is contradicted by the paper's own text.

claims.claim: Table 1 shows ECL is the only compared method that simultaneously handles covariate shift, supports class-wise and canonical calibration, tolerates unbounded density ratios, and is mini-batch trainable, while Figure 2 reliability diagrams and Appendix Table 3 (source-vs-target calibration gap) further corroborate the approach on simulated data and the PACS dataset (Table 1, Figure 2, Appendix Table 3).
claims.evidence: The 'mini-batch trainable' conjunct of the Table 1 exclusivity claim is defined by the unbiased-gradient identity of Theorem 3.3, which Claim 3's exact counterexample shows is false for Algorithm 1's same-batch auxiliary mechanism; since one conjunct of the five-capability conjunction is false, the 'only compared method with all five capabilities' claim is false regardless of the remaining checkmarks or corroborating figures.

ProCreations/icml2026-repro-gfpptokv9c.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the theoretical claims (Theorems 3.1, 3.2, and the soft-binning extensions) via exact arithmetic, independent derivations, and finite-difference gradient checks, while falsifying Theorem 3.3 with an exact counterexample showing nonzero mini-batch gradient bias. Claims 5 and 6 are falsified through careful source-text auditing: the benchmark scope is misstated as MNIST-only when the paper uses merged digit sources, and the Table 1 exclusivity conjunction inherits the false mini-batch-trainability conjunct.

DineshAI/SOlPHMdSY3.paper_title: Finite-Width Neural Tangent Kernels from Feynman Diagrams

claims.claim: Feynman-diagram graphical rules are introduced that simplify layer-wise recursion relations for finite-width Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) statistics at order 1/n (Section 4).
claims.evidence: An executable verifier (claim1_verifier.py) reconstructs the Section 4 rules—external signatures, F-channel partitions, D/F/A/B quartic vertices, translation to algebra—and passes six checks including rejection of an invalid unpaired color as a negative control, concretely demonstrating the rules uniquely determine the order-1/n layer recursions.

claims.claim: A recursion relation for the first-order (1/n) finite-width correction to the NTK mean is derived using five Feynman diagrams containing quadratic and quartic vertices (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: The enumerator and independent checker return exactly five unique diagrams (two quadratic: K1 coeff 1/2, Theta1 coeff 1; three quartic: V coeff 1/8, D coeff C_W/2, F coeff C_W) matching Appendix E, with a missing-vertex negative control that exits nonzero.

claims.claim: For scale-invariant activation functions (ReLU and LeakyReLU), the infinite-width NTK diagonal Theta(x,x) has no finite-width corrections (Section 5.3).
claims.evidence: A symbolic verifier reconstructs the homogeneity cancellation, and a paper-scale experiment with 5,000,000 initializations at widths 20 and 80 for ReLU and LeakyReLU shows diagonal means within 0.19% of infinite-width predictions (all |z|<1.2) while off-diagonal controls detect 1.3–8.3% corrections at z>10, confirming the diagonal cancellation is specific.

claims.claim: Experiments on four-layer ReLU MLPs sampled over 5x10^6 initializations, with hidden-layer widths n>=20, confirm the finite-width kernel corrections predicted by the recursion relations (Figure 2, Section 6).
claims.evidence: The logbook identifies that the paper's Figure 2 uses GeLU (not ReLU as stated in the claim) with 100k samples per width; it tests four widths (32, 56, 100, 220) with 100k networks each, finding all measured means closer to first-order predictions than infinite-width (median residual ratio 0.1283), with an infinite-width substitution negative control that fails. The activation and sample-count discrepancy from the claim text is explicitly documented as a source clarification against paper v4.

claims.claim: Gradient-stability experiments on 200-hidden-unit ReLU MLPs with up to 30 layers, averaged over 1000 initializations, show linear scaling with depth at the critical initialization C_W=2 (Figure 1, Section 6).
claims.evidence: Width-200 ReLU MLPs at depths 1–30 with 1,000 initializations per regime show observed through-origin slope 0.6795±0.0122 vs predicted 0.6691 (z=0.85, R²=0.9999, max deviation 2.5%), with low-C_W control showing exponential decay (log-slope −2.03) and high-C_W showing exponential growth (log-slope +0.75), matching the claim's exact specifications.

DineshAI/SOlPHMdSY3.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental and symbolic evidence for all five claims at or near the paper's stated scale, with independent checkers and negative controls throughout. The main caveat is Claim 4, where the logbook documents that the paper's Figure 2 actually uses GeLU with 100k samples rather than the ReLU/5M stated in the claim, though the core finding of confirmed finite-width corrections is supported.

DineshAI/ga20H0vR6f.paper_title: Reinforcement Learning for Reachability: Guaranteeing Asymptotic Optimality

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes a PAC guarantee that, for a sufficiently small guessed minimum transition probability p_k, there exists a number of simulations N_k such that the learned policy is ε_k-optimal with probability at least 1-δ_k (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Success rates increase with N ({8: 0.15, 40: 0.662, 200: 0.938}) on small MDPs (3-4 states per Claim 4 evidence), qualitatively consistent with a PAC guarantee but at toy scale without specified δ_k, p_k, or verification that the rate meets 1-δ_k.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 shows that once the approximation error ε_k falls below a threshold ε_diff—the minimum value gap between optimal and suboptimal memoryless deterministic policies—any ε_k-optimal policy is guaranteed to be exactly optimal, not merely near-optimal (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Checked on a single MDP where eps_diff=1.0000 and near-optimal set equals optimal set, which is consistent with the theorem but on a trivially simple case with an extremely large value gap.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 proves that using a summable failure schedule δ_k = 1/2^k, the Borel-Cantelli lemma guarantees only finitely many stages fail, so the algorithm's policy is exactly optimal from some finite stage onward with probability 1 (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: Fraction of MDPs where policy becomes exactly optimal is 1.00, but this is a finite-sample empirical check on small MDPs of a probability-1 theoretical result, not a proof or large-scale demonstration.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 bounds ε_diff via transition-complexity parameter D, showing ‖v_π − v_π'‖_1 ≥ (2D)^(-2|A|·|S|) 2^(-2|S|) for any two distinct memoryless deterministic policies, giving an explicit MDP-structure-dependent characterization of when exact optimality is reached (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: All three test cases report min_gap=0.0 alongside positive bounds (e.g., 2.27e-13), which would mean 0.0 >= positive_bound is false—either contradicting the theorem or indicating a bug; the core.py implementation is not shown, making the result uninterpretable.

claims.claim: Empirical evaluation on standardized benchmarks shows the algorithm's policy becomes exactly optimal at a median stage k=2, far earlier than the stage (k≈16) at which the theoretical worst-case value-bound guarantees convergence (empirical validation section).
claims.evidence: Uses 20 small random MDPs (not the 'standardized benchmarks' specified in the claim) and finds median first-exact stage k=1, not the claimed k=2; the simplified setup and mismatched result preclude full verification or falsification.

DineshAI/ga20H0vR6f.overall: The logbook provides toy-scale empirical checks on very small MDPs (3-4 states, 2-3 actions) that are qualitatively consistent with some theoretical claims but do not constitute full verification, and Claim 4's evidence (min_gap=0.0 with positive bounds) is ambiguous or contradictory. The core implementation is not shown, no standardized benchmarks are used, and the self-reported 'full scale' assessment is contradicted by the actual MDP sizes in the evidence.

DineshAI/j4c3i3a5kH.paper_title: DPO Unchained: Your Training Algorithm is Secretly Disentangled in Human Choice Theory (and Its Loss' Convexity is Dispensable)

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 proves that for any strictly increasing function ψ, there exists a strictly proper loss pair (ℓ0, ℓ1) such that ψ decomposes as a composition of that loss with a strictly increasing function, generalizing DPO's link beyond the fixed logistic loss (Theorem 4.3, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Z3 returns UNSAT for the witness ψ(z)=z, F(z)=sigmoid(z): properness at p=0 requires ℓ0(q)≥ℓ0(0) for all q, but decomposition at z=ℓ0(0)−1 gives ℓ0(sigmoid(ℓ0(0)−1))=ℓ0(0)−1<ℓ0(0), a contradiction confirmed by five 60-digit Decimal checks and a SAT negative control when the inequality is reversed.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows that when the RLHF regularizer R is the regret of a proper loss, R equals a Bregman divergence, generalizing DPO's KL-based regularization to arbitrary Bregman divergences (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Symbolic expansion of D_φ,G(p||q)=φ(p)−φ(q)−(p−q)·G(q) with φ(p)=−L(p,p) and G(q)=−ℓ(q) yields residual 0, corroborated by 200 exact-Fraction trials of quadratic scoring rule across dimensions 2–9 all matching squared Euclidean divergence, with a sign-mutation negative control producing residual 4.

claims.claim: The paper introduces a 'KLST*' choice-theoretic structure built on expandability, local choice structure, and monotonicity axioms (Definitions 3.2-3.4) to generalize Bradley-Terry-Luce while allowing abstention (Section 3, Definition 3.4).
claims.evidence: SymPy factorization and Z3 both show that expandability plus atomic and lottery bearability force α(1−α)(p(a>b)+p(b>a)−1)=0 for all α∈(0,1), implying p(a>b)+p(b>a)=1 for every atomic pair, so abstention is impossible; dropping mixed-lottery bearability makes an abstaining model SAT (negative control).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 shows any choice probability with a KLST* structure can be represented as a strictly increasing link function F applied to a difference of latent utility functions, generalizing DPO's BTL-derived link r_theta = f(pi_theta) (Theorem 4.2, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: Four routes were attempted: a proof-step gap was identified (mixed-lottery vs atomic domain), exhaustive search over 125 reciprocal models on a 5-point grid found all 19 KLST*-satisfying models representable, and adversarial search found 5,987 candidate counterexamples all rejected by monotonicity—but no proof certificate closes the universal theorem and no valid counterexample falsifies it.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 and Corollary 4.5 show that DPO's standard logistic loss and symmetric link are recovered as one special case within the general (proper loss, link function, proper loss) triptych the paper constructs (Theorem 4.4, Corollary 4.5, Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: Symbolic computation confirms general subgradient and Fenchel residuals are both 0, and exact log-loss identities H(sigmoid(z))−z=0, ℓ0−log(1+exp(z))=0, ℓ1−log(1+exp(−z))=0 hold after substitution x=exp(z)>0 covering all real z; 19 exact-Fraction asymmetric Brier controls preserve the canonical identity while rejecting symmetry, and a sign-reversal control yields residual 2.

DineshAI/j4c3i3a5kH.overall: The logbook provides rigorous symbolic and exact-arithmetic evidence (Z3, SymPy, Decimal/Fraction) with negative controls for all five theorem-claims: Claims 2 and 5 are verified algebraically, Claims 1 and 3 are falsified by concrete contradictions, and Claim 4 remains unresolved with a documented proof gap but no valid counterexample.

DineshAI/PUIivg3GrO.paper_title: On the Existence of Consistent Adversarial Attacks in High-Dimensional Linear Classification

claims.claim: Proposition 1 gives the geometric existence condition for a consistent (label-preserving) adversarial attack: ε·d*_q*(ŵ_⊥) ≥ |⟨ŵ,x⟩|, where ŵ_⊥ is the component of the classifier orthogonal to the ground-truth direction (Section 3.1, Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: The extremal orthogonal certificate agrees in 400/400 trials (200 feasible, 200 infeasible) with maximum target residual 2.22e-16 and budget excess 5.55e-17, directly confirming the condition ε·||ŵ_⊥|| ≥ |⟨ŵ,x⟩| predicts attack feasibility; a full-norm mutation control is rejected in 20 designed cases.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 shows that, for the well-specified Gaussian model, the consistent robust-error and consistent boundary-error metrics concentrate to closed-form integrals depending on √(q-m²), in contrast to the standard (inconsistent) robust error which depends on √q, formally explaining why consistent attacks are less effective at fixed perturbation budget (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The printed Theorem 3.1 formulas (eqs. 24–25) give robust error 0.5 and boundary error 0.0957, while the definition-faithful computation gives 0.6915 and 0.1915 respectively, confirmed by 4M-draw Monte Carlo (0.6916±0.0002) and d=512 constructions (0.6925); the printed event omits a sign factor, producing incorrect closed-form values.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 characterizes the asymptotic robust-ERM performance in a latent-space (misspecified) linear classification model via a system of self-consistent equations in the proportional limit n,p,d→∞, distinguishing underparameterized (γ≤1) from overparameterized (γ>1) regimes (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The printed equations (37)–(42) are ill-defined: left sides do not define P, V, m, or q, and eq. (37) assigns the same RHS to all four conjugates while Appendix (119) gives distinct expressions, creating conflicts for P̂, V̂, and q̂; an appendix-consistent repair with four distinct conjugate updates exists but differs from the printed theorem.

claims.claim: Section 4.3 shows overparameterization has a dual effect: the consistent boundary error E_bnd^cns increases with overparameterization (greater vulnerability to label-preserving attacks), while the aggregate consistent robust error E_rob^cns decreases because overparameterization improves clean generalization (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: The current-verification page marks this BLOCKED: the exact evaluation contract (budget, loss, tuning, seeds, large-ψ threshold) is absent, and the historical sweep was rejected for assumption mismatch; the reported E_bnd_cns values [0.9977, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0] are saturated and E_rob_cns [0.7875, 0.5068, 0.6598, 0.6238] is non-monotonic, so the dual effect is not convincingly demonstrated.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 gives the exact asymptotic characterization of the consistent error metrics (E_rob^cns and E_bnd^cns) for the latent-variable classification model under misspecification (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: The printed event {ν>0, μ<c} ∪ {ν<0, μ>c} omits the set {ν<0, −c<μ≤c} compared to the definition-faithful event; at correlations −0.75, −0.25, 0.25, 0.75 with 500K draws each, omitted counts [95578, 95931, 95398, 95540] exactly equal the robust-error count gaps, and boundary ratios are ~2.0 instead of 1.0, confirming the printed formula is incorrect for positive thresholds.

DineshAI/PUIivg3GrO.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification of Proposition 1's geometric condition (400/400 trials) but presents concrete evidence that Theorems 3.1, 4.1, and 4.2 contain errors as printed (wrong event signs, ill-defined equations, omitted probability sets), while the overparameterization dual-effect claim remains unverified due to missing setup details and saturated/non-monotonic metrics.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 proves that mean-shift-induced spiked eigenvalues (set Λ_A) are spectrally separable from the covariance-induced spikes (set Λ_P) in high dimensions, using tools from Random Matrix Theory under the additive low-rank perturbation model (Section 3, Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: Exact rational arithmetic shows that at c=1/2, ell=3, theta²=3 (both above BBP threshold), g(ell)=g(theta²)=14/3, producing a spectral location collision between a covariance-induced spike and a mean-shift-induced spike, contradicting universal disjointness of Λ_A and Λ_P.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.11 (Eigenspace Invariance) shows that the eigenspace of the uncontaminated sample covariance matrix remains asymptotically invariant under mean-shift mixture contamination, regardless of the mixture weight π (Section 3, Theorem 3.11).
claims.evidence: A rank-one counterexample (X=u·1_n^T, Haar mean direction, Bernoulli(1/5) membership) satisfying the cited assumptions shows the perturbation residual staying flat at ~0.20 across 200 trials per size from n=250 to 8000 (log-log slope 0.000052), so sqrt(n)·residual diverges; the centered control decays at slope -0.503 as expected.

claims.claim: The proposed two-stage Mean-Shift PCA (MS-PCA, Algorithm 1) deliberately injects an artificial knockoff mean-shift perturbation A'_n = m'γ'^T with mixture weight π' (e.g., π'=0.5 or π'=1) and threshold ϵ=Cn^(-1/2) to identify and remove the mean-shift eigenvalues while leaving covariance-induced eigenvalues invariant (Section 2, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Literal Algorithm 1 run at c=1, pi=0.05, covariance strength 2, mean norm sqrt(80) with 12 trials each at n=500, 1000, 2000: mean-shift spike removed in 100% of trials, covariance spike retained in 91.7% aggregate (100% at n≥1000), with dense eigensolver agreement (1.64e-14) and zero-injection negative control confirming the mechanism.

claims.claim: Both mean-shift-induced spikes and covariance-induced spikes fluctuate at order O(n^-1/2), except the largest eigenvalue at the spectral edge which fluctuates at order O(n^-2/3), as used to set the matching threshold in the algorithm (Section 2, citing Theorem 2.19/2.16/2.15 of prior RMT results).
claims.evidence: The empirical fluctuation route was explicitly inconclusive: fitted slopes of -0.440 (covariance), -0.608 (mean), and -0.806 (edge) did not match the claimed rates of -0.5, -0.5, and -0.667. The accepted alternative is a described mathematical derivation chaining RMT CLTs, but this is an assertion of a proof check rather than concrete experimental evidence confirming the rates.

claims.claim: Section 4 numerical experiments show that existing Robust PCA methods fail to recover the true principal component even with only 5% outlier proportion when the aspect ratio d/n does not vanish (e.g., d/n=1), whereas MS-PCA consistently recovers it (Figure 2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: At d/n=1 with 5% mean-shift contamination, 36 trials across n=500, 1000, 2000 show MS-PCA alignment averaging 0.940 vs PCA 0.086 (paired bootstrap 95% CI for difference [0.759, 0.926]); 12 paired Robust PCA trials at n=500 average 0.079, with MS-PCA difference CI [0.637, 0.955].

DineshAI/ISNSiAC3n1.overall: The logbook provides concrete exact-arithmetic and Monte-Carlo evidence falsifying the universal spectral separability (Claim 1) and eigenspace invariance (Claim 2) claims, while verifying the MS-PCA algorithm's spike-removal mechanism (Claim 3) and its superiority over PCA/Robust PCA at d/n=1 with 5% outliers (Claim 5). The fluctuation-rate claim (Claim 4) remains inconclusive because the empirical slopes did not match the theoretical predictions and the supporting evidence is a described but non-experimental mathematical derivation.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 derives a variational dual form of entropic optimal transport, EOT_eps(p0,p1) = sup_f L(f) = sup_{f,xi} L(f,xi), replacing the intractable log-partition function with a tractable variational minimization over an auxiliary normalizer xi (Section 3, Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies the variational dual identity on a grid-discretized EOT setup (numpy, CPU), reporting L(f*,xi_f)-L*=0.00e+00 and L(f,xi)<=L(f) with excess 0.00e+00. This is a simplified discretized check of a continuous theorem, not a full-scale reproduction with continuous distributions and neural network potentials.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows the optimality gap equals a scaled KL divergence, eps*KL(pi* || pi_{f,xi}) = L* - L(f,xi), so optimizing the variational objective directly controls approximation of the ground-truth EOT plan (Section 3, Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: The grid-discretized verification reports max abs err 1.85e-12 for eps*KL(pi*||pi_f)=L*-L(f), confirming the identity at machine precision on a small grid. This is a valid but simplified numerical check, not evidence at the paper's continuous scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 gives a finite-sample estimation error bound of order O(N^(-1/(1+D))) + O(M^(-1/(1+D))) for Lipschitz-constrained function classes on compact supports (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports estimation errors [0.273, 0.178, 0.177, 0.056, 0.045] over N=[64..1024] with log-log slope -0.686, roughly consistent with N^{-1/2}. However, this is measured on a grid-based proxy, not the Lipschitz-constrained function classes on compact supports specified by the theorem.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.7 proves the approximation error vanishes as neural network capacity grows under universal function approximation, giving a full generalization guarantee together with Theorem 3.5 (Section 3.3, Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence: Approximation error decreases [0.269, 0.033, 0.001, 5e-05, 0, 0] over grid-based features [4..128], but these are not neural networks with universal approximation capacity as the theorem requires. The logbook also labels this as Theorem 3.6, not 3.7 as claimed.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 trains VarEOT in a simulation-free manner by jointly optimizing the potential f_theta and auxiliary function xi_psi via stochastic gradient ascent, avoiding the MCMC simulations required by EgNOT (Section 3, Algorithm 1; Table 1).
claims.evidence: The grid-based optimization reports KL(pi*||pi_f_hat)=0.0053 and simulation-free MC estimator errors, but this does not implement Algorithm 1 with neural network potentials f_theta and xi_psi trained via stochastic gradient ascent on real distributions—it is a grid-discretized proxy.

DineshAI/DgRd1uu8dj.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence on a grid-discretized numpy setup for all five claims, with real runs and specific numbers, but the grid-based verification is a clearly simplified proxy for the paper's continuous EOT setting with neural network function classes. No claim is verified at the paper's actual scale involving continuous distributions, neural networks, or the real Algorithm 1.

abdullahbinaqeel/repro-rex-solvers.paper_title: Rex: A Family of Reversible Exponential (Stochastic) Runge-Kutta Solvers

claims.claim: Rex converts explicit Runge-Kutta and stochastic Runge-Kutta schemes into algebraically reversible exponential solvers for diffusion ODEs and SDEs (Section 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook implements the McCallum-Foster coupling (Rex construction) from scratch and demonstrates machine-precision ODE round-trip errors (log10: Euler −14.09, Midpoint −14.53, RK4 −14.30) and SDE round-trip error 2.68e-14 on a nonlinear mixture probability-flow ODE and Gaussian VP SDE, with a non-reversible Lawson-Euler contrast drifting to −0.90 (8 orders worse).

claims.claim: The ODE Rex construction inherits arbitrary order of convergence and a non-zero linear stability region from the base McCallum-Foster method (Theorem A.1).
claims.evidence: Convergence study on a nonlinear mixture ODE with fine RK4 reference (N=8192) yields measured orders Euler 1.175, Midpoint 2.002, RK4 3.968, matching predicted 1/2/4; exact spectral-radius test on the 2×2 amplification matrix over 88,831 complex-plane grid points shows genuinely 2D stability regions for ζ<1 (e.g., Euler 6718 stable points at ζ=0.05 with off-axis extent), while leapfrog has only 105 points all on the imaginary axis.

claims.claim: Rex achieves near-machine-precision reconstruction under exact inversion in image-generation inversion experiments (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: The image-generation inversion experiments (Figure 7) were not run; the logbook explicitly states these require GPU hardware and trained model checkpoints (SD v1.5) unavailable in the CPU-only build.

claims.claim: Rex improves or remains competitive on unconditional generation, text-conditioned generation, and image editing benchmarks versus prior reversible solvers (Figures 7-9).
claims.evidence: The unconditional generation, text-conditioned generation, and image editing benchmark comparisons (Figures 7-9) were not run; the logbook states these require GPU and trained model checkpoints not available.

claims.claim: Rex enables accurate likelihood-based Boltzmann sampling on tri-alanine with flow models (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The tri-alanine Boltzmann sampling experiments (Table 1) were not run; the logbook states these require GPU and flow model checkpoints unavailable in the CPU-only build.

abdullahbinaqeel/repro-rex-solvers.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the mathematical foundations of Rex—algebraic reversibility to machine precision, convergence order inheritance, and 2D linear stability—on a self-contained CPU problem with closed-form score and exact spectral-radius computations. The three empirical application claims (image generation/editing and Boltzmann sampling) are not addressed at all due to GPU and checkpoint limitations.

snaykey/repro-bregman-levy-smd.paper_title: Bregman meets Lévy: Stochastic Mirror Descent with Heavy-Tailed Noise in Continuous and Discrete Time

claims.claim: Under the Lévy Mirror Flow model with centered Lévy noise having finite p-th moments (1<p≤2), time-averaged orbits achieve ε-optimality within Õ(ε^(-p/(p-1))) time for convex objectives (Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: Fitted ergodic rate exponents (-0.040, -0.251, -0.598, -0.883, -0.996) do not match theory (-0.231, -0.333, -0.412, -0.474, -0.500), diverging in both directions; for p=1.3 and p=1.5 the measured rate is slower than the upper bound, potentially violating it, while for p≥1.7 the rate is faster than theory due to instance-specific concentration, so the minimax exponent is neither verified nor falsified.

claims.claim: For strongly convex objectives, the process converges geometrically to an uncertainty ball whose radius scales as O(ησ²_tame + η^(p-1)σ^p_heavy), despite jump discontinuities of arbitrary magnitude (Theorem 4).
claims.evidence: Noise-floor η-exponent tracks p-1 (0.155/0.370/0.682/1.01 vs theory 0.3/0.5/0.7/1.0) with good match for p≥1.7, geometric contraction at rate μη observed for p=2 (slope -0.079 vs -0.06), and jumps of magnitude >10³ confirm convergence survives arbitrary-magnitude discontinuities.

claims.claim: The first-passage (hitting) time to within δ of the optimum for strongly convex objectives is Õ(δ^(-2p/(p-1))) (Theorem 3).
claims.evidence: Only the tame case p=2 was tested (measured exponent -3.3 to -3.8 vs theory -4, consistent with the upper bound); the heavy-tailed case p<2 — the paper's main contribution — was not measured at all due to computational infeasibility, so the p-dependent exponent δ^{-2p/(p-1)} is not verified.

claims.claim: The discrete-time Stochastic Dual Averaging analogue achieves an O(T^(-(p-1)/p)) ergodic convergence rate on convex functions, matching the continuous-time rate (Theorem 5).
claims.evidence: Fitted SDA ergodic exponents (-0.110, -0.488, -0.613, -0.983) do not match theory (-0.231, -0.333, -0.412, -0.474), diverging in both directions with the bound potentially violated at p=1.3; the Figure 1 reproduction tests strongly convex objectives, not the convex functions of Theorem 5, so the claimed convex rate is not directly verified.

claims.claim: For strongly convex functions, the discrete-time method requires Ω((σ^p/ε)^(1/(p-1)) log(1/ε)) iterations to reach ε-accuracy (Corollary 1).
claims.evidence: Iteration complexity exponent for p=1.5 matches theory almost perfectly (fitted slope -2.002 vs theory -2.000, r²=1.000) with clear scaling T(ε)=6249→173 across the ε range; p=2 gives ≈-1.0 on the resolvable range, consistent with classical O(1/ε) complexity.

claims.claim: A novel 'weak Itô formula' for Lipschitz-smooth convex functions under Lévy integrators is proved to enable the analysis despite discontinuous sample paths and potentially infinite noise variance when p<2 (Section 2).
claims.evidence: Second moment diverges for p<2 (ratio 15.8× at p=1.3, 3.3× at p=1.5) while first moment stays stable, confirming the classical Itô obstruction; energy budget scales as η^{p-1} (0.426/0.591/0.759 vs theory 0.3/0.5/0.7), confirming the weak Itô formula's finite p-th-moment control despite infinite variance.

snaykey/repro-bregman-levy-smd.overall: The logbook provides a real-scale simulation of the Lévy Mirror Flow and discrete SDA under genuine α-stable noise at n=100 with hundreds of trials, verifying the strongly convex claims (floor scaling η^{p-1}, iteration complexity ε^{-1/(p-1)}, and weak Itô energy bounds) with reasonable quantitative accuracy. The convex ergodic rate claims show correct qualitative features (clean power laws, p-ordering) but significant exponent mismatches that the logbook attributes to instance-specific concentration rather than minimax tightness, and the hitting-time claim is largely untested for the heavy-tailed regime.

claims.claim: A weighted set is defined as a β-approximation preserving coreset (β-APC) if any α-approximate k-means solution computed on it yields an αβ-approximate solution on the full dataset (Definition 1.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook demonstrates the β-APC contract on real data: Euclidean (β=1+ε) on MNIST (n=30000) and Adult (n=48842) with β_eff q90 values of 0.764/0.755/0.738 and 0.914/0.897/0.868 across ε=0.30/0.20/0.10, all ≤ 1+ε; arbitrary-metric (β=4+ε) on MNIST (n=32000) with β_eff max 1.327 ≤ 4+ε. A negative control on Adult shows the coreset is not strong (adversarial q90 error 0.152 > ε at m=120), confirming the definition sits strictly between weak and strong coresets.

claims.claim: For Euclidean k-means, sensitivity sampling constructs a (1+ε)-APC of size Õ(kε^-3), improving on strong coreset size requirements (Theorem 1.2).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 2 is implemented on MNIST (n=30000, d=50) and Adult (n=48842) with β_eff q90 ≤ 1+ε for 40 solutions per setting, good-solution relative error ≤ ε at all ε values, and coreset size m = c·(k/ε³)·log(k/ε) (e.g., 4891 points at k=10, ε=0.20). The ~16× size saving over strong coresets is demonstrated via the negative control, and the Figure-1 cost-ratio curve (≈1.12 at m/k=10, decaying to 1) reproduces across three datasets and three algorithms.

claims.claim: For arbitrary metrics, an iterative downsampling approach constructs a (4+ε)-APC of size Õ(kε^-2) (Theorem 1.3).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 4 is implemented on MNIST as a finite metric (n up to 64000, k=8, ε=0.3). Coreset size is flat at 4670 for n ≥ 8000 (independent of n), matching Õ(kε⁻²). The (4+ε)-APC contract holds with β_eff max 1.327 ≤ 4+ε across 80 solutions, and the nearest-point lifting factor (Lemma 4.3) is bounded by max 1.342 ≤ 4. Cost preservation on Ω-centred solutions has q90 error 0.0077 ≤ ε.

claims.claim: Sensitivity sampling with m = Cε^-2(k log(k/δ) + log N) points gives strong coreset concentration guarantees for a solution family of size N (Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: On MNIST (n=30000, d=50), the concentration rate is confirmed: log-log slope of max error vs m is −0.486 (theory −0.5), and error grows as √log N (corr(err², log N)=0.795, observed ratio 1.22 vs theoretical 1.33). The sample-size formula m = Cε⁻²(k log(k/δ)+log N) is shown sufficient with empirical failure probability ≪ δ=0.1 across ε ∈ {0.10,0.12,0.15} and k ∈ {5,10,20,40}, with m growing ∝ k log k as predicted.

claims.claim: For finite n-point metrics, sensitivity sampling yields strong coresets of size O(kε^-2 log n), matching known lower bounds without extra polylogarithmic factors (Corollary 2.3).
claims.evidence: On Adult (k=8, ε=0.2, δ=0.1) sweeping n from 1000 to 16000, the minimal sufficient coreset size satisfies min_m/(kε⁻² log n) = 0.120 constant across the entire 16× range (corr(min_m, log n)=1.000), confirming O(kε⁻² log n) with no extra polylogarithmic factors. The ratio's constance directly rules out log log n or log⁵ε⁻¹ factors, matching the known lower bound.

claims.claim: A lower bound of Ω(log N / log log N) is proved showing that APC guarantees below β=4 are not achievable for the arbitrary-metric setting (Theorem 4.6).
claims.evidence: The packing family (Lemma 4.5) is verified numerically: mean intersection = r²/n = 1.0 with zero violating pairs (|S∩T| ≤ τr, τ=0.25) for n ≥ 400. The core impossibility gap is confirmed: best common approximation ratio across all centres is 3.70 (median 3.88 ≥ 4−3τ=3.25), so no centre β-approximates both inputs for β < 4. Pigeonhole gives coreset size s/r ≈ 0.34 constant (Ω(r)), and r = Θ(log N/log log N) is confirmed with ratio in [0.741, 0.799] over n ∈ [400, 10⁴].

snaykey/repro-approx-preserving-coresets.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence on real datasets (MNIST, Adult, CoverType at n up to 64k) for all six claims, with verbatim algorithm implementations, specific numerical results, negative controls, and SHA-256 hashes for reproducibility. Every claim is supported by real-scale runs with quantified β_eff values, concentration rates, size scaling, or lower-bound construction steps — not merely assertions.

snaykey/repro-first-order-diffopt.paper_title: A Fully First-Order Layer for Differentiable Optimization

claims.claim: FFOLayer computes an ε-approximate hypergradient using an active-set Lagrangian oracle that requires no Hessian evaluations, achieving Õ(1) first-order oracle calls per hypergradient estimate (Section 4.2, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Dimension sweep dy=20–800 (paper's synthetic scale) shows exactly 2 black-box solves per hypergradient at every dimension with 0 Hessian factorizations (vs 1 for implicit diff), cos(FFO,exact)=1.0 to ≥10 digits, and O(δ) truncation error confirmed on a non-quadratic lower level (log-log slope 1.0005).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that the 'ghost bilevel optimization' reformulation, which treats active constraints as equalities, preserves the accuracy of the hypergradient computed at the original constrained-optimization solution (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Four-way comparison (original full-KKT, ghost-reduced KKT, FFO, model-free numerical) on QPs up to d=150 with strict complementarity shows max relative error 2.9e-05 between original and ghost gradients; negative control with wrong active set yields 0.27 error (8-order-of-magnitude gap), confirming the identity is non-trivial.

claims.claim: For constrained bilevel optimization, the method achieves an oracle complexity of Õ(δ⁻¹ε⁻³), matching best-known rates for non-smooth non-convex optimization, while extending prior guarantees from linear to general convex constraints (Section 4, complexity analysis).
claims.evidence: FFO per-hypergradient cost is constant (2 solves) across target ε from 1e-1 to 1e-6, while penalty oracle shows O(1/ε) scaling (slope −0.96); QCQP general-convex extension verified (max rel. error 1.0e-9 vs exact implicit diff); end-to-end Goldstein method reaches (δ=0.2, ε=0.1)-stationarity at 2 solves/call. Outer Õ(δ⁻¹ε⁻³) rate is cited from Zhang 2020b, not re-derived, but the load-bearing new factors are directly verified.

claims.claim: On synthetic decision-focused-learning QP tasks and 9×9 Sudoku constraint-learning tasks formulated as linear programs, FFOLayer matches the convergence of exact differentiable-optimization solvers CvxpyLayer and qpth while using a substantially faster backward pass (Experiments section, synthetic QP and Sudoku benchmarks).
claims.evidence: DFL QP training (dy=100) shows max |loss_FFO−loss_exact|=2.5e-06 over 40 steps; 9×9 Sudoku (729 variables) gradient verified vs model-free numerical (1.4e-06); 4×4 Sudoku training parity (5.6e-10); backward speedup up to 22× with near-linear vs cubic scaling. Sudoku training parity is at 4×4 with 9×9 verified at gradient level, and own exact implicit diff substitutes for CvxpyLayer/qpth, but core convergence and speed claims are supported.

claims.claim: FFOLayer's PyTorch implementation is objective-agnostic, exposing task-loss influence via a single detached gradient coefficient c := detach(dF/dy*), allowing users to substitute it for CvxpyLayer with minimal code changes (Section on practical implementation).
claims.evidence: Lemma E.1 surrogate identity confirmed (max error 1.8e-06 over 20 instances); five distinct upper objectives (linear, isotropic quadratic, weighted quadratic, Huber, log-cosh) all reproduce exact implicit-diff gradient through a single code path with max rel. error 6.3e-08; drop-in torch.autograd.Function with CvxpyLayer signature matches exact (2.3e-09) and numerical (1.2e-09) gradients.

claims.claim: FFOLayer outperforms the gradient-unrolling baseline LPGD in the reported experiments while eliminating the cubic-complexity Hessian inversion required by standard implicit differentiation (Experiments section, comparison with LPGD).
claims.evidence: FFO achieves machine-precision hypergradients (5e-12) at solver tolerance 1e-5 while LPGD needs 1e-11 for comparable accuracy (10³–10⁶× tighter tolerance gap, matching paper's 1e-4→1e-12 finding); exact backward scales ~d^2.69 vs FFO ~d^1.11 (36× speedup at d=600) with 0 vs 1 Hessian factorizations. LPGD training instability on ill-conditioned Sudoku is not reproduced (both converge on benign task), but the tolerance gap and cubic elimination are directly measured.

snaykey/repro-first-order-diffopt.overall: The logbook provides concrete, non-toy experimental evidence supporting all six claims through an independent reimplementation of Algorithm 1, with dimension sweeps up to the paper's own scale, multiple independent gradient references (exact implicit differentiation and model-free numerical), negative controls, and pinned result files. Key limitations include Sudoku training parity demonstrated at 4×4 (9×9 at gradient level only), the outer complexity rate cited rather than re-derived, and LPGD training instability not reproduced on benign tasks.

michaldobiezynski/repro-reusing-trajecto.paper_title: Reusing Trajectories in Policy Gradients Enables Fast Convergence

claims.claim: Introduces RPG (retrospective/reusing-trajectories policy gradient), which combines a power-mean-corrected multiple importance weighting estimator with on-policy and off-policy data drawn from the most recent ω iterations of trajectories (Section 3).
claims.evidence: MSE of the MPM estimator against the exact gradient falls with log-log slope −0.976 (ideal −1) as ω grows from 1 to 64 on a d_Θ=128 Gaussian linear policy using real consecutive RPG iterates as behavior policies (χ² up to 14.06), and the power-mean correction beats naive MIW 1.6× at the widest window (15.53 vs 24.92).

claims.claim: Derives a concentration bound on the power-mean estimator's error of order O(√(D·d_Θ·log(1/δ)/(N·k))), where D bounds the χ² divergence between behavior and target policies (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Across 35 configurations on two policy classes (including a softmax class where G1, χ² divergence, and grad J are all exact by enumeration), the exponent in N·ω_k measures −0.505 vs predicted −0.500, the bound is satisfied in every configuration (max measured/bound = 0.113), and N and ω_k are interchangeable at fixed product to within 1.22× while ω_k varies 16-fold.

claims.claim: Proves RPG attains Õ(ε^-1) sample complexity to reach an ε-stationary point using a constant batch size N (including N=1), which the paper identifies as the best known rate among policy gradient methods (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: On a non-concave saturating-reward instance, n(ε)·ε decreases monotonically from 24960 to 1135 across 256× in ε, consistent with Õ(ε^-1); RPG reaches ε=0.0625 in 18160 trajectories while REINFORCE at the same constant batch never reaches it in 50000, though the N=1 case shows no advantage at 6000 trajectories (0.5712 vs 0.4995).

claims.claim: Compares against REINFORCE (O(ε^-2)), SVRPG (O(ε^-5/3)), SRVRPG and STORM-PG (O(ε^-3/2)), showing RPG's trajectory-reuse strategy improves on all of these gradient-based variance-reduction baselines (Table 1).
claims.evidence: All four baselines implemented from their own update rules and run on the identical non-concave instance, seeds, and budget; RPG needs 1.86×–3.02× fewer trajectories than each baseline at their common ε=0.25 and achieves the lowest final ‖grad J‖² (0.0221 vs 0.1819–0.1934), though the baselines' internal Table-1 ordering does not reproduce.

michaldobiezynski/repro-reusing-trajecto.overall: The logbook provides thorough empirical validation of all four claims on synthetic MDPs with exact ground-truth gradients (d_Θ up to 2048), demonstrating the estimator's variance reduction, the concentration bound's scaling, Õ(ε^-1) sample complexity on a non-concave instance, and RPG's improvement over all four implemented baselines. The main limitation is the absence of real RL benchmarks (MuJoCo/gym), but the synthetic setups are appropriately designed for testing the paper's theoretical claims with exact ground truth.

ProCreations/icml2026-repro-sj7ngz2eqx.paper_title: A Unifying View of Variational Generative Wasserstein Flows

claims.claim: The Generative Wasserstein Flows (GWF) framework shows that Variational Wasserstein Gradient Flow (VWGF) and Scalable JKO (S-JKO) objectives, despite different formulations, are mathematically equivalent (Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: Independent optimization of VWGF (inf_T sup_g) and S-JKO (sup_g inf_T) on continuous 2D anisotropic Gaussians yields duality gaps of 6.66e-16 to 8.88e-16 across three step sizes, with a mismatched-conjugate negative control separating by 0.14–0.37, and both sides recovering the same rebalanced measure to ~7e-09.

claims.claim: The paper shows explicit Wasserstein gradient descent with a regularized f-divergence is equivalent to JKO steps for the corresponding unregularized f-divergence under specific parameter relationships (Proposition 3.2).
claims.evidence: The γ=1/2, ε=2τ Wasserstein-gradient-descent step matches the independently computed JKO iterate to ≤3.7e-08 across KL, reverse KL, and χ² at three step sizes, with the first-variation identity confirmed by finite differences to 1e-06, and perturbed γ/ε controls missing by 0.07–0.29.

claims.claim: The paper introduces a Donsker-Varadhan formulation for the KL divergence within the JKO scheme that yields tighter lower bounds than classical variational representations while preserving equivalence at optimality (Section 3).
claims.evidence: A SymPy certificate proves DV−classical = Z/e−log Z ≥ 0 with unique zero at Z=e; 755 continuous quadratic critics show zero sign violations with DV strictly closer to KL; both bounds equal exact KL at the optimal critic with error 0.0; a pinned-offset critic class shows a 0.4125-nat DV advantage.

claims.claim: The GWF framework is extended beyond f-divergences to integral probability metrics, including Wasserstein-1 and squared Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD²), introducing a JKO-regularized version of MMD-GAN that does not require explicit discriminator optimization (Section 4, Equation 18).
claims.evidence: The paper's own Equation 18 includes a maximization over the learned embedding (identified as a discriminator), Algorithm 2 updates it by gradient steps, and an exact PSD-kernel counterexample on point masses shows that fixing vs. optimizing the embedding yields different transport minimizers (t=0 vs. t=2/3), demonstrating the embedding optimization is mathematically load-bearing.

claims.claim: Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 measured by Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) show JKO regularization gives moderate but consistent improvements for f-divergences (KL, Jensen-Shannon, χ²) and more pronounced gains for MMD, up to 20 FID points (Section 6/7 experiments).
claims.evidence: Exact decimal-to-Fraction arithmetic on the paper's own CIFAR-10 Table 4 shows the Jensen-Shannon (source-labeled 'Shannon') row has no-JKO FID 14.60 versus JKO FIDs of 32.24, 15.92, and 15.23—all worse—directly contradicting the claim of consistent improvements across all named f-divergences.

claims.claim: Parametric JKO updates are shown to approximate preconditioned Wasserstein gradient flows in the small-step-size regime (τ→0) (Proposition 6.3).
claims.evidence: The Proposition 6.3 residual R(τ) decays from 3.11e-02 to 2.38e-04 over τ∈[0.001, 0.2] with fitted exponent 0.9857±0.0033 on a 3-parameter nonlinear map family with condition-11.5 metric, while the identity-G control stays flat (slope −0.018), confirming the G-weighting is load-bearing.

ProCreations/icml2026-repro-sj7ngz2eqx.overall: The logbook verifies four mathematical propositions (Claims 1, 2, 3, 6) through rigorous numerical experiments on continuous 2D anisotropic Gaussian instances with closed-form integrals, independent codepaths, and falsifying negative controls, and falsifies two claims (4, 5) using the paper's own equations, algorithm, and FID tables.

michaldobiezynski/repro-flatland-the-adv.paper_title: Flatland: The Adventures of Gradient Descent with Large Step Sizes

claims.claim: Definition 2.3 formalizes 'large' step sizes using only local Lipschitz continuity of the gradient, requiring the step size to periodically exceed twice the local smoothness threshold, matching empirically observed edge-of-stability behavior (Definition 2.3).
claims.evidence: On the paper's 89,610-parameter MLP with real MNIST data, condition (i) of Def 2.3 held in 100% of 33 sampled steps and condition (ii) in 61% (max gap P≤45) at δ=0.5, and 100%/100% at δ=0.9; the EoS phenomenon was independently reproduced via fixed-step GD settling at η·λ₁=2.04 (range [1.94, 2.16]) against the predicted 2/η=2.

claims.claim: Proposition 2.5 establishes that the proposed equality line-search method (Algorithm 2) is Lipschitz-aware without requiring second-order information (Proposition 2.5).
claims.evidence: The Prop 2.5 lower bound η≥2δ(1−c)/l held in 100% of 33 sampled steps at both δ settings (min ratio 1.32), and a controlled objective-rescaling experiment over a 64× range yielded d log η/d log s = −1.000 at all five tested iterates with η·l invariant at 1.81±0.34, confirming Lipschitz-awareness with zero Hessian calls inside the line search.

claims.claim: Lemma 3.1 shows sharpness converges to its global minimum of 2/K, where K is the number of classes (Lemma 3.1, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The last-layer-bias Hessian block equals (2/K)I_K to 1e-14 for K=2,5,10, and large-step GD converges to sharpness exactly 2/K (0.400000 at K=5, 0.200000 at K=10, ratio 1.0000) with the full signature: top-K eigenvalues all at 2/K, remaining spectrum at 0, all gradient norms 0, loss frozen at the random-guess value, and accuracy exactly 1/K.

claims.claim: Empirically, the loss decreases nonmonotonically while the product of step size and sharpness stays above the edge-of-stability threshold of 2 throughout training, with methods reaching edge-of-stability right from the start (Abstract, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: η·λ₁ exceeds 1−c in 100% of samples and exceeds 2 in 79% at δ=0.5 (100% at δ=0.9), EoS is reached at the first iterate (η·λ₁=2.58), and the loss is genuinely nonmonotone (40% of 447 steps increase) while training converges to 88.9% test accuracy—matching the paper's own hedged wording ('very often greater than 2').

claims.claim: Reaching the globally minimal sharpness too early in training slows convergence and generalization; the proposed NLS-ub variant, which caps step sizes below K, avoids this and achieves better practical performance (Section 3.2, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The first half is strongly verified: the run reaching 2/K early freezes at 10.0% train/test accuracy with loss stuck at the random-guess value 0.09, versus 88.9% for runs staying above the floor; however, the NLS-vs-NLS-ub comparison is not separable because NLS never selected η>4<K=10, leaving the cap inactive and the two variants within seed noise (+0.17±0.4 points), so the key practical claim about NLS-ub's advantage remains untested on this setup.

michaldobiezynski/repro-flatland-the-adv.overall: The logbook provides rigorous numerical evidence supporting Claims 1–4 on the paper's own 89,610-parameter MLP with real MNIST data, including exact verification of the 2/K sharpness floor, Lipschitz-awareness via a controlled scaling experiment, and the EoS phenomenon. Claim 5's premise (early flatness is catastrophic) is verified, but the NLS-ub advantage cannot be tested because the MLP setup never triggers the precondition (NLS entering the flat region) that the paper's CNN/ResNet experiments create.

claims.claim: The federated bilevel performatively stable (FBPS) point is defined as the fixed point at which each client's deployed model induces a distribution under which the aggregated upper-level risk is minimized at that same point (Section 2.1.1).
claims.evidence: At d=100, M=50, N=500 across 5 seeds, ||R(x_s)-x_s|| ≤ 2.11e-15 and frozen UL gradient ≤ 1.23e-14; independent L-BFGS-B recovers x_s to 7.22e-08 and FBi-GD to 1.28e-14; 200 random probes show x_s strictly minimizes frozen risk by ≥2.43e-03; negative controls show residual bounded away from zero off the fixed point.

claims.claim: Under Assumptions 1-4, the update operator R(·) is contractive whenever L̄ᶠᶜˣ(εc,εd)/γf ≤ 1, which guarantees existence, uniqueness, and linear convergence of FBi-RRM to the FBPS point (Theorem 1, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: All Assumption 1-4 constants measured numerically (γf=0.6009, γg=0.5742, C_d=2.543, C_cd=1.291e5); eqn (7) holds at all sensitivities (L_emp/bound ratios 1.1e-14 to 1.5e-05); eqn (11) envelope holds for r≤40; 8/8 random starts converge to same point for ε≤1 (6.47e-14 apart); contraction loss between ε=1 and ε=10 matches Fig 1(a).

claims.claim: FBi-SGD, a communication-efficient stochastic variant using local updates and hypergradient estimation via an auxiliary variable, converges at rate E‖xr−xs‖²=O(1/r) under sufficiently small distribution sensitivities (Theorem 2, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Full three-term Lyapunov P_r tracked over 10,000 rounds at d=100 with Algorithm 2 as written (10/50 participation, 3 local steps, separate η^(c)/η^(s), projected v): log-log slopes -0.965/-0.878 at ε=0.01 and -0.968/-0.886 at ε=0.1 on successive tail windows against target -1, across 3 realizations; P_r drops by factor 2.8e4.

claims.claim: The distance between the federated bilevel performatively optimal (FBPO) point and the FBPS point is bounded by an expression proportional to the product of upper- and lower-level distribution sensitivities εc and εd (Theorem 3, Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: RHS of eqn (30) with measured constants dominates ||x_o-x_s|| in all 13 heterogeneous configurations (ratio 1.65e-07 to 7.46e-04); ε̄c exponent converges to 1.021/1.042; Remark 8 aggregate-only dependence confirmed across 4 profiles. A counterexample exists at ε̄c=0, ε̄d>0 (gap up to 3.79e-03 vs bound of 0), but this is a degenerate corner outside the main regime.

claims.claim: This work is presented as the first to combine federated bilevel optimization with performative prediction under decision-dependent distribution shifts at both objective levels (Section 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook shows the combined problem is not reducible to either feeder literature (residuals 1.31e-01 and 2.84e-02 vs 2.11e-15 for FBi-RRM) and a literature search finds no prior work in the fourth corner, but a claim of being 'first' requires exhaustive literature coverage that no reproduction experiment can provide.

michaldobiezynski/repro-federated-bileve.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous from-scratch reproduction at d=100, M=50, N=500 (10x the paper's scale) with measured theorem constants, multiple independent solvers, and negative controls, verifying Claims 1-4 with concrete numerical evidence. Claim 5 (novelty/priority) is inherently not decidable by computation, and the logbook correctly identifies this limitation.

claims.claim: The HJ-Prox estimator's approximation error is uniformly bounded by sup_x ||prox^δ_{tf}(x) - prox_{tf}(x)|| ≤ sqrt(n t δ) (Theorem 3.2, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The exact-integral HJ-prox error was measured against sqrt(n t δ) across 3 penalty families (ℓ1, indicator, group-ℓ2) from the paper, with worst-case ratio 0.7979 ≤ 1 over n∈[50,1000], δ∈[1e-1,1e-6], t∈{0.1,1.0}, and the measured δ-exponent (0.47–0.50) matches the theoretical 0.5; quadrature self-check confirms numerical error is far below measured proximal error.

claims.claim: Replacing exact proximal steps with HJ-Prox in the proximal point method and proximal gradient descent preserves almost-sure convergence under mild assumptions (Theorem 3.5, Theorem 3.6, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: On the paper's 250×500 LASSO instance, 3 independent MC streams of HJ-PGD all converge to within 2.09e-02 relative of the FISTA-certified optimum; Assumption 3.4 is tested directly via a constant-δ sweep showing a monotonically shrinking bias floor (7.14e-02→1.97e-02 as δ falls by 64×) that stays inside the √(n t δ) envelope, while the summable-δ arm reaches 2.76e-02, below every constant-δ floor ≥ 0.0625.

claims.claim: The HJ-Prox substitution extends convergence guarantees to Douglas-Rachford splitting and Davis-Yin splitting for composite objectives f+g+h with h L-smooth (Theorem 3.8, Theorem 3.9, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: DYS on the 300×60 sparse-group LASSO with both proxes replaced by HJ-Prox matches the paper (447.045/447.319 vs 447.045/447.388, rel gap 6.13e-04); DRS on the 256-point trend-filtering instance at 150000 iterations gives analytical baseline 2.0028 (paper 2.003) and DRS-HJ 2.2375 (paper 2.184, rel gap 2.45e-02), sitting above its matched-γ exact control as expected from MC error.

claims.claim: HJ-Prox is also applied within the primal-dual hybrid gradient algorithm via conjugate operator approximations (Theorem 3.10, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: On the paper's 4096-unknown TV-deblurring instance at 20000 iterations, exact PDHG gives 34.385 (paper 34.393) and PDHG-HJ gives 35.014 (paper 34.770, rel gap 7.02e-03); a conjugate-step ablation replacing only prox_(σg*) tracks the exact solution to 9.20e-05 relative at δ=1e-02 and degrades where J*=exp(2L²t/δ) exceeds the sample budget, matching the theory.

claims.claim: Splitting reduces the effective Lipschitz constant relative to non-split approaches, and hybrid exact/approximate strategies outperform fully approximate proximal methods in experiments (Section 3.3, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: All four Fig.4 objectives on the 250×500 non-negative LASSO match the paper to 3-4 significant figures (105.174/105.685/109.187/114.055 vs 105.174/105.730/109.259/113.870) with both claimed orderings (objective and fixed-point residual) holding exactly; the J* ratio of 7.94e10 is corroborated by a measured 4.12× MC-std ratio between split and combined prox evaluations.

michaldobiezynski/repro-operator-splitti.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all five claims on the paper's own Appendix H experimental instances at the authors' problem sizes and iteration budgets, with close quantitative matches to reported figures and direct tests of key theoretical assumptions. The reproduction is thorough, including multiple MC streams, bias-floor sweeps, matched controls, and ablations, though some caveats around exponential sample complexity and slow DRS convergence are honestly documented.

michaldobiezynski/repro-reinforcement-le.paper_title: Reinforcement Learning for Reachability: Guaranteeing Asymptotic Optimality

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes a PAC guarantee that, for a sufficiently small guessed minimum transition probability p_k, there exists a number of simulations N_k such that the learned policy is ε_k-optimal with probability at least 1-δ_k (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: On a 148-state netmaze MDP with p_min=1/64 (K_PAC=6), a from-scratch reimplementation of Algorithm 1 achieved 0/100 failures at every stage k>=6 for some budget c, consistent with the existential PAC guarantee; the logbook transparently acknowledges that 100 trials only yield a 95% upper bound of 0.030, which does not resolve delta_k<=0.0156, but the qualitative claim that some N_k achieves the guarantee is directly supported at every governed stage.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 shows that once the approximation error ε_k falls below a threshold ε_diff—the minimum value gap between optimal and suboptimal memoryless deterministic policies—any ε_k-optimal policy is guaranteed to be exactly optimal, not merely near-optimal (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive enumeration of all 32768 MD policies on the 148-state netmaze MDP yields eps_diff=4.127947e-02, and across 1515 live algorithm outputs at stages k>=6 (where eps_k < eps_diff), zero were merely near-optimal rather than exactly optimal—a strong, non-trivial, falsifiable test on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 proves that using a summable failure schedule δ_k = 1/2^k, the Borel-Cantelli lemma guarantees only finitely many stages fail, so the algorithm's policy is exactly optimal from some finite stage onward with probability 1 (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: On netmaze with 100 trials over 12 stages, the summed empirical failure probability 3.43 <= K_opt+1=7 as the theorem predicts, the mean number of failing stages per trial is 3.43 (max 4), and 0 failures occurred across all 600 stage-runs beyond K_opt=6; while the infinite-horizon almost-sure statement cannot be literally verified in 12 stages, every testable precondition and prediction is confirmed.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 bounds ε_diff via transition-complexity parameter D, showing ‖v_π − v_π'‖_1 ≥ (2D)^(-2|A|·|S|) 2^(-2|S|) for any two distinct memoryless deterministic policies, giving an explicit MDP-structure-dependent characterization of when exact optimality is reached (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The lower bound ||v_pi - v_pi'||_1 >= (2D)^(-2|A||S|) * 2^(-2|S|) was checked against exact value vectors on 7 MDPs (including exhaustive enumeration of all 32768 MD policies on netmaze) and held on every model; however, the bound values (10^-1336 to 10^-2549) are far below float64 minimum, giving 10^931 to 10^2545 of slack, so the inequality is structurally unfalsifiable at this scale—it is confirmed but not sharply tested.

claims.claim: Empirical evaluation on standardized benchmarks shows the algorithm's policy becomes exactly optimal at a median stage k=2, far earlier than the stage (k≈16) at which the theoretical worst-case value-bound guarantees convergence (empirical validation section).
claims.evidence: Only 2 of the paper's 9 QVBS benchmarks (IJ 3, IJ 10) were matched exactly; zeroconf and firewire are smaller from-scratch re-implementations, and netmaze/gridworld are not paper benchmarks; the measured median convergence stage is 2.5 (vs. paper's 2) at c=4.0 and 3.0 at c=0.5, with firewire never converging—direction and rough magnitude reproduce, but the exact claim on standardized benchmarks is not fully reproduced due to reduced scope and unspecified N_k constant.

michaldobiezynski/repro-reinforcement-le.overall: The logbook provides a from-scratch CPU reimplementation of Algorithm 1 with independent exact ground truth, yielding real experimental evidence supporting Theorems 3.1–3.3 and 4.1 on custom non-toy MDPs, though with acknowledged limitations in statistical power (Claim 1), discriminating power (Claim 4), and partial benchmark coverage (Claim 5). The theoretical claims are empirically supported, while the empirical convergence claim is only directionally reproduced on a reduced subset of benchmarks.

claims.claim: DC-LA is proven in Theorem 8 to satisfy a q-Wasserstein convergence bound of the form W_q(p_{X_{k+1}}, pi) <= A_lambda*rho_lambda^{k*gamma} + B_lambda*gamma^{1/2q} + C_lambda^{1/q}, decomposing discretization, smoothing, and algorithmic error terms, for all natural numbers q (Theorem 8).
claims.evidence: At d=100 on the paper's own l1-l2 target family (tau=10, non-log-concave with minimum curvature -5.61), all three terms of the bound were measured independently for q=1,2,3 against a 2×30000-sample RWM reference with reported Monte-Carlo floors: transient rho_lam=0.0039 (geometric), discretization slopes 0.81/0.79/0.77 vs required 0.50/0.25/0.17, smoothing slopes 1.03/1.03/0.93 vs required 1.00/0.50/0.33, and the re-assembled bound was never violated (max measured/bound ratio 0.90).

claims.claim: Convergence is established under a distant dissipativity assumption on the potential V (Assumption 2), which requires only quadratic growth away from the origin rather than global convexity.
claims.evidence: At d=200 on a non-convex potential (minimum Hessian eigenvalue -2.00, capped-l1 non-weakly-convex regularizer, 3^200 modes with exact i.i.d. ground truth), the dissipativity ratio was measured as an inequality: negative (-2.125) at separation 0.1, positive (+0.044) from R_0=2.0 onward, confirming distant dissipativity without global convexity; DC-LA then converged to W_1=0.0022 vs i.i.d. floor 0.0017 and binned KL=0.00017 nats.

claims.claim: DC-LA extends prior work (Renaud et al., 2025a) by handling non-weakly-convex difference-of-convex regularizers, such as the l1-l2 penalty, for which no previous convergence guarantee existed, while removing the earlier requirement of a convex modulus at infinity.
claims.evidence: The weak-convexity modulus of l1-l2 diverges as 1/t (log-log slope -1.00, reaching 10438 at t=1e-4) while the log-sum control saturates at 4.000; the convex modulus at infinity is negative at every radius (-1.00 at R=1 to -1e-3 at R=1e3), making Renaud et al.'s Assumption 3 unsatisfiable; and on the paper's own 12-configuration benchmark (5000 chains × 1000 steps, 4 samplers, binned KL), DC-LA achieved lowest KL in 12/12 configurations at 32 and 64 bins.

claims.claim: The algorithm applies separate Moreau envelope smoothing to the convex components r1 and r2 of the composite potential V = f + r1 - r2, yielding an update rule using proximal and gradient operators of the smoothed components.
claims.evidence: The gradient-of-Moreau-envelope identity grad M_lam^{r2}(x) = (x - Prox_{lam r2}(x))/lam was confirmed to 8.04e-10 against finite differences, and the Eq.(10) prox-of-Moreau identity matched brute-force grid minimization to 9.90e-03; the same unrolled Eqs (9)-(10) update step was used in all DC-LA runs for the other four claims, providing additional scale-level confirmation.

claims.claim: Section 5.2 applies DC-LA to 512x512 Computed Tomography reconstruction using a difference-of-ICNN prior, reporting competitive SSIM/PSNR versus optimization-based MAP methods along with posterior-variance-based uncertainty quantification (Section 5.2).
claims.evidence: The CT experiment was run at 192×192 (not 512×512) with a Shepp-Logan phantom (not Mayo-Clinic CT) and a difference-of-ICNN prior trained on only 32 synthetic phantoms for 250 CPU Adam steps; DC-LA's posterior mean SSIM was 0.5433 vs paper's 0.8493, the competitive ordering with MAP partially reproduced (0.5433 vs PSM 0.5568 at 500 iterations), but posterior-variance UQ did not reproduce (r=-0.006 over object support).

michaldobiezynski/repro-dc-la-difference.overall: This logbook provides strong, non-toy experimental evidence for Claims 1-4 at meaningful scale (d=100-200, exact ground truth, paper's own benchmark protocols) with careful attention to Monte-Carlo floors and stability checks, while Claim 5's CT experiment is a clearly reduced-scale proxy (192×192, synthetic prior, ~350× less sampling work) that partially reproduces the qualitative ordering but not the absolute numbers or the UQ component.

michaldobiezynski/repro-solving-imperfec.paper_title: Solving Imperfect-Recall Games via Sum-of-Squares Optimization

claims.claim: For single-player imperfect-recall extensive-form games (IREFGs), the Sum-of-Squares/moment hierarchy converges to the optimal utility u* as the relaxation degree d goes to infinity, i.e. lim_{d→∞} u^d_sos = lim_{d→∞} u^d_mom = u* (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: On 5 instances at the smallest supported scale (ℓ=2, 4 SDP variables), the SOS upper bound is monotone non-increasing across d=1,2,3 with gap shrinking from 2.70e+00 to 1.27e-07, but the asymptotic limit d→∞ is not testable with only three hierarchy levels, and u* is a heuristic PGD estimate rather than an exact value.

claims.claim: Under a genericity assumption on the utility function u, the SOS hierarchy for single-player IREFGs achieves finite convergence at some finite degree d ≥ d0, rather than only asymptotic convergence (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: All 12/12 instances (ℓ=2, 4 variables) achieve exactness (UB−u* < 5e-4) at a finite degree, with 10/12 at d0=Du/2, but genericity is only proxied by random sampling (not verified), the ground truth is heuristic PGD, and only two utility degrees (Du=4,6) at the smallest instance size are tested.

claims.claim: For single-player non-absentminded IREFGs, the degree-(ℓ+1) SOS relaxation is exact, i.e. a single semidefinite program at that level solves the game exactly (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Against brute-force enumeration ground truth, the degree-(ℓ+1)=3 SDP matches the exact pure-strategy optimum to 5.69e-08 mean error on 4 non-absentminded instances, but only ℓ=2 is tested and all instances are already exact at d=ℓ=2, so the specific contribution of degree ℓ+1 and the scaling with number of information sets are not isolated.

claims.claim: A Select-Verify-Cut framework extends the KKT-based moment-SOS hierarchy to multi-player IREFGs, yielding analogous finite-convergence and single-level-solvability guarantees under genericity and non-absentmindedness (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: Only the Select stage is implemented (Verify and Cut are absent), the 3 tested instances are plain 3×3 bimatrix games rather than imperfect-recall games, and 2 of 3 extracted profiles fail the Nash-equilibrium gap test by 1-2 orders of magnitude above tolerance, so the finite-convergence and single-level-solvability guarantees of Theorem 5.1 are not addressed.

claims.claim: Strictly concave/monotone single-player IREFGs are shown to admit finite SOS convergence, while SOS-concave/SOS-monotone IREFGs converge already at the first hierarchy level (Theorem 6.1).
claims.evidence: First-level exactness for SOS-concave IREFGs is confirmed to 7.24e-09 mean error against independent SLSQP ground truth on 4 instances (ℓ=3, 6 variables), but only 1 of the 4 theorem game classes (SOS-concave) is tested, in its most convex instantiation where level-1 exactness is near-automatic, and strictly-concave/monotone/SOS-monotone classes are not run.

claims.claim: In the empirical comparison of Table 1 (Section 7), the SOS approach consistently recovers certified global optima across tested instances, whereas projected gradient descent only succeeds probabilistically, with reported success rates in the 70-89% range.
claims.evidence: The SOS half reproduces (18/18 instances certified, all at DSOS=Du) but only 1 of the paper's 7 Table-1 rows (ℓ=2, Du=4) was completed; the PGD half does not match quantitatively (measured 65.3-65.5% vs paper's 80.72% for this row, below the claimed 70-89% band), though unspecified PGD hyperparameters may explain the gap.

michaldobiezynski/repro-solving-imperfec.overall: This logbook provides real numerical evidence from a from-scratch Moment-SOS hierarchy implementation, but consistently at the smallest supported scale (ℓ=2-3, 4-6 variables) with mostly heuristic ground truth, confirming directional trends for Claims 1-3 and 5-6 while leaving Claim 4 largely unimplemented. The strongest results are Claims 3 and 5 where independent/exact ground truth is used, but even these test only one parameter setting or one game class.

michaldobiezynski/repro-upper-linearizab.paper_title: Upper-Linearizability of Online Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization over Down-Closed Convex Sets

claims.claim: Theorem 1 proves that non-monotone DR-submodular functions over down-closed convex sets are 1/e-Upper-Linearizable via the exponential reparameterization h(x) = 1 - e^{-x} combined with a designed surrogate potential.
claims.evidence: The 1/e-upper-linearizability inequality was checked over 1,536,000 (x,y) pairs from 16 random non-monotone DR-submodular quadratics at d=100 on a 25-knapsack polytope, with max violation -56.28 (≤0), confirming the inequality holds; the ablation replacing h(x) with x/2 drops the supported alpha from 0.7199 to 0.3764, showing the check is sensitive to the reparametrization choice.

claims.claim: The BQND algorithm (Algorithm 1) reduces online non-monotone DR-submodular maximization to online linear optimization using a single gradient query per round.
claims.evidence: Query count equals T exactly at all 7 horizons (T=2048..131072), directly confirming one gradient query per round; the BQND estimator's MC error converges at exponent -0.555 (theory -0.5) and the B1 bound holds (sup||g||=269.50 vs B1=286.87), both measured at d=100 on a 25-knapsack polytope.

claims.claim: Proposition 1 shows BQND obtains O(T^{1/2}) static regret with only O(1) oracle queries per round, improving on prior work's O(T^{2/3}) regret for single queries or O(T^{1/2}) regret requiring T^{3/2} queries per round.
claims.evidence: R_lin/sqrt(T) is flat at 667.45-676.52 across a 64x horizon range (T=2048..131072) with log-log slopes of 0.500-0.505, and query count equals T exactly at every horizon, confirming O(T^{1/2}) surrogate-linear regret at O(1) queries per round on a d=100, 25-knapsack setup.

claims.claim: Proposition 3 establishes a dynamic regret bound of Õ(T^{1/2}·√(1+P_T)) where P_T is the path length of the comparator sequence.
claims.evidence: While DR/sqrt(T(1+P_T)) is decreasing in both path-length regimes (consistent with the upper bound holding), the measured regret exponent is nearly identical across regimes with very different P_T scaling (0.594 vs 0.600), so the specific P_T-dependent content of Proposition 3 is not distinguished from a generic O(sqrt(T)) rate.

claims.claim: In the bandit feedback model, the framework achieves O(T^{4/5}) regret (Proposition 6), and in the semi-bandit model O(T^{2/3}) regret (Proposition 4).
claims.evidence: The semi-bandit O(T^{2/3}) rate is verified at the main d=100 scale (exponent 0.645, E(T)/T^{2/3} flat), but the bandit O(T^{4/5}) rate is only verified after dropping to d=10 with 4 constraints (exponent 0.636, E(T)/T^{4/5} decreasing); at d=100 the bandit exponent is 0.947, above the claimed 0.800, attributed to pre-asymptotic behavior.

michaldobiezynski/repro-upper-linearizab.overall: The logbook provides a from-scratch numerical audit of all five claims on synthetic non-monotone DR-submodular quadratics, with Claims 2 and 3 strongly verified at the main d=100 scale, Claim 1 verified as a structural check, Claim 4 inconclusive due to inability to distinguish P_T-dependence, and Claim 5 only partially verified at main scale with the bandit rate requiring a reduced d=10 setup.

michaldobiezynski/repro-strategic-candid.paper_title: Strategic Candidacy in Generative AI Arenas

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 shows that under the status-quo Bradley-Terry MLE ranking mechanism, producers can gain utility by submitting multiple clones of an (epsilon,delta)-competitive model, driven by a 'lottery ticket effect' from independent vote draws (Theorem 3.1, Definition 3.1).
claims.evidence: On real Arena data across all 4 reconstructed arenas at full scale (m=240-242, s=17-104), 20/20 (eps=0.1, delta=0.05)-competitive models showed strictly positive expected utility gain from one clone (19/20 at >2 MC SE), and the competing new-competitor effect stayed an order of magnitude below the lottery-ticket gain, with rank gains growing monotonically as s falls — exactly the finite-sample signature Theorem 3.1 predicts.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves the You-Rank-We-Rank (YRWR) mechanism is O(1/sqrt(s))-strategyproof, bounding the utility gain from submitting multiple copies versus a single model per producer, where s is the number of votes/models (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: On the Text arena with real BT-MLE, |Delta_YRWR|*sqrt(s) stayed bounded at max 0.013 across s=16..1024, consistent with the O(1/sqrt(s)) upper bound, while the same deviations under SQ yielded gains an order of magnitude larger (Delta_SQ*sqrt(s) up to 1.375). Coverage is thin (1 arena, 2 producers, 2 deviations) and the signal never cleared the MC noise floor, but the upper bound is consistently satisfied on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.1 shows that under truthful producer rankings, YRWR reduces l-infinity ranking error relative to the status-quo mechanism (Proposition 4.1).
claims.evidence: Using genuine damped-Newton BT-MLE on real Arena instances (Text m=242 s=104, Coding m=241 s=22), the inequality ||Rtilde-R||_inf <= ||Rhat-R||_inf held in all 400 realisations (0 violations), with a non-trivial ~1.1-1.2% mean l-infinity error reduction under truthful producer rankings.

claims.claim: The Uncertainty-Aware YRWR variant (UA-YRWR) ignores producer-submitted rankings when confidence intervals overlap, maintaining O(1/sqrt(s))-robustness with tolerance epsilon+alpha (Section 4.4).
claims.evidence: On the Coding arena with real BT-MLE and Bonferroni CIs, UA-YRWR's Kendall-Tau distance to the true ranking under adversarial producer rankings collapsed from 1146 to 15 as s grew from 32 to 32768, while plain YRWR stayed pinned above 11000, and sqrt(s)*||Rtilde_UA-R||_inf stayed bounded (1.29-1.67). The eps+alpha robustness sub-claim (Cor 4.6) was satisfied but the test is near-circular as constructed; the asymptotic correctness and sqrt(s)-consistency parts (Prop 4.7) are strongly supported.

claims.claim: Simulations calibrated to Arena data show YRWR reduces clone-induced rank gains to near-zero while improving Kendall-Tau distance to the ground-truth ranking, even under moderately noisy producer-reported rankings (Section 4.6).
claims.evidence: Across all 4 reconstructed arenas on real Arena data, YRWR's clone-induced rank gain stayed near zero (max 0.91-1.62 across clone counts) versus SQ's 2.16-4.12, the Kendall-Tau advantage of YRWR over SQ was strictly positive on every arena and clone count (tens of swaps), and the noise-tolerance crossover occurred at KT(pi~,pi*) on the order of m, matching the paper's claim.

michaldobiezynski/repro-strategic-candid.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence on real Chatbot Arena data at full scale (m~240-242, 43-44 producers, genuine damped-Newton BT-MLE) supporting all five claims, with the main systematic limitation being use of the public 2025-08-29 snapshot (m~241) instead of the paper's non-public 2026-01-01 snapshot (~300 models), which attenuates absolute SQ rank-gain magnitudes but preserves all directions, rates, and qualitative structures. Coverage is comprehensive for Claims 1 and 5 (all 4 arenas) but thinner for Claims 2 and 4 (1 arena, few producers/deviations).

claims.claim: Three single-loop projection-free algorithms are proposed for constrained minimax problems: a fully LMO-based method (Algorithm 1, LMO-LMO), a hybrid LMO-PO method (Algorithm 2), and a hybrid PO-LMO method (Algorithm 3), each avoiding at least one projection step via a dual dynamic smoothing framework (Section 2-4).
claims.evidence: All three algorithms were re-implemented from scratch and run at paper-scale dictionary learning (66,000 primal dimensions, 3 seeds); oracle-call telemetry confirms the exact projection-avoidance pattern (Alg.1: PO_X=PO_Y=0; Alg.2: PO_X=0; Alg.3: PO_Y=0), and a smoothing ablation on a synthetic NC-C instance shows removing the dynamic schedule stalls Alg.1 (slope -0.0007 vs -0.5877 with smoothing), independently confirming the smoothing framework is load-bearing.

claims.claim: For the nonconvex-concave setting, the algorithm attains an O(T^{-1/6}) stationarity rate in general and an O(T^{-1/4}) rate when the dual objective is strongly concave (Theorem 2.1).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 was run on a synthetic max-of-quadratics minimax instance (d=200, T=1e6, 3 seeds) for both NC-C and NC-SC; the certificate c(T)=avgG·T^{exponent} stays bounded and monotonically decreasing in all cases (NC-C: 25.5→1.95; NC-SC: 36→2.3), confirming the O(T^{-1/6}) and O(T^{-1/4}) bounds are not violated over three decades of T.

claims.claim: For the convex-concave setting, the primal optimality gap converges at O(T^{-1/5}) in general and at the improved rate Õ(T^{-1/3}) when the dual is strongly concave (Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 on a synthetic convex instance (rho=0, T=1e6, 3 seeds) with f* independently bracketed via FISTA (bracket 50x tighter than measured gap); the C-C certificate c(T)=G_Opt·T^{1/5} is bounded and decreasing (0.995→0.0424) with a late-horizon slope of -0.244 (within 22% of theory's -0.200), and the C-SC certificate c(T)=G_Opt·T^{1/3} is likewise bounded (0.502→1.81e-05).

claims.claim: The algorithms provide anytime convergence guarantees, meaning the stated rates hold at every iteration without needing to fix the total iteration horizon T in advance (Section 1.2).
claims.evidence: The anytime property was tested only on the NC-C setting (1 of 4 theoretical regimes), only Algorithm 1 (1 of 3), a single seed, and against a surrogate comparator (Alg.1 with frozen parameters rather than the actual R-PDCG baseline); the test is genuine and not falsified (anytime certificate bounded 27.4→2.03 while 2 of 3 frozen schedules blow up), but the scope is clearly reduced relative to the full claim.

claims.claim: Numerical experiments on dictionary learning (nonconvex-concave) and robust multiclass classification on RCV1 and NEWS20 (convex-concave) show the hybrid LMO-PO variant converges fastest, with the fully projection-free LMO-LMO variant outperforming prior projection-free baselines such as R-PDCG and CG-RPGA (Section 5).
