claims.evidence: RCV1 was never run, R-PDCG was omitted from NEWS20, baselines were surrogates rather than published implementations, compute budget was cut 8-12x (25-60s vs 300s), and the dictionary-learning geometric-mean aggregate is corrupted by sub-machine-precision tail values including a negative number; the face-value rankings contradict the paper (LMO-PO fastest on 0/3 seeds, SP-FW fastest on NEWS20) but the setup departs too far from the paper's protocol to adjudicate.

michaldobiezynski/repro-projection-free-.overall: The logbook provides solid independent evidence for the theoretical contributions: the three-algorithm structure is confirmed by oracle telemetry and a smoothing ablation at paper scale, and both convergence-rate theorems pass a bounded-certificate test over three decades of T with 3 seeds (C-C fit within 22% of the claimed exponent). The anytime property is only narrowly tested, and the Section 5 experimental ranking is unresolved due to missing datasets/baselines, surrogate comparators, and a severely reduced compute budget.

michaldobiezynski/repro-belief-propagati.paper_title: Belief Propagation Converges to Gaussian Distributions in Sparsely-Connected Factor Graphs

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that variables in pairwise chain factor graphs develop increasingly Gaussian-distributed beliefs as topological distance from prior factors increases, driven by repeated convolution via the Central Limit Theorem (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Log-log slopes measured at k3=-0.4988, k4=-0.9999, D_KL=-1.0015 over N=1000..10000 across 8 seeds on a growing lattice with no truncation, matching the theoretical rates of -0.500/-1.000/-1.000 to three decimals; a heterogeneous-chain run decays faster, consistent with the bound.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 extends the Gaussian convergence result to tree-topology factor graphs, provided the message non-Gaussianity ε satisfies ε² ≪ ε with increasing distance from the nearest prior factor (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: On a degree-3 branching tree spine (d=1..10000, 6 seeds), D_KL falls monotonically from 2.07e-02 to 1.18e-06 and the Lemma 4.3 condition was checked directly: resid/eps² decreases from 0.1229 to 0.0535 as eps falls, confirming eps²≪eps holds at every branching node; the paper states no rate for trees, only that convergence occurs.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.5 uses computation-tree equivalence to show loopy factor graphs exhibit the same Gaussian convergence mechanism as tree graphs under identical assumptions (Theorem 4.5).
claims.evidence: The computation-tree equivalence is exact to float64 round-off (max|Δ|=6.9e-17) but only on tiny instances (16-variable grid, 3-variable cycle, T≤6); the Gaussian-emergence half used a single 64x64 loopy topology where D_KL plateaus at 2.06e-03 after 2-3 hops and |k4_hat| never decays (0.253→0.272), only partially supporting 'the same convergence mechanism as tree graphs.'

claims.claim: Lemma 4.2 identifies an 'exclusion zone' in which non-Gaussian prior factors prevent Gaussian convergence when the prior-to-pairwise variance ratio R is less than or equal to approximately 6 (Lemma 4.2).
claims.evidence: Solving Eq (28) numerically gives R*=6.0168 matching the paper's R~6, and a dominance criterion evaluated on the measured BP fixed point (10 seeds, 8192-bin lattice, R swept 0.019–179.9) flips sign at R=6.316 vs analytic 6.017 (5% agreement); the physical D_KL crossing at R=2.17 is consistent with the paper's own stated conservatism.

claims.claim: Figure 4 shows all tested topologies reach a KL divergence below 0.02 within 3 hops from prior factors, and that higher node degree increases non-Gaussianity in star graphs while weaker priors enable faster Gaussian emergence (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Sub-claims (a) and (b) reproduce quantitatively (all topologies below D_KL=0.02 at 3 hops: chain 0.0012, tree 0.0006, grid 0.0019; star-graph degree effect r=+0.998), but sub-claim (c) fails under the paper's own Appendix-I lattice settings (D_KL non-monotone, never crosses 0.02) and only reproduces after switching to an untruncated 1024-bin lattice; topologies are small (13–127 variables).

claims.claim: Figure 5 applies the theory to stereo depth estimation belief propagation, showing Gaussian convergence in textureless image regions while non-Gaussian beliefs persist at high-contrast edges (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: On the real Middlebury 2003 Cones stereo pair (30000 variables, 250 BP iterations), textureless-quintile median D_KL=0.0136 (below 0.02) vs high-contrast-quintile median D_KL=0.0322 (above 0.02), a 2.4x gap with gradient/D_KL correlation rho=+0.33, directly supporting the claimed spatial split at the paper's own threshold.

michaldobiezynski/repro-belief-propagati.overall: The logbook provides strong quantitative evidence for the paper's core theoretical results: chain convergence rates match to three decimals (Claim 1), the tree extension and its eps²≪eps condition are directly verified (Claim 2), the R≈6 exclusion-zone boundary is recovered from simulation (Claim 4), and the stereo-depth application reproduces the Gaussian/non-Gaussian spatial split on real data (Claim 6). Two claims are only partially supported: the loopy-graph theorem is confirmed structurally but on tiny instances with a single emergence topology that plateaus (Claim 3), and one of three Figure-4 sub-claims fails under the paper's own lattice settings (Claim 5).

snaykey/repro-noneuclidean-gd-eos.paper_title: Non-Euclidean Gradient Descent Operates at the Edge of Stability

claims.claim: Directional smoothness D is defined so that, for non-Euclidean gradient descent with step size eta, the loss decreases if and only if D <= 2/eta (Definition 2.1).
claims.evidence: On full-batch CIFAR-10-5k MLP training (float64), the iff ΔL≤0 ⇔ D≤2/η holds at 100% of steps for both ℓ₂ and ℓ∞ geometries, and D computed from its definition (eq. 5) matches D from the identity (eq. 6) to max relative gap 4.4e-10, confirming the directional smoothness identity on real neural-network trajectories.

claims.claim: Generalized sharpness S is defined as the maximum of d^T times the Hessian of the loss times d subject to the norm of d being at most 1 under an arbitrary norm, generalizing the largest-eigenvalue sharpness used for vanilla gradient descent (Definition 2.2).
claims.evidence: The generalized sharpness definition is validated against exact references across three geometries: ℓ₂ power iteration matches eigh λ_max to ≤1e-11, ℓ∞ Frank–Wolfe matches brute-force Ising ground state to ≤1.9e-16, and spectral Frank–Wolfe matches exact ‖A‖_*² to ≤8.6e-16, with the ℓ₂⊆ℓ∞ containment inequality S_ℓ∞≥S_ℓ₂ confirmed.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 proves non-Euclidean gradient descent on quadratic objectives converges linearly when the step size eta < 2/S, where S is the generalized sharpness (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: All 25 quadratic runs with η=frac·2/S (frac∈{0.3,…,0.99}) across ℓ₂ (dims 10–100) and ℓ∞ (dims 10–16) geometries converge linearly (L_end/L₀≈1e-24), with empirical contraction rates increasing toward 1 as η→2/S, using exact S (eigh or brute-force Ising).

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 proves divergence occurs from some initialization when eta > 2/S for non-Euclidean gradient descent on quadratics (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Lemma 5.3's invariant direction (H d̂)*=d̂ holds to ≤2.8e-16 across ℓ₂ and ℓ∞ geometries, and the invariant-line dynamics w_t=(1−ηS)^t w₀ are reproduced exactly: η=1.5·2/S gives |1−ηS|=2 and ‖w_T‖/‖w₀‖=1.2e+18 (divergence), while η=0.5·2/S gives convergence to ≈0.

claims.claim: Experiments show l-infinity-descent on CIFAR-10 and Tiny Shakespeare exhibits generalized sharpness stabilizing slightly above the 2/eta threshold, unlike vanilla GD which stabilizes at 2/eta (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: On full-batch CIFAR-10-5k MLP and Tiny Shakespeare transformer, ℓ∞-descent generalized sharpness plateaus at S/(2/η)=1.06–1.44 (above threshold) while vanilla GD plateaus at 1.04–1.1 (at threshold), with a negative control at small step size showing no EoS (max S/(2/η)=0.419), reproducing the qualitative at-vs-above contrast across two datasets and two architectures.

claims.claim: SignGD and Muon (without momentum) are shown to exhibit normalized sharpness converging near the 2/eta edge-of-stability threshold, extending the phenomenon to optimizers used in practice (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: On full-batch CIFAR-10-5k MLP, SignGD normalized sharpness plateaus at S̃/(2/η)=1.25–1.41 and Muon-without-momentum at 0.945–0.96, both in the neighborhood of the 2/η threshold across multiple step sizes, with representative trajectories showing convergence toward the threshold from both sides.

snaykey/repro-noneuclidean-gd-eos.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all six claims: theoretical claims (1–4) are verified to machine precision against exact references on quadratic and real NN setups, and the neural-network EoS claims (5–6) are reproduced on real full-batch training of MLPs and transformers with appropriate negative controls. The main limitation is sub-sampled datasets and modest networks for the NN claims, but the qualitative phenomena are robust across step sizes, seeds, and architectures.

snaykey/repro-convex-distance-ot.paper_title: Convex Distance Operator Transport: A Convex and Geometry-Preserving Formulation

claims.claim: CDOT formulates cross-domain distribution alignment as a convex quadratic program over transport polytopes, with Theorem 3.4 establishing existence of an optimal coupling and convexity of the objective (Theorem 3.4).
claims.evidence: The logbook computes the analytic Hessian H = 2n_X n_Y M^T M on 120 random mm-space pairs and finds it PSD (min eigenvalue ratio +4.30e-14) on all instances, verifies midpoint convexity on 400 random configs (worst value -3.67e-6 ≤ 0), and shows FW converges to a single optimum from 20 random inits (spread 3.5e-7), with a GW negative control failing all three tests.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 proves the CDOT discrepancy is a valid pseudometric on attributed compact metric-measure spaces, while Theorem 3.7 derives a 'dispersion gap' relating CDOT to Gromov-Wasserstein via ℛ_GW,2(π) − ℛ(π) = 𝒱(π) (Theorem 3.5, Theorem 3.7).
claims.evidence: The dispersion gap identity R_GW,2(π) - R(π) = V(π) is verified to worst relative error 2.71e-15 across n=10,30,60,100, with an independent cross-check of the Γ-form vs operator-commutator form to 7e-16. All four pseudometric axioms are tested across hundreds of instances with 0 triangle-inequality violations (min slack 0.413), identity to 9.67e-9, and symmetry to 1.16e-15.

claims.claim: On synthetic 2D clustered point clouds with n=500 samples, CDOT achieves a matching MSE of 0.0016±0.00, lower than both FGW (0.0034±0.00) and IsoRank (0.0033±0.00) (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The claim specifies n=500 (N=2000), but the reproduction only runs n=100, 200, 300 due to CPU budget. While the same protocol is used and CDOT is lowest at every tested n with values matching the paper within ~5%, the specific n=500 headline row is not directly tested; the trend is extrapolated rather than measured.

claims.claim: On the OASIS-3 brain connectome dataset (696 subjects, 170-node networks), CDOT attains 0.6136 matching accuracy under diffusion distance versus 0.1853 for FGW, though FGW outperforms CDOT under geodesic distance (0.5375 vs 0.4640) (Table 3).
claims.evidence: Real OASIS-3 is DUA-gated and replaced with a synthetic 170-node connectome proxy using only 12 subjects (vs 696 in the paper). The primary diffusion-distance finding (CDOT 0.695 > FGW 0.458) is reproduced, but the secondary geodesic reversal (FGW > CDOT) is not reproduced on the synthetic data, and the dataset is synthetic at drastically reduced subject count.

claims.claim: On TUDataset graph classification benchmarks, CDOT outperforms FGW on MUTAG (0.8617±0.07 vs 0.8249±0.08) and ENZYMES (0.5133±0.04 vs 0.4450±0.03) using an RBF-kernel SVM with 10-fold cross-validation (Table 4).
claims.evidence: Only MUTAG is addressed, on a 90-graph subsample (vs 188 in the paper), yielding CDOT 0.778±0.157 vs FGW 0.756±0.130 — the direction is reproduced but absolute accuracies are substantially below the paper's values. ENZYMES (the second half of the claim) is not run at all due to CPU budget, leaving half the claim unaddressed.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.6 gives a non-asymptotic risk bound decomposing into an O(1/T) optimization error and a statistical error term, with Corollary 5.7 establishing asymptotic consistency under Frank-Wolfe optimization (Theorem 5.6, Corollary 5.7).
claims.evidence: The FW optimization gap is measured at T=2 through 1280 on an n=80 instance; the paper's explicit bound 32α·n_min/(T+3) holds at every T, and the gap decays with log-log slope -1.88 (at least as fast as O(1/T)). Statistical consistency is shown by monotone decrease of sampling error as N grows from 40 to 640, providing concrete numerical evidence for both the non-asymptotic bound and the consistency corollary.

snaykey/repro-convex-distance-ot.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical verification of the three theoretical claims (convexity/PSD Hessian, pseudometric/dispersion-gap identity, O(1/T) convergence) with matched GW negative controls and hundreds of test instances. The three empirical claims are only partially reproduced at reduced scale or on synthetic proxies due to CPU and data-access constraints, with the specific headline configurations (n=500, real OASIS-3, full MUTAG+ENZYMES) not directly tested.

Srishti280992/repro-a-fully-first-order-.paper_title: A Fully First-Order Layer for Differentiable Optimization

claims.claim: FFOLayer computes an ε-approximate hypergradient using an active-set Lagrangian oracle that requires no Hessian evaluations, achieving Õ(1) first-order oracle calls per hypergradient estimate (Section 4.2, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: On active-set QPs with d up to 200 and up to 806 total inequalities, the FFO hypergradient matched exact implicit differentiation with max L∞ error 3.41e-10 and cosine 1.0, using exactly 2 solves and 2 first-order gradient evaluations per estimate with zero Hessian/Jacobian evaluations; a non-quadratic equality problem confirmed O(δ) error scaling (log-log slope 1.031).

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves that the 'ghost bilevel optimization' reformulation, which treats active constraints as equalities, preserves the accuracy of the hypergradient computed at the original constrained-optimization solution (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The code computes 'original' and 'ghost' hypergradients identically—both call exact_hypergradient(prob, x) with no extra_equalities—so the reported max error of 0.0 is tautological. The negative control (forcing an inactive constraint active) is meaningful but only shows wrong active-set identification fails, not that the ghost reformulation preserves the hypergradient versus the full inequality-constrained solution.

claims.claim: For constrained bilevel optimization, the method achieves an oracle complexity of Õ(δ⁻¹ε⁻³), matching best-known rates for non-smooth non-convex optimization, while extending prior guarantees from linear to general convex constraints (Section 4, complexity analysis).
claims.evidence: The Õ(δ⁻¹ε⁻³) oracle complexity is neither rederived nor empirically validated; the timing audit measures wall-clock solve times on small CPU problems with highly erratic speedups (3.6× to 134.8×) and does not count oracle calls or measure convergence to a target accuracy.

claims.claim: On synthetic decision-focused-learning QP tasks and 9×9 Sudoku constraint-learning tasks formulated as linear programs, FFOLayer matches the convergence of exact differentiable-optimization solvers CvxpyLayer and qpth while using a substantially faster backward pass (Experiments section, synthetic QP and Sudoku benchmarks).
claims.evidence: The QP training uses a small problem (d=36, nx=10, 60 steps, 3 seeds) comparing 'exact' vs 'FFO' but does not use CvxpyLayer or qpth as the claim requires; the Sudoku test is a single gradient-direction check on the 729-variable equality polytope, not a full LP training run. The logbook explicitly states these are scaled proxies.

claims.claim: FFOLayer's PyTorch implementation is objective-agnostic, exposing task-loss influence via a single detached gradient coefficient c := detach(dF/dy*), allowing users to substitute it for CvxpyLayer with minimal code changes (Section on practical implementation).
claims.evidence: The surrogate comparison is tautological (original = direct_x + dy.T @ c vs surrogate = direct_x + dy.T @ c.copy(), yielding error 0.0 by construction); the FFO check across 5 objectives on a small problem (d=28) shows the detached-coefficient math works (max error 2.63e-11), but the actual PyTorch implementation and CvxpyLayer-substitutability claim are never tested.

claims.claim: FFOLayer outperforms the gradient-unrolling baseline LPGD in the reported experiments while eliminating the cubic-complexity Hessian inversion required by standard implicit differentiation (Experiments section, comparison with LPGD).
claims.evidence: A custom finite-difference-through-unrolling proxy for LPGD on a small problem (d=70, nx=9) shows FFO is more accurate (L2 error 1.07e-10 vs 0.065 for 200-step LPGD), but the FFO timing (0.021ms) measures only vector ops after the solve, not the full backward pass, and the logbook acknowledges it is not the paper's LPGD training curve.

Srishti280992/repro-a-fully-first-order-.overall: The logbook provides solid independent verification of the core FFO oracle mechanism (Claim 1) on non-trivial QPs, but the ghost-reformulation test (Claim 2) is tautological, the complexity claim (Claim 3) is not empirically validated, and the benchmark claims (Claims 4, 5, 6) are only addressed on reduced-scale proxies without the paper's actual baselines (CvxpyLayer, qpth, LPGD).

michaldobiezynski/repro-online-social-we.paper_title: Online Social Welfare Function-based Resource Allocation

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows that monotonicity of the social welfare function alone suffices to lift coordinate-wise anytime-valid confidence sequences on individual utilities into a valid confidence sequence for the optimal social welfare M(mu ⊙ p*) (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Sandwich inequality tested with zero violations over 12,000 random triples and 6,000,000 live SWF-UCB rounds (n=50–200, T=10,000, 600 trajectories), with lifted-CS miscoverage 0/200 at nominal δ=0.1 for WPM, Kolm, and Gini — concrete evidence on a non-toy setup supporting the theorem's lifting mechanism.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 establishes that SWF-UCB attains regret R(T) = O(L(n + sqrt(nkT))) with probability 1-delta (up to polylog log log T and log(2n/delta) factors), matching lower bounds up to polylogarithmic terms (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Upper bound checked on 120 trajectories at T=4.096M (max ratio 0.011 with leading constant 1, ~100x headroom, exponents ≤0.51), but the 'matching lower bounds' minimax half is not tested, only a single n=50 instance is used (n-dependence untested), and the loose headroom makes the upper-bound check a sanity check rather than a tight confirmation.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 provides efficient policy oracles per SWF family: an O(n log n) water-filling solution for the Weighted Power Mean and Kolm families, and an O(kn) greedy block algorithm for the Gini family (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: Oracle exactness confirmed to ≤1.6e-15 relative gap over 450 instances cross-checked against CLARABEL and HiGHS, and complexity timed to n=262,144 with log-log exponents matching predictions (WPM 1.112 vs 1.091, Kolm 1.083, Gini 1.104; Gini k-scaling confirms Θ(k) block iterations and 1.944 exponent vs 2.0 for O(kn)).

claims.claim: Experiments across the Weighted Power Mean, Kolm, and Gini social welfare families show consistent sqrt(T) regret scaling, but regret depends non-monotonically on the resource budget k, peaking at intermediate k values (Section 6).
claims.evidence: Non-monotone-in-k reproduced in 7/7 SWF configurations with interior peaks (egalitarian peaks at k=20 matching the paper) and R(k=n)=0 in all configurations; R(T)/√T bounded (max ratio 1.261 over 3.5 decades) across all families at T=4.096M with 2100 trajectories for the k-sweep.

claims.claim: Allocation feasibility under the cardinality constraint |S_t|=k is enforced via dependent rounding that preserves the marginal selection probabilities P(i in S_t) = p_{t,i} (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Dependent rounding applied to 10 real oracle-produced allocation vectors with 2,000,000 draws each (20M total): 0 cardinality violations, max marginal deviation 9.04e-4, max z-score 2.83 (within null expectation for 500 coordinates), confirming P(i∈S_t)=p_{t,i} preservation.

michaldobiezynski/repro-online-social-we.overall: This logbook provides strong numerical evidence for the algorithmic claims (Theorem 5.1 oracles, dependent rounding) and the experimental claims (non-monotone k-dependence, bounded √T regret), all tested at substantial scale (n up to 262K, T up to 4M, 20M rounding draws). The regret upper bound (Theorem 5.2) is only loosely checked with ~100x headroom and its minimax lower-bound matching is unaddressed, making that claim a partial test.

michaldobiezynski/repro-high-dimensional.paper_title: High-Dimensional Learning Dynamics of Quantized Models with Straight-Through Estimator

claims.claim: In the high-dimensional limit, the microscopic dynamics of straight-through estimator (STE) training converge to a stochastic differential equation governed by Eq. (15) (Section IV, Theorem IV.3).
claims.evidence: A quantitative Wasserstein-1 distance test between STE coordinate laws and the SDE law at d=750 and d=3000 shows mean W1 shrinking from 0.0065 to 0.0024, with the d=3000 residual below the sampling floor (0.0076) and moments tracking to 4 significant figures — concrete convergence evidence at the paper's own Fig. 1 scale.

claims.claim: The macroscopic summary statistics of STE training concentrate onto a deterministic ODE trajectory (Eqs. (24)-(25)) with concentration rate O_d(d^{-1/2}) as dimension d grows (Section V-B, Theorem V.3).
claims.evidence: The exact d^{-1/2} rate with flat C(d)≈0.52 holds only in setting (a) where weights are unquantized (psi_w=identity); in the faithful weight-quantized setting (b, the paper's Fig. 2 config), the slope degrades to -0.408 and C(d) grows from 1.12 to 1.50 with a persistent d-independent bias of ~0.02, so the concentration claim is neither confirmed nor refuted in the intended regime.

claims.claim: STE training exhibits an extended plateau followed by a sharp drop in generalization error across bit-widths b in {2,3,4,5}, with the plateau length depending on the quantization range ω (Section VI-A1/VI-A2, Figures 2-3).
claims.evidence: At d=900 with 5 independent STE runs, plateau-then-drop in eps_g is present for all bit-widths b∈{2,3,4,5} with monotone-decreasing floors (0.5027>0.2782>0.2563>0.2523) matching closed-form predictions to within 2.5%, and the omega sweep at b=3 covers all five named omega values showing the claimed dependence.

claims.claim: For input-only quantization, a closed-form stable fixed point exists under the learning-rate condition 0 < η < 2(σ_ψ^2 + λ)/σ_ψ^4 (Section VI-C1, Proposition VI.1).
claims.evidence: The 1e-10-level agreement in the Jacobian sweep (a) is algebraic self-consistency against the paper's own ODEs; the genuinely independent finite-d test (b) at d=1000 confirms the threshold to within 4% but the stability sign criterion fails in 4 of 16 configurations near r=0.9, and steady-state agreement (c) at d=1200 is within 1% — partial finite-d confirmation with material gaps, not a full reproduction.

claims.claim: The asymptotic deviation of the STE-trained quantized model from the unquantized linear model is characterized across three regimes, with a leading-order correction term of size O_Δ(Δ^2) depending on the fractional quantization level position (Section VI-C2, Theorem VI.3).
claims.evidence: The headline results (slope exactly 2.0000, ratios 1.0000, worst error 7.7e-8) come from solving the paper's own fixed-point equations and comparing to its own closed-form expansion — an algebraic self-consistency check; Regime II is visited 0/234 times in the systematic sweep, the paper's Fig. 6 STE simulation (d=100, tau to 8e6) was never executed, and the only finite-d evidence is recycled d=900 floors from Claim 3 agreeing to within 3.1%.

michaldobiezynski/repro-high-dimensional.overall: The logbook provides solid quantitative evidence for the microscopic SDE convergence (Claim 1) and the plateau-then-drop phenomenology (Claim 3) at the paper's own scale, but the concentration-rate claim (Claim 2) is inconclusive in the weight-quantized regime, and the two closed-form asymptotic results (Claims 4–5) are primarily validated as algebraic self-consistency checks with only thin and partially failing finite-d evidence.

michaldobiezynski/repro-natural-hypergra.paper_title: Natural Hypergradient Descent:  Algorithm Design, Convergence Analysis, and Parallel Implementation

claims.claim: NHGD approximates the Hessian inverse in bilevel optimization using the empirical Fisher information matrix, updated via the Sherman-Morrison formula from stochastic gradients already computed during inner-loop SGD, enabling parallel rather than sequential computation (Section on algorithm design).
claims.evidence: The Sherman-Morrison EFIM update matches brute-force inversion to 4.9e-14 relative error, uses exactly 3000 gradient oracle calls for 3000 SGD+EFIM steps (zero extra gradients), scales as d^2.03 vs d^2.78 for explicit inversion matching the O(d^2)/O(d^3) claim, and produces bit-identical parallel-vs-serial hypergradients (0.000e+00 difference) with 47.7% of Hessian-inverse work hidden; corroborated at paper-scale d_theta=12801 in the PDE run.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.7 establishes a high-probability error bound on the Hessian-inverse approximation, ‖A_k^T − H(θ*(v_k))^{-1}‖ = O((1/√T)·√(1+log((1+T)/δ))), for T inner iterations with probability at least 1−δ (Theorem 4.7).
claims.evidence: Across 24 independent runs to T=100,000, the measured asymptotic log-log slopes (-0.458 and -0.528) bracket the theory-implied slopes (-0.462, -0.465) within 0.07, and across 160 runs at T=10,000 the delta-dependence fits the predicted sqrt(1+log((1+T)/delta)) shape with R²=0.993, directly confirming both the T^{-1/2} rate and the high-probability tail form.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.10 shows NHGD attains an ε-stationary point with overall sample complexity Õ(ε⁻²) using T = O(ε⁻¹ log(δ⁻¹ε⁻¹)) inner iterations and K = O(ε⁻¹) outer iterations, matching the sample complexity of optimize-then-approximate methods such as stocBiO and AmIGO while reducing computational overhead (Theorem 4.10, Table 1).
claims.evidence: On a small synthetic bilevel problem (d_theta=192), NHGD meets the ε-stationarity criterion at all six tested ε values with slopes matching stocBiO/AmIGO, but the slope agreement is largely tautological (T and K are set directly from the theorem's formulas) and a frozen-T control also meets the criterion at every ε, so the evidence does not establish that the prescribed T=O(ε⁻¹ log) schedule is necessary.

claims.claim: Table 1 shows NHGD is the only compared method offering a high-probability bound (rather than an MSE bound) together with parallel EFIM-based Hessian inversion and constant O(1) batch size (Table 1).
claims.evidence: On a d_theta=192 synthetic benchmark, the H.P. tail shape tracks empirical quantiles within 3% (vs 8.85x looser for Chebyshev) and the parallel critical-path advantage over 5 reimplemented baselines is confirmed, but the measured batch-size scaling of baselines (~B⁻³·³) contradicts Table 1's stated Õ(ε⁻¹) batch dependence, and the proof-type uniqueness (MSE vs H.P. for each baseline) is asserted from the paper rather than independently verified.

claims.claim: In PDE-constrained optimization on a 2D heat equation, NHGD converges 3-4x faster than a Broyden-based baseline while reaching a comparable final objective value (Section on experiments).
claims.evidence: On a faithful paper-scale PINN setup (d_theta=12801, correct architecture and collocation points), NHGD is consistently faster than Broyden with a comparable final objective (ratio 1.22 vs paper's 1.12), but three reasonable speedup metrics give 2.92x, 7.79x, and 7.83x—straddling rather than confirming the claimed 3-4x—and both runs settle at objectives ~2x above the paper's Table 5 values, indicating the runs are not at the paper's exact convergence point.

michaldobiezynski/repro-natural-hypergra.overall: This logbook provides strong concrete evidence for the algorithmic core (Claim 1: Sherman-Morrison EFIM update with machine-precision exactness, gradient reuse, and verified parallelism) and the per-update error bound (Claim 2: Theorem 4.7's rate and delta-dependence confirmed across 184 runs), while the sample-complexity theorem (Claim 3) and Table 1 uniqueness (Claim 4) are tested only on small synthetic instances with key controls failing to discriminate, and the flagship PDE speedup (Claim 5) reproduces qualitatively but not at the stated 3-4x factor.

michaldobiezynski/repro-lions-and-muons-.paper_title: Lions and Muons: Optimization via Stochastic Frank-Wolfe under Heavy-Tailed Noises

claims.claim: Lion with weight decay is shown to be a special instance of Stochastic Frank-Wolfe under an l-infinity norm constraint (Theorem 1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Lion and SFW trajectories match to worst relative deviation 8.17e-14 across 4 hyperparameter configs on a 2000-param logistic regression, with a discriminative negative control (wrong gamma mapping) failing at 7.07e-01 — confirming the exact algebraic identity of Theorem 1 to float64 round-off.

claims.claim: Muon with weight decay is shown to be a special instance of Stochastic Frank-Wolfe under a spectral-norm constraint (Theorem 2, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Exact-oracle Muon and SFW trajectories match to worst relative deviation 2.28e-15 across 3 configs on a 256×128 weight matrix, including the Nesterov-Muon variant (Theorem 7), with negative control failing at 1.35e-01; the practical Newton-Schulz gap (1.67e-01) is honestly reported as outside the theorem's stated exact-oracle scope.

claims.claim: Under standard smoothness and bounded-variance assumptions, the proposed Stochastic Frank-Wolfe framework achieves an expected Frank-Wolfe gap of O(1/sqrt(T)) plus a variance term, and convergence in Frank-Wolfe gap corresponds to convergence to a KKT point of the norm-constrained problem (Theorem 3, Section 4).
claims.evidence: On a single hand-constructed synthetic d=200 non-convex objective, the 1/√T rate is confirmed (slopes −0.457 then −0.504 over successive decades) and the KKT/Lemma-1 correspondence holds to 5.2e-14 identity error, but the variance term's specific functional form is not matched: the β/(γ(1−γ)) factor is anti-correlated with measurements (−0.951) and the bound is loose by 10–50×.

claims.claim: With heavy-tailed (p-th moment, p in (1,2]) gradient noise, a clipped variant achieves a high-probability convergence rate of O(log(T/delta) T^((1-p)/(3p-2))) without requiring large batch sizes, improved to O(log(T/delta) T^((1-p)/(2p-1))) when combined with variance reduction (Theorems 5-6, Section 4).
claims.evidence: On the same synthetic d=200 objective with Pareto noise, measured exponents land within 0.06 of theory at p=1.5 and p=2.0, but at p=1.2 the decay is a third of the claimed rate; the theorem's literal step-size constants stall the iterate entirely (η=1.19e-08), requiring a 1e+05 rescaling, and only a single geometry is tested.

claims.claim: On a 10M-parameter nanoGPT trained on Shakespeare, the clipped variant Lion+ reaches a validation loss of 1.46 in 3,200 steps versus 4,000 steps for standard Lion, a 20% reduction, while Muon+ reduces steps from 4,400 to 4,150 versus standard Muon (Section 5).
claims.evidence: At 1/6 the paper's parameter count (1.83M vs 10.6M), 1/5 the steps, and 2 seeds, the qualitative step-reduction ordering reproduces (LION+ 25.0% fewer steps, MUON+ 5.1% fewer), but the paper's absolute clipping thresholds never bind at this scale, the 1.46/1.47 loss target is unreachable, and exact step counts do not transfer.

michaldobiezynski/repro-lions-and-muons-.overall: The logbook provides machine-precision verification of the two core algebraic equivalence theorems (Claims 1–2) with discriminative negative controls, establishing the paper's theoretical foundation. The convergence-rate and empirical claims (3–5) are addressed only on reduced or synthetic setups with partial quantitative agreement — the 1/√T rate and KKT correspondence confirm cleanly, but variance-term scaling, heavy-tailed rates at p=1.2, and the full-scale nanoGPT results remain incompletely verified.

DineshAI/HMyCBL2yMV.paper_title: Beyond First-order Asymptotics in Sequential Mean Testing

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 establishes a central limit theorem for the empirical KL_inf statistic, showing sqrt(n)(KL_inf(q_hat_n, m_o) - KL_inf(q, m_o)) converges in distribution to N(0, sigma^2(q, m_o)) (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Monte Carlo with 5,000 replicates at n∈{50,200,1000,5000} for Beta(3,2) and Bernoulli(0.6) at m₀=0.7 shows variance ratios of 1.0093 and 0.9957 at n=5000, KS distances of 0.0124 and 0.0185, and Gaussian 95% coverage of 0.9530 and 0.9522, all improving from n=50; 40,000 raw replicates with independent checker confirmation.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 extends this result to the stopping time tau_alpha, proving sqrt(log(1/alpha))(tau_alpha/log(1/alpha) - 1/KL_inf(q,m_o)) converges to a Gaussian limit N(0, sigma^2_bd(q,m_o)) as alpha to 0 (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: 10,000 paths per level for Bernoulli(0.6) at m₀=0.2 across b=log(1/α)∈{4.6,...,10000} show variance ratio converging from 2.4271 to 0.9923, KS from 0.4895 to 0.0349, coverage from 0.6463 to 0.9477, and centering error from 106.7% to 0.10% at b=10000, with 160,000 raw paths and first-hit inequality verification.

claims.claim: The proof decomposes the normalized KL_inf statistic into a term from the dual optimization (shown to vanish in probability) and a standard empirical-mean term that converges to Gaussian, combined with verification of Anscombe's condition to transfer the CLT to the stopping time (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Decomposition at n∈{200,1000,5000,50000} with 10,000 paths shows dual term T₁ RMS decreasing from 0.0617 to 0.0039 (factor 15.8), T₁/T₂ ratio 0.0044 at n=50000, full/linear variance ratio 1.0001, and machine-precision identity; Anscombe condition verified with 5,000 paths across all integer prefixes in windows δ∈{0.2,...,0.01}, with Wilson upper bounds far below η=0.1 at δ=0.01 for n≥10000.

claims.claim: Proposition 4.5 constructs asymptotically valid confidence intervals for the stopping time using only a single simulation run, without requiring multiple independent replicates (Proposition 4.5).
claims.evidence: The logbook's own numerical evidence contradicts its 'falsified' label: at b=10000, single-run CIs show 95% coverage of 0.9513 (Wilson [0.947,0.955] containing 0.95) and 50% coverage of 0.5010 (Wilson [0.491,0.511] containing 0.50), with plug-in variance ratio 1.00043—all constructed from individual paths without multiple replicates. The 'falsification' rests on a semantic argument that 'confidence intervals for the stopping time' must mean prediction intervals for the random variable, but the proposition provides standard confidence intervals for the asymptotic centering parameter 1/KL_inf, w

claims.claim: Numerical experiments on synthetic Beta and Bernoulli distributions and on real crop-yield data show empirical stopping-time distributions converging to the theoretical Gaussian limit, with stronger agreement at smaller significance levels alpha (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Synthetic stopping-time experiments show KS improvement from α=1e-4 to 1e-8 (growing boundary: 0.4006→0.3324; constant boundary: 0.0912→0.0766); real DSSAT crop-yield bootstrap with 3,000 paths at m₀=0.5, α=1e-4 on 44 public maize yields shows KS 0.0890, variance ratio 0.9396, and coverage 0.9693, with KS improving across α∈{1e-2,1e-3,1e-4}. The real-data pool differs from the authors' undisclosed Figure 5 data but uses the same protocol on official same-domain DSSAT data.

DineshAI/HMyCBL2yMV.overall: The logbook provides substantial Monte Carlo evidence with proper convergence trends, independent checkers, negative controls, and raw data artifacts supporting all five claims. The only notable issue is Claim 4, where the logbook's self-assigned 'falsified' verdict is contradicted by its own numerical evidence showing well-calibrated single-run confidence intervals.

michaldobiezynski/repro-geometric-entrop.paper_title: Geometric Entropy and Retrieval Phase Transitions in Continuous Thermal Dense Associative Memory

claims.claim: For continuous Dense Associative Memory with exponential pattern capacity p=e^(αN) on the N-sphere, the maximum retrieval capacity at zero temperature is α_c(0) = 0.5 for both LSE and LSR kernels (Section 4.3, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The T→0 limit α_c→0.5 is confirmed only by numerically re-solving the paper's own closed-form equations (Eq 22/26/33/37), yielding 0.49999 at T=1e-6 — an algebra check, not a measurement on real pattern ensembles near α=0.5. Real measurements of the key ingredient φ_max on N-sphere ensembles (0.366 vs predicted 0.447 at α=0.1, N=50) contradict the Gaussian-tail assumption underpinning the derivation, but the T→0 endpoint itself was never directly tested at capacity.

claims.claim: The geometric entropy density depends only on the alignment φ via s(φ) = (1/2)ln(1-φ²), independent of the choice of energy kernel (Section 3.2, Equation 19).
claims.evidence: A real spherical Metropolis-Hastings sampler at N=50,100,200,400 with multiple-histogram stitching directly measures s(φ), with deviation from (1/2)ln(1-φ²) shrinking from 0.0682 to 0.0034 (N=50→400), consistent with 1/N convergence. Kernel-independence is measured directly: max|s_LSE−s_LSR| ≤ 0.0101 at N=50/100 on common support, confirming the claim across both kernels and four scales.

claims.claim: The LSE and LSR kernels have distinct finite-temperature phase boundaries, given respectively by α_c^LSE(T) = (1/2)[1-f_ret^LSE(T)]² (Equation 35) and α_c^LSR(T) = (1/2)[1-f_ret^LSR(T)]² (Equation 39) (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: The LSE boundary Eq(35) matches the self-consistent inversion of the paper's own Eq(22) to 1.1e-16, but the LSR boundary Eq(39) departs by up to 0.249 in α from the self-consistent inversion of Eq(22)+Eq(30) (the paper's own LSR noise floor), with non-monotonic behavior above T~1.5. The paper's own LSR noise floor diverges at α_th, implying T_max=∞ rather than the finite T_max≈0.22 from Eq(39), showing Eq(39) is internally inconsistent with the paper's framework.

claims.claim: For the LSR kernel with shape parameter b=3.41, there exists a support threshold α_th = (1/2)(1-1/b)² ≈ 0.25 below which retrieval is perfect at any temperature, a behavior absent for the LSE kernel (Section 4.2-4.3).
claims.evidence: Sub-threshold behavior is confirmed at α=0.05/0.10, N≤100: zero spurious occupancy (mean count=0, max=0) and sustained cold-start LSR retrieval (<φ>≥0.7291 over T∈[0.25,20]). However, the threshold value 0.25 is questioned — the exact N-sphere tail places it at 0.346, and Gaussian-tail counting over-predicts above-threshold occupancy by 120x-820x. 'Perfect retrieval at any temperature' is cold-start only; hot-start LSR never enters the retrieval basin (<φ>∈[−0.0019,0.0124]), indicating metastable trapping rather than equilibrium retrieval.

claims.claim: Monte Carlo simulations at N=50, α=0.1 confirm the theoretical predictions, showing the LSE kernel undergoes a retrieval-to-disorder transition around T≈0.7-0.8, while the LSR kernel below its threshold maintains retrieval across all tested temperatures (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Faithful reproduction of the paper's Fig 2 protocol (N=50, α=0.1, M=148, 50 trials, cold-start) gives MC T_c^LSE=0.745, inside the claimed 0.7-0.8 band and matching theory's 0.7512; below the transition, MC tracks the finite-N Boltzmann curve to ~0.002. LSR cold-start shows no transition (min <φ>=0.7291 above support edge 0.7067) and curves overlap across loads (A/B within 0.006), as predicted. The hot-start control showing no retrieval contextualizes the result as a spinodal but does not contradict the claim, which concerns the paper's own cold-start protocol.

michaldobiezynski/repro-geometric-entrop.overall: The logbook provides direct sampler-based verification of the kernel-independent geometric entropy (Claim 2) and the Fig 2 Monte Carlo protocol (Claim 5), while demonstrating an internal-consistency defect in the LSR finite-temperature boundary Eq(39) (Claim 3) and showing that the T→0 capacity and LSR threshold claims rest on a Gaussian-tail approximation contradicted by real N-sphere measurements (Claims 1, 4).

claims.claim: The AIPW U-statistic estimator using augmented inverse probability weighting is proven unbiased, satisfying E[U_AIPW^π] = θ* (Proposition 2.1).
claims.evidence: On real ACS 2018 California PUMS data (n=16000, 600 replicates, budget 960), the AIPW estimator averaged 69851.79 vs target 69884.27 (bias -32.48, MC-SE 148.14, z=-0.22, relative bias -4.6e-4), while the uncorrected plug-in showed -37.9% relative error, confirming AIPW removes large observable bias as Proposition 2.1 predicts.

claims.claim: The variance-minimizing (optimal) sampling probability is proportional to the square root of a residual-uncertainty term derived from the Hoeffding projection, depending on h1(Y) − h1^μ(Ŷ) rather than the raw prediction error |Y − Ŷ| (Theorem 2.2, Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: Both a local synthetic run (n=5000) and a HF GPU Job (n=20000, 2500 replicates) show projection-based sampling minimizes MC variance: raw-residual sampling was 1.66x worse locally and 2.14x worse in the HF Job, with projection and raw scores distinct (correlation 0.708), directly supporting the theorem's core distinction.

claims.claim: A central limit theorem is established for the normalized AIPW U-statistic under data-adaptive sampling, enabling computable asymptotic confidence intervals via a common-random-number coupling argument (Theorem 2.4).
claims.evidence: On scaled ACS data (n=4000–16000), 90% coverage was 0.92–0.943 with z_sd approaching 0.95, and the simulated CRN coupling error had log-log slope -0.7575 versus the Lemma A.3 target of -0.750, matching the theorem's predicted asymptotic behavior on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: On the ACS income dataset, active sampling for the Gini index achieves roughly 60% labeling-budget reduction relative to uniform sampling while maintaining 90% confidence-interval coverage (Section 4.1, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The claimed ~60% budget reduction is not reproduced: the only completed code (revise_claims45_fast.py, exit 0) yields 16.3% mean saving vs classical via first-order analytical variance, and even the MC table of unclear provenance (the script that may have produced it was interrupted, exit 130) shows only 43%—neither matches 60%.

claims.claim: On the VitalDB perioperative dataset, the active Wilcoxon signed-rank test for hemoglobin shifts requires approximately 20% less labeling budget than the classical baseline for equivalent precision (Section 4.2, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: With cross-fitted, strongly regularized XGBoost on the exact VitalDB cohort (n=1520, 4000 MC replicates), active sampling saved only +7.0% vs classical (range +3.4% to +8.7%), far below the claimed ~20%; the companion ~10% vs uniform claim was approximately reproduced at +9.9%, but the central magnitude claim fails.

claims.claim: On the political-bias dataset, active estimation of Kendall's τ for LLM label quality reduces the labeling budget by about 20% versus the classical baseline and about 10% versus uniform sampling (Section 4.3, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: On the CDI political-bias dataset with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o labels, active sampling lost on average -29.8% vs classical and -19.1% vs uniform; for GPT-4o specifically, active was -67.5% worse than classical, directly contradicting the claimed ~20% saving.

Srishti280992/repro-learning-u-statistic.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting the three theoretical claims (AIPW unbiasedness, projection-based optimal sampling, and CLT/coupling behavior) on real or controlled non-toy setups. The three empirical budget-reduction claims are falsified: ACS shows at best 43% (not 60%), VitalDB shows 7% (not 20%) vs classical, and political-bias shows active sampling performing worse than baselines.

ProCreations/icml2026-repro-tjshrzdydw.paper_title: Statistical Early Stopping for Reasoning Models

claims.claim: The nonparametric Maxwise Conformal Stopping method (Proposition 2.1) guarantees P(∃j: u_{n+1}(L_j) > τ*) ≤ α by setting the threshold to the (1-α)(1+1/n) quantile of maximum uncertainty-density scores from calibration traces, giving finite-sample false-positive-rate control without negative examples (Proposition 2.1).
claims.evidence: A native Monte Carlo simulation with 100,000 trials, n=99 calibration traces, and 8 sequential looks yields a 3.693% crossing rate under the paper-faithful exchangeable setup (below α=0.05), while broken controls (final-look-only calibration, distribution shift) inflate to 36.473% and 35.351%, directly confirming the finite-sample guarantee and its exchangeability/simultaneous-calibration requirements.

claims.claim: The parametric Renewal Process method models inter-arrival times of uncertainty keywords, computes a Sidak-corrected normalized test statistic Z_t, and halts generation once Z_t exceeds threshold (Section on renewal process stopping).
claims.evidence: A native simulation with 400 calibration traces and 100,000 test traces confirms the Sidak-corrected Z_t statistic achieves 3.608% familywise error rate (below α=0.05) versus 14.068% uncorrected, and source-code inspection verifies the exact formula Z_t = (X_t - t/μ̂)/√(t·σ̂²/μ̂³) with Sidak threshold Φ⁻¹((1-α)^(1/m)) = 2.4898 for m=8 looks.

claims.claim: Uncertainty keywords are extracted semi-supervised from 800 paired reasoning traces, yielding 102 keywords split into Impossibility (34), Speculation (14), and Insufficiency (56) categories (keyword construction section).
claims.evidence: Reconstruction of the released classifier artifact confirms 800 paired reasoning traces and category memberships of 34 (Impossibility), 14 (Speculation), and 56 (Insufficiency), with two overlapping strings yielding 102 unique keywords after union—exactly matching the claimed counts.

claims.claim: On GSM-MC, the Renewal method achieves 3.75% false-positive rate with 69.75% detection power and the Maxwise method achieves 5.42% FPR with 70.92% power, both far exceeding a length-based baseline's 32.17% power at 4.50% FPR (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Independent reaggregation of the released 12-model stopping-rule artifacts at a pinned commit reproduces Table 1 values exactly (Renewal 3.75%/69.75%, Maxwise 5.42%/70.92%, Length 4.50%/32.17%), and a separate raw Qwen3-8B replay on 200 GSM8K calibration traces and 100 GSM-MC pairs shows 0.00 percentage-point deviation from stored metrics.

claims.claim: Both methods reach roughly 82-85% of oracle detection power on math benchmarks, with regression slopes of 0.8238 (Renewal) and 0.8532 (Maxwise) against oracle power (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Exact OLS computation over 48 released data points (12 models × 4 math datasets) yields origin-constrained slopes of 0.8238439 (Renewal) and 0.8532302 (Maxwise), rounding precisely to the claimed 0.8238 and 0.8532 values.

claims.claim: On out-of-domain scientific reasoning benchmarks GPQA and HULE, calibrating on GSM8K yields 1.37-2.56% FPR but detection power drops to only 47-58% of the oracle baseline due to domain shift (Table 11).
claims.evidence: Reconstruction of the released scientific-domain result rows shows HLE false-positive rates of 4.76% (Renewal) and 5.96% (Maxwise), both outside the claimed 1.37–2.56% FPR range, while the power slopes (0.4702 and 0.5897) do support the separate 47–58% oracle-power claim.

ProCreations/icml2026-repro-tjshrzdydw.overall: The logbook provides concrete evidence for claims 1–5 through native Monte Carlo simulations (100K trials each for the two stopping rules), released-artifact reconstruction and replay, and exact arithmetic replay, all at non-toy scale. Claim 6 is falsified by a direct source-internal counterexample: HLE FPR values of 4.76% and 5.96% contradict the claimed 1.37–2.56% range.

Srishti280992/repro-clipping-makes-distr.paper_title: Clipping Makes Distributed and Federated Asynchronous SGD Robust to Stragglers

claims.claim: In the homogeneous setting, Clipped ASGD achieves oracle complexity Õ(σ²/ε⁴ + σ·τ_C/ε³ + τ_C/ε²), which depends on the concurrency τ_C but not on the maximum delay τ_max (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: The active invariant audit (4000 cases, max ratio 0.9616) and oracle rate algebra audit (10000 cases, 0 failures) are numerical checks on synthetic setups with d=50 and a toy gradient function. The delay stress test shows clipped ASGD median updates staying flat (264→254) as τ_max goes 16→1024 while vanilla grows 2.42x, supporting the τ_max-independence signature, but only on a synthetic nonconvex function, not a real ML task.

claims.claim: In the heterogeneous setting, Clipped ASGD achieves oracle complexity Õ((σ²+ζ²)/ε⁴ + (σ+ζ)·τ_C/ε³ + τ_C/ε²), where ζ measures data heterogeneity, again independent of τ_max (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: The same oracle rate audit includes heterogeneous terms with zero failures, and the synthetic heterogeneous stress test shows clipped updates flat (330.5→331.5, ratio 1.003) while vanilla grows 2.61x. However, heterogeneity is modeled as a fixed worker-specific shift on a d=50 synthetic gradient, not a real federated/distributed learning scenario.

claims.claim: The paper establishes the first high-probability convergence guarantees for asynchronous SGD, with a polylogarithmic dependence on the failure probability δ governed by the sub-Weibull tail parameter θ (Theorem 4.3, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: The high-probability algebra terms (with log^θ(1/δ) factors) pass the 10000-case termwise inversion audit, and a 200-seed concentration check on the synthetic setup shows 99.5%-to-median ratio of 1.176 for clipped ASGD, approximately linear in log(1/δ). The 'first high-probability guarantee' priority claim is not independently verifiable, and the concentration check uses the same toy d=50 synthetic problem.

claims.claim: Gradient noise is modeled as sub-Weibull (Definition 3.1), generalizing sub-Gaussian (θ=1/2) and sub-exponential (θ=1) noise, and empirical measurement of ResNet-18 gradient noise on CIFAR-10 yields a fitted tail parameter θ=2.71 (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The gpu_cifar_repro.py script was written to measure ResNet-18 gradient noise tails on CIFAR-10, but all three execution attempts failed: the first with a torch._six compatibility error, the second interrupted during CIFAR-10 download, and the third (with --synthetic-data) also interrupted. No theta measurement was ever produced from real CIFAR-10 data.

claims.claim: On CIFAR-10 with delay factor D=4, Clipped ASGD achieves a 1.8x wall-clock speedup over vanilla ASGD (Figure 2), and on Shakespeare it achieves 2.0-2.2x speedup depending on the delay regime (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The CIFAR-10 asynchronous experiment (part of gpu_cifar_repro.py) never completed due to repeated execution failures. No Shakespeare experiment was attempted at all. The synthetic delay stress test is not comparable to the paper's CIFAR-10 D=4 or Shakespeare speedup claims.

claims.claim: Under label-skew data heterogeneity on CIFAR-10, Clipped ASGD shows a 1.2-1.3x improvement over vanilla ASGD (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The label-skew CIFAR-10 experiment was part of the same gpu_cifar_repro.py script that never completed. The synthetic heterogeneous stress test uses artificial worker shifts, not CIFAR-10 label-skew, and does not produce the 1.2-1.3x speedup figure claimed in the paper.

Srishti280992/repro-clipping-makes-distr.overall: The logbook provides toy-scale numerical evidence (synthetic d=50 gradient, 4000+10000 algebraic audits, delay stress tests) that supports the structure of the theoretical complexity claims but does not reproduce any of the paper's empirical results. All GPU/CIFAR-10 experiments failed to execute, and no Shakespeare experiments were attempted.

claims.claim: Single-head softmax attention parameters can be exactly recovered using O(d^2) value queries via a two-phase algorithm that first recovers the output projection vector v with length-1 queries, then recovers the attention matrix W column-by-column with length-2 queries (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Full two-phase algorithm implemented and run at d∈{8,16,32,64} with 100 random trials each: v recovered to 0.0, W recovered to ≤8.8e-11 Frobenius error, instrumented query count equals d+d² exactly, and a negative control with d-3 probes collapses to error 7.14.

claims.claim: When rank(W) <= r << d, the attention matrix can instead be recovered with only O(rd) queries using rank-one projections and nuclear norm minimization from compressed sensing (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Nuclear-norm minimization via cvxpy/SCS on rank-one projections at (d=20,r=2) and (d=30,r=3): recovery succeeds (rel. error ~1e-5) above m≈5·rd with total queries 220 and 480 respectively, well below d²=400 and 900, with a clear phase transition from 0% to 100% success.

claims.claim: Under norm bounds and margin conditions on the parameters, epsilon-accurate approximate recovery is achievable with O(d^2) queries tolerating additive noise tau = O(min{mu, epsilon_v/sqrt(d), mu*epsilon_w/(W^2 d)}) (Theorem 6.2).
claims.evidence: Scaled/clipped noisy estimator tested at d=12 with 40 trials per point: exact at τ=0 (3.4e-14), within eps_W=0.1 for all τ≤τ*=6.5e-6 (max error 9.5e-3), linear error scaling with τ, and degradation to 0.99 error at 100×τ* confirming the tolerance threshold.

claims.claim: Multi-head attention parameters are non-identifiable from queries: distinct parameter sets can produce identical input-output maps, ruling out exact parameter extraction without further structural assumptions (Proposition 7.1).
claims.evidence: Proposition 7.1 collision family constructed explicitly at d∈{8,16,32,64} with H∈{2,4,8,8}: 200 random constructions per config show max I/O discrepancy 7.1e-15 between distinct parameter sets whose per-head value vectors differ by at least 0.18.

claims.claim: Length-2 queries reduce the softmax attention weight to a sigmoid, alpha = sigma(s1 - s2), enabling inversion via sigma^-1 into linear equations in the unknown parameters (Section preceding Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Three sub-identities verified across d∈{4,8,16,32,64} with 200 random instances each (1000 total): softmax-to-sigmoid equality to 1.1e-16, linearity of score gap in W to 8.5e-14, sigmoid inversion round-trip to 3.2e-10, and Theorem 4.1 probe reduction to 2.2e-16.

snaykey/repro-learning-attention-queries.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence for all five claims through real algorithm implementations with instrumented query counts, negative controls, and multiple random trials at meaningful dimensions. Every claim is supported by actual experimental runs with specific error metrics rather than mere assertions.

snaykey/repro-adaptive-gradient-heavy-ta.paper_title: Can Adaptive Gradient Methods Converge under Heavy-Tailed Noise? A Case Study of AdaGrad

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 gives the first convergence guarantee for AdaGrad under heavy-tailed noise with tail index p in (4/3, 2], showing a convergence rate of tilde-O(1/T^((3p-4)/(4p))) (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: AdaGrad (Algorithm 1) was run on a non-convex objective with α-stable heavy-tailed noise (d=10, 300 seeds, T=30000), yielding measured convergence exponents 0.189/0.233/0.255 for p=1.5/1.7/2.0 that are monotone in p, recover ~1/4 at p=2, and respect the upper bound (measured ≥ theory). The SGD negative control flatlines under the same noise (13.55→13.41 at p=1.5), supporting the claim that AdaGrad converges where SGD fails.

claims.claim: This convergence rate is achieved without prior knowledge of the tail index p or the noise level, with AdaGrad adapting automatically to both (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: With a single fixed schedule (γ=0.5, λ=0.1) never given p or σ, the measured exponent is flat across a 10× noise-scale sweep (≈0.20 at p=1.5, ≈0.26 at p=2.0 across σ∈{1,3,10}) while remaining p-dependent, directly demonstrating adaptivity to both the noise level and the tail index as claimed.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 provides an algorithm-dependent lower bound for the one-dimensional case of AdaGrad, implying the minimax-optimal rate for heavy-tailed stochastic optimization is not attainable by AdaGrad (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook does not reproduce the d=1 hard-instance construction of Theorem 3.3 (the adversarial oracle forcing slow convergence), which is the core of the lower bound. Part A is arithmetic comparing two known formulas ((p-1)/(3p-2) vs (3p-4)/(4p)), not experimental evidence; Part B merely shows AdaGrad's measured exponent on a benign instance does not exceed the minimax rate, which is expected for any algorithm and does not test the lower bound itself.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 shows that a normalized AdaGrad-Norm variant achieves a faster rate of O(1/T^((p-1)/(2p))) under a bounded-objective assumption, valid for all p in (1, 2] (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: AdaGrad-Norm (Algorithm 2) was run on a genuinely bounded non-convex objective (f=Σaᵢ(1-cos xᵢ), d=5, 300 seeds, T=30000) alongside vanilla AdaGrad. The measured exponents for AdaGrad-Norm exceed vanilla at every p (0.306>0.198, 0.403>0.232, 0.332>0.260), confirming the faster-rate prediction, with all measured exponents sitting above their theoretical upper bounds as expected for benign instances.

claims.claim: The authors identify the regime p in (1, 4/3] as unresolved and a primary limitation of their analysis (Section 5, Limitations).
claims.evidence: The paper's Section 5 explicitly states the (1, 4/3] regime as a limitation; the exponent formula (3p-4)/(4p) is arithmetically ≤0 for p≤4/3 (exactly 0 at p=4/3), confirming the bound is vacuous there; and empirical runs show convergence stalling below the threshold (final/init metric 0.527 at p=1.2 vs 0.167 at p=2.0), all consistent with the stated limitation.

snaykey/repro-adaptive-gradient-heavy-ta.overall: The logbook provides solid empirical support for 4 of 5 claims by faithfully re-implementing AdaGrad and AdaGrad-Norm with α-stable heavy-tailed noise at meaningful scale (300 seeds, T=30000) with appropriate controls, demonstrating convergence rate ordering, adaptivity, and the bounded-objective advantage. The lower-bound claim (Claim 3) is not substantiated: the actual adversarial hard-instance construction of Theorem 3.3 is not reproduced, and the provided evidence reduces to arithmetic on known formulas and expected behavior on a benign instance.

Srishti280992/repro-adalina-adaptive-lin.paper_title: Adalina: Adaptive Linear Approximation for the Shapley Value and Beyond

claims.claim: Adalina (Algorithm 1) is a randomized adaptive linear-approximation algorithm achieving O(n/ε² log(1/δ)) utility-query complexity while using only Θ(n) space (Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The theory mode swept n=8..3072 and fitted query-bound slopes of 1.001 in n, -2.000 in ε, and a delta-normalized spread of 5.96e-7, matching O(n/ε² log(1/δ)); streaming-state bytes grew with log-log slope 0.991 versus 2.000 for a quadratic control, confirming Θ(n) space.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 shows that under an optimal sampling distribution q*_s, Adalina attains query complexity O(nD*C²/ε² log(2/δ)) where D*∈O(1) for both Beta Shapley and weighted Banzhaf semi-values, improving on OFA's O(n log n/(ε²δ)) bound (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: D* was computed for weighted Banzhaf (w∈{0.1..0.9}) and Beta Shapley {(1,1),(2,3),(8,8)} up to n=1024; max D* was 11.09 for weighted Banzhaf and 5.54 for beta(2,3), confirming boundedness, while the uniform-vs-optimal D ratio at n=512 was 1.499, confirming q* improves the dominant complexity factor.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 proves that paired sampling reduces the estimation problem to approximating (U−U^c)/2 and provably lowers MSE whenever E[U(S)·U([n]\S)] > 0 (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: In an exact n=8 enumeration, the paired estimator and the (U−U^c)/2 estimator agreed to max absolute difference 0.0; a positive-constant utility with E[U·U^c]>0 yielded paired/unpaired MSE ratio 1.36e-31, while an anti-complement control with E[U·U^c]<0 worsened the ratio to 1.935, matching Theorem 3.2's predictions.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows Adalina achieves improved mean-square error approaching the optimal E[‖ϕ̂^γ*−ϕ‖²₂] while preserving O(n/ε² log(1/δ)) query complexity for symmetric semi-values, and the paper shows SHAP-IQ does not minimize query complexity under this framework (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: On an exact n=8 Beta(2,2) game, Adalina's MSE matched the oracle-gamma* estimator (ratio 0.988 at T=512, 1200 reps) while SHAP-IQ's MSE was ~10× worse; separately, D(q_SHAP-IQ)/D* was strictly >1 (1.029–1.499) across n up to 512 for Shapley, confirming SHAP-IQ does not minimize query complexity.

claims.claim: Experiments on spambase (n=57), FOTP (n=51), MinibooNE (n=50), and philippine (n=308) datasets, using 1000 queries per player averaged over 10 seeds, empirically validate the theoretical complexity/variance predictions (Figures 1-4).
claims.evidence: The official OpenML pipeline was smoke-tested on all four named datasets at 10 queries/player × 1 seed (confirming n=57,51,50,308), but the full 1000 queries/player × 10 seeds replay was still running at publication time with only 8/10 spambase seeds visible; the reduced-scale run does not reproduce the paper's figure-level results.

Srishti280992/repro-adalina-adaptive-lin.overall: The logbook provides rigorous independent numerical audits (exact enumeration, Monte Carlo with 1200 reps, scaling sweeps to n=3072) that verify the theoretical Claims 1–4, but the empirical Claim 5 is only addressed at a clearly reduced scale (10 qpp, 1 seed) with the full-scale replay incomplete.

ProCreations/icml2026-repro-mjgkpafdik.paper_title: Deep networks learn to parse uniform-depth context-free languages from local statistics

claims.claim: Introduces the Varying-tree Random Hierarchy Model, a tunable class of uniform-depth PCFGs with m2 binary and m3 ternary production rules per symbol scaling asymptotically as m2=f2*v and m3=f3*v^2 in vocabulary size v (Section 2).
claims.evidence: Exact arithmetic validation confirms m2=f2*v, m3=f3*v^2 are integers within available tuple counts, and length bounds [2^L, 3^L] hold for tested settings (4,2,1,4), (8,2,1,8), (12,3,3,36), (16,3,4,64).

claims.claim: Identifies a phase transition at critical ambiguity parameter f_c = 3/8, below which sentences are globally unambiguous (unique parse/class label) and above which multiple valid parse trees exist, driven by spurious nonterminals in the inside algorithm (Section 3, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook's theoretical analysis cites the paper's own Eq. 28 and top-down argument (F*N_t~1), both yielding f_c=1/2, which contradicts the claimed f_c=3/8 by a difference of 1/8; the paper itself reportedly warns that finite-v entropy crossover is not the asymptotic critical value.

claims.claim: Derives a closed-form sample complexity formula P* = O((p2^2/2)^(1-L) · v · m3 · m2^(L-1)) for learning the grammar via root-to-substring covariance clustering (Section 4, Equation 8).
claims.evidence: Exact rational substitution confirms the formula: with p2=1/2, f=1/v, L=2 gives (1/8)^(-1)*v*v*1=8v^2, and f=1/4, L=3 gives (1/8)^(-2)*v*(v^2/4)*(v/4)^2=v^5, matching both advertised regimes.

claims.claim: Confirms P* ~ v^2 scaling (with f=1/v) for CNNs via test-loss collapse when training set size is rescaled by the theoretical P* (Section 5.1, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: A threshold-free collapse estimator on 86 released (v,P) points yields alpha=1.9610±0.0488 (95% CI contains 2), with alpha=2 only 0.9% above the minimum residual while alpha=1 and alpha=3 are 5.8x and 6.3x worse; fresh from-scratch CPU training at v=6,8,10 independently reproduces alpha≈2.16.

claims.claim: Shows P* ~ v^5 scaling for f=1/4 and depth L=3 as vocabulary size v increases, validated against CNN training curves (Section 5.1, Figure 7a).
claims.evidence: Fresh CPU training at f=1/4, L=3 for v=4 and v=8 measures the threshold ratio P_thr(v=8)/P_thr(v=4)=32=2^5 across multiple loss levels (exponent 5.164±0.038), discriminating v^5 from v^2 by ~9x; budget controls confirm the anchors are sample-limited, not optimizer-limited.

claims.claim: Demonstrates the same P* ~ v^2 sample-complexity scaling law holds across CNNs, an Inside Neural Network (INN), and an encoder-only Transformer, with INN having the best prefactor due to task-aligned architecture (Section 5.2, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: Collapse exponents on released data are 1.9610±0.0488 (CNN), 1.8798±0.0464 (INN), 1.9473±0.1086 (Transformer), all pairwise differences non-significant (z<1.3) and all CIs contain 2; INN prefactor is 2.17x better than CNN and 2.98x better than Transformer at loss 0.5, holding in 11/11 per-vocabulary comparisons.

ProCreations/icml2026-repro-mjgkpafdik.overall: The logbook provides rigorous evidence for five claims via exact arithmetic validation, a threshold-free collapse estimator on 86 released data points, and fresh from-scratch CPU training with budget controls. Claim 2 is falsified by theoretical analysis showing the paper's own equations yield f_c=1/2 rather than the claimed 3/8.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-corruption-tolerant-.paper_title: Corruption-Tolerant Asynchronous Q-Learning with Near-Optimal Rates

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows Robust Async-Q achieves a finite-time convergence rate of O(1/√T), matching classical asynchronous Q-learning, plus an additive O(√ε) term where ε∈[0,1/2) is the fraction of adversarially corrupted rewards (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook tests O(1/√T) convergence on a 4-state, 3-action MDP with a fitted slope of -0.452 at ε=0 (R²=0.913), and demonstrates magnitude-independence (naive error grows 307x vs robust 0.9x over attack magnitude 1→1000). However, the claim is about a finite-time rate on a general MDP class; the 4-state MDP is a clearly simplified setup, and the additive O(√ε) term is only indirectly probed via magnitude-independence rather than directly measured.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 gives an information-theoretic lower bound of Ω(√ε), proving the additive corruption term in the upper bound is unavoidable (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook reproduces the paper's Appendix D two-MDP construction (Eq. 74-78): contaminated distributions are bit-identical (max pmf diff < 1e-12) across ε∈{0.05,0.1,0.2,0.3}, Q* gaps meet theoretical minimums (e.g., 1.7568 vs 1.5811 at ε=0.1), and two-point testing error stays at ~0.5 (no-better-than-chance), confirming the Ω(√ε) information-theoretic indistinguishability on the paper's own construction.

claims.claim: Theorem 4 extends the guarantee to a reward-agnostic setting where the algorithm needs no prior knowledge of the reward distribution's bounds (Section 5.1).
claims.evidence: The reward-agnostic variant (using m(t)=t^p as proxy for unknown σ̃) is tested on a 4-state, 3-action MDP, showing comparable convergence (slope=-0.466, R²=0.961) and p-robustness across p∈{1,2,4}. This is a real implementation of the mechanism on a clearly simplified MDP, confirming qualitative behavior but not a full-scale demonstration.

claims.claim: Theorem 6 extends the near-optimal finite-time rate to single-trajectory Markovian sampling with time-correlated data, with the bound inflated by the chain's mixing time (Section 6).
claims.evidence: Markovian sampling is tested on the 4-state MDP across 4 self-loop-probability settings with measured mixing times (τ=1,1,2,5), showing positive error-vs-τ slope (0.135) and bounded convergence. The setup is simplified and the mixing-time variation range is narrow (1 to 5), providing only a toy-scale demonstration of the mixing-time inflation mechanism.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 (Robust Async-Q) combines a trimmed-mean reward estimator with an adaptive threshold G_t to filter corrupted rewards before the standard Q-learning update, requiring only knowledge of the corruption fraction ε and minimum state-action visitation probability λ_min (Algorithm 1, Assumption 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook separately verifies all three Algorithm 1 mechanisms: (a) TRIM estimator bias grows only 0.25x vs naive 282x over magnitude 1→2000, (b) λ_min dependence confirmed (balanced λ_min=0.0485/error=0.0421 vs skewed λ_min=0.0084/error=0.1284), and (c) adaptive threshold discards ~0% when clean vs non-trivial fraction when corrupted (ε=0.3). These are direct, concrete tests of each component on a real MDP.

sabaridsnfuji/repro-corruption-tolerant-.overall: The logbook provides genuine from-scratch implementations with real bugs found and fixed, testing all five claims on a small 4-state, 3-action MDP with Huber-contaminated rewards. The Algorithm 1 mechanism tests and the Theorem 3 lower-bound construction are the strongest results, while the convergence rate, reward-agnostic, and Markovian sampling claims are only demonstrated at toy scale.

sci-m-wang/repro-structured-multi-modal-.paper_title: Structured Multi-modal Graph Disentanglement for Psychiatric Diagnosis

claims.claim: SMGD achieves improved in-domain diagnosis and more reliable cross-dataset generalization under modality gap
claims.evidence: The reproduction used a simplified setup: 480 of 1071 ABIDE-I subjects (240/120/120 split), only 20 epochs vs the paper's 100, CPU-only, and SRPBS-SC schizophrenia graphs as a proxy stress test instead of the paper's actual ABIDE-I→SRPBS-ASD transfer protocol (which was not executable due to missing data/scripts). In this proxy comparison, the structured variant showed no consistent advantage: mean accuracy dropped by 0.008 on ABIDE-I test and 0.009 on SRPBS-SC, MCC dropped by 0.017 and 0.014 respectively, while F1 improved only marginally (+0.009 and +0.004).

claims.claim: Achieves this without expert-crafted features
claims.evidence: A source-code audit of the released code confirmed that the classifier uses only disentangled core/shared latent variables (not expert-crafted diagnostic features), the shortcut component is separated from the classifier, FC matrix rows serve directly as node features, atlas-region gray-matter distributions are used for structural graphs, and demographic covariates (age/sex) are loaded but never passed to the model. No handcrafted diagnostic biomarker vector was found in the codebase.

sci-m-wang/repro-structured-multi-modal-.overall: The logbook provides a controlled but reduced-scale comparison (subset of ABIDE-I, 20 epochs, CPU, proxy cross-dataset task) that does not reproduce the paper's headline in-domain or transfer results, and the actual ABIDE-I→SRPBS-ASD transfer protocol was not testable from the release. A thorough code audit does confirm the design claim that no expert-crafted diagnostic feature vector enters the classifier.

sci-m-wang/repro-si-igcl-subject-invaria.paper_title: SI-IGCL: Subject Invariance-aware Inverse Graph Contrastive Learning for Psychiatric Disorder Identification

claims.claim: Outperforms all state-of-the-art methods for psychiatric disorder identification
claims.evidence: The official SI-IGCL main.py never executed (hardcoded Windows paths caused FileNotFoundError), no SI-IGCL training was run, and none of the 14 baselines were reproduced. The Table 1 audit merely re-derives descriptive statistics from the paper's own reported mean±SD values, and the only independent experiment—a linear FC baseline on 215 ABIDE subjects (61.86% accuracy)—does not test SI-IGCL or any baseline method at all.

claims.claim: Constructs inverse contrastive objective to repel intra-subject and attract inter-subject embeddings
claims.evidence: An exact gradient audit of the released HCNT_Xent function (commit fc6f818) across 128 random trials showed the diagonal gradient is always negative and off-diagonal gradient always positive, meaning minimizing the loss increases same-subject similarity and decreases inter-subject similarity—the opposite of the claimed inverse objective. Direct embedding optimization confirmed this: same-subject cosine rose 0.9859→0.9879 while inter-subject cosine fell 0.3849→0.3671. The function also ignores its temperature parameter entirely.

sci-m-wang/repro-si-igcl-subject-invaria.overall: The logbook provides a rigorous mathematical falsification of Claim 2 by exactly auditing the released loss function's gradient directions, but fails to produce any independent experimental evidence for or against Claim 1 because SI-IGCL never ran and no baselines were reproduced.

snaykey/repro-nonconvex-heavytail-stabil.paper_title: Stability and Generalization of Nonconvex Optimization with Heavy-Tailed Noise

claims.claim: Under Assumption 3.1 (bounded p-th centered moment, p-BCM, for p in (1,2]), Theorem 4.2 bounds the generalization gap between population and empirical gradients by 4ε + C_p σ_p n^{-(p-1)/p} using a truncation argument to handle heavy-tailed noise (Theorem 4.2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: On a real 2-layer MLP (610 params) trained on UCI digits with injected α-stable heavy-tailed noise, the logbook recovers the n^{-(p-1)/p} median exponent to 1–3% accuracy (0.344/0.419/0.499 vs 0.333/0.412/0.500) across 200 subsamples per n, verifies the closed-form C_p constants, and confirms the full Theorem 4.2 inequality holds at every n for all p, Jensen-tight at p=2.

claims.claim: For Clipped SGD (Algorithm 1), Proposition 5.1 gives an on-average stability bound ε_c ≤ 2Lγ√(T/n) Σ η_t, and Theorem 5.2/Corollary 5.3 derive a resulting population gradient bound with rate O(n^{-(p-1)/(3(3p-2))}) (Section 5.1, Theorem 5.2, Corollary 5.3).
claims.evidence: Proposition 5.1's stability bound holds on the real MLP with the distinctive γ-linear signature confirmed (log-log slope 1.019 vs predicted 1.0), and the population gradient decreases with n for all p. However, the fitted rate exponents (0.011–0.020) are far below the predicted O(n^{-(p-1)/(3(3p-2))}) rate (~0.067–0.083), so the rate itself is not recovered; the ordering (clipped slower than NSGD-B) is confirmed.

claims.claim: For Mini-Batch Normalized SGD (Algorithm 2), Theorem 5.5 and Corollary 5.6 establish an improved generalization rate of O(n^{-(p-1)/(7p-6)}) compared to the clipped-SGD rate (Section 5.2, Theorem 5.5, Corollary 5.6).
claims.evidence: The √B stability growth signature is confirmed (log-log slope 0.873 in batch size, bound holds at all points), and NSGD-B achieves a strictly lower population gradient than clipped SGD at n=1024 for every p with a larger fitted decay exponent, confirming the Corollary 5.6 improvement. As with Claim 2, the absolute rate exponents (0.018–0.038) are much smaller than the theoretical prediction (~0.111–0.125).

claims.claim: For Normalized SGD with Momentum (Algorithm 3), Theorem 5.9 matches the O(n^{-(p-1)/(7p-6)}) rate of the normalized batch variant (Section 5.3, Theorem 5.9).
claims.evidence: The γ-free and B-free stability of Proposition 5.8 is confirmed (stability flat in β at 0.0010–0.0016, bound holds), and NSGD-M's population gradient decreases with n, matches NSGD-B's rate class, and beats clipped SGD for every p. The rate matching is supported by comparable fitted exponents between NSGD-M and NSGD-B, though both are far below the asymptotic prediction.

claims.claim: The combined clipping-plus-momentum method (Algorithm 4) achieves the same stability bound as momentum alone (Proposition 5.12) and a matching rate of O(n^{-(p-1)/(7p-6)}) without dependence on the linear step-size term γ (Theorem 5.13, Section 5.4).
claims.evidence: The key prediction of γ-independent stability is decisively confirmed: NSGD-CM's stability is flat in γ (slope 0.053 vs clipped SGD's 1.019), and the fitted rate exponent is exactly γ-invariant (spread 0.000 across an 8× γ range). NSGD-CM also matches the momentum variant's population gradient at n=1024 for all p.

snaykey/repro-nonconvex-heavytail-stabil.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence on a real nonconvex MLP trained on UCI digits with injected heavy-tailed noise, verifying the stability functional forms, method ordering, and γ-invariance predictions of all five theoretical claims. The main limitation is that the population-gradient rate exponents are not recovered (consistently 3–8× smaller than predicted), which the logbook transparently attributes to finite-scale optimization floors, but the load-bearing qualitative predictions are confirmed.

snaykey/repro-gradflow-dro.paper_title: Gradient Flow Sampler-based Distributionally Robust Optimization

claims.claim: The paper introduces a unified PDE gradient flow framework for distributionally robust optimization (DRO) with six concrete algorithms, including Wasserstein Gradient Flow (Algorithm 3) and Wasserstein Fisher-Rao flow (Algorithm 4) variants for entropy-regularized Wasserstein DRO (Section 4, Algorithms 3-4).
claims.evidence: The WGF (Algorithm 3, ULA update) and WFR (Algorithm 4, birth-death resampling) samplers are implemented faithfully from the paper's equations and tested against a closed-form Gaussian worst-case distribution, achieving KL ≤ 0.0024 across d=1,2,5 with 20,000 particles and 4000 steps.

claims.claim: Proposition 1 shows the Wasserstein gradient flow sampler must run for time at least on the order of O((1/λ) log(L/√(λε))) to produce an ε-accurate gradient estimate (Section 4, Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: Mixing time scaling is measured directly: t* ∝ 1/λ (log-log slope −1.003, r=1.0000) and λ·t* ∝ log(1/ε_grad) (r=1.0000), with the particle sampler matching the analytic ULA recursion to 0.1% rel. err., confirming the O((1/λ)log(L/√(λε))) form.

claims.claim: Theorem 1 proves the outer loop of the gradient-flow-sampler-based DRO algorithm requires O(1/ε²_opt) iterations to reach an ε-stationary point (Section 5, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: On a non-convex surrogate with known ∇Φ and bounded-variance stochastic gradients, E‖∇Φ(θ_R)‖² decays as S^{−0.53} (target −0.5, r=−0.9998), yielding S(ε_opt) ∝ ε_opt^{−1.89} (target −2, r=−1.0000) across 7 horizon values and 48 runs.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 bounds the total computational complexity of the WGF-based DRO algorithm (Algorithm 3) as Õ(L_Φ L²_U L²_f d² / (λ³_U ε⁴_opt)) (Section 5, Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: By composing the measured outer-loop 1/ε² scaling with the inner ULA step-size/bias laws, the total work scales as d^{2.002} (r=1.0000) and ε_opt^{−4.27} (r=−1.0000), confirming the d²/ε⁴_opt dominant exponents of Theorem 2.
