SabaPivot/repro-explanations-are-a-means.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence from a completed HF Job on the full Ames Iowa dataset, real behavioral data from 998 human participants, exact symbolic verification of the garbling proposition, and executed worked examples, all supporting the six claims. The main caveat is that local runs failed due to an XGBoost/OpenMP architecture mismatch, and the authoritative results come from a remote HF Job whose full execution logs are summarized rather than fully displayed.

SabaPivot/repro-optimal-transport-under-.paper_title: Optimal Transport under Group Fairness Constraints

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 (FairSinkhorn) modifies the Sinkhorn algorithm with an additional group-level projection step to compute exact F-fair transport plans as defined in Definition 3.3 (Section 4, Algorithm 1, Definition 3.3).
claims.evidence: 78 instances across Gaussians/Circles at 50×50 and 100×1000 plus 7×7 groups show worst group-mass residual 1.11e-16 (machine precision) with marginals at 2.43e-17; plain Sinkhorn control gives 0.2730 residual; optimality certified by weak duality (1.13e-14 suboptimality), independent L-BFGS-B dual (sandwich width -2.22e-16), and independent SLSQP primal solve.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 derives a finite-sample complexity bound showing the expected deviation of the penalized entropic OT solution from the population optimum scales as O(1/√n), matching standard entropic OT sample-complexity rates (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: 169 GCG solves at n=25–1600 with 24 seeds show √n·error decreasing 0.655→0.118 (bound holds at every n); sharpness test on continuous Gaussian population gives two-sample exponent -0.464 vs theory -0.5; fixed-n₀ negative control correctly fails with √n·error growing 12.3×.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 bounds the fairness deviation of the bilevel cost-learning approach on unseen data uniformly over a parameterized cost family, with a dependence of the form exp(5R_Θ/ε)√n (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Bilevel eq. (7) with Mahalanobis cost reduces fairness loss 79.5% (sign-flip control increases it); 6 fixed θ values show per-θ decay slopes -0.438 to -0.785 with sup_θ at -0.438 and √n·sup bounded by 0.329; ε-sweep shows C(ε) growing as exp(0.0644/ε), inside the theorem's 5R_Θ=38.07 ceiling, confirming the exponential-in-1/ε form.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 and 3.2 establish existence, uniqueness, and dual-variable characterization of fair OT plans under compactness assumptions, ensuring the Sinkhorn-compatible structure used by Algorithm 1 (Section 3, Propositions 3.1-3.2).
claims.evidence: 200/200 random valid targets solved to <1e-12 (existence); 8 initializations agree to 7.81e-18 and projected Hessian λ_min=70.84>0 certifies uniqueness; dual form verified by blockwise rank-1 defect 1.10e-15, zero duality gap 3.33e-16, and independent dual-only L-BFGS-B solve matching Algorithm 1 to 3.09e-10; perturbed-plan control shows rank-1 defect 2.58e-02 (non-vacuous); infeasible F correctly causes failure.

claims.claim: Section 4.3 contrasts the two proposed strategies: the penalized formulation stays convex but must be re-solved per batch, while the bilevel cost-learning approach yields a reusable cost function at the expense of non-convex optimization (Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Penalized objective projected Hessian λ_min=68.25>0 with 0/2000 midpoint-convexity violations (convex); bilevel outer objective has 23/400 violations and min directional second difference -0.198<0 (non-convex); paper's Sec 5.1.4 protocol shows reused learned cost gives L_F=0.00661 at 7ms vs re-solved penalized L_F=0.0000681 at 1234ms (190× faster); penalized drives L_F to 1.951e-06 vs Mahalanobis floor 6.729e-03 (3450× gap, confirming flexibility difference).

SabaPivot/repro-optimal-transport-under-.overall: All five claims are supported by concrete numerical experiments on the paper's own datasets, target matrices, and scales, with independently written code, multiple cross-validation methods, and negative controls that fail when mechanisms are removed. The reproduction is rigorous with honest documentation of limitations (sampled universal quantifiers, exponential prefactor verified in form not magnitude, neural cost parameterization not tested).

SabaPivot/repro-incentivized-exploration.paper_title: Incentivized Exploration with Stochastic Covariates: A Two-Stage Mechanism Design for Recommender System

claims.claim: The RCB algorithm achieves an O(sqrt(KdT)) regret bound, where K is the number of arms, d the feature dimension, and T the time horizon (Section 4.3, Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: Confound-controlled fixed-gap environment sweeps over K∈{2..40}, d∈{2..20}, W∈{4096..131072} with 8 seeds show horizon exponents 0.516/0.515 and dimension exponent 0.547 against theory 0.5; the K-exponent of 0.7027 is explained by RCB's own IPGS rule yielding R=(σ/2)·((K−1)/√K)·√(dW), which fits all 20 configurations with R²=0.9974 and 2.4% mean error, confirming Θ(√(KdT)).

claims.claim: RCB simultaneously satisfies an epsilon-Dynamic Bayesian Incentive Compatibility (epsilon-DBIC) constraint, requiring a minimum cold-start sample size N(epsilon) that scales cubically with the number of arms K and linearly with dimension d (Section 4.2, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: N(ε) is exactly cubic in K (exponent 3.000) but its d-exponent over the paper's own dimensions {2,3,5,10,70} is 0.045 (essentially flat, not linear); additionally, running the real mechanism shows ε-DBIC is violated in 5.6% of cold-start rounds at K=10 (worst gain −1.83 vs budget 0.05), with violation rate growing with K.

claims.claim: The two-stage mechanism separates a Cold Start Stage (Algorithm 1), which explores products while preserving incentive compatibility, from an Exploitation Stage (Algorithm 2) using inverse proportional gap sampling (Section 3.1-3.2).
claims.evidence: On a real run (K=5, d=5, T=30000), all 5 structural checks pass: both stages reached, all 4 phases exercised, organic recommendations never corrupt statistics (0/1537 miscounted), every arm saturates before transition; the cold-start mechanism respects ε-DBIC in 95.1% of rounds vs 28.5% for a uniform-random baseline, and the two stages have distinct entropy profiles (0.82 vs 0.93).

claims.claim: The analysis reveals a tradeoff in which larger incentive budgets epsilon reduce required cold-start sample sizes but affect the regret guarantee (Section 4, Theorem 1 and Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: N(ε) is strictly monotonically decreasing in ε (closed form confirmed numerically), and running the real mechanism with 3 seeds per ε shows T_cold falling from 196,520 to 2,453 and total regret falling from 47,550 to 628 as ε rises from 0.02 to 0.12, confirming the tradeoff operationally.

claims.claim: In warfarin-dosing simulations using real data, RCB achieves a weighted risk score of approximately 0.29 compared to a physician baseline of 0.20, with error rates around 35% (Section 5.2, Table 1, Figure 2).
claims.evidence: On the real 5,528-patient IWPC cohort, the physician baseline (0.2236, close to paper's 0.20) and error rate (0.3882, matching paper's ~0.388) reproduce, but RCB's measured weighted risk score of 0.2599–0.2636 across three ε values falls well short of the claimed ≈0.29, though it does exceed the physician baseline in the correct direction.

SabaPivot/repro-incentivized-exploration.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous from-scratch reproduction with controlled confounds, multiple seeds, and real data, verifying the regret rate, two-stage structure, and incentive-budget tradeoff while falsifying the linear-in-d sample complexity claim and the specific warfarin risk score magnitude.

SabaPivot/repro-vlm-robustbench-a-compre.paper_title: VLM-RobustBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Robustness of Vision-Language Models

claims.claim: VLM-RobustBench evaluates 49 augmentations, including 42 severity-based corruptions across nine categories and 7 binary transforms (Table 1).
claims.evidence: An independent re-implementation (audit_taxonomy.py) enumerates 9 categories containing 42 severity augmentations and 7 binary transforms, summing to 49 types, with category counts (blur 5, noise 4, weather 5, digital 2, geometric 5, occlusion 3, color_tone 10, resolution 5, vlm_specific 3) confirmed by a fresh CPU audit with seed 1082026.

claims.claim: The benchmark yields 133 corrupted settings per model-dataset pair by applying three severities to 42 corruptions plus seven binary transforms (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The audit computes 42×3 + 7 = 133 corrupted settings (126 severity + 7 binary), with 135 including clean and no-image baselines, and independently realizes all 133 configurations as deterministic valid RGB uint8 images (133/133 byte-identical on re-run, 133/133 valid RGB).

claims.claim: The evaluation covers 11 VLMs from Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5, Molmo2, and Gemma 3 families on MMBench and MMMU-Pro (Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Cross-referencing the paper's Table 2 confirms 4 families (Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5, Molmo2, Gemma 3), 9 instruct checkpoints + 2 Qwen-Think = 11 total, evaluated on 2 benchmarks (MMBench EN dev 869 samples, MMMU-Pro 532 samples). This is a structural/count claim about the paper's experimental design, confirmed by table audit and fresh CPU audit (n_families=4).

claims.claim: Low-severity glass blur causes an average 8.1 percentage-point MMBench accuracy drop, larger than high-severity brightness reduction, illustrating a severity mismatch (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: On Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct at N=1000 MMBench-dev (parse rate 1.00, zero errors), low-severity glass_blur (imagecorruptions severity 1) causes a 1.4pp drop, not 8.1pp; the ~8.1pp magnitude appears at mid severity (8.9pp at severity 3). InternVL3-8B at N=300 corroborates with 2.7pp at low severity. The model substitution (Qwen2.5-VL vs Qwen3-VL) is a documented backend change at similar class, but the 5.8× discrepancy at the claimed severity level is concrete contradictory evidence.

claims.claim: The study finds that spatial and resampling perturbations such as upsample and elastic_transform can cause drops up to 34 percentage points (Section 1).
claims.evidence: Across six geometric/resampling transforms at maximum severity on Qwen2.5-VL-7B at N=1000 (elastic_transform s5 12.2pp, upsample×8 8.7pp, rotate 45° 2.7pp, shear 1.6pp, perspective 1.7pp), the largest drop is 12.2pp—roughly one-third of the claimed 34pp. InternVL3-8B at N=300 corroborates with a maximum drop of 11.7pp across all tested conditions. No tested configuration comes within 20pp of 34pp.

claims.claim: Robustness is reported to vary by model family rather than simply by parameter count, producing family-specific vulnerability fingerprints (Section 1).
claims.evidence: At matched parameter count (Qwen2.5-VL-7B vs InternVL3-8B, 1.14× scale ratio) on identical 300 MMBench-dev items with identical preprocessing, the two families invert their vulnerability ordering: Qwen shows geometric mean 4.8pp > photometric mean 3.5pp while InternVL shows photometric mean 7.2pp > geometric mean 5.0pp, with the worst single corruption also inverting (geometric elastic_transform for Qwen vs photometric glass_blur for InternVL). Parameter count is held approximately constant and cannot explain the divergence.

SabaPivot/repro-vlm-robustbench-a-compre.overall: The logbook independently verifies the benchmark's structural composition claims (49 augmentations, 133 settings, 11 VLMs across 4 families) via re-implementation and table audit, and confirms the family-fingerprint claim via a controlled matched-scale contrast. The two headline magnitude claims (8.1pp low-severity glass blur, 34pp spatial/resampling drops) are contradicted by full-scale GPU runs on two open-weight model families, though using earlier-generation model versions (Qwen2.5-VL/InternVL3 vs Qwen3-VL/InternVL3.5) and only 2 of 9 models.

SabaPivot/repro-full-batch-gradient-desc.paper_title: Full-Batch Gradient Descent Outperforms One-Pass SGD: Sample Complexity Separation in Single-Index Learning

claims.claim: For quadratic activation σ(z) = z², when the sample size n = o(d log d), spherical gradient flow fails to achieve weak recovery, showing full-batch updates offer no statistical advantage over one-pass SGD in this regime (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: Power iteration on M̂=(1/n)ΣyᵢxᵢxᵢT with quadratic activation across d=32–1024 (10 seeds, 13 ratios) shows the weak-recovery threshold ratio n*/d grows with log d (slope +0.562, R²=0.900), and at fixed n/d=6 the mean overlap decays with log d (slope -0.0292), both consistent with failure below the d log d scale.

claims.claim: With a truncated quadratic activation, full-batch spherical gradient flow achieves weak recovery with only n ≳ d samples, compared to the n ≳ d log d samples required by one-pass SGD, establishing a sample complexity separation (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Same power-iteration mechanism with truncated activation y=clip(z²,0,6) shows threshold ratio n*/d stays flat (slope +0.102, under a third of the quadratic slope +0.562) across d=32–1024, with the threshold confined to a narrow 3.89–4.44 band, consistent with Θ(d) rather than Θ(d log d) sample complexity.

claims.claim: Using the truncated activation on squared loss with small initialization (r₀ = d^-15), full-batch gradient descent achieves strong recovery in T ≳ log d gradient steps given n ≥ CM⁴d samples (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Full-batch squared-loss GD with literal r0=d^-15 (down to ~2.3e-41 at d=512) and truncated activation M=16 shows median steps-to-‖β̂-β*‖<1e-4 scaling linearly with log d (slope 77.04, R²=0.9915) across d=32–512, with 20/25 runs achieving exact recovery; the 80% success rate is honestly reported and the median is robust to stalls.

claims.claim: The trajectory of full-batch gradient descent decomposes into an initial angle-reduction phase lasting O(log d/η) steps followed by geometric convergence during a refinement phase (Section 4).
claims.evidence: From the same GD trajectories: search-phase length (cos>0.9 threshold) scales with log d (slope 80.79, R²=0.9632) and with 1/η (η×search_time CV=0.099 across an 8× η range at d=256), while the refinement phase shows geometric convergence (log(error) vs step median R²=0.9986, slope -0.0273).

claims.claim: Full-batch methods with truncated activation match the information-theoretic sample lower bound of n ≳ d, removing the extra log d factor that is unavoidable for one-pass SGD under quadratic activation (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Streaming one-pass Oja SGD with the same truncated activation (best-of-3 learning rates) shows threshold ratio n*/d growing steeply with log d (slope +2.548, R²=0.922) while full-batch truncated stays flat (slope +0.102), yielding a measured gap of +2.45 that directly demonstrates the algorithmic separation; the information-theoretic lower bound itself is cited from the paper, not re-derived.

SabaPivot/repro-full-batch-gradient-desc.overall: This logbook provides concrete, independently-implemented experimental evidence (pure numpy, unit-tested, no paper code) across all five claims at the paper's native scale (d up to 1024 for weak recovery, 512 for trajectory), measuring real power-iteration thresholds, GD trajectories from literal d^-15 initialization, and a one-pass SGD baseline that together reproduce the predicted sample-complexity separation and two-phase dynamics. The main limitations are finite-d rather than asymptotic evidence and an honestly-reported 80% success rate for strong recovery, but the numerical trends are statistically robust and directly support each claim.

SabaPivot/repro-on-the-convergence-rate-.paper_title: On the Convergence Rate of LoRA Gradient Descent

claims.claim: LoRA gradient descent converges to a stationary point at rate O(1/log T) in the general case without assuming Lipschitz smoothness of the reparameterized objective (Theorem 3, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: On the paper's own separable-logistic family at d=100, 3 seeds, T=5000, the two proof-critical inequalities (norm-growth bound and harmonic step-size lower bound) each hold at 100% of all 15,000 step×seed checks, Eq.(10) holds at every step, and the measured guarantee curve 4(J₀−L*)/Σηₜ fits a 1/log(t)-linear form with R²=0.964. The adapter norm genuinely grows unboundedly (tail exponent 0.289>0), confirming the general-case regime is actually entered.

claims.claim: When adapter norms are bounded, the same LoRA gradient descent algorithm converges at the faster rate O(1/T) (Theorem 3, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: With the bounded-norm hypothesis literally enforced by projection (max‖V‖=4.40<5.0) and a flat-minimum loss ψ(u)=u⁴/(1+u²) avoiding strong-convexity flooring, Σηₜ grows with log-log slope 0.881 (R²=0.9924) and the Eq.(10) guarantee decays at slope −0.881, matching Θ(1/T) rather than Θ(1/log T). The actual min‖∇J‖² decays even faster (slope −2.80), staying strictly under the guarantee.

claims.claim: The analysis relies only on Assumption 1 (Lipschitz smoothness of the original, non-reparameterized loss) and Assumption 2 (the loss is lower bounded), avoiding artificially imposed smoothness on the LoRA-reparameterized objective (Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: Measured local-Lipschitz ratios confirm L is globally smooth for two loss families (least-squares: 0.0123→0.0122 across 10⁴× scale, both ≤0.0223; logistic: 0.0036→0.00028, both ≤0.0055), while the reparameterized J(V)=L(BA) has local-Lipschitz ratio growing as ‖V‖^2.00 (R²=0.9990) over a 100× range — no finite global smoothness constant exists for J, directly supporting the minimal-assumption premise.

claims.claim: The proof derives a Lipschitz-like descent lemma (Lemma 1) accounting for higher-order terms from the bilinear BA^T reparameterization, paired with an adaptive step-size rule ηt = min{1/(5√2 L(‖Vt‖^2+‖∇L(·)‖)), 1} (Lemma 2, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: Lemma 3.3 (higher-order descent bound with bilinear terms) and Lemma 3.4 (one-step descent under adaptive step) were checked pointwise at floating-point tolerance (1e-9·(|J|+1)) on the exact T=5000 trajectory across 3 seeds, holding at 100% of all 15,000 step×seed checks. The implementation correctly uses the paper's actual 4√2 constant from arXiv v3, not the registry's 5√2 typo.

claims.claim: The paper shows the derived convergence rate is independent of the chosen LoRA rank, since gradient descent on the low-rank factors operates dimension-free (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: A 16× rank sweep (r∈{1,2,4,8,16}) with identical X/y/seed/T shows the rate-governing Σηₜ growth exponent is {0.541, 0.547, 0.547, 0.559, 0.559} with std=0.0072<0.05, demonstrating rank-invariance. Although d=30 (reduced from d=100 for sweep speed), the mechanism and loss family are identical and the claim is specifically about rank-independence, not absolute scale.

SabaPivot/repro-on-the-convergence-rate-.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous from-scratch numpy re-implementation of the paper's LoRA gradient descent algorithm, verifying all five theoretical claims through concrete pointwise inequality checks, measured growth exponents, and direct Lipschitz-ratio measurements on non-toy synthetic problems at the paper's own d=100 scale (d=30 only for the rank sweep). The evidence is honest about the distinction between worst-case asymptotic bounds and finite-T observables, and correctly verifies the proof machinery rather than attempting to observe unobservable asymptotic slopes directly.

SabaPivot/repro-upper-linearizability-of.paper_title: Upper-Linearizability of Online Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization over Down-Closed Convex Sets

claims.claim: Theorem 1 proves that non-monotone DR-submodular functions over down-closed convex sets are 1/e-Upper-Linearizable via the exponential reparameterization h(x) = 1 - e^{-x} combined with a designed surrogate potential.
claims.evidence: Theorem 1's inequality (1/e)f(y)-f(h(x)) ≤ (1-1/e)⟨∇F(x),y-x⟩ holds 1800/1800 random trials at d∈{3,5,8} with worst slack 0.2357≥0, plus exhaustive 2^d box-corner stress tests; Lemma 1 holds 6000/6000 trials; surrogate potential F and gradient ∇F computed via independent Gauss-Legendre quadrature and cross-checked against finite differences (max|diff|<2e-4).

claims.claim: The BQND algorithm (Algorithm 1) reduces online non-monotone DR-submodular maximization to online linear optimization using a single gradient query per round.
claims.evidence: Exactly one oracle query per round confirmed by direct counting across 2,372,800/2,372,800 rounds; BQND estimator is unbiased (Monte-Carlo convergence rate n^-0.473 vs CLT -0.5, R²=0.961) and norm-bounded (max‖g‖=3.8884 ≤ B₁=3.8889); three structurally different OLO base learners (projected OGA, 8-expert Improved Ader, OGA over SFTT blocks) consume the identical BQND stream with Theorem 3 transfer holding 100/100 and 252/252.

claims.claim: Proposition 1 shows BQND obtains O(T^{1/2}) static regret with only O(1) oracle queries per round, improving on prior work's O(T^{2/3}) regret for single queries or O(T^{1/2}) regret requiring T^{3/2} queries per round.
claims.evidence: Linear-surrogate regret fits log R = 0.3086 + 0.5009·log(T) at R²=0.9999 (exponent 0.501 vs paper's 0.500), independently re-measured at 0.5017 on a disjoint T grid; √T fits the measured curve 49x better than T^{2/3} in log-log RMSE (0.0112 vs 0.5487); single query per round verified across 256,000/256,000 rounds; Theorem 3 transfer holds 100/100.

claims.claim: Proposition 3 establishes a dynamic regret bound of Õ(T^{1/2}·√(1+P_T)) where P_T is the path length of the comparator sequence.
claims.evidence: Improved Ader run for 2,116,800 single-query rounds on a down-closed knapsack polytope with measured P_T from 0 to 166.254; R/√(T(1+P_T)) stays within a 5.37x band while T(1+P_T) spans ~5,300x; the P_T exponent converges monotonically toward 0.5 (0.800→0.737) while the switched-off OGA control diverges (1.204→1.465); two-term fit attributes 93.8% of regret at T=25,600 to the paper's √(T(1+P_T)) term at R²=0.9731; transfer holds 252/252.

claims.claim: In the bandit feedback model, the framework achieves O(T^{4/5}) regret (Proposition 6), and in the semi-bandit model O(T^{2/3}) regret (Proposition 4).
claims.evidence: Semi-bandit O(T^{2/3}) is supported (measured exponent 0.6457, T^{2/3} best fixed-exponent fit by 3.7x, prescribed block size L=T^{1/3} at empirical minimum), but the bandit claim is contradicted: the paper's own Proposition 6 body states O(T^{2/3}) (not O(T^{4/5}) as the claim asserts), and the measured STB envelope exponent of 0.8614 rules out T^{2/3} across all eight tunings (all ≥0.736) and sits above Table 1's T^{4/5}=0.8, with T^{5/6} being the best fixed-exponent fit.

SabaPivot/repro-upper-linearizability-of.overall: The logbook provides strong independent experimental support for Claims 1-4 at the paper's native scale (d up to 8, T up to 128,000, 2.6M+ online rounds), with proper DR-submodular test functions, exhaustive corner checks, and multiple base learners confirming the reduction. Claim 5's semi-bandit rate reproduces but the bandit rate is falsified: the paper is internally inconsistent about Proposition 6's rate, and the measured envelope exponent (0.8614) contradicts both the claimed T^{4/5} and the paper's own Proposition 6 body text of T^{2/3}.

SabaPivot/repro-bandit-social-leaning-dy.paper_title: Bandit Social Leaning Dynamics with Exploration Episodes

claims.claim: In the Episodic Bandit Social Learning (EpiBSL) model with two-armed Bernoulli bandits and episode length m≥2, aggregate exploration fails with probability at least q_P^m > 0 for any symmetric utility aggregation function, even though each agent explores within its own episode (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive 135-configuration grid (9 priors × {sum,max,min} × m∈{2..6}) confirms arm-2 abandonment within N_P pulls with 0/135 exceptions, and exact rational computation of the witness event probability Pr[Ev2]=(1-μ2)^N_P for m=2..9 yields a log-slope matching the theoretical q_P^m decay to |diff|=4.4e-16, providing a concrete positive lower-bound witness as Theorem 4.1 requires.

claims.claim: When exploration failure occurs, Bayesian regret grows linearly in the time horizon T, satisfying BReg(T) ≥ c0(T − N0) for constants c0, N0 depending only on the prior (Corollary 4.5).
claims.evidence: The Theorem 3.6 deterministic backbone Reg(t)≥(t−N_t)·G(μ) holds with 0 violations across 30,000 checks (150 realizations × T=200), mean regret 82.54 exceeds the fail-fraction·T·G lower bound of 66.0, and the control with arm 1 truly best yields Reg(T)=0 confirming linear regret is specific to the failure event.

claims.claim: For episode length m=2, learning failure occurs with positive probability even for non-symmetric per-episode utility aggregation functions, not just sum/min/max (Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: The paper's own Appendix G.2 hard instance is reproduced digit-for-digit in exact rational arithmetic (optimal value 1223/2000=0.6115, policy arm2→skip/arm1, alternatives 0.6045 and 0.53 all matching), plus a second independently chosen non-symmetric utility f=r1+2r2 shows arm-2 exploration then abandonment with Pr[tape]=0.4>0.

claims.claim: For m=2 with symmetric utility functions, or for max/min aggregation at any episode length m, failure probability remains positive even without imposing exploration costs on agents (Theorem 4.7).
claims.evidence: Lemma 3.9 closed-form utility-gap bounds verified with 0 violations across 1,152 exact rational configurations (576 min + 576 max), with exact tightness at csel=0; additionally, 24/24 (f,csel,m) cases for max and min at costs up to the maximal csel=1.0 confirm failure without any cost restriction.

claims.claim: The stronger failure event StrongFail_{c,N} (at most N episodes ever try the good arm) occurs with probability at least 1/2 conditional on the base failure event FAIL_{c,N} (Lemma 3.4).
claims.evidence: Per-good-episode arm-2 pull probability verified ≥ c^m over 320 grid points (min 0.0711 ≥ 0.008), exhaustive enumeration of all 2^10=1024 good-episode sequences yields Pr[Bridge]=0.9453≥1/2, the paper's own N' formula gives exact binomial tail 1.0≥1−δ/2, and an undersized-N' control yields Pr[Bridge]=1.01e-5≪1/2 confirming the bound is non-vacuous.

SabaPivot/repro-bandit-social-leaning-dy.overall: This logbook presents a clean-room exact rational-arithmetic reimplementation of the EpiBSL backward-induction engine, verified against independent brute-force enumeration (15/15 unit tests), and provides concrete numerical evidence across exhaustive configuration grids, exact probability computations, and destructive controls for all five claims. The evidence operates at the paper's own native scale (finite decision trees of depth m≤6, two-armed Bernoulli bandits) rather than a reduced proxy, and every claim is supported by measured numbers rather than formula substitution.

claims.claim: The optimal collaborative prediction set C*(x) has a two-threshold form: it augments the human-proposed set H(x) with labels whose score exceeds threshold a*, and prunes labels within H(x) whose score exceeds threshold b* (Theorem 2.1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: The two-threshold rule (exact kink-based separable search) vs the unconstrained ILP optimum shows relative gap shrinking from 0.0105 (L=40) to 0.0041 (L=200) as the label grid refines toward the continuous limit, while a shuffled-score control stays flat at 1.40–1.73, confirming the near-zero gap reflects the theorem's structure rather than a vacuous test.

claims.claim: The counterfactual harm principle requires P(Y not in C(X) | Y in H(X)) < epsilon, i.e., the AI must not remove correct labels the human already proposed (Section 1).
claims.evidence: CUP-Offline's split-conformal pruning threshold controls realized harm to 0.063 (target ε=0.08) at n_cal=80,000 with 90% of seeds satisfying the bound, while a model-drift control (frozen threshold, drifted test-time scorer) breaks the guarantee with harm jumping to 0.377 and 100% of seeds violating.

claims.claim: The complementarity principle requires P(Y in C(X) | Y not in H(X)) >= 1-delta, i.e., the AI must recover correct labels the human missed (Section 1).
claims.evidence: CUP-Offline's augmentation threshold tracks complementarity coverage to mean 0.7821 (target 1-δ=0.78) at n_cal=80,000, with the model-drift control collapsing coverage to 0.516 and 100% of seeds falling below target, confirming the guarantee rests on exchangeability.

claims.claim: The offline calibration procedure gives distribution-free finite-sample coverage guarantees whose bounds depend on the sizes of the calibration sets used to fit a* and b* (Proposition 4.1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: The 1/(n+1) slack shrinks monotonically from 0.01977 (n=150) to 0.000202 (n=15,000) with frac_slack_shrinks=1.0, directly demonstrating calibration-size dependence; lower bounds hold 100% of n_cal settings, and a noise-inflation control breaks them (out-H coverage drops to 0.658 vs target 0.82).

claims.claim: The CUP-Online algorithm updates thresholds a_t and b_t via stochastic approximation steps (a_{t+1}=a_t+eta(1{s(x_t,y_t)>a_t}-delta), and analogously for b_t) to track target error rates under arbitrary distribution shift, including shifts caused by humans adapting their behavior to the AI (Section 4.2, Proposition 4.2).
claims.evidence: The SA recursion implemented exactly as specified tracks targets under all three shift regimes (in-rate ~0.097 vs target 0.09, out-rate ~0.244 vs target 0.24) within the Proposition 4.2 bound for 12/12 seeds, and under the human-sharpening shift the frozen baseline degrades to out-dev 0.0450 vs CUP-Online's 0.0036.

SabaPivot/repro-human-ai-collaborative-u.overall: All five claims are supported by concrete experimental evidence on synthetic but non-trivial setups (calibration sizes up to 80,000, label grids up to 200, online streams of 22,000 steps) with controls that break specific preconditions to validate the tests are non-vacuous. The reproduction targets the paper's theoretical guarantees directly rather than its application experiments, which is appropriate given the claims are theorems and propositions about distribution-free properties.

SabaPivot/repro-softjax-softtorch-empowe.paper_title: SoftJAX & SoftTorch: Empowering Automatic Differentiation Libraries with Informative Gradients

claims.claim: SoftJAX and SoftTorch provide differentiable soft surrogates for hard primitives including thresholding (sign, abs, round, ReLU, clip via Heaviside relaxations), Boolean/fuzzy logic operators, discrete indexing (SoftIndex), and sorting/ranking (Sections 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: Ran the real softjax v0.1.1 library on 11 operators across all 4 claimed families, measuring jax.grad on hard vs. soft paths: sign/round/heaviside have exactly-zero hard gradients with non-zero soft gradients (65-100% nonzero), logical_and/or/xor have exactly-zero hard gradients with soft gradient norms 51-53, SoftIndex gives 0.0 hard vs 0.31-0.99 soft at 7 test points, and hard rank has all-zero gradient vs soft rank norm 0.1280.

claims.claim: The libraries identify an 'STE pitfall' where applying straight-through estimation separately to each factor of a multiplicative composite operation causes gradients to vanish, and show this is avoided by applying STE to the composite function as a whole (Section 2, Equation 1).
claims.evidence: 40,000 gradient evaluations across 8 heaviside composite pairs × 5000 points show per-factor STE vanishes at 36.25% of points while whole-composite STE vanishes at only 0.605%, a 60× reduction directly demonstrating the Eq. 1 mechanism using real softjax primitives.

claims.claim: Four families of differentiable sort/rank operators are implemented: optimal-transport-based, unit-simplex-projection-based (SoftSort, NeuralSort), permutahedron-projection-based (FastSoftSort, and a novel entropy-regularized SmoothSort variant), and sorting-network-based (Sections 4.1-4.4).
claims.evidence: All 6 real sj.sort method strings (ot, softsort, neuralsort, fast_soft_sort, smooth_sort, sorting_network) spanning the 4 claimed families were invoked on identical input, with 6/6 producing monotone sorted output and 6/6 having finite non-zero Jacobians (max|grad| 0.40-1.98) verified via jax.jacobian.

claims.claim: FastSoftSort achieves the lowest memory footprint (~420KB) among benchmarked soft-sorting methods at n=4096, while the sorting-network approach is fastest at ~1.0ms (3.8x the hard baseline), versus ~16ms for SoftSort and ~37ms for NeuralSort (Section 5, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: At n=4096 on CPU, FastSoftSort has lowest memory (2273KB via XLA cost_analysis vs 29760-41805KB for others) and sorting_network is fastest backward pass (3.555ms = 3.42× hard baseline vs paper's 3.8×), with softsort (52ms) < neuralsort (99.6ms) preserving the paper's relative ordering; absolute values differ by hardware but the two superlative claims and ordering are confirmed at full scale.

claims.claim: A case study applies SoftJAX operators (sj.argmax, sj.dynamic_index_in_dim) to soften the manifold-point-selection step of MuJoCo XLA's collision detection pipeline, enabling gradient flow through a previously non-differentiable physics operation (Appendix B).
claims.evidence: Built a real mujoco.mjx box-on-plane model, ran mjx.forward() to obtain a genuine 4-point contact manifold, reproduced MJX's _manifold_points selector verbatim, and measured jax.grad of selected points w.r.t. all 8 vertices: hard selector gives exactly 0.0 gradient at non-selected vertices while the softened version (sj.argmax + sj.dynamic_index_in_dim) gives gradient norm 0.03376 at those same vertices.

SabaPivot/repro-softjax-softtorch-empowe.overall: This logbook provides concrete experimental evidence for all 5 claims by running the real softjax/softtorch v0.1.1 libraries with measured jax.grad/jax.jacobian outputs, wall-clock and memory benchmarks at n=4096, and a genuine MuJoCo-XLA physics scene. The reproduction is rigorous and honest, including disclosure of 2/19 failed finite-difference unit tests and CPU-only hardware caveats for claim 4, while all relative ordering claims and mechanism-level evidence hold.

Frame17/repro-xskill-continual-learning-.paper_title: XSkill: Continual Learning from Experience and Skills in Multimodal Agents

claims.claim: XSkill maintains two complementary knowledge stores extracted in a training-free Phase I (Accumulation): visually-grounded rollout summaries and cross-rollout critiques of successful versus failed trajectories, later consolidated hierarchically to reduce redundancy (Section on Architecture/Phase I).
claims.evidence: Codebase analysis confirms two stores (skills as Markdown, experiences as JSON) with consolidation mechanisms (batch_merge at 0.7 threshold, skill merging), and local runs showed the experience library growing online from E0-E3 to E4 with dedup-merging, but only on 2-4 samples with local Ollama models — not at the paper's scale.

claims.claim: Across five benchmarks (VisualToolBench, TIR-Bench, MMSearch-Plus, MMBrowseComp, and AgentVista) and four backbone models, XSkill yields average improvements of 2.58 to 6.71 points over tool-only baselines, with a maximum single-benchmark improvement of 11.13 points on challenging visual reasoning tasks (Evaluation section, Performance Results).
claims.evidence: Local runs on gemma4:12b show XSkill beating tools-only (0.500 vs 0.250 on Tool_Test, 0.500 vs 0.375 on VisualProbe_Test), directionally consistent with the paper, but only 2-4 samples with one local model — the claimed 2.58-6.71 point gains across 5 benchmarks and 4 backbone models were not reproduced; paper Table 2 numbers are quoted, not independently generated.

claims.claim: XSkill is compared against Agent Workflow Memory, Dynamic CheatSheet, and Agent-KB baselines, with the proposed method winning consistently, particularly on tasks requiring complex visual reasoning and multi-step tool composition (Evaluation section).
claims.evidence: A head-to-head comparison with proxy baselines on 2 samples (run 065f180c) shows XSkill at 0.500 accuracy, tying Agent-KB proxy (0.500) and Dynamic CheatSheet proxy (0.500) and beating AWM proxy (0.250) — XSkill does not consistently win as claimed, but the scale is too small to falsify; the logbook itself notes the paper's margin over Agent-KB was not reproduced.

claims.claim: Ablation-style analysis shows the 'skills' stream reduces structural/syntax errors from 20.3% to 11.4% via tool templates and workflow guidance, while the 'experiences' stream shifts tool-usage patterns contextually, e.g., code-interpreter usage rising from 66.63% to 76.97% on visual tasks (Methodology Insights section).
claims.evidence: A local ablation (run ea83cb59, 2 samples) showed no accuracy delta between skills-only, experiences-only, and full pipeline (all 0.500), and skills-only actually produced parse failures in 4/4 rollouts — the specific claimed numbers (20.3%→11.4% structural errors, 66.63%→76.97% code-interpreter usage) were not reproduced, though experiences-only showing more focused responses is directionally consistent.

claims.claim: XSkill's Phase II (Inference) applies retrieved knowledge through task decomposition into subtasks, context-aware visual adaptation of retrieved knowledge, and non-prescriptive injection that preserves agent flexibility (Architecture, Phase II section).
claims.evidence: Codebase analysis confirms the Phase II components exist (experience_retriever.py for retrieval, rewrite_experiences_for_task for context adaptation, inference_prompts.yaml for injection), and local runs exercised the full pipeline with retrieval engaging during rollouts, but the specific mechanisms of task decomposition, context-aware visual adaptation, and non-prescriptive injection were not isolated or tested separately — only run end-to-end at 2-4 sample scale.

Frame17/repro-xskill-continual-learning-.overall: The logbook provides thorough codebase verification and toy-scale local runs (2-4 samples with Ollama models like gemma4:12b and qwen3-vl:8b) that show directional consistency with some paper claims, but none of the five claims are reproduced at the paper's stated scale (5 benchmarks × 4 backbone models). The reproduction is limited by lack of access to proprietary model APIs and benchmark datasets, resulting in all claims being addressed only at toy scale.

amkkk/repro-projection-head-geometry-con.paper_title: The Geometry of Projection Heads: Conditioning, Invariance, and Collapse

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 shows that smooth nonlinear projection heads (e.g., using Swish or GELU) destabilize collapsed equilibria by injecting negative eigenvalues into the effective Hessian, while linear heads preserve collapse since the interaction term vanishes (Theorem 4.1, Section 4)
claims.evidence: Exact autograd Hessian eigenvalues at near-collapsed equilibria show Swish min eigenvalue -0.0352 and GELU -0.0357, while linear and ReLU are exactly 0.0 across all 15 configurations (4 activations × 5 seeds × 3 variances), with a symbolic derivation confirming the interaction term ∝ σ''(c)·(h²+h₀²) vanishes when σ''≡0.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes that linear projection heads perform implicit local subspace whitening, achieving isotropy only on the active subspace determined by the loss rank (Theorem 3.1, Section 3)
claims.evidence: Exhaustive numerical verification across 2400 trials (d=4..12, r=2..5) confirms the whitening map W=diag(1/√λ)U_r^T yields WHW^T=I_r on the active subspace (max error 2.2e-15) and annihilates the null subspace (max error 1.4e-15), with symbolic derivation showing full-space isotropy is impossible when r<d.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.3 shows that when the loss geometry has nonvanishing Riemann curvature, no global linear map can produce everywhere-isotropic conditioning, motivating the use of nonlinear heads (Proposition 3.3, Section 3)
claims.evidence: Symbolic argument shows W^T M(x) W = I for all x forces M(x) constant (flat), confirmed numerically: global linear isotropization residual is 0.0 for flat fields (k=0) but 4.23–9.42 for curved fields (k=0.5–2), while pointwise nonlinear maps achieve residuals of 8.5e-4–2.5e-5.

claims.claim: Figure 3 tracks the Hessian spectrum during training and shows that smooth-activation heads inject negative eigenvalues enabling escape from collapse, whereas ReLU-based heads fail to do so, relying instead on discrete dynamics and BatchNorm (Figure 3, Section 6)
claims.evidence: On the reduced setup (n=64, d=8, k=4, no BatchNorm), ReLU spread grew 0.0006→0.417 and linear 0.0008→0.513, meaning every head escaped near-collapse, contradicting the paper's ReLU-fails claim; however, the setup lacks BatchNorm and discrete dynamics that the claim itself identifies as necessary for ReLU's behavior, so the claim cannot be properly tested.

claims.claim: The geometric analysis is applied across both contrastive methods (InfoNCE, SimCLR, MoCo, DINO) and non-contrastive/decorrelation-based methods (BYOL, SimSiam, VICReg, Barlow Twins) (Section 6)
claims.evidence: All eight SSL losses (InfoNCE, SimCLR, MoCo, DINO, BYOL, SimSiam, VICReg, Barlow Twins) were implemented and decomposed into alignment+uniformity components on synthetic batches (n=32, d=8) with effective-rank Hessian analysis, demonstrating the framework's applicability but at drastically reduced scale.

claims.claim: Figure 5 shows PCA visualization demonstrating 21.85x compression of augmentation orbits under the learned projection head geometry (Figure 5, Section 6)
claims.evidence: A synthetic setup (6 classes × 32 augmented views, 24-d base vectors, 6-d tanh head) shows orbit compression (1264x under balanced protocol), qualitatively matching the claim's direction, but the exact 21.85x magnitude is not reproduced and the official dataset, augmentation family, and head geometry are unavailable.

amkkk/repro-projection-head-geometry-con.overall: The logbook provides rigorous formal derivations and exhaustive numerical verification for the three theoretical claims (Theorems 4.1, 3.1, and Proposition 3.3), but the empirical claims about training dynamics and orbit compression are only addressed on reduced synthetic setups lacking the paper's official architectures, datasets, and BatchNorm.

nmaher/repro-worldcomp2d-spatio-semantic.paper_title: WorldComp2D: Spatio-semantic Representations of Object Identity and Location from Local Views

claims.claim: WorldComp2D reduces parameter count by up to 4.0x (from 9.7M to 2.4M parameters) and FLOPs by up to 2.2x compared to the PoPos SoTA lightweight baseline, with the full breakdown across its proximity-dependent encoder (PdEnc, 1.1M params), localizer (1.3M params), and auxiliary localizer (AuxLoc, 4.0K params) modules given in Table 1.
claims.evidence: FLOPs match within 0.7% across all three configurations (295.4M vs 293.7M, 548.4M vs 546.8M, 258.6M vs 256.9M after MACs→FLOPs convention). Parameter count is ~8% higher than stated (2.57–2.62M vs 2.4M, yielding 3.7–3.8× not 4.0× reduction), traced to the localizer module measuring 1.48M vs the paper's 1.3M via direct checkpoint state_dict enumeration, but the overall reduction claim and FLOPs are substantively confirmed.

claims.claim: WorldComp2D achieves real-time CPU inference on an Intel i5-13400 of 138.4 FPS on COFW, 78.48 FPS on 300W, and 163.55 FPS on AFLW, while attaining normalized mean error (NME) of 5.16 on COFW, 5.06 on 300W, and 1.52 (NME_Diag) on AFLW, competitive with but slightly behind SoTA regression methods (Table 2, Table 1).
claims.evidence: COFW NME matches near-exactly (5.165±0.052 vs 5.16±0.05) on the full 507-image test set, but 300W and AFLW NME are untested due to dataset access restrictions, and FPS was measured on a different, weaker CPU (i7-8550U laptop vs i5-13400 desktop) yielding 5–18× lower absolute numbers with only ordering preserved—insufficient to confirm the specific FPS claims or 2 of 3 NME values.

claims.claim: Under degradations such as blur, JPEG compression, motion blur, and occlusion, WorldComp2D shows a maximum accuracy degradation of about 10.2% (extreme occlusion on 300W), with consistently moderate degradation across other corruption types (Table 4).
claims.evidence: On COFW, 10 of 12 corrupted conditions match within ~0.05 NME of the paper across blur, JPEG, motion blur, and occlusion, but the specific claim about 'maximum degradation of about 10.2% on 300W extreme occlusion' is untested because 300W and AFLW test sets are inaccessible; only 1 of 3 datasets was evaluated.

claims.claim: In zero-shot cross-dataset transfer from a model trained on 300W and evaluated on COFW-68, WorldComp2D's NME degrades by only 20.2%, compared to 27-32% degradation for regression-based baselines (Table 6).
claims.evidence: Zero-shot 300W→COFW-68 transfer NME_IO measured at 6.082±0.145 vs the paper's 6.08±0.14, with the 20.2% degradation figure matching to one decimal place, on the full 507-image COFW-68 test set using the released pretrained checkpoint; the 300W in-distribution baseline (5.06) was taken from the paper rather than independently re-derived, but the transfer result itself is a direct independent measurement.

claims.claim: WorldComp2D's latent space explicitly structures object identity and spatial proximity, exhibiting intra-class clustering by landmark class, inter-class separation between landmark identities, and latent L2 distances that correlate with real-world spatial proximity within the receptive field (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Using the pretrained COFW PdEnc on real test images, the reproduction quantified all three panels: intra-class clustering inter/intra L2 ratio of 4.54×, inter-class separation Spearman ρ of 0.995 (p<0.0001) for left-pupil-vs-other-classes latent distances, and distance-preservation Spearman ρ of 1.000 (p<0.0001) for radial offset vs latent distance within the receptive field—concrete quantitative evidence supporting the structured-latent-space claim.

nmaher/repro-worldcomp2d-spatio-semantic.overall: The logbook provides strong, non-toy evidence supporting Claims 1, 4, and 5 on the full COFW test set with near-exact quantitative matches, while Claims 2 and 3 are only partially addressed on COFW due to 300W/AFLW dataset access restrictions and different FPS measurement hardware, leaving those claims' full scope unverified.

amkkk/repro-relative-entropy-estimation-.paper_title: Relative Entropy Estimation in Function Space: Theory and Applications to Trajectory Inference

claims.claim: The paper derives a tractable estimator for the KL divergence between trajectory distributions in function space, expressed via squared discrepancies between the associated velocity fields under Functional Flow Matching (Theorem 3.6).
claims.evidence: The Theorem 3.6 identity is numerically verified only on the Gaussian special case with exact velocity fields (MC estimate 3.6601 vs analytic 3.6698, Lemma 3.5 max error 1.07e-14, quadrature relative error 2.9e-06), using a truncated spectral basis and no trained pipeline — a simplified validation of the analytic core, not the paper's full estimator at scale.

claims.claim: On synthetic Gaussian-measure validation cases, the estimator's KL values range from 3.95 to 45.73 across 8 configurations, closely matching analytic ground-truth values of 3.64 to 45.43 (Table 1).
claims.evidence: The 8-configuration Gaussian validation is run with a reduced spectral model; 7/8 analytic values match within ~1%, but the measured estimated range is 3.70–85.11 rather than the paper's 3.95–45.73, with case 4 deviating 17.9% due to a different Matérn eigenvalue discretization — the specific numerical range claim is not reproduced, though the estimator-vs-analytic matching pattern holds on the simplified model.

claims.claim: The functional KL estimator is benchmarked against five methods (vSB, SBIRR, MSBM, MFL, AM, TIGON) on synthetic dynamical systems (Lotka-Volterra, Repressilator, Petal) and four real single-cell RNA-seq datasets (EB, hESC, ME, HF), using marginal metrics (EMD, W2, SWD, MWD, MMD) alongside forward and reverse functional KL (Tables 2-3).
claims.evidence: The benchmark protocol is demonstrated on three simulated synthetic systems with six simplified proxy stand-ins (not official codebases) and a MINO-lite estimator; the four real scRNA-seq datasets (EB, hESC, ME, HF) are not used, and Tables 2-3 numerical values are not reproduced.

claims.claim: On the Repressilator dataset, TIGON ranks above SBIRR according to marginal metrics but below SBIRR according to functional KL, illustrating that marginal-metric-based evaluation can be inconsistent with trajectory-level evaluation (Section on TI benchmark evaluation, Tables 2-3).
claims.evidence: The Repressilator ordering inconsistency is reproduced using two deliberately constructed proxies (TIGON-like smooth interpolation vs SBIRR-like noisy oscillation) that were designed to exhibit the phenomenon, not the actual TIGON/SBIRR methods; the qualitative ordering is replicated on a simplified analog but absolute values differ substantially from Table 2b.

claims.claim: Figure 3 shows that marginal-metric-based rankings on Lotka-Volterra and Repressilator are often statistically indistinguishable despite apparently large numerical differences between methods, undermining confidence in marginal-only evaluation (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The Nemenyi CD analysis is run on Lotka-Volterra and Repressilator analogs with six proxy stand-ins, finding 83.3% of pairs statistically indistinguishable at α=0.05; however, the proxies are simplified and the paper's full task list, official trajectories, and Wilcoxon-Holm post-hoc procedure are not reproduced.

claims.claim: The estimator uses a Mesh-Informed Neural Operator (MINO) architecture with a subtraction-based parameterization enforcing boundary conditions and Monte Carlo integration that does not require simulating the full generative dynamics via ODE integration (Section 4).
claims.evidence: A small MINO-lite stand-in (shared-MLP, 64-point grid, 1500 functions, 500 steps) verifies the subtraction parameterization boundary residual (4.77e-07) and ODE-free MC structure, but the FKL estimate has 17.5% relative error (4.311 vs 3.670) and the paper's full MINO-T transformer at 256 resolution with 50k functions is not reproduced.

amkkk/repro-relative-entropy-estimation-.overall: All six claims are addressed only at reduced scale with simplified proxies, truncated spectral models, or MINO-lite stand-ins on CPU; no claim is verified at the paper's full scale (256-resolution FFM, MINO-T, official TI codebases, real scRNA-seq datasets). The logbook provides real numeric evidence on toy setups for each claim, but the specific quantitative claims (e.g., Table 1 ranges, Tables 2-3 values) are not reproduced.

AakashJammula/repro-dln-symmetry-multipa.paper_title: Gradient Descent with Large Step Size Restores Symmetry in Deep Linear Networks with Multi-Pathway

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 shows equal distribution of target singular values across H parallel pathways reduces sharpness by a factor of H^(2/L-1) relative to single-pathway (winner-takes-all) solutions, where L is network depth (Section 4.1, Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: Part B measured the true Hessian of a real 2-mode d×d multi-pathway matrix network via finite-differenced analytic gradients, matching the closed-form Prop 4.1 formula to rel. error 1.88e-11 across 9 (L,H) configs; Part B2 confirmed the balanced/concentrated sharpness ratio equals H^(2/L-1) to rel. error 3.22e-11.

claims.claim: Below the stability threshold (learning rate eta < 2/S_1), gradient descent reproduces gradient-flow symmetry-breaking into a winner-takes-all pathway, while eta > 2/S_1 triggers edge-of-stability oscillations that re-balance singular values across pathways (Section 5.1, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: Part C ran actual GD with H=2, L=20 (matching Fig. 1): at eta=0.5×(2/S1) the final pathway values were (0.9987, 0.0013) confirming winner-takes-all, while at eta=1.5×(2/S1) they were (0.7584, 0.2416) confirming re-balancing, with converged sharpness 13.17 tracking 2/eta=13.33 to 1.2% error.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.2 establishes a depth-dependent worst-case-return learning-rate ceiling eta_WCR, with the tolerance ratio gamma_WCR(L) scaling as Theta(log L), so deeper networks tolerate a wider range of large step sizes during re-balancing (Section 6, Theorem 6.2, Proposition 6.3).
claims.evidence: Part 1 computed gamma_WCR(L) by direct bisection on Definition 6.1 (independent of the paper's closed-form reduction), matching the paper's table to max rel. error 1.17e-4; Part 2 brute-force-simulated the two-step-return property confirming safety holds at 0.98×alpha_WCR and fails at 1.02×alpha_WCR for all 6 tested L; Part 3 fit gamma_WCR(L) vs log(L) over L=2..200 with R²=0.9992 in the asymptotic tail.

claims.claim: With heterogeneous pathway depths (e.g., L_1, L_2 in {3,5,7}^2), large-step gradient descent still converges to the theoretically predicted equilibrium that equalizes marginal sharpness 2(L_h-1)sigma_hi^(1-2/L_h) across pathways, overriding the architectural depth asymmetry (Section 5.3, Proposition 5.1, Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook contains no experiments involving heterogeneous pathway depths (L_1, L_2 in {3,5,7}), no test of Proposition 5.1, no Figure 4 reproduction, and no measurement of marginal sharpness equalization 2(L_h-1)*sigma_hi^(1-2/L_h) across asymmetric-depth pathways.

claims.claim: Nonlinear MLPs with Tanh activations and multi-pathway structure exhibit an analogous large-step re-balancing phenomenon to the deep linear network case (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook contains no experiments with nonlinear MLPs, Tanh activations, or any Figure 3 reproduction; all experiments use deep linear networks only.

AakashJammula/repro-dln-symmetry-multipa.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies Claims 1–3 with multiple independent numerical methods (measured Hessians, GD dynamics, direct bisection, brute-force boundary checks) achieving near machine-precision or ~1% agreement with the paper's formulas and tables. Claims 4 and 5 are entirely unaddressed—no heterogeneous-depth or nonlinear-MLP experiments were run.

AakashJammula/repro-pomdp-value-function.paper_title: The Value Function Semi-Algebraic Set in Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes

claims.claim: The feasible set of value functions in POMDPs is proven to be a semi-algebraic set defined by explicit polynomial equalities and inequalities, in contrast to the polyhedral (piecewise-linear) feasible set of fully observable MDPs (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: The semi-algebraic structure and polyhedral contrast were verified on the minimal |S|=|A|=|O|=2 case: symbolic exact-arithmetic matching of determinantal polynomial conditions plus 1400/1400 numeric agreement across two instances, with β=I yielding linear factors (MDP polytope) and partial observability yielding irreducible quadratics. However, only the minimal possible POMDP size and only the top-rank stratum were tested.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.9 first characterizes feasible POMDP value functions via infinitely many piecewise-linear inequalities derived from the Bellman equation parameters.
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states Theorem 3.9's semi-infinite y-sweep characterization 'was not implemented in its own indexed form' and instead used a provably-equivalent LP ground truth, so the specific infinite piecewise-linear inequality characterization was never directly tested.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 reduces the infinite characterization to a finite description using a zonotope containment condition on deviation matrices and midpoint residuals.
claims.evidence: Although the executive summary claims Theorem 4.2 is verified 'by construction,' no experiment directly tests the zonotope containment condition on deviation matrices and midpoint residuals; the code only exercises Theorem 4.4's LP and determinantal formulations.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 gives an explicit quantifier-free semi-algebraic description of the feasible value-function set, stratified by matrix rank via determinantal polynomial conditions on submatrices.
claims.evidence: The determinantal polynomial conditions were symbolically verified and numerically cross-validated (1400/1400 agreement with LP oracles) on the minimal 2x2x2 case, but the logbook explicitly notes 'only the top (full-rank) stratum of Theorem 4.4's rank-stratified union was tested' and lower-rank strata were never exercised.

claims.claim: Partial observability is shown to induce nonlinear coupling constraints between decision variables absent in MDPs, making optimal policies dependent on the initial state distribution (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The nonlinear coupling aspect is partially supported by the observation that partial observability produces irreducible quadratic constraints versus linear factors under full observability, but the claim that optimal policies become dependent on the initial state distribution was never addressed experimentally.

AakashJammula/repro-pomdp-value-function.overall: This logbook provides a rigorous but narrow verification of Theorem 4.4's determinantal/semi-algebraic construction on the minimal 2x2x2 POMDP case, with exact symbolic matching and 1400/1400 numeric cross-validation across three independent code paths, plus a well-demonstrated erratum in one appendix polynomial. Theorems 3.9 and 4.2's specific characterizations, the full rank stratification, larger instances, and the initial-state-distribution dependence claim remain unaddressed.

claims.claim: Thompson Sampling admits an online optimization form that mimics the Bellman-optimal policy structure.
claims.evidence: The logbook numerically verifies Theorem 1's identity x^TS_t = argmin_x[(E[max(θ1,θ2)]−x)² + ν^TS·x] across 192 Gaussian and 124 Beta-Bernoulli posterior settings using four independent comparison routes, achieving machine-precision agreement (max_abs_err ≤ 4.44e-16) for closed-form checks and ~1e-6 agreement for fully Monte-Carlo checks with Pearson r = 1.0000000000.

claims.claim: Thompson Sampling regularizes greediness by a measure of residual uncertainty in the optimization framework.
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly computes the regularizer ν^TS = Cov(θ1−θ2, sign(θ1−θ2)) in all checks and confirms that the argmin of the regularized objective (E[max]−x)² + ν^TS·x equals TS's pull rule, with the closed-form solution x* = E[max] − ν/2 demonstrating that the regularizer shifts the solution away from the greedy value E[max] by an amount proportional to residual uncertainty about which arm is better.

AakashJammula/repro-ts-online-optimizati.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence for both claims by exhaustively verifying Theorem 1's algebraic identity across two posterior families (Gaussian, Beta-Bernoulli), hundreds of parameter settings, and four independent comparison routes including closed-form, numerical optimization, quadrature, and fully Monte-Carlo approaches. The reproduction is rigorous and the setup matches the paper's actual two-armed bandit setting rather than a reduced proxy.

algorise/repro-softmax-as-linear-attenti.paper_title: Softmax as Linear Attention in the Large-Prompt Regime: a Measure-based Perspective

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 establishes non-asymptotic concentration bounds of order σ⁶ln(L)/L^(c₂/σ²) showing finite-prompt softmax attention outputs converge to their infinite-prompt counterparts as prompt length L grows, for i.i.d. Gaussian inputs (Section 3, Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: Only two sparse data points are reported (0.5199 at L=64, 0.129965 at L=4096) with no methodology, no comparison to the predicted σ⁶ln(L)/L^(c₂/σ²) rate, no code, and no description of how the concentration bound was computed. Two numbers without context do not constitute verification of a specific convergence rate.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.4 extends the concentration result to gradients, giving comparable convergence rates for gradient stability along the training trajectory (Section 3, Proposition 3.4).
claims.evidence: No numerical results are presented at all — the logbook merely states 'gradient concentration along training trajectory verified with rate matching output concentration,' which is an unsupported assertion with zero quantitative evidence.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 shows that under Gaussian input measures, the infinite-prompt softmax attention operator reduces to an affine map T^(U,V)[μ](z) = Vm + VΓK^⊤Qz, i.e., structurally equivalent to linear attention (Section 2, Lemma 2.1).
claims.evidence: A single residual error value (< 0.012997) is reported with no description of the experimental setup, input dimensions, how the affine map was compared, or what the residual measures. One number without context cannot verify a structural equivalence claim.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.3 proves that the asymptotic training risk of finite-prompt softmax attention under gradient flow is bounded by the infinite-prompt linear-attention risk plus an error term ε, allowing optimization analyses to transfer from linear to softmax attention (Section 4, Theorem 4.3).
claims.evidence: No numerical results whatsoever — the logbook only states 'asymptotic training risk under gradient flow bounded by infinite-prompt operator risk,' which is a bare assertion with no data, no gradient flow implementation details, and no risk values.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 shows that in the large-prompt regime, softmax attention achieves Bayes-optimal risk for in-context linear regression with anisotropic Gaussian covariates, extending prior results restricted to the isotropic case (Section 5, Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: No numerical results are provided — the logbook merely asserts 'Bayes-optimal risk achieved for in-context linear regression in large-prompt regime L -> inf' without any simulation of anisotropic Gaussian covariates, risk measurements, or comparison to the Bayes-optimal benchmark.

algorise/repro-softmax-as-linear-attenti.overall: This logbook provides almost no concrete experimental evidence for any of the five claims. It reports a handful of numbers without methodology, code, or comparison to theoretical predictions, and most claims are supported by bare assertions only. The entire reproduction reportedly took under 5 seconds on CPU, which is inconsistent with a rigorous verification of concentration bounds, gradient stability, and Bayes-optimality across multiple prompt lengths and training trajectories.

claims.claim: The Stackelberg-Littlestone (SL) dimension characterizes the optimal mistake bound for online learning in structured Stackelberg games: deterministic algorithms require at least SLdim_G(H) mistakes and randomized algorithms require at least half that in expectation (Theorem 3.8).
claims.evidence: The logbook only states 'SLdim_G(H)=4 tight mistake bound verified' with no game construction, hypothesis class definition, adversary strategy, deterministic vs. randomized comparison, or any code/trajectory shown. A single bare number with no experimental detail is insufficient to verify a lower-bound theorem.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 (the Stackelberg Standard Optimal Algorithm) achieves a regret bound matching this lower bound, i.e. regret bounded by SLdim_G(H), making it provably optimal (Theorem 3.10).
claims.evidence: The logbook asserts 'worst-case mistakes = 4 <= SLdim_G(H)=4' but provides no Algorithm 1 implementation, no adversary, no learning trajectory, and no evidence this is a worst-case sequence rather than a trivial instance.

claims.claim: There exist Stackelberg game instances where the standard Littlestone dimension is infinite (Ldim(H)=∞) yet the leader's learning problem remains learnable, showing that standard multiclass complexity measures fail to characterize the learning task's true difficulty (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: The logbook claims 'standard Littlestone dimension is infinite (inf) while SLdim=4' but shows no construction of the separating instance, no proof or computational method for establishing Ldim=∞, and no code. A simulation cannot demonstrate infinity without detailed construction.

claims.claim: In the agnostic online setting, the paper's algorithm achieves a regret bound of Õ(√(SLdim_G(H)·T)) (Section 3.2, Theorem 3.15).
claims.evidence: Only a single data point is given: 'regret 158.11 at T=1000'. There is no variation of T to verify the √T rate, no comparison to baselines, no algorithm implementation, and no analysis of log factors. One number cannot verify a rate bound.

claims.claim: For distributional learning with contexts, the Stackelberg-Natarajan (SN) dimension satisfies dSN,G(H) ≤ dN(H) with strict inequality possible, and Stackelberg ERM achieves sample complexity Õ(dSN,G(H)·log(dSN,G(H)·K/ε)/ε), improving over vanilla ERM which scales with the (larger) Natarajan dimension dN(H) (Section 4.2, Theorem 4.10, Theorem 4.12, Proposition 4.7).
claims.evidence: The logbook states 'd_SN,G(H) <= d_N(H) verified with strict inequality' but provides no actual dimension values, no game/hypothesis construction, no sample complexity experiments varying ε or K, and no comparison of Stackelberg ERM vs. vanilla ERM sample complexity.

algorise/repro-learning-in-structured-st.overall: The logbook provides only single-sentence assertions with at most one bare number per claim, accompanied by identical boilerplate 'theoretical context' text. No code, game constructions, algorithm implementations, adversary strategies, learning trajectories, or multi-parameter experiments are shown, making it impossible to independently assess any claim.

algorise/repro-dynamic-regret-via-discou.paper_title: Dynamic Regret via Discounted-to-Dynamic Reduction with Applications to Curved Losses and Adam Optimizer

claims.claim: Theorem 1 gives a modular discounted-to-dynamic (D2D) reduction converting a rescaled-regret bound of the form sum_s beta^{-s}(f_s(x_s)-f_s(u)) <= phi_t(u) + sum_s Lambda_s into an explicit dynamic regret bound via stability terms Lambda_s and path variation P_T^beta (Section 2.2, Theorem 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook provides no numerical results, no implementation details, and no comparison between predicted and observed dynamic regret bounds. The only evidence is the assertion 'rescaled regret translates directly to dynamic regret bound' with no supporting data.

claims.claim: For online linear regression, discounted Vovk-Azoury-Warmuth achieves dynamic regret O(d log T + sqrt(d*T*P_T^beta)) without Bregman-divergence arguments, recovering optimal rates (Section 3.1, Theorem 2).
claims.evidence: A single regret value of 623.73 at T=2000 is reported, but without specifying d, P_T^beta, or the theoretical bound value, it is impossible to assess whether this matches O(d log T + sqrt(d*T*P_T^beta)). No scaling experiments are presented.

claims.claim: For online logistic regression, the discounted AIOLI algorithm avoids exponential dependence on the comparator norm B, and a two-layer ensemble achieves dynamic regret O(d*B*log(BT) + sqrt(d*B*T*P_T^{beta*})) via automatic discount-factor tuning (Section 3.2, Theorems 3-4).
claims.evidence: No numerical results whatsoever are presented. The logbook merely asserts 'regret linear in d, polynomial in B' without any data, scaling experiments, or comparison to the stated O(d*B*log(BT) + sqrt(d*B*T*P_T^{beta*})) bound.

claims.claim: Theorem 5 proves clipped Adam converges with a relaxed beta_2 condition, max{1-nu/(G+sigma), beta_1^4} <= beta_2 < 1 (versus the prior requirement beta_2 >= beta_1^2), attaining the optimal O(F*G^2*c^{1/2}*epsilon^{-7/2}) iteration complexity (Section 4.3.1, Theorem 5).
claims.evidence: The only 'evidence' is checking that 0.9333 <= 0.9990 < 1.0, which is trivial arithmetic, not an experiment. No convergence curves, iteration counts, or comparison with the O(F*G^2*c^{1/2}*epsilon^{-7/2}) complexity are provided.

claims.claim: Theorem 7 shows a clip-free variant of Adam, using a composite loss with a tuned damping term, achieves the same optimal convergence rates under the standard condition beta_2 >= beta_1^2 (Section 4.4, Theorem 7).
claims.evidence: No numerical results, convergence curves, or iteration counts are presented. The logbook only asserts 'optimal O(T^(1/2)) convergence under heavy-tailed noise' without any supporting data or experimental details.

algorise/repro-dynamic-regret-via-discou.overall: This logbook provides essentially no concrete experimental evidence for any of the five claims. It consists almost entirely of assertions with minimal numbers (one regret value without context, one arithmetic inequality check), and the total wall time of <5 seconds for all experiments indicates no substantive reproduction was performed.

tomyimkc/repro-learning-high-dimensional.paper_title: Learning High-Dimensional Parity Functions with Product Networks using Gradient Descent

claims.claim: Product networks trained with gradient descent under controlled stochastic data sparsity are shown to learn high-dimensional parity functions, with the problem formalized in Section 3 and main theoretical results developed in Section 4.
claims.evidence: Full-scale reproduction at N up to 100,000 (matching the paper's own maximum) with real minibatch SGD: sparse training (pe=1/N) achieved support-recovery accuracy 1.0 and L1 distance ~6e-9 at all four N values, while the dense-input control (pe=0.5) collapsed to chance accuracy (0.48-0.57), confirming the sparsity precondition is load-bearing.

claims.claim: Theorems F.5-F.7 in Appendix F establish core convergence guarantees for the product-network learning dynamics on parity functions (Theorem F.5-F.7, Appendix F).
claims.evidence: Run at 10,000 of the paper's 1,000,000 steps: symmetry preservation held well (symmetry error 0.00091→0.00020, control with asymmetric init stayed at 0.112), but Gaussian preservation showed measurable drift (excess kurtosis 0.045→0.424, normality test rejected at p=6.94e-82), providing only partial, reduced-scale validation of the convergence guarantees.

claims.claim: Theorems F.10-F.12 give polynomial scaling laws relating required network width to input dimension N under the sparsity conditions studied (Theorem F.10-F.12, Appendix F).
claims.evidence: The experiment tests steps-to-converge scaling (a proxy) rather than the literal claim about network width vs N, and the logbook confirms F.10-F.12 are foundational approximation lemmas, not a width-scaling law. The proxy test at full N scale showed essentially constant steps-to-converge (slope 0.0018) under the paper's constant-effective-rate recipe, with the fixed-alpha control diverging as predicted.

claims.claim: Theorems F.14-F.16 provide sample complexity bounds for learning parity functions with the product-network architecture (Theorem F.14-F.16, Appendix F).
claims.evidence: The claim says 'sample complexity bounds' but F.14/F.16 actually bound the learning rate alpha; the experiment tests the theorems' real content at N up to 20,000 (below the paper's 100,000). The proven-safe zone (0.5x and 1.0x alpha1) always succeeded (success rate 1.0), the bound was shown conservative (5x alpha1 still worked at N=200), and the 2000x control always failed, confirming the thresholds' directionality.

claims.claim: Section 5 reports experimental validation of the theoretical predictions across varying input dimensions and network configurations, complementing the initialization analysis in Theorems H.1-H.9 (Section 5, Appendix H).
claims.evidence: Part A tested a genuine multi-node P-parallel network but at reduced scale (P up to 64 vs paper's 1000, N up to 8000 vs 100,000): baseline accuracy was 1.0 across all (N,P,pw) configurations with the M-only normalization, while the M*P control degraded to 0.54 at P=64. Part B verified Prop H.1's bound (0 violations across 200K points) and Thm H.5's envelope contraction (slack 0.0 baseline, 126.7 control), but Appendix H is general convergence machinery, not the 'initialization analysis' the claim describes.

tomyimkc/repro-learning-high-dimensional.overall: The logbook provides a strong full-scale verification of the core empirical claim (Claim 1) at N=100,000 with proper sparsity controls, while Claims 2-5 are tested at reduced scale or via proxy experiments due to terminology mismatches between the claim text and the actual theorem content, yielding partial but directionally consistent evidence.

tomyimkc/repro-adaptive-bandit-algorithm.paper_title: Adaptive Bandit Algorithms for Contextual Matching Markets

claims.claim: For stochastic contexts, the paper defines a minimum preference gap (Definition 2) and proves the Batched Adaptive Regret-Balancing (BARB) algorithm achieves an instance-dependent regret upper bound depending on log T and 1/∆_min^2 (Theorem 3.1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: The 1/Delta_min^2 scaling is confirmed (log-log slope -1.913 vs theory -2.0, R^2=1.0, 25 seeds) and T-independence is confirmed (slope 0.054 vs linear control slope 1.0), but BARB is warm-started with Delta_1 near the true gap, bypassing the algorithm's blind multi-batch search mechanism, and the market is small (N=K=3, d=2, T up to 32,000).

claims.claim: Under a regularity condition on the CDF of the minimum utility difference (Assumption 5), BARB's regret is shown to be Θ̃(T^{2/3}) asymptotically, with Theorem 3.2 giving the O(T^{2/3}) upper bound and Theorem 3.3 giving a matching Ω(T^{2/3}) lower bound for N=K=3 (Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: With gap scaled as 2.0*T^{-1/3}, BARB's regret grows with log-log slope 0.732 (theory 0.667, R^2=1.0) versus a near-flat 0.073 control at fixed gap, but the same warm-start simplification is used, the lower bound (Theorem 3.3) is not tested at all, and the market is small (N=K=3, d=2, T up to 64,000).

claims.claim: For adversarial contexts, the paper introduces a tractable α-approximate ∆-optimal stable regret (Equation 7) and proposes the Adaptive Explore-Choose Oracle (AdECO) algorithm, proving a regret upper bound of O(Nd log^2(T)/(∆-ε)^2 + ((∆+ε)/2)T) that becomes O(T^{2/3}) when ∆ = O(T^{-1/3}) (Theorem 4.1, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The U-shaped Delta-dependence is confirmed (mean worst/best degradation ratio 5.93x across three horizons), but the T^{2/3} asymptotic rate is not observed (measured slope 1.06 vs target 0.667), and the setup is small (N=K=3, d=3, 3-8 seeds, only 3 T values).

claims.claim: Numerical experiments simulate a matching market with N=4 players, K=4 arms, and context dimension d=3 over a horizon of T=200,000 rounds averaged over 20 trials, comparing BARB against Batched-ETC and ETC baselines, and AdECO against alternatives (Section 5, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: At N=4, K=4, d=3 with all paper constants matched but T reduced to 30,000 (paper: 200,000) and 10 trials (paper: 20), the main Figure 1 ordering is not reproduced (Batched-ETC median 2988.1 beats BARB 3919.4, contradicting the paper's narrative), though the Appendix H control finding is matched (ETC beats BARB under large eigenvalue) and the AdECO Delta-grid U-shape is confirmed at the paper's market size.

tomyimkc/repro-adaptive-bandit-algorithm.overall: The logbook tests core scaling mechanisms of BARB and AdECO on simplified setups with warm-starting and reduced scale, confirming the 1/Delta_min^2 and T^{2/3} scaling relationships and the U-shaped Delta trade-off, but does not fully reproduce any claim at the paper's scale and fails to reproduce the main numerical ordering in Claim 4.

algorise/repro-asymptotic-universal-alig.paper_title: Asymptotic Universal Alignment: A New Alignment Framework via Test-Time Scaling

claims.claim: The paper proves the optimal convergence rate for universal (U-)alignment under test-time scaling with k samples is f(k)=k/(k+1), and shows this rate cannot be improved upon by any method (Propositions 2-3, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook only states f(k)=k/(k+1) was 'verified from k=1 (0.5000) to k=32 (0.9697)' but provides no code, no methodology, no data tables, and no description of what was actually simulated. Computing the formula k/(k+1) for various k is not an independent verification of a proof of optimality.

claims.claim: Theorem 3 shows there exists a family of single-output policies whose test-time-scaled versions achieve U-alignment at the optimal rate k/(k+1) (Theorem 3, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook merely restates the claim ('Single-output policy family achieves U-alignment at rate f(k)') with zero numerical results, no code, no methodology, and no description of the policy family tested.

claims.claim: Theorem 2 shows that symmetric Nash equilibrium policies of the (k+1)-player alignment game achieve (k, k/(k+1))-robust alignment, guaranteeing a win rate of at least 1-1/(k+1) against any competing policy (Theorem 2, Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook only restates the claim verbatim with no experimental setup, no win-rate measurements, no comparison against competing policies, and no code.

claims.claim: Proposition 5 shows that fixed points of gradient ascent dynamics in the alignment game correspond to symmetric Nash equilibria (Proposition 5, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook only restates the claim with no simulation of gradient ascent dynamics, no fixed-point computation, no Nash equilibrium verification, and no code or results.

claims.claim: Proposition 6 shows that no-regret learning dynamics yield (k, k/(k+1) - Reg_T/T)-robust alignment, giving a finite-time learning guarantee that approaches the optimal rate as regret vanishes (Proposition 6, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook mentions 'Reg_T/T = 0.0050' but provides no context on what was simulated, no learning dynamics description, no regret trajectory, no code, and no methodology.

algorise/repro-asymptotic-universal-alig.overall: This logbook provides essentially no concrete experimental evidence for any of the five theoretical claims. Each claim page merely restates the claim, labels it 'VERIFIED', and cites a vague 'CPU non-toy simulation' with a <5 second wall time, but no code, methodology, data tables, or meaningful results are presented anywhere.

algorise/repro-full-batch-gradient-desce.paper_title: Full-Batch Gradient Descent Outperforms One-Pass SGD: Sample Complexity Separation in Single-Index Learning

claims.claim: For quadratic activation σ(z) = z², when the sample size n = o(d log d), spherical gradient flow fails to achieve weak recovery, showing full-batch updates offer no statistical advantage over one-pass SGD in this regime (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook states 'fails weak recovery when n = 102.0 samples' but never specifies d, provides no alignment/recovery metrics, no trajectories, and no comparison across multiple n values. A single unsubstantiated number without context cannot verify a sample complexity threshold claim.

claims.claim: With a truncated quadratic activation, full-batch spherical gradient flow achieves weak recovery with only n ≳ d samples, compared to the n ≳ d log d samples required by one-pass SGD, establishing a sample complexity separation (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook says 'n = 60 >= d samples' without specifying d or showing any recovery metric, and critically provides no comparison to one-pass SGD at n ≳ d log d, which is essential to establishing the separation claim.
