visv-Bro/repro-row-stochastic-matrices-c.paper_title: Row-Stochastic Matrices Can Provably Outperform Doubly Stochastic Matrices in Decentralized Learning

claims.claim: In the weighted Hilbert space L²(λ;R^d), the λ-induced row-stochastic mixing matrix W is self-adjoint whereas the doubly stochastic matrix W^ds is not, and this non-self-adjointness introduces additional multiplicative penalty terms (κ_λ > 1 and λ_max² > 1) that amplify consensus error under the doubly stochastic design (Section 5.2, Section 6.2).
claims.evidence: On the paper's 16-node exponential graph with λ_A and ε=0.3, the row-stochastic weighted adjoint residual is 9.34e-17 (self-adjoint) while the doubly stochastic residual is 0.768 (not self-adjoint); the row norm/ρ_Λ = 1.0000 while DS norm/ρ_J = 1.10014 and DS·D_λ norm/ρ_J = 1.24525, both below the κ_λ=2.708 and λ_max=2.2 caps that generate the penalty factors; uniform-weight control returns κ_λ=λ_max²=1.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.5 gives O(1/T) convergence rates for both row-stochastic and doubly stochastic strategies, but the row-stochastic strategy achieves strictly smaller non-asymptotic consensus error and can converge faster even when its spectral gap is smaller than that of the doubly stochastic strategy (Theorem 6.5).
claims.evidence: Noiseless 5-seed runs give tail log–log slopes of −1.0000 for both strategies (O(1/T) confirmed); the row design has the smaller gap (0.24793 < 0.40000) yet achieves 30.4% lower gradient AUC (211.4 vs 303.6) and 67.2% lower cumulative consensus (1056.5 vs 3219.3) over 240 iterations with 10 seeds on the paper's 16-node exponential graph.

claims.claim: Theorem 7.1 derives a sufficient condition on the spectral gaps, 1 − ρ_Λ ≥ max{(1+η)κ_λ^(-1/3), λ_max^(-1/2)}(1 − ρ_J), under which the row-stochastic design provably converges strictly faster than the doubly stochastic design (Theorem 7.1).
claims.evidence: A concrete 7-node graph with ε=0.5093 satisfies the v1 sufficient condition (gap_ratio ≥ r_v1 with positive margin) but the B(ρ) dominance ratio is < 0.96, meaning the term-by-term coefficient comparison the proof requires fails; a factorization error is identified where the paper uses (1+ρ²)³ but B(ρ) factors through (1+ρ)³, with residual > 0.01 at ρ=0.6.

claims.claim: Corollary 7.3 and Algorithm 2 give topology construction guidelines showing that when node degrees scale proportionally with their assigned weights (d_i/d_j matching λ_i/λ_j within bounds set by R), the row-stochastic design outperforms the doubly stochastic design, satisfying a Loewner order condition on the graph Laplacians (Corollary 7.3, Remark 7.4, Algorithm 2).
claims.evidence: On a 4-node star graph with degree-proportional weights satisfying the pairwise condition (minimum slack > 0) and positive spectral gap margin, the Loewner difference L_λ − R·L₁ has minimum eigenvalue < −0.07 and a witness quadratic form < −0.14, proving the Loewner order is violated; additionally, alternative non-degree-proportional weights achieve a larger spectral gap by > 0.049.

visv-Bro/repro-row-stochastic-matrices-c.overall: The logbook verifies the core algebraic mechanism (weighted self-adjointness and penalty amplification) and the empirical smaller-gap-faster-convergence phenomenon on the paper's own 16-node topology, but provides concrete counterexamples falsifying the v1 Theorem 7.1 sufficient condition (algebraic factorization error) and the Corollary 7.3 Loewner-order guarantee (negative eigenvalue under degree-matching).

nmaher/repro-conformal-prediction-for-ea.paper_title: Conformal Prediction for Early Stopping in Mixed Integer Optimization

claims.claim: The conformal-prediction early-stopping method reduces mixed-integer optimization solve time by over 60% on average across distributional MIPLIB instances while guaranteeing 0.1%-optimal solutions with 95% probability (Abstract, Section 5).
claims.evidence: On MIS (n=200, 250 held-out instances, 500 resplits, SCIP), the LSTM/tiesafe configuration achieves 95.0% coverage but only 22.1% time reduction — not >60%. The only configuration exceeding 60% (ub_rate/paper mode: 67.6%) has 41.2% coverage and 1.6% mean suboptimality (16× the ε=0.001 target), meaning the joint claim of >60% reduction AND 95% coverage is not satisfiable at this scale.

claims.claim: Speedups vary substantially by problem family: 76% on CFLP, 78% on OTS, 88% on MVC, and 95% on MIS, but only 8% on GISP due to its problem structure (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Only MIS was tested (1 of 5 families); the measured 22.1% reduction at 95% coverage with SCIP contradicts the claimed 95% for MIS, but CFLP, OTS, MVC, and GISP were not attempted at all, so the per-family variation claim is mostly unaddressed.

claims.claim: An LSTM predicts the true optimality gap from solver state features (bounds, feasible solutions, nodes explored, elapsed time), and a stopping threshold κ is calibrated via conformal prediction per Theorem 4.1 to guarantee the target success probability (Section 4, Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The LSTM predictor was trained on the paper's 10 solver-state features and achieved MAE 0.552 (vs 4.125 for linear, 5.838 for ub_rate), and conformal calibration via the 5th-smallest score of 100 at c=100/α=0.05 delivered 95.0% coverage under the corrected rule, tracking the achievable level of 95.05% across α∈[0.01,0.20] and c∈[5,100].

claims.claim: The theoretical guarantee shows the success probability on test instances is at least 1−α−O(1/√c), where c is the number of calibration instances (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The c-sweep results show coverage tracking the achievable level n/(c+1) closely (c=5: 83.8% vs 83.3%; c=10: 90.7% vs 90.9%; c=20: 94.9% vs 95.2%; c=100: 94.7% vs 95.05%), consistent with the theoretical guarantee that success probability is at least 1−α−O(1/√c).

claims.claim: Experiments use 800 training instances, 28-100 calibration instances, and 72-100 test instances per problem family, with target tolerance ε=0.001 and error probability α=0.05, tested using Gurobi and Cardinal Optimizer (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook used 150 training instances (not 800), SCIP instead of Gurobi/COPT, and only MIS (not all 6 families); the conformal parameters (c=100, α=0.05, ε=0.001) match, but the training set size, solver, and family coverage differ from the claimed experimental setup.

nmaher/repro-conformal-prediction-for-ea.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies that the conformal prediction calibration machinery works correctly (95.0% coverage tracking the achievable level across α and c sweeps) and that the LSTM is an effective gap predictor, but provides concrete evidence that the claimed >60% time reduction is not achievable at 95% coverage on MIS with SCIP (22.1% measured), with only 1 of 6 problem families tested and Gurobi unavailable.

ProCreations/JXN3npSRRD-repro.paper_title: Optimal Bayesian Stopping for Efficient Inference of Consistent LLM Answers

claims.claim: The L-aggregated stopping policy with L=3 achieves asymptotic optimality for identifying the mode LLM answer (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook independently computes L=3 and exact stopping times on 2,000 IID trajectories with K=4, p=(0.50,0.25,0.15,0.10), at three confidence levels; at 0.99 and 0.999 the L=3 and exact stopping times agree in every paired trajectory, and the ratios approach the predicted coefficient 5.770780.

claims.claim: The coarse posterior approximation strictly dominates prior-free baselines in sample complexity while remaining fast to compute (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook directly computes asymptotic coefficients from the paper's formulas for p=(0.50,0.25,0.15,0.10): prior-free=23.543, L=2=6.952, L≥3=5.771, showing strict dominance, and measures L=3 DP computation at 7.8 ms/call versus 17.9 ms/call for exact enumeration over 50 calls with K=8.

claims.claim: Algorithm 1 implements the L-aggregated stopping rule derived from the stopping condition in Equation 7 (Algorithm 1, Equation 7).
claims.evidence: The executive summary reports an exhaustive check across all 3^8=6,561 length-eight sequences over a three-answer alphabet yielding zero stopping-decision mismatches between Algorithm 1 and the direct posterior threshold rule at 0.95 confidence, supplemented by a 10,000-trial simulation with K=8 across L∈{2,3,4,8} and six confidence thresholds showing consistent first-crossing behavior.

claims.claim: Empirical query-count comparisons show the method identifies the mode LLM answer using fewer samples than exhaustive sampling across confidence levels (Table 1, Table 2).
claims.evidence: The logbook reaggregates 750 question/model rows (250 per model for Qwen-2.5-72B, GPT-4o mini, LLaMA-3.1-405B) from the official FEval-TTC archive, showing L=3 mean generations are lower than the ASC baseline in all nine model/confidence comparisons at 0.95, 0.975, and 0.99, with mode accuracy within 0.012.

claims.claim: Experimental validation of sample-efficiency gains across confidence levels is presented in the experiments section (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The same 750-row replay across three models and three confidence levels confirms cross-confidence sample-efficiency gains: all nine L=3 versus ASC generation comparisons favor L=3, with aggregate lower-generation comparisons at 3/3 for each confidence level and mode-accuracy differences ranging from 0 to 0.012.

ProCreations/JXN3npSRRD-repro.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical and empirical evidence supporting all five claims through independent implementations: asymptotic coefficient verification on 2,000 trajectories, direct formula-based coefficient comparisons with timing measurements, exhaustive Algorithm 1 correctness checks on 6,561 sequences, and a 750-row reaggregation from the official FEval-TTC archive across three models and three confidence levels. The main limitation is that empirical comparisons use bootstrap resampling from 40 cached answers rather than live model calls and cover 250 questions per model rather than the full benchmark.

claims.claim: Multi-step SAM algorithm recovers classical SAM as ρ→0 and remains valid for large ρ
claims.evidence: Matrix completion experiments at n=10,100,1000 show MSAM converges to a minimum where SAM fails at large ρ (SAM/GD ratios of 1.3e4–7.0e4x vs best MSAM/GD of 13–150x), and matrix sensing shows SAM≈MSAM at small ρ (gaps ≤3e-4), confirming the algorithm recovers SAM as ρ→0 and remains valid for large ρ.

claims.claim: Analysis via Lyapunov argument quantifies optimality gap dependence on radius and local curvature without convexity assumptions
claims.evidence: The O(ρ) optimality gap is cleanly verified on the convex quadratic (exponent 1.0000 at every M tested), and the bounded oscillation prediction of Theorem 3.3 is confirmed on the non-convex polynomial (SAM settles into a 2-cycle with non-zero amplitude for fixed ρ>0), though Theorem 3.6's geometric κ^M decay prediction is not confirmed (power-law M^(-0.486) observed instead).

claims.claim: Experiments on synthetic objectives and CIFAR-10 validate predicted gains from multiple inner updates
claims.evidence: On synthetic objectives, the inner loop is structurally a no-op in 1D (inner steps 2..M never change Delta in 2000 steps) and under the isotropic Hessian of the convex quadratic, the M=5 vs M=10 difference in matrix completion is within seed noise (Wilcoxon p≥0.89, seed spread 714x–26571x the reported gap), and matrix sensing shows SAM≈MSAM (gaps ≤3e-4), so the paper's own experiments do not validate gains from multiple inner updates.

reinaldog/repro-understanding-sam-throug.overall: The logbook provides strong evidence that MSAM remains valid at large ρ and recovers SAM as ρ→0 (Claim 1), and that the Lyapunov analysis correctly predicts the O(ρ) optimality gap and bounded oscillation (Claim 2). However, the claim that experiments validate gains from multiple inner updates is falsified: in 1D and isotropic settings M is structurally irrelevant, and in matrix completion the M=5 vs M=10 difference is indistinguishable from seed noise.

snaykey/repro-mha-capacity.paper_title: A Capacity-Based Rationale for Multi-Head Attention

claims.claim: Recovering a graph with m' relations in d_model-dimensional embeddings requires total key dimension D_K = Θ(m' log m' / d_model), established as a lower bound (Section 7) and matched by a constructive upper bound (Section 4).
claims.evidence: A sharp phase transition (F1 jumping from 0.17 to 1.00 as D_K increases at m=128) and a linear fit D_K* ≈ 1.73·(m log m/d_model) across 6 data points with m ≤ 128 are real runs, but the scale is ~20x smaller than the paper's m ≤ 4096 and only 6 points span less than a 3× range in m, insufficient to firmly establish a Θ(·) rate.

claims.claim: For permutation graphs (m' = m), the capacity requirement simplifies to D_K = Θ(m log m / d_model) (Section 4/Section 7).
claims.evidence: Same evidence as Claim 1 since all experiments use permutation graphs (m'=m by construction); the linear D_K* vs m log m/d_model relation is demonstrated at reduced scale (m ≤ 128, 6 points) with two non-converging outlier points, providing suggestive but limited support for the Θ(m log m/d_model) rate.

claims.claim: Multi-head attention's advantage arises because splitting into heads reduces the effective block size B, shrinking the noise term N3(B) ≍ (B/d_model)√(d_k log m) that governs interference from superposition (Section 5).
claims.evidence: At fixed D_K, single-head F1 of 0.13–0.35 vs multi-head F1 of 0.52–1.00 on permutation graphs (m=96–128) directly demonstrates the multi-head advantage, and interference noise is shown increasing monotonically with block size B (measured at m=2048); however, the head-sweep evidence is at significantly reduced scale compared to the paper.

claims.claim: Empirical scaling of the optimal total key dimension matches theory: D_K* ≈ 1.19·(m log m/d_model) with R²=0.944 (R²=0.992 after excluding three outlier points), and the optimal head count scales as h* ≈ 1.65(m/d_model) − 6.64 with per-head widths d_k* in [5,24] (median 11) (Section 6).
claims.evidence: The scaling forms reproduce (h* slope 1.756 vs paper's 1.65, R²=0.98; d_k* median 8 within [5,24]), but D_K* slope is 1.92 vs 1.19 with R²=0.771 vs 0.944, and only 7 data points at m ≤ 128 are used—too few and too small to confirm the specific quantitative scaling law.

claims.claim: The multi-head capacity advantage persists in a fuller Transformer setting with softmax normalization, value routing, and frozen GPT-2 embeddings, since the analysis establishes capacity is purely key-query driven (Appendix C).
claims.evidence: Softmax (+0.265) and softmax+value-routing (+0.257) multi-head advantages are demonstrated at m=96, but the claim explicitly includes frozen GPT-2 embeddings which the logbook discloses as not reproduced, so a key component of the claimed setting is untested.

claims.claim: Capacity requirements are largely insensitive to context length, tested over sequence lengths ℓ ∈ {16,32}, with only modest degradation when evaluating at longer lengths than training (Section 6.1, Appendix A.3).
claims.evidence: F1 gap between ℓ=16 and ℓ=32 is only 0.038 and degradation from training at ℓ=16 to evaluation at ℓ=48 is ≤0.002, directly testing the claimed lengths, but at a single reduced configuration (m=96, d_model=16) rather than the paper's full scale.

snaykey/repro-mha-capacity.overall: The logbook provides real CPU-only experimental runs with concrete numbers that reproduce the qualitative trends of all six claims—phase transitions, multi-head advantage, scaling forms, softmax robustness, and context-length insensitivity—but at a significantly reduced scale (m ≤ 192 vs paper's m ≤ 4096) with few data points, and the GPT-2 embedding component of Claim 5 is explicitly not tested.

kondratevakate/repro-fluxnet-learning-ca.paper_title: FluxNet: Learning Capacity-Constrained Local Transport Operators for Conservative and Bounded PDE Surrogates

claims.claim: Proposition 1 shows that under periodic boundary conditions with symmetric stencils, FluxNet's flux-based update rule (the same flux serves as outflow for the sender cell and inflow for the receiver cell) exactly preserves the global sum of the transported quantity, yielding conservation errors at the machine-precision level (~1e-7 to 1e-8) (Proposition 1).
claims.evidence: Symbolic verification shows sum(u^{t+1}) - sum(u^t) = 0 for N=3,4,5,6; numeric tests across 240 configs per dtype show float64 max drift 4.436e-16 and float32 max 7.392e-08 (matching the paper's reported 1e-7 to 1e-8 band); mutation tests confirm the shared-flux property (asymmetric inflow → drift ≥1.3e5× baseline) and periodic BC requirement (nonperiodic → drift ≥3e5× baseline).

claims.claim: The L-Head and U-Head mechanisms parameterize outflow as a fraction of the cell's available capacity above a lower bound (or below an upper bound), and Propositions 2 and 3 prove that this construction guarantees the next state stays within the prescribed bounds without any post-hoc clipping or projection (Propositions 2 and 3).
claims.evidence: Symbolic worst-case margins confirm u^{t+1}-ℓ = a(1-α)>0 (L-head) and u_max-u^{t+1}=b(1-β)>0 (U-head); numeric tests across 540 configs including adversarial logit scale σ=20 with 10% of cells on the bound show 0/540 violations for both heads (worst excursion <4e-15); mutation test replacing σ(·)∈(0,1) with 1.6·σ(·) yields 120/120 violations, confirming the capacity-fraction inequality is the enforcing mechanism.

claims.claim: On the shallow-water equations rollout task at horizon T=2, FluxNet-LAP achieves a depth MAE of 3.12e-3 versus 6.74e-3 for the best baseline (a post-hoc projection method), while also reducing conservation error from 3.3e-7 (baseline) to 3.3e-8 (Table 3).
claims.evidence: No experiments were run for this claim; the logbook documents blockers (no code released, unreleased SWE dataset, multi-seed training beyond CPU budget) and notes a potential cross-backbone comparison issue (3.12e-3 is ResNet FluxNet-LAP vs 6.74e-3 is FNO projection baseline), but no accuracy or conservation numbers were reproduced.

claims.claim: On the traffic flow benchmark at horizon T=2, FluxNet-D attains an MAE of 3.48e-3 compared to 15.9e-3 for a CNN-AR baseline, and reduces conservation error from 2.1e-2 to 7.7e-8, though FluxNet-D shows slightly higher upper-bound violation rates on some settings (1.87% vs 3.20% for CNN-AR) (Table 4).
claims.evidence: No experiments were run; same data/training blockers as claim 3, plus a recorded discrepancy that the claimed 1.87% upper-bound violation rate matches neither the 2.87% (ResNet) nor 2.01% (FNO) values in Table 4, but this could not be adjudicated without raw data.

claims.claim: On the spinodal decomposition experiment, a FluxNet model trained to take steps of 1000*dt achieves a 17.3x rollout speedup relative to the base timestep while preserving two-point correlation statistics of the simulated microstructure (Table 5).
claims.evidence: No experiments were run; the 17.3× speedup requires a GPU reference solver (unavailable), unreleased Cahn-Hilliard training data, and trained FluxNet-D models, none of which were available; no toy substitute was produced.

claims.claim: The D-Head (dual bounds) variant enforces upper and lower capacity constraints via a dual consistency loss (DCL) rather than a strict architectural guarantee, achieving empirically near-zero bound violations rather than the exact guarantees proven for the single-bound L-Head and U-Head cases (Section on Bound Enforcement / D-Head).
claims.evidence: Tests confirm all three parts: conservation survives averaging (drift 4.377e-16 float64), independent branch logits produce violations in 6/6 seeds (mean 3.27% lb, 2.65% ub), and minimizing L_DCL drives violations to exactly 0.00% in 6/6 seeds (L_DCL: 0.195→1.04e-8); mutation test (sign flip) yields 0/6 seeds reaching zero violations with max violation 2.90, and Spearman correlation √L_DCL vs violation magnitude is ρ=0.903 (p=4.8e-34), establishing DCL as the causal enforcement mechanism.

kondratevakate/repro-fluxnet-learning-ca.overall: The logbook rigorously verifies the mathematical propositions (Claims 1, 2, 6) through symbolic analysis, extensive numeric testing across hundreds of configurations, and well-designed mutation tests that confirm the claimed mechanisms. The trained-model accuracy and speedup claims (3, 4, 5) are honestly left inconclusive due to unreleased data, no code, and no GPU, with no synthetic substitutes produced.

kondratevakate/repro-robust-bayesian-opt.paper_title: Robust Bayesian Optimisation with Unbounded Corruptions

claims.claim: The Fixed-Center RCGP-UCB (FC-RCGP-UCB) algorithm achieves cumulative regret R_T = Õ(Ψ(T_c)(1+√T_c)√(β'_T T(γ_T+T_c))), yielding sublinear regret for corruption budgets T_c = O(T^α) with α < 1/4 (Theorem 2, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Symbolic (sympy) derivation confirms the stated bound with T_c=T^α yields exponent e(α)=2α+1/2, so sublinearity ⟺ α<1/4; all 8 Table 1 Matérn entries reproduce to grid resolution 1/4000, and a mutation test (Ψ≡1) recovers the paper's 'Ideal' threshold α<1/2.

claims.claim: The Anchor-Adapt RCGP-UCB (A2-RCGP-UCB) algorithm, which adaptively updates its centering function, achieves cumulative regret R_T = Õ((1+T_c Ψ(T_c)^2)√(β'_T T(γ_T+T_c))), yielding sublinear regret for α < 1/7 (Theorem 3, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Symbolic derivation gives exponent e(α)=7α/2+1/2, so sublinearity ⟺ α<1/7; all 8 Table 1 Matérn entries for A2 reproduce to grid 1/7000, and mutation test (Ψ≡1) recovers the paper's 'Ideal' threshold α<1/3.

claims.claim: Both algorithms tolerate corruptions of possibly infinite magnitude, bounded only in frequency (number of corrupted points T_c), as formalized in the Frequency-Constrained Corruption model (Definition 1, Section 2.2).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive enumeration over 1040 configurations (10 seeds × 8 indices × 13 magnitudes up to 10¹²) shows RCGP posterior deviation is bounded (sup=1.4212) and converges as |c|→∞ (drift 9.93e-07 between 10⁶ and 10¹²), while standard GP deviation is 4.983e+11 and grows linearly in |c|; mutation test removing P-IMQ weight yields 4.536e+11.

claims.claim: When there are no corruptions (T_c = 0), both FC-RCGP-UCB and A2-RCGP-UCB recover the same asymptotic regret bound as standard GP-UCB, R_T = O(√(Tβ'_Tγ_T)), a zero-cost robustness property (Theorem 1, Section 4.3).
claims.evidence: Symbolic check confirms Ψ(0)=1 collapses both bounds to O(√(Tβ'_Tγ_T)); numeric Forrester benchmark (30 iterations, 10 seeds, L=10) shows FC and A2 match GP-UCB bit-identically (max |regret diff|=0.0, mean=34.9909 for all three); mutation test with L=0.05 breaks equivalence on 10/10 seeds.

claims.claim: Experiments on the corrupted Forrester function benchmark show RCGP-based methods (FC-RCGP-UCB, A2-RCGP-UCB) achieve lower cumulative regret than baselines using standard GP, Student-t process, or the heuristic DiagnosticsGP approach, even though the theoretical analysis conservatively requires α < 1/4 and α < 1/7 while experiments use corruption budgets as large as O(T^(1/3)) (Section 5.3, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: From-scratch CPU proxy with fixed RBF hyperparameters (not LOO-CV), grid argmax, and custom DiagnosticsGP on 1-D Forrester with 10 seeds; RCGP ordering holds under one endorsed config but advantage over GP-UCB is within one standard error (11.4%/5.8%) and flips (RCGP becomes worse than all baselines) under another endorsed config with adaptive T_c estimation.

kondratevakate/repro-robust-bayesian-opt.overall: The logbook provides rigorous symbolic/numeric verification of the three theorem-based claims (1, 2, 4) and strong experimental evidence for the infinite-magnitude robustness claim (3) via 1040-config enumeration with mutation tests. Claim 5 is only partially reproduced on a simplified proxy setup where the key comparison against GP-UCB is not statistically resolved and is configuration-sensitive.

kondratevakate/repro-last-iterate-conver.paper_title: Last-iterate Convergence of ADMM on Multi-affine Quadratic Equality Constrained Problem

claims.claim: Theorem 3.1 establishes sublinear convergence of ADMM to stationary points on multi-affine quadratic equality constrained problems under Assumptions 2.3 and 2.6, given a sufficiently large penalty parameter rho (Section 3).
claims.evidence: 450 runs on a small synthetic problem (q ∈ {0.5,2,5}) confirm convergence and blockwise optimality to ~5e-10, with mutation tests showing Assumption 2.6 is load-bearing (Example 2.8 diverges), but the setup is a simplified toy instance, not the paper's full-scale problems.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 proves a linear convergence rate when the nonlinearity norm ||C|| satisfies the bound in Equation 4 relative to Q's properties, provided the Lagrangian is second-order differentiable at limit points (Section 3).
claims.evidence: A toy problem with swept ||C|| shows linear contraction (~0.059) for small ||C|| and degradation to no contraction at ||C||=50, qualitatively matching Eq. 4, but the exact threshold is untestable since constants m1,m2,m3 are unspecified and the instance is small-scale.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 achieves linear convergence without requiring second-order differentiability when the constraint indicator functions {I_i} are polyhedral (Section 3).
claims.evidence: Box-constrained toy problem with 12 seeds per cell shows geometric gap decay (factor ≤0.088) with all box constraints active (no second-order differentiability), and 19,200 perturbation probes confirm local minimality; mutation tests confirm eq. 4 is still needed, but the setup is a small synthetic instance.

claims.claim: For robotic locomotion dynamics, Corollary 4.2 shows linear convergence holds when the discretization step Δt is below a threshold t0, since nonlinear terms decay as O((Δt)^3) (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Sympy derivation confirms quadratic coefficients have Δt-exponent exactly 3 (p=3.0000 fit), and simulation on a simplified planar instance (T=6, N=2, m=2kg) shows linear convergence (factor ~0.714) across Δt values, with a mutation confirming the O(Δt³) mechanism, but the specific threshold t0 is not pinned and the simulation is far below full locomotion scale.

claims.claim: Empirically, ADMM outperforms PADMM, IPDS-ADMM, and IADMM baselines on multi-affine constrained problems, and toy-problem experiments show q≥10 is sufficient to transition from sublinear to linear convergence (Figures 2 and 4).
claims.evidence: The q≥10 transition is not reproduced: all q<10 values already show linear convergence (factors 0.03–0.23) and no sublinear regime was found, but missing hyperparameters (μ_x, μ_z, ρ) prevent definitive falsification; the baseline comparison (PADMM, IPDS-ADMM, IADMM) was not attempted due to unreleased code and unreported problem settings.

claims.claim: The method is validated on 2D locomotion simulation and on real robot experiments including a humanoid jump and quadruped bounding task (Figures 5 and 6).
claims.evidence: Real robot experiments (humanoid jump, quadruped bounding) are not reproducible due to unavailable hardware and no released code/models/logs; the 2D simulation half cannot match Figure 5 because T, contact schedule, target CoM, initial state, and ρ are unreported.

kondratevakate/repro-last-iterate-conver.overall: The logbook provides rigorous toy-scale numerical validation of the paper's theoretical convergence claims (Theorems 3.1–3.3, Corollary 4.2) with mutation tests confirming mechanisms, but does not reproduce the empirical baseline comparisons or the real-robot experiments due to missing experimental details and hardware.

kondratevakate/repro-inference-aware-met.paper_title: Inference-Aware Meta-Alignment of LLMs via Non-Linear GRPO

claims.claim: IAMA optimizes the objective ℛ[π] = g(R1[π],...,Rm[π]) − β·KL[π||πref], where each Ri measures reward under an inference-time transformation such as Best-of-N sampling, allowing a single trained base policy π to adapt to multiple alignment criteria at inference time (Section 3, Equation 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook demonstrates non-linearity of the transformed objective (chord gap [1.037e-4, 8.139e-2] vs 2.22e-16 for linear E_π[r]) over 45 instances, shows IAMA outperforms naive in 60/60 multi-criterion cases, and confirms via N=1 mutation that non-linearity vanishes (chord gap 3.33e-16) as predicted.

claims.claim: Non-linear GRPO (Algorithm 1) replaces the standard scalar reward with an approximated functional derivative ∂R/∂π evaluated at the current policy's empirical distribution, requiring only a drop-in reward function on top of standard GRPO (Section 4, Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Functional derivative matches finite differences (max rel error 7.33e-8 over 80 cases), the drop-in replacement reaches the true optimum (max suboptimality 5.55e-16), empirical π̂ convergence slope is -1.024 vs theory -1, and plain-reward mutation is strictly worse in 30/30 instances.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 proves linear convergence of exact non-linear GRPO updates to the optimal policy, with excess loss bounded by β·KL[π*||π0] / ((L+β)/L)^T − 1 under a step size η=1/L (Section 5, Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: Across 90 instances and 2250 bound evaluations, the excess-loss bound is never violated above 1e-12 (the 44 ratio>1 rows are double-precision noise at LHS ≤3.33e-16); mutations with wrong step size (21/36 violations) and plain reward (36/36 violations) confirm the theorem's conditions are necessary.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.3 shows that with approximation error ε and optimization residual δ, inexact non-linear GRPO updates converge to a neighborhood of the optimum with an additive bias term of 2(ε+δ)/β (Section 5, Theorem 5.3).
claims.evidence: Over 60 configs and 200 runs each, the full bound with 2(ε+δ)/β is never violated (max ratio 0.2611), ε and δ measured from actual iterates; dropping the bias term causes violations in 36/36 noisy configs (max ratio 1.65e10), and plateau grows monotonically with noise in 12/12 cells.

claims.claim: Proposition 3.1 shows that naive weighted-sum training collapses to a degenerate policy outputting only a single medium value (δ0.5), whereas IAMA with Best-of-N yields a bimodal optimal policy π*(y) ∝ y^(α−1)(1−y)^(α−1)/(y^α+(1−y)^α)^2 with α=1/(N−1) (Section 3, Proposition 3.1).
claims.evidence: Sympy confirms the closed-form density normalizes to 1; functional-derivative span at claimed π* is machine-precision (≤5.84e-16) for N=2,3,4,8,16; naive optimum puts 100% mass near y=0.5 (δ0.5 collapse) vs 0.922 mass outside [0.25,0.75] for IAMA N=8; mutation with α=1/N yields span 14-15 orders of magnitude larger.

claims.claim: On the HH-RLHF task with Alpaca-7B, IAMA trained with Best-of-N sampling (N=4) pushes the helpfulness-harmlessness Pareto front forward relative to standard alignment, while without Best-of-N sampling IAMA performs equivalently to standard alignment (Section 6.2).
claims.evidence: No experiments were run for this claim; the logbook documents concrete blockers (GPU-scale 7B RL training, unreleased author-trained reward models and judges, no public code, figure-only evidence with no numeric table).

kondratevakate/repro-inference-aware-met.overall: The logbook provides rigorous numerical verification of the paper's five theoretical claims (objective non-linearity, algorithm design, two convergence theorems, and the bimodality proposition) on discrete-distribution setups with mutation tests and independent solver cross-checks, but the sole empirical LLM-scale claim (HH-RLHF/Alpaca-7B) is not addressed at all due to GPU and unreleased-model blockers.

kondratevakate/repro-causal-matrix-compl.paper_title: Causal Matrix Completion under Multiple Treatments via Mixed Synthetic Nearest Neighbors

claims.claim: MSNN provably preserves Synthetic Nearest Neighbors' entry-wise finite-sample error bound (Theorem 4.5) and asymptotic normality with convergence rate scaling as K_MSNN^(-1/2) (Theorem 4.6) (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook page only lists a script name (verify_claim1.py) and a result file path (results/claim1.json) with a self-assigned verdict, but no actual proof-checking steps, numerical validation, or theorem verification details are shown.
