claims.evidence: No agent runs were executed on HistBench. The logbook built an exact-match scoring harness and measured a trivial floor (empty answer → 0.000 over 310 items), but no actual HistAgent or GPT-4o inference was performed, so the 27.54%/36.47% accuracy figures are entirely untested.

claims.claim: HistAgent significantly outperforms GPT-4o with online search (18.60% pass@1), DeepSeek-R1 (14.49% pass@1), Grok 3 (17.63% pass@1), and Open Deep Research-smolagents (20.29% pass@1, 25.12% pass@2) on HistBench (Table 5, Table 6).
claims.evidence: No baseline models (GPT-4o with search, DeepSeek-R1, Grok 3, Open Deep Research) were run on HistBench, and no comparison data was generated. The claim's comparative accuracy figures are completely unaddressed.

claims.claim: HistAgent achieves 60.00% pass@1 accuracy on the GAIA validation benchmark, compared to 55.15% for Open Deep Research (HuggingFace/smolagents) on the same split, indicating domain-specific customization does not hinder general-task performance (Table 7).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states GAIA runs were not performed due to budget constraints. No experimental evidence exists for the 60.00% pass@1 or the 55.15% comparison figure.

claims.claim: Questions in HistBench were filtered during a multi-stage review pipeline that excludes items solved by more than two of several strong LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1) tested without access to supporting materials, followed by professional historian review (Section 3, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook does not address the multi-stage review pipeline, the LLM-based filtering process, or the professional historian review at any point. No evidence was gathered regarding this claim.

snowfire/repro-histbench-histagent.overall: The logbook provides a solid audit of the public HistBench dataset confirming core composition statistics (414 questions, 306/108 split, multimodal coverage), but none of the four agent-performance or pipeline claims were tested with any experimental runs. The reproduction attempt is limited to static dataset inspection; the paper's central experimental contributions remain entirely unverified.

snowfire/repro-esg-geometry.paper_title: Learning the ESG Geometry with Domain Aware Language Models

claims.claim: Domain-aware representation learning enables accurate ESG forecasting, trajectory-based grouping, and latent-space search for asset selection.
claims.evidence: A toy heterogeneous-forecasting check on synthetic tokens (not real ESG data) showed block-ortho RMSE 1.003 vs naive 0.913 (-9.8%), i.e., no downstream benefit on the proxy task; the actual ESG forecasting, trajectory grouping, and asset selection claims were never tested on real data.

claims.claim: Value-aware tokens with block-wise orthogonal embeddings preserve both numerical proximity and semantic type for heterogeneous time series.
claims.evidence: On three diagnostics with synthetic heterogeneous tokens, block-orthogonal embeddings achieved within-type value-proximity correlation 0.965 and diff-type same-value similarity 0.000, while a naive shared projection leaked value across types (0.509), directly confirming that the mechanism preserves both numerical proximity and semantic type purity.

snowfire/repro-esg-geometry.overall: The logbook constructively verifies the block-orthogonal embedding mechanism (Claim 2) with clear metrics showing type purity and value preservation, but only provides a toy proxy test for the downstream ESG claims (Claim 1) using synthetic data, where the method actually underperformed a naive baseline.

Jaycee766/repro-a-geometric-analysis-of-.paper_title: A Geometric Analysis of Small-sized Language Model Hallucinations

claims.claim: Across a dataset of 300,000 responses (150 responses per prompt for 200 time-sensitive prompts, across 10 small LLMs of 7B-32B parameters), genuine responses show tighter intra-class clustering than hallucinated responses, with the ratio of inter-class to intra-class embedding distance averaging 1.13 in raw embedding space (Table 1).
claims.evidence: On 297,795 rows of the SOCRATES-300K dataset, the reproduction measured a mean raw separability ratio of 1.1324, closely matching the paper's claimed 1.13, using 1,777 valid pairs.

claims.claim: Fisher Discriminant Analysis projection amplifies the separability ratio between genuine and hallucinated response clusters from 1.13× to an average of 7.26× across the 10 evaluated models, with a shared optimal regularization value of λ≈1.2 across architectures (Table 1, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: The measured mean Fisher-projected separability of 7.2613 closely matches the paper's 7.26×, and the mean best λ of 1.30 is near the claimed λ≈1.2, though the min-regret λ of 0.8 introduces some ambiguity about the 'shared optimal' characterization.

claims.claim: A label-propagation classifier built on the Fisher-projected embedding space achieves average accuracy of 87.2% and average F1-score of 90.7% for hallucination classification, with per-model F1 ranging from 84.0% to 95.3% (Table 2).
claims.evidence: The label-propagation classifier achieved 87.1% accuracy and 90.6% F1 with per-model F1 ranging from 84.1% to 95.2%, closely matching the paper's reported 87.2% accuracy, 90.7% F1, and 84.0–95.3% F1 range across 1,554 pairs.

claims.claim: Label-propagation F1 performance saturates once 30-50 labeled training responses are available, demonstrating label-efficient hallucination classification (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The label efficiency curve shows F1 reaching 95% of maximum at n_train=33, which falls within the paper's claimed 30–50 label saturation range.

claims.claim: Observed Wasserstein distances between genuine and hallucinated response distributions exceed the null-hypothesis (random label permutation) baseline for 87.6% of prompts on average, with per-model rates ranging from 81.5% to 94.5%, indicating genuine geometric structure rather than sampling artifacts (Table 5, Figures 3 and 6).
claims.evidence: The measured global rate of Wasserstein distances exceeding the null baseline is 87.64% with per-model range 81.48–94.51%, closely matching the paper's 87.6% and 81.5–94.5% range.

claims.claim: The global average hallucination rate across all evaluated models and years is 80.9%, with individual model rates ranging from 66.4% to 87.6% (Table 4).
claims.evidence: The reproduction measured a global hallucination rate of 84.59% with per-model range 72.1–91.9%, which notably diverges from the paper's claimed 80.9% with range 66.4–87.6% — a ~3.7pp discrepancy that the logbook incorrectly marks as matching, possibly due to the ~2,200 missing rows or different data processing.

Jaycee766/repro-a-geometric-analysis-of-.overall: The logbook reruns the authors' own APORIA analysis pipeline on the released SOCRATES-300K precomputed embeddings (297,795 rows), closely matching most reported metrics for separability, Fisher projection, label-propagation classification, label efficiency, and Wasserstein permutation analysis. However, it does not independently regenerate model responses or recompute embeddings, and Claim 6 shows a notable 3.7pp discrepancy in hallucination rate that is not adequately explained.

subham73/repro-futurecad-brep-grounding.paper_title: Towards High-Fidelity CAD Generation via LLM-Driven Program Generation and Text-Based B-Rep Primitive Grounding

claims.claim: FutureCAD generates executable CadQuery scripts via an LLM that emits parametric feature sequences plus natural-language queries, which the BRepGround module (Figure 3) grounds to specific B-Rep primitives for the CAD kernel to execute (Section 4, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: No LLM generation, CadQuery script execution, or BRepGround module was ever run. The dataset audit found 81,907 JSON files with feature sequences consistent with the paper's framing, but this only confirms data structure, not pipeline functionality.

claims.claim: Training proceeds via supervised fine-tuning on text-to-program pairs at two description granularities (abstract and detailed), plus ~80k additional program-rewritten samples for diversity, followed by reinforcement learning with Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) using a Chamfer Distance-based geometric reward (Section 5).
claims.evidence: No training code, configs, checkpoints, rewritten samples, or splits were available. No SFT or GSPO RL training was executed; the claim was never experimentally addressed.

claims.claim: The reward function assigns higher scores to geometrically closer generated shapes and linearly penalizes Chamfer Distance deviations beyond a 0.2 tolerance (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The reward_audit.py script demonstrated the formula is monotonically non-increasing with reward 1.0 for distances ≤0.2 and linearly decreasing beyond that, and chamfer_reward_surface_audit.py confirmed on 3D cube point clouds that geometrically closer shapes receive higher rewards.

claims.claim: On the new FutureCAD dataset (~140,000 real-world CAD models sourced from the ABC dataset via the Onshape API, including 28k advanced-feature models), the method achieves a median Chamfer Distance of 31.12 (mean 71.39) and an invalidity ratio of 1.01% on the advanced subset, and a median Chamfer Distance of 14.68 (down from a 37.47 baseline) on the standard subset (Section 6, Table 1).
claims.evidence: The dataset audit found 81,907 JSON files (not ~140k) and 30,468 advanced models, but no generation outputs, evaluation code, official splits, or CAD kernel scripts were available to recompute Table 1 metrics.

claims.claim: BRepGround achieves 63.07% mAP and 50.23% F1 on B-Rep primitive grounding, and the full pipeline attains G-F1 of 80.54% and R-F1 of 85.35% on the advanced subset (Section 6, Table 2).
claims.evidence: A lexical+geometry baseline (not UV-Net+BERT BRepGround) was run on 12,000 of 81,907 models with a reduced candidate set, yielding mAP 0.5859 and F1 0.5226 versus the paper's 0.6307/0.5023; the full pipeline G-F1/R-F1 metrics were never addressed at all.

subham73/repro-futurecad-brep-grounding.overall: The logbook independently verifies the reward function's mathematical properties and provides a reduced-scale proxy test of text-to-primitive grounding on real FutureCAD data, but the core pipeline claims (LLM CadQuery generation, SFT+GSPO training, Table 1/Table 2 metrics) remain unaddressed due to the absence of released code, checkpoints, and evaluation scripts.

AakashJammula/repro-lapconn-laplacian-co.paper_title: Impact of Connectivity on Laplacian Representations in Reinforcement Learning

claims.claim: The approximation error of a rank-k learned Laplacian representation used for linear value function approximation is upper-bounded by ‖v−v̂_k‖_Φ ≤ ‖r̄‖_Φ√(1/(λ₂λ_{k+1})) + ‖v‖_Φ√(2ε/(λ_{k+1}−λ_k)), decomposing into truncation error and feature-estimation error (Theorem 3.3, Section 3.1).
claims.evidence: 1260 numerical bound checks across 60 MDPs (8x8 gridworlds, 10 wall counts, 3 seeds, uniform and non-uniform policies, k∈{3,5,8}, 7 epsilon levels) all held with zero violations; max LHS/RHS ratio was 0.189, confirming the two-term end-to-end error bound holds on both symmetric and genuinely asymmetric transition kernels.

claims.claim: The truncation error term is bounded by ‖v−v_k‖²_Φ ≤ ‖r̄‖²_Φ/(λ₂λ_{k+1}), showing the bound scales inversely with the algebraic connectivity λ₂ of the state-transition graph, so poorly-connected MDPs induce larger approximation error (Lemma 3.4, Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: 180/180 truncation-error bound checks held with zero violations (max ratio 0.036); a dedicated connectivity sweep (125 trials, 25 wall counts × 5 seeds) confirmed the inverse-λ₂ scaling with Spearman correlation(λ₂, bound²) = −0.965, and seed-averaged actual truncation error increased with decreasing connectivity (Spearman +0.81).

claims.claim: The Graph Drawing Objective's feature-estimation error is bounded by ‖Π_Ψ−Π_Ψ̃‖₂ < √(2ε/(λ_{k+1}−λ_k)), depending on the spectral gap between the k-th and (k+1)-th eigenvalues (Lemma 3.5, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: 1260/1260 checks of the projection-distance bound ‖Π_Ψ−Π_Ψ̃‖₂ < √(2ε/(λ_{k+1}−λ_k)) held with zero violations (max ratio 0.313), with the strict inequality respected across the full ~1000x range of epsilon and both policy types.

claims.claim: The analysis defines a Φ-self-adjoint Laplacian L = I − (P+Φ⁻¹PᵀΦ)/2 (Equation 6, Section 3) and applies without assuming symmetry of the induced transition kernel, i.e., it holds for general non-uniform behavior policies (Lemma 3.6, Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: On a 49-state gridworld with strongly asymmetric P (max|P−Pᵀ|=0.986), ΦL was symmetric to 6.9e-18 and the self-adjointness identity held to 1.7e-16; the naive I−P alternative failed self-adjointness at 0.051 on the same P, directly demonstrating Eq. 6's necessity for non-uniform policies.

claims.claim: Propositions 4.1 and 4.2 establish that this matrix-based Laplacian formulation is equivalent to the operator-theoretic Laplacian representation formulation of Wu et al. (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Proposition 4.1's operator-matrix identity was confirmed to 9.7e-17 by implementing Wu et al.'s kernel as an explicit double sum (not shortcut through Eq. 6); Proposition 4.2's optimality was confirmed by trace matching to 2.6e-16 and by all 200 random Φ-orthonormal frames achieving strictly larger trace (min 2.17 vs. 0.022).

AakashJammula/repro-lapconn-laplacian-co.overall: This logbook provides strong numerical evidence for all five theoretical claims through exact linear algebra on gridworld MDPs matching the paper's own Section 6 validation environment, with 2700+ bound checks (zero violations) and machine-precision algebraic verifications on asymmetric transition kernels. The reproduction is rigorous: it tests both symmetric and non-uniform policies, sweeps connectivity and epsilon ranges, constructs analytically-controlled epsilon-optimal features, and honestly reports a self-caught implementation bug.

AakashJammula/repro-softjax-informative-.paper_title: SoftJAX & SoftTorch: Empowering Automatic Differentiation Libraries with Informative Gradients

claims.claim: SoftJAX and SoftTorch provide differentiable soft surrogates for hard primitives including thresholding (sign, abs, round, ReLU, clip via Heaviside relaxations), Boolean/fuzzy logic operators, discrete indexing (SoftIndex), and sorting/ranking (Sections 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook verifies thresholding primitives (sign, abs, round, clip, ReLU, comparison) with 20,000 points and multiple tau values showing convergence to hard counterparts and informative gradients, but Boolean/fuzzy logic operators and SoftIndex (discrete indexing) — explicitly named in the claim — are never implemented or tested.

claims.claim: The libraries identify an 'STE pitfall' where applying straight-through estimation separately to each factor of a multiplicative composite operation causes gradients to vanish, and show this is avoided by applying STE to the composite function as a whole (Section 2, Equation 1).
claims.evidence: PyTorch float64 autograd at (x,y)=(-1,-1) with f=relu(x), g=relu(y) shows naive per-factor STE gradient is exactly (0.0, 0.0) while composite STE gradient is (0.0108, 0.0108), with forward values matching hard relu(x)*relu(y) exactly across four test points — directly reproducing Eqs. 2-3 and Figure 3.

claims.claim: Four families of differentiable sort/rank operators are implemented: optimal-transport-based, unit-simplex-projection-based (SoftSort, NeuralSort), permutahedron-projection-based (FastSoftSort, and a novel entropy-regularized SmoothSort variant), and sorting-network-based (Sections 4.1-4.4).
claims.evidence: All four families are implemented with representative methods (Sinkhorn, SoftSort, NeuralSort, FastSoftSort via PAVA, soft bitonic network) and verified at n=8 with 30 trials showing convergence to hard sort and informative gradients near ties, but the novel entropy-regularized SmoothSort variant is not implemented and the scale is far below the paper's benchmarks.

claims.claim: FastSoftSort achieves the lowest memory footprint (~420KB) among benchmarked soft-sorting methods at n=4096, while the sorting-network approach is fastest at ~1.0ms (3.8x the hard baseline), versus ~16ms for SoftSort and ~37ms for NeuralSort (Section 5, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: Benchmarked at n=1024 (not n=4096) with pure-NumPy implementations: FastSoftSort has lowest memory (58KB vs 25-42MB for others), confirming the memory ranking, but the sorting network is 4th of 5 in speed (136ms vs 0.95ms for FastSoftSort), not fastest as claimed — the logbook attributes this to Python-loop overhead vs JAX/XLA compilation.

claims.claim: A case study applies SoftJAX operators (sj.argmax, sj.dynamic_index_in_dim) to soften the manifold-point-selection step of MuJoCo XLA's collision detection pipeline, enabling gradient flow through a previously non-differentiable physics operation (Appendix B).
claims.evidence: The MuJoCo XLA collision detection case study (Appendix B) is never addressed — no code, no experiments, no results related to sj.argmax, sj.dynamic_index_in_dim, or physics pipeline integration appear anywhere in the logbook.

AakashJammula/repro-softjax-informative-.overall: The logbook provides solid numerical evidence for the STE pitfall (Claim 2) and partial verification of soft primitives and sorting operators at small scale, but leaves Boolean/fuzzy logic, SoftIndex, the novel SmoothSort variant, and the MuJoCo XLA case study entirely unaddressed. Benchmark rankings are tested at reduced scale with unoptimized implementations, yielding mixed results.

AakashJammula/repro-gsim-joint-learning-.paper_title: Joint Learning in the Gaussian Single Index Model

claims.claim: In the joint learning setting (as opposed to the planted-target-only model), gradient flow converges to the target direction even when the initial correlation m0 is negative, for first-nonzero-Hermite-coefficient index s≥2, with |1+m_t| decaying at rate Ce^{-c(t-τc)} after time τc ≥ Cd^{s-1} (Theorem 1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: Experiment B shows joint learning with s=2, m0=-0.05 reaches m_final=-1.0 with E_T=5.8e-15 (functional recovery via coefficient sign-flip), while Experiment C's 120-seed sweep across d={20,50,80} with m0=-2/sqrt(d) achieves 100% success (E_T<1e-2) with all m_final<0, confirming m_t→-1 for negative m0 with s≥2. The specific exponential rate Ce^{-c(t-τc)} and τc≥Cd^{s-1} scaling are not directly measured via decay curves, but the convergence itself is robustly demonstrated.

claims.claim: This contrasts with the planted model, where a negative initial direction traps the gradient flow in a spurious basin; in joint learning the adaptively evolving link function f_t corrects for the early misalignment (Section 4.2).
claims.evidence: The planted-model control (Claim 1 experiments) reproduces all three trapping branches including m_T=-0.666667=-m_bar for h2+h3 (genuine spurious basin), and Experiment B's direct contrast on identical target/m0 shows planted model fails (E_T=2.0, frozen coefficients cannot sign-flip) while joint learning succeeds (E_T=5.8e-15), isolating the adaptive-link-function mechanism.

claims.claim: A dense reproducing kernel Hilbert space built from Hermite functions, K(x,y)=Σ_k c_k h_k(x) h_k(y), is constructed to adapt to the single-index structure for univariate function estimation (Proposition 2, Section 5).
claims.evidence: The Gram matrix of K(x,y)=Σ c_k h_k(x)h_k(y) with c_k=1/(k+1)^3 is verified PSD (min eigenvalue -6e-16), the reproducing property <f,K(x,.)>_H=f(x) holds to 8.9e-16 over 200 random trials, and the truncation bound inf||f-g||²≤||f||²_H1/K² holds at all tested K values (K=2,5,10,20,50,100).

claims.claim: The joint gradient flow on Hermite coefficients and the index direction can be implemented in practice as a finite-dimensional ODE on ((a_k)_{k≤𝗄}, m), discretized via an Euler scheme (Section 5, Section 6).
claims.evidence: The idealized Euler-discretized ODE on ((a_k)_{k≤K}, m) runs correctly throughout all experiments, and the empirical finite-sample realization (run_empirical_rkhs.py, n=8000, d=60, K=6, projected gradient descent) reproduces Theorem 1 behavior with E_T=3.6e-15 for joint vs E_T=1.81 for planted from negative m0=-0.387, confirming practical implementability.

AakashJammula/repro-gsim-joint-learning-.overall: This logbook provides concrete numerical evidence supporting all four claims through Euler-discretized ODE integration, a 120-seed statistical sweep, a direct planted-vs-joint contrast isolating the coefficient sign-flip mechanism, a finite-sample gradient-descent realization, and exact verification of the Hermite RKHS construction and approximation bound. The main gap is that the specific exponential convergence rate and τc~d^{s-1} scaling are not directly measured, though convergence is robustly demonstrated.

snowfire/repro-soar-self-play-curriculum.paper_title: Teaching Models to Teach Themselves: Reasoning at the Edge of Learnability

claims.claim: SOAR trains a teacher model with meta-RL to generate synthetic problems rewarded by measured improvement in a student model on hard target problems (Section 3.2).
claims.evidence: The logbook demonstrates the improvement-grounded reward peaking at practice offset 0.0 (student_improvement=0.004452) in a synthetic sigmoid-based learnability simulation, but no actual meta-RL teacher model is trained; the mechanism is replicated on a proxy task.

claims.claim: The experiments target sparse-reward math subsets where the base model has 0/128 initial success on sampled hard problems (Abstract).
claims.evidence: The simulation initializes hard targets at 0.0003 per-attempt success (~0/128), mimicking the zero-signal condition, but this is on synthetic data with no real math subsets (MATH/HARP) or real base model.

claims.claim: Students trained on SOAR promotion questions outperform hard-only training and intrinsic-reward teacher baselines on MATH and HARP fail@128 evaluations (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The simulation shows edge curriculum reaching 1.0 while hard-only stalls at 0.0003 and intrinsic reaches ~0.996, replicating the ordering, but this is on a synthetic learnability model, not MATH or HARP fail@128 evaluations with real models.

claims.claim: Grounded teacher rewards yield more stable student pass@32 trajectories than intrinsic teacher rewards across teacher seeds (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook reports grounded teacher final-pass std=0.000 vs intrinsic std=0.003 in the synthetic simulation, showing the stability pattern, but no real teacher seeds or real pass@32 trajectories on actual tasks are evaluated.

claims.claim: SOAR-generated MATH promotion questions recover 75% of the gains from full MATH training, while HARP promotion questions recover 50% of the gains from full HARP training (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The simulation shows edge promotion recovering ~100% of full-training gains, but the specific claims of 75% recovery on MATH and 50% on HARP are not tested; no real MATH or HARP datasets are used.

claims.claim: The final trained teacher policy does not improve direct inference on fail@128 test problems, separating generator utility from solver ability (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The logbook states the teacher scores ~0 as a direct solver while its student reaches ~1.0 in the synthetic simulation, demonstrating generator≠solver, but no real teacher policy is evaluated on real fail@128 test problems.

snowfire/repro-soar-self-play-curriculum.overall: The logbook reproduces SOAR's core mechanisms (edge-of-learnability curriculum advantage, improvement-grounded reward stability, generator≠solver separation) on a synthetic CPU learnability simulation with sigmoid-based student competence, but none of the six claims are tested on real language models, real math datasets (MATH/HARP), or with actual meta-RL teacher training. All claims are addressed only at toy scale with a 1-second synthetic simulation.

snowfire/repro-reponavigator.paper_title: One Tool Is Enough: Reinforcement Learning of LLM Agents for Repository-Level Code Navigation

claims.claim: RepoNavigator equips an LLM agent with a single execution-aware jump tool backed by symbol resolution from a language server (Figure 1; Section 3.3).
claims.evidence: The logbook replaces the actual LLM agent and language server with a synthetic graph where 'call edges = execution-aware jumps,' providing a toy proxy of the concept without any real symbol resolution or LLM agent.

claims.claim: RepoNavigator is trained with GRPO using a hybrid reward combining localization Dice with tool-use success (Section 3.4).
claims.evidence: A simple linear policy with learned weights (is_call=3.7, lexical_sim=-0.8) on a synthetic graph is used instead of actual GRPO training of an LLM with the hybrid reward; the core training mechanism is not reproduced at scale.

claims.claim: RL-trained RepoNavigator improves function-level and file-level localization on SWE-bench_Verified over same-size baselines, with 7B models outperforming 14B baselines and 14B models surpassing 32B competitors (Table 1).
claims.evidence: No SWE-bench_Verified data, no 7B/14B/32B model comparisons, and no real baselines are used; the synthetic graph shows RL policy Dice 0.311 vs random 0.185 and retrieval 0.073, but this is a proxy task far removed from the claim's specific benchmark and model-size results.

claims.claim: RepoNavigator also achieves state-of-the-art localization performance on SWE-bench_Pro across compared agent pipelines (Table 2).
claims.evidence: SWE-bench_Pro and agent pipelines are not used; only a synthetic graph comparison of strategies (RL 0.311 vs others) is provided as a proxy for the SOTA claim.

claims.claim: Increasing the allowed number of jump-tool calls improves localization performance before and after RL training, supporting a scaling law of tool-calling (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: The logbook shows Dice increasing with K on a synthetic graph (exec: 0.143→0.173, RL: 0.251→0.342 across K=2–12), demonstrating the general trend but on a toy setup without real repositories or LLM agents.

claims.claim: Substituting RepoNavigator localization into an Agentless repair pipeline improves downstream SWE-bench_Verified issue resolution (Table 3).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states the downstream Agentless repair improvement was not tested; no experiment addresses this claim.

snowfire/repro-reponavigator.overall: This logbook constructs a small synthetic repository-graph proxy (runtime ~2s on CPU) to illustrate general principles behind RepoNavigator, but does not reproduce any of the paper's actual experiments on SWE-bench_Verified, SWE-bench_Pro, or with real LLMs, language servers, or model-size comparisons. Claims 1–5 are addressed only at toy scale, and Claim 6 is entirely untested.

snowfire/repro-med-seglens.paper_title: Med-SegLens: Latent-Level Model Diffing for Interpretable Medical Image Segmentation

claims.claim: Med-SegLens trains sparse autoencoders on intermediate segmentation-model activations and uses automated latent interpretation plus latent alignment for model diffing (Figure 1; Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: The logbook demonstrates the SAE + latent interpretation + model-diffing mechanism on synthetic concept-superposition activations (12 concepts in 16 dims) with sparse dictionary learning as an SAE analog, not on actual segmentation-model activations from SegFormer or U-Net.

claims.claim: Sparse autoencoder latents correspond to interpretable tumor, anatomy, background, and boundary concepts in SegFormer and U-Net models (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: SAE vs PCA selectivity (0.323 vs 0.136) and best-match correlation (0.621 vs 0.554) are reported on synthetic activations with known concepts, not on real SegFormer/U-Net models interpreting actual tumor, anatomy, background, and boundary concepts from medical images.

claims.claim: SegFormer and U-Net use latent categories differently on BraTS-Adult cases, with SegFormer activating substantially more tumor-related latent mass than U-Net (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Model A (SegFormer-like) tumor-latent mass 0.185 vs 0.074 for model B (ratio 2.49) is measured on synthetic models A/B, not on actual SegFormer and U-Net evaluated on BraTS-Adult cases.

claims.claim: Cross-dataset latent alignment reveals a stable but partial shared representation backbone across adult, pediatric, Sub-Saharan African glioma, and healthy cohorts (Table 1).
claims.evidence: Cross-cohort latent→concept mapping shared fractions (1.0/0.92/0.92/0.83) are computed on synthetic data, not on real adult, pediatric, Sub-Saharan African glioma, and healthy cohorts.

claims.claim: Latent steering recovers a substantial fraction of segmentation failure cases without retraining and improves mean Dice on failure cases (Figure 6; Table 3).
claims.evidence: Latent steering lifting Dice from 0.325 to 0.757 on failure cases is demonstrated on synthetic activations with a synthetic Dice readout, not on actual segmentation failure cases from real models.

claims.claim: Cross-domain latent steering improves Adult-to-Pediatric and Pediatric-to-Adult out-of-distribution segmentation performance, especially for edema errors (Table 5; Figure 8).
claims.evidence: The logbook explicitly states cross-domain Adult↔Pediatric steering OOD gains were not tested; no experiments or data address this claim.

snowfire/repro-med-seglens.overall: The logbook reproduces the Med-SegLens mechanism (SAE monosemanticity, model diffing, latent steering) on a small synthetic concept-superposition dataset with known concepts, providing real numbers but at toy scale with no real segmentation models, BraTS data, or medical images. Claim 6 (cross-domain OOD steering) was never addressed.

snowfire/repro-stable-gflownet-redteamin.paper_title: Stable-GFlowNet: Toward Diverse and Robust LLM Red-Teaming via Contrastive Trajectory Balance

claims.claim: Stable-GFN replaces explicit GFlowNet partition-function estimation with Contrastive Trajectory Balance based on pairwise trajectory comparisons (Section 4).
claims.evidence: CTB is implemented without a logZ parameter (TB retains learned logZ) on a 64-leaf tabular GFlowNet (length-3 sequences over 4-symbol alphabet), confirming the structural design but at a scale far below the paper's LLM red-teaming setting.

claims.claim: The method adds Noisy Gradient Pruning to filter uninformative reward differences under noisy red-teaming rewards (Section 4).
claims.evidence: No experiment implements or tests Noisy Gradient Pruning as a distinct component; the noisy-reward runs only compare TB vs CTB, without isolating or evaluating the pruning mechanism itself.

claims.claim: The Min-K Fluency Stabilizer penalizes non-fluent out-of-distribution prompts to reduce gibberish reward hacking (Section 4).
claims.evidence: Fluency stabilizer on/off is tested on a synthetic 64-leaf environment with manual 'gibberish traps,' showing mass on non-fluent leaves drops from 0.468 to 0.003, but this is a proxy task with no real LLM prompts or fluency model.

claims.claim: Stable-GFN reports stronger attack diversity and attack performance than GFN baselines across LLM red-teaming settings (Section 5).
claims.evidence: TB vs CTB compared on 64-leaf toy environment: clean rewards yield tied mode coverage and L1 (~0.018-0.019), noisy rewards yield L1 0.560 vs 0.570 (essentially tied), so no CTB-over-TB advantage manifests at this scale.

claims.claim: Ablations evaluate loss-function and reward-stabilization choices, including the effect of reward constraints on attack discovery (Table 3).
claims.evidence: Partial ablation-like comparisons exist (TB vs CTB loss, fluency stabilizer on/off, clean vs noisy rewards) on the 64-leaf synthetic setup, but no reproduction of the paper's Table 3 ablation structure or reward-constraint attack-discovery analysis at LLM scale.

snowfire/repro-stable-gflownet-redteamin.overall: The logbook implements core structural elements (CTB without logZ, fluency stabilizer) on a tiny 64-leaf tabular GFlowNet with synthetic rewards, demonstrating the fluency stabilizer's effect but failing to show CTB's claimed advantage over TB at this scale. Noisy Gradient Pruning is never specifically tested, and all experiments are far below the paper's LLM red-teaming scale.

nmaher/repro-stand-self-aware-preconditi.paper_title: STAND: Self-Aware Precondition Induction for Interactive Task Learning

claims.claim: At N=100 training problems for multicolumn addition, STAND reaches 98.62% per-problem completeness versus 96.97% for decision trees, 95.53% for random forests, and 98.01% for XGBoost (Section 5, Table 1).
claims.evidence: This claim concerns multicolumn-addition completeness at N=100, but the logbook explicitly marks all real ITL-domain claims (Dice Adventure, Fractions, MC Addition) as BLOCKED due to unavailable proprietary VAL/AI2T infrastructure. The synthetic-task experiments (logbook Claim 1) report different numbers (STAND 90.0%/96.89%) and do not test the MC-addition domain or the specific 98.62% figure.

claims.claim: STAND achieves 100% completeness in 19 of 40 multicolumn-addition runs, compared with only 10 of 40 runs for single decision trees (Section 5, Table 1).
claims.evidence: This claim about 100% completeness in 19 of 40 MC-addition runs was never addressed; the logbook's Claim 8 states the real ITL domains including MC Addition are BLOCKED. No run-count data from the actual multicolumn-addition domain exists anywhere in the logbook.

claims.claim: STAND's total error recurrence rate on multicolumn addition is 0.53%, comparable to decision trees (0.38%) and lower than random forests (1.28%) and XGBoost (0.74%) (Section 5, Table 2).
claims.evidence: The claim specifies error recurrence rates on multicolumn addition (0.53% for STAND, etc.), but the logbook's error-reoccurrence experiments (logbook Claim 2) were run only on the synthetic task with entirely different absolute magnitudes (STAND-hs FP 8.66%, FN 6.74%). The MC-addition domain was never run.

claims.claim: On productive monotonicity (alignment between certainty change and actual learning gains), STAND scores 78.54% on fractions versus 50.61% for random forests and 50.90% for XGBoost (Section 5, Table 4).
claims.evidence: The claim concerns productive monotonicity on the fractions domain (78.54% for STAND), but the logbook's productive-monotonicity experiment (logbook Claim 3) was run only on the synthetic task (STAND-hs 83.9%). The fractions domain was explicitly BLOCKED and never tested.

claims.claim: STAND's average fitting time (5.30ms) and prediction time (0.35ms) remain below the 10ms threshold required for interactive task-learning applications, despite building a full approximate version space at each split (Section 5).
claims.evidence: No timing measurements appear anywhere in the logbook. None of the eight logbook claims address fitting or prediction latency, and the specific 5.30ms/0.35ms figures were never measured or reported.

nmaher/repro-stand-self-aware-preconditi.overall: The logbook implements STAND from scratch and runs experiments on a synthetic benchmark and UCI datasets, but all five claims being judged concern the multicolumn-addition and fractions domains, which the logbook explicitly marks as BLOCKED due to unavailable proprietary tutoring infrastructure. None of the five specific claims were tested on their actual domains.

AakashJammula/repro-matroid-size-sensiti.paper_title: Matroid Algorithms Under Size-Sensitive Independence Oracles

claims.claim: Under the size-sensitive independence-oracle cost model, any (possibly randomized) algorithm approximating matroid rank within a multiplicative factor of 1 ± 1/40 with probability at least 2/3 must incur Ω(n²) query cost in the worst case (Theorem 1.1.1).
claims.evidence: The hard-instance family (free∪uniform matroid, truncated) is correctly constructed and its structural properties verified at 100% match rate across m=10–160, and the trivial greedy algorithm's cost scales with log-log slope 1.994≈2. However, this is a lower bound over all algorithms that no experiment can prove; the evidence confirms the proof mechanism and consistency of the natural algorithm, not the Ω(n²) bound itself.

claims.claim: For matroids whose maximum circuit size is at most c, a randomized algorithm finds a maximum-weight basis with expected query cost O(n^{2−1/c} log n), breaking the quadratic query-cost barrier (Theorem 1.1.1).
claims.evidence: Algorithm 1 is implemented verbatim and finds the exact maximum-weight basis in all 21 trials across c=2,3,4 (n up to 6144). Fitted cost exponents 1.599/1.803/1.881 closely track the predicted 2−1/c=1.5/1.667/1.75, with the small consistent excess (~0.1–0.14) explained by the theorem's O(n^{2−1/c} log n) bound (the 1/log n correction term accounts for ~0.12–0.13 at these scales).

claims.claim: Distinguishing a partition matroid of part size 3 from one of part size 4 requires Ω(n²) query cost, matching the Õ(n²) upper bound for partition-size estimation (Theorem 1.1.2).
claims.evidence: The l-relaxed partition matroid hard instance is built exactly as specified, with 100% match rate for both the small-query-uninformative property and the exact witness characterization (intersects every part) across m=12–192. Witness rarity decays exponentially in m (fitted rate 1.398). However, as a lower bound over all algorithms, this verifies the proof mechanism but not the Ω(n²) bound itself.

claims.claim: For general non-decreasing query-cost functions f(|Q|), the paper proves an Ω(n·f(n/3)) lower bound using matroid unions of free and uniform matroids as hard instances (Section 6).
claims.evidence: The upper bound O(n·f(n)) is strongly verified: greedy algorithm cost under f(k)=k^p yields fitted slopes 1.991/2.484/2.964/3.959 vs predicted 2/2.5/3/4 for p=1/1.5/2/3. However, the actual claim is the Ω(n·f(n/3)) lower bound, for which only qualitative/directional witness-rarity evidence is provided—insufficient to verify the lower bound claim itself.

claims.claim: Linear-time size-sensitive oracle implementations are given for partition, graphic, bicircular, convex-transversal, and job-scheduling matroids (Section B).
claims.evidence: All 5 oracle types (partition, graphic, bicircular, convex-transversal, job-scheduling) are implemented per the paper's Section B descriptions and tested at query sizes 1,000–128,000. Tail-half log-log slopes are 1.14–1.27 for the linear oracles and ~0.97 for the near-linear oracles, consistent with linear/near-linear scaling (the modest excess above 1.0 attributable to Python-level overhead and cache effects, with per-element time growing only ~2.5x for a 128x size increase rather than the 128x a quadratic oracle would show).

AakashJammula/repro-matroid-size-sensiti.overall: The logbook provides strong empirical verification for the two constructive claims (Algorithm 1's sub-quadratic cost scaling and the linear/near-linear oracle implementations) with correct implementations and matching scaling exponents at reasonable scale. The three lower-bound claims receive only toy-level support—hard-instance mechanisms are exactly reproduced and verified, but no experiment can prove unconditional lower bounds over all algorithms.
