RyeCatcher/repro-perceptrons-and-localiz.paper_title: Perceptrons and Localization of Attention’s Mean-Field Landscape

claims.claim: For non-analytic ReLU-type perceptron potentials in dimension d=2, every stationary measure of the mean-field energy is proved to be purely atomic with finite support (Theorem 3.1).
claims.evidence: The logbook only performed a source-text token-matching audit (checking that the LaTeX theorem block contains 'd=2', 'σ(s)=s_+', etc.), with no proof replay, no numerical experiment, and no independent construction of stationary measures. This confirms the paper says the claim, not that the claim holds.

claims.claim: For analytic activation functions such as GeLU in d=2, strict second-order-positive-definite (SOPD) Wasserstein critical points are shown to be purely atomic with finite support (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Same source-local theorem-statement audit only — 4/4 token checks on the LaTeX block. No proof verification, no numerical construction of SOPD critical points, no experimental evidence of any kind.

claims.claim: In dimensions d≥2, stationary measures are proved singular (zero Lebesgue measure), and for an open dense set of parameters with analytic activation they are purely atomic (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: Source-text aggregation of theorem parts with 5/5 token checks, but no proof replay and no experimental verification of singularity or purely atomic structure in d≥2.

claims.claim: In the descent (repulsive) regime, clusters forming at interaction scale sqrt(beta) are bounded in mass by approximately 0.5742 + O(e^{-beta}), preventing full collapse to single atoms (Theorem 3.5).
claims.evidence: The 'negative control' merely constructs a two-atom example with mass 1.0 > 0.5742 when the cluster-diameter premise is dropped, which is trivially obvious and does not test the actual theorem. No descent dynamics were simulated and no proof was replayed.

claims.claim: Global maximizers of the combined attention-perceptron energy reduce to a single Dirac mass at the point maximizing the perceptron potential, while the global minimizer is unique and rotationally invariant (Proposition 3.7).
claims.evidence: Source-text audit found the Dirac-maximizer part matches but the exact phrase 'rotationally invariant' is absent from the proposition block. The 'toy symmetry check' (sampling rotations fixing two orthogonal directions yields only [0.0]) is a trivial geometric observation, not a test of the proposition's mathematical content.

claims.claim: Numerical simulations across dimensions d in {1,2,...,50} confirm that the number of atomic clusters scales approximately as sqrt(beta), for both ascent and descent regimes and under softmax-normalized attention (Section 4).
claims.evidence: No simulations were rerun. The logbook only visually inspected the paper's own PDF figures and noted that patterns are 'setup-dependent' with some rows saturating or behaving non-monotonically. Without independent numerical runs across d∈{1,…,50}, the √β scaling claim is neither confirmed nor refuted.

RyeCatcher/repro-perceptrons-and-localiz.overall: This logbook is a source-text audit, not a reproduction: it checks that the paper's LaTeX contains the right theorem statements but runs no mathematical proof verification and no independent numerical simulations for any of the six claims. None of the claims are supported or refuted by concrete experimental evidence.

ai-sherpa/feasible-payoff-set-estimation.paper_title: Optimal Rates for Feasible Payoff Set Estimation in Games

claims.claim: For exact equilibria (α=0) with support-restriction πmin>0, the paper proves a sample-complexity lower bound of Ω(log(1/δ)/log(1/(1-πmin)) + (n+log(1/δ))/ϵ²) (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: Real geometric-hitting-time Monte Carlo (40,000 trials/cell, 54 cells) confirms the exact support-discovery threshold m*=⌈log(δ)/log(1-πmin)⌉ is minimal in 100% of cells (miss-rate ≤δ at m*, >δ at m*-1), and real multinomial sampling across 63 cells (n up to 1024) achieves 99.8% mean success at the claimed (n+log(1/δ))/ε² budget vs 2.9% at a quarter of it, directly testing both components of the lower bound mechanism.

claims.claim: For approximate equilibria with α∈(0,1/4) and ϵ≤1/128, the lower bound scales as Ω((n+log(1/δ))/(ϵ²α)), showing the approximation parameter α multiplies the sample complexity (Theorem 3.3).
claims.evidence: Exact KL computation of the paper's own Theorem A.4 Bernoulli hard pair across 35 cells shows KL/(αε²)∈[1.762,2.012] (bounded, finite, positive), the Theorem A.5 categorical hard family (n up to 257, 84 cells) shows per-sample KL exactly n-invariant (spread 1.000000×), and a genuine Gilbert-Varshamov greedy packing exceeds the 2^(dim/5) threshold in all 4/4 tested dimensions — all three mechanisms driving the lower bound are concretely verified.

claims.claim: An upper-bound algorithm (Procedure 1) achieves Õ(log(1/δ)/log(1/(1-πmin)) + (n+log(1/δ))/ϵ²) samples for exact equilibria in both general-sum and zero-sum bimatrix games, matching the lower bound (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: The paper's Eq.(7) alternative-matrix construction is executed on 64 freshly-sampled Nash-consistent games (n=4–512, both general-sum and zero-sum): all 64/64 certificates hold with nonvacuous ratio ‖A-Â‖∞/(4‖y-ŷ‖₁)∈[0.380,0.626] and equality gaps ~6.6e-17, and an end-to-end budget sweep (48 cells) achieves 98.6% mean success at the claimed budget vs 58% max at a quarter budget.

claims.claim: For approximate equilibria with α>0, the proposed algorithm attains O((n+log(1/δ))/(ϵ²α) + √n·log(1/δ)/(ϵα)) samples, which matches the lower bound for ϵ≲n^{-1/2} (Theorem 4.2).
claims.evidence: The paper's alpha-Nash scaled-matrix construction (Â=(α/g_A)A when g_A≥α) is executed on 144 cells (n=4–512, both game classes, α∈{0.02,0.1,0.2}) with all 144/144 satisfying the exact α-Nash condition, and a budget sweep in the paper's stated matching regime ε~0.5/√n (32 cells) achieves 99.2% mean success at the claimed budget vs 50% max at a quarter.

claims.claim: The analysis identifies a fractional-knapsack structure underlying the approximate-equilibrium error, showing actions played with probability ~α create multiplicative α⁻¹ dependence in the convergence rate (Section 4).
claims.evidence: The paper's Eq.(9)-(10) fractional-knapsack greedy solution matches an independent HiGHS LP to 6.94e-18 across 112 cells (n up to 512), a destructive raw-deviation-ordering control is suboptimal in 93.8% of cells confirming the specific ratio-ordering matters, and real multinomial sampling with one action at probability exactly α yields a log-log slope of required-m vs α of -1.126 (theory: -1), cross-checked against the closed-form Binomial variance identity to 0.0004.

ai-sherpa/feasible-payoff-set-estimation.overall: This logbook provides concrete experimental evidence for all five claims by executing the paper's own hard instances, proof constructions, and algorithmic mechanisms at non-trivial scale (n up to 512, thousands of Monte Carlo trials, exact KL computations, independent LP cross-checks), rather than merely evaluating closed-form rate expressions. The reproduction is transparent about its limitations (finite sweeps cannot certify universal minimax bounds, zero-sum construction is partially reconstructed, packing tested at smaller dimensions), but the evidence directly tests the underlying mechanisms of each theorem.

ai-sherpa/robust-maximal-lotteries-repro.paper_title: Robust AI Evaluation through Maximal Lotteries

claims.claim: Robust lotteries are computed via a distributionally robust linear program of size O(mK) that maximizes worst-case win probability across plausible shifts in the annotator/preference distribution (Theorem 17).
claims.evidence: The Theorem-17 LP is implemented from scratch in scipy/HiGHS and its optimum agrees with an independent primal recomputation (separate per-action LP over the TV ball sharing no dual variables) on 200/200 random instances (worst gap 1.4e-15); variable/constraint counts fit a·mK+b·m+c with R²=1.000000, directly confirming O(mK) size.

claims.claim: Theorem 19 establishes a regret bound of 4√(K/n) + 4√(2 log(2/δ)/n) for the robust lottery's worst-case win-rate guarantee, and Theorem 18 shows ε-optimal solutions can be sparse with logarithmic support size (Theorem 18, Theorem 19).
claims.evidence: Theorem 19's regret bound holds on 100% of 150 resampling trials using real LMArena margin matrices (mean regret 0.0158 vs bound 1.0272, coverage 100% ≥ 1−δ=0.90); Theorem 18's sparsity is verified by a constructive greedy truncation + restricted-LP re-solving algorithm on 32/32 instances (up to m=150), using only 2.18% of the theoretical allowance when the bound is tighter than m.

claims.claim: On LMArena, the standard (non-robust) maximal lottery concentrates support on a single model, whereas the robust lottery spreads probability across 4 complementary models while substantially improving the worst-case win-rate guarantee (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: On the full real LMArena release (135,634 votes, top-16 models, 4 languages), the standard lottery concentrates on gemini-2.5-pro (weight 1.0, worst-group win rate 0.3636) matching the paper, while the robust lottery (ρ=1) spreads across 3 models with worst-group win rate 0.4592 (+0.0956); the K=1 pooling control forces an exact null (diff 0.0), confirming the mechanism requires real multi-group structure. The claim says '4 models' but the reproduction finds 3, a minor discrepancy attributed to slightly different model selection.

claims.claim: On the HUMAINE dataset with ethnic-group-based population splits, preference reversals occur in 42%-47% of cases across language/demographic groups, and increasing the robustness radius ρ reduces the train-test worst-group performance gap from about 6% (ρ=0) to about 2% (ρ=1) (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: On real pinned HUMAINE data (6,802 comparisons matching the paper's protocol exactly), the core mechanism is verified: preference reversals are measured at 77.4–84.2% (top-5 pairs) and held-out worst-group win rate rises 0.200→0.314 as ρ goes 0→1 with support expanding 1→4. The logbook identifies that the claim's specific '42–47%' and '6%→2%' numbers are about LMArena per the paper's own Section 5 text, not HUMAINE, and reports HUMAINE's own directly-measured numbers instead.

claims.claim: Theorem 8 and Theorem 11 establish that robust lotteries satisfy robust Condorcet consistency and weak-clone invariance, respectively, as axiomatic guarantees not generally satisfied by standard Bradley-Terry aggregation (Theorem 8, Theorem 11).
claims.evidence: Theorem 8 (robust Condorcet consistency) is verified by solving the Theorem-17 LP on 400 random instances with a forced strict Condorcet winner, recovering the exact point-mass lottery on 400/400 (max off-support mass 0.0); Theorem 11 (weak-clone invariance) is verified on 300 random instances where adding 1–2 weak clones leaves the game value unchanged (max gap 1.9e-16), non-cloned weights unchanged, and support membership preserved on 300/300.

ai-sherpa/robust-maximal-lotteries-repro.overall: This logbook provides a thorough, independent from-scratch reproduction of all five claims using real pinned datasets (LMArena 135,634 votes, HUMAINE 174,225 rows), independent LP certification via separate primal recomputation, destructive controls (K=1 pooling, label shuffling), and transparent reporting of discrepancies including a provenance correction for Claim 4's misattributed numbers. The reproduction is notably rigorous for a $0 CPU-only effort, with machine-precision agreement across hundreds of random instances and honest disclosure of limitations.

ai-sherpa/on-policy-dpo-coverage-converg.paper_title: Coverage Improvement and Fast Convergence of On-policy Preference Learning

claims.claim: Theorem 3.2 shows on-policy DPO converges exponentially (linearly per round) in the number of iterations K once the per-round batch size exceeds a generalized coverage threshold C*_p(R), with total sample complexity O~(R^2/ε^2 ∨ (ln R/ε)·C*_p(R)) (Theorem 3.2).
claims.evidence: A d=20-action Bradley-Terry bandit with adversarial base policy (coverage 536.1) shows coverage improving 46× after one on-policy update, per-round KL contracting geometrically (log-KL slope -0.920/round, R²=0.869), and rounds-to-ε growing logarithmically (K(ε) = 1.131 + 0.660·ln(1/ε), R²=0.759), all measured from real MLE refits on current-policy samples.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.2 proves any offline learner sampling from a fixed base policy π0 requires Ω(1/ε^2 · C*_p(R)) samples to reach error ε, a quadratic-in-1/ε separation from the on-policy rate (Theorem 2.2).
claims.evidence: Fixed-base-policy offline estimator (coverage=16.67 constant) shows empirical sample complexity N_off(ε) scaling as ε^{-2.099} (R²=0.996), closely matching the predicted quadratic rate, and a direct coverage-skew intervention shows error monotonically increasing with the coverage constant across 5 steps.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 shows a hybrid sampler using preferential G-optimal experimental design (via Kiefer-Wolfowitz equivalence with centered features) achieves ‖θ̂_2 − θ*‖ ≤ ε in just two rounds with sample complexity O~(dR^2/ε^2 · log(1/δ)), removing dependence on the coverage constant (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: An exact Fraction-arithmetic counterexample (V=diag(1/100,1), e=(9,0), ε=1) shows the V(π*)-weighted norm bound (e^T V e = 81/100 ≤ 1, holds) does not imply the plain Euclidean norm bound (e^T e = 81 > 1, fails), and SHA-256-verified source confirms Theorem 4.4 states the weighted norm, not the Euclidean norm claimed.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.1 shows on-policy reward-distillation methods that learn reward differences rather than preferences converge at rate O(n^-1 ∨ e^{-Ω(K)}), faster than preference-based on-policy DPO but inheriting reward-model error ε_RM (Theorem 5.1).
claims.evidence: Exact arc-intersection version-space computation matches n^{-1} rate (slope -1.006, R²=0.9992), direct reward-difference regression achieves near-machine-precision recovery vs. Bradley-Terry MLE's slower rate (slope -0.604), and reward-model-error perturbation transfers 1-for-1 to the downstream floor (slope 0.996, R²=0.9999).

claims.claim: On the general-chat UltraFeedback benchmark, the proposed on-policy distillation approach achieves a 45.44% AlpacaEval win-rate versus 41.26% for the offline baseline, while naive REBEL-style distillation degrades performance unless calibrated (RDRC) (Section on experimental validation).
claims.evidence: SHA-256-verified source-text parsing shows 45.44% is attributed to on-policy DPO (iter 3) and 41.26% to offline DPO (epoch 3)—both plain DPO, not distillation—while the paper's actual distillation methods report distinct values (PDFR=43.99, REBEL=43.81, RDRC=44.07), contradicting the claim's method attribution.

ai-sherpa/on-policy-dpo-coverage-converg.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, independently-run bandit simulations and exact geometric/arithmetic computations that verify the on-policy exponential convergence (Claim 1), offline quadratic lower bound (Claim 2), and reward-distillation rate structure (Claim 4), while falsifying Claims 3 and 5 through an exact norm-mismatch counterexample and source-text provenance audit respectively. The reproduction is high-quality but limited to the theoretical bandit framework, with no LLM training experiments attempted.

ai-sherpa/linear-contracts-sample-comple.paper_title: The Optimal Sample Complexity of Linear Contracts

claims.claim: Theorem 1.1 establishes uniform convergence: for sample size s ≥ 3456 ln(4/δ)/ε², with probability at least 1−δ, the empirical and expected utility of every linear contract differ by at most ε (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: Across 20 (model × ε,δ) cells with 4,096 Monte-Carlo trials each, exact breakpoint enumeration of the sup deviation never exceeded ε (0 failures total, worst deviation 0.686% of ε), with a destructive n=16 control producing up to 31.9% failure rate, confirming the test is non-vacuous at the paper's sample size s ≥ 3456 ln(4/δ)/ε².

claims.claim: Corollary 1.2 shows the Empirical Utility Maximization algorithm achieves an ε-approximation of the optimal linear contract using s ≥ 6912 ln(4/δ)/ε² samples and O(1/ε) oracle queries (Corollary 1.2).
claims.evidence: EUM implemented on the {0, ε/4, …, 1} grid (O(1/ε) queries: 21–81 contracts) with true regret measured over 20 cells × 4,096 trials; 0 runs exceeded ε regret, worst being 9.93% of ε, at s ≥ 6912 ln(4/δ)/ε² with sample sizes up to 16,565,202.

claims.claim: The O(ln(1/δ)/ε²) sample complexity matches the lower bound of Dütting et al. (2025) up to constant factors, and is independent of the action space size n and the number of outcomes m (Theorem 1.1).
claims.evidence: An explicit two-type binomial instance with exact tail computation yields normalized critical count n*ε²/ln(1/δ) in [0.1129, 0.1780] across four (ε,δ) settings with quarter-sized controls breaching δ; action independence verified via 0 failures across 4–24 actions (2,048 trials each), and outcome invariance confirmed to machine precision (2.22e-16) for m ∈ {2,4,8,16}.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.1 shows the expected reward of a linear contract is non-decreasing in the contract parameter α, a structural property exploited to build fine-grained covering arguments where general pseudo-dimension bounds fail (Lemma 2.1).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive exact audit of 262,529 consecutive reward steps across 4 models found 0 decreases in agent best-response expected reward, while the principal's utility (1−α)·reward was non-monotone at 86,525 of the same steps, providing a specificity control confirming the check targets the reward property specifically.

claims.claim: Lemma 2.2 constructs an L2 cover of the reward function class of size O(1/ν²), obtained by discretizing empirical rewards into ν-intervals, taking pullbacks to parameter space, and combining with grid discretization of the outcome axis (Lemma 2.2).
claims.evidence: The Lemma 2.2 cover was constructed literally for 4 models × 4 ν values (16 cells): cover size ≤ 0.3467 × 12/ν² (within O(1/ν²) budget), realized L2 error ≤ 0.2935 × ν (within ν target), and 0 missing pullback bins, with coverage evaluated at action-switch sides and Voronoi boundaries.

ai-sherpa/linear-contracts-sample-comple.overall: This logbook provides concrete computational evidence supporting all five claims through exact breakpoint enumeration, Monte-Carlo trials (4,096 per cell), exhaustive monotonicity checks (262,529 steps), exact binomial lower-bound computation, and literal L2-cover construction at non-trivial scale (up to 16 types × 24 actions, millions of samples). The reproduction includes destructive and specificity controls that confirm the tests are non-vacuous, and all experiments directly instantiate the paper's mechanisms rather than proxy tasks.

claims.claim: The optimal collaborative prediction set C*(x) has a two-threshold form: it augments the human-proposed set H(x) with labels whose score exceeds threshold a*, and prunes labels within H(x) whose score exceeds threshold b* (Theorem 2.1, Section 2).
claims.evidence: At n=300,000 on a synthetic K=10-class setup with random logits and a Dirichlet-perturbed simulated human, the two-threshold construction achieves harm coverage 0.90001 and complementarity coverage 0.80002 (matching targets), while human-only fails complementarity (0.0) and single-threshold fails complementarity (0.761). Real runs and numbers, but entirely synthetic data with no real human predictions or real-world task.

claims.claim: The counterfactual harm principle requires P(Y not in C(X) | Y in H(X)) < epsilon, i.e., the AI must not remove correct labels the human already proposed (Section 1).
claims.evidence: The counterfactual harm principle is used as a constraint in the experiments (harm coverage measured at ~0.90), but it is a definitional principle, not a testable hypothesis, and the logbook does not separately address or verify it as a standalone claim.

claims.claim: The complementarity principle requires P(Y in C(X) | Y not in H(X)) >= 1-delta, i.e., the AI must recover correct labels the human missed (Section 1).
claims.evidence: The complementarity principle is used as a constraint in the experiments (complementarity coverage measured at ~0.80), but it is a definitional principle, not a testable hypothesis, and the logbook does not separately address or verify it as a standalone claim.

claims.claim: The offline calibration procedure gives distribution-free finite-sample coverage guarantees whose bounds depend on the sizes of the calibration sets used to fit a* and b* (Proposition 4.1, Section 4.1).
claims.evidence: 1,500 Monte Carlo replicates on synthetic K=10 data show mean harm coverage 0.9014 (lower bound 0.90, upper bound 0.9017) and mean complementarity coverage 0.8018 (lower bound 0.80, upper bound 0.8049), confirming both finite-sample bounds. Real runs and numbers, but on a simplified synthetic setup with no real data or human predictions.

claims.claim: The CUP-Online algorithm updates thresholds a_t and b_t via stochastic approximation steps (a_{t+1}=a_t+eta(1{s(x_t,y_t)>a_t}-delta), and analogously for b_t) to track target error rates under arbitrary distribution shift, including shifts caused by humans adapting their behavior to the AI (Section 4.2, Proposition 4.2).
claims.evidence: CUP-Online run for 40,000 steps with an abrupt distribution shift at t=20,000 on synthetic K=10 data shows final running error rates 0.10033 (target 0.10) and 0.20069 (target 0.20), with the finite-sample bound checked numerically. Real runs and numbers demonstrating tracking under shift, but on a simplified synthetic setup with no real data or human predictions.

AakashJammula/repro-haiuq-collaborative-.overall: The logbook provides concrete numerical evidence on a synthetic K=10-class simulation that supports the paper's three central theoretical results (Theorem 2.1, Propositions 4.1 and 4.2), with well-designed experiments including baselines, Monte Carlo replicates, and distribution shift. However, the entire setup is synthetic with no real datasets, no real human predictions, and a small class space, making it a toy-scale verification rather than a full reproduction.

ai-sherpa/swe-bench-pro-dataset-statisti.paper_title: SWE-Bench Pro: Can AI Agents Solve Long-Horizon Software Engineering Tasks?

claims.claim: SWE-Bench Pro comprises 1,865 problems sourced from 41 actively maintained software repositories (abstract only).
claims.evidence: The logbook downloaded the released public split and directly measured 731 instances across 11 repositories, matching the paper's stated public-split figures exactly; the full 1,865/41 total is arithmetically reconstructed (731+276+858=1865; 11+18+12=41) from the paper's own stated split numbers, with the private portions being inherently unverifiable.

claims.claim: SWE-Bench Pro is split into a public set of 11 openly accessible repositories, a held-out set of 12 repositories not publicly accessible, and a commercial set of 18 proprietary repositories obtained via partnership agreements with startups (abstract only).
claims.evidence: The public split's 11 repositories and 731 instances were directly measured from the released dataset and match the paper exactly; the held-out (12) and commercial (18) repository counts cannot be independently recomputed since those sets are deliberately unreleased, but this is an inherent constraint of the dataset's design rather than a methodological gap.

claims.claim: Tasks in SWE-Bench Pro are long-horizon, potentially requiring hours to days for a professional software engineer to complete and often involving patches across multiple files (abstract only).
claims.evidence: A from-scratch, unit-tested unified-diff parser applied to all 731 public patches measured mean 169.6 changed lines across mean 5.1 files per task, with 47.7% exceeding 100 lines and 100% exceeding the paper's ≥10-line floor (min=20), providing concrete evidence for the multi-file and substantial-effort aspects of the claim; the 'hours to days' qualitative framing is supported by this proxy but not directly timed.

claims.claim: All SWE-Bench Pro tasks underwent human verification to ensure they include adequate context for resolution (abstract only).
claims.evidence: All 731/731 public instances were checked and found to have non-empty, non-trivial human-augmentation fields: requirements (mean 1483 chars, min 124), interface (mean 670 chars), problem_statement, fail_to_pass, pass_to_pass, and test_patch — 100% completeness across all six fields, providing concrete evidence of the human verification artifacts, though only the public split (731/1865) is checkable.

claims.claim: SWE-Bench Pro is designed as a contamination-resistant testbed spanning business applications, B2B services, and developer tools to more faithfully capture real-world software engineering complexity than the original SWE-Bench (abstract only).
claims.evidence: Independent GitHub API and LICENSE-file lookups confirmed all 11 public repos use copyleft licenses (8× GPL-3.0, 3× AGPL-3.0, including a corrected classification of element-web as AGPL-3.0), and all three claimed domains (business applications, B2B services, developer tools) are represented among the public repositories; the comparison to original SWE-Bench complexity is not directly measured.

ai-sherpa/swe-bench-pro-dataset-statisti.overall: The logbook independently verifies all five abstract-level dataset-composition claims against the paper's full released public split (731/1865 instances, 11/41 repos) using from-scratch diff parsing, field-completeness checks, and independent license/domain lookups. The private commercial and held-out sets are inherently unverifiable since they are not released, but every measurable public component matches the paper's stated figures exactly.

ai-sherpa/efficient-inference-noisy-llm-.paper_title: Efficient Inference for Noisy LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation

claims.claim: The efficient influence function (EIF) estimator, the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE), and optimally-tuned PPI++ all attain the same asymptotic variance, which is strictly smaller than that of vanilla PPI, which in turn is strictly smaller than that of the Rogan-Gladen estimator except when sensitivity q1 and specificity q0 both equal 1 (Proposition 7).
claims.evidence: Independent symbolic derivation via Fisher information matrix yields V_MLE−V_EIF=0 and V_PPI++(λ*)−V_EIF=0 as exact symbolic zeros; V_PPI−V_PPI++(λ*) and V_RG−V_PPI factor into manifestly signed expressions with boundary collapse at q0=q1=1. A 12,000-point numeric grid audit confirms 0 violations (max |diff| 4.5e-14).

claims.claim: For binary outcomes, optimally tuned PPI++ matches the efficiency of the EIF estimator because the regression function E[Y|Ŷ] is necessarily affine, so no further efficiency gain is possible from nonparametric calibration (Section on efficiency comparison).
claims.evidence: Exact algebra shows any function on a 2-point support is affine (a=μ0, b=μ1−μ0). Monte Carlo across 3 cells with 4,000 replicates gives variance ratios linear/EIF of 1.002–1.011. A 3-level non-affine positive control produces a 20% efficiency gap, confirming the mechanism is causal.

claims.claim: In simulations with N=2,000 and 1,000 replicates on binary outcomes, when judge quality is low (q0+q1=1.2), Rogan-Gladen confidence intervals are roughly 10x wider than EIF/PPI++ intervals, and EIF/PPI++ intervals are 35-55% narrower than vanilla PPI intervals (simulation study section).
claims.evidence: From-scratch Monte Carlo on the paper's own grid (9 θ × 3 budgets, q0=q1=0.6, 2 seeds × 1,000 replicates, 54 cells) yields median RG/EIF width ratio of 4.96× (only 4/54 cells in 8–12× band) and median PPI++ reduction of 29.2% (only 22/54 cells in 35–55% band), contradicting the claimed magnitudes.

claims.claim: On real Chatbot Arena preference data across three model pairs (414-494 samples each) using 10% calibration splits, PPI++, EIF, and MLE achieve near-nominal 90% coverage with mean interval widths of 0.27-0.30, while Rogan-Gladen achieves 0.76-0.96 width with 100% coverage, indicating over-conservatism (real-data application section).
claims.evidence: Released data files contain 325/276/275 rows per pair, not the claimed 414–494. Across 1,000 real 10%/90% splits, PPI++/EIF mean widths fall below the claimed 0.27 floor in 4/6 combinations (as low as 0.230), and the joint MLE fails to return an interval on 175–514 of every 1,000 splits, contradicting the compound coverage/width claim.

claims.claim: The efficient influence function for the target parameter θ=E[Y] is φ*(R,Y,Ŷ;P) = μ(Ŷ) − θ + [R/P(R=1)]{Y − μ(Ŷ)}, where μ(ŷ)=E[Y|Ŷ=ŷ] is the optimal translation of the surrogate label (Proposition 5).
claims.evidence: Symbolic derivation for a fully generic discrete (Y,Ŷ) law confirms E[φ*]=0 under MCAR via the tower property and E[(R/π)(Y−μ(Ŷ))]=0, with exact collapse to Y−θ at π=1. Monte Carlo (400,000 draws) gives mean(φ*)=−0.00142 (1.31 SE from 0); a non-MCAR positive control pushes it to 0.0803 (94.9 SE from 0).

ai-sherpa/efficient-inference-noisy-llm-.overall: The logbook provides rigorous independent evidence—symbolic algebra, dense numeric audits, and Monte Carlo with positive controls—confirming the paper's core theoretical claims (1, 2, 5) to machine precision, while falsifying the specific empirical magnitudes in claims 3 and 4 through from-scratch simulation and analysis of the paper's own released data.

rakshi-the-neural-nexus/repro-stage-bo-a.paper_title: Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization via Adaptive $\varepsilon$-Constraint Decomposition

claims.claim: STAGE-BO provides uniform Pareto coverage without hypervolume computation
claims.evidence: Destructive control shows removing the hypervolume block produces bit-identical trajectories (max abs diff 0.0 on ZDT1, 8 steps), confirming point selection never consults HV. Fill distance and IGD results show STAGE-BO best on 5 of 6 problems (margins 2.4–13.8 SE), but on DTLZ7 (m=5, disconnected front) Sobol covers 5.4× better (7.55 vs 40.63 fill distance, ~18 SE), a real limitation on one problem.

claims.claim: Naturally applies to constrained and preference-based multi-objective optimization settings
claims.evidence: Constrained mode reaches feasible fraction 0.40–0.45 vs Sobol control of 0.000–0.045 on three hard problems (SRN, C2DTLZ2, MW7_4), 10/10 seeds each. Preference mode lifts in-box containment from ~0.30 to ~0.77 on ZDT1/ZDT2 (10/10 seeds) and from 0.073 to 0.313 on rocket injector (10/10 seeds), with coil spring weak (4/10 seeds).

claims.claim: Achieves competitive hypervolume performance against state-of-the-art baselines
claims.evidence: Against qEHVI and qParEGO (2 of 8 paper baselines) on 6 problems with 5–10 seeds: STAGE-BO wins HV on ZDT1 (+0.86, 4.7 SE), ZDT2 (+7.89, 5.8 SE), DTLZ7 (1.76× qParEGO), ties on coil spring and water planning, loses on rocket injector to qEHVI (−0.063, 9.6 SE). 'Competitive' is supported against the baselines tested, though 6/8 baselines were not run.

rakshi-the-neural-nexus/repro-stage-bo-a.overall: The logbook provides rigorous, non-toy evidence supporting all three claims: a destructive control conclusively shows HV is inert, coverage and HV benchmarks run on the paper's 6 problems with 5–10 seeds each, and constrained/preference modes are shown to do real work against controls. Key limitations include a coverage reversal on DTLZ7 (Sobol 5.4× better), only 2 of 8 baselines tested for claim 3, and several code defects in the released artifact that do not refute the paper's claims.

SabaPivot/repro-deep-networks-learn-to-p.paper_title: Deep networks learn to parse uniform-depth context-free languages from local statistics

claims.claim: Introduces the Varying-tree Random Hierarchy Model, a tunable class of uniform-depth PCFGs with m2 binary and m3 ternary production rules per symbol scaling asymptotically as m2=f2*v and m3=f3*v^2 in vocabulary size v (Section 2).
claims.evidence: From-scratch numpy VRHM generator checked across 8 settings (v=8–24, L=2–3): observed m2 and m3 match f2·v and f3·v² exactly in every case, log-log fits give slopes 1.0000 (m2) and 2.0000 (m3), RHS distinctness and sentence-length bounds all verified.

claims.claim: Identifies a phase transition at critical ambiguity parameter f_c = 3/8, below which sentences are globally unambiguous (unique parse/class label) and above which multiple valid parse trees exist, driven by spurious nonterminals in the inside algorithm (Section 3, Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Paper's own vendored inside algorithm run on freshly sampled grammars across f∈[0.15,1.0], L=2,3,4, v=8,16: parse-class count is ≈1 below the transition and grows above it, sharpening with depth. Measured onset at v=8, L=2 lands exactly on f=0.375=3/8; other settings are noisier but show the same qualitative signature.

claims.claim: Derives a closed-form sample complexity formula P* = O((p2^2/2)^(1-L) · v · m3 · m2^(L-1)) for learning the grammar via root-to-substring covariance clustering (Section 4, Equation 8).
claims.evidence: Independent covariance-clustering implementation achieves AUC=1.0 separating genuine production rules from non-rules on real generated VRHM data (v=8–20), and the closed-form P* reduces algebraically to exactly 8v² (f=1/v, L=2) and v⁵ (f=1/4, L=3) across multiple v values. The Eq. 13 per-rule signal-decay exponent sub-point is reported as inconclusive (measured slope ≈−0.012 vs paper's −0.86).

claims.claim: Confirms P* ~ v^2 scaling (with f=1/v) for CNNs via test-loss collapse when training set size is rescaled by the theoretical P* (Section 5.1, Figure 1).
claims.evidence: Paper's own vendored hCNN_Gen trained on real VRHM data at f=1/v, L=2 across v=8,12,16,24 (9× range in P*=8v²): normalized test-loss curves collapse under P/P* rescaling with mean cross-v spread 0.057 on a 0.777-wide loss axis, despite raw training sizes differing by 9×. Single seed per cell and modest step budgets limit precision.

claims.claim: Shows P* ~ v^5 scaling for f=1/4 and depth L=3 as vocabulary size v increases, validated against CNN training curves (Section 5.1, Figure 7a).
claims.evidence: 54 GPU runs (2 seeds/cell) of vendored hCNN_Gen at f=1/4, L=3 across v=4,8,12,16 (1024× range in P*=v⁵, up to P=2,097,152) with validation-based early stopping: test-loss curves collapse under P/v⁵ (cross-v spread 0.0199), exponent fitted from curves is 4.792±0.044 (R²=0.9998), collapse optimum at α=5.4, and α=2 collapses 4.5× worse.

claims.claim: Demonstrates the same P* ~ v^2 sample-complexity scaling law holds across CNNs, an Inside Neural Network (INN), and an encoder-only Transformer, with INN having the best prefactor due to task-aligned architecture (Section 5.2, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: All three vendored architectures (CNN, INN, Transformer) trained fresh at v=8,12 with f=1/v, L=2: each collapses under the same P*=8v² rescaling (cross-v spread 0.036/0.056/0.057), and INN achieves the lowest normalized loss at P/P*=1 (0.732 vs CNN 0.818, Transformer 0.809), matching the claimed prefactor ranking. Limited to only 2 vocabulary sizes, so the v² exponent itself is weakly tested for INN/Transformer.

SabaPivot/repro-deep-networks-learn-to-p.overall: This logbook provides concrete experimental evidence supporting all six claims: a from-scratch VRHM generator verifying rule-count scaling, the paper's own inside algorithm demonstrating the ambiguity phase transition with onset at 3/8, covariance clustering with AUC=1.0 and exact algebraic formula reduction, and real network training (CNN/INN/Transformer) showing test-loss collapse under the predicted P* rescaling for both v² and v⁵ regimes. The main limitations are single-seed runs and limited step budgets for claims 4 and 6, only 2 vocabulary sizes for claim 6, and an inconclusive Eq. 13 signal-decay sub-point in claim 3.

SabaPivot/repro-adaptive-personalized-fe.paper_title: Adaptive Personalized Federated Learning via Multi-task Averaging of Kernel Mean Embeddings

claims.claim: Theorem 4.4 establishes finite-sample guarantees for a Q-aggregation estimator of kernel mean embeddings, with a bound that trades off bias governed by the maximum distributional distance ΔV against variance controlled by the combined sample size nV (Theorem 4.4).
claims.evidence: A real mirror-descent Q-aggregation optimizer was executed on a 15-config (δ, n_group) grid with Gaussian sources, showing collaboration gain monotonically increasing in n_V (4.23×→7.86× at δ=0) and decreasing in δ (7.86×→1.23× at n_V=4160), with a first-principles bias(Δ_V)²+variance/n_V envelope holding at all 15/15 grid points. The logbook honestly notes this is a self-constructed envelope, not the paper's exact Eq. 14, but the qualitative bias-variance tradeoff is demonstrated on a non-toy setup.

claims.claim: Corollary 4.6 bounds the excess risk of the personalized model by 2RΘ·E[MMD(P̂(ω̂), P₁)], where RΘ controls the RKHS norm of the loss class, linking the KME estimation error directly to downstream task risk (Corollary 4.6).
claims.evidence: The bound excess ≤ 2·R_Θ·MMD was tested on 3000 randomized instances with 0 violations, but using a finite (K=8–32) linear-in-RFF-feature loss class — a clearly simplified proxy for the general RKHS loss class the corollary addresses. The ERM, MMD, and excess-risk computations are real, but the function class is a reduced/simplified setup rather than the paper's full scope.

claims.claim: Per Example 4.5, the learned collaboration weights automatically shift toward local-only learning (ω₁ ≈ 1) recovering the naive O(n₁^{-1/2}) rate when no beneficial collaborators exist, and toward pooling when other agents share similar distributions, without prior knowledge of heterogeneity (Example 4.5).
claims.evidence: Regime A (29 far agents): learned own-weight ω₁ rises 0.525→0.908 as n₁ grows 25→800, with measured MMD² log-log slope −0.821 (theory: −1), demonstrating retreat-to-local with approximate naive-rate recovery. Regime B (9 identical collaborators + 20 distractors): weight mass on matching group reaches 0.304 with 2.61× gain over local — both regimes from actual learned weights with no heterogeneity label provided.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.2 quantifies the communication-statistical efficiency tradeoff when the method is implemented with D-dimensional random Fourier features, adding an approximation error term of order C√(log B/D) (Theorem 5.2).
claims.evidence: 30 independent RFF draws at D∈{16,…,1024} with B=100 agents, comparing RFF kernel estimates against exact Gaussian kernel: measured median |k̂−k| is strictly decreasing in D with log-log slope −0.4955 (R²=0.9998), closely matching the theorem's predicted −0.5 exponent for the C√(log B/D) approximation term.

claims.claim: On a synthetic concept-shift experiment with 100 agents and 10 samples each, the method's adaptive weighting correctly improves performance once intra-group similarity crosses the transition point σc² = 0.5 (Section 6.1).
claims.evidence: Full generate→weight→weighted-ridge pipeline at the paper's own B=100, n=10 scale: Q-aggregation beats local for σ_c²≤0.3 (ratio 0.965) and crosses to worse-than-local in (0.4, 0.5), tightly bracketing the paper's stated σ_c²=0.5 transition. Above the transition, Q-aggregation damps degradation to 1.18× vs the naive oracle's 1.71× at σ_c²=1.0, demonstrating adaptive weighting behavior.

claims.claim: On the FEMNIST handwriting benchmark with 192 agents, the adaptive weighting scheme consistently outperforms a uniform-weighting baseline using fixed, untuned hyperparameters (Section 6.3).
claims.evidence: Real LEAF FEMNIST data with 192 writers (54,441 train / 13,613 test images): Q-aggregation achieves mean accuracy 0.6694 vs GrandMean 0.5430 (Local 0.6449), with 95.8% of writers strictly beating GrandMean and worst-case deficit of only −0.030. The regression head is closed-form weighted ridge (not the paper's MLP), but this is a reasonable backend substitution since the adaptive weighting — not the regression head — is the research contribution, and the same head is used for both methods.

SabaPivot/repro-adaptive-personalized-fe.overall: The logbook provides concrete experimental evidence from a from-scratch mirror-descent Q-aggregation optimizer run on real sampled data and real FEMNIST data, supporting five of six claims at non-toy scale and one claim (Corollary 4.6) on a simplified finite-linear function class. Key limitations include self-constructed envelopes/theorems rather than the paper's exact constants, a simplified loss class for Claim 2, and a ridge regression head substituting for the paper's MLP in Claim 6.

SabaPivot/repro-minimizing-upper-confide.paper_title: Minimizing Upper Confidence Bounds: A Data-Driven Framework for Stochastic Programming

claims.claim: The Average Percentile Upper Bound (APUB) is defined as U^apub[μ|P̂_n] := (1/α)∫₀^α U^efron[μ|P̂_n] dτ, integrating Efron's percentile upper bound over confidence level τ from 0 to α (Definition 2.2, Section 2)
claims.evidence: Closed-form CVaR matches a literal 3000-point Riemann-sum integration of Definition 2.2's integral to max residual 2.083e-05 across 168 exact Binomial count-law cells (n up to 65536, 6 populations, 4 confidence levels), directly confirming the integral definition. The brute-force pmf enumeration shows large residuals (0.19 at n=8, α=0.05) which are unexplained, but the Riemann-sum cross-check directly validates the definition itself.

claims.claim: Theorem 2.7 proves APUB converges almost surely to the true population mean as sample size n approaches infinity, for every confidence level in (0,1] (Theorem 2.7)
claims.evidence: Exact nested-Binomial expectation (no Monte Carlo) over 100 (p,α,N) cells shows expected |APUB−p| contracts monotonically in 20/20 population/α combinations from N=50 to N=204800, with sqrt(N)-scaled ratio median 0.996, providing strong finite-scope exact-law evidence consistent with a.s. convergence.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.3 shows the APUB-embedded stochastic optimization model achieves first-order asymptotic correctness, with coverage probability exceeding the nominal confidence level up to an O(N^{-1/2}) term (Theorem 3.3)
claims.evidence: Exact outer-law coverage computation (no sampling) over 18 (N,α) cells on a newsvendor-style decision problem shows the deficit max(0,(1−α)−coverage) is exactly 0 in 100% of cells, with worst sqrt(N)·deficit = 0.0000, directly confirming the theorem's coverage inequality. The decision problem is simple (binary outcome, 101-point grid) but tests the actual coverage property the theorem asserts.

claims.claim: Theorem 3.5 establishes that both the optimal values and optimal solution sets of the APUB-based optimization problem converge almost surely to their true counterparts as sample size increases (Theorem 3.5)
claims.evidence: Using the same exact outer-law machinery, expected optimal-value error contracts from ~0.13 (N=40) to ~0.02 (N=40960) and expected solution error contracts from ~0.5 to ~0 for every α tested, providing concrete exact-law evidence of convergence consistent with Theorem 3.5.

claims.claim: On a Gamma(2,1) numerical example with nominal level α=0.05 and sample sizes ranging from 80 to 10,000, APUB's coverage probability approaches the 0.95 nominal level faster than Efron's percentile bound and standard large-sample approximations (Figure 1, Example 2.5)
claims.evidence: Independent bootstrap Monte Carlo (200 trials, 400 bootstrap resamples per N, N=80–10000) shows at N=10000: APUB coverage 0.985, Efron 0.940, large-sample 0.945 — APUB overshoots 0.95 while Efron and large-sample are the methods tracking toward 0.95, contradicting the registered claim that APUB approaches 0.95 faster. The logbook notes this matches the paper's own text which states the opposite direction.

claims.claim: The framework is validated on two-stage product mix and multi-product newsvendor problems, showing APUB balances robustness and practicality compared to Sample Average Approximation (SAA) and Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) (Section 5)
claims.evidence: All three paper application instances (20×8 random-recourse product mix, 4×2 fixed-recourse with Wasserstein DRO, 10-product newsvendor Cases I/II) are rebuilt at the paper's own dimensions and Appendix-C parameters, solved as deterministic-equivalent LPs via HiGHS with 4–25 replications per cell and 20,000-point test sets. Concrete results show APUB at N=120 achieves −4459.07 vs SAA's −4358.10 with 2.99× lower dispersion and beats SAA trained on twice the data, coverage β of 0.875–1.000 vs SAA's 0.438–0.500, and DRO's decision-independence on the newsvendor (max|x_DRO−x_SAA|=0 across all 36 c

SabaPivot/repro-minimizing-upper-confide.overall: The logbook provides concrete exact-law and bootstrap-Monte-Carlo evidence supporting claims 1–4 and 6 at meaningful scale, including the paper's own application instances at full dimensions. Claim 5 is falsified: the registered text states APUB approaches 0.95 faster than comparators, but independent measurement shows APUB overshoots 0.95 while Efron and large-sample approach it — the opposite direction.

SabaPivot/repro-black-box-assisted-regre.paper_title: Black-Box Assisted Regression: Phase Transitions and Minimax Optimality

claims.claim: The critical phase-transition threshold for black-box assisted regression is characterized as δc(n) ≍ n^(-β/(2β+d)), separating a prior-dominated regime from a sample-dominated regime (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Four (β,d) combinations yield fitted exponents 0.3334/0.3972/0.2513/0.2008 against theory 0.3333/0.4000/0.2500/0.2000, computed deterministically over 8 decades of n using the paper's own Appendix-D.2 hard construction with exact Bayes risk (disjoint bump supports make the posterior factorize).

claims.claim: The proposed safe residual estimator achieves the minimax risk rate min{δ², n^(-2β/(2β+d))} up to a validation-selection cost, with the lower bound given in Theorem 5.4 and the matching upper bound in Theorem 5.5 (Theorem 5.4, Theorem 5.5).
claims.evidence: Lower-bound (Thm 5.4) exponents match theory to within 0.0022 with normalized constant flat to under 4% across 9 decades of n, computed as exact Bayes risk over all measurable estimators; the upper-bound (Thm 5.5) half is weaker (noisy MC, coarse supremum) but the bounded ratio and O(1) C'/n form are supported.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.7 provides an oracle inequality showing the validation-based selection between f0 and f0+r̂ performs nearly as well as the better of the two candidate predictors (Theorem 5.7).
claims.evidence: The smallest constant C making the oracle inequality hold at the 95% quantile measures 0.501/0.446/0.406 at n=200/1000/5000 — finite and decreasing in n as the theorem requires — across 27 settings with 150 replications each, running Algorithm 1 verbatim at the adversarial operating point δ≈δc.

claims.claim: In synthetic experiments at n=20 and δ=0.0, the safe residual estimator achieves risk 0.0027 compared to 0.1894 for learning from scratch (Tables 1-2).
claims.evidence: The parameter-free ratio RES(SAFE)/RES(RAW) at δ=0 (provably independent of unstated σ and f*, verified numerically to 2.9e-15) measures 0.1834 ± 0.0164 over 12,000 seeds vs the paper's implied 0.0806; absolute risks measure 0.0062 ± 0.0010 and 0.2933 ± 0.0331 vs claimed 0.0027 and 0.1894, with the entire (fallback, ratio) frontier over ρ∈[0.10,0.50] and four selection variants staying clear of the paper's point.

claims.claim: On CIFAR-100 with CLIP features at n=2000, the residual learning method achieves 66.7% accuracy versus 63.9% for a weighted-ensemble baseline, improving over the 59.4% zero-shot baseline (Section 6, CIFAR-100/CLIP experiments).
claims.evidence: On real CIFAR-100 with frozen CLIP ViT-B/32 and the paper's Appendix-F head at n=2000, the RES−WGT gap measures −0.09 (standardized) and +0.58 (L2-normalized) vs the claimed +2.8; the measured RES (68–69%) actually exceeds the paper's 66.7% but the baselines improve by more, closing the gap.

claims.claim: On AG News with Qwen3-8B at n=16, residual learning achieves 75.2% accuracy while the weighted-ensemble baseline exhibits negative transfer, dropping to 71.2% (Section 6, AG News/Qwen3-8B experiments).
claims.evidence: Using the paper's own frozen Qwen3-8B on real AG News at n=16 with 10 seeds: zero-shot BB 73.85% (paper 74.06%), RES 74.41 ± 2.12% (paper 75.23%, within 0.8 and above BB), WGT 53.94% — far below the black box, confirming the asserted negative transfer via validation-tuned α collapsing to 0.

SabaPivot/repro-black-box-assisted-regre.overall: The logbook provides strong numerical evidence confirming the paper's theoretical core (phase-transition exponents, minimax lower bound, oracle inequality) via deterministic exact-Bayes-risk computations on the paper's own hard construction, and confirms the AG News empirical claim with the paper's own Qwen3-8B model. Two empirical claims are falsified: the synthetic n=20 δ=0 table entry fails on a provably parameter-free ratio, and the CIFAR-100 claimed advantage vanishes because straightforward baselines are much stronger than the paper reports.

SabaPivot/repro-delayed-momentum-aggrega.paper_title: Delayed Momentum Aggregation: Communication-efficient Byzantine-robust Federated Learning with Partial Participation

claims.claim: D-Byz-SGDM (DeMoA) maintains convergence under partial client participation with participation probability p=0.5 and Byzantine fraction δ up to 0.2, while FedAvg and FedAvg-M diverge when the sampled subset contains a Byzantine majority (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The 300-round T4 run (n=20, p=0.5, δ=0.2, ALIE, CCLIP) shows DeMoA converges (0.9178 mean acc) and FedCM/FedAvg-M collapses under majority-conditioned seeds (0.5048), but FedAvg recovers to 0.9197 in those same majority-conditioned seeds, directly contradicting the claim that FedAvg diverges when the sampled subset contains a Byzantine majority.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 proves D-Byz-SGDM converges to an O(cδζ²/p) neighborhood of a stationary point, where c is the robust-aggregator constant, δ the Byzantine fraction, ζ² the data heterogeneity bound, and p the participation probability.
claims.evidence: Source audit of all .tex files found 0 occurrences of 'Theorem 4.1' and 0 occurrences of 'c\delta\zeta^2/p'; the main theorem (labeled theorem:main_result_hetero in Section 3) has a non-vanishing neighborhood of O(cδζ²) without the /p factor, and the discussion explicitly states the non-vanishing term remains O(cδζ²) under partial participation.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.2 establishes a matching Ω(δζ²/p) lower bound, showing the O(cδζ²/p) convergence neighborhood in Theorem 4.1 is information-theoretically unimprovable.
claims.evidence: Source audit found 0 occurrences of 'Theorem 4.2' and 0 occurrences of '\Omega(\delta\zeta^2/p)'; no registered Theorem 4.2 proving a matching Ω(δζ²/p) lower bound exists in the paper source, though the source discusses unimprovability of the O(cδζ²) term without the /p factor.

claims.claim: On MNIST with a CNN (n=20-25 clients, momentum α=0.9), D-Byz-SGDM is evaluated against FedAvg, FedAvg-M, and Byz-VR-MARINA-PP under six Byzantine attacks (BF, LF, mimic, IPM, ALIE, INF) combined with five robust aggregators (average, Krum, coordinate-wise median, centered clipping, RFA) (Section 5).
claims.evidence: Source audit found INF=0 occurrences (only 5 attacks: BF, LF, mimic, IPM, ALIE, not 6), and the source lists 4 robust aggregators (Krum, CM, CCLIP, RFA) not 5; 'avg' appears only as a non-Byzantine baseline, not as a robust aggregator. The paper also primarily uses 'FedCM' not 'FedAvg-M'.

claims.claim: Even in the non-Byzantine setting, D-Byz-SGDM exceeds FedAvg-M performance under partial participation, indicating the delayed-momentum caching mechanism yields a regularization benefit beyond robustness (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The 300-round T4 non-Byzantine run (n=20, p=0.5, δ=0, average aggregator, α=0.9, seeds 0-2, best LR=0.1) shows DeMoA at 0.9550 mean final accuracy, below FedCM at 0.9566 and FedAvg at 0.9572, directly contradicting the claim that DeMoA exceeds FedAvg-M in the non-Byzantine setting.

claims.claim: The delayed momentum aggregation scheme caches stale momentum for non-sampled clients (m_i^t ← m_i^{t-1}) so that Byzantine clients cannot dominate the aggregated update even if they form a majority of the sampled set, and it requires no additional communication overhead versus full participation (Algorithm 1).
claims.evidence: Source audit confirms the no-extra-communication property, but the claimed update m_i^t ← m_i^{t-1} is not Algorithm 1; the actual source update for non-sampled clients is m_i^t ← (1 - α_t p_t) m_i^{t-1} (multiplicative decay), so the conjunction as stated is falsified.

SabaPivot/repro-delayed-momentum-aggrega.overall: The logbook provides a thorough source audit and paper-scale MNIST CNN experiments (300 rounds, T4 GPU) that falsify all six registered claims: the theorem statements don't match the source, the experimental matrix dimensions are wrong, FedAvg does not diverge as claimed, DeMoA underperforms in the non-Byzantine setting, and the cache update formula is incorrect.

tomyimkc/repro-the-fisher-dimension-inst.paper_title: The Fisher Dimension: Instance-Dependent Complexity for Causal Discovery

claims.claim: Fisher dimension governs sample complexity for Markov equivalence class recovery
claims.evidence: Across 500 random linear-Gaussian DAG instances (p=18, 14-36 edges each), log(empirical n* for 90% edge recovery via Fisher-z tests with exact Wishart sampling) correlates with log(d_F) at r=0.9917 (r²=0.9835) with log-log slope 0.951 (theory ~1), while the marginal-correlation control collapses to r=0.0029, isolating the correctly-conditioned partial correlation as the governing quantity.

claims.claim: Provides both lower and upper bounds (tight up to logarithmic factors) for sample complexity
claims.evidence: Across p=8 to 96 (20 reps per p, 300 MC trials per n), n*_uncorrected/d_F has CV=0.028 (lower-bound scaling) and n*_corrected/(d_F·ln E) has CV=0.115 (upper-bound scaling), with measured cor/unc ratio correlating with the Bonferroni-predicted ratio at r=0.988; the fixed-sample control shows family-wise recovery dropping from 0.899 to 0.0 as p outgrows the budget, confirming the log(#tests) gap is necessary.

claims.claim: Under spectrally well-conditioned models, Fisher dimension is uniformly bounded regardless of graph structure
claims.evidence: Under a subcriticality condition (in-degree×max-coeff²=0.75<1), the log-log slope of max d_F vs p stays below 0.066 for all four structural families (chain/star/tree/dense) from p=20 to 800 with a bound ratio of 1.153; the control that grows only the dense family's in-degree produces a steeper slope of 0.263 and 2151× eigenvalue blow-up for that family alone, while chain/star/tree remain flat, isolating the bounded-eigenvalue precondition.

tomyimkc/repro-the-fisher-dimension-inst.overall: The logbook provides strong, non-toy experimental evidence for all three claims through 500-instance (Claim 1) and multi-p-scale (Claims 2-3) simulations using exact Wishart sampling and closed-form population computations, each with an isolating control that behaves as theory predicts. The main caveat is that all definitions are reconstructed from the abstract since no full paper text was available, so the experiments verify the stated mechanisms rather than the paper's specific formal definitions.

visv-Bro/repro-envy-free-allocation-of-i.paper_title: Envy-Free Allocation of Indivisible Goods via Noisy Queries

claims.claim: A naive non-adaptive algorithm achieves envy-freeness using O(m^3/Δ^2) noisy queries, where m is the number of items and Δ is the gap parameter of the optimal negative envy (Theorem 1, Section 3).
claims.evidence: Exhaustive Algorithm 1 was tested only on m ∈ {8,10,12,14} with a single fixed gap Δ=0.5 and one synthetic balanced-instance type; while 100% success at the theorem bound and normalized constant ≈32 are confirmed, the scale is far too small to constitute a full reproduction of the O(m³/Δ²) claim.

claims.claim: An improved polynomial-time algorithm using non-adaptive queries achieves envy-freeness with q ≤ Õ(m^2.5/Δ^2) queries, valid when Δ ≥ m^(1/4) log^2 m and Δ ≤ Cm for a sufficiently small constant C (Theorem 2, Section 4).
claims.evidence: The threshold allocation mechanism was tested at m ∈ {40,000, 160,000, 640,000} with Δ=0.1m satisfying the stated conditions; at q = m²·⁵/Δ², success rates were 97.2%, 100%, and 94.4% respectively, reaching 100% at 2× scaling, confirming the Õ(m²·⁵/Δ²) scaling mechanism at non-trivial scale.

claims.claim: An algorithm-independent lower bound of Ω̃(m^2.5/Δ^2) queries is proven to hold even under adaptive querying strategies and unbounded computation time, matching the upper bound up to logarithmic factors (Theorem 3, Section 5).
claims.evidence: The lower bound is algorithm-independent by nature and cannot be verified by simulation; the logbook itself acknowledges testing only 'one concrete algorithm.' Critically, the specific algorithm tested shows 0% failure even at 0.001× the base query budget, which does not demonstrate the hardness the lower bound claims.

claims.claim: The problem setup assumes agent valuations are accessed only through queries corrupted by Gaussian noise, formalized as the noisy query model (Section 2).
claims.evidence: Gaussian sample-mean variance was confirmed to follow σ²/τ across τ ∈ {1,…,128} with 5,000–50,000 repetitions, variance ratios within rounding of 1.0, cross-agent correlations near zero, and log-log slope ≈ −1, confirming the formal noisy-query model properties.

claims.claim: The paper extends its analysis of general noise levels beyond the Gaussian model and discusses extension of the results from two agents to n-agent scenarios (Section 6, Section 7).
claims.evidence: The logbook only runs a control showing that Laplace and Student-t distributions have different tail behavior than Gaussian; it explicitly states 'non-Gaussian and n>2 results are future work in Section 7' and does not implement or test any extension to general noise models or n-agent scenarios.

visv-Bro/repro-envy-free-allocation-of-i.overall: The logbook provides a credible numerical audit of the Gaussian query model and the improved upper-bound mechanism at large scale (m up to 640,000), but the naive upper bound is tested only on toy-sized instances, and the algorithm-independent lower bound is inherently unverifiable by simulation with the tested algorithm showing no failures.

tomyimkc/repro-approximation-error-upper.paper_title: Approximation Error Upper and Lower Bounds  for Hölder Class with Transformers

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 (Section 4) shows a Transformer with at most O(epsilon^{-d0/alpha}) blocks can approximate any bounded Holder-alpha function of d0-dimensional input to error less than epsilon.
claims.evidence: The experiment measures the piecewise-constant projector (a proof intermediate) rather than an actual Transformer, at small scale (d0≤3, M≤24). The upper-bound exponent holds in only 4/6 settings (upper_bound_holds_all_settings=false); the two failures at α=1,d0=2,3 show measured exponents slightly more negative than predicted (-2.032 vs -2.0, -3.016 vs -3.0), while the checkerboard control correctly yields slope ~0.

claims.claim: Theorem 5.3 (Section 5) establishes a matching-type lower bound: any Transformer achieving epsilon approximation accuracy on this Holder class must have at least Omega(epsilon^{-d0/(4*alpha)}) blocks, derived via VC-dimension analysis.
claims.evidence: The entropy exponent match to machine precision (MAE 6.2e-16, R²=1.0) is tautological—log2N is set to M^d0 by construction and eps=M^{-α}, so the slope is -d0/α by algebra. The VC-dimension O(D^4) (Theorem 5.2) is assumed as input, not independently verified, and no actual Transformer is instantiated.

claims.claim: The gap between the upper bound exponent -d0/alpha (Theorem 4.1) and lower bound exponent -d0/(4*alpha) (Theorem 5.3) leaves a factor-of-4 gap in the exponent that the authors note as room for tightening (Section 5).
claims.evidence: The experiment is pure arithmetic: computing (-d0/α)/(-d0/(4α))=4 across 7 settings yields exactly 4.0 (trivially correct by construction), plus a band-width check that is also arithmetic. No non-trivial experimental setup is involved; the claim is a mathematical observation about the paper's own formulas.

claims.claim: Theorem 6.2 (Section 6) gives a statistical convergence rate of N^{-alpha/(2 d0 + alpha)} for Transformer-based nonparametric regression on Holder-alpha functions, under the constraint d0 > 2*alpha (Theorem 6.2).
claims.evidence: The experiment uses a cell-average regressor proxy instead of a Transformer ERM, at moderate sample sizes (N≤64000). Measured rates deviate substantially from predicted (e.g., -0.594 vs -0.111 for d0=2,α=0.5; rate_max_rel_dev_on=4.34), with one setting having very poor fit (R²=0.171). The off-precondition control shows weak degradation (off MAE 0.246 vs on MAE 0.182).

tomyimkc/repro-approximation-error-upper.overall: All four claims are addressed only through simplified proxy constructions (piecewise-constant projectors, entropy packing, arithmetic ratios, cell-average regressors) rather than actual Transformers, at small to moderate scale. The experiments include useful controls but the results are either tautological (Claims 2, 3), mixed (Claim 1: 4/6 settings hold), or show large deviations from predicted rates (Claim 4), so no claim receives full verification.

visv-Bro/repro-alignment-between-brains-.paper_title: Alignment between Brains and AI: Evidence for Convergent Evolution across Modalities, Scales and Training Trajectories

claims.claim: Brain alignment correlates with task performance more strongly for language models (Pearson r=0.89, p<7.5×10⁻¹³, on LLM Leaderboard 2 performance) than for vision models (Pearson r=0.53, p<2.0×10⁻⁴⁴, on ImageNet accuracy) (Figure 1d-e, Table 1).
claims.evidence: Full-scale reproduction on 36 language and 594 vision models from released parquet tables yields language r=0.8853 (p=7.52e-13) and vision r=0.5305 (p=2.03e-44), matching the paper's r=0.89/p<7.5e-13 and r=0.53/p<2.0e-44 with the claimed modality gap.

claims.claim: For language models, a logarithmic fit between brain alignment and performance (R²=0.80) outperforms a linear fit (R²=0.78), with individual benchmark correlations ranging r=0.66–0.84 (Table 1).
claims.evidence: On the 36-model language set, linear R²=0.7838 and log R²=0.8017 reproduce the reported 0.78 vs 0.80; log fit also wins on AIC (117.6 vs 120.7) and BIC. Individual benchmark Pearson r spans 0.658 (MUSR) to 0.836 (BBH), matching the stated 0.66–0.84 range.

claims.claim: Layer-wise analysis shows vision models exhibit progressively increasing brain alignment with network depth, whereas language models peak in brain alignment at middle layers (3/8 to 5/8 normalized depth), with deeper vision layers converging toward language-model-like organization (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: Vision median alignment is strictly increasing across all depth bins for every subject (Spearman ρ=1.0 for S01–S07); language peaks at depth 3/8 in all four subjects (within claimed 3/8–5/8); cross-modal regional-vector correlation rises from r=0.9914 at depth 2/8 to r=0.9973 at depth 6/8, supporting deeper convergence.

claims.claim: Across Pythia model checkpoints, brain alignment stabilizes by approximately 10% of training tokens for language models, while vision models show a sharp early increase in alignment reaching about 85% of maximum by 20% of training samples, indicating alignment emerges before performance gains (Figure 3, Pythia correlations r=0.73–0.95).
claims.evidence: Pythia alignment–performance correlations span r=0.734–0.951, exactly matching the claimed r=0.73–0.95. Alignment reaches 91.2% of maximum at ~10% of tokens for Pythia and 93.6% at ~20% for MixNet (higher than the paper's approximate 85%, still directionally consistent with early emergence before performance gains).

claims.claim: Kernel-size (spatial scale) analysis shows brain alignment decreases at larger scales in primary visual areas V1, V2, V3 (Δ=−5.30, −2.81, −1.05) while increasing in limbic regions such as orbitofrontal cortex (Δ=+1.56), with sign consistency of 0.83 across subjects (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: Normalized language-model deltas match the paper to 2–3 decimals: V1=−5.304, V2=−2.810, V3=−1.052, OFC=+1.561. Sign consistency is 0.821 for language and 0.818 for vision, slightly below the reported 0.83 but matching the committed derived CSV; the core directional pattern is exactly reproduced.

claims.claim: Inter-subject consistency of alignment scores is very high for both language models (r=0.997–1.000) and vision models (r=0.970–0.999), supporting a shared, near-universal organizational principle underlying brain-model correspondence (Tables 2–3).
claims.evidence: Off-diagonal inter-subject Pearson correlations from the full 36-language and 594-vision model matrices are r=0.9971–0.9998 for language and r=0.9701–0.9993 for vision, reproducing the reported ranges of 0.997–1.000 and 0.970–0.999.

visv-Bro/repro-alignment-between-brains-.overall: This logbook provides a full-scale reproduction using the released BrainAlign parquet tables (36 language, 594 vision models, 4 NSD subjects) with commit-pinned provenance, DuckDB-based aggregation following the paper's CKA σ=36 and top-five selection protocol, and independent recomputation of all statistics. All six claims are numerically reproduced with only minor discrepancies in the sign-consistency statistic (0.82 vs 0.83) and the MixNet early-alignment percentage (93.6% vs ~85%).

rakshi-the-neural-nexus/repro-gradient-b.paper_title: Gradient-Based Causal Tree Ensembles: A Backbone Architecture for Heterogeneous Treatment Effects

claims.claim: GRACE consistently surpasses neural network and tree-based baselines across diverse HTE benchmarks, often by substantial margin.
claims.evidence: Only 2 of the paper's 11 datasets were tested (toy_1 and sim_1), with 5 seeds instead of 30, a reduced training budget (3,000 vs 50,000 steps), and scikit-learn meta-learner baselines rather than the paper's own comparators (CFR, TARNet, causal forests). GRACE leads all baselines on both datasets, but decisively only on toy_1 (0.0471 vs 0.0802, ~13 SE); on sim_1 the gap to the best baseline is 1.1 SE, not statistically significant. This reduced scope cannot test the claim's 'consistently across diverse HTE benchmarks' quantifier.

claims.claim: GRACE can be seamlessly integrated into existing models as replacement for fully-connected neural network layers.
claims.evidence: A controlled swap experiment replaces one nn.Linear hidden layer with GRACE_layer in an S-learner network, keeping everything else identical (same loop, seed, budget, optimizer). GRACE_layer accepts the same constructor role, returns the same shape, trains through standard loss.backward() with no tuning changes, and improves PEHE on both benchmarks (8.9 SE on toy_1, 2.3 SE on sim_1). This is concrete evidence that the layer integrates seamlessly as a drop-in replacement, which is what the engineering claim asserts.

rakshi-the-neural-nexus/repro-gradient-b.overall: The logbook provides real runs on the paper's own synthetic benchmarks with published code and raw results, but at substantially reduced scope (2/11 datasets, 5 seeds, shortened training, custom baselines). The layer-replacement engineering claim is concretely verified; the superiority claim is only partially tested and cannot establish 'consistency across diverse benchmarks' at this scale.

gopaljigaur/repro-a-general-neural-backb.paper_title: A General Neural Backbone for Mixed-Integer Linear Optimization via Dual Attention

claims.claim: The dual-attention backbone combines intra-type self-attention (variables and constraints separately) with inter-type, sparsity-aware cross-attention over the coefficient matrix structure, computed in parallel rather than via sequential GNN message passing (equations 5-8, 11-14).
claims.evidence: Using the official unmodified Dual_Attention_layer code on a controlled bipartite chain graph (8 vars, 7 constraints), gradient-flow analysis shows BGNN has exactly zero gradient beyond ceil(k/2) hops (0 at v2+ for L=1, v3+ for L=2) while Dual-Attention has nonzero gradient at all variables regardless of hop distance after just 1 layer — confirming the parallel global receptive field property architecturally.

claims.claim: On the element-level binary-variable-prediction benchmark, the proposed model improves over the BGNN baseline on all four datasets, e.g. MCC on the CA dataset rises from 0.3488 to 0.3825 (+9.65%) and error rate on IP drops from 20.88% to 17.72% (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Only 2 of 4 datasets could be tested, at toy scale (60 items/nodes vs paper's 8000/3000, 100 train/40 test vs 400/100). On toy-IS DA edges out BGNN (MCC 0.5418 vs 0.5382), but on toy-CA BGNN beats DA even after fixing an optimization-collapse artifact (MCC 0.2635 vs 0.2241), so the 'all four datasets' claim is not reproduced.

claims.claim: On instance-level feasibility prediction on challenging 'foldable' synthetic datasets, the proposed model attains 0% error compared to 6% error for an enhanced BGNN baseline (Section on instance-level prediction).
claims.evidence: On 1000 train/1000 test foldable instances with SCIP solver and 3000 training epochs, DA achieves 49.9% error and BGNN 50.0% — both pinned at the 50% chance floor — directly contradicting the paper's claimed 0% for DA and 6% for BGNN. The unfoldable control (23%/26% vs 42.3% majority baseline) confirms the pipeline works, isolating the failure to the foldable construction itself.

claims.claim: In a component ablation on the WA dataset, removing self-attention drops MCC from 0.8411 to 0.7985, and removing cross-attention drops MCC further to 0.5724, showing both attention types are necessary (Table 7).
claims.evidence: The WA dataset was never tested (ML4CO competition download unavailable); the toy-CA substitute produced all-zero MCC for every ablation variant (full, no-self, no-cross) across 3 seeds due to optimization collapse, yielding no reproducible ranking signal to confirm or refute the paper's specific MCC ordering (0.8411 > 0.7985 > 0.5724).

claims.claim: Using predict-and-search frameworks built on the model's predictions, the approach achieves 14.5-36% average improvement in primal gap over BGNN-based predict-and-search baselines (Table 3, Table 4).
claims.evidence: On toy-IS with hard variable-fixing (simplified from the paper's soft trust-region method), pooled k=0.7/0.9 gives 19.9% improvement (within the 14.5–36% band), but on toy-CA DA-PS is worse than BGNN-PS at every k (−11% to −70%) due to the known collapsed upstream predictor; only 2 of 4 operating points were included in the headline.

claims.claim: On 215 real-world MIPLIB instances with up to 550,539 variables and severe 42:1 class imbalance, the proposed model generalizes out-of-distribution and outperforms BGNN on MCC, balanced accuracy, and macro-F1 (Table 9).
claims.evidence: Only 9 of 215 MIPLIB instances were tested (156–4516 vars vs up to 550,539) using toy-scale checkpoints; pooled metrics favor DA (MCC 0.478 vs 0.006) but 22.6% of pooled variables come from one easy instance (splice1k1, DA MCC=1.0), and excluding it both models are indistinguishable from random (MCC −0.021 vs −0.023).

gopaljigaur/repro-a-general-neural-backb.overall: The logbook cleanly verifies the architectural mechanism (Claim 1) via gradient-flow analysis with official code, but provides only toy-scale or inconclusive evidence for the empirical claims due to Gurobi license limits, missing ecole wheels, and inaccessible competition datasets. Claim 3 is actively falsified on a non-toy 1000/1000-instance setup where both DA and BGNN sit at chance level, contradicting the paper's 0%/6% split.

visv-Bro/repro-a-graphop-analysis-of-gra.paper_title: A Graphop Analysis of Graph Neural Networks on Sparse Graphs: Generalization and Universal Approximation

claims.claim: Graphops are introduced as self-adjoint, positivity-preserving operators over probability spaces, unifying dense graphons and sparse graphs as a single class of limit objects (Definition 3.1).
claims.evidence: Finite n=256 discretizations of three simple operator families (cosine kernel, cycle, rotation) pass 128 randomized linearity/symmetry/positivity checks with residuals ~1e-16, plus a singular scaling table showing density 2/n→0 while fiber mass stays 1. This is a basic sanity check of definition properties on small, simple finite matrices, not a demonstration of the infinite-dimensional unification framework.

claims.claim: A restricted subclass called bounded-fiber operators (bofops) is defined via fiber measures nu_x satisfying ess sup_{x in Omega} nu_x(Omega) < infinity, capturing sparse connectivity patterns within the graphop framework (Definition 3.1).
claims.evidence: Fiber masses computed as matrix row sums for cycle (max=2.0), rotation (max=1.0), dense graphon (max=0.6), and star control (max=n-1 growing to 4095) across n=16–4096, plus random-sign probes confirming induced norm ≤ row-sum norm. These are trivially correct finite analogs verifying the bounded-fiber concept on small simple operators, not a reproduction of Theorem 3.3.

claims.claim: Theorem 4.1 establishes that message passing neural networks (MPNNs) are Lipschitz (Holder) continuous with respect to an action metric d_M on bofop-signals: ||H(A_1,f_1) - H(A_2,f_2)||_2 <= C'_{D,r} d_M((A_1,f_1),(A_2,f_2)) (Theorem 4.1).
claims.evidence: A concrete mathematical counterexample on singleton probability spaces: with A1=0, A2=I, f1=f2=0, and MPNN phi_0(x)=M (Lipschitz constant 0), the exact action distance d_M=Σ k/2^k=2 is numerically verified (partial sums converging to 1.999998), yet the output gap equals M. For any proposed constant C, choosing M=2C+1 yields M>C·d_M=2C, violating the theorem's output inequality. The control adding |phi_0(0)|≤1 blocks the counterexample, confirming the defect is a missing range/offset bound in the formal MP_D class.

claims.claim: Corollary 5.3 shows the space of bofop-DIDMs (degree-indexed distribution measures) is compact under the DIDM-mover's distance, forming a proper subset of the corresponding dense-graph structure (Corollary 5.3).
claims.evidence: At depth L=0, taking Omega=H^0, A=0 (self-adjoint, positivity-preserving, norm 0<r), and f=id gives Gamma_0=(id)_#pi=pi for arbitrary pi, so Gamma_0(BF_d^r)=P(H^0) and the inclusion is equality rather than strict. The logbook explicitly does not challenge the compactness clause and notes strictness may hold for L≥1, but the proper-subset quantifier in the claim is contradicted at L=0.

claims.claim: Section 6.1 uses this compactness and continuity to prove a universal approximation theorem: any continuous function on bofop-DIDMs can be uniformly approximated by MPNNs directly on sparse graphs (Section 6.1).
claims.evidence: A single-layer sum-aggregation MPNN with random fixed weights and ridge-regression readout is trained on 1200 small graphs (12–64 nodes) and tested on 600 graphs (80–160 nodes) for one specific continuous target. Held-out MAE improves with width (up to 256), but the scope explicitly states 'this tests one continuous target, not the universal quantifier,' and the architecture is a simplified proxy rather than the full MPNN class in the theorem.

claims.claim: Section 6.2 derives generalization bounds showing generalization error vanishes as sample size grows, exploiting the uniform equicontinuity and compactness established in Theorem 4.1 and Corollary 5.3 (Section 6.2).
claims.evidence: Using the same singleton-space counterexample as Claim 3 with phi_0(x)=M, the generalization gap is |N1/N−1/2|·(M−2) for M≥2, which is infinite whenever N1/N≠1/2. The sample-size sweep (N=5–1000) shows P(infinite gap)→1 for the unbounded class, while the repaired bounded class (0≤M≤1) decays with slope −0.5. Additional proof audit identifies an invalid L∞/L1 inference and a union-vs-intersection event error in Appendix N.

visv-Bro/repro-a-graphop-analysis-of-gra.overall: The logbook provides mathematical counterexamples that falsify Claims 3, 4, and 6 as stated (missing output-range bounds in MP_D, equality at L=0, and infinite generalization gap without output envelopes), while Claims 1, 2, and 5 receive only finite-dimensional numerical audits or simplified proxy experiments that do not constitute full reproductions.
